units.la: REVERENDISSIME, Quotiescunque istius diei recordor, recordor autem sæ-pius, qui Anglis, an Belgis effusiori ac-ceptus lætitiâ fuerit, incertum, omnibus certe pro miraculo habitus fuit, quo Re-gem venistis vestrum repetitum in Bel-gio, quod non quidem Reges parit, at Regum proximos, atque hos, & illos etiam, excipit, tuetur, servat tum juri suo, tum suis; & Tu, unà cum aliis, pro
units.tr: REVERENDISSIME, Whenever I recall that day, and I recall it often, it is uncertain whether it was welcomed with greater joy by the English or by the Dutch. Yet it was certainly regarded by everyone as a miracle that you brought your King back from Belgium. Belgium does not indeed produce kings, but it receives, shelters and keeps safe the close kin of kings, and it protects them both by its own right and by its own people. And you, together with others, on behalf of

units.la: DEDICATIO.
units.tr: DEDICATION.

units.la: Ecclesiis vestris, adfuisti, Regem redu-cturus & comitaturus; meque, cum viris Reverendis, itineris & negotiorum so-ciis, invisere, ac domum meam & mu-saeum intrare dignatus fuisti, & spectare laborum, quibus in veritatis defensionem tum temporis forte occupabamur, seriem, hoc etiam quod imprasens[?] in lucem damus: aequum visum, idipsum Ti-bi, facto inde Episcopo, nunc inscribere, & sub amplissimi tui Nominis praesidio edere, reverentiae erga Te nostrae & gratitudinis symbolum atq; monumentum.
units.tr: You were present in your churches, intending to bring back and accompany the King. You also deigned to visit me, together with reverend men who were companions of your journey and business, to enter my house and museum, and to view the series of labours with which we were then occupied, perhaps, in defence of the truth, and this too which we now bring to light. It seemed fitting to me, now that you have been made a bishop, to inscribe this to you and to publish it under the protection of your most distinguished name, as a token and memorial of our reverence and gratitude towards you.

units.la: Jam & ante haec tempora eo in Eccle-sia & Academia fuisti loco, ea functus dignitate & munere, ut non apud An-glos modo, sed Belgas, & ad exteros quoscunque, Nominis tui fama pervagata sit, & Reformatae Ecclesiae non JOHANNEM modò RAYNOLDUM, τὸν πάνυ[?] cognatum tuum, celeberrimum contra Papistas disputatorem⌣; sed & EDUARDUM loquantur, scriptis Pra-cticis clarum: bina gentilitiæ pietatis & eruditionis illustria nomina. Cumque duo in Ecclesia maximopere sint necef-saria, veritatem doctrinæ tueri adversus extraneos, & sanctitatem ejus urgere⌣ apud suos, neque enim sine sanctitatis studio doctrina, neque extra Christi doctrinam vera sanctitas est; ita qui in utraque promovenda operam omnem ponunt & ætatem, inter præcipua Ec-clesiæ decora reputandos arbitror. Fuit tempus, quo Ecclesia à Papatus corrup-telis, superstitione, & tyrannide vindi-canda ac reformanda, Primoribus ejus vix aliud agere licuit præterquam hoc unum, ut cum jurato in bonorum perni-ciem, & Papis solis mancipato clero, assi-duè confligerent, averterentque extrema saluti & libertati nostræ intentantes hostes Romanos. Ut verò respirare aliquibus licuit, & feriari, non quiescere, mox totâ mente & studio ad tractandam jucundissimam & saluberrimam Theologiæ partem, quæ in moribus & vitâ ad Reformationem componendâ versatur, impigre se transtulerunt. Quæ præsertim vobis Anglis contigit temporum & rerum felicitas, à gloriss.[?] mem. Reginâ, in exemplum datâ Regum omnium, Principumque, ELISABETA. Unde factum, ut Ecclesiæ Anglicæ in hoc genere doctrinæ supra alias emicuerint, & paucæ idem potuerint, nisi earum exemplum gnaviter æmulari.Neque enim pudet agnoscere[?], quæ divina liberalitas aliis indulsit, præsertim talia, quæ in nostros non minus usus redundant, quam ipsorum. Præter Papismum autem Ecclesiis omnibus pariter infestum, sua singulæ experiuntur mala propria & domestica: stica : omnibus item letale virus inten-dit hæresis à Socino nomen ferens ; hoc Papismo perniciosior , quo præcipua, & catholica Christianismi dogmata evertit , quæ etiam Papismus retinet quadantenus, quamvis superstitionibus suis obruta multum & suppressa. Hic autem ultimus videtur Diaboli in Eccle-siam conatus : per Socinianos , fidem ; per dissolutum vivendi genus, pietatem impetere : licentiam ubique & agendi & credendi, sub specie & prætextu su-nestæ libertatis urgendo , in perniciem fidei pariter & pietatis. Libertati quidem ingeniorum , fateor , aliquid tri-buendum ; nonnihil etiam novitati ; sed in melius, sed in subsidium veritatis, non detrimentum, non ut facile contra Do-ctorum , minus Ecclesiarum sententiam & consensum , ex temerario novandi pruritu, & quærendi nomen per devia quod via regia non possis, disputando conturbes omnia, misceasque ima summis, & quasi, quod olim planxit in Ecclesiâ Alvares Pelagius, non sit sciens hodie qui notates non invenit: sed ut Dei Verbo eo firmius te adstringas, & subjicias ingenium, & placita omnia cum aliorum, tum tua. Utinam vero novitatem piè vivendi af-fectarent homines æque, ac sentiendi & dissentiendi! Sed quæ est nostra perversitas, & ingeniorum vertigo, non diu placent eadem, quamvis recta, quamvis optima: neq; sanè immerito gentem nostram notavit olim, apud Coloniensem Episcopum Hermannum, Bucerus, elatâ manu & huc conversâ dicens: væ Belgio, à petulantiâ ingeniorum! Forte, sic exigente[?] hominum improbitate, instat aliud Ec-clesiæ sæculum, priori multum dissimile, & quod dixit Tertullianus, ultimant patriæ tempora: sed laudabilius equidem duxero, cum prioribus censeri, & haberi vel in-ter reliquias illius ævi, quod à Reforma-tione calens, eodem spiritu suos vegeta-vit; quam primum alterius, sed pejoris, daturi mox progeniem vitiosorem, quia dissolutiorem. Eat tandem post alios to-tus mundus, nobis stat sententia non re-cedere à viâ, quam monstravit Christus, & Apostoli docuerunt, & Martyres riga-runt suo sanguine, & Reformati ad principia sua revocarunt, & Majores com-mendarunt, quo minus eandem trada-mus nostris, nostri aliquando nepotibus. Apud extraneos regnent errores atque vitia: accurabimus vero, ne per dolosos cuniculos irrepat in Ecclesiam malum alibi ortum, quod heic vix deprehensum antequam notum, antequam clarum, jam profectu suo audax, vim trahat ex loco, quem forte occuparit. Salvis vis-ceribus, quamdiu in externis hæret impetigo, minus nocet, quia arcetur. Sed neq; argùmenti difficultas aut hominum odium absterrere ab officio nos debet. Quandoquidem impossibile est placere simul Christo & mundo, Ecclesiæ & hæ-reticis, hostibus atque amicis. Male de nobis loquantur, & oderint, & perse-quantur, quæ nunc sunt mollia perse-quutionum tempora præ prioribus, non cedemus malis, nec movebimur per Dei gratiam, nisi in meliora, & hoc contrà ibimus audentiores, & lætiores à prælio, ab insectatione, quo plura exceperimus pro Christi causâ, nostrâ conscientiâ, aliorum salute & instructione, vulnera, jacturam, & quoque, si res ita ferat, graviora. Scitè Cyprianus, Si odio seculi labora-mus, odium seculi sustinuit prior Christus. Nolim laudari nisi illis, quos laudat Christus: omnibus probari nec cupio, nec quæro. Atque ubi veri & optimi Christi athletæ proscinduntur omnes & lacerantur, ibi laudari non id quidem laudabile, ne-que laudabunt admodum, quorum, pro dignitate repressa à te insania, & veris, non ludicris armis petita fuit, atque ex-pugnata. Sic tuti causâ, & Deo, pergi-mus ad victoriam, quæ incruenta esse non potest, quia non sine cruore suam adeptus est Christus, quæ & nostra. Au-dio acclamantem Augustinum : quid times homo, in sinu Dei? Certe nil timendum, non si fractus illabatur orbis, in opere quam-vis gravi & invidioso, quale est, quod impræsentiarum, Venerande Domine, Tibi venio oblatum. Post quod sequetur bre-vi, uti spero, pars ejus postrema ; si vi-res Deus & vitam benigne concesserit. Nam ad frequentem mortis cogitatio-nem, & maturam omnium ad eam præ-parationem cum alia, tum assiduus mor-talitatis mihi monitor calculus identidem vocant, jubentque in novissimam horam omnia expedire, & ex Sapientis monito, agere pro viribus, quia nullum in sepulchro, quò innus [?], opus, nulla cogitatio. Hac propter uti festinamus, sic facile contemnit omnia, qui se semper cogitat esse mo-riturum. Quæ Hieronymi verba ita mea facio, ut Tibi ætatis provectæ viro, & mortem in proximo præstolanti non importuna credam vel ingrata. Deum veneror, ut & vitam nobis, & excessum largiatur, sibi honorificum, & salutarem nobis, atque Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Even before these times you held such a place and office in that Church and Academy that the fame of your name has spread abroad, not only among the English but among the Dutch and all foreigners. The Reformed Church speaks not only of John Rainolds, your very kinsman [τὸν πάνυ], the most celebrated disputant against the Papists, but also of Edward, known for his practical writings: two illustrious names of hereditary piety and learning. Since two things are most necessary in the Church, to defend the truth of doctrine against outsiders and to press its holiness upon its own members (for doctrine is not without zeal for holiness, nor is true holiness found outside the doctrine of Christ), I judge that those who put all their effort and life into promoting both are to be reckoned among the chief ornaments of the Church. There was a time when the Church had to be vindicated and reformed from the corruptions, superstition and tyranny of the Papacy, and its leaders could scarcely do anything but this one thing: to struggle constantly with the clergy, sworn to the destruction of goods and devoted to the Papists alone, and to turn aside the Roman enemies who threatened the utmost danger to our safety and liberty. But when some were allowed to breathe and take a holiday (not to rest), they soon turned with their whole mind and zeal, and with energy, to handling the most pleasant and wholesome part of theology, the part which concerns the shaping of morals and life for reformation. This happy condition of times and affairs fell especially to you English, under the most glorious Queen Elizabeth, given as an example to all kings and princes. Hence it came about that the English Churches shone above others in this kind of doctrine, and few others could achieve the same unless they earnestly emulated their example. For we are not ashamed to acknowledge what divine generosity has granted to others, especially such gifts as bring no less benefit to our people than to theirs. Besides Popery, which is equally hostile to all churches, each one suffers its own particular and domestic evils; and a deadly poison threatens all alike, the heresy bearing the name of Socinus. It is more pernicious than Popery, inasmuch as it overthrows the chief and catholic doctrines of Christianity, which Popery still retains to some extent, though they are much buried and suppressed beneath its superstitions. This seems to be the last attempt of the Devil against the Church: through the Socinians he assails faith, and through a loose manner of living he assails piety, everywhere pressing a licence both to act and to believe under the appearance and pretext of a baneful liberty, to the ruin of faith and piety alike. I admit that some allowance must be made for freedom of mind, and some also for novelty; but this must be for the better and for the support of truth, not to its detriment. It must not be that, from a rash itch for innovation and a desire for a name by byways which the royal road would not give you, you throw everything into confusion in disputing, mix the lowest with the highest, and (as Alvarus Pelagius once lamented in the Church) he is not knowing today who does not find what he has marked. Rather, you should bind yourself the more firmly to the Word of God, and subject your intellect and all opinions, both those of others and your own. Would that men pursued novelty in living piously as eagerly as in thinking and dissenting! But such is our perversity and the giddiness of minds that the same things, though right and very best, do not please for long. Not without reason did Bucer once remark on our nation, before Hermann, the bishop of Cologne, lifting his hand and turning towards us: Woe to Belgium, from the wantonness of minds! Perhaps, as men's wickedness demands, another age of the Church is at hand, very unlike the former, of which Tertullian said the last times of the fatherland. But I would rather think it more praiseworthy to be reckoned with the former, and to be counted even among the remnants of that age which, glowing since the Reformation, quickened its own people with the same spirit, than soon to bring forth another, worse offspring, more vicious because more dissolute. Let the whole world go after the others; our resolve stands: not to depart from the way that Christ showed, the Apostles taught, the Martyrs watered with their blood, the Reformers recalled to their first principles, and our forebears commended. We will hand the same down to ours, and ours one day to our grandchildren. Let errors and vices reign among foreigners. We will take care, however, that no evil born elsewhere creeps into the Church through deceitful tunnels, an evil which, scarcely detected here before it is known and clear, already bold in its advance, draws strength from whatever place it may have occupied. While the vital organs are safe, a rash that sticks to the surface does less harm, because it is kept off. But neither the difficulty of the subject nor men's hatred ought to frighten us from our duty, since it is impossible to please Christ and the world at once, the Church and heretics, enemies and friends at the same time. Let them speak ill of us, hate us and persecute us; these are now soft times of persecution compared with earlier ones. We shall not yield to evils, nor be moved, by God's grace, except towards better things. On the contrary, we shall go forward the bolder and the more cheerful from the battle and the harrying, the more wounds, loss, and, if the matter so requires, graver injuries we have received for Christ's cause, for our conscience, and for the salvation and instruction of others. Cyprian rightly says: If we labour under the hatred of the world, the hatred of the world was first borne by Christ. I would not be praised except by those whom Christ praises; I neither desire nor seek to be approved by everyone. And where the true and best athletes of Christ are all torn apart and mangled, there to be praised is not indeed laudable, nor will those praise much whose madness, checked by you as its dignity deserved, was assailed and overcome with true, not playful, weapons. So, secure in our cause and in God, we press on to victory, which cannot be bloodless, since Christ did not win his own without blood, and neither shall we. I hear Augustine crying out: Why do you fear, man, in the bosom of God? Surely nothing is to be feared, even if the broken world should fall in upon us, in a work however weighty and odious as this which I now offer to you, Venerable Lord. After it there will follow, as I hope, shortly, its last part, if God graciously grants strength and life. For the frequent thought of death, and the timely preparation of all for it, along with the constant reminder of my mortality (the stone that calls me again and again), bid me settle all things for the final hour, and, following the Wise Man's counsel, to act with all my strength, since in the grave, whither we hasten, there is no work and no thought. For this reason, as we hurry, he who always thinks he is about to die easily despises all things. I make these words of Jerome my own, so that I may think them neither unwelcome nor unpleasant to you, a man of advanced years who awaits death at hand. I pray God to grant us both life and a departure that is honourable to himself and beneficial to us and to the Church.

units.la: In quibus respondetur ad lib. Irenicum Irenicorum, & Novam ejus confirmationem.
units.tr: In which a reply is given to the book Irenicum Irenicorum and to its new confirmation.

units.la: Emere praescribit Autor libro suo titulum infallibilitatis. Cur pro argumento Irenici sumserit quaestionem de Deitate Christi. An, & unde SocinIani, vel qui ipsorum sententiae sunt, quascunque alias sectas facile admittant. An Lutherani, & Pontificii doceant articulum de Christi Deitate verâ, ex Scripturis probari non posse. De Petavio. Idololatria, & contemtus Christi nullus apud nos, apud Adversarios maximus. Neque neganda est Christi deitas, in gratiam infidelium, ut convertantur. Status controversiae non est formandus de summo Deo, sed vero, an Christus ille sit. Solvitur argumentum Adversarii ex natura petitum, à disparatis, quod simul de uno tertio non possunt esse vera. Quid sit, in argumentando petere principium. Quomodo in rebus fidei disputandum ex ratione. De traditione, sive doctrinâ Veteris Ecclesiae, de Christi deitate. Ostenditur fidem de eâ nostram blasphemè adscribi, tamquam autori primo, Simoni Mago, inde Cerintho, haereticis. De versibus Orphei, Justino citatis. Iterum de Petavio. Primi Patres an docuerint, Filium Patre inferiorem esse aevo, dignitate, & potestate, seu non verum & eundem Patre Deum? De Hermâ. De Clemente Romano. Ignatio. Polycarpo. Justino. Athenagorâ. Theophilo. Tatiano. Irenaeo. De sententiâ Novatiani, in libro de Trinitate. De Tertulliano. De Symbolo. Sectâ Artemonitarum. Denique de Luciani, & Plinii testimonio, de Christianis, eorumque in Christum fide.
units.tr: The author prefixes to his book the title of infallibility. Why he took as the subject of his Irenicum the question of the deity of Christ. Whether, and from where, the Socinians, or those who share their opinions, readily admit any other sects. Whether the Lutherans and the Papists teach that the article on the true deity of Christ cannot be proved from Scripture. On Petavius. Idolatry and contempt of Christ are nowhere among us, but are very great among our opponents. The deity of Christ is not to be denied in order to win unbelievers, that they may be converted. The state of the controversy is not to be framed concerning the supreme God, but concerning the true God, and whether that Christ is he. The opponent's argument from nature is answered, which is drawn from things disparate: that things which are said of one third thing cannot both be true at once. What it is to beg the question in argument. How one should dispute on matters of faith by reason. On the tradition, or teaching, of the Ancient Church concerning the deity of Christ. It is shown that our faith in this is blasphemously ascribed, as if its first author were Simon Magus, then Cerinthus and the heretics. On the verses of Orpheus cited by Justin. Again on Petavius. Whether the first Fathers taught that the Son is inferior to the Father in age, dignity and power, or is not the true and same God as the Father. On Hermas. On Clement of Rome. Ignatius. Polycarp. Justin. Athenagoras. Theophilus. Tatian. Irenaeus. On the opinion of Novatian in his book On the Trinity. On Tertullian. On the Creed. The sect of the Artemonites. Finally, on the testimony of Lucian and Pliny concerning the Christians, and their faith in Christ.

units.la: Supra decennium est, Benevole Lector, quod edidimus primum, adversus errores Socinianorum, Tomum: ubi disputavimus de principiis religionis, de Scripturâ, Deo, Creatione, & similibus capitibus. A quo quidem tempore aliquamdiu feriandum censuimus, & exspectandum, si quid contra nostra illa reponeretur ab Adversariis, quod interea discuti deberet & examinari, ad illa quae jam scripseramus pertinens, forte & moneret quomodo in caeteris quae sequi debebant, gerere, ad uberiorem Christianae rei fructum, nos oporteret. At nihil istius generis prodiit jam satis diu: & praeter animi sententiam accidit, quod in secundi hujus Tomi editione tardantem Ty-pographum variare necesse fuit, & prior negligentior non modo in longum protraxit opus, sed neque satis ex voto in excudendo versatus fuit; quod postea deprehendi, & cujus singulatim reddenda erit suo loco ratio, atque corrigenda vitia. Praeterito autem anno prodiit liber Anonymus, cujus autorem, quia sic amat, latere sino, scriptus adversus venerandum senem & amicum nostrum Johannem Amosum Comenium, tit. Irenicomastix, sive Confirmatio Irenici Irenicorum, ubi me quoque ad partes citari vidi, non propter ea quae in primo Tomo scripseram, sed in Disputationibus Theologicis, de Vera Christi Deitate, ex primaeva Antiquitate, ubi quae hujus rei in Irenico illo legeram, examinavi & discussi, quae locum quoque reperiunt, in hoc Tomo secundo. Exspectaram vero responsum ad Tomum nostrum, & adversarium designaram[?] mihi virum satis doctum, & acutum disputatorem, Jonam Schlichtingium, quem Petavius, Theologic. Dogmat. Tom. IV. lib. XVII. in Praefat. teterrimum & pestilentissimum appellat inter Adversarios, ubi de ejus opere, adversus Meisnerum, loquitur.
units.tr: More than ten years ago, kind reader, I first published the first volume against the errors of the Socinians, in which I discussed the principles of religion, Scripture, God, creation, and similar topics. From that time I thought it best to rest for a while and wait to see whether our opponents would bring out anything against those views that ought to be examined in the meantime, and that might, as it bore on what we had already written, also advise us how we should handle the remaining matters in the volumes still to come, for the greater benefit of the Christian cause. But nothing of that kind has appeared for a long time now. Beyond my intention, the printer's delay in the edition of this second volume made it necessary to change type, and the earlier compositor, who was more careless, not only drew out the work at great length but also did not follow my wishes closely in setting it. I have since noticed this, and I will give an account of it individually in its proper place and correct the faults. Last year, however, an anonymous book appeared, whose author I will allow to remain hidden, since he prefers it. It was written against our venerable elder and friend Johann Amos Comenius, under the title Irenicomastix, or a Confirmation of the Irenicum of the Irenics. In it I saw that I too was cited on their side, not for what I had written in the first volume, but for my Theological Disputations on the True Deity of Christ from Primitive Antiquity, where I examined and discussed what I had read on this subject in that Irenicum. These matters also find their place in this second volume. I had expected a reply to our volume, and I had marked out as my opponent a man learned enough and a sharp disputant, Jonas Schlichting, whom Petavius, in the preface to book XVII of the fourth volume of his Theologica Dogmata, calls a most foul and pestilent man among the opponents, where he speaks of Schlichting's work against Meisner.

units.la: Atque ego scripseram jam ann. MDCL in Apparatu, ad Controversias & Disputationes Socinianas, pag. 68. Jonam Schlichtingium Adversarium mihi cupio, designo: hic in vivis superest, & qualis sit, in disputationibus suis cum Balthasare Meisnero ostendit, eumque eo lubentius hoc meo in scripto ad partes nonnunquam cito. Vir, si quid judico, ingenuus, & doctus, neque enim vel in ipso hoste virtutes quae sunt, dissimulandae: sufficit hoc unum culpare, quod hostis est. Nunc vero obiisse eum, accepi. Quare quod unum superest, ad Anonymum Irenici autorem conferre me debeo, & hujus, quae adversus nos, & causam nostram attulit, expendere. Quem vellem modestius argumentum tractasse hoc religionis primarium, & Adversarium quoque suum; atque nominis, quod induit, magis in tota disputatione fuisse memorem. Jam nihil minus vel agere visus fuit, vel curare, quam pacem inter Christianos dissidentes, non modo quod horrendo istum in finem utitur medio, sublatae videlicet ex Christianorum fide & animis vera Christi Salvatoris Deitate, sed quoque quod in disputatione tam impotenter versetur, ut in isto genere Scriptorum non viderim alium immodestius se gerentem: quum aliis fere solent illi affectare quandam animi & styli lenitatem. Dicendum enim est, quod ita se habere unusquisque in Scriptore nostro, si modo inspexerit, quamvis me a modestia, prae D. Comenio, laudare videatur, depredeprehendet, & magnam certe libri partem personalibus impleri criminationibus non sine stomacho videbit.
units.tr: And I had already written in the year 1650, in the Apparatus to the Socinian Controversies and Disputations, page 68: I wish to mark out Jonas Schlichting as my opponent. He is still alive, and in his disputations with Balthasar Meisner he shows what sort of man he is. I am the more willing to address him now and then in this writing of mine. He is, if I judge rightly, an honest and learned man, for one must not conceal the virtues that are present even in an enemy. It is enough to blame him for this one thing, that he is an enemy. Now, however, I have heard that he has died. Therefore, the one remaining task is that I must address the anonymous author of the Irenicum and weigh what he has brought against us and against our cause. I could have wished that he had handled this chief matter of religion more modestly, and had been more mindful, throughout the whole disputation, of the name he has taken on, even toward his opponent. As it is, nothing seems to have been further from his aim or his care than peace among Christians who disagree. This is not only because he uses for that dreadful end the means of removing from the faith and minds of Christians the true deity of Christ the Saviour, but also because he conducts the dispute so intemperately that I have not seen any other writer of this kind behave more immodestly. Others of that sort usually affect a certain gentleness of mind and style. For it must be said that anyone who looks closely at our author, though he may seem to praise me for my moderation in comparison with Comenius, will find him out, and will see with no little irritation that a large part of the book is filled with personal accusations.

units.la: Probare autem intendit, Jesum Christum non esse verum, sive summum Deum, ex natura, Scriptura, hanc enim illa, apud disputatores nostros, in hac etiam materia, antecedit; & denique ex antiquitate, sive traditione Ecclesiastica. Primum vero, nescio quid hoc est, quod in libri utriusque titulo praefigit Autor elogium infallibilitatis: in posteriori, Nova Confirmatio infallibilitatis Irenici Irenicorum. An infallibile putat suum Irenicum? Profecto maximae arrogantiae hoc est argumentum: nam utcunque verum esset, quod Irenico suo scripsit, non proinde est infallibile. Nam aliquid verum potest esse, utcunque non eo genere & gradu veritatis, ut sit infallibile. Veritas probatur ex convenientia rei cum suo archetypo, idea, vel verborum aut conceptuum nostrorum cum ea; infallibilitas vero oritur ex qualitate seu dignitate personae, ut errare in hoc, quod docet, non possit. Multa dicimus quae vera, at non propterea infallibilia, quandoquidem fallibiles sumus ipsi. Saepe non falli, at semper fallibiles. Jam vero neque etiam vera ratio Irenici est, nec exempli, seu doctrinae ejus, cui placuit insistere, de Christo; sed prorsus salsissima. Ut turpiter admodum in limine impingat & imponat, quando infallibilitatis praeconium Irenico suo praescribere ausus temere fuit: & sibi imprimis dicta aestimet, quae ipse Comenio, statim in initio, pag. 2. Apostolus, ubi Pseudo-Apostolos perstringebat, summa doctrina sua certitudine infallibilitateque ejusdem praeditus erat, adeo ut contradicentes sibi convincere, iisque os obstruere potuerit. Tu vero aequis es, qui te hic cum Apostolo conferre velis? Et unde doctrina tua certitudo aut infallibilitas patet, ut alii te itidem Ducem ac Magistrum suum agnoscere aut revereri teneantur?
units.tr: He intends, however, to prove that Jesus Christ is not the true, or supreme, God: from nature, from Scripture (for among our disputants, even in this matter, Scripture comes before nature), and finally from antiquity, or the ecclesiastical tradition. As for the first, I do not know what it means that the author prefixes to the title of each book the praise of infallibility: in the latter he calls it A New Confirmation of the Infallibility of the Irenicum of the Irenics. Does he think his Irenicum infallible? Surely this is an argument of the greatest arrogance. For however true it may be that he wrote in his Irenicum, it does not on that account become infallible. Something can be true without being true in that kind and degree of truth which makes it infallible. Truth is proved from the agreement of a thing with its archetype or idea, or of our words or concepts with it; but infallibility arises from the quality or dignity of a person, such that he cannot err in what he teaches. We say many things that are true, yet not for that reason infallible, since we ourselves are fallible. We often do not err, but we are always fallible. Moreover, neither the reasoning of the Irenicum nor the example or doctrine about Christ that he chose to insist upon is true at all; rather it is wholly foolish. So he shamefully stumbles and trips at the threshold, when he has rashly dared to prescribe to his Irenicum the praise of infallibility. He should rather consider as said to himself what he himself says to Comenius at the very beginning, on page 2: The Apostle, when he rebuked the false apostles, was endowed with the utmost certainty and infallibility of his teaching, so that he could convict those who contradicted him and stop their mouths. But are you so fair-minded that you would compare yourself here with the Apostle? And where is the certainty or infallibility of your teaching made plain, so that others are likewise bound to acknowledge you and revere you as their leader and master?

units.la: Jam quod hunc articulum de Christo, quod non sit verus & aeternus ac summus Deus, sumserit pro exemplo, in Irenicorum Irenico, dat rationes, à pag. 14. quatuor. Et primo quidem, quod putat sibi observasse, homines si quando relicta priori sententia & secta, amplectantur[?] Socinianorum seu Monarchianorum de Christo sententiam, ex lupis fieri opes[?], sive qui antea alias à sua diversas sectas fuerant prosecuti odio implacabili, protinus mutari & amare incipere reliquas sectas omnes, & cum iis pacem colere velle. Quod an satis bene observarit, multum dubito: certe id non experti sumus in aliis, non in hoc Autore nos ipsi. Et si tale quid forte unquam evenerit, nec veram pacem interpretamur, quâ isti cæteras Sectas prosequantur, neque ex mutatione animi in melius ortam, sed potius ex veræ & purioris doctrinæ contemtu & fastidio, omnia porro in religione suisque deque habente, & parum curante quid quis dicat, doceat, aut credat: quomodo facile reliqua parvi pendunt, qui semel gravissimum & primarium de Christo prodiderunt articulum.
units.tr: As for his taking this article, that Christ is not the true and eternal and supreme God, as an example in the Irenicum of the Irenics, he gives four reasons, from page 14. The first is that he thinks he has observed that when men, having abandoned their former opinion and sect, embrace the opinion of the Socinians or Monarchians about Christ, they turn from wolves into lambs. Those who before had pursued with implacable hatred the sects differing from their own at once change, begin to love all the other sects, and want to cultivate peace with them. Whether he has observed this well enough, I very much doubt. Certainly we have not experienced it in others, and not in this author himself. And if something of the sort ever happens, we do not take it for true peace with which they pursue the other sects, nor do we think it arises from a change of mind for the better. It arises rather from contempt and distaste for true and purer doctrine, and from a habit of holding everything in religion, and their own affairs, in light regard, caring little what anyone says, teaches or believes. Thus those who have once put forward the most serious and chief article about Christ easily make little of the rest.

units.la: Secundam causam dicit, quia nullum dogma brevius, certius, & clarius poterat demonstrare, quam istud, Christum nimirum non esse summum Deum. Hoc autem negamus. Probat, autoritate Pontificio-rum, & Lutheranorum, qui fateantur, Socinianorum sententiam ex Scripturis convinci aut refutari nequaquam posse. Lutheranorum vero nominat neminem, & valde metuo ne producere aliquem possit. Ex Pontificiis solum producit Jesuitam Petavium: ad quod & antehac respondimus: neque admodum mirum, ita si loquuntur Papistæ, ad commendandas quâ vi, quâ injuriâ suas traditiones. Fac vero idem dicere & Pontificios, & Lutheranos omnes, quod neutiquam tamen ita se habet, non propterea illud quod dixit, vel eorum testimonio pro-bare annisus fuit Autor noster, est verum. Jam vero ex Scripturis non refutarunt Socinianorum errores Lutherani, non Pontificii? & quid-quid etiam fecerint, annon tentarunt saltem? ut certe noluerint sup-peditare argumentum alicui dicendi, ex Scripturâ Socinianam senten-tiam redargui non posse. Quid quod ipse Petavius illo, ad quem hic remittimur, loco ex Scripturis Socinianam sententiam refutat: tantum abest, ut refutari posse neger. §. III. Ad hanc igitur exponenda Scriptu-ra præscriptionem omnia nostra dirigentes duo universe contra Crelliana sophismata præscribimus, tam ex divina Scripturarum auctoritate, quam ex majorum decreto ac sententia. — Hæc nos catholica veritatis firmamenta duo, nempe de Christi utraque naturâ, divinâ & humanâ; atque æternâ ejus generatione à Patre, tam in Scripturis, ut dixi, quam in facultorum omnium approbatione, ad hunc fixa diem, atque fundata, contra Crelianas artes, & interpretandi temeritatem & calumniam objecimus. Disputavit enim toto libro Petavius, & ex Scriptura, & aliunde, adversus Crellii librum de uno[?] Deo Patre, eumque exarmavit. Eat nunc Noster, & scribat, uti facit pag. 15. quod Pontificii ipsi cum Lutheranis nonnullis ingenue fateantur, Socinianorum seu Monarchianorum sententiam ex scripturis convinci aut refutari nequaquam posse. Notetque Petavium, Dogmat. Theol. Tom. II. lib. III. cap. XI. ubi quidem scribit §. IX. qui sola scriptura, hoc est scriptis verbis fidem suam alligant, qui præter hanc nullam credendi sibi normam, ac regulam constituunt, quoties cum talibus pestibus pugnam conferunt, quæ se solis itidem scriptura verbis tegunt, ac tuentur, sudare plus satis eos necesse est, & suo artificio superari. Quod iis sæpius in Colloquiis, ac disputationibus, quas cum Photinianis, Arianisque contulerunt, superiore illis accidisse sæculo, memoria proditum est. verùm hoc non est dicere, Socinianorum sententiam ex Scripturis convinci aut refutari nequaquam posse: quamquam sæpius in colloquiis & disputationibus cum Photinianis plus satis fudasse eos, & illorum artificio etiam superatos, constaret. Deinde loquitur illo paragrapho Petavius, de tali homine, coram quo disputatio cum Photinianis instituta eum ancipitem animi reddiderat, in quam partem inclinaret, quem ad fidem porro permoveri posse accedente Ecclesiæ autoritate & judicio, contendit, nec aliter. Notum autem, ex quâ illud hypothesi Jesuita urgeat. Sed verò hoc iterum non est, errorem Photinianum ex scripturis convinci aut refutari nequaquam posse. Accipe Petavii verba :sed hoc demum illos consequi vi & subtilitate sua, ut in utrumvis difficile veri judicium reddant. Erit tunc videlicet anceps, & incertus auditoris, vel lectoris animus, & ne usquam errore labatur, assensum suum sustinebit. Quid igitur sic affecto, & constituto homini faciendum vel illi ipsi suadeant? in hoc, inquam, partium conflictu, cum nec Photiniani nostro, neque nos illorum judicio, & scripturarum interpretatione stare velimus, quis erit, obsecro, rixarum ac jurgiorum modus; nisi tamquam ex compromisso controversia arbiter aliquis, ac disceptator adhibeatur? Quis autem magis idoneus capi potest, quam Ecclesia ipsa, quæ columna est, & firmamentum veritatis? Quis autem ignorat communem Pontificiorum, pro judice controversiarum Ecclesiā, argumentationem, & ad hoc adstruendum adhiberi solitum ex 1 Tim. iii. 15. Scripturæ locum? Petavius loquitur, de movendo animo ad fidem; noster Autor, de refutandā sententiā aut errore: Jesuita, de homine dubio & sententiæ amplectendæ incerto, quid tunc videlicet agi conveniat, quodve porro adhibendum sit argumentum; Scriptor Irenici, de disputatione & partibus inter se contendentibus, vel ubi de refutandā agitur alterius sententiā. Ubi nos contrā tuemur, instandum esse iterum ex Scriptura, & permovendum eā animum, & non esse necessarium, in ejus subsidium advocare, pro ingenerandā & fundandā fide, Ecclesiæ sive antiquæ, sive hodiernæ autoritatem. Etenim si inde quod sic colligit & argumentatur Petavius, tu rite concludas, ipsum statuere, Sociniano-rum doctrinam ex Scripturā erroris convinci non posse, poteris æque Petavio impingere, & omnibus adeo Pontificiis, quod doceant, nullam prorsus controversiā ex Scripturis refutari posse,& non tantum illam de Christi deitate: quia in quācunque controversiā ipsis non cedirur, eo mox accurrunt argumento, ut necessariam faciant judicis Ecclesiae autorita-tem, sine quā decidi controversias vel fidem suaderi posse, negant.
units.tr: The author gives a second reason: no doctrine could be proved more briefly, more certainly, and more clearly than this one, namely that Christ is not the supreme God. We deny this. He argues from the authority of the Papists and the Lutherans, who admit that the opinion of the Socinians cannot in any way be convicted or refuted from the Scriptures. He names no Lutheran, and I greatly fear he could not produce one. From the Papists he produces only the Jesuit Petavius, to whom we have already replied. It is not surprising that Papists speak this way, since they urge their own traditions by force and wrong. But suppose that all Papists and all Lutherans said this, which is by no means the case; our author has not thereby proved what he said, whether by their testimony or otherwise. Indeed, did the Lutherans and the Papists not refute the errors of the Socinians from the Scriptures? And whatever they did, did they not at least attempt it? Surely they did not wish to supply anyone with the argument that the Socinian opinion cannot be refuted from Scripture. What is more, Petavius himself, in the very passage to which we are referred, refutes the Socinian opinion from the Scriptures; so far is he from denying that it can be refuted. §. III. Directing all our efforts to the explanation of this Scriptural rule, we set against the Crellian sophisms two firm propositions, drawn as much from the divine authority of the Scriptures as from the decree and judgment of our predecessors. These two foundations of Catholic truth, namely Christ's two natures, divine and human, and his eternal generation from the Father, fixed and grounded both in the Scriptures, as I have said, and in the approval of all the faculties up to this day, we have opposed to the Crellian arts, to their rash interpretation and their calumny. For Petavius, throughout his whole book, disputed against Crellius's book On the One God the Father, both from Scripture and from other sources, and disarmed him. Let our author now go and write, as he does on page 15, that the Papists themselves, with some Lutherans, frankly admit that the opinion of the Socinians or Monarchians cannot in any way be convicted or refuted from the Scriptures. Let him note Petavius, Dogmatic Theology, vol. II, book III, chapter XI, where indeed he writes, §. IX. Those who bind their faith to Scripture alone, that is to the written words, and who set up no rule of belief except this, must necessarily sweat more than enough, and be overcome by their own craft, whenever they engage in combat with such plagues as shelter and defend themselves by the words of Scripture alone. This is recorded in memory as having happened to them very often in the colloquies and disputations which they held with the Photinians and Arians in the previous century. But this is not to say that the Socinian opinion cannot in any way be convicted or refuted from the Scriptures; although it was established that in colloquies and disputations with the Photinians they had sweated more than enough and were overcome by their craft. Next, in that same paragraph Petavius speaks of a certain man, before whom a disputation with the Photinians had made his mind so wavering that he might incline to either side; and he contends that such a man can be moved further toward the faith by the added authority and judgment of the Church, and in no other way. It is well known from what hypothesis the Jesuit is pressing this. But again this is not to say that the Photinian error cannot in any way be convicted or refuted from the Scriptures. Hear Petavius's own words: But they achieve only this, by their force and subtlety, that they make a true judgment difficult either way. Then, of course, the mind of the hearer or reader will be doubtful and uncertain, and lest it slip anywhere into error, it will withhold its assent. What, then, should be done for, or suggested to, a man so disposed? In this conflict of parties, I say, since neither the Photinians are willing to stand by our judgment and interpretation of Scripture, nor we by theirs, what, I ask, will be the end of such quarrels and wrangling, unless some arbiter and judge is called in, as in a compromise? And who can be found more fit for this than the Church itself, which is the pillar and foundation of truth? Who does not know the common argument of the Papists, that the Church is the judge of controversies, and the passage of Scripture usually adduced for establishing this, 1 Tim. iii. 15? Petavius speaks of moving the mind to faith; our author speaks of refuting an opinion or an error. The Jesuit speaks of a doubtful man, uncertain which opinion to embrace, and of what then ought to be done and what argument should further be applied; the writer of the Irenicum speaks of a disputation and of parties contending with one another, or where the question is about refuting another's opinion. Where we, on the contrary, maintain that one must press on again from Scripture, and move the mind by it, and that it is not necessary to call in the authority of the Church, ancient or present, to produce and found faith. For if from what Petavius thus infers and argues you rightly conclude that he holds the doctrine of the Socinians cannot be convicted of error from Scripture, you could equally charge Petavius, and indeed all the Papists, with teaching that no controversy whatever can be refuted from the Scriptures, and not only that concerning Christ's deity. For in whatever controversy they are not yielded to, they at once run to this argument, so as to make the authority of a judge in the Church necessary, and they deny that controversies or faith can be settled without it.

units.la: Quis autem illam ipsis propterea adscribat opinionem, quod propter hanc de Ecclesiae autoritate, vel traditionum necessitate, putent, controversiam vel dogma controversum aliquod ex Scripturis convinci aut refutari nequaquam posse? Et quod in gratiam tum illarum hypothesium, tum quoque alterius his vicinae & consectaneae, de Scripturae imperfectione ita loquitur Jesuita, tum ex animo & instituto ejus, tum ex cursu totius disputationis, imo ex solâ denominatione honorificâ scilicet Calvinianorum & Lutheranorum, potest reddi manifestum. Hoc ipso capite §. III. Scripturas non tantum obscuras, sed & instar propheticorum oraculorum ambiguas, ait. Denique non esse mentem Petavii, uti Noster colligit, sententiam Socini ex Scripturis refutari minime posse, & ex claris ipsius verbis, & facto seu disputatione in contrarium ex Scripturâ, ad refutandam illam sententiam, satis superque patet. Imo è solis Scripturis disputationem se inire paratum ostendit: Negat utrumque Photi-nianus Crellius; ac tum unam numero & singularem esse Dei personam; tum Christum nihil esse praeter hominem affirmat. Non possunt ambo ista esse vera, sed vincat alterutra pars oportet. Vincet autem, opinor, ea, quae hoc asseverat, quod Deus dixerit. Jam quid dixerit, vel solis e Scriptura verbis, vel praeter hac, alunde necesse est petere. Nolo hic de scripto, vel non scr pto Dei verbo controversiam facere. Differamus hanc in aliud tempus, & in unis Scripturis hereat nostra contentio. Et vis, hunc docere, sententiam illam ex Scripturis convinci aut refutari nequaquam posse? quam eopse loco ex Scripturis per-git refellere.
units.tr: But why should anyone attribute to them that opinion, merely because, on account of this doctrine of the authority of the Church or the necessity of traditions, they think a controversy or some disputed doctrine cannot be convicted or refuted from the Scriptures? And that the Jesuit speaks as he does about the imperfection of Scripture, in favour of those hypotheses and of another akin to them and consequent upon them, can be made plain both from his purpose and design and from the course of the whole disputation, indeed from the very honorific label he gives to the Calvinists and Lutherans. In this same chapter, §. III, he says that the Scriptures are not only obscure but also, like the prophetic oracles, ambiguous. Finally, that it was not Petavius's mind, as our author infers, that the opinion of Socinus cannot be refuted from the Scriptures at all, is sufficiently and more than sufficiently clear both from his plain words and from his deed, that is, his disputation against it from Scripture in order to refute that opinion. Indeed he shows that he is ready to enter into a disputation from the Scriptures alone: The Photinian Crellius denies both propositions; he affirms that the person of God is one and singular, and that Christ is nothing but a man. Both of these cannot be true, but one side must win. Yet he who asserts what God has said will win, I think. Now what God has said must necessarily be sought either from the words of Scripture alone, or else from elsewhere besides them. I do not wish here to make a dispute over the written or unwritten word of God. Let us postpone that to another time, and let our contention rest on the Scriptures alone. Do you wish to teach that this opinion cannot be convicted or refuted from the Scriptures? On this very point he goes on to refute it from the Scriptures.

units.la: De Petavio haec evidentius ob oculos ponenda fuerunt, quia in ejus testimonio Scriptor noster mirum quam gloriatur, in tota hac disputa-tione, & passim lectores suos ad eum ablegat: quin-& pag. 24. tam-quam ipsa Petavii verba recitaret, scribere non veretur, quod in modo allegatis verbis victoriam a parte Socinianorum necessario esse innuit. Quae si cui liberet exagitare, quem ad modum ille Comenium solet, non defuturam materiam satis video: sed [?]ἡμεῖς τοιαύτην συνήθειαν οὐκ ἔχομεν. Annotat & alium ex Petavio locum, quasi huic similem, Tom. iv. lib. xvi. cap. i. §. 8. Sed bene est, quod ipse addiderit, in eandem fere sententiam isthic scribere Petavium. Revera & hic Petavius argumentum illud à traditione seu autoritate Ecclesiae adhibendum censet, non quod causa illud postulet, ceu quae non satis ex Scriptura defendi queat, quem in sensum verba Petavii male adducuntur, sed ad pervicaces tantum convincendos & constringendos. Quod haec ipsa Petavii satis clare docent: non quod ex illis Scripturis satis magna lux ad veritatem dignoscen-dam non affluat. Viden' quod ad rem requiritur, satis clare & copiose ex Scriptura haberi posse? sed quod pervicacibus & obstinatis in sua quoque modo tuenda opinione mentibus promtum ac facile sit innumeras excogitare cavil-lationes &c. & propter hos putat nihil ultra Scripturam adferri commodius, praeter traditiones posse. Quare in ipso capitis argumento praefixit, non posse illis ex Scriptura verbis litem componi ob illorum pervicaciam.
units.tr: These matters about Petavius had to be set out more plainly, because our author boasts remarkably of his testimony throughout this whole disputation, and everywhere sends his readers off to him. Indeed, on page 24, as if he were reciting Petavius's own words, he does not hesitate to write that by the words cited, he implies that victory necessarily belongs to the side of the Socinians. If anyone wishes to castigate this, in the way he usually treats Comenius, I see that there will be no lack of material. But we do not have such a custom [ἡμεῖς τοιαύτην συνήθειαν οὐκ ἔχομεν]. He also notes another passage from Petavius, as if similar to this, Tom. iv, book xvi, chapter i, §. 8. But it is well that he himself added that Petavius writes almost to the same effect in that place. Indeed Petavius here too holds that the argument from tradition or the authority of the Church is to be applied, not because the cause requires it, as if it could not be defended sufficiently from Scripture (the words of Petavius are wrongly cited to that sense), but only to convict and constrain the stubborn. This Petavius's own words make quite clear: not because from those Scriptures a sufficiently great light for discerning the truth does not flow. Do you see that what the matter requires can be had clearly and abundantly from Scripture? But because it is easy for minds that are obstinate, and pertinacious in defending their opinion in whatever way, to devise countless cavils, etc. And on account of these people he thinks nothing more suitable can be brought forward beyond Scripture, except traditions. Therefore at the head of the chapter's own argument he has prefixed: that controversies cannot be settled by those words of Scripture on account of the obstinacy of those men.

units.la: Nos vero censemus, minus Ecclesiae autoritate commotum iri, qui Scripturis non cesserit, adeoque talem cum sua pervicacia sibi relinquendum esse, & Deo. Quam animi pravitatem si deponant, & soli rei studeant, facile ex Scriptura convincendos ipse etiam Petavius asserit. Nihil ergo dixit in praejudicium causae, quidem adversariorum. Et quid si dixisset, quid ad nos? neque enim ex Petavio pendemus.
units.tr: We, however, think that someone who has not yielded to the Scriptures will be moved less by the authority of the Church, and so such a person must be left to his own obstinacy and to God. If such people lay aside their perversity and devote themselves only to the matter itself, Petavius himself asserts that they can easily be convinced from Scripture. He therefore said nothing to the prejudice of our cause, or of the adversaries' cause either. And what if he had said so? What is that to us? We do not depend on Petavius.

units.la: Communis autem illa & trita est Pontificiorum sententia, adversus Reformatos omnes, non peculiaris Jesuitae unius, in hoc argumento: quapropter etiam cap. II. quod de Socinianis dicto, idem & ad Lutheranos, & Calvi-nistas pertinet, adeoque recentiores haereses omnes: nempe quae ad solas scripturas adhaerescere se profitentur. Quare frustra pro se, tamquam doctrinae suae faventem producit Irenicus Petavium. Qui idem prorsus dicet de quacumque alia controversia sive cum Socinianis, sive cum aliis:è quibus temere quis concludat, ipsum innuere victoriam esse penes nos, penes alios, quia in omnibus, propter adversariorum sive constantiam, sive tergiversationes, deveniendum tandem ad Ecclesiae autoritatem statuit, & sine eâ frangi aut convinci alios non posse. Et quod ad Socinianos, tantum abest ut illis de se, de doctrinâ, & fide suâ catholicâ victoriam largiatur, ut ex Scripturâ, & eâ solâ illos refellat. Sunt enim quamplurima, eaque difertissima Scriptura testimonia, qua Christum Dominum ambo hac esse, Deum & hominem, perspicue demonstrant. inquit hoc ipso cap. I. & aliquoties in eundem sensum loquitur. Exiis omnibus Scriptura locis manifeste consequuntur illa, qua de filio Dei, deque divinitate ipsius, & incarnatione fides catholica profitetur: neque clarius, ac differtius exprimi ista potuerunt. §. IV. Atenim de singulis illis locis controversiam movent; & aliter intelligenda illa pugnant Adversarii, quam nos volumus.
units.tr: That opinion, however, is common and well worn among the Papists, held against all the Reformed, and is not peculiar to one Jesuit, on this subject. For this reason, too, in chapter II he says: "What has been said of the Socinians applies equally to the Lutherans and the Calvinists, and so to all the more recent heresies," namely those which profess to cling to Scripture alone. So Irenicus vainly produces Petavius as if he favoured his doctrine. Petavius would say exactly the same about any other controversy, whether with the Socinians or with others. From this one could rashly conclude that he is hinting that victory lies with us, or with others, because in all of them, on account of the adversaries' either firmness or evasions, he finally decides that one must come to the authority of the Church, and that without it others cannot be overthrown or convicted. And as for the Socinians, he is so far from conceding to them the victory over him, over his doctrine and his catholic faith, that he refutes them from Scripture alone. For, in chapter I of this same work, he says: "There are very many and very clear testimonies of Scripture which plainly demonstrate that Christ our Lord is both God and man." And he speaks several times to the same effect. "From all these passages of Scripture, those things follow clearly which the catholic faith professes concerning the Son of God, concerning his divinity and incarnation; nor could these things have been expressed more clearly and more fully." §4. "But the adversaries stir up controversy over each of these passages, and they struggle to understand them differently from how we wish."

units.la: Quid tum? Minusne propterea convenienter ex sacrarum auctoritate Scriptu-rarum Catholicum, & omnibus retro saeculis sic intellectum, ac praedicatum dogma defendimus? Scilicet qui ita loquitur, ex Scripturis sacris victoriam à parte Socinianorum necessario esse innuit? innuit victoriam penes eos esse, & quidem etiam necessario? Quid non persuaderi hominibus credant isti homines, qui sic nobiscum agunt, & ad quaevis omnia rapiunt? Nimirum sic scripsit, atque ea concessit de illa parte vel doctrinâ Petavius, quam passim Christiani nominis inimicam teterrimam.——putidam, & fatuam odioque dignam Christianorum omnium haeresim, scribit locis istis, ad quae allegamur?
units.tr: "So what? Do we defend the catholic dogma, which has been understood and preached in this way in all past ages, any less appropriately from the authority of the holy Scriptures?" Surely the man who speaks like this does not hint that victory necessarily lies on the side of the Socinians? Does he hint that victory lies with them, and indeed necessarily? What will these men not persuade themselves of, who deal with us in this way and twist every statement to suit themselves? Surely this is how Petavius wrote, and conceded in that place or doctrine, which he elsewhere calls "most foul and an enemy of the Christian name… a foul and foolish heresy, worthy of hatred by all Christians," in the passages to which we are referred?

units.la: Denique quod neque antiquitatis doctrinam cum Socinianâ parem fuisse voluerit, sed cum Catholicâ nostrâ, indicant ejus disputationes, & verba. lib. III. de Trinit. cap. XI. §. III. Etenim quamvis eorum ali-qui nondum plenam Catholici decreti professionem expresserint; sed loquendi saltem genere ipso dissenserint ab eâ regulâ, quae post Nicaenam constituta Synodum est, ut in primo libro disputavimus: tamen & personas tres divinas reipsa distinctas, & harum secundam assumtâ carne hominem factam, diserte omnes edocent, & contra sentientes Ebionitas refellunt. & postea, Satis ista sunt ad Socinianorum refrenandam, qui cum suo dogmate consentientem se veterem Ecclesiam, ad Nicaenum usque, & aliquanto post, Concilium vel imperite, vel sine ulla fronte praedicant. In quo praeterea quam habetes, ac stupidi sunt! Nam qui ad id etiam tempus, quod Nicaenam Synodum secutum est, veram in Ecclesia de Deo fuisse fidem fatentur; necesse est ea pro veris complectantur[?], quae de eadem fide tam illa ipsa Nicaena Synodus, quam qui eiinterfuere, Catholici Patres professi sunt; imprimis autem Athanasius. Atqui pro duobus istis nusquam fere non Petavium nominat Irenaeus noster, ut ejus testimonio sententia Sociniani vincat, tum ex Scripturis, tum ex primâ Ecclesiae antiquitate. Quod utrumque ostendimus (opinor) nunc satis, praeter Petavii mentem, ipsi affingi, & praeter veritatem ex Scripturis, & Patribus ab ipso luculenter assertam. Et hoc scripti Irenici praecipuum est fundamentum, cui totum fere innititur: quod propterea & primò examinandum fuit, & nunc satis convulsum subrutumque arbitror. Diximusque ista ad secundam rationem, quam dedit, quare in Irenico exem-plum de Christi. Deitate sumserit potius, quam aliud, nempe quia judice scilicet Petavio, ea ex Scripturis probari non posset. Quod si etiam Petavius, si alii, si omnes Jesuitae, quin & Pontificii, & Lu-therani therani omnes dicerent, parum nos moveret, non magis quam alia, quæ vel illi, vel alii communia habent adversus Ecclesiam nostram, & veritatem.
units.tr: Finally, that he did not wish the doctrine of antiquity to be equal to the Socinian doctrine, but to our catholic one, is shown by his discussions and words. Book III, On the Trinity, chapter XI, §3: "For although some of them have not yet expressed a full profession of the catholic decree, but have at least differed in the very manner of speaking from that rule which was established after the Nicene Synod, as we argued in the first book, nevertheless they all plainly teach that the three divine persons are really distinct, and that the second of these, having assumed flesh, was made man, and they refute the Ebionites who thought otherwise." And afterwards: "These things are enough to restrain the Socinians, who foolishly, or without any shame, proclaim that the ancient Church agreed with their dogma, up to the Nicene Council and for some time after. How dull and stupid they are in this respect! For those who confess that the true faith concerning God existed in the Church even until the time that followed the Nicene Synod, must necessarily embrace as true those things which both that Nicene Synod itself and the Catholic Fathers who were present there professed concerning the same faith, above all Athanasius." Yet our Irenicus almost always names Petavius in support of these two points, so that by his testimony the Socinian opinion may be overcome, both from Scripture and from the earliest antiquity of the Church. We have now, I think, shown sufficiently that both of these are attributed to Petavius against his mind, and that the truth is luminously asserted by him from Scripture and the Fathers. And this is the chief foundation of the Irenicus' writing, on which almost the whole of it rests; therefore it had to be examined first, and I think it has now been sufficiently overturned and undermined. We have said these things in reply to the second reason he gives why in the Irenicus he took the example of Christ's deity rather than another, namely because, in the judgement of Petavius, it cannot be proved from Scripture. But if Petavius, or others, or all the Jesuits, and indeed all the Papists and all the Lutherans, were to say so, it would move us little, no more than other things which they, or others, hold in common against our Church and the truth.

units.la: Pro tertia adfert causa, quia illa unâ, de Christi vid. deitate, senten-tia cognita, multæ difficiles quæstiones mox simul cognoscuntur, & evadunt faciliores. Quod hactenus in genere dictum, nihil habet adversum nos, vel pro adversariis. Sed & periculum, quod vult esse in nostra de Christo sententia, sic simul putat tolli. Ecquodnam illud? Nempe quid in nostra sententia, si falsa sit (quemadmodum omnino falsa est, ) inquit, aperta & manifesta idololatria reperiatur, dum is, qui summus Deus non est, pro summo tamen Deo colitur & habetur. Adde, quod vos (sic loquitur) Christum quoque si summus Deus non est, (quemadmodum etiam omnino non est, neque esse potest,) prorsus contemnere, ne dicam abnegare, videamini, dum eum ut humanam tantum naturam habentem, præeunte vobis Augustino, de Verb. Dom. Serm. §8[?]. & Damasceno, lib. 3. cap. 8. NB. adorare, & pro Mediatore recipere, inque eum credere, prorsus dedignamini, eo quod creaturæ venerationi talis non debeatur. Numquid illa non est principii petitio, quam nobis aliquoties objiciunt, ubi sententiam nostram dicit falsam semel & iterum, & non probat? Nec metuit dicere, duplex periculum illud se nobis ad oculum quasi monstrasse, qua idololatria, quâ contemtus Christi hominis, ejusque abnegationis? Idololatriæ, quia colimus pro summo Deo, qui talis non est: contemtus, quod Christum, si non nisi homo sit, adorare detrectamus.
units.tr: For the third reason he offers: because once that one opinion about the deity of Christ is known, many difficult questions are at once known together with it and become easier. This, stated thus in general, has nothing against us or in favour of our adversaries. But he also thinks that the danger which he claims exists in our opinion about Christ is removed at the same time. What danger is that? Namely, he says, if our opinion were false (as indeed it is entirely false), there would be found a clear and manifest idolatry, since one who is not the highest God is worshipped and held as the highest God. He adds: "Since you (so he speaks) seem to despise Christ, if he is not the highest God (as indeed he is not, and cannot be), not to say to deny him, while, following Augustine in On the Words of the Lord, sermon 8 [?], and Damascene, book 3, chapter 8, NB, you regard him as having only a human nature, you utterly disdain to worship him and to receive him as Mediator and to believe in him, because such worship is not owed to a creature." Is this not a begging of the question, which they often throw at us, when he calls our opinion false once and again and does not prove it? Nor does he fear to say that he has shown us, as if before our eyes, a twofold danger: idolatry on one side, and on the other contempt and denial of Christ the man. Idolatry, because we worship as the highest God one who is not such; contempt, because we refuse to worship Christ if he is only a man.

units.la: Primùm, si illa idololatria est, ejus ipsi quoque rei sunt, quod pro Deo habent, & colunt, qui tamen Deus non est: & verum etiam dicunt Deum, qui verus non est. Nam passim se jactant Christum Deum agnoscere, & verum. Nos verò inde ita pergimus: quod si Chri-stus Deus, & verus Deus, uti Scriptura hoc tam clare docet, ut Ad-versarii reclamare, & aliter loqui non audeant, facile & lubentius hoc facturi, si non illa luce cogerentur; non ergo idolum colit, qui Christum colit verum Deum. Credimus autem Scripturam Christum dicentem Deum, & docentem quoque nonnisi unum esse Deum, vera loqui, præ-sertim quum non tantum passim eum Deum nominet, sed probet quoque omnibus argumentis, quibus probari ulla veritas potest. Quare qui Christum pro uno vero Deo colit, nihil præter Scripturam facit. Neque enim Scriptura plures veros Deos docet, aut eos adorari usquam imperat. Cedo, si ex vestro doctamine Scriptura testari vellet Christum esse Deum, quod nos credimus; quo demum sermone, quibus verbis, phrasibusque id faceret? age, explica: & audiamus terminum aut dicendi modum, qui si occurreret, tum vos crediturus, ut hinc constare nobis queat. Jam enim Deum vocat, nec loco uno, nec modo, & attributive, & subjective, & divina ei attribuuntur, praeterquam nomina, etiam attributa, & opera, & cultus: quid post illa & singula requiras amplius? Certe utcunque de nonnullis inter nos & Adversarios non conveniat, non tamen negant, nonnulla eorum quae vere divina sunt, praeterquam nomen, Christo passim in Scripturis attribui: ubi ergo nomen habemus, per divina alia explicatum, quid peccamus si vera esse credimus, & ex vero dici in Scriptura, potius quam vobiscum metaphorice? Praesertim quia in materia de Deo, eoque colendo, Scripturam satis cautam novimus, ut ne quid doceat, quod in idololatriae argumentum rapi possit.
units.tr: First, if that is idolatry, then they themselves are guilty of it, who hold and worship as God one who is not God, and who also call God one who is not the true God. For they everywhere boast that they acknowledge Christ as God and as true. But we go on thus: if Christ is God, and the true God, as Scripture teaches this so clearly that the adversaries cannot protest and dare not speak otherwise (they would do so easily and gladly, if they were not compelled by that light), then he who worships Christ does not worship an idol but the true God. We believe, moreover, that Scripture, which calls Christ God and also teaches that there is only one God, speaks true things, especially since it not only names him God everywhere, but also proves it by every argument by which any truth can be proved. Therefore he who worships Christ as the one true God does nothing beyond Scripture. For Scripture does not teach that there are several true gods, nor does it anywhere command that they be worshipped. Come now, if, according to your doctrine, Scripture wished to testify that Christ is God, as we believe, in what language, with what words and phrases would it do so? Come, explain, and let us hear the term or mode of speaking which, if it occurred, would make you believe, so that it might be established for us. For he already calls him God, and not in one place or in one way, both attributively and substantively, and divine attributes are ascribed to him, not only names but also attributes, works and worship. What more do you require after these and each of them? Certainly, however far there may be disagreement between us and the adversaries about some things, they do not deny that many things which are truly divine, apart from the name, are everywhere in Scripture ascribed to Christ. Where then we have the name, explained by other divine things, why do we sin if we believe these to be true, and that they are said in Scripture truly rather than, as you do, metaphorically? Especially since we know that Scripture, in matters concerning God and his worship, is cautious enough not to teach anything that could be seized upon as an argument for idolatry.

units.la: Dices forte, in Scripturis non tradi Christum esse summum Deum, quod si extaret, tum vos crediturus. Ego vero primùm quaero, num etiam aliud quid sit, quod ad rei hujus fidem & doctrinam desideretis, scilicet verbum vel loquutio alia? Atqui si vel illud καὶ λέγειν[?] in Scripturis totidem syllabis & apicibus de Christo expresse legeretur, nec defuturas etiam sic vobis praevideo exceptiones & responsiones, quas ad hoc, aeque ac ad alia quae nunc à nobis proferuntur, promtum quoque foret comminisci. Videlicet summum Deum diceretis, id est, summo inter creaturas officio, honore, loco decoratum, summum supra creaturas, non tamen parem seu aequalem aut unum cum Deo. Quare etiam Noster,pag.135.inquit, hac ratione ego quoque Christum summum (i.e. Angelis quoque superiorem) Deum esse concedo. Viden' ut ne sic quidem tergiversandi praecisa erit occasio, imo praeripi nullâ, ne quidem à vobis ipsis promendâ & excogitandâ, loquutione poterit, quamdiu ejusmodi exceptionibus ludere constitutum est, ac fit à vobis in locis aliis? Age profer mihi ullam vocem aut dictionem, quâ vos acquieturos si Scripturâ continueretur, in fide verae & unius Christi deitatis nobiscum, profiteamini: & ego, quamvis quid prolaturi fitis divinare nequeam, spondeo tamen me ad istud ex solitis vestris responsionibus & cavillationibus allaturum, quod ejus vim enervabit, & ostendet vel istis modis, quibus Christi deitatem probavimus ex Scripturâ, factum satis, vel aliis non posse: & sic vestras expositiones debere aeque cedere claritati verborum & sensuum, quem nunc habemus, ac quibusvis aliis ex vestro ipsorum placito demum proferendis. Deinde quid attinuit Christum summum[?] Deum dici, quando eum Scriptura toties Deum appellat? Quum nullus alius Deus sit, quam summus, nec Scriptura alium, quam summum norit vel tradat. Non enim aut multitudinem, aut divisionem Deorum Scriptura docet, & Deum alterum summum, alterum non summum. Imo quia nota relativa non additur in Scripturis, ubi de deitate Christi sermo est, Dei vel supremi, vel inferioris, hoc pro argumento est, absolute summum esse, quem Deum testatur. Ergo toties Christus Deus summus dicitur, ac docetur esse Deus: & quod is est, in quem, uti in Deum, credere, sperare, & reclinare absolute debemus. Porro annon satis summus Deus nuncupatur, quando in principio fuisse dicitur, non tantum ante omnia, sed & supra omnia, & apud Deum, & Deus ipse, denique per ipsum facta esse omnia? Joan. 1. 1. 2. quan-do Paulus ipsum scribit Deum benedictum supra omnia in fæcula? Rom. ix. 5. & Phil. ii. 6. quod in forma Dei fuit æqualis ἴσα Θεῷ? Ne alia huic in finem addam, quæ, ubi de Christo Deo disputamus, adferri solent. Porro quid per summum Deum intelligunt? an summum supra creaturas omnes: sic etiam, ex ipsorum confessione Christus summus Deus est. Si summum supra Deos alios? Nec isto sensu summitatem Dei Scriptura tradit, quæ plures Deos non agnoscit, sed damnat; uti nec Deum ullum factum docet ullibi, vel fieri posse. Adeo ut, quâ ratione Deus summus est, eâdem & Christus sit quoque. Summum enim dicitur in ordine ad alia.
units.tr: You may perhaps say that Scripture does not teach that Christ is the supreme God, and that if it did, you would believe it. But first I ask whether you also require some other thing for faith in and doctrine of this matter, namely a particular word or some other form of expression. For if even that phrase and to say [καὶ λέγειν] were read in Scripture of Christ, in as many syllables and letters, I foresee that you would not lack exceptions and answers even then, and it would be just as easy for you to devise them against this as against the other things we now bring forward. Of course you would say that he is the supreme God, that is, adorned with the highest office, honour and rank among creatures, supreme above creatures, but not equal or one with God. That is why our author also says, on page 135, in this sense I too concede that Christ is the supreme God (that is, superior even to the angels). Do you see how, even in this case, there would be no cut-off point for evasion? Indeed, no expression, not even one you yourselves would have to produce and invent, could forestall it, so long as you have decided to play with such exceptions, as you do elsewhere. Come, name for me any word or phrase which you would accept, if it were found in Scripture, and which you would profess along with us in the faith of the true and only deity of Christ. Although I cannot guess what you are going to offer, I promise that I will bring from your usual answers and cavils something that will weaken its force and show that either by those very ways in which we have proved the deity of Christ from Scripture enough has been done, or else that it cannot be done by others. And so your interpretations must yield just as much to the clarity of the words and of the sense we now have as to any others that you might devise according to your own opinion. Next, what is the point of calling Christ the supreme God, when Scripture so often calls him God? Since there is no other God than the supreme one, and Scripture knows and teaches no other than the supreme one. For Scripture does not teach a multitude or a division of gods, one supreme and another not supreme. Indeed, because no relative qualifier is added in Scripture when the deity of Christ is discussed, saying God of the highest or of the lower, this is the proof that he who is attested as God is supreme in an absolute sense. Therefore Christ is so often called the supreme God, and is taught to be God; and he is the one in whom, as in God, we must absolutely believe, hope and rest. Moreover, is he not named supreme God enough, when he is said to have been in the beginning, not only before all things but also above all things, and with God, and God himself, and finally when all things were made through him? (John 1:1, 2.) When Paul writes that he is God blessed above all for ever? (Rom. 9:5.) And when he was in the form of God, equal to God [ἴσα Θεῷ]? (Phil. 2:6.) I will not add other passages to this purpose, which are usually brought forward when we dispute about Christ as God. But what do they understand by supreme God? Is it supreme above all creatures? Then, by their own confession, Christ is the supreme God in that sense too. Or supreme above other gods? Scripture does not teach the supremacy of God in that sense either, since it acknowledges no plurality of gods but condemns it; nor does it teach anywhere that any God has been made, or could be made. So that, by the same reasoning by which God is supreme, Christ too is so. For supreme is said in relation to other things.

units.la: Jam ad priora redeundo, nec idololatriæ rei, nisi per grandem calumniam, postulamur, quia non idolum, sed Deum, ab ipsa Scriptura innumeris locis testatum ac probatum, colimus: nec contemtus, quia summum credimus & veneramur. At hominem eum non adoramus, ac proinde contemnimus. Itane qui hominem, qui creaturam non adorat, contemnit? Qui adorat Christum, & hoc magis, quod Deum credit, ullâ fronte aut Christi, aut cultus ejus contemti argui potest? Imo ne con-temtores Dei, & jussionis divinæ videamur rei, quâ severe cavet invocari ullum, præter verum, & unum Deum, in Novo pariter Testamento, ac Veteri, ᾧ[?] αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις, Matth. iv. 10. addens hic μόνῳ, quod in verbis textus Deut. vi. tamen non est, sed quidem in ejus διανοίᾳ, ut non minus nunc unum solum Deum colendum ostenderet, quam unquam antea, adde Apoc. xix. 10. & xxii. 9. & ut ne idolo-latriæ ullius communione nos commaculemus, non alium invocamus, præterquam verum Deum. Quanto majori jure ista in Adversarios retorqueamus? dum, si vera sit nostra sententia, uti omnino vera est (sic enim nobis æque licer[?] agere, ac illis adversum nos, ad ostendendum quoque periculum in sententia ipso-rum) improbi in Christum contemtus rei sunt, quando pro Deo vero non agnoscunt, qui seipsum, quem Pater, quem omnia toties tamque diser-te Deum esse comprobant, & pro tali tamen non recipiunt, quin, Ju-dæorum instar, contrà nituntur, & adimunt ei, quantum in ipsis, hoc quod est summum, nempe deitatem summam. Iterum idololatriæ de-bent argui, dum divino cultu prosequuntur illum qui Deus non est. Neque aliud idololatria est, quam unum verum Deum præterire, & alium non Deum pro Deo habere ac colere. Si dicas, vos ex contuma-ciā non peccare, vel contemtu in Christum; sed quia illud de ipso vobis non videatur in Scripturis doceri? An autem nos convicistis erroris vel contumaciæ, aut contemtus Christi? & non putatis æque nos dicere, nisi Scriptura illud testaretur nostro saltem judicio, nos illud non esse credituros? Ergo hactenus dum ex Scripturis, in disputatione de Christo Deo, aliter evictum sit, abstinere à recensendis illis cau-sis, & exprobrandis nobis idololatriæ, & contemtus Christi criminibus, quod tamen facit Noster debuisset. Scriptura semper ponit unum Deum adorandum, nunquam secundum, aut tertium, aut plures. Eadem Scri-ptura Christum dicit, & probat Deum, atque jubet adorari. Quid cer-tius hinc colligatur, quam Christum esse illum unum Deum? Non gra-dus aut species Deitatis usquam tradit, non etiam cultus divini: uti hoc adversus Papistas rite ostenditur à Reformatis, & repeti idem adversus Socinianos debet, qui non minus ac illi necesse habent cultum religiosum distribuere quasi in duliæ & hyperduliæ, vel latriæ & duliæ, pro diversitate veri Dei, aut facti. Neque enim qui non est summus Deus, summo honore coli potest. Noster, pag. 16. inquit: an Christi honori quicquam derogo aut detraho? & annon potius eundem summe & prout decet, extollo? Nota illud summe. Qui summo honore debet adorari, is summus est Deus. Vel, qui non est summus Deus, eundem summe extollere aut honorare non licet. Hominem tantum, à Deo exaltatum Dominum factum, uti de Christo loquitur, pag. 17. non licet summo cultu prosequi, non etiam divino aut religioso: atqui talis Christus est, aperta ipsorum confessione & doctrina. Quare quod periculum in ipso-rum sit sententia, hinc apparet: & quomodo, non nos, sed ipsi, Chri-stum prorsus de folio suo deturbent, deitatis nimirum, & cultus summi: & denique num nihil referat, sive de ejus naturâ divinâ constet, sive non, quum nisi illud fit, divinus ipsi honor competere non possit. Et quando corpus glorificatum, uti hic loqueris, brachium tuum statuis, quamvis non infirmam, carnem tamen, & hoc contra voluntatem & mandatum Dei, habes, Jerem.xxx. 9. Nec magis eludes divinam sententiam, distinctione inter corpus glorificatum, & non glorificatum, quam Pontificii dicendo, se non nisi glorificatos & beatos adorare. Neque Deus istam praeformavit, in cultus divini negotio, distinctionem, inanem prorsus ac futilem. Quum fundamentum divini & religiosi cultus, uti contra Pontificios & idololatras omnes hactenus bene Ecclesia asseruit, non sit corpus, non homo tantum; sed Deus, ejusque divina natura: non corporis aut hominis glorificatio, neque Christi etiam, qui etiam nondum glorificatus adorari tamen debuit, & proinde pro ratione adorabilitatis glorificationem non habuit, sed aliud est, quod quia ipsi auferunt Adversarii, non sine turpi absurditate & contradictione cultum divinum ei vindicare possunt: uti ipsis ostensum à Christiano Francken, Francisco Davidis, aliisque, qui quamvis in hypothesi errarent, negantes Christum adorandum esse, in thesi tamen rite constringebant Socinum, quod qui non est Deus, religiose etiam cultu adorari non debeat. Jam quando Deus dixit, se gloriam suam alteri non daturum, ita generaliter, & ob causam generalem hoc asseruit, ut non tantum de Gentilium idolis & sculptilibus, sed quocunque non-Deo intelligi debeat. Annon & ipsi adversus Pontificiorum Deos id intorquebitis? Nempe quicunque non est verus ille unus Deus, alter ab ipso est, & huic, quicumque etiam sit, gloriam suam nec velle, nec posse dare se Deus testatur. Eamque à propria essentia suâ causam hic exprimit, dicens, ego sum Jehova, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. id est, alteri non, qui non sit ille mecum Jehova, & de nomine, ut essentia, mecum communicet. Et nos hinc culpari non possumus, quia Christum, non alterum Deum facimus, & non alteri à se Deo Deus gloriam illam communicat, sed suo ejusdem secum & essentiae & gloriae filio Pater. Caeterum 1 Cor. xv. 27. 28. & Joan. xiv. 28. agitur de Christo oeconomice considerato, uti Mediator est, & Mediatoris munere fungitur sub Patre, quod ejus Deitati, Theologicè considde-ratae, nequicquam adversatur.
units.tr: Now returning to what came before: we are charged with idolatry only by a great calumny, since we worship not an idol but God, whose existence and whose nature Scripture itself attests and proves in countless places; nor are we charged with contempt, since we believe him to be supreme and venerate him. But we do not adore a man, and therefore we do not despise him. Does one who does not adore a man or a creature despise him? Can anyone, with a straight face, accuse one who adores Christ, and all the more because he believes him to be God, of despising either Christ or his worship?
