Indeed, lest we seem to be despisers of God and of the divine command, which in the New Testament as in the Old strictly forbids any invocation of anyone except the true and one God—him only shalt thou serve [αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις], Matt. 4:10, adding here only [μόνῳ], which is not in the words of the text in Deut. 6, but is indeed in its sense, so as to show that the one God alone is to be worshipped now no less than ever before; add Rev. 19:10 and 22:9. And so that we may not defile ourselves by any communion with idolatry, we call upon no other than the true God. With how much greater right can we turn these charges back upon our adversaries? For if our view is true, as it entirely is (for it is just as lawful for us to argue thus against them, as they do against us, in order to show also the danger in their own opinion), then the wicked are guilty of contempt towards Christ, since they do not acknowledge as the true God him whom the Father and all things so often and so plainly prove to be God, and yet do not receive him as such; but, like the Jews, they strive against him and take from him, as far as in them lies, that which is supreme in him, namely supreme deity. Again, they ought to be charged with idolatry, since they pay divine worship to one who is not God. Idolatry is nothing other than passing over the one true God and having and worshipping another who is not God as God. If you say that you do not sin out of obstinacy or contempt towards Christ, but because this about him does not seem to you to be taught in Scripture: have we convicted you of error, or obstinacy, or contempt of Christ? And do you not think that we say the same, unless Scripture attested it, at least by our judgement, that we would not believe it? Therefore, so long as the matter has been decided otherwise from Scripture in the disputation about Christ as God, our author ought to have refrained from enumerating those charges and from throwing up to us the crimes of idolatry and of contempt of Christ, which nevertheless he does. Scripture always sets one God to be adored, never a second, or a third, or several. The same Scripture says and proves that Christ is God, and commands him to be adored. What can be more certainly inferred from this than that Christ is that one God? Scripture nowhere teaches degrees or kinds of deity, nor of divine worship either; as the Reformed rightly show against the Papists, and the same must be urged against the Socinians, who no less than those are obliged to distribute religious worship as if into dulia and hyperdulia, or latria and dulia, according to the difference of the true God or of the made one. For one who is not the supreme God cannot be worshipped with supreme honour. Our author says on page 16: Do I detract from or take away anything from the honour of Christ? Do I not rather exalt him in the highest degree and as is fitting? Note that word in the highest degree. One who must be adored with supreme honour is the supreme God. Or, one who is not the supreme God may not be exalted or honoured in the highest degree. To pay the highest worship to a mere man, exalted by God and made Lord, as he speaks of Christ on page 17, is not lawful, nor is divine or religious worship; yet such is Christ, by their own open confession and doctrine. Hence it is evident what danger lies in their opinion, and how it is not we but they who utterly cast Christ down from his throne, that is, of deity and of supreme worship. And finally, whether it makes no difference if it is agreed about his divine nature or not, since without it divine honour cannot belong to him. And when you set up the glorified body, as you put it here, as your arm, you have, though not a weak flesh, yet flesh, and this against the will and command of God (Jer. 30:9?). Nor will you elude the divine sentence any more by the distinction between a glorified and a non-glorified body than the Papists do by saying that they adore none but the glorified and blessed. For God has not prescribed any such distinction in the matter of divine worship, a distinction utterly empty and futile. Since the foundation of divine and religious worship—as the Church has rightly always asserted against the Papists and all idolaters—is not the body, not a man only, but God and his divine nature, the glorification of the body or of the man is not the ground, not even of Christ's, who ought to have been adored even before he was glorified and therefore did not have glorification as the basis of his worthiness of adoration. Rather, there is something else, which, since the adversaries take it away from him, they cannot attribute divine worship to him without shameful absurdity and contradiction. This was shown to them by Christian Francken, Francis David, and others, who, although they erred in their hypothesis by denying that Christ is to be adored, nevertheless rightly constrained Socinus in principle, since one who is not God ought not to be adored with religious worship either. Now, when God said that he would not give his glory to another, he asserted this in general terms, and for a general reason, so that it must be understood not only of the idols and graven images of the Gentiles, but of any non-God whatsoever. Will you not turn this also against the gods of the Papists? Whoever is not that one true God is other than he, and God declares that he neither wills nor is able to give his glory to whoever this is. And here he states the cause of it from his own essence, saying, I am Jehovah, this is my name, and my glory I will not give to another; that is, to another who is not that Jehovah along with me, and who does not share with me in name as in essence. Nor can we be blamed for this, since we do not make Christ another God, and God does not communicate that glory to another God apart from himself, but the Father communicates it to his Son, who with him is of the same essence and glory. Moreover, 1 Cor. 15:27, 28 and John 14:28 treat of Christ as considered economically, as he is Mediator and performs the office of Mediator under the Father; which does not in the least conflict with his deity considered theologically.

units.la: At Christo homini etiam data gloria adorationis. Homini mero? & denum homini, sive facto, sive glorificato? hoc negatur. Christum in mundum adducens jussit Deus adorari, præsertim ubi summâ post adscensionem decoratus in cœlis gloriâ, significatum fuit, omnibus agnoscendum & venerandum illum esse. Sed si principium, fundamentum, formalis causa quæratur ejus adorandi, est ipsius Deitas, quâ si careret, non esset adorandus, quacunque etiam gloriâ aut loco præfulgeret: loquimur de adoratione religiosâ, & cultu divino, non de veneratione aliâ communi aut civili, quod ad suum genus: neque etiam de causâ ob quam, sive argumento, propter quod adoretur, cujusmodi plura sunt; sed de principio formali adorabilitatis in ipso quærimus, & non tantum cur à nobis adoretur. Adoratur, quia nimirum est adorabilis; hactenus imus unâ; at in fundamentum si pergimus inquirere adorabilitatis, in diversa deflectimus. Adversarii accidentale aliquod in Christo, vel datam ipsi gloriam allegant ejus causam; nos verò adorabilitatis fundamentum agnoscimus nullum, præter naturam Deitatis. Qui Deus est, hoc ipso adorari debet; qui verò non est Deus, ideo non debet. Alia accedunt quidem confirmantia adorabilitatem, & ostendentia quod adorandus sit, & moventia animum ad adorationem, sed ipsius adorabilitatis ex quo fluat, principium est in naturâ, vid. divinâ. Multæ causæ sunt adorationis; una adorabilitatis. Uti Deus adoratur, propter varia, & quæcunque unquam præstitit opera, sed quamvis illa non essent, nullum opus ejus vel creatura extaret, non quidem adoraretur, non propter istas, ob quas nunc, causas; esset tamen semper adorabilis: quare? quia adorabilitas fundatur in Dei naturâ, non demùm oritur vel accedit ipsi aliunde, ex ullo suo opere. Adorabilitas attributû, & proprietatis est divinæ naturæ: adoratio, actio nostra, illo quidem fundamento nixa respectu adorandi, sed ad quam nos variis insuper movemur causis. Ita in Christo plurima sunt, ob quæ nos eum adoramus; sed prima causa, ob quam adorabilis est, natura est divina. Adoramus etiam quia carnem assumsit, homo factus pro nobis est, Mediatorem agit, glorificatus nunc in cælis vivit, aliquando revertetur judicaturus nos & salvaturus; sed hæc non sunt prima & formalis causa, quæ rei dat esse, sive quæ ipsi confert adorabilitatem, quæ est proprietas solius naturæ divinæ, neque aliunde fluere aut haberi potest, quam ab illâ. Propter creationem etiam adoratur, quemadmodum & propter alia, Deus, sed quamvis nunquam creator, fuisset tamen semper adorabilis, quia Deus. Ergo Deitas, sive natura divina sola fundamentum est adorabilitatis; non actio ulla, nedum passio, sive hoc quod forte Christus accepit gloriæ in tempore. Christi adorabilitas consideratur vel relate ad nos, qui ipsum adoramus; vel ad ipsum, qui adorandus est: illo modo dici potest, adorari, & adorandum, & adorabilem nobis esse propter illa etiam, quæ dicta; sed respectu ipsius, in ordine ad fundamentum proprium, & formale principium, unde per fe adorabilitas, tamquam proprietas fluit, nec est aliud præter divinam naturam, nec dari, vel concipi rite aliud potest. Certe eum ut hominem tantum, quamvis à Deo exaltatum, & Dominum factum, nec jubemur ullibi adorare, nec ut sic adorare licet. Sed causa formalis quâ, & reciproca adorabilitatis in Christo, ob quam positam adorari debet, & quâ negatâ non deberet adorari, est vera & sola ipsius deitas. Hæc ad tertiam Irenæi nostri causam, cur in exemplo de Christi Deitate tractando voluerit insistere.
units.tr: But glory of adoration was also given to Christ as man. Given to man merely? And indeed to man, whether made or glorified? This is denied. When God brought Christ into the mundum, he commanded him to be worshipped, especially since, after the ascension, he was adorned in heaven with the highest glory, which signified that all should acknowledge and venerate him. But if we ask for the principle, the foundation, and the formal cause of his being worshipped, it is his Deitas, and without it he would not be worthy of worship, however much glory or rank he might shine with. We are speaking of religious adoration and divine worship, not of other common or civil veneration, which is a different kind. Nor are we asking about the cause on account of which he is worshipped, or the argument for which he is worshipped, of which there are many. We are asking about the formal principle of his adorability, and not merely why he is worshipped by us. He is adored because he is indeed adorable; so far we go together. But if we press on to inquire into the foundation of his adorability, we turn in different directions. Our opponents allege some accidental feature in Christ, or the glory given to him, as its cause. We, however, acknowledge no foundation of adorability except the nature of the Deity. Whoever is God ought for that very reason to be worshipped; whoever is not God is for that reason not to be worshipped. There are indeed other things that confirm his adorability, show that he is to be worshipped, and move the mind to adoration. But the source from which his adorability itself flows lies in his nature, namely the divine nature. There are many causes of adoration; there is one cause of adorability. God is worshipped on account of the various works he has performed, and whatever works he has ever done. But even if those works had never existed, and no creature had ever come into being, he would not indeed be worshipped on those grounds on which he is now worshipped, yet he would always be adorable. Why? Because adorability is grounded in the nature of God, and does not arise or accrue to him from anywhere else, from any of his works. Adorability is an attribute and property of the divine nature; adoration is our act, which rests on that foundation with respect to the one adored, but to which we are moved besides by various other causes. So in Christ there are very many reasons why we worship him, but the first cause why he is adorable is the divine nature. We also worship him because he took on flesh, was made man for us, performs the office of Mediator, now lives glorified in heaven, and will at some time return to judge and save us. But these are not the first and formal cause, which gives the thing its being, or which confers on him adorability. That is the property of the divine nature alone, and it cannot flow from or be had from anything other than that nature. God is worshipped also on account of creation, as well as on account of other things; but even if he had never been Creator, he would still always have been adorable, because he is God. Therefore the Deity, or the divine nature alone, is the foundation of adorability; no action at all, still less a passion, or what Christ perhaps received of glory in time, is that foundation. Christ's adorability is considered either in relation to us, who worship him, or in relation to himself, who is to be worshipped. In the former sense it can be said that he is worshipped, and is to be worshipped, and is adorable to us, on account of the things already mentioned. But with respect to himself, in reference to the proper foundation and formal principle from which adorability flows as a property through itself, it is nothing other than the divine nature, and nothing else can rightly be given or conceived. Certainly we are nowhere commanded to worship him as man only, although he was exalted by God and made Lord, nor is it lawful to worship him as such. But the formal and reciprocal cause of adorability in Christ, on account of which he must be worshipped when it is posited, and without which he ought not to be worshipped, is his true and sole deity. This is what I have said in reply to the third reason of our Irenicus, why in treating the example of Christ's Deity he wished to dwell on it.

units.la: Quartam & ultimam allegat, quod si ista sua sententia de Christo tantum homine passim inter Christianos reciperetur & doceretur, spem concipit, infideles sic melius ad fidem Christianam convertendos. Ergo omnia fidei & Euangelii mysteria deserat potius, & invertat, ut Gentiles vid. eo commodius lucretur, faciatque ne Christus porro sit offendiculum Judæis & Gentilibus, nec prædicatio ejus stulta amplius, ut eos pertrahat ad fidem, qui illis offenduntur. Viderit etiam, ut neget Christi crucifixionem, quâ maxime quidem offenduntur: & quam objicere illos quidem memini, non vero adeo sententiam de ejus Deitate. Tum quæ illa foret conversio, aut fides, ad quam perducerentur, illis demtis? certe non Christi, vel Euangelii: vel omnia capita controversa, ex quibus lites & odia Christianorum inter se oriuntur, per accidens improbitatis hominum, tollat ergo, & cedat infidelibus, ut Christianos faciat, si modo tales tum Christiani dicendi forent.
units.tr: He alleges a fourth and last reason: that if this opinion of his about Christ as mere man were generally received and taught among Christians, he hopes that unbelievers might thus be converted to the Christian faith more easily. So he would rather abandon and overturn all the mysteries of faith and the Gospel, so that he might win over the Gentiles more conveniently, and so that Christ would no longer be a stumbling block to Jews and Gentiles, and his preaching would no longer be foolishness, so as to draw to the faith those who take offence at it. He will also see to it that he denies the crucifixion of Christ, at which they are most offended, and which I recall they do object to, though not so much the opinion about his Deity. Then what conversion or faith would it be to which they would be led, with these things taken away? Certainly not a faith in Christ or in the Gospel. Or let him remove all the controverted articles, from which the quarrels and hatreds among Christians arise, through the accidental wickedness of men, and let him give way to unbelievers, so that he may make them Christians, if at least such people could then be called Christians.

units.la: Porro in formando statu Controversiæ, quem hunc perpetuo constituit, An scilicet Christus summus sit Deus? ita loquitur, ac si verus aliquis Deus esset, vel esse posset, qui non sit summus: vel quasi plures & diversi essent Dii, alius summus, alius minus summus, vel inferior: quod in prima impingit non fidei tantum, sed rationis & naturæ principia. Non est Deus ullus, nisi summus: neque aliter de Deo loquitur Scriptura, aut philosophatur sana ratio. Tum quare non in controversiæ statu addit affirmative & exponit sententiam de Christo, videlicet esse eum hominem tantum, uti loquitur, pag. 17? ut definiat sententiam suam, non contra nos tantum, sed & Arianos, quos scit pag. 98. Christum & summum Deum negare nobis, & tantum esse hominem docere, atque ita sententiam facere tertiam. Controversia autem formanda potius erit de Dei veritate, quæ & summitatem comprehendit: An Christus sit verus Deus? Pag. 134. inquit, inauditum est in Scripturis plures esse summos Deos. Dico ego, æque inauditum est, plures esse veros Deos; vel, esse alium verum Deum, à summo.
units.tr: Furthermore, in framing the state of the controversy, which he constantly sets as this, whether Christ is the supreme God? he speaks as though there were, or could be, some true God who is not supreme, or as though there were several and different gods, one supreme and another less than supreme or inferior. In the first place this offends against the principles not only of faith but of reason and nature. There is no God unless he is supreme; nor does Scripture speak otherwise of God, nor does sound reason reason otherwise. Then why does he not, in stating the controversy, add affirmatively and set out his opinion about Christ, namely that he is man only, as he says at p. 17? So that he might define his opinion not only against us but also against the Arians, whom he knows (at p. 98) deny to us that Christ is the supreme God and teach that he is only man, and so make a third opinion. But the controversy ought rather to be framed concerning the truth of God, which also includes his supremacy: Is Christ the true God? At p. 134 he says: It is unheard of in the Scriptures that there are several supreme Gods. I say that it is equally unheard of that there are several true Gods, or that there is another true God besides the supreme one.

units.la: Cæterum argumentum, quod ex ratione continuò urget adversus sententiam de Christo nostram, est illud à Disparatis: quod ita in Irenico „propositum erat primum: Quicunque est homo, patitur, resurgit &c. is „non est summus Deus. Atqui Christus est homo &c. Ergo. — per „regulam de disparatis. Nam duo disparata de eodem dici subjecto „impossibile est. Hoc nunc identidem repetit, ad nauseam usque. Sed primum in Disparatorum naturam propius inquirendum, saltem quæ disparata intelligat, videndum. Disparata ergo sumit substantiva, non accidentalia: hæc enim de eodem subjecto prædicari, uti de Julio Cæsare, quod & bellator fuit, & scriptor egregius, agnoscit: substantialia non item, ut de uno dicatur, quod homo sit, & Deus. pag.40 Deinde disparata intelligit, quæ vere subjecto insunt, non improprie & figurate de eo dicuntur: quomodo de Christo, quod sit homo, & vitis ac lapis: de Deo, quod spiritus sit, & membra habeat corporis; per figuram nimirum, non proprie. pag. 41. Sed non bene disparatorum naturam assequitur, quando cum contrariis confundit, minus autem quando cum contradictoriis: passim conjungendo disparata & contradictoria, pag. 52. 53. 101. & pag. 126. duo contraria aut contradictoria simul posse esse vera. quare pag. 55. hoc format argumentum: quæcunque diversa naturis & proprietatibus suis sibi invicem contradicunt, ea de uno eodemque subjecto dici nequeunt. At non de talibus, sive contradictoriis, sive contrariis instituta erat disputatio; sed de disparatis. Atque reponimus ei, quod ipse dicit Comenio, pag. 58. ignorationem Elenchi hic committis, dum — pro disparatis sumis, quæ tamen proprie disparata non sunt. Quare frustra est, quando hoc de disparatis ita capit, ac si contenderemus, absurda de eodem prædicari posse. pag. 67. nam cum quæstio hic sic: utrum duo disparata de eodem subjecto dici possint, i. e. utrum vere absurda unquam vera esse possint? &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the argument which he constantly presses from reason against our opinion about Christ is that drawn from Disparates. In the Irenicum it was proposed first in this form: "Whoever is man suffers, rises again, etc., is not the supreme God. But Christ is man, etc. Therefore..." — by the "rule of disparates", for two disparates cannot be said of the same subject. This he repeats again and again, to the point of nausea. But first we must inquire more closely into the nature of disparates, at least to see what he understands by disparates. He takes disparates to be substantive, not accidental, for accidental things can be predicated of the same subject, as of Julius Caesar, who was both a warrior and an outstanding writer, as he acknowledges; but substantial things cannot likewise be said of one thing, that it is man and God (p. 40). Next, he understands by disparates those which are truly in a subject, and not those said of it improperly and figuratively: as of Christ, that he is man, and also a vine and a stone; of God, that he is a spirit, and has the members of a body, by figure, that is, not properly (p. 41). But he does not grasp the nature of disparates well when he confuses them with contraries, and still less when he confuses them with contradictories, everywhere joining disparates and contradictories together (pp. 52, 53, 101, and p. 126), saying that two contraries or contradictories can both be true at once. Hence at p. 55 he forms this argument: whatever things are by their natures and properties mutually contradictory cannot be said of one and the same subject. But the disputation was not set up concerning such things, whether contradictory or contrary, but concerning disparates. And we reply to him what he himself says to Comenius at p. 58: here you commit a fallacy of ignoratio elenchi, while you take as disparates those things which are not properly disparate. Therefore it is vain when he takes this about disparates as though we contended that absurdities could be predicated of the same subject (p. 67): for since the question here is this: whether two disparates can be said of the same subject, i.e. whether things truly absurd could ever be true? etc.

units.la: Jam ad argumentum respondemus ita: verum est, duo disparata vera & substantialia, de eodem subjecto non possunt prædicari formaliter, vel in eo vera esse per formalem identitatem eorundem, ut vid. eadem sit forma, natura & ratio hujus disparati, ac illius: sed hoc non obstat, quare non duo disparata subjective queant concurrere, & de eodem tertio enunciari, diverso modo. Neque enim sunt contraria, nedum contradictoria, minime vero absurda. Et pridem Logica nos docuit diversas esse oppositorum species, disparata, contraria, & contradicentia. Disparata sibimet non contrariantur sub eodem genere; quomodo album & nigrum, virtus vitium, justitia & injustitia; nedum ut sibi contradicant, quemadmodum album non album, homo non homo &c. quae inter se opponuntur ut ens, & non ens; ista, ut ens, & ejus contrarium; illa, uti ens, & ens, quorumque varia duntaxat & dispar invicem est ratio. Quid autem hic contrarii, aut contradictorii, aut denique absurdi, si talia, quorum dispar est ratio, praedicentur de eodem diversimode? uti anima & corpus, de Petro: homo & Deus, de Christo? Anima & corpus vere sunt disparata, & substantialia; non contraria, vel sibi mutuo inimica & destruentia: non contradictoria, qualia demum sunt anima non anima, corpus non corpus; non autem corpus & anima: atque secundum aliam rationem praedicatur de Petro, anima; secundum aliam, corpus. Ita Deus ac homo nec contradictoria sunt, nec contraria, sed opponuntur ut vere disparia: sed, quidquid etiam aliunde ostenderetur, ob quod non possent congredi, saltem nulla ex regula de disparatis sequitur repugnantia. Fac verum Angelum cum vero humano cotpore conjungi, annon ibi duo disparata substantialia de eodem subjecto vera erunt, & dicetur illum esse Angelum, & hominem? Si per rerum naturam illud non implicet, neque impossibile sit per absolutam Dei potentiam, opinor non erit per regulam de disparatis. Ipse pag. 99. ad argumentum Adversarii, quo concluderet, ergo Christum non esse tantum hominem, respondet, non sequi propterea, esse summum Deum: posset namque esse Angelus! quemadmodum Origenes, citante Hieronymo in Commentar. in cap. 1. Aggai, existimavit, Prophetas nonnullos fuisse Angelos, ad modum Christi incarnatos. Videatur Bibliot. Sanct. Sixti Senens. annotat. 177. in Johannis cap. 1. Posset quoque esse Deus, sed minor Patre; prout Arianos sentire paulo ante dictum est. Quod si hoc posset esse, utique posset quoque verum esse quod dico, disparata substantialia de eodem praedicari. Atque ita sibi fecit responsum ad argumentum suum, quod duo disparata dici de subjecto impossibile sit. Jam & pag. 59. sic colligit: si Angelum aut spiritum aliquem, lapidi se insinuantem, eoque tum quasi vestitum — & Angelum recte appello, propter id, quod principaliter est, & lapidem, propter id quod assumsit. Utique & Christus, lapidea natura praeditus (hanc substituit humanae, ut absurdum vid. aliquod inferat, sed quod ad rem nostram de duobus disparatis uni subjecto aptandis perinde est) & vere homo, & vere lapis est, aut esse potest. Ergo saltem duo disparata, qualia homo & lapis sunt, de eodem dici subjecto possunt.
units.tr: Now we answer the argument thus: it is true that two substantial and true disparates cannot be predicated of the same subject formally, or be true of it through a formal identity between them, that is, if the form, nature and reason of the one disparate were the same as those of the other. But this does not prevent two disparates from concurring in the same subject subjectively and being affirmed of one and the same third thing in different ways. For they are not contraries, much less contradictories, and by no means absurdities. Logic taught us long ago that there are different kinds of opposites: disparates, contraries and contradictories. Disparates are not opposed to one another as contraries within the same genus, as white and black, virtue and vice, justice and injustice, much less do they contradict one another, as white and not-white, or man and not-man, etc., which are opposed as being and non-being; the one is opposed as being and its contrary, the other as being and being, whose reasons differ only in variety and disparity. But what is contrary, contradictory or absurd here, if things whose reasons differ are predicated of the same thing in different ways, as soul and body of Peter, or man and God of Christ? Soul and body are truly disparates and substantial; they are not contraries, nor do they oppose or destroy one another; they are not contradictories, which would be soul and not-soul, body and not-body, but not body and soul. And in one respect soul is predicated of Peter, and in another respect body. So God and man are neither contradictories nor contraries, but are opposed as truly disparate things. But even if it were shown from elsewhere that they could not come together, at least no contradiction follows from the rule about disparates. Suppose a true angel were joined to a true human body: would there not be two substantial disparates truly predicated of the same subject, and would he not be called both an angel and a man? If this does not imply a contradiction in the nature of things, and is not impossible by the absolute power of God, I think it will not be excluded by the rule about disparates. In page 99, he answers the opponent's argument, by which he would conclude that Christ is therefore not merely a man, by replying that it does not follow for that reason that he is the highest God: for he could be an angel! Just as Origen, as Jerome cites him in his commentary on the first chapter of Haggai, thought that some prophets were angels, incarnated in the manner of Christ. See the Bibliotheca Sancta of Sixtus of Siena, annotation 177 on John chapter 1. He could also be God, but less than the Father, as shortly before it was said the Arians think. But if this could be so, then surely what I say could also be true, that disparate substantials are predicated of the same thing. And so he has made his answer to his own argument, that it is impossible for two disparates to be said of one subject. Again, on page 59 he concludes thus: if an angel or some spirit insinuates itself into a stone, and is then as it were clothed in it, I call it rightly an angel because of what is principal, and a stone because of what it has assumed. Likewise Christ, endowed with a stony nature (he substitutes this for the human, so that he may draw some absurdity, but as far as our matter is concerned, of two disparates fitted to one subject, it makes no difference) is truly man and truly stone, or can be. Therefore at least two disparates, such as man and stone are, can be predicated of the same subject.

units.la: Quodque ibidem addit, pag. 60. omnino tam absurdum est dicere, Christum proprie esse Hominem & Deum, quam si cum Lutheranis dicas, Hominem (in Christo) esse Deum, & Deum esse Hominem? (quod tu tamen dicere cum iis vereris? Aut si dicas: Uxor Lothi est simul statua salis? aut statua salis est simul uxor Lothi? Ipse Paulus est simul Petrus? Ipse Goliath est simul David? Ipse panis est simul corpus Christi? i.e. Unum est simul duo, & duo sunt simul unum? aut eadem res potest simul esse hic & alibi? Negatur, parem esse istorum rationem cum disparatis, quae de eodem praedicantur subjecto: nam unum esse hic & alibi, unum & duo, Davidem & Goliatum, Petrum simul esse & Paulum, statuam salis & uxorem Lothi, contraria sunt, se mutuo tollentia, quae propterea in eodem subjecto locum habere non possunt; at disparatorum alia est ratio, quia sibi non contrariantur, vel se mutuo non destruunt, sed conspirare bene & convenire in unum possunt. Deinde proprie de Christo dicitur, esse hominem & Deum, subjective videlicet, non ut formaliter in eo idem sit esse Deum, & hominem. Atque ita putamus, facili negotio expugnatum arietem, quo tantopere superbit Autor, sive argumentum ejus unicum hoc & palmariam, de disparatis. Quamvis etiam si bene attendamus, nec rite con-cludat,vel concludet contra ipsos, quando Christum etiam voluntDeum: quia argumento illo de disparatis quod nequeant dici de eodem, sequetur etiam Christum non esse Deum, quia nimirum Deus & homo de eodem praedicari non poterunt, æque & prius, quam eum non esse summum Deum. Semper enim contendunt Christum Deum esse, atque hoc debere dici: sed vel illud argumentum de disparatis omittere debebas contra nos, vel Tibi reponemus, ut cogaris de caetero Christum nunquam appellare Deum. At valde solent indignari, quando in suspicionem trahuntur negatae Christo deitatis, istiusque nomenclationis.
units.tr: And what he adds in the same place, on page 60: Is it not altogether as absurd to say that Christ is properly man and God, as if you were to say with the Lutherans that man (in Christ) is God, and God is man? (Do you yourself fear to say this with them?) Or if you say: Is Lot's wife at the same time a pillar of salt? Or is a pillar of salt at the same time Lot's wife? Is Paul himself at the same time Peter? Is Goliath himself at the same time David? Is bread itself at the same time the body of Christ? That is, one is at the same time two, and two are at the same time one? Or can the same thing be here and elsewhere at once? We deny that the reason for these is the same as for disparates predicated of the same subject. For to be here and elsewhere, one and two, David and Goliath, Peter and Paul at once, a pillar of salt and Lot's wife, are contraries that cancel one another, and therefore cannot have a place in the same subject. But disparates have a different reason, because they are not contrary to one another, nor do they destroy one another, but can agree well and come together into one. Further, it is properly said of Christ that he is man and God, subjectively, that is, not in the sense that being God and being man are formally the same in him. And so we think that the battering ram, in which the author takes such pride, namely his only argument and his chief point, the one about disparates, has been overthrown with little effort. Even if we attend carefully, it does not rightly conclude, nor will it conclude against them even when they also say that Christ is God. For by that argument about disparates, that they cannot be said of the same thing, it would follow also that Christ is not God, because God and man could not be predicated of the same thing, just as much and just as early as that he is not the highest God. For they always contend that Christ is God, and that this must be said. But you ought either to omit that argument about disparates against us, or we shall reply to you so that you are forced henceforth never to call Christ God. Yet they are very wont to be indignant when they are brought under suspicion of denying the deity of Christ and this way of naming him.

units.la: Magis autem ex regulâ illâ de disparatis sequitur, Christum non esse dicendum Deum, quia homo est; quam non esse dicendum summum, ubi dicitur Deus. Etiam antea cavit, disparata hic intelligi debere substantiarum, non accidentium: quare concludere per suam argumentationem cogetur adversus Christi deitatem, & non adeo adversus Deitatis ejus summitatem.
units.tr: But more truly, from that rule about disparates it follows that Christ is not to be called God because he is man, than that he is not to be called the highest where he is called God. He has also already taken care that the disparates here must be understood as of substances, not of accidents. Therefore, by his own argument he will be compelled to conclude against the deity of Christ, and not so much against the supremacy of his deity.

units.la: Denique magna mihi videtur inter argumentum Adversariorum istud, à disparatis, adversus à nos, affinitas cum argumento Judæorum, adversus Christum, super eâdem prorsus materiâ, Joan. x. 33. non pro-pter malum opus te lapidamus, sed blasphemiam, & quod tu homo cum sis facis teipsum Deum. Nos quidem scimus, Christum non-blasphemasse; deinde Deum se dixisse & probasse satis evidenter, etiam quando non-dum erat glorificarus, & nihil perperam dixisse: ac quomodo contrà argumentantur Judæi, nisi quod frustra se dicat Deum, vel dicatur Deus, quum sit homo? quia vid. duo ista disparata de eodem non possunt esse vera. Quod quid obsecro aliud est, quam uti Adversarius in formâ disputat & scribit: quicunque est homo, is non est summus Deus. Atqui Chri-stus est homo; Ergo. Major mea firma est per regulam de disparatis. Nam duo disparata de eodem dici subjecto impossibile est. Certè ovum ovo non potest esse similius. Neque alium Deum esse, quam summum, credebant Judæi, & agnovit ac docuit quoque Christus.
units.tr: Finally, there seems to me to be a great affinity between this argument of the Adversaries from disparates, against us, and the argument of the Jews against Christ on exactly the same matter, John 10:33: We stone you not for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because you, being a man, make yourself God. We indeed know that Christ did not blaspheme; further, that he said he was God and proved it quite evidently, even when he was not yet glorified, and that he said nothing amiss. And how else do the Jews argue against him, except that he says in vain that he is God, or is called God, since he is a man? Because, as they see it, these two disparates cannot both be true of the same thing. What, I ask, is this but the way the Adversary argues and writes in form: Whoever is a man is not the highest God. But Christ is a man; therefore. My major premise is firm by the rule about disparates, for it is impossible for two disparates to be predicated of the same subject. Surely an egg could not be more like an egg. Nor did the Jews believe, and Christ also acknowledged and taught, that there is any God other than the highest.

units.la: Et sic respondendo, non puto quod aliquis objiciet, nos petere principium. Præterquam quod non argumentamur, sed ad alterius tantummodo respondemus argumentum, nihil prorsus petimus, neutiquam illud quod est in controversiâ. Petere principium vitium opponentis est, & argumentantis, non respondentis; qui quidem tuetur principium suum, at non proinde petere dicendus est. Aliud est, in disputatione principium defendere, vel petere. Nisi Respondens partes suas deponat, & alias opponentis assumat, tum petere principium potest, sed hoc tum ut Opponens committit, non facit ut Respondens. Confer ad hæc Andreæ Kesleri Logica Photiniana Examen, Sect. iv. pag. 271. & seq.
units.tr: And in answering thus, I do not think anyone will object that we beg the question. Besides, we do not argue, but only reply to another's argument, and we assume nothing at all that is in controversy. To beg the question is a fault of the opponent and the arguer, not of the respondent; he indeed maintains his principle, but he is not to be said to beg the question on that account. It is one thing in a disputation to defend a principle, and another to beg it. Unless the respondent lays down his own role and takes up that of the opponent, he may beg the question, but then he does so as an opponent, not as a respondent. On these matters compare Andreas Keslerus, Logica Photiniana Examen, section iv, page 271 and following.

units.la: Porrò in formando seu retorquendo argumento mire quam est fasti-diosus. Quicunque, inquit, Deus quidem dicitur, ita tamen, ut homo sit, Deum-que supra se, dum Deus dicitur habeat, quem & se majorem esse ipsemet expresse profiteatur, &c. de eo non necessario sequitur, quod Deus summus sit. pag. 90. Multa in hoc argumento sunt, quæ desideramus, & egent correctione.
units.tr: Moreover, in framing or turning back the argument, he is remarkably fussy. Whoever is said to be God, yet in such a way that he is a man, and has above himself the God whom, while he is called God, he expressly professes to be greater than himself, etc., it does not necessarily follow from this that he is the highest God. p. 90. There is much in this argument that we miss, and that needs correction.

units.la: Atque ut à conclusione ordiamur, mirum est, ut semper concludat, adversus Christum, eum non esse summum Deum, quasi Deum quidem velit concedere, modo ne sit summus, & de gradu potius contendere, quam de rei veritate. Sed Deum negare quia reformidant, quando tam sæpe, & clare Deus dicitur, hinc eam impugnare malunt sub ejus summitate, quam deitatem ipsam. Neque argumentatio fluit, nisi sic dicat: qui Deus quidem dicitur, ita tamen ut homo sit, & Deus quidem etiam; at Deum supra se habeat &c. Alioqui nulla vis videtur in illatione, ut simplisimpliciter is qui Deus dicitur, & nulla ratione sit, inde putetur esse Deus summus. Jam illud sive subintelligat, sive addat, manifestum, in argumento connotari duorum disparatorum de uno Christo prædicationem: nullius alias pretii est argumentum, ut cum eo qui vere & substantialiter homo est, jungatur externa & impropria ac catachrestica nominatio Dei. Quæ enim quæso esset illa argumentatio, qui quidem Deus dicitur, at improprie & abusive, non tamen vere & essentia hoc est, quod dicitur, quare supra se Deum habet &c. is non est summus Deus. Quis enim talem vellet summum Deum facere, qui Deus modo dicatur, at non sit. Præterea ambiguum est in argumento illud, dum Deus dicitur: nam Christus, dum Deus dicitur, uti in statu humiliationis Deus dictus fuit, Deum supra se agnovit; sed, an in ratione Deitatis, quæritur; an istius, quod gerebat, officii? illud negamus, quia sic dicitur fuisse Deus, & Verbum erat Deus: istud vero non tangit quæstionem. De eo, inquit, non necessario sequitur, quod Deus summus sit: certe, non ex eo quod tantum Deus dicitur, quod solum potuit in antecedente; nisi Deus sit, atque hoc probetur esse. Quare quam multis scatere vitiis argumentum illud vidimus, in antecedente, & consequente, & denique conclusione. Neque quidquam contra nos concludit, quandoquidem ex eo quod aliquis simpliciter Deus dicitur, & homo est, & Deum supra se majorem habet, nos nequaquam inferimus, talem esse summum Deum.
units.tr: To begin from the conclusion: it is remarkable that he always concludes against Christ that he is not the highest God, as if he were willing to grant that he is God, provided he is not the highest, and contends about rank rather than about the truth of the matter. But since they shrink from denying God, when God is so often and so clearly called God, they prefer to attack his supremacy rather than his deity itself. Nor does the argument hold unless he says: whoever is called God, yet so as to be man, and God indeed also, but has God above himself, etc. Otherwise there seems to be no force in the inference that one who is simply called God, and has no basis for it, is therefore thought to be the highest God. Now whether he understands or adds that, it is plain that the argument implies the predication of two disparate things of the one Christ. It is an argument of no value when an external, improper and catachrestic naming of God is joined to one who is truly and substantially man. For what argument, I ask, would that be: whoever is called God, but improperly and abusively, and not truly and in essence what is said, therefore has God above himself, etc., is not the highest God? For who would want to make the highest God one who is merely called God but is not? Besides, the phrase "while he is called God" is ambiguous in the argument. For Christ, while he was called God in the state of humiliation, acknowledged God above himself; but the question is whether this is said with respect to the reason of deity, or with respect to the office he bore. We deny the former, because thus he is said to have been God, and the Word was God; but the latter does not touch the question. It does not necessarily follow, he says, that he is the highest God. Certainly not from the fact that he is only called God, which he could have only in the antecedent, unless he is God and this is proved. Hence we have seen how many faults that argument abounds in, in the antecedent, the consequent and finally the conclusion. Nor does it conclude anything against us, since from the fact that someone is simply called God, and is man, and has a greater God above himself, we by no means infer that such a one is the highest God.

units.la: Et quemadmodum ille se ex abundanti ita argumentari profitetur, sic non video quare non etiam Comenius, quascunque partes gesserit, sive Opponentis, sive Defendentis, ad ostendendam argumenti infirmitatem reponere potuerit: quicunque homo quidem dicitur, ita tamen, ut simul dicatur verus super omnia Deus benedictus in sæcula, is homo tantum esse nulla ratione potest. Quia vis quæstionis tota in hoc recidit, an Christus, non dicatur tantum, sed vere dicatur, & sit verus Deus. Quod ego nego refelli tali argumento Anthropomorphitæ, ac habet, pag. 95[?]. „ Quicunque homo quidem esse negatur, spiritusque esse pronunciatur, „ ita tamen, ut passim quoque membra humana habere dicatur, is non „ simpliciter homo esse negari, neque simpliciter aut proprie spiritus esse pronunciari potest. Quam propositionem, utcunque nonnulla in ea etiam notari possint, & ex pluribus de Deo quæ dicuntur, dicamus ejus quoque esse spiritualitatem, simpliciter negamus: eamque ubi Anthropomorphita confirmare laborabit, tum quod statim diximus, hic repetendum, nim. quæ verè dicantur de Deo, quæ non sed impro-prie, quale est quod Deus habet humana membra: contrà verò de Christo utrùmque verè prædicatur, quod sit homo, & quod sit Deus.
units.tr: And just as he professes to argue thus "out of abundance," so I do not see why Comenius, in whatever role he has played, whether of opponent or of defender, could not likewise have replied to show the weakness of the argument: whoever is indeed called man, yet so that at the same time he is said to be true God over all, blessed for ever, cannot in any way be merely man. For the whole force of the question comes down to this: whether Christ is not merely called, but truly called and truly is, true God. This I deny can be refuted by such an argument, as the Anthropomorphite has it, p. 95[?]: "Whoever is denied to be man, and is pronounced to be spirit, yet so that he is also said everywhere to have human members, cannot be simply denied to be man, nor simply or properly pronounced to be spirit." This proposition, although some things in it may be noted, and although from the many things said of God we say that spirituality also belongs to him, we simply deny; and when the Anthropomorphite labours to confirm it, we must repeat here what we have just said: that some things are truly said of God, and others not truly but improperly, as that God has human members; whereas on the contrary, of Christ both are truly predicated, that he is man and that he is God.

units.la: Atque hoc responsum, ad argumentum, quod primo loco, adversus Christi Deitatem veram adfert, petitum ex ratione: quam frustra ante Scripturas ponunt. vel hinc petita argumenta. Quum in rebus fidei semper primùm Scriptura audienda sit, tum ratio, si quis locus, non viceversa. Ex Scriptura enim petuntur universæ, sive ex supernaturali revelatione, quia mysteria sunt, non ex naturali ratione. Hilarius, lib. v. de Trinitate: ex verbis igitur sensum sequamur, & ex sensu ratio-nem intelligamus, & ex ratione veritatem apprehendamus. Ratione vid. Scripturarià. Neque nos aliter, sive contra Pontificios, sive Lutheranos, quod nobis objicit pag. 50. disputamus ex ratione, quod unum corpus in pluribus locis esse nequeat, quam post ostensam & probatam rei fidem ex Scripturâ: & tum quis dedignetur, idem confirmari ex ratione? Non primùm rationem consulimus, tum Scripturam, ut hæc ad illam flectatur; neque rationem contra Lutheranos pro normâ habent Calviniani, uti notat in Indice: sed uti veritas ubique sui similis est, juvat admodum eandem quæ in Scripturis lucet, etiam ratione corroborari. Et argumentum quod hinc petitur, pro naturâ medii termini, quoque rationis & philosophiæ habendum est, non proprie fidei. Verum quidem est, quod Scriptura & fides contra rationem nihil doceat, & veritas nullibi sibi ullâ parte contrarietur, sed non proinde ex ratione res Scripturæ & fidei probandæ primò sunt, tum Dei testimonio, sed contrà: eo magis, quo facilius nominare licet sanam omnium hominum rationem, quod hominibus nostris in hac disputatione admodum est familiare, quam ubi sit ostendere & probare. Atque bene Keslerus in Examine Logicæ Photinianæ scribit pag. 21. nec de rectâ ratione è cujuscunque hominis, nec de Philosophia ex hujus vel illius philosophi mente judicandum esse.
units.tr: This is the answer to the argument, which he brings first against the true deity of Christ, taken from reason, which they set before the Scriptures in vain, or arguments drawn from this. Since in matters of faith Scripture must always be heard first, and reason afterwards, if at all, and not the reverse. For all things are sought from Scripture, whether from supernatural revelation, because they are mysteries, or from natural reason. Hilary, book v, On the Trinity: Therefore let us follow the sense from the words, and understand the reason from the sense, and grasp the truth from the reason. On reason, see the Scriptural argument. Nor do we argue otherwise, whether against the Papists or the Lutherans, when he objects to us on p. 50 that one body cannot be in several places, arguing from reason, after the matter of faith has been shown and proved from Scripture. Then who would disdain to have the same thing confirmed by reason? We do not consult reason first and then Scripture, so that the latter may be bent to the former; nor do the Calvinists hold reason as the standard against the Lutherans, as he notes in the index. Rather, since truth is everywhere like itself, it greatly helps to corroborate by reason the very same truth that shines in the Scriptures. And the argument drawn from this must be held to belong, by the nature of the middle term, to reason and philosophy, not properly to faith. It is indeed true that Scripture and faith teach nothing contrary to reason, and truth is nowhere in any part contrary to itself; but for this reason the matters of Scripture and faith are not to be proved first by reason and then by the testimony of God, but the reverse; the more so because it is easier to name the sound reason of all men, which is quite familiar to our opponents in this dispute, than to show and prove where it is. And Kessler rightly writes in his Examination of the Photinian Logic, p. 21, that one must judge neither by the right reason of any man whatever, nor by philosophy according to the mind of this or that philosopher.

units.la: Sed ad Scripturam quod pertinet, quæ totam decidere controversiam debet, & à quâ unâ fidei rationem petere æquum est, quia nihil in transfecursu attulit Adversarius, quod non in opere hoc à nobis examinetur, & quod ex iis solvi non possit, ideo iisdem immorari supersedeo, ne mihi primum, inde & aliis molestâ repetitione tædium creare necesse habeam: atque ipse subinde significat de Scripturæ locis nunc non esse quæstionem, præsertim ubi evertimus ejus λογισμόν de disparatis, ex quo etiam Scripturam interpretari jubet, quum passim, tum pag. 263. Ad quæ satis habemus dicere cum Tertulliano, adversus Praxeam: Porro non periclitatur Scriptura, ut illi de tua argumentatione succurras, ne sibi contraria videatur.
units.tr: But as far as Scripture is concerned, which ought to settle the whole controversy, and from which alone it is right to seek the reason of faith, since the adversary has brought forward nothing in passing that is not examined by us in this work, and that cannot be solved from it, I therefore refrain from dwelling on these matters, lest I be obliged to create weariness for myself first, and then for others, by tiresome repetition. He himself at times signals that the question is not now about the passages of Scripture, especially where we have overturned his reasoning about the disparates, from which he also orders Scripture to be interpreted, both here and there, as on p. 263. To these things we are content to say with Tertullian, against Praxeas: Moreover, Scripture is not put in peril, so that you may come to the aid of your argument, lest it seem to contradict itself.

units.la: Pergo ad eas, quas vocat, traditiones, sive doctrinam Veterum de Christi deitate. Intolerandâ autem calumniâ gravat fidem nostram, quando eam reducit, tamquam ad autorem suum, Simonem Magum, Cerinthum, aliosque hæreticos, qui sententiam illam primi sc. invexerint in Ecclesiam. Tum ostendere conatur, primos Patres, Hermam, Clementem Romanum, Ignatium, Polycarpum, Justinum, Athenagoram, Theophilum, Tatianum, Irenæum, & Tertullianum docuisse Christum, ut Deum, Patre vero Deo fuisse essentiâ & naturâ inæqualem, & inferiorem ævo, dignitate, & potestate, sive solum Patrem, & non etiam Filium, ac Spiritum S. esse summum & verum Deum. Hæc verò ut confirmet videamus.
units.tr: I proceed to what he calls traditions, that is, the teaching of the ancients concerning the deity of Christ. But he burdens our faith with an intolerable calumny when he traces it back, as to its author, to Simon Magus, Cerinthus, and other heretics, who, he says, first introduced that opinion into the Church. Then he tries to show that the first Fathers, Hermas, Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, Justin, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Tatian, Irenaeus and Tertullian, taught that Christ is God, but unequal in essence and nature to God the Father, and inferior in age, dignity and power; or that only the Father, and not also the Son and the Holy Spirit, is the highest and true God. But let us see how he confirms these things.

units.la: Simonem Magum, dicit Adversarius primò, negasse, Jesum esse Christum: contra verò asseruisse, se unum & Filium esse, & Patrem, & Spiritum sanctum. Se unum Deum, sub diversis formis, & modo tamquam Patrem, nunc tamquam Filium, & nunc tamquam Spiritum S. inter homines apparuisse, variaque effecisse; seseque infinitam potentiam esse, quæ etiam varias mentis conceptiones, mentem scilicet, Vocem, & Rationem producere possit, produxeritque. pag. 166. 167. Ergo, inquit, Simon Magus novam Christi generationem, extra eam, quâ homo generatus fuit, extra hominem Christum, seu prorsus negato homine Christo, alium filium Dei, descripsit. pag. 161. videlicet qualem nos credimus. Resp. Negamus syllogismi majorem, & minorem. Simon Magus illa docuit: ergo nos à Simone illo habemus nostra, vel Veteres, qui idem hic nobiscum senserunt? deinde negamus, quod eadem, quæ nos, Simon Magus docuit. Videamus, quid ille. Ita de eo Irenæus, lib. 1. cap. xx. Hic igitur à multis quasi Deus glorificatus est, & docuit semetipsum esse qui inter Judæos quidem quasi filius apparuerit, in Samaria autem quasi pater descenderit, & in reliquis vero gentibus quasi spiritus sanctus adventaverit. Esse autem se sublimissimam virtutem, hoc est, eum qui sit super omnia pater, & suslineri vocari se quodcunque eum vocant homines. Simon autem Samaritanus, ex quo universæ hæreses subsisterunt, habet hujusmodi sectæ materiam. Nos verò idem, vel simile quid docemus, credimus? & Christiani omnes? Sed distinxit Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum. An verò errasse in eo ipsum hactenus, Irenæus scripsit, vel ullus unquam Autor? vel vos ipsi? qui saltem in Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum S. creditis, uti in symbolo profitemini, quocunque demum sensu à vobis fiat. An autem præter illud aliquid est, in Simonis dogmate, quod ullam cum doctrinâ Christianâ ostendit convenientiam? An quod de mente vel conceptione suâ docuit? Docuit autem, Helenam suam esse primam mentis suæ conceptionem, matrem omnium, per quam initio mente concepit Angelos facere, & Archan-gelos, & quæ plura ejus farinæ leguntur porrò apud Irenæum, putidiora quam ut referantur, indignissima profecto, ut cum re Christianâ ulla parte conferantur. Epiphanius, de Simone, lib. i. tom. ii. dicebat seipsum esse magnam virtutem Dei, & ex supernis descendisse. Patrem vero dicebat seipsum esse apud Samaritas, apud Judæos vero Filium se esse dicebat. passim autem se non pas-sim esse, sed solum apparenter. Augustinus, in Catal. hæref. cap. i. dixerat enim se in monte Sina legem Moysi in Patris persona dedisse Judæis. Tempore Tiberii in Filii persona putative apparuisse: postea se in linguis igneis Spiritum Sanctum super Apostolos venisse: Christum autem nec venisse, nec à Judæis quicquam pertulisse. Tu hinc dices, nos similia cum Mago illo statuere, vel ab eo edo-ctos esse? Quem quæso non pudeat contumeliæ, & quis non miretur adeo frontem posuisse Scriptorem, quod hoc afferere non erubuerit? Filium aliquem Dei dixit Simon, fateor, ac proinde à Patre generatum: sed, vel eundem Filium, quem nos? vel eandem ejus generationem? Falsum. Se Filium illum dixit, se Patrem, & se quoque Spiritum Sanctum, ac nescio, quo pacto, genitum, & concipientem, & quæ porro de miris & infandis ennæis & ille, & alii, de quibus videlis Irenæum, lib. i. vel solum ejus caput xxxiii. Vel, crediderit Filii in Deitate generationem à Patre: an proinde magis ab eo hoc habent Christiani, quo id credunt modo, quam Patris, & Filii, in genere? & non ipse id ex communi doctrinâ Christianorum? quemadmodum Irenæus, cap. ii.
units.tr: Our opponent first says that Simon Magus denied that Jesus is the Christ, but on the contrary asserted that he himself is one and the Son, and the Father, and the Holy Spirit. He appeared among men as one God under different forms and in different modes, now as the Father, now as the Son, and now as the Holy Spirit, and he produced various effects; and he is infinite power, which can produce, and has produced, various conceptions of the mind, namely mind, voice, and reason. p. 166, 167. Therefore, he says, Simon Magus described a new generation of Christ, apart from that by which the man was begotten, apart from the man Christ, or wholly denying the man Christ, another son of God, p. 161, namely such as we believe. Answer: We deny both the major and the minor premise of the syllogism. Simon Magus taught those things: therefore do we have our doctrines from that Simon, or from the ancients who here thought the same as we do? Next, we deny that Simon Magus taught the same things as we do. Let us see what he did teach. Irenaeus says of him, book 1, chapter 20: This man, therefore, was glorified by many as a god, and he taught that he himself is the one who appeared among the Jews as a son, who in Samaria came down as a father, and who among the other nations came as the Holy Spirit. He said that he is the highest power, that is, the father who is above all things, and that he allows himself to be called by whatever name men give him. Simon the Samaritan, from whom all heresies have arisen, has provided the material for this kind of sect. But do we believe the same or something similar? Do all Christians? But Simon did distinguish the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Has Irenaeus written, or has any author ever written, that this is an error, or have you yourselves, who at least believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as you profess in the creed, whatever sense you give it? Is there anything in Simon's teaching that shows any agreement with Christian doctrine? Or is it what he taught about his mind or his conception? He taught that his Helena was the first conception of his mind, the mother of all, through whom he first conceived in his mind to make angels and archangels. Many more things of this sort are read further on in Irenaeus, too foul to be repeated, and most unworthy of being compared in any part with the Christian religion. Epiphanius, on Simon, book 1, vol. 2: He said that he himself was the great power of God, and that he had come down from above. He said that he was the Father among the Samaritans, but among the Jews he said that he was the Son. Yet he said that he was not everywhere, but only in appearance. Augustine, in the Catalogue of Heresies, chapter 1: For he had said that on Mount Sinai he gave the law of Moses to the Jews in the person of the Father; that in the time of Tiberius he appeared in the person of the Son, seemingly; that afterwards he came as the Holy Spirit upon the apostles in tongues of fire; but that Christ neither came nor suffered anything from the Jews. Will you say from this that we hold similar views to that magician, or that we were taught them by him? Whom, I ask, would this insult not shame, and who would not wonder that the writer had the face to assert this without blushing? Simon said that there was some Son of God, I grant, and therefore one begotten by the Father; but was it the same Son that we mean, or the same generation? That is false. He said that he himself was that Son, that he himself was the Father, and that he himself was also the Holy Spirit, and that he was somehow begotten and conceiving; and what else he and others said of the wonderful and unspeakable aeons, of which you may see in Irenaeus, book 1, or at least chapter 33 of it. Or did he believe in the generation of the Son in the Deity from the Father? Do Christians therefore have this belief from him, in the way they believe it, more than the Father and the Son in general? Is it not rather from the common doctrine of Christians that he himself had it, as Irenaeus says in chapter 2?

units.la: Ecclesia enim, inquit, per universum orbem usque ad fines terræ seminata, & ab Apostolis, & a discipulis eorum accepit eam fidem, quæ est in unum Deum, patrem omnipotentem, qui fecit cælum, & terram, mare & omnia quæ in eis sunt, & in unum Jesum Christum filium Dei, incarnatum pro nostra salute, & in Spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: For the Church, scattered throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the apostles and their disciples that faith which is in one God, the Father almighty, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; and in one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, made flesh for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Successor Simonis Menander primam quidem virtutem incognitam ait omnibus, se autem eum esse qui missus sit ab invisibilibus salvatorem pro salute hominum. Mundum autem factum ab angelis, quos & ipse similiter, ut Simeon, ab Ennoia emissos dicit. Irenæus, cap. xxi. An propterea vel Christus non fuit missus ad hominum salutem? vel hanc fidem Ecclesia mutuata est ab haereticis? Denique si tantus vir ille Simon fuit, ut ab eo doctrina, quae in Nicaena Synodo ab Ecclesiis Orientali-bus, & Occidentalibus, & postea passim agnita fuit & celebrata, habuerit originem, nonne vel haereticorum catalogo ob hanc saltem rationem exemtus, vel nominatus & probatus doctrinae hujus saltem de-fensor fuisset? & non potius pro patrono doctrinae catholicae, quam haeresis, ab aliquo saltem fuisset notatus & memoratus? quem nunc omnes, & propter ea, quae in eo Irenaeus notat, pro monstro blasphe-miarum habuerunt semper, non fidei assertore, nedum autore primo aut patrono.
units.tr: Simon's successor Menander says that the first power is unknown to all, but that he himself is the one who was sent by the invisible beings as savior for the salvation of men. He says that the world was made by angels, whom he too, like Simon, says were sent forth from Ennoia. Irenaeus, chapter 21. Does it follow that Christ was not sent for the salvation of men? Or has the Church borrowed this faith from the heretics? Finally, if that great man Simon was so important that the doctrine which was acknowledged and celebrated at the Nicene Synod by the Eastern and Western Churches, and afterwards everywhere, had its origin from him, would he not at least have been excluded from the catalogue of heretics for this reason alone, or would he not have been named and approved as a defender of this doctrine? Would he not rather have been noted and remembered by someone, at least as a champion of Catholic doctrine rather than of heresy? Yet now everyone, and on account of what Irenaeus notes against him, has always regarded him as a monster of blasphemies, not as an asserter of the faith, much less its first author or patron.

units.la: Cerinthi similis est ratio, a quo, cum Simone Mago, nescio quomodo doctrinam nostram derivare improbitas ausa fuit. nempe quia primi abnegatores Jesu Christi hominis, novique Christi inventores illi fuerunt, ait pag. 19. Adeone tales nos vobis videmur? nosne Christi abnegatores? nos illum negamus hominem? nos novum praedicamus Christum? Et haec scilicet asserere, satis est. Nam quid adfert? Expolivit, inquit, dogma de nova Christi generatione. pag. 168. & pag. 169. primus quasi, non ergo Simon Magus primus, homini Jesu divinam aliquam naturam, imperfectius licet adhuc, conciliare voluit, Filium Dei e coelis ei jungendo & tribuendo. & pag. 224. Quare huic Cerintho primo attribuit introductam distinctionem divinae in Christo naturae, ab humana. Resp. De Cerintho sic Irenaeus, lib. 1. cap. xxv. Cerinthus autem quidam in Asia non a primo Deo factum esse mundum docuit, sed a virtute quadam valde separata & distante ab ea principalitate, quae est super universa, & ignorante eo, qui est super omnia Deo. Jesum autem subjecit non ex virgine natum, impossibile enim hoc ei visum est, fuisse autem eum Joseph & Maria filium similiter ut reliqui omnes homines, & plus potuisse justitia & prudentia & sapientia pra omnibus, & post baptismum descendisse in eum Christum ab ea principalitate quae est super omnia figura columba, & tunc annunciasse incognitum patrem & virtutes perfecisse, in fine autem revolasse iterum Christum de Jesu, & Jesum passum esse & resurrexisse, Christum autem impassibilem perseverasse existentem spiritualem. Anne illa eadem sunt cum doctrina nostra, ut ab eo quidem habere nos eandem, & tamquam a primo quidem autore, dicendi simus? Nam si primus docuit in Christo distingui divinam naturam ab humana, prorsus etiam distinctam ab humana divinam agnovit: quicunque enim agno-scit, eo ipso debet quoque distinguere. Sed tantum abest, ut ista in Christo distinxerit, ut quamvis diversa posuerit Christum, & Jesum, & Christum Jesu supervenisse in baptismo, postea iterum ab eo evo-lasse, non tamen illum Christum dixit esse divinam naturam, sed, nescio quid forte virtutis ejusdem separatae & distantis à Deo, à qua mundum conditum somniavit. Spiritum sanctum interpretatur Epiphanius, & virtutem Dei quod intellexerit, in Jesum ex supernis ve-nisse, & hinc fecisse virtutes suas. Nam nunquam divinam in Jesu naturam, vel Jesum Deum agnovit, sed hominem tantummodo, inquit Augu-stinus, cap. viii. Distinxit autem in Christo Jesu aliud impassibile, passibile aliud; aliud quod è coelo, aliud è terrâ ortum. Sed an propterea divinam in Christo agnovit naturam? vel idem quod nos sensit, & non nos tantum idem quod ipse, sed & ab ipso quoque primo autore docti tenemus nostra? Constitues forte inter illa aliquam convenientiam. Bene ergo & dic nos Ophitas esse, quia docemus, in V. T. Chri-stum fuisse: quia illi colubrum, qui decepit Adamum & Evam, Christum fuisse asseruerunt. Et quae non inde portenta & haereses singulis imputari possent, si consequentias vel convenientias & analogias ejusmodi sententiarum formare satis esset. Quomodo autem vel à Simone Mago, & Cerintho, similibusque, Ecclesia doctrinam de Christi deitate hauserit primum, vel aliquid sibi cum illis commune voluerit, quos non modo constanter omnes & singuli in haereticorum catalogum retulerunt, sed in omnibus haeresium capitibus condemnarunt pariter, neque unus alio quidpiam in illis plus aut minus tulit, & qui post Concilium Nicenum, atque qui ante illud de iis scripserunt, prorsus eadem semper carpse-runt, neque aliquis unquam in illis excepit quidquam ad doctrinam de Christi deitate pertinens. Quin Nicetas Choniates in Thesauro Ortho-doxae Fidei, lib. iv. inter Ante-Arianas haereses primam constituit Si-monianam illam, non inter Anti-Arianas, ut in iis suam vidisset senten-tiam de Christo, aut ejus deitate.
units.tr: The reasoning about Cerinthus is similar. Somehow impudence has dared to derive our doctrine from him together with Simon Magus, namely because, he says on p. 19, they were the first deniers of Jesus Christ the man, and the inventors of a new Christ. Do we seem such people to you? Are we deniers of Christ? Do we deny that he is a man? Do we preach a new Christ? And it seems that it is enough simply to assert these things. For what does he bring forward? He says, he polished the doctrine of a new generation of Christ, p. 168, and p. 169, as it were the first, not therefore Simon Magus the first, wished to attribute to the man Jesus some divine nature, though still more imperfectly, by joining and ascribing to him the Son of God from heaven; and p. 224, wherefore he attributes to this Cerinthus, as the first, the introduced distinction of the divine nature in Christ from the human. Answer: Irenaeus says this of Cerinthus, book 1, chapter 25: Cerinthus, a certain man in Asia, taught that the world was not made by the first God, but by a certain power far separated from and distant from that sovereignty which is over all things, and ignorant of the God who is over all. He held that Jesus was not born of a virgin, for this seemed to him impossible, but that he was the son of Joseph and Mary, just like all other men, and that he was more capable of justice, prudence and wisdom than all others. And after his baptism, that Christ came down upon him from that sovereignty which is over all, in the form of a dove; and then he announced the unknown Father and performed mighty works. But at the end, Christ flew back again from Jesus, and Jesus suffered and rose again, while Christ remained impassible, being spiritual. Are these things the same as our doctrine, so that we might be said to have the same doctrine from him, and as from him as the first author? For if he was the first to teach that the divine nature is distinguished in Christ from the human, he also recognized the divine nature as entirely distinct from the human; for whoever recognizes it must at the same time distinguish it. But he was so far from distinguishing these things in Christ, that although he posited Christ and Jesus as different, and said that Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism and afterwards flew away from him again, he nevertheless did not say that Christ was the divine nature, but, I know not what power, perhaps, separated from and distant from God, by which he dreamed the world was made. Epiphanius interprets the Holy Spirit, and the power of God, as meaning that it came from above upon Jesus, and that from it he performed his mighty works. For he never recognized the divine nature in Jesus, or Jesus as God, but only a man, says Augustine, chapter 8. But he distinguished in Christ Jesus one thing impassible and another passible; one thing born from heaven and another from earth. But does that mean that he recognized the divine nature in Christ? Or that he thought the same as we do, and that we hold our doctrines not only as he does, but also as taught by him, the first author himself? Perhaps you will establish some agreement between those things. Therefore you may well say that we are Ophites, because we teach that Christ was present in the Old Testament, since they asserted that the serpent who deceived Adam and Eve was Christ. And what monsters and heresies could not be imputed to each man in this way, if it were enough to form consequences, or agreements and analogies of such opinions! But how the Church first drew its doctrine of the deity of Christ from Simon Magus, Cerinthus and the like, or how it could wish to have anything in common with them, whom not only all of the heresy-writers, one and all, have consistently listed in the catalogue of heretics, but whom they have likewise condemned in all the heads of heresy, and none of them has brought forward anything in them more or less, and those who wrote about them both after the Council of Nicaea and before it have always criticized them in exactly the same way, and no one has ever excepted anything in them pertaining to the doctrine of the deity of Christ. Indeed Nicetas Choniates, in the Treasury of Orthodox Faith, book 4, places that Simonian heresy first among the heresies before Arius, not among the anti-Arian ones, as he would have done if he had seen his own opinion about Christ or his deity in them.

units.la: Jam ex Orphei versibus, & Platonis philosophiâ, nam ab Haereticis Chri-stianis ad Gentilium Poëtas & Philosophos adscendere debuit, Justinum ait sententiam suam de Christo, ejusque à Patre generatione, accepisse. Quodque Impostor aliquis, Simonis Magi discipulus versus sub Orphei nomine inter Christianos sparserit, quos Justinus, tamquam ex Mosis doctrinâ haustos, sibi & aliis fecerit sacros. Versus illi sunt:
units.tr: Now, he says that Justin took his view of Christ, and of his generation from the Father, from the verses of Orpheus and from the philosophy of Plato, for he had to climb from the heretical Christians to the Gentile poets and philosophers. He also says that some impostor, a disciple of Simon Magus, spread verses under the name of Orpheus among the Christians, and that Justin, as if they had been drawn from the teaching of Moses, made them sacred for himself and for others. The verses are these:

units.la: Vocem juro Patris primum quam prodidit ore, Consilio ipse suo mundum cum conderet omnem. Vide Confirmat. Irenici, pag. 179. 180. & 191. præsertim cum manifestum quoque fit, Platonem & Platonicos Verbum aliquod, quod Deus sit, & quod omnia creaverit, quodque à summo Deo, quem & Patrem nominant, ante conditum Mundi genitum sit, introduxisse: adeoque Verbum hoc à Justino quoque, ceu Philosopho Platonico, nullo negotio, productaque insuper Orphei auctoritate, retentum, inque fidem Christianam invectum introductumque fuisse, pateat.
units.tr: "I swear by the Voice of the Father, which he first uttered from his mouth, when he himself by his own counsel was founding the whole world." See the Confirmatio Irenici, pp. 179, 180 and 191, especially since it is also plain that Plato and the Platonists introduced a Word which is God, which created all things, and which was begotten by the highest God, whom they also call Father, before the world was made. It is therefore evident that this Word was retained by Justin too, as a Platonic philosopher, without any difficulty, and moreover with the authority of Orpheus, and was brought into and introduced into the Christian faith.

units.la: Quodque dicit, confirmare se putat testimonio Petavii. Ut quatuor im-præsentiarum veniant examinanda: quæ fuerit Justini sententia, de generatione Filii à Patre ? an sententiam suam, quæcunque fuerit, habeat ex Orphei versibus, vel hos ejus fecerit fundamentum? an ex philosophiâ Platonicâ ? & quid super istis dicat Petavius ? Atque ut à postremo incipiam, in quo tota vis est collectionis apud Adversarium, quodque in initio adhibet, & porrò passim, Petavii loca citat imprimis ex lib. I. de Trinitate, cap. v. §. 10. & cap. III. §. 1. ubi scribit quidem, nonnullos nonnulla ex Platonicâ maxime philosophiâ attulisse in Theologiam, atque in doctrinam de Trinitate; & quod in modo generationis Verbi à Patre constituendo nimis sæpe ad dogmata Platonica deflexerint, & ad hoc etiam citatos versus Orphei à Justino fuisse: sed non docet, vel Justinum, vel alios cum eo, ante Nicænam Synodum Patres, non convenisse in tradendâ Trinitatis in Deo, qualem & Nicæni Patres, & Ecclesia post eos tenuit, fide; quamvis modo loquendi, & in definiendis rei circumstantiis ac modis discreparint, & erraverint non-nunquam: summam ejus & substantiam professi fuerunt, & hanc illos vel ex Platonis schola, vel Orphei versibus hausisse, & non ex Scripturâ, nunquam somniavit Petavius. Et hoc tamen est hujus loci , non illud.
units.tr: As for what he says, he thinks he confirms it by the testimony of Petavius. Four questions must be examined at present: what was Justin's view of the generation of the Son from the Father? Did he take his view, whatever it was, from the verses of Orpheus, or did he make those verses its foundation? Did he take it from Platonic philosophy? And what does Petavius say about these matters? To begin with the last point, which is where the whole force of his collection lies for the Adversary, and which he cites at the outset and again everywhere, he quotes Petavius's passages, chiefly from book I of On the Trinity, chapter 5, section 10, and chapter 3, section 1. There Petavius does indeed write that some theologians drew a good deal from Platonic philosophy into theology and into the doctrine of the Trinity, and that in fixing the manner of the Word's generation from the Father they too often turned aside to Platonic doctrines, and that the verses of Orpheus cited by Justin belong to this too. But he does not teach that Justin, or others with him, the Fathers before the Nicene Synod, disagreed in handing down the faith of the Trinity in God, such as the Nicene Fathers and the Church after them held it. Their manner of speaking and their definitions of the circumstances and modes of the matter differed, and at times they erred, but they professed its sum and substance. Petavius never dreamed that they had drawn this from the school of Plato or from the verses of Orpheus rather than from Scripture. Yet this belongs to the present place, not to that other point.

units.la: Hinc Petavius, in Præfatione librorum de Trinitate, in quâ & lib. III. cautius egit multum, quam lib. I., sic cap. I. loquitur: Atenim complures antiquorum illorum, quos auctores & testes appellamus fidei nostrae, de plurimis dogmatibus, præsertim vero de Trinitate, multum à nobis diversa scripserint. Verum & paucissimi illi sunt, qui in re differunt à communi fide; & si sinceros purosque catholicos quærimus, omnino nulli. In re ipsa dixi. Nam in loquendi modo paullulum quosdam variasse, in tertio & quarto capite primi libri de Trinitate monstravimus. Deinde cujusquemodi tandem istorum scripta, & testimonia sunt; in præcipuis tamen, & quæ ad summam spectant mysterii totius, ut concordes invicem sunt, ita nobiscum congruunt. Jam an bonâ fide Noster in Irenico versatus sit, & cum Patribus, & cum Petavio, qui ex eo tantum institit in referendis illorum næuis & incommodis loquu-tionibus, in præjudicium catholici dogmatis, & reliqua ipsorum bona præterm sit, neque ista æque accepit, Lector judicet.
units.tr: Hence Petavius, in the Preface to the books On the Trinity, where he also proceeds much more cautiously in book III than in book I, speaks thus in chapter 1: "Indeed, many of those ancients whom we call authors and witnesses of our faith have written much that differs from us on very many doctrines, above all on the Trinity. Yet very few of them differ from the common faith in the matter itself, and if we seek sincere and pure Catholics, there are simply none. I have said so in the matter itself. For I have shown in the third and fourth chapters of the first book On the Trinity that some of them varied a little in their manner of speaking. Furthermore, whatever kind of writings and testimonies these men left, in the principal points, and in those that concern the sum of the whole mystery, they agree with one another and so agree with us." Whether our author has dealt with these writers in good faith, both with the Fathers and with Petavius, whom he follows only in pointing out their flaws and inconvenient expressions, to the prejudice of the Catholic doctrine, and passes over their other merits, and whether he has not received these things equally, the reader may judge.

units.la: Petavius ex omni Patrum numero qui Nicænam præcessere Synodum, paucos commemorat, & distinctos in classes duas. Præter manifestos hæreticos & hæresium conditores, qualem facit Tatianum, & veterum etiam judicio, Tertullianum, alios esse docet, qui communem rectamque fidem, sive dogmatis substantiam tenentes, in consectariis quibusdam nonnihil à regulâ deflexerunt: alios, in omnibus re consentientes, loquendi duntaxat modo discrepasse, ab usitatâ præscriptione. Et prioris generis ponit tres, non amplius, Justinum Martyrem, Athenagoram, & Theophilum Antiochenum; posterioris, Irenæum, Clementem Alexandrinum, &, Basilio (ut putat) teste, Gregorium Neocæsariensem, tum Methodium, & Tertullianum, & Origenem collocat inter hæreticos. Verùm præter paucos illos, quamplurimos ait esse, quorum scripta aut non supersunt, aut fragmenta ab aliis descripta, aut nomina à posterioribus indicata fuerunt, qui verœ fidei testimonium perhibuerunt, quale adversus Arianos post-modum proferri, neque ab Adversariis negari potuit, ut ex disputa-tionibus constat Athanasii, Basilii, Gregoriorum Nysseni, & Na-zianzeni &c.
units.tr: Of all the Fathers who came before the Nicene Synod, Petavius mentions a few, and divides them into two classes. Besides the openly heretical and the founders of heresies, such as he makes Tatian, and, by the judgment of the ancients too, Tertullian, he teaches that there are others who, while holding the common and right faith, or the substance of the doctrine, departed somewhat from the rule in certain consequences; and others who agreed in every matter and differed only in manner of speaking from the customary formula. Of the first kind he names only three, no more: Justin Martyr, Athenagoras and Theophilus of Antioch.
