Of the second kind he places Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and, on the witness of Basil (as he thinks), Gregory of Neocaesarea, then Methodius; he counts Tertullian and Origen among the heretics. But, besides those few, he says there were very many whose writings either no longer survive, or survive only in fragments copied by others, or whose names were recorded by later writers, and who bore witness to the true faith. Such testimony could afterwards be brought forward against the Arians, and the Adversaries could not deny it, as is clear from the disputations of Athanasius, Basil, the Gregories of Nyssa and Nazianzus, and others.

units.la: In cujus rei fidem cap. II. varios adducit autores. & cap. III. Justi-num, qui quamvis in quibusdam, quæ ad hoc mysterium spectant, usurpavit aliqua, quæ ab exacta Theologorum regulâ, & loquendi modo dissident; quod tamen in eo primarium est, & ὁμοούσιος, præclare, inquit, complexus est. Probatque tum ex duobus ejus Apologiis, tum Dialogo cum Tryphone. Adde Petavium, lib. III. de Trinit. cap. XI. §. XII. ubi Justinum ostendit utramque in Christo probare naturam, adversus Photinianam, & Socinianam impietatem. Quamvis ergo & illi & alii in explicando dogmate non satis rectè loquuti sæpe fuerint, & ex philosophiâ nonnihil corrupisse simplicitatem fidei constet, non censet tamen Petavius, neque hoc aliquis de Patribus ostendet, quod vel cum Adversariis Christum tantùm esse hominem, ex Mariâ natum, statuerint, vel non fundamenta verœ personarum in Deo Trinitatis retinuerint. Neque novum est, non ita exacte loqui Autores de re aliquâ, priusquam in controversiam adducta, & quæstionibus agitata sit, quam postea. Quem in finem dicta citat Hieronymi, & Augustini, Petavius, lib. I. cap. III. Quemadmodum & Erasmus scribit, ad lib. v. Irenæi, in præfat. sed in hujusmodi multis veteres illi cum candore, nonnunquam & cum venia legendi sunt, quod hæc tum temporis nondum in quæstionem venerant. Denique non illa, in quibus recte & senserunt & loquuti fuerunt Veteres, de dogmatis nostri substantia, sed in quibus modum ejus temere explicare conati fuerunt ex philosophia Platonica, & sic philosophiæ illius abusum, seu intempestivam in res fidei introductionem, causam fuisse erroris ipsis, & occasionem errandi postea Arianis, verum est, & Petavio quoque observatum. Etenim quidquid hæreseon, opinionumque falsarum primis illis Ecclesiæ temporibus emersit, ac præsertim Ariana tota perfidia, ex illo Platonicorum commento caussum & originem accepit. inquit, lib. i. cap. i. & lib. ii. in procem. illam de trium inæqualitate personarum, ac multiplici divinitatis gradu sententiam, à Platonicis mutuatos fuisse antiquiores aliquot, qui Nicænam Synodum antecesserunt, & ab Ario postmodum defensam & amplificatam fuisse, non negat.
units.tr: In confirmation of this, in chapter 2 he adduces various authors, and in chapter 3 he says that Justin, "although in some things which pertain to this mystery he used some expressions which differ from the exact rule and manner of speaking of the theologians; yet what is chief in him, and the ὁμοούσιος [homoousios], he has expressed admirably." He proves this both from his two Apologies and from the Dialogue with Trypho. Add Petavius, On the Trinity, book III, chapter 11, section 12, where he shows that Justin proves both natures in Christ, against the Photinian and Socinian impiety. Although, then, both he and others have often not spoken quite correctly in explaining the doctrine, and it is clear that they somewhat corrupted the simplicity of the faith by philosophy, Petavius does not judge, and no one will show from the Fathers, that they held Christ to be merely a man born of Mary, as the Adversaries do, or that they failed to retain the foundations of the true persons of the Trinity in God. Nor is it a new thing for authors not to speak so exactly about some matter before it was brought into controversy and debated by questions, as they did afterwards. To this end Petavius, in book I, chapter 3, cites the sayings of Jerome and Augustine: "As Erasmus also writes in the preface to his notes on book v of Irenaeus, but with such matters the ancients must be read with candour and sometimes with indulgence, because these things had not yet come into question at that time." Finally, it is true, and Petavius has also observed it, that the ancients were not wrong in the substance of our doctrine, where they thought and spoke rightly, but in those points where they rashly tried to explain its manner from Platonic philosophy. From this abuse of that philosophy, or its untimely introduction into the matters of faith, arose their error, and afterwards an occasion for erring for the Arians. For, as he says in book I, chapter 1, and in the preface to book II, "whatever heresies and false opinions emerged in those first times of the Church, and especially the whole Arian perfidy, took their cause and origin from that Platonic invention." He does not deny that some of the earlier writers, who preceded the Nicene Synod, borrowed from the Platonists that opinion "of the inequality of the three persons and of a manifold grade of divinity," and that it was afterwards defended and enlarged by Arius.

units.la: Quare uti in Veteribus Theologis distinguendi sunt, qui doctrinam de fide Trinitatis rectius tenuerunt, quorum autoritate pugnarunt etiam adversus Arianos Catholici, ab iis, qui in ea exponenda hæsitarunt, & imprudenter ei admiscuerunt conceptus philosophicos; sic in iis, substantia doctrinæ recte secernenda semper est, à temeraria philosophiæ admixtione, & quamvis hanc ex philosophia hauserunt, & confirmarunt Gentilium aut Orphei versibus, non proinde illam totam, & quod ex Scripturis petitum in fide Trinitatis est, ex illis quoque manasse affirmari debet. Quemadmodum si quis nunc ex placitis Scholasticorum vellet judicare de communi fide Trinitatis, & propter nonnullas, quas illi de suo, & ex philosophia addunt explicationes, afferere totum quidquid ejus fidei est, ex philosophia definitum, & ejusdem esse commatis, certe maximam veritati faceret injuriam: sic qui, propter aliquos ex Veteribus, philosophiæ nimium addictos, & qui ab ejus professione, quod Justino contigit, transierunt ad fidem, hinc nonnulla philosophemata fidei temere admiscuerunt, dicat, totam doctrinam de Personarum in Deo Trinitate humanam aut philosophicam & sequioris notæ esse, gravi contumelia afficeret Patres, eorumque doctrinam, nostram etiam, quatenus eam cum illis habemus communem. Quæ vero ex Justino, in confirmationem communis fidei spectari debent, sua Petavius, nostra etiam Tuo loco adducimus, lib. i. de Christo Deo.
units.tr: Therefore, just as among the old theologians we must distinguish those who held the doctrine of the faith of the Trinity more rightly, and by whose authority the Catholics fought even against the Arians, from those who hesitated in setting it out and rashly mixed philosophical concepts into it; so in these writers the substance of the doctrine must always be rightly separated from the rash admixture of philosophy. And although they drew this from philosophy, and confirmed it by the verses of the Gentiles or of Orpheus, it must not be asserted on that account that the whole of it, and what in the faith of the Trinity is taken from Scripture, also flowed from those sources. Just as, if someone now wished to judge the common faith of the Trinity from the opinions of the Schoolmen, and because of some explanations which they added from their own resources and from philosophy, were to assert that whatever belongs to that faith has been defined by philosophy and is of the same stamp, he would certainly do the greatest injustice to the truth; so whoever, on account of some of the ancients who were too devoted to philosophy, and who, when they passed from its profession to the faith (as happened to Justin), rashly mixed some philosophical notions into the faith, should say that the whole doctrine of the persons in the Trinity of God is human or philosophical and of inferior quality, would do grave injury to the Fathers, and to their doctrine, and to ours too, insofar as we hold it in common with them. But what must be looked for in Justin in confirmation of the common faith, Petavius, and we too in our own place, adduce, "book I, On Christ God."

units.la: Neque lib. Expositionis fidei, qui sub nomine Justini legitur, genuinum esse Justini asserui: ut dicere nequiverit, quod facit acerbo satis, pro more, stylo, pag. 332. qui & Expositionem fidei ingratiis licet cordatorum omnium, vel progenuino Justini scripto, vel saltem pro ejus aevi parte, introdu-cere allaborant: sic sui loquutus, ut expresse dixerim, Doctos eum non censere Justini esse, at non propterea velle, quod minus recte senserit Justinus de illis articulis, vel quod eandem etiam veritatem non fuerit professus: sed antiquum autorem dixi, & Veteribus citatum, quos etiam nominavi, & elegantem, ac pro orthodoxa fide disertum atque copiosum. Quæ leviter præteriens Noster alio arripuit, de quibus inter se collatis, exhibentur enim hoc in Opere, expeto recte uniuscujusque judicium & censuram. Neque enim video ipsum novum quid aut singulare produxisse, nisi indignas & innumeras per totam disputationem criminationes.
units.tr: I have not asserted that the book Exposition of the Faith, which is read under Justin's name, is genuine, so he could not say (as he does, rather bitterly and in his usual style, at p. 332) that they labour, against the wishes of all sensible people, to introduce the Exposition of the faith either as a genuine writing of Justin or at least as belonging to his age. He quotes me in such a way that I expressly said the learned do not consider it to be Justin's; but I did not therefore want to say that Justin judged those articles less rightly, or that he did not profess the same truth. I called it an ancient author, cited by the Fathers, whom I also named, and elegant, and eloquent and full in its defence of the orthodox faith. Our author, passing lightly over these points, has seized on other matters. I would welcome each reader's right judgment and assessment of them when they are compared, for they are set out together in this work. For I do not see that he has produced anything new or singular, apart from unworthy and countless accusations throughout the whole disputation.

units.la: Videamus ad singulos Patres, è quibus suam de illis sententiam roborare annisus fuit, & ad responsiones de illis nostras, quid reposuerit. Ac primum de Herma. Quem concludit, Christum Patre multo minorem facere. Quod solum, inquit pag. 227. ad rem faciebat, & satis erat. Id vero nos negamus, vel satis esse, vel solum ad rem facere. Sed illum, quemadmodum reliquos Veteres, nam hoc addit, docuisse, Christum homi-nem tantum, quemadmodum loquitur pag. 17. & non etiam Deum esse, monstrandum fuerat. Neque, an Christus Patre multo minor fuerit. Nam hoc lubens fatemur, eum qua ratione Christus est, Patrem esse multo inferiorem. Sed non inde sequitur, eum omni alia ratione Patre esse inferiorem, & non quoque Patri ἴσον, uti est Joan. v. 18. & Phil. ii. 6. ubi & ἴσα Θεῷ fuisse dicitur ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ[?], antequam μορφὴν δούλου[?] assumeret, & ut homo deprehensus se humiliaret ad mortem. Hilarius, contra Constantium: non est æqualitas Dei in forma Dei esse, si non æqualitas hominis est esse in forma servi. Quod si in forma servi homo Christus est, quid aliud in forma Dei quam Christus Deus est ? Qui ergo in conclusione errat toto cœlo, qualem in præmissis formandis se gerat, vel hinc conjicere promtum est. Profert pro se, quod & olim Ariani fecerunt, teste Theodoreto, hist. lib. i. cap. viii. quod Hermas dixit, primo omnium crede quoniam unus est Deus, qui omnia constituit, & consummavit, & fecit ex eo quod non erat, ut essent omnia, omnium capax, & qui a nemine capiatur. Quod de Deo quidem dicitur, omnium creatore; verum adversus Filium dici, probare non potest. Jam lib. iii. Similit. v. legitur, ad interrogationem ab Hermâ factam, quare Filius Dei, in similitudine istâ, servili loco poneretur? Pastorem respondisse: in servili conditione non ponitur Filius Dei, sed in magna potestate & imperio. ad quod Noster, in potestate magna & imperio positum Filium post mortem demum: & sic illa explicat. Sed, quamvis non negemus, Christum post mortem, gloriâ, potestate & imperio insignem, & hoc denotari Matth.xxviii.18. quod nihil necesse fuerat operose, & adductis plurimorum Theologorum testimoniis probare, non efficit, ideo post mortem demum, pag. 234. 235. Christum in gloriâ fuisse, & nullâ ratione antea, non etiam antequam in terram venit, & mortem, hujus acceptae gloriae antecedaneam, fuit passus. Nam uti in Christo Theologi distinguunt considerationem Theologicam, ab oeconomicâ; ita quoque regnum ejus naturale, quod quâ Deus est, habet; & oeconomicum, quod, quâ Mediator, in tempore accepit. Neque mihi dicat, hanc esse petitionem principii: quia non argumentor, sed argumentum modò meum tueor & expono, osten-doque frustra ipsum ex accessorio Christo, ut Mediatoris, & oeconomico regno divinum naturale evertere, hoc solo, quod Christus tale regnum accepit, quod non negamus, sed consequentiam, quam inde format, probari non videmus. Quod & ipse hinc enervat, dum statuit, Veteres Christianos ad unum omnes, Christum creaturis antiquiorem esse credidisse, pag. 258.159. ergo hoc saltem ante-creaturas omnes, & ante istam ex Maria existentiam, & ante mortem suam, habuit. Et quando putat, illos Christum, utcunque creaturis antiquiorem, Patre tamen inferiorem fecisse cum aevo, tum dignitate, & potentiâ, suam ergo ei etiam, pro istâ antiquitate, dignitatem & potentiam, creaturis omnibus potiorem, attribuerunt: & sic necesse est nobiscum distinguere gloriam, quam Christus ante mundum habuit, & quam in mundo post mortem demum accepit. Porro pro sententiâ nostrâ adfertur ex lib. iii. Simil. ix. quod dicitur, Filius quidem Dei omni creaturâ antiquior est, ita ut in consilio Patri suo adfuerit, ad condendam creaturam. Porta autem propterea nova est, quia in consummatione in novissimus diebus apparet, ut qui assecuti sunt salutem, per eam intrent in regnum Dei. Respondet Ad-versarius, locum esse suppositium. Compendiosa profecto & elegans elabendi ratio. Tua, quae forte adducis, ex Autore eodem, pro veris-simis habere; at quae adversus te faciunt, esse suppositia. Quare mihi quoque non integrum erit idem de tuis respondere & statuere? Habesne codicem, qui aliter legat, vel Autorem, qui aliter legerit unquam?
units.tr: Let us look at the individual Fathers from whom he has tried to strengthen his view of them, and see what he has replied to our answers about them. And first, concerning Hermas. He concludes that he makes Christ much less than the Father. This alone, he says at p. 227, was relevant, and was enough. But we deny either that it is enough or that it alone is relevant. Rather it had to be shown that he taught just as the other Ancients did, for he adds this, that Christ was only a man, as he puts it at p. 17, and not also God; and not whether Christ was much less than the Father. For we gladly admit that, in the respect in which Christ is Christ, the Father is far superior to him. But it does not follow from this that he is inferior to the Father in every other respect, and not also equal to the Father (ἴσον), as is said in John 5:18 and Phil. 2:6, where he is also said to have been ἴσα Θεῷ [equal to God] ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ [in the form of God] before he took the μορφὴν δούλου [form of a servant], and as a man humbled himself, even unto death. Hilary, against Constantius: It is not the equality of God to be in the form of God, unless it is the equality of man to be in the form of a servant. But if Christ is a man in the form of a servant, what else is he in the form of God than God? It is therefore easy to see from this how completely wrong he is in his conclusion, and what manner of man he is in forming his premises. He puts forward in support of himself what the Arians also once did, as Theodoret witnesses (Hist. book 1, ch. 8): that Hermas said, first of all believe that God is one, who created and completed all things, and made from what did not exist that all things might be, capable of all things and seized by no one. This is indeed said of God, the creator of all; but he cannot prove that it is said against the Son. Again, in Similitude 5, book 3, it is read that when Hermas asked why the Son of God was placed in a servile position in that parable, the Shepherd answered: The Son of God is not placed in a servile condition, but in great power and dominion. To this our author replies that the Son was placed in great power and dominion only after death, and so explains the passage. But although we do not deny that Christ after death was distinguished by glory, power and dominion, and that this is denoted at Matt. 28:18, which was not necessary to prove laboriously, and with the testimonies of many theologians, it does not follow that therefore Christ was in glory only after death, pp. 234-235, and in no respect before, not even before he came into the world and suffered death, the forerunner of this glory he received. For, just as theologians distinguish in Christ the theological consideration from the economic, so also his natural kingdom, which he has as God, is distinguished from the economic kingdom, which he received in time as Mediator. Nor let him say to me that this is begging the question; for I am not arguing but only maintaining and setting out my argument, and I show that he vainly tries to overthrow the divine natural kingdom from an accident of Christ as Mediator and his economic kingdom, from the sole fact that Christ received such a kingdom. This we do not deny; but we do not see that the consequence he draws from it is proved. He himself weakens this when he states that the early Christians all without exception believed that Christ was older than the creatures, pp. 158-159. Therefore he had this at least before all creatures, and before that existence from Mary, and before his own death. And when he thinks that they, however much they made Christ older than the creatures, made him nevertheless inferior to the Father both in age and in dignity and power, they therefore attributed to him, on account of that antiquity, a dignity and power superior to all creatures; and so it is necessary, with us, to distinguish the glory that Christ had before the world from that which he received in the world after death. Moreover, in support of our view there is cited from book 3, Similitude 9, the statement: The Son of God is indeed older than every creature, so that he was present with his Father in counsel when creation was made. But the gate is new for this reason, that it appears at the consummation in the last days, so that those who have obtained salvation may enter through it into the kingdom of God. The Opponent replies that the passage is spurious. This is certainly a concise and elegant way of escaping. You may hold your own citations, which you perhaps bring from the same author, to be most true, but whatever tells against you to be spurious. Why then should I not be equally free to reply and decide the same about your passages? Do you have a manuscript which reads otherwise, or an author who ever read it otherwise?

units.la: Sed, ista, inquis, non fuerunt ab Athanasio, non à Nicaenis Patribus allegata, quum maxime quidem è re ipsorum fuisset, illis pugnare contra* Arianos. An nunquam vel ab iis, vel aliis allata fuerint, non dicam ego, neque tu. Et non alia etiam, ex quibus hic disputas, ab illis adducta: proinde ergo suppositicia? Notum est, argumentum tale negativum non concludere.
units.tr: But, you say, these were not alleged by Athanasius, nor by the Nicene Fathers, although it would have been most to their purpose to fight the Arians with them. Whether they were never brought forward by them or by others, I will not say, nor will you. And are the other passages from which you argue not also adduced by them? Therefore are they to be regarded as spurious too? It is well known that an argument of this negative kind does not prove anything.

units.la: Putat etiam hinc verba illa suppositicia esse, quia scilicet non conveniunt cum iis, quae ex Similitudine v. adduxit, prose. Sed hoc jam dis-solvimus, etiamsi de gloriâ ibi verba accipiantur Christo data in tempore. Quia non de eodem fuit sermo, ac proinde neque oppositio ad idem. Et quare non aliquis dicat, forte verba, quae adducis pro te quasi facientia, quamvis talia neque sint, esse interpolata, si minus probentur convenire cum iis quae dicuntur Similitudine nona; aeque ac tu id dicis de verbis hisce, propter illa? Deinde, inquit, absurdum, ut non Pastor dixisset in consilium à Deo adhibitum esse quoque Christum, cum Spiritu S. & Angelis, de Christo in coelestem gloriam evehendo, si illum credidisset fuisse rerum omnium creatorem. Quod tamen non facit. Sed Christus in consilium hoc vocari, ut Christus non potuit: hoc enim in tempore fuit, ex officio, ad quod erat unctus. An verò prout idem est Dei Filius, non intelligatur in consilium illud quoque adhibi-tus, haud facile dixeris, quia duplicem hic nescio annon Filium nomi-net, Spiritum Sanctum, & Christum: credo quia forte processionem Spiritus S. tamquam filiationem aliquam conceperunt, ideo & nominarunt: Filius autem, Spiritus Sanctus est. Servus vero ille Filius Dei. Per servum absque dubio intelligit Christum, vel ejus corpus, sive ipsum in corpore consideratum. Hoc ergo corpus, in quod inductus est Spiritus Sanctus, servavit illi spiritui, recte ambulans &c. Advocavit ergo Deus Filium, & nuncios bonos, ut & huic scilicet corpori, quod servivit Spiritui Sancto sine querela, locus aliquis consistendi daretur, ne videretur mercedem servi-tutis suâ perdidisse. Certe Spiritum Sanctum credidit esse personam, non tantum Filium eum nominando, sed quod in consilium adhibitus, sen-tentiam etiam dixerit aut comprobarit, quemadmodum Angeli, & Deo dicitur fuisse charus & haeres. Quae simpliciter de virtute Dei, ut notat attributum essentiale, exponi non possunt. Credens autem personas in Deo Patrem, & Spiritum Sanctum, Filium non credere non potuit. Et quid, quod dixit, abhibitum à Deo Filium, quem charum & haeredem habebat? Nunquam enim dicitur haeres Patri Spiritus S. Dubito ergo, an-non non per Filium in consilium adhibitum, praeter Spiritum etiam subintelligat secundam personam Filium. Quod aeque hic potest fieri, ac quando de corpore Christi passim dicens, Spiritui paruisse, in ea habitasse Deum, ei infusum fuisse Spiritum &c. intelligi hoc debet saltem una de ejus quoque anima. Sed harum Similitudinem ea est, valde intricata & crassa admodum, ratio, ut quemadmodum in isto argumentorum genere, sic hic non certe omnia ad vivum resecanda sint vel rigidius examinanda.
units.tr: He also thinks that these words are spurious because they do not agree, of course, with what he quoted above from Similitude 5. But we have already resolved this, even if those words are taken as referring to the glory given to Christ in time. For there was not talk of the same thing, and consequently there is no opposition about the same thing. And why should someone not say that perhaps the words you bring forward in your favour as if they supported you, though they are not such, have been interpolated, if they are shown not to agree with what is said in Similitude 9? Just as you say this about these words, because of those. Next, he says, it is absurd that the Shepherd should not have said that Christ too was taken into counsel by God, together with the Holy Spirit and the angels, in exalting Christ to heavenly glory, if he had believed him to be the creator of all things. Yet he does not do so. But Christ could not be called into this counsel as Christ, for that was in time, from the office for which he was anointed. But whether, as the Son of God, he is not understood to have been taken into that counsel too, you could hardly say easily, since I do not know whether he names the Son here as a double reference, the Holy Spirit and Christ. I believe perhaps that they conceived the procession of the Holy Spirit as a certain sonship, and therefore also named him: But the Son is the Holy Spirit. Indeed that servant is the Son of God. Through the servant he undoubtedly means Christ, or his body, or Christ himself considered in the body. This body, therefore, into which the Holy Spirit was brought, kept that spirit, walking rightly, etc. God therefore called the Son and the good messengers, so that some place of standing might be given also to that body, which served the Holy Spirit without fault, lest it should seem to have lost the reward of its servitude. Certainly he believed the Holy Spirit to be a person, not only by naming him Son, but because, taken into counsel, he also gave or approved an opinion, just as the angels are said to have been dear to God and heirs. These things cannot be explained simply of the power of God, as an essential attribute. But since he believed there are persons in God, the Father and the Holy Spirit, he could not fail to believe in the Son. And what of his saying that the Son, whom he had as dear and heir, was taken into counsel by God? For the Holy Spirit is never called heir of the Father. I doubt therefore whether he does not also understand, under the Son who was taken into counsel, the second person, the Son, besides the Spirit. This can be done here just as, when he speaks of Christ's body generally, saying that it obeyed the Spirit, that God dwelt in it, that the Spirit was poured into it, and so on, it must be understood at least of one of its souls as well. But the likeness of these is a very intricate and rather crude method, so that, as in this kind of argument, not everything is to be cut down to the quick or examined too rigidly.

units.la: Autor noster aliud adhuc comminiscitur, ad verba Simil. ix. , explicatque Christum respectu Spiritus Sancti in ipso habitantis posse dici omni creatura antiquiorem, & Patri adfuisse in opere creationis. Filius quidem Dei omni creatura antiquior est, ita ut in consilio Patri suo adfuerit, ad condendam creaturam. 'Petra autem propterea nova est, 'quia in consummatione in novissimis diebus apparuit. id est, inquit, respectu Spiritus S in ipso habitantis. Sic ergo & nos poterimus dici omni creatura, & nobis ipsis, antiquiores, respectu ejusdem Spiritus, nobis quoque dati. Sed Filius ille Christus, nam de hoc est sermo, & non de Spiritu Sancto, dicitur antiquior omnibus, & in consilio Patri adfuisse. Denique repugnat adversativa, Petra autem nova: quod de solo Christo, appposite ad antiquitatem illam, intelligendum. Tandem probat ex Visione 2. Filium Dei, ex mente Hermae, a Patre primo, & ante omnes alias creaturas creatum, mundumq; per & propter eum conditum fuisse. Saltem ergo non credidit Hermas, tantum esse hominem, ex Maria natum. Et creatum si dicar, potest in commodum sensum exponi verbum durius, quemadmodum id ostendit Petavius, ad Prov. viii. 22.
units.tr: Our author devises yet another idea, on the words of Simil. ix., and explains that Christ, with respect to the Holy Spirit dwelling in him, can be called older than every creature, and was present with the Father in the work of creation. The Son of God is indeed older than every creature, so that he was present with his Father in counsel when the creature was founded. 'But the rock is therefore new, 'because in the consummation, in the last days, he appeared. That is, he says, with respect to the Holy Spirit dwelling in him. So then we too may be called older than every creature, and older than ourselves, with respect to the same Spirit, who is given to us also. But that Son, Christ (for it is of him that the discourse is, and not of the Holy Spirit), is said to be older than all and to have been present with the Father in counsel. Finally, the adversative contradicts: But the rock is new, which must be understood of Christ alone, as opposed to that antiquity. Lastly, from Vision 2 he proves that, in Hermas's mind, the Son of God was created by the Father first and before all other creatures, and that the world was made through him and for him. So at least Hermas did not believe that he was merely a man born of Mary. And if I say that he was created, the harsher word can be explained in a more suitable sense, as Petavius shows on Prov. viii. 22.

units.la: Denique Christum Patri in creatione adfuisse, & omni creatura antiquiorem putat Noster dici posse, respectu decreti & praedestinationis, etiamsi eundem, hominem tantum esse crediderit Hermas. Nam si primo creata dicitur vetula, per quam Ecclesia designatur, Visione 2. quare anus est? Quoniam, inquit, omnium prima creata est, ideo anus: & propter illam mundus factus est. Nego, quod ibi creata significet, praedestinata vel decreta; vel primo creata, quod est, primo decreta. Quod nec verum, neque Adversarii credunt, neque Hermae mentem fuisse, ostenditur. Sed revera primo creata fuit, non primo ante creaturas omnes, & Angelos, & coelum: nam humana, post coelestia facta sunt, & Adversarius, tum Hermae, tum aliorum sententiam fuisse dicit, Christum esse primam creaturam. Sed primo revera creata, sive inter prima, & statim cum homine,hi enim Ecclesiam constituunt; & propter Ecclesiam,ut eam haberet Deus, hæc, & alia creata sunt. Ut nec necesse sit ad Dei decretum confugere, neque id verba patiantur, sive hæc de Ecclesia, sive illa de Christo.
units.tr: Finally, our author thinks that Christ can be said to have been present with the Father in creation, and to be older than every creature, with respect to the decree and predestination, even though Hermas believed him to be only a man. For in Vision 2 the old woman, through whom the Church is designated, is said to have been created first. Why is she an old woman? Because, he says, she was created first of all, therefore old; and for her sake the world was made. I deny that "created" there means "predestined" or "decreed", or that "created first" means "decreed first". That this is neither true, nor believed by our adversary, nor the meaning of Hermas, is shown. Rather, she was truly created first, not first before all creatures, and the angels, and heaven; for human beings were made after the heavenly things. Our adversary says that the opinion of Hermas, and of others, was that Christ is the first creature. But she was created first in fact, or among the first, and at once together with man; for these two constitute the Church, and for the sake of the Church, that God might have it, these and other things were created. So there is no need to take refuge in God's decree, nor do the words allow it, whether these things are said of the Church or those of Christ.

units.la: Cum Clemente Romano haud aliter atque cum Herma agit Adversarius, ostensurus eundem quoque (post Hermam) Christum Patre minorem credidisse. pag. 268. quod nos credimus quoque, sed non negamus propterea, eum cum Patre esse verum Deum. Quod nec Clemens inficiatus fuit. Minor Patre Christus, quod ad naturam humanam, & officium hinc pendens; non quod ad deitatem, quæ minorem, aut majorem non fert. Ubi enim unus Deus creditur, ibi minor & major excluditur, inquit Autor Breviarii Fidei, adversus Arianos. Dixerat, nam nos, sicut eum Deum legimus, ita nec majorem, nec minorem Deum usquam legimus, nec credere religiosa mente debemus. Et postea, adducto loco 1 Joan. v. 20. & simus, inquit, in vero filio ejus Jesu Christo. hic est verus Deus, & vita æterna. Audis verum Deum, & præsumis dicere minorem, & non confiteris æqualem? Dicit etiam beatus Apostolus ad Titum, Expectantes beatam spem, & adventum gloriæ magni Dei. Nescio qua fronte minor esse dicatur, quem magnum Deum Apostolus profitetur. ——Iterum, sed credamus scripturæ dicenti, tam noviquam veteris Testamenti, quia Deus unus est. & si unus major, alter minor est, ut Ariani dicunt, unus dici non potest, inæqualitas unitatem excludit. Sed ita argumentatur Noster, pag. 269: Si a Clemente Deus quidem verus, unus, & omnipotens describitur, ab hoc vero Christus tum simul distinguatur, adeoque excludatur &c. Ergo. Distingui, concedo: prorsus excludi, nego. Imo, addit, si magnificentissime licet descriptus Christus, splendor tantum & radius magnificentiæ Dei appellatur &c. Ita appellatur, ut tantum hoc sit, & non quoque verus Deus? nego Minorem. Ita appellatur tantum? nam multum situm est in particulæ hujus sensu, & cum quibus conjungas, non ut alia propterea excludantur, quemadmodum excludi solâ illâ denominatione non possunt: iterum nego. Quin verba ista, esse splendorem & radium magnificentiæ Dei adeo quidem veritatem naturæ divinæ non excludunt, ut connotent, quo sensu ea Apostolus usurpavit, Hebr.1.3. unde illa mutuatum Clementem fatetur, pag.273. uti de eo suo loco disputamus. Nam impræsentiarum, quod testatur pag.273. de locis Scripturæ non est quæstio, sed de sententiâ Veterum: ac propterea & nos invindicandis Scripturæ locis non immoramur, nedum ut Apostolus illo loco de eo egerit, quod Christus tantum in tempore accepit, adeoque ex gratia. Quod denique addit Noster, Christum, à Clemente, cum Angelis, duntaxat ob acceptam à Deo potestatem, comparari: nec verum est, neque si verum esset, faceret elenchum. Uti neque, quod postremò ait, Christum cum Deo, à Clemente non exæquari. Nam quamvis in terminis hoc non fiat, modo fiat reipsâ: fit autem, quando in cultus paritate cum Patre Christus con-jungitur, quodque hoc tollat vel destruat additur nihil. Aliter enim non adoratur cum Patre, nisi quia idem, & verus cum Patre Deus est. Ful-gentius, contra Arianos: Nos idcirco filium Dei de patris substantia natum, hoc est, de id quod pater est, credimus & fatemur, quoniam quicquid substantia Dei non est, non possumus ut Deum vel adorare vel colere, (præceptum legis sollicitus observantes, quo dicitur: Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus Dominus unus est, & Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illi soli servies) quem Deum, non patrem solum credimus, sed patrem & filium & spiritum sanctum: fides enim nostra, qua unum Deum colimus & timemus, nec unione personali con-trahitur, nec substantia diversitate defungitur, ne aut Deos gentiliter colamus, diversas colendo substantias, aut filium & spiritum cum Sabellio denegemus, non servantes in trinitate personas. & postea: quod si Dominum Deum, solum patrem accipere debemus, filio ergo nec ut Deo serviamus, nec eum adoremus. Quicquid enim ad naturam domini Dei solius non pertinet, ut Deus à nobis adorari non debet. & Novatianus, de Trinitate: si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ipse dicit: Et omnis qui videt & credit in me, non morietur in æternum? Sed enim qui in hominem solitarium credit & nudum, maledictus dicitur: Hic autem qui credit in Christum non maledictus, sed in æternum non moriturus refertur. Ex quo si aut homo est tantum, ut hæretici volunt, quomodo quisquis in eum credit, non morietur in æternum, quum maledictus esse teneatur qui confidit in homine? aut si non maledictus, sed potius ad æternæ vitæ consecutionem, ut legitur, destinatus, non homo tantummodo Christus, sed & Deus, in quem qui credit, & maledictionis periculum deponit, & ad fru-ctum justitiæ accedit.
units.tr: Our adversary deals with Clement of Rome in much the same way as with Hermas, intending to show that he too (after Hermas) believed Christ to be less than the Father, p. 268. We too believe this, but we do not on that account deny that he, together with the Father, is the true God. Clement did not deny this either. Christ is less than the Father as regards his human nature and the office that depends on it, not as regards his deity, which does not admit of being less or greater. For where one God is believed, there the less and the greater are excluded, says the author of the Breviary of Faith against the Arians. He had said: for we, as we read that he is God, so nowhere do we read that he is a greater or lesser God, nor ought we to believe it with a religious mind. And afterwards, citing 1 John 5:20: "and we are in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life." Do you hear "true God", and do you presume to call him less, and not confess him equal? The blessed Apostle also says to Titus: "Looking for the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God." I know not with what face he is said to be less, whom the Apostle professes to be the great God. Again: but let us believe Scripture, which says, both in the New and in the Old Testament, that God is one; and if one is greater and the other less, as the Arians say, he cannot be called one; inequality excludes unity. But our author argues thus, p. 269: If Clement describes God as true, one and almighty, and Christ is at the same time distinguished from this true God, and so is excluded, etc. Therefore... I grant that he is distinguished; I deny that he is wholly excluded. Indeed, he adds: if Christ is described most magnificently, he is called only the splendour and ray of God's majesty, etc. Is he called so only, so that he is not also the true God? I deny the minor premise. Is he called so only? For much depends on the sense of this particle, and on what you join it with, so that other things are not thereby excluded, as they cannot be excluded by that designation alone: again I deny it. Indeed, these words, that he is the splendour and ray of God's glory, do not so exclude the truth of the divine nature, but rather connote in what sense the Apostle used them, Heb. 1:3, from which Clement, as our author admits on p. 273, borrowed them, as we discuss in its place. For what he attests on p. 273 is not a question about the words of Scripture at present, but about the opinion of the ancients; and therefore we do not linger here over vindicating the passages of Scripture, much less as though the Apostle in that place spoke of what Christ received only in time, and so by grace. Finally, as to what our author adds, that Clement compares Christ with the angels only on account of the power received from God, this is not true, and even if it were, it would not make a refutation. Nor does it matter that he says, lastly, that Clement does not equate Christ with God. For although this is not done in so many words, it is done in fact: and it is done when Christ is joined with the Father in parity of worship; and nothing is added that would remove or destroy this. For otherwise Christ is not worshipped with the Father, unless because he is the same and true God with the Father. Fulgentius, against the Arians: We therefore believe and confess that the Son of God was born of the substance of the Father, that is, of that which the Father is, because whatever is not the substance of God, we cannot adore or worship as God (carefully observing the precept of the law, which says: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord; and you shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone"), whom we believe to be not only the Father but the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For our faith, by which we worship and fear the one God, is neither contracted by personal union nor dissolved by diversity of substance, lest we either worship gods in the manner of the Gentiles, worshipping diverse substances, or deny the Son and the Spirit with Sabellius, not preserving the persons in the Trinity. And afterwards: but if we ought to take the Lord God as the Father alone, then we should serve the Son neither as God nor adore him. For whatever does not pertain to the nature of the one Lord God is not to be adored by us as God. And Novatian, On the Trinity: If Christ is only a man, how does he himself say: "And everyone who sees and believes in me shall not die for ever"? For he who believes in a solitary and bare man is called accursed; but he who believes in Christ is not called accursed, but is said to be destined not to die for ever. Therefore if he is only a man, as the heretics wish, how is it that whoever believes in him shall not die for ever, when he who trusts in a man is bound to be accursed? Or if he is not accursed, but rather destined, as is read, to the attainment of eternal life, then Christ is not only a man but also God, in whom whoever believes both puts away the danger of the curse and comes to the fruit of righteousness.

units.la: Putat Noster, pag. 271. satis esse, quod à Clemente Filius Patri non æquatur. 1. Quia Doctorem agebat Clemens. Ideone omnia ubique omnes docere debuit, vel si id minus fecerit, & aliquid forte omiserit, hoc propterea non agnovisse dicendus est? II. & optimam ad illud docendum occasionem habuit. Non etiam ad alia, quæ forte omisit quoque? Et satis sæpe habet Doctor, res attigisse aliquas, quamvis non plane explicet, non ad tuum placitum & sensum, non illis terminis, quibus, re in controversiam adducta, postmodum explicari solet, sive pro, sive contra.
units.tr: Our author, at p. 271, thinks it is enough that Clement does not make the Son equal to the Father. (1) Because Clement was acting as a teacher. Must he then have taught everything everywhere? And if he did less, and perhaps omitted something, is he to be said not to have known it? (2) He also had an excellent opportunity to teach that doctrine. Is he not likewise to be excused for other things he may have left out? A teacher often has enough if he has touched on some matters, even without explaining them fully, not in your manner and sense, nor in the terms which, once the question has been raised, are usually used afterwards to explain it, whether for or against.

units.la: Ad Ignatium pergit, quem Patrem Filio majorem credidisse, asserit. Sed jam ostenderat Petavius, hoc etiam Veteres nonnunquam dixisse, qui tamen Christum verum, & ejusdem cum Patre essentiæ crediderunt. Respondimusque, quamvis Ignatius ostenderit, Christum non esse ipsum illum super omnia Deum, id est, Patrem, non tamen negasse simpliciter, esse Deum super omnia. Neque contrarium eo probatur, quod Christus est Filius Dei, quod adscendit ad Deum suum &c. Et Adverf. pag. 278. agnoscit, Veteres Patrem hoc proprio quasi epitheto Deum super omnia appellasse, & sic Ignatium perstrinxisse hæreticos illos, qui Filium cum Patre confundebant, id est, personas illas duas. Neque enim inter hæreticos unquam collocati fuerunt, qui Patrem & Filium ejusdem dixerunt esse essentiæ personas. Ut nunc omittamus disputationem de Epistolarum Ignatiarum veritate, & numero, sed sumamus prout eæ circumferuntur & leguntur, unde non unum alterumque, sed plura loca attulimus pro Christi verâ Deitate, quæ suo loco videri possunt, & discussimus quoque quod ex epistolâ ejus ad Philippenses adducitur, & alterâ ad Ephesios: quæ verba à Theodoreto, Dial. 1. apud Petavium, in Præfat. lib. de Trinitate, cap. 11. ita quidem citantur, εἷς ἰατρὸς ἐστι σαρκικὸς καὶ πνευματικός, γεννητὸς καὶ ἀγέννητος, ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ Θεός, ἐν θανάτῳ ζωὴ ἀληθινή, καὶ ἐκ Μαρίας, καὶ ἐκ Θεοῦ, πρῶτον παθητὸς καὶ τότε ἀπαθὴς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν. Unus est medicus carnalis & spiritualis, genitus ex ingenito, in homine Deus, in morte vera vita, & ex Maria, & ex Deo, primum patibilis & tunc impatibilis Jesus Christus Dominus noster. Athanasius autem in libro de Synodis legit, γεννητὸς καὶ ἀγέννητος [?]: quandoquidem & recte scripsit beatus Ignatius, factum illum vocans propter carnem: etenim Christus caro factus est: increatum vero, quoniam non est ex operum & creaturam numero, sed Filius ex Patre. Græca sunt, ὅτι γὰρ ὁ μακάριος Ἰγνάτιος ὀρθῶς ἔγραψε, γεννητὸν αὐτὸν λέγων διὰ τὰ σαρκικά. ὁ γὰρ Χριστὸς σὰρξ ἐγένετο· ἀγέννητον δέ, ὅτι μὴ τῶν μητέρων, καὶ γεννητῶν ἐστιν, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐκ πατρός. Quæ nescio quare non æque adduxerit Noster, pag. 286. ac Theodoreti illa, cum utraque junctim legeret apud Petavium. Vel illa etiam quæ apud Theodoretum, ex Ignatio leguntur, τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ κατὰ θεότητα [?] καὶ δύναμιν, Dominum nostrum Filium Dei secundum deitatem & potentiam. Et, ex epistolâ ad Ephef. apud Theodoretum, eodem Dialogo, ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐκυοφορηθὴς[?] ὑπὸ Μαρίας, καὶ οἰκονομίαν Θεοῦ[?]. Deus enim noster Jesus Christus in Maria utero gestatus est, secundum dispensationem Dei. Qui in eadem epist. Christum nominat Filium hominis, secundum carnem, & Filium Dei.
units.tr: He goes on to Ignatius, whom he asserts believed the Father to be greater than the Son. But Petavius has already shown that the ancients sometimes said this too, although they nonetheless believed Christ to be true God and of the same essence as the Father. We replied that, although Ignatius showed that Christ is not that very God over all, that is, the Father, he did not simply deny that God is over all. Nor is the contrary proved by the fact that Christ is the Son of God, that he ascended to his God, and so on. In his Adversus, at p. 278, he admits that the ancients called the Father "God over all" as a peculiar epithet of his, and that in this way Ignatius struck at those heretics who confused the Son with the Father, that is, those two persons. For those who said that the Father and the Son are persons of the same essence were never counted among the heretics. To pass over for now the question of the genuineness and number of the Epistles of Ignatius, and to take them as they are circulated and read, we have adduced not one or two but several passages for Christ's true Deity, which may be seen in their place, and we have also examined what is cited from his letter to the Philippians and from the other to the Ephesians. Theodoret, in his first Dialogue, as cited by Petavius in the preface to his book On the Trinity, chapter 11, quotes these words thus: εἷς ἰατρὸς ἐστι σαρκικὸς καὶ πνευματικός, γεννητὸς καὶ ἀγέννητος, ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ Θεός, ἐν θανάτῳ ζωὴ ἀληθινή, καὶ ἐκ Μαρίας, καὶ ἐκ Θεοῦ, πρῶτον παθητὸς καὶ τότε ἀπαθὴς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν. There is one physician, carnal and spiritual, begotten and unbegotten, God in man, true life in death, both of Mary and of God, first passible and then impassible, Jesus Christ our Lord. Athanasius, however, in his book On the Synods, reads γεννητὸς καὶ ἀγέννητος [?]: since blessed Ignatius also wrote rightly, calling him begotten on account of the flesh, for Christ became flesh; but unbegotten, because he is not of the number of works and creatures, but a Son from the Father. The Greek is: ὅτι γὰρ ὁ μακάριος Ἰγνάτιος ὀρθῶς ἔγραψε, γεννητὸν αὐτὸν λέγων διὰ τὰ σαρκικά. ὁ γὰρ Χριστὸς σὰρξ ἐγένετο· ἀγέννητον δέ, ὅτι μὴ τῶν μητέρων, καὶ γεννητῶν ἐστιν, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐκ πατρός. I do not know why our author did not cite these words equally at p. 286, since he read both passages together in Petavius, nor those which are read in Theodoret from Ignatius: τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ κατὰ θεότητα [?] καὶ δύναμιν, our Lord, the Son of God according to deity and power. And from the letter to the Ephesians, in Theodoret in the same Dialogue: ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐκυοφορηθὴς[?] ὑπὸ Μαρίας, καὶ οἰκονομίαν Θεοῦ[?]: "For our God, Jesus Christ, was carried in the womb of Mary according to the dispensation of God." In the same letter he names Christ the Son of man according to the flesh, and the Son of God.

units.la: Ex quibus, & citatis alibi, clarum est quæ fuerit Ignatii, de Christo, mens & fides, neque voluisse ipsum, propterea quod Patrem vocaret Deum super omnia, Filium à Deitate eădem excludere, ad Antiochenos scribens, nec multitudinem Deorum introducendam esse, neque, specie unitatis Dei negandum Christum, ἢ μὴ πλήθη[?] ... ἐπαγαγεῖν[?], μήτε τὸν Χριστὸν ... φαντασίᾳ[?] ... ἑνὸς Θεοῦ[?]. Christum simpliciter & sæpe appellat Deum: Deum verbum: Filium Dei verum: docens, ante mundum extitisse: & πρὸ αἰώνων ante fæcula apud Patrem fuisse, & in fine apparuisse, in epist. ad Magnesianos, ὃς πρὸ αἰῶνος[?] τῷ Πατρί. & paulo post, ἦν γὰρ αὐτὸς ὡς ἓν αὐτῷ λόγῳ, ἀ ῥήτης[?], ἀλλ' ἀσιωπήτης[?], verbum ipsum, non prolativum, sed substantiale. quæ plane, & minio non signata sic leguntur etiam in editione Usserii. Petavius, lib. xvi. de incarnatione, cap. 11. pag. 626. ita citat, ὃς ἦν αὐτῷ λόγῳ αἰδίῳ. alibi vocat Ignatius ἀνάρχον, per quem facta in mundo omnia: quod probat ex Joan. 1. & Prov. viii. Deum esse omnium intelligibilium & sensibilium. Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum S. non esse Deum trinominem, aut nominis duntaxat inter illos distinctionem, sed alterius, & alterius esse nomina, quamvis unius Dei. Filium Dei à Maria in utero gestatum, secundum œconomiam: neque ex Maria accepisse exordium: assumsisse corpus: fuisse incarnatum, & in carne habitasse: non esse merum hominem, constantem ex solâ animâ & corpore: nec secundum idem esse Deum & hominem: ἀνθρωπολάτρας[?] Ebionitas adorare merum hominem, quos damnat. Jam qui talia de Christo sentit & docet, eum dices, vel cum Adversariis stare, vel contra nos?
units.tr: From these passages, and from others cited elsewhere, it is clear what Ignatius's mind and faith concerning Christ were. He did not wish, because he calls the Father "God over all," to exclude the Son from that same Deity, when writing to the Antiochenes that a multitude of gods is not to be introduced, nor is Christ to be denied under the appearance of the unity of God: ἢ μὴ πλήθη[?] ... ἐπαγαγεῖν[?], μήτε τὸν Χριστὸν ... φαντασίᾳ[?] ... ἑνὸς Θεοῦ[?]. He simply and often calls Christ God, the Word of God, the true Son of God, teaching that he existed before the world, and was with the Father before the ages, and appeared at the end. In his letter to the Magnesians: ὃς πρὸ αἰῶνος[?] τῷ Πατρί; and shortly after: ἦν γὰρ αὐτὸς ὡς ἓν αὐτῷ λόγῳ, ἀ ῥήτης[?], ἀλλ' ἀσιωπήτης[?], the Word itself, not uttered but substantial. These words, plainly and without any red mark, are read thus also in Ussher's edition. Petavius, in book 16 On the Incarnation, chapter 11, page 626, cites them as: ὃς ἦν αὐτῷ λόγῳ αἰδίῳ. Elsewhere Ignatius calls him ἀνάρχον, through whom all things were made in the world, which he proves from John 1 and Proverbs 8, that God is the maker of all intelligible and sensible things. He teaches that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not one God with three names, or a mere distinction of names among them, but that the names are of different persons, though of one God. That the Son of God was carried in the womb of Mary according to the economy; that he did not take his beginning from Mary; that he assumed a body, was made flesh, and dwelt in the flesh; that he is not a mere man consisting of soul and body alone; and that he is not both God and man in the same respect. He condemns the Ebionites, who worship a mere man, as idolaters of man (ἀνθρωπολάτρας[?]). Now, when someone thinks and teaches such things about Christ, will you say that he stands with our adversaries, or against us?

units.la: Quo minus audiendus Noster, quando Polycarpum, Ignatii æqualem, jubet Christum hominem tantum credidisse. Quod nunquam ostendet. Non certe hinc, quod eum à Patre distinguit, vel Patrem Deum Domini nostri Jesu Christi dicit, vel Christum ejus ministrum, à Patre suscitatum, & exaltatum; vel quod denique non plura ex unâ ejus epistolâ, pro Christi Dei-
units.tr: Our author is the less to be heard when he orders us to believe that Polycarp, a contemporary of Ignatius, held that Christ was only a man. He will never show this. Certainly not from the fact that he distinguishes him from the Father, or calls the Father the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, or calls Christ his minister, raised and exalted by the Father; nor from the fact that many arguments for Christ's divin-

units.la: Deitate, & cum Patre æqualitate, produci argumenta possunt. Nam aliter ac Ignatius, vel contra ipsum, credidisse Polycarpum de Christo, nemo, opinor, dicet. Etiam Orthodoxi post Nicænam Synodum, Filium Dei Patris ministrum quidem appellarunt, qui tamen de Filii deitate optime senserunt. Apud Hilarium, de Synodis, adversus Arian. quoniam si quis Christum Deum filium Dei ante secula subsistentem & ministrantem patri ad omnium perfectionem non dicat, sed ex quo de Maria natus est, ex eo & Christum & filium nominatum esse & initium accepisse, ut sit Deus, anathema sit. & post: namque origo sua innascibilis substantia est. Non unum subsistentem, sed unam substantiam. Non differentem, non unum in dissimilibus naturis Dei nomen, sed unius nominis atque naturæ indissimilem essentiam. Non prastantem quenquam cuiquam genere substantiæ, sed subjectum alterum alteri nativitate naturæ. Patrem in eo majorem esse quod Pater est, filium in eo non minorem esse quod filius est. Significationem interesse, non interesse naturam. Denique quando Polycarpus in solemni oratione & doxologia, Patrem, cum Filio, & Spiritu S. adoravit, Christum hominem tantum fecisse, sive ἀνθρωπολάτρας fuisse, quos homuncionistas vocant Veteres, aut Scripturam hominem Christum juxta cum Deo adorari, coli & glorificari velle, probabitur nunquam.
units.tr: nity and equality with the Father cannot be drawn from his one epistle alone. For no one, I think, will say that Polycarp believed about Christ otherwise than Ignatius did, or contrary to him. Even the orthodox after the Nicene Synod called the Son of God the minister of the Father, yet they thought most rightly about the Son's deity. In Hilary, On the Synods, against the Arians: For if anyone does not say that Christ is God, the Son of God, subsisting before the ages and ministering to the Father for the perfection of all things, but says that from the time he was born of Mary, from that point he both was named Christ and Son and received a beginning, so that he is God, let him be anathema. And afterwards: For his origin is an unbegotten substance. Not one subsisting, but one substance. Not a different one, not one name of God in dissimilar natures, but an essence not dissimilar in name and nature. Not one excelling another in the kind of substance, but another subject from another by the nativity of nature. The Father is greater in that he is Father, the Son is not less in that he is Son. The signification differs, the nature does not differ. Finally, when Polycarp in his solemn prayer and doxology adored the Father together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, it will never be proved that he made Christ a mere man, or was a worshipper of man (ἀνθρωπολάτρας), whom the ancients called homuncionists, or that Scripture wishes the man Christ to be adored, worshipped and glorified together with God.

units.la: De Iustino, quasi primus vid. excogitaverit generationem seu productionem Verbi, ante mundum conditum, ex Platonica nim. philosophia, & insuper Orphei auctoritate motus; pag. 191. & 194. ad illa jam ante satis dictum: nihilque hic repetit Adversarius, quod non suo loco discussum fuit. Quare cum eo quid ni dicere hic nobis liceat, pag. 310. altum enim agere nolo, nec opus est. De Synodo Nicæna, quod intermisicet, postea dicemus. Sed ad quatuor rationes, quas fingit, quibus Justinum, & sequaces ejus permotos vult, ad novum sc. Christum facilius recipiendum, & in Ecclesiam introducendum, facitque pag. 189. has, prima ut fuerit, Platonica philosophia cognitio & amor. II. Gentilismi, pluriumque Deorum non prorsus obliterata memoria. III. Homines præstantes mox in numerum Deorum reponendi consuetudo. & IV. eum, qui homo tantum fit, colendi religio ac horror: dicimus, illas totidem esse in Christianum nomen ac fidem atroces contumelias. Quam vero futiles sint rationes, inde facili opera unusquisque deprehendet, si in formam tentarit redigere syllogisticam. e. g. Qui ex Schola Platonis venerunt olim ad fidem Christi, quive in scriptis lubenter Platonizarunt, ii generationem Filii a Patre ante mundum conditum, ex philosophia illa attulerunt, & non didicerunt ex Scripturis: vel, si aliqua apud Platonem sunt, quorum similia nonnulla sive in Scripturis occurrunt, sive Veterum theologiâ; sequitur quod hæc à Platonicis accepta, & falsa sunt? Vide ut ineptæ sint & non ferendæ istæ consequentiæ. Jam instet in exemplo Justini, & viderit quo medio termino probet, quod scribere ausus, pag. 190. quod philosophia Platonica Justinum, ad novum Christum, eo facilius recipiendum publiceque introducendum, permoverit. Falsum est, quod novum Christum introduxerit Justinus. Quod neque dixit Petavius; neque ullus, neque Autor noster probat. Falsum, quod Justinus Christum suum, ejusque generationem à Platone dedicit. Falsum denique, nos illa à Justino habere, nedum à Platonicis, & non ex Scripturâ. Sed Amelius, scriptor Platonicus, apud Eusebium, Præparat. lib. xi. cap. x. utitur verbis Johannis, ex Evangelio, cap. i. de verbo: & tacito nomine, Barbarum, quia Johannes Judæus erat, appellat. Ecquid tum? Traxit Platonicus illa in mentem suam: ergo bene intellexit? nego. ergo, philosophia Platonica Justinum ad novum Christum facilius recipiendum publiceque introducendum permovit? nam de eo hic quærebatur, uti sedulo monet, pag. 190. Quin potius sequeretur, quod ergo Johannes sua à Platone habeat, & quod ille de Verbo docet, ex Platonis philosophiâ desumtum sit, quam quod Justinus: prius enim & propius illa ad Johannem referuntur, quam ad Justinum. Proba, Justinum à Platonicis sua accepisse, & non à Johanne, quod ad Christum, ejusque, ante mundum, nativitatem. Proba, Justinum alienum Christum, à Johanne, prædicasse & introducere conatum. Atque eò hæc citavit Eusebius, non ut ex Platonicis illa de Verbo in Christianam theologiam venisse doceret, nequidquam: sed ut similitudinem aliquam innueret inter utraque, & Platonicos illa habere, sive mediate, sive immediate, ex Sacris Scripturis, ostenderet. Hinc primum in initio capitis exponit, quid de unigenito Dei Filio, sive Verbo, dicat Scriptura, tum similia istis profert ex Platone, & Platonicis. Unde, nonne tibi videtur, Plato Hebræorum scriptis infudasse? inquit. Atque prolatis ex Numenio Platonico nonnullis, ista illis Psalmistæ similia sunt, ait: & Numenius consentanea iis scripsit, quæ Christus alicubi tradit. Ita Platonici omnes, & ante Platonicos ipse Plato ab Hebræis ea nomina videntur habuisse, quibus excelluerunt. Nam & si non recte intellexerunt, verbis tamen suis manifesti sunt, cuncta ab Hebræis accepisse. Viderit hinc Noster, ut argumentum suum colligat, & convincat Adversarium, de Justino, ejusque novo introducto Deo, & Christo, quomodo contumeliose loquitur. Quid Augustinus? ante lectos Platonicorum libros, Christum hominem tantum, ut Photiniani, credidit, post lectos autem, & ex illis alium filium Dei, & novum Christum acceptavit? Sic quidem Noster: at ipse hoc de se non fatetur Augu-stinus: & quamvis fateretur, non probaret etiam Justinum, hujusque sequaces alios idem fecisse. Nihil enim testatur Augustinus, Confess. lib. vii. cap. xx. in Platonicorum libris de Christo, de Filio Dei se legisse, nedum ut inde fecisset alium, à Scripturæ mente, & novum Christum, vel illum promovisset; tantummodo se in istis quidem stricturas aliquas veritatis de Deo, ejusque essentiâ infinitâ observasse, sed inflatiorem vanâ scientiâ, in divinis demum Scripturis manuefactum, & edoctum de viâ veritatis, & salute per solum Chri-stum, quod ex Platonicis illis habere non poterat. Demum ergo ex Scri-ptura didicit, Christum non esse tantum excellentis sapientiæ virum, quod antea putarat, cap. xix. Ego autem aliquanto posterius, quam Ali-pius, didicisse me fateor, in eo quod verbum caro factum est, quomodo catholica veritas à Photini falsitate dirimatur. Non à Platone hoc didicit, sed à Johanne. Et cap. xxi. ubi quid in sacris libris invenerit, non inventum in Platonicis, exponit, quid faciet miser homo? inquit. Quis eum liberabit de corpore mortis hujus, nisi gratia tua per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, quem genuisti coæternum, & creasti in principio viarum tuarum, in quo princeps hujus mundi non invenit quicquam morte dignum, & occidit eum, & evacuatum est chirographum quod erat contrarium nobis? Hoc illa[?] litera non habent. Non habent illa[?] pagina vultum pietatis hujus. Vide, ut quoque creatum dicat, ex Prov. viii. 22. coæternum à Patre genitum Filium: & locum illum etiam usurparint Patres, nec tamen adversus Filii æternitatem, & æternam generationem, secus ac Arianis, & Nostro visum. Hac mihi in-viscerabantur miris modis, cum minimum Apostolorum tuorum legerem Paulum, inquit, non Platonem, quem cum sylvestri cacumine confert, unde utcunque videre patriam pacis, non tamen iter ad eam invenire, possis.
units.tr: Concerning Justin, that he was the first to have devised the generation or production of the Word before the world was made, drawn from Platonic philosophy and moved besides by the authority of Orpheus, see pp. 191 and 194, and what has already been said enough on that point. The Adversary repeats nothing here that was not discussed in its proper place. So why should I not say to him, as he says on p. 310, I do not want to be lofty, nor is there need? As for the Synod of Nicaea, which he passes over, we will speak of it later. But as to the four reasons he invents, by which he wants Justin and his followers to have been moved to receive the new Christ more easily and to introduce him into the Church (he sets them out on p. 189), they are these: first, knowledge and love of Platonic philosophy; second, the not wholly erased memory of Gentilism and of the many gods; third, the custom of placing outstanding men at once in the number of the gods; and fourth, the cult and dread of one who is only a man. We say these are four atrocious insults against the Christian name and faith. How feeble these reasons are, anyone can easily see if he tries to reduce them to syllogistic form. For example: those who once came from the school of Plato to the faith of Christ, or who gladly philosophised like Plato in their writings, brought the generation of the Son from the Father before the world was made from that philosophy and did not learn it from the Scriptures; or, if some things are found in Plato, of which some similar things occur either in the Scriptures or in the theology of the Ancients, it follows that these things were taken from the Platonists and are false? See how inept and intolerable these inferences are. Now let him press the matter with the example of Justin, and let him see by what middle term he proves what he has dared to write on p. 190: that Platonic philosophy moved Justin to receive the new Christ more easily and to introduce him publicly. It is false that Justin introduced a new Christ. Neither Petavius said this, nor anyone else, and our author does not prove it. It is false that Justin derived his Christ and his generation from Plato. And finally it is false that we have those things from Justin, let alone from the Platonists, and not from Scripture. But Amelius, a Platonic writer, in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 11, chapter 10, uses the words of John from the Gospel, chapter 1, about the Word, and, without naming him, calls him a barbarian, because John was a Jew. What follows? The Platonist took those things into his own mind; therefore he understood them well? I deny it. Therefore Platonic philosophy moved Justin to receive the new Christ more easily and to introduce him publicly? For this is what was being asked here, as he carefully warns on p. 190. Indeed it would rather follow that John has his teaching from Plato, and that what he teaches about the Word was taken from Platonic philosophy, than that Justin did; for those things are referred to John earlier and more closely than to Justin. Prove that Justin received his doctrines from the Platonists and not from John, as regards the birth of Christ before the world. Prove that Justin tried to preach and introduce a Christ alien to John. And Eusebius cited these passages for this purpose: not to teach that those things about the Word came into Christian theology from the Platonists (that would be pointless), but to point out some likeness between the two and to show that the Platonists had them, either mediately or immediately, from the Holy Scriptures. Hence at the beginning of the chapter he first sets out what Scripture says about the only-begotten Son of God, or the Word, and then brings forward similar things from Plato and the Platonists. Whence he says: Does it not seem to you that Plato had poured in the writings of the Hebrews? And after quoting some passages from the Platonist Numenius, he says: these are like those of the Psalmist, and Numenius wrote things consistent with those which Christ somewhere delivers. Thus all the Platonists, and Plato himself before them, seem to have had from the Hebrews those names by which they excelled. For although they did not understand them rightly, they are nevertheless plain from their own words to have received everything from the Hebrews. Let our author see how he will draw his argument from this and convince the Adversary about Justin, his newly introduced god, and Christ, and how he speaks reproachfully. What of Augustine? Did he, before reading the books of the Platonists, believe Christ to be only a man, like the Photinians, and after reading them, accept from them another Son of God and a new Christ? Our author says so; but Augustine does not confess this about himself, and even if he did confess it, he would not prove that Justin too, and his other followers, did the same. For Augustine, in Confessions book 7, chapter 20, testifies that he read nothing in the books of the Platonists about Christ or the Son of God, much less that from them he made another Christ, alien to the mind of Scripture, or promoted a new Christ. He says only that in those books he observed certain glimpses of truth about God and his infinite essence, but that, puffed up with vain learning, he was at last made tame in the divine Scriptures, and taught the way of truth and salvation through Christ alone, which he could not have from those Platonists. Therefore he learned from Scripture that Christ was not merely a man of excellent wisdom, as he had previously thought (chapter 19): But I confess that I learned, somewhat later than Alypius, in what sense the Word was made flesh, and how catholic truth is distinguished from the falsehood of Photinus. He did not learn this from Plato, but from John. And in chapter 21, where he explains what he found in the sacred books that was not found in the Platonists, he says: What will wretched man do? Who will deliver him from the body of this death, unless your grace through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom you begot coeternal and created in the beginning of your ways, in whom the prince of this world found nothing worthy of death, and he killed him, and the handwriting that was against us was blotted out? Those books do not have this. Those pages do not have the face of this piety. Note how he also calls the Son created, from Prov. 8:22, though begotten coeternal with the Father; and the Fathers also used that passage, yet not against the eternity of the Son and his eternal generation, as it seemed to the Arians and to our author. These things were wonderfully impressed upon me, he says, when I read the least of your Apostles, Paul, whom he compares with Plato, the wooded height, from which one may somehow see the land of peace, yet not find the way to it.

units.la: Jam quod ad secundam ejus rationem, quâ scilicet Justinum, ejusque sequaces motos scribit ad novum Christum facilius recipiendum, inque Ecclesiam introducendum, nimirum Gentilismi & plurium Deorum non prorsus obliteratam memoriam: execrabilis certe est impietatis, religionem nostram derivare ex Gentilismo, & cum abominandis Diis conferre Christum quem Christiani colunt, & hinc eos polytheismi accusari etiam à Christianis. Et hoc scilicet Justinus fecerit, fecerint & alii, polytheismi Gentilium accerrimi hostes & adversarii constantissimi? Nempe inde si illis sententia de Christo Deo, atque hinc Deorum multitudine, adhaesisset, tam absolute & acriter omnem πολυθεότητα[?] damnassent & evulsissent hominum animis, nulla adhibita distinctione, qua excepissent saltem & salvassent alium & novum suum Deum Christum? & nunquam in disputationibus suis aut indicassent illud, aut ex Gentili polytheismo sibi vendicassent, vel hoc ipsis etiam objecissent Gentiles? Nunquam vero ubi Christum Deum probant, ex Gentilium facto id probant Christiani, & non ex Scriptura. Vel saltem ergo quando Adversarii Christum Deum dicunt, ex Gentilismo hoc habebunt: eo magis, quo uti Gentiles, merum hominem Deum faciunt, & sic Deorum multitudinem revera introducunt; non vero nos, qui eundem illum & unum credimus cum Patre Deum. Quod ut nihil cum Gentilium superstitione commune habet, ita hinc non nisi summa cum blasphemia derivatur. Quare Ambrosius, lib. 1. de fide, cap. 1. Assertio autem nostra fidei haec est, ut unum Deum esse dicamus. Neque ut Gentes Filium separamus. Neque ut Photinus, initium Filii ex virgine disputemus. Neque ut Arius plures credendo & dissimiles potestates, plures Deos gentili errore faciamus, quia scriptum est, audi Israel! Dominus Deus tuus, Deus unus est. Quid vero ad haec facit, quod vel Cornelius, Act. x. 25.26. Petrum adorare voluit? vel Simon Magus a Samaritanis pro Deo habitus fuit? vel Pontificii, rejectâ quamvis Deorum gentilium multitudine, plures tamen Divos, quos colant, faciunt? neque enim ignoramus, rejectione Deorum gentilium non protinus indicari, homines ab ἀποθεώσεως[?] seu praestantium virorum deificatione liberos prorsus esse ac immunes: sed parem esse in Ecclesia Christiana Christi, pro Deo agniti & adorati, rationem, hoc pernegamus.
units.tr: Now as to his second reason, by which he writes that Justin and his followers were moved to receive the new Christ more easily and introduce him into the Church, namely the not wholly erased memory of Gentilism and of many gods: it is surely an execrable impiety to derive our religion from Gentilism, and to compare with abominable gods the Christ whom Christians worship, and thence to have them accused of polytheism even by Christians. Did Justin do this, and did others too, the most bitter enemies and most constant opponents of the polytheism of the Gentiles? Indeed, if their opinion about Christ as God had clung to them from this, and from it the multitude of gods, would they have condemned all polytheism [πολυθεότης] so absolutely and sharply and torn it out of men's minds, with no distinction made, by which they would at least have excepted and saved their new god Christ? And would they never have indicated this in their disputations, or claimed it from Gentile polytheism, or would the Gentiles not have thrown this very thing back at them? But indeed, where Christians prove Christ to be God, they do not prove it from the practice of the Gentiles but from Scripture. Or at least, when the Adversaries say that Christ is God, they will have this from Gentilism, all the more so since, like the Gentiles, they make a mere man God, and so in fact introduce a multitude of gods; but we, who believe that the same one God with the Father is one, do not. This, since it has nothing in common with Gentile superstition, is derived from it only with the greatest blasphemy. Therefore Ambrose, On the Faith, book 1, chapter 1: Now our assertion of the faith is this, that we say there is one God. Nor, like the Gentiles, do we separate the Son. Nor, like Photinus, do we dispute about the beginning of the Son from the virgin. Nor, like Arius, by believing in several and unlike powers, do we make several gods with Gentile error, because it is written: Hear, O Israel! The Lord your God is one God. But what bearing on these points has the fact that Cornelius wished to adore Peter (Acts 10:25–26), or that Simon Magus was held to be God by the Samaritans, or that the Papists, though they have rejected the multitude of Gentile gods, still make several divi whom they worship? For we do not ignore that the rejection of Gentile gods does not at once show that men are wholly free and exempt from the deification [ἀποθεώσεως] of outstanding men; but we deny that in the Christian Church there is a like reasoning about Christ, who is acknowledged and adored as God.

units.la: Idem dictum sit ad tertiam rationem, quae cum priori coincidit, consuetudinem scilicet homines praestantes mox in Deorum numerum reponendi: ad quod allegat factum Lystrensium & Melitensium, qui Apostolum Paulum faciebant Deum e coelis descendentem, Act. xiv. 9. 10. & xxviii. 6. Adriani, & Alexandri Impp. Christum inter Deos recipientium; & Abgari Edesseni, Christum ob editas virtutes mox Deum e coelis delapsum cogitantis, apud Eusebium, lib. 1. cap. xiii. & Cornelii, quod exemplum modo etiam attulit, ut videat rationem hanc a secunda non differre, qui Petrum adorare voluit: quae omnia neutiquam probant hoc quod probandum est. Exponat enim, quinam, pari modo, & ubi, & quomodo Christum deificarint unquam Christiani: vel id Justinum fecisse, aliosque. Quid, quaso, mirum, inquit, Christianos ex Gentibus, Deificationi talis praestantium Virorum jam inde a pueritia assuetos, Christoque cultum divinum post Deum Patrem, competere videntes, ac de divinitate ejus per nonnulla obscura Scriptura loca quoddammodo persuasos, eidem Christo divinam naturam tribuisse, eumque Deum ipsum e caelis venientem, & in uterum Maria delapsum, credidisse? Probanda autem haec fuerant, non leviter promenda; astruenda, non asserenda. i. Christianos ex Gentibus, deificationi hominum assuetos fuisse. ii. Si per Scriptura loca persuasi fuerunt Christiani, de Christi divinitate, & Christo cultum divinum competere; non ergo ex errore Gentilium id traxerunt. iii. dum Christo divinam naturam ex Scripturae locis illis putarunt tribuendam, non ergo Christum deificarunt ad illum modum, quo Gentiles alios nonnunquam deificandos consuerunt. iv. neque ex multitudine Deorum huc prolapsi fuerunt, quum Christo tribuerent naturam divinam, & Deum ipsum crederent ex caelis venisse, atque incarnatum. v. Atque ad hoc quidem Christi opera fecerunt, ut illis tamquam σημείοις crederent homines inesse ipsi naturam supra humanam & creatam, quare Lactantius dixit, ut etiam Deus ex operibus adseratur: & Novatianus nefas habet, Christum hominem tantummodo dicere: non vero ut propterea Deum facerent, qui Deus non erat. vi. Nedum ut ostendi possit, hoc mox ab illis factum a Christi apparitione & miraculis. Denique ex factis nonnullorum temerariis, tumultuariis, & praecipitantibus ad impartiendam hominibus sive piis, sive impiis, Apostolis aut magis, & a Gentilium opinione erga Christum gentili, fluxisse apud Christianos exemplum, & doctrinam Christum habendi pro Deo, nec probat Noster, nec si probaret, nos magis constringeret, quam ipsum, Christum quoque pro Deo, & adorando, habentem, quamvis alia ex causa quam nos, sed cujus diversitatem non premunt illae ipsius ratiunculae; ac propterea non nos magis, imo nos non adeo feriunt, quam ipsum.
units.tr: The same may be said of the third reason, which coincides with the earlier one: the custom of quickly placing outstanding men among the gods. To support this he cites the case of the Lystrans and the Maltese, who took the Apostle Paul for a god come down from heaven (Acts 14:9, 10; 28:6); the emperors Hadrian and Alexander, who received Christ among the gods; Abgarus of Edessa, who thought Christ, because of the miracles he performed, had quickly come down from heaven as God (Eusebius, bk. 1, ch. 13); and Cornelius, whom he has just mentioned as wishing to worship Peter, so that he may see this reason does not differ from the second. None of these things proves what needs to be proved. Let him explain who, in the same way, and where, and how, Christians ever deified Christ, or whether Justin and others did so. "What is so surprising, I ask," he says, "that Christians from the Gentiles, accustomed from childhood to the deification of such outstanding men, and seeing that divine worship is owed to Christ after God the Father, and being in some measure persuaded of his divinity by certain obscure passages of Scripture, should have attributed a divine nature to him and believed that he, God himself, came from heaven and descended into the womb of Mary?" But these claims ought to have been proved, not lightly advanced; established, not merely asserted. (i) That Christians from the Gentiles were accustomed to the deification of men. (ii) If Christians were persuaded by passages of Scripture of Christ's divinity and that divine worship is due to Christ, then they did not derive this from the error of the Gentiles. (iii) While they thought a divine nature was to be attributed to Christ from those passages of Scripture, they did not therefore deify Christ in that manner in which the Gentiles were accustomed sometimes to deify others. (iv) Nor did they fall into this from a multitude of gods, since they attributed a divine nature to Christ and believed that God himself had come from heaven and been made flesh. (v) And to this end Christ performed works, so that men might believe, as in signs, that a nature above human and created dwelt in him; wherefore Lactantius said, that God may also be shown from his works; and Novatian holds it wrong to say that Christ is merely a man; yet they did not make him God in order to do so, though he was not God. (vi) Nor can it be shown that this was done by them immediately after Christ's appearance and miracles. Finally, from the rash, tumultuous and headlong deeds of some, in bestowing divine honour on men, whether pious or impious, rather than on the Apostles, and from the pagan opinion of the Gentiles concerning Christ, there arose among Christians the example and doctrine of holding Christ to be God. Our author does not prove this, nor, even if he did prove it, would it press us more than it presses himself, who also holds Christ to be God and to be worshipped, though for a different reason from ours. Those little arguments of his do not remove that difference; and therefore they strike us no more, indeed not so much, as they strike him.

units.la: Postremo ultima, quam adfert ratio, qua Justinum & sequaces permotos scribit ad novum Christum faciendum, & recipiendum, erat religio & horror colendi eum, qui tantum fit homo. Haec priores refutat ratio: si enim id animo sedit Justino, & Veteribus Christianis, non colere pro Deo, qui tantum sit homo; ergo non voluerunt Christum tantum hominem deificare, ex veteri superstitione. Simul enim non constiterunt, non audere hominem pro Deo colere, & velle eum, propterea ut hoc facias, deificare: neque enim per deificationem aliquid poterant Christo tribuere, solum hoc agnoscere quod in ipso erat. Si autem illud religio vetet,& prohibeat Christianum facere;etiam & iflud. Vel an Chri-stiana religio magis permittit, ut hominem Deum facias, quam ut colas? Hoc tantum quaerebatur, inquit, annon religio & horror hominem colendi, Justinum & alios permoverit ad novum Christum eo facilius recipiendum? & hoc vult vel affirmari, vel negari. Affirmo illud, ut propterea nec Chri-stum tantum ut hominem consideraverint, vel adorarint; sed ut verum, & unum Deum: neque novum Christum aut fecerit Justinus, aut aliis reci-piendum praescripserit. Imo ex hac ratione concludo, Veteres, religio-ne prohibitos fuisse Christum statuere merum esse hominem. Colligit tandem, Veteres, non tam propter loca aliqua Scriptura, quam quod hominem Christum colere horruerint, divinitatem Christo tribuisse, eumque inter Divos retulisse. Male colligit: nec ullo modo probat. Et quomodo religio Ve-teres ab ἀνθρωπολατρεία[?] abstterruit, quam per Scripturam? Vel si pagana religio illud docuit, an minus Scripturaria[?], vel ex eâ magis vitam suam instituerunt Christiani, quam istâ? Quis Veterum dixit, scripsit, se Christo divinitatem tribuere, quia hominem eum colere reformidavit? & non se Christum agnoscere Deum, propter testimonia Scripturae? Vel quis, & quo ritu, Christum inter Divos retulit? nedum ut hoc tali, quâ vos dicitis, causâ fecerit Ecclesia Christiana & catholica. Sed vos scilicet Christum hominem inter Divos refertis. At de hisce satis.
