units.tr: Lastly, the final reason he brings forward, by which he writes that Justin and his followers were moved to make and receive a new Christ, was religion and the horror of worshipping one who is only a man. This reason refutes the former ones: for if this was in Justin's mind and in that of the early Christians, not to worship as God one who is only a man, then they did not wish to deify Christ, a mere man, out of ancient superstition. For they did not at the same time hold that it was not lawful to worship a man as God and yet wish him to be deified for the purpose of doing so; for by deification they could attribute nothing to Christ, but only acknowledge what was in him. But if religion forbids this, it forbids that too. Or does the Christian religion more permit you to make a man God than to worship him? The only question, he says, was whether religion and horror of worshipping a man moved Justin and others to receive the new Christ more readily? And he wants this either affirmed or denied. I affirm it, so that they did not therefore regard or worship Christ merely as a man, but as the true and only God; nor did Justin make a new Christ, nor did he prescribe that he be received by others. Indeed, from this reasoning I conclude that the ancients were forbidden by religion to hold that Christ is a mere man. He finally concludes: The ancients attributed divinity to Christ and counted him among the gods, not so much because of certain passages of Scripture as because they shrank from worshipping Christ as a man. He concludes badly, and by no means proves it. And how could religion have deterred the ancients from anthropolatry [ἀνθρωπολατρεία] more than Scripture did? Or if pagan religion taught that, were Christians less shaped by Scripture, or did they order their lives more by pagan religion than by Scripture? Which of the ancients ever said or wrote that he attributed divinity to Christ because he shrank from worshipping him as a man, and did not acknowledge Christ as God on account of the testimonies of Scripture? Or who, and by what rite, counted Christ among the gods? Still less did the Christian and catholic Church do so for the reason you allege. But of course you count Christ, a mere man, among the gods. Enough of these matters.

units.la: Athenagoras non simpliciter docet, Filium à Patre creatum, sed de Christo verba faciens adducit tritum ex Prov. viii. 20. locum, ex vulgatâ Graecorum lectione, Dominus ἔκτισέ[?] με, pro ἔκτισε[?], de quo alibi diximus, & Petavius lib. ii. de Trinit. cap. i. qualia Noster in Petavio prorsus dissimulat. Atque in verbo ἔκτισε[?] non istam vim Veteres constituerunt, quam postea Ariani, sed pro eodem fere habebant saepe, sic dicerent, vel aliter, creatum an genitum, vel factum: Filio nihil hac ratione derogari sciebant: credentes scilicet, parum interesse, sive eum ... genitum dicas, sive creatum, agnoscit quoque Noster, pag. 342. & confirmat ex Tertulliano, ubi is, prior abysso genita sum. — Ut credas, abyssum quoque geni-tam, id est, factam, quia & filios facimus, licet generemus. An verò cum generatione Filius initium habuerit, jam non quaeritur, dum solummodò de usu vocis agitur. & Psalm. cii. 19. populus dicitur creandus, id est, generandus.
units.tr: Athenagoras does not simply teach that the Son was created by the Father; but in speaking of Christ he adduces the well-worn passage from Proverbs 8:22, from the common Greek reading, the Lord created [ἔκτισέ με] me, in place of created [ἔκτισε], about which we have spoken elsewhere, and Petavius, bk. 2 of On the Trinity, ch. 1, which our author entirely passes over in Petavius. Moreover, the ancients did not assign to the word created [ἔκτισε] the sense that the Arians later did; they often used it almost as the same thing, whether they said created or begotten or made. They knew that nothing was taken from the Son by this usage, believing, of course, that it made little difference whether you call him begotten or created. Our author also acknowledges this, p. 342, and confirms it from Tertullian, where he says: I was begotten before the abyss. — That you may believe the abyss too was begotten, that is, made, since we also make sons, though we beget them. Whether the Son had a beginning with his generation is not now in question, since we are concerned only with the use of the word. And at Psalm 102:19 the people is said to be created, that is, to be begotten.

units.la: Jam etiam perperam in aeternitate, vel duratione Dei aeternâ Adverfarius constituit partes, seu prius & posterius: quod non probatur ex voce ante Deo tributâ, quando de illis sermo est, quæ de eo dicenda ante creationem, quia hoc in ordine ad creaturas dicitur, non quod in ipso Deo sit ante vel post, prius & posterius, uti ostendimus Socinianismi Confut. Tom. I. lib. II. cap. I. Quare qui Christum seu Filium Dei genitum fuisse dicunt ante creationem, & ante concreatum tempus, in perpetuâ & æternâ illâ duratione, non etiam possunt non agnoscere æternum Filium, ex generatione, nullâ vel temporis, vel prioris & posterioris notâ interstinguendâ. Hilarius, lib. II. de Trinit. jam sine principio est apud Deum, quod erat ante principium. Dixerat: quid est illud, in principio erat? transeuntur tempora, transcenduntur sæcula, tolluntur ætates, pone aliquid quod voles tua principium opinione, non tenes tempore. & lib. III. hic ergo ingenitus ante omne tempus ex se filium genuit, non ex aliqua subjacente materia, quia per filium omnia, non ex nihilo, quia ex se filium, non ut partum, quia nihil in Deo demutabile aut vacuum est, non partem sui vel divisam, vel discissam, vel extensam, quia & impassibilis & incorporeus Deus est, hæc autem passionis & carnis sunt, & secundum Apostolum in Christo inhabitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter. Sed incomprehensibiliter, inenarrabiliter ante omne tempus & sæcula unigenitum ex his quæ ingenita in se erant, procreavit: omne quod Deus est per charitatem atque virtutem nativitati ejus impartiens, ac sic ab ingenito, perfecto æternoque patre unigenitus & perfectus & æternus est filius. Autor Breviarii Fidei, contra Arianos: sed adhuc forte dicis, sicut habet carnalis intellectus, inter gignentem patrem & genitum filium non potuisse fieri nisi ut aliquod fuisset spatium. Spatium hora faciunt, hora tempus designant: ac sic, si tempus anteponis filio, non omnia per ipsum facta fateris. Et ubi est illud, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt? Sic & Ambrosius, neque ex tempore Deus poterat esse, qui fecit tempora. Quorum testimonia non ideo adfero, ut iis admodum constringam Adversarium, quem illis non moveri scio, sed ut ex illis etiam Veterum ante eos explanetur, de eadem re, sententia.
units.tr: Now too the adversary wrongly assigns parts, that is a before and an after, within the eternity or eternal duration of God. This is not proved from the word before [ante] applied to God when we speak of those things which are to be said of him before creation, since this is said with respect to creatures, and not because there is before or after, prior or posterior, in God himself, as we have shown in Socinianismi Confut., Tom. I, bk. II, ch. I. Therefore those who say that Christ or the Son of God was begotten before creation, and before time was created, in that perpetual and eternal duration, cannot fail to acknowledge an eternal Son by generation, without any mark of time, or of prior and posterior, to be distinguished. Hilary, bk. II On the Trinity: That which was before the beginning is already without beginning with God. He had said: What is that "in the beginning was"? Times are passed over, ages are passed beyond, eras are removed; name whatever you like as a beginning in your opinion, you do not hold it in time. And bk. III: This unbegotten one, therefore, before all time, begot a Son out of himself, not from any underlying matter, because all things are through the Son, not out of nothing, because he is from himself, not as a birth, because nothing in God is changeable or empty, not a part of himself, either divided, cut off or extended, because God is both impassible and incorporeal; these things belong to passion and flesh, while according to the Apostle in Christ dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. But incomprehensibly and ineffably, before all time and ages, he produced the only-begotten from those things which were unbegotten in himself, imparting to his birth all that God is through love and power; and thus the only-begotten and perfect and eternal Son is from the unbegotten, perfect and eternal Father. The author of the Breviary of Faith, against the Arians: But perhaps you still say, as carnal understanding has it, that between the begetting Father and the begotten Son there could not be anything but some interval of space. Spaces make hours, hours designate times; and so, if you place time before the Son, you do not confess that all things were made through him. And where is that: All things were made through him? So too Ambrose: God could not be from time, who made the times. I do not adduce these testimonies so as to press the adversary greatly with them, for I know he is not moved by them; but so that the opinion of the ancients before them on the same matter may be explained by them.

units.la: Sed quacunque ratione probare Noster satagit, Veteres, quando Sermonem Dei in Deo extitisse ab æterno dixerunt, & Patrem absque eo non fuisse, sed semper in eo fuisse Mentem, Rationem, Sapientiam seu Sophiam, eique consiliarium, uti Theophylus loquitur; non tamen attribuisse Verbo subsistentiam, sed intellexisse non aliter in Deo fuisse, quam cogitationem & conceptum aliquem mentis in homine, unde dein Filius genitus fuerit ac processerit. Quare Filium Patri non statuisse coæternum. Ad hoc semel respondendum, quia aliquoties, & ad variorum Patrum explicandam sententiam, Athenagoræ, Theophili, & aliorum eadem semper facit recurrere. Quare primo di-cimus, haud ignorare nos, Patres, ubi ad modum generationis Filii exponendum accedunt, sæpe errasse, sive ex intemperantiâ ingenii, non acquiescentis in re ὅτι ἐστὶ[?], nisi & διότι[?] & τὸ πῶς[?] penetrarent; vel ex securitate errandi eo majore, quo nondum exorti erant illi, qui post-modum varias hæreses & errores super hoc in Ecclesiam introduxerunt, & proinde exactius cautiusque ad rem loqui jusserunt: præsertim sibi aliquanto liberalius indulserunt in rationem cur Filius Verbum appella-retur, & quid esset ejus generari à Patre: quæ nullus scripta ipsorum attente perlegens non observet. In quæ non æque facile prolabitur, qui carni & ingenio novit fibulam imponere, nec laxat fræ].num temeraria curiositati, satis habens credere quod sit, licet intelligere vel explicare non possit, quomodo sit, magis fidei argumentum existimans esse hoc, de quo agimus, quam rationis. Ambrosius, de fide, ad Gratianum, lib. 1. cap. v. tu quoque manum ori admove, scrutari non licet superna mysteria, li-cet scire quod natus sit, non licet discutere, quemadmodum natus sit. Illud negare mihi non licet, hoc quærere metus est. & post, noli Ariane, ex nostris æstimare divina, sed divina crede, ubi humana non invenies. Et scite Leporius presbyter, in libello Emendationis, nostrum namque est credere, illius nosse. Attamen vel in Arii, qualis postmodum fuit, nedum Photini sententiâ prorsus fuisse Veteres illos, quod ad ipsam rem, non probabitur. Quam-vis ita incogitanter nonnunquam loquutos videamus, ut hinc non alii æque, ac Ariani ansam postmodum arripuerint, illorum verba usurpandi, & contra Ecclesiam, & contra ipsos; qui antequam in Alexandria quasi dæ-monium meridianum Arius nasceretur, innocenter quædam, & minus caute locuti sunt, uti in secundâ adversus Ruffinum Apologiâ scripsit Hieronymus. Nam quidquid fuerit de ipsorum verbis, mentem, quod ad rei summam, fuisse rectiorem, & credidisse in tres divinas personas, Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, verum, & unum, & ejusdem essentiæ Deum, & non in tempore demum Filium factum, vel in Christum hominem tantùm, certum est. Quod illis omnibus probatur testimoniis, quæ nos, quæ alii, ex illis, pro sententiâ nostrâ, & ipsorum fide, adferimus. Interim dum incuriosius conantur dicere quomodo, aut quando Filius sit genitus, non leviter sæpe impegerunt: quod illa ostendunt, quæ Adversarii, ex ipsis producunt. Jam quando illa utraque conjunguntur, uti nolumus omnino negare, intercurrere conceptus notiones sæpe non fatis rectas, ita religio quoque est propterea expun-gere & negare velle omnia quæ melius dicta, & testari possunt catholi-cam ipsorum fidem, quod ad rei summam & fundamentum, sanctam atque rectam.
units.tr: But by whatever reasoning our author labours to prove his point, the ancients, when they said that the Word of God had existed in God from eternity, and that the Father was never without it but always had in himself Mind, Reason, Wisdom or Sophia, his counsellor, as Theophilus puts it, did not thereby attribute subsistence to the Word. They understood only that in God there was nothing other than a thought and some concept of the mind, as in a man, from which the Son was then begotten and proceeded. Hence they did not hold the Son to be co-eternal with the Father. This must be answered once for all, since the point keeps recurring, both in explaining the views of various Fathers and in the case of Athenagoras, Theophilus and others. First, I say that we are not unaware that the Fathers often erred when they came to explain the manner of the Son's generation. Sometimes this was from the impatience of their intellect, which would not rest content with the fact (that it is, [ὅτι ἐστὶ]) unless it also penetrated the reason why (why, [διότι]) and the how (the manner, [τὸ πῶς]). Sometimes it was from a security in erring that was all the greater because those who later introduced various heresies and errors on this matter had not yet arisen, and so they had not been required to speak of it more exactly and cautiously. They especially indulged themselves rather freely in explaining why the Son is called Word and what it means for him to be begotten of the Father. No one who reads their writings attentively fails to notice this. Into such errors does not so easily slip the man who knows how to put a bridle on his flesh and his intellect, and does not give rash curiosity its head. He is content to believe that a thing is, even if he cannot understand or explain how it is, and he thinks the matter we are discussing is more a matter of faith than of reason. Ambrose, On Faith, to Gratian, book 1, ch. 5: you too, put your hand to your mouth; it is not permitted to scrutinise the heavenly mysteries. It is permitted to know that he was born; it is not permitted to examine how he was born. It is not permitted me to deny the former; to inquire into the latter is dangerous. And afterwards: do not, Arian, judge divine things by our standards, but believe divine things where you will not find human things. And Leporius the presbyter, shrewdly, in his little book of Amendment: "For it is ours to believe, his to know." Yet it will not be proved that those ancients held, even in the matter itself, the opinion of Arius as he later became, much less that of Photinus. Although we sometimes see them speaking so carelessly that others, and the Arians above all, afterwards seized on their words and used them both against the Church and against the Fathers themselves. These were men who, "before Arius was born in Alexandria like a noonday demon, spoke innocently and somewhat less cautiously," as Jerome wrote in his second Apology against Rufinus. For whatever may be said of their words, it is certain that their mind, as regards the sum of the matter, was more upright. They believed in three divine persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one true God of the same essence, and they did not hold that the Son was made only in time, or that Christ was only a man. This is proved by all the testimonies which we and others bring from them in support of our view and of their faith. Meanwhile, when they less carefully try to say how or when the Son was begotten, they have often stumbled, and not lightly. This is shown by the passages which the opponents produce from them. Now, when these two things are joined, we are by no means willing to deny that somewhat inaccurate notions sometimes intrude. Yet it is equally wrong to wish to erase and deny all the things they said better, which can attest their catholic faith as holy and right in the sum and foundation of the matter.

units.la: Juftinus ipse, cum quo, & ex quo reliquos componunt, de Filio à Patre genito, & vocato non Verbo tantum, sed Deo, etenim Deum appellat sermo Propheticus, inquit, docet eum non tantum esse virtutem & δύναμιν aliquam Patris, sed quoque subsistens ab eo distinctum numero, & eandem habere essentiam, non aliam, uti ignis ab igne accensus, quod Nicæni dixerunt, Deus de Deo, lumen de lumine, Deus verus de Deo vero. Hilarius, de Trinitate, lib. vi. sed quia vera fidei professio est, ita Deum ex Deo natum ut lumen ex lumine, quod fine detrimento suo naturam suam præstat ex sese, ut det quod habet, & quod dederit habeat, nascaturque quod fit, cum non aliud quam quod est natum fit, & nativitas acceperit quod erat, nec ademerit quod accepit, fitque uterque unum, dum ex eo quod est nascitur, & quod nascitur, neque aliunde, neque aliud est. Est enim lumen ex lumine. Sic Juftiuus, in Dialogo, cum Tryphone, pag. 281. Et quod virtus ista quæ Deum propheticus sermo vocat, prout pluribus similiter est probatum, & An-gelum, non ita ut Solis lumen nomine tantum numeratur ὀνόματι μόνον ἀριθ-μῷ, ἀλλὰ ἡ ἀριθμῷ ἕτερόν τι ἐστι verum numero quoque aliud quiddam est, supra pluribus explicui. Virtutem hanc dicens à Patre genitam, virtute & consilio ejus, sed non per recifionem ἀποτομὴν, tamquam Patris effentia dispertita ὡς ἀπομερι-ζομένης τῆς ἐν πατρὸς οὐσίας, prout alia omnia divisa & secta non eadem sunt quæ antequam scinderentur. Atque exempli gratia ea sumsi quæ ab igne accensa, ignem alium cernimus, illo nihil diminuto, sed manente eodem.
units.tr: Justin himself, with whom and from whom the others agree, teaches that the Son was begotten of the Father and is called not only Word but God: for the prophetic word calls him God. He is not merely some power or virtue of the Father, but a subsistent being distinct from him in number, and having the same essence, not another, like fire kindled from fire. This is what the Nicenes expressed: God of God, light of light, true God of true God. Hilary, On the Trinity, book 6: But since it is the true profession of faith that God is born of God as light is born of light, which without loss of its own nature gives forth from itself, so as to give what it has and to have what it has given, and what is born comes into being, since nothing else comes into being than what is born, and the birth has received what it was and has not taken away what it received, and each becomes one, while what is born is born from what is, and is neither from elsewhere nor other. For light is from light. Thus Justin, in the Dialogue with Trypho, p. 281: And that this power which the prophetic word calls God, as has been shown at length in a similar way, and also the Angel, is not counted merely in name, as the light of the sun is [by name alone, ὀνόματι μόνον ἀριθμῷ], but is something other in number [ἀλλὰ ἡ ἀριθμῷ ἕτερόν τι ἐστι]; truly also something other in number, as I explained at more length. In saying that this power was begotten of the Father by his power and counsel, Justin did not mean by cutting off [ἀποτομήν], as if the essence of the Father were divided and parted (ὡς ἀπομεριζομένης τῆς ἐν πατρὸς οὐσίας), since other things that are divided and cut do not remain the same as they were before they were split. And for example I have taken those things which, when kindled from fire, we see as another fire, nothing being diminished from the first, but the first remaining the same.

units.la: Cæterum quod in proferendo ex Athenagorá loco, falsi crimen, pro foli-tá immodestiá & πνεῦμα, pag. 344. & in Indice iterum, nobis impingit Autor, in eo officii oblitus & veritatis omnino fuit: nam, ut ipse non Græca, sed Latina tantum allegarat ex Athenagorâ, sic Latinum duntaxat exemplar, quale extat in Bibliothecâ Patrum primæ editionis, fequuti istam simpliciter versionem fuimus, ac proinde crimen falsi commisisse dici non possumus. Latinum Interpretem fallendi animo sic transtulisse, ut probat? etenim nil præter mentem Autoris expressit, alibi etiam significatam. Quid ergo? dicit Athenagoras, apud Latinum interpretem, quippe ut Deum afferimus, & Filium ipsius verbum, & Spiritum Sanctum: tria quidem secundum potentiam, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum: aliu vero & essentia unum. Filius enim Patris mens, verbum, & sapientia est: & (ab eodem) Spiritus, ut lumen ab igne, profluit. Hic admodum carpit positum, tria, ubi apud Athenagoram legitur, unita ἑνὰμα[?]; & inter Filium, ac Spiritum, interserta verba ista, aliu vero & essentia unum. At vero unita[?] illa, annon sunt tria? vel annon tres commemoravit, Patrem, & Filium,&Spiritum? hactenus ergo contra mentem Autoris nil fecit interpres Latinus,qui fuit Conradus Gesnerus. Sed post nominatum Spiritum Sanctum, addidit haec, aliu vero & essentia unum: fateor, me illa in textu Graeco non legere: sed primo annon in suo codice legerit Interpres, non possum dicere: hoc passum, quod vel illa, vel alia verba addi debeant propter praemissam conjunctionem μὲν, cui aliàs nihil est quod respondet, ἑνὰμα μὲν τῇ δυνάμει, τὸν πατέρα, τὸν υἱὸν, τὸ πνεῦμα· ὅτι νοῦς &c. unita quidem secundum potentiam, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum, mens enim &c. apparet quod sit hiulca oratio, nisi quid inter illa, ante mens enim vel legatur vel subintelligatur, quod illis μὲν quidem, per ἡ vero congruat. Hoc autem, tres istos aliu & essentia unum esse, an in nullo exemplari legatur non dixero, viderint quibus codicum copia est: non alienum vero esse à mente Athenagorae cum ex hoc loco, tum ex aliis redditur manifestum. Nam, uti tres nominavit, sic & Deum asseruit, neque alium, quam unum, & Filium dicens Patris esse mentem, verbum, sapientiam, & ἀπόρροιαν, Spiritum quoque uti lumen ab igne procedens, satis indicavit ejusdem essentiae & actus essentialis tres illos esse. Accedit, quod ante etiam aliquoties idem dixit, agnoscentes & tenentes Deum hunc, cujus verbo fabricata, & spiritu continentur omnia. atque probat, unum esse Deum, universi opificem. Sequitur, Filius Dei est verbum Patris in idea & efficacia. ab ipso enim & per ipsum facta sunt omnia, ἑνὸς οὖ[?] quum Pater & Filius unum sint, ita ut Filius sit in Patre, & Pater in Filio, per unionem & potentiam ἑνότητι ἡ δυνάμει Spiritus, mens & verbum Patris, Dei Filius. Postea, quem Deum cum verbo suo agnoscere optamus, τῆς ἡ ἐκ παιδὸς πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἑνότης qua Filii ad Patrem sit unio, qua Patris cum Filio communio κοινωνία, quid Spiritus, τῆς ἡ τῶν πατέρων ἑνώσεως, καὶ διαιρέσεως ἐνεμφῶν, ἐκ πνεύματος, ἐκ παιδός, ἐκ πατρός. qua trium unitas & unitorum discretio, Spiritus, Filii, Patris. Sunt tria, vel tres uniti, ex communicatione nimirum Patris. Quid ergo tantum falsi crimen commisit Interpres, quod scripsit in loco nostro, & intelligi voluit ex Autoris mente tria unita, actu vero & essentiâ unum ?
units.tr: As for the charge of falsehood which the author brings against us, for quoting Athenagoras, on account of his usual immodesty, [πνεῦμα], p. 344, and again in the Index, he has forgotten both his duty and the truth. For just as he himself cited Athenagoras only in Latin and not in Greek, so we followed only the Latin version, as it stands in the first edition of the Bibliotheca Patrum, and therefore we cannot be said to have committed a falsehood. How does he prove that the Latin translator meant to deceive? For he expressed nothing except the author's meaning, which is also indicated elsewhere. What then? Athenagoras says, as rendered by the Latin translator: For as we affirm God, and his Son the Word, and the Holy Spirit: three indeed according to power, the Father, the Son and the Spirit; but one in essence. For the Son is the mind, word and wisdom of the Father, and the Spirit flows from the same, as light from fire. Here the author sharply criticises the word three, where in Athenagoras the Greek reads united unita [ἑνὰμα], and the words but one in essence inserted between the Son and the Spirit. But are those united things not three? Or did he not mention three, the Father, the Son and the Spirit? So far, then, the Latin translator, who was Conrad Gesner, did nothing against the author's meaning. But after naming the Holy Spirit he added: but one in essence. I confess I do not find those words in the Greek text. But whether the translator read them in his own copy, I cannot say. This passage shows that either those words or others must be added, because of the preceding conjunction μέν, to which nothing otherwise corresponds: [ἑνὰμα μὲν τῇ δυνάμει, τὸν πατέρα, τὸν υἱὸν, τὸ πνεῦμα· ὅτι νοῦς &c.] united indeed according to power, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit; for mind &c. It is clear that the sentence is broken unless something is read or understood before mind enim, to match the quidem with the ἡ, the vero. Whether these three are one in essence and act is read in no copy, I will not say; let those who have an abundance of manuscripts see to it. It is not foreign to Athenagoras's meaning, as is shown both from this passage and from others. For as he named three, so he also asserted God, not another but one. Calling the Son the Father's mind, word, wisdom and emanation, and the Spirit flowing like light from fire, he sufficiently indicated that these three are of the same essence and of one essential act. Add that earlier he also said several times: acknowledging and holding this God, by whose word all things are made and by whose spirit they are held, and he proves that God is one, maker of the universe. There follows: the Son of God is the Word of the Father in idea and in operation; for all things were made by him and through him, [ἑνὸς οὖ] since the Father and the Son are one, so that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, by union and power [ἑνότητι ἡ δυνάμει]; the Spirit, the mind and word of the Father, God's Son. Afterwards: which God we desire to acknowledge with his Word [τῆς ἡ ἐκ παιδὸς πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἑνότης], by which there is union of the Son with the Father, by which there is communion of the Father with the Son [κοινωνία], and what of the Spirit [τῆς ἡ τῶν πατέρων ἑνώσεως, καὶ διαιρέσεως ἐνεμφῶν, ἐκ πνεύματος, ἐκ παιδός, ἐκ πατρός], by which there is the unity of the three and the distinction of the united, of Spirit, Son and Father. There are three, or three united, by communion from the Father. What, then, is the falsehood the translator committed, in writing in our passage, and wishing it understood from the author's mind, three united, but one in essence and act?

units.la: Adversus Theophilum, vel nos, ex Theophilo, Noster adfert, quod dixerit, non Deum, sed Filium ejus in Paradyso, cum homine fuisse locutum, quia nempe Deus nec loco includi, nec in eo inveniri possit, sed tantum Filius, qui abipso mutatur: unde colligit, ipsum sensisse, solum Patrem summum esse Deum, pag. 346. An vero dixit, Filium Deum non summum, aut inferiorem? an duos Deos, vel tres? Nunquam Veteres alium, praeter unum Deum, somniant. Et dum Christum credunt Deum, putant verum. non est Dei Filius Deus falsus, nec adoptivus, nec Deus nuncupativus, sed Deus verus, Hilarius, de Trinitate, lib. v. & Ambrosius, de fide, lib. v. cap. v. non legi, non audivi, nec aliquem in Deo invenio gradum. Nusquam secundum, nusquam tertium Deum legi, primum legi, primum ac solum audivi. Quando autem solum, neutiquam excluso Filio. Sed Theophilum audiamus ipsum. Objicias, inquit, igitur mihi: supra tradidisti, Deum loco non comprehendi, nunc vero ais, eum in Paradyso ambulare? Audi responsum: Deus quidem universorum pater loco nec includitur, neque in loco inventur. Non enim est locus in quo ipse quiescat. Caeterum sermo ejus, per quem omnia creavit, existens potentia & sapientia Patris; assumit faciem seu personam Patris & domini universorum. Is venit in Paradysum sub persona Dei, & colloquebatur cum Adamo. Siquidem Scriptura Sacra diserte ponit, Adamum dixisse, vocem tuam audivi. At vocem quid aliud dixerit, quam sermonem Dei, qui ejus est Filius. Ubi primum nota, Deum universorum, ipsi, quemadmodum aliis, Patrem dici, quum tamen etiam Filium Deum, & creatorem universorum agnoscant. Deinde de Patre quidem dicere, quod loco nec includitur, nec tenetur, sed neque id de Filio afferere. Filium autem cum Adamo locutum, & ambulasse in Paradyso, ait, quum sit Dei sermo & sapientia, per quem Deus omnia fecerit, faciatque. Quae non negant Filium verum Deum, & aeternum cum Patre, eaque ratione summum, & cum Patre unum esse. Etenim ibidem Filium Dei τὸν λόγον semper apud Deum fuisse memorat, internum quasi in corde Dei ἐνδιάθετον; singulari ratione prolatum & genitum factumque προφορικὸν ad creationem. [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] ἀλλὰ λόγον φρονήσεως, ἐν τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ [?] ὁμιλῶν. Semper in Deo fuit λό-γῳ, νοῦς, φρόνησις, συμβουλία, δύναμις ἡ σοφία: at hic idem est Filius, neque enim creatum putat ἐκ τῶν ὄντων, sed, nescio, quomodo productum & genitum ante creationem, ut per eum tamquam ὑπηρέτην Deus omnia ageret perficeretque. Sic secundum sui substantiam, & quâ etiam in Patre distinguitur, & consiliarius ipsi fuit, semper extitit; qui secundum aliquem modum generationis emanarit à Patre, ad œconomiam creationis & gubernationis omnium admovendus. Neque duplicem facit λόγον, sed eundem, diversâ sui ratione, ἐνδιάθετον, & προφορικόν, non alterum, & alterum. Qui conceptus quamvis non sint usquequaque recti, non tamen impedimento fuerunt ut non prædicaret etiam Trinitatem in Deo, tres primos creationis dies faciens typos τῆς τριάδος ἐν Θεῷ, ἡ ἐν λόγῳ αὐτοῦ, ἡ σοφίας αὐτοῦ.
units.tr: Against Theophilus, or rather from Theophilus, our author cites his statement that it was not God but his Son who spoke with man in Paradise, because God can be contained in no place nor found in one, but only the Son, who changes himself [ab ipso mutatur]. From this he infers that Theophilus held that the Father alone is the supreme God, p. 346. But did he say that the Son is not the supreme God, or is inferior? Did he say that there are two Gods, or three? The ancients never dreamed of any God besides the one God. And while they believe Christ to be God, they think him to be the true God. The Son of God is not a false God, nor an adoptive God, nor a God in name only, but the true God, Hilary, On the Trinity, book 5, and Ambrose, On the Faith, book 5, chapter 5. I have not read, I have not heard, and I do not find in God any degree. I have never read of a second God, or a third God; I have read of, and heard of, a first and only God. But when he says "only," he by no means excludes the Son. Let us hear Theophilus himself. You may object, then, that I have said before that God is not contained in a place, and now you say that he walks in Paradise. Hear the answer: God, the Father of all things, is neither contained in a place nor found in one, for there is no place in which he may rest. But his Word, through whom he created all things, existing as the power and wisdom of the Father, assumes the face or person of the Father and Lord of all. He came into Paradise under the person of God, and spoke with Adam. For Holy Scripture plainly says that Adam said, "I have heard your voice." But what else is that voice than the word of God, who is his Son? Here first note that Theophilus, like others, calls God the Father of all, although they also acknowledge the Son to be God and the creator of all things. Next, he says indeed that the Father is not contained or held in a place, but he does not assert this of the Son. He says that the Son spoke with Adam and walked in Paradise, since he is the Word and wisdom of God, through whom God made and makes all things. These statements do not deny that the Son is the true God and eternal with the Father, and that for this reason he is supreme and one with the Father. Indeed, in the same place he records that the Word of God, logos [τὸν λόγον], was always with God, internal as it were in the heart of God [ἐνδιάθετον]; and that it was brought forth in a unique manner, and begotten and made as a uttered word [προφορικὸν] for the work of creation. [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] but a word of wisdom, conversing in his word [ἀλλὰ λόγον φρονήσεως, ἐν τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ]. Always in God there was word, mind, prudence, counsel, power, and wisdom [λόγος, νοῦς, φρόνησις, συμβουλία, δύναμις, σοφία]. But this is the same Son; for he does not think that he was created out of existing things, but that he was somehow produced and begotten before creation, so that God might act and accomplish all things through him as through a servant [ὑπηρέτην]. Thus, according to his substance, by which he is also distinguished in the Father, he was always present and was a counsellor to him; he who, by some mode of generation, proceeded from the Father to be employed in the economy of the creation and government of all things. Nor does he make a double Word, but the same Word, in a different aspect of his being, inward and uttered, not one and another. Although these conceptions are not altogether correct, they did not prevent him from also preaching the Trinity in God, making the first three days of creation types of the Trinity in God, which is in his Word and in his wisdom.

units.la: Jam Tatianus, in Oratione contra Græcos, quod dixit, Patrem nondum condito mundo solum fuisse, & , cum voluit, productum fuisse primum opus ejus Verbum, valde urget Adversarius, ut probet, Filium non fuisse semper, & esse voluntate Dei productum, sive creatum. Ipsa autem videamus Tatiani verba, & fidem in istis citandis explicandisque liberemus nostram. Nunc vero, inquit, manifestius exponam nostra. Deus erat in principio, principium vero ipsum Dei potentiam esse accepimus. Quare vero hoc non carpit? quum & in Græco, & versione Latinâ fit Verbi potentia, τῷ ἡ ὑ ἐν λόγῳ δύναμιν παρεληφαμεν. Neque aliud voluit Autor, quam quod Johannes, cap. I. 1. ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. & antea vidimus, Veteres λόγον dixisse δύναμιν. Ut quia hoc, in principio statuunt fuisse, agnoverint quoque ante illud non fuisse tempus, sive principium ante principium, sed in Deo, & cum Deo, in æternâ, ante temporis omne principium, duratione; in quâ non est prius & posterius, vel tempus, quod quidem in rebus creatis, sive Angelis, sive aliis rebus, ex quo creatæ sunt, quamvis etiam ante hexaëmeron creatos esse Angelos statuatur. Temporis sive ævi hic quidem sunt differentiæ, quæ extra hoc in Deo, & ejus æternitate vel durationem, ejus sapientiâ, potentiâ &c. & quidquid ex ea dicitur genitum & constare totum, esse non possunt. Quippe Dominus universi, verba sunt Tatiani, ipse existens omnium hypostasis, secundum quidem creationem nondum factam solus erat, videlicet solus absque ullâ creaturâ, non solus absque Verbo. quod ad potentiam vero, καθ' ἡ πᾶσα δύναμις, five quatenus omnis aut omnium potentia, visibilium & invisibilium ipse erat potentia: id est, erant in potentiâ causæ. cum eo omnia : cum ipso, per Verbi, vel rationalem potentiam διὰ λογικῆς δυνάμεως. Nam, inquit Adversarius, & hanc rationalem particulam miratur nos omisisse, cum tamen in textu Graeco habeatur, & nescio quid suspicatur. Imo in Textu Graeco non est. En verba : συν αὐτῷ] τὰ πάντα, συν αὐτῷ διὰ λογικῆς δυνάμεως, αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ λόγος ὃς ἦν ἐν αὐτῷ ὑφίστατο. Nullibi est γάρ. neque aliter fe verba habent, ac ego verti. Exponitque Autor porrò, quomodo omnia dixerit cum eo fuisse, vid. διὰ λογικῆς δυνάμεως. Tum de Verbo addit, & ipsum Verbum, quod in ipso erat subsistebat. Quod interpretatur, Verbum, prout alia omnia fubfiftiffe, & de Verbo non aliter, quam de omnibus aliis rebus creatis intelligi. Id quod ego nego. Ambrosius, de fide, lib. iv. cap. vi. inter omnia Filius non est, quia omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & omnia in ipso constant. Verbum dicitur in ipso fuisse, ἐν αὐτῷ : non tantum uti alia, συν αὐτῷ. & quod ὑφίστασθαι. quod non dicitur de aliis: sed Deum ipsorum fuisse hypostasim, vid. in potentiâ suâ. At substitisse reliqua in isto Verbo, seu potentiâ. Quomodo enim reliqua pariter substitissent cum Verbo, vel Verbum cum illis, quod per potentiam suam illa produxit, & creator ipsorum fuit ? quomodo denique, quum nunquam non adfuerit Patri ille λόγος, δύναμις, σοφία, νοῦς & consiliarius Patri exstitit, non ita caetera ? Sensus ergo verborum, αὐτὸς ὁ λόγος ὃς ἦν ἐν αὐτῷ ὑφίστατο, est, ipsum etiam Verbum, quod erat in eo, subsistebat, vel subsistebat etiam cum eo συν αὐτῷ, sed longe aliâ ratione ac caetera. Quod & sequentia declarant, voluntate autem suâ vel simplicitatis suæ, θελήματι ἁπλοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγος, quod ita vertit Interpres Latinus, cum voluit autem ipse, Verbum ex ejus simplicitate prosiliit. ὁ λόγος Verbum autem non in vanum proferens, ἡ κενὴ χωρήσεως, ἔργον πρωτότοκον πνεύματος γεννῆ primigenium opus fuit spiritus. opus dicit, propter generationem, non propter similem cum aliis creationem. Ambrosius, de fide, lib. iv. cap. iv. sed nihil in sempiterna generatione precedit nec velle nec nolle, ergo nec invitum dixerim, nec volentem, quia generatio non in voluntatis poffibilitate est, sed in jure quodam & proprietate paterni videtur esse secreti.
units.tr: Now Tatian, in his Oration against the Greeks, where he said that the Father was alone before the world was made, and that his first work, the Word, was produced when he willed, is greatly pressed by our opponent, to prove that the Son was not always, but was produced or created by the will of God. Let us look at Tatian's own words, and free our own faith from the burden of citing and explaining them. Now, however, he says, I shall set out our teaching more plainly. God was in the beginning, and we have received that the beginning itself is the power of God. Why then does he not take issue with this? For both in the Greek and in the Latin version it reads power of the Word [τῷ ἡ ὑ ἐν λόγῳ δύναμιν παρεληφαμεν]. Nor did the author mean anything other than what John says, chapter 1, verse 1: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God [ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος]. And we saw earlier that the ancients called the Word "power." So, because they affirm that he was in the beginning, they also acknowledge that before that beginning there was no time, or a beginning before the beginning, but that he was in God and with God, in eternal duration before every beginning of time; in which there is no before and after, nor time. Time exists among created things, whether angels or other things, from the moment they were created, although it is held that the angels were created even before the six days of creation. Here there are differences of time or age, which cannot exist outside this, in God and in his eternity, whether duration, or his wisdom, power, and so on, and whatever is said to be begotten from it, and to consist as a whole. For the Lord of the universe, Tatian's words are, himself being the substance of all things, was alone before creation had been made, that is, alone without any creature, not alone without the Word. As to power, indeed [καθ' ἡ πᾶσα δύναμις], that is, insofar as he himself was the power of all or of all things, visible and invisible: that is, they existed in the power of their cause. All things were with him; with him, through the Word, or rational power [διὰ λογικῆς δυνάμεως]. For, says our opponent, who marvels that we omitted this rational particle, since it is found in the Greek text, and he suspects something or other. But indeed it is not in the Greek text. Here are the words: συν αὐτῷ] τὰ πάντα, συν αὐτῷ διὰ λογικῆς δυνάμεως, αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ λόγος ὃς ἦν ἐν αὐτῷ ὑφίστατο. Nowhere is there a "for" [γάρ], and the words do not read otherwise than as I have translated them. The author then goes on to explain how he said all things were with him, namely through the rational power [διὰ λογικῆς δυνάμεως]. Then he adds about the Word: and the Word itself, which was in him, subsisted. Our opponent interprets this as the Word subsisting just as all other things did, and as meaning that the Word is to be understood in no other way than all other created things. This I deny. Ambrose, On the Faith, book 4, chapter 6: The Son is not among all things, because all things were made through him, and all things consist in him. The Word is said to have been in him [ἐν αὐτῷ], not merely as other things were with him [συν αὐτῷ]; and it is said to have subsisted [ὑφίστασθαι], which is not said of other things. For God himself was the substance of these things, namely in his power. But the rest subsisted in that Word, or power. For how could the rest have subsisted equally with the Word, or the Word with them, when he produced them through his power and was their creator? And finally, since that Word, power, wisdom, mind (logos, dynamis, sophia, nous) was always with the Father and was the Father's counsellor, how could the rest not be so? The sense of the words, therefore, the Word itself, which was in him, subsisted [αὐτὸς ὁ λόγος ὃς ἦν ἐν αὐτῷ ὑφίστατο], is: the Word itself, which was in him, subsisted, or subsisted also with him [συν αὐτῷ], but in a very different way from the rest. The following sentences make this clear: but by his own will, or by his simplicity [θελήματι ἁπλοῦ αὐτοῦ], the Word leapt forth from his simplicity; the Latin translator renders it: when he himself willed, the Word leapt forth from his simplicity. [ὁ λόγος] But the Word, not uttering in vain [ἡ κενὴ χωρήσεως], begot the firstborn work of the Spirit [ἔργον πρωτότοκον πνεύματος γεννῆ]: the firstborn work was the Spirit. He calls it a work on account of generation, not on account of a creation like the others. Ambrose, On the Faith, book 4, chapter 4: But in eternal generation nothing precedes, neither willing nor not willing; therefore I would not say either that it is unwilling or willing, since generation is not within the possibility of the will, but seems to be a certain secret of the paternal right and property.

units.la: Tom. 2. secreti. Nam sicut bonus pater non aut ex voluntate est aut necessitate, super naturam, ita non generat ex voluntate aut necessitate pater. Esto tamen, sit generatio in voluntate generantis, quando hanc voluntatem fuisse dicunt? Si in principio, utique si sempiterna voluntas, sempiternus & filius. Et Hilarius, ad citatum locum Joan. 1. 1. distinguit inter inter esse, & inesse, & adesse. Id enim quod in principio erat, non in altero prædicatur esse, sed cum altero. lib. II. de Trinitate.
units.tr: Tom. 2. secreti. For just as a good father does not beget either from will or from necessity, above nature, so the Father does not beget from will or from necessity. Yet grant that generation lies in the will of the one who begets: when do they say this will existed? If in the beginning, then surely if the will is eternal, the Son is eternal too. And Hilary, on the cited passage John 1.1, distinguishes between being (esse), being in (inesse), and being with (adesse): For what was in the beginning is not said to be in another, but to be with another. Book 2, On the Trinity.

units.la: Denique Tatianum facit Noster argumentantem, quod Filius, quia genitus est, principium habeat, neque paris sit, propterea cum Patre potentiæ: & sic Athenagoram quoque concludentem, illud tantum generari posse, quod antea non fuerit. Athenagoras quidem ita loquitur, sed quoniam omnis sermo noster Deum unum celebrat, conditorem illum universitatis, qui ingenitus ipse (neque enim generari potest quod est, sed quod non est) omnia Verbo suo creavit. Ingenitum Deum dicit, oppositè ad alia in universo: ab ipso genita vel facta: & ipsum Filium conditorem universitatis. Quo ipso satis indicat alterius à reliquis substantiæ esse Filium, videlicet Creatorem, à creatura. Uti enim Alexander, Alexandrinus episcopus, inquit, in epistolâ ad Alexandrum Constantinopolitanum, apud Theodoretum, lib. I. cap. IV. nulla enim ratio vult, ut quod creat, ejusdem sit cum creatis naturæ. & Fulgentius Afer, lib. II. de immensitate divinitatis filii Dei, statim in initio: quæ essentia se hoc præsertim indicio sempiternam, increatam, immutabilemque monstravit, cum ex nihilo, id est, ex eo quod non esset, creare potuit, quod fuisset. Nam quid ni ex sequentibus priores, ubi de eodem agunt, exponamus? Esse, & non esse, & à non esse generari ad esse, creaturarum sunt, deque istis ab Athenagorâ dicuntur: uti quando de materia mundi postea disserit, & concludit propterea eam pro Deo à Christianis non haberi: nos vero discrimen facimus, inquit, inter genitum & ingenitum, inter ens & non ens, inter id quod intellectu, quoque sensu percipitur. Et sic Tatianus, neque enim materia est ἀνάρχῳ [?] καὶ ἀγένητος ὁ Θεὸς principii expers quemadmodum Deus, & quia principii non est, expers parem cum Deo potentiam habere non potuit: siquidem genita est, & non ab alio facta, sed uno omnium conditore perdućta. Loquuntur de rerum omnium materiâ, & ejus à Deo productione, quare & inæqualitate cum Deo; non verò pari ratione de Filio: quem dicit Athenagoras materiam fecisse, quamvis in principio genitum, neque tamen principium habuisse, uti materia & alia, existimat. In principio fuit, ante materiæ principium, quæ & naturam & initium habet ab eo: & natus, sive ex Patris potentiâ progressus fuit [?προελθὼν ἐκ τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς] [?δυνάμεως], sive λογικῆς δυνάμεως: certe non ἐκ τῶν ὄντων, uti materia, & reliqua, neque etiam principium temporis habuisse eum asserit. Uti propterea Novatianus, de Trinitate, citatus Autori nostro, pag. 364. Filium Dei ante omne tempus constituit. Nec enim illi tempus assignari potest, qui ante tempus est, inquit. Non ergo de Filio illa loquitur, sive Athenagoras, sive Tatianus, quæ Noster tamquam de Filio ab ipsis dicta allegat, quæ æque exagitare possemus, si liberet, ac ille solet multa perperam & inclementer in suis Adversariis. Quin Tatianus Christum prædicari à Christianis, quapropter & credi, affirmat Deum in hominis formâ natum, [?θεὸν ἐν ἀνθρώπου μορφῇ γενόμενον]. Quod & Deitatis Christi, & incarnationis illustre est argumentum.
units.tr: Finally, our author makes Tatian argue that the Son, because he has been begotten, has a beginning and is therefore not equal, and so with the Father in power; and in the same way he makes Athenagoras conclude that only what did not previously exist can be begotten. Athenagoras indeed speaks thus: But since our whole discourse honours one God, the maker of the universe, who himself is unbegotten (for what is cannot be begotten, but only what is not), and who created all things through his Word. He calls God unbegotten, in contrast to other things in the universe, which are begotten or made by him; and he calls the Son the maker of the universe. By this very fact he sufficiently indicates that the Son is of a different substance from the rest, namely the Creator, distinct from the creature. For as Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, says in his letter to Alexander of Constantinople, cited by Theodoret, Book 1, chapter 4: For no reason requires that what creates should be of the same nature as the things created. And Fulgentius of Africa, Book 2, On the Immensity of the Divinity of the Son of God, at the very beginning: This essence showed itself eternal, uncreated and unchangeable, especially by this sign, that it was able to create out of nothing, that is, out of that which did not exist, what had existed. For why should we not explain the earlier passages from what follows, where they treat the same subject? Being and not-being, and coming to be from not-being, belong to creatures, and it is of these that Athenagoras speaks; as when he later discusses the matter of the world and concludes that Christians therefore do not regard it as God: But we make a distinction, he says, between the begotten and the unbegotten, between being and not-being, between what is perceived by the intellect and what is perceived by the senses. So also Tatian: For matter is not [ἀνάρχῳ [?] καὶ ἀγένητος ὁ Θεὸς] without beginning as God is, and since it is without beginning, it could not have a power equal to God's; for it was begotten, and was not made by another, but brought forth by the one Creator of all. They are speaking of the matter of all things and its production by God, and therefore of its inequality with God; not in the same way of the Son. Athenagoras says that the Son was begotten "in the beginning," yet he does not think he had a beginning, as matter and other things do. He was in the beginning, before the beginning of matter, which has both its nature and its origin from him; and he came forth from the Father's power [προελθὼν ἐκ τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς δυνάμεως], or from a rational power [λογικῆς δυνάμεως]; certainly not out of existing things, as matter and the rest are, nor does he assert that he had a beginning of time. So too Novatian, On the Trinity, cited by our author on p. 364, sets the Son of God before all time. For no time can be assigned to him who is before time, he says. Therefore neither Athenagoras nor Tatian is speaking of the Son in the passages which our author cites as said of the Son by them; and we could equally criticise these, if we chose, as he often does, unfairly and harshly, against his opponents. Indeed Tatian affirms that Christ is preached by Christians, and therefore believed, as God born in the form of man [θεὸν ἐν ἀνθρώπου μορφῇ γενόμενον]. This is a notable proof both of the divinity of Christ and of the incarnation.

units.la: Pergamus ad Irenæum, quem statuisse, Filium ante mundum conditum jam extitisse, nemo est qui neget, pag. 356. Quod primò est contra ejus, quam de Christo tenet, sententiam. Nec tantum ante mundum conditum fuisse Filium, Irenæus docet, sed quoque quod Filius semper cum Patre erat, lib. iv. cap. xxxvii. Et quia in adducendo & describendo illo loco, qui prolixior est, abruperam per &c. omittens loca quæ citabantur ex Proverbiis Salomonis; comparat me, pro solitâ humanitate & modestiâ, cum iniquo dispensatore in parabolâ Luc. 16. nempe quia omisi ex Irenæo adducere quod citat ex Prov. viii. Dominus creavit me principium viarum suarum. ad quod tamen antè respondera m. Unde nec probaverit, Irenæum non credidisse Filium coæternum; quia illa quidem verba adduxerunt alii etiam, qui tamen de Filii æternitate non dubitarunt: uti nec hinc idem illud evincit, quod forte Irenæus de Filio loquens, non iisdem utitur loquendi formulis, quibus aliàs Patris describit majestatem. Ostendat verò aliquid omissum à nobis in citando loco, quod ad sententiam vel expositionem nostram de Irenæo evertendam faciat, antequam fidem nostram sugillet: quod dum non facit, viderit ut nodum in scirpo quæsierit, & calumniari, præter caussam.
units.tr: Let us proceed to Irenaeus, whom no one denies to have held that the Son already existed before the world was made, p. 356. This is first of all against his own view concerning Christ. Irenaeus teaches not only that the Son existed before the world was made, but also that the Son was always with the Father, Book 4, chapter 37. And since, in citing and describing that passage, which is rather long, I broke off with "etc.," omitting the places cited from the Proverbs of Solomon, he compares me, with his usual humanity and moderation, to the unjust steward in the parable of Luke 16, namely because I omitted to cite from Irenaeus what he quotes from Proverbs 8: The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, to which, however, I had already replied earlier. Hence he has not proved that Irenaeus did not believe the Son to be coeternal; for others too have adduced those very words, and yet have not doubted the eternity of the Son. Nor does it follow from this that Irenaeus, speaking of the Son, does not use the same forms of speech with which he elsewhere describes the majesty of the Father. Let him show that something has been omitted by us in citing the passage, which would overturn our interpretation of Irenaeus or support his, before he impugns our faith; and as long as he does not do so, he will see that he has sought a knot in a bulrush and made a false accusation without cause.

units.la: Porrò conatur ostendere, Veteres, quamvis dixerint Verbum vel Filium semper in Patre fuisse, non tamen credidisse Filium Patri esse coæternum: in quem finem adducit Novatianum, in libro de Trinitate, apud Tertullianum, dicentem, Filium semper in Patre esse, quod ita explicat, semper autem sic dico, ut non innatum, sed natum probem. Negamus autem, Nostrum hoc ex loco probare sententiam vel consequentiam suam : nempe quod qui illud dicit, eo non credat Filium Patri esse coæ-ternum. Nam propterea Filium in Patre ponit, quia certe à Patre est genitus, & non innatus. Et quia semper in Patre, semper ita quoque natus fuit. Sed & principium nativitatis, addit Novatianus, Filium ante omne tempus accipientem: dumque ante tempus dicit, non principium aliquod temporis, sed nativitatis, ut sic, intelligit: postmodum etiam dicens, quod principium nativitatis ante omne tempus accepit. Voce illa non-nunquam utuntur Veteres, non ad negandam æternitatem, sed ad expo-nendam à Patre, quem Filii principium & causam & originem subinde vocant, generationem. Quod & Petavius ostendit ac tractavit argu-mentum suo loco.
units.tr: Furthermore he tries to show that the Ancients, although they said that the Word or the Son was always in the Father, did not believe that the Son was coeternal with the Father. To this end he cites Novatian, in his book On the Trinity, as quoted by Tertullian, saying that the Son is always in the Father, which he explains thus: I say always in such a way that I prove him to be begotten, not unbegotten. We deny, however, that our author proves his point or his conclusion from this passage, namely that whoever says this does not believe the Son to be coeternal with the Father. For Novatian places the Son in the Father precisely because he is certainly begotten of the Father, and not unbegotten; and because he was always in the Father, he was always begotten in this way too. But Novatian adds that the Son also received the beginning of his birth before all time; and when he says "before time," he means not some beginning of time, but of birth, in this sense; and afterwards he says, that he received the beginning of birth before all time. The Ancients sometimes use this expression not to deny eternity, but to explain the generation from the Father, whom they also frequently call the beginning, cause and origin of the Son. Petavius also shows this and has treated the question in its proper place.

units.la: Confirmant de Novatiano, quæ dixi, & ejus sententiâ, ipsa illa, quæ ex eo Noster adducit, dicente, sed qui ante omne tempus est, semper in Patre fuisse dicendus est. Nec enim illi tempus assignari potest, qui ante tempus est. Semper enim in Patre, ne Pater non fit Pater. Qui ante omne tempus, etiam extra omne tempus est, & non habet temporis aliquod principium vel momentum, quo assignari quod non fuerit, possit. Semper ergo fuit Filius, & qui in Patre semper, semper etiam extitit. Atque uti semper Pater, ita semper Filius, quia neuter hoc quod est, potest esse absque altero. Tam Patri necessarius Filius est, ut sit Pater, quam Filio Pater, ut sit Filius, ne Pater non semper fit Pater. Pater ergo semper est Pater, & in illo Filio: quare uti ille æternus, sic iste non potest non esse coæternus, alioqui nec æternus fuerit Pater. Ambrosius, de Fide, lib. i. cap. v. cum enim patrem dixeris, ejus etiam Filium designasti, quia nemo ipse sibi pater est. Cum filium nominas, etiam patrem ejus fateris, quia nemo ipse sibi filius est. Itaque nec filius sine patre, nec pater potest esse sine filio. Semper igitur pater, semper & filius. Et lib. de fide, contra Arianos, cap. ii. ac proinde cujus origo principium non habet, sempiternus cum Patre credendus est: quia nec pater potest unquam sine filio nominari, nec filius sine patre vocari, ac per hoc semper filius, quia semper pater.
units.tr: The very words which our author cites from Novatian confirm what I have said, and his opinion, when he says: But he who is before all time must be said always to have been in the Father. For no time can be assigned to him who is before time. For always in the Father, lest the Father should not be Father. He who is before all time is also outside all time, and has no beginning or moment of time to which it could be assigned that he did not exist. The Son, then, always was, and as he was always in the Father, so he always existed too. And just as the Father is always Father, so the Son is always Son, since neither can be what he is without the other. The Son is as necessary to the Father, that he may be Father, as the Father is to the Son, that he may be Son, lest the Father should not always be Father. The Father therefore is always Father, and that in relation to the Son; so that as the one is eternal, the other cannot fail to be coeternal, otherwise the Father would not be eternal either. Ambrose, On Faith, Book 1, chapter 5: For when you have named the Father, you have also designated his Son, because no one is father to himself. When you name the Son, you also acknowledge his Father, because no one is son to himself. Therefore the Son cannot be without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. Therefore always Father, always also Son. And in his book On Faith, against the Arians, chapter 2: And therefore he whose origin has no beginning must be believed to be eternal with the Father: because the Father can never be named without the Son, nor the Son be called without the Father, and so always Son, because always Father.

units.la: Sed addit Novatianus: quin & Pater illum etiam præcedit, quod necesse est, prior fit, qua Pater fit. Quoniam antecedat necesse est eum, qui habet originem ille qui originem nescit. Ergo non temporis, vel æternitatis ratione Patrem priorem facit, sed duntaxat generationis, qua Pater est, non quâ uter-que Deus:* Et expositurus Filii generationem, à Patre non genito, alterum originem habere dicit, alterum nescire. Vocibus originis, & prin-cipii utens, ad relationem personalitatis invicem declarandam, & chara&terifticam[?] Patris proprietatem à Filio distinctam, quâ Pater est in-genitus, Filius à Patre genitus. Et propterea prioritatem Patris nullam agnoscit praeterquam qua Pater sit, & Filium Patre hoc minorem qua nascitur. Id enim restrictivae hae denotant. Patri tamen hoc etiam ipso satis vicinum, nam sic loquitur, facit in nativitate, dum ex Patre, qui solus originem non habet, nascitur. Etiam Autor noster ita exponit, ut dicatur Novatiano Filius, quoque propter generationem vicinus quasi æternitati aut perpetuitati: quod quantum distet ab æternitate, viderit.
units.tr: But Novatian adds: Indeed the Father even precedes him, which must be so: he becomes prior by the very fact that he is the Father. For it must be that he who has an origin comes after him who does not know origin. So he makes the Father prior not by reason of time or eternity, but only of generation, by which he is Father, and not by which each is God. And intending to explain the generation of the Son from the Father who was not begotten, he says that the one has an origin and the other does not know it. Using the words origin and beginning to declare the relation of persons to one another, and the characteristic property of the Father distinguished from the Son, by which the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten of the Father, he therefore acknowledges no priority in the Father except in that he is Father, and the Son as less than the Father in that he is born. For these restrictive words denote this. Yet this comes very close to the Father itself, for he speaks thus, and makes it so in birth, while he is born from the Father, who alone has no origin. Our author also explains it so that it may be said to Novatian that the Son too, because of his generation, is near, as it were, to eternity or perpetuity. How far that is from eternity, let him see.

units.la: Deinde ait Novatianus, Filium, quando Pater voluit, ab ipso ptocef-sisse, & quia ex Patre fuit, postmodum cum eo semper fuisse. Urget Adversarius illud postmodum: at frustra. Nam non temporis aliquod momentum eo notavit Autor, quem ante omne tempus semper fuisse asseruit; sed distinctionem rei, sive generationis, aut generati à generante. Nam nihil ista facere ad differentiam essentialem utriusque, hoc confirmat, quod additur, Verbum seu Filium esse substantiam divinam; sub-stantia scilicet illa divina, cujus nomen est Verbum, per quod facta sunt omnia &c. Quare quamvis Filium dicat post Patrem, quà Filius, nihil tamen adimit essentiae, vel ejus in utroque identitati. Quò & ista spectant, Deus utique procedens ex Deo, plane uti in Concilio Nicaeno loquuti Patres, secundam personam efficiens.
units.tr: Next Novatian says that the Son proceeded from him when the Father willed, and because he was from the Father, afterwards was always with him. The Adversary presses that word afterwards, but in vain. For the author did not mark by it any moment of time, since he asserted that the Son was always before all time; he marked a distinction of the thing, that is, of generation, or of the begotten from the begetter. That these things have nothing to do with an essential difference between the two is confirmed by what is added, that the Word or Son is the divine substance: that divine substance, namely, whose name is the Word, through which all things were made, etc. So although he says the Son is after the Father, as Son, he nonetheless takes nothing from the essence, or from its identity in both. To this also belongs the phrase God indeed proceeding from God, just as the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea spoke, effecting the second person.

units.la: Ergò quod Deitatem, ejusque substantiam concernit, eadem est Patris atque Filii: differentia tantum est secundum personam, quae vel Pater est, vel Filius, & originem generationis alter habet, alter non. Propterea non duos Deos, sed unum dicit, & Patrem quidem invisibilem, incomprehensibilem, & Christum Patri obedientem & ministrantem, ad singularem vid. oeconomiae rationem explicandam, κατ᾽ οἰκονομίαν[?] dicunt Veteres, ad opus: neque est quod distinctio ista in nobis perstringatur: καὶ κατὰ θεολογίαν[?] verò de eo loquuntur, quando de unâ Deitate, & divinâ substantiâ disputant. Alius est Filius à Patre, non verò aliud. Fulgentius, lib. 1. de fide, ad Pet. una est Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti essentia, in qua non est aliud Pater, aliud Filius, aliud Spiritus Sanctus; quamvis personaliter sit alius Pater, alius Filius, alius Spiritus Sanctus. Hilarius, lib. 11. alius ab alio, quia Pater & Filius. Non natura divinitatis alia & alia, quia ambo unum. Deus à Deo. Ab uno ingenito unigenitus Deus. & Tertullianus, adversus Praxeam: ecce enim dico alium esse Patrem, & alium Filium, & alium Spiritum Sanctum. Male accepit idiotes quisque, aut perversus hoc dictum, quasi diversitatem sonet, & ex diversitate separationem protendat Patris & Filii & Spiritus. Ut minime evertantur ex Novatiano, ea quae ad Irenaeum annotavimus, qui non tantum dixit, quod ille, Filium semper fuisse in Patre, sed & cum Patre, quin confirmentur & illustrentur. Nec qui dicit Filium semper in Patre fuisse, atque adeo ne Pater non semper sit Pater, & substantiae esse divinae, Deum ex Deo; negat ejusdem esse essentiae, & propterea quoque aeternitatis Deum, cum Patre, Filium, unum.
units.tr: Therefore, as far as the Deity and its substance are concerned, the Father and the Son are the same; the difference is only in the person, which is either Father or Son, and one has the origin of generation while the other does not. For this reason he says there are not two Gods but one: the Father invisible and incomprehensible, and Christ obedient to the Father and ministering to him. The ancients call this according to the economy [κατ᾽ οἰκονομίαν], namely to explain the particular plan of the economy with respect to the work; and this distinction is not to be disparaged. But when they dispute about the one Deity and the divine substance, they speak according to theology [καὶ κατὰ θεολογίαν]. The Son is other than the Father, but not another thing. Fulgentius, book 1 on the faith, to Peter: There is one essence of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, in which the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Hilarius, book 11: other from another, because Father and Son. Not a different and different nature of divinity, because both are one. God from God. From the one unbegotten, the only-begotten God. And Tertullian, against Praxeas: For behold, I say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. Some simpleton or perverse person has misunderstood this saying, as if it sounded like diversity, and drew from the diversity a separation of the Father and the Son and the Spirit. So what we noted on Irenaeus is by no means overturned by Novatian, who not only said, as he did, that the Son had always been in the Father, but also with the Father; rather it is confirmed and illustrated. Nor does he who says the Son was always in the Father, and that the Father is always Father, and that the Son is of divine substance, God from God, deny that the Son, God with the Father, is one with him in essence and therefore also in eternity.

units.la: Porro carpit Adversarius, quod verba Irenaei ex lib. III. cap. VIII, ipse enim infectus, & sine initio, & sine fine, & nullius indigens, ipse sibi sufficiens, & adhuc reliquis omnibus, ut sint hoc ipsum praestans, etiam de Filio intelligimus, quae de Patre vult accipienda: quod non quaeritur: At, annon etiam de Filio, hoc quaerebatur. Id vero propterea verum est, quia in Filio passim Veteres agnoscunt, quod omnibus ut sint praestat. Filium autem una comprehendi sub reliquis omnibus, de quibus hic sermo, nec probabit Noster, neque cum Christi aut Filii omnium creatoris dignitate convenit, in classem reliquorum omnium isto modo referri.
units.tr: Further, the Adversary carps that we understand the words of Irenaeus from book III, chapter VIII, for he himself is unmade, without beginning and without end, needing nothing, sufficient to himself, and yet giving to all the rest that they may be, also of the Son, whereas he wants them taken of the Father. That is not the question; the question was whether this too is to be said of the Son. And it is true, because among the ancients the Son is everywhere recognised as giving to all that they may be. But that the Son is included among all the rest, of whom the discussion here is, our author will not prove. Nor does it agree with the dignity of Christ, or of the Son, creator of all, to be placed in this way in the class of all the rest.

units.la: Ipse Irenaeus, nec quidem ex his quae constituta, & in subjectione sunt comparabitur verbo Dei, per quem facta sunt omnia, quae est Dominus noster Jesus Christus. Ecce ut distinguantur reliqua omnia, quae facta sunt, a Verbo omnium creatore. Et quod Patrem cum Filio conjunctim consi-derat, haec ejus ultima ostendunt verba, a nobis adducta, Adversario autem, nescio qua de causa, non enim ei lubet sua reponere, omissa, uti & alia: ita ut is quidem qui omnia fecerit cum verbo suo, juste dicatur Deus & Dominus solus, quae autem facta sunt, non jam ejusdem vocabuli perceptibilia esse, neque juste id vocabulum sumere debere, quod est creatoris. Distinguit omnia quae facta sunt, a creatore: conjungit autem Deum, cum Filio: tum in creationis communitate, tum nominis Dei, ac Domini, & creatoris: quae factis a Deo competere, negat: & cum Verbo Deum dicit Deum & Dominum solum: ergo quando solus Deus nominatur ipsi aut Dominus, non intelligi debet, secludere Filium: etiam, quando altera vocat, quae constituta sunt ab eo qui constituit, & quae facta sunt; & , reliquis omnibus, ut sint hoc ipsum praestans, non notat sub reliquis istis Filium: sed eum designat hisce, ab eo qui constituit ---- ab eo qui fecit. ipse enim infectus, & sine initio, & , sine fine, & nullius indigens, ipse sibi sufficiens, & adhuc reliquis omnibus, ut sint hoc ipsum praestans. Nempe is, qui omnia fecit cum Verbo suo. Non ergo illis opponitur Deus Verbo, uti aliis a se à se factis rebus, sed cum eo conjungitur. Neque aliud docetur lib. II. cap. LXVII. ubi ostensurus, Prophetas non de aliis diis, sed de uno eodemque semper vaticinatos, contra Gnosticos, ait, per qua unum Deus & Pater ostenditur qui continet omnia, & omnibus ut sint praestans. Patrem notat, fateor: non vero Filium? nego. & Noster, pro more, satis habet illa dicere, non probare. Omnibus ut sint, periphrasis est creaturarum, & creationis, quae semper, ab Irenaeo, & aliis, Filio attribuitur cum Patre: neque ostendet, omnibus ut sint Filium consignificari. Sed Pater cum Filio, ex mente Irenaei, omnibus ut sint, praestat. Neque plures hinc Dii, vel Patres, sed unus Deus & Pater, cum Filio, & Spiritu Sancto. Uti dixit lib. IV. cap. XVII. ministrat ei Patri ad omnia sua progenies, & figuratio sua, id est, Filius, & Spiritus, Verbum & sapientia, quibus serviunt & subjecti sunt omnes Angeli, id est, & omnia: omnibus ut sint praestans, dixit enim ad omnia; & omnia ipsi servire & subjecta esse, necessum. Quare quando illo cap. ultimo, sive LXVII. lib. II. Patrem nominat, & a solo Deo Patre visibilia atque invisibilia, & omnia omnino, quaecunque facta sunt existere, & creatorem & fabricatorem omnium, docet; Patrem non intelligit absque Filio, Verbo, sed absque Diis aliis: quia contra Gnosticos disputat, plures Deos fingentes, inquit etiam Noster, non adversus nos, vel imo seipsum, qui passim tradit, Verbum omnia fecisse. Unde in initio capitis inquit, omnes Prophetas unum Deum & Dominum praedicasse, & ipsum factorem coeli & terra, & omnium quae in eis sunt, & quod adventum Filii ejus significaverint.
units.tr: Irenaeus himself says: nor indeed is he compared with the things that are constituted and in subjection to the Word of God, through whom all things were made, who is our Lord Jesus Christ. See how all the other things that were made are distinguished from the Word, the creator of all. And that he considers the Father together with the Son, the last words we quoted show; but the Adversary, for some reason I do not know (for he does not care to set out his own passages), omitted them, as also other things: so that he who made all things with his Word is justly called God and Lord alone, but the things that were made are no longer capable of the same name, nor ought they justly to take that name, which belongs to the Creator. He distinguishes all the things that were made from the Creator, but he joins God with the Son, both in the community of creation and in the names of God, Lord and Creator, which he denies to things made. And with the Word he calls God alone God and Lord. Therefore when alone is named of God or of Lord, it must not be understood to exclude the Son. Nor, when he calls the others what is constituted by him who constituted, and what was made, and , all the rest, so that they may be, giving this very thing, does he mark the Son among those rest; he designates him by these words: by him who constituted ... by him who made. For he himself is unmade, without beginning, without end, needing nothing, sufficient to himself, and yet giving to all the rest that they may be. Namely, he who made all things with his Word. So God is not opposed to the Word as to other things made by him, but is joined with him. Nor is anything different taught in book II, chapter 67, where, intending to show against the Gnostics that the Prophets did not prophesy about other gods but always about one and the same God, he says: through whom the one God and Father is shown, who contains all things, and gives to all that they may be. I admit he denotes the Father; but the Son? I deny it. And our author, as is his way, is content to say these things without proving them. To all that they may be is a periphrasis for creatures and creation, which Irenaeus and others always attribute to the Son along with the Father; nor will he show that the Son is co-signified in to all that they may be. But the Father, with the Son, in Irenaeus' view, gives to all that they may be. Nor from this are there more Gods or Fathers, but one God and Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit. As he says in book IV, chapter 17: his offspring and his figure, that is, the Son and the Spirit, the Word and Wisdom, to whom all the Angels minister and are subject, serve that Father for all his purposes; that is, and all things. For he says for all things, and it is necessary that all things serve him and be subject to him. Therefore when in that last chapter, that is chapter 67 of book II, he names the Father, and teaches that visible and invisible things, and all things whatsoever that were made, exist from God the Father alone, and that he is the creator and maker of all, he does not understand the Father without the Son, the Word, but without other Gods, because he disputes against the Gnostics, feigning many Gods, as our author also says, and not against us, or rather against himself, who everywhere hands down that the Word made all things. Hence at the beginning of that chapter he says that all the Prophets preached one God and Lord, and the maker of heaven and earth and of all that is in them, and that they signified the coming of his Son.

units.la: Non ergo, uti Noster explicat, Patrem non vero Filium, sed Patrem, cum Filio, Irenaeus significat; quia & cum eo fecit omnia, & factorem cum Patre Filium, & fabricatorem omnium vulgo praedicat, & Filium non ut alium Deum, cum Gnosticis aut habere videtur, aut haberi vult. Sic & lib. II. cap. II. non Angelos probat mundum fecisse, sed solum Patrem, per Filium verbum: quoniam nullius indigens omnium Deus, verbo condidit omnia & fecit, neque Angelis indigens adjutoribus ad ea quae fecit. — & idoneus est & sufficiens ad formationem omnium proprium ejus verbum, quemadmodum & Joannes domini Discipulus ait de eo, omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil, in omnibus autem est & hic qui est secundum nos mundus. Et hic ergo a verbo ejus factus est. Non autem in horum omnium ordinem redigit Filium, non una cum mundo Filium mundi factorem. Cui non refragatur, quod lib. III. cap. VIII. & IX. Christum facit docentem, quod Pater tantum is Deus & Dominus sit, qui solus est Deus & dominator omnium, & nullus alius praeter ipsum. Quia haec aliis Diis, vel mundi fabricatoribus aut Dominis opponun-tur, non Filio. Quemadmodum significat illâ conclusione capitis secundi, lib. II. in principio fecit Deus cœlum & terram, & deinceps reliqua omnia, sed non Dii, neque Angeli. Ex quibus cognoscere licet, quibus unum omnium creatorem Deum, in totâ hac disputatione, opponat Irenæus, & quæ per reliqua omnia passim intelligat, vid. neutrobique Filium, quem cum Patre semper conjungit & unit. Ut falso, vel nos corrumpere Irenæi locum, vel nulla ratione de Filio intelligi illa posse, Adversarius afferat. Huc faciunt & illa lib. III. cap. IX. ad quæ nos allegat: Ostenso igitur sic plane, & adhuc ostendatur manifestius neminem alterum Dominum vel Deum, neque Prophetas neque Apostolos, neque dominum Christum confessum esse ex sua persona, sed præcipue Deum & Dominum, Prophetis quidem & Apostolis Patrem & Filium confitentibus, alterum autem neminem neque Deum nominantibus, neque Dominum confitentibus. Et deinde: Unus igitur & idem Deus est, Pater Domini nostri, qui & præcursorem per Prophetas missurum se promisit, & salutare suum, id est, verbum suum visibile effecit omni fieri carni, incarnatum & ipsum, ut in omnibus manifestus fieret rex eorum.
units.tr: Therefore, as our opponent explains, Irenaeus does not mean "the Father, but not the Son." He means the Father together with the Son. He says that the Son made all things with him, and he commonly proclaims the Son as maker and framer of all things along with the Father. He neither appears to hold, nor wishes to be held, that the Son is another God, as the Gnostics do. So also in book II, chapter 2, he proves that it was not angels but the Father alone who made the world, through the Word, the Son: "since God, lacking nothing, made and created all things by his Word, and needing no angels as helpers for the things he made. — And his own Word is fit and sufficient for the formation of all, as John, the disciple of the Lord, says of him: 'All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made' (John 1:3); and in all things is this world which is according to us. And so it was made by his Word." He does not, however, reduce the Son to the rank of all these things, nor make the Son, together with the world, a maker of the world. Nor does he contradict this in book III, chapters 8 and 9, where he makes Christ teach that the Father alone is God and Lord, the only God and ruler of all, and that there is no other beside him. For these things are set against other gods, or against makers and lords of the world, not against the Son. He signals this by the conclusion of chapter 2 of book II: "in the beginning God made heaven and earth, and all the rest, but not gods or angels." From this it may be known whom Irenaeus, throughout this whole discussion, sets against the one Creator of all, and what he means by "all the rest." Clearly in neither case is the Son meant, whom he always joins and unites with the Father. So the opponent's claim, that either we corrupt Irenaeus' words or those words cannot in any way be understood of the Son, is false. Those words of book III, chapter 9, to which he appeals us, also tend this way: "Having therefore shown this plainly, and let it be shown still more clearly, that neither the Prophets nor the Apostles nor the Lord Christ has confessed any other God or Lord from his own person, but especially God and Lord; the Prophets and Apostles confessing the Father and the Son, and naming no one else as God or confessing anyone else as Lord. And then: One and the same God is the Father of our Lord, who promised through the Prophets that he would send his forerunner, and who made his salvation, that is, his visible Word, to become flesh for all flesh, himself also incarnate, so that he might be made manifest as king of them all."

units.la: Alteram deinde corruptionem in dicto Irenæi loco,lib. iii.cap.viii. mihi impingit acerbe satis ac contumeliose: nempe dixit Irenæus, Ita ut is quidem qui omnia fecerit cum verbo suo, juste dicatur Deus & Dominus solus. Neque aliter citavimus. Dicit autem, nos verba Irenæi ita protulisse, ac si dixisset, Solus is, Pater ac verbum suum, Dominus ac Deus appellandus. Quasi hæc, verbum suum construxerim cum verbo dicatur, cum debeat construi tantum cum verbo fecerit. Egone vel protuli verba aliter, vel construxi, vel denique interpunxi, quam apud Irenæum leguntur, & ipse Adversarius legit? Intellexi aliter, ac ille: verum est. Sed an illud quis vocabit locum corrumpere, per manifestam falsationem, quod ille hic facit? Falsat, qui locum, ipsum varie, & aliter citat, quam legitur; non qui locum aliter intelligit, quam adversarius suus cupiat. Alioqui quot non falsationum haberi ipse debebit reus? Dicit, in loco Irenæi intelligendum Patrem, non vero Filium, &c, nulla ratione de Filio intelligi posse. Hoc ego nego, & doceo contrarium. Ipsa verò Irenæi verba pari modo à nobis leguntur.
