Non ergo mihi magis falsationem objicere potest, quam ego ipsi, quum non de verbis inter nos sit disputatio, sed eorum vero sensu. Neque id admodum spectavi, vel specto, utrum verbum suum construatur cum dicatur, an cum fecerit, tantum doceo Verbum esse conjungendum cum Patre, quod facit Irenæus; non ab eo separandum, quod Adversarius. Pater cum Verbo est, & facit omnia, & sic cum Verbo dicitur Deus & Dominus solus. Nusquam potest Pater à Filio, vel à Patre Filius sejungi. Tum argumentum, quo utitur Irenæus, idem confirmat: nam probaturus, nec Prophetas, nec Apostolos alium Deum vel Dominum appellasse, præter verum & solum Deum, quod in capitis initio præmittit, omnia alia ab hac nomenclatura dicit excludi, cum Patre comparata, & Verbo Dei per quem facta sunt omnia, qui est Dominus noster Jesus Christus. quem & Dominum & Deum esse, ac dici, probat; non ita sive angeli, sive archangeli, sive throni, sive dominationes ab eo qui super omnes est Deus, & constituta, & facta per Verbum ejus. Reliqua vero ab eo facta, propterea etiam omnino differens vocabulum habere asserit, qua autem facta sunt, non jam ejusdem vocabuli perceptibilia esse, neque juste id vocabulum sumere debere. Quodnam? Dei & Domini, quod proprium est Patri cum Filio. Filium quemadmodum cum Patre jungit, & discernit ab aliis creaturis, uti creatorem, sic & nominis istius facit perceptibilem, & juste eum illam quoque sumere sibi appellationem. Ita ut is quidem qui omnia fecerit cum Verbo suo, juste dicatur Dominus & Deus solus. Non ita alia. Quæ aut quia facta sunt, non jam ejusdem vocabuli percipibilia esse, neque juste id vocabulum sumere debere, quod est creatoris. Adde lib. III. cap. VI. cujus argumentum est, quod in Scripturis nemo alius Deus nominatur, nec Dominus nuncupatur, quam solus verus Deus Pater omnium, & Verbum ejus. Quæ suo loco à nobis adducta & descripta, sicco pede Adversarius transit. Provocamus ad omnium conscientiam, qui legere ista & examinare apud Irenæum dignentur, an, quod vult Noster, Filium excludant, & tantum intelligant Patrem, & de Filio nulla ratione possint intelligi? vel, an falsationis hic ullius simus accusandi? annon ipse vero contortæ & contumeliosæ interpretationis, adversus Filium æque, ac adversus nos? Denique uti majorem modestiam, ita meliorem in hisce mentem, & fidem Adversario, pro omnibus maledictis, ab eodem illo Filio, ex animo apprecamur.
units.tr: Next, he harshly and insultingly charges me with another corruption of Irenaeus' passage in book III, chapter 8. Irenaeus said: "So that he who made all things with his Word is rightly called God and Lord alone." I did not cite it otherwise. But he says that we have given Irenaeus' words as if he had said: "He alone, the Father and his Word, is to be called Lord and God." As if I had construed "his Word" with "is called," when it ought to be construed only with "made." Did I give the words differently, construe them differently, or indeed punctuate them differently from how they are read in Irenaeus, and as our opponent himself reads them? I understood them differently from him: that is true. But will anyone call it corrupting a passage, through manifest falsification, when he does what this man does? He falsifies who cites a passage differently from how it is read, and not he who understands it differently from what his opponent would like. Otherwise, how many falsifications must he himself be held guilty of? He says that in Irenaeus' passage "the Father, not the Son," etc. must be understood, and that it cannot be understood of the Son in any way. I deny this and teach the opposite. Irenaeus' own words are read in the same way by both of us. So he cannot charge me with falsification any more than I can charge him, since our dispute is not about the words but about their true sense. Nor have I been much concerned, or am I concerned, whether "his Word" is construed with "is called" or with "made." I only teach that the Word is to be joined with the Father, as Irenaeus does, and not separated from him, as the opponent does. The Father is with the Word, and makes all things, and so with the Word he is called God and Lord alone. The Father can never be separated from the Son, nor the Son from the Father. Moreover, the argument Irenaeus uses confirms the same thing. For, intending to prove that neither the Prophets nor the Apostles called any other God or Lord except the true and only God, he says at the start of the chapter that all other things are excluded from this name when compared with the Father and "the Word of God, through whom all things were made, who is our Lord Jesus Christ," whom he proves to be and to be called both Lord and God. That is not so with "whether angels, or archangels, or thrones, or dominations, which were established and made by the Word of him who is God over all." The other things made by him, he says, have for that reason a "name altogether different," and "those things that were made are not capable of receiving the same name, nor ought they justly to take that name." What name? That of God and Lord, which belongs properly to the Father together with the Son. Just as he joins the Son with the Father, and distinguishes him from other creatures as creator, so he makes him capable of this name, and says that he rightly takes that title to himself. "So that he who made all things with his Word is rightly called Lord and God alone." Not so with the other things: "Because they were made, they are not capable of this name, nor ought they justly to take the name that belongs to the Creator." Add book III, chapter 6, whose argument is "that in the Scriptures no other is named God, or called Lord, than the one true God, the Father of all, and his Word." These words I have cited and set out in their place, and the opponent passes over them dry-shod. We appeal to the conscience of all who deign to read these things and examine them in Irenaeus: do they exclude the Son, as our opponent wishes, so that only the Father is understood and the Son cannot in any way be meant? Or are we here accused of any falsification, or is it rather he who is guilty of a twisted and insulting interpretation, against the Son no less than against us? Finally, for all his abuse, we pray from our hearts to that same Son that our opponent may have more modesty, a better mind in these matters, and faith.

units.la: Jam & cætera, quæ addit ex eodem Irenæo, & contra ipsum, facili operā est diluere. Uti quod ex eo citat, dicente, id quod magis potest, antiquius est omnibus, quod eo, quem indicat loco, lib. I. cap.v. non lego: quidem, quod adversus Valentinianos disputans, eorum errores recen-
units.tr: Now the rest of what he adds from the same Irenaeus, and against him, is easily answered. As for what he cites from him, saying "that which can do more is older than all things," I do not read this in the passage he indicates, book I, chapter 5. Indeed, in that chapter Irenaeus, disputing against the Valentinians, lists their errors, and their errors against Christ and the Holy Spirit. And he confirms the faith of the Trinity by setting forth the most ancient of all creeds at the beginning of his books, chapter 2.

units.la: Tom. 2. fer, & adversus Christum, & Spiritum Sanctum; & quod fidem Trinita-tis confirmat prolato Symbolo omnium antiquissimo, in librorum suo-rum initio, cap. II. Ecclesia enim per universum orbem usque ad fines terra seminata, & ab Apostolis, & a discipulis eorum accepit eam fidem, qua est in unum Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, qui fecit coelum, & terram, mare & omnia qua in eis sunt, & in unum Jesum Christum filium Dei, incarnatum pro nostra salute, & in Spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: Tom. 2. "For the Church, scattered through the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the Apostles and their disciples that faith by which we believe in one God, the Father Almighty, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them; and in one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, made flesh for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Cæterum neque hæc verba, id quod magis potest, antiquius est omnibus; nec quod alibi dicitur, Christum deseruire Patri; vel, principalitatem in omnibus habere Deum, & priorem esse omnium, & omnibus, ut sint, esse causam, reliqua omnia autem ipsi esse subjecta; vel, quod Filium appellat potens verbum, forte non omnipotentem ifthic loci, quem notat, lib. v. in initio: &, Filium vel Verbum portari a Patre; unum Deum Patrem esse, qui est super omnia, & per omnia, & in omnibus, & caput Christi: hæc, dico, veræ & æternæ Christi Deitati nequaquam incommodant: quia vel dicuntur de Patre in ordine ad creaturas, non ad Filium; vel de Filio, non respectu substantiæ divinæ, & quatenus in, ac cum Patre esse, ipsi Irenæo dicitur; sed, vel generationis personalis, aut incarnationis, quam passim docet, & apud Epiphanium, hæref.xxxi. vel officii Mediatorii ratione: aut de Filio non negant, eum esse quod credimus, aut contrarium adstruunt: denique illa de Patre affirmant, quæ & Filio conveniunt, quin etiam ut argumentum pro Filii Deitate adferri possunt.
units.tr: Moreover, neither these words, which can more properly be said, are older than all others; nor is it the case that Christ serves the Father, or that God has the first place in all things and is prior to all, and the cause of all things being, and that all else is subject to him; nor that he calls the Son "powerful Word," perhaps not "almighty" in the place he refers to in book 5 at the beginning; nor that the Son or Word is carried by the Father; nor that the Father is the one God, who is above all, through all, in all, and the head of Christ. These things, I say, by no means conflict with the true and eternal deity of Christ, because they are either said of the Father in relation to creatures, not to the Son; or said of the Son, not with respect to the divine substance, but in so far as he is said to be in and with the Father, as Irenaeus himself says; but with respect to his personal generation or incarnation, which he teaches everywhere, and in Epiphanius, heresy 31; or with respect to his mediatorial office. Or else they do not deny that the Son is what we believe him to be, or they assert the contrary. Finally, they affirm of the Father things which also belong to the Son, and indeed these can be brought forward as an argument for the deity of the Son.

units.la: Quemadmodum quod lib. iv. cap. v. Irenæus de Chri-sto ait, quod fabricatorem omnium appellat Deum & magnum regem, quod non fieret, nisi alius effet ipso superior; qui autem super se habet aliquem superiorem, & sub alterius potestate est, hic neque Deus, neque magnus rex dici potest, inquit Noster: at Christus & Deus, & rex dici-tur, & magnus etiam, & formator seu creator omnium. Loquitur au-tem de superiore, & altero Deo Irenæus, qualem nec Pater habet, nec Filius. Jam lib. iv. cap. lxxv. dicens, infectum Deum, & priorem omnibus, reliqua vero omnia in subjectione manere Dei, quod Noster addit, puta ne Filio quidem excepto, majori jure possemus falsationem dicere verborum, ac ipse nobis eam supra affingere conatus fuit. De creaturis enim intelligitur reliquis, non de Filio ipso creatore. Quemadmodum aliter de eo & tota mox Trinitate loquitur, hominem dicens factum ad similitudinem infecti Dei. Quis ille? Patre quidem bene sentiente, Filio vero ministrante & formante, spiritu vero nutriente & augente. Et post quam differentiam infecti Dei à reliquis omnibus putet, significat, iis, contra quos agit, impingens, quod, antequam fiant homines, jam volunt similes esse factori Deo, & nullam esse differentiam infecti Dei, & nunc facti hominis, qui plus irrationales sunt, quam muta animalia. Ergo diversum dicit infectum à factis, sive creatorem à creaturis, Deum ab homine, non Patrem à Filio. Ex quibus, & aliis, quæ suo loco adduximus, apparet, vere nos dixisse, ista eandem Filii cum Patre probare Deitatem, & Deitatis æqualitatem seu identitatem.
units.tr: Likewise, when Irenaeus says of Christ in book 4, chapter 5, that he calls the maker of all things God and great King, which would not be so unless there were another superior to him; and that one who has someone superior above himself and is under another's power cannot be called God or great King, says our author; yet Christ is called both God and King, and great too, and the former and creator of all things. But Irenaeus is speaking of a superior and other God, such as neither the Father nor the Son has. Again, in book 4, chapter 75, where he says that God is unmade and prior to all, but all other things remain in subjection to God, which our author adds, namely, not even the Son excepted, we could with greater right call it a falsification of words, and he himself has tried to fasten it upon us above. For it is understood of the other creatures, not of the Son himself, the creator. In the same way he speaks differently of him and of the whole Trinity shortly after, saying that man was made in the likeness of the unmade God. Who is he? The Father indeed willing well, but the Son ministering and forming, and the Spirit nourishing and increasing. And after this, he thinks there is a difference between the unmade God and all others; he signifies this, striking at those against whom he is writing, that before men are made, they already want to be like the maker God, and that there is no difference between the unmade God and the now-made man, who are more irrational than dumb animals. Therefore he says that the unmade differs from the made, that is, the Creator from creatures, God from man, not the Father from the Son. From these and other passages which we have cited in their place, it is clear that we were right to say that these very things prove the same deity of the Son with the Father, and the equality or identity of the deity.

units.la: Denique Tertullianum, ultimum allegatorum autorem, quod concernit, ex quo satagunt probare, ipsum solum Patrem summum Deum, Filium autem eo minorem, credidisse: Patri monarchiam principaliter competere, Filio vero & Spiritui S. minus principaliter & secundario: ad ea i jam respondimus, & nihil ad rei substantiam nobis officere, demonstratum. Nam & Personarum in Deo Trinitatem illum statuisse, negari non potest, & eas substantiâ convenire. Sic enim loquitur, etiam apud Nostrum, pag. 374. Caeterum qui Filium non aliunde deduco, sed de substantiâ Patris, nihil facientem sine Patris voluntate, omnem a Patre consecutum potestatem, quomodo possum de fide destruere monarchiam, quam a Patre filio traditam in filio servo. Hoc mihi & in tertium gradum dictum sit, quia spiritum non aliunde puto, quam a Patre per Filium. De substantiâ Patris Filius est: citra cujus voluntatem nihil facit, habetque omnem potestatem, & monarchiam sive divinam unitatem, à Patre. Sic & Spiritus Sanctus. Etenim nequaquam unitatem à Trinitate everti, multis docet. Jam vero quando monarchiam Filio dicit traditam, & reddendam Patri, hodie apud Filium est, inquit, sed in suo statu, quo restituendam docet, cum tradiderit regnum Deo & Patri: quod uti de ipsa Filii persona, & geni-to Filio resorbendo aliquando à Patre intelligi nequit, ita de regno, seu œconomiâ istâ regni debet intelligi, quâ Pater nunc omnia regit per Filium Mediatorem, qui modus regni aliquando desiturus est, at nunquam propterea ipse Filius.
units.tr: Finally, as for Tertullian, the last author cited, from whom they strive to prove that he believed the Father alone to be the supreme God and the Son inferior to him, that the sovereignty belongs chiefly to the Father, but to the Son and Holy Spirit less chiefly and in a secondary way: to these points I have already replied, and it has been shown that they do nothing against the substance of the matter. For it cannot be denied that he also held a Trinity of Persons in God, and that these agree in substance. For he speaks thus, also in our author's citation, p. 374: Moreover, I do not derive the Son from anywhere else but from the substance of the Father, who does nothing without the Father's will, who has received from the Father all power; how can I destroy the monarchy from the faith, when it was handed down by the Father to the Son, who remains a servant? This is said to me also concerning the third degree, because I think the Spirit comes from nowhere else than from the Father through the Son. The Son is from the substance of the Father, does nothing without his will, and has all power and the monarchy, or divine unity, from the Father. So also the Holy Spirit. And indeed he teaches in many places that unity is by no means overturned by the Trinity. Now when he says that the monarchy was handed over to the Son and is to be returned to the Father, today it is with the Son, he says, but in its own state, into which he teaches it is to be restored, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father. Just as this cannot be understood of the very person of the Son, nor of the Son being at some time reabsorbed by the Father, so it must be understood of the kingdom, or of that economy of the kingdom, by which the Father now rules all things through the Son as Mediator, a mode of reign which will at some time cease, but the Son himself never on that account.

units.la: Quod vero subjungit, Trinitatis illam œconomiam à Tertulliano introductam, novam tum fuisse, neque pluribus receptam, & de Simone Mago istius primo autore hic iterum, non pro figmentis tantum, sed calumniis in S. fidem, & ejus doctores, merito habemus. Nam, ne de Simone iterum dicam, quum id supra satis discussum sit; quæ hic mirum in modum accumulat, paris omnia sunt fidei: ut quod Catholicam & communem Christianorum sententiam de homoufio, Sabbellianam esse contendit: hanc fluere, & sic nostram quoque, ex schola Simonis Magi: à Juftino vero, & Tertulliano pòst, de Trinitate personarum doctrinam cepisse originem: Quæ alia aliis sunt salsiora.
units.tr: As for what he adds, that that economy of the Trinity was introduced by Tertullian, that it was then new and not received by many, and that Simon Magus was its first author, we rightly hold this to be not only fiction but slander against the holy faith and its teachers, which he here again piles up in wonderful measure. For, not to speak again of Simon, since this has already been sufficiently discussed above, all these things he gathers here are of the same kind: as when he contends that the Catholic and common opinion of Christians concerning the homoousion is Sabellian, that this flows from it, and that ours too comes from the school of Simon Magus; and that the doctrine of the Trinity of persons received its origin from Justin and afterwards Tertullian. Some of these are more absurd than others.

units.la: Profert Gregorium Neocaesarienfem, in disputatione contra Ælia-num, apud Basilium, epist.64. quod dixerit, Patrem & Filium ἑτεροίᾳ μὲν ἐννοίᾳ δύο, ὑποστάσει δὲ ἕν, mentis quidem consideratione duos, hypostasi vero unum. quæ primùm non sunt verba Basilii de Gregorio, sed Adversariorum Sabellianorum, qui ista quasi Gregorii in suam rem proferebant. Et perstringit Basilius, non satis bonâ fide ab Adversariis producì, quasi à Gregorio fuissent dicta, quæ vel non dixerat, vel saltem non eo sensu: sed illos in eo ingenii sui prodere vafritiem, quemadmodum in aliis, quod sub nomine Gregorii illa jactarent, in præjudicium fidei, καθήκων δέ τινα πεῖραν ἀπ' ἐπιστολῆς, καὶ πρὸς τὸν ὁμόψυχον ἡμῶν Ἀνθιμον τὸν Τυάνων ἐπίσκοπον· ὡς ἀφ' Γρη-γορίου εἰπόντι[?], dederunt autem experimentum aliquod per epistolam etiam adejusdem nobiscum sententia Anthymum Tyanorum episcopum: quasi Gregorium dixerit. Ut hic possem perstringere Adversarium, quod non consideraret in Græco illud ὡς ac, quasi, & citarit illa quasi à Basilio de Gregorio dicta, quum sint Adversariorum; si luberet ipsi mutuum rependere? sed nobis satis est convinci hominem, & quærimus aliorum conversionem, non confusionem. Præterea, ad sensum verborum, subdit Basilius, nequaquam in Sabellianorum sententia Gregorium fuisse, sed illa in disputatione dicta fuisse adversus Ælianum, ἢ δογματικῶς ἀλλ' ἀγωνιστικῶς, non dogmatice, sed in contentione; nec recte ab illis intelligi, τὴν ἡ οὐκ ἠδυνήθησαν[?] ζωὴν[?] intelligere nequiverunt, qui propter intelligendi subtilitatem beatos se reputant. Porro in fidei Expositione Gregorii, unde verba illa desumta, multos alios errores occurrere descriptorum, aperte testatur Basilius, ἐν ᾗ πολλὰ τ' ὑπογραψαμένων ἐς[?] σφάλματα, quemadmodum ex ipsis verbis se recipit ostensurum. Tum Gregorium ibi egisse cum Gentili, quem ad fidem adducere nitebatur: & propterea non existimasse sibi de verbis exactius disceptandum esse, ὡς ἡγεῖτο χρῆναι ἀκριβολογεῖσθαι περὶ τὰ ῥήματα. Quapropter & plu-res ibi occurrere voces, quibus hæretici abutantur, quasi ipsis faverent, inter quas ponit τὰ κτίσματα, ποίημα, creatura, factura & similia. Denique multa illic reperiri, ait, dicta de conjunctione cum homine, quæ ad divinidivinitatis rationem referunt imperite, ἀτωσβεύτως[?], quale & hoc ipsum est quod ab istis circumfertur. Atque hæc de Gregorii illo dicto, apud Basilium: in quo adducendo, magis autem interpretando, ut fe gesserit Noster, apparere arbitror. Quamvis etiam commodum sensum dare verbis Gregorii, etiamsi prout adducuntur, legantur, non fit difficile: quod & Petavius facit, lib. i. de Trinitate, cap. iv. §. xi. & Bellarminus, de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, voce hypostasis, quod Veteribus frequens fuit, acceptâ pro effentiâ. Quemadmodum Hieronymus scribit, in epift. ad Damasum, tota facularium littarum Schola nihil aliud hypoftafin, nisi ufian novit. Et sic est una Patris Filiique hypostasis, id est, effentia; ὑπόστασις[?] verò differunt. Uti vicissim alii substantias accipiunt pro personis. Hilarius, lib. iv. de Trinit. quapropter tres substantia sunt, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus. Ubi in margine posuit Erasmus, tres substantia ὑποστάσεις[?]: Similiter loquitur Hilarius, lib. iv. Quod dici adversus Sabellianos, explicat in lib. de Synodis, volens igitur congregata sanctorum Synodus impietatem eam perimere, qua veritatem patris & filii & Spiritus Sancti, nominum numero eluderet, ut non subsistente causa uniuscujusque nominis, triplex nuncupatio obtineret sub falsitate nominum unionem, ut pater solus atque unus idem atque ipse haberet & Spiritus Sancti nomen & Filii, idcirco tres substantias esse dixerunt, subsistentium personas per substantias edocentes, non substantiam Patris, & Filii & Spiritus Sancti diversitate dissimilis effentia separantes. Quapropter ex diversa vocis hypostasis acceptione, quæ apud Veteres, uti & substantiæ, non semper fuit eadem, ob diversas adeo causas, male colligit Adversarius, aut Gregorium Neo-Cæsariensem fuisse Sabellianum; aut hoc à Basilio doceri; aut omnes fere, quod scribit, pag. 377. Sabellii sententiâ fuisse commaculatos. Quamvis enim Basilius dicat, errorem illum olim extinctum infandæ hæresis autores iterum renovare: non propterea scribit, omnes eo infectos. Nam quoties id non fit, ut vetera errorum portenta quasi ex orco revocentur & reviviscant? An qui diceret, per Servetum ante fæculum, per similes ei socios hodie nefandæ hæresis extincta olim dogmata in scenam reproduci, eo testaretur cunctos aut plurimos, habitâ ad Catholicos comparatione, illâ esse imprægnatos? Certe id de Sabellianis, ætate Basilii, dici non potuit. Minime autem ptobabit Noster, aut per homousion, à Christianis Sabellianismum adoptatum; vel Sabellium sententiam suam à Simone Mago mutuatum fuisse. Nam quamvis Sabellius unam dixerit trium essentiam, quod etiam Catholici, non proinde hi in Sabellii sententiam concedere dici debent, nisi omnium haereticorum singulas etiam sententias Catholicis affricare velis, propter hoc quod forte in illis rectae fidei est. Nulla etenim tam deformis & tetra unquam haeresis, quae non aliquid semper agnoverit boni. Primo quidem dicam tibi, non ideo non utatur & veritas vocabulo isto, & re ac censu ejus, quia & haeresis utitur: imo haeresis potius ex veritate accepit, quod ad mendacium suum strueret: ut verba Tertulliani hic usurpem, quae habet adversus Praxeam, cap. vi. Fides enim inter Sabellianos, & Arianos ita incedit media & & recta, ut nec ad hos deflectat propter illos, nec in illos recidat, quando ab his abhorret. Ambrosius, de fide, lib. ii. cap. ii. nec juxta Sabellianos Patrem Filiumque confundens, nec juxta Arianos Patrem Filiumque secernens. Pater enim & Filius distinctionem habent ut Pater & Filius, separationem divinitatis non habent. Vel, quamvis Simon Magus se dixerit jam ut Patrem, tum ut Filium, demum ut Spiritum Sanctum appa-ruisse, proinde idem voluit, vel ab illo mutuatus fuit Sabellius, quod de Deo personâ uno, triplici tantum nomine diversum, & jam ut Patrem, aliquando ut Filium, nonnunquam ut Spiritum Sanctum, asseruit.
units.tr: The author cites Gregory of Neocaesarea, in his disputation against Aelianus, as quoted by Basil in Epistle 64: that he said the Father and the Son are two in mental conception, but one in hypostasis [ἑτεροίᾳ μὲν ἐννοίᾳ δύο, ὑποστάσει δὲ ἕν]. First, these are not Basil's words about Gregory but the words of the Sabellian opponents, who put them forward as Gregory's in support of their own cause. Basil also rebukes the Adversary, who was not honest enough, for quoting as if from Gregory things that he either did not say or did not say in that sense. Those men, he says, betrayed their cunning in this, as in other matters, by bringing forward under Gregory's name things that would prejudice the faith: they produced some sample also from an epistle, sent to Anthymus, bishop of Tyana, who shares our view, as if Gregory had said it [καθήκων δέ τινα πεῖραν ἀπ' ἐπιστολῆς, καὶ πρὸς τὸν ὁμόψυχον ἡμῶν Ἀνθιμον τὸν Τυάνων ἐπίσκοπον· ὡς ἀφ' Γρηγορίου εἰπόντι]. Here I might have charged the Adversary in turn: he failed to notice the Greek word as, or as if, and cited as said by Gregory, through Basil, words that belong to the Adversaries. Why should I not repay him in kind? But it is enough for us to convict the man; we seek his conversion, not his confusion. Further, as to the sense of the words, Basil adds that Gregory was in no way of the Sabellian opinion, but that those words were spoken in the disputation against Aelianus, not dogmatically but polemically, in contention; and they were not rightly understood by those who could not grasp the life [τὴν ἡ οὐκ ἠδυνήθησαν ζωὴν] and failed to understand it, though they count themselves blessed for their subtlety of understanding. Moreover, Basil openly testifies that in Gregory's exposition of the faith, from which those words are taken, many other errors occur, put down by those who wrote it out [ἐν ᾗ πολλὰ τ' ὑπογραψαμένων ἐς σφάλματα], as he says he will show from the words themselves. Then, he says, Gregory was there dealing with a Gentile whom he was trying to bring to the faith; and so he did not think he had to dispute about words more exactly, since he thought it right to be precise about the words [ὡς ἡγεῖτο χρῆναι ἀκριβολογεῖσθαι περὶ τὰ ῥήματα]. For this reason, several words occur there which heretics misuse as if they favoured them, among them the terms creatures, a making, a creature, a work and the like [τὰ κτίσματα, ποίημα]. Finally, Basil says, many things are found there about the union with man which clumsily refer to the nature of the Godhead [ἀτωσβεύτως], and this very thing is what those men now circulate. So much for that saying of Gregory's as cited by Basil; I think that in citing it, or rather in explaining it, our author's conduct is plain. Yet it is not hard to give a fair sense to Gregory's words even as they are quoted and read, as Petavius does, On the Trinity, book 1, chapter 4, section 11, and Bellarmine in On Ecclesiastical Writers, under the word hypostasis, which the Ancients often took to mean essence. Thus Jerome writes in his letter to Damasus: the whole school of the grammarians knows of no hypostasis but the substance. And so there is one hypostasis of the Father and the Son, that is, one essence; but hypostasis and person differ. In turn, others take substance for person. Hilary, in book 4 of On the Trinity: wherefore there are three substances, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Erasmus put in the margin there: three substances, hypostases. Hilary speaks in the same way in book 4. He explains what is said against the Sabellians in his book On the Synods: the synod of the saints, wishing to destroy that impiety which, by counting names, would mock the truth of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, so that, with no underlying reality for each name, a threefold naming might hold under a false unity of names, so that the one Father alone should also have the name of the Holy Spirit and of the Son, therefore they said there are three substances, teaching that the persons subsist through the substances, not separating the Father, Son and Holy Spirit by a difference of unlike essence. Therefore, from the differing use of the word hypostasis, which among the Ancients, like substance, was not always the same, and for various causes, the Adversary wrongly infers either that Gregory of Neocaesarea was a Sabellian, or that this was taught by Basil, or that almost all, as he writes at page 377, were tainted with the opinion of Sabellius. For although Basil says that the authors of an unspeakable heresy renew that error, long since extinguished, he does not therefore write that all were infected with it. For whenever this does not happen, how are the old monsters of error not called back, as it were from the underworld, and brought to life again? Would anyone who said that through Servetus, a century ago, and through similar companions today, long-extinguished doctrines of an abominable heresy are being revived on the stage, thereby be declaring that all or most, compared with the Catholics, were steeped in it? Certainly that could not be said of the Sabellians in Basil's time. Nor will our author prove that Sabellianism was adopted by Christians through the word homoousion, or that Sabellius borrowed his opinion from Simon Magus. For although Sabellius spoke of one essence of three, which the Catholics also do, these men should not on that account be said to concede to the opinion of Sabellius, unless you wish to lay against the Catholics every single opinion of every heretic, on the ground that perhaps some part of right faith is in them. For there has never been a heresy so deformed and foul that it did not always recognise some good. In the first place, I tell you, truth does not therefore refrain from using that word, and its reality and worth, because heresy uses it too; rather, heresy took from truth what it might build upon for its lie, to use here the words of Tertullian against Praxeas, chapter 6. For faith among the Sabellians and the Arians walks in the middle and straight way, so that it neither bends toward these on account of those, nor falls back into those when it shrinks from these. Ambrose, On the Faith, book 2, chapter 2: neither confounding Father and Son after the manner of the Sabellians, nor separating Father and Son after the manner of the Arians. For the Father and the Son have a distinction as Father and Son; they do not have a separation of the Godhead. Or, although Simon Magus said that he had appeared first as the Father, then as the Son, and last as the Holy Spirit, either Simon meant the same thing, or Sabellius borrowed from him the claim that one person of God, differing only in threefold name, is now the Father, at another time the Son, and at another the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Sed ad Tertullianum, quem Autorem Noster facit introductae apud Christianos Trinitatis personarum, post Justinum; atque à plerisque Christianis, tum adhuc rejectae: adducit illum in libro adversus Praxeam scribentem: Simplices enim quique ne dixerim imprudentes & idiotae (quae ma-jor semper credentium pars est) quoniam & ipsa regula fidei à pluribus diis seculi, ad unicum & verum Deum transfert: non intelligentes unicum quidem, sed cum sua οἰκονομίᾳ esse credendum, expavescunt ad οἰκονομίαν. Quae non dicunt, ut inde colligitur, Trinitatis oeconomiam à plerisque Christianis rejectam fuisse, sed rudes & idiotas, ex imprudentiâ & simplicitate, illam non rectè statim percepisse, sed magis ac magis instruendos fuisse, praesertim adversus Praxeanorum & similium tentationes, & Diaboli ipsius; de quo in initio dixerat: Varie Diabolus æmulatus est veritatem. Adfectavit illam aliquando defendendo concutere. Unicum dominum vindicat omnipotentem mundi conditorem, ut & de unico hæresim faciat.
units.tr: But as for Tertullian, whom our author makes the introducer, after Justin, of the doctrine of the persons of the Trinity among Christians, and one rejected at that time by most Christians, he cites him as writing in the book against Praxeas: For simple people, I would not say foolish and unlearned (and these are always the greater part of believers), since the rule of faith itself turns them from many gods of the world to the one and true God, not understanding that the one God must indeed be believed with his economy, they shrink from the economy. These words do not say, as one may gather, that the economy of the Trinity was rejected by most Christians; they say that the simple and unlearned, through lack of thought and simplicity, did not at once rightly grasp it, and had to be instructed more and more, especially against the temptations of the Praxeans and the like, and of the Devil himself. Of him Tertullian had said at the outset: The Devil has variously imitated the truth. At one time he aimed to shake it by defending it. He claims the one Lord, the almighty Creator of the world, so that he may make a heresy out of the one God too.

units.la: An verò haec jam probant, plerosque Christianos Diabolo occupatos in admittendis ejus tentationibus fuisse? Etiam in pluribus aliis fidei articulis probe cognoscendis & defendendis haerere Christianorum multos, praesertim simplices & rudiores, compertum est: de quo videsis Augustini tractatum, de Catechizandis rudibus: quod ideo non probat concontrarias fidei sententias à Christianorum pluribus admitti, vel illos nolle, uti pag. 382. Noster loquitur, communia Ecclesiæ dogmata, vel Doctorum ejus recipere, & Filium à Patre distinguere. Et quid si illud etiam dixisset Tertullianus, tantumque Praxeanæ in seducendis hominibus perversitati tum temporis tribuisset, quando fructificaverant avenæ Praxeanæ, hic quoque superseminatæ, dormientibus multis in simplicitate doctrinæ: an propterea vel actum de veritate doctrinæ, vel non etiam evulsæ, & postquam eruptæ iterum avenæ istæ, non quoque eradicandas scribit, & quod die suo colligentur omnes adulteræ fruges, & cum cæteris scandalis igni inextinguibili cremabuntur? Neque dicit Tertullianus, vel dicere potuit, quod nec Græci œconomiam Trinitatis intelligere aut admittere voluere: sed Græce loquentes intelligit, qui circa explicationem tum μοναρχίας, tum οἰκονομίας hærebant, à se edocendos: nam de linguæ usu vel sono disserit, non de Græcis aliis. Et ita sonum ipsum vocaliter exprimunt etiam Latini, etiam opici, ut puto illos tam bene intelligere μοναρχίαν quam enunciant. Sed μοναρχίαν sonare student Latini, οἰκονομίαν intelligere volunt etiam Græci. At ego si quid utriusque linguæ præcepsi &c. ostenditque porro μοναρχίαν, cum οἰκονομίᾳ personarum rite consistere: & quamvis Patri principalitatem attribuat, à quo communicatur in Filium, tamen eandem utriusque dicit & substantiam, & monarchiam, quæ à duobus tam unicis continetur. Quale est ut Deus divisionem & dispersionem pati videatur in Filio & Spiritu Sancto, secundum & tertium sortitis locum, tam consortibus substantiæ Patris. Cæterum, qui Filium non aliunde deduco, sed de substantia Patris, nihil facientem sine Patris voluntate, omnem à Patre consecutum potestatem, quomodo possum de fide destruere monarchiam, quam à Patre Filio traditam, in Filio servo? Hoc mihi & in tertium gradum dictum sit, quia Spiritum non aliunde puto, quàm à Patre per Filium. Explicat sententiam & doctrinam de Trinitatis œconomiâ, simplicioribus inter credentes, atque tuetur eam contra adversarios Praxeanos. Nam adversarios eum habuisse, uti & nos semper, doctrinæ & fidei, nec mirum, nec novum: unde neque adversus eam, neque ejus credentes quidquam colligi potest, quod non adversus quoscunque alios fidei articulos, & quæcunque ejus tempora, ab hostibus & adversariis concludi possit. Jam & ante dixerat Tertullianus: quasi non sic quoque unus sit omnia, dum ex uno omnia, per substantiam scilicet unitatem: & nihilominus custodiatur οἰκονομίας sacramentum, qua unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens, patrem, & filium, & spiritum sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu: nec substantia, sed formanes nec potestate, sed specie: unius autem substantiæ, & unius status, & unius potestatis: quia unus Deus, ex quo & gradus isti & formæ, & species, in nomine patris, & filii, & spiritus sancti deputantur. Ex quibus explicari possunt & debent, quæ aliàs dicit de Filio, esse eum substantiæ Patris derivationem & portionem. Ad quod suo loco respondimus, & quod dictum nobis de stylo Tertulliani fuit, ejusque duritie & stridore, quo, si bene memini, verbo Junius de Tertulliano loquens, usus fuit, inficiari hoc nemo potest, nisi qui Autorem non attente legerit, ut frustra illud judicium in me suggillet. Accipe Hieronymum, in epist. ad Paulinum; Tertullianus creber est in sententiis, sed difficilis in loquendo. Lactantium Firmianum, lib. v. cap. 1. Septimius quoque Tertullianus, fuit omni genere litterarum peritus, sed in eloquendo parum facilis & minus comptus & multum obscurus fuit. Accedit, quod primus Latinorum de hac materia scripsit; & librum hunc adversus Praxeam, postquam ad prophetias Montani fuerat delapsus. Interim utcunque distributionem inter Trinitatis personas, non tamen diversitatem fecit; distinctionem, non divisionem; eandem dicens trium substantiam, potestatem, statum: ex quibus, etiam secundum regulas exponendi ab Autore nostro datas, de phrasibus ejus aliis & magis duris pronunciari debet, & ferri judicium. Atque ita iterum diximus de decem ex primis in Ecclesiâ Christianâ scriptoribus, qui adversus fidem & doctrinam nostram de Trinitate identidem proferuntur, ostendimusque, quamvis loquendi forte & exponendi ardua mysteria modo, quod in primis scriptoribus ferri à sequentibus æquum est, à nobis diffidere videantur, in rei tamen summâ non dissentire, sed agnoscere veram in Deo Personarum Trinitatem, ejusdem substantiæ, &, ut loquitur Terrullianus, status, ac potestatis: unde quidquid aliàs de distinctione aut differentiâ loquuntur, cum illis debet conciliari, & convenire in re unius substantiæ, & unius status, & unius potestatis. Sic Christum postea, cap. xvii. utriusque substantiæ fuisse dicit: & paulò post, Quanquam cum dua substantiæ censeantur in Christo Jesu divina & humana, constet autem immortalem esse divinam cum mortalem qua humana sit, apparet quatenus eum mortuum dicat: id est qua carnem & hominem & filium hominis, non qua spiritum & sermonem & dei filium. Alia ex Tertulliano, & Cypriano, ejus discipulo, cujus non potuit alia esse à Magistro sententia, facile proferri possunt, & prolata sunt à Petavio, in Præfat. cap. v. & à nobis, Tom. I. lib. II. cap.v. Quæ, ut & alia à nobis in hanc rem scripta, quia non attingit Noster, vel quæ in iteratâ Irenici Confirmatione ponit multa, nos non tangunt, neque causam, prætermittimus, & duo quæ prioribus superaddit, ex Symbolo nempe, & Artemonitarum sectâ, quamvis ad ea jam responderi-mus, tamen iterum expendenda sunt, & videndum fi quæ meliora vel certiora prioribus attulerit:
units.tr: But do these arguments prove that most Christians were caught up in accepting the Devil's temptations? It is well known that many Christians, especially simple and less learned people, have stuck in their understanding and defence of several other articles of faith. On this see Augustine's treatise On Catechizing the Uninstructed, which does not show that contrary opinions on the faith were accepted by most Christians, or that they did not want to hold the common doctrines of the Church and its teachers and to distinguish the Son from the Father, as our author says on p. 382. And what if Tertullian had also said this, and had attributed so much to the perversity of Praxeas in misleading people at that time, when the oats of Praxeas had borne fruit, sown here too while many slept in the simplicity of doctrine? Does it follow that the truth of the doctrine was ruined, or that those oats were not also uprooted? Once they had sprung up again, he writes that they must be eradicated too, and that on its day all the adulterous crops will be gathered and burned with the other offences in unquenchable fire. Tertullian does not say, nor could he have said, that the Greeks also refused to understand or admit the economy of the Trinity. He is speaking to Greek speakers, who were stuck over the explanation of both monarchy and economy, and who were to be taught by him; for he is discussing the use and sound of a word, not other Greeks. Thus Latins too pronounce the sound itself aloud, and even the rustics, as I suppose, understand monarchia as well as they pronounce it. But Latins try to pronounce monarchia, and Greeks want to understand oikonomia too. But if I have anything of either language [...] and he further shows that monarchy stands properly together with the economy of the persons. Although he attributes principality to the Father, from whom the Son is communicated, he still says that both have the same substance and monarchy, which is contained in two so unique. How is it that God seems to suffer division and dispersion in the Son and the Holy Spirit, who hold the second and third places, companions of the same substance as the Father? Moreover, I do not derive the Son from anywhere else but from the substance of the Father, doing nothing without the Father's will, having received all power from the Father. How can I, in faith, destroy the monarchy handed down from the Father to the Son, when the Son is a servant? Let this also be said to me about the third degree, because I think the Spirit comes from nowhere else than from the Father through the Son. He explains the doctrine of the economy of the Trinity to the simpler believers, and defends it against the Praxean opponents. That he had opponents, as we always do, of doctrine and faith, is neither surprising nor new. Hence nothing can be inferred against this doctrine or its believers that could not equally be inferred by enemies and adversaries against any other article of faith and any other period. Already before, Tertullian had said: as if one is not also thus all things, since all things are from one, namely by the unity of substance; and nevertheless the sacrament of the economy is kept, which arranges the unity into a Trinity, setting out three, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. But the three are not of condition but of degree, not of substance but of form, not of power but of appearance; yet of one substance, one condition and one power, because it is one God from whom these degrees, forms and appearances are reckoned in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. From these passages can and must be explained what he says elsewhere about the Son, that he is a derivation and portion of the substance of the Father. We have replied to this in its place. As for what was said to us about Tertullian's style, and its harshness and grating, which, if I remember rightly, Junius used the word for when speaking of Tertullian, no one can deny it except one who has not read the author carefully, so that the judgement he brings against me is in vain. Take Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus: Tertullian is rich in sentiments, but difficult in speech. Lactantius Firmianus, book 5, chapter 1: Septimius Tertullian too was skilled in every kind of literature, but in speaking he was little easy, less polished and very obscure. Moreover, he was the first of the Latins to write on this matter, and this book against Praxeas was written after he had fallen into the prophecies of Montanus. Meanwhile, however he distributed the persons of the Trinity, he did not make a diversity; he made a distinction, not a division, saying that the three are of one substance, power and condition. From these, and according to the rules of interpretation given by our author himself, his other and harder phrases ought to be pronounced upon and judged. Thus again we have said of the ten earliest writers in the Christian Church, who are repeatedly brought forward against our faith and doctrine of the Trinity: we have shown that although in manner of speaking and in explaining the lofty mysteries they seem to differ from us, which is fair for later writers to bear from the earliest, nevertheless in the substance of the matter they do not disagree, but acknowledge the true Trinity of persons in God, of one substance and, as Tertullian says, of one condition and power. Hence whatever else they say about distinction or difference must be reconciled with those, and agree in the matter of one substance, one condition and one power. So later, in chapter 17, he says that Christ was of both substances; and a little after: Although two substances, divine and human, are reckoned in Christ Jesus, and it is clear that the divine is immortal while the human is mortal, it appears in what respect he says that he died: namely in respect of the flesh, the man and the son of man, not in respect of the spirit, the word and the Son of God. Other passages from Tertullian and from Cyprian, his disciple, whose view could not differ from his master's, can easily be quoted, and have been quoted by Petavius in the Preface, chapter 5, and by us in Tome I, book II, chapter 5. Since our author does not touch these, nor the many things he puts in the repeated Confirmation of the Irenicum, which do not concern us or the cause, we pass them over. The two points he adds to the earlier ones, namely from the Creed and from the sect of the Artemonites, although we have already answered them, must nevertheless be considered again, and we must see whether he has brought anything better or more certain than before.

units.la: Atque in Symbolo urget, quod nihil continetur, præterquam quod Christus fit unigenitus Dei Filius, non verò natus ante mundi constitu-tionem. Sed, an hoc negatur Symbolo? annon & plura sunt, quæ eo non continentur, nec exponuntur plenius? non etiam qualia Veteribus credita palam constat de Filio Dei, & Christo? Tertullianus, in expo-nendâ regulâ fidei, lib. de Præfcript. cap. i v. dicit Filium, verbum primò omnium emissum, & Deum omnia per Verbum istud ex nihilo produxisse, Id Verbum Filium ejus appellatum, in nomine Dei varie visum à Patriarchis in Prophetis semper auditum, postremo delatum ex Spiritu Patris Dei & virtute in virginem Mariam. ergo regulâ illâ etiam significatum, ante constitu-tionem mundi natum Dei Filium, & per hunc omnia fuisse creata: quæ tamen totidem verbis in Symbolo non legas. Ex quibus patet, vocem Filii Dei, in Symbolo, non tantum de homine Jesu Christo intelligi debere: nec sequi, de Christo ibi recensetur, quod natus, quod passus, & mortuus, ergo hominem tantum vult credi, nec Deum. Nam & vos Deum jactatis, quamvis Deus hic non dicatur. Nec mirum, quia Symbolum inter prima, quod ad hunc articulum, factum, & rudioribus prima exhibens fidei fundamenta, non omnia explicare neceffum duxit, uti contra vim hæresium postea factum: quandoquidem in primis quarumcunque rerum, legum, scientiarum compendiis ac tabulis, breviter duntaxat notari præcipua capita solent, non omni modo eadem exponi. Porro nec in Symbolo multa habes de Deo, quæ etiam necessariò credenda sunt; neque sex illa, quæ proferre Sociniani solent, ibi sunt expressa: non de Dei providentiâ, beneficiis Christi, justificatione, sanctificatione & similibus, quæ comprehensa sensu dicere solemus, verbis αὐτολέξει non extant. Accedit, quod, dum Patres vulgo statuisse, ais, Christum Dei Filium, natum ante mundi creationem, quamvis inferiorem Patre, non potes ex Patrum symbolo probare illa de Dei Filio intelligi debere tantum de Christo facto homine, & ex Mariâ nato &c. non etiam nato, ex ipsorum sententiâ, ante mundi creationem. Satis habuerunt Filium Dei confiteri, & hoc exprimere, antequam conceptum & natum dicerent. Fortius verò sic instruamus ex Symbolo argumentum contra vos & vestram sententiam : qui Patres (nam hos Symboli autores fuisse, non Apostolos, satis notum) crediderunt, Christum esse Filium Dei unigenitum, antequam conceptus, natus, & homo ex Maria factus fuit, illi verbis istis noluerunt significare, Christum tantum Filium Dei factum, postquam conceptus & natus homo fuit. Accipe & aliud: qui, ubi mentionem adscensionis Chri-sti faciunt unius tantum, post resurrectionem, neque meminerunt unquam alterius adscensionis Christi, tempore quadragesimalis jejunii, ad accipiendam a Patre doctrinam & mandata, illi adscensionem talem nunquam crediderunt: quam tamen docent Sociniani. Possem & alia addere ex Symbolo adversus illos argumenta, sed illa arbitror sufficere.
units.tr: And in the Creed he presses that it contains nothing except that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God, not that he was born before the foundation of the world. But is this denied in the Creed? Are there not many things which it does not contain and does not explain more fully? Are there not also things which were clearly believed by the ancients concerning the Son of God and Christ? Tertullian, in expounding the rule of faith in the book On Prescription, chapter 4, says that the Son is the Word, first of all things sent forth, and that God produced all things out of nothing through this Word, this Word being called his Son, seen in various ways in the name of God by the patriarchs, always heard in the prophets, and at last brought down from the Spirit and power of God the Father into the virgin Mary. Therefore the same rule also signifies that the Son of God was born before the foundation of the world, and that all things were created through him; yet you will not find these things in the Creed in so many words. From these things it is plain that the expression Son of God in the Creed ought not to be understood only of the man Jesus Christ. Nor does it follow that, because what is recounted there of Christ is that he was born, suffered and died, he is therefore meant to be believed only a man, and not God. For you too boast of God, although God is not named here. Nor is this surprising, because the Creed, which was made among the first against this article and presents the first foundations of faith to the less learned, did not think it necessary to explain everything, as was done later against the force of the heresies. For in the first outlines of any subjects, laws or sciences, only the principal heads are usually noted briefly, not each set out fully. Moreover, you do not find in the Creed many things about God which must also be believed of necessity, nor are those six points which the Socinians are accustomed to bring forward expressed there: not God's providence, Christ's benefits, justification, sanctification and the like, which we are accustomed to say are comprehended in sense, though they do not appear there in those words. Add that, while you say the Fathers commonly held that Christ, the Son of God, was born before the creation of the world, although inferior to the Father, you cannot prove from the Fathers' creed that those words must be understood only of Christ made man and born of Mary, and not also of one born, in their opinion, before the creation of the world. They were content to confess the Son of God and to express this, without going on to say that he was conceived and born. But we shall construct a stronger argument against you and your view from the Creed in this way: those Fathers (for it is well known that these were the authors of the Creed, not the Apostles) believed that Christ is the only-begotten Son of God before he was conceived, born and made man of Mary. They did not wish by these words to signify that Christ became the Son of God only after he was conceived and born a man. Take also another point: when they mention only one ascension of Christ, after the resurrection, and never recall any other ascension of Christ, during the time of the forty-day fast, to receive doctrine and commands from the Father, they never believed in such an ascension; yet the Socinians teach it. I could add other arguments against them from the Creed, but I think these are sufficient.

units.la: Addit autem vel monet, se loqui de Symbolo non quatenus id variis illis additionibus articuli tertii jam auctum fuerat: Et in Spiritum S. Sanctum, Ecclesiam Catholicam, Sanctorum communionem, carnis resurrectionem, & vitam aeternam: sed quatenus tertius ille dictus articulus de Fide in Spiritum S. nondum additus erat: Prout scilicet Tertullianus quoque in allegatis (pag. 69. Iren.) fidei Regulis, fidei in Spiritum S. nullam adhuc mentionem facit, sed fidei tantum in Deum Patrem, & Filium ejus Jesum Christum. Ad illa dico, nunquam Symbolum constitit absque articulo fidei in Spiritum Sanctum. Neque additio ad Symbolum consistit in illo articulo, sed in sequentibus post eum, de Ecclesia, remissione peccatorum &c. Et Tertullianus quidem in libro, de Virg. Velandis, cap. 1. referens fidei regulam seu symbolum, praeterit articulum de Spiritu S. recensere suo ordine & forma, sed non reipsa, mox subjungens, quod Paracletum Dominus miserit, aliaque de illo vicario Domini Spiritu Sancto, uti loquitur. Unde non magis ex formula exulasse fidem illam dici potest, quam ex Oratione Dominica conclusio ista, quam Lucas omittit, cap. xi.4. nam tuum est regnum &c. Et de praescript. adverf. haeret. cap. xxxvi. ita summam omnium perstringit, ut si inde argumentari liceat, plures articulos in Symbolo defuisse sequeretur: nam meminit tantum Dei creatoris, & Jesu ex Maria nati filii Dei, & resurrectionis carnis: nil de Christo crucifixo, resuscitato, aliisque quae in priori loco Symboli capita commemoravit. Explicatlus autem eodem libro, cap. xiii. illam fidei regulam posuit, tertium sic commemorans articulum, misisse vicariam vim Spiritus Sancti qui credentes agat: venturum Christum nem-pe cum claritate ad sumendos sanctos in vita aeterna & promissorum caelestium fustum, & ad prophanos judicandos igni perpetuo, facta utriusque partis refuscitatione cum carnis resurrectione. Quæ verò antiquior & purior fidei professio, quam apud Irenæum occurrit, lib. i. cap. ii. ubi expresse, & in Spiritum Sanctum? Et longè hæc ante tempus concilii Nicæni, vel motas ab Ario, & Macedonio controversias. Atque uti non solebant baptizare homines, nisi editâ fidei confessione & Symbolo, ita in omnibus sermonibus, de Symbolo ad Competentes habitis, fides præcipuè memoratur in Spiritum Sanctum. Basilius, de Spiritu, ad Amphil. cap. xi. quid autem professi sunt, & quando? professi sunt se credere in Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum S. quum renunciantes Diabolo & Angelis ejus saluti ferâm illam vocem ediderunt.
units.tr: He adds, or warns, that he is speaking of the creed not as it had already been enlarged by those various additions to the third article: And in the Holy Spirit, the Catholic Church, the communion of saints, the resurrection of the flesh, and life everlasting; but as far as that third article, concerning faith in the Holy Spirit, had not yet been added. In this way, he says, Tertullian too, in the rules of faith he cites (p. 69, Irenaeus), makes no mention of faith in the Holy Spirit but only faith in God the Father and in his Son Jesus Christ. To this I reply that the creed never existed without an article of faith in the Holy Spirit. Nor does the addition to the creed consist in that article, but in the clauses that follow it, concerning the Church, the forgiveness of sins, and so on. Tertullian, indeed, in the book On the Veiling of Virgins, chapter 1, when he recites the rule of faith or creed, omits to recount the article on the Spirit in its proper order and form, but not in substance, immediately adding that the Lord has sent the Paraclete, and other things about that Holy Spirit, the Lord's vicar, as he puts it. So it can no more be said that this faith was dropped from the formula than that the closing words of the Lord's Prayer, which Luke omits (Luke 11:4), for yours is the kingdom, were dropped from the prayer. And in the book On Prescription against Heretics, chapter 36, he sums up the whole so briefly that, if one may argue from that, it would follow that several articles were missing from the creed: for he mentions only God the Creator, Jesus born of Mary the Son of God, and the resurrection of the flesh; nothing about Christ crucified and raised again, or the other points he had recorded in the earlier place of the creed. But in the same book, chapter 13, where he sets out the rule of faith more fully, he records the third article thus: that the Lord sent the power of the Holy Spirit, a vicar, to guide believers; that Christ will come with glory to take the saints into eternal life and the promised heavenly goods, and to judge the profane with eternal fire; with the resurrection of both parties, the raising up of the flesh. But what is the more ancient and purer profession of faith, found in Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 2, where we read expressly and in the Holy Spirit? And this is long before the time of the Council of Nicaea, or the controversies stirred up by Arius and Macedonius. Moreover, just as men were not accustomed to be baptized unless the confession of faith and the creed had first been given, so in all the sermons delivered on the creed to the candidates for baptism, faith in the Holy Spirit is especially mentioned. Basil, On the Spirit, to Amphilochius, chapter 11: But what did they profess, and when? They professed that they believed in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, when, renouncing the Devil and his angels, they uttered that saving word.

units.la: Nullum unquam in Ecclesiis notum receptumque fuit Symbolum, in quo non fuit expressa confessio fidei, & in Spiritum Sanctum. In initio solùm fuit, credo in Deum Patrem, & in Jesum Christum, & in Spiritum Sanctum. Postea alia fuerunt interserta, & vel lectum, credo in Spiritum Sanctum; vel, & in Spiritum Sanctum, intelle&to ἀπὸ κοινῆς[?], credo; nunquam verò omissus, neque in Arianis, vel ab Arianis agnitis Symbolis, etiam in Nicæno Concilio, articulus fidei in Spiritum Sanctum. Et Eunomius apud Basilium, adversus eum lib. i. antiquam referens Patrum confes‑sionem, hanc ponit: credimus in unum Deum Patrem omnipotentem, à quo sunt omnia, & in unum unigenitum Dei filium, Deum verbum, Dominum nostrum Jesum, per quem sunt omnia, ergo non merum hominem: & in unum Spiritum Sanctum paracletum. Vide Athanasium, de Synodis, & quotquot hic recenset variorum Confessiones. Vide & Vossium, Dif-fert. i. de symbol. thef. xxxviii. Ufferium, de Symbolis: cedo unum ex multis, & primis Symbolum, quæ ab illo referuntur, refert autem plura, quod articulum illum omittat. Neque id absre, quum si articulorum natura introspiciatur & momentum, præter illum de Patre, & de Filio, non sit alius magis necessarius & illis conjunctus, quam de Spiritu S. Primaque Symboli illud continet delineatio & rudimentum, unde omnia post sumta fuerunt, Matth. xxviii. 19. discipulos facientes omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti. Quæ verò post articulum de Spiritu S. postmodum addita, in aliis omis‑sa fuere, vel posita brevius aut longius, nunquam ita tamen lecta ullibi, ut non continuerint fidem in Spiritum Sanctum. Sed qui adversus Fi‑lium, eos quoque necesse fuit insurgere in Spiritum Sanctum, & im‑petere Symboli articulum utrumque, vel neutrum. Uti Athanasius, in epistolâ ad Serapionem loquitur, ἄπαξ[?] γὰρ ἀρνούμενοι τὸν τῆς Θεοῦ λόγον, ἕκαστος τὰ αὐτὰ κατὰ τὸ Πνεῦμα αὐτῆς δυσφημίας[?].
units.tr: No creed ever known and received in the churches has lacked an express confession of faith and in the Holy Spirit. At first it had only I believe in God the Father, and in Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit. Afterwards other clauses were inserted, and either the words I believe in the Holy Spirit were read, or and in the Holy Spirit was read with I believe understood ἀπὸ κοινῆς [?] (in common, from the preceding clause); but never was the article of faith in the Holy Spirit omitted, not even in the creeds of the Arians, or creeds acknowledged by the Arians, nor in the Nicene Council itself. Eunomius, too, in Basil's Against Eunomius, book 1, when he recalls the ancient confession of the Fathers, gives this: We believe in one God the Father almighty, from whom are all things, and in one only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, our Lord Jesus, through whom are all things, therefore not a mere man; and in one Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. See Athanasius, On the Councils, and all the various confessions he there lists. See also Vossius, Dissertation 1 on the creeds, thesis 38, and Ussher, On Creeds. I challenge anyone to name one creed among the many, and the earliest, that is reported by them, though they report several, which omits that article. Nor is this surprising, since if one looks at the nature and importance of the articles, there is no other article more necessary and more closely bound to those on the Father and the Son than the one on the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the earliest form of the creed contains that outline and rudiment from which everything afterwards was drawn: Matthew 28:19, making disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Whatever was added afterwards following the article on the Holy Spirit was omitted in other creeds, or stated more briefly or at greater length, yet never so read anywhere as not to retain faith in the Holy Spirit. But those who rise against the Son must also rise against the Holy Spirit, and must attack either both articles of the creed or neither. As Athanasius says in his letter to Serapion: For once they deny the Word of God, each of them speaks the same blasphemies against his Spirit [ἄπαξ γὰρ ἀρνούμενοι τὸν τῆς Θεοῦ λόγον, ἕκαστος τὰ αὐτὰ κατὰ τὸ Πνεῦμα αὐτῆς δυσφημίας].

units.la: Instat Noster, pag. 446. Antiquissimos Christianos, quemadmodum tantum in hominem Christum crediderunt; ita in Spiritum Sanctum nunquam credere jussos fuisse: & proinde Basilium, lib. de Spirit. Sanct. cap. xxvii. expresse quaesivisse, ipsam fidei confessionem, quod credimus in Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum S. ex quibus scriptis habemus? quasi vid. innuat, fidem in Spirit. S. nusquam in Scripturis mandatam esse. Quemadmodum & Apostoli unice tantum & fidem in Christum inculcarint, & tantum in nomen Christi baptizasse leguntur. Ad quae resp. Probari quidem, fidem in Christum fuisse praedicatam passim; sed non, exclusive ad Patrem, aut ad Spiritum Sanctum. Uti nec tantum in hominem Christum credere jussos fuisse Christianos. Annon & Deus Christus? Annon & Spiritus Sanctus est, praeter Christum, & in ejus nomen tum discipulos conscribi Christus voluit, tum baptizari? & quomodo dicitur, tantum in hominem Christum nos juberi credere? Committitque elenchum Adversarius, quando probat in Christum credi à nobis debere, & non hoc probat, quod unicè controvertitur, tantum in hominem Christum nos debere credere. Quid quod ipsi Adversar. in Expositione symboli, art. Credo in Spiritum S. variis ex Scripturâ locis confirmant? Quod factum à Schlichtingio, in exponendâ Fidei Confessione, nomine Ecclesiarum suarum editâ. Quodque in nomen Christi fideles dicuntur baptizari, neque probat in Christum tantum ut hominem; neque de Christo, oppositè ad Spiritum Sanctum, magis quam ad Patrem, accipi debere. Ostenditque Basilius, ad Amphilochium, de Spiritu S. cap. xii. adversus eos qui dicunt sufficere baptisma tantum in nomine Domini, quando in Scripturis commemoratur baptismus Christi, Spiritum S. eo etiam connotari: aliquando & eum solum nominari, uti 1 Cor. xii. omnes in unum Spiritum baptizati sumus. Et cap. xxvii. quidem interrogat, ipsam fidei professionem, quâ credimus in Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum S. e quibus habemus scriptis? non verò quod dubitet ex Scripturis illam probari: contrarium enim ostendit, per totum tractatum, & mox, ex traditione baptismi, quemadmodum baptizamur, sic & credere debentes; sed formam edendae confessionis, cujus materia in Scripturis satis superque habeatur, ex traditione confirmat: ut evincat bene à se in doxologiâ dictum in Spiritu, vel cum Spiritu: super quo mota ipsi fuerat quaestio, nu-per orante me apud populum, & utroque modo glorificationem absolvente Deo ac Patri, interdum cum Filio, & cum Spiritu Sancto, μετ᾽ οὗ τῆς σὺν τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ, interdum διὰ οὗ τῆς ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι per Filium in Spiritu Sancto, alii quidam ex his qui tum aderant in nos irruerunt. cap. I. & Patri quidem dicendum contendebant, ex quo ἐξ οὗ, Filio, per quem δι᾽ οὗ, at Spiritui Sancto, in quo ἐν ᾧ: adversus quos prolixe probat, & ex Scriptura, & ex traditione, cap. IX. syllabarum & articulorum istorum usum de illis saepe inverti, & rationem esse manifestam, quare de Spiritu S. etiam possit dici, cum quo: quandoquidem sunt συνδυναμούντα, in & cum cap. XXV. XXVI. Hoc autem nolebant Adversarii, glorificari cum Patre, & Filio, Spiritum. Quapropter quaerit cap. XXIV. quem alium locum Spiritui deputare possit, num gloriae consortio spoliare eum qui ubique conjunctus est divinitati, in professione fidei, in baptismate redemtionis, in operatione virtutem, in inhabitatione sanctorum, in beneficiis in subditos conferendis? Ergo modum illum dicendi cum Spiritu ita derivat ex traditione, ut Scripturae doceat consentaneam τῇ γραφῇ σύμφωνον. Minime ut dubitet fidem in Patrem, & Filium, & Spirit. Sanct. ex Scripturis probari posse, in quem sensum ejus verba perperam accepit Noster. Quum eandem doceat trium personarum essentiam, cap. XVIII. quod in professione trium personarum pium dogma monarchia servatur. Unus Deus & Pater, & unus unigenitus Filius, & unus Spiritus Sanctus. Unamquamque personam singulariter efferimus. Deum in personis unum novit, non plures, non primum, secundum, & tertium. Secundum autem Deum nunquam antehac, ac ne hodie quidem audimus, eo quod Deum ex Deo adorantes, etiam proprietatem profitemur personarum, manemusque in uno principatu, non dissipantes divina natura rationem in multitudinem subdivisam: eo quod unam in Deo Patre, & Deo unigenito formam, ut ita loquar, contemplamur inseparabili Deitatis essentia unitam. Unus autem est & Spiritus Sanctus, qui & ipse per se profertur, ac per seipsum complet super omnia conglorificandam ac beatam Trinitatem. — Sed non hinc solum probatur naturae communio: verum illinc quoque, quod ex Deo esse dicitur, non sic ex Deo veniens, quemadmodum ex Deo sunt omnia, sed tamquam ex Deo procedens: neque per generationem, quemadmodum Filius, sed tamquam Spiritus oris ejus. — Caeterum qui subnumerationem ponunt, dicentes, primum, secundum, ac tertium, sciant sese Deorum multitudinem, juxta gentium errorem, in illibatam Christianorum de Deo professionem inducere. Subnumerationem haudquaquam fert, aeque minus inter Spiritum & Filium, ac inter Filium & Patrem : cap. xvii. Etenim si Filium subnumeratis, rursus in ejusdem impietatis sermonem reciditis, videlicet in disparilitatem essentiae, in dignitatis dejectionem, in nativitatem tempore posteriorem. Quod si soli spiritui putant convenire subnumerationem, discant spiritum simul eodem modo pronunciari cum Domino, quomodo Filius pronunciatur cum Patre. Nomen enim Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti similiter editum est. Distinctionem quidem inter tres illos ponit, & distinctionem personalem, sed substantiae imitatem agnoscit quoque & identitatem. Cap. xvi. ac nemo me credat tres originales subsistentias ponere, aut Filii operationem imperfectam esse. Principium enim eorum qua sunt, unum est, per Filium condens, per Spiritum Sanctum perficiens &c. Cap. xix. probat, Spiritum Sanctum bonum esse ὡς ἀγαθὸς ὁ πατήρ· ἡ ἀγαθὸς ὁ υἱὸς ἡ ἀγαθὴ γεννηθείς, ἔχων τὴν ἀγαθότητα: atque ita communia esse nomina Patri, & Filio, & Spiritui Sancto. ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως οἰκειότητος. & naturae inter illos communionem, cap. xxii. ἡ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως κοινωνίας.
units.tr: Our author presses on, p. 446: the most ancient Christians believed only in the man Christ, and so they were never bidden to believe in the Holy Spirit. Therefore Basil, in his book On the Holy Spirit, ch. 27, expressly asked what written sources do we have for the very confession of faith, that we believe in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit? as if he were hinting that faith in the Holy Spirit is nowhere commanded in the Scriptures. Just so, the Apostles are read to have urged only faith in Christ, and to have baptized only into the name of Christ. To this I reply: it is indeed proved that faith in Christ was preached everywhere, but not in a way that excludes the Father or the Holy Spirit. Nor were Christians bidden to believe only in the man Christ. Is Christ not also God? Is the Holy Spirit not also God? Did Christ will that his disciples be enrolled, and baptized, in his name and besides it in the name of the Spirit? And how can it be said that we are bidden to believe only in the man Christ? The adversary also begs the question: when he proves that we ought to believe in Christ, he does not prove what alone is in dispute, that we ought to believe only in the man Christ. And what of the fact that the Socinians themselves, in their Exposition of the Creed, under the article I believe in the Holy Spirit, confirm it from various passages of Scripture? This was also done by Schlichting in expounding the Confession of Faith published in the name of their churches. And the statement that the faithful are baptized into the name of Christ does not prove faith in Christ only as man, nor should it be understood of Christ as opposed to the Holy Spirit any more than to the Father. Basil shows, in his letter to Amphilochius, On the Holy Spirit, ch. 12, against those who say that baptism in the name of the Lord alone is enough, that when the baptism of Christ is mentioned in Scripture, the Holy Spirit is implied as well; and sometimes the Spirit alone is named, as in 1 Cor. 12: we were all baptized into one Spirit. In ch. 27 he indeed asks what profession of faith do we have from the Scriptures, in which we believe in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit? not because he doubts that it is proved from Scripture; for the contrary appears throughout the whole treatise, and soon after, from the tradition of baptism: just as we are baptized, so we ought to believe too. Rather, he confirms from tradition the form of the confession to be made, whose matter is in Scripture more than enough. His aim is to show that he rightly said, in the doxology, in the Spirit or with the Spirit. On this a question had been raised to him: lately, when I was praying before the people and ending the glorification to God the Father in both ways, sometimes with the Son and with the Holy Spirit [μετ᾽ οὗ, σὺν τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ], and sometimes through the Son in the Holy Spirit [διὰ οὗ, ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι], some of those who were present attacked us. (ch. 1) They contended that to the Father one should say from whom [ἐξ οὗ], to the Son through whom [δι᾽ οὗ], but to the Holy Spirit in whom [ἐν ᾧ]. Against them he proves at length, from both Scripture and tradition (ch. 9), that these syllables and prepositions are often interchanged, and that the reason is plain why one may also say of the Holy Spirit with whom: since the Persons are co-operating [συνδυναμούντα], in and with (ch. 25, 26). But the adversaries did not want the Spirit glorified together with the Father and the Son. Therefore in ch. 24 he asks what other place could be assigned to the Spirit: should he be robbed of the fellowship of glory, who is everywhere joined to the Godhead, in the profession of faith, in the baptism of redemption, in the working of powers, in the indwelling of the saints, in the bestowing of benefits upon his subjects? So he derives that manner of speaking with the Spirit from tradition, in such a way as to show that it agrees with Scripture [τῇ γραφῇ σύμφωνον]. He by no means doubts that faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit can be proved from Scripture, whatever sense our author has wrongly given his words. For he teaches the same essence of the three Persons (ch. 18): in the profession of the three Persons the pious dogma of monarchy is preserved: one God and Father, and one only-begotten Son, and one Holy Spirit. We name each Person singly. He knows God as one in the Persons, not more, not a first, a second and a third. Yet we have never heard, not even today, of a "second God", since in adoring God from God we also profess the properties of the Persons, and we remain in one principality, not dissipating the account of the divine nature into a subdivided multitude; because we contemplate in God the Father and in the only-begotten God one form, as I may say, united in the inseparable essence of the Deity. There is also one Holy Spirit, who is himself brought forth through himself, and through himself completes the Trinity to be glorified together and blessed above all things. But the communion of nature is proved not only from this, but also from the fact that he is said to be from God, not coming from God as all things are from God, but as proceeding from God: not by generation as the Son is, but as the Spirit of his mouth. Moreover, those who posit a subnumeration, saying first, second and third, should know that they bring a multitude of gods, after the error of the Gentiles, into the unblemished Christian profession concerning God. He by no means admits a subnumeration, and least of all between the Spirit and the Son, or between the Son and the Father (ch. 17). For if you subnumber the Son, you fall back into the same impiety of speech: namely inequality of essence, a lowering of dignity, a nativity later in time. But if they think subnumeration belongs to the Spirit alone, let them learn that the Spirit is named together with the Lord in the same way as the Son is named with the Father, for the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit is given in like manner. He indeed posits a distinction among those three, a personal distinction, but he also acknowledges the likeness and identity of substance. (ch. 16) Nor let anyone think that I posit three original subsistences, or that the operation of the Son is imperfect. For the principle of the things that are is one: creating through the Son, perfecting through the Holy Spirit, etc. (ch. 19) He proves that the Holy Spirit is good, as the Father is good and the Son is good, begotten good, having goodness; and thus the names are common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, [from the kinship of his own nature, ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως οἰκειότητος], and the communion of nature among them (ch. 22) [ἡ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως κοινωνίας].

units.la: Objicit deinde Noster, quod Thaddaeus apud Edeffenos praedicaverit Christum tantum, non vero etiam fidem in Spiritum Sanctum. Eusebi. lib. i. cap. xiii. & lib. ii. cap. i. Id vero non dicitur, apud Eusebium, quod vel tantum Christum ipsis praedicaverit; vel non etiam Spiritum Sanctum. Alioqui & potuissent dicere cum Ephesiis, neque an Spiritus Sancti sit, audivimus. Act. xix. 2.
units.tr: Next our author objects that Thaddaeus, among the Edessenes, preached Christ only, and not also faith in the Holy Spirit (Eusebius, bk. 1, ch. 13, and bk. 2, ch. 1). But Eusebius does not say that he preached to them either only Christ, or not also the Holy Spirit. Otherwise they could also have answered as the Ephesians did: "we have not so much as heard whether there is a Holy Spirit" (Acts 19:2).

units.la: Similis commatis reliqua sunt, quae addit, in antiquissima historia ante Justinum Martyrem, unice tantum de fide in Deum, & Christum actum, auditumque fuisse. nullo nec nominato, nec indicato Historico. Quod Christiani, tempore Polycarpi dixerunt, se praeter Deum, nullum alium, vid. Deum, colere posse, quam Christum. Quod Smyrnensis Ecclesia, & Polycarpus, in epistolis, tantum a Deo Patre, & Christo misericordiam ac gratiam suis adprecantur. Unde negamus sequi, quod concludit, illos in Spiritum Sanctum minime credidisse: vel eos nullum Symbolum, aut formulam de fide in Spiritum Sanctum habuisse. Sunt enim argumenta omnia negativa, non probativa. Neque alia porro sunt, quod Justinus cum Judaeis agens de solo Christo disputat, & ejus inculcat fidem, neminemque docet, praeter Deum & Christum esse adorandum: quod Irenaeus scribit, fidem in N. Test. additamentum accepisse per Filium Dei, & omittit Spiritum Sanctum: quod multi Veterum Christum non vocant Deum: vel etiam orationes suas ad ad ipsum speciatim non dirigunt. Ad quæ facilis est responsio, quod nihil directe probant, non, vel nescivisse eos, vel noluisse, aut non ausos fuisse Spiritum Sanctum confiteri Deum. Etenim ex Veteribus, & Veterum Symbolis, atque doxologiis rem aliter se habere & nunc ostendimus, & olim Tom. I. Socin. Confut. lib. ii. cap. v. Atque Basilius, ad Amphilochium, cap. xxix. antiquiores profert, Dionysium Alex. scribentem: Deo Patri, & Filio Domino nostro Jesu Christo, cum Spiritu Sancto gloria & imperium in secula seculorum, Amen. Clementem, sic docentem, Vivit Deus & Dominus Jesus Christus & Spiritus Sanctus. Irenæum addit, & Eusebium, & Origenem multis in locis expositionum in Psalmos, cum Spiritu Sancto gloriam deferentem Deo. Advocat ejusdem rei testes & professores Africanum historicum, Gregorium Thaumaturgum, Firmilianum, & denique Meletium. Quid, dicemusne illos vel non agnovisse Spir. Sanct. Deum, vel non unâ cum Patre & Filio conglorificasse, aut eos qui cum illis, vel etiam post eos vixerunt tantundem non scivisse, vel fateri ausos fuisse de Spir. Sanct Deo, & religiosum in modum honorando? Quodque in Nicæno Concilio, vel apud alios tenuis Spiritus S. videtur mentio, non factum sive ex ignorantia, sive incredulitate, sed [illegible, ~14 letters] quod hæc quæstio nondum esset agitata, uti Gregorius Nazianzenus loquitur, epist. ii. ad Cledonium, sive Orat. LII.
units.tr: The rest is of the same kind: he adds that in the most ancient history, before Justin Martyr, only faith in God and Christ was treated and heard of, with no historian named or indicated. But the Christians in Polycarp's time said that they could worship no one besides God, that is, besides Christ. And the Smyrnean Church and Polycarp, in their letters, ask for mercy and grace for their people only from God the Father and Christ. From this we deny that it follows, as he concludes, that they did not believe in the Holy Spirit at all, or that they had no creed or formula of faith in the Holy Spirit. All these arguments are negative, not probative. Nor is it of any more weight that Justin, when dealing with the Jews, disputes about Christ alone and urges faith in him, teaching that no one is to be worshipped besides God and Christ; or that Irenaeus writes that faith received an addition in the New Testament through the Son of God and omits the Holy Spirit; or that many of the ancients do not call Christ God, or do not specially direct their prayers to him. The answer to these is easy: they prove nothing directly. It does not follow that they either did not know, or were unwilling, or did not dare to confess the Holy Spirit as God. For that the matter stands otherwise we have now shown from the ancients, from the ancient creeds and doxologies, and before this in Tom. I, Socinianism Confuted, bk. 2, ch. 5.
