And Basil, in his letter to Amphilochius (ch. 29), brings forward more ancient witnesses: Dionysius of Alexandria, writing: To God the Father, and to the Son our Lord Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen. Clement, teaching thus: God lives, and the Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit. He adds Irenaeus, Eusebius and Origen, who in many places in their commentaries on the Psalms ascribe glory to God together with the Holy Spirit. He calls as witnesses and professors of the same matter the historian Africanus, Gregory Thaumaturgus, Firmilian and finally Meletius. What then? Shall we say that these either did not recognize the Holy Spirit as God, or did not glorify him together with the Father and the Son; or that those who lived with them, or even after them, were equally ignorant, or dared to say of the Holy Spirit that he is God and to honour him in a religious manner? As for the fact that at the Council of Nicaea, or among others, the Holy Spirit is only slightly mentioned, this happened not from ignorance or unbelief, but because this question had not yet been raised, as Gregory Nazianzen says (letter 2 to Cledonius, or Oration 52).

units.la: Ad ea, quæ de Artemonitis respondimus, nihil prorsus Noster annotat, & nescio quid adeo hinc posset concludere, nisi fuisse & olim tales, qui Christum negarunt Deum: quod nemo ignorat: vel se istorum sequi opinionem & errorem, quod quoque non est obscurum. Et de Nazaræis etiam diximus, ad quæ nihil reponit. Frustra autem cum Apostolis jungit Nazaræos Ebionitas, qui inter hæreticos à Veteribus collocantur, quod nec negat, pag. 456. scribens, legis Mosaicæ pariter observantissimi, & hinc propterea quoque à sequentibus Christianis pro hæreticis tandem habiti: Vel frustra recipit magis hoc, quod de se Artemonitæ, & omnes pariter hæretici, dixerunt, sententiam suam antiquam, Apostolos, & ipsum Dominum habere autorem; quam quod scriptor antiquos apud Eusebium, lib. v. cap. ult. & ei valde laudatus, Adversus hæresim, quæ servatorem solum hominem esse asseveravit, scribit, [illegible, ~20 letters] non longe antea exortam. unde Noster in Scriptoris istius vertitur contumeliam, & fidem ejus accusat palam, cui nec credi possit aut debeat, pag. 462. 463. 464. cum absque eo tamen nesciret hoc ipsum, quod de Artemonitarum jactat antiquitate, & in quo totum fundat argumenti sui præsidium, imo in quo Scriptore etiam cogitur ingenuitatem comprobare, quando ad refutandam Artemonitarum hæresim accedens [?]συγχωρητικῶς[?] præmittit primum, forte verisimilem videri ipsorum narrationem posse, [?]ὡς δ' ἂν τύχοι πνευμάτων τὸ λέ-γειν[?], vid. de Christi & Apostolorum consentiente secum doctrinâ, nisi refragarentur ipsis Scriptura Sacra. Non verò probi disputatoris est, ex Autore petere ea tantum, quæ in rem tuam vertas, de cætero contemnere eum & convitiari. Vel quare nobis non liceat adversus Artemonitarum, & Autoris nostri collectionem, dogma suum ab Apostolis repetentium dicere, quod ipse pag. 480. de Justino, quod scilicet nihil hoc faciat, sive Justini Martyris, aliorumque recentiorum scripta, Christum esse dicant, sive non dicant, cum Apostoli aliquid sentire & docere potuerunt, a quo Justinus, dico ego, Artemonitæ, cum nonnullis aliis, deinceps aberra-verit. Sed & Athanasius, lib. de Synodis, Eusebianis exprobrat, quasi nescierint jam ante Concilium Nicænum,hæresim istam abominabilem fuisse, quo tempore Artemas ejus fundamenta jaciebat. Alexander, Alexandrinus episcopus, in epist. ad Alexandrum Constantinopolitanum,apud Theodoretum, lib. 1. cap. iv. cum non ignoretis tum Ebionis, tum Artemæ doctrinam, quæ non itapridem veram Ecclesiæ pietatem oppugnare capit.
units.tr: Our author makes no answer at all to what we said about the Artemonites, and I do not know what he could conclude from it, except that there were such people in former times who denied that Christ is God, which nobody doubts, or that he follows their opinion and error, which is also not hidden. We also spoke of the Nazarenes, and he has no reply to that. But he wrongly joins the Nazarene Ebionites with the Apostles, although the Fathers count them among the heretics. He does not deny this, writing on page 456: "They were most strict observers of the Mosaic law, and for this reason were finally regarded as heretics by the Christians who followed." Or else he is wrong to accept more readily what the Artemonites and all heretics said about themselves, namely that their opinion is ancient and that the Apostles and the Lord himself were its authors. Yet the ancient writer whom he quotes from Eusebius, book 5, last chapter, and praises highly, writes "against the heresy which asserted that the Saviour was only a man," and says it arose "[illegible, ~20 letters] not long before." For this reason our author heaps abuse on that writer and openly accuses his trustworthiness, saying he "cannot and should not be believed," on pages 462, 463 and 464. And yet he did not know this very thing, which he boasts about as the antiquity of the Artemonites, and on which he rests the whole support of his argument. Indeed, he is forced to vouch for that same writer's candour, when, coming to refute the Artemonite heresy, he first grants, by way of concession, that their account may perhaps seem plausible, "as it might happen to be said by spirits" [ὡς δ' ἂν τύχοι πνευμάτων τὸ λέγειν], namely about the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles agreeing with itself, unless the Holy Scripture contradicted them. But it is not the mark of an honest disputant to take from an author only what suits his purpose, and to despise and revile him for the rest. Or why should we not be allowed to say, against the Artemonites and our author's collection, that they trace their doctrine back to the Apostles? Our author himself says this on page 480 about Justin: "that is, this does nothing, whether the writings of Justin Martyr and other more recent men say that Christ is God or do not say it, since the Apostles could have thought and taught something, from which Justin, and, I say, the Artemonites with some others, afterwards strayed." But Athanasius also, in his book On the Synods, charges the Eusebians with acting as if they did not know that this abominable heresy existed even before the Council of Nicaea, "at the time when Artemas was laying its foundations." Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, in his letter to Alexander of Constantinople, quoted by Theodoret, book 1, chapter 4: "Since you are not ignorant of the doctrine both of Ebion and of Artemas, which has only lately begun to attack the true piety of the Church."

units.la: Cæterum Artemonitarum sententiam Noster dissimulat: quo fine non est admodum obscurum. Pag. 475. dicit, Apostolos & Nazaræos credidisse, hominem Christum Filium esse Dei, & quod sententia Artemonitarum eadem fuit, & non alia, quæ fuit [?]ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον φύσει τὴν σω-τῆρα[?], quod Servator fuit merus homo: quæ aliud sonant, quam simpliciter illud; quod in bonum etiam sensum accipi potest; non item istud.
units.tr: Besides, our author conceals the opinion of the Artemonites, and the purpose of this is not very hidden. On page 475 he says that the Apostles and the Nazarenes believed "that the man Christ is the Son of God," and that "the opinion of the Artemonites was the same and not different," which was that "the Saviour was by nature a mere man" [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον φύσει τὴν σωτῆρα], that is, that the Saviour was a mere man. These words mean something other than the first, which can be taken in a good sense, but the second cannot.

units.la: Denique stramineum prorsus est, cui superstruit vim argumenti ex Scriptore illo adversus Artemonitas, quod eos refutaturus, antiquiorem adversus ipsorum sententiam nullum memoret Justino, hinc enim ego quoque collegeram, Artemonitarum sententiam de Christo, saltem ante Justinum, in Ecclesia inde ab Apostolis viguisse. Sed oppidò vana est illa collectio. Nam primò quis tibi dixit, Scriptorem illum non potuisse etiam alios Justino antiquiores pro se citare, quod audacter asseris? pag. 472. neminem citare, citareque potuisse. Deinde ne dicam illum ad Scripturam provocare, autoritatem omnium antiquissimam, propositum erat non quoscunque sententiæ suæ adducere testes antiquos, uti ejus verba accipis, sed ex illis, qui adversus Gentiles, aut Hæreticos scripserant, argumentari, inter quos primus occurrit Justinus: nisi primùm Sacræ Scripturæ testimonia illis contradicerent: deinde Fratrum quorundam scripta superessent, Victoris temporibus multo antiquiora: quæ illi cum contra Gentiles pro veritatis defensione, tum contra hæreses quæ id temporis grassabantur, scripserunt, ut Justini, Miltiadis, Tatiani, Clementis, & aliorum nonnullorum: in quorum omnium libris Christus verus Deus esse confirmatur. Quis Irenæi, quis Melitionis, quis caeterorum libros ignorat, qui Christum Deum & hominem constanter adseverant? Vides, quare Justinum, & similes Scriptores allegat. III. Fac, quoscunque ipsum citare voluisse; an proinde qui non citat omnes & singulos, eos propterea putandus est sibi adversarios existimare, aut non favent es? Quis scriptor ad duram & iniquam illam legem velit adstringi, vel sua, in citandis autoribus? præsertim ubi testatus non fuit, forte nec testari potuit, se omnes illos adducere, vel nosse. IV. Imprimis quando non quaecunque scripta sive epistolas, sed tractatus, & tales, ac dictum, & celebriores, adversus hæreses singulorum temporum, adducere constituit, adducitque insuper in eandem fidem psalmos & hymnos, à quibusvis vulgo cantari solitos: quod hic facit Autor: quot item psalmi, quot hymni à fratribus fidelibus antiquitus conscripti, qui Christum, verbum Dei, verum Deum esse concentu quodam concelebrant Θεολογοῦνται. Cum igitur ex tot annorum spatio, doctrina Ecclesiastica vere annunciata fuerit, quomodo fieri potest, ut illi Patres, qui ad Victorem usque vitam produxerunt, sic, ut isti asserunt, prædicarint? Ergo ante Victorem Patres, & in hymnis suis Ecclesia passim confessa fuit Christum Deum, Θεὸν ὡς ἄνθρωπον [?], & non, quod Artemonitæ docebant, ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον. Denique vide ἀνακολουθίαν [?] argumenti: qui scriptor, adversus hæresim Artemonitarum, ante Justinum neminem recenset, adversus illos facientem, ille neminem novit, vel credit ante illud tempus adversus tales homines, & istiusmodi sententiam fuisse, sensisse, vel scripsisse? negatur. Pergo ulterius, & fac Scriptorem nullum extitisse: ergo non fuerunt passim istius sententiæ & fidei Christiani? neque hoc sequitur. Minimè vero, quod ergo Artemonitarum sententia de Christo, ante Justinum, inde ab Apostolis viguit. Quod quæso quâ ratione vel medio termino comprobat, dum pugnat solo testimonio negativo, id est, nullo; vel eorum, qui in suâ testari causa non possunt, dum nil probant, & à melius sentientibus convincuntur.
units.tr: Finally, he builds an argument from that writer against the Artemonites on a foundation that is entirely of straw: that in refuting them the writer mentions no earlier witness against their opinion than Justin. "For I too had concluded from this that the Artemonite opinion about Christ, at least before Justin, had flourished in the Church from the Apostles onward." But that inference is utterly empty. For, first, who told you that the writer could not also cite other writers older than Justin in his favour, as you boldly assert on page 472: "he cites no one, and could not have cited anyone"? Next, not to say that he appealed to Scripture, the most ancient authority of all, his purpose was not to bring forward every ancient witness to his opinion, as you take his words, but to argue from those who had written against the Gentiles or the heretics, among whom Justin comes first: "unless first the testimonies of Holy Scripture contradicted them, and then there survived the writings of certain brethren, much older than the time of Victor, which they wrote both against the Gentiles in defence of the truth and against the heresies that were then spreading, such as those of Justin, Miltiades, Tatian, Clement and some others, in all of whose books Christ is affirmed to be true God. Who does not know the books of Irenaeus, of Melito, and of the others who constantly assert that Christ is God and man?" You see why he cites Justin and writers like him. III. Suppose he wished to cite all of them; does it follow that one who does not cite each and every writer must be thought to regard them as opponents, or that they do not favour him? What writer would wish to be bound by that harsh and unjust law, even in choosing his own authorities? Especially when he did not declare, and perhaps could not declare, that he was bringing forward or knew all of them. IV. Above all, when he has decided to bring forward not every writing or letter, but treatises, and those famous and notable ones, against the heresies of each period, and moreover brings in for the same faith psalms and hymns commonly sung by anyone, as this author does here: "Likewise how many psalms and how many hymns were composed in antiquity by faithful brethren, which together celebrate in harmony that Christ, the Word of God, is true God [Θεολογοῦνται]. Since, then, over so many years the ecclesiastical teaching was truly proclaimed, how can it be that those Fathers who lived down to Victor taught it in the way these men assert?" Therefore, before Victor, the Fathers and the Church, in their hymns everywhere, confessed that Christ is God, [Θεὸν ὡς ἄνθρωπον], and not, as the Artemonites taught, a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον]. Finally, see the lack of sequence [ἀνακολουθία] in the argument: the writer, against the Artemonite heresy, mentions no one before Justin who favours his side. Does he therefore know of no one, or believe that before that time there was no such opinion, no such view, no such writing against such men? That is denied. I go further, and suppose that no writer had existed: does it follow that there were no Christians of that opinion and faith everywhere? Nor does this follow. Certainly it does not follow that the Artemonite opinion about Christ flourished from the Apostles onward before Justin. What reason, or what middle term, does he offer to prove this, when he argues only from a negative testimony, that is, from none at all, or from the testimony of men who cannot give evidence in their own cause, and who prove nothing and are refuted by those who think better?

units.la: Paulo aliter ipsi procedit res, non dico honestius, quando sententiæ suæ, post Artemonitas, & similes priorum temporum, à seculo quarto socios secum recenset hæreticos Priscillianistas, in Hispaniâ; alios inter Theopaschitas, Jacobitas, & Armenos; præterea Alcoranum Muhammedis, ex quo pag. 499. citat testimonium adversus Trinitatem, & deitatem Christi: quod ei facile largimur, & confirmat ita nostrum argumentum de consonantiâ Socinianæ cum Muhammedicâ, ut nihil sit quod in eo proinde amplius laboremus. Mitto quæ allegat de dogmatis sui revivif-centiâ in Elipando, Felice Urgelitano, & similibus, qui Christum contenderunt esse, instar aliorum, Filium Dei adoptivum, & nuncupativum, non verum. Taceo Bogomilos; & quos Parisienses olim damnarunt: an verò ejusdem sententiæ fuerit Abaliardus, disputatur: atque ita haud gravate finimus Nostrum per illos desinere in Serveto , suo magistro & patrono: nobis vicissim concedat aliis acquiescere ducibus, & fidei Christianæ assertoribus magis claris & probatis.
units.tr: The matter goes rather differently for him, not more honestly I say, when after the Artemonites and others of earlier times he counts among his companions, from the fourth century onward, the heretics known as the Priscillianists in Spain, and among others the Theopaschites, the Jacobites and the Armenians; and besides, the Koran of Muhammad, from which on page 499 he quotes a testimony against the Trinity and the deity of Christ. We readily grant him this, and it so confirms our argument about the agreement of Socinianism with Muhammadanism that we need not labour any further over it. I pass over what he alleges about the revival of his doctrine in Elipandus, Felix of Urgel, and similar men, who maintained, like others, that Christ is the adoptive and merely nominal Son of God, not the true one. I say nothing of the Bogomils, and of those whom the Parisians condemned long ago. Whether Abelard held the same opinion is disputed. And so we gladly finish our author's catalogue of those who end in Servetus, his master and patron. In return, let him allow us to rest with other leaders, and with defenders of the Christian faith who are more famous and better tested.

units.la: Quod verò ultimò de Baronio dicit, locum pro traditione Ecclesiasti-cā de fide Trinitatis proferente ex Luciano, in Philop. ubi Christianus Ethnicum catechizans, jubet eum Deum alte regnantem, magnum, æthereum, atque æternum Filium Patris, & Spiritum Sanctum, ex Patre procedentem, Unum ex tribus, & ex uno tria, credere Deum: quam veritatem impio homini nonnisi ex communi Christianorum sententiâ innotescere potuisse, qua omnes, qui crediturî erant, imbuebantur, Baronius scribit: nescio quid Noster de Baroniano periculo, de nostro erga ipsum fulcimine, paratragædiat. Nempe negaram, Baronium eo fine Lucianum citare, vel, quod tali autore fides Trinitatis niteretur, vel quod ex illo demum patere conficique traditio de Trinitate posset, uti in Irenico scri-pserat. Jam unirè exagitat, quod negare ausus sum, Baronium dixisse aut innuisse, unum Lucianum ad Traditionem ipsius conficiendam sufficere. 2. eundem Lucianum affirmare, Ecclesiam tempore Apostolorum, Trinitatis doctrinam fideles docuisse. Primo quum tam rigide censeat aliorum verba, non debet pro eodem habere, dixisse aut innuisse. Nam aliquid innuere, quod tamen non dicat. Et Baronius non dixit, unum Lucianum sufficere ad probandam thesim, sensu quo id accepit Noster, vid. ut ex illo demum patere conficique traditio possit, reliquis neglectis aut exclusis: sed, uti qui ex superabundanti disputant, sic Baronius dicit, vel uno hoc argumento, ex veteri traditione, de communi sententia Ecclesiæ, unde illa nota gentilibus & profanis fuit, judicari posse. Non dicit unum simpliciter Lucianum; sed ex externis & impiis vel unum illum sufficere ad istud probandum: hanc autem traditionem —— externi etiam & impii produnt, fidemque faciunt, ut illud Luciani &c. —— quo omnis impietas convicia prorsus remaneant & extincta. Deinde, Baronius agnoscit quidem, uti & nos, Ecclesiam, tempore Apostolorum, & semper ac ubique, Trinitatis doctrinam fideles docuisse; sed hoc ipsum a Luciano asseri, non dicit, neque id etiam loquitur Lucianus; sed Baronius inde deducit, ac bene. Neque aliter id docuisse Apostolos, affirmari a Luciano verbis illis, Baronius dicere potuit, quam ratione rei & materiae, sic se habentis. Ex quibus viderit Autor, num rationem habuerit impotenter exaestuandi super iis, quae respondera m ad ea quae in Baronium dixerat, quasi audacter & invereunde Baronium fulcire & confirmare annisus fuisset, nam ita haec in Indice scilicet etiam notanda fuerunt, quae mea, ut scripsi, cum Autoris αὐτοχρολόγοις[?], uti in aliis omnibus, sic & heic, conferri desidero & judicari.
units.tr: As for what he says last about Baronius, that he cites a passage from Lucian in the Philopatris, where a Christian instructing a heathen bids him believe that God is the high-reigning God, great, ethereal, and eternal, the Son of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, one out of three and three out of one, and Baronius writes that this truth could have been known to an impious man only from the common opinion of Christians, by which all who were about to believe were imbued, I do not know what our author is making such a tragedy about, concerning the danger to Baronius and our support for him. I did deny that Baronius cited Lucian for this purpose, either because the faith of the Trinity rests on such an author, or because a tradition about the Trinity could be shown and established from him alone, as I had written in the Irenicum. Now he rails at me for daring to deny that Baronius said or hinted that Lucian alone is enough to establish the tradition itself. 2. That the same Lucian affirms that the Church in the time of the Apostles taught the faithful the doctrine of the Trinity. First, since he judges the words of others so strictly, he ought not to treat "said or hinted" as the same thing, for one can hint at what one does not say. Baronius did not say that Lucian alone is enough to prove the thesis in the sense our author took it, namely that a tradition can be shown and established from him alone, with all else neglected or excluded. Rather, as those who argue from surplus do, Baronius says even by this one argument alone, from ancient tradition and the common opinion of the Church, whence that doctrine was known to Gentiles and profane people, the matter can be judged. He does not say Lucian alone simply, but that from outsiders and impious men that one witness suffices for proving this: but this tradition (even outsiders and impious men reveal it and give assurance of it, as that passage of Lucian etc.), by which all impious reproaches are utterly silenced and extinguished. Further, Baronius acknowledges, as we do, that the Church in the time of the Apostles, and always and everywhere, taught the faithful the doctrine of the Trinity. But he does not say that Lucian asserts this itself, nor does Lucian speak to it; Baronius draws it from Lucian, and rightly. Nor could Baronius say that the Apostles taught this in any other way than by the reason of the thing and matter as it stands, which Lucian asserts in those words. Let the author consider whether he had reason for raging without restraint at my answers to what he had said against Baronius, as if he had boldly and shamelessly striven to prop up and confirm Baronius. For these points too were to be noted in the Index, as I have written, and I desire that my remarks, here as in all other matters, be compared with the author's own words [αὐτοχρολόγοις] and judged.

units.la: Porro, non dico, Lucianum sententiam Christianorum velut Apostolorum tempore jam exortam aut communem, commemorare; sed, rite Baronium, rite alios, ex verbis illis colligere communem illam Christianorum fuisse fidem, & derivatam ab Apostolis, quum tam vulgariter eam commemoret homo exterus & infidelis: &, utcunque in libris catechetici nonnunquam inspergantur aliqua minus antiqua, tamen in illa instructione, qua primum initiari conversi ex gentibus debent, non solent nova & minus nota vel certa tradi. Atque ita & in Spiritum Sanctum Veteres quoque credidisse, ex antiquissima fidei formula, liquet; & Symboli sensum esse pro nobis. Hilarius. lib. II. dixerat Dominus baptizandas gentes in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Forma fidei certa est, ex illa nempe primum sumta, sed quantum ad haereticos omnis sensus incertus est. Quos nec pudet Ecclesiæ fide contra ecclesiæ fidem pugnare, uti alibi inquit.
units.tr: Moreover, I do not say that Lucian recalls the opinion of Christians as already arisen or common in the time of the Apostles. I say that Baronius and others rightly gather from those words that this was the common faith of Christians and derived from the Apostles, since an outsider and unbeliever mentions it so commonly. And although some less ancient matters are sometimes mixed into catechetical books, yet in that instruction by which converts from the Gentiles are first initiated, new and less known or uncertain things are not usually handed down. Thus it is clear from the most ancient formula of faith that the ancients too believed in the Holy Spirit, and that the sense of the Creed is on our side. Hilary, book II: the Lord had said that the nations are to be baptised in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The form of faith is certain, taken from that very first formula; but as far as the heretics are concerned, every sense is uncertain. They are not ashamed to fight against the faith of the Church with the faith of the Church, as he says elsewhere.

units.la: Denique in epistolâ Plinii ad Trajanum, quâ Christiani narrantur carmen dixisse ut Deo, ait, idem etiam Nazaræos suos fecisse, qui tamen Christum ut merum hominem habebant. Id vero similiter ostendi cupio de Nazaræis illis, apud Scriptorem ullum Ecclesiasticum: dici simpliciter ab Adversario, aut fingi non est satis. Neque verba ut Deum explico, tamquam aliquem Deum post Patrem: quia talis nec est, neque ut Deus coli potest, aut debet. Sed bene, uti id dicitur Joan. xiv. 1. & v. 23. quod non abusive isthic de Filio, sed vere & proprie praedicatur, & similitudinem docet cultus, & fidei, & honoris Christo debiti, cum Patre. Si virtus eadem est, si honor idem est, quaero in quo defit æqualitas? Hilarius, contra Constant. Augustum. Atque ita bene colligo ex Plinii verbis, sive ut ejus, sive Christianorum accipiantur, nam ejus non alia ratione sunt, quam quod de Christianis perhibet testimonium, ex vero illos id, & quia faciunt, ex sensu animi facere, ex verbis (dico) illis bene colligo, primos illos, optimosque, quia tentationibus exercitatos, Christum, non ut merum hominem habuisse, quem ut Deum colebant. Quod idem, eodemque sensu de Christianis testatur antiquus adversus Artemonitas Scriptor ille, qui supra, quot item Psalmi, quot hymni à fratribus fidelibus antiquitus perscripti, qui Christum, verbum Dei, verum Deum esse concentu quodam concelebrant? Græce est Θεολογύσεις[?].
units.tr: Finally, in Pliny's letter to Trajan, in which the Christians are said to have sung a hymn as to God, he says the same of his Nazarenes, who nevertheless held Christ to be a mere man. I wish, however, to have this likewise shown about those Nazarenes from some ecclesiastical writer; it is not enough for the Adversary simply to say it or to invent it. Nor do I explain the words as to God to mean as some God after the Father, since no such god exists, nor can one or should one be worshipped as God. Rather, the words are used as in John xiv. 1 and v. 23, where it is said of the Son not abusively but truly and properly, and it teaches the likeness of the worship, faith, and honour owed to Christ with the Father. If the power is the same, if the honour is the same, I ask, where is the lack of equality? Hilary, against Constantius Augustus. So I rightly gather from the words of Pliny, whether they are taken as his or as the Christians', for his are nothing other than what he bears witness to about the Christians: that they did this from the truth, and because they did it from the sense of their minds. From those words, I say, I rightly gather that those first and best men, being tried by temptations, held Christ not as a mere man but worshipped him as God. The same, and in the same sense, an ancient writer against the Artemonites, the one mentioned above, testifies about the Christians: how many psalms, how many hymns have been written from antiquity by the faithful brethren, which celebrate in harmonious chorus that Christ is the Word of God and true God? In Greek it is Θεολογύσεις[?].

units.la: Ultimum refugium in hoc ponit, quod apud Tertullianum, ubi verba Plinii citantur, legitur & Deo, non ut Deo. Scilicet ex Tertulliano Plinius corrigetur, non ex Plinio Tertullianus: etiam ad mentem Plinii hæc facile conciliabuntur, etiamsi legas & Deo, modo non sit vitium codicis scribentis vocalem unam pro altera. Sæpe autem in incitationibus non ipsa adducuntur verba. Eusebius, lib. iii. cap. xxvii. ᾧ τὸν Χριστὸν θεῷ ὑμνῷ[?], quod Interpres Latinus, ex Plinii magis verbis, exponit, ad canendum Christo ut Deo. & in Tertulliano Georgii Ambianatis legitur, Christo ut Deo. Similiter apud Nicephorum, lib. iii. cap. xvii. & Ufferium, in Appendice Ignatianâ, aliosque passim.
units.tr: His last refuge is this: that in Tertullian, where the words of Pliny are cited, it is read and to God, not as to God. Evidently Pliny is to be corrected from Tertullian, not Tertullian from Pliny. Even on Pliny's meaning these things are easily reconciled, even if you read and to God, provided it is not a fault of a copyist writing one vowel for another. Often, however, the words themselves are not given in citations. Eusebius, book iii, ch. xxvii: ᾧ τὸν Χριστὸν θεῷ ὑμνῷ [sing hymns to Christ as God], which the Latin translator, drawing more on Pliny's words, renders to sing to Christ as to God. And in Tertullian, in the edition of Georgius Ambianas, it is read to Christ as to God. Similarly in Nicephorus, book iii, ch. xvii, and in Usher's Ignatian Appendix, and in others everywhere.

units.la: Cæterum Nicænam Synodum quod spectat, quâ Arius condemnatus fuit, habitam ann. cccxxv. graviter, neque hoc adeò mirum, invehitur in eam Adversarius, à pag. 313. iterumque pag. 406. & alia in Alexandrum dicit, Alexandriæ episcopum; alia in Concilium, & ejus acta; alia denique in Constantinum Imperatorem: & pro Ario, sive contra concilium, quod inaudita causa; per vim & tyrannidem; postremò à simpliciori-bus & imperitis fuit damnatus. Qualia nemo mirari potest ab Adversa-riis dici, quum ab omnibus soleant oggeri adversus latam sententiam, in hæresi & contumacia perseverantibus. Non quod velimus quævis omnium facta probare & defendere, vel Nicænorum acta omnia, quod nec lubet nec necesse est; sed,quod ad rei summam, non videmus sententiam Synodi à Scripturâ alienam, vel Arianis, aut sequacibus causam fuisse justæ adversus Synodi doctrinam querelæ & criminationum atque invectivarum, quas etiam Noster in illam congerit. Nam quomodocunque origo controversiæ se habuerit inter Arium, & Alexandrum, quam aliter hi, aliter illi referunt, & in dissertationem Alexandri alii conjiciunt, de Trinitate sic philosophantem, ac si Sabellianis visa fuisset favere ipsius oratio, alii in Arii ambitionem, in episcopatu Alexandro postpositi: sic enim refert Theodoritus, lib. 1. cap. 11. Arius cum videret Alexandrum ad episcopatus gubernacula designatum, invidia flammam, qua incendebatur minime reprimere, sed ea vehementius inflammatus, materiam contentionis & discordia indies aucupari laboravit: ac tametsi in praestabilem eximiamque Alexandri vivendi rationem aciem acriter intendendo, nihil ad falsam criminationem contra eum confingendam potuit omnino reperire, tamen ejus invidia eum quiescere non sivit. Istum igitur cum hostis veritatis diabolus nactus esset, ejus conatibus Ecclesiam procellis miscere, exagitareque instituit. Nam persuasit illi, ut Apostolica Alexandri doctrina aperte resisteret. Itaque ut Alexander Sacrarum literarum disciplina obsecutus, filium patri honore parem, eandemque habere cum Genitore subsistentiam docuit: sic Arius palam contra veritatem pugnans, eum creatum & factum affirmavit. Quinetiam adjecit, tempus aliquando fuisse, cum non erat: & alia nonnulla, quae ex ejus libris multo apertius possunt intelligi. Atque ista non in Ecclesia solum, verum etiam extra in circulis & congressibus hominum differere coepit. Per aedes quoque circum circa grassari, ut quos posset, in istorum errorum laqueos induceret. Socrates tamen, qui commemorat orationem Alexandri de unitate Trinitatis occasionem Ario praebuisse sequius quid de convenientia ejus cum Sabellianismo cogitandi, Arium dicit ἐx φιλονεικίας contentionis studio se oppositisse, acerbe satis atque aspere.
units.tr: As for the Nicene Synod, at which Arius was condemned, held in 325, the Adversary attacks it severely, and this is not surprising: from p. 313 and again p. 406. He says some things against Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, some against the Council and its acts, and finally some against the Emperor Constantine. He says that Arius was condemned against the council without a hearing, by force and tyranny, and finally by the simpler and unskilled. No one can wonder that such things are said by adversaries, since they are usually thrown at every judgment passed against those who persist in heresy and obstinacy. Not that we wish to approve and defend every deed of everyone, or all the acts of the Nicenes, which neither pleases us nor is necessary. But as to the substance of the matter, we do not see that the Synod's decision was foreign to Scripture, or that the Arians or their followers had any just cause for the complaints, accusations, and invectives against the Synod's doctrine which our author heaps upon it. For however the origin of the controversy between Arius and Alexander stood (and some report it one way, others another), and some conjecture about Alexander's discourse, philosophising about the Trinity in such a way that his speech seemed to favour the Sabellians, while others point to Arius's ambition, since he had been passed over for the bishopric in favour of Alexander (for so Theodoret relates, book 1, ch. 11): when Arius saw Alexander designated to the helm of the episcopate, he did not at all suppress the flame of envy by which he burned, but, inflamed all the more by it, laboured to seize daily material for strife and discord; and although he sharpened his gaze keenly on Alexander's excellent and outstanding way of life, he could find nothing at all with which to invent a false accusation against him, yet his envy did not let him rest. The devil, enemy of truth, having got hold of him, set about stirring the Church with storms and harassing it through his efforts. For he persuaded him to openly resist Alexander's apostolic doctrine. So while Alexander, following the discipline of the holy letters, taught that the Son is equal in honour to the Father and has the same subsistence with the Begetter, Arius, openly fighting against the truth, affirmed that he was created and made. He added, moreover, that there was a time when he was not, and some other things which can be understood much more clearly from his books. These matters he began to dispute not only in the Church but also outside, in circles and gatherings of men, and he roamed through houses round about so that he might lead into the snares of these errors whomever he could. Socrates, however, who recalls that Alexander's discourse on the unity of the Trinity gave Arius the occasion, though he thought otherwise of its agreement with Sabellianism, says that Arius opposed it out of contentiousness [ἐx φιλονεικίας], bitterly and harshly enough.

units.la: Fluctuasse autem & dubium fidei diu haesisse Alexandrum in controversia Ariana, vel mediam inter utrosque sententiam sequutum, Christoque aliam attribuisse, inter divinam & creatam, naturam, quod Noster ait, pag. 313. non est verum: neque id testatur Theodoretus. Docuit quidem Filium à Patre in hoc differre, quod genitus est à Patre ingenito, sed non aliam, mediam, aut diversam habuisse naturam. Quin contrà ibidem expresse asserit, hinc filium praeterea agnoscimus, perinde atque Patrem, nec converti, nec mutari posse, nullius rei indigentem, perfectum Filium, similem Patris: & ab eo solum quia ingenitus sit, discrepantem. Non essentia ergo & natura discrepare à Patre facit Filium, tantum generationis modo ἀνάρχῳ carentis initio: ita ut divinitatem ejus minime infringat, τὴν μὲν Θεότητα αὐτῷ μὴ παραλλάττειν[?], ἀλλὰ τῇ εἰκόνι καὶ τῷ χαρακτῆρι τῷ πρὸς ἀπηκριβωμένῳ ἐμφέρειαν καὶ πάντα ἀναλ- [illegible, ~5 letters], exquisitam per omnia Patris imagini & charactèri attribuentes similitudinem, tudinem. Patet etiam ex dissertationis scopo: quia adversus eos disputat, qui hinc quod negaret Filium Dei ex nihilo ortum, colligebant duo ipsum docere ingenita: quod negat sequi; sed Filium dicit genitum a Patre ingenito, hoc solo excepto ipsi per omnia similem. Inter Patrem ingenitum, & cætera ex nihilo facta, Filium quasi mediæ naturæ facit, ex Patre genitum, & per quem reliqua producta sint, non Patrem inter & Filium. Nec magis Sozomenus, lib. 1. cap. XVI. Alexandrum sententiæ facit ancipitem, sed quidem, quum quæstio illa ab Ario mota esset, & vigeret inter Diæcesis suæ clericos, quod eos coram se vocaverit, & audita disputatione litem componere, atque in viam reducere Arianos, omni modestia prius fuerit conatus, sed frustra. Nam causam institutæ illius coram episcopo collationis scribit fuisse, quod accusaretur nimiæ lenitatis, accusabant Alexandrum, quod has novas adversus Christianam religionem opiniones contra quam debuerat, pertulisset. At ille, ratus multo satius esse, ut rationes de rebus ambiguis ab utraque parte proponerentur, quo videretur adversarios non necessitate coegisse, sed persuadendo ad desistendum a contentione induxisse: ipse cum quibusdam ex clero sedens ut judex utramque partem in certamen adducit: & uti in disceptationibus litigiosis usu venire solet, utraque vincere conatur. Nam Arius opiniones quas protulerat, acriter defendere laborat: alii autem, filium consubstantialem esse patri & coæternum, afferunt. Convocato rursus concilio, tanta cum contentione disceptatum est, ut nullo modo consentire inter ipsos posset. Itaque cum adhuc quæstio anceps & controversa videretur, ita primo quidem Alexander animo affectus erat, ut modo hos, modo illos laudaret. Ad extremum tamen, his qui filium consubstantialem patri, coæternum asseverabant, assensus est: jussitque Ario, ut contrariis rationibus rejectis, eandem cum eo sententiam sequeretur. Verum cum ei persuadere non posset, & complures tum episcopi tum clerici ejus diœcesEos Arium vere dicere censerent, illi, cum ceteris clericis ejusdem opinionis fautoribus, interdixit ecclesia. Quæ lenitatis & prudentiæ in Episcopo fuerunt argumenta, non lubricitatis vel præcipitantiæ, aut denique contentionis: quæ vitia ei temere a Nostro impinguntur. Arium vero movisse & jactasse scribit Sozomenus, illud quod a nemine ante dictum fuerat, Filium Dei ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γεγενῆσθαι, ἦν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν[?]. Ut non Arii antiqua fuerit Patrum sententia, sed contraria. Similiter Socrates, lib. 1. cap. iii. inquit, Arium nova quadam & maudita ratione litem hanc inchoasse. & Theodoretus, lib. 1. cap. ii. Alexander igitur doctrinæ Apostolicæ patronus, primum primum hortatione & consilio eum a sententia deducere tentat. Caterum ubi Corybantum more insanire vidit, & impiam doctrinam palam praedicare, de dignitate Sacerdotali dimovet, Euangelii praecepto obsecutus, si oculus tuus dexter scandalizet te, erue eum, & projice abs te. Quo non obstante, quum pergeret Arius, & conventus praeterea seorsim celebrare, cap. iv. & seditiones porro concitare, graves ciere persecutiones, & interdum lites per mulierculas impurarum sermones, quas ipsi in fraudem impulerant, intendere, nonnunquam religionem Christianam, suas tenellas meretriculas per singulas plateas turpiter circumducendo, gravissimis contumeliis afficere; quinetiam inconsutam & indissolubilem Christi tunicam quam tortores noluerunt discindere, hi discerpere non dubitarunt. Nos igitur, sicut scelerata eorum vita & conatus execrabilis postulat suffragiis omnium tandem, licet fero propter rei ignorationem istud summus aggressi, Ecclesia, quae Christi divinitatem sanctè adorat, ejecimus, inquit Alexander, in litteris ad Alexandrum Constantinopolitanum episcopum, apud Theodoretum, cap. iv. Denique fac Alexandrum vel non recte sensisse aliquando, vel non recte aliquando egisse, quod tamen non probas, causae id nequaquam praejudicare in genere potest, vel Ario patrocinari, ejusque novis & perniciosis in Ecclesiam & fidem molitionibus, quominus in Synodum deduci, atque ab eā condemnari debuerit.
units.tr: That Alexander wavered for a long time in the Arian controversy, doubting the faith, or followed a middle opinion between the two sides and assigned to Christ a nature between the divine and the created, as our author says on p. 313, is not true, and Theodoret does not bear witness to it. He did teach that the Son differs from the Father in this, that he was begotten of the unbegotten Father, but he did not hold that the Son has another, intermediate, or different nature. On the contrary, in the same place he expressly asserts that we also acknowledge the Son, just as the Father, to be incapable of change or alteration, lacking nothing, perfect, like the Father, and differing from him only in being begotten, not unbegotten. So the Son differs from the Father not in essence or nature, but only in the mode of generation, which is without beginning [ἀνάρχῳ], and this does not in any way impair his divinity: indeed not differing from him in divinity, but in the image and the exact impress [χαρακτῆρι] of the Father, he ascribes a complete likeness in all things [illegible], attributing to the image and character of the Father an exact likeness in every respect. This is also clear from the purpose of the dissertation, since he argues against those who, because he denied that the Son of God was made out of nothing, concluded that he taught that the Son was unbegotten. He denies this consequence, and says that the Son was begotten of the unbegotten Father, and that, apart from this one thing, he is in all respects like him. He does not make the Son, begotten of the Father and through whom the rest were produced, a being of a middle nature between the unbegotten Father and the things created out of nothing; and he does not place him between the Father and the Son. Nor does Sozomen, book 1, chapter 16, make Alexander ambivalent in his opinion. Rather, when that question had been raised by Arius and was being debated among the clergy of his diocese, he summoned them before himself, and, after hearing the dispute, first tried with all moderation to settle the quarrel and to bring the Arians back to the right path, but in vain. For Sozomen writes that the reason for that conference held before the bishop was that he was accused of excessive leniency: they accused Alexander of having tolerated these new opinions against the Christian religion more than he ought. But he, thinking it much better that the arguments on the disputed matters should be set forth by each side, so that it might appear that he had not compelled his opponents by necessity but had led them to give up the contention by persuasion, sat as judge with some of the clergy and brought both parties into the contest, and, as usually happens in litigious disputes, each side tried to win. For Arius laboured to defend vigorously the opinions he had put forward; others, however, asserted that the Son is consubstantial with the Father and co-eternal. When the council was convened again, the dispute was conducted with such contention that they could not in any way agree among themselves. Therefore, while the question still seemed doubtful and disputed, Alexander was at first so disposed in mind that he praised now these, now those. At last, however, he assented to those who maintained that the Son is consubstantial with the Father and co-eternal, and he ordered Arius, having rejected the contrary arguments, to follow the same opinion as they did. But since he could not persuade him, and several bishops and clergy of his diocese judged that Arius spoke truly, he, together with the other clergy who favoured the same opinion, was excluded by the Church. These were tokens of leniency and prudence in the bishop, not of levity or rashness, or finally of contentiousness, which faults our author rashly charges against him. Sozomen writes that it was Arius who started and put forward that which had been said by no one before, namely that the Son of God was made out of things that were not, and there was when he was not. So the opinion of the Fathers was not the ancient opinion of Arius, but the opposite. Likewise Socrates, book 1, chapter 3, says that Arius began this strife by a certain new and unheard-of reasoning. And Theodoret, book 1, chapter 2: Alexander, therefore, the champion of the apostolic doctrine, first tried to turn him from his opinion by exhortation and counsel. But when he saw him raging like the Corybantes and openly preaching an impious doctrine, he removed him from the dignity of the priesthood, obeying the precept of the Gospel: If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. Notwithstanding this, when Arius went on, and moreover held assemblies apart, chapter 4, and further stirred up seditions, roused grave persecutions, and sometimes pressed quarrels through silly women, whom they had driven into deceit by their impure words, sometimes insulted the Christian religion with the gravest affronts by parading their tender little harlots through every street in a shameful way; yea, they did not hesitate to tear apart the seamless and indissoluble tunic of Christ, which the executioners had not wished to rend. Therefore, as their wicked life and their detestable attempts demanded, we, having at last undertaken this with the votes of all, though with reluctance on account of our ignorance of the matter, have cast out those who devoutly worship the divinity of Christ from the Church, says Alexander in his letter to Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, as cited by Theodoret, chapter 4. Finally, suppose that Alexander at some time did not think rightly, or at some time did not act rightly, which you do not prove; this can by no means prejudice the cause in general, or excuse Arius, or prevent his novel and pernicious attempts against the Church and the faith from being brought before the Synod and condemned by it.

units.la: Ejusdem commatis sunt, quae in Synodum dicit Noster, & Patres ejus, quod fuerunt rerum imperiti & simplices: quam a Sabino episcopo Macedoniano calumniam mutuatus, non omittere debuerat, quae contra Sabinum, & temerarium illud ejus judicium annotavit Socrates, lib. i. cap. v. & vi. atque quod Theodoretus, lib. i. cap. vii. in Patrum commendationem scribit, multos inter ipsos fuisse ἀπο-[?]στολικοὶς χαρίσμασι[?] excellentes, & qui stigmata Domini Jesu gestarent in corpore.
units.tr: Of the same kind are the things our author says about the Synod and its Fathers, that they were unskilled and simple men. He borrowed this calumny from Sabinus, bishop of Macedonia, and should not have omitted what Socrates noted against Sabinus and his rash judgement, book 1, chapters 5 and 6, and what Theodoret, book 1, chapter 7, writes in praise of the Fathers, that many among them were eminent in the apostolic gifts and bore the marks of the Lord Jesus in their bodies.

units.la: Neque inaudita causa, per vim & tyrannidem condemnati Ariani; sed habita primum diligenti causae inquisitione, & disputatione. Epistola Synodi, ad Alexandrinos, apud Socratem, lib. i. cap. vi. Primum impia & perversa dogmata Arii, eorumque qui ejus sectam sequuntur, coram sanctissimo imperatore Constantino perquisita sunt: unde placuit Concilio, communibus suffragiis anathema denunciare ejus nefaria opinioni, & verbis sententiisque execrabilibus, quibus usus est ad filium Dei blasphemus afficiendum. Et in epistola Constantini, ad Ecclesias: atque eò usque de omnibus rebus accurate quaesitum est, quoad sententia Deo omnium contemplatori grata acceptaque, propter concordiam & animorum consensum palàm pronunciata effet: sic ut nihil quod vel ad discordiam, vel fidei controversiam spectaret, omnino in posterum reliquum fieret. Subscripseruntque omnes in Synodo, exceptis quinque. Socrates, cap. v. hanc fidem approbarunt trecenti decem & octo episcopi, eique omnes assensi sunt: & uti scriptum est apud Eusebium, consentientibus animis opinionibusque eidem subscripserunt: quinque solum exceptis, qui hanc vocem ὁμοούσιον[?], id est, consubstantiale, repudiarunt: Eusebio videlicet, Nicomedia episcopo, Theognide, Nicaea, Mari Chalcedonis, Theona Marmarica, Secundo Ptolemaidis. Mox autem Eusebium, & Theognidem facti paenituit, atque subscripserunt ii quoque. Cumque Ariani aliam fidei formulam Concilio offerrent, eam ilico discerptam quidem Theodoretus memorat, cap.vii. sed, ratione addita, quia non sana, sed Apostolicis dogmatibus contraria erat, & propterea non sine indignatione rejecta.
units.tr: Nor were the Arians condemned unheard, by force and tyranny; rather, a diligent inquiry into the case and a disputation were first held. The letter of the Synod to the Alexandrians, in Socrates, book 1, chapter 6: First the impious and perverse dogmas of Arius and of those who follow his sect were examined before the most holy emperor Constantine; whereupon the Council resolved, by common vote, to pronounce anathema on his nefarious opinion and on the execrable words and sentences by which he used to blaspheme the Son of God. And in the letter of Constantine to the Churches: and all matters were investigated so carefully, until the opinion pleasing and acceptable to God, the beholder of all things, was publicly declared, for the sake of concord and agreement of minds, so that nothing which might pertain to discord or to controversy about the faith should remain at all in the future. All in the Synod subscribed, except five. Socrates, chapter 5: three hundred and eighteen bishops approved this faith, and all assented to it; and, as is written in Eusebius, with minds and opinions in agreement, they subscribed to it, five only excepted, who rejected the word ὁμοούσιον [homoousion], that is, consubstantial: namely Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theona of Marmarica, and Secundus of Ptolemais. Soon, however, Eusebius and Theognis repented, and they too subscribed. And when the Arians offered the Council another formula of faith, Theodoret records that it was at once torn up, chapter 7, but with the reason added that it was not sound but contrary to the apostolic doctrines, and therefore was rejected not without indignation.

units.la: Perperam autem Constantinum Imp. criminatur, p. 320. & 407. tum temporis adhuc catechumenum, atque inde concilium Catechumenorum verius dicendum fuisse censet, quam Episcoporum: quasi non ultra trecentum fuerint episcopi, & Imperator quamvis nondum baptizatus, qui baptismum in finem vitae distulerat, non provectae satis aetatis, & rerum princeps callentissimus fuerit: quod & ex curâ ejus ad componendam controversiam, per Hosium Cordubensem, apud Socratem, lib. i. cap. iv. & sermone atque factis in Synodo, apparuit, ejusdem libri cap. v. denique epistolis, post Synodum, ad diversos scriptis, cap. vi. quamvis à sorore Arianâ, Lucinii viduâ, sub vitae finem circumventum, & tum de zelo in Arianos remisisse, tum presbyterum Arianum ipsi commendatum, cui moriens testamentum suum reliquerit, narret Ruffinus, Socrates, Theodoretus, Sozomenus, Nicetas, lib. iv. cap. x. Unde scite Hieronymus, adversus Pelagium, Arius, ut orbem deciperet, sororem Principis ante decepit.
units.tr: Our author wrongly accuses the Emperor Constantine, pp. 320 and 407, who at that time was still a catechumen, and therefore thinks the council should more truly be called a council of catechumens than of bishops, as if there were not more than three hundred bishops, and as if the Emperor, though not yet baptized, having postponed baptism to the end of his life, was not a man of sufficiently mature age and a most experienced ruler. This appeared both from his concern to settle the controversy through Hosius of Cordoba, in Socrates, book 1, chapter 4, and from his speech and conduct in the Synod, chapter 5 of the same book, and finally from his letters written to various persons after the Synod, chapter 6, although Ruffinus, Socrates, Theodoret, Sozomen and Nicetas, book 4, chapter 10, relate that he was, near the end of his life, won over by his Arian sister, the widow of Licinius, and at that time relaxed his zeal against the Arians, and commended to him an Arian presbyter, to whom he left his testament when dying. Whence Jerome rightly says against Pelagius: Arius, in order to deceive the world, first deceived the sister of the prince.

units.la: Vox autem Consubstantialis, quamvis ab Imperatore urgeretur ut fidei confessioni adderetur, idque ad omnem ambiguitatem & tergiversationes evitandas, non tamen vel ab ipso excogitatam, vel à Nicaenis Patribus primùm usurpatam, ipse Eusebius Caesareensis testatus fuit, qui de admittendâ illâ in Synodo haesitarat, atque inter Arianos à plurimis recensetur. Vide Billium, Observat. S. lib. i. cap. xxvii. Jacobum Gothofredum, Observat. in Philostorgium, lib.i.cap. viii. Namque ubi percepisset, non aliam de istâ voce Patrum esse sententiam, quam Filium ex Patre esse, non verò partem Patris, neque ex aliâ, quam Patris substantiâ & essentiâ genitum, approbandam sibi communi assensu nomenclaturam existimavit, nam nonnullos veteres episcopos & Scriptores, viros sane distortos atque illustres, in Patris & Filii divinitate explicanda hoc verbo Consubstantiali usos fuisse cognovimus, inquit apud Socratem, lib. 1. cap. v. & apud Athanasium, in epist. de Synodis Arimin. & Seleuc. Cui quidem, addit Eusebius, omnes ad unum assensi sumus, non temere & inconsulto, sed secundum sententias coram ipso sanctissimo Imperatore propositas, discussasque, & communi omnium consensu approbatas. Unde Theodoritus, lib. 1. cap. xiii. quod autem vox Consubstantialis non sit nova, neque a Patribus id temporis Nicaea congregatis inventa, sed antiquitus a majoribus ad posteros deducta, Eusebius locuples testis est. Atque Athanasius, lib. de Decretis Synodi Nicænæ, Patres illos vocem non primos finxisse, sed a Majoribus accepisse, ostendit testimoniis Theognosti, in Secundo Hypotyposeon, & Dionysii Alexandrini, contra Sabellium, & Dionysii Romani, & Origenis. Neque vox erat, quam adeo oderant Adversarii, nisi quod ea una omnia ipsorum subterfugia præciderentur, & detegeretur eo modo multiplex ipsorum vafrities. Quid quod ipsi occasionem dederunt illius usurpandæ, adversus ὁμοουσίας[?], quibus in hoc argumento utebantur, dicendo Filium ex non existentibus factum. Athanasius: quod si rursus quia voces ista in Scripturis solennes non sint, obmurmurationes faciant, æquum profecto est, ut ea de causa ipsi potissimum rejiciantur, utpote logodædali novorum vocabulorum, & quod magis est, sanis sententiis non utentes, seque ipsi in hoc negotio incusent, quod primi hujus rei occasionem præbuerunt, dum ex non scriptis vocibus Deo bellum indicere cœperunt. Simul autem eognoscat quisquis est studiosioris animi, has voces quamvis ita in Scripturis non reperiantur, habere tamen Scripturarum sententiam, & porpterea id ipsum sonare apud illos, quibus aures ad pietatem sunt integræ & minimè vitiatæ.
units.tr: The word Consubstantial, although the Emperor pressed for it to be added to the confession of faith, in order to avoid all ambiguity and evasion, was not devised by him, nor was it first used by the Nicene Fathers. Eusebius of Caesarea himself bore witness to this. He had hesitated about admitting it at the Synod, and he is counted among the Arians by many. See Billius, Observations on Scripture, book 1, chapter 27, and Jacob Gothofredus, Observations on Philostorgius, book 1, chapter 8. For when Eusebius had learned that the Fathers held no other view of this word than that the Son is from the Father, not a part of the Father, and begotten from no other substance and essence than the Father's, he thought that the term should be approved by common assent, for we know that some ancient bishops and writers, men truly distinguished and illustrious, used this word Consubstantial in explaining the divinity of the Father and the Son, he says, as reported by Socrates, book 1, chapter 5, and by Athanasius, in his letter on the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia. To this, Eusebius adds, we all agreed without exception, not rashly or without consideration, but according to opinions set out and discussed before the most holy Emperor himself, and approved by the common consent of all. Hence Theodoret, book 1, chapter 13: that the word Consubstantial is not new, nor was it invented at that time by the Fathers gathered at Nicaea, but was handed down from the elders to their successors of old, is shown by Eusebius, a copious witness. Athanasius too, in his book on the Decrees of the Nicene Synod, shows by the testimonies of Theognostus in the second book of his Hypotyposes, of Dionysius of Alexandria against Sabellius, of Dionysius of Rome, and of Origen, that those Fathers did not first coin the word but received it from their predecessors. Nor was it a word which their opponents so hated, except that by this one word all their evasions were cut off, and their manifold cunning was exposed. Moreover, they themselves gave the occasion for its use against the homoousion [ὁμοούσιον], which they employed in this dispute when they said that the Son was made out of things that did not exist. Athanasius: But if, again, they grumble because these words are not solemn in Scripture, it is surely fair that they themselves should be rejected for that very reason, as being coiners of new words and, what is worse, not using sound sentiments; and they should blame themselves in this matter, since they gave the first occasion for it, when they began to declare war on God with words not written. At the same time, let whoever has a more earnest mind understand that these words, although they are not found in this form in Scripture, nevertheless have the sense of Scripture, and therefore they sound the same thing to those whose ears are sound for piety and not at all corrupted.

units.la: Quod autem in Ariminensi postmodum, & Seluciensi Synodo Ariani conati fuerunt & Consubstantiale demere ex fidei Confessione, & Nicænam inducere, favente ipsis Imperatore Constantio, temporum vicissitudinibus imputandum, & pervicaci Sectæ, quæ nunquam desiit frænum illud Nicænæ Synodi admordere. Quod tamen nec ita obtinuerunt, quin potiores alii in Ariminensi Synodo, cognitâ illorum fraude, antesignanos factionis Ursacium & Valentem, principes Arianorum vocat Sulpitius, & nonnullos alios pronunciarint hæreticos, & Synodum Nicænam comprobarint : uti est apud Athanasium, de Synodis : Nice- tam, Thesauro Fid. Orthod. lib. v. cap. xvii. Igitur frequentibus concilis nihil actum , nostris in fide manentibus, illis de perfidia non cedentibus, ait Sulpitius, lib. ii. Tandem circumventos pios in Ariminensi Syno- do, & ad ingenium rediisse Arianos , illorum facilitate abusos, com- pertum. Hieronymus, adversus Luciferianos; Idem regi & bonis omni- bus cura fuerat, ut Oriens atque Occidens communionis sibi vinculo nectieren-tur[?]. Sed diu scelera non latent : & cicatrix male obducta, incosto[?] pure dirum- pitur. Caperunt postea Valens & Ursacius, caterique nequitia eorum socii, egregii videlicet Christi sacerdotes, palmas suas jactitare[?] : dicentes se Filium non creaturam negasse, sed similem caeteris creaturis. Tunc usia nomen abolitum est, tunc Nicæna fidei damnatio conclamata est. Inginuit totus orbis, & Arianum se esse miratus est. Dolis videlicet Arianorum , metu Imperato- ris, illis patrocinantis, & Orthodoxorum supina credulitate atque fa- cilitate nimia. Idem a nobis dictum sit de Sirmiensi Concilio: (per erro- rem in Apparatu nostro ad Controversias & Disp. Socin. ad primum Tom. aliquoties pro Sirmiensi, scriptum Smyrnensi: uti in ipso opere, per nominum similitudinem, pro Meisnero, Mentzérus.) Augustinus lib. iii. contra Maximinum, Arian. Episc. hoc est illud homousion quod in concilio Nicæno adversus hæreticos Arrianos a catholicis patribus veritatis authoritate & authoritatis veritate firmatum est : quod postea in concilio Ariminensi, propter novitatem in verbis minus quam oportuit intellectum , quam tamen fides antiqua pepererat , multis paucorum fraude deceptis , hæretica impietas sub hæretico Imperatore Constantio labefactare tentavit. Sed post non longum tempus libertate fidei Catholica prævalente , postea quam vis verbi sicut debuit , intellecta est , Homousion illud Catholicæ fidei sanitate longe lateque defensum est. Quid est enim Homousion , nisi unius ejusdemque substantiæ ? Quid est inquam Homousion, nisi, Ego & pater unum sumus? Sed nunc nec ego Nicænum, nec tu debes Ariminensi, tanquam prejudicaturus proferre concilium: Neq; ego hujus authoritate , nec tu illius detineris : Scripturarum authoritatibus , non quorumque propriis , sed utrisque communibus testibus , res cum re , causa cum causa , ratio cum ratione concertet.
units.tr: As for the Arians' later attempts, at the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia, to remove Consubstantial from the confession of faith and to bring in the Nicene formula, with the support of the Emperor Constantius, this must be put down to the changing fortunes of the times, and to that stubborn sect, which never ceased to chew on that bit of the Nicene Synod. Yet they did not succeed so completely that others of greater standing at the Synod of Ariminum, having recognised their fraud, did not declare Ursacius and Valens, the standard-bearers of the faction and princes of the Arians, as Sulpicius calls them, and some others to be heretics, and approve the Nicene Synod, as Athanasius reports in his book on the Synods, and Nicetas in his Treasury of Orthodox Faith, book 5, chapter 17. Therefore nothing was achieved by the frequent councils, our side remaining firm in the faith, and they not giving up their treachery, says Sulpicius, book 2. At last it was discovered that the godly had been outwitted at the Synod of Ariminum, and that the Arians had returned to their old nature, having taken advantage of the others' readiness. Jerome, against the Luciferians: The same concern had been felt by the king and by all good men, that East and West should be bound together by the tie of communion. But wicked deeds do not stay hidden for long, and a poorly healed scar bursts open again. Afterwards Valens and Ursacius, and the others who shared their wickedness, those splendid priests of Christ, began to boast of their palms, saying that they had denied the Son to be a creature, but only a likeness to other creatures. Then the name of substance was abolished, then the condemnation of the Nicene faith was proclaimed. The whole world groaned and wondered that it had become Arian. Clearly this was by the deceits of the Arians, who were protected by the fear of the Emperor, and by the supine credulity and excessive ease of the Orthodox. I have said the same of the Synod of Sirmium (by mistake, in my Apparatus to the Controversies and the Disputation against the Socinians, on the first volume, I have sometimes written Smyrnensi for Sirmiensi; and in the same work, through a similarity of names, Mentzer for Meisner). Augustine, book 3, against Maximinus the Arian bishop: This is that homoousion which, against the Arian heretics, was affirmed at the Nicene council by the Catholic Fathers, with the authority of truth and the truth of authority. Later, at the Council of Ariminum, because of novelty in the words, it was understood less than it should have been; and although the ancient faith had produced it, through the fraud of a few, many were deceived, and heretical impiety under the heretical Emperor Constantius tried to weaken it. But not long afterwards, when the freedom of the Catholic faith prevailed, the word was understood as it ought to be, and that homoousion was defended far and wide by the soundness of the Catholic faith. For what is homoousion, if not of one and the same substance? What is homoousion, I say, if not, I and the Father are one? But now neither I should bring forward the Nicene council, nor should you the Council of Ariminum, as if to prejudge the matter. I am not bound by its authority, nor are you by that one. Let the matter contend with the matter, the cause with the cause, and reason with reason, by the authorities of the Scriptures, not of individuals, but of witnesses common to both.

units.la: Atque ita, nisi fallor, vindicavi fidem nostram, de Filio Dei vero Deo, cum adversus alios, tum Autorem Irenici, saltem in iis, quae nos tangebant, & nihil studio praeterii, quod quidem ad rem faciat, consisus aliorum venena nulli infirmorum facile nocitura, si quis hanc nostram ex fide praebiberit, vel etiam superbiberit potionem, uti loquar cum Tertulliano, adversus Gnosticos.Neque unum,sed plures selegi Adversarios,quamvis ejusdem census omnes, dum materia plene & ex professo disputanda erat, si forte alius quid haberet prioribus aut melius, aut copiosius, ut cuncta quae vel pro, vel contra argumentum dici possunt, annotarem & expenderem, vel, uti loquitur Lactantius, lib. v. cap. iv. ut omnes, qui ubique idem operis efficiunt, aut effecerunt, uno simul impetu profligarem. Nudâ ac simplici veritatis, & mansuetudinis ἀποδείξει [?] agendum nobis putavi: neque vincendi gloriâ tenemur, sed ardore & studio convincendi, atque convertendi. Quamvis nec vinci fit, sed vincere, ubi quis erroris admonitus corrigit eum, & sequitur meliora. Cyprianus, de hæreticis baptiz. ad Quintinum, nec enim vincimur, quando offeruntur nobis meliora, sed instruimur, maxime in his, quae ad Ecclesiae unitatem pertinent, & spei ac fidei nostrae veritatem. Quemadmodum Cæcilius dicit, in Dialogo Minutii, Octavio: nam ut ille mei victor est, ita ego triumphator erroris. Et Luciferianus, apud Hieronymum, in Dialogo, palmam refer tu mei, & ego erroris.
units.tr: And so, unless I am mistaken, I have vindicated our faith concerning the Son of God, the true God, both against others and against the author of the Irenicum, at least in those points which concern us; and I have neglected nothing that might bear on the matter, relying on the labours of others. Their poisons are not easily harmful to anyone weak, if anyone has drunk, or even drunk to the full, this our draught drawn from the faith, to use the words of Tertullian against the Gnostics. I have chosen not one but several opponents, although all of the same rank, since the subject had to be disputed fully and expressly, so that if by chance another had something better or fuller than the earlier ones, I might note and weigh everything that can be said for or against the argument. Or, as Lactantius says, book 5, chapter 4: so that I might overthrow in a single assault all who pursue or have pursued the same aim throughout their work. I thought I should proceed with the bare and simple demonstration [ἀπόδειξις] of truth and gentleness, for we are bound not by the glory of conquering but by the zeal and eagerness to convince and convert. Yet it is not losing but winning, when someone, warned of his error, corrects it and follows the better course. Cyprian, on heretics' baptism, to Quintinus: For we are not beaten when better things are put before us, but we are instructed, especially in those matters which concern the unity of the Church and the truth of our hope and faith. As Caecilius says in Minucius's Dialogue, to Octavius: For as he is my conqueror, so I am the triumphant over error. And the Luciferian in Jerome's Dialogue: You carry back the palm of me, and I of error.

units.la: Judicabit autem aliquando ipse Christus, quo animo, integritate, pro ipso steterim, adversus ejus, & nostros hostes: neque aliud, præterquam ab eo, præmium exspecto, & mercedem in cælis eo majorem, quo in terris nil nisi odium referimus & contumelias. In animo semper gerens illud quod ipse dixit, Luc. vi. 22. 23. beati estis ubi oderint vos homines &c. Jam finire lubet iisdem, quibus Hilarius libros suos de Trinitate, vel eadem ad Deum facta precatione: Conserva, oro, hanc fidei meae incontaminatam religionem, & usque ad excessum spiritus mei dona mihi hanc conscientiae meae vocem, ut quod in regenerationis meae symbolo bapti-zatus in Patre, & Filio, & Spiritu Sancto professus sum, semper obtineam, Patrem scilicet te nostrum, Filium tuum una tecum adorem, & Sanctum Spiritum tuum, qui ex te per unigenitum tuum est, promerear. Quia mihi idoneus ad fidem testis est, dicens: Pater omnia mea tua sunt, & tua mea, Dominus meus Jesus Christus manens in te, & ex te, & apud te semper Deus, qui est benedictus in saecula saeculorum, AMEN.
units.tr: Christ himself will one day judge with what sincerity and integrity I have stood for him against his enemies and ours. I expect no reward from anyone but him, and a greater recompense in heaven, the more on earth we receive nothing but hatred and insults, always bearing in mind what he himself said, Luke 6:22-23: Blessed are you when men hate you, etc. Now I am glad to finish, with the same prayer to God with which Hilary ended his books on the Trinity: Preserve, I pray, this unpolluted religion of my faith, and grant me, until the last breath of my spirit, this voice of conscience, that I may always hold to what I professed when baptised, in the creed of my regeneration, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that I may worship together with you the Father, and your Son, and your Holy Spirit, who proceeds from you through your only-begotten Son. For he is a faithful witness to me, saying: All my things are yours, and yours are mine; my Lord Jesus Christ, remaining in you, and from you, and with you, is God forever, who is blessed for ever and ever. AMEN.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

Chrium, l. Christum. p. 119. in fine ad verba Enjedini adde, postea, quomodo humanitati sit unita doceant. Deinde tum Apostoli, tum ipse Christus testantur cum & in Christo, Deum Patrem fuisse, non autem aliquem Filium aut Spiritum, & omnia operatum in Christo & per Christum. p. 153. lin. 4. hinc quae sequuntur usque ad medium paginae 161. (pro creationis autem opere &c.) debent legi p. 146. ante argum. petitum ex omniscientia Christi. p. 187. lin. 3. adde, Enjedinus in Heb. 1. p. 205. lin. 24. ὁμοσ[?]ίᾳ, l. ὁμοιώσει. p. 215. lin. 1. veritat. l. veritatis. p. 352. lin. 14. sermone, l. femine. p. 459. l. 36. post habeant, adde, ignoro. p. 533. lin. 1. post diversi, l. sententiae. p. 571. lin. 14. semper deleatur. lin. 17, 18. causam denotet impulsivam. l. non denotet causam impulsivam. p. 578. lin. 2. units.tr: P. 23, line 14: primogenitum, read unigenitum. P. 29, line 22: voluntate est, read voluntatem. P. 29: the note exceptio, dicunt Rem. &c. is to be placed on p. 22, line 4, before "exc. ad Rom. viii. 34." P. 48, line 15: quia, read qua. P. 62: Chrium, read Christum. P. 119, at the end, after the words of Enjedinus add postea, "they teach how it is united to the humanity." Then both the Apostles and Christ himself testify that God the Father was in Christ, and not some other Son or Spirit, and that he worked all things in Christ and through Christ. P. 153, line 4: what follows from here to the middle of p. 161 (pro creationis autem opere &c.) should be read after p. 146, before the argument taken from the omniscience of Christ. P. 187, line 3: add "Enjedinus in Heb. 1." P. 205, line 24: ὁμοσ[?]ίᾳ [homos?ia], read homoiōsei [ὁμοιώσει]. P. 215, line 1: veritat, read veritatis. P. 352, line 14: sermone, read femine. units.la: SOCINIANISMI CONFUTATI TOMUS SECUNDUS. LIBER PRIMUS, DE CHRISTO. CAPUT PRIMUM, De verâ Christi Deitate, seu Christo vero Deo.
units.tr: SOCINIANISMI CONFUTATI, VOLUME TWO. BOOK ONE, ON CHRIST. CHAPTER ONE: On the True Deity of Christ, or Christ as True God.

units.la: CONTROVERSIA: An Christus sit verus Deus, æternus Dei Filius?
units.tr: THE CONTROVERSY: Whether Christ is true God, the eternal Son of God?

units.la: Conjunctio hujus Tomi, cum priori. Argumentum quæstionum deinceps tractandarum. Momentum controversiæ, de naturâ Christi. Status quæstionis, de naturâ Christi divinâ. Fallaces Adversariorum, quibus Christum quasi insigniunt, tituli. Christus cur Filius Dei dicatur, juxta Socinianos, tum Remonstrantes. Vera, unicaque ejus causa, æternæ à Patre generationis argumentis adstruitur, & ab Adversariorum impugnationibus vindicatur. Discrimen sententiæ Socini, ab Erasmi Johannis, de Christo. Ariana ista. Uti & Episcopii. Fides de Christo Deo catholica. Argumentorum classes quatuor. Prima, ex Dei nominibus Christo verè tributis. Philipp. ii. 6. Joann. xx. 28. 1 Joann. v. 20. Ostenditur, nomen Dei proprie non esse officii vel dignitatis, sed naturæ, non appellativum, sed proprium; refutatis in contrarium objectionibus. Argumentum alterum, ex divinæ naturæ attributis, Christo propriis. Vindicatur Joann. viii. 18. contra perversissimas Socini, Ministrorum Transylvaniæ, atque Enjedini, expositiones. Argumentum à divinis Christi operibus. Exponitur initium Euang. Johannis. Col. i. 16. Heb. i. 2. 3. Ultimum arg. ex cultu Christo debito. De ejus adoratione. Controversia super eo inter Socinum, & Franciscum Davidis. Sententia Episcopii. Muhammedanorum confessio, de Christo, quod prædicatur Deus in epistolis Paulinis. Objectiones Adversariorum contra Christi Deitatem, ex Joann. xvii. 3. 1 Cor. viii. 6. aliæque diluuntur.
units.tr: The connection of this volume with the previous one. The subject of the questions to be treated next. The importance of the controversy over the nature of Christ. The state of the question concerning Christ's divine nature. The deceptive titles with which the adversaries, as it were, label Christ. Why Christ is called the Son of God according to the Socinians and then the Remonstrants. His true and only cause, the eternal generation from the Father, is established by arguments and defended against the attacks of the adversaries. The difference between the opinion of Socinus and that of John Erasmus concerning Christ. This Arian view, and likewise that of Episcopius. The Catholic faith that Christ is God. Four classes of arguments. The first, from the names of God truly given to Christ: Philippians 2:6; John 20:28; 1 John 5:20. It is shown that the name of God belongs properly not to an office or dignity but to nature, that it is not a common appellation but a proper one, and the objections to the contrary are refuted. The second argument, from the attributes of the divine nature proper to Christ. John 8:18 is vindicated against the thoroughly perverse interpretations of Socinus, of the ministers of Transylvania, and of Enjedinus. The argument from Christ's divine works. The beginning of the Gospel of John is explained. Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2-3. The last argument, from the worship due to Christ, and his adoration. The controversy on this point between Socinus and Francis David. The view of Episcopius. The confession of the Mohammedans concerning Christ, that he is proclaimed God in the Pauline epistles. The objections of the adversaries against Christ's deity, drawn from John 17:3 and 1 Corinthians 8:6, and others, are answered.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA
units.tr: SECTION ONE

units.la: Postquam tribus libris Socinianismi Confutati, Tomo primo, egimus de Scripturâ & religione, de Deo, de Creatione, iisque quæ titulis istis annexa sunt; sequitur de Christo tractatio, quam favente eodem, cujus agimus causam, suscipimus, ad examen vocaturi Theologiam, si ita fas sit dicere, sive doctrinam Socini, suorumque, methodo ac ordine eodem, quem hactenus fuimus sequuti, ita ut primò in statum Controversiæ diligenter inquiramus; tum sententiæ ac doctrinæ veræ adferamus nostra argumenta; denique objectiones confutemus Ad-versariorum. Neque unum alterumve ad partes vocamus, sed quoscunque nobis videre contigit & legere, interque eos, quibus ab aliis non ita, quod scimus, re-sponsum. Bene acti[?] operis Auctoribus suis reservata agnitaque, uti decet, laude. Ut tamen nec pro ea disputemus, neque adeo nobis, sed veritati, & Deo, qui labo-ris omnis sibi impensi satis augustum & gloriosum est ipse praemium ac merces.
units.tr: Having treated, in the three books of the first volume of Socinianismi Confutati, of Scripture and religion, of God, of creation, and of the matters annexed to those headings, we now take up the treatment of Christ. With the favour of the same God whose cause we are defending, we undertake to bring to examination the theology, if we may so call it, or the doctrine of Socinus and his followers, by the same method and order we have followed so far. First we shall carefully inquire into the state of the controversy; then we shall set out our arguments for the true doctrine; finally we shall refute the objections of our opponents. We summon not just one or two to the field, but whomever we have had the chance to see and read, and among them those whom, as we know, others have not answered adequately. The good work of its authors is reserved and acknowledged with the praise due to them. Yet we do not argue for that praise, nor for ourselves, but for the truth and for God, who is himself the most exalted and glorious reward and wage for all the labour expended on him.

units.la: Uti Christi consideramus personam, & status, & officia: in illa naturas duas, divinam, atque humanam; isthic, conditionem humiliationis, tum exaltationis; hic, Propheticum, Sacerdotale, & Regium: ita cum Socinianis quidem de duobus praecipue contendimus, Christi persona, & officio: ibi, de natura ejus divina; hic de Salvatoris officio Prophetico, & ejus doctrina; tum de sacerdotali officio, atque ejus satisfactione, seu Christo servatore; denique quae illam sequitur, estque ejus effectum & fructus, hominis coram Deo justificatione. De illis hoc Tomo secundo: ac primum quidem de vera Christi Deitate, seu Christo Deo, hoc dicemus libro, & quod ejusdem argumenti est, de filiatione ejus a Patre, unde Dei Filius?
units.tr: As we consider the person, the states, and the offices of Christ: in the person, his two natures, divine and human; in the states, the condition of humiliation and then of exaltation; in the offices, the prophetic, priestly, and kingly. So with the Socinians we contend chiefly over two things, the person and the office of Christ. In the person, we contend over his divine nature; in the office, over the prophetic office of the Saviour and his teaching; then over the priestly office and its satisfaction, that is, Christ as Saviour; and finally over what follows from it and is its effect and fruit, the justification of man before God. Of these we treat in this second volume. First, then, we shall speak in this book of the true Deity of Christ, that is, of Christ as God, and, which belongs to the same subject, of his sonship from the Father, whence he is the Son of God.

units.la: In principio notanda & refellenda Socini ea est sententia, qua statuit, inter quaestiones de Christo, quas partiti sumus in illas quae de ejus persona atque officio agunt, priores de persona non adeo esse cognitu necessarias. Quare in Catechesi, pag. 16. interrogans: Primum igitur, quid censes de Christi natura sive essentia nobis cognitu esse necessarium? Respondet: Id, ut antea dixi, fine cujus cognitione voluntas Dei erga nos per ipsum Christum patefacta, a nobis vel sciri, vel servari nequeat. Interrog. Quid igitur ex iis, quae ad Christi naturam sive essentiam pertinent, ejusmodi esse censes? Respondetur, Vix quidquam, &c. Similiter Ostorodus, Instit. cap. vi. Nihil necesse est ad cognoscendam Dei erga nos voluntatem, quantum ad salutem requiritur, Christi cognoscere essentiam, solummodo ejus officium. Cognitionem naturae Christi haud adeo faciunt necessariam ad salutem, vel ad religionem. Quamvis quidem cognoscendam ejus naturam alibi dicant, in Brevi Catechismo, Cap. v. Doce me, quae de Iesu Christo cognoscenda sint? R. Haec duplicia sunt: quaedam ad personam, quaedam ad munus ipsius referuntur. Quaenam sunt ea, quae ad personam ejus referuntur? Quod natura fit verus homo, qui olim quidem, cum in terris viveret, mortalis fuerit, nunc vero immortalis fit. Opinio haec originem habet ex illa, qua dicunt, duas modo esse religionis partes, praecepta, & promissiones, non adeo veritatis notitiam: quod examinavimus lib. i. cap. viii. Quare speciatim nunc ad id, quod de Christi persona vel essentia cognoscenda dicunt, quodque ejus necessitatem insuper habent, annotamus i. Varietatem opinionis hinc a Socino, inde ab Ostorodo propositae: illo dicente, Vix quidquam illius cognitu esse necessarium; isto, nihil tale esse. Quibus, quod alibi ajunt, cognoscenda quaedam de Christo esse quae ad ejus personam, quaedam quae ad munus referuntur, haud adeo videtur convenire. ii.
