Ubi Scriptura discrimen illud cognitionis utriusque, & momenti indicat, ubi agnoscit? Nusquam. Atq; huc jam applicemus id, quod Schlichtingius ait in Hebr. i. p. 45. argumenta etiam ex negato Scripturae testimonio aliquando duci posse, nempe cum agitur de rebus haud exigui momenti. iii. Quin contra Scriptura, ut summam utriusque doceret necessitatem, utrumque eodem modo, & copiose tractat, doctrinam de Christi officio non solum, sed quoque de ejus natura & essentia: ut nihil minus dicere fas sit, quam solummodo Christi officium cognosci necessario debere, non item essentiam. Sive Christi naturam spectemus divinam, sive humanam, Scriptura passim primo loco satisque abundanter quod eo spectat exponit, tum quae ad ejus officium. Vide initia Evangeliorum, & Scriptorum Apostolicorum, Matth. i. Marc. i. Luc. i. Johan. i. Rom. i. Hebr. 1. istis primum locis de Christi natura agitur, exinde officia exponuntur: neque minorem illius tractationis aut dignitatem, aut pondus, & necessitatem observaveris, quam sequentium. iv. Imo absque naturae Christi notitia, altera de ejus officiis haberi nequit, quae tota in priori fundatur, & sine ea dextre & sane explicata credita-que miserè aberrat: quare & ejus saltem ratione habenda necessaria, certè magis, quam ut Socino dicere liceat, vix quidquam; aut Oftorodo, nihil necessarium hic esse. Imo, non quaedam, sed multa ad Christi personam pertinentia, quaeque naturalia illi sunt, praeter ea quae à Deo postmodum ipsi data & concessa, quaeve ad Dei voluntatem cognoscendam aut ejus operationes referuntur, nobis cognita esse debent: secus ac Socino visum. Propterea quoque tam luculenter illa & saepius, quae ad naturam, conceptionem, & nativitatem ejus pertinent Scriptura relata voluit. v. Qua ratione in cognitione Dei quaedam dicunt de natura Dei cognitu necessaria esse, ut quod Deus sit, unus, aeternus, justus, sapiens, & non similiter quoque in notitia de Christo alia cognitu necessaria, concernentia ejus naturam, praeter ea quae ad Dei voluntatem spectant, vel Christi officium? Siquidem haud dissimilis hac in re utrobique ratio. Melior hac in parte Vorstius, quem alias nimis frequenter seu sequi amant, seu ad se pertrahere, in Delineat. fidei Christianae, cap. vii. ubi inquit: Hujus Mediatoris universa cognitio, quatenus ad salutem necessaria est, duabus potissimum partibus continetur. Nam partim ad personam, partim ad officium ipsius pertinet. Denique sententia Socini illa eo spectat, ut quamvis ejus opinione videamur errare nostra in personam Christi fide, tamen error iste salutem non evertat. Quod hactenus quidem pro nobis facit; nobis autem de ipsius sententia idem dicere, integrum haud est. In Catechesi, ad interrogationem: Quid isti tam multis tamen fiet qui illam ex ipsius Dei subsistantia Christi generationem mordicus tenent? Respondetur: Modo alioqui Christo ipsi obediant, & charitatem adversus eos exerceant, qui aliter sentiunt, nec praefracte illis eorumve sententiae sese opponant, censendum est, errorem illis ad aeternam salutem consequendam impedimento non futurum. Et in Paraenesi, vel libro de officio hominis Christiani, Socinus, cap. iv. istos nostros errores constituit in Catalogo eorum, qui licet per se ipsi aeternam salutem non adimant, tamen facile impediunt, quo minus quis recte viam, quae ad illam ducit, cognitam habeat, perque eam gradiatur.
units.tr: At the outset, the view of Socinus that must be noted and refuted is this: among the questions about Christ, which we have divided into those that concern his person and those that concern his office, he holds that the former, concerning the person, are not so necessary to know. Hence in the Catechism, p. 16, asking: First, then, what do you think is necessary for us to know about the nature or essence of Christ? he answers: That, as I said before, without knowing which the will of God towards us, revealed through Christ himself, cannot be known or kept by us. Question: Then which of those things that pertain to the nature or essence of Christ do you think are of this kind? Answer: Scarcely anything, etc. Similarly Ostorodus, Institutes ch. vi.: It is not necessary to know the essence of Christ in order to know God's will towards us, as far as salvation requires; only his office. They do not make knowledge of the nature of Christ so necessary for salvation or for religion. Yet they say elsewhere that his nature is to be known, in the Short Catechism, ch. v.: Teach me what is to be known about Jesus Christ? A. These are twofold: some relate to his person, some to his office. What are those that relate to his person? That by nature he becomes a true man, who indeed was once mortal while he lived on earth, but now becomes immortal. This opinion arises from the view that religion has only two parts, precepts and promises, and not so much the knowledge of truth; which we examined in book i, ch. viii. Therefore we now note specifically what they say about knowing the person or essence of Christ, and what they hold concerning its necessity. i. The opinion proposed by Socinus on the one hand and by Ostorodus on the other differs: the former says scarcely anything of that is necessary to know; the latter, nothing of the kind. With these views, what they say elsewhere, that some things about Christ are to be known which pertain to his person, and some which pertain to his office, scarcely seems to agree. ii. Where does Scripture indicate that distinction between the two kinds of knowledge and their importance? Where does it acknowledge it? Nowhere. And here let us apply what Schlichting says on Heb. 1, p. 45: arguments can sometimes also be drawn from a denied testimony of Scripture, namely when the matter concerns things of no small importance. iii. Indeed, on the contrary, Scripture, to teach the necessity of both, treats both in the same way and at length: not only the doctrine of Christ's office, but also that of his nature and essence. So that one could hardly say anything less than that only the office of Christ must necessarily be known, and not likewise his essence. Whether we look at the divine or the human nature of Christ, Scripture everywhere sets forth first, and abundantly, what pertains to that nature, and then what pertains to his office. See the beginnings of the Gospels and the apostolic writings: Matt. 1, Mark 1, Luke 1, John 1, Rom. 1, Heb. 1. In these first places the nature of Christ is treated, and then his offices are set out. Nor will you find that treatment any less dignified, weighty, or necessary than what follows. iv. Indeed, without knowledge of the nature of Christ, the other doctrine, of his offices, cannot be had. It rests wholly on the former, and without it, believed and explained rightly and soundly, it goes miserably astray. Therefore it must be taken into account at least for that reason, and certainly more so than to allow Socinus to say that scarcely anything, or Ostorodus that nothing, is necessary here. Indeed, not some but many things pertaining to the person of Christ, and which are natural to him, besides those things given and granted to him afterwards by God, or which refer to the knowledge of God's will or to his operations, ought to be known to us; contrary to what seemed right to Socinus. For this reason Scripture also chose to relate so clearly and so often those things which pertain to his nature, conception, and birth. v. On what reasoning do they say that in the knowledge of God some things about the nature of God must be known, such as that God is one, eternal, just, and wise, but that likewise in the knowledge of Christ other things concerning his nature, besides those which regard God's will or Christ's office, are not necessary to know? For the reasoning in both cases is not dissimilar. Vorstius is better on this point, whom they often either love to follow or love to draw over to themselves; in the Delineatio fidei Christianae, ch. vii., where he says: The whole knowledge of this Mediator, as far as it is necessary for salvation, is contained in two main parts. For it partly pertains to his person, partly to his office. Finally, the purpose of the view of Socinus is that, although in his opinion we seem to err in our faith concerning the person of Christ, that error does not overthrow salvation. This so far works in our favour, but it is not open to us to say the same of his own view. In the Catechism, to the question: What will become of those many who stubbornly hold that generation of Christ from the very substance of God? the answer is: Provided that they otherwise obey Christ himself, and exercise charity towards those who think otherwise, and do not stubbornly set themselves against them or their opinion, it is to be judged that their error will not be an impediment to obtaining eternal salvation. And in the Paraenesis, or the book On the Duty of a Christian Man, Socinus, ch. iv., places our errors in the catalogue of those which, although they do not of themselves take away eternal salvation, nevertheless easily hinder a person from knowing rightly the way that leads to it, and from walking along it.

units.la: Quaestionem autem ipsam, quae hic agitatur praecipue, de persona Christi, est, an verus sit Deus? sive an praeter humanam naturam, de qua inter nos constat, habeat quoque divinam? Hoc modo proposita quaestio de natura in Christo divina magis presse exponit τὸ ξενοφυὲς[?] quam si de Christo quaeratur in concreto, quem multis titulis Adversarii insigniunt, & divinitatem ei attribuunt, merum hominem negant, jam Deum etiam dicunt, & divinae naturae participem, atque Dei Filium: sed naturam habere divinam, aliam praeter humanam, eam unicam & veram, quae Deitatis est, pernegant. Inde librorum illi apud Socinianos fastuosi & mendaces tituli. Smalcii, de divinitate Iesu Christi. Ejusdemque alter, contra Smiglecium, de Christo vero & naturali Dei Filio: nempe, inquit, non controvertitur, an Christus Dei filius sit, sed unde & cur talis dicatur, aut sit. Contra autem Sommerus dixit, lib. ii. adversus Carolium, cap. v. Christus nusquam naturalis Dei filius dicitur: sed est υἱὸς φύσει[?] filius Dei, sicut gentes υἱοὶ φύσει[?] in bonam oleam insitae sunt. Hic apertius pro sententia sua loquutus, ille fallacius. Smalcius contra Frantzium, Disp. i. pag. 5. filium personam esse non diffitemur, eamque divinam. In Paraenesi libri de divinitate Christi: hæc sunt quæ in præsentia de Iesu Christi præstantiâ & breviter differere (longior enim harum rerum omnium tractatio librum non minimum conficeret) & omnium hominum judicio & censuræ subjicere voluimus, ut scilicet juste judicent, an ii, qui talem de Christo habent sententiam, jure dici possint, in divinitatem ejus involare, & eum illâ privare. Sic Socinus, hominem plane divinum, Discursu de officio Christi, pag. 18. & alii ejusdem classis Christum passim appellant. quare nec merum hominem dicere sustinent quasi, scilicet qualitatis & accidentium respectu, non naturæ. Catechef. Racoviensis, cap. 1. de nat. Christi: ergo Christus est merus homo? Neutiquam. Socinus, in Disp. cum Erasmo Johannis, de Filii Dei existentia: Quærimus enim, utrum Christus fuerit unigenitus Dei filius, nec ne, antequam ex virgine nasceretur, non autem utrum fuerit purus homo: Nihil autem impedit, quominus Christus non fuerit unigenitus Dei filius, nisi postquam natus est ex virgine, nec tamen sit aut fuerit unquam purus homo: At enim as, tu eum purum hominem fuisse doces: primum non credo me unquam de Christo ad ipsum modum locutum esse. Imo Deum nominant.
units.tr: The question chiefly debated here concerns the person of Christ: is he truly God? That is, besides the human nature, about which we agree, does he also have a divine nature? Put this way, the question about the divine nature in Christ is framed more pointedly [τὸ ξενοφυὲς] than if one asked about Christ in the concrete. Our opponents load Christ with many titles and attribute divinity to him. They deny that he is a mere man, and now even call him God, a partaker of the divine nature, and the Son of God. But they flatly deny that he has a divine nature other than the human, the one true nature that belongs to Deity. Hence the proud and deceptive book titles among the Socinians: Smalcius, On the Divinity of Jesus Christ; and his other work, against Smiglecius, On Christ the True and Natural Son of God. In it, he says, the question is not whether Christ is the Son of God, but whence and why he is so called, or what he is. Socinus, on the other hand, said in book 2 against Carolus, ch. 5: "Christ is nowhere called the natural Son of God, but he is the Son of God [υἱὸς φύσει], just as the Gentiles, sons by nature [υἱοὶ φύσει], were grafted into the good olive." The one speaks more openly for his view, the other more deceptively. Smalcius, against Frantzius, Disp. 1, p. 5: "We do not deny that the Son is a person, and a divine one." In the Paraenesis of the book on the divinity of Christ: "These are the matters we wished to set out and briefly discuss concerning the excellence of Jesus Christ (for a fuller treatment of all these things would make no small book), and to submit to the judgement and censure of all men, so that they may justly decide whether those who hold such a view of Christ can rightly be said to assail his divinity and deprive him of it." So Socinus calls Christ "plainly a divine man" in his Discourse on the Office of Christ, p. 18, and others of the same party call him so everywhere. Hence they do not venture to call him a mere man, as if they meant that in respect of quality and accidents, not of nature. Racovian Catechism, ch. 1, on the nature of Christ: "Is Christ then a mere man?" "By no means." Socinus, in his disputation with Erasmus Johannis on the existence of the Son of God: "For we ask whether Christ was the only-begotten Son of God before he was born of the virgin, not whether he was a pure man. Nothing prevents Christ from not being the only-begotten Son of God, except after he was born of the virgin; yet he is not, and never was, a pure man. But you, Erasmus, teach that he was a pure man. First, I do not believe I ever spoke of Christ in that way." Indeed, they call him God.

units.la: Quin dicunt Ministri Transsylvaniæ, lib. 11. de cognitione Dei, cap. VII. nec dubitatum fuit unquam, an Christus Deus dicendus esset. Smalcius, de divin. Christi, cap. XII. scribit, Iesum Christum, tunc etiam, cum in terris mortalis degeret, Deum appellatum, & reipsa fuisse. De eo enim, quod nunc, cum immortalis evasit, Deus appelletur & sit, non est ullum dubium, ut ex iis, quæ paulo post de ipsius divino regno dicturi sumus, constabit. Appellatus est igitur D. Iesus Deus, respectu muneris, quod in terris gessit, à D. Iohanne bis. Primum, quid litteræ illæ sibi volunt D. ante Christum, & Iohannem positæ? an ibi Dominus Jesus; hic Divus Johannes? Id est, ut in illam divinitatem non tantum socius veniat Johannes, neque hujus & illius divinitas specie differant; sed & pro vulgari loquendi forma Christus dicatur vulgo Deus, & Johannes excellentiori titulo decoretur, quam Christus? nisi D. significet Dominum Johannem, & sic saltem pari cum Christo fruatur fede & elogio. At quidquid sit de illa Christi divinitate, vel Deitate, liquet accidentariam, & ministerialem ipsis esse, nominis, non rei; denominativam, non essentialem; creatam, non increatam, id est, non veram, & Deo propriam vel dignam, titularem duntaxat, & Adversariis non alio fine adhibitam, quam ut Christo, nobilsque ejusmodi verbis & elogiis imponerent. Catechesis Racoviensis, de essentia Christi, cap. 1. pag. 76. Dominus Christus autem, quamvis quidem verus fit Deus, tamen non est unicus, verus Deus, qui solus à se, & perfectissime Deus est. Notate obsecro fucum, contradictionem, blasphemiam: Christus quamvis verus fit Deus, tamen non est verus Deus. Quasi vero plures Dii sint, vel alius Deus, & verus, quam unicus. In Brevi Institut. religionis succ. cap. 11. Nonne & Christus est Deus? Est quidem Deus, sed non ille summus, quandoquidem ipsius est filius. Imo non est Deus, si non ille summus: nisi & Ethnicorum more non plures modo Deos introducere velitis, sed & in classes superiorum & inferiorum eos dispositos. Præterea, quia est Filius Dei, non communi aliquâ ratione, sed singulari, quæ nec Angelis competat, neque hominibus, ut sit Patris ὁμοούσιος, & ἰσοούσιος, patet, eum Deum cum Patre summum unicumque esse. Eadem Institut. cap. ix. Ergo Dominus Iesus est purus homo? Non. Nam divinæ naturæ particeps evasit, cum spiritus vivificans sì factus, 1. Cor. 15. 45. & ex reliquorum omnium hominum numero est exemtus, quia est Dei filius, & quidem Unigenitus. Nempe jam est factus Deus, non naturâ, non etiam verus Deus. Quæso, an patereris vel te, vel alium quempiam donis, beneficiis, & imperio à Deo egregie ornatum, Deum dici, & verum Deum? Propter illa tamen, ejusejusdem speciei bona, magis enim & minus non variant speciem, Christum Deum clamatis, & verum Deum. Interim & suo se hic saepe produnt indicio, quando verum Deum à Christo distinguunt. In proœmio ad Smalcii librum, de Divinit. Christi: eosque per solam veri Dei, & filii ejus Iesu Christi gloriam rogamus. Sed & addunt Christum natura Deum, ut summam Adversariorum vafritiem agnoscamus. In Notis ad Disput. Socini, cum Christiano-Francken, de Adorat. Christi, pag.37. In hoc argumento est fallacia aequivocationis in voce Natura. Ea enim in loco ad Gal. nihil aliud significat quam Reipsa, Et opinioni opponitur, quemadmodum ibidem annotavit Theodorus Beza. Atqui hoc sensu Christus Socini sententia est natura Deus. Quid, ergo dicetis, superest, in quo disputationis cardinem figamus in controversia de Christo Deo? audivimus etenim dicentes, Christum non esse merum, non purum hominem, nec hominem solum plane divinum, sed Deum, & verum Deum, & naturâ Deum, & naturalem Dei filium, adeoque unigenitum. Sic enim Smalcius scripsit, sub eodem titulo ac Smiglecius, quasi pro Christi gloria & divinitate haud minus contendens ac ille, de Christo vero & naturali Dei filio. Socinus, contra Wiekum, cap. v. dixi-mus, nos concedere, Christum esse naturalem Dei filium. Servetus, lib. 1. de Erroribus Trinitatis concedit tria, primo, hic est Christus. Secundo, hic est filius Dei. Tertio, hic est Deus. Sed de homine accepta & intellecta. Nam pag. 12. ait, sed pro nomine denotante invisibilem Deum, horrescoconcedere. Iterum, lib. 11. pag. 57. dico, quod tota Dei natura & essentia est in Christo. Nempe
units.tr: Moreover, the ministers of Transylvania, book 2 On the Knowledge of God, ch. 7, say that it was never doubted whether Christ should be called God. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 12, writes that Jesus Christ was called God, and was indeed God, even while he lived as a mortal on earth. For there is no doubt that he is now called God and is God, now that he has become immortal, as will be clear from what we shall say shortly about his divine kingdom. Jesus was therefore called God, with respect to the office he discharged on earth, twice by Divus John. First, what do the letters "D." placed before Christ and John mean? Is it "Dominus Jesus" here and "Divus Johannes" there? That is, does John come into that divinity as a companion, so that the divinity of the one and the other does not differ in kind? Or, according to the common manner of speaking, is Christ commonly called God, while John is adorned with a more excellent title than Christ? Unless "D." signifies "Dominus John," so that at least he enjoys the same honour and title as Christ. But whatever the case with that divinity or Deity of Christ, it is clear that it is accidental and ministerial to him: a matter of name, not of thing; denominative, not essential; created, not uncreated. That is, it is not true, or proper or worthy of God, but merely a title, used by the adversaries for no other purpose than to impose on Christ and to adorn him with such words and honours. Racovian Catechism, on the essence of Christ, ch. 1, p. 76: "The Lord Christ, although he is indeed true God, is nevertheless not the only true God, who alone is from himself and most perfectly God." Note, I beg you, the trickery, the contradiction, the blasphemy: Christ, although he is true God, is nevertheless not the true God, as if there were several gods, or another God who is true besides the only one. In the Brief Institution of the Successive Religion, ch. 11: "Is not Christ also God? He is indeed God, but not the highest, since he is the Son of the highest." Indeed, he is not God if he is not the highest, unless, after the manner of the heathens, you wish to introduce not merely several gods but also to arrange them in classes of superiors and inferiors. Furthermore, because he is the Son of God not by some common reason but by a singular one, which belongs neither to angels nor to men, so as to be homoousios and isoousios with the Father [ὁμοούσιος, ἰσοούσιος], it is clear that he is God, the highest and only one, together with the Father. The same Institution, ch. 9: "Then is the Lord Jesus a mere man? No. For he became a partaker of the divine nature when he was made a life-giving spirit (1 Cor. 15:45), and he is removed from the number of all other men, because he is the Son of God, and indeed the only-begotten." Namely, he has now been made God, not by nature, and not even a true God. I ask: would you tolerate it if you yourself, or someone else excellently endowed by God with gifts, benefits and dominion, were called God, and true God? Yet on account of those goods of the same kind (for greater and less do not change the kind), you cry out that Christ is God, and true God. Meanwhile they often betray themselves by their own indication, when they distinguish the true God from Christ. In the preface to Smalcius's book On the Divinity of Christ: "and we beseech them through the glory of the true God and of his Son Jesus Christ alone." But they also add that Christ is God by nature, so that we may recognise the great cunning of the adversaries. In the notes to the disputation of Socinus with the Christian Franck, On the Worship of Christ, p. 37: "There is a fallacy of equivocation in the word 'nature' in this argument. For in the passage to Galatians it signifies nothing other than 'in reality,' and is opposed to opinion, as Theodore Beza noted there. But in this sense Christ is God by nature, according to the opinion of Socinus." What, then, you will say, is left on which to fix the hinge of the dispute about Christ as God? For we have heard them say that Christ is not a mere man, nor a pure man, nor a man only plainly divine, but God, and true God, and God by nature, and the natural Son of God, and so the only-begotten. For Smalcius wrote under the same title as Smiglecius, as if contending no less than he for the glory and divinity of Christ: On Christ the True and Natural Son of God. Socinus, against Wiekius, ch. 5: "We have said that we concede that Christ is the natural Son of God." Servetus, book 1 On the Errors of the Trinity, concedes three things: first, this is Christ; second, this is the Son of God; third, this is God. But he means this of a man taken and understood. For at p. 12 he says: "but for the name denoting the invisible God, I shudder to concede." Again, book 2, p. 57: "I say that the whole nature and essence of God is in Christ." Namely,

units.la: Pergula pictorum veri nihil, omnia falsa.
units.tr: A painter's booth: nothing true, everything false.

units.la: Omnia quae de Christo tam magnifice asserunt Adversarii, in fraudem composita sunt & dolum inanem, ut verbis & locutione sola se nobis assimilarent & veritati, reipsa longissime diversi. Nam quidquid etiam de Christo dicant, & quantumcunque ei adscribant divinitatem, ultra humanam non adscendunt naturam: omnem ejus divinitatem in donis & accidentibus constituunt. Atqui hoc est fallere velle, non docere, vel disputare. Ipsumque illud, si bene expendamus, malae causae evidens argumentum. Nam uti veritas nullas quaerit latebras, obvolucra nulla, sed se gestit ingenue planeque exponere, ita quod pigmenta amat & figmenta, seque verbosa fraude commendatum cupit, non alterius rei, quam falsitatis indicium esse potest. Eodem animo & modo, nec Trinitatem à se negari, contendunt. Eques Polonus, in Apologia, adversus Edictum D D. Ordinum, pag. 3. inquit, in margine, se'S. Trinitatem non negare, & in ipso libro, an enim nobis inquam in mentem venit negare Trium Unitatem? Similiter pag. 10. se non evertere Christi & Spiritus S. divinitatem. Ajunt, inquit, nos evertere Christi & Spiritus S. divinitatem. Atqui nos Christum Deum esse confitemur, divinitatemque Christo, quae Dei sermoni, quae Regi & judici omnium a Deo constituto, propria est, pag. 27. Unionem duarum in Christo naturarum suos non irridere. Smalcius, qui omnium copiosissime scripsit de Christi divinitate, remque istam ex suorum mente pertractavit valde plene, unde etiam librum istum communi nomine approbarunt, in proœmio: Nunc vero data opera, in hunc ipsum finem, hunc libellum edimus, in quo, quid nos, & omnes nobiscum in uno coetu congregati, de Iesu Christi praestantia & divinitate sentiant, breviter quidem, sed tamen non omnino insufficienter describimus. Iste dico Smalcius, omnem illam Christi divinitatem hisce rebus complexus fuit, primo ea, quam habuit nempe ante suam ex Maria nativitatem; deinde quam post eam. Illam iterum duplicem facit, vel quae ejus fuit ante mundum conditum, vel quae post. Prima nimirum Christi praestantia, & divinitas, quamque habuit ante mundum conditum, secundum Smalcium fuit, ejus à Deo praedestinaito. Altera, & post mundum conditum, ejus facta olim à Deo multiplex promissio. Divinitas, quae innotuit ab eo tem-pore, quo in mundo esse coepit, duum iterum constituitur generum, vid. dum mor-talis fuit, vel à quo tempore coepit immortalis esse. Quare tertia ejus divinitas sita in miraculosa conceptione & nativitate. Quarta in munere, illiusque ad hoc initiatione; tum tractatione, quando Dei revelavit voluntatem praeceptis, ac promissis divinis; denique ejus confirmatione per sanctitatem, ac vitae puritatem; potestatem, & miracula; demum afflictiones, & mortem. Porro quintam divinitatis Christi notam constituit in appellatione, quod Deus etiam hic in terris vocatus fit. Sextam, in ejus resurrectione. Septimam, in adscensione. Octavam, in regno. Nonam, in ejus pro nobis cura: in quo solo omne Christi situm vult sacerdotium. Decima ei est in fide in Christum, ejusque adoratione & invocatione. Non hæc isto numero à Smalcio pro-posita, quo nos fecimus, sed ordinis causa sic in hoc schemate distribuimus, quò compendio constaret quid quantumque divinitatis Adversarii intelligant, quando tam operose eam jactant, ut unam veram Christi Deitatem tollant. Videlicet nihil nisi donorum, operumque divinorum. Quemadmodum idem genus deitatis, licet impari gradu, in aliis quoque est agnoscere. Socinus, Disp. de natura Christi, pag. 20. Ea enim omnia vel sanctitatem vitaeque innocentiam, vel rerum humanarum, vel divinarum scientiam, vel admiranda faciendi potestatem, vel in universa dominationem atque impe-rium, vel denique illi debitam adorationem respiciunt, nihil praeterea in eo homine quod hu-manam conditionem exsuperet, inveniri posse videtur.
units.tr: Everything that our opponents assert so magnificently about Christ is composed as a deceit and an empty trick, so that by words and speech alone they may make themselves resemble us and the truth, while in reality they are far removed from it. For whatever they say about Christ, and however much divinity they ascribe to him, they do not rise above a human nature: they place all his divinity in gifts and accidents. But this is to wish to deceive, not to teach or to dispute. And this itself, if we weigh it well, is clear evidence of a bad cause. For just as truth seeks no hiding-places or coverings, but delights to set itself forth openly and plainly, so what loves paint and fictions, and wishes to commend itself by wordy deceit, can be a sign of nothing but falsehood. In the same spirit and manner they also contend that they do not deny the Trinity. The Polish knight, in his Apology against the Edict of the Lords of the Orders, p. 3, says in the margin that he does not deny the Trinity, and in the book itself: for, I ask, has it come into our minds to deny the Unity of the Three? Similarly on p. 10, that he does not overthrow the divinity of Christ and of the Holy Spirit. "They say," he says, "that we overthrow the divinity of Christ and of the Holy Spirit." Yet we confess that Christ is God, and we attribute to Christ the divinity that belongs to the Word of God, to the King and judge of all appointed by God, p. 27. The union of the two natures in Christ, they say, does not mock their own people. Smalcius, who wrote most copiously of all on the divinity of Christ and handled that matter very fully according to the mind of his people, whence they also approved that book under a common name, says in the preface: Now indeed, with this very end in view, we publish this little book, in which we describe briefly, yet not altogether insufficiently, what we, and all who are gathered with us in one assembly, think about the excellence and divinity of Jesus Christ. This Smalcius, I say, embraced all that divinity of Christ under these heads: first, that which he had before his birth from Mary; then that which he had after it. He again makes this twofold: either that which was his before the world was made, or that which was after. The first excellence and divinity of Christ, which he had before the world was made, was according to Smalcius his predestination by God. The second, after the world was made, is the manifold promise once made by God to him. The divinity which became known from the time when he began to be in the world is again constituted in two kinds, namely whether while he was mortal, or from the time when he began to be immortal. Therefore his third divinity lies in the miraculous conception and birth. The fourth lies in his office and his initiation to it; then in his handling, when he revealed God's will through the divine precepts and promises; lastly in his confirmation through holiness and purity of life, power and miracles; finally in afflictions and death. Moreover he sets up as the fifth mark of Christ's divinity his appellation, that God was called even here on earth. The sixth is in his resurrection. The seventh in his ascension. The eighth in his kingdom. The ninth in his care for us, in which alone he wishes all of Christ's priesthood to lie. The tenth is in faith in Christ, and in his adoration and invocation. These are not set out by Smalcius in this number, which we have made; but for the sake of order we distribute them thus in this scheme, so that it may be clear in brief what and how great a divinity our opponents understand, when they boast of it so laboriously in order to remove the one true Deity of Christ. Namely, nothing but gifts and divine works. Just as the same kind of deity, though of unequal degree, is to be recognised in others also. Socinus, Disp. on the nature of Christ, p. 20: For all those things look either to holiness and innocence of life, or to knowledge of human and divine things, or to the admirable power of doing, or to universal lordship and rule, or lastly to the adoration due to him; nothing else in that man which surpasses the human condition seems possible to be found.

units.la: Sed praestantiam ista dicunt, non veram arguunt divinitatem, ut Deus aliquis appellari non modo possit, sed & reipsa fit, quemadmodum Smalcius cap. XII. loqui-tur. Imo inde est, quod is fere ubique dixerit praestantiam Christi, & divinitatem, non Deitatem, quia proprie nec hanc, nec istam, illis ostendi novit, solummodo illam. In Refutatione Smiglecii, de erroribus Arian. l. II. p. 179. Veram enim Christo di-vinitatem tribuimus, qualis scilicet ei, salva sacra Scriptura & sana ratione, tribui potest. Nem-pe quia naturalis divinitas ut numero una est, sic alteri dari non potest, participata ut tribuatur, necessarium omnino est. En nugas. Quomodo est vera divinitas, si non sit naturalis? naturale & verum annon hic reciprocantur? qui non est natura Deus, neque est vere Deus. Hinc Apostolus dicit, Gal. iv. 8. [illegible, ~60 letters] Quare Christus, quum non sit natura Deus, nec vere Deus erit. Sed Deus, quemadmodum Smiglecius in Novis Monstris novi Arianismi scripserat, erit, & filius Dei metaphoricus; Semideus & Semidominus: eruntque Christianis colendi Dii duo. Tum, quomodo Christus ex mente Socini, quod supra vidimus, dici poterit natura Deus, si careat, quod Smalcius fatetur, naturali divinitate? Denique, si quod Smalcius hoc libro contra Smiglecium dicit, cap. I. rectissime Christi divinitatem potestate illius definiri, verum; quomodo ad Christi divinitatem trahunt alia, quam quae ad potestatem ejus pertinent, quae nimirum vel ante mundum, vel ante ortum Christum, vel datam ei potestatem locum habent, & de Christo totidem divinitatis argumenta ipsis constituunt?
units.tr: But they say that these are excellence, not that they prove true divinity, such that someone could be called God not only in name but in fact too, as Smalcius speaks in chapter 12. Indeed for this reason he has nearly everywhere spoken of the excellence and divinity of Christ, not of Deity, because he knew that neither this nor that could properly be shown to them, only the former. In the Refutation of Smiglecius, on the errors of the Arians, book 2, p. 179: For we attribute to Christ true divinity, such as can be attributed to him, saving holy Scripture and sound reason. For since natural divinity is one in number, it cannot be given to another; to be attributed by participation it is altogether necessary. Behold the trifles. How is it true divinity if it is not natural? Do not natural and true go together here? He who is not God by nature is not truly God either. Hence the Apostle says, Gal. 4:8 [illegible]. Therefore Christ, since he is not God by nature, will not be truly God either. But he will be God, as Smiglecius had written in his New Monsters of the New Arianism, and a metaphorical Son of God; a Demigod and Demi-lord; and there will be two gods to be worshipped by Christians. Then, how can Christ, according to the mind of Socinus which we saw above, be called God by nature, if he lacks, as Smalcius confesses, natural divinity? Finally, if what Smalcius says in this book against Smiglecius, chap. 1, is true, that the divinity of Christ is most rightly defined by his power; how do they draw to Christ's divinity other things than those which pertain to his power, namely those which have their place either before the world, or before Christ's birth, or in the power given to him, and from these constitute for themselves as many arguments of divinity about Christ?

units.la: Jam inter illa comprehensae quoque causae sunt, quare Christum Filium Dei dictum autument. Videlicet ob quatuor causas. I. conceptionem ejus ex Spiritu Sancto. II. san-ctificationem ad obeundum munus. III. resuscitationem à mortuis. IV. Potestatem, ac re-
units.tr: Now among these are also comprised the reasons why they claim that Christ is called the Son of God. Namely, for four reasons. I. his conception by the Holy Spirit. II. his sanctification to undertake the office. III. his resurrection from the dead. IV. the power, and the re-

units.la: Note: the Greek line of Gal. 4:8 above is too faint to read letter by letter and is marked illegible. gnum ei à Patre collatum. Smalcius, lib. de divinitate Christi. Et, de vero & naturali Dei filio. Restat igitur, ut aliae causae inquirantur, ob quas filius Dei censendus sit. Eae autem sunt duplices. Partim enim ob modum, quo Christus extitit, hoc est, propter miraculosam conceptionem & natiuitatem, filius Dei appellatur: partim ob similitudinem, quam cum ipso Deo habuit in hac mortali vita, & nunc in vita illa immortali habet, quae consistebat in perfecta illius sanctitate, sapientia, potentia, & nunc consistit in divina ejus natura, hoc est immortalitate, juncta cum summo illo in omnia, quae ad salutem pertinent, imperio. Libro alio contra Smiglecii Nova monstra pag. 149. In examine clvii. errorum Smiglecii pag. 6. putat se singulare quid observasse, quando ait, Christum à nativitate quidem legi appellatum Dei filium, Deum vero nusquam. Propter hanc scilicet rationem, quod ab ipsa conceptione & nativitate aliquid in Christo fuit, quod eum suo modo filium Dei probaret, nihil autem, quod eum Deum esse ostenderet. Quasi vero vel non eodem rediret, vere esse filium Dei, & ejusdem naturae Deum: & non dicatur expresse, Verbum, quod Deus erat, carnem factum, Joann. 1.1.14. & Deum esse manifestatum in carne, 1.Tim.iii.16. Annon Isaias, c.ix.6. ab ipsa pueri nativitate, & datione filii eum nominat Deum fortem [?]. Et quid si statim a nativitate non fuisset appellatus Dei filius, haud ideo minus esset, id quod semper fuit: aeque ac si ponamus non statim nuncupatum Jesum aut Christum, sequeretur eum id non esse, quod nunc vel ibi non fuit dictus. Neque enim tota rei aut personae veritas pendet ab ejus nominatione. Oftorodus similiter, contra Tradelum p. 131. Catechesis Racov. de essent. Christi, cap. 1. Volkelius, de Relig. lib. v. cap. xii. & lib. iii. c. 1. Schlichtingius, in Heb. 1.1. pag. 16. Breviter ipsorum Institutio Relig. cap. v. quae & Scripturae loca addit, communiter huc adferri solita, quae a nobis hoc in loco examinanda: Cur Dei Filius appellatur? Quatuor ejus rei sunt causae. Prima est, quia e Spiritu Sancto conceptus fuit, & sic nullum alium patrem praeter Deum habuit, quam causam expressit Angelus, Mariam virginem sic alloquens: Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te, & virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi: ideoque quod ex te nascetur sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei. Quae est secunda causa? Quia a Patre sanctificatus, & in mundum missus fuit: quam causam ipse Christus apud Iohannem expressit. Quomodo vero ea sanctificatio & in mundum missio illum Dei filium constituit? Quod hoc modo Deo sanctitate, sapientia & potentia similis evasit, ejusque personam in praedicando Euangelio maxima cum auctoritate sustinuit, qua in re etiam singularissima ac plane paterna erga ipsum Dei charitas cernitur. Quae est tertia causa? Quia Deus eum a mortuis excitavit, & ad sempiternam vitam denuo veluti genuit. Unde & primogenitus ex mortuis dicitur. Quae est quarta causa? Quia cum Deus non tantum immortalitate, sed & potestate ac imperio simillimum sibi effecit, cum eum caelestem aeternumque Pontificem ac Regem constituit. Blandrata, in Disputatione Albanensi, Actione vi. diei, dixit, Non agnoscimus aliquem Dei filium, qui non fit homo, & dicimus hunc esse Deum. 1.Quia de spiritu S. conceptus est, 2. Quia data est illi potestas in caelo & in terra. 3. Quia ubique testatus est Christus se esse filium Dei.
units.tr: ...gnum conferred on him by the Father. Smalcius, in his book on the divinity of Christ. And, on the true and natural Son of God. It remains, therefore, that other causes be inquired into, for which he is to be deemed the Son of God. These are of two kinds. For partly it is on account of the manner in which Christ came into being, that is, because of his miraculous conception and birth, that he is called the Son of God; partly on account of the likeness which he had with God himself in this mortal life, and now has in that immortal life, which consisted in his perfect holiness, wisdom and power, and now consists in his divine nature, that is, immortality, joined with that supreme authority over all things that pertain to salvation. In another book against Smiglecius' New Monsters, p. 149. In the examination of Smiglecius' 157th errors, p. 6. he thinks he has observed something singular when he says that Christ was indeed called the Son of God from his birth, but nowhere God. For this reason, namely, that from the very conception and birth there was something in Christ which proved him to be the Son of God in his own way, but nothing which showed him to be God. As if it would not come to the same thing, to be truly the Son of God and God of the same nature; and as if it were not expressly said: the Word, which was God, was made flesh, John 1:1, 14, and God was manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16. Does not Isaiah, chap. 9:6, from the very birth of the child and the giving of the Son, name him mighty God [?]. And what if he had not been called the Son of God immediately from his birth? He would be no less what he always was; just as, if we suppose that he was not named Jesus or Christ immediately, it would not follow that he was not what he is now, or was not there when he was not yet named. For the whole truth of a thing or person does not depend on its naming. Oftorodus likewise, against Tradelius, p. 131; the Racovian Catechism, on the essence of Christ, chap. 1; Volkelius, On Religion, book 5, chap. 12, and book 3, chap. 1; Schlichting, on Hebrews 1:1, p. 16. Briefly, the Institution of Religion of these men, chap. 5, which also adds the passages of Scripture usually brought forward here, and which we must examine in this place: Why is he called the Son of God? There are four causes of this. The first is that he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, and so had no other father than God; which cause the Angel expressed, addressing the Virgin Mary thus: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow you; therefore that which shall be born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God." What is the second cause? Because he was sanctified by the Father and sent into the world; which cause Christ himself expressed in John. But how does that sanctification and sending into the world make him the Son of God? In that in this way he became like God in holiness, wisdom and power, and sustained his person in preaching the Gospel with the greatest authority; in which matter also the singular and altogether fatherly love of God towards him is seen. What is the third cause? Because God raised him from the dead, and begot him again, as it were, to eternal life. Whence he is also called the firstborn from the dead. What is the fourth cause? Because, since God made him most like himself not only in immortality but also in power and rule, he appointed him the heavenly and eternal Priest and King. Blandrata, in the Albanian Disputation, Act 6 of the day, said: We do not acknowledge any Son of God who is not man, and we say that this one is God. 1. Because he was conceived of the Holy Spirit. 2. Because power was given to him in heaven and on earth. 3. Because Christ everywhere testified that he is the Son of God.

units.la: Conveniunt Remonstrantes, Apol. cap. iii. pag. 48. Ubi Christum pluribus modis & variis de causis vocari in Scripturis Filium Dei contendunt, nempe quatuor modis, quos Socinians dicunt, atque ex iisdem Scripturae locis, male expositis. Et Episcopius, Instit. Theolog. lib. iv. cap. xxxiii. Christum hominem quatuor modis vocari Dei filium ostendere allaborat. Qui in hoc quidem cum Socinianis conveniunt, quod quatuor istas causas filiationis probent, sed in hoc discrepant, quod
units.tr: The Remonstrants agree, Apol. ch. iii, p. 48. There they contend that Christ is called Son of God in Scripture in several ways and for various causes, namely in four ways, which the Socinians also name, and from the same passages of Scripture, badly expounded. Episcopius too, Instit. Theolog. bk iv, ch. xxxiii, labours to show that Christ the man is called Son of God in four ways. In this they agree with the Socinians, that they prove those four causes of sonship; but they differ in this, that

units.la: aliam etiam causam videntur agnoscere, quam sanè, modo videbimus, filiationis Christi, nempe ejus à Patre generationem, quandoquidem genitum à Patre afferunt, non tamen ὁμοούσιον; sed tum ordine, tum dignitate, tum potestate differentem à Patre, eique non collateralem vel coordinatum, aut potius consubstantialem, sed verò subordinatum: uti Episcopius exponit, cap. xxxv. libri jam citati. Neutiquam verò generatio ista divina cum humana vulgari comparanda, sive ad eam examinanda & exigenda venit. Uti enim opera Dei longe excedunt vias nostras, & Deus ipse, & praecipuè hæ personales actiones, ita non absque contumelia & blasphemia gravi quæsivit Servetus, lib. ii. de erroribus Trinitatis, pag. m. 52. Si logos filius erat natus ex patre sine matre, dic mihi quomodo peperit cum, per ventrem, an per latus? Quæ horrenda admodum, sola execratione digna verba sunt.
units.tr: they seem to acknowledge another cause as well, namely Christ's generation by the Father, which, as we shall presently see, is indeed the cause of his sonship. For they affirm that he was begotten by the Father, yet not of the same substance [ὁμοούσιον], but differing from the Father in order, in dignity and in power; not collateral or co-ordinate with him, or rather consubstantial, but truly subordinate, as Episcopius sets out in ch. xxxv of the book already cited. Yet this divine generation must by no means be compared with, or brought to the test and measure of, ordinary human generation. For just as the works of God far exceed our ways, and God himself, and especially these personal actions, so Servetus, in book ii of De erroribus Trinitatis, p. 52, was not without insult and grave blasphemy when he asked: If the Logos Son was born of the Father without a mother, tell me how he was brought forth, with the womb, or through the side? These are words most horrible, worthy of nothing but execration.

units.la: Pro verâ autem, æterna, & divina prorsus Filii à Patre generatione, eaque unicâ filiationis ejus causâ, nos primum argumentabimur; inde responsuri ad argumenta, & loca Adversariorum. Ac primo quidem ita: Qui filius Dei fuit, eâque ratione Deus ejus Pater, ante conceptionem ac nativitatem ex Mariâ, & Filius Patris, per generationem ex eo, is non demum à nativitate illâ vel post eam, coepit Filius Dei fieri: sed Christus Filius Dei fuit, ejusque ratione Deus ejus Pater, per generationem à Patre, ante conceptionem ac nativitatem ex Mariâ: Ergo. Consequentia certa est. Quare ad Minorem probandam pergimus, & ostendemus, tum Christum, ante suam ex Mariâ generationem humanam, Filium Dei fuisse; & Filium ex generatione; tum, ejus ratione, Deum ejus Patrem. Psal. ii. 7. filius meus es tu, ego hodie ילדתיך genui te. Heb. i. 4. 5. Eo major factus Angelis, quanto excellentius supra illos adeptus est nomen. Cui etenim Angelorum unquam dixit: filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? Nota 1. Angelos quoque, filios Dei aliquando appellari. Schlichtingius in locum istum ad Hebræos: appellantur quidem aliquando in Scripturâ Angeli filii Dei, ut apud Iob. cap. i. Episcopius, Instit. lib. iv. cap. xxxiii. Angeli etiam vocantur filii Dei. Iob. i. i. & xxxviii. 7. & Psalm. xxxix. 7. Deinde Angelis omnibus præponit Apostolus hunc filium Christum. iii. Atque præponit in ratione filiationis. iv. Nec ut superiorem modo, χρείττονα, sed differentem in hoc ab Angelis ἀλλοφορώτερον. v. Ergo filiationis differentia inter Christum, Angelosque debet poni toto genere diversa: nam nullo modo competit Angelis, quod in solo Christo Filio considerat Apostolus, adeoque effert. vi. Quo longius humana omnia excedit, & superat. vii. Jam vero differentia ista non constituitur in solo nomine Filii, utpote pluribus communi, sed in generatione, quâ hunc suum Filium, & à se genitum Pater solemni & singulari ratione, quod nulli usquam alteri, dixit. Schlichtingius: pronomen tu vim habet cæteros omnes præter Christum excludendi, & à tituli isti participatione arcendi, q. d. tu, & non alius: ut vel inde appareat, Christo filii Dei appellationem peculiariter convenire. viii. Propterea nequit verum esse, quod ipse, aliique cum eo dicunt, Filium Dei esse nomen imperii & dignitatis, non naturæ & generationis: quare filius nempe Dei h. l. significat eum, qui imperium ac potentiam, eamque in terris summam accepit: quemadmodum & Iudices Psal. 82. & Dii, & filii altissimi eandem ob causam vocantur. Nam hoc modo præcellentia, vel differentia Christi ab aliis in filiatione, neque tanta, neque totius generis diversa esset, nec in generatione consisteret, uti hic docemur, ix. Benè hoc exponit Schlichtingius: ego hodie genui te. q.d. quia ego te genui, idcirco te filium meum voco. Sed omnino male, Genui te, id est, te ex morte ereptum, treptum, mihi similem effeci, & Regem populi mei constitui. Nam primo, nec loco ullo, nec ratione probat, gignere illud quidem significare. Deinde, id significare, quando additur explicativum filii. Denique, quamvis forte metaphoricè alicubi accipere-tur, quod nec verum, nec probat; hoc loco extra proprium sensum, simili haud uno, haud facili ac plano, exponendum esse, ostendet nunquam. Ad locum Act. xiii. 32. 33. postea respondebimus, & quam nihil ipsos juvet, ostendemus.
units.tr: For the true, eternal and wholly divine generation of the Son from the Father, and this as the sole cause of his sonship, we shall first argue; then we shall answer the arguments and passages of our opponents. First, then, thus: whoever was the Son of God, and on that ground God was his Father, before the conception and birth from Mary, and is the Son of the Father by generation from him, did not begin to become Son of God only from that birth or after it. But Christ was the Son of God, and on that ground God was his Father, by generation from the Father, before his conception and birth from Mary. Therefore the conclusion follows. The consequence is certain. We proceed, then, to prove the minor premise, and we shall show that Christ, before his human generation from Mary, was the Son of God, and Son by generation; and that on that ground God was his Father. Ps. ii. 7: You are my son; today I have begotten you [ילדתיך]. Heb. i. 4, 5: He became as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say, You are my son, today I have begotten you? Note 1: that angels too are sometimes called sons of God. Schlichting, on that passage in Hebrews: Angels are indeed sometimes called sons of God in Scripture, as in Job chapter 1. Episcopius, Instit. bk iv, ch. xxxiii: Angels too are called sons of God, Job i. 1, xxxviii. 7, and Ps. xxxix. 7. Next, the Apostle places this Son, Christ, above all the angels. iii. And he places him above them on the ground of sonship. iv. Not merely as superior [χρείττονα], but differing from them in this [ἀλλοφορώτερον]. v. Therefore the difference of sonship between Christ and the angels must be laid down as totally different in kind; for what the Apostle considers in the Son alone, and so extols, in no way belongs to the angels. vi. And it rises as far above all human things as it surpasses them. vii. Now this difference is not founded on the name of Son alone, since that is common to many, but on generation, by which the Father, in a solemn and singular manner which he used of no other anywhere, called this his Son, begotten by himself. Schlichting: The pronoun thou has the force of excluding all others except Christ, and of barring them from sharing that title; as if to say, thou, and not another; so that from this alone it appears that the appellation Son of God belongs to Christ peculiarly. viii. Therefore it cannot be true, as he and others with him say, that Son of God is a name of office and dignity, not of nature and generation: wherefore the Son of God here means one who received dominion and power, and that the highest on earth; just as judges in Ps. 82 and gods and sons of the Most High are called so for the same reason. For in that way the pre-eminence or difference of Christ from others in sonship would be neither so great, nor of a wholly different kind, nor would it consist in generation, as we are taught here. ix. Schlichting explains this well: I have begotten you today, that is, because I begot you, therefore I call you my son. But altogether wrongly. I begot you means: I have snatched you from death, made you like myself, and appointed you king of my people. For, first, he proves by no passage and no reason that to beget means that. Second, that it means that when the explanatory word son is added. Finally, though it might perhaps be taken metaphorically somewhere, which is neither true nor proved, he will never show that in this place it must be expounded away from its proper sense, by a likeness that is not single, not easy and not plain. We shall answer the passage in Acts xiii. 32, 33 later, and show how little it helps them.

units.la: Objicit, non posse, ego hodie genui te, ad æternam Christi ex Patre generationem applicari, quia illud demum Christo dictum, quando ad dexteram Dei collocatus est. Filium autem suum Deus Christum tum temporis vocavit, & tum temporis genuit, cum eum a morte vindicatum regem cœlestem populi sui constituit. quo tum etiam vox hodie, ei facere videtur. Sed 1. ipse hoc evertit, quando mox subdit, Christum filium fuisse, & sic appellatum quoque, antequam ad dextram Dei consideret. non quod antea cum filium suum non vocaverit, aut etiam non genuerit. II. Imo hoc Scriptura fortiter & perspicue convellit, quando Christo illud dictum memorat, jam olim Psalm. II. & non demum tempore Euangelii. Iehova dixit mihi, tu es filius meus. Unde Heb. I. 5. cui enim dixit? III. Et jam tum in præsenti de hoc Filio dictum, Osculamini filium, & ne pereatis, & beati qui confidunt in eo: quæ indicant, filium jam tum etiam existentem, & Deum, id est, divinæ generationis filium: de quo & verf. penult. Servite Iehovæ. IV. Proba, usquam gignere significare, vel ex morte eripere, vel regem facere. Et hoc si voluisset, quare non plane loquutus fuisset Spiritus Sanctus, hoc quod ipsum dixisse vis, præsertim quum ita soleat, ubi rem istam loquitur? hoc ipso Psalmo, tum in præcedenti, tum in sequentibus versibus, & Regem te constitui, &c. ut omnino appareat ab hoc, quod Regem eum constituit, diversum esse, genuisse sibi filium. Uti & Psalm. cx. Denique vox hodie quando de Deo usurpatur, quidem ad nos relata tempus notat, sed non ad Deum. Heb. xiii. 8. Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem. Examinemus compendio ea quæ Enjedinus in illum locum Psalm. II. 7. adfert, qui itâ:
units.tr: They object that today I have begotten you cannot be applied to the eternal generation of Christ from the Father, because it was said to Christ only when he was set at God's right hand. But God then called his Son Christ, and then begot him, when he vindicated him from death and set him up as heavenly king of his people. On this view the word today seems to favour them. But, first, the objection undermines itself, since it at once adds that Christ was the Son and was so called even before he sat at God's right hand, not that before this he had not called him his son, or even had not begotten him. Second, Scripture itself strongly and plainly overthrows this, when it records that this was said to Christ long ago in Ps. ii, and not only in the time of the Gospel: Jehovah said to me, You are my son. Hence Heb. i. 5: For to which of them did he say it? Third, the words spoken of this Son were already applicable at that time: Kiss the Son, lest you perish, and blessed are all who trust in him, which show that the Son was already then existing and God, that is, the Son of divine generation; of whom also, in the penultimate verse, Serve Jehovah. Fourth, prove that to beget anywhere means either to snatch from death or to make a king. And if he had meant that, why did the Holy Spirit not speak plainly, as you would have it, especially since he usually does so when he speaks of that matter? In this same Psalm, both in the preceding and the following verses: and I have set you as king, and so on; so that it plainly appears that to set him as king is one thing, and to have begotten a son is another. So also Ps. cx. Finally, the word today, when it is used of God, does indeed denote time as it relates to us, but not as it relates to God. Heb. xiii. 8: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today. Let us briefly examine what Enjedinus brings forward on that passage, Ps. ii. 7, who says thus:

units.la: Psalm. II. v. 7. Iehova dixit ad me: Filius meus es tu. ego hodie genui te. Vt hic locus, quem Trinitarii, ad æternitatem Filii comprobandam producere solent, rectius intelligatur, duo quædam prius observanda sunt. Primum: duos esse præcipuos interpretandi scripturam modos. Vnum, literalem & historicum. Alterum mysticum & spiritualem. Quod omnes tam Hebræi quam Christiani doctores, uno ore fatentur; & res ipsa docet. Atque ne huic rei immoremur; certissimum est, illud Exod. II. v. 46. nec os illius confringetis, literaliter & historicè de Agno paschali: spiritualiter autem de Christi corpore esse dictum. Sic Osea II. ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum: literaliter de Israele, spiritualiter de Iesu Christo accipi. Secundum quod hic notetur, est: Psalmum secundum, literaliter de Davide, spi-
units.tr: Ps. ii. 7: Jehovah said to me: You are my son; today I have begotten you. So that this passage, which the Trinitarians are wont to produce to prove the eternity of the Son, may be understood more rightly, two things must first be observed. The first: there are two principal ways of interpreting Scripture, one literal and historical, the other mystical and spiritual. Both Hebrew and Christian teachers confess this with one voice, and the thing itself teaches it. And not to dwell on this: it is most certain that that passage, Exod. xii. 46, "nor shall you break its bone", is said literally and historically of the paschal lamb, but spiritually of the body of Christ. So Hosea xi., "Out of Egypt I have called my son", is to be taken literally of Israel, spiritually of Jesus Christ. The second point to be noted here is: the second Psalm is said literally of David, spiritually

units.la: Resp. Quæ duo præmittit ad loci expositionem, de interpretandi Scripturam modo litterali uno, altero mystico; & secundum hunc Psalmum de Davide literaliter, spiritualiter de Christo loqui, iis non tam reclamant Nostri, ac quidem argumentis, quibus illa nititur comprobare, quibus non sunt acquieturi, non secundo, tertio, & quarto. Nam quod illic concludit, contra Christum fremere & insurgere populos ac reges non potuisse, quia tempore conscripti illius Psalmi Christus secundum humanitatem nondum erat, futile est, & responso indignum. Nam Psalmus non tantum de re vel transactâ vel præsenti loquitur, sed, uti in sermone de Messiâ prophetico solet, quam maxime de futurâ. Et Christo nunritualiter de Messia, seu Christo loqui. Quod quia apud nonnullos fortasse dubium est, argu-mentis aliquot confirmabimus. Primum igitur hoc persuadeat, non tantum Hebraeorum omnium, quorum auctoritatem in scripturis in-terpretandis, nemo sanus temere contemserit, verum etiam Christianorum interpretum, & quidem aeterni Filii ac Trinitatis assertorum, consensus. Qui fatentur, historice Psalmum hunc de Davide esse conscriptum, sicut videre & legere quivis, apud Bucerum, Calvinum, Musculum, Tremellium, & alios potest. Secundo, perspicuum etiam est, autorem Psalmi hujus, de re vel transacta, vel certe praesenti hic loqui. At Iesus Christus, tempore conscripti hujus cantici, secundum humanitatem quidem, (ut cum Trinitariis loquar) nondum erat. Ergo contra eum fremere & insurgere populi ac reges, non potuerunt. Secundum divinitatem vero, si extitit, hostes & reges terrae, qui ipsum ex solio regio deturbare conati fuissent, nullos habuit. Unde liquet, literaliter haec, de Christo non fuisse scripta. Tertio, ea quae hic dicuntur, si litera urgeatur, nunquam in Iesu Christo completa sunt. Nam ejus divinitati haec non competere, clarum est. Iam vero, ne cum natus quidem ex Maria est, historice haec illi evenerunt. Qui enim sunt isti quaesopuli, quae gentes, qui Reges, qui contra Iesum jam regem constitutum consurrexerunt? Certe nec Pilatus, qui tamen rex non erat, nec Herodes, ei hoc nomine, ut illum solio & dignitate regia deturbarent, molesti fuerunt, neque consilia adversus ejus regnum contulerunt, nec copias collegerunt. Imo Pilatus, quamvis illum Regem dici audiret, tamen liberare & dimittere paratus erat. Et Herodes adversus eum non fremuit, sed hominem contemsit, & illaesum, cum in potestate sua haberet, dimisit. Pilatus Joh. 18. fatetur: Gens tua, & Pontifices tradiderunt me tibi. Soli ergo Iudaei, fuerunt hostes Iesu, & eorum consilia adversus eum, non fuerunt irrita, sed optatum finem consecuta. Cujus contrarium hic narratur. In summa, tantus concursus, tanta consultatio, quid suo tempore non acerrime restitue-runt reges ac populi universi? annon id in primis Ecclesiae initiis expresse observatum Apostolis fuit? Act. iv. 29. revera congregati sunt contra sanctum filium tuum Iesum, quem unxisti, Herodes & Pontius Pilatus cum gentibus & populis Israelis. Quin annon semper, pro ratione militantis Ecclesiae, & opposuerunt se Christo terrae filii, & opponent? Deinde, quamvis nondum homo Christus sub V.T. existebat, fungebatur tamen jam tum officio Mediatoris, vi & certitudine ejus quod aliquando futurus, & facturus erat. III. Qua ratione & tertio ejus responsum argumento. Etenim in Christum, non modo regem constitutum, sed & simul ac natus esset, consurrexerunt reges Herodes, Archelaus, & alii, sive primores, sive populi. Nam, quod in Psalmo de regibus terrae, non ita praecise de regibus accipiendum, ut non in genere de quibuscunque magnatibus & gentibus intelligendum sit: ac propterea Pilato, qui tamen rex non erat, & populo Israelis illud etiam attribuere, Apostoli non fuerunt veriti. Neque id solum spectatur in hostibus istis, num Christum regem de solio conentur deturbare, sed in genere quod ei resistunt, & obedientiam ejus excutiunt, disrumpamus vincula eorum, &c. Mirari satis nequeo quorsum interroget Adversarius, qui sint isti populi, quae gentes, qui reges, qui contra Iesum jam regem constitutum consurrexerunt? nescitne illos, nescit quid gestum in Ecclesia, ab ejus primordio, vel contra eam fit? & qui istam[?], certe eum Christum persequi, ignotum nemini esse potest. Tot populi, reges, gentes, ac unquam Christo adversati, contra eum insurrexerunt, illiq; magno certe ubique numero, ignoti nostris? Non Pilatus, inquit, nec Herodes: imo alii innumeri, & isti quoque. Sed non ut illum solio, vel dignitate regia exuerent, quid audio? tantus armorum strepitus, & apparatus belli-cus, qualem haec verba Psalmi significant, nunquam contra Iesum extitit. Praeterea, isti Reges & populi dicunt: Dirumpamus vincula eorum, &c. At Iesus, nec Iudaei, nec Gentibus imperitavit, nec vincula injecit, nulla tributa imposuit, non leges praescripsit, quibus illos constrictos tenuisset, & a quibus illi liberari concupivisset. Nam si quis haec ad doctrinam Iesu accommodet; spiritualem & mysticum introducet sensum. Quarto, haec non posse literaliter de Iesu Christo accipi,illud quoque ostendit, quod hic continua textitur historia, de eadem persona, & tempore continuato cuncta narrantur. At Novi Testamenti scriptores, cum hujus Psalmi verba, & sententias citant, diversis personis, & temporibus illa accommodant. Nam initium Psalmi, Apostoli Act.4. sibi, & persecutioni, quam post Christi ascensionem paticbantur, applicant. Dictum vero illud: Filius meus es tu, &c. Paulus Act. 13. ad Iesu Christi resurrectionem: Auctor vero epistolae ad Hebraeos, ad ascensionem ejusdem in coelum refert. Denique illud: Reges illos in virga ferrea: Ipse Christus Apoc.2. pius in vita futura regnantibus, Iohannes vero Apoc.19. v.15. ipsi Christo jam regnanti accommodat. Quae quidem, secundum sensum mysticum apte omnia dicuntur, secundum historicum vero consistere non possent. Quare ex his patet, istum Psalmum literaliter, non de Iesu, sed David loqui. Quod vero spiritualiter, de Messia, & regno Christi scriptus sit, non modo omnes Christiani, verum etiam Hebraeorum magistri fatentur.
units.tr: Reply. The author first sets out two principles for explaining the passage: that Scripture is to be interpreted in one literal sense and another mystical sense, and that on this basis the Psalm speaks literally of David and spiritually of Christ. Our side does not seriously object to this, but it does not accept the arguments by which he tries to prove it, and it does not agree with his second, third and fourth points. For his conclusion that the peoples and kings could not have raged against Christ or risen up against him, because when this Psalm was written Christ did not yet exist according to his humanity, is trifling and unworthy of an answer. The Psalm does not speak only of a thing either past or present, but, as is usual in prophetic speech about the Messiah, most of all of the future. And it speaks of the Messiah, or Christ, spiritually. Since this may perhaps be doubtful to some, we shall confirm it by several arguments. First, let the agreement not only of all the Hebrews, whose authority in interpreting Scripture no sane person would lightly despise, but also of Christian interpreters, and indeed of those who defend the eternal Son and the Trinity, persuade us. They acknowledge that this Psalm was written historically by David, as anyone can see and read in Bucer, Calvin, Musculus, Tremellius and others. Second, it is also plain that the author of this Psalm speaks here of a thing either past or certainly present. But Jesus Christ, at the time this song was written, did not yet exist, according to his humanity (to speak with the Trinitarians). Therefore the peoples and kings could not rage against him or rise up against him. According to his divinity, if he existed, he had no enemies or kings of the earth who tried to thrust him from his royal throne. From this it is clear that these words were not written literally of Christ. Third, what is said here, if the letter is pressed, was never fulfilled in Jesus Christ. For it is clear that these things do not apply to his divinity. Indeed, even after he was born of Mary, these things did not happen to him historically. For who are those peoples, those nations, those kings who rose up against Jesus, now established as king? Certainly neither Pilate, who was not a king, nor Herod was troubled on this account, so as to cast him from his throne and royal dignity, nor did they plan counsels against his kingdom or gather forces. Indeed Pilate, although he heard that Jesus was called King, was still ready to release him and let him go. And Herod did not rage against him, but despised the man and, although he had him in his power, let him go unharmed. Pilate says in John 18: Your nation and the chief priests have delivered me to you. So the Jews alone were the enemies of Jesus, and their counsels against him were not in vain but reached their desired end. The opposite is related here. In short, such a great assembling, such a great consultation, what kings and peoples in their own time did not most fiercely resist? Was this not expressly seen in the first beginnings of the Church? Acts 4:27: For truly they were gathered together against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel. Indeed, have not the sons of the earth always set themselves against Christ, according to the condition of the militant Church, and will they not continue to do so? Next, although Christ as man did not yet exist under the Old Testament, he already discharged the office of Mediator, by the power and certainty of what he would one day be and do. This is the reason, and the third point, by which his answer is refuted. For against Christ, not only when he was appointed king but as soon as he was born, there rose up the kings Herod, Archelaus and others, whether the chief men or the peoples. As for the statement in the Psalm about the kings of the earth, it is not to be taken so strictly that it cannot be understood generally of any great men and nations. For this reason the apostles did not hesitate to attribute it also to Pilate, who was not a king, and to the people of Israel. Nor is it only considered in these enemies whether they try to cast Christ from his throne, but in general that they resist him and shake off his obedience: let us break their bonds asunder, etc. I can scarcely wonder enough why my opponent asks: who are those peoples, what nations, what kings, who rose up against Jesus, now established as king? Does he not know them? Does he not know what has been done in the Church from its beginning, or is done against it? That they persecute Christ and it is not unknown to anyone. So many peoples, kings and nations have always opposed Christ and risen up against him, and surely in great numbers everywhere, unknown to our people? Not Pilate, says he, nor Herod; indeed countless others, and these too. But not to strip him of his throne or royal dignity: what do I hear? Such a din of arms and such warlike preparation as these words of the Psalm signify has never arisen against Jesus. Moreover, these kings and peoples say: let us break their bonds asunder, etc. But Jesus neither ruled over Jews nor Gentiles, nor laid on chains, nor imposed any tributes, nor prescribed laws by which he would have held them bound and from which they might desire to be freed. For if anyone applies these words to the teaching of Jesus, he will introduce a spiritual and mystical sense. Fourth, that these words cannot be taken literally of Jesus Christ is also shown by the fact that here a continuous history is woven, and everything is related of one and the same person and in continuous time. But the writers of the New Testament, when they cite the words and sentences of this Psalm, apply them to different persons and times. For the apostles in Acts 4 apply the beginning of the Psalm to themselves and to the persecution they suffered after Christ's ascension. Paul in Acts 13 applies that saying, You are my Son, etc., to the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews refers it to his ascension into heaven. Finally, You shall rule them with a rod of iron: Christ himself, in Revelation 2, applies it to the faithful who will reign in the life to come, while John in Revelation 19:15 applies it to Christ already reigning. All of these are aptly said according to the mystical sense, but according to the historical sense they could not stand. From these things it is therefore clear that this Psalm speaks literally not of Jesus but of David. That it was written spiritually of the Messiah and the kingdom of Christ is acknowledged not only by all Christians but also by the teachers of the Hebrews.

units.la: Quibus praecognitis, ad explicationem verborum accessuri, primo haec literaliter, quo modo Davidi conveniant, exponamus. Haec igitur verba Iehova dixit ad me, &c. a David, vel certe in persona Davidis dicta sunt. Vbi notetur primo, Davidem hic loqui, jam adultum, & regno ac imperio aptum. Non ergo hic de generatione naturali, seu nativitate externa agitur, nam isto modo, jam pridem David, ex suis parentibus erat genitus. Dein-id[?] annon palam praese tulit Herodes?non-ne eo incitatus Christum de medio sustulit Pilatus? Si mihi non credis, at saltem Apostolis crede, iisdem adductis ex Psalmo verbis, illud de utroq; asseverantibus. Act. iv. 25. 26.27. qui per os Davidis filii tui dixisti; quare fremuerunt gentes, & populi agitarunt inania? consurrexerunt reges terrae, & principes congregati una sunt adversus Dominum & Christum ejus. Congregati enim revera sunt adversus sanctum filium tuum Iesum, quem unxisti, Herodes & Pontius Pilatus cum gentibus & populis Israel. Vide ut conveniat Enjedino cum Apostolis: hi dicunt impletum adversus Christum Psalmi secundi vaticinium, & quoque ab Herode & Pilato:ille & hos eximere culpa allaborat, & quando, vel a quibus factum illud, quaerit. Jam illis quaeso oggerat, & quod Pilatus non fuerit rex, & quod Herodes Christum solio dejicere non studuerit, vel adversus eum non fremuerit: non Herodes magnus, nec Antipas, ejus filius, quorum alter Christum sub vitae initium, sub finem ejus alter crudeliter fuit persequutus. Prodeat Herodis & Pilati advocatus, atque in os Apostolis regerat, quod non illi, sed soli Iudaei fuerunt hostes Christi; quae totidem & aperta sunt Enjedini verba, contra rei veritatem, Apostolorum fidem, & communem Christianorum omnium sententiam, quam & in symbolo profitentur, ubi non alio sensu Christum sub Pilato passum, quam & ab eo, credunt. Neque consilia adversus ejus regnum contulerunt illi, si Enjedinum; longe vero aliter, si Euangelium audimus. Annon manifeste, &, quem regem audiebant, Christum, & ejus regnum evertere moliti fuerunt? id est, tum personam Christi, tum ejus doctrinam, & Ecclesiam? Sed, non copias collegerunt, non apparatum bellicum adversus Christum adhibuerunt. Quid tum, proinde nec molesti, nec consilia adversus ejus de notandum etiam est, cum dicitur David, filius Dei, & genitus à Deo, eo non significari physicam generationem, quasi Deus naturaliter, ex sua essentia aut natura genuisset Davidem: sed hoc intelligendum esse, de gratia, favore, & amore Dei paterno, quo Davidem amplexus est, honore, dignitate & beneficio affecit. Nam & Deus gignere, & homo ex Deo nasci dicitur, cum protectio, auxilium, & beneficium aliquod singulare à Deo homini contingit. Perspicuum autem est, nullum illustrius benevolentiæ Dei signum in Davide apparuisse, quam cum imperium & regnum ei super Israelem concessit. Ergo procul dubio, hic se à Deo genitum gloriatur David, quando hunc honorem consecutus est. Hæc autem divinæ benignitatis declaratio, tribus præcipuè temporibus facta est. Primo, cum à Samuele Propheta, coram parentibus & fratribus, in Regem Israelis David unctus est. Secundo, cum post Saulis mortem, Rex ab Israelitis creatus est. Tertio, cum interfecto Absolomo, denuo regnum recuperavit. Ita enim ipsemet, de hoc tempore, loquitur, 1 Reg. 19. v. 12. An ignoro, hodie me factum esse regem super Israel? Possunt igitur hæc Davidis [?] verba: Iehova dixit ad me, &c. ad aliquod horum temporum referri. Et cum expresse ex scriptura non constet, quando hic Psalmus fit scriptus: meo judicio, liberum est cuivis, ad illud tempus, quod ipsi accommodatissimum videbitur, sine ulla pietatis & scripturæ injuria, applicare. Verumtamen, videntur ad tempus illud medium, quando post mortem Saulis, ab universo Israële, Rex David electus & proclamatus est, commodissime referri. Tunc enim legimus Ammonitas, Philistæos, Moabitas, & alias gentes contra Davidem, sed nullo cum successu, ut hic canitur, consurrexisse. Atque hic est literalis, & historicus verborum istorum sensus: nunc veniamus ad mysticum.
units.tr: With these things previously noted, we shall now come to the explanation of the words, and first set out how these things literally fit David. The LORD has said to me, etc. These words were spoken by David, or at least in the person of David. Here it should first be noted that David is speaking here as one already grown up and fit for kingship and rule. Therefore this does not concern natural generation or outward birth, for in that way David had long before been begotten of his parents. Next, did Herod not openly show this? Was Pilate not incited by this to remove Christ from the midst? If you do not believe me, at least believe the apostles, who, quoting the same words from the Psalm, assert this of both: Acts 4:25–27: who by the mouth of David your son said: why do the nations rage and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood up and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. For truly they were gathered together against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel. See how Enjedinus agrees with the apostles: they say that the prophecy of the second Psalm was fulfilled against Christ, and by Herod and Pilate also; he labours to exempt these from blame, and asks when and by whom that was done. Now I would ask him to answer this: that Pilate was not a king, and that Herod did not strive to cast Christ from his throne, nor rage against him. Neither Herod the Great nor Antipas his son, of whom the one persecuted Christ at the beginning of his life and the other cruelly at its end. Let the advocate of Herod and Pilate come forward and throw in the apostles' faces that it was not they but only the Jews who were the enemies of Christ; these are the very words of Enjedinus, contrary to the truth of the matter, the faith of the apostles and the common opinion of all Christians, which they also profess in the creed, where Christ is said to have suffered under Pilate in no other sense than that they believe he was also killed by him. Nor did they plan counsels against his kingdom, if we follow Enjedinus; but it is far otherwise if we hear the Gospel. Did they not clearly, and against him whom they heard called king, strive to overthrow Christ and his kingdom? That is, both the person of Christ and his doctrine and the Church? But, they did not gather forces, nor did they bring warlike preparations against Christ. What then? Therefore neither were they troubled, nor did they plan counsels against his — it must also be noted that when David is called the son of God and begotten of God, this does not signify physical generation, as if God had begotten David naturally from his own essence or nature; but it is to be understood of the grace, favour and fatherly love of God, by which he embraced David and endowed him with honour, dignity and benefit. For God is also said to beget, and man to be born of God, when some singular protection, help and benefit comes from God to a man. It is plain that no clearer sign of God's goodwill appeared in David than when he granted him rule and kingdom over Israel. Therefore, without doubt, David here glories that he was begotten of God when he obtained this honour. Now this declaration of divine kindness was made especially at three times. First, when David was anointed king of Israel by the prophet Samuel, in the presence of his parents and brothers. Second, when after the death of Saul the king was made by the Israelites. Third, when, after Absalom was killed, he recovered the kingdom again. For David himself speaks thus of this time, 2 Sam. 19:22: Do I not know that today I have been made king over Israel? These words of David, The LORD has said to me, etc., can therefore be referred to one of these times. And since it is not expressly established from Scripture when this Psalm was written, in my judgement it is free for anyone to apply it, without any injury to piety or Scripture, to whatever time seems most suitable to him. Yet it seems most conveniently referred to that middle time, when after the death of Saul King David was chosen and proclaimed by all Israel. For then we read that the Ammonites, Philistines, Moabites and other nations rose up against David, but with no success, as is sung here. And this is the literal and historical sense of these words; now let us come to the mystical sense.

units.la: Confitemur igitur, una cum adversariis nostris, hæc verba: Iehova dixit ad me, spiritualiter dici à Christo, vel in Christi persona. Sed desensu, inter nos non convenit. Ajunt regnum contulerunt? adeoque nec hostes Iesu fuerunt? quæ hic dicere Noster non reformidat. Omnis ergo in Christum inimicitia, & persequutio in bello sita externo & corporali? nonne & aliis multis modis contra eum hostes se produnt? annon & bello, armorumque strepitu alii eum, ejusque regnum oppugnarunt? Quid Saulus egit, & alii sui similes contra Christum, & ejus discipulos? absque armis venit, & apparatu bellico? Non dicitur in Psalmo, vel quod omnes bello Christum adorarentur, vel pari omnes modo & hostilitatis genere.
