Alii sic, vel aliter, quotquot Christo repugnant, hic intelliguntur, quocunque id fecerint armorum apparatu, corporali an spirituali, dolo an vi. Pilatus Ioh. 18. fatetur: gens tua & Pontifices tradiderunt me tibi. Rectè, sed ita ut omnino insons in toto negotio propterea fuerit, insons Herodes, nec ii etiam hostes Jesu, soli alii Judæi? falsum. Reclamat Euangelio aperto ore, & quod ex Actis modo attulimus.
units.tr: We therefore confess, together with our opponents, that these words, "Jehovah said to me," are spoken spiritually by Christ, or in the person of Christ. But we do not agree about the sense. They say did they not confer the kingdom? And so were they not enemies of Jesus either? Our author does not shrink from saying these things here. Is every enmity against Christ, then, confined to external and bodily warfare? Do not men show themselves his enemies in many other ways? Have not others attacked him and his kingdom with war and the clash of arms? What did Saul, and others like him, do against Christ and his disciples? Did they come without weapons and without military preparation? The Psalm does not say that all were to attack Christ with war, or all in the same way and with the same kind of hostility. Whoever opposes Christ, in whatever way, is meant here, whether with an apparatus of arms, bodily or spiritual, by treachery or by force. Pilate says in John 18: "Thy nation and the chief priests have delivered thee unto me." Rightly so, but was he therefore wholly innocent in the whole affair? Was Herod innocent, and were those men not enemies of Jesus, only the other Jews? That is false. It cries out against the open Gospel, and against what we have just quoted from the Acts.

units.la: Dicat forte, tum nondum regem Christum constitutum. Quidquid sit, adversus Christum tamen hostiliter insurrexerunt. Et contra regem certe Messiam: cui & nomen & jus regis jam debebatur, propediē etiam clarissimis documentis rex manifestandus. Unde quam præter omnem veritatem scribere sit ausus Enjedinus, quod ea quæ hic dicuntur, si litera urgeatur, nunquam in Iesu Christo completa sunt, quilibet videt. Imo contrà assero, nunquam illa vere, nisi in Christo adimpleta. Nam 1. nec gentes in genere & terrarum populi ita contra Davidem insurrexerunt omnes, ac contra Christum. II. neque illo irrito conatu, quem in oppugnando Christo & ejus regno experti sunt. III. neque dominium, vincula gentibus impone David aut voluit, aut potuit, uti doctrinâ, & disciplinâ sua Christus. IV. Nec vicissim illa rumpere, & Davidi immo-enim enim illi, hic Christum loqui, de sua aeterna, ex essentia Patris generatione. Id nos pernegamus, & probari cupimus. Respondent, Christum dici Filium Dei; At Filius nascitur naturaliter. Quare Christus quoque ex Deo naturaliter genitus est. Si objiciamus, Israelem, pios homines & Reges terrae dici filios Dei; nec tamen eos ex essentia Dei esse genitos: Excipiunt, alio modo homines, & alio Christum, esse Dei filium. Nam primo, Christus tum alii, tum hic, non tantum Filius Dei dicitur, sed genitus ex Deo. Quo naturalis significetur productio. Sed hoc nihil est. Nam Israel, non tantum primogenitus Dei filius vocatur, sed etiam ex Deo genitus dicitur. Deut.32. v.18. Deum qui te genuit, dereliquisti. Et omnes regenerati, Iohan. 1. geniti ex Deo dicuntur. Imo, quod mujus [?] est, Deus se, non tantum Patrem, sed & matrem ac nutricem Israelitarum fatetur, Isaiae 46. v.3. Audite me domus Iacob, & omne reliduum domus Israel, qui portamini a meo utero, qui gestamini a mea vulva. SED instant, & adjiciunt, homines, esse tantum adoptivos Dei filios, Christum autem naturalem. At nos dicimus naturaliter illum esse genitum ex homine Maria, ideoque tum ipse Iesus se, tum alii ipsum, Filium hominis vocant. Hic cum constricti tenentur: exclamant, Christum duplicem naturalem habuisse generationem. Unam ex Patre, sine matre. Alteram ex Matre, sine Patre. Et cum haec, ut nobis ex sacris offendant, rogamus: ajunt se ex multis sacrae scripturae locis illud colligere, ex quorum numero fit, unus ille. Sed de aliis, ad hanc rem ab ipsis productis testimoniis alias, nunc hunc locum praesentem excutiamus.
units.tr: Perhaps someone will say that Christ had not yet been established as king at that time. Whatever the case, they nevertheless rose up in hostility against Christ. And certainly against the king, the Messiah, to whom both the name and the right of king were already due, and who was soon to be made manifest as king by the clearest proofs. Hence anyone can see how far beyond all truth Enjedinus dared to write that the things said here, if taken literally, were never fulfilled in Jesus Christ. On the contrary, I maintain that they were never truly fulfilled except in Christ. For: (1) the Gentiles and the peoples of the earth in general did not all rise up against David as they did against Christ; (2) nor did they achieve that futile attempt which they made in attacking Christ and his kingdom; (3) nor did David wish, or was he able, to impose a dominion and bonds upon the nations, as Christ did by his doctrine and discipline; (4) nor, conversely, did they break those bonds, and [...] to David [...] for that, here, Christ speaks, concerning his eternal generation from the essence of the Father. This we deny, and we desire to prove it. They answer: Christ is called the Son of God; but a son is born naturally. Therefore Christ too was naturally begotten of God. If we object that Israel, pious men and kings of the earth are called sons of God, and yet were not begotten from the essence of God, they reply that men are sons of God in one way and Christ in another. For first, Christ is called not only the Son of God, but begotten of God, which signifies natural production. But this is nothing. For Israel is called not only God's firstborn son, but is also said to be begotten of God. Deut. 32:18: "Thou hast forgotten God who begat thee." And all the regenerate are said to be begotten of God, John 1. Indeed, what is more, God confesses himself not only as Father, but also as mother and nurse of the Israelites, Isa. 46:3: "Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb." But they press on and add that men are only adoptive sons of God, but Christ is natural. We, however, say that he was naturally begotten of the man Mary, and therefore both Jesus himself and others call him the Son of man. Here they are held fast, cornered: they cry out that Christ had a twofold natural generation: one from the Father without a mother, and another from the mother without a father. And when we challenge them to show these things from the sacred writings, they say they gather this from many places of Holy Scripture, one of which is that one. But concerning the others, the testimonies they bring forward for this matter, we will examine them elsewhere; now let us examine this present passage.

units.la: Negamus igitur hic de Christi aeterna generatione ex essentia Patris, loqui scripturam. Idque his argumentis demonstramus. Primum, Aeternus ille, ex essentia Patris genitus Filius, ut ipsi docent, nec major, nec minor, nec inferior ulla ex parte, sed prorsus & per omnia aequalis est Deo Patri. At de quo Filio hic est sermo, minor & inferior est Patre. Ergo hic non est sermo, de Filio aeterno. Minor pro-
units.tr: We deny, therefore, that Scripture here speaks of the eternal generation of Christ from the essence of the Father. And we demonstrate this by these arguments. First, that eternal Son, begotten from the essence of the Father, as they themselves teach, is neither greater, nor less, nor inferior in any respect, but is altogether and in every way equal to God the Father. But the Son of whom this passage speaks is less than and inferior to the Father. Therefore this passage does not speak of the eternal Son. The minor pro-

units.la: rigeros se praebere gentiles, populi & terrae reges, ac quidem Christo, ejus in se respuentes imperium & regulas, quibus refraenarentur & regerentur. v. Neque adeo ob rejectum & contemtum Davidem gentes Dei iram senserunt, ac propter repudiatum Christum: risitque conatus ipsorum fruftraneos Deus contra Christum verius, quam Davidem. vi. Et in Christum potius, plenius certe quadrat, quod Rex constitutus sit super montem sanctitatis Dei, id est, Ecclesiam, quam Davidem, cujus tempore nondum templum erectum in monte sancto erat, quo Ecclesia designabatur. vii. Jam ad nullum quam Christum applicari illud Dei pn [?] vel decretum potest, quo ei dictum, filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. viii. Neque quod sequitur, pete a me, & dabo gentes haereditatem tuam, & fines terrae in tuam possessionem. vii. Quos, vasorum instar conterere, non in Davidis, sed Christi demum fuit protestate. viii. Atque ad Christi fidem & cultum invitati terrae reges, judices, populi; non Davidis. Denique ad ferendum illi submissionis & reverentiae osculum; collocandam in eo fiduciam, quod in homine ullo plane nefas: & metu quidem irae ejus, quia concidere in via alioqui possent, & perire. Illa dico, in Christum quadrant, non Davidem. Ut fi etiam de Davide in Psalmo aliquid, certe potiffima de Christo quidem, & eo solo explicari debeant, sensu spirituali & mystico, uti quae in Psalmo xlv. & alibi de Christo enunciata & praedicta occurrunt.
units.tr: [...] showing themselves stubborn, the Gentiles, the peoples and the kings of the earth, rejecting and spurning the rule of Christ and the laws by which they might be restrained and governed. v. Nor, indeed, did the Gentiles feel God's wrath because they rejected and despised David, nor because they repudiated Christ: and God mocked their vain attempts against Christ more truly than against David. vi. And it fits Christ rather, and certainly more fully, that he was set as king upon the holy mountain of God, that is, the Church, than David, in whose time the temple had not yet been erected on the holy mountain, by which the Church was designated. vii. Now that decree of God, or the decree [...], by which it was said to him, "Thou art my son, this day have I begotten thee," can be applied to no one other than Christ. viii. Nor does what follows: "Ask of me, and I will give the nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession." vii. Which he would break like vessels, this power belonged not to David, but at last to Christ. viii. And the kings, judges and peoples of the earth are invited to the faith and worship of Christ, not of David. Finally, to bring to him the kiss of submission and reverence; to place trust in him, which is clearly wicked in any man; and indeed through fear of his wrath, lest they otherwise perish and fall on the way. I say these things fit Christ, not David. So that even if something in the Psalm concerns David, what chiefly concerns Christ must certainly be explained of him alone, in a spiritual and mystical sense, as those things that occur in Psalm 45 and elsewhere, pronounced and foretold concerning Christ.

units.la: Nunc iv. videamus, ut ostendat Adversarius, illa in Psalmo non posse literaliter de Jesu Christo accipi. Quia, inquit, in Psalmo continua texitur de eadem persona historia; at in Novo Test. verba & sententiae hinc citatae diversis personis & temporibus accommodantur. Quid tum? fac argumentum, & negabitur consebatur, tam ex antecedentibus, quam confequen-tibus verbis. Nam versu 6. ita loquitur Iehova: Et ego constitui regem meum, super Sion. At hic Rex à Iehova constitutus, postea dicit illa verba: Iehova dixit ad me: Filius, &c. Item statim, v.8. eidem Regi dicit Iehova: Postula à me, & dabo Gentes, &c. Iam vero, qui ab alio constituitur Rex, qui petit & accipit ab alio regnum & imperium, certè minor est eo, à quo constituitur, petit & accipit potentiam. Iste autem est qui dicit, fe esse Filium Iehovæ, & genitum ab eo. Secundum: De eo Filio, loquitur hic scriptura, qui certo tempore, à Deo genitus est: dicit enim: Ego hodie genui te. Atqui hodie, certum & determinatum tempus; genui actionem præteritam significat; Sed Filius ille æternus neque certo tempore genitus est, fuit enim semper, initio & fine carens. Neque ejus generatio transacta est; quia ajunt ipsum semper gigni, semper genitum, & semper esse gignendum. Quod verò hic quidam per vocem hodie æternitatem significari affirmant, valde ineptum & ridiculum est. Nunquam enim ostendent in scriptura voce illa æternitatem significari, nos autem monstrare possumus, semper tempus determinatum ea denotari, ut Exod. 14. v. 13. Luc. 19. v.9. &c. Ideoque etiam Trinitarii, hoc commentum conspuunt, & frivolum esse affirmant. Tertio, hanc interpretationem evertimus, testimonio Apostolorum. Nam illi quotiescunque hoc dictum producunt, non alteri, quam homini Iesu, ex Maria virgine nato applicant. Et quidem ita, ut nullo modo ad divinam naturam referri possit. Tribus autem in locis, hæc sententia in Novo Testamento profertur. Primo Act. 13. v. 31. ubi inquit ad Iudæos Paulus: Quoniam hanc (repromissionem) Deus adimplevit filiis nostris, resuscitans Iesum, sicut & in Psalmo fecundo scriptum est: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Vbi Apostolus manifestissime, hanc prophetiam ei applicat, qui mortuus & resuscitatus est. At Filius ille æternus, nec mortuus est unquam, nec re-surrexit. Ergo hic locus ad eum nihil spectat.
units.tr: Now iv. let us see how the opponent shows that those things in the Psalm cannot be taken literally of Jesus Christ. Because, he says, in the Psalm a continuous history is woven concerning the same person; but in the New Testament the words and sentences cited from here are applied to different persons and times. What then? Grant the argument, and the consequence will be denied. For the exposition of a passage is distinguished from its application, so that the latter may be different although the former is one and the same; and why should one thing not be applied in different ways to different things and persons, especially at different times? For nothing is less [...] than the sense was considered, both from the preceding words and from the following ones. For in verse 6 Jehovah speaks thus: "Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion." But this king, set up by Jehovah, afterwards says those words: "Jehovah said to me, Thou art my son," etc. Likewise immediately, in verse 8, Jehovah says to the same King: "Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations," etc. Now indeed, he who is made king by another, who asks and receives kingdom and rule from another, is certainly less than the one by whom he is made king, and asks and receives power. But this one is he who says that he is the Son of Jehovah, and begotten by him. Second: the Scripture here speaks of that Son who was begotten by God at a certain time, for it says: "This day have I begotten thee." But "this day" signifies a certain and determined time, and "begotten" signifies a past action. But that eternal Son was neither begotten at a certain time, for he always was, without beginning or end. Nor is his generation past, because they say he is always being begotten, always begotten, and always to be begotten. That some here affirm that by the word "today" eternity is signified is very foolish and ridiculous. For they will never show that eternity is signified by that word in Scripture, whereas we can show that a determined time is always denoted by it, as in Exod. 14:13, Luke 19:9, etc. Therefore even the Trinitarians spit upon this fiction and affirm it to be frivolous. Third, we overturn this interpretation by the testimony of the Apostles. For whenever they cite this saying, they apply it to no one other than the man Jesus, born of the virgin Mary. And indeed in such a way that it can in no way be referred to the divine nature. Now this sentence is quoted in the New Testament in three places. First, Acts 13:31, where Paul says to the Jews: "That God has fulfilled this promise to our children, in that he raised up Jesus, as it is also written in the second Psalm: Thou art my son, this day have I begotten thee." Here the Apostle most clearly applies this prophecy to him who died and was raised again. But that eternal Son neither ever died nor rose again. Therefore this passage has nothing to do with him.

units.la: quentia. Nam & distinguitur loci alicujus expositio, ab ejus applicatione: ut hæc possit esse diversa, quamvis illa una fit eademque: & quid ni diversis rebus ac personis diversimode unum aliquid applicari possit? præsertim diversis temporibus. Nihil enim minus aut sensus aut rei unitatem tollit, quam diversis temporibus illius facta applicatio. Quot non temporibus & rebus sæpissime unus idemque Scripturæ locus applicatur, de unâ & eadem re loquens? Ecquis ita argumentantem ferat, diversis personis, rebus, temporibus idem accommodatur dictum, ergo non est unius sensus, non de uno eodemque agit? Quæso quid ni & initium Psalmi, ubi de Christi perfequutoribus, applicetur ab Apostolis, Act. iv. persecutioni, quam post Christi adscensionem patiebantur? & verf. 7. filius meus es tu, &c. Christo, tum in resurrectione ejus, tum adscensione? quibus efficaciter & clarissime declaratus est Christus esse iste Dei filius. Jam an ad resurrectionem & adscensionem Christi, annon ad Christum ipsum, quamvis adscensionis aut resurrectionis ejus forte illis in locis fiat mentio, referatur illud ex Psalmo allegatum, ut non quod resurrexerit vel adscenderit, sed quis, denotetur, suo loco examinabitur. Ita nec quod reges illos virga ferrea, in Apoc. Christo regnanti, piisque, cum & per eum regnantibus attribuitur, nam & additur in textu, Apoc. 1. 27. quemadmodum & ego accepi à Patre, nihil efficit, quare non de Jesu Christo Psalmus possit, certe illa debeant, & non item de Davide, vere ac proprie intelligi.
units.tr: consequence. For the exposition of a passage is distinguished from its application, so the two can differ even though the exposition is one and the same. And why should one thing not be applied in different ways to different things and persons, especially at different times? A change of time does nothing to remove the unity of the sense or of the matter by its application. How often is one and the same passage of Scripture applied at different times and to different things, while speaking of one and the same matter? Who would tolerate this argument: the same saying is applied to different persons, things and times, therefore it does not have one sense and does not speak of one and the same thing? I ask, why should the opening of the Psalm, where it speaks of Christ's persecutors, not be applied by the Apostles (Acts 4) to the persecution they suffered after Christ's ascension? And why should verse 7, "You are my Son, etc.," not be applied to Christ, both at his resurrection and at his ascension, by which Christ was most clearly and effectively declared to be that Son of God? Whether the passage quoted from the Psalm refers to the resurrection and ascension of Christ, or to Christ himself, even though mention of his ascension or resurrection may happen to occur in those places, and whether it denotes not that he rose or ascended but who he is, will be examined in its own place. Likewise, the fact that in Revelation the rule with the iron rod is attributed to Christ reigning and to the pious who reign through him (for the text adds, Rev. 2:27, "as I also received from my Father") proves nothing about why the Psalm cannot be understood truly and properly of Jesus Christ, and not equally of David.

units.la: Ostensurus porro de Davide debere exponi ista, Iehova dixit ad me, &c. notat primo, Davidem loqui adultum; tum non de sua generatione naturali, quasi ex Deo naturaliter effet genitus: verum ita non probat, quod probandum erat, sed ScSecundo citatur hic locus, in epistola ad Hebr. cap. 1. Vbi cum dixisset Apostolus, Deum nouissimis diebus, nobis locutum esse per Filium, quem haeredem universorum constituit; addit ad eundem, haec illum verba dixisse: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. At certe, nouissimis diebus, locutus est, & a Deo haeres constitutus est, non aliquis Filius aeternus, qui a nemine constitui, utpote omnipotens, haeres omnium potest: sed Filius ille Mariae, homo Iesus Christus. De hoc ergo, non de illo hic agitur. Tertio, hic idem auctor, cap.5.v.5. iterum citat hoc dictum: Sic & Christus non semetipsum clarificavit, ut Pontifex fieret, sed qui locutus est ad eum: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Hic quoque illi applicatur dictum illud, qui clarificatus est a Deo, & ab eodem Pontificatum accepit. At aeternus Filius, nec clarificatus est, nec Pontificatum a quoquam accepit. Ergo haec Prophetia Psalmi, nihil ad illum pertinet. Postremo accedat etiam confessio adversariorum, qui etsi aeternam Filii Deitatem adstruunt: tamen fatentur, hic omnino agi de Filio exaltato, & in summum dignitatis gradum evecto. Sicut videre, in eorum, quos supra nominavimus, Commentariis quilibet potest. Hac igitur falsa opinione repudiata, explicemus genuinam verborum prophetae sententiam. Iam antea diximus, ne ἰσηχῶς[?] quidem posse haec verba de nativitate externa, & generatione naturali accipi. Ergo multo minus eam significabunt, mystice & spiritualiter accepta. Cum ea etiam, quae literaliter accepta, naturalia sunt, si ad mysticum sensum transferantur, spiritualia evadant. Sicut ergo de Davide dicebamus generationem ejus ex Deo, significare amorem, favorem, beneficium, & evectionem ad regiam dignitatem; quod praecipue tribus temporibus in illo declaratum fuit: ita etiam affirmamus, Christi a Deo generationem, significare favorem, protectionem, gratiam, & regiam dignitatem ei divinitus collatam. Quae tribus similiter temporibus, praecipue declarata est. Nam etsi tempore quoque conceptionis, dixerit An-
units.tr: Intending to show further that these words, "The LORD said to me, etc.," must be explained of David, he first notes that David speaks as an adult, and then not of his natural generation, as if he were naturally begotten of God. But in this way he does not prove what needed proof. Secondly, this passage is cited in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1. There, after the Apostle has said that God in these last days has spoken to us by the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, he adds that God said to him these words: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you." But surely it was not some eternal Son who spoke in these last days and was appointed heir by God; one who is appointed by no one, since as almighty he can be heir of all things. It was that Son of Mary, the man Jesus Christ. So it is of him, not of that other, that this is spoken. Thirdly, the same author, Hebrews 5:5, again cites this saying: "So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who said to him, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'" Here too that saying is applied to one who was glorified by God and received the priesthood from him. But the eternal Son was neither glorified nor received the priesthood from anyone. Therefore this prophecy of the Psalm has nothing to do with him. Finally, let the confession of our opponents be added: although they assert the eternal Deity of the Son, they nevertheless admit that this passage is wholly about the exalted Son, raised to the highest degree of dignity. Anyone can see this in the commentaries of those whom we named above. Therefore, with this false opinion rejected, let us explain the genuine sense of the prophet's words. We said earlier that these words cannot be taken even as the outward birth and natural generation. Therefore they will signify this much less when taken mystically and spiritually. Things which, taken literally, are natural, become spiritual when transferred to a mystical sense. Just as we said that David's begetting from God signifies love, favour, benefit and elevation to royal dignity, which was declared in him chiefly at three times, so we also affirm that Christ's begetting from God signifies favour, protection, grace and the royal dignity divinely conferred on him, which was likewise declared chiefly at three times. For although at the time of conception also, the angel said

units.la: temere id praesupponit, & quod in quaestione est turpiter assumit: nempe Davidem de se hic loqui. Loquitur David adultus, omnino, prout Psalmi divinus auctor; sed non de se adulto: non de sua generatione, sed alterius, Messiae nempe ut filii Dei, atque de eo sermo ejus accipi debet, non de ipso. Quare omnia illa quae hic habet de Davidis promotione in regnum, variisque ejus periodis, ut ad rem praesentem non admodum facientia, sicco pede praeterimus: dicimusque, verba illa litteraliter & historice de Christo solo explicari debere, non de Davide: de Christi filiatione & generatione ex Deo, spirituali & aeterna. Quod probamus, praeterquam ex antecedentibus, & consequentibus, quae in Christo impleta, & de eo, non aeque de Davide sumenda ostendimus, ex hoc ipso versu, & primum ab exordio ejus & introductione, augustiore, quam pro Davidis conditione, qua se enarraturum [illegible, ~3 letters] Dei singulare statutum commemorat, non quod regem constituerit, hoc enim praecesserit, sed quod sibi dictum, filius meus es tu, &c. Cedo ubi, & quando illud Davidi dictum, a Deo, singulari adeo ratione? Nec est, quod adferat Dei in Davidem collata beneficia, nominis praesertim & dignitatis regiae, nam de eo hoc versu nego agi, sed jam versu antecedente de rege in Zionem constituto praecesserat: hoc versu ut de re alia, & longe excelsiori verba facturus, praefatur, se Dei statutum aliquod commemoraturum, non quod ex statuto illo filius factus, sed quod qui filius singulariter a Deo genitus, peteret a Deo gentes in haereditatem, de quo versu seq. & sic redit ad vim & conditionem potestatis regiae Christo datae, cujus fundamentum in ejus filiatione; prout eundem suum filium Deus quoque constituit κληρονόμον πάντων[?]. Ergo non modo nulli unquam Deus, neque gelus Iesum nasciturum, Dei filium: tamen in futuro loquitur: magnus erit, inquit, & filius Altissimi vocabitur, Luc. 1. v. 32. Ergo post istam naturalem & externam generatio-nem, genitus etiam a Deo est. Primo, cum in Iordane, a Iohanne baptizatus est. Tunc enim illa vox intonuit: Hic est Filius meus dilectus. Et ipse Christus, Ioh. 3. fatetur, eum, qui aqua, & Spiritu sancto baptizatur, quod ipsi tunc accidit, denuo nasci. Secundo, genitus a Deo est, cum est a Patre suscitatus, & resurrexit. Tunc enim teste Paulo ad Rom. 1. declaratus, & definitus est esse Filius Dei. Tertio, genitus est a Deo, cum coelos ascendit, sedit ad dextram Dei patris, & omnia pedibus ejus subiecta sunt. Iam ergo hanc prophetiam, possumus libere ad quodvis horum temporum salva pietate referre. Qua in re ipsi nobis Apostoli praeunt, & quo modo hoc dicto uti debeamus ostendunt. Nam Paulus quidem, ut jam diximus, Act. 13. refert hanc prophetiam, ad tempus resurrectionis Christi. Et idem confirmat ad Rom. 1. v. 4. Auctor vero Epistolae ad Hebraeos, refert ad ascensionem & Pontificatum Christi. Neque in hoc vel secum pugnant, vel peccant Apostoli. Quod ad diversa referunt, eadem verba, tempora. Quin licet illa ad quodvis exaltationis Christi tempus referre. Ideo recte faciunt etiam illi, qui ista ad tempus baptismatis Christi accommodant. etiam Davidi dixit, tu es meus filius, non ita nuncupative & solenniter uti & hic, & in Euangelio aliquoties de caelo palam de Christo testatus fuit; & explicationem ejus ipse mox addit, ego hodie genui te, quod simpliciter, & nulla improprietatis addita nota, de propria & filiatione & generatione omnino accipiendum est: sed, quod omnem dubitationem & controversiam tollit, Apostolus Heb. 1. adeo singulariter Christo Dei filio dictum observat, ut non modo hominum nulli, sed nec Angelorum, id est, nulli plane creaturae tribui vel dici illud, aut tale quid potuerit, quippe in quo situm [illegible, ~16 letters], quod Christum supra omnia & omnes plane efferat. Neque haec infringit ullo modo, quod Israel dicitur Dei filius, & ex Deo genitus, similiter omnes pii & spiritualiter regeniti, vel quod Deus, Iesa. xlvi. 1. se Israelem portasse, ait, ab utero, & a vulva gestasse. nam illa omnia in tertia persona dicuntur, non in secunda, non tam emphatice & solemniter, uti hic, tu es filius meus, ego hodie genui te: non ut eo singulare aliquid denotetur, quod ne Angelorum quidem ulli communicari queat: caeteraenim illa communia sunt vel Israeli, vel piis. Tum quod adfert ex Iesaia, non cap. xlvi. 1. nihil enim tale ibi occurrit, sed cap. xlix. 1. non legitur, uti ille vertit qui portamini a meo utero, qui gestamini a mea vulva: sed, audite me insulae, & advertite populi a longinquo. Iehova me vocavit ab utero, a visceribus matris meae recordatus est nominis mei" Deinde facit, nos instare, atque adjicere, homines esse quidem filios aliquos. Dei adoptivos, Christum vero naturalem. Ad quod respondet, Christum esse ex Maria genitum, ac propterea dictum filium hominis. Hic, inquit, cum conflicti tenentur. O miserum disputatorem! Nos ita constrictos putat, & illa quidem responsione ad incitas redactos, quae ne elenchum quidem facit: nam ubi nos Dei naturalem filium Christum in argumento dicimus: respondet ille, esse filium Mariae. Quis negat? sed num inde sequitur, non esse item Dei filium, vel solum esse Mariae filium, neque ex Deo genitum filium naturalem, aeque unde filius Dei dicitur, ac propterea quod ex Maria genitus [illegible, ~20 letters] filius hominis? hoc inferendum fuerat, exclusive ad illud, si ad argumentum respondere, nedum nos constringere, voluisset.
units.tr: rashly presupposes this and shamefully assumes what is in question, namely that David is speaking here of himself. David, an adult, speaks indeed, as the divine author of the Psalm; but not of himself as an adult, not of his own generation, but of another's, namely the Messiah's as Son of God, and his speech must be understood of him, not of himself. Therefore we pass over dryly all those things which he has here about David's promotion to the kingdom and the various stages of his life, as not very relevant to the present matter. And we say that those words must be explained literally and historically of Christ alone, not of David: of Christ's sonship and begetting from God, spiritual and eternal. We prove this not only from what precedes and follows, which we show was fulfilled in Christ and must be taken of him rather than of David, but from this very verse, and first from its beginning and introduction, which is more august than David's condition warrants, where he recalls a singular decree of God by which he will recount… not that God made him king, for this came earlier, but that it was said to him, "You are my Son, etc." Tell me where and when was that said to David by God in so singular a manner? Nor is there any force in the objection that God's benefits conferred on David are mentioned, especially his name and royal dignity; for I deny that this verse is about these, since the preceding verse had already spoken of the king set on Zion. In this verse, as one about to speak of another matter and of a far higher one, he introduces it by saying that he will recount some decree of God, not that by that decree he became a son, but that he who as Son was singularly begotten by God asks God for the nations as his inheritance, of which the following verse speaks. So he returns to the force and condition of the royal power given to Christ, whose foundation lies in his sonship, just as God also appointed this same Son "heir of all things" [κληρονόμον πάντων]. Therefore God not only never said this to anyone, nor did an angel say that Jesus, the Son of God, would be born; yet he speaks in the future tense: "He will be great," he says, "and will be called the Son of the Most High," Luke 1:32. Therefore after that natural and outward generation he was also begotten by God. First, when he was baptized by John in the Jordan. For then that voice sounded: "This is my beloved Son." And Christ himself, John 3, affirms that the one who is baptized with water and the Holy Spirit, which happened to him then, is born again. Secondly, he was begotten by God when he was raised by the Father and rose again. For then, as Paul testifies in Romans 1, he was declared and defined to be the Son of God. Thirdly, he was begotten by God when he ascended into heaven, sat at the right hand of God the Father, and all things were subjected to his feet. Now, therefore, we may freely refer this prophecy to any of these times without harm to piety. In this the Apostles themselves go before us and show how we ought to use this saying. For Paul indeed, as we have already said, Acts 13, refers this prophecy to the time of Christ's resurrection, and he confirms it in Romans 1:4. But the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews refers it to Christ's ascension and priesthood. Nor in this do the Apostles contradict themselves or sin: that they refer the same words to different times is no fault. Indeed it is lawful to refer them to any time of Christ's exaltation. Therefore those also do rightly who apply these words to the time of Christ's baptism.

units.la: Videamus autem, quae contra naturalem & divinam Christi ex Patre generatio-nem, nem, & contra argumentum ex præsenti loco sumtum adferat. Sunt illa quatuor· Ad primum, neque enim repetere ea, vel ex vicina columna in hanc transferre, necessum. Is de quo in hoc Psalmo, est minor Patre: Filius non est minor Patre: Ergo non est is, de quo in hoc Psalmo. Is de quo in hoc Psalmo, secundum aliam rationem est minor, secundum aliam æqualis Patri, & idem. Certe de Christo sermonem haberi, apud nos extra partes est. Et Christus, quamvis, quod quoque in con-fesso, Patre sit minor aliquâ ratione, annon etiam & æqualis Patri, & idem unum-quecum Patre esse, docetur? ergo vides, haud repugnare, ut idem & minor dica-tur, & æqualis cum Patre, secundum aliam nempe & aliam rationem. Minor Christus Patre secundum id quod homo, & Mediator, à Patre constitutus inter se & homines, κατ᾽ οἰκονομίαν [?], non κατ᾽ θεολογίαν [?] minor, non quatenus aut Deus, aut Dei filius.
units.tr: Let us see what they bring against the natural and divine generation of Christ from the Father, and against the argument drawn from the present passage. There are four points. First, there is no need to repeat them or to carry them over here from the neighbouring column. (1) He of whom this Psalm speaks is less than the Father. (2) The Son is not less than the Father. (3) Therefore he is not the one of whom this Psalm speaks. But he of whom this Psalm speaks is less in one respect and equal to the Father in another, and is the same. Certainly, among us it is beyond dispute that the discourse is about Christ. And is it not also taught that Christ, although, as is granted, he is in some respect less than the Father, is also equal to the Father and one and the same being with the Father? So you see that there is no contradiction in the same person being called both less and equal to the Father, namely in one respect and in another. Christ is less than the Father according to what he is as man and Mediator, appointed by the Father between God and men, [κατ᾽ οἰκονομίαν], according to the economy, [not κατ᾽ θεολογίαν], according to theology. He is not less insofar as he is God or the Son of God.

units.la: Ad fecundum. De quo Filio Scriptura loquitur, certo tempore genitus est, ita ut & generatio ejus præterierit, ego hodie te genui: ergo non de æterna & propria à Patre ge-neratione. Resp. Vox quidem hodie proprie tempus, & certam ejus notat periodum, & sic verbum præteriti temporis, si in se, & prout in humanis vel terrenis accipi consuevit: aliter, vero ubi de Deo. Hinc nihil frequentius omnes norunt, quam ut vocibus & sermone ab humanis accepto, sed ῥηματικῶς [?] exponendo, summa mysteria passim tradantur: sic temporis momenta Deo attribuuntur, qui supra tempus est, & vicissitudinum illarum plane expers. Humano more nempe, quia sic in nostri gratiam balbutire Deus voluit, qui æternitatis illud ἅπαξ [?] completi animo vel cogitatione haud quaquam possumus. Verum proprie quando illa exponuntur, tum dicitur, quod χίλια ἔτη [?] apud eum sunt uti ἡμέρα μία. 2 Pet. iii.8. Quæ ubi de Dei æternitate egimus, latius fuerunt explicata. Non vero volunt Nostri, vocem hodie æternitatem significare, sed pro subjecta materia exponi debere, & quando Deo tribuitur, non infringere ejus æternitatem, sed ei propter nos & ἀνθρωπίνως [?] duntaxat adjungi. Sic & in alio sermone de Christo, dicitur heri & hodie, & in sæcula idem, Heb. xiii.8. id est, semper. Non ergo vox hodie, sed ipsa res, de qua usurpatur, æternitate notans, illa pro rei, cui adhibetur, natura explicanda venit. Nihilque magis obvium, quam ut Deus de se utatur verbis quidem temporis periodos connotantibus, non tamen ista temporis ratione exponendis. Præterquam, quod apud Hebræos usitatissimum, verbi præteritum adhibere, pro præsenti. Quare neque nos dicimus, filium semper gigni, semper genitum, & semper esse gignendum: id quod nos dicentes facit. Secludimus enim ab hac Dei actione prorsus omnem temporis habitudinem, neque vel semper gigni, vel semper genitum, aut gignendum dicimus, sed genitum supra omnem temporis rerumque temporalium ordinem & rationem. Servetus, lib. ii. de errorib. Trinit. pag. 53. Propterea dictum est, ego hodie genui te, quia ab initio mundi usque ad Christum est una dies, qua Christi generatio agitur. Quid vero id sibi vult? longe commodius universa apud Deum duratio, quasi aliquod hodie dicatur.
units.tr: Second, the Scripture speaks of this Son as begotten at a certain time, so that his generation lies in the past: "I have today begotten you." Therefore it is not a question of an eternal and proper generation from the Father. Reply: the word "today" properly denotes time and a definite period of it, and so is a word of past time, when it is taken in itself and as it is customarily understood in human or earthly matters. But it is otherwise when it is said of God. Nothing is more common, as everyone knows, than that the highest mysteries are everywhere set forth in words and language taken from human usage, but explained figuratively [ῥηματικῶς]. Thus moments of time are attributed to God, who is above time and wholly free of its changes. This is done in the human manner, because God was pleased to speak thus, as it were stammering, for our benefit, since we can in no way grasp in mind or thought that "once for all" [ἅπαξ] of eternity. But when these things are explained properly, it is said that "a thousand years are with him as one day" (2 Pet. 3:8). These matters were explained more fully where we treated of God's eternity. Our people, however, do not wish the word "today" to signify eternity, but to be explained according to the subject matter, and when it is attributed to God, not to impair his eternity, but to be joined to him only on our account and in a human manner [ἀνθρωπίνως]. So also in another passage about Christ it is said "yesterday and today, and the same for ever" (Heb. 13:8), that is, always. Therefore it is not the word "today" but the thing itself of which it is used, denoting eternity, that must be explained according to the nature of the thing to which it is applied. Nothing is more usual than for God to use of himself words that indeed signify periods of time, yet are not to be explained by that temporal reckoning. Besides, it is most usual among the Hebrews to use the past tense for the present. Hence we do not say that the Son is "always being begotten, always begotten, and always to be begotten," which is what those who say so would make of him. For we wholly exclude from this action of God every relation to time, and we do not say that he is always being begotten, or always begotten, or to be begotten, but that he is begotten above all order and reckoning of time and temporal things. Servetus, book 2 of On the Errors of the Trinity, p. 53: "For this reason it is said, I have today begotten you, because from the beginning of the world until Christ there is one day, in which Christ's generation is carried out." But what does this mean? It is far more fitting that the whole duration with God should be called, as it were, a single "today."

units.la: Ad tertium. Certe quotiescumque dictum illud producunt Apostoli, id non alteri, quam Christo applicatum eunt. Neque alteri etiam competit. Sed ita ut nullo modo ad divinam naturam referri possit, vel aliter quam prout ex Maria Virgine natus filius hominis fuit, nunquam est probaturus. Primo enim Act.xiii.33. quod citatur ex Psalmo sec. non ad probandam Christi resurrectionem facit, sed eum, qui re-
units.tr: Third, certainly whenever the Apostles produce that saying, they apply it to no one but Christ, nor does it belong to anyone else. But they will never prove that it can in no way be referred to the divine nature, or otherwise than insofar as the Son of man was born of the Virgin Mary. First, Acts 13:33, which is quoted from the second Psalm, does not serve to prove the resurrection of Christ, but that he who rose again

units.la: Tom.2. resurrexit. Quemadmodum sequenti versu resurrectionem Christi confirmaturus, & aliter loquitur, & locum, vel Psalmum adducit alium, sic: quod vero eum suscitavit e mortuis, nunquam iterum reversurum ad corruptionem, sic dixit, quod daturus vobis sum sancta fidelia Davidis. Propterea & alibi dixit, non sines sanctum tuum videre corruptionem[?].
units.tr: Tom. 2. rose again. In the following verse, which is to confirm Christ's resurrection, the Apostle both speaks differently and adduces another passage or Psalm, thus: "But that he raised him from the dead, never to return to corruption, he has spoken thus: I will give you the holy and sure mercies of David. Therefore he also says elsewhere: You will not suffer your Holy One to see corruption."

units.la: Verba illa, quod vero eum, &c. denotant jam demum ad probandam Christi resurrectionem eum accedere. Et quamvis Apostolus prophetiam illam Psalmi sec. applicat ei qui mortuus & resuscitatus est; non sequitur, ergo quatenus mortuus vel resuscitatus: nam certe qua mortuus, nulla id potest ratione: & de eo qui resuscitatus, agitur, non tamen de ejus resuscitatione. Denique & sume, quod Christi resuscitationi illa verba applicentur, non hinc tamen sequitur, id proprie denotasse, sed resuscitationi Christi applicari, ut argumento veritatis illius evidentissimo & singulari, quo non jam demum factus, sed potenter declaratus fuit Dei filius. Nam nec ipsi volunt, Christum tum primo Dei filium factum vel genitum; ergo, quemadmodum resuscitatio, cui explicandae verba illa aptantur, non evertit Christum Filium Dei antea factum, juxta Adversarios; sic neque juxta nos, aliam ejus, & vere divinam filiationem impugnabunt: sed cum anteriori ejus in filium generatione, tam bene, imo melius, consistere poterunt, juxta sententiam nostram, quam Adversariorum.
units.tr: The words "But that he raised him," and so on, show that now at last he is coming to prove Christ's resurrection. And although the Apostle applies that prophecy of the Psalm to "him who died and was raised," it does not follow that it is so as dead or as raised. For certainly it cannot be so in any way as dead; and it concerns one who was raised, but not his resurrection. Finally, grant that those words are applied to Christ's resurrection: it does not follow that they properly denote it, but that they are applied to the resurrection of Christ as a most evident and unique argument of that truth, by which the Son of God was not then first made, but powerfully declared. For they themselves do not wish that Christ was then first made or begotten Son of God. Therefore, just as the resurrection, to which those words are fitted for explanation, does not overturn Christ's being made Son of God earlier, according to the Adversaries, so neither will they, according to us, impugn his other and truly divine sonship. Rather, they can agree with his earlier generation as Son, as well as, or better than, on the Adversaries' view, according to our opinion.

units.la: Idem responsum esto ad citationem ejusdem loci in ep. Heb. cap. i. ubi dicitur, quod Deus Filium suum haeredem constituit: sed filium æternum haeredem constitui, qui dici potest? omnino vero. Nam si filium antea factum generatione ex Mariâ; quare non ante genitum ex se? Sed ita omnipotens existens, hæres constitui non potuisset. Imo non quasi eo eguisset sibi, sed quidem propter nos, ut idem qui propter nos factus erat homo Jesus Christus, & Mariae filius, post humiliationem spontaneam exaltaretur, & eveheretur in regem, haeredemque omnium oeconomicum; uti naturale regnum, Deitatis suae ratione, in omnia habet cum Patre.
units.tr: The same answer holds for the citation of the same passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, where it is said that God appointed his Son heir. But who can say that an eternal Son was appointed heir? Altogether no one, indeed. For if he was a Son made earlier by generation from Mary, why was he not begotten earlier from himself? But being omnipotent, he could not have been appointed heir in that way. Nor indeed as if he lacked it for himself, but for our sake: so that the same Jesus Christ, who for our sake had been made man and the son of Mary, after his voluntary humiliation, should be exalted and raised up as king and heir of all things in the economy, just as he has a natural kingdom over all things together with the Father by reason of his Deity.

units.la: Heb. v. 5. Christus seipsum non glorificavit, sed qui ei dixit, filius meus es tu. Quid hic quaeso est, quod neget ista dicta Christo, æternæ generationis ratione? At æternus filius, inquit, nec clarificatus est, nec Pontificatum a quoquam accepit. Æternus filius, acceptâ in tempore humanâ naturâ, & conditione servili, glorificatus a Deo non fuit? negatur. Nam ideo quod in statu illo exinanitionis obediens factus fuit Deo, etiam usque ad crucis mortem, exaltavit eum Deus, & gloriâ coronavit supra ipsos adeo angelos. Sed hæc de statu, quem in tempore accepit intellecta, nihil omnino præjudicant ejus conditioni & naturae divinae, quâ faciens [illegible, ~6 letters] Dei æternus filius est, ejusdemque naturae & dignitatis. Ut nobis nihil contradicamus, quando in Psalmo, & de filio exaltato sermonem fieri dicimus, & quoque ab æterno a Patre, quia vere & ejusdem naturae, genito: quae haud magis sibi repugnant, quam quando eodem loci de Christo saepe agitur humiliato, & glorificato. Nam & verbis, & versibus aliis tum haec, tum illa significantur. Non ergo nostra sententia vel falsa, vel repudianda est. De caetero ut suam probet Adversarius, vel explicet, videamus.
units.tr: Hebrews 5:5: "Christ did not glorify himself, but he who said to him, You are my Son." What, I ask, is there here that denies these words to Christ on the ground of eternal generation? But, it is said, the eternal Son was neither glorified nor received the priesthood from anyone. Is it denied that the eternal Son, having taken human nature and a servile condition in time, was glorified by God? For because in that state of emptying he became obedient to God, even to the death of the cross, God exalted him and crowned him with glory, above the very angels. But these things, understood of the state which he received in time, do not in any way prejudice his condition and divine nature, by which the eternal Son is the one who makes all things and is of the same nature and dignity. So we contradict nothing when we say that in the Psalm there is talk of the exalted Son, and also of the one begotten from the Father from eternity, since he is truly of the same nature. These are no more in conflict with each other than when, in the same place, the humiliated and the glorified Christ is often spoken of. For both these and those are signified both by these words and by other verses. Therefore our opinion is neither false nor to be rejected. As for the rest, let us see how the Adversary proves or explains his own view.

units.la: Si verba ista, de nativitate externa accipi non possunt, quod concedimus, viderint tum Adversarii, an etiam propter humanam suam ex Mariâ generationem Christus factus sit Dei filius. Nos autem nec litterali sensu, nec mystico, nativitatem externam & generationem naturalem hic innui statuimus. Quare quum nequaquam probaverit, generationem ullam Davidis, ex Deo, significari, neque per eam divinum favorem Davidi, in ejus evectione ad dignitatem regiam exhibitum, non etiam mystica ejus sive explicatio, sive applicatio admittitur, de Dei amore erga Christum, in beneficiis quibusdam, & praesertim collatione potestatis regiae ostenso, ut nec in tempora, quibus illa declarata fuerint, varia inquirere, opus sit. Videtur autem Enjedinus, singulariter a suis, statuere Christum externa & corporali ex Maria generatione, non esse factum Dei filium, vel genitum: quod baptismo, & resurrectioni, & adscensioni attribuit: quum alii huc etiam trahant verba Lucae, & filius altissimi vocabitur: ille tamen post istam suam generationem genitum a Deo Christum, & primo quidem in Jordane, disputat. Quae omnia nobis, ejusdem sunt pretii, & suis locis singula diluuntur. Nam quod de baptismo Christi in Jordane, tum quidem vox caelo delata testataque fuit, hic est filius meus dilectus, non per eam, vel tum temporis Christus genitus, aut Dei filius factus est, declaratus: uti & Matth. xvii. 5. in monte, quando idem auditum e caelo, non vero iterum genitus Christus fuit, quamvis de multiplici Christi a Deo genitura hic philosophetur Adversarius, perperam & inepte. Sic est, Christus Joann. iii. 5. testatur eum, qui aqua & Spiritu Sancto baptizatur, regenerari, & quod nisi quis regenitus sit, regnum caelorum intrare nequeat: sed istudne de se Christus intellexit? apage cum ista expositione. Quid illa ad Christum? certe haud magis, ac quod cap. i. dictum, quotquot acceperunt eum, dedit iis potestatem filios Dei fieri, quotquot nimirum in ipsum crediderunt. Denique, imo certe licet illa Psalmi verba ad varia referre tempora: per nos licet referas ad tempus baptizati Christi, & resuscitati, & quum adscendit, & gloriam adiit supremam: non vero quod illis filius Dei factus & genitus demum, vel aliquoties, sed quod singularibus illis temporibus & documentis manifestatus fuit & confirmatus. Apparet etiam inde, quam verum scilicet & naturalem Dei filium Adversarii Christum statuant, & vere a Deo genitum. Non enim illa veram generationem denotant, sed impropriae & metaphoricae sunt locutiones: metaphora autem deflectit vocem a vera & naturali sua significatione. Quae enim illa generatio vera, quae totuplex, & variis adeo temporibus & rebus facta, ut monstrum potius hinc aliquod oriatur, quam verus & naturalis filius, nedum Dei?
units.tr: If these words cannot be taken of the external birth, which we grant, let the Adversaries consider whether Christ was made the Son of God on account of his human generation from Mary. We, however, hold that the external birth and natural generation are not hinted at here, either in the literal sense or in a mystical one. Therefore, since he has by no means proved that any generation of David from God is meant, or that by it the divine favour shown to David in his elevation to royal dignity is signified, the mystical explanation or application is not excluded, namely of God's love towards Christ, shown in certain benefits and especially in the conferral of royal power. Nor is there any need to inquire into the various times in which these things were declared. Enjedinus alone among his people seems to hold that Christ was not made the Son of God or begotten by the external and bodily generation from Mary. He attributes this to baptism, to the resurrection and to the ascension, whereas others draw here also the words of Luke, and he shall be called the Son of the Most High. Yet he argues that Christ was begotten by God after that generation, and first of all in the Jordan. All these things are of equal worth to us, and each is refuted in its own place. For as to Christ's baptism in the Jordan, when the voice from heaven was then indeed delivered and testified, this is my beloved Son, Christ was not begotten or declared to be the Son of God then through that voice. The same holds for Matthew 17:5 on the mountain, when the same was heard from heaven, and Christ was not begotten again, although the Adversary here philosophises, wrongly and foolishly, about a manifold begetting of Christ by God. Likewise, Christ in John 3:5 testifies that the one who is baptised with water and the Holy Spirit is born again, and that unless someone is born again he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. But did Christ understand this of himself? Away with that interpretation! What has that to do with Christ? Certainly no more than what is said in chapter 1, that to as many as received him he gave the power to become sons of God, namely to as many as believed in him. Finally, indeed, it is certainly allowed to refer those words of the Psalm to various times: by all means refer them to the time of Christ's baptism, and of his resurrection, and when he ascended and entered into supreme glory. But this is not because he was then made and begotten the Son of God, or was so at several times, but because he was manifested and confirmed by those singular times and proofs. From this it also appears how truly and naturally the Adversaries hold Christ to be the Son of God, and truly begotten by God. For those expressions do not denote a true generation, but are improper and metaphorical forms of speech, and a metaphor turns a word away from its true and natural meaning. For what true generation is that, which is so manifold and made at such various times and in such various matters, that from it some monster rather than a true and natural son, let alone of God, would arise?

units.la: Praeterea Christum Dei Filium fuisse jam ante suam ex Maria nativitatem, probamus ex hoc eodem capite primo ad Hebraeos, verf. 8. Ad filium vero dixit, Psalmo nempe xlv. Thronus tuus o Deus, in saecula. Ille jam tum erat Dei filius, cui Deus Pater ista dicebat.
units.tr: Moreover, we prove that Christ was the Son of God even before his birth from Mary, from the same first chapter of Hebrews, verse 8: but to the Son he said, namely in Psalm 45, Thy throne, O God, is for ever. He who was then addressed by God the Father with those words was already the Son of God.

units.la: Excipit Enjedinus, in Heb. i. Haec verba, si literalem & verum sensum quaerimus, de Solomone in Psalmis scripta esse, & tantum mystice ac propter similitudinem nonnullam hic Jesu Christo applicari: non tantum consensus omnium doctissimorum interpretum; sed res ipsa docet: ut quivis per se deprehendere, si Psalmum 44. perlegat, unde haec verba depromta sunt, potest. Sed de quocunque accipiantur, certe non Deum, sed hominem describunt. Nam qui unctus est, qui Deum, hoc est
units.tr: Enjedinus objects, on Hebrews 1: If we seek the literal and true sense, these words were written in the Psalms about Solomon, and are applied to Jesus Christ here only mystically and on account of some resemblance. This is taught not only by the agreement of all the most learned interpreters, but by the matter itself, so that anyone can perceive for himself, if he reads through Psalm 44, from which these words are taken. But whatever they are taken to refer to, they certainly describe not God but a man. For he who is anointed, who God, that is

units.la: Resp. Haec verba non de Salomone dicta, sed Christo soli proprie, & non tantum mystice, vel propter similitudinem nonnullam applicanda esse, & res ipsa, & doctissimorum interpretum consensus docent. 1. Quia illa sic dicuntur, ut innuatur, eum de quo illa intelligenda, eo majorem esse Angelis. Quod de Salomone dici nequit. Ecce vers. 7. & ad Angelos quidem dixit, &c. Jam vers. 8. ad Filium vero. Hic ergo indicatur aliquid se superiorem & majorem, qui consortes & socios regni habet: non Deus æternus, cui ista repugnant, sed homo, vel certe creatura fit, necesse est. Itaque ridiculi sunt, qui ex hoc loco, æternam Christi deitatem excidere conantur, cum totum inde contrarium necessario sequatur. Denique possunt illa verba, sic commode explicari, ut vox Deus, nec de Solomone, nec de Christo dicatur, neque fit Vocativi casus, sed Nominativi, & intelligatur de Deo Patre tum Solomonis, tum Christi, hoc sensu: Deus est thronus tuus in saeculum: id est, Deus tibi thronum firmabit usque in saeculum. Psalmi de Christo, Vnxit te o Deus, Deus tuus? quid clarius, quam Christum dici, &c.
units.tr: Reply: These words are not said of Solomon, but are to be applied properly to Christ alone, and not merely mystically or on account of some resemblance. Both the matter itself and the agreement of the most learned interpreters teach this. 1. Because they are said in such a way as to indicate that the one of whom they are to be understood is greater than the angels. This cannot be said of Solomon. See verse 7: and of the angels indeed he said, etc. Then verse 8: but to the Son. Here, therefore, something is indicated that is superior and greater, who has partners and companions in the kingdom. It must be that he is not the eternal God, to whom these things are inconsistent, but a man, or at least a creature. So they are ridiculous who try from this passage to destroy the eternal deity of Christ, since the entire contrary necessarily follows from it. Finally, those words can be explained suitably in such a way that the word God is said neither of Solomon nor of Christ, and is not in the vocative case but the nominative, and is understood of God the Father, both of Solomon's and of Christ's, in this sense: God is your throne for ever, that is, God will establish your throne for ever. The Psalm about Christ says, God, thy God, hath anointed thee. What could be clearer than that Christ is called...?

units.la: III. Et hominem describunt, fateor, sed ἀνθρώπων. non non Deum sed hominem, sed Deum & hominem. Neque inde contrarium Deitatis aliquid sequitur, quod continentur talia quæ hominem sonant & Mediatorem.
units.tr: III. They do describe a man, I grant, but [ἀνθρώπων]: not God but man, but God and man. Nor does anything contrary to deity follow from this, since such things are contained which signify a man and a Mediator.

units.la: IV. Non certe possunt illa sic commode explicari, ut vox Deus nec de Salomone, nec de Christo dicatur, quum ad Filium expresse referat Apostolus, & ad eum, thronus tuus, Deus. ὁ θεός σου ὁ θεός. Et postea iterum, propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo lætitiæ supra consortes tuos: nota intercisionis inter ὁ θεὸς & ὁ θεὸς σε. Denique quis ille sensus esset, thronus tuus, Deus in saeculum: scilicet, Deus est thronus tuus in saeculum, & hoc iterum sic, Deus tibi thronum firmabit usque in sæculum. Prov. viii. 22. 23. 24. Sapientia λόγος loquitur: Iehova possidebat me principio viæ suæ; ante opera sua, ante ullum tempus. Ante sæculum inuntta fui, ante principium, ante primordia terræ. Quum nullæ essent abyssi, edita eram [illegible, ~8 letters] cap. xxx. 4. Quis adscendat cælos, &c. quod nomen hujus, & quod nomen filii ipsius, si noveris? Hic i. Filius Deus, ex divinis operibus. ii. Æque incomprehensibilis ac Pater. iii. Christus. Schlichtingius in Commentario Epist. ad Hebr. pag.43. ad locum modo discussum: quandocumque Dei filius simpliciter nominatur, nullus alius intelligitur quam Christus. Jesa. ix.6. Filius nobis natus est. Mich. v. 2. cujus exortus, inde a principio, a diebus sæculi.
units.tr: IV. Certainly those words cannot be explained suitably in such a way that the word God is said neither of Solomon nor of Christ, since the Apostle expressly refers them to the Son, and says to him, thy throne, God [ὁ θεός σου ὁ θεός]. And afterwards again, therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. Note the break between ὁ θεὸς and ὁ θεὸς σε. Finally, what would that sense be, thy throne, God for ever? Namely, God is your throne for ever, and again this way: God will establish a throne for you for ever. Proverbs 8:22, 23, 24. Wisdom, [λόγος], speaks: Jehovah possessed me at the beginning of his way, before his works, before any time. I was anointed from eternity, from the beginning, before the origins of the earth. When there were no depths, I was brought forth [illegible]. Chapter 30:4: Who has ascended into heaven, etc.? What is his name, and what is the name of his Son, if you know it? Here (1) the Son is God, from the divine works; (2) he is as incomprehensible as the Father; (3) he is Christ. Schlichting, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, p. 43, on the passage just discussed: whenever the Son of God is named simply, no one else is understood than Christ. Isaiah 9:6: a son is born to us. Micah 5:2: whose going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

units.la: Qui Filius Dei dicitur, atque est, proprius, unigenitus, imago & character personæ Patris, par & æqualis, unus cum eo, ille non propter aliqua humanæ suæ naturæ communicata, propter miraculosam conceptionem, potestatem, vel per id quod hominis, filius Dei est; sed per propriam a Patre & divinam generationem, quā & coessentialis Patri. Atqui talis est Christus, non solum Filius Dei, quia genitus a Patre, quæ argumento primo vidimus; sed filius ille dilectus Patri. Matth. iii. 17. & filius Dei viventis. Matth. xvi. 16. qui, quemadmodum Pater vitam habet in semetipso, ita & filio dedit vitam habere in semetipso. Joann. v. 26. filius proprius. Roman. viii. 32. qui proprio filio non pepercit. à Patre proprio. Joann. v. 18. patrem proprium dixit Deum. Hinc unigenitus, unius Dei, unica filiatione, unicus filius. Joan. i. 14. vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam ut unigeniti à Patre. 18. Deum nemo vidit unquam; unigenitus ille filius, qui in sinu Patris est, is declaravit. Patris imago, & expressa, & character. Col. i. 15. qui imago est invisibilis Dei. Heb. i. 3. qui est ἀπαύγασμα δόξης, & χαρακτὴρ ὑποστάσεως ipsius. Inde ἐγὼ Deo. Joann. v. 17. 18. 19. Pater meus usque hodie operatur, & ego operor. Eo igitur magis Iudæi eum conabantur occidere, quod etiam Deum diceret proprium patrem, seipsum parem Deo faciens. Respondit Jesus, &c. quæ enim ipse facit Pater, ea & filius similiter facit. Phil. 11. 6. qui in forma Dei existens, non arbitratus est rapinam, esse Deo parem ἴσα[?]. Distinguit formam Dei, & hominis, verf. 7. 8. ut opposita. illiusque ratione Christo adscribit ἰσότητα[?] cum Patre. Altiora hæc non solum sunt, quam humana natura statusque, sed alterius formæ, & formis, id est, totis essentiis inter se differunt. Unus cum Deo. Joann. x. 30. Ego & Pater unum sumus. Unde blasphemiam Christo impingunt, vers. 33. sed lapidamus te propter blasphemiam, quod, cum tu fis homo, Deum te facis. 36. Vos dicitis blasphemare, quod dixi, filius Dei sum? Ergo i. Filium Dei esse, qualis Christus, indicat unum cum Deo, & Deum esse. ii. Estque aliud, quam homini vel humanæ naturæ attribui possit. 1 Joann. v. 7. Pater, & Verbum, & Spiritus Sanctus: & hi tres unum sunt. Ex quibus omnibus tria hæc luce clariora apparent. i. Christum esse Filium Dei, non per aut propter humanum aliquid: quia hactenus dicta formam & naturam humanam infinitè superant. ii. Sed per propriam, veram & divinam Filii, ut Filii, à Patre suo generationem: quò omnia spectant, quæ de Filio, & Patre dicta. iii. Et hinc Filium esse revera Patri coessentialem, quia paria, & eadem cum Patre habet, formam, & ἰσότητα[?], & τὸ ἓν[?] Dei. Age & vide, num adducta loca homini, vel humanæ alicui naturæ, & potestati essentialiter tali, utcunque modo & accidentibus excellenti, attribui queant: senties, quantam vim facturus sis tum locis illis, tum tuo animo, siquidem illa cogas servire tuæ hypothesi, & non veritati locum des, ac Deo, atque isti vero, de quo Johannes i. cap. v. 20. & sumus in isto vero, in filio ejus Iesu Christo: hic est verus ille Deus, & vita æterna.
units.tr: He who is and is called the Son of God, the proper, only-begotten, image and character of the person of the Father, equal and co-equal, one with him, is not the Son of God because of some things communicated to his human nature, because of his miraculous conception, by power, or in that he is the Son of God through what is human. He is the Son of God through his own divine generation from the Father, by which he is co-essential with the Father. Now such is Christ: he is not only the Son of God because he was begotten by the Father, as we saw in the first argument, but he is that Son beloved of the Father (Matthew 3:17), and the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16), who, as the Father has life in himself, so has he given the Son to have life in himself (John 5:26); the proper Son (Romans 8:32), who did not spare his own Son; from his own Father (John 5:18), where he called God his own Father. Hence he is the only-begotten, of the one God, by the one sonship, the only Son. John 1:14: we saw his glory, the glory of the only-begotten from the Father; verse 18: No one has ever seen God; that only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him. He is the image of the Father, both express and the character (Colossians 1:15: who is the image of the invisible God; Hebrews 1:3: who is the brightness [ἀπαύγασμα] of glory and the express image [χαρακτὴρ] of his substance). Hence the claim to equality with God (John 5:17, 18, 19): My Father works until now, and I work. "Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God." Jesus answered, etc.: "For whatever things the Father does, these the Son also does in like manner." Philippians 2:6: who, existing in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God [ἴσα]. He distinguishes the form of God from the form of a man, verses 7 and 8, as opposites, and on that basis ascribes to Christ equality [ἰσότητα] with the Father. These things are not only higher than the human nature and condition, but differ from it in another form, indeed in forms, that is, in their whole essences. One with God: John 10:30, I and the Father are one. Hence they charge Christ with blasphemy (verse 33): "but we stone you for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God." Verse 36: "Do you say that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God?" Therefore: (1) the Son of God, such as Christ is, indicates one with God, and God; (2) and it is something that cannot be attributed to a man or to human nature. 1 John 5:7: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. From all these things, three points appear clearer than light: (1) Christ is the Son of God not through or on account of anything human, since the things said so far far exceed the human form and nature. (2) But he is so through his own true and divine generation from the Father as Son, to which all the things said of the Son and the Father look. (3) And hence the Son is truly co-essential with the Father, since he has the same equality [ἰσότητα] and the oneness [τὸ ἓν] of God as equal and identical with the Father. Come now, and see whether the places cited can be attributed to a man, or to some human nature and power essentially such, however excellent it may be in some way or accidents: you will perceive how great a violence you will do to those places and to your own mind, if you force them to serve your hypothesis and do not give place to the truth, and to God, and to that truth of which John says in chapter 5, verse 20: and we are in that true one, in his Son Jesus Christ: this is the true God, and eternal life.

units.la: Argum. tertium. Qui non per propriam & veram generationem est filius, sed propter quædam & varia accidentia, is filius magis dicitur, quam est, idque communi modo, non proprio; metaphorico, non vero; æquivoco & homonymo, non adæquato. Sed talis est Filius Dei, juxta Socinianos, Christus. Unde apparet, utri magis pro Christo, Dei filio, ejusque veritate & dignitate loquantur, nos, an Adversarii, & quinam proprietatem & veritatem magis sequantur tum vocum, tum rei.
units.tr: Third argument. One who is a son not by proper and true generation, but on account of certain various accidents, is called a son more than he really is, and that in a common, not a proper, sense; metaphorically, not truly; equivocally and homonymously, not univocally. But such, according to the Socinians, is Christ, the Son of God. From this it appears which side speaks more for Christ, the Son of God, and for his truth and dignity, we or our opponents, and which side follows more closely the propriety and truth both of words and of the thing.

units.la: Ut non adeo ægre ferre debeant Socinianï, quando libros alii contra eos scripse-runt, de Deo apud ipsos metaphorico, Christo Semideo, & Semidomino, de colendis Diis duobus. Juxta Socinianos, Christus filius Dei erit quasi adoptivus, à nostri filiatione distans modo & gradibus, non totâ formâ ac genere. Jam adoptio est assimilata filiatio, non propria, naturam imitans, in eorum solatium inventa, qui liberos non habent, attamen habere possunt. nam adoptio in his personis locum habet, in quibus etiam natura potest habere. l. 16. D. de adoption. & emancip. adeo ut qui omnino generare nequit, is neque adoptare queat. Error vel hæresis de Christo filio Dei adoptivo damnata olim fuit in Felice Urgelitano, & Elipando Toletano Episcopis, Ann. Dccxciv. in Concilio Francofurtensi. De quibus vide præter, & post alios, copiose agentem Joh. Forbesium, Instruct. Historico-Theolog. lib. vi. cap. i. & lib. i. cap. xxx. Atque valde convenit Felicis illius sententia cum Fausto nostro, Christum ex Mariâ natum filium Dei adoptivum, & Deum nuncupativum asserentis; & cum Episcopio, qui addit etiam filium naturalem dici Christum, propter generationem à Patre in natura divinâ, sed non ejusdem naturæ vel essentiæ, cum Patre Filium. Sed Filium Dei naturalem docebat ille Deo etiam coæqualem, secus ac Episcopius. In Apologia cap. iii. p. 49. concedunt Remonstrantes, assimilationem gratiosam, qua Christus etiam sit filius Dei, non esse propriam generationem, quamvis veram. Sed Christus filius Dei est, ejusque filiatio non vera solum, sed propria. Unde proprius Dei Filius,* & Pater ejus proprius dicitur.
units.tr: So the Socinians should not take it too badly that others have written books against them, calling God metaphorical among them, Christ a demigod and demilord, and speaking of the worship of two gods. According to the Socinians, Christ will be the Son of God in an adoptive sense, differing from our sonship in mode and degree, not in its whole form and kind. Now adoption is a sonship by resemblance, not a proper one, imitating nature, and it was devised for the comfort of those who have no children but are able to have them. For adoption has a place in those persons in whom nature too can have a place. Law 16, D. de adoption. & emancip. So one who cannot beget at all cannot adopt either. The error or heresy of Christ as an adoptive Son of God was condemned long ago in the bishops Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo, in the year 794, at the Council of Frankfurt. On these matters see, among others and after them, John Forbes, who treats them at length in Instruct. Historico-Theolog. book 6 chapter 1 and book 1 chapter 30. And Felix's opinion agrees well with our Faustus, who asserts that Christ born of Mary is an adoptive Son of God and God only by name; and with Episcopius, who adds that Christ is also called a natural Son, on account of his generation from the Father in the divine nature, but that the Son is not of the same nature or essence as the Father. Yet Felix taught a natural Son of God who was also co-equal with God, unlike Episcopius. In the Apologia, chapter 3, page 49, the Remonstrants concede that the gracious likeness by which Christ is also the Son of God is not a proper generation, although it is a true one. But Christ is the Son of God, and his sonship is not only true but proper. Hence he is called the proper Son of God, and God is called his proper Father.

units.la: Excipit ad Rom. viii. 32. Schlichtingius contra Meisnerum, de Trinitate pag. 445. Christum proprium dici Dei filium, id est, non alienum: Negamus enim idcirco Christum Filium Dei proprium dici, quod proprie a Deo fit genitus vel quod fit Filius proprie dictus: proprius enim Dei Filius jure optimo dicitur propterea, quod non fit alienus, nec cujusquam alterius. Num vero solius Dei Filius esse non potest Christus, nisi etiam ab ipso, proprie loquendo, fit genitus? quid prohibet quominus etiam adoptivus Filius, proprius alicujus dicatur Filius, quatenus scil. nemo alius in eum paternum jus habeat, quam qui eum sibi adoptavit in Filium? quanto magis id in Christo locum habet, qui non solum adoptionis, sed etiam ipsius ge-nerationis jure, nullius alterius Patris, quam Dei Filius fuit? Nec sane dicere Paulus dubuit, ut charitatem Dei summam erga nos ex-primeret, quod Deus nostra causa non peper-cerit Filio proprie dicto, sed quod non peperce-rit suo Filio. Nam si vel maxime ipse Filius esset Filius proprie dictus, nisi esset ipsius Dei Filius, nullum hinc argumentum divinae charitatis erga nos duci potuisset. Denique, ut in-fra videbimus, talem hic proprium Dei filium intelligit Paulus, cui Deus non parcere, sed quem tradere pro nobis in mortem potuit; in eo enim tota ratio divinae ipsius charitatis consi-stit; qualis profecto non est Filius ex Dei essen-tia ab aeterno genitus, idem numero cum Patre Deus. Itaque ut paucis concludamus, vox proprii in verbis Pauli non apponitur per si-militudinem dicto, sed tantum communi vel alieno. quo sensu & in quotidiano sermone cre-berrime, & in S. L. non infrequenter usurpa-ri solet: illo autem fere tantum in Philoso-phorum, non vero in Piscatorum scholis.
units.tr: Objection on Rom. 8:32, from Schlichting against Meisner, On the Trinity, page 445: "We say that Christ is called the proper Son of God, that is, not alien. For we deny that Christ is called the proper Son of God because he was properly begotten by God, or because he is the Son in the strict sense. For the proper Son of God is rightly so called because he is not alien, nor belongs to anyone else. But can Christ not be the Son of God alone unless he was also begotten by him in the proper sense? What prevents an adoptive son from being called the proper son of someone, inasmuch as no one else has paternal right over him except the one who adopted him as son? How much more does this hold for Christ, who was the Son of God, and of no other father, not only by right of adoption but also by right of generation itself? Nor did Paul hesitate, to express God's supreme love toward us, to say that God did not spare his Son in the strict sense for our sake, but that he did not spare his own Son. For even if the Son were the Son in the strict sense, unless he were the Son of God himself, no argument of divine love toward us could be drawn from this. Finally, as we shall see below, Paul understands by the proper Son of God one whom God did not spare but could hand over to death for us; for in this the whole reason of God's own love consists. That is certainly not the Son begotten from the essence of God from eternity, numerically the same God as the Father. Therefore, to conclude briefly, the word proper in Paul's words is not applied by way of likeness to what is said, but only in the common or foreign sense. In this sense it is very often used in everyday speech, and not infrequently in Holy Scripture; but that sense is used almost only in the schools of the philosophers, not in the schools of the fishermen."

units.la: Resp. I. Negat jam audacter Christum esse proprie dictum Dei filium, & tamen alibi clamant, esse filium Dei verum & naturalem. Quid vero minus admitti po-test, quam filium dici proprium, nec tamen proprie dictum? proprium, ut improprius habeatur? II. proprium non tantum communi, sed etiam improprie dicto, & propriissime quidem, opponitur. Ut qua ratione proprie aliquid esse omnino potest, ita & intelligatur, sic filius proprius, non solum non communis, sed etiam proprie dictus, & a Patre, cujus ita dicitur filius, genitus. Nam quum de proprietate rei tota hic fit quaestio, pro quibus decidi eam intelligemus a Scriptura, quam pro iis qui propriam filiationem accipiunt, Scriptura expresse adeo filium proprium nominante? Ut provide huic disceptationi illo addito nomine occurrere voluisse videatur. III. Et nos, quo sensu Dei filii appellemur, non sumus alieni filii, nec cujusquam alterius, quam solius Dei; neque tamen aliquis se proprium Dei filium sine sacrile-gio dicere audeat. IV. Ut propterea bla-sphemiam sonare Judaeis videbatur, quando Christus Deum patrem suum proprium nominabat. Joan.v. 18. Sed & Pa-trem proprium dixerat Deum, aequalem Deo faciens. Quaque ratione Deus Christi Pater proprius, eadem & ipse filius Dei proprius. v. In materia & negotio filiationis, proprius & adoptivus opponuntur: ut proprius non fit adoptivus, & adoptivus non fit proprius; sed adoptivus naturali opponitur & proprio, & naturalis non est adoptivus, adoptivis liberis opponuntur naturales ac veri, dicunt JCti.vi. Quo-modo ad proprium Dei filium sufficit, ut non fit cujusquam alterius? non alterius Dei? Atqui sic in Christo id nihil singulare dicet prae aliis. Si non cujusquam alterius parentis? at Christus proprius fuit & proprie dictus Mariae filius. Si non alterius adoptantis? hoc iterum Christo non proprium. Dicet, nullius alterius Dei Patris. Sed hoc eodem redit, cum primo. Neque enim nos alterius Dei Patris sumus, & non tamen Dei filii, quomodo Christus filius Dei proprius est. Quare potest quidem aliquis esse solius Dei filius, utcunque non ab eo proprie genitus, uti nos: sed non proprius, quemadmodum Christus, nisi ab eo genitus. VII. Non tantum Christus est solius Dei filius, sed & solus, μονογενὴς[?], ut ea ratione nullus cum eo conveniat. Jam quid id est, Christum esse Dei filium, & genitum à Deo, & proprium, & unigenitum, ut tamen omnia illa non dicantur proprie generationis ergo, sed improprie proprius, & genitus, & primogenitus: quare non etiam tum & filius improprie? Certè filius proprius est ob propriam filiationem & generationem, nisi aequè dicas filium improprium, & improprie genitum: nam & filium, & genitum Scriptura nominat. Ne exciperes in Filio, & quod aliud fundamentum vel argumentum ejus constituteres à generatione, addit, genitum: & ne in hoc iterum haereres, neq; proprie genitum arbitrareris, adjunxit primogenitum. VIII. Uti autem adoptivus Filius est minor proprio, & propter similitudinem modo dictus, ita Christo illud non citra contumeliam tribui posse Ecclesia Christiana semper judicavit, & opinionem de Christo Filii Dei adoptivo constanter proscripsit. IX. Deinde uti adoptio naturam imitari dicitur, atque in solatium inventa ejus, qui liberos non habet, sic Deo objici non debet, qui praejudicium Filii proprii, quousque probari non potest, cum natura Dei pugnare, ut habeat Filium proprie dictum, cujus in Scripturis adeo frequens mentio. l. 16. D. de Adopt. Adoptio enim in his personis locum habet, in quibus etiam natura potest habere. X. Non potest aliquis ejusdem simul dici Filius, adoptionis & generationis jure: quomodo de Christo philosophatur Schlichtingius. Si ex generatione, supervacua non solum, sed impossibilis adoptio. Nam haec illius locum & defectum quasi supplet, & qui non genitus, in filium tamen benigne adoptatur. Sin ajat, per similitudinem omnia intelligenda: respondemus, quomodocumque ex generatione factus Filius, idem ex adoptione fieri nec potest, nec necesse est. Multis quidem modis Filius aliquis declarari potest & probari, non item fieri. Neque in hoc Philosophorum, & Piscatorum scholae, vel sacrae litterae quotidiano sermoni contrariae.
