Antea Filium Dei per similitudinem genitum docuerat, quanto magis si per similitudinem genitus esse dicatur? quod ipsum nos contendimus. Quemadmodum enim Filius Dei nominatur Christus, sumta similitudine ab hominibus, sic etiam per eandem similitudinem genitus a Deo dicitur. Omnia ergo ex similitudine de Christo dicta, non vere & proprie Filius, nec genitus. Fruantur illi similitudine, modo nos gaudeamus ipsa rei veritate. Certe totam fere religionem convertunt isti homines in schema aliquod & metaphoram, Christum Dei Filium, Deum, mediatorem, redemtionem nostram, & quid non? Atque ubi Scriptura proprium dicit, reclamant audacter & reponunt, improprium. XI. Jam & quid dicere Paulus debuit, praescribunt, nempe non quod Deus nostra causa non pepercerit Filio proprie dicto, sed quod non pepercerit suo Filio. Dixit tamen, Filio proprio. I, & castiga tu hoc in Paulo. Infert, Nam si vel maxime iste Filius esset Filius proprie dictus, nisi esset ipsius Dei Filius, &c. quasi vel esset, vel esse posset Filius Dei proprie dictus, & non ipsius Dei Filius? Denique ait, quod Deus proprie dictum suum filium in mortem tradere pro nobis non potuerit: sed id non probat. Nam uti nostro loco voluit eum humanam & servikem[?] formam induere, ita quoque ad mortem usque se demittere: eoque superabundantem suam erga nos charitatem ostendere Deus voluit, quod eum in finem proprium & naturalem suum exhibuerit & tradiderit Filium. Et in hoc sita vis argumenti Paulini, tum testati amoris divini, quod proprio suo non pepercerit in nostri gratiam Filio: tum connexionis additae, quomodo non cum eo omnia nobis gratifi-caretur? Ergo, ut concludamus, vox proprii in verbis Pauli non opponitur tantum communi vel alieno, sed & per similitudinem dicto. Utrumque enim vox proprius proprie acceptus, & in quotidiano sermone, & S.L. sua vi & latitudine comprehendit. Sic dicitur fructus proprius, Luc. vi. 44. [illegible, ~20 letters], id est, vero ac naturaliter proprio.
units.tr: Reply. I. He now boldly denies that Christ is properly called the Son of God, and yet elsewhere they cry out that he is the true and natural Son of God. But what can be less admitted than that a son should be called one's own, and yet not be properly so called? Is he to be regarded as not one's own, so as to be considered improper? II. "One's own" is opposed not only to what is common but also to what is improperly so called, and most properly so. Just as a thing can be properly its own in every sense, so it can be understood: thus a proper son is not only not common but also properly so called, and begotten by the Father whose son he is called. For since the whole question here concerns the propriety of the thing, by which side shall we understand it to be decided: by Scripture, which expressly calls him the proper Son, or by those who take it to mean a proper sonship? As if he had wished to meet this dispute in advance by adding that word. III. And we, in the sense in which we are called sons of God, are not the sons of strangers, nor of anyone but God alone; yet no one may dare to say without sacrilege that he is God's proper Son. IV. Therefore it seemed blasphemous to the Jews when Christ called God his own Father. John 5:18. But he had also called God his proper Father, making himself equal to God. By whatever reason God is Christ's proper Father, by the same reason he himself is the proper Son of God. V. In the matter and business of sonship, proper and adoptive are opposed: a proper son does not become adoptive, and an adoptive son does not become proper; the adoptive is opposed to the natural and the proper, and the natural is not adoptive; natural and true children are set against adopted children, as the jurists say. VI. How is it sufficient for a proper Son of God that he is not of anyone else? Not of another God? But then nothing peculiar would be said of Christ compared with others. Not of another parent? But Christ was indeed the proper son, and properly so called, of Mary. Not of another adopter? Again this is not peculiar to Christ. He will say: not of another God the Father. But this comes back to the first point. For we too are not of another God the Father, and yet we are not sons of God in the way that Christ is the proper Son of God. Therefore someone may indeed be the son of God alone, however not begotten by him properly, as we are; but not the proper son, as Christ is, unless he was begotten by him. VII. Christ is not only the Son of God alone, but also the only one, monogenēs [μονογενής], so that by this reasoning no one else is comparable to him. Now what does it mean that Christ is the Son of God, begotten by God, proper and only-begotten, yet all these things are not said properly on account of generation, but improperly? Proper, and begotten, and firstborn: why then is he not also improperly a son? Surely he is a proper son because of his proper sonship and generation, unless you equally say that he is an improper son and improperly begotten; for Scripture names him both Son and begotten. Lest you should make an exception in the case of the Son, and set up some other foundation or argument for him apart from generation, it adds "begotten," and lest you should still cling to this and think he was not properly begotten, it has added "firstborn." VIII. Just as an adoptive son is less than a proper son, and is so called only on account of resemblance, so the Christian Church has always judged that this cannot be attributed to Christ without insult, and has consistently rejected the opinion that Christ is an adoptive Son of God. IX. Next, just as adoption is said to imitate nature, and was devised as a consolation for one who has no children, so it ought not to be objected to God that, unless it can be proved, it is contrary to the nature of God to have a Son properly so called, of whom mention is so frequent in the Scriptures. D. 1.7.16, On Adoption: "For adoption has its place among those persons who can also have natural children." X. No one can at the same time be called a son by the right of adoption and of generation, as Schlichting philosophizes about Christ. If he is a son by generation, adoption is not only superfluous but impossible; for adoption supplies, as it were, its place and lack, and one who is not begotten is nonetheless kindly adopted as a son. But if he says that everything must be understood by resemblance, we reply that a son made by generation in whatever way cannot also be made by adoption, nor need he be. A son may indeed be shown and proved in many ways, but not likewise made. Nor is this contrary to the school of the philosophers and fishermen, or to Scripture, or to ordinary speech. Before, he had taught that the Son of God was begotten by resemblance: how much more if he is said to be begotten by resemblance? This is exactly what we contend. For just as Christ is named the Son of God by taking the resemblance from men, so too he is said to be begotten by God through the same resemblance. Therefore everything said about Christ from resemblance is not truly and properly a Son, nor begotten. Let them enjoy the resemblance; we rejoice in the very truth of the thing. Certainly these men turn almost the whole of religion into some figure and metaphor: Christ the Son of God, God, mediator, our redemption, and what not? And where Scripture says "proper," they cry out boldly and reply: "improper." XI. Now they also lay down what Paul ought to have said: namely, not that God did not spare his proper Son for our sake, but that he did not spare his Son. Yet he said "his proper Son." Go on, and find fault with this in Paul! He adds: "For even if this Son were most truly a Son properly so called, unless he were the Son of God himself, etc." As if he were, or could be, a Son of God properly so called and not the Son of God himself? Finally he says that God could not deliver up his Son properly so called to death for us; but this does not prove it. For just as God willed that he should put on human and servile form in our place, so also that he should lower himself even to death; and God willed to show his love for us abounding in this way, in that to this end he displayed and gave up his own and natural Son. In this lies the force of Paul's argument: both the attested proof of divine love, that he did not spare his own Son for our sake, and the added connection, how would he not with him graciously give us all things? Therefore, to conclude: the word "proper" in Paul's words is opposed not only to what is common or foreign, but is also said by way of resemblance. For the word "proper," taken in its proper sense, in both ordinary speech and Scripture, comprehends both in its force and breadth. Thus it is said "proper fruit," Luke 6:44, [illegible], that is, truly and naturally one's own.

units.la: Socinus, contra Wiekum, cap. v. ad locum istum, & petitum inde argumentum, inquit, nomen proprii duplicem habere expositionem, ut significet, non alienum; deinde omnino & singulari ratione suum: nihil vero aliud in Novo Testamento designare, neque tertiam aliam ejus ibidem extare acceptionem, non qua sumatur pro vere & proprie naturali, oppositum metaphorico:
units.tr: Socinus, against Wiek, chapter 5, on that passage, and the argument drawn from it, says that the word "proper" has a twofold meaning: first, that it signifies "not foreign"; then, "wholly and in a singular way one's own." He says that nothing else is designated by it in the New Testament, nor is there any third sense of it there, in which it is taken for truly and properly natural, as opposed to metaphorical.

units.la: Respondeo, vocem Proprij in novo testamento non habere aliam vim majorem, quam interdum significandi aliquid omnino suum, id est, quale nemo alius habeat: ut in loco illo, Et unicuique feminum proprium corpus, 1 Cor. 15. v. 38. & saepissime nihil aliud significare, quam simpliciter, Suum, aut Suum ipsius, id est, non alienum: ut, cum dicitur, Christum non per sanguinem hircorum & taurorum, sed per proprium sanguinem ingressum fuisse in sancta, Hebr. 9. 12. aut, cum Paulus dicit, 1 Corinth. 6. v. 18. eum, qui scortatur, in proprium (ἰδίον enim est in Graeco) corpus peccare: ubi latina editio habet suum. tertiam aliam significationem non credo hujus vocabuli in novo testamento inveniri. utracunque autem significatione dixerit Paulus, Deum non pepercisse proprio filio, nihil, ex ipsius vocabuli vi, concludi potest de generatione ex Dei Patris substantia. nihil enim vetat, quominus Christus sit Dei Filius peculiaris & suus, non autem alienus, & tamen non sit generatus ex ipsius Dei substantia. Et certe vis rationis adversariorum in eo tota est, si Proprius apponatur Metaphorico: quod nec unquam sit in novo testamento, & in illo Pauli loco, qui solus est, ubi Christus vocetur Proprius Dei Filius, haec significatio non potest habere locum: cum non addatur vox Suo, quae omnino requiritur in tali locutione videtur, ad istam vocis
units.tr: I reply that the word "proper" in the New Testament has no greater force than sometimes to signify something wholly one's own, that is, such as no one else has: as in that place, "to each seed its own proper body," 1 Cor. 15:38; and very often it signifies nothing else than simply "one's own," or "his own," that is, not foreign: as when it is said that Christ entered into the holy places not through the blood of goats and bulls, but through his own blood, Heb. 9:12; or when Paul says, 1 Cor. 6:18, that he who commits fornication sins against his own body (for in Greek it is idion [ἰδίον]); where the Latin edition has "his own." I do not believe a third meaning of this word is found in the New Testament. But in whatever sense Paul spoke, that God did not spare his own Son, nothing can be concluded from the force of the word itself about generation from the substance of God the Father. For nothing prevents Christ from being the peculiar and own Son of God, and not foreign, and yet not be begotten from the very substance of God. And indeed the whole force of the opponents' argument lies in this: if "proper" is applied to the metaphorical; which never occurs in the New Testament, and in that passage of Paul, which alone is where Christ is called the proper Son of God, this meaning cannot apply, since the word "his" is not added, which seems altogether required in such an expression for that word.

units.la: Resp. I. in loco 1 Cor. xv. 38. & uni-cuique feminum proprium corpus, id quidem est, omnino suum, & quale aliud semen non habet; sed etiam naturale, & vere ac proprie naturale corpus: quod imo fundamentum illius proprietatis est. Deus singulis dat suum corpus, animalibus, feminibus, rebus quibuscunque: nempe pro singulorum natura, unicuique suum, proprium, naturale. Ut in expositione proprii, non debeant opponi, corpus non alienum, & vere naturale, sed conjungi, tanquam alterum alterius causa. Sic veri. 35. quaeritur, in exordio hujus disputationis, quomodo resurgent mortui? quali veniunt corpore? responsio est, proprio, ac naturali, non alieno, non alio, quam quo iis, pro sua singula conditione, natura vestit. Quod II. item respondemus ad istum locum, quem adfert Socinus, ut ostendat vocem proprii significare suum ipsius, uti Heb. ix. 12. & 1 Cor. vi. 18. certe per proprium sanguinem Christus dicitur ingressus in sancta, id est, non per alienum, uti sacerdotes V. T. agebant: sed neque illud quovis modo proprium, & non alienum, sed naturaliter proprium: quod quum tale omnino fuerit, quare non & sic etiam hic intelligatur? Quemadmodum Paulus dixit, Act. xx. 28. Proprij significationem exprimendam. nam alioqui, ut dixi, Proprius suum simpliciter significare solet: quin etiam tum demum solet Proprius Metaphorico opponi, cum dicitur, exempli caussa, Hoc nomen, seu, hoc vocabulum est proprium, Hæc significatio, five hic sensus est proprius, &c, sed cum alicui nominatæ rei simplex vox Proprij adjungitur, ut Filius proprius, Pastor proprius, Vitis propria, numquam fortasse, five in Græca, five in Latina lingua, cum ista significatione inveniatur[?], tunc enim ad sensum istum exprimendum dici solet, Filius proprie dictus, Pastor proprie dictus, &c.
units.tr: Answer I. On 1 Cor. xv. 38, "to each seed its own body": this is indeed its own, such as no other seed has, but it is also natural, truly and properly natural. This is in fact the foundation of that propriety. God gives each thing its own body, to animals, to seeds, to things of every kind, namely according to the nature of each, so that each has its own, proper, natural body. In explaining proprium, these should not be set against one another, a body that is not alien and a body that is truly natural. They should be joined, one being the cause of the other. So in ver. 35 the question is raised at the start of this discussion: how do the dead rise? with what body do they come? The answer is: with a proper and natural body, not an alien one, and not any other than the one which nature, according to each one's condition, clothes them with. Our second answer is to the passage which Socinus cites to show that the word proprius means "one's own", as in Heb. ix. 12 and 1 Cor. vi. 18. Certainly Christ is said to have entered the holy places through his own blood, that is, not through alien blood, as the priests of the Old Testament did. But that blood was not proper in just any way, and not alien, but naturally proper. Since it was altogether of this kind, why should it not be understood in this way here too? As Paul said in Acts xx. 28, the meaning of proper must be expressed. For otherwise, as I said, proprius usually means simply "one's own". Indeed it is only then that proprius is usually opposed to the metaphorical, when one says, for example, "this name or word is proper", "this meaning or sense is proper", etc. But when the bare word proprius is added to a named thing, as proper son, proper shepherd, proper vine, it is perhaps never found, whether in Greek or in Latin, with that meaning; for to express that sense people usually say "son properly so called", "shepherd properly so called", etc.

units.la: Satis sane fuerat ad hanc tertiam rationem labefactandam monuisse, & exemplis prolatis ostendisse, vocem Proprij nihil aliud quàm Suum, aut Suum ipsius, in novo testamento solere significare. alia tamen addidimus, ut rudioribus etiam & morosioribus, hac in re, satis fieri posset.
units.tr: It would certainly have been enough to refute this third argument by pointing out, and showing with examples, that the word proprius in the New Testament usually means nothing other than suus, or one's own. Yet we have added other points, so that the matter might be fully satisfactory even to the less learned and more fastidious.

units.la: quod Christus Ecclesiam redemit pro-prio sanguine, idem Hebræ. xiii. 12. & 1 Cor. vi. 18. scortator peccare dicitur in proprium corpus, id est, non alienum, sed suum naturale corpus, uti aliter peccans quicunque dicitur peccare non in corpore alieno, sed simpliciter extra corpus, ἐκτὸς δ᾽ σώματος[?], huic opponitur peccans in corpore, vel in corpus, idque ἴδιον, id est, suum proprissimum. III. Jam videre licet, an tertia vocis proprii significatio, sive proprissima illa, in Scriptura N. T. non reperiatur, qua non simpliciter significat, non alienum, & quid omnino suum, quæ non tollimus, sed insuper naturaliter & proprissime proprium, præsertim ubi naturis rerum, aut actionibus naturalibus adjungitur. Immo an usquam accipiatur aliter. Itaque quando aut Filius dicitur proprius alicujus, aut Pater, cur non, uti in tali sermone & argumē-
units.tr: That Christ redeemed the Church with his own blood (proprio sanguine), the same is found in Heb. 13:12; and in 1 Cor. 6:18 the fornicator is said to sin against his own body (in proprium corpus), that is, not against another's body but against his own natural body. Just as whoever sins otherwise is said to sin not in another's body but simply outside the body [ἐκτὸς δὲ σώματος], so the one who sins in or against the body is opposed to him, and this is idion, that is, his very own [ἴδιον]. III. Now one may see whether the third sense of the word proprius, or rather its most proper sense, is not found in the New Testament, the sense in which it means not merely what is not another's, or anything at all that is one's own, which we do not deny, but what is one's own in the most natural and proper way, especially when it is joined to the natures of things or to natural actions. Indeed, one may ask whether it is ever taken otherwise. Therefore, when a son is called the proprius son of someone, or a father, why should it not, in such a discourse and argument, denote by the proper and not transferred or restricted meaning of the word, a true and natural generation, which alone is the foundation of that true relation? We follow the native and full use of the word; our opponents do the reverse. Which is more correct? Especially where nothing compels us to move from the proper sense to another.

units.la: to solet, pro vocis propriâ, & non translatâ aut restrictâ significatione, denotabit generatione vera & naturali proprium[?]: quæ sola fundamentum verae illius relationis est. Nos nativum & plenum vocis usum sequimur: Adversarii contra: utri rectius[?] præsertim ubi nihil est quod in alium à proprio sensum abire[?] nos cogat. IV. Proprium, inquit, nusquam opponi metaphorico, in Novo Testamento. ergo nusquam proprie sumitur[?]: quid absurdius dici vel fingi potest, præcipue quum vox ista saepissime usurpetur[?] Ego contra assero, in omnibus hactenus auditis locis non aliter sumi, & nusquam non opponi metaphorico. Quæso quando dicitur proprium corpus, sive feminis, sive hominis, & proprius sanguis, annon opponitur metaphorico, annon intelliguntur proprie talia, & non dicta per metaphoram[?]? Vel quando proprius frater Andreæ Simon dicitur, Joann. i. 41. ἐκ τ[?] ἰδίων loqui Satanas, cap. viii. 44. & mundus τὰ ἴδια diligere, cap. xv. 19. unumquemque proprio sensu debere abundare, ἰδίῳ τοῦ[?] Rom. xiv. 5. habens cauterizatā propriam conscientiam, 1 Tim. iv. 2. secundum proprias concupiscentias, 2 Tim. iv. 3. & Iac. i. 14. reprehensionem accepit propriæ transgressionis, 2 Pet. ii. 16. 22. ἰδίον ἐξεγχω[?]: quid, an hæc & alia ejusmodi non proprie accipienda, & oppositâ sensui eorundem metaphorico[?] v. Et Deo quando ἰδία adscribuntur, ea nunquam aliter accipi possunt. Uti 2 Tim. i. 9. ἀλλ᾽ κατ᾽ ἴδιον πρόθεσιν[?] & Heb. iv. 10. Quemadmodum à propriis Deus. Annon propria ista opponuntur metaphoricis[?] Quod si ad illa regerat, istis quidem vocem proprii contineri, non autem proprii Filii. Hoc vero valde ineptum: quia non de hac, sed illâ voce nunc disputatur, ejusque sensu & in N.T. usu, quem ostendimus ubique metaphorico opponi, & non tantum denotari quid quovis modo suum, aut non alienum, sed propriissime etiam & naturaliter suum. VI. Quemadmodum in relationibus aliis similibus, fratrum, & conjugum, sic omnino in consimili parentum, requiritur ut quando quis proprius
units.tr: IV. Proprius, they say, is nowhere opposed to the metaphorical in the New Testament; therefore it is nowhere taken in its proper sense. What could be more absurd to say or imagine, especially since this word is very often used? I, on the contrary, maintain that in all the passages heard so far it is not taken otherwise, and is nowhere not opposed to the metaphorical. I ask: when we speak of one's own body, whether of a woman or of a man, and one's own blood, is it not opposed to the metaphorical? Are such things not understood properly and not said by way of metaphor? Or when Simon is called the own (proprius) brother of Andrew, John 1:41; or Satan speaks from his own (ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων) [λαλεῖ], John 8:44; or the world loves its own (τὰ ἴδια), John 15:19; or each one should abound in his own mind (ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ), Rom. 14:5; or having a seared own conscience, 1 Tim. 4:2; or according to their own lusts, 2 Tim. 4:3, and James 1:14, where one is tempted by his own desire; or he received a reproof for his own transgression, 2 Pet. 2:16, 22, ἰδίου ἐλέγχου: are not these and similar expressions to be taken properly, and opposed to the metaphorical sense of the same words? V. And when ἰδία is ascribed to God, these can never be taken otherwise, as in 2 Tim. 1:9, ἀλλὰ κατ᾽ ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν, and Heb. 4:10, Quemadmodum à propriis Deus. Are not these proprii words opposed to the metaphorical? But if they were to refer them to those passages, the word proprius would indeed be contained in those, but not the proprius Son. This, however, is very inept, because it is not this word but that one which is now under dispute, and its meaning and use in the N.T., which we have shown is everywhere opposed to the metaphorical, and not merely denotes what is in any way one's own or not another's, but also what is one's own most properly and naturally. VI. As in other similar relations, of brothers and spouses, so altogether in the like relation of parents, it is required that when someone is called proprius, this is understood of the property of that foundation on which the relation rests, whether it be in nature or in a natural affinity or bond. Thus, not to repeat it again, Peter is called the own brother of Andrew in that sense. When a man is called proprius of his wife, unaquaeque habeat proprium virum, 1 Cor. 7:2, and in verse 4, Mulier autem ἰδία proprii corporis potestatem non habet, etc., Eph. 5:22, Mulieres propriis viris estote obedientes, and Col. 3:18: is it not understood that a true and proper marriage is the foundation of that relation? So why should not the ἰδίας of the proper Son, and the generation of the Father, likewise be properly so called?

units.la: Tom.2. nominatur, id intelligatur de proprietate istius fundamenti, quo relatio nitítur, sive in natura sit, aut naturali affinitate vel vinculo. Sic, ne iterum dicamus, illo sensu Petrum appellari Andreæ fratrem proprium: quando vir dicitur proprius conjugis, unaquaeque habeat proprium virum, 1 Cor. vii. 2. & vers. 4. Mulier autem ἰδία[?] proprii corporis potestatem non habet, &c. Eph. v. 22. Mulieres propriis viris estote obedientes, & Col iii. 18. annon intelligitur verum ac proprium conjugium relationis illius fundamentum esse? Sic quid ni ἰδίας[?] proprii Filii, ac Patris, generatio item proprie dicta? In loco, inquit, Rom. viii. 32. vox proprii non potest habere significationem illam propriam, quia non additur vox sui. Negatur omnino, id requiri ad istam vocis proprii significationem exprimendam. Quasi non vox proprii tantundem valeat ac proprium suum? Joan. xv. 19. mundus τὸ ἴδιον diligeret, id est suum proprium. Act. i. 7. Tempestates, quas Pater posuit in propria, id est, sua propria potestate. 1 Cor. xii. 11. Spiritus, distribuens propria ἰδία[?] sive sua, quae sibi propria sunt. Perinde ergo est, an vox proprius, an suus usurpetur. Quod in nostro argumento exigit, ut in N. T. ostendamus ubi Christus dicatur non modo Patris Filius proprius, sed suus proprius, id valde est absonum. Nam cui non satis est, quod Pater eum testatur Filium suum, & appellatur proprius Filius Patris, ei neque satisfaciet si vel junctum alicubi legeretur, suus proprius. Quasi non in voce sui æque exceptionem aliquam reperire vel fingere possent, ac proprii? & non paris esset potestatis, dicere, Deum non pepercisse Filio proprio, ac suo proprio? Præterquam quod sermonis Græci ratio non ita ferat, exigatve, dicere ἴδιῳ αὐτοῦ υἱῷ, ac quidem Latini, sui proprii Filii. Proprius non simpliciter significare solet suum, sed proprie suum, & pro subjecta materia, naturaliter suum. Et metaphorico oppo-nitur, non tantum ubi dicimus, hoc nomen, seu vocabulum &c. proprium, in quibus significationem denotat propriam, sed & ubi alias vox proprii adhibetur: etiam quando dicitur, Filius proprius, vitis propria, pastor proprius: nisi quod in voce pastoris possit esse metaphora, sed utcunque sumatur vel pro pastore pecudum, hominumve, adjunctum proprii omnino metaphorico opponitur. Neque necesse est semper addi, proprie dictus Filius, &c. quia id satis sola proprii nomenclaturâ continetur: atque ad grammaticam, & vocis expositionem illud potius addi in sermone solet, quam in continua tractatione & expositione rei. Quare nihil fuit, quod se in rudiorum & morosiorum gratiam Socinus dixit multa corrogasse ut ostenderet, vocem proprii nihil aliud quam suum, aut suum ipsius in N. T. significare: quod nec ostendit, nec si ostendisset, vel ita rationem nostram labefactasset, hinc petitam, quod Christus Filius Dei appellatur proprius, quod, quia nihil in contrarium adferri potest, quod expositionem illam impediat vel tollat, non aliter sumendum quam Filius proprie dictus, & hoc, proprie genitus.
units.tr: Tom. 2. "In the passage, they say, Rom. 8:32, the word proprius cannot have that proper meaning, because the word suus is not added." This is denied altogether: that is not required to express this sense of the word proprius. As if the word proprius did not have the same force as proprium suum! John 15:19, mundus τὸ ἴδιον diligeret, that is, his own. Acts 1:7, Tempestates, quas Pater posuit in propria, that is, in his own power. 1 Cor. 12:11, Spiritus, distribuens propria ἰδία, that is, his own gifts, which are proper to him. It is therefore all one whether the word proprius or suus is used. What our argument requires is that we show in the N.T. where Christ is called not only the proper Son of the Father, but his own proper Son; this is quite absurd. For whoever is not satisfied that the Father testifies that he is his Son, and that he is called the proper Son of the Father, will not be satisfied even if suus proprius were read somewhere joined together. As if they could not find or invent some exception in the word suus just as in proprius! And would it not be of no less force to say that God did not spare his proper Son than his own proper Son? Besides, the nature of the Greek language does not allow or require saying ἰδίῳ αὐτοῦ υἱῷ, nor, in Latin, sui proprii Filii. Proprius does not usually mean simply suum, but properly suum, and, with respect to the subject matter, naturally suum. It is also opposed to the metaphorical, not only where we say hoc nomen, seu vocabulum, etc., proprium, in which it denotes the proper meaning, but also where the word proprius is used in other ways: even when it is said Filius proprius, vitis propria, pastor proprius; except that in the word pastor there may be a metaphor, but however it is taken, whether for a shepherd of flocks or of men, the adjunct proprius is wholly opposed to the metaphorical. Nor is it always necessary to add proprie dictus Son, etc., since that is sufficiently contained in the word proprius alone; and this is usually added in grammatical discussion and explanation of a word rather than in a continuous treatment and exposition of a matter. Therefore there was no need for Socinus to say that he had gathered many things for the sake of the less learned and more fastidious, to show that the word proprius in the N.T. means nothing else than suum, or one's own. He neither showed this, nor, had he shown it, would he thereby have weakened our argument, drawn from the fact that Christ is called the proper Son of God, which, since nothing can be adduced to the contrary that impedes or removes that explanation, must be taken no otherwise than as the Son properly so called, and, this, properly begotten.

units.la: Eadem valent ad vindicationem ejus, quod Christus Joan. v. 18. Deum dixit Patrem proprium. Propterea ergo magis quaesiverunt Judæi Iesum occidere, quod non modo[?] solvisset Sabbatum, sed & πατέρα ἴδιον ἔλεγε τὸν Θεόν, ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ. Dixerat autem, Pater meus usque hodie operatur, & ego operor. Unde sequitur, quod plane alia ratione Christus Dei Filius, & Deus Christi Pater est, quam qua nos; & tali quidem, qualis in nos, vel in creaturas alias non cadit. Quodque Christi ut Filii Pater, sit ejus Pater proprius: & quod hoc tantundem sit, ac esse æqualem, parem Deo, ἴσον τῷ Θεῷ. Quod certe creaturæ ulli tribui nequit. Apostolus dixit, Christum ἴσα[?] τῷ θεῷ[?]: id est, plane æqualem Deo: quod ei idem, cum esse ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ, in forma Dei. Quis autem creaturæ ulli adscribat formam Dei, æqualem, eandem & illa in Christo veneratur, antequam homo factus, antequam seipsum exinanivit, formâ servi accepta, & in similitudine repertus hominum, &c. Quid ad hæc Socinus negat sequi Christum esse verum, seu æternum & summum Deum, ex eo quod æqualis Deo.
units.tr: The same holds for the claim that Christ, in John 5:18, called God his own Father. "For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father [πατέρα ἴδιον ἔλεγε τὸν Θεόν], making himself equal to God [ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ]." He had said, "My Father is working until now, and I am working." From this it follows that Christ is the Son of God, and God is the Father of Christ, in a way clearly different from our way, and in a manner that does not apply to us or to any other creatures. And since the Father of Christ as Son is his own Father, and this amounts to being equal, on a par with God [ἴσον τῷ Θεῷ], this certainly cannot be attributed to any creature. The Apostle says that Christ was equal to God [ἴσα τῷ θεῷ], that is, plainly equal to God, and that he was in the form of God [ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ]. Who would ascribe the form of God, equal to God, to any creature? The Church also reveres this in Christ before he became man, before he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was found in the likeness of men, and so on. To this Socinus replies that it does not follow from Christ's being equal to God that he is the true, eternal and supreme God.

units.la: Respondeo, consequentiam hujus argumenti nullam esse, immo argumentum in adversa-rios facile retorqueri. tantum enim abest, ut ex eo, quod Christus sit æqualis Deo, sequatur, ipsum esse æternum & summum Deum, ut potius ex hoc ipso necessario consequatur, Christum non esse æternum & summum Deum. nemo enim sibi ipsi æqualis esse potest. certum est autem, Deum, cui Christus sit æqualis, esse æternum & summum Deum: idque ad argumentum adversariorum concludendum, neces-sarium est: si tamen concludi ullo modo posset. sed quo minus concludi posset, obstat, quod summus & æternus Deus unus tantum est: adeo ut ex hoc consequatur, argumentum in ipsos adversarios, ut diximus, merito retorque-ri. Præterea hic est fallacia à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter. neque enim Chri-stus simpliciter se Deo æqualem fecit, immo æqualitatis suæ cum Deo nihil diserte memi-nit: sed tantummodo dixit, Pater meus usque modo operatur, & ego operor: unde colligitur, ipsum se æqualem Deo fecisse. Itaque Christi cum Deo æqualitas, de qua evangelista loquitur, huc tantum pertinet, atque hactenus tantum extenditur, quatenus ipse operatur, quemadmodum Deus seu Pater operatur. quam æqualitatem in hoc ipso non esse omnimodam, declarant subsequentia verba ipsius Christi, quibus antecedentia ista explicat, & rem totam dilucide exponit. inquit enim, Amen, Amen dico vobis, Non potest Filius à se facere quidquam, nisi quod viderit Patrem facientem. quæcunque enim ille fecerit, hæc & Filius similiter facit. Audis hic æqualitatem, quæ est inter Christum & Deum, seu Filium & Patrem, in ope-rando, & simul eadem in re inæqualitatem. æqualitas est, quatenus Filius ea facit, quæ
units.tr: I answer that the consequence of this argument is null, and indeed that the argument can easily be turned against our opponents. For it is so far from being the case that, because Christ is equal to God, it follows that he is the eternal and supreme God, that rather, from this very fact, it necessarily follows that Christ is not the eternal and supreme God. For no one can be equal to himself. It is certain, however, that the God to whom Christ is equal is the eternal and supreme God; and this is necessary for drawing the conclusion of our opponents, if indeed it could be drawn in any way. But what prevents it from being drawn is that the supreme and eternal God is only one; so that from this it follows that the argument, as we have said, is rightly turned back against our opponents themselves. Moreover, here is a fallacy from a statement qualified in some respect to a statement taken absolutely. For Christ did not make himself simply equal to God; indeed he does not expressly mention any equality of his with God, but only said, "My Father is working until now, and I am working." From this it is inferred that he made himself equal to God. Therefore the equality of Christ with God, of which the evangelist speaks, pertains only to this and extends only so far as he himself works, just as God or the Father works. That this equality is not complete in every respect is shown by the words of Christ that follow, by which he explains the preceding words and sets out the whole matter clearly. For he says: "Truly, truly I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing; for whatever he does, the Son does likewise." Here you hear the equality that exists between Christ and God, or Son and Father, in working, and at the same time the inequality in the same matter. There is equality insofar as the Son does those things which

units.la: Resp. 1. Ad retorsionem, quam facit, argumenti contra nos, quod nemo sibi ipsi æqualis esse possit, quodque seque-retur, si Christus æqualis Deo, inde pro-baretur idem Deus esse; dicimus, eidem non competere esse æquale sibimetipsi, secundum idem, ad idem: sed quidem duo-bus alia ratione distinctis, alia iisdem & æqualibus: id est, duabus distinctis per-sonis, quales sunt Pater & Filius, diversis quod ad personam, iisdem quoad essentiam. Cur enim Filius non potest, non debet esse ejusdem cum Patre essentiæ, eique ea ratione per omnia æqualis? Æqua-lis dicitur persona personæ, respectu ejuf-dem essentiæ, dignitatis, honoris. Cu-jus ratione summa inter illas est identitas. Ergo uti in persona spectatur esse essentiæ, & personæ, respectu demum habito ad istam, æqualitas dicitur, ad illam vero identitas, neque nisi hujus ratione illa ha-bet locum. Deinde ait, Christum se æqualem facere Deo Patri, non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, ratione operatio-nis, non essentiæ: quia antea dixit, Pater meus usque modo operatur, & ego operor; & quod Christi cum Patre æqualitas huc tantum pertineat, & hactenus tantum ex-tendatur, quatenus ipse operatur, quem-admodum Deus seu Pater operatur. Sed ex eo sane temere quis concluserit, se esse æqualem Deo, quod operatur simplici-ter, uti & Pater operatur. Præsertim si attendatur, quod alio semper modo & alia omnino Pater operatur, alia homo, quicunque is demum fit: & quod inter il-los, & illa, semper infinita maneat distan-tia, utcunque in eodem forte opere occu-pentur, & nihil iste agat, nisi quod faciendi Pater facit: inæqualitas vero, quatenus Fi-lius nihil potuit facere à seipso, quod profectò sa-tis est, ad demonstrandum, Filium non esse illum summum & æternum Deum. quid enim absurdius aut impossibilius, quam summum illum & æternum Deum nihil à seipso facere posse? Pater igitur, qui sine controversia est summus ille & æternus Deus, à seipso, absque dubio, omnia facere potest: & sic magna inæqualitas, in operando, inter Patrem & Filium apparet, præsertim, si rectè intelligatur, quid sibi velit, Filium à seipso nihil posse facere, id autem, quamvis alioqui per se clarissimum, declarat Christus illico subsequentibus verbis, nisi viderit Patrem facientem. hoc enim perinde est, ac si dixisset, Nisi quod faciendi potestatem & jussum à Patre habuerit. Nullus unquam dicet, inde æqualitatem utri-usque legitimè probatam, aut probari posse: ut non tali dumtaxat argumento nixus Christus debeat dici probasse suam cum Patre deitatem, & æqualitatem. Quod si illud argumentum procederet, jam quis non, licet impari aliquantum modo & gradu, posset cum Christo suam jactare cum Patre æqualitatem? quis non saltem æqualitatem cum Christo? At tam hoc, quam illud merito piis omnibus horrori est atque detestationi. III. Quod si ex operatione Christi cum Patre, concludatur ejus cum isto æqualitas, necessario intelligenda quoque operationis æqualitas: alias non magis æqualitas, quam inæqualitas isto argumento probaretur. Quare si vel hic omnimoda similitudo intelligatur, quæ intelligi sanè debet ad conficiendam æqualitatem, jam & potestatis, & essentiæ quoque paritas connotabitur. Quod eodem, cum argumento nostro, redit. Quod enim dicit, non omnimodam hic indicari æqualitatem, æque negare posset æqualitatem ipsam, quin ejus loco inæqualitatem suggerere: atque ita vim sermonis, & illationis, seu argumenti quod in verbis textus est, tollere. Neq; propterea quod aliquam suorum operum cum divinis convenientiam prædicaret, occidendus videbatur Christus, sed quod sui paritatem cum Deo haud obscure significabat: ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ θεῷ [?]. IV. Non æqualitatem, operum nedum eam, quæ non sit omnimoda, impugnabant adeo in Christo Judæi, vel damnabant, quam personarum. Et de hac verba textus sumenda, non tantum de illa. Patet ex loco, nam primo dicitur, propterea autem magis quærebant ipsum Judæi interficere, non modo quod Sabbatum solvisset, opere nimirum illo suo fanationis: haec de ejus operatione. Sed & Patrem proprium dixerat Deum, seipsum faciens æqualem Deo. Æqualem se faciens Deo, eo quod dixerat Patrem suum. Non ergo opera, & operationem, eorumque cum Deo æqualitatem duntaxat quandam impetebant Judæi: sed imprimis sui cum Deo æqualitatem: quod seipsum ἴσον [?] faceret æqualem Deo. v. Et sic etiam in sermone Christi, Pater meus usque hodie operatur, & ego operor. Duo sunt, quod Deum dicit Patrem suum, singulari appropriatione; & sua opera cum Deo conjungit: utrumque ita, ut omnino appareat, indicari ab eo sui cum Deo ἰσότητα [?]. Jam hoc Judæos offendit, & hoc vindicare satagunt, quod Christi spectat æqualitatem cum Deo Patre, tum verbis, tum operibus significatam. vi. Quod autem verf. 19. addit, Filium à seipso nihil facere posse nisi quod Patrem viderit facientem, & quæ Pater facit, eadem & Filium facere ὁμοίως [?]: duo includit, & Christum, pro ratione officii sui, nihil posse aut velle præter id quod sibi à Patre imperatum, eidemque gratum sciret: & hoc eo significatur, quod filius dicitur nihil à seipso facere; & sua illa opera, ob quæ Judæi ipsum exagitabant, docet non esse alia, quam qualia & Patris sui, quod est facere, quæ Patrem viderit facientem; deinde fundamentum istorum adjungitur, quod quæcunque Pater, eadem & Filius faciat ὁμοίως[?] : quod nisi posita ejus cum Patre æqualitate, verum esse non potest. Etenim faciamus ex Adversariorum sententia Christum non nisi hominem, quamvis valde excellentem, quomodo non Patrem ea facere, quæ ipse Patris jussu ac potestate agit, sed & se facere similiter ea quæ Pater, nota, & eadem, & similiter, ἀ[?], πάντα[?], ᾧ ὁμοίως[?], dicere ausit? nisi agnoscat similitudinem, & æqualitatem, & proprietatem omnimodam Filii cum Patre, ὁμοῖον[?], ἴσον[?], ἰδιον[?].
units.tr: Reply 1. As to the turning back of the argument against us, that no one can be equal to himself, and that it would follow, if Christ is equal to God, that the same God is proved: we say that it does not belong to the same thing to be equal to itself, in the same respect and in regard to the same thing; but rather to two things distinguished in one way and equal in another, that is, to two distinct persons, such as the Father and the Son, different as to person but the same as to essence. For why can the Son not, and why should he not, be of the same essence as the Father, and in this respect in every way equal to him? A person is called equal to a person with respect to the same essence, dignity and honour. By this reasoning there is the greatest identity between them. Therefore, just as in a person we look at the essence and the person, and with respect to the latter, equality is spoken of, but with respect to the former, identity, and the one applies only in virtue of the other. Next, he says that Christ made himself equal to God the Father, not simply, but in some respect, by reason of the operation and not of the essence, because he said before, "My Father is working until now, and I am working," and because the equality of Christ with the Father pertains only to this and extends only so far as he himself works, just as God or the Father works. But from this one would certainly conclude rashly that he is equal to God, because he works simply, as the Father also works. Especially if one considers that the Father always works in a different way and in an entirely different manner from man, whoever he may be; and that between the one and the other there always remains an infinite distance, however they may be occupied in the same work; and that the Son does nothing except what he sees the Father doing: whereas the inequality, insofar as the Son could do nothing of himself, which is quite enough to demonstrate that the Son is not that supreme and eternal God. For what is more absurd or more impossible than that the supreme and eternal God could do nothing of himself? Therefore the Father, who is without controversy that supreme and eternal God, can certainly do all things of himself; and so a great inequality in working appears between Father and Son, especially if one rightly understands what it means that the Son can do nothing of himself. Christ himself declares this, although it is clear enough in itself, in the words that immediately follow: unless he sees the Father doing it. For this is just as if he had said: unless he has the power and command to do it from the Father. No one will ever say that from this a legitimate proof of the equality of the two has been drawn, or can be drawn; so that Christ should not be said to have proved his deity and equality with the Father merely by such an argument. But if that argument held, who would not, though in a somewhat unequal manner and degree, be able to boast of equality with Christ and with the Father? Who would not at least claim equality with Christ? Yet this, as much as that, is rightly abhorrent and detestable to all the godly. III. If from Christ's working together with the Father one were to conclude an equality between them, the equality of the working must necessarily be understood as well; otherwise the argument would prove not equality any more than inequality. Therefore, if here one understands complete likeness, which must indeed be understood to establish equality, then the parity of power and of essence will also be implied. This comes to the same thing as our argument. For one who says that no complete equality is indicated here could equally deny equality itself, and instead suggest inequality in its place; and so would destroy the force of the statement and of the inference, or argument, that is in the words of the text. Nor was Christ thought to deserve death because he claimed some agreement of his works with divine works, but because he plainly signified his parity with God: making himself equal to God [ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ θεῷ]. IV. The Jews did not attack, or condemn in Christ, an equality of works, still less one that is not complete, but an equality of persons. And the words of the text must be taken of this and not merely of the former. This is clear from the place itself: for it is first said, therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, not only because he had broken the Sabbath, namely by that work of his, the healing; this concerns his working. But he had also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. He made himself equal to God in that he called God his Father. Therefore the Jews did not attack only the works and operation of Christ and some equality of them with God, but chiefly his equality with God, because he made himself equal [ἴσον] to God. V. And so also in the saying of Christ, "My Father is working until now, and I am working." There are two things: he calls God his Father in a unique appropriation, and he joins his works to God's; both in such a way that it plainly appears he indicates by this his equality [ἰσότητα] with God. Now this offends the Jews, and they strive to defend it, because it regards Christ's equality with God the Father, signified both by his words and by his works. VI. But what he adds in verse 19, that the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing, and that whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise [ὁμοίως], includes two things: that Christ, according to the nature of his office, can do or will nothing except what he knows has been commanded him by the Father and is pleasing to him; and this is signified by the fact that the Son is said to do nothing of himself; and that those works of his for which the Jews harassed him show that they are no other than those of his Father, which is to do what he sees the Father doing. Then the foundation of these is added, that whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does [ὁμοίως]; which cannot be true unless his equality with the Father is assumed. For suppose, on the view of our opponents, that Christ is only a man, though a very excellent one: how could he dare to say that he does in the same way, and likewise, and in all things [πάντα], what the Father does, when he does by the Father's command and authority the things which the Father does? Unless he acknowledges a likeness, an equality, and a complete identity of the Son with the Father, like [ὅμοιον], equal [ἴσον], own [ἴδιον].

units.la: Pergit Filius illa explicare. Etenim Pater amat Filium, & omnia ostendit ei quæcunque ipse facit: & majora horum ei ostendet opera, ut miremini. Quomodo enim Pater exsuscitat mortuos & vivificat, ita & filius quos vult vivificat. Adeo quando dixit Filius, se nihil posse, extra id quod Patri placitum, intelligendum, se præter id nihil velle. Nam qui quos vult, vivificat, & quæ vult, facere credendus est. Non potest ergo; impotentia morali nempe, non physica, cujus causa hæret in voluntate, quod quis nolit, non in viribus, quod non valeat. Uti Marc. vi. 5, Et non poterat ibi ullam facere virtutem, non ob defectum potentiæ, sed quod non placeret, non videretur congruum, vulgi infidelitati, se, suasque virtutes prostituere. Æqualitas, inquit Socinus, Filii cum Patre in hoc sita, quod Filius ea facit, quæ Pater. Verum plus dicitur in textu, nempe quod quæ Pater facit, illa & Filius similiter facit. Inæqualitatem vero in hoc ponit Adversarius, quod Filius nihil potest facere à seipso: sed quod diximus ita accipi nequaquam posse aut debere, quasi in præjudicium potestatis Christi, sed ad demonstrandam ejus cum Patre convenientiam: atque in officio suo peragendo, uti hæc de Christo ejus ratione dicta, & accipienda sunt, ita se in omnibus prorsus habuit ad nutum & voluntatem est Patris: quod nequaquam adversatur isti ejus naturæ, secundum quam Patris proprius, & cum Patre æqualis est Filius. Uti vulgatum & antiquum est in Scholis Theologorum, distinguere in Christo considerationem Theologicam, ab œconomicâ; & naturam, ab officio. Et hoc ubique obvium, inter homines etiam, ut alia de quopiam sui & naturæ, aut conditionis propriæ respectu dicantur, alia officii ratione, qua aliis se submittit & inservit. Nihil potest Christus facere à seipso, nihil alienum, seorsim à Patre, aut præter ejus voluntatem ac mandatum. Interim nec definit Patri per omnia esse similis, & æqualis: ad hoc enim demonstrandum, Patrem Deum suum dixit proprium. Quod non ita à Judæis modo, sed ipso quoque Euangelista acceptum, & à Christo significatum Socinus agnoscit, sentitque ex modoloquendi, quo usus est Euangelista, cum omnino una cum Iudæis censuisse, Christum, verbis illis, se æqualem Deo fecisse.
units.tr: The Son goes on to explain these things. "For the Father loveth the Son, and sheweth him all things that himself doeth: and he will shew him greater works than these, that ye may marvel. For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom he will." So when the Son said that he can do nothing, this must be understood as meaning nothing beyond what pleases the Father; he wills nothing apart from that. For one who quickens whom he wills and does what he wills is believed to be able to do so. Therefore he cannot, but this is moral impotence, not physical: its cause lies in the will, in that a man is unwilling, not in his powers, in that he lacks strength. Compare Mark 6:5, "And he could there do no mighty work," where the lack was not of power but because it would not please him, nor seem fitting, to prostitute himself and his powers to the unbelief of the crowd. The equality of the Son with the Father, says Socinus, lies in this, that the Son does the things that the Father does. But the text says more, namely that what the Father does, the Son also does in like manner. The Adversary, on the other hand, places the inequality in this, that the Son can do nothing of himself. But what we have said cannot and must not be taken in such a way as to prejudice the power of Christ; it is rather to demonstrate his agreement with the Father. Just as these things said about Christ, in respect of his office, are to be understood in that sense, so in all things he has conformed himself entirely to the nod and will of the Father. This is in no way opposed to that nature according to which the Son is the Father's own and equal with the Father. It is the common and ancient practice in the schools of the theologians to distinguish in Christ the theological consideration from the economic, and the nature from the office. This is also obvious among men: some things are said of a person with respect to his own nature or proper condition, and other things with respect to his office, by which he submits and serves others. Christ can do nothing of himself: nothing foreign to, or apart from, the Father, or contrary to his will and command. Yet he does not cease to be in all things like and equal to the Father; for to demonstrate this he called God his own Father. Socinus acknowledges that this was understood thus not only by the Jews but also by the Evangelist himself, and by Christ's own meaning, and he feels "from the manner of speaking which the Evangelist used, since he indeed agreed with the Jews that by those words Christ made himself equal to God."

units.la: Dicunt Remonstrantes, loco citato, pag. 49. Nemo etenim adeo amens est, ut gratiosam filiationem sive generationem, proprie dictam generationem sive filiationem vocet. Assimilatio gratiosa, vere ac recte dicitur filiatio, sed non proprie, nec enim propria generatio est. Sic nos recte ac vere filii Dei sumus, ac vocamur in Scripturis, imo divinæ naturæ consortes dicimur, etiamsi proprie Filii Dei non sumus. Sed clarissime in adoptione res patet. Is qui naturaliter filius alterius est, vere quidem filius adoptantis fit, etsi non pro-
units.tr: The Remonstrants say, in the place cited, p. 49: "For no one is so mad as to call gracious sonship or generation, generation or sonship properly so called. A gracious assimilation is truly and rightly called sonship, but not properly; for it is not a proper generation. Thus we are rightly and truly sons of God, and are so called in the Scriptures; indeed we are said to be partakers of the divine nature, even though we are not properly sons of God. But the matter is very clearly seen in adoption. He who is naturally the son of another truly becomes the son of the one who adopts him, although not properly; for he is not begotten of the adopter..."

units.la: Resp. 1. At Christi Filiatio, sive generatio nullo modo gratiosa est. Talis est nostra: & in hoc Christi nostrique filiatio differt. Quod Patres, & ii qui contra Felicem Urgelitanum disputarunt olim, significatum volunt istis Christi verbis, Joann. xx. 17. adscendo ad Patrem meum, & Patrem vestrum. non dixit, adscendo ad nostrum Patrem, sed distincte ad meum, & vestrum. ἄλλως ἡμῶν[?], ἐξ φύσιν ἄλλως ὑμῶν[?], ἐξ[?] uti Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus inquit; quod idem Ambrosius observat, prie, quia in jura omnia filii succedit, non ali-& Augustinus. Ambrosius, lib. 1. de fide, ter quam si proprie ex adoptante genitus cap. VI. Et addidit: Deum meum & Deum esset. vestrum. Quia licet ipse & Pater unum sint, & illi proprius proprietate naturae, nobis Deus proprius esse coepit per Filium: non naturae jure, sed gratiae: tamen utramque naturam hic significare videtur in Christo & divinitatis & carnis. Divinitatis ex Patre, carnis ex matre. Illamque ante omnia: ipsamque ex virgine. Denique ante Patrem ut Filius nominavit, Deum postea ut homo nuncupavit, ubique autem Deum suum.
units.tr: Reply 1. But the sonship or generation of Christ is in no way gracious. Ours is such, and in this the sonship of Christ and ours differs. The Fathers, and those who long ago disputed against Felix of Urgel, wished these words of Christ, John 20:17, "I ascend to my Father and your Father," to be understood to mean this. He did not say "to our Father," but distinctly "to my" and "your" Father. [Ἄλλως ἡμῶν, ἐξ φύσιν ἄλλως ὑμῶν]: as Cyril of Jerusalem says, the one is of nature, the other of grace. Ambrose observes the same thing, and Augustine too. Ambrose, in book 1 On the Faith, chapter 6, adds: "He said 'my God' and 'your God.' For although he and the Father are one, and he is God by the property of nature, God has become ours through the Son, not by the right of nature but by grace. Yet here he seems to signify both natures in Christ, of divinity and of flesh: of divinity from the Father, of flesh from the mother. And he named him Son before the Father, and afterwards named God as man, but everywhere his own God."

units.la: II. Neque Christi Filiatio est assimilatio, ὁμοίωσις sed ὁμοούσια consubstantialitas, ἰσότης.
units.tr: II. Nor is the sonship of Christ an assimilation, [ὁμοίωσις], but consubstantiality, [ὁμοούσια], equality, [ἰσότης].

units.la: III. Imo quia ista non est propria generatio, non talis est Christi Filiatio, quia haec propria est, & utrumque relatorum habet proprium, Patrem proprium, & proprium Filium, ex fundamento proprio, ego genui te, quod nulli alteri dictum, ὡς μονογενής, ἰδικῶς.
units.tr: III. Indeed, because that is not a proper generation, such is not the sonship of Christ, for this one is proper, and has each of the correlatives proper: a proper Father and a proper Son, on the proper ground, "I have begotten thee," which was said to no other, [ὡς μονογενής], [ἰδικῶς].

units.la: IV. Nos filii Dei sumus, sed non eodem ordine & genere, quo Christus.
units.tr: IV. We are sons of God, but not in the same order and kind as Christ.

units.la: V. Adoptio in Christum non quadrat.
units.tr: V. Adoption does not fit Christ.

units.la: VI. Nam non potest fieri Filius Dei, qui jam naturaliter est. φύσει υἱὸς θεοῦ, dicunt Veteres. Ideoque Patri non extraneus. Scholastici in III. Dist. X. & inter illos Gabriel Biel, qu. unica: primo requiritur ad hoc quod aliquis sit filius adoptivus alicujus, quod sit ei extraneus, id est, non sit ejus naturalis filius. Unde concludunt, Christum non posse esse Filium Dei adoptivum. Sic omnes tenent, contra Durandum.
units.tr: VI. For one who is already naturally the Son of God cannot become the Son of God: the Ancients call him [φύσει υἱὸς θεοῦ], "Son of God by nature." Therefore he is not a stranger to the Father. The Schoolmen, on III Dist. X, and among them Gabriel Biel, question unique: "First it is required, for someone to be an adopted son of another, that he be a stranger to him, that is, not his natural son." Hence they conclude that Christ cannot be an adopted Son of God. All hold this, against Durandus.

units.la: VII. Dic, quando, vel quomodo adoptatus?
units.tr: VII. Say when, or how, he was adopted?

units.la: VIII. Vel nega, Christum proprie à Deo genitum, qui Filius est viventis Dei. Matth. XVI. 16. Confer Scholasticos, ad III. Dist. X. ubi Magister inquit: Si vero quaeritur, an Christus sit adoptivus Filius secundum quod homo, sive alio modo: respondemus, Christum non esse adoptivum Filium aliquo modo, sed tantum naturaliter: quia natura Filius Dei est, non adoptionis gratia. Similiter Thomas, III. qu. XXIII. art. IV. atque in hunc locum disputantes, Medina, Suarez, Disp. XLIX. sect. II. Vasquez, Disp. XXXIX. Petrus de Lorca, Disp. LXXXIV. alii.
units.tr: VIII. Or deny that Christ was properly begotten of God, who is the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16). Compare the Schoolmen on III Dist. X, where the Master says: "But if it is asked whether Christ is an adoptive Son according to his humanity, or in some other way, we answer that Christ is not an adoptive Son in any way, but only naturally, because he is the Son of God by nature, not by the grace of adoption." Similarly Thomas, III q. 23 art. 4, and those disputing on this passage: Medina, Suárez, Disp. 49 sect. 2; Vásquez, Disp. 39; Pedro de Lorca, Disp. 84; and others.

units.la: Argumentum quartum. Verae propriaeque filiationis non possunt esse plures causae; sed una sola, scilicet generatio: quemadmodum assimilatae, adoptio. Plura possunt esse seu argumenta seu documenta, per quae quis demonstratur filius esse; sed per quam fit, non nisi una. Nam non hic quaerimus, quibus rationibus, quis fuisse dicatur filius, sed fit. Illae sint variae, haec ex ipsa rei natura non potest esse nisi unica. Adeo quidem, ut plurimis visum, in Christo, quamvis duas habeat naturas, & sic duas generationes, uti dicunt, passivas, tamen unam esse realem filiationem. Ita Thomas, Quodlibet. I. art. II. & quodlib. IX. art. IV. ubi ex professo de hoc disputat. Quem plurimi Theologi sequuntur.
units.tr: Fourth argument. A true and proper sonship cannot have several causes, but only one, namely generation; just as an assimilated sonship has adoption. There may be several arguments or proofs by which someone is shown to be a son, but there is only one through which he is made a son. For we are not here asking by what reasons someone is said to be a son, but how he is one. The former are various; the latter, from the very nature of the thing, can only be single. So much so that it has seemed to most, that in Christ, although he has two natures, and so two generations, which they call passive, there is nevertheless one real sonship. So Thomas, Quodlibet I art. 2 and Quodlibet IX art. 4, where he disputes this expressly, and whom very many theologians follow.

units.la: Nam quamvis in persona Christi, respectu duarum naturarum, fit duplex generatio, atque ex hac duae naturae; quia tamen filiatio non in natura videtur terminari, sed suppositio, quod hic unum, ideo unam etiam defendunt filiationem, quemadmodum Filium unicum, cui Filium Mariae dici accedat ut relatio rationis, sicuti relationes quae de Deo dicuntur ad creaturas, quamvis ex ad Deum relatae reales sint, quomodo etiam naturae Christi humanae generatio ad matrem realis est, sed quae juxta Thomam, non habeat rationem veram filiationis. Nam hoc ille quidem nititur fundamento, quod filiatio non posset aliud habere subjectum, quam suppositum. Verum id si negetur, quemadmodum negant Scotus, Durandus, & alii, dicentes filiationem non fundari in suppositio, sed in sola natura, & ejus generatione, seu in productione alicujus naturaliter similis productio, misso necessario ad suppositum respectu, tum relatio realis filiationis plurificabitur juxta numerum merum generationis, & quia haec duplex, totuplex quoque erit filiatio. Adfert certe hunc in finem acutas rationes Johannes de Rada, Controverf. Theolog. inter Thomam ac Scotum, Part. III. Controv. VI. art. III. quibus duas in Christo astruat reales filiationes, unam aeternam divinae naturae, qua refertur ad Patrem: alteram temporalem humanae, qua ad matrem. De qua quidquid sit controversia, & filiatione sive una, sive duabus, filiationis in Christo divinae non aliam quam unam causam, unamque relationem ponunt. Id est, unius filiationis, causam unicam. Et filiationis divinae, non aliam, quam divinam & aeternam generationem. Unde, quomodo argumentantur, quod filiatione aeterna Christus non refertur ad matrem, sed per aliam, quae in tempore ei accedit; ita nos nunc, quod per id, quod Christo in tempore advenit sive naturae sive potestatis, nequit acquirere relationem filiationis divinae, & hinc dici Filius Dei. Non quod Scholasticorum agamus authoritate, sed rationibus & argumentis: quae vel huc faciunt, ut unam modo in Christo filiationem realem ponant, nempe divinam personae, vel si duas reales, alteram divinae filiationis, ad Patrem; & alteram humanae, ad Matrem, tamen divinam filiationem modo unam statuunt, & unam ejus causam, nempe generationem aeternam. Dictante hoc satis ipsa rei natura, quod unius filiationis queat esse modo unica causa. Et quamvis illorum quidam duas dicant filiationes, nulli tamen duos filios. Hoc enim utrimque cavent. Nempe, uti Durandus distinguit in III. Dist. VIII. qu. 2. non sequitur, habet duas filiationes, ergo sunt duo filii, quia secundum ipsum, filiatio dupliciter accipitur, vel pro relatione tantum; vel non solum pro relatione, at quoque proprietate personali. Priori modo concedit in Christo duas esse filiationes reales, & praeter filiationem, qua refertur ad Patrem, esse aliam, qua ad matrem referatur, quae sit aeque realis, ac quaelibet alia in creaturis filiatio: Verum quod si accipiatur filiatio, non solum pro relatione, sed quoque proprietate personali, tum negat in Christo posse esse filiationem, nisi unam. Rada distinguit, quod tamen eodem redit, inter filiationis formam, & suppositum, tum abstractum, & concretum. Quare sequi negat, a plurificatione filiationum, plurificatio filiorum, quia, inquit, concreta non plurificantur, nisi plurificentur tam forma, quam suppositum. Sola autem plurificatio formae non sufficit. Quemadmodum Christus non est plures volentes, licet habeat plures volitiones, nec habens plures scientias, ob id est plures scientes. Unde neque consequentia valet a plurificatione abstracti ad plurificationem concreti. Unus ergo, juxta omnes, Christus Dei filius; & unica ejus, ut Dei Filii, filiatio; propter unam ejus causam, nempe aeternam a Patre generationem, ad quam uti nihil addi potest ex temporali nativitate, seu donis, ita praeter eam filiationis verae causam aliunde alias petere, a re, uti quod maxime, est alienum.
units.tr: For although in the person of Christ, with respect to his two natures, there is a twofold generation, and from this two natures, yet because sonship does not seem to terminate in the nature but in the supposit, which here is one, they therefore also defend one sonship, just as one only Son. To this is added, as a relation of reason, the Son of Mary, just as the relations which are said of God with respect to creatures, although they are real relations from the side of the creature, not from God. In the same way the generation of Christ's human nature with respect to the mother is real, but according to Thomas it does not have the true character of sonship. For he indeed rests on this foundation, that sonship cannot have any subject other than a supposit. But if this is denied, as Scotus, Durandus and others deny, saying that sonship is grounded not in the supposit but in nature alone, and in its generation, or in the production of something naturally similar, apart from any necessary respect to the supposit, then the real relation of sonship will be multiplied according to the mere number of generations, and since this is twofold, the sonship will also be twofold. John de Rada certainly brings sharp arguments to this end, in his Controversies of Theology between Thomas and Scotus, Part III, Controversy VI, art. 3, by which he maintains two real sonships in Christ: one eternal, belonging to the divine nature, by which he is related to the Father; the other temporal, belonging to the human nature, by which he is related to the mother. Whatever be the controversy about this, and whether the sonship is one or two, they posit for the divine sonship in Christ no other cause and no other relation than one. That is, a single cause of one sonship, and for divine sonship no other than the divine and eternal generation. Hence, just as they argue that Christ is not related to the mother by his eternal sonship but by another which comes to him in time, so we now argue that by what comes to Christ in time, whether of nature or of power, he cannot acquire the relation of divine sonship and hence be called Son of God. Not that we proceed on the authority of the Schoolmen, but on reasons and arguments; which either serve to make them posit only one real sonship in Christ, namely the divine sonship of the person, or, if they posit two real ones, one of divine sonship with respect to the Father, and another of human sonship with respect to the Mother, yet they establish only one divine sonship and one cause of it, namely eternal generation. The very nature of the thing dictates this sufficiently: that a single sonship can have only one cause. And although some of them speak of two sonships, none speak of two sons; for they are careful on both sides about this. Indeed, as Durandus distinguishes in III Dist. VIII q. 2: it does not follow that he has two sonships, therefore there are two sons, because according to him sonship is taken in two ways: either for relation only, or not only for relation but also for personal property. In the former sense he concedes that there are two real sonships in Christ, and besides the sonship by which he is related to the Father there is another by which he is related to the mother, which is equally real as any other sonship in creatures. But if sonship is taken not only for relation but also for personal property, then he denies that there can be more than one sonship in Christ. Rada distinguishes, which nevertheless comes to the same thing, between the form of sonship and the supposit, and between the abstract and the concrete. Hence he denies that from a multiplication of sonships follows a multiplication of sons, because, he says, concretes are not multiplied unless both the form and the supposit are multiplied; but the multiplication of the form alone does not suffice. Just as Christ is not several willers, although he has several volitions, nor, having several knowledges, is he on that account several knowers. Hence the inference from a multiplication of the abstract to a multiplication of the concrete does not hold. Therefore, according to all, Christ is one Son of God; and his sonship, as Son of God, is one, on account of its one cause, namely the eternal generation from the Father, to which nothing can be added from temporal birth or from gifts; and so, apart from that, to seek the true cause of sonship elsewhere, from a thing which is most of all foreign to it, is absurd.

units.la: Francifcus Junius, in Determinatione &c. Quaestionum MSS. qu. XCI. concedit duas in Christo filiationes, quamvis unica sit persona: atqui duas relationes negat facere totidem supposita [?], tantum diversos suppositi modos. Respectu divinae naturae, inquit, Dei filius; respectu humanae, filius virginis. Relatio non tantum notat suppositum, sed duos etiam modos suppositi, Relatio non statuit subsistentiam, sed est in subsistentia. Filiatio non notat, sed connotat. Matthias Martinius libellum conscripsit, de duabus Christi nativitatibus, & unica filiatione, statuens, filiationem terminari in persona. Similiter Amesius, Medull. Theol. lib. I. cap. XXI. Neque idcirco duae sunt in Christo filiationes realiter distinctae, vel duo filii conjuncti. Temporalis enim illa filiatio, qua refertur ad Matrem, fuit respectus rationis tantum. Natura quidem in Christo humana realem relationem habuit ad Mariâ, ut ad causam. Filiatio autem nullo modo convenit naturæ, sed personæ soli. Differentia ista facile componi potest, prout Filiatio ad personam tantũ putatur referenda, aut non. Id est, quum quinque hic occurrant notiones, naturæ, generationis, filiationis, Filii, & personæ: naturæ in Christo duæ sunt, etiam duplex generatio, æterna & temporalis, altera qua ad Deum, altera qua refertur ad Matrem, prout aut Deus, aut homo est; & similiter de duabus postremis notionibus constat, esse in Christo non nisi unum Filium, & personam unam; de Filiatione, uti in medio posita totus videtur dissensus, prout aut ad generationem refertur, quæ hic duplex, vel ad Filium, qui est unicus. Ergo ut filiatio duntaxat generationem essentiæ dicit, concedunt duas filiationes, si modum suppositalitatis, seu personæ Filii, unica est Filiatio, uti persona Filii una. In generatione licet distinguere subjectum, & terminum: illud substantia est, hoc substantia & persona. Qua ratione commodius dicitur, duas hic quidem esse generationes, pro duplici substantiâ; unam vero filiationem: quia non duo filii, vel personæ aut substantiæ, aut generatio duplex sortita diplicem terminum, sed duæ in una persona naturæ, & solius Filii personæ, cui in tempore accessit relatio, non persona humanitatis, quodque dictus etiam filius hominis, in eodem suppositò, ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ[?] ὑποστάσει[?], inquit Damascenus. Augustinus, in Enchiridio, cap. xxxiv. Unus Dei Filius, idemque hominis Filius, unus hominis Filius, idemque Dei Filius, non duo Filii Dei, Deus & homo, sed unus Dei Filius, Deus sine initio, homo a certo initio, Dominus noster Jesus Christus.
units.tr: Francis Junius, in his Determinatio of the unpublished Quaestiones, question 91, grants that there are two sonships in Christ, although there is only one person. Yet he denies that the two relations make two supposits, and says they are only different modes of the one supposit. With respect to the divine nature, he says, He is the Son of God; with respect to the human nature, the son of the Virgin. A relation does not merely denote the supposit but also two modes of the supposit. A relation does not establish subsistence but exists in subsistence. Sonship does not denote but connotes. Matthias Martinius wrote a little book, On the two nativities of Christ and the one sonship, holding that sonship terminates in the person. Amesius likewise, Medulla Theologiae, book 1, chapter 21. Yet there are not on that account two sonships in Christ really distinct, or two conjoined sons. For that temporal sonship, by which he is related to his Mother, was a relation of reason only. The human nature of Christ did indeed have a real relation to Mary, as to a cause. But sonship belongs in no way to the nature, only to the person. This difference can easily be reconciled, depending on whether sonship is thought to be referred to the person alone or not. That is, since five notions occur here, nature, generation, sonship, Son, and person: there are two natures in Christ, and also a twofold generation, eternal and temporal, the one by which he is related to God, the other by which he is related to his Mother, according as he is God or man. Likewise it is agreed concerning the last two notions that there is in Christ only one Son and one person. Concerning sonship, which stands in the middle, the whole disagreement seems to lie in whether it is referred to generation, which here is twofold, or to the Son, who is unique. Therefore, if sonship signifies only the generation of the essence, they concede two sonships. If it signifies the mode of supposit or person of the Son, the sonship is one, just as the person of the Son is one. In generation one may distinguish the subject and the term: the subject is the substance, the term is substance and person. For this reason it is more fitting to say that there are indeed two generations here, corresponding to the twofold substance, but one sonship: not because there are two sons or persons, or because the substance or the generation, having a twofold term, has a twofold term, but because there are two natures in one person, the person of the Son alone, to whom in time a relation was added, not the person of the humanity. And for this reason he is also called the Son of man in the same supposit [ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ ὑποστάσει], says Damascene. Augustine, in the Enchiridion, chapter 34: One Son of God, and also the same Son of man; one Son of man, and also the same Son of God; not two Sons of God, God and man, but one Son of God, God without beginning, man from a certain beginning, our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Arg. quintum. Uti filiationis divinæ in Christo modo una causa, non plures, in specie eâ nequeunt esse, quas Sociniani, & Remonstrantes proferunt, nempe Christi miraculosa ex Virgine conceptio, missio ab obeundum munus, resuscitatio ex mortuis, & regnum. 1. Quia Scriptura, quando Christum Filium Dei dicit, sedulo restringit & distinguit, secundum Deum, & hominem; secundum Spiritum, & carnem: illa adeo sejungens, ut non juxta aliquid quod carnis vel humanæ naturæ fit, Filius Dei dici debeat. Huc enim facit sollicita ista distinguendi ratio in Scripturis observata. II. Significat quoque, per illa declaratum & demonstratum fuisse Deum, Deique Filium. Jam diversa sunt, declarari, & fieri: imo quod declaratur, eo non fit, sed esse demonstratur. Utrumque evidens satis est illo, quem Adversarii hic quidem, sed frustra adferunt, loco. Rom. 1. 3. 4. De Filio (qui factus est ex semine Davidis quoad carnem: & ὁρισθέντος (Castellio, definito. Racovienśis versio, der bestimmt ist. Episcopius, qui constitutus est.) Filii Dei in potentia, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, per resurrectionem ex mortuis) Jesu Christi Domini nostri. Primo hujus loci membro distinctio ponitur; altero, Filii Dei declaratio. De Filio ejus, non facto, non ex semine Davidis, sed interposita divisionis notâ, tum addita restringente particulâ, quod ex semine Davidis, quod natus, secundum carnem est; at Dei Filius non secundum hæc. Jam per resurrectionem ex mortuis definitus, constitutus Filius Dei. at quomodo? an ut fieret hinc Dei Filius? non dices, nam etiam ante jam Filium Dei fecisti. Sed ut ostenderetur, declararetur, poteti hoc documento, Filius Dei esse. Sic Chrysostomus exponit, sic Theophylactus, qui & ὁρισθέντος[?], [illegible, ~12 letters], κρατοῦντος[?], [illegible, ~25 letters]. Nam cuncti definierunt, judicaruntque ipsum esse Filium Dei. Undenam? in virtute, hoc est ex potentia & efficacia signorum, quæ faciebat. Præterea, secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, hoc est, ex Spiritu per quem sanctificabat credentes. Dei enim est donare talia. Quin etiam, ex resurrectione mortuorum: nam primus ille & solus seipse excitavit. Itaque ex resurrectione definitus est ac declaratus filius Dei. Magnum enim & hoc est, perinde atque ipse ait: cum exaltaveritis me a terra, tum cognoscetis quod ego sum. Joann. viii. 28. ὁρίζει [?] ἐστι, declarare & ostendere. Quemadmodum Psalm. ii. 7. Decretum enarraturus sum, &c. Ita & Tertullianus Rom. i. vertit, declaratum. Vide Bezam, in suis Notis. Atque ita respondemus ad pleraque ab Adversariis adducta in hoc negotio Scripturae loca, agi iis de Filio Dei declarato, non primum facto.
units.tr: Argument the fifth. Just as there can be only one cause of the divine sonship in Christ, not several, so in kind there cannot be those which the Socinians and the Remonstrants put forward: namely, Christ's miraculous conception from the Virgin, his sending to undertake his office, his resurrection from the dead, and his kingdom. First, because Scripture, when it calls Christ the Son of God, carefully qualifies and distinguishes, according to God and man, according to the Spirit and the flesh, separating these so strictly that he ought not to be called the Son of God in respect of anything that belongs to the flesh or the human nature. For this careful manner of distinguishing observed in the Scriptures serves exactly this purpose. Second, it also signifies that he was declared and demonstrated to be God and the Son of God by those things. Now to be declared and to be made are different. Indeed what is declared is not made by that, but is shown to be. Both are clear enough from the passage which the adversaries here cite, but in vain: Romans 1:3–4, Concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and who was [ὁρισθέντος] (Castellio: defined; the Racovian version: who is appointed; Episcopius: who was constituted) the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord. In the first member of this passage a distinction is made; in the second, a declaration of the Son of God. Concerning his Son, not as made, not as of the seed of David, but with a mark of division inserted, and then the restrictive particle added: who was made of the seed of David, that is, born according to the flesh; but the Son of God not according to these things. Now he is defined and constituted the Son of God by the resurrection from the dead. But how? Was he thereby made the Son of God? You will not say so, for you had already made him the Son of God before. But it was so that by this proof it might be shown and declared that he is the Son of God. So Chrysostom explains it, so Theophylact, who [...]. For all defined and judged him to be the Son of God. Whence? In power, that is, from the might and efficacy of the signs which he performed. Besides, according to the Spirit of sanctification, that is, from the Spirit through whom he sanctified believers. For it is God's prerogative to give such things. Moreover, from the resurrection of the dead: for he alone raised himself, the first and only one to do so. Thus he was defined and declared the Son of God by the resurrection. For this too is a great thing, just as he himself says: When you have lifted up the Son of man, then you will know that I am (John 8:28). ὁρίζειν means to declare and to show, as in Psalm 2:7, I will declare the decree, etc. So Tertullian also translated Romans 1 as declared.
