See Beza in his notes. And thus we answer that most of the passages of Scripture cited by the adversaries in this matter speak of the Son of God as declared, not as first made.

units.la: Argumenta autem contra sententiam & fidem nostram, ut ostendat Socinus, Christum non posse dici Dei Filium, per essentiam, atq;ab aeterno a Patre genitum, haec sunt: primum, quod pugnet cum Dei singularissima unitate.
units.tr: The arguments against our opinion and faith, by which Socinus seeks to show that Christ cannot be called the Son of God by essence, begotten from eternity by the Father, are these. First, that it conflicts with the most singular unity of God.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 394. Primum sumptum est ab unitate & summa Dei perfectione, quae periret, si Deus ex essentia seu essentia sibi similem generaret. Si Deus, inquit Socinus, sibi omnino similem generat, non est ipse natura sua & necessario singularissimus, & sic neque summe perfectus, cum summe perfectus esse nequeat, nisi unus tantum. Quid hac ratione est evidentius?
units.tr: Schlichting, p. 394: The first is taken from the unity and the supreme perfection of God, which would perish if God generated from his essence a being like himself. If God, says Socinus, generates one wholly like himself, he is not by his own nature necessarily most singular, and so not most perfect either, since he cannot be most perfect unless he is only one. What could be more evident than this argument?

units.la: Resp. 1. Negatur majoris consequentia, quod si Pater Deus generat Filium, Deus non sit natura sua & necessario singularissimus, & sic neque summe perfectus. Quod additur, cum summe perfectus esse nequeat, nisi unus tantum, ad minorem pertinet, quae non negatur, haud ad majorem. Quid nunc illa Socini ratione invidentius, vel infirmius? 11. Pater Filium generat non similem sibi, sed essentia eundem, generat non ὁμοιούσιον sed ὁμοούσιον, quod cum credere nos haud ignoret Socinus, frustra argumentum format ex Filio simili Deo, & non eodem. Jam reformet argumentum, uti profecto debet, ne velit peccare elencho, & dicat: Si Deus Pater generans Filium, generat eum qui secum essentia unus idemque fit, ergo non est ipse natura sua & necessario singularissimus? negatur. III. Deus Pater non generat ex essentia, vel fecunditate essentiae suae, uti alii loquuntur, quasi Filius sit essentiatus, vel essentia generet essentiam; sed persona personam, Pater Filium generat, qua generatione communicatur Filio eadem Patris essentia. Nam essentia idem sunt. Joann. v. 3. 1 Joann. v. 7. personis distincti: alius, & alius; non aliud & aliud; distincta personarum nomina ὑπόστασις, non distinctae res.
units.tr: Reply: first, the consequence of the major premise is denied, namely that if God the Father generates a Son, God is not by his own nature necessarily most singular, and so not most perfect. What is added, since he cannot be most perfect unless he is only one, pertains to the minor premise, which is not denied, but not to the major. What, then, could be more unfair or weaker than this argument of Socinus? Second, the Father begets a Son not like himself but the same in essence; he begets not homoiousion but homoousion. Since Socinus is not unaware that we believe this, he vainly frames an argument from a Son like God and not the same. Now let him reframe the argument, as he certainly ought, lest he wish to sin against the rules of refutation, and let him say: If God the Father, generating a Son, generates one who becomes one and the same in essence with himself, therefore he is not by his own nature necessarily most singular? This is denied. Third, God the Father does not generate from the essence, or the fecundity of his essence, as others speak, as if the Son were "essenced," or the essence generated the essence; but the person generates the person. The Father begets the Son, and by this generation the same essence of the Father is communicated to the Son. For the essences are the same. John 5:3; 1 John 5:7. The persons are distinct: one and another, not one thing and another thing. The names of the distinct persons are hypostases, not distinct things.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 400. Si persona significet personam, una essentia unam essentiam, implicatur contradictio: cum unius numero essentiae plures statuuntur personae, & plurium personarum una numero essentia.
units.tr: Schlichtingius, p. 400. If 'persona' signifies a person and 'una essentia' one essence, a contradiction is implied: since several persons are posited in one numerically single essence, and one numerically single essence of several persons.

units.la: Resp. Hoc autem debebat ostendere, contradictione implicari; non asserere: quare dico, imo persona significat personam, una essentia unam essentiam, & unius numero essentiae plures statuuntur personae, & plurium personarum una numero essentia, neq;tamen ulla contradictio.
units.tr: Reply: But he ought to have shown that a contradiction is implied, not merely asserted it. So I say: yes indeed, 'persona' signifies a person, and one essence signifies one essence, and several persons are posited in a numerically single essence, and one numerically single essence of several persons, and yet there is no contradiction.

units.la: Pergit: Vel essentiam Filii generat Pater, vel tantum personam. Si tantum personam, cur dicitur ex essentia generare, essentiam communicare? Num ergo quidpiam aliud ex essentia generat Pater quam essentiam?, & essentiam communicando, non communicat essentiam? Adde quod persona, sive Patris, sive Filii, ipsius sit essentia. Nemo enim extra
units.tr: He goes on: Either the Father generates the essence of the Son, or only the person. If only the person, why is it said that he generates from the essence, that he communicates the essence? Does the Father, then, generate anything else from the essence than the essence? And by communicating the essence, does he not communicate the essence? Add that the person, whether of the Father or of the Son, is itself the essence. For nothing exists outside

units.la: Resp. 1. Pater generat personam. Neque in essentia Patris, aut Filii, alia est generans, alia generata, sed persona: generatio, uti a persona oritur, sic in ea terminatur, non proprie in essentia. Non ergo ex essentia Deitatis generat Pater, nedum essentiam aliam. Quamvis generatione communicetur essentia Filio; uti prosuam essentiam quidquam est. Itaque persona sive Patris, sive Filii, vel nihil est, vel ipsa Patris & Filii essentia est. Quod si tamen aliquid aliud est quam essentia, vel suam habet peculiarem essentiam, vel non habet. Si non habet, nihil est: quod enim essentiam non habet, non est. Si habet, cum tres sint distinctae in Deo personae, tres erunt distinctae essentiae, eaeque tales, quarum una alteram generat seu produ-cit. At hoc ipsum pugnat cum unitate, & summa Dei perfectione. Plures enim nihilo-minus una erunt illius unius Dei naturae & es-sentiae, eaeque tales, quae ipsas personas consti-tuant. Si vero essentiam Filii generat, suam generat: eandem enim numero cum Filio ha-bet. Num vero quispiam suam ipsius essen-tiam generare potest, & se ipso prior esse? Ad-de, quod hac ratione non sibi similem, sed eun-dem numero secum Deus gigneret. tia, cum illo singulari subsistendi modo. processione, Spiritui sancto. Verum no-strum haud est modum & rationem generationis indagare, aut exponere non solum inexplicabilem, sed imperceptibilem. Nempe qui adeo haeremus in generatione nostra explicanda, & tot tan-tosque ibi recessus & nodos experimur, quid miseri homunciones in divinitatis ardua nos ingerimus, & generatione Filii, qui uti ipse פלא[?] admirabilis, Iesa. ix. 6. ita quoque ejus generatio, enarrandā nos fati-gabimus? sufficit τὸ ὅτι[?] credere, quod Pater Filium genuit, unde aut quomodo, edisserere nostrum haud est. ii. Persona, sive Patris, sive Filii, ipsius est essentia: formaliter essentia Deitatis? nego. Neque tamen est extra suam essentiam. Neque persona est essentia, vel nihil. Sed personalitas, est modus: persona, essen-tia, cum illo singulari subsistendi modo. Confundit Adversarius personalitatem, cum persona: essentiam, cum modo essentiae: essentiam, & rei quiditatem. Perso-nalitas est quidem quid aliud quam Deitatis essentia, sed non habet aliam essentiam: nam & de hac iterum quaeri posset, an aliam haberet, & sic porro: sed quid proprie Dei persona sit, uti personalitas, perfecte a nobis explicari haud potest: id dicere licet, quod non est formaliter ipsa Dei essentia, neque etiam essentia alia. Jam vero exponant Adversarii, quid sit persona, quid personalitas Patris, unam etenim perso-nam Patris esse semper clamitant. Quippe personalitas differt ab essentia, neque valet argumentatio, vel suam habet peculiarem essentiam, vel non habet. Si non ha-bet, nihil est: quod enim essentiam non habet, non est. Si habet, erunt distinctae essentiae. iii. Negamus enim, quod id quod essentia non habet, non fit, essentiae voce stricte accepta, uti modo opponitur, qui nec nihil est nec proprie ens, sed medium ali-quod, seu entis essentiae affectio, meliusque dici potest quid non fit, quam quid imo. Quare non sunt tres in Deo distinctae essentiae, quamvis tres personae, tribus subsisten-di modis distinctae, sed unius omnino essentiae, non plures unius Dei naturae & es-sentiae, quae ipsas personas constituant. Neque Pater essentiam Filii generat, quam eandem cum Filio habet. Sed, quod in fine dixit Adversarius, non Pater sibi simi-lem, sed eundem numero secum, personam vid. genuit.
units.tr: Resp. 1. The Father generates the person. In the essence of the Father or of the Son there is not one thing that generates and another that is generated; there is a person. Generation, as it arises from the person, so it terminates in the person, not properly in the essence. Therefore the Father does not generate from the essence of the Deity, much less another essence. Although the essence is communicated to the Son by generation, just as something has its own essence. So the person, whether of the Father or of the Son, either is nothing or is itself the essence of the Father and of the Son. But if the person is something other than the essence, it either has its own peculiar essence or it does not. If it does not, it is nothing, for what does not have an essence is not. If it does, then since there are three distinct persons in God, there will be three distinct essences, and of such a kind that one generates or produces the other. But this itself clashes with the unity and the supreme perfection of God. For there would nevertheless be several essences of that one nature and essence of God, and these would be such as to constitute the persons themselves. But if the Father generates the essence of the Son, he generates his own, for he has the same essence as the Son, numerically the same. Can anyone generate his own essence and be prior to himself? Add that in this way God would beget not one like himself, but one numerically the same as himself. Procession belongs to the Holy Spirit. But it is not for us to inquire into or set out the manner and reason of generation, which is not only inexplicable but imperceptible. Indeed, since we get stuck so hard in explaining our own generation, and experience so many and such great recesses and knots there, why do we wretched little men thrust ourselves into the lofty matters of the Godhead, and labour to recount the generation of the Son, who, as he himself is wonderful [פלא], Isaiah 9:6, so also his generation is wonderful? It is enough to believe [τὸ ὅτι] that the Father begot the Son; how or in what manner, it is not for us to explain. ii. The person, whether of the Father or of the Son, is the essence itself: formally the essence of the Deity? I deny it. Nor is it outside its essence. The person is neither the essence nor nothing. But personality is a mode: the person is the essence with that singular mode of subsisting. The Adversary confuses personality with the person, the essence with the mode of the essence, and the essence with the quiddity of the thing. Personality is indeed something other than the essence of the Deity, but it does not have another essence; for one could ask again about this too whether it had another, and so on indefinitely. But what the person of God properly is, as personality, cannot be perfectly explained by us; we may say this much, that it is not formally the very essence of God, nor yet another essence. Now let the Adversaries set out what the person is, and what the personality of the Father is, for they constantly cry out that there is one person of the Father. Personality indeed differs from essence, and the argument, "either it has its own peculiar essence or it does not," does not hold. If it does not have one, it is nothing, for what does not have an essence is not. If it does, there will be distinct essences. iii. For we deny that what does not have an essence is not, taking the word essence strictly, as it is here opposed; such a thing is neither nothing nor properly a being, but some middle thing, an affection of the being of the essence, and it can better be said what it is not than what it is. Hence there are not three distinct essences in God, although there are three persons, distinguished by three modes of subsisting, but there is altogether one essence, not several essences of the one nature of God constituting the persons themselves. Nor does the Father generate the essence of the Son, which he has in common with the Son. But what the Adversary said at the end, that the Father begot not one like himself but one numerically the same as himself, namely the person, is beside the point.

units.la: Alterum argumentum Socinus petit a Dei aeternitate & perpetuitate, cui adversa-ri putat Christum esse Filium Dei, ab aeterno a Patre genitum.
units.tr: The second argument Socinus draws from the eternity and perpetuity of God, against which he thinks that Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father from eternity, is opposed.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 403. Quid, inquit Socinus, cum incommutabili aeternitate ac perpetuitate alicujus excellentissimi individui, cujusmodi Deus est, magis pugnare potest, quam sibi simile gignere, cum sui similis generationem propterea in natura inveniri constet, ut geni-
units.tr: Schlichtingius, p. 403. What,' says Socinus, 'can conflict more with the unchangeable eternity and perpetuity of any most excellent individual, such as God is, than to beget one like himself, since the generation of a like thing is found in nature for this reason, that the begotten

units.la: Resp. Fiat argumentum: Deus incom-mutabiliter aeternus ac perpetuus non potest sibi simile generare: Pater est Deus incommutabiliter aeternus ac perpetuus: ergo. Negatur major. Probat: Quod propterea in natura invenitur, ut genitum tum in generantis locum quodammodo succedat, id est, hoc intereunte, illud remaneat, & sic subinde perpetuo fiat, quo rerum genera conserventur?
units.tr: Reply. Let the argument be set out: God, unchangeably eternal and perpetual, cannot beget one like himself; the Father is God, unchangeably eternal and perpetual; therefore. The major is denied. He proves it: since the begotten succeeds in some way into the place of the begetter, that is, while the one perishes the other remains, and so continually, from time to time, so that the kinds of things may be preserved?

units.la: in generantis locum quodammodo succedat, &c. id cum incommutabili aeternitate ac perpetuitate Dei pugnat: sed gene-ratio propterea in natura inveniri constat, ut illud fiat: ergo. Respondeo, fieri μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος [?], à Deo ad naturam, à divina & spirituali generatione ad temporalem & corporariam, ab incommutabili aeternitate, ad successionem quae fit in tempore, quasi hinc divina aestimanda essent, & Deus ab inferioribus acciperet regulam ac modum: Cum sui similis generationem propterea in natura inveniri constet. Non probandum fuerat, quid in natura inveniatur, sed quid in Deo locum habere possit, quod ex natura petendum non est. Vel hoc ipso indicio, quod in natura est sui similis generatio, in Deo ejus qui ejusdem, & non similis duntaxat cum generante fit essentiae. Negatur etiam quod finis generationis per se fit, ut genitum succedat quodammodo in locum generantis, quod locum non habet nisi interventu mortis: at finis generationis per se est sola individui multiplicatio, פרו ורבו [?] dicunt Hebraei, ex Genef. 1.28. Generare quidem Deo competit, sed non ad istum modum, quo naturalibus & pereuntibus: uti videre, audire, & reliqua, quae de Deo & creaturis aequivoce dicuntur, non univoce.
units.tr: succeeds in some way into the place of the begetter, etc. This conflicts with the unchangeable eternity and perpetuity of God; but generation is found in nature for this reason, that this should happen; therefore. I answer: there is a passing over into another genus [μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος], from God to nature, from divine and spiritual generation to temporal and corporeal, from unchangeable eternity to succession, which happens in time, as if divine things were to be measured by lower things, and God were to take his rule and measure from inferiors. Since the generation of a like thing is found in nature for this reason. It was not to be proved what is found in nature, but what can have a place in God, which is not to be sought from nature. Indeed, by this very sign, that in nature there is generation of a like thing, in God there is generation of one of the same essence, not merely similar to the begetter. It is also denied that the end of generation comes about of itself, so that the begotten succeeds in some way into the place of the begetter, which has no place except by the intervention of death; but the end of generation is of itself only the multiplication of the individual, be fruitful and multiply [פרו ורבו], as the Hebrews say, from Genesis 1:28. To beget indeed befits God, but not in that manner by which natural and perishable things do; just as seeing, hearing, and the rest, which are said of God and of creatures equivocally, not univocally.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag.407. Deinde tanto magis verum erit, aeternum a parte ante non generare sibi essentia similem, quomodo enim ejusdem essentiae esse potest id quod non semper fuit, cum eo quod semper fuit? at generari aliquid, & semper fuisse, implicat contradictionem. Omnis enim generatio progreditur a non ente ad ens, quod qui negat, generationem esse genera-tionem negare simul debebat.
units.tr: Schlichtingius, p. 407. Further, it will be all the more true that the eternal, from the beginning, does not beget one of like essence to himself: for how can that which did not always exist be of the same essence as that which always existed? But for something to be begotten and to have always existed involves a contradiction. For every generation proceeds from non-being to being, and whoever denies this must at the same time deny that there is generation.

units.la: Resp. Id quod non semper fuit. Dixi-mus, non generatam essentiam: & deinde huic divinae generationi temporis articu-li vel momenta, praeteriti, praesentis, aut futuri accommodari non debent. Nam uti supra rerum creatarum, ita & tempo-ris feriem est. Cui proinde non debet praescribi simile quod in rebus est, aut in temporum apud nos periodis. Essentia ergo Filii Dei non minus semper fuit, ac Patris, quum sit eadem. Generari & semper fuisse, in naturalibus, & in ordine temporis, sunt contraria: sed hactenus divinae generationi applicari non debent. Omnis generatio progreditur à non ente ad ens, scilicet, in generatione novae essentiae: & generatione temporaria. Haec vero in Deo, aut generatione Filii locum minime habent.
units.tr: Reply. That which did not always exist. We have said the essence was not begotten; and then, moments or points of time, past, present or future, ought not to be fitted to this divine generation. For, just as of created things, so also of time there is a series, to which therefore what is found in things, or in the periods of time among us, ought not to be prescribed. Therefore the essence of the Son of God has been no less always, as that of the Father, since it is the same. To be begotten and always to have existed are contraries in natural things and in the order of time; but so far they ought not to be applied to divine generation. Every generation proceeds from non-being to being, namely, in the generation of a new essence, and in temporal generation. But these have no place in God, or in the generation of the Son.

units.la: Schlichtingius, Pergit, nempe Meisne-rus: quâ Pater aeternus, inquit, Filium coaeternum ineffabili modo producit. Producit? igitur nondum produxit. Nondum igitur nec Pater est, nec Filius; imo nec unquam aut Pater erit aut Filius. Pater aeternus, Filium coaeternum? at si Filius est, Patri coaeternus esse non potest. Si enim filius est, productus est: at qui productus est, non semper fuit, cum omnis productio fit a non ente ad ens: qui vero non semper fuit, ei qui semper fuit, coaeternus esse non potest.
units.tr: Schlichtingius goes on, namely Meisnerus: by which the eternal Father, he says, produces the coeternal Son in an ineffable manner. Produces? Then he has not yet produced. Then neither is there yet a Father nor a Son; indeed neither will there ever be a Father or a Son. The eternal Father, a coeternal Son? But if he is a Son, he cannot be coeternal with the Father. For if he is a Son, he has been produced; but whatever has been produced has not always existed, since every production goes from non-being to being; and whatever has not always existed cannot be coeternal with that which always existed.

units.la: Resp. Producit, ergo nondum produxit. Negatur. Quia temporis illae dif-ferentiae locum hic non habent, supra re-rum temporisque ordinem & quaestiones posita divina Fillii generatione. Nun-quam caepit, nunquam etiam defuit, nullis temporum cancellis inclusa filiatio. Su-pra & extra tempus est. Quare ad mo-dum & periodos praeteriti vel futuri fru-stra revocatur. Si Filius est, Patri coae-ternus esse nequit: Negatur. Qui produ-ctus est, non semper fuit: Imo proprie
units.tr: Answer: "He produces, therefore he has not yet produced." This is denied. For those distinctions of time have no place here, since the divine generation of the Son is placed above the order of things and times and above such questions. The filiation, enclosed within no bounds of time, never began and never was absent. It is above and outside time. So it is in vain that it is called back to the mode and periods of past or future. "If he is a Son, he cannot be coeternal with the Father": this is denied. "Whoever has been produced has not always existed": indeed, properly speaking,

units.la: productus, scilicet à non ente ad ens. Talis autem productio hic non est. Non productio alterius, vel novae essentiae, vel à non existente ad existens, quasi ἦν πότε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν[?]; sed in aeternitate, ubi nec prius, nec posterius, non praeteritum vel futurum, nullave mutatio, nempe in propria aeternitate, quae Dei est, generatio Filii incommutabilis, de quo nec essentiae, nec personae ratione affirmare fas est, quod non semper fuerit.
units.tr: produced, namely from non-being to being. But such a production does not occur here: it is not the production of another, or of a new essence, or from not existing to existing, as if "there was when he was not" [ἦν πότε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν]; rather, it takes place in eternity, where there is neither before nor after, neither past nor future, nor any change. In that proper eternity, which belongs to God, the generation of the Son is unchangeable, and concerning it, neither in respect of essence nor of person is it right to affirm that he has not always been.

units.la: Adversus Wiekum, aliud adhuc argumentum profert Socinus, contra aeternam Filii à Patre generationem ὁμοούσιας[?], ex absurdo, quod illinc videatur sequi, Filium sui ipsius Filium esse.
units.tr: Against Wiek, Socinus brings forward yet another argument against the eternal generation of the Son from the Father, the consubstantiality [ὁμοουσίας], from the absurdity that seems to follow from it, namely that the Son would be the son of himself.

units.la: Cap. v. pag. 244. Quinimo hoc argumentum contra ipsos retorquetur, estque unum ex potioribus ad eos falsae opinionis redarguendos, nemo enim sui ipsius Filius esse potest: quare si Christus est illius unius veri Dei Filius, nequit ullo pacto fieri, ut ipse Christus sit ille unus verus Deus.
units.tr: Chapter 5, page 244: Indeed this argument is turned back against them, and it is one of the stronger ones for refuting their false opinion. For no one can be the son of himself. Therefore if Christ is the Son of that one true God, he cannot in any way be that one true God himself.

units.la: Resp. Sed Christus non est Filius essentiae, sed personae; non Dei essentiae, sed Dei Patris. Genitus enim est, non essentiatus: ergo non essentiae suae, vel sui Filius. Est Filius unius veri Dei, vid. Patris, non divinae in Patre essentiae. Quare & ille unus verus Deus est, habens eandem divinam naturam, sibi à Patre per generationem communicatam, ac proinde & Patris Filius, & unus verus cum Patre Deus. Ego & Pater unum sumus.
units.tr: Answer: But Christ is not the Son of the essence but of the person; not of God's essence but of God the Father. For he is begotten, not essenced; therefore he is not the son of his own essence or of himself. He is the Son of the one true God, namely the Father, not of the divine essence in the Father. Hence he too is that one true God, having the same divine nature, communicated to him by the Father through generation; and therefore both the Son of the Father and one true God with the Father. I and the Father are one.

units.la: Adversarii vero causam filiationis Dei in Christo, repudiatâ aeternâ à Patre generatione, perque eam ὁμοούσιαν[?], in genere in solâ humanitate constituunt, & hominis cum Deo excellentiori aliquâ similitudine. Similitudinem autem faciunt duplicem, in persona, & personae ortu. Hoc in Christo singulare: illud ei cum aliis Dei Filiis commune, collocant in donis, sapientiae, sanctitatis, immortalitatis, atque Dominii.
units.tr: But the adversaries, rejecting the eternal generation from the Father and with it the consubstantiality, place the cause of God's sonship in Christ in general in his humanity alone, and in a certain more excellent likeness of man to God. They make the likeness twofold: in the person, and in the origin of the person. The former they place in Christ alone; the latter they place in gifts, wisdom, holiness, immortality and dominion, which he shares with the other sons of God.

units.la: Socinus, contra Wiekum, cap. v. pag. 346. Apparet igitur, necesse esse, ut, quando nullo prorsus pacto fieri potest, ut Deus ex sua substantia generet, qui ejus dicuntur filii, atque ab eo geniti, per similitudinem aliquam ita dicantur, quam cum iis habeant, qui ex substantia alicujus generantur: haec siquidem demum, proprie dicta, est tum generatio, tum filiatio: habeant, inquam, considerati respectu Dei, quemadmodum illi respectu ejus, ex quo sunt geniti. Haec autem similitudo duplex esse potest: aut, videlicet, in ipsa persona, aut in modo existendi. In ipsa persona intelligo, ut, quemadmodum ij, qui ex substantia alicujus generantur, similes sunt & substantia & qualitatibus illi, ex quo sunt geniti, sic isti Deo sint similes in iis, quae Dei sunt propria: cujusmodi sunt sapientia, sanctitas, immortalitas, dominatio, &c. In modo autem existendi intelligo, vel quia, ut existerent tales, Dei actio & operatio intervenit illius, ex cujus substantia quis fit generatus, ad hoc, ut ei similis existeret: vel
units.tr: Socinus, against Wiek, chapter 5, page 346: It appears, then, that when it is by no means possible for God to beget from his own substance, those who are called his sons and begotten by him must be so called through some likeness which they have with those who are generated from the substance of someone. For this alone, properly speaking, is both generation and filiation. They have it, I say, when considered with respect to God, just as those have it with respect to him from whom they were begotten. This likeness can be twofold: namely, either in the person itself or in the mode of existing. By "in the person itself" I mean that, just as those who are generated from the substance of someone are like, in both substance and qualities, the one from whom they were begotten, so these are like God in those things which are proper to God: such as wisdom, holiness, immortality, dominion, etc. By "in the mode of existing" I mean either that, in order that they should exist as such, the action and operation of God intervened of him from whose substance someone is generated, so that they might exist like him; or

units.la: Praesupponit frustra, Deum non generare, communicando essentiam, solummodo per similitudinem: & quod in eo tertio omnes Dei Filii conveniant, etiam Christus, quem nos eo eximimus, & singulari ab aliis ratione, non per similitudinem, sed naturam dicimus Dei esse Filium, quia proprius iste, seu proprie dictus Dei Filius: quum proprie dictam generationem, seu filiationem, in communione essentiae consistere, etiâ Adversarius fateatur. Deinde nunquam sola similitudo facit filiationem aut Filium: quidem Filii similes sunt parentibus, & se parentum filios moribus & gestibus similibus ostendunt, non tamen hinc filii fiunt, sed probantur. Et filios Dei docet illa cum Deo similitudo, sed ea filios sequitur, non demum constituit. Nam & Angelorum debemus esse, erimusque; adeo similes postmodum, ut ἰσάγγελοι[?] dicendi simus, non autem eorum propterea filii: & hovel quia ipsum suum esse, seu quod simpliciter existerint, ex tali Dei actione & operatione habeant, quae aliqua ratione actioni & operationi respondeat illius, ex cujus substantia quis[?] generatus, inde habuit, ut existeret. Hujus autem rei, quam postremo diximus, nullum revera exemplum habemus, nisi in Christo Iesu: qui, ut supra docuimus, hoc ipsum, quod exiterit, id est, conceptus & natus fuerit, ex tali Dei actione & operatione habet, quae viri gignentis actioni & operationi respondet: quod nec in angelis, nec in ulla alia re creata contigit, adeo ut, quatenus simpliciter existunt, non geniti a Deo, sed creati tantum dici possint, quicunque praeter Christum filii Dei appellantur: Christus vero, quatenus simpliciter existit, non creatus modo a Deo, sed etiam ab ipso genitus merito dicatur. Ex quo, ut dictum fuit, consequitur, ut naturalis Dei filius jure appellari queat, & quidem solus naturalis, ac propterea unigenitus: praesertim inter homines, quorum respectu potissimum unigenitus Dei filius est appellatus.
units.tr: He presupposes in vain that God does not beget by communicating his essence, only by likeness; and that all the sons of God agree in this third respect, Christ too, whom we exempt from this and, by a unique manner distinct from the others, say to be the Son of God not by likeness but by nature, because he is the proper or properly so-called Son of God. For the opponent himself concedes that proper generation, or filiation, consists in communion of essence. Next, likeness alone never makes filiation or a son. Indeed sons are like their parents, and show themselves to be sons of their parents by similar manners and gestures, yet they do not become sons by this; they are shown to be such. Likewise that likeness to God teaches us that they are sons of God, but it follows the sons; it does not constitute them as sons in the first place. For we are, and shall be, like the angels, so much so that we may afterwards be called equal to the angels [ἰσάγγελοι], yet we are not on that account their sons. Or [the second mode is] because they have their very being, that is, that they simply exist, from such an action and operation of God, which in some way corresponds to the action and operation of him from whose substance someone is generated, and from it has the power to exist. Yet we truly have no example of this last thing we have mentioned, except in Christ Jesus, who, as we taught above, has from such an action and operation of God that very thing which is to have existed, that is, to have been conceived and born, which corresponds to the action and operation of the begetting man. This happens neither in angels nor in any other created thing, so that, insofar as they simply exist, all who are called sons of God besides Christ can be said only to be created, not begotten, by God. But Christ, insofar as he simply exists, is rightly said to be not merely created by God but also begotten by him. From this, as was said, it follows that the natural Son of God can rightly be so called, and indeed he alone is natural, and therefore only-begotten; especially among men, with respect to whom the Son of God is chiefly called only-begotten.

units.la: mines aliis similes quoque, quam parenti-bus, non tamen illorum filii: ita ergo in fo-la aliqua similitudine filiatio nunquam fi-ta. Quemadmodum, inquit Socinus, qui ex substantia alicujus generantur, similes sunt & substantia & qualitatibus illi, ex quo sunt geniti. Recte, praesupponit generationem similitudini, & hanc ex illa, non vice versa colligit: similitudo, ex substantiali generatione; similitudo qualitatum, ex similitudine substantiae. Et sic, quia in Christo non similitudo cum Deo, sed paritas ἰσότης, identitas ἑνότης, talis quoque est ejus generatio vera & propria ejusdem essentiae: in aliis filiatio impropria, sive per creationem, ut Angelis, & Adamo; sive adoptionem, quomodo in fidelibus, & hinc morum illa vel qualitatum similitudo cum Deo, toto genere & forma distans a filiatione Christi. III. Quod si illud facit Filium Dei non modo, sed quoque naturalem, quod ipsum suum esse, seu
units.tr: Men are like others as well as their parents, yet they are not sons of those others; thus filiation is never established on a mere likeness. As Socinus says, those who are generated from the substance of someone are like, in both substance and qualities, the one from whom they were begotten. Rightly so: he presupposes generation before likeness, and infers the likeness from the generation, not the reverse. Likeness arises from substantial generation; likeness of qualities arises from likeness of substance. And so, because in Christ there is not likeness to God but equality [ἰσότης] and identity [ἑνότης], his generation is also true and proper, of the same essence. In others, filiation is improper, either through creation, as with the angels and Adam, or through adoption, as with believers; and the likeness of manners or qualities to God in these is, in its whole kind and form, distant from the filiation of Christ. III. But if that makes the Son of God not only but also natural, because they have their very being, that is, that they simply exist,

units.la: quod simpliciter existunt, ex tali Dei actione & operatione habent, quae aliqua ratione actioni & operationi respondet illius, ex cujus substantia quis generatus, inde habuit, ut existeret: jam non fideles, non homines tantum, sed creaturae omnes Dei filii dicendae erunt, quia omnes quod existunt, ex tali Dei actione habent, quae aliqua ratione respondet actioni generationis. Sic jam egregie Christum fecerit singularem Dei Filium, ea ratione scilicet, quae in omnes adeo cadit creaturas. Annon creatio est actio similis generationi? Et regeneratio nostra annon propterea etiam dicitur nova creatio? Et quandocunque generamur naturaliter, talis Dei actio intervenit & operatio, quae aliqua ratione actioni generationis respondeat, imo quae vim omnem naturae ad generandum conferat, & absque qua omnis alia actio aut facultas sit fruitra? IV. Explicet & probet Adversarius hoc actionis divinae quid sit in generatione Christi humana, quod viri gignentis operationi respondederit, praeterquam vis prolificandi virgini concessa, immediata operatione. Annon in creatione hominis similis aliqua ratione Dei operatio intercesserit, qua terram faecundavit, in producendo hominem, cum actione generantis? Vel, annon in regeneratione aliquid habituale in nobis creatur, principium & quasi semen novae vitae, quod conferri potest cum actione generantis? annon propterea dicimur regeniti, & ex Deo geniti; & hactenus simpliciter ut existimus tales, geniti a Deo appellamur? Quare si Christus non alia ratione Dei Filius, & naturalis erit, nos etiam & filii Dei, & naturales, propter similem rationem, dicendi erimus: non certe Christus unigenitus.
units.tr: from such an action and operation of God, which in some way corresponds to the action and operation of him from whose substance someone is generated, and from it has the power to exist: then not only believers and men but all creatures will have to be called sons of God, since all of them, insofar as they exist, have it from such an action of God, which in some way corresponds to the action of generation. Thus Christ will have been made a singular Son of God in a way that applies equally to all creatures. Is not creation a action similar to generation? And is not our regeneration for this reason also called a new creation? And whenever we are naturally generated, does not such an action and operation of God intervene, which in some way corresponds to the action of generation, indeed which confers every power of nature for generating, and without which every other action or faculty would be in vain? IV. Let the opponent explain and prove what this divine action in Christ's human generation was, which corresponded to the operation of the begetting man, apart from the power of procreation granted to the Virgin by an immediate operation. Did not some similar operation of God intervene in the creation of man, by which he made the earth fruitful in producing man, together with the action of the begetter? Or, in regeneration, is not something habitual created in us, a principle and as it were a seed of new life, which can be compared with the action of the begetter? Are we not on that account called regenerate and begotten of God, and so far as we simply exist, are we not called begotten of God? Therefore if Christ is the Son of God and natural for no other reason, we too shall have to be called sons of God and natural, for a similar reason; certainly not Christ the only-begotten.

units.la: In specie autem & primum, Christum Filium Dei factum contendunt, admirandâ sui ex Mariâ conceptione & nativitate. Quo referunt locum, Luc. 1. 35. Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi: ideoque quod ex te nascetur sanctum, vocabitur filius Dei. Hoc loco ad illud probandum, omnes utuntur, SocIniani, & Remonstrantes. Socinus, in Catechismo, Divina ista Christi filiatio, eatenus tantum ad ejus naturam aliquo modo referri potest, quatenus id respicit, quod Christus divini spiritus, sine viri ope in virginis utero conceptus & formatus fuit. nam hujusce rei causam eum Dei Filium vocatum iri ipsius Dei angelus ipsimet virgini, ex qua natus est, praedixit. Luc. 1.35. Resp. in Textu dicitur quidem vocabitur, non, fiet. iv. vocabitur sic, ex argumento probante & demonstrante illum esse Dei Filium; non efficiente. Atqui non quaeritur, an hinc Filius Dei dici potuerit debueritque, tanquam ex argumento seu signo, unde constabat eum istum esse; sed an hinc primum, vel num hinc factus sit Dei Filius. iii. Aliud est quia, aliud, qua. Christus Filius Dei appellari potuit, quia extraordinario illo modo conceptus ac natus; non formaliter qua ita natus. iv. Nempe sic praedictum fuerat, Jes. vii. 14. Ecce virgo concipet, & pariet Filium, & vocabit nomen ejus Immanuel. Ut omnino, quando jam Angelus dicit, hanc virginem concepturam & pariturum istum, addere debuerit ideo hunc vocandum habitumque meri-to iri pro Immanuele illo, Deique Filio. Matth. 1. 22. 23. Hoc vero totum factum est ut impleretur dictum a Domino per Prophetam, dicentem: ecce, virgo concipiet, & pariet Filium, & vocabunt nomen ejus Emmanuel: quod interpretatum, Deus est nobiscum. Quare Persica versio Luc. 1.35. habet: qui enim ex te nascetur, sanctus est, & Filius Dei vocabitur. Sic quoque Aethiopica, & qui nascetur a te.
units.tr: In particular, and first, they contend that Christ was made the Son of God by his wonderful conception and birth from Mary. To this they refer Luke 1:35: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born of you will be called the Son of God. All the Socinians and Remonstrants use this passage to prove the point. Socinus, in the Catechism: This divine sonship of Christ can be referred to his nature in some way only insofar as it concerns the fact that Christ was conceived and formed by the divine Spirit in the virgin's womb without the help of a man. For the angel of God himself foretold to the virgin, from whom he was born, that he would be called the Son of God for this reason. Luke 1:35. Reply: the text says will be called, not will be made. It says will be called in the sense of an argument proving and demonstrating that he is the Son of God, not one effecting it. Nor is the question whether he could and should be called the Son of God from this, as from an argument or sign by which it was evident that he was such; the question is whether he became the Son of God from this, or first from this. Iii. It is one thing to say because, and another to say in that. Christ could be called the Son of God because he was conceived and born in that extraordinary manner, not formally in that he was so born. Iv. Indeed this had been foretold in just this way, Isaiah 7:14: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. So, when the angel now says that this virgin will conceive and bear this child, he ought to have added that for this reason he will be called and will rightly be held to be that Immanuel, the Son of God. Matthew 1:22-23: Now all this came about so that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel, which means, God is with us. Hence the Persian version of Luke 1:35 has: for he who is born of you is holy, and will be called the Son of God. So too the Ethiopic: he who will be born of you.

units.la: Smiglecius, lib. de Dei filio, cap. iii. propterea Christum Dei Filium in nativitate factum exponit, quia Deus viri vices supppleverit, creata, additaque Mariae sanguini materia, ex qua natus Christus sit. Secundum illa, quae ex Socini disputatione & libro contra Wiekum mox adferemus. Nos Christum Filium Dei, secundum carnem, vel ob conceptionem & nativitatem esse dicimus, propterea quod Deus in nativitate Christi, viri vices supppleverit.----interim verum manet, generationem & hanc dici posse, quatenus in Deum ea cadere potest, si ad sanguinem Mariae addita sit ex parte Dei materia, ex qua, cum sanguine Mariae juncta, natus sit Christus. Nam si generatio Dei id dici potest, cum nihil prorsus materiae accedit, quanto magis ea generatio dici potest, cum aliquid a Deo creatur, & ad generandum aliquid adjicitur ? Jam Christus, secundum carnem non Filius Dei, sed hominis dicitur, facti ex semine Davidis quoad carnem: declarati filii Dei cum potentia, secundum spiritum sanctitatis. Rom. 1. 3. & IX. 5. Ex quibus Patribus Christus est quod ad carnem, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in saecula. Deinde Deum Patrem viri vices in Christi conceptione supplevisse, nuspiam docetur: quum contra, uti Maria nullas viri vices, ita Christus nullas Patris agnovit, ἀπάτωρ[?]. Deinde si eo fundetur divina generatio, quod ad Christi nativitatem Deus aliquid per creationem attulit, eadem ratione omnes homines poterunt dici Dei Filii naturales, quia in eorum generatione Deus, ad ipsorum formandam essentiam, animam creat & introducit. Et sic non erit id Christo proprium. Quod adeo hic agnoscit Adversarius, ut scribere haud erubescat, nulla de causa Christus proprie (si vox ista accipiatur ut vulgo solet accipi) filius Dei dicitur, aut dici potest. Quod certe contra Scripturam est evidentissime, quae Christum Filium Dei appellat proprium, & proprium ejus Patrem Deum.
units.tr: Smiglecius, in his book on the Son of God, chapter 3, therefore explains that Christ was made the Son of God at his birth because God supplied the part of a man, by creating matter and adding it to Mary's blood, from which Christ was born. This is in line with what we shall presently cite from Socinus's disputation and his book against Wiecki. We say that Christ is the Son of God according to the flesh, or because of his conception and birth, because in the birth of Christ God supplied the part of a man.---Yet it remains true that this generation can also be said of God, insofar as it can apply to God, if matter from God was added to Mary's blood, from which Christ was born, joined with Mary's blood. For if generation can be said of God when nothing of matter is added at all, how much more can that generation be said of God when something is created by God and added to effect the generation? Now, Christ according to the flesh is not called the Son of God but of man: made of the seed of David according to the flesh, declared the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness. Romans 1:3; and 9:5: from whom, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Furthermore, nowhere is it taught that God the Father supplied the part of a man in the conception of Christ; whereas, just as Mary knew of no part of a man, so Christ knew of no part of a father, being without father [ἀπάτωρ]. Furthermore, if the divine generation is founded on the fact that God brought something by creation at the nativity of Christ, then by the same reasoning all men could be called natural Sons of God, because in their generation God creates and introduces the soul to form their essence. And so this would not be peculiar to Christ. Our opponent so acknowledges this that he does not blush to write: for no reason is Christ properly called (if that word is taken as it is commonly taken) the Son of God, or can be called so. This is certainly against Scripture, which most clearly calls Christ the Son of God in the proper sense, and God his own proper Father.

units.la: Secundam Filiationis Dei in Christo causam collocant Adversarii, in ejus missione & sanctificatione ad obeundum suum munus. Quo trahunt Joan. x. 35. 36. Si illos dixit Deos, ad quos verbum Dei factum, & Scriptura solvi nequit: Quem Pater sanctificavit & misit in mundum, vos dicitis: quod blasphemat, quia dixi, Filius Dei sum? Resp. est arguargumentatio à minori ad majus: tum ex benè observatâ conclusione, quæ est, Christum non blasphemasse, facilis redditur expositio. Quare I. dum Christus concludit, defenditque se non blasphemasse, quod se dixerit Dei Filium, ideo quod plures alii sint, qui dicuntur Dii, λεγόμενοι θεοί. I Cor. viii. 5. eo Christus non inquirit in causam filiationis suæ, neque eam adeo ostendit, quam se tuto posse dici Dei Filium. Non quod Christus sit solum λεγόμενος θεὸς, nequidquam; sed quod ille sit scopus præsentis argumentationis & versus, quod extra blasphemiam sit, quod se dixit Deum. Est modus agendi συλλογιστικός[?]. Si illi, quibus loquitur Psalmus lxxxii. citra blasphemiam dicuntur Dii, ergo ego blasphemiæ non sum accusandus, ideo quod me Deum dixi. Probatur, à majore. Nam ego illis multum præsto, qui sum missus à Patre in mundum, & sanctificatus. Hoc jam non dicit causam suæ Filiationis, sed præstantiæ supra alios, unde potius queat nuncupari Dei Filius, quam illi Dii. Juxta regulam, qui aliis non est inferior dignitate, etiam nec nomine: Atqui ego: ergo. Dices, ergone Christus probat solum se dici posse Dei Filium, non unde talis sit? imo vero: neq; enim aliàs quadrat argumentatio ex Psalm. lxxxii. An ergo Christus ejus ordinis Deus est, quo illi λεγόμενοι Dii? nihil minus. Sed hoc non ex Psalmo allegato, vel verbis textus, quibus ille Psalmus urgetur, ostenditur, sed plurimis aliis quæ præcedunt, tum sequuntur. II. Quem Pater sanctificavit, & in mundum misit, merito, & absque blasphemiâ dicitur Filius Dei. Hoc totum est, quod versu illo 36. & argumento hinc facto, continetur. Sed non dicit, illam sanctificationem & missionem, esse causam Filiationis in Christo. Quem Pater sanctificavit, is est Filius Dei, specificative is talis est; non, quia sanctificavit, talis. Vel, quia sanctificavit, talis dignoscitur; non, quâ eum sanctificavit, talis, id est, filius Dei est. Ratio hæc, sanctificavit, &c. referri debet ad Deos λεγομένους, quibus Christus omnino præponitur; non ad sequens, non tanquam formalis vel adæquata ratio aut causa filiationis Dei. III. Imo si vel ex naturâ rei, vel ex textu causam indagemus filiationis, ea non est sanctificatio & missio filii, sed hæc illius consequens. Nam, quem Pater sanctificavit, & in mundum misit, is est Dei filius; non filius, quia sanctificavit; sed sanctificavit & misit, quia filius. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum dederit. Joann. iii. 16. Non Deus ex missio in mundum Christo, hoc lucrari putandus est, ut filium hinc receperit: sed in hoc amorem testatus est suum, quod filium misit, non missione filium fecit. Filius jam erat ante missionem, non factus demum ex eâ, & post eam. Hinc ubique adeo deprædicatur, quod Deus nobis Filium suum dedit, filium in mundum misit, filio non pe-percit. Ergo sensus loci (quem Pater sanctificavit & misit in mundum, vos dicitis blasphemare, quod se dixit filium) non est, se filium Dei esse consequenter & effective ex illa missione, sed jam in illa, & ante, atque ad eam Dei filium fuisse. Adeo verum & undiquaque certum est, eum esse Dei Filium. IV. Longe aliam Christus filiationis suæ causam exponit, quam illam sui missionem, nempe verf. 30. ego & Pater unum sumus. Unde quod se Deum dixerat, quod alioqui revera in homine blasphemum fuisset, non negat Christus, sed tuetur benè à se factum. Quum simplici alias negatione potuisset toto negotio breviter & solide defungi. Verum non negandam sibi assumptionem sciebat, sed majorem istam propositionem: qui se dicit Deum, est blas-sphemus. sphemus. Cujus negationem primùm probat ex Psalmo. Deinde assumtionis veritatem: ego me dico Deum, probat verf 39. ex suis operibus, si non facio opera Patris mei, ne mihi credite. vid. me Dei Patris Filium esse: quæ opera eum non Deum aut Dei Filium faciebant, sed monstrabant.
units.tr: Second, our opponents place the cause of the sonship of God in Christ in his being sent and sanctified to perform his office. To this they draw John 10:35-36: If he called them gods, to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken; do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, You blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God? Reply: this is an argument from the less to the greater, and its explanation is easily given once the conclusion is rightly observed, which is that Christ did not blaspheme. First, when Christ concludes and defends that he did not blaspheme in saying that he is the Son of God, because there are many others who are called gods, [so-called gods, λεγόμενοι θεοί], 1 Corinthians 8:5, Christ does not here inquire into the cause of his sonship, nor does he show the cause by which he could safely be called the Son of God. Not that Christ is only a so-called god, which is absurd; but that this is the aim of the present argument and verse, that it is outside blasphemy for him to have called himself God. It is a syllogistic mode of arguing [συλλογιστικός]: if those to whom Psalm 82 speaks are rightly called gods, then I am not to be accused of blasphemy for calling myself God. It is proved from the greater premise: for I am far superior to them, I who am sent by the Father into the world and sanctified. This does not state the cause of his sonship, but his pre-eminence over others, by which he may rather be named the Son of God than those gods. According to the rule: whoever is not inferior to others in dignity, is not inferior in name either. But I am such; therefore. You will say, does Christ then prove only that he can be called the Son of God, not whence he is such? Indeed, for otherwise the argument from Psalm 82 would not fit. Is Christ then God in the same order as those so-called gods? By no means. But this is shown not from the psalm cited, or from the words of the text on which that psalm is pressed, but from the many other things that precede and follow. II. He whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world is rightly and without blasphemy called the Son of God. This is the whole of what is contained in verse 36 and the argument drawn from it. But he does not say that that sanctification and mission are the cause of Christ's sonship. He whom the Father sanctified is the Son of God: he is such specifically, not because he sanctified him. Or: because he was sanctified he is recognised as such; not that in that he was sanctified he is the Son of God. This reason, sanctified, etc., must be referred to the so-called gods, over whom Christ is altogether preferred; not to what follows, nor as a formal or adequate reason or cause of the sonship of God. III. Indeed, if we search for the cause of sonship either from the nature of the thing or from the text, it is not the sanctification and mission of the Son, but these are its consequence. For he whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world is the Son of God; he is not the Son because he was sanctified, but he was sanctified and sent because he is the Son. God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son. John 3:16. God is not to be thought to gain from the mission of Christ into the world that he has received him as a son from this; rather, in this he showed his love, that he sent his Son, and by sending did not make him Son. He was already Son before the mission, not made so by it and after it. Hence everywhere it is proclaimed that God gave us his Son, sent his Son into the world, and did not spare his Son. Therefore the sense of the passage (whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, you say he blasphemes because he called himself the Son) is not that he is the Son of God consequently and effectively from that mission, but that he was already the Son of God in that mission, and before it, and as leading to it. So true and certain on every side is it that he is the Son of God. IV. Christ sets out a quite different cause of his sonship from his mission, namely verse 30: I and the Father are one. Hence Christ does not deny that he called himself God, which otherwise would in a mere man have been blasphemy, but defends it as rightly said by him. Whereas he could have dealt briefly and soundly with the whole matter by a simple denial of the other proposition. But he knew that the assumption was not to be denied, but the major premise: whoever calls himself God is a blasphemer. He first proves the denial of this from the psalm. Then he proves the truth of the assumption, that he calls himself God, verse 38, from his own works: if I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me, so that you may see that I am the Son of the Father God; which works did not make him God or the Son of God, but showed it.

units.la: Aliunde constare, hoc ipsum quod Christus & Pater unum sint, nullo modo ad essentiæ unitatem referendum esse, & verbis, videlicet illa ipsius Christi ad Patrem, Ioh. 17. 22. de discipulis suis, Et ego claritatem, quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis, ut sint unum, sicut & nos unum sumus. Ubi nequeat intelligi unitas essentiæ. Contra Wiekum cap. v. classe III. arg. IV. Resp. 1. Negatur consequentia, quod unitas illa Dei Christique, interpretanda veniat ex unitate, quæ de fidelibus prædicatur cum Deo, & Christo. Neque etiam ex eo quod à Christo additur, ut unum sint, quemadmodum nos unum sumus. Ratio est, quia diversitas modi adjungitur à Christo, ipso illo in loco, quo eam docet; præterquam quod res ipsa indubium omnibus faciat, unitatem istam inter Deum ac fideles, de unitate essentiali accipiendam nequaquam esse. Haud ita de unitate Dei Patris ac Filii, quam Christus priori loco docet. Nam & Patrem, & se Filium appellat, Ego & Pater, verf. 30. quod dixi Filius Dei sum? Quum vero se hinc dicat unum, quam aliam unitatem intelligemus, quam quæ est Patris ac Filii, sive essentiæ. Ista enim ratione illi unum dicuntur passim ac primo, atque id sunt. II. Attende mihi connexionem, verf. 30. cum 29. & vim argumenti Christi: Pater meus qui dedit mihi, vid. oves, major est omnibus: & nemo poterit rapere eas de manu Patris mei. Ego & Pater unum sumus. Quomodo unum? nempe quomodo Filius unum est cum Patre: ubi non tantum est conjunctio voluntatis & rerum, de qua unitatem istam Socinus exponit, sed & essentialis, quinimo hanc illa sequitur, & habet pro fundamento. III. Quum vis argumenti Christi in hoc sita sit, quod nemo rapturus esset oves ex manu suâ, vel Patris, quia hoc unum sit; non potest solam suam tum voluntatis tum rerum cum Patre conjunctionem innuere, quia hæc causam illius non indicat, non saltem manifeste. Faciamus enim Christi argumentum: qui unum sum cum Patre, voluntate, & rerum, præsertim ovium mearum, possessione, ex ejus an è Patris manibus oves quis rapiat, perinde est. Quid ista major, an videtur satis certa? annon eadem oves habere cum alio, & ejusdem animi ac consensus in iis conservandis quis esse potest, ut tamen illud non sequatur, vel quod nemo eas rapere possit è manu suâ, vel quod ejus cum altero manus idem sit: sive inter homines accipias, sive etiam de homine quocunque; relate ad Deum. Si Christus tantum unum cum Patre se dicit, ut ejusdem voluntatis sit, ac res possideat eandem, id nondum probat, quod propterea nemo vel ex suâ vel Patris manu oves rapere possit, nisi & alia significetur unitas quæ istius rei causa sit. Et in hanc Christus nos adducit. Quod Socinus advert, non rejicimus, id est Christum unius cum Patre voluntatis esse, & habere res easdem, sed hoc totum esse quod hic docetur, negamus: & negamus propterea, quia Christi argumento non satisfacit. IV. Quum Christus expresse satis aliud ponat, quam voluntatem; vel res sibi cum Patre unas eandemque, vid. manum, & posse seu potentiam Patris, Pater meus major est omnibus, & nemo potest eas rapere de manu Patris mei. Oves sibi significat easdem esse cum Patre, & manum seu potentiam eandem, quo nititur hoc quod docet, neminem ex suâ vel Patris manu eas rapturum. quur? quia perinde est, sive ex suâ, an Patris manu id dicatur fieri: cum eadem utriusque sit manus & potestas. Smalcius, contra Ravenspergerum, pag. 44. Ratio est, quia tanta est meæ cum Patre voluntatis, & (ut recte addit Socinus) rerum conjunctio, ut si quis velit meas oves de manu mea rapere, prorsus idem fit, ac si de ipsius Patris manu eas rapere vellet. quare? quandoquidem ego & Pater unum sumus. v. Intellige prorsus & omni modo idem. Quidni? dum non restringit textus, non Christus: certe non restringitur ad ea, quæ Socinus, neque salva argumenti vi, ad ea restringi potest. Nota est communis Theologorum regula, ubi textus non restringit vel limitat, nobis limitandum non esse. vi. Vide vero, ut ex nostra sententia & expositione argumentum constet, neque aliter: nemo rapiet oves meas, sunt enim & Patris, qui omnibus major, & ex cujus, sive mea manu nemo eas rapere potis est, quia id idem est sive ex Patris, sive mea manu eæ rapiantur, eadem cum utriusque manus sit & potentia, quandoquidem ego & Pater unum sumus, omni modo, essentiâ, viribus, voluntate, rebus. Sic exposito argumento, nihil est quod adversus ejus vim & formam excipi possit. vii. Nisi quod rei solum superest, ex Socini vero expositione locum non habet, blasphemum videri, quod homo se Deum faciat. Id vero ex Socini expositione non datur sequi: quomodo enim ex eo quod quis dicat se id velle quod Deus, & Dei oves possidere, trahat, eum blasphemiam committere, vel se Deum facere? Verum omni modo, si quis se unum dicat cum Deo, profecto blasphemiam, nisi talis revera sit, haud effugiet. viii. Certe si Christus non alius fuerit, ac eum Sociniani faciunt, homo, justus, missus ad istud singulare officium, oves curans sibi à Patre datas, & in hoc divinæ voluntati prorsus consentiens, præterea in illo humili adhuc statu, non glorificatus, haud potuit adeo simpliciter atque absolute dicere, sine gravi offensione, ego & Pater unum sumus. Non enim inde unitatem sibi cum Deo ullus arrogare jure potest, non simpliciter. Neque dixit, ego cum Patre, sed, ego & Pater: non unus, sed unum; quemadmodum & Syriaca habet versio, & Persica, Arabica, Æthiopica. Dein quare non Christus clarius aperti-usq; significasset, se non aliam sibi arrogare cum Patre conjunctionem, quam voluntatis & rerum, eam si intellexisset solam, uti in altero loco Joan. xvii. satis manifeste exponit unitatem illam, quæ est fidelium cum Deo, ut nullum dubium oriri possit, quin spiritualem unitatem intellexerit, non essentialem vel absolutam. ix. De unitate potentiæ deinceps subjungit Socinus: Se libenter concedere unitatem istam Christi cum Patre referri ad potentiam: sed interim eam non esse extendendam ultra limites ejus rei, de qua agatur & similium: atque intelligendum, non quidem simpliciter & absolute, unam & eandem esse potentiam Christi & Patris, sed secundum quid: quatenus scilicet Pater cum Chri-sto in regendis & servandis iis, quos ille dedit, suam potentiam communicarit: & quidem qua-lem, seu tam magnam, ut ea in re ipse Pater, id est, Deus habet. Passim autem & lubentius referunt eam Adversarii ad unitatem concordiæ ac voluntatis inter se & Patrem. Sinalcius, adversus Ravenspergerum, pag. 44. Et hactenus quidem ita respondimus, ac si certum esset Christum in hoc loco de unitate potentiæ cum Patre agere. Iam vero si verba Christi de unitate non potentiæ, sed concordiæ & voluntatis intelligenda esse, vel saltem rectissime de ea intelligi posse constet, quidnam virium habebit argumentatio adversariorum? Sic nec licuisset Christo dicere, se unum potentia esse cum Patre, si non aliud habuerit, ac ei Adversarii concedunt. Quis enim hominum audit ita de se loqui, se unum esse cum Deo potentia, vel simpliciter unum, utcunque amplam alicujus rei haberet à Deo potestatem, & forte, qualis aliquando Mosis & Davidis fuit, majorem, vel parem, saltem non multo inferiorem, ac Christus, ex mente Adversariorum, cum hæc loqueretur, habuit? Tum non vult Socinus simpliciter & absolute intelligi, unam & eandem esse Christi & Patris potentiam. Attamen simpliciter & absolute id Christus dixit: nec potentia unum, sed simplicius & absolute, unum. Idne, ut Deus potentiam suam communicet cum creatura, satis est, ut hinc dicatur creatura unum esse cum Deo, unum potentia, etiam in regendis & salvandis hominibus? Nam illam Christi potentiam pertinere tantum ad oves protegendas, hoc est, ad salutem humani generis, Smalcius scribit. Et quomodo illam potentiam Christo, ante sui exaltationem, velint communicatam, peto ut planius Adversarii explicent: praesertim quod illa talis, seu tanta fuerit, ut ea in re ipse Pater habet. Quod cum veritate conciliabunt nunquam, Christo accepto ex mente Adversariorum, pro homine, & in tantum humiliato, atq; non Deo. Smalcius, contra Ravenspergerum, pag. 45. Quis enim non cre-debat, Patrem posse nos servare? De Christo vero, tunc id reipsa credere, nec necesse erat, nec requirebatur. Ipse enim adhuc mortalis erat, cum ista diceret. Qui vero mortalis est, vitam aeternam reipsa nemini dare potest. Quare nec tum temporis ei adeo competiisse Deitatem, Smalcius affirmat, pag. 54. Nempe sanctificationem & missionem Christi in mundum, quo etiam opera pertinent, non esse praecipua & potissima argumenta ejus, quod Christus est Filius Dei, vel etiam Deus. Haec enim ad illud tempus tantum pertinent, quo Christus in terris commoratus est. Non vero Christus in aliqua re potentiae, ut ipse Pater habet, capax est. Sed haec iterum in fumum abibunt, adhibita distinctione infiniti proprie vel improprie, simpliciter & secundum quid. Quemadmodum Socinus alibi in Disputatione cum Christiano Francken respondit, de adoratione Christi, ad ejus argumentum, quod finita Christi substantia non fit capax scientiae infinitae, ergo neque potentiae: ergo neque adorationis: sic Francken. Socinus vero: Proprie fortassis ac simpliciter infinita. Seu minus proprie, & secundum quid, ut hic infiniti vocabulum accipitur, potest omnino finita substantia infinitae scientiae esse capax. Quid enim vetat, quominus homo quispiam omnia sciat, quae de re aliqua sciri possunt? & post iterum: haec infinitas non proprie & simpliciter, sed, ut dictum est minus proprie, & secundum quid accipitur: pag. 78. & 20. Atqui Christus in sermone nostro proprie, simpliciter & absolute se unum dicit cum Patre, quod & in genere, & secundum potentiam, proprie quoque accipiendum est. IX. Jam quod ad locum, quem nobis objicit, Joann. XVII. 22. ut unum sint, quemadmodum nos unum sumus: negamus, quod illud quemadmodum καθ᾽ ὡς [?] probet parem rationem unitatis esse inter Deum & Christum, quae est hominum ad Deum. Similitudo aliqua notatur modo, non paritas, ad exemplum, non ad aequalitatem. Quemadmodum alibi saepe, & hoc ipso cap. verf. 23. & dilexisti eos, καθ᾽ ὡς [?] quemadmodum me dilexisti. Luc.vi. 36. Sitis ergo misericordes, quemadmodum καθ᾽ ὡς [?] & Pater vester est misericors: quod alibi dicitur, ὥσπερ [?], Mat. v. 48. Act. xv. 8. Dans ipsis Spiritum sanctum, quemadmodum καθ᾽ ὡς [?] & nobis. Eph. v. 28. Viri diligite uxores vestras, quemadmodum & Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & seipsum tradidit pro ea. Adde verf. 2. & 29. Col. iii. 13. Denique in loco Joann. xvii. multa sunt, quae unitatem illam exponunt & declarant. verf. 21. ut illi in nobis unum sint. verf. 23. ego in ipsis, & tu in me, ut sint consummati in unum, εἷς ἕν [?]: nempe ut accipiant gloriam Christi, in quo unitatem illam constituit, & ego gloriam quam dedisti mihi, dedi iis: ut sint unum, quemadmodum nos unum sumus, & verf. seq. ad unum, εἷς ἕν [?]. Instat Socinus, atque addit alia ad argumentum, ex Christi verbis extractum penitus dis-solvendum: ut cum Paulus ait, 1. Cor. 3. 8. eum, qui plantat, & eum, qui rigat, unum esse: vel, cum ad Galatas scribens, cap. 3. 28. inquit, omnes enim vos unum estis in Christo Iesu. Sive, ut Graeca exemplaria habent, unus; quod ad unitatem essentiae declarandam multo magis pertinere videtur. Resp. Non necesse est probare, illa, vel illos, qui quovis modo in idem aliquod conveniunt, & sunt εἷς τὸ ἓν, eâ ratione dici quoque posse unum: sed propterea non potest isto sermone denotari unitatem essentiae, non illis Christi verbis, quibus dixit se unum esse cum Patre, hoc probandum. Imo dicuntur fideles esse unum corpus, vid. spirituale, ἐν σῶμα. 1 Cor. vi. 16. & x. 17. Eph. ii. 14. τὸ ἀμφότερα ἐν. & verl. 16. & iv. 4. Col. iii. 15. 1 Joann. v. 7. & hi tres unum sunt. Fac deniq; illud Christum, quod dicimus, voluisse, quibus quaeso verbis commodius declarasset, quam quibus nunc fecit? Ut tam clarum sit, Christum eo sensu id dixisse de se, ac alio dicta illa ab Apostolo fuisse, de quo nemo potest ambigere. Explicat se Apostolus utroque in loco. In priori, plantans & rigans unum sunt, nempe uti verl. dixerat 5. Quis ergo est Paulus, quis autem Apollo, nisi ministri, per quos credidistis? Unum sunt, in communi Ecclesiae ministerio. verl. 9. Dei enim sumus co-operarii, &c. In posteriori loco significat Apostolus, quod unus vid. quasi homo, vel unum sunt in Christo. verl. 29. Si vero vos Christi, dixerat verl. 27. Eos in Christum baptizatos, Christum induisse. Hac ergo ratione voluit unum esse in Christo: non simpliciter unum, sed in isto tertio, Iesu Christo. Unus an unum dicatur, eodem redit. Nisi quod ad vocem unus aliquid videatur subintelligendum, non ita ad unum. In loco ad Galatas, dicitur unus, quod tantundem est ac unum. Smalcius, adversus Ravensperger um, pag. 24. Illud, nempe unum, de alia unitate quam essentiae intelligi potest: hoc vero, communi more loquendi observato, necessario unitatem essentiae, si scilicet unitas in eadem alio detur, indicat. Verum quid, illud unum de ipsa unitate essentiae intelligi non potest? Hoc vero unum Gal. iii. 28. non notat essentiae unitatem; neque probabit, magis necessario unitatem essentiae denotare, quam illud: ut, cui constitutum reluctari, aeque facile quid reperire possit adversus unum, quam alterum. Nam paulo post inquit Smalcius, ex mente Oftorodi, verisimilius fore, quod nos volumus, si dictum esset unus sumus, quam nunc cum scriptum est, unum sumus: ergo non necessario, nec sic denotata essentiae fuisset unitas. Age ergo & praescribat non nobis, sed Deo, quomodo tandem, & qua voce loqui debuisset, illud si significare, & satisfacere istiusmodi ingeniis voluisset.
units.tr: It is clear from elsewhere that the statement that Christ and the Father are one must in no way be referred to the unity of essence, and this from Christ's own words to the Father, John 17:22, about his disciples: And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one. Here the unity of essence cannot be understood. Against Wiekus, chap. 5, class III, arg. IV. Reply: (1) The consequence is denied, namely that the unity of God and Christ must be interpreted from the unity that is predicated of the faithful with God and with Christ. Nor does it follow from what Christ adds, that they may be one, even as we are one. The reason is that Christ adds a difference of manner in the very place where he teaches the unity, and the matter itself makes it indubitable to all that the unity between God and the faithful is not to be taken as an essential unity. It is otherwise with the unity of God the Father and the Son, which Christ teaches in the earlier place. For he calls both the Father and himself the Son: I and the Father are one, v. 30; do you say of me, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, You blaspheme, because I said I am the Son of God? Since he here says that they are one, what other unity shall we understand than that of the Father and the Son, which is of essence? For on this reasoning they are everywhere and first called one, and they are so. (2) Observe for me the connection between v. 30 and v. 29, and the force of Christ's argument: My Father, who gave them to me, that is, the sheep, is greater than all; and no one is able to snatch them out of my Father's hand. I and the Father are one. In what way one? Namely, in the way the Son is one with the Father. Here there is not merely a conjunction of will and of possessions, by which Socinus explains this unity, but an essential one, and indeed the latter follows from it and has it as its foundation. (3) Since the force of Christ's argument lies in this, that no one would snatch the sheep out of his hand or out of the Father's, because they are one, he cannot be indicating only his conjunction with the Father in will and possessions, since this does not show the cause of that, at least not clearly. For let us frame Christ's argument thus: I am one with the Father in will and in possessions, especially in possession of my sheep; so it makes no difference whether anyone snatches the sheep out of his hand or out of the Father's. What is the major premise here; does it seem certain enough? Can there not be the same possession of sheep with another, and a like mind and agreement in keeping them, and yet it not follow that no one can snatch them out of his hand, or that his hand is the same as the other's? Whether you take this of men or of any man at all, relate it to God. If Christ says only that he is one with the Father so that he has the same will and possesses the same things, this does not yet prove that for this reason no one can snatch the sheep out of his hand or out of the Father's, unless some other unity is also signified which is the cause of this. And to this Christ leads us. What Socinus notes we do not reject, namely that Christ is one with the Father in will and has the same possessions, but we deny that this is the whole of what is taught here, and we deny it for the reason that it does not satisfy Christ's argument. (4) Since Christ plainly sets down something other than will, or than the things that are one and the same for him and the Father, namely the hand and power of the Father: My Father, who is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of my Father's hand, he signifies that the sheep are the same with the Father, and the hand or power the same, on which rests his teaching that no one will snatch them out of his own hand or the Father's. Why? Because it makes no difference whether it is said to be done from his own hand or from the Father's, since the hand and power of both are the same. Smalcius, against Ravensperger, p. 44: The reason is that the conjunction of my will with the Father's is so great, and (as Socinus rightly adds) of possessions too, that if anyone should wish to snatch my sheep out of my hand, it is exactly the same as if he wished to snatch them out of the hand of the Father himself. Why? Since I and the Father are one. (5) Understand: exactly and in every way the same. Why not? Since the text does not restrict it, and Christ does not restrict it; certainly it cannot be restricted to what Socinus allows without weakening the force of the argument. It is a common rule of the theologians that where the text does not restrict or limit, we must not limit. (6) See further how the argument stands according to our opinion and exposition, and in no other way: no one shall snatch my sheep, for they are both the Father's, who is greater than all, and mine; out of whose hand, or out of mine, no one is able to snatch them, because it is the same whether they are snatched out of the Father's hand or out of mine, since the hand and power of both are the same, since I and the Father are one, in every way, in essence, in strength, in will, in possessions. So expounded, there is nothing that can be objected against the force and form of the argument. (7) Except that the thing alone remains: on Socinus's own exposition, which has no place here, it is seen as blasphemous for a man to make himself God. But this does not follow from Socinus's exposition: for how can it be inferred from the fact that someone says he wishes what God wishes, and possesses God's sheep, that he commits blasphemy or makes himself God? Certainly, in every way, if anyone says that he is one with God, he will not escape blasphemy, unless he is truly such. (8) Surely if Christ were not other than the Sociniani make him, a mere man, just, sent to this singular office, caring for the sheep given him by the Father, and in this wholly consenting to the divine will, and moreover still in that humble state, not glorified, he could not have said so simply and absolutely, without grave offence, I and the Father are one. For no one can rightly claim for himself a unity with God on this ground, not simply. Nor did he say, I with the Father, but I and the Father: not one [masculine], but one [neuter]; as the Syriac version also has, and the Persian, Arabic and Ethiopic. Further, why did Christ not more clearly and openly signify that he claimed no other conjunction with the Father than of will and of possessions? If he had meant only that, he would have expressed it plainly, as in the other place, John 17, where he explains that unity which is of the faithful with God, so that no doubt could arise that he meant a spiritual unity and not an essential or absolute one. (9) Next Socinus adds, about the unity of power: that he is willing to grant that this unity of Christ with the Father is referred to power, but that it is not to be extended beyond the limits of the matter in question and similar matters; and that it must be understood not simply and absolutely that the power of Christ and of the Father is one and the same, but in a certain respect: namely, insofar as the Father has communicated his power to Christ in governing and preserving those whom he has given him; and indeed of such a kind, or so great, that in that matter the Father himself, that is God, has it. Our opponents, however, more often and more willingly refer it to a unity of agreement and will between him and the Father. Smalcius, against Ravensperger, p. 44: Thus far we have answered as if it were certain that Christ in this place is speaking of unity of power with the Father. But now, if it is established that the words of Christ are to be understood not of unity of power but of agreement and will, or at least can rightly be understood of it, what strength will the argument of the opponents have? So neither could Christ have been permitted to say that he is one with the Father in power, if he had nothing more than our opponents concede to him. For who among men hears anyone speak of himself thus, that he is one with God in power, or simply one, however ample a power of some kind he might have from God, and perhaps greater, or equal, or at least not much inferior, such as that once possessed by Moses and David, than Christ, on the view of our opponents, had when he spoke these words? Then Socinus does not want it understood simply and absolutely that the power of Christ and of the Father is one and the same. Yet Christ did say it simply and absolutely: one not in power, but simply and absolutely one. Is it enough, for God to communicate his power to a creature, that the creature should on this account be said to be one with God, one in power, even in governing and saving men? For Smalcius writes that that power of Christ pertains only to the protecting of the sheep, that is, to the salvation of the human race. And I ask that the opponents explain more plainly how they suppose that power was communicated to Christ before his exaltation, especially that it was of such a kind, or so great, that the Father himself has it in that matter. They will never reconcile this with the truth, since on the view of our opponents Christ was then a man, and so humbled, and not God. Smalcius, against Ravensperger, p. 45: For who did not believe that the Father could save us? But concerning Christ, to believe this in actual fact then was neither necessary nor required. For he was still mortal when he said these things. But one who is mortal cannot in actual fact give eternal life to anyone. Hence Smalcius affirms that the deity did not then belong to him so fully, p. 54: Namely, that the sanctification and mission of Christ into the world, to which also his works pertain, are not the chief and principal arguments that Christ is the Son of God, or even God. For these pertain only to that time in which Christ dwelt on earth. But Christ is not capable of any power in the way the Father himself has it. Yet these things will again vanish into smoke, once the distinction of the infinite is applied, properly or improperly, simply and in a certain respect. As Socinus elsewhere replied in his disputation with Christian Francken, about the worship of Christ, to Francken's argument that a finite substance of Christ is not capable of infinite knowledge, therefore neither of power, therefore neither of worship: so Francken. But Socinus: Perhaps properly and simply infinite. Or less properly, and in a certain respect, as the word infinite is taken here, a finite substance can altogether be capable of infinite knowledge. For what forbids some man from knowing everything that can be known about some matter? And afterwards again: This infinity is not taken properly and simply, but, as has been said, less properly and in a certain respect, p. 78 and 20. Yet Christ in our text says properly, simply and absolutely that he is one with the Father, which must be taken properly also in respect of essence and of power.
