(9 [sic]) Now as to the place that they object to us, John 17:22, that they may be one, even as we are one: we deny that the word even as (καθὼς) proves that the unity between God and Christ is of the same kind as that of men with God. Only some likeness is noted, not equality, an example and not an equality. As elsewhere often, and in this very chapter, v. 23: and hast loved them, as (καθὼς) thou hast loved me. Luke 6:36: Be ye therefore merciful, as (καθὼς) your Father also is merciful; which elsewhere is said by ὥσπερ, Matt. 5:48; Acts 15:8: giving them the Holy Spirit, as (καθὼς) to us also; Eph. 5:28: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for it. Add v. 2 and 29; Col. 3:13. Finally, in the place of John 17 there are many things which explain and declare that unity. v. 21: that they also may be one in us. v. 23: I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one (εἰς ἓν); namely, that they may receive the glory of Christ, in which he places that unity: and the glory which thou gavest me I have given them, that they may be one, even as we are one, and in the following verse into one (εἰς ἕν). Socinus presses on and adds other things to dissolve entirely the argument drawn from Christ's words: as when Paul says, 1 Cor. 3:8, he that planteth and he that watereth are one; or when writing to the Galatians, chap. 3:28, he says, for ye are all one in Christ Jesus; or as the Greek copies have it, one (εἷς), which seems much more to pertain to declaring unity of essence. Reply: It is not necessary to prove that those, or they who in any way come together into something and are (εἷς τὸ ἓν) one, may be called one for that reason too; but it cannot be proved by that word that the unity of essence is denoted, nor by those words of Christ in which he said that he is one with the Father. Indeed the faithful are said to be one body, that is, a spiritual body (ἓν σῶμα), 1 Cor. 6:16; 10:17; Eph. 2:14 (τὰ ἀμφότερα ἕν); and v. 16; 4:4; Col. 3:15; 1 John 5:7: and these three are one. Suppose finally that Christ meant what we say: by what words, I ask, would he have declared it more conveniently than by those he now used? So clear is it that Christ said this of himself in the same sense as those words were said by the Apostle, about whom no one can doubt. The Apostle explains himself in both places. In the first, planting and watering are one, namely as v. 5 had said: Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers through whom ye believed? They are one in the common ministry of the Church. v. 9: For we are God's fellow-workers, etc. In the second place the Apostle signifies that they are one, as it were one man, or are one in Christ. v. 29: And if ye are Christ's, he had said in v. 27, those baptized into Christ have put on Christ. In this way, therefore, he wished them to be one in Christ: not simply one, but in that third thing, Jesus Christ. Whether it is said one or one thing, it comes to the same. Except that with the word one something seems to be understood which is not so with one thing. In the place to the Galatians, it is said one, which is the same as one thing. Smalcius, against Ravensperger, p. 24: That, namely one, can be understood of some unity other than that of essence; but this, one thing, observing common usage of speech, necessarily indicates unity of essence, if indeed a unity in the same thing is given elsewhere. But what, can that one not be understood of the unity of essence itself? Yet this one in Gal. 3:28 does not signify unity of essence; nor will it prove that it denotes unity of essence more necessarily than the other, so that whoever has set out to resist can find something against the one as easily as against the other. For shortly after Smalcius says, from the mind of Ostorodus, that what we want would be more likely if it had been said we are one, than now that it has been written we are one thing: therefore it would not have been necessary, nor would the unity of essence have been denoted in this way. Come then, let him prescribe not to us, but to God, how at last, and in what words, he ought to have spoken, if he had wished to signify that and to satisfy minds of this kind.

units.la: Tertiam Filii Dei in Christo causam faciunt Adversarii, ejus à mortuis resuscitatio-nem.
units.tr: The Adversaries make the third cause of Christ's being the Son of God his resurrection from the dead.

units.la: Nam Christum in resurrectione factum esse Dei Filium, contendit Smalcius, lib. de Dei Filio, cap. xi. & pag. 103. Argumentum autem est sumtum à testimonio Davidis, in quo dicitur, quod Deus Filium suum certo die genuerit. Unde rectissime infertur, Deum tunc, cum Christum ex mortuis resuscitavit, eundem genuisse, & ita promissiones de servatore implevisse. Locus est, Act. xiii. 32. 33. Et nos vobis evangelizamus promissionem Patribus factam, quod Deus eam nobis ipsorum filiis implevit, resuscitans Iesum: quomodo etiam in secundo Psalmo scribitur: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Atq; Rom. i. 4. Col. i. 18. dicitur, primogenitus ex mortuis. Resp. Fiat argumentum, & negabitur consequentia. In sermone de Christo, ejusque resuscitatione adhibetur locus ille ex Psalm. ii. ergo resuscitatione ex mortuis Christus factus est Filius Dei, vel effectus, uti loquitur Schlichtingius tingius,negatur. 11. Applicatio loci alicujus non est ideo propria ejus & litteralis ex-plicatio. Sic in sermone de Christi suscitatione ex mortuis, applicatur Psalmus se-cundus: nemo tamen dicet, isto loco de suscitatione agi, ut ex hac ille explicari vel possit, vel debeat: Nedum,quod ait Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum, pag. 428. quod verba Psalmi de ea Filiatione loquuntur, quae in Christi resuscitatione a mortuis, & quae eam est consequuta dominatione, tota constitit. 111. Revera locus ille Psalmi non adducitur ad resurrectionis, sed ad Christi, sive non ad praedicati, sed subjecti expositionem. Nam cum praecesserat, Deum promissionem suam implevisse resuscitando Ie-sum; quis Jesus ille, plenius exponitur obiter.vers. 33. ex Psalm. 11. resuscitatio autem vers. 34. ex alio Davidis Psalmo. Quod utrumque confirmat ratio con-nexionis; ibi ὡς κ̣ῷ[?] in Psalmo secundo scribitur, id est, de quo, vel uti de eo, Iesu sc. resuscitato, in Psalmo 11. dicitur, tu filius meus: hic, ὅτι ὁ ἀνέστησεν αὐτὸν, quod vero eum resuscitavit ex mortuis, &c. ita dixit, &c. Ut plane appareat, ad aliud, atque aliud adhiberi illum locum, atque hunc. iv. Suscitationem ex mortuis generationem appellari posse, ait Episcopius, figurate, & Christum Dei Filium. Ergo sic Christus dicetur Filius Dei figuratus. Non quaerimus jam de figura aliqua locutionis; sed de rei veritate, de causa filiationis, unde Christus Filius Dei, non dicatur, sed sit. Nam sic Remonstrantes ipsi dicunt, Apol. sol. 49. Ex hisce liquet, quam inconsiderate Censor hic affirmet, Scripturam Christo Domino nostro unicam filiationem tantum attribuere, ex unico ad divinam ipsius & aeternam generationem respectu; & contra quam recte, quam solide Remonstrantes cum Scriptura asseruerint, Christum pluribus modis Filium Dei esse ac vocari. Ergo non solum agitur de eo, quod vocetur Christus Dei Filius, sed quoque quod sit. Paulo ante dixerat Episcopius: Per suscitationem autem ex mortuis aliquem recte & merito Filium Dei vocari posse. In Institutionibus addidit, figurate licet. Et suscitationem illam ex mortuis, generationem recte, licet figurate, vocari posse. Quis autem capiat, per resurrectionem aliquem fieri filium Dei? Resuscitatio simpliciter est ad vitam, & quemadmodum distincta sunt ab hac dona, quae forte resuscitato dantur, ita ut resuscitatio fundamentum praebeat relationis filii, perperam asseritur. Vel dicantur ergo omnes fieri Dei filii, quotquot a Deo resuscitabuntur. Illustre vero Christo quod Filius Dei esset, documentum perhibuit ejus resuscitatio. Ad locum Rom. 1. 4. quem Syrus vertit, agnitus Filius Dei; Versio Arabica, Filio Dei destinato; Æthiopica, Quem declaravit esse Filium Dei, jam ante respondimus. Col. 1. 18. dicitur πρωτότοκος ex mortuis; quia nempe primus, ut in omnibus sit πρωτεύων[?] manifesta & sola metaphora, a primogenitis sumta. Quod Luc. xx. 36. dicuntur υἱοὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως[?], Hebraismus est, & metaphora, quae non magis dicit, eum qui suscitatur ideo gigni a Deo, quam Matth. ix. 15. υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος[?], qui a sponso gignuntur. Praeterea, Grotius observat, apud Lucam τῆς ἀναστάσεως non significare resurrectionem, sed ἀναστάσεως nomen hic vitam aeternam ac beatam significat, inquit, ut Heb. xi. 35. & alibi saepe.
units.tr: Smalcius contends, in his book on the Son of God, chapter 11 and page 103, that Christ became the Son of God in his resurrection. The argument is taken from the testimony of David, where it is said that God begot his Son on a certain day. From this it is rightly inferred that God then begot him, when he raised Christ from the dead, and so fulfilled the promises concerning the Saviour. The place is Acts 13:32–33: "And we preach to you the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled it to us their children, in raising up Jesus; as it is also written in the second Psalm: You are my Son, this day have I begotten you." And Romans 1:4 and Colossians 1:18 call him "the firstborn from the dead." Answer: let the argument be framed, and the consequence will be denied. Because that passage of Psalm 2 is applied in a sermon on Christ and his resurrection, it does not follow that Christ was made the Son of God, or became so by his resurrection from the dead, as Schlichting puts it; this is denied. (2) The application of a passage is not for that reason its proper and literal explanation. Thus in a sermon on Christ's raising from the dead the second Psalm is applied, yet no one will say that the passage is about the resurrection, so that it can or must be explained by it. Still less is it true, as Schlichting says against Meisner, page 428, that the words of the Psalm "speak of that sonship which consists wholly in Christ's resurrection from the dead, and in the dominion that followed it." (3) Indeed that passage of the Psalm is not cited to explain the resurrection, but Christ; that is, it explains not the predicate but the subject. For when it had been said that God fulfilled his promise "in raising up Jesus," what sort of Jesus he was is explained in passing in verse 33 from Psalm 2, and the resurrection itself in verse 34 from another Psalm of David. The connection of the words confirms both points: there it is written in the second Psalm [ὡς], that is, of whom, or as of him, Jesus, namely the one raised, it is said in Psalm 2, "You are my Son"; here [ὅτι ὁ ἀνέστησεν αὐτὸν], "that he raised him up from the dead, etc., thus he said, etc." So it plainly appears that the one passage is adduced for something other than the other. (4) Episcopius says that the raising up from the dead can be called a generation, figuratively, and Christ the Son of God. So Christ would be called the Son of God figuratively. We are not now asking about some figure of speech, but about the truth of the matter, about the cause of the sonship, whereby Christ is not said to be the Son of God but is so. For the Remonstrants themselves say this, Apology, p. 49: From these things it is clear how thoughtlessly this Censor here affirms that Scripture attributes to our Lord Christ only one sonship, from his one divine and eternal generation; and on the contrary how rightly and how soundly the Remonstrants have asserted with Scripture that Christ is the Son of God and is called so in several ways. So the question is not only whether Christ is called the Son of God, but also whether he is so. A little before, Episcopius had said: But by the raising up from the dead, someone can rightly and deservedly be called the Son of God. In the Institutes he added: figuratively, it is true. And that raising up from the dead can rightly, though figuratively, be called a generation. But who can grasp how a man is made the Son of God by the resurrection? Resurrection is simply a going over to life; and just as these gifts, which may perhaps be given to the one raised, are distinct from it, so that the resurrection provides the foundation of the relation of sonship, this is wrongly asserted. Or let it then be said that all are made sons of God whom God shall raise up. But his resurrection bore evidence that Christ was the Son of God in a notable way. As for Romans 1:4, which the Syriac renders acknowledged Son of God, the Arabic version Son of God appointed, and the Ethiopic Whom he declared to be the Son of God, we have already answered this earlier. Colossians 1:18 says firstborn from the dead [πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν] because he is plainly the first, so that in all things he may be pre-eminent [πρωτεύων]; it is a plain and sole metaphor, taken from firstborns. That in Luke 20:36 they are called sons of the resurrection [υἱοὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως] is a Hebraism and a metaphor, which no more says that the one who is raised is therefore begotten by God than Matthew 9:15 sons of the bridechamber [υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος] says that they are begotten by the bridegroom. Moreover, Grotius observes that in Luke τῆς ἀναστάσεως does not signify the resurrection, but that the word resurrection here means eternal and blessed life, he says, as in Hebrews 11:35 and often elsewhere.

units.la: Quartam denique Filiationis in Christo constituunt Adversarii causam, in collata Christo potestate, ac regno. Eoq; trahunt Heb.v.5. Sic & Christus non seipsum ἐδοξασε[?] ut fieret sacerdos supremus, sed qui dixit ei, tu es filius meus,ego hodie genui te. Resp. Non ali-bi magis misere disputant Adversarii, quam hic, & ex hoc loco. 1. Non enim agi-tur de collata Christo summa potestate & regno, sed sacerdotio. Sacerdotium autem ejus confundere cum regno, ineptum & ἀξιόλογον[?] esse alias plenius indicabimus. II. ἐδόξασε[?] non est glorificavit, qualis Christo gloria contigit post adscen-sionem, sed sibi honorem tribuere sacerdotii, vel vocationis ad sacerdotium. quem-admodum proxime ante dicitur: neque sibi ipsi quisquam sumit hunc honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo, sicut & Aaron. Unde & Castalio vertit: Sic Christus quoque non ipse sibi eum honorem vendicavit. III. Qui dixit Christo, filius meus tu es, ipsum destinavit sacerdotio; ergo ex sacerdotio factus est Dei filius? quae sequela. Quinimo contrarium manifestum est, ei jam dictum, filius meus tu es, antequam sacerdos fieret. verf. 8. & quamvis filius esset, didicit ab iis quae passus obedientiam. Filius fuit ante exaltationem. IV. Sacerdos factus est, non per illud, filius meus es tu; sed, quod in alio dixit: tu es sacerdos in aeternum, juxta ordinem Melchisedek, quod proximo verf. 6. sequitur. V. Sacerdotio autem Christus functus fuit etiam in terris; verf. 7. seq. qui in diebus carnis suae, &c. 9. & consummatus factus est auctor salutis. 10. cognominatus a Deo Pontifex. Nihil autem ad causam Adversariorum spectant loca, Matth. xvi. 16. Tu es Christus, filius illi viventis Dei. Marc. viii. 29. Luc. 9. 20. Sed contra illa dicunt, Filium eum Dei etiam fuisse, ante caelestem suam gloriam & regnum. Vel quid huc facit, quod illis locis, & 1 Joann. v. 1. 5. Jesus Christus appellatur? an vero idem fit esse Dei Filium in Christo, & esse Christum, vel, an Scriptura pro eodem accipiat Iesum esse Christum, & Iesum esse Dei Filium, uti Socinus loquitur, in Catechesi, p.39. mox exami-nabimus.
units.tr: Finally, the Adversaries make the fourth cause of Christ's sonship the power and kingdom conferred on Christ. On this they rely on Hebrews 5:5: "So also Christ did not glorify himself [ἐδόξασε] so as to become the supreme priest, but he who said to him, You are my Son, this day have I begotten you." Answer: (1) Nowhere do the Adversaries argue more wretchedly than here, and from this text. For it is not a question of the supreme power and kingdom conferred on Christ, but of the priesthood. To confuse his priesthood with his kingdom is absurd and [ἀξιόλογον] unworthy of notice, as we shall show more fully elsewhere. (2) [ἐδόξασε] does not mean "glorified," as the glory which came to Christ after the ascension; it means that he did not assume to himself the honour of the priesthood, or of being called to the priesthood, as is said just before: Nor does anyone take this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. Hence Castalio also translates: So Christ too did not claim that honour for himself. (3) He who said to Christ, You are my Son, appointed him to the priesthood; therefore he was made the Son of God from the priesthood? What a consequence! On the contrary, the opposite is plain: that You are my Son was said to him already, before he became priest. Verse 8: And although he was a Son, he learned obedience from the things he suffered. He was Son before his exaltation. (4) He was made priest not by that word, You are my Son, but by what was said in another place, You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek, which follows in verse 6. (5) Christ also discharged the priesthood on earth, as verse 7 and following show: who in the days of his flesh, etc.; verse 9: and having been made perfect, became the author of salvation; verse 10: named by God a High Priest. But the passages Matthew 16:16, You are Christ, the Son of the living God, Mark 8:29 and Luke 9:20 have nothing to do with the Adversaries' cause. Nor do they say against those passages that he was also the Son of God before his heavenly glory and kingdom. Or what does it matter to this that in those places, and in 1 John 5:1, 5, Jesus Christ is named? Is it indeed the same thing to be the Son of God in Christ and to be Christ? Or does Scripture take Jesus to be Christ and Jesus to be the Son of God as the same thing, as Socinus puts it in his Catechism, p. 39? We shall examine this shortly.

units.la: Atque ita vindicavimus fidem nostram, & Christum, ejusque veram à Patre filiationem, per aeternam generationem, vel communicationem essentiae divinae, ab adulterina expositione Adversariorum, qua Socinianorum, qua Remonstrantium, quibus egregie quoque responsum, ab Altingio, in Theol. Elenctica, pag. 149. &c. & Triglandio, Disp. ix. contra Apol. Remonstr. Atque illis, quae ad hoc argumentum jam diximus, enervatam existimamus operosam Smalcii de divinitate Christi tractationem, quaeque prolixe admodum de divinitate Christi conquisivit multa, ut variis quasi deitatibus fictitiis unam veram eluderet. Cui scripto aliud oppositum Cloppen-burgius. Ut quae dicunt Adversarii de Christo, vero & naturali Dei Filio, omnia nullius facienda sint, ad fucum modo compota & impostu-ram, quasi magnum aliquod Christo tribuerent, & Deitatem, interim supra hominem, & humanam conditionem, quamvis divinis donis decoratam, & sic quasi deificatam, non adscendentes. Adeo, quod de Arianis olim Hilarius, Adversariis nostris summo jure adscribimus: Tri-buunt[?] Christo Dei nomen, quia hoc & hominibus fit tributum. Fatentur Dei vere filium, quia sacramento Baptismi vere Dei filius unusquisque perficitur. Ante tempora & secula confitentur, quod de angelis & diabolis non est negandum. Ita Domino Christo sola illa tribuuntur, quae sunt vel angelorum propria, vel nostra. Caeterum quod Deo Christo legitimum & verum est, Christus Deus verus, id est, eadem esse filii, quae patris divinitas, denegatur. libro contra Auxentium Mediolanensem. Apertius vero Johannes Sommerus contra Carolium, lib. 2. cap. v. suorum mentem de Christo dicto naturali Dei filio exponit, & palam asserit: Christus nusquam naturalis Dei filius dicitur: sed est [illegible, ~2 letters] φύσει filius Dei, sicut gentes κατὰ[?] φύσιν in oleam insitæ sunt. Quando concesssimus ista dici posse, eo sensu concesssimus, quo proprius dicitur, nempe valde amatus & charus.
units.tr: And so we have vindicated our faith, and Christ's true sonship from the Father, through eternal generation, or the communication of the divine essence, against the adulterated exposition of the Adversaries, both the Socinians and the Remonstrants. These have been answered admirably by Altingius in his Theologia Elenctica, page 149 and following, and by Triglandius, Disputation 9 against the Remonstrant Apology. By what we have already said on this subject we consider laboured Smalcius' treatise on the divinity of Christ to be enervated, and the many things he has so lengthily sought out about the divinity of Christ, so that by various fictitious deities he might evade the one true God. Against that writing Cloppenburg has set another. Whatever the Adversaries say about Christ, the true and natural Son of God, is all to be disregarded, put together only as a veneer and a deception, as if they attributed to Christ something great, and yet did not rise to a Deity above man and the human condition, though adorned with divine gifts, and so as it were deified. So, what Hilary once said of the Arians we rightly attribute to our Adversaries with the highest justice: They attribute to Christ the name of God, because this is also given to men. They confess him to be truly the Son of God, because every one is made truly a son of God by the sacrament of baptism. They confess him before times and ages, which must not be denied of angels and devils. Thus to the Lord Christ are attributed only those things which are either proper to angels or to us. But what is lawful and true for God, that Christ is true God, that is, that the Son has the same divinity as the Father, is denied; so Hilary in his book against Auxentius of Milan. More openly still, John Sommer, against Karl, book 2, chapter 5, sets out the mind of his party about the so-called natural Son of God, and openly asserts: Christ is nowhere called the natural Son of God; but he is the Son of God by nature [φύσει], just as the Gentiles, contrary to nature [κατὰ φύσιν], have been grafted into the olive tree. When we conceded that these things can be said, we conceded them in the sense in which "proper" is used, namely greatly beloved and dear. They nevertheless say that Christ is the natural Son of God; but the deception must be exposed in the word or concession "natural Son": a son is not natural if he is begotten from nature, or is of the same nature, a partner by generation; but he is the Son of God as soon as he is born, or greatly beloved, and not...

units.la: Dicunt tamen Christum naturalem Dei Filium: sed detegendus fucus est in verbo vel concessione filii naturalis: quod non est ex natura genitus filius, vel ejusdem naturæ, per generationem, consors; sed quam primum natus, Dei filius, vel amatus valde, non autem naturæ ejusdem generatione talis.
units.tr: They say, however, that Christ is the natural Son of God. But the trick lies in the word "natural" as applied to the Son: it does not mean a son begotten from the nature of God, or one who by generation shares that same nature. It means one who, as soon as he is born, is a son of God, or one who is greatly loved, and not one who is such by generation of the same nature.

units.la: Socinus, contra Wiekum, cap. v. Dico igitur, Naturalem filium hic, secundum ipsorum adversariorum verba, opponi Adoptivo sive Ascititio filio, id est, ei qui, cum aliquando non esset filius, postea ex gratia & beneficio factus est filius. Ergo, qui filius natus est & filius semper fuit, ut profecto adoptivus sive ascititius filius non erit, & consequenter erit naturalis filius. nam quid alioqui etiam aliud Naturalis est, quam Natura sua talis, id est natus talis? natus, sed quod à natura & vi ejus, cumque ea conveniens, naturale dicitur. Namq;liberi fidelium, vel ab alterutro parente fideli nati, statim ac ex fœderatis nati, sancti sunt & filii Dei, non tamen naturales Dei filii. 1 Cor. vii.14. Et filius statim ac natus, Rex aut princeps est, non naturalis propterea, quia non vi & jure naturæ, sed politico ordine talis evadit aut nascitur. Ergo, si nihil aliud fit, Christus propterea filius Dei naturalis dicendus non est, quod statim ac natus talis fuit. Deinde aliquid singulare in eo constituunt, quod, ut ferant Christum dici naturalem Dei Filium, ajunt, statim ac natus fuit, quod non tantum ipsis sonat, statim ac extitit, sed statim ac genitus fuit, id est, ut ex generatione, quamvis non ejusdem essentiæ communione, habeat istam filiationem naturalem. Nam Angelos fatentur quidem etiam nunquam non fuisse Dei filios, utpote tales ab ipso initio creatos, sed non natos: Christum vero in ipsa nativitate accepisse vel conceptione, materiæ aliquid à Deo Patre in virgine creatum, quod cum materia ex matris substantia sumtâ corpus ejus constituerit, unde non minus Deus ejus Pater dici debeat, ac Maria mater. Et hinc sc. naturalis ille Dei Filius.
units.tr: Socinus, against Wiekus, ch. v. I say, then, that "natural son," according to our opponents' own words, is here opposed to an adoptive or ascititious son, that is, one who, since at some time he was not a son, was afterwards made a son by grace and favour. Therefore, one who was born a son and always was a son will certainly not be an adoptive or ascititious son, and consequently will be a natural son. For what else is "natural" besides being such by its nature, that is, born such? It is not born, but what comes from nature and its power and agrees with it is called natural. For the children of believers, or those born of one believing parent, are holy and sons of God as soon as they are born within the covenant, yet they are not natural sons of God. 1 Cor. 7:14. Likewise a son who is king or prince from the moment of his birth is not natural for that reason, because he does not become such by the right and force of nature but by political order. Therefore, if nothing else is the case, Christ is not to be called the natural Son of God merely because he was such as soon as he was born. Next, they make something singular of him: to justify calling Christ the natural Son of God, they say that he was such as soon as he was born, which for them does not merely mean as soon as he existed, but as soon as he was begotten; that is, by generation, though not by communion of the same essence, he has that natural sonship. For they admit that the angels too were never not sons of God, as created such from the beginning, but they were not born. Christ, however, in his very birth or conception, received from God the Father something created in the virgin as matter, which, together with matter taken from the substance of the mother, formed his body. Hence God his Father ought to be called no less his Father than Mary is his mother. And hence that natural Son of God.

units.la: Resp. Sic & Smalcius, contra Smiglecium, se explicat, de vero & naturali Dei filio, cap. iv. & viii. Negant Christum vel proprie, vel tantum adoptivum filium, quia nunquam non Dei filius fuit; quia autem à nativitate, & per nativitatem talis, quamvis non ejusdem cum Deo naturæ, seu essentiæ, naturalem appellant, id est, natum talem. Verum id non dicitur naturale, quod quis habet vel est, statim ac natus, sed quod à natura & vi ejus, cumque
units.tr: Reply. Smalcius, against Smiglecius, explains himself in the same way: concerning the true and natural Son of God, ch. iv. and viii. They deny that Christ is an adoptive son, either properly or merely, because he was never not the Son of God. But because he is such from and by his birth, although not of the same nature or essence as God, they call him natural, that is, born such. But that is not called natural which someone has or is as soon as he is born; what is natural is what comes from nature and its power and agrees with it.

units.la: Socinus,contra Wiekum. cap. v.classe iii. arg. 1. p. 337. Nam cum ipsa Virgo ad Angelum dixisset, Quomodo fiet istud? quoniam virum non agnosco, statim Angelus respondit, Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Quod omnino perinde est, ac si dixisset, Quod viri opera in homine gignendo fieri solet, hic virtutis divinæ opera fiet. Nec sane consequitur, quia Christus homo in virgine utero, ex ipsa Dei substantia non fit genitus, idcirco ex sola Virginis substantia eum fuisse generatum. nec Mennonitæ danda est occasio, ejusmodi male conclusis rationibus, in suo er-
units.tr: Socinus, against Wiekus, ch. v., class iii., arg. 1, p. 337. For when the Virgin herself said to the angel, "How shall this be, since I know not a man?", the angel at once answered, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." This is entirely the same as if he had said: what is usually done by the work of a man in begetting a human being will here be done by the work of divine power. Nor does it follow that because Christ as man was not begotten from the very substance of God in the virgin's womb, he was therefore begotten from the substance of the Virgin alone. Nor should the Mennonites be given an occasion, by such badly drawn conclusions, in their error.

units.la: Resp. Quando Angelus dixit, quod Spiritus Sanctus superventurus esset Mariæ atque eam obumbraturus, non id prorsus voluit, quod effecturus esset Spiritus Sanctus in Maria, quod viri opera in gignendo fieri solet; sed simpliciter non necesse esse ut exciperet se viru non nosse, & putaret sine eo concipere se non posse aut parere, Dei Spiritum hoc effecturum opus, & pro absente viro satis fore: non autem quod ista spiritus operatio futura esset in virgine, quæ alias viri. Nam quod dicit, non ex sola matris substantia Christi corpus generatum fuisse, sed & rore perseverandi: sed quemadmodum urgendum est, Christum hominem ex Virgine matre non minus sumpsisse, quàm alii homines ex suis matribus sumant: sumere autem, ex ipsis sacris litteris & physicis etiam, si opus sit, rationibus demonstrandum: sic non est negandum, Dei virtutem in Virginis uterum substantiam aliquam creatam immisisse, aut ibi creasse, ex quo Christus, iuncto eo, quod ex ipsius Virginis substantia sumpsit, verus homo generatus fuerit: qui propterea, ut homo, non matrem tantum, nempe Virginem ipsam, habuerit, sed patrem quoque, nempe ipsum Deum. alia insuper aliquâ à Deo Patre in virgi-nis uterum immissâ, vel ibi creatâ, hoc, praeterquam quod ex illo Lucae testimonio ostendi minime potest, nulla nititur ratione. Inter Mennonitas haud defuerunt, qui nescio quae de femine Patris, ex quo Christus prodiisset, fuerunt nugati, neque dissimilia sunt, quae Socinus hic profert. Reponimus autem, quum, uti palam omnibus notum, entia haud sint multiplicanda citra necessitatem, quod ex ingenio, citra necessitatem, & ullum sacrum testimonium, talia sive de femine aliquo Pa-tris, vero an analogico, aut substantia à se demissa in Virginis uterum, ibive creatâ, prolata locum apud nos ullum haud mereantur. Praeterea & obscurare videntur virginis concipientis miraculum, ubi nec viri, nec similis aliqua accesserit opera, sed ejus sola materia, per singularem Dei & miraculosam operationem, citra aliud femen, vel feminis aliquod instar, vim & potentiam accepit faetificandi. Augustinus quatuor facit generationis humanae modos vel exempla, Serm. xx. ad fratres in eremo: Primus sine masculo & sine fæmina, ut Adam: secundus, de masculo sine fæmina, ut Eva de Adam. Tertius, de masculo & fæmina, ut Abel. Quartus, de fæmina, sine masculo, ut Salvator mundi, qui de beata Virgine pro nobis nasci dignatus est.
units.tr: Reply. When the angel said that the Holy Spirit would come upon Mary and overshadow her, he did not mean at all what the Holy Spirit would bring about in Mary, namely what is usually done by a man's work in begetting; he meant simply that it was not necessary for her to object that she knew no man, and to think she could neither conceive nor bear without him: the Spirit of God would accomplish this work and would be enough in place of an absent husband. He did not mean that this operation of the Spirit would be in the virgin in the way it is in a husband's begetting. For as to his saying that the body of Christ was begotten not from the substance of the mother alone but also by the dew of ... [the text here is corrupt; the sense is that the Socinian claim must be met by showing from Scripture and, if need be, physical reasons, that Christ as man took no less from the Virgin mother than other men take from theirs; and it must not be denied that God's power introduced or created in the Virgin's womb some created substance, by which, joined to what he took from the Virgin's own substance, Christ was begotten a true man; who therefore, as man, had not only a mother, the Virgin herself, but also a father, God himself.] Some other substance, sent in or created by God the Father in the virgin's womb, can in no way be shown from that testimony of Luke and rests on no reason. Among the Mennonites there were not lacking those who babbled about I know not what seed of the Father from which Christ came forth, and what Socinus advances here is not unlike it. We reply, however, that since, as is plainly known to all, beings are not to be multiplied without necessity, and since no sacred testimony, but only invention, supports such things, whether a seed of the Father, real or analogical, or a substance sent forth from him and created in the Virgin's womb, they deserve no place among us. Moreover, such things seem to obscure the miracle of the virgin's conception, where no husband's work or any similar thing has intervened, but her matter alone received, through a singular and miraculous operation of God, and without other seed or anything in the place of seed, the power of bringing forth. Augustine makes four modes or examples of human generation, Sermon 20 to the brethren in the desert: The first without male and without female, as Adam; the second from a male without a female, as Eve from Adam; the third from a male and a female, as Abel; the fourth from a female without a male, as the Saviour of the world, who deigned to be born for us of the blessed Virgin.

units.la: Christum adoptivum Dei Filium nunc ajunt Adversarii, nunc iterum negant. Quomodo & Filium naturalem alia ratione ajunt, alia inficiantur. Socinus, pag. 351. Nec tamen illas naturales habuit, id est, cum iis non est conceptus & natus, & idcirco, earum respectu, naturalis Dei filius dici nequit. Quin proprie nullum putant dicendum Filium Dei adoptivum: quia adoptivum significet tantum pro filio quempiam habere, non autem esse reverafilium, quum qui Filii Dei dicuntur, tales etiam sint. Adoptionem autem iis attribui, non propter similitudinem aliquam adoptionis, sed quia uti adoptivi non sunt geniti, ita filii Dei non ex prima sui generatione tales, sed postea facti Dei filii, sive Deo aliquo modo assimilati, qualitatibus quibusdam & donis. Socinus contra Wiekum, jam dicto capite, pag. 237.
units.tr: The adversaries now say that Christ is an adoptive Son of God, and now again they deny it. In the same way they call him a natural Son in one sense and deny it in another. Socinus, p. 351: Nor did he however have those natural sons, that is, he was not conceived and born with them, and therefore cannot be called a natural Son of God with respect to them. Indeed they think that one should properly not call the Son of God adoptive at all, because "adoptive" signifies only having someone as a son, not actually being a true son, whereas those who are called sons of God are truly such. They attribute adoption to them not because of any likeness to adoption, but because, just as adopted sons are not begotten, so the sons of God are not such from their first generation but were made sons of God afterwards, or assimilated to God in some way by certain qualities and gifts. Socinus, against Wiekus, the chapter already cited, p. 237.

units.la: Smalcius, contra Smiglecium, de [illegible, ~3 letters] & naturali Dei Filio, cap. viii. pag. 347. Proprie loquendo, ne homines quidem ipsi, qui Dei filii sunt, adoptivi Dei filii dici debent, quamvis nec nati sint ab initio, nec creati Dei filii, adoptivus enim filius is est, qui pro filio quidem habetur, sed tamen revera non est filius. Atqui homines, qui Dei filii sunt aut dicuntur, praesertim Christiani, revera sunt Dei filii, ut quidem filios Deus generat. propterea eos ge-nuisse Deus dicitur, ut supra, sacris testimoniis citatis, ostendimus. nemo vero dicet, se genuisse
units.tr: Smalcius, against Smiglecius, concerning the natural Son of God, ch. viii., p. 347: Properly speaking, not even men themselves who are or are called sons of God ought to be called adoptive sons of God, although they were neither born from the beginning nor created sons of God; for an adoptive son is one who is indeed held as a son but is not really a son. But men who are or are called sons of God, especially Christians, really are sons of God, since God does indeed beget sons. Therefore God is said to have begotten them, as we have shown above from the sacred testimonies cited. But no one will say that he begot

units.la: Resp. Adoptivus filius, non est quidem proprius filius, seu genitus, attamen revera est filius. Transit enim in nomen, jus, & bona familiae, & cum genito ac naturali paria omnia habet, excepto eo, quod non sit genitus, cujus in locum adoptio inventa, quasi adsimilata generatio. Definitur à Jcc. quod sit legitima alicujus in locum filii electio. Adoptivus ergo vere filius, quamvis non genitus, & cum filiis caetera omnia habet communia. Hinc adoptio aliis adfiliatio dicta. Graecis υἱοθεσία[?], inter filios collocatio. Et si revera parens adoptivus, est revera & filius adoptivus. II. Adoptio fidelibus vere adscribitur & proprie, ut significetur, non natura eos esse filios, sed jure adoptionis, quae adoptio non solum indicat, quid non, sed etiam quid, atque unde sint Dei Filii. Parum enim est dicere, ideo adoptivos filios appellari, quod ab initio nec nati, nec creati sint Dei filii: neque in regeneratione, quae nobis a Deo contingit, fundanda ratio nostrae filiationis, sed in adoptione. Quando Paulus dixit, nos expectare υἱοθεσίαν [?], Rom. viii. 23. intellexit ejus perfectionem, & consummationem, in plena hominis liberatione & gloria. Nam certe plene quidem erimus Dei filii, facti filii resurrectionis, sed non quasi non etiam nunc filii Dei sumus, namque Rom. viii. 15. inquit Apostolus, nos jam accepisse spiritum adoptionis, quo clamamus Abba Pater, & verf. 14. quotquot spiritu Dei aguntur, ii sunt Filii Dei. Et Gal. iv. 5. 6. 7. Vt adoptionem filiorum adipisceremur. Quoniam vero estis filii, misit Deus spiritum Filii sui in corda vestra, clamantem, Abba, Pater. Adeo ut non sis jam servus, sed filius. III. Fundamentum autem filiationis nostrae est adoptio, non vero regeneratio, seu ea actio, quia nos Deus dicitur regignere: non quod haud a Deo in conversione regignamur, vel regeneratio non fit necessaria, sed quod ad aliud tendat, quam ad filiationem. Probatur a. quia haec fundata est non in nobis, sed, extra nos, in Christo, & conjuncta cum nostri justificatione. Quos enim Deus justificat, adoptat quoq; in filios, & Christus est fundamentum hujus, atque illius, Rom. viii. 17. Si vero filii, & haeredes: haeredes quidem Dei, coharedes autem Christi. Non propter aliquid in nobis, sed propter solum Christum, in quo & per quem fideles justificamur, & in hoc nos constitutos Deus pro filiis adoptat: unde Pater Christi & nostrum dicitur. Deus Christi & nostrum. Ioann. xx. 17. Deinde, Filium Dei fieri est res juris & dignitatis, easque excellentissimae, non virtutis alicujus nostrae, aut in probitate nostra vitae vel operibus acquirendae: ἐξουσία [?], dicitur Joann. 1.12. Quotquot eum acceperunt, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri. Gal. iv. 5. Vt eos qui sub lege redimeret, ut υἱοθεσίαν [?] adoptionem acciperemus. Est dignitas, quam in Christo, ex ejus justificatione & redemtione adipiscimur. γ. filiatio nostra est perfecta, regeneratio imperfecta: ergo non hinc fluit, sed ex justificatione, quae similiter perfecta est, & simul ac semel fidelibus contingit [?] in Christo. δ. Nedum ut talis regeneratio filiationis fundamentum sit, qualem Adversarii docent, quae nequidem singularem Dei in homine actionem, qua ei novae vitae habitus efficaciter ingeneretur, significat; tantummodo vitae in melius mutationem, quam ipse homo, ad hoc praedicatione Evangelii incitatus, peragit. Regeneratio tamen, quamvis ad hoc non faciat, ut relationem filiationis nostrae proprie constituat, omnino tamen necessaria est, ad novam vitam, quae absque singulari illa Dei in nobis actione non est, qua sola, & nequidquam ex nobis, principium novae ac sanctioris vitae confertur, efficiendam vel progignendam. Et hujus mutationis vel novationis ipsetu, propter similem tum Dei vim, tum nostram ad spiritualem nostri vivificationem impotentiam, actio illa Dei appellatur generatio, creatio, suscitatio a mortuis, &c. Igitur non in nostra ulla actione, vel etiam regeneratione proprie, sed adoptione gratiosa, quae cum justificatione jungitur, & ejus quasi pars est, filiatio nostra sita est. Nos adoptivi Dei filii; Christus naturalis.
units.tr: The adoptive son is not indeed a son by birth or begotten, yet he is truly a son. For he passes into the name, the right and the goods of the family, and has all things equal with the begotten and natural son, except that he is not begotten. Adoption was devised in place of generation, as a kind of imitated generation. The jurists define it as the lawful choice of someone in the place of a son. So the adoptive son is truly a son, though not begotten, and he has all other things in common with the sons. Hence adoption is also called affiliation by others, and by the Greeks sonship by adoption [υἱοθεσία], that is, placement among the sons. And if the adoptive parent is truly a parent, so the adoptive son is truly a son. II. Adoption is rightly and properly ascribed to believers, to signify that they are sons of God not by nature but by the right of adoption. This adoption shows not only what they are not but also what they are, and from what source they are sons of God. For it is not enough to say that they are called adoptive sons because they were neither begotten nor created as sons of God from the beginning. The ground of our sonship is not to be laid in regeneration, which comes to us from God, but in adoption. When Paul said that we await the adoption [υἱοθεσία] (Rom. 8:23), he meant its perfection and completion in the full deliverance and glory of man. For certainly we shall be fully the sons of God, having become sons of the resurrection, yet we are not, as it were, not even now the sons of God. For in Rom. 8:15 the Apostle says that we have already received the spirit of adoption, by which we cry, Abba, Father; and in v. 14, as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. And Gal. 4:5–7: that we might receive the adoption of sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. So that you are no longer a servant, but a son. III. The foundation of our sonship, however, is adoption, not regeneration, or that act by which God is said to beget us again. This is not because we are not begotten again by God in conversion, or because regeneration is not necessary, but because it aims at something other than sonship. This is proved first: adoption is grounded not in us but outside us, in Christ, and is joined with our justification. For whom God justifies, he also adopts as sons, and Christ is the foundation of both, Rom. 8:17: if indeed sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, but fellow heirs with Christ. It is not on account of anything in us, but on account of Christ alone, in whom and through whom believers are justified, and God, placing us in him, adopts us as sons; hence he is called the Father of Christ and of us: my God and your God (John 20:17). Second, to become a son of God is a matter of right and dignity, and a most excellent one, not something acquired by any virtue of ours or by the uprightness of our life or works. It is called power [ἐξουσία] in John 1:12: as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God. Gal. 4:5: that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive adoption [υἱοθεσία]. It is a dignity which we obtain in Christ through his justification and redemption. Third, our sonship is perfect, while regeneration is imperfect; therefore sonship does not flow from regeneration but from justification, which is likewise perfect, and which comes to believers in Christ at once and once for all. Fourth, regeneration is by no means the foundation of sonship in the way the Adversaries teach it, since it does not even signify that singular action of God in a man by which a habit of new life is effectively engendered in him. It signifies only a change for the better in life, which man himself accomplishes, spurred on to this by the preaching of the Gospel. Yet regeneration, although it does not properly constitute the relation of our sonship, is nonetheless wholly necessary for the new life, which does not exist without that singular action of God in us, by which alone, and not from ourselves (which would be in vain), the principle of a new and holier life is conferred so that it may be brought about and begotten. And because of the very nature of this change or renewal, and because of the similar power of God on the one hand and our powerlessness for our own spiritual quickening on the other, that action of God is called generation, creation, raising from the dead, and so on. Therefore our sonship rests not in any action of ours, nor even properly in regeneration, but in gracious adoption, which is joined with justification and is, as it were, a part of it. We are adoptive sons of God; Christ is the natural Son.

units.la: Adoptivum tamen etiam Filium Christum appellari posse hactenus concedit Socinus, quatenus & nos Christiani, id est, quod postquam genitus Christus, similitudinem illam cum Deo adeptus est; in qua-formam filiationis constituit.
units.tr: Socinus concedes so far that Christ too may be called an adoptive Son, inasmuch as we Christians are such, namely because, after Christ was begotten, he obtained that likeness to God in which he established the form of sonship.

units.la: Iam dictum est, cum filium naturalem esse, propterea quia natus sit Dei filius. verum cum filiatio ex Deo similitudine potissimum continetur, quam quis cum Deo habeat, potest ipse Christus, quatenus propter hanc causam, praeter illam, quod existentiam suam per Dei actionem & operationem habet similem ei, per quam exsistunt ii, qui ex patris sui substantia sunt geniti, Dei filius est, non modo naturalis, sed etiam adoptivus Dei filius dici, eo sensu, quo, ut dictum est, scriptura homines Christianos adoptivos Dei filios vocat: nempe, quia similitudinem, quam cum Deo habet, non in ipsa conceptione et nativitate habuit, sed postea ex Dei dono & gratia illam adeptus est: quae quanto major & multiplicior (ut ita dicam) in dies in illo fuit, tanto excellentior Dei filius est factus, & non semel, neque una ratione a Deo genitus: non declaratione tantum, ut ex parte sensisse Hilarius (in Psalm. 2.) videtur, qui cum & in nativitate ex virgine, & in baptismo, & in resurrectione a mortuis generatum a Deo fuisse, agnoscit: sed etiam effectu ipso, id est, per adeptionem ejus cum Deo similitudinis, quam antea vel omnino non habebat, vel non tantam.
units.tr: It has already been said that he is a natural Son because he was born as the Son of God. But since sonship is contained chiefly in the likeness which someone has to God, Christ himself, as far as this cause is concerned, besides that other reason (that he has his existence through the action and operation of God, similar to that by which those who are born of their father's substance come into being), can be called not only the natural Son of God but also the adoptive Son of God, in the sense in which, as has been said, Scripture calls Christian men adoptive sons of God. Namely, because the likeness which he has with God he did not have in his very conception and birth, but afterwards obtained it by the gift and grace of God. And the greater and the more manifold this likeness became in him from day to day (so to speak), the more excellent a Son of God he was made, and he was begotten by God not once nor in one way only. Not merely by declaration, as Hilary seems in part to have thought (on Psalm 2), who acknowledges that he was begotten by God both at his birth from the Virgin, and at his baptism, and at his resurrection from the dead. But also by the effect itself, that is, through his obtaining that likeness with God which before he either did not have at all or did not have to such a degree.

units.la: Resp. Nequaquam vero Christus adoptivus Dei Filius nuncupari potest, non ob hoc etiam, quod Christiani tales: quia ejus filiatio diversissimi generis haberi semper debet a nostra. Quod bene contra Nestorium primo, tum etiam seculo octavo contra Elipandum Toletanae urbis, & Felicem UrgelitanumEpiscopum tuita fuit pia antiquitas, qui Christum, saltem secundum humanam naturam docebant, filium Dei esse adoptivum: sed condemnati, cum in aliis Synodis fuere, tum praesertim Francofurtensi, a. DCCXCIV. In hoc tamen diffabat illorum sententia a Sociniana, quod etiam fatebantur in Christo divinam naturam, quodque ejus ratione Dei filius esset naturalis & proprius, sed humanae naturae respectu dicendum esse adoptivum, urgebant. Contra, unum Dei Filium dixerunt Patres, ab aeterno a Patre genitum, non alium, non secundum adoptivum etiam aliquem, e Maria natum, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum verum Dei Filium, non putativum: proprium, non adoptivum: aequalem & coaeternum Patri sanctoque Spiritui. uti loquitur Paulinus, Aquilejensis episcopus, in libello Sacrosyllabo, exhibito in Concilio Francofurtensi, & seorsim quoque excuso, una cum Opusculo Caroli Magni, contra imagines, a. DCCXLIX. legiturque in Bibliotheca Patrum, Tomo quarto. Opponebant passim adoptivum Filium proprio, ut simul nemo posset dici filius Dei adoptivus, & proprius. Carolus M. in epistola ad Elipandum Toletanum, in Actis Concilii Francofurtensis, Ut qui erat in divinitate Dei Patris Filius, esset & in humanitate hominis Matris filius: perfectus in divinitate Deus, perfectus in humanitate homo: Deus ante omnia saecula, homo in fine saeculi: verus in utraque substantia Dei Filius: non putativus, sed verus: non adoptione, sed proprietate. Paulinus, in illo suo libro: adoptivus dici non potest, nisi is qui alienus est ab eo, a quo dicitur adoptatus: & gratia ei adoptio tribuitur; quoniam non ex debito, sed ex indulgentia tantummodo adoptio praestatur: sicut nos aliquando, cum essemus peccando Filii irae, alieni eramus a Deo, per proprium & verum Filium ejus, qui non egui t adoptione, adoptio nobis filiorum donata est: Paulo attestante, qui ait, cum ergo venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum sub lege, ut eos qui sub lege erant, redimeret, ut adoptionem filiorum reciperemus per filium ipsum. Proprius factus est ex muliere, non adoptivus. Quia ergo proprium tuebantur Christum Dei Filium, uni-eumque, negabant adoptivum. In aliquo Fausto nostro, cum Felice illo conveniebat (felix nomine, actu infelix, dicebat de eo Jonas, Aurelianensis episcopus, lib. 1. contra
units.tr: Reply: Christ cannot by any means be called the adoptive Son of God, not even on this ground that Christians are such, because his sonship must always be held to be of a wholly different kind from ours. This was rightly maintained by ancient piety against Nestorius first, and then in the eighth century against Elipandus, bishop of the city of Toledo, and Felix, bishop of Urgel, who taught that Christ, at least according to his human nature, was the adoptive Son of God. But they were condemned, both at other synods and especially at Frankfurt in 794. Yet their opinion differed from the Socinian one in this: they also confessed the divine nature in Christ, and they insisted that on account of it he was the natural and proper Son of God, while with respect to his human nature he was to be called adoptive. On the contrary, the Fathers spoke of one Son of God, begotten from the Father from eternity, not another, nor one who was also adoptive in some sense, born of Mary: our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, not putative; proper, not adoptive; equal and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. So speaks Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, in the little book Sacrosyllabus, presented at the Council of Frankfurt and also printed separately, together with the work of Charlemagne against images, in 794; it is read in the Bibliotheca Patrum, volume four. Everywhere they set the adoptive Son against the proper Son, so that no one could be called both adoptive and proper Son of God. Charlemagne, in his letter to Elipandus of Toledo, in the Acts of the Council of Frankfurt: He who was the Son of God the Father in divinity, was also the son of man's mother in humanity: perfect God in divinity, perfect man in humanity; God before all ages, man at the end of the age; true Son of God in each substance: not putative but true, not by adoption but by property. Paulinus, in that book of his: He cannot be called adoptive except one who is a stranger to him by whom he is said to be adopted; and adoption is granted to him by grace, since adoption is bestowed not from debt but only from indulgence. Just as we, when we were sons of wrath through sinning, were strangers to God, adoption as sons was given to us through his proper and true Son, who did not need adoption, as Paul bears witness, who says: when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons through the Son himself. He was made proper of a woman, not adoptive. Therefore, because they defended Christ as the proper and only Son of God, they denied that he was adoptive. In one of our Faustus, they agreed with that Felix (Jonas, bishop of Orléans, in book 1 against

units.la: Tom.2. Claudium Taurinensem: non minus ac noster infaustus Faustus) quod adoptivum Christum uterque admittit: diffensus vero, quod Felix etiam concedebat Filium esse, essentiae divinae ratione, naturalem. Paulinus, in Sacrofyllabo, Dei ergo filius qua ratione credi potest adoptivus, qui infeperabiliter adsumpto homine in una persona, coeunte utraque natura, non duo filii, alius Dei, & alius hominis, ut, sicut illi errando aestimant, adoptivus sit hominis filius, & sine adoptione Dei filius, sed in una persona unus idemque Dei & hominis filius?
units.tr: Tom. 2. against Claudius of Turin: no less than our unlucky Faustus) that both admit an adoptive Christ. They differ, however, in that Felix also conceded that the Son is natural by reason of the divine essence. Paulinus, in the Sacrosyllabus: By what reason, then, can the Son of God be believed to be adoptive, when, with the human nature assumed ineffably into one person, both natures come together, so that there are not two sons, one of God and another of man, such that, as those men wrongly suppose, he is an adoptive son of man and a son of God without adoption, but in one person there is one and the same Son of God and man?

units.la: Jam & Filium Dei unigenitum μονογενῆ [?] appellari vere Christum, & esse, ita evertere conatur Socinus, quod talis dicatur propter excellentiam dumtaxat supra alios Dei filios, quia pluribus modis aliis Dei filiis omnibus antecellit, licet non ipse solus sit ex cogenitus. Quam excellentiam praesertim in duobus collocat, quod prae aliis omnibus a Patre sit dilectus, & paternus haeres: addit tertium, quod primus omnium sub N. T. Dei filius fuerit, ante suam etiam resurrectionem, quo tempore nullus adhuc talis erat Dei filius, ac pro conditione N. T. oportet esse eos, qui ista appellatione sint digni.
units.tr: Socinus also tries to overturn the view that Christ truly is and is called the only-begotten [μονογενῆ?] Son of God, arguing that he is so called only on account of his excellence above the other sons of God, since he surpasses all the other sons of God in several respects, although he is not the only one begotten of him. He places this excellence chiefly in two things: that he is loved by the Father above all others, and is the Father's heir. He adds a third: that he was the first of all the sons of God under the New Testament, even before his own resurrection, at a time when no one else yet was such a son of God, and under the New Testament conditions it is fitting that those who are worthy of that title should be such.

units.la: Contra Wiekum, cap.v.
units.tr: Against Wiekum, chapter 5.

units.la: Respondeo, imo jure Christum vocari unigenitum, id est, unicum Dei filium, nec tamen hinc sequi, illum genitum esse ex substantia Dei Patris. nec sane debuit ex tam debili ratiocinatione concludi id, quod, ut antea docuimus, nulla ratione fieri potest. Christus enim unigenitus Dei filius merito appellatur, quia pluribus modis, aliis Dei filiis omnibus antecellit, licet non ipse solus sit ex eo genitus: siquidem & alij ex Deo geniti seu nati sunt, Ioh. 1. v. 13. Iac. 1. v. 18. 1 Ioh. 3. v. 9. & 10. nam alibi etiam in sacris litteris unigenitum filium, sive unicum, dici illum, qui non solus ex patre suo est genitus, probat exemplum Isaaci, qui unigenitus Abrahami filius appellatur, Gen. 22. v. 2. & 12. Heb. 11. v. 17. certum siquidem est, eo ipso tempore, pro quo ita appellatur, non solum ipsum Isaacum extitisse, Abrahamo genitum, sed etiam Ismaelem. quod exemplum rei nostrae accommodatissimum censeri debet: cum dubium non sit, quin Isaacus Christi typus fuerit. Quemadmodum igitur Isaacus propterea unigenitus Abrahami filius est appellatus, quia pluribus modis fratrem suum Ismaelem ex eodem patre genitum antecellebat: sic Christus merito unigenitus Dei filius est dictus, quia fratres suos ex eodem patre Deo genitos pluribus modis antecellit.
units.tr: I reply: rather, Christ is rightly called the only-begotten, that is, the unique Son of God, and yet it does not follow from this that he was begotten of the substance of God the Father. Indeed, that which, as we taught above, cannot be brought about in any way, ought not to have been inferred from so weak an argument. For Christ is rightly called the only-begotten Son of God because he surpasses all the other sons of God in several ways, although he is not the only one begotten of him. For others too are begotten or born of God, John 1:13, James 1:18, 1 John 3:9–10. Elsewhere in Sacred Scripture the example of Isaac proves that the only son, or the unique son, is called the one who is not the only one begotten of his father. Isaac is called the only-begotten son of Abraham, Gen. 22:2 and 12, Heb. 11:17. It is certain that at the very time for which he is so called, not only Isaac himself but also Ishmael had been begotten of Abraham. This example ought to be considered most suitable to our case, since there is no doubt that Isaac was a type of Christ. Just as Isaac was therefore called the only-begotten son of Abraham because he surpassed his brother Ishmael, begotten of the same father, in several ways, so Christ is rightly called the only-begotten Son of God because he surpasses his brothers, who were begotten of God the same Father, in several ways.

units.la: Primum, ut ille, paterna erga se dilectione: quae potissima hujus rei videtur esse causa. Hinc Resp. 1. Mirum vero, cum Scriptura non modo Christum Dei Filium dicat, sed & a Deo genitum, & unigenitum, quod tamen Adversarii illum a Deo proprie genitum nolint, sed metaphorice tantum & per excellentiam sic dictum. Quid si Deus dixisset, Filium ex substantia Dei Patris natum? neque sic defuturam Adversariis exceptionem autumo. Adeo ingeniosa & felix ad inveniendam quaecumq; effugia haeresis. [illegible, ~5 letters] Quod autem addit, nulla ratione generationem illam fieri posse, non docebit unquam. 11. Appellatur, inquit Socinus, unigenitus Dei Filius, licet non sit solus ex eo genitus: hoc vero est negare, eum esse unigenitum: contra apertum Scripturae testimonium, & manifestissimam veritatem, qua qui Dei est filius, uti Christus, unigenitus Dei filius est, & non alius esse potest. Uti enim alii plures dicuntur Dei filii ex communi generatione, vel adoptione, nemo tamen eorum, utcunque multis saepe modis excellentior aliis non potest tamen dici unigenitus; ita Christus qui solus Patris est unigenitus, id habere nequit propter aliquod sibi cum aliis Dei filiis commune, licet excelsiori modo sibi communicatum, sive dilectionis divinae, gloriae, aut haereditatis: sed uniSalomon Prov. 4. v. 3. dicit, se fuisse unigeni-tum coram matre sua, quamvis non esset solus ex eadem matre Davidi natus, ex expresse habetur 1 Paral. 3. v. 3. nempe, quia praeter alios matri suae carus erat. Propterea Graeca translatio tam in duobus illis Genef. locis c. 22. quam in hoc Proverb. 4. pro eo, quod in Latina habetur unigenitum, habet ἀγαπητὴν seu ἀγαπητωμένην [?], id est Dilectum seu Amatum, est autem in Hebraeo vox Iehid, quae proprie significat Unicum: quae, cum ad filium refertur, eandem vim omnino habet, quam vox unigenitus, ut, prae-ter rationem manifestam, docet locus Heb. 11. v. 17. ibi enim vox ista Hebraea non in versione tantum Latina unigeniti voce, sed in ipsius auctoris Graecis verbi voce μονογενής, quae unigenitum plane significat, reddita fuit. Atqui eadem vox ad unicam dilectionem significandam usurpata invenitur: ut Pf. 22. (secundum Hebraici codicis numerum) v. 20. & Psal. 35. v. 17. ubi David animam seu vitam suam Iehidathi, id est, unicam meam, vocat. nihil enim homini vita carius. Atque utrobique Graeca translatio habet μονογενῆ [?], id est, unigenitam. Quin Deus ipse, Christi Pater, videtur declarasse, quid sibi vellet excellens ista unigeniti appella-tio Christo tributa, & nomini Filii Dei addita, cum tam in ejus baptismo, quam in transfigu-ratione, ubi illum quam maxime commendare voluit, Filium illum suum dilectum eum appel-lavit, in quo sibi complacuisset: nec quidquam amplius illi tribuit. Ex quo concludi potest, unigeniti appellationem, utpote ad eum commendandum omnium appositissimam, appella-tionem ista illius dilecti filii, fuisse expressam.
units.tr: First, as with Isaac, by the Father's love towards him, which seems to be the chief cause of this. Hence, the first reply. It is strange, however, that Scripture not only calls Christ the Son of God but also says he was begotten of God and is the only-begotten, while our opponents refuse to hold that he was properly begotten of God, saying that he is so called only metaphorically and by excellence. What if God had said that he was born of the substance of God the Father? I suppose our opponents would not then lack an objection either. So ingenious and fortunate is heresy in finding escapes of every kind [illegible]. As for his further claim, that the generation cannot happen in any way, he will never prove it. "He is called," says Socinus, "the only-begotten Son of God, although he is not the only one begotten of him." But this is to deny that he is the only-begotten, against the plain testimony of Scripture and the most manifest truth, by which whoever is the Son of God, as Christ is, is the only-begotten Son of God, and no other can be. For just as many others are called sons of God by common generation or adoption, yet none of them, however much he may often excel others in many ways, can be called the only-begotten, so Christ, who alone is the Father's only-begotten, cannot have this on account of anything he shares with the other sons of God, even if it is communicated to him in a higher way, whether of divine love, glory or inheritance. Rather, Solomon in Prov. 4:3 says that he was an only-begotten before his mother, although he was not the only son born to David from the same mother. This is expressly stated in 1 Chron. 3:3, namely, because he was dear to his mother beyond the others. Therefore the Greek translation, both in those two passages of Genesis 22 and in this one, Prov. 4, has for what the Latin renders as unigenitum [only-begotten] the word ἀγαπητήν or ἀγαπητουμένην [?], that is, beloved or loved. In the Hebrew, however, the word is Iehid, which properly means unique. When referred to a son, it has altogether the same force as the word only-begotten, as the passage Heb. 11:17 shows, apart from the clear reason. For there this Hebrew word was rendered not only by the Latin word unigenitus, but by the very Greek word of the author, μονογενής, which plainly means only-begotten. Yet the same word is found used to signify a unique love, as in Ps. 22 (by the Hebrew numbering) v. 20 and Ps. 35:17, where David calls his soul or life Iehidathi, that is, my unique one, for nothing is dearer to a man than life. In both places the Greek translation has μονογενῆ [?], that is, only-begotten. Indeed God himself, the Father of Christ, seems to have declared what he meant by this excellent title of only-begotten given to Christ and added to the name of Son of God, since both at his baptism and at the transfiguration, where he wished to commend him most highly, he called that Son his beloved, in whom he was well pleased, and gave him nothing further. From this it can be concluded that the title only-begotten, being most suitable for commending him, was expressed in that title of the beloved Son.

units.la: Deinde, quemadmodum Isaac, ut verisimile omnino est, propterea etiam est unigenitus Abrahami filius appellatus, quia solus ei in universa haereditate successurus erat, Gal. 3. v. 40. sic Christus unigenitus Dei filius est dictus, quia solus universorum haeres fuit a Deo constitutus, Heb. 1. v. 2. & sicut in Isaac tantum vocandum erat semen Abrahamo, unigenitus sit oportet, propter aliquid sibi soli proprium, & verae a Patre generationis respectu, non metaphoricae. iii. Quod fideles & pii dicuntur ex Deo geniti, metaphorice intelligendum omnes agnoscimus; sed proinde Christum non posse esse proprie ex Deo genitum laborat [illegible, ~6 letters] τὸ ἐπιμένον [?]. Quia longe alterius generis est Christi filiatio, a nostra, διαφορώτερον ὄνομα. Quod vel ipsa loca adducta, & modus loquendi in iis observatus innuit. De fidelibus dicitur, quod ex Deo geniti, Joann. 1. 13. at verf. 14. seq. Christum esse unigenitum a Patre, ᾧ πατρὸς ibi ἐκ θεοῦ ἐγεννήθησαν, oppositae ad generationem humanam ἐξ αἱμάτων, & σαρκὸς. Quamvis multi illi, qui ex Deo geniti, unus tamen est a Patre genitus Christus: alterius plane generis hic ab illis. Quod nisi esset, Apostolus non simpliciter statim post nominatos plures illos filios appos-uisset, unigenitum a Patre: quin si ex illorum genere habuisset Christum, dixisset potius praecipuum & excellentiorem ex illis filium, non, absque ulla expositione, unigenitum. iv. Deinde & quae ista consequentia? alibi unigenitus dicitur, qui non genitus est ex patre suo solus: ergo hic. Alibi unigenitus significat eum, qui fratribus suis antecessit, vel qui prae caeteris dilectus: ergo hic quoque, ubi de Christo est sermo? negamus sequi. Dicet forte, ergo posse saltem ita hoc exponi quoque de Christo, ubi Dei di-citur unigenitus, & non obstare vocis u-sum aut rationem. Ego contra regero, nec obstare, quamvis multi dicantur Dei filii, ut Christus singulari ratione talis dicatur, quae nequaquam cadat in alios, & ut ob eam vere nominetur unigenitus. Contra sequitur ex argumento Adversarii, quod Christus non sit unigenitus: nam uti quis abusive & non proprie dicisic in solo Christo semen filiorum Dei vocandum fuit, Gal. 3. v. 17. quod, ad unigeniti appellationem tribuendam, maximi momenti esse, nemo, opinor, negaverit.
units.tr: Secondly, just as Isaac was most probably also called the only-begotten son of Abraham because he alone was to succeed to the whole inheritance (Gal. 3:40), so Christ is called the only-begotten Son of God because he alone was appointed heir of all things by God (Heb. 1:2). And just as in Isaac alone the seed of Abraham was to be called, so he must be only-begotten on account of something proper to himself alone, and with respect to a true generation from the Father, not a metaphorical one. Third, we all acknowledge that the faithful and pious are said to be born of God in a metaphorical sense. But from this it does not follow that Christ cannot be properly begotten of God; the sonship of Christ is of a quite different kind from ours, a more distinctive name [διαφορώτερον ὄνομα]. This the passages cited themselves, and the manner of speaking in them, indicate. Of the faithful it is said that they are born of God, John 1:13. But in v. 14 following, Christ is said to be the only-begotten of the Father, ᾧ πατρὸς, where ibid. they are born ἐκ θεοῦ, set over against human generation ἐξ αἱμάτων and σαρκὸς. Although those many who are born of God are many, Christ alone is begotten of the Father; he is of a quite different kind from them. If this were not so, the Apostle would not have simply added, straight after naming those many sons, the words only-begotten of the Father; indeed, if he had reckoned Christ among their kind, he would have said rather that he was the foremost and most excellent of those sons, not, without any further explanation, the only-begotten. Fourth, what kind of inference is this? Elsewhere someone is called only-begotten who is not the only one begotten of his father; therefore here too. Elsewhere "only-begotten" signifies one who surpassed his brothers, or who was loved beyond the rest; therefore here too, where the subject is Christ? We deny that it follows. Perhaps he will say that it can at least be explained in this way also of Christ, where he is called the only-begotten of God, and that the usage of the word and the reasoning do not stand in the way. I reply on the contrary that they do not stand in the way: although many are called sons of God, Christ is called such by a singular reason, which in no way applies to others, and on account of which he is truly named the only-begotten. On the contrary, it follows from the argument of our opponent that Christ is not the only-begotten. For just as someone is abusively and not properly called [...], so in Christ alone was the seed of the sons of God to be called, Gal. 3:17, which, for the bestowing of the title only-begotten, is of the greatest importance, no one, I think, will deny.

units.la: Adde, quod si quis animadverterit, pro quo tempore Christus unigenitus Dei filius est appellatus, videbit, illi ipsam appellationem convenisse, non modo, quia aliis Dei filiis longe praestabat, sed etiam, quia revera nullus alius homo adhuc talis Dei filius erat, qualem esse oportet cum, qui sub Novo testamento ista appellatione fit dignus, Christus enim pro eo tempore appellatus est unigenitus Dei filius, quod ejus resurrectionem & glorificationem, spiritusque sancti missionem antecessit: quibus rebus factum est, ut tales inter homines Dei filii esse coeperint, quales in hac mortali vita esse possunt. Unde, ut diximus, pro eo tempore, quo sic appellatus fuit, merito Christo unigeniti filii Dei appellatio convenit, etiamsi ea omnino hanc vim haberet, ut omnes alios a vera ex Deo filiatione excluderet. Sed ex ante dictis, ni fallor, constat, eam hanc vim non habere, & singularitatem tantum quandam in eodem ex Dei filiationis genere significare. qua de re, antequam responsionem ad hoc primum hujus tertiae classis argumentum concludamus, aliquid iterum dicemus, & alias causas, cur Christus unigenitus Dei filius dicatur, explicabimus.
units.tr: Add that if anyone considers the time at which Christ was called the only-begotten Son of God, he will see that this title belonged to him not only because he far surpassed the other sons of God, but also because in truth no other man was yet such a son of God as ought to bear that title under the New Testament. For Christ was called the only-begotten Son of God at a time before his resurrection and glorification and the sending of the Holy Spirit. By these things it came about that men began to be sons of God in the way they can be in this mortal life. Hence, as we have said, at the time when he was so called, the title of only-begotten Son of God rightly belonged to Christ, even if it had the force of excluding all others from true sonship from God. But from what has been said before, unless I am mistaken, it is clear that it does not have this force, and signifies only a certain singularity within the same kind of sonship from God. On this account, before we conclude our answer to this first argument of this third class, we will say something more and explain the other reasons why Christ is called the only-begotten Son of God.

units.la: tur unigenitus, ubi ex eodem plures secum geniti: vel non vere Isaac fuit Abrahami, juxta nostros, unigenitus, quamvis ita dictus: ita nec Christus revera unigenitus, cum ejusdem conditionis plures sint una cum eo. v. Isaac appellatur Abrahami, יחיד[?]. Genef. xxii. 2. 12. μονογενὴς Heb. xi. 17. quamvis non solus ex Abrahamo genitus, sed prior eo ex eodem Patre, Ismael. At vero יחיד[?] non proprie & per se significat μονογενὴ unigenitum, sed quavis ratione unicum, unde יחיד[?] solitarii, Psalm. lxviii. 7. & ubique fere vertitur ἀγαπητὸς, exceptis Psalmis; ubi tamen Aquila vertit μονάχον[?]. Sed Judic. xi. 39. ad denotandam unigenitam, plus additur, [illegible, ~6 letters] ip-fa unica, neq; erat ei praeter eam filius aut filia. Apostolus tamen unigenitum dixit. Sed semel ita. Quod certe Christo objici non potest, qui non quovis modo tantum unigenitus, sed unigenitus à Patre, & unigenitus qui in sinu Patris est, verf. 18. & aliquoties unigenitus, & filius unigenitus, ut filiationis, non demum alterius cujusdam excellentiae ratione intelligi debeat, appellatus, Joann. i. 18. & iii. 16. 18. 1 Joann. iv. 9. Quare non est par utriusque, Christi & Isaaci causa, in denominatione unigeniti. vi. Non probat Adversarius, propterea Isaacum fuisse dictum unigenitum, quia pluribus modis fratrem suum Ismaelem ex eodem Patre genitum antecellebat. Contrà imo revera fuit unigenitus, ex Sara nempe; neque enim haec alium unquam filium marito peperit, praeter Isaacum. Atque hic unicus fuit ex promissione filius. Denique is, qui mutati & amplificati nominis parenti causa exstitit. Illud ergo, quod ex Sara, & promissione solus Abrahamo genitus satis causae est, cur dicatur יחיד[?] unicus & unigenitus: propriae genituraे respectu, non alterius cujusdam excellentiae. vii. Non ergo paterna erga se dilectio, potissima hujus rei causa: quia ea exprimitur postquam dictus יחיד[?] filium quem diligis, & in historia Iosephi, illud sic effertur, cap. xxxvii. Et Israel dilexit Iosephum supra omnes filios suos, quia filius senectutis ipsi ei erat. Et hoc modo illud significatur in Scriptura, non per esse יחיד[?] vel unigenitum. Quamvis hoc ipsum, quod quis unigenitus, causa dilectionis singularis exstat. Quae & ratio quod Graeci verterint, utrumque una jungendo, λαβὲ τ̔ ἡὸν σ̔ ἀγαπητόν. Prov. iv. 3. ἡ ἀγαπώμενον ἐν πρόσωπῳ μητρός. viii. Atque ad hunc locum Prov. respondere possum, quamvis יחיד[?] quod[?] proprie unicum sonat, significaret unice dilectum, ex ratione argumenti cui adhibe-tur, non tamen μονογενὴς idem denotare, non ubi de Christo agitur, & saepissime is di-citur Patris sui unigenitus. Deinde in parabolasic dici a Salomone, & introduci filium unigenitum ita loquentem, non proprie ipsum. Tertio & seipsum, pro eo vide-licet tempore, quo matri omnino fuit unigenitus. Ut omnino nihil hinc sequatur ar-gumento nostro adversum. ix. & in Psalmo anima sua Davidi dicitur unica, יחידה [?] quam unicam habuit, & unice caram. Uti quo quid parcius, vel magis unum, carius quoque esse solet. Job 17.4. Sed anima non dicitur unigenita: & si vel ita per similitudinem diceretur, non officeret propriae voci ubi de filio, & generatione ac-cipitur. x. Porro Christum a Patre suo proclamatum palam Filium suum dilec-tum, quis nescit? Sed eo declaratum, quid velit excellens ista unigeniti appellatio Christo tributa & nomini filii Dei addita. Sit ita: sed nec quidquam amplius illi tribui, praeter dilectionem, non etiam generationem veram nomine filii declara-tam, probabit nunquam, vel ut dilectum esse objici vel opponi debeat vere ac pro-prie unigenito: quasi non & unigenitus vere, & dilectus filius simul esse debeat.
units.tr: ...is called only-begotten, where there are several born from the same father with him. Or else, according to our opponents, Isaac was not truly the only-begotten of Abraham, although so called; so neither is Christ truly the only-begotten, since there are several of the same condition along with him. Isaac is called Abraham's יחיד (yachid), Gen. 22:2, 12, and μονογενής (monogenēs), Heb. 11:17, although he was not the only one begotten of Abraham, since Ishmael, from the same father, was born before him. But יחיד does not properly and of itself signify μονογενής, only-begotten, but "unique" in any sense; hence יחיד means solitary, Ps. 68:7, and is almost everywhere rendered ἀγαπητός (beloved), except in the Psalms, where however Aquila renders it μονάχος (solitary). But in Judg. 11:39, to denote the only-begotten, more is added: [illegible, about six letters], she herself the only one, and she had no son or daughter besides her. The Apostle, however, did say only-begotten, but only once. This certainly cannot be objected to Christ, who is called not merely only-begotten in some way, but only-begotten from the Father, and the only-begotten who is in the bosom of the Father, v. 18, and often the only-begotten and the only-begotten Son, so that this must be understood as a matter of his sonship and not on account of some other excellence, John 1:18, 3:16, 18, 1 John 4:9. Therefore the case of Christ and the case of Isaac are not alike in the naming of the only-begotten. vi. The opponent does not prove that Isaac was called the only-begotten because in several ways he surpassed his brother Ishmael, begotten of the same father. On the contrary, he really was the only-begotten, namely of Sarah; for she never bore another son to her husband besides Isaac. And he alone was the son of the promise. Finally, he was the cause of the father's name being changed and enlarged. Therefore that Isaac alone was begotten of Abraham, of Sarah and by promise, is enough reason why he is called יחיד, unique and only-begotten, with respect to his proper begetting, not on account of some other excellence. vii. Therefore paternal love toward him is not the chief cause of this: since that love is expressed after יחיד, "the son whom you love," and in the story of Joseph it is put thus, chap. 37: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he was the son of his old age to him." And in this way Scripture signifies it, not by being יחיד or only-begotten. Although the fact that someone is only-begotten is itself a cause of singular love. This is also why the Greeks translated the two together: λαβὲ τὸν υἱόν σου τὸν ἀγαπητόν, Prov. 4:3, ἠγαπώμενον ἐνώπιον μητρός. viii. And to this passage of Proverbs I can answer that although יחיד properly means "unique," it signifies "uniquely beloved" from the nature of the subject to which it is applied; yet μονογενής does not mean the same thing, nor where it is spoken of Christ, who is very often called the only-begotten of his Father. Further, Solomon is said to speak this in a parable, and the only-begotten son is introduced speaking thus, and not properly himself. Third, Solomon speaks of himself also, namely at that time when he was altogether the only-begotten of his mother. So nothing whatever follows from this against our argument. ix. And in the Psalm, his soul is called יחידה, unique, David's soul, which he had as his only one and dearly loved. Just as what is rarer, or more one, is usually also dearer. Job 17:4.
