But a soul is not called only-begotten; and even if it were so called by way of likeness, this would not hinder the proper term where the son and begetting are meant. x. Moreover, who does not know that Christ was proclaimed by his Father as his beloved Son? But by that it is declared what this excellent title of only-begotten, given to Christ and added to the name of Son of God, means. So be it: but he will never prove that nothing more is attributed to him than love, and not also true begetting declared by the name of Son, so that it ought to be objected or opposed to being truly and properly the only-begotten, as if one could not be at once truly the only-begotten and the beloved Son.

units.la: Deinde alteram in Christo, cur unigenitus dicatur Dei filius, causam, seclusa vera a Patre generatione, constituit Adversarius in hoc, quod, quomodo ab Abraham patre Isaac, sic a Deo Patre haeres universorum constitutus sit Christus. Verum haeredem constitui, est consequens generationis, & proprium quod unigenitis debetur, non propria ipsorum forma. Non quia Christus universorum haeres, ideo filius Dei unigenitus est dictus, sed quia filius unigenitus, ideo & haeres: quemadmodum nos quoque, non quia haeredes, filii; sed quia filii, idcirco haeredes. Rom. viii. 17.
units.tr: Next, the opponent establishes the other reason why Christ is called the Son of God as only-begotten, setting aside the true begetting from the Father: that just as Isaac was made heir by Abraham his father, so Christ was made heir of all things by God the Father. But to be made heir is a consequence of begetting, and belongs to the only-begotten as a proper due, not to their proper form. Christ is not called the only-begotten Son of God because he is heir of all things, but he is heir because he is the only-begotten Son; just as we too are not sons because we are heirs, but are heirs because we are sons. Rom. 8:17.

units.la: Quod addit, tum temporis Christum Filium Dei unigenitum appellatum, quo nullus alius homo adhuc Dei filius sub N.T. erat, valde frivolum, & si vel verum, nihil tamen juvaret causam. Sed nec verum. Nam quo tempore de Christo dictum fuit quod filius Dei esset unigenitus, verum quoque fuit, filios Dei esse, quicunque vera fide eum acciperent. Joann. 1. 12. 14. Et hoc ante ejus resurrectionem & glorificationem aeque, ac postea. Quocumque tempore quis in Christum credit, & Servatorem am-plectitur, jus accipit & dignitatem filii Dei. Verum quidem est, quod ejus resurrectione & gloria illud adipiscimur; sed non quasi ex isto demum tempore penderet, bene ex re:quae, quod in moralibus frequens, propter certitudinem suam, etiam ante actualem existentiam, & exhibitionem, vim suam habet ac pondus. Nam & ante tempus re-surrectionis Christi, filii Dei exstiterunt permulti, ex Deo geniti, & ab ipso Christo illo titulo insigniti. Jam ponamus, quod toto illo quod dicit, tempore Christus solus Dei filius fuisset appellatus: numquid hinc solide sequeretur, quod ergo solus filius Dei esset, & propter eam causam dictus unigenitus? Non res a nominatione pendet, sed haec ab illa. Quid si ante resurrectionem suam nec filius Dei, nec unigenitus fuisset appellatus, eo id minus fuisset, quod tamen revera fuit? Hocne ab ap-pellatione pendet, vel, quod latius, ab ejus tempore? Imo videretur hinc sequi, quod uti Christus fuit unigenitus ante resurrectionem & adscensionem, quando nullus N. T. filius, & propter hanc causam ita dictus, post istud tempus nomen unigeniti amittere debuerit, ubi multi facti Dei filii, & quidem, quod non erubescit addere, eodem ex Deo filiationis genere. Tota ergo Christi filiatio, & praesertim si dicendus unigenitus, pendebit a nostra. Eoque quod nos facti filii, unigenitus ille esse desierit. Certe, siquidem unius generis cum Christo filii simus. Nam ubi plures ejusdem generis filii, ibi nemo istorum fe potest dicere unigenitum. Quod vero ait, Christum pro tempore unigenitum fuisse, quamvis ei plures postmodum additi ejusdem generis filii, confirmat id quod diximus ad Prov. iv. 3. Salomonem posse unigenitum appellari matris suae, pro eo tempore quo talis fuit, quamvis non semper unigenitus manserit, natis praeter fe matri postmodum & filiis aliis.
units.tr: What he adds, that at that time Christ was called the Son of God as only-begotten, when no other man was yet a son of God under the New Testament, is very trifling, and even if it were true it would not help his cause. But it is not true. For at the time when it was said of Christ that he was the only-begotten Son of God, it was also true that all who received him with true faith were sons of God. John 1:12, 14. And this was so before his resurrection and glorification just as it was afterwards. At whatever time anyone believes in Christ and embraces him as Saviour, he receives the right and dignity of a son of God. It is true that we obtain this through his resurrection and glory; but it does not follow that it depended on that time alone, but rather it is by reason of the thing itself, which, as is frequent in matters of morals, has its force and weight on account of its certainty, even before its actual existence and manifestation. For even before the time of Christ's resurrection there were very many sons of God, begotten of God, and marked with that title by Christ himself. Now let us suppose that during the whole time of which he speaks, Christ alone had been called the Son of God: would it follow soundly that he was therefore the only Son of God, and for that reason called the only-begotten? The thing does not depend on the naming, but the naming on the thing. What if before his resurrection he had been called neither Son of God nor only-begotten; would he for that reason have been less what in truth he was? Does this depend on the title, or, more broadly, on his time? Indeed it would seem to follow from this that, just as Christ was the only-begotten before his resurrection and ascension, when no son under the New Testament existed and was so called for this reason, so after that time he ought to have lost the name of only-begotten, since many have become sons of God, and indeed, as he is not ashamed to add, "of the same kind of sonship from God." Therefore the whole sonship of Christ, and especially if he is to be called only-begotten, will depend on ours, and he will have ceased to be that only-begotten because we have become sons. Certainly this would be so, if we are sons of the same kind as Christ. For where there are several sons of the same kind, none of them can call himself the only-begotten. But when he says that Christ was the only-begotten for a time, even though several sons of the same kind were afterwards added to him, this confirms what we said on Prov. 4:3, that Solomon could be called the only-begotten of his mother at the time when he was such, although he did not always remain the only-begotten, since other sons were afterwards born to his mother besides him.

units.la: Quas porro Socinus ait causas, cur Christus unigenitus Dei dicatur filius, Schlichtingius persequitur contra Meifnerum, quem haud abs re erit audire. Causam istius, inquit, appellationis in S. L.
units.tr: Schlichting goes on to pursue, against Meisner, the reasons Socinus gives why Christ is called the only-begotten Son of God, and it will not be out of place to hear him. The cause of this designation, he says, in Holy Scripture

units.la: Quod ad priorem attinet, ea est ab ipsius Dei Angelo Gabriele[?] expressa, cùm virginem Mariam alloquens ait; Spiritus sanctus super-veniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbra-bit tibi: ideoque quod nascetur ex te Sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei. Quibus in verbis luculentiffimè testatur Angelus, causam, cur ipse homo Iesus Nazarenus filius Dei appel-letur, hanc esse, quòd Spiritus Sanctus, & virtus altissimi ejus conceptionem, & primam existentiam fit operata, & sic Patris generantis loco Deus fuerit. Quae porro causa non tantùm facit, ut homo ille Iesus in virginis utero conce-ptus, & ex virgine natus, Dei Filius appelletur; sed etiam ut appelletur singularis proprie & unicus, ac proinde unigenitus Dei Filius, quandoquidem nemo alius unquam hoc pacto a Deo generatus est.
units.tr: As for the first, it is expressed by the angel Gabriel himself, when speaking to the Virgin Mary he says: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is to be born of you will be called the Son of God." In these words the angel most clearly testifies that the cause why this man Jesus of Nazareth is called the Son of God is that the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High brought about his conception and first existence, and so God took the place of a generating Father. This cause does not only make it so that this man Jesus, conceived in the virgin's womb and born of the virgin, is called the Son of God; it also makes him to be called singular and properly the only one, and therefore the only-begotten Son of God, since no one else has ever been begotten by God in this way.

units.la: Resp. Non dicitur Luc. 1. causam, cur Jesus filius Dei appelletur, esse, quod Spi-ritus sanctus ejus conceptionem & primam existentiam fuerit operatus. nego, ista adducto loco contineri. Dicitur quidem, Spiritum Sanctum superventurum Mariae, & virtutem altissimi ei obumbraturam, ideoque quod nasceretur ex ea, vocandum Filium Dei: non vero inter illa, quod intrudit Schlichtingius, quod Spiritus Sanctus & virtus altissimi ejus conceptionem & primam existentiam fit operata. Sin dicat, hoc significari illa Spiritus obumbratione, id probandum ei, nam nos de prima fi-lii Dei existentia intellectum, quod facit Adversarius, negamus. Bene qui-dem de eo quod in Maria conceptum, na-tumque intelligi potest, quod Spiritus ejus fit auctor & causa; nec tamen Patris generantis loco, quia nil materiae vel substantiae de suo Deus contulit, ut Pater, & generatione propria esse queat: sed materiam in & ex matre Virgine foecundam Deus reddidit ad ferendam prolem, quod citra singularem Dei vim & operationem fieri non potuisset. Verum ille sic natus, sic miraculose conceptus editusque ostendit, deberi sibi appellationem filii Dei, non quod hinc de-mum Filius Dei factus, sed declaratus fuerit & probatus. Quemadmodum ὅτι[?], sic & διὸ[?] causam non semper formalem denotat, vel efficientem a priori, sed saepe a posteriori aut ab adjuncto rationem quamvis declarantem & significantem, propter aut per quam res ostenditur esse talis, ac est. Deinde, in textu ratio datur, cur appellandus ef-set Dei filius: non propter quam effet unigenitus. Quod addit, solum Christum illo singulari modo natum fuisse, in hoc quidem nihil a vero alienum, sed ita ex re argu-mentatur, non ex textu. Causas, inquit, afferimus, non ob quas Christus non fit ex effentia Patris ab aeterno genitus; sed ob quas ex nomine unigeniti id colligi non possit. Non vero id ex nomine redarguitis, quod hic non extat, sed e re, vel vestra potius opinione teme-raria. Nempe propter singularem nativitatis rationem, & per eam Christum factum Filium Dei unigenitum. Quod negamus. Nusquam modus generationis unigenitum facit, sed ipsa. Adamus etiam singulari modo filius Dei fuit, quo nemo aliùs, vid. per creationem: an propterea filius Dei unigenitus? Nos iterum alia generationis ratione filii Dei sumus: vel fac unum modo hominem ita filium Dei factum: istæne singulares rationes faciunt totidem unigenitos? Ridicule sane: hoc enim est, unige-nitum[?] tollere, quando plures constituis ejusdem generis filios, quamvis diversimode factos. Denique quod si daremus, Christum etiam propter admirandam illam ex Maria nativitatem suo modo Filium Dei appellatum, non tamen sequeretur, veram & propriam filiationis ejus causam non esse aliam sublimiorem: vel non eam posse consistere cum verbis textus: quod ostendendum Socino, siquidem hinc probari causam suam, exclusa nostra, arbitretur. Quod agnoscens Schlichtingius, inquit, Neque enim Socinus ex eo, quod Christus dicatur unigenitus Dei Filius, propter conceptionem ex Spiritu S. & virtute ipsius Dei, colligit, vel nullam aliam esse istius appellationis causam, vel eam, quam afferunt adversarii, esse falsam; sed tantum eam ex ista unigeniti appellatione necessario colligi non posse, & aliunde, si vera sit, prius colligendam esse. Verum ex unigeniti appellatione, & explicatione id colligimus, nim. propria, quam improprie præferendam, res ipsa, & communis Scripturam exponendi usus, docent. Imo quando Socinus dixit, causam appellationis unigeniti in S. L. esse duplicem illam, quam ponit, vid. Christi nativitatem, & muneris excellentiam, annon aliam omnem præterea condemnat? & nullam esse istius appellationis causam, vel eam, quam nos adferimus, esse falsam, clare satis innuit? Schlich. pag. 534. Licet, inquit, ut genitus a gignendo, sic unigenitus ab unica generatione nomen habeat, quod hic commemorat Meisnerus: tamen, quemadmodum genitus non semper proprie loquendo genitum, sed genito similem, sic unigenitus non semper generatione unicum, sed illi similem declarare & potest & solet. Unigenitus proprie nomen habet ab unica generatione: a generatione, eaque unica: non plures ejus causæ, non aliæ a generatione. Adversarii in hoc operam collocant, ut Christum faciant unigenito similem: nos vere & proprie unigenitum tenemus, ac tuemur.
units.tr: Reply. It is not said in Luke 1 that the cause why Jesus is called the Son of God is that the Holy Spirit brought about his conception and first existence. I deny that this is contained in the passage cited. It is indeed said that the Holy Spirit will come upon Mary and the power of the Most High will overshadow her, and therefore the child born of her is to be called the Son of God; but it is not said among these things what Schlichting thrusts in, that the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High brought about his conception and first existence. But if he says that this is signified by that overshadowing of the Spirit, that must be proved by him, for we deny that the Adversary's reading of the first existence of the Son of God is correct. It can indeed rightly be understood of what was conceived and born in Mary, that the Spirit is its author and cause; yet God did not take the place of a Father generating, since God contributed nothing of matter or substance from his own, as a Father does, and so could not be begotten in the proper sense. Rather, God made the matter in and from the virgin mother fruitful for bearing offspring, which could not have happened without the singular power and working of God. But that he was born thus, conceived and brought forth thus by a miracle, shows that the title Son of God is due to him, not because he was made the Son of God from this point on, but because he was declared and proved to be so. Just as hoti [ὅτι], so also dio [διὸ] does not always denote a formal cause, or an efficient cause in the sense of prior, but often an a posteriori or accompanying reason that declares and signifies, on account of which or through which a thing is shown to be what it is. Further, in the text a reason is given why he ought to be called the Son of God, not the reason why he would be the only-begotten. As to his adding that Christ alone was born in that singular manner, this is indeed not foreign to the truth, but he argues from the matter, not from the text. We give, he says, reasons why Christ is not begotten from the essence of the Father from eternity; but from them it cannot be gathered from the name of only-begotten. But you do not refute this from the name, which is not present here, but from the matter, or rather from your rash opinion. Namely, you say, on account of the singular manner of his birth, and through it Christ is made the only-begotten Son of God. This we deny. The manner of generation never makes someone only-begotten; the thing itself does. Adam also was the Son of God in a singular manner, which no one else was, namely through creation: is he therefore the only-begotten Son of God? Again, we are sons of God by another mode of generation; or suppose only one man were made the Son of God in this way: do those singular modes make as many only-begotten? Truly ridiculous; for this is to remove the only-begotten, when you set up many sons of the same kind, though made in different ways. Finally, even if we granted that Christ was called the Son of God in his own way on account of that wonderful birth from Mary, it would not follow that the true and proper cause of his sonship is not another, higher one, or that it cannot stand with the words of the text; which the Socinian ought to show, if he thinks that his cause is proved from this with ours excluded. Schlichting, recognising this, says: "For Socinus does not gather from the fact that Christ is called the only-begotten Son of God, on account of his conception by the Holy Spirit and the power of God himself, either that there is no other cause of that designation, or that the cause the adversaries give is false; but only that it cannot necessarily be gathered from that designation of only-begotten, and must be gathered elsewhere first, if it is true." But from the designation and explanation of only-begotten we do gather it, namely that the proper sense, not the improper, is to be preferred; the thing itself and the common usage of interpreting Scripture teach this. Indeed, when Socinus said that the cause of the designation only-begotten in Holy Scripture is the double one he lays down, namely Christ's birth and the excellence of his office, does he not also condemn every other cause besides, and clearly enough hint that there is no cause of that designation except that which he gives, and that the one we give is false? Schlichting, p. 534: "Although," he says, "just as begotten has its name from begetting, so only-begotten has its name from a unique generation, which Meisner here mentions; nevertheless, just as the begotten does not always properly mean one begotten, but one similar to the begotten, so the only-begotten can and does often signify not one unique by generation, but one similar to him." The only-begotten properly has its name from a unique generation: from a generation, and that a unique one; it has not several causes, or causes other than generation. The Adversaries labour to make Christ similar to the only-begotten; we truly and properly hold and defend him as the only-begotten.

units.la: Quod ergo ad alteram appellationis unigeniti in Christo causam, quam dat Socinus, ea est muneris Christi dignitas. Contendit enim, idem in Scripturis sonare Dei Filium, quod Christus: & quia unicus est Christus, proinde & unigenitum illum dici Dei Filium.
units.tr: As for the second cause of the designation only-begotten in Christ, which Socinus gives, it is the dignity of Christ's office. For he contends that Son of God in the Scriptures means the same as Christ, and because Christ is unique, therefore that one is called the only-begotten Son of God.

units.la: Posteriorem, inquit Socinus, causam exprimunt loca illa, ex quibus apparet, unicum illum & singularem Dei Filium, idem esse quod Christus. Nam Christus præcipue ac potissimum regem populi Dei significat. Vides hic rursus hominis illius Iesu Nazareni summam post Deum dignitatem, & regiæ personæ, quam in ipso Dei populo sustinet, omnium maximam excellentiam, causam esse, cur sit ille unicus & singularis Dei filius.
units.tr: The second cause, says Socinus, is expressed by those passages from which it appears that that unique and singular Son of God is the same as Christ. For Christ chiefly and above all signifies the king of the people of God. You see here again that the highest dignity of this man Jesus of Nazareth after God, and the greatest excellence of the royal person he sustains among the people of God itself, is the cause why he is the unique and singular Son of God.

units.la: Resp. Videmus omnino Iesu Christi summam post Deum dignitatem, & excellentiam regiam, sed istam causam esse cur sit unigenitus Dei filius, non videmus, nec Socinus vel leviter probat. Primum autem ut de vi & intentione argumenti constet, dein visuri ejus formam, inquit Schlichtingius, pag. 534. Argumenti Socini vim non percepit Meisnerus. Neque enim Socinus hoc argumento excludit eam, quam
units.tr: Reply. We see indeed the highest dignity after God and the royal excellence of Jesus Christ, but that this is the cause why he is the only-begotten Son of God we do not see, nor does Socinus even slightly prove it. But first, that the force and intent of the argument may be established, and then that its form may be seen, says Schlichting, p. 534: Meisner did not grasp the force of Socinus's argument. For Socinus does not by this argument exclude that which

units.la: Adversarii putant, appellationis istius causam, sed tantum negat eam ex appellatione ista posse probari. Quare posset consistere nihilominus sententia nostra, & appellationis unigeniti, quam damus, causa, etiamsi constaret argumento Socini sua vis. Bene est. Res modo salva sit, de argumento aliquo, hinc inde ducto, quod magis aut minus firmum sit, non adeo ac quidem de ipsa erimus solliciti. Sed quare non verae rei vera & propria vocis subserviat acceptio? cum illa propria sit unigeniti acceptio, uti ipse hic fatetur. Ut genitus a gignendo, sic unigenitus ab unica generatione nomen habet. Verumtamen quomodo non excludit suo argumento Socinus causam appellationis uniunigeniti, qua nos damus, quando negat eam ex appellatione ista probari posse? Velim hoc ut ostenderet. Forte dicet, se impetere isto modo non causam, sed causae probationem. Sed qui propriam rei probationem convellit, ex propria ejus appellatione sumptam, eum ipsam quoque causam impugnare, mihi videtur. Jam ad argumenti formam: Quod Jesu impositum est, ob divinum officium & dignitatem regiam, ex eo non potest probari divina ejus natura, seu aeterna ex Patre generatio: verum tale nomen est unigeniti filii Dei: ergo. Negatur minor. Neque enim nomen aut filii, aut unigeniti Dei Filii Jesu impositum, quemadmodum nomen Christi: vel officium ejus causa, ob quam filius Dei unigenitus fuerit. Propterea quod filius Dei, impositum istud ei munus; non propter munus factus Dei filius. Quis ex munere aut dignitate aliqua filius fit: & non ex eo quod filius est, dignitate ornatur? Certe non potest exemplum ejus dari, aut ratio, nequidem conceptus, ut per & post munus aliquod singulare quis evadat filius unigenitus. Filiatio, & officium adeo diversa sunt, ut idem esse prorsus nequeant. Neque idem, filius Dei unicus & singularis, ac Christus. Aliud nomen personae, aliud officii. Apparet, inquit, unicum illum & singularem Dei filium, idem esse quod Christum. Negamus. Eundem si dicat esse, qui Christus, sive eandem personam, verum est. Sed quae eidem conveniunt, & debentur uni, non propterea formaliter in se idem sunt. Nam, addit, Christus praecipue ac potissimum regem populi Dei significat. Quae in hoc sequela? Unigenitus Dei filius, & Christus idem sunt, quia Christus regem significat Ecclesiae, seu populi Dei. In forma: Quod regem populi Dei significat, id idem est cum unico & singulari Dei filio: Christus id significat: ergo. Negatur Major. Christus quidem etiam regem significat, sed & alia. Cur autem praecipue, & potissimum regem, neque etiam prophetam aeque, & sacerdotem? Qui vero ista idem possunt dici cum filio Dei unigenito? Quidquid in Christo singulare, non propterea idem est cum singularitate suae filiationis. Si Christus praecipue & potissimum regem populi Dei significat, & propterea Dei Filium unigenitum, minus ergo praecipue etiam aliud, quare nec omnino idem est Christus & Dei unigenitus filius, seu non idem sonant vel identificantur, aut ejusdem sunt significationis & latitudinis. Vides hic, &c. Neutiquam vero id videmus, summam & regiam Christi dignitatem causam esse, cur sit unigenitus Dei filius. Fiat argumentum: Christus denotat regiam dignitatem, ergo Filium Dei unigenitum. Negatur. Praeterea subdole mutat terminos Adversarius, & pro unigenitus substituit unicus & singularis Dei filius. Quod non ita ferimus, siquidem minus & generalius quid istud nobis sonat, quam illud. Qui unigenitus, is est unicus & singularis; sed non qui quovis modo unicus & singularis, proinde est unigenitus. Quare ad enervandam vim appellationis unigeniti, variationem terminorum illam faciunt Adversarii, quam minime probamus.
units.tr: the adversaries think is the cause of that designation, but only denies that it can be proved from that designation. Therefore our view, and the cause of the designation only-begotten which we give, could nonetheless stand, even if the force of Socinus's argument were granted. Well and good. Provided the matter itself is safe, we shall not be so anxious about some argument, drawn one way or the other, that is more or less firm. But why does the true and proper meaning of the word not serve the true thing? Since that is the proper meaning of only-begotten, as he himself here admits: just as begotten has its name from begetting, so only-begotten has its name from a unique generation. And yet how does Socinus not, by his argument, exclude the cause of the designation of the unique only-begotten which we give, when he denies that it can be proved from that designation? I would like him to show this. Perhaps he will say that he attacks not the cause but the proof of the cause in this way. But it seems to me that whoever overthrows the proof of a thing, taken from its proper designation, also attacks the cause itself. Now to the form of the argument: What has been imposed on Jesus because of his divine office and royal dignity cannot prove his divine nature, or his eternal generation from the Father; but such a name is that of the only-begotten Son of God; therefore. The minor is denied. For neither the name of Son, nor of only-begotten Son of God, was imposed on Jesus like the name Christ, or was the cause of his office the reason why he was the only-begotten Son of God. For the Son of God is the designation given to him, not the office; he did not become the Son of God on account of his office. Who becomes a son from some office or dignity, rather than being adorned with a dignity because he is a son? Certainly no example of this can be given, nor any reason, nor even a concept, by which someone becomes the only-begotten son through or after some singular office. Sonship and office are so different that they cannot be entirely the same thing. Nor is the unique and singular Son of God the same as Christ: one is the name of the person, the other of the office. It appears, he says, that that unique and singular Son of God is the same as Christ. We deny it. If he means that they are the same person, that is, the same person as Christ, that is true. But things that agree with and are due to the same one are not for that reason formally the same in themselves. For, he adds, Christ chiefly and above all signifies the king of the people of God. What follows from this? The only-begotten Son of God and Christ are the same, because Christ signifies the king of the Church, or of the people of God. In form: What signifies the king of the people of God is the same as the unique and singular Son of God: Christ signifies this; therefore. The major is denied. Christ indeed also signifies the king, but also other things. But why chiefly and above all the king, and not equally the prophet and the priest? And how can these be called the same as the only-begotten Son of God? Whatever is singular in Christ is not on that account the same as the singularity of his sonship. If Christ chiefly and above all signifies the king of the people of God, and therefore the only-begotten Son of God, then by the same token he chiefly signifies something else less; so Christ and the only-begotten Son of God are not altogether the same, or do not sound the same or are not identified, or are not of the same signification and extent. You see here, etc. But we by no means see that the highest and royal dignity of Christ is the cause why he is the only-begotten Son of God. Let the argument stand: Christ denotes royal dignity, therefore the only-begotten Son of God. Denied. Moreover, the Adversary craftily changes the terms, and for only-begotten substitutes unique and singular Son of God. We do not accept this, since that sounds to us as something less and more general than the other. Whoever is only-begotten is unique and singular; but whoever is unique and singular in some way is not for that reason only-begotten. Therefore, to weaken the force of the designation only-begotten, the Adversaries make this change of terms, which we by no means approve.

units.la: Dixerat Meisnerus, quod filius Dei quidem est idem, qui Christus, non idem quod Christus. ad quod Schlichtingius: Si filius Dei est ille idem, qui Christus, hoc solum nobis sufficit ad convincendos adversarios. Quis enim est Christus? Is sane qui ungi ab alio, & regia dignitate ac nomine afficI potuit. Si vero Filius ille Dei singularis is ipse est, sane summus ille Deus esse non potest. Alioquin enim unum idemque subjectum duo disparata simul esse, imo potius unum disparatorum esset alterum, quod implicat contradictionem. Nequaquam id satis est, ad nos convincendos, quod filius Dei est idem ille qui Christus, post videlicet Christi ex Maria nativitatem, post incarnationem, dixerat Meisnerus. Is qui ungi ab alio potuit, est Christus; filius autem Dei ab alio ungi non potuit, si fit summus Deus. Quid hinc jam sequitur? ergo non est idem filius iste, & Christus, id est, non est idem hic quod iste, negatur. Filius Dei, accepta humana forma, ἀνθρωπῷ[?], Christus factus fuit, & haec persona ad officium suum χρισθέντα[?] uncta. Qua Christus, qua unctus, qua homo, non est summus ille Deus: idem tamen, secundum diversas sui rationes, est homo, & Deus; filius hominis, & filius Dei. Neque inde sequitur, unum disparatorum esse alterum, vel duo disparata esse unum subjectum, quidem in uno subjecto: quod non munus hic, quam quod in uno homine disparata duo anima & corpus, locum habere potest. Schlichtingius, pag. 538. Si Christi appellatio formaliter est officii, Regem, Sacerdotem, & Prophetam denotans: itemque si Christus a temporali unctione nomen habet; quomodo Christum esse divinae naturae conveniet, ut paulo ante idem, sicut vidimus, asserit? Num divinae naturae, non jam dico Regium & Sacerdotale officium, sed officium Propheticum competere poterit? Num temporalis unctio & donorum spiritualium collatio? Bene illa conveniunt, ut Christus sit divinae naturae, & quoque homo, & hactenus qua homo, qua ἀνθρωπῷ[?] fungatur officio regis, sacerdotis, prophetae, & ab hac temporali unctione nomen Christi habeat, aliunde Dei & Dei Filii. Non divinae naturae competunt illa officia, sed quidem Deo in carne manifestato, Deo humanam formam induto, verbo caro facto, & hinc ἀνθρώπῳ[?], respectu humanae naturae unctio, & donorum spiritualium collatio.
units.tr: Meisnerus had said that the Son of God is indeed the same as Christ, but not the same thing as Christ. To this Schlichtingius replies: If the Son of God is the same as Christ, this alone is enough for us to convict our opponents. For who is Christ? He is surely one who could be anointed by another and invested with royal dignity and name. But if that singular Son of God is that very one, he cannot surely be the supreme God. For otherwise one and the same subject would be two disparate things at once, or rather one of the disparates would be the other, which involves a contradiction. Meisnerus's statement that the Son of God is that same person who is Christ, after the nativity of Christ from Mary and after the incarnation, is by no means enough to convict us. He who could be anointed by another is Christ, but the Son of God, if he is the supreme God, could not be anointed by another. What follows from this? Therefore this Son and Christ are not the same, that is, this is not the same as that. I deny the inference. The Son of God, having taken human form, was made Christ as man [ἀνθρωπῷ], and this person was anointed [χρισθέντα] for his office. As Christ, as anointed, as man, he is not the supreme God; yet in respect of his different natures he is at the same time man and God, Son of man and Son of God. Nor does it follow from this that one of two disparates is the other, or that two disparates are one subject. There is no such contradiction here, any more than there is in one man, where the two disparates, soul and body, are present. Schlichtingius, p. 538: If the appellation Christ formally denotes an office, signifying King, Priest and Prophet, and if Christ takes his name from a temporal anointing, how will it fit with the divine nature that Christ should be God, as he has just asserted? Can the prophetic office, let alone the royal and priestly office, belong to the divine nature? Can a temporal anointing and the bestowal of spiritual gifts? These things agree well enough: Christ is of the divine nature and is also man, and insofar as he is man, he discharges the office of king, priest and prophet as man [ἀνθρωπῷ], and he has the name Christ from this temporal anointing, which comes from elsewhere, namely from God and the Son of God. These offices belong not to the divine nature, but to God manifested in the flesh, to God clothed in human form, to the Word made flesh; and hence the anointing and the bestowal of spiritual gifts belong to him as man, with respect to the human nature.

units.la: Veniamus nunc ad testimonia a Socino allata, quibus demonstrat, unicum illum ac singularem esse Dei Filium, id significare quod esse Christum. inquit
units.tr: Let us now come to the testimonies adduced by Socinus, by which he demonstrates that the unique and singular Son of God signifies the same as being Christ. So he says.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 541. Primum testimonium sumit, ex collatione locorum Mat. 16. 16. Luc. 9. 20. In quibus locis refertur confessio Apostolorum de Iesu. & a Matthaeo quidem narratur, quod Petrus dixerit: Tu es Christus Filius Dei vivi: a Marco autem, & a Luca: Tu es Christus, Tu es Christus Dei. Unde apparet sola Christi, vel Christi Dei appellatione id contineri, quod significat appellatio illius filii Dei vivi (est enim in Graeco articulus nomini filii praefixus,) sic ut Filii Dei nomen voci Christi additum, non quidpiam plus significet, quam vox Christi, sed tantum vocis Christi significationem magis declaret & explicet. Hinc autem id quod dicimus apparere merito affirmamus, quia alioquin Marcus & Lucas eandem Apostolorum confessionem referentes, illud quod longe maximum foret, seu multo potiorem confessionis Apostolicae partem omisissent, quod fieri non potuit, seu non debuit. Illud etiam indicio est, rem eandem utraque appellatione designari, quod inter vocem Christi, & filii Dei nulla interjecta sit copula, quae res diversas conjungi
units.tr: Schlichtingius, p. 541. He takes his first testimony from the comparison of Matthew 16:16 and Luke 9:20. In these passages the confession of the Apostles concerning Jesus is reported. Matthew relates that Peter said: "You are Christ, the Son of the living God"; but Mark and Luke say: "You are Christ," and "You are the Christ of God." Hence it appears that the same thing is contained in the bare appellation Christ, or Christ of God, that is signified by the appellation of that Son of the living God (for in the Greek there is an article prefixed to the word Son). So the name Son of God, added to the word Christ, signifies nothing more than the word Christ, but only declares and explains more fully the meaning of the word Christ. We rightly affirm that this appears from what we have said, because otherwise Mark and Luke, reporting the same confession of the Apostles, would have omitted what was by far the greatest part, or a much more important part, of the Apostolic confession; which could not or ought not to have happened. This is also a sign that the same thing is designated by each appellation, since no conjunction is placed between the word Christ and Son of God, a thing that joins different things.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non facit Adversarius Elenchum: neq; enim quaeritur, an appellatione Christi, vel Christi Dei contineatur hoc quod Christus Filius Dei est: sed, an duo illa idem significent. Eundem significare, scimus: idem, negamus. II. Nomen filii Dei non quidpiam significare ait, praeter vocem Christi. Verum est, quod filius Dei Christum notat, & Christus Dei Filium: non autem quod voces propterea sint synonymae vel idem significet. Jesus Christum, & Christus Jesum notat, an propterea vox una nil aliud significat, qua altera? Jesus Filium Dei, & filius Dei Jesum designat, an proinde voces sunt idem, nec quidpiam plus significantes? III. Sed Lucas omisit referre & Marcus, quod Matthaeus dixerat, de Christo filio Dei, satis habentes dixisse Christum simpliciter, vel Christum Dei. Negatur consequentia: ergo illae voces idem, & non quidpiam plus una quam alia significat. Verum omisissent ita illi potiorem confessionis Apostolicae partem: nego iterum consequentiam, ergo voces Christi, & Dei fiindicio fit, sed (ut in oppositionibus fieri solet, lii idem significant. Quae obsecro sequela cum prius declaratur per posterius, dicatur: ista est? Vin tu ex omissis omnibus vocibus Tu es ille Christus, ille Filius Dei ventis. apud hunc aut illum Euangelistam, vel scriptorem alium, idem forte cum aliis referentem, inferre omissas voces cum memoratis altero in loco esse synonimas? Atque istud tamen nunc vis. Sic est, dum commemorant alii Christum, non aliud volunt, quam quod alter, Christum Filium Dei, sed propter identitatem rei, non vocum. Et quoties non id evenit, ut alia omittant Scriptores sacri, ab aliis commemorata, & longe maximi saepe momenti? Quod frustra in praejudicium omissae rei, tanquam certum adducas argumentum. Exempla ejus rei innumera. Titulum crucis Matthaeus dicit fuisse, Iste est Iesus Rex Iudaeorum. Marcus, Rex Iudaeorum. Johannes, Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum. Conveniunt ista satis in designanda re, eademque persona; sed an voces propterea idem significant, Iesus Rex, vel Nazarenus & Iesus? Concionem Christi primam ita refert Matthaeus, ut Christus dixerit, resipiscite, Matth. iv. 17. Marcus, quod addiderit & credite Euangelio, cap. i. 15. ergo voces illae idem significant? Omisit Lucas in recensenda oratione Dominica, ejus epilogum, Matthaeo narrante; an propterea non quidpiam plus significat quam antecedentia, vel non potuit aut debuit fieri, ut Lucas tam egregiam & necessariam quoque orationis partem omitteret? Viderit nunc Schlichtingius, quam bene negarit, quemquam Euangelistarum sermonis alicujus necessariam relatu partem omisisse, praesertim non simplicis alicujus sermonis, seu tam sanctae, qualis est confessionis. Nisi non sanctam dixerit Orationis partem illam, quam Matthaeus quidem, non item Lucas, recenset. Innumera istiusmodi proferri ex V. & N. T. posse nemo ambigit. Nempe horum hominum erit statuere, quid caeteri post Matthaeum Euangelistae referre, vel omittere potuerint aut debuerint. Quasi non multa alia haud minus momentosa omiserint saepe sequentes Euangelistae? vel ex omissione liceat, aut rerum, aut Scriptorum fidem elevare. Denique etiam ex copulae omissione argumentatur, eoque indicari putat rem eandem utraque appellatione designari. Hoc modo si agendum censeat Adversarius, concludat quoque Iesum & Christum esse voces synonymas, quia non solum copula, sed & incisionis omissa nota passim conjunguntur: an propterea vox Christus non quidpiam plus significat quam vox Iesus? Rom. i. i. Paulus servus Iesu Christi, vocatus Apostolus, non interjicitur & vocatus Apostolus, an propterea voces illae & istae idem, neque quidpiam plus significat Apostolus, quam servus Christi? Apoc. i. 5. Et a Iesu Christo, qui fidelis ille testis, primogenitus ille & mortuus, an ista, quia non interjicitur copula, idem sunt, neque res diversae, quamvis eandem denotent personam? Atque talia passim observare est. Sic Christus, & filius Dei, copula addita aut omissa, significant quidem eundem, non tamen idem. Non de verbis nunc agimus, inquit, sed de rebus. Annon de verbis quando nomen filii Dei idem sonare, quod appellatio Christi, idem significare, non quidpiam plus significare, quam vox Christi, eandem utriusque vocis esse significationem, aperte & aliquoties dictum fuit? nam si id solum velit, in re & persona convenire Christum, ac Dei Filium, neminem habebit repugnantem, sed noverit tum se deferere secundum Socini argumentum, quo probare satagebat appellationem filii Dei, nihil denotare quam nomen Christi.
units.tr: Reply 1. The opponent does not make an argument: for the question is not whether the appellation Christ, or Christ of God, contains the fact that Christ is the Son of God, but whether those two expressions mean the same thing. We know that they mean the same thing; we deny that they are the same. II. He says the name Son of God signifies nothing more than the word Christ. It is true that Son of God denotes Christ, and Christ denotes the Son of God; but it does not follow that the words are synonyms or mean the same thing. Jesus denotes Christ, and Christ denotes Jesus: does the one word therefore signify nothing other than the other? Does Jesus designate the Son of God, and the Son of God designate Jesus: are the words therefore the same, and signify nothing more? III. But Luke and Mark omitted to report what Matthew had said about Christ the Son of God, being content to say simply Christ, or Christ of God. I deny the inference: therefore those words are the same, and one signifies no more than the other. Indeed they would have omitted by this means the more important part of the Apostolic confession: I again deny the inference. Therefore the words Christ and Son of God mean the same thing? What kind of sequence is this, I beg you, when what is previously declared is proved by what is later? (as is usual in objections, the less clear should be explained by the clearer). Do you want to infer, from the omission of all the words You are that Christ, that Son of God in one or another evangelist, or another writer who happens to report the same thing as others, that the words omitted are synonymous with those mentioned in the other place? And yet this is what you now want. It is so, you say, since other writers, when they mention Christ, mean nothing other than what the other does, Christ the Son of God, but because of the identity of the thing, not of the words. And how often does it not happen that the sacred writers omit other things which others have mentioned, and which are often of the greatest importance? Your citing of an omitted thing against the others as a certain argument is in vain. Examples of this are countless. Matthew says the title of the cross was This is Jesus the King of the Jews. Mark says The King of the Jews. John says Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. These agree well enough in designating the thing and the same person; but do the words therefore mean the same thing: Jesus the King, or Nazarene and Jesus? Matthew reports Christ's first sermon as saying repent, Matt. 4:17. Mark adds and believe the gospel, ch. 1:15. Therefore do those words mean the same thing? Luke, in reciting the Lord's Prayer, omitted its conclusion, which Matthew reports; does Luke therefore signify nothing more than what precedes, or could not or ought not to have happened, that Luke should omit so excellent and so necessary a part of the prayer? Let Schlichtingius now consider how wrongly he has denied that any of the evangelists omitted a necessary part of any discourse, especially of a discourse that is not simple, but as holy as a confession. Unless he says that the part of the prayer which Matthew, but not Luke, recounts is not holy. Nobody doubts that countless instances of this kind can be brought forward from the Old and New Testaments. It will be for these men to decide what the other evangelists after Matthew could or ought to have reported or omitted. As if the later evangelists had not often omitted many other things no less important! Or may one, from an omission, weaken the credibility either of things or of writers? Finally, he also argues from the omission of the conjunction, and thinks that by this it is indicated that the same thing is designated by each appellation. If the opponent thinks he ought to proceed in this way, let him also conclude that Jesus and Christ are synonymous words, because they are frequently joined not only without a conjunction but also without the mark of a break: does the word Christ therefore signify nothing more than the word Jesus? Rom. 1:1: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle; here and called is not interposed. Are those words and these therefore the same, and does apostle signify nothing more than servant of Christ? Rev. 1:5: And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn, the dead; because no conjunction is interposed, are these things therefore the same, and not different things, though they denote the same person? And such instances are to be observed everywhere. So Christ and the Son of God, with a conjunction added or omitted, signify indeed the same person, yet are not the same. We are not speaking now of words, he says, but of things. Has it not been said plainly and more than once that when the name Son of God sounds the same as the appellation Christ, it signifies the same, signifies nothing more than the word Christ, and that the meaning of each word is the same? For if he wants only this, that Christ and the Son of God agree in the thing and the person, he will have no one contradicting him; but let him know that he is then abandoning Socinus's argument, by which he laboured to prove that the appellation Son of God denotes nothing but the name Christ.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 547. Non simpli- Resp. 1. Tune dices, quid omittendum citer ab omissione licet inferre identitatem eo- fuerit, quid minus? ut, quod tibi videarum, quae ponuntur & quae omissa sunt: sed etiam demum, quando quidpiam a Sacris scrip-toribus omittitur, quod, nisi in eo quod ponitur comprehensum significatumque esset, omitten-dum nullo pacto fuerat; praesertim vero colle-ctio ista locum habet tum, cum id quod ponitur ita est comparatum, ut id quod omittitur includere ac significare sua natura possit: qualis est Christi appellatio, quae filii Dei appellationem omnino in se continet, cum nemo possit esse Christus seu unctus Dei, quin eo ipso sit filius Dei. Unde & supremi Judices ac Magistratus, a Deo uncti & constituti, filii altissimi, imo Dii nominantur.
units.tr: Schlichting, p. 547: "One may not simply infer an identity of things from the omission of things put and things left out, but even when something is omitted by the sacred writers, which could not have been omitted in any way unless it were included and signified in what is stated; and this inference especially holds when what is stated is of such a nature that it can by its very nature include and signify what is omitted, as with the appellation Christ, which entirely contains within itself the appellation Son of God, since no one can be Christ or anointed of God without being by that very fact the Son of God. Hence also the supreme judges and magistrates, anointed and appointed by God, are called sons of the Most High, indeed gods." Reply, 1. Will you say that what should or should not have been omitted, and what less so? For example, what you think should not have been omitted is already contained in what precedes? As if, when the weight of things is not carefully considered, let alone prejudged, many things are often omitted for the sake of brevity, or because the discourse hastens on to other matters, or because it was written chiefly for other purposes.

units.la: & voces idem sonare vel significare. III. Atque ita judices, & Magistratus filii altissimi nominantur: sed non idem propterea sonant voces illae: nam & Angeli, & alii filii Dei nuncupantur: neque uti illi sunt solummodo Dei nuncupativi, λεγόμενοι θεοί, ejusdem census Christus; sed est Filius Dei verus, proprius, naturalis.
units.tr: and that the voices sound or signify the same. III. And so judges and magistrates are called sons of the Most High, but for that reason those voices do not sound the same: for angels too, and other sons of God, are so named; and not as those are merely called gods by name, λεγόμενοι θεοί, of the same rank is Christ; but he is the true, proper, natural Son of God.

units.la: tur non omittendum fuisse, id jam conti-neatur antecedentibus? Quasi non haud considerata, nedum praejudicata rerum gravitate, multa saepe omittantur, brevitatis ergo, vel quia ad alia festinat oratio, vel propter alia potissimum instituta fuit.
units.tr: should not have been omitted, is that already contained in what precedes? As if many things are not often omitted, out of brevity, or because the discourse hastens to other matters, or was written chiefly for other purposes, without careful consideration, let alone prejudgment, of the weight of the matters.

units.la: II. Dilabitur a quaestione & ab argumento suo, quando a re ad vocem, vult natura rei inclusum aliquando, quod verbis omissum. Sic fatemur, nominato Christo includi quoque Filium Dei, quum nemo possit esse Christus, nisi Dei Filius, sed propterea non sequitur, quod initio disputationis constitutum, appellationes illas & voces idem sonare vel significare. III. Atque ita judices, & Magistratus filii altissimi nominantur: sed non idem propterea sonant voces illae: nam & Angeli, & alii filii Dei nuncupantur: neque uti illi sunt solummodo Dei nuncupativi, λεγόμενοι θεοί, ejusdem census Christus; sed est Filius Dei verus, proprius, naturalis.
units.tr: II. He strays from the question and from his own argument when, moving from the thing to the word, he holds that what is omitted in words is sometimes included in the nature of the thing. Thus we grant that when Christ is named, the Son of God is included as well, since no one can be Christ except the Son of God; but it does not follow, as was established at the beginning of the dispute, that those appellations and voices sound or signify the same. III. And so judges and magistrates are called sons of the Most High, but for that reason those voices do not sound the same: for angels too, and other sons of God, are so named; and not as those are merely called gods by name, λεγόμενοι θεοί, of the same rank is Christ; but he is the true, proper, natural Son of God.

units.la: Secundum testimonium sumit Socinus, ex collatione locorum Matth. 26. 63. & Mar. 14. 61. cum loco Luc. 22. 67. Nam Matthaeus & Marcus scivit a summo Sacerdote interrogatum esse Christum, num is esset Filius Dei, aut benedicti? Hanc ipsam vero interrogationem Lucas referens, narrat eos interrogasse, num esset Christus? Unde sane constat, Christi nomen in ipso Christo per se idem significare, ac si illi addatur nomen Filii Dei.
units.tr: Socinus takes his second testimony from a comparison of Matthew 26:63 and Mark 14:61 with Luke 22:67. For Matthew and Mark tell us that Christ was asked by the high priest whether he was the Son of God, or of the Blessed One. Luke, however, reporting this same question, says that they asked whether he was the Christ. Hence it is clear that the name Christ, in Christ himself, signifies the same thing as if the name Son of God were added to it.

units.la: Pergit cum Socino, Schlicht. adstruere, Christum & Filium Dei idem significare.
units.tr: He goes on with Socinus and Schlichting to maintain that Christ and the Son of God signify the same thing.

units.la: Resp. Ex eo, quod Matthaeus & Marcus referunt, Christum a summo sacerdote interrogatum, num esset filius Dei, Lucas vero simpliciter, an esset Christus, omittens istud, filius Dei constat quidem, facile eundem designari, sive Christum nomines, sive Filium Dei, quia is unus idemque est, non vero probabit, eo animo ad Lucam fecisse, ut indicaret, eandem rem appellationis, istis significari. No-tant quidem personam, non rem eandem. Praeteriit brevitatis ergo alterum illud
units.tr: Reply. From the fact that Matthew and Mark report that Christ was asked by the high priest whether he was the Son of God, while Luke simply asks whether he was the Christ, omitting the former, it is certainly established that the one who is designated is easily the same, whether one names Christ or the Son of God, because he is one and the same; but he will not prove that Luke meant by this to indicate that the same thing is signified by these appellations. They indeed denote the person, not the same thing. He passed over that other point for the sake of brevity.

units.la: Lucas, quia omnium vis in hoc sita erat, num se Christum fateretur, ac Messiam, eo ipso, non vi nominis, sed rei, connotatum quoque Dei Filium. Fac illos interrogasse an Jesus esset, quemadmodum titulus crucis istud nomen praetulit, non rite inde colligeretur, illa idem significare, quidem eundem, & quod satis Adversariis videretur ad condemnandum Christum & crucifigendum.
units.tr: Luke, because the whole force lay in this: whether he confessed himself to be the Christ and the Messiah; and by that very fact, not by the force of the name but of the thing, the Son of God was also implied. Suppose they had asked whether he was Jesus, as the title on the cross put forward that name: it would not rightly be inferred from this that those names signify the same thing, nor would it have seemed enough to the adversaries for condemning Christ and crucifying him.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 556. Tertio idem probat Socinus, Iohannis Apostoli verbis, qui Iesum esse Christum, & Iesum esse Dei Filium nempe unicum & singularem, pro eodem habet. Nam pro eo quod 1. Epist. cap. 5. ver. 1. dicit: omnis qui credit Iesum esse Christum ex Deo genitus est: paulo post, v. 4, 5. dicit, Omne quod genitum est ex Deo, vincit mundum. Et haec est victoria, quae
units.tr: Schlichting, p. 556: "Thirdly, Socinus proves the same from the words of the Apostle John, who holds that Jesus is the Christ and that Jesus is the Son of God, that is, the only and unique one, to be the same thing. For in 1 John 5:1 he says: 'Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God'; and shortly after, in verses 4 and 5, he says: 'Everything that is born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory which

units.la: Resp. Eodem modo in hisce Nostri argumentantur, ac si quis ex varia baptismi forma, in Iesum, vel in nomen Patris, Filii, & Spiritus S. colligeret aut ista omnia idem significare & esse appellationes idem sonantes, aut diversas fidei poni confessiones. Num obsecro varias id infert fidei confessiones, quod in objecto ejus explicando, alia prolixius nonnunquam refevincit mundum, fides nostra. Quis est qui vincit mundum, nisi qui credit Jesum esse illum Dei Filium? & supra cap. 4.15. qui confitetur Jesum esse illum Dei Filium, Deus in ipso manet, & ipse in Deo. Num enim Iohannes diversas fides hic exprimit, & non eandem ac unicam? quomodo igitur verum effet, omnem qui unam tantum habeat fidem, ex Deo esse genitum, aut in Deo esse & Deum in illo esse, aut mundum vincere? quomodo alibi Paulus quoque dicere potuisset, fi ore confessus fueris Iesum esse dominum & credideris, quod Deus eum resuscitavit ex mortuis (quibus in rebus totum id continetur quod hic Ioannes Christi voce complexus est,) salvus eris, fi praeter hanc fidem requiritur etiam alia, nempe ut credas eum ex Patris effentia genitum, eundem esse cum Patre Deum. runtur & explicatius, alias brevius, nuf-piam rejectis quae ad fidei complementum alibi exprimuntur? Vera & salutaris fides est in Jesum, Christum, Dei Filium, regem, Dominum, Prophetam, Sacerdotem nostrum, &c. fi nunc plura, nunc pauciora istius posuero membra, an vel omissiorum ideo notavi minus pretium, aut varias indicavi fidei confessiones, aut denique ita omnia idem significare volui? nequaquam certe. Fidem in Deum aliquando summatim, aliquando per partes magis describimus, in Deum Patrem, omnipotentem creatorem caeli & terrae: fi simpliciter, vel in Deum creatorem,aut Patrem omnipotentem dixero, varias innuere fidei confessiones videbor, aut significare synonyma esse cum recensitis aliis ista quae forte omisi? Quando Paulus dixit,
units.tr: Reply. In the same way our opponents argue as if someone were to infer, from the varying form of baptism, into Jesus, or into the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, either that all these signify the same thing and are appellations sounding the same, or that different confessions of faith are laid down. Pray, does it follow that there are different confessions of faith because, in explaining its object, some passages are sometimes more fully, sometimes more briefly, expressed in one way and another, without rejecting anything that is expressed elsewhere for the completion of faith? "overcomes the world, our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?" And above, chapter 4:15: "Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God." For does not John here express different faiths, rather than one and the same single faith? How then would it be true that everyone who has only one faith is born of God, or abides in God and God in him, or overcomes the world? How could Paul elsewhere also have said: "If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe that God raised him from the dead" (things in which is contained all that John here comprehended in the words of Christ), "you will be saved," if besides this faith it were also required that you believe he was begotten of the substance of the Father and is God together with the Father? Is the faith in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, king, Lord, prophet, our priest, etc., true and saving? If I now state more members of this faith and now fewer, do I on that account either think less of what I have omitted, or indicate different confessions of faith, or finally mean that all these signify the same thing? By no means. We sometimes describe faith in God in summary, sometimes more in parts: in God the Father, almighty, creator of heaven and earth. If I say simply "in God," or "in God the creator," or "the almighty Father," shall I seem to hint at different confessions of faith, or to signify that these are synonyms with the others recounted, and that I have perhaps left out some? When Paul said

units.la: credendum quod Deus Christum è mortuis suscitavit,ideo minus putavit necessarium creditu, quod Christus pro nobis mortuus,aut etiam adscendit? vel voluit,voces istas idem significare inter fe, & in Christo? Uti ergo dicens, fi credideris Christum Iesum esse Dominum, atque è mortuis à Patre suscitatum, eris salvus, non negat credendum quoque ad salutem, Christum adscendisse, & reversurum ad judicium, aliaque fide in Christum comprehensa, ita nec illo excludit ut credas Christum à Patre ab aeterno genitum, eundemque cum eo Deum, & Dei Filium, quod alias docemur, & loco isto tamen Apostolus non commemoravit, Rom. x. 9. nec quod Dei filius, nec quod Christus,neq; tamen minus necessaria.
units.tr: that one must believe that God raised Christ from the dead, did he therefore think it less necessary to believe that Christ died for us, or even ascended? Or did he wish these words to signify the same thing among themselves and in Christ? So when he says, "If you believe that Christ Jesus is Lord, and that he was raised from the dead by the Father, you will be saved," he does not deny that it is also necessary for salvation to believe that Christ ascended and will return to judgement, and other things comprehended in faith in Christ; nor does he exclude thereby that you should believe that Christ was begotten by the Father from eternity, and is God together with him, and the Son of God, which we are taught elsewhere, though the Apostle did not mention it in that passage, Rom. x. 9. Neither the Son of God nor Christ is named there, yet neither is less necessary.

units.la: Quartum à Socino allatum testimonium, ex eadem Ioannis Epistola petitum est. Idipsum, inquit Socinus, intelligitur exeo, quod scriptum est cap. 2. v. 22.23. Ex isto enim loco apparet, idem esse, negare Iesum esse Christum, quod negare Filium. Ioannis verba sunt: Quis est ille mendax, nisi qui negat Iesum esse Christum. Hic est Antichristus, qui negat Patrem & Filium. Omnis qui negat Filium, neque Patrem habet. Ex his enim verbis apparet, negato eo, quòd Iesus fit Christus, eo ipso negari Filium. Hoc vero qui fieret, nisi Christum esse idem significaret, quod esse Dei Filium? Si dicas, idcirco istud fi, quod Christum esse, & illum Dei Filium esse, tam arcte cohaerent, ut uno negato alte-
units.tr: The fourth testimony brought forward by Socinus is taken from the same Epistle of John. "The same is understood," says Socinus, "from what is written in chapter 2, verses 22 and 23." For from this passage it appears that to deny that Jesus is the Christ is the same as to deny the Son. The words of John are: "Who is the liar, but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the Antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father." From these words it appears that by denying that Jesus is the Christ, the Son is thereby denied. But how could this be, unless to be the Christ signified the same as to be the Son of God? If you say that this is so because being the Christ and being that Son of God are so closely connected that, when one is denied, the other

units.la: Resp. 1. Non dicitur in Textu, super quod tamen fundat non modo prolixam suam orationem Adversarius, sed fere triumphum, ita ut non alium locum pro sententia sua putet commodiorem,non,in-quam, dicitur, negato eo, quod Iesus fit Christus,negari quoque Filium. Non quod verum esse istud negem, sed quod id textu contineri, ut inde argumentum in nos vibrare possit, nequeat ostendere. Illum mendacem ait[?] Iohannes, qui negat Iesum esse Christum: Antichristum, qui negat Patrem & Filium. Non dicit, quod negato Christo, negetur quoque filius. Uti nec, quod negato Christo, negetur & Pater. Quod non minus verum, ac illud. Et qui unum,alterum quoque docere, putansitm[?] negari oportet; non vero, quod unum idemque significent. 1. Si id propter cohaerentiam iam fieret, non vero propter eandem utriusque vocis significationem, non debuisset Ioannes unum pro altero ita simpliciter substituere, quemadmodum fecit, sed aliquam consequentiae rationem insinuare. 2. Aut Filii Dei voce significatur is, qui supremum in omnia imperium ex Patris gratia adeptus est: aut is, qui ab aeterno ex ipsius essentia sit genitus. Si prius; nihil aliud Filii vox designabit quam Christi; meritoque Ioannes pro eodem habet, negare Christum, & negare Filium. Si posterius; falsum est haec inter se cohaerere, ut uno negato protinus negetur & alterum: id est, negato Christo negetur & Dei Filius. Quid enim, si quis Iudaeus vestra de Trinitate sententia imbutus esset, (quandoquidem etiam sub Veteri Foedere dogma Trinitatis ignotum non fuisse docetis, imo inde etiam testimonia pro eo adstruendo petere soletis) num idcirco negaret Patrem, qui ab aeterno ex essentia sua genuerit: negaret Filium ab aeterno ex Patris essentia genitum, quia Iesum illum Nazarenum, qui in carne venit, quiqué infami supplicio affectus fuerit, Christum esse negaret: ac proinde Christum nondum venisse, nondum esse, contenderet? Imo, si necessarium esse sciret, ut is, qui Christus esset, simul etiam ille Dei Filius esset, vel idcirco maxime Iesum negaret esse Christum, quod cum Filium illum Dei esse nollet concedere. Itaque si quis alius, hic certe Ioannis locus pro nostra sententia militat. alioqui enim nunquam negationem Christi, & negationem Patris ac Filii Ioannes inter se permutare potuisset, & unum pro altero, praesertim ita simpliciter, substituere. dus est. Haud tamen inde effici, opinor, statues, quod Christus & Pater idem sonant, vel esse eandem utriusque vocis significationem. Atque certum est, quamvis id textu non dicatur, eum, qui Christum, negare etiam Patrem & Filium. Sed id satis habuit dixisse Auctor, quod mendax sit, qui Iesum Chhristum negat: Antichristus, qui Patrem & Filium. Quae vero inter illa connexio sit, vel ad mutuam sive positionem, sive destructionem sequela, ex rei natura potius, quam nudis illis verbis constare potest. II. Verum tamen est, eo ipso quod quis Christum, negare quoque Filium & Patrem; vel qui in textu servatur ordo, Patrem & Filium. Nam Christus est filius, & nisi filius, Christus non esset, uti nec sine filio Pater. Haec ergo ita conjuncta, ut alterum sine altero esse, & negari nequeat. Et notetur, quod jam cohaerentiam rerum illam rejicit Adversarius, urgeat vero eandem utriusque vocis significationem, qui modo dixit, se non de verbis agere, sed de rebus. Atqui de vocibus, negamus, Iohannem unum pro altero substituisse. Consequentiae rationem ipsa rei natura satis insinuat. III. Filii Dei voce significatur is, & qui supremum in omnia imperium ex Patris dono adeptus est, & qui ab aeterno ex ejus essentia genitus. Neque tamen filii vox nihil aliud designat, quam Christi: quidem neminem alium. Quaesierat enim, aut filii Dei voce significatur is, &c. non id. Atqui respectu personae, merito Iohannes pro eodem habet, negare Christum, & negare Filium. Deinde, omnino illa inter se cohaerent, negare Christum, & negare aeternum Dei Filium, ut qui illum, hunc etiam inficietur. Quia enim non alius est filius, quam Christus, neque Christus alius quam ille idem Filius, qui hunc illum, & vice versa, qui Christum, idem Filium negat. Neque enim satis est ad hoc eludendum, ut aliquem Filium tibi formes & fingas, qui non sit Christus; vel Christum alium, quam qui sit filius: sed Filium Christum, & Christum Filium habeas necesse est, si verum. Non est filius absque Christo, non Christus absque filio: quare qui unum, is & alterum habeat, aut tollat, simul requiritur. Imo certe Iudaeus ille, aut quicumque alius, qui Trinitatem credere se profitetur, & negat ChriChristi Messiam, negare eo ipso veram, non aliquam suam fictitiam, Trinitatem dicendus esset. Postquam enim Deo placuit, Filium suum huic operi in mundum mittere, quod nomine & officio Christi comprehenditur, non verum Filium is teneret, quare nec etiam verum Patre, qui alium a Christo. Nam Pater filii, est etiam Pater Christi, nam qui diceret, Christum non esse illum Dei Filium, & Patrem non esse filii Christi Patrem, annon & Patrem negaret, & Filium: id est, non aliquem esse Patrem & Filium, sed illum, qui verus Pater, & filius est, negaret. Neque apud Iohannem intelligitur, quacumque ratione dictus aut dicendus Pater, & sic quoque Filius: sed Pater filii Christi,& filius Patris Christus. Propter istam causam,qui Patrem,is & Filium negat; & qui Filium, Patrem. Quare quam nihil ille locus pro sententia adversaria militet, constat. Neque enim negationem Patris ac Filii Johannes inter se permutat, quidem conjungit, ut necessario inter se cohaerentia, non vero unum pro altero, nedum simpliciter, substituit. Sequeretur etiam alias, quod non tantum idem significarent voces filii Dei, & Christi: sed quoque Patris. Non autem dicent, opinor, Adversarii, eandem vocis Patris, & Filii esse significationem.
units.tr: Reply 1. The text does not say what the opponent builds on, and on which he rests not only his long argument but almost his whole triumph, so that he thinks no other passage better suits his view. The text does not say, I repeat, that when Jesus is denied to be the Christ, the Son is denied too. I do not deny that this is true; my point is that he cannot show it is contained in the text, so that he could hurl an argument from it against us. John calls the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ a liar, and the one who denies the Father and the Son an antichrist. He does not say that when Christ is denied, the Son is denied as well, nor that when Christ is denied, the Father is denied too. That is no less true than the other, and whoever thinks one must be taught along with the other is wrong to infer that they mean the same thing. (1) If this followed from their connection, and not from the same meaning of each term, John would not have substituted one for the other so simply, as he did, but would have hinted at some reason for the consequence. (2) The term Son of God signifies either him who has obtained supreme rule over all things by the Father's grace, or him who has been begotten from eternity out of the Father's essence. If the first, the term Son signifies nothing other than Christ, and John rightly regards denying Christ and denying the Son as the same thing. If the second, it is false that the two are so connected that denying one at once denies the other, that is, that denying Christ denies the Son of God. For suppose some Jew, imbued with your doctrine of the Trinity (since you teach that the doctrine of the Trinity was not unknown even under the Old Covenant, and indeed you are accustomed to seek testimonies from there to establish it), were to deny that Jesus the Nazarene, who came in the flesh and suffered an infamous death, is the Christ, and to maintain that the Christ has not yet come and does not yet exist. Would he for that reason deny the Father who begot the Son from eternity out of his own essence, and deny the Son begotten from eternity out of the Father's essence? Indeed, if he knew it was necessary that he who is the Christ should also be the Son of God, he would most of all deny that Jesus is the Christ precisely because he was unwilling to grant that he is the Son of God. So if any other passage, this passage of John certainly fights for our view; otherwise John could never have interchanged the denial of Christ with the denial of the Father and the Son, and substituted one for the other, especially so simply. Yet, I think, it does not follow from this that Christ and Father sound the same, or that the meaning of each term is the same. And it is certain that, although the text does not say it, whoever denies Christ also denies the Father and the Son. But the author was content to have said that the one who denies Jesus Christ is a liar, and the one who denies the Father and the Son is an antichrist. What connection exists between those things, whether a mutual consequence of affirmation or of destruction, can be established from the nature of the thing rather than from those bare words. II. It is nevertheless true that by the very fact that someone denies Christ he also denies the Son and the Father; the order in the text is Father and Son. For Christ is the Son, and unless he were the Son he would not be Christ, just as the Father is not without the Son. These things, then, are so conjoined that one cannot exist without the other or be denied apart from it. And it should be noted that the opponent now rejects that connection of things, yet insists on the same meaning of each term, though he just said he was not dealing with words but with things. But we deny that John substituted one word for another. The nature of the thing itself sufficiently suggests the reason for the consequence. III. By the term Son of God is signified him who has obtained supreme rule over all things by the Father's gift, and who has been begotten from eternity out of his essence. Nor does the term Son designate nothing other than Christ, since it designates no one else. For the question was whether by the term Son of God is signified him, etc., not that. Yet with respect to the person, John rightly regards denying Christ and denying the Son as the same thing. Moreover, these things cohere entirely: to deny Christ and to deny the eternal Son of God, since whoever denies the one also denies the other. For since the Son is no other than Christ, nor Christ other than that same Son, whoever denies this one also denies that one, and vice versa, whoever denies Christ denies the same Son. It is not enough to escape this by inventing for yourself some Son who is not Christ, or some Christ who is not the Son; you must hold that the Son is Christ and Christ is the Son, if it is to be true. There is no Son without Christ, no Christ without the Son; therefore whoever affirms or removes one, at the same time requires the other. Indeed, that Jew, or anyone else who professes to believe in the Trinity and denies that Christ is the Messiah, would rightly be said by that very fact to deny the true Trinity, not some fictitious one of his own. For once it pleased God to send his Son into the world for this work, which is comprehended in the name and office of Christ, whoever holds that he is not the true Son does not hold the true Father either, since the Father is other than Christ. For the Father of the Son is also the Father of Christ; for whoever said that Christ is not that Son of God, and that the Father is not the Father of the Son Christ, would he not deny both the Father and the Son? That is, he would deny not some Father and Son, but the one who is the true Father and Son. Nor is it understood in John in whatever way the Father is called, or ought to be called, and thus also the Son, but the Father of the Son Christ and the Son of the Father Christ. For this reason, whoever denies the Father, denies also the Son; and whoever denies the Son, the Father. Hence it is plain how little that passage favours the adversary's view. For John does not interchange the denial of the Father and of the Son, but conjoins them as things necessarily cohering with each other, and does not substitute one for the other, much less simply. Otherwise it would follow that the terms Son of God and Christ signify not only the same thing, but also the Father. The opponents, I think, will not say that the terms Father and Son have the same meaning.

units.la: Quintum Socini argumentum, ex ipsius Christi apud Ioannem verbis petitum est, cap. 10. v. 36. in quibus causam, cur se Dei Filium (singulari nimirum, caeterisque minime communi ratione,) appellasset, afferens, eam attulit, quae tota Christi nomine continetur. Haec autem est, quod a Patre sanctificatus, id est, ut Petrus loquitur, a Deo Spiritu Sancto & virtute unctus, (unde Christi nomen) & in mundum missus, id est, ad hoc ipsum, ad quod unctus fuit, munus, inter homines obeundum, ablegatus fuerit.
units.tr: The fifth argument of Socinus is taken from the very words of Christ in John, chap. 10, v. 36, in which, giving the reason why he called himself the Son of God (in the singular, and in a way quite unlike other men), he gave the one that is wholly contained in the name Christ. This reason is that he was sanctified by the Father, that is, as Peter says, anointed by God with the Holy Spirit and power (whence the name Christ), and was sent into the world, that is, dispatched to perform among men the very office for which he was anointed.

units.la: Resp. 1. Si Christus ibi causam adfert, quare sit Dei filius, quae toto nomine Christi continetur, ergo non idem significant duae illae appellationes Christi, & filii Dei; sed differunt, uti causa, & causatum: & sequetur quidem, unicum esse Filium, quia unus Christus, non vero voces illas ejusdem esse significationis.
units.tr: Reply 1. If Christ there gives the reason why he is the Son of God, which is contained in the whole name Christ, then the two appellations, Christ and Son of God, do not signify the same thing, but differ as cause and effect. And it would follow indeed that there is one Son, because there is one Christ, but not that those terms have the same meaning.

units.la: II. Vox Christi in textu non occurrit, ergo hinc non potest evincere eandem utri-que vocis significationem. Nec re, nec voce, aut vocum significatione eadem sunt, esse Filium Dei, & esse Christum, quamvis quidem una persona, sed in quo aliud significat esse Christum, aliud Dei Filium.
units.tr: II. The word "Christ" does not occur in the text, so one cannot prove from this that both terms have the same meaning. Being the Son of God and being Christ are not the same in thing, in word, or in the meaning of the words, although it is one person. In this case, "Christ" signifies one thing and "Son of God" another.

units.la: III. Causam non adfert Christus hoc versu propriam suae filiationis, sed cur non debeat censeri blasphemasse, quod se Dei Filium, vel cum Patre unum, ἓν[?] dixisset, & σεαυτὸν θεόν[?]. Si illos dixit Deos, ad quos sermo Dei factus, & non potest Scriptura solvi. Quem Pater sanctificavit & misit in mundum, vos dicitis, quod blasphemas, quia dixi, filius Dei sum?
units.tr: III. In this verse Christ does not give the cause of his own sonship. He gives the reason why he should not be thought to have blasphemed when he called himself the Son of God, or said that he was one with the Father, "ἓν" [ἓν], and "making himself God" [σεαυτὸν θεόν]. "If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken..." "Do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world that he blasphemes, because I said, I am the Son of God?"

units.la: IV. Mitti in mundum, & sanctificari fuit causa quidem indicans Dei Filium, nonef- ficiens.
units.tr: IV. Being sent into the world and being sanctified indicate that he is the Son of God, but they do not make him so.

units.la: V. Talis ista est intelligenda filiatio, ex qua filius cum Patre idem est, & αὐτὸς θεὸς[?], verf. 30. 33. quod quia non est ex sanctificatione & munere, quod obvit in terris, hoc pro causa illius formali & adaequata adferri non potest.
units.tr: V. The sonship that must be understood here is one by which the Son is one with the Father and "himself God" [αὐτὸς θεὸς], vers. 30, 33. Because this is not from sanctification and the office he undertook on earth, it cannot be advanced as its formal and adequate cause.

units.la: VI. Missio Christi in mundum, ejusque sanctificatio, prout ab ad versariis exponitur, non est ita Christo propria, ut non aliqua etiam ratione communis sit aliis: quare ea non potest causa dici cur filius Dei, nedum unigenitus, appelletur.
units.tr: VI. The sending of Christ into the world and his sanctification, as our opponents explain them, are not so proper to Christ that they are not in some respect common to others also. Therefore they cannot be called the cause why he is called the Son of God, much less the only-begotten.

units.la: Sexto ait Socinus: Cum Christi nomen & munus in Iesu Nazareno unicum ac perpetuum eundemque coelestem populi Dei regem Schlichtingius, pag. 570.
units.tr: Sixthly, Socinus says: Since the name and office of Christ in Jesus of Nazareth is unique and perpetual, and the same heavenly king of the people of God, Schlichtingius, p. 570.

units.la: Resp. 1. Christi nomen, regium ejus munus atque imperium significat, sed non solum; nam & plures ejus muneris par-tes, quod nomine illo significatur. Quae significet, & ita omne divinum imperium ac majestatem, quam Jesus habet, aperte declaret, quid amplius, quod huc pertineant, Filii Dei nomen significare potuit? Respondet Meisnerus: appellationem Filii respicere aeternam generationem & ὁμοούσιον cum Patre. Et paulo post ait. Imo formaliter & directe solam filiationem, vel aeternam productionem & nullatenus officium vel regnum significat. At nos dicimus, I. Aeternam illam generationem & ὁμοούσιον, non ante nobis in Filii Dei nomine obtrudendam esse, quam aliunde liquidis documentis demonstrata fuerit. 2. Magno praejudicio causam aggravat Meisnerus.
