Nam cum res ipsa loquatur, fieri non posse, quin tam augusto Filii Dei titulo divinum Christi ac sublime imperium significetur, quo & maxima illius cum Deo similitudo, & omnibus Regibus, qui tamen & ipsi Filii Dei nuncupantur, longe celsior continetur majestas: ipso autem Meisnero teste, nullatenus ad hoc imperium pertineat aeterna Christi filiatio, quid aliud restat, quam ut fateatur, hujus tituli Christi veritatem majestatemque sine ea posse constare? quia, vel Adversario teste, non idem denotant quod Dei Filius, consequitur, nomina Christi & Dei Filii ejusdem significationis non esse, aut latitudinis. II. Nomen filii Dei id significat, quod Christus ante officii sui adoptionem fuit. Nam id muneris Dei filio impositum, quod nulli alteri imponi debuit, aut potuit. Quare significat & divinam suam, ex generatione, non officio, naturam; & par ei imperium, cui postea officium & dominium mediatorium tributum, per quod Ecclesia Deo reconciliaretur & regeretur. Atque sic fieri quidem non potest, quin augusto filii titulo divinum imperium denotetur, sed non quod in tempore ei datum demum Mediatori, verum essentiale, quod cum Patre ἐν unus idemque habet, quo & maxima illius cum Deo similitudo non tantum, sed ἑνότης, & omnibus Regibus, qui tamen & ipsi filii Dei nuncupantur, longe celsior majestas continetur. Ergo omnino ad Filium Dei pertinet imperium, sed non restringendum ad hoc quod in tempore accepit: sed aeternum, & vere divinum. Christi autem ὁμοούσια vel hinc demonstratur, quod verus Dei filius, id est, naturae ejusdem per generationem vere & proprie particeps. Metaphoram si contra illi clament; ergo metaphorico se obiectent, nos propriam verborum significationem sequendam docti, & proprium amplectemur Dei Filium, & divinum regem. Filium nempe, qui eo est ἐν cum Patre, & αὐτῆς Θεὸς : quae ὁμοούσιον fatis declarant & ostendunt.
units.tr: Reply 1. The name Christ signifies his kingly office and rule, but not only that, for it also signifies several other parts of that office. Yet how could the name Son of God, if it signifies all divine rule and majesty which Jesus has and clearly declares, signify anything more that pertains to this? Meisner replies that the name Son refers to eternal generation and consubstantiality [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father. And a little later he says: Indeed it signifies formally and directly only sonship, or eternal production, and in no way office or kingdom. But we say, first, that that eternal generation and consubstantiality must not be forced upon us in the name Son of God until it has been demonstrated from clear proofs elsewhere. Second, Meisner makes his case worse by a great prejudice. For since the thing itself speaks, it cannot fail that by so august a title as Son of God the divine and lofty rule of Christ is signified, by which both his greatest likeness to God and a majesty far higher than that of all kings, who are nevertheless also called sons of God, is contained. But by Meisner's own testimony, the eternal sonship of Christ does not pertain at all to this rule. What remains, then, except that he must confess that the truth and majesty of this title of Christ can stand without that sonship? Because, even on the testimony of the opponent, they do not denote the same thing as Son of God, it follows that the names Christ and Son of God are not of the same signification or breadth. II. The name Son of God signifies what Christ was before the adoption of his office. For that is a title imposed on the Son of God which could be imposed on no other. Hence it signifies his divine nature, from generation and not from office, and a rule equal to God's, to which afterwards the office and mediatorial dominion was given, through which the Church is reconciled to God and governed. And so it cannot but be that by the august title of Son a divine rule is denoted, not however that which was given to him in time as Mediator, but the essential rule which he has as one and the same with the Father, "ἐν" [ἐν], by which not only his greatest likeness to God but oneness [ἑνότης] is contained, and a majesty far higher than that of all kings, who are nevertheless also called sons of God. Therefore rule certainly belongs to the Son of God, but it must not be restricted to what he received in time; it is eternal and truly divine. And the consubstantiality of Christ is demonstrated from this, that he is the true Son of God, that is, truly and properly a partaker of the same nature by generation. If they cry out that this is metaphor, then they are objecting to a metaphor; we, taught to follow the proper meaning of words, embrace the proper Son of God and the divine King: the Son who is "one" [ἐν] with the Father and "himself God" [αὐτὸς θεὸς]. These things sufficiently declare and show consubstantiality [ὁμοούσιον].

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 570. Septimum Socini argumentum: Quod illi, qui imperium aliquod & judicium habent, & exercent, Filii Dei & nominentur, & sint; quemadmodum docet locus ab ipso Christo citatus, Ego dixi, Dii estis, & filii Excelsi omnes. Quare & Christus ob imperium ac judicium, quod a Deo accepit, recte Filius Dei nominatur: Et, quia unicum ac singulare prorsus imperium accepit, quod alia infinitis partibus superat, quodque nullus alius praeter ipsum nec
units.tr: Schlichtingius, p. 570. The seventh argument of Socinus: Those who have and exercise some rule and judgment are both called and are sons of God, as the passage which Christ himself cited teaches: "I said, You are gods, and you are all sons of the Most High." Therefore Christ also is rightly called Son of God because of the rule and judgment which he received from God. And since he has received a unique and altogether singular rule, which surpasses others by infinite degrees, and which no one else but himself nor

units.la: Resp. Si non alia de causa Christus esset Dei filius, ita appellari posset, & propter imperium ac judicium, quod a Deo accepit. Sed ea ratione foret modo λεγόμενος[?] θεός, non φύσει, non ἐν cum Patre, neque inde liceret se facere Deum, σεαυ-τὸν θεόν, magis quam alii reges aut principes. Quum vero ita Christus sit Dei filius ut hoc explicetur non solum excel-lentiori gradu, quem supra alios reges ha-beat, habet, nec habere potest: idcirco etiam optimo jure unicus ille ac singularis Dei Filius & est, & appellatur. Hoc autem, ut dictum est, ipsa una Christi appellatione totum continetur. beat, sed diversa plane forma, ut in nemi-nem, praeterquam verum ipsum Deum cadat, liquet, appellationem filii Dei in Christo non esse exponendam ex vulgari alia nomenclatione simili regum aut prin-cipum terrenorum, aut similitudine quam ad istos habeat, sed similitudine ejus aut paritate ad Deum. Cæterum non propter imperium, quamvis singulare, haberi eum Dei Filium, sed propterea quod Dei filius, imperium ei datum, vel ipse rerum ordo evincit. Ut nec eo filius, nedum unigenitus factus, aut dictus fuerit. Neque una Christi appellatione totum continetur, sensu vocis nimirum, bene quidem cohærentia rei, & reductive.
units.tr: Reply. If Christ were not the Son of God for any other reason, he could be so called on account of the rule and judgment which he received from God. But on that ground he would be merely a god by name [λεγόμενος θεός], not by nature, not "one" [ἐν] with the Father, and it would not then be lawful for him to make himself God [σεαυτὸν θεόν] any more than other kings or princes. But since Christ is the Son of God in such a way that this is explained not only by a higher degree which he has above other kings, nor can he have it, therefore that unique and singular Son of God is also rightly both and called so. This, as has been said, is wholly contained in the one name Christ. It is clear that the name Son of God in Christ is not to be explained from the common nomenclature of kings or earthly princes, nor from the likeness he bears to them, but from his likeness or equality with God. Moreover, he is not regarded as the Son of God on account of a rule, however singular, but because he is the Son of God, which the given rule, or the very order of things, proves. Nor was he made or named the Son, much less the only-begotten, by that. Nor is everything contained in the one name Christ, in the sense of the word, rightly cohering with the thing, and by reduction.

units.la: Atque illa quidem Socini argumenta sunt septem, quæ recollegit & vindicare ausus fuit Schlichtingius, ut probaret, appellationem filii Dei idem significare, quod Christi: quorum quinque Scripturæ eodem fere redeunt, nempe ut eundem Iesum, jam nomine Christi, jam filii Dei designari, alias omitti hanc vel istam nomenclationem, ostendant: nisi quod Joann. x. 36. vox Christi non occurrat, quamvis quidem res: & argumenta duo ultima è ratione petita, idem urgent, Christi vid. imperium, ut Dei filius propterea dicatur. Sed in disputatione non erat propositum, agere jam de filio Dei, sed de notione unigeniti: quæ in omnibus illis locis non occurrit, & tantum huc pertrahitur, ut unigenitus nil significet aliud, quam unicum Christum. Id vero dixit quidem, & argumentationi annexuit, non vero probavit: nec probabit ullo aut Scripturæ loco, aut alicujus demum Scriptoris, ullave ratione aut unum dominum, unigenitum, aut unigenitum, qui unus forte singulari modo dominetur, unquam appellatum. Et tam temerarie, addo profane, licebit ludere in sacris, & hoc sacrorum altissimo mysterio, ubi de Christo agitur, & Dei filio, adeoq; & de Deo Patre? Quod Filius Dei unigenitus dicat, unicum Christum, probetur ullo vel minimo aut Scripturæ, aut rationis indicio. Quin fit unus modo Christus, probatione non eget, neq; hoc ut ostendatur peto, sed quod unigenitus Dei filius nihil aliud quam istud significet, id demum probari mihi peto. Et fac, quod vox filii Dei Christum significet, non tamen ideo probatum, vocem unigeniti nihil aliud significare quam Christum vel Dominum unum. Diversæ voces sunt, & sensus earum diversi. Quæcunque allata haftenus, de filio Dei loquuntur, de unigenito nihil. Quis unquam unigenitum dixit, unum vel singularem Dominum intelligens? contrà quando unigenitus filio additur, quod non generationis id fit respectu? Non semel aliquando Christus aut Dei filius dicitur, aut unigenitus, sed genitus, filius, unigenitus, proprius, ut proprie omnia accipienda ne ignoraremus. Adversarii unigenitum interpretantur quasi κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν[?] dictum Filium. Schlichtingius, pag. 572. Iesum Nazarenum propter illud non tantum simpliciter Dei filium, sed etiam Dei Filium κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν[?], id est, unicum, singularem, propterea q; unigenitum, merito posse appellari. Hoc vim unigeniti est enervare, & detrudere ad communem fortem, quando per solam exponitur excellentiam. Unitatem dicit, & unitatem generationis, non quandam simpliciter excellentiam. Quia est unigenitus Dei filius, ideo unicus, & singulariter excellens, non quia talis, ideo unigeni-tus. Falsum est, inquit, filiationem Christi ad idem genus cum aliorum hominum filiatione non pertinere. Potest enim & fingularissima ratione Christus esse filius Dei, & tamen in generali ali-qua qua filiationis ratione cum caeteris hominibus convenire. Generalis ratio filiationis in similitudine cum Deo posita est: singularissima vero in singularissima similitudine, nec alii ulli communi.
units.tr: These, indeed, are the seven arguments of Socinus, which Schlichtingius gathered together and dared to defend, in order to prove that the name Son of God signifies the same as Christ. Five of them come back to almost the same thing, namely that they show that the same Jesus is designated now by the name Christ, now by the name Son of God, and that otherwise this or that designation is omitted. Except that the word Christ does not occur in John 10:36, though the thing does; and the last two arguments, drawn from reason, press the same point, namely the rule of Christ, so that he is called the Son of God on that account. But in the disputation it was not my purpose to treat now of the Son of God, but of the meaning of "only-begotten," which does not occur in any of those passages, and is dragged in only so that "only-begotten" signifies nothing other than the one Christ. He indeed said this and attached it to the argument, but did not prove it, nor will he prove by any passage of Scripture, or of any writer whatever, or by any reason, that "only-begotten" was ever used for "the one Lord," or for one who perhaps rules in a singular way. And shall it be so rashly, I add profanely, permitted to play with sacred things, and with this most lofty mystery of the sacred, where Christ is treated of, the Son of God, and so also God the Father? That the Son of God, the only-begotten, means the one Christ, let it be proved by any, even the smallest, indication of Scripture or of reason. That Christ is only one needs no proof, nor do I ask for it to be shown; but that the only-begotten Son of God signifies nothing else than this, that I ask to be proved. And grant that the term Son of God signifies Christ; it does not follow that it has been proved that the term only-begotten signifies nothing else than Christ or the one Lord. The words are different, and their meanings are different. Whatever has been adduced so far speaks of the Son of God; nothing of the only-begotten. Who ever called anyone "only-begotten," meaning one or a singular Lord? On the contrary, when "only-begotten" is added to "Son," how is this not with respect to generation? Christ or the Son of God is not called at any time simply "only-begotten," but "begotten," "son," "only-begotten," "proper," so that all things are to be taken properly, lest we be ignorant. The opponents interpret "only-begotten" as the Son spoken of by way of pre-eminence [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν]. Schlichtingius, p. 572: that Jesus of Nazareth can be called, on account of that, not only simply Son of God, but also the Son of God by pre-eminence [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν], that is, the unique, singular one, and therefore rightly called only-begotten. This is to weaken the force of "only-begotten" and to drag it down to the common lot, since it is explained only by excellence. It signifies unity, and the unity of generation, not some simple excellence. Because he is the only-begotten Son of God, he is therefore unique and singularly excellent; not because he is such, is he therefore only-begotten. It is false, he says, that the sonship of Christ does not belong to the same kind as the sonship of other men. For Christ can be the Son of God in a most singular way, and yet in some general respect of sonship agree with other men. The general ground of sonship is placed in likeness to God; but the most singular in the most singular likeness, and not common to any other.

units.la: Non certe ejusdem generis est filiatio Christi, cum nostra, sed toto genere differt, ἀδιαφορώτερον [?] ὄνομα. Quantum distat filiatio naturalis, a morali, quarum illa fundamentum habet in generatione naturali, ista in morali aliqua similitudine, illamque imitatur & solo nomine refert, tantum differt filiatio Christi, a nostra: nemini enim vel Angelorum unquam dixit Deus, tu es filius meus ego hodie genui te. Nemo ex filiatione sua concluserit citra blasphemiam, quod fit unum cum Patre, aut fecerit οὕτω τὸν θεὸν [?], uti Christus, nemo hinc filius Dei proprius, quod ille. Nostra quidem filiatio in similitudine fundatur aliqua, Christi vero in unitate vel identitate. Estq; hic non similitudo aliqua, quamvis nostra gradu excelsior, sed ἑνότης [?] nulli alii communis.
units.tr: Certainly the sonship of Christ is not of the same kind as ours; it differs from ours in its whole kind [ἀδιαφορώτερον ὄνομα]. As far as natural sonship differs from moral sonship, the former resting on natural generation and the latter on some moral likeness, which imitates the former and bears only its name, so far does the sonship of Christ differ from ours. For God never said to any of the angels, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you." No one may rightly infer from his own sonship, without blasphemy, that he is one with the Father, or make himself equal to God [οὕτω τὸν θεὸν] as Christ did, or that he is the proper Son of God in the way that he is. Our sonship is founded on some likeness, but Christ's on unity or identity. This is not some likeness, however much higher in degree than ours, but a unity [ἑνότης] shared with no other.

units.la: Tandem urget Socinus, Ipsum Dei Filium proprium & unigenitum esse mortuum, Ioan. 3. 16. Rom. 5. 10. & 32. Act. 3. 13. 26. 1 Thess. 1. 10. Hinc infert: Cum igitur, sicut omnes fatentur, sic etiam divinitus testatissimum sit, Dei Filium Unigenitum fuisse mortuum, mori autem non potuerit substantia ulla divina, quae in Christo fuerit, sed tantum humana: sequitur, non divinam ullam, sed tantum humanam substantiam in Christo esse Unigenitum Dei Filium. Syllogismum ita format Schlichtingius ipse: Quicumque vere mortuus est, is non est, aut illius non est divina aliqua substantia; sed filius Dei unigenitus vere mortuus est. Ergo, &c. Resp. Negatur major. Neque enim illa magis vera, quam haec, quicumque vere mortuus est, is non est, aut illius non est immortalis aliqua substantia. Quippe homo vere moritur, immortali quamvis anima. Et quid morti magis opponi in terminis potest, quam quod est immortale? Ut instantiam illam illudat Adversarius, inquit, Licet enim in homine qui moritur sit anima, quae est incorruptibilis quaedam substantia: tamen homo ipse, aut hominis ipsius non est incorruptibilis substantia; quemadmodum Meisnerus Filium Dei, aut Filii Dei divinam substantiam proprie esse, asserit. Imo hominis ipsius est aliqua incorruptibilis substantia, quemadmodum Christi aliqua prorsus divina. Et homo ipse, quemadmodum & Christus, moritur, sed non id propterea quod in homine immortale, vel in Christo divinum. Salva ergo manente animae immortalitate homo moritur, & salva divina sui substantia Christus: ut non ex morte Christi magis contra divinam naturam, ac ex morte hominis contra animam ejus immortalem arguere fas sit. At quemadmodum anima aliquando dicitur mori in homine, anima quae peccavit, ipsa moritur, id est homo anima, sed ipsa immortali, praeditus: ita filii Dei mors dicitur, id est, Christi, qui & Dei filius. Quo pacto responsum etiam ad syllogismi minorem. Nempe qui filius Dei unigenitus, Christus puta, vere mortuus est: non qua filius unigenitus. Nam quemadmodum Pater non potuit desinere esse Pater, sic neque Filius; atqui eo moriente nec ille tantisper saltem fuisset Pater. Praeterea si filius Dei juxta Adversarios non fit substantia, sed accidens, quomodo vere dicetur mori, neque enim accidentia proprie, sed substantia vivens moritur. Denique, jam divinam in Christo substantiam negant. Unde apparet, quem Dei Filium velint, id est, absque divina substantia: quod est, quasi Filium hominis formarent, absque humana substantia. Sed neque inde quod filius Dei dicitur mortuus, sequitur Dei Filium, & Christum idem significare. Nec certe idem significant voces, quae etymologia ac origine, natura sua, & usu perpetuo & universali diversum habent sensum, qualia sunt filius Dei, & Christus, utcunque res eadem personae conveniat. Secundo, & quae separari possunt, ut filius Dei non sit Christus, atque etiam juxta Adversarios, ut filius Dei ex singulari nativitate, non autem ad istam dignitatem & imperium perveniat, quod jam Christo datum. Tertio, multi Dei filii, qui tamen non dicendi Christi: ergo ista non idem significant. Denique quis unquam dixerit, filiationem alicujus perfici, & de gradu in gradum consummari? ita quidem generatio naturalis sua momenta habet & partes, quibus tandem absolvitur, filiatio nunquam.
units.tr: Finally, Socinus presses the point that the proper and only-begotten Son of God died (John 3:16; Rom. 5:10 and 32; Acts 3:13, 26; 1 Thess. 1:10). From this he infers: since it is as certain as everyone admits, and as clearly attested by divine testimony, that the only-begotten Son of God died, and since no divine substance that was in Christ could die, but only the human substance, it follows that in Christ the only-begotten Son of God is not any divine substance but only a human substance. Schlichting himself puts the syllogism in this form: whoever truly died either is not, or has no divine substance; but the only-begotten Son of God truly died. Therefore, etc. I reply: the major premise is denied. For it is no more true that whoever truly died is not, or has no immortal substance, than the other way. Indeed a man truly dies, although his soul is immortal. And what can be more directly opposed in terms than death and immortality? To evade this instance, the opponent says: "For although in a man who dies there is a soul, which is an incorruptible substance, yet the man himself, or the man's own substance, is not incorruptible, just as Meisner asserts that the Son of God, or the divine substance of the Son of God, is properly so." But in fact the man himself does have an incorruptible substance, just as Christ has a wholly divine one. And the man himself dies, just as Christ does, but not because of what is immortal in the man, or divine in Christ. So the man dies while the immortality of his soul remains, and Christ dies while his divine substance remains; thus it is no more right to argue from the death of Christ against his divine nature than from the death of a man against his immortal soul. But just as the soul is sometimes said to die in a man ("the soul that sins, it itself dies"), meaning the man who is endowed with an immortal soul, so the death of the Son of God is spoken of, that is, of Christ, who is also the Son of God. This also answers the minor premise: the only-begotten Son of God, Christ that is, truly died, but not as the only-begotten Son. For just as the Father could not cease to be Father, so neither could the Son; yet while he died, the Father would not have been Father even for that time. Besides, if according to our opponents the Son of God is not a substance but an accident, how can he be said truly to die? For accidents do not die in the proper sense; only a living substance dies. Finally, they now deny the divine substance in Christ. From this it is clear what Son of God they want, namely one without divine substance; which is as if they were fashioning a Son of Man without human substance. But it does not follow, from the fact that the Son of God is said to have died, that the Son of God and Christ signify the same thing. Nor do words that differ in etymology and origin, in their nature, and in their constant and universal usage, signify the same, as "Son of God" and "Christ" do, however much the same person is meant by both. Second, things that can be separated: the Son of God need not be Christ; indeed, according to our opponents, he may be the Son of God by singular birth without attaining that dignity and rule which has now been given to Christ. Third, there are many sons of God who are not rightly called Christ; therefore these terms do not mean the same. Finally, who has ever said that the sonship of anyone is completed and brought to perfection step by step? For natural generation has its moments and parts by which it is at last finished; sonship never is.

units.la: At cum Filium Dei in Christo exponant Adversarii per imperium, & esse dominum, illud quoq; addunt imperite, & contra omnem filiationis naturam, quod certis passibus progressa sit, donec ad fastigium perveniret. Schlichtingius, pag.563. Filiatio quippe Christi divina, quae similitudine ejus cum Deo continetur, pari, ut sic dicam, passu cum ejus unctione ac sanctificatione progressa est, & tum demum ad summum fastigium pervenit, cum Christus perfectissima ratione unctus & sanctificatus fuit. Quae de filiatione dicere, atque omnium perfectissima Dei, valde a re est alienum. Ne nostra quidem filiatio, quae in gratuita nostri adoptione consistit, & similitudine aliqua, non natura, formaliter non perficitur variis ejusmodi actibus & tempore, sed simul ac semel una cum hominis justificatione peragitur: nedum ut illa Christi filiatio tanto constet tempore atque diversitate. Varia quidem possunt accedere, ad filii dignitatem perficiendam; non vero ad ipsam filiationem. Atque haec de Christo Dei Filio; jam de ipso ut Deo, non quod essentia differant, sed diverso modo tractentur, magis ex professo dicemus. Quia Dei filius, atque ita filius, proinde verus Deus. Atque uti in agnoscendo Christum, pro Dei filio, ita & pro Deo passim multis verborum utuntur Adversarii fallaciis.
units.tr: But although our opponents explain the Son of God in Christ as rule and lordship, they also foolishly add, and contrary to the whole nature of sonship, that it advanced by fixed stages until it reached its summit. Schlichting, p. 563: "The divine sonship of Christ, which is contained in his likeness to God, advanced, so to speak, at the same pace as his anointing and sanctification, and then at last reached its highest summit when Christ was anointed and sanctified in the most perfect way." To say such things about sonship, and especially about the most perfect sonship of God, is very far from the matter. Even our own sonship, which consists in our gratuitous adoption and in some likeness, not in nature, is not formally completed by various acts of this kind over a period of time, but is accomplished at once and in one act together with a person's justification. How much less should the sonship of Christ take such a long time and such variety! Various things may be added to complete the dignity of the Son, but not to complete the sonship itself. But these are enough about Christ the Son of God; we shall speak more deliberately about him as God, not because they differ in essence, but because they are treated in different ways. For he is the Son of God, and so the Son, and therefore true God. And just as our opponents use many verbal fallacies in acknowledging Christ as the Son of God, so they do throughout in acknowledging him as God.

units.la: Servetus, & quam is in Christum maledicus! in libris de erroribus. Trinitatis quos scripsit, Christum non Dei tantum filium, sed Deum, & quoque magnum Deum subinde nuncupat. Lib. i. pag. 2. Primo, hic est Iesus Christus: Secundo, hic est Filius Dei. Tertio, hic est Deus. Et pag. 9. Tertio, istam dixi esse veram, Christus est Deus, dicitur enim esse specie Deus, quia, ut inquit Apostolus, erat in forma Dei. Pag. 11. Cum Christo latius erit privilegium, ut non modo Filius Dei, sed etiam dicatur, & sit Deus noster. Pag. 11. Pronomine enim demonstrante Christum, concedo, hoc est Deus noster, Deus benedictus, Deus fortis. Pag. 13. Quid enim si Iesum Christum magnum Deum esse dico, &c.? Pag. 14. Sed hoc adhuc parum est, ut de Christo integre sentias, donec Verbi arcana noveris, & scies, Christum huic ipsum esse & fuisse ab æterno Deum. Lib. ii. pag. 53. Hæc sola ratio, si sursum respicias, sufficit ad hoc ut non modo filius Dei, sed Deus & Dominus mundi dicatur. Lib. vii. in initio, pag. 110. Ab initio fuisse dico filiationem in divinis, non realem, sed personalem, Verbum erat filius, non realis, sed personalis erat filius. Haec in illis libris, quibuscum blasphemum caput dignas poenas luit. Et quomodocumque de Christo speciose aliquando, alibi deridiculo filium mathematicum, pag. 59. metaphysicum, pag. 111. appellat. Et pag. 52. horresco referens: si logos filius erat natus ex patre sine matre, dic mihi quomodo peperit eum, pervertrem, an per latus? aliis referendis supersedeo. Istud tamen citavi ex eo, quia aliquando dubitatum & quaesitum, an id quidem potuisset auctor, quae illa, quam dixi, pagina in libris ejus lego, dignis scilicet, qui ferventibus per partiam tumultibus Remonstranticis in Belgicum conversi fuerint, & hominibus nostris expositi, ann. MDCXX. per R. T. Servetum vero Adversarii nostri, non tantum inter antecessores suos numerant, sed & pro martyre venerantur. Eques Polonus, in Apologia, martyrium Serveti nominat. De quo Serveto videri etiam possunt epistolæ Oecolampadii, inter Zuinglii Epistolas, pag. i. & 18. & 173.
units.tr: Servetus, how abusive he is against Christ! In the books he wrote "On the Errors of the Trinity," he repeatedly calls Christ not only the Son of God but God, and even great God. Book 1, p. 2: "First, this is Jesus Christ; second, this is the Son of God; third, this is God." And p. 9: "Third, I have said that this is true: Christ is God, for he is said to be God in appearance, because, as the Apostle says, he was in the form of God." P. 11: "With Christ the privilege will be broader, so that he is called and is our God not only as the Son of God." P. 11: "For by the demonstrative pronoun pointing to Christ, I grant that this is our God, the blessed God, the mighty God." P. 13: "For what if I say that Jesus Christ is the great God, etc.?" P. 14: "But this is still too little for you to think rightly of Christ, until you know the secrets of the Word, and you will know that Christ himself is and has been God from eternity." Book 2, p. 53: "This one reason, if you look upward, is enough for him to be called not only Son of God but God and Lord of the world." Book 7, at the beginning, p. 110: "I say that from the beginning there was sonship in the divine persons, not real but personal; the Word was Son, not really but personally Son." These are the things in those books, for which the blasphemous author paid the punishment he deserved. And although he speaks sometimes in a showy way about Christ, elsewhere he mockingly calls him the "mathematical" Son (p. 59) and the "metaphysical" Son (p. 111). And on p. 52, I shudder to report it: "If the Logos was a Son born of the Father without a mother, tell me how he bore him, through the side or through the womb?" I forbear to report others. I have cited this one, however, because it was once doubted and asked whether the author could have written it; I read that passage in his books. These, no doubt, are worthy of being turned into Belgian and exposed to our people, when the Remonstrant tumults were raging among us in the year 1620, by the Reverend Servetus. Our opponents not only count Servetus among their predecessors but also venerate him as a martyr. The Polish knight, in his Apology, calls the death of Servetus a martyrdom. Concerning this Servetus, the letters of Oecolampadius among the letters of Zwingli may also be consulted, pp. 1, 18 and 173.

units.la: Inter illos, quibuscum res nobis in hac disputatione, de Deitate Christi, Adversarios, alii sunt, qui cum antiquo Photino, & nupero Socino, Christum negant omnino exstitisse, antequam è Maria nasceretur: alii, eum conditum, & primum a Deo creatum, ante reliquas omnes creaturas, statuunt, juxta sententiam Arii; quae inter Adversarios est Erasmi Iohannis, qui super illa re cum Socino per biduum palam disputavit. Arius Christum ante omnes creaturas a Deo factum, seu creatum asserebat: ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, unde & Exoucontii dicti, perque eum, seu instrumentum aliquod, mundum a Deo factum. Ipsum vero in tempore corpus assumsisse, non animam, quia ipsum pro anima erat. Theodoretus in ἀσυγχ.[?]· σῶμα γὰρ τὸν Θεὸν λόγον μόνον αὐτὸν ἀνειληφέναι φασίν. Et de ejus existentia divulgatum ipsorum verbum erat, ἦν ποτέ[?], ὅτε οὐκ ἦν[?]. fuit aliquando tempus, quo non erat. Atque uti ante Arium alii fuerunt ejusdem, saltem similis cum eo, contra veram aeternamq; Christi Deitatem, sententiae, de quibus Nicetas Choniates, lib. iv. Thesauri Orthodoxae fidei, de Ante-Arianis haeresibus: ita & post eum, varie interpolata haeresis fuit, unde Homoianorum, & Anomoio-rum diversae sectae, & alii Ariani dicti, alii Semi-Ariani. Photinus autem, & qui ante eum Pauliani dicti, Christum extitisse demum a nativitate ex Maria, & nequaquam ante, statuebant.
units.tr: Among those adversaries with whom we have to deal in this dispute about the Deity of Christ, some, with the old Photinus and the recent Socinus, deny altogether that Christ existed before he was born of Mary. Others hold that he was founded and first created by God, before all other creatures, according to the opinion of Arius. Among our adversaries this opinion belongs to Erasmus Johannes, who disputed openly with Socinus on this matter for two days. Arius asserted that Christ was made or created by God before all creatures, out of nothing [ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων], whence they were also called Exoucontians, and that the world was made by God through him, or through some instrument. Moreover, he assumed a body in time, but not a soul, because he himself stood in the place of the soul. Theodoret says: "They say that God the Word alone assumed a body" [σῶμα γὰρ τὸν Θεὸν λόγον μόνον αὐτὸν ἀνειληφέναι φασίν]. Concerning his existence, their common saying was: there was once a time when he was not [ἦν ποτέ, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν]. Just as before Arius there were others of the same, or at least a similar, view against the true and eternal Deity of Christ, of whom Nicetas Choniates speaks in book iv of the Thesaurus of the Orthodox Faith, under the heading On the heresies before Arius, so after him a heresy arose in various forms, whence came the different sects of the Homoians and Anomoians, and others who were called Arians, and others Semi-Arians. Photinus, and those before him called Paulians, held that Christ had existed only from his birth from Mary, and in no way before it.

units.la: Erasmus Iohannis Rector primum fuit Scholae Antverpiensis, ubi quum Arianismum saperet atque doceret, profugus in Poloniam ad Socinum propere contendit. Deque eo Henricus Antonii, in Praefat. Systematis Theol. haec habet: ex ipso Ecclesiae sinu Scholae Antverpianae Rector Iohannes Erasmus (Erasmus Johannes nomen erat) clam edito libro Arianismum molitur. Vigilantia & pietate Principis Auraici laudatiss. memoriae institutum hoc evanescit. Liber ille Erasmi prodiit ann. MDLXXXIV. & memoratur celebri nostro historico Borrio, Annal. lib. xix. fuitque hoc titulo:
units.tr: Erasmus Johannis was first rector of the school at Antwerp. There, because he savoured of Arianism and taught it, he fled to Poland and hurried to Socinus. Henricus Antonii, in the preface to his Systema Theologiae, says of him: The rector of the Antwerp school, Johannes Erasmus (that was his name), from the very bosom of the Church, secretly published a book stirring up Arianism. The vigilance and piety of the Prince of Orange, of most praiseworthy memory, put an end to this. That book of Erasmus appeared in 1584 and is mentioned by our well-known historian Borrius, Annals, book 19. It bore this title:

units.la: <bl>Klare Ueberwysinge[?] dat d'Antichrist, terstont na den doodt der Apostelen begost heeft in den kerken Christi te regneren.</bl>
units.tr: Clear proof that the Antichrist began to reign in the churches of Christ immediately after the death of the Apostles.

units.la: Atque eo valde invehitur in Veterum Concilia, praecipuè Nicaenum. Unde, ubi constare de hominis mente ac haeresi, & turbis quas moliretur, sedulo investigatus variis, ubi delitescere credebatur, urbibus ac locis, clam aufugit ad perfidiae similes socios, in Transylvaniam & Poloniam. Ubi & mox factus coetus Claudiopolitani minister. Hinc statim sub annum MDLXXXV. Cracoviam venit, uti cum Socino conferret, & disputaret de existentia Filii Dei. Conveniebat quidem cum illo, in negandâ & oppugnandâ Trinitate, sed non item in principio Christo assignando, in quo Arium sequebatur, & Christum fuisse unigenitum Dei Filium affirmabat, etiam antequam ex virgine nasceretur, quod Faustus negabat. Disputatio ab utroque postea edita fuit. Et Socinus in Praefat. de Erasmo, & suorum sententiâ, ita: Arii similes, eumve imitati, Iesum Nazarenum subsistantiam quandam spiritualem primam omnium divinitus creatam esse statuunt, quae humanum corpus seu carnem induerit. Sententiam suam ipse sic Erasmus propositu[?], in Disputationis initio: Primum omnium fateor, me tecum facere in articulo de uno vero Deo patre, nec Trinitatem cognoscere, quamobrem patior persecutionem a Germanis. Verum in doctrina de persona & officio Christi nego, me tecum sentire. Deinde, inquit, tum demum Christus vere honoratur, si habeatur non solum pro Filio Mariae, sed etiam unigenito Filio Dei, cujus essentia longissime excedat claritate & splendore omnium angelorum essentiam quamvis spiritualem, quique fuerit ante initium rerum omnium, ac per quem Deus non solum redemit mundum, sed etiam ex nihilo creavit. Haec autem Socini sententiae valde sunt contraria. Unde Sociniani graviter ferunt, se Arianos appellari. Socinus in titulo libri, de Officio hominis Christiani, quod Regni Poloniæ & Magni Ducatus Lithuaniæ homines, vulgò Euangelici dicti, qui solidæ pietatis sint studiosi, omnino deberent se illorum cœtui adjungere, qui in iisdem locis falso & immerito Ariani & Ebionitæ vocantur. Extant Erasmi & Socini epistolæ, inter Epistolas Socini, pag. 441. Erasmi Iohannis autem de Christi existentia opinionem cum ipse Socinus, tum alii passim redarguunt & confutant. Ille, in Catechesi, à pag. 32. Volkelius, lib. v. cap. xiii. alii alibi.
units.tr: He attacks the ancient councils with great vehemence, especially the Council of Nicaea. Because of this, when his views and his heresy became known, and the disturbances he was thought to be stirring up, he was diligently sought in various cities and places where he was believed to be hiding. He escaped secretly to fellow-traitors to the faith, into Transylvania and Poland. There he soon became minister of the congregation at Klausenburg. From there, around the year 1585, he came straight to Cracow, in order to confer with Socinus and dispute about the existence of the Son of God. He agreed with him indeed in denying and attacking the Trinity, but not in assigning a beginning to Christ, in which he followed Arius and affirmed that Christ was the only-begotten Son of God even before he was born of the virgin, something Faustus denied. The disputation was afterwards published by both of them. Socinus, in his preface about Erasmus and his followers' opinion, says: Those who are like Arius, or who imitate him, hold that Jesus of Nazareth was a certain spiritual substance, the first of all things created by God, which put on a human body or flesh. Erasmus himself set out his view in this way at the beginning of the disputation: First of all, I confess that I agree with you on the article concerning the one true God the Father, and that I do not acknowledge a Trinity; for this reason I suffer persecution from the Germans. But in the doctrine concerning the person and office of Christ, I deny that I agree with you. Then, he says, Christ is truly honoured only if he is held not merely to be the Son of Mary but also the only-begotten Son of God, whose essence far surpasses in brightness and splendour the essence of all angels, however spiritual, and who existed before the beginning of all things, and through whom God not only redeemed the world but also created it out of nothing. But these views of Socinus are very much opposed to one another. Hence the Socinians take it hard that they are called Arians. Socinus, in the title of his book on the duty of the Christian man, says that the men of the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, commonly called Evangelicals, who are zealous for solid piety, ought altogether to join the assembly of those who in those same places are falsely and undeservedly called Arians and Ebionites. The letters of Erasmus and Socinus survive, among the letters of Socinus, p. 441. The opinion of Johannes Erasmus about the existence of Christ is refuted and confuted everywhere, both by Socinus himself and by others. He does so in the Catechesis, from p. 32; Volkelius, book 5, chapter 13; and others elsewhere.

units.la: Aut ego nihil video, aut Simon Episcopius, Remonstrantium primipilus, in eadem est cum Erasmo Johannis sententia, Christum Dei Filium extitisse ante suam ex Maria nativitatem, & ante alia à Deo conditum, certè non unius ejusdemque cum Patre esse essentiæ. Contra Socinum disputat quidem, Instit. Theolog. l. v. sect. ii. cap. xxxiii. contenditque, quod Iesus Christus revera exstiterit, & subsisterit tamquam vera atque unica Patris sui proles, antequam ex Maria matre sua homo nasceretur; neque aliter explicanda esse verba Ioann. i. i. saltem verosimiliter illum in modum exponi (neque enim fas sibi existimat durius vel apertius contra Socinum loqui) ostendit. 1. Quia oratio, ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν, respondet orationi sive locutioni isti, quia Moses in principio Genesios usus est [?]. 2. Quia sic facillime & planissime intelligitur locutio sive phrasis sequens bis repetita, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν. Antequam enim quicquam in rerum natura esset, non poterat alibi λόγος esse, quam apud Deum. 3. Quia diserte statim v. 3. sequitur, Omnia per λόγον illum facta esse, & absque eo factum est nihil quod factum sit. Unde per τὸν ἀρχὴν intelligi principium temporis illius, quo omnia ea fieri coeperunt, quæ facta sunt, prorsus verosimile est. Verum non ejusdem essentiæ Filium esse cum Patre, non leviter indicat, dum acrius & manifestius, quam illic contra Socinum, hic cum Orthodoxis disputat, adversus τὸ ὁμοούσιον; statuitque, modum aliquem filiationis esse, absque quo rei veritas tamen teneri bene ac credi possit: sic sibi objiciens, cap. xxxv. Si hic modus peculiaris filiationis Iesu Christi non est ad salutem creditu necessarius, tum non potest salvari Personarum Trinitas: Resp. Negatur consequentia. Insto: Non potest salvari ὁμοούσιον Filii cum Patre & S. Sancto. Ergo. Resp. Esto. At absque illa salvari potest Trinitas, id est, fides quod revera sit Pater, Filius & S. Sanctus. Hoc enim Scriptura diserte affirmat. Insto. At non salvatur Trinitas in unica essentia numerica. Ergo non salvatur Trinitas. Resp. Consequentia laborat. Non salvatur Trinitas ipso modo: Ergo non salvatur Trinitas. Inst. Atque sine ipso modo Trinitas non est Trinitas. Resp. Hoc est illud ipsum, quod hic quæritur. eo ipso enim quod asseritur, Iesum Christum non esse Filium Dei peculiari ipso modo, quia videlicet ex essentia Patris ante secula genitus est, asseritur etiam Trinitatem sine modo ipso esse, & simul ipsa Trinitas agnoscitur cum Scriptura. Quasi Scriptura aliam vel Trinitatem, vel generationem personarum doceat, quam in eadem essentia? vel hoc modum rei aut fidei concernat, & non rem ipsam? Verum nondum disputamus, tantummodo sententiam exploramus Adversariorum, & indagamus. Itaque hac in re suos facit adversarios Episcopius, qui Filium Dei unius numero essentiæ esse affirmunt cum Deo Patre suo. pag. 343. Et quorsum adeo τὸ [illegible, ~6 letters] exagitat in Christo, quod dicitur à Theologis, intelligiturque essentiæ & naturæ divinæ respectu, quod nempe Filius habet à Patre eandem cum Patre essentiam, quæ alia Dei non est, quam [illegible, ~8 letters] nisi ut ὁμοούσιον eo fortius neget, convellatque? Si enim ὁμοούσιος Filius, est quoque αὐτόθεος, nam talis est essentia, & Deitas Patris. Periculose ei errant, qui Filium Dei αὐτόθεον, scribendum αὐτόθεον, esse contendunt, sic ut qua Deus est, sit a seipso, qua Filius est, sit a Patre. Ecquae videlicet causa periculosi istius erroris? cum hac ratione subordinatio vera inter Patrem & Filium tollatur. Subordinatio ista, quam tuetur, merum constituit Arianismum.
units.tr: Either I see nothing, or Simon Episcopius, the chief of the Remonstrants, holds the same opinion as Erasmus Johannes, that the Son of God existed before his birth from Mary, and before other things created by God; certainly he does not hold that he is of one and the same essence with the Father. He does indeed dispute against Socinus, in the Institutes of Theology, book v, section ii, chapter xxxiii, and contends that Jesus Christ really existed and subsisted as the true and only offspring of his Father before he was born as a man of his mother Mary; and he shows that the words of John i. 1 are not to be explained otherwise, or at least that it is probable they should be explained in that way (for he does not consider it right to speak more harshly or openly against Socinus). He gives these reasons. 1. The phrase in the beginning was [ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν] answers to that phrase or expression, because Moses used it at the beginning of Genesis. 2. Because the phrase that follows, repeated twice, and the Word was with God [καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν], is understood most easily and plainly in this way: before anything existed in the nature of things, the Word could be nowhere but with God. 3. Because at once in verse 3 it clearly follows that all things were made through that Word, and without him nothing was made that was made. Hence it is quite probable that by the beginning is meant the beginning of that time when the things that were made began to be made. But Episcopius does not lightly suggest that the Son is not of the same essence as the Father; he argues this more sharply and more clearly than he does against Socinus, and here with the Orthodox, against the homoousion; and he holds that there is some mode of sonship, without which the truth of the matter may nevertheless be held and believed well enough. Thus, objecting to himself in chapter xxxv: "If this particular mode of the sonship of Jesus Christ is not necessary to be believed for salvation, then the Trinity of Persons cannot be saved." Answer: the consequence is denied. I press: the homoousion of the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit cannot be saved. Therefore... Answer: Granted. But the Trinity, that is, the faith that there really are the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, can be saved without it, for Scripture affirms this expressly. I press: but the Trinity is not saved in a single numerical essence. Therefore the Trinity is not saved. Answer: the consequence is faulty. The Trinity is not saved in this very mode; therefore the Trinity is not saved. Objection: and without this very mode the Trinity is not a Trinity. Answer: this is just the very thing that is being asked here. For by the very fact that it is asserted that Jesus Christ is not the Son of God in this particular mode, namely because he was begotten of the essence of the Father before the ages, it is also asserted that the Trinity exists without this mode, and at the same time the Trinity itself is acknowledged in agreement with Scripture. As if Scripture taught another Trinity, or another generation of the Persons, than in the same essence? Or as if it concerned the mode of the thing or of the faith, and not the thing itself? But we are not yet disputing; we are only exploring and investigating the opinion of the adversaries. Accordingly, in this matter Episcopius makes his own those adversaries who affirm that the Son of God is one in number of essence with God his Father, p. 343. And why does he so vigorously attack what is said by the theologians about Christ with respect to the essence and divine nature, namely that the Son has from the Father the same essence as the Father, which is no other than the essence of God, [illegible], except in order to deny and overthrow the homoousion the more strongly? For if the Son is homoousios, he is also autotheos, for such is the essence and Deity of the Father. They err dangerously who contend that the Son of God is autotheos (it should be written autotheos), so that as God he is from himself, and as Son he is from the Father. What, I ask, is the cause of this dangerous error? Because by this reasoning the true subordination between the Father and the Son is removed. That subordination which he defends constitutes sheer Arianism.

units.la: Episcopius, certum, inquit, personis tribus divinitatem divinasque perfectiones tribui, non collateraliter, aut coordinate, sed subordinate. Qua subordinatione posita, certum est Patri soli proprie istam divinitatis perfectionem sive αὐτόθεότητα competere, quod eam a seipso, id est, a nullo alio habeat. Unde consequitur, Patrem sic esse primum, ut etiam summus sit, tum ordine, tum dignitate, tum potestate. Non ponimus essentiae collateralitatem inter personas divinas, credimus identitatem. Quam si non admittas, certo certius est te introducere τριθεότητα. Tres illi habent vel eandem essentiam, vel aliam: si eandem, ergo non subordinatam, & differentem ordine, dignitate, potestate; sed ὁμοούσιον, & αὐτόθεον: sin aliam, ergo alia & alia Dei essentia, multiplex Deitas, & plures Dii, non ii λεγόμενοι, sed essentia Dii. Respondeat, si potest. Hinc pressius argumento ex adoratione sumpto, quod cum solus adorari possit, debeatque (quod Reformati accurate semper tuentur adversus Pontificios,) Filius Dei non posset adorari nisi unus ille idemque Deus sit, respondet, licere etiam alium a Deo adorare, modo Deus jubeat, adeoq; adorationem ad solum Deum, aut Deitatem non esse restrictam, vel ei propriam. Sufficit ad hoc, ut quis adorari & divino honore adsici possit, ut Deus cum tali honore dignetur, etiamsi non sit verus Deus, inquit, cap. xxv. Quare concludo, sententiam & doctrinam Episcopii, de Christo Dei Filio, ante nativitatem ex Maria, non esse aliam, quam Erasmi Johannis, & Arianorum, certe non satis orthodoxam. Quod magis etiam confirmat Curcellaei praefatio, in Episcopii Opera, ubi ille utile non esse asserit, in hac materia adhibere voces Trinitatis, Essentiae, personae, ὁμοούσιος, ob primariam hanc videlicet rationem, quod voces istae sint ὁμώνυμοι, & quo significatu accipi debeant ignoretur. Quod manifeste falsum. Porro subjungit, alios non habere legitimam causam cur admodum succensent illis qui unam tantum in Deo personam agnoscunt. Nam in hoc quod praecipuum est conveniunt, essentiam sive naturam divinam esse unam, & eam totam in Patre esse, nihilique essentiae Dei decedere, sive una sive plures censeantur esse personae. Hoccine praecipuum, in quo convenire oportet? nequaquam, nisi dicatur, unam eandemque naturam, quae in Patre, esse in Filio quoque, & Spiritu Sancto. Neque parum refert, unam: an plures Personas statuas. Istas personas agnoscere oportet & credere. Tum ex male adductis Patribus temere conatur ostendere Curcellaeus, illos censuisse, non aliter Patrem & Filium in divinis esse ὁμοουσίως, quam prout duo homines sunt ὁμοούσιοι, qui eandem speciem humanitatem inter se communem habent. Contra, recentiorum dicit sententiam loqui de eadem Personarum consubstantialitate: se vero ab illis diversum facit, & tertium. Sed recentiores Theologi, ut ex omnibus ipsorum scriptis liquet, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum S. putant esse ὁμοουσίως, quia unam numero essentiam inter se communem habent, non vero specie tantum. Quam sententiam adeo non probat, ut dicat ἀκατα-ληπτον. & hoc putido[?] argumento convellere allaborat: Nam cum essentia sit illud, quo[?] maxime quaeque res id quod est, & ab aliis omnibus distinguitur, plures in divinitate distinctae[?] personae esse non posse videntur, quin plures etiam sint essentiae; & dicere tres personas unam numero halere[?] essentiam, idem esse videtur atque afferere eas unam tantum esse personam, Sabelliique haeresi accedere, qui Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum S. unam, eandemque personam esse dixit, sed quā diversis nominibus appellatur, & ita mirum in modum totam salutis nostrae œconomiam perturbavit.
units.tr: Episcopius says: it is certain that divinity and divine perfections are attributed to the three persons, not collaterally or coordinately, but subordinately. With this subordination laid down, it is certain that this perfection of divinity, or autotheotes [αὐτόθεότης], belongs properly to the Father alone, because he has it from himself, that is, from no other. Hence it follows that the Father is so first that he is also highest, in order, in dignity, and in power. We do not hold a collateral essence among the divine persons; we believe in their identity. If you do not admit this, you will most surely introduce tritheism [τριθεότης]. Those three either have the same essence or a different one. If the same, then they are not subordinate and differ in order, dignity and power, but are consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] and autotheos [αὐτόθεον]. If a different one, then there are different essences of God, a manifold Deity, and several gods, not so called but gods in essence. Let him answer, if he can. More closely, he takes an argument from worship: since God alone can and must be worshipped (which the Reformed always defend accurately against the Papists), the Son of God could not be worshipped unless he were that one and the same God. Episcopius answers that it is lawful to worship another besides God, provided God commands it, and so worship is not restricted to God alone, or proper to the Deity. It is enough for someone to be worshipped and to receive divine honour that God deigns to honour him with such honour, even if he is not the true God, he says, chapter 25. Therefore I conclude that the opinion and doctrine of Episcopius concerning Christ the Son of God, before his birth from Mary, is no other than that of Johannes Erasmus and the Arians, and certainly not sufficiently orthodox. The preface of Curcellaeus to the works of Episcopius confirms this still more, where he asserts that it is not useful in this matter to employ the words Trinity, essence, person, consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος], for this chief reason, that these words are equivocal [ὁμώνυμοι], and the sense in which they ought to be taken is unknown. This is manifestly false. He goes on: the others have no lawful reason to be very angry with those who acknowledge only one person in God. For in what is chief they agree, that the divine essence or nature is one, and that it is wholly in the Father, and that nothing of the essence of God is lost, whether there are thought to be one or several persons. Is this the chief point in which they ought to agree? By no means, unless it is said that the one and the same nature which is in the Father is also in the Son and in the Holy Spirit. And it matters not a little whether you posit one person or several. We must acknowledge and believe these persons. Then, from badly cited Fathers, Curcellaeus rashly tries to show that they held that the Father and Son are consubstantial [ὁμοουσίως] in the divine nature no otherwise than two men are consubstantial, who have the same species of humanity in common. On the contrary, he says the opinion of the more recent writers speaks of the same consubstantiality of the persons, but he sets himself apart from them and makes a third view. But the more recent theologians, as is clear from all their writings, think that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are consubstantial [ὁμοουσίως], because they have one essence in common among themselves numerically, not merely in species. He so little approves this opinion that he calls it incomprehensible [ἀκατάληπτον], and he labours to overturn it with this stinking argument: for since essence is that by which each thing most of all is what it is and is distinguished from all others, it seems that there cannot be several distinct persons in the Godhead without there being also several essences; and to say that three persons have one essence numerically seems the same as asserting that they are only one person, and approaches the heresy of Sabellius, who said that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one and the same person, but called by different names, and so wonderfully disturbed the whole economy of our salvation.

units.la: Multa dicit, sed quorum nihil probat. Essentia est id, quo res ab aliis omnibus distinguitur, vid. essentiis. Sic Deus per essentiam distinguitur ab aliis omnibus essentiis: sicut in eo personae, a personis; non per essentiam, sed diversas personalitates: ut omnino plures possint esse personae, quamvis non plures essentiae. Unde sententia, quae tres unius essentiae distinctas personas statuit, œconomiam salutis non invertit, sed fundat: invertere vero dicenda est sententia contraria, aut Sabellii, aut Arianorum, & Remonstrantium, personas in divinitate, & earum ὁμοούσιον, non, quod dicit, ὁμοιούσιος, ne-gantium. Ut nihil quidem manifestius, quam Remonstrantes, Episcopium sequutos, omnes esse Arianos. Quod dubio procul Johannes Sartorius, Socinianus, significavit litteris suis Amstelda mo scriptis, ann. MDCXXXVIII. quas interceptas Princeps Transylvaniae Georgius Rakoci huc misit: plurimi inter ipsos sunt Ariani, aut Arianis proximi, qui sentiunt Filium Dei similem habere essentiam cum Patre, ex cujus essentia, ut putant, in tempore genitus fit: & ex quo, dicunt, Spiritum Sanctum tanquam personam procedere: interim fatentur hoc dogma non esse necessarium, neque negant se nos pro fratribus habituros. Differt quidem, fateor, Arianorum sententia, & Socinianorum, super Filii Dei existentia; sed utcunque positiva eorum alia sit & alia, negativa tamen contra nos eadem est, parique ratione & modo refutanda, quod vid. Christus Filius Dei non sit verus ille unus Deus.
units.tr: He says many things, but proves none of them. Essence is that by which a thing is distinguished from all others; see "essences." Thus God is distinguished by essence from all other essences, just as the persons are distinguished from one another in him, not by essence but by distinct personalities; so that there can be several persons without there being several essences. Hence the opinion which posits three distinct persons of one essence does not overturn the economy of salvation but establishes it. It is rather the contrary opinion, that of Sabellius, or of the Arians and Remonstrants, that must be called overturning, which denies the persons in the Godhead and their consubstantiality, and says homoiousios [ὁμοιούσιος] instead. Nothing is more manifest than that the Remonstrants, following Episcopius, are all Arians. This Johannes Sartorius, a Socinian, undoubtedly made clear in his letters written from Amsterdam in 1638, which the Prince of Transylvania, George Rakoczi, intercepted and sent here: most of them among themselves are Arians, or close to the Arians, who hold that the Son of God has an essence similar to that of the Father, from whose essence, as they think, he was begotten in time, and from whom, they say, the Holy Spirit proceeds as a person; yet they confess that this doctrine is not necessary, and they do not deny that they will count us as brothers. The opinion of the Arians and that of the Socinians indeed differ, I admit, concerning the existence of the Son of God; but however their positive views may differ, their negative view against us is the same, and it must be refuted in the same way and manner, namely that Christ the Son of God is not the true and one God.

units.la: Quaestio ergo est & manet, an Christus, praeter naturam humanam, habeat aliam divinam, veram, & cum Patre eandem? quum una tantum sit vera essentia, & natura divina. Atque in natura divina, quamvis supra audivimus fucosas Adversariorum de Christo etiam natura Deo, & Filio Dei naturali locutiones, statum cardinemque quaestionis etiam Adversarii constituunt. Catechesis Racov. cap. 1. de Christo, pag. 55. An non Iesus Christus habet quoque divinam naturam? Non, non habet, adde pag. 150. Sic & Socinus, lib. de natura Christi, pag. 4. Et lib. contra Wiekum, cap 1. pag. 7.8. Ostorodus, Instit. cap. VI. pag. 39. 40. 44. 48. Volkelius, pag. 38. & alii passim.
units.tr: The question therefore is and remains whether Christ, besides his human nature, has another, divine nature, true and the same as the Father's? since there is only one true essence and divine nature. And as for divine nature, although above we heard the Adversaries' specious expressions about Christ also having the divine nature, and about the natural Son of God, the Adversaries themselves set out the state and hinge of the question. Racovian Catechism, chapter 1, on Christ, page 55: Does not Jesus Christ also have a divine nature? No, he does not have it; add page 150. So also Socinus, book on the nature of Christ, page 4, and book against Wiekus, chapter 1, pages 7–8. Ostorodus, Institutes, chapter 6, pages 39, 40, 44, 48. Volkelius, page 38, and others everywhere.

units.la: Catholica sententia & fides manifesta est, ex Confessionibus: Helvetica posteriori, cap. XI. Eundem quoque Christum, aeterni Dei aeternum Filium credimus, & agnoscimus ergo in uno atque eodem Domino nostro Iesu Christo, duas naturas, divinam & humanam. Helvetica priori, art. XI. Hic Christus verus Dei Filius, verusque Deus. Basileensi, art. IV. Bohemica, cap. VI. Gallica, art. XIV. Anglica, art. II. Belgica, art. XVIII. XIX. quapropter confitetur, ipsum verum Deum, & verum hominem esse: verum quidem Deum, ut mortem sua potentia vinceret: & verum hominem, ut in carnis sua infirmitate pro nobis mortem obiret. Catechesis, qu. 15. & 18. quis autem est ille mediator, qui simul est verus Deus: & verus perfectéque justus homo? Dominus noster Iesus Christus. qu. 33. Quia solus Christus est coaeternus & naturalis aeterni Patris filius. Confessio Augustana, art. III. Wirtembergica, cap. II. Suevica, cap. II.
units.tr: The catholic opinion and faith is plain from the Confessions: the Second Helvetic, chapter 11: We believe that the same Christ is the eternal Son of the eternal God, and so we acknowledge in one and the same Lord our Jesus Christ two natures, divine and human. The First Helvetic, article 11: This Christ is the true Son of God and true God. The Basel, article 4; the Bohemian, chapter 6; the Gallican, article 14; the English, article 2; the Belgic, articles 18 and 19: wherefore it confesses that he is true God and true man: true God, that he might overcome death by his power; and true man, that he might die for us in the weakness of his flesh. Catechism, questions 15 and 18: But who is that Mediator who is at once true God and truly and perfectly just man? Our Lord Jesus Christ. Question 33: Because Christ alone is the coeternal and natural Son of the eternal Father. Augsburg Confession, article 3; the Württemberg, chapter 2; the Swabian, chapter 2.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA.
units.tr: SECTION TWO.

units.la: Nunc ad Disputationem pergimus, & argumentationem: ac primo quidem pro sententia nostra: quæ per illa, quæ hactenus diximus, reddetur haud parum facilior ac brevior. Sequemur autem communem & usitatam argumentorum seriem ac clas-ses: quæ probatæ quoque Episcopio, Institut. lib. IV. cap. XXXII. & Arminio, Disput. de Persona Patris & Filii. Quare primum agemus, ex nominibus divinis Christo adscriptis, tum attributis, inde operibus, quarto loco ejus urgebimus cultum, atque invocationem religiosam. Ut quatuor nascantur argumentorum genera, quæ singula & omnia probant, Christum Deum, vel; in Christo, præter naturam humanam, esse quoque divinam, seu Deum esse divina essentia præditum: ne in ullis verborum ambiguitatibus, aut fucis hæreant ultra Adversarii ac nidulentur.
units.tr: We now proceed to the disputation and its arguments. First we take up the argument for our own view, which will be made much easier and shorter by what we have said so far. We shall follow the usual sequence and classes of arguments, which Episcopius also approved (Institut. lib. IV. cap. XXXII.) and Arminius (Disput. de Persona Patris & Filii.). So we shall first argue from the divine names given to Christ, then from the attributes, then from the works, and fourthly we shall press the religious worship and invocation of him. In this way four kinds of argument arise, each of which, singly and together, proves that Christ is God, or that in Christ, besides a human nature, there is also a divine one, that is, that he is God endowed with the divine essence. Thus our opponents may have no room to hide or nest in any ambiguity of words or in any pretence.

units.la: Primum. Cui nomen Dei, & Deitatem proprie significans, in Scripturis passim & vere, proprieque tribuitur, uti Patri, is est verus, idemque cum Patre natura Deus: sed Christo nomen Dei ita tribuitur in Scripturis: Ergo. Major certa est, & pro Filio æque militat, ac Patre, ut, nisi Filius concedatur Deus esse, nec Pater Deus esse probari possit. Quare ad Minorem. Cujus probationem non male complectitur hac thesi Arminius, in Disputatione suprà memorata; Ex nominibus, quæ illi in Script. tribuuntur id patet, 1. Quia Deus appellatur, & non attributive tantum, ut, sermo est Deus: qui est Deus benedictus in sæcula, sed etiam subjective, Deus manifestatus in carne. O Deus, Deus tuus te unxit oleo lætitiæ: imo & magnus Deus. II. Filii vox idem evincit, præsertim quatenus illi ista propriè & unicè competit, juxta id quod dicitur proprius, & unigenitus Filius Dei; quas voces tantundem valere dicimus, ac si naturalis esset appellatus. II. Quia vocatur Rex Regum, & Dominus Dominantium; item Dominus gloriæ. Quæ nomina longè fortius evincunt, quod volumus, si cum V. T. Scripturis conferantur, ubi eadem illi, qui Iehovah dicitur, attribuuntur. IV. Ex nomine Λόγῳ pia antiquitas idem adstruit, quod sermonem [illegible, ~8 letters] & propria subsistentia carentem significare non potest, propter ea, quæ illi in Scripturis tribuuntur. Dicitur n. fuisse in principio; fuisse apud Deum: Esse Deus: & per illum creata esse omnia, &c. Distinctè singula ponemus, atque considerabimus.
units.tr: First. He to whom the name of God, signifying Deity properly, is truly and properly given throughout Scripture, as it is to the Father, is the true God and, by nature, God together with the Father. But the name of God is so given to Christ in Scripture. Therefore Christ is God. The major premise is certain and applies to the Son just as much as to the Father, so that unless the Son is granted to be God, it cannot be proved that the Father is God either. So we come to the minor premise. Arminius, in the disputation mentioned above, sums up its proof well in this thesis: That this is so is clear from the names which are given to him in Scripture. 1. Because he is called God, and not merely by way of attribute, as in "the word was God," or "who is God blessed for ever" [Rom. 9:5], but also as the subject, as in "God manifested in the flesh" [1 Tim. 3:16]; "O God, thy God hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness" [Ps. 45:7]; and even "the great God" [Tit. 2:13]. II. The name Son proves the same, especially as it belongs to him properly and uniquely, according to the words "the proper and only-begotten Son of God." We say these words have the same force as if he were called natural Son. III. Because he is called King of kings and Lord of lords, and likewise Lord of glory. These names prove what we want far more strongly if they are compared with the Scriptures of the Old Testament, where the same names are given to him who is called Jehovah. IV. From the name Logos, ancient piety holds the same thing, since it cannot signify a mere word lacking a proper subsistence, on account of what is ascribed to him in Scripture. For it is said that he was in the beginning, that he was with God, that he was God, and that all things were created through him, and so on. We shall set out and consider each of these points distinctly.

units.la: 1. Deus dicitur, oppositè ad hominem. Gal. 1. 1. non ab hominibus, neque per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum. Ubi Christus opponitur hominibus, ne videatur Paulus ab homine vocatus, & non à Deo. Excipit Enjedinus, Christum eximi, non quasi non sit homo, sed quia non vulgaris homo, non certe homo abjectus nunc & miser, uti sæpe vocabulum hominis pro ista hominis conditione magis sumitur, quam natura.
units.tr: 1. He is called God, in contrast to man. Gal. 1:1, not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ. Here Christ is set against men, lest it seem that Paul was called by a man and not by God. Enyedinus objects that Christ is excepted, not as if he were not a man, but because he is not an ordinary man, certainly not a man now abject and wretched, as the word "man" is often taken for that condition of man rather than for his nature.

units.la: Negat hic Paulus, se ab homine munus Apostolicum, sed à Iesu Christo accepisse. Unde videtur negare Iesum, esse hominem. Si autem non sit homo, sequitur, ut adversarii concludunt, esse Deum. Sed primo, talis collectio, admodum infirma, & sophistica est. Neque enim necessa-
units.tr: Here Paul denies that he received the apostolic office from a man, but from Jesus Christ. Hence they seem to deny that Jesus is a man. If, however, he is not a man, it follows, as our opponents conclude, that he is God. But first, such an inference is very weak and sophistical. For it does not necessarily follow

units.la: Resp. 1. Fatemur, non necessario sequi, si quis negetur esse homo, ut sit Deus: sed in hujusmodi negatione, ac est in nostro tex-tu, id adeo certum est, ut nihil aliud reddi in opposito membro vel possit, vel debeat, quam Deus. Non vocatus ab hominibus, rio sequitur, si quis negetur esse homo, ut sit Deus. Nam Deus & homo, non sunt oppositä immediata. Deinde, si ea fuisset mens Apostoli, ut homines Deo opponeret, satis habuisset Dei nomen ponere, in altero oppositionis membro; neque opus fuisset, seorsim a Deo, nominare Iesum Christum. Praeterea, si haec collectio firma est, non minus nostram, quam Christi, Pauli, & ipsorum denique adversariorum de Christo sententiam evertit. Nam Iesus semper se hominis filium, Paulus eundem fere ubique virum & hominem, & ipsi adversarii cum verum esse hominem affirmat. Non ergo hic Paulus negavit Iesum esse hominem. Sed ut verus huius loci sensus magis illucescat, paulo fusius & diligentius de eo differamus. Usitatum hoc est, tam prophanis, quam sacris, tam Graecis, quam Latinis scriptoribus, ut unum aliquem, propter excellentiam, & singulare aliquod privilegium, e numero & ordine caeterorum, ejusdem generis & speciei, eximant & segregent. Ut Aristophanes, Plutum suam sic orditur:
units.tr: Reply 1. We grant that it does not necessarily follow that, if someone is denied to be a man, he must be God. But in a negation of this kind, such as is in our text, it is so certain that nothing else can or should be supplied in the opposite member but God: "not called by men," and so on. For God and man are not immediate opposites. Next, if it had been the Apostle's intention to set men against God, it would have been enough for him to put the name of God in the second member of the opposition; there would have been no need to name Jesus Christ separately from God. Moreover, if this inference were sound, it would overturn our view of Christ no less than the view of Christ held by Paul, and by the opponents themselves. For Jesus always calls himself the Son of man, Paul almost everywhere calls him a man, and our opponents themselves affirm that he is truly a man. Therefore Paul did not here deny that Jesus is a man. But so that the true sense of this place may shine out more clearly, let us discuss it at somewhat more length and with more care. It is the usual practice, in profane writers as in sacred, in Greek writers as in Latin, to single out one person from the number and order of others of the same kind and species, on account of his excellence or some singular privilege. Thus Aristophanes begins his Plutus in this way:

units.la: ὡς ἔγγε λέων[?] πρᾶγμ' ὅδ', ὦ Ζεῦ καὶ θεοί.
units.tr: ὡς ἔγγε λέων[?] πρᾶγμ' ὅδ', ὦ Ζεῦ καὶ θεοί.

units.la: Ubi Iupiter non excluditur, e numero Deorum, sed propter excellentiam seorsim nominatur. Sic Mar. 16. v.7. Dicite discipulis ejus, & Petro. Certe hic Petrus, non excluditur e numero discipulorum, sed propter eximium in Christum amorem, aut aliquam aliam ob causam, seorsim nominatur. Ita Matt. 3. & Mar. 3. post Iu-daeam totam, nominatur Ierosolyma, non quod Ierosolyma non comprehenderetur in Iudaea tota, sed quia caput erat Iudaeae. Plura exempla qui volet observare, passim poterit. Secundo, illud etiam observetur, vocabulum Hominis in sacris praesertim, non tantum certam animalis speciem, verum etiam imbecillitatem, & mortalitatem de-notare. Ad quod confirmandum sufficiat illud unicum Esaiae dictum cap. 31. Aegyptus homo, & non Deus. Ergo saepe fit, ut qui excellenti aliquo dono est ornatus, & aliquid supra vulgares homines obtinet, e numero hominum eximatur, ut cum ille Pharisaeus Luc. 11. ait : Non sum sicut caeteri homines. Sed accommodatius habe-mus exemplum Iudicum cap. 16. ubi Samson neque per ho-minem, sed, intellige per Deum. Quid enim, vel quis hac in re ho-minibus opponitur, quam Deus? Deinde quamvis non solius Dei nomen posuerit Apostolus, in altero oppositionis membro, & nominarit Iesum, non sequitur, negasse eum Deum, quum adeo ipsi Adversarii non negent Christum, Deum esse: verum egit hoc, ad significandum, Christum quoque Deum esse, oppositae ad homines.
units.tr: Here Jupiter is not excluded from the number of the gods, but is named apart on account of his excellence. So too Mark 16:7: "Go, tell his disciples and Peter." Here Peter is certainly not excluded from the number of the disciples, but is named separately on account of his outstanding love for Christ, or some other cause. Likewise in Matt. 3 and Mark 3, after the whole of Judaea, Jerusalem is named, not because Jerusalem was not included in the whole of Judaea, but because it was its head. Anyone who wishes may find many more examples everywhere. Secondly, let this also be noted: the word "man," especially in sacred writings, denotes not only a certain species of animal but also weakness and mortality. To confirm this one saying of Isaiah, chap. 31, is enough: "The Egyptians are men, and not God." Therefore it often happens that one who is adorned with some excellent gift and possesses something above ordinary men is singled out from the number of men, as the Pharisee in Luke 11 says, "I am not as other men are." But we have a more suitable example in Judges 16, where Samson is not described as "by man," but, understand, "by God." For what, or who, in this matter is set against men, if not God? Next, although the Apostle did not put only the name of God in the second member of the opposition, but named Jesus, it does not follow that he denied him to be God, since our opponents themselves do not deny that Christ is God. Rather he did this to signify that Christ is also God, set against men.

units.la: III. Neque tamen eo negat Paulus, Chri-stum hominem, sed merum esse hominem. Verum esse hominem, affirmamus omnes, sed non merum, sive humanae tantum, & non quoque divinae naturae. Neque negavit Paulus, Iesum esse hominem; sed affirma-vit, esse Deum. Quod nec Adversarii refu-giunt, sed alio, ac Paulus, sensu. IV. Non est quaestio, an aliquando apud Scriptores aliquis propter excellentiam, e numero caeterorum eximatur, quum in nostro loco non fit exemtio Christi e numero caetero-rum, sed oppositio, ἀλλὰ: neque enim magis exemtio vel exceptio de Christo potest intelligi, quam de Deo Patre Christum e mortuis vel resuscitante, quum de utroque eadem praedicetur oppositio sed. Quare nec loca allegata aliquid probant, in quibus excellentia unius praedicatur prae aliis ejusdem generis, uti apud Aristophanem, Pluti inter & supra Deos; apud Marcum, Petri, inter discipulos; denique Jero-solymae, in Judaea: neque enim in loco-rum istorum ullo est oppositio, ἀλλά, vel Jovis ad Deos, vel Petri ad discipulos, vel Ierosolymae ad Iudaeam, qualis foret si fuisset dictum, non Dii, sed Jupiter, non discipuli sed Petrus, non Judaea sed Jero-solyma: ac proinde elenchus est dissimi-lium. In quo quaeso te, istorum locorum, ullove alio occurrunt particulae oppositionis οὐχ, ὅτι[?], ἀλλά? quare non denotatur sola exceptio vel excellentia, sed oppositio? v. Vox hominis in sacris, & ubiubi denotet hominis simul imbecilli-tatem ; negat quodammodo, se esse hominem. Nam v. 7. ait: Infirmus ero, ut caeteri homines. Et v. 11. Infirmus ero, & aliorum hominum similis: Hinc etiam gentiles, eos qui eximia virtute excellebant, non homines, sed heroas vocabant. Qua tamen appellatione, non excludebant eos a natura humana. Tertio, & illud notetur; Petrum, & caeteros a Christo electos Apostolos, fuisse in magna auctoritate, post ascensionem Christi, in Ecclesia, ut patet cum ex aliis locis, tum ex cap. 15. Actorum: Sed & ex hac eadem Pauli epistola. Nam quod ad Petrum attinet, ait hoc eodem capite, se post conversionem, Ierofolymam ad Petrum venisse, & apud eum solum aliquot dies mansisse. Sequenti vero capite, praecipuos Apostolos vocat columnas Ecclesiae. Quarto, observetur & illud, fuisse quosdam Iudaeos pseudapostolos, qui affirmabant se a Petro, & caeteris praecipuis Apostolis, habere docendi auctoritatem, atque Gentes ad circumcisionem, & reliquas Mosis leges observandas cogebant. His cum adversaretur Paulus, & ejus doctrina: pseudapostoli elevabant auctoritatem Pauli, & doctrinam calumniabantur, afferentes Paulum, non esse a Petro & caeteris Apostolis ordinatum, & vocatum ad munus Apostolicum, ideoque non ei tantum tribuendum esse, neque mirandum, si erret in doctrina, cum non sit Apostolorum discipulus. Hoc Paulo ubi innotuit, ne doctrina sua apud auditores in contemtum veniret, & discipuli ipsius de salute periclitarentur: sui Apostolatus dignitatem, graviter tuetur. Affirmat igitur, se eandem habere, cum caeteris Apostolis auctoritatem, illis vero qui ab Apostolis ordinati sunt, longe esse superiorem. Nam istos ab hominibus esse vocatos, ipsum vero a Deo, & Iesu Christo. Ex his omnibus, verborum Apostoli sensus satis manifestus est. Opponit enim homini, id est, Petro, etiam in summa auctoritate, inter Apostolos praedito: Deum Patrem: Hominibus autem, id est, Apostolis reliquis, Iesum Christum. In qua quidem oppositione, non hoc vult, Iesum non esse hominem, sicut nec Petrus excluditur, e numero discipulorum, cum seorsim nominatur a caeteris; nec Sum-tatem; non vero uspiam hominem negat, sed eundem ubique connotat & comprehendit, praesertim Deo oppositâ, uti in loco Iesaiae, Aegyptus homo, & non Deus.
units.tr: III. Yet Paul does not thereby deny that Christ is a man, but that he is merely a man. We all affirm that he is truly a man, but not merely a man, that is, not only of human nature and not also of divine nature. Paul did not deny that Jesus is a man; he affirmed that he is God. Our opponents do not shrink from this, but they take it in another sense than Paul does. IV. The question is not whether sometimes among writers someone is singled out from the number of others on account of excellence, since in our passage Christ is not singled out from the number of others, but set in opposition, by the word ἀλλά ("but"). Nor can an exception or exclusion concerning Christ be understood any more than concerning God the Father raising Christ from the dead, since the same opposition with "but" is affirmed of both. Therefore the places cited prove nothing in which the excellence of one is asserted above others of the same kind, as in Aristophanes, of Plutus among and above the gods; in Mark, of Peter among the disciples; and finally, of Jerusalem in Judaea. For in none of those places is there an opposition with ἀλλά, whether of Jupiter to the gods, or of Peter to the disciples, or of Jerusalem to Judaea. It would be such an opposition if it had been said, not "gods" but "Jupiter," not "disciples" but "Peter," not "Judaea" but "Jerusalem"; and so the argument is one of dissimilar things. In those places, I ask you, or in any other, do the particles of opposition οὐχ, ὅτι, ἀλλά appear? Why, then, is not merely an exception or excellence signified, but an opposition? V. The word "man" in sacred writings, wherever it occurs, denotes at the same time human weakness; in a sense he denies that he himself is a man. For in v. 7 he says: "I will be weak, as other men are." And in v. 11: "I will be weak, and like other men." Hence also the Gentiles called those who excelled in outstanding virtue not men but heroes. Yet by this title they did not exclude them from human nature. Thirdly, let this also be noted: Peter and the other Apostles chosen by Christ were held in great authority in the Church after Christ's ascension, as is clear both from other places and from Acts 15, and also from this same Epistle of Paul.
