For as regards Peter, Paul says in this same chapter that after his conversion he went up to Jerusalem to Peter and stayed with him alone for some days. In the following chapter he calls the chief Apostles the pillars of the Church. Fourthly, let this also be observed: there were some Jewish false apostles who claimed that they had the authority to teach from Peter and the other chief Apostles, and who compelled the Gentiles to observe circumcision and the rest of the laws of Moses. Paul opposed them and his teaching. The false apostles disparaged Paul's authority and slandered his doctrine, asserting that Paul had not been appointed and called to the apostolic office by Peter and the other Apostles, and that therefore he was not to be given so much credit, nor was it surprising if he erred in doctrine, since he was not a disciple of the Apostles. When this came to Paul's notice, lest his teaching be despised among his hearers and his disciples be endangered as to their salvation, he defends the dignity of his apostleship with vigour. He therefore affirms that he has the same authority as the other Apostles, and that he is far superior to those who were ordained by the Apostles. For these, he says, were called by men, but he himself by God and by Jesus Christ. From all this the sense of the Apostle's words is sufficiently plain. For he sets against man, that is, against Peter, who had the highest authority among the Apostles, God the Father; and against men, that is, the other Apostles, Jesus Christ. In this opposition he does not mean that Jesus is not a man, just as Peter is not excluded from the number of the disciples when he is named separately from the others. Nor does he deny man anywhere; rather he everywhere implies and includes the same, especially when set against God, as in the passage of Isaiah: "The Egyptians are men, and not God."

units.la: Neque hinc probat Adversarius, eum, qui excellenti aliquo dono est ornatus, & aliquid supra vulgares homines obtinet, è numero hominum eximi, quidem è numero vulgarium, uti Pharisaeus ille dicens, non sum sicut caeteri homines, à caeteris segregatur, non è numero hominum; & Samson, infirmus ero, ut caeteri homines; cum caeteris hominibus interim se comparat quoad communem infirmitatem, non vero è numero hominum eximit. At in textu nostro nihil tale, quod indicet Christum è numero hominum eximii, tamquam iis in eodem genere dumtaxat excellentiorem. Cedo aliquid in textu simile cum locis hic, sive è prophanis, sive sacris, allegatis. Vel quid huc demum facit, quod Gentiles vocarint suos, aut coluerint heroas? vi. Petrum, ac caeteros Apostolos magnae semper in Ecclesia fuisse autoritatis, nemo negat, aut nescit; verum Paulum Apostolum, post agnitum ejus apostolatum atque vocationem, opus habuisse se adversus illos, aut ab ipsis vocatos, & qui eorum auctoritate in vilipendium missionis suae abutebantur, suam confirmare, & hinc doctrinae suae parare patrocinium, non probat Adversarius: neque quod fingit & pingit, Pseudoapostolos auctoritatem Pauli elevasse, & doctrinam ejus calumniatos, asserentes Paulum non esse à Petro & caeteris Apostolis ordinatum & vocatum ad munus Apostolicum, ideoque non ei tantum tribuendum esse, vel non mirandum, si erret in doctrina, cum non sit Apostolorum discipulus. Unde quaeso ista probat? vel quod proinde Apostolus coactus dignitatem Apostolatus & ministerii sui assistere, se affirmarit non ab hominibus vocatum, id est Apostolis illis, sed Deo & Christo Iesu. Primum autem in textu dicitur, à
units.tr: Nor does the Adversary prove from this that a man who is adorned with some outstanding gift and holds a place above ordinary men is thereby taken out of the number of men. He is taken out of the number of common people, as that Pharisee who said, "I am not as other men," sets himself apart from the rest, not from the human race; and Samson, "I shall be weak, as other men," compares himself with other men in respect of common weakness, but does not exclude himself from mankind. In our text there is nothing like this, nothing which indicates that Christ is removed from the number of men as one who excels only within the same kind. Let him show me something in the text similar to the passages cited here, whether from profane or from sacred writers. Or what does it matter that the Gentiles called their own men heroes or worshipped heroes? That Peter and the other Apostles always had great authority in the Church, no one denies or is ignorant of. But that Paul the Apostle, after his apostleship and calling had been acknowledged, had need to assert himself against those men, or against those called by them, who abused their authority to disparage his mission, and so to secure a defence for his doctrine, the Adversary does not prove. Nor does he prove what he invents and paints, that the false apostles diminished Paul's authority and slandered his teaching, asserting that Paul had not been ordained and called to the apostolic office by Peter and the other Apostles, and that therefore he should not be given so much credit, and it is no wonder if he erred in doctrine, since he was not a disciple of the Apostles. From what, I ask, does he prove these things? Or that the Apostle, compelled to defend the dignity of his apostleship and ministry, therefore affirmed that he had been called not by men, that is, by those Apostles, but by God and Christ Jesus. But first, the text says "by Christ, or through Christ and God." Next, if by men the Apostles are meant, why did Enjedinus make those remarks he made earlier about the word "man," as signifying the common weakness of men and not their excellence, since surely it here denotes the excellence of the apostleship, and not a common excellence? Moreover, there was no need to prove that he had not been called to the apostolic office by Peter or the other Apostles, since no one can be called to that office by men, but by Christ and God alone. And in that matter, others rashly aspired to something above Paul, namely that they had been called by Peter or the Apostles; which rather shows that they were not Apostles at all, let alone superior to Paul. And so the Apostle, both here and elsewhere, proclaims that his calling to the apostolic office was immediate, from Christ and not from men. Nor is this his meaning here, that he signifies Peter by "man," or sets God the Father against him. For who has ever supposed that the Apostle, in the words "not through man," meant to denote Peter, and not man indefinitely, in general? Hence the Arabic version has "nor through any man." To this end the Apostle also placed "not through men" first. The Ethiopic version reads: Paul an Apostle, not of men nor through men, but through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc. But who understands by those men the remaining Apostles, the followers of Peter, or thinks that Christ Jesus is set by the Apostle against them? And are these things said by the Adversary without any proof, or even a shadow of proof? Let him make a paraphrase of the passage and see whether it can be proved to learned and sensible readers: "Paul the Apostle was called not by the Apostles, nor by Peter, but by the divine and altogether excellent man Jesus Christ, and by God the Father, etc." Finally, in whatever state Christ is considered, that he is set against men not only in respect of condition but of nature is shown by the addition "of God," unless you are willing to say that the Father too is set against men in respect of condition, and not of nature.

units.la: Tom. 2. Samson propterea negatur esse homo, quia tum demum se fore hominibus similem, cum vires ami-sisset, affirmat: sed quia sicut Petrus inter discipulos, & Samson inter homines, supra vulga-rem & communem sortem, ac conditionem, ali-quid eximium & peculiare habebant: ita etiam Christus, praesertim post ascensionem in caelum, quo tempore haec scribebat Apostolus, (id quod diligenter observandum est) fuit e communi hominum forte exemtus, & longe excellentior, non modo hominibus, verum etiam Angelis sa-stus[?]. Quare opponi omnibus in terra viventi-bus hominibus, quantumvis excellentibus, non quidem ratione naturae, sed conditionis, merito potuit. Christo, vel per Christum & Deum. De-inde si per homines intelligantur Apostoli, quorsum ista fecerunt, quae antea dixit En-jedinus, de vocabulo hominis ut significat hominum vulgarem infirmitatem, non ex-cellentiam, quum certe Apostolatus excel-lentiam designet, eamque non vulgarem. Praeterea nil necesse fuit probare, ad mu-nus Apostolicum se non esse vocatum a Pe-tro aut caeteris Apostolis, quum ad munus istud nemo ab hominibus vocari possit, sed a solo Christo ac Deo, atque in eo temere alii supra Paulum quidpiam affectassent, quod a Petro vel Apostolis vocati essent, quum id arguat potius eos non esse Aposto-los, nedum Paulo superiores. Ac propterea Apostolus & hic, & alibi deprædicat im-mediatam suam a Christo, non ab hominibus, vocationem ad munus Apostolicum: non vero hic ejus sensus, ut vel per hominem Petrum significet, vel ei Deum Patrem opponat. Quis enim unquam cogitavit Apostolum verbis istis, non per hominem, denotare voluisse Petrum, & non indefinite, hominem in genere? unde versio Arabica habet, ne-que per ullum hominem. In quem finem & praemisit Apost. non per homines. Versio Aethio-pica, Paulus Apostolus, ejus qui non fuit per homines, & non fuit ab hominibus, sed per Domi-num nostrum, &c. Quis autem vel per homines illos intelligat reliquos a Petro Apostolo-los, vel iis opponi ab Apostolo, Christum Jesum? & haec ita dici ab Adversario, citra ullam probationem, vel probationis umbram? Faciat loci paraphrasim, & videat ut pro-bari ea doctis & cordatis possit: Paulus Apostolus non ab Apostolis, neque a Petro voca-tus, sed a divino & prorsus excellenti viro Jesu Christo, & Deo Patre, &c. Deniq; quo-cumque in statu consideretur Christus, opponi eum hominibus, non solius conditionis, sed naturae respectu, arguit adjunctum Dei, nisi & Patrem aequae velis conditionis, & non naturae respectu, opponi hominibus.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Samson is not therefore denied to be a man because he declares that he would then be like other men when he had lost his strength; but because, just as Peter among the disciples and Samson among men had something outstanding and peculiar above the common lot and condition, so also Christ, especially after his ascension into heaven, at which time the Apostle was writing these things (which must be carefully observed), was taken out of the common lot of men and was far more excellent, not only than men but even than the holy angels. Wherefore he could rightly be set over against all men living on earth, however excellent, not indeed in respect of nature but of condition. Christ, or through Christ and God. Next, if by men the Apostles are understood, why did they do those things which Enjedinus said before about the word man, as signifying the common weakness of men and not their excellence, since surely it designates the excellence of the apostleship, and an uncommon excellence? Moreover, there was no need to prove that he had not been called to the apostolic office by Peter or the other Apostles, since no man can be called to that office by men, but only by Christ and God; and in that matter others rashly aspired to something above Paul, namely that they had been called by Peter or the Apostles, which rather proves that they were not Apostles, let alone superior to Paul. And so the Apostle, both here and elsewhere, proclaims that his calling to the apostolic office was immediate, from Christ and not from men; and his sense here is not that he signifies Peter by "man," or sets God the Father against him. For who ever thought that the Apostle, in the words "not through man," meant to denote Peter and not man indefinitely, in general? Hence the Arabic version has "nor through any man." To this end the Apostle also placed "not through men" first. The Ethiopic version: Paul an Apostle, of one who was not through men, and not from men, but through our Lord, etc. But who understands by those men the remaining Apostles of Peter, or that Christ Jesus is set against them by the Apostle? And are these things said by the Adversary without any proof, or even a shadow of proof? Let him make a paraphrase of the passage and see whether it can be proved to learned and sensible people: "Paul the Apostle was called not by the Apostles, nor by Peter, but by the divine and altogether excellent man Jesus Christ, and by God the Father, etc." Finally, in whatever state Christ is considered, that he is set against men, not in respect of condition only but of nature, is shown by the adjunct "of God," unless you are willing that the Father also be set against men in respect of condition, and not of nature.

units.la: Christus non solum praedicative & attributive, sed quoque subjective nuncupatur Deus. Satis quidem fidenter Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum, de Trinitate, pag. 145. Negamus (inquit) uspiam Dei nomen, cum subjective ponitur, aut etiam cum illi articulum in Graeco additur, quo illud pluribus alioqui natura sua commune ad summum illum Deum significandum determinet, Christo usquam in Scriptura tributum esse. Duo negat 1. nomen Dei subjective Christo tribui. ii. Et cum articulo. Quorum utrumque sumus probaturi. At-que illud primum: etiam Arminio bene notatum, & Episcopio. Illius verba modo audivimus. Hic, Instit. lib. iv. cap xxxii. de Filio res clara etiam est: quia is appellatur Deus, non attributive tantum, Ioh. 1.1. & sermo ille erat Deus. sed & subjunctive, Heb. 1.8.9. Ad Filium autem, thronus tuus Deus, in seculum seculi. Virga recta, virga regni tui. Dilexisti justi-tiam, & odisti iniquitatem: propterea unxit te, o Deus, Deus tuus oleo laetitiae supra consortes tuos. Haec loca habemus, pro subjectiva locutione de Christo, Deo. 1. Tim. iii. 16. Deus manifestatus in carne. Heb. 1.8.6. Ad Filium autem, thronus tuus, Deus, &c. propte-rea unxit te, o Deus, Deus tuus. Tit. ii.[?] 12. Magni Dei & Servatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Quibus duobus articulus quoque additur, ὁ μεγάλῳ θεὸς [?]. & ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ θεὸς. ἐξεῖσι σε ὁ θεὸς, ὁ θεὸς σε. Act. xx. 28. pascere Ecclesiam ὃν θεὸς [?] quam per proprium sanguinem redemit. Deus dicitur, & pariter Dominus, ὁ Κύριος [?] quod in N.T. respondet Hebraeae voci Jehova. Matth. xxii. 43. ex Psalm. cx. 1. εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος τῷ Κυρίῳ μου. Luc. 1. multos filiorum Israel convertet ad Dominum Deum ipsorum. Et ipse praecedet coram eo: Christo nempe, uti notum. Κύριον τὸν θεὸν dicitur, vers. 76. Et tu puerule, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis: praecedes enim ante faciem Domini, parraturus vias ejus. Joann. xx. 28. Et respondit Thomas, & dixit ei· ὁ Κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ θεός μου. Ubi utrumque jungitur, & tribuitur Christo, subjective etiam, addito-que articulo; Κύριος, quo nomine Hebraeum Jehova a Graecis Interpretibus passim exprimitur; deinde vox θεός. Sed articuli ista nec vis, nec usus est in sacris, qui promiscue aliquando additur, aliquando omittitur, sive de vero Deo, sive falsis Diis, sit sermo. Omittitur etiam in sermone de vero Deo, Matth. iv. 4. διὰ [?] cap. v. 9. υἱοὶ θεοῦ. non θεοῦ. cap. vi. 24. θεῷ δουλεύειν. ibid. verl. 30.33. cap. xiv. 33. & xxvii. 43. 54. & innumeris aliis locis. Iterum additur articulus, Act. vii. 43. τὴν ἄστρον τοῦ θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ῥεμφάν. 2 Cor. iv. 4. ὁ θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου. Gal. 4. 8. τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς. Phil. iii. 19. ὧν ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοιλία: quibus locis minime agitur de vero Deo. Enjedinus, in Tit. ii. 18. infinita ostendunt exempla, magnam varietatem & licentiam esse Graecis, in articulis addendis, omittendis, transponendis. Iam & ubi Christo nomen θεὸς, cum articulo, subjecti loco tribuatur, annotavimus.
units.tr: Christ is called God not only predicatively and attributively, but also subjectively. Schlichting, against Meisner, On the Trinity, p. 145, rather confidently says: "We deny (he says) that the name of God is anywhere in Scripture given to Christ when it is used subjectively, or even when the article is added to it in Greek, which otherwise by its nature is common to many and determines it to signify that highest God." He denies two things: first, that the name of God is attributed to Christ subjectively; second, that it is so with the article. We shall prove each of these. And first, that point has been well noted also by Arminius and Episcopius. We have just heard his words. Here, in Institutes book iv, chapter 32, the matter concerning the Son is also clear: for he is called God, not only attributively, John 1:1, "and the Word was God," but also subjectively, Heb. 1:8–9, "But unto the Son, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom. Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows." We have these passages as subjective expressions concerning Christ as God: 1 Tim. 3:16, "God was manifested in the flesh"; Heb. 1:8, "But unto the Son, Thy throne, O God, etc., therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee"; Tit. 2:13, "the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ." In these two the article is also added: τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ [of the great God]; and ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ θεός [Thy throne, O God]; ἔχρισέ σε ὁ θεὸς ὁ θεός σου [God, thy God, hath anointed thee]. Acts 20:28, "to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood," τῆς ἐκκλησίας τοῦ θεοῦ, ἣν περιεποιήσατο διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος. He is called God, and likewise Lord, ὁ Κύριος, which in the New Testament corresponds to the Hebrew word Jehovah. Matt. 22:43, from Psalm 110:1, εἶπεν ὁ Κύριος τῷ Κυρίῳ μου [The Lord said unto my Lord]. Luke 1:16, "And many of the children of Israel shall he turn to the Lord their God. And he shall go before him": namely Christ, as is well known. In verse 76 he is called Lord God: "And thou, child, shall be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord, to prepare his ways." John 20:28, "And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God," ὁ Κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου. Here both are joined and attributed to Christ, subjectively too, with the article added: Κύριος, by which name the Greek interpreters commonly express the Hebrew Jehovah; then the word θεός. But the article has neither force nor fixed use in Holy Scripture, since it is sometimes added and sometimes omitted, whether the discourse concerns the true God or false gods. It is also omitted in speech about the true God, Matt. 4:4, διὰ παντὸς ῥήματος [by every word of God]; ch. 5:9, υἱοὶ θεοῦ [children of God], not τοῦ θεοῦ; ch. 6:24, θεῷ δουλεύειν [serve God]; ibid. vv. 30, 33; ch. 14:33; ch. 27:43, 54; and in countless other places. The article is added again, Acts 7:43, τὸ ἄστρον τοῦ θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ῥομφάν [the star of your god Rephan]; 2 Cor. 4:4, ὁ θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου [the god of this world]; Gal. 4:8, τοῖς μὴ φύσει οὖσι θεοῖς [to those which by nature are no gods]; Phil. 3:19, ὧν ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοιλία [whose god is their belly]; in which places there is by no means any question of the true God. Enjedinus, on Tit. 2:18, says: "Infinite examples show that the Greeks have great variety and licence in adding, omitting and transposing articles." Now we have also noted where the name θεός, with the article, is given to Christ in the place of the subject.

units.la: Sed ad Ioann. xx. 28. excipiunt, Thomam illis verbis non Christum compellare, sed magna admiratione tactum exclamare, Deum! alium intelligendo, quam Christum. Ita illud intorquet Enjedinus: quibus quidem verbis non Christum compellat, neque eum Dominum & Deum suum vocat: sed rem inusitatam, & admirationem suam summam significat, sicut cum repente aliquid sive horrendum, sive admirabile nonnullis occurrit, exclamant, Iesus, Maria: vel quomodo, inquit, Gentiles exclamare solebant, Dii boni, Hercules, o Iupiter, &c. Nempe adeo non potuit loco huic solutio excogitari, nisi a perversa & temeraria hominum vulgarium per Deum, per Jesum, Mariam, &c. jurantium. Sic Thomas, praesentibus caeteris, & apud Christum, dixit? Imo expresse in textu vides, quod id Thomas Christo dixerit, ut. Versio Persica, Dominus quidem meus es, & Deus meus. Unde Adversariorum alii haec Christo dicta inficiari nequeunt. Servetus, lib. 1. pag. 10. Et Thomas Iohannis 20. cum appellat Deus meus, Dominus meus. Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, cap. xxiv. pag. 146. Theophilus Nicolaides, contra Miedzibozium, pro Socino, pag. 33. Ab ipso denique Socino, epist. ad Franciscum Davidis, qui quoque ea Thomae verba ad Christum dirigi negabat, inter epist. Socini, pag. 186. & 189. Iam vero haec tua interpretatio nullo modo sustineri potest. Primum, quia, ut diximus, non potuisset Iohannes simpliciter dicere, Thomam respondisse, si ad alium quam ad Iesum, qui ipsum allocutus fuerat, verba tua direxisset. Deinde, quia nullum ejusmodi eclipsis exemplum in tota scriptura, sed neque etiam in alio probato auctore, fortasse invenies. Praeterea, cum Christus verbis illis a Thoma prolatis, statim dicat, Quia vidisti, Thoma, credidisti, nemo dubitare potest, quin ex ipsis Thomæ verbis aperte constiterit eum jam credidisse. Atqui, si ad Deum patrem illa referantur, id nullo modo constare potest, cum nullam sententiam explicent, & varia possint subaudiri; immo talia, quae Thomam nec credidisse, nec credere voluisse, demonstrent. Pag. 192. Verum quid proclivius est, quam sine ulla vera eclipsi, aut insolente atque incerta interpretatione verbum substantivum quod vocant, simpliciter subaudire? Persimilis autem (ut explicationi nostræ, quæ multo uberius confirmari posset, colophonem hunc addamus) huic loco est locus ille apud eundem Iohannem cap. 13. v. 13. Vos vocatis me magister & dominus. Namin Græco est ὁ διδάσκαλος καὶ[?] ὁ κύριος. Quemadmodum enim dominum agnoscebant, & confitebantur, sic Thomas Christo dicens, Dominus meus, & Deus meus, cum Dominum & Deum suum agnovit, & confessus est.
units.tr: But against John 20:28 they object that Thomas, in those words, is not addressing Christ but exclaiming in great astonishment, "God!", meaning someone other than Christ. Enjedinus twists the passage thus: by these words he does not address Christ or call him his Lord and God, but expresses something unusual and his great amazement, just as when something either dreadful or wonderful suddenly occurs to some people, they cry out, Jesus! Mary! or, as he puts it, as the Gentiles used to cry out, Good gods, Hercules, O Jupiter, etc. Indeed no such solution could have been devised for this passage except from the perverse and rash habit of common people who swear by God, by Jesus, by Mary, and so on. So did Thomas say this while the others were present, and to Christ? Indeed, you plainly see in the text that Thomas said it to Christ. The Persian version reads: My Lord indeed you are, and my God. Hence some of our adversaries cannot deny that these words were spoken to Christ. Servetus, book 1, p. 10: "And Thomas, John 20, when he calls him my God, my Lord." Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 24, p. 146. Theophilus Nicolaides, against Miedzibozius, for Socinus, p. 33. Finally, from Socinus himself, in his letter to Francis David, who likewise denied that those words of Thomas were directed to Christ, among the letters of Socinus, pp. 186 and 189: But this interpretation of yours cannot be sustained in any way. First, because, as we have said, John could not simply have said that Thomas replied, if your words were directed to someone other than Jesus, who had addressed him. Then, because you will perhaps find no example of such an ellipsis in all of Scripture, nor even in any other approved author. Moreover, since Christ, immediately after those words spoken by Thomas, says, "Because you have seen, Thomas, you have believed," no one can doubt that Thomas's own words clearly showed that he had already believed. But if those words are referred to God the Father, this cannot be established in any way, since they express no complete sentence and can be supplied in various ways; indeed, they show things which Thomas neither believed nor wished to believe. p. 192. But what is more obvious than simply to supply the so-called substantive verb, without any true ellipsis or any strained and uncertain interpretation? Quite similar to this passage (so that we may add this conclusion to our explanation, which could be confirmed far more fully) is that other passage in the same John, ch. 13, v. 13: "You call me Teacher and Lord." For in Greek it is [ὁ διδάσκαλος καὶ ὁ κύριος]. Just as they acknowledged and confessed him as Lord, so Thomas, saying to Christ, "My Lord and my God," acknowledged and confessed him as his Lord and God.

units.la: Volkelius aliam dat in hunc locum exceptionem, libro v. de religione sua, cap. x. pag. 423. Si nomini Deus aliqua restrictio adjiciatur, articulus ille vim suam non retinet: veluti cum Thomas Christo dicit: ὁ κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ θεός μου: tunc pronomen μου, voci θεὸς adjunctum, articulo eidem præpositio vim consuetam ita adimit, ut jam non unum illum Deum, sed eum significet, quem Thomas ut Divinum Dominum sibi colendum, ex refusi-tatione[?] ipsius a Deo fatta, agnovit. Nota pervicaciam. Iam volunt vocem θεὸς, ut verum Deum designet, debere articulum habere additum ὁ. Præterquam quod non probent, hoc ita debere fieri: loca damus de Christo loquentia, cum isto articulo. Sed hæc iterum ex alio articulo addito enervant, scilicet, quia additur voci θεὸς, μου, meus. Quod si non fuisset additum, aliam procul dubio iterum confingerent elabendi rationem. Ut scias non ex animo, vel sensu veritatis disputare istos homines, sed pro solis suis hypothesibus, ex mera animi pertinacia. Probent, articulum ὁ, additum vel negatum, eam vim habere, ut Deum notet, vel non. Probent, istum vim suam perdere, ubi additur ei pronomen μου. Hæc pro somniis, & inanibus ulcerosi animi dictatis habemus, quousque non probant, neque vel probare intendunt. II. Thomas non agnoscit Christum sibi colendum ut divinum Dominum, quæ perpetua eorum est perversio & loquela de Christo, sed Deum: hoc enim in textu est, non illud. III. Nec potest hic locum habere illa expositio, non modo propter præpositum utrobique articulum ὁ, & adjunctum μου, verum & propter interjectam incisionem, confirmatam connectivâ particulâ καὶ, ὁ κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ θεός μου, ut nequeat verti vel explicari, ô Dominus meus divinus! sed non aliter possit, quam, ô Dominus meus, & Deus meus! Quemadmodum Racoviensis versio etiam habet: mein Herr, und mein Gott. IV. Neque illo pacto adjunctum μου infringet adeo vim articuli, quam ipsius nominis θεὸς, faciens nempe ut hoc de Deo non accipiatur, quod aliás solet ac debet. V. Ego contra dico, adjunctum pronomen μου vim præcedentis articuli ὁ non adimere, sed sententiam valde confirmare. Et quomodo quæso auferret, quo hoc aut jure faceret, aut regula, aut quæ illa inter utrumque articulum repugnantia, vel diversitas, unde id fieret? Non magis hoc pronomen vim infringit praecedentium, quam ἡμῶν, in Pater noster : vel μή in Christi exclamatione, Θεέ μή, Θεέ μή. Quae non μείωσιν [?], sed singularem facere αὔξησιν [?] nemo quidem diffiteri potest. Versio Persica Joann. xx. 28. habet, Dominus quidem meus es, & Deus meus: vi. Quam vanae illae Adversariorum nostrorum observationes & exceptiones sint in articulo ὁ, vel μή, etiam inde patet, quod illa passim in simili locutione promiscue jam adduntur, jam omittuntur, citra ullam sensus, aut rei variationem. Christus, Matth. xi. 25. 26. primum dicit, ἐξομολογοῦμαί σοι, πάτερ. Dein addit articulum, Ναί ὁ πατήρ. Ecquis putabit, aliud quid, vel magis aut minus denotare nomen Patris hic, aut ibi, quamvis in uno membro articulus addatur, in altero non? Socinus tamen, contra Wiekum, cap. v. pag. 280. &c. quem sui hic sequuntur, audet pro se adferre verba illa Christi in cruce, Θεέ μή, Θεέ μή, uti Matthaeus, quae Marcus habet ὁ Θεὸς μή, ὁ Θεὸς μή. Quam vero frustra, nunc vidimus. Nam casus iste vocativi, nominativum non enervat, sed vim ejus auget ac confirmat. Et dum fateri cogitur, Christum a Thoma Deum nuncupari, hoc exponit, non simpliciter Deum, sed suum ipsius Deum: id est, non modo Dominum quod prius expresserat, sed divinum Dominum: quem nimirum colere, cuique confidere debeat. Id jam non est vim articuli tantum, quam alias solam urgent, sed & vocis Dei prorsus evacuare ac tollere. Qua ratione loci quivis alii, ubi de Deo, sive addito articulo, sive omisso, sermo fit, enervari atque in alium plane sensum mutari possunt. Adfert etiam Matth. vii. 9. quis est ex vobis homo, quem si petierit filius suus panem, ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ, ut ostendat, nullam articuli vim esse, propter additum pronomen. Sed nos nomos istam vim in articulo collocamus: nec ille probat, articuli vim imminui, propter additum nomini pronomen. Certe, inquit, non intelligit aliquem singularem seu unicum Filium, sed quemlibet: adde vero, suum: quod vim sermonis, tum rem omnem satis denotat.
units.tr: Volkelius gives another exception to this passage, in book 5 of his On his Religion, ch. 10, p. 423: If some restriction is added to the word God, the article loses its force; for example, when Thomas says to Christ [ὁ κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ θεός μου]: then the pronoun μου, joined to the word θεός, takes away from the article ὁ its usual force, so that it no longer signifies that one God, but him whom Thomas acknowledged, from his resurrection effected by God, as the divine Lord to be worshipped by himself. Note the obstinacy. Now they want the word θεός, to designate the true God, to have the article ὁ added. Besides not proving that this must be done so, we give passages speaking of Christ with this article. But these again they weaken by another added word, namely, because μου, "my," is added to θεός. Had it not been added, they would doubtless have devised yet another way of escape. So that you may know that these men dispute not sincerely or from a sense of truth, but solely for the sake of their own hypotheses, out of mere stubbornness of mind. Let them prove that the article ὁ, added or omitted, has this force, of denoting God, or not. Let them prove that it loses this force where the pronoun μου is added. We hold these claims as dreams and empty dictates of an ulcerated mind, until they prove them, or even intend to prove them. II. Thomas does not acknowledge Christ as the divine Lord to be worshipped by himself, which is their constant perversion and manner of speaking about Christ, but he acknowledges God: for this is what the text says, not that. III. Nor can that explanation hold here, not only because of the article ὁ placed before each noun and the added μου, but also because of the intervening break, confirmed by the connective particle καὶ [ὁ κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ θεός μου], so that it cannot be rendered or explained as "O my divine Lord!", but can only be rendered "O my Lord, and my God!" As the Racovian version also has: "my Lord, and my God." IV. Nor will the added μου in that way weaken the force of the article so much as the force of the name θεός itself, by causing this not to be taken of God, which it otherwise usually and rightly is. V. I on the contrary say that the added pronoun μου does not take away the force of the preceding article ὁ, but greatly strengthens the sense. And how, I ask, would it take it away, and by what right or rule would it do so, or what conflict or difference between the two articles would be the cause? This pronoun weakens the force of the preceding word no more than ἡμῶν in the Our Father, or μή in Christ's cry, [Θεέ μή, Θεέ μή]. No one can deny that these make not a diminution but a remarkable increase. The Persian version of John 20:28 reads: "My Lord indeed you are, and my God." VI. How empty the observations and exceptions of our adversaries about the article ὁ, or μή, are, is also clear from the fact that these are used everywhere in similar expressions, sometimes added and sometimes omitted, without any change in sense or meaning. Christ, Matt. 11:25-26, first says [ἐξομολογοῦμαί σοι, πάτερ], "I thank you, Father." Then he adds the article: [Ναί ὁ πατήρ], "Yes, Father." Who would think that the name Father denotes something different, or more or less, here or there, just because the article is added in one clause and not in the other? Socinus, however, against Wiek, ch. 5, p. 280 etc., whom his followers here follow, dares to bring forward in his favour those words of Christ on the cross, [Θεέ μή, Θεέ μή], as Matthew has them, which Mark has as [ὁ Θεὸς μή, ὁ Θεὸς μή]. How vainly, we have now seen. For that vocative case does not weaken the nominative, but increases and confirms its force. And while he is compelled to admit that Christ is called God by Thomas, he explains this as not simply God, but his own God: that is, not only Lord, which he had expressed before, but divine Lord, whom he ought indeed to worship and in whom he ought to trust. This is no longer a matter only of the force of the article, which they alone otherwise press, but also entirely empties and removes the force of the word God. By this method any other passages where God is spoken of, whether with the article added or omitted, could be weakened and turned into a quite different sense. He also cites Matt. 7:9, What man is there among you, whom if his son asks for bread, [ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ], to show that the article has no force because of the added pronoun. But we, on the contrary, place that force in the article, nor does he prove that the force of the article is diminished by a pronoun added to the noun. Certainly, he says, it does not mean some single or unique son, but any son. Add, however, "his own," which sufficiently indicates the force of the saying and the whole matter.

units.la: Ad 1 Tim. iii. 16. excipiunt, non agi ibi de Christo, vel non eum intelligi per Deum manifestatum in carne, sed Deum Patrem.
units.tr: They object that at 1 Tim. 3:16 nothing is said about Christ, or that he is not meant by "God manifested in the flesh," but God the Father.

units.la: Enjedinus, pag. 368, 369: Nec propositum Apostoli ferre, nec necessitate requirere, nec connexionem verborum & sententiarum permittere, ut hic de incarnatione Dei disputetur; sed potius, ut instituta de excellentia Ecclesiae, & muneris Ecclesiastici dignitate oratio, pertexatur. Ergo quicquid hic dicitur, de manifestatione, & justi-ficatione, & aliis, ita debet accipi & exponi, ut non ad Dei essentiam describendam, sed ad doctrinae Christianae auctoritatem & commendationem pertineant. Sed demus, haec de incarnatio-ne, vel incarnato Deo esse accipienda, videamus, an stare haec interpretatio possit. Cū dicitur Deus esse in carne manifestatus, quaerimus, quid per Deum intelligant. Certe horum aliquid respondere debent, Deum, aut significare Trinitatem, seu Essentiam communem tribus Personis aut
units.tr: Enjedinus, pp. 368, 369: The Apostle's purpose does not bear, nor does necessity require, nor does the connection of words and sentences allow, that the incarnation of God be discussed here; rather, the discourse is to proceed as it was begun, concerning the excellence of the Church and the dignity of the ecclesiastical office. Therefore whatever is said here about manifestation, justification and the rest must be so understood and explained that it pertains not to describing the essence of God but to the authority and commendation of Christian doctrine. But grant that these things must be taken of the incarnation, or of God incarnate. Let us see whether this interpretation can stand. When it is said that God was manifested in the flesh, we ask what they mean by God. Surely one of these must answer: they mean either God, that is, the Trinity or the essence common to the three Persons, or

units.la: Resp. Non est hic ab Apostolo institu-ta disputatio de excellentia Eccle-siae, & muneris Ecclesiastici dignita-te, sed ubi de variis Ecclesiasticorum muniis egisset, & commendasset obiter Ecclesiam, pergit explicare myste-rium fidei, & praecipua quaedam ejus capita. Vel, fac de illis instituisse dis-putationem, non probat tamen Adver-sarius, vel propositum Apostoli non ferre, vel verborum & sententiarum connexionem, ut commemoret mysterium incarnationis Christi: praesertim quum hoc etiam ad doctrinae Christianae auctoritatem & commendationem pertineat, ad quam describendam Apostolum transfire, Patrem, aut Christum totum, ut alteram Christi naturam, Deitatem nempe, seu λόγον illum. Si primum dicatur, sequetur totam Trinitatem & Deitatem incarnatam. Si secundū, similiter sequitur Patrem esse incarnatum, justificatum, visum, &c. Totus Christus ea voce intelligi non potest, eo quod non totus Christus, sed pars ejus tantum, natura nimirum divina, dicitur carnem assumsisse, & homo factus esse: alias dicendum esset, etiam humanitatem, seu humanam naturam, esse incarnatam. Praeterea hic diserte opponitur Deus carni. Ergo si caro humanam significat naturam, Deus non poterit nisi divinam significare naturam. Iam vero si per vocem Deus, intelligatur aeternus: sequitur illum esse concretum, visum, justificatum, assumtum in coelum. Quae λόγῳ aeterno, omnipotenti, infinito, non competunt, quia cum sit invisibilis Spiritus, & omnia complens, nec cerni, nec de loco in locum transferri potest. Deinde, unde probabunt, manifestari in carne, idem esse quod incarnari? Nisi eadem ratione dicant, vitam Jesu quoque esse incarnatam, vel incorporatam, eo quod 2 Cor. 4. v. 10. dicitur, illa manifestari in carne seu corpore piorum. Paulus manifestus est in Corinthiis 2 Cor. 11. v. 6. Propterea Paulus, unitus est & quasi incorporatus Corinthiis? Deus ipse, quam saepe, & quam in multis rebus se inde ab initio manifestavit? Ergone illis unitus hypostatice? Christus manifestavit gloriam suam in conversione aquae in vinum. An ideo vel Christus, vel gloria ipsius, incorporata est vino, aut, ut ita loquar, inaquata vel invinata est? Apparet igitur, quam vana sit haec interpretatio. Sed tamen, etiamsi haec lectio retineatur, poterit recte hic locus exponi, ita ut nec incarnationem Christi significet, & nihil absurdi habeat. Nam per vocem Deus, si Pater intelligatur, etsi secundum adversariorum sententiam, stare non poterit, quia sequeretur Patrem esse incarnatum; tamen, si vere & in genuina sua significatione vox manifestandi transfire, ait. Vel denique quare connexio non finit, ut de Christo Deo ea aeque intelligamus, ac de Patre & manifestatione ejus in Christo,& rebus Christi, prout Adversarii expount? Non ergo ullius hoc argumentum. II. Ita argumentatur, vel per Deum intelligi Dei essentiam communem tribus personis, aut Patrem, aut Christum totum, aut alteram ejus partem, seu Deitatem. Respondeo, intelligi Dei essentiam, non prout in tribus est personis, vel Trinitatem, sed prout est in Filio, sive Personam in Trinitate alteram, quae Christi non est proprie dicta pars aliqua, quum in compositionem venire nequeat. III. Quodque addit, Deum λόγον conspici non potuisse, haud magis nostram, quam ipsorum expositionem evertit. Nam nec Deus Pater potest conspici, & hunc tamen intelligunt, manifestatum in carne fuisse. IV. Christum autem hic denotari per Deum, apparet ex singulis hujus versus membris; tum re ipsa tota. Quodnam enim in Euangelio mysterium adeo, quam Christi? Cui & nomen, & res mysterii propius quadrat, quam Christo, & mysterium, in quod ipsi Angeli concupiverunt introspicere? 1 Pet. 1. 12. & Col. 1. 26. mysterium a seculis & generationibus, nunc vero manifestatum ejus sanctis: quibus Deus voluit notum facere quae sint divitiae gloriosi istius mysterii inter gentes, ὃς ἐστιν[?] Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν. Christus ergo est istud mysterium. Subjungit, quem nos annunciamus. & in loco hoc ad Tim. praedicantur inter gentes. Annon Christus ipse substantia & argumentum est praedicationis Evangelicae, & quem ubique annunciarunt? dein fidei ac religionis? ut de nullo prius queat intelligi, creditus in mundo, quam de Christo. & sic, quod justificatus, de Christo commodius, quam de Patre, intelligas. denique & primum illud, manifestatus in carne. Non quod Pater non etiam fuerit manifestatus in Filio, sed in carne proximius filius, quum Pater,
units.tr: Reply: The Apostle's discussion here is not about the excellence of the Church or the dignity of the ecclesiastical office. Having treated the various offices of the ministers and touched in passing on the Church's commendation, he goes on to explain the mystery of the faith and certain of its chief articles. Or grant that he had begun a discussion of those things: the Adversary still does not prove that the purpose of the Apostle does not bear, or that the connection of words and sentences does not allow, that he should recall the mystery of the incarnation of Christ, especially since this too pertains to the authority and commendation of Christian doctrine, which the Apostle goes on to describe. Either the Father, or the whole Christ, or the other nature of Christ, namely his Deity, or that Word. If the first is said, it will follow that the whole Trinity and Deity was incarnate. If the second, it similarly follows that the Father was incarnate, justified, seen, and so on. The whole Christ cannot be understood by the word, because it is not the whole Christ but only a part of him, namely the divine nature, that is said to have assumed flesh and to have been made man; otherwise it would have to be said that the humanity, or human nature, was also incarnate. Moreover, here God is expressly set over against the flesh. Therefore if flesh signifies the human nature, God can signify only the divine nature. Now if by the word God we understand the eternal one, it follows that he was seen, justified, and taken up into heaven, which do not befit the eternal, almighty, infinite Word, since, being an invisible Spirit who fills all things, he can be neither seen nor transferred from place to place. Next, from what will they prove that to be manifested in the flesh is the same as to be incarnate? Unless by the same reasoning they say that the life of Jesus was also incarnated or embodied, since at 2 Cor. 4:10 it is said that this life is manifested in the flesh, that is, the body, of the godly. Paul was manifest among the Corinthians (2 Cor. 11:6). Is Paul therefore united with the Corinthians and as it were embodied in them? How often, and in how many things, has God himself manifested himself from the beginning? Is he therefore hypostatically united with them? Christ manifested his glory in the changing of water into wine. Is therefore either Christ or his glory embodied in the wine, or, to put it so, watered down or winified? It is clear, then, how vain this interpretation is. But even if this reading is retained, the passage can be rightly explained so that it does not signify the incarnation of Christ and has nothing absurd in it. For if by the word God the Father is understood, even though this cannot stand according to the opinion of the adversaries, since it would follow that the Father was incarnate; nevertheless, if the word manifest is taken truly and in its proper signification, Paul passes over ... Finally, why does the connection not allow us to understand, of Christ as God, these things just as we understand them of the Father and of his manifestation in Christ and in Christ's affairs, as the Adversaries expound them? So this argument is worth nothing. II. He argues thus: either by God is meant the common essence of God belonging to the three persons, or the Father, or the whole Christ, or his other part, namely the Deity. I answer: the essence of God is meant, not as it is in the three persons, or the Trinity, but as it is in the Son, or as the other Person in the Trinity, who is not properly any part of Christ, since he cannot enter into composition. III. And what he adds, that God the Word could not be seen, overturns our exposition no more than theirs. For neither can God the Father be seen, and yet they understand that he was manifested in the flesh. IV. That Christ is here denoted by God appears from each member of this verse, and indeed from the whole matter itself. For what mystery in the Gospel is so great as that of Christ? To whom does both the name and the matter of the mystery fit more closely than to Christ, and which mystery did the very angels long to look into? (1 Pet. 1:12; Col. 1:26) The mystery hidden from ages and generations, but now manifested to his saints, to whom God willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you [ὃς ἐστιν Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν]. Christ therefore is that mystery. He adds: whom we proclaim, and in this place of Timothy are preached among the Gentiles. Is not Christ himself the substance and the subject of the Gospel preaching, and the one whom they everywhere proclaimed? And then of faith and religion? So that the phrase believed in the world could be understood of no one before Christ, and so you understand justified more fittingly of Christ than of the Father. Finally, the first of these, manifested in the flesh. Not that the Father was not also manifested in the Son, but more nearly the Son is manifested in the flesh, since the Father

units.la: {y} Ex singulis: Textus Col. 2. 2. Ibid.: Cap. 1. 27. accipiatur: vera & approbanda nascetur huius loci expositio. Nam certum est Deum Patrem apparuisse, sese manifestasse, conspicuum praebuisse, patefecisse mundo, in carne, hoc est vili & abjectae conditionis ac fortis hominibus, quales fuerunt Christus & Apostoli. Nam vocabulum carnis in hac significatione saepissime accipi, notissimum est, & nos supra, in illa Iohannis verba: Verbum caro factum est, fusius demonstravimus. factum? quod quid aliud est, quam Verbum
units.tr: {y} On the individual points: take the texts of Col. 2:2 and Col. 1:27. The true and approved exposition of this passage will then emerge. For it is certain that God the Father appeared, showed himself, made himself conspicuous, and revealed himself to the world in the flesh, that is, among men of low and abject condition, such as Christ and the Apostles were. For it is well known that the word flesh is very often taken in this sense, and we have shown more fully above, on those words of John, "The Word was made flesh." Made? What else is that than the Word

units.la: Pater, ac propterea Deus manifestatus de eo intelligendum. Quod non ob aliud negant Adversarii, quam quia Deus appellatur, quo se fortiter admodum constringi sentiunt. Nam quin praedicata hoc loco recensita, omnia propriissime & commodissime Christo debeantur, nemo potest dubitare. Et hoc, Deus manifestatus in carne, quo alio exponetur, quam simili loco Ioannis, cap. 14. & verbum caro fa- in carne manifestatum? & Deus erat hoc
units.tr: the Father, and therefore God manifested must be understood of him. The Adversaries deny this for no other reason than that God is named, and they feel themselves strongly constrained by that. For that all the predicates recounted in this place belong to Christ most properly and most suitably, no one can doubt. And this, God manifested in the flesh, how else is it to be explained than by a similar passage of John, ch. 1, "The Word was made flesh"? And "the Word was God" [ver. 1], manifested in the flesh?

units.la: verbum, verf. 1. Quod quia per nativitatem in carne factum, quid aliud est, quam σαρκωσις incarnatio, vel inhumanatio? v. Non autem simplex vox manifestari, sed manifestari in carne, & caro fieri, isto, quo id de Christo Scriptura tradit modo, incarnari denotant. Ut ad rem hic neutiquam faciat, vel quod 2Cor.xi.6. Apost.semet, ait, manifestari in Corinthiis: quae planam & indubiam secum adferunt expositionem, de manifestatione virtutis, & non simpliciter, sed & apud quos vel in quibus factam indicant manifestationem: at in textu nostro est, Deum ipsum, se manifestare, vel manifestari, simpliciter, in carne: carne ergo sua, vid. assumta, manifestatus fuit Deus. Quid vero huc facit, quod alias Deus, vel Christus gloriam & potentiam suam in operibus demonstrat? uti in conversione aquae in vinum, &c. non enim nos ex quacumque Dei manifestatione argumentamur, ad incarnationem: vel an illud factus Christus dici potest, quemadmodum verbum caro factum? vi. Qua ratione mirificam suam expositionem confirmabit Adversarius, ut Deus manifestatus in carne significet, Deus Pater se manifestarit in vili carne vel conditione hominum, quales fuerint Christus & Apostoli? ad quod non necesse est, eum ostendere vel vocem carnis quandoque designare abjectam & fragilem hominum conditionem, vel Deum se operibus patefacere; praeterea, Christum & Apostolos, quadam: ratione valde abjectos fuisse ac viles; sed, Deum carne manifestari, illam ferre expositionem; & applicationem, vel restrictionem ad Christum atque Apostolos. vii. Ejusdem commatis est expositio, quam dat ultimi in loco nostro membri, ἀνεληφθη ἐν δόξῃ id est, gloriose a gentibus acceptus est, seu admissus.
units.tr: [ver. 1]. And since this was done in the flesh through birth, what else is it but incarnation [σάρκωσις], or becoming human? But the simple word manifest, not in the flesh but made flesh, in the way in which Scripture records this of Christ, signifies to be incarnate. Nor does it bear on the matter at all that Paul says of himself that he was manifest among the Corinthians (2 Cor. 11:6); that passage brings a plain and certain explanation, concerning the manifestation of power, and it indicates not simply the manifestation but also among or in whom it was made. But in our text it is God himself who manifests himself, or is manifested, simply, in the flesh: God was therefore manifested in his own flesh, that is, the flesh he assumed. What, moreover, does it have to do with this that elsewhere God or Christ demonstrates his glory and power in works, as in the changing of water into wine, and so on? For we do not argue from any manifestation of God whatever to the incarnation, nor whether Christ could be said to have been made, as the Word was made flesh. The Adversary will confirm his wonderful exposition by what reasoning, that God manifested in the flesh means that God the Father manifested himself in the lowly flesh or condition of men, such as Christ and the Apostles were? For it is not necessary for him to show that the word flesh sometimes designates the abject and frail condition of men, or that God reveals himself by works; moreover, that Christ and the Apostles were in a certain sense very abject and base. Rather, to be manifest in the flesh bears that exposition, and the application, or restriction, to Christ and the Apostles. vii. The exposition he gives of the last member of the same clause in our passage is of the same kind: [ἀνεληφθη ἐν δόξῃ], that is, he was gloriously received, or admitted, by the Gentiles.

units.la: Sciendum itaque est ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι non semper significare, in altum sublevari, sursum assumi, sed simpliciter, recipi, assumi, admitti, accipi: ut Act. 20. v. 13. & 14. bis dicitur Paulus ἀναλη-φθῆναι, id est, assumi, adjungi, seu ut Beza vertit, recipi. Et capite 13. v. 31. idem Beza vertit eandem vocem, per verbum accipiendi. Sic ad Eph. 6 ἀναλαμ-βάνετε τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, id est: Assumite, (vel accipite) armaturam
units.tr: It should be noted, then, that ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι [analambanesthai] does not always mean to be lifted up on high or taken up aloft, but simply to be received, taken up, admitted, or accepted. Thus in Acts 20.13 and 14 Paul is twice said to be ἀναληφθῆναι [analēphthēnai], that is, taken up, joined on, or, as Beza translates it, received. And in chapter 13.31 Beza renders the same word by the verb "to accept." So in Ephesians 6 ἀναλαμβάνετε τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ [analambanete tēn panoplian tou Theou] means: take up (or accept) the armour of God.

units.la: Resp. 1: Saltem ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι significare in altum sublevari & assumi, negare nequit: uti nec quod ἀνελήφθη in sermone de Christo, & simpliciter positum, semper significet ejus ἀναλήψιν in cælos: quo nos etiam hoc in loco trahit plana acceptio ejus & familiaris quod mox additur, ἐν δόξῃ. II. Neque inlocis ab Adversario adductis, Act. xx. 13. & cap. xxiix.31. vel Eph.vi.16. alium habet cmnem Dei. Ergo hic quoque citra ullam scripturae iniuriam, rectè sic, ista vox verti potest, hoc sensu: [?]A Gentibus acceptum, receptum, admissum esse Deum. Si quis objiciat, hac interpretatione admissa, Paulo ταυτολογίαν inuri, nam antea quoque affirmavit, creditum esse Deum in mundo: Respondeo, aliud esse credere, & aliud assumere, admittere Deum: illud praecedit, hoc sequitur. Multi credebant Iesum, esse Messiam, ut Nicodemus & alii, de quibus Iohannes cap. 12. v. 41. sed non recipiebant, propter metum, ne ejicerentur è synagoga. Deinde, antea dixit Deum esse creditum, hic vero non simpliciter creditum, sed gloriose admissum; proinde, non bis dixit idem. Nam illud, in gloria, idem valet quod gloriose, sicut paullo ante quoque in illa particula, in spiritu, annotabamus. Et hoc confirmatur, ex epistola ad Colossenses 3. v. 4. tunc & vos apparebitis cum ipso, in gloria, id est, gloriose, vel ut Beza vertit, gloriosi. Haec autem gloria intelligi potest, vel de gentibus, vel de Deo. Nam & gentes per hanc doctrinam, atque cognitionem Dei, gloriosae sunt redditae, & Deus glorificatus est, celebriorque evasit.
units.tr: Response 1: At least the opponent cannot deny that ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι means to be lifted up on high and taken up. Nor can he deny that ἀνελήφθη [anelēphthē], used absolutely in a statement about Christ, does not always mean his ascension into heaven. Here, too, the plain and familiar sense of the word, and the phrase that immediately follows, ἐν δόξῃ [en doxē], draw us in that direction. II. Nor do the passages the opponent cites, Acts 20.13, chapter 13.31, or Eph. 6.16, have any other meaning at all. So here too, without any violence to Scripture, the word can rightly be rendered in this sense: that God was received, accepted, and admitted by the Gentiles. If someone objects that on this interpretation Paul is guilty of tautology, since he had already said that God was believed in the world, I answer: to believe is one thing, and to take up or admit God is another; the first comes before, the second follows. Many believed that Jesus was the Messiah, as Nicodemus and others did, of whom John speaks in chapter 12.41, but they did not receive him, for fear of being cast out of the synagogue. Again, he had said earlier that God was believed, but here he says not merely that he was believed but that he was gloriously admitted. So he has not said the same thing twice. For the phrase "in glory" means the same as "gloriously," just as I noted a little earlier with the phrase "in spirit." This is confirmed by Colossians 3.4: "then you also shall appear with him in glory," that is, gloriously, or as Beza translates it, "glorious." This glory may be understood either of the Gentiles or of God. For through this teaching and the knowledge of God the Gentiles were made glorious, and God was glorified and made more renowned.

units.la: habet sensum, quam assumere sursum, ἀνα assumere ad, non in, non quovis modo accipere vel admittere, non recipere, quo sensu significat aliquid animo accipere, & Adversarius id hic vult exponi pro acceptione vel fide Euangelii, aut Dei nec tamen a consueta & propria verborum significatione est recedendum, inquit alibi Socinus. III. Cum vero praecessisset in textu, quod fuerit creditus in mundo, atque videretur tautologia si assumtus exponatur pro admissus, vel acceptus animo & fide, haec ita distinguunt, ut differentiam constituant inter credere & admittere, quod sunt qui credunt in Iesum, neque tamen eum recipiunt. Valde perperam. Imo impossibile est, credere aliquid, credere Iesum, nisi eum admittas, accipias animo & fide: & quodnam aliud admittere hic potest intelligi? Multi quidem possunt credere Christum Messiam, qui tamen eum non aeque audeant profiteri; sed ut non admittant vel recipiant Iesum, qui in eum credunt, idne cogitari quidem potest. At ἀναλαμ-
units.tr: …has the sense, as to take up on high, ἀνά [ana] meaning "to," not "in," and not in any chance manner to receive or admit, not to accept; in which sense it means to take something into the mind. The opponent wants this to be explained here as the reception or faith of the gospel, or of God. But we must not depart from the usual and proper meaning of words, as Socinus says elsewhere. III. Since the text had already said that he was believed in the world, and it would seem tautological if "taken up" were explained as "admitted" or "received in mind and faith," the opponents distinguish the two so as to set up a difference between believing and admitting, saying that there are some who believe in Jesus and yet do not receive him. This is very wrong. Indeed it is impossible to believe something, to believe in Jesus, without admitting him, accepting him in mind and faith. And what other sense of admitting could be understood here? Many indeed may believe that Christ is the Messiah and yet not dare to profess him to the same extent; but that those who believe in Jesus do not admit or receive him, can that even be thought? But analam-

units.la: βανέσθαι[?] non significat profiteri. Citat Adversarius Joann. xii. 42[?]. ubi dicuntur multi credidisse in Christum: sed an, non recepisse eum? sed propter Pharisaeos eum non profitebantur, dicitur, non, quod non receperint. Proba, non fateri, idem esse, quod non recipere. Qui non recipiunt, eum non confitentur, sed non sequitur, quod qui prae metu non confitentur, prorsus non recipiant. iv. Ἐν δόξῃ eadem emphasi atque relatione ponitur, qua in praecedentibus ἐν ἔθνεσι[?], ἐν σαρκί. Ut terminum, vel statum notet assumtionis, vid. in gloriam: vel fit, gloriose assumtus. Sed gloriose creditus, aut admissus, peregrinum sonat, sive de Gentibus exponatur, vel de Dei in gentibus, per Euangelii praedicationem & fidem, glorificatione. De Christo autem, & ejus in gloriam assumtione, tum caeteraque antecedunt, ut manifestatum fuisse in carne, &c. tum alii passim locum exponunt omnes. Syrus interpres: & certe magnum est hoc arcanum justitiae, quod manifestatus sit in carne, & justificatus in Spiritu, visusque Angelis, & praedicatus inter Gentes, & creditus in mundo, denique assumptus in gloria. Arabs: haec dogmata memora, nempe magnitudinem mysterii bonae pietatis: quod Deus apparuit in carne, &c. adscendit cum gloria. Versio Aethiopica, quia magnum est, quod profitentur, mysterium veritatis, quod apparuit in carne humana, &c. & adscendit in gloria.
units.tr: banesthai [ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι] does not mean to profess. The opponent cites John 12.42, where many are said to have believed in Christ. But does that mean they had not received him? They did not profess him because of the Pharisees; it is not said that they did not receive him. Prove that not confessing and not receiving are the same thing. Those who do not receive him do not confess him, but it does not follow that those who through fear do not confess him do not receive him at all. IV. ἐν δόξῃ [en doxē] is placed with the same emphasis and relation as the preceding ἐν ἔθνεσι [en ethnesi] and ἐν σαρκί [en sarki]. It either denotes the goal or state of the assumption, see "into glory," or it becomes "gloriously assumed." But "gloriously believed" or "gloriously admitted" sounds strange, whether it is explained of the Gentiles, or of God in the Gentiles, through the preaching of the gospel and faith, as a glorification. But concerning Christ and his assumption into glory, both the things that precede, such as that he was manifested in the flesh, and the rest, and the other translators explain the whole passage in the same way. The Syriac translator: And surely great is this mystery of righteousness, that he was manifested in the flesh, and justified in the Spirit, and seen by angels, and preached among the Gentiles, and believed in the world, and finally taken up in glory. The Arabic: Recall these doctrines, namely the greatness of the mystery of good piety: that God appeared in the flesh, etc., ascended with glory. The Ethiopic version: Because great is the mystery of truth which they profess, that appeared in human flesh, etc., and ascended in glory.

units.la: Schlichtingius vero, contra Meisnerum, de Trinitate, pag. 479. ad istum respondens locum, evidenter satis ac turpiter id committit, quod perperam alias nobis impingunt Adversarii, vid. petitionem principii. Nequaquam concedimus, inquit, Dei nomine Christum significari, sed unum illum Deum, qui Pater est, designari contendimus. Negamus enim, Deum manifestari in carne, significare, Deum carne seu humana natura assumta conspicuum fieri. Nam 1. absoluta vox Dei subjecti loco posita, addito insuper articulo, nunquam pro Filio posita esse demonstrabitur. 2. Manifestatio Dei sub Novo Foedere non solet significare personae divinae exhibitionem, sed tantum eorum, quae ad cognitionem Dei, ejusque voluntatis spectant, revelationem. 3. Spiritus mentio in sequenti membro offendit, carnem hic opponi spiritui: quemadmodum & alibi semper. At spiritus non designat naturam divinam, hoc praesertim in loco, (quo enim sensu diceretur, Deum esse justificatum in divina natura?) sed tantum divinam virtutem & efficaciam. quocirca nec caro naturam humanam simpliciter designabit. 4. Quod hic magnum & multiplex pietatis (id est, religionis Christianae,) mysterium pandat Apostolus. At, si hic de Dei incarnatione loqueretur, quale quaesito in eo esset mysterium, quod Deus incarnatus ab Angelis fuerit visus? quasi, vel postquam incarnatus esset, cum non videre potuerint, vel, antequam incarnaretur, non viderint. quale item & illud, quod sursum, id est, in coelos assumtus fuerit? 5. Denique, quo sensu ista dicerentur aut cohaerent, Deus incarnatus est, & justificatus est in spiritu? Quid est, petere principium, si hoc non est? Id enim quaeritur, an vox Dei subjecti loco nunquam ponatur pro Filio. Quod nos etiam ex hoc loco demonstrare confidimus. Etiam quaeritur, an manifestatio Dei sub Novo foedere non significet divinae personae exhibitionem. An Spiritus carni oppositus, in sermone nempe de Christo, non divinam denotet naturam. Jam vero nullum adeo mysterium videtur Adversariis Christi incarnatio? quam vel ideo, quia mysterium est, rejiciunt. Certe Angelis, & hominibus non potuit non maximi mysterii loco esse, quod Deus in carne se exhibuit contemplandum, & contrectandum. Ioann. 1. 14. & 1 Joann. 1. 1. Quem ut Deum incarnatum videre, nisi ab incarnatione, non potuerunt. Deinde & hoc adeo exiguum ipsis, Christum gloriose in coelos assumtum fuisse? Denique satis bene cohaerent, Deum incarnatum, & justificatum esse spiritu, id est, utcumque in carne fuerit humiliatus, sua tamen Deitate, & Deitatis operibus se probasse Deum, & non hominem tantum seu carnem. Tandem addit: Susceptus in gloria, quod non solum creditum fit Deo, sed etiam quod summa sua cum gloria fit receptus: voces enim in gloria idem valent, quod eum gloria, id est, gloriose, consuetudo Hebraismi: non vero, ut vos explicatis, in gloriam, nullo Scripturae exemplo. Fac me totum concedere, & ἐν δόξῃ exponere cum gloria, sive gloriose Christum receptum fuisse. Certe gloriose fuit receptus in caelum, cum gloria in gloriam. Quare utrumque potest verti & intelligi. Ἐν pro εἰς consuetum apud Graecos, & vicissim εἰς pro ἐν: uti quoque apud Hebraeos particulae ב & ל. Luc. vii. 13. καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ὁ λόγος οὗτος ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ, καὶ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ περιχώρῳ, id est εἰς, in Iudaeam universam, & regionem totam circumjacentem. πιστεύειν dicimur in Evangelio, & in Euangelium, in Christo, & in Christum, ἐν & εἰς. De Christo, quod venerit ἐν σαρκί, & εἰς σάρκα. 1 Joann. iv. 2. 9. Matth. xvi. 38. donec viderint Filium hominis venientem ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ. pro εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν. Sic Graeci dicunt, εἶναι ἐν οἴκῳ, pro εἰς οἶκον. Homerus, κατῆντησεν ἐν Ἄῤῥῳ dixit, pro ὡς Λήμνου[?], decidi in lemnum.
units.tr: Schlichting, however, answering this passage against Meisner in his work On the Trinity, p. 479, does so plainly and shamefully, committing the very fault our opponents wrongly charge us with elsewhere, namely begging the question. We by no means concede, he says, that Christ is signified by the name of God, but we contend that the one God who is the Father is designated. For we deny that to manifest God in the flesh signifies that God becomes visible by the assumption of the flesh or human nature. For, first, it will be shown that the absolute word "God," placed as the subject, with the article added, is never used for the Son. (2) The manifestation of God under the New Covenant does not usually signify the exhibition of a divine person, but only the revelation of those things which concern the knowledge of God and his will. (3) The mention of Spirit in the following clause is out of place, since flesh is here opposed to spirit, as it always is elsewhere. But spirit does not designate the divine nature, especially in this place (for in what sense would it be said that God was justified in the divine nature?), but only the divine power and efficacy. Therefore neither will flesh simply designate the human nature. (4) The Apostle here sets forth the great and manifold mystery of piety (that is, of the Christian religion). But if he were speaking here of the incarnation of God, what mystery would there be in the fact that God incarnate was seen by angels? As if they could not see him after he was incarnate, or did not see him before he was incarnate. Likewise what about the fact that he was taken up on high, that is, into heaven? (5) Finally, in what sense would these things be said, or cohere: God was incarnate, and was justified in the Spirit? What is begging the question, if this is not? For what is being asked is whether the word "God" as subject is never used for the Son. We are confident that we can demonstrate from this passage that it is. It is also asked whether the manifestation of God under the New Covenant does not signify the exhibition of a divine person. And whether Spirit, opposed to flesh, in a statement about Christ, does not denote the divine nature. Yet does the incarnation of Christ seem to our opponents to be so small a mystery? They reject it for no other reason than that it is a mystery. Surely it could not but be to angels and men a matter of the greatest mystery that God showed himself in the flesh to be seen and handled, John 1.14 and 1 John 1.1, which they could not see as God incarnate except from the incarnation. Then is it also so trivial to them that Christ was taken up gloriously into heaven? Finally, that God incarnate was justified in the Spirit fits together quite well: that is, however humbled in the flesh, he nevertheless proved himself God by his Deity and the works of Deity, and not merely a man or flesh. Finally he adds: Received in glory: not only is it believed by God, but it is received by him with his great glory. For the words "in glory" mean the same as "with glory," that is, gloriously, a Hebraism by custom; not as you explain it, "into glory," with no example in Scripture. Grant that I concede everything and explain ἐν δόξῃ as "with glory," or that Christ was gloriously received. Certainly he was gloriously received into heaven, with glory into glory. So both can be translated and understood. ἐν [en] is used for εἰς [eis] as is customary among the Greeks, and conversely εἰς for ἐν, as also the Hebrew particles ב [beth] and ל [lamed] are interchanged. Luke 7.13: καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ὁ λόγος οὗτος ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ, καὶ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ περιχώρῳ [kai exēlthen ho logos houtos en holē tē Ioudaia, kai en pasē tē perichōrō], that is, "went out into all Judaea and the whole surrounding region." In the Gospel we are said to believe in and into the Gospel, in Christ and into Christ, ἐν and εἰς. Concerning Christ, that he came ἐν σαρκί [en sarki] and εἰς σάρκα [eis sarka], 1 John 4.2, 9; Matthew 16.28: "until they see the Son of man coming ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ [en tē basileia autou]," for εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν [eis tēn basileian]. So the Greeks say εἶναι ἐν οἴκῳ [einai en oikō] for εἰς οἶκον [eis oikon]. Homer wrote κατῆντησεν ἐν Ἄῤῥῳ [katēntēsen en Arrhō] for ὡς Λήμνου [hōs Lēmnou], "he fell into Lemnos."

units.la: Ad Heb 1. 8. excipit Enjedinus, verba uti ex Psalmo xlv. desumta, ita Salomoni proprie, Christo non nisi mystice ac propter similitudinem applicanda esse, cuicumq; demum, ei non Deo, sed homini. Nam qui unctus est, qui Deum, hoc est, se superiorem & majorem, qui consortes & socios regni habet, non Deus æternus, cui ista repugnant, sed homo, vel certe creatura fit, necesse est. Resp. Negatur consequentia, quod qui etiam, & secundum aliquam sui rationem unctus elt, & habet Deum, &c. ille non potest simul esse Deus: id est, qui homo, non etiam potest esse Deum, seu θεάνθρωπον[?]. Deinde, utcunque in Psalmo nonnulla sint, quæ de Salomone etiam intelligantur, illa certe verba, quæ Apostolus adducit, nec Salomoni, nec ulli conveniunt, præter Christum. Quod Apostolus etiam significat, qui ubi verf. 7. notasset illa dicta Angelis, qui facit Angelos, &c. adducturus nunc ista de Christo dicta Psalm. xlv. præmittit, dixit, sed soli filio. Uti quod verf. 9. propterea unxit te. verf. 10. tu ab initio Domine fundasti terram. Quare & Syrus de filio dictum exponit. Similiter & Æthiops. An vero non majori jure dicimus Schlichtingio, in Commentario ad Heb. sic explicanti. Vocatur Salomon Deus Elohim, propter sublimem illam potestatem & regiam dignitatem, quam in populo divino in terris habuit, ut locum vel argumentum ullum proferat, quo ostendat, homini alicui & subjecti loco, simpliciter, cum articulo etiam, nomen Dei tribui, quam ut contra Deitatem Christi excipiat, nisi ei vox Dei, tali modo, tribuatur, se non recipere? quo dum nuncupari Christum hoc docemus textu, adeo nec ita tamen denotari Deum vult, ut potius ad alium, præter Christum, ista trahat, & quovis alio modo alteri applicet. Nempe Christus, inquit, longe majori jure dicitur Deus, quam Salomon. Egregie certe vindicata Christi Deitas.
units.tr: Ad Heb 1. 8. Enjedinus makes this exception: the words, taken from Psalm 45, are to be applied properly to Solomon, and to Christ only mystically and by way of resemblance; they apply to someone who is not God but a man. For he who is anointed, who has God (that is, one who is superior and greater than himself), who has partners and associates in his kingdom, must necessarily be not the eternal God, to whom these things are repugnant, but a man, or at least a creature. Reply: the consequence is denied. The one who is anointed in some respect, and who has God, and so on, cannot at the same time be God; that is, one who is a man cannot also be God or the God-man [θεάνθρωπον]. Further, although some things in the Psalm may also be understood of Solomon, the words which the Apostle quotes apply neither to Solomon nor to anyone but Christ. The Apostle himself indicates this. In verse 7 he had noted that those words were said of the angels, who makes his angels, and so on; now, about to quote what is said of Christ in Psalm 45, he prefaces it with the words "but to the Son". So also in verse 9, therefore he has anointed you, and in verse 10, you, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning. For this reason the Syriac also explains these words as spoken of the Son, and likewise the Ethiopic. Indeed, with better right do we say to Schlichting, who explains it thus in his commentary on Hebrews: Solomon is called God, Elohim, on account of that exalted power and royal dignity which he held among the divine people on earth, that he cannot produce any place or argument to show that the name of God is simply given, even with the article, to some man in a subordinate position, except to make an exception against the Deity of Christ; unless he says he does not accept that the word God is given to Christ in such a manner. By teaching that Christ is named God in this text, we do not want him to be so designated as God that he refers these words to someone other than Christ and applies them to another in any other way. Indeed, he says, Christ is called God with far greater right than Solomon. Certainly a splendid vindication of the Deity of Christ!

units.la: At Tit. 11. 13. ubi Christus dicitur magnus Deus, expectantes beatam spem, & manifestationem gloriæ magni Dei & salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi, τ[?] μεγάλα θεοῦ[?] ἡ σω-τῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ[?], ubi & subjective, & cum articulo appellatur Christus Deus, excipit Enjedinus duo, nec si magnus Deus Christus dicatur, ideo sequi esse verum, seu æternum Deum; nec ita eum hic appellari, sed Patrem.
units.tr: But in Titus 2:13, where Christ is called the great God, looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ [τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ], where Christ is called God both by the construction and with the article, Enjedinus takes two exceptions: that even if Christ is called the great God, it does not follow that he is the true or eternal God; and that here he is not called that, but the Father is.

units.la: Volunt adversarii, in his verbis, Iesum Christum, dici magnum Deum: unde consequatur, illum æternum, & æqualem, ac eundem esse cum Patre, Deum. At etiamsi Antecedens concedetur, consequens tamen jure negari posset. Nam qui Deus est, ut inquit Erasmus, eo ipso, magnum etiam esse eum oportet: nihil tamen vetat alterum esse majorem, qui sic magnus fit, ut nihil illo fit majus. Et sane, si quis contendat, Magni Dei epitheton hic pertinere ad Christum, consideret simul illud, de eo statim affirmari, ipsum esse mortuum pro peccatis nostris. Quod an Deo magno, id est summo competat: prudens rerum æstimator perpendat. Neque hic ad illam communicationem idiomatum confugere possunt. Nam fateri coguntur, Christum dici magnum
units.tr: Our opponents want it that in these words, Jesus Christ, he is called the great God, from which it follows that he is eternal, equal to the Father, and the same God as the Father. But even if the antecedent is conceded, the consequent can nevertheless rightly be denied. For he who is God, as Erasmus says, must for that very reason also be great; yet nothing prevents there being another who is greater, one who is so great that nothing is greater than he. And indeed, if anyone contends that the epithet of the great God applies here to Christ, let him consider at the same time that it is immediately affirmed of him that he died for our sins. Whether this befits the great God, that is, the supreme God, let the prudent judge of things weigh. Nor can they here take refuge in that communication of idioms. For they are forced to admit that Christ is called great

units.la: Resp. 1. Ergo Deus erit alius major, alius minor, & quoque alius maximus: quæ Theologia sit Gentilium, certe non est Christianorum. Habuerunt illi varia Deorum genera ac classes; Christianorum autem Deus, nisi unus, non est Deus. Ostendat nobis in Scriptura Deum vel majorem, vel minorem, simpliciter talem, vel comparativum, vel denique superlativum: si non, tali hactenus ergo inter Christianos prorsus abstineat sermone, ac doctrina, tam Gentilismo propriâ, quam à Christianismo aliena & abhorrens.
units.tr: Reply 1. Then God will be one who is greater, another who is less, and another who is greatest. That may be the theology of the Gentiles, but it is certainly not the theology of Christians. Those people had various kinds and classes of gods; but the God of Christians, unless he is one, is not God. Let them show us in Scripture a God who is greater or less, simply so, or in the comparative, or finally in the superlative. If they cannot, then let them at least refrain from such language and doctrine among Christians, a doctrine both peculiar to Gentilism and alien to and abhorrent from Christianity.

units.la: 11. Quod mox additur in loco, qui tradidit seipsum, certe probat de Christo antecedentia, uti & hoc ipsum, intelligenda esse, nec iis repugnare Deum, respectu divinæ naturæ. At statim subjicitur: qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, &c. Ubi Relativum illud qui, refert illum, qui proxime nominatus erat, nempe Iesum Christum, magnum scilicet Deum. Ergo ille magnus Deus, dicitur se dedisse in mortem: At magnus Deus non humanam naturam, quæ mori potuit, sed divinam, quæ immortalis est, respicit & denotat. Ergo eatenus dicitur esse mortuus, quatenus erat magnus Deus. Quare patet, Deo magno non repugnare, quin moriatur. At ille qui moritur, pro summo Deo haberi non debet. Ergo hic magnus Deus, summum, æternum, & immortalem Deum non significat, sed aliquem in summam dignitatem a vero Deo evectum, & cæteris Diis mortalibus antelatum. Sed veniamus ad antecedens, nam illud quoque falsum est. Duorum enim in hoc loco fit mentio, Magni Dei, qui est Pater, & Salvatoris, qui est Iesus Christus. Idque Conjunctio, &, interposita, satis manifeste demonstrat. Ad Philip. I. v. 1. legimus: Paulus & Timotheus, servi Iesu Christi. Num Pauli nomen, hic Timotheo attribuitur, & non potius duæ distinctæ res nominantur. pugnare, quum Christus fit θεάνθρω-πος[?] & alterum ei, qua homo; alterum competat, qua est Deus. In quo nullam facimus idiomatum communicationem, tantummodo propria naturarum singulis applicamus. III. Certe qui est magnus Deus, seipsum tradidit pro nobis in mortem; sed non qua talis est: at mortem subiit, qua est homo. Uti homo, qui animæ est immortalis, mortem substinet, at non qua talis. Christus, qui etiam homo, adoratur; non qua homo. IV. Et a veritate, & usu Scripturarum, ac religionis alienum est, ut qui in summam dignitatem a Deo evehitur, & cæteris Diis antefertur mortalibus, dicatur magnus Deus. Etenim hic contra Adversarios argumentari licet, quo pacto ipsi solent adversus nos; qui evehitur ad dignitatem illam a Deo, quomodo Deus, & Deus magnus erit? Neque est quod excipiant, dici illum Deum, at non esse: quum textus ajat, eum talem esse, nec dici tantum, & quidem cum articulo τῷ μεγάλῳ θεῷ[?].
units.tr: 11. What is added soon after in the place, who gave himself, certainly proves that the preceding words are to be understood of Christ, and also that this very thing is to be understood in the same way, and that it does not conflict with them: God, with respect to the divine nature. But immediately it is added: who gave himself for us, etc. Here the relative who refers to him who was named immediately before, namely Jesus Christ, the great God of course. Therefore that great God is said to have given himself to death. But the great God regards and denotes not the human nature, which could die, but the divine, which is immortal. Therefore he is said to have died only in so far as he was the great God. Hence it is plain that it is not repugnant to the great God that he should die. But he who dies ought not to be regarded as the supreme God. Therefore this great God does not signify the supreme, eternal and immortal God, but someone raised to the highest dignity by the true God and placed above the other mortal gods. But let us come to the antecedent, for that too is false. For mention is made of two in this place, of the great God, who is the Father, and of the Saviour, who is Jesus Christ. And the conjunction "and", placed between them, demonstrates this quite clearly. In Philippians 1:1 we read: Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ. Is not the name of Paul here attributed to Timothy, but rather are two distinct things named? [it is not repugnant] since Christ is the God-man [θεάνθρωπος], and one thing belongs to him as man, another as he is God. In this we make no communication of idioms; we merely apply the proper qualities of the two natures to each. III. Certainly he who is the great God gave himself for us to death; but not in so far as he is such, but he underwent death in so far as he is man.
