Just as a man, who is immortal in soul, endures death, yet not as such. Christ, who is also man, is adored, but not as man. IV. And it is foreign to the truth, to the usage of the Scriptures and to religion, that one who is raised by God to the highest dignity and placed before the other mortal gods should be called the great God. For here we may argue against our opponents in the way they are accustomed to argue against us: how will he who is raised to that dignity by God be God, and the great God? Nor is there any reason for them to object that he is called God but is not God, since the text says that he is such, and is not merely called so, and indeed with the article, [τῷ μεγάλῳ θεῷ].

units.la: Hinc ad Minorem vel antecedens, negant de Christo intelligendum id quod in textu est de magno Deo; verum de Patre, idque conjunctionem denotare interpositam ἡ[?] &, magni Dei & servatoris. Sed quare non etiam observant intermissam incisionem vel comma, ut quoniam de eodem intelligi utrumque potest, Christo nempe, quod concedunt, de eodem utrumque accipiatur: quod clarum est alibi non posse, uti de Paulo ac Timotheo quod idem sint, in exemplo allato. Duorum, inquit, fit mentio, magni Dei, & salvatoris, ergo duo diversi intelliguntur. negatur. Ecce, Dominum & Christum eum, Act. 11. 36. Deus & Pater Domini nostri, 1 Pet. 1. 3. ubi & conjunctio intervenit, neque tamen duo intelliguntur. Apoc. 1. 6. Deo & Patri. Nullus autem similior locus, quam 2 Pet. 1. 1. Dei nostri & salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Ubi idem procul dubio intelligitur, & intercedit conjunctio, & eadem, quæ in textu nostro, verba. Versio Æthiopica, in loco nostro, conjunctionis notam omittit, Dei nostri magni, Iesu Christi servatoris nostri. Denique Adversariis reponimus hæc Enjedini, ad præsentem locum, verba: infinita ostendunt exempla, magnam varietatem & licentiam esse Græcis, in articulis addendis, omittendis, transponendis.
units.tr: Hence, as to the minor premise or antecedent, they deny that what is in the text about the great God is to be understood of Christ, but of the Father, and they say that the conjunction "and", placed between "of the great God" and "Saviour", denotes this. But why do they not also observe the intervening break or comma? If both can be understood of the same person, namely Christ, which they concede, then both are taken of the same person; that this is clearly not always the case elsewhere is shown by the example given of Paul and Timothy, which are not the same. Two are mentioned, he says, the great God and the Saviour; therefore two different persons are understood. This is denied. Look at "the Lord and Christ" in Acts 11:36, God and Father of our Lord, 1 Peter 1:3, where a conjunction also intervenes, and yet two are not understood; Revelation 1:6, to God and Father. But there is no more similar place than 2 Peter 1:1, of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ. There the same person is undoubtedly understood, a conjunction intervenes, and the words are the same as in our text. The Ethiopic version, in our place, omits the sign of the conjunction: of our great God, Jesus Christ our Saviour. Finally, to our adversaries we reply with these words of Enjedinus about the present passage: countless examples show that the Greeks have great freedom and latitude in adding, omitting and transposing the articles.

units.la: Ad locum vero Act. xx. 28. excipiunt, dici Deum suo sanguine redemisse Ecclesiam, non Christum, sed Deum Patrem, per sanguinem Christi, seu filii sui. Enjedinus:
units.tr: As for Acts 20:28, they object that it says God redeemed the Church with his own blood, and that this means God the Father, not Christ, through the blood of Christ or of his Son. Enjedinus:

units.la: Dicunt hic manifeste Christum, vocari Deum. Nam Deus Pater, sanguinem non habet: iste autem, qui hic redemisse aut acquisivisse dicitur
units.tr: They here plainly call Christ God. For God the Father has no blood; but he who is said here to have redeemed or acquired

units.la: Resp. Primum concedunt, Christum esse Deum, sed non æternum ac omnipotentem, id est, Deum, non Deum, vel sanguine Ecclesiam, Deus dicitur: Ergo alius est a Deo Patre. Atqui, ut ex aliis scripturae locis apparet, Christus est is, cujus sanguine pii sunt redempti. Ergo de Christo est hic locus intelligendus. Resp. Ut omnis lapis moveatur, hinc nihil aliud obtineri potest, quam Christum esse Deum. Quod nos non gravate concedimus: sed addimus, non statim qui Deus est, esse etiam creatorem coeli & terrae, aeternum ac omnipotentem. Deinde, usitatum est, ut ea quae sunt carissimorum, nostra reputemus, imo alteros nos exiimemus. Hinc audimus Deum dicentem: Non te rejecerunt, sed me. Qui vos tetigerit, tangit pupillam oculi mei, Zach. 2. v. 8. Et Christus Matt. 25. Quod uni horum fecistis, mihi fecistis. Paulus dum persequitur Christianos, audit a Christo. Saule, quid me persequeris? Ergo etiam sanguis Iesu Christi, quia erat hominis Deo carissimi, & filii dilectissimi, dicitur esse, Dei sanguis, non quod Deus sanguinem habeat, sicut neque pupillam habet, sed quod illum Deus pro suo reputet, & tam pretiosus illi sit, quam si esset ipsius. Praeterea, notissimum est, Graecos, ablativo casu carere, eumque per Genitivum exprimere. Illud quoque manifestum est, elliptica nonnunquam eos uti oratione: atque Substantivum ὑος fere semper, opposito Patris tantum aut gentis nomine, in casu Genitivo, omittere & subintelligendum relinquere, ut cum alibi, tum Luc. 3. videre licet. Sed & Hebraei, quorum in loquendo usum, saepe Novi testamenti scriptores sequi, certum est: quaevis Substantiva, oppositis tantum Adjectivis, subintelligenda relinquere, confuserunt, ut Cevallerius in sua Syntaxi Canone 19. docet. Itaque etiam hoc loco, salva tum Graecorum tum Hebraeorum Grammatica, imo utrorumque consuetudinem secuti, interpretari verba ista sic ponimus: acquisivit sanguine sui (vel proprii) subaudi Filii. Ne autem haec Ellipsis cuiquam dura videri possit, primo illud efficit, quod alias quoque vox Filii omissa, subaudiri solet, ut ἰάκωβος ὁ ζεβεδαίου [?]non verum Deum. Atqui in loco nostro Deus subjective appellatur, & cum articulo, quae Adversarii volunt esse veri Dei indicia & argumenta. II. Quod si istum in modum liceat exponere Scripturam, quo id hoc loco faciunt Adversarii, cedo mihi vel aliquod paradoxum maxime portentosum, quod ex Scriptura non probem; vel argumentum quodvis, pro quacumque etiam veritate, fortissimum, quod non eludam. Quis nescit, communi usu, etiam Scripturae receptum, ut ea quae sunt carissimorum, reputemus nostra; sed an propterea vel similis ratio est textus nostri, vel fieret, ita interpretandus? Christus certe Deo Patri charissimus, verum ideo ei vel sanguis, vel Christi sanguis, & tamquam proprius, quoque Ecclesiam redemerit, hoc in loco, attribuitur? Quidem tangere Deum dicuntur ea etiam quae sui experiuntur, & quasi proxime eum attingunt, non item agere ea, & praestare quae sui per passiones, proinde dicitur. III. Praeterea quid huc faciunt ista, Graecos casu carere ablativo; dein, elliptica uti oratione; denique substantivum ὑος saepe omittere: iterum ad Hebraeos recurrere, qui subst antiva, oppositis tantum adjectivis, subintelligunt. Eheu in quot, quantosque modos & modos induere se necesse habent, qui planam veritatis fastidiunt simplicitatem! nempe ut aliquo colore aut specie possit subaudiri filii vox, acquisivit sanguine sui filii. Verum nec ullum indicium est ellipsis, non ejusmodi, non ulla mentio facta Patris, ut nec possit nec debeat aliud intelligi: quemadmodum id clarum in locis, vel exemplis allegatis, Luc. 3. ὁ ἡλί, &c. vel ἰάκωβος τοῦ ζεβεδαίου Matth. IV. 22. ubi & articulus ellipsis index additur, Ἰάκωβος τοῦ Ζεβεδαίου & opponitur mox, ὁ Ζεscilicet υἱός. Matth. 4. Deinde, quod similia Substantiva subaudiri sæpe solent: ut Ioh. 13. v. 1. ἀγαπητὸς τῆς ἰδίας, subaudi μαθητής. Et Ioh. 1. v. 11. καὶ οἱ ἴδιοι αὐτὸν οὐ παρέλαβον, subaudi ἄνθρωποι, aut aliquid simile, Matth. 10. v. 41. ποτήριον ψυχροῦ, scilicet ὕδατος, &c. Ad hæc, scimus tam apud Græcos vocem αἷμα, quam apud Latinos vocem Sanguis, sæpe poni pro Filio: ut Homer: Οὐνος. δ. Αἷμα[?] εἰς ἀγαπητὸν φίλον τέκος[?], id est, Ex sanguine bono es, care fili. Et Οὐνος. τ. ὁ ἐμὸς υἱός ἐστι καὶ αἷμα[?] ἡμέτερος[?], id est, Si vere meus es, & è sanguine nostro. Sic apud Theocritum Heraclisco Γεγενημένον αἷμα. Apud Latinos etiam sic usurpatur sanguis. Virg. Æn. 6.
units.tr: Reply: First, they concede that Christ is God, but not eternal and almighty; that is, God, but not God in the sense in which the true God is meant. Their own argument shows this. Scripture says that God redeemed the Church with blood. Therefore he is different from God the Father. But, as other passages of Scripture make plain, Christ is he by whose blood the godly are redeemed. Therefore this passage must be understood of Christ. Reply: However hard one pushes, nothing more can be obtained from this than that Christ is God. We do not hesitate to concede that. But we add that whoever is God is not at once the creator of heaven and earth, eternal and almighty. Moreover, it is a common usage, even in Scripture, to regard as our own what belongs to those we love most, and indeed to count them as ourselves. Thus we hear God saying: "They have not rejected you, but me. He who touches you touches the apple of my eye" (Zech. 2:8). And Christ says in Matthew 25: "What you have done to one of these, you have done to me." When Paul persecuted Christians, he heard from Christ: "Saul, why do you persecute me?" So also the blood of Jesus Christ, since it was the blood of a man most dear to God and of his most beloved Son, is called the blood of God. This is not because God has blood, any more than he has an apple of the eye, but because God regards it as his own, and it is as precious to him as if it were his own. Besides, it is well known that the Greeks lack the ablative case and express it by the genitive. It is also plain that they sometimes use elliptical speech, and that they very often omit the substantive υἱός in the genitive, leaving it to be understood, when it is opposed only to the name of a father or a people, as can be seen both elsewhere and in Luke 3. But it is also certain that the Hebrews, whose manner of speaking the writers of the New Testament often follow, leave any substantive to be understood when it is opposed only to an adjective, as Cevallerius teaches in his Syntax, Canon 19. Therefore in this place too, keeping the grammar of both Greek and Hebrew, and indeed following the custom of both, we render the words thus: he acquired with his own blood (or his proper blood), understand "Son". Lest this ellipsis seem harsh to anyone, I first point out that the word "Son" is in many other places also omitted and usually understood, as in "James the son of Zebedee" [ἰάκωβος ὁ ζεβεδαίου] — not the true God. Yet in our passage God is named as a subject and with the article, which the adversaries wish to be signs and proofs of the true God. II. But if it is allowed to expound Scripture in the way the adversaries do here, name me any most monstrous paradox that I cannot prove from Scripture, or any argument, however strong for any truth whatever, that I cannot elude. Who does not know that by common usage, which Scripture too has received, we regard as our own what belongs to those we love? But is there for that reason a similar reasoning in our text, or should it be so interpreted? Is it certainly said in this place that Christ, most dear to God the Father, redeemed the Church, and that the blood, or the blood of Christ, is attributed to God as his own? Indeed, those things are said to touch God which he also suffers in his own people, and which in a sense reach him closely; but it is not said that he acts or performs those things which are done by his people through their sufferings. III. Moreover, what do these points help: that the Greeks lack the ablative case; then that they use elliptical speech; finally that they often omit the substantive υἱός; and again that they resort to the Hebrews, who understand substantives when only adjectives are opposed? Alas, in how many and how great ways must they clothe themselves, who scorn the plain simplicity of truth! Namely, so that the word "Son" can be understood with some colour or appearance: "he acquired with the blood of his Son." But there is no sign of an ellipsis, none of this kind, no mention of the Father made, such that anything else could or should be understood. This is clear from the passages or examples alleged: Luke 3, "Heli," etc., or "James of Zebedee" in Matthew 4:22, where the article is added as a sign of the ellipsis, "James the (son) of Zebedee," and immediately after it is opposed, "the Zebedee" that is, the son. Matthew 4. Further, similar substantives are often wont to be understood: as in John 13:1, "his own (beloved)," understand "disciple"; and in John 1:11, "and his own did not receive him," understand "men" or something similar; Matthew 10:41, "a cup of cold (water)," namely "water," etc. Besides, we know that among the Greeks the word αἷμα, and among the Latins the word "blood," are often put for "son." As in Homer: "Thou art of good blood, dear son" [Ex sanguine bono es, care fili]. And again: "If you are truly my son, and of our blood" [Si vere meus es, et e sanguine nostro]. So in Theocritus, to Heracliscus: "one born of blood" [Γεγενημένον αἷμα]. Among the Latins too "blood" is so used. Virgil, Aeneid 6:

units.la: Projice tela manu, sanguis meus.
units.tr: Cast the weapons from your hand, my blood.

units.la: Tibullus ad matrem de filia:
units.tr: Tibullus, to the mother, about the daughter:

units.la: Quicquid agit, sanguis est tamen illa tuus.
units.tr: Whatever she does, she is still your blood.

units.la: Posset ergo non incommode dici, Deum sanguine suo (vel proprio) hoc est, Filio suo redemisse Ecclesiam. Denique sanguinem victimarum & sacrificiorum, notum est fuisse sanctificatum Deo, ideoque & comedi illum nefas erat, & ad Dei aram effundi jubebatur. Iam vero Christus dicitur victima, & sacrificium. Ergo sanguis Christi effusus, potest dici sanguis Dei, erat enim illi sacer, quo quidem sanguine fuit redemta Ecclesia. Cum igitur tot modis explicari, locus iste, secundum scripturam, possit: nihil ex eo, contra nostram sententiam, colligi potest.
units.tr: It could therefore not inappropriately be said that God redeemed the Church with his own blood (or proper blood), that is, with his Son's. Finally, it is well known that the blood of victims and sacrifices was consecrated to God; therefore it was unlawful to eat it, and it was commanded to be poured out at God's altar. Now Christ is called a victim and a sacrifice. Therefore the blood of Christ, when shed, can be called the blood of God, for it was sacred to him, and with this blood the Church was redeemed. Since, then, this passage can be explained in so many ways consistent with Scripture, nothing can be drawn from it against our opinion.

units.la: quale nihil in nostro loco, vel subesse nemo unquam supficatus fuit. Nihil in eo gentilitium, vel genealogicum, nihilque poni conveniens fuit. Non dicitur in textu ὁ ἀληθινὸς τ. ἰδίας[?], sc. Filii; sed διὰ τὸ ἴδιον αἷμα[?], ut ἰδίον ad αἷμα referatur, non ad υἱόν[?], atque hoc demum subintelligatur: neque sensus, acquisivit sanguine sui, sed, acquisivit suo sanguine, vox ἴδιον ad αἷμα, non contra; tum ejusdem utrumque casus, non diversi; denique proprium est, non simpliciter suum. Idēst, non alterius sanguine, non sanguine taurorum & hircorum, Heb. ix. 12, 13. vel aliorum hominum, sed suo proprio redemit Ecclesiam, inde etiam suam. iv. Cæterum, uti sanguis in N.T. in argumento nempe redemtionis, Christi intelligitur, ita & Ecclesia, & redemptio Christi: ut certe Christo, hoc in loco, quæ tam clare commemorantur, non possint non attribui. v. υἱός omnibus istis, quæ indicat, locis, usurpatum nuspiam subaudit υἱοῦ[?]: imo neque aliud quippiam: sed designat simpliciter suos. Aliud prorsus, neque ad rem quidpiam faciens est Matth. x. 42. poculum frigidæ, sc. aquæ. Quasi vero negaremus nos, aliqua in sermone subinde intelligi? vi. Denique, ut anxiam horum hominum videamus sollicitudinem in exquirendâ præsentis loci expositione aliqua, confugiunt & huc, ut per sanguinem intelligant filium: quia nimirum filius
units.tr: Nobody has ever suspected that anything of the kind lies beneath our passage. Nothing in it is tribal or genealogical, nor was anything of that kind fitting to put here. The text does not say ὁ ἀληθινὸς τῆς ἰδίας, that is, of the Son; but διὰ τὸ ἴδιον αἷμα, so that ἴδιον refers to αἷμα, not to υἱός, and only then is something supplied. The sense is not "he acquired with his own (Son's) blood" but "he acquired with his own blood": the word ἴδιον refers to αἷμα, not the reverse; and both cases are the same, not different. Finally, the word means "proper," not simply "his own." That is, he redeemed the Church not with another's blood, not with the blood of bulls and goats (Heb. 9:12, 13), nor with the blood of other men, but with his own proper blood, and therefore it is also his own. IV. Moreover, just as in the New Testament "blood" is understood of Christ in the matter of redemption, so also "the Church" and "the redemption" are of Christ: so that these things, which are so clearly mentioned here, cannot but be attributed to Christ in this place. V. The word υἱός is used in none of the passages that these people cite, and nowhere does it supply υἱοῦ, nor anything else of the kind; rather it simply denotes "his own people." The example of Matthew 10:42, "a cup of cold (water)," that is "water," is quite different and has nothing to do with the matter. As if we denied that some things are sometimes understood in speech! VI. Finally, so that we may see the anxious concern of these men in seeking some explanation of the present passage, they flee here too, to understand "blood" as "son," because, of course, a son is naturally of the blood.

units.la: naturaliter est ex sanguine: & hoc necesse videtur aliquot testimoniis ex profanis Auctoribus confirmare, quasi id nimirum tanti sit: & quidem ex Poëtis, quos metri ratio ad id sæpe cogit vel invitat. Sed ex sacris nihil adducunt, nihil ex ullo, quo de Christo filio Dei agitur, loco. Neque etiam ex sanguine Patris Christus, ob quam causam alii vulgo filii, parentum sanguis appellantur. Non certe Christus, ex sanguine Patris proprio, ut proprius ejus sanguis dici ulla ratione queat. Denique in argumento de redemptione Ecclesiæ per Christum, vox sanguis proprie sumi solet: nunquam sanguis, pro filio, pro Christo, semper autem pro vero Christi sanguine. cogitat rationem, quia nimirum Deo effunditur. Ergo jam proprie vox sanguis usur-patur. Atq; deinde in effusione sanguinis ergo Christus sacerdote egit, non demum in caelis. Nec in textu dicitur sanguis Dei, sed quod Deus sanguine suo redemerit Ecclesiā. Jam vero si ille modus vel exponendi Scripturam, vel respondendi ad argumentum aliquod ex ea formatum valeat, ut excogitatis quibuscumque miris detorsionibus tandem dicatur, nihil solidi ex ea colligi posse, quia multis aliis modis forte explicetur, nihil certi constare amplius poterit ex Scripturis, vel probari. Nos vero nullum istorum modorum, quos Adversarius attulit, subsistere, neque aliter quam de Christo, & quod hic Deus appelletur, voce Dei subjecti loco, & cum articulo posita, exponi posse, planum, uti arbitror, fecimus.
units.tr: It is naturally from the blood, and this seems necessary to confirm by some testimonies from profane authors, as if that mattered so much. They draw these from the poets, whom the demands of metre often compel or invite to it. But from the sacred writings they adduce nothing, nothing from any passage in which the Son of God is spoken of as Christ. Nor is Christ said to be of his Father's blood, which is why others are commonly called the sons of their parents' blood. Certainly Christ is not from his Father's own blood, so that it could in any way be called his proper blood. Finally, in the argument about the redemption of the Church through Christ, the word blood is usually taken properly: never does blood stand for the Son or for Christ, but always for the true blood of Christ. The reason is that it is poured out to God. So the word blood is already being used properly. Then, in the shedding of blood Christ acted as priest, and not only later in heaven. Nor does the text speak of the blood of God, but says that God redeemed the Church with his own blood. Now if that method, either of expounding Scripture or of answering an argument formed from it, holds good, so that after any strange distortions whatever have been devised it may finally be said that nothing solid can be gathered from it, because perhaps it can be explained in many other ways, then nothing certain can any longer be established or proved from the Scriptures. But we have made it plain, as I think, that none of those methods which the Adversary has brought forward can stand, and that the word God cannot be explained in any other way than of Christ, and that he is called God here, the word God being placed in the subject position and with the article.

units.la: Sed & Christus dicitur non modo Dominus, verum Dominus gloriae, addito etiam articulo, τὸν Κύριον τῆς δόξης [?] crucifixerunt. 1 Cor. ii. 1. Ubi si non nomen Κυρίου, certe adjunctum τῆς δόξης ostendit, Deum verum intelligi. Christus Deus dicitur, & Dominus, & Dominus gloriae, ac pariter cum tali descriptione Deus, ut de vera ejus Deitate nemo, sine grandi facinore, dubitare hic queat. Deus nempe verus. 1 Joann. v. 20. addito etiam articulo, ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ, in Filio ejus Iesu Christo: est ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος.
units.tr: But Christ is called not only Lord but Lord of glory, with the article added: "they crucified the Lord of glory" [τὸν Κύριον τῆς δόξης], 1 Cor. 2:1. Here, if not the name of Lord, at least the addition of "of glory" shows that the true God is meant. Christ is called God, and Lord, and Lord of glory, and so equally with such a description as God that no one here can doubt his true deity without great wickedness. Indeed true God: 1 John 5:20, with the article also added, "in the true one" [ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ], in his Son Jesus Christ: "he is the true God [ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς], and eternal life" [καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος].

units.la: Excipit post Socinium, contra Wiekum, cap. 4. Volkelius, lib. v. cap. x. pag. 423.
units.tr: After Socinus, against Wiek, chap. 4, Volkelius, book 5, chap. 10, p. 423.

units.la: Primo igitur non diffitemur quidem, Christum verum & nequaquam imaginarium Deum esse; hoc tamen nomen nusquam, quod sciamus, in S. lit. ei expressè tribuitur. tametsi enim Iohannes sic vocare videtur: attentius tamen locum illum inspicienti facile patebit, verba illa, Hic est verus Deus, & vita aeterna, non ad Christum, sed ad Patrem referenda esse, in cujus notitiam Christum nos deduxisse, ibidem dictum fuerat, quem patrem solum verum Deum esse, apud eundem Ioannem scriptum legimus. Quo fit, ut nisi cum Christo Apostolum pugnare volumus, Filius verus Deus, ea significatione, quae hic spectatur, esse non possit. Accedit, quod articulus vocibus vero Deo in Graeco praefixus, de illo vero Deo sermonem esse ostendit, cui omnium perfectissima ratione hoc nomen convenit. Eum autem non nisi Christi patrem esse, ex iis, quae supra a nobis disputata sunt, patet. Praeterea Deus ille, de quo sermo est, in his Apostoli verbis idolis opponitur, quod de patre saepissime, de Christo nusquam legitur. Denique in hoc eodem Iohannis loco, Christus bis ab illo vero Deo distinguitur. Nam & Filius venisse, nobisque
units.tr: First, then, we do not deny that Christ is a true God and by no means an imaginary one; yet as far as we know this name is nowhere expressly given to him in the sacred writings. For although John seems to call him so, yet anyone who looks more attentively at that passage will easily see that the words "This is the true God and eternal life" are to be referred not to Christ but to the Father, into whose knowledge, it had been said in the same place, Christ had led us; and we read in the same John that the Father alone is the true God. Hence, unless we wish to set the Apostle against Christ, the Son cannot be the true God in the sense that is intended here. In addition, the article prefixed in Greek to the words "the true God" shows that the discourse is about that true God to whom this name belongs in the most perfect way. That he is none other than the Father of Christ is clear from what we have argued above. Moreover, that God of whom the discourse is spoken is in these words of the Apostle set over against idols, which is read very often of the Father, but nowhere of Christ. Finally, in this same passage of John, Christ is twice distinguished from that true God. For both the Son has come and has given us...

units.la: Resp. 1. Verum exponit, id est, non fictitium, non imaginarium. Sed veritas, non est affectio entis negativa, sed positiva: non sufficit, ut quis verus dicatur Deus, ne sit falsus, requiritur insuper, ne fallamus, vel fallamur, ut vera ejus ratio, natura, definitio eidem competat. Enjedinus: certum enim est, verum fictitio & imaginario opponi. At quoscumque Deus evehit, & Deos facit, non umbratitii, sed veri sunt Dii; quales sunt reges & judices, & Prophetae. Neque tamen sequitur, eos propterea quod sunt veri Dii, esse aeternos, & eosdem cum Patre Deos.
units.tr: Answer 1. Verum means "real", that is, not fictitious, not imaginary. But truth is not a negative affection of being but a positive one. It is not enough that someone be called a true God, so that he is not false; it is further required that we not deceive or be deceived, so that the true account, nature and definition of him belong to him. Enjedinus: for it is certain that verum is opposed to fictitious and imaginary. But whomever God exalts and makes gods are not shadowy but true gods, such as kings and judges and prophets. Yet it does not follow that, because they are true gods, they are eternal and the same gods as the Father.

units.la: Verum non solum fictitio opponitur, sed praeterea positivam dicit rei cum natura ejus, quod dicitur, convenientiam. Quod Deus deos facit, eosque veros, nuspiam astruitur. Nedum ut aliquis in singulari, & subjective, & cum articulo, & in sacris, non solum dicatur Deus, sed & Deus verus. Smalcius, in Exam. c. errorum, pag. 4. aperte affirmat, non tantum Deum Patrem, sed alios etiam, & inter hos suo modo Iesum Christum, esse veros Deos. Duro, diroque, inter Christianos, sermone, plures esse non Deos tantum, sed & veros Deos. illius veri, nempe Dei, cognoscendi mentem de- ad praesentem locum expositione pa-diffe, & nos per eundem Dei Filium in illo vero, tet. patebit etiam ex responsione, quam nempe, ut diximus Deo, esse affirmatur. daturi estis ad hoc nostrum argumentum: verus Deus est, qui habet essentiam Dei: nam veritas entis est affectio, & cum suo ente convertitur: at Christus vester non habet essentiam Dei: ergo non est Deus, non verus Deus. III. Nescis, uspiam nomen Dei Christo in S. litteris expresse tribui? quorsum ergo Deum dicis. Tu hoc nescis, quod ipsi Muhammedani in Scripturis vident & testantur, Christum Deum ibi dici? Hoc nescis, quod ego nescio an ulli Sociani palam ausint dicere. IV. Quod Johannis locum pro nobis adducimus, vobis mirum videri non debet, quum & hoc fateamini, quod Iohannes cum sic vocare videtur. V. Negas tamen ad Christum verba referenda esse, sed ad Patrem: idque quatuor argumentis: Quomodo & Enjedinus disputat, in hunc locum.
units.tr: But verum is not only opposed to fictitious; it also expresses a positive agreement of the thing with its nature, of what is said. Nowhere is it asserted that God makes gods, and true ones. Still less that someone in the singular, and as a subject, and with the article, and in the sacred writings, is called not only God but the true God. Smalcius, in Examen of errors, p. 4, plainly affirms that not only God the Father but others also, and among these, in his own way, Jesus Christ, are true gods. Duro, in a harsh and hard manner of speaking among Christians, that there are many not only gods but true gods. Of that true one, namely God, the mind of knowing... to the exposition of the present passage... it will be clear also from the reply which you will give to this argument of ours: the true God is he who has the essence of God; for the truth of a being is an affection and is convertible with its being; but your Christ does not have the essence of God; therefore he is not God, not the true God. III. Do you not know that the name of God is nowhere expressly given to Christ in the sacred letters? Why then do you call him God? Do you not know this, which the Muhammadans themselves see and testify in the Scriptures, that Christ is called God there? You do not know this, which I do not know whether any Socinian dares openly to say. IV. That we bring forward the passage of John on our side ought not to seem strange to you, since you also admit this, that John seems to call him so. V. Yet you deny that the words are to be referred to Christ but to the Father, and this by four arguments, as Enjedinus also disputes on this passage.

units.la: Primo, quia Christus Patrem verum Deum appellat Joann. xvii. 3. cum quo Apo-lus pugnare non potest. Resp. 1. Certe pugnaret, si alium Deum Christum diceret a Patre: quem quia verum dicit, eundem intelligit, uti & nos. Quare non pugnare hac ratione dicendus est cum Christo Apostolus, sed adeo quidem convenire, ut de eodem vero Deo identificetur eorundem sermo uterque. Quippe Pater est solus verus Deus, & Filius Christus est solus verus Deus, atque ὁ ἀληθινὸς idem ille verus Deus. II. Quae nisi confirmem ex ipsis vestris hypothesibus, ne credite. Deus verus opponitur Diis falsis: atqui vos Christum non redigitis in censum Deorum falsorum, sed dicitis vos eum habere pro Deo vero: Ergo verus Deus in sermone seu Christi, seu Apostoli, Christo opponi non potest, nec debet, sed Diis aliis, iisque non veris. III. Deus verus opponitur Diis falsis, estque modo unus verus Deus, & is Pater, & Filius, & S.
units.tr: First, because Christ calls the Father the true God, John 17:3, with whom the Apostle cannot disagree. Answer 1. He would indeed disagree if he called Christ a God other than the Father; but since he calls him true, he means the same one, as we also do. Hence it must be said that the Apostle does not disagree with Christ in this way, but indeed agrees so fully that the discourse of each is about the same true God. For the Father is the only true God, and the Son Christ is the only true God, and the true one [ὁ ἀληθινὸς] is that same true God. II. Which things, unless I confirm them from your own hypotheses, do not believe them. The true God is opposed to false gods; but you do not reckon Christ among false gods, but say that you hold him to be the true God. Therefore the true God, in the discourse either of Christ or of the Apostle, cannot and ought not to be opposed to Christ, but to other gods, and those not true. III. The true God is opposed to false gods, and there is only one true God, and he is the Father, and the Son, and the

units.la: S. Pater, & Filius non opponuntur Deitatis ratione, sed ἐν sunt. Oppositio est respectu Personarum, relativa, non essentialis diversarum naturarum. Atqui in utroque loco Deitas consideratur contra Deos falsos, non personalitas inter Patrem, Filiumque, in ordine ad verum Deum, qui Deus uterque dicitur, & bene, & vere, citra ullam repugnantiam.
units.tr: Holy Spirit. The Father and the Son are not opposed in respect of their deity, but are one [ἐν]. The opposition is relative, with respect to the Persons, not essential, between different natures. Yet in both passages the Deity is considered against false gods, not the personality between Father and Son in relation to the true God, who is called God in each case, both rightly and truly, without any contradiction.

units.la: Secundo ait, locum 1 Joann. v. 20. de Christo accipi non posse, propter articulum ὁ & τῷ vocibus vero Deo praefixum. Sed jam ostendimus, quam inane hoc sit. Imo articulus clare & fortiter ostendit, Christo omnia haec applicanda esse, ita conjunctionis etiam vicem supplet, ut cognoscamus τὸν ἀληθινόν. καὶ simus ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ, ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ: hic est ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος. Videmus, omnia per articulum innecti firmarique, ad demonstrandum, de eodem subjecto intelligenda commodè esse. Uti τῷ ὑῷ [?], eodem modo dicitur τῷ ἀληθινῷ, deque eodem. Articulus ostendit, inquit, de illo vero Deo sermonem esse, cui omnium perfectissima ratione hoc nomen convenit. Ne dicam, perfectissima ratione hoc nomen Christo tribui, ut uni, eidem, vero Deo, quantae ineptiae, ut ipsum nomen Christo vere tribuatur, (ex mente Adversariorum, Deo imperfecto) & ut articulus seu pronomen perfectionem majorem, imo omnem connotet & significet, plus quam ipsum nomen?
units.tr: Secondly, he says that 1 John 5:20 cannot be understood of Christ, because of the article ὁ and τῷ placed before the words "the true God" [ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεός]. But we have already shown how empty this objection is. Indeed the article clearly and strongly shows that all these things are to be applied to Christ. It even takes the place of a conjunction, so that "we may know the true one" [τὸν ἀληθινόν], "and may be in the true one" [ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ], "in his Son Jesus Christ" [ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ]: "this is the true God" [ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς], "and eternal life" [καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος]. We see that everything is linked and confirmed by the article, to show that it is conveniently to be understood of the same subject. Just as the article is used with the Son, so it is used with "the true one", and of the same one. "The article shows," he says, "that the discourse is of that true God, to whom this name belongs in the most perfect way of all." Not to mention that this name is attributed to Christ in the most perfect way, as to one and the same true God. How great is the absurdity that the name itself is truly attributed to Christ (in the opinion of our opponents, to an imperfect God), and yet the article or pronoun signifies and implies a greater perfection, indeed all perfection, than the name itself does!

units.la: Tertia ratio. Deus verus idolis opponitur: & hoc de Christo nusquam legitur. Resp. 1. Negare nos consequentiam: qui non legitur opponi idolis, is non est verus Deus. Revera opponitur Christus Deus idolis. Sed quamvis hoc nullibi legeretur: & pone, ut nullibi legatur de Deo Patre, non ideo definit verus Deus esse. Non omnia necesse est omnimodo exprimi, & legi. Quamvis alicujus rei subticeatur forte aliquod argumentum aut signum, haud ideo amittit esse vera. II. Quoties Christus Deus dicitur in Scripturis, annon opponitur idolis? Vos negatisne eum idolis opponi? vel, an eodem ordine habetis cum idolis? quorsum ergo Deum, & verum Deum, & naturâ talem, ac naturalem Dei filium appellatis? Deus τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς oppo-nitur, Gal. IV.8. III. Proba, Christum hoc loco idolis non opponi. Hoc fumere, abs-que probatione, futile est & ineptum. IV. Christus aeque ac Pater idolis opponitur, 1 Cor. VIII. 6. Nobis unus Deus Pater, ex quo omnia, & nos ad ipsum: & unus dominus Iesus Christus, per quem omnia, & nos per eum. opponitur idolis, de quibus vers. 4. 5. 7. Scimus quod idolum nihil est in mundo. Quaero, annon huic etiam Christus opponatur? Additur: nobis autem non est Deus alius quam unus. Vel cum hoc uno Deo idem facit Christus, contra idola, vel non? fit enim oppositio Deum inter, & idola. Et cum Deo expresse Christus jungitur vers. 6. tum ante, & post istum locum de idolis agitur. Atque etiamnum dubitas, Christum idolis opponi? Vel an Deus opponitur Christo κυρίῳ, ut idolo? Christus Patri conjungitur in eadem oppositione contra idola, & τῆς ψευδωνύμους θεοῦς, de quibus vers. 5. Ergo Christus unus ille verus Deus, atque verae naturae divinae, non ψευδώνυμος, saltem qui idolis opponi ut debet, ita hoc loco satis clare objicitur.
units.tr: Third argument. The true God is set over against idols, and this is nowhere read of Christ. Answer 1. We deny the consequence: one who is not read of as set over against idols is not therefore not the true God. Indeed Christ, God, is set over against idols. But even if this were read nowhere, suppose it were read nowhere of God the Father either; he does not thereby cease to be the true God. It is not necessary that everything be expressed and read in every way. Although some argument or sign of a thing may perhaps be passed over in silence, it does not on that account lose its truth. II. Whenever Christ is called God in the Scriptures, is he not set over against idols? Do you deny that he is set over against idols? Or do you place him in the same rank as idols? Why then do you call him God, and the true God, and the natural Son of God by nature? God is set over against "those that are not gods by nature" [τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς], Gal. 4:8. III. Prove that Christ is not set over against idols in this passage. To assume this without proof is futile and absurd. IV. Christ is set over against idols just as the Father is, 1 Cor. 8:6: "To us there is one God the Father, of whom are all things, and we unto him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him." He is set over against the idols of which verses 4, 5 and 7 speak: "We know that an idol is nothing in the world." I ask, is Christ not set over against these too? It is added: "But to us there is not another God but one." Either Christ does the same with this one God against the idols, or he does not; for there is an opposition between God and the idols. And since Christ is expressly joined with God in verse 6, and since the passage about idols is discussed both before and after that place, do you still doubt that Christ is set over against idols? Or is God set over against Christ the Lord as an idol? Christ is joined with the Father in the same opposition against idols and "the so-called gods" [τῆς ψευδωνύμους θεοῦς], of which verse 5 speaks. Therefore Christ is that one true God, of the true divine nature, not a false-named god; at least he is clearly set forth in this passage as one who is opposed to idols, as he ought to be.

units.la: Denique quarto loco, Christus bis (inquit) ab illo vero Deo distinguitur. Resp. Negari majorem, & minorem. Potest distingui ab illo vero Deo, & tamen idem quoque esse ille verus Deus. Distingui nempe non in Deitate, ejusque veritate, sed personaliter, non essentialiter. II. Negamus, Christum a vero Deo hic distingui, qui ipse verus Deus ille significatur, in Filio ejus Christo: hic est verus ille Deus. Quod conjunctio indicat de eodem accipi & praedicari. Non quod negemus, subinde pronomen relativum referri non ad proximum, sed ad remotius antecedens, quod nobis hic objicit Enjedinus; sed quod nulla ejus hoc in loco fit indicatio, & omnia contrarium efflagitent. Praeterquam enim quod planam & simplicem verborum expositionem sectari semper debemus, & ab ea non recedere nisi cogente admodum necessitate, alia sunt in textu, quae non ferunt contrariam expositionem, ἐν τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ. οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος. Istud οὗτος dicimus, hic referendum ad proxime antecedens Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ: juxta consuetum & maxime commodum explicandi modum, qui pro nobis stat. Adversatur & remotius antecedens. Age & hoc concedamus, antecedit autem τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ. Non, sed ad solum αὐτοῦ contendunt referri debere istum, de quo intellexit ejus αὐτοῦ, est ille Deus. Vide quam contorte & coacte. Primum inter αὐτοῦ & οὗτος, interponitur Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ, quod mala fide Enjedinus omittit, ita locum in fronte praescribens: & sumus in vero filio ejus. Hic est verus Deus: Non dicitur, & sumus in vero filio ejus. Sed, & sumus in vero isto, in filio ejus Iesu Christo. Non quadrat connexio αὐτοῦ οὗτος. Dixisset Iohannes, non οὗτος, sed ὅς. Et conjunxisset immediate, cum αὐτοῦ. Imo nec ita, quin potius dixisset, αὐτοῦ, τῷ ἀληθινῷ θεῷ. Nullum dabitur simile exemplum, ut aliquis οὗτος ἐστιν nec ad proximum nomen, quod hic est, Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς[?], nec ad remotius, quod est ὑπὲρ[?] referatur, sed ad interjectum pronomen αὐτὸς[?]. Neque aliter ἀληθινὸς[?] debet accipi, quam de Patre & Filio; ut propterea etiam dicatur, quod qui in uno, etiam est in alio. Inque eo sita recta τὸ ἀληθινὸν[?] cognitio, & hoc demum est in ipso esse; ἐν τῷ ὑπὲρ[?] æque dicitur, ac ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ[?] & pari modo τὸ ἐν[?] exponendum. Versio Æthiopica, ipse qui vere Deus est. iv. Tum quod sequitur, & vita æterna, argumento est Christum designari, qui passim in Novo Testamento hac phrasi describitur. v. Præterquam quod in Christo finire, uti hic finit epistola, Novi Testamenti stylus est vulgaris. vi. Vt cognoscamus verum illum, designat & Patrem, & Christum, utrumque. Et quod si eorsim illum velis, nihil hoc Christo præjudicabit, qui ei statim adjungitur, ut verus ille, nempe & Dei Filius, & Deus, & vita. Denique adferimus testimonium primùm Serveti, locum de Christo accipientis, lib. i. de Trinitate, pag. 13. de Christo dicitur apud Ioannem, ad differentiam simulacrorum, & eorum, quos falso Deos jactabant, 1 Ioann. 5. deinde Ministrorum Transylvaniæ, in blasphemo libro, de Vnius Dei cognitione, lib. ii. cap. iv. ubi ita loquuntur: Hunc eundem Jesum Christum & verum quoque Deum esse confitemur 1 Ioannis 5. Luc. 20. & Matth. 28. Apocalypsis 5. & Ioannis 10.
units.tr: Finally, in the fourth place, he says, Christ is distinguished twice from that true God. Answer. We deny the major and the minor premise. He can be distinguished from that true God and yet be also that true God. He is distinguished, of course, not in deity and its truth, but personally, not essentially. II. We deny that Christ is distinguished here from the true God, who is himself signified as the true God "in his Son Jesus Christ: this is the true God." The conjunction indicates that the same is spoken of and predicated. We do not deny that a relative pronoun is sometimes referred not to the nearest but to a more remote antecedent, as Enjedinus objects here; but in this place there is no indication of this, and everything demands the contrary. For apart from the fact that we must always follow the plain and simple sense of the words and not depart from it except under very compelling necessity, there are other things in the text which do not allow a different interpretation: "in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life." We say that this "this" [οὗτος] is to be referred here to the immediately preceding "Jesus Christ", according to the customary and most convenient mode of explanation, which stands in our favour. The more remote antecedent also opposes this. Come, let us grant this too: "his Son" does precede. But they contend that the "this" must be referred only to "his" [αὐτοῦ], so that the one whose "his" it is, is that God. See how twisted and forced this is! First, between "his" and "this" there intervenes "Jesus Christ", which Enjedinus omits in bad faith, so setting out the passage at the front: "and we are in his true Son. This is the true God." It does not say "and we are in his true Son", but "and we are in that true one, in his Son Jesus Christ." The connection of "his" and "this" does not fit. John would have said not "this" but "who" [ὅς], and would have joined it immediately with "his". Indeed he would not even have done it so, but rather would have said "his, the true God" [αὐτοῦ, τῷ ἀληθινῷ θεῷ]. No similar example will be found where "this is" [οὗτός ἐστιν] refers neither to the nearest name, which here is "Jesus Christ", nor to the more remote one, but to the intervening pronoun "he himself" [αὐτός]. Nor is "true" [ἀληθινός] to be understood otherwise than of the Father and the Son, so that it is also said that whoever is in the one is also in the other. In this consists the right knowledge of the true one [τὸ ἀληθινόν], and this at last is what it is to be in him; "in him" [ἐν τῷ ὑπὲρ] is said in the same way as "in the true one" [ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ], and "in" [τὸ ἐν] is to be explained in the same way. The Ethiopic version: "he who is truly God." IV. Then, what follows, "and eternal life", is an argument that Christ is designated, who is described in this phrase throughout the New Testament. V. Besides, to end with Christ, as this epistle here ends, is the common style of the New Testament. VI. "That we may know the true one" designates both the Father and Christ, both of them. And if you wish to take it separately, this will not prejudice Christ, who is immediately joined to it as "the true one", namely both the Son of God, and God, and life. Finally, we adduce first the testimony of Servetus, who takes the passage as about Christ, Book 1 on the Trinity, p. 13: "Of Christ it is said by John, in contrast to images and those whom they falsely boasted as gods, 1 John 5." Then the ministers of Transylvania, in their blasphemous book On the Knowledge of the One God, Book 2, chapter 4, where they speak thus: "We confess that this same Jesus Christ is also the true God: 1 John 5; Luke 20; Matt. 28; Revelation 5; and John 10."

units.la: Dicitur Christus in Scripturis Deus, & veritas, & benedictus. Rom. ix. 5. Ex quibus Christus est quoad carnem, qui est supra omnia Deus benedictus in sæcula. Amen. Quod de Christo dictum intelligunt etiam Ministri Transsylvaniæ, de Dei cognitione, lib. ii. cap. iv. & vii. Servetus, lib. i. de Erroribus Trinitatis, pag. 10. & Rom. nono Christus dicitur in omnibus Deus laudandus & benedicendus.
units.tr: Christ is called God in the Scriptures, and truth, and "blessed." Rom. 9:5: "Of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen." The ministers of Transylvania also understand this as said of Christ, On the Knowledge of God, Book 2, chapters 4 and 7. Servetus, Book 1 on the Errors of the Trinity, p. 10, and in Romans 9 Christ is called God to be praised and blessed in all things.

units.la: Excipiunt Sociniani passim duo. i. Non esse ista de Christo, sed Deo Patre accipienda, quod confirmant auctoritate & sententia Erasmi. ii. Et si de Christo intelligantur, eum Deum quidem evincere, non vero æternum illum, & unum. Socinus, contra Volanum, Resp. pri. pag. 25. ut Erasmus pluribus in locis annotat, possunt hæc verba ita interpungi, ut nomen Deus non referatur ad Christum. Et alicubi ait, verba Pauli nullum sensum evidentius reddere, quam hunc: Deus, qui est super omnia, est benedictus in sæcula. Deinde contra Wiekum, Cap. v. cl. iii. arg. viii.
units.tr: The Socinians commonly make two exceptions. (i) These words should not be understood of Christ but of God the Father, and they support this with the authority and opinion of Erasmus. (ii) Even if they are understood of Christ, they prove him to be God, but not that eternal and one God. Socinus, against Volanus, first reply, p. 25: "As Erasmus notes in many places, these words can be punctuated so that the name God is not referred to Christ. And somewhere he says that Paul's words express no sense more clearly than this: God, who is above all things, is blessed for ever." Then against Wiekus, ch. 5, cl. 3, arg. 8.

units.la: Enjedinus: Nostri adversarii nihil possunt adferre, quo suam sententiam confirment, præter quàm quod aiunt, distinctionem illam post vocem, Carnem, in codicibus non reperiri. Sed hoc valde infirmum est. Primo, quia non illi omnes bibliothecas excussere, neque omnia exemplaria inspexerunt. Deinde, nihil est usitatius, quàm distinctiones omittere, aut male collocare. Vnde nullus unquam ita religiosus fuit, qui eas mutare, tollere aut apponere, loci sententia ita postulante, non fuerit ausus. Nos verò pro altera lectione adferre possumus argumentum, in sacris literis admodum validum: quod nimirum ubicunque hoc elogium legitur, illud semper attribuitur Patri, nusquam Christo. Ergo ut
units.tr: Enjedinus: Our adversaries can offer nothing to confirm their view except that they say the punctuation mark after the word "flesh" is not found in the manuscripts. But this is very weak. First, because they have not searched all the libraries or examined all the copies. Second, nothing is more common than for punctuation to be omitted or misplaced. For this reason no one has ever been so scrupulous that he did not dare to change, remove or add punctuation when the sense of the passage required it. For our reading, however, we can bring an argument that is very strong in Holy Scripture: namely that wherever this praise is read, it is always attributed to the Father, never to Christ. Therefore, that

units.la: Resp. I. Hoc si permittatur, ut quisque pro lubitu, & ut viderit hypothesi suæ convenire, textuum distinctiones & interpunctiones omittat, vel mutet, jam nihil certi ex Scripturâ haberi poterit, quod non facile corrumpi possit, & in alium prorsus inverti sensum. Quinimo signum est succumbentis malæ causæ, in ejus subsidium temeritate istâ uti. II.[?] Quod si illud valde infirmum sit, aliquid in codicibus non reperiri, tum quid firmum sit, vel pro firmo haberi, aut probari possit, equidem video nihil. Sin dicant, distinctionem, quamcunque facias, aut mutes, rem esse nihili, iterum nihil erit quod ego vel proba-
units.tr: Reply I. If it is allowed that each man, as he pleases and as he sees fit to his hypothesis, omits or changes the divisions and punctuation of the texts, then nothing certain can be had from Scripture, which could not easily be corrupted and turned into an entirely different sense. Indeed, it is a sign of a failing bad cause to use such recklessness in its support. II.[?] But if it is very weak that something is not found in the manuscripts, then I see nothing at all that is firm, or that can be held or proved to be firm. But if they say that whatever punctuation you make or change is a matter of no importance, then again there will be nothing which I could prove or

units.la: Tom. 2. analogia scripturae salva fit, hic quoque de eodem intelligendum est. Verbi gratia Luc. 1. v. 68. Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, Et ad Rom. cap. 1. v. 25. Et servierunt creaturae potius quam creatori, qui est benedictus in secula. Amen. 2 Cor. 1. v. 3. & cap. 11. v. 31. Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui est benedictus in secula, scit quod non mentior. Eph. 1. v. 3. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Eadem sunt verba 1 Pet. 1. v. 3. Imo usque adeo peculiare epitheton est Deo Patri εὐλογητῆς, ut nulli praeter quam ipsi attributum in Novo testamento legatur. Nam Maria, Christus, caeteri, non εὐλογητοὶ in voce Activa, sed εὐλογημένοι in voce Passiva dicuntur, inter quas voces, discrimen Latine exprimi non possit, testatur Beza, Mar. cap. 14. Hinc fit, ut posita solum illa εὐλογητὸς voce, Deus Pater intelligatur, ut Mar. 14. v. 61. Tunc es ille Christus, filius εὐλογητοῦ, id est, Benedicti? Si igitur & vox εὐλογητὸς, quae in hoc Pauli loco legitur, & aliae similes ac prorsus eadem phrases, nunquam de alio, quam de solo Patre dicuntur: cur non etiam hoc loco, de illo accipi debeat? cum citra ullam, sicut dictum est, & verborum, & linguae injuriam fieri possit? Nam quod fortasse alicui durum videri posset, quod Relativum ὃς qui, prius ponitur, quam antecedens Θεός: ut sciat, hoc satis usitatum esse. Tremell. in Cap. 10. Deut. v. 6. Et 1 Sam. 23. v. 7. & elegantiae nonnunquam dari. Sic ad Rom. 16. v. 25. Ei qui potens est vos confirmare, soli sapienti Deo, per Iesum Christum honor & gloria, in secula seculorum, Amen. Verum, etiamsi priorem distinctionem admittamus: quid hinc aliud consequentur adversarii, quam quod Christus sit super omnia, sit Deus, sit benedictus in secula? Quae omnia nos de Christo, utpote alibi quoque testata, singillatim confitemur. Nam quod super omnia esse dicitur: hoc idem de eo Baptista affirmat Ioh. 3. v. 31. Qui desursum venit, super omnes est. Et illa idem re, vel invertere non possim, data distinctionum faciendarum, aut mutandarum potestate. Et si non standum sit codicibus, non omnibus, nihil superest, cuius fide moveamur, vel certis nobis ac securis esse liceat.
units.tr: ...the analogy of Scripture is kept safe, the same must be understood here too. For example, Luke 1:68: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel." And Rom. 1:25: "and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen." 2 Cor. 1:3 and 2 Cor. 11:31: "The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows that I do not lie." Eph. 1:3: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." The same words occur in 1 Pet. 1:3. Indeed, the epithet eulogētos [εὐλογητός] is so peculiar to God the Father that in the New Testament it is applied to no one but him. For Mary, Christ and the others are called not eulogētoi [εὐλογητοί] in the active voice but eulogēmenoi [εὐλογημένοι] in the passive voice, and Beza, on Mark ch. 14, testifies that the difference between these forms cannot be expressed in Latin. Hence it follows that when the word eulogētos [εὐλογητός] stands alone, God the Father is understood, as in Mark 14:61: "Are you that Christ, the Son of the Blessed [eulogētou, εὐλογητοῦ], that is, of the Blessed One?" If therefore the word eulogētos [εὐλογητός], which is read in this passage of Paul, and other similar and entirely identical phrases, are never said of anyone but the Father alone, why should it not be understood in this place as well, since, as has been said, this can be done without any injury to the words or to the language? For what might perhaps seem harsh to someone, that the relative hos [ὃς], "who", is placed before its antecedent theos [Θεός], "God", is known to be quite common, and sometimes even counted as an elegance. Tremellius on Deut. 10:6 and 1 Sam. 23:7 says so. So also in Rom. 16:25: "To him who is able to establish you, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen." But even if we admit the former punctuation, what else would the adversaries gain from it than that Christ is above all things, is God, and is blessed for ever? All of which we confess individually of Christ, as is attested elsewhere too. For that he is said to be above all things, the Baptist affirms the same of him in John 3:31: "He who comes from above is above all." And I could not change that same thing, given the power of making or changing punctuation at will. And if one must not stand by the manuscripts, and not all of them, nothing remains by whose trustworthiness we may be moved, or be allowed to be certain and secure.

units.la: III. Sed nos exemplaria omnia non inspeximus. Quis autem? & an propterea nihil certi esse potest iis, qui non omnia consuluerunt, non vobis, non denique nobis omnibus? & si hoc non fit causa primum malitiam agnoscere, quando in ejus gratiam cogeris lectionem mutare Scripturae, contra codicum omnium fidem, deinde desperationem, ubi pro illa tua mutatione adversare nihil potes, quam quod Adversarius tuus non omnes forte codices perluftrarit, id quod unicuivis prorsus est impossibile, quid demum eam possit arguere, velim alius clariori argumento demonstret.
units.tr: III. But we have not examined all the copies. Who has? And can nothing be certain for those who have not consulted all of them, not for you, not finally for all of us? And if this is not the case, first, you must recognise malice, when for its sake you are compelled to change the reading of Scripture against the faith of all the manuscripts; second, despair, when against that change of yours you can urge nothing except that your opponent perhaps has not gone through all the manuscripts, which is utterly impossible for anyone. Finally, let someone else show by a clearer argument what could prove it.

units.la: IV. Nihil, inquit, usitatius, quam distinctiones omittere, aut male collocare. In Scripturis sacris, aliquid male collocatum a Scriptoribus suis, ego non concedo. De scriptis vulgaribus humanis non est quaestio. Scilicet nostri homines, id quod male collocatum in sacris, corrigent & emendabunt. Denique loci sententiam postulante, mutationem distinctionis ab Adversariis hic fieri, & non ab ipsorum mala hypothesi, & animi pervicacia, non persuadebunt.
units.tr: IV. "Nothing," he says, "is more common than to omit or misplace punctuation." In the holy Scriptures I do not concede that anything has been misplaced by its writers. The question does not concern common human writings. Of course our people will correct and emend whatever is misplaced in the sacred text. Finally, the adversaries will not persuade us that a change of punctuation is being made here, when the sense of the passage demands it, rather than by their own faulty hypothesis and stubbornness of mind.

units.la: V. Videamus argumentum: elogium benedicti Dei ubique tribuitur Patri, ergo Christo hic adscribi non potest. Negatur consequentia. Namque ipsi fatebuntur, plura & Patri, & Filio eadem attribui: quare ergo non & hoc? Tum in citatis locis est, benedictus Deus, & benedictus praeponitur, non uti in textu nostro postponitur, Deus benedictus: ibi εὐλογητὸς Θεὸς & cum articulo, ὁ Θεὸς, non Θεὸς εὐλογητὸς, quod praedicati loco est in sermone textus nostri; in aliis, subjecti, hic habet appositum suum verbum subsistantivum, ὁ ὢν Θεὸς εὐλογητὸς, qui est Deus significant, Ephes. 1. v. 21. constitutus super omnem principatum, & potestatem, & virtutem & dominationem, & omne nomen: &c. Et Philip. 2. v. 9. Donavit illi nomen, quod est super omne nomen. In quibus tamen omnibus illud observandum est, de quo admonet Apostolus 1 Cor. 15. v. 27. Cum autem dicat: Omnia subjecta sunt ei, sine dubio, praeter eum, qui subjecit ei omnia. Similiter caetera quoque epitheta, passim Christo attributa legimus. Ex quibus tamen non efficitur, illum aeternum, Patri coessentialem, coeli terraeque creatorem esse. Quod solum nos negamus, nam omnibus creatis Christum praelatum, & praeferendum esse, libenter & ingenue confitemur. Denique notum est ex Annotationibus Erasmi, vocem Deus, hic suspectam esse: neque enim eam Cyprianus, Hilarius & Chrysostomus legerunt, sed videtur esse addita ab aliquo divinitatis Christi nimis studiose, & Arianorum hoste. Quod quidem si admittatur, sententia erit perspicua, neque quidquam hic dicetur, quod Christi aeternam divinitatem confirmet.
units.tr: V. Let us look at the argument: the praise "blessed God" is everywhere given to the Father; therefore it cannot be ascribed to Christ here. The inference is denied. For they will themselves admit that many things are attributed both to the Father and to the Son in the same way; why then not this as well? Moreover, in the passages cited it is "blessed God", with the adjective placed before the noun, not "God blessed" as in our text, where it is placed after. There it is eulogētos Theos [εὐλογητὸς Θεὸς] with the article, ho Theos [ὁ Θεὸς], not Theos eulogētos [Θεὸς εὐλογητὸς], which in the wording of our text is in the position of a predicate; in other places it is the subject, here it has its own appended substantive verb, ho ōn Theos eulogētos [ὁ ὢν Θεὸς εὐλογητὸς], "who is God". Compare Eph. 1:21: "set above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name" etc., and Phil. 2:9: "He gave him a name which is above every name." Yet in all these passages one must observe what the Apostle warns of in 1 Cor. 15:27: "But when he says, 'All things are put under him', it is clear that this excludes him who put all things under him." Similarly we read the other epithets too, applied to Christ in many places. Yet from these it does not follow that he is eternal, co-essential with the Father, the creator of heaven and earth. This alone we deny; for we gladly and frankly confess that Christ is preferred and to be preferred above all creatures. Finally, it is well known from Erasmus's Annotations that the word God in this place is suspect: for Cyprian, Hilary and Chrysostom did not read it, but it seems to have been added by someone too eagerly zealous for the divinity of Christ, and an enemy of the Arians. If this is admitted, the sense will be plain, and nothing will be said here that confirms the eternal divinity of Christ.

units.la: Deus benedictus, in aliis subintelligitur, benedictus fit Deus. atque argumentum illud ex praeposita, vel postposita benedicti voce tantum fecit Socinus, contra Wiekum, ut propterea Erasmi interpunctionem deserere coactus fuerit, & agnoscere, verbi prolati Paulini testimonii omnia ad Christum referenda esse. Praeterea in omnibus locis, quibus dicitur, benedictus Deus, essentialiter intelligitur de Deo, & non de solo Patre opposite ad Christum, quamvis nonnunquam statim addatur Pater: ut illud non ad excludendum Christum adferri possit, quod eum connotat atque comprehendit, ejusdem essentiae ac naturae Deum. Quare εὐλογητὸς non est peculiare epitheton Deo Patri, sed Deo, quod propterea etiam Christo tribuitur, Deo, cum Patre, ὁμοούσιῳ. Nullibi vero sic Patri ut Patri, ut non quoque Christo adscribitur, qui & εὐλογημένος, quatenus inter homines versatus fuit Mediator, & εὐλογητὸς Deus super omnia. Denique nec sequitur, si vox εὐλογη-τὸς, & aliae similes quae hic leguntur, nunquam de alio, quam de solo Patre dicuntur; ergo Christo non applicandae: quidem si probaretur, nunquam de alio, quam de solo Patre dici illa posse. Nam alias argumentum stringit pro nobis, quando id quod solius Dei proprium, Christo quoque tribuitur. Etenim benedictum esse, ita soli Patri potest proprium dici, ut intelligatur in ordine ad creaturas, non ad Filium proprietas. Nam Patri tribuitur, qua Deo, cum sit elogium Dei, qui passim etiam in hoc sermone solet conjungi. Quare hinc argumentum nostrum pro vera Christi, unicaque & eadem cum Patre, deitate, confirmatur valde, neutiquam infringitur.
units.tr: "Blessed God" is understood in the other passages as "God is blessed." Socinus alone built his argument on the placing of the word "blessed" before or after, against Wiekus, and so he was forced to abandon Erasmus's punctuation and admit that everything said in the Pauline testimony must be referred to Christ. Moreover, in all the places where it is said "blessed God," it is understood essentially of God, and not of the Father alone as opposed to Christ, even though "the Father" is sometimes added straight away. Therefore that passage cannot be cited to exclude Christ, since the phrase implies and includes God of the same essence and nature as the Father. So εὐλογητὸς [blessed] is not a peculiar epithet of God the Father, but of God, and for that reason it is ascribed also to Christ, who is God, consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father. Nowhere is it ascribed to the Father as Father without also being ascribed to Christ, who is both "blessed" [εὐλογημένος], insofar as he lived among men as Mediator, and "blessed God over all" [εὐλογητὸς]. Finally, it does not follow that, because the word εὐλογητός and other similar words read here are never said of anyone but the Father alone, they must therefore not be applied to Christ. That would hold only if it were proved that they could never be said of anyone but the Father alone. Otherwise the argument works for us, when what belongs only to God is also attributed to Christ. For to be blessed can be called a property of the Father alone only in the sense that it is understood in relation to creatures, not as a property relating to the Son. It is attributed to the Father as God, since it is an epithet of God, and in this discourse it is commonly joined with the Father. Hence our argument for the true deity of Christ, one and the same with the Father, is greatly confirmed and in no way overturned.

units.la: v. Praeterea interpretationi Adversariorum, vel temerariae transpunctioni, unde illam conficiunt, repugnat non solum relativus ὁ, qui praemittitur, non postponitur voci Θεὸς, sed & substantivum verbum ὤν, qui est, qui est existens super omnia Deus benedictus: quemadmodum Rom. 1. 25. & servierunt creaturae potius quam creatori, qui est benedictus in saecula. Amen. est eadem connexio, qui est benedictus, cum antecedentibus, ac in nostro textu: neque magis hic, quam ibi potest fieri talis transmutatio, ac volunt. Deinde exire quidem in ejusmodi δοξολογίαν [?] sermonem, videmus, non vero abrumpi in epiphonema, quale adversarii fingunt, & omni connexione destitutum orationi obtrudunt atque ἀσυγκλώστως [?] interponunt. Neque una post σάρκα, sed & alia atque alia figenda iterum transpunctio erit post πάνττῶν, & post ϟ̈ς. Jam & eandem distinctionem servant antiquæ versiones. Arabica, ex quibus sunt Patres, & ex quibus est Christus, quantum attinet ad carnem, qui est immobiliter super omnia Deus benedictus in secula, vere. Æthiopica, Et illi sunt sacerdotes, & illi sunt patres nostri, & ex illis natus est Christus secundum carnem hominis, qui est Deus benedictus in secula, Amen. Syriaca quidem paulo aliter distinguit, in rem tamen haud dissimiliter, ex quibus apparuit Christus in carne, qui est Deus supra omnes. Cui sint laudes & benedictiones in secula seculorum, Amen. Denique concedamus lectionem vel mutationem distinctionum, quamcunque etiam Adversarii cupiunt, nihilominus de eodem Christo non solum poterunt, sed debebunt quoq; exponi quæ de Deo benedicto hic dicuntur, utpote proximè ei conjuncta, & non aliter commodius explicanda. Siquidem dixerat, Christum, secundum carnem: cui subjungit, qui est super omnia Deus: quacunque interpunctionis distinguantur notâ, res docet jungenda adeo invicem esse, deque eodem omnia interpretanda. Quod & confirmat restrictio in priori membro adhibita κῇ σαρκὶ, & τῷ κῇ σαρκὶ, ex quibus Christus quantum ad hoc, quod carnem spectat; cui quid magis oppositum & necessarium adjungi altero in membro debuit, ad tollendum Judæorum de Christo, ejusque humiliatione præjudicium, quam ut pergeret in exponendâ naturâ divinâ, & in ejus commemoratione ac laudatione desinaret? VII. Tandem & de Christo concedunt omnia fumi atque exponi, sed neque ita probari Christum verum Deum. Quibus si non probetur, tum quibus aliis probari possit, dicant. Cedo formulam verborum, quibus supra omnem suam exceptionem putent deitatem doceri: fallor si ipsi eam inventuri vel daturi sint ex voto. Christus Deus dicitur absolute, quomodo nemo usquam, præter solum verum Deum. Deus benedictus quoque nulli, quam vero Deo, attributum. Deus super omnia, absolute, non demum in aliqua, non nunc, sed in omnia prorsus & semper. neque enim Scriptura distinguit, vel limitat. I Cor. VIII. 6. per quem omnia, & nos per eum, & Col. I. 16. τὰ πάντα. Quod aperte negant Auctores lib. de falsa & vera unius Dei cognitione lib. II. cap. IV. Filium esse super omnia Deum. Uti quoque in omnia fæcula. Et clausula Amen in religiosa vera Dei nuncupatione locum habere solet. VIII. Quod autem Erasmus testatur, Cyprianum lib. II. adversus Iudæos, cap. V. adducere hunc locum, omissa Dei mentione: nec dicit, eum ita legisse in suo codice, vel alios, ac citavit; vel, si legisset, non esse sequendam lectionem nostram vulgarem & communem, quam, teste eodem Erasmo, confirmat omnium exemplarium consensus. Et hoc certe loco, inquit, Paulus palam Christum pronunciavit Deum, & consentiunt, quæ quidem viderim, Græcorum exemplaria. Non autem nos latet, in quam suspicionem venerit Erasmus apud cujusque gentis & professionis Theologos, quasi non bene de Christi deitate sensisset: de quo quidquid sit, id certo scimus, Adversarios nostros eum pro suo passim vindicare & adferre. Unde Auctores librorum, de falsa & vera unius Dei Patris, &c. cognitione lib. I. cap. IX. Erasmum, cum Servetò, quibus & Martinum addunt Cellarium, inter patriarchas suos constituerat: atque cap. VII. ex Annotationibus Erasmi per totum N. T. adferunt sequiores expositiones: tum inter illas etiam, id quod statuit de loco nostro, Rom. IX. 5. Præterea Christus appellatur magnus Deus, & cum articulo, magnus ille Deus, Tit. II. 13. ex-spectantes beatam spem & apparitionem gloriæ ἡμῶν μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Ubi Jesus servator dicitur, quamvis absque articulo, non minus tamen verè ille servator: at & Deus ille magnus, cum articulo, atque sine notâ in-tercisionis, uti & in versione Arabica. Ut & nomen Dei, & propria Dei elogia veri, benedicti, magni in eum competant, sintque totidem argumenta verae & supremae deitatis. Servetus, lib. 1. de Trinitate, pag. 15. non solum enim illa divinitatis nomina non rejicio, sed per excellentiam Christo convenire dico. Ideo ad notandam differentiam ab aliis diis, additur; Deus omnis terrae, Deus magnus, terribilis, fortis, mirabilis, & super omnia benedictus.
units.tr: v. Moreover, the relative ὁ [ho], which stands before the word Θεὸς [God] and not after it, is opposed to the Adversaries' interpretation, or to the rash repunctuation by which they make it. So too is the substantive verb ὤν [being]: "who is, who is God over all, blessed." Compare Rom. 1.25: "and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen." The connection of "who is blessed" with what precedes is the same here as in our text, and such a change cannot be made here any more than there, as they wish. Next, we see that the discourse does pass into a doxology [δοξολογίαν], but it does not break off into an exclamation of the kind the Adversaries invent, which lacks all connection with what precedes and is forced into the sentence asyndetically [ἀσυγκλώστως]. Nor would the punctuation have to be placed once after "flesh," but another and another punctuation would have to be placed again after "all things" and after the next word. Also, the ancient versions keep the same punctuation. The Arabic version, from which come the Fathers and from which Christ comes as far as the flesh is concerned: "who is immovably God over all, blessed for ever, truly." The Ethiopic: "And they are priests, and they are our fathers, and from them Christ was born according to the flesh of man, who is God blessed for ever, Amen." The Syriac punctuates somewhat differently, but to much the same effect: "from whom Christ appeared in the flesh, who is God over all. To whom be praises and blessings for ever and ever, Amen." Finally, let us grant any reading or change of punctuation the Adversaries like: still, what is said here of the blessed God can and must be explained of the same Christ, since it is joined most closely to him and cannot be explained more fittingly in any other way. For he has just said "Christ, according to the flesh," and then adds "who is God over all." Whatever mark of punctuation is used, the sense shows that the two must be joined and everything interpreted of the same person. The restriction used in the first clause, "according to the flesh" [κατὰ σάρκα] and "as to the flesh" [τῷ κατὰ σάρκα], confirms this: Christ is spoken of in respect of what concerns the flesh. What could more fittingly and necessarily be added in the second clause, to remove the Jews' prejudice concerning Christ and his humiliation, than to go on to speak of his divine nature and end with its commemoration and praise? VII. Finally, they concede that everything is taken and explained of Christ, but they deny that Christ is proved to be true God. If it is not proved by this, let them say by what other means it can be proved. Let them give me the form of words by which, beyond all exception, they think the deity is taught. I am mistaken if they are ever going to find or give one to their liking. Christ is called God absolutely, which nobody is anywhere, except the only true God. Blessed God is also attributed to no one but the true God. God over all, absolutely, not only in some respect, not for now, but over all things, entirely and always. For Scripture does not distinguish or limit it: 1 Cor. 8.6, "by whom are all things, and we by him," and Col. 1.16, τὰ πάντα [all things]. The authors of the book On the False and True Knowledge of the One God, book 2, chapter 4, clearly deny this, namely that the Son is God over all, and for ever. The closing "Amen" also customarily belongs to the true and religious naming of God. VIII. As for Erasmus's statement that Cyprian, in book 2 Against the Jews, chapter 5, cites this passage with the mention of God omitted, he does not say that Cyprian read it so in his codex, or other codices, as he cited it; or, if he did read it so, that our common and usual reading should not be followed, which, as Erasmus himself testifies, is confirmed by the agreement of all the copies. And in this passage, he says, Paul plainly declared Christ to be God, and the Greek copies, so far as I have seen, agree. We are not unaware of the suspicion Erasmus fell under among theologians of every nation and profession, as if he had not thought rightly about Christ's deity. Whatever the truth of that, we know for certain that our Adversaries everywhere claim him for their own and cite him. Hence the authors of the books On the False and True Knowledge of the One God the Father, etc., book 1, chapter 9, placed Erasmus among their patriarchs, together with Servetus, and they add Martin Cellarius. In chapter 7 they cite from Erasmus's Annotations, throughout the whole New Testament, the later expositions, including the one he proposed for our passage, Rom. 9.5. Moreover, Christ is called "the great God," with the article, "that great God," in Titus 2.13: "looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great God [τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ] and of our Saviour Jesus Christ." Here Jesus is called Saviour without the article, yet he is none the less truly that Saviour; but the great God is with the article, and without any mark of division, as also in the Arabic version. So both the name of God and the proper epithets of God, true, blessed, great, belong to him, and they are so many proofs of true and supreme deity. Servetus, book 1 On the Trinity, p. 15: For I do not only not reject those names of divinity, but I say that they belong to Christ pre-eminently. Therefore, to mark the difference from other gods, it is added: God of all the earth, great God, terrible, strong, wonderful, and blessed over all.

units.la: Exceptio aliqua generalis Adversariorum solvenda ante omnia venit, de nomine Dei, quod dicunt, non esse naturae, sed dignitatis tantum: non significare naturam divinam, sed potestatem, dignitatem, dominium: quare, exinde quod quis Deus nominatur, verum & naturâ Deum argui non posse. Socinus, contra Volanum, Resp. pri. pag. 26. Sed an nescis, hoc nomen Deus non esse nomen proprium, sed appellativum, & idem significare, quod dominator, judex, seu gubernator, potens, seu fortis, benefactor, & ejusmodi alia nomina? in Catechesi, pag. 25. Nempe divinum ipsius Christi in nos imperium ac majestas, unde merito & Deus, & noster Deus esse dicitur. Dei siquidem nomen non substantiam sive essentiam ipsam illius, cui tribuitur, significat, nec alicujus substantiae sive essentiae est revera proprium, sed est nomen, ut vocant, appellativum, quo in Hebraica lingua, cujus idiotismis referta sunt ipsa novi testamenti Graeca scripta, significatur potentia, & inde potestas, & idcirco ii qui potentia aut potestate aliqua sunt praediti, dii in sacris litteris vocantur, ita ut non modo angeli, quorum robur & virtus major est, quam hominum dominationem aliquam habentium, sed ipsi homines qui munere aliquo cum potestate quadam conjuncto funguntur, Dei nomine decorentur. Adeo ut simpliciter atque absolute Dii esse dicantur. De Angelis testimonia habes Psal. 8. & 97. interprete praesertim scriptore epist. ad Hebr. cap. 1. & 2. De hominibus vero potestate aliqua praeditis, testantur hi loci, Exod. 21. v. 6. & 22. v. 8. & 28. atque ut alia non pauca omittam, insigne est illud testimonium Psa. 82. Ego dixi Dii estis. Eadem Crellius, lib. de Deo & attributis, cap. xiii. & in Praef. contra librum Grotii, de satisfactione. Smalcius, in Exam. c. error. pag. 5. Volkelius, lib. v. pag. 422. Oftorodus, Institut. cap. x. & caeteri passim. Atque ante eos Servetus, lib. 1. Deus, non est nomen naturae. Franciscus Davidis, in Confessione, quam ex carcere exhibuit, a. & 1 lxxxix [?]. d. xvii. Aprilis, in initio, Iesum Christum Messiam promissum, filium Dei in plenitudine temporis exhibitum, non natura, sed officio Deum fuisse, fateor. Sommerus, contra Carolium, lib. 11. cap. 11. illud enim nescire non potest, vocabulum Dei dignitatis & officii esse nomen, non autem naturae. & cap. iii. est enim officii & dignitatis nomen, Deum esse, non naturae. Cap. vi. Sequitur igitur officii ratione eum appellari Iehovah.
units.tr: First of all, a general objection of the Adversaries has to be answered, namely that the name God is not a name of nature but of dignity only: that it signifies not the divine nature but power, dignity, dominion; so that from the fact that someone is called God, it cannot be argued that he is God by nature and in truth. Socinus, against Volanus, first answer, p. 26: But do you not know that this name God is not a proper name but an appellative, and that it means the same as ruler, judge or governor, mighty or strong, benefactor, and other names of that kind? In the Catechism, p. 25: that is, the divine rule and majesty of Christ over us, from which he is rightly called both God and our God. For the name of God signifies not the substance or essence itself of him to whom it is given, nor is it truly proper to any substance or essence, but it is a name, as they call it, appellative, by which in the Hebrew language, whose idioms fill the Greek writings of the New Testament itself, power is signified, and from that authority; and therefore those who are endowed with some power or authority are called gods in Holy Writ, so that not only the angels, whose strength and virtue are greater than that of men exercising some dominion, but men themselves who discharge some office joined with a certain authority, are adorned with the name of God. So much so that they are called gods simply and absolutely. On the angels you have testimonies in Psalms 8 and 97, especially as interpreted by the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapters 1 and 2. On men endowed with some power, these passages bear witness: Exodus 21.6 and 22.8 and 28, and, to omit many others, that famous testimony of Psalm 82: I have said, You are gods. Crellius says the same in his book On God and His Attributes, chapter 13, and in the preface against Grotius's book on satisfaction. Smalcius, in the Examination of the Chapter of Errors, p. 5. Volkelius, book 5, p. 422. Ostorodus, Institutes, chapter 10, and the others everywhere. And before them Servetus, book 1: God is not a name of nature. Franciscus Davidis, in the Confession which he presented from prison, on 17 April, at the beginning: I confess that Jesus Christ, the Messiah promised, the Son of God revealed in the fullness of time, was God not by nature but by office. Sommer, against Carolus, book 2, chapter 2: for he cannot be ignorant that the word God is a name of dignity and office, not of nature. And chapter 3: for it is a name of office and dignity, that he is God, not of nature. Chapter 6: It follows therefore that by reason of office he is called Jehovah.

units.la: Nam non de solo nomine Dei ita sentiunt Adversarii, sed & de omnibus aliis, quibus Deus notari solet, sive Hebraicis nominibus, sive Graecis, appellativa esse, non propria, & Deo quidem κατ' ἐξοχὴν tribui, sed naturâ suâ esse communia, & significare eum, qui vel potentia seu viribus, vel potestate, atque imperio, vel utraque re eminet, praesertim ita ut rerum naturalium modo supergrediatur.
