Sed in excellentissima significatione accepta, designare eum, cujus & vires, & potestas, atque imperium absolute summum est, & independens, inquit Crellius, lib. de Deo, pag. 90. atque ita duplicem nominum divinorum constituunt significationem; unam laxiorem & communem, alteram angustiorem, & supremo Numini peculiarem. Atque eodem modo, sive de voce Θεὸς Deus, sive de nomine El. cap. viii, sive Eloah, & Elohim cap. ix. Adonai, cap. x. Κυρίος, cap. xiv. sive etiam Iehovah, philosophatur, cap. xi. quod quoque originis ac naturæ significationis ratione commune esse afferere haud dubitat.
units.tr: Nor do our Adversaries hold this only of the name of God, but of all the other names by which God is usually designated, whether Hebrew or Greek: they say these are appellatives, not proper names, and that they are indeed attributed to God [κατ' ἐξοχήν] by preeminence, yet are common by their nature, and signify one who excels either in strength or power, or in authority and command, or in both, especially in a way that surpasses the nature of created things. But when taken in its most excellent sense, they say, the name designates him whose strength, power and command is absolutely supreme and independent, as Crellius says in his book on God, p. 90. In this way they set up a twofold signification of the divine names: one looser and common, the other narrower and peculiar to the supreme Deity. In the same way, whether he is speaking of the word Θεός [God], or of the name El (ch. 8), or Eloah and Elohim (ch. 9), Adonai (ch. 10), Κύριος [Lord] (ch. 14), or even Jehovah (ch. 11), he philosophises, and he does not hesitate to assert that this name too is common, by reason of its origin and the meaning of its nature.

units.la: Ex adverso non quidem negamus, Deo etiam tribui nomina communia & appellativa; sed sola talia, nulla propria, hoc negamus. 11. Propria Dei nomina connotent & consignificent Dei quoque potestatem & dominium, prout Dei natura illa includit, & nunquam à se amovet, sed ut Dei nomina omnia, & propria quæ dicimus, verbi causa nomen Dei, Iehovæ, &c. primo denotet illud, & non Dei naturam, & proprie hoc, ac solum, pernegamus: sed dicimus esse nomina naturæ & essentiæ, & hanc primo designare. Quare in hoc vertitur controversia, an nulla Deus habeat nomina propria; verum omnia ejus nomina sint appellativa? Quod negamus, & duplici argumento, primum generali, de Dei nominibus; inde speciali, de nominibus istis Dei, Jehovæ, & quæ ejusdem ordinis ac naturæ.
units.tr: On the other side, we do not deny that common and appellative names are also attributed to God; but we deny that only such names are attributed to him, and that none are proper. We deny flatly that the proper names of God, such as the name of God, Jehovah, and so on, primarily denote that power and dominion (which the nature of God includes and never puts away from itself) and not the nature of God, and that they denote this properly and only this. We say rather that they are names of nature and essence, and that they primarily designate this. Hence the controversy turns on this: whether God has no proper names, and all his names are appellatives. This we deny, on a twofold argument: first a general one, about the names of God; then a particular one, about those names of God, Jehovah, and others of the same order and nature.

units.la: Arg.. Qui habet essentiam, nulla ratione communem, sed distinctam & singularem; qui proprietates essentiæ suæ propriissimas; cujusque actiones similes, id est, propriæ, non communes, is ut inter nomina sua etiam habeat propria, requiritur: sed Deus habet essentiam, proprietates, actiones proprias: ergo. Huc accedit, quod illa Dei, quibus denotatur, nomina, ex ejus vel essentia vel proprietatibus petita sint vel actionibus, ut proprie proximeque designent ea, quæ Deo propriissima: Quare ejusdem quoque rationis nomina ut sint, id est, propria est necessum. Quid indignius, quam ubi omnes res sua habent nomina, & Adamus sua animalibus dedit, Genes. 11. 19.20. solus Deus non nominibus careat, sed nullum habeat sibi proprium, omnia cum creaturis communia? Quando dicitur, Deum nomine non egere, hoc non ita accipiendum est, quasi nullum nomen proprium habeat, sibi soli conveniens, sed quod nullo nomine opus habeat distingui ab aliis, ceu Diis. Cæterum uti nominis officium duplex est, designare, & distinguere, atq; hoc ab aliis, præsertim sui similibus, hac sola ratione postremâ Deus non eget nomine, nisi quod quo designatur, etiam distinguitur satis: ut hoc quod Dei nobis essentiam notat, eoq; Deo proprium nomen est, & designat, & distinguit eum nobis ab aliis omnibus, à quibus Deus vel Dei essentia non quidem necesse a-deo habet distingui per se, quasi citra hoc vel communis, vel non distincta satis, ac nos quidem eum distinguere per illa sæpe cogimur, designare semper. Ut caute admodum, & cum diligenti respectu ad hos scopulos de nominibus Dei propriis, vel disputatione super eo cum Socinians præsenti accipiendum fit, quod quandoque dici solet, Deum non habere nomen. Nomen appellativum est, quod multis commune est ob communem naturam, ut homo, urbs, flumen: sic olim ex Grammatica recitavimus. Proprium, quod uni rei singulatim datum est, ut Petrus, Colonia, Rhenus, Interrogo nunc Adversariorum nostrorum conscientiam: an nomen Dei, nomen Jehova, proprium debeat dici, an appellativum? Num ob naturam Deo cum aliis communem, Deo nomen illud tribuitur? An Deo non tam singulatim, ut enti singulari, competit suum nomen, ac huic nomen Petri, Coloniæ, Rheni? Certe nisi contra omnem rationem, sensumque, atque adeo proprium animi loqui velimus, manifestum est, Dei illa nomina, si quæ usquam alia, propria & singularia esse, non appellativa, vel communia. Inspiciamus eorum aliqua. Esse ens αὐτὸν[?], quodque propterea dicitur Jehova; vel ex proprietatibus, omnipotens, יהוה[?]; vel ex operibus creator, an aliquid dicunt commune aliis, & non tota sui ratione uni competunt Deo, uti res, ita & nomina? Etenim nomina rerum sunt, earum signa, & quales res, talia nomina. Seu res hic intueamur, seu nomina, nihil uspiam est quod non soli Deo sit proprium, & propriissimum.
units.tr: Argument. He who has an essence that is not common in any way, but distinct and singular; who has properties most proper to his essence; and whose actions are of a like kind, that is, proper and not common, must of necessity have proper names among his names. But God has an essence, properties and actions that are his own. Therefore God has proper names. Moreover, the names by which God is designated are taken from his essence, his properties or his actions, so that they designate, properly and most closely, what is most proper to God. Hence names of the same kind must be proper. What could be more unworthy than this: that all things have their names, and Adam gave names to the animals (Gen. 2.19-20 [printed "Genes. 11. 19.20"]), yet God alone should lack names, having none proper to himself but all in common with creatures? When it is said that God has no need of a name, this is not to be taken to mean that he has no proper name belonging to him alone, but that he has no need of a name to distinguish him from others, such as gods. For the office of a name is twofold, to designate and to distinguish; and as for distinguishing him from others, especially from his like, God has no need of a name for this reason alone, since whatever designates him also distinguishes him sufficiently. So the name which expresses to us the essence of God, and is therefore proper to God, both designates him and distinguishes him for us from all others. God, or the essence of God, does not indeed need to be distinguished of itself, as if without this it were either common or not sufficiently distinct; but we are often forced to distinguish him by these names, while we always designate him by them. This must be understood with great caution, and with careful regard to these rocks concerning the proper names of God, or in the present dispute with the Socinians, whenever it is sometimes said that God has no name. An appellative name is one common to many because of a common nature, as man, city, river; so we recited from grammar long ago. A proper name is one given singly to a single thing, as Peter, Cologne, Rhine. I now ask the conscience of our Adversaries: ought the name of God, the name Jehovah, to be called proper or appellative? Is that name given to God because of a nature he shares with others? Or does his name belong to God not in common, as to some one of a kind, but singly, to a single being, as the names Peter, Cologne and Rhine belong to their objects? Certainly, unless we wish to speak against all reason and common sense, and indeed against our own mind, it is plain that those names of God, if any names anywhere, are proper and singular, not appellative or common. Let us look at some of them. That he is the one who is [ὁ ὤν], and is therefore called Jehovah; or, from his properties, Almighty; or, from his works, Creator: do they say anything here which is common to others? Do not these names, in their whole nature, belong to God alone, just as things do, and so do their names? For names are the signs of things, and such as the things are, such are the names. Whether we look here at things or at names, there is nothing anywhere that is not proper and most proper to God alone.

units.la: Hoc in genere: in specie de Dei nominibus, primum de nomine Deus. Dicimus naturam Dei notare & significare per se ac primo, non solam oteftatem[?], aut dominium. Quod probamus hoc quidem modo. 1. Quia nihil praeter eum Deus vel dici potest, vel esse. II. Nihil natura Deus. III. Is verus Deus. IV. Atque solus.v. De-nique ex abstracto Deitas, quod naturam denotat, ergo ejus quoque concretum, Deus. Nihil aliud Deus dici potest, nihil Deus esse, praeter unum illum verum: ergo no-men Dei non est commune. Probo, quia quae praeter Deum Dii dicuntur, λεγό-μενοι ϑεοί, non in singulari, & simpliciter vel absolutè Deus dici possunt. Imò in hoc illis opponitur supremum Numen, quòd solus Deus sit, dicaturque, non ita re-liqua. 1 Cor. VIII. 4. Scimus, quòd idolum nihil est in mundo, & quòd non sit alius Deus, quam unus. 5. Nam quamvis sint multi dicti Dii, sive in terrâ, quemadmodum sunt Dii multi & Domini multi. 6. Verum nobis unus Deus est Pater, &c. Opponuntur Dii, & Deus: illi, sive idola, sive dignitate aliquâ in caelo, ut Angeli, aut in terrâ, ut Magistratus, praediti, quotquot Dii appellantur λεγόμενοι ϑεοί, ne de solis idolis accipiamus, non sunt Deus, nam Deus est modo unus, id est, unus cui ut natura, ita nomen Dei competit, caeteri propter aliquam, non communitatem, sed similitudinem, seu veram, uti Magistratus & Angeli, seu fictam, ut idola, non ϑεὸς, sed ϑεοί sunt, iisque λεγό-μενοι, non ὄντως tales. Hi per catachresim, isti per metaphoram λεγόμενοι Dii, omnes improprie, solus Deus proprie sic dicitur. Diximus, quid appellativum sit, nunc etiam tenendum, quid metaphora, ut utrumque bene distinguatur à nomine proprio, pateatque omni ratione, Dei nomen esse proprium, nunquam appellativum, quamvis aliquando fiat metaphoricum. Metaphora, uti ex Rhetoricis repetimus, est tropus, quo verbum à propria significatione in alienam transfertur, ob similitudinem. Et quemadmodum tria hic spectantur, ita primi loci est significatio propria, tum im-propria, propter aliquam nempe similitudinem; verum praesupponit semper significationem propriam. Ut quando vox Dei per metaphoram aliis tribuitur, hoc ipsum ostendat vocem alteri propriam esse, id est, summo Numini. Unde ita arguimus. Vox Dei quando Deo tribuitur, & hominibus, illi simpliciter, his cum relatione aliquâ, & quando aliqui dicuntur Dii, vel proprie utrumque fit, vel improprie, vel hoc, aut illud proprie, & improprie. Non potes dicere, utrumque improprie, nam impro-pria loquutio aliam semper praesupponit propriam: & si alterutri proprium nomen, non opinor denegabis hoc Deo. Superest modò, ut aliis praeter Deum vox eadem proprie competat, aut improprie. Illud dici nequit, quia non communem habent essentiam aut naturam; sed suam Deus propriam: ergo aliis tribuitur improprie, & per metaphoram. Quod evincit, nomen hoc, super quo contendimus, Deo soli proprium esse, aliis nullis commune. Hinc Smiglecius Jesuita haud male in Notis monstris novi Arianismi, part. III. scripsit de Deo, & Filio Dei Metaphorico quem statuere videantur & colere Adversarii. Nec certe ex hoc loco argumentamur, quomodo argumentantes nos facit Enjedinus: Galatae cognoverunt natura Deum: At Galatae cognoverunt Christum: Ergo Christus est natura Deus, non magis quam sic: Galatae cognoverunt natura Deum: Galatae cognoverunt Paulum Apostolum: Ergo Paulus Apostolus est natura Deus. Non nescii, syllogismum ex puris particulari-bus non concludere, & eum qui quatuor constat terminis, ineptum esse. Verum inde concludimus, nomen Dei naturæ nomen esse, & Deitatis designare naturam: quaré Christum, qui absolute Deus appellatur, esse natura Deum, non ex eorum numero, qui natura non sunt Dii. Deinde, Deus dicitur, atque est natura Deus, alii non natura Dii: ergo Deus naturæ nomen est. Quomodo enim dicimus, Deus est natura potens, natura Dominus; sic etiam natura Deus. Quod dici neque intelligi potest, nisi vox Dei, naturam denotans vox sit. Gal. iv. 8. Tunc non nosceutes Deum, serviistis τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς. Nec Deus sunt, nec dici possunt alii non natura Dii. Non noviistis Deum. Hic verus solus Deus est, atque nominari Deus potest: alii minimè. Neque enim qui in aliis defixus, ignorare dicitur supremum & solùm viventem, sed Deum: nam non alius Deus præter eum, neque Deum esse, ulla ratione commune habet cum aliis. Deinde in textu, majoris explicationis causa, additum, non natura Dii. quorsum? nisi ut notet, unum illum natura Deum esse, atque idcirco solum sic nominandum. Uti si dixero, non natura homines, de fictis pictisque; significabit, nomen hominis designare naturam: sic Deus, naturâ Deus, naturam notat, non communem, sed singularem Dei.
units.tr: So much in general. In particular, concerning the names of God: first, concerning the name God itself. We say that the name God signifies and designates the nature of God primarily and of itself, and not merely his power or dominion. We prove this in the following way. 1. Because nothing but him can be called God, or be God. 2. Nothing is God by nature except him. 3. He is the true God. 4. And he alone is God. Finally, from the abstract noun Deity, which denotes his nature, it follows that its concrete term, God, does too. Nothing else can be called God, and nothing else is God, except that one true God; therefore the name of God is not common. I prove this, because those who are called gods besides God, [λεγόμενοι θεοί] (as they are called), cannot be called God in the singular, or simply and absolutely. Indeed, the supreme Deity is set against them in this, that he alone is God and is so called, and the others are not. 1 Cor. 8.4: "We know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one." 5: "For though there be that are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth (as there be gods many, and lords many)." 6: "But to us there is but one God, the Father, etc." Here gods and God are set against each other. Those gods, whether idols, or beings endowed with some dignity in heaven, such as angels, or on earth, such as magistrates, however many are called gods [λεγόμενοι θεοί] (not to be taken only of idols), are not God; for God is one only, that is, the one to whom the nature of God belongs and the name of God belongs too. The others are called gods because of some resemblance, not a common nature but a likeness, either true, as magistrates and angels, or false, as idols; they are not θεὸς but θεοί, and are called gods, not really such. The latter are called gods by catachresis, the former by metaphor; all are improperly so called, and God alone is properly so called. I have said what an appellative is; now we must also grasp what a metaphor is, so that both are well distinguished from a proper name, and it is clear in every respect that the name of God is proper and never appellative, although it sometimes becomes metaphorical. A metaphor, as we recall from the rhetoricians, is a trope by which a word is transferred from its proper meaning to an alien one, on account of a likeness. And as three things are looked at here, so the first place belongs to the proper meaning, then to the improper, on account of some likeness; yet it always presupposes a proper meaning. So when the word God is applied metaphorically to others, this very thing shows that the word is proper to another, that is, to the supreme Deity. Hence we argue thus. When the word God is applied both to God and to men, it is applied to God simply and to men with some relation; and when some are called gods, either both uses are proper, or both are improper, or one is proper and the other improper. You cannot say that both are improper, for an improper usage always presupposes a proper one; and if the name is proper to either, I do not think you will deny it is proper to God. It remains only that the same word applies to others besides God either properly or improperly. The first cannot be said, because they do not have a common essence or nature, but God has his own. Therefore it is applied to others improperly, and by metaphor. This proves that this name, about which we are contending, is proper to God alone and common to none others. Hence the Jesuit Smiglecius rightly wrote in his Notes on the Monsters of the New Arianism, part III, about a metaphorical God and Son of God, such as our Adversaries seem to set up and worship. Nor indeed do we argue from this passage in the way that Enjedinus makes us argue: "The Galatians knew God by nature; but the Galatians knew Christ; therefore Christ is God by nature," no more than in this way: "The Galatians knew God by nature; the Galatians knew Paul the Apostle; therefore Paul the Apostle is God by nature." I am not unaware that a syllogism made of purely particular premises does not conclude, and that one with four terms is faulty. But we conclude from this that the name God is the name of a nature, and that the name of Deity designates a nature; therefore Christ, who is called God absolutely, is God by nature, and not one of those who are not gods by nature. Further, God is called God and is God by nature, while others are gods but not by nature; therefore God is the name of a nature. For just as we say that God is powerful by nature and Lord by nature, so too we say God by nature. This could neither be said nor understood unless the word God were a word denoting nature. Gal. 4.8: "Then, not knowing God, you served those which by nature are not gods [τοῖς μὴ φύσει θεοῖς]." Those others are neither God nor can they be called gods by nature. You did not know God: this one is the true and only God, and can be named God; the others not at all. For he who is fixed on other things is not said to be ignorant of the supreme and only living being, but of God; for there is no other God besides him, and his being God has nothing in common with others in any way. Moreover, in the text, added for greater explanation, "not gods by nature": why? Unless to show that he alone is God by nature, and therefore is alone to be so named. Just as if I said "men not by nature" of fictitious or painted ones, it would signify that the name man designates a nature; so God, God by nature, signifies the nature of God, not common but singular.

units.la: Quâ ratione verus Deus dicitur, nisi vox Dei naturam significet? ut verus homo; verus lapis: vel ut in re potius singulari instemus, verus sol. Ac proinde, quum alia, præter illum, non sint verus Deus, id est, nihil verè Dei, aut verae Deitatis, vel divinæ veritatis habeant, Deus etiam vere dici nequeunt.Et quando jam Deus alicujus, vel Dii appellantur, non vere, sed metaphorice, & catachrestice sic dicuntur. Joann. xvii. 3. ut te cognoscant verum Deum. 1 Joann. v. 20. hic est verus ille Deus, 1 Thess. i. 9. Deo vivo & vero. Quod etiam aliud suppeditat argumentum, nempe ut solus Deus, & verus Deus sit, qui vitam Dei habet; quod certe nullis commune. Adeoque significatur etiam, nomen Dei, vitæ esse, & naturam Dei viventem significare: quod si vitam notet, ergo naturam, ergo non est nomen solius potestatis. Matth. xvi. 16. Tu es Filius Dei viventis. Enjedinus, in Col. ii. 9. certe negari non potest, quin vox θεὸς etiam denotet subsistentiam.
units.tr: By what reasoning is he called the true God, unless the word God signifies his nature? It is like calling something a true man or a true stone, or, to take a more specific example, a true sun. Therefore, since there are no other true gods besides him, that is, since the others have nothing truly divine, nor any true Deity or divine truth, they cannot truly be called God either. Whenever others are called gods, or a god, they are so called not truly but metaphorically and catachrestically. John 17:3: that they may know thee the true God. 1 John 5:20: this is the true God. 1 Thess. 1:9: to serve the living and true God. This supplies a further argument: only he who has the life of God is the sole and true God, and this certainly belongs to no one else. So the name God is also shown to signify life, and to denote the living nature of God. If it denotes life, then it denotes nature, and so it is not the name of power alone. Matt. 16:16: Thou art the Son of the living God. Enjedinus, on Col. 2:9: it certainly cannot be denied that the word θεὸς [theos] also denotes subsistence.

units.la: iv. Est solus Deus. Quod directè contrariatur formæ nominis appellativi: nam hoc non soli alicui, sed pluribus debetur; & fundatur in natura communi, quæ ubi non est, neque appellativi ratio esse potest. Observandumque, jungi in notatione Dei, solum, & verum. Joann. xvii. 5. te solum verum Deum. Marc. xii. 32. Unus est Deus, neque est alius præter eum. 1 Cor. viii. 4. & non est Deus alius, nisi unus. Valde συγγενικῶς[?], non est Deus alius primò; tum, nisi unus. v. Concretum nomen est synonimum abstractivo: atqui abstractivum Deitas, quod occurrit Col. ii. 9. est naturæ nomen, atque essentiæ: expresseque distinguitur à potestate & potentia Dei. Rom. i. 20. æterna ejus δύναμις ἡ θειότης[?]. Non est ergo Deus solius potestatis nomen vel imperii. Athanasius, in epist. de decretis Nicænæ Synodi: Cum dicimus Deum, & nominamus Patrem, nihil nos eorum, quæ circa eum sunt, sed ipsius substantiam significamus.
units.tr: iv. He is the only God. This directly contradicts the form of an appellative name, for an appellative is owed not to one alone but to many, and it rests on a common nature, and where there is no common nature there can be no appellative. It should also be noted that only and true are joined in the designation of God. John 17:3: thee, the only true God. Mark 12:32: There is one God, and there is none other but he. 1 Cor. 8:4: and there is none other God but one. Very closely related [συγγενικῶς], first: "there is not another God"; then: "except one." v. A concrete name is synonymous with the abstract. But the abstract term Deity, which occurs at Col. 2:9, is a name of nature and essence, and it is expressly distinguished from the power and might of God. Rom. 1:20: his eternal power and divinity [δύναμις ἡ θειότης]. So God is not a name of power or dominion alone. Athanasius, in his letter on the decrees of the Nicene Synod: When we say God, and name the Father, we signify nothing of those things which are about him, but his very substance.

units.la: Facilius idem demonstrabimus in nomine Iehova, Deo hoc proprium esse, non commune aut appellativum. Sive respexerimus, 1. ejus etymologiam & originem, quæ est ab הָיָה[?] vel מִן[?] fuit, ut suâ vi vox naturam, vel essentiam Dei denotet. Unde Hebræi appellant שם הוה[?] nomen substantiæ, vel essentiæ. Quam ejus vim & notationem Deus prodidit, Exod. iii. 14. 15. ubi quærebatur de Dei nomine, nam quando dicent mihi Israëlitæ, inquiebat Moses, quis misit te, quod nomen ejus, quid dicam illis? & respondit Deus Mosi אהיה אשר אהיה ero qui ero. & dixit, ita dices filiis Israel, ero misit me ad vos. Dixitque insuper Iehova ad Mosem, ita dices filiis Israël, Iehova Deus Patrum vestrorum, Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci, & Deus Iacobi misit me ad vos, hoc nomen meum in æternum, & hoc memoriale meum de generatione in generationem. Deus hic prodit nomen suum Iehova, quod suum dicit nomen esse æternum, & memoriale perpetuum, ejusque expositionem vel etymologiam præmittit, ero qui ero. Idem denotatur utroque: nam utrumque ei datur pro nomine mittentis Mosem ad populum, atque de hoc & illo pariter inquit Deus, hoc est nomen meum, quo ego denotari & jam, & in posterum semper debeo. Confer Gabrielis Vasquez Disputat. lix. in i. Thomæ. Ero qui ero, sum qui sum, non ab aliquo attributo Deum notat, sed ab ejus essentia, essentia absolutissimè consideratâ, non sub aliquo ejus modo, aut restrictiva consideratione; sed nominat ipsum pelagus substantiæ infinitum, inquit Thomas bene, i. qu. xiii. art. xi. Atq; essentiam Dei significat immutabilem, eandem semper, sive in præsenti nostro, præterito, aut futuro. Unde triplicis temporis notas in hoc nomine Hebræi observant, characteristicum futuri in ';& ' participii præsentis; ' præteriti. Johannes in Apocalypsi, cap. i. 4. ὁ ὢν, ἡ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [?], id est, ad omnes temporis differentias semper idem, qui à seipso & per essentiam est id quod est, omnisque extra se essentiæ alterius auctor. Quare nomen hoc est Deo proprium, satisq; manifeste essentiam Dei propriam significans. Crellius ipse, cap. xi. de Deo & attrib. pag. 79. nomen hoc Deum unum ita significat, ut diversæ ejus attributa, naturæ vinculo inter se colligata, animis nostris insinuet. Deinde ex Scripturâ idem probatur, esse nomen hoc Deo proprium. Quia Deus toties dicit hoc nomen suum, memoriale. Exod. iii. 15. hoc est nomen meum. & vi. 22. 24. 25. Iesa. xvi. 21. & xlii. 8. Ierem. xvi. 21. & xliv. 26. Hos. xii. 5. Quo nomine denotari voluit, solitusq; est notari solum. Psalm. lxxxviii. 19. ut cognoscant te, qui soli nomen est Iehova, אתה שמך יהוה לבך, excelsus עליון super omnem terram. Distinguitur nomen Iehova, ab Excelso עליון: non ergo illud est nomen potestatis solum. atque Dei dicitur nomen esse Iehova suum, solum, שמך, & לבך. Amos. v. 6. 8. i. Reg. xviii. 21. Si Iehova Deus אם יהוה האלהים, sequimini eum &c. 36. ô Iehova, Deus Abrahami. 39. Dixerunt, Iehova ipse Deus est, Iehova ipse Deus est, היה הוא [?] האלהים. Atq; inde Judæi appellant שם המיוחד, nomen proprium Dei. R. David Kimchi, in Iesa. xl. ii. 8. Iehova, hoc est nomen meum, הוא שמי המיוחד לי, inquit, hoc nomen meum mihi proprium. Qui & in Hos. xii. 5. Iehova, memoriale ejus, inquit: ובשם אל ואלהים, הוא משתתף עמהם אבל בזה השם אינו משתתף עם זולתי. Et in nomine El, ac Elohim communicat cum illis; at in hoc nomine non communicat cum alio. Hinc idem שם חעצם vocant, quod cum priori significat nomen proprium. vide Aben Ezram, in Exod. iii. 14. ubi latè de hoc nomine agit, & in Exod. xxiii. 21. atque rationes exponit Grammaticales, quæ nomen hoc ostendant esse proprium: quod non assumit he demonstrativum he hajediah, neque enim dicitur hajehova, uti nec haabraham, haisaak, &c. pro natura singularium individuorum. ii. Neq; sic. admittit pronomina affixa. iii. Nec formam constructam. iv. Neque declinationem vel flexionem singularis in pluralem. Maimonides, in More Nebuchim, part. i. cap. lxi. Sed illud nomen, cujus litteræ sunt jod,he,vau,he, non habet etymologiam notam, neque communicatur alteri. Magnificentia hujus nominis & prohibitio lectionis ejus inde provenit, quia docet de sub-
units.tr: We shall demonstrate more easily that the name Jehovah is proper to God, not common or appellative. Whether we look at its etymology and origin, which is from הָיָה [hayah] or מִן [min], "to be," the word by its own force signifies the nature or essence of God. Hence the Hebrews call שם הוה [shem havah] "the name of substance or essence." God himself disclosed this meaning and force, Exod. 3:14–15, where the name of God was being asked about: for when the Israelites shall say to me, Moses says, What is his name? what shall I say to them? And God answered Moses, אהיה אשר אהיה [ehyeh asher ehyeh], I am who I am, and said, thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel, I am hath sent me unto you. And Jehovah further said to Moses, thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel, Jehovah the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me unto you: this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation. Here God makes known his name Jehovah, and says that it is his name for ever and his perpetual memorial, and he sets before it its explanation or etymology, I am who I am. Both denote the same thing, for both are given to Moses as the name of the one who sent him to the people, and God says of both alike: this is my name, by which I ought to be designated both now and always in the future. Compare Gabriel Vasquez, Disputation 59 on the first part of Thomas. I am who I am does not denote God by any attribute but by his essence, considered in the most absolute way, not under any mode or restricted consideration; it names the infinite ocean of substance itself, as Thomas rightly says, I, q. 13, art. 11. It signifies the immutable essence of God, always the same, whether in our present, past or future time. Hence the Hebrews note the marks of the three tenses in this name: the characteristic of the future in יְ [y] and the participle of the present in ' and of the past in ה [h]. John in the Apocalypse, ch. 1:4: ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [ho on, kai ho ēn, kai ho erchomenos], that is, always the same in all differences of time, who is from himself and through his essence what he is, and the author of all other essence outside himself. Therefore this name is proper to God, and it clearly enough signifies God's own essence. Crellius himself, ch. 11, On God and his attributes, p. 79: this name so signifies the one God that it insinuates into our minds his various attributes, bound together among themselves by the bond of nature. Further, the same is proved from Scripture, that this name is proper to God, because God so often calls this name his own and memorial: Exod. 3:15, this is my name; and 6:22, 24, 25; Isa. 16:21 and 42:8; Jer. 16:21 and 44:26; Hos. 12:5. By this name he willed to be designated, and he is accustomed to be noted by it alone. Ps. 83:19: that they may know that thou, whose name alone is Jehovah, art most high over all the earth [אתה שמך יהוה לבך, עליון על כל הארץ]. The name Jehovah is distinguished from the Most High עליון [elyon], so it is not the name of power alone; and God says that Jehovah is his own, sole name [שמך, ולבך]. Amos 5:6, 8. 1 Kings 18:21: If Jehovah be God [אם יהוה האלהים], follow him, etc. 36: O Jehovah, God of Abraham. 39: They said, Jehovah, he is God, Jehovah, he is God [יהוה הוא האלהים]. And thence the Jews call it the שם המיוחד [shem hameyuhad], the proper name of God. Rabbi David Kimchi, on Isa. 42:8: Jehovah, this is my name, [הוא שמי המיוחד לי], he says, this is my name proper to me. He says the same on Hos. 12:5: Jehovah, his memorial: [ובשם אל ואלהים, הוא משתתף עמהם אבל בזה השם אינו משתתף עם זולתי]. In the name El and Elohim he shares with them, but in this name he does not share with another. Hence they also call it שם העצם [shem ha'etzem], the name of essence, which together with the former means the proper name. See Aben Ezra on Exod. 3:14, where he treats of this name at length, and on Exod. 23:21, and sets out the grammatical reasons that show this name is proper: (i) it does not take the demonstrative he, he hajediah, for one does not say hajehovah, any more than haabraham, haisaak, etc., as for the nature of individual singulars; (ii) nor does it admit affixed pronouns; (iii) nor the construct form; (iv) nor does the singular pass into the plural by declension or inflection. Maimonides, in the Guide of the Perplexed, part 1, ch. 61: But that name whose letters are yod, he, vav, he has no known etymology, nor is it communicated to another. The magnificence of this name and the prohibition of its reading arise from this, that it teaches about the sub-

units.la: Tom. 2. stantiâ Dei, quo respectu vel in quâ significatione nulli creaturæ communicatur, sicut deo Rabbini nostri dicunt; nomen meum proprium mihi. Adde Menassem ben Israel Conciliat. in Exod. quæst. III. Eundemque in sensum putatur à multis dictum nomen hammephorasch, המפורש שם, quasi nomen segregatum ab aliis Dei nominibus, Deoque proprium: quamvis alii exponant, nomen explicatum. Passim שם, nomen istud, per synedochem, ex Levit. XXIV. 11. & expressit שם יהוה [?]. E re quoque est audire Adversariorum de hoc Iehovæ nomine testimonia. Servetus, lib. v. de Erroribus Trinit. in initio: nomina divinitatis insigniora sunt Elohim & Iehovah, alterum Christi, alterum Patris nomen. Socinus, Resp. contra Vujekum, cap. VI. pag. 368. Alioqui nomen Iehovæ est nomen proprium, Κυρίος [?] vero seu Dominus appellativum & plurimùm vulgo tributum. Crellius, de Deo & attrib. cap. XI. Quare nomen hoc, loquitur de nomine Iehova, unum Deum itâ significat, ut diversa ejus attributa, naturæ vinculo inter se colligata, animis nostris insinuet. pag. 82. Relinquitur ergo, non Christo, nec Angelis, cum in seipsis spectantur, hoc nomen absolutè positum convenire; sed Deo summo, cujus ille Filius est, hi servi, esse proprium. Cap. XIV. pag. 102. Quia vero vox Iehova magis, quam cætera Dei nomina, proprium naturam sequitur, ideo etiam Græca Κυρίος [?], cum pro illa ponitur, proprium indolem, qua licet, æmulatur.
units.tr: Vol. 2. stance of God, in which respect or in what sense it is communicated to no creature, as our rabbis say of God: my name is proper to me. Add Menasseh ben Israel, Reconciliations, on Exodus, question 3. Many think the same sense is meant by the name hammephorash, המפורש שם [ha-shem ha-meforash], as if it were a name set apart from the other names of God and proper to him, though others explain it as the explicit name. Everywhere the word שם [shem], that name, is used by synecdoche, from Lev. 24:11, where it expresses שם יהוה [shem Yehovah]. It is also useful to hear the testimonies of our adversaries about this name Jehovah. Servetus, book 5, On the Errors of the Trinity, at the beginning: the more distinguished names of divinity are Elohim and Jehovah, the one the name of Christ, the other the name of the Father. Socinus, Reply to Vujek, ch. 6, p. 368: Otherwise the name Jehovah is a proper name, but Κύριος [Kyrios] or Lord is an appellative and very commonly given. Crellius, On God and his attributes, ch. 11. Wherefore this name, speaking of the name Jehovah, so signifies the one God that it insinuates into our minds his various attributes, bound together among themselves by the bond of nature, p. 82. It follows, then, that this name, absolutely stated, belongs not to Christ, nor to the angels when they are regarded in themselves, but to the highest God, of whom the one is the Son and these are the servants. Ch. 14, p. 102. For since the word Jehovah follows the proper nature more than the other names of God do, therefore also the Greek Κύριος [Kyrios], when it is put in its place, imitates, as far as it can, its proper character.

units.la: Obiiciunt I. Nomina Dei originis communis esse: ergo & ipsa. Nomen Θεὸς venire vel à Θέειν, currere, vel ab αἴθω urere, aut Θεάσθαι cernere, quæ variis modis Gentilium Numinibus, aut vero etiam Deo adscripta, significationis communis sint. היה [?] ab היה, fuit. Quare nomina inde deducta communia quoque esse & appellativa. Crellius, lib. de Deo cap. XIII. & XI. Resp. negari consequentiam, ut verbalia à communis significationis radice venientia ideo quoque communia sint. v. g. Adam venit ab אדמה terra, Eva à חיה vixit; Noah à נחם consolatus est; Moses à משה traxit. neque illa ideo minùs propria: sic apud alios, Philo, Hippias, Plato, &c. Non attenditur in nominibus, appellativis aut propriis, unde unumquodque veniat, sed ad quod applicetur, ad communem, an vero singularem denotandam naturam. Quemadmodum Scholastici, & inter illos Thomas, I. qu. XIII. art. VIII. ubi etiam disputat, utrum hoc nomen Deus sit nomen naturæ? respondet: non est semper idem id, à quo impositur nomen ad significandum, & id ad quod significandum nomen impositur. Sicut enim substantiam rei ex proprietatibus vel operationibus ejus cognoscimus, ita substantiam rei denominamus quandoque ab aliqua ejus operatione vel proprietate. Sicut substantiam lapidis denominamus ab aliqua actione ejus, quia lædit pedem: non tamen hoc nomen impositum est ad significandum hanc actionem, sed substantiam lapidis. Quamvis neque de etymologia lapidis, quam dat, neque Dei, velimus contendere, vera an sit. II. Deum vel Θεόν, ab istis, quæ dicta sunt, verbis derivari, aut actionibus, nondum satis certum est. Nam Θεὸς, cum quo Copticum seu Ægyptiacum Θωύθ [?] convenire videtur, cujus originis fit, non satis exploratum. III. Jehova quidem ab היה venit, sed non ab esse quod commune fit Deo & creaturis, sed ab esse Dei, quod ei proprium ac singulare, non ejusdem aut generis, aut naturæ cum creaturis, quare neque nominis.
units.tr: They object, first, that the names of God have a common origin, so the name itself must be common too. The name Theos [Θεὸς] comes either from theein [Θέειν], to run, or from aithō [αἴθω], to burn, or from theasthai [Θεάσθαι], to see, and these ideas have been ascribed in various ways to the deities of the Gentiles, or indeed to God. The Hebrew name [היה] comes from hayah [היה], to be. Therefore names derived from these are common and appellative as well. Crellius, book on God, chapters 11 and 13. The answer: the inference is denied. Words derived from a root of common meaning are not for that reason common. For example, Adam comes from adamah [אדמה], earth; Eve from chayah [חיה], she lived; Noah from nacham [נחם], he comforted; Moses from mashah [משה], he drew out. Yet these names are no less proper for that. So among other writers, Philo, Hippias, Plato and others. In names, whether appellative or proper, what matters is not where each comes from, but what it is applied to, whether it denotes a common nature or a singular one. So the Scholastics, and among them Thomas, Part I, question 13, article 8, where he also asks whether this name God is a name of nature. He answers that the thing from which a name is imposed is not always the same as the thing which the name is imposed to signify. For just as we know the substance of a thing from its properties or operations, so we sometimes name the substance of a thing from some one of its operations or properties. Thus we name the substance of a stone from one of its actions, because it hurts the foot; yet the name was not imposed to signify this action, but the substance of the stone. Although we do not wish to contend whether the etymology he gives of stone, or of God, is true. II. That God, Theos [Θεόν], is derived from the words just mentioned, or from actions, is not yet certain enough. For the origin of Theos, with which the Coptic or Egyptian Thoth [Θωύθ] seems to agree, has not been sufficiently investigated. III. Jehovah indeed comes from hayah [היה], but not from "to be" in the sense in which it is common to God and creatures, but from the being of God, which is proper and singular to him, not of the same kind or nature as the creatures. Therefore neither is the name common.

units.la: II. Objiciunt, In Scripturis vocem Dei & Jehovæ aliis quoque tribui, quam uni Deo, quare videri nomina communia esse & appellativa, non propria. Socinus, in Cathechesi, loco supra adducto, Scripturae textus attulit, in quibus de Angelis at-que hominibus aliquoties dictum, quod Deus sunt: ubi Angelo videtur tribui nomen Jehovae, vel de loco aliquo dici, Jehova ibi, Jehova pax, &c. loca nota, eademque attulit Socinus, contra Vujekum, pag. 360. Catechel. Racovien. pag. 72. Crellius, cap. xi. Remonstrantes, Apolog. cap. iii. pag. 51. Resp. i. Loca quidem aliqua in Scripturis ostendi possunt, quibus vel Angeli vel homines aliqui Dii nuncu-pantur: at non ubi Deus, in singulari. ii. Non ubi absolute & simpliciter: sed cum re-latione ad aliquam rem, vel officium, aut personam. Sic Moses dicitur אלהים Pha-raonis, Exod. vii. i. iii. Dicuntur illi Dii, aut metaphorice, aut catachrestice: at quaerimus hic de acceptione vocis propriâ. iv. Nomen Jehovae, alicui tribui praeterquam vero Deo, constanter nego. Quando Angelo adscribitur, est is Angelus Deus, Angelus foederis, increatus, Mal. iii. 2. Hos. xii. 5. 6. non creatus. Nam ex toto sermone apparet, & ratione qua Angelus se habet, quod loquitur, agit, denique uti colitur, esse Deum ipsum. v. At quando vel de altari dicitur, יהוה נסי Jehova vexillum meum. Exod. xvii. 15. de monte, quem Abrahamus vocavit יהוה יראה [?] Jehova providebit. de urbe Jerusalemo, Jezech. ult. יהוה שמה [?], Jehova ibi, nequaquam sunt pro nominibus habenda aut altaris, aut montis, urbive; sed elogiis, testimoniis, symbolis, occasione istorum, pronunciatis & celebratis. Uti si dixero, ibi habitat Petrus, Petrus regnat, &c. ad singulare aliquod factum, seu argumentum; non significat Petri nomen illis tribui, ac desinere esse proprium. Ita in illis, Jehova vexillum, &c. non Jehovae nomen rebus aliis attribuitur, sed proprie professio fidei editur atque religionis. Crellius, de Deo, pag. 84. Cernimus enim in sacris literis integram nonnunquam sententiam seu orationem, unius instar nominis usurpari. Sic jussus fuit Esaias filium suum appellare, Accelera, detrahe spolium, festina praedari. Confer & Georgii Dor-schei Differt. de nomine Jehova, pag. 34. & seq.
units.tr: II. They object that in Scripture the words God and Jehovah are also given to others besides the one God, so that they seem to be common and appellative names, not proper ones. Socinus, in his Catechesis, in the place cited above, brought forward passages of Scripture in which it is said several times of angels and men that they are God; where the name Jehovah seems to be given to an angel, or it is said of some place, Jehovah is there, Jehovah is peace, and so on. These well-known passages Socinus also cited contra Vujekum, page 360; the Racovian Catechism, page 72; Crellius, cap. 11; and the Remonstrants, Apolog. cap. 3, pag. 51, Resp. 1. The answer: i. Some passages can indeed be shown in Scripture in which angels or certain men are called gods; but not where God is said in the singular. ii. Not where it is used absolutely and simply, but in relation to some thing, office or person. So Moses is called elohim [אלהים] of Pharaoh, Exod. 7:1. Those are called gods either metaphorically or catachrestically; but we are asking here about the proper use of the word. iv. I constantly deny that the name Jehovah is given to anyone other than the true God. When it is ascribed to the angel, that angel is God, the angel of the covenant, uncreated, Mal. 3:2; Hos. 12:5, 6. For from the whole discourse it appears, and from the way the angel behaves, in that he speaks and acts, and finally from the way he is worshipped, that he is God himself. v. But when it is said of an altar, Jehovah is my banner (Jehovah nissi [יהוה נסי]), Exod. 17:15; of the mountain which Abraham called Jehovah-jireh [יהוה יראה], Jehovah will provide; of the city of Jerusalem, in the last chapter of Ezekiel, Jehovah shammah [יהוה שמה], Jehovah is there; these are by no means to be taken as names of the altar, the mountain or the city. Rather they are eulogies, testimonies and symbols, uttered and celebrated on the occasion of those things. Just as if I say, Peter lives there, Peter reigns, and so on, with reference to some single deed or argument, I do not mean that Peter's name is transferred to those things and ceases to be proper to him. So in the phrases Jehovah is my banner, and so on, the name of Jehovah is not being given to other things; rather a profession of faith and of religion is properly put forward. Crellius, on God, page 84: We see in the sacred letters that sometimes a whole sentence or saying is used as if it were a single name. So Isaiah was ordered to call his son, Hurry, take the spoil, hasten to plunder. Compare also Georg Dorschei's Dissertation on the name Jehovah, page 34 and following.

units.la: Jam Christum Jehovam etiam, uti Deum, appellari, constat tum directe ex illis locis, ubi hoc aperte fit. Jerem. xxiii. 6. Jehova iustitia nostra. Jesa. xl. 3. parate viam Jehovae. tum magis indirecte ex locis Vet. Test. de Deo Jehova enunciatis, & Christo in Nov. Test. applicatis. Quales sunt Jesa. vi. 9. & Joann. xii. 41. Haec dixit Esaias, quando vidit gloriam ejus, & loquutus est de eo. Exod. xvii. 2. Deut. xxxii. 12. Num. xxi. 5. Psalm. xcv. 8. & 1. Cor. x. 9. Neque tentemus Christum, sicuti quidam eorum tentarunt, & a serpentibus perierunt. Psalm. xcvii. 7. cum Heb. i. 6. ubi verba illa Psalm. 97. & adorent eum omnes angeli Dei, manifeste ad Christum referuntur, inquit Socinus, Epist. iii. ad Radecium pag. 147. & Psalm. cii. 26. cum Heb. i. 10. Tu Domine in principio terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt caeli. Jesa. xliv. 6. cum Apoc. i. 11. ego sum, inquit Christus, cum articulo, τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω[?]. ὁ πρῶτος[?] καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος. & cap. xxii. 13. Ita a Petro dicitur, Prophetas olim ex Spiritu Christi vaticinatos. 1. Pet. i. 11. Indagantes in quod & quale tempus indicaret in illis Spiritus Christi, praetestificans Christi passiones, & post eas glorias.
units.tr: Now that Christ too is called Jehovah, as God is, is clear both directly from those passages where this is openly done: Jer. 23:6, Jehovah our righteousness; Isa. 40:3, prepare the way of Jehovah; and more indirectly from passages of the Old Testament in which God Jehovah is spoken of and which are applied to Christ in the New Testament. Such are Isa. 6:9 and John 12:41, These things said Isaiah, when he saw his glory, and spoke of him; Exod. 17:2; Deut. 32:12; Num. 21:5; Ps. 95:8 and 1 Cor. 10:9, Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and perished by serpents; Ps. 97:7 with Heb. 1:6, where the words of Psalm 97, and let all the angels of God worship him, are plainly referred to Christ, says Socinus, Epistle 3 to Radecius, page 147; and Ps. 102:26 with Heb. 1:10, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of thy hands; Isa. 44:6 with Rev. 1:11, where Christ says, I am with the article, the Alpha and the Omega [τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω], the first and the last [ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος]; and chapter 22:13. So Peter says that the prophets of old prophesied by the Spirit of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:11: searching what, or what manner of time, the Spirit of Christ within them indicated, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow them.

units.la: Ad Jerem. xxiii. 6. Excipit Socinus, epist. ad Andream Voidovium, iii. Locutio ista vocabit cum[?], ex idiotismo hebraeo latine sic resolvitur & explicatur, n[?] vocabitur; & nihilominus tamen sensus revera non est, ipsum vocatum iri Jehovam simpliciter & absolute, sed per eum a Jehova datum iri iustitiam, propter quam causam poterit nomen ejus dici Jehova, iustitia nostra. Verum non quid poterit dici, sed debeat, docetur. Nec tantum, quod per eum Jehova daturus esset iustitiam, sed quod inde sic etiam nuncuparetur, affirmatur. Haud negamus, quod Socinus ait, nobis per Christum dari iustitiam, sed nec negare debebat, quod textus asserit, eum esse Iehovam iustitiam. Duo dicuntur, quod sit iustitia nostra, & Iehova: unum & alterum nuncupatur, quodque nuncupatur, est. Non enim frustra Deus nomen imponit, non suum proprium. Quis dubitat, Christum esse iustitiam nostram? quod aliquoties in N. T. asseritur. Rom. 1. 17. & x. 4. 1. Cor. 1. 30. Phil. iii. 9. & hoc vere ac propriissime Christum dici: ita quoque Iehovam. Denique aliter non potuit tantum, sed nec debuit vocari. Unde quam dissimilis sit praedicatio, ab oratione illa, in qua de loco aliquando affirmatur, quod Iehova ibi sit, apparet. Nam uti proprie Christus dicitur iustitia, non improprie, ita & Iehova. Estque, quod vocatur, vere Iehova iustitia nostra.
units.tr: Socinus, in his third letter to Andreas Voidovius, on Jer. 23:6, makes this exception: That locution, "will be called," is resolved and explained in Latin according to the Hebrew idiom as "will not be called"; and nevertheless the sense is really not that he himself will be called Jehovah simply and absolutely, but that through him Jehovah will give righteousness, for which reason his name can be said to be Jehovah our righteousness. But what is taught is not what can be said, but what ought to be said. Nor is it affirmed merely that Jehovah would give righteousness through him, but that he is so named from this. We do not deny what Socinus says, that righteousness is given to us through Christ; but he ought not to deny what the text asserts, that he is Jehovah our righteousness. Two things are said: that he is our righteousness, and that he is Jehovah; the one and the other are named, and what is named, is. For God does not impose a name in vain, and certainly not one that is not his own. Who doubts that Christ is our righteousness? This is asserted several times in the New Testament: Rom. 1:17 and 10:4; 1 Cor. 1:30; Phil. 3:9. And it is said of Christ truly and most properly; so also Jehovah. Finally, he could not only be called this, but ought to be called it. From this it appears how unlike this predication is to that statement in which it is affirmed of a place that Jehovah is there. For just as Christ is properly called righteousness, not improperly, so too is he Jehovah. And that which is called is truly Jehovah our righteousness.

units.la: Ad locum Ioann. xii. 41. ita Eniedinus: Ex hoc loco ita quidam ratiocinantur: Esaias vidit gloriam Christi; Ergo Esaiae aetate extitit Christus. Ac proinde, antequam nasceretur ex Maria, revera fuit.
units.tr: On the passage John 12:41, Enjedinus says: Some people reason from this passage as follows: Isaiah saw the glory of Christ; therefore Christ existed in Isaiah's time, and so before he was born of Mary he truly was.

units.la: Resp. Negatur consequentia prior. Non enim sequitur, si quis videat alicujus gloriam, eum iam revera existere. In Deo enim omnia sunt praesentia, & in ipso licet speculari omnia quae sunt, fuerunt, & erunt. Potuit igitur Propheta in visione, tam Christi gloriam, quam alia quamplurima, per extasin & in spiritu videre, & loqui de illis, etiam antequam re vera existerent. Sic Abraham dicitur vidisse diem Christi: Ita Balaam, Num. 14. vers. 17. Video illum, sed non modo, intueor illum, sed non de prope. Quam multa dicunt Prophetae se videre, tanquam praesentia, quae tamen postmodum eveniunt, quam multa praeteriisse, quae nondum adsunt. Nempe vident illi sane, nec mentiuntur, nec fallluntur, sed re vera vident in Deo praesentia, quae apud homines nondum existunt. Ita ergo potuit Esaias, vel in Deo, vel in similitudine aliqua futuram Christi gloriam videre, quae tamen re vera apud homines nondum exiterit. Nam tantum abest, ut Christus glorificatus exstiterit revera aetate Esaiae, ut nec vivens quidem, ante resurrectionem glorificatum fuisse dicatur, Ioh. 7. vers. 39. sed gloriam accepisse post mortem, 1. Pet. 1. vers. 21. Heb. 2. vers. 9. Apoc. 5. vers. 12. ad Philip. 2. vers. 9. Osius Propheta vidit gloriam omnium credentium, nec tamen illi tunc extitisse per revelationem? sed, quomodo cum in Deo
units.tr: Answer: The first consequence is denied. It does not follow that, if someone sees another's glory, that person already really exists. For all things are present to God, and in him one may contemplate all things that are, have been, and will be. The prophet could therefore, in vision and in the Spirit, by ecstasy, see both the glory of Christ and very many other things, and speak of them, even before they really existed. So Abraham is said to have seen the day of Christ. So too Balaam, Num. 14:17: "I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not nigh." How many things the prophets say they see as present, which nevertheless happen afterwards; how many things they have seen past, which are not yet present! Those men see truly, and do not lie or deceive, but they really see in God things that are present, though they do not yet exist among men. So Isaiah could see the future glory of Christ, either in God or in some likeness, though it had not yet really come into being among men. For it is far from the case that Christ was glorified in reality in Isaiah's time: he was not said to be glorified even while living, before the resurrection, John 7:39, but to have received glory after his death, 1 Pet. 1:21, Heb. 2:9, Rev. 5:12, Phil. 2:9. The prophet Hosea saw the glory of all believers; yet was it not then made manifest to him by revelation? But how, when in God...

units.la: Resp. I. Esaias non vidit, vel praevidit gloriam alicujus futuram, sed praesentem, & praesentis. vers. 1. & vidi Dominum sedentem supra solium amplum & elevatum, &c. plena est tota terra gloria ejus. Illam, & illius gloriam Esaias conspexit: quod de Christo interpretatur Iohannes, visam a Propheta fuisse ejus gloriam. Nempe secundum id quod Christus alibi testatur, ego & Pater unum sumus. atque Philippo: Philippe, qui me vidit, vidit Patrem. Ioann. xiv. 6. Sed Esaias non vidit aliquid, vel aliquem non existentem: sed quem & contuebatur & alloquebatur Angeli caelestes, Seraphim. Nihil est in textu, quod significet, Prophetam aliquid in Deo vidisse futurum, vel gloriae Christi futurae. Non quod diem Christi praeviderit, quemadmodum Abrahamus: non, quod viderit Christum, at non prope, quod Bileam dixit, sed coram eum vidit, & loquutus cum eo praesente fuit Propheta. Alioqui non negamus, Prophetas futura, tamquam praesentia, praedicere; sed, aliud est, praesentem gloriam videre, & eam praedicare. Ut quemadmodum Seraphim non videbant & celebrabant in Deo gloriam duntaxat futuram, sed praesentem, ita eandem conspexit quadantenus & collaudavit Propheta. Quid vero hoc est, in Deo videre futuram Christi gloriam? an ut in speculo aliquo, quale Iesuitae in Deo fingunt? an in decreto, vel essentia Dei? an per revelationem? sed, quomodo cum in Deo ipsa. Ad Rom. 9. vers.13. 14.15. Atque ut familiari exemplo declaramus, posse gloriam videri, sine eo, cujus est gloria: Fingamus aliquem regem constituisse, eum qui propositum a se certamen subierit, purpurea veste, sceptro aureo, dignitate amplissima, gemmis & annulis pretiosissimis ornaturum, quae omnia habeat in promtu parata, ita ut possit aliis ostendere & videnda exhibere: Certe potest quis gloriam athletha victoriosi videre, etiamsi non videat, nec sciat adhuc an in rerum sit natura ille athleta: Ita Deus praeparaverat gloriam Iesu Christo, & quidem ab aeterno, ut legimus Iohann. 17. vers.5. & 24. Sicut praeparavit eodem modo, etiam piis omnibus, ut legimus Matth. 25. v. 34. Eph. 1. v. 5. Haec gloria potest, & potuit videri, imo visa est a Prophetis, etiam Christo & piis nondum existentibus, ut docet Petrus 1. Epist. cap. 1. ut mox referemus. Præterea, in verbis præscriptis, nulla fit mentio Christi, neque ulla necessitas cogit pronomen αὐτῷ, ejus & eo ad Christum referre, cum potius referendum videatur ad vocem κυρίῳ, quae ponitur in versu 33. neque est ullum vicinius nomen, ad quod referri possit. Ibi autem per κυρίου, non alium intelligi, quam Deum Patrem, nemo est, puto, qui dubitet. Hanc sententiam non esse absurdam, primo patet ex eo, quod Euangelista illud excaecavit & induravit, procul dubio retulit ad vocem κυρίῳ, alias verba Prophetae non immutasset, quae tamen esse immutata, nemo negare potest, cum aliter apud illum ista legantur, sed Euangelista voluit significare, illam execrationem auctore Deo esse factam. Si ergo excaecavit & induravit, refertur ad vocem κυρίῳ, certe etiam Pronomen αὐτῷ, recte eodem referri potest. Deinde confirmatur haec sententia, auctoritate codicum Graecorum, in quibusdam enim, loco Pronominis seu Relativi αὐτῷ, positum est ipsum antecedens nomen Θεός. [illegible, ~3 letters] Hanc scripturam legesapud eos, qui in Deo dicetur ea vidisse[?] vel quando Prophetae praevident & praedicunt futura, quod ea in Deo revera videant praesentia, velim ut quis nobis clarius exponat. Deo quidem omnia praesentia, non item aliis, qui Deo praesentes sunt, vel eum quovis modo vident. Tum, aliud est videre res, seu cognoscere; aliud, uti objectivae illae offeruntur in visione aliqua contemplandae, sic eas videre. Atque ita intelligitur visa a Prophetâ Christi gloria, non aliquo tantum modo praecognita. Praeterea Christus, ut Christus, non fuit glorificatus tempore Iesaiae, fuit tamen secundum quod filius Dei, in gloria, quam habuit etiam antequam mundus fieret. Ioann. xvii. 5. id est, ab aeterno, uti ipse id hic explicat Enjedinus. Quomodo vero ex Hosea probet, vidisse eum gloriam omnium credentium, inde quod Apostolus dicit Rom. ix. 23. ut notas faciat divitias gloriae suae in vasa misericordiae quae praeparavit ad gloriam. 24. quos & vocavit non solum ex Iudaeis, sed quoque ex gentibus: quemadmodum & apud Hoseam dicit, non populum meum vocabo populum meum, & non dilectam, dilectam, ego non satis perspicio: nam de vocatione disserit Hoseas, in eo, quem Apostolus adducit, loco: quamvis certum, nec ipsum, uti nec fideles alios latere, credentium, & filiorum Dei gloriam. Sed non certe eam vidit hic Hoseas, qua ratione gloriam Dei, & Christi dicitur vidisse Esaias. Ut quomodo huc illa spe-ctent, quae adducit Noster, minime appareat. Denique potest aliqua gloria videri, etiam absque eo, cui ea postmodum datur, vel quoque sine eo, cujus illa fit, uti in proposito, satis sterili & ludicro, exemplo athletae; sed non uti ab aliquo prominens & effulgens gloria, qualis est in exemplo Prophetę, ut non simul is existat, cujus sit illa gloria. Ostende nobis, quomodo Christi gloriam paraverit Deus ab aeterno, & hoc tempore videndam obvarias Novi Testamenti lectiones collegerunt, ut in Roberti Stephani, & Crispini editionibus.
units.tr: Answer I. Isaiah did not see or foresee the future glory of someone, but the present glory of one who is present. Verse 1: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne, etc. The whole earth is full of his glory." Isaiah beheld him and his glory; John interprets this of Christ, that the prophet saw his glory. Indeed, this agrees with what Christ elsewhere testifies: "I and the Father are one," and to Philip: "Philip, he who has seen me has seen the Father," John 14:6. But Isaiah did not see something or someone not existing; he gazed upon and was addressed by him, and the heavenly angels, the seraphim, did likewise. There is nothing in the text to signify that the prophet saw in God something future, or the future glory of Christ. It is not that he foresaw the day of Christ, as Abraham did; nor that he saw Christ but not nearby, as Balaam said; but he saw him face to face, and the prophet spoke with him while he was present. Otherwise we do not deny that the prophets foretell future things as if they were present; but it is one thing to see present glory and proclaim it, another to see it in prospect. Just as the seraphim did not see and celebrate in God a glory merely future but a present one, so the prophet to some extent beheld and praised the same. But what does it mean to see in God the future glory of Christ? As in some mirror, such as the Jesuits imagine in God? Or in the decree or essence of God? Or by revelation? But how, when in God itself. Rom. 9:13-15. And, to make the point with a familiar example, that glory can be seen without him whose glory it is: let us suppose that a king has appointed a contest, and that he who undertakes the contest is to be adorned by him with a purple robe, a golden sceptre, the highest dignity, and most precious jewels and rings, all of which the king has ready at hand, so that he can show them to others and exhibit them to be seen. Surely someone may see the glory of the victorious athlete, even if he does not yet see, or know, whether that athlete exists in reality. So God had prepared glory for Jesus Christ, and indeed from eternity, as we read in John 17:5 and 24, just as he prepared it in the same way for all the pious, as we read in Matt. 25:34, Eph. 1:5. This glory can be, and could be, seen, indeed it was seen by the prophets, even when neither Christ nor the pious yet existed, as Peter teaches in 1 Pet. 1, as we shall presently show. Moreover, in the words cited, there is no mention of Christ, and no necessity compels us to refer the pronoun autō [αὐτῷ], "his" or "to him," to Christ, since it seems rather to be referred to the word kyrio [κυρίῳ], "Lord," which is found in verse 33; nor is there any nearer noun to which it could refer. That by kyriou [κυρίου] nothing other than God the Father is meant, I think no one doubts. That this opinion is not absurd appears first from the fact that the Evangelist, when he says "he blinded and hardened," undoubtedly referred this to the word kyrio [κυρίῳ]; otherwise he would not have altered the words of the prophet, which nevertheless have been altered, as no one can deny, since they are read differently there; but the Evangelist wished to signify that this curse was made by God as its author. If, then, "he blinded and hardened" refers to the word kyrio [κυρίῳ], certainly the pronoun autō [αὐτῷ] can rightly be referred to the same. Next, this opinion is confirmed by the authority of Greek manuscripts, for in some, in place of the pronoun or relative autō [αὐτῷ], the antecedent noun itself, Theos [Θεός], is put. [illegible] I should like someone to explain to us more clearly how, in those who are said to have seen these things in God... [illegible], or when the prophets foresee and foretell future things, because they really see them present in God. God indeed has all things present, but not so others, who are present to God or see him in any way. Moreover, it is one thing to see things, that is, to know them; another, to see them as objects offered in some vision to be contemplated. Thus it is understood that the glory of Christ was seen by the prophet, not merely foreknown in some way. Besides, Christ, as Christ, was not glorified in Isaiah's time; yet according as he is the Son of God, he had glory, which he had even before the world was made, John 17:5, that is, from eternity, as Enjedinus himself here explains. But how he proves from Hosea that the glory of all believers was seen, from the fact that the Apostle says, Rom. 9:23, "that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy which he had prepared for glory," 24, "whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, as also he says in Hosea, I will call them my people who were not my people, and her beloved who was not beloved," I do not sufficiently see: for Hosea speaks of calling in the passage the Apostle adduces, although it is certain that the glory of believers and sons of God was not hidden from him, nor from the other faithful. But certainly Hosea did not see here the glory by which Isaiah is said to have seen the glory of God and Christ. How these things which our author adduces bear on this is by no means apparent. Finally, some glory can be seen even without him to whom it is afterwards given, or without him whose it is, as in the case of the athlete, a rather barren and frivolous example, in our instance; but not as a glory standing out and shining forth from someone, such that he to whom that glory belongs does not exist at the same time. Show us how God prepared the glory of Christ from eternity, and how it is to be seen at this time; the variant readings of the New Testament have been gathered in the editions of Robert Stephanus and Crispin.

units.la: Ad hæc, etiamsi concedamus, per pronomen αὐτῷ[?] intelligendum esse Christum: observandum est, vocabulum videre poni sæpe in sacris pro prævidere, seu prophetare. Est enim familiare his scriptoribus simplex ponere pro compositō. Unde etiam Prophetæ, apud Hebræos vocantur videntes. Et Esa. cap. 30. verf. 10. legimus. Qui dicunt videntibus, ne videatis, & prospicientibus, ne prospiciatis nobis recta. Ita ergo dicetur hic Esaias vi-disse gloriam, id est, prophetasse de gloria: Non quod tunc viderit, sed quod prædixerit gloriam Christi. Qui sensus & probus, & no-bis non est contrarius. Confirmatur hæc interpretatio ex dicto Petri, qui primæ epistolæ, cap. 1. v. 10. ait & piorum gratiam, & Christi gloriam à Prophetis prævisam & prædi-[?]stam esse: De qua inquit, salute inquisiverunt, & quam scrutati sunt Prophetæ, qui ventu-ram in vos gratiam prædixerunt, scrutantes in quem, aut cujusmodi temporis articulū prænuncius ille, qui in ipsis erat Spiritus Christi declararet eventuras Christo perpessiones, & gloriam illas consecuturā.
units.tr: Moreover, even if we grant that the pronoun αὐτῷ [αὐτῷ] is to be understood of Christ, it must be observed that the verb "to see" is often used in Scripture for "to foresee" or "to prophesy." It is familiar to these writers to use the simple verb for the compound. Hence the prophets are also called "seers" among the Hebrews. And we read in Isaiah 30:10: "Who say to the seers, Do not see; and to the prospectors, Do not prospect for us right things." So Isaiah is said here to have "seen the glory," that is, to have prophesied about the glory: not that he saw it then, but that he foretold the glory of Christ. This sense is sound and is not contrary to us. The interpretation is confirmed by the saying of Peter in the first epistle, chapter 1, verse 10, who says that both the grace toward believers and the glory of Christ were foreseen and foretold by the prophets. Of this salvation, he says, "the prophets have inquired and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that would come to you, searching what time or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did point to, when he testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow."

units.la: Quarto respondemus: Observandum est, hic duos Esaiæ locos citari ab Euangelista, unum ex cap. 53. alterum ex cap. 6. Nunc quæri potest, cum subjicit Euangelista: Hæc dixit Esaias &c. per pronomen Hæc, an locum utrumque simul, an alterutrum tantum intellexerit: & si alterutrum, priusne an posterius citatum? Adversarii nostri videntur, Pronomen hæc, referre tantum ad locum posteriorem, ex cap. 6. citatum: Aiunt enim Euangelistam significare voluisse, majestatem illam, quam se vidisse Esaias refert, in principio capitis sexti, fuisse gloriam Christi. Sed hæc sententia stare non potest. Primo, quia Esaias ibi non gloriam se vidisse ait, sed Dominum sedentem super solium. & audivisse canentes Angelos, terram esse plenam gloria Domini. Deinde, illam visionem non pertinere ad Chritulerit Prophetæ: an vero aliquo loco ea continebatur, quæ quomodo triumphale athletæ apparatum, sceptrum, vestimen-ta, & quæ huc cætera crepitacula nostrer profert, ostendere Deus Prophetæ volue-rit: sed nihil adeo excelles in Christi gloria Adversarius hic vidit, ut non piis omnibus commune faciat, habere tum gloriam ita paratam, tum videri eam à Prophetis posse. Atque si hoc totum fit, quod Propheta gloriam Christi in Deo vidit, quando ejus gloriam vidisse scribitur, tum & piorum omnium gloriam æque vidisse dici poterit, ac Christi, nihilque singulare hic de Christo Iohannes, quando ait, eum vidisse Christi gloriam, quod tamen abs-que singulari emphasi & elogio dictum accipiet nemo.
units.tr: Fourthly we reply: it must be observed that the evangelist here cites two passages of Isaiah, one from chapter 53 and the other from chapter 6. Now it may be asked, when the evangelist adds, "These things said Isaiah," etc., by the pronoun "these" (haec), whether he meant both passages together or only one of them, and if only one, whether the first or the second that was cited. Our opponents seem to hold that the pronoun "these" refers only to the second passage, cited from chapter 6. For they say that the evangelist meant that the majesty which Isaiah reports having seen at the beginning of chapter 6 was the glory of Christ. But this view cannot stand. First, because Isaiah there does not say that he saw glory, but that he saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, and heard the angels singing that the earth is full of the glory of the Lord. Next, that vision does not pertain to Christ... [the text here is corrupt] ...whether God wished to show the prophet somewhere in that passage the things which our opponent brings forward, such as the triumphal equipment of an athlete, a sceptre, garments, and other such rattles; but this adversary has seen nothing so excellent in the glory of Christ that he does not make it common to all the godly: to have such a glory prepared, and to be able to be seen by the prophets. And if this is all there is, namely that the prophet saw the glory of Christ in God, then when his glory is said to have been seen, it could equally be said that the glory of all the godly was seen, just as the glory of Christ was, and John's words that he saw the glory of Christ would contain nothing singular about Christ. Yet no one would take it that this was said without a singular emphasis and praise.

units.la: Quod ad secundam responsionem, qua Auctor relativum αὐτὸς non ad Christum refert, sed ad Deum Patrem, vel Κύριον, qui verf. 38. bis commemoratur, ex Iesa. liii. 1. Domine, quis credidit auditui nostro, & brachium Domini &c. ei reponimus, 1. obstare totam sermonis rationem & contextum, ut aliter quam de Christo intelligatur, quod ejus gloriam vidit Propheta. Verum enim 37. fundamentum sermonis est, tanta ipso coram iis faciente signa, non crediderunt in eum: certe Christum. Nempe id factum, ait verf. 38. ut impleretur quod dictum à Iesaia, Domine quis credidit auditui nostro? Iterum hoc unde factum, verf. 39. 40. ex eodem exponit, dicente, excæcavit eorum oculos, & induravit ipsorum cor, &c. Iesa. vi. cui immediate adjungit, verf. 41. ista dixit Iesaias, quando gloriam ejus vidit & de eo est loquutus. Quis αὐτὸς[?], nisi Christi? qui argumentum est sermonis, & objectum, in quod infidelitate sua impegerant, cujus infidelitatis exponit & probat ex Iesaia τὸ quod, & quale, ὅτι, & διότι[?]. 11. Commemoratur quidem stum, sed peculiariter ad Deum Patrem, appa-ret ex Apocal. cap. 4. ubi vel eadem, vel certe similis visio describitur, & Deo Patri tribuitur, & aperte distinguitur Christus capite sequenti, ab illo super thronum sedente, ad quem pertinet visio. Tertio, cum non semel, sed aliquoties locus ille Esaiae cap. 6. in Novo Testamento citetur; nunquam Christo attribuitur. Quare neque hic ei applicari debet. Itaque si separanda sunt illa Esaiae duo dicta, certe potius, de eo qui prius, quam eo qui posterius est citatus loco, pronomen Haec accipi debet. Manifestissimum enim est, quod quemadmodum caput sextum, de Deo Patre : ita Caput 53. semper de Christo citatur, in Novo Testamento. Quin textus ipse docet, caput 53. non de Deo, sed de Christo loqui, sicut cap. 6. de Deo, non de Christo. Si quis autem objiciat, locum illum Esa. cap. 53. non de gloria, sed de ignominia potius Christi agere: Respondemus; idem de loco cap. 6. objici posse, ubi de poena gentis Iudaicae perfida agitur; quod non pertinet ad gloriam Christi. Deinde dicimus a versu 11. capitis 53. usque ad finem, agi luculenter de gloria & honore Christi; quo respexerit Euangelista. Quin imo post passiones ac cruciatus, fuisse Christo ingrediundum in suam gloriam, testatur ipsemet Christus Luca ultimo. Si igitur a fine, ut decet, aestimatio & judicium fiat: passiones, ab Esaia descriptae, non ignominia, sed gloria fuerunt Christi, tendebant enim & ducebant ad gloriam. Verum, si quis diligenter Euangelistae verba & sensum introspiciat & perpendat: deprehendet omnino Pronomen haec referendum esse ad Caput 53. Nam voluit reddere rationem, cur Christo Iudaei non crederent: rationem adducit hanc ex Esaia, quia praedixit ille cap. 53. fore multos incredulos. Et haec est ratio, qua etiam Paulus utitur in re simili, ad Rom. cap. 10. Sed cum videret Euangelista, posse aliquem huius rationis, rationem postulare: addidit alium ejusdem Prophetae locum, in quo explicatur, cur quidam sint increduli. Adduxit igitur dictum capitis sexti, non
units.tr: As to the second reply, in which the author refers the pronoun αὐτὸς [αὐτὸς] not to Christ but to God the Father, or to the Lord [κύριος], who is mentioned twice in verse 38, from Isaiah 53:1, "Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed," etc., we answer: first, the whole reasoning and context of the discourse stand in the way of understanding it otherwise than of Christ, that he saw his glory. For the foundation of the discourse is in verse 37: although he had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, certainly Christ. Indeed, the evangelist says in verse 38 that this happened so that what was said by Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed our report?" Again, in verses 39 and 40 he explains from the same passage how this came about, saying: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart," etc., from Isaiah 6, to which he immediately adds in verse 41: "Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him." Who is αὐτὸς [αὐτὸς], unless Christ? He is the subject of the discourse and the object against which they had stumbled through their unbelief, and the evangelist explains and proves from Isaiah both the fact (ὅτι) and the reason (διότι) of that unbelief. Second, although God the Father is indeed mentioned there, this is plain from Revelation chapter 4, where either the same or a similar vision is described and attributed to God the Father, and Christ is clearly distinguished in the following chapter from him who sits upon the throne, to whom the vision pertains. Third, although that passage of Isaiah chapter 6 is cited in the New Testament not once but several times, it is never attributed to Christ. Therefore it ought not to be applied to him here either. So if the two sayings of Isaiah are to be separated, the pronoun "these" must certainly be taken as referring to the earlier cited passage, the one concerning him who is the first, rather than the one cited second. For it is most evident that just as chapter 6 is cited in the New Testament of God the Father, so chapter 53 is always cited of Christ. Indeed the text itself teaches that chapter 53 speaks of Christ, not of God, just as chapter 6 speaks of God, not of Christ. If anyone objects that the passage of Isaiah 53 treats not of glory but rather of the ignominy of Christ, we reply that the same objection could be made to the passage of chapter 6, where the punishment of the faithless Jewish nation is treated, which does not pertain to the glory of Christ. Further, we say that from verse 11 of chapter 53 to the end, the glory and honour of Christ is plainly treated, and this is what the evangelist had in view. Indeed, that after his sufferings and torments Christ was to enter into his glory is attested by Christ himself in the last chapter of Luke. If therefore the judgment is made from the end, as it should be, the sufferings described by Isaiah were not the ignominy but the glory of Christ, for they tended toward and led to glory. But if anyone carefully examines and weighs the words and sense of the evangelist, he will discover that the pronoun "these" must be referred altogether to chapter 53. For the evangelist wished to give the reason why the Jews did not believe Christ, and he brings this reason from Isaiah, because that prophet had foretold in chapter 53 that many would be unbelievers. This is also the reasoning which Paul uses in a similar matter in Romans chapter 10. But since the evangelist saw that someone might demand a reason for this reason, he added another passage of the same prophet, in which it is explained why some are unbelievers. He therefore brought the saying of chapter 6, not...

units.la: κύ[?] verf. 38. sed non in sermone Euangelistae, at in loco Iesaiae: versus autem 41 est Euangelistae, non Prophetae, quando vidit ejus gloriam. III. Nec κύ[?] exclusive dicitur, aut oppositae ad Christum, sed est nomen essentiale, tam huic personae conveniens, quam isti. IV. de quo est accipiendum, ista dixit Iesaias, quando loquutus est de eo; de eodem, quod jungitur, quando ejus vidit gloriam, utrobique est idem relativum, αὐτοῦ αὐτῷ, neque ulla distinctionis nota divulsum. Denique quod ad aliam lectionem, quam alicubi forte occurrere observatum, Ἰησοῦ[?] pro αὐτοῦ, quis, qualisve ille codex fuerit, non addit: plures saltem aliter legere, negari non potest. Et quid si legamus Ἰησοῦ[?], id quoque facit ad confirmationem argumenti nostri, quod Christus ille Deus, quia de eo loquutum Prophetam Euangelista asserit, cujus, utpote Dei, gloriam visam Iesaiae, attestatur.
units.tr: Lord [κύριος] in verse 38, but this is not in the evangelist's own words, but in the passage of Isaiah. Verse 41, however, is the evangelist's, not the prophet's, when he says that he saw his glory. Third, "Lord" [κύριος] is not used exclusively or in opposition to Christ, but is an essential name, belonging as much to this person as to that. Fourth, of whom it is to be understood, "these things Isaiah said, when he spoke of him"; of the same person, which is joined in "when he saw his glory." In both places it is the same relative, αὐτοῦ, αὐτῷ, and it is not separated by any mark of distinction. Finally, as to the other reading, which perhaps is observed to occur somewhere, Jesus [Ἰησοῦ] instead of αὐτοῦ, he does not add what manuscript it was or what kind it was; but it cannot be denied that several read it differently. And even if we read Jesus [Ἰησοῦ], this also serves to confirm our argument: the evangelist asserts that the prophet spoke of him, and that Christ, who is God, is the one whose glory, as God's, Isaiah saw; he bears witness to this.

units.la: Tertio excipit, vocem videre exponi posse praevidere, seu prophetare. Verum quidem videre prophetarum idem aliquando valere, quod praevidere, aut prophetare; quin & ii de Christi gloria subinde prophetarint, non negamus, quod locus Petri confirmat, 1. Pet. 1. 10. sed in hoc loco videre distinguitur a praedicare vel prophetare: nam distincte dicit, eum vidisse Christi gloriam, & loquutum de eo fuisse: deinde revera in visione ei obtigisse cospiciendam gloriam, & vidit Dominum sedentem super solium amplum & excelsum. Iesa. vi. vi. 1. denique quid hic legitur prophetasse de Christi gloria? ut de prophetia ejusmodi, & non de visione gloriae ipsa, exponi locus deberet.
units.tr: Third, he objects that the word "to see" can be explained as "to foresee," or "to prophesy." It is true indeed that to see in the prophets sometimes has the same force as to foresee or to prophesy, and we do not deny that they also at times prophesied of the glory of Christ, as the passage of Peter confirms, 1 Peter 1:10. But in this passage "to see" is distinguished from "to preach" or "to prophesy," for the evangelist plainly says that he saw the glory of Christ and spoke of him; and further, that in the vision the glory was actually granted to him to behold: "he saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne," Isaiah 6:1. Finally, what is read here about prophesying of the glory of Christ? The passage ought to be explained as a matter of prophecy of that kind, and not of the vision of the glory itself.

units.la: Quarto respondet, verba ista Euangelistae, super quibus est disputatio, nempe verf. 41.
