Ista dixit Iesaias, &c. non de loco Iesa. vi. sed Iesa. lIII.[?] accipi debere, nam utrumque principaliter; Itaque cum respiciendum semper sit ad illud quod principale est: verisimile, imo necessarium est, Iohannem in censura ac iudicio ferendo, non illius quod obiter & ad alius confirmationem adduxerat, sed ejus quod erat principale, rationem habuisse: ac proinde illud hæc de loco capitis liii[?]. intelligi voluisse. Illud tamen non incitus concesserim, secundario, & quatenus posterior ratio, in priore, virtute includitur, etiam ad posterius dictum, illud hæc pertinere. Ex quibus manifeste apparet, locum capitis sexti, ad Christi gloriam visam, non tam directe trahi. utrque fuerat allegatus. Verum obstat, quod Iesa. vi. fuerat ultimo allegatus & proxime. Atque nihil obstat, quominus commodissime ad eum referatur. Deniq; ibi visa fuit Dei gloria & Christi, non ita cap. liii[?]. Sed, regerit primo, Iesaiam non gloriam vidisse Domini, sed eum sedentem super solium, & Angelis acclamasse, plenam esse terram gloria Domini. Quasi illa non pro eodem habenda essent, videre alicujus gloriam, aut in gloria sedentem, vel admodum gloriose se exhibentem? 2. inquit, illa visio Apoc. 4. ad Pa-trem refertur, non ad Christum: imo ad Deum refertur, uti quoque illa Iesa. vi. & non ad Patrem, opposite, vel exclusive ad Christum, nam & Christus Deus. Deinde etiam opposite accipiatur ad Christum, sed prout est agnus mactatus, Apoc. v. 6. non prout est filius Dei. Et dicitur tamen quoque fuisse in medio throno, ibidem. Iam 3. inquit, aliquoties locum Iesa. vi. citari in Nov. Test. nunquam vero Christo tribui, semper Patri. Citatur vero Matth. xiii. 14. & Act. xxviii. 25. atque utrobique Christo applicatur, & in eodem argumento incredulitatis Iudaeorum erga Christum, ac in loco praesenti. Deinde non in illis locis epiphonema istud subjungitur, quod hoc in loco, Prophetam ista dixisse, quando gloriam ejus vidit, deque eo loquutus fuit, nempe de Christo. Ut Euangelista sua ista expositione indubium relinquat, de Christo debere intelligi; atque uti hic, sic & alibi. Quod si velimus, utrique citationi, tum ex Iesa. liii[?]. tum cap. vi. applicari debere ea, quae Euangelista post utriusque citationem subjungit: ista dixit Iesaias, &c. non admodum refragor, modo non excludatur id, quod proxime adduxerat ex Iesa. vi. ad quod pronomen relativum τωῦτο[?], & αὐτῷ[?] ultro se refert. Et hoc de visa gloria ad cap. vi. id vero quod de eo loquutus dicitur Propheta, principalius ad cap. liii[?]. applicetur. Neque nisi aperta vi id quod Euangelista de Iesaia, quae dixerit visa ejus gloria, a cap. vi. abduci poterit, & ad caput trahi liii[?]. ubi quamvis in fine subjiciatur id, quod ad Christi facere gloriam debuit, non tamen argumentum capitis est, Christi gloriam exponere, sed passiones: non certe in visione ei obtigit Christi gloria, uti cap. vi. Prophetae conspicienda datur gloria Domini. Et quantumvis à cap. vi. post exhibitam illam gloriae visionem, subjungatur prophetia de poena gentis Iudaicae, propter suam incredulitatem, hoc non tollit praecedentis visionis veritatem, vel majestatem. Denique quamvis ad Christi παθήματα[?] sequutae sint δόξαι[?], atque tenderint ad gloriam, diversa tamen illa in se fuerunt, & diversis vicibus modisque tum a Prophetis, tum ab Apostolis expósita & confirmata: atque non impediunt, quo minus & Iesa. liii[?]. magis explicata fuerit veritas passionum Christi, & in visione Iesa. vi. ejus gloria. Quod vero tandem vult, pronomen omnino referendum esse ad Jes. liii[?]. quandoquidem quod inde citat pro principali argumento habendum, & quod ex Ies. vi. pro minus principali, quodque obiter tantum attulerit ad prioris confirmationem. Sed primo non probat istam differentiam inter illa duo loca, & ca. & fac probasse, non minus tamen momenti est in hoc, quam illo, seu loco, seu facto inde argumento. Postremo quidquid fit, Euangelista subjuncta sua obser-vatione, quod quando ista scripserit Jesaias, vidit ejus gloriam, manuducit nos satis evidenter ad Jesa. vi. Quod tandem nec negare Adversarius potuit, sed, tanquam secundarium aliquod admittere coactus fuit. Imo primario hoc ad Iesa. vi. referri debet, quod de vita Prophetae, Christi gloria Iohannes commemorat: & Christum probat Deum, cujus gloriam Jesaias isto loco tanta cum majestate vidit, atque veneratus fuit.
units.tr: Fourthly, he replies that the Evangelist's words under discussion, namely verse 41, "These things said Isaiah," etc., must be taken not of the passage in Isaiah 6 but of Isaiah 53, since both were cited principally; therefore, since one must always look to what is principal, it is likely, indeed necessary, that John, in pronouncing his judgement, took account not of what he had adduced incidentally and to confirm another point, but of what was principal, and so meant these words to refer to the passage in chapter 53. Yet I would not be unwilling to grant that, secondarily, and insofar as the later reason is included in the earlier, these words also pertain to the later saying. From this it clearly appears that the passage of chapter 6, concerning the vision of Christ's glory, is not so directly drawn into the argument. Both had been cited. But it is objected that Isaiah 6 was cited last and nearest. Yet nothing prevents its being most fittingly referred to that passage. Finally, there the glory of God and of Christ was seen, which is not so in chapter 53. But, he objects first, Isaiah did not see the glory of the Lord, but saw him sitting upon the throne, and the angels cried out that the whole earth is full of the glory of the Lord. As if these were not to be regarded as the same thing: to see someone's glory, or to see him sitting in glory, or presenting himself very gloriously? Second, he says that the vision in Revelation 4 is referred to the Father, not to Christ. But it is referred to God, as is also that of Isaiah 6, and not to the Father in opposition to, or exclusively of, Christ, for Christ is also God. Moreover, it is taken in opposition to Christ too, but as he is the slain Lamb (Apoc. v. 6), not as he is the Son of God. And yet he is also said to have been "in the midst of the throne" in the same place. Third, he says that Isaiah 6 is cited several times in the New Testament, but is never attributed to Christ, always to the Father. Yet Matthew 13:14 and Acts 28:25 are cited, and in both places it is applied to Christ, in the same argument about the Jews' unbelief towards Christ as in the present place. Furthermore, in those places that clause is not added which here says that the Prophet spoke these things when he saw Christ's glory and spoke of him, namely of Christ; so that the Evangelist, by this exposition of his, leaves no doubt that it must be understood of Christ, and that this is so here as elsewhere. If we wish that both citations, from Isaiah 53 and from chapter 6, should be applied to what the Evangelist adds after both citations, "These things said Isaiah," etc., I do not greatly object, provided it is not excluded that what he had just adduced from Isaiah 6, to which the relative pronoun [τοῦτο] and [αὐτῷ] refer of their own accord, is included. And the saying about the vision of glory applies to chapter 6, while what is said of the Prophet's speaking of him applies more principally to chapter 53. Nor can what the Evangelist says of Isaiah, that his glory was seen when he spoke these things, be drawn away from chapter 6 and carried to chapter 53 except by open force; there, although at the end is added what ought to have served Christ's glory, the subject of the chapter is not to set forth his glory but his sufferings. Certainly in that chapter the glory of Christ was not granted to the Prophet to behold in a vision, as in chapter 6 the glory of the Lord is given to be seen. And however much, after the vision of that glory in chapter 6, the prophecy of the punishment of the Jewish nation for their unbelief is added, this does not take away the truth or majesty of the preceding vision. Finally, although the glories [δόξαι] followed the sufferings [παθήματα] of Christ and tended towards glory, these were nonetheless different things in themselves, and were set forth and confirmed in different ways and manners both by the Prophets and by the Apostles; and they do not prevent the truth of Christ's sufferings from being explained more fully in Isaiah 53, and his glory in the vision of Isaiah 6. As for what he finally wishes, that the pronoun must wholly be referred to Isaiah 53, since what he cites from there is to be held the principal argument, and what he cites from Isaiah 6 is less principal, and was adduced only incidentally to confirm the former: but first, he does not prove this difference between the two passages; and even if he had proved it, the argument drawn from the one place or the other is no less weighty in this matter. Lastly, whatever be the case, the Evangelist, by his added observation that when Isaiah wrote these things he saw his glory, leads us quite plainly to Isaiah 6. This the Adversary could not even deny, but was compelled to admit it as something secondary. Indeed, it must be referred primarily to Isaiah 6, that John records of the life of the Prophet the glory of Christ, and proves Christ to be God, whose glory Isaiah saw in that passage with such majesty and worshipped.

units.la: Ex loco vero, 1. Cor. x. 9. neque tentemus Christum, sicut quidam eorum tentave-runt, constat & Christum extitisse eo tempore, quo tentatus ab Israelitis fuit, ergo non demum cepisse a nativitate ex Maria, & fuisse Deum illum, quem passim dicuntur tentasse Israelitae. Exod. xvii. 2. quapropter contendens ריב populus cum Mose, dixerunt, date nobis aquam ut bibamus: quibus dixit Moses, quid contenditis תריבון mecum, quid tentatis תנסון יהוה [?] Iehovam? cum Mose quidem contenderunt, at Iehovam tentarunt, & hoc ipsum fuit argumentum contentionis, inter Mosem, ac populum, & vers. 3. vocavit autem nomen illius loci Massam & Meribam, propterea quod contenderant filii Israelis, & propterea quod tentaverant Iehovam, dicendo, estne Iehova inter nos, an non? Num. xxi. 6. tum immisit Iehova in populum illum serpentes spesteres, qui morderent populum: ita moriebatur populus multus ex Israele. Psalm. lxxviii. 18. & tentantes Deum cum animo suo, petiverunt cibum pro desiderio animi sui: ac obloquentes contra Deum, dixerunt, &c. 56. attamen tentarunt & exacerbarunt Deum excelsum. Psalm. xcv. 9. ubi tentaverunt me majores vestri, probaverunt me. Heb. iii. 9. & Psalm. cvi. 14. Sed ducti concupiscentia tentarunt Deum in solitudine. Ubique dicuntur tentasse Deum: quem Apostolus ait, fuisse Christum. Quare Christus idem est cum illo Deus.
units.tr: From the passage in 1 Corinthians 10:9, "Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted," it is evident both that Christ existed at the time when he was tempted by the Israelites, and therefore that he had not only begun to exist from his birth of Mary, and that he was that God whom the Israelites are everywhere said to have tempted. Exodus 17:2: "Wherefore the people contended [ריב] with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink. To whom Moses said, Why do you contend [תריבון] with me? Why do you tempt [תנסון] Jehovah?" They contended with Moses, but they tempted Jehovah, and this very thing was the ground of the contention between Moses and the people. Verse 3: "And he called the name of that place Massah and Meribah, because the children of Israel contended and because they tempted Jehovah, saying, Is Jehovah among us or not?" Numbers 21:6: "Then Jehovah sent fiery serpents among the people, which bit the people, so that many of Israel died." Psalm 78:18: "And they tempted God in their heart, asking food for their desire; and they spoke against God, and said, etc." Verse 56: "Yet they tempted and provoked the Most High God." Psalm 95:9: "When your fathers tempted me, they proved me." Hebrews 3:9, and Psalm 106:14: "But lusting exceedingly, they tempted God in the wilderness." Everywhere they are said to have tempted God, and the Apostle says that this was Christ. Therefore Christ is the same God.

units.la: Enjedinus: Ex his verbis, tum quod Deus sit, tum quod re ipsa ante nativitatem ex Maria, extiterit Christus, probari solet. Cum enim constet, ab Israelitis, in deserto, Deum esse tentatum; & hic dicatur, Christus ab illis fuisse tentatus: sequi videtur, Christum esse Deum. Sed primo, hanc argumentandi formam esse fallacem, jam saepe ostensum est; Non enim propter idem attributum, plura, unum & idem sunt. Deinde syllogismi talis Major, universaliter non est vera. Nam non solum Deum tentarunt Israelitae in deserto. Hic enim Paulus tentationem vocat, murmur illud populi cujus fit mentio Num.21. At ibi expresse legimus vers.5. Locutusque est populus contra Dominum, & Mosem. Et mox vers.7. Locuti sumus contra Dominum, & te. Sic Psal. 105. vers. 16. Et irritaverunt Mosem in ca-stris, Aaron sanctum Domini. Ibidem vs. 31. Vexatus est Moses propter eos, quia exacerba-verunt spiritum ejus, &c. Non ergo omnis, quem tentaverunt Israelitae, est Deus. Ac
units.tr: Enjedinus: From these words it is usually proved both that Christ is God and that, in fact, before his birth from Mary, Christ existed. For since it is agreed that God was tempted by the Israelites in the desert, and here it is said that Christ was tempted by them, it seems to follow that Christ is God. But first, this form of argument is fallacious, as has often been shown; for things are not one and the same merely because they share one attribute. Then, the major premise of such a syllogism is not universally true. For the Israelites did not tempt God alone in the desert. Here Paul calls it temptation, that murmuring of the people mentioned in Numbers 21. But there we read expressly in verse 5: "And the people spoke against God and against Moses." And soon after, verse 7: "We have spoken against the Lord and against you." So Psalm 105:16: "They also provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron the saint of the Lord." Verse 31 of the same: "Moses was troubled because of them, because they provoked his spirit, etc." Therefore not everyone whom the Israelites tempted is God. And

units.la: Resp. 1. Sic est, non propter quodvis idem attributum, aliqua sive aliqui sunt unum & idem: sed hic, uti non de quo-rumvis unitate, ita nec de qualicunque agimus: sermo vero est de unitate Dei, & Christi, Christum autem & Deum esse, & unum cum Deo non negant Adversarii: quaeritur, de modo, quo & hoc, & istud accipiendum sit. Ergo non est ut ex aliqua attributorum similitudine probemus demum unitatem, eam enim & Adversarii utcunque concedunt, sed explicemus. Ostendimus vero ex identita-te attributorum, eandem, quod ad rem seu essentiam, personarum. Nempe, non potuerint tentare Christum Israelitae, nisi jam tum exsistentem. Id autem Adversarii perperam negant. Et non tenta-runt eum aliter, quam qua Deum: hoc enim passim asseritur, illos Deum tentas-se. Neque aliter quam ut Deum tentare potuerunt. Et in hoc sita vis argumenti nostri prcinde syllogismus iste constabit expurũ particularibus. Et etiamsi Christus fuisset in deserto tentatus, non consequeretur eum propterea Deum esse habendum. Nam & Mosem & Aaronem, & Angelum Dei tentaverunt Israelitae, qui tamen non sunt Deus ipse. Quod vero ad alteram collectionem attinet, qua concluditur Christus fuisse ante matrem, eo quod dicatur tentatus esse in deserto: falsa & fallax etiam est. Nam primo, non dicit Apostolus, Christum fuisse tentatum, verba enim sic iacent: Neque tentemus Christum, sicut quidam eorum tentaverunt. Ubi verbum illud tentaverunt, non est transitive sed Absolute accipiendum, hoc sensu, tentationem fecerunt, sicut Graeci dicunt πεῖραν ποιεῖσθαι[?], pro πειράζων, ut est apud Hesychium; aut aliquod simile. Hanc interpretationem esse illi loco consonam, tum ea quae praecedunt, tum quae sequuntur, ostendunt. Subjicitur statim: Sicut quidam eorum murmurarunt. Ubi non exprimitur, contra quem murmurarint, sed vox murmurarunt absolute, non transitive ponitur, pro, murmurationem fecerunt, vel murmur ediderunt. Hoc enim tantum vult Apostolus, ne illorum scelera imitemur; & prohibet non ea ipsa, quae jam transacta erant, sed similia facinora. Sicut ergo potuerunt Corinthii fornicari, non cum iisdem quibus Iudaei, sed cum aliis similibus: ita potuerunt tentare, non eum quem Iudaei, sed alium praesentem, similem illi Iudaeorum duci. Deinde, si quis omnino contendat, verbum illud, tentaverunt, esse transitivum, & subaudiendum aliquem Accusativum: dicimus Ellipsin non esse supplendam ex antecedente, sed subintelligendum illud, quod alibi expressit scriptura. Notissimum autem erat, Israelitas tentasse Deum, id quod itentidem inculcatur. Psal. 77. vers. 18. 41. 56. Et Psal. 105. vers. 7. 14. 29. 32. 43. &c. Vide & Heb. 3. vers. 9. Ubi dicitur Spiritus sanctus fuisse tentatus in deserto. Hoc tanquam protritum & vulgare, subintelligi a quovis facile poterat ac debebat, ideoque nostri est. 11. Dicuntur quidem Israelitae loquuti contra Mosem, Num. xxi.5. וידבר העם[?] & vers. 7. atque contendisse cum eo. & Psalm. cvi. 16. ad iram eum provocasse יקניאוהו[?]. & spiritum ejus exacerbasse, vers. 32. הִמְרוּ אֶת רוּחוֹ[?] sed tentasse semper dicuntur Deum, dicentes, an possit Deus adstruere mensam in hoc deserto? Psalm. lxxviii. 18. quo non Mosem, sed Deum ipsum probare, fuit animus.
units.tr: Answer 1. That is so, but not because any one shared attribute makes some things or persons one and the same. Here, just as we are not speaking of unity in any sense whatever, we are speaking of the unity of God and Christ. The adversaries do not deny that Christ is God and one with God. The question is how this and that are to be understood. So we do not prove the unity from some similarity of attributes, which the adversaries in some measure grant anyway, but we explain it. We show, however, from the identity of attributes that the persons are the same as to the thing, or essence. The Israelites could not have tempted Christ unless he already existed, and the adversaries wrongly deny this. Nor did they tempt him otherwise than as God. This is asserted everywhere: that they tempted God. Nor could they have tempted him except as God. In this lies the force of our argument, and the syllogism will stand even when the particulars are stripped away. Even if Christ had been tempted in the wilderness, it would not follow that he must be regarded as God, for the Israelites also tempted Moses and Aaron and the angel of God, who are nevertheless not God himself. As for the other inference, by which it is concluded that Christ existed before his mother because it is said that he was tempted in the wilderness, this too is false and deceptive. First, the Apostle does not say that Christ was tempted. The words stand thus: Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted. Here the verb tempted is not to be taken transitively but absolutely, in the sense of they made a trial, as the Greeks say πεῖραν ποιεῖσθαι [peiran poieisthai], for πειράζων [peirazōn], as is found in Hesychius, or something similar. That this interpretation suits the passage is shown both by what comes before and by what follows. It is immediately added: as some of them also murmured. Here it is not stated against whom they murmured, but the word murmured is put absolutely, not transitively, meaning they made a murmuring or raised a complaint. This is all the Apostle wishes: that we should not imitate their sins. He forbids not those very deeds that had already been done, but similar wickedness. Just as the Corinthians could commit fornication, not with the same partners as the Jews, but with others like them, so they could tempt not him whom the Jews tempted, but another present person, like that leader of the Jews. Next, if anyone insists that the word tempted is transitive and that some accusative must be supplied, we say that the ellipsis is not to be filled from the preceding words but from what Scripture states expressly elsewhere. It was very well known that the Israelites tempted God, and this is repeatedly stressed: Psalm 77 verse 18, 41, 56; and Psalm 105 verses 7, 14, 29, 32, 43, and so on. See also Hebrews 3 verse 9, where it is said that the Holy Spirit was tempted in the wilderness. Since this was a familiar and common expression, anyone could and should easily supply it, and so it is our point. (11.) It is true that the Israelites are said to have spoken against Moses, Numbers 21:5, וידבר העם [vaydabber ha-am], and verse 7, and to have contended with him, and in Psalm 106:16 to have provoked him to anger, יקניאוהו [qinne'uhu], and to have embittered his spirit, verse 32, הִמְרוּ אֶת רוּחוֹ [himru et ruḥo]. But they are always said to have tempted God, saying, can God prepare a table in this wilderness? Psalm 78:18, where the intention was to test not Moses but God himself.

units.la: III. Verbum tentarant, in sermone Apostoli, no debet intransitive accipi vel absolute, quia ipsum est verbum activum, & requirit necessario suum accusativum, qui tentetur: vox murmurarunt absolute potest accipi, quamvis etiam subintelligatur alius, contra quem murmurent; & fornicati sunt consignificat foeminas, quibuscum peccarunt. Absurde vero infertur, quasi dubium, an cum iisdem quibuscum fornicati fuerunt Israelitae, intelligendum, ne fornicarentur Corinthii. Neque ad fornicationis mentionem addit objectum vel materia, cum quibus: uti in prohibitione tentationis. IV. Sed, inquit, subintelligatur quod tentarunt, sc. Deum. Omnino vero, neque Christum aliter tentarunt, quam quod ille Deus. Verùm Christus Deo non opponendus, qui cum eo non jungitur, sed identificatur. Et propterea Apostolus nil necesse duxit, nomen Dei addere, quum nominasset Christum. Deum autem ab Israelitis tentatum, tam non eget probatione, quam, non tentatum fuisse Christum, non nisi contra Apostolum intendi potest. Psalm. cvi. 29. est, ויכעיסו[?] & irritarunt. Ubi ellipsim non negamus: sed neque id quispiam dubitat, etiam in Sacris ellipses dari. In nostro vero loco non est necesse alio recurrere, quum expresse nominetur Christus, qui ab iis tentatus fuit. Praeterea, Christum intelligendum esse, quem Israelitae tentarunt, confirmatur ex conjungendi adverbio ab Apostolo non fuit adjectum. Illustratur & probatur hoc ex Psal. 105. verf. 29. Et irritaverunt operibus suis, & crevit in eis plaga. Vbi similis est prorsus ellipsis, quam si quis supplere velit, indicat verf. 14. quid ibi subintelligendum sit, ubi haec habentur: tentaverunt Deum in solitudine. Ergo hic quoque idem subintelligi debet. Sensus enim admonitionis Apostoli est: Ne nos modo tentemus Christum, sicut illi olim tentarunt Deum. Non est ergo hoc Erasmi cavillum, ut scribit Calvinus, sed vera, & genuina loci expositio. Quae confirmatur etiam ex vocabulo Christus, quod significat unctum. At unctio pertinet ad corpus, & ut Trinitarii loquuntur, ad humanitatem. Constat autem etiam ipsorum confessione, tunc corpus, & humanitatem Christi, re ipsa non extitisse. Quomodo ergo, quod non erat, tentari potuit? Neque hic illa, ab ipsis conficta communicatio idiomatum, quidquam valet. Nam nemo unquam ab eo quod nondum est, & quod non habet, denominari solet. Si igitur ille λό-γος seu spiritus, nondum habebat, in deserto, carnem & corpus: vocari Christus nullo modo potuit. Praeterea, etiam si concedamus, repetendum esse vocabulum, Christus; tamen nihil efficient. Nam & ante & post haec verba docet Apostolus, omnia quae Patribus illis contigerunt, fuisse figuras & typos. Scimus autem Christum in figura, & occisum, & venditum, & crucifixum fuisse, etiam in veteri Testamento. Ergo si tentatus etiam est, in figura tentatus est, hoc est, in re aliqua Christum repraesentante & significante, verbi gratia, in Mose. Quod illis libenter concedimus, neque quidquam contra nos facit. Denique, cum Christi vox generalis sit, & omnibus regibus ac ducibus attribui soleat, possumus dicere, Iudaeos tentasse Christum, sed non illum cujus tentationem hic prohibet Corinthiis Paulus, verum suum, & a Deo sibi datum Christum, nempe Mosem, qui non tantum propterea poterat dici Christus, quia figuram gerebat Iesu, filii Mariae, qui postea maxime pro-
units.tr: III. The verb tentarunt [they tempted] in the Apostle's words should not be taken intransitively or absolutely, because it is an active verb and necessarily requires its accusative, the one who is tempted. The verb murmured can be taken absolutely, although some other object, against whom they murmur, may also be understood; and committed fornication implies women with whom they sinned. It is absurd to infer, as if it were doubtful, that the sense is "do not commit fornication with the same women as the Israelites did," as if the Corinthians were warned against fornication. Nor does the mention of fornication add an object or material, with whom, as the prohibition of tempting does. IV. But, they say, let it be understood that they tempted God. Certainly they did not tempt Christ otherwise than as God. But Christ is not to be set against God, as one who is joined to him, but is identified with him. For this reason the Apostle thought it unnecessary to add the name of God when he had named Christ. That the Israelites tempted God needs no more proof than that Christ was not tempted can be maintained only against the Apostle. Psalm 106:29 reads ויכעיסו [vayakisu], and they provoked. We do not deny an ellipsis there, but no one doubts that ellipses occur even in Sacred Scripture. In our passage, however, there is no need to look elsewhere, since Christ, who was tempted by them, is expressly named. Moreover, that Christ is the one whom the Israelites tempted is confirmed by the connecting adverb, which the Apostle did not add. This is illustrated and proved from Psalm 105 verse 29: And they provoked him by their works, and a plague broke out among them. Here the ellipsis is entirely similar, and if anyone wishes to supply it, verse 14 indicates what must be understood there, where we read: they tempted God in the wilderness. So here too the same must be understood. For the sense of the Apostle's admonition is this: Let us not now tempt Christ, as those men of old tempted God. Therefore this is not Erasmus's quibble, as Calvin writes, but the true and genuine exposition of the passage. It is also confirmed by the word Christ, which means anointed. But anointing pertains to the body and, as the Trinitarians speak, to the humanity. It is admitted by their own confession that at that time the body and humanity of Christ did not actually exist. How then could what did not exist be tempted? Nor does the so-called communication of idioms, invented by them, help here. For no one is ever named from what does not yet exist and does not yet have something. If, therefore, that Logos or spirit did not yet have flesh and body in the wilderness, he could in no way be called Christ. Furthermore, even if we concede that the word Christ must be repeated, they will gain nothing. For both before and after these words the Apostle teaches that all the things that happened to those fathers were figures and types. We know that Christ was also in the Old Testament prefigured as slain, sold, and crucified. Therefore if he was also tempted, he was tempted in a figure, that is, in some thing representing and signifying Christ, for example in Moses. We gladly concede this, and it does nothing against us. Finally, since the word Christ is general and is usually applied to all kings and leaders, we may say that the Jews tempted Christ, but not the one whom Paul here forbids the Corinthians to tempt, rather their own Christ, given to them by God, namely Moses. He could be called Christ not only because he bore a figure of Jesus, son of Mary, who was later chiefly…

units.la: [illegible, ~1 letters] ne tentemus Christum, quemadmodum & quidam eorum tentarunt. Quorsum alias istud & ? conjungit tentationem hanc & istam, ne tentemus, &c. quemadmodum tentarunt, & idem utrobique objectum, Christum. Hunc ne tentent Corinthii, quem eundem tentarant & Israelitae. Non similitudine aliqua generali ne tentent, sed in specie, ne Christum tentent, quomodo se culpae istius reos fecerant Israelitae. v. Jam & faciamus ita legi, quemadmodum & quidam eorum tentarunt Deum: non certe sic peribit nobis argumentum nostrum. Nam, praeterquam quod & Christus sub nomine Dei continetur, aequiparatur tentatio ejus, & Dei. Non autem commode ista conjungentur, tentatio Christi, & Dei, sive prohibitio illius, ad normam istius, si Christus non alia sit persona, quam Adversarii volunt. Quid enim videtur, auderet ne aliquis de homine, in quantavis dignitate constituto, ita loqui, v. g. de Apostolo aliquo, & quod Apostolo majus inter homines dari potest, ne tentemus eum, quemadmodum & quidam Israelitarum tentarunt Deum? Ne dicam, haud fuere sensum & contextum orationis: quis ferat, istum in modum de homine fieri, in comparatione ad Deum, & ad flagitium, quod tanto ardore ac vindicta in suos prosequutus Deus fuit? Taceo, quod alias Adversarii tam cupide solent ampletti, sicubi se diversa lectio offerat, quae favere ipsis videatur, quod hoc in loco nonnulla exemplaria habent, quemadmodum & quidam eorum tentarunt αὐτὸν eum,vid. Christum: nulla vero hic legere ,θεόν. v 1. Elumbe vero & tritum istud est argumentum, Christum non posse intelligi ab Israelitis tentatum, quandoquidem tum nondum fuerat unctus,& homo: quia non secundum id, quod unctus, is tamen, qui jam prie[?] dictus est Christus: verum etiam quia re-vera erat a Deo unctus, in ducem & principem populi Israelitici, hoc enim est, esse Christum. Ergo potest in posteriori clausula quoque Chri-sti vox repeti, sed in alia significatione. Quod fieri necesse est in caeteris quoque Apostoli ad-monitionibus: ne fornicemur, inquit: Intelli-ge cum scortis praesentibus: sicut quidam ex ipsis fornicati sunt, scilicet cum scortis ea aetate viventibus. jam tum unctus erat, quum id scriberet Apostolus, sed secundum aliam sui ratio-nem, intelligitur. Neque hic ad confi-ctam aliquam idiomatum recurrimus communicationem: & scimus satis, non appellatum Christum fuisse in deserto, uti hoc jam tempore a Paulo appellari potuit, debuitque, fuisse tamen eundem, qui nunc Christus erat & humanatus.
units.tr: Lest we tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted. Why does he otherwise join this temptation and that one, lest we tempt, etc., as they tempted, and the same object in both, Christ? The Corinthians are not to tempt him whom the Israelites tempted. The warning is not general, that they should not tempt by some general likeness, but specifically, that they should not tempt Christ, as the Israelites made themselves guilty of this offence. V. Even if we read it thus, as some of them also tempted God, our argument will certainly not be lost. For, apart from the fact that Christ is included under the name of God, his temptation and God's are placed on the same level. But these cannot be fittingly joined, the temptation of Christ and of God, or the prohibition of the one according to the rule of the other, if Christ is not a different person from what the adversaries want. For what would seem to follow? Would anyone dare to speak thus of a man, however high his dignity, for example of some Apostle, or of anyone greater than an Apostle among men: let us not tempt him, as some of the Israelites tempted God? Not to mention that this would not fit the sense and context of the discourse. Who could bear that a man should be spoken of in such a way in comparison with God, and with the crime which God pursued with such zeal and vengeance against his own people? I pass over the fact that the adversaries are usually so eager to seize on a different reading whenever one appears that seems to favour them. In this passage some copies have as some of them also tempted αὐτὸν [auton], him, that is, Christ; but none reads θεόν [theon] here. VI. Moreover, the argument that Christ cannot be understood as tempted by the Israelites, since at that time he had not yet been anointed and become man, is stale and worn out. Not only is he who was already named Christ, not according to what he was anointed, but in truth he was anointed by God as leader and prince of the Israelite people, for that is what it means to be Christ. Therefore the name of Christ can be repeated also in the latter clause, but in another sense. This must happen with the Apostle's other admonitions too: let us not commit fornication, he says. Understand this with the present harlots, as some of them committed fornication, that is, with harlots living in that age. He was already anointed when he wrote this, but he is understood according to another aspect of his office. Nor do we here have recourse to any invented communication of idioms. We know well that he was not called Christ in the wilderness as he could and should be called by Paul now, yet he was the same one who is now Christ and made man.

units.la: VII. Longius vero abit, quod Christum in deserto tentatum exponant (nam pariter Socinus respondet, & eodem passim modo Enjedinus ac Socinus) de Christo tentato in Mose, seu in sui aliqua figura: nam dicuntur omnia illa contigisse in figuris. Non in figuris, sed τύποι[?], figurae, exemplaria, uti quorum exemplo nos admonemur, ne in simile genus peccati labamur, & poenae. Deinde Mosem Christi typum hic gessisse, quando vel populus Deum tentavit, vel fatigavit Mosem, non probatur. Dicant ergo & in reliquis omnibus rebus Mosem Christi egisse typum, sive quas egit, sive passus fuit. Et Christum illa eadem posse dici passum, vel egisse. Porro si Mosem indicare, Apostolo fuisset animus, id non ita siluisset, vel involvisset obscure, qui quotiescunque de Mose dicendi offert se vel levis occasio, aperte satis eum nominare consuevit & praedicare.
units.tr: VII. They go further astray in explaining that Christ was tempted in the wilderness as Christ tempted in Moses, or in some figure of himself. (Socinus answers in the same way, and Enjedinus everywhere follows Socinus.) For all those things, they say, happened in figures. But they did not happen in figures; they happened as types [τύποι], figures and examples, by whose example we are warned not to fall into the same kind of sin and punishment. Next, that Moses was here a type of Christ, when either the people tempted God or wearied Moses, is not proved. Let them say, then, that Moses was a type of Christ in all the other things too, whether those he did or those he suffered, and that Christ could likewise be said to have suffered or done those same things. Moreover, if the Apostle had meant to indicate Moses, he would not have kept silent about it or wrapped it up obscurely, since whenever even a slight occasion for speaking of Moses presents itself, he is accustomed to name and proclaim him plainly enough.

units.la: Quod pariter valet, ad ultimam, seu quartam Enjedini expositionem, qua per Christum, in priori etiam orationis membro, Mosem intelligit, voce Christi accepta appellative pro quovis uncto. Quid non isti homines audent, & in Scriptura exponenda, atque ad se trahenda? Velit, nolit, sibi suisque hypothesibus servire eam jubent & morem gerere. Jam verbum tentarunt, intransitive volunt accipi: ac si cogantur ejus accusativum admittere, substituunt in textu vocem Dei, ut Christum sc. praeterant: vel si hoc non succedat modo, Christum tentatum exponunt in persona Mosis: denique ipsum Mosem intelligendum contendunt, atque hic appellari Christum. Itane ambiguè tandem & periculose loquutus fuisset Apostolus, & tam temere usurpasset nomen Christi, quod in Novo Testamento de nullo usurpatum, quam de Jesu Christo? de alio, vel de Mose hoc in loco accipere nemo potuisset, nemo etiam potuit, his solum Novatoribus exceptis. Dicant vero, quorsum Apostolus non aperte nominasset Mosem, siquidem eum designare voluisset. Et noluerit eum vocare, annon alia erant nomina, vel tituli, quibus notaretur, quam voce Christi, adeo dubia, & plena istum in sensum periculi? Nequidem in veteri unquam Testamento Moses unctus aut Christus fuit appellatus, nedum in Novo. Neque is etiam legitur fuisse tentatus. Et si per nomen Christi intelligere voluisset eum ducem populi fuisse, principemque, quanto certius meliusque ducem aut principem dixisset populi tentatum fuisse Mosem, quam Christum? & hoc simpliciter, sine ullo additamento, quod indicium vel minimum praebeat nomen istud aliter, ac de alio sumendi, quam soleat? Quam deniq; elumbe est, expositionem istam inde probare vel confirmare, quod ad prohibitionem de scortatione intelligi deberet, ne fornicetur sc. cum scortis ea aetate viventibus. Quasi vel fornicari aliquis absq; scortis queat; vel periculū videatur, ne quis fornicetur cum aliis, quam cum suae aetatis scortis.
units.tr: The same holds for Enjedinus's last, or fourth, explanation, by which he understands Moses even in the first clause of the sentence, taking the word Christ appellatively for any anointed person. What do these men not dare, in expounding Scripture and bending it to themselves? Whether it likes it or not, they order it to serve and obey their own hypotheses. Now they want the verb tempted taken intransitively; and if they are forced to admit an object, they substitute the word of God in the text, so as to pass over Christ. Or if that does not work, they explain that Christ was tempted in the person of Moses. Finally they contend that Moses himself must be understood, and that Christ is named here. Would the Apostle have spoken so ambiguously and dangerously, and so rashly used the name of Christ, which in the New Testament is used of no one but Jesus Christ? No one could take it in this place of anyone other than Jesus Christ, or of Moses. No one ever has, except these innovators alone. Let them say why the Apostle did not openly name Moses, if he had wished to designate him. And if he did not want to call him that, were there not other names or titles by which he could have been marked, rather than the word Christ, so doubtful and so full of danger in that sense? Moses was never called anointed, or Christ, even in the Old Testament, much less in the New. Nor is he read to have been tempted. And if by the name of Christ he had meant that Moses was the leader and prince of the people, how much more certainly and better would he have said that Moses, the leader or prince of the people, was tempted, than that Christ was! And he would have said it simply, without any addition that might give the slightest sign that the name is to be taken otherwise than usual, and of someone else. Finally, how feeble it is to prove or confirm that explanation from the fact that it ought to be understood of the prohibition of fornication, let us not commit fornication, namely with prostitutes living in that age! As if anyone could commit fornication without prostitutes, or as if there were any danger that someone might commit fornication with anyone other than the prostitutes of his own age.

units.la: Porro ad id quod Psalm. xcvii. 8. de Deo dicitur, & pariter Christo tribuit Apostolus Heb. 1. 6. & adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei, iterum Enjedinus:
units.tr: Next, concerning what is said of God in Psalm xcvii. 8, and which the Apostle likewise attributes to Christ in Heb. 1. 6, "let all the angels of God worship him," Enjedinus again:

units.la: Duobus modis solent, ex hoc loco, Christi divinitatem adversarii probare. Primo ajunt, Angelos, cum praestantissima sint Dei creatu-ra, nullos adorare, nisi Deum verum. Si ergo adorant Christum, patet illum aeternum esse Deum. Sed hoc valde infirmum est: Nam primo vocabulum adorandi saepe pro honoris exhibitione, & civili cultu ponitur, neque statim, qui adoratur, pro Deo habetur. Cum autem Deus ipse Pater, Iesum hominem, propter obedientiam honoraverit, 1. Reg. 2. v. 30. Quicunque honoraverit me, honorabo eum, & honorari voluerit, quid mirum est, si Angeli quoque illum adoraverint, hoc est, honoraverint? Deinde, quantum interest, inter adorationem, & ministerium? Certe aut paria haec sunt aut ministerium sive servitus videtur majorem subjectionem significare, quam adoratio. Sed Angeli servierunt & ministrarunt, Deo jubente, hominibus, ut cum Tobiae, tum aliorum exempla monstrant: Et hic in fine Capitis Apostolus testatur. Et tamen hoc ipso, homines Dii non sunt effecti aut habiti. Ergo minus hoc ipsum adoratio efficiet. Sed fortius instant, cum sic ratiocinantur: Apostolus, inquiunt, hic citat locum ex Psal. 96. v. 8. At certum est ibi sermonem haberi, de*Deo vero Israelis. Ergo cum idem dictum hic applicet Apostolus Christo, indicat Christum esse verum Israelis Deum. Sunt, qui assumtum hujus syllogismi negent, & contendant non de vero Israelis Deo, illo Psalmi loco agi, sed de futuro novi orbis Domino, cujus proxime facta est mentio, qui non Iehova, sed Adon vocatur, quo non Deus, sed simpliciter, herus & Dominus significatur. Ego autem censeo, Propositionem esse hic negandam, aut potius distinguendam & explicandam. Nam dictum aliquod, dupliciter dici potest citari, primo cum eadem verba, & idem sensus verborum retinetur utrobique. Secundo cum allusio tantum quaedam fit ad locum, & vel sensus, vel utrumque influitur & immutatur. Sive ut planius loqua-
units.tr: From this passage, the adversaries usually prove the divinity of Christ in two ways. First, they say that angels, since they are the most excellent of God's creatures, worship no one but the true God. If therefore they worship Christ, it is plain that he is the eternal God. But this is very weak. For first, the word to worship is often used for showing honour and for civil reverence, and the one who is worshipped is not at once regarded as God. Since God the Father himself honoured Jesus, a man, on account of his obedience (1 Kings 2. 30: whoever honours me, I will honour him), and wished to be honoured, why is it strange if the angels also worshipped him, that is, honoured him? Next, how much difference is there between worship and ministry? Surely these are either equal, or else ministry or service seems to signify greater subjection than worship. But the angels served and ministered to men at God's command, as the examples of Tobias and others show, and the Apostle testifies to this at the end of the chapter. Yet by this very fact men have not been made or regarded as gods. Therefore worship will accomplish even less. But they press more strongly when they reason thus: the Apostle, they say, here cites a passage from Psalm xcvi. 8. But it is certain that there the discourse is about the true God of Israel. Therefore, since the Apostle applies the same saying to Christ here, he indicates that Christ is the true God of Israel. Some deny the assumption of this syllogism, and contend that the psalm is not about the true God of Israel but about the future Lord of the new world, whose mention was just made, who is called not Jehovah but Adon, which signifies not God but simply lord and master. I, however, think the proposition should be denied here, or rather distinguished and explained. For a saying can be cited in two ways: first, when the same words and the same sense of the words are kept on both sides; second, when there is only some allusion to the passage, and either the sense or both are influenced and altered. Or, to speak more plainly...

units.la: Resp. I. Non quaeritur hoc loco, quid saepe vocabulum adorandi significet, & an etiam pro civili cultu vel veneratione accipiatur, sed quomodo hic accipiendum sit. Neque, an qui adoratur, statim idcirco pro Deo habeatur: sed, an non hic intelligenda Dei adoratio sit, tum in Psalmo, tum in Epist. ad Hebraeos.
units.tr: Reply I. It is not asked here what the word to worship often signifies, and whether it is also taken for civil honour or veneration, but how it is to be taken here. Nor is it asked whether the one who is worshipped is for that reason at once regarded as God, but whether the worship of God is not to be understood here, both in the Psalm and in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: II. Quando civilis adoratio intelligenda, hoc ipsa res manifeste satis indicat: at ubi objectum ponitur, cui religiosa convenit, quemadmodum Deo, Christoque eam convenire Adversarii haud negant, etiam talem intelligendum esse, ex rei tum natura quoque evincitur.
units.tr: II. When civil worship is meant, the thing itself indicates this clearly enough. But where an object is set forth to which religious worship belongs, as the adversaries do not deny it belongs to God and to Christ, it is also shown from the nature of the matter that such worship is to be understood.

units.la: III. Aliud longe diversumque est, quando Deus dicitur aliquem honorare, vel creatura Deum, seu Christum adorare. Aliter Deus honorat suos, aliter sui Deum. Ille effective honorem iis tribuendo, sed non uti creaturae Deum, cum humili, subjectione, agnitione, & reverentia animi erga adorandam majestatem, atque ὑπεροχὴν [?] honorant, quae est religiosa & pia adoratio.
units.tr: III. It is far different when God is said to honour someone, or a creature to worship God or Christ. God honours his people in one way, and his people worship God in another. He honours them effectively, by bestowing honour on them, but not as a creature worships God, with humble subjection, acknowledgement, and reverence of mind towards the majesty to be worshipped. They honour him with pre-eminence [ὑπεροχήν], which is religious and pious worship.

units.la: IV. Non sunt paria, adoratio, & ministerium: ministerium debemus multis, & suum Angeli nobis impendunt, haud propterea adorationem. Neutiquam vero ministerium sive servitus videtur majorem subjectionem significare, quam adoratio. Adoratio ministerium comprehendit, non vicissim ministerium, nisi religiosum, adorationem.
units.tr: IV. Worship and ministry are not equal. We owe ministry to many, and angels render their own ministry to us, yet not on that account worship. Nor by any means does ministry or service seem to signify greater subjection than worship. Worship includes ministry; conversely, ministry, unless it is religious, does not include worship.

units.la: V. Multo minus per ministerium, seu adorationem aliquis Deus efficitur: bene quidem in religiosa adoratione, is, cui ista tribuitur, pro Deo agnoscitur & habetur.
units.tr: V. Still less is anyone made God through ministry or worship. Indeed, in religious worship, the one to whom it is given is acknowledged and held as God.

units.la: VI. Addit: esse, qui negent in isto Psalmi loco agi de vero Israelis Deo. Quibus quia se non dicit accedere, ejus probatione possumus facile supersedere: ne tamen forte alius isti sententiae adstipuletur, probamus tot ex ipso mur, id quod historice & literaliter uno in loco accipitur, in alio spiritualiter & mystice usurpatur. Si igitur adversarii asserant, ut omnino asserere videntur, dictum illud Psalmi, ab Apostolo, primo modo esse citatum: id illis negamus. Si posteriori modo, dicemus argumentum nihil concludere, & objectionem esse dissolutam. Nam erunt quatuor in syllogismo termini. Atque Apostolum non iisdem verbis, neque in eodem sensu citare locum Psalmi, quo a Davide scriptus est, his argumentis demonstrare possumus. Primo, verba ipsa utrobique sunt diversa, & immutata. Nam in Psalmo legimus: Adorate. At Apostolus, & Modo & Persona verbi mutata dixit, adorent. Hic legimus: & Adorent. apud Davidem conjunctio, &, nusquam est. Secundo, apud Davidem est Elohim, apud Apostolum, Angeli. Etsi autem Elohim, aliquando Angelos significant, id tamen perpetuum non est, & hoc loco interpretes peritiores interpretantur Deos potius, vel potentes, quam Angelos. Denique apud Davidem est ejus, Pronomen relativum, apud Apostolum est Dei, Nomen antecedens. Itaque apparet, non eadem verba esse utrobique posita. Iam, neque sensum esse eundem, apparet primo, quia hic applicatur dictum istud Primogenito. At in Psalmo nulla Primogeniti fit mentio, sed Dei, totius orbis terrarum Domini. Quod autem Primogeniti nomen, non possit significare verum & aeternum Deum, primo patet inde, quia Deus nunquam Primogenitus vocatur, neque etiam vocari recte potest, cum omne genitum, causam & principium ortus sui habeat. Deinde ipsi adversarii fatentur, hic Christum primogenitum vocari, respectu incarnationis, & temporis illius, quo dominium accepit post resurrectionem a mortuis. At tempore Davidis, neque incarnatio, neque resurrectio Christi extabat, ergo de illo in praesenti dicere non potuit, Adorate eum. Postremo verba & praecedentia & sequentia ostendunt, mystico, non historico & literali sensu citari hunc locum. Nam testimonia illa quae praecesserunt, ut illud: Filius meus es tu, &c. Et: Ero illi
units.tr: VI. He adds that there are some who deny that the passage of the Psalm is about the true God of Israel. Since he does not say that he agrees with them, we can easily pass over their proof. Yet lest perhaps another should side with that opinion, we prove by so many arguments from it that which is taken historically and literally in one place is used spiritually and mystically in another. If therefore the adversaries assert, as they seem altogether to assert, that the said saying of the Psalm is cited by the Apostle in the first way, we deny it to them. If in the second way, we shall say that the argument concludes nothing and the objection is dissolved, for there will be four terms in the syllogism. And that the Apostle does not cite the Psalm passage in the same words, or in the same sense in which David wrote it, we can show by these arguments. First, the words themselves are different and changed on each side. For in the Psalm we read: worship (adorate). But the Apostle, with the mood and person of the verb changed, says: let them worship (adorent). Here we read: and let them worship. In David there is no conjunction, and, anywhere. Second, in David it is Elohim; in the Apostle, angels. Although Elohim sometimes signifies angels, that is not invariable, and in this place more skilled interpreters explain it as gods or mighty ones rather than angels. Finally, in David there is the relative pronoun his, while in the Apostle there is the noun of God as antecedent. So it appears that the same words are not placed on each side. And that the sense is not the same appears first because this saying is here applied to the Firstborn. But in the Psalm there is no mention of a Firstborn, only of God, the Lord of the whole earth. That the name Firstborn cannot signify the true and eternal God is shown first by the fact that God is never called Firstborn, nor can he rightly be so called, since everything begotten has a cause and principle of its origin. Next, the adversaries themselves admit that here Christ is called Firstborn with respect to the incarnation, and that time when he received dominion after his resurrection from the dead. But in David's time neither the incarnation nor the resurrection of Christ existed, and therefore he could not say of him in the present, worship him. Lastly, both the words that precede and those that follow show that this passage is cited in a mystical, not a historical and literal, sense. For those testimonies that went before, such as You are my son, etc., and I will be to him

units.la: Psalmo argumentis, quot sunt versus, imo pluribus, quia uno versu aliquando plura continentur. Accipe initium: Iehova regnat. & propterea exsultet terra. vers. 2. Nubes & caligo circumstant eum, &c. 3. ignis ante eum, &c. 4. Perlustrant fulgura ejus, &c. 5. Montes, ut cera liquefiunt a praesentia Iehovae, a praesentia Domini totius terrae. Quis Iehova? quis dominus totius terrae? quis, a cujus conspectu & praesentia montes liquefiunt, nisi Deus verus Israelis? 6. indicant coeli justitiam ejus, & omnes populi vident honorem ejus. 7. pudore suffundantur omnes colentes sculptile, qui se jactant de idolis: incurvent se ei omnes Dii, vel angeli אלהים. Quis passim Diis aliis opponitur, & praefertur, & cui jubentur omnes se incurvare, quam vero Israelis Deo? Mitto sequentia, in quibus singuli versus, uno excepto, Iehovam nominant, aut compellant. 8. o Iehova. 9. Tu enim es Iehova. 10. Amantes Iehovae, a manu improborum eripit eos. 12. Laetamini justi in Iehova, & celebrate memoriam sanctitatis ejus. Eant nunc, qui volunt isto tamen Psalmo de Deo non agi: certe pio & intelligenti persuadebunt id, opinor, nunquam. Sed, adon vocatur. Semel nempe, at sexies Iehova: & adon, seu dominus totius terrae: quę solius Dei est periphrasis & elogium. Ne caetera dicam, quibus dominus ille ita describitur, ut alius praeter Deum, cogitari non possit. Denique adon dominus & alibi Deum notat. En similem valde locum, Psalm. cxiv. 7. a praesentia Domini adon tremuit terra, a praesentia Dei Iacobi.
units.tr: Psalm by its arguments, as many as there are verses, indeed more, since sometimes several are contained in one verse. Take the beginning: Jehovah reigns, and therefore let the earth rejoice. Verse 2: clouds and darkness surround him, etc. 3: fire goes before him, etc. 4: his lightnings light up the world, etc. 5: the mountains melt like wax at the presence of Jehovah, at the presence of the Lord of the whole earth. Who is Jehovah? Who is the Lord of the whole earth? Who is it at whose sight and presence the mountains melt, if not the true God of Israel? 6: the heavens declare his righteousness, and all peoples see his glory. 7: let all who serve graven images be put to shame, who boast in idols; let all gods, or angels, elohim, bow down before him. Who is set against other gods everywhere, and preferred to them, and before whom all are commanded to bow, if not the God of Israel? I pass over what follows, in which each verse, with one exception, names or addresses Jehovah. 8: O Jehovah. 9: For you are Jehovah. 10: Jehovah delivers those who love him from the hand of the wicked. 12: Rejoice in Jehovah, you righteous, and celebrate the memory of his holiness. Let those now go who want to say that this Psalm is not about God; surely they will never, I think, persuade a pious and intelligent person of it. But he is called adon. Indeed, Jehovah occurs once and six times adon, that is, Lord of the whole earth, which is a periphrasis and epithet of the God alone. Not to mention the other things by which that lord is so described that no one other than God can be thought of. Finally, adon, lord, also elsewhere denotes God. See a very similar passage, Psalm 114:7: at the presence of the Lord adon the earth trembled, at the presence of the God of Jacob.

units.la: Sententia denique Enjedini est, Psalmum esse mysticum, proprie de Davide intelligendum, & per accommodationem quandam Christo applicari, vel per allusionem. Quod si diceret, Psalmum propheticum esse de Christo, verum diceret: de Davide vero nihil est in toto Psalmo, quod indicet, ad eum referendum esse; plurima, quae nunc partim vidimus, quae in Patrem &c. Nemo est ita indoctus & perpudens, qui ausit negare, mysticè Christo applicari, imò non solum Christo, sed omnibus piis. Apocal. cap. 21. v. 7. cum literaliter, de David & Solomone loquatur. Similiter locus sequens: Thronus tuus Deus, &c. manifestissimè literaliter, de Solomone dicitur, & tamen mysticè ad Christum hic transfertur. Cum igitur & praecedentia & subsequentia testimonia, mysticè intelligantur: clarissimum est, haec quoque verba eodem modo esse accipienda. Res igitur ita se habet: Celebrat illo carmine David, seu quicunque illius Psalmi auctor est, victoriam Dei, qua universos Israelitas, & multas gentes, imperio Davidis subjecerat, ac propterea illum colendum, & adorandum censet. Pari ratione, cum Christus victa morte, & doloribus inferni superatus, resurrexisset, & plenariam potestatem, regnumque super omnes tam Israelitas quam Gentes obtinuisset, videbatur similis esse illi Deo, qui Davidi subjecerat plurimas gentes. Sicut igitur Deus verus merebatur adorationem, ob suam illam potentiam, ita etiam Christus propter simile imperium, adorationem meretur. Quae tamen non eadem neque æqualis, sed quodammodo similis est illi, quæ Deo debetur. Et propterea Apostolus alludens ad dictum Psalmistæ, conformibus verbis majestatem Christi expressit. Denique Davidem & ejus imperium, fuisse typum Iesu Christi & regni ejus, ex plurimis sacræ scripturæ locis apparet. Et qui mysticè sacras literas interpretabantur, quales erant Pharisæi, illum quoque Psalmum spiritualiter de Messia explicabant, quos hic Apostolus sequitur. prorsus reclamant. Verùm verba, prout in Psalmo leguntur, vel apud Apostolum, variant, atque sunt immutata. Ibi est, adorate; hic, adorent. Ibi simpliciter, adorate;hic,& adorent. Apud Davidem, elohim; apud Apostolum, angeli. Denique apud Davidem est, ejus; hic, Dei. Postremum hoc, ut ab eo ordiamur, manifestus error est, neque enim apud Davidem est, ejus, sed quod ipse statim dixit, simpliciter Elohim. Sed in Vulgata, quam nimis imperite noster passim sequitur,etiam in Psalmorū designando numero, ita quidem legitur, adorate eum omnes angeli ejus. in Hebræo verò, cujus non admodum callens fuit Enjedinus, [?] השתחוו־לו [?] כל אלהים adorate eum, quod pro modo loquendi Hebræo idem est quod, adorent: ut frustra in eo quædam rei notetur differentia. Uti & in eo, quod Apostolus interpretatur Elohim, angelos: nam Enjedinus ipse scit, quod Elohim aliquando Angelos significant. Sed hoc loco interpretes peritiores interpretantur Deos potius, vel potentes,quam Angelos. Ego vero peritiores Apostolo interpretes ignoro. & hic sequuntus Græcos, qui ita vertunt, προσκυνήσατε αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι αὐτοῦ [?]. ex qua versione tum temporis utpote ab omnibus receptâ, divini viri testimonia potere solebant, inquit Schlichtingius,in h. l. ad Hebræos, qui etiam Angelos vertit. Et quamvis aliqui Deos interpretentur,tamen eo intelligunt Angelos, nó certe excludunt. Schlichtingius: per istos autem Elohim, quia nulli melius, quam Angeli intelligi possunt, idcirco merito Græcus textus in locum Elohim Angelos Dei reposuit. Id saltem verum est, Angelos in hac voce omnino includendos esse.
units.tr: Finally, the opinion of Enjedinus is that the Psalm is mystical, to be understood properly of David, and applied to Christ by a certain accommodation or by allusion. If he were to say that the Psalm is prophetic about Christ, he would say what is true; but there is nothing in the whole Psalm about David that indicates it should be referred to him; most of what we have now partly seen, which in the Father, etc. No one is so unlearned and shameless as to dare to deny that it is applied to Christ mystically, indeed not only to Christ but to all the godly, Apocalypse 21:7, although it speaks literally of David and Solomon. Similarly the following passage, "Your throne, O God, etc.," is said most plainly literally of Solomon, and yet here it is mystically transferred to Christ. Since therefore both the preceding and following testimonies are understood mystically, it is most clear that these words too must be taken in the same way. The matter therefore stands thus: David, or whoever is the author of that Psalm, celebrates in that song the victory of God, by which he had subjected all the Israelites and many nations to David's rule, and therefore judges that God is to be honoured and worshipped. In the same way, when Christ, having conquered death and been overcome by the sorrows of hell, had risen, and had obtained full power and a kingdom over all, both Israelites and Gentiles, he seemed to be like that God who had subjected many nations to David. Just as the true God deserved worship because of that power, so Christ too deserves worship because of his like dominion. This worship, however, is not the same or equal, but in some way similar to that which is owed to God. And therefore the Apostle, alluding to the saying of the Psalmist, expressed the majesty of Christ in conformable words. Finally, that David and his rule were a type of Jesus Christ and his kingdom appears from very many places of Holy Scripture. And those who interpreted the sacred letters mystically, such as the Pharisees, explained that Psalm also spiritually of the Messiah, and this Apostle follows them. utterly cry out against it. But the words, as they are read in the Psalm and in the Apostle, differ and are changed. There it is adorate, here adorent; there simply adorate, here et adorent. In David elohim; in the Apostle angeli. Finally, in David it is ejus, here Dei. This last, to begin from it, is a manifest error, for in David it is not ejus but simply Elohim, as he himself says immediately. But in the Vulgate, which our author follows too carelessly everywhere, even in designating the number of the Psalm, it reads thus: adore him, all his angels. In the Hebrew, however, of which Enjedinus was not very skilled, [השתחוו־לו כל אלהים] adore him, all gods, which, according to the Hebrew idiom, is the same as adorent, so that in vain is some difference of the matter noted in it. The same holds for the fact that the Apostle renders Elohim as angels; for Enjedinus himself knows that Elohim sometimes signifies angels. But in this place more skilled interpreters render it gods, or the mighty, rather than angels. I, however, do not know more skilled interpreters than the Apostle, and here I follow the Greeks, who translate thus: [προσκυνήσατε αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι αὐτοῦ] worship him, all his angels. From this version, then received by all, the divine man's testimonies were wont to be used, says Schlichting on this passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews, who also renders it as angels. And although some interpret it as gods, nevertheless by it they understand angels, and certainly do not exclude them. Schlichting: But by these Elohim, since they can be understood best of all as angels, therefore the Greek text rightly put the angels of God in place of Elohim. At least this is true, that the angels must altogether be included in this word.

units.la: Cæterum ex sensu adhuc miserius disputat, ut non eundem ostendat esse verborum apud Davidem, atque apud Apostolum, Enjedinus. Eccur non? quia Paulus ea tribuit primogenito, dicens, quando verò iterum introducit primogenitum in mundum, dicit, & adorent &c. At in Psalmo nulla primogeniti fit mentio. Fiat argumentum, & negabitur consequentia Majoris. Ille, qui primogenitus, non est etiam Deus adorandus: vel, Deo primogenitum orbi exhibente, non potest huic dici, quod in Psalmis Deo, adorent eum, &c. Negamus. Verùm Deus non potest vocari primogenitus; neque qui primogenitus, Deus: negatur & hoc, quidem qua primogenitus ex mortuis, non est Deus, vel qua Deus non est talis: at nil obstat, quare non qui Deus, etiam, sed alia, quam Deitatis ratione, dicatur primogenitus, & vi-cissim. Ne jam de eo disputem, an ratione resurrectionis suæ hic dicatur primoge-nitus. Quod sequentia & antecedentia dicit quoque mystico sensu ad Christum applicari, litteraliter vero sive ad Davidem, sive Salomonem, id saltem de locis istis filius meus es tu, &c. & Thronus tuus Deus, &c. dici nequit, nemini, præter Christum, applicanda. Quemadmodum quod in Psalmo nostro legitur, adorate eum, &c. neutiquam Davidi, (quod & Socinus vult) tribuendum, imo ne unum quidem istorum verbum: non adorate, quod Davidi non debetur, nec competit: non enim, quod refertur ad Jehovam dominum totius terræ, de quo in toto Psalmo: omnes angeli, vel Dii, Davidi non subjecti, neque ei venerationem debuerunt vel detulerunt: nedum si juxta versionem Vulgatam, quam Enjedinus sequitur, legamus, Angeli ejus, non enim Davidis sunt Angeli, sed Dei. Quare omnino negamus, rem ita se habere, quod Auctor Psalmi celebret victoriam Dei, qua universos Israelitas, & multas gentes, imperio Davidis subjecerat, ac propterea eum colendum & adorandum censeret. Nihil est in toto Psalmo, quod istorum aliquid subindicet: nihil etiam Noster profert, quo illud confirmet: omnia denique, uti ostendimus, contraria, non aliter quam de Deo, & Christo ejus accipienda. Quomodo docet, Christum adorationem, propter simile cum Deo imperium, & ab Angelis, meritum? nec tamen eandem, sed quoquomodo ei similem: denique Apostolum alludere ad Psalmistæ dictum, & non proprie Christo applicare, uti de eo dictum atque intelligendum? Postremo non negamus, Psalmum de Christo exponendum, sed ut propheticum, non ut litteraliter de Davide, sed vere & proprie de Christo intelligendum.
units.tr: Otherwise Enjedinus argues more wretchedly from the sense, so as not to show that the words in David are the same as in the Apostle. Why not? Because Paul ascribes them to the firstborn, saying, "But when again he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, let them adore him," etc. But in the Psalm there is no mention of a firstborn. Let an argument be made, and the consequence of the major premise will be denied: he who is firstborn is not also to be worshipped as God; or, if God presents the firstborn to the world, it cannot be said to him what is said in the Psalms, "let them adore him," etc. We deny it. But God cannot be called firstborn, nor is he who is firstborn God; this too is denied, indeed as firstborn from the dead he is not God, or as God he is not such; but nothing hinders that he who is God may also be called firstborn, though on a different ground than that of his deity, and conversely. I will not now dispute whether here he is called firstborn on account of his resurrection. That what precedes and follows is also applied to Christ in a mystical sense, but literally either to David or to Solomon, is at least not possible to say of those passages, "You are my Son, etc." and "Your throne, O God, etc.," which must be applied to no one but Christ. Likewise, what is read in our Psalm, "adore him, etc.," is by no means to be ascribed to David (as Socinus also wishes), nor even one of these words: "do not adore," which is not owed to David nor fitting for him; "for," which refers to Jehovah, the Lord of the whole earth, of whom the whole Psalm speaks; "all angels," or "gods," not subject to David, who neither owed nor offered him veneration; much less if, according to the Vulgate version which Enjedinus follows, we read "his angels," for the angels are not David's but God's. Therefore we altogether deny that the matter stands thus, that the author of the Psalm celebrates the victory of God, by which he had subjected all the Israelites and many nations to David's rule, and therefore judged him to be honoured and worshipped. There is nothing in the whole Psalm that hints at any of these things; our author brings forward nothing to confirm it; finally, all things, as we have shown, are contrary to it and must be taken only of God and of his Christ. How does he teach that Christ deserves worship because of a dominion like God's, and from the angels, yet not the same worship but somehow similar to it; and that the Apostle alludes to the saying of the Psalmist, and does not properly apply it to Christ, as it is said and to be understood of him? Finally, we do not deny that the Psalm is to be expounded of Christ, but as prophetic: not literally of David, but truly and properly to be understood of Christ.

units.la: Valde perperam a Schlichtingio asseritur, Psalmum litteraliter de Deo, & mystice de Christo exponendum esse. Nunquam enim hoc, & non satis datur intelligi, quomodo Deus typum sustineat Christi. Nam neque Deus in typi rationem venit; neque aut par paris, aut major minoris, quemadmodum Deus ut sic, major est Christo, ut Mediatore, typus esse solet, aut potest.
units.tr: Schlichting is quite wrong to assert that the Psalm should be explained literally of God and mystically of Christ. It is never made clear, and it is not sufficiently explained, how God can serve as a type of Christ. For God does not come under the notion of a type, and a type is not usually, nor can it be, either equal to what it prefigures or greater than it in the way that God as such is greater than Christ as Mediator.

units.la: Ad id, quod Heb. 1. 10. Christo applicatur locus Psalmi c11. 26. Tu in principio domine, terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli, præter alias exceptiones, & hanc dat Enjedinus, intelligi mundi reformationem, non primam ejus creationem. Ubi primum id sumunt, quandoquidem hic cum præcedentibus locus jungitur, per solam copulativam καὶ[?], subintelligi vel repeti e prioribus debere, quod ista Pater dixerit ad Christum, quod ad alia hic etiam a V. T. citata loca præmittitur. Verum non sequitur, quamvis ad alia id fuerit prænotatum, hic pari modo intelligi debere, quod id sc. Pater dixerit Christo, non, quin dictum Christo fuerit. Nec enim valet consequentia, ut pari ubique modo omnia adducantur, aut par ratio citatorum, vel ubique talis subintelligenda necessario [illegible, ~9 letters] Patris, ad Filium: sed imper-sonaliter accipere convenit, illa de filio Christo nunc & tunc fuisse dicta. Ut vers. 8. ad filium vero, supple, dicitur: Thronus tuus Deus, &c. non quod Pater ita dixerit. Similiter & hoc loco vers. 10. &[?], subintellige, de eodem dicitur, vel dictum: tu in principio Dominine, &c. Nam non est ille stylus loquendi divinus, ut Pater ad Christum dicat ipse, in vocativo casu, Domine: quod impium dicit Enjedinus, vel Adversariorum alii, & blasphemum: neque Pater Christo adscribet opus creationis: neque etiam de orbis reformatione, ad Christum dicet, opus manuum tuarum est, quasi minus id sibi arrogaret, vel conveniret. Accedens deinde ad loci explicationem Adversarius, primam ponit illorum, qui negant haec verba, tu in principio, &c. de Christo, id volunt de Deo Patre esse dicta, atque accipienda.
units.tr: As for the fact that Heb. 1. 10 applies to Christ the passage of Psalm 101. 26, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast founded the earth, and the works of thy hands are the heavens, Enjedinus gives, among other explanations, this one: it refers to the reformation of the world, not its first creation. They take this as their starting point, since this passage is joined to what precedes by the single conjunction [καὶ], and so it must be understood or supplied from the earlier verses that the Father said this to Christ, as is stated before the other passages cited here from the Old Testament. But it does not follow that, because this was signalled in the other cases, it must likewise be understood here, that the Father said it to Christ, rather than that it was said to Christ. Nor is the inference valid that all the citations must be taken in the same way everywhere, or that the same manner of supplying a speaker from the Father to the Son must necessarily be assumed everywhere. Rather, it is proper to take these words impersonally, as having been spoken now and then of the Son Christ. So at verse 8, where it is said to the Son, the words Thy throne, O God, etc. are supplied, but it is not that the Father said them in this way. Similarly here at verse 10, the words Thou, Lord, in the beginning, etc. must be understood as said, or to be said, of the same person. For it is not a divine manner of speaking for the Father himself to address Christ with the vocative Lord. Enjedinus, or some other of our opponents, calls this impious and blasphemous. Nor would the Father ascribe to Christ the work of creation, nor would he say to Christ, concerning the reformation of the world, the works of thy hands, as if that were less becoming for himself to claim or less fitting. Our opponent then comes to the explanation of the passage and sets out the first view, of those who deny that the words Thou, in the beginning, etc. are spoken of Christ and maintain that they are said and must be taken of God the Father.

units.la: Quam suam sententiam his argumentis confirmant. Primo, si haec de Christo intelligantur, scriptor epistolae sibi contrariabitur, qui supra vers. 2. dixit, Deum Patrem creasse mundum per Filium. His autem verbis expresse Filio attribueretur creatio Mundi. Atqui ex instrumento causam principalem efficere, & ejusdem rei creationem, eodem loco, diversis autem attribuere, & inconstantis & secum pugnantis est. Confirmatur haec ratio, ex perpetuo consensu scripturae; nusquam enim creatio tribuitur Christo, sed ubique Deo, qui per Filium creaverit omnia. Ergo neque hoc testimonium aliter accipi ac intelligi debet. Praeterea, hoc ipsum probatur, ex proposito Apostoli, Nam vult Christum supra alios homines & Angelos extollere, ad quod probandum varia undique sollicite colligit testimonia. At si Christo creationem mundi attribueret, Creatorem creaturae compararet[?], quod certe fatuum & ineptum esset. Quis enim nescit, Creatorem infinitis partibus praestantiorem esse, suis creaturis? Et tamen videmus Apostolum, in suo proposito confirmando esse admodum diligentem & sollicitum, ex quo apparet illum rem apud quosdam dubiam & non creditam, velle confirmare, & persuadere. At nemo unquam dubitavit, Creatorem esse excellentiorem creatura: proinde res ea probatione non indigebat. Et peccatum est fieri per plura, quod potest fieri per pauciora. Cum igitur unico argumento evincere potuisset, Christum esse praestantiorem Angelis & hominibus, dicendo illum esse creatorem, hos autem creaturas, quid opus fuisset tot argumenta & testimonia conge-rere ?
units.tr: They confirm this view with the following arguments. First, if these words are understood of Christ, the writer of the epistle will contradict himself, since above, at verse 2, he said that God the Father created the world through the Son. Yet by these words the creation of the world would be expressly attributed to the Son. But to make a cause the principal agent through an instrument, and in the same place to attribute the creation of the same thing to different agents, is inconsistent and self-contradictory. This reasoning is confirmed by the constant agreement of Scripture; nowhere is creation attributed to Christ, but everywhere to God, who created all things through the Son. Therefore this testimony too must not be received or understood otherwise. Moreover, this very point is proved from the Apostle's purpose. For he wants to exalt Christ above other men and the angels, and to prove this he carefully gathers various testimonies from every side. But if he attributed the creation of the world to Christ, he would be comparing the Creator with the creature, which would certainly be foolish and absurd. For who does not know that the Creator is infinitely more excellent than his creatures? And yet we see the Apostle being very diligent and careful in confirming his purpose, from which it appears that he wished to confirm and persuade of a matter that was doubtful and not believed among some. But no one has ever doubted that the Creator is more excellent than the creature; therefore that matter did not need such proof. And it is a fault to do by many means what can be done by fewer. Since, then, he could have proved by a single argument that Christ is more excellent than the angels and men, by saying that he is the Creator and they are creatures, what need was there to heap together so many arguments and testimonies?

units.la: Resp. Ad primum argumentum, negari, repugnantiam in Apostolo fore, si nempe Filio attribuat creationem, quam antea adscripsit Patri, vers. 2. Nam non propterea eam negavit Christo, sed asseruit, quia Patri eam vendicavit, Deo. vers. 1. ὁ Θεός, vers. 2. ἐποίησε[?]: hoc enim ab isto regi, liquet, propterea idem Christo opus debetur quia idem cum Patre Deus. Nec per Filium dicitur Pater mundum creasse, tamquam per instrumentum: non magis quam cum v.3. δι᾽ ἑαυτοῦ[?] per semetipsum purgationem fecisse peccatorum. Ubi non instrumentum intelligitur, sed causa utrobique principalis. Neque diversis auctoribus creatio attribuitur, sed uni Deo, Patri, Filio, atque etiam Spiritui Sancto. Non etiam in Scriptura semper Patri adscripta creatio, sed & Christo, praesertim Ioann. 1. Col. 1. Heb. 1. vel Deo, & Patri per Christum. Jam & hoc accipimus, quod saltem ista responsione tum concedunt, agi hoc in loco, & vers. 2. de rerum omnium prima creatione, & non de spirituali aliqua mundi reformatione per Christum. Sed, quid opus, inquit, Apostolo, tot argumentis Christi excellentiam asserere, si creato-rem eum esse credat? quo solo probato confecta omnia. Verum praeterquam quod nostrum, non est, aliis, praesertim sacris Auctoribus, scribendi modum praefigere, & istud tamen, & aliaperegit Apostolus satis clare ac copiose, ut quae ad excellentiam Christi, Dei, & mediatoris
units.tr: Reply. To the first argument: it is denied that there would be any inconsistency in the Apostle if he attributes to the Son the creation which he had earlier ascribed to the Father, at verse 2. For he did not deny it to Christ on that account, but asserted it, because he claimed it for the Father, God, at verse 1 [ὁ Θεός] and verse 2 [ἐποίησε]. For it is plain that the one subject is governed by the other; therefore the same work is owed to Christ because he is the same God with the Father. Nor is it said that the Father created the world through the Son as through an instrument, any more than in verse 3 [δι᾽ ἑαυτοῦ], where he made purification of sins "through himself." In both places the principal cause is meant, not an instrument. Nor is creation attributed to different authors, but to the one God: to the Father, to the Son, and also to the Holy Spirit. Nor is creation in Scripture always ascribed to the Father; it is ascribed also to Christ, especially in John 1, Col. 1 and Heb. 1, or to God and the Father through Christ. Now we also accept this point, which in this reply at least they concede: that the passage, and verse 2, deals with the first creation of all things, and not with some spiritual reformation of the world through Christ. But, they say, why should the Apostle need so many arguments to assert Christ's excellence, if he believed him to be the Creator? By which alone, once proved, everything would be settled. But apart from the fact that it is not our place to prescribe to other writers, especially sacred authors, the manner in which they write, the Apostle did indeed deal with this point, and others, quite clearly and abundantly, so that he might gather from the Old Testament among the Hebrews, and set forth, whatever would serve the excellence of Christ as God and Mediator.

units.la: facerent, ex V. T. apud Hebraeos, conquireret & enarraret. Minime vero si creationem mundi Christo attribuit, creatorem creaturae comparat, sed creaturam auctori suo vindicat adstruitque. Neque necesse duxit Hebraeis suis, vel ullis denique hominibus persuadere, creatorem esse excellentiorem creaturâ, quorsum enim hoc
units.tr: Indeed, if he attributes the creation of the world to Christ, he does not compare the Creator with the creature; rather, he claims the creature for its author and establishes it so. Nor did he think it necessary to persuade his Hebrews, or any men at all, that the Creator is more excellent than the creature; for why would he say this?

units.la: Tom. 2. sed Christum creaturis omnibus non tantum esse praecellentiorem, sed quoque creatorem ipsum, rem apud Hebraeos suos maxime dubiam & non creditam, confirmare voluit. Denique nisi de Christo verba illa accipienda sint, quorsum adduxit? quare non illa aeque de Christo interpretanda ac reliqua, in toto capite? & hoc ejusdem cum caeteris esse naturae ac instituti, probat conjunctio, &c. Adversarii vero sensum ita expediunt: ac primo conjunctionem & non separandam, sed conjungendam cum verbis sequentibus volunt. Tum sententiam hoc modo efferunt, Deus, scilicet Pater unxit te, &c. & tu Domine, scilicet, qui unxisti Christum, in principio terram fundasti, ita ut apostrophe fiat ad Patrem. Mira verborum, & sensus inversio. Quid hic loci illa apostrophe, ubi toto capite de Christo agit, & ad probandam ejus excellentiam praesertim ex Scriptura disputat?
