Quid attinebat de Patre hoc docere, & transitione tam dura, inusitata, & nemini perceptibili orationem suam abrumpere & convertere ad Patrem? & si quid hujus rei agere voluisset, quorsum simpliciter allegare locum Vet. Test. & neque ante, neque post significare, isto animo aut fine citari, diversimodo ab allegatis? atque tam longum textum, per tres integros versus inserere, abrupta admiratione quadam, quasi extra se raptus, nulla adeo necessitate vel usu? denique & contra fidem codicum, & stylum Apostoli in variorum locorum citatione, ut aliqua distinctionis & applicationis nota utatur, ꝶ & non disjungere a sequentibus, uti disjungitur ꝶ, sed connectere, & distinctionis notam abjicere. Nam & res ipsa, & diversa Scripturae loca, distinctionis notam effiagitant. Quemadmodum quoque diversa Scripturae loca adducuntur & connectuntur per copulam ꝶ & ꝶ, Act. 1. 10. quemadmodum in libro Psalmorum scriptum est, fiat commoratio ejus deserta & non sit qui habitet in ea. Et, episcopatum ejus accipiat alius. Alterum ex Psalmo lxix. 25. alterum, Psalm. cix. 8. Secundam expositionem, quae etiam Socini, hanc fecit Enjedinus, ut, quae ex Psalmo isto hic citantur, ad Christum etiam pertineant, sed non omnia, non primus versus, qui est 10. Domine tu in principio fundasti terram, & opus manuum tuarum sunt coeli. verum sequentia, ipsi peribunt, &c.
units.tr: Vol. 2. But he wanted to confirm among his Hebrews a matter that was most doubtful and not believed: that Christ is not only far more excellent than all creatures, but is himself also their Creator. Finally, unless those words must be taken of Christ, why did he cite them? Why should they not be interpreted of Christ just as the rest are, throughout the whole chapter? The conjunction proves that this passage is of the same nature and purpose as the others, etc. Our opponents, however, explain the sense as follows. First, they want the conjunction not to be separated but joined with the words that follow. Then they render the sentence thus: God, namely the Father, anointed thee, etc.; and thou, Lord, namely, you who anointed Christ, in the beginning hast founded the earth, so that an apostrophe is made to the Father. This is a strange inversion of words and sense. What is the point of that apostrophe here, where he deals with Christ throughout the whole chapter and argues for his excellence especially from Scripture? What was the point of teaching something about the Father in this way, and of breaking off and turning his discourse to the Father by such a harsh, unusual transition, one that no one could perceive? And if he had wished to make some point of this kind, why simply cite a passage of the Old Testament, not signalling in any way before or after that it was cited with this intention or purpose, unlike the other citations? And why insert so long a text, over three whole verses, with a sort of abrupt admiration, as if carried out of himself, with no such necessity or use? Finally, this is contrary both to the reading of the manuscripts and to the Apostle's manner in citing various passages, which uses some mark of distinction and application, and does not detach it from what follows, as is done elsewhere, but connects it and drops the mark of distinction. For both the matter itself and the different passages of Scripture demand a mark of distinction. Just as different passages of Scripture are also cited and connected by the conjunction, as in Acts 1. 10: as it is written in the book of Psalms, let his habitation be desolate, and let no one dwell in it; and, let another take his bishopric. The first is from Psalm 69. 25, the second from Psalm 109. 8. Enjedinus has adopted a second explanation, which is also that of Socinus: the passages cited here from that Psalm also pertain to Christ, but not all of them. Not the first verse, which is verse 10: Lord, thou in the beginning didst found the earth, and the works of thy hands are the heavens, but the following: they shall perish, etc.

units.la: Alii vero sic explicant. Certum est, Apostolum hoc loco de dignitate regia, & regni Christi excellentia loqui, quod ipsum haereditario jure a Patre accepisse verf. 2. testatus est, quod non esse hunc mundum, neque ex isto mundo, cum ipse Christus alibi fatetur, tum hic cap. 2. verf. 5. Apostolus indicat, cum ait se de futuro orbe loqui. De hoc autem futuro orbe, cui praeficiendus erat, cujus pater & princeps erat Christus, insignis extat in hoc loco Psalmi prophetia, sicut illa verba ostendunt: Ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanebis, & omnes ut vestimentum veterascent, & velut amictum mutabis eos. Volens igitur Apostolus, haec verba producere, & illis novum Christi regnum, & veteris mundi abolitionem describi, ostendere, totum & integrum Psalmi locum adscripsit: Non
units.tr: Others, however, explain it differently. It is certain that the Apostle in this passage is speaking of royal dignity and the excellence of Christ's kingdom, which he testifies that Christ received from the Father by hereditary right (verse 2). That this is so, the Apostle shows both where Christ himself says that he is not of this world, and here in chapter 2, verse 5, where he says he is speaking of the world to come. The prophecy of this psalm about that future world, over which Christ was to be set as Father and Prince, stands out clearly in these words: They shall perish, but thou shalt endure; yea, they all shall wax old like a garment, and as a vesture shalt thou change them. The Apostle therefore wished to bring forward these words, and to describe by them the new kingdom of Christ and the abolition of the old world. So he cited the whole and entire passage of the Psalm: Not

units.la: Resp. I. Quis, quodve argumentum Adversarios nostros docuit, illa sic distribuere, & conjuncta adeo in uno loco, & una citatione divellere, ut unum ad Christum pertineat, aut Patrem, non item alterum? Annon tribus continuo versibus est, σὺ κύρἱε, σὺ δὲ, σὺ δὲ [?] ? tu vero ista sic unita divelles, & nec σὺ, nec δὲ, nec σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς ἐι [?], neque ἐπὶ σὺ respicies, ut ad eundem omnia referri agnoscas; sed distrahes pro arbitrio vel imperio res & verba conjunctissima? Quod si is responendi, vel exponendi Scripturam admittatur modus, jam nihil non negari porro vel affirmari poterit in Scriptura tota.
units.tr: Reply, first. Who, or what argument, taught our opponents to divide these verses in this way, and to tear apart in one passage and one citation things so closely joined, so that one part refers to Christ or to the Father and another does not? Do not three verses follow one another with thou, Lord and thou, and thou [σὺ κύριε, σὺ δὲ, σὺ δὲ]? But you will divide these things, so united, and you will not see that thou [σὺ], and [δὲ], and thou [σὺ δὲ] are the same, nor will you look at thou [σὺ] in the same way, so that you may recognise that all things are referred to the same person. Instead you will tear apart, at your own pleasure or by your own command, words and things that are most closely bound together. If such a method of answering or of expounding Scripture were admitted, then nothing at all could henceforth be denied or affirmed anywhere in the whole of Scripture.

units.la: II. De Christi regno & futuro orbe, hoc
units.tr: II. On Christ's kingdom and the world to come, that

units.la: quod illa verba: Tu in principio Domine, &c. quiddam ad propositum ipsius facerent, sed quia verba posteriora, quae adducere volebat, ab his pendebant, & eis cohaerebant, ideo illa quoque attulit, interim tamen rationem habuit tantum illorum, quibus mutatio & renovatio mundi significabatur. Solere autem tam sacros, quam alios scriptores, unius sententiolae, aut etiam vocula causa, integras & aliquando prolixiores etiam sententias adducere, in confesso est. Ita inter se connexio comprobat. Et quaeso cur magis posteriora, quam priora ad scopum Apostoli facere videntur, nisi quod haec Adversarii jugulant sententiam & hypothesim? Vel, quomodo ostendet, Apostolum tantum rationem habuisse illorum verborum, quibus mutatio mundi significatur? Vel an ista forte non potuisset citare, absque prioribus, si sola ea, non etiam haec spectasset? Eidem tribuit mundi mutationem, qui factionem: neque ullum, vel minimum in textu, aut allegatione, est indicium, quod verba priora magis quam posteriora, vel viceversa magis haec quam illa, ad Patrem respiciunt, quam Filium, & non omnia uno in loco, de eodem sint intelligenda. Æque facile dices, nec posteriora de Christo accipienda esse, quin debeas, quia omnia patri modo interpretanda, & sic frustra ac incongrue adhibitum locum illum ab Apostolo fuisse. Quae quantum religioni & Scripturae inferant praejudicium, nemo non videt. Age proferant simile aliquod exemplum, non ubi in citatione nonnulla ex abundanti adduntur propter unum forte aliquod, in cujus gratiam citatio instituitur; sed ubi unius loci citati verba ita diripiuntur, ut quamvis in textu manifesta fiat personae allocutio, & semper ejusdem, per nescio quam apostrophen divellantur omnia a se atque diversis adscribantur personis; nulla vel personarum, vel sermonis in textu occurrente diversitate, aut diversitatis vel tenuissima indicatione.
units.tr: those words, "Thou, Lord, in the beginning," and so on, were somewhat to his purpose; but because the following words, which he wished to bring forward, depended on these and were joined to them, he therefore also quoted these, while having regard only to those words by which the change and renewal of the world are signified. It is agreed that both sacred and other writers are accustomed to cite, for the sake of a single little phrase or even a single word, whole and sometimes rather long passages. So the connection between them proves it. And I ask, why do the following words seem to serve the Apostle's purpose more than the preceding ones, except that these overthrow our opponents' opinion and hypothesis? Or how will they show that the Apostle had regard only to those words by which the change of the world is signified? Or could he perhaps not have cited those words without the preceding ones, if he had looked only to these and not to those? He attributes the change of the world to the one who makes it; and there is no indication at all, not even the slightest, in the text or in the citation, that the preceding words refer to the Father rather than the following, or the reverse, that the following refer to the Father rather than the preceding, nor that all things in one passage must be understood of the same person. You might just as easily say that the following words too must not be taken of Christ, because everything must be interpreted of the Father, and so the Apostle would have used that passage in vain and inappropriately. How much prejudice this brings to religion and to Scripture, no one fails to see. Come, let them produce some similar example, not where some things are added in a citation out of abundance, perhaps for the sake of one particular word for which the citation is made, but where the words of a single cited passage are so torn apart that, although the address to the person is plainly made in the text, and always to the same person, all of them are separated by some apostrophe I know not what, and are ascribed to different persons, with no difference of person or of speech appearing in the text, and not the faintest indication of any difference.

units.la: Denique nec per apostrophen illa accipi possunt, quia non sunt Pauli verba, sed Davidis: Apostolus vero simpliciter adducit & applicat Christo. Quaero, apud Davidem, vel verba illa omnia de eodem sunt exponenda, vel de diversis, atque prima per apostrophen ad Patrem, de eo, & reliqua de Filio, vel non: si ita, quaeso, ut id illis hoc in Psalmo ostendatur indiciis. Sin non, ergo praeter sensum ea allegavit Apostolus, aliterque expositit, quam exponenda erant. Praeterquam quod nullo modo significavit, se apostrophen instituere, vel diversimode verba illa explicare velle. Ut certe nemo unquam illum Apostoli in adducendis illis sensum fuisse perspicere hactenus potuit.
units.tr: Finally, these words cannot be taken by way of apostrophe, because they are not Paul's words but David's; the Apostle simply quotes them and applies them to Christ. I ask: in David, are those words all to be expounded of the same person, or of different persons, so that the first is addressed by apostrophe to the Father, and the rest to the Son? If not, then the Apostle cited the words against their sense and expounded them otherwise than they ought to be expounded. Moreover, he gave no sign at all that he meant to make an apostrophe or to explain those words in different ways. Indeed, no one has yet been able to discern what the Apostle's sense was in citing them.

units.la: Denique suam addit Enjedinus expositionem, quam diximus initio, mysticam, nempe Apostolum disputare de Novo seu de renovato mundo, ut ipsemet testatur cap. 2. v. 5. cujus princeps & pater, ut testatur Esaias, & ut ait Paulus Ephes. 2. verf. 14. ipse [illegible, ~8 letters] duo in unum. Quod ergo Psalmista de Deo Patre, & veteri mundo dixerat, illud Apostolus mystice applicat ad Christum & novum mundum. Verum nec de novo, seu renovato mundo Apostolum hoc in loco disputare, probat. Non enim agimus impraesentiarum de cap. 11. verf. 5. Neque sensu mystico, & non proprio, adduci illa ex Psalmo. Denique nec verba Psalmi ad mundum renovatum applicari commode possunt; & applicari debuisse, nullo argumento vel indicio Apostolus significavit.
units.tr: Finally, Enjedinus adds his own explanation, which we mentioned at the beginning, a mystical one: namely, that the Apostle is discussing the New, or renewed, world, as he himself testifies in chapter 2, verse 5, whose prince and father, as Isaiah testifies and as Paul says in Ephesians 2, verse 14, is [illegible] the two into one. What therefore the Psalmist had said of God the Father and the old world, that the Apostle mystically applies to Christ and the new world. But he does not prove that the Apostle is discussing in this passage the new or renewed world. For we are not dealing at present with chapter 11, verse 5. Nor can those words be cited from the Psalm in a mystical sense and not a proper one. Finally, the words of the Psalm cannot conveniently be applied to a renewed world; and the Apostle gave no argument or indication that they ought to have been so applied.

units.la: Huc, ubi Christi divina spectamus nomina, quæ ipsum Deum arguunt, referendum quoque, de quo etiam in antecedentibus, quod Filius Dei dicitur, nempe non eâ ratione, qua nos, sed, uti in præcedentibus explicatum, propter æternam & divinam à Patre generationem. Unde Filius Dei dicitur, & æqualis Deo, habens eadem cum Patre omnia, quique in Patre est, cum eo unus, & idem, ita ut hinc in ipso etiam habitet omnis Deitas, & Deitatis plenitudo. Quæ ita de aliis hominibus, vel de se enunciari posse, haud arbitror ullus Adversariorum admittet. Quare arguunt personam, supra humanam, aliâque quam humanâ solâ, natura præditam. Tues Christus, Filius ille Dei vivi. Ideoque sanctum quod nascetur, Filius Dei vocabitur. Adeo enim Deus mundum dilexit, ut Filium suum unigenitum dederit, & c. Vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam ut unigeniti à Patre. sed & proprium Patrem dixerat Deum, parem seipsum faciens Deo. qui offensus Dei Filius potenter. & qui proprio Filio non pepercit. misit Deus Filium suum factum ex muliere. Cui etenim Angelorum unquam dixit; Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te.
units.tr: Here also belongs the consideration of the divine names of Christ, which prove that he is God himself; and of which, also in what goes before, it is said that he is the Son of God, not in the way we are, but, as was explained above, on account of his eternal and divine generation from the Father. Hence he is called the Son of God, and equal to God, having all things in common with the Father, and being in the Father, one and the same with him, so that in him also dwells all the Godhead and the fullness of the Godhead. I do not think any of our opponents will admit that these things can be said in the same way of other men or of themselves. Therefore they prove that he is a person above human nature, endowed with a nature other than human alone. Thou art Christ, that Son of the living God. Therefore that holy thing which shall be born shall be called the Son of God. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, and so on. We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father. But he had also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. He, being the Son of God, [...] powerfully, and who spared not his own Son; God sent forth his Son, made of a woman. For to which of the angels did he ever say, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee?

units.la: Æqualis Deo quod sit, præterquam ex citatis, liquet etiam Ioann. v. 18. ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ. & verf. 19. quæ Pater facit, eadem etiam Filius facit ὁμοίως. Phil. II. 6. qui ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ [?] in formâ Dei existens, rapinam non duxit τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ [?] esse æqualem Deo. Habens omnia cum Patre, eădem. Omnia quæcunque Pater habet, mea sunt. In Patre, ut credatis quod Pater in me, & ego in Patre. Unus cum Patre, Philippe, qui vidit me, vidit Patrem; & quomodo tu dicis; ostende mihi Patrem? In quo omnis Deitas revera habitat, Nam in eo habitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter.
units.tr: That he is equal to God is clear, besides from the passages cited, also from John v. 18: making himself equal to God [ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ]; and verse 19: what the Father does, the Son also does likewise [ὁμοίως]. Phil. ii. 6: who, being in the form of God [ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ], did not count it robbery to be equal with God [τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ]. He has all things in common with the Father: All things that the Father has are mine. He is in the Father: that you may believe that the Father is in me, and I in the Father. He is one with the Father: Philip, he who has seen me has seen the Father; and how do you say, Show us the Father? In him all the Godhead truly dwells: For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily.

units.la: Excipiunt Adversarii, exponendum hoc esse de plenitudine donorum divinorum in Christo habitante, non de Dei ipsius essentiâ.
units.tr: Our opponents object that this must be explained of the fullness of the divine gifts dwelling in Christ, and not of the essence of God himself.

units.la: Enjedinus: Patroni Trinitatis, duo ex hoc loco eliciunt dogmata: Unum, duas esse in Christo naturas. Per illa enim verba: in ipso, & corporaliter: significari humanam naturam putant: Per plenitudinem divinitatis, naturam divinam. Cum ergo dicatur plenitudo divinitatis, habitasse in Christo, affirmant, eo significari divinam naturam esse unitam humanitati. Ac proinde Christum constare ex duabus naturis. Alterum dogma, Christum esse æternum & verum Deum, quia dicatur in eo habitasse, omnis divinitas, vel, ut quidam loqui malunt, Deitas. Si autem omnis Deitas in Christo est; sequitur non esse alium præter ipsum, Deum, seu quicquid usquam Dei est, id in Christo esse, ac proinde ipsum esse verum & æternum Deum. Sed horum nihil esse verum, facile est, diligenter verborum Apostoli sententia, demonstrare. Nam primum, inhabitatio, discrimen potius quam unionem & identitatem in-
units.tr: Enjedinus: The defenders of the Trinity draw two doctrines from this passage. The first is that there are two natures in Christ. They think that the words "in him" and "bodily" signify the human nature, and "the fullness of the Godhead" the divine nature. Since it is said that the fullness of the Godhead dwelt in Christ, they affirm that this means the divine nature is united to the humanity, and so Christ consists of two natures. The second doctrine is that Christ is eternal and true God, because it is said that all the Godhead, or, as some prefer to say, the Deity, dwelt in him. If all the Deity is in Christ, it follows that there is no other God besides him; whatever there is of God anywhere is in Christ, and so he himself is the true and eternal God. But that none of this is true is easy to show by carefully weighing the sense of the Apostle's words. For first, indwelling signifies a distinction rather than a union and identity in

units.la: Resp. I. Duo dat Adversarius argumenta, contra expositionem nostram, quorum neutrum concludit; deinde expositionem aliam, suam. Primum, ex voce inhabitationis, quod dum discrimen notat ab eo, quod inhabitatur, non posse hic denotari unionem utriusque in Christo naturæ, autumat. Verum, negamus consequentiam: nam quamvis inhabitans, & id cui inhabitat, sint diversa, non sequitur, quod in Christo, vel in humana ejus natura, non possit dici inhabitare divina. Nam hic imo discrimen est, sed quoque unio: unio autem non est absque aliquo unitorum discrimine: unio quippe est, non identitas. Neque enim naturæ inter se unitæ, vel divina cum humana natura, aut Deitas cum Christo identificantur. Humana vero in Christo natura non est instar loci, vel continentis, aut uti domus, addinuit. Certè enim alius est qui inhabitat, & alius in quo habitatur, nisi quis dicere velit, locus & locatum, continens & contentum esse eadem: aut idem posse in seipso habitare. Homo habitat in domo, & tamen domus, non est homo. Præterea, sic & plurima alia, veri Dii & æterni erunt habenda. Nam Deus, & deitas, multis reibus inhabitare dicitur, quæ tamen nihil nànus sunt, quàm Dii. Primum enim, esse in aliquo, manere in aliquo, habitare in aliquo, templum habere aliquem, æquipollent: ut apparet ex Levit. 26. vers. 11. Et 1. Cor. 6. vers. 16. Et hac de re plurbus nos disseruimus supra, in locum Ioh. 10. vers. 38. Pater in me est, &c. & 1. Cor. 3. & 6. & 2. Cor. 6. Iam verò, quot, & quibus in rebus, dicitur Deus habitare, esse, manere? In Israelitis, Lev. 26. In Sione, Psalm. 131. vers. 13. Quoniam elegit Deus Sion, elegit eam in habitationem sibi, hæc requies mea in seculum seculi, hic habitabo, quoniam elegi eam, &c. In templo Salomonis, Matth. 23. vers. 22. Num Israël aut Sion, propterea sunt dicendi Dii æterni? Quod verò argutantur, vocem κατοικεῖν significare non temporariam mansionem, sed perpetuam unionem: falsum & vanum est. Nam & κατοικεῖν, non significat uniri, sed incolere, inhabitare, & Deus in iis rebus dicitur κατοικεῖν, quibus non est unitus, ut testimonia, tum nunc citata, tum alia quam plurima ostendunt. Præterea, si diuturna mansio, quod videtur significare vox κατοικεῖν, efficit unionem, etiam pìs dicendus est Deus unitus esse, quia in illis manere sæpe dicitur, Iohann. 14. vers. 21. 1. Ioh. 3. vers. 24. &c. Sic spiritus Eliæ dicitur requievisse super Elisæum, 4. Reg. 2. vers. 15. Insuper, etsi fatemur cum Scriptura, Deum, & deitatem fuisse, & habitasse in Christo, tamen hic Paulus illud non asserit. Non enim Deum aut deitatem, sed plenitudinem dicit in Christo habitasse. At plenitudo non essentiam, aut substantiam, sed qualitatem denotat. Male ergò hinc unio essentialis colli-
units.tr: Reply, I. The Adversary offers two arguments against our interpretation, and neither proves its conclusion. Then he offers his own interpretation. First, from the word "indwelling", he claims that since it denotes a distinction from that which is indwelt, it cannot here denote the union of both natures in Christ. But we deny the consequence. For although the one who dwells and that in which he dwells are different, it does not follow that in Christ, or in his human nature, one cannot say that the divine dwells. Here there is indeed a distinction, but there is also a union; and a union is not without some distinction of the things united, for a union is not an identity. Nor are the natures united to one another, or the divine nature with the human, or the Godhead with Christ, identified. Moreover, the human nature in Christ is not like a place or a container, or like a house, as he has added. For certainly the one who dwells is other than that in which he dwells, unless someone wishes to say that place and the thing placed, container and contained, are the same, or that the same thing can dwell in itself. A man dwells in a house, and yet a house is not a man. Besides, on this reasoning many other things would have to be counted as true and eternal gods. For God and Deity are said to dwell in many things, which are nonetheless no more gods than anything else. First, to be in something, to remain in something, to dwell in something, and to have someone as a temple, are equivalent, as appears from Lev. 26.11 and 1 Cor. 6.16. And we have discussed this matter at length above, on John 10.38, "the Father is in me", etc., and on 1 Cor. 3 and 6 and 2 Cor. 6. Now, in how many and what kinds of things is God said to dwell, to be, or to remain? In the Israelites, Lev. 26. In Zion, Ps. 131.13: "For the LORD has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it", etc. In Solomon's temple, Matt. 23.22: "Is Israel or Zion therefore to be called eternal gods?" As for their quibble that the word κατοικεῖν [katoikein] signifies not a temporary dwelling but a perpetual union, it is false and empty. For κατοικεῖν does not mean to be united, but to inhabit, to dwell; and God is said to κατοικεῖν [katoikein] in those things to which he is not united, as both the testimonies cited just now and many others show. Furthermore, if a long stay, which the word κατοικεῖν [katoikein] seems to signify, produces a union, then God must also be said to be united to godly men, because he is often said to remain in them: John 14.21, 1 John 3.24, etc. Thus the spirit of Elijah is said to have rested upon Elisha, 2 Kings 2.15. Moreover, although we admit with Scripture that God and the Godhead were and dwelt in Christ, yet Paul does not assert this here. For he does not say that God or the Godhead dwelt in him, but that the fullness dwelt in Christ. But fullness denotes not essence or substance but quality. Therefore it is wrongly inferred from this that an essential union

units.la: ad divinam, neque in humanâ proprie natura dicitur quod Deitas habitat, sed in Christo, in ista videlicet personâ. Præterea non est, tamquam in loco aliquo inclusa vel locata Deitas, quando in Christo esse dicitur. Athanasius, de incarnatione Verbi, λόγῳ non est colligatus corpori, sed ipse corpus continet, ut & in eo sit, & extra omnia, & in sinu Patris, neque cum sit in omnibus, sit pars aliorum. Secundo ait, quod in multis admodum dicitur Deus habitare vel deitas, quæ tamen nihil minus sunt, quàm Dii. Quasi verò nos pro Diis concludamus: & non sit unus Deus, vel una Deitas, quæ habitare dicitur in Christo. Jam & in aliis habitet Deus, an propterea non singulari modo in Christo? atque si singulari modo, quantumvis & de plurimis idem dicatur, an propterea non potest significare istum singularem inhabitationis modum, quo in ipso habitat Deitas essentialiter, personali naturarum unione? Sed unum cedo exemplum, quo, quod de Christo, omnis plenitudo deitatis dicatur in aliquo corporaliter habitare, præterquam in ipso. iii. Hoc autem non probatur ex phrasibus, quibus Deus dicitur esse, manere, habitare in aliquo, uti in Israelitis, Sione, &c. neque enim in omnibus istis similis locutio est, cum præsenti: non ibi deitas, non plenitudo deitatis, non omnis plenitudo deitatis dicitur habitare corporaliter, uti hoc in loco enunciatur de Christo. Committit ergo elenchum Adversarius dissimilium. Nec ex unâ aliquâ voce argumentamur, sed ex omnibus, & tota adeoratione. iv. Videri vult fateri cum Scriptura, Deum & deitatem habitasse in Christo: iterum negat, id doceri hoc in loco. Proferat ergo, si possit, unum aliquem locum, hoc clariorem. Ego enim si eo id non doceatur, quo probari possit, non video. Peto autem locum talem, ad-vergitur. Confirmatur hoc ex praecedentis capitis verf. 19. ubi simpliciter dicitur in Christo habitare omnis plenitudo, id est quaevis perfectio: quod recte Beza his verbis explicat: Plenitudinem nomine significatur cumulatissima omnium divinarum rerum copia. Atque ita etiam ipse Paulus interpretatur, hoc eodem capite verf. 3. In quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae abscondite. Ex quibus apparet, hic per plenitudinem divinitatis, nihil aliud quam dona Dei excellentissima, & spiritus sancti copiam esse intelligendam. Deitas contra essentiam notat vel substantiam, non qualitatem. Cui non magis debet objici notio plenitudinis, quam magnitudinis, & similes: quibus pro infirmitate conceptuum nostrorum, & consuetudine utimur humana, θεοπρεπῶς [?] semper exponendis. Versio Arabica, nam in eo inhabitavit tota perfectio Deitatis corporaliter. Πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα, cap. 1. 19. non est diversum à plenitudine, quae hoc in loco commemoratur: quam etiam non evertit plenitudo donorum, & cumulatissima rerum divinarum copia, sive in humana Christi natura, sive persona. Sed nihil aliud hic intelligi, quam dona Dei excellentissima, inde non sequitur. Namque aliud est, plenitudo donorum; aliud, plenitudo ipsius deitatis, ut haec inhabitare alicubi dicatur, & corporaliter: quae personalia sunt, non accidentalia, sive personam designant, ejusque personalem actionem, non accidens. Et quod est hoc capite verf. 3. in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae abscondite, commodissime refertur ad antecedens nomen mysterii, ut in mysterio illo dicantur abscondite esse illi sapientiae thesauri: ad cognitionem mysterii Dei & Patris & Iesu Christi. In quo omnes thesauri, &c. Vel si de Christo malis intelligere, non hoc negatur, neque nobis adversatur quidquam. Nihil vero plus de Christo dici iis verbis, quod in eo plenitudo deitatis habitet corporaliter, haud probat.
units.tr: to the divine; nor is it said that the Godhead dwells in the human nature properly, but in Christ, that is, in that person. Besides, the Godhead, when it is said to be in Christ, is not enclosed or placed in some place as if in a container. Athanasius, in his work on the incarnation of the Word: "The Word [λόγῳ] is not bound to the body, but himself contains the body, so that he is both in it and outside all things, and in the bosom of the Father; and although he is in all things, he is not a part of others." Secondly, he says that God or the Deity is said to dwell in many things, which are nonetheless no more gods than anything else. As if we concluded that they are gods! As if there were not one God or one Deity who is said to dwell in Christ! And if God dwells in others, is he therefore not in Christ in a singular manner? And if he dwells in a singular manner, even though the same may be said of very many, can this not signify that singular mode of indwelling, in which the Deity dwells essentially in him by the personal union of the natures? But let him cite one example in which the fullness of the Godhead is said to dwell bodily in anything other than him, as is said of Christ. iii. This, however, is not proved from the expressions by which God is said to be, remain, or dwell in something, as in the Israelites, in Zion, etc. For in none of those is the wording like the present: there it is not "Deity", not "fullness of the Godhead", not "all the fullness of the Godhead" that is said to dwell "bodily", as is declared of Christ in this passage. The Adversary therefore commits the fallacy of dissimilar things. Nor do we argue from one word, but from all of them and from the whole context. iv. He wishes to appear to admit with Scripture that God and the Godhead dwelt in Christ, but again denies that this is taught in this passage. Let him therefore produce, if he can, one passage that is clearer on this point. For if it is not taught here, I do not see by what passage it could be proved; and I ask for such a passage, but I cannot see one. This is confirmed from verse 19 of the preceding chapter, where it is simply said that all the fullness dwells in Christ, that is, every perfection, which Beza rightly explains in these words: "By the name fullness is signified the most complete abundance of all divine things. And Paul himself so interprets it in the same chapter, verse 3: 'In whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden.' From which it appears that here by the fullness of the Godhead nothing else is to be understood than the most excellent gifts of God and the abundance of the Holy Spirit." Deity, on the other hand, denotes essence or substance, not quality; and the notion of fullness should no more be objected to here than that of greatness and the like, which we use, because of the weakness of our concepts and by human custom, and which must always be explained in a manner worthy of God. The Arabic version: for in him dwelt all the perfection of the Deity bodily. The πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα [pan to plērōma] of chapter 1.19 is not different from the fullness mentioned in this passage; nor does the fullness of gifts and the most complete abundance of divine things, whether in the human nature of Christ or in his person, rule it out. But it does not follow from this that nothing else is to be understood here than the most excellent gifts of God. For it is one thing to say "fullness of gifts", and another "fullness of the Deity itself", so that this is said to dwell somewhere, and bodily: these are personal, not accidental; they designate the person and his personal action, not an accident. And what follows in this chapter, verse 3, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden, is most fittingly referred to the preceding noun mystery, so that in that mystery those treasures of wisdom are said to be hidden: to the knowledge of the mystery of God, the Father and Jesus Christ. In whom are all the treasures, etc. Or if you prefer to understand it of Christ, this is not denied, and nothing opposes us in it. But that the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him is not proved by those words to say anything more about Christ.

units.la: Objicit locum Eph. iii. 19. ubi inquit Apostolus, ut impleamini in omnem plenitudinem Dei, quod idem censet, cum plenitudine Deitatis. Verum errat; nam aliud est plenitudo Dei, vel accrescere aut impleri in plenitudinem Dei, id est, plenitudinem gratiarum omnium à Deo, & ad Deum; atq; plenitudo Deitatis. Deitas semper naturam designat; plenitudo Dei, ejus effectum & beneficium. Neque in plenitudinem Deitatis aliquis potest assurgere: nedum ut plenitudo Deitatis, & omnis plenitudo alteri inhabitet, quae simplici illa loquutione, in omnem plenitudinem Dei, non exhauriuntur. Deitas, θεότης, & θειότης, Rom. 1. 20. aeterna ejus potentia & divinitas, de substantia Dei accipitur, fatente Enjedino. τὸ Θεῖον, Act. xvii. 29. natura nomenclationes sunt, non divinorum beneficiorum ant donorum. Et θείας φύσεως, 1. Pet. 1. 3. quod improprie sumi in communione illa, quam scribit Apostolus, nemo nescit: vox autem ipsa satis aperte est naturam notans. Praeterea σωματικῶς corporaliter, in Christo habitat tota Deitatis plenitudo: non, quemadmodum olim in populo Iudaico, in arca foederis, in Prophetis, in templo Salomonis, sed vere & quasi palpabiliter, hoc enim vox illa significat σωματικῶς, inquit Enjedinus, quasi diceret: Deum olim in aliis habitasse umbratice, spiritualiter, particulariter, typicos: in Christo autem vere, perfecte, abundantissime & totaliter. adde, & substantialiter. Nam etiam substantiale aliquid ista voce denotari, contra ac Adversarius vult, certum est: quia Deitas, de qua praedicatur, quod corporaliter in Christo habitarit, nunquam aliter quam substantiam Deitatis significat: & habitare proprie substantiae est, praesertim ubi tria ista conjunguntur, quod Deitas inhabitet corporaliter. Deinde, quia in corpore, dicitur corporaliter in eo habitasse omnis Deitas. Quare enim non id quoque intelligatur, quod verum est? Versio Aethiopica, Quia super eum habitat omnis perfectio Deitatis suae in corpore hominis. Melius, quam quod Adversarius illud σωματικῶς, correctionis loco addi censet, postquam Apostolus dixisset, in Christo omnem Deitatis plenitudinem habitare, nempe ut hoc corrigeret & excusaret per vocem σωματικῶς, quasi dixisset, ut nos crasso modo loqui solemus, ut corporaliter & ruditer cum vulgo loquar. Verum hoc si voluisset, dixisset, σωματικῶς εἰπεῖν, & praefixum ante σωματικῶς fuisset comma. Vel, uti alias solet, dixisset, ἀνθρώπινον λέγω, vel καθ' ἄνθρωπον, vel simile quid aliud: non in una & continua oratione, omnis plenitudo deitatis corporaliter.
units.tr: He objects to Eph. 3:19, where the Apostle says, that you may be filled unto all the fulness of God, and he thinks this means the same as the fulness of the Deity. But he is wrong. The fulness of God, or to be increased and filled up unto the fulness of God, means the whole fulness of gifts that come from God and return to God, and this is something other than the fulness of the Deity. Deity always designates the nature, while the fulness of God designates its effect and benefit. Nor can anyone rise up to the fulness of the Deity, much less can the fulness of the Deity and all fulness dwell in another, which are not exhausted by that simple phrase unto all the fulness of God. Deity [θεότης, theotēs] in Rom. 1:20, his eternal power and Godhead, is taken from the substance of God, as Enjedinus admits. The Divine [τὸ Θεῖον, to Theion] in Acts 17:29 are names of nature, not of divine benefits or gifts. And of the divine nature [θείας φύσεως, theias physeos] in 1 Pet. 1:3 is taken figuratively in that fellowship which the Apostle writes of, as everyone knows; but the word itself plainly signifies nature. Moreover, the whole fulness of the Deity dwells in Christ bodily [σωματικῶς, sōmatikōs]: not, as once in the Jewish people, in the ark of the covenant, in the prophets, in Solomon's temple, but truly and as it were palpably, for that word σωματικῶς signifies this, says Enjedinus, as if it said: God formerly dwelt in others in shadow, spiritually, in part, typically; but in Christ truly, perfectly, most abundantly and wholly. Add: and substantially. For it is certain that something substantial is denoted by this word, contrary to what the adversary wants; because the Deity, of which it is predicated that it dwelt bodily in Christ, never signifies anything other than the substance of the Deity; and to dwell properly belongs to substance, especially where these three things are joined together, that the Deity dwells bodily. Next, because in the body it is said that all the Deity dwelt bodily in him. Why, then, should not that also be understood which is true? The Ethiopic version reads: For in him dwells all the perfection of his Deity in the body of a man. This is better than what the adversary thinks should be added as a correction, after the Apostle had said that all the fulness of the Deity dwells in Christ, namely to correct and excuse this by the word bodily, as if he had said, as we are wont to speak in a crude manner, that I speak bodily and rudely with the common people. But if he had wanted this, he would have said σωματικῶς εἰπεῖν [somatikōs eipein], and a comma would have been placed before σωματικῶς. Or, as is usual elsewhere, he would have said ἀνθρώπινον λέγω [anthrōpinon legō], or καθ' ἄνθρωπον [kath' anthrōpon], or something similar; not in one continuous sentence, all the fulness of the Deity bodily.

units.la: Enjedinus: Quaerimus, quaenam sit illa plenitudo deitatis, quae inhabitat in Christo? Certe horum aliquod esse, cogentur fateri: Aut esse illam communem tribus personis essentiam: Aut illum aeternum & invisibilem spiritum, quem Pater ab aeterno genuisse dicitur, & vocatur ab illis λόγῳ. Aut vero essentiam, vel personam peculiarem, vel Patris, vel Spiritus sancti. At quodvis horum affirment, in absurditatem manifestam incident. Si enim primum dicant, sequeretur, totam Deitatem, seu Trinitatem esse humanitati hypostatice unitam, incarnatam, &c. Nam communis essentia totam Trinitatem complectitur, neque sine Personis intelligi aut dici potest communis. Deinde, cum illa essentia communis, sit ipse Deus infinitus, quomodo est verisimile, in parvo Christi corpore, eam fuisse conclusam? Si dicant, illam plenitudinem divinitatis, esse aeternum illum λόγον, ante secula natam, primo hoc probandum illis esset, talem aliquem Filium existere, nos enim in Scriptura tota non legimus neque agnoscimus, genitum ab aeterno Deum vel aliquem Spiritum. Primum ergo probent Filium talem esse, & po-
units.tr: Enjedinus: We ask what that fulness of the Deity is which dwells in Christ? Certainly they will be compelled to admit that it is one of these: either that common essence of the three persons; or that eternal and invisible Spirit whom the Father is said to have begotten from eternity, and whom they call the Word [λόγῳ, logō]. Or else the essence or a peculiar person, either of the Father or of the Holy Spirit. But if they affirm any of these, they will fall into manifest absurdity. For if they say the first, it would follow that the whole Godhead, or Trinity, is hypostatically united to the humanity, incarnate, etc. For the common essence embraces the whole Trinity, and cannot be understood or called common apart from the Persons. Next, since that common essence is the infinite God himself, how is it likely that it was enclosed in the small body of Christ? If they say that the fulness of the Godhead is that eternal Word, born before the ages, they would first have to prove that such a Son exists; for we do not read or acknowledge in the whole of Scripture that God or any Spirit was begotten from eternity. Let them therefore first prove that the Son is such, and

units.la: Respondemus, Est essentia Deitatis, communis tribus Personis, subsistens in secunda persona, seu Filio, aut Dei Verbo, quae inhabitat in Christo corporaliter, id est, substantialiter, hypostatice. In Christo, id est, persona Christi.
units.tr: We reply: there is the essence of the Deity, common to the three Persons, subsisting in the second Person, or the Son, or the Word of God, which dwells in Christ bodily, that is, substantially and hypostatically. In Christ, that is, in the person of Christ.

units.la: II. Studiose confundit Adversarius, quae, dum interrogat sententiam nostram, ex ea novit distingui, essentiam vid. in Deo, & personam. Essentiam, inquit, vel personam. Non vero ista idem sunt. Essentia est in persona, quae supra essentiam dicit peculiarem subsistendi modum, vel personalitatem: quemadmodum illa explicuimus suo loco, Tom. I. ubi de Trinitate actum.
units.tr: II. The adversary studiously confuses things which, while he asks our opinion, he himself knows are distinguished, namely the essence, that is, in God, and the person. The essence, he says, or the person. But these are not the same. The essence is in the person, which, beyond the essence, denotes a peculiar mode of subsisting, or personality, as we explained in its place, in Vol. I, where we treated of the Trinity.

units.la: III. Iam absurdum hoc inde trahit, quod sequetur ex nostra expositione, totam Deitatem seu Trinitatem humanitati hypostatice unitam, incarnatam. Tota Deitas, sed quae, & prout in secunda persona, incarnata est, non tres personae, vel Trinitas. Haec nunc tueri sufficit ab absurdo, quo ista gravare nituntur, quae alibi demonstramus. Ne dicant, a nobis principium peti: non enim nos argumentamur, sed contra Adversariorum argumentationem, sentensententiam nostram defendimus. Ut perperam admodum mox in sua argumentatione, probaturus, filii personam non posse intelligi per Deitatis plenitudinem, primo loco hoc adferat, probandum nobis esse talem filium existere. Quod suo loco, sed quando nostrae argumentandi partes sunt, non omittimus. iv. Revera Deitas est infinita, neque parvo Christi corpore conclusa fuit, vel concludi potuit, sed quidem cum eo personaliter conjungi. Longe autem aliud est, jungi cum aliqua re; vel, ea concludi. v. Christus & Apostoli testantur, non solum Patrem in Christo fuisse, & per eum operatum, communi nimirum ratione, & non hypostatica unione; sed Filium a Patre exivisse, carnem factum, ex muliere, & servi formam accepisse, &c. quae non de Patre, sed de Filio Verbo intelligi possunt ac debent.
units.tr: III. Next he draws from this the absurdity that would follow from our exposition, that the whole Godhead or Trinity is hypostatically united to the humanity, incarnate. The whole Deity, but it is so as incarnate in the second Person, not three persons or the Trinity. It is enough now to defend these points from the absurdity with which they strive to burden them, which we demonstrate elsewhere. Let them not say that we beg the question: for we do not argue, but defend our opinion against the adversaries' argument. As he very wrongly, in his argument which he is about to prove, that the person of the Son cannot be understood by the fulness of the Deity, first brings this forward, that we must prove that such a Son exists. This we do not omit in its place, but when it is our turn to argue. iv. Indeed the Deity is infinite, and was not, or could not be, enclosed in the small body of Christ, but it was personally joined with it. It is far otherwise to be joined with something than to be enclosed by it. v. Christ and the Apostles testify not only that the Father was in Christ, and worked through him, by a common manner, and not by a hypostatic union; but that the Son went forth from the Father, was made flesh, was born of a woman, and took the form of a servant, etc., which can and must be understood not of the Father but of the Son, the Word.

units.la: Enjedinus: Postremo, vel hoc unicum, omnes ineptias adversariorum confutaverit, quod si ipsorum admittatur expositio, nihil faciet ad propositum Apostoli. Constat enim hic Paulum hortari Colossenses, ne a doctrina jam recepta deficiant, aut abstrahi se patiantur, neve fidem in Christum, sterilem, aut insufficientem ad salutem existiment, quia in Christo inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis. Iam si adversariorum expositio admittatur, qualis quaesito erit ista consequentia: In Christo ambulate, super quem aedificati & radicati estis, nec patiamini vos per philosophiam inanem, fraudem, aut traditionem antiquorum decipi, quia aeterna Deitas unita est humanitati Christi. An non res ipsa flagitare videtur, eam quam nos attulimus interpretationem? Nolite alienam doctrinam sectari, ne pleniorem eo, quem accepistis, justificationis modum quaerite, quia in Christo omnia invenietis, omnia bona & dona, quae Deus conferre piis & Ecclesiae solet, in eo continentur. In ipso enim latent abscondite omnes sapientiae Dei thesauri.
units.tr: Enjedinus: Finally, this one thing alone will refute all the absurdities of the adversaries: if their exposition is admitted, it will have nothing to do with the Apostle's purpose. For it is clear that Paul here exhorts the Colossians not to fall away from the doctrine already received, nor to allow themselves to be drawn away, nor to think that faith in Christ is barren or insufficient for salvation, because in Christ dwells all the fulness of the Deity. Now if the adversaries' exposition is admitted, what kind of consequence will this be: Walk in Christ, in whom you are built up and rooted, and do not let yourselves be deceived by empty philosophy, fraud, or the tradition of the ancients, because the eternal Deity is united to the humanity of Christ? Does not the matter itself seem to demand the interpretation we have brought? Do not follow the doctrine of others, nor seek a fuller manner of justification than the one you have received, because in Christ you will find all things, all the good things and gifts which God is accustomed to confer on the pious and the Church, are contained in him. For in him are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom of God.

units.la: Respond. Bona verba. Non nos ineptias adferimus, qui locum explicamus, ex fidei analogia, & consensu orbis Christiani antiquo, & catholico: denique ad sensum Apostoli appositissime. Nempe, ut fideles in Christo maneant, & secundum eum se gerant, non ad philosophiam, vel deceptiones alias deflectant, quandoquidem in Christo habeant omnia. Certe omnia, quum in ipso corporaliter & substantialiter inhabitet omnis plenitudo Deitatis. In Christo ambulate, &c. nolite alienam sectari doctrinam, nec pleniorem eo, quem accepistis, justificationis modum quaerite, quia in Christo omnia invenietis, omnia bona & dona, quae Deus conferre piis & Ecclesiae solet, in eo continentur. In ipso enim latent abscondite omnes sapientiae Dei thesauri. Adde, nam & in ipso tota habitat Deitas, ex unione nempe cum natura humana. Ut ex nostra expositione eo fortiter assurgat Apostoli commonitio, quo plura in Christo constituit, & majorem ejus dignitatem.
units.tr: Reply: Fair words. It is not we who bring forward absurdities, who explain the passage from the analogy of faith, from the ancient and catholic consensus of the Christian world, and finally most aptly to the sense of the Apostle. Namely, that the faithful should remain in Christ and conduct themselves according to him, and not turn aside to philosophy or other deceptions, since they have all things in him. Certainly all things, since in him dwells bodily and substantially all the fulness of the Deity. Walk in Christ, etc. Do not follow the doctrine of others, nor seek a fuller manner of justification than the one you have received, because in Christ you will find all things, all the good things and gifts which God is accustomed to confer on the pious and the Church, are contained in him. For in him are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom of God. Add that in him the whole Deity dwells, namely from union with human nature. So that, from our exposition, the Apostle's admonition rises more strongly, in that he sets forth more things in Christ and his greater dignity.

units.la: Aliam praeterea loci expositionem dat Volkelius, Lib. v. cap. x.
units.tr: Volkelius gives another explanation of this passage, Book 5, chapter 10.

units.la: Quod Divinitatis nomine, nec Dei, nec Christi naturam, sed divinae voluntatis notitia, Deique colendi ratio intelligi potest, atque adeo debet. Quam quidem plenitudinis vocabulo amplificare, & corporaliter Christo, id est, ipsius doctrinae inesse, ideo afferre voluit Paulus, ut divinae veritatis cognitionem perfectam, solidam, nullaque ex parte adumbratam, ut in Lege fiebat, Christi institutis contineri intelligeretur, id quod satis ostendit, Divinitatis
units.tr: By the name of Divinity, one can understand, and therefore ought to understand, neither the nature of God nor the nature of Christ, but the knowledge of the divine will and the manner of worshipping God. Paul wanted to amplify this with the word "fullness," and to say that it dwells bodily in Christ, that is, in his doctrine, so that the perfect and solid knowledge of divine truth, not shadowed in any respect as it was under the Law, might be understood to be contained in the institutions of Christ. This sufficiently shows the divinity

units.la: Resp. I. In Christo, inquit, id est, in ejus doctrina. Omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter, id est, divinae veritatis cognitio perfecta. Ut vero probat: quia nomen Christi saepenumero non personam aut naturam, sed tantum aliquid denotat, ad Christi respiciens. In quo nulla est consequentia. Nam Christus quidem etiam aliquando quid significat praeter ejus essentiam & naturam, sed ut ea semper connotetur, nomine, essentiam ipsius Dei altissimi intelligi nequaquam debere. Quod enim alioqui necesse fuisset plenitudinis istius Divinitatis, & quidem omnis, meminisse ? quasi vero suspicari quispiam potuisset, eam in illo, in quo habitet, non plenam, vel non usquequaque plenam esse. non vero negligatur aut rejiciatur. Quem-admodum Adversarius hic caepit, nomen Christi, non Christi personam aut naturam denotare: & divinitatis nomine essentiam ipsius Dei altissimi intelligi nequaquam debere. Christus designet alibi Christi doctri-nam, aliudve ejus beneficium aut opus, sed nonne ipsum quoque notet ejus naturam. Sic Deitatis nomen nunquam non naturam significat. Applicet vero singulis verbis expositionem suam Adversarius, & videbit, quam ea dura sit, & non conveniens. Quomodo exponet, in eo ? quomodo, deitatem ? ejus plenitudinem omnem ? inhabitare ? & corporaliter inhabitare ? si corporaliter, sit perfect[?] quid tum per omnem plenitudinem intelligetur ? & si per Christum, ejus doctrina, & divinae voluntatis notitia, quid, per deitatem ? Denique nihil est in textu, quod suadeat, in Christo, hic accipi, pro doctrina Christi: Dissuadent vero cum alia, tum connexio versus hujus, cum praecedente, ubi fuit, ἐν ᾧ ἐν Χριστῷ[?]; & sequente, & estis in eo adimpleti, qui est caput omnis principatus, potestatis. demum, in quo & circumcisi estis. Ubique intelligitur Christus ipse, nullibi vero sola ejus doctrina. Caeterum quamvis ubicunque Deitas, ibi tota est, & nullibi non plena, hic tamen placuit Apostolo nominare omnem Deitatis plenitudinem, ad dignitatem & omnisufficientiam Christi, oppositae ad quaevis alia, eo melius explicandam.
units.tr: Reply, first: "In Christ," he says, that is, in his doctrine. "All the fullness of the Godhead bodily," that is, the perfect knowledge of divine truth. But he proves this because the name of Christ often denotes not a person or a nature but only something relating to Christ. In this there is no consequence. For Christ indeed sometimes signifies something beyond his essence and nature, but that he should always be connoted by it, so that the essence of the most high God itself by no means ought to be understood by the name, is not to be granted. For why would it have been necessary to mention the fullness of this Godhead, and indeed of all of it? As if anyone could suspect that it is not full in him in whom it dwells, or not fully full. Nor is it to be neglected or rejected. Our opponent here begins by saying that the name of Christ denotes not the person or nature of Christ, and that by the name of Divinity the essence of the most high God by no means ought to be understood. Elsewhere Christ designates the doctrine of Christ, or some other benefit or work of his, but does it not also here denote his nature? Thus the name of Deity never fails to signify nature. Let our opponent apply his explanation to each word, and he will see how harsh and unsuitable it is. How will he explain "in him"? How "deity"? "all its fullness"? "to dwell"? "to dwell bodily"? If bodily, is it perfect? What then is meant by "all the fullness"? And if by Christ is meant his doctrine and the knowledge of the divine will, what is meant by "deity"? Finally, there is nothing in the text that suggests that "in Christ" is here to be taken as the doctrine of Christ. Both the connection of this verse with the preceding one, where it reads "[ἐν ᾧ ἐν Χριστῷ]" [in whom, in Christ], and with the following one, "and you are complete in him, who is the head of all principality and power," and finally "in whom you were also circumcised," argue against it. Everywhere Christ himself is meant, and nowhere his doctrine alone. Moreover, although wherever the Godhead is, there it is whole, and nowhere not full, the Apostle nevertheless chose here to name "all the fullness of the Godhead," so that the dignity and all-sufficiency of Christ, set over against all other things, might be the better explained.

units.la: Jam & examinemus ea, quae Adversarii excipiunt ad illustrem de Christi deitate locum Philipp. II. 6. &c. ubi id omnino verum est, quod agnoscit Enjedinus, Apostolum hic agere de triplici statu & conditione Christi, cujus primus est dignitatis, alter humilitatis, denique tertius exaltationis. Praeterea & hoc verum est, quod addit, Christum vere fuisse humilem, id est, qui se sponte humiliarit, cum aliter potuisset: Non enim ille est humilis, inquit, qui ideo se contrahit, & abjecte se gerit, quia nec vires habet sese efferendi, ostentandi & superbiendi, verum ille qui cum potest se extollere, & vires habet sese magnificandi, sponte se submittit. Itaque ne quis dicere posset, non esse mirum, si Christus se humilem praebuit, qui in vili & abjecta fuit conditione, neque potuit splendide se gerere ac proinde non fuisse vere humilem: ideo ante omnia affirmat Apostolus, habuisse Christum vires, potentiam, auctoritatem, & modum sese extollendi, qua potuisset se, si voluisset, ostentare. Nam fuit in forma Dei, aequalis Deo. Fatetur quippe, istis verbis describi primum Christi statum dignitatis. Verum verba illa non aeque recte exponit. Primum rationibus nonnullis genuinam & orthodoxam illorum explicationem impugnat: tum aliam suam substituit. Quid autem planius, quam dignitatis conditionem illis verbis in Christo denotari, quae praecesserit ejus ex Maria nativitatem? Hoc tamen audacter negat. Quasi non humilitatem suam in hoc etiam ostendisset Christus, quod ita nasci voluit? & humilitatis statum secundum praecessit ille primus dignitatis, juxta ipsius confessionem. Et Apostolus istud de Christo in forma Dei aequali Deo, quo se humiliavit, praemittit acceptioni formae humanae & servitutis. Ergo antequam hoc fecit, talis tantusque Christus fuit.
units.tr: Let us now also examine the objections that our opponents raise against the illustrious passage on the deity of Christ, Philippians 2:6, etc. Here it is entirely true what Enjedinus acknowledges, that the Apostle here treats of a threefold state and condition of Christ, the first of which is of dignity, the second of humility, and the third of exaltation. Moreover this too is true, that he adds that Christ was truly humble, that is, one who humbled himself of his own accord when he could have done otherwise. For, he says, he is not humble who draws himself together and conducts himself abjectly because he has no strength to raise himself, to display himself and to be proud; rather he is humble who, when he can exalt himself and has the power to magnify himself, submits himself of his own accord. Therefore, lest anyone could say that it is no wonder if Christ showed himself humble, since he was in a base and abject condition and could not conduct himself splendidly, and that therefore he was not truly humble, the Apostle first of all affirms that Christ had the strength, power, authority and means to exalt himself, by which he could, if he wished, display himself. For he was in the form of God, equal to God. Indeed he confesses that by these words the first state of Christ's dignity is described. But he does not explain those words rightly. First, he assails by several arguments their genuine and orthodox explanation; then he substitutes his own. Yet what is clearer than that by those words is denoted in Christ a condition of dignity which preceded his birth from Mary? This however he boldly denies. As if Christ had not shown his humility in this also, that he willed to be born in this way? And that first state of dignity preceded the state of humility, according to his own confession. And the Apostle puts this before the acceptance of the human form and of servitude, the point at which he humbled himself, namely that Christ was in the form of God, equal to God. Therefore, before he did this, Christ was such and so great.

units.la: Sed rationes ejus attendamus. loquitur, inquit, Apostolus de Christo Jesu, qui nullus fuit, nisi natus ex Maria homo, non ergo aliquis hoc prior. Deinde putat, non confi-stere posse vim exempli & argumentationis, qua utitur Apostolus, nisi accipiatur ab
units.tr: But let us consider his arguments. The Apostle, he says, speaks of Christ Jesus, who was not anything but a man born of Mary; therefore this is not earlier. Then he thinks that the force of the example and argument which the Apostle uses cannot stand unless it is taken from

units.la: Tom. 2. illo statu, qui in hominem cadit, & non alio divino, qui supra hominis vires sit & conditionem. Tum & seriem orationis sibi, non nobis favere autumat; & loquendi modum Apostolo inusitatum; dictum denique aliquod Ambrosii, quod Erasmus citat. Singula expendamus.
units.tr: Vol. 2. that state which falls to man, and not from another divine state, which is above the strength and condition of man. Then he also claims that the sequence of the discourse favours him and not us; and calls the mode of speaking unusual to the Apostle; and finally cites some saying of Ambrose which Erasmus quotes. Let us weigh each point.

units.la: Etiamsi consideremus, quod tamen nun-quam concedemus, Messiam, ante Mariam matrem re ipsa extitisse: tamen manifestum esset, hic Paulum non de eo loqui. Nam ipse loquitur de Christo Iesu: hoc inquit, sentite in vo-bis, quod & in Christo Iesu. At neque Iesu, neque Christi nomen ulli alii competit quam genito homini. Nam Iesus est nomenclatura & appellatio non alicujus Spiritus, Angeli, aut Dei, sed tantum hominum, qui solent hoc nomine vocari. Ille autem qui ante Mariam exti-tit, non fuit homo, sed Spiritus, imo, ut ipsi aiunt, Deus aeternus. Ergo Iesu appellatio illi minime competit, neque unquam talis Spiritus hoc nomine vocatus est, aut vocari potuit. Deinde, primus hujus appellationis Messiae, auctor seu interpres, fuit Angelus, qui Mariae dixit: Paries filium, & vocabis nomen ejus Iesum. Hanc autem appellationem attribuit Angelus, non Spiritui alicui invisibili, sed homini nascituro. Clarum igitur est, nomen Iesu non nisi homini competere. Iam quod ad alteram appellationem, Christi nimirum attinet, perspicuum est, ne illam quidem alteri quam homini competere. Christus enim, ut notum est, nihil aliud significat quam unctum, ad regiam vel sacerdotalem dignitatem erectum & elec-tum. Sed Spiritus ille aeternus, seu λόγος[?] nunquam inunctus est, aut inungi potuit, er-go neque Christus esse, aut dici potuit. Hic autem Paulus Iesum Christum, id est, eum, cui hae appellationes conveniunt, ait fuisse in forma Dei, & aequalem Deo, ergo non loquitur de eo qui ante matrem extiterit. Ac proinde hic Messiae statum referri ad tempus illud, pro non-dum a matre genitus erat, non potest.
units.tr: Even if we consider, which however we shall never concede, that the Messiah existed in fact before Mary the mother, yet it would be clear that Paul is not speaking here of him. For he himself speaks of Christ Jesus: "this," he says, "think among yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus." But neither the name Jesus nor the name Christ belongs to anyone other than a man who has been born. For Jesus is the designation and appellation not of some spirit, angel or God, but only of men, who are wont to be called by this name. But he who existed before Mary was not a man but a spirit, indeed, as they themselves say, the eternal God. Therefore the appellation Jesus by no means belongs to him, nor was such a spirit ever called, or could be called, by this name. Further, the first author or interpreter of this appellation of Messiah was the angel who said to Mary: You shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. Moreover the angel gave this appellation not to some invisible spirit but to a man about to be born. It is therefore clear that the name Jesus belongs only to a man. Now as to the other appellation, namely that of Christ, it is evident that not even that belongs to anyone other than a man. For Christ, as is known, signifies nothing else than "anointed," raised up and chosen to a royal or priestly dignity. But that eternal Spirit, or [λόγος] Logos, was never anointed, nor could he be anointed; therefore he could neither be nor be called Christ. Here, however, Paul says that Jesus Christ, that is, the one to whom these appellations belong, was in the form of God and equal to God; therefore he is not speaking of one who existed before the mother. And accordingly the state of the Messiah cannot be referred to that time, when he had not yet been born of the mother.

units.la: Resp.: Ambiguum est, dicere Messiam reipsa extitisse ante Mariam matrem. Is quidem reipsa extitit, qui Messias fuit, at non hoc ipsum, quod Messias fuit. Messias enim missus in mundum, unctus ad hoc a Deo, & ex Maria natus est: sed idem quoque secundum aliam sui rationem, ante suscepturam istam conditionem, extitit: & quia certissime eam erat suscepturus, vi ejus jam ante fruebantur fide-les atque salvabantur. Fere ea ratione, qua post mortem extitisse Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Jacobum dici potest, quia Deus etiam tum illorum Deus dicitur, non mortuorum, sed vivorum: Messias etiam fuit, ante suam ex Maria nativitatem, non secundum plenariam sui existentiam, & muneris functionem, sed quod is existeret, qui futurus Messias erat, omniaque pro nominis istius ratione exequuturus: id est, Deus, at nondum θεάνθρωπος[?]. Quo solo facile nunc solvuntur ejus pri-mariae adversum nos rationes. Neque Iesu, inquit, neque Christi nomen ulli alii competit, quam genito homini. Sed hoc nihil obstat, quo minus de isto genito homine, aliqua dicantur, quae ejus generationem ante-cedunt. Uti nomen Abrahami, & Isaaci nulli alii competit, quam genitis istis hominibus, attamen & post mortem existentibus: sic nomen Christi, in sermone de eo, quid ni referatur ad id quod & ante-quam Christus natus, ipse quoque fuit? At tum nondum fuit Christus, vel Mes-sias, & Christum Apostolus nominat. Quasi id inusitatum fit, Christum appel-
units.tr: Reply: It is ambiguous to say that the Messiah in fact existed before Mary the mother. He in fact existed who was the Messiah, but not this very thing, that he was the Messiah. For the Messiah, sent into the world, anointed for this by God, was born of Mary; but he also existed according to another aspect of himself, before taking up that condition; and because he was most certainly going to take it up, the faithful already enjoyed his power before it and were saved. In much the same way it can be said that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob existed after death, because God is still called their God, not of the dead but of the living. The Messiah also existed before his birth from Mary, not according to his full existence and the discharge of his office, but in that he existed who was going to be the Messiah, and was going to accomplish all things according to the meaning of that name; that is, he was God, but not yet [θεάνθρωπος] theanthropos, God-man. By this alone his primary arguments against us are now easily resolved. "Neither the name Jesus," he says, "nor the name Christ belongs to any other than a man who has been born." But this does not prevent some things being said of that born man which precede his generation. Just as the names of Abraham and Isaac belong to no one other than those men who were born, and yet they also exist after death, so why should the name of Christ, in speaking of him, not be referred to what he also was before Christ was born? But then he was not yet Christ or Messiah, and the Apostle names him Christ. As if it were an unusual thing to call someone Christ when you tell of something about him which was true before he became such.

units.la: lare, quando de eo aliquid narras, quod antequam talis factus, verum fuit. Sicut[?] dixero, Apostolum Paulum à prima aetate Deo serviisse, & in Scripturis exercita-tum à teneris fuisse ejus discipulum Timotheum, quis me reprehendat, quia non a pueritia, sed adulta fere aetate aut ille Apostolus fuit, aut ille ejus discipulus. Ille qui postmodum factus Apostolus, & Christi discipulus Timotheus, etiam antea ta-les les fuerunt: sic & Christum haud male quis nominat, quando eum docet etiam ante istius nominis proprium usum ac vim, fuisse, eique competere istam existentiam & gloriam, quam Apostolus significat. Faciat Adversarius argumentum,& videbit mox ejus ἀνακολλυθίαν[?]: Christus, Messias notat hominem natum,ergo eum nominando, non potes simul dicere quod & quid fuerit ante illam nativitatem? Negantur prorsus. Manifestam rei retro considerationem indicant ista verba,qui cum esset in forma, esset in forma Dei,&c. De Christo Jesu loquitur, enarratque quid fuerit,fecerit-que ante. Quemadmodum si Davidem regem nominans, ejusque ad imitationem proponens exemplum, dixero, id sententiæ sit in vobis, quod & in Davide rege, qui cum pastor ovium esset,&c. temere quis hoc infringeret,argueretque de vita Davidis anteacta intelligi non posse, quia Davidem regem dico,quo tempore pastoritiam non exercuit: nam quamvis regem nomino, non propterea id solum explico quod a Regia conditione & officio fuit, sed & sic æque mihi licet vitam ejus anteactam commemorare, ac quæ sequuta sunt: ita quamvis Christum Jesum Apostolus vocat, & Christus Jesus revera fuit a nativitate, non tamen sequitur quod non ad istud queat assurgere ejus oratio, & exponere quod fuit, antequam proprie & plenarie Christus esset. Quia de eodem sermo est, qui est Christus Jesus, licet non hoc exponatur quod, aut quatenus est Christus Jesus. Et quid vel usitatius eo, vel rectius? Si non esset Christus etiam Deus, & ante humanam suam nativitatem quoque æternus, huc reflectere Apostoli oratio non posset: sed posito quod talis sit, uti id doceri ab Apostolo evincemus, eo illud everti non potest, quod ratio appellationis Jesu Christi ei demum competit abhinc quod homo factus: nam id docere intendit,quanta ille sui humiliatione huc devenerit. Ergo ad ista Adversarii verba, quod neque Ie-su, neque Christi nomen ulli alii competit quam genito homini, addatur, & qui simul Deus, vel ante humanam hanc generationem in forma Dei, eique æqualis: quo tum omnia redduntur plana, & scopus Apostoli liquet, exponentis, quantum se dimiserit Deus, quum humanam acciperet carnem & conditionem. Sit Iesus nomenclatura & appellatio, non alicujus Spiritus, Angeli, sed hominum: id nihil ad rem, dummodo nomen proprium hoc Iesu Christi ejus sit, qui non tantum homo, uti reliqui, sed homo Deus θεάνθρωπος. Qui autem ante Mariam extitit, non fuit homo, sed Deus: ergo Iesu appellatio ei minime competit, qui simul ex Maria, & ante Mariam, diversa sui ratione? qui sequitur? Non Iesu appellatio, fateor, propter hoc ei convenit, quod & quatenus ab æterno Deus; sed τῷ θεανθρώπῳ: in quo exponendo licet ad humanam deflectere naturam, vel divinam spectare, prout ratio instituti exposcit.
units.tr: to speak of Christ Jesus, when you tell something about him that was true before he became such. If I say that the Apostle Paul served God from his earliest age and that Timothy, his disciple, was trained in the Scriptures from childhood, who would rebuke me because it was not from boyhood but in roughly adult life that the Apostle became an apostle and Timothy his disciple? Timothy, who afterwards became a disciple of Christ, was already such before. So too one may quite properly name Christ when one teaches what he was even before the proper use and meaning of that name, and that existence and glory which the Apostle describes belong to him. Let the Adversary frame an argument and he will soon see his own anacoluthon [ἀνακολλυθίαν]: Christ means a man who was born; therefore, when you name him, you cannot at the same time say what he was and what he was before that birth? This is utterly denied. The words "who, being in the form of God, was in the form of God, etc." indicate a clear looking back over the matter. He speaks of Christ Jesus, and describes what he was and what he did before. Just as if, in naming King David and setting him forth as an example for imitation, I were to say, "Let this be your mind, which was also in King David, who, when he was a shepherd of sheep, etc.", someone might rashly object to this and argue that David's earlier life cannot be understood, because I call him king at a time when he did not exercise the shepherd's trade. For although I name him king, I do not therefore explain only what pertained to the royal condition and office; I am equally free to recall his earlier life as well as what followed. So, although the Apostle calls him Christ Jesus, and Christ Jesus truly was from his birth, it does not follow that his discourse cannot rise to that point and set forth what he was before he was properly and fully Christ. For the discourse concerns the same one who is Christ Jesus, even if it does not set forth what, or in what respect, he is Christ Jesus. And what could be more usual or more correct than this? If Christ were not also God, and eternal even before his human birth, the Apostle's discourse could not look back to that point; but granted that he is such, as we shall show from the Apostle's own teaching, it cannot be overturned by the argument that the ground of the appellation Jesus Christ belongs to him only from the time he became man. For the Apostle intends to teach how far he humbled himself in coming down to this. Therefore to the Adversary's words, "that neither the name Jesus nor the name Christ belongs to anyone other than a man who has been born," let there be added: "and who at the same time is God, and before this human generation was in the form of God and equal to him." Then all things are made plain, and the purpose of the Apostle is clear, who sets forth how far God lowered himself when he took on human flesh and condition. Let Jesus be a name and designation not of some spirit or angel but of men: this is nothing to the point, provided that this proper name Jesus Christ belongs to him who is not merely a man, as the rest are, but God-man [θεάνθρωπος]. But he who existed before Mary was not a man but God; therefore the appellation Jesus does not belong to him, who is at once from Mary and before Mary, in a different respect of his being? What follows? I grant that the appellation Jesus does not belong to him on account of that by which and insofar as he is God from eternity; but it belongs to him as God-man [θεάνθρωπος]. In setting this forth, one may turn to the human nature or regard the divine, as the purpose of the undertaking requires.

units.la: Angelus, Matth. 1. nomen Messiæ seu Iesus attribuit homini ex Maria nascitu-ro, ergo nulla is ratione fuit ante istam nativitatem, vel non quoque Deus: nullo modo sequitur. Neque nos volumus, nomen illud competere Spiritui alicui invisibili, non Deo etiam formaliter & præcise considerato, sed τῷ θεανθρώπῳ. Semper malè Adversarius concludit, jam quod nomen Iesus non competat spiritui, Angelo, aut Deo; tum, quod nonnisi homini; denique quod idem spiritus nequeat esse aut dici Christus: illa etenim sunt præter quæstionem: concludendum fuerat, quod is qui Christus Iesus appellatur, nequeat esse θεάνθρωπος, ex hoc quod nomen illud Iesu lud Iesus Christus humanam etiam naturam & conditionem connotat. Caeterum non quidem divina natura seorsim & theologice considerata inuncta est vel inungi potuit, sed quatenus Christi unctio non externam aliquam aut corporalem unctionem significat, verum destinationem divinam, atque aptitudinem ad munus sibi injunctum, quatenus Dei filius ad hoc a Patre destinatus missusque est, ut unita sibi per generationem humana natura opus perageret redemtionis, uncti & Christi appellatio ei quoque attribui potest. Vnde tandem quam aliter concludere debeamus, atque Adversarius, apparet: nempe, quod Paulus Iesum Christum, i. e. eum, cui hae appellationes conveniunt, dicens fuisse in forma Dei & aequalem Deo, significat Deum simul esse, quare & ante matrem extitisse, & hoc fuisse etiam tum: quando nondum a matre genitus erat, ostendisse vero in hoc summam & inexplicabilem suam humiliationem, quod, illo non obstante, se exinanire quasi, & homo in hominum gratiam fieri voluit. Hoc primum Adversarii, contra expositionem nostram, argumentum: sequitur alterum, a ratione exempli.
units.tr: The angel in Matthew 1 gives the name Messiah, or Jesus, to the man who is to be born of Mary; therefore he was in no way before that birth, or was not also God: this does not follow in any way. Nor do we wish that name to belong to some invisible spirit, not to God even considered formally and precisely, but to the God-man [θεάνθρωπος]. The Adversary always concludes badly: first, that the name Jesus does not belong to a spirit, an angel, or God; then, that it belongs only to a man; finally, that the same spirit cannot be or be called Christ. For these points are beside the question. He ought to have concluded that the one who is called Christ Jesus cannot be God-man, from the fact that the name Jesus Christ also connotes a human nature and condition. Moreover, the divine nature considered apart and theologically was not, and could not be, anointed; but insofar as Christ's anointing signifies not some external or bodily anointing but the divine destination and fitness for the office laid upon him, in that the Son of God was destined and sent by the Father for this purpose, that the human nature united to himself by generation might accomplish the work of redemption, the appellation anointed and Christ can also be attributed to him. From this it appears at last how differently we ought to conclude than the Adversary does. Namely, when Paul says that Jesus Christ, that is, the one to whom these appellations belong, was in the form of God and equal to God, he signifies that God is at the same time, and therefore existed before the mother, and that this was so even then, when he had not yet been born of the mother; but in this he showed his supreme and inexplicable humiliation, that, notwithstanding this, he was willing, as it were, to empty himself and to become man for the sake of men. This is the Adversary's first argument against our exposition; the second follows, from the reasoning of the example.

units.la: Secundo vanitas huius opinionis patet ex proprietate exemplorum, quando enim per exempla aliquos docere volumus, ea afferre debemus, quae apta sint, quae imitari is quem docemus possit, & quae repudiare docendus ne-quicquat[?]. Alias, exemplorum usus erit inutilis. Verbi gratia, si quis ad celeritatem hortari quempiam ab exemplo volens, tali uteretur sermone: Esto celer, sicut vides illam avem cele-rem esse. Hoc exemplum esset ineptum. Posset enim respondere qui monetur: se neque avem esse, nec alas habere, nec volare posse, ac proinde non debere se esse celerem. Pari ratione, si adversariorum sententia esset vera, Pauli adhortatio esset inepta & inanis. Nam secundum ipsius hic est Pauli verborum sensus: Estote humiles, sicut Christus, qui cum ante matrem esset aeternus Deus, factus est postea homo, seu incarnatus est. At poterant respondere Phi-lippenses, se nec fuisse ante matrem Deos aeternos, nec fieri potuisse aut posse homines: itaque non sequi, si Christus fuit humilis, se quoque debere esse humiles.
units.tr: Secondly, the vanity of this opinion appears from the nature of examples. For when we wish to teach someone by examples, we ought to bring forward those that are apt, that the one we are teaching can imitate, and that the learner ought to reject nothing. Otherwise the use of examples will be useless. For instance, if someone wished to exhort another to speed by an example, and used such a speech as: "Be swift, as you see that bird is swift," this example would be inept. For the one who is admonished could reply that he is neither a bird, nor has wings, nor can fly, and therefore ought not to be swift. In the same way, if the Adversaries' opinion were true, Paul's exhortation would be inept and empty. For according to them the sense of Paul's words is this: "Be humble, as Christ, who, though before his mother he was eternal God, was afterwards made man, or was incarnate." But the Philippians could answer that they were not eternal gods before their mother, nor could they be made or become men: therefore it does not follow that, if Christ was humble, they too ought to be humble.

units.la: Respond. Nihil fere ineptius & inanius adferri potest, quam hoc quod pro fecundâ adducit Auctor ratione. Nam ita quidem est, exempla debere apta semper esse; sed non bene observavit, in quo apti-tudo illa sita fit. non certe in eo, ut idem semper faciat, qui propositio commonea-tur exemplo, sed vel idem, vel simile, in uno tertio modo conveniatur, salva exemplorum res est.
