Atque alias exemplorum usus erit inutilis. Si quis, inquit, ad celeritatem volens hortari quempiam, exemplo avis celeriter volantis, exemplum ineptum foret. Imo, addo ego, si eum hortari vellet ad celeritatem volandi. Quae tum ineptitudo foret, non in exemplo, sed ejus stulta applicatione. At proposita materia, in qua celeritas adhiberi ab homine debeat, & possit, ut moneatur ad officium celeriter peragendum, adinstar avis celeriter, non tarde, ad sua volantis, quid in hoc inepti foret obsecro, vel reprehensione dignum ? Nisi adhorta-tiones omnes ad officium ex exemplo non avium tantum, sed & reliquorum animalium, quae non magis praestare homo posset, ac volatum avium, respuere velit ac condemnare. Quid de avibus dico ? altiora petuntur ab exemplis, quam ista, quaeque multo minus imitari aliquis possit vel assequi. A coelo, ab Angelis, ipso adeo Deo argumenta petuntur apud homines officii sui. Quando Christus in-quit Matth. v. 45. Vt sitis filii Patris vestri in coelis, qui solem suum oriri facit super malos & bonos, & pluit super justos & injustos; quis vitiligantem hunc in modum ferat, at ego nec splendere instar solis possum, nec emittere pluviam. Atque hoc tantundem est, ac qui objecto sibi avium exemplo, ad praestandam celeritatem non certe in volando, sed in suo officio, regereret ineptissime, se neque avem esse, nec alas habere, nec volare posse: denique turpissimum hinc concludere, addereque, ac proinde non debere se esse celerem. Apage istos λῆρας λόγας[?]. imo si juberem esse celerem volatu, ut tum exciperes te nec alas habere, nec volare posse; at hortatus simpliciter ad celeritatem, vid. in curandis tuis, uti aves ad sua, talis certe exceptio fustigatione potius digna foret, quam responsione. Et sic de caeteris. Ne dicam isthoc pacto eludi aeque posse omnes, quas Scriptura vel ab avibus, vel ab aliis animalibus format similitudines. Quam ergo futilis est ista ad Pauli similitudinem responsio? Paulus jubet humiles nos esse exemplo Christi, qui cum in gloria Dei esset, ea paulum sepositá, voluit pro nobis homo fieri, & induere formam & conditionem servilem, ut ad hoc faciat respondentes Philippenses Enjedinus, se nec Deos fuisse ante matrem, &c. quae fere taedet repetere. at quis ab iis postulat, ut plane eadem in re, eodemque modo se humilient; verum ut suo, quo possunt ac debent modo, & in suis se humilient, quo modo id in suis praestitit Christus hoc agebatur. Quamque ineptam facit Philippensium conclusionem, ideo quod Dii non potuerint esse, uti Christus, vel eundem in modum fieri homines, non sequi, si Christus fuit humilis, se quoque debere esse humiles. Quis ita argumentari poterit, vel argumentantem facere Apostolum, aut colligentes Philippenses? Quocunque demum modo ab exemplo Christi horteris aliquos, semper patebit magna inter utrumque disparitas, neque conveniet argumentum, nisi in simili aliquo tertio. Restringe Pauli argumentionem ad Christi vitam & conditionem humanam, nonne pariter Philippenses respondere possent, se non esse Christos, nec fieri, aut praestare posse, id quod Christus, proindeque non sequi, si Christus fuit humilis, se quoque debere esse humiles? Unde quam elumbis illa sit responsio, viderint Adversarii.
units.tr: Reply. Almost nothing more inept and empty can be brought forward than what the author adduces as his fruitful reason. For it is indeed true that examples ought always to be apt; but he has not rightly observed in what that aptness consists. Certainly it does not consist in this, that the one who is admonished by an example should always do the very same thing; but the example stands good if the same, or something similar, is found in one third respect. And otherwise the use of examples will be useless. "If someone," he says, "wishing to exhort another to speed, used the example of a bird flying swiftly, the example would be inept." Indeed, I add, if he wished to exhort him to swiftness of flying. What inaptness there would then be would lie not in the example but in its foolish application. But when the matter is proposed in which a man ought and is able to show speed, so that he may be admonished to perform his duty swiftly, like a bird that flies swiftly and not slowly to its own nest, what in this, I beg you, is inept or worthy of reproof? Unless he wishes to reject and condemn all exhortations to duty from the example not only of birds but also of the other animals, which man can no more surpass than the flight of birds. Why do I speak of birds? Higher things are sought from examples than these, and things which one can far less imitate or attain. Arguments for men's duty are drawn from heaven, from the angels, indeed from God himself. When Christ says in Matthew 5:45, "That you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust," who would bear with such a comparison? Yet I neither can shine like the sun nor send rain. And this is just as if someone, having the example of birds set before him, should reply most ineptly, not with regard to flying but to his own duty, in order to show speed: "I am neither a bird, nor have wings, nor can fly"; and finally should shamefully conclude from this and add: "and therefore I ought not to be swift. Away with those idle words [λῆρας λόγας]." Indeed, if I were bidden to be swift in flight, then you could take exception that you have no wings and cannot fly; but when simply exhorted to speed in looking after your affairs, as birds do to theirs, such an exception would certainly deserve a whipping rather than an answer. And so with the rest. Not to mention that in this way all the likenesses that Scripture forms from birds or from other animals could be evaded just as well. How futile, then, is this response to Paul's comparison? Paul bids us to be humble after the example of Christ, who, though he was in the glory of God, set that aside for a little while and willed to become man for us, and to put on the form and condition of a servant. To this the Philippians' reply, which Enjedinus makes, that they were not gods before their mother, etc., is almost wearisome to repeat. But no one demands of them that they humble themselves in exactly the same matter and in exactly the same way; rather that they humble themselves in their own way, which they can and ought to use, and in their own affairs, in the way in which Christ did so in his. This is what was being treated. And how inept the Philippians' conclusion makes it, that because gods could not be, as Christ was, or become men in the same way, "it does not follow that, if Christ was humble, they too ought to be humble." Who could argue thus, or who could make the Apostle, or the Philippians gathering their conclusion, argue thus? In whatever way you exhort anyone from the example of Christ, there will always be a great disparity between the two, and the argument will not hold unless there is some third thing in common. Restrict Paul's argument to the life and human condition of Christ: would not the Philippians equally be able to reply that they are not Christs, nor can they become or perform what Christ did, and therefore it does not follow that, if Christ was humble, they too ought to be humble? How feeble that reply is, let the Adversaries see.

units.la: Tertio, hoc ipsum confirmatur, ex serie, & συνεχείᾳ verborum Apostoli. Eundem enim, quem in forma Dei, & aequalem Deo fuisse scribit, illum ipsum inquam, & formam Dei exuisse, se exinanivisse, servum, humilem, similem hominibus effectum, mortuum, crucifixum & exaltatum fuisse affirmat. At nihil horum λόγῳ adversariorum competit. Ergo neque illa forma Dei ad illum quidquam pertinet competit, ut totidem verbis scripserit Iohannes, & verbum caro factum est: & habitavit inter nos, ( & vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam uti unigeniti a Patre. )
units.tr: Third, this same point is confirmed by the sequence and connection (συνεχείᾳ) of the Apostle's words. For he affirms that the very one whom he writes was in the form of God and equal to God, I say that same one, also laid aside the form of God, emptied himself, was made a servant, humble, made like men, died, was crucified and was exalted. But none of these things fits the opponents' account [λόγῳ]. Therefore that form of God does not pertain to him at all fits, just as John wrote in so many words, and the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (and we saw his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father).

units.la: Quarto, hoc ipsum, loquendi modus, quo Apostolus utitur confirmat. Ita enim loquitur, ut satis aperte demonstret, eodem ipso tempore, fuisse Christum in forma Dei, quo fuit humilis, & exinanitus, haec enim sunt verba Apostoli: ὃς ἐν μορφῇ Θεῷ[?] ὑπάρχων, ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε. Hoc est, eodem ipso tem-
units.tr: Fourth, the manner of speaking that the Apostle uses confirms this same point. For he speaks in such a way as to show quite plainly that Christ was in the form of God at the very time when he was humble and emptied, for these are the Apostle's words: who, being in the form of God [ὃς ἐν μορφῇ Θεῷ ὑπάρχων], emptied himself [ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε]. That is, at that very time.

units.la: Resp. Nos vero id totum invertimus, atque argumentamur ipsi ex συνεχείας[?] verborum Apostoli: Eundem, n. qui in forma Dei, aequalis Deo, docet Ap. semetipsum exinanivisse & hominis induisse formam, &c. hoc autem fecit, quum generaretur, id est, eo ipso quod homo fieret, se humiliavit: ergo illud fuit jam tum quum nondum a matre esset genitus. Quod tam vere certeque τῷ λόγῳ ἡμῷ[?]
units.tr: Answer: We, on the contrary, turn the whole thing around and argue from the sequence of the Apostle's words ourselves. For the Apostle teaches that the same one, who was in the form of God and equal to God, emptied himself and took on the form of a man, and so on. Now he did this when he was begotten, that is, by the very fact that he became man, he humbled himself. Therefore it was already so when he had not yet been born of the mother. This is as true and certain as our word [τῷ λόγῳ ἡμῷ].

units.la: Resp. Iterum ex loquendi modo, quo Apostolus utitur, ipsi sententiam & expositionem nostram confirmamus. Nam non desiit omnino Christus esse in formâ Dei & aequalis Deo, quomodocunque etiam humiliatus, in natura assumta, vel ejus statu, morte denique exosissimâ; & quoque ante haec talis existebat, quare pore, quo humiliabat se, erat in forma Dei, quod indicat participium praesentis temporis ὑπάρχων. Si enim adversariorum sententia esset vera, Paulus non scripsisset ὑπάρχων, sed ὑπάρξας. Iam vero, etiam adversarii fatentur, humiliationem Christi, fuisse post incarnationem, vel nativitatem. Ergo tunc debuit esse etiam in forma Dei, sed & in ac cum eâ, quam primus gloriae antecessit.
units.tr: Answer: Again, from the manner of speaking that the Apostle uses, we confirm our own view and exposition. For Christ did not cease altogether to be in the form of God and equal to God, however much he was humbled in the assumed nature, or in its condition, and finally in death, most hateful as it was; and he also existed thus before these things. Therefore, at the time when he humbled himself, he was in the form of God, which the present participle ὑπάρχων [being] indicates. For if the opponents' view were true, Paul would not have written ὑπάρχων, but ὑπάρξας [having been]. Now, the opponents themselves admit that the humiliation of Christ came after the incarnation or the nativity. Therefore he must then have been also in the form of God, and indeed in and with that form which preceded his glory.

units.la: Denique Ambrosius, ut annotat Erasmus, dicit Christum tunc fuisse in forma Dei, cum mortuos suscitat, surdis reddidit auditum, leprosos mundavit. At ista Christus fecit post nativitatem, ergo in forma quoque Dei fuit post nativitatem. Ex quibus & similibus apparet, male ab istis primum conditionis Christi tempus assignatum esse.
units.tr: Finally, Ambrose, as Erasmus notes, says that Christ was then in the form of God when he raised the dead, gave hearing to the deaf, and cleansed the lepers. But Christ did these things after his nativity; therefore he was in the form of God after his nativity as well. From these and similar points it appears that the opponents have wrongly assigned the first time of Christ's condition.

units.la: esse in formâ Dei, & æqualem Deo, præ-mittit ejus humanationi, ut eo verbo utar.
units.tr: to be in the form of God and equal to God, goes before his humanation, to use that word.

units.la: Ac propterea non alio verbo, nec verbi tempore uti debuit Apostolus, quam fecit, ὑπάρχων. Ad ostendendum, & quod antea Christus fuit, & quod postea semper idem mansit. Atque fatemur, humiliationem Christi fuisse non tantum post incarnationem ejus vel nativitatem, & majestatis Christi status nunquam non.
units.tr: And therefore the Apostle ought not to have used any other word or tense than the one he used, ὑπάρχων [being], to show both that Christ was before and that afterwards he always remained the same. And we admit that the humiliation of Christ was not only after his incarnation or nativity, but that the state of his majesty was never absent.

units.la: Respond. In eo, quod ex Ambrosio, vel Erasmo citat, non facit elenchum. Ergo Christus in forma quoque Dei fuit post nativitatem. Conceditur. Non hoc concludendum erat: sed eum non fuisse in forma & æqualitate Dei, etiam ante nativitatem. Id autem Ambrosium non statuere, qui ex professo multis pro fide ortho-doxa contra Arianos, similesque veritatis hostes disputat, nemini non est manifestum.
units.tr: Answer: The objection drawn from Ambrose or Erasmus does not hold. Therefore Christ was also in the form of God after his nativity. Granted. But this was not the conclusion to be drawn; rather, that he was not in the form and equality of God even before his nativity. That Ambrose does not teach this, though he argues it professedly against the Arians and similar enemies of the truth, in defence of the orthodox faith, is clear to everyone.

units.la: Quare nos bene primum conditionis Christi statum assignamus dignitatis, quam habuit ante suam ex Maria nativitatem, eaque factum sui humiliationem.
units.tr: Therefore we rightly assign the first state of Christ's condition to the dignity that he had before his birth from Mary, and by which he made his humiliation.

units.la: Pergit hinc ad singula Adversarius, atque primum illa in textu expendit, quibus Christus dicitur fuisse ἐν μορφῇ θεῷ, ἴσα θεῷ, in formâ Dei, & æqualis Deo, eaque non significare divinam naturam & majestatem, contendit. Quia si substantiam seu naturam aliquam hic voluisset Paulus significare, non dixisset Christum fuisse in forma Dei, sed Deum, &c. Resp. Mirum, ut hi homines varie se torqueant. Quando Apostolus Christum Deum vocat, quod facit aliquoties, tum dicunt, si Apostolus substantiam seu naturam voluisset significare, non dixisset Christum Deum, sed nescio quid non. Jam ubi explicatissime dicit in forma Dei existere, & æqualem Deo esse, jubent eum potius Christum appellare Deum. Alias prolixe negant, nomen Dei substantiam seu naturam denotare: nunc, si substantiam seu naturam aliquam hic voluisset Paulus significare, non aliter dicturum fuisse dictitant, quam Deum. Ergo vox Dei naturam significat & substantiam, ipsique eam Paulo suppeditant, si velit Dei naturam & substantiam significare, eaque propriorem aut commodiorem ipsi ignorant. Quare ergo adversus nos, & clarissimam veritatem, propriamque confessionem ita alibi tergiversantur, ubi negare non possunt infinities Christum in sacris Deum appellari? longe aliud dicunt esse in forma alicujus, quam esse aliquid. Imo illud, & hoc, & plus dicit, ipsam & totam ejus vim atque naturam.
units.tr: The opponent next goes through the individual points, and first examines those passages in the text where Christ is said to be ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ [in the form of God], ἴσα θεῷ [equal to God], and contends that these do not signify the divine nature and majesty. For if Paul had wished to signify any substance or nature here, he would not have said that Christ was in the form of God, but God, etc. Answer: It is strange how these men twist themselves about in various ways. When the Apostle calls Christ God, which he does several times, then they say that if the Apostle had wanted to signify substance or nature, he would not have called Christ God, but something or other else. Yet where he says most explicitly that he exists in the form of God and is equal to God, they urge that he should rather be called God. Elsewhere again they deny at length that the name of God denotes substance or nature; now they insist that if Paul had wished to signify any substance or nature here, he would have said nothing other than God. Therefore the word God signifies nature and substance, and they supply it to Paul if he wishes to signify the nature and substance of God, while they do not know a word more proper or more fitting for it. Why then do they evade in this way against us and against the very clear truth and their own confession elsewhere, where they cannot deny that Christ is called God in Scripture countless times? They say that to be in the form of someone is quite different from being something. Nay, that expression signifies both that and more: indeed it signifies his whole force and nature.

units.la: Qui dicunt, sive Calvinus, Beza, sive alii, per formam Christi, notari ejus majestatem, divinam substantiam seu naturam non excludunt, sed connotant. Quasi qualitates appellant, non enim proprie qualitates in Deo locum habent: sed quemadmodum Deus aliquando consideratur Theologis in quid, aliquando in quale, non quasi hoc illud vel neget, vel destruat, sed pro varia conceptuum nostrorum ratione & ordine, ita hic ajunt ab Apostolo attendi qualitates & gloriam Christi divinam, opposite ad statum servilem humanum, quem sub forma servi describit. At quemadmodum ista, utcunque qualitates significantia, proxime conditionem Christi inter homines denotant quidem, μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν, ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος, καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, attamen & naturam humanam designant: ita & illud in divinitatis Christi consideratione, quod de forma Dei, opositum formae servi, qualitatem & conditionem divinam notat, hoc humanam, simul intellecta utrobique propria cujusque natura. De illo dubitare minime finit adducta ista paritatis omnimodae cum Deo nota, τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ. Quaerit Adversarius, quod si iis verbis, cum in forma Dei esset, proponitur natura divina qualitatibus vestita, utra vox istam naturam significet? Respondeo, utraque, & vox Dei, & vox formae Dei. Addo, & vox forma, praeter naturam, etiam qualitatem seu majestatem ejus denotat. Ac proinde cum dicit Apostolus, Christum fuisse in forma Dei, idem est ac si dixisset, Christum parem per omnia Deo fuisse, natura, qualitate, conditione, & statu, sive majestate.
units.tr: Those who say, whether Calvin, Beza, or others, that by the form of Christ his majesty is noted, do not exclude the divine substance or nature, but connote it. They call these qualities, for properly speaking qualities have no place in God. But just as God is sometimes considered by theologians in quid (as to what he is) and sometimes in quale (as to what he is like), not as if the one denied or destroyed the other, but according to the varying manner and order of our concepts, so they say that the Apostle here regards the qualities and divine glory of Christ, set against the servile human state which he describes under the form of a servant. But just as those expressions, though they signify qualities, mainly denote Christ's condition among men, [μορφὴν δούλου λαβών] taking the form of a servant, [ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος] being made in the likeness of men, and [καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος] being found in fashion as a man, yet they also designate the human nature; so also in the consideration of Christ's divinity, that phrase about the form of God, set against the form of a servant, denotes the divine quality and condition, just as the other denotes the human, each proper nature being understood in both cases. Concerning the first, the cited note of complete equality with God, [τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ] to be equal to God, leaves no room for doubt. The opponent asks, if by those words, while he was in the form of God, the divine nature clothed in qualities is set forth, which word signifies that nature? I answer: both, the word God and the word form of God. I add that the word form, besides the nature, also denotes its quality or majesty. Accordingly, when the Apostle says that Christ was in the form of God, it is the same as if he had said that Christ was in every respect equal to God, in nature, quality, condition, and state, that is, majesty.

units.la: Deinde quamvis quis dicat, potius hic qualitates à Paulo, quam substantias considerari, & principalem hunc vel praecipuum scopum ejus constituat, non ideo substantias tollit, sed ponit, praecipuè in considerandis qualitatibus Dei formalibus, quae à Dei naturâ separari non possunt, sed cum eâ identificantur. Verbi causa, quando Iesaias cap. vi. principaliter vidit Dei gloriam τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ, uti Ioann. xii. 41. proptereane minus notavit Dei propriam naturam seu essentiam? Denique si Apostolus naturas, quamvis oblique & minus principaliter, innuit tamen, neque solae qualitates, sed & naturae quoque spectandae nobis sunt, in mente Apostoli rite percipienda. Jam id parum refert, in ordine considerationis sive principali sive minus principali, veram modo Christi divinam doceri hic naturam agnoscas.
units.tr: Further, although someone may say that Paul here considers qualities rather than substances, and makes this his principal or chief aim, he does not thereby remove the substances but posits them, chiefly in considering the formal qualities of God, which cannot be separated from the nature of God but are identical with it. For example, when Isaiah in chapter 6 principally saw the glory of God [τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ], as John 12:41 says, is it therefore that he noticed less the proper nature or essence of God? Finally, if the Apostle hints at the natures, though obliquely and less principally, nevertheless neither the qualities alone, but the natures too, must be regarded by us, to be rightly grasped in the mind of the Apostle. Now it matters little, in the order of consideration, whether principal or less principal, that you recognise here that the true divine nature of Christ is taught.

units.la: At regerit, hic per vocabulum μορφὴ forma, non substantiam, sed accidens significari, ex perpetuo Scripturae Sacrae usu. Verùm vocis istius expositio peti ex subjectâ materiâ debet. Neque negamus, illam apud Graecos & Latinos qualitatem saepe significare & rei modum: sed, quemadmodum ipsi fatentur Adversarii, in sermone hoc nostro notat statum & conditionem Dei, & statum dignitatis, dignitatis autem divinae, quae spectrum aut φάντασμα vel μόρφωσις inanis aliqua esse nequit, qualis Apostolo notatur II. Timot. iii. 5. quae careat vi sua & δυνάμει: quapropter veram Dei gloriam notet est necesse, quae propria Dei est, & ab eo separari nequit, adeoque & aequalitatem cum Deo infert. Proptereaque nec rejici acceptio vocis formae philosophica debet, qua rei denotatur essentia, sed connotari & includi. Praeterea non sola vox attendenda est, qua Apostolus utitur, formae: sed phrasis, exist-ere in forma, qua omnino indicatur natura existens in divina illa forma, quae quidquid Dei, tamquam formam suam recipit.
units.tr: But he replies that here the word μορφή (forma) signifies an accident, not a substance, because of the constant usage of Holy Scripture. But the meaning of that word must be drawn from the subject matter under discussion. We do not deny that among Greeks and Latins that word often signifies a quality and the manner of a thing. But, as our opponents themselves admit, in this passage of ours it denotes the state and condition of God, and the state of dignity, and divine dignity, which cannot be some empty appearance, phantasm, or mere outward shape [φάντασμα, μόρφωσις], such as the Apostle describes in 2 Tim. 3:5, lacking its own power and strength [δύναμις]. Therefore it must signify the true glory of God, which belongs to God's own nature and cannot be separated from him, and so it implies equality with God. For this reason the philosophical sense of forma, by which the essence of a thing is denoted, should not be rejected, but rather understood as connoted and included. Moreover, we must consider not only the word forma which the Apostle uses, but the phrase to exist in the form of God, which plainly indicates a nature existing in that divine form, which receives whatever belongs to God as its own form.

units.la: Denique opponitur ei, sed seipsum exinanivit, non exinanivit formam, sed seipsum quasi forma. Ergo substantia connotatur formâ seu gloriâ illâ vestita, & non, quomodo colligit Adversarius, nihil aliud, quam accidens. Quod autem ipse urget, Christum Dei formam depositasse, exuisse, ac eâ se abdicasse, quod non de natura, sed de solo accidente possit intelligi, non id de totali & plena evacuatione intelligere quifpiam potest, tantummodo de occultatione, obscuratione, pro statu humiliationis, χξ' τι[?], non ἀπλῶς. Atque uti in assumenda servi forma, quod illius contrarium est, intelligitur cum servili conditione, natura humana, ita in illo cum divina gloria & dignitate, quoque ejus natura. Tandem ex proposito Apostoli argumentatur, sed per-peram. Nam vult quidem Apostolus, Philippenses exemplo Christi esse humiles: sed nostra non est opinio, humilitatem in Christo significare substantiae mutationem vel essentialem transfigurationem, sed tantum mutationem status, assumtâ ad hoc humana & servili forma. Quis autem somniet, Apostolum suadere, ut Philippenses sibi uniant & associent humanitatem, quemadmodum Christus id fecit: nam revera hoc impossibile & absurdum nimis esset: sed nec similium ea est ratio, ut idem, sed quo-cunque modo simile duntaxat imperent, id est, ut in rebus suis omnem humilitatem affectent Philippenses, quemadmodum suo eam commendavit exemplo Christus, quando existens Deus, in gloria, aequalitate & forma Dei, haud dubitavit se ad homines usque demittere, quin & eorum assumere naturam, atque conditionem vilissimam. Istudne evincit, uti colligit Adversarius, vocem formae hic non substantiam seu naturam significare, quando Christo attribuitur, quod in forma Dei extitit, ante suam humiliationem? Quare quod alii annotarunt, sive Erasmus, sive Calvinus, aut Beza, hic de Christi qualitate & conditione disseri, nobis haudquaquam adver-satur, dummodo non negetur, eam praesupponere, includere, connotare divinam etiam naturam in Christo, una cum gloriae ista conditione, ante humiliationis statum, & vitae hujus. Quod videamus porro, ut Adversarius conetur infringere: nempe, quod non connotatur divina in Christo essentia: quod Apostolus proprie & principaliter designat Christi gloriam; eamque, per formam Dei & aequalitatem cum eo summam, qualem se alteri non daturum Deus testatur Jesa. xlii.
units.tr: Finally, the words but he emptied himself are set against it: he did not empty the form, but himself, as it were, of the form. Therefore substance is connoted by the form, or by the glory with which it is clothed, and not, as our opponent infers, nothing but an accident. As for his insistence that Christ laid aside, stripped off and renounced the form of God, which can be understood only of an accident and not of the nature, no one can understand this as a total and complete emptying, but only of a concealment or obscuring for the state of humiliation, [κατά τι] in some respect, not absolutely [ἁπλῶς]. And just as in the assumption of the form of a servant, which is its opposite, what is meant is the servile condition together with human nature, so in the case of the form of God what is meant is the divine glory and dignity together with his divine nature. Finally, the opponent argues from the Apostle's purpose, but wrongly. For the Apostle does indeed wish the Philippians to be humble after Christ's example. But it is not our view that humility in Christ signifies a change of substance or an essential transformation, only a change of state, the human and servile form having been assumed for this purpose. Yet who would dream that the Apostle urges the Philippians to unite and join humanity to themselves as Christ did? For in truth that would be impossible and altogether absurd. Nor is it the way of comparisons to command the same thing, but only something similar in whatever way; that is, that the Philippians should aim at all humility in their own affairs, as Christ recommended it by his own example, when, though existing as God, in glory, equality and the form of God, he did not hesitate to lower himself to men, and even to take on their nature and most abject condition. Does this prove, as our opponent concludes, that the word form here does not signify substance or nature when it is attributed to Christ that he existed in the form of God before his humiliation? Therefore, what others have noted, whether Erasmus, Calvin or Beza, that here is discussed Christ's quality and condition, does not in the least oppose us, provided it is not denied that it presupposes, includes and connotes the divine nature also in Christ, together with that glorious condition, before the state of humiliation and this life. Let us see further what the opponent tries to overturn: namely, that the divine essence is not connoted in Christ, the Apostle properly and principally designating Christ's glory, and that glory by the form of God and the supreme equality with him, such as God testifies he will not give to another, Isa. 42:8.

units.la: Primum ait, qualitates istas, quas recitat Apostolus, non modo separabiles esse, sed prorsus separatas fuisse à Christo, atque ab ejus divinitate: vid. quia Christum Apostolus scribit, formam Dei & aequalitatem cum eo, abjecisse, exuisse, & depo-suisse, cum eum exinanitum & formam servi assumsisse testatur. At vero ista exinanitio, uti jam dictum, non est intelligenda de totali ablatione vel extinctione, sed χξ' τι[?] de obscuratione & occultatione ad tempus, quando obducto velo humanitatis se continuit, & majestatem suam non palam ostentare voluit, pro peragendo, in humiliatione & crucifixione sui corporis, redemtionis opere. Quae certe quia tanta, & tantae gloriae fuit obnubilatio, & quasi quaedam ad tempus sepositio, merito κένωσις exinanitio Apostolo appellata fuit. Nam cujuscunque demum dignitatis exponas eam fuisse exinanitionem, nunquam tantam licebit semper statuere, ut omni se omnino Christus exuerit, qui ubique haud dubios nominis virtutisque suae radios exeruit. Quare ex loquendi modo ad totalem seu gloriae seu naturae divinae in Christo depositionem argumentari nemo poterit.
units.tr: First he says that those qualities which the Apostle recites are not only separable but were completely separated from Christ and from his divinity. For the Apostle writes that Christ laid aside, stripped off and renounced the form of God and equality with him, when he testifies that he emptied himself and took the form of a servant. But this emptying, as has already been said, is not to be understood as a total removal or extinction, but [κατά τι] in some respect, as a concealment and obscuring for a time, when, with the veil of humanity drawn over him, he restrained himself and chose not to display his majesty openly, in order to accomplish the work of redemption in the humiliation and crucifixion of his body. Since this obscuring of glory was so great, and was in a sense a temporary setting aside, the Apostle rightly called it kenōsis, emptying. For whatever kind of dignity you explain that emptying to be, it can never be so great that Christ should be said to have stripped himself entirely of it, since he everywhere shone forth with unmistakable rays of his name and power. Therefore no one can argue from this way of speaking to a total laying aside of either the glory or the divine nature in Christ.

units.la: Deinde non quidem dicimus, Paulum de gloria Christi principaliter differere, qui principaliter agit de ejus humiliatione, sed hanc ut exponat, illam praemittere dicimus & praesupponere, ut quanta ea fuerit, clarius ostenderet. Qualitates deitatis Apostolum de Christo recitare, Adversarius affirmat. Sed illae à Deitate adeo sunt inseparabiles, ut cum ea revera sint idem. Quae autem Deitatis verae qualitates dici possunt, ut quodammodo tantum, & non omni modo ad gloriam Deitatis faciant, & sic Christi? An vero verba immediate gloriam significent, an mediate, non est quod multum contendamus, dummodo & eam notent, & ejus cum natura divina conjunctionem, atque adeo identitatem. De re modo constet, haud admodum de verbis, eorumve significatione, mediatâ an immediatâ, litigabimus. Certe forma Dei non aliam significat regiam dignitatem, majestatem, & auctoritatem, jus & potestatem imperandi, quam quae Dei est: nam profecto Deus rex noster est, eique ista competunt: & dicitur in textu, forma Dei, non forma regis. Dignitas ergo & majestas vere & proprie divina intelligitur, quam Christus habuit ante omnem humiliationem, nam ab eo statu se demisit in inferiorem conditionis humanae & servilis. Æqualitas vero cum Deo, uti & forma illa Dei, quidem significat quod supra naturam humanam est, sed nec praecise nec proprie mirifica Christi opera, potentiam & vires ista patrandi: plus certe dicit εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ[?], aequalem esse Deo. Nam utut multis attribui mirifica opera possint, nemo tamen sibi arrogare ausit aequalitatem cum Deo. Dignitas, & potentia sunt cognata gloriae, & non eadem, sed ab ipsa distincta, at non dignitas & potentia vere divina, non quae formam Dei complectitur, & ejus aequalitatem, qualis hic expresse nominatur: haec adjuncta divinitatis sunt inseparabilia, quin divinitas Dei ipsa.
units.tr: Next, we do not say that Paul treats principally of Christ's glory, since he treats principally of his humiliation. But in explaining the humiliation he states the glory beforehand and presupposes it, so as to show more clearly how great the humiliation was. The opponent asserts that the Apostle recites the qualities of deity concerning Christ. But these are so inseparable from deity that they are really the same thing. Yet what can be called true qualities of deity, which contribute to the glory of deity only in some measure and not in every way, and so to Christ's glory? Whether the words signify glory immediately or mediately is not a matter we need contend over much, provided they denote both it and its conjunction, and thus identity, with the divine nature. If the thing itself is agreed, we shall not quarrel much over the words, or over their meaning, whether mediate or immediate. Certainly the form of God signifies no other royal dignity, majesty and authority, right and power of ruling, than that which belongs to God. For surely God is our King, and these things belong to him; and the text says the form of God, not the form of a king. Therefore dignity and majesty are rightly and properly understood as divine, which Christ had before all humiliation, for from that state he lowered himself to the lesser condition of human and servile existence. But equality with God, like that form of God, certainly signifies what is above human nature, but not precisely or properly the wonderful works, power and strength by which these things are accomplished. Surely the words to be equal to God say more. For although wonderful works may be attributed to many, no one would dare to claim equality with God for himself. Dignity and power are akin to glory, not the same as it, but distinct from it; yet they are not truly divine dignity and power, not that which embraces the form of God and his equality, which is expressly named here. These are inseparable attributes of divinity, indeed they are the very divinity of God.

units.la: Unde similiter sequitur, gloriam illam, de qua Paulus disserit, & quam in Christo ante ejus humiliationem deprædicat, fuisse summam. Non enim quaelibet gloria intelligitur, sed summa, quae formam & aequalitatem Dei arguit, ac proinde ab æterna Deitate est inseparabilis. In argumento Adversarii, quo evincere conatur, haud posse significari gloriam in Christo summam, negamus simpliciter Minorem: quod sc. Christus forma Dei & aequalitate cum Deo postea habuit gloriam majorem. Probat, quia Christus dicitur in forma Dei & aequalis Deo fuisse ante mortem. Immo, sed & ante vitam, antequam etiam homo fieret, & deprehenderetur σχήματι ἀν-θρώπῳ[?]. Sed Christus, inquit, hanc dignitatem abjecit, & deposuit. Non omnino, nec dignitatem illam, majestatem, auctoritatem ejus, & potestatem, quam tu dicis, quae & retinuit in ipsa morte multisque modis ubivis exeruit; neque gloriam, formam & aequalitatem Dei veram, quam nos credimus. Accepit autem post humiliationem suam, gloriam exaltationis, in persona Mediatoris & humanâ naturâ, tantam ac antea in humiliationis statu non habuit; sed & qua Deus recepit manifestationem divinæ suæ gloriæ, & majestatis cum Deo æqualis, quam habuit etiam ante mundum conditum, quæque, quod ad formam & essentiam suam, perire, tolli, aut deponi nequit, tantummodo quoad sui usum, vim, manifestationem, & actum, uti loquuntur, secundum inhiberi. Denique de illa priori gloriâ exaltationis, postmodum in naturâ humiliatâ acceptæ, intelligendus Christus est, quando Luc. ult. ait, prius se debere pati, antequam in gloriam suam intret. De altera vero, ejusque non nova datione, sed redhibitione, quod dixit Ioann. xvii. 5. de gloriâ, quam apud Patrem habuit, antequam mundus fieret. Quare nihil ab Adversario allatum, quod infringat formam Dei, & hoc æqualitatem cum eo connotare summam, divinamque gloriam.
units.tr: Hence it similarly follows that the glory of which Paul discourses, and which he proclaims in Christ before his humiliation, was supreme. For it is not any glory that is meant, but the supreme glory, which proves the form and equality of God, and therefore is inseparable from eternal deity. In the opponent's argument, by which he tries to prove that supreme glory cannot be signified in Christ, we simply deny the minor premise, namely that Christ afterwards had a greater glory in the form of God and equal to God. He proves it because Christ is said to have been in the form of God and equal to God before death. Indeed, he was so even before his life, before he became man and was found in the fashion of a man [σχήματι ἀνθρώπῳ]. But Christ, says he, laid aside and renounced this dignity. Not entirely, nor that dignity, majesty, authority and power of his which you speak of, which he retained even in death and displayed in many ways everywhere; nor the true glory, form and equality of God, which we believe. But after his humiliation he received the glory of exaltation, in the person of the Mediator and in his human nature, greater than he had in the state of humiliation before; but also, as God, he received a manifestation of his divine glory and majesty, equal with God, which he had even before the world was made, and which, as to its form and essence, cannot perish, be removed or laid aside, but can only be restrained as to its use, power, manifestation and action, as they say. Finally, it is of that former glory of exaltation, afterwards received in his humbled nature, that Christ must be understood when in Luke's last chapter he says that he must suffer before entering into his glory. But of the other glory, and of its restoration rather than new bestowal, he spoke in John 17:5, concerning the glory which he had with the Father before the world was made. Therefore nothing brought forward by the opponent overturns the form of God, and that equality with him which connotes supreme and divine glory.

units.la: Quam facit deinde instantiam Adversarius, eam non agnoscimus nostram, quasi Christus summam Deitatis gloriam accepisset demum post mortem, & non habuisset antea: nam summam illam, seu æqualem Deo, habuit semper, & non accepit in tempore, sed gloriam οἰκονομικῶ[?], mediatoriam, nomen supra omne nomen, ὑπερύψωσεν[?] adeptus post supremum humiliationis gradum tandem fuit. Formam autem Dei & æqualitatem cum Deo non significare summam gloriam, & indivisibilem à Deitate qualitatem, haud tali ratione probare Adversarius debet, qua argumentum nobis impingit quale minime agnoscimus. Neque deinde etiam ex Iesaiæ loco ita argumentamur, quod Christo data sit illa summa gloria; sed quia Deus testatur, se gloriam suam non daturum alteri, hinc sequi, eum, qui gloriam illam habet, non esse à Deo alium. Gloria enim illa Dei propria, & coæqualis in Christo, non cadit sub datione temporali. Præterea mire confundit Adversarius gloriam, à Deo quæ venit, & gloriam Dei, quam se daturum nemini affirmat: nam certe quidem omnis gloria à Deo est, & nisi fit ab honorante se honorantem hominem Deo, non est vera, 1. Sam. ii. 30. sed alia est gloria hominis, alia Dei; & illam quamvis Deus homini de suo largiatur, non de alieno, omnia enim Dei sunt, terra & tota ejus plenitudo, omniaque ab eo & per eum, tamen distincta manet à gloria illa, quam Deus suam, & se communicaturum ait cum nemine. Quæcunque vero deinceps de datione gloriæ in Christo disserit, aut quasi in argumento collocat, aut ad locum annotat Iesaiæ, nos non feriunt: nam nec aliquo tempore datam Christo summam aut Dei propriam gloriam dicimus, sed eam habuisse ab æterno, nec vel argumentum, quemadmodum dictum, ita formamus uti Adversarii, nec probamus ita. Gloria absolute summa, est eadem peculiaris gloria Dei, quam suam asserit, & hanc negamus Christo primum datam in sui exaltatione, sed dicimus, eum ab æterno & naturaliter semper possidere. Quare nos non ad probationem adferimus id, quod sibi hoc in loco objicit Adversarius, ex Apostolo: donavit Deus. Hoc enim de exaltatione Christi quæ in tempore contigit, novimus accipiendum, non de illa forma Christi & æqualitate divina, quam Apostolus præmisit. Illiusque ratione scimus Christum Patre donante inferiorem esse; uti istâ æqualem.
units.tr: The Adversary's next objection is one we do not recognise as ours, as if Christ had received the highest glory of the Godhead only after death, and had not possessed it before. For he always had that highest glory, or equality with God, and did not receive it in time. What he attained after the lowest step of humiliation was an economic [οἰκονομικῶς], mediatorial glory, the name above every name, and a being highly exalted [ὑπερύψωσεν]. The Adversary ought not to prove by such an argument that the form of God and equality with God do not signify the highest glory and a quality indivisible from the Godhead. It is an argument we do not accept. Nor do we argue from the passage of Isaiah that the highest glory was given to Christ. Our point is that God declares he will not give his glory to another, and from this it follows that the one who has that glory is not other than God. That glory, proper to God and equal in Christ, does not fall under a temporal gift. Moreover, the Adversary badly confuses the glory that comes from God with the glory of God which he affirms he will give to no one. Certainly all glory is from God, and unless a man who honours God is himself honoured by God, it is not true glory (1 Sam. 2.30). But the glory of man is one thing, and the glory of God is another. Although God bestows the former on man out of his own store, not out of another's (for all things are God's, the earth and all its fullness, and all things are from him and through him), that glory remains distinct from the glory which God calls his own and says he will share with no one. As for whatever the Adversary goes on to say about the giving of glory in Christ, whether he sets it up as an argument or annotates it on the passage of Isaiah, it does not touch us. We do not say that the highest glory, or the glory proper to God, was given to Christ at any time. We say he had it from eternity, and we do not frame the argument as the Adversary does, nor do we prove it in that way. Absolutely highest glory is that same peculiar glory of God which he claims as his own, and we deny that it was first given to Christ in his exaltation. We say rather that he has always possessed it from eternity and by nature. Therefore we do not bring forward, as proof, what the Adversary here objects from the Apostle: "God has given" [donavit Deus]. We know this must be understood of Christ's exaltation, which took place in time, and not of that form of Christ and divine equality which the Apostle put first. By reason of that form we know that Christ is inferior to the Father in that he is given by the Father, but equal to him in the other respect.

units.la: Argumentum autem quod hactenus frustra oppugnavit Adversarius, ita reformamus: Cuicunque competit absolute summa Dei gloria, est ipsemet Deus æternus: Sed Christo competit absolute summa Dei gloria: ergo. Jam vero illud probamus ex Iesaia, ubi Deus pronunciat, se gloriam suam non daturum alteri: quæ est gloria absolute summa, & ubique eadem. Istud cum ex aliis locis, tum ex adductis, Ioann. xvii. 5. & Phil. ii. 6. Hoc vero negat Advers. videlicet Christum absolute & simpliciter summam gloriam habuisse, duobus, ut sibi videtur, nixus fundamentis: primum 1. Cor. xv. 27. 28. ubi, quantumvis Christus extollatur, Deus Pater semper excipitur Christo exaltato major. At respondemus, sermonem ibi esse de Christi exaltatione, quâ non fuisse Christo collatam absolute summam, seu Dei propriam, & coessentialem vel coæqualem gloriam scimus, sed summam suo ordine & κ[?]τί[?], non vero de gloria quam Christus antè habuit, adeoque ex illius affirmatione & positione, istam non everti: Deinde argumentatione ex Ioann. xvii. ad quam simili ratione respondemus. Christi gloriam, ait, fuisse eam, pro qua Patri supplicat: atqui ea gloria non fuit absolute summa. Concedi-tur totum. Sed inde non sequitur, ergo præter eam gloriam, quam sibi Christus precatur & Apostolis, non habuit quoque aliam æternam, coæqualem Deo, & indivisibilem atque insepa-rabilem à Deitate, cujus vel illa quoque oratione mentionem facit, dicens se eam habuishabuisse ante constitutionem mundi, quæ certe non erat hæc, quam nunc exspectabat & precabatur. Postremo, non accipimus, quod ex intempestiva liberalitate nobis videtur concedere, Deū Patrem suam gloriam dedisse Christo in tempore. Non ex singulari aliqua donatione eam Christus habet, sed natura, & generatione, ab omni æternitate. Sed quidem etiam identitatem essentiæ Dei & Christi Dei filii ostendi dicimus inde, quod eam Christus habet, quia eam se daturum nemini Deus affirmat. Quæ ver-ba quidem proxime referuntur ad idola & sculptilia, ut ea Deus primo perstringat, sed non ita ad ea restringi debent, ut solis iis applicentur, atque testimonium reddant particulare, quod in genere dictum, de quibuscunque accipiendum est, ratione addi-tâ generali, quia ipse est Jehova. Sed Christus non est alius & alter seu diversus à Deo, sed unum cum eo. Certè & unum non voluntate tantum & consensu, sed essen-tia. Quandoquidem sola illa voluntatis concordia non efficeret, quo minus Christus etiam alter & alius esset, neque tantam cum Deo unitatem, ac Scriptura in eo agnoscit. Præterquam quod ista unitas sit reciproca vel mutua Christi cum Patre, & vicissim Patris cum Christo, quod nemo utcunque maxime cum voluntate & mandato Dei conspiret, ausit[?] de se affirmare, se proinde ita unum esse cum Deo, & Deum secum. Certe Christus non erat sculptile, sed viva Dei imago, adeoque idem, & ejusdem cum Deo essentiæ gloriæque. In dicto Jesaiæ non negat Deus, se gloriam aliquam daturum aliis, sed suam gloriam, sibique propriam & singularem. Atque hanc Christo competere Adversarii maximè reclamant. Præsertim dum mox ipsi significant, eandem esse Christi & sanctorum gloriam, ejusdemque generis utrorumque cum Deo unitatem. Est quidem aliqua communis, sed & alia propria Dei, quæ quoque Christi, & quæ tum gloria, tum unitas Christum evincit Deum, atque eun-dem essentia esse cum Patre. Jam in Syllogismo, prout ab Adversario refectus est, nihil ineptius poni quam ista Major potest: Cuicunque, à Deo alio & diver-so, summa datur gloria, est ipsemet Deus æternus. Quis enim ita concludere & sibi tam manifeste velit contradicere, ut ipsummet Deum æternum, ajat, qui à Deo sit diversus & alius? vel qui pro Christo Deo argumentari volens, dicat eum Deum alium & diversum? Sed si in formâ velit argumentum ex dicto Jesaiæ, ita habeat: Cui revera competit propria Dei gloria, is est ipsemet Deus: sed Christo illa competit. Ratio Majoris est, quia eam in nullo alio agnoscit Deus, quam in se. Minor evidens est hinc, quia in formâ Dei Christus est æqualis Deo.
units.tr: We restate the argument which the Adversary has so far attacked in vain as follows: whoever possesses the absolutely highest glory of God is the eternal God himself. But the absolutely highest glory of God belongs to Christ. Therefore Christ is the eternal God himself. We prove the minor from Isaiah, where God declares that he will not give his glory to another. This is the absolutely highest glory, and it is everywhere the same. This we prove both from other passages and from those cited, John 17.5 and Phil. 2.6. The Adversary denies this, namely that Christ had absolutely and simply the highest glory, relying, as he thinks, on two grounds. The first is 1 Cor. 15.27-28, where, however much Christ is exalted, God the Father is always excepted as greater than the exalted Christ. We answer that the discussion there concerns Christ's exaltation, by which we know that the absolutely highest glory, that is, the glory proper to God and co-essential or co-equal with him, was not conferred on Christ. It was conferred in its own order and manner. But the passage does not concern the glory Christ had before, and so by affirming or positing the former, it does not overturn the latter. The second is an argument from John 17, to which we reply in a similar way. He says Christ's glory was that for which he prays to the Father, and that glory was not absolutely highest. We grant the whole of this. But it does not follow that, besides the glory which Christ asks for himself and for the apostles, he did not also have another, eternal, co-equal with God, and indivisible and inseparable from the Godhead. Even in that prayer he mentions this, saying that he had it before the foundation of the world. That was certainly not the glory which he now looked for and prayed for. Finally, we do not accept what he, out of ill-timed generosity, seems to concede to us: that God the Father gave his glory to Christ in time. Christ does not have that glory by some special gift, but by nature and generation, from all eternity. We say, however, that the identity of essence between God and Christ the Son of God is also shown by this, that Christ has that glory because God affirms he will give it to no one. These words, to be sure, are immediately referred to idols and graven images, in order that God may first rebuke them. But they should not be so restricted that they apply only to those, and give a particular testimony. What is said in general is to be understood of whatever things, with the general reason added, because he is Jehovah. But Christ is not another or different from God, but one with him. Indeed, they are one not merely in will and agreement but in essence. For the agreement of will alone would not prevent Christ from being also another and different, nor would it establish the unity so great with God which Scripture acknowledges in him. Besides, this unity is reciprocal or mutual, of Christ with the Father and in turn of the Father with Christ, and no one, however much he agrees with the will and command of God, would dare to affirm of himself that he is so one with God, and God with him. Certainly Christ was not a graven image but the living image of God, and therefore the same, and of the same essence and glory as God. In the saying of Isaiah, God does not deny that he will give some glory to others, but he denies that he will give his own glory, which is proper and singular to himself. The Adversaries most vigorously protest that this glory belongs to Christ. Especially since they soon say that the glory of Christ and of the saints is the same, and that the unity of both with God is of the same kind. There is indeed a common glory, but there is also another glory proper to God, which is also Christ's, and which both glory and unity prove to be Christ, God, and of the same essence as the Father. Now, as to the syllogism as the Adversary has recast it, nothing more absurd can be put forward than this major premise: whoever is given the highest glory by a God other than and different from himself is the eternal God himself. For who would so conclude, and so plainly contradict himself, as to say that the eternal God himself is one who is different from God and other than God? Or who, wishing to argue that Christ is God, would say that he is another and different God? But if he wishes to frame the argument from the saying of Isaiah in form, let it run thus: whoever truly possesses the glory proper to God is God himself. But that glory belongs to Christ. The reason for the major is that God acknowledges that glory in no one but himself. The minor is evident from this: in the form of God, Christ is equal to God.

units.la: De hac autem Christi cum Deo æqualitate porrò disputaturus Adversarius, primo expositionem producit quandam, quam nec ipse probat, & nos proinde quoque missam facimus. Interim negare non audet, Christum esse æqualem Deo, victus tum hoc loco admodum evidenti, tum simili alio Joann. v. 18. Sed negat, inde rectè elici identitatem essentiæ & naturæ. Quid ita? nempe vox ἴζον[?] sæpe idem significat, quod ὅμοιον simile. Hoc est quasi ipse impugnare & tollere vellet id quod jam concesserat, Christum æqualem hic dici Deo. Sic enim potius similis diceretur, quam æqualis. Sed ejusdem inquiet esse utrumque hic significationis. Verùm ut aliquando ἴζον[?] significet ὅμοιον, & æquale nil aliud velit quam simile, primò non dicitur Christus tantum ἴζος[?] Joann. v. sed hic loci τὸ εἶναι ἴζα[?]. Ut de vocis in hac quidem materia nihil remittendum videatur, sed accipienda ea proprie & strictè. Quemadmodum ἐχθρᾳ[?] Rom. viii. 7. consueto Hebraismo, qualis [illegible, ~3 letters] Psalm. 1. 1. &c, quæ sunt ἀνθρωπικά[?] & vim vocum intendunt, non diminuunt: sive Græcismus sit, ut Adversario placet, parum refert. Deinde in sermone de Deo, insuper æqualitate cum eo, plenum est discriminis, licenter loqui & plus quam se res habet: plane ut ex vulgari & profano sermone non sit petenda ratio sacri & divini. Ut minime valeat collectio ista, sic Homerus, sic Trismegistus loquuntur, ergo etiam in hoc loco Apostoli, &c. Præterea utut facile agnoscimus, id quod simile alteri, aliquando etiam æquale appellari, tamen nec id eo trahendum, ut ubique vim verborum istorum confundat, & nullam amplius faciat istorum differentiam, aut tollat τὸ ἀξιόσον καὶ ἴσον[?] vel æqualis supra simile, præsertim non ubi in oratione ea adduntur, quæ omnino significant, non similitudinem doceri aliquam, sed veram justamque æqualitatem. Quod est in loco Apostoli. Denique si solam similitudinem cum Deo denotaret ista loquutio, quid tantæ offensionis præbere Iudæis potuisset, ut propterea Christum voluissent interficere?
units.tr: Turning next to this equality of Christ with God, the Adversary first produces a certain interpretation, which he does not himself prove, and so we too set it aside. Meanwhile he does not dare to deny that Christ is equal to God, being overcome both by the very evident passage here and by a similar one in John 5.18. But he denies that from this one may rightly infer identity of essence and nature. Why so? Because, he says, the word ἴσον [isos] often means the same as ὅμοιον [homoion], like. This is as if he wished to attack and remove what he has already conceded, that Christ is here called equal to God. For in that case he would be said to be similar rather than equal. But, he will say, both words have the same meaning here. Yet even granting that ἴσον sometimes means ὅμοιον, and that "equal" sometimes means nothing more than "like," first, Christ is not said in John 5 merely to be ἴσος [isos], but here the phrase is τὸ εἶναι ἴσα [to einai isa], "to be equal." So in this matter nothing should be yielded from the meaning of the word, but it should be taken properly and strictly. Just as ἐχθρά [echthra] in Rom. 8.7 is a Hebraism of usage, and such as [illegible in the scan] in Ps. 1.1, and so on, these are anthropic [ἀνθρωπικά] expressions and they intensify the force of words rather than diminish it. Whether this is Graecism, as the Adversary wishes, matters little. Further, in speaking of God, and especially of equality with him, there is great danger in speaking loosely and more than the reality warrants. This is so plainly the case that one should not seek the account of the sacred and divine from common and profane speech. This inference is therefore of no force: Homer and Trismegistus speak thus, therefore the Apostles also speak thus in this passage. Moreover, although we readily acknowledge that what is like something else is sometimes also called equal, yet this should not be stretched so as to confuse everywhere the force of these words and make no difference between them, or to remove the distinction between ἀξιόσον [axioson] and ἴσον [ison], or between "equal" and "like." This holds especially where the context adds things which plainly signify not some likeness being taught, but true and just equality. And this is the case in the Apostle's passage. Finally, if that expression signified only likeness to God, what great offence could it have given the Jews, that they wished on that account to kill Christ?

units.la: Deinceps ad aliud recurrit Adversarius, & retentā, inquit, usitatiori vocabuli interpretatione, ut ἴσον vertatur æquale, nihil aliud quam accidens eo denotabitur. Ergo saltem illa usitatior est acceptio. Et advertere secundo debet, pro vi vocis & rei eā significatæ dici ἴσα, & ἐναντί ἴσα, non simpliciter esse ἴσον Θεῷ. Iam ait, accidens eo denotari. In genere, & vulgo? de hoc non est quæstio. In specie, & hoc in loco? probat, ex Philosopho, in prædicamento quantitatis. Quam ista est egregia probatio? fateor, nomen æqualitatis inter res quascunque creatas, & vulgo, ex quo tota philosophia nata est, accidens denotare, & quantitatis paritatem. Sed uti nemo arrogare sibi ausit paritatem ac æqualitatem cum Deo, nempe ejus qui in forma Dei esse dicitur; ita id statui non potest accidentis ratione, quod in Deo locum non habet, solummodo substantiæ. Et sic inter plures nempe personas æqualitas est, in ratione ejusdem substantiæ. Quare non sequitur, quod si Christus à Deo est alius, necessario aliam ab eo naturam & essentiam habere, dummodo non sit aliud essentiæ, quamvis alius personæ. Sic ergo duo sunt, ut tamen etiam sint ἓν unum.
units.tr: The Adversary next turns to another point. He says that if the usual meaning of the word is kept, so that ἴσον is rendered "equal," then it denotes nothing but an accident. So at least that is the more common sense. He ought to notice, secondly, that according to the force of the word and the thing it signifies, things are called ἴσα and ἐναντί ἴσα [equal and equal in opposition], but they are not simply ἴσον to God. He now says that it denotes an accident. In general and in common usage? That is not in question. Specifically, and in this passage? He proves it from the Philosopher, in the category of quantity. What an excellent proof! I grant that the name of equality, among all created things and in common usage, from which all philosophy arose, denotes an accident and a sameness of quantity. But just as no one dares to claim parity and equality with God, namely with him who is said to be in the form of God, so that cannot be asserted in respect of an accident, which has no place in God, but only in respect of substance. Thus there is equality among several persons, in respect of the same substance. Therefore it does not follow that, if Christ is other than God, he must have a different nature and essence from him, provided he is not other in essence, although he is other in person. So there are two, and yet they are also one [ἓν].

units.la: Non autem à Peripateticis, ullisve philosophis discenda est Theologia, vel mysteria fidei adstringenda regulis Dialecticis. Ipsa natura divina non est speciei instar ad suas personas, sed individua & singularis eadem in illis tribus. Quibus cæteroquin verbis exprimeretur id quod nos credimus, dicant Adversarii. Si solum similis fuisset Christus dictus Patri, regererent, at non æqualem propterea doceri: jam & æqualis dicitur, neque id sufficit. Dicitur insuper unus, & unum cum Patre. Quibus ista non sunt satis, exponant necesse est, quibus tandem verbis explicare id debuisset Spiritus Sanctus, ut fidem impetraret. Nobis illa abunde sufficiunt. Non vero nos hic insurgimus, uti perperam sibi imaginatur noster, & æqualitatem essentiæ inter Personas divinas colligimus, ex æqualitate accidentium. Non enim quandam accidentium æqualitatem inter Personas fingimus, quasi accidentibus convenirent (in quibus potest esse convenientia, utcunque res ipsis formis & essentiis differant, quod hic docere supervacaneum fuit) sed essentiæ nullis accidentibus subjectæ paritatem atque identitatem inter Personas statuimus. Quare neutiquam huc quadrant, quæ sive de nobis ἱστορίας[?], sive de æqualibus mercede operariis adducit Adversarius, ubi res, & voces, phrasesque diversissimæ. Tandem ergo ubi nihil solidi vidit aut dixit Adversarius contra fidem,& loci Pau-lini expositionem nostram, aliam procudere satagit, nobis deinceps examinandam. Ubi vel id videri posset fatis esse ad arguendam causæ imbecillitatem, quod tantas per ambages & tergiverfationes demum pervenit ad rem, &, quam agitat, conclu-fionem. Iam,inquit, fi Apostolus Christum expresse dixisset Deum, non tamen inde concludi posset, esse natura Deum. Verum de hoc jam non disputamus: notum quippe nobis est quidem, quid ad istam appellationem, & argumentationem inde nostram excipiant Adversarii: ut autem probent, non videmus. Nam utcumque Magistratus ob aliquam excellentiam & metaphoram vocentur Dii, aliam tamen esse rationem Christi, quando vocatur Deus, nemo non videt. Quis autem ex im-proprià vocis appellatione, ejus tollat proprietatem, & eo quidem loci, ubi maxi-me proprietas attendi debet? Tum hoc nobis fatis est, quod agnoscat, Dei voca-bulum non semper in Scriptura naturam, sed sæpe excellentiam denotare. ergo, naturam etiam, & sæpius, adeoque vox est naturam proprie significans, non officium vel di-gnitatem. Quod alias in dubium trahunt. Quæ autem hic est consequentia, Principes & Reges appellantur Dii, ergo pari modo Christus Deus, vel esse in forma Dei? sic enim debet concludere, non quod haud mirum fit, Christum dici in-forma Dei fuisse. Vel quomodo sequitur, Christus fuit Rex, & peculiariter Rex Iudæorum, ergo id significat Paulus cum ait, eum fuisse in forma Dei? Et non alio modo defungitur primo expositionis suæ membro, quando illud, in forma Dei esse, conatur pertrahere in alium, à nostro, sensum.
units.tr: Theology, however, is not to be learned from the Peripatetics or any philosophers, nor are the mysteries of faith to be bound by the rules of dialectic. The divine nature itself is not like a species in relation to its persons, but is one individual and singular nature in those three. Let the Adversaries say by what other words they would express what we believe. If Christ had been called merely like the Father, they would reply, but not therefore taught to be equal; yet he is also called equal, and that is not enough for them. He is further called one, and one with the Father. If these expressions are not enough for them, they must explain in what words the Holy Spirit should have explained it, in order to win faith. For us those words are amply sufficient. We do not here make the mistake our Adversary imagines, nor do we infer equality of essence between the divine Persons from equality of accidents. For we do not invent some equality of accidents between the Persons, as though they belonged to accidents (among which there can be agreement, however different the things are in their forms and essences, which it was superfluous to teach here). Rather, we affirm a parity and identity of essence, which is subject to no accidents, between the Persons. Therefore the things the Adversary brings forward, whether from histories or from workmen equal in wages, have no bearing here, since the things, words and phrases are wholly different. Finally, then, since the Adversary has seen or said nothing solid against the faith and against our exposition of the Pauline passage, he labours to forge another argument, which we shall examine next. Here one might think it enough to show the weakness of his cause that he arrives, through so many circumlocutions and evasions, at the matter and the conclusion he is pursuing. Now, he says, even if the Apostle had expressly called Christ God, it could not therefore be concluded that he is God by nature. But we are not disputing this now. We know well enough what the Adversaries make of that title and of our argument drawn from it; but we do not see that they prove it. For however magistrates may be called gods because of some eminence and by metaphor, no one fails to see that there is another reason when Christ is called God. Who, moreover, takes away the proper sense of a word by the improper use of its name, and that in the very place where the proper sense most needs to be considered? Yet this is enough for us, that he admits the word God does not always denote nature in Scripture, but often excellence. Therefore it also denotes nature, and more often, so that the word properly signifies nature, not office or dignity. Other people draw this into doubt. But what kind of consequence is this: princes and kings are called gods, therefore in the same way Christ is God, or is in the form of God? For he ought to conclude that, not that it is no wonder that Christ is said to have been in the form of God. Or how does it follow: Christ was a king, and in particular king of the Jews, therefore this is what Paul means when he says that he was in the form of God? Nor does he acquit himself any differently with the first member of his exposition, when he tries to draw that phrase "to be in the form of God" into a sense other than ours.

units.la: Quod ad alterum attinet, in quo Christus affirmatur fuisse æqualis Deo, dictat Adverf. uti per formam Dei, regia Christi majestas; ita per æqualitatem Dei significa-ri magnifica ejus opera & miracula, quæ patravit: quo videlicet demonftrarit, non fe frustra regem esse aut dici, sed veritatem ejus tituli factis ostendere, & reipfa declarare, fe esse vere regem & Meffiam Israelis, voluerit. Respond. I. Mirum autem, quod hoc ipsum, in quo cardo rei vertitur, nullo argumento probet Ad-verfarius, neque etiam vel aggrediatur probare, statim ac illa dictaffet, ad nos impugnandum iterum prosiliens, & vocis ἴσα [?] vim enervare omni studio fata-gens. II. Ubi, aut qua ratione, forma Dei significat esse regem Iudæorum? Quamvis enim is, qui in forma Dei, etiam Rex Iudæorum fuit, non ideo illa-idem significant, sed in eodem diverfiffima. Neque magis forma Dei regem divi-num, ac forma hominum regem humanum denotat. Præterea, dicitur esse in forma Dei: quod evidentius declarat, vim istius phrafis esse longe aliam, quam Adversarii videlicet faciunt, effeipfum Deum. Hinc Versio Æthiopica, qui quum fuit vultus Dei. Arabica, qui semper existens ad imaginem Dei. III. Et plures fue-runt Iudæorum reges, qui nulla tamen ratione propterea dici potuerunt esse in formâ Dei. IV. Sed & ubi, vel quomodo, æqualis esse Deo, significare potest magnifica edere opera & miracula? dicitur ἔναρ [?] in textu, non ποιεῖν, de eo quod fuerit Christus disseritur, non, istis certe verbis, quid fecerit. Æqualitas cum Deo derivatur ex Dei forma, in quâ fuerit, non ex operibus, quæ egerit. Et nisi in formâ Dei proprie fuerit, & æqualis essentiâ Deo, ἴσα [?] æqualia Deo opera patrare non potuit: Magnifica opera non sunt ἴσα ϑεῷ. Illiusmodi opera etiam Apostoli ediderint, haud propterea ἰζῶ ϑεῷ fecerunt, nedum fuisse dicendi sunt.
units.tr: As for the other point, where Christ is said to have been equal to God, the Adversary dictates that, just as the form of God signifies Christ's royal majesty, so the equality with God signifies his magnificent works and miracles which he performed. By these, he says, Christ wished to show that he was not in vain king or called king, but that by his deeds he proved the truth of his title and declared in fact that he was truly the king and Messiah of Israel. Reply I. It is strange that our Adversary proves nothing by argument on the very point on which the matter turns, and does not even attempt to prove it. Once he has made this assertion, he leaps back again to attack us and labours with all his effort to weaken the force of the word ἴσα [ἴσα]. II. Where, or by what reasoning, does form of God signify that someone is king of the Jews? For although the one who was in the form of God was also king of the Jews, the two expressions do not therefore mean the same thing; on the contrary, they are very different. Nor does the form of God denote a divine king any more than the form of men denotes a human king. Moreover, it is said that he was in the form of God, which shows more clearly that the force of this phrase is quite different from what our Adversaries make it, namely that he was God himself. Hence the Ethiopic version renders it who was the face of God, and the Arabic who always existed in the image of God. III. There were also several kings of the Jews who could in no way for that reason be said to be in the form of God. IV. But where, or how, can being equal to God signify performing magnificent works and miracles? The text says ἔναρ [ἔναρ], not ποιεῖν, and what is being discussed is what Christ was, not, in those words, what he did. Equality with God is derived from the form of God in which he was, not from the works which he performed. Unless he was truly in the form of God and equal to God in essence, he could not perform works equal to God (ἴσα [ἴσα]): magnificent works are not ἴσα θεῷ. Apostles also performed such works, yet they did not for that reason become ἴσα θεῷ, much less are they to be called so.

units.la: v. Denique & hoc demus, non autem concedamus, denotari verbis illis regiam Christi dignitatem & potestatem patrandi opera prorsus divina, habuisse illam, dicendum est, ante omnem sui humiliationem, id est, antequam etiam in forma humana apparuit, seu homo fieret. Nam id contextus & ordo verborum Apostoli satis clare arguit, praecessisse illa, antequam formam humanam Christus assumsit.
units.tr: Finally, let us grant this, though we do not concede it: that those words denote Christ's royal dignity and power to perform works that are wholly divine, it must be said that he had this before all his humiliation, that is, before he even appeared in human form or became a man. For the context and the order of the Apostle's words argue quite clearly that these things came before Christ assumed the human form.

units.la: Iam redit ad vocem ἰζα, & vocem θεὸς, repetitque vel amplificat quae ante dixerat, & quibus suo loco respondimus. ἰσὼ an more loquendi Graeco, an Hebraeo dicatur, parum refert, sed ejus vim infringere, & expositionem petere ex dicendi more poëtico aut profano de Diis, haud aeque tolerabile. Praeterquam quod similis nostrae phrasis nulla adducitur. Non aliquam cum Deo similitudinem proferre satis est, ad phrasim nostram explicandam, neque dicere quod significet dunta-xat aliquem supra communem & vulgarem sortem constitutum. Nam hujusmodi plures dari possunt, haud tamen aliquis, cui ea quae hic de Christo, possint attribui. Quod ad vocem Dei, de qua tamen hic non est quaestio, sed de phrasi, esse in forma Dei, & ἰζα θεῶ, non probabit, non certe ex sacris, absolute & simpliciter Deum dici, quodcunque aliqua ratione in suo genere excellit, vel vulgarem ac usitatam sortem superat. Neque Cicero, cujus testimonium praemittit, & Paulum potius cum Cicerone videtur velle conciliare, quam hunc cum illo, non absolute Deum appellat, sed relative, in dicendo Deum: & Apostolus Phil. iii. 19. similiter relative inquit, Quorum Deus venter est. At Eph. v. 5. ne quidem vocem Dei usurpat, tantummodo ait, avarum esse idololatram. Quid haec quaeso simile habent cum phrasi, εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ? Id significat, inquit, Christum esse excellentissimum, & in suo genere eminentissimum, & inter homines quasi Deum. Id vero est Apostolo in os reclamare, qui ne quis leviter simile aliquod de Christo confingeret, quibus maxime potuit verbis devitavit, & ad exprimendam vim substantiae divinae dixit, in forma Dei eum fuisse, prorsus ei aequalem, ne quis in verbo aliquo technas quaereret frivolasque elusiones. Quale & illud est quod addit, per vocabulum Dei non substantiam vel ipsum Deum denotari videtur suadere non appositus ei articulus: quod alibi multis refellimus exemplis, praeterquam quod ipse hoc Auctor seipsum: nam in loco, quem adfert Phil. iii. 19. addito articulo dicitur venter ipsorum ὁ θεὸς, & tamen non substantiam ibi, sed accidens, & eximium aliquid denotari, dixit. Adeo in articulo addito, sive omisso vis θεὸς constituenda non est. Hanc modo percurrat Apostoli epistolam, videbitque quoties vox θεὸς de Deo ponatur sine articulo, cap. i. 2. ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρός. vers. 11. ὡς ἐπαγγελίαν θεὸς. vers. 28. ἡ τῶν ἀπὸ θεοῦ. cap. ii. 15. τέκνα θεοῦ ἀμώμητα. cap. iii. 3. θεῷ λατρεύοντες. vers. 9. τῷ ὄντι θεοῦ δικαιοσύνῃ. Eat, atque ex articuli omissione contra Deum argumentari pergat.
units.tr: Now he returns to the word ἰσὼ [ἴσα] and the word θεός [θεὸς], repeating or enlarging what he said before, and to which we have replied in its place. Whether ἴσα [ἴσα] is said in the Greek manner of speaking or the Hebrew hardly matters, but to weaken its force and seek an explanation from the poetic or profane manner of speaking about the gods is not at all tolerable. Besides, no phrase similar to ours is adduced. It is not enough to bring forward some likeness to God in order to explain our phrase, nor to say that it means merely that someone has been placed above the common and ordinary lot. For there can be several such people, yet none to whom the things said here about Christ could be attributed. As for the word God, which is not, however, the question here, but the phrase to be in the form of God and ἴσα θεῷ [ἴσα θεῷ], he will not prove, certainly not from the sacred writings, that anything is called God absolutely and simply whenever it in some way excels in its kind or surpasses the common and usual lot. Nor does Cicero, whose testimony he puts forward, and whom he seems to want to reconcile Paul with rather than Paul with Cicero, call him God absolutely but relatively, when speaking of a god. And the Apostle in Phil. 3:19 likewise speaks relatively: whose god is the belly [ὧν ὁ θεὸς ἡ κοιλία]. But in Eph. 5:5 he does not even use the word God, but only says that the covetous man is an idolater. What do these have in common, I ask, with the phrase εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ [εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ]? It means, he says, that Christ is the most excellent and most eminent in his kind, and among men as it were God. But this is to contradict the Apostle to his face, who, so that no one might lightly invent anything similar about Christ, avoided this as far as he could, and to express the force of the divine substance he said that he was in the form of God, altogether equal to him, so that no one might look for tricks and worthless evasions in some word. Such also is what he adds: that the lack of the article before the word God seems to suggest that the substance or God himself is not denoted by it. We refute this by many examples elsewhere, and besides, this Author refutes himself: for in the passage he cites, Phil. 3:19, with the article added, the belly of such people is called ὁ θεὸς [ὁ θεὸς], and yet he said that there not the substance but an accident and something outstanding is denoted. So the force of θεὸς is not to be determined by whether the article is added or omitted. Let him only run through this Epistle of the Apostle, and he will see how often the word θεὸς is used of God without the article: ch. 1:2, ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρός [from God our Father]; v. 11, ὡς ἐπαγγελίαν θεὸς [as God promised]; v. 28, ἡ τῶν ἀπὸ θεοῦ [those from God]; ch. 2:15, τέκνα θεοῦ ἀμώμητα [blameless children of God]; ch. 3:3, θεῷ λατρεύοντες [serving God]; v. 9, τῷ ὄντι θεοῦ δικαιοσύνῃ [the righteousness of God]. Let him go and read it, and then continue to argue against God from the omission of the article.

units.la: Explicaturus porro, quid in Apostoli verbis fit, non rapinam arbitratus est, praemittit, quod Christus aequalitatem cum Deo habuerit ex donatione Patris, quasi id Apostolus voluerit istis verbis: donavit illi nomen. non attendens, haec de alia gloria Christo mediatori post humiliationem data intelligi debere, quam ante omnem humiliationem habuit, & in Lactantio rhetoricationem magis, quam ἀρπάζεσθαι[?] esse, quando de Christo ait, quod Dei nomen accepit. Sit proverbialis ista locutio, cujus exempla occurrant apud Heliodorum: verum non evincet, sensum ejus hoc in loco esse quem dat, vid. Christum non arbitratum rapinam, fieri regem Judaeorum, neque voluisse oblatam istam dignitatem statim amplecti, eaque frui, sed humiliari prius & mori. Nam I. quod & supra monuimus, nihil hic de imperio Judaico. ii. Neque Christus imperium populi istius corporalis expetebat, vel affectabat, uti de eo accipienda Adversarii verba. iii. Neque in eo collocari aequalitas cum Deo potuit. iv. Æqualitatem cum Deo autem constituit in potestate patrandorum miraculorum, sed hanc Christus non neglexit, at habuit posseditque omni tempore: & formam Dei, de regia dignitate fuit interpretatus: dicitur tamen in textu, quod rapinam non fuit arbitratus esse aequalem Deo, non, esse in forma Dei, conjungitur illud cum isto, non cum hoc, sed praesupponitur jam in forma Dei fuisse: ut si rapinam non arbitratus aequalis Deo esse, congruenter praecedentibus esset interpretandum, ita ex Adversariorum mente accipienda haec essent, Christus cum regia polleret dignitate, haud tamen oblatam sibi conditionem patrandorum operum maxime magnificorum amplecti voluit. Quae nec cum rei veritate, nec verborum Apostoli sensu, denique nec satis cum explicatione ipsorum Adversariorum, conveniunt. Sit autem ἀρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο proverbialis loquutio, saltem metaphorica, significetque rem maximi facere, habere admodum gratam, charam, optatamque, quam summe aestimes, & concessam arte teneas, ut qui rapinam solent, quem sensum optime ferunt & nostris proxime accedunt illa apud Heliodorum verba, οὐχ' ἁρπαγμα, ἀλλ' ἐμαυτὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ πρᾶγμα: sensus resultat ex Apostoli verbis iste commodissimus, vid. quod Christus, quum Deus esset, in ipsa Dei forma, & aequalitate omnimoda, haec tamen quasi posthabere visus sit suae, in nostri gratiam, humiliationi, ut illa quantumvis tanta, non tamen ita chara quasi habuerit & pretiosa, ac nostri salutem, nos prae se quasi amans, Rom. v. 8. & propterea se eo usque pro nobis demittens. Sic Deus Pater nec Filio suo pepercit, nec Filius sibi, ut nobis parceretur. Ergo οὐχ' ἡγήσατο Christus hoc quod ipse erat, non τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ[?], quamvis ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ ὑπάρχων[?]; non illud sibi tanti, ac vulgo homines ἁρπαγμὸν facere soliti, quin neglexit ad tempus, & statum, dignitatem, ac gloriam seponere voluit, ut se quasi exinaniret illis, & formam humanam servilemque induere.
