Nisi sit, quod aliis placet, haud Christus illam Dei formam, aequalitatem, in quâ erat, voluit in mundo palam ostentare & quasi in triumphum ducere, uti quandoque rapinas suas gloriabunde homines solent, sed occultare & humili specie σχήματι vestire.
units.tr: Intending next to explain what the Apostle means by the words he did not think it robbery, the opponent first states that Christ had equality with God by the Father's gift, as though the Apostle meant by these words: he gave him a name. He does not notice that these things must be understood of another glory given to Christ the Mediator after his humiliation, which he did not have before any humiliation. And in Lactantius, when he says of Christ that he received the name of God, it is more a rhetorical flourish than a seizing [ἀρπάζεσθαι]. Let this be a proverbial expression, of which examples occur in Heliodorus. Yet it will not prove that its sense here is what they give, namely that Christ did not think it robbery to become king of the Jews, and that he did not wish to embrace that offered dignity at once and enjoy it, but first to be humbled and to die. For first, as we noted above, there is nothing here about a Jewish empire. Second, Christ did not seek or aspire to the empire of that bodily people, as the opponent's words would have it. Third, equality with God could not consist in that. Fourth, the opponent places equality with God in the power of working miracles, but Christ did not neglect this; he had it and possessed it at all times. He has interpreted form of God as regal dignity. Yet the text says that he did not think it robbery to be equal to God, not that he was in the form of God. The clause is joined with the one that follows, not with the one that precedes, and it presupposes that he was already in the form of God. If did not think it robbery to be equal to God were to be interpreted in agreement with what precedes, then, in the opponents' mind, the sense would be: Christ, though he had regal dignity, nevertheless did not wish to embrace the offered condition of performing very great works. These readings agree neither with the truth of the matter, nor with the sense of the Apostle's words, nor even sufficiently with the opponents' own explanation. Let the expression [ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο] be a proverbial phrase, or at least a metaphorical one, meaning to set great store by a thing, to hold dear, pleasing and longed-for what one values most highly and keeps firmly once it is granted, as those who plunder are wont to do. Heliodorus's words, not a robbery, but he thought the thing to be himself [οὐχ' ἁρπαγμα, ἀλλ' ἐμαυτὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ πρᾶγμα], express this sense best and come closest to ours. From the Apostle's words there follows the most suitable sense: that Christ, though he was God, in the very form of God and in complete equality with him, nevertheless seemed as it were to set aside his own glory for our sake, so that he did not hold that equality, however great, as so precious and dear to himself, and, loving us as if we were before him (Rom. 5:8), lowered himself so far for our sake. Thus God the Father did not spare his own Son, nor did the Son spare himself, that we might be spared. Therefore Christ did not count it a prize [οὐχ' ἡγήσατο] to be what he himself was, not to be equal to God [τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ], though he existed in the form of God [ἐν μορφῇ Θεοῦ ὑπάρχων]. He did not hold this as dear as men commonly do, who are wont to make a prize of such things. Rather, he set aside for a time his state, dignity and glory, so that he might empty himself and put on the human and servile form. Unless it is the case, as others prefer, that Christ did not wish to display openly in the world that form and equality of God in which he was, nor to lead it about as in triumph, as men are wont to boast of their plunder at times, but rather to hide it and clothe it in a humble appearance [σχῆμα].

units.la: Jam in secundo Christi statu, quem Apostolus persequitur usque ad verf. 9. exponendo, qui est humiliationis, disputat Adversarius, illa non esse accipienda, de toto vitae Christi cursu ac tempore, sed tantummodo ad tempus mortis, & quae mortem proximè praecesserunt, ut quod captus, vinctus, flagellatus, illusus, denique crucifixus & sepultus fuit. Quod nos negamus, & humiliationem Christi de tota ejus vita, & ipso vitae exordio accipiendam esse, contendimus. i. Quia toto illo tempore etiam humilis & abjectus fuit, monstrante id tota vitæ ejus historia, inde à prima nativitate, Luc. ii. 7. & peperit filium ejus primogenitum, & involvit fascijs, & reposuit cum in præsepi; quandoquidem ibi locus non erat in diversorio. Non hæc nota argumentum fuit abjecti satis & humiliati Christi? Quid reliqua dicam, fuga & in Ægyptum, persequutiones passas, contemptus, laborem, servitutem, quæ omnia sustinuit assiduo vitæ suæ tractu? Quæ opinor nemo negare ausit [?] humilitatis in Christo documenta fuisse perquam manifesta. ii. Similiter apud Prophetas significata jam olim fuerat humilitas ortus Christi, & vitæ, non tantum mortis, quod instar virgulti ex radice succisi, & natali admodum abjecto prodiret. iii. Apostolus humilitatem Christi orditur ab eo quod homo factus, non tantum quod mortuus: verum exinanivit seipsum: factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem vero crucis. Duo, vel tria Apostolus considerat momenta, hominis conditionem, tum servilem, & mortem; primum, quod Christus hominis assumsit formam & conditionem, ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος, καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος [?]: deinde inter homines, statum servi μορφὴν δούλου λαβών [?]. Denique & mortem subiit, eamque dirissimam crucis. iv. Ipse Adversarius ita sermonem Apostoli partitus fuit, ut verf. 6. acciperet de statu & conditione dignitatis Christi; secundum vero Christi statum qui est humiliationis, descriptum dicat ab Apostolo his verbis: sed semetipsum exinanivit, formam servi accipiens, &c. usque ad verf. 6. Denique in N. T. Christi humilitas explicatur etiam de ejus ortu, vitaque. Gal. iv. 4. quando autem venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere, factum sub lege. & Rom. i. 3. factum esse ex semine Davidis quoad carnem, opponitur ei, quod potenter declaratus fuit esse filius Dei.
units.tr: Now in the second state of Christ, which is that of humiliation and which the Apostle pursues in his exposition up to verse 9, the opponent argues that these words are not to be understood of the whole course and time of Christ's life, but only of the time of his death and of what immediately preceded it, such as his being seized, bound, scourged, mocked, and finally crucified and buried. We deny this, and we contend that Christ's humiliation must be understood of his whole life, from its very beginning. First, because throughout that whole time he was also humble and lowly, as the whole history of his life shows, from his first birth: And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn (Luke 2:7). Is this not sufficient proof of the lowliness and humiliation of Christ? What shall I say of the rest: his flight into Egypt, the persecutions he suffered, the contempt, the toil, the servitude, which he bore throughout the continual course of his life? I think no one would dare to deny that these were most manifest proofs of humility in Christ. Second, the humility of Christ's birth and life, not merely of his death, was likewise signified long before by the prophets, as that which would come forth like a shoot from a cut root, in a most lowly birth. Third, the Apostle begins the humiliation of Christ not merely from his death but from his being made man: but he emptied himself, being made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. The Apostle considers two or three stages: the condition of man, then the servile condition, and death. The first is that Christ took on the form and condition of man, being made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man [ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος, καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος]. Then, among men, he took the state of a servant [μορφὴν δούλου λαβών]. Finally, he underwent death, and that the most dreadful death of the cross. Fourth, the opponent himself divided the Apostle's discourse in such a way that he takes verse 6 as referring to the state and condition of Christ's dignity, but says that the second state of Christ, which is that of humiliation, is described by the Apostle in these words: but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and so on, up to verse 6. Finally, in the New Testament, the humility of Christ is also explained with reference to his birth and life. Gal. 4:4: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law. And Rom. 1:3, that he was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, is set against his being declared powerfully to be the Son of God.

units.la: Argumenta vero, quibus in contrarium militat Adversarius, ea adfert, ut primum sit petitio ejus quod in quæstione, nempe, inquit, si tempus hoc humiliationis Christi completeretur omne tempus vitæ, haud assignari posset tempus primo statui & conditioni dignitatis ejus, quam constitui ante nativitatem ex matre haud posse putat, sed quod nullis rationibus demonstravit. Secundo, quia Christus per omne post nativitatem tempus non fuit in humili & abjecto statu, sed glorioso, & auctoritatis pleno. Ad quod nonnulla adfert Scripturæ dicta, quæ testantur, Christum crevisse, adeoque plenum fuisse sapientia, gratia, gloria, & auctoritate ac potentia instructum supra modum. Unde argumentum format: ille, qui celebris est, qui cum auctoritate docet, qui gloriosus est, quem totus mundus sequitur, observat, qui admiranda loquitur, & facit, non est in vili, abjecta & humili conditione. Hanc vero propositionem nos similiter negamus. Adeoque nihil sententiæ suæ probavit Adversarius. Nam Christus in statu humiliationis illa opera exhibuit, & talem se esse demonstravit, ut sub servili forma cognoscerent homines Deum latere & existere. Ad quod confirmandum hoc unum nunc sufficerit, quod Christus idem ille fuit, talemque sed dictis [?] & factis præstitit quoque tempore passionis & mortis suæ: quare illa non significant, quando talis fuit Christus, non fuisse in vili, abjecta & humili conditione. Denique nimis abjecte & carnaliter de Christo loquitur Adversarius, in exponendis causis humiliationis ejus, quod viderit humano generi fore salubrius, si ad tempus aliquod, ab imperio & regno Iudaico abstineret, insuper & mortem subiret, plures subditos, majus imperium, potentiam ampliorem se habiturum, maluerit cupiditati, quæ præsentibus statim frui suadet, per mortem, frænum injicere, & cruciatus, ad tempus, sustinere, ut duplicatum postea consequeretur honorem, quam fine ulla molestia regnum Judaicum obtinere, & delicate vivere. Quare per istam humiliationem hoc adeptus fit, ut & prior dignitas illi non auferretur, & adjiceretur novum imperium, regnum scilicet gentium. Ita ut loco unius regionis & nationis, omnes gentes, & totum mundum acceperit in haereditatem, &c. Quasi vero Christus imperium aliquod terrenum regionum aut nationum, imprimis autem regnum Judaicum, affectarit. Non certe tanquam de regno & rege spirituali hic loquitur noster, cujus ne quidem verbum admiscet, sed tanquam fi plane carnalis fuisset Meffias, & Judaicus aliquis, ita eum introducit agentem, & secum consultantem. Qui cupiditatibus suis fraenum injecerit: credo ne ipsum transversum agerent, & per intempestivam ambitionem fraudarent meliori occasione. Qui hoc sibi habuerit propositum, delicate vivere, & duplicato frui imperio. Quis vero existimet, ita Christianum loqui de Christo? & quum in margine moneat, fe explicare causas humiliationis Christi, ita in solis Christi commodis, adeoque carnalibus haerere, neque nostri fere & redemtionis spiritualis, per ejus humiliationem, meminisse? Sed & hinc disce, qualis Adversariis nostris Christus, redemptio qualis, qualis & religio ipsorum, fi placet, Christiana. Et tamen huc etiam trahitur locus II. Cor. viii. 9. quod Christus quum effet dives, propter nos egenus factus fit, id est, inquit, quum regiam dignitatem & imperandi inter Judaeos potestatem haberet in manu Christus, spretis istis divitiis, mendicum fe & pauperem fecit, ut Gentes, quales erant Corinthii, divites faceret, &c. de Christo quod dicit, nimis jejunum est, quando illud quod Christi divinitatis, ad humanitatem; quod aeternae gloriae, ad temporalem conditionem trahit, & minus vilem facit ejus humiliationem, ad mendicitatem usque, nec majorem gloriam, quam nimis impotenter ad imperium refert Judaicum. Denique perpetuae ejus expositioni id unum hic reponimus, quod regiam dignitatem, qua unctus Christus a nativitate fuit, nunquam deposuit, nec ea fe prorsus evacuavit, quum πλυτεόπως[?] eam variis vicibus ostenderit, & post fui exaltationem fecerit maxime illustrem.
units.tr: The arguments by which the opponent fights on the other side are these. The first is a petitio principii of the very question: namely, he says, if this time of Christ's humiliation were to extend over his whole life, no time could be assigned to the first state and condition of his dignity; and he thinks that this state cannot be placed before his birth from the mother, but he has demonstrated this by no reasons. Second, because for every time after his birth Christ was not in a humble and lowly state, but in a glorious one, full of authority. To this he adduces several sayings of Scripture which testify that Christ grew, and was therefore full of wisdom, grace, glory and authority, and endowed beyond measure with power. Whence he forms the argument: he who is renowned, who teaches with authority, who is glorious, whom the whole world follows, who observes, who speaks and does admirable things, is not in a vile, abject and humble condition. We likewise deny this proposition. Thus the opponent has proved nothing for his view. For in the state of humiliation Christ displayed those works and showed himself such that men, under a servile form, might recognise that God lay hidden there and was present. To confirm this, let the following one point now suffice: that Christ was the same person, and that he displayed the same kind of words and deeds also at the time of his passion and death. Therefore those things do not show that, at the time when Christ was such, he was not in a vile, abject and humble condition. Finally, the opponent speaks of Christ too abjectly and carnally, in setting out the causes of his humiliation: that he saw it would be more profitable for the human race if for some time he abstained from the empire and kingdom of the Jews, and moreover underwent death; that he would have more subjects, a greater empire and wider power; that he preferred to put a bridle on his desire, which urges one to enjoy present things at once, through death, and to endure torments for a time, so that afterwards he might obtain a doubled honour, rather than obtain the Jewish kingdom without any trouble and live delicately. Hence, through this humiliation, he achieved that his former dignity was not taken from him, and that a new empire was added, namely the kingdom of the Gentiles, so that instead of one region and one nation he received all nations and the whole world as his inheritance. As if Christ aspired to some earthly empire of regions or nations, and above all to the Jewish kingdom! Our author certainly does not speak here of a kingdom and king who are spiritual, nor does he mix in a word about them; rather, he introduces Christ as if he were a wholly carnal Messiah, a Jewish sort of man, acting and deliberating with himself: he who would put a bridle on his desires, lest, I suppose, they should lead him astray, and through untimely ambition defraud himself of a better opportunity; he who had this purpose, to live delicately and enjoy a doubled empire. But who would think that a Christian speaks thus of Christ? And while he warns in the margin that he is explaining the causes of Christ's humiliation, does he so cling to Christ's advantages alone, and so to carnal ones, that he scarcely remembers our salvation and our spiritual redemption through his humiliation? But from this learn also what kind of Christ, what kind of redemption, and what kind of religion, if you please, Christian, our opponents have. And yet the passage II Cor. 8:9 is also dragged into this, that Christ, though he was rich, for our sake became poor, that is, says the opponent, since Christ had regal dignity and the power of ruling among the Jews in his hand, he spurned those riches, made himself a beggar and a poor man, so that he might make rich the Gentiles, such as the Corinthians were. What he says about Christ is far too meagre: he draws what belongs to Christ's divinity down to his humanity, what belongs to eternal glory down to a temporal condition, and makes his humiliation less vile than it is, even to the point of beggary, and assigns to him no greater glory than the Jewish empire, which he too feebly ascribes to it. Finally, to his whole exposition we here set against this one thing: that Christ, anointed with regal dignity from his birth, never laid that dignity down, nor did he at all empty himself of it, since he displayed it in various ways while he was on earth, and after his exaltation made it most illustrious.

units.la: Deinceps ipsa Apostoli verba sigillatim cosiderat Adversarius. Ac primum verba illa, exinanivit seipsum, non posse ex nostro sensu, de incarnatione Christi intelligi hinc cotendit, quia non dicit Apostolus, λόγον se exinaniisse, sed Iesum Christum: quae appellatio est nulli, nisi homini nato competens. Ad quod jam antea respondimus, quod quamvis ratio appellationis, fi plena ejus vis spectetur, competat Christo homini, attamen nihil impediat de ista persona ea dicere, non minus vera, quae ei alia ratione, & longe ante eam, competunt. Praeterquam quod appellatio illa Iesu Christi non simpliciter homini nato, sed homini Deo θεανθρώπω conveniat, de cujus Deitate alia, alia de humanitate ejusque ortu docet Apostolus, & tota passim Scriptura Sacra. Denique annon id, quod a Paulo nunc exigit, a Iohanne discere potuit, qui dixit λόγον carnem factum? Joann. I. 14.
units.tr: Next the Adversary examines the Apostle's words one by one. First, he argues that the words "emptied himself" cannot be understood of the incarnation of Christ, on our interpretation, because the Apostle does not say that the Word emptied himself, but that Jesus Christ did. That name, he says, belongs only to a man who has been born. We have already answered this: although the reason for the name, taken in its full force, applies to Christ as man, nothing prevents us from saying of this person things that are just as true and that belong to him on another ground, and long before that. Moreover, the name Jesus Christ belongs not simply to a man who was born, but to a man who is God [θεανθρώπῳ], of whose Deity the Apostle teaches one thing, and of whose humanity and birth he teaches another, as does all of Holy Scripture throughout. Finally, could he not have learned from John, who said that the Word was made flesh, what he now demands from Paul? John 1:14.

units.la: Aliud fecundo argumentum instruit, dicitque, exinanitionem nec divinae, juxta nos, neque humanae attribui naturae posse, quare nec eam defendi. Non illi, quae nec diminui, nec decrescere, neque mutari potest, ac proinde nec exinaniri. Isti non, quia affumta humana natura in unionem hypostaticam cum divina, non exinanita, vel humiliata, sed decorata & impleta fuit. Respondemus, divinae naturae compe-
units.tr: He brings forward a second argument: the emptying can be attributed neither to the divine nature, on our view, nor to the human nature, and therefore it cannot be defended. Not to the divine nature, which can be neither diminished, nor decreased, nor changed, and so cannot be emptied. Not to the human nature, because the assumed human nature, in hypostatic union with the divine, was not emptied or humbled but adorned and filled. We reply that this emptying belongs to the divine nature

units.la: Tom. 2. (printed volume mark at the foot, left) tit[?] ista exinanitio, non quoad mutationem vel diminutionem essentiae, sed quod se eo dimittere summa Majestas voluit, & assumere atque adjungere sibi vilem admodum naturam, eaque inter homines ambulare, & pro eo statu ac tempore gloriam suam in assumta natura & conditione humana occultare, seponere & quasi sequestrare. Hæc ista est exinanitio. Quemadmodum Angelus, qui sub Vet. Test. aliquoties apparuit Patribus sub humana specie, vere dicitur hactenus seipsum exinanivisse, quamvis essentiam suam propterea non evacuarit: ita jam Dei Filius assumens ex generatione naturam humanam, exinanivit seipsum, non essentiae ratione, sed accidentaliter quoad nos, non quoad seipsum: videlicet, quod pro nobis humiliari, & non se gerere pro majestate sua, eamque ubivis ostentare voluit, id est, variationem quidem status subiit, non naturae, citra ullam sui realem mutationem. Deinde inanitio humanae naturae competit, quoad servilem conditionem, quam in natura & statu illo subiit.
units.tr: Tom. 2. (printed volume mark at the foot, left) ... this emptying, not with respect to any change or diminution of the essence, but in that the supreme Majesty willed to lower itself thereby, to assume and join to itself a very lowly nature, to walk among men, and for that state and time to hide its glory in the assumed nature and human condition, to set it aside and as it were to sequester it. This is that emptying. Just as the Angel who in the Old Testament appeared several times to the Fathers in human form is truly said to have emptied himself up to that point, though he did not on that account lose his essence, so now the Son of God, assuming human nature by generation, emptied himself: not in respect of essence, but accidentally as regards us, not as regards himself. That is, he was willing to be humbled for us and not to conduct himself according to his majesty, nor to display it everywhere. He underwent a change of state, not of nature, without any real change in himself. Then, emptying belongs to the human nature as regards the servile condition which it underwent in that nature and state.

units.la: In explicatione deinde formae servilis pari modo progreditur, ac supra, ubi de forma Dei disseruit. Dicit, illa accidens notare, non substantiam. Quod non id proprie est, quod quaeritur: sed annon & essentiam connotent. Certe hic denotatur servilis Christi conditio, sed quae humanam naturam praesupponit & includit, utpote in qua sola haereat. Neque enim de servili forma in abstracto hic philosophamur, vel ex Aristotele ejus petimus rationem, sed de homine servo loquimur, qui & homo, & servus fieri voluit, non naturae suae divinae mutatione, sed sola variatione externi status. Hoc autem quamvis sit accidentarium, substantiae assumtionem & conjunctionem tamen necessario exigit, nec Scripturae, nec Adversariis (opinor) negatam. Ut de eo multum verba facere nihil sit necesse. Ad humilitatem hortatur Apostolus Philippenses, exemplo Christi, non ad eandem speciem, quis enim tam insanus ut hoc putet, vel in argumentatione ab exemplo requirat? sed ad similem, ad eam quae ipsis conveniat. Ut, quemadmodum Christus admirabilem in eo sui humiliationem declaravit, quod gloriosus Deus ad infirmam humanae fortis conditionem se demittere voluit, sic Philippenses quoque in omni re humilitatem Christi sequi, seque demissos præbere haud erubescerent: non ut per hypostaticam unionem diversas naturas sibi copularent. Idem glossema adaptat Adversarius sequentibus, ubi Apostolus dicit, Christum in similitudinem hominum factum, & habitu inventum, ut homo: quae de sola hominis similitudine accipit, non natura. Nos de utraque. Probat quidem, accidentalem istis verbis notari Christi hominis conditionem, sed non item naturam haud connotari posse, vel debere. Quum verba illa ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων, & ὡς ἄνθρωπος, præsertim in sermone de Christo, absque consignificatione humanae naturae vix intelligi queant. Æque minus ac hoc, quod Apostolus dixit, Hebr. 11. 17. ὄφειλεν [?] κατὰ πάντα τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ὁμοιωθῆναι. & Rom. viii. 3. ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας.
units.tr: In explaining the "form of a servant" he proceeds in the same way as above, where he discussed the "form of God." He says that this term signifies an accident, not a substance. But that is not really the point at issue: the question is whether it may not also connote the essence. Certainly the servile condition of Christ is here denoted, but this presupposes and includes the human nature, since it inheres in that alone. For we are not here philosophizing about the servile form in the abstract, nor seeking its definition from Aristotle, but speaking of a man who became both man and servant, not by any change of his divine nature but by a mere variation of his external state. Although this is accidental, it necessarily requires the assumption and conjunction of a substance, and this is not denied by Scripture, nor (I suppose) by the Adversaries. So there is no need to say much more about it. The Apostle exhorts the Philippians to humility by the example of Christ, not to the same kind of humility (for who would be so mad as to think this, or to demand it in an argument from example?), but to a similar humility, one that suits them. Just as Christ displayed his admirable humility in this, that the glorious God was willing to descend to the weak condition of human frailty, so the Philippians too should not be ashamed to follow Christ's humility in everything and to show themselves humble and lowly, not so as to join diverse natures to themselves by the hypostatic union. The Adversary applies the same gloss to the following verses, where the Apostle says that Christ was made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man. He takes this of the likeness of man alone, not of the nature; we take it of both. He indeed proves that these words signify an accidental condition of Christ as man, but he does not show that the nature cannot or should not be connoted as well. Since the words "in the likeness of men" [ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων] and "as a man" [ὡς ἄνθρωπος], especially in a discourse about Christ, can scarcely be understood without co-signifying the human nature. No less so is what the Apostle said in Heb. 2:17, that he ought in all things to be made like unto his brethren [ὤφειλεν κατὰ πάντα τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ὁμοιωθῆναι], and Rom. 8:3, in the likeness of sinful flesh [ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας].

units.la: Quod in responsione ad objectiunculam, quam sibi format, ait, Christum satis alibi in Scriptura dici hominem, docere eum debuerat, istum sensum a verbis Pauli præsentibus proinde non ita arcendum vel rejiciendum fuisse, quem non solum ferant, sed quoque exigant: & de voce hominis quod subjungit, significare eam aliquando accidens, vid. mortalitatem & infirmitatem, in nullo quidem exemplo satis comprobavit, non certe iis, quæ adduxit, sive e sacris, sive profanis: ubique enim notat naturam cum infirmitate, non hanc solam, absque ea, aut merum accidens. Ubique designat non mortalem vel infirmum praecise, sed hominem mortalem & corruptibilem, ejus vid. naturae pariter & conditionis. Caetera de Christi humiliatione{*}, morte & cruce sunt ἐξαγώνια[?].
units.tr: In reply to a small objection which he frames for himself, he says that Christ is elsewhere in Scripture sufficiently called man. He ought to have taught that this sense, which not only the words of Paul here allow but even require, should not therefore be excluded or rejected. And concerning the word "man," which he adds, that it sometimes signifies an accident, namely mortality and infirmity, he has by no means proved this sufficiently from any example, certainly not from those he has adduced, whether from sacred or profane writers. For everywhere it denotes the nature together with infirmity, not infirmity alone, apart from the nature, or a mere accident. Everywhere it designates not what is precisely mortal or infirm, but a man who is mortal and corruptible, that is, of that nature and condition alike. The rest about the humiliation, death and cross of Christ are [ἐξαγώνια] beside the point.

units.la: In tertio autem vitae Christi statu, qui exaltationis est, explicando, praecipua in praecognitis, quae facit, castiganda veniunt. Primum personale est, quod Calvino blasphemiam immerito impingit. Nam id revera blasphemum, dicere Christum pro se potius, quam nobis passum, ut sibi mereretur, non nobis, & potius gloriam acquireret, quam satisfaceret pro nobis & mereretur justitiam ac salutem. Christus per passionem & mortem quidem adeptus est supremam gloriam mediatoris, & in humana natura, non autem divina, non, quod in secundo dicit praecognito, totam suam dignitatem. Sed & hic committit elenchum divisionis, ea in Christo divellens, quae omnino sunt conjungenda. Non enim λόγῳ simpliciter, sed λόγῳ χριστῷ[?] Messias est; non Deus, non homo, sed Deus-homo Christus est. Qua ratione negamus in argumentatione Adversarii, Minorem: λόγῳ nihil unquam quidquam a quoquam accipit, nunquam passus, nunquam mortuus est: Imo vero accipit, non praecise & formaliter in se, sed persona ἀνθρώπος[?]. In tertio sive argumento, sive praecognito, negamus in textu dici, Christum, propter rejectionem, depositionem, & abdicationem formae Dei, fuisse exaltatum: Nam nec sensu Adversariorum verum est, quod Christus plane formam Dei rejecerit, vel ea se prorsus evacuarit. Sic in sui humiliatione Christus naturam non abdicavit, sed gloriam inhibuit, & velo humanae ac servilis conditionis quasi obduxit. Quarto Christus excellentior factus postea, quam ante erat, non quam ante erat in forma Dei, sed a forma Dei humiliatus in servili forma, atque obedientia mortis. Denique nec id probabit Adversarius, Christum ante mortem designatum fuisse tantum Regem Judaeorum, & non etiam gentium. Nam & in Vet. Test. designatus Rex Messias fuit idemque agnitus semper in Nov. Test. totius populi Dei, Judaeos inter ac Gentiles.
units.tr: In explaining the third state of Christ's life, which is that of exaltation, the chief points to be censured are those which he makes in his preliminary remarks. The first is personal, which he unjustly charges against Calvin as blasphemy. For it is truly blasphemous to say that Christ suffered for himself rather than for us, so that he might merit for himself, not for us, and might rather acquire glory than make satisfaction for us and merit righteousness and salvation. Christ indeed obtained by his passion and death the supreme glory of the Mediator, and in the human nature, not the divine, and not, as he says in the second preliminary point, "his whole dignity." But here too he commits the fallacy of division, separating in Christ what must altogether be joined. For the Messiah is not simply the Word, but the Word-Christ [λόγῳ χριστῷ]: Christ is not God, nor man, but God-man. On this ground we deny the minor premise of the Adversary's argument, that the Word never receives anything from anyone, never suffers, never dies. Indeed he receives it, not precisely and formally in himself, but in the person of the man. As to the third point, whether as argument or as preliminary remark, we deny that the text says that Christ was exalted on account of the rejection, laying aside, and renunciation of the form of God. For, even in the Adversaries' sense, it is not true that Christ plainly rejected the form of God or utterly emptied himself of it. Thus in his humiliation Christ did not abdicate his nature, but restrained his glory and as it were drew over it a veil of the human and servile condition. Fourthly, Christ became more excellent afterwards than he was before, not than he was before in the form of God, but humbled from the form of God into the servile form and the obedience of death. Finally, the Adversary will not prove that Christ before his death was designated only King of the Jews and not also of the Gentiles. For in the Old Testament the Messiah the King was also designated, and the same was always acknowledged in the New Testament as the King of the whole people of God, among Jews and Gentiles alike.

units.la: Agnoscunt Adversarii, per genuflexionem quae hic omnibus imperatur in nomine Iesu, intelligi debere, cultum, venerationem atque observantiam religiosam, sive verba ista, ut in nomine Iesu flectatur omne genu, ex Isaia petita sint, sive non; ex honore illo cultuque argumentamur, pro vera Christi Deitate, quandoquidem cultus ille nulli nisi vero Deo tribui debet. Quod vero de dignitate Christi Adversarius habet, quam a Deo Patre acceperit, ambiguum est, nam non accepit Christus demum post humiliationem, & mortem suam, dignitatem adorationis; sed quidem dignitatem exaltationis. Illam enim & ante habuit, & ratione divinae naturae ei debetur, non ex dono aliquo succedaneo. At ex gloria & nomine seu potestate superexcellenti voluit Pater eum agnosci, cui per se, & jure naturae divinae, cultus atque adoratio competit. Est enim religiosa adoratio soli Deo, atque propter Deitatem, conveniens. Ad argumentum autem, illi Christo flectetur omne genu, &c. respondemus ad Minorem: aeternus Deus nec exaltatus est, nec resuscitatus, nec obedivit Deo; non qua Deus, sed quidem ἀνθρώπῳ[?] Christus: persona ista exaltata, resuscitata, & obedivit Deo, in natura altera humana, quae persona quoque Deus. Ergo concedimus, aeternum Deum in se non fuisse exaltatum, &c. non quod non fuerit exaltatus is qui etiam æternus Deus, non secundum hanc quidem rationem & naturam, sed alteram humanam. Interim personæ tribuuntur actiones, passiones, & accidentia sive gloriæ, sive miseriæ, singula ad suum accommodata principium. Deinde non argumentamur ex eo, quod ante Christi tribunal omne flectetur genu, extremi judicii tempore, Christum habere eandem cum Patre naturam divinam: sed quia ista genuflexio, quæ religiosam notat venerationem ac cultum, Deum significat, cui ea exhibeatur, hinc eandem Christi cum Patre naturam colligimus, non simpliciter ex judicio, quod sit administraturus. Quare instantiæ, quas adfert, Cancellarii, vel Apostolorum, quasi supremi judicii, & Christi assessorum, nihil ad rem faciunt.
units.tr: The Adversaries acknowledge that the bowing of the knee which is here enjoined on all at the name of Jesus must be understood as worship, veneration and religious observance. Whether or not the words "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" are taken from Isaiah, we argue from that honour and worship for the true Deity of Christ, since that worship ought to be paid to no one but the true God. As to what the Adversary holds about the dignity Christ received from God the Father, it is ambiguous. For Christ did not receive the dignity of adoration only after his humiliation and death, but indeed the dignity of exaltation. For he had that even before, and it is due to him by reason of the divine nature, not by some substitute gift. But the Father willed that he be acknowledged by a surpassing glory and name or power, to whom worship and adoration belong by himself and by the right of the divine nature. For religious adoration is fitting for God alone, and on account of his Deity. As to the argument, "to him every knee shall bow," etc., we reply to the minor premise: the eternal God was neither exalted, nor raised up, nor obedient to God, not as God, but Christ as man. That person, who is also God, was exalted, raised up, and obedient to God in the other, human, nature. Therefore we concede that the eternal God in himself was not exalted, etc. not because he who is also eternal God was not exalted, though not according to this reason and nature but according to the other, human nature. Meanwhile, actions, sufferings and accidents, whether of glory or of misery, are attributed to the person, each according to the principle to which it is suited. Further, we do not argue from the fact that every knee shall bow before the judgment seat of Christ at the time of the last judgment that Christ has the same divine nature as the Father; but because this bowing, which denotes religious veneration and worship, signifies the God to whom it is rendered, we infer from it the same nature of Christ with the Father, not simply from the judgment which he is to administer. Hence the instances he brings forward, of chancellors, or of the Apostles as assessors of the supreme judgment and of Christ, have nothing to do with the matter.

units.la: Ad extremum in ultimis verbis, & omnis lingua confiteatur, &c. duo notat, primum, quod Christus non vocatur Deus, sed Dominus; alterum, quod Christi finis est, gloria Dei Patris: unde colligit, Deum Patrem etiam ipso Christo præstantiorem esse atque digniorem. Quod quando concedimus, nihil plane nobis adversatur. Sic & alibi dicitur, Christum esse Dei. 1. Cor. iii. ult. Nam Christi, ut Christus est, Dominus est Pater, qui Filium suum Christum fecit & constituit, Act. ii. 36. Hebr. iii. 2. sed hoc non pugnat, quominus Christus, ut est Dei Filius, sit quoque ejusdem cum Patre naturæ, atque verus Deus, nec hac ratione Patre minor aut inferior, sed cum eo ἐν[?]. Aliud est Christus, aliud in Christo ea natura, cui in tempore accessit, esse Christum. Hujus finis est, ut rerum aliarum omnium, gloria Dei, & non illius naturæ in Christo divinæ. Denique quod Christus hic non Deus appellatur, sed Dominus, nihil habet momenti ad evincendum, eum non esse Deum, quam nemo negare audit sæpius Deum in Sacris nominari. Quid tum refert, si hic forte non Deus vocetur, sed Dominus, nimirum ubi de ejus potestate agitur & imperio? At hoc habet non à seipso, sed ab alio. Dominatum œconomicum, mediatorium, ut est Christus, habet a Patre; sed hoc nihil derogat vel alteri naturæ, vel dominatui, quem secundum eam habet cum Patre eundem, non vero in tempore accepit. Illi ergo sit laus & gloria in sæcula sæculorum. Amen. Atque ita respondimus Enjedino, ad celebrem istum locum Phil. ii. 6. excipienti, & in eo reliquis, sive quæ Socinus habet, contra Vujekum, Cap. v. classe iii. arg. ix. sive Volkelius, lib. v. cap. x. sive alii: omnium enim omnia eodem redeunt.
units.tr: Finally, in the last words, and every tongue shall confess, etc., he notes two things: first, that Christ is called not God but Lord; second, that the end of Christ is the glory of God the Father. From this he infers that God the Father is even more excellent and worthy than Christ himself. We grant this, and it is in no way opposed to us. So it is also said elsewhere that Christ is God's (1 Cor. 3, last verse). For as Christ, in so far as he is Christ, the Father is his Lord, who made and appointed his Son Christ (Acts 2:36; Heb. 3:2). But this does not prevent Christ, as he is the Son of God, from also being of the same nature as the Father and true God, and in this respect not less or inferior to the Father, but equal with him in (?). It is one thing to be Christ, and another for that nature, to which he was joined in time, to be in Christ. The end of the latter, like that of all other things, is the glory of God, and not that of the divine nature in Christ. Finally, that Christ is here called not God but Lord has no weight in proving that he is not God, since no one fails to hear that God is named in the Sacred Writings very often. What does it matter if here he is perhaps called not God but Lord, namely where his power and rule are under discussion? But he has this not from himself but from another. He has the economical and mediatorial dominion, as Christ, from the Father; but this detracts nothing either from the other nature or from the dominion which, according to that nature, he has equally with the Father, and which he did not receive in time. To him therefore be praise and glory for ever and ever. Amen. In this way we have answered Enjedinus, who objects to that famous passage, Phil. 2:6, and in it the rest, whether what Socinus says against Vujek (ch. 5, class 3, arg. 9), or Volkelius (book 5, ch. 10), or others: for all their arguments come back to the same thing.

units.la: Atque hæc de primo nostro argumento, ad probandam veram Christi Deitatem, ex appellatione & nominibus, dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: So much for our first argument, drawn from the appellations and names, for proving the true Deity of Christ.

units.la: Sec. pro Christi Deitate vera & essentiali argumentum petitur ex attributis & proprietatibus divinis, quæ ipsi competunt, ut sunt æternitas, omniscientia, omnipræsentia, omnipotentia, & similia. Unde sic argumentamur: Qui est revera æternus, omniscius, omnipræsens, omnipotens, is est Deus: nam illa Deo propria sunt attributa, neque ulli, præter eum, communia vel communicabilia. Sed Christus est revera æternus, omniscius, omnipræsens, omnipotens: ergo. Ad probandam ejus primo æternitatem, sic progredimur. 1. Fuit ante suam ex Maria nativitatem. 11. Ante generis sui humani progenitorem, qui in βίβλῳ γενέσεως primum occupat ordinem, Abrahamum. 111. Ante mundum conditum. 1v. Et cum Deo æternus. De quo, quæso te, homine ista dici posse, vel dicta autumes? Ecquis talis, nisi qui sit Deus verus?
units.tr: Second, the argument for the true and essential Deity of Christ is drawn from the divine attributes and properties which belong to him, such as eternity, omniscience, omnipresence, omnipotence, and the like. We argue thus: whoever is truly eternal, omniscient, omnipresent and omnipotent, is God; for these are attributes proper to God, and common to no one else, nor communicable to anyone else. But Christ is truly eternal, omniscient, omnipresent and omnipotent; therefore he is God. To prove first his eternity, we proceed as follows. (1) He existed before his birth from Mary. (2) He existed before the progenitor of the human race, who holds the first place in the book of Genesis [βίβλῳ γενέσεως], namely Abraham. (3) He existed before the world was made. (4) He is eternal with God. Of whom, I ask you, can such things be said, or do you suppose they have been said? Who is such a one, except he who is true God?

units.la: Primo fuit ante suam ex matre nativitatem, nam ante se fuisse Iohannes Baptista his testatus verbis fuit, Joann. 1. 15. qui post me venit, ἐμπροσθέν μου γέ-γονεν. ὅτι πρῶτός μου ἦν[?]. Dicit absolute de Christo, tam hoc, quam istud, & simpliciter debent intelligi, non secundum aliquam restrictionem. Versio Arabi-ca, ipse erat ante me, quia antiquior me est. Persica, eo quod me antiquior est. Syriaca, fuit ante me, quoniam prior me est. Æthiopica, qui erat ante me, quia anteivit me. Castellio: ante me fuit, quippe prior me. Racoviensis versio: Der nach mich kommt ist mir zuvor kommen : denn er war fürtzefflicher / als ich. At in margine apponunt: Ꝯ[?]. für mir her wozden. Et ad fürtreffliher / Ꝯ[?]. erster. & versu iterum 27. ipse est qui post venit, & ante me fuit. ideoque & ἰσχυρότερος[?] Iohanne : quemadmodum dicitur apud Matthæum, cap. III. 11. Marc. 1. 7. Luc. III. 16.
units.tr: First, he existed before his birth from his mother. For John the Baptist bore witness that he existed before him, in these words, John 1:15, he who comes after me, [ἐμπροσθέν μου γέγονεν, ὅτι πρῶτός μου ἦν], has become before me, for he was before me. He says this absolutely of Christ, and both this and that clause must be understood simply, without any restriction. The Arabic version: he was before me, because he is older than I. The Persian: because he is older than I. The Syriac: he was before me, since he is prior to me. The Ethiopic: he who was before me, because he went before me. Castellio: he was before me, indeed as prior to me. The Racovian version in German: "He who comes after me has come before me: for he was more excellent than I." But in the margin they add: "has become before me," and for "more excellent" they give "first." And in verse 27 again: he it is who comes after, and was before me. Hence also he is said to be stronger [ἰσχυρότερος] than John, as it is said in Matthew 3:11, Mark 1:7, Luke 3:16.

units.la: Atque ante Abrahamum se fuisse Christus palam dixit, Ioann. viii. 58. Dixit iis Iesus, amen amen dico vobis, antequam Abraham existeret, ego sum. πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι, ἐγὼ εἰμί. Non est locus alius, in quo mire pervertendo majorem audaciam Adversarii adferunt atque improbitatem. Antequam Abraham esset, ego sum, id est, dicunt, antequam Abraham fieret pater multarum gentium & populorum, id scilicet quod nomen ejus designat, per prædicationem Euangelii Apostolicam demum ad Dei fidem cultumque vocandorum. Et certe ante istud tempus Christus extitit. Inque ea expositione, ceu valde ingeniosâ, supra modum gloriatur Socinus, in Responso primo, contra Andr. Volanum, pag. 32. Aliam esse ejus loci sententiam, quam plerique omnes existimare videntur, aliterque ac hactenus factum est, verba Græca interpretanda esse, quam brevissime fieri poterit demonstrabimus. Ita Socinus ibi, & in Responsione altera, pag. 177. ubi pag. 179. indicat, non à se tamen primo inventam expositionem illam esse, quæ de ipsa voce dicebam, sententiam atque interpretationem meam juvare posset, quæ tamen mea revera non est. Sed, qui primus nostra ætate de Christi essentia, atque persona exactissimam (ni fallor) veritatem in lucem protulit, idem hanc illius loci explicationem primus repetit: & porro, dum viveret, non paucis piis hominibus prorsus probavit. Is autem ejusmodi vir fuit, cui Volanus inter suos omnes vel sanctarum literarum cognitione, vel vitæ innocentia vix parem inveniet. Existimo, quod patruum suum Lælium Socinum intelligat, saltem ex alio quam sui furfuris authore expositionem illam probare non sustinebit, non ex Patribus, aliisque probæ notæ Theologis. Atque in illam me sententiam ducunt, quæ de eadem illa expositione Socinus habet in Disputatione cum Erasmo Iohannis, pag. 67. ubi thrasonice admodum in expositione illa, ejusque authore gloriatur, sic dicens: Cum primum fatendi verbum, in tuis verbis animadverti, sperabam, te potius fassurum nullam in vita tua Scripturæ interpretationem te audivisse, quæ hac sit aut acutior aut verior, quæve magis divinum quid sapiat, & à Deo ipso patefactum fuisse præ se ferat. Ego quidem certe non leves conjecturas habeo, illum, qui primus ætate nostra eam in lucem protulit, (hic autem is fuit, qui primus quoque sententiam de Christi origine, quam ego constanter defendo, hæc ætate renovavit) precibus multis ab ipso Christo illam impetrasse. Hoc profecto affirmare ausim, cum Deus illi viro permulta aliis prorsus tunc temporis incognita patefecerit, vix quidquam inter illa omnia esse quod interpretatione hac divinius videri queat. Eandem explicationem multis locis Socinus repetit atque inculcat: post eum reliqui. Ille, ad Articulos Posnanienses, pag. 35. Contra Vujekum, de divinitate Filii, pag. 17. & 399. Lib. contra Eutropium, pag. 258. Epist. III. ad Dudithium, pag. 52. Catechesis Racoviensis, pag. 61. Etiam Sommerus, contra Carolium, Lib. II. pag. 69. Oftorodus, Inftitut. cap. VIII. pag. 57. ac contra Tradelum part. II. cap. VI. pag. 122. Smalcius de Dei Filio, cap. XIII. pag. 121. & contra Ravenspergium. denique contra Frantzium, pag. 27. 82. Volkelius, pag. 485. Enjedinus, in Explicat. hujus loci, pag. 223. Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum de Trinitate pag. 462. in Explicatione quatuor Scripturae locorum, Deitatem Christi concernentium, scripta Polonice primum, atque in Belgicum translata, editaque Ann. MDCXLIX. Unde locum ita vertunt Germanice, in Editione Racoviensi: Amen/Amen ich sage euch ehe denn Abraham wirb [?] / ich bin.
units.tr: And Christ plainly said that he existed before Abraham, John 8:58: Jesus said to them, Verily, verily I say to you, before Abraham was, I am [πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι, ἐγὼ εἰμί]. There is no other place where the adversaries bring greater boldness and wickedness by a strange perversion. Before Abraham was, I am, they say, that is, before Abraham became the father of many nations and peoples, which is what his name signifies, through the apostolic preaching of the Gospel, to be called to the faith and worship of God at last. And certainly Christ existed before that time. And Socinus boasts beyond measure in this explanation, as if it were very ingenious, in his First Reply against Andreas Volanus, p. 32: that the meaning of that passage is other than most men seem to think, and that the Greek words must be interpreted otherwise than has been done hitherto; this we shall demonstrate as briefly as possible. So Socinus there, and in his second Reply, p. 177, where at p. 179 he points out that yet this explanation was not first discovered by himself; it is what I said about the word itself, which could help my interpretation and opinion, though it is not really mine. But he who first in our age brought to light the most exact (unless I am mistaken) truth about the essence and person of Christ, the same first repeated this explanation of that passage; and moreover, while he lived, he fully approved it to not a few pious men. He was such a man that Volanus will scarcely find his equal among all his own people, either in knowledge of the Holy Scriptures or in innocence of life. I suppose he means his uncle Lelius Socinus; at least he will not be able to prove that interpretation from the Fathers or other theologians of sound repute, rather than from its own author, who is of a different sort of chaff. And these things lead me to that opinion which Socinus holds about the same explanation in his disputation with Erasmus Johannis, p. 67, where he boasts very boastfully of that explanation and of its author, saying: When I first noticed the word of acknowledgment in your words, I hoped that you would rather confess that in your life you had heard of no interpretation of Scripture sharper or truer than this, or one that savours more of the divine and shows itself revealed by God himself. I certainly have no slight conjecture that he who first in our age brought that explanation to light (and he was also the one who first revived in our age the opinion about the origin of Christ, which I constantly defend) obtained it from Christ himself by many prayers. I would venture to affirm this: since God at that time revealed to that man many things entirely unknown to others, there is scarcely anything among all of them that can seem more divine than this interpretation. Socinus repeats and inculcates this same explanation in many places: after him the rest do likewise. He does so in his Against the Posnanian Articles, p. 35; against Vujek, On the Divinity of the Son, pp. 17 and 399; in the book against Eutropius, p. 258; in Letter III to Dudith, p. 52; in the Racovian Catechism, p. 61. Also Sommer, against Carolus, book 2, p. 69; Ostorodt, Institutes, ch. 8, p. 57, and against Tradel, part 2, ch. 6, p. 122; Smalcius, On the Son of God, ch. 13, p. 121, and against Ravenspergius; finally, against Frantz, pp. 27 and 82. Volkelius, p. 485; Enjedinus, in his explanation of this passage, p. 223; Schlichting, against Meisner On the Trinity, p. 462, in the Explanation of Four Passages of Scripture concerning the Deity of Christ, written first in Polish, and translated into Dutch, published in 1649. Hence they render the passage thus in German, in the Racovian edition: "Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."

units.la: Resp. 1. Attendenda ante omnia sermonis Christi occasio. In disputatione cum Judaeis, injecta haud semel mentio fuerat Abrahami. Primum verf. 33. responderunt ei, semen Abrahae sumus, & nulli unquam servivimus: quomodo tu dicis, liberi fietis? Ad quae Christus regerit, illos non esse dignos Abrahamo filios, adeo ei dissimiles operibus; verum similiores esse patri Diabolo, &c. Ad aliud, quod dixerat Salvator, quod, qui verba ejus servaret, non visurus esset mortem, iterum Abrahamum objiciunt, qui fuisset mortuus, quo non videretur major propheta Christus, verf. 53. ad quae is, inter alia, verf. 56. Abraham Pater vester gavisus fuit videre diem meum, & vidit, & laetatus fuit. Hinc jam Judaei: nondum habes quinquaginta annos, & vidisti Abrahamum? Dixit iis Jesus: amen amen dico vobis, antequam Abraham esset, ego sum. Sunt verba prolata α. in disputatione. β. In responsione ad motam objectionem. γ. De Christi aetate. Ad haec ergo illa exponenda, ut cum veritate, & sensu bono conciliari queant.
units.tr: Answer 1. Before all else, the occasion of Christ's words must be considered. In the disputation with the Jews, mention of Abraham had been made more than once. First at verse 33: they answered him, We are Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free? To this Christ replied that they were not worthy to be Abraham's sons, being so unlike him in their works, but were rather more like their father the devil, etc. Next, to another saying of the Saviour, that whoever kept his word would not see death, they again object Abraham, who had died, so that Christ would not seem greater than the prophets (verse 53). To this he answers, among other things, at verse 56: Abraham your father rejoiced to see my day, and he saw it, and was glad. Hence the Jews: Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast thou seen Abraham? Jesus said to them: Verily, verily I say unto you, before Abraham was, I am. These are words uttered α. in the disputation, β. in reply to the objection raised, γ. concerning Christ's age. These must therefore be explained so that they can be reconciled with the truth and with a good sense.

units.la: II. Expositio nostra est plana, dilucida: imo ante Abrahamum ego fui, extiti, ante illum natum notumque. Ut Adversarios provocare nobis liceat, atque interrogare, num alia qua ratione, vel oratione aut verbis potuisset clarius certiusque proponi sententia nostra, quam illis factum verbis fuit? Contra Adversariorum explicatio est non obscura, sed violenta, contorta, nulli hactenus visa nisi huic hominum generi, eaque nulla alia magis potest dari inversa, insolens, & tota sui specie horrenda.
units.tr: II. Our explanation is plain and clear: indeed, before Abraham I was, I existed, I was known before he was born. We may therefore challenge our opponents and ask whether, by any other means, or in any other language or words, our view could have been set forth more clearly and certainly than it was by these words. The opponents' explanation is not obscure but forced and twisted, seen hitherto by no one except this class of men, and no other explanation could be more inverted, unusual, and in its whole character more horrible.

units.la: III. Nam primo, ex subjecto faciunt praedicatum, unde totam verborum rerumque feriem transformant. Antequam fieret Abraham, vel antequam nasceretur Abraham, subjectum est, Abraham; praedicatum, [illegible, ~6 letters]. Illi hinc praedicatum faciunt, [illegible, ~6 letters].
units.tr: III. For first, they make the predicate out of the subject, and so transform the whole sequence of words and things. "Before Abraham was made" or "before Abraham was born" is the subject, Abraham; the predicate is [illegible]. They make the predicate [illegible].

units.la: IV. Atque subjectum tollunt, & nullum faciunt in oratione reliquum.
units.tr: IV. And they remove the subject and leave nothing remaining in the sentence.

units.la: Non minus contra stylum & sensum orationis, ac illud. V. Coguntur ex ingenio suo intrudere pro fecunda vice nomen Abraham, pro subjecto, quod primo fuftu-lerant, antequam Abraham fieret Abraham. Qui agendi & explicandi modus fi semel concedatur, jam tantum non quidlibet ex quolibet faciendi dabitur potestas.
units.tr: No less contrary to the style and sense of the sentence is the fifth point: they are forced by their own invention to introduce, for a second time, the name Abraham as the subject, in place of the subject they had first removed, namely "before Abraham became Abraham." If this method of construing and explaining is once conceded, there will soon be almost unlimited licence to make anything out of anything.

units.la: VI. Contrà, siquidem hoc voluisset Scriptura, pro more suo non repetiisset, vel repetere voluisset nomen, sed ejus reddidisset explicationem, praesertim quum in eà totius orationis pendeat vis atque efficacia. Quemadmodum Hebr. VII. 1. 2. Hic enim Melchifedeck, rex Salem, &c. primum quidem interpretatus rex justitiae, deinde & rex Salem, quod est rex pacis, Matth. 1. 23. Emmanuel, quod exponitur, Deus nobiscum.
units.tr: VI. On the contrary, if Scripture had meant this, it would not, according to its usual manner, have repeated the name, or wished to repeat it, but would have given its explanation, especially since the force and efficacy of the whole sentence depend on it. So Heb. 7:1–2: For this Melchisedec, king of Salem, … being first by interpretation king of righteousness, and after that also king of Salem, which is king of peace. Matt. 1:23: Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.

units.la: VII. Et quare non aperte & explicate Christus, haud solum interpretatus nomen Abrahami fuisset, illud fi, quod Adversarii, voluisset, sed planius pleniusque exponeret rem ipsam vocationis gentium, non modo Judaeis, sed ipsis quoque suis disci-pulis procul dubio, ut ex aliis similibus colligere licet, haud adeo perspectam, saltem non ita tecte & involute hoc proponere debuisset, quod ex isto certe sermone nullus unquam divinare potuisset. viii. Negatur, Abrahamum demum factum fuisse patrem multarum gentium, id est, vere juxta promissionem sibi factam fundatamque in nomine, aut nominis mutatione, Abrahamum cum vocatione gentium per Apostolos, sed jam olim etiam, quando & quousque seu homines quicumque, exemplum, fidemque ejus imitati, in Christum crediderunt. Gen. xvii. 6, 7. Ut tamen, si vel accipiamus nomen Abrahami eo hic sensu, quo Socinus vult, Christus ante Abrahamum dici non potuerit fuisse, nisi ante eum natum, saltem credentem, & fideles post patrem filios, populosque, extiterit. Nam quamvis plurium, a vocatione gentium per Apostolos, factus sit fidelium populorum spiritualis pater, tamen & Abraham fuit olim, pater omnium credentium, inquit Apostolus, Rom. iv. 11. & in praeputio, & in circumcisione credentium, verf. 12. & patrem circumcisionis, non in solum qui ex circumcisione, sed insistentibus vestigiis fidei patris nostri Abrahami in praeputio. 16. Abraham, qui est pater nostrum omnium. ix. Imo quod horrendum est, perfectum Sophistam egit Christus hoc si egerit, quod Sociniani volunt. Objiciunt Judæi, quod inaniter se Christus fecisset Abrahamo ætate anteriorem, & diem suum diebus illius.
units.tr: VII. And why did Christ not plainly and explicitly interpret, not merely the name of Abraham, if he had meant what the opponents say, but expound more clearly and fully the very matter of the calling of the Gentiles? Without doubt this was not well understood even by the Jews, and even by his own disciples, as may be gathered from other similar passages. At the very least he ought not to have set it forth so covertly and obscurely, since from that speech no one could ever have guessed it. VIII. It is denied that Abraham was made the father of many nations only then, that is, truly according to the promise made to him and founded in the name, or in the change of his name, with the calling of the Gentiles through the Apostles; rather, this happened long before, when and as often as men of any kind, imitating his example and faith, believed in Christ (Gen. 17:6–7). Yet even if we take the name of Abraham here in the sense Socinus wishes, Christ could not have been said to be before Abraham unless he had existed before him as one born, or at least as one believing, with the faithful being sons and peoples after the father. For although he was made the spiritual father of many peoples of the faithful through the calling of the Gentiles by the Apostles, nevertheless Abraham was once the father of all believers, as the Apostle says (Rom. 4:11), both of those in uncircumcision and of believers in circumcision (v. 12): and the father of circumcision, not only to those who are of the circumcision, but who walk in the steps of the faith of our father Abraham in uncircumcision. (v. 16): Abraham, who is the father of us all. IX. Indeed, and this is horrible, Christ would have acted as a perfect sophist if he had done this, as the Socinians want. The Jews object that Christ had made himself, to no purpose, older than Abraham, and his day to be of those days.

units.la: NegatChristus inaniter a se factum, & confirmat tu gravi addita asseveratione: amen amen dico vobis. tum addit quod ante natum etiam Abrahamum fuerit, πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι[?].
units.tr: Christ denies that he did so to no purpose, and confirms it with a solemn addition of asseveration: Verily, verily I say unto you. Then he adds that he was even before Abraham was born [πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι].

units.la: Juxta Socinianos Christus indigna captione fuit usus, nec respondit ad difficultatem, quomodo verum quiret esse illud, ipse quum nondum esset ætate quinquagenarius? sed ad aliud deflectit, quod nec agebatur, nec quaerebatur, nec cuiquam in mentem venire poterat eo a Christo respici. Quod contra Christi morem animumque, ita implicate, & finistre rem proponere. Ex verbis Judæorum, satis aperta mens est, sc. quomodo potuisset Christus vixisse ante Abrahamum; id quod verbis suis significarat. Quid ad hæc Christus? An negat, sua id significasse verba, quod ex iis Judæi collegerant, istumque illorum sensum esse? non. Sed confirmat, amen amen,&c. Fatetur imo, se vixisse ante Abrahamum.
units.tr: According to the Socinians, Christ made use of an unworthy evasion and did not answer the difficulty of how it could be true, since he was not yet fifty years old. Instead he turns to another matter, which was neither under discussion nor asked about, and which could not come into anyone's mind as something Christ would refer to. This is contrary to Christ's manner and mind, to propose a matter so intricately and sinisterly. From the Jews' words the meaning is quite clear, namely how Christ could have lived before Abraham, which he himself had signified by his words. What does Christ say to this? Does he deny that his words signified what the Jews gathered from them, and that this was their meaning? No. Rather he confirms it: amen, amen, etc. Indeed he confesses that he lived before Abraham.

units.la: Verum ad mentem nunc Socini examinemus verba. Christus an concedit, vel negat, Judæos verba sua bene accepisse, quod se videretur facere ætate Abrahamo anteriorem? refutat, aut reprehendit, an confirmat illa? Et certe ad hoc Christum respondere oportuit, si velimus ad scopum respondisse, in disputatione, contra Adversarios. At nihil hujus egit Christus, juxta Socinum. Dixit, se esse, antequam Abraham fieret pater multarum gentium; per Apostolos demum vocandarum. Sed non quod esset, sed quando fuisset, quæsitum fuit. Tu Abrahamum vidisti? Nec ad Judæorum objecta verba, neque ad sua quæ præcedunt, unde quæstionis arrepta ansa fuerat, convenienter responderit Christus. Neque instruxerit homines aut responso, aut alia sive doctrinâ, sive argumento, in re propositâ. Dixit se esse, sc. antequam gentes vocentur, & sic Abram factus sit Abraham. Quam futile? Num hoc Judæi quærebant? hoc ullus ignorabat? Hoc dicere, docereque Christum necesse fuit, vel decuit, ego jam sum, ante vocandas postea gentes? Annon id etiam de quovis verum erat? annon præsentes id omnes de se æque dicere poterant, ac Christus? annon inanius est, quam ut dici, nedum a Christo, & tali occasione, debeat, ego sum ante diem crastinum, ante illud quod futuro tempore contingit? an de futuro, & non de præterito tempore erat instituta disputatio, & tum Christi sermo, tum objectio Judæorum? Ohe, quam elumbis, inanis, ridicula hoc pacto redditur Christi oratio! annon risum movisset auditoribus ejusmodi responsio & indignationem? Tu videri vis prior esse Abrahamo, & grandævior dævior, atque jam tute hoc explicas ea ratione, ut & nos omnes Abrahamo æque priores dici debeamus, atque tu : quin & omnia quæ contingunt priora debent dici, antequam illa vocatio gentium instituitur, impleturque. Quare Versio Æthiopica, Amen dico vobis, antequam Abraham nasceretur, fui ego. Arabica, Amen dico vobis, quod ego sum antequam esset Abraham. Persica, quod nondum Abraham factus erat, cum ego eram. & Syriaca, antequam fieret Abraham, ego sum.
units.tr: But now let us examine the words according to Socinus' mind. Does Christ concede or deny that the Jews rightly understood his words, that he seemed to make himself older than Abraham? Does he refute or rebuke that, or confirm it? Certainly Christ ought to have answered this, if we wish to say he answered to the point in the disputation against his opponents. But according to Socinus, Christ did nothing of the kind. He said that he was before Abraham became the father of many nations, to be called only later through the Apostles. But it was not asked what he was, but when he had been. Hast thou seen Abraham? Christ answered neither the Jews' objection nor his own preceding words, from which the occasion of the question had been taken. Nor did he instruct the people, either by his answer or by any doctrine or argument concerning the matter proposed. He said that he was, that is, before the Gentiles are called, and so Abram became Abraham. How trifling! Did the Jews ask this? Did anyone not know it? Was it necessary, or fitting, for Christ to say and teach this: "I am now, before the Gentiles are afterwards called"? Was this not true of anyone? Could not all those present say of themselves just as much as Christ did? Is it not more empty than should be said, let alone by Christ and on such an occasion: "I am before tomorrow, before what will happen at a future time"? Or was the disputation, both Christ's speech and the Jews' objection, concerned with the future and not with the past? Oh, how feeble, empty and ridiculous Christ's speech becomes in this way! Would such an answer not have provoked laughter and indignation in the hearers? You want to seem prior to Abraham and older, and now you explain it in such a way that we all ought to be called equally prior to Abraham as you are; indeed, all things that happen would have to be called prior, before the calling of the Gentiles is instituted and fulfilled. Hence the Ethiopic version: Verily I say to you, before Abraham was born, I was. The Arabic: Verily I say to you, that I am before Abraham was. The Persian: that before Abraham had become, I was. And the Syriac: before Abraham became Abraham, I am.

units.la: Certe Socinus in loco Ioann. viii. 58. perfectum se præbet veteratorem, ita singula intorquet & corrumpit verba. Abraham, non de persona accipit, sed promissione ei facta. γενέσθαι [?] non fieret, exponit; sed, fiat, contra & vocis vim, & præpositionem additam, πρίν [?]. Ego sum, non ei est, existo, fui; sed sum Iesus Nazarenus. Abraham exultavit, & vidit diem meum, explicat; exultasset videre diem meum, atque si vidisset, gavisus fuisset. Unde & sic vertunt: Abraham ewer [?] Vater hette gefrolocket/das er meinen tag sehen mochte: bnd so er ihn gesehen hette/so hette er sich gefreuet. Adeo nihil tutum ab illorum depravatione nec in Theologia, nec in Scriptura. Atque nisi quis affectibus ducatur partibusque, placere istorum hominum doctrina cuiquam sano, & Christiano homini non potest. Unde hæc Erasmi Johannis de Socino querela fuit & judicium, hoc loco nobis annotandum, ex ejus cum Soci-no [?] Disput. de Unigeniti Filii Dei existentia, pag. 17. multi abstrerrentur ejusmodi contortis Scripturæ interpretationibus, quas plerique vestrorum sequuntur in doctrina de Christo, usque adeo offenduntur, ut ea etiam suspecta ipsis fiant, quæ rectissime de uno vero Deo contra Trinitatem docentur. Verum ne temere id affirmare videar, aliquot argumentis demonstrare aggrediar. Atque ad illam, quam hactenus examinavimus, loci Ioann. viii. 58. explicationem eum ducit: namque eadem hic ei cum illo controversia, quæ & nobis, pag. 67. fateor me per omnem vitam meam, dixit, non magis contortam Scripturæ interpretationem audivisse; ideoque eam penitus improbo. Quod si versionem Castellionis audire placet, ad locum hunc, ea sic habet: Abrahamus ille parens vester meam diem videre gestivit, & vidit, idque lætatus est, &c. Hoc mihi certo certoque credite, priusquam Abrahamus esset, ego sum. non dixit, priusquam Abrahamus fiat.
units.tr: Certainly Socinus, on the passage John 8:58, shows himself a complete trickster, twisting and corrupting each word. He takes "Abraham" not of the person but of the promise made to him. He explains "would be made" [γενέσθαι] as "was not made", but "let it be made" runs against both the force of the verb and the added preposition, before [πρίν]. He takes "I am" not as "I exist, I was" but as "I am Jesus of Nazareth". He explains "Abraham rejoiced" and "saw my day" as: he would have rejoiced to see my day, and if he had seen it he would have been glad. Hence they also render it in German: "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; and when he had seen it he was glad." So nothing is safe from their distortion, either in theology or in Scripture. Unless a man is driven by passions and party, the teaching of these men cannot please any sound and Christian person. Hence the complaint and judgment of Erasmus Johannes against Socinus, which we should note here, from his disputation with Socinus on the existence of the only-begotten Son of God, page 17: "Many are put off by such twisted interpretations of Scripture, which most of your people follow in the doctrine of Christ, and they are so offended that even things taught most rightly about the one true God against the Trinity become suspect to them." But lest I seem to affirm this rashly, I shall undertake to demonstrate it by several arguments. Socinus is led to this explanation of the passage John 8:58, which we have examined so far; for here he has the same dispute with us, which he has on page 67: "I confess," he said, "that in my whole life I have never heard a more distorted interpretation of Scripture"; and therefore he utterly rejects it. But if you care to hear the version of Castellio on this passage, it reads thus: "That Abraham, your father, longed to see my day, and saw it, and rejoiced in it, etc. Believe me of a certainty: before Abraham was, I am." He did not say "before Abraham is made".

units.la: Aliam loci interpretationem Ministri Transylvaniæ, quamvis nec hanc veram, dederunt, lib. II. de Dei cognitione, cap. x. ubi dicunt: fuit ergo ante Abrahamum Christus in virtute, cognitione, & figuris, quemadmodum dicitur, heri & hodie Christus & in sæcula. Cap. xi. Sic se ante Abrahamum fuisse dicit ille homo Christus, Ioannis 8. (non enim alius ibi loquitur) Ab initio enim mundi, ante Abrahamum erat promissus, cognitus, & expectatus. Sed, quemadmodum non agitur hic de Abrahamo, ut Patre gentium vocandarum futuro, sed persona, eoque quando natus fuerit, quod hactenus contra Socinum defendimus; ita nec de Christo promisso, aut præfigurato, sed exhibito, vivente, & cum Iudæis loquente: nam ratio temporis quando est id, quod in controversiam hic venit de Abrahamo, & Christo, quando, vel quamdiu extiterint ambo. Deinde quærimus, ut exponant Adversarii, ubi & quibus locis ante Abrahamum Christus promissus, cognitus, & exspectatus fuerit: quum alias cognitionem de Christo in V. T. ejusque exspectationem tam exilem solent facere, & fere nullam. Præterquam quod iisdem hæc expositio premi potest & refelli absurditatibus, quibus prior illa Socini, prout utraque extra verborum scopum est, & mentem.
units.tr: The ministers of Transylvania gave another interpretation of the passage, though this too is not the true one, in book II of On the Knowledge of God, chapter 10, where they say: "Christ was therefore before Abraham in power, knowledge and figures, just as it is said: Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever." Chapter 11: "Thus that man Christ says that he was before Abraham, John 8 (for no other speaks there). For from the beginning of the world, before Abraham, he was promised, known and expected." But just as the passage is not here about Abraham as the future father of the nations to be called, but about the person, and when he was born, which we have so far defended against Socinus, so it is not about Christ as promised or prefigured, but as present, living and speaking with the Jews. For the question of time, when, is what comes into controversy here, concerning Abraham and Christ: when, or how long, each of them existed. Next we ask that the opponents explain where and in which passages Christ was promised, known and expected before Abraham; since otherwise they are accustomed to make the knowledge of Christ in the Old Testament and its expectation so slight, and almost nothing. Besides, this explanation can be pressed and refuted by the same absurdities by which that earlier explanation of Socinus is refuted, since both lie outside the scope and meaning of the words.

units.la: Addit aliam insuper expositionem Schlichtingius: nempe quod Christus ante Abrahamum fuerit, quin & ante mundum conditum, sed in præordinatione divina, non propriâ existentiâ. Resp. 1. Non dicit Christus, se fuisse praeordinatum, antequam Abraham esset, sed se esse, existere, ἐγὼ εἰμί. Socino etiam agnoscente hoc absolutè hic poni. Non negamus quidem Christum praeordinatum fuisse, quod Petrus testatur 1. cap. 1. 20. sed à Christo id dici, & loco quidem isto, vel in hoc Christi Deitatem sitam esse, quod Smalcius contendit, negamus. 11. Frigidam reddit responsionem ad Iudaeorum de Christi aetate, atque praecellentia supra Abrahamum, interrogationem, loqui de sui à Deo praeordinacione. 111. Imo non hoc solius Christi est, praeordinatum à Deo fuisse. Etiam Iudaei isti malefici in supremo suo scelere egerunt, Herodes & Pontius Pilatus, quae manus & consilium Dei praeordinarat προέγνω [?] προώρισεν [?] γενέσθαι ut fierent. Act. iv. 28. Quin omnes electos Deus προέγνω [?] προώρισεν [?] Rom. viii. 29. Quam egregia scilicet jam isthaec elabendi ratio, quando quis dicit se ante alios aetate esse, eo quod, antequam illi existerent, praeordinatus à Deo fuerit? Et non illi alii, non quoque Abraham à Deo praeordinatus fuit? Atque ita ventosa & superba Socini gloriatio de nova sua in praedictum locum expositione est discussa.
units.tr: Schlichting adds yet another explanation: namely that Christ was before Abraham, indeed before the world was created, but in the divine predestination, not by his own existence. Reply: (1) Christ does not say that he was predestined before Abraham was, but that he is, that he exists, "I am" [ἐγὼ εἰμί]. Even Socinus acknowledges that this is stated here absolutely. We do not deny that Christ was predestined, as Peter testifies in 1 Peter 1:20, but we deny that Christ said this, or that Christ's deity is located in this passage, as Smalcius contends. (2) He makes a cold reply to the Jews' question about Christ's age and his pre-eminence over Abraham, by speaking of his predestination by God. (3) Indeed, to have been predestined by God is not peculiar to Christ alone. Those wicked Jews also, and Herod and Pontius Pilate, in their supreme crime did what the hand and counsel of God had foreordained [προώρισεν] to be done [γενέσθαι] (Acts 4:28). Moreover God foreknew and predestined [προέγνω, προώρισεν] all the elect (Romans 8:29). What an excellent way of escaping this, then, when someone says that he is older in age than others because, before they existed, he was predestined by God! And was not Abraham also predestined by God, as well as those others? Thus the empty and proud boast of Socinus about his new explanation of the said passage is shattered.

units.la: De qua plura dicere supersedeo, cùm & egregie, praeter alios multos, eâ profligârit Josua Placeus, in Disputationibus, de Christi existentia, antequam in utero Virginis, secundum carnem conciperetur: qui videndus. Nec modo ante matrem, & generationem ex ea suam Christus fuit, ante Johannem, ante Abrahamum, sed & ante mun-dum conditum. Qua ratione aeternitatem designari, Crellius testatur, lib. de Deo, cap. xviii. pag. 124. Nunc de ratione agendum est, qua sacrae literae antegressam aeternitatis divinae partem significare consueverunt; facere autem id ferè solent comparate. Ita enim eam indicare solent, ut Deum ante mundum conditum extitisse dicant, aut aperte significent. Atqui de Christo dictum Ioan. 1. 1. 2. 3. In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Col. 1. 15. Hebr. 1. 2. Imo & tum jam se habuisse gloriam suam dixit, Ioann. xvii. 5. Et nunc glorifica me tu Pater apud te eâ gloriâ, quam habui, antequam hic mundus fieret, apud te. Ioann. vi. 62. Si ergo videritis filium hominis adscendentem, ubi erat prius? Hinc venisse in mundum dicitur, & exivisse à Patre. Iohann. xvi. 28. Exivi à Patre, & veni in mundum. Iterum relinquo mundum, & vado ad Patrem. Ioann. iii. 16. Et nemo adscendit in coelum, nisi qui ex coelo descendit, filius hominis qui est in coelo. Eph. iv. 9. 10. Quod adscendit, quid est, nisi quod descendit primum ad inferiores partes terrae? qui descendit, idem est qui etiam adscendit. Gal. iv. 4. Misit Deus filium suum, factum ex muliere. 1. Ioann. iv. 2. Omnis spiritus qui confitetur Iesum Christum in carnem venisse. 1. Tim. iii. 16. Deus manifestatus in carne. Hebr. ii. 14. & xiii. 8. Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem, & in saecula. Adeo fuit ante suam nativitatem, & apud Patrem, in coelo, unde missus in terram, & homo factus fuit. Denique aeternitatem suam Christus confirmat, quando ait, Apoc. 1. 11. Ego sum α & ω, primus ille & ultimus. cap xxii. 13. Ego sum α & ω, principium & finis, primus & ultimus. Quem locum ab exceptionibus Socinianorum vindicatum vide à Becmanno, Exercit. Theol. v. Slichtingius, contra Meisnerum, de Trinitate, pag. 473. primum negat, verba illa de Christo cap. 1.8. intelligenda; sed de Patre. Deinde, non significari, cap. xxii. Christum esse omnium simpliciter rerum principium & finem, duntaxat certarum.
units.tr: I shall refrain from saying more about this, since Josua Placaeus has also refuted it admirably, among many others, in his Disputations on the existence of Christ before he was conceived according to the flesh in the womb of the Virgin; he should be consulted. Christ existed not only before his mother and his generation from her, before John, before Abraham, but also before the world was created. Crellius testifies that eternity is designated in this way, in his book On God, chapter 18, page 124: "Now we must deal with the manner in which the sacred writings have been accustomed to signify the earlier part of divine eternity; and they generally do this comparatively. For they are accustomed to indicate it so that they either say or plainly signify that God existed before the world was created." Yet of Christ it is said in John 1:1-3: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him." Also Colossians 1:15 and Hebrews 1:2. Indeed he also said that he already had his glory then, John 17:5: "And now glorify me, Father, with you, with the glory which I had with you before the world was." John 6:62: "If then you see the Son of man ascending, where was he before?" Hence he is said to have "come into the world" and to have "gone out from the Father", John 16:28: "I went out from the Father and came into the world. Again I leave the world and go to the Father." John 3:13: "And no one has ascended into heaven, except him who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven."
