Ephesians 4:9-10: "That he ascended, what is it but that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who also ascended." Galatians 4:4: "God sent his Son, made of a woman." 1 John 4:2: "Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ to have come in the flesh." 1 Timothy 3:16: "God manifested in the flesh." Hebrews 2:14 and 13:8: "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and for ever." So he was before his birth, and with the Father, in heaven, whence he was sent into the earth and was made man. Finally Christ affirms his eternity when he says, Revelation 1:11: "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last." Chapter 22:13: "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last." For the defence of this passage against the Socinian objections, see Becmann, Theological Exercises, and Schlichting against Meisner, On the Trinity, page 473. Schlichting first denies that those words of Christ in chapter 1:8 are to be understood of Christ, but of the Father. Then he says that in chapter 22 it does not signify that Christ is the beginning and end of all things simply, but only of certain things.

units.la: Quarum ergo rerum, inquis, Christus dici- Resp. 1. Ergo alteri debentur eadem tur α & ω, principium & finis? Nostræ salutis, inquam; quemadmodum & res ipsa, & loci circumstantiæ, in quibus de salute ac mercede piorum agitur, demonstrant. Unde & alibi Christus dicitur esse dux & consummator salutis nostræ, quæ verba istorum, de quibus agimus, explicatio sunt. verba, cap. 1. alteri vero, cap. xxii. Existi-mat, quia cap. 1. 8. post illa, Ego sum α & ω, principium & finis, statim additur, dicit Dominus, qui est, qui erat, & qui veniens est, (id est, qui semper futurus est) ille omnipotens, ad Christum verba illa referenda non esse. Frustra, nam & per tres proxime antecedentes versus de solo Christo verba facta, & nihil in textu de Christo dicitur, quod non aliunde etiam confirmari possit, de Christo esse verum. Quin ex hoc ipso capite:
units.tr: Of which things, you ask, is Christ called the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end? Answer 1: Of our salvation, I say, as both the thing itself and the circumstances of the passage, in which the salvation and reward of the godly are discussed, show. Hence Christ is also elsewhere called the leader and perfecter of our salvation, and the words of those (texts) with which we are dealing are an explanation of this. The words in chapter 1 belong to God, those in chapter 22 to Christ. They think that, because in chapter 1 verse 8, after I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, it is immediately added, says the Lord, who is, who was, and who is to come (that is, who will always be), the Almighty, those words are not to be referred to Christ. This is in vain, for the three verses immediately preceding speak of Christ alone, and nothing is said in the text about Christ that cannot also be confirmed from elsewhere to be true of Christ. Indeed, from this very chapter:

units.la: ubi enim ad vocem istam, Ego sum α & ω, primus ille & ultimus, respexerat Iohannes, ut videret cujusmodi vox illa esset, vidit similem filio hominis, verf. 13. Hujus ergo illa vox, qui & post alia, iterum hoc repetit verf. 13. 18. Ne metue. Ego sum primus ille & ultimus: & vivens ille, & fui mortuus, & ecce vivo in sæcula sæculorum, & habeo claves inferni & mortis. Quæ à Christo dicta nemo potest dubitare, uti eadem cap. II. 8. & tantundem continent, ac verf. 8. dictum fuerat. Ut hinc de victoria causæ nostræ judicium ferre omnes possint, dicente contra Wiekum Socino, cap. III. classe I. arg. X. certe si ibi de Christo sermo esset, jam vicissent Adversarii. II. Certe est illud epitheton veri Dei, Iesa. xliv. 6. Ego sum primus & ultimus, neque præter me est Deus alius. tum cap. xlviii. 12. Sed & inde nos argumentamur, pro vera Christi Deitate, quod idem ei attribuitur. Adde Exod. iii. 14. Tertio, salutis certe, & rerum denique omnium Christus simpliciter est α & ω, quandoquidem id simpliciter & absolute de Christo asseritur, de eo æquè ac de Patre, & non tantum vel salutis nostræ vel officii sui ratione. Quemadmodum Enjedinus, in Apoc. I. 17. dicit se Iesus primum & novissimum, non respectu substantiæ & existentiæ, sed ratione officii. IV. Quod si absolute primum & ultimum dicere Spiritus S. velit Christum esse, pari cum Patre ratione, quo id quæso modo aptius clariusque faceret, quam nunc fecit? ut apertæ luci, & communi verborum sensui repugnare videantur Adversarii, in gratiam suarum hypothesium, nos vero, ut oportet, illa sequi. V. Neque salutis ratione, sensu Adversariorum, Christus poterit dici principium & finis, α & ω, sed Deus. Non certe seipsum ita homo ullus vocabit, qualem se hic eodem titulo, cum Deo, designat Christus, nisi magna temeritate & valde indecenter, quod in Christum non cadit. Denique Christus diserte dicitur, Iesai e cap. ix. 6. pater æternitatis אבי־עד[?], sive, pater æternus, & per spiritum æternum dicitur se obtulisse Deo. Heb. ix. 14.
units.tr: For when John had looked back at this saying, I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, to see what sort of saying it was, he saw one like the Son of man, verse 13. Therefore it is his voice which, after other things, repeats this again in verses 13 and 18: Fear not; I am the first and the last, and I am he that lives, and was dead, and behold, I am alive for evermore, and have the keys of hell and of death. No one can doubt that these words were spoken by Christ, just as the same words in chapter 2, verse 8, contain the same as what had been said in verse 8. So from this all may judge the victory of our cause, since Socinus, against Wiek, says in chapter 3, class 1, argument 10: Certainly if there were talk of Christ there, our opponents would already have won. II. Certainly the epithet of the true God is also in Isaiah 44:6: I am the first and the last, and beside me there is no other God; and again in chapter 48:12. But from this too we argue for the true Deity of Christ, because the same is attributed to him. Add Exodus 3:14. Third, Christ is certainly simply the Alpha and the Omega of salvation, and indeed of all things, since this is asserted of Christ simply and absolutely, equally as of the Father, and not merely by reason of our salvation or his office. As Enjedinus says on Revelation 1:17, Jesus says he is the first and the last not with respect to substance and existence, but by reason of office. IV. But if the Holy Spirit wished to say absolutely that Christ is the first and the last, by the same reason as the Father, in what more fitting and clearer way could he have done so than he has now? So that the opponents seem to contradict the plain light and the common sense of the words, for the sake of their own hypotheses; but we, as we ought, follow those words. V. Nor, in the sense of the opponents, can Christ, by reason of salvation, be called the beginning and end, Alpha and Omega, but God. Certainly no man would call himself thus, as Christ here, with God, designates himself under the same title, except with great rashness and very unbecomingly, which does not fall upon Christ. Finally, Christ is expressly called in Isaiah 9:6 Father of eternity [אבי־עד], or eternal Father, and through the eternal Spirit he is said to have offered himself to God, Hebrews 9:14.

units.la: Jam & ex aliis divinis attributis seu proprietatibus argumentamur, pro vera Christi Deitate. Atque ejus quidem omniscientiam testantur hæc. Ioann. xxi. 17. Domine tu nosti omnia, tu nosti quod te diligo. Apoc. ii. 9. 23. novi opera tua, &c. 23. Nam ego sum scrutans renes & corda. Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, cap. x. pag. 45. Præterea, (quod huc omnino pertinet) Christus instar Dei, omnia, quæcunque ad munus ipsius, & salutem humani generis quoquo modo pertinebant, scire potuit, ut ne abditissimi humani cordis sensus cum laterent. Quod sane ita Dei proprium est, ut nemo, nedum hominum, sed ne Angelorum tam bonorum, quam malorum, exacte scire possit, quid unus homo cum animo suo cogitet.
units.tr: Now we also argue for the true Deity of Christ from the other divine attributes or properties. And these texts bear witness to his omniscience. John 21:17: Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you. Revelation 2:9, 23: I know your works, etc.; verse 23: For I am he who searches the reins and hearts. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, chapter 10, page 45. Moreover (which pertains wholly to this point), Christ, like God, could know all things that in any way pertained to his office and the salvation of mankind, so that even the most hidden feelings of the human heart were not hidden from him. This is indeed so proper to God that no one, not only of men but not even of the Angels, good or evil, can know exactly what a single man thinks in his mind.

units.la: Excipit autem post Socinum, contra Wiekum, cap. IIX[?]. Enjedinus, nosse quidem Christum cogitata & affectus animi occultos, verum non ex se, sed dono Patris.
units.tr: Enjedinus, however, after Socinus, against Wiek, chap. IIX[?], makes this exception: that Christ indeed knows the thoughts and hidden affections of the mind, but not from himself, rather by the gift of the Father.

units.la: Scrutatio cordium & renum, hoc loco sive significet notitiam, & cogitationum perspectionem; sive potius, justi & aequissimi judicii administrationem, & executionem: Christum, non facit aeternum Deum. Quia Christus, omnia haec habet a Patre. Sicut multi Prophetae & Apostoli, cogitationes hominum, etiam tacentium & absentium, intellexerunt & perspexerunt: Non tamen inde sequitur, eos fuisse Deos aeternos.
units.tr: The searching of hearts and reins, whether it here means knowledge and the perception of thoughts, or rather the administration and execution of a just and most equitable judgment, does not make Christ the eternal God. For Christ has all these things from the Father. Just as many Prophets and Apostles understood and perceived the thoughts of men, even of those who were silent and absent; yet it does not follow from this that they were eternal Gods.

units.la: Quod autem omnem scientiam, judicium, atque adeo scipsum Christus a Patre acceperit; non tantum alibi saepe, & hic cap. 5. verf. 12. dicitur, verum etiam hoc in loco verf. 27. ipse met fatetur Christus: Sicut & ego accepi a Patre meo. Pater igitur, seu verus & solus aeternus Deus, eam notitiam, qua perspicit abditissima quaeque cordis cogitata, a nemine accepit: Christus autem omnia a Patre habet. Ille ergo vere & a se Deus est: hic autem a Patre creatus & factus.
units.tr: But that Christ received all knowledge and judgment, and indeed himself, from the Father, is not only said often elsewhere, and here in chapter 5, verse 12, but Christ himself also confesses it in this passage, verse 27: As I also have received from my Father. Therefore the Father, or the true and only eternal God, received that knowledge by which he perceives all the most hidden thoughts of the heart from no one; but Christ has all things from the Father. Therefore he is truly God and from himself; but this one is created and made by the Father.

units.la: Resp. i. Serutatio cordium & renum hic significat notitiam & perspectionem cogitationum: tum quod haec propria verborum illorum sit significatio; tum quod de judicio ex eo administrando statim addatur, & dabo unicuique versum secundum opera vestra. ii. Aliquando Prophetae, ex singulari Dei revelatione sciverunt[?] cogitationes aliorum; sed non per se, quomodo Christus. iii. extraordinario, & non ita saepe: Christus semper. iv. Numquam ut sibi adscribere fuissent ausi, se esse scrutatores cordium, & renum. Unde Socinus concedit, nullum Prophetarum ausurum esse ita loqui. v. Est loquutio Deo propria, & solemnis ad describendam ejus omniscientiam, mutuata ex V. T. Psalm vii. 10. & xxvi. 2. Jerem. xi. 20. & xx. 12. & xvii. 10. ego Iehova scrutator cordis, probator renum: idque ut dem unicuique fecundum vias suas, fecundum tractum actionum suarum. Act. 1.24. Tu Domine, qui corda omnium nosti. Quare in nostro loco aliqui vertunt, uti Erasmus, ille scrutans renes & corda. Et Syrus, [illegible, ~5 letters] quod ego sum ille qui scrutatur, &c. vi. dicit quidem Christus, idque versu demum 27. se a Patre accepisse, ut regeret gentes virga ferrea, idque pro officio mediatoris; non vero quod eodem modo norit omnium corda. vii. Est quidem, & habet omnia a Patre Christus, ex generatione sui aeterna, ut Filii, non constitutione in mediatorem, vel officio in tempore suscepto. viii. Ut simpliciter & absolute, quod fatetur Socinus, attribuatur Christo, quod corda omnium noscat & scrutetur, quod de nullo Prophetarum unquam dictum fuit, vel dici potuit; ex dono aliquis habere, vel cuipiam communicari non potest, quia est proprietas solius Dei, illa fieri ex propria facultate, & per directum intuitum in animam. Nam qui ista abditissima cordium, & in omnibus novit, ille etiam reliqua omnia, & proinde infinita ejus ut sit scientia, est necesse. Quare omnes Ecclesiae dicuntur hoc sci-turae, quod Christus ille est, qui renes & corda scrutatur. Omnipotentiae Christi tot testes ac documenta sunt, quot miracula edidit. tum quod ipse dixit, Joan. v. 19. Quae enim Pater operatur, eadem & filius operatur similiter. Hinc Deus fortis dicitur, Jesa. ix. & Apoc. i. 8. Ego sum α & ω, &c. omnipotens ille. Phil. iii. 21. τὸ δύνασθαι τὰ πάντα.
units.tr: Answer 1. The searching of hearts and reins here means knowledge and perception of thoughts: both because this is the proper meaning of those words, and because concerning the judgment to be administered from it, it is immediately added, and I will give to each one according to your works. 2. Sometimes the Prophets, by a singular revelation of God, knew the thoughts of others; but not through themselves, as Christ does. 3. (They did so) by an extraordinary means, and not so often; Christ always. 4. They never would have dared to claim for themselves that they were searchers of hearts and reins. Hence Socinus concedes that no Prophet would have dared to speak thus. 5. It is an expression proper to God and solemn for describing his omniscience, borrowed from the Old Testament: Psalm 7:10, and 26:2; Jeremiah 11:20, 20:12 and 17:10: I, Jehovah, am the searcher of the heart and the tester of the reins, and that I may give to each one according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds. Acts 1:24: You, Lord, who know the hearts of all. Therefore in our passage some translate, as Erasmus does, he who searches the reins and hearts. And the Syriac, [illegible], that I am he who searches, etc. 6. Christ indeed says, and that only in verse 27, that he received from the Father in order to rule the nations with an iron rod, and that for the office of mediator; but not that he knows the hearts of all in the same way. 7. Christ indeed has and receives all things from the Father, by his eternal generation as Son, not by appointment as mediator or by an office undertaken in time. 8. That simply and absolutely, as Socinus confesses, is attributed to Christ, that he knows and searches the hearts of all, which was never said, or could be said, of any Prophet; it cannot be had from a gift, nor communicated to anyone, because it is a property of God alone, that it is done by one's own faculty and by direct insight into the soul. For he who knows those most hidden things of the hearts of all men must necessarily know all other things too, and therefore his knowledge must be infinite. Therefore all the Churches are said to know this, that Christ is he who searches the reins and hearts. There are as many witnesses and proofs of the omnipotence of Christ as there are miracles he performed; and he himself said, John 5:19: For whatever the Father does, the Son also does in like manner. Hence God is called mighty, Isaiah 9, and Revelation 1:8: I am the Alpha and the Omega, etc., the Almighty. Philippians 3:21: the ability to subject all things [τὸ δύνασθαι τὰ πάντα].

units.la: Verum ad Joann. v. 19. excipit Enjedinus:
units.tr: But Enjedinus objects to John 5:19:

units.la: Vrgent adversarii voculam ὁμοίως, id est, similiter, & ex ea aequalitatem, vel potius identitatem Christi & Patris eliciunt. Qui enim similiter operantur, habent easdem vires. Ergo sunt aequales, vel iidem.
units.tr: The adversaries press the little word ὁμοίως, that is, "similarly" [ὁμοίως], and from it they draw the equality, or rather the identity, of Christ and the Father. For those who work similarly have the same powers. Therefore they are equal, or the same.

units.la: Sed primo sciendum est, vocem ὁμοίως Respon. i. Non ex simplici vocula ὁ-μοίως argumentamur, ad eliciendam inde Christi cum Patre aequalitatem vel identitatem: sed ex toto Christi sermone, tum hoc textu. Dixerat Christus, verf. 17. quod Pater suus usque hodie operarenor invehere æqualitatem, multo minus identi-tatem. Simile enim, ut dicitur, non est idem: Et possunt plures similiter operari, qui tamen inæqualibus viribus sint præditi. Nam recte dicimus de viro & muliere, vel Patre & filio in opere aliquo versantibus: Vir operatur, & mulier similiter operatur. Pater laborat, & similiter filius laborat. Sicut enim vir non otiatur, ita nec mulier, ut Pater, ita filius laborat. Sed hinc tamen non sequitur, in muliere vim tantam esse, quanta est in viro, & in filio æquales patri vires. Nam vox similiter, non quantitatem, sed qualitatem, seu rem in qua plures conveniunt, vel participes sunt, licet non æqualiter, denotat. Ut: Absfolon peccat cum patrem persequitur, similiter peccat filius, cum reluctatur patris imperio. Neque tamen sequitur, Absfolonis & inobedientis filii peccata esse æqualia, aut eadem. Sic 1. Cor. 7. verf. 36. dicitur, eum qui virginem nuptum dat, non peccare: verf. 37. qui non dat, bene facere. Quæ possunt, eodem sensu, sic efferri: Qui virginem nuptum dat, non peccat, similiter qui nuptum non dat, non peccat. Et tamen in hac oratione vox similiter, non facit æqualitatem inter dantem aut non dantem; subjicit enim Apostolus verf. 38. Itaque qui dat nuptum bene facit, qui vero non dat nuptum melius facit. Gradus enim diversi, non destruunt similitudinem. Atque in his & similibus locutionibus, vox similiter, non tam est comparativa, quam copulativa. Proinde pari ratione dicere possumus: Patrem operari & similiter filium operari, neque tamen inde consequetur, in Patre & Filio æquales esse vires, aut ipsos ejusdem esse essentiæ. Verum si quis præscripta Euangelistæ diligentius consideret, non hoc simpliciter dicitur, quod Pater faciat, & Filius similiter faciat: sed, eadem quæ Pater facit, Filium similiter facere: & καὶ ὁ υἱὸς, &c. [?] quo significatur, Patrem non operari sine filio, atque ejusdem effectus seu operis, causas esse tam Patrem quam filium. Unde Beza vocem ὁμοίως vertit, non similiter, sed pariter, ita ut denotetur in agendo, conjuncta Patris ac filii virtus. Hæc interpretatio congrua est hitur, & ipse una cum Patre. Ob quam cau-tela, tam quum eum lapidare Judæi conarentur, non adeo quod solvisset sabbathum, quam quod 1. Deum dixisset proprium Patrem, ἴδιον πατέρα. & 2. ita se parem fecisset cum Deo; ἴσον τῷ θεῷ. respondit Christus, verum id esse, neque lapidatione dignum: comprobavitque inde, quod filius non tantum nil seorsim ageret à Patre, nempe qui proprius filius esset proprii Patris, sed quæcunque Pater facit, eadem & filius faceret ὁμοίως: inde quod ἴσος Patri, ut illud ὁμοίου fluat ex illo ἴσῳ, & hinc, non vi vocis, ὁμοίως hic idem fit quod ἴσως, æqualiter, pariter. Non quod, qui quovis modo similiter operantur, propterea easdem vires habeant, vel sint æquales: sed qui ita similiter operantur, uti hic Filius, cum Patre. Adeo ut non quadrent exempla, quæ Enjedinus affert, viri & mulieris, patris ac filii, vel quæ aliquam duntaxat similitudinem notant, non talem, ac in nostro textu. 11. Plus Christus hic vult, quam quod Pater non operetur sine filio, vel operatur non ipsius adeo essent, quam Patris; sed ostendeda ei erat sua cum Patre ἴσότης, quam confirmatum it argumento sumpto à potentia vel operibus, quod nempe quæcunque Pater, eadem possit & Filius. Non tantum, quod quæ filii, eadem sint Patris, sed & quæcunque Patris, eadem & Filii. III. Imo universalissima est Christi assertio, quod quæ Pater, eadem & Filius faciat similiter. Neque vel ulla verba, aut circumstantiæ rei vel temporis contrarium indicant, vel id patitur propositæ res aut argumentum, quod erat, Christi probare cum Deo æqualitatem, & proprietatem. Ingenere enim inquit, ὅσα, quæ, vel quæcunque, eadem. Quemadmodum ei oppositum membrum quoque est universale ὅσον, Filius non potest facere quidquam, nisi viderit facientem Patrem. storiæ, ideoque meo judicio vera. Nam Christus hoc ipso se tuebatur contra calumnias Iudæorum, quod opera ipsius, non essent hominis atque sua, sed Dei Patris, proinde ea quæ ipse faciat, non esse ipsi tribuenda, sed præcipuè Patri, ita ut in Filio intelligatur operari Pater, atque possint & debeant hæc opera tribui conjunctim Patri & Filio. Nam sicut Filius nihil potest à se ipso facere, nisi Patre præeunte ac monstrante: ita Pater non vult nisi per Filium & in Filio operari; atque ita Filius facit, quæ Pater facit. Hunc sensum putant adversarii favere ipsorum causæ, quod Patri quasi collega & socius addatur Filius, unde colligenda sit utriusque æqualitas. Sed falluntur. Nam primò, non est universalis hæc Christi assertio, quasi nihil unquam fecerit, faciat aut facturus sit Pater, quod non una fecerit, faciat aut facturus sit Filius: sed hæc intelligenda sunt, ut verba quoque & temporis, ac rei circumstantiæ docent, de miraculis, quæ Christus vi à Patre accepta, & nomine Patris faciebat.
units.tr: But first it must be understood what the word ὁμοίως means. Answer 1. We do not argue from the bare particle ὁμοίως to infer from it the equality or identity of Christ with the Father; we argue from the whole of Christ's discourse, and from this passage in particular. Christ had said in v. 17 that his Father works even until now, so the word does not bring in equality, much less identity. For, as the saying goes, a similar thing is not the same thing. Several may act similarly and yet be endowed with unequal powers. We rightly say of a man and a woman, or of a father and a son, engaged in some task: "The man works, and the woman works similarly. The father labours, and the son similarly labours." For just as the man does not idle, neither does the woman; so the father labours, and the son likewise labours. Yet it does not follow from this that the woman has as much strength as the man, or that the son has powers equal to the father's. For the word similarly denotes not quantity but quality, that is, a thing in which several agree or share, though not equally. For example: "Absalom sins when he pursues his father; likewise his son sins when he resists his father's command." Nor does it follow that the sins of Absalom and of the disobedient son are equal or the same. So in 1 Cor. 7:36 it is said that he who gives his virgin in marriage does not sin, and v. 37 that he who does not give her does well. These may be put in the same sense thus: "He who gives his virgin in marriage does not sin; likewise he who does not give her in marriage does not sin." Yet in this sentence the word similarly does not make the giver and the non-giver equal, for the Apostle adds in v. 38: "So he who gives her in marriage does well, but he who does not give her does better." Different degrees do not destroy the similarity. Indeed, in these and similar expressions the word similarly is less comparative than copulative. Therefore by the same reasoning we may say, "The Father works, and likewise the Son works," and yet it will not follow that the Father and the Son have equal powers, or that they are of the same essence. But if anyone considers the evangelist's words more carefully, it is not simply said that the Father does something and the Son similarly does it; rather, the Son likewise does the very things the Father does, and [καὶ ὁ υἱὸς] etc. By this is signified that the Father does not work without the Son, and that the Father and the Son are both causes of the same effect or work. Hence Beza translates ὁμοίως not "similarly" but "equally", so that the combined power of Father and Son in acting is shown. This interpretation agrees with the context, and with the Son himself working together with the Father. On account of this, when the Jews tried to stone him, it was not so much because he had broken the Sabbath as because 1. he had called God his own Father [ἴδιον πατέρα], and 2. had thereby made himself equal to God [ἴσον τῷ θεῷ]. Christ answered that this was true and not deserving of stoning, and he proved it by showing that the Son does nothing apart from the Father; he is the proper Son of the proper Father; and whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise [ὁμοίως]. From this, since he is equal [ἴσος] to the Father, the word ὁμοίως flows from that ἴσως, so that here ὁμοίως, by the force not of the word but of the context, means the same as ἴσως, equally, in like manner. This does not mean that whoever works in any way similarly therefore has the same powers or is equal; it means those who so work similarly as this Son works with the Father. So the examples Enjedinus brings, of man and woman, father and son, or those which indicate only some slight similarity, do not fit, and are not like the case in our text. 2. Christ here means more than that the Father does not work without the Son, or that the works are not so much the Son's as the Father's; he was showing his equality [ἴσότης] with the Father, and he confirmed it by an argument drawn from power or works, namely that whatever the Father can do, the Son can do too. It is not only that what belongs to the Son belongs to the Father, but also that whatever belongs to the Father belongs to the Son. 3. Indeed, Christ's assertion is most universal: whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. Neither any words nor the circumstances of the thing or the time indicate the contrary, nor does the matter under discussion allow it, since the point was for Christ to prove his equality and proper deity with God. For he says in general ὅσα [whatever], "whatever things"; and the opposite member is equally universal: ὅσον [whatever], "The Son can do nothing of himself unless he sees the Father doing it." This is the sense of the history, and therefore in my judgement true. For Christ defended himself in this very way against the slanders of the Jews: that his works were not those of a mere man, nor his own, but of God the Father; therefore what he does is not to be attributed to himself but chiefly to the Father, so that the Father is understood to work in the Son, and these works can and should be attributed jointly to the Father and the Son. For just as the Son can do nothing of himself except as the Father goes before and shows him, so the Father wills to work only through the Son and in the Son; and thus the Son does what the Father does. The adversaries think this sense favours their cause, because the Son is added to the Father as a kind of colleague and partner, from which equality of both is to be inferred. But they are mistaken. For first, this assertion of Christ is not universal, as if the Father had never done, does, or will do anything which the Son has not also done, does, or will do; rather, these words must be understood, as the words, the time, and the circumstances of the thing teach, about the miracles which Christ performed by the power received from the Father and in the Father's name.

units.la: Deinde cooperarii, seu ii qui una laborant in eadem re conficienda, non ideo pares aut iidem censentur, alias Apostoli & Christus & Deus ipse, essent pares ac eiusdem essentiæ. Legimus enim Marci ultimo: Illi vero egressi prædicarunt ubique Domino cooperante. Et 1. Cor. 3. vers. 9. Paulus & cæteri Apostoli vocantur Θεοῦ συν-εργοί. Sic etiam non sequitur, si Christus Deo Patri cooperatur, aut simul cum Patre agit, ip-sam esse æqualem Deo, aut eundem cum eo.
units.tr: Next, co-workers, that is, those who labour together to accomplish the same thing, are not for that reason regarded as equal or the same; otherwise the Apostles, Christ and God himself would be equal and of the same essence. For we read at the end of Mark: "And they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them." And in 1 Cor. 3:9 Paul and the other Apostles are called God's fellow-workers [Θεοῦ συνεργοί]. So too it does not follow that, if Christ co-operates with God the Father, or acts together with the Father, he is equal to God or the same as him.

units.la: Patrem, ita, quæcunq; Pater, eadem & Filius ὁμοίως, pariter, uti quæ Filii, Patris, ita & quæ Patris, Filii. Et omnia tua mea sunt, & tua mea. Joann. xvii. 10. Quarto, quemadmodum in antecedenti versu, quod hujus fundamentum continet & causam, generaliter ac absolute dictum, quod Christus se faceret æqualem Deo ἴσον θεῷ: ita argumentum ad hoc probandum, ex operibus non minus universale est, idque tale esse debuit ad faciendum elenchum. Quod si vero illa intelligenda fuissent cum ista restrictione & diminutione, quam Adversarii faciunt, id si significasset Christus, difficultate sua caruisset negotium totum. Et certe significare id, uti facile poterat, ita debuisset Christus: non ut Iudæos solum & auditores suos, sed & nos quoque liberasset incommodo: Nam verba absolute posita non aliter quam absolute accipi possunt & debent. Interpres Syrus, vers. 18. Quod se-ipsum coæqualem faceret Deo. ומשוה הוא את נפשו עם אלהים[?] Versio Arabica, quia dicebat, quod Deus pater meus est: & coæquabat se Deo. Persica, Propterea quod dixisset, Deus pater meus est, & seipsum cum Deo unum fecisset. Et vers. 19. Syriaca versio, Ea enim quæ Pater facit, hæc itidem & Filius facit. Arabica, Quia opera quæ facit Pater, hæc etiam facit Filius. Persica, Quidquid Deus fecerit, Filius etiam simile ei facit. Denique quod de cooperariis Adversa-rius argumentatur, nos haudquaquam ferit, qui non pro ejusmodi cooperariis habemus Patrem & Filium, ut nec ejusmodi formemus consequentiam, si Christus Deo Patri cooperatur, vel, quicunque Deo cooperatur, est ejusdem cum eo essentiæ & virium: Christus enim non ut cooperator hic simpliciter introducitur, sed qui eadem operatur cum Patre ἴσος θεῷ. quod longe aliud quid est, quam simpliciter cooperari.
units.tr: Likewise, whatever the Father does, the Son does in like manner [ὁμοίως], equally, as the things of the Son are the Father's, so the things of the Father are the Son's. "All my things are yours, and yours are mine" (John 17:10). Fourth, just as in the preceding verse, which contains the ground and cause of this, it is said generally and absolutely that Christ made himself equal to God [ἴσον θεῷ], so the argument for proving this from the works is no less universal, and it had to be so in order to make the refutation effective. But if those things had to be understood with that restriction and diminution which the adversaries make, then, had Christ meant it, the whole difficulty would have been avoided. And certainly, as he could easily have said so, so he ought to have said so, and not only freed the Jews and his hearers but also spared us this difficulty. For words stated absolutely can and must be taken in no other way than absolutely. The Syriac interpreter, v. 18: "because he made himself equal to God" [umashweh hu et nafsho im Elohim]. The Arabic version: "because he said that God is my Father, and made himself equal to God." The Persian: "because he said, God is my Father, and made himself one with God." And v. 19, the Syriac version: "For whatever the Father does, these things also the Son does likewise." The Arabic: "Because the works which the Father does, these also the Son does." The Persian: "Whatever God does, the Son also does a like thing." Finally, what the adversary argues about co-workers does not touch us at all, since we do not regard the Father and the Son as such co-workers, nor do we form the inference that if Christ co-operates with God the Father, or whoever co-operates with God, is of the same essence and powers with him. For Christ is not introduced here simply as a co-worker, but as one who does the same works with the Father, equal to God [ἴσος θεῷ], which is quite a different thing from merely co-operating.

units.la: Christi omnipræsentiam loquitur Ioann. iii. 13. Et nemo adscendit in cœlum nisi qui ex cœlo descendit, Filius hominis qui est in cœlo. Matth. xviii. 20. Vbi fuerint duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, in medio illorum sum. cap. xxviii. 20. Ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem sæculi.
units.tr: He speaks of Christ's omnipresence: John 3:13. And no one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven. Matt. 18:20. Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them. Ch. 28:20. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.

units.la: Ad Iohann. iii. 13. excipit Enjedinus, post Servetum, lib. ii. de Errorib. Trinit. in initio; Socinum, contra Wiekum, cap. vii. istud esse in cœlo, spirituali modo esse intelligendum, pro cœlestia cogitare & intelligere. Esse in Coelo, non est hoc loco aliud, quam frui intelligentia & cognitione rerum Coelestium. Sicut de omnibus pijs dicit Paulus, Phil. 1.verf. 10. Nostra conversatio est in Caelis. item Ephes. 2. verf. 6. Collocavit nos Deus in Coelestibus. Certe qui versatur in Caelis, & collocatus est in Coelestibus: in Coelo est. Non recte igitur colligitur, ex eo quod quis in terris existens, dicitur esse in Coelo, aeterna divinitas.
units.tr: Regarding John 3:13, Enjedinus, following Servetus (book 2 of On the Errors of the Trinity, at the beginning), and Socinus, against Wiekus (ch. 7), take the words to be in heaven to be understood in a spiritual way, as meaning to think and understand heavenly things. To be in heaven here means nothing other than to enjoy understanding and knowledge of heavenly things, just as Paul says of all the godly, Phil. 1:10: Our conversation is in heaven; and Eph. 2:6: God has seated us in the heavenly places. Surely whoever lives in heaven and is placed among heavenly things is in heaven. Therefore it is not rightly concluded, from the fact that someone who exists on earth is said to be in heaven, that he has eternal divinity.

units.la: Resp. 1. Adscendere & descendere in coelum & terram, nunquam Christo tri-buuntur, nisi de persona, & tum de ejus adventu in terram, tum locali in coelos ascensione intellecta. Similis locus est Eph. iv. 9. Quod adscendit, quid est nisi quod descendit primum in inferiores partes terrae &c.:
units.tr: Answer 1. To ascend and descend into heaven and earth are never attributed to Christ except of his person, and that with reference both to his coming down to the earth and to his local ascension into the heavens. A similar passage is Eph. 4:9: That he ascended, what is it but that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth, etc.

units.la: II. Esse in coelo, nuspiam aliud nihil significat, quam frui intelligentia & cogni-tione rerum coelestium. Aliud est, quod piorum conversatio dicitur esse in coelis, quando id immediate opponitur iis qui terrena sapiunt, uti Phil. iii. 19. 20. & Eph. ii. 6. cum Christo dicuntur fideles vivificati, & consuscitati, & constituti seu collocati in coelestibus in Christo Iesu. Non ergo ipsi dicunt se esse in coelo, sed in & cum Christo in coelestibus: quod Col. iii. 3. dixit, Et vita vestra occultatur cum Christo in Deo. Vita nostra est in Christo, qui coelestia nunc occupavit, & hinc cum eo coelestium nos sumus participes & accolae. iii. Non simpliciter ex eo quod quis in terris existens dicitur quovis modo esse in coelo, colligimus aeternam ejus divinitatem: verum inde quod Christus non tantum descendisse de Coelo, & adscensurus iterum, verum & esse in coelo, quamvis descenderit, dicitur, ejus primo omnipraesentiam concludimus, quandoquidem coelum simul & terram occupat; tum ex divina proprietate natu-ram.
units.tr: II. To be in heaven nowhere means anything other than to enjoy understanding and knowledge of heavenly things. It is different when the conversation of the godly is said to be in heaven, where this is directly set against those who mind earthly things, as in Phil. 3:19–20, and Eph. 2:6, where the faithful are said with Christ to be made alive, raised up, and seated or placed among heavenly things in Christ Jesus. So they do not say of themselves that they are in heaven, but that they are in and with Christ among heavenly things. This is what Col. 3:3 says: And your life is hidden with Christ in God. Our life is in Christ, who now occupies heavenly things, and from him we are sharers and inhabitants of heavenly things with him. III. We do not conclude his eternal divinity simply from the fact that someone who exists on earth is said in any way to be in heaven. Rather, from the fact that Christ, who not only came down from heaven and will come again, but who is said to be in heaven although he came down, we first conclude his omnipresence, since he fills heaven and earth at once; and then, from the divine property, his nature.

units.la: Aliter ad hoc excipit Socinus: Qui est in Coelo, posse reddi, qui erat in Coelo: quemadmodum & ab Erasmo, & a Beza, & ab aliis annotatum fuerat. Verum an non potest retineri illud, qui est in Coelo? an non propius id significatur istis, ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ? quemadmodum cap. 1. 18. ὁ ὢν qui est in sinu Patris. Syrus, Filius hominis ille qui in coelo est. הו ראיתוה [?]. Arabs: Filius hominis existens in Coelo. Translatio Persica, Filius hominis qui in Coelo est. Denique qui admittunt, exponi etiam posse, qui erat in Coelo, non hoc ideo volunt, quasi non possit, non debeat intelligi quoque ipsum pro praesenti in coelo fuisse; sed pariter hoc, & illud, juxta Apoc. 1.8. ὁ ὢν [?] ὁ ἦν [?] ὁ ἐρχόμε-νος. Caeterum Erasmus, & Beza vertunt, qui est in coelo, quamvis ille dicat, quod participium verti poterat per praeteritum imperfectum, qui erat in coelo, videlicet antequam descenderet. Sic enim Filius hominis dicitur fuisse in Coelo, sicut Dominus gloriae dicitur crucifixus, ob proprietatum in hypostasi duas complectentem naturas communionem. Et Beza, vel qui erat in coelo, ut idem ipse Christus loquitur infra cap. 6. 62.
units.tr: Otherwise Socinus objects to this: "who is in heaven" can be rendered "who was in heaven," as was noted by Erasmus, Beza, and others. But can "who is in heaven" not be retained? Does it not more properly signify for them who is in heaven [ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ]? So in ch. 1:18, who is [ὁ ὢν] in the bosom of the Father. The Syriac: the Son of man, he who is in heaven. The Arabic: the Son of man existing in heaven. The Persian translation: the Son of man who is in heaven. Finally, those who admit that it may also be explained as who was in heaven do not mean it in this way, as if it could not or should not also be understood of his being present in heaven; rather, both this and that alike, in accordance with Rev. 1:8, who is [ὁ ὢν], who was [ὁ ἦν], who is to come [ὁ ἐρχόμενος]. Moreover, Erasmus and Beza translate it who is in heaven, although he says that the participle could be rendered by the imperfect past, who was in heaven, that is, before he came down. For in this way the Son of man is said to have been in heaven, just as the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified, because of the communion of properties in one person embracing two natures. And Beza: or who was in heaven, as Christ himself speaks below in ch. 6:62.

units.la: Ad Matth. xviii. 20. Socinus excipit, contra majorem argumenti, seu consequen-tiam; & minorem:
units.tr: On Matt. 18:20, Socinus objects, against the major premise of the argument, or its consequence, and against the minor:

units.la: Respondeo, negans primum consequentiam hujus argumentationis, etiamsi, ut in ipsa pro concessso sumitur, Christi verba de reali & essen-tiali praesentia accipienda essent. Posset enim Christus, in omnibus locis, ubi sint duo aut tres aut plures congregati, in nomine ipsius, essentia-liter adesse: nec tamen esse ubique quemadmo-
units.tr: I answer, first denying the consequence of this argument, even if Christ's words were to be taken, as is assumed in the argument itself, of a real and essential presence. For Christ could be essentially present in all places where two or three or more are gathered in his name, and yet not be everywhere in the same way

units.la: Resp. 1. Non id nobis demonstrat Socinus, quomodo Christus pluribus in locis, & omnibus iis, quibus congregatio-nes habentur in ejus nomine, essentialiter praesens esset, & non posset, non deberet praesens esse locis omnibus. Nam quum illa multipraesentia necessario deberet esse dum,ad hoc ut immensus fit,omnino requiritur. Neque enim (arbitror) in aere, aut sub aquis, vel etiam in ipso Coelo, congregationes aliquando fiunt duorum aut trium, aut plurium in Christi nomine. Sed deinde quis non videt aut negare potest, Christum, in isto & similibus locis, de praesentia sua, quod ad favorem & auxilium attinet, verba facere? naturae multipraesentis,multipraesentia e-iusdem [?] invidiae naturae non potest esse nisi ex eadem facultate aut vi naturali, qua possit esse omnipraesens. Quodque omnipraesens potest esse, id eo ipso omnipraesens est. Quemadmodum quod Deus esse potest, eo ipso necessario Deus est. Non disputamus hic cum Pontificiis,& Luthe-ranis, super omnipraesentia humanae naturae in Christo; sed cum Socino nobis res est, cui aeque illa invisa sunt, ac nobis. 11. Haud negamus, hac Christi, in medio suorum praesentia connotari etiam praesentiam gratiae, sed hoc, uti in praesentia Dei, naturae ejus praesentiam non tollit aut negat, sed ponit & confirmat. Quod & phrasis significat, esse in medio ipsorum, neque tantum cum ipsis. Quemadmodum, Cor. xiv.
units.tr: Answer 1. Socinus does not show us how Christ could be essentially present in several places, and in all those where assemblies are held in his name, and how he could not, and ought not, be present in all places. For since that multipresence would necessarily belong to a multipresent nature, and for this to be immense it is wholly required, the multipresence of that same nature cannot be except from the same faculty or natural power by which it could be omnipresent. And whatever can be omnipresent is by that very fact omnipresent, just as whatever God can be, he necessarily is God. We are not disputing here with the Papists and the Lutherans about the omnipresence of the human nature in Christ; we are dealing with Socinus, to whom that doctrine is as hateful as it is to us. II. We do not deny that by this presence of Christ in the midst of his people there is also implied the presence of grace; but this, as in the presence of God, does not remove or deny his natural presence, but posits and confirms it. The phrase also means to be in the midst of them, not merely with them, just as in 1 Cor. 14:

units.la: 25. Annuncians quod revera Deus in vobis, vel inter vos est. Vti ἐν μέσῳ εἶναι [?] semper, ubi usurpatur, denotat praesentiam personae. Quemadmodum Apoc. 1. 13. In medio septem candelabrorum. & cap. 11. 1. & hoc ipso capite xviii. Math. verf. 2. Stitit in medio ipsorum puerulum. Matth. xiv. 6. Luc. 11. 46. In medio doctorum. Luc. x. 3. In medio luporum. cap. xxii. 27. Ego sum in medio vestri ut ministrans. cap. xxiv. 36. Ipse Iesus stetit in medio ipsorum. Act. 1. 15. & 11. 22. & xvii. 21. 1. Thess. 11. 7. & alibi.
units.tr: 25. Declaring that God is truly in you, or among you. Wherever to be in the midst [ἐν μέσῳ εἶναι] is used, it always denotes the presence of a person, as in Rev. 1:13, in the midst of the seven candlesticks; and ch. 11:1; and in this very chapter of Matthew, v. 2, He set a little child in the midst of them. Matt. 14:6; Luke 11:46, in the midst of the teachers; Luke 10:3, in the midst of wolves; ch. 22:27, I am in the midst of you as one who serves; ch. 24:36, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them; Acts 1:15, and 11:22, and 17:21; 1 Thess. 2:7, and elsewhere.

units.la: Denique hoc argumentum nostrum fecundum pro Christi Deitate, sumptum ex attributis & proprietatibus divinis concludimus verbis Smalcii, in lib. de divinitate Christi, cap. ix. pag.43. Quod sane quoties apud animum meum confidero, ita me percellit, & tantam Iesu Christi divinitatem testatur, ut, quemadmodum nobis per omnia similis quo ad naturam fuerit, sic Deo per omnia similis, quoad qualitates & proprietates, fuisse, jure dici possit. Arg.tertium. Cui opera foli Deo propria tribuuntur, ejus etiam agnoscenda est vera & Deo propria Deitas: Christo opera foli Deo propria tribuuntur: ergo. Primo,in genere, Ioann. v. 19. Quae enim Pater facit, ea similiter & Filius facit. verf. 21. Sicut Pater suscitat mortuos & vivificat, sic & Filius quos vult vivificat. Tum in specie,ac primum creatio. Ioann. 1. 3. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quodcunque factum. Scio quidem quam audacter & improbe haec invertant Adversarii, eo impudentius, quo illustriora de Christo, & ejus Deitate perhibent testimonia, totam hanc periculpen trahentes ad statum & initium Euangeli à Iohanne Baptista praedicati, quod in ejus initio Christus fuerit,non vero in initio creationis. Quae quia tum sua se satis inanitate evertunt,tum à plurimis viris egregiis doctisque copiose examinata & refutata sunt,praesertim à Clariss. Collega nostro D.Coccejo in Consideratione principii Euang. Iohannis, ubi ad partes vocavit Adversariorum primarios, Socinum, Enjedinum, Smalcium, & Schlichtingium, nos eo opere lubenter supersedemus, eoque Lectorem & Adversarios remittimus, quae ubi ulteriori responso impetierint, tum nos de vindiciis cogitabimus, quibus nil poterit dari facilius, quando singula loci verba ponderamus ceu totidem argumenta. Ἐν ἀρχῇ ὦ [?], בראשית [?]. Simpliciter positum, nil denotans quam rerum omnium principium simpliciter: nam sine relatione est ad hoc vel illud. 11. Atque ut illud cogitemus, jubet nos Euangelista altius ascendere, & Christum in illo principio apud Deum contemplari, adeo ab humanis, & tempore Euangelii, quando in carne inter homines Christus ἐσκήνωσε [?], lectores suos Jos[?] revocans. In principio Euangelii, vel praedicationis Euangelicae fuit Christus apud homines; in principio, quod Iohannes dicit, rerum apud Deum. iii. Quin si in principio Euangelii Christus extitit, fuit etiam in principio mundi; nam statim Euangelium a mundo condito lapsoque, promulgatum, ante Abrahamum, uti dixerunt supra ex Adversariis nonnulli. iv. Nec solum apud Deum fuit Christus λόγος, sed & Deus ipse. Admiranda gradatio. Primum in principio fuisse dicitur: tum ne inter creaturas collocaretur, apud Deum: denique & Deus. Illud Photinianos jugulat & Socinianos; istud Arianos; hoc fidei articulum plane aperteque exponit. Primo membro notatur ejus existentia, quando extiterit; secundo subsistentia, quod persona fuit distincta apud Patrem; tertio eadem ejus essentia, & fuit Deus. v. Jam illud ulterius ostenditur ex effecto, vid. creatione. Hoc enim primum Dei opus: in principio creavit Deus. vi. Atque omnia creavit, & nihil sine eo conditum: per regulam de omni, & de nullo. Quemadmodum etiam Hebr. xv. 13. & non est creatura occulta coram eo; omnia vero nuda & decollata oculis ejus, de quo nobis sermo. Non per ipsum, juxta Socinum, omnia facta in initio praedicationis Euangelii; neque omnia tum renovata. Sed in initio rerum fecit, creavitque Christus res omnino omnes. Syrus, omnia per manum ejus fuere, & sine ipso ne unum quidem fuit, אף לא חרא[?], ex eo quod fuit. Versio Persica, omne per manum ejus erat, & absque eo non factum est, unum, quod factum est. Versio Arabica, in initio Euangelii habet, in nomine Dei unius, Patris, & filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Aethiopica etiam aliud hoc versu pro Christo argumentum habet, quod videlicet non tantum omnia per ipsum facta sint, sed etiam ad ejus gloriam: & unumquodque per ipsum factum est, & absque ipso non fuit quod factum est quidquam, & etiam quod factum est propter ipsum est. vii. In super Christus hoc in loco dicitur Vitae omnis auctor. viii. Hominumque, & vitae in ipsis. Perrumpat haec sua mala opinione atque hypothesi, pervertatque Adversarius, nunquam sibi veritas deerit illis ex capitibus se defendendi; neque alii, veritati.
units.tr: Finally, we conclude this second argument for Christ's deity, taken from the divine attributes and properties, in the words of Smalcius, in his book on the deity of Christ, chapter 9, page 43: Indeed, whenever I consider this in my own mind, it so moves me and attests to such a great divinity of Jesus Christ that it can rightly be said that, just as he was in every way like us in nature, so he was in every way like God in qualities and properties. The third argument runs: Whoever is credited with works proper to God alone must also be acknowledged as true God, having the deity proper to God; Christ is credited with works proper to God alone; therefore (Christ is true God). First, in general, John 5:19: For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. Verse 21: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills. Then in particular, and first, creation. John 1:3: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. I know well how boldly and wickedly our opponents twist these words, all the more shamelessly because the passage bears such clear testimony to Christ and his deity. They drag this whole passage down to the state and beginning of the gospel preached by John the Baptist, claiming that Christ was at the beginning of that, and not at the beginning of creation. These claims overthrow themselves by their own emptiness, and they have been fully examined and refuted by many outstanding and learned men, especially by our distinguished colleague, Dr. Cocceius, in his Consideration of the Beginning of John's Gospel, where he called to the field the chief of our opponents, Socinus, Enjedinus, Smalcius and Schlichting. We therefore gladly spare ourselves that work and refer the reader and our opponents to it. When they have attempted a further reply, we shall then consider our vindication, which can be given very easily, since we weigh each word of the passage as so many arguments. En archē ēn ho logos [Ἐν ἀρχῇ ... ]; bereshit [בראשית]. Simply put, it signifies nothing but the beginning of all things, without any reference to this or that. 2. And so that we may grasp that, the evangelist bids us to ascend higher and to contemplate Christ in that beginning, with God, calling his readers back from human things and from the time of the gospel, when Christ tabernacled in the flesh among men. In the beginning of the gospel, or of the gospel preaching, Christ was among men; in the beginning that John speaks of, he was with God. 3. Indeed, if Christ existed in the beginning of the gospel, he also existed in the beginning of the world; for the gospel was promulgated at once after the world was created and fell, before Abraham, as some of our opponents said above. 4. Nor was Christ only the Word with God, but he was also God himself. An admirable gradation: first it is said that he was in the beginning; then, that he was with God, so as not to be placed among creatures; and finally, that he was God. The first statement overthrows the Photinians and Socinians, the second the Arians, and the third sets out the article of faith plainly and openly. In the first member is noted his existence, and when he existed; in the second his subsistence, that he was a distinct person with the Father; in the third his very essence, and that he was God. 5. This is further shown from his effect, namely creation. For this is God's first work: In the beginning God created. 6. And he created all things, and nothing was founded without him, by the rule of "of all" and "of none." So also Hebrews 4:13: and no creature is hidden before him; but all things are naked and laid open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do. It is not, according to Socinus, that all things were made through him at the beginning of the preaching of the gospel, nor that all things were then renewed. Rather, at the beginning of things, Christ made and created all things without exception. The Syriac: all things were by his hand, and without him not even one thing was, aph la chra, from what was made. The Persian version: everything was by his hand, and without him not one thing was made that was made. The Arabic version, at the beginning of the gospel, has: in the name of the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Ethiopic also has, for Christ, another argument in this verse: that not only were all things made through him, but also for his glory, and each thing was made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made, and whatever was made was made for him. 7. Moreover, in this place Christ is called the author of all life. 8. And of men, and of the life in them. Let the adversary break these claims with his evil opinion and hypothesis and distort them; the truth will never fail us on these grounds for defending ourselves, nor will others fail the truth.

units.la: Ut nihil quidem sit quam solita Adversariorum & thrasonica jactantia, quando tam insolenter sua solùm, quia nova & impudentia, contra omnem Scripturae & Christianismi sensum, extollunt. Quo spiritu Socinus suam istam expositionem: Multa profecto sunt in quibus adhuc Christianus orbis caecutit, &c. statim initio. Pag. 3. Longiores tantummodo fuimus in iis explicandis, quorum verus sensus omnes prorsus (qui quidem extarent) explanatores latuisse videtur. Quae quidem sibi habeat inventa sua vanamque gloriam, nos magis securi certique sumus in ea Scripturae hujus expositione, quam Catholica Christi Ecclesia, non jam modo, sed a primis ejus incunabulis, id est, a principio Euangelii, quod hic adeo vexant Adversarii, tenuit atque venerata fuit. Socinus iterum, pag. 29. Quid autem hoc loco sibi velit Iohannes, a nemine (quod sciam) adhuc recte expositum fuit, quare conabimur nos verum sensum elicere. In initio Disputationis, de Christi natura, Scripsimus ante annos non paucos, amicorum hortatu, perbrevem expositionem sententiae nostrae in Iohannis Euangelii principio interpretando, quam, cum non tantum nostra aetate, sed etiam multis ante saeculis inauditam sciremus, nostrum nomen supprimentes, aliorum de ea judicium cognoscere decrevimus. Et paulo post, pag. 4. Veruntamen ut unicuique sua constet laus, iisque in Ecclesia agnoscantur perpetuo, quos Deus donis suis praeclarissimis, suaeque veritatis praestantissima cognitione dignatus est, meam sententiam illam in Iohannis Euangelistae verbis explicandis, & quae ad eam afferendam vel jam dixi, vel posthac dicturus sum, magna ex parte ex Lælii Socini Senensis sermonibus, dum adhu[?] adhuc viveret, & post ejus mortem ex aliquibus ipsius scriptis, quae in manus meas non absque mirabili Dei opera atque consilio pervenerunt, & hausisse & desumpsisse, non minus libenter, quam ingenue fateor. Verum missum faciamus infaustum novatorem.
units.tr: Nothing, indeed, is more than the usual boasting and bragging of our opponents, when they so insolently exalt their own views, merely because they are new and shameless, against the whole sense of Scripture and of Christianity. With such a spirit Socinus begins his exposition: Indeed, there are many matters on which the Christian world is still blind, etc. right at the start, page 3: We have been longer only in explaining those things whose true sense seems to have been hidden from all their expounders (at least those who existed). Let him keep his discoveries and his empty glory. We are more secure and certain in our exposition of this Scripture than the Catholic Church of Christ has held and venerated it, not only now but from its earliest cradle, that is, from the beginning of the gospel, which our opponents here so harass. Socinus again, page 29: What John means by this passage, as far as I know, has not yet been rightly explained by anyone; therefore we shall try to bring out the true sense. At the start of the disputation on Christ's nature: Some years ago, at the urging of friends, I wrote a very brief exposition of our view in interpreting the beginning of John's Gospel. Since we knew it had not only not been heard in our own age but was unheard of for many centuries before, we decided, suppressing our name, to learn the judgment of others about it. And a little later, page 4: However, so that each may have his own praise, and so that those whom God has honoured with his excellent gifts and the most outstanding knowledge of his truth may always be acknowledged in the Church, I freely confess that I have drawn and taken that view of mine, both what I have already said and what I shall say hereafter in explaining the words of the evangelist John, for the most part from the discourses of Lelio Socino of Siena while he was still living, and after his death from some of his writings, which came into my hands not without a wonderful work and plan of God. But let us dismiss this unfortunate innovator.

units.la: Locum Ioann. XVII. 5. & nunc glorifica me tu Pater ea gloria, quam habui antequam hic mundus fieret apud te. ita explicat Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum, de Trinitate, pag. 465. ut non reipsa gloriam istam habuisse Christum apud Patrem, antequam mundus esset, dici possit, quod tamen Christus aperte asserit, sed divino tantum decreto ac destinatione.
units.tr: Schlichting, against Meisner, in On the Trinity, page 465, explains John 17:5, "And now, Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was made," in such a way that it can be said that Christ did not actually have that glory with the Father before the world existed, although Christ plainly asserts it, but only by divine decree and destination.

units.la: Neque hic locus aeternam Filii generationem & ὁμοούσιον[?] demonstrat. cum aliud sit gloriam apud Deum ante mundum conditum habere: aliud ab aeterno ejusdem numero cum ipso essentiae participem factum esse. Deinde, aut Christus iam gloriam re ipsa habuit, aut non re ipsa, sed tantum divino decreto ac destinatione. Si re ipsa habuit, quaero, num eam etiam tum re ipsa habuerit, cum in terris versaretur, & has preces ad Patrem funderet: an vero eam habere tum desierit? Si illud, cur ergo rogat Patrem, ut sibi hanc gloriam conferat? Irridere hoc Deum est, non orare. An dices eum rogare Patrem, non ut sibi gloriam donet, quam habeat, sed istius gloriae praedicationem tantum, quam non habeat?
units.tr: This passage does not demonstrate the eternal generation of the Son or the homoousion. For it is one thing to have glory with God before the world was created, and another to have been made a partaker of the same essence with him from eternity. Next, either Christ actually had glory already, or he did not have it in fact, but only by divine decree and destination. If he actually had it, I ask whether he still actually had it when he was living on earth and pouring out these prayers to the Father; or did he then cease to have it? If the former, why then does he ask the Father to confer this glory on him? To do so is to mock God, not to pray. Or will you say that he asked the Father not to give him glory which he has, but only the proclamation of a glory which he does not have?

units.la: Resp. 1. Neque hinc adeo, vel primo probamus Filii a Patre generationem, aut ὁμοούσιον[?], nisi consequenter, quod istius gloriae alius, quam qui talis, capax esse non possit. Adfertur autem locus, ad probandam Christi, ante conditum mundi, existentiam, & gloriam divinam. Unde caetera tum sequuntur sponte. II. Gloriam istam Christus habuit, etiam cum in terris versaretur, sed non usum ejus & manifestationem gloriosam: ut quam pro ratione οἰκονομίας[?] & humiliationis, quam pro eo tempore obibat, explicare noluit, vel exerere. Istam manifestationem, probationem, exhibitionem a Patre petit, nec tan-tummodo ejus praedicationem. Ideoque dixit, glorifica me Pater ea gloria, non eam nunc primum mihi confer, ea gloria, quam habui: non prorsus novam, sed veterem & postliminio quasi reddendam, repetit. Quando vero eam ante habuit? antequam mundus esset. Habuit ergo, & jam tum habuit: ex quo imprasentiarum argumentamur. III. Atque hoc plus dicit, quam habere divino decreto ac destinatione tantum. Quod revera est, non habere, uti nondum revera existere. Aliud est, habere sibi aliquid destinatum; aliud, simpliciter habere. Schlichtingius, quando sibi facit Meisnerum respondere, intelligi hic gloriae praedicationem potius quam gloriam ipsam, ait, at quis tibi istud concedet? Majore jure hoc reponimus, quaerimusque, quis ei concessurus sit, quum gloriam se habuisse Christus testetur, ut hoc exponat, de gloriae destinatione vel ea destinata, non habita, quodve habuerit destinatione, non vi & reipsa? Deinde vide, quam multa hoc evertant. I. Simpliciter Christus habendi verbo utitur, non decernendi vel destinandi. II. Et habuisse, ait in praeterito. III. Habuisse gloriam, quam habere, quamdiu quis nondum existit in rerum natura, haud potest. IV. Habuisse etiam antequam mundus existeret. V. Cui opponit τὸ[?] nunc: petens, ut nunc eadem glorificetur gloria, sua illa aeterna: nimirum quam ad tempus & dies carnis ac humiliationis suae quasi seposuerat & usurparat minus.
units.tr: Answer 1. Nor do we prove the Son's generation from the Father, or his homoousion [ὁμοούσιον], from this passage, except as a consequence: that only one who is such can be capable of that glory. The passage is cited to prove Christ's existence and divine glory before the world was made, and the rest follows of its own accord. II. Christ had this glory even while he was on earth, but not its use and glorious manifestation, which he was unwilling to explain or display because of the economy [οἰκονομία] and the humiliation he then underwent. It is this manifestation, proof and exhibition that he asks of the Father, not merely its proclamation. So he said, "Glorify me, Father, with that glory." He does not say, "Now first confer on me that glory which I had." He asks for it again, not as a wholly new glory but as the old one, to be restored as if by right of return. When did he have it before? "Before the world was." He therefore had it, and had it already then, and from this we argue now. III. And this says more than having it only by divine decree and destination. That is in truth not having, just as not yet really existing is not existing. It is one thing to have something destined for oneself and another simply to have it. When Schlichting makes Meisner reply that here the proclamation of the glory is meant rather than the glory itself, he asks, "But who will grant you that?" With greater right we answer him in turn, and ask who will concede that, since Christ testifies that he had glory, this should be explained as a destination of glory, either destined and not possessed, or had by destination and not in power and in fact. Next, see how many things overturn this. I. Christ simply uses the verb "to have," not "to decree" or "to destine." II. He says "had," in the past tense. III. He had glory, which one cannot have while one does not yet exist in nature. IV. He had it even before the world existed. V. To this he opposes "now" [τὸ νῦν], asking that now he be glorified with that same glory, his own eternal glory, which he had, as it were, set aside and used less for the time and days of his flesh and humiliation.

units.la: Quid ergo restat aliud, quam ut fatearis, Christum non re ipsa gloriam ante mundum conditum habuisse, sed divino decreto ac de-
units.tr: What remains, then, but that you confess that Christ did not in reality have glory before the world was made, but only by divine decree and de-

units.la: Resp. 1. Tum quod credentes dicuntur a Deo electi ante constitutionem mundi, Eph. 1. 4. tum gratia nobis data
units.tr: Answer 1. Both because believers are said to have been chosen by God before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1.4), and because grace was given to us

units.la: Tom. 2. stinatione tantùm. Sic de credentibus in Christum dixit Paulus, eos esse à Deo in Christo electos ante constitutionem mundi; iis datam esse gratiam ante tempora secularia, quia nimirum Deus ante secula & mundi constitutionem iis gloriam ac regnum suum destinârit: Multa id evincunt. 1. quòd gloriam istam sibi à Patre conferri petat. 2. quòd gloriam apud Patrem seu in cœlis dari sibi postulet. 3. quòd promissum sibi dari flagitet. quò etiam spectare videntur illa verba, quàm habui apud te: quasi dicat, quod observavit & Augustinus, habui gloriam apud te, sed fac, ut eam nunc habeam apud me. 4. ipsum Jesu Christi subjectum id requirit. Jesus Christus enim, id est, homo ille ex Spiritu Sancto conceptus & ex Maria natus, à Deo unctus, gloriam ante mundum conditum re ipsa habere non potuit. 5. Ipsa gloria idem postulat, quæ est potestas omnis [?] Christo homini post resurrectionem ad dandam hominibus vitam æternam tributa: quemadmodum hanc gloriam ipse Christus vers. 2. describit. 6. quòd hanc gloriam Christus à Patre sibi datam esse asserat, datam autem non per æternam generationem, sed ex gratia, ex amore ac dilectione. ait enim Christus vers. 24. Pater quos dedisti mihi, volo ut, ubi ego sum, & illi sint mecum, videant gloriam meam, quam dedisti mihi. Cur verò? quia dilexisti me ante constitutionem mundi. 7. quòd eandem illam gloriam Christus discipulis suis se dedisse dicat, id est, juris eorum fecijse, vers. 22. quod ejusdem generis & Christi & discipulorum ejus gloriam esse indicat, licèt gradu multùm differat. At Deum ipsum summum esse, toto genere à fidelium gloria differt. in Christo ante tempora secularia, II. Tim. 1.9. longe aliud est, quam quod dicatur ea aliquis habere, vel habuisse.
units.tr: Tom. 2. stination only. So Paul said of those who believe in Christ that they were chosen by God in Christ before the foundation of the world, and that grace was given them before the secular times, because God, before the ages and the foundation of the world, had destined his glory and kingdom for them. Many things prove this. 1. That he asks that this glory be conferred on him by the Father. 2. That he asks that it be given to him with the Father, or in heaven. 3. That he begs that what was promised be given to him. To this also seem to point the words "which I had with you," as if he says what Augustine also observed: "I had glory with you, but grant that I may now have it with me." 4. The very subject, Jesus Christ, requires this. For Jesus Christ, that is, that man conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of Mary, anointed by God, could not in reality have had glory before the world was made. 5. The glory itself demands the same, namely the power over all flesh given to Christ as man after the resurrection to give eternal life to men, as Christ himself describes this glory in verse 2. 6. That Christ asserts this glory was given to him by the Father, but given not through eternal generation but from grace, from love and affection. For Christ says in verse 24: "Father, those whom you have given me, I wish that where I am they also may be with me, and may see my glory which you have given me." Why? Because you loved me before the foundation of the world. 7. That Christ says he gave that same glory to his disciples, that is, made it theirs by right (verse 22), which shows that the glory of Christ and of his disciples is of the same kind, though it differs greatly in degree. But God himself, the highest, differs wholly in kind from the glory of believers. To be in Christ before the secular times (2 Tim. 1.9) is far different from saying that someone has or had it.

units.la: Certè Deus credentes omnes & singulos elegit, ante mundi constitutionem, quamvis id alias negent Sociniani, & singulare divinitatis Christi argumentum in eo constituant, quod electus vel prædestinatus fuit ab æterno. Sed hæc Dei tota actio, & nihil inde adhuc homo habet, habebit quidem suo tempore. Christus verò dicitur habuisse illam gloriam. Et gratia data ante tempora secularia, sive destinata, sive promissa, & collocata in Christo; non à nobis habita, dicitur. Actiones Dei significantur, non nostræ. Non nos habuisse illam gratiam dicimur: quod etiamsi dictum, facilius in alium sensum exponere-tur, quam habere gloriam. Ut exemplorum maxima & manifesta appareat differentia. Nam dare etiam bene dicitur, qui proponit & concludit dare: sed quamvis dare, non item hic alter habere, quod ei destinatum ut longissimè post demum detur. Alioqui & nos omnes debebimur dici gloriam cœleste habuisse ante creatum mundum, quæ nobis tum destinata à Deo fuit. Quis verò non singulare hic videt aliquid de Christo dici, non tantum gloriæ, sed ejus habitæ ante mundum ratione, quod in aliis item locum non habeat? fac omnes dicere, se illud habuisse ante mundum conditum, quod ipsis à Deo tum destinatum, & videbis, ut inepte ac perperam phrasis, habere ante conditum mundum, exponatur de Dei tantum decreto ac destinatione. Præterquam, quod nullum istiusmodi acceptionis exemplum proferant, quod aliàs gnaviter, ubi possunt, solent Adversarii. Locum II Tim. 1.9. vertit Castalio: sed ob suum decretum & beneficium, quod nobis in Christo Jesu ante omnem temporum æternitatem donatum, nunc repræsentatum est adventu servatoris nostri Jesu Christi. Translatio Æthiopica, & dedit nobis gratiam in Christo Jesu, qui ante mundum erat. Adeo Christus quidem solus ante mundum: non vero nos tum vel fuisse, vel habuisse aliquid dici possumus. Non simpliciter dicitur, data nobis gratia, ante tempora secularia, sed data in Christo, id est, reposita in eo ut ex eo eam tandem & suo[?] tempore adipisceremur. ii. Videamus quæ evincere putet, Christum non reipsa gloriam ante mundum conditum habuisse, sed divino decreto ac destinatione tantum. i. Non petit Christus sibi demum conferri gloriam, sed suâ, quam habuit etiam ante mundum conditum, glorificari. Et fac, quod conferri sibi petat, an propterea dicit, destinatam sibi gloriam, & non quod reipsa eam habuit? Conferri sibi gloriæ suæ illustrationem & manifestationem petere jure potuit, hactenus velo mortalitatis & humilitatis admodum obscuratam: ut nihil minus tamen inde sequatur, quam quod Adversarius cupit. ii. Christus quidem postulat sibi gloriam apud Patrem, sed non exponit, in cælis. Quomodo vero in cælis, si in decreto tantum & destinatione? Non nego quin in cælis, sed & in terra, & ubique apud Patrem, atque à Patre, glorificatus post humiliationem Christus, & redditus pristino suo apud Patrem statui ac loco fuit, qui in passionibus & morte hactenus iram Patris sustinebat, & maledictio pro suis factus, dilectus in se nunquam non filius. Ad hanc conditionem & gloriam, apud Patrem, inde apud se, & alias, restitui Christus petit, idque ab ima & maledicta morte in quam sese jamjam erat dimissurus. iii. Gloria, quam habui, inquit Christus, non, quam mihi promisisti: promissionis hic non magis sit mentio, quam destinationis. Et quomodo promiserit, ante conditum mundum? Denique intelligatur promissio postmodum facta, & quod ex promissione petat sibi reddi plenissimam gloriam, neque inde sequitur, ipsum non reipsa istam gloriam ante mundum conditum habuisse, quam ad tempus quasi sequestratam redhiberi sibi nunc postulat. iv. Jesus Christus, qua Jesus Christus, reduplicative, ut ajunt, gloriam ante mundum conditum non habuit, sed quidem ille qui Jesus Christus, at qua Dei Filius, qua ratione ante suam è Maria nativitatem, & unctionem à Patre, extitit. Neque est quod regerant, sic respondendo peti, principium: nam nos hic non argumentamur, sed ad rationem ab Adversario allatam respondemus, eamque ostendimus nullarum esse virium. Quin ipsi ita agendo, istaque pro argumento adferendo, turpem committunt petitionem principii, ejusque quod est in quæstione. v. Quemadmodum in aliis hactenus responsionibus, ἀρνητικῶς primum egimus, & tum συγχωρητικῶς, ita quoque hic, negamus primo quod dicit, & deinde concesso eo, negamus quoque consequentiam. Negamus, quod gloria sit potestas omnis carnis Christo homini post resurrectionem data: cujus manifesta est ratio, quia hanc post resurrectionem demum, illam Christus habuit ante conditum mundum. Et quomodo potestatem omnis carnis habuit, antequam caro ulla fuit? Sin iterum dicant, destinatione: at sibi jam datam illam potestatem, testatur vers. 2. Et potestas hæc in omnem carnem, qua ratione dicitur, apud Patrem esse, apud quem se glorificari jam petit. Denique intelligatur etiam potestas in omnem carnem, sibi data, sub illa gloria, neque ita sequitur, Christum hanc non reipsa habuisse ante conditum mundum: neque enim ista se evertunt mutuo vel tollunt. Reddatur illa mihi gloria, quam ab æterno apud te habui, & post nebulam infirmitatis passionum mihi iterum refulgeat, uti nunc dedisti mihi potestatem in omnem carnem, post peractum præstitumque huc usque opus mediatorium: illud Pater, mihi Filio; istud, Christo.
units.tr: Certainly God chose all believers, each one, before the foundation of the world, although the Socinians deny this elsewhere and find in it a singular argument for the divinity of Christ, that he was chosen or predestined from eternity. But this is entirely God's action, and man has nothing from it yet, though he will have it in his time. Christ, however, is said to have had that glory. And grace given before the secular times, whether destined or promised and placed in Christ, is said not to have been had by us. The actions of God are signified, not ours. We are not said to have had that grace, and even if it were said, it would be more easily explained in another sense than "to have glory." So the great and clear difference between the examples appears. For one who proposes and resolves to give is also rightly said to give; but although we may say "give," the other cannot likewise say "have," since that is destined for him to be given much later. Otherwise we would all have to be said to have had heavenly glory before the world was created, since it was then destined for us by God. Who does not see that something singular is said here about Christ, not only of the glory but of the manner in which he had it before the world, which likewise has no place in others? Suppose everyone said that they had before the world was made what was then destined for them by God: you will see how foolish and wrong the phrase "to have before the world was made" becomes if it is explained only of God's decree and destination. Besides, they produce no example of such a sense, which the Adversaries, where they can, usually and diligently do produce elsewhere. Castalio translates 2 Tim. 1.9: "but on account of his decree and benefit, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before all the eternity of times, and now has been made manifest by the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ." The Ethiopic translation has: "and gave us grace in Christ Jesus, who was before the world." So Christ alone was before the world; we cannot be said then to have been, or to have had anything. It is not simply said that grace was given to us before the secular times, but given in Christ, that is, laid up in him, so that we might at last obtain it from him in its time. ii. Let us see what they think proves that Christ did not in reality have glory before the world was made, but only by divine decree and destination. i. Christ does not ask that glory be conferred on him at last, but that he be glorified with his own glory, which he had even before the world was made. And suppose he asks that it be conferred on him: does he therefore speak of glory destined for him, and not of his actually having it? He could rightly ask that the illustration and manifestation of his glory be conferred on him, since it had been much obscured, so far as mortality and humility went; yet nothing less follows from this than what the Adversary wants. ii. Christ indeed asks for glory with the Father, but does not say "in heaven." But how in heaven, if only in decree and destination? I do not deny that it is in heaven, but also on earth and everywhere, and with and from the Father, Christ was glorified after his humiliation and restored to his former standing and place with the Father, who until then, in his sufferings and death, had borne the Father's wrath and was made a curse for his own, the Son who was never not beloved. To this condition and glory, with the Father, and thence with himself and otherwise, Christ asks to be restored, and that from the lowest and accursed death into which he was about to be sent forthwith. iii. "The glory which I had," says Christ, not "which you promised me." There is no more mention of promise here than of destination. And how would he have promised before the world was made? Finally, let it be understood as a promise made afterwards, and that from the promise he asks that his full glory be restored to him. Nor does it follow from this that he did not in reality have that glory before the world was made, which he now asks to be given back to him as if set apart for a time. iv. Jesus Christ, as Jesus Christ, reduplicatively as they say, did not have glory before the world was made; rather, he who is Jesus Christ, as the Son of God, existed before his birth from Mary and his anointing by the Father. Nor is there reason for them to reply that by answering thus one begs the question, for we are not arguing here, but answering the argument brought by the Adversary and showing it to have no force. Indeed, by acting so and bringing this forward as an argument, they themselves commit a shameful begging of the question, and of the very point in dispute. v. As in the other responses so far, we first acted negatively [ἀρνητικῶς], and then concessively [συγχωρητικῶς]; so here too we first deny what he says, and then, granting it, we deny the consequence as well. We deny that glory is the power over all flesh given to Christ as man after the resurrection. The clear reason is that he had the one only after the resurrection, the other before the world was made. And how did he have power over all flesh before any flesh existed? But if they again say, by destination, yet verse 2 attests that this power had already been given to him. And this power over all flesh, in what sense is it said to be with the Father, with whom he now asks to be glorified? Finally, let it be understood that the power over all flesh given to him falls under that glory too; and it does not follow from this that Christ did not in reality have that glory before the world was made, for these do not overturn or cancel each other. Let that glory be given back to me, which I had with you from eternity, and after the cloud of the infirmity of my sufferings let it shine again for me, just as now you have given me power over all flesh after the mediatorial work so far done and accomplished. The former is the Father speaking to the Son; the latter is to Christ.

units.la: Quis vero futurus sensus, si per potestatem in omnem carnem, vers. 2. & gloriam apud Patrem vers. 5. intelligatur, sicut mihi dedisti potestatem, & ita da mihi eam? vi. gloriam istam filii non datam ex æterna generatione, ut probat? ex vers. 24. probet ergo primum, de eadem isthic agi gloria. Nam distinguimus nos in Christo, gloriam divinam, essentialem, naturalem, aeternam, ab oeconomica, & mediato-ria, quam etiam in humana natura, in tempore, accepit: & de utraque agitur hoc in capite, non ubique de eadem. Quidquid sit, illam haec non evertit. Pater dilexit Filium ab aeterno, & huic omnia etiam dedit, uti essentiam, ita gloriam dedit: coessentialem esse & conglorificandum secum. 7.
