Non dicit Christus verf. 22. se eandem suam gloriam discipulis dare, sed cum ejus gloria sit varia, & ex ejus plenitudine sui capiant quidquid habent, de gloria ejus participant fideles, tamquam ejus membra, & hoc vult verf. 22. & ego gloriam, quam dedisti mihi, dedi iis. Non vero dicit, omnem suam gloriam esse ejusdem generis, & a discipulorum gloria tantum gradu differre, cum sit διαφορώτερον ὄνομα [?]. Heb. 1.4.
units.tr: What would the meaning be if "power over all flesh" (v. 2) and "glory with the Father" (v. 5) were understood as "as you have given me power, so give it to me again"? See whether he proves from verse 24 that this glory of the Son was not given by eternal generation. He should first prove that the glory in question here is the same. For we distinguish in Christ the divine, essential, natural, eternal glory from the economic and mediatorial glory, which he also received in his human nature, in time. This chapter treats of both, not of the same glory everywhere. Whatever the case, this does not overturn the former. The Father loved the Son from eternity and gave him everything, including essence and glory, so that he is co-essential and to be glorified together with the Father. In verse 22 Christ does not say that he gives the disciples his own glory, but since his glory is manifold, and they receive whatever they have from his fullness, the faithful share in his glory as his members. This is what verse 22 means: "And the glory which you gave me I have given to them." He does not say that all his glory is of the same kind, differing from the disciples' glory only in degree, since it is a more excellent name [διαφορώτερον ὄνομα]. Heb. 1.4.

units.la: Ad Joan. xvi. 28. exivi a Patre, & veni in mundum: iterum relinquo mundum, & vado ad Patrem, Enjedinus excipit, non hic aliquem e caelo descensum notari, sed Deo mittenti obtemperare.
units.tr: On John 16:28, "I came out from the Father, and came into the world: again I leave the world, and go to the Father," Enjedinus objects that no descent from heaven is meant here, but obedience to God who sends.

units.la: Iam vero quod illa phrasi, neque aliquis e caelo descensus in terram, vel aliorsum denotetur, hinc patet. Certum est, secundum adversariorum sententiam, Christum antequam ex Maria nasceretur, solum quoad divinam naturam, fuisse in caelo, quae divina natura, etiam post incarnationem, non desiit esse in caelo, neque locum mutavit, quippe quae omnia, tanquam Deus, replet & ubique sit. Quomodo ergo Christus dicere potest, se exiisse, id est, progressum esse, & revera descendisse de caelo? Neque hoc etiam de natura humana Christi verum est, quae ante nativitatem in caelo non fuit, ideoque e caelo descendisse, atque a Deo exiisse non potuit. Cum ergo neutri naturae, hoc est, Christo iste sensus verborum competat, alia omnino interpretatio quaerenda est. Nos, exire a Deo, nihil aliud significare dicimus, quam auctore Deo, & illo jubente ac mittente, aliquid facere. Sicut ipsemet Christus explicat in sequentis capitis verf. 8. Et cognoverunt vere quia a te exivi, & crediderunt quia tu me misisti. Atque cum hoc eodem Capite verf. 17. dixisset discipulis: vos me amastis, & credidistis, quia ego a Deo exivi, explicat cap. 17. verf. 15. Pater juste, mundus te non cognovit, ego autem te cognovi, & hi cognoverunt quia tu me misisti. Ex quibus apparet, exire a Deo, esse, mitti a Deo. Venire autem in mundum, nihil est aliud quam missioni & mandato obtemperare, Mun-
units.tr: Now that in this phrase, "neither any descent from heaven to earth," or anything else is denoted, is clear from this. It is certain, according to the opponents' view, that Christ, before he was born of Mary, was in heaven only in respect of his divine nature. This divine nature, even after the incarnation, did not cease to be in heaven, nor did it change place, since as God it fills all things and is everywhere. How then can Christ say that he has gone out, that is, has proceeded, and has truly descended from heaven? Nor is this true of the human nature of Christ, which was not in heaven before its birth, and so could not have descended from heaven or come out from God. Since, then, this sense of the words belongs neither to the one nature nor to the other, that is, to Christ, an entirely different interpretation must be sought. We say that to go out from God means nothing other than to do something with God as its author, and at his command and sending. Christ himself explains this in verse 8 of the following chapter: "And they have known surely that I came out from you, and they have believed that you sent me." And when in this same chapter, verse 17, he had said to the disciples, "You have loved me and believed, because I came out from God," he explains it in chapter 17, verse 15: "Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me." From these passages it appears that to go out from God is to be sent from God. To come into the world, moreover, is nothing other than to obey the sending and command. Mun-

units.la: Resp. I. Nos adoritur κατὰ τὴν βίαιον [?], & studet evincere, neque secundum divinam, neque humanam naturam, Christo attribui posse illum e caelis descensum: ergo nulla prorsus ratione. Ad quod respondemus, illam Christi a Patre exitionem, & quod venit in mundum non intelligi de humana natura, sed de persona illa, secundum naturam divinam. Non quod divina proprie locum possit mutare, & caelum derelinquere, sed quod hic de ea dicatur, quemadmodum de Deo saepe in V. T. quod descendit in terram, & in hunc vel illum locum, non proprie & localiter, & cum ulla loci vel essentiae suae mutatione, sed quoad effectum, quando singulare aliquod opus in mundo, & hoc vel illo loco statuit perficere: sic quando Dei Patris Filius carnem assumere, & sub ea in mundo versari voluit, hac ratione de caelo venisse in mundum dicitur. Quod nisi extitisset antea, vere dici de eo nequaquam posset.
units.tr: Reply I. He attacks us [κατὰ τὴν βίαιον] and strives to prove that the descent from heaven cannot be ascribed to Christ either according to the divine or the human nature, and therefore in no way at all. To this we reply that this going out of Christ from the Father, and his coming into the world, is not understood of the human nature but of that person according to the divine nature. Not that the divine nature can properly change place and leave heaven, but that it is said of it here in the way that God is often said in the Old Testament to descend to the earth and to this or that place: not properly and locally, nor with any change of place or of his essence, but in respect of effect, when he decides to accomplish some singular work in the world at this or that place. So when the Son of God chose to assume flesh and to live in the world under it, in this way he is said to have come from heaven into the world. And unless he had existed before, it could in no way truly be said of him.

units.la: II. Exire a Deo dicit Adversarius, nihil aliud significare, quam auctore Deo & illo jubente ac mittente quidpiam facere. Sed hoc est finem & opus commiscere cum causa. Hoc enim ad prius istud sequitur, ejusque est effectum. Quemadmodum illa distinguit Christus, Joann. VI. 38. descendi de caelo, non ut facerem voluntatem [?] [?]do manifestum fieri, [?]ta quæ iussa sunt, perficere et exsequi. Ait igitur Christus, a Deo se exiisse, id est, missum esse: Se autem mittenti obtemperasse, et venisse in mundum. illo, sed ad eum sequebatur, ut cujus rei gratia Christus descenderat. III. Neque contrarium probatur, ex verf. 8. cap. seq. et cognoverunt vere quia a te exivi, et crediderunt quia tu me misisti: nam id non dicit, exire a Deo nihil aliud esse, quam Deo mittente aliquid facere. In eo quod Christus a Patre missus, exivit a Patre, et exivit missus, sed hæc aliud sunt, significant saltem, ab eo, quod Christus ita exiens a Patre, et missus peregit. Crediderunt discipuli, eum a Patre missum; verum aliud est, ad quod sit missus: in his vero verbis non est, quod Christus ex missione sua fecit, nedum ut idem illa, et nihil aliud significent.
units.tr: II. The adversary says that to go forth from God signifies nothing other than to do something at God's authority, at his command and by his sending. But this confuses the end and the work with the cause. For the one follows from the former and is its effect. Christ distinguishes these things in John 6:38: "I came down from heaven, not that I might do my own will," ... to make it manifest, but to perform and carry out what has been commanded. Christ therefore says that he went forth from God, that is, was sent; but that he obeyed the one sending and came into the world. That follows from it, but it is not the same thing; it is rather the purpose for which Christ came down. III. Nor is the contrary proved from v. 8 of the following chapter: "They have truly known that I came forth from you, and have believed that you sent me." For it does not say that going forth from God is nothing other than doing something at God's sending. That Christ, sent by the Father, went forth from the Father, and went forth as one sent, is true, but these are different things. They signify at least what Christ accomplished in going forth from the Father and being sent. The disciples believed that he was sent by the Father; but being sent is one thing, and the purpose for which he was sent is another. In these words there is not what Christ made of his mission, much less that these things signify the same thing and nothing else.

units.la: IV. Et hoc cap. XVI. verf. 27. quod dicit, exivi a Deo, mox explicat verf. 28. exivi a Patre; et veni in mundum. Quibuscum non pugnat, quod cap. XVII. 24. dicitur, et hi cognoverunt quia tu me misisti: etenim omnia illa in Christo agnoscenda, quod exivit a Patre, quod ab eo missus, quod venit in mundum: atque unum est quidem explicativum alterius, sed ad confirmationem mutuam faciens, et amplificationem, non ad diminutionem. Non ut exire a Deo nihil aliud fit, quam mitti a Deo; vel, aliquid facere Deo mittente. Præterquam quod nec ista pro eodem sumenda sint, mitti a Deo, et mittente Deo aliquid facere. Tum, si venire in mundum, nihil aliud fit, quam missioni obtemperare; et exire a Patre nihil aliud, quam Deo mittente ac jubente aliquid facere, quid adeo ista inter se distant? v. Revera Christus, qui a Deo Patre exivit, missus ab eo fuit, et mittenti perfectissime obtemperavit; sed non propterea phrases istæ hoc in loco usurpatæ nihil insuper aliud significant. Certe notant etiam eum, qui missus, ante suam istam missionem extitisse, fuisse apud Patrem, et extra mundum hunc, in quem missus. Quod ipsum illud est, quod ex hoc textu intendimus probare; et citra quod plenitudo ejus non satis accipitur. Quippe exire a Patre plus aliquid dicit, quam simpliciter mitti a Patre. Non quicunque a Patre mittitur, eo modo exit a Patre. Præsupponit certe, eum apud Patrem prius existere, qui ab eo ita missus exit. Sic enim cap. I. explicatum id Johanni, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum, verf. 11. in propria venit. 14. Et Verbum caro factum. Deinde idem ex opposito membro colligitur, et vado ad Patrem: quod est, ut apud Patrem agat: ita, quum venit a Patre, apud eum fuisse, intelligi debet. Simili modo, venire in mundum, et relinquere mundum, opponuntur, ut hoc venire in mundum connotet eum prius extra mundum fuisse, quemadmodum postea iterum extra mundum istum ivit.
units.tr: IV. And in this ch. 16, v. 27, where he says "I came forth from God," he immediately explains it in v. 28: "I came forth from the Father, and came into the world." This does not conflict with what is said in ch. 17, v. 24: "And these have known that you sent me." For all those things must be acknowledged in Christ: that he came forth from the Father, that he was sent by him, that he came into the world. One explains the other, certainly, but it serves to confirm and amplify each other, not to diminish. So "to go forth from God" is not nothing other than "to be sent from God", or "to do something at God's sending". Besides, these are not to be taken as the same: to be sent from God, and to do something at God's sending. Further, if to come into the world is nothing other than to obey the sending, and to go forth from the Father nothing other than to do something at God's sending and command, how then do these differ from each other? V. Indeed Christ, who went forth from God the Father, was sent by him, and most perfectly obeyed the one sending; but for that reason these phrases, used in this place, do not signify nothing beyond that. Certainly they also note that he who was sent existed before this sending of his, was with the Father, and outside this world into which he was sent. This is precisely what we intend to prove from this text, and without which his fullness is not sufficiently grasped. Indeed to go forth from the Father says something more than simply to be sent from the Father. Not everyone who is sent by the Father goes forth from the Father in that way. It certainly presupposes that he who so goes forth from the Father existed with the Father beforehand. For thus it is explained in ch. 1 of John: "and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (v. 1); v. 11, "he came to his own"; v. 14, "and the Word was made flesh." Then the same is inferred from the opposite member, "and I go to the Father", which means that he acts with the Father; so when he comes from the Father, it must be understood that he was with him. In a similar way, to come into the world and to leave the world are opposed, so that this coming into the world implies that he was outside the world beforehand, just as afterwards he went out of this world again.

units.la: Quod vero huiusmodi exitus et missio, nullam præexistentiam in coelo significat, ex similibus dictis facile ostendi potest. Nam Christus inquit Ioh. 17. verf. 18. Sicut tu (Pater) me misisti in mundum, et ego misi eos in mundum. Et cap. 20. verf. 21. Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos. Si ergo ex eo, quod Christus missus est a Deo in mundum, colligendum est, ipsum prius fuisse in coelo; idem de Apostolis quoque dicendum erit; nam dicit
units.tr: That such a going forth and sending does not signify any pre-existence in heaven can easily be shown from similar sayings. For Christ says in John 17:18, As you (Father) sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. And in chapter 20:21, As the Father sent me, so I send you. If therefore it must be inferred from the fact that Christ was sent by God into the world that he existed in heaven before, the same must also be said of the Apostles; for he says...

units.la: Resp. 1. Johann. XVII. 18: quemadmodum misit me Pater, &c. similitudo est in tertio missionis, non in modo ejus undiquaque et absolute pari. Quis enim hoc aufert adstruere, uti nec illud negare quisquam. Sensus est, tu me misisti Pater, sic et ego illos: non est paritas ubique modi urgenda, uti nec loci aut dignitatis. Καθὼς ergo est, uti sæpe Hebræorum ב, similitudinis, non paritatis. Deinde Christus similiter se illos misisse. At si quis infert, Christum quidem à Deo e coelo: Apostolos vero, e Iudaea a Christo esse missos. Respondebimus, tunc perire similitudinem, quam tamen Christus expressit. Deinde si Christus a coelo missus est, aut missus est, tunc cum natus est, aut postea cum docendi munus suscepit. Si primum dicatur: certe Christus & discipuli non poterunt dici similiter missi. Nam Apostoli postquam missi sunt, statim docuerunt; at Christus, non statim cum natus est, docuit. Deinde, Christi missio, erit nativitas. Apostolorum missio, erit ablegatio ad praedicandum Euangelium. Quae nullam habent similitudinem. de aliud est, mitti à Deo; aliud, venire, vel exire à Deo: iterum aliud, mitti in mundum; vel, venire in mundum. Mittuntur quidem Apostoli à Deo; non vero exeunt à Deo: & mittuntur à Christo in mundum, in mundo jam existentes ipsi; non vero veniunt in mundum Apostoli, sicut Christus dicitur venisse in mundum. Quis denique Apostolorum aut hominum audet de se dicere in singulari, ego exivi à Patre, & ego veni in mundum, uti id Christus de se asseruit? Non ergo ex eo simpliciter, quod Christus à Deo in mundum missus est, colligimus ipsum prius fuisse in caelo, sed ex caeteris quae adduntur, quod apud Patrem fuit, à Patre prodiit vel exivit, in mundum venit, ut iterum mundum relinqueret, & rediret ad Patrem. iv. Neque eo perit similitudo in Christi oratione, quando Christus statuitur à Deo è caelo missus; & Apostoli à Christo, ex Iudaea: quia manet istud tertium in quo vis similitudinis consistit, nempe utrobiq; missionis. Enjedinus, in Joann. v. 19. Simile enim, ut dicitur, non est idem. v. Christus à Deo missus est, tunc cum natus, & à Deo venit, ut mundum subintraret, ex qua missione post singulas officii partes curavit, & docendi munus, quemadmodum & alia, suo tempore adimplevit. Jam vero quamvis Christus, non statim ac natus, docuit, uti quidem Apostoli statim ac missi praedicarunt, & in eo temporis ordine non conveniant, possunt tamen & debent dici similiter missi à Deo, quia in missione conveniunt, non in singulis ejus circumstantiis, & omni τοίω[?]. Neque id in ulla, nedum hac, similitudine requiritur. Non in oratione Dominica, remitte nobis debita nostra sicut & nos, &c. ὡς ϰ̣[?], neque Eph.[?] v. 25. viri diligite uxores vestras, quemadmodum καθὼς ἡ[?] & Christus dilexit Ecclesiam. atque plurimis aliis in locis, seu exemplis. Joann. 11.6. & 111.3.7. qui facit justitiam justus est, quemadmodum καθὼς ipse justus est. non tamen omni prorsus modo, quemadmodum Christus; sed aliquo simili. & hoc ipso capite Joann. xvii. aliquoties καθὼς non aliter accipiendum venit: verf. 11. uti sint unum quemadmodum nos. verf. 16. non sunt ex mundo, quemadmodum ego non sum ex mundo. & verf. 21. 22. 23. quod dilexisti eos, quemadmodum me dilexisti. vel denique admittat illam τῷ καθὼς ergo expositionem in Joann. v.23. ut omnes honorent Filium, quemadmodum καθὼς honorant Patrem. vi. Christi missio non est nativitas, sed haec ex illa quidem, uti ex eadem, post nativitatem, reliqua: sic ex Apostolorum à Christo missione est, quod praedicarunt apud omnes Euangelium, & caeteras missionis suae partes administrarunt.
units.tr: Reply 1. On John 17:18, just as the Father sent me, etc.: the likeness lies in the third point of the sending, not in its manner, which is not altogether and absolutely the same. For who denies this, or who would deny that the one can be asserted? The sense is: you sent me, Father, so also I have sent them. It is not necessary to press the parity of manner everywhere, any more than of place or dignity. So [καθὼς] is used here, as the Hebrew [ב] often is, to express likeness, not equality. Then Christ likewise says that he sent them. But if someone infers that Christ was sent from heaven by God, while the Apostles were sent from Judea by Christ, we reply that then the likeness which Christ himself expressed would perish. Next, if Christ was sent from heaven, it was either when he was born or later, when he took up the office of teaching. If the first is said, then certainly Christ and the disciples cannot be said to have been sent in the same way. For the Apostles taught immediately after they were sent, but Christ did not teach immediately when he was born. Further, the sending of Christ would be his birth, while the sending of the Apostles would be their dispatch to preach the Gospel. These have no likeness. For it is one thing to be sent by God, another to come or go forth from God; and again one thing to be sent into the world, another to come into the world. The Apostles are indeed sent by God, but they do not go forth from God; and they are sent by Christ into the world, they themselves already existing in the world; but the Apostles do not come into the world as Christ is said to have come into the world. Lastly, which of the Apostles or of men dares to say of himself in the singular, I went forth from the Father, and I came into the world, as Christ asserted of himself? We therefore do not infer from the bare fact that Christ was sent into the world by God that he existed in heaven before; we infer it from the other things added: that he was with the Father, proceeded or went forth from the Father, came into the world, so that he might leave the world again and return to the Father. (iv.) Nor is the likeness in Christ's words destroyed when Christ is said to be sent from heaven by God, and the Apostles from Judea by Christ, because that third point in which the force of the likeness consists remains, namely, the sending in both cases. Enjedinus, on John 5:19: For a likeness, as it is said, is not the same thing. (v.) Christ was sent by God when he was born, and he came from God in order to enter the world; in this sending he afterwards fulfilled, in its proper time, the individual parts of his office, and the office of teaching, as well as the rest. Now although Christ did not teach as soon as he was born, whereas the Apostles preached as soon as they were sent, and although they do not agree in the order of time, they can and should nevertheless be said to be similarly sent by God, because they agree in the sending, not in its individual circumstances and every manner. Nor is such a likeness required in this passage alone. It is not required in the Lord's Prayer: forgive us our debts as we also [etc.], nor in Eph. 5:25, husbands, love your wives, just as [καθὼς] Christ loved the Church, nor in very many other places or examples. In John 11:6 and 3:3, 7, he who does righteousness is righteous, just as [καθὼς] he himself is righteous, the comparison is not in every respect like that of Christ, but in some similar way. And in this very chapter of John 17, καθὼς occurs several times and must be understood no differently: v. 11, that they may be one, just as we are; v. 16, they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world; and vv. 21–23, that you have loved them, just as you have loved me. Or, finally, let him admit that exposition of the phrase καθὼς in John 5:23, that all may honour the Son, just as [καθὼς] they honour the Father. (vi.) The sending of Christ is not his birth, but the rest follows from it, as from the same source, after his birth; so from the sending of the Apostles by Christ comes their preaching of the Gospel among all men and their performance of the other parts of their mission.

units.la: Quod diximus, non idem esse, mitti in mundum, ac exire à Patre, illud multis attribui, hoc soli Christo posse, conatur sic evertere Enjedinus:
units.tr: That we have said that to be sent into the world is not the same as to go forth from the Father, and that the former may be attributed to many but the latter only to Christ, Enjedinus tries to overturn thus:

units.la: Neque etiam obstat, quam alii quoque Pro-
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that others also...

units.la: Resp. 1. Nullum vel locum, vel exem-plum phetæ & Sancti, sunt à Deo sæpe, ad homines in mundum missi, qui tamen à Deo non dicuntur exiisse & in mundum venisse. 1. Nam primum de Iohanne legimus, illius doctrinam fuisse è cœlo. 2. Deinde Christus majori cum potentia & auctoritate, quàm quisquam unquam alius, est in mundum missus, ideo peculiari modo loquendi, ejus adventus significari potuit & debuit. 3. Præterea, non ideo dicendum est ipsum de Sanctis & Prophetis non esse dictum quia hodie in sacris literis id non legimus. Multa enim & dicta facta sunt, quæ literis consignata aut non sunt, aut consignata perierunt. 4. Denique, si non eadem verba: similes tamen sententias, legimus, etiam de Sanctis. Nam cum dicunt: Hæc dicit Dominus. Et Esaias: Dominus misit me. cum servos se Dei esse Prophetæ scribunt; tantumdem est ac si dicerent, se à Deo exiisse, & venisse in Mundum. fuisse, nunc vero perierit. Quod telum pertinaciæ semel datum, nihil ex Scripturis argui ultra poterit, neque ullius revinci contumacia: quia semper in promtu erit regerere, hoc & illud, quamvis nunc non legatur in scripturis, olim tamen Sacris literis consignatum fuisse, nunc autem periisse. Quemadmodum istum prorsus in modum Muhammedani respondent de suo Muhammedo, nomen ejus scriptum lectumque olim in Scripturis fuisse, Ioannis vid. cap.xv. 26. cum Paracleto illo alio, quem se missurum Christus ibi pollicetur; verius quod à Christianis ex malitia nomen illud deletum erasumque fuerit. Tale quid si etiam pro suis aliquibus hypothesibus dicere nunc Christiani incipiant, quid quæso impudentia non dicet, non tuebitur? Deinde quæ suspicio, vel levissima etiam suspicandi ratio, quod istud, à Deo scilicet exivisse & venisse in mundum, de prophetâ ullo vel sancto olim dictum fuerit, & nunc non legatur? Neque enim ita aliquid in sacris, vel de sacris dicendum est, absque ulla prorsus rationis specie. Denique negamus, tantundem esse quando Prophetæ scribunt, hæc dicit Dominus, vel, Dominus misit me, cum, exivisse à Patre, & venisse in mundu: illa enim doctrinæ ratione dicuntur & muneris Prophetici; hoc præsertim personæ, & ad significandam ejus ante hæc præexistentiam, quam manifeste ipsa verba continent & declarant.
units.tr: Reply 1. There is no place or example of the prophets and saints being sent often by God to men in the world who are nevertheless not said to have gone forth from God and come into the world. 1. For first we read of John that his teaching was from heaven. 2. Next, Christ was sent into the world with greater power and authority than anyone else ever was; therefore his coming could and should be signified by a particular manner of speaking. 3. Moreover, it should not be said that he was not spoken of concerning the saints and prophets merely because we do not read it today in the Holy Scriptures. For many things were both said and done which either were never committed to writing or, having been committed, have perished. 4. Finally, even if not the same words, we read similar statements also concerning the saints. For when they say, Thus says the Lord, and Isaiah, The Lord has sent me, when the prophets write that they are servants of God, it amounts to the same as if they said that they had gone forth from God and come into the world. ...had been, but now has perished. Once this weapon of obstinacy is given, nothing further can be argued from the Scriptures, nor can anyone's stubbornness be refuted; for it will always be ready to reply that this or that, though it is not now read in the Scriptures, was once committed to the sacred writings but has now perished. In exactly this way the Muslims answer about their Muhammad, that his name was once written and read in the Scriptures, in John 15:26, with that other Paraclete whom Christ there promises to send; more truly, that name was deleted and erased by the Christians out of malice. If the Christians now begin to say something of this kind even about some of their own hypotheses, what, I ask, will impudence not say or not defend? Moreover, what suspicion, or even the slightest ground for suspecting, is there that this, namely that someone went forth from God and came into the world, was once said of any prophet or saint and is now not read? For nothing ought to be said in or about the sacred things without some appearance of reason at all. Finally, we deny that it amounts to the same thing when the prophets write, Thus says the Lord, or the Lord has sent me, as when they write, went forth from the Father, and came into the world; for the former are said by reason of the teaching and the prophetic office, the latter especially by reason of the person, and to signify his pre-existence before these things, which the words themselves plainly contain and declare.

units.la: Deinde, quia argumentamur ex voce πάλιν iterum relinquo mundum, quod Christus eo significet, se etiam alias extra mundum fuisse, nempe antequam exiens à Patre, in mundum veniret, excipit Adversarius primum, istud adverbium non semper denotare iterationem, aut idem quod denuo, quod neque nos negamus, & suo loco sumus annotaturi ad expositionem loci Heb. vi. 6. iterum renovari, unde adversus nos argumentantur, & contra perseverantiam sanctorum: sed, præterquam quod nihil in hoc textu Ioann. xvi. 28. fit quod illam τὸ πάλιν[?] significationem, quam frequentissimam Adversarius fatetur, haud ferat, sermonis ratio eam prorsus efflagitat. Neque chiasmum statuere hic necesse; sed ipsa, quò referri debeant, indicant verba, & veni in mundum, iterum relinquo mundum, ut juncta proximè in oratione, ita & sibimet opposita: quemadmodum ex altera parte, exivi à Patre, & vado ad Patrem.
units.tr: Next, since we argue from the word πάλιν [palin] that Christ says "I leave the world again," and that he therefore was outside the world at some earlier time, namely before he went out from the Father and came into the world, our opponent first objects that this adverb does not always denote repetition or mean "again." We do not deny this, and we will note it in its place when we explain Heb. 6:6, "to be renewed again," where they argue against us and against the perseverance of the saints. But apart from this, nothing in the text of John 16:28 is such that it would not bear the meaning of πάλιν which our opponent admits to be the most frequent. The sense of the passage demands it outright. We need not posit a chiasm here. The words themselves show what each clause refers to: I came into the world, and again I leave the world, which are placed next to each other in the sentence and also set against each other, just as on the other side are I went out from the Father and I go to the Father.

units.la: Ad argumentum verò quod hic iterum ingerit Adversarius, jam in praecedentibus respondimus: Deinde, ne ipsi quidem possunt, ista eodem modo explicare. Nam certè illud: Exivi à Patre, dictum volunt respectu divinae naturae, Humana enim natura, nec genita est ex Dei essentia, nec è coelo descendit. At hoc posterius: Vado ad Patrem, dicunt verum esse respectu humanae naturae; quia divina jam erat, imo semper fuit in coelo, nec unquam recessit à Patre. Ergo non potest proprie de ea dici, quod profecta sit ad Patrem; sed hoc tribuendum est carni & humanae naturae, quae proprie ad Deum, in coelum sublata est. Apparet ergo, neque secundum adversarios, in eodem sensu sumi utrumque oppositionis membrum: ac proinde nec nobis vitio esse vertendum si diversimode illa explicemus. Nam, exire à Patre, & ad eum reverti, dicimus de persona intelligendum, Christo, sed, quoad naturas diversimode: exivit à Patre, quod ad effectum singulare divinae naturae, in sui incarnatione; rediit ad Patrem, cum humanâ.
units.tr: As for the argument which our opponent raises again here, we have already answered it in the preceding discussion. He says: Further, they themselves cannot explain these things in the same way. For they certainly want the words "I went out from the Father" to be said with respect to the divine nature, since the human nature was neither begotten of the essence of God nor came down from heaven. But of the latter, "I go to the Father," they say it is true with respect to the human nature, since the divine nature was already there, indeed had always been in heaven, and never departed from the Father. Therefore it cannot properly be said of the divine nature that it went to the Father; this must be attributed to the flesh and the human nature, which was properly taken up to God into heaven. It is evident, then, that neither according to our opponents are both members of the opposition taken in the same sense; and therefore we should not be blamed if we explain them in different ways. For we say that to go out from the Father and to return to him is to be understood of the person, of Christ, but differently with respect to the natures: he went out from the Father with respect to the singular effect of the divine nature, in his incarnation; he returned to the Father with the human nature.

units.la: Ad locum Eph. iv. 9. 10. quod adscendit; quid est, nisi quod descendit primum ad inferiores partes terrae, ita excipit Enjedinus: Quod verò Christus descendisse in infimas terrae partes dicitur; & rursus, ascendisse supra coelos: dupliciter interpretari possumus. Primo ut illa verba proprie: Secundo, ut figurate accipiantur. Si proprie accipiantur, per descensum in intimas terrae partes, intelligatur Mors & Sepultura Christi. Nos verò haud negamus, hic intelligi Christi humiliationem, & adscensionem, atque adeptam ex eâ gloriam & majestatem: tum in descensu ejus ad infimas terrae partes, connotari quoque ejus mortem, & sepulturam: sed plus, nempe quoque ejus descensum è coelo: atque eo facere praesertim haec verba, qui descendit, idem est qui & adscendit supra omnes coelos. Uti nempe in coelos istos adscendit, sic & ex iis descenderat idem, quando in terram venit, atque in terram coelo oppositam descendit. Nam, ut annotant eruditi, hic tota terra consideratur, & confertur toti coelo, seu aetherea regioni, non autem pars una terrae, cum caeteris. Sicut ergo nihil est coelo superius: ita nihil terra humilius, & magis deorsum.
units.tr: On Eph. 4:9–10, "that he ascended, what is it but that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth," Enjedinus answers as follows: But as for the statement that Christ descended into the lowest parts of the earth, and again that he ascended above the heavens, we may interpret this in two ways. First, that these words are taken properly; second, that they are taken figuratively. If they are taken properly, the descent into the lowest parts of the earth is understood as the death and burial of Christ. We, however, do not deny that the humiliation and the ascension of Christ are meant here, and the glory and majesty gained from it; and that in his descent to the lowest parts of the earth his death and burial are also implied. But more is meant, namely also his descent from heaven; and the words he who descended is the same who also ascended above all the heavens especially make this clear. Just as he ascended into those heavens, so the same one also came down from them when he came into the earth and descended into the earth, which is set over against heaven. For, as learned men observe, here the whole earth is considered and compared with the whole heaven, that is, the ethereal region, and not one part of the earth with the others. Therefore just as nothing is higher than heaven, so nothing is lower than the earth, and more downward.

units.la: Ad Heb. xiii. 8. Iesus Christus heri & hodie, ipse & in saecula, sic iterum Enjedinus:
units.tr: On Heb. 13:8, Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, the same also for ever, Enjedinus again says as follows:

units.la: Quia Iesu Christi existentia, in his verbis, per omnes differentias temporis, praeteritum nimirum, praesens & futurum, adstrui videtur: inde colligunt quidam, Christum esse aeternum Deum. Sed hoc pacto[?] argumentari, nimis frivolum est. Nam istae temporis differentiae, quae hic iis[?] nominibus exprimuntur, non aeternitatem, sed certum, determinatum, & definitum tempus denotant. Unde qui sunt prudentiores, neque hic de Christi essentia, sed cognitione agi, neque etiam per vocem heri, aliud quam veteris testamenti tempus significari putant. At neque cognitio Christi, aeterna dici potest, quia homines[?], ad quos ista cognitio pertinet, aeterni
units.tr: Because the existence of Jesus Christ is asserted in these words through all the distinctions of time, namely past, present and future, some conclude from this that Christ is the eternal God. But to argue in this way is too frivolous. For these distinctions of time, which are expressed here by these names, do not denote eternity but a certain, determined and defined time. Hence the more prudent men think that here it is not about the essence of Christ but about the knowledge of him, and that by the word yesterday nothing else is meant than the time of the Old Testament. But neither can the knowledge of Christ be called eternal, because the men to whom this knowledge pertains are not eternal.

units.la: Resp. I. Qui de cognitione Christi haec intelligenda afferunt, haud negant ideo & de essentia Christi accipienda esse, vel eum extitisse toto illo tempore, quo agnitus etiam sub V.T. fuit; & propterea in textu dici, non cognitus Christus, sed ipse, supple, est. II. Adverbia haec temporis, secundum omnes ejus differentias, indicant Christum semper fuisse eundem, & qui hodie, eundem & olim fuisse, & mansurum in perpetuum. III. Quod homines Iobo dicuntur fuisse ἐφήμεροι, hoc ipsum satis innuit aliam esse phrasis rationem, quando aliquis non ab hesterno non sunt, sed certo tempore a Deo creati; neque etiam vetus testamentum, aeternum est, quoniam certo tempore, hoc est, cum Abrahamo coepit. Unde sequitur, nullam hic aeternitatem describi.
units.tr: Answer, I. Those who maintain that these things are to be understood of the knowledge of Christ do not deny that they must therefore also be taken of the essence of Christ, or that he existed through the whole time in which he was also known under the Old Testament; and that for this reason the text says not that Christ was known, but that he himself (supply: is the same). II. These adverbs of time, in all their distinctions, indicate that Christ has always been the same, both he who is today and he who was the same formerly, and who will remain for ever. III. That men are said in Job to be ephemeral (ἐφήμεροι), this itself sufficiently suggests that another manner of speaking is used when someone is not from yesterday, but was created by God at a certain time; nor is the Old Testament eternal, since it began at a certain time, that is, with Abraham. From this it follows that no eternity is described here.

units.la: Quin potius per voces Heri & hodie, videtur significari res recens, nupera, & quae non ita pridem initium habuerit. Nam homines, dicuntur Iobi 8. verf. 9. hesterni, & apud Graecos idem ἐφήμεροι, id est, hodierni: propter ae-tatis brevitatem, & parvam durationem. Citius igitur voces hae Heri & hodie, momentaneam durationem, quam aeternitatem significaverint.
units.tr: Rather, through the words yesterday and today there seems to be signified something recent, of recent date, which has not begun very long ago. For men are called yesterday's in Job 8:9, and among the Greeks the same word ἐφήμεροι means "of the day," that is, of today, on account of the brevity of their life and their short duration. Therefore these words yesterday and today will sooner have signified a momentary duration than eternity.

units.la: hesterno, sed idem heri ac hodie, esse dicirur.. Deinde additum iis, & in saecula idem, designat hoc pari modo de anteriori tempore accipiendum esse; ut in tempore praeterito, praesenti, & futuro semper idem sit ac maneat Christus. iv. Nec primo & proprie voces has heri & hodie aeternitatem notare statuimus, sed temporis omnem rationem ac periodos, quibus Christus fuerit semper idem, & non demum hodie factus: nempe ut idem semper omnium salvandorum fuerit mediator ac salus: nam uti bene Enjedinus inquit:
units.tr: Yet not "yesterday" in the sense of the past, but that the same is said to be yesterday and today. Next, the addition to these, and for ever the same, designates that this must be taken in the same way of the former time, so that in past, present and future time Christ is always the same and remains so. IV. Nor do we hold that these words yesterday and today primarily and properly denote eternity, but rather every reckoning and period of time in which Christ has been always the same and was not only made so today; namely that he has always been the same mediator and salvation of all who are to be saved. For, as Enjedinus rightly says:

units.la: Similes sunt huic phrasis illae: Ego sum primus & novissimus. Et 1 Cor. 1. verf. 12. Fundamentum aliud poni non potest, praeter id quod positum est, Iesus Christus. Et Actor. 4. verf. 12. Non est aliud nomen sub coelo datum, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri, &c. Denique. Quinto. Hoc saltem in loco, heri & hodie non potest significare recens aliquid & momentaneum, quia id & Christi dignitati, & huic, quae hoc in loco est, de eo praedicationi, & posteriori denique sermonis membro, & in saecula ipse, nimis quam adversatur. Quid enim hoc, & in saecula ipse? si momentaneus, & brevis admodum durationis?
units.tr: Similar to this are those phrases: "I am the first and the last." And 1 Cor. 3:11, "No other foundation can be laid than that which is laid, Jesus Christ." And Acts 4:12, "There is no other name under heaven given, by which we must be saved," etc. Finally, fifthly: in this place at least, yesterday and today cannot mean something recent and momentary, because that is utterly opposed both to the dignity of Christ, and to the predication about him which is in this place, and finally to the latter member of the sentence, and for ever the same. For what does this "and for ever the same" mean, if he is momentary and of very brief duration?

units.la: Pro creationis autem opere, Christo attributo, praeter Ioan. 1. etiam haec sunt Scripturae S. loca. Col. 1. 16. Nam per ipsum, ἐν αὐτῷ (Castellio, per eum. Racovienfis versio, durch ihn) creata sunt omnia quae in coelis, & quae in terra, visibilia & invisibilia, sive throni, sive dominationes, &c. Nempe, inquit Schlichtingius, cuncta quae sub Evangelio creata. In disputatione contra Balthasarem Meisnerum, de Trinitate, pag. 346.
units.tr: Moreover, for the work of creation attributed to Christ, besides John 1, these passages of Holy Scripture also occur. Col. 1:16, For through him (ἐν αὐτῷ [en autō]; Castellio, through him; the Racovian version, durch ihn, "through him") all things were created, which are in heaven and which are on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions, etc. Namely, says Schlichting, all things that were created under the Gospel. In his disputation against Balthasar Meisner, on the Trinity, p. 346.

units.la: In posteriore vero Col. 1.16. agitur de nova creatione. Multa id evincunt. 1. Ipsum Iesu Christi Nomen, quod non alium, quam hominem illum ex Spiritu S. conceptum, & ex Virgine natum indicat. 2. Mentio causae creationis istius mediae, quae in veteri creatura locum non habet. 3. Quod istius creaturae primogenitus, i. e. inter has omnes creaturas, & tempore & dignitate primus esse dicatur, & sic in earum numerum referatur. Iam vero Christus eo modo ad veteres creaturas, nisi Arriani esse velimus, referri non debet. 4. Quod non ipsum coelum & terra, sed tantum ea, quae sunt in coelo, & quae in terra, per Christum creata dicuntur. At cum de veteri rerum omnium creatione agitur, nunquam coelum & terra omittitur, praesertim eorum, quae in coelo & in terra sunt, distincta mentione facta: quin potius coeli & terrae creatio pro omnium etiam reliquarum rerum crea-
units.tr: But in the latter passage, Col. 1:16, the new creation is in view. Many things prove this. 1. The very name of Jesus Christ, which indicates no one other than that man conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin. 2. The mention of the cause of this intermediate creation, which has no place in the old creature. 3. That he is said to be the firstborn of this creature, that is, first among all these creatures both in time and in dignity, and so is counted among their number. Now Christ should not be referred to the old creatures in that way, unless we wish to be Arians. 4. That it is not heaven and earth themselves, but only those things which are in heaven and which are on earth, that are said to be created through Christ. But when the old creation of all things is in view, heaven and earth are never omitted, especially with a distinct mention made of those things which are in heaven and on earth; rather, the creation of heaven and earth is put for the creation of all other things too.

units.la: Nos breviter respondemus. Ad primum. 1. Ipsum Iesu Christi nomen non occurrit isto loco, quem jam urgemus, pro ejus Deitate, vel creationis opere divino, id est, verf. 15. 16. 17. Deinde, quamvis occurreret, subjectum sermonis denotaret, non tolleret, ut de isto subjecto praedicaretur opus creationis, vel creatorem illum esse. Quemadmodum Iesu Christi nomen si occurrat, & hominem illum denotet (Adversariis loquor) ex Spiritu S. conceptum, & ex virgine natum, non impedit quo minus tamen dicatur divinus, Deus, & ante Abrahamum olim fuisse, sensu etiam Adversariorum, in quo Christi divinitatem collocant: ita neque etiam si de Christo praedicetur vera Deitas. Nam uti illud, sic istud alia ratione de eodem intelligitur, quam qua conceptus, aut natus. Varia
units.tr: We reply briefly. To the first point. 1. The name of Jesus Christ does not occur in the passage we are now pressing, either for his Deity or for the divine work of creation, that is, in verses 15, 16 and 17. Moreover, even if it did occur, it would only denote the subject of the discourse, and would not prevent the work of creation, or being the creator, from being predicated of that subject. Just as the name of Jesus Christ, if it occurs and denotes that man (I speak to our opponents) conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of a virgin, does not prevent him from also being called divine, God, and from having existed before Abraham, even in the sense of our opponents, in which they locate the divinity of Christ, so neither does the name prevent true Deity from being predicated of him. For the one thing is understood of the same person in one way, and the other in another way, just as the conception and the birth are. III. The name of Jesus Christ does not denote any other man than the one born of Mary, but it can also be used when a generation other than the human one is meant, for example Matthew 16:16, "You are Christ, the Son of the living God."

units.la: Tom. 2, tione ponitur. 5. Quod omnia ista, quæ per Christum, sive in cœlis, sive in terra creata esse dicuntur, quemadmodum ex sequentibus Pauli verbis apparet, ad solos angelos & homines, seu creaturas mente præditas referantur. 6. Quia alibi etiam idem Paulus non de alia, quam de nova creatione, seu omnium rerum per Christum immutatione facta loquens, dicit Deum omnia creasse per Iesum Christum, Eph. 3. 9. 7. Quod ex sequentibus liquido appareat, ad Christi resurrectionem a mortuis, & ad tempora novi fœderis, eaque res, quæ per illum sub N. fœdere sunt peratta, respici. Quæ eadem habet in explicatione loci istius, seorsim edita, aliisque. de eodem dici possunt, secundum alium & alium modum. III. Jesu Christi nomen non alium denotat hominem quam Mariâ natum, sed adhiberi tamen potest etiam quando alia ejus generatio designatur, quam humana. v. g. Matth. xvi. 16. Tu es Christus, Filius Dei viventis.
units.tr: Vol. 2, can be said of the same person in different ways and according to different modes. 5. That all those things which are said to have been created through Christ, whether in the heavens or on the earth, as appears from the following words of Paul, refer only to the angels and to men, or to creatures endowed with mind. 6. Because Paul himself elsewhere, speaking not of any other creation than the new creation, or the renewal of all things through Christ, says that God created all things through Jesus Christ, Ephesians 3:9. 7. Because it is clear from what follows that the reference is to the resurrection of Christ from the dead and to the times of the New Covenant, and to those things which have been accomplished under him in the New Covenant. He has the same things in his separately published explanation of this passage, and in other works.

units.la: Ad secundum, Resp. 1. non fit mentio Christi, tamquam causæ creationis media. II. Ἐν αὐτῷ [?] per eum, de Deo, vel Patre (ut cum Adversariis loquar) etiam dicitur, Act. xvii. 29. ἐν αὐτῷ, in ipso enim vivimus & movemur, & sumus, quod est, per ipsum, ejus vim, influxum & providentiam. Pari ratione aliquando de Christo dicitur idem quod de Patre, juxta expositionem Adversariorum, 1 Ioan. v. 20. & sumus in vero illo, quod de Deo Patre exponunt, & in filio ejus Iesu Christo. III. Pater per Filium operatur, & creat, non tamquam per causam mediam, in opere simpliciter divino: Aliter in opere œconomico, & mediatorio.
units.tr: To the second point, the reply is: 1. There is no mention of Christ as the means of creation. II. "In him" [ἐν αὐτῷ] is also said of God, or of the Father (to speak with our opponents), Acts 17:28, "in him" [ἐν αὐτῷ], for in him we live and move and have our being, that is, through him, by his power, influence and providence. For the same reason, something is sometimes said of Christ that is said of the Father, according to the interpretation of our opponents, 1 John 5:20: and we are in that true one, which they explain of God the Father, and in his Son Jesus Christ. III. The Father works and creates through the Son, not as through an intermediate cause, in the work that is simply divine. In the economic and mediatorial work it is otherwise.

units.la: Ad tertium, Resp. 1. Christus dicitur πρωτότοκος [?] primogenitus omnis creaturæ, non quod propterea ex censu creaturarum sit, quarum respectu primus dicatur; sed per metaphoram, in hoc solo sitam, quod primus omnium sit, verf. 18. ut sit in omnibus πρωτεύων [?]. Non ut ejusdem ideo generis sit cum aliis. II. Neque, juxta Adversarios, Christus ejusdem census est cum creaturis (ita ad hominem loquor) Euangelicis. Namque Schlichtingius in Explicatione quatuor locor. ideo notat Christum non dictum primo creatum inter creaturas, sed primogenitum, quo ostenderetur, inquit, hanc Christi creationem non communem, sed singularem esse, unde peculiariter factus sit Dei Filius. Quemadmodum, ait, ab altera parte, Christum non nominat primogenitum omnium filiorum Dei, vel fratrum suorum. Nempe quia hæc Christi primogenitura in se talem comprehendit generationem ex Deo, ut eo respectu Deus non alios ullos filios habeat, neque Christus fratres. Quare, infero, Christum primogenitum dici creaturarum, eum etiam in earum numerum referendum non probat. III. Neq; phrasis magis obstat, ut explicetur primogenitus creaturarum, omnibus creaturis & dignitate & tempore prior, per generationem æternam ex Patre; quam ut per aliam quam singularem à reliquis fidelibus, quam Adversarius fingit.
units.tr: To the third point, the reply is: 1. Christ is called the firstborn [πρωτότοκος] of every creature, not because he therefore belongs to the number of creatures, with respect to which he might be called first; but by a metaphor lying in this alone, that he is first of all, verse 18, so that he may have the first place [πρωτεύων] among all things. Not so that he is therefore of the same kind as the others. II. Nor, according to our opponents, is Christ of the same rank as the evangelical creatures (I speak to the man in his own terms). For Schlichting, in his Explanation of Four Passages, notes that Christ is not called the first created among creatures, but the firstborn, by which, he says, it is shown that this creation of Christ is not common but singular, whence he was made the Son of God in a peculiar way. Just as, he says, on the other hand, Christ does not call himself the firstborn of all the sons of God, or of his brothers. Clearly, because this firstbornship of Christ contains in itself such a generation from God that, in that respect, God has no other sons and Christ has no brothers. Therefore, I conclude, the fact that Christ is called the firstborn of creatures does not prove that he is to be reckoned in their number. III. Nor does the expression stand in the way of explaining "firstborn of creatures" as prior to all creatures both in dignity and in time, through his eternal generation from the Father; which is no less acceptable than the singular explanation, distinct from that of the other faithful, which the opponent invents.

units.la: Ad quartum, Resp. 1. Elumbe argumentum, dicuntur per Christum creata ea quæ in cælo & in terra, ergo non agitur de illorum creatione. Quis non talem argumentationem rideat, vel potius multa cum indignatione rejiciat? II. Imo quis dubitet, creata intelligi cælum & terram, ubi creata dicuntur quæcumq; in illis omnia τὰ πάντα τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, &c. III. Ubi & omnium rerum subjungitur mox distributio, in τὰ ὁρατὰ, & τὰ ἀόρατα.. IV. Dicitur πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως omnis creaturæ primogenitus, id est, primus, & creator, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη: quod si omnis creaturæ, ergo & cæli terræque. v. Vos omnem creaturam accipitis Euangelicam, citra ullius exceptionem: quare ergo verba eadem, ad nostrum sensum, non poterunt sumi de omni creatura mundanâ? vi. Dicuntur creata per Christum quæ sunt in cælo, & quæ in terra: falsum, quod ea tantum dicuntur. vii. Proba hoc discrimen subesse inter duas locutiones, creare cælum & terram, atque creare ea quæ in cælo & terra, ut illud creationem rerum denotet, hoc renovationem Euangelii. viii. Proba, ullam rei & materiæ tractandæ diversitatem ista ratione significari. ix. Renovatio Euangelii non complectitur omnia quæ ubique sunt τὰ πάντα τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς[?]: at creatio imo: quare illud istis non significatur. x. Phrasis, τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίοις καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς[?], significat omnia, quæ ubicumque sunt. Deut. III.24. quis Deus est in cælo aut terra qui faciat secundum opera tua? adde 1 Reg.viii.23. xi. Illud ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίοις καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς[?], omnes, quæ in mundo sunt, creaturas designat. Apoc. v.13. καὶ πᾶν κτίσμα ὃ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ[?], καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ, καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς θαλάσσης ἃ ἐστί[?], καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς πάντα. ad quæ se non extendit renovatio Euangelii, & creatio nova spiritualis in Christo. xii. Qui dicitur creasse omnia quæ in cælo, & quæ in terra, eo intelligi satis debet creasse quoque ipsum cælum & terram. Quid obstat? Nam ita junguntur illa sæpe; opponuntur nunquam. Exod. xx.11. nam sex diebus fecit Dominus cœlos & terram & mare, & omnia quæ in iis. Psalm. lxxx. ix. 12. Tuum cœlum, & tua terra, mundum & plenitudinem ejus tu fundasti. Psalm. xcv.4.5. & cxlvi.6.
units.tr: To the fourth point, the reply is: 1. A feeble argument: things in heaven and on earth are said to have been created through Christ, therefore the creation of those things is not the subject. Who would not laugh at such an argument, or rather reject it with great indignation? II. Indeed, who would doubt that heaven and earth are to be understood as created, when all the things in them are said to have been created: all things in the heavens [τὰ πάντα τὰ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς], etc.? III. Where also a division of all things into things visible and invisible [τὰ ὁρατὰ and τὰ ἀόρατα] is added immediately. IV. He is called the firstborn of all creation [πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως], the firstborn of every creature, that is, the first, and the creator, because in him all things were created [ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη]; but if of every creature, then of heaven and earth too. V. You accept every evangelical creature without any exception: why, then, can the same words, in our sense, not be taken of every worldly creature? VI. It is said that things in heaven and things on earth are created through Christ: it is false that they are only said so. VII. Prove that there is this distinction between the two expressions, to create heaven and earth, and to create the things that are in heaven and on earth, namely that the former denotes the creation of things, the latter the renewal of the gospel. VIII. Prove that any difference of subject and matter is signified by this way of speaking. IX. The renewal of the gospel does not embrace all things that are everywhere on earth [τὰ πάντα τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς]; but creation does: therefore that phrase is not meant for the former. X. The phrase, things in the heights and on the earth [τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίοις καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς], signifies all things wherever they are. Deuteronomy 3:24, what God is there in heaven or on earth who does works like yours? Add 1 Kings 8:23. XI. That were created [ἐκτίσθη] of all things in the heights and on the earth designates all the creatures that are in the world. Revelation 5:13, "and every creature [κτίσμα] which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the sea, and all the things in them," to which the renewal of the gospel and the new spiritual creation in Christ do not extend. XII. He who is said to have created all things in heaven and on earth must surely be understood to have created heaven and earth themselves too. What stands in the way? For these are often joined together; never opposed. Exodus 20:11, for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and sea, and all that is in them. Psalm 89 (Vulgate 88):12, Yours is the heaven, and yours is the earth; you founded the world and its fullness. Psalm 95:4-5 and 146:6.

units.la: Ad quintum, Resp. i. Negatur, ad solas creaturas mente præditas, seu Angelos, seu homines referri, quæ Paulus dicit de omnibus per Christum creatis. ii. Aliud est, per illa prius explicari, & exponi per hæc ut præcipua creaturarum, quod de omnibus per Christum creatis dicitur; aliud, ad illa, tanquam sola restringi. iii. Imo contra textum restringit, quia universim omnia dicuntur per ipsum facta, multoties. πάσης κτίσεως[?], ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα. Τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ. Καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων, καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε. Jam autem creaturæ rationales solæ non sunt omnia illa. iii. Imo si creaturæ omnes rationales per eum factæ, facile idem est concludere de reliquis.
units.tr: To the fifth point, the reply is: i. It is denied that Paul, when he speaks of all things created through Christ, refers only to creatures endowed with mind, whether angels or men. ii. It is one thing to have those things explained first through these, and expounded by them as the chief of creatures, which is said of all things created through Christ; it is another to be restricted to those alone. iii. Indeed, he restricts the text against its wording, since all things are said universally, many times, to have been made through him: of all creation [πάσης κτίσεως], all things were created [ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα], all things through him [Τὰ πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ], and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him [Καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων, καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε]. Now, rational creatures alone are not all those things. iii. Indeed, if all rational creatures were made through him, it is easy to conclude the same of the rest.

units.la: Ad sextum. Resp. i. Hic se prodit Theologiæ Socinianæ methodus, vocis alicujus inquirere aliam forte acceptionem quocunq; demum in loco, ut inde tum contra clarissimum & proprium textus sensum obnitantur. Sic, quia alibi vox creationis sumitur de nova & spirituali creatione; ergo hic quoque, & non de creatione Physica? Negamus consequentiam. ii. Eph. iii. agitur de Euangelio, ejusque revelatione & prædicatione, quod in loco Col. i.15.16.17. ostendi nequit. iii. Non solum verbum κτίσεως occurrit Col.i.15.16.17. sed tum verba, tum res creationis, ejusq; explicatio, ut manifestius exprimi ea non potuerint. iv. Deniq; & nego Eph. iii.9. τῷ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ[?] exponenda esse de nova creatione per Euangelium; dico intelligenda esse, quemadmodum in loco nostro, de creatione propriâ rerum omnium in initio, ut hoc obiter de Christo commemoret Apostolus, per eundem redimi mundum, per quem, utpote Deum, & Dei Filium, mundus olim creatus fuerat. Theophylactus in hunc locum: καλῶς κτίσεως[?] ἐμνημόνευσεν, pulchre creationis meminit, Qui omnia condidit, Deus, inquit, est per Christum. Sine ipso enim, inquit, factum est nihil. Quae eadem habet ante eum Chrysostomus.
units.tr: To the sixth. Reply: Here the method of the Socinian theology reveals itself: to look for some other meaning of a word, wherever it may be, so that they may then resist the clear and proper sense of the text. Thus, because the word creation is elsewhere taken of a new and spiritual creation, therefore here too it is not of physical creation? We deny the inference. (2) Ephesians 3 deals with the gospel, its revelation and preaching, which cannot be shown in the passage of Colossians 1:15, 16, 17. (3) The word creation [κτίσεως] occurs not only in Colossians 1:15, 16, 17, but also the words and the thing of creation, and its explanation; they could not have been expressed more plainly. (4) Finally, I deny that Ephesians 3:9, "who created all things through Jesus Christ" [τῷ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ], is to be explained of a new creation through the gospel. I say it is to be understood, as in our passage, of the proper creation of all things at the beginning, so that the Apostle may mention in passing that Christ redeemed the world through the same one through whom, as God and the Son of God, the world had once been created. Theophylact on this passage: rightly [καλῶς κτίσεως ἐμνημόνευσεν] he mentions creation: "He who made all things," he says, "is God through Christ. For without him, he says, nothing was made." Chrysostom, before him, has the same.

units.la: Ad septimum, Resp. Consequentiam itidem negari: in sequentibus agitur de Christi resurrectione & temporibus N. T. ergo his versibus nequit agi de creatione rerum omnium per Christum facta. 11. Aliud est respici, aliud restringi eo omnia. Scopus Apostoli est quidem, de Euangelio, & praedicatione, fructibusque ejus loqui; sed tamen interserit nonnulla, quae, quamvis tandem huc referantur, alterius tamen generis sunt ac ordinis.
units.tr: As to the seventh, the reply is likewise that the inference is denied: in what follows the subject is Christ's resurrection and the times of the New Testament; therefore these verses cannot be about the creation of all things through Christ. (2) It is one thing to be looked at, another to be restricted by it. The Apostle's aim is indeed to speak of the gospel, its preaching and its fruits; but he nonetheless inserts some things which, although in the end they are referred to this, are nevertheless of another kind and order.

units.la: Postquam vero ostendimus, coactam & violentam esse Adversariorum expositionem loci Paulini, neque de spirituali creatione & renovatione Euangelii intelligieum posse, videamus ea, quae aliter explicari non debere, quam de creatione vera, propria, Physica rerum omnium in initio, arguant. 1. Vox κτίσεως & κτίσματος ter usurpata, absque minimo improprie significationis indicio: unde & postea vers. 23. πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει, significatione eadem, nempe propria. 11. Additum quinquies syncategorema omnis, & omnia. 111. Distributio creationis & rerum creatarum, neque nisi hinc, commode exponenda, juxta loca, ἐν οὐρανοῖς καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς[?]. Species, εἴτε ὁρατὰ εἴτε ἀόρατα[?]. Gradus, εἴτε θρόνοι, &c. Ut non huic cavillationi locus sit, quam ad postremum membrum dat Schlichtingius, in Expositione loci, Christum non creasse Angelos ipsos, sed quidem eorum dignitates & gradus. Nam si hoc, quare non illud etiam? tum non solos gradus creasse dicitur, vel hos primo, sed tertio loco, postquam ipsos Angelos satis sub specie invisibilium creatos innuerat: & quamvis etiam non addidisset illud, nemo nisi praefractae mentis sententiaeque statuet per Christum creatos quidem Angelorum thronos dignitatesque, & non ipsos quoque a Christo conditos Angelos. 1v. Omnia per ipsum creata, & in ipsum dicuntur, id est, ad ejus gloriam. Quod Dei creatoris proprium. v. Additur, ut creationi opus conservationis, καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε. vi. Sequitur demum de officio Christi mediatorio, & praedicatione Euangelii, a vers. 18. Denique per Ecclesiam Christi significata fuit Angelis ταῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις[?] multiformis Dei sapientia, Eph. 111. 10. non illi tum demum facti.
units.tr: But now that we have shown that the opponents' interpretation of the Pauline passage is forced and violent, and that it cannot be understood of a spiritual creation and renewal of the gospel, let us see what things show that it ought to be explained only of true, proper, physical creation of all things at the beginning. (1) The word creation [κτίσεως] and created thing [κτίσματος] is used three times, without the least sign of an improper meaning; whence also afterwards, in verse 23, to every creature [πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει], with the same meaning, namely the proper one. (2) The syncategorematic words all and all things are added five times. (3) The distribution of creation and created things is properly explained only in this way, according to places: in heaven and on earth [ἐν οὐρανοῖς καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς]; kinds: visible or invisible [εἴτε ὁρατὰ εἴτε ἀόρατα]; degrees: whether thrones, etc. [εἴτε θρόνοι, &c.]. So there is no room for the quibble which Schlichting offers at the last member, in his exposition of the passage: that Christ did not create the angels themselves, but only their dignities and degrees. For if this, why not that as well? Moreover, it is not said that he created only the degrees, or these first, but in the third place, after he had already indicated, under the aspect of invisible beings, that the angels themselves were created. And even if he had not added that, no one who is not perverse in mind and judgement will maintain that thrones and dignities of angels were created through Christ, but the angels themselves were not also made by Christ. (4) All things are said to be created through him and unto him, that is, to his glory, which is proper to God the Creator. (5) There is added, as a work of preservation after creation: and in him all things consist [καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε]. (6) Finally it follows concerning Christ's mediatorial office and the preaching of the gospel, from verse 18 on. Lastly, through the Church of Christ there was made known to the angels, to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places [ταῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις], the manifold wisdom of God, Ephesians 3:10; they were not then made for the first time.

units.la: Lubet ad partes etiam vocare Enjedini in locum hunc expositionem. Nam revera multa sunt in loco, quae aeternam Christi deitatem probant, ac confirmant, sive qualis Christus esse, sive quae fecisse dicatur, observemus. Inter quae aliud alio fatemur fortius praebere argumentum contra refragantes Adversarios, nihil non suppeditare eximium fidei subsidium credentibus. Humanam Christi naturam significarat in praecedentibus Apostolus, quibus sanguinem ejus commemorat, in quo habemus redemtionem, per ejus sanguinem: adjungit nunc divinam naturam, qui est εἰκὼν imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus omnis creaturae. Inde ad opera ejus pergit pariter divina, ac primum creationis, vers. 16. quoniam in ipso, vel per ipsum creata sunt omnia quae in coelis, & quae in terra, visibilia & invisibilia, &c. Deinde conservationis, vers. seq. & omnia in ipso constiterunt. Denique redemptionis, ad ecclesiam, vers. 18, & ipse est caput corporis ecclefiæ, &c. Quæ sigillatim perpendere & examinare, operæ fuerit pretium. Sic ergo Enjedinus:
units.tr: It is worth also calling Enyedi's exposition of this passage to the field. For in truth there are many things in the passage which prove and confirm the eternal deity of Christ, whether we observe what sort of being Christ is, or what he is said to have done. Among these we confess that one provides a stronger argument than another against the opposing adversaries, and that there is nothing in them which does not supply an outstanding support to believers. In the preceding words the Apostle signified Christ's human nature, when he recalls his blood: in whom we have redemption through his blood. Now he adds the divine nature: who is the image [εἰκὼν] of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature. From there he goes on to his works, equally divine, and first of creation, verse 16: for in him, or through him, all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, etc. Then of preservation, the following verse: and in him all things consist. Finally of redemption, toward the Church, verse 18: and he is the head of the body of the church, etc. It would be worth our while to weigh and examine these one by one. So Enyedi says:

units.la: In hoc Pauli loco, multa Christo attribuntur, quibus æternam ejus divinitatem confirmari posse, existimant nonnulli. Quare illa singillatim perpendere & examinare, operæ fuerit pretium. Ex eo igitur, quod Christus dicitur imago inconspicui, nullam probationem firmam ad ejus divinitatem æternam posse elici, & su-prain[?] cap. 4. Epistolæ 2. ad Corinthios, ostendimus: & adversarii acutiores ac saniores contendunt. Ubi tamen mirari libet Calvini inconstantiam, qui etsi fatetur nimis infirmum hinc duci posse, ad Christi divinitatem confirmandam, argumentum; imo illud ab ipso Paulo refelli asserit: tamen ipse post pauca verba, in idem impingit, & ex his verbis, venatur Christi cum Deo Patre æqualitatem & identitatem: quasi per imaginem Dei, deitas æterna Christi denotetur. Sed hæc imaginatio quam vana sit, præter supra dictas rationes, etiam Paulus hic demonstrat: Nam in proxime præcedentibus verbis, loquitur de Christo, ut homine, ita enim scribit: in quo habemus redemtionem, per sanguinem ejus remissionem peccatorum, qui est imago Dei inconspicui. Ubi clarissimum est, vocem Qui, referre eum qui sanguinem effudit. Ac divinitas illa æterna, sanguine caret, non ergo illa dicitur hic imago Dei.. Fatentur enim etiam adversarii, Christum in tempore accepisse corpus & sanguinem. Unde patet, non de aliquo æterno, sed de eo, qui certo tempore initium habuit, hoc in loco agi, & eum esse imaginem Dei. Denique illud etiam hic observandum est, vocem εἰκὼν conjungi posse, cum πρωτότο-κῳ[?], hoc sensu: Christum esse imaginem Dei inconspicui primogenitam, id est, primam seu præstantissimam omnis creaturæ. Sed plures, πρωτότοκον ἀπὸ[?] superioribus sejungentes, novum epitheton Christi esse volunt, & eo confirmari, illius ante veterem & primam creationem subsistentiam. Sic enim verba interpretantur: Primogenitus omnis creaturæ, hoc est, genitus ante res omnes conditas. In qua interpretatio-
units.tr: In this passage of Paul many things are attributed to Christ, by which some think his eternal divinity can be confirmed. Therefore it would be worth our while to weigh and examine them one by one. From the fact, then, that Christ is called the image of the invisible God, no firm proof of his eternal divinity can be drawn; we have shown this above, in chapter 4 of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians; and the more acute and sounder of the adversaries contend the same. Yet here it is worth wondering at the inconsistency of Calvin, who, although he admits that too weak an argument can be drawn from this to confirm the divinity of Christ, and even asserts that Paul himself refutes it, nevertheless, after a few words, falls into the same thing himself, and from these words hunts out the equality and identity of Christ with God the Father, as if the eternal deity of Christ were denoted by the image of God. But how vain this imagining is, apart from the reasons mentioned above, Paul himself demonstrates here as well. For in the words immediately preceding he speaks of Christ as man; for thus he writes: in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God. Here it is most clear that the word who refers to him who shed the blood. But that eternal divinity is without blood; therefore it is not called here the image of God. For even the adversaries grant that Christ in time received a body and blood. From this it is plain that the passage is not speaking of something eternal, but of him who had a beginning at a certain time, and that he is the image of God. Finally, this too is to be observed here: the word image [εἰκὼν] can be joined with firstborn [πρωτότοκος] in this sense: that Christ is the firstborn image of the invisible God, that is, the first or most excellent of every creature. But many, separating firstborn [πρωτότοκον] from what precedes, want it to be a new epithet of Christ, and claim that his existence before the old and first creation is confirmed by it. For they interpret the words thus: firstborn of every creature, that is, begotten before all things were created. In which interpretation

units.la: Resp. primo quidem Calvinus sibi hic loci nequaquam contradicit, negans in solo imaginis vocabulo totum causæ præsidium collocandum esse, quia etiam vir imago & gloria Dei dicitur: nihilominus tamen constare hinc nobis argumentum adstruit, quia non simpliciter imago Dei Christus, sed ista ac talis imago est. Deinde quod dicitur Christus imago Dei, non simpliciter in se & abstracte sumtum, si vel a sequentibus verba divellantur, vel non ex aliis quoque Scripturæ locis petatur expositio ejus, quæ inter Patrem ac Filium est, convenientiæ, concludit Christi deitatem, quasi ista solum verba, imaginem Dei esse, probarent ipsam essentiam deitatem; sed conjuncta cum iis, quæ dicimus, sic illam confirmant. Verum est, homo etiam vocatur εἰκὼν καὶ[?] δόξα θεοῦ 1 Cor. xi. 7. sed & in promtu est ratio, quia ad imaginem Dei factus: quia autem non propter eandem, sed aliam, eamque longe excelsiorem causam Christus imago Dei dicitur, non omnis istius appellationis ratio ex illo deducenda venit. Apostolus vero & hic, & alibi altius quid in Christo, & ejus cum Patre similitudine consideratur: nempe quando eum dicit ἀπαύ-γασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ[?] χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. Hebr. 1.3. quæ longe aliud quid dicunt, quam quod est in imagine, ad quam homo dicitur creatus. Quod non infringitur eo, quod Adversarius, ex præcedentibus Apostoli verbis format, argumento, ubi loquitur de Christo ut homine, deque ejus sanguine. Negamus enim sequelam: Divinitas caret sanguine, ergo quum Apostolus de Christi sanguine loquatur in præcedentibus, hisce, quibus Christum ait esse imaginem Dei, nequit significare ejus deitatem. ne, illud primo notandum est, quod etiamsi ea vera esset, nihil inde aliud sequeretur, quam Christum primo creatum, & conditum esse à Deo; non autem, quod sit æternus, & principio carens. Nam quod quidam objiciunt, Christum hic non dici creatum, sed genitum, & aliud esse gignere, & aliud creare: valde infirmum est. Nam scimus has voces sæpe ἐκ πυρ' ἀλ-λήλʒ [?] poni, neque quidquam differre, ut Deut. 32. vers. 18. Deum, qui te genuit, dereliquisti, & oblitus es Domini, creatoris tui. Et Gen. 2. vers. 4. Istæ sunt generationes cœli & terræ, quando creatæ sunt, &c. Deinde alibi quoque Christus creatura Dei dicitur, quod primo patet ex collatione locorum istorum:
units.tr: Reply: first, Calvin does not contradict himself here at all, denying that the whole support of the cause is to be placed in the word image alone, since even man is called the image and glory of God; nevertheless he holds that an argument is established from it for us, because Christ is not simply the image of God, but such and such an image. Next, when Calvin concludes Christ's deity from the fact that Christ is called the image of God, not taken simply in himself and in the abstract, if the words are torn from what follows, or if the explanation of the agreement between the Father and the Son is not sought also from other passages of Scripture, he argues as if these words alone, to be the image of God, proved the essential deity itself; but joined with what we say, they confirm it in this way. It is true that man too is called image and glory of God (1 Corinthians 11:7); and the reason is at hand, because he was made in the image of God. But since Christ is called the image of God not on the same ground, but for another and far loftier cause, not every reason for that appellation is to be derived from that. The Apostle, both here and elsewhere, considers something higher in Christ and his likeness to the Father, namely when he calls him the brightness of his glory and the express image of his substance [ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ] (Hebrews 1:3), which say something quite different from what is in the image to which man is said to have been created. This is not overturned by the adversary's argument drawn from the Apostle's preceding words, where he speaks of Christ as man and of his blood. For we deny the consequence: divinity is without blood, therefore since the Apostle speaks of Christ's blood in the preceding words, in these, where he says Christ is the image of God, he cannot signify his deity. But first of all this must be noted: that even if that were true, nothing else would follow from it than that Christ was first created and made by God, and not that he is eternal and without beginning. For as to what some object, that Christ is here not said to be created but begotten, and that to beget is one thing and to create another: this is very weak. For we know that these words are often used interchangeably [ἐξ ἀλλήλων] and differ in nothing, as in Deuteronomy 32:18: you have forsaken God who begot you, and have forgotten the Lord your creator. And Genesis 2:4: These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, etc. Then elsewhere too Christ is called the creature of God, which appears first from a comparison of these passages:

units.la: ⊿Ad Rom. cap. 13. vers. 14. suadet Apostolus, ut novum hominem, Iesum Christum pii induant. ⊿At ad Eph. 4. vers. 24. Et ad Coloss. 3. vers. 10. ait, novum hominem à pris induendum, esse creatum à Deo.
units.tr: At Rom. 13:14 the Apostle urges the godly to put on the new man, Jesus Christ. But at Eph. 4:24 and Col. 3:10 he says that the new man, who is to be put on, has been created by God.

units.la: ⊿Ad hæc, locus ille Efaiae 45. vers. 8. Rorate cœli, &c. mystice de Christo intelligitur. At ibi de Salvatore gignendo dicitur. Ego Dominus creavi eum. Sic Apoc. 3. vers. 14. Christus vocatur principium creaturæ Dei. Ex quibus apparet, jure Christum, inter creaturas numerari. Quod etiam ex similibus phrasibus confirmari potest. Nam Christus & in hoc loco, & 1 ad Corinth. 15. vers. 20. Et Apoc. 1. vers. 5. vocatur primogenitus mortuorum. Unde recte infertur, Christum fuisse mortuum, seu unum ex mortuis. Sic Abel dicitur Gen. 4. vers. 4. obtulisse Deo sacrificium, de primogenitis gregis sui. Ergo illa primogenita, fuerunt ex grege. Pari ratione Christus, est primogenitus creaturæ, ergo unus ex creatura Dei. Secundo de hac interpretatione etiam illud observetur, quod ea destruit ipsorum adversariorum, de Christi generatione sententiam. Si enim Christus ante omnem creaturam genitus est, certe suum esse completum habuit, antequam quidquam à Deo crearetur.
units.tr: Besides this, the passage of Isaiah 45:8, "Drop down, ye heavens," etc., is understood mystically of Christ. But there it is said of the Saviour's begetting: "I the Lord have created him." So in Rev. 3:14 Christ is called "the beginning of the creation of God" [ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ θεοῦ]. From these passages it appears that Christ is rightly numbered among the creatures. This can also be confirmed from similar phrases. For in this place, and in 1 Cor. 15:20 and Rev. 1:5, Christ is called "the firstborn of the dead." Whence it is rightly inferred that Christ was dead, or one of the dead. So Abel is said in Gen. 4:4 to have offered to God a sacrifice from the firstborn of his flock. Therefore those firstborn were from the flock. By the same reasoning Christ is the firstborn of the creature, therefore one of God's creatures. Secondly, this interpretation also deserves notice because it destroys our opponents' own opinion about Christ's generation. For if Christ was begotten before every creature, certainly he had his full being before anything was created by God.

units.la: ⊿At ipsi dicunt, Christum, etiam hodie gigni, & ejus generationis finem nunquam fore. Quod nihil est aliud, quam Christum nondum esse. Quod enim est in Nulla in isto est consequentia.
