Fatemur, Christum in tempore accepisse corpus & sanguinem; sed & præter hæc, ab æterno, secundum aliam sui rationem fuisse Deum: ergo de eodem, & quod ab æterno fuit, & certo tempore initium habuit, secundum variam rationem, & loquendi modum, prædicari, citra contradictione ullam vel repugnantiam potest. Denique vox εἰκὼν cum πρωτοτόκῳ jungi non potest, tum quia intercisio, ne jungatur, intercedit; tum quia nisi πρωτότοκος conjungatur cum πάσης κτίσεως, horum commodus sensus dari non potest: quo enim referas ista, omnis creaturæ? vel quomodo exponas? nam non simpliciter in textu est πρωτότοκος, sed omnis creaturæ πρωτοτόκος, ut ad ista vox debeat referri, non ad præcedentia εἰκὼν imago Dei. Exponere πρωτοτόκον præstantissimum, sive imaginem præstantissimam & primam omnis creaturæ, id primo præter rationem enervat vim vocis πρωτοτόκος, totiusque sententiæ, & hoc si intendisset, aliis tum verbis, tum constructione usus fuisset Spiritus Sanctus. Quod Christus genitus est ante res omnes creatas, id eum ostendit æternum & principio carentem. Non quod Deus non potuisset aliquid constituere & facere ante creationem hexaemeri, quod non fuisset æternum, sed quia ita id verum, omnia cum creatione mundi extitisse, ut in Scripturis æquipolleant, esse ante mundum conditum, & esse ab æterno, quandoquidem initium rerum temporisque sumitur à principio, in quo Deus omnia creavit. Utcunque pro eodem aliquando sumantur gigni & creari, hominesque à Deo & creari dicantur & gigni, Filius Dei tamen à Deo creatus non est, neque creatus dicitur; de Christo, vel eo, quatenus filius Dei fieri, nondum est, neque suam perfectionem ad-ptum est. Ex quibus apparet, tantum abesse, ut ex hoc Apostoli dicto, Christi aeterna divinitas probari possit: ut contra, firmissime probari queat, illum & creaturam esse, & principium habuisse. Sed ut vera interpretatio huius loci habeatur: sciendum est vocabulum primogenitus, varia in sacris literis significare. Nam illud saepe nihil aliud, quam quod vox simplex primus significat. Ut Ierem. 4. verf. 31. quae primum enititur, vocatur primogenitum pariens, quod una voce Latine dici posset primipera. Sic fructuum & panum primitiae, vocantur primogenita, Levit. 23. verf. 17. & 20. Sic praecoces fructus, Nahum. 3. vocantur primogenitae, quas Horatius vocat ficus primas lib. 1. epist. 7. Eodem modo dicitur Christus primo-genitus mortuorum, hoc est, primus. Nam alias, si vocis etymon spectetur, absurda erit sententia. Qui enim moritur, aut mortuus est, certe gigni non dicitur: cum etiam ea quae per gene-rationem acquisita erant, in morte amitti solent. Sic dici potest Christus hoc loco primoge-nitus creaturae, non quod genitus primo fit, sed quod fit simpliciter primus creaturarum. Nam compositum primogenitus, idem significat quod vox simplex primus. Hinc factum est, ut sicut primus, ita etiam primogenitus, in sacris, non semper significet eum, qui prior est tempore, sed saepe ad dignitatem & excellentiam referatur, & principem ac praestantissimum denotet. Ut Iob. 18. verf. 13. Primogenitus Mortis, vocatur princeps mortis, qui praecipue Mortis imperium habet. Ita Iudas Gen. 49. Ita Ephraim Ierem. 31. verf. 9. vocantur primogeniti, quam-vis aliis, essent aetate & tempore posteriores. Sic Esai. 14. verf. 30. Pascentur primogeniti pau-perum, id est, qui inter pauperes principatum tenent, hoc est, pauperrimi quique. Hoc sensu recte Christus dicitur primogenitus creaturae, hoc est, Princeps, praestantissimus, & excellentissimus omnium creaturarum Dei. Praeterea, quia primogeniti solent parentibus esse charissi-mi, saepe primogenitus ponitur pro dilecto: ut in illum locum Exod. 4. verf. 22. primogenitus Dei ordinatus, unctusque est in Mediatorem, ut factus hoc vel creatus etiam aliquando dicatur, res est alia. Quamvis nec iis, quae citat Adversarius, Scripturae locis creatura Christus dicatur. Non Rom. xiii. 14. ubi jubet induere Christum Apostolus, quae impropria est loquutio: & quamvis Ephes. i v. 24. regeneratio & novus homo dicatur nova creatura, hoc non vult Christum ea ratione esse creaturam, sed hanc esse nostram Christi induitionem, vel ad Christi formam renovationem. Quae sunt diversissima. Quae Jesa. xlv. 8. legun-tur, de Salvatore bene exponuntur mysti-ce; sed tali in casu non debent singula verba exigi ad propriam significationem, & Christo attribui. [?]אֶת־בְּרִית is in textu, quod de Cyro proprie accipiendum. vide cap. xliv. 28. & xliii. 7. vel in neutro accipi potest, ego creavi illud, nimirum feci ut coelum & terra proferrent salutem ac justitiam, quemadmodum verf. praec. formans lucem & creans tenebras, faciens pa-cem & creans malum, ego Iehova facio omnia illa. adde cap. xli. 20. & Psalm. cix. 27. Quamvis, uti jam dictum, si de Christo accipiamus, ejusque beneficiis, nihil nobis adversetur. Apocal. iii. 14. Christus appellatur ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ θεοῦ[?], quod eum ante creaturas quidem, non inter eas locat. Primogenitus mortuorum vocatur, eo quod is sit, qui omnium suorum resur-rectionem, & resurgendorum quasi gregem sanctificat, ut post quem, & in quo re-surgut. Sed & notatur eo, dices, quod inter mortuos, & eorum unus fuerit: Sic quo-que primogenitus creaturarum, quia e numero creaturarum? non sequitur. nam πρωτότοκος designat anterioritatem, quare fuisse πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως, fuisse ante creaturas, quarum ratione dicitur primogenitus. Jam vero sic docet Apostolus Christum, secundum id quod imago est invisibilis Dei, esse primum ante-omnes meus Israel, annotat Tremellius, primogenitus, id est, summe mihi dilectus. Ad Hebr. 12. verf. 23. Omnes Israelitae vocantur primogeniti. De Davide in Psalmis: Primogenitum ponam eum, Psal. 88. verf. 28. Iam vero scimus Christum, ἀγαπητὸν[?] Dei vocari, qua voce summum significari amorem, supra alicubi diximus. Atque haec de voce Primogenitus.
units.tr: But they themselves say that Christ is being begotten even today, and that his generation will never come to an end. This is nothing other than saying that Christ does not yet exist, for there is no consequence in that. We admit that Christ took on body and blood in time; but besides these, from eternity, according to another aspect of himself, he was God. Therefore of the same one, both what was from eternity and what had a beginning at a certain time can be predicated, according to different reasons and modes of speaking, without any contradiction or repugnance. Finally, the word image [εἰκὼν] cannot be joined with firstborn [πρωτοτόκῳ]: first, because a break intervenes to prevent their joining; second, because unless firstborn is joined with "of all creation" [πάσης κτίσεως], no sensible meaning can be given to these words. For to what would you refer "of every creature," or how would you explain it? The text does not simply have firstborn [πρωτότοκος], but firstborn of every creature [πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως], so that this word must be referred to these words, not to the preceding "image of God" [εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ]. To explain firstborn [πρωτότοκον] as "most excellent," or "the most excellent and first image of every creature," first of all weakens against reason the force of the word firstborn and of the whole sentence. And if the Holy Spirit had intended this, he would have used other words and another construction. That Christ was begotten before all created things shows him to be eternal and without beginning. This is not because God could not have set up and made something before the creation of the six days which was not eternal, but because it is true that all things came into being together with the creation of the world, so that in Scripture "to be before the world was made" and "to be from eternity" are equivalent; for the beginning of things and of time is taken from the beginning in which God created all things. However, although "to beget" and "to create" are sometimes taken for the same thing, and men are said both to be created and to be begotten by God, the Son of God was nevertheless not created by God, nor is he said to be created. Of Christ, or insofar as he is the Son of God, it is not yet being made, nor has it attained its perfection. From these things it appears that so far is this saying of the Apostle from proving Christ's eternal divinity, that on the contrary it can most firmly be proved that he both is a creature and had a beginning. But so that the true interpretation of this passage may be had, it must be noted that the word firstborn signifies various things in the sacred letters. For it often means nothing other than what the simple word first means. So in Jer. 4:31 she who first gives birth is called "firstborn bearing," which in Latin could be said in one word, primipara. Thus the first-fruits and first loaves are called firstborn, Lev. 23:17 and 20. Likewise the early fruits are called firstborn, Nahum 3, which Horace calls "first figs," Epist. 1.7. In the same way Christ is called "firstborn of the dead," that is, first. For otherwise, if the etymology of the word is considered, the sense would be absurd. For one who dies, or is dead, is certainly not said to be begotten, since even those things which were acquired by generation are usually lost in death. So Christ can be called firstborn of the creature in this place, not because he was first begotten, but because he is simply the first of the creatures. For the compound firstborn means the same as the simple word first. Hence it has come about that, just as first, so also firstborn in sacred usage does not always mean one who is earlier in time, but often refers to dignity and excellence, and denotes a prince and the most excellent. So in Job 18:13 the "firstborn of death" is called the prince of death, who especially holds the power of Death. So Judah (Gen. 49), and Ephraim (Jer. 31:9), are called firstborn, although they were later in age and time. So Isa. 14:30, "the firstborn of the poor shall feed," that is, those who hold the leading place among the poor, that is, the very poorest. In this sense Christ is rightly called firstborn of the creature, that is, the prince, the most excellent and most eminent of all God's creatures. Moreover, because firstborn sons are usually most dear to their parents, firstborn is often used for beloved; as in that place, Exod. 4:22, "firstborn of God," that is, one ordained and anointed as Mediator. That he is said to have been made, or even created, at some time, is another matter. Although the Scripture passages which our opponent cites do not call Christ a creature. Not Rom. 13:14, where the Apostle bids us put on Christ, which is an improper expression; and although Eph. 4:24 calls regeneration and the new man a new creation, this does not mean that Christ is a creature in that way, but that this is our putting on of Christ, or renewal into the form of Christ, which are very different things. The words in Isa. 45:8 are rightly explained mystically of the Saviour; but in such a case the individual words must not be forced to their proper meaning and attributed to Christ. The Hebrew "et-berith" [את־ברית] stands in the text, which is properly to be taken of Cyrus; see chap. 44:28 and 43:7. Or it may be taken in the neuter: "I created it," namely, I made heaven and earth bring forth salvation and righteousness, just as in the preceding verse "forming the light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil, I, Jehovah, do all these things." Add chap. 41:20 and Ps. 109:27. Although, as already said, if we take it of Christ and his benefits, nothing opposes us. In Rev. 3:14 Christ is called "the beginning of the creation of God" [ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ θεοῦ], which places him before the creatures, not among them. He is called firstborn of the dead because he is the one who sanctifies the resurrection of all his own and of those who are to rise, as a kind of flock, so that they rise after him and in him. But, you will say, he is also called so because he was among the dead, and one of them. Likewise he is firstborn of the creatures because he is of their number? That does not follow. For firstborn [πρωτότοκος] designates priority, so that to have been firstborn of every creature [πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως] means to have been before the creatures, by reason of which he is called firstborn. Now indeed the Apostle teaches this: that Christ, insofar as he is the invisible image of God, is first before all. "My Israel," Tremellius notes, "firstborn," that is, most dear to me. Heb. 12:23: All the Israelites are called firstborn. Of David in the Psalms: "I will make him firstborn," Ps. 89:28. Now we know that Christ is called the beloved [ἀγαπητόν] of God, a word by which the highest love is signified, as I have said somewhere above. And these things concerning the word firstborn.

units.la: Quod vero attinet ad vocabulum creaturae, & illud ambiguum est. Nam etsi fere illud omnes ad primam mundi creationem, & rerum omnium constitutionem referant: potest tamen recte pro regeneratione & regeneratis accipi. Eo quod illa vox saepe pro nova creatione ponitur, ut mox ostendemus. Deinde, hic ille dicitur primogenitus creaturae, qui effudit sanguinem. At Christus, etiamsi extitisset ante primam Mundi creationem: tamen tunc, etiam adversariis consentientibus, non habuit sanguinem. Ergo tunc non fuit, nec esse potuit primogenitus. Quare interpretari debemus per creaturam, vel creationem; posteriorem creationem seu renovationem, quando Christus sanguinem fundere potuit. Atque si hic sensus admittatur, concedere poterimus, Christum, etiam tempore, creationem antecessisse. Nam in secunda creatione, Christus & tempore, & ordine, & dignitate, omnibus prior est. Sequitur in verbis Apostoli, Quoniam in ipso, (vel ut alii, per ipsum) condita sunt universa, in coelis & in terra. Quae clausula urgetur praecipue ab adversariis, quia Christus in ea, auctor & creator omnium statui videtur. Notum autem est, illum esse solum & aeternum Deum, qui mundum condidit. Unde etiam Pythagoras veri Dei notam mundi creationem esse affirmat in his versibus: Εἰ τίς ἐρᾷ θεὸς εἰμί, παρὰ ἐμὲ ἔστω[?], ὀφειλὴ κόσμον ἴσην τῷ σήμᾳ[?] εἴπειν ἐμῷ ἔστω[?], ἴδε ἐστί[?], idest, Si quis, excepto uno, dicat, Deus sum, debet mundum aequalem, huic constituens, dicere, hic meus est. Nos vero neque hic Christum appellari creatorem, neque de veteri creatione agi, affirmamus, omnes creaturas, ut omnia per ipsum fuerint creata: ergo non pari prorsus ratione intelligendus est Christus esse primogenitus omnis creaturae, atque primogenitus mortuorum. Verum in hoc est accipienda similitudo, ex ratione primitiarum olim ad totam massam, quam benedicebant, quod quemadmodum Christus resurrectione sua antecessit resurgendos, imo & faciet per eam illos resurgere, sic quoque ante omnes creaturas extitit Christus, & iussit esse eas, seu creavit.
units.tr: As for the word "creature," that too is ambiguous. For although almost everyone refers it to the first creation of the world and the constitution of all things, it can rightly be taken of regeneration and of the regenerate, since that expression is often used of new creation, as we shall soon show. Next, the one who shed his blood is called the firstborn of the creature. But Christ, even if he had existed before the first creation of the world, did not then have blood, as even our adversaries agree. Therefore then he was not, and could not be, the firstborn. So we must interpret "creature" or "creation" as the later creation or renewal, when Christ was able to shed blood. And if this sense is admitted, we can concede that Christ preceded creation even in time. For in the second creation Christ is prior to all in time, in order, and in dignity. There follows the Apostle's phrase: "for in him (or, as others read, through him) all things were created, in heaven and on earth." This clause is pressed chiefly by our adversaries, because Christ seems to be set forth in it as the author and creator of all. It is known, however, that the one who made the world is the only and eternal God. Hence Pythagoras also affirms that the creation of the world is the mark of the true God, in these verses: "If anyone, excepting one, says 'I am God,' he ought to say, establishing a world equal to this one, 'this is mine'" [Εἰ τίς ἐρᾷ θεὸς εἰμί, παρὰ ἐμὲ ἔστω, ὀφειλὴ κόσμον ἴσην τῷ σήμᾳ εἴπειν ἐμῷ ἔστω]. But we affirm that Christ is not here called creator, and that the old creation is not the subject here, but that all creatures were created through him. Therefore Christ is not to be understood in exactly the same way as "firstborn of every creature" and "firstborn of the dead." Rather the likeness is to be taken from the ancient rule concerning the firstfruits, which were blessed along with the whole mass: just as Christ by his resurrection went before those who are to rise, and indeed by it will make them rise, so also Christ existed before all creatures and commanded them to be, or created them.

units.la: Quod ad alteram contra nos argumentationem spectat, negamus, Christi generationem, vel principium capere, vel finem, ullamve temporis circumstantiam aut mutationem: istis enim non subjacet, qui supra tempus est, & nec regulatur aut modificatur superexcedens omnem creatam entitatem, & temporalis rei modum, Deus. Quare negamus Minorem illam: Christum etiam hodie gigni, & ejus generationis finem nunquam fore. Nam est alterius generis illa, quam ea quae tempore constant. Nec principium temporis habet, nec praesens, nec futurum, supra & ante tempus, nequidquam temporali vel corporali modo facta ipsius generatio. Adexistit quidem nostro tempori omnibusq; ejus momentis, quemadmodum tota Dei aeternitas, & indivisibilis unitas, non autem temporis vicissitudini subjacet eâve regulatur. Ergo nunquam est in fieri, neque ita ut aliquando perfectionem suam nondum fuerit adeptus.
units.tr: As for the other argument against us, we deny that the generation of Christ admits of a beginning or an end, or any circumstance or change of time. For God, who is above time and is neither governed nor modified by it, surpassing every created being and the mode of a temporal thing, is not subject to these. Therefore we deny that minor premise: that Christ is begotten even today, and that the end of his generation will never come. For that generation is of another kind than those things which exist in time. It has no beginning in time, nor present nor future, but is above and before time; his generation was not effected in a temporal or bodily manner. It indeed coexists with our time and all its moments, just as the whole eternity and indivisible unity of God does, but it is not subject to the vicissitude of time nor governed by it. Therefore it is never in process of becoming, nor is it such that at some time he had not yet attained his perfection.

units.la: Verbum autem primogeniti Adversarius primum accipit simpliciter de primo, & quomodocunq;, quamvis non proprie per generationem, ante alia exsistente. Neque adversamur, ut quod ita primum, per translationem metaphoricam appelletur primogenitum. Certe omnis primogenitus est primus: & de iis, quae generatione exsistunt, quare non exponatur primum natus, nulla apparet ratio. & IeProbamus utrumque, & primo, prius. Nam Paulus, non dicit hic Christum creasse omnia, sed in eo, vel, per ipsum, creata esse omnia. Qua loquendi forma, non primariam causam, & primum efficiens, sed instrumentum tantum & medium significatur. Alius ergo est qui creavit, & alius in quo creata sunt omnia. Iam vero, ille est verus & aeternus Deus, qui omnia creavit. Hic vero non est de eo sermo, qui creavit omnia, sed de eo, per quem omnia sunt creata. Ergo clarum est, hic non agi de creatore rerum omnium. Vbi observandum est, quod hic locus videtur quidem aliquid favere Arianis, sed nihil Homousianis. Nam hinc videtur consequi, iam tempore creationis extitisse Christum: sed tamen non esse ipsum rerum auctorem, & creatorem, quia vox in, vel per, instrumentum denotat. Verum, non loqui Paulum hic de veteri creatione Mundi, sic demonstramus. Quo & Arianorum & Homousianorum opinio evertitur: Primo: Quotiescunque scriptura veteris creationis meminit, semper illam soli Deo, exclusis omnibus instrumentis & sociis, attribuit, ut Iob. 9. verf. 8. Qui extendit coelos solus. Et ipse Deus, Isa.40. verf.13. Quis adjuvit Spiritum Domini? aut quis Consiliarius ejus fuit? & ostendit illi? Cum quo iniit consilium, & instruxit eum, &c. & 44. Ego sum Dominus faciens omnia, extendens coelos solus, stabiliens terram, & nullus mecum. Et cap. 45. verf. 7. Ego Dominus, & non est alter, formans lucem, & creans tenebras. Et ipse Christus, Matt. 11. Apostoli, Actor. 4. hanc creationem soli Deo Patri adscribunt. Quin ut omnia instrumenta & media hinc excluderentur, Rom. 11. verf. 36. ad Hebr. 2. verf. 10. dicitur Deus Pater esse, ex quo, per quem, & propter quem omnia sunt condita. Quibus verbis omne instrumentum, & omne externum auxilium a creatione excluditur, ac principale efficiens, instrumentum, & finis creationis, solus Deus dicitur. Nam quod alicubi scriptura videtur Deo administros, & media quaedam, etiam in hoc opere adjungere, ut quum per Verbum, Spiritum, Sa-pientiam suam cuncta creasse dicitur, id nihil rem. iv.31. מבכירה est primipera pariens primogenitum. Deinde exponit primogenitum, non eum qui prior sit tempore, aut generatione, sed dignitate & praestantia. Quorsum autem ad improprias vocis recurramus exceptiones, ubi propriae locus? Quamvis etiam primogenitus, propterea quia primogenitus, excellentior caeteris habeatur. Neque negamus, Christum esse principem, praestantissimum, & excellentissimum omnium creaturarum: sed etiam ante eas fuit: & sic ante eas, ut non sit πρωτόκτιστος, sed πρωτότοκος, & πρωτοπλάστος. Genef. xlix. non dicitur Juda, sed Ruben primogenitus: ad illum Jacobus, verf. 9. בני ; ad istum verf. 3. בכור. Neque Ierem. xxxi. 9. Ephraim appellatur primogenitus, respectu fratrum suorum, sed de populo suo Deus testatur, eum sibi esse primogenitum: nempe ipse ejus pater, illi vero ejus filius primogenitus.
units.tr: The adversary first takes the word "firstborn" simply of the first, and in whatever way, even though not properly through generation, as one who existed before other things. Nor do we oppose the view that what is first in this way may be called firstborn by a metaphorical transfer. Certainly every firstborn is first, and there appears to be no reason why, of things that come into being by generation, "firstborn" should not be explained as "first-born." We grant both: that he is first, and that he is prior. For Paul does not say here that Christ created all things, but that all things were created in him, or through him. By this form of speech is signified not the primary cause and first efficient, but only an instrument and means. Therefore the one who created is different from the one in whom all things were created. Now, the one who created all things is the true and eternal God. But the discussion here is not about him who created all things, but about him through whom all things were created. Therefore it is clear that the subject here is not the creator of all things. We must observe that this passage seems indeed to favour the Arians somewhat, but the Homoousians not at all. For from it it seems to follow that Christ already existed at the time of creation, yet was not himself the author and creator of things, since the preposition "in" or "through" denotes an instrument. But that Paul is not speaking here of the old creation of the world, we demonstrate as follows, by which the opinion of both the Arians and the Homoousians is overturned. First: whenever Scripture mentions the old creation, it always ascribes it to God alone, excluding all instruments and associates, as in Job 9:8, "who alone stretches out the heavens"; and God himself in Isa. 40:13, "Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord? or who was his counsellor, and has taught him?" "With whom did he take counsel, and instruct him?" etc.; and in ch. 44, "I am the Lord who makes all things, stretching out the heavens alone, stabilizing the earth, and no one with me." And in ch. 45:7, "I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness." Christ himself, in Matt. 11, and the Apostles, in Acts 4, ascribe this creation to God the Father alone. Moreover, that all instruments and means may be excluded from it, Rom. 11:36 and Heb. 2:10 say that God the Father is the one from whom, through whom, and for whom all things were made. By these words every instrument and every external help is excluded from creation, and God alone is called the principal efficient, instrument, and end of creation. For although Scripture in some places seems to join to God certain ministers and means in this work too, as when it says that he created all things through his Word, Spirit, or Wisdom, that is nothing to the point. In Jer. 31:9 [מבכירה] is "a bearer of firstborn," the one who bears a firstborn. Next, he explains "firstborn" not as one who is prior in time or in generation, but in dignity and pre-eminence. Why, then, should we have recourse to the improper exceptions of the word when its proper place is available? Although the firstborn, precisely because he is firstborn, is also regarded as more excellent than the rest. Nor do we deny that Christ is the prince, most excellent and most outstanding of all creatures; but he also was before them, and so before them that he is not πρωτόκτιστος (first-created) but πρωτότοκος (first-born) and πρωτοπλάστος (first-formed). In Gen. 49 it is not Judah but Reuben who is called firstborn: of the latter Jacob says in verse 3 [בכור], and of the former in verse 9 [בני]. Nor in Jer. 31 is Ephraim called firstborn with respect to his brothers; rather God testifies concerning his own people that he is his firstborn, namely, he is his father and Ephraim his firstborn son.

units.la: Tertio & hanc addit vocis primogeniti expositionem, ut notet dilectum, ut Christus dicatur primogenitus, id est, ἀγαπητός. Quin sit unice Deo dilectus, nemo dubitat; sed nihil aliud voce primogeniti designari, est in quaestione. Revera Christus est primus, & praestantissimus, & charissimus: sed quod primogenitus, plus aliquid notat, magisque proprium. Atque si singularem Dei dilectionem exprimere voluisset Apostolus, aliis magisque usitatis & claris id fecisset verbis. Non simpliciter πρωτότοκον appellat, vel Dei primogenitum, ut leviter exponeres dilectum Dei, sed πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως, quod in ordine ad creaturas dicitur; & dilutum foret, neque satis conveniens phraseologiae, exponere de dilectione Dei erga eum, supra creaturas reliquas.
units.tr: Third, he also adds this explanation of the word "firstborn," so as to note the beloved, so that Christ is called firstborn, that is, ἀγαπητός (beloved). That he is uniquely beloved of God no one doubts; but it is in question whether nothing else is designated by the word "firstborn." Indeed Christ is first, and most excellent, and most dear; but "firstborn" signifies something more, and something more proper. And if the Apostle had wished to express God's singular love, he would have done so in other and more common and clear words. He does not simply call him πρωτότοκον (firstborn) or the firstborn of God, as if to lightly express God's beloved, but πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως (firstborn of every creature), which is said in relation to creatures; and it would be weak, and not well suited to the phrasing, to explain it of God's love towards him above the other creatures.

units.la: Atque haec de voce primogenitus. Quod vero attinet ad vocabulum creaturae, hoc non minus vexat quam praecedens Adveraliud significat quam Deum sua vi, & propria potestate mundum creasse. Idem enim est dicere, Deus creavit, & Deus per verbum, spiritum, sapientiam creavit. Sicut similes phrases id confirmant, ut cum dextera sua, & manibus suis dicitur Deus coelum & terram formasse: Isa. 45. vers. 12. Ierem. 27. vers. 5. Quibus verbis, nullum Deo auxiliatorem aut socium creationis attribui intelligimus. Sic Nabugodonosor, cum significare vellet, se propria vi condidisse Babylonem, ait: In robore fortitudinis suae, aedificasse urbem eam. Quod idem est, ac si dixisset, ego a nullo adjutus, neque ullius ope usus, hoc feci. Cum igitur scriptura, creationis veteris mentionem faciens, nullius instrumenti aut medii meminisse soleat: sequitur, ut quum de tali creatione loquitur, in qua instrumenti alicujus fit mentio, ibi non agat de veteri creatione. At hic Apostolus de tali loquitur creatione, in qua instrumenti quoque meminit; ait enim in ipso, vel per ipsum condita omnia. Hic certe non tantum creatio, sed & instrumentum nominatur. Ergo hic non agitur, de prima & veteri creatione. Secundo id ipsum confirmatur hac ratione: Quandocunque scriptura veterem & externam creationem describit, mentionem facit creationis coeli & terrae. Imo saepissime, vel potius semper, harum duarum mundi praecipuarum partium nomine, intelligitur universus mundus. Et scriptura, cum vult indicare, Deum esse creatorem mundi; eum coeli & terrae artificem, & creatorem nominat. Gen. 1. in principio creavit Deus coelum & terram. Act. 14. Deum vivum, qui fecit coelum & terram, & mare, & omnia quae in eis sunt. Et Act. 17. Hic caeli & terrae cum sit Dominus. Quin etiam in Symbolo Apostolico sic verus Deus describitur: Patrem omnipotentem, creatorem coeli & terrae. Ex quibus & similibus dictis apparet, creationem veterem praecipue in coeli terraeque creatione consistere, neque cum de ea fit sermo, illarum creationem praetermitti solere. Atque in hoc Pauli loco, non fit creationis coeli & terrae mentio. Non enim dicitur Christus coelum & terram creasse, neque per illum terrae co-
units.tr: And this is enough on the word firstborn. As for the word creatures, it troubles us no less than the preceding one. The adversary's claim amounts to saying that God created the world by his own power and by himself alone. For to say "God created" and to say "God created through the Word, the Spirit, or wisdom" are not the same thing. Similar phrases confirm this, such as when God is said to have formed heaven and earth with his right hand and his own hands (Isa. 45:12; Jer. 27:5). By such words we understand that no helper or companion in creation is ascribed to God. So too Nebuchadnezzar, wishing to say that he had built Babylon by his own power, says: "In the strength of my might I have built this city." This is the same as if he had said: "I did this without any help from anyone, and with no one's aid." Since Scripture, when it speaks of the old creation, is accustomed to make no mention of any instrument or means, it follows that when it speaks of a creation in which some instrument is mentioned, it is not speaking of the old creation. But here the Apostle speaks of such a creation, and he does mention an instrument, for he says that all things were created in him, or through him. Here not only creation but also an instrument is named. Therefore this passage is not about the first and old creation. Secondly, the point is confirmed by this reasoning: whenever Scripture describes the old and external creation, it mentions the creation of heaven and earth. Indeed, very often, or rather always, the whole world is understood by the name of these two chief parts of the world. And when Scripture wants to show that God is the Creator of the world, it calls him the maker and creator of heaven and earth (Gen. 1:1: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth"; Acts 14:15: "the living God, who made heaven and earth, and the sea, and all that is in them"; Acts 17:24: "since he is Lord of heaven and earth"). Indeed, in the Apostles' Creed the true God is described in this way: "Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth." From these and similar sayings it appears that the old creation consists chiefly in the creation of heaven and earth, and that when there is talk of it, these are not usually passed over. And in this passage of Paul there is no mention of the creation of heaven and earth. For it is not said that Christ created heaven and earth, nor that through him heaven and earth were...

units.la: farius, & intelligi vult creationem secundam, seu renovationem, per Christum factam, non creationem rerum aut mundi. Potest, inquit, vocabulum illud pro regeneratione & regeneratis accipi: unde colligit, quod sic interpretari debemus. Perperam, a posse argumentari, ad debere. Potest, ait, illud, quia saepe pro nova creatione ponitur. Nunquam simpliciter, nisi quando totus textus & connexio illud manifeste exigunt: nunquam, ubi additur particula universalis omnis, uti hic, omnis creaturae. Deinde ille dicitur primogenitus, non creaturae simpliciter, sed omnis creaturae, qui effudit sanguinem: at non, qua effudit sanguinem. Et Christus ille, qui postea homo, eatenus habuit sanguinem, non vero ante primam mundi creationem, ergo tunc non fuit, nec esse potuit primogenitus. Quae sequela? Naturas, & pro ratione naturarum distingue tempora vel periodos, & videbis elumbem plane argumentationem.
units.tr: ...our opponent, and wants it to be understood as a second creation, or renewal, brought about through Christ, not as the creation of things or of the world. "It can," he says, "be taken for regeneration and the regenerate"; and from this he concludes that we ought to interpret it so. He argues badly, moving from "can" to "must." "It can," he says, "because it is often put for new creation." Never simply, except when the whole text and its connection clearly demand it; never where the universal particle all is added, as here: of all creation. Next, he is called firstborn not of the creature simply, but of all creation, who shed his blood; but not as he shed his blood. And that Christ who afterwards became man had blood only from then, not before the first creation of the world; therefore at that time he was not, and could not be, firstborn. What does this follow from? Distinguish the natures, and according to the reason of the natures distinguish the times or periods, and you will see that the argument is plainly feeble.

units.la: Sequitur in verbis Apostoli, quoniam in ipso, vel, per ipsum condita sunt universa in coelis & in terra. adversus quae Auctor noster insurgit, & negat, Christum esse creatorem; vel, hic agi de rerum creatione: illud, quia non creasse omnia, sed in ipso, vel per ipsum omnia creata dicuntur, & significatur Christus causa instrumentalis, non primaria. Verum fac dictum, per Christum facta omnia, id non magis derogat causae primae, quam quando Paulus alibi de Deo simpliciter scripsit, ex eo, & per eum, & propter eum sunt omnia, ei gloria in secula. Amen. Non hic significat per, causam instrumentalem, vel inferiorem, sed vim primi efficientis. Deinde in textu nostro est in eo, ἐν αὐτῷ, quemadmodum Act. xvii. 28. ἐν αὐτῷ, in eo enim vivimus, & movemur, & sumus. Qua loquendi forma non instrumentum tantum medium, sed primaria causa, & primum efficiens signilumque creata, sed ea quae in coelo & terra sunt. Haec autem diversa sunt. Aliud enim est dicere, ego creavi domum, & aliud, ego creavi ea quae in domo sunt. Aliud est domus, & alia quae sunt in domo. Imo domum prius constructam esse oportet, quam ea quae in domo sunt. Ita etiam, hoc loco, aliud esset, si diceret Apostolus, coelum & terram per Christum esse creata, quam cum dicit, ea quae in coelo & terra sunt, per eum esse condita. Illud enim videretur primam creationem significare posse, hoc autem minime. Quin potius sequitur, prius creatum esse coelum & terram, quam ea quae in eis sunt; quin id quod continet, prius esse oportet iis, quae in eo continentur. Ergo jam coelum & terra erant, cum ea, quae in iis sunt, per Christum condebantur. Quare cum ab ista creatione, de qua hic agit Apostolus, excludantur coelum & terra, & prima creatio, absque his, nec esse, nec intelligi possit, imo non soleat aliter describi, quam per has principales mundi partes: necessario sequitur, hic non agi de prima creatione.
units.tr: There follows in the Apostle's words: for in him, or through him, all things were created in heaven and on earth. Against this our author rises up and denies that Christ is the Creator, or that the creation of things is meant here: on the ground that all things are not said to have been created by him, but in him or through him, and that this signifies Christ as the instrumental, not the primary, cause. But grant that it was said that all things were made through Christ: this takes nothing away from the first cause any more than when Paul elsewhere wrote simply of God: "from him, and through him, and to him are all things; to him be glory for ever. Amen" (Rom. 11:36). Here through does not signify an instrumental or subordinate cause, but the power of the first efficient cause. Further, in our text the phrase is in him, [ἐν αὐτῷ], as in Acts 17:28, [ἐν αὐτῷ], "for in him we live, and move, and have our being." By this form of speech there is signified not merely an intermediate instrument but the primary cause and first efficient. The adversary's argument also mixes up two things. The Apostle does not say that heaven and earth were created through Christ, but that the things which are in heaven and on earth were created through him. These, however, are different things. It is one thing to say "I built the house," and another to say "I made the things that are in the house"; the house and the things in it are different. Indeed, the house must first be built before the things that are in it. So in this passage, it would be one thing if the Apostle said that heaven and earth were created through Christ, and another when he says that the things which are in heaven and earth were created through him. For the former could seem to signify the first creation, but the latter not at all. Rather it follows that heaven and earth were created before the things in them; for what contains must be prior to what is contained in it. Therefore heaven and earth already existed when the things in them were being created through Christ. Since heaven and earth, and the first creation, are excluded from that creation of which the Apostle here speaks, and since that creation can neither exist nor be understood without these, indeed is not usually described otherwise than through these chief parts of the world, it necessarily follows that the first creation is not meant here.

units.la: Confutata adversariorum sententia, ut verus Apostoli verborum sensus illustrior fit: sciendum est, duplicem esse creationem, quorum prior vetus, altera vocari solet nova. Ad quod confirmandum, cum res sit notissima, & ab omnibus concessa, non est opus multis scripturae testimoniis. De prima, quae & vetus est, loquitur Moses Gen. 1. In principio creavit Deus coelum & terram. De secunda quae & nova est, cum alii tum Paulus 2 Cor. 5. verf. 17. si quis ergo in Christo est, nova creatura est, vetera transierunt: ecce facta sunt omnia nova, &c. Utriusque autem creationis auctor & origo est Deus Pater, ut tum Moses, tum Paulus, in locis citatis testantur. Sed priorem creationem Deus immediate, nullo administro aut medio usus, ut dictum est, absolvit: Novam autem peregit per Christum, cumque praecipuum instrumentum, & medium in hoc opere habuit. Unde fit, ut fere semper, quoties novae creationis fit mentio, illa per Christum esse perfecta dicatur. Hinc illa: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum. Per quem fecit & secula, seu significatur. Quare hic omnino est sermo de eo qui creavit omnia, sive in quo & per quem sunt creata: nam illa aequipollent. Adeoq; nec Arianis favet locus, nec Photinianis, sed fortissime adstruit sententiam catholicam, quam tribuit Adversarius Homousianis.
units.tr: Having refuted the opponents' view, so that the true sense of the Apostle's words may be clearer, we must note that there are two creations: the first is called the old, the other is usually called the new. To confirm this, since the matter is very well known and granted by all, there is no need of many testimonies of Scripture. Of the first, which is also the old, Moses speaks in Genesis 1: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." Of the second, which is also the new, both others and Paul speak, in 2 Corinthians 5:17: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new," and so on. Now the author and origin of both creations is God the Father, as both Moses and Paul bear witness in the passages cited. But God completed the first creation immediately, using no minister or means, as has been said; the new he accomplished through Christ, and had him as the chief instrument and means in this work. Hence it happens that almost always, whenever the new creation is mentioned, it is said to have been completed through Christ: hence the words, "All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made" (John 1:3); and "through whom he also made the worlds" (Heb. 1:2). Therefore here there is altogether talk of him who created all things, or in whom and through whom they were created, for these amount to the same thing. Thus the passage favours neither the Arians nor the Photinians, but very strongly establishes the Catholic doctrine, which the adversary attributes to the Homoousians.

units.la: Jam etiam audiamus, quomodo studeat evincere, non agi hic de creatione mundi & rerum prima. Sic infert: in mundi creatione remota fuit omnino causa instrumentalis, exclusa fuerunt omnia instrumenta & media, & soli Deo illa tributa. Quod concedimus totum, neque ut nobis probet, ullatenus est necesse: sed negamus consequentiam, ergo Christo creatio illa adscribi non potest: nam Christo non adscribitur ut socio, adjutori, vel instrumento infra Deum, sed Deo eidem ac uni. Et quando illum in modum disputat Adversarius, non Homousianorum videtur in animo habuisse sententiam, quam impugnaret, sed Arianorum. Ariani enim tale quid de Christo statuebant, non Catholici. At hic Apostolus, inquit, de tali loquitur creatione, in qua instrumenti quoque meminit. Id vero negamus. Negaturque ostendi vocibus, in ipso, vel per ipsum.
units.tr: Now let us also hear how he tries to prove that the creation of the world and of things in their first beginning is not meant here. He infers thus: "In the creation of the world the instrumental cause was altogether set aside; all instruments and means were excluded, and that work was ascribed to God alone." We concede all of this, nor is it at all necessary for our case that he prove it. But we deny the consequence: "therefore that creation cannot be ascribed to Christ." For Christ is not ascribed as an associate, helper, or instrument subordinate to God, but as one and the same God with him. And when the adversary argues in this way, he seems to have had in mind not the view of the Homoousians, which he would be attacking, but that of the Arians. For the Arians held something of this kind about Christ, not the Catholics. But here, he says, the Apostle speaks of such a creation in which he also mentions an instrument. This we deny. And we deny that this is shown by the words in him, or through him.

units.la: Pro secunda ratione adfert, quod apud Apostolum non dicitur Christus creasse coelum & terram: quod tamen solemne verbum est, quo in creationis historia vel opere designando Scriptura solet uti. Negamus iterum consequentiam. Non eadem utitur, qua alias, formula, ergo non de eadem loquitur re. Quis neget satis clarum esse expressionem Apostoli, quam adhibet, ad creationem significandam? Argumento est, quod locum omnes hactenus de creatione rerum acceperunt.
units.tr: For his second argument he points out that the Apostle does not say that Christ created heaven and earth, although that is the customary expression Scripture uses to describe creation or the work of creation. Again we deny the inference. The Apostle does not use the same formula as elsewhere, therefore he is not speaking of the same thing. Who would deny that the expression the Apostle uses to signify creation is clear enough? The proof is that everyone has hitherto understood the passage as referring to the creation of things.

units.la: Fatetur Adversarius, hic dici, per Christum creata ea quae in coelo & in terra sunt; & praemittitur, πρώτης κτίσεως [?]. Quis ea audiens, ambigat de creatione mundi sermonem esse? Aliud quidem est domus, aliud mundum. Nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per ipsum, &c. Nos igitur affirmamus, etiam hoc loco Paulum loqui de nova creatione. Primo, quia offensum jam est, hic non agi de prima & veteri creatione. Ergo de nova & secunda. Deinde, hic fit mentio instrumenti, seu medii, scimus autem Christum esse novae creationis praecipuum instrumentum, quem hic Apostolus nominat. Ergo haec de nova creatione sunt intelligenda. Tertio, usitatum est sacris scriptoribus, ut quae brevius & obscurius primo dicunt, postea dilucidius & copiosius explicent. Ergo hic quoque quod prius dixerat Apostolus obscure, universa in Christo esse condita, clarius postea explicat vers. 20. omnia per ipsum esse reconciliata, & pacificata. Quod non nisi de nova creatione intelligi potest. Si quis autem hic forte objiciat, scripturam, quando facit novae creationis mentionem, claris & disertis verbis id significare, ut apud Esa. & Ioh. Apoc. 22. Ecce nova facio omnia. Et 2 Cor. 5. Ecce facta sunt omnia nova, &c. Quod cum in his Pauli verbis expresse non dicatur, sed simpliciter creatio nominetur, sequi videtur, ista Apostoli verba, non esse de nova creatione intelligenda: facile est diluere. Non enim hoc perpetuum est, ut nova creatio semper diserte exprimatur, sed simpliciter saepe & absolute, creatio & creatura dicitur. Exempla huius rei plura sunt, uno & altero contenti erimus. Isa. 65. vers. 18. Sed gaudebitis & exultabitis usque in sempiternum in his, quae ego creo. Quia ecce ego creo Ierusalem exultationem, &c. Quae de nova creatione dici, nemo ambigit. Sic 2 Ep. vers. 10. Ipsius enim sumus factura, creati in Christo Iesu in operibus bonis, &c. ad Coloss. 3. vers. 10. --- secundum imaginem ejus qui creavit illum. Sic ad Eph. 3. vers. 9. dicitur Deus, omnia condidisse per Christum. Quem locum de regeneratione & reformatione, seu nova creatione intelligendum esse, etiam adversarii fatentur. Sic Iacobus cap. 1. vers. 18. Apostolos sive pies, ea aetate viventes, initium seu primitias vocat creaturae Dei. Quod non potest, nisi de creatura nova intelligi. Causa autem, cur haec aliud ea quae in domo: iterum, facere hoc, vel ista: sed, qui potest omnia facere quae in domo, quid ei deerit ad efficiendam quoque domum ipsam? Jam quod ea quae in mundo, vel fecisse ea quae in coelo & in terra, evertat aut non admittat etiam ipsam mundi ab eode facturam, & ut exceptio valeat, quod fecerit Christus ea quae in mundo, & non ipsum, qui probabitur? Debet dici, Christum fecisse omnia, & non tantum ea quae in mundo, esseque πάσης κτίσεως auctorem, nam & hoc dicitur, & bis τὰ πάντα, τὰ πάντα: & cui hoc jure imputatur, dubitabis eidem adscribere ipsam mundi creationem? Quod si in textu totidem verbis dictum fuisset, quod poscunt Adversarii, Christum coelum creasse ac terram, formidarent scilicet excogitare ad eludendam argumenti ac sententiae vim aliquod [illegible, ~9 letters]; vel non idè, quod nunc, applicare potuissent illis verbis φάρμακον[?]. Praeterea, an quia Marc. xiii. 19. dicitur ab initio creationis quam creavit Deus, & non creationis coeli ac terrae, haud innuitur creatio mundi? Atque uti illic simpliciter est, κτίσεως ἧς ἔκτισεν ὁ Θεὸς, ita hic, πάσης κτίσεως ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη. sic quoque Marc. x. 6. ἀπὸ δὲ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως. & II Pet. III. 4. I Pet. iv. 19. fideli creatori, quamvis non additur, coeli terraeque, haud eo minus rerum intelligitur creator ac creatio. Neque, quamvis coelum & terra non nominetur, idcirco a creatione, quam Apostolus commemorat, coelum & terra excluditur.
units.tr: Our opponent admits that the text says the things in heaven and on earth were created through Christ, and he adds the words "of the first creation" [πρώτης κτίσεως]. Who, hearing this, could doubt that the discourse concerns the creation of the world? One thing is a house, another the world. "No one comes to the Father except through him," etc. So we affirm that Paul is speaking here too of the new creation. First, because it has already been shown that the first and old creation is not what is in view here. Therefore it is the new and second creation. Second, mention is made here of an instrument or means, and we know that Christ is the chief instrument of the new creation, and this is the one the Apostle names here. Therefore these words are to be understood of the new creation. Third, it is the custom of the sacred writers to explain more fully and clearly afterwards what they first said briefly and obscurely. So here too, what the Apostle had said obscurely at first, that all things were created in Christ, he explains more clearly afterwards in verse 20, that all things were reconciled and pacified through him. This can only be understood of the new creation. But if anyone objects here that Scripture, when it mentions the new creation, signifies this in clear and explicit words, as in Isaiah and in John's Apocalypse, "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev. 21), and 2 Cor. 5, "Behold, all things are become new," etc., and since this is not expressly said in Paul's words but creation is simply named, it seems to follow that these words of the Apostle are not to be understood of the new creation: this is easily answered. For it is not a fixed rule that the new creation is always expressly named; rather creation and creature are often mentioned simply and absolutely. There are many examples of this, and we shall be content with one or two. Isaiah 65:18: "But you shall rejoice and exult for ever in what I create. For behold, I create Jerusalem a exultation," etc. No one doubts that this speaks of the new creation. So also 2 Eph. 2:10: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works," etc.; Col. 3:10: "according to the image of him who created him." So also Eph. 3:9 says God created all things through Christ. Our opponents themselves admit that this passage is to be understood of regeneration and reformation, that is, of the new creation. So also James 1:18, where he calls those living in that age, the Apostles or the godly, the beginning or firstfruits of God's creature. This can only be understood of the new creature. Now the reason why these things are said... [the sentence here is corrupt in the scan]. Again, to do this or that: but he who can do all the things in the house, what will be lacking to him for making the house itself? Now, that the things in the world, or the things in heaven and on earth, were made by him, should overturn or not admit that the world itself was made by the same person; and for the exception to hold, that Christ made the things in the world and not himself, who will prove it? It must be said that Christ made all things, and not only those in the world, and that he is the author of "all creation" [πάσης κτίσεως]. For this is also said, and twice "all things" [τὰ πάντα, τὰ πάντα]. And if this is rightly attributed to him, will you doubt that the creation of the world itself is ascribed to him? And if the text had said in so many words what the adversaries demand, that Christ created heaven and earth, they would surely have been afraid to devise some [evasion] to elude the force of the argument and the sense; or they could not, as now, have applied to those words... Besides, does the fact that Mark 13:19 speaks of "the beginning of the creation which God created," and not of "the creation of heaven and earth," imply that the creation of the world is not meant? And just as there it is simply "of the creation which God created" [κτίσεως ἧς ἔκτισεν ὁ Θεὸς], so here it is "of all creation was created in him" [πάσης κτίσεως ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη]. So also Mark 10:6, "from the beginning of creation" [ἀπὸ δὲ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως], and 2 Pet. 3:4, and 1 Pet. 4:19, "a faithful Creator," where although "of heaven and earth" is not added, the Creator and creation of things is nonetheless understood. Nor, although heaven and earth are not named, is heaven and earth for that reason excluded from the creation which the Apostle mentions.

units.la: Non negamus, regenerationem dici quoque creationem, propter similitudinem operationis in rerum creatione, & in hominis renovatione, sed id rarius, & de homine, deque regeneratione, ubi verba sunt ita clara, ut dubium esse nequeat, & nova creatio, simpliciter aliquando vocatur creatio, esse potest prima haec. Quia Hebraei vocibus compositis vel carent, vel certe simplicibus pro compositis utuntur. Notum autem est, etiam Novum testamentum Hebraismum scatere. Deinde, quia voluerunt sacri scriptores, hanc secundam creationem, quodammodo aequiparare priori, & indicare, non minorem gratiam, potentiam, & benignitatem, Deum in hac posteriori creatione ostendisse, quam in prima. Itaque etiamsi Paulus non expresse scribat, se loqui de secunda creatione: tamen circumstantiae, antecedentia & consequentia, & rationes firmae, de ea hic agi docent. Sed hic insurgunt nostri adversarii, & contra hanc nostram interpretationem valide torquent, & urgent sequentia Apostoli verba: in eo, inquit, sunt condita universa, quae in coelis & terra sunt, visibilia & invisibilia, sive throni, &c. Nova, inquiunt, creatio, spectat tantum ad homines, nam Deus per Christum non plantas, bestias, aves, pisces, & alias creaturas, sed solum genus humanum restauravit, & renovavit. At hic Apostolus, primo quidem universaliter utitur voce, τὰ πάντα. Quam ne quis synechdochice, ad particulare aliquod restringeret, mox addit explicationem, & quid per omnia intelligendum sit, clarius exprimit, ac cuncta in duas classes distribuit, in ea quae in coelis, & ea quae in terra sunt. Illa vocat invisibilia, haec visibilia. Et quia invisibilia, erant ignotiora, ea singillatim statim enumerat; sive throni, inquit, sive dominationes, sive principatus, sive potestates. Atque haec omnia per Christum esse condita affirmat; unde apparet haec ad novam creationem, hoc est, ad solos homines restringi non posse. Non levis sane objectio, sed cui tamen, Deo nos juvante, abunde satisfaciemus. Et primo ad ista omnia respondemus, etiamsi daremus, quod non damus, haec de prima creatione esse intelligenda: non tamen principale adversariorum intentum hinc elici posset. Nam hic Apostolus, Christum instrumentum tantum facit; non dicit haec Christum creasse, sed alium, per ipsum, haec creasse. Major autem & subjunctâ explicatione, quae istud confirmet: at in hoc textu non de hominibus, sed de rebus fit mentio, iisque omnibus, unde τὰ πάντα aliquoties, non πάντες[?]; & status, dominationes, dignitates adduntur, nihil quod indicet de solis per Christum regenitis sermonem esse, & κτίσεως, ἐκτίσθη[?], ἐκλήρω[?] dicitur, nulla indicatâ explicatione, quod illa improprie & spiritualiter accipere oporteat. Quemadmodum non ita accipienda in locis quae annotat, omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil quod factum. Et, per quem fecit & secula.
units.tr: We do not deny that regeneration is also called creation, on account of the similarity of the work in the creation of things and in the renewal of man; but this is rarer, and is said of man and of regeneration where the words are so clear that there can be no doubt. And that the new creation is sometimes simply called creation, this may be the first reason: the Hebrews either lack compound words or certainly use simple words for compound ones, and it is well known that even the New Testament abounds in Hebraisms. Second, because the sacred writers wished to make this second creation in some way equal to the first, and to indicate that God showed no less grace, power and goodness in this later creation than in the first. Thus, even if Paul does not expressly write that he is speaking of the second creation, nevertheless the circumstances, the preceding and following context, and the solid reasons show that this is what is treated here. But here our adversaries rise up, vigorously twist against this our interpretation, and press the following words of the Apostle: "in him," he says, "were created all things that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones," etc. The new creation, they say, pertains only to men; for through Christ God restored and renewed not plants, beasts, birds, fish and other creatures, but only the human race. But here the Apostle, first of all, uses the word "all things" (τὰ πάντα) in a universal way. Lest anyone restrict this by synecdoche to some particular part, he immediately adds an explanation, expresses more clearly what is to be understood by "all things," and distributes everything into two classes: those in heaven and those on earth. He calls the former invisible and the latter visible. And because the invisible things were more unknown, he at once enumerates them one by one: "whether thrones," he says, "or dominions, or principalities, or powers." And he affirms that all these were created through Christ; whence it appears that these cannot be restricted to the new creation, that is, to men alone. This is certainly no slight objection, but we shall, God helping us, answer it amply. And first we reply to all these points: even if we granted, which we do not, that these are to be understood of the first creation, the principal aim of the adversaries could not be drawn from this. For here the Apostle makes Christ only an instrument; he does not say that Christ created these things, but that another created these things through him. As for the major premise and the added explanation which confirms it: in this text mention is made not of men but of things, and of all of them, whence "all things" (τὰ πάντα) is used several times, not "all men" [πάντες]; and thrones, dominions, and dignities are added, nothing indicating that the discourse is only about those regenerated through Christ. And it is said "of creation," "was created" [κτίσεως, ἐκτίσθη], and "was allotted" [ἐκλήρω], with no explanation indicating that these words must be taken improperly and spiritually. Just as they are not to be so taken in the passages he notes: "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made," and "through whom he also made the ages."

units.la: Contendit tamen, Paulum loqui de nova creatione, & non veteri: sed in cujus probatione mire deficit. Nam in primo argumento putidè petit hoc, quod est in quaestione. In secundo, itidem. In tertio nihil concludit, quum de versu 20. respondeat, & de alio, vid. 15. 16. sit instituta quaestio.
units.tr: He contends, however, that Paul is speaking of the new creation and not the old, but in proving this he fails badly. In his first argument he shamelessly begs the very question at issue. The second does the same. The third concludes nothing, since he answers concerning verse 20, whereas the question was raised about another passage, see verses 15 and 16.

units.la: Jam verò alia sunt & fortiora, quae nos contrà, pro catholica sententia & explicatione loci adferre possumus, quo constet hic agi de primâ rerum creatione, eamque Christo diserte attribui. Nam rarius vox creationis & creaturae, renovationem significat spiritualem, quàm proprie creationem mundi. Atq; illud ubi fit in transcursu magis & breviter, non ita prolixe, ut in hoc textu, ubi ad minimum ter vox illa occurrit. Et nusquam additur explicatio, vel aliquid rei, vel verbi, quod indicet improprie accipiendum sermonem esse de creatione spirituali gratiae, & non naturae. Ubi de renovatione agitur, in particulari ea attribuitur hominibus, iisque certis aliquibus: ubi vero de creatione sermo est, universali omnium, & rerum, τὰ πάντα, τὰ πάντα, & πίστης κτίσεως. Non universaliter de Christi gratia Scriptura loquitur, neque adeo universanobilior ille est; qui creat, eo, per quem creat.
units.tr: There are other and stronger arguments which we can bring against him, on behalf of the Catholic opinion and the explanation of the passage, to show that it treats of the first creation of things and that this is expressly attributed to Christ. The words creation and creature rarely signify spiritual renewal; they properly signify the creation of the world. Where they do signify renewal, it is done in passing and briefly, not at such length as in this text, where the word occurs at least three times. Nowhere is there any added explanation, either of the thing or of the word, to indicate that the language must be taken improperly, of the spiritual creation of grace and not of nature. Where renewal is in view, it is attributed in particular to men, and to certain men at that; where creation is spoken of, it is universal, of all and of everything, τὰ πάντα [all things], and πάσης κτίσεως [of every creature]. Scripture does not speak universally of Christ's grace, nor is there any universal grace of Christ. He who creates is more noble than that through whom he creates.

units.la: At Deo æterno, qualem isti Christum facere volunt, nemo major, nemo nobilior. Itaque hæc verba, Arianos videntur aliquo modo, sed homousianos nullo modo juvare. Sed ut ad veram verborum interpretationem accedamus, Concedimus & fatemur novam creationem, proprie & principaliter ad solos homines pertinere: Attamen, in scriptura sæpe generali voce, omnium creatio vocatur. Ut vel ille unicus Pauli locus docere potest, 2 Cor. 5. Si quis in Christo est, nova creatura est, vetera transierunt, ecce facta sunt omnia nova. Omnia autem ex Deo, qui nos reconciliavit sibi per Christum. Ubi dicit eos esse novam creationem, qui in Christo sunt, & qui Deo per Christum reconciliati sunt.
units.tr: But to the eternal God, such as these people wish Christ to be, no one is greater and no one more noble. Thus these words seem to help the Arians in some way, but the Homoousians in no way. But to come to the true interpretation of the words: we concede and confess that the new creation pertains properly and principally to men alone. Nevertheless, in Scripture the creation of all is often called by a general word, as that single passage of Paul can teach, 2 Cor. 5: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ." There he says that those who are in Christ, and who have been reconciled to God through Christ, are the new creation.

units.la: At isti sunt soli homines. Et tamen ait: ecce facta sunt omnia nova. Similiter ad Eph. 3. vers. 9. --- quæ sit dispensatio sacramenti absconditi à seculis in Deo, qui omnia creavit, ut innotescat principibus, &c. Ubi per omnium creationem, restaurationem generis humani, seu novam creationem intelligi, etiam Trinitarii fatentur. Nemo igitur admiretur, neque contra scripturam fieri putet, si nos hic quoque, per creationem universorum, seu omnium, posteriorem seu novam creationem, significari & describi affirmamus. Sed instabit aliquis, sequentia verba hujus vocis πᾶσα[?], nostram expositionem refellere. Nam hæc omnia, vocantur cœlestia & terrestria, visibilia, & invisibilia, throni, potestates, &c. At homines non sunt cœlestes, neque invisibiles, ergo hæc descriptio, seu σωμα[?], ad solos homines, ac proinde, nec ad novam creationem, pertinere non potest. Ad hanc instantiam removendam, duas afferemus responsiones. Unam generalem; alteram specialem. Generali responsioni fundamenta hæc præmittimus. Unum: Homines, in sacris litteris sæpe vocari, omnem creaturam, & totum mundum. Cujus rei clarissima extant testimonia: Marc. 16. vers. 15. Prædicate Euangelium, omni creaturæ, id est, homini, seu generi humano. Et in hoc eodem
units.tr: But these are only men, and yet he says: behold, all things have become new. Similarly, Eph. 3:9: "what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that it might be made known to the principalities," etc. Here even the Trinitarians admit that by the creation of all things is understood the restoration of the human race, or the new creation. Therefore no one should wonder, or think it contrary to Scripture, if we also affirm that here, by the creation of all things, or of the universe, the later or new creation is signified and described. But someone will object that the following words, "every" [πᾶσα], refute our interpretation. For all these things are called heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible, thrones, powers, and so on. But men are neither heavenly nor invisible; therefore this description cannot pertain to men alone, and consequently cannot pertain to the new creation. To remove this objection we will offer two replies: one general, the other special. For the general reply we lay down these foundations. First: in the sacred letters men are often called every creature and the whole world. There are very clear testimonies to this: Mark 16:15, "Preach the gospel to every creature," that is, to man, or the human race. And in this same

units.la: verse, aliter ... verbis, ... ille capite verf. 23. Immobiles a spe Euangelii, quod audivistis, quod praedicatum est in universa creatura, quae sub caelo est, hoc est, cuius homini. Ad Rom. 8. Et Ioh. 12. verf. 19. Ecce totus mundus post eum abit, id est, homines. Hinc etiam Philosophi, hominem μικρο-κοσμον appellant, quicquid enim in magno & spatioso mundo est, id summatim in homine parvo comprehensum est. Secunda hypothesis haec esto: Mundum, seu omnem creaturam, cuncta comprehendere quaecunque sunt. Sive ergo quis una voce dicat Mundus, sive vero per enumerationem partium, caelum, terra, visibilia, invisibilia, throni, dominationes, principatus, potestates, idem esse, atque hoc tantum differre, quod ibi eadem res, unica voce, hic pluribus effertur; illud est definitum, hoc definitio. Tertium fundamentum ponatur hoc: Cuicunque competit definitum, eidem & definitio. Et, de quocunque praedicatur definitum, de eodem etiam definitio. Cuius ratio est, quia definitum & definitio, re ipsa, idem sunt: definitum est contracta definitio, & definitio est dilatatum & expansum definitum. Quibus praemissis, ita argumentor. De homine praedicatur mundus, & omnis creatura. Ergo de eodem praedicatur caelum, terra, visibilia, throni, potestates, &c. Antecedens probatum est in prima hypothesi. Consequentia patet ex secunda & tertia hypothesi. Nam mundus, seu omnis creatura, est definitum: caelum vero, terra, visibilia, invisibilia, & caetera, sunt definitio. Neque re ipsa haec quidquam differunt. An non igitur imprudens & ineptus est, qui definitum alicui attribuens, definitionem attribuere veretur? qui totum concedit, & partes negat? qui totius nomine alicui concesso, partium attributione conturbatur? Quid est absurdi si dicamus, per ea quae in caelo & terra sunt, per visibilia & invisibilia, intelligi solos homines, si antea probavimus, omnem creaturam, & totum mundum solos homines significare? An ea quae in caelo, & in terra, quae visibilia, & invisibilia sunt, creaturae, & mundi partes mundi rerumque omnium.
units.tr: verse, otherwise ... in the words ... chapter 1, verse 23: "unmoved from the hope of the gospel which you have heard, which has been preached in every creature under heaven," that is, to every man. Rom. 8; and John 12:19: "Behold, the whole world has gone after him," that is, men. Hence the philosophers also call man a microcosm, for whatever is in the great and spacious world is summarily comprehended in the small man. Let the second hypothesis be this: the world, or every creature, comprehends all things that exist. Whether therefore one says in one word "world," or by enumerating the parts, "heaven, earth, visible things, invisible things, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers," it is the same thing, differing only in that the same reality is expressed there by one word and here by several; the former is the defined, the latter the definition. Let the third foundation be this: whatever belongs to the defined belongs also to the definition, and whatever is predicated of the defined is predicated also of the definition. The reason is that the defined and the definition are in fact the same: the defined is a contracted definition, and the definition is the defined expanded and spread out. With these premises I argue thus. The world and every creature is predicated of man. Therefore heaven, earth, visible things, thrones, powers, etc., are predicated of the same man. The antecedent was proved in the first hypothesis. The consequence is clear from the second and third hypotheses. For the world, or every creature, is the defined; heaven, earth, the visible, the invisible and the rest are the definition, and in fact these differ in no way. Is it not then imprudent and foolish to fear attributing the definition to someone to whom one has attributed the defined? Who concedes the whole and denies the parts? Who, having conceded the name of the whole to someone, is disturbed by the attribution of the parts? What is absurd if we say that by those things which are in heaven and on earth, the visible and the invisible, only men are understood, when we have already proved that every creature and the whole world signifies only men? Or are those things which are in heaven and on earth, which are visible and invisible, creatures and parts of the world and of all things?

units.la: Ad quod multum facit, quod ipse Adversarius fatetur in sequentibus verbis haud exiguum latere causae nostrae momentum, quando dicuntur condita in Christo universa, quae in caelis & terra sunt, visibilia & invisibilia, sive throni, &c. verum putat, non ita nos principale intentum obtinere, & Arianis aliquo modo videri favere locum, non nobis. Un-de? quia Christum instrumentum tantum facit creationis. Hoc nos in superioribus refutavimus. Deinde fatetur, novam creationem, proprie & principaliter ad solos homines pertinere. Sed & putat, in Scriptura saepe generali voce, omnium creationem vocari. Hoc negamus, & sive ita esset, nihil adhuc contra nos evinceret, quia in textu dicitur & omnium creatio, atq; universalitas ista ita mox explicatur, ut nisi de omnium rerum creatione exponi non possit.
units.tr: To this the Adversary himself greatly contributes, since in the following words he confesses that no small weight of our cause lies hidden: when it is said that all things, visible and invisible, which are in heaven and on earth, or thrones, etc., were created in Christ. He thinks, however, that we do not thereby obtain our principal aim, and that the passage seems to favour the Arians somewhat rather than us. On what ground? Because he makes Christ merely the instrument of creation. We have refuted this above. Next he confesses that the new creation pertains properly and principally to men alone. But he also thinks that in Scripture the creation of all is often called by a general word. We deny this; and even if it were so, it would prove nothing further against us, because in the text the creation of all is mentioned, and this universality is then explained in such a way that it cannot be expounded except of the creation of all things.

units.la: 1 Cor. v. 17. inquit quidem Apostolus, ecce facta sunt omnia nova. Sed & praemiserat proxime ante, in Christo, & nova creatura, & vetera praeteriisse; atque subjunxerat statim, omnia ista nova intelligi reconciliata Deo per Christum, nempe nos fideles in Christo. Hac ergo ratione omnia nova dixit. Et creationem non dixit nisi novam, non creationem simpliciter, nedum creationem omnium. Quod & videt Adversarius, inquiens, quod Apostolus dicit eos esse novam creationem. Similiter ad Eph. iii. 9. dicitur de Deo, qui omnia creavit: quod non adeo certum est, de sola nova creatione intelligi debere. Sed sic ita, circumstantiae textus istud patiantur, at nunc regerimus Adversario, quod ille nobis supra, non addi, in caelis, & in terra, qua loquendi formula, sive quarum duarum mundi praecipuarum partium nomine intelligitur universus mundus. Atqui in loco Col. i. non tantum omnium sit mentio a Christo creatorum, sed omnium in caelis &c in non sunt? An cum totum alicui tribuitur, partes eidem negantur? Certè si totus mundus significare potest tantum homines, partes quoque mundi eosdem significare poterunt. Quid est ergo, quod adversarii nostri, cum audiunt homines solos, vocari universam creaturam, totum mundum: non conturbantur, sed totum agnoscunt, explicant, & excusant: Si vero vident, hoc idem, per partes, iisdem hominibus attribui, si voces, cœli & terræ, visibilium & invisibilium audiunt, obstupescunt, hærent? titubant? Atqui, ô inepti, hoc idem dicebatur de homine, cum vocabatur universa creatura; tantum modo ea, quæ antea breviter & summatim proposita erant, hic per partes, & copiosius exponuntur. Res eadem prorsus est: modus loquendi tantum variat. Hæc est generalis responsio: nunc specialem adjiciamus, & excussis singulis clausulis, ostendamus, hanc nostram sententiam esse veram. Ait igitur Apostolus, per Christum esse condita, ea quæ sunt in cœlis, & quæ in terra. Quæ phrasi nihil aliud significari existimo, quam humanum genus à Deo per Christum renovatum & redemptum. Credo hic imperitos aliquos exclamaturos, quis unquam credat, per cœlum & terram, homines intelligi? Sed hæc admiratio & exclamatio oritur ex φρασεων[?] & proprietatis linguæ sanctæ ignoratione; in qua hujusmodi hyperbolicæ locutiones usitatæ sunt, & cœli terræque nomine passim homines intelligi solent. Quod si cui absurdum & insolens videtur, cogitet, nullam esse linguam, cui quædam phrases, & loquendi formulæ peculiares non sint, quas si quis ad verbum, in aliam linguam transferat, ridicula, absona & absurda videantur. Non consueverunt fortasse Græci & Latini, per cœlum & terram, intelligere homines; sed Hebræis hoc elegans & vulgaris loquendi formula est. Quis autem præscribere potest variis nationibus, ut hoc aut illo modo loquantur? Si spiritui sancto placuit ita loqui, quis est qui ausit[?] reprehendere? Iam verò ἓ πᾶν[?] nomine, homines solos significari, sæpè demonstravimus, ut
units.tr: The Apostle indeed says, 2 Cor. 5:17: "behold, all things have become new." But shortly before he had said "in Christ, a new creature," and that old things had passed away; and he had immediately added that all these new things are understood to be reconciled to God through Christ, namely we faithful in Christ. In this way, therefore, he called them all new. And he did not speak of creation except as new, not of creation simply, much less of the creation of all. The Adversary also sees this, saying that the Apostle says that those are a new creation. Similarly at Eph. 3:9 it is said of God, who created all things, which is not so certainly to be understood of the new creation alone; but so the circumstances of the text allow. Now we turn back on the Adversary what he objected to us above: that "in heaven and on earth" is not added, a form of speech by which the whole world is understood under the name of two principal parts, of the two chief parts of the world the name signifies the whole universe. Yet in Col. 1 there is mention not only of all things created by Christ, but of all things in heaven and on earth. Is it when something is attributed to the whole that the parts are denied to it? Certainly if the whole world can signify only men, the parts of the world will also be able to signify the same. Why is it, then, that our adversaries, when they hear that men alone are called the whole creature, the whole world, are not disturbed but acknowledge the whole, explain it and excuse it; yet if they see the same thing attributed to the same men through its parts, if they hear the words heaven and earth, visible and invisible, they are astonished, stick fast and stagger? Yet, you fools, the same was said of man when he was called the whole creature; only the things previously set forth briefly and summarily are here expounded by parts and more fully. The thing itself is entirely the same; only the mode of speaking varies. This is the general reply. Now let us add the special one, and, having examined the individual clauses, show that our opinion is true. The Apostle therefore says that those things which are in heaven and which are on earth were created through Christ. By this phrase I think nothing else is signified than the human race renewed and redeemed by God through Christ. I believe that some unskilled people will here cry out, "Who would ever believe that by heaven and earth men are understood?" But this wonder and exclamation arises from ignorance of the idioms and proper usage of the holy tongue, in which such hyperbolical expressions are in use, and by the name of heaven and earth men are commonly understood. If this seems absurd and strange to anyone, let him consider that there is no language without certain peculiar phrases and forms of speech which, if someone translates word for word into another language, would seem ridiculous, incongruous and absurd. Perhaps the Greeks and Latins are not accustomed to understand men by heaven and earth, but for the Hebrews this is an elegant and common form of speech. Who, moreover, can prescribe to the various nations that they must speak in this or that way? If it pleased the Holy Spirit to speak thus, who dares to find fault? Now, that by the name "all" [πᾶν] only men are signified, we have often demonstrated, as

units.la: & in terra, & porro magis distributive, omnium visibilium & invisibilium, &c. quin & πάσης κτίσεως.
units.tr: and on earth, and further, more distributively, of all things visible and invisible, etc.; indeed of all creation [πάσης κτίσεως].

units.la: Ad quæ iterum ecce nova effugia. Unum, hominem in Sacris litteris sæpe vocari omnem creaturam, & totum mundum. Verùm non tum homo, sed humanum genus dicitur omnis creatura. Non proprie, sed improprie. Non junctim cum creatione, sed cum prædicatione: unde tum satis liquet, prædicatione, quæ dicitur fieri omni creaturæ, exponi debere de omni homine. Creatura illic non potest non intelligi humana: hic exponitur sive de humana, sive angelica, cœlesti & terrestri. Denique prædicatio quidem contingit cuivis homini, non item renovatio, & creatio per Christum secunda: quare quantumvis illa dicatur fieri omni creaturæ, ista non potest. Nec magis hoc stringit, quod homo μικρόκοσμος[?] appellatur. Nam id ratione cujuscunq; hominis dicitur. Quid ergo an unus homo posset in sermone dici omnis creatura & totus mundus? Num propterea id hic loci debet? Eversâ primâ hypothesi, corruunt reliquæ.
units.tr: Against these he again offers new escapes. The first is that in Holy Scripture a man is often called every creature and the whole world. But it is not the man himself that is called every creature, but the human race. The term is used improperly, not properly. It is not joined with creation but with preaching, and from this it is clear enough that the preaching said to be made to every creature must be understood of every man. The creature there cannot but be understood as human; here it may be understood either of humans or of angels, heavenly and earthly beings. Finally, preaching does indeed reach every man, but renewal and the second creation through Christ do not; so however much the one is said to be made to every creature, the other cannot be. Nor does it press the point any more that man is called a microcosm [μικρόκοσμος]. For that is said of any man whatever. What then? Could a single man be called in speech every creature and the whole world? Is it therefore to be so understood in this place? Once the first hypothesis is overturned, the rest collapse.

units.la: Mundus, inquit, comprehendit omnia quæ sunt in mundo.
