Et perinde est, sive mundum nomine collectivè, sive distributivè eas, per singulas mundi partes, visibilia, invisibilia, &c. scilicet quando mundum ipsum physicè consideras, non ubi voce mundi uteris in quavis oratione. Neque hominem nominando, ideo statim intelligis totum humanum genus. Nam eo nihil fingi potest absurdius. Nam quando dicitur Ioan. xii. 19. quod totus mundus post Christum ivit, quis ferat dicentem, visibilia & invisibilia, thronos, potestates, &c. omnia post Christum ivisse[?]? Mundus quidem simpliciter, per se, & proprie acceptus illa complectitur, sed non propterea vox mundi ubicunque in fer-
units.tr: The world, he says, comprehends all the things that are in the world. And it makes no difference whether the world is taken collectively or distributively, through its individual parts: visible things, invisible things, and so on. Clearly, this holds when you consider the world itself physically, not when you use the word world in any speech whatever. Nor, when you name a man, do you at once understand the whole human race; nothing could be more absurd than that. For when it is said in John 12:19 that the whole world went after Christ, who could bear someone saying that visible and invisible things, thrones, powers, and so on, all went after Christ? The world, taken simply, in itself and properly, does embrace those things; but for that reason the word world does not occur everywhere in speech even in an improper sense. Or, when Christ ordered the gospel to be preached to every creature, will you therefore explain it so that the apostles went to preach to all creatures in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, etc.?

units.la: 2 Cor. 5. verf. 17. Ad Eph. 3. verf. 9. Per cœlum & terram homines significari, ut illud praetermittam, homines sæpe apud Prophetas, Solem, Lunam, Luciferum, stellas, quæ in cœlo, & magna pars cœli sunt, nominari; patet vel ex illo Esaiæ dicto, cap. 51. verf. 16. Posui verba mea in ore tuo, & in umbra manus meæ protexi te, ut plantes cœlos & fundes terram. Certè locus ipse sive de Propheta, sive de Christo intelligatur: clarum est ibi per cœlos & terram, nihil nisi pios homines significari: sicut omnes hodie testantur. & ipse Esaias statim explanat, cum subjicit: Et dicas ad Sion: Populus meus es tu. Quæ verba, explicatio sunt superiorum. Similis est locus Ieremiæ, cap. 1. verf. 9. Ecce constitui te hodie super gentes & super regna, ut evellas & destruas, & dispergas & dissipes, & ædifices & plantes. Sic Aggæi cap. 2. verf. 7. Adhuc unum modicum est, & ego commovebo cœlum & terram, & mare & aridam. Quod quid sit statim explicat, cum subjicit: Et movebo omnes gentes. Ergo clarum est per cœlum & terram, sæpe solos homines in scriptura intelligi. At si quis forte instet, ac dicat, hic non cœlum & terram (quæ sæpe denotant) dici creata esse, sed ea quæ in cœlo & terra sunt: Respondeo, nihil referre utrum modo loquatur scriptura, sensum esse eundem. Ac ne quis tergiversetur, dabimus exemplum aliud, huic omnino par: Apoc. 5. verf. 13. Et omnem creaturam, quæ in cœlo est, & super terram, & sub terra, & quæ sunt in mari, & quæ in eo, omnes audivi dicentes. Hoc est, pios homines audivi. Nihil igitur miri, nihil absurdi, nihil inusitati est, per ea quæ in cœlo, & in terra sunt, per visibilia & invisibilia, homines solos intelligere. Quod subjicitur, visibilia & invisibilia, illud terrestria, hoc cœlestia significant. Ergo, idem de hiis vocibus dicendum: quod de cœlo & terra. Denique throni, dominationes, &c. significant omnes cujuscunque gradus & dignitatis homines, ut apparet ex Rom. 8. Et ad Eph. 3. verf. 9. Quasi dicat, ad omnes hominum ordines, parvos, magnos, divites & pauperes, Dei, per sermone occurrit, etiam improprio. Vel, quando Christus jussit Euangelium prædicare omni creaturæ, idne propterea ex-pones, ut prædicatum irent Apostoli crea-turis omnibus in cœlis, & terra, visibili-bus & invisibilibus? &c. Denique si idem fit, sive quis unâ voce dicat mundus, sive per enumerationem partium, cœlum, terra, visibilia, throni, dominationes, principatus, potestates, atque hoc tantum diffe-rant, quod ibi eadem res unica voce, hic pluribus effertur, illud est definitum, hoc definitio, ergo quando Christus dicitur omnia creasse quæ in cœlis & terra, &c. per istam partium enumerationem, tantundem est ac si fuisset dictum, eum mundum creasse. Et consequenter male in hoc constituit responsionem suam Adversa-rius supra, quod quidem à Christo dicerentur facta illa esse in mundo, non autem mundus, quæ jam vult nihil differre. Atque ita sibi mirum in modum contradicit.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5:17. Eph. 3:9. That heaven and earth signify men, to pass over that point, is shown by the fact that in the prophets men are often named by heaven and earth; the sun, moon, Lucifer, and the stars, which are in heaven, and a large part of heaven, are named for men. This is plain from that saying of Isaiah, ch. 51:16: "I have put my words in your mouth, and covered you in the shadow of my hand, that I may plant the heavens and found the earth." Certainly, whether this place is understood of the prophet or of Christ, it is clear that by heavens and earth only pious men are signified there, as all today testify; and Isaiah himself straightway explains it when he adds: "And say to Zion, You are my people." These words are an explanation of what precedes. Similar is the place in Jeremiah, ch. 1:9: "Behold, I have set you this day over nations and kingdoms, to root out and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant." So in Haggai ch. 2:7: "Yet once, a little while, and I will shake the heaven and the earth, the sea and the dry land." What this means he explains at once when he adds: "And I will shake all nations." Therefore it is clear that by heaven and earth, which often denote the heavens and the earth, Scripture often means only men. But if someone perhaps presses and says that here it is not heaven and earth (which often denote them) said to be created, but those things which are in heaven and earth, I answer that it makes no difference whether Scripture speaks in this way or that; the sense is the same. And lest anyone evade, we will give another example wholly like this: Rev. 5:13: "And every creature which is in heaven, and upon the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, I heard saying..." That is, I heard pious men. Nothing therefore is strange, nothing absurd, nothing unusual, in understanding by the things which are in heaven and on earth, by visible and invisible things, men alone. What is added, visible and invisible, the former signifies earthly things, the latter heavenly things. Therefore, the same must be said of these words as of heaven and earth. Finally, thrones, dominions, etc. signify men of every rank and dignity, as appears from Rom. 8 and Eph. 3:9. As if he said, to all the orders of men, small and great, rich and poor, of God, through the word, even in an improper sense. Or, when Christ commanded the gospel to be preached to every creature, will you on that account explain it so that the apostles went to preach to all creatures in heaven and earth, visible and invisible? Finally, if it is the same whether someone says the world in one word, or enumerates its parts, heaven, earth, visible things, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, and the only difference is that there the same thing is expressed by one word and here by many, then the one is the term defined and the other the definition. Therefore, when Christ is said to have created all things that are in heaven and earth, etc., by this enumeration of parts, it is just as if it had been said that he created the world. And consequently the adversary, above, wrongly bases his reply on this, that those things were indeed said by Christ to be made in the world, but not the world itself; and yet now he wants to say there is no difference. So in a wonderful way he contradicts himself.

units.la: Nam & nobis hinc adaptamus tertium ejus fundamentum, quodque ei superstruit, argumentum. Cui enim competit definitio, eidem & definitum competit, & de quocunque prædicatur definitio, de eodem & definitum. Quia definitio & definitum reipsa idem sunt. Definitio est di-latatum & expansum definitum, & contra definitum con-tracta definitio. Jam de quo prædicatur, creatum cœlum, terra, visibilia, throni, potestates, &c. de eodem prædicatur mundus & omnis creatura: sed de Christi creatione prædicatur cœlum, terra, visibilia, &c. ergo. Nam cœlum, terra, visibilia, invisibilia, &c. sunt definitio, vel partes definiti, & mundus, seu omnis creatura est definitum. Nec re-ipsa hæc quidquam differunt. Neque ei licet jam excipere, in textu non dici cœ-lum, & terram creata, sed ea quæ in cælis, & terrâ; nam ipse illa ita accipit, & hic, & in sequentibus, in argumentatione, ex Christum, gratiam exundasse. Et ita est amplificatio beneficii divini. Si quis autem quaerat, cur huiusmodi formulis loquendi utatur scriptura? responderi potest, in venerem & gratiam orationi quaeri. Sunt enim illae αὐξη[?]σὶς ὑπερβολικαί. Neque est iniusta-tum, ut cum quippiam amplificare, & constanter affirmare volumus, pluribus vocibus, idem significantibus, atque etiam rei veritatem superantibus, utamur: Talis est illa enumeratio Pauli, ad Rom. 8. verf. 38. Certus sum enim, quia neque mors, neque vita, neque Angeli, neque principatus, neque virtutes, neque instantia, neque futura, neque fortitudo, neque altitudo, neque profundum, neque creatura alia poterit nos separare à charitate Dei. Quorum verborum simplex sensus est, nihil potest nos separare ab amore Dei. Sic ad Ephef. 1. verf. 21. Supra omnem principatum & potestatem, & virtutem & dominationem, & omne nomen quod nominatur non solum in hoc seculo, sed etiam in futuro. Hoc est, supra omne id, quicquid usquam est. Tale est in Epistola eadem cap. 3. verf. 18. & illud: ut possitis comprehendere cum omnibus Sanctis, quae sit longitudo & latitudo, & sublimitas & profundum, id est, penitus & omnino intelligere. Pari ratione, cum Apostolus hoc loco vellet significare, omnia in creatione nova per Christum esse facta, hac enumeratione αὐξηλυκὴ [?] ὑπερβολικὴ usus est, quae aequipollet illi voci generali, τὰ πάντα. Sed quia sunt qui pertendant, & indocta superstitione excaecati, hac simplici & vulgari interpretatione non contenti, omnino hic aliquid mysterii latere, neque hyperbolicas locutiones in sacris agnoscere, aut admittere volunt: videamus, an ipsis alio etiam modo satisfacere possimus. Hoc igitur ipsis omnibus commune est, per ea quae in coelis sunt, per invisibilia, per thronos, dominationes, principatus, potestates, intelligi debere Spiritus quosdam, & substantias abstractas, sive Angelos. Qui quoniam in duplici sunt differentia, textu, pro voce homo: quare non aliter nos accipere debemus in argumentatione pro Christo, ejusque creatione, quae tam clare textu continentur. Adversarius postmodum: at si quis forte instet, ac dicat, hic non coelum & terram (quae saepe homines denotant) dici creata esse, sed ea quae in coelo & terra sunt: Respondeo, nihil referre, utrovis modo loquatur Scriptura, sensum esse eundem. Annon igitur imprudens & ineptus est, qui definitionem alicui attribuens, definitum attribuere veretur? qui ea quae in mundo omni à Christo creata dici concedens, effugium in eo quaerit, quod non dicatur mundum fecisse, & non fecisse coelum ac terram, quamvis dicatur fecisse ea quae in coelis & in terra? qui partes concedit, ut totum neget? qui partium attributione concessa, totius nomine conturbetur? Res eadem prorsus est, modus loquendi tantum variat. Sed de voce hominis, ejusque significatione vel acceptione ita argumentari, uti facit Adversarius, valde ineptum est. De homine praedicatur mundus, & universa creatura: negamus. Ergo de eodem praedicatur coelum, terra, visibilia, &c. iterum negamus sequi. Aliud est, si de voce mundi quaeratur, quomodo aliquando in sermone usurpetur, vel improprie: aliud rem considerare, & mundi non vocem grammatice, sed rem physice. Non de homine praedicatur mundus, sed quidem humanum genus, vel hominum multitudo, mundus dicitur: idque propter multitudinem, non quod propterea partes mundi eidem queuant attribui, vel in sermone aequipollent. Quae quaesito ista consequentia? de homine, vid. de hominibus in genere praedicatur sive dicitur in sermone, quod sint mundus & omnis creatura: ergo de eodem praedicatur coelum, terra, visibilia, &c. ex impropria loquutione argumentari ad veritatem, & partes rei in se, proprie & physice? id est, omnem vocis traquidam enim sunt boni, quidam mali, quos & Diabolos vocamus: Sunt qui per prædictas appellationes intelligant Angelos bonos, quia scilicet indignum videbatur ipsis, Diabolos per Christum creatos dicere. Cum enim extollere aliquem volumus (quod hic facit Apostolus) non imperfectiorum & noxiorum operum, sed utilium & præstantium facere solemus & debemus mentionem. Ex his titulis ornantur etiam Angeli boni. Rom. 8. Eph. 1. & 3. Alii contra, per ipsos spiritus, intelligunt Diabolos, eo quod ad Eph. 6. vers. 11. his iisdem epithe-tis ornentur Diaboli; vocantur enim Principes, potestates, mundi potentes, &c. Verum omisso eo in quo dissentiunt, utrique hoc pacto ex ipso loco ratiocinantur: Angeli tam boni, quam mali, creati sunt ante visibilis mundi creationem. Si ergo Angeli sunt per Christum creati, sequitur, Christum ante mundi creatio-nem revera extitisse. Et si nos dicamus, per creationem hic intelligi reformationem & rege-nerationem, hoc stare non posse confirmant. Nam Angeli, sicut regeneratione non indigue-runt, ita nec regenerati sunt, neque Deus, Iesum, Messiam & mediatorem Angelorum, sed hominum esse voluit. Ergo non potest hæc creatio de regeneratione accipi, sed de prima rerum omnium origine. Ad hæc nos primo, repetimus id quod antea diximus: hoc argumentum, etiamsi esset solidum, non probare tamen æternitatem Christi, quia ex eo saltem colligitur, Christum extitisse ante Angelos: ac proinde si quid habet roboris, Arianorum sententiam confirmat. Secundo dicimus, Paulum Apostolum, tam hic, quam alibi, reconciliationem & restaurationem rerum in cœlo existentium, tribuere non Spiritui alicui æterno, sed homini, sanguinem habenti, ita enim hic loquitur vers. 20. pacificans per sanguinem crucis ejus, sive quæ in terris, sive quæ in cœlis sunt. Et ad Eph. 1. vers. 10. Proposuit Deus in dispositione plenitudinis temporum, instaurare omnia in Chri-sto, quæ in cœlis & in terra sunt. Ubi per dispo-sitionem plenitudinis temporum, nihil aliud quàm Christi exhibiti tempus significari, clalationem[?]
units.tr: For we also apply to our own case his third foundation and the argument he builds upon it. For whatever belongs to a definition belongs also to the thing defined, and whatever is predicated of a definition is predicated of the thing defined, since definition and thing defined are really the same. A definition is the thing defined spread out and expanded, and conversely the thing defined is a definition contracted. Now, what is predicated of created heaven, earth, visible things, thrones, powers, and so on, is predicated of the world and of all creation; but heaven, earth, visible things, and so on are predicated of Christ's creation. Therefore: heaven, earth, visible and invisible things, and so on are the definition, or the parts of the defined, and the world or all creation is the defined. Nor do these really differ at all. Nor is it open to him now to object that the text does not say that heaven and earth were created, but the things that are in heaven and on earth; for he himself takes them in this way, here and in what follows, in the argument from Christ's grace overflowing. And so it is an amplification of the divine benefit. If anyone asks why Scripture uses such forms of speech, it can be answered that they are sought for the sake of ornament and grace in the discourse. For they are hyperbolic amplifications. Nor is it unjust, when we wish to magnify something and affirm it firmly, to use several words that mean the same thing and even go beyond the truth of the matter. Such is that enumeration of Paul in Romans 8:38: "For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God." The plain sense of these words is: nothing can separate us from the love of God. So also Ephesians 1:21: "Far above all principality and power, and might and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world but also in that which is to come." That is, above everything whatever that exists anywhere. Such is also, in the same Epistle, chapter 3:18, and that: "that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth and height and depth", that is, to understand thoroughly and completely. By the same reasoning, when the Apostle here wished to signify that all things were made new in creation through Christ, he used this enumeration, which is an amplifying hyperbole and is equivalent to the general term "all things". But since there are some who insist, blinded by an unlearned superstition, and who, not content with this simple and common interpretation, hold that some mystery lies hidden here and will not acknowledge or admit hyperbolic expressions in the sacred writings, let us see whether we can satisfy them in another way as well. Therefore all of them agree on this: that through the things that are in heaven, through invisible things, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, certain spirits and abstract substances, that is, angels, must be understood. Since these are of two kinds, Christum, gratiam exundasse (the text, for the word man); therefore we ought not to understand the argument concerning Christ and his creation otherwise than as it is clearly contained in the text. The Adversary afterwards: but if someone perhaps presses and says that here it is not heaven and earth (which often denote men) that are said to be created, but the things that are in heaven and earth: I answer that it makes no difference in which way Scripture speaks, the sense is the same. Is he not then foolish and inept who, when he attributes a definition to something, hesitates to attribute the thing defined? Who, granting that the things in the whole world were created by Christ, seeks an escape in the claim that the world is not said to have been made, and that heaven and earth were not made, although the things in heaven and on earth are said to have been made? Who grants the parts and denies the whole? Who, having conceded the ascription of the parts, is disturbed by the name of the whole? The matter is entirely the same; only the mode of speaking varies. But to argue about the word "man" and its meaning or acceptance in the way the Adversary does is very inept. "The world and the whole creation are predicated of man": we deny it. Therefore "heaven, earth, visible things, etc. are predicated of the same": again we deny that it follows. It is another matter if one asks how the word "world" is sometimes used in speech, whether improperly; it is another to consider the thing itself, not the word of the world grammatically, but the thing physically. The world is not predicated of man; rather, when the human race or a multitude of men is called the world, this is because of the multitude, and not because parts of the world can therefore be attributed to men or are equivalent in speech. What kind of consequence is this? "Of man, that is, of men in general, it is said in speech that they are the world and all creation: therefore heaven, earth, visible things, etc. are predicated of the same": to argue from an improper mode of speaking to the truth and to the parts of the thing in itself, properly and physically? That is, to pass over every figure of speech... For some are good, some evil, whom we also call devils. Some by the aforesaid appellations understand good angels, because it seemed unworthy to them to say that devils were created through Christ. For when we wish to extol someone (as the Apostle does here) we are accustomed, and ought, to mention not imperfect and harmful works but useful and excellent ones. Good angels too are adorned with these titles: Romans 8, Ephesians 1 and 3. Others, on the contrary, understand devils by these same spirits, because in Ephesians 6:11 devils are adorned with the same epithets; for they are called princes, powers, rulers of this world, and so on. But, setting aside the point on which they disagree, both sides reason in this way from the passage itself: angels, both good and bad, were created before the creation of the visible world. If therefore the angels were created through Christ, it follows that Christ truly existed before the creation of the world. And if we say that by creation is meant here reformation and regeneration, they maintain that this cannot stand. For angels did not need regeneration, and so they were not regenerated; nor did God will that Jesus, the Messiah and Mediator, be the mediator of angels, but of men. Therefore this creation cannot be understood of regeneration, but of the first origin of all things. To these points we answer first: we repeat what we said before, that this argument, even if it were sound, would not prove the eternity of Christ, since from it one can at most conclude that Christ existed before the angels; and so, if it has any strength, it confirms the opinion of the Arians. Secondly, we say that the Apostle Paul, both here and elsewhere, ascribes the reconciliation and restoration of things existing in heaven not to some eternal Spirit but to a man having blood; for he speaks thus here in verse 20: "having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in earth or things in heaven." And in Ephesians 1:10: "God has purposed in the dispensation of the fullness of times to gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven and which are on earth." Here by "the dispensation of the fullness of times" nothing else is signified than the time of Christ's manifestation, and to neglect the trope

units.la: lationem negligere, & à voce, eaque tro-picè sumta transfire, & aucupari ipsas res? Fateor valde imprudens atque ineptus est, qui definitum alicui attribuens, definitionem attribuere veretur. Verum id uti in rebus verissimum, ita à vocibus quomo-docunque sumtis ad res argumentari velle, est ineptissimum. Jam quod infert, si totus mundus significare potest tantum homines, partes quoque mundi eosdem significare posse, hoc est à grammaticâ transfire ad physicam, atq; si id non sit μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος, quid hoc demum sit, ego certe nescio. Dein quod ait, quid hoc, quod cum audimus homines vel humanum genus vocari universam creaturam, totum mundum, tropum agnoscimus, & non item, quando hominibus attribuuntur voces cæli, terræ, visibilium &c.? respondemus, quia illud usus obtinuit, ut sic aliquando humanum genus, & multitudo aliqua appelletur, non ita in cæteris: non certe ubi mundus per partes illas explicatur. Probet vel uno loco, vel ullius sermone, in quavis lingua Adversarius, post usurpatam vocem mundi, additas partes cœli, terræ, visibilium, invisibilium &c. de solo homine accipi. Nos inficiamur, hoc unquam ullibi fieri. Contrarium age ostendat.
units.tr: to neglect the trope, and to pass over from the word, taken figuratively, and to snatch at the things themselves? I grant that he is very unwise and inept who, when he attributes the thing defined to something, hesitates to attribute the definition. But, while this is most true in matters themselves, to wish to argue from words, however they are taken, to things is most absurd. Now as to what he infers, that if the whole world can signify only men, then the parts of the world can also signify the same men, that is, to pass from grammar to physics; and if this is not "passing into another genus" (μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος), I certainly do not know what it is. Next, as to his question: why, when we hear that men or the human race are called the whole creation, the whole world, do we recognize a trope, and not likewise when the words heaven, earth, visible things, etc. are attributed to men? We answer: because usage has established that the human race or some multitude is sometimes called in this way, but not so with the rest; certainly not where the world is explained through those parts. Let the Adversary show, in one passage or in the writing of anyone, in any language, that after the word "world" has been used, the added parts, heaven, earth, visible things, invisible things, etc., are taken of man alone. We deny that this has ever been done anywhere. Let him show the contrary.

units.la: Jam ineptum est dicere, hoc de homine dicebatur, quando vocabatur universa creatura: nam argumentum inde si formetur, negabimus & Majorem, & Minorem. Nam quamvis homines aliqui multi dicantur universa creatura, intelligitur creatura humana, atq; hyperbolica est locutio; ut nō propterea possint eidem attribui, vel perinde de eo prædicari ipsi mundi partes, cœlum, terra, visibilia, & invisibilia. Per ea ergo, quæ in cœlis & terrà à Christo dicuntur condita, intelligit Adversarius nihil aliud, quam humanum genus à Deo per Christum renovatum, & rissimum est. Unde apparet, nihil nos absurdi dicere, cum affirmamus, Angelos (si tamen per illa epitheta ipsi intelligantur) per hominem Christum in novissimo tempore, esse regeneratos & reformatos, cum ipse Apostolus, per crucem & sanguinem, tempore exhibiti Messiae, ista esse facta testetur. At ante mundi huius visibilis creationem, certe nec crux, nec sanguis Christi, nec tempus fuit novissimum. Si autem regeneratio caelestium fieri potuit per sanguinem hominis Christi, cur non etiam creatio? Cum praesertim demonstraverimus, creationem saepe pro regeneratione usurpari? Quamcunque igitur responsionem & solutionem ipsi adferent locorum Apostoli, a nobis citatorum, eandem nos quoque, nostrae sententiae & explicationis, esse affirmabimus. Idem enim est cuneus, utrique nodo adhibendus. Dicant nobis, quid sit, caelestia per sanguinem Christi esse instaurata? idem nos dicemus esse, Angelos per Christum esse creatos. Si vero ipsi a nobis quaerant, quid illud, vel hoc putemus esse? Respondemus istud supra a nobis explicatum esse. Sed etiam si demus, quod supra negavimus, hic per caelestia & invisibilia, debere intelligi Angelos, stabit tamen nostra sententia, hic agi de reformatione rerum, non de prima creatione. Nam si postulant a nobis, ut explicemus, quomodo Angeli sint reformati? respondere primo possumus, Nos nescire. Quam responsionem, sufficere debere modestis & piis viris, hoc modo ostendimus. Deus ea omnia, quae ad salutem nostram, & gloriam nominis sui, necessaria sunt, copiose, luculenter & perspicue nobis per Prophetas & Apostolos exponi jussit & patefecit. Quae autem minus videbantur necessaria, & in aliud tempus differenda, ea parce & obscure tantum, innuit potius quam explicuit. Qualis est disputatio de Angelis, seu spiritibus illis abstractis, de quorum & creatione, & lapsu, & statu, perpauca nobis Spiritus sancti administri tradiderunt, ex quibus suspicari potius, quam certi aliquid statuere & discere possumus. Ex quo apparet non debere nos curiosius in ista inquirere, sed necessaria magis & saepe inculredemtum. Ut jam nihil dicamus de metaphorica Christi redemtione, quam iidem faciunt, ut aeque redemtio haec in summum tandem abeat, atque illa creatio, quomodo probabit, per ea quae in caelis & terra, solos in terra homines denotari, & solos renovatos ac reformatos per Christum ? respondet, unicuique linguae suas esse peculiares phrases. quis nescit? Concedit, fortasse nec Graecos, neque Latinos ita consuevisse loqui, sed esse elegantiam Hebraeis vulgarem. Audiamus. ἓ πνεῦμος [?] nomine homines solos significari se demonstrasse ait, ex 11 Cor. v. 17. & Eph. iii. 9. quibus etiam suo loco respondimus. Sed hoc non quaeritur, an vox πᾶς [?] aliquando omnes & solos homines significet, quod ex sermonis & textus sententia constare debet: uti Rom. iii. 12. πᾶς ἐξεκλιναν [?], & alibi: verum an τῷ πᾶν [?] explicatum per ea quae in caelis, & terra, & visibilia, & junctu aliquoties cum creatione, citra quod vel minimum in ista pericope addatur indicium redemtionis, debeat ita exponi, quemadmodum Adversarii cupiunt, quaeritur.
units.tr: Now it is absurd to say that this was said of man when the whole creation was being named. If one builds an argument on that basis, we will deny both the major and the minor premise. Many men may indeed be called the whole creation, but the human creature is what is meant, and the expression is hyperbolical. It does not follow that the parts of the world, heaven, earth, things visible and invisible, can be attributed to him or predicated of him in the same way. So by the things said to have been created in heaven and on earth through Christ, the Adversary understands nothing other than the human race renewed by God through Christ, and that is most absurd. From this it appears that we say nothing absurd when we affirm that the angels (if those expressions are indeed understood of them) were regenerated and reformed in the last times through the man Christ, since the Apostle himself testifies that these things were done through the cross and blood of Christ at the time of the manifested Messiah. But before the creation of this visible world, certainly neither the cross nor the blood of Christ nor the last time existed. If, however, the regeneration of heavenly beings could come about through the blood of the man Christ, why not also their creation? Especially since we have shown that creation is often used for regeneration. Therefore whatever answer and solution they bring to the passages of the Apostle that we have cited, we shall likewise affirm it to be the same for our opinion and explanation. For it is the same wedge to be applied to both knots. Let them tell us what it is for heavenly things to be restored through the blood of Christ; we shall say the same thing, that the angels were created through Christ. If, however, they ask us what we think that or this means, we reply that this has been explained by us above. But even if we grant what we denied above, that by heavenly and invisible things the angels must be understood here, our view still stands: this passage is about the reformation of things, not their first creation. For if they demand that we explain how the angels were reformed, we can first answer: we do not know. That this answer ought to suffice for modest and pious men we show as follows. God ordered and revealed through the Prophets and Apostles, fully, clearly and plainly, all those things that are necessary for our salvation and for the glory of his name. Those things which seemed less necessary and to be deferred to another time, he only sparingly and obscurely hinted at rather than explained. Such is the discussion about the angels, or those abstract spirits, about whose creation, fall and state the ministers of the Holy Spirit have handed down very few things, from which we can rather surmise than determine and learn anything certain. From this it appears that we ought not to inquire into these things too curiously, but rather to insist often on what is necessary. Let us now say nothing of the metaphorical redemption of Christ, which they also do, so that this redemption too ends at last in the highest degree, just as that creation does. How will they prove that by the things in heaven and on earth only men on earth are denoted, and only men renewed and reformed through Christ? They answer that each language has its own peculiar idioms. Who does not know that? They concede, perhaps, that neither the Greeks nor the Latins were accustomed to speak in this way, but that this elegance is common to the Hebrews. Let us hear them. They say they have shown that by the word [πνεῦμα] only men are signified, from 2 Cor. 5:17 and Eph. 3:9, to which we have also replied in their place. But the question is not whether the word [πᾶς] sometimes signifies all men and only men, which must be established from the sense of the discourse and the text, as in Rom. 3:12 [πάντες ἐξέκλιναν] and elsewhere. The question is whether [τὸ πᾶν], explained by the things in heaven and on earth, and things visible, and joined several times with creation, without the slightest indication of redemption being added in that passage, ought to be interpreted as the Adversaries wish.

units.la: Per caelum & terram homines significari contendit, inde quia homines apud Prophetas sol, luna, lucifer, stellae nominantur. Quis autem disparem illorum non videt rationem? ut in sermone homines aliqui comparentur aliquando cum sole, luna, stellis, propter quandam inter haec similitudinem, & tamen nequeat in textu quod dicitur, ea quae in caelis, quae in terra, &c. exponi de solis hominibus renovatis & redemtis? Illic sermo in specie nominat hanc vel istam creaturam, cum qua homines confert; hic nihil tale: ergo nequaquam simile exemplum, ex quo nostra explicari queant. Nec magis ad rem facit, quod citat ex Ierem. i. 9. qui locus ne quidem caelum & terram nominat, Hagg. ii. 7. proprie intelligi potest tata, ac perspicuè tradita versare. Sufficiat nobis quod clare affirmat Apostolus, per crucem Christi, etiam coelestia esse reformata: quo modo id factum sit, quia scriptura non docet, quaerere mittamus. Nam etiam in iis, quae copiosius perscripta sunt, curiosa & inquieta ingenia desiderare multa solent, & praetermissa esse plurima, conqueri possunt. Vt, quamvis prima creatio copiosè satis & perspicuè sit à Mose descripta, tamen cum Epicureo illo clamant quidam? Quibus oculis intueri potuit vester Moses fabricam illam tanti operis quae constituit à Deo atque aedificari mundum fecit? quae molitio, quae ferramenta, qui vectes, quae machinae, qui ministri tanti numeris fuerunt? &c. At ille sapit, qui non supra quam opus est sapit, sed sapit ad sobrietatem; Rom. 12. verf. 3. Sed ut curiosis quoque, quantum possumus, satisfaciamus: afferimus hic Angelos dici conditos & creatos per Christum esse, eo quod, ut idem Apostolus, tum hic, tum ad Eph. 1. explicat, sint restaurati, reformati, renovati, pacificati: neque hic aliud significare creationem, quam immutationem, adeptionem conditionis & status melioris. Quod vero quaerunt, quomodo Angeli sint reconciliati, & renovati, cum constet, bonos quidem non fuisse invisos Deo, ubi autem odium non est, ibi non est opus reconciliatione, malos autem etiam hodie hostes & adversarios esse Dei? Respondemus, quod ad malos attinet Angelos, sunt qui censent eos per Christum restauratos, quia multi Spiritus mali, post adventum Christi, respuerunt, ac Deo reconciliati sunt. Quam sententiam confirmat illa de Antonio eremita seu fabula, seu historia: Satyrum nimirum quendam in sylvis factum obvium, ac cum se daemonem esse fassus fuisset, ex iis, quos superstitio gentilium coleret, petiisse ut communem Deum oraret, pro suo grege cujus legatione fungeretur, orari pro salute sua voluit. Huc facit etiam Origenis opinio, qui aliquando etiam diabolos salutem, per Christum, consecuturos esse opinatus est. Alii restaurationem Diabolorum sic explicant: Certum est Diabolos quoque Christo,
units.tr: He contends that by heaven and earth men are signified, because in the Prophets men are called sun, moon, morning star and stars. But who does not see the disparity of these cases? In a discourse some men are sometimes compared with the sun, moon and stars, on account of some likeness between them; yet can what is said in the text, the things in heaven, the things on earth, etc., be explained of men alone, renewed and redeemed? There the discourse names expressly this or that creature with which it compares men; here nothing of the kind occurs. So this is by no means a similar example by which our reading could be explained. Nor does it help the matter more that they cite Jer. 1:9, a passage which does not even name heaven and earth, or Hag. 2:7. The Apostle clearly affirms that through the cross of Christ even heavenly things were reformed; how this came about, since Scripture does not teach it, let us not seek to ask. For even in those matters which have been written about more fully, curious and restless minds are wont to desire many things, and to complain that very many have been passed over. So that, although the first creation has been described by Moses fully enough and plainly, some still cry out with that Epicurean: With what eyes could your Moses have seen that vast work which he records was established by God and built as the world? What labour, what tools, what levers, what machines, what workmen were there in such numbers? etc. But he is wise who is not wiser than is necessary, but is wise with sobriety (Rom. 12:3). Yet, that we may also satisfy the curious as far as we can: we here affirm that the angels are said to have been founded and created through Christ, because, as the same Apostle explains both here and at Eph. 1, they have been restored, reformed, renewed and pacified; and here creation signifies nothing other than a change and the attainment of a better condition and state. As to what they ask, how the angels were reconciled and renewed, since it is established that the good angels were not hateful to God (where there is no hatred there is no need of reconciliation), while the evil angels are even today enemies and adversaries of God? We reply that, as far as the evil angels are concerned, there are those who think they were restored through Christ, because many evil spirits, after the coming of Christ, renounced their error and were reconciled to God. The story of Antony the hermit, whether fable or history, confirms this opinion: that a certain satyr met him in the woods, and when he confessed himself to be a demon, he asked him to pray to the common God on behalf of his flock, from those whom the superstition of the Gentiles worshipped, since he acted as their envoy; he wished to be prayed for for his own salvation. The opinion of Origen also favours this, who at one time supposed that even the devils would attain salvation through Christ. Others explain the restoration of the devils thus: It is certain that the devils too will be reconciled to Christ,

units.la: de commotione coeli ac terrae, rerumque omnium cum adventu Christi. Caeterum per coelum ac terram, praesertim ubi appellantur nova vel novari dicuntur, intelligantur homines per Christum regeniti vel regenerandi, quod locus ubi id fit, satis docet, id non adaequat vim locutionis in nostro textu, quando dicuntur primum omnia per Christum creata; tum id explicatur per coelum & terram, eaque quae in iis, & hoc iterum per visibilia ac invisibilia, deniq; & illud per potestates, principatus: nam ut non in uno, sed pluribus argumenti nostri vis fundatur, & locus ipsum, ne quod dubium subesse queat, variis modis exponit.
units.tr: by the shaking of heaven and earth and of all things at the coming of Christ. Moreover, by heaven and earth, especially where they are called new or are said to be renewed, let us understand men regenerated or to be regenerated through Christ. The place where this happens teaches enough that this does not match the force of the expression in our text, where it is said that all things were first created through Christ; then this is explained by heaven and earth, and those things in them; and this again by things visible and invisible; and finally by powers and principalities. For the force of our argument rests not on one point but on several, and the passage itself, lest any doubt should be able to lie hidden, sets it out in various ways.

units.la: Tandem profert Apoc. v.13. & omnem creaturam, quae in coelo est & super terram, & sub terra & quae sunt in mari & quae in eo, omnes audivi dicentes: & exponit, pios homines audivi dicentes. solos homines? in terra agentes? nego. Nam omnino illud debet intelligi de omnibus creaturis, quibus per prosopopoeiam attribuit illam Dei laudationem. Quemadmodum id est frequens in Sacris, praesertim Psalmis, Psalm. XIX. 1. 2. 3. & CXLVIII. Quae neutiquam possunt exponi aut restringi ad solos homines. Levissime transcurrit caetera Adversarius, & visibilia atque invisibilia dicit terrestria significare & coelestia. Quare idem de iis vocibus dicendum, quod de coelo & terra. Imo eo plus, quo explicativa sunt praecedentium, & coelum & terra aliquando improprie sumuntur, non ita visibilia & invisibilia, quando explicationis loco post illa subjunguntur.
units.tr: At last he produces Apoc. v.13: "And every creature which is in heaven and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, I heard saying," and he explains it: "I heard pious men saying." Only men, and men living on earth? I deny it. For that passage must certainly be understood of all creatures, to whom the praise of God is ascribed by prosopopoeia. This is frequent in the Sacred Writings, especially in the Psalms, Psalm 19:1-3 and 148. These cannot in any way be explained or restricted to men alone. Our Adversary passes very lightly over the rest, and says that "visible and invisible" signify earthly and heavenly things. So what must be said of those words is the same as what must be said of heaven and earth. Indeed, all the more so, since they are explanatory of what precedes; and heaven and earth are sometimes taken improperly, but "visible and invisible" are not so, when they are added after those words by way of explanation.

units.la: Denique thronos, dominationes, &c. dicit significare cujuscunque gradus & dignitatis homines. Sed in textu non restringitur ad ea quae in terra, nedum ad homines. Neque ad cujuscunque status homines illa applicari possunt, etiam parvos, pauperes, &c. quia solum de gradibus. à Deo esse subiectos, & per Christum eorum vires & potestatem immunitas atque immutatas. Unde illa: Venisti ante tempus perdere nos? Marc. 1. verf. 24. Princeps mundi ejicietur foras. Vidi Satanam de coelo cadentem, ut fulgur. Fortis armatus spoliatus a robustiore est, &c. Quae mutatio licet ipsis Diabolis in bonum non cessit, cessit tamen in bonum iis, qui praecipue ad hanc mundi reformationem pertinent, & cum universi reformatio facta sit, ac Diaboli quoque sint pars universi, ipsi quoque Diaboli, reformati per Christum fuisse, dici a Paulo potuerunt. Hoc enim pacto nova quaedam forma in hierarchiam introducta est, quae antea talem dominum & rectorem non habebat. Et Christus potestatem habet omnium eorum, qui in illa continentur, munera mutandi, augendi, minuendi, prout ipsi visum fuerit; quemadmodum fieri videmus, si quis alicujus Reip. Princeps ac Dominus fiat; quam Remp. vel ob id, quod principem, ac Dominum, quem antea non haberet, fit nata, novam simul formam esse natam, nemo negare audebit. Qui vero per Angelos, Spiritus bonos intelligunt, illi primo contendunt de duplici reconciliatione & pacificatione hic loqui Apostolum. Primo de ea, quae concernit concordiam, & pacem rerum creatarum inter se, ita ut Dei cultu & veneratione, omnes conspirent & consentiant. Deinde, de altera, quae pertinet ad concordiam Dei cum rebus creatis. Atque de priore reconciliatione, loqui Apostolum in illis verbis verf. 20. Placuit Deo per Christum reconciliare omnia in ipsum, pacificando per sanguinem crucis ejus, sive quae in terris, sive quae in coelis sunt. De altera autem pacificatione, & reconciliatione, quae facta est inter Deum & homines, agi in verf. 32. Nunc autem reconciliavit in corpore carnis ejus, &c. Etsi autem utraque haec reconciliatio facta sit per eundem Christum, tamen in hoc differunt: quod prior reconciliatio, in genere pertinet tam ad homines quam Angelos; posterior autem tantum ad homines. Nam in priori fit coelestium quoque mentio, in posteriori tantum hominum. Quibus sic excellentiae loquitur Apostolus, & thronos, dominationes, principatus, & potestates, non conditiones inferiores aut afflictas: quare satius illa ad Angelos applicare, ubi solae excellentiae locum habent, non ullae afflictiones. Jam vero si notare eos Apostolus voluisset, ad quos beneficium Christi pervenit, non certe ita appellasset, quod non modo nunquam facit, neque id significat, sed planius, uti solet, expressisset; quin revera ad alios potius Christi beneficium spectat, quam ad magnates, & honorum gradus, quos hic solos nominat, nam non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, inquit idem, 1 Cor. 1. 26. Denique per Christum dicit creata illa, dominationes, thronos, &c. quod aliud est, quam an ad illa Christi beneficium pertigerit. Non vero gratiae aut beneficii Christi vel redemtionis est, efficere gradus dignitatis inter homines. Et tamen gradus illos vel dignitates dicit Ap. a Christo factas. Aliud ergo spectavit, quam eum voluisse, opinantur Adversarii.
units.tr: Finally, thrones, dominions, etc., he says, signify men of every rank and dignity. But in the text it is not restricted to things on earth, much less to men. Nor can those words be applied to men of every condition, even the small, the poor, and so on, since they refer only to the degrees, which are made subject to God, and through Christ have their powers and authority stripped and changed. Hence those words: Have you come to destroy us before the time? Mark 1:24. The prince of this world shall be cast out. I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning. A strong man armed is spoiled by one stronger than he, etc. Although this change did not turn out for the good of the devils themselves, it did turn out for the good of those who are chiefly concerned in this reformation of the world. And since the whole universe has been reformed, and the devils too are part of the universe, the devils themselves could be said by Paul to have been reformed through Christ. For in this way a new kind of order has been introduced into the hierarchy, which previously had no such lord and ruler. And Christ has the power to change, increase, and diminish the offices of all who are contained in it, as he pleases; just as we see happen when someone becomes the prince and lord of some commonwealth. No one will dare deny that such a commonwealth, because it has acquired a prince and lord it did not previously have, has at the same time come to have a new form. But those who understand good spirits or angels by these words first contend that the Apostle is speaking here of a twofold reconciliation and peacemaking. The first concerns the concord and peace of created things among themselves, so that all conspire and agree in the worship and veneration of God. The second concerns the concord of God with created things. The Apostle speaks of the first reconciliation in verse 20: It pleased God through Christ to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven. But the second peacemaking and reconciliation, which was made between God and men, is treated in verse 22: But now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh, etc. Although both these reconciliations were made by the same Christ, they differ in this: the first reconciliation extends in general to men as well as angels, but the second only to men. For in the first mention is made also of heavenly beings, in the second only of men. In listing these, the Apostle speaks of excellences: thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, not inferior or afflicted conditions. Therefore it is more fitting to apply them to angels, where only excellences have a place and no afflictions. Now indeed, if the Apostle had wished to mark those to whom the benefit of Christ came, he would certainly not have named them in this way, which he not only never does, nor does it signify this, but he would have expressed it more plainly, as he usually does. Indeed, the benefit of Christ concerns others rather than the great men and the grades of honour, whom alone he names here; for not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, says the same writer, 1 Cor. 1:26. Finally, he says that those created things, dominions, thrones, etc., were created through Christ; which is something other than whether the benefit of Christ has reached them. But it is not the work of grace or of Christ's benefit or redemption to establish degrees of dignity among men. And yet the Apostle says that those degrees or dignities were made by Christ. He therefore had in view something other than what our Adversaries suppose he meant.

units.la: Sed sua expositione putant se venerem & gratiam conciliare verbis Apostoli. Quasi illud venentur Scriptores Sacri, & non potius gravem & sanctam simplicitatem ament. Neque ii fumus, qui loquutionum hyperbolicarum usum sacris denegamus: sed hic loci hyperbolem constituendam esse non judicamus. Amplificasse vero orationem suam, & per sequentia magis explicuisse, haud negamus. Et quemadmodum verborum Pauli Rom. viii. 38. quae adducit Noster, is simplex sensus est, nihil nos separare ab amore Dei posse; & Eph. 1. 21. Christum evectum supra omne id, quodcunque uspiam est: pari fateor ratione intelligendum, quod Apostolus hic docet, omnia omnino, & quidquid uspiam, a Christo creatum, sive in coelis, sive in terra, fuisse.
units.tr: But by their own interpretation they think they win favour and grace for their views from the Apostle's words, as if the Sacred Writers were hunting for that, rather than loving a grave and holy simplicity. Nor are we those who deny the use of hyperbolical expressions in Scripture; but we do not judge that a hyperbole is to be assumed in this passage. We do not deny, however, that he amplified his discourse and explained it more fully by what follows. And just as the simple sense of the words of Paul in Romans 8:38, which our author cites, is that nothing can separate us from the love of God, and of Eph. 1:21, that Christ is exalted above everything that is anywhere: by the same reasoning, I maintain, what the Apostle teaches here must be understood as all things absolutely, and whatever is anywhere, to have been created by Christ, whether in heaven or on earth.

units.la: Valde vero se constrictos sentiunt Adstantibus, affirmant, cum dicit Apostolus: re-conciliata & pacificata esse omnia in ipsum, voces illas in ipsum, sensum hunc habere, inter se, ut dicantur omnia non Deo reconciliata esse, sed ipsa sibi invicem amica esse reddita, & quæ antea dissidebant, ad concordiam redacta, ut unanimi consensu Deum colerent & celebrarent. Erant enim antea inter ea, quæ in cœlis sunt, id est, Angelos, & quæ in terris sunt, id est, homines, inimicitiæ. Nam primo, Iudæi dissidebant cum gentilibus. Deinde, Angeli boni, infesti erant hominibus. At Christus & Gentes cum Iudæis, & Angelos hominibus reconciliavit, & pacem inter illos, ac concordiam fecit.
units.tr: The Adversaries, however, feel themselves greatly pressed. They affirm that when the Apostle says, "all things have been reconciled and pacified in him," the words "in him" have this sense among themselves: that all things are said to have been reconciled not to God but to have been made friendly to one another, and those things which previously disagreed were brought into concord, so that with unanimous consent they might worship and celebrate God. For previously there were enmities between those things which are in heaven, that is, the angels, and those which are on earth, that is, men. For first, the Jews disagreed with the Gentiles. Then the good angels were hostile to men. But Christ reconciled both the Gentiles with the Jews and the angels with men, and made peace and concord between them.

units.la: De hominum inter se reconciliatione, per Christum factâ, non est opus pluribus agere, quandoquidem res est notissima, & apud Paulum frequenter repetita, ad Ephef. 2. vers. 14. Ipse enim, inquit, est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum, & medium parietem maceriæ solvens inimicitias in carne sua, legem mandatorum decretis evacuans, ut duos condat in semetipso in unum novum hominem, faciens pacem, & reconciliet ambos in uno corpore Deo per crucem, interficiens inimicitias in semetipso. Et veniens euangelizavit pacem vobis qui longe fui-stis, & pacem iis qui prope, quoniam per ipsum habemus accessum ambo in uno Spiritu ad Patrem, &c.
units.tr: There is no need to say much about the reconciliation of men among themselves, made through Christ, since the matter is very well known and is repeated frequently by Paul, Ephesians 2:14. "For he himself," he says, "is our peace, who has made both one, and has broken down the middle wall of partition, the enmity in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in ordinances, so that he might create in himself of the two one new man, making peace, and might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, slaying the enmity in himself. And coming he preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near; for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father," etc.

units.la: De Angelis verò reconciliatis, ita differunt. Certum est, Angelos ad custodiam & ministerium non tantum Dei, sed hominum quoque piorum creatos, ut castra metentur circa illos, tueantur & defendant ab omni malo. Sed post peccatum Adami, inimicos & infestos esse hominibus factos. Unde statuitur Cherubin in ostio Paradisi, qui ancipitem & districtum en-sem manu vibrans, hominem ab ingressu horti deliciarum arceret & repelleret. Hinc factum est, ut Satan seu Diabolus inciperet regnare in mundo, & imperium obtinere in homines, unde vocatur Deus & princeps huius seculi, & maxi-ma pars hominum, utpote omnes gentes, exceptis Israelitis, sub ditione & imperio Diaboli fue-runt. At ubi Christus advenit, & ostium fidei gentibus est apertum, Satanæ imperium fractum
units.tr: But concerning the reconciliation of the angels they differ as follows. It is certain that angels were created for the guard and ministry not only of God but also of pious men, so that they encamp around them, watch over them, and defend them from every evil. But after the sin of Adam they became enemies and hostile to men. Hence the cherub was set at the gate of Paradise, who, brandishing a two-edged and drawn sword in his hand, kept man away and drove him from entering the garden of delights. From this it came about that Satan, or the Devil, began to reign in the world and to obtain dominion over men; hence he is called "the god and prince of this age," and the greater part of men, namely all the nations apart from the Israelites, were under the power and dominion of the Devil. But when Christ came, and the door of faith was opened to the Gentiles, the dominion of Satan was broken.

units.la: versarii, quomodo de Angelis queant ex-ponere, si quidem eos per Christum creatos admittere cogantur. Affirmant ergo, Angelos per hominem Christum in novissimo tempore esse regeneratos & reformatos. Quare? quia Apostolus testatur ista facta esse tempore exhibiti Mes-siæ, per ejus sanguinem & crucem. Negatur, quod Apostolus dicat, creationem, de qua loquitur, factam per sanguinem Christi, vel demum tempore Christi exhi-biti. Per Christum quidem, ait, illa fa-cta, sed non per Christi in carnem exhi-bitionem, sed per hoc Christi, quod ante erat, imago invisibilis Dei & primogenitus omnis creaturæ.
units.tr: ...the Remonstrants, how they can explain the angels, since they are compelled to admit that the angels were created through Christ. They therefore affirm that the angels were regenerated and reformed in the last times through the man Christ. Why? Because the Apostle testifies that these things were done at the time when the Messiah was revealed, through his blood and cross. I deny that the Apostle says that the creation he is speaking of was made through the blood of Christ, or even at the time of Christ's revelation in the flesh. He says indeed that those things were made through Christ, but not through Christ's manifestation in the flesh; rather through that in Christ which existed before, namely the invisible image of God and the firstborn of every creature.

units.la: Sed præmiserat de sanguine Christi, in quo habemus remissionem peccatorum. Hoc dicit vers. 14. tum vers. 15. adscen-dit ad Christi considerationem theologi-cam & divinam. Cui vers. 16. attribuit omnium creationem, etiam Angelorum. Quomodo autem probabit aliquis, vers. 14. cum 16. eundem esse, vel hisce quæ vers. 16. de Angelis dicuntur, attribui pari modo debere ea quæ vers. 14. dixerat? Nam & expresse ibi vim sanguinis Chri-sti, & remissionem peccatorum ad homi-nes applicarat, in quo habemus inquit &c. nisi quis velit omnia, quæ quovis modo in oratione junguntur, confundere, & non agnoscere progressum sermonis ad res sæ-pe diversissimas. Sanguini Christi attri-buitur vers. 14. remissio nostrorum peccatorum: sed vers. 16. neque de Christi sanguine, neq; de remissione peccatorum aliquid dicitur, sed docetur, per Christum res factas etiam longe alias, vid. creata ab eo omnia in cælis & in terra, non per ejus sanguinem & crucem, sed divinitatem.
units.tr: But he had premised the blood of Christ, "in whom we have the forgiveness of sins." He says this in verse 14, and then in verse 15 he rises to the theological and divine consideration of Christ, to whom in verse 16 he attributes the creation of all things, including the angels. But how will anyone prove that verse 14 and verse 16 are the same, or that what verse 14 says should be attributed in the same way to the things said of the angels in verse 16? For there he had expressly applied to men the efficacy of Christ's blood and the forgiveness of sins, when he said, "in whom we have," and so on. Unless one wishes to confuse everything that is joined together in a sentence, and fail to recognise the progress of the discourse to matters that are often very diverse. In verse 14 the forgiveness of our sins is attributed to Christ's blood; but in verse 16 nothing is said either of Christ's blood or of the forgiveness of sins, but it is taught that things, even very different ones, were made through Christ, namely that all things in heaven and on earth were created by him, not through his blood and cross but through his divinity.

units.la: Tandem etiam affirmat Adversarius, Angelos per Christum renovatos esse & reformatos. Verùm si quæramus, quo-modo? respondet, se nescire. Nempe id est respondendo effugere, non satis facere. & abolitum est, fortis armatus expoliatus, à Christo robustiore & separatus est. Quo facto, hominibus resipiscentibus, & verum Deum ac Dominum suum agnoscentibus, Angeli quoque, sublata dissidii & odii causa, coeperunt esse amici hominibus, hinc laetantur super uno pec-catore resipiscente. Obtinent ergo prius suum, quod in prima creatione habuerant, dominium, officium & imperium, quo antea, regnante Satana, privati erant. Hoc igitur modo restaurati & renovati ipsi quoque esse dicuntur. Praeter-ea, saepe testatur Paulus, mysterium vocationis gentium, fuisse absconditum a mundi initio, & ignotum etiam Angelis, quod est illis, & toti mundo, per Christum, & ejus passionem pate-factum. At qui aliquid addiscunt, & quod prius ignorabant, resciscunt, quodammodo novum statum induisse, & reformati dici pos-sunt. Alia quaedam his similia, possunt ex Apostolorum scriptis colligi. Nam ita in qui-busdam locis loquuntur, ut videantur significa-re, non tantum homines, sed totum universum, peccato Adae deformatum, & perturbatum fuisse, quae omnia in ordinem rectum & priorem statum, per Christum fuerint restituta, aut certe olim sint restituenda, quandoquidem hic nunc, initia tantum quaedam restitutionis hujus videmus. Lege hac de re quae scribuntur ab Apostolo ad Rom. 8. Quamvis ibi quoque per hyperbolicas locutiones, solius humani generis, atque adeo tantum piorum statum & restaurationem describere Paulus videatur. Quam ego sententiam, tam illi, quam huic loco, accommo-datissimam esse existimo. Postremo, ubi dicitur Christus, ante omnes, (vel omnia) esse: hoc non ad tempus, sed ad dignitatem referendum esse, cum ex sequentibus liquidissime apparet, tum ex aliis scripturae locis. Sic Baptista Christum ante se factum, & super omnes esse affirmat. Quanquam in nova creatione, etiam tempore, omnes praecedit Christus.
units.tr: Finally, the Opponent also affirms that the angels were renewed and reformed through Christ. But if we ask how, he replies that he does not know. Certainly this is to escape by answering, not to give satisfaction. "...and it has been abolished; the strong armed man has been stripped and his armour taken away by the stronger Christ" (cf. Luke 11:22). When this was done, and men repented and acknowledged the true God and their Lord, the angels too, the cause of discord and hatred having been removed, began to be friends to men; hence they rejoice over one sinner who repents. They therefore recover what they had in the first creation, their dominion, office and rule, of which they had been deprived before, while Satan reigned. In this way they are said to be restored and renewed themselves as well. Moreover, Paul often testifies that the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles had been hidden from the beginning of the world, and unknown even to the angels, and that it was made known to them, and to the whole world, through Christ and his passion. But those who learn something and come to know what they had previously been ignorant of, are in some sense put into a new state and can be said to be reformed. Other things similar to these can be gathered from the writings of the Apostles. For in certain places they speak in such a way that they seem to signify that not only men but the whole universe was deformed and disturbed by the sin of Adam, and that all these things have been or will certainly be restored to their right order and former state through Christ, since here and now we see only certain beginnings of this restoration. Read on this matter what the Apostle writes in Romans 8, although there too Paul seems to describe, through hyperbolical expressions, only the state and restoration of the human race, and indeed only of the godly. This opinion I judge to be most suitable both to that passage and to this one. Lastly, where it is said that Christ is before all (or all things), this must be referred not to time but to dignity, as is quite clear both from what follows and from other passages of Scripture. So John the Baptist affirms that Christ was made before him and is above all. Yet in the new creation Christ also precedes all, even in time.

units.la: Adeone sufficit verba dare, & id spectare duntaxat ut aliis quid regeras, non habita ratione quale illud sit? Vult credo, ut re-sponsionem illam accipiamus, quam ne ipse quidem capit. Certe si hoc fit respon-dere, tum licebit effutire, quidquid in buccam venerit, & ubi rogaberis exposi-tionem vel probationem dicere, te nesci-re. Jam quilibet securus sit de disputatio-ne, quamdiu talia afferre concessum erit. Rationis tamen loco adfert, non debere nos curiosius investigare in ea, quae Ma-gister optimus celare voluit, praesertim in negotio de Angelis, quod parce admo-dum Deus revelavit. Sed propterea non idipsum dicere de Angelis debuerat, quod dixit: quia id nullo in Scripturis funda-mento nititur, indicio nullo. Curiositatis est ea scire & afferere velle, quae Deus non manifestavit, vel in ratione modum-que rerum quamvis revelatarum altius quam decet, inquirere, ὑπὲρ φρονεῖν παρ' [?] ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν. Sed assertionis alicujus temeraria causam quaerere, adeo non est vitiose curiosum esse, ut hoc demum modo curiositas optime castigetur, & coerceatur. Neque verum est, quod praesupponit, clare affirmare Apostolum, per crucem Christi, etiam caelestia esse refor-mata.
units.tr: Is it enough, then, to give words, and to aim only at telling others something, without regard to what kind of thing it is? He wishes, I suppose, that we accept the answer which he himself does not even understand. Certainly if this is what answering means, then one may babble whatever comes into one's mouth, and whenever one is asked to give an explanation or proof, say that one does not know. Anyone may then be secure in a dispute, so long as such assertions are permitted. Instead of a reason, however, he brings forward that we ought not to investigate too curiously those things which the best Master wished to keep hidden, especially in the matter of the angels, about which God has revealed very sparingly. But for that reason he ought not to have said about the angels what he said, because it rests on no foundation in the Scriptures and no indication. It is curiosity to wish to know and assert things which God has not manifested, or to inquire into the manner and reason of things, even revealed ones, more deeply than is fitting: "to be wise beyond what one ought to be wise" [ὑπὲρ φρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν]. But to seek rashly the cause of some assertion is by no means a faulty curiosity; indeed in this way curiosity is best rebuked and restrained. Nor is it true, as he presupposes, that the Apostle clearly affirms that even heavenly things have been reformed through the cross of Christ.

units.la: Deinde probat assertionem suam, ex Ephes. 1. ubi Apostolus testetur, Angelos per Christum esse restauratos, refor-matos, renovatos, pacificatos. Quo primum ostendit, non fuisse damnatae curio-fitatis, rationem ejus efflagitare, cujus probationem putat se ex Apostolo adfer-re posse. Sed ostendere debuerat, illud ab Apostolo doceri, Ephes. 1. quod non ibi magis reperimus, quam alibi: & ego mihi persuadeo, si credidisset Adversarius, à Paulo tale quid dici, non tam leviter id annotasset atque transfivisset, sed explicuisset, pro more ubi vel minimum opinatur causae suae momentum habere, latius atque prolixius. Dicit Ephes. 1, 21. Apostolus, Christum evectum esse super omnem principatum; & potestatem, & potentiam, & dominationem, & omne nomen quod nomi-natur sive hoc in seculo, sive in futuro: an hoc est, Angelos docere per Christi san-guinem reformatos, renovatos, restauratos esse? nihil minus. Non magis quam in hoc sæculo omnem potestatem, dignitatem, & nomen, per Christum renovata & ite-rum creata esse.
units.tr: Next he proves his assertion from Ephesians 1, where the Apostle testifies that the angels were restored, reformed, renewed and reconciled through Christ. By this he first shows that it was not a condemned curiosity to demand the reason for a thing whose proof he thinks he can bring from the Apostle. But he ought to have shown that this is taught by the Apostle in Ephesians 1, which we do not find there any more than elsewhere. And I am persuaded that if the Opponent had believed that such a thing was said by Paul, he would not have noted it so lightly and passed over it, but would have explained it, as is his custom wherever he thinks his cause has even the slightest weight, at greater length and in more detail. He says that in Ephesians 1:21 the Apostle says that Christ was exalted above every principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, whether in this age or in the age to come. Does this mean that the angels are taught to have been reformed, renewed, restored through the blood of Christ? Not at all. No more than that in this age every power, dignity and name has been renewed and created anew through Christ.

units.la: Hinc etiam pergit Adversarius ostendere, quomodo Angeli sint per Christum re-conciliati & renovati, cum boni quidem reconciliatione non egeant, mali verò extra spem reconciliationis constituti. De malis primùm ita respondet, ut exponat, quid alii censeant, non quid ipse. Primò, quod multi spiritus mali, post adventum Christi resipuerint, ac Deo sint reconciliati. Ut probat[?] Fabulâ Satyri, seu Diaboli Anto-nio oblati, & pro salute sua petentis ejus preces atque intercessionem. Futilis pro-batio, cui non existimo, quod ipse qui eam adfert, fidem suam accommodat. Tum Origenis advocat opinionem, statuentis, Diabolos etiam salutem aliquando per Christum obtenturos. Sed de Origenis sententia, num ista fuerit, adhuc hodie dispu-tant; & quod si fuerit, passim est condemnata. Denique non opinionibus stamus alie-nis, sed ratione propria ac solidâ.
units.tr: Hence the Opponent also goes on to show how the angels have been reconciled and renewed through Christ, although the good indeed have no need of reconciliation, and the wicked are placed beyond the hope of reconciliation. Concerning the wicked he first responds by setting out what others think, not what he himself thinks. First, that many evil spirits repented after the coming of Christ and were reconciled to God. He proves this by the fable of a satyr, or devil, presented to Antony, who begged his prayers and intercession for his own salvation. A futile proof, and I do not think that he who brings it puts his own faith in it. Then he calls in the opinion of Origen, who held that the devils too will at some time obtain salvation through Christ. But whether this was Origen's view is still disputed today; and even if it was, it has been condemned everywhere. Finally, we stand not on the opinions of others but on our own reason, and a solid one.

units.la: Porro etiam aliter Diabolorum reformationem explicat. Nempe, quod ipsi à Deo Christo subjecti fuerunt, & per Christum eorum vires & potestas imminuta atque immutata. Verùm id non est renovatum esse & restauratum: non per sanguinem Christi. Neque ista mutatio, agnoscente quoque Adversario, Diabolis in bonum cedit. Verùm inquit, in bonum cessit aliis. At non de aliis nunc agitur, quam Dia-bolis, & hos volebat ostendere, per Christi sanguinem esse quoque restauratos. Quia, subjicit, universi reformatio per Christum contigit, ipsi Diaboli, universi pars, per Christum reformati dici quoque possunt. Uti propter aliam Reipub. formam, tota sæpe mutatur. Reformatio per Christum, & ejus vis ac beneficium ad Ecclesiam per-tinuit, non ad universum, vel ad alia in universo, nisi quatenus omnia Christo Media-tori subjecta. Sed, quemadmodum in Rebusp. ita hic, illa subjectio contingere po-test, sine reformatione & renovatione singulorum, præsertim eorum, quos diuturna malitia & conditio facit inemendabiles. Novam formam capit Resp. ubi ejus muta-tur regimen; sed nusquam testatur Scriptura, quod cum Christi novo imperio refor-matio sequuta fuerit in ipso etiam inferno, apud Diabolos; non quod in Christo illi noviter creati, & æque ac alii in mundo, renovati & restituti: nam in Christo dicun-tur creata tam quæ in cœlis, quam quæ in terrâ.
units.tr: Further, he explains the reformation of the devils in another way. Namely, that they have been made subject to Christ, God, and that through Christ their powers and authority have been diminished and changed. But this is not to be renewed and restored, not through the blood of Christ. Nor does this change, as the Opponent too acknowledges, turn to the good of the devils. But, he says, it turned to the good of others. But we are not now dealing with others than the devils, and it was these he wished to show were also restored through the blood of Christ. Because, he adds, the reformation of the whole universe took place through Christ, the devils themselves, being part of the universe, can also be said to be reformed through Christ. Just as, for another form of commonwealth, the whole is often changed. But reformation through Christ, and his power and benefit, pertains to the Church, not to the whole universe or to other things in the universe, except insofar as all things are subject to Christ the Mediator. But, as in a commonwealth, so here that subjection can happen without the reformation and renewal of individuals, especially of those whom long-standing malice and condition make incorrigible. A commonwealth takes a new form when its government is changed; but Scripture nowhere testifies that, with the new rule of Christ, a reformation followed even in hell itself, among the devils; nor that those who were created anew in Christ, and like others in the world, were renewed and restored. For in Christ are said to have been created both the things in heaven and the things on earth.

units.la: Transit deinceps Adversarius, ad bonos Angelos, eosque, ait, de novo quasi creatos in Christo, & restauratos per reconciliationem inter eos constitutam ac homines, illis se nunc mutuo in Christo amantibus, qui per peccatum hominum antea erant divulsi & dissidentes. Quidquid sit de versu seq. 20. ubi omnia dicuntur per Chri-stum & in eo pacificata, sive quæ in terrâ, sive quæ in cœlis, atque de hominibus in-ligi potest, sive in terrâ adhuc militantibus, sive in cœlo, sed per Christum beatis, ex-serte dicuntur reconciliata & pacificata: in versu autem 16. non hoc, sed bis dicun-tur per Christum creata. Hoc aliud: atque illud antecessit. Neque aliquid est in versu nostro, vel verborum, vel rei, quod expositionem illam reconciliationis ferat. Nam in ipso creata omnia quæ in cœlis & quæ in terra, visibilia & invisibliia, non dicit, creata in unum. Quod si velis, primò intelligi debere renovationem moralem, tum in specie pacificationem eorum inter se; quidni ita quodvis ex quovis educi possit ac probari[?] Neutrum illorum probare potest, atque in disputatione dictare velle, incongruum. Denique quorsum, si reconciliationem illorum intendisset Apostolus docere, vel non iisdem verbis fuisset usus, quibus postea, vel non aliquam connexionis particulam adhibuisset cum, vel inter? vel denique priora, & mentem suam plenius explicare voluisset per thronos, potestates, &c.' Quorsum ista? neque enim hæc ad reconciliationem exponendam quidquam faciunt.
units.tr: The Adversary next turns to the good angels, and says that they were, as it were, created anew in Christ and restored through the reconciliation established between them and men, since they now love each other in Christ, whereas before they had been divided and at odds through the sin of men. Whatever may be said of the following verse 20, where all things are said to be through Christ and made peace in him, whether things on earth or things in heaven, and which may be applied to men, whether still fighting on earth or blessed in heaven through Christ, they are expressly said to be reconciled and made peace. But in verse 16 it is not this that is said; there it is twice said that they were created through Christ. That is a different matter, and the one went before the other. Nor is there anything in our verse, either in the words or in the sense, that supports that explanation of reconciliation. For it does not say "created into one". And if you wish it to be understood first of moral renewal, and then specifically of their peace with one another, why could not anything be drawn and proved from anything else in the same way? Neither of these can be proved, and it is out of place to want to dictate them in a disputation. Finally, to what purpose, if the Apostle had intended to teach their reconciliation, would he not have used the same words as afterwards, or would he not have added some connecting particle such as "with" or "between"? Or at last, if he had wished to explain his meaning more fully, would he not have done so through thrones, powers, and so on? Why these things? For none of them contributes anything to explaining reconciliation.

units.la: Inde iterum aliud adfert, quo illud, creari per Christum, de Angelis exponat, vid. quod patefacto per Christum mysterio vocationis gentium, hoc, quod antea ignoratum fuit, inde clarius & ipsi Angeli perspexerint: jam qui aliquid resciscere, quodammodo novum statum induere & reformari dici potest. Ad quæ non declinat, & quot opus habet adferre, qui ab unâ desciscit veritate, & hujus rejecta simplicitate in varia se induit præjudicia ac errores? Quæcunq; etiam excogitat & producit Adversarius, non adæquant tamen vim verborum Apostoli, de creatione omnium per Christum. Minus hoc, quod ultimo loco dicit, de acquisita Angelis aliqua notitia experimentali. Hoc si creari sit, jam quotidie & Angeli, & nos dicendi erimus creari. Quo quid absurdius? præsertim in Theologia, de sermone sacro, ubi alia & propria sunt atque usurpantur, tum hic, tum illud significantia, nomina.
units.tr: Then he brings forward yet another point, by which he explains the words "created through Christ" as referring to the angels: namely, that once the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles had been revealed through Christ, the angels themselves came to see more clearly what had previously been unknown to them; and one who comes to know something can in a way be said to put on a new state and be reformed. He does not shrink from such things, and how many must one bring forward, when one has departed from a single truth and, having rejected its simplicity, clothes oneself in various prejudices and errors? Whatever the Adversary also devises and produces does not, however, match the force of the Apostle's words about the creation of all things through Christ. Still less does what he says last, about some experiential knowledge acquired by the angels. If that were what it means to be created, then the angels and we too would be said to be created every day. What could be more absurd, especially in theology, where in sacred speech other and proper names are used, each with its own meaning?

units.la: Rursum ad aliud dilabitur, & nunc ex Rom. viii. ubi omnium restitutionem jubet Apostolis exspectare cum Christo, argumentatur: tum id ipse mox rejicit, & ad solos homines restringit. Nescius, quid ipse velit, ac dicere porro debeat. Bene interim, quod agnoscit variis Scripturæ locis doceri, non tantum homines, sed totum universum[?], peccato Adæ deformatum & perturbatum fuisse, quum alias peccatum illud adeo soleant extenuare Adversarii, & vix ad homines derivare.
units.tr: Again he slips off to another point, and now argues from Romans 8, where the Apostles are bidden to await with Christ the restitution of all things. Then he himself soon rejects this and restricts it to men alone. He does not know what he himself wants, or what he ought to say further. Meanwhile it is good that he admits that various passages of Scripture teach that not only men but the whole universe was deformed and disturbed by the sin of Adam, since otherwise the Adversaries are accustomed to belittle that sin and hardly to extend it beyond men.

units.la: Postremo & idarrodit, quod Christus dicitur πρὸ πάντων[?] ante omnia, & primum ad dignitatem referendum esse contendit, non vero ad tempus, tandem concedit etiam de tempore, at non simpliciter, sed restrictè ad novam creationem. Nos simpliciter, atque de omni absolute prioritate intelligendum esse, censemus: quia hoc Apostolus in animo habuit, omnimodam Christo assignare prioritatem, ἵνα γένηται ἐν πᾶσιν αὐτὸς[?] πρωτεύων. ergo etiam ratione creationis primæ, de qua ante egerat, & speciatim dixerat eum esse πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως, non minus quam πρωτότοκον ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν. Eaque ratione Baptista dixit, Christum, non dignitate solum & potentia, sed quoque tempore priorem fuisse, ante me natus fuit, quandoquidem omni ratione & absolute me prior est, πρῶτός μου ἦν.
units.tr: Finally, he also scoffs that Christ is said to be πρὸ πάντων [before all things], and he contends that this must be referred to dignity and not to time. At last he concedes even the point about time, but not simply; he restricts it to the new creation. We judge that it must be understood simply, and of every absolute priority, because this is what the Apostle had in mind: to ascribe to Christ every kind of priority, ἵνα γένηται ἐν πᾶσιν αὐτὸς πρωτεύων [that in all things he might have the preeminence].
