Therefore it applies also in respect of the first creation, of which he had spoken before, and where he had specifically said that Christ is the πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως [firstborn of all creation], no less than πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν [firstborn from the dead]. And on this reasoning the Baptist said that Christ was prior not only in dignity and power but also in time: "He was before me" [πρῶτός μου ἦν], since he is before me in every respect and absolutely.

units.la: Quod hactenus argumentum ursimus à creatione, idem epist. ad Hebræos suppeditat, cap. 1. 2. 3. cum loco Col. 1. valde conveniens. Quem Filium Deus constituit hæredem omnium, per quem & sæcula fecit. Qui est resplendescentia gloriæ, & charaćter hypostasis ejus, ferens omnia verbo potentiæ suæ. Uti Col. 1. 15. Apostolus primum dixerat, quis esset Christus, εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου[?]: ita hic vers. 3. resplendescentia gloriæ, & charaćter hypostasis ejus. Tum ejus enarrat opera, primum creationis, ibi vers. 16. Nam per ipsum facta sunt omnia: hic, vers. 2. per eum sæcula fecit. Deinde conservationis: ibi, τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε: hic, ferens omnia verbo potentiæ suæ. Denique redemtionis, vers. 18. nam ipse est caput corporis Ecclesiæ, &c. hic, per seipsum expiatione factâ peccatorum nostrorum. Idem ordo, ac series etiam observatur Ioan. 1. Adde Hebr. 1. 10, de Christo dictum: Tu, Domine, in initio terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli.
units.tr: The argument we have so far drawn from creation is supplied in the same way by the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapters 1, 2 and 3, which agrees very closely with the passage in Colossians 1. "Whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds; who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, upholding all things by the word of his power." As the Apostle had first said in Colossians 1:15 who Christ is, εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου [the image of the invisible God], so here in verse 3 he says "the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person". Then he recounts his works: first creation, there in verse 16, "for by him were all things created"; here in verse 2, "by him he made the worlds". Then preservation: there, τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε [in him all things consist]; here, "upholding all things by the word of his power". Finally redemption: in verse 18, "for he is the head of the body, the Church", and so on; here, "by himself, having made purification of our sins". The same order and sequence is observed in John 1. Add Hebrews 1:10, said of Christ: "Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of thine hands."

units.la: Vt demus hic agi de prima creatione, non tamen hinc ulla Christi æternitas, vel Deitas colligi potest. Nam primo, in confesso est, Angelos antiquiores esse mundo visibili, nec tamen sunt æterni. Deinde, etiam ex his verbis apparet, Christum minorem esse Patre, nam non Christo, sed Patri tribuitur creatio. Christus enim tantum instrumentum, & medium fuisse dicitur creationis. Semper autem principale efficiens, præstantius est instrumento. Præterea sunt qui illud: διʼ ἅ [?] interpretentur, non per quem, sed propter quem, quod posse & solere fieri, & Grammatica, & infinita exempla docent. Atque tunc verborum sensus erit, in gratiam Filii esse conditum mundum. Quod cum Hebræorum doctissimorum sententia congruit, qui affirmant, Deum propter Messiam condidisse mundum. Qua de re aliquid etiam apud Galatinum legitur, lib. 7. cap. 2. Atque hæc afferre possumus, si constaret, hic per Secula, intelligi mundum visibilem: verum illud valde ambiguum, imò falsum est. Nam primo, ipsemet Apostolus, paulo post, cap. 2. vers. 5. de loqui de futuro orbe testatur. Deinde, hoc ipsum confirmari hoc pacto potest: Per eum Deus dicitur condidisse secula, quem constituit hæredem, & per quem locutus est novissimis diebus. Nam Relativum quem, omnino refert eum de quo proximè habitus erat sermo. At Deus constituit hæredem, & locutus est, per hominem, seu per Filium, ut isti loquuntur, incarnatum. Ergo per Filium incarnatum Deus condidit secula. At cum Christus est incarnatus, jam ante aliquot centenos annos creatus erat mundus visibilis, ergo de alia quàm prima hic agitur creatione. Confirmatur hoc ex eo, quod scribitur Deus prius esse locutus per Filium, quàm condiderit per eum secula. At cum locutus est per Filium, jam mundi machina pridem erat constituta.
units.tr: Let us grant that the first creation is treated here; yet from this no eternity or Deity of Christ can be inferred. For, first, it is agreed that the angels are older than the visible world, and yet they are not eternal. Next, even from these words it appears that Christ is less than the Father, since creation is ascribed not to Christ but to the Father. For Christ is said to have been only the instrument and means of creation, whereas the principal efficient cause is always more excellent than the instrument. Moreover, there are those who take the phrase διʼ οὗ [through whom] to mean not "through whom" but "on account of whom", which both grammar and countless examples show can and does happen. Then the sense of the words will be that the world was made for the sake of the Son. This agrees with the opinion of the most learned Hebrews, who affirm that God made the world on account of the Messiah. Something on this matter is also read in Galatinus, book 7, chapter 2. And we could bring forward these points if it were established that "the ages" here means the visible world; but that is very doubtful, indeed false. For, first, the Apostle himself, a little later in chapter 2, verse 5, testifies that he is speaking of the future world. Next, this very point can be confirmed in this way: God is said to have made the ages through him whom he has constituted heir, and through whom he spoke in the last days. For the relative "whom" plainly refers to the one who was the immediate subject of discourse. But God appointed the heir, and spoke through a man, or through the Son, as those people say, incarnate. Therefore God made the ages through the incarnate Son. But when Christ was incarnate, the visible world had already been created some centuries earlier; therefore the creation here treated is other than the first. This is confirmed by the fact that it is written that God spoke through the Son before he made the ages through him. But when he spoke through the Son, the frame of the world had long since been established.

units.la: Resp. I. Non simpliciter quod antiquius possit esse mundo visibili, est æternũ; sed id quod ante omnem, omniumq; creatione, hoc est æternum,& Deus. II. Non est verum, nedum ut sit in cofesso, Angelos antiquiores esse mundo visibili,& ante hexaemerum extitisse. Quod refutavimus, Tom. I. lib. III. cap. I. Adde Rivetum, Exercit. XI. in Genesin. III. Non inde Christus minor est Patre, quod Patri tribuitur creatio; quinimo par & æqualis Patri, quandoquidem ipsi eadem quoque attribuitur, & hic, & alibi. Neq; tantum instrumentum & medium dicitur fuisse creationis, quale nec dari vel esse aliquid potest: sed causa principalis, propria, & vera. Quod vero dicitur Pater per eum fecisse, non id secunditatem causæ indicat, sed in agendo ordinem, & S. Trinitatis in operando œconomiam. IV. διʼ ἑαυτῷ non hic est propter, sed per quem: uti & vers. 3. διʼ ἑαυτῷ per seipsum. & sic passim. Rom. XI. 36. quia ex ipso, & per ipsum, διʼ αὐτοῦ, & in ipsum omnia. Illud est δι, οὗ, ut in Hebr. II. 10. decuit enim cum δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα, δι' ὃν τὰ πάντα, propter quem omnia & per quem omnia. & vers. 3. quæ cæpit enarrari ἀρξά δὲ Κυρίᾳ [?]. & cap. XIII. 15. διʼ αὐτοῦ: per eum ergo offeramus sacrificium laudis. Syris hoc loco ܒܗ [?] & per eum. Sic & Arabica, & Æthiopica legunt. Præterea si propter Filium creatus mundus, ita ut is creationis sit habendus finis, sequitur eo etiam Deum esse, quia hoc in nullum cadit, nisi in ipsum Deum, & Deus quæcunque facit non propter alium facit,quam propter se. Prov.xvi.4.
units.tr: Reply. I. It is not simply that what can be older than the visible world is eternal; rather, that which is before every creation and before all creatures, that is eternal, and that is God. II. It is not true, far from being agreed, that the angels are older than the visible world and existed before the six days. We have refuted this in Tome I, book III, chapter 1. Add Rivetus, Exercitation XI on Genesis. III. Christ is not less than the Father because creation is ascribed to the Father; rather he is equal and like the Father, since the same is also ascribed to him, both here and elsewhere. Nor is he said to have been merely the instrument and means of creation, which cannot be given or exist as such, but the principal, proper and true cause. And when the Father is said to have made all things "through him", this does not indicate a subordinate causality, but the order of acting and the economy of the Holy Trinity in working. IV. Here διʼ ἑαυτῷ does not mean "on account of", but "through whom"; so also in verse 3, διʼ ἑαυτῷ [through himself]. And so throughout. Romans 11:36: "for of him, and through him [διʼ αὐτοῦ], and to him, are all things." That is the δι' οὗ construction, as in Hebrews 2:10: "for it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things [δι' ὃν τὰ πάντα, δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα], in bringing many sons unto glory." And verse 3: which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord [ἀρχὴν λαλεῖσθαι διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου]. And chapter 13, verse 15: "by him [διʼ αὐτοῦ] therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise." The Syriac here has bēh, "by him" and "through him". The Arabic and Ethiopic versions read so as well. Moreover, if the world was created on account of the Son, so that this is to be regarded as the end of creation, it follows that he is also God; for this cannot apply to anyone but God himself, and God does whatever he does for no other end than himself. Proverbs 16:4.

units.la: Porro negat Adversarius, hic de mundo, ejusque creatione sermonem esse, nempe quia paulo post Apostolus cap. 11. 5. loquitur de orbe futuro: negatur sequi, quod ergo cap. 1. 2. non loquatur de creatione mundi visibilis: non magis, quam quod non etiam quae cap. 1. 6. de mundo, in quem Deus introduxit suum primogenitum, & ver. 10. tu Domine in initio fundasti terram, de mundo visibili sint exponenda, praesenti nempe, non demum futuro. VI. Per eum, quem Deus constituit haeredem, per quem loquutus est diebus ultimis, quique incarnatus, Deus mundum condidit, sed non dicitur quod postquam incarnatus, & constitutus, a praedicatione, omnium haeres: per eum, qui talis, non qua talis, creata a Deo sunt omnia. VII. Et sic, quamvis prius dicatur Deus fuisse locutus per Filium, quam condidisse per eum saecula, non sequitur in serie & ordine temporis illa ita sequi: neque enim hic vel historia panditur, vel ordo temporis designatur, narratur vel docetur tantum quis ac qualis ille Dei filius, nempe per quem olim saecula facta, & nunc redemti ejus sanguine homines. Denique dicuntur per eum saecula condita αἰῶνες, quod de visibili mundo passim intelligitur. Sic Hebr. XI. 3. fide credimus firmata saecula verbo Dei.
units.tr: The Adversary further denies that this passage speaks of the world and its creation, namely because a little later (chapter 11, verse 5) the Apostle speaks of the world to come. It does not follow, he says, that in chapter 1, verse 2, the Apostle is not speaking of the creation of the visible world. Nor does it follow that what is said in chapter 1, verse 6, about the world into which God brought his firstborn, and in verse 10, "You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth," must be explained of the visible world, meaning the present world and not the world to come. 6. God made the world through him whom he appointed heir, through whom he spoke in the last days, and who was made flesh. But it is not said that after he was made flesh and appointed, he became heir of all things by his preaching. All things were created by God through him who is such, not through him as such. 7. And so, although it is said that God first spoke through the Son and only afterwards made the ages through him, it does not follow that these things happen in that order of sequence and time. For here neither a history is unfolded nor an order of time marked out; rather it is only narrated or taught who and what kind of Son of God he is, namely the one through whom the ages were once made and through whose blood men are now redeemed. Finally, the ages are said to have been created through him [αἰῶνες], which is commonly understood of the visible world. So Heb. 11:3: "By faith we believe that the ages were framed by the word of God."

units.la: Respondet Enjedinus, se non negare, quinvox αἰὼν, quemadmodum κόσμος, etiam mundum significet hunc visibilem, sed illa, quemadmodum sunt πολύτμημα[?], pro subjecta materia diversimode esse accipienda. Verum unum cedo locum, ubi vel vox αἰὼν simpliciter posita, vel ποιεῖν[?] αἰῶνας aliter, quam de hoc saeculo, vel mundo intelligitur. Idem dico de voce κόσμος. Quando αἰὼν futurum notat saeculum, semper additur nota futuri vel μέλλον[?], aut ἐρχόμενον, vel praepositio εἰς illud indicans, uti Hebraice לעולם הבא[?]; quod opponitur עולם & αἰῶνι simpliciter posito, vel τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι. Syrus hoc in loco, לעלמא[?]. Caeterum duo adfert argumenta Adversarius, ut ostendat hic intelligi non creationem mundi visibilis hujus, sed futuri.
units.tr: Enjedinus replies that he does not deny that the word αἰών, like κόσμος, also means this visible world; but these words, being of many senses, must be taken in different ways according to the subject matter. Yet let him show me one place where the word αἰών, used by itself, or the phrase ποιεῖν αἰῶνας, is understood otherwise than of this age or world. I say the same of the word κόσμος. When αἰών denotes the age to come, a mark of the future is always added, either μέλλον or ἐρχόμενον, or the preposition εἰς indicating that age, as in the Hebrew לעולם הבא [le-olam ha-ba], "the world to come," which is opposed to עולם [olam] and to αἰῶνι simply put, or to τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ and τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι. The Syriac in this place has לעלמא [le-alma]. Besides this, the Adversary brings two arguments to show that what is meant here is not the creation of this visible world but of the future one.

units.la: Propositum Apostoli est, Filium Dei supra omnes creaturas extollere, & ejus excellentiam deprædicare. Sed, quid opus est Deum æternum, creaturis suis excellentiorem esse demonstrare? Annon hoc notius est etiamnis, quae sensibus externis comprehendimus? Oportet ergo de re humiliori, quam sit Deus æternus, Apostolum loqui. Loquitur autem de homine Iesu Christo. At certissimum est, per hominem non potuisse condi mundum veterem visibilem, eum post illum ipse fit formatus. Ergo necessa-rio sequitur, hic non agi de creationes veteris mundi. Deinde, hoc ipsum circumstantiae ostendunt. Nam & ante, & post haec verba, de tali Filio agitur, qui locutus est hominibus in diebus novissimis, qui constitutus a Deo est haeres, qui est splendor gloriae, qui purgavit peccata, qui collocatus est ad dextram Dei.
units.tr: The Apostle's purpose is to exalt the Son of God above all creatures and to proclaim his excellence. But why is it necessary to show that the eternal God is more excellent than his creatures? Is not this more widely known even now, from what we perceive by the external senses? It must therefore be that the Apostle speaks of something lower than the eternal God. But he speaks of the man Jesus Christ. Yet it is most certain that the old visible world could not have been created by a man, since the man himself was formed after it. It therefore follows necessarily that the creation of the old world is not what is meant here. Furthermore, the context itself shows this. For both before and after these words, the discussion concerns such a Son as spoke to men in the last days, who was appointed heir by God, who is the brightness of glory, who purged sins, and who was set at the right hand of God.

units.la: Resp. 1. Apostoli propositum est, Chri-sti excellentiam supra omnes homines, Angelos, & creaturas evehere apud suos Hebræos, qui humili ejus statu passim erant offensi. 1 Cor. 1. 2, 3. Prædicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudæis quidem scandalum. Quare hoc agit, ut ostendat, eum esse Dei filium, & Deum. Sic quidem est, ubi agnoscitur Deus, nil ne-cesse insuper ejus excellentiam ostendere; sed illud probari aliis, aliis confirmari semper opus est. Quidquid sit, hoc ipsum nunc docere Apostolus instituit, & nulli magis id docendi fuerunt, quam Hebræi. Loquitur Apostolus de homine Iesu, sed quem docet, alia quam humanitatis suae ratione, esse supra creaturas, Deum. Quare per eum, non ut hominem, sed Deum, condiAt nihil horum competit, nisi homini, per quem conditus hic visibilis mundus fuit, & in certe vetus mundus fieri non potuit. eo omnia, coelum, & terra, & mare,& omnia quae in iis. Act. xiv. 16. Ergo necessario sequitur, hic agi de creatione veteris mundi.
units.tr: Answer 1. The Apostle's purpose is to raise the excellence of Christ above all men, angels and creatures among his own Hebrews, who were everywhere offended by his humble condition (1 Cor. 1:2, 3: "We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews"). He therefore sets out to show that he is the Son of God and God. This is so: where God is acknowledged, there is no need to show his excellence further; but it always needs to be proved to some and confirmed to others. Whatever the case, this is what the Apostle now sets out to teach, and no people needed to be taught it more than the Hebrews. The Apostle speaks of the man Jesus, but he teaches that, by a reason other than his humanity, he is God above the creatures. Therefore, it is through him, not as man but as God, that all things were created, "in him all things were created, in heaven and earth, visible and invisible." But none of this applies except to the man through whom this visible world was created; and certainly the old world could not have been made except through him, "who made heaven, and earth, and sea, and all that is in them" (Acts 14:16). Therefore it necessarily follows that the creation of the old world is what is meant here.

units.la: In secundo Adversarii argumento negatur consequentia: ubi in antecedentibus & consequentibus agitur de tali filio, qui locutus est hominibus in diebus novissimis, &c. ibi non potest intelligi filius, per quem mundus sit conditus: negatur. At illud loqui competit homini, per quem certe mundus fieri non potuit. Non per hominem, non quatenus loquutus hominibus, mundus est factus, sed per Deum, qui postea & homo factus ἀνθρώπῳ[?].
units.tr: To the Adversary's second argument, the consequence is denied: where, in what goes before and after, the discussion concerns such a Son as spoke to men in the last days, etc., there the Son through whom the world was created cannot be understood. This is denied. For speaking belongs to the man, while the world certainly could not have been made through the man. The world was made not through the man, nor insofar as he spoke to men, but through God, who was afterwards also made man [ἄνθρωπος].

units.la: Opus providentiae divinae Christo adscribitur, praeterquam dictis, etiam Ioann. v. 17. Pater meus usque hodie operatur, atque ego operor. verf. 19. quae enim ille Pater facit, eadem & Filius similiter facit. Unde imperavit coelo ac ventis. Matth. viii. 26. Tum resurgens increpuit ventos & mare: & facta fuit tranquillitas magna. Mirati vero homines dixerunt: quantus hic est, ut & venti & mare ei obediant? Hoc autem Dei est, & Deo passim adscribitur, quod imperat coelo, ac mari, & quod omnia ei subjecta sunt, atque obtemperant. Psalm. cxxxv. 6. 7.
units.tr: Besides the passages cited, the work of divine providence is also ascribed to Christ, in John 5:17: "My Father works until now, and I work," and verse 19: "For whatever that Father does, the Son also does in like manner." Hence he commanded the heavens and the winds (Matt. 8:26): "Then he arose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. But the men marvelled and said, 'What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?'" But that he commands the heavens and the sea, and that all things are subject to him and obey him, is God's work and is everywhere ascribed to God (Ps. 135:6, 7).

units.la: Ad locum vero Heb. i. 3. ubi Christus dicitur portans omnia verbo potentiae suae, duo excipit Enjedinus.
units.tr: Enjedinus takes exception to two points in the passage Heb. 1:3, where Christ is said to be "upholding all things by the word of his power."

units.la: Quod hic Christus dicitur omnia portare, hoc est, gubernare, administrare potenter: non inde sequitur, eum esse Deum aeternum & omnipotentem. Quia omnis in coelo & terra potestas ei data est. Matth. 21. Et Iob. 13. Sciens Iesus, quia omnia dedit ei Pater in manus. At Deo aeterno, nemo quidquam unquam dedit. Deinde, per vocem Omnia, saepe jam docuimus significari mundum renovatum, orbem futurum, Ecclesiam, duos populos: Iudaeos nimirum & gentes, super quos Christus accepit imperium & dominium. Est ergo Dominus in domo Patris, sed constitutus a Deo. Resp. I. Ut a posteriori responso incipiam, in quo etiam prioris vis sita est, per vocem omnia simpliciter acceptam denotari orbem futurum, aut Ecclesiam, nemo ullo docuit unquam testimonio vel argumento. Si in sermone diceretur aliquo, omnia Ecclesiae, vel similiter, tum non vox omnia, sed additum subjectum limitaret orationem. In nostro vero loco absolute dicitur, omnia, portans omnia, non portans Ecclesiam, vel omnia Ecclesiae. II. Atque in praesenti dum dicitur, portans omnia, frustra explicatur de orbe futuro.
units.tr: That Christ is said here to bear all things, that is, to govern and administer them with power, does not follow from this that he is the eternal and almighty God, because all power in heaven and earth has been given to him (Matt. 28), and (John 13): "Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands." But no one has ever given anything to the eternal God. Further, by the word "all things" we have often shown already that the renewed world, the world to come, the Church, and the two peoples are meant: namely the Jews and the Gentiles, over whom Christ received rule and dominion. He is therefore Lord in the house of the Father, but appointed by God. Answer I. To begin with the second reply, on which the force of the first also rests: no one has ever shown, by any testimony or argument, that the word "all things," taken simply, denotes the world to come or the Church. If in some discourse it were said "all things of the Church" or something similar, then the added subject, not the word "all things," would limit the sense. But in our passage it is said absolutely, "all things, upholding all things," not "upholding the Church" or "all things of the Church." II. And in the present passage, where it is said "upholding all things," it is vainly explained of the world to come.

units.la: III. Dumque potentiae fit mentio, qua omnia portat, τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῆς[?], illa quae divina potentia nituntur, non gratia, intelligit, quae a Theologis dicuntur esse regni divinae potentiae, ex creatione; non gratiae, ex Christo. IV. Per omnia, duos populos intelligi, Judaeos & Gentiles, quomodo probabit? & quare non aeq; populos omnes? V. Differunt ista, omnem Christo in coelo & terra datam potestatem, & portare ipsum, postquam fecit saecula, omnia verbo potentiae, seu potenti, aut potenter. Deniq; portare, non est simpliciter gubernare, sed & conservare, ac facere ne intereant. Quod praestare solius Dei est, & ejusdem, quae in creatione, virtutis.
units.tr: III. And when mention is made of the power by which he upholds all things, [τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῆς, "by the word of his power"], he is understood to mean the divine power on which created things rest, not grace; which the theologians say belongs to the kingdom of divine power by creation, and not to grace through Christ. IV. How will he prove that "all things" means the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles? And why not all peoples equally? V. These points differ: the power given to Christ in heaven and earth, and his upholding all things by the word of his power, or powerfully, after he made the ages. Finally, to uphold is not simply to govern, but also to preserve and to keep things from perishing. This belongs to God alone, and to the same power which operated in creation.

units.la: Potestas patrandorum miraculorum in Christo arguit divinam naturam, quippe quae alia longe ratione edidit, quam caeteri homines ex peculiari quandoque dono, prout hoc discrimen, & simul certitudo cum argumenti nostri, tum divinae Christi naturae, ex hisce patefecit: I. quod fecit Christus miracula, sua propria vi & virtute: Apostoli per Christum. Act. iii. 12. 13. Videns autem Petrus respondit populo: Viri Israelitae quid miramini hoc, aut in nos quid intenti estis, quasi potentia propria aut pietate fecissemus ambulare istum ? Deus Abrahami, Isaaci, Iacobi, Deus Patrum nostrorum glorificavit Filium suum Iesum, &c. atque per fidem nominis ejus, ipsum, quem videtis & nostis, firmavit nomen ejus: & fides quæ per ipsum est dedit ei incolumitatem istam coram vobis omnibus. Ideoque dixerant Apostoli, in homine sanando, verf.6. in nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni surge & ambula. Christum autem sua virtute miracula patrasse, cum ex hoc satis constat loco, ubi aliis confert, per se, suoque nomine miracula facere; tum hinc, quod alia prorsus ratione in edendis miraculis se habuit, ac Apostoli, & non aliter quam propria virtute visus miracula fecisse: quod & palam agnovit. Matth. ix. 28. inquit cæcis: creditis quod ego hoc possum facere ? dicunt ei: ita Domine. 29. Tunc attigit eorum oculos, dicens: secundum fidem vestram fiat vobis, atque aperti fuerunt eorum oculi. Huc applicandum illud Psalm. cxxxvi. 4. qui facit נפלאות mirabilia magna solus. Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, cap. x. pag. 46. Sed & hoc addendum omnino est, quod Iesu Christi divinitatem in hac parte omnium fere maxime arguit, quod Iesus Christus, non alii, vel ante vel post eum, hanc tantam potestatem ita possedit, ut illa ab eo abesse potuerit, tanquam accidens vagum; vel quod opus habuerit, ut alii omnes, quicunque miracula unquam fecerunt, ipsam potestatem precibus à Deo impetrare, & eandem perpetuo studio conservare; sed ut verus verorum bonorum Dei possessor, ita eam secum communicatam habuit, ut ipsius propria effecta fuerit, & in eo perpetuo habitarit.
units.tr: The power to work miracles in Christ proves his divine nature, since he worked them in a quite different way from other men, who had such gifts only at times, as a special gift. In this difference, and at the same time in the certainty of my argument, both about the divine nature of Christ, the following points make it clear. (I) Christ worked miracles by his own power and virtue, whereas the apostles worked them through Christ. Acts 3:12, 13: But when Peter saw it, he answered the people: Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as if we had made this man walk by our own power or piety? The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus, etc.; and through faith in his name, his name has strengthened this man whom you see and know; and the faith which is through him has given him this soundness in the sight of you all. Hence the apostles said when healing the man, v. 6: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk. That Christ worked miracles by his own virtue is clear enough from this passage, where he is contrasted with the others: he works miracles through himself and in his own name. It is also clear from the fact that he went about working miracles in a quite different way from the apostles, and did so only by his own virtue, which he himself openly acknowledged. Matt. 9:28: he said to the blind men, Do you believe that I can do this? They say to him, Yes, Lord. 29. Then he touched their eyes, saying, Let it be done to you according to your faith, and their eyes were opened. To this applies Ps. 136:4: who alone does great wonders [נפלאות]. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 10, p. 46: But this must certainly also be added, that the divinity of Jesus Christ is proved in this respect almost more than anything else, because Jesus Christ, and not any other before or after him, possessed this so great power in such a way that it could be absent from him like a wandering accident, or because he needed, as all others who ever worked miracles did, to obtain this power from God by prayer and to keep it by constant effort. Rather, as the true possessor of the true goods of God, he had it communicated to him in such a way that it became his own and dwelt in him perpetually.

units.la: II. Facit Christus miracula pro arbitrio, quando & ubi vult, quod est eorum qui sua agunt potestate, non aliena. Unde Apostoli aliquando non potuerunt dæmonium ejicere, utcunque maxime etiam conarentur. Sed de Christo, Matth. viii. 2. Domine, si velis, potes me mundare. Ioann. v. 21. ita & filius quos vult vivificat. Etenim hic Dei Filius est. Psalm. cxv. 3. atque Deus noster in cœlis est, כל אשר חפץ [?], quodcumque vult facit. & Psalm. cxxxv. 6. Quidquid Iehova vult, facit in cœlo & in terra, in mari, & abysso omni. III. Porrò singularia Christus facit miracula, & Deo propria. Ioann. ix. 32. à sæculo non auditum quod aliquis cæci nati oculos aperuit. IV. Facit ea Christus in gloriam suam, quod nulli fas, neque competit nisi soli Deo, in gloriam suam operari. Prov. xvi. 4. Matth. vi. 1,2. & v. 16. Act. xiv. 13. Ioann. ii. 11. hoc initium miraculorum fecit Christus in Cana Galilæa, & manifestavit gloriam suam: atque crediderunt in ipsum discipuli ejus. Cap. ii. 4. Audiens Iesus dixit: hæc infirmitas non est ad mortem, sed pro gloria Dei, ut per illam Filius Dei glorificetur. Ad gloriam Filii Dei, hoc ab ipso factum miraculum, cujus eadem est cum gloria Dei. Act. iii. 13. dicitur ad miraculum sanati claudi: Deus Patrum nostrorum glorificavit Filium suum Iesum. v. Atque aliis Christus donum miraculorum impertit, quod solius Dei est. Matth. x. 1. Luc. x. 17. Marc. xvi. 17. &c. Smalcius, de divin. Christi, cap. x. pag. 44. Deinde non unius, sed omnis generis miracula D. Iesus fecit, qua de causa etiam tot vocibus, virtutum, signorum, prodigiorum, exprimuntur; imo inter Christi miracula, & confirmationes Euangelii, numerantur etiam Spiritus S. distributiones, ut scilicet vera divinitas ex illis I. Christi appa-reat, qui & omnis generis miracula fecerit, & ipsa etiam dona spiritualia, loco miraculorum, aliis, aliquo modo, dum mortalis esset, deinde perfecte, cum ex mortuis resuscitatus esset, do-narit, quod nemo, etiam si miracula facere fortasse, Deo permittente, posset, nisi Deus, aut ab eo missus, potest.
units.tr: (II) Christ works miracles at his own will, when and where he pleases, which belongs to those who act by their own power, not by another's. Hence the apostles sometimes could not cast out a demon, however hard they tried. But of Christ, Matt. 8:2: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. John 5:21: So also the Son gives life to whom he will. For he is the Son of God. Ps. 115:3: But our God is in the heavens; he does whatever he pleases [כל אשר חפץ]. And Ps. 135:6: Whatever the LORD pleases he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all deeps. (III) Moreover, Christ works unique miracles, which are proper to God. John 9:32: It has never been heard since the world began that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. (IV) Christ works them for his own glory, which is right for no one, and fits no one but God alone, to work for his own glory. Prov. 16:4; Matt. 6:1, 2 and 5:16; Acts 14:13; John 2:11: This beginning of miracles Jesus made in Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory; and his disciples believed in him. Ch. 11:4: When Jesus heard it, he said: This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it. The miracle wrought by him is for the glory of the Son of God, and this glory is the same as the glory of God. Acts 3:13, speaking of the healing of the lame man: The God of our fathers has glorified his Son Jesus. (V) And Christ bestows on others the gift of miracles, which belongs to God alone. Matt. 10:1; Luke 10:17; Mark 16:17, etc. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 10, p. 44: Moreover, Lord Jesus worked not one kind of miracle but every kind of miracle, for which reason he is also described by so many words: powers, signs, wonders. Indeed, among the miracles of Christ and the confirmations of the Gospel are numbered also the distributions of the Holy Spirit, so that the true divinity of Christ appears from them: he who worked every kind of miracle, and who also, while mortal, gave to others, in some way, spiritual gifts in place of miracles, and afterwards perfectly, when he had been raised from the dead, gave them; which no one else can do, even if he can perhaps work miracles by God's permission, unless he is God or sent by him.

units.la: Inter opera Deo propria, est etiam nostra redemtio, quæ Christo non tributa solum, sed & singulari modo propria, eum arguit esse Deum. Quod nos redemit, clarum est, ex innumeris*Scripturæ locis, atque ex substantia religionis Christianæ, quæ potissimum in hoc consistit, quod Christum agnoscimus, credimus, colimus Redemtorem nostrum. Jam autem redimere aliquem a peccato, & miseria omni peccato debita, expiare, & propitiare Deo, non est hominis, neque creaturæ alicujus. Pfalm. xlix. 8, 9. 1 Pet. 1. 18, 19. sed opus Dei, unde passim Deo attribuitur, & ei adjungitur. Tit. ii. 13. exspectantes manifestationem gloriæ magni Dei, addito articulo, τοῦ [?] μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Act. xx. 28. pascere Ecclesiam Dei, quam redemit proprio sanguine. 1 Ioann. 1. 7. Sanguis Iesu Christi Filii ejus purgat nos ab omni peccato. Matth. 1. 21. Vocabis nomen ejus Iesum: ipse enim servabit populum suum a peccatis ipsorum. 23. Et vocabunt nomen ejus Immanuel, quod exponitur, Deus nobiscum. Deo adscribitur opus redemtionis, ut ei proprium & peculiare. Et quod huc spectat, remissio peccatorum Christo convenit, opus adeo divinum, ut & Deus suum hoc solemniter proclamet, Jef. xliii. 25. ego ego ipse sum ille [?]אנכי אנכי הוא qui delco transgressiones tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Quare Judæi hinc blasphemiam Christo intentabant, quod hominibus peccata remitteret, gnari hoc solius Dei esse. Matth. ix. 2, 3. Rom. viii. 33, 34. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus justificat. Quis damnat? Christus mortuus pro iis est &c. Jef. i. 8. Denique salvatio Dei opus est, & Christo ita proprium, ut hinc Servator & Iesus appelletur. Salvatorem esse Christum Christianus nemo negat; atque hoc Dei opus esse, nemo etiam inficiari potest, ab eo solo exspectandum, dandumque. Domine exfpectio salutare tuum. Genef. xlix. 18. Luc. i. 47. & exultavit spiritus meus in Deo salvatore meo. Tit. ii. 13. Unde Christum dicunt, Actor. iii. 15. τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς ζωῆς. Hebr. ii. 10. τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας. Denique cap. xii. 2. ἀρχηγὸν [?] καὶ τελειωτὴν.
units.tr: Among the works proper to God is also our redemption, which is not only ascribed to Christ but, in a singular way, belongs to him as proper, and this proves that he is God. That he redeemed us is clear from countless places of Scripture, and from the substance of the Christian religion, which consists chiefly in this, that we acknowledge, believe in and worship Christ as our Redeemer. But to redeem someone from sin and from all the misery owed to sin, to make expiation and to propitiate God, is not the work of a man or of any creature. Ps. 49:8, 9; 1 Pet. 1:18, 19. It is the work of God, and therefore it is everywhere attributed to God and joined to him. Titus 2:13: looking for the manifestation of the glory of the great God, with the article added, τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ [of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ]. Acts 20:28: to feed the Church of God, which he redeemed with his own blood. 1 John 1:7: The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin. Matt. 1:21: You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins. v. 23: And they shall call his name Immanuel, which means, God with us. The work of redemption is ascribed to God as his own and peculiar. And what bears on this, the forgiveness of sins, belongs to Christ, a work so divine that God himself solemnly proclaims it as his own, Isa. 43:25: I, I am he [אנכי אנכי הוא] who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and will not remember your sins. Therefore the Jews charged Christ with blasphemy on this ground, that he forgave men's sins, knowing that this belongs to God alone. Matt. 9:2, 3; Rom. 8:33, 34: Who shall accuse God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died for them, etc. Isa. 1:8. Finally, salvation is the work of God, and it is so proper to Christ that he is therefore called Saviour and Jesus. No Christian denies that Christ is the Saviour, and no one can deny that this is the work of God, to be expected and given from him alone: Lord, I wait for your salvation. Gen. 49:18. Luke 1:47: and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour. Titus 2:13. Hence they call Christ, Acts 3:15, τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς ζωῆς [the Prince of life]; Heb. 2:10, τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας [the author of salvation]; and finally Heb. 12:2, ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν [the author and finisher].

units.la: Quartum argumentum, vel argumentorum classis ad probandam divinam in Christo naturam, sumitur ex cultu divino, seu religioso, Christo debito. sic: Qui cultu divino & religioso colitur, is est Deus: sed Christus cultu divino & religioso colitur: ergo. Ex Adversariis alii negant majorem; minorem alii. Socinus, & qui cum eo faciunt, atque Episcopius, negant majorem, putantque religiosum cultum quidem deferri etiam alicui, quamvis non sit natura Deus: Deumque honorum istum communicare quoque alteri, & ex hac causa Christum adorari vel solâ, quod Socinani, vel etiam, quod Remonstrantes censent. In coetu Anti-Trinitariorum Franciscus Davidis, Christianus Francken, aliiq; istius commatis, minorem syllogismi negarunt propositionem, & Christum putarunt invocari non debere, ideo quod non est Deus. Quæ paulo plenius exponenda veniunt. Socinus agnoscit, in argumento hoc à cultu seu invocatione Christi sumto magnam causæ nostræ vim sitam, quin, uti temere loquitur, fere unicam. In Epist. iii. ad Radecium, pag. 143. Video nihil hodie edi posse in totâ Christiana religione majoris momenti, quam hoc sit, demonstratio videlicet, quod Christo, licet rei creatæ, tamen invocatio & adoratio, seu cultus divinus conveniat, &c. si enim hoc demonstratum fuerit, concident omnes Trinitariorum munitiones, quæ revera uno hoc fundamento adhuc nituntur, quod Christo adoratio & invocatio conveniat, quæ solius Dei illius altissimi omni ratione videtur esse propria. Non certe vel uno hoc fundamento nituntur nostræ munitiones; vel hoc, haud magis quam reliqua, ab Adversariis subrui ac everti potest. Sed satis à sociis suis Francisco Davidis, & Christiano Francken hac in parte Socinus prostratus fuit ac debellatus, videlicet quod ad illam propositionem, quam hic facit suam. Errarunt quidem isti in eo, quod Christum negarent invocandum : sed non in hoc, quod dicerent, rei creatae invocationem & adorationem seu cultum divinum non convenire. Imo hic convenienter Theologiae, & sanae rationi loquuti fuerunt, iisque argumentis Socinum adorti, quibus solvendis plane impar, nec illis, neque suorum aliis satisfecit. Christianus Francken, in Disp. de adoratione Christi, pag. 35. Nec divina ista potestas est adoratione religiosa digna, nisi eam ad divinam usque natu-ram extendamus, quemadmodum faciunt Trinitarii, existimantes indissolubili nexu colliga-tam esse divinam potestatem cum essentia & adoratione divina, verumque esse idololatram qui adorationem a Deitate sejungit. Distinguit Socinus passim inter adorationem, & invocatio-nem: illam pro corporis vel animi inclinatione, & reverentia modo aliqua, ut tamen nihil petas, accipit? hanc, ubi alterius etiam imploras opem. Illam Christo nos debere, istam licere tantum tribuere, affirmat. Quam differentiam ita exponit Smalcius, lib. de divinit. Christi, cap. xxiv. Hujus fidei in Iesum Christum, consequentia quaedam rursus sunt, divina, quae ei debetur, adoratio & invocatio: quae quidem ita inter se differunt, ut adoratio sit, cum quis alicui corpus aut animum reverenter inclinat; & coram eo venerabun-dus procumbit, etiamsi nihil petat, quemadmodum legimus angelos Christum adorare, vel genua ei flectere, quod idem est, qui tamen eum non invocant. Invocatio vero est, cum quis in ne-cessitate constitutus, ut aliquid percupiens, confidenter alienam opem & benignitatem implorat. Illam, nempe adorationem, debet Iesu Christo omne genu coelestium, terrestrium, & inferiorum, hoc est, omnes angeli, tam boni, quam mali, omnes homines tam vivi quam mortui, & quicun-que vivorum hominum non semper adorat Iesum Christum, is procul dubio Christianus esse de-sistit. Socinus, Epist. iii. ad Radecium, pag. 151. Hic primum adorationem cum invocatione confundis, quod tamen fieri non debet, cum utriusque sit diversa quaedam ratio; adeo ut ego, quamvis nihil prorsus dubitem, praeceptum extare de Christo invocando, & etiamsi non extaret, tamen eum omnino adorari a nobis debere, non idem tamen existimem de eodem invocando, cum videlicet invocatio pro ipsa opis implorations, & directione precum nostrarum accipitur. Hic enim statuo, id quidem merito a nobis fieri posse, id est, posse nos jure ad ipsum Christum preces nostras dirigere, ejusque opem nominatim implorare; nihil tamen esse, quod nos id facere cogat.
units.tr: The fourth argument, or class of arguments, for proving the divine nature in Christ is drawn from the divine, or religious, worship owed to Christ. It runs thus: whatever is worshipped with divine and religious worship is God; but Christ is worshipped with divine and religious worship; therefore Christ is God. Among our opponents some deny the major premise, others the minor. Socinus, and those who agree with him, and Episcopius deny the major, and think that religious worship may be paid even to someone who is not by nature God, and that God may communicate this honour to another; on this ground they hold that Christ may be adored, either only as the Socinians hold, or also as the Remonstrants think. Within the company of the Anti-Trinitarians, Francis Davidis, Christian Francken, and others of that sort denied the minor premise, and held that Christ ought not to be invoked, because he is not God. These points must be set out somewhat more fully. Socinus acknowledges that the strength of our cause lies to a great degree in this argument, drawn from the worship or invocation of Christ, indeed, as he rashly puts it, almost its only strength. In his third letter to Radecius, p. 143: "I see that nothing of greater importance can be put forward today in the whole Christian religion than this, namely the demonstration that divine worship, namely invocation and adoration, belongs to Christ, although he is a created thing. For if this is demonstrated, all the fortifications of the Trinitarians will fall, which in truth still rest on this one foundation alone, that adoration and invocation belong to Christ, which seems in every way to be proper to the one most high God alone." Our fortifications certainly do not rest on this one foundation alone, and they cannot be undermined and overthrown by the opponents on this point any more than on the rest. But Socinus was sufficiently overthrown and defeated on this point by his own associates, Francis Davidis and Christian Francken, namely with respect to that proposition which he makes his own. These men did indeed err in that they denied that Christ ought to be invoked; but not in saying that invocation and adoration, that is, divine worship, do not belong to a created thing. Indeed, in this they spoke in agreement with theology and sound reason, and they attacked Socinus with arguments to which he was utterly unequal, and he satisfied neither them nor others of his party with a solution. Christian Francken, in his disputation on the adoration of Christ, p. 35: "Nor is that divine power worthy of religious adoration, unless we extend it even to the divine nature, as the Trinitarians do, who think that the divine power is bound by an indissoluble tie to the divine essence and to divine adoration, and that whoever separates adoration from the Deity is truly an idolater." Socinus everywhere distinguishes between adoration and invocation: he takes the former as an inclination of body or mind, a reverence of some kind, which nonetheless asks for nothing; the latter as when you also implore another's help. He affirms that we owe the former to Christ, while the latter may be given to him only as permitted. Smalcius explains this difference thus, in his book on the divinity of Christ, ch. 24: "Along with this faith in Jesus Christ there follow certain further things, namely the divine adoration and invocation which are due to him. These differ from each other in this way: adoration is when someone bows his body or mind reverently to another, and falls down humbly before him, even if he asks nothing, just as we read that the angels worshipped Christ, or bowed their knees to him, which is the same thing; yet they did not invoke him. Invocation, however, is when someone, placed in need and wishing eagerly for something, confidently implores another's help and kindness. The adoration, namely, every knee of the heavenly, the earthly and the under-earthly owes to Jesus Christ, that is, all angels, both good and evil, all men both living and dead; and whoever among living men does not always adore Jesus Christ, he without doubt ceases to be a Christian." Socinus, third letter to Radecius, p. 151: "Here you first confuse adoration with invocation, which ought not to be done, since each has a different nature of its own; so that I, although I have no doubt at all that there is a command to invoke Christ, and even if there were no such command, that he must altogether be adored by us, yet do not think the same about invoking him, since invocation is taken for the very imploradditon of help and the directing of our prayers. For here I hold that this may indeed rightly be done by us, that is, that we may lawfully direct our prayers to Christ himself and implore his help by name; yet there is nothing that compels us to do so."

units.la: Distinctio ergo Sociniana inter adorationem,& invocationem in his consistit. i. Ut adoratio significet modo reverentem nostri coram aliquo inclinationem; invocatio, ejus insuper religiosam compellationem, opisque implorationem. ii. Quod illa ab omnibus, Angelis etiam praestanda sit; haec a solis hominibus, qui Christi ope egeant. iii. Illa praecepta sit, & necessaria; haec non praecepta, sed licita modo in se atque conve-niens. iv. Illius fundamentum in Christo, majestas; hujus sit, potentia. Saltem adoran-dum, invocandumque, & religioso cultu prosequendum Christum, Socinus & Socinia-ni non negant, non autem per aut propter naturam in Christo divinam, sed ex gra-tuito dono & communicatione, qua ei Pater istius cultus copiam fecit, concessitque, ut, quamvis non verus natura Deus, sic tamen etiam coleretur, ut subordinatus & inferior Deo, tanquam secundaria causa, & a primaria plane pendens, inquit Socinus, contra Franc. Davidis pag. 193. & non secus atque ipsi Deo confidere jubet Smalcius, de divinit. pag. 140. Contra autem Franciscus Davidis, Christianus Francken, Bud-naeus, aliique similes impudenti ore negabant Christum religiose adorandum, aut in-vocandum esse, ideo quod eum non haberent pro Deo. In quo si de majore pro-positione solum actum fuisset: qui non est Deus, religiose coli aut invocari non po-test, nec debet, stabant quidem illi; at assumentes, vel Christum Deum non esse, aut ejus simpliciter negando adorationem, & se, & Christianam religionem turpissime prostituerunt. Unde Socinus, & sui illos pro Christianis agnoscere renuunt. Ille in Catechesi, pag. 32. Quid igitur censes de iis, qui ista Christo non tribuunt? Resp. Censeo, illos non esse Christianos, quippe qui re ipsa Christum non habeant, & Iesum esse Christum, licet fortasse aperte verbis non audeant, re tamen ipsa omnino negent. Sic & Catechesis Racovien-sis, pag. 177. Volkelius, pag. 201. Theophilus Nicolai, de Ecclesia, pag. 81. Quod Budnaeum & Franciscum Davidis nostrae sectae homines appellat, in eo affectui potius indulgere, quam veritati patrocinari videtur. Illi enim cum nostris perpetua fuit pugna, & tandem etiam excommunicatus, diem suum obiit. Hic vero a nostris plane pro impio habitus fuit, & hodie nos pro fratre nostro neminem eorum agnoscimus, qui sententiam Francisci Davidis impiam sectetur vel defendat. De quibus prolixe dicimus, in Apparatu ad Controvers. & Disput. Socin. pag. 31.44. &c. Uti negata Christi Deitate, perrexerunt ad negandam Christi adorationem, ita hoc posito, jam non Christum aliter consideraverunt quam alium quem ex hominum vel Doctorum coetu, nihilque in universa Christi religione intactum reliquerunt, quod non plane inverterent. Quod aliter fieri nequit, quin transformato Christo, abolerent omnem quoque ejus religionem. Mirum, quibus hoc factum gradibus, & quam tandem illi homines nobis cuderint Theologiam. Eam hic exhibere ob oculos, prout ex illorum scriptis habere potui, haud gravabor. Namque eo delata nunc est nostra disputatio.
units.tr: The Socinian distinction, then, between adoration and invocation consists in these points: (i) adoration signifies only a reverent inclination of oneself before someone, whereas invocation adds to this a religious addressing of him and an imploring of his help; (ii) adoration is to be rendered by all, even angels, whereas invocation is to be made only by men who need Christ's help; (iii) adoration is a command and necessary, whereas invocation is not commanded but merely permitted, lawful in itself and fitting; (iv) the foundation of adoration in Christ is his majesty, while that of invocation is his power. Socinus and the Socinians do not deny that Christ is to be adored, invoked and honoured with religious worship, at least in some measure; but not through or on account of the divine nature in Christ. It is from the free gift and communication by which the Father granted and conceded to him the fullness of this worship, so that, although he is not by nature true God, he may nevertheless be worshipped as one subordinate and inferior to God, as a secondary cause wholly dependent on the primary cause, as Socinus says against Francis Davidis, p. 193; and Smalcius bids us to trust in him "no differently than in God himself," in his book on the divinity, p. 140. On the other hand, Francis Davidis, Christian Francken, Budnaeus, and others like them denied with shameless mouths that Christ is to be adored or invoked with religious worship, because they did not hold him to be God. If the discussion had turned only on the major premise, namely that what is not God cannot and ought not to be worshipped or invoked with religion, they would have stood firm; but in assuming either that Christ is not God, or in simply denying that he is to be adored, they have shamefully prostituted both themselves and the Christian religion. Hence Socinus and his followers refuse to acknowledge them as Christians. He, in his Catechism, p. 32: "What then do you think of those who do not attribute these things to Christ?" Answer: "I think they are not Christians, since in fact they do not have Christ, and although perhaps they do not dare to say openly in words that Jesus is Christ, yet in actual fact they wholly deny it." So also the Racovian Catechism, p. 177; Volkelius, p. 201; Theophilus Nicolai, on the Church, p. 81: "That he calls Budnaeus and Francis Davidis men of our sect seems rather to indulge a feeling than to defend the truth. For Budnaeus was in constant conflict with our people, and at last, excommunicated, he died. Francis Davidis, indeed, was regarded by our people as altogether impious, and today we acknowledge none of them as our brother who follows or defends the impious opinion of Francis Davidis." Concerning these men we speak at length in our Apparatus to the Controversies and Disputations of the Socinians, p. 31, 44, etc. Just as, once the deity of Christ was denied, they went on to deny Christ's adoration, so, with this granted, they no longer regarded Christ otherwise than as any other man or teacher from the company of men, and they left nothing in the whole Christian religion untouched that they did not utterly overturn. This cannot happen otherwise than that, Christ having been transformed, they should also abolish all his religion. It is remarkable by what steps this came about, and what kind of theology those men have forged for us. I will not hesitate to set it before our eyes, as far as I have been able to gather it from their writings, for to that point our disputation has now come.

units.la: 1. Trinitate de throno deturbata, II. facile fuit Christi impugnare Deitatem. Socinus, in Disput. de adorat. Christi, contra Franciscum Davidis, pag. 128. tu ipse in iis scriptis, quae hactenus communiter cum aliis edidisti, satis aperte adversus Trinitarios, &c. Atque de Christo Franciscus Davidis, in Thesibus; & in suis Antithesibus Socinus, eodem modo loquuntur: Homo ille Iesus Nazarenus, qui Christus appellatur. III. Franciscus Davidis ulterius Christum nec dici Deum sustinebat, Thes. 8. Non igitur Deus amplius dici potest, quemadmodum fortasse, cum in mundo versaretur, poterat ratione officii. Nam ab officio, ut dictum est, nunc plane cessat. IV. Neque invocandum Christum, docebat. pag. 172. Quandocumque vocabulum invocationis pro cultu & fiducia accipitur, qua petimus a Deo bona corporalia & spiritualia, Christo invocationem in Scriptura sacra attributam fuisse non legitur. 2. Christus invocari nec debet nec potest. v. Ut qui, ex ejus sententia, nos non possset juvare aliqua in re. Unde pag. 182. blasphemae dicit: non perperam fingitur in Alchorano, Christum suis cultoribus opem ferre non posse. vi. Christi doctrinam negabat esse authenticam. pag. 184. Homo ille Iesus Nazarenus, qui Christus appellatur, non per spiritum propheticum, sed tantummodo per Spiritum Sanctum locutus est. vii. Quare doctrinam Christi ad Mosaicam examinari volebat, ut ea inferiorem & minus certam. Ibidem: Hinc fit, ut illius & Apostolorum ejus verba, ad Mosaicae legis, & aliorum propheticorum oraculorum normam expendenda sint. Et si quid vel contrarium, vel diversum ab his in illis reperitur, aut reperiri videtur, id aut rejiciendum, aut certe ita interpretandum sit, ut cum Mosis & prophetarum doctrina plane consentiat, quae sola morum, vitae, & divini cultus regula nobis esse debet. viii. Observandam legem Mosis, in omnibus, etiam caeremoniatibus. Ibidem: Nam inter vetus per Mosem, & novum per Christum percussum foedus, nulla penitus vel in doctrina (ea praesertim quae ad mores spectat) vel in divinis promissionibus differentia statuenda est, sed in hoc tantummodo differre dicenda sunt, quod in foedere litterae, in novo vero spiritus ministerium fuit, adeo ut caeteroquin per hoc illud nec antiquatum, nec immutatum ullo modo, sed confirmatum dici debeat. Et Socinus ideo, in Disput. de Adorat. Christi, adversus Erasmum Johannis, dixit, Alioqui (quod tamen aliqui ex vobis sen-tiunt) ceremonialia (quae vocant) Mosaicae legis praecepta, adhuc inviolabilia permanerent, cum nec Deus Pater de coelo, nec Christus ipse ore proprio ea unquam abrogaverit, sed tantummodo ab Apostolis, & discipulis Iesu Christi, praesertim vero a Paulo id factum fuerit. IX. Nec credere in Christum ei aliud sonabat, quam quod olim credere in Mosem. pag. 180. In Christum credere, & Christo confidere, hodie nihil plus continet, quam olim continuerunt credere in Mosem, ut Israelitae fecerunt, quod attinet ad utriusque personam. X. Dubitabat an Christus sacerdos noster esset, de quo ita, pag. 190. Porro ejus sacerdotium (si modo re vera sacerdos unquam fuit) tunc re ipsa finem habuit, cum in cruce exspiravit, nec alia ratione ejus oblatio nobis prodest, aut prodesse potest, quam propter ipsius oblationis, quamvis jam transactae, efficaciam, quae perpetuo durat, propter quod etiam ejus sacerdotium perpetuum, & ipse sacerdos in aeternum esse dicitur, & adhuc peccata nostra eum expiare alicubi fortasse scriptum est. XI. Faciebat eum regem terrenum, & simile ejus regnum. pag. 186. ex omnium Prophetarum oraculis certum, Christum illum a Deo promissum, nullum aliud regnum quam terrenum, & quale supra dictum est, habiturum. ut ejusmodi regnum statim haberet missus fuit in mundum Iesus a Deo, &c. XII. Judaeos, inquiebat, Christum regem, iustudque ejus regnum repudiasse; quodque Deus eum ideo e terra in coelum sustulisset, ibique quiescere jussisset, donec, sumta de inimicis vindicta, Christum remitteret in orbem, intermissum regnum Jerosolymis meliori omine scilicet instituturum. Christus ergo ei jam in coelis securus & otiosus sedet sub protectione divina, nullam curam Ecclesiae gerens aut regimen. pag. 174. Christus cum in terris fuit, curam gessit suae Ecclesiae: At postquam hinc abiit, eam curam Patri commendavit, quam denuo usque ad praefinitum tempus suscipiet. pag. 176. Ex quo apparet, Christum ad dexteram Dei sedere, &c. nihil aliud esse, quam tutum & firmum sub protectione Dei expectare, ut sibi a Deo subjiciantur omnes inimici. quod Christus nunc habeat clavem Davidis, & claves mortis & inferni, hoc nihil amplius illi tribuit, quam Petro & aliis sanctis mortuis hoc tempore tribuant, quod aliquando habuerint claves regni coelorum. pag. 186. Interim Iesus est quidem Christus, sive rex populi Dei, sed designatione tantum, cum ex omnium prophetarum oraculis certum sit, Christum illum a Deo promissum, nullum aliud regnum quam terrenum, quale supra dictum est, habiturum. Ut hujusmodi regnum statim haberet missus fuit Iesus a Deo in mundum, sed quia noluerunt eum Judaei, quibus promissus fuerat & quorum rex esse debebat, recipere, postquam ab ipsis contra Dei propositum interemptus fuit, sustulit eum Deus ab illis, & in locum translulit, ubi tuto in Dei protectione quiescit. Hoc siquidem est cum sedere vel esse in coelis, a dexteris sive in dextera Dei. Itaque ibi expectat, donec subjiciantur illi a Deo omnes inimici ejus, & ita regnum sibi promissum habeat, nihil interea habet. XIII. Scilicet rediens ex coelo Christus regnum in hoc mundo terrenum Jerosolymis in Judaeos erecturus est. pag. 186. Praesertim cum novum illud foedus vere hactenus ad tempus tantum, idque perbreve, exiterit, id est, usque ad Hierosolymae excidium, nec postea locum, nisi ex parte aliqua habuerit, aut habiturum sit, donec Iesus iterum ad nos redierit, & in hoc mundo, in ipsa urbe Hierosolyma instaurata, super carnali populo Iacob, ut ceteri reges terrae solent, justissime tamen & sanctissime regnaverit.
units.tr: 1. With the Trinity cast down from its throne, II. it was easy to assail the deity of Christ. Socinus, in the Disputation on the Worship of Christ, against Franciscus Davidis, p. 128: you yourself, in those writings which you have hitherto published jointly with others, speak quite openly against the Trinitarians, etc. And concerning Christ, Franciscus Davidis in his Theses, and Socinus in his Antitheses, speak in the same way: that man Jesus of Nazareth, who is called Christ. III. Franciscus Davidis further would not allow that Christ be called God, Thes. 8: Therefore God can no longer be said to be what he perhaps could be, by reason of his office, while he was in the world. For he has now altogether ceased from that office, as has been said. IV. He also taught that Christ is not to be invoked, p. 172: Whenever the word invocation is taken for worship and trust, by which we ask God for good things, bodily and spiritual, it is not read that invocation was attributed to Christ in holy Scripture. 2. Christ neither ought nor can be invoked. V. For, on his view, he could not help us in any matter. Hence on p. 182 he says blasphemously: It is not wrongly imagined in the Alcoran that Christ is unable to bring help to his worshippers. VI. He denied that the doctrine of Christ was authentic, p. 184: That man Jesus of Nazareth, who is called Christ, spoke not by the prophetic Spirit, but only by the Holy Spirit. VII. Therefore he wished the doctrine of Christ to be examined by the Mosaic, so that it might be judged inferior and less certain. In the same place: Hence it follows that his words and those of his apostles are to be weighed by the rule of the Mosaic law and of the other prophetic oracles. And if anything is found, or seems to be found, in them that is contrary or different to these, it is either to be rejected or at least so interpreted that it wholly agrees with the teaching of Moses and the prophets, which alone ought to be for us the rule of morals, of life, and of divine worship. VIII. The law of Moses is to be observed in all things, even the ceremonial ones. In the same place: For between the old covenant struck through Moses and the new struck through Christ, no difference at all is to be established, either in doctrine (especially that which concerns morals) or in the divine promises; but they are to be said to differ only in this, that in the old covenant there was the letter, and in the new the ministry of the Spirit, so that by this the former is in no way said to be abolished or changed, but rather to be confirmed. And so Socinus, in the Disputation on the Worship of Christ, against Erasmus Johannis, said: Otherwise (which nonetheless some of you hold) the ceremonial precepts of the Mosaic law, as they are called, would remain still inviolable, since neither God the Father from heaven nor Christ himself with his own mouth ever abrogated them, but this was done only by the apostles and disciples of Jesus Christ, and especially by Paul. IX. Nor did believing in Christ mean to him anything other than believing in Moses once did. P. 180: To believe in Christ and to trust in Christ today contains no more, as far as the person of either is concerned, than what the Israelites once contained when they believed in Moses. X. He doubted whether Christ was our priest, of which he says, p. 190: Moreover, his priesthood (if indeed he was ever really a priest) then in fact came to an end when he breathed his last on the cross; nor does his oblation benefit us, or can it benefit us, in any other way than by the efficacy of that oblation, though already past, which lasts for ever; on account of which his priesthood is also said to be perpetual, and he himself a priest for ever; and it is perhaps written somewhere that he still expiates our sins. XI. He made him an earthly king, and his kingdom likewise. P. 186: It is certain from the oracles of all the prophets that Christ, promised by God, would have no other kingdom than an earthly one, and such as has been described above. So that Jesus was sent by God into the world to have such a kingdom at once, etc. XII. He said that the Jews had rejected Christ as king and his just kingdom; and that God had therefore taken him up from the earth into heaven and ordered him to rest there until, having taken vengeance on his enemies, he should send him back into the world, to establish at Jerusalem the kingdom that had been interrupted, under better auspices, of course. Christ therefore now sits in heaven idle and at ease, under divine protection, bearing no care or government of the Church. P. 174: While Christ was on earth he took care of his Church; but after he departed hence he committed that care to the Father, which he will take up again at the appointed time. P. 176: From this it appears that Christ's sitting at the right hand of God, etc., is nothing other than to wait safely and firmly under the protection of God until all his enemies are made subject to him by God. That Christ now has the key of David and the keys of death and of hell, this attributes to him no more than the saints who are dead attribute to Peter and others at this time, namely that they once held the keys of the kingdom of heaven. P. 186: Meanwhile Jesus is indeed Christ, that is, king of the people of God, but only by designation, since it is certain from the oracles of all the prophets that Christ, promised by God, would have no other kingdom than an earthly one, such as has been described above. So that such a kingdom he might have at once, Jesus was sent by God into the world; but because the Jews, to whom he had been promised and of whom he ought to be king, were unwilling to receive him, after he was put to death by them against God's purpose, God took him away from them and transferred him to a place where he rests safely in God's protection. For this is what it is to sit or be in heaven, at or in the right hand of God. So there he waits until all his enemies are made subject to him by God, and so he will have the kingdom promised to him; meanwhile he has nothing. XIII. Clearly, Christ, returning from heaven, is to set up in this world an earthly kingdom among the Jews at Jerusalem. P. 186: Especially since that new covenant has truly up to now existed only for a time, and that a very short one, that is, until the destruction of Jerusalem, and afterwards it has had, or will have, no place except in some part, until Jesus returns to us again and reigns in this world, in the city of Jerusalem restored, over the carnal people of Jacob, as the other kings of the earth do, yet most justly and most holily.

units.la: Habes doctrinae & religionis istorum hominum systema. De quo videri etiam poterit Possevinus, lib. de Atheismis haereticorum, cap. xxx. horrendum sane, quod in Christianismo quis audiat. Sed eo prolabi homines oportuit, qui semel constituerunt veritatem & Deum tormentis impetere, & deturbare throno. Veteres Valentinianorum, Ebionitarum, & Marcionitarum haereses recoctas puta, atque ex Judaismo & Muhammedismo conflatam professæ impietatis doctrinam. Nempe quibus leve fuit maximos fidei articulos evertere, nihil porro sani relinquere & habere, justa ultione, quâ solet veritatis suæ illusæ destitutæque pœnam exposcere, Deus voluit. Neque opus est ut illa refutatione dignemur ulla, quæ cognita Christianus execrari, quam refutare malit. Satis Socino negotii fuit illis cum hominibus, facile perspicienti quantum sibi hinc periculum crearetur, quod illos à partibus suis haberet, vel quod sui in ejusmodi insanias atq; blasphemias haud difficulter prolaberetur. Mortis Fr. Davi-dis (nam in carcerem à Principe Transylvaniæ conjectus, mœrore atq; phrenesi, vel quâ alia ratione misere extinctus fuit) causam & invidiam multi Socino adscripserunt. De quo alibi diximus: hæc vero occasione controversiæ de adorando & invocando Christo.
units.tr: You have here the system of doctrine and religion of these men. On it Possevino may also be consulted, in his book on the atheisms of heretics, chapter 30. It is indeed a horrible thing to hear within Christianity. But these men had to come to this, having once resolved to assail truth and God with torments and to cast them down from their throne. You may think of them as the old heresies of the Valentinians, Ebionites and Marcionites revived, and a doctrine of professed impiety fused together out of Judaism and Muhammadanism. For God willed that it should be a light matter for them to overturn the greatest articles of faith and to retain nothing sound thereafter, as a just retribution, by which he is wont to exact punishment for the mocking and desertion of his truth. Nor is there any need that we deign to refute these views, which a Christian, once he knows them, would rather execrate than refute. Socinus had trouble enough with these men, since he easily perceived how much danger was being created for himself, both because he had them on his side and because his own followers might not too easily slip into such madness and blasphemy. The death of Franciscus Davidis (for he was thrown into prison by the Prince of Transylvania and wretchedly died of grief and frenzy, or by some other means) was ascribed by many to Socinus as its cause and as the object of odium. Of this we have spoken elsewhere; but these matters arise on the occasion of the controversy about worshipping and invoking Christ.

units.la: Cum Socino super adoratione Christo communicatâ paria facit Simon Episcopius, Instit. lib. iv.[?] v. sect. ii. cap. xxxv. dum Christum non propter essentiæ ὁμοούσιον[?], & eandem cum Patre naturam adorari, neque necesse hoc esse ut qui adoretur summus omnium Deus sit, contendit. Verùm adorationem facit duplicem, aliam, quæ Deo, propter divinam suam naturam; aliam, quæ etiam creaturis, ex Dei voluntate, ex gratia & donatione libera, datur. Et hac Christum, etiam quatenus filius hominis est, & quidem ex gratia, id est, ex liberalitate & magnificentia gratiosa, adorandum ait. Neque Christum solum hac ratione, sed etiam Angelos sub V. T. Deo sic volente, adoratos fuisse. Quod tamen non licuerit sub Testam. Novo. Unde, quod ridiculum, Iohannem, ait, primo Angelum adorasse, ex ritu scilicet V. adhuc Testam. quod nesciret morem istum jam tunc abrogatum. Hæc ejus verba: Sed vero alia ratio est veteris, alia Nov. Testam. sub isto, Deum seu voluisse, seu permisisse adorari Angelos suos, vel Angelum[?] aliquem suum aliquando, quando videlicet is personam Dei repræsentabat, & ad speciale aliquod ministerium nomine & autoritate Dei exequendum destinatus erat, ex nonnullis locis liquet. Exod. iii. 5. & xxiii. 21. Jos. v. 14. 15. Jud. xiii. 19. &c. Sed in Novo Testamento id non licere manifestum est ex Apoc. xix. 10. & xxii. 8. 9. Quod tamen Ioannes Angelum ad se missum prima instantia pronus adorasse dicatur, id videri potest ex ignorantia profectum, quod morem sub Veteri Testamento usitatum, jam tum abrogatum esse nesciret, quod vero monitus tum ab Angelo, idem iterum nihilominus deinde non multo post fecisse legatur, id ex infirmitate, inadvertentia, aut subita quadam animi perturbatione, quæ vel ex Majestate & splendore Angeli, vel eo quod afferebat nuntio, oriri potuit, profectum videri debet. Resp. i. Vel Iohannes non eo se animo projiciebat ad Angeli pedes, ut eum religiose adora-ret, sed confessernatus adorationem προσκύνησιν[?] adhibuit civilem, quam externo ritu religiosæ similem Angelus non tam increpare, quam prævenire voluit & præpedire à peccato. ii. Vel, si religiose adorare intendit, peccavit. Quod verba tamen non necessario efflagitant. iii. Interim omnem religiosi cultus speciem à se amovit Angelus. iv. Quâ ex causa? non quod id olim quidem concessum, hoc vero tempore prohibitum esset. Nam i. istam causam nec allegat, nec indicat. ii. Sed aliam, quia Angelus esset. Argumento, non ex tempore, sed naturâ suâ sumto, & officio. Quod nullum fuisset, si ad id usque temporis id licuisset & propter istam causam. Quin satis significavit, propter id nefas esse quempiam adorare. iii. Alteram addit causam, positive adorationem suo vero adsignantem objecto, Deum adora. Cujus hæc vis est, non se, non alium, sed solum Deum adorandum, neque ulli præter ipsum fas esse honorem istum attribuere. iv. Proba, sub V. T. licuisse Angelum adorare, & non sub Novo. Vel quare, hoc si concessum unquam, non etiam hodie? Vel si nunc nefas, olim licuit? Ubi hoc Deus aut concessit, aut nunc vetuit? v. Contrà hoc sibi soli semper Deus proprium habuit voluitque, religiose coli atque adorari. Et Angelum, qui legitur in V. T. aliquando adoratus, Deum intelligi, non creaturam, haud ignoravit Episcopius: idque discutere debuisset primo, quam praeterire leviter, & in suam hypothesin torquere. vi. Communicare adorationem si Deus potuit soleatque, quare non in N. T. aeque ac in Veteri? Vel quare jam Angeli eo privilegio exuti & gratia? Contrà vero sola Dei natura atque ὑπεροχὴ[?] fundamentum cultus est, atque etiam esse potest, uti plenius nunc exponemus. Argumentum nostrum fuit: Cui competit divinus cultus, is est Deus: Christo competit divinus cultus: ergo. Negant majorem Socinians, & Remonstrantes. Deum autem nos haud alium agnoscimus, quam unum verum Deum. Minorem Syllogismi negavit Franciscus Davidis, & suae fortis homines. Ut in Minoris probatione nobis minus negotii haereat. Confirmanda tamen breviter, eo magis, quo hinc etiam Major elucidatur, probaturque.
units.tr: Simon Episcopius takes the same line as Socinus on whether Christ may be worshipped with divine worship. In his Institutes, book 4 (?), section 5 (?), chapter 35 (Instit. lib. iv.[?] v. sect. ii. cap. xxxv.), he contends that Christ is not to be adored on account of consubstantiality [ὁμοούσιον] and sharing the same nature with the Father, and that it is not necessary for the one who is adored to be the supreme God of all. He makes worship twofold: one kind is due to God alone, on account of his divine nature; the other is also given to creatures, by God's will, through grace and free gift. By this second kind, he says, Christ is to be adored even as the Son of man, and indeed by grace, that is, by generous and gracious magnificence. He adds that not only Christ was worshipped in this way, but also angels under the Old Testament, with God so willing. This, however, has not been permitted under the New Testament. Hence, he says (and this is ridiculous), John first worshipped the angel, following the custom of the Old Testament, because he did not know that this custom had already been abrogated. These are his words: But the situation under the Old Testament is one thing, and under the New Testament another. That God either willed or permitted his angels to be worshipped, or some angel of his at some time, namely when he represented the person of God and was sent to carry out some special ministry in the name and authority of God, is clear from some passages: Exod. 3:5 and 23:21; Josh. 5:14, 15; Judg. 13:19, etc. But that this is not allowed under the New Testament is plain from Rev. 19:10 and 22:8, 9. That John is said to have fallen prostrate and worshipped the angel sent to him at first instance may be seen to have arisen from ignorance, because he did not know that the custom used under the Old Testament had already been abrogated. But that, when he was then warned by the angel, he is nevertheless read to have done the same again not long afterwards, should be seen as arising from weakness, inattention, or some sudden disturbance of mind, which could have come either from the majesty and splendour of the angel or from the message he brought. Our reply: (i) Either John did not throw himself at the angel's feet with the intention of worshipping him religiously, but, being accustomed, offered a civil reverence [προσκύνησιν], which an angel wished to forestall and prevent from becoming sin, rather than rebuke, since it resembled religious worship in its outward form. (ii) Or, if he intended to worship religiously, he sinned. Yet the words do not necessarily demand this. (iii) Meanwhile, the angel removed every appearance of religious worship from himself. (iv) For what reason? Not because this was once permitted but is now forbidden. For (i) Episcopius neither alleges nor indicates this reason. (ii) Instead he gives another reason, that the angel is an angel. This argument is taken not from time but from his nature and office. This would have been no reason at all if such worship had been permitted up to that time and for that cause. Indeed, the angel sufficiently signified that it is wrong for anyone to worship such a being. (iii) He adds a second reason, positively assigning adoration to its true object: Worship God. The force of this is that not himself, not another, but God alone is to be worshipped, and that it is right to ascribe this honour to no one but him. (iv) Prove that under the Old Testament it was permitted to worship an angel, and not under the New. Or why, if this was ever permitted, is it not permitted today as well? Or if it is now wrong, was it once permitted? Where has God either permitted this or now forbidden it? (v) On the contrary, God has always held and willed that worship and adoration be paid to himself alone as his own. And Episcopius was not unaware that the angel who is read in the Old Testament as having been worshipped was understood to be God, not a creature; he ought to have examined this first, rather than passing over it lightly and twisting it to suit his own hypothesis. (vi) If God could and did communicate worship, why not under the New Testament as well as under the Old? Or why have angels now been stripped of this privilege and grace? On the contrary, the nature of God alone, and his pre-eminence [ὑπεροχὴ], is the foundation of worship, and can be so, as we shall now set out more fully. Our argument was this: whoever is due divine worship is God; Christ is due divine worship; therefore Christ is God. The Socinians and the Remonstrants deny the major premise. We, however, acknowledge no other God than the one true God. Francis David and his fellows denied the minor premise of the syllogism. So that the proof of the minor premise may give us less trouble, let us confirm it briefly, all the more because the major premise is thereby also made clear and proved.

units.la: Christum divino cultu prosequendum, probant in genere alia, alia in specie, per singulos divini cultus modos. Illud, Ioan. v.23. Ut omnes honorent filium, quemadmodum honorant Patrem. Qui non honorat filium, non honorat Patrem, qui misit eum. Socinus, Epist. 111. ad Radecium, Hic primum audis, Deum velle ut Christus honoretur, sicut ipse honoratur. Ex quo aperte intelligitur, Christum eo genere honoris a nobis afficiendum esse, quo ipse Deus a nobis afficitur, & consequenter a nobis adorandum esse. Annotanda in loco Christi duo. Res primum: ut omnes honorent filium. 11. Rei modus: καθὼς quemadmodum Patrem. Ioan. xiv. 1. Creditis in Deum, etiam in me credite. Sed hoc ad specialem cultus divini modum spectat, fundatum in illa cum Deo identitate.
units.tr: That Christ is to be given divine worship is proved, in general, by some passages, and in particular, by individual modes of divine worship, of which the first is John 5:23: That all may honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him. Socinus, in Epistle 111 to Radecki: Here you first hear that God wills that Christ be honoured just as he himself is honoured. From this it is clearly understood that Christ is to be honoured by us with the same kind of honour with which God himself is honoured by us, and consequently that he is to be adored by us. Two things are to be noted in this passage of Christ. The first is the thing itself: that all may honour the Son. The second is the manner of the thing: even as [καθὼς] the Father. John 14:1: You believe in God; believe also in me. But this pertains to the special mode of divine worship, grounded in that identity with God.

units.la: Sed in specie: nam Christo cultus religionis tribuitur verus, & omnis. 1. Ipsum credimus. Loco jam adducto, aliisque per Euangelium plurimis. Cujus istud totum argumentum est, ut in Christum credamus. Ioan. 111.15. 16. 18. 36. & vi. 29. Act. xxvi. 18. &c. 11. Ipsum speramus. Matt. xii. 21. Eph. 1. 11. 12. 13. 111. Eum adoramus. Hebr. 1. 6. 1 Cor. 1. 2. Rom. xiv. 9. Act. vii. 59, 60. & ix. 13, 14. Rom. 1. 2. iv. Inque ejus baptizamur nomen. Matth. xxviii. 19. Actor. 11. 38. 1 Cor. 1. 13.
