Socinus, in Catechesi, pag. 17. ut Christum divino cultu afficiamus, ut Deus; ejus generis inquam cultu, cujus is est, quem ipsi Deo exhibere debemus. Atque in margine annotat Scripturae loca, Ioh. 5. 23. Psalm. 45. 12. Hebr. 1. 6. Phil. 2. 10. Addo Smalcium, lib. de divinitate Christi, cap. xxxiv. ubi tractat de fide in Christum, & de adoratione & invocatione Christi.
units.tr: But specifically: for the worship of religion is ascribed to Christ as true and as complete. (1) We believe in him, by the passage just cited and by very many others throughout the Gospel; indeed the whole argument of that is that we should believe in Christ: John 3:15, 16, 18, 36; 6:29; Acts 26:18, etc. (2) We hope in him: Matt. 12:21; Eph. 1:11, 12, 13; 3:11. (3) We adore him: Heb. 1:6; 1 Cor. 1:2; Rom. 14:9; Acts 7:59, 60; 9:13, 14; Rom. 1:2; 4. (4) And we are baptized into his name: Matt. 28:19; Acts 2:38; 1 Cor. 1:13. Socinus, in his Catechesis, p. 17: that we honour Christ with divine worship, as God; with that kind of worship, I say, of which he is the one whom we ourselves must render to God. And in the margin he notes passages of Scripture: John 5:23; Psalm 45:12; Heb. 1:6; Phil. 2:10. I add Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, chapter 34, where he treats of faith in Christ, and of the adoration and invocation of Christ.

units.la: Verum ad confirmationem majoris, quod qui adoratur, verus inde probatur Deus: quod Adversarii negant. At neque negant Christum verum Deum. Socinus, contra Wiekum, cap. 11. aperte salsissimum est, nos palam affirmare, Christum non esse verum Deum: immo contrarium publice profitemur, & in nostris, tam Latina, quam Polonica lingua non paucis editis scriptis, Christum verum Deum esse, asserimus. An verum Deum, prout Deus, verus Deus est? Non, dicent. Sic ergo fucus detegitur sermonis. In hac enim materia nec ludere verbis licet, neque aliter quam ex vero & veritate Deo digna, loqui. Eodemque sensu negant se Jesum adorare, tanquam nudum hominem: Eques Polonus[?] in Apologia: & passim alii: nempe quia Jesus non est vilis homo, & eximius admodum, & singulari ratione à Deo in nativitate, vita, & nunc ab adscensione honoratus: sed merum hominem quando nos dicimus, intelligimus naturæ ratione, non donorum: quomodo Imperator, quamvis cæteris præcellat, homo tamen est, nec naturam exuit. Quibus prælibatis, ita porro progredimur.
units.tr: But to confirm the major premise, that the one who is adored is thereby proved to be the true God: this the adversaries deny. Yet they do not deny that Christ is the true God. Socinus, against Wiekus, chapter 11: It is most utterly false that we openly affirm that Christ is not the true God; indeed we publicly profess the contrary, and in our many writings published both in Latin and in Polish we assert that Christ is the true God. But is he the true God in the sense that God is true God? No, they will say. Thus the deceit of their language is exposed. For in this matter one may neither trifle with words nor speak otherwise than in truth and in a way worthy of God. In the same sense they also deny that they adore Jesus as a bare man: the Polish knight in his Apology, and others everywhere. That is because Jesus is not a common man, but a most distinguished one, honoured in an singular way by God at his birth, in his life, and now since his ascension. When we call him a mere man, we mean in respect of nature, not of gifts: just as an emperor, though he excels the rest, is nonetheless a man and does not lay aside his nature. With these preliminaries settled, we proceed as follows.

units.la: I. Adoratio (non enim admittimus Socini distinctionem inter adorationem, & invocationem, ubi Deo tribuitur, aut Christo, & de eo seu adorando, seu invocando sermo est, quia hic semper intelligitur adoratio non alia quam religiosa, προσκυνήσεως [?]) soli Deo semper adscribitur in Scripturis, ut ei propria, debitaque. Matth. iv. 10. Scriptum est enim, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis προσκυνήσεις [?], & ipsi soli servies λατρεύσεις [?]. Deut. vi. 13. & x. 20. Quæ loca hic respici, Racoviensis versio ad marginem habet. Utrobique dicitur: Iehovam Deum tuum timebis, & ipsi servies תַּעְבֹּד [?]. Quibus Christus nihil addidit, quum scriptum dixit, soli servies, quantumvis id in textu, quem allegat, non legatur, quandoquidem ista verborum illorum vis est, ex ipsa rei natura, servies Deo, nempe soli. At quare hoc? nisi quod unus solus Deus sit, & propterea solus colendus: ut servitus ista nulli nisi Deo competat, atque Deum certissime arguat. Neque aliter explicueris, quomodo Christo licuerit pro verbis, Deo servies, substituere, soli Deo servies. Nempe, nisi Deo servire significet, & idem valeat cum soli Deo servire. Dices tu, servire Deo, non arguere soli Deo ut servias, sed permittere etiam ut alteri servias non Deo: atqui hoc directe est contraire, & enervare Christi verba, argumentum, & autoritatem. At dices, nisi Deus velit vel præcipiat, ut quoque alteri, præter eum, creaturæ quoque religiose serviamus. Verum respondeo, Deus hoc præcipere non potest, quia non potest contraria præcipere: nam sub præcepto serviendi, sibi soli serviendum, nulli alteri, præcepit. Estque præceptum morale, immutabile, & perpetuum, inque N. T. ab ipso Christo confirmatum, in disputatione, ubi de alio colendo agebatur, & Christus non retundebat Satanam hinc, quod indignus esset qui coleretur, argumento ab ipso, & ejus ineptitudine, sed à Deo, Dei natura, cultuque sumto, ideo quod dictum, Deo servies, quod hoc perinde valeret ac si fuisset dictum, soli Deo servies. Quod certe Christus non vere collegisset, siquidem & antea, & post, non soli sibi serviendum Deus, quin etiam alteri, & creaturis, seu Angelis, seu hominibus, voluisset. Crellius, lib. de Deo, pag. 117. Etenim unitate Dei, tanquam fundamento quodam, omnia illa nituntur præcepta, aliaque Spiritus sancti dicta, quibus vel universus cultus divinus, vel pars ejus aliqua, soli Deo vindicatur atque asseritur.
units.tr: I. Adoration (for we do not accept Socinus's distinction between adoration and invocation, whether worship is ascribed to God or to Christ, and whether we speak of him as to be adored or to be invoked, since here adoration is always understood as nothing other than religious worship [προσκυνήσεως]) is always ascribed in Scripture to God alone, as his proper and due. Matt. 4:10: For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God [προσκυνήσεις], and him only shall you serve [λατρεύσεις]. Deut. 6:13 and 10:20. The Racovian version notes in its margin that these passages are in view here. In both places it reads: You shall fear Jehovah your God, and serve him [תַּעְבֹּד]. Christ added nothing to these words when he said, "you shall serve him only," even though the word "only" is not found in the text he cites, since the force of those words arises from the very nature of the matter: you shall serve God, namely him alone. But why so? Unless because there is only one God, and therefore he alone is to be worshipped; so that such service belongs to no one but God and most certainly proves him to be God. Nor can you explain otherwise how Christ could substitute "you shall serve the Lord only" for "you shall serve the Lord." Namely, unless to serve God means the same as to serve God alone. You will say that to serve God does not require that one serve God alone, but permits one also to serve another who is not God. But this is directly contrary to Christ's words, argument and authority, and undermines them. But you will say: unless God wills or commands it, we also serve creatures religiously besides him. I answer that God cannot command this, because he cannot command contrary things; for under the precept to serve, he commanded that he alone be served, and no other. It is a moral precept, immutable and perpetual, and in the New Testament it was confirmed by Christ himself, in a dispute where the worship of another was at issue. Christ did not refute Satan on the ground that he was unworthy to be worshipped, by an argument from himself and his unfitness, but from God, from the nature of God and the worship due to him. Therefore the words "you shall serve God" would carry exactly the same force as if it had been said "you shall serve God alone." Christ certainly would not have rightly drawn that inference, since both before and after, God did not wish to be served alone, but also wished another, whether angels or men, to be served. Crellius, book on God, p. 117: For all those precepts, and the other sayings of the Holy Spirit, rest upon the unity of God as upon a foundation, by which either the whole divine worship or some part of it is claimed and asserted for God alone.

units.la: I. Excipit Ostorodus, contra Tradelum, part. II. cap. III. verbum soli non præponi voci adorabis, sed, servies. Quantæ ineptiæ! quasi non & hoc, & illo verbo notetur cultus religiosus, σεβασμὸς λατρείας [?], & λατρεία προσκυνήσεως [?]? Credo si vox soli isto loco ante adorabis collocata fuisset, quod nec ita cavillatio defuisset auctoribus alia. Quin eo magis stringit, quod vox illa addita τῷ servies: quia sic in textu Hebræo, ubi non est adorabis, sed timebis. In Græcâ versione: Κύριον τὸν θεόν σου φοβηθήσῃ, καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις, Deut. vi. Adeo omni tempore judicatum, Deo servire, non esse aliud quam soli servire.
units.tr: I. Ostorodus objects, against Tradelius, part II, chap. III, that the word alone is not placed before you shall worship but before you shall serve. What trifling! As if both words did not denote religious worship, sebasmos latreias [σεβασμὸς λατρείας] and latreia proskynēseōs [λατρεία προσκυνήσεως]! I think that if the word alone had been placed before you shall worship in that passage, the authors would not have lacked some other quibble. Indeed the point presses all the more because that word is added to serve in the Greek, since in the Hebrew text there is no worship but fear. In the Greek version: Kyrion ton theon sou phobēthēsē, kai autō monō latreusis [Κύριον τὸν θεόν σου φοβηθήσῃ, καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις], Deut. 6. So at all times it has been judged that to serve God is nothing other than to serve God alone.

units.la: II. Excipit, præceptum hoc arguere si quos colas Deos tuo arbitrio & sponte, non si Dei jussu, quemadmodum Christus colitur. Resp. Imo non illud solum arguit, si quos colas tuo arbitrio; sed simpliciter, si modo colas alios, vel alium. Duo hic sunt, non alios colere: non tuo arbitrio. Res, & rei modus seu ratio. Hoc fateor prohibitum; sed & illud: imo illud prius, & clare, & directe. Neque enim hic attenditur, qua authoritate, nomine, jussu colas alios, an tuo motu proprio: ne verbulum quidem est, quod eo spectet. Sed ipsa illa res prohibetur colendi alios, ideoque (nam hoc re illa includitur) etiam tuo arbitratu, vel quocumque alterius. Sed quid si Deus praecipiat, nam praecipit aliquando alia & alia. Contraria? & quae praeceptis moralibus praecepta opponantur, quae praecepto primo? nunquam. Non potest Deus alio praecepto injungere, cultum religiosum suum aliis impendere, quia non se negare, non praeceptum primum tollere, non hoc, quo dicens sibi serviendum, eo sensu id praecepit, ut solus coleretur. Qui sensus fuit praecepti illius semper & usquam, in Veteri, atque in Novo Test.
units.tr: II. It is objected that this precept proves only that one must not worship other gods of one's own choice and will, not if one worships them by God's command, as Christ is worshipped. Reply. Indeed it proves not only this, that one must not worship others of one's own choice, but simply that one must not worship others or another at all. Two things are here: not to worship others; and not of one's own choice. The thing and the manner or reason of it. I grant that the one is forbidden, but so is the other: indeed the first is forbidden, and clearly and directly. For here it is not considered by what authority, in what name, or by what command you worship others, or by your own motion: there is not even a little word that bears on this. But the very thing itself is forbidden, namely worshipping others, and therefore (for this is included in the thing itself) even by your own choice or by anyone else's. But what if God commands it, for he sometimes commands one thing and sometimes another? Contrary things? And what precepts are set against the moral precepts, or against the first precept? Never. God cannot by another precept enjoin that his religious worship be bestowed on others, because he cannot deny himself, cannot abolish the first precept, and did not command this in the sense in which he said that he should be served, namely that he alone be worshipped. That was the sense of that precept always and everywhere, in the Old and in the New Testament.

units.la: Sec. argumentum. Uti soli Deo adscriptus cultus religiosus & adoratio, ita eidem soli semper attributa: neque exempla ullorum probata dari possunt, qui alium adorarint. Adeo ut quemadmodum adoratione saepe omnis Dei comprehenditur cultus & religio, ita ab ullo pio rite alteri tributa quam Deo, non legitur, non probatur.
units.tr: Second argument. Just as religious worship and adoration are ascribed to God alone, so too praise is always attributed to him alone; nor can examples be given of any who have approved of worshipping another. So that just as by adoration all the worship and religion of God is often comprehended, so it is not read or proved that anyone pious has rightly ascribed it to another than God.

units.la: Arg. tertium. Ita sibi soli vendicat Deus cultum divinum ac religiosum, ut alteri dare eum, vel dari, nullo modo velit. Jes. XLII. 8. Ego Iehova, hoc est nomen meum. Et gloriam meam alteri non dabo, & laudem meam sculptilibus. Idemque cap. XLVIII. 11. Excipiunt tria 1. per alterum non debere intelligi alterum, qui Deo subordinatus sit, qualis Christus; sed contrarius. 11. quod dare hic significat non concedere, sed permittere. 111. Gloriam meam, esse gloriam Deo propriam, neque Christo communicabilem, uti esse causam primam. Primum habet Socinus, epist. ad Radecium 111. pag. 149. Disp. de adoratione cum Christiano Francken habita a. 1584. d. 14 Martii, pag. 40.41. Catechesis Racovien(sis), pag. 145. 146. Tria autem illa conjuncta, Theophilus Nicolaides, Tractatu de Ecclesia, contra Borcorium, cap. VII. pag. 80. Ex eo Volkelius, lib. v. de Religione Socinianâ, cap. x. pag. 440. Atque ex illis eadem Episcopius, Inst. Theol. Sect. 11. cap. xxxv. pag. 343. Verba Theophili ita habent:
units.tr: Third argument. God claims divine and religious worship for himself alone in such a way that he wills in no way to give it to another, or to have it given. Isa. 42:8: I am Jehovah, that is my name. And my glory I will not give to another, nor my praise to graven images. And likewise chap. 48:11. They object three things: (1) that by another one must not understand one who is subordinate to God, as Christ is, but one who is contrary to him; (2) that to give here means not to grant but to permit; (3) that my glory is glory proper to God, not communicable to Christ, as is being the first cause. The first is held by Socinus, letter to Radecki III, p. 149; in the disputation on worship held with Christian Francken in 1584, on 14 March, pp. 40–41; and the Racovian Catechism, pp. 145–146. These three points taken together are found in Theophilus Nicolaides, treatise On the Church, against Borcorius, chap. VII, p. 80; from him Volkelius, book V On the Socinian Religion, chap. X, p. 440; and from those same sources Episcopius, Institutes of Theology, sect. II, chap. XXXV, p. 343. The words of Theophilus are as follows:

units.la: Prophetae autem verbis sobrius quaerendus sensus. Is porro est, quod per vocem alteri, intelligatur, qui Deo non sit subordinatus, sed contrarius. Id constat ex verbis apud Prophetam mox sequentibus, quae praecedentium explicatio censenda sunt: Nec laudem meam sculptilibus. Praeterea si quis rem accuratius consideret, non dixit Deus, semetipsum non daturum alteri gloriam, sed se non permissurum, ut ab alio detur gloria sua alteri. Vox enim dare, permittere interdum significat. Denique non dedit Deus gloriam suam Christo. Gloria enim Dei est, esse omnium rerum causam primam. Hanc autem nemini dedit, nec ipsi Iesu Christo: Dedit autem gloriam ejusdem generis, cujus ea est, quae Dei est.
units.tr: But the sense of the prophet's words must be sought soberly. It is this: that by the word another is understood one who is not subordinate to God but contrary to him. This is clear from the words in the prophet immediately following, which should be taken as an explanation of the preceding: nor my praise to graven images. Moreover, if anyone considers the matter more carefully, God did not say that he would not give glory to another himself, but that he would not permit his glory to be given to another by someone else. For the word to give sometimes means to permit. Finally, God did not give his glory to Christ. For the glory of God is to be the first cause of all things. This he gave to no one, not even to Jesus Christ himself. But he did give a glory of the same kind as that which belongs to God.

units.la: Resp. ad primum illud. 1. Intelligi etiam idola, & quoscunque Deo contrarios alios, non nego; sed hoc in secundo verborum membro: primum latissimè, simpliciter, atque absolute positum est, non alteri cuicunque. 11. Praeterquam ex hac voce, idem constat ex gloriae divinae adjuncta explicatione, meam, nam gloria mea est, vult Deus dicere. 111. Si sufficiat, & vim praecepti aut prohibitionis declinet, quando alteri divinus honor conciliatur, modo in subordinatione ad Deum, jam quidni aliis idem detur, non refragaturis ut subordinate ad Deum, & in ordine ad eum omnes cultum illum interpretentur? Scimus enim ita Pontificios, aliosque fo-lere idololatriam suam explicare & extenuare, quod omnia fiant in honorem Dei, & quod quidquid sculptilibus, Sanctis & numinibus impendunt, in iis subsistat mi-nimè, nimè, sed in Deum vergat, ultimum omnium terminum, & finem. Neque est quòd dicas, illos præter voluntatem Dei facere. Nam in hoc nondum inquirimus, velit Deus neque, rem ipsam in se spectamus, an hoc quod subordinatus honor divinus alicui contingit, sufficiat ad intelligendum, quod non alteri detur, id quod in hoc textu primo considerandum fuit loco.
units.tr: Reply to the first point. (1) I do not deny that idols and any other beings contrary to God are also understood, but this is in the second part of the statement: the first is put very broadly, simply and absolutely, not to any other whatever. (2) Apart from this word, the same is shown by the explanation attached to the divine glory, my, for God means to say that it is his glory. (3) If it suffices, and it evades the force of a precept or prohibition, when divine honour is bestowed on another, provided it is in subordination to God, why should it not then also be given to others, who will not object, as long as they interpret all such worship as subordinate to God and directed toward him? For we know that the Papists and others customarily explain and extenuate their idolatry in this way: that everything is done to the honour of God, and that whatever they bestow on graven images, saints and divinities does not rest in them at all, but tends to God, the ultimate end and goal of all. Nor is there reason for you to say that they act against the will of God. For at this point we are not yet inquiring whether God wills it, nor are we considering the matter in itself; we are asking whether the fact that subordinate divine honour falls to someone suffices to show that it is not given to another, which was the first thing to be considered in this text.

units.la: Ad secundum, Resp. ut dare tum alibi sumatur, tum & hic exponatur permittere, nihil reclamo. Sed etiam, non solum. II. Imo ideo hoc permissurus Deus non est, ut recte sc. tuto vel impune fiat, (cæteroquin aliquoties fieri & factum omnes novimus) quia dari suam aliis gloriam non vult, & hoc, quia dare nolit. III. Utcunque dare hic fit permittere, & fac dixisse Deum, non sinam aliis tribui gloriam meam, hinc autem recte jam & debite colligitur, nec Deum velle dare eam alteri cuicunque. Ut quocunque te vertas, istud hic, si non aperte, quod tamen verum, saltem implicite ac virtualiter significarum agnoscere cogaris.
units.tr: As to the second point, I answer that "to give" may be taken elsewhere as "to permit," and it is explained here in that sense; I make no objection. But also, not only. II. Indeed God would not permit this so that it might be done rightly, that is, safely or with impunity (otherwise we all know that it has happened many times, and does happen), but because he does not wish to give his glory to others, and this is because he is unwilling to give it. III. However "to give" is here taken as "to permit," and even if God had said, "I will not allow my glory to be given to others," it is then rightly and properly inferred that God does not wish to give it to anyone whatever. Whichever way you turn, you are forced to acknowledge that this is signified here, if not openly, yet at least implicitly and virtually, and it is in fact true.

units.la: Ad tertium. Resp. I. Gloria Dei est, esse omnium rerum causam primam. Sed an illa sola? nego. II. Quod Deus gloriam cultus intelligat, patet tum ex re ipsa, quia hæc sua gloria: tum ex subjuncta explicatione תהלתי[?], laudem meam. III. Quid est gloria ejusdem generis, cujus ea est, quæ Dei? an hæc non est gloria Dei, & laus Dei? atqui illam negat Deus se daturum. IV. Quando Smalcius dixit, nos Christo non secus atque ipsi Deo confidere, annon gloriam Dei Christo tribuit? eam tamen hac responsione tribuendam Christo aperte negant. Socinus, contra Wiekum cap. 1. Cui homini eam potestatem atque imperium à Deo ipsius Patre datum & donatum esse afferimus, ut merito ac necessario illi ipsi per se, & Dei nomen & divinus cultus tribuatur. Si propter illa debetur isti cultus divinus, non jam per se, uti neque proprie: & propter dona aliqua in hominem collata non potest ei deberi vel tribui ejusdem generis cultus qui Deo, propter naturam, competit; quod per se Deo, idem propter effecta & dona aliqua Dei, alteri non-Deo non convenit.
units.tr: As to the third point, I answer. I. It is the glory of God to be the first cause of all things. But is that alone his glory? I deny it. II. That God understands glory to mean worship is clear both from the thing itself, since this is his glory, and from the explanation that follows, tehillati [תהלתי], my praise. III. What is glory of the same kind as that which belongs to God? Is this not the glory of God and the praise of God? Yet God denies that he will give it. IV. When Smalcius said that we trust in Christ no less than in God himself, did he not ascribe the glory of God to Christ? Yet by this answer they plainly deny that it is to be ascribed to Christ. Socinus, against Wiek, chapter 1: We affirm that the power and dominion given and granted to this man by God the Father himself is such that the name of God and divine worship are rightly and necessarily ascribed to him, through himself. If divine worship is owed to him on account of these things, it is not owed through himself, nor properly. And on account of some gifts bestowed upon a man, the same kind of worship that belongs to God by nature cannot be owed or ascribed to him; what belongs through itself to God, on account of his effects and gifts, does not belong to any non-God.

units.la: Arg. quartum. Cui non possunt communicari fundamenta adorationis necessaria & propria, ei neque adoratio potest: sed nulli non Deo illa communicari possunt: ergo. Fundamenta illa præcipua sunt, omniscientia, & omnipotentia: hæc autem in hominem, vel humanam naturam non cadunt. Ipse Christus disertis verbis testatus est, se esse eum qui renes & corda scrutetur, inquit Socinus in Catechesi. pag.32. consequenter & se Deum esse. Non vero cadunt illa in quemquam nisi ὀλοτρόπως Deum. Cyrillus Alexandrinus, lib. vi. de adorat. in spir. & verit. προσκυνητὸν ἐν [?]ἀγίῳ μόνῳ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ[?] Κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ τῆς γραφῆς[?], ἐπεὶ δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγει[?].
units.tr: The fourth argument. To whom the necessary and proper grounds of adoration cannot be communicated, to him adoration cannot be given either; but these grounds cannot be communicated to anyone who is not God; therefore. The chief of these grounds are omniscience and omnipotence; but these do not fall upon a man or human nature. Christ himself testified in plain words that he is the one who searches the reins and hearts, says Socinus in the Catechism, page 32, and consequently that he is God. But these things do not fall upon anyone except God in every respect (ὀλοτρόπως). Cyril of Alexandria, book 6 on worship in spirit and truth: "Worship is to be offered to the Lord God of Scripture alone in spirit and truth" [προσκυνητὸν ἐν ἀγίῳ μόνῳ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ Κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ τῆς γραφῆς], since he speaks thus to him...

units.la: Excipit Socinus, primo, in Disput. cum Christiano Francken, pag. 15. Haud recte conclusa est ratio illa. Adoratio enim seu divinus cultus non requirit necessario omnipotentiam & participationem reliquarum, id est (ut nos interpretamur) aliarum omnium proprietatum Dei. Sed satis est, si is, qui adorari debet, iis, qui eum sunt adoraturi, divina ratione imperet ac dominetur. Nam quemadmodum iis, qui humana ratione nobis dominan-
units.tr: Socinus objects, first, in the disputation with Christian Francken, page 15: That argument is not rightly drawn. For adoration, or divine worship, does not necessarily require omnipotence and the participation of the other attributes, that is (as we interpret it) of all the other properties of God. It is enough, however, if he who is to be adored rules and has dominion by divine reason over those who are going to adore him. For just as those who rule over us by human reason

units.la: Resp. I. Quid est, divinâ ratione impera-re? an, formaliter divinâ? an divinâ metaphoricè? hoc inquiet. atqui, ne homines multos dicam, divina ratione nobis sæpe imperantes, Angeli sic dici possunt divinâ ratione imperare: ergo & adorari quoque poterunt ab iis, quibus præficiuntur? Hoc si satis est, fac etiam sanctum aliquem nobis imperare, quod Pontificii opinantur de quamplurimis, iste ergo adotur,humanus cultus à nobis debetur, sic divinus rari non modo poterit, sed & debebit. iii. ci, qui divinâ.
units.tr: Answer. I. What is it to rule by divine reason? Is it formally divine? Or divine in a metaphorical sense? He will say this. But angels, not to mention many men who often rule over us by divine reason, can thus be said to rule by divine reason; therefore may they also be worshipped by those over whom they are set? If that is enough, then suppose some saint rules over us, as the Papists suppose of very many; then this one is to be worshipped, and human worship is owed to us, and so not only could he be worshipped by us but he ought to be. iii. ... those who by divine [reason].

units.la: Hactenus Socinani dixerunt, illud non satis esse, ut quis nobis imperet, sed debere accedere voluntatem & jussionem Dei, ut adoretur. Potest enim Deus velle ut aliquis imperet, quacunque etiam optimâ & divina ratione, neque tamen ideo ut adoretur. iv. Imo in adorando requiritur necessario omnipotentia, aliæque Dei proprietates. Nam omnia ab ipso petimus, quem invocamus; ergo & præstare posse, credendum: & omnes petimus; ergo omnium vota scire, atque necessitates, debet. Denique, annon sic semper argumentati fuimus contra Pontificios, & bene: Sancti non sciunt, neque possunt omnia: ergo non sunt ab omnibus religiose invocandi? Deinde concedit Socinus Christo omniscientiam quandam, & omnipotentiam, sed non plenam; non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, improprie, & restricte, ut omnia sciat, & possit, quæ Ecclesiam suam concernunt, & homines in ea regendos. Pag. 16. Potestas Christi est infinita in Ecclesia, simpliciter autem finita; utpote certis finibus inclusa: cum tantummodo ad ea extendatur, quæ sunt intra Ecclesiam. Quumque ei Francken objecisset, quod finita substantia, qualis Christi hominis, infiniti non esset capax, non scientiæ, neque potentiæ infinitæ: respondit Socinus, proprie fortassis ac simpliciter infinita. Sed minus proprie, & secundum quid, ut hic infiniti vocabulum accipitur, potest omnino finita substantia infinitæ scientiæ esse capax. Quid enim vetat, quo minus homo quispiam omnia sciat, quæ de re aliqua sciri possunt? Et pag. 20. Atque hæc infinitas non proprie & simpliciter, sed, ut dictum est, minus proprie & secundum quid accipitur. Pag. 23. Verum jam dictum est, Christi scientiæ effectâ, infinita hoc loco dici, non proprie & simpliciter, sed minus proprie & secundum quid, & hujus infinitatis finitam substantiam capacem esse posse ostensum fuit. Additque similia exempla: quasi vero vilissimæ, præsertim præ ipso Christo, creaturæ non inveniantur, quæ longissime à se distantia perspiciunt, ut de lynce compertum est. ne quid dicam de aliis sensibus, auditu & olfactu. Aper enim sonos remotos exaudit. Milvus verò quàm remotissimos cadaverum odores sentit. Unde intelligere licet, Christum glorificatum, creaturam omnium creaturarum quacunque ratione excellentissimam, longe remotissima à substantia sua & abstrusissima videre, audire, & cognoscere nihil absurdi in se continere. Præsertim cum certissimum sit, dæmones, creaturas Christo haud paulo inferiores, plurima nosse, licet alioquin occultissima, & ab ipsorum substantia remotissima.
units.tr: Thus far the Socinians have said that it is not enough for someone to rule over us; the will and command of God must also be present for him to be worshipped. For God may wish someone to rule, even by the best and most divine reason, and yet not wish him to be worshipped. iv. Indeed, in adoring, omnipotence and the other properties of God are necessarily required. For we ask all things of him whom we invoke; therefore we must believe that he is able to grant them; and we all ask; therefore he must know the prayers and needs of all. Finally, have we not always argued thus against the Papists, and rightly: the saints do not know all things, nor can they do all; therefore they are not to be invoked religiously by all? Then Socinus concedes to Christ a certain omniscience and omnipotence, but not full; not simply, but in a certain respect, improperly and in a restricted sense, so that he knows and can do all those things that concern his Church and the men to be governed in it. Page 16: The power of Christ is infinite in the Church, but simply finite, being enclosed within certain limits, since it extends only to those things that are within the Church. And when Francken objected to him that a finite substance, such as the human substance of Christ, is not capable of infinite knowledge or infinite power, Socinus replied: Perhaps properly and simply infinite. But in a less proper sense, and in a certain respect, as the word infinite is taken here, a finite substance can altogether be capable of infinite knowledge. For what prevents some man from knowing all the things that can be known about any matter? And on page 20: This infinity is taken not properly and simply, but, as has been said, less properly and in a certain respect. Page 23: It has already been said that the knowledge of Christ is here called infinite, not properly and simply, but less properly and in a certain respect, and it has been shown that a finite substance can be capable of this infinity. He adds similar examples: as if the lowliest creatures, especially in comparison with Christ himself, were not found which perceive things very far from themselves, as has been discovered of the lynx; not to mention the other senses, hearing and smell. For the boar hears distant sounds, and the kite perceives the smells of corpses from the most remote distances. Whence it may be understood that it contains nothing absurd that Christ glorified, the most excellent creature of all creatures in whatever respect, should see, hear, and know things very remote and most hidden from his substance. Especially since it is most certain that demons, creatures not a little inferior to Christ, know very many things, though otherwise most hidden and very remote from their substance.

units.la: Resp. i. Omniscientia & omnipotentia non propriæ haud possunt esse fundamentum propriæ adorationis. ii. Quod simpliciter finitum est, illud non potest dici infinitum. iii. Proba, infinitatem Christo communicatam esse respectu suæ Ecclesiæ, & non habere infinitatem scientiæ potentiæque in omnia. iv. Absolute & simpliciter, proprieque ei dixit Petrus, Domine tu scis omnia. Ioann. xxi.17. Non limitatur, vel ad Ecclesiam, quam non multam adeo tum adhuc habebat Christus; vel ad alia: sed omnia complectitur. v. Imo qui Christus novit Ecclesiam suam per totum mundum dispersam, omniaque ejus negotia, & potest in ea omnia, si non habeat immensitatem scientiæ potentiæque in omnia, in ea etiam quæ interposita inter varias Ecclesias fidelesque loca sunt & res? vi. Bene est, quod scientia Christi confertur cum sagacitate animalium, cum lyncis visione, auditu apri, odore milvi, denique & cum scientia dæmonum, ut illis omnibus merito excellentior. Nempe hoc meretur Socinianorum Christus, cum illis comparari. Noster collationibus illis & exemplis haud eget. Veri Christi scientia & potentia ejusdem generis non est cum illis. Vim illa aliquam majorem notent in naturis harum rerum illarumque, in hominibus nihil adeo concludunt, ut non proinde sequatur in Adamo illa fuisse, vel Christo, vel in corporibus futura beatorum. vii. Ecquis dicit, absurdi aliquid in se continere, quod Christus longe remotissima a substantia sua & abstrusissima videat, audiat & cognoscat? cui diluendo misera illa & ferina argumenta congessit Socinus. Sed quaeritur, an infinita cognoscat? vel, quomodo finita substantia infinitam capiat scientiam? sed jam dixisti scilicet, Christum vestrum illa videre, audire, cognoscere, uti lynx remotissima etiam videt, aper audit, milvus sentit; quin ne cui ullus praeterea haereat scrupulus, uti daemones Christo (adde vestro, neque enim aliter haec vel legi volo) haud paulo inferiores creaturae plurima noscunt, licet alioquin occultissima, & ab ipsorum substantia occultissima.
units.tr: Answer. I. Omniscience and omnipotence cannot properly be the foundation of proper adoration. II. What is simply finite cannot be called infinite. III. Prove that infinity was communicated to Christ with respect to his Church, and that he does not have infinite knowledge and power over all things. IV. Peter said to him absolutely and simply, and properly, "Lord, you know all things" (John 21:17). He is not limited either to the Church, which Christ then did not yet have in great number, or to other things; but it embraces all things. V. Indeed, if Christ knows his Church dispersed through the whole world and all its affairs, and can do all things in it, if he does not have immensity of knowledge and power over all things, does he also know the things and places that lie between the various churches and faithful people? VI. It is well that the knowledge of Christ is compared with the sagacity of animals, with the sight of the lynx, the hearing of the boar, the smell of the kite, and finally with the knowledge of demons, so that he is rightly more excellent than all of them. Indeed the Christ of the Socinians deserves to be compared with these things; ours has no need of such comparisons and examples. The knowledge and power of the true Christ are not of the same kind as those. Those things may indicate some greater force in the natures of these creatures, but they conclude nothing about men, so that it does not follow that such powers were in Adam, or in Christ, or will be in the bodies of the blessed. VII. Who says that it contains something absurd that Christ sees, hears, and knows things very remote and most hidden from his substance? To refute this, Socinus has heaped up those wretched and brutish arguments. But the question is whether he knows infinite things, or how a finite substance can hold infinite knowledge. But you have now said, of course, that your Christ sees, hears, and knows those things just as the lynx sees very remote things, the boar hears, and the kite smells; and lest any scruple remain for anyone, that demons (add "yours," for I do not wish these things to be read otherwise) not a little inferior creatures know very many things, though otherwise most hidden, and most hidden from their substance.

units.la: Adoratio ita soli Deo propria est, ut, adorare alium, quam Deum, vera sit idololatria. Ne dicas, quod continuo & satis promte regerere hac in causa solent Adversarii, imo quando Deus non jubet alium adorare. At vero Deus, tum natura sua, tum praecepto vel prohibitione de idololatria, non potest neque vult imperare ut alteri cultum deferamus divinum, religiosum, praeterquam sibi. Sed tunc Deum non noscentes, serviistis iis qui natura Dei non sunt. Unde hoc fluit argumentum: servire iis, qui natura non sunt Dii, idololatria est & ignorantia veri Dei. Quae ipsa thesis est nobis probanda. Atque ii revera sunt Dii אלהים[?], praecepto notati damnatique. Non inde modo, quod eos Deus coli nolit, sed quod coli, ideo quod Deus non sunt, haud possint.
units.tr: Worship belongs so exclusively to God that to worship anyone other than God is true idolatry. Do not say what the Adversaries usually answer quickly and readily in this matter, namely, "Yes, but even if God does not command us to worship another." God, however, both by his nature and by his precept or prohibition concerning idolatry, cannot and will not command that we give divine, religious worship to anyone besides himself. But then, not knowing God, you served those who by nature are not gods. From this follows the argument: to serve those who by nature are not gods is idolatry and ignorance of the true God. This very thesis is what we must prove. And they are indeed "gods" [אלהים], noted and condemned by the precept. Not only because God does not want them worshipped, but because, since they are not God, they cannot be worshipped.

units.la: Audiamus, quid Socinus excipiat. In Disputatione cum Christiano Francken, In hoc argumento est fallacia aequi-vocationis, in voce Natura. Ea enim in loco ad Gal. nihil aliud significat quam reipsa, & opinationi opponitur. Quemadmodum ibidem annotavit Theodorus Beza. Atqui hoc sensu Christus Socini sententia est natura Deus. Ista autem vel similis ejus vocis significatio animadversa est a vetustioribus & recentioribus etiam quibusdam cap. 2. Epistolae ad Ephesios in illis verbis: Eramus natura filii irae. Vbi Hieronymus fatetur, vocem Graecam φύσει[?] esse ambiguam.
units.tr: Let us hear what Socinus objects. In his Disputation with the Christian Francken: In this argument there is an equivocation in the word "nature". For in the passage on Galatians it means nothing other than "in reality", and it is opposed to opinion, as Theodore Beza noted in the same place. But in this sense Christ, according to Socinus's view, is God by nature. This meaning, or one similar to it, has been noticed by some older and more recent writers on chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, in those words: "We were by nature children of wrath." Where Jerome admits that the Greek word φύσει [physei] is ambiguous.

units.la: Resp. i. Vox natura φύσις[?] significat reipsa, & opinationi opponitur, quia ipsam divinae naturae rem, & veram Deitatem significat. Non reipsa erant Dii, quos coluerant, quia non natura. Quod natura dixit, reipsa includit, & utrumque opinationi opponitur. Quare in versione Aethiopica illud natura omittitur, uti satis inclusum in verbis Dii: ut sive Deum, & natura Deum, aut Deos dicas, idem videatur, quia qui non natura, non est Deus. Adeo illud, argumentum non solvit. ii. Non ostendit Socinus aequivocationem in voce natura, quia non oppo-nitur natura, & reipsa. Sed idem hic sunt, nisi quod naturae vox fortius exprimat & declaret id quod reipsa designat. Et utrumque opinationi opponitur, non hoc solum.
units.tr: Reply first. The word nature [φύσις] means in reality, and is opposed to opinion, because it signifies the very thing of the divine nature and true Deity. They were not gods in reality whom they worshipped, because they were not by nature. What "by nature" says, "in reality" includes, and both are opposed to opinion. Hence in the Ethiopian version the word "nature" is omitted, as being sufficiently included in the word "gods". So whether you say God, or God by nature, or gods, it seems to be the same, because whoever is not by nature is not God. Thus that argument does not solve the problem. Second, Socinus does not show any equivocation in the word "nature", since it is not opposed to "in reality". Rather these are the same here, except that the word "nature" expresses and declares more strongly what "in reality" designates. And both are opposed to opinion, not this one alone.

units.la: iii. Quo sensu Socino Christus natura Deus fit, supra vidimus, scilicet sensu, qui reipsa Deus non est, qui naturam Dei, & rem Deitatis ipsam non habet. v. Christus Socini sensu vir divinus est, propter excellentem dignitatem, naturam, opera: atqui talis eodem pacto Deus appellari potest & natura Deus, quemadmodum is qui excellens aliquod edit facinus, & regium quod solemus vocare, rex natura dici posset: non distinguendo inter metaphoricum, & proprium. vi. Qui non est proprie Deus, non est natura Deus. vii. Christus Socini opinione tantum Deus est, non reipsa, non proprie, non naturaliter, opinantis virum ita excellentem Deum appellandum esse, quamvis propria Deitatis natura careat. viii. Exponas licet Eph. ii. eramus natura filii iræ, id est, reipsa, non opinione. Jam autem unde & quare reipsa? nimirum, quia natura. adeo hæc non pugnant, vel se destruunt, sed explicant, & hoc illud continet, neque absque eo explicari potest. ix. Non lego apud Hieronymum, vocem φύσις esse ambiguam: sed hæc, Et eramus natura filii iræ, &c. Ita nos fraternæ, existimo legendum paternæ, traditionis consuetudo potuerat, ut omnes ad damnationem nasci videremur. Denique nullus Veterum negabit vocem natura proprie hic sumendam esse, nisi qui ex Pelagii, quam Christi Schola, edoceri & philosophari maluerit.
units.tr: Third, in what sense Christ becomes God by nature for Socinus we saw above: namely, in the sense that he is not God in reality, who does not have the nature of God and the very thing of Deity. Fourth, in Socinus's sense Christ is a divine man, on account of excellent dignity, nature and works; yet someone of this kind can in the same way be called God and God by nature, just as one who performs some excellent deed, and whom we usually call a king, could be called king by nature, without distinguishing between the metaphorical and the proper. Fifth, whoever is not properly God is not God by nature. Sixth, Christ in Socinus's opinion is God only in opinion, not in reality, not properly, not naturally, since the opinion holds that a man so excellent is to be called God, although he lacks the proper nature of Deity. Seventh, you may explain Ephesians 2, "we were by nature children of wrath", as meaning in reality, not in opinion. Now, whence and why "in reality"? Surely because "by nature". So these do not conflict or destroy each other, but explain each other, and the one contains the other, nor can the one be explained without the other. Eighth, I do not read in Jerome that the word φύσις is ambiguous; but these words: "And we were by nature children of wrath, etc." So I think we should read "paternal" for "fraternal": "the custom of tradition could have made us all seem born to damnation." Finally, no one among the ancients will deny that the word "nature" is to be taken properly here, except one who would rather be taught and philosophise by Pelagius than by Christ's school.

units.la: Act. x. 25.26. Cornelius, cadens ante pedes, adoravit. Petrus autem erexit eum, dicens: surge: nam & ego homo sum. Quod in hoc fundatur axiomate, qui est homo, cultu religioso adorari non potest. Unde Athanasius dixit, Orat. III. contra Arianos, Πέτρος μὲν οὖν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, προσκυνῆσαι θέλοντα τὸν Κορνήλιον, κωλύει λέγων, ὅτι κἀγὼ ἄνθρωπός εἰμι. ἀγγέλῳ δὲ θέλοντι προσκυνῆσαι τὸν Ἰωάννην ἐν τῇ ἀποκαλύψει, κωλύει λέγων, &c. οὐκοῦν δεῖ εἷς μόνῳ τῷ προσκυνεῖσθαι. ὅτι καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῆς δόξης ὑπερέχωσι, ἀλλὰ κτίσματα πάντες εἰσί. [?] Apoc. xix. 10. Cecidi coram pedibus ejus adoraturus eum: atque dixit mihi, vide ne: sum enim conservus tuus, & fratrum tuorum habentium testimonium Iesu. Deum adora. Adorare alium, præterquam Deum, adorare eum, qui ulla ratione nobis servit, nefas est & idololatria.
units.tr: Acts 10:25–26. Cornelius, falling at his feet, worshipped. But Peter raised him up, saying: Rise; for I too am a man. This rests on the axiom that one who is a man cannot be worshipped with religious worship. Hence Athanasius said, Oration III against the Arians: Peter the Apostle, when Cornelius wished to worship him, forbids him, saying, "I too am a man". And when an angel wished to worship John in the Apocalypse, he forbids him, saying, etc. Therefore worship must be given to the one alone, since the others, though they surpass in glory, are all creatures. [Πέτρος μὲν οὖν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, προσκυνῆσαι θέλοντα τὸν Κορνήλιον, κωλύει λέγων, ὅτι κἀγὼ ἄνθρωπός εἰμι. ἀγγέλῳ δὲ θέλοντι προσκυνῆσαι τὸν Ἰωάννην ἐν τῇ ἀποκαλύψει, κωλύει λέγων, &c. οὐκοῦν δεῖ εἷς μόνῳ τῷ προσκυνεῖσθαι. ὅτι καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῆς δόξης ὑπερέχωσι, ἀλλὰ κτίσματα πάντες εἰσί.] Apoc. 19:10. I fell at his feet to worship him; and he said to me, See that you do not; for I am your fellow servant, and of your brethren who have the testimony of Jesus. Worship God. To worship anyone other than God, that is, to worship one who in any way serves us, is wicked and idolatry.

units.la: Excipit Socinus, in Disp. cum Francken, pag. 37. Immo Christus homo est Dominus omnium nostrum, adeoque angelorum omnium. Sic, ut nunc non modo conservus noster simplici-ter dici nequeat, quod nec unquam potuit, sed ne Dei quidem ipsius servus proprie dici posse videatur. Unde & ad verba illa Pauli 1 Cor. 15. tunc & ipse filius subjectus erit, qui subjecit ipsi omnia, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus, ait: Hinc enim aperte constat, Paulum sensisse, non posse Christum hominem, cui Deus omnia subjecit, hoc tempore proprie Deo sub-jectum dici; quare neque etiam proprie ejus servum. Resp. 1. Quin Dominus omnium Christus sit, non ambigimus. Quod & servus Dei, quodcunque sit de præsenti ejus statu, olim dici potuerit, patet ex Jesa. liii. 11. Phil. ii. 7. Matth. xx. 28. ii. Verba Pauli 1 Cor. xv. 28. non sunt de hoc tempore exponenda, sed tempore post resurrectionem, quando finis erit, & regnum traditurus Deo ac Patri. vers. 24. iii. Quomodo Paulus non senserit, Christum hominem haud posse dici subjectum Deo? nam & natura hoc hominis, & officium ejus declarant. Jam Jer. xvii. 5. Sic inquit Iehova, maledictus vir ille qui confidit in homine & ponit carnem pro brachio suo, atque à Iehova deflectit corde suo. Ubi duo continentur. i. Nefas esse confidere in homine. & ii. Hoc qui facit, eo deflectere à Deo. Quare hominem, vel creaturam adorare, & adorando ei confidere, præsertim non secus atque ipsi Deo, quod Smalcius dixit, peccatum atque idololatria est manifesta.
units.tr: Socinus objects, in his Disputation with Francken, p. 37: "Indeed Christ as man is Lord of all of us, and so of all the angels. So that now he can not only not simply be called our fellow servant, which he never could be, but not even the servant of God himself seems properly to be called." Hence also on those words of Paul, 1 Cor. 15: "Then the Son also shall be subjected, who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all", he says: "For from this it clearly appears that Paul thought that Christ as man, to whom God subjected all things, cannot at this time properly be called subject to God; therefore neither properly his servant." Reply, first: that Christ is Lord of all we do not doubt. That he could once be called the servant of God, whatever his present state, is clear from Isaiah 53:11, Philippians 2:7, Matthew 20:28. Second, the words of Paul at 1 Cor. 15:28 are not to be expounded of this time, but of the time after the resurrection, when the end will come and he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father (v. 24). Third, how did Paul not think that Christ as man could not be said to be subject to God? For both the nature of man and his office declare it. Now Jeremiah 17:5: "Thus says Jehovah: cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and turns his heart away from Jehovah." Where two things are contained: first, that it is wrong to trust in man; second, whoever does this turns away from God. Hence to worship a man or a creature, and by worshipping to trust in him, "not otherwise than to God himself", as Smalcius said, is sin and manifest idolatry.

units.la: Columns below the text: see notes. da[?] constitutus non fit, & quatenus nihil aliud est, quam homo, id est, divinis viribus non est præditus; unde fiat, ut, qui in hujusmodi homine fiduciam collocet, ab ipso Deo recedat. Propterea ibidem post verba à Francken recitata statim subjungitur, & à Jehova recedit cor ejus. Qui igitur ita in homine fiduciam habet, ut interim nullo pacto à Deo ejus cor recedat, quippe qui hominem, cui confidit, divina potestate præditum esse agnoscat, idque, ipsius Dei consilio, in eum finem ut sibi opem ferat, is sane Dei sententia illa maledictus non est. Immo maledictus est eadem Dei sententia is, qui ejusmodi homini confidere renuit. Deo enim ipsi renuit confidere; atque ita à Iehova recedit cor ejus. Sic enim in re simili loquitur Paulus 1 Thess. iv.8. Itaque, inquit, qui spernit, non hominem spernit, sed Deum, qui etiam dedit spiritum suum sanctum in nobis. Adde, quod ex verbis illis, & statuit carnem brachium suum, non obscure ob vocem carnis colligitur, ibi hominem significari non solum mortalem & caducum, sed etiam divina potentia destitutum. Quorum hoc nunquam revera de Christo dici potuit; illud vero post ejus glorificatione plane est falsum. Nam præterea carnis appellationem glorificatis hominibus non convenire docet Paulus, cum ait, Caro & sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt. 1 Cor. xv. 50. stitutus sit, quales multi passim fuerunt, atque sunt, non tamen illis, juxta hunc locum aliosque similes, erit confidendum.
units.tr: ...is not constituted, and insofar as he is nothing other than a man, that is, is not endowed with divine powers; whence it comes about that whoever places trust in such a man recedes from God himself. Therefore in the same place, immediately after the words recited from Francken, it is added: "and his heart recedes from Jehovah." Whoever therefore has trust in a man in such a way that in the meantime his heart by no means recedes from God, since he acknowledges that the man in whom he trusts is endowed with divine power, and that by God's own counsel, to the end that he may bring help to him, that person is certainly not cursed by that sentence of God. Rather, he is cursed by the same sentence of God who refuses to trust such a man. For he refuses to trust God himself, and so his heart recedes from Jehovah. For Paul speaks thus in a similar matter, 1 Thess. 4:8: "Therefore, he says, he who despises, despises not man but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us." Add that from those words, "and makes flesh his arm", it is gathered, not obscurely from the word flesh, that man is signified there not only as mortal and frail, but also as destitute of divine power. Of these, the first could never truly be said of Christ; the second is plainly false after his glorification. For Paul also teaches that the name of flesh does not belong to glorified men, when he says: "Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God." 1 Cor. 15:50. However constituted such men were, and as many as there have been and are everywhere, yet in trust in them, according to this place and others like it, one should not place confidence.

units.la: III. Homo, quamvis divinis viribus præditus, est tamen, atque manet homo. IV. Qui in quocunque homine fiduciam collocat, ab ipso recedit Deo. V. Impossibile est, ut, qui in homine fiduciam habet, nullo pacto à Deo recedat. VI. Quamvis hominem scias divina potestate præditum, idque ipsius Dei consilio, tibi ut opem ferat, non tamen in eum confidere licet, vel adorare eum, atque si ei confidas, sane Dei sententia illa omnino es maledictus. VII. Quomodo maledictum dicis, qui ejusmodi homini confidere renuit? nam dixeras ante, consilium Dei esse, ut isti homini sideremus, duntaxat ut nobis opem ferret: non ut omittentes id, essemus maledicti. VIII. Si jam dicas, Deum jubere, ejusque consilium esse, ut homini confidamus, falsum dicis, & quod Deus pro maledicto palàm habet. IX. Quid huc facit locus Pauli? qui agit de spernendis Apostolis, non de adorandis: & qui illos spernit, certe Deum spernit, & magis adhuc, qui Christum. At non qui hominem non adorat, vel in eum non confidit, Deum spernere interpretandus est: sed revera qui spreto Dei mandato & comminatione, illud committit, revera læsæ Dei Majestatis reus haberi debet.
units.tr: III. A man, although endowed with divine powers, is nevertheless and remains a man. IV. Whoever places his trust in any man turns away from God himself. V. It is impossible that someone who trusts in a man should in no way turn away from God. VI. Although you know that a man is endowed with divine power, and that this is by the counsel of God so that he may bring you help, it is still not lawful to trust in him or to worship him; and if you do trust in him, you are certainly accursed by that sentence of God. VII. In what sense do you call accursed the one who refuses to trust such a man? For you said before that it is God's counsel that we should rely on this man, only so that he might bring us help, not that we should be accursed if we neglected to do so. VIII. If you now say that God commands, and that it is his counsel, that we trust in a man, you speak falsely, and say what God openly regards as accursed. IX. What does the passage of Paul have to do with this? It speaks of despising the apostles, not of worshipping them; and whoever despises them certainly despises God, and even more so whoever despises Christ. But he who does not worship a man, or does not trust in him, is not to be understood as despising God. Rather, one who, having spurned the command and threat of God, commits that act, ought truly to be held guilty of offending the majesty of God.

units.la: X. Carnem in loco Prophetæ quomodocunque sumas, nam non tantum pro carne caduca, sed substantiâ in Scriptura usurpatur, & pro homine in genere, prius illud de homine adeo non tollit, ut confirmet, & de homine quomodocunque accepto exponi debere indicet. XI. Non negat Apostolus carnem & sanguinem glorificatis competere, quod ad substantiam eorum, sed quod ad corruptionem, quando dixit, caro & sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt. quod patet ex addito, eodem versu, neque corruptio incorruptionem.
units.tr: X. However you take the word "flesh" in the prophet's passage, for it is used in Scripture not only of frail flesh but of substance, and of man in general, the former point does not remove the sense "man" but confirms it, and shows that the passage must be explained of man, in whatever sense that term is taken. XI. The Apostle does not deny that flesh and blood belong to the glorified as to their substance, but as to corruption, when he said, "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God." This is clear from what is added in the same verse: "nor does corruption inherit incorruption."

units.la: Atque hæc ad argumentum nostrum dicta, de adoratione & cultu religioso nemini tribuendo, quàm uni & vero Deo, ex quo proinde Christum Deum esse juste collegimus. Jamque argumenta catholica pro asserendâ Christi verâ Deitate, ex nominibus divinis, proprietatibus, actionibus, cultu vindicavimus: ea prosequuti, quæ maximam in hac causa habere vim videbantur. Tertullianus, vel sub ejus nomine Novatianus, de Trinitate, pag. 610. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quo modo adest ubique invocatus? cum hæc hominis natura non fit, sed Dei, ut adesse omni loco possit? si homo tantummodo Christus, cur homo in orationibus mediator invocatur? cum invocatio hominis ad praestandam salutem inefficax judicetur? Si homo tantummodo Christus, cur spes in illum ponitur, cum spes in homine maledicta referatur?
units.tr: And these things have been said to our argument, that worship and religious cult are to be given to no one but the one and true God, from which we rightly conclude that Christ is God. We have also already vindicated the Catholic arguments for asserting the true Deity of Christ from the divine names, properties, actions, and worship, pursuing those which seemed to have the greatest force in this cause. Tertullian, or Novatian under his name, On the Trinity, p. 610: If Christ is only a man, how is he invoked as present everywhere? For this is not the nature of man but of God, to be able to be present in every place. If Christ is only a man, why is a man invoked as mediator in prayers, since the invocation of a man is judged ineffective for obtaining salvation? If Christ is only a man, why is hope placed in him, when hope in a man is pronounced accursed?

units.la: Antequam ad Adversariorum argumenta seu objectiones solvendas progrediamur, hoc denique justi argumenti loco omnibus considerandum relinquimus, quod ex testimonio & confessione Muhammedanorum petere nobis licet: qui utcunque fortiter etiam negent Christum Deum esse, unde & Servetus argumentatur, ex Alkorano nimirum, lib. 1. de Trinit. pag. 43. attamen Deum vere doceri in epistolis Paulinis palam fatentur: & concedunt minorem istam nostram assumtionem, quam alii Christiani scilicet nobis negant, miranturque stuporem eorum qui id eunt inficias: sed, inquiunt, non hanc Pauli sententiam, vel Pauli verba, sed a Christianis infarta & supposita pro Paulinis fuisse. Quod uti Christiani nulli dicunt vel credunt, ita eorum nonnullos minus in Scriptura perspicaces esse, quam sint Muhammedani, & hoc non videre, quod ii quidem vident, valde probrosum merito videri debet. Perinde ac Judaei olim in Christo id videre non potuerunt vel noluerunt, quod gentilis Centurio, aliique cum eo milites Romani de Christo profitebantur: vere hic Filius Dei erat. Ita hoc esse, quod de Muhammedanis dicimus, videri potest ex disputatione Ahme-dis filii Zin Alabedin, Persae Asphahanensis, adversus quem Philippus Guadagnolus pro Religione Christianâ responsum scripsit satis vastum & prolixum, quod Arabice extat, & Latine. Ad quae liceat aliquo modo dicere, quod Chrysostomus, Homil. VII. in Matth. Erubescat Marcion, erubescat & Samosatenus ille Paulus, qui nolunt videre quod Magi viderunt, Ecclesiae progenitores. Nequaquam sic erubuerim nuncupare eos. Confundatur, inquam, videns dominum Marcion in assumptione carnis adorari: Confundatur & Paulus, videns non sicut hominem adorari, quem tantummodo hominem suspicatur. Ne Gentiles dicam, qui idem de Christianis exiftimarunt olim, eos Christum pro Deo habere. Unde illa Plinii epistola, ad Trajanum, lib. x. epist. 97. Affirmabant autem hanc fuisse summam vel culpae suae, vel erroris, quod essent soliti stato die ante lucem convenire: carmenque Christo, quasi Deo, dicere secum invicem.
units.tr: Before we proceed to solve the arguments or objections of our opponents, we leave to everyone this final consideration, as a point of just argument, which we are entitled to draw from the testimony and confession of the Muhammedans. However strongly they deny that Christ is God, whence Servetus also argues from the Alcoran, book 1 On the Trinity, p. 43, they nevertheless openly confess that God is truly taught in the Pauline epistles, and they concede that minor premise of ours which other Christians deny us, and they marvel at the stupidity of those who deny it. But, they say, this is not Paul's opinion or Paul's words; they were inserted and foisted into the Pauline writings by Christians. As no Christians say or believe this, it deserves to be considered very shameful that some of them are less perceptive in Scripture than the Muhammedans, and do not see what the Muhammedans do see. Just as the Jews formerly could not or would not see in Christ what the Gentile centurion and the other Roman soldiers with him professed about Christ: truly this was the Son of God. That this is what we say about the Muhammedans may be seen from the disputation of Ahmed, son of Zin Alabedin, a Persian of Ispahan, against whom Philip Guadagnolo wrote a response for the Christian religion, quite large and lengthy, which exists in Arabic and in Latin. To these things we may say, in some measure, what Chrysostom says, Homily 7 on Matthew: Let Marcion blush, let that Samosatene Paul blush too, who refuse to see what the Magi saw, the forefathers of the Church. I would not at all blush to call them that. Let Marcion be confounded, I say, seeing the Lord adored in the assumption of flesh; let Paul also be confounded, seeing him adored not as a man, whom he only suspects to be a man. To say nothing of the Gentiles, who formerly thought the same of Christians, that they held Christ to be God. Hence that letter of Pliny to Trajan, book 10, letter 97: They affirmed, however, that the sum of their fault or error was this: that they were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn, and to sing a hymn to Christ among themselves in turn, as to God.

units.la: Visis jam illis de natura Christi divina, facile est explicare & tueri veritatem incarnationis Christi, qua persona in ipso divina creditur assumsisse in sui unitatem naturam humanam, quo tum agere, tum pati posset quae absque natura humana fieri haud poterant, & tamen ad munus mediatorium peragendum requirebantur. Indigne quidem & malitiose Adversarii veritatem istam insectantur & blasphemant, appellantes fabulam, quod Smalcius facit contra Frantzium, & contra Graweium. Socinus, Disput. de Christi natura, pag. 8. Dei metamorphosim. Pag. 10. Humanationem, merum humani ingenii commentum. Pag. 15. Divinae humanaeque substantiae constitam copulationem. Ostorodus, Instit. cap. xvii. commentum. caeteraque ejusmodi: Nobis autem εἰς ἐλαχίστην ἐστί[?], quod ab illis haereticorum monstris & veritas, & propter eam nos audimus male. Primo enim veritas incarnationis probatur iis Scripturae locis, quae Christum probant Deum. Quae hactenus produximus. II. Iis, quae hominem, satis nota & confessa. III. Quibus conjungitur utrumque, vid. esse Deum simul & hominem. Rom. 1. 3, 4. & ix. 5. Gal. iv. 4. Act. xx. 28. 1 Joann. 1. 7. Phil. ii. 6 &c. IV. Quibus Deus dicitur factus caro: assumsisse naturam nostram: & manifestatus fuisse in carne. Joann. 1. 14. Heb. ii. 14. 1 Tim. iii. 16. V. denique unam tamen esse personam. Unde unus Mediator dicitur, 1 Tim. ii. 5. Unus Dominus. Ephes. iv. 6. Vnus Christus : qui Deus & homo est, θεάνθρωπος[?]. uti hac voce Patres Græci utuntur, & Clemens Alexandrinus, in initio Protreptici ad Gentes, νῦν δὲ ἐπιφάνῃ ἀνθρώποις αὐτὸς ἥτ[?]ο ὁ λόγος, ὁ μόνος ἀμφὼ θεὸς τε ἡ ἀνθρώπος[?], ἀπάντων ἡμῖν αὐτὸς ἀρχηγὸς[?]. Hinc Christus, Deitatis ratione Theologis dictus αὐτόθεος[?]. Christum autem dicimus αὐτόθεον, id est, à se Deum ; etiam αὐτοθέον, eundem illum Deum : sed in hac quæstione quia prius illud spectatur, quod à se Deus, sic quoque pungenda vox videtur. Dicitur Christus ita, essentiæ suæ ratione, non personæ : etenim ut persona, est à Patre , Filius à Patre genitus, non ergo αὐτιὸς[?], quamvis αὐτόθεος. Et non tres αὐτοθεοὶ, uti nec Dii dicendi, sed tres αὐτόθεος[?]; quemadmodum neque tres ὁμοούσιοι, sed tres ὁμοούσιοι Θεοί. Atque esse à se dicitur Deus, Filius, non esse à se productus, sed habere eandem cum Patre Deitatis essentiam, quæ à nullo alio sit Deo, neque alium Deum faciat. Recte dixeris, Filium habere essentiam à se ; conjungendo essentiam à se ; & non, conjungendo hæc prioribus, dices, Filium à se, habere essentiam divinam : sed, Filius habet, essentiam à se, id est, essentiam vere divinam, ἀνάρχον, ἀναίτιον, αὐτούσιον[?], eandem cum Patre unam.
units.tr: Having now considered the divine nature of Christ, it is easy to explain and defend the truth of the incarnation of Christ, in which the divine person is believed to have taken human nature into its own unity, so that it could act and suffer those things which could not be done without human nature, and which were nevertheless required for carrying out the mediatorial office. Our opponents unworthily and maliciously attack and blaspheme this truth, calling it a fable, as Smalcius does against Frantzius and against Grawer. Socinus, Disputation on the Nature of Christ, p. 8: a metamorphosis of God; p. 10: humanation, a mere invention of human wit; p. 15: a copulation constituted of divine and human substance. Ostorodt, Institutes, ch. 17: an invention; and other things of this kind. But for us, the truth itself and the abuse heaped on it by those monstrous heretics are both to be borne with patience. First, the truth of the incarnation is proved by those passages of Scripture which prove Christ to be God, which we have hitherto set forth. Second, by those which prove man, which are sufficiently known and acknowledged. Third, by those which join both together, namely that he is God and man at once: Rom. 1.3, 4; 9.5; Gal. 4.4; Acts 20.28; 1 John 1.7; Phil. 2.6, etc. Fourth, by those in which God is said to have been made flesh, to have assumed our nature, and to have been manifested in the flesh: John 1.14; Heb. 2.14; 1 Tim. 3.16. Fifth, finally, that there is nevertheless one person. Hence he is called the one Mediator, 1 Tim. 2.5; one Lord, Eph. 4.6; one Christ, who is God and man, [θεάνθρωπος], a word the Greek Fathers use, as Clement of Alexandria does at the beginning of his Exhortation to the Greeks. Hence Christ is called by theologians, with respect to his deity, [αὐτόθεος], self-God. We call Christ autotheon, that is, God from himself, and also the same God; but since in this question the first sense is the one in view, the word seems to be pointed in this way. Christ is so called by reason of his essence, not of his person; for as a person, the Son is from the Father, begotten of the Father, and so is not [αὐτίος], though he is self-God. And there are not three self-Gods, nor are they to be called gods in that sense, but three [αὐτόθεοι] ; just as they are not three consubstantials, but three consubstantial Gods. And God the Son is said to be from himself, not in the sense that he was produced from himself, but that he has the same divine essence as the Father, which is from no other God and does not make another God. You would rightly say that the Son has his essence from himself, joining "essence" to "from himself"; and you will not say, joining these to what precedes, that the Son, from himself, has the divine essence; but that the Son has essence from himself, that is, essence truly divine, unbegotten, without cause, self-subsisting, one and the same with the Father.

units.la: Exagitarunt istud in Calvino Pontificii, interque eos primi Bellarminus, Genebrardus, & Gregorius de Valentia ; postea super eodem disputatum etiam inter Gomarum, & Arminium ; successit Episcopius ; & huic Curcellæus : sed quum Arminius videretur à Gomaro maxime dissentire in voce, iste & rem aggressus, ὁμοούσιον, tantis viribus ac constantia ab Ecclesiâ Catholicâ semper defensum contra Hæreticos, impugnare palam cæpit, damnatam ab Ecclesiis Reformatis Valentini Gentilis doctrinam, quam ipsarum, malens sequi. Arminius enim Disp. de Persona Patris, & Filii, thes. XVI. agnoscit etiam Nicænorum Patrum ὁμοούσιον, rejecto ὁμοιουσίῳ, & convenientiam utriusque personæ, ratione unius ejusdemque naturæ & essentiæ, secundum quam Filius in forma Dei esse dicitur, Patrique æqualis, & juxta Nicænæ Synodi decretum ὁμοούσιον Patri, non ὁμοιούσιον. & in Epistolâ ad Uyttenbogardum, quemad- modum esse Filium à se, ita esse à se Deum pari modo dici haud posse, existimat, Deitatem tamen habere non aliam, quam quæ Patris, & à se sit, id est, à nullo : Pater enim est, inquit, principium filii, & non deitatis filii. Nam filii deitas est eadem, quæ Pa- tris ; at illa simpliciter est sine principio, & originis expers ; est tamen causa, quod filius ha- beat deitatem. Quare & istas loquendi formulas rejicit, essentia gignit, essentia gignitur. -- At quia filius habet ἴδιον[?] quæ est à nullo, hinc non sequitur, quod filius sit Deus ex se- ipso. --- Ista est enim orthodoxa formula, filius est Deus ea deitate, quæ est originis expers & à nullo : vel, ut ille, Polanus sc. loquitur, quæ est à se ipsa. Denique magis loquendi formam castigavit, quam rem. Quare conclusit tandem, abstinendum esse ab illis loquendi formulis, & omnino operam dandam, ut de tam altis mysteriis, non tantum cum Scri- ptura sentiamus, sed etiam loquamur, quantum fieri potest. Quod per nos licet, modo li- ceat per adversarios, quorum latibula & in istis, & per ista sæpe sunt deregenda. Gomari verò, præceptoris sui sententiam, singulari expressam diatribe, additis no-tis edidit, in parte prima Disputationum Theologicarum, præceptor, & Collega nu-per noster, Gisbertus Voetius, qui super argumento isto videatur.
units.tr: The Papists attacked this in Calvin, and among them first Bellarmine, Genebrardus and Gregory of Valencia. Later the same question was also disputed between Gomarus and Arminius, then Episcopius took it up, and after him Curcellaeus. But since Arminius seemed to differ from Gomarus chiefly over a word, Curcellaeus took up the matter itself and began openly to attack the ὁμοούσιον, which the Catholic Church had always defended against heretics with such strength and constancy. He preferred to follow the doctrine of Valentinus Gentilis, which the Reformed Churches had condemned, rather than their own. For Arminius, in his disputation On the Person of the Father and the Son, thesis 16, acknowledges the ὁμοούσιον of the Nicene Fathers, rejecting the ὁμοιουσίῳ, and acknowledges the agreement of both persons in respect of one and the same nature and essence, according to which the Son is said to be in the form of God and equal to the Father, and, according to the decree of the Nicene Synod, ὁμοούσιον with the Father, not ὁμοιούσιον. In his letter to Uytenbogaert he judges that, just as the Son cannot be said to be from himself, so God cannot in the same way be said to be from himself. Yet he holds that the deity of the Son is not other than that of the Father and is from himself, that is, from no one. For the Father, he says, is the principle of the Son, but not of the Son's deity. For the deity of the Son is the same as that of the Father, and that deity is simply without beginning and free of origin; it is, however, the cause of the Son's having deity. Wherefore he also rejects those formulas of speech, "the essence begets" and "the essence is begotten." But because the Son has his own [ἴδιον] deity, which is from no one, it does not follow that the Son is God from himself. For the orthodox formula is this: the Son is God by that deity which is free of origin and from no one; or, as Polanus puts it, which is from itself. In the end he corrected the form of speech rather than the matter itself. He therefore concluded that we should abstain from those formulas and should above all take pains to think and speak about such deep mysteries not only in agreement with Scripture but as far as possible. What is permitted to us should be permitted to our adversaries too, whose hiding-places in these matters, and through these very formulas, must often be dragged out. Gomarus's own opinion, expressed in a separate treatise with added notes, was published in the first part of the Theological Disputations by our teacher and recent colleague Gisbertus Voetius, who may be consulted on that subject.

units.la: Sed & diu ante idem in doctrinâ nostrâ oppugnarunt Socinianì[?], quiq; ejusdem sectæ, Ministri Transylvaniæ, in maledicentissimo libro, de falsa & vera unius Dei cognitione, lib. II. cap. x. tum, præter Socinum, Crellius, & Schlichtingius. Nec mirum, quum à seipso, & natura Deum esse, sciant reciprocari, ut de eodem utrumque vel affirmari debeat, vel negari. Sommerus contra Carolium, lib. II. cap. II. Si verum Deum intelligit, natura Deum, vel à seipso, concedam. Crellius quidem, in libro de Uno Deo Patre, lib. I. cap. II. ita:
units.tr: But long before this, the Socinians also attacked it in our doctrine, and the ministers of the same sect in Transylvania did so in a most abusive book, On the False and True Knowledge of the One God, book II, chapter 10; besides Socinus, Crellius and Schlichting did so as well. Nor is this surprising, since they know that being God from oneself and being God by nature are reciprocal, so that of the same thing either both must be affirmed or both denied. Sommer, against Carolus, book II, chapter 2: If he understands the true God, I shall grant that God is by nature, or from himself. Crellius, indeed, in the book On the One God the Father, book I, chapter 2, says the following:

units.la: Sed non deerunt qui dicant, Christum qui-dem qua Filius est, sed habita ratione personæ suæ, à Patre esse; non verò qua Deus est, seu habita ratione naturæ divinæ. Hujus enim re-spectu cum non minus, quam Patrem, esse à se-ipso, & ut loquuntur, αὐτόθεον. Unde conse-quatur, Patri præ Filio, qua Filius est, non qua Deus, ὑπεροχὴν seu præ-rogativam atque excellentiam quandam competere. Hanc verò non prohibere, quominus Christus Deus su-premus sit. Verum hac responsione nihil proficiunt. Nam illud ipsum, quod fatentur, suffi-cit nobis ad probandum id, quod non fatentur. Primò enim docuimus, Deo supremo neminem ulla ratione posse esse excellentiorem. At illi fatentur, faterique coguntur, Patrem Filio, qua Filius est, seu habita ratione personæ, excellen-tiorem esse. Adde, quod Deus supremus, nul-latenus, hoc est, nec ratione naturæ suæ, nec ratione personæ, (ut nunc ista cum adversariis ita distinguamus) ab alio est. Quicquid enim ab alio est, id à causa efficiente pendet. At Deus supremus nullatenus à causa efficiente pendet. Quare si Christus ratione personæ à Patre est; Deus supremus esse non potest. Præ-terea male illi personam Christi à naturâ ipsius divina ita distinguunt, ut dicant, illam à Pa-tre esse, hanc non esse. Siquidem persona divi-na nil est aliud, quam ipsa natura divina sub-sistens, ut libro secundo docebimus, & multi ex adversariis fatentur. Nam quod isti, cum qui-bus nunc nobis res est, ajunt, personam, qua talis est, nihil esse aliud, quam τρόπον ὑ-
units.tr: But there will not be lacking those who say that Christ, indeed as Son, but with regard to his person, is from the Father, and not as God, or with regard to the divine nature. For with respect to this he is no less than the Father from himself, and as they say, αὐτόθεον [autotheon]. Whence it follows that the Father has, before the Son as Son (not as God), a certain superiority or prerogative and excellence. This, however, does not prevent Christ from being the supreme God. But by this answer they gain nothing. For what they confess is enough for us to prove what they do not confess. For first we have taught that no one in any way can be more excellent than the supreme God. But they confess, and are compelled to confess, that the Father is more excellent than the Son as Son, or with regard to his person. Add that the supreme God is in no way from another, that is, neither in respect of his nature nor of his person (as we now distinguish these things against our adversaries). For whatever is from another depends on an efficient cause, but the supreme God does not depend on an efficient cause in any way. Therefore, if Christ with regard to his person is from the Father, he cannot be the supreme God. Moreover, they wrongly distinguish the person of Christ from his divine nature, so as to say that the one is from the Father and the other is not. For the divine person is nothing other than the divine nature itself subsisting, as we shall show in book II, and many of our adversaries confess this. For what those with whom we now have to deal say, that the person, as such, is nothing other than a mode [τρόπον ὑ-

units.la: Resp. I. Imo nulla proprie Patri præ Filio est ὑπεροχὴ, sive prærogativa, atque excellentia, neque id fatemur: quare ex eo argumentari ad aliud, adversum nos, haud licet. Nam excellentia, & sic ex-cellentius esse alio, sunt attributa atque af-sectiones essentiæ, non personalitatis aut personæ, ut sic, essentiæ contradistinctæ. Deo tribuitur excellentia, & debetur, su-pra omnes creaturas; sed illa est proprie-tas essentialis, Patri, Filio, Spiritui San-cto eadem, & pari modo conveniens. Non Patri, qua Patri, aut Filio, qua Filio, Spi-ritui Sancto, qua Spiritui, sed qua Deo. Hinc ergo nec majoritas, nec minoritas, excellentia vel inferioritas concludi de-bet. Primo enim docemus, Deo supre-mo neminem ulla ratione posse esse excel-lentiorem. Neque fatemur, aut fateri co-gimur, Patrem Filio, qua Filius est, seu habita ratione personæ, excellentiorem esse. II. Deus supremus, inquis, nec ra-tione naturæ suæ, nec ratione personæ: at, quando dicis Deum, supremum, na-turæ ratione dicis, non personæ: & sic non esse ab alio fatemur. Sed quidem per-sona, quæ est Deus supremus, non quia Deus supremus, sed qua persona aliqua, est ab alio. Eaque ratione negamus verum esse, quod quidquid ab alio est, id à causa pendeat efficiente. Atqui certe Deus su-premus nullatenus à causa efficiente pen-det. Sed nequaquam inde consequitur, si Christus ratione personę à Patre est, quod Deus ὑπάρξεως[?], hoc est, modum existendi, quem alii subsistentiam vocant; in eo mirum in modum falluntur. Poterant id vel inde discere, quod persona Patris generat, Filii generatur. At modus existentiae, seu subsistentiae, nec generat, nec per se generatur, sed ipsa natura subsistens. Accedit, quod tum ex aliis, tum imprimis ex Ioh. 10. 34. & seqq. satis appa-ret, Christum eatenus jure dici posse Deum, quatenus est Dei Filius. Docet enim ibi Christus exemplo eorum, quos Deus ipse olim Deos appellavit, se, quem Pater sanctificaverit, & in mundum miserit, multo magis appellari posse Filium Dei. Ubi eandem ob rationem conclu-dere poterat, se multo magis appellari posse Deum. quanquam non conclusit, ut hac ipsa ratione ostenderet, se sibi divinitatem supremam haud sumsisse, sed eo ipso, quod Deum Patrem suum appellasset, & se Filium ipsius hoc pacto asseruisset, à supremo Deo se distinxisse, ut alibi est à nobis explicatum. Certe illi ipsi quoque, quos in exemplum adduxit Christus, eandem ob caussam & Dii, & Filii Dei in eo scriptura loco, cujus partem Christus adducit, fuerunt appellati. Id tantum discriminis appella-tiones illæ habent, quod prior personas illas à Deo sermone per se non distinguit, posterior di-stinguit: illa dependentiam divinitatis à supremo numine non exprimit, utut divinitatem illam, quæ à supremo numine dependet, exprimat: hæc etiam dependentiam illam exprimit. Ex quibus intelligitur, si Christus, qua Filius Dei, à Patre est, & sic Pater ipso est excellen-tior; Christum etiam qua Deus est, à Patre esse, & sic Patrem ipso esse excellentiorem. Po-stremo, si Christus naturam suam non accepit à Patre, non fuit proprie generatus. Quisquis enim ab altero proprie generatur, naturam suam ab altero accipit. Atqui illi, uti & cæteri adversarii, omnino volunt atque urgent, Filium proprie à Patre generatum esse, & nisi id statuatur, Christum unigenitum Dei Filium non fore. Quare sua vineta cadunt, dum na-turam suam divinam Christum à Patre accepisse negant, sed personam tantum ab eo habere Deus supremus esse non possit. iii.
