Non di-cimus, quod persona nihil aliud sit quam τρόπος ὑπάρξεως, non id persona est, sed personalitas. Et natura subsistens dicitur generare, vel generari, non termi-native ad naturam, sed ad personam. A persona ad personam; non, à natura ad naturam. Id est, non natura Patris alia est, & Filii; generans alia, vel generata essentia, ut essentiæ ratione fit aliud & aliud, sed persona quidem est alia, & alia, & quamvis persona non sit sine natura vel essentia, in hac tamen non fuit facta vel terminata generatio, sed, cum communicatione ejusdem essentiæ, in diversâ per-sonâ. Non natura seorsim, nec persona seorsim generat, sed uti distincta sunt natura & persona, ita generatio & communicatio, tum generationis subjectum & terminus. Natura, per generationem, communicatur; generatio autem personæ est. Persona generatur, non natura. Persona non communicatur, sed generatur. Et subjectum generationis est quidem natura, quæ hoc modo communicatur, sed terminus est persona, vel personalitas. Termini voce utimur, in signo rationis, non rei, improprie, quia ita hic cogimur balbutire. iv. Constat ex Ioann. x. 34. Christum eatenus jure dici Deum, quatenus est Dei Filius. Et hoc si verum, uti omnino est, tantundem est ac si Christus ipse aperte ita concluderet, quatenus nempe id ex loco illo apparet. Dixerit autem Christus, an non, res arguit, quatenus est Dei Filius, jure eum dici posse ac debere Deum. Ut causa, cur id aperte non concluserit, ista nequeat esse, quod sibi divinitatem supremam haud sumeret: quod & antecedentibus satis manifeste repugnat, quibus se unum cum Patre asseruerat; & hinc, quod ex loco isto satis apparere ait Adversarius, Christum eatenus jure dici posse Deum, quatenus est Dei Filius. Quod cum non quadrat, neque ullo afferunt. quamquam nec in eo satis sibi semper constant, ut ab aliis adversariis est animad-versum. modo sequitur argumentum, quod Chri-stus se Filium appellans Dei, eo distingue-re à supremo Deo voluerit. Quod nemo unquam est probaturus. Filium se nominans, distinguit à Patre, personam a persona, non se à supremo Deo, quia se & unum aperte dixerat cum Patre, & σεαυτὸν[?] Θεόν.
units.tr: Reply I. Indeed, there is no preeminence [ὑπεροχή] of the Father over the Son properly so called, nor any prerogative or excellence, and we do not concede it. So it is not permitted to argue from this to something else against us. For excellence, and being more excellent than another, are attributes and affections of the essence, not of personality or of the person as such, as distinct from the essence. Excellence is ascribed to God and is due to him above all creatures, but it is an essential property, the same and equally belonging to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. It belongs not to the Father as Father, or to the Son as Son, or to the Holy Spirit as Spirit, but to God. Hence neither greater nor lesser, nor excellence or inferiority, ought to be inferred. For first, we teach that no one can in any way be more excellent than the supreme God. Nor do we confess, or are we compelled to confess, that the Father is more excellent than the Son as the Son is, or in respect of the person. II. You say that the supreme God is neither by reason of his nature nor by reason of his person. But when you say God supreme, you speak by reason of nature, not of person, and so we do not confess that he is from another. Yet the person who is the supreme God is not from another because he is supreme God, but as some person. On this ground we deny that it is true that whatever is from another depends on an efficient cause. Yet certainly the supreme God does not depend on an efficient cause in any way. But it by no means follows from this that, if Christ is from the Father by reason of his person, then God [ὑπάρξεως], that is, the mode of existing, which others call subsistence; in this they are wonderfully mistaken, and the supreme God cannot be such. They could have learned this at least from the fact that the person of the Father begets and the person of the Son is begotten. But the mode of existence or subsistence neither begets nor is itself begotten; it is the subsisting nature itself. Besides, it is sufficiently clear, both from other passages and especially from John 10:34 and following, that Christ can rightly be called God only so far as he is the Son of God. For there Christ teaches, by the example of those whom God himself formerly called gods, that he, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, can much more be called the Son of God. There he could have concluded by the same reasoning that he could much more be called God, although he did not conclude it. He did this so as to show that he had not assumed supreme divinity for himself, but, by the very fact that he called God his Father and so asserted himself to be his Son, he distinguished himself from the supreme God, as we have explained elsewhere. Certainly those very persons whom Christ adduced as examples were called both gods and sons of God in that passage of Scripture, part of which Christ cites, for the same reason. The only difference between those appellations is this: the former does not by its own wording distinguish those persons from God, while the latter does distinguish them. The former does not express the dependence of divinity on the supreme deity, though it expresses a divinity that depends on the supreme deity; the latter also expresses that dependence. From these points it is understood that if Christ, as Son of God, is from the Father, and so the Father is more excellent than he, then Christ also as God is from the Father, and so the Father is more excellent than he. Finally, if Christ did not receive his nature from the Father, he was not properly begotten. For whoever is properly begotten by another receives his nature from another. But they, like the other adversaries, insist and urge entirely that the Son was properly begotten of the Father, and that unless this is granted, Christ would not be the only begotten Son of God. So their own arguments fall, while they deny that Christ received his divine nature from the Father and say that he has only the person from him. The supreme God cannot be such. iii. We do not say that the person is nothing other than the mode of existence; the person is not that, but the personality is. A subsisting nature is said to beget or be begotten not terminatively with respect to the nature, but with respect to the person: from person to person, not from nature to nature. That is, the nature of the Father is not another, and the begetting essence is not another, or the begotten essence another, as happens with respect to essence when one essence differs from another. Rather the person is one and another, and although the person does not exist without nature or essence, the generation was not made or terminated in this nature, but, with communication of the same essence, in a different person. Neither nature alone nor person alone begets; just as nature and person are distinct, so generation and communication are distinct, as also the subject and the terminus of generation. The nature is communicated by generation, but generation belongs to the person. The person is begotten, not the nature. The person is not communicated, but begotten. The subject of generation is indeed the nature, which is communicated in this way, but the terminus is the person or personality. We use the word terminus in the sense of a sign of reason, not of the thing, and improperly, because in this matter we are compelled to stammer in this way. iv. It is established from John 10:34 that Christ can rightly be called God only so far as he is the Son of God. And if this is true, as it entirely is, it amounts to the same as if Christ himself had plainly concluded thus, namely, to the extent that this appears from that passage. Whether Christ said it, however, the matter itself shows: insofar as he is the Son of God, he can and ought to be rightly called God. The reason he did not openly conclude this cannot be that he would not assume supreme divinity for himself; this is clearly contrary even to what precedes, where he had asserted that he was one with the Father. And from this, the adversary says that it sufficiently appears from that passage that Christ can rightly be called God only so far as he is the Son of God. Since this does not fit, nor do they bring any proof for it, though they are not always consistent with themselves in this, as other adversaries have noted, it only follows that the argument, that Christ in calling himself the Son of God wished to distinguish himself by this from the supreme God, is one that no one will ever prove. In calling himself Son he distinguishes himself from the Father, person from person, not himself from the supreme God, because he had plainly said that he and the Father are one, and called himself God [αὐτὸν Θεόν].

units.la: Iique, quos Christus illo loco in exemplum adduxit, quod eos Scriptura Deos nominasset, & Dei filios, non certe seipsos aut unum vel eundem ἐν, vel αὐτὸν Θεόν[?] dixissent, quod de se Christus: ut non illorum exemplum attulerit, quasi omnino simile, sed latis ad diluendam calumniam faciens, quod non confestim blasphemaret, qui diceretur Deus, aut Dei Filius.
units.tr: And those whom Christ in that passage adduced as examples, because Scripture had called them gods and sons of God, certainly did not call themselves one [ἕν] or God himself [αὐτὸν Θεόν], as Christ did of himself. So he did not bring their example as though it were altogether similar; rather he did so to refute the calumny, namely that one who was called God, or Son of God, would not immediately be blaspheming.

units.la: In sequentibus obscurior est Crellius, ut quid sibi velit, haud satis pateat, quam priorem innuat appellationem, quam posteriorem, quod dependentiam divinitatis à supremo numine non exprimat, & tamen divinitatem, quae à supremo numine dependet. Nam verae divinitatis à supremo numine dependentia nulla est. Neque in censum τῶν λεγομένων Θεῶν[?] Christi vera Deitas reduci potest aut debet. Ex quibus intelligitur, quod, quamvis Christus, qua Filius Dei, à Patre est, Pater tamen ipso non fit excellentior: nec Christum, qua Deus est, à Patre esse, vel quod sic Pater ipso fit excellentior. Quandoquidem & eandem habet cum Patre Deitatem, quae est à seipsa, id est, non ab alio aliquo, quare eandemque excellentiam: & excellentia non personae respectu dicitur, sed essentiae, ut quae est attributum hujus, non illius. Postremo Christus, qua Dei Filius, naturam accepit à Patre, uti ab eo genitus Filius, sed naturam eandem, quae Patris, sive quae est à se, quod essentiae respectu dicitur, & est attributum essentiale, non personale. Quare non naturam Christum à Patre accepisse negamus, neque ei obloquimur, quando personam tantum ab eo habere asserimus: quia, uti ipse ante dixit, persona est natura subsistens, & id modo significatum volumus, generationem terminari in personam, non in essentiam, vel non alterius essentiae aut essentiatum esse Filium, sed in communione ejusdem individuae essentiae generatum, personā alium, non essentia, quamvis non nudam tantum personalitatem, sed cum ea naturam eandem accepit in persona alia.
units.tr: In what follows, Crellius is rather obscure, so that it is not sufficiently clear what he means, namely that the former appellation suggests something other than the latter: that it does not express the dependence of divinity on the supreme deity, and yet it expresses a divinity that depends on the supreme deity. For there is no dependence of true divinity on the supreme deity. Nor can or ought the true deity of Christ be counted among those called gods [τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν]. From these points it is understood that, although Christ as Son of God is from the Father, the Father is not made more excellent than he, nor is Christ, as God, from the Father, nor does it follow that the Father is thereby more excellent than he. Since he has the same deity with the Father, which is from itself, that is, not from any other, and therefore the same excellence, and excellence is said with respect not to the person but to the essence, as it is an attribute of this and not of that. Finally, Christ as Son of God received his nature from the Father, as the Son begotten by him, but the same nature which is the Father's, or which is from itself, which is said with respect to essence, and is an essential, not a personal, attribute. Therefore we do not deny that Christ received his nature from the Father, nor do we contradict anyone when we assert that he has only the person from him; because, as he himself said before, the person is a subsisting nature, and we want this only to be signified: that generation terminates in the person, not in the essence, or that the Son is not of another essence or of an essence that has been made another, but is begotten in communion with the same undivided essence, another in person, not in essence, although he received with the person not merely bare personality, but along with it the same nature in another person.

units.la: Ex illis nunc facile solvi possunt quaecunque, eadem fere, Schlichtingius, adversus Christum αὐτοθεὸν protulit, in Disp. contra Meisnerum, de Trinitate, pag. 375. & deinceps. Pag. 377.
units.tr: From these points, nearly all the objections that Schlichting, in his disputation against Meisner on the Trinity (p. 375 and following), brought against Christ as autotheos [αὐτοθεὸν] can now easily be resolved.

units.la: Et sane Socino sufficit, si fateamini, Filium, quatenus unus cum Patre Deus est, essentiam habere improductam; quatenus enim unus cum Patre Deus est, hactenus & simpliciter Deus est, nisi forte plures uno Deos esse dicatis: quatenus igitur Deus est, improductus est, & à se ipso Deus est. At si Filius à se ipso Deus est, ubi erit praerogativa Patris? ubi tot Theologorum, qui etsi Trinitatis hanc opinionem tutati sunt, contrarium tamen senserunt, ubi ipsius Niceni concilii, quod Christum Deum de Deo; lumen de lumine esse dicit, auctoritas?
units.tr: And indeed it is enough for Socinus, if you grant that the Son, insofar as he is one God with the Father, has an unproduced essence. For insofar as he is one God with the Father, so far he is simply God, unless perhaps you say that there are several Gods besides the one. Insofar, then, as he is God, he is unproduced and is God from himself. But if the Son is God from himself, where will the prerogative of the Father be? Where is the authority of so many theologians who, although they defended this doctrine of the Trinity, nevertheless held the contrary? Where is the authority of the Nicene Council itself, which says that Christ is God of God, light of light?

units.la: Resp. Duo potissimum urget, quod Filius, si genitus, debet habere essentiam à Patre productam; id est, aliam à Patre, alioqui non futurus Filius, quum extra essentiam suam Filius esse non possit. Deinde, si non habeat essentiam productam Filius, nullam fore Patris, præ Filio, praerogativam. Ad quae ita respondemus. Nullam hic quidem locum habere veram & propriam productionem, quae aut rei ex nihilo, aut novae ortum significat, & rebus creatis atque naturalibus aptior nomenclatura[?] est,quam Deo. Schlichtingius postmodum pag.385. fi vera est productio, temporalis est, id est, in tempore fit : quidquid enim producitur, in tempore producitur. Quare alio sensu vox ista hic adhiberi debet, quam illic, quum generatio in divinis non fit novae rei productio, vel effectio aliqua libera actione a Deo instituta, sed actio Patris aeterna, naturalis, necessaria, & in ejusdem essentiae communicatione sita, non formatione novae. Habet ergo improductam essentiam Filius, quia eandem cum Patre. Eaque ratione, quatenus unus cum Patre Deus est, essentiam habet improductam ; quatenus enim unus cum Patre Deus, hactenus & simpliciter Deus est, nisi forte plures uno Deos esse dicas : quatenus igitur Deus est, improductus, & a seipso Deus est.
units.tr: Reply. They press mainly two points: first, that the Son, if begotten, must have an essence produced by the Father, that is, one different from the Father's, since otherwise he would not be Son, the Son being unable to exist outside his own essence; second, that if the Son does not have a produced essence, there will be no prerogative of the Father over the Son. To these we answer as follows. Here there is no true and proper production, which signifies either the origin of a thing from nothing or the origin of something new, a term more fitting for created and natural things than for God. Schlichting later says (p. 385): if production is true, it is temporal, that is, it takes place in time, for whatever is produced is produced in time. The word must therefore be taken here in a different sense than there, since generation in the divine nature is not the production of a new thing, or some effect brought about by a free action instituted by God, but an eternal, natural and necessary action of the Father, consisting in the communication of the same essence and not in the forming of something new. The Son therefore has an unproduced essence because it is the same as the Father's. And for this reason, insofar as he is one God with the Father, he has an unproduced essence; for insofar as he is one God with the Father, so far he is simply God, unless perhaps you say that there are several Gods besides the one. Insofar, then, as he is God, he is unproduced, and is God from himself.

units.la: Deinde , quod ad praerogativam Patris, hanc aeque minus in Patre agnoscimus supra Filium, ac in Filio productionem aliquam inferiorem a Patre. Non est hic proprie praerogativa vel excellentia, solummodo ordo, ut Pater fit prima persona, Filius fecunda, neutra alteri major vel minor. Praerogativa, uti excellentia Deo tribuitur, in ordine ad creaturas, estque attributum essentiale, non in Deo ipso locum habet in ordine & relatione mutua ad personas.
units.tr: Next, as for the prerogative of the Father, we recognise this no less in the Father over the Son than we recognise in the Son some inferior production from the Father. Here there is properly no prerogative or excellence, only order: the Father is the first person, the Son the second, and neither is greater or less than the other. Prerogative, like excellence, is ascribed to God in relation to creatures, and is an essential attribute; it has no place in God himself, in the order and mutual relation of the persons.

units.la: Et quod Nicaenum Concilium habet de Christo, Deus de Deo, lumen de lumine, perfonaliter accipiendum est, non essentialiter. Si enim effentia Filii non est genita, nec producta, inquit, nec Filius est genitus, atque productus. Effentia Filii ambigue dicitur. Vel enim notat essentiam in Filio formaliter spectatam, quae nec producta nec genita est, sed eadem quae Patris. Vel personam Filii notat, quae est genita. Fiat nunc argumentum: Si effentia in Filio non est proprie & formaliter genita, ergo nec Filius, seu persona Filii. Negatur. Nam Filius extra suam essentiam esse non potest. Iterum argumentum: Si Filius extra suam essentiam esse non potest, ergo, non genita in Filio sua formaliter effentia, ipse vel ejus persona genita esse non potest. Negatur. Namque ejusdem essentiae genitus est a Patre Filius. Num enim, rogat, persona Filii aliud quiddam est, quam ipsa Filii effentia individua ? Non inquam, sed tamen effentia potest ac debet distingui, ab ipsa ejus persona: quae effentia, & perfonalitate sua, ut ita loquamur, constat. Num potest persona aliqua produci seu gigni, & tamen effentia illius non gigni ? Omnino vero, in generatione divina, ubi Pater ejusdem essentiae suae communione genuit sibi Filium. Et mysterium istud nulla ex inferioribus regula aut exemplo adstringitur aut mensuratur. Relatio enim omnis requirit fundamentum: fundamentum autem relationis inter Patrem & Filium generatio est: generationis vero subjectum effentia est. At una numero effentia fui ipsius respectu generare, & generari nequaquam potest. Qui igitur relationem Patris & Filii unius ejufdemque essentiae respectu ponunt; perinde faciunt, ac fi domum esse dicant, fundamentum omne amoveant. Generationis subjectum effentia est: non simpliciter spectata, sed in communicatione, five generatione. Et effentia, fui ipsius respectu, neque generat, neque generatur. Relationem Patris denique & Filii non ponimus unius ejufdemque essentiae respectu, sed generationis. Itâ pergere atque sequi Adversarios nostros debemus, in retundendis importunis interrogationibus: absque quibus effet, ut in nuda fidei simplicitate, & sanctâ [illegible, ~3 letters] defensione acquiescere mallemus, quam spineta illa ingredi, quae tamen ipsa, ut omnis tergiversandi ansa illis auferatur, sic etiam caedi debere videntur. Porro Calvini verba adfert, eaque contradictione laborare frustra ostendere satagit.
units.tr: And what the Nicene Council says of Christ, God of God, light of light, must be understood personally, not essentially. For if the essence of the Son is not begotten nor produced, it says, neither is the Son begotten and produced. The phrase "the essence of the Son" is ambiguous. For it either denotes the essence considered formally in the Son, which is neither produced nor begotten but is the same as the Father's, or it denotes the person of the Son, which is begotten. Let us now construct an argument: if the essence in the Son is not properly and formally begotten, then neither is the Son, or the person of the Son. Denied. For the Son cannot exist outside his essence. Again the argument: if the Son cannot exist outside his essence, then, since his formal essence is not begotten in the Son, the Son himself or his person cannot be begotten. Denied. For the Son is begotten of the Father, of the same essence. For does the person of the Son, he asks, differ at all from the Son's individual essence? No, I say, yet the essence can and must be distinguished from his person itself, which essence consists also, so to speak, of its personality. Can any person be produced or begotten while its essence is not begotten? Certainly, in the divine generation, where the Father, by communion of his own essence, begot the Son for himself. And this mystery is bound by and measured by no rule or example from lower things. For every relation requires a foundation; the foundation of the relation between Father and Son is generation; but the subject of generation is the essence. Yet one numerically identical essence can in no way generate or be generated with respect to itself. Therefore those who posit a relation of Father and Son with respect to one and the same essence do the same as those who say there is a house and remove every foundation. The subject of generation is the essence: not considered simply, but in communication, or generation. And the essence, with respect to itself, neither generates nor is generated. Finally, we do not posit the relation of Father and Son with respect to one and the same essence, but with respect to generation. Thus we ought to proceed and follow our opponents in repelling troublesome questions; without these we would prefer to rest in the bare simplicity of faith and its holy [illegible] defence, rather than enter those thickets, which yet, so that every excuse for evasion is taken from them, seem to need to be cut through as well. Further, he brings forward Calvin's words, and tries in vain to show that they labour under a contradiction.

units.la: Ipsum Calvinum cur non audiamus? Quum de Filio fine Patris respectu simpliciter loqui-
units.tr: Why should we not hear Calvin himself? When we speak of the Son simply, without respect to the Father—

units.la: Contradictionem, quae in verbis Calvini non deprehenditur, iis mire affingit :
units.tr: He attributes to Calvin's words, in a remarkable way, a contradiction which is not found in them:

units.la: Tom. 2. mur, bene & proprie ipsum a se esse asserimus: & ideo unicum vocamus principium: quum vero relationem, quae illi cum Patre est, notamus, Patrem Filii principium merito facimus. Poteratne Calvinus clarius mentem suam exponere, id est, apertius sibi ipsi contradicere? quid enim hoc aliud est, quam si diceret; Filius quatenus per seipsum consideratur, sine relatione ad Patrem, id est, quatenus consideratur, ut improductus, eatenus a se ipso est, nec ab ullo est productus: quatenus autem consideratur cum relatione ad Patrem, h. e. quatenus consideratur, ut a Patre genitus, eatenus non est a se ipso, sed a Patre. Num vero haec contradictio non est? Nonne simul Filium & productum esse asserit, & productum esse negat? tionem, quam exserte Calvinus expressit,
units.tr: Vol. 2: we say, well and properly, that he is from himself; and therefore we call him the sole principle. When, however, we take note of the relation which he has with the Father, we rightly make the Father the principle of the Son. "Could Calvin have expressed his mind more clearly, that is, contradicted himself more openly? For what else is this than if he had said: the Son, insofar as he is considered through himself, without relation to the Father, that is, insofar as he is considered as unproduced, is so far from himself and is produced by no one; but insofar as he is considered in relation to the Father, that is, insofar as he is considered as begotten of the Father, so far he is not from himself but from the Father. Is this not a contradiction? Does he not assert at once that the Son is produced and deny that he is produced?" tion, which Calvin expressly set forth,

units.la: neque enim iste illorum sensus est, Filius, quatenus per seipsum consideratur, sine relatione ad Patrem, id est, quatenus consideratur ut improductus, eatenus a se ipso est, nec ab ullo producto; sed hic, quod Filius, in mera sua consideratur sententia, sine illo Filii respectu & relatione ad Patrem, est a se & non ab alio, sive eam habet essentiam, quae non venit ab alio; quatenus vero consideratur cum relatione ad Patrem, est a Patre: non autem ut, quatenus consideratur a Patre genitus, non fit a Patre genitus. Qui sensus foret futilis, non autem contradictorius. Neque enim simul afferere Filium esse genitum, & non genitum, secundum diversam rationem, contradictorium est: cum inter leges
units.tr: For that is not their meaning: that the Son, considered in his bare sense, without that respect of the Son and relation to the Father, is from himself and not from another, or has an essence which does not come from another; but insofar as he is considered in relation to the Father, he is from the Father. It is not that, insofar as he is considered as begotten by the Father, he is not begotten by the Father. That sense would be silly, not contradictory. For to assert at once that the Son is begotten and is not begotten, according to different aspects, is not a contradiction, since among the laws

units.la: oppositionis, uti notum, requiratur, ut sit ad idem, & secundum idem. Quod hic aliter se habet.
units.tr: of opposition, as is known, it is required that it be in the same respect and according to the same thing. Here it stands otherwise.

units.la: Sed sive personam Calvinus, sive essentiam Filii, duplici ratione considerat, vel absolute & in se, vel respective ad Patrem: illo modo considerata, sive persona, sive essentia dicas, nil refert, Filium a se ipso esse statuit; hoc vero modo considerata, Patrem Filii principium esse concedit. Verum haec, ut diximus, aperta contradictio est.
units.tr: But whether Calvin considers the person or the essence of the Son in a twofold way, either absolutely and in itself, or with respect to the Father: considered in the first way, whether you call it person or essence makes no difference, he holds that the Son is from himself; considered in the second way, he concedes that the Father is the principle of the Son. But this, as we have said, is a plain contradiction.

units.la: Jam certe pervertit manifestissime Calvini mentem Adversarius, qui quidem Filium duplici ratione considerat, non sive personam, sive essentiam Filii duplici citer. In Filio considerat vel essentiam, & hanc [absolute ac in se; vel personam, respective ad Patrem. Ut prorsus male, ex sententia Calvini, nil referre dicat, personam dicas, sive essentiam. Et quod utrovis modo Filium a seipso esse statuat. Qui id demum intelligi vult, habita essentiae divinae ratione in se, dici αὐτόθεον[?]: personae autem ratione, & in relatione ad Patrem spectato Filio, Patrem Filii principium esse, seu originem, vocibus his lata significatione, & non ut a creaturis ad Deum proprie, vel pari utrobique modo acceptis.
units.tr: Now the Adversary certainly and most plainly distorts Calvin's meaning. He considers the Son in a twofold way, but not, as he says, whether the person or the essence of the Son is meant. In the Son he considers either the essence, and this absolutely and in itself, or the person, with respect to the Father. So it is quite wrong to say, by Calvin's view, that it makes no difference whether you call it person or essence, and that Calvin holds the Son to be from himself in either way. Whoever wants this to be understood must take it this way: considering the divine essence in itself, the Son is called autotheos [αὐτόθεον]; but considering the person, and the Son in relation to the Father, the Father is the principle, or origin, of the Son. These words are used in a broad sense, and not in the proper sense in which they are applied to God from creatures, or in the same sense on both sides.

units.la: Si illam ipsam naturam habet Filius, quam Pater, a nemine ortam aut dependentem; Ergo essentiam seu naturam divinam non habet ab alio, sed a se ipso. Nam essentiam a nemine ortam aut dependentem habere, & eam habere ab alio, contradictoria sunt, & sese perimunt. alio, sunt contradictoria: negatur id quoque. Etenim ab alio habere, attribuitur vel essentiae, vel personae: haec ab alio est, non illa. Persona secunda a Patre, per generationem, accepit essentiam eandem, quae a nemine orta vel dependens. Aliud est considerare, quin, aut quid acceperit. Filius ab alio accepit, sed quod accepit, idipsum, naturae suae ratione, a nemine est. Neque haec contradictoria, quia non ad idem, sed diversimode accipiuntur. Sophisma ergo est compositionis & divisionis, Filius habet ab alio essentiam, prout vel sic accipis, Filius habet ab alio, essentiam;
units.tr: If the Son has that very nature which the Father has, a nature not begotten of anyone nor dependent on anyone, then he does not have the divine essence or nature from another, but from himself. For to have an essence not begotten of anyone or dependent on anyone, and to have it from another, are contradictory and destroy each other. Are contradictory: this too is denied. For to have something from another is ascribed either to the essence or to the person. The person is from another, not the essence. The second person, by generation, receives from the Father the same essence, which is not begotten or dependent on anyone. It is one thing to consider what he has received, and another to consider that he has received it. The Son has received from another, but what he has received is, by reason of its nature, from no one. Nor are these contradictory, since they are not taken in the same respect but in different ways. It is therefore a sophism of composition and division: "The Son has from another the essence," according to whether you take it so, or "The Son has from another, the essence."

units.la: Resp. Negatur utriusque argumenti Major propositio, seu consequentia: Si habet essentiam Filius a nemine ortam aut dependentem: ergo non est ab alio. Deinde: habere essentiam independen-tem, nec ortam ab alio, & eam habere ab alio, sunt contradictoria: negatur id quoque. vel, Filius habet, ab alio essentiam: ut ab alio conjungatur cum essentia, vel cum Filio. Clare dicendum, Filius habet ab alio, Patre videlicet, essentiam cum Patre eandem, seu quae non est ab alio.
units.tr: Answer: the major premise of each argument, or the inference, is denied: "If the Son has an essence not begotten of anyone or dependent on anyone, then he is not from another." Next, to have an independent essence, not begotten from another, and to have it from another, are contradictory: this too is denied. Or "The Son has from another the essence," where "from another" is joined either with the essence or with the Son. It must clearly be said that the Son has from another, namely from the Father, an essence the same as the Father's, that is, one which is not from another.

units.la: Porro, nam insequendus nobis Adversarius, quousque aliquid argumenti nectere videtur:
units.tr: Next, since the Adversary seems to be building up some argument, let us follow him further.

units.la: Nec video quorsum hic istam personae diver-sitatem, una numero essentia posita fingatis, cum idem dicere possitis de persona, quod de natura, nempe, licet eadem sit Patris & Filii persona; Filium tamen personam hanc non habere a seipso, sed a Patre. Praeterea, dic quaeso, num personam Filii idem re ipsa esse putes, quod ejus essentiam divinam, num quidpiam diversum? Si idem, non minus Filius eandem cum Patre personam habebit, quam eandem cum illo habet essentiam: proinde tam ratione personae, quam ratione essentiae a Patre genitus & productus non erit. Si diversum, quaero, num istius ipsius respectu Filius erit Deus, nec ne? Si prius dicas, poterit aliquis esse Deus extra divinam essentiam: imo duplex erit Deus, tum ratione personae, tum ratione essentiae. Si posterius dicas, non tantum Filius respectu personae non erit αὐτόθεος[?], seu per seipsum Deus, sed simpliciter ne Deus quidem ullus. Quomodo ergo verum erit, cum hoc sensu esse Deum de Deo, Patrumque Nicenorum hanc fuisse mentem?
units.tr: Nor do I see why you invent this diversity of person with one numerically identical essence, since you could say of the person the same thing you say of the nature, namely that although the person of the Father and the Son is the same, the Son does not have this person from himself, but from the Father. Moreover, tell me, pray, do you think the person of the Son is really the same thing as his divine essence, or something different? If the same, the Son will have the same person with the Father no less than he has the same essence; so he will not be begotten and produced by the Father as much by reason of the person as by reason of the essence. If different, I ask, will the Son be God with respect to that very thing or not? If you say the former, someone could be God outside the divine essence: indeed God would be twofold, both by reason of the person and by reason of the essence. If you say the latter, the Son will not only not be autotheos [αὐτόθεος], that is, God through himself, with respect to the person, but will simply not be God at all. How then will it be true that in this sense he is God of God, and that this was the mind of the Nicene Fathers?

units.la: Non nos fingimus personae diversitatem, una numero essentia: nisi & Johannes fingere dicendus sit, qui tres personas, testes, nominavit, eosque unum esse; & Christus, se a Patre aliam personam, & quoque unum esse. Quare non idem de persona dicere fas est, quod de natura, quodve eadem Patris & Filii sit persona. Praeterea, putamus Filii personam idem, quod ad essentiam, & realiter esse cum natura: formaliter aut modaliter ab essentia diversam. Id est, diversas quidem naturae, & personae, ut sic, esse definitiones, non tamen rei substantia differre. Si idem, inquit, non minus Filius eandem cum Patre personam habebit, quam eandem cum illo habet essentiam: imo si prorsus & omni modo idem. Sed hoc negamus. Pergit: si diversum, num istius ipsius respectu Filius erit Deus? Formaliter, quasi in hoc respectu vel modo singularis constituenda foret Deitas? negatur. In re tamen ipsa ac substantia, sensu identico, istius respectu Filius est Deus, quia persona talis non potest non esse Deus: non duplex Deus, tum ratione essentiae; sed persona, ratione essentiae, quam connotat, Deus. Infert, quod tum Filius, respectu personae non erit αὐτόθεος. concedimus: nam αὐτόθεος est, uti nunc aliquoties dictum, ratione essentiae, non personae.
units.tr: We do not invent a diversity of person with one numerically identical essence; otherwise John too would have to be said to invent it, who named three persons, witnesses, and said that they are one; and Christ too, who said that he is another person from the Father, and also that they are one. Therefore it is not right to say of the person what we say of the nature, or that the person of the Father and the Son is the same. Moreover, we hold that the person of the Son is the same as the essence, and really one with the nature, but formally or modally different from the essence. That is, the definitions of nature and of person are indeed different, but they do not differ in the substance of the thing. "If the same," he says, "the Son will have the same person with the Father no less than he has the same essence": indeed, if it were the same altogether and in every way. But this we deny. He goes on: "If different, will the Son be God with respect to that very thing?" Formally, as if a singular Godhead were to be constituted in this respect or mode? Denied. Yet in the thing itself and in substance, in the same sense, the Son is God with respect to that, because such a person cannot but be God: not a twofold God, by reason of the essence, but the person, by reason of the essence which it connotes, is God. He infers that then the Son, with respect to the person, will not be autotheos [αὐτόθεος]. We concede this: for autotheos [αὐτόθεος], as has been said several times now, is by reason of the essence, not of the person.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: SECTION THREE.

units.la: AD argumenta & objectiones quod spectat Adversariorum, contra Christi Deitatem, & nostram de ea fidem, adferunt multas quidem, sed inanes, & easdem quas antiqui Haeretici contra eundem articulum olim adduxere, quasque in eadem disputatione Muhammedani, uti patet, cum ex aliis, tum ex Samlate Isphachane, Persa, in epistola ad Monachum Meletium, cui pro Meletio, Ann. MCCCLX. respondit Iohannes Cantacutzenus Rex, in Orationibus & Apologiis, quae una cum Alkorano Latino, editae, ex translatione Rudolphi Gualteri, Ann. MDL[?]. Omnia omnium argumenta contra Christum collegit Crellius, libris duobus, de uno Deo Patre, sed quibus plene responsum a Bisterfeldio, & Botsacco, & Placaeo. Quinquaginta fere sunt illius argumenta, contra Christi Deitatem, quæ ad quinque commode referi-mus. I. Quod solus Pater dicitur Deus. II. Christus autem à Deo distinguitur. III. Aliqua sibi negat Christus divina, & Deo propria. IV. Atque ex adverso alia ei competunt humana prorsus, & cum Deitate non bene concilianda. V. Quod passim refertur inter creaturas. VI. Denique ex ratione, quod in unâ personâ nequeunt esse duæ naturæ. De singulis breviter videamus. Namque hæc tam sæpe à viris doctis & eximiis tractata, quia arcem causæ petunt & fidei, atque in eo argumento supra alia Adversarii multi sunt & prolixi, ut breviores esse ideo liceat: non autem prorsus præterire, quia & hæc pars ad plenam materiæ tractationem addenda, ut non mi-nus necessaria, fuit.
units.tr: As for the arguments and objections that our opponents bring against Christ's deity and our faith in it, they offer many, but empty ones, and the same ones that the ancient heretics once raised against this article. The Mohammedans also raised them in the same dispute, as is clear both from others and from Samlates Isphachanus, a Persian, in his letter to the monk Meletius. Ioannes Cantacuzenus the King answered that letter on Meletius's behalf in his Orations and Apologies, which were published along with the Latin Koran, from the translation of Rudolph Walter, in the year 1550 [?]. Crellius gathered all the arguments of everyone against Christ in two books, On the One God the Father. Bisterfeld, Botsacus and Placaeus have answered them fully. Crellius has nearly fifty arguments against Christ's deity, which we conveniently refer to five headings: (I) that only the Father is called God; (II) that Christ is distinguished from God; (III) that Christ denies to himself things that are divine and proper to God; (IV) that, on the other hand, things wholly human, and not easily reconciled with deity, belong to him; (V) that he is commonly listed among the creatures; (VI) and finally, from reason, that two natures cannot exist in one person. Let us look briefly at each. These matters have been treated so often by learned and distinguished men, because they go to the heart of the cause and of the faith, and because on this question the opponents are many and long-winded, that I may be allowed to be briefer here. Still, I must not pass them over altogether, since this part, no less necessary than the others, had to be added to a full treatment of the subject.

units.la: Primò illa objiciunt Scripturæ loca Adversarii, quibus Pater Deus, & solus verus Deus dicitur. Joann. xvii. 3. 1 Cor. viii. 6. Ephes. iv. 6. Ita disputant Ministri Transylvaniæ, lib. II. de Dei cognit. cap. v. Socinus, contra Posnanienses. Catechesis Racoviensis, pag. 57. Ostorodus, contra Tradelum, cap. III. & contra Ravenspergerum. Smalcius, contra Grawerum, pag. 10. Volkelius. pag. 458. Crellius. omnes. Locus ita habet Joann. xvii. 3. hæc autem est vita æterna, ut cognoscant σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν [?], & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Totam vim argumenti constituunt in eo, quod Christus Patrem alloquens, eum non modo Deum, sed Deum unicum appellat, se proinde, cum cæteris, exclusō. Resp. I. Observare oportet, quo hæc loco Christus dixit, & statu, humiliationis nempe & pro conditione suâ œconomicâ, uti Veteres loquuntur, qua, quæ depressionem sui testantur, solet significare, non quæ gloriam: nam Christus orans hæc dixit, verf. 1. & de iis, quæ ex Patris mandato in terris habuerat peragenda. Interim tamen nec neglexit alteram suam conditionem, quam subindicavit potius, quam ut nunc prædicaret, commemorans se à Patre exivisse, omnia Patris sua esse, se unum cum Patre, & gloriosum apud eum fuisse etiam antiquam hic mundus existeret. II. Patrem testatur esse illum solum verum Deum. Quis dubitat? est quippe hoc Patris prædicatum essentiale. III. Non dicit, σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν [?], te solum illum verum Deum; sed σὲ τὸν μόνον te illum solum verum Deum. Nempe quandoquidem verus ille Deus est tantum unus solus, Patrem hunc esse, non quod solus Pater, vel sola ejus persona ille Deus sit. τὸν μόνον illum solum, ad prædicatum refertur, non ad subjectum. IV. Facetiam, ad subjectum pertinere, neque sic evincent, quod volunt, ut cognoscant te solum, esse verum Deum: nam non propterea sequitur, illud solum, ita soli Patri adscribi, ut excludat Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum: neque vi vocis, neque rei designatæ. Non illud, quia sæpe generaliter & illa, & similes voces ponuntur, ut tamen non universaliter excludant, sed cum restrictione. V. g. 1 Tim. vi. 15. 16. μόνος δυνάστης [?], solus potens, rex regum, & dominus dominantium, qui solus habet immortalitatem, sive de Patre intelligas, non excluditur Christus; sive de Christo, non excluditur Pater: ita & hoc in loco, solum verum Deum. Joann. xvi. 32. ecce, venit hora, & jam venit, ut dispergamini unusquisque ad sua, & me relinquitis solum, μόνον ἀφῆτε [?], & non sum solus. Solus dicitur, & non tamen solus: id est non usquequaque, omni modo & simpliciter solus, sed solus respectu ipsorum, non Patris, nam Pater mecum est: ita hic Patrem dicit solum quidem, exclusis aliis, at non proinde exclusò se. Atque 1 Cor. 11. 2. non enim statui scire inter vos quippiam, nisi Iesum Christum. Quid? non etiam Patrem? Non ergo ex solo vocum sono tutò argumentaberis, utcumque generali, quia non tamen ita universaliter accipiendæ. Minus autem procedit argumentum ex rei naturâ, quia sic præsupponerent Adversarii id, quod est in quæstione, atque peterent principium, vide Christum esse diversæ à Patre essentiæ, qua Deus est, quod falsum. Sin regerant, nos id dicendo, idem committere vitium, & petere quod in quæstione, responsio facilis, quia nos hic non argumentamur, sed ipsi, illi ergo pro medio termino petunt id quod in quæstione, nos nihil petimus, quia non hinc adstruimus, hactenus saltem non, ac propterea non possumus dici petere principium, quod solum defendimus & tuemur adversus illorum hinc structam argumentationem. Quæ duo quia sæpe confundunt, & non observant diversas defenden-tis ab opponente partes, hinc frustra aliquando nobis exprobant, cujus ipsi sunt rei. Quare quandoquidem Christus unius ejusdemque cum Patre est essentiæ, se hoc dicto à Patris essentiâ & deitate secludere non potuit. Nullo modo hoc eum hic fecisse, ullis è textu ostendi potest indiciis. Fac, Christum ejusdem esse cum Patre essentiæ, istis Christi ad Patrem verbis, ut cognoscant te illum solum verum Deum, nullus senties se-cludi Christum, quidem alia, vel alios μὴ φύσει θεός [?]. Iterum, dicamus esse al-terius essentiæ, tum illis verbis quoque notabitur quidem seclusus, at non vi verborum, sed rei, & essentiæ diversæ. Hoc autem aliunde tum debebit constare & pro-bari rationibus aliis, non autem ex hoc probabitur textu. v. Nec potuit Christus se-met excludere, quia Patrem notando, non magis Filium removet, quam dicendo se, Patrem. Si ergo vita æterna in hoc sita, ut cognoscatur Pater, non ergo ut ne co-gnoscatur Filius, vel non absque Filio. Ac propterea se etiam in hoc sermone con-jungit cum Patre ut ἐν [?], verf. 11.22. Sin objicias, idem illum dicere quoque de aliis secum, ut sint unum, quemadmodum nos unum sumus: extra dubium est, uti id in utroque membro non potest pari modo accipi, ita debere explicari de singulis, suo ἑνότητι [?] genere ac modo, qui alibi clarius exponitur: quare conjungimus Ioan. v. 18. & x. 33. 1 Ioan. v. 7. Præterea non potuit Christus se oratione illa excludere, quia est in Patre, & Pater in ipso, mutua personarum ἐμπεριχωρήσει [?]. Ioann. x. 38. ut sciatis & cognoscatis quod Pater in me, & ego in ipso. Quomodo ergo nunc Patrem nominando, se excluderet? vel ad quid quæso id pertineret, si vel directe id fecisset Christus, aut intendisset, vel indirecte? vi. Christus Patrem nominando solum illum verum Deum, seclusit procul dubio omnia alia quæ non sunt Deus: certe ergo non seipsum: quia in horum censum Christus non venit. Profecto non se notavit ista sua oratione, sed alios non Deos. vii. Quare ad construendam plene Christi orationem, repetendum κατὰ κοινὴν [?] est, hæc est vita æterna ut te cognoscant solum illum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum, quoque solum illum verum Deum: nam non minus in cognitione Christi sita vita æterna est, quam Patris; & quoque verus ille Deus est; & loquendi is modus, vel repetendi ex priori membro, satis omnibus in linguis usitatus. 1 Ioann. 11. 22. Quis est mendax, nisi qui negat Iesum esse Christum? hic est Antichristus, qui negat Patrem & Filium, nempe & hunc esse Jesum Christum. Ioann. xv. 4. manete in me, & ego in vobis, sc. manebo. 5. ὁ μένων in me, & ego in ipso, sc. μέγων[?]. 1 Cor. iv. 15. Si enim mille pædagogos habeatis in Christo, sed non multos Patres, nempe habetis in Christo. 11 Cor. xi. 22. Hebræi sunt ? & ego, nempe Hebræus sum, Israelitæ sunt ? & ego, sum Israelita. Semen Abrahæ sunt ? & ego talis sum. Et talia innumera. Denique & Adversarii nostri fatentur Christum Deum, & verum Deum; ergo quum non solus Pater, sed etiam Christus sit verus Deus, neque Patrem potuit ita solum verum dicere, ut semetipsum excluderet, vel seipsum illo sermone spoliare veritate & dignitate sibi debita. Sin dicant, alio modo verum Deum Patrem, alio modo Christum: jam ergo non ex vi verborum argumentantur, quibus differentia illa nequicquam notatur: &, quod dicunt, præterquam quod nec aliunde possint probare, pugnat cum ipsa rei natura, ut verus Deus sit alio & alio modo. Qui est ullo modo verus Deus, est eo modo quo aliquis verus Deus, nam veritas ubique est eadem & uniformis. Per quod Pater est verus Deus, per idem & Christus, si est verus Deus. Unde Deus verus est, nisi per veritatem essentiæ divinæ? Verum, & ens convertuntur. Ubi non est vera rei essentia, ibi nec veritas. Minime omnium convenit æquivocatione ulla uti in sermone de Deo, & quidem ubi agitur de ipsius Dei veritate. Iterum dico, si Christus verus Deus, habet ergo veram Dei essentiam, & per id est Deus, per quod Pater verus Deus. Nisi & plures Deos, & plures veros Deos, statuamus. Quis autem nescit, omnes in materia de Deo, & de Diis semper dixisse, unum esse verum Deum, non plures? Ut inaudita & prorsus insolens sit loquendi ratio, quam Adversarii nunc sequuntur, plures non tantum, sed & veros scilicet Deos statuere. Atque loca alibi adduximus, quibus Christum ajunt verum Deum, & verum ac naturalem Dei Filium. Socinus, adversus Wiekum, pag. 48. Aperte salsissimum est, nos palam affirmare Christum non esse verum Deum, imo contrarium publice profitemur, & in nostris tam Latina, quam Polonica lingua non paucis editis scriptis Christum verum Deum esse, asserimus. Smalcius, Refut. lib. 1. de Errorib. cap. iii. Christus Deus noster, & Deus verus summo jure appellandus est, & reipsa est. & Refut. lib. de divina Verbi incarnati natura, cap. x. pag. 61. confitetur Christum nunc perfectissimo modo esse Deum. Quod si Christus perfectissimo modo Deus, & summo jure ac reipsa Deus verus est, ergo habet veram Dei naturam, quin non homines, sed & Christum, & Deum sermone nostro turpiter ludimus, atque improbissime hic cavillamur. Verus homo ecquis dicitur, nisi qui naturam habet vere humanam? ut verus ignis, aqua, aurum, &c. Improprie quidem illa nomina quandoque aliis tribuuntur, quam quibus vere competunt, sed per metaphoram, sive deflexionem vocis à significatu proprio, non vere. Sic hominis imago & effigies non est vere homo, aurea virtus non vere aurea, sed improprie, & sic de aliis: qui autem vere Deus nemo, nisi qui essentiam Dei vere habet, eoque opponitur τοῖς λεγομένοις θεοῖς. Quare Christus si verus Deus, jam vere, id est, essentiæ veritate Deus fit, est necesse. Et quomodocumque etiam id sumas, dummodo Deus verus, excludi nequit hac sua oratione, nec quando Patrem verum Deum dixit, nec quando solum, nam certe solus verus Deus, est Deus. Quacumque ergo ratione locum accipiant Adversarii, perit ipsis suum ex eo argumentum. Dicitur Pater, solus verus Deus: atque id est: non solus Pater. Atque intelligatur vel legatur etiam, solus Pater, verus Deus: non tamen excepto Filio, qui in Patre, & cum eo Deus verus, Filius in Patre, atque Pater in Filio. Quare Syrus interpres legit, אלהא רשרא בלהוריך [?] Deum veritat solum, nomen solum postponendo: & Deum verum, dixit Deum veritatis. Id nempe est, Deum verum esse. Versio Persica, quod tu es Deus in veritate solus. Certe non excluso, sententia nostra non tantum, sed & Adversariorum, Filio à veritate Dei, quo minus sit verus Deus. Si Deus, si verus Deus, & verus Deus est solus Deus, jam & Christus istis verbis notatur quoque, non secluditur.
units.tr: First, the Adversaries object to those passages of Scripture in which the Father is called God, and the only true God. John 17:3; 1 Cor. 8:6; Eph. 4:6. The Ministers of Transylvania argue this way, lib. II, de Dei cognit., cap. v; Socinus, against the Posnanians; the Racovian Catechism, p. 57; Ostorodus, against Tradelus, cap. III, and against Ravenspergerus; Smalcius, against Grawerus, p. 10; Volkelius, p. 458; Crellius, and all of them. The text of John 17:3 reads: "And this is eternal life, that they may know σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν [?], and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." They rest the whole force of the argument on this, that Christ, addressing the Father, calls him not only God but the one God, thereby excluding himself along with the others. Answer. I. We must observe the circumstances in which Christ spoke these words, namely his state of humiliation and his economic condition, as the Ancients put it, which usually signifies the things that bear witness to his lowliness, not to his glory. For Christ spoke these words while praying (v. 1), and about the tasks he had received on earth to carry out by the Father's command. Yet he did not neglect his other condition, which he hinted at rather than proclaimed, when he recalled that he had come forth from the Father, that all things of the Father are his, that he is one with the Father, and that he was glorious with him before the world existed. II. He testifies that the Father is that only true God. Who doubts it? For this is an essential predicate of the Father. III. He does not say σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν [?], you, the only true God, but σὲ τὸν μόνον, you, that only one [the true God]. Since the true God is indeed only one, the Father is said to be this one, not because the Father alone, or his person alone, is that God. τὸν μόνον, that only one, refers to the predicate, not to the subject. IV. Even if the word belongs to the subject, they will not thereby prove what they want, namely that "they may know you alone to be the true God." For it does not follow that only is so ascribed to the Father as to exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit, neither by the force of the word nor by the thing signified. Nor does it follow from the fact that such words as this and similar ones are often put in a general sense, yet do not exclude universally but with a restriction. For example, 1 Tim. 6:15–16: μόνος δυνάστης [?], the only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality; whether you understand this of the Father, Christ is not excluded, or whether of Christ, the Father is not excluded. So also in this place, the only true God. John 16:32: "Behold, the hour comes, and now is come, that you shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone, μόνον ἀφῆτε [?], and yet I am not alone." He is said to be alone, and yet not alone: that is, not alone in every way, in every respect, and simply, but alone in respect of them, not of the Father, for the Father is with me. So here he says the Father is alone, indeed, with others excluded, yet he does not thereby exclude himself. And 1 Cor. 2:2: "For I determined not to know anything among you, save Jesus Christ." What? Not the Father also? So you cannot argue safely from the mere sound of words, however general they may be, since they are not to be taken universally in every case. The argument from the nature of the thing is still weaker, for in that way the Adversaries would presuppose what is in question and beg the principle, namely that Christ is of a different essence from the Father, in respect of which he is God, which is false. But if they retort that we commit the same fault in saying this, and beg the question, the answer is easy: we are not arguing here, but they are. They therefore beg as their middle term what is in question; we beg nothing, since we do not draw our conclusion from this point, at least not so far, and so we cannot be said to beg the principle, which we only defend and maintain against their argument built upon it. Since they often confuse these two things and do not observe the different roles of defender and opponent, they sometimes reproach us in vain for a fault of which they themselves are guilty. Therefore, since Christ is of one and the same essence with the Father, he could not have excluded himself from the Father's essence and deity by this saying. That he did so here cannot be shown from any indication in the text. Grant that Christ is of the same essence as the Father: from these words of Christ to the Father, "that they may know you, the only true God," no one will sense that Christ is excluded, but only other things or other beings that are μὴ φύσει θεός [?], not God by nature. Again, let us say he is of a different essence: then, by these words too, he will be noted as excluded, but not by the force of the words, rather by the reality and the different essence. This, however, must be established from other grounds, and cannot be proved from this text. V. Nor could Christ exclude himself, since by pointing to the Father he removes the Son no more than by saying "I" he removes the Father. If, then, eternal life consists in this, that the Father be known, it does not follow that the Son is not known, or is not known apart from the Son. And therefore in this very discourse he joins himself with the Father as ἐν [?], verses 11 and 22. If you object that he says the same about others with himself, "that they may be one, as we are one", it is beyond doubt that as this cannot be taken in the same way in both members, so it must be explained of each according to its own kind and mode of unity, which is set forth more clearly elsewhere. Therefore we join John 5:18 and 10:33 and 1 John 5:7. Moreover, Christ could not exclude himself by that speech, since he is in the Father and the Father in him, by the mutual indwelling [ἐμπεριχωρήσει] of the persons. John 10:38: "that you may know and understand that the Father is in me, and I in him." How then, by naming the Father now, would he exclude himself? Or, I ask, to what would that pertain, if Christ had done so either directly or intended it, or indirectly? VI. By naming the Father the only true God, Christ undoubtedly excluded all other things that are not God, certainly not himself, since Christ does not belong to their number. Surely he did not mark himself off by that saying of his, but other things that are not gods. VII. Therefore, to construe Christ's prayer fully, the words must be repeated by a common construction: "this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent," so that the only true God is also repeated; for eternal life consists no less in the knowledge of Christ than of the Father, and he too is the true God; and this mode of speaking, or repeating from the preceding member, is common enough in all languages. 1 John 2:22: "Who is a liar but he that denies that Jesus is the Christ? He is Antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son," namely, he denies that this one is Jesus Christ. John 15:4: "Abide in me, and I in you," that is, I will abide. Verse 5: ὁ μένων [?], he who abides in me, and I in him, that is, μένων [?]. 1 Cor. 4:15: "For though you have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet not many fathers," namely, you have them in Christ. 2 Cor. 11:22: "Are they Hebrews?" so am I, namely, I am a Hebrew; "are they Israelites?" so am I, I am an Israelite; "are they the seed of Abraham?" so am I. And countless such examples. Finally, our Adversaries themselves confess that Christ is God and the true God; therefore, since not the Father alone but Christ also is the true God, the Father could not have been called the only true God in such a way as to exclude himself, or to strip himself by that speech of the truth and dignity owed to him. But if they say that the Father is the true God in one way and Christ in another, then they are not arguing from the force of the words, by which that difference is in vain marked; and what they say, besides the fact that they cannot prove it from anywhere else, is at odds with the very nature of the thing, that one should be the true God in one way and another in another way. Whatever is truly God is God in that same way in which anyone is the true God, for truth is everywhere the same and uniform. Whereby the Father is the true God, by the same is Christ also, if he is the true God. For whence is God true, except through the truth of the divine essence? The true and being are convertible. Where there is no true essence of a thing, there is no truth either. Least of all does it suit anyone to use any equivocation in discourse about God, and certainly where the very truth of God is at issue. I say again: if Christ is the true God, then he has the true essence of God, and he is God by the same thing by which the Father is the true God. Unless we posit more gods, and more true gods. Yet who does not know that in the matter of God, and of gods, everyone has always said there is one true God, not several? So that the manner of speaking that the Adversaries now follow, positing several gods, and indeed several true gods, is unheard of and altogether novel. And we have elsewhere cited passages in which they call Christ the true God and the true and natural Son of God. Socinus, against Wiekius, p. 48: "It is plainly most absurd that we should openly affirm that Christ is not the true God; on the contrary, we publicly profess, and in our many writings published in both Latin and Polish we assert that Christ is the true God." Smalcius, Refutation, book 1, de Erroribus, cap. iii: "Christ our God and the true God is to be called so by the highest right, and is so in very deed." And in his Refutation, book on the divine nature of the incarnate Word, cap. x, p. 61, he confesses that Christ is now God in the most perfect manner. But if Christ is God in the most perfect manner, and is God by the highest right and in very deed, then he has the true nature of God; so that we are not playing shamefully with words, nor are we wickedly quibbling here. Who is called a true man except one who has a truly human nature? As true fire, water, gold, and so on. Those names are sometimes applied to other things improperly, rather than to those to which they truly belong, by metaphor, or by a turning of the word from its proper meaning, not truly. Thus the image or effigy of a man is not truly a man, a golden virtue is not truly gold, but improperly, and so on for other cases; but no one is truly God except one who truly has the essence of God, and such a one is opposed to τοῖς λεγομένοις θεοῖς [?], those so-called gods. Therefore, if Christ is the true God, he necessarily is now truly God, that is, God by the truth of essence. And however you take it, provided he is the true God, he cannot be excluded by this saying of his, neither when he called the Father the true God, nor when he called him the only one; for certainly the only true God is God. Whatever reasoning the Adversaries use to take the passage, their own argument from it perishes. It is said: the Father is the only true God. And that means: not the Father alone. And let it be understood or read even as: the Father alone is the true God; yet not with the Son excluded, who is in the Father, and with him the true God, the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son. So the Syriac translator reads אלהא רשרא בלהוריך [?], Deum veritat solum (Elaha reshra b'lahuria, roughly "God of truth alone"), placing the word solum after the noun; and he renders "the true God" as "God of truth." That is, that he is the true God. The Persian version: "that you are God alone in truth." Certainly, with no one excluded, our opinion, and not only ours but that of the Adversaries as well, holds that the Son is not thereby hindered from being the true God, from the truth of God. If he is God, and the true God, and the only true God is God, then Christ too is noted by these words, not excluded.

units.la: Loco altero, quem objiciunt, 1 Cor. viii. 6. dicitur, Sed nobis unus Deus Pater, ex quo omnia, & nos in illum. Unde se Vnitarios appellant, & Monarchianos, uti Auctor Irenici Irenicorum loquitur, Monarchianae, vulgo Socinianae Ecclesiae: sed quomodo Tertullianus inquit adversus Praxeam, Vnicum dominum vindicat omnipotentem mundi conditorem, ut & de unico haeresim faciat. & cap. iii. Itaque duos & tres jam jactitant a nobis praedicari, si vero unius Dei cultores praesumunt: quasi non & unitas irrationaliter collecta haeresim faciat, & trinitas rationaliter expensa, veritatem constituat. μοναρχίαν (inquiunt) tenemus. Ad locum vero illum 1 Cor. viii. 6. velimus primum fieri ab Adversariis argumentum, quo constabit de ejus aut vi, aut infirmitate. Quibus est unus Deus Pater, iis non est unus Deus Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus: negatur haec propositio. Si unus Pater est Deus, ergo non Filius, non Spiritus Sanctus: sed unus Pater est Deus: ergo. Praeterquam quod id in textu non dicitur, quod unus Pater est Deus, negatur & major, & minor. Unus Pater est Deus, & non idola, Pater vid. opposi-tus idolis, quibus in hac oratione opponitur; non autem oppositus Filio & Spiritui Sancto. Dicitur in textu verf. 4. & non' est Deus alius praeterquam unus. De Dei es-sentiâ, & eâ unica, contra quoscumque alios ita nominatos Deos sermonem institu-tum, omnes vident: tum inquit, & nobis unus Deus Pater. Id est, nobis unus Deus, non plures: & unus ille Deus est Pater. Sic certe. Praeterquam enim quod vox Pa-ter hic potest essentialiter accipi, relate ad creaturas, ex quo omnia, ut sic & Filio attribuatur; illa quae essentialiter de persona Patris praedicantur, conveniunt etiam Filio, eumque non excludunt, sed comprehendunt. Neque sic petimus principium: non enim hactenus argumentamur nos, sed Adversarii: ipsorum vero est tale hinc extruere argumentum, quod principium vel thesim nostram evertat, alioqui nihil effecerint. Isto autem modo id non fit, neque concluditur, propterea quod Pater est verus ille atque unus Deus, idem de Filio non posse verum esse ac praedicari. ii. Quidquid Adversarii ex isto loco conentur concludere, refelli similibus instantiis poterit, à Christo sumtis, qui dicitur esse solus Dominus, verf. 6. & unus Dominus Jesus Christus, sc. nobis est, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum. Quid enim, an nobis liceret hoc pacto argumentari: quibus est unus Dominus Jesus Christus, iis non est unus Dominus Pater? vel, si unus Jesus Christus est Dominus, ergo non Pater? Quomodocumque formabunt argumentum illi suum de uno Deo Patre, sic & nos formaturi sumus nostrum, de uno Domino Christo. Et quidquid responsuri sunt illic, apparebit retundi simili à nobis responsione posse hinc. Quare liquet, quamvis quae hoc in loco dicuntur, de Patre, & Christo accipiantur oppositia idolis, vel nominatis aut metaphorice, aut catachrestice in mundo Diis, non tamen ut sibi mutuo oppositia, vel de Patre & non de Filio illa, vel de Christo ista & non de Patre quoque accipienda esse. iii. Saepissime in Scripturis occurrunt ejusmodi loquutiones, & strictiores, quae tamen non sunt prorsus exclusivae. Praeter id quod ad praecedens diximus argumen-tum, quod nihil se scire Apostolus arbitratus fuit, praeter Jesum Christum, eum-que que crucifixum 1 Cor. ii. 2. quid, an nihil praeter Christum? non etiam Patrem? solum crucifixum, & non etiam resuscitatum, evectum in caelos, hinc regnantem, & rediturum, &c? Act. iv. 12. non est aliud nomen ἕτερον ὄνομα, in quo oporteat nos servari, praeter nomen Christi: num propterea hinc excluditur Pater? Si ore confessus fueris Dominum Iesum, & credideris eum a mortuis suscitatum, salvaberis, inquit Apostolus, Rom. x. 9. an ita solos illos indicat articulos, ut nullos alios admittat ad salutem necessarios, & excludat quae de Patre credenda nobis sunt, ne dicam alia? Joann. v. 22. neque enim Pater judicat quempiam, quomodo, an ut iudicandi actione prorsus excludatur Pater? Atque talia adferri possunt innumera.
units.tr: The second passage they object to is 1 Cor. viii. 6: But to us there is one God the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him. Hence they call themselves Unitarians and Monarchians, as the author of the Irenicum of the Irenica speaks of the Monarchian, commonly called Socinian Church. But as Tertullian says against Praxeas: He claims one Lord, the almighty creator of the world, so that he may make a heresy out of the one. And in chapter 3: So they now boast that we preach two and three, if they presume to be worshippers of the one God. As if the unity, gathered irrationally, does not make a heresy, and the trinity, weighed rationally, does not constitute the truth. They say, we hold monarchy [μοναρχίαν]. First, however, let us have the Adversaries make an argument from that passage, 1 Cor. viii. 6, so that it becomes clear whether its force or its weakness lies there. Those to whom there is one God the Father, to them there is not one God the Son and the Holy Spirit: this proposition is denied. If the Father alone is God, then not the Son, not the Holy Spirit: but the Father alone is God: therefore. Besides, this is not said in the text, that the Father alone is God; both the major and the minor premise are denied. The Father is one God, and not idols: the Father is opposed to idols, which are opposed to him in this discourse, not to the Son and the Holy Spirit. In the text, at verse 4, it is said: and there is no other God but one. Everyone sees that the discourse is about the essence of God, and about that one essence, against any others so named as gods. Then it says: and to us one God the Father. That is, to us there is one God, not many, and that one God is the Father. Surely so. For, apart from the fact that the word Father here may be taken essentially, in relation to creatures, of whom are all things, so that it may also be attributed to the Son, those things which are predicated essentially of the person of the Father also belong to the Son, and do not exclude him but include him. Nor in this way do we beg the question: for we are not arguing thus; it is the Adversaries who do. It is their task to build from this an argument that overturns our principle or thesis, otherwise they will have achieved nothing. But in this way it is not done, nor is it concluded that because the Father is the true and only God, the same cannot be true and predicated of the Son. ii. Whatever the Adversaries try to conclude from this passage can be refuted by similar instances taken from Christ, who is called the only Lord, verse 6: and one Lord Jesus Christ, namely to us, through whom are all things, and we through him. For could we argue in this way: to those to whom there is one Lord Jesus Christ, there is not one Lord the Father? Or: if Jesus Christ alone is Lord, then not the Father? However they form their argument about the one God the Father, so shall we form ours about the one Lord Christ. And whatever answer they give there, it will appear that it can be refuted by a similar answer from us here. Hence it is clear that although what is said in this place is taken of the Father and of Christ as opposed to idols, or to those called gods in the world, either metaphorically or catachrestically, nevertheless these things are not to be taken as opposed to each other, nor the former of the Father and not of the Son, nor the latter of Christ and not of the Father also. iii. Such expressions, both restricted and yet not wholly exclusive, occur very often in Scripture. Besides what we said with the preceding argument, that the Apostle thought he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. ii. 2), what of this: nothing except Christ? Not also the Father? Crucified alone, and not also raised, taken up into heaven, reigning from there, and to come again, etc.? Acts iv. 12: there is no other name [ἕτερον ὄνομα] by which we must be saved, except the name of Christ: does the Father therefore get excluded here? If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved, says the Apostle (Rom. x. 9). Does he so indicate those articles alone, that he admits no others necessary to salvation, and excludes what must be believed about the Father, not to mention others? John v. 22: For the Father judges no one: how so? Is the Father wholly excluded from the act of judging? And countless such examples can be brought.

units.la: iv. Imo quandoquidem Christum tam arte mox conjungit cum Patre Deo, uti Patrem cum Christo Domino, docet non separandum alterum aut hinc, aut isthinc esse, sed jungendum pariter utrobique esse utrumque. v. Vers. 4. dixit, & non est alius Deus, praeterquam[?] unus. Quandoquidem ergo & Christus est Deus, & verus Deus, est quoque ille unus Deus, non ἕτερος, אחד[?]. Et sic quemadmodum inde ducit Apostolus vers. 6. nobis unus Deus Pater; simili ratione dici idem de Christo potest: nobis unus Deus Christus. Vel duos dicam Deos Patrem & Filium, vel unum. Si duos, reclamant verbis Apostoli, quibus testatus fuit, nobis unum esse Deum: sin unum, ergo verbis istis, nobis unus Deus Pater; Filius non excluditur. Denique & haec testantur; Christum doceri Deum illum, non tantum quia Κύριος[?] dicitur, qua ratione nobis unus est dominus, quo a Graecis interpretibus semper Hebraeorum יהוה[?] dicitur, quemadmodum & Eph. iv. 5. unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma, de domino Deo unico illud accipitur: sed & quia additur, omnia per ipsum Dominum esse, & nos propter ipsum: quae solius Dei sunt, deque eo solo efferri possunt, & usurpantur, Rom. xi. 35. non aliqua, sed omnia, & per eum, & ad eum: ut sit & efficiens, & finis tum nostri, tum omnium, quae de nullo vere dici, quam vero & uno Deo, possunt. Neque obest particula per, quasi instrumentum denotaret a Deo diversum. Nam Deo attribuitur, praeterquam Rom. xi. 35. etiam 1 Cor. i. 9. Fidelis Deus, per quem vocati estis. Et Christus dicitur suscitatus per gloriam Patris, Rom. vi. 4. 1 Cor. vi. 14. Deus autem & Dominum suscitavit, & exsuscitabit vos per suam potentiam.
units.tr: iv. Indeed, since he so closely joins Christ with God the Father, just as he joins the Father with Christ the Lord, he teaches that neither one is to be separated from the other, here or there, but each must be joined to the other on both sides. v. Verse 4 says: and there is no other God but one. Since, then, Christ is both God and the true God, he is also that one God, not another [ἕτερος], not one [אחד]. And just as the Apostle draws from this in verse 6, to us one God the Father, the same can be said of Christ by a similar reasoning: to us one God Christ. Either I should say there are two Gods, the Father and the Son, or one. If two, they contradict the words of the Apostle, by which he testified that for us there is one God. But if one, then by those words, to us one God the Father, the Son is not excluded. Finally, these things also testify that the God taught here is Christ: not only because he is called Lord [Κύριος], by which title there is for us one Lord, which the Greek translators always render as the Hebrew יהוה [YHWH], as also in Eph. iv. 5, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, which is understood of the one Lord God; but also because it is added that all things are through him the Lord, and we are for him. These belong to God alone, and can be said and are used only of him, Rom. xi. 35: not some things, but all things, and through him and to him, so that he is both the efficient and the final cause of us and of all things, which can truly be said of no one but the one God. Nor does the particle through stand in the way, as if it denoted an instrument distinct from God. For it is attributed to God, besides Rom. xi. 35, also in 1 Cor. i. 9: God is faithful, through whom you were called. And Christ is said to be raised through the glory of the Father (Rom. vi. 4), and 1 Cor. vi. 14: But God both raised up the Lord and will raise us up through his power.

units.la: Similiter neque ex loco Eph. iv. 6. argumentari pro sua opinione Adver-sariis licet, ubi dicitur, unus Deus & Pater omnium, qui super omnia & per omnia, & in omnibus vobis. Dictum fuerat vers. 5. unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma, & paulo superius, vers. 4. unum corpus & unus spiritus: sicut & vocati estis in una spe vo-cationis vestrae. Adhortatur Apostolus ad concordiam & unitatem: ad quod argu-mentum, cum aliunde, tum etiam petit ab unitate Dei: unum vero dicit Deum & Patrem omnium. Quid? anne sunt, qui dicunt plures esse veros Deos, quam adver-sarii Socciniani? de Christianis loquor. Anne ulli, qui plures Patres, quam unum? sive vox Patris essentialiter sumatur, sive personaliter. Quomodo ergo hinc quippiam possunt concludere? ii. Accipient vocem Patris Adver-sarii personaliter. Sit ita, at de Filio non minus potest dici, unus Deus & Filius; unus Deus & Spiritus Sanctus, quam unus Deus & Pater. iii. Non dicitur in textu, unus Deus Pater, quam-visi & ita dictum fuisset, non tamen faceret quidpiam pro Adversariis, sed, unus Deus & Pater: ubi si Patrem personaliter intelligas, significatur ista copulativa & hunc hanc, quemadmodum & Spiritum & Filium quoque Deum esse. Nisi potius denotet, essentialiter accipiendam Patris hoc in loco notionem esse, praesertim quando attendimus ad ea quae sequuntur, ut sensus sit, unus Deus omnium, unus Pater omnium: quemadmodum Malach. 11. 10. annon Pater unus est omnium? annon Deus unus creavit nos? IV. Certe Christo illa negari nequeunt, quae hic Patri attribuuntur, esse supra omnia, & per omnia, vel, omnes, & in omnibus vobis. Quare non est ita hic versus de Patre exponendus, ut secludat Filium. v. Imo exserte nominarat jam in antecedentibus Apostolus Spiritum, & Dominum; unus Dominus. Et Crellius, Deum unum, inquit, hoc loco distinxit, & a Domino uno, & a Spiritu uno. ---- Vidimus autem jam superiori capite, per unum Dominum, nominatim Christum intelligi. At quemadmodum Christus quando nominatur unus Dominus, non excluditur Pater, ita nec Christus a deitate Patris, quando is dicitur unus Deus, uti ille unus Dominus. Imo Christus quando dicitur & Dominus, & unus Dominus notantur ea, quae Patri hic adscripta, esse omnium vid. dominum, & supra omnia, vel per omnia, & in omnibus vobis, quemadmodum cap. i. 23. quod omnia in omnibus impleat.
units.tr: Likewise the Adversaries may not argue for their opinion from Eph. iv. 6, where it is said: one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all of you. It had been said at verse 5, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and a little earlier, at verse 4, one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. The Apostle exhorts to concord and unity, and for this argument he draws, among other things, on the unity of God: and he calls God the Father of all one God. Well? Are there those who say there are more true Gods than the Socinian Adversaries? I speak of Christians. Are there any who say there are more Fathers than one, whether the word Father is taken essentially or personally? How then can they conclude anything from this? ii. Let the Adversaries take the word Father personally. So be it; yet of the Son it can be said no less: one God and the Son; one God and the Holy Spirit, as much as one God and the Father. iii. The text does not say one God the Father; even if it had been so put, it would not help the Adversaries. It says one God and Father, where, if you understand the Father personally, the conjunction and signifies that the Spirit and the Son are also God, in the same way. Unless it rather indicates that the notion of Father is to be taken essentially in this place, especially when we attend to what follows, so that the sense is: one God of all, one Father of all, just as in Malach. ii. 10: Has not one Father of all? Has not one God created us? iv. Certainly the things attributed here to the Father, that he is above all, and through all, or all, and in all of you, cannot be denied to Christ. Therefore this verse is not to be explained of the Father in such a way as to shut out the Son. v. Indeed the Apostle had already named the Spirit and the Lord explicitly in what precedes: one Lord. And Crellius says: In this place he distinguished God the one, both from the one Lord and from the one Spirit. ---- But we have already seen in the earlier chapter that by the one Lord, Christ is specifically meant. Yet just as when Christ is named the one Lord, the Father is not excluded, so Christ is not excluded from the deity of the Father when God is called one God, as that one Lord is.
