Indeed, when Christ is called both Lord and one Lord, the things attributed here to the Father are also marked as belonging to him, that is, to be of all, namely Lord, and above all, or through all, and in all of you, just as in chapter 1, verse 23, he fills all in all.

units.la: Secunda objectio: Christus a Deo distinguitur: ergo Deus ipse non est. Illud apparere, ajunt, ex omnibus illis locis, quibus se ut Filium & Christum, a Patre saepissime fecerunt. Joann. v. 19: Non potest Filius facere quidquam a seipso, nisi quod videt Patrem facientem. Cap. xii. 44. Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum, qui misit me. Crellius, lib. 1. sect. 11. Ostorodus, contra Tradelum, pag. 20. aliique.
units.tr: Second objection: Christ is distinguished from God, therefore he is not God himself. They say this appears from all those passages in which they very often set Christ forth as Son and Christ, distinct from the Father: John 5:19: The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. John 12:44: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me. See Crellius, book 1, sect. 11; Ostorodus, against Tradelius, p. 20; and others.

units.la: Crellius:
units.tr: Crellius:

units.la: Ex hoc autem loco argumentamur: Deus ille summus a seipso omnia facere potest. Christus a semetipso nihil facere potest. Ergo Christus non est Deus ille supremus. Propositio major, ut in scholis appellant, per se manifesta est. Deus enim supremus prima atque suprema omnium rerum causa est; ac porro quicquid facere potest, a seipso potest, non ab alio: aliquin ipse prima ac suprema causa non esset; sed is potius, a quo haberet, ut facere aliquid posset. Assumtio autem, seu minor, ipsius Christi est.
units.tr: From this passage we argue as follows: that highest God can do all things from himself; Christ cannot do anything from himself; therefore Christ is not that supreme God. The major premise, as the schools call it, is self-evident. For the supreme God is the first and highest cause of all things, and whatever he can do, he can do from himself and not from another. Otherwise he would not be the first and highest cause, but that from which he had the ability to do anything. The assumption, or minor premise, concerns Christ himself.

units.la: Resp. I. Non dicitur in loco Joann. v. 19. quod Christus nihil a seipso facere possit simpliciter, sed quod nihil isto tali modo, seorsim a Patre, verum omnia unum cum Patre, & ὁμοίως. Nam postquam dixerat, Patrem suum usque hodie operari & se quoque: atque inde intulissent Judaei, quod ergo Deum Patrem suum proprium fecisset, & se ei aequalem ἴσον ἑαυτὸν τῷ θεῷ, respondens Christus id adeo non negat, quod facere, nisi
units.tr: Reply, first: in John 5:19 it is not said that Christ can do nothing from himself absolutely, but that he can do nothing in that manner, separately from the Father, but that he does all things one with the Father, and [ὁμοίως] in like manner. For after saying that his Father works until now, and that he works too, the Jews inferred that he was calling God his own Father and making himself equal to God [ἴσον ἑαυτὸν τῷ θεῷ]. Christus does not deny this, as he would have had to if it were false. Instead he confirms both points: that God is his own Father, and that he does all things with him.

units.la: verum fuisset, debuerat, sed confirmat utrumque, & Deum suum esse Patrem proprium, & facere se cum eo omnia: hinc dictum, non potest Filius facere aliquid a se ipso, nisi viderit Patrem facientem: quae enim ille faciat, eadem & Filius facit similiter ὁμοίως. Non ergo simpliciter inquit Christus, quod Filius nihil possit a seipso, ex quo solo, & a reliquis divulso frustra argumentatur Adversarius, fallacia divisionis, sed nihil nisi illo modo, & una cum Patre eum posse. Uti illud non posse, cum restrictione saepe accipi debet, pro re subjecta. 1 Joann. iii. 9. & non potest peccare, quia ex Deo natus est. Non quod prorsus non possit peccare, sed quod non isto modo, quo ii qui ex phrasi Scripturae dicuntur peccatum facere; quicumque natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit, quia semen ejus in ipso manet. ii. Nihil potest Filius a se ipso, sed a Patre. Recte. Nam a Patre est, & quidquid potest, quidquid est, est a Patre. Sed;
units.tr: Hence the words: the Son can do nothing from himself, unless he sees the Father doing it; for whatever that one does, the Son too does in like manner [ὁμοίως]. Christ therefore does not say simply that the Son can do nothing from himself. Our opponent argues from this alone, cutting the words off from the rest, which is a fallacy of division. Christ says only that the Son can do nothing in that way, but can do all things together with the Father. Such a "cannot" should often be understood with a restriction according to the subject matter, as in 1 John 3:9: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. This does not mean that he absolutely cannot sin, but that he cannot do so in the way of those who are said, in the phrase of Scripture, to commit sin; whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him. Second, the Son can do nothing from himself, but from the Father. That is correct, for he is from the Father, and whatever he can do and whatever he is, he has from the Father. But—

units.la: Tom. 2. quemadmodum ea quae a Patre potest, non tantum eadem, sed eodem modo potest ὁμοίως, ita & suum idem esse habet a Patre, & cum Patre. Nihil ista adversus nos, qui quoque dicimus Filium esse a Patre, & ab eo habere omnia sua. iii. Nihil potest, pro phrasi Scripturę significat non adeo quid aliquis non possit, quam quid non faciat, quid non recte, moraliter potius, quam physice ut accipiatur. Non facit Filius quidquam, nisi quod fit ex sententia Patris, & neque potest quidem: quia uti nil absque, ita nil contra Patrem. Quod confirmatur vers. 30. ubi Christus dicit, ego non possum facere quidquam a me ipso, uti audio, iudico: & iudicium meum iustum: quia non quaero voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem Patris qui misit me. Confer cap. xii. 49. 50. Versio Persica, Filius ex voluntate sua non potest quidpiam facere. Quemadmodum Matth. vi. 24. nemo potest duobus dominis servire. Marc. vi. 5. & non potuit ibi virtutem ullam facere. 1 Cor. x. 21. non potestis poculum Domini bibere, & poculum daemoniorum. Apoc. ii. 2. non potes ferre malos. iv. Denique perquam multa sunt in textu, quae sententiam nostram confirmant. Nam, quemadmodum vers. 17. dixerat, se facere quod Pater, Pater meus usque hodie operatur, & ego operor: ita hoc versu, Patrem facere ait, quae ipse, & se nihil extra Patrem seorsim: quae enim ille, eadem & Filius facit. Sed nec tantum eadem, ἁ, τῶν τα; sed ὁμοίως similiter ea facit Filius. Versio Aethiopica, quod ille fecit, sic Filius faciet, in similitudine ejus. Non diluit, sed admittit Christus, quod Judaei ex ejus sermone trahunt, quod & Deum significet proprium suum Patrem, non communi aliqua ratione; deinde & hoc ratione ita propria, ut se aequalem fecerit Deo, ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ [?]; Syrus, אלהים נפשו עשה [?], & seipsum coaequalem faceret Deo. Versio Persica, & seipsum cum Deo unum fecisset. Arabica, & coaequabat se Deo. Aethiopica, & aequalem fecit seipsum cum Deo. Unum ergo se & coaequalem cum Deo facit Christus, ex unitate operationum tum Patris secum, tum suarum cum Patre. Jam & vers. 21. quemadmodum enim Pater suscitat mortuos & vivificat, sic & Filius quos vult vivificat. Quos vult, nimirum eosdem vult & Pater: neque enim nisi cum Patre & operatur, & vult; eadem Patris & sua cum sit & operatio, & potentia, & voluntas, nempe quia unus & aequalis cum Patre Filius. ὥσπερ quemadmodum Pater, ὥτω ὡς sic & Filius; eodem modo, versio Persica. Vers. 22. neque enim Pater judicat quempiam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio. Quomodo, nisi unus & aequalis cum Patre esset Filius? deniq; quorsum id ut omnes honorent Filium, quemadmodum honorant Patrem. Qui non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem, qui misit eum. Par cultus utriusque, quia in omnibus pares. Adeo hoc sermone docetur aequalis Filii cum Patre essentia, voluntas, potentia, operatio omnis, & denique honor, sibi ab omnibus debitus, & ex prioribus pari modo consequens. Atque ita ex isto loco nobis surgit argumentum haud unum, contra Adversarios; ipsis, adversum nos, nullum.
units.tr: As he can do what he does from the Father not only the same things, but in the same manner [ὁμοίως], so he has his own being from the Father and with the Father. Our opponents' argument does not touch us, for we too say that the Son is from the Father and has all that he has from him. Third, he can do nothing, in the phrase of Scripture, means not so much that someone cannot do something, as that he does not do it, or does not do it rightly; it should be understood morally rather than physically. The Son does nothing except what is done according to the Father's will, and indeed he cannot do otherwise, for just as he does nothing apart from the Father, so he does nothing against him. This is confirmed in verse 30, where Christ says: I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, so I judge; and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me. Compare chapter 12:49–50. The Persian version reads: the Son cannot do anything from his own will. Compare Matthew 6:24: no one can serve two masters; Mark 6:5: and he could do no mighty work there; 1 Cor. 10:21: you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; Rev. 2:2: you cannot bear evil men. Finally, there are very many things in the text that confirm our view. For just as in verse 17 he had said that he does what the Father does, my Father works until now, and I work, so in this verse he says that the Father does what he does, and that he does nothing apart from the Father on his own. For whatever that one does, the Son too does; and he does these things not only the same, [ἁ, τῶν τα], but in like manner [ὁμοίως]. The Ethiopic version reads: what he did, so the Son will do, in his likeness. Christ does not refute but admits what the Jews draw from his words: that he means God as his own Father, not in some common sense, but in a sense so proper that he made himself equal to God [ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ Θεῷ]. The Syriac reads: elohim nafsho 'asah, and he made himself coequal with God. The Persian reads: and he had made himself one with God. The Arabic: and he made himself equal to God. The Ethiopic: and he made himself equal with God. Christ therefore makes himself one with God and coequal with him, from the unity of his operations both with the Father and with his own with the Father. Also in verse 21: for as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son too gives life to whom he wills. Whom he wills, clearly the same the Father also wills; for he does not act or will except with the Father, and the operation, power and will of the Father and of the Son are the same, because the Son is one with and equal to the Father. [ὥσπερ] as the Father, [ὥτω ὡς] so also the Son; in the same manner, says the Persian version. Verse 22: for the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. How could this be, unless the Son were one with and equal to the Father? Lastly, to what end is it that all should honor the Son, just as they honor the Father? He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. The worship of each is equal, because they are equal in all things. So this saying teaches the equal essence, will, power and entire operation of the Son with the Father, and finally the honor due to him from all, which follows in the same way from what has gone before. Thus from this passage a argument arises for us, not one only, against our opponents; against us, none for them.

units.la: Cap. xii. 44. Qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum, qui misit me. Hinc quod Christus non sit ultimum & principale fidei objectum, sed Deus Pater, contra nos concludunt: at frustra. Nam 1. non negatur, nos credere in Christum, neque hic, neque usquam: quin contrarium ubique docetur per totum Euangelium. Vers. 46. ut omnis credens in me. 1). ergo, non credit in me, est non simpliciter non credit in me, sed, non in me solum, non in me alium a Patre Deum, sive, non adeo in me, quam in Patrem. Quemadmodum 1 Sam. viii. 7. non te rejecerunt, sed me, inquit Deus ad ad Samuelem. Et passim negativa illa sic accipitur in Scripturis, omnique adeo sermone, non simpliciter, sed comparate, & tali cum restrictione, ac diximus iii. Act. v. 4. non mentitus es hominibus, sed Deo. Non hominibus tantum, sed etiam Deo. ii Thess. iv. 8. itaque qui spernit, non hominem spernit, sed Deum, misericordiam volo & non sacrificium. Matth. ix. 13. non enim vos estis loquentes, sed Spiritus Sanctus. Marc. xiii. 11. quod si caeci essetis, utique non haberetis peccatum, Ioann. ix. 41. & cap. xv. 22. si non venissem, & loquutus iis fuissem, non haberent peccatum. iii. Quare sensus verborum Christi est, quod qui in ipsum credit, & in ipsum, & in Patrem credat, & non in se solum. Ut argumentum praebeat pro se, & pro nobis. Quemadmodum vers. seq. & qui videt me, videt eum, qui me misit: iterum quasi dixisset, non me videt, sed Patrem, id est, me non tantum, sed & me, & Patrem, cap. xiv. 9. Philippe, qui me videt, videt Patrem. Marc. ix. 37. qui me suscipit, non suscipit me, sed eum qui misit me, id est, non me tantum, sed & me, & Patrem, qui me misit. Quare dixit cap. xiv. 1. creditis in Deum, & in me credite. Rationem istarum conjunctionum dat, cap. xiv. 9. qui me videt, videt Patrem: & quomodo tu dicis, ostende nobis Patrem? Non credis quod ego in Patre, & Pater in me est? Haec ergo ratio, quare eodem redeat credere in Christum, & in Deum. iv. Non vero probabunt Adversarii, hanc istius locutionis subesse causam, quod Christus minus sit Deus, quam Pater, vel quod non in Christum, aeque ac in Deum, credendum sit. Non ex negativa particula, qua Christus utitur, non ex sermone toto, vel ejus ratione. Denique sit ita, nec credamus in Christum ut ultimum fidei scopum, sed per eum in Deum, pro ratione Christi oeconomica, & mediatoria, non sequitur inde, quod pro ratione Theologica non sit unus ac summus ille Deus, & objectum fidei ultimum atque supremum. Etenim pro duplici sua ratione Christus est utrumque, atque dicimur in Scripturis in eum credere, & per eum.
units.tr: Chapter 12:44: He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me. From this they conclude that Christ is not the ultimate and principal object of faith, but God the Father; but in vain. For, first, it is not denied that we believe in Christ, either here or anywhere; rather the contrary is taught everywhere throughout the Gospel. Verse 46: that everyone who believes in me. 1) Therefore he does not believe in me means not simply that he does not believe in me, but that he does not believe in me alone, not in me as another God apart from the Father; or, not so much in me as in the Father. So 1 Samuel 8:7: they have not rejected you, but me, says God to Samuel. And throughout Scripture, and indeed in all speech, such negatives are understood not absolutely but comparatively, with such a restriction as we said in iii. Acts 5:4: you have not lied to men, but to God: not to men only, but also to God. 2 Thessalonians 4:8: therefore he who rejects does not reject man, but God. Hosea 6:6 (Matthew 9:13): I desire mercy and not sacrifice. Matthew 10:20: for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. Mark 13:11. John 9:41: if you were blind, you would have no sin. And chapter 15:22: if I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin. iii. Therefore the sense of Christ's words is that he who believes in him believes both in him and in the Father, and not in himself alone; so that it may serve as an argument for himself and for us. Just as in the following verse: and he who sees me sees him who sent me: again, as if he had said, he sees not me but the Father, that is, not me only but both me and the Father; chapter 14:9: Philip, he who sees me sees the Father. Mark 9:37: he who receives me does not receive me, but him who sent me, that is, not me only but both me and the Father who sent me. Hence he says in chapter 14:1: you believe in God, believe also in me. He gives the reason for these conjunctions in chapter 14:9: he who sees me sees the Father; how can you say, show us the Father? Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? This, then, is the reason why believing in Christ and believing in God come to the same thing. iv. The adversaries will not prove that the reason for this manner of speaking is that Christ is less God than the Father, or that one must not believe in Christ equally as in God. This is shown neither by the negative particle Christ uses, nor by the whole discourse, nor by its reasoning. Grant that we do not believe in Christ as the ultimate goal of faith, but through him in God, according to Christ's economic and mediatorial office; it does not follow from this that, according to his theological nature, he is not the one and supreme God and the ultimate and highest object of faith. For in his twofold capacity Christ is both, and we are said in Scripture to believe in him and through him.

units.la: III. Objectio. Aliqua sibi Christus negat, Deo propria, & quae de Deo negari haud possunt; ergo non est ille Deus. Matth. xxiv. 36. de die autem illo & hora nemo scit, neque Angeli caelorum, nisi solus Pater. Marc. xiii. 32. de die autem illo vel hora nemo scit: neque Angeli in caelo, neque Filius, nisi Pater. Matth. xix. 17. quid me dicis bonum? nemo bonus, nisi unus Deus. Crellius, lib. i. sect. i. & ii. Resp. Illa Christus sibi negat, ut homini, qualem modo credebant Adversarii, atque ille Juvenis, quem hoc responso perstringere Christus voluit & percellere. ii. Neque Filius Marc. xiii. 32. intellige similiter Filium hominis, uti vers. 26. in hoc ipso sermone: & tunc videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nubibus. iii. Quomodo Christus, qua Filius Dei, illud nesciret, quum de eo dictum Joann. v. 22. neque enim Pater quempiam judicat, sed omne judicium tradidit Filio; ut omnes honorent Filium, quemadmodum honorant Patrem? iv. Denique & quum Christus dicatur, omnia nosse? Joann. xxi. 17. Quare Ambrosius, quomodo potest nescire partem, qui facit omnia, cum minus sit scire, quam facere? lib. v. de fide, cap. vii. Petavius, lib. ii. de Trinit. cap. iii. & lib. iii. cap. i. sic locum primum interpretatur, ut Christus nescierit diem judicii, id est, non debuerit, non potuerit eloqui, & patefacere illum hominibus.
units.tr: III. Objection. Christ denies of himself things that belong to God and that cannot be denied of God: therefore he is not God. Matt. 24:36: But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only. Mark 13:32: But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father. Matt. 19:17: Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God. Crellius, bk. 1, sects. 1 and 2. Answer: (1) Christ denies these things of himself as man, in the way the opponents themselves believed, and as the young man was meant to be rebuked and struck by this reply. (2) In Mark 13:32, understand "the Son" in the same way as "the Son of man" in verse 26 of this same discourse: And then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds. (3) How could Christ, as the Son of God, not know that, when it is said of him in John 5:22: For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son: that all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father? (4) Finally, Christ is said to know all things: John 21:17. Hence Ambrose: How can he who makes all things not know a part, since it is less to know than to make? Book 5 on Faith, ch. 7. Petavius, bk. 2 On the Trinity, ch. 3, and bk. 3, ch. 1, interprets the first passage thus: that Christ did not know the day of judgment, that is, that he ought not, or could not, declare and reveal it to men.

units.la: IV. Obj. Sibi Christus attribuit, quae Deo non conveniunt: ergo ipse non est Deus. uti Joann. xiv. 28. Pater major me est. quod a Patre in mundum missus: quod; ad Patrem preces fudit: quod omnia a Patre sibi donata dicit, &c. Ex quibus argumentatur Catechesis Racov pag. 57. 58. Ostorodus, contra Tradelum, pag. 9. Crellius, lib. i. sect. i. Resp. Christus aliquando Patri se dicit ἴσον, aliquando minorem. Utrumque verum est. Neque enim hoc illi, vel illud huic contrarium haberi debet: quia non de eodem praedicatur ad idem, eodem modo. Patri æqualis est, ratione Deitatis suæ: inæqualis & minor, ratione humanæ naturæ, & officii Mediatorii, cujus respectu sub Patre est. ὁ δὲ μεσίτης, ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστιν. Gal. iii. 20. Atque hujus ratione, ex data distinctione, explicanda sunt & reliqua. Vide ad locum illum Johannis, quoque Petavium, Tom. ii. Theol. Dogmat. lib. ii. de Trinit. cap. ii.
units.tr: IV. Objection. Christ attributes to himself things that do not belong to God: therefore he is not God. For example John 14:28: My Father is greater than I. Also that he was sent into the world by the Father; that he poured out prayers to the Father; that he says all things have been given him by the Father, and so on. The Racovian Catechism, pp. 57–58, argues from these; Ostorodus, against Tradelius, p. 9; Crellius, bk. 1, sects. 1. Answer: Christ sometimes calls himself equal to the Father, and sometimes less. Both are true. Nor should one be held contrary to the other, since they are not predicated of the same thing, in the same respect. He is equal to the Father in respect of his deity, and unequal and less in respect of his human nature and mediatorial office, in regard to which he is under the Father. "But a mediator is not of one" (Gal. 3:20). By this distinction the rest also must be explained. See on that passage of John, and also Petavius, vol. 2 of the Dogmatic Theology, bk. 2 On the Trinity, ch. 2.

units.la: v. Obj. Christus inter creaturas recensetur: quare non est Deus. Catechef. Racov. pag. 57. Ostorodus, Apolog. pag. 15. & contra Tradelum, pag. 55. 67. Crellius: alii. Resp. Ergo Christus inter creaturas referendus est: conceditur. at, etiam; non, solum. Et qua homo, etiam creatura est. 11 Col. i. 15. dicitur quidem primus, & quasi primogenitus creaturarum, non creatus: πρωτότοκος [?], non πρωτόκτιστος [?].
units.tr: V. Objection. Christ is counted among the creatures: therefore he is not God. Racovian Catechism, p. 57; Ostorodus, Apology, p. 15, and against Tradelius, pp. 55, 67; Crellius and others. Answer: Therefore Christ is to be reckoned among the creatures: this is granted, but not only that; he is so too, but not only so. As man he is also a creature. In Col. 1:15 he is indeed called the first and, as it were, firstborn of the creatures, not created: [πρωτότοκος], not [πρωτόκτιστος].

units.la: iii. Quod si ibi cum creaturis censeatur Christus, certe fuit tum ante creaturas, quare & ante suam ex Maria nativitatem, quod Adversarii nolunt. iv. Apocal. iii. 14. nominatur ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ: non principium passivum, sed activum, quod in principio, ἐν ἀρχῇ omnia condidit.
units.tr: (3) If Christ is counted with the creatures there, then surely he was before the creatures, and therefore before his birth from Mary, which the opponents do not want. (4) In Rev. 3:14 he is called the beginning of the creation of God [ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ]: the word means not a passive beginning but an active one, since he created all things in the beginning [ἐν ἀρχῇ].

units.la: vi. Obj. Cum ratione non congruit, ut duæ naturæ inter se uniantur, vel ut natura singularis non sit persona, vel duæ in una persona naturæ. Atque hoc argumentum quidem priore loco ponunt ante argumenta Scripturaria. Catech. Racov. pag. 55. illud non solum rectæ rationi, sed etiam Scripturæ adversum est. Volkelius, lib. 5. cap. xi. in principio, constanter dicimus, hanc opinionem nec cum sanæ mentis ratione conciliari, nec ullo sanctarum litterarum testimonio comprobari posse. Rationis judicium & repugnantiam, quam sibi fingunt, priori collocantes sede, ante, & satis supra Scripturam. Quem errorem Libro primo ex professo discussimus. Similiter argumentantur omnes, ex sua ratione. Socinus, Disp. de natura Christi, pag. 14. 15. In Catechesi, pag. 34. Smalcius, contra Frantzium, pag. 63. Contra Grawerum, pag. 10. Ostorodus, Institut. pag. 40. Crellius, &c. Resp. i. Nulla ratio philosophica dari potest, quare quum duæ substantiæ diversissimarum formarum & proprietatum uniri possunt unione substantiali; non etiam possint, ubi sic Deo placet, uniri duas naturas, in una hypostasi, unione personali. Vel enim repugnantia erit ex parte rei, vel Dei: non hoc, neque illud: ergo. Imo quidquid obganniunt Adversarii, exemplo unionis substantialis animæ & corporis refutare possumus. Non quod eam statuamus eandem, cum unione personali: sed quod eo minus putandum sit, hanc pugnare cum ratione, vel implicare, cum in inferiori unionis genere quæcunque Adversariorum difficultates vel objectiones facile nobis sit infringere & superare. ii. In natura fatemur simile exemplum dari non posse. Ut ex communi natura argumenta non recte promantur contra mysterium supernaturale: quum divina non debeant in ordinem redigi & paritatem cum naturalibus; sed quidquid in his, illi subservire & fasces [?] submittere oportet. Da simile in natura concepti ex virgine hominis, natique. Ut in hoc non modo Christus sit נִפְלָא [?] admirabilis, quod utramque habet unam naturam; sed in ipsa humana natura: cujus quia simile exemplum dari in natura non potest, videmus quam temerarium fit, ex communi natura, & hujus axiomatibus mere naturalibus velle illa eversum ire, quæ supra naturam fides agnoscit; & Deus, non ratio fundavit; singularia ut essent, non communia; mysteria, non vulgaria; gratiæ dealdenique, & solius Dei, non naturæ. Tolle argumenta, inquit Ambrosius, ubi fides quæritur. lib. 1. de fide, cap. 11. Fides nimirum in Deum Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, juxta id quod dicit Iohannes 1. epist. v. 7. quia tres sunt qui testificantur in coelo, Pater, Verbum, & Spiritus Sanctus, & illi tres unum sunt. De quo quamvis dubitatum disputatumque sæpius fuerit loco, & eum omittant versiones Syriaca, Arabica, & Æthiopica, aliique tam Græci, quam Latini codices varii, Cyprianus tamen, qui ante ortam Arianam hæresim floruit, sub annum CCL. locum citat illum, lib. de Unitate Ecclesiæ; & Athanasius, qui Concilio Nicæno interfuit, lib. ad Theophilum, de unita Deitate Trinitatis; & Idacius Clarus, ad a. CCC LXXX. lib. adversus Varimadum Arianum, in Bibl. PP. tom. iv. ut Hieronymus, qui sub annum vixit paulo minus quam quadringentesimum a Christi passione, uti ipse refert in Hof. iii. scribat in prologo Epistol. Canonic. ad Eustochium, hic ab infidelibus translatoribus multum erratum esse a Fidei veritate, trium tantummodo vocabula, hoc est, Aquæ, sanguinis, & Spiritus in ipsa sua editione ponentibus, & Patris, Verbique, ac Spiritus testimonium omittentibus, in quo maxime & fides Catholica roboratur, & Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti una divinitatis substantia comprobatur. Unde non tantum in diversis Antiquorum codicibus lectum illud comma, sed & ab aliis citatum, atque in Ecclesiis in publicis lectionibus Dominica in albis, & in Ritualibus Græcorum recitari solitum, ostendit variis exemplis Jo. Seldenus, lib. ii. de Synedrii, cap. iv. & Johannes Gerhardi, Disputat. Ienensium, part. ii. pag. 1293.
units.tr: VI. Objection. It does not agree with reason that two natures should be united with each other, or that a single nature should not be a person, or that two natures should be in one person. The opponents indeed put this argument first, before the arguments from Scripture. Racovian Catechism, p. 55: That is opposed not only to right reason but also to Scripture. Volkelius, bk. 5, ch. 11, at the beginning: We maintain constantly that this opinion can be reconciled neither with the reasoning of a sound mind nor proved by any testimony of the holy letters. By placing the judgment of reason and the repugnance they imagine in the first seat, before and well above Scripture, they commit an error which we have expressly discussed in the first book. All of them argue in the same way from their own reasoning: Socinus, Disputation on the Nature of Christ, pp. 14–15; in the Catechism, p. 34; Smalcius, against Frantzius, p. 63; against Grawerus, p. 10; Ostorodus, Institutes, p. 40; Crellius, etc. Answer: (1) No philosophical reason can be given why, when two substances of very different forms and properties can be united by a substantial union, two natures should not also be able to be united in one hypostasis by a personal union, where God so pleases. For either the repugnance will lie on the side of the thing or on the side of God; it is neither this nor that; therefore. Indeed, whatever the opponents snarl, we can refute them by the example of the substantial union of soul and body. Not that we hold it to be the same as the personal union, but that it must be thought all the less to fight against reason or to involve a contradiction, since in the lower kind of union we can easily break down and overcome whatever difficulties or objections the opponents raise. (2) In nature we admit that no similar example can be given. Arguments drawn from common nature cannot rightly be brought against a supernatural mystery, since divine things ought not to be brought into order and parity with natural things; rather, whatever is in the natural order must serve and bend to them. Give a similar case in nature of a man conceived and born of a virgin. Then not only is Christ admirable [נִפְלָא] in this, that he has both natures in one person, but also in the human nature itself. Since a similar example cannot be given in nature, we see how rash it is to wish to overturn, from common nature and its purely natural axioms, those things which faith acknowledges above nature, and which God, not reason, founded: singular things, not common ones; mysteries, not ordinary ones; things of grace and of God alone, not of nature. Take away arguments, says Ambrose, where faith is sought. Book 1 On Faith, ch. 11. Faith, of course, is in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in accordance with what John says in 1 John 5:7: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. Although this passage has often been doubted and disputed, and the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions omit it, along with various other Greek and Latin codices, nevertheless Cyprian, who flourished before the Arian heresy arose, about the year 250, cites this passage in his book On the Unity of the Church; and Athanasius, who was present at the Council of Nicaea, in his book To Theophilus, On the Unity of the Deity of the Trinity; and Idacius Clarus, about the year 380, in his book Against Varimadus the Arian, in the Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 4. Jerome, who lived a little less than four hundred years after Christ's passion, as he himself reports on Hosea 3, writes in the prologue to the Catholic Epistles to Eustochium: Here the unfaithful translators have strayed much from the truth of the faith, since they put in their edition only three words, that is, water, blood, and Spirit, and omit the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, in which above all the Catholic faith is strengthened, and the one divine substance of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is proved. Hence John Selden, bk. 2 On the Sanhedrin, ch. 4, and Johann Gerhard, Jena Disputations, part 2, p. 1293, show by various examples that this verse was not only read in the diverse codices of the ancients and cited by others, but was also customarily recited in the churches in public readings on Low Sunday and in the Ritual of the Greeks.

units.la: Atque ita tractavimus, bono cum Deo, arduum & magnum hoc pietatis mysterium, quod Deus manifestatus in carne, quod Christus θεάνθρωπ[?]ος, & verus natura Deus est. Quam tum argumentis confirmavimus veritatem, tum vindicavimus à cavillis & objectionibus Adversariorum Christi, & Dei. Nihilque scimus momenti aut ponderis alicujus à nobis præteritum, certe data operâ nihil, quin ex dictis commode responderi possit ad omnia, quæ hic agitari, quæri, ac disputari solent. Facillimeque ad ea etiam quæ alii, quæ Dominicus Montanus, in Disputatione epistolica Belgicæ, Ann. MDCXXV. pridem edita Ann. MDCI[?]. cum Petro Johanne Twisck, Anabaptista attulit, cum per totum, tum pag. 125. &c. Nam quomodo illos homines, juxta cum Remonstrantibus, sollicitent Sociniani, & per illos irrepere conentur, nimis quam notum omnibus. Narratque Petrus Twisck epistolâ ad Montanum primâ, pag. 7. sibi cum Christophoro Ostorodo, & Andrea Voidovio, quum in Belgium venissent, Amsteldami sermonem fuisse, atque abinde tum à se ad illos in Poloniam (quos Fratres appellat), tum ab Ostorodo sibi libros missos, ut non exiguum illorum inter se sciamus fuisse commercium, & nimium sæpe eos convenire. In quod tempestive invigilare debent, cum cætus ab hac labe adhuc magis immunes, tum præsertim nos, quorum est videre, ne qua via sive per alios, sive recta hæresis ingruat, vel aliquod inde veritas capiat detrimenti.
units.tr: And so, with God's good help, we have treated this arduous and great mystery of godliness, that God was manifested in the flesh, that Christ is theanthropos [θεάνθρωπος], and true God by nature. We have confirmed this truth by arguments, and defended it against the cavils and objections of the adversaries of Christ and of God. We know of no point of weight or moment that we have passed over, and certainly none deliberately omitted: from what has been said, a fitting answer can be given to all the things that are usually raised, asked and disputed on this subject. Those things can also be answered very easily which others have brought forward, such as Dominicus Montanus, in the Dutch Epistolary Disputation, published some time before, together with Petrus Johannes Twisck, an Anabaptist, both throughout and at p. 125 and following. For how the Socinians, together with the Remonstrants, try to draw those men over and creep in through them, is all too well known to everyone. Petrus Twisck relates, in his first letter to Montanus, p. 7, that he had a conversation in Amsterdam with Christophorus Ostorodus and Andreas Wojdowski when they came into Belgium; and that afterwards books were sent to him by Ostorodus, and by him to those men in Poland (whom he calls "Brethren"). So we know that there was no small intercourse among them, and that they met very often. Against this the congregations, still more free from this taint, ought to be on guard in good time, and especially we, whose duty it is to see that no heresy breaks in, whether by indirect or direct means, and that the truth suffers no harm from it.

units.la: Sed & levi admodum operâ respondere potest ad rationes ab Autore Irenici Ireni-rorum nuper allatas, quibus probare conatur Christum non esse summum Deum nempe titulo libri promittens lectori ea, quæ, uti ipse scribit, imo ab ipso Apostolorum ævo inaudita fuere: quo non leve rebus suis ipsum creare præjudicium prudentiores facile vident. Jam hoc ejus primum argumentum: Quicumque est homo, patitur, moritur, resurgit &c. non est summus Deus. Atqui Christus est homo &c. Ergo. Resp. 1. Perperam ab Adversariis in disputatione, ubi de Deo vero quæritur, & non absque sophistica addi summum Deum: quasi alius sit Deus à summo, & vel in-seriores alii Dii, vel aliquis etiam verus Deus, quamvis non sit summus. Quin quoties dicunt summum Deum, toties suam sententiam tacite condemnant, de Deo apud ipsos alio à summo, & suo Christo non Deo, vel semi Deo. Qui Gentilium error à Christianis semper merito castigatus fuit, tantum abest ut inter eos unquam repe-rerit locum. Certe nisi summus Deus, non est Deus, non verus. Fraudulenter ergo in totâ hac disputatione dicunt Adversarii, solum Patrem esse summum Deum: significantes sc. Christum esse quidem etiam Deum, sed non summum, summo vid. inferiorem, & huic quid ni inferiores etiam alios? ii. Præsertim quandoquidem nomen Dei negant naturæ nomen, tantummodo dignitatis esse & officii. Summus Deus Adversariis significat, summæ esse potestatis ac officii: & hoc summum Chri-sto derogare qui possunt, vel qua ratione in dubium trahere summam ejus Deitatem, quodque dicatur summus Deus? Nam certe summum ejus est officium, dignitas summa. Non ergo solus Pater, sed & Christus, etiam ex Adversariorum de Deo sententia & expositione, Deus summus est vel officio summo. Quid si nullæ essent creaturæ, in quas potestatem aliquam Deus exerceret, nullusne esset Deus? nempe si nihil præter dignitatem & officium vox Dei designet. iii. Summum Deum quando intelligunt, ita ut ab illâ summitate submoveatur Christus, in ipsis terminis turpiter petunt id quod est in quæstione, quod contra leges disputandi est, atque vitium, cujus nos volunt arguere, ipsi autem maximè sunt rei. iv. Solum Patrem esse summum Deum nusquam Scriptura dicit, quidem illum esse Deum, & verum Deum: atque uti à veritate Deus non patitur diversitatem & gradus, ita nec in summitate. v. Solus Pater est summus Deus, & solus Christus est summus Deus,& solus quoque Spiritus Sanctus: solus dicitur, ad exclusionem eorum qui non sunt Deus, non qui Deus. Pariter dicam, solus Christus est summus Dominus, respectu vid. aliorum, non Patris: sic & Deus summus, inferiorum aliorum ratione dicatur, non Filii, vel Spiritus Sancti. Summitas est attributum relativum ad creaturas, tam in Deo, quam in Domino. Nuspiam dicitur summus respectu Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Hæc ad quæstionis prædicatum: utrum Christus sit summus Deus? vi. Nunc ad majo-rem; quicunque est homo &c. is non est Deus, vel, in quo termino lubenter ludunt Adversarii, non summus Deus: reformamus eam, vel limitamus: quicunque est homo, is, ea ratione, non est Deus: concedo. vel, quicunque est homo, is nullâ prorsus ratione potest esse Deus: negatur. Quicunque est homo, quatenus talis, qua homo, non est Deus: rectè. Et hinc sequitur, quod ergo Christus homo, qua talis, non est Deus. Atque nisi ita restringamus propositionem, erunt quatuor termini. Qui est homo, non est Deus: atqui Christus est homo: ergo Christus homo, non est Deus: vid. qui & quatenus homo: non autem debes concludere simpliciter, ergo Christus non est Deus: prout nomen homo collocas, vel exponis aut restringis. vii. Quicunque est homo, &c. is non est Deus: certe non omnis & quicunque est homo, Deus est: non hinc quod homo, est Deus: neque quid sit, inferendum; sed, quid, vel non, etiam esse possit: hoc modo, Qui est homo, patitur, moritur, resurgît, &c. is non potest etiam esse summus Deus? negatur tum ista propositio. viii. Jam ego retorquebo argumentum, & formato eo ad mentem Adversariorum, qui dicunt passim Christum Deum, & verum Deum esse, quam non concludat, vel quo laboret vitio, videbitur: Quicunque est homo, patitur, moritur, resurgit &c. is non est Deus: Atqui Christus est homo &c. Ergo Christus non est Deus. Conclusio etiam contra ipsos est, & sensum ipsorum istum, quo eum contendunt, non quaero quomodo, contendunt tamen Deum esse. Quare ut salvent conclusionem suam, & minorem negari non potest, majorem vel negare debent, vel limitare. Atque hoc idem sece-ramus nos. Vident ergo majoris propositionis vitium aut defectum. ix. Alia instantia: Quicunque habet corpus, quo ambulat, edit, &c. is non est Angelus: Qui Abrahamo, aliisque Patribus apparet, habet corpus, &c. Ergo non est Angelus. Li-mitabis, sat scio, majorem meam: sic nempe & ego tuam. Vel denique sic, Quicunque moritur, is non est immortalis: Homo moritur: ergo non est immortalis.
units.tr: But the reasons recently brought forward by the author of Irenicum Irenicorum can also be answered with very little effort. By these he tries to prove that Christ is not the supreme God, promising the reader in the title of his book things which, as he himself writes, were indeed unheard of from the very age of the apostles. Prudent readers easily see that this is no slight prejudice against his own cause. Now here is his first argument: Whoever is man, suffers, dies, rises again, etc., is not the supreme God. But Christ is man, etc. Therefore... Answer 1. The adversaries wrongly add "supreme" in a dispute where the question is about the true God, and they do so not without sophistry, as if there were one God apart from the supreme one, and lesser gods, or some true God who is not supreme. Indeed, whenever they say "the supreme God", they tacitly condemn their own opinion, namely that there is a God other than the supreme one, and that their Christ is not God but at most a demigod. The error of the Gentiles has always been rightly rebuked by Christians, and it has never found a place among them. Certainly, if he is not the supreme God, he is not God, not the true God. The adversaries therefore fraudulently say, throughout this whole dispute, that only the Father is the supreme God, meaning that Christ is indeed God but not supreme, that is, inferior to the supreme God; and why not other inferiors as well? ii. Especially since they deny that the name God is a name of nature, and say that it is only a name of dignity and office. The adversaries mean by "supreme God" one who has supreme power and office; and how can they deprive Christ of this supremacy, or on what ground can they call in question his supreme Deity and say that he is the supreme God? For certainly his office is supreme and his dignity is the highest. So it is not only the Father but also Christ who is the supreme God, according to the adversaries' own opinion and explanation, or at least by his supreme office. What if there were no creatures over which God exercised any power? Would he then not be God, if the word God signifies nothing but dignity and office? iii. When they understand "supreme God" in such a way that Christ is removed from that supremacy, they shamefully beg in the very terms the question that is in dispute. This is against the rules of disputation, and it is the fault with which they want to charge us, though they themselves are most guilty of it. iv. Scripture nowhere says that only the Father is the supreme God; it says that he is God, and the true God. And just as God does not admit of diversity and degrees in truth, so neither does he in supremacy. v. Only the Father is the supreme God, and only Christ is the supreme God, and only the Holy Spirit too. "Only" is said to exclude those who are not God, not those who are God. In the same way I would say that Christ alone is the supreme Lord, in relation to others, not to the Father; so too "supreme God" is said in relation to other inferiors, not in relation to the Son or the Holy Spirit. Supremacy is an attribute relative to creatures, both in God and in Lord. Nowhere is he called supreme in relation to the Son and the Holy Spirit. So much for the predicate of the question: whether Christ is the supreme God? vi. Now to the major premise: "Whoever is man, etc., is not God," or, at the point where the adversaries gladly play, "is not the supreme God." I reform or limit it: "Whoever is man, is not God in that respect": I grant it. But if it means "whoever is man can in no way at all be God": I deny it. "Whoever is man, as such, insofar as he is man, is not God": that is right. And from this it follows that Christ, as man, is not God. Unless we restrict the proposition in this way, there will be four terms. "He who is man is not God; but Christ is man; therefore Christ as man is not God": here the phrase "who" and "insofar as" are needed. You must not conclude simply, "Therefore Christ is not God," according to how you place, explain or restrict the word "man". vii. "Whoever is man, etc., is not God": certainly not every man is God, and it does not follow from the fact that he is man that he is God; nor should we infer what he is, but what he can or cannot also be. In this way: "He who is man, suffers, dies, rises again, etc., cannot also be the supreme God?" That proposition too is denied. viii. Now I will turn the argument back, and, framing it in the mind of the adversaries, who everywhere say that Christ is God and the true God, it will be seen whether it concludes, or what fault it suffers from: "Whoever is man, suffers, dies, rises again, etc., is not God. But Christ is man, etc. Therefore Christ is not God." The conclusion also tells against them, and I do not ask how they contend that he is God, though they do contend it. So, if they want to save their conclusion, and the minor cannot be denied, they must either deny the major or limit it. And this is exactly what we have done. They therefore see the fault or defect in the major premise. ix. Another instance: "Whoever has a body by which he walks, eats, etc., is not an angel. He who appeared to Abraham and the other fathers has a body, etc. Therefore he is not an angel." I know well that you will limit my major premise; so, by the same token, I limit yours. Or finally in this way: "Whoever dies is not immortal. Man dies. Therefore he is not immortal."

units.la: Respondent, hoc quidem manifeste verum esse, quod homo secundum animam est immortalis, non autem quod Christus aliam ab humana habet naturam: & illud dum dicimus, petere nos quaestionem: nam illud esse controversum, non ita hominis quod ad animam immortalitatem. Verum non ego argumentor, & peto mihi dari id quod in quaestione, vid. in Christo praeter humanam naturam, esse quoq; divinam. Sed dico, quod id ipsum per Adversarii argumentum non evertitur. Etenim defendenti licet adversus Opponentem thesim suam tenere, quam tuetur, modo nil eo probet. Deinde quemadmodum illud de hominis immortalitate adferre licet, quia manifeste verum, non quod ab altera disputantium parte assumitur, sic illud propterea attulimus, quia manifesta sua veritate ostendit majorem argumenti adversus nos & Christum formati non esse simpliciter & universaliter veram. Misso ergo hoc, an a partibus illud vel illud accipiatur, an non, rerum veritate nitimur, non partium concessione.
units.tr: They reply that it is manifestly true that man is immortal according to the soul, but not that Christ has a nature other than the human one; and while we say that, they say, we beg the question, because it is not the immortality of man as to the soul that is in controversy. But I am not arguing, and I ask only that what is in question be granted, namely that in Christ, besides the human nature, there is also a divine nature. What I say is that this very point is not overturned by the adversary's argument. For it is permitted to a defender, against an opponent, to hold the thesis he defends, provided he proves nothing by it. Furthermore, just as we may adduce the truth about man's immortality because it is manifestly true, and not because it is assumed by the other party of the disputants, so we adduced that point because by its manifest truth it shows that the major premise of the argument formed against us and Christ is not simply and universally true. Setting aside, then, whether that is accepted or not by the parties, we rest on the truth of the matter, not on the concession of the parties.

units.la: Major mea firma est per regulam de disparatis,” inquit Autor. Nam duo disparata de eodem dici subjecto impossibile est. Quid disparata? imo contraria possunt dici de eodem subjecto: uti de eodem homine, non solum quod albus, & longus, & doctus, sed quoque quod albus & niger, mortalis est & immortalis: modo, quod etiam tyrones norunt, non ad idem, atque eodem modo illa dicantur de eodem homine; secundum aliud albus, aliud niger est, sic mortalis & immortalis. Atque sic exponimus (nam expositionis causa illud adducimus, non probationis) Christum secundum aliud esse hominem, & passum, & mortuum; secundum aliud, Deum.
units.tr: "My major premise is firm by the rule of disparates," says the author. "For two disparates cannot be predicated of the same subject." What disparates? Indeed contraries can be predicated of the same subject. Of the same man one can say not only that he is white, tall and learned, but also that he is white and black, mortal and immortal. Provided, as even beginners know, that these are not said of the same man in the same respect and in the same way, there is no problem: in one respect he is white, in another black; in one respect mortal, in another immortal. So we explain (for we adduce this for the sake of explanation, not as proof) that Christ, according to one nature, is man, and suffered, and died; according to another, he is God.

units.la: Quocirca, immota nunc veritatis manet haec argumentatio: Quaecunque se perimunt, sive in naturalibus, sive divinis, ea, cum stare simul non possint, falsa sunt. Agnosco: sed ap-plicatum ad varia de eodem subjecto disparata, quasi aut se mutuo perimerent, aut simul stare non possent, & in naturalibus, & in divinis est aeque falsum. Quare non ut sibi facit respondentem suum Adversarium, ita loquentes deprehendet Autor no-ster omnes.
units.tr: "Therefore the argument stands unshaken in its truth: whatever destroy each other, whether in natural or in divine things, those things, since they cannot stand together, are false." I agree. But when this is applied to various disparates predicated of the same subject, as if they either destroyed each other or could not stand together, it is equally false in natural things and in divine things. Therefore our author will not catch all who speak in this way, just as he makes his opponent reply to himself.

units.la: Secundum probationis membrum oppositum rationibus, uti eas formant, nostris r.[?] ex eo, quod Christus in Scripturis Deus dicitur, imo ut alicubi, Deus verus, & Iehova dici videatur: Ier. 23. 5. I Ioh. 5. 20. &c. vel 2. quod ei tribuitur descriptio Dei: Rom. 9. 5. vel 3. quod ei attributa divina tribuuntur: ut, immutabilitas, seu duratio, Heb. 13. 8. aeternitas, Ef.[?] 9. 6. Mich. 5. 2. Omniscientia, Ioh. 21. 17. Omnipotentia, Apoc. 1. 5. Phil. 3.21. vel 4. opera divina, ut Creatio & conservatio mundi, Ioh. 1. 3. Col. 1. 16. resuscitatio mor-tuorum, Ioh. 5. 21, 26. miracula alia omnia, Ioh. 10. 36, 37. & 5. demum cultus divinus, Ioh. 5. 21, 22, 23. hunc in modum instituit: Quicunque Deus quidem dicitur (prout in Thesi tua, modo citata, probas,) ita tamen, ut verus homo sit, Deumque supra se, vel eo ipso, quod Deus dicitur, habere dicatur, quem & se majorem esse expresse ipsemet profiteatur, & a quo omnia sua habeat, cum a seipso nihil habeat aut possit; quicunque durat quidem, sed a certo tantum & definito tempore; quicunque homo existens, Pater quidem aeternitatis aut seculorum dicitur, (prout tu itidem in Thesi tuâ urges & probas,) sed non, vel aeternus, vel ab aeterno esse, imo non sine principio esse, dicitur; quicunque porro omnisciens quidem dicitur, ita tamen, ut d'em ultimum sese ignorare diserte profiteatur; quicunque omnia quidem potest, sed per Patrem tantum; cuicunque Creatio quidem tribuitur, sed nova, idque, ut causae tantum secunda aut mediae, nunquam vero, ut primae; & quicunque demum cultu quidem divino affici debet, ita tamen, ut Mediator tantum & legatus Patris &c. si[?] Deus summus nulla ratione esse potest: Ratio est, quandoquidem, summum Deum supra se Deum habere; aut ab alio accipere quicquam, imo omnia; & nonnulla ignorare quoque, quae aliis sciat; esseque causam tantum secundam, non primam, &c. contradictoria sunt.
units.tr: The second part of the proof, set against our arguments as they frame them: (1) from the fact that Christ is called God in the Scriptures, and in some places even seems to be called true God and Jehovah: Ier. 23. 5; 1 Ioh. 5. 20, etc.; (2) from the fact that a description of God is ascribed to him: Rom. 9. 5; (3) from the fact that divine attributes are ascribed to him, such as immutability or duration, Heb. 13. 8; eternity, Isa. 9. 6; Mic. 5. 2; omniscience, Ioh. 21. 17; omnipotence, Apoc. 1. 5; Phil. 3. 21; (4) from divine works, such as the creation and preservation of the world, Ioh. 1. 3; Col. 1. 16; the resurrection of the dead, Ioh. 5. 21, 26; and all other miracles, Ioh. 10. 36, 37; and (5) finally from divine worship, Ioh. 5. 21, 22, 23. He sets it up in this way: whoever is indeed called God (as you prove in your thesis, cited just now), yet so that he is a true man, and is said to have God above himself, or, by the very fact that he is called God, whom he himself expressly professes to be greater than himself, and from whom he has all that he has, since he has nothing and can have nothing from himself; whoever indeed endures, but only from a certain and defined time; whoever, existing as a man, is indeed called Father of eternity or of ages (as you likewise urge and prove in your thesis), but is not said to be eternal, or to be from eternity, nay, is said not even to be without beginning; whoever further is indeed called omniscient, yet expressly professes that he is ignorant of the last day; whoever can indeed do all things, but only through the Father; to whom creation is indeed ascribed, but a new creation, and that only as a secondary or intermediate cause, never as the first; and whoever finally ought indeed to be honoured with divine worship, yet only as Mediator and envoy of the Father, etc.: such a one can in no way be the Most High God. The reason is that to have the Most High God above oneself, or to receive anything, indeed everything, from another, and also to be ignorant of some things which others know, and to be only a secondary and not a first cause, etc., are contradictory.

units.la: Resp. I. Observari ante omnia debet istorum hominum in disputando methodus; ex ratione scilicet nostra primo argumentantur in rebus fidei & summis[?]; tum secundo demum loco per Scripturam, sanam scilicet omnium hominum rationem, & S. Scripturam: quasi nempe vel satis fana nunc fit hominum ratio, vel facile constet quaenam fit omnium hominum, vel denique isto etiam modo in rebus ejusmodi praemitti debeat Scripturae Sacrae, & primo haberi loco ratio. Neque enim primo videndum, quid ratio hominibus dictet, & deinde ad eam flectenda vel interpretanda S. Scriptura: sed primum ex Scriptura, de ejus mente oportet esse certos, tum ad eam accommodare se debet omnium hominum sana ratio, sin minus sana, corrigenda. Judex rerum fidei est sola Scriptura Sacra, non ullorum hominum, quaecunque etiam, ratio. Apprehendit quidem ista illas res, & dijudicat, sed ad Scripturam, ejusque sensum; non ad se, vel ad suum placitum. Est instrumentum rerum recipiendarum, non judicandarum canon aut regula. Ut nec titulum disputationis hujus feram, prout eam praescripsit Auctor, Norma triplex, fana omnium hominum ratio, Scriptura Sacra, & Traditiones: nam neque ratio rerum Theologicarum est norma, neque, quamvis esset, praemitti Scripturae Sacrae, citra gravem ejus contumeliam, deberet.
units.tr: Answer. I. First of all, the method of these men in disputing must be observed. They argue first from our reason in matters of faith and the highest things; and only in the second place from Scripture, the sound reason of all men, and holy Scripture. As if, forsooth, the reason of men is now sufficiently sound, or it is easily agreed what is of all men, or finally, in such matters, reason ought to be placed before holy Scripture and given the first place. For we must not first consider what reason dictates to men and then bend or interpret holy Scripture to suit it; rather, we must first learn from Scripture, and be certain of its meaning, and then the sound reason of all men must accommodate itself to it, or, if it is not sound, be corrected. The judge of matters of faith is holy Scripture alone, not the reason of any men, however many. Reason apprehends those things and judges them, but with reference to Scripture and its sense, not to itself or its own pleasure. It is an instrument for receiving things, not a canon or rule for judging them. Nor would I bear the title of this disputation as the author has prescribed it: "A threefold norm: the sound reason of all men, holy Scripture, and traditions." For reason is not the norm of theological matters, and even if it were, it ought not to be placed before holy Scripture without grave dishonour to the latter.

units.la: II. Jam ad argumentum, ex abundanti tantum, & majoris claritatis ergo positum inquit, scilicet satis sufficiens ex ratione prolata argumentatio est, & Scriptura ad abundantiam facit magis quam ad necessitatem, & claritatis ergo duntaxat ad illustrandam rationem: ad argumentum, dico, illud, quod Scripturae locis hic adferri solitis complectitur, sed quae non vindicantur vel urgentur, levis sufficit responsio, quod nimirum ex iis non probatur thesis, nec adstruitur argumentum: quid a nobis in singulorum locorum examine antea copiose ostensum.
units.tr: II. As to the argument, which he says is put forward "only out of abundance and for the sake of greater clarity", namely that the argument from reason as set forth is sufficient, and that Scripture serves for abundance rather than necessity, and only for clarity, to illuminate the reason: to that argument, I say, which embraces the passages of Scripture usually cited here, but which are neither vindicated nor pressed, a slight reply suffices: that these passages clearly do not prove the thesis, nor establish the argument. We have already shown this copiously in our examination of each passage.

units.la: III. Christus dicitur Deus, non a nobis tantum, quoque ab Adversariis, ita tamen ut etiam verus homo sit, atque hac ratione, idem qui & Deus, Deum supra se habet se majorem, & a quo omnia, qui ut à Patre est, sic ab eo habet quidquid est & potest, & non a certo aliquo tempore existit, sed ante omne tempus ac semper, aeternus & ante rerum omnium principium, qui scit omnia, quamvis humanae ejus naturae non fuerit revelatus dies ultimus, omnia potest & à Patre, tribuiturque ei creatio rerum omnium etiam prima, ut causae proprię & primae, & cultu divino afficitur, ut Deus. Ita levi verborum transpositione satis ostenditur infirmitas argumenti, & quam in toto hoc negotio id quod in quaestione ipsi petant, non probent. Namque id vitium uti in argumento, ita committitur quoque in argumenti, quam institutis, probatione, quando ea ceu probata sumis, quae tibi nequaquam concessum iri non ignoras. Ut iterum, quando hoc argumentum format, repetat Sophisticam suam, non emendet. Cum alioquin fundamenta thesis tuae vel sequente tantum syllogismo examinari, refringi, & refutari potuissent: Quicunque Deus quidem dicitur, ita tamen, ut homo sit, Deumque supra se, dum Deus dicitur, habeat, quem & se majorem esse ipsemet expresse profitentur, &c. de eo non necessario sequitur, quod Deus summus sit. Ratio est in promptu, ut ante: quandoquidem, summum esse Deum, summoque Deo subesse, aut eo minorem esse, contradictoria sint. Adeone hoc tantum syllogismo oppido leves ac imbelles fingit Adversarios, qui tam facilem sibi spondet victoriam. Et totum negotium uno hoc argumento, nulla instantia, vel exceptione firmando, aut infringendo: Id prorsus facile censendum est, tum quia nuda tantum sit affirmatio, tum quia mera petitio principii. Quid ni enim verbis Smalcii nunc utar e libro ejus de vero & naturali Dei filio, cap. XI. pag. 104: Nude enim aliquid dicere, & illud adversario obtrudere, non est disputare, sed est, eum opprimere velle: sumere vero illud, quod est in controversia, cujus est, qui a rationibus destituitur, & desperabundus quidvis dicere mavult, quam veritati cedere. Caeterum ad palmarium vid. illud argumentum: quid hoc est, quicunque Deus quidem dicitur? an λεγόμενον θεόν[?] vult Christum, & qui dicis causa vulgo habetur talis, at non est? Illa quidem ipsorum est sententia, sed cujus invidiam semper aliis verbis studet obtegere & declinare. Christus certe est Deus, ita tamen ut homo sit, nempe est θεάνθρωπος[?]: dumque talis dicitur, Deum habet supra se, & se majorem: nihilominus ergo & Deus. Jam Deum alium, quam summum, ignorat fides, ignorat ratio, ignorat denique religio. De eo non necessario sequitur, quod Deus summus sit. Quis enim inferat, ut dum commemorat, aliquem dici quidem Deum, ita tamen ut homo sit, Deumque supra se, dum Deus dicitur, habeat, & quem se majorem esse ipsemet expresse fateatur, hinc sequatur, eum esse Deum? & conclusio ejus nostra debet directe opponi, ut nos affirmemus, quod ille negat: vel, ut inde aliquis concludat, necessario sequi, eum esse Deum? vel, Deum summum? Non necessario qui est homo, & Deum se majorem habet, proinde est Deus: uti nec necessario, qui Deus dicitur, talis est homo. Necessario sequitur, Christum esse Deum ex iis quae de eo hanc in rem testata Scriptura Sacra fuit. Non necessarium fuit, vel eum hominem fieri, vel ut hinc quod homo testatus Deum se superiorem, ejus Deitas necessario probetur. Jam quod ad rationem, quam subjungit, contradictoria quidem sunt in se, summum esse Deum, & non summum Deum, sed non sunt contradictoria, ut idem, secundum diversas rationes, summus sit Deus, & summo Deo subsit, eo minor: probet ista sic esse contradictoria, non petat, vel ajat tantum.
units.tr: III. Christ is called God, not only by us but also by our adversaries, yet so that he is also a true man. In this way the same one who is also God has God above himself, as greater, and from whom all things come; who, as he is from the Father, so has from him whatever he is and can be; who exists not from a certain time, but before all time and always, eternal and before the beginning of all things; who knows all things, although the last day has not been revealed to his human nature; who can do all things, and that from the Father; to whom the creation of all things is ascribed, even the first creation, as to a proper and first cause; and who is honoured with divine worship as God. Thus by a slight transposition of words it is sufficiently shown how weak the argument is, and how in this whole business they do not prove what they seek in the very question. For this fault is committed both in the argument and in the proof of the argument you set up, when you take as proved what you well know will by no means be granted to you. And again, when he forms this argument, he repeats his sophism rather than correcting it. Yet otherwise the foundations of your thesis could have been examined, broken and refuted by the following syllogism alone: "Whoever is indeed called God, yet so that he is a man, and has God above himself while he is called God, whom they also expressly profess to be greater, &c., does not necessarily follow to be the Most High God. The reason is ready, as before: since being the Most High God, and being subject to the Most High God, or being less than him, are contradictory." Do they imagine our adversaries so feeble and unwarlike that they promise themselves so easy a victory by this syllogism alone, and think the whole business can be settled by this one argument, with no instance or exception to confirm or overturn it? "That is altogether easy to judge, both because it is a bare assertion, and because it is a mere petitio principii." Why should I not now use the words of Smalcius from his book on the true and natural Son of God, chap. XI, p. 104: "For to say something bare, and to thrust it upon an adversary, is not to dispute, but is to wish to crush him; but to assume what is in controversy belongs to one who is destitute of reasons, and who, in despair, prefers to say anything rather than yield to the truth." Moreover, consider the chief argument: what is this, "whoever is indeed called God"? Does he mean Christ as a so-called God [λεγόμενον θεόν], who is commonly held to be such for the sake of argument but is not? That is indeed their opinion, but they always take pains to conceal and deflect its odium with other words. Christ is certainly God, yet so that he is a man; namely, he is God-man [θεάνθρωπος]. And while he is called such, he has God above himself, and as greater; nevertheless, therefore, he is also God. Now faith does not know another God than the Most High; reason does not know one; finally, religion does not know one. "It does not necessarily follow that he is the Most High God." For who would infer, from his recounting that someone is indeed called God, yet so that he is a man, and has God above himself while he is called God, and whom he himself expressly confesses to be greater, that it follows from this that he is God? And his conclusion ought to be directly opposed by us, so that we affirm what he denies; or, so that someone may conclude from it that it necessarily follows that he is God, or the Most High God? He who is a man and has a God greater than himself is not necessarily God on that account, just as he who is called God is not necessarily such a man. It necessarily follows that Christ is God from those things which Holy Scripture has testified concerning him to this effect. It was not necessary either that he should become a man, or that, from the fact that the man testified that he is superior to God, his Deity should necessarily be proved. As for the reason he adds: it is true that "to be the Most High God, and not to be the Most High God," are in themselves contradictory; but they are not contradictory, that the same being, according to different respects, is the Most High God and is subject to the Most High God, less than him. Let him prove these to be contradictory in such a way, and not beg the question or merely assert it.

units.la: Quare frustra tandem concludit, omnia ea, quae de Christo probata sunt, ei tanquam homini, competere posse. Quod secus se habere, ex disputatione nostra manifestum. Et, si quicquam Respondens adhuc agere velit, necesse habet probare. 1. Duo contradictoria posse simul esse vera. 2. Christum κατ' ἐξοχὴν & secundum excellentiam, in Scripturis dici Deum, quemadmodum alioquin ipse Pater, summus esse Deus dicitur. Prius probare nil necesse est, quia id non dicimus. Alterum peti a nobis non debet, quia Scriptura ignorat, alium secundum excellentiam dici Deum, & κατ' ἐλάττω[?], alium minus: & quem verum Deum testatur, docet, probat, eum hoc ipso summum esse affirmat.
units.tr: Therefore he concludes in vain that all those things which have been proved concerning Christ may belong to him as man. That this is otherwise is clear from our discussion. And if the Respondent still wishes to make any point, he must prove: 1. that two contradictories can be true at the same time; 2. that Christ is called God by way of excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν] and in the highest sense in the Scriptures, just as the Father himself is otherwise called the highest God. There is no need to prove the first, since we do not say it. The second ought not to be demanded of us, because Scripture does not know that one is called God in the highest sense and another in a lesser sense [κατ' ἐλάττονα]; and whoever it is that it attests, teaches and proves to be the true God, by that very fact it affirms him to be the highest.

units.la: Denique etiam ex Antiquitate primaeva confirmare fidem & sententiam nostram de vera Christi Deitate parati fumus, imprimis adversus Autorem libri illius, tit. Irenicum Irenicorum, ubi per traditiones decurrens, nobis impingere conatur, primis duobus seculis extitisse neminem, qui Filium docuerit unum cum Patre verum Deum, sed quod Patre ætate[?], dignitate, & potentia inferiorem omnes, quotquot extant, Scriptores asseruerint. Qui sententiam nostram originem suam debere Simoni Mago, ait, vel Cerintho, à Justino Martyre diligentius postmodum interpolatam & excultam.
units.tr: Finally, we are also ready to confirm our faith and opinion concerning the true Deity of Christ from the earliest antiquity, especially against the author of that book entitled Irenicum Irenicorum, where, running through the traditions, he tries to force upon us the claim that in the first two centuries there was no one who taught that the Son is one with the Father as the true God, but that all the writers who are extant asserted that the Son is inferior to the Father in age, dignity and power. He says that our opinion owes its origin to Simon Magus or Cerinthus, and was later more carefully embellished and polished by Justin Martyr.

units.la: Quamvis idem quoque præstitimus in disp. de Trinitate, Tom. I. Socin. Confutati, lib. II. cap. V. contra Ministros Transylvaniæ, & Jonam Schlichtingium, ubi Patres vindicavimus, ex quibus Autor Irenici iterum disputat, Ignatium puta, Irenæum, Tertullianum, alios. Age tamen, & expendamus quoque, quæ hic de novo recens scriptor attulit.
units.tr: Although we have already done the same thing in our disputation on the Trinity, in Tom. I. Socin. Confutati, lib. II. cap. V., against the ministers of Transylvania and Jonas Schlichting, where we vindicated the Fathers, from whom the author of the Irenicum again argues, namely Ignatius, Irenaeus, Tertullian and others. Nevertheless, come, let us also weigh what this recent writer has newly brought forward here.

units.la: Ex libro Pastoris primùm, seu Hermæ ad a. C. 80. hæc citat: crede, quoniam unus est Deus, qui omnia constituit, & fecit, ut essent omnia, omnium capax, & qui à nemine capitur. Nego, ista in Filium dicta, eive[?] adversa esse. Rebus omnibus aliis opponitur Deus, non Filio Pater. Aliter verò Deus ad creaturas se habet, aliter Pater ad Filium, & viceversa. Jam verò probaturus Noster, ab Hermâ Filium pro homine tantum fuisse agnitum, aut Patre & Spiritu S. minorem, hæc ex lib. III. Simil. v. profert: & propterea corpus Christi, seu Filii Dei, cui infusus erat Spiritus Sanctus, huic Spiritui servivit. Et mox, corpus Christi, inquit, Spiritui S. semper obediverat, &c. & propterea placuit Deo, & receptum est in gloria; eo quod tam pius cursus, tamque pia vita Filii sui, corporisque ejus sancti, Deo valde accepta fuerit, placueritque. Verum ex hisce non ostenditur, Hermam Filium Dei agnoscere pro homine tantum; non, Patre, per omnia minorem, vel Spiritu Sancto; at quidem corpus Filii Dei, vel eum quatenus in corpore vixit, minorem. Inter alia enim & sic loquitur: quia nuncius audit illum Spiritum Sanctum, qui infusus est omnium primus in corpore, in quo habitaret Deus. — Hoc ergo corpus, in quod inductus est Spiritus Sanctus, servivit illi spiritui. In illo ergo corpore Deus & spiritus habitavit. Neque solum Spiritum S. & Angelos dicit Hermas à Deo in consilium vocatos, de Christo in cœlestem hæreditatem evehendo, sed & Filium: Advocavit ergo Filium, & nuncios bonos, ut & huic scilicet corpori, quod servivit Spiritui S. sine querela, locus aliquis confiscendi daretur, ne viderentur mercedem servitutis suæ perdidisse. & Simil. IX. Filium Dei facit omni creaturâ antiquiorem: Filius quidem Dei omni creatura antiquior est, ita ut in consilio Patri suo adfuerit, ad condendam creaturam. Porta autem propterea nova est, quia in consummatione in novissimis diebus apparuit, ut qui affecturi sunt salutem, per eam intrent in regnum Dei. nam viderat petram candidam & ingentem, quæ erat altior montibus, & quadrata, ita ut posset totum orbem sustinere. Vetus autem videbatur esse, sed habebat novam portam quæ nuper videbatur exculpta. Quæsieratque tandem, Petra hæc & porta quid sunt? respondsum, petra hæc & porta Filius Dei est. Ille vero, quonam pacto Domine, petra vetus est, porta autem nova? Audi, inquit, insipiens & intellige. Filius quidem Dei omni creatura antiquior est, &c. Porta autem propterea nova est, quia in consummatione in novissimis diebus apparuit. Hic vero non alius, quam Christus. Idem, secundum aliam rationem, antiquus; aliam, novus est: petra, & porta. Antiquior omni creaturâ, & Dominus creaturæ, quapropter dicitur, totum orbem sustinere: iterum, & totus ab eo sustentatur orbis. Hic tandem apparuit in corpore, Deus manifestatus in carne, ut esset via vel porta suis ad salutem. Porta vero Filius Dei est, qui solus est accessus ad Deum. Aliter ergo nemo intrabit ad Deum, nisi per Filium ejus. Et hac quidem ratione, tum quod servus Patris dictus, eo minor, quatenus vero Filius, antiquior omni creatura, non docetur Patre fuisse minor, vel Pater solus summus Deus, excluso Filio. Id vero quod Aristides librum dicitur scripsisse, hoc titulo, quod Christus Jesus filius esset Deus, iterum eludit Adversarius, Christum Jesum solum esse Deum, scilicet a Deo factum & constitutum: ut, sive dicatur Deus, & solus Deus, sive non, parata semper habeant Adversarii sua κρησφύγετα[?], quibus elabantur, ut nihil videlicet iis facile sit satisfacturum. Nempe primi isti & puriores Christiani, quibus assidue cum Gentilibus, eorumque Diis pluribus confligendum erat, plures ipsi fecissent & coluissent Deos, fictum alium, alium non factum; verum hunc, alium titularem & metaphoricum; summum, & inferiorem: qualia in Gentilismo passim ac perpetuo condemnabant ipsi?
units.tr: First, from the Shepherd, that is, the Hermas, about AD 80, he cites this: believe that God is one, who created and made all things, that they might exist, who is able to contain all things, and who is contained by no one. I deny that these things, said of the Son, or anything like them, are said. God is set over against all other things, not the Father over against the Son. God relates to creatures in one way, and the Father relates to the Son in another, and vice versa. Now, our author, intending to prove from Hermas that the Son was acknowledged as merely a man, or less than the Father and the Holy Spirit, brings forward these words from Similitude 5 of Book III: and therefore the body of Christ, or of the Son of God, into which the Holy Spirit had been poured, served this Spirit. And soon after: the body of Christ, he says, had always obeyed the Holy Spirit, etc. And therefore it pleased God, and it was received into glory, because the so pious course and so pious life of his Son, and of his holy body, had been very acceptable to God, and had pleased him. But from these words it is not shown that Hermas acknowledges the Son of God as merely a man, nor as in every respect less than the Father or the Holy Spirit; rather, that the body of the Son of God, or him as he lived in the body, was less. For among other things he speaks thus: because the messenger hears that Holy Spirit which was poured first of all into the body in which God would dwell. This body therefore, into which the Holy Spirit was brought, served that Spirit. Therefore God and the Spirit dwelt in that body. And Hermas says that not only the Holy Spirit and the angels were called by God into counsel about exalting Christ to the heavenly inheritance, but also the Son: He therefore called the Son and the good messengers, so that some place might be granted to this body which served the Holy Spirit without complaint, lest they seem to have lost the reward of their service. And Similitude 9: The Son of God is indeed older than every creature, so that he was present at the counsel of his Father in creating the creature. But the gate is new for this reason, because it appeared in the last days, at the consummation, so that those who are going to obtain salvation may enter through it into the kingdom of God. For he saw a white and huge rock, which was higher than the mountains and square, so that it could sustain the whole world. But the gate seemed to be old, yet it had a new gate which had recently seemed to be carved out. And he asked at last, what are this rock and gate? It was answered: this rock and gate is the Son of God. And he: how, Lord, is the rock old, but the gate new? Hear, he said, foolish one, and understand. The Son of God is indeed older than every creature, etc. But the gate is new for this reason, because it appeared at the consummation in the last days. Here, however, it is none other than Christ. He is the same, old in one respect, new in another: rock and gate. Older than every creature, and Lord of the creature; for this reason he is said to sustain the whole world; again, and the whole world is sustained by him. He at last appeared in the body, God manifested in the flesh, so that he might be the way or gate for his people to salvation. Now the gate is the Son of God, who alone is the access to God. Otherwise therefore no one will enter to God except through his Son. And in this way, namely because he is called the servant of the Father, he is less in that respect; but insofar as he is the Son, older than every creature, it is not taught that he was less than the Father, or that the Father alone is the highest God to the exclusion of the Son. As for the book which Aristides is said to have written under this title, that Christ Jesus is the Son of God, the adversary again evades it, claiming that Christ Jesus alone is God, namely made and established by God; so that whether he is called God, and the only God, or not, the opponents always have their ready hiding-places [κρησφύγετα], by which they slip away, so that nothing can easily satisfy them. Indeed, those first and purer Christians, who had constantly to contend with the Gentiles and their many gods, would themselves have made and worshipped many gods: one made, another not made; but this one a titular and metaphorical god, another supreme and inferior. Did they not themselves constantly condemn such things in Gentilism?

units.la: Clemens Romanus, ad a. xcii. in epistolis nullibi declarat, quod Adversarius ei impingit, quod solus Pater, excluso Christo, sit unus verus Deus: neque id inde probatur, si vel dixisset, Patrem Filio majorem esse; quod secundum rationem istam, qua Filius se demisit, & obediens Patri factus est usque ad mortem, verum, non autem secundum omnem ejus rationem. Neq; damus Adversario, Clementem facere Filium prorsus inaequalem Patri, quamvis aequalitatem forte in terminis non exprimat. Nedum quod Christum ita describat, ut vix aliam, quam humanam naturam in ipso cognoscere videatur. Quando vero fatetur, nos habere ἕνα Θεόν[?], ἐ ἕνα Χριστὸν[?], καὶ[?] ἐν Πνεύματι[?], haud obscure Trinitatem significare voluit, prout agitata semper fuit & docta in Christi Ecclesia, ex fidei simplicitate magis, quam ad disputationum modos explicata doctrina. Nam non ab omnibus, omni tempore, loco, & occasione aeque clara & copiosa cujuslibet veritatis testimonia expectanda: praesertim non vel eo tempore, vel ab iis, qui contrariis disputationibus minus fuerunt divexati.
units.tr: Clement of Rome, about AD 92, nowhere in his epistles declares what the adversary charges him with, namely that the Father alone, to the exclusion of Christ, is the one true God. Nor is this proved from his words even if he had said that the Father is greater than the Son; that would be true according to that aspect by which the Son humbled himself and became obedient to the Father unto death, but not according to every aspect of him. Nor do we grant to the adversary that Clement makes the Son altogether unequal to the Father, although perhaps he does not express equality in so many words. Much less does he describe Christ in such a way that he seems to recognise in him scarcely any nature other than the human. When, however, he says that we have one God, and one Christ, and one Spirit [ἕνα Θεόν, ἕνα Χριστόν, ἐν Πνεύματι], he clearly meant to signify the Trinity, as this doctrine has always been debated and taught in the Church of Christ, set forth more from the simplicity of faith than in the modes of disputation. For clear and abundant testimonies of every truth are not to be expected at all times, in all places and on all occasions, least of all at that time, or from those who were less harassed by contrary disputations.

units.la: Ignatium ad a. C. alibi vindicavimus, neque taedet denuo ejus suscipere patrocinium. Ex duabus ejus epistolis adversus nos disputat Adversarius, ea quae est ad Tarsenses, & ad Philippenses.
