Ubi primo sciendum, de istarum epistolarum, ne dicam omnium, fide disputari inter doctos, & illas saltem non haberi pro Ignatianis, sed quas mediae aetatis Graeci, sub illius nomine, procuderint. Videamus autem, an etiam hinc, vel pro se, vel contra nos, bene disputet. Ex epistola ad Tarsenses adducit, quasi Ignatii ista: novi, quoniam quidam ministrorum Satanae voluerunt vos turbare: quorum quidam dicunt, quasi Jesu putative natus est, & putative crucifixus; quidam vero quia non est Filius ejus, qui fecit mundum; alii autem, quia ipse est ille, qui est super omnia Deus. Hoc postremum nobis objicit, quo aperte negare videtur Ignatius, vel quicunque epistolae istius autor, Christum esse eundem, qui est super omnia Deus. At primum, quare non exhibet locum integrum? plura enim sunt, quae epistolae autor rejicit, nimirum sic pergens: alii quoque, vid. ex ministris Satanae, qui vos conturbant, dicunt, quia Christus homo est merus ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος[?]. quidam vero, quia caro ejus non resurrexit, &c. Quando ergo illos rejicit, qui docebant, Christum esse eundem super omnia Deum, non voluit Christum privare divina natura, & solam in eo agnoscere humanam: nam eos, qui hoc vellent, non minus impetit, quam alios: sed neque homo merus est, per quem & in quo facta sunt omnia. Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt. Quando faciebat coelos, una ipsi aderam, & ibi aderam illi, coaptans singula, & congratulabatur mihi quotidie, congaudebatque. Quomodo merus homo audiit, Sede a dextris meis? Quomodo vero dicebat dicebat: Antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum? Et glorificabis me gloria, quam habui ante quam esset mundus. Qualis vero homo dicet: Descendi de coelo, non ut faciam voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me? De quo porro homine dicebat: Erat lux vera quae illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc modum? In mundo erat, & mundus per ipsum factus est, & mundus illum non cognovit. In propria venit, & sui eum non receperunt. Quomodo igitur hic natus homo, & qui ut esset, ex Maria coepisset exordium? & non potius Deus verbum? & unigenitus Filius? In principio enim erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat verbum. & alibi: & Dominus creavit me initium viarum suarum, in opera sua, ante saecula fundavit me, & ante omnes colles generat me. Quae sententiam ac errorem Adversariorum penitus jugulant, & non causam tantam nostram, sed & argumenta pro eadem adduci solita confirmant. Jam quomodo intellexit, quod Christus non esset idem qui super omnia Deus? videlicet, quod non esset Pater, sed Filius; contra Patripassianos, eosque qui docebant Christum ipsum esse Patrem, & Spiritum Sanctum: quem errorem Noetus postmodum, unde Noetiani, in Ecclesia Smyrnensi, renovavit, de quibus Augustinus, Haeresi cap. xxxvi. Adversarius noster fatetur, Veteres pro uno eodemque habuisse, sive quis Patrem diceret, sive Deum super omnia. Interim Christum Auctor haud semel in hac epistolâ Deum vocat, [?]τὸ σωτῆρ[?] μου [?]ὁ θεὸν [?]. [?]πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως ὁ θεὸς λόγος[?]. Ex epistolâ vero ad Philippenses haec profert Adversarius, quibus Christum introducit praecipientem baptizare in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti, & addit: non in unum quendam trinonymum, neque in tres unius ejusdemque honoris. Graeca autem longe aliter habent, & in editione Plantiniana, ann. MDLXXII. & Ufferii castigatissima, hoc modo: ὑπ᾽ εἰς ἕνα τριάνυμον, ὑπ᾽ εἰς τρεῖς ἀνθρώπους σαρκωθέντας, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τρεῖς ὁμοτίμως, non in unum trinomium, neque in tres incarnatos, sed tres ejusdem honoris. Sequitur, & haec quorsum Adversarii omittunt? unus enim est tantum ὁ ἀνθρωπήσας qui homo factus, non Pater, neque Paracletus, sed solus Filius, non putative, neque in phantasia, sed veritate: verbum enim caro factum est: nam sapientia sibi aedificavit domum, & factus est sicut homo, Deus verbum, cum corpore quod susceperit ex virgine. Praecesserat, ergo neque tres sunt Patres, neque tres Filii, neque tres Paracleti: sed unus Pater, & unus Filius, & unus Paracletus. Incarnationem dum docet, id ipsum docet, quod Adversarios nostros maxime offendit. Tres, Patrem, Filium, ac Spiritum S. dicit ejusdem honoris: quare & ejusdem essentiae. Disputat contra eos, qui unam personam faciebant, eamque τρίωνυμον, quare & Patrem hominem factum aferebant, & passim τὸ ἀγέννητον ingenitum, quo nomine Patrem designant, natum; & τὸ ἀνάρχον carentem principio cruci affixum, uti postea loquitur. contra Ignatius, non Patrem, sed Patris Filium, idque non δοκήσει, quod alii somniabant, contra quos quoque alibi invehitur, ἀλλ᾽ ἀληθείας. Autor epistolae ad Mariam Cassobolitam: Ignatius ad Trallianos; idem ad Smyrnenses. Et in hac epistola iterum offendit, quod Christus non sit merus homo ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐν ψυχῇ καὶ σώματι μόνον, verum Deus: quomodo autem non est Deus ille, qui mortuus resuscitavit, clausos fapavit, &c. — Parva tibi videntur cunabula, passiones, circumcifio, lasciua[?] nutritio. Indigna tibi haec Deo esse videntur. Vocat & Deum omnium intelligibilium ac sensibilium, Diabolum objurgans, qui ϑεωρότῃ τηλικούτῳ, ϑεῷ πάντων τ νοητῶν ϗ αἰσθητῶν dicere ausus fuit, si procidens me adoraverit. Autor epistolae, sub Ignatii nomine, ad Polycarpum, Christum dicit Filium Dei, intemporalem in tempore, invisibilem natura, visibilem in carne; impalpabilem & intactum, ut incorporeum, corporeum vero propter nos & contrectabilem; impassibilem ut Deum, passibilem vero propter nos ut hominem. In epistola, ad Antiochenos: Et Euangelistae dicentes unum Patrem solum verum Deum, non reliquerunt ea quae propria sunt Domino nostro, sed scripserunt: In principio erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat verbum. Hoc erat in principio apud Deum: omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Et de incarnatione ipsius: Verbum, inquit, caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis. Et: Liber generationis Iesu Christi filii David, filii Abraham. Apostoli vero dicentes quod Deus unus est, iidem dixerunt, quod unus & mediator Dei & hominum: nec de incarnatione; nec de passione ejus erubuerunt. Quid enim inquit? Homo Iesus Christus qui dedit semetipsum pro mundi vita & salute. Omnis itaque qui annuntiat unum & solum Deum, ut tollat Christi divinitatem, is est diabolus, & hostis omnis justitiae. Non ergo ita docetur unus Deus, ut Christi Deitati praejudicet, vel intercedat: quare & ipse est ille unus ac solus Deus. Et quicunque, inquit statim potest, incarnationem rejicit, & quem crucis pudet, propter quam vinctus sum, hic est Antichristus. Patrem appellat ingenitum; Filium vero ante secula natum: incolumes vos servet ille qui est solus ingenitus, per illum qui est ante secula natus, ὁ ὢν μόνῳ ἀγεννήτῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ αἰώνων γεγεννημένῳ. Epistola ad Heronem, diaconum: si quis merum hominem dixerit Dominum, Iudaeus est, Christi interfector. Ignatius, in epistola ad Ephesios: Habemus etiam medicum Iesum Christum ante secula unigenitum, & verbum: postea vero & hominem factum ex Maria virgine. Verbum enim caro factum est, incorporeus in corpore, impassibilis in corpore passibili, immortalis in corpore mortali, vita in corruptione, ut a morte & corruptione liberaret. Et postea, Dominus autem noster & Deus Iesus Christus. — Filius autem Dei (qui ante secula genitus est, & omnia dispositione Patris constituit) ipse in utero portatus est a Maria, secundum Dei dispositionem, ex semine David, & Spiritu Sancto. In epistola ad Trallianos, castigat eos, qui Filium merum hominem esse dicebant, & eundem esse Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum. — Obturate igitur aures vestras, cum vobis quispiam loquitur, excludens Iesum Christum Filium Dei, qui natus est ex David, qui ex Maria, qui vere genitus est ex Deo, & ex virgine, verum non similli modo. Non enim secundum idem est Deus & homo. Vere assumpsit corpus, verbum enim caro factum est. Vetus interpres, apud Ufferium legit, qui vere natus est ex Deo, & ex virgine; quia hoc ipsum est quod & Deus. Denique & Hebionitas perstringit, ut ἀνθρωπολάτρας hominis cultores, quos maledictos esse Ieremias Propheta asserit. In epistola ad Romanos, Christi, Dei & Salvatoris nostri. Ad Philadelphenos, & unus est ingenitus Deus Pater; & unus unigenitus Filius, Deus Verbum & homo: & unus Paracletus Spiritus veritatis. Tres intelligit Personas, & per ingenitum, Patrem: Filium autem esse Deum, & ϑεάνθρωπον. Siquis dicat unum quidem esse Deum, & confiteatur Christum Iesum, sed eundem nudum esse hominem putet, non autem Deum unigenitum, sapientiam & verbum Dei, sed sola anima & corpore illum constare censet, hujusmodi serpens est, fraudem & errorem praedicans in exitium hominum, & est ejusmodi inops sensu, cognomento Ebion. Ad Smyrnenses, Verbum in carne habitavit, sapientia enim aedificavit sibi domum. Verbum ergo templum sui ipsius, ab Adversariis resolutum, resuscitavit tertia die. Verbum utique exaltata carne sua, velut illo aeneo serpente in eremo, omnes attraxit ad se, ad salutem aeternam. Ex quibus constat, certe Ignatium non statuisse, Christum demum extitisse a nativitate ex Maria; vel, merum esse hominem, constantem anima & corpore, neque aliam quam humanam habere naturam, quod in Ebione, aliisque passim damnavit, de quibus ad Trallianos, τὸ μὲν γὰρ Χριστὸν ἀλλοτρίωσιν[?] ἀπὸ Πατρός, quod Christum a Patre alienarent. Ipse vero constanter docet, Christum Deum, Patris ingeniti unigenitum Filium, ante secula natum, & in temporis plenitudine incarnatum, vel hominem factum: ad quod etiam ista adfert Scripturae loca, quae hoc docent, & ab Ecclesia, inque disputationibus nostris, adferri solent: ἐνσωμάτωσιν[?] dicit, epist. ad Philadelphenos; alibi ἐνανθρωπήσαντα[?]. Docet quidem, Christum non esse Patrem, & alium ab eo, non vero non esse Deum, vel alium a vero Deum.
units.tr: We have defended Ignatius elsewhere, and I am not weary of taking up his cause again. The Adversary argues against us from two of his letters, the one to the Tarsians and the one to the Philippians. First, we must note that among scholars the authenticity of these letters, not to say of all of them, is disputed, and that at least these are not regarded as genuinely Ignatian, but as works which Greeks of the middle ages put out under his name. Let us see, however, whether he argues well from them, either for his own view or against us. From the letter to the Tarsians he cites these words as Ignatius's: I know that certain ministers of Satan have wished to trouble you. Some of them say that he was born in appearance only, and suffered in appearance only; others that he is not the Son of him who made the world; others again that he is himself that God who is above all things. He objects to us this last clause, by which Ignatius, or whoever the author of the letter was, seems plainly to deny that Christ is the same as the God who is above all things. But first, why does he not give the passage whole? For the author rejects more than this, going on thus: Others also, namely among the ministers of Satan who trouble you, say that Christ is a mere man [ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος]. Others again say that his flesh did not rise, and so on. When therefore he rejects those who taught that Christ is the same as the God who is above all things, he does not wish to strip Christ of the divine nature and acknowledge in him only the human; for he assails those who hold this no less than the others: But neither is he a mere man, through whom and in whom all things were made. For all things were made through him. When he was making the heavens, I was present with him, and there I was beside him, arranging each thing, and he rejoiced in me daily and was glad. How could a mere man hear, Sit at my right hand? And how does he say, Before Abraham was, I am? And, Glorify me with the glory which I had before the world was? What kind of man would say, I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me? And of what man does he further say, It was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world? He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. How then could this man, born and having his beginning from Mary, be the Word of God and the only-begotten Son? For in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And elsewhere: The Lord created me the beginning of his ways, for his works; before the ages he founded me, and before all hills he begets me. These passages utterly overthrow the opinion and error of the Adversaries, and confirm not only our cause but the arguments usually brought forward for it. Now how did he understand that Christ is not the same as the God who is above all things? Clearly, that he is not the Father but the Son, against the Patripassians, and those who taught that Christ himself is the Father and the Holy Spirit. This error Noetus afterwards renewed in the Church of Smyrna, whence the Noetians, of whom Augustine speaks in his book on heresies, chapter 36. Our Adversary admits that the ancients held the one and same to be meant whether one said the Father or God above all things. Meanwhile the author of this letter calls Christ God more than once: my Saviour, God [τὸ σωτῆρ μου ὁ θεός]; the firstborn of all creation, the Word of God [πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως ὁ θεὸς λόγος]. From the letter to the Philippians the Adversary brings forward these words, in which Christ is introduced commanding to baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and he adds: not into one certain trinominal being, nor into three of the same honour. But the Greek reads quite differently, both in the Plantin edition of 1572 and in Ussher's most accurate edition, thus: not into one trinominal, nor into three incarnate men, but into three equal in honour [ὑπ᾽ εἰς ἕνα τριάνυμον, ὑπ᾽ εἰς τρεῖς ἀνθρώπους σαρκωθέντας, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τρεῖς ὁμοτίμως]. Why do the Adversaries omit what follows? For there is only one who became man, not the Father, nor the Paraclete, but the Son alone, not in appearance nor in fancy but in truth; for the Word was made flesh, and wisdom built itself a house, and God the Word was made as man, with the body which he took from the virgin. He had said before that there are neither three Fathers, nor three Sons, nor three Paracletes, but one Father, one Son, and one Paraclete. In teaching the incarnation he teaches just what most offends our Adversaries. He calls the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit of the same honour, and therefore of the same essence. He disputes against those who made one person, and that a trinominal one, and so said that the Father himself was made man; and everywhere they call the Father unbegotten [τὸ ἀγέννητον], by which name they designate the Father, and the Son begotten; and without beginning [τὸ ἀνάρχον] the one fixed to the cross, as he speaks afterwards. Against these Ignatius sets not the Father but the Son of the Father, and this not in appearance [δοκήσει], as others dreamed, against whom he also inveighs elsewhere, but in truth [ἀληθείας]. The author of the letter to Maria of Cassobola, Ignatius to the Trallians, and likewise to the Smyrnians. And in this letter again he takes offence that Christ is not a mere man [ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος], in soul and body only, but is God. How, however, is he not that God who, being dead, rose again, opened the closed doors, and so on? — The cradle, the sufferings, the circumcision, the wanton nursing seem to you small things. These things seem to you unworthy of God. He also calls him God of all intelligible and sensible things, rebuking the devil, who dared to say to so great a divinity, God of all intelligible and sensible things [ϑεῷ πάντων τῶν νοητῶν καὶ αἰσθητῶν], if falling down he should worship me. The author of the letter, under Ignatius's name, to Polycarp, calls Christ the Son of God, timeless in time, invisible in nature, visible in the flesh; impalpable and untouchable as incorporeal, but corporeal and touchable for our sake; impassible as God, but passible for our sake as man. In the letter to the Antiochenes: And the evangelists, saying that the one Father is the only true God, did not leave out what is proper to our Lord, but wrote: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God: all things were made through him, and without him was made nothing that was made. And of his incarnation: The Word, he says, was made flesh, and dwelt among us. And: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. But the apostles, saying that God is one, said also that there is one mediator between God and men; nor were they ashamed of his incarnation or of his passion. For what, he says, is the man Jesus Christ, who gave himself for the life and salvation of the world? Therefore everyone who proclaims the one and only God so as to take away the divinity of Christ, he is the devil and the enemy of all righteousness. The one God is therefore not taught in such a way as to prejudice or hinder the Deity of Christ; wherefore he too is that one and only God. And whoever, he says at once, rejects the incarnation, and is ashamed of the cross, for which I am bound, he is Antichrist. He calls the Father unbegotten, but the Son born before the ages: may he preserve you unharmed who alone is unbegotten, through him who was begotten before the ages [ὁ ὢν μόνῳ ἀγεννήτῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ αἰώνων γεγεννημένῳ]. The letter to Heron the deacon: If anyone calls the Lord a mere man, he is a Jew and a murderer of Christ. Ignatius, in the letter to the Ephesians: We have also Jesus Christ, the physician, the only-begotten and Word before the ages, but afterwards also made man of Mary the virgin. For the Word was made flesh, incorporeal in a body, impassible in a passible body, immortal in a mortal body, life in corruption, so that he might free us from death and corruption. And afterwards: But our Lord and God Jesus Christ. — The Son of God, who was begotten before the ages and established all things by the Father's disposition, was himself carried in the womb by Mary, according to God's disposition, of the seed of David, and by the Holy Spirit. In the letter to the Trallians he rebukes those who said that the Son was a mere man and that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit were the same. — Stop your ears, therefore, when anyone speaks to you apart from Jesus Christ the Son of God, who was born of David, of Mary, who was truly begotten of God and of the virgin, but not in the same way. For God and man are not the same according to the same thing. He truly took a body, for the Word was made flesh. The old translator, as read in Ussher, has who was truly born of God and of the virgin, because this very thing is also God. Lastly, he also attacks the Hebionites, as worshippers of man [ἀνθρωπολάτρας], whom the prophet Jeremiah declares to be accursed. In the letter to the Romans: of Christ, our God and Saviour. To the Philadelphians: and there is one unbegotten God the Father, and one only-begotten Son, God the Word and man, and one Paraclete, the Spirit of truth. He understands three Persons, and by the unbegotten he means the Father, but the Son is God and God-man [ϑεάνθρωπον]. If anyone says that there is indeed one God, and confesses Christ Jesus, but thinks that he is a bare man and not the only-begotten God, wisdom and Word of God, and judges that he consists only of soul and body, such a man is a serpent, preaching deceit and error to the destruction of men, and is of such a sort, empty of sense, a man of the name of Ebion. To the Smyrnians: The Word dwelt in the flesh, for wisdom built itself a house. The Word therefore, the temple of himself, being destroyed by the adversaries, raised it up on the third day. The Word indeed, having lifted up his flesh, as that brazen serpent in the wilderness, drew all to himself, to eternal salvation. From which it is clear that Ignatius certainly did not hold that Christ came into existence only at his birth from Mary, or that he was a mere man, consisting of soul and body, and having no nature other than human, which he condemned in Ebion and others everywhere, of whom he says in the letter to the Trallians that they estrange Christ from the Father [τὸ μὲν γὰρ Χριστὸν ἀλλοτρίωσιν ἀπὸ Πατρός]. He himself teaches constantly that Christ is God, the only-begotten Son of the unbegotten Father, begotten before the ages and incarnate, or made man, in the fulness of time; and to this he also brings those Scripture passages which teach this and which are usually brought forward by the Church and in our disputations. He says incorporated [ἐνσωμάτωσιν] in the letter to the Philadelphians, and elsewhere having become man [ἐνανθρωπήσαντα]. He does indeed teach that Christ is not the Father, and is other than him, but not that he is not God, or other than the true God.

units.la: Quod modo dixi, iterum, ubi de Polycarpo, repetendum videtur. Non ab omnibus, ubique, & semper fidem in Trinitatem, & Deitatem Filii aeque testatam & confirmatam fuisse, prout non semper ejus oblata occasio, non controversia, quae hoc exigeret: at nihil tamen in contrarium proferri ex illis, ab Adversariis, posse. Et negativum argumentum in hujusmodi nil concludere, omnibus notum. Non certe Polycarpus ullibi id docuit, quod eum Filium hominem tantum credidisse, uti ait, arguat. Contrarium enim vel ex Ignatio colligas, cum quo paria credidisse Polycarpum, quem in epistola sua magnopere commendat, extra dubium haberi debet. Distinguit quidem Christum a Deo, misericordia vobis & pax a Deo omnipotente, & Iesu Christo Salvatore nostro. — Sicut Deo & Christo. — Deus autem & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & ipse sempiternus Pontifex, Dei Filius, Iesus Christus. — qui credituri sunt in Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, & in ipsius Patrem, qui resuscitavit eum a mortuis: sed uti eo non negatur, Christum quoq; semetipsum suscitasse, quod Ignatius aperte docet; ita & Dei Filium extitisse antequam Christus esset, & ante secula a Patre genitum, ex eodem probari poterit. Ubi vero dicitur Polycarpo, Christus homo tantum, & qui in carne venit? quod contendit Noster, non probat, vel, quod Filium hominem tantum crediderit? Quin contra fidei potius suae argumentum illustre exhibuit, in oratione, sub ultimam martyrii horam martyrii, dicens: Pater dilecti & benedicti Filii tui Iesu Christi, &c. tibi gratias ago — per immortalem Spiritum S. virtutem, &c. Ac propterea prae caeteris omnibus te laudo, te benedico, te glorifico, per Iesum Christum dilectum tuum Filium, pontificem aeternum, per quem tibi cum eo in Spiritu S. gloria nunc & in futura saecula saeculorum. Amen.
units.tr: What I have just said about Polycarp seems to need repeating. It is not that the faith in the Trinity and in the Deity of the Son was equally attested and confirmed by all, everywhere, and always. The occasion did not always arise, and there was not always a controversy that demanded it. Yet our opponents can bring forward nothing to the contrary from those writings. Everyone knows that an argument from silence proves nothing in such matters. Certainly Polycarp nowhere taught what they say, that he believed the Son to be only a man. The contrary may be gathered even from Ignatius, and it must be beyond doubt that Polycarp, whom Ignatius greatly commends in his letter, believed the same things as Ignatius. Polycarp does indeed distinguish Christ from God: mercy to you and peace from God Almighty and from Jesus Christ our Saviour. As to God and Christ. But God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the eternal High Priest himself, Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Those who are about to believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, and in his Father, who raised him from the dead. But just as it is not denied by this that Christ also raised himself, which Ignatius plainly teaches, so it can be proved from the same passages that the Son of God existed before Christ was made flesh, and was begotten by the Father before the ages. As for the words said to Polycarp, Christ a mere man, who came in the flesh?, which our author contends, do they prove that he believed the Son to be only a man? On the contrary, Polycarp gave a notable proof of his faith in his prayer at the last hour of his martyrdom, saying: Father of your beloved and blessed Son Jesus Christ, etc. I give you thanks, through the immortal Spirit, etc. And therefore above all others I praise you, I bless you, I glorify you, through Jesus Christ your beloved Son, the eternal High Priest, through whom be glory to you with him and the Holy Spirit, now and for the ages to come. Amen.

units.la: Qualis usitata semper in Ecclesia fuit δοξολογία eorum, qui fidem suam in Trinitatem ὁμοούσιον testari ista formula voluerunt, nempe qui & Filium, & Spiritum S. Patri aequalem statuebant ac credebant. Non quod nihil argutari contra eam male sani possint: quid enim tale dari aut praescribi queat, quod non arrodere aliquo pacto homines audeant? sed quod modestis ac piis confessio istiusmodi facile satisfaciat, & comprehendere censeatur, quae Orthodoxa Ecclesia contra haereticos, eorumque errores constanter agnovit ac tenuit. Nec tria hic tantum nomina vel τριώνυμον[?] celebravit martyr, sed tres, distinctos quidem, at una conglorificandos, Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum. Verum, inquit Noster, etiam Eph. vi. 18. docemur orare in Spiritu, sine ulla aequalitatis Spiritus, cum Patre, notâ. Resp. Incertum esse, an non in spiritu, ibi sit, quod mente, ac animo, quemadmodum Joan. iv. 23. in spiritu & veritate: vel si Spiritum Sanctum intelligas, quaero, quaenam inaequalitatis cum Patre addita hic sit nota?
units.tr: Such has always been the usual doxology in the Church of those who wished to declare their faith in the consubstantial Trinity by this formula, namely those who held and believed that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father. It is not that wicked men cannot quibble against it in some way, for what can be given or prescribed that men do not dare to gnaw at in some way? But such a confession easily satisfies modest and pious people, and is held to comprehend what the Orthodox Church constantly acknowledged and held against heretics and their errors. Nor did the martyr here celebrate merely three names, or a triad, but three persons, distinct indeed, yet to be glorified together: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But, says our author, Eph. vi. 18. teaches us to pray in the Spirit, without any mark of the Spirit's equality with the Father. Reply: It is uncertain whether in spirit there means something else, namely in mind and soul, as in John iv. 23., in spirit and truth. Or if you understand the Holy Spirit, I ask, what mark of inequality with the Father is added here?

units.la: Pergit ad Iustinum, qui vixit circa annum Christi cL. de quo falsò primum annotat, quod tum temporis primum recepta fuit in Ecclesia, de duabus in Christo naturis, sententia, cuius adeo manifesta documenta dedimus, in epistolis Ignatii. Neque verum, quod vel primus Justinus, vel post eum alii, versus Orphei
units.tr: He goes on to Justin, who lived about the year of Christ 150. Concerning him our author first wrongly notes that at that time the doctrine of the two natures in Christ was for the first time received in the Church, though we have given clear evidence of this view in the letters of Ignatius. Nor is it true that either Justin first, or others after him, adopted as some divine foundation the verses of Orpheus,

units.la: Vocem juro Patris, primum quam prodidit ore, Consilio ipse suo mundum cum conderet omnem.
units.tr: I swear by the voice of the Father, which first he uttered from his mouth, when with his own counsel he founded the whole world,

units.la: pro fundamento aliquo iecerint divino, ad quod sententiam de Christo accommodarent & conformarent. Quamvis nimis avide forte religionem Christianam è scriptis gentilium, sive Poetarum, sive Philosophorum, comprobare sategerint, animo magis bono, quam prudenti, quasi ea quae videntur vera, undiquaque ab exteris vindicaturi, & adscripturi religioni. Juxta id, quod Justinus habet, Apol. i. quaecunque apud omnes recte dicta sunt, nostra Christianorum sunt. Praeterea exponere quidem nonnunquam modum aeternae generationis tentarunt, & negative potius quam affirmative; non vero de eo admodum disputare, nisi postquam haereticorum in sensum detorqueri illa caeperunt. Denique Scriptor antiquus, apud Eusebium, lib. v. cap. ult. contra Artemonitarum haeresim, quae Christum ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον merum esse hominem docebat, nominat inter primos Justinum, qui illam rejecerit: non quod vel nemo ante hunc idem docuerit, contrarium enim jam ostendimus; vel quod à Justino tantum sententiae istius professio inchoarit: sed quod illos intenderit commemorare, qui tum contra Gentiles, pro veritatis defensione, tum contra haereses eo tempore grassantes scripserant, interque eos primum collocat Justinum, citra alterius ullius praejudicium vel neglectum. Tum iste Autor haeresim, quae vid. Servatorem merum hominem dicebat, & quam ejus patroni ad Apostolos usque perducebant, suo tempore, vel non longe antea ὑ' ἀπὸ [illegible, ~7 letters] exortam, inquit, & impium ac blasphemum commentum, βλάσφημον ψευδηγορίαν[?], cujus Theodotus coriarius fuerit auctor: referens, quod Victor, Romanus episcopus, Theodotum illum coriarium τὸν ἀρχηγὸν [?] ἐκ πατρὸς τῆς Θεότητος ἀπεκήρυξε τῆς κοινωνίας, πρῶτον εἰπόντα ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν Χριστόν, qui primus dixit Christum esse merum hominem, ducem & patrem ipsius Deum negantis defectionis, communione interdixit. Porro in scriptis Justini, Miltiadis, Tatiani, Clementis, Christum vere Deum esse, idem Author confirmari ait, ὡς ἐν εἷς ἅπαξ θεολογεῖται[?] ὁ Χριστός. Irenaei enim, & Melitonis, & reliquorum libros quis ignorat Christum praedicare Deum & hominem? Quot item Psalmi, quot hymni à fratribus fidelibus antiquitus perscripti, qui Christum verbum Dei, verum Deum esse concentu quodam concelebrant?
units.tr: to which they might adapt and conform their view of Christ. Although perhaps they too eagerly strove to prove the Christian religion from the writings of the Gentiles, whether poets or philosophers, with a good rather than a prudent intention, as if they would claim for their religion whatever seems true from outsiders and ascribe it to religion. Accordingly, Justin says in his first Apology: whatever has been rightly said among all men belongs to us Christians. Moreover, they sometimes attempted to explain the manner of eternal generation, and negatively rather than affirmatively, but they did not discuss it much until heretics began to twist those doctrines to their own sense. Finally, an ancient writer, in Eusebius, book v, last chapter, against the heresy of the Artemonites, who taught that Christ was a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον], names Justin among the first who rejected it. Not that no one had taught this before him, for we have already shown the contrary; nor that the profession of this view began only with Justin; but the writer intended to mention those who wrote at that time both against the Gentiles, in defence of the truth, and against the heresies then raging, and he places Justin first among them, without prejudice to or neglect of anyone else. Then the same author says that the heresy which called the Saviour a mere man, and which its adherents traced back to the Apostles, arose in his own time, or not long before, as an impious and blasphemous fiction [βλάσφημον ψευδηγορίαν], whose author was Theodotus the tanner. He reports that Victor, bishop of Rome, excommunicated that tanner Theodotus, the leader [τὸν ἀρχηγὸν] of the defection that denied the Deity, who first said that Christ was a mere man [πρῶτον εἰπόντα ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν Χριστόν]. Further, the same author says that in the writings of Justin, Miltiades, Tatian and Clement it is confirmed that Christ is truly God, since Christ is spoken of as God in one way throughout. For who does not know that the books of Irenaeus, Melito and the rest preach Christ as God and man? How many psalms and hymns, how many written down of old by the faithful brethren, celebrate in a certain harmony Christ as the Word of God and true God?

units.la: Caeterum quamvis Expositionem fidei, quae sub Justini nomine venit, ejus haud esse Docti censeant, propterea quia clarius & distinctius de Trinitate & Deitate Christi differat, quam eo tempore, vel ante motas controversias, solebat, non propterea vel minus recte sensisse Justinum de fidei articulis illis volunt, vel eandem ipsum veritatem non fuisse professum. Tum quisquis istius libri Auctor, & antiquus, nam etiam Veteribus citatur, in Concilio vi. Act. x. in Lateranensi i. sub Martino i. à Leontio Hierosolymitano, lib. contra Monophysitas, sive in Ἀ[?]ντιρρητικὸς [?] περὶ τῆς μιᾶς φύσεως σωθέντων [illegible, ~12 letters] ab Euthymio Zigabeno, Panopliae tit. xvi. qui est, κατὰ μονοφυσιτῶν [?]: elegans quoque est, & pro orthodoxâ sententiâ oppido planus ac copiosus, περὶ τῆς ἁγίας τῆς ὁμοουσίου τριάδος [?], uti titulus libri habet. Unus ergo revera est universitatis hujus Deus, qui in Patre & Filio & Sancto Spiritu cognoscitur. Cum namque & substantia sua Pater Filium progenuerit, atque ex eadem Spiritum produxerit, jure optimo, quæ unam eandemque participant essentiam, una eademque dignantur divinitate. Περὶ τῆς οὐσίας, μία πίστις, ἐν ἁγίᾳ πίστει [?]. Et egregie Christum è numero creaturarum eximi, probat ex Rom. viii. ubi Apostolus, recensitis omnibus creaturis, Christum Dominum iis opponit, nam persuasum habeo, quod neque vita, neque mundus, neque mors, neque Angeli, neque virtutes, &c. neque creatura alia poterit nos separare à dilectione Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. quod nisi Filium & Spiritum non esse τῆς κτίσεως ἀρχὴς [?] credidisset, haud isto exposuisset modo. Quin & à Patris potestate non posteriores esse Filii & Spiritus S. partes, è divina didicimus Scriptura. Itaque si in mundi disciplina, & in baptismi doctrina, & insuper in creationis ratione, potestatisque virtute conjunctis unum Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti nomen traditum est: quænam ratio & oratio infitiando afferre poterit, Filium & Spiritum divinæ beatæque naturæ & essentiæ non esse? Tum de Filii Dei œconomia disserens, qua factus homo, utriusque naturæ esse Deum & hominem, docet. Jam vero Justinus Christum passim Deum docet, & ante secula genitum, πρῶτον γέννημα τοῦ Θεοῦ, Apol. ii. ἐξ ἰδίας οὐσίας τὴν κοινὴν γέννησιν γεγεννημένος αὐτὸν ἐκ θεοῦ λόγον θεόν [?]: perq; eum mundum creatum, Patribus in V.T. sæpius apparuisse, ipsumq; esse Deum Abrahami, & Isaaci, & Jacobi, tandem autem incarnatum, σαρκοποιηθέντα ἄνθρωπον [?], in Apol. ii. haud semel, & una cum Spiritu S. religiose colendum, atque adorandum. Apol. i. ὁ ἐξ ὧς ἐκεῖνος, ὁ μὲν λεγόμενος λόγος κυρίως ὁς ὁ λόγος τῶν ποιημάτων ἡ σωμάτων ἐγενόμενος, ὅτι τὸ [illegible, ~30 letters] ἐκλογῆς & κοσμογονίας. — Ingeniti quamquam & ineffabilis Dei Rationem ac Verbum secundum Deum, adoramus & complectimur: quoniam nostra causa id homo factum est, ut perfectionum nostrarum participatione medicinam nobis faceret. Apol. ii. Verum hunc ipsum Patrem, & qui ab eo venit, atque ista nos &c. docuit, Filium, & Spiritum propheticum, colimus & adoramus. — Iesum Christum, ipsius veri Dei Filium edocti ὁμοίως Θεοῦ [?], secundo loco, ac spiritum propheticum tertio ordine, nos cum ratione venerari & colere demonstrabimus. — Et Iesus Christus, unus & solus proprie Filius Deo genitus, qui nimirum Verbum ejus & Primogenitus & Virtus est, atque de consilio voluntateque ejus, instaurandi & restituendi humani generis ergo, homo factus. Platonem, quia super aquas legerat à Mose narrari, Spiritum Dei ferri, secundum locum Dei Verbo dedisse putat; tertium vero ei, qui super aquas dicebatur ferri, Spiritui. Quidquid de Platone sit, ipse saltem Justinus ita sensit, eoque Scripturæ testimonio sententiam suam comprobavit: & in istam homines fidem baptizari, mox adjunxit: eo regenerationis modo, quo ipsi regenerati fumus, regenerantur. nam in nomine rerum cunctarum Patris & Domini Dei, & Servatoris nostri Iesu Christi, & Spiritus S. in aqua lavantur. — Benedicendo laudamus factorem omnium, per Filium ejus Iesum Christum, & Spiritum Sanctum. Quae ex Apologia illa adducta nostram juvant sententiam, non certe Adversariorum: Trinitatem quippe docent in Deo personarum, & τὸ ἰσοτιμον, ut pari honore atque cultu sint prosequendi Pater, & Filius, & Sp. Sanctus: neque Trinitatem quovis modo: nam uti Autor Expositionis fidei loquitur, in initio: Non simplex Patris & Filii gloriae depredicatio salutem nobis adfert; sed fana Trinitatis confessio, eorum quae vere religiosis piisque reposita sunt, bonorum fructum donat. Nam & eos qui aliter sentiunt aliquis audiat Patrem & Filium hymnis concelebrare; verumtamen non secundum rectam notionem, cultum praestare. At & cultum singulis istis praestandum Juftinus docet. In Dialogo, cum Tryphone, Judaeus inquit: crucifixum nobis persuaderi petis cum Mose & Aaron fuisse, & cum eis in columna ignis colloquutum: ac deinceps hominem factum & in cruce suspensum esse, & in coelum ascendisse: atque inde rursus in terram venturum, adeoque adorandum esse. — qui Christum Dei Filium cognoverunt, salvabuntur. qui & ante luciferum, & ante lunam fuit, & ex virgine ista generis Davidici caro factus natus sustinuit. — ante secula Deum fuisse Christum. — ante mundum conditum Deus fuit. — Utrum ergo aliquem alium vos asseritis Spiritum Sanctum Dominum & Deum dicere, extra Patrem universorum, & Christum ejus? Ergo tres illi Deus, & numero alii, uti postea dicit: & satis bene Veteres, contra ac Adversarius noster loquitur, Spiritum S. Deum dicere audebant. Tum a Patre editum germen hoc ante creaturas omnino universas, tum germen ipsum numero aliud a generante. Haec ipsa a Patre revera edita progenies, ante creaturas omnes una cum Patre fuit, & cum ea Pater colloquitur Gen. 1.26. prout Verbum per Salomonem declaravit, Prov. VIII.
units.tr: Although scholars judge that the Exposition of the Faith, which goes under Justin's name, is not his, because it speaks more clearly and distinctly of the Trinity and the Deity of Christ than was usual in his time or before the controversies arose, they do not therefore wish to say that Justin held those articles of faith less rightly, or that he did not profess the same truth himself. Moreover, whoever the author of that book was, he was an ancient one: he is cited by the ancients, in the Sixth Council, Act 10, and in the First Lateran Council under Martin I, by Leontius of Jerusalem in his book against the Monophysites, or in the work on the one nature [words illegible] by Euthymius Zigabenus, Panoplia, title 16, which is "against the Monophysites." It is also elegant, and very plain and full in support of the orthodox opinion, "concerning the holy consubstantial Trinity," as the title of the book has it. There is therefore in truth one God of this whole universe, who is known in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. For since the Father has begotten the Son from his own substance, and has brought forth the Spirit from the same, those who share one and the same essence are rightly honoured with one and the same divinity. [Concerning the essence, one faith, in holy faith.] And he proves admirably from Romans 8 that Christ is not to be counted among the creatures, for the Apostle, after listing all creatures, sets Christ the Lord over against them: "I am persuaded that neither life, nor the world, nor death, nor angels, nor powers, etc., nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." He would not have expressed it in this way unless he believed that the Son and the Spirit are not [the beginnings of creation]. Indeed, we learn from divine Scripture that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not inferior to the power of the Father. Therefore, if in the governing of the world, in the doctrine of baptism, and besides in the account of creation and the power of its virtue, the one name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit has been handed down together, what reasoning or speech could assert by denial that the Son and the Spirit do not belong to the blessed divine nature and essence? Then, discussing the economy of the Son of God, by which he was made man, he teaches that in both natures he is God and man. Justin indeed teaches everywhere that Christ is God and was begotten before the ages, [the firstborn offspring of God] (Apol. 2), begotten from his own substance in a common generation, he who is God from God the Word, [words illegible]; and that through him the world was created, that he appeared often to the Fathers in the Old Testament, that he himself is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and at last was incarnate, [made flesh and man], as he says more than once in the Second Apology, and that he is to be worshipped and adored religiously together with the Holy Spirit. (Apol. 1) [words illegible]. (Apol. 2) "We adore and embrace the Reason and Word of the ingenerate and ineffable God, according to God; for because of us he became man, so that by sharing our perfections he might be a medicine for us." (Apol. 2) "Indeed we worship and adore the Father himself, and the Son who came from him and taught us these things, and the prophetic Spirit." "We will show that we worship and honour, with reason, Jesus Christ, the Son of the true God himself, in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third order." And Jesus Christ, the one and only Son properly begotten of God, who is his Word, both firstborn and power, and who by his counsel and will became man for the restoring and renewing of the human race. Justin thinks that Plato, because he had read that Moses said the Spirit of God was borne over the waters, gave the second place to the Word of God, and the third to the Spirit who was said to be borne over the waters. Whatever Plato's view, Justin himself at least thought so, and confirmed his opinion by that testimony of Scripture: and that men are baptised into that faith, he added at once: they are regenerated in the same manner in which we ourselves were regenerated; for in the name of the Father and Lord God of all things, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they are washed in water. By blessing we praise the Maker of all things, through his Son Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit. What is brought from that Apology supports our opinion, not that of our opponents: for they teach a Trinity of persons in God, and equal honour [τὸ ἰσοτιμον], so that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are to be honoured and worshipped with equal honour and cult; and not a Trinity in any manner whatever. For as the author of the Exposition of the Faith says at the beginning: The bare proclamation of the glory of the Father and the Son does not bring us salvation, but the sound confession of the Trinity, which is laid up for those who are truly religious and pious, gives the fruit of good things. For let anyone hear that those who think otherwise also praise the Father and the Son with hymns; yet they offer worship not according to the right notion. But Justin also teaches that worship is to be offered to each of these. In the Dialogue with Trypho, the Jew says: You ask us to be persuaded that the one crucified appeared with Moses and Aaron, and talked with them in a pillar of fire; and afterwards that he was made man and hanged on the cross, and ascended into heaven; and that from there he will come again to earth, and so is to be worshipped. Those who have known Christ the Son of God will be saved. He who was before the morning star and before the moon, and was born of the virgin of the line of David, having been made flesh. Christ was God before the ages. Before the world was made, God was. Do you therefore assert that some other Holy Spirit is called Lord and God, apart from the Father of all and his Christ? Therefore those three are God, and other in number, as he says afterwards; and the ancients, contrary to what our opponent says, dared to call the Holy Spirit God quite rightly. This offspring, brought forth by the Father, existed before all creatures, and the offspring itself is numerically other than the one who begets it. This very progeny, truly brought forth by the Father, was together with the Father before all creatures, and with it the Father speaks (Gen. 1:26), as the Word declared through Solomon (Prov. 8).

units.la: Haec vero omnia sententiae Adversariorum non modo non adaptari possunt, verum ē diametro repugnant. Patrem, & Filium facit Deum, illi creationem adscribit rerum, ac proinde conditorem universi passim appellat; Filium, ejus administrum.
units.tr: Yet all these statements cannot be fitted to the opinions of our opponents; indeed they flatly contradict them. Justin makes both the Father and the Son God, ascribes the creation of things to the Father, and accordingly calls him everywhere the maker of the universe; the Son he calls his minister.

units.la: Quare, quando vel Filium Parenti universorum ministrasse, vel eum non esse conditorem universi, affirmat, denique Dominum universi Patribus non apparuisse, variam Personarum in agendo respicit oeconomiam ac modum, ut Pater omnia per Filium, Filius a Patre agat, eique ministret, & Filii sint propria, non Patris, venire ad homines, cum iis loqui, versari &c. quibus sibi non proposuit Filii, vel Spiritus S. Deitatem ullo pacto laedere aut imminuere; sed distinctionem Filii a Patre significare, praesertim contra eos, qui nullam hic admittentes, Filium & Patrem commiscebant, & Filium dicebant esse Patrem, quos & Ignatio notatos ac castigatos vidimus. Quo faciunt & haec Justini verba, Apol. II. Qui enim Filium Patrem esse dicunt, comperiuntur neque Patrem scire, neque Filium esse Patri universorum nosse: qui quod Verbum & primogenitus Deus fit, Deus etiam est. Erant ergo, qui Filium Patrem esse, dicerent, eosque sibi refutandos censuit: sed nec minus semper Filium agnovit Deum. Pro synonymis habuit Patrem Christi, & Patrem universi, non quod Filium excluserit a creatione, sed a Patre omnium originem putarit repetendam esse. Nam per Christum, mundum creatum, aliquoties adstruit. Unde nec erubescit dicere, Christum alterum Deum, praeter opificem universi, in Dial. cum Tryphone, cum tamen pro uno Deo scripserit librum totum de monarchia, sive de unitate Dei. Nisi nonnulla incommode a Justino in hoc argumento dicta fateamur, praesertim ubi arcanorum rationem edere & modum generationis Filii exponere tentavit, quae postmodum ab aliis deterioris sententiae in malam partem capi potuerint: uti securius loqui solemus de re nondum in controversiam adducta, quam postea, & quandoque ita intenti in errorem unum expatiamur liberius, ut alterius fere obliviscamur, & incauti proferamus ea, quae in contrarium extremum alii postea perperam interpretantur. Ita prudenter & dextre accipiendum, quod in Dialogo cum Tryphone dixit, quod nemo, cui vel minimum mentis fit, Autorem & patrem universi supercoelestia omnia reliquisse, & in pusilla terrae parte sese exhibuisse, dicere fit ausurus. nempe ut intelligatur, quod se Pater in carne manifestarit, non Filius. Quare postmodum dixit, quod non debeant putare, ipsum ingenitum Deum vel ascendisse vel descendisse quopiam. nam ineffabilis ille Pater & Dominus universitatis hujus, non venit in locum aliquem, neque deambulat, neque dormit, neque surgit, &c. Plane differentiam inter Patrem, & Filium sumit, ex diversa oeconomia, & operandi modo, qui Patri non competit.
units.tr: Therefore, when he asserts either that the Son ministered to the Parent of all, or that he is not the maker of the universe, or finally that the Lord of the universe did not appear to the Fathers, he has regard to the varied economy and manner of the Persons in acting: that the Father does all things through the Son, and the Son acts from the Father and ministers to him, and that the works are the Son's and not the Father's: to come to men, to speak with them, to dwell among them, and so on. By these things he did not intend in any way to harm or diminish the Deity of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, but to signify the distinction of the Son from the Father, especially against those who, admitting no such distinction here, confused the Son and the Father and said that the Son is the Father, whom we have seen noted and rebuked by Ignatius. To this purpose also are these words of Justin in the Second Apology: For those who say that the Son is the Father are found neither to know the Father nor to know that the Son is the Father of all; who, since the Word and firstborn is God, is also God. There were therefore some who said that the Son is the Father, and he judged that they were to be refuted; yet he never acknowledged the Son as less than God. He held the Father of Christ and the Father of the universe to be synonymous, not because he excluded the Son from creation, but because he thought the origin of all must be traced back to the Father. For he asserts in several places that the world was created through Christ. Hence he is not ashamed to say, in the Dialogue with Trypho, that Christ is another God, besides the maker of the universe; yet he wrote a whole book on monarchy, or on the unity of God, as if for one God. Unless we admit that some things said by Justin on this subject were unfitting, especially where he tried to set out the secrets and explain the manner of the Son's generation, which afterwards others could take in a worse sense, of the kind we are wont to speak about a matter not yet brought into controversy, but which we later, when intent on one error, wander into more freely, and forgetting almost the other, carelessly put forward things that other men afterwards wrongly interpret toward the opposite extreme. Thus what he said in the Dialogue with Trypho must be received prudently and fairly: that no one who has even the least understanding will dare to say that the Author and Father of the universe left all the heavenly things and showed himself in a small part of the earth. That is, it is to be understood that the Father, not the Son, manifested himself in the flesh. Therefore he afterwards said that they ought not to think that the unbegotten God himself ascended or descended anywhere; for that ineffable Father and Lord of this universe does not come to any place, nor walk about, nor sleep, nor rise, and so on. He clearly takes the distinction between the Father and the Son from the different economy and mode of acting, which does not belong to the Father.

units.la: An vero Athenagoras nostrae fuerit sententiae, an adversae, ex ejus judicabitur verbis, quae extant in Apologia, vel Legatione pro Christianis. inscripta Imperatoribus M. Aurelio Antonino, & Aurelio Commodo, Armeniacis, Sarmaticis, & quod maximum est, Philosophis: sic enim habet inscriptio, & legitur in Bibliotheca Patrum: fuit autem Athenagoras Justini ferme aequalis. Is dicto libro: Nec est quod aliquis ridiculum putet, Deo Filium a me attribui &c. Dicit, Patrem & Filium esse unum: Filium in Patre, Patrem esse in Filio; unione, vel in unitate Sp. Sancti. Per Filium omnia creata, & esse rerum omnium ideam, atque efficaciam, nunquam non hoc Verbum Patri adfuisse, & sine eo, uti sine ratione, esse non posse. Non, quo Pater ipse, tanquam forma sua sit λογικὸς, sed qui Patri sit substantiale Verbum, λόγος Filius, per quem Pater omnia efficit. Citat, vulgata Graecorum lectione, locum Prov. VIII. 20. Dominus creavit me, Κύριος ἔκτισέ[?] με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ[?] quod in Hebraeo est קָנָנִי[?] possedit me: non vero significat, se proprie vocem ἔκτισε[?] hic accipere, & non lata significatione. Aquila, Κύριος ἐκτήσατό[?] με. Tum de Spiritu S. inquit, quae verba Adversarius noster omittit: & ipsum Spiritum S. agentem in illis, qui propheticos sermones fundunt, ita a Deo emanare, ad ipsumque reflecti[?] dicimus, ut emissi a Sole radii reciprocant. Quis igitur non miretur, nos qui Deum Patrem praedicamus, & Deum Filium, & Spiritum S. ita ut & unionis eorum vim, & ordinis distinctionem exponamus, impios & sine Deo homines vocari? Uti & quae postea occurrunt verba: Denique asserimus, & Filium ipsius Verbum, & Spiritum Sanctum: tria quidem secundum potentiam, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum: actu vero & essentia unum. Filius enim Patris mens, verbum & sapientia est: & ab eodem Spiritu, ut lumen ab igne, profluit. Quid clarius potuit dici, quam essentia unum esse Filium cum Patre? etenim nunquam diversas Dei, vel Deorum essentias agnoverunt Patres; & quomodo apertius Trinitatem praedicare potuit, quam tali professione? Et hunc tamen etiam Autorem pro se adferre, aut contra nos, Adversarius haud erubuit.
units.tr: Whether Athenagoras was of our opinion or of the opposing one will be judged from his own words, which are found in his Apology, or Embassy, for the Christians, addressed to the emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Aurelius Commodus, the Armeniacs, Sarmatics, "and, what is greatest, philosophers." For that is how the inscription reads, and it is read in the Bibliotheca Patrum. Athenagoras was roughly a contemporary of Justin. In that book he says: "Nor is there any reason for anyone to think it ridiculous that I attribute a Son to God," and so on. He says that the Father and the Son are one, the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Through the Son all things were created; the Son is the idea and the active power of all things; this Word has always been with the Father, and without him, as without reason, God could not exist. He is not the Word in the sense that the Father himself is rational, as if rationality were his form, but the Son is the substantial Word of the Father, the logos, through whom the Father makes all things. He cites Proverbs 8:20 according to the common Greek reading, "The Lord created me" [Κύριος ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ], though in the Hebrew it is "possessed me" [קָנָנִי]. He does not mean that the word "created" is to be taken here in its proper sense and not in its broader meaning. Aquila has "The Lord acquired me" [Κύριος ἐκτήσατό με]. Then he speaks of the Holy Spirit, which words our opponent omits: "We say that the Holy Spirit, acting in those who utter prophetic words, emanates from God and is reflected back to him, as rays sent out from the sun are reflected back." Who then would not be astonished that we, who preach God the Father and God the Son and the Holy Spirit, and who set out both the power of their union and the distinction of their order, are called impious men without God? And the words that follow: "In short, we affirm that his Son is the Word, and the Holy Spirit: three in power, the Father, the Son and the Spirit, but one in act and in essence. For the Son is the mind, word and wisdom of the Father, and the Spirit flows from the same source as light flows from fire." What could be said more clearly than that the Son is one in essence with the Father? For the Fathers never acknowledged different essences of God or gods; and how could he have professed the Trinity more openly than by such a confession? Yet our opponent has not been ashamed to cite this very author on his own side, or against us.

units.la: Theophilus, Antiochenus Episcopus, nihil omnino dicit de Filio, vel ejus a Patre generatione, quod ab Adversario quidem adfertur, & non ex iis, quae ad praecedentia jam diximus, exponi possit. Metaphorice inquit, Patrem genuisse Filium, quem in visceribus suis habebat: neque tempus distinguit, vel dicit Patrem fuisse antequam Filium habebat, non magis quam ut fuerit sine sapientia, quam ipsum Filium esse, dicit. Per hoc Verbum ait, Patrem omnia creare, & operari; atque sic exponit Ioann. 1. non de principio Euangelicae praedicationis, sed rerum omnium creationis. Nunquam non Deo adfuisse suum λόγον docet, sed singulari eum modo prolatum, quod genitum appellat, ad mundi creationem, ut per eum Pater conderet omnia, regeret-que. Distinguit in hoc etiam argumento, quod vulgo solet, an recte, non dico, λόγον ἐνδιάθετον, & προφορικόν: hunc productum ait, ad mundi creationem, illum semper fuisse apud Deum. λόγον ergo istum facit aeternum, & cum Deo unum. ἔχων ἐν ὁ Θεὸς τ' ἑαυτῷ λόγον ἐνδιάθετον ἐν τοῖς ἰδίοις σπλάγχνοις [?], habens ergo Deus Verbum insitum in visceribus suis: dura admodum metaphora: postea, τ' οὖν ἀλλὰ πρωτοῖς ἐνδιάθετον ἐν καρδίᾳ Θεῦ [?], genuit cum cum sapientia sua eruditans ante omnia, ἐγέννησεν αὐτὸν μὴ τ' ἑαυτοῦ σοφίας ὑπερ-ἀξιόμων [?] τ' ὅλων [?]. postea iterum, ὅτε δὲ ἠθέλησεν ὁ Θεὸς ποιῆσαι ὅσα ἐβούλετο [?], τὸν τ' λόγον ἐγέννησεν προφορικόν [?], quando autem voluit Deus facere ea quae statuerat, genuit hoc Verbum prolatum, primogenitum omnis creaturae, non interim ipse exinanitus Verbo, sed Verbum gignens, & Verbo suo semper conversatus. Denique & hoc Verbum Deus habuit ὑπάρχον τ' ὢν αὐτῷ γεννηθὲν [?], & per eum fecit omnia, &c. Non fecit aliud Verbum προφορικόν, aliud ἐνδιάθετον. Illud tantum de Verbo dicit, in ordine ad creationem. Verum semper in Deo fuisse idem istud Verbum asserit: non autem creatum ἐν τ' ὧν ὄντων [?], nedum tantum, ut extitisset a nativitate ex Maria. Non quod omnes hujus, aut aliorum Doctorum expositiones, sive de Trinitatis mysterio, sive Filii, & generationis ipsius, approbemus: sufficit ostendere, ipsam thesim & veritatem ab iis agnitam, & non docuisse idem, quod postmodum haeretici, quodve eo nomine palliare studuent, vel defendere alii. Sic Dei Trinitatem agnovit, & ejus typum aliquem constituit in tribus primis creationis diebus, ὡσαύτως ἡ αἱ τρεῖς ἡμέραι τ' φωστήρων γεγονυῖαι τύπι εἰσὶν τ' τριάδος τ' Θεῦ [?], ἡ τ' λόγου αὐτοῦ, ἡ τ' σοφίας αὐτοῦ [?]. Ita & tres dies qui praecesserunt creationem luminarium, typi sunt Trinitatis in Deo, & Verbi ejus, & sapientiae ejus. Non dicimus; typum hunc bene constitui; non, an per Verbum & Sapientiam, Trinitatem declaret; an tantum Filium in Trinitate Personarum secundum: &, an eundem intelligat per Verbum & Sapientiam, an vero per Sapientiam, Spiritum Sanctum. Haec incerta, uti illud satis certum ac manifestum, Trinitatem saltem ab eo creditam probatamque fuisse: quae veritas, uti & aliae, a sequentibus semper magis ac magis enucleata fuit, ac probata.
units.tr: Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, says absolutely nothing about the Son or his generation from the Father, which our opponent does bring forward, but which cannot be explained from what we have already said. He says metaphorically that the Father begot the Son, whom he had in his bowels. He does not distinguish a time, nor say that the Father existed before he had the Son, any more than he says that God was once without wisdom, which he says the Son himself is. Through this Word, he says, the Father creates and works all things; and in this way he explains John 1, not of the beginning of the Gospel preaching, but of the creation of all things. He teaches that his logos was never not present with God, but was brought forth in a singular manner, which he calls being begotten, at the creation of the world, so that through him the Father might found and govern all things. In this argument he also draws the distinction that is commonly made (whether rightly, I do not say) between the logos endiathetos and the logos prophorikos: he says the one was brought forth at the creation of the world, while the other was always with God. He therefore makes that logos eternal and one with God: "God, having the Word inherent in his own bowels" [ἔχων ἐν ἑαυτῷ λόγον ἐνδιάθετον ἐν τοῖς ἰδίοις σπλάγχνοις], a very harsh metaphor. Later: "he begot him, with his own wisdom, instructing before all things" [ἐγέννησεν αὐτὸν ... σοφίας ...]. Again: "when God willed to make what he had purposed, he begot this Word brought forth, the firstborn of all creation, not being himself emptied by the Word, but begetting the Word and always conversing with his Word." Finally, God had this Word existing with him, begotten, and "through him he made all things," etc. He did not make one Word prophorikos and another endiathetos. He speaks of the Word only in relation to creation; but he asserts that this same Word was always in God, and not created "among the things that are," much less that it began to exist only at the birth from Mary. We do not approve of all the explanations of this author or of other teachers, whether concerning the mystery of the Trinity or concerning the Son and his generation. It is enough to show that they acknowledged the thesis and the truth itself, and that they did not teach what the heretics later taught, or what others have tried to cover with that name or to defend. Thus he acknowledged the Trinity of God, and set up a certain type of it in the first three days of creation: "Likewise the three days before the creation of the lights are types of the Trinity of God, of his Word, and of his wisdom" [ὡσαύτως ... τύποι εἰσὶν τῆς τριάδος τοῦ Θεοῦ, τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ, τῆς σοφίας αὐτοῦ]. We do not say that this type is well chosen; nor whether through the Word and Wisdom he declares the Trinity; nor whether he means only the Son as second in the Persons of the Trinity; nor whether by Word and Wisdom he means the same thing, or whether by Wisdom he means the Holy Spirit. These matters are uncertain; but this is quite certain and manifest, that he at least believed and approved the Trinity. This truth, like others, was afterwards more and more clearly unfolded and proved by those who followed.

units.la: Tatianus, circa annum Christi clxx. & Justini Martyris discipulus, in Oratione contra Graecos, de arcanis religionis nostrae acturus, Deum dicit fuisse in principio, principium autem Verbi fuisse potentiam, in ea apud Deum fuisse omnia. Considerat autem λόγον, seu Verbum dupliciter, in Deo Patre, & in ordine ad creationem: ibi dicit, exstitisse semper apud Deum, vel in Deo; hic ad oeconomiam creationis, & ad hoc perficiendum opus, a Deo quasi genitum. Ita novam quasi Verbi productionem imaginati sibi fuerunt illi Theologi, quando ad opus illud extra se producendum Deus se accingeret; sed non propterea æternam Verbi negarunt subsistentiam. Videtur omnino respexisse ad Johannis illa verba, in principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum. Non quod probemus quæcunque ad explicationem hujus argumenti forte adfert Tatianus; sed quod appareat, eum æternitatem Λόγω agnovisse, & subsistentiam. Exserte enim inquit, αὐτὸς γ' [?] ὁ Λόγος ὡς ἐν αὐτῷ ὑπέστησε [?], ipsum istud Verbum, quod in ipso erat, subsistit. Et hypostasis vocem bis usurpat, dicens, quod Dominus universi ipsi erat omnium ὑπόστασις, in se quidem solus, respectu vero potentiæ, & potentiæ Λόγω, λογικῆς δυνάμεως, cum eo omnia, quandoquidem αὐτῆς ὁ Λόγος ἐν αὐτῷ ὑπέστησε. Sic enim habent verba: [illegible, ~60 letters] ὁ δὲ [?] μόνος ἦν, καὶ ἐδὲ πάσαι δυνάμεις [?], ἐξ ὧν [?] ἦν, σὺν αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα [?]. Nunc vero manifestius ex-ponam nostra. Deus erat in principio, principium vero istud Dei potentiam esse accepimus. Quippe Dominus universi ipse existens omnium hypostasis, secundum quidem creationem nondum factam solus erat, quod ad potentiam vero, visibilium invisibiliumque fuit hypostasis. cum eo omnia: cum ipso per Verbi vel rationalem potentiam, & ipsum Verbum quod fuit in ipso subsistebat. Inde, ab illa Verbi tum existentia, tum subsistentia, æterna & necessaria, pergit ad ejus considerationem, quatenus se habuit in creatione mundi: ad quam quasi prolatum, genitumque observat, & hinc mundi cæptam originem: prolatumque vel progressum a Deo per distinctionem, κατὰ μερισμὸν, ἢ κατὰ [?] non per divulsionem, [illegible, ~25 letters] quod autem dividitur, suam sumens œconomiam, non imminuit sum, a quo sumitur, quod porro exponit similitudine tum facis ab alia, citra prioris diminutionem, accensæ; tum sermocinationis, per quam qui sermocinatur, non fit propterea ipse vacuus sermone, vel ἢ λόγος κενός.
units.tr: Tatian, about the year of Christ 170, and a disciple of Justin Martyr, in his Oration against the Greeks, when he is about to speak of the mysteries of our religion, says that God was in the beginning, and that the beginning was the power of the Word, and that in it all things were with God. He considers the logos, or Word, in two ways: in God the Father, and in relation to creation. There he says it has always existed with God or in God; here, with respect to the economy of creation and the carrying out of that work, he says it was as it were begotten by God. Those theologians therefore imagined a kind of new production of the Word when God was about to bring that work forth outside himself; but on that account they did not deny the eternal subsistence of the Word. He clearly had regard to those words of John: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." I do not approve of everything Tatian perhaps brings forward in explaining this matter; but it appears that he acknowledged the eternity and the subsistence of the Logos. For he says plainly: "the Word itself, which was in him, subsists" [αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ Λόγος ὡς ἐν αὐτῷ ὑπέστησε]. He uses the word hypostasis twice, saying that the Lord of the universe was himself the hypostasis of all things, alone in himself, but in respect of power, and of the rational power of the Word [λογικῆς δυνάμεως], with him all things; since the Word itself subsisted in him. For his words are: "... but he alone was, and all powers were from him, with him all things ..." Now I will set out our view more clearly. "God was in the beginning, and we have received that this beginning is the power of God." Indeed, the Lord of the universe, himself existing as the hypostasis of all things, was alone according to creation, which was not yet made; but as to power, he was the hypostasis of things visible and invisible, with him all things: with him, through the rational power of the Word, and the Word itself, which was subsisting in him. Then, from that existence and subsistence of the Word, both eternal and necessary, he goes on to consider it insofar as it stood in the creation of the world; and he observes that it was, as it were, brought forth and begotten for that purpose, and hence the beginning of the world; and the Word was brought forth or proceeded from God by division [κατὰ μερισμόν], not by separation, [illegible in the scan]: "what is divided, taking up its own economy, does not diminish that from which it is taken." He explains this further by the likeness of one fire kindled from another without diminishing the first, and by the likeness of speech, in which the speaker is not thereby emptied of speech, or made a "empty word" [λόγος κενός].

units.la: Irenæus, ad ann. Christi c L xxx. quando dicit, Deum gratiam potius in novissimis temporibus per Filium suum humano generi donasse, eum qui incomprehensibilis per comprehensibilem, & invisibilis per visibilem, Filium quidem facit visibilem & comprehensibilem, sed consideratum ab incarnatione, & humano generi a Patre donatum: neque Filium a Deo illo uno excludit, quum exserte dicat, quod extra eum non fit, sed in sinu Patris existit, lib. III. cap. XI. Itaque non tanquam diversos Deos facit, Patrem invisibilem, & Filium visibilem ac comprehensibilem, sed Patrem docet per Filium visibilem & comprehensibilem factum a nativitate humana, voluntatem suam hominibus declarasse, Patrem enim invisibilem existentem, ille qui in sinu ejus est Filius, omnibus enarrat: & Filius extra eum Patrem non est. Neque quod dicit, unum esse Deum, & Evangelia nec alterum Deum scire, præter universi fabricatorem, neque alterum, quam Christi Patrem, nobis quidquam adversatur, qui nec plures Deos novimus, nec plures Patres, sed Deum unum, & Patrem, uti & Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, unum. Sed non alter Deus, nec alter Pater, neque Bythus, neque pleroma[?] triginta Aeonum, nec mater Ogdoados, inquit: nam contra ista haeresium portenta ibidem disputat: & non, quemadmodum illi dicunt, alterum quidem fabricatorem, alium autem Patrem Domini, & alium quidem fabricatoris Filium, alterum vero de superioribus Christum, &c. Christum vero ipse confitetur incarnatum, & quod Filius Dei factus filius hominis, ad hoc ut & homo fieret filius Dei.
units.tr: Irenaeus, about the year of Christ 180, when he says that God gave grace rather in the last times to the human race through his Son, who is incomprehensible in the comprehensible, and invisible in the visible, makes the Son indeed visible and comprehensible, but only as considered from the incarnation and given to the human race by the Father. Nor does he exclude the Son from the one God, since he plainly says that the Son is not outside him, but exists in the bosom of the Father, book III, chapter XI. So he does not make two Gods, an invisible Father and a visible and comprehensible Son, but teaches that the Father, through the Son made visible and comprehensible by his human birth, declared his will to men: for the Son, who is in the bosom of the invisible Father, declares him to all. And the Son is not outside the Father. Nor does what he says, that there is one God, and that the Gospels know no other God besides the maker of the universe, nor any other Father than the Father of Christ, go against us, since we also know not many Gods or many Fathers, but one God and Father, and likewise one Son and one Holy Spirit. But there is not another God, nor another Father, neither Bythus, nor a pleroma of thirty Aeons, nor a mother of the Ogdoad, he says; for against these monstrous heresies he argues in the same place: and not, as they say, one maker, another the Father of the Lord, and another the Son of the maker, and another Christ from the higher regions, and so on. Indeed, Irenaeus himself confesses Christ incarnate, and that the Son of God became the son of man, so that the son of man might become the son of God.

units.la: Neque in altero Irenaei loco, quem adducit Noster, lib. iv. cap. xxxvii. aliquid nobis adversum occurrit, quinimo aliqua haud parum faventia. Quamvis enim doceat Irenaeus, Patrem nunquam hominibus visum vel apparuisse, sed & fecisse & loquutum omnia per Filium, Verbum suum; deinde & eum, a Patre ad haec & ista facienda, potestatem accipere, non propterea vel solam Patris personam Deum dicit; vel Filium, eundem cum Patre Deum esse, negat. Quin Filium semper cum Patre fuisse, docet. Et quoniam Verbum, id est, Filius semper cum Patre erat, per multa demonstravimus. Quoniam & Sapientia, quae est Spiritus, erat apud Deum ante omnem constitutionem, per Salomonem ait, &c. Est autem hic Verbum ejus Dominus noster Iesus Christus, qui in novissimis temporibus homo, in hominibus factus est, ut finem conjungeret principio, id est, homini Deo. Et propterea prophetae ab eodem verbo prophetieum accipientes charisma, praedicaverunt ejus secundum carnem adventum, per quem commixtio & communio Dei hominis secundum placitum Patris facta est, ab initio praenunciante verbo Dei, quoniam videbitur Deus ab hominibus, & conversabitur cum eis super terram. Quare locum citans Joan. i. 18. non uti in codicibus nostris est, adducit, unigenitus Filius, sed, unigenitus Deus; tum, quasi a Domino dictum esset, quemadmodum & Dominus dixit, Unigenitus Deus qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit. Quin & clare satis Trinitatem Personarum docet hoc in capite, neque uno modo. Primum: non Angeli fecerunt nos, nec nos plasmaverunt, nec Angeli potuerunt imaginem facere Dei, nec alius quis, praeter verbum Domini, nec virtus longe absistens a Patre universorum. Nec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum, quae ipse apud se praefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suis non haberet manus. Adest enim et semper verbum & sapientia filius, & spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere & sponte fecit, ad quos & loquitur, dicens, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Iterum, videbitur autem & in regno coelorum paternaliter, spiritu quidem praeparante hominem in Filium Dei, Filio autem adducente ad Patrem, Patre autem incorruptelam donante in aeternam vitam, quae unicuique evenit ex eo quod videat Deum. Denique, Sic igitur manifestabatur Deus, per omnia enim haec Deus Pater ostenditur, spiritu quidem operante, Filio vero administrante, Patre vero comprobante, homine vero consummante ad salutem. Et cap. xvii. Patrem non indigere, aiet, ministerio Angelorum, ad fabricationem hominis, sed habere copiosum & inenarrabile ministerium. Ministrat enim ei ad omnia sua progenies, & figuratio sua, id est, Filius, & Spiritus, Verbum & sapientia, quibus serviunt & subjecti sunt omnes Angeli. Filium appellat Patris progeniem, & Verbum; Spiritum S. ejus figurationem, & sapientiam: neque quod ministrare Patri dicit, aliud vult, quam Patrem per illos operari. Nam semper cum Patre, nec extra eum, & Patris progeniem ac figurationem esse, aliter ac creaturae, & inter eas praestantissimae Angeli, neque magis a Patre posse divelli, quam ejus sapientiam & verbum, docuit. Lib. ii. cap. XLVIII. agens contra eos, qui frustra modum generationis Filii a Patre conabantur ingenio suo metiri, & explicare, generationem ejus ex Patre divinantes, & contendens, à nobis illam cognosci & enarrari haud posse, eo etiam utitur argumento, quod vel Christus aliqua se dicat ignorare, quandoquidem & Dominus ipse Filius Dei, ipsum judicii diem & horam concessit scire solum Patrem, manifeste dicens, de die illa & hora nemo scit, neque Filius, nisi Pater solus. Si igitur scientiam diei illius, Filius non erubuit referre ad Patrem, sed dixit quod verum est, neque nos erubescimus quae sunt in quaestionibus majora secundum nos, reservare Deo. Nemo enim super magistrum est. Si quis itaque nobis dixerit, quomodo ergo Filius prolatus a Patre est, dicimus ei, quia prolationem istam, sive generationem, sive nuncupationem, sive adapertionem, aut quomodolibet quis nomine vocaverit, generationem ejus inenarrabilem existentem nemo novit. Non Valentinus, non Marcion, neque Saturninus, neque Basilides, neque Angeli, neque Archangeli, neque principes, neque potestates, nisi solus qui genuit pater, & qui natus est filius. Ine-narrabilis itaque generatio ejus cum fit, quicunque niituntur generationes & prolationes enar-rare, non sunt compotes sui, ea quae inenarrabilia sunt enarrare promittentes. An vero Filius secundum id, quod à Patre natus, & quod alias in se inenarrabile nobis, solus cum Patre novit, eftq; Dei sapientia, & non extra eum, non sciverit diem & horam ultimam, haud asserit. Capite autem seq. ubi non tantum idem repetit, quod Christus dicitur diem & horam judicii ignorare, sub eadem commonefactione, dimittere ita oportet cognitionem hanc Deo, quemadmodum & Dominus horae & diei; sed & in ejus rei causam inquirit, quomodo id Christus dicatur ignorare: Etenim si quis exquirat causam, propter quam in omnibus Pater communicans Filio, solus scire & horam & diem Domino manifestatus est, neque aptabilem magis, neque decentiorem, nec sine periculo alteram, quam hanc inveniat in praesenti, quoniam cum solus verax magister est Dominus, ut discamus per ipsum, super omnia esse Patrem. etenim Pater, ait, major me est, & secundum agnitionem itaque praepositus esse Pater annuntiatus est à Domino nostro, ad hoc ut & nos, inquantum in figura hujus mundi sumus, perfectam scientiam, & tales quaestiones concedamus Deo, & ne forte quaerentes altitudinem Patris investigare, in tantum periculum incidamus, uti quaeramus an super Deum alter fit Deus. Primum concedens, quod Pater in omnibus communicat Filio, Filii cum Patre communia docet omnia: interim quod Domino manifestatum, ignorare diem atque horam illam, de alia Domini accipit σχέσει [?], Christi nempe, pro statu manifestationis, non communionis omnium, atque hinc singulariter hujus ignoratae vid. rei causam aperit, ex humiliationis Christi sub Patre conditione, agnoscentis Patrem se majorem, neque omnia se in figura hujus mundi scire, quo magis nos doceret, multorum scientiam soli Deo resignare, neque vel in Patris altitudinem curiose nimis investigare, vel Patre alium Deum superiorem constituere. Aliud vero, secundum eum, est, Filium considerare in ratione communionis omnimodae cum Patre, vel ma-nifestationis singularis à Patre, quomodo quod super omnia est Pater, id vero non praejudicat dignitati isti primae, qua cum Patre Filius habet communia: uti & noster magister est, non secundum hanc, sed illam rationem, qua est Christus Dominus. Atque commode Patri super omnia esse Deum tribuitur, creaturarum respectu, & mundi, dein quod is nunquam se ita humiliarit, quemadmodum quidem Filius. Ut ex illa phrasi contra Filium, & ejus cum Patre communem rationem argumentari Adversariis haud liceat. Tum lib. III. cap. VIII. Irenaeus, docens quod nunquam Prophetae, neque Apostoli alium Deum nominaverunt, vel Dominum appellaverunt, praeter verum & solum Deum; Christum vero Dominum appellando, & ejusdem cum Deo nominis participem faciendo, non item alia quaevis, significat eum cum Patre eundem Deum esse. Cui nihil obstat, quod docet Patrem, per eum omnia fecisse, creasse, & loquutum, vel ipsum ex praecepto Patris omnia egisse, quia haec oeconomiam notant, ad operationes externas, qua Pater per Filium omnia agit, non contra. Atque ita per Filium, uti cum Filio, & Filius Deus nomen commune cum Patre habeat, quod nemo aliás. Quoniam enim sive Angeli, sive Archangeli, sive throni, sive dominationes ab eo qui super omnes est Deus, & constituta sunt, & facta per verbum ejus, Ioannes quidem sic significavit: cum enim dixisset de verbo Dei, quoniam erat in Patre, adjecit, Omnia per eum facta sunt, & sine eo factum est nihil. Cui ergo praecepit ? Verbo scilicet ; per quod, inquit, coeli firmati sunt, & spiritu oris ejus omnis virtus eorum. Altera autem sunt, quae constituta sunt ab eo qui constituta sunt ab eo qui constituit, & quae facta sunt ab eo qui fecit. ipse enim infectus, & sine initio, & sine fine, & nullius indigens, ipse sibi sufficiens, & adhuc reliquis omnibus, ut sint hoc ipsum praestans. Quae vero ab eo sunt facta, initium sumpserunt. Quaecun-que autem initium sumpserunt percipere, & subjecta sunt, & indigens ejus qui se fecit, necesse est omnino uti differens vocabulum habeant apud eos, qui vel modicum sensum in discernendo talia habeant. Ita ut is quidem qui omnia fecerit cum verbo suo, juste dicatur Deus & Dominus solus, quae autem facta sunt, non jam ejusdem vocabuli percipibilia esse, neque juste id vocabu-lum sumere debere, quod est creatoris. Omnia vero fecit Verbum, vel Deus cum Verbo, de quo dixerat, nec quidem ex his quae constitutione, & in subjectione sunt comparabitur Verbo Dei, per quem facta sunt omnia, qui est Dominus noster Iesus Christus. Duplex hic oppositio inter factorem, & facturam, nominis, ac rei: ille est infectus, sine initio, sine fine, & nullius indigens, sibi soli sufficiens, & reliquis, ut hoc sint, praestans; reliqua contra: deinde solus is, Pater ac Verbum suum, Dominus ac Deus appellandus, cujus appellationis consors nihil est aliud. Verbum ergo non modo non ex genere factorum illorum, sed vere Deus, cum Patre idem, tum proprietatibus divinis, tum & nomine. Vide totum caput sextum hujus libri, ubi ostenditur multis, quod nemo alius Deus nominatur, nisi solus verus Deus Pater omnium, & ejus Verbum. Quo etiam spectat, quod Idem habet lib. iv. cap. viii. Filium Patris esse mensuram, vel Deum qui omnia in mensura fecit, & apud quem nihil non mensum, sibi quoque ipsius mensuram dedisse Filium: omnia enim mensura & ordine, Deus facit, & nihil non mensum apud eum, quoniam nec incompositum. Et bene, qui dixit ipsum immensum Patrem in Filio mensuratum. Mensura enim Patris Filius, quoniam & capit eum. Quoniam & c-pit eum, immensum videlicet, ergo mensura immensi immensa: imo quum nequeat esse multiplex immensum, sui ipsius mensura quasi est Pater in Filio.
