Non vero istam mensuram Filii respectu Patris, intelligendam esse de eo quod Filius omnia legis implet, perficiat & capiat, quae hactenus apud Patrem mensa & determinata fuerant; vel de mensura cognitionis perfecta apud Filium, in suo genere, non absolute, uti vult Autor Irenici, probat hoc, quod universaliter & absolute loquitur de rerum omnium apud Deum, & a Deo mensura, non de hac tantum aut illa, ubi de mensura agit: omnia enim mensura & ordine Deus facit. Et sui, non modo cognitionis, nedum imperfectae, uti hactenus voluit colligere, ex cognitione Christi imperfecta, ad eandem Filii, Autor, Irenaeus dicit Filium esse mensuram Patris. Deniq; in conclusione, quam facit Noster, manifesta ludit ambiguitate, dicens, Irenaeum juxta cum Iustino, & sequentibus Christianis Patrem Verbo statuisse superiorem, minime vero aequalem: nam istud, Patrem esse Verbo superiorem, & non aequalem, intelligi potest vel de Verbo incarnato, & prout incarnatum est, reduplicative, & sic concedimus, Patrem esse majorem; majorem ; vel de Verbo, quod fuit, atque est, præter, & ante ἐνσαρκωσιν [?], & sic non negant æqualitatem ejus cum Patre, quin potius hoc loco Irenæus tradit, mensuram Patris esse Filium, atque ab eo capi. Quæ est ipsissima æqualitas. Atque ejus incarnationem passim docet, per quam communixtio & communio Dei & hominis secundum placitum Patris facta est. lib. iv. cap. viii. & lib. v. in initio, Verbum existens, homo factus fuit. Quare lib. i. cap. ii. in lymbolo, ait, nos credere Christum Filium Dei, incarnatum pro nostra salute: & in Spiritum Sanctum. Jam non dicit tantum, sed & probat verum unicumque cum Patre Filium Deum , lib. iii. cap. vi. Neque igitur Dominus, neque Spiritus Sanctus, neque Apostoli eum qui non effet Deus, definitive & absolute Deum nominaffent aliquando, nisi effet verus Deus, neque Dominum appellaffent aliquem ex sua persona, nisi qui dominatur omnium Deum Patrem & Filium ejus, qui dominium accepit a Patre suo omnis conditionis, quemadmodum habet illud: dixit Dominus Domino meo, sede a dextris meis, quoadusque ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Patrem enim Filio collocutum ostendit, qui & dedit ei haereditatem gentium, & subjecit ei omnes inimicos. Vere igitur cum Pater sit Dominus, & Filius vere sit Dominus, merito Spiritus Sanctus Domini appellatione signavit eos. Et iterum in eversione Sodomitarum Scriptura ait: Et pluit Dominus super Sodomam & Gomorram, ignem & sulphur a Domino de cœlo. Filium enim hic significat, qui & Abrahae conloquutus fit, a Patre accepisse potestatem ad judicandum Sodomitas, propter iniquitatem eorum. Similiter habet illud: Sedes tua Deus in æternum, virga directionis, virga regni tui; Dilexisti justitiam, & odisti iniquitatem, propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus. Utrosque enim Dei appellatione significavit spiritus, & eum qui ungitur Filium, & eum qui ungit, id est Patrem. — Nemo igitur alius, quemadmodum prædixi, Deus nominatur, aut Dominus appellatur, nisi qui est omnium Deus & Dominus, qui & Moysi dixit; ego sum qui sum, &c. & hujus Filius Iesus Christus Dominus noster. — Per Filium itaque qui est in Patre, & habet in se Patrem, &c. Qui fecisti cœlum & terram, & dominaris omnium, qui es solus & verus Deus, super quem alius Deus non est praeter Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, dominatione quoque dominaris Spiritus Sancti &c. Lib. iv. cap. ix. Ipse igitur Christus cum Patre vivorum est Deus, qui & locutus est Moysi, qui & Patribus manifestatus est. Hæc autem Filii eandem cum Patre Deitatem probant, & Deitatis æqualitatem, seu identitatem.
units.tr: Nor does the second passage of Irenaeus that our author cites, book 4, chapter 37, present us with anything against us; on the contrary, it contains several things that favour us considerably. Although Irenaeus teaches that the Father was never seen or made visible to men, but that he made and spoke all things through the Son, his Word, and that the Son receives from the Father the power to do these and those things, he does not for that reason call the Father alone God, nor deny that the Son is the same God as the Father. Indeed, he teaches that the Son has always been with the Father. And since we have shown in many ways that the Word, that is, the Son, was always with the Father. For Wisdom, which is the Spirit, was with God before all creation, as he says through Solomon, etc. Now this Word of his is our Lord Jesus Christ, who in the last times became man among men, so that he might join the end to the beginning, that is, God to man. And therefore the prophets, receiving the prophetic gift from the same Word, proclaimed his coming according to the flesh, through which the mingling and communion of God and man was brought about according to the good pleasure of the Father, the Word of God announcing it from the beginning, that God would be seen by men and would live among them upon the earth. Accordingly, when he cites John 1:18, he does not give it as it stands in our copies, the only-begotten Son, but the only-begotten God, as if it had been spoken by the Lord himself, just as the Lord said, The only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him. Moreover, in this same chapter he teaches the Trinity of Persons quite clearly, and in more than one way. First: It was not angels who made us, nor did they form us, nor could angels make the image of God, nor anyone else except the Word of the Lord, nor a power far removed from the Father of all things. For God had no need of these to do what he had himself determined beforehand should be done, as if he did not have his own hands. For the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, are always present, through whom and in whom he freely and spontaneously made all things, to whom also he speaks, saying, Let us make man in our image and likeness. Again: Moreover, he will be seen in the kingdom of heaven in a fatherly manner, the Spirit indeed preparing man for the Son of God, the Son leading him to the Father, and the Father bestowing incorruption for eternal life, which falls to each one from seeing God. Finally: So God was thus made manifest. For through all these things God the Father is shown forth, the Spirit indeed working, the Son ministering, the Father approving, and man being brought to salvation. And in chapter 17 he says that the Father did not need the ministry of angels for the fashioning of man, but had an abundant and unspeakable ministry. For his offspring and his figure, that is, the Son and the Spirit, the Word and the Wisdom, minister to him in all his works, and all the angels serve them and are subject to them. He calls the Son the offspring of the Father and his Word, and the Holy Spirit his figure and Wisdom. When he says that they minister to the Father, he means nothing other than that the Father works through them. For he taught that the Son is always with the Father and not outside him, and is the offspring and figure of the Father in a way different from creatures, and that the angels, the most excellent among creatures, cannot be separated from the Father any more than his Wisdom and Word can. In book 2, chapter 48, when he is arguing against those who vainly tried to measure and explain the manner of the Son's generation from the Father with their own wit, guessing at his generation from the Father, and maintaining that it cannot be known or declared by us, he also uses this argument: that Christ himself says he does not know certain things. Since the Lord himself, the Son of God, granted that the Father alone knows the day and hour of judgment, plainly saying, Of that day and hour no one knows, neither the Son, but the Father only. If therefore the Son did not blush to refer the knowledge of that day to the Father, but said what was true, neither should we blush to leave to God the greater questions that are beyond us. For no one is above the master. If anyone therefore says to us, How then was the Son brought forth by the Father? we answer him that this bringing forth, whether one calls it generation, or naming, or opening, or by whatever name, is his generation, which is ineffable, and no one knows it. Not Valentinus, not Marcion, nor Saturninus, nor Basilides, nor angels, nor archangels, nor principalities, nor powers, but only the Father who begot and the Son who was begotten. Since, therefore, his generation is ineffable, all those who try to declare generations and emanations are not in their right mind, promising to declare things that cannot be declared. Yet he does not assert that the Son, according to that which was born of the Father, and which, being otherwise ineffable to us, the Son alone knows with the Father, being the Wisdom of God and not outside him, did not know the last day and hour. In the following chapter, however, he not only repeats that Christ is said to be ignorant of the day and hour of judgment, under the same warning, that this knowledge must be left to God, just as the Lord left the hour and the day, but he also inquires into the cause of this, why Christ is said to be ignorant of it: For if anyone asks the reason why the Father, sharing all things with the Son, alone was shown by the Lord to know both the hour and the day, he will find no more fitting, no more becoming, and no other reason that is free from danger than this one at present: since the Lord is the only true teacher, we may learn through him that the Father is above all things. For the Father, he says, is greater than I; and so the Father was declared by our Lord to be pre-eminent in knowledge, so that we, while we are in the figure of this world, should allow perfect knowledge and such questions to God, and lest perhaps, seeking to search out the height of the Father, we fall into such danger as to ask whether there is another God above God. First, granting that the Father shares in all things with the Son, he teaches that all the things of the Son are common with the Father; but that what was made known to the Lord, namely, that he did not know that day and hour, he takes in another relation [σχέσει], that is, of Christ in the state of manifestation, not of the communion of all things; and from this he reveals the particular cause of this ignorance, from the condition of Christ's humiliation under the Father, acknowledging the Father as greater and that he does not know all things in the figure of this world. By this he teaches us the more to leave the knowledge of many things to God alone, and not to search too curiously into the height of the Father, nor to set up another God above the Father. But another thing, in his view, is to consider the Son in the respect of the complete communion with the Father, or of the singular manifestation from the Father; and that the Father is above all things does not in fact prejudice that first dignity, by which the Son has things in common with the Father; just as our teacher is so, not according to this respect, but according to that by which he is Christ the Lord. And it is fittingly ascribed to the Father that he is God above all things, with respect to creatures and the world, and then because he never so humbled himself as the Son did. So that the adversaries may not argue from that phrase against the Son and his common nature with the Father. Then in book 3, chapter 8, Irenaeus, teaching that the prophets and apostles never named another God, or called anyone Lord, except the true and only God, and by calling Christ Lord and making him a sharer in the same name of God, and not in any other name whatever, signifies that he is the same God as the Father. Nothing stands in the way of this, that he teaches that the Father made, created, and spoke all things through him, or that the Son himself did all things by the command of the Father, because these phrases denote the economy, the external operations by which the Father works all things through the Son, and not the contrary. And so the Son is God through the Father, as with the Son, and the Son has the name God in common with the Father, which no one else has. For whether angels, or archangels, or thrones, or dominions were constituted and made by him who is God above all, and were made through his Word, John indeed has signified this: when he had said of the Word of God that he was in the Father, he added, All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. To whom then did he give the command? To the Word indeed; through whom, he says, the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth. But other things are those that were constituted by him who constituted them, and were made by him who made them. For he himself is uncreated, without beginning and without end, lacking nothing, sufficient for himself, and giving to all the rest that they should be what they are. But those things that were made by him had a beginning. And whatever has received a beginning must be subject to him who made it, and needs him altogether; so that those who have even a modest understanding in discerning such things must necessarily have a different name for them. Thus he who made all things with his Word is rightly called God and Lord alone, while the things that were made must not receive the name of the Creator, nor is it right for them to take that name. Now the Word made all things, or God with the Word, of whom he had spoken; nor are those things that are in the order of constitution and subjection to be compared with the Word of God, through whom all things were made, who is our Lord Jesus Christ. Here there is a twofold opposition between the Maker and the made, in name and in reality: the one is uncreated, without beginning, without end, lacking nothing, sufficient to himself alone, and giving to the rest that they should exist; the rest, on the other hand, are such. Then, the one who alone is to be called Lord and God is the Father and his Word, and nothing else is a partner in that name. Therefore the Word is not only not of the kind of those made things, but is truly God, the same as the Father, both in divine properties and in name. See the whole sixth chapter of this book, where it is shown at length that no one else is named God except the one true God, the Father of all, and his Word. To this also belongs what he says in book 4, chapter 8, that the Son is the measure of the Father, or the God who made all things in measure, and with whom nothing is unmeasured; and that the Son has given to himself also his own measure: For God makes all things with measure and order, and nothing is unmeasured with him, since nothing is without composition. And rightly he who said that the immeasurable Father was measured in the Son. For the Son is the measure of the Father, since he also contains him. Since he contains him, that is, the immeasurable, therefore the measure of the immeasurable is itself immeasurable; indeed, since the immeasurable cannot be multiplied, the Father is in a sense the measure of himself in the Son. Nor does the proof of our author's view, that this measure of the Son with respect to the Father should be understood of the Son's fulfilling, perfecting, and containing all the things of the law which had hitherto been measured and determined in the Father, or of the perfect measure of knowledge in the Son in his own kind, and not absolutely, as the author of the Irenicum wishes, hold. For Irenaeus speaks universally and absolutely of all things with God and from God being measured, not only of this or that in which he is speaking of measure: For God makes all things with measure and order. And he does not say that the Son is the measure of the Father in respect of knowledge only, nor even of imperfect knowledge, as the author hitherto wanted to infer from the imperfect knowledge of Christ, to the same Son. Finally, in the conclusion which our author draws, he plays on an obvious ambiguity, saying: Irenaeus, together with Justin and the Christians who followed them, held that the Father is superior to the Word, but by no means equal; for this, that the Father is superior to the Word and not equal, can be understood either of the incarnate Word, and as he is incarnate, by reduplication, and so we concede that the Father is greater; greater; or of the Word who was and is, before and beyond the [ἐνσάρκωσιν] incarnation, and so they do not deny his equality with the Father; rather, in this very place Irenaeus teaches that the Son is the measure of the Father and is contained by him. This is the very equality itself. And he teaches his incarnation everywhere, by which the mingling and communion of God and man was brought about according to the good pleasure of the Father (book 4, chapter 8, and book 5 at the beginning): the Word, existing, was made man. Therefore in book 1, chapter 2, in the creed he says that we believe in Christ the Son of God, incarnate for our salvation, and in the Holy Spirit. Now he not only says but also proves that the Son is true God together with the Father, in book 3, chapter 6: Neither the Lord, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the apostles would ever have called definitively and absolutely God one who was not God, unless he were the true God; nor would they have called anyone Lord from his own person, unless he were the one who rules over all, God the Father and his Son, who received dominion from his Father over every creature, as that text has it: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. For he shows the Father speaking to the Son, who also gave him the inheritance of the nations and subjected all his enemies to him. Truly, therefore, since the Father is Lord and the Son is truly Lord, the Holy Spirit has rightly marked them with the appellation of Lord. And again, at the overthrow of the Sodomites, Scripture says: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah fire and brimstone from the Lord out of heaven. For here it signifies the Son, who also spoke with Abraham, and who received from the Father the power to judge the Sodomites for their iniquity. Similarly, that text has: Thy throne, O God, is for ever, the sceptre of direction is the sceptre of thy kingdom; thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, thy God, has anointed thee. For the Spirit signified both by the name of God: the one who is anointed, the Son, and the one who anoints, that is, the Father. — No one else, therefore, as I have said before, is named God or called Lord, but only he who is God and Lord of all, who also said to Moses, I am who I am, etc., and whose Son is Jesus Christ our Lord. — Therefore through the Son, who is in the Father and has the Father in himself, etc. You who made heaven and earth and rule over all, who alone are the true God, beside whom there is no other God except our Lord Jesus Christ, you also rule by the dominion of the Holy Spirit, etc. Book 4, chapter 9: Christ himself, therefore, is God together with the Father of the living, who also spoke to Moses, and who was also made manifest to the fathers. These statements, moreover, prove the same Deity of the Son with the Father, and the equality, or identity, of the Deity.

units.la: Ultimus sequitur Tertullianus, qui ad annum vixit cc. & ex quo sententiam suam, quod Filius non sit ejusdem cum Patre essentiæ, sed quod Pater Filio omni modo major, antiquior, & potentior, confirmare nituntur Adversarii, Ministri Transsylvaniæ, in lib. de unius Dei cognitione; Schlichtingius, in præfat. adversus Meisnerum, de Trinitate; Autor Irenici Irenicorum, quem ad examen imprælens vocamus. Non vero illud quod volunt, probat Tertullianus, eo, quod dicit lib. ii. contra Marcionem, cap. vi. Filium Patris nomine egisse & locutum cum Patribus, sub V.T.: neq; enim inde conficitur hoc, quod contendunt Adversarii: sed imo contrarium, quando ait, Filium esse sermonem Patris, quem ex semetipso proferendo, Filium fecit. nota, proferendo ex semetipso, non ex nonexistentibus, vel ex nihilo. & hinc Filium istum suum omni dispositioni suæ voluntatique præfecit — in cujus autoritate & nomine ipse erat Deus, qui videbatur, invisibili manente Patre, Dei Filius. In libro contra Praxeam, distinguit in Deo Λόγον, & ejus in creatione prolationem, quando nimirum emisit Deus vocem, & dixit, reliqua ut fierent, ipsum primum protulit Sermonem, habentem in se indiviiduas suas rationes, Sophiam, ut per ipsum fierent universa, per quem erant cogitata atque disposita. — Tunc igitur etiam ipse sermo speciem & ornatum suum sumit, sonum & vocem, cum dicit Deus, fiat lux. Haec accipit, uti Λόγῳ[?] & personae divinae, quam Sophiam & Λόγον appellat, externam manifestationem, non vero propriam & primam generationem. Cap. VI. Quid enim sapientius ratione Dei, sive sermone? itaque Sophiam quoque exaudi, ut secundam personam conditam. Illa vero ratio & sermo semper in Deo & cum Deo, juxta eum. Sed distinguit, Sermonem emittere, vel proferre, quod in creatione fecit; & apud se habere: habuisse dicit semper, neque absque eo fuisse solitarium Deum, at protulisse vel emisisse demum in creatione. Nam etsi Deus sermonem suum nondum miserat, proinde eum cum ipsa & in ipsa ratione intra semetipsum habebat, tacite cogitando & disponendo secum, quae per sermonem mox erat dicturus. Sermonem semper habebat, & hic ex aeterno penes Deum, uti adversarius noster ex Tertulliano loquitur, fuit; sed suo demum tempore per sermonem dixit in creatione ea, quae dicendo fecit. Non autem persona secunda secundum se tantum facta in creatione, sed quidem manifestata, prolata, emissa. Distinguit Tertullianus, in Deo rationem, & sermonem, atque hinc Deum rationalem, & sermonalem, eumque fuisse ait, ante istum, sed non quasi plane non fuisset apud Deum Λόγος, sermo, secunda persona, genitaque fuisset demum sermonis creatifici prolatione, sed quod tum declarata & prolata foras; habuisse, inquit, Deum in semetipso rationem, & in ratione sermonem, quem secundum a se faceret. Qua ratione, ait, Deum ante universitatis constitutionem solum non fuisse. Paulo ante, Caeterum ne tunc quidem solus; habebat enim secum, quam habebat in semetipso, rationem suam scilicet. Rationalis enim Deus, & ratio in ipso prius; & ita a ipso omnia. Quae ratio sensus ipsius est, hanc Graeci Λόγον dicunt, quo vocabulo etiam Sermonem appellamus. Quare non statuit, productione sive pronunciatione sermonis, qua res singulas creavit Deus, alteram Trinitatis personam, hoc est, Sermonem sive Verbum, ac Dei Filium, tum demum in se ac substantia propria productum fuisse, qui ante & semper cum Deo una fuit, & in eo. Quamvis externam sermonis prolationem, quatenus significatio fuit interni & aeterni Verbi, quasi ad perfectionem, non nati sed noti, & ad operandum se componentis, facere significet. Cap. VII. Haec est nativitas perfecta sermonis, dum ex Deo procedit, conditus ab eo primum ad cogitatum in nomine Sophiae. Dominus condidit me in initium viarum suarum. Dehinc generatus ad effectum: Cum pararet coelum, aderam illi simul. Quae nemo non benigne interpretanda esse, videt. Quid enim primum condi, dehinc generari ad effectum, & nativitas perfecta, nisi in eum, quem modo dedi, sensum? Unde & istum in creatione sermonem, adversus Praxeam tenet substantivum fuisse, ut res & persona quaedam videri possit: & ita capiat secundus a Deo constitutus duos efficere, Patrem & Filium, Deum & sermonem. Docens, duas personas esse Patrem, & Filium, & Filium in substantia ipsius propria productum, uti agnoscit Adversarius, non vero totum, quantus quantus est, in creatione demum factum. Quaecunque ergo substantia sermonis fuit, illam dico personam, & illi nomen Filii vindico; & dum Filium agnosco, secundum a Patre defendo. Non ergo ea Tertulliani est sententia, tum primum Filium a Patre factum vel progenitum, quando res omnes creatas e nihilo fabricatus est, ad idque usus sermone: quamvis tum de sermone substantivo, qui a Deo prolatus est, tum Dei corpore, nonnulla haud admodum accurate philosophetur. Nam sermo ei, & in Patre semper, sicut dicit, ego in Patre. Et apud Deum semper, sicut scriptum est: & sermo erat apud Deum. Et nunquam sepa-
units.tr: The last to follow is Tertullian, who lived down to about the year 200 and from whom our opponents, the ministers of Transylvania in their book de unius Dei cognitione, Schlichting in the preface to his adversus Meisnerum, de Trinitate, and the author of the Irenicum Irenicorum, which we summon to examination here, try to confirm their view that the Son is not of the same essence as the Father, but that the Father is in every respect greater, older and more powerful than the Son. Tertullian does not prove what they want, however, from what he says in book 2 against Marcion, chapter 6, that the Son acted and spoke with the Fathers under the Old Testament in the Father's name. For it does not follow from this what our opponents contend. On the contrary, the opposite follows, when he says that the Son is the Word of the Father, whom he made Son by bringing him forth out of himself. Note: by bringing him forth out of himself, not out of non-existent things or out of nothing. And from this he set this Son of his over all his disposition and will, in whose authority and name he himself was God, who was seen, while the Father remained invisible, as the Son of God. In the book against Praxeas he distinguishes in God the Logos [Λόγον] and its utterance in creation, namely when God uttered a voice and said, and the rest came to be: he first brought forth the Word itself, having in itself its own undivided reasons, Sophia, so that all things might come to be through him, through whom they had been thought out and arranged. Then therefore the Word itself also takes on its appearance and adornment, its sound and voice, when God says, Let there be light. He takes this as the external manifestation of the divine person, whom he calls Sophia and Logos [Λόγος], and not as its proper and first generation. Chapter 6: For what is wiser than the reason of God, or the Word? So hear Sophia too, as the second person created. That reason and Word were always in God and with God, beside him. But he distinguishes between uttering or bringing forth the Word, which he did in creation, and having it within himself; he says that he always had it, and that God was never solitary without it, but that he brought it forth or uttered it only in creation. For although God had not yet sent forth his Word, nevertheless he had it with himself and in his own reason, silently thinking and arranging within himself what he was soon to speak through the Word. He always had the Word, and this Word was from eternity with God, as our opponent speaks from Tertullian; but in its own time he spoke, through the Word, the things he made by speaking in creation. Yet the second person was not made in creation merely in himself, but was indeed manifested, brought forth and sent out. Tertullian distinguishes in God reason and word, and thence calls God rational and verbal, and says that the one existed before the other, not as if the Logos, the Word, the second person, had not been with God at all, and had been begotten only by the bringing forth of the creative Word; rather that it was then declared and brought out. He says God had within himself reason, and in reason a word, which he would make second to himself. By this reasoning, he says, God was not alone even before the constitution of the universe. A little earlier: Yet not even then was he alone; for he had with him, that is, his own reason, which he had within himself. For God is rational, and reason was first in him; and so all things come from him. This reason is his sense, which the Greeks call Logos, a word we also use for Word. Therefore he does not hold that by the production or pronouncement of the Word, by which God created the individual things, the other person of the Trinity, that is the Word or Son of God, was then at last produced in himself and in his own substance, though he was before and always one with God and in him. Yet he may mean by the external utterance of the Word, insofar as it was the sign of the inner and eternal Word, that he made it for perfection, not born but known, and arranging itself for action. Chapter 7: This is the perfect birth of the Word, when it proceeds from God, first created by him for thought under the name of Sophia. The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways. Then begotten for effect: when he prepared the heavens, I was there with him. Everyone sees that these must be interpreted charitably. For what does it mean to be first created, then begotten for effect, and to have a perfect birth, unless in the sense I have just given? Hence also he holds, against Praxeas, that this Word in creation was substantive, so that it could appear as a thing and a person, and so the second, constituted by God, might make two, Father and Son, God and Word. Teaching that there are two persons, the Father and the Son, and the Son brought forth in his own proper substance, as our opponent acknowledges, but not that he was made in creation as a whole, however great he is. Whatever the substance of the Word was, I call that a person, and I claim for it the name of Son; and while I acknowledge the Son, I defend him as second to the Father. So it is not Tertullian's view that the Son was made or begotten by the Father only when he fashioned all created things out of nothing, using the Word for this; though he does reason somewhat inaccurately, then, about the substantive Word that was brought forth by God and about the body of God. For the Word is with him and in the Father always, as he says, I am in the Father. And with God always, as it is written: and the Word was with God. And never separated from the Father, or other than the Father, because I and the Father are one.

units.la: Tom. 2. ratus à Patre, aut alius à Patre: quia, ego & Pater unum sumus. Qui unum cum Patre, nunquam separatus, aut alius à Patre, & apud Deum, & in Deo semper, ille non tum demum factus, quando creari caeptum, neque externa vocis prolatio fuit, vel inde demum generatus extitit. Certe Trinitatem, hoc cap. VII. aperte nominat & docet; secundus autem ubi est, duo sunt. Et tertius ubi est, tres sunt. Tertius enim est Spiritus à Deo & Filio, sicut tertius à radice fructus ex frutice, &c. Ita Trinitas per confertos & connexos gradus à Patre decurrens, & Monarchiae nihil obstrepit, & οἰκονομίας[?] statum protegit. Monarchiam appellat Dei unitatem, quemadmodum & Justinus librum hoc titulo scripsit, de Dei unitate. Tertullianus, cap. IX. Ecce dico, alium esse Patrem, & alium Filium, & alium Spiritum. Male accepit Idiotes quisque aut perversus hoc dictum, quasi diversitatem sonet, & ex diversitate separationem portendat Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus. & cap. XII. Immo quia jam adhaerebat Patri Filius, secunda persona, sermo ipsius; & tertia, Spiritus in Sermone, ideo pluraliter pronunciavit, faciamus (hominem) & nostram, & nobis. Cum quibus enim faciebat hominem, & quibus faciebat similem? Filio quidem, qui erat induitu-rus hominem, Spiritu vero, qui erat sanctificaturus hominem, quasi cum ministris & arbitris ex unitate Trinitatis loquebatur. Postrema haec, quasi cum ministris & arbitris Trinitatis, eo sensu explicanda, quod Pater per illos operetur, juxta ordinem divinae oeconomiae, non contra. At quod dicit cap. IX. Pater enim tota substantia est, Filius vero derivatio totius & portio, uti venit ex ista ejus loquutione, qua Deo corpus visus attribuere, qui enim negabit Deum corpus esse, etsi Deus spiritus est? & similitudine alia, qua generationem Filii à Patre expo-suerat, uti fructicis à radice, fluvii à fonte, & à sole radii; ita incommodius dictum est, dum explicare satagit, & Filii à Patre generationem, & ejus à Patre differentiam, quodque hinc principium communicatae Deitatis habeatur in Filio. Hujus saltem sententiae eum fuisse indicat, quod ejusdem substantiae sit Pater & Filius, & in Deo Personarum Trinitas: quod nec Adversarius diffitetur, de Tertulliano inquiens, quod Sermonem, sive Verbum ac Dei Filium, in se & in substantia ipsius Patris propria productum esse, non ex nihilo, sed ex ipsius Dei substantia, testatur. Unde cap. XII. Tertullianus, quod Noster hic quoque adducit: Alium autem quomodo accipere debeas, jam professus sum, personae, non substantiae nomine, ad distinctionem, non ad divisionem. Caeterum ubique teneo unam substantiam in tribus cohaerentibus. Sed explicandi & declarandi, quem adhibet, modus non usquequaque convenit. Ad id vero, quod Patrem invisibilem, & Filium visibilem dicit, jam ante etiam respondimus, quamvis & secundum eam rationem, quam cum Patre communem habet, sive substantiam, invisibilem quoque Filium agnoscat. Visibilem autem Dei Filium, id est, Sermonem Dei, quia, qui caro factus est, Christus dictus est: & hac quoque ratione mortalis, & accessibilis.
units.tr: Vol. 2. He who is one with the Father, never separated, or other than the Father, and with God, and always in God, was not made only when he began to be created, nor did he come to be begotten only through the external utterance of a voice. Certainly in this chapter 7 he clearly names and teaches the Trinity; but where the second is, there are two, and where the third is, there are three. For the third is the Spirit from God and the Son, just as the third fruit from the root is from the shrub, and so on. Thus the Trinity, descending from the Father through linked and connected degrees, neither disturbs the Monarchy nor violates the state of the economy [οἰκονομίας]. He calls the unity of God the Monarchy, just as Justin also wrote a book under this title, on the unity of God. Tertullian, chapter 9: Behold, I say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Spirit another. Any ignorant or perverse person misunderstands this saying, as if it sounded like diversity, and from diversity portended a separation of the Father, the Son and the Spirit. And chapter 12: Indeed, because the Son, the second person, his Word, already clung to the Father, and the third, the Spirit, was in the Word, therefore he spoke in the plural: let us make (man) in our image and likeness. With whom was he making man, and to whom was he making him like? Certainly with the Son, who was about to put on man, and with the Spirit, who was about to sanctify man; he spoke as with ministers and assessors from the unity of the Trinity. This last phrase, as with ministers and assessors of the Trinity, must be explained in the sense that the Father works through them, according to the order of the divine economy, and not against it. But when he says in chapter 9: For the Father is the whole substance, while the Son is a derivation of the whole and a portion, as comes from that manner of speaking by which he attributed a body to God, for who will deny that God is a body, even though God is spirit? and by another likeness, by which he had explained the Son's generation from the Father, as of a shrub from a root, of a river from a spring, and of rays from the sun, it is said too awkwardly, while he labours to explain both the Son's generation from the Father, and his difference from the Father, and that from this there is held to be a beginning of the communicated Deity in the Son. At least that he held this view is shown by the fact that the Father and the Son are of the same substance, and that in God there is a Trinity of persons; which our opponent does not deny, when he says of Tertullian that he attests that the Word, or Son of God, was brought forth in himself and in the proper substance of the Father, not from nothing but from the very substance of God. Hence in chapter 12 Tertullian, whom our author also cites here, says: How you ought to understand the other, I have already professed: by the name of person, not of substance, for distinction, not for division. Moreover I everywhere hold one substance in three cohering. But the mode of explanation and declaration he uses does not agree in every respect. As for his saying that the Father is invisible and the Son visible, we have already answered this too, although according to that reason which he holds in common with the Father, that is substance, he also acknowledges the Son as invisible. But the Son of God as visible, that is the Word of God, because he who was made flesh was called Christ; and by this reason too he is mortal and accessible.

units.la: Contra Hermogenem, sic pro materiae, ex qua Deus omnia condiderit, aeternitate argutantem, quia cum Deus ab aeterno fuerit, ut Deus, ita & Dominus, necessario quoque adesse debuerit materia, cujus respectu Deo nomen istud competat, Tertullianus, negans materiam ab aeterno, negat quoque Deum ab aeterno fuisse Dominum, accepisse vero hanc nomenclaturam, ait, in tempore, quando ista fecit, in quae dominaretur. Agnoscit quidem, semper fuisse Deum; at non semper Dominum. Haec ejus verba: Dei nomen dicimus semper fuisse, apud semetipsum, & in semetipso, Dominum vero non semper: diversa enim utriusque conditio. Deus substantiae ipsius nomen, id est, divinitatis; Dominus vero non substantiae, sed potestatis. Substantiam semper fuisse cum suo nomine nomine, quod est Deus, postea Dominus, accedentis scilicet rei mentio. Nam ex quo esse coepe-runt, in quae potestas Domini ageret, ex illo per accessionem potestatis & factus est, & dictus Do-minus. Hinc pergit, a Deo Domino, ad Deum Patrem, atque judicem: & similia loquitur, quia & Pater Deus est, & judex Deus est, non tamen ideo pater & judex semper, quia Deus semper. Nam nec pater potuit esse ante filium, nec judex ante delictum. Fuit autem tem-pus, cum & delictum, & filius non fuit, quod judicem, & qui patrem Dominum faceret. Sic & Dominus non ante ea, quorum Dominus existeret, sed Dominus tantum futurus quandoque, sicut & Pater per Filium, sicut judex per delictum, ita & Dominus per ea, quae sibi servitura fecisset. Non dubito, quin si post tempus & disputationes Arii vixisset, cautius hac in parte scripsisset Auctor, cujus sententia, nunquam hinc in Ecclesia notata, vel damnata, potius ex perpetua fidei in Trinitatem confessione, & quod Filium ὁμοού-σιον, hoc est eadem substantia praeditum docuit, expositia fuit. Ista vero de Deo, quod fuerit, antequam Pater esset, sic expono, quod, uti dum negat Deum fuisse semper Dominum, id non aliter accipit, vel accipere etiam potest, quam non fuisse actu dominatum vel dominari non potuisse in res nondum in mundo existentes; ut ita etiam non ἁπλῶς[?], sed κατὰ τι[?], & secundum istum modum, vid. quod ad Filii in mundo, & per mundi creationem, manifestationem, non fuisse hactenus Patrem, intelligat. Quemadmodum enim aliquis potest esse dominus, quamvis actu non dominetur, quod & in aliis dominationibus passim verum, ubi inter habitum distinguimus & actum, quemadmodum Imperator, Princeps, qui tamen id non agunt, ita Deus Dominus aeternus & ab aeterno, quamvis in tempore demum dominatus fuerit in mundum, a se in tempore factum: sic & Pater cum Filio quidem ab aeterno, utpote quem in semetipso, uti alibi dixit, habuit Filium Verbum, qua ratione nec solus fuit, uti antea dixit; sed non fuit manifestatus Pater nisi in Filio, per opera & verba, exhibito. Alias Hilarius dixit, lib. de Synod. si quis seniorem tempore Patrem dicat Filio ex se unigenito, juniorem autem Filium Patre, anathema sit. & Tertullianus noster, cap. seq. quis enim alius Dei census, quam aeternitas? quis alius aeternitatis status, quam semper fuisse & futurum esse, & prærogativa nullius initii & nullius finis? Cap. xvii. Patrem ait, Sophiam condidisse, & generasse in semetipso, statim ut necessariam sensit ad opera mundi: agnoscat ergo Hermogenes, idcirco etiam Sophiam Dei, natam & conditam praedicari, ne quid innatum & inconditum praeter solum Deum crederemus. Conditum appellat Dei Filium, ex vulgato usu loci Prov. viii. 22. non tamen eo sensu, ut putet proprie creatum, quandoquidem Filium natum docet non ex nihilo, sed ex ipso & in ipso Deo: ut de sententia alicujus in hoc argumento non fit judicandum, ex communi & perversa citatione loci, Deus ἔκτισε[?] creavit, vel condidit me: quam loci lectionem, ut non congruere cum Hebraeo omnes vident, quare neque sequendam esse; ita, etiamsi maneat, alii de humana natura Christi, & ejus corpore; alii ad divinam relatum, simpliciter etiam pro generatione accipiunt, non proprie creatione, quem verbi usum nonnullis confirmant, ac creationem dici, ut verbi substantia & hypostasis significetur, non mera ἐνέργεια: alii vocem accipiunt pro constituere, id est, constituit, ordinavit me: denique alii, non de Verbo Dei substantiali, seu Filio acceptum, sed de sapientia, per prosopopoeiam, ad quam Deus omnia crearit, tanquam ideam: quam expositionem sequitur Petavius, Tom. II. lib. II. de Trinitate, cap. I. qui videndus. Certe Filius non est ingenitus, uti Deus Pater. Si enim intra Dominum, quod ex ipso & in ipso fuit, sine initio non fuit: Sophia scilicet ipsius exinde nata & condita, ex quo in sensu Dei ad opera mundi disponenda coepit agitari: multo magis non capit sine initio quicquam fuisse quod extra Dominum fuerit: quale quid foret, materia Hermogenis. Negat, sine initio fuisse Verbum, quandoquidem ab alio processit: dure, & nullo habito ad controversias post natas respectu, tantummodo ad Hermogenis materiam, ut ejus initium astrueret a Deo, negaretque carere principio. Ita nondum nata & agitata controversia, licentiosius loqui homines solent, quae in sequiorem partem postmodum frustra rapiuntur. Deinde mirum in modum magis, quam vere & accurate, antea adversus Praxeam, cap. xii. distinxit Autor noster, esse Sophiae apud Patrem, & generationem ejus ad effectum, quasi tum quando in creatione Pater produxit seu manifestavit Verbum, per quod omnia effecit, & dixit, omnia ut fierent, nova conditio fuerit ejus & generatio: de quo liberius loquitur, quam rectius, conditus ab eo primum ad cogitatum in nomine Sophiae: dehinc generatus ad effectum. qua quasi generatione aliqua, Patrem facit antiquiorem: Si vero Sophia eadem Dei sermo est sensu Sophia, & sine quo factum est nihil, sicut & dispositum sine Sophia, quale est ut Filii Dei Sermone unigenito & primogenito aliquid fuerit praeter Patrem antiquius: & hoc modo utique generosius, nedum quod innatum nato fortius &c. vid. materia Hermogenis, nato ex Deo Filio foret major, si ea non a Deo nata vel facta esset, quum sit natus & factus, uti loquitur, Filius. De Filio usurpat verba, quae de materia, non vero ut pari modo intelligantur.
units.tr: Against Hermogenes, who argues for the eternity of the matter from which God made all things: since God has been from eternity, as God, so also as Lord, matter must necessarily have existed too, with respect to which that name belongs to God. Tertullian, denying that matter is eternal, also denies that God was Lord from eternity. He says that God received this title in time, when he made the things over which he would rule. He does acknowledge that God has always existed, but not that he has always been Lord. His words are these: We say that the name of God has always existed, with himself and in himself, but not that of Lord, for the condition of the two is different. God is the name of his substance, that is, of his divinity; but Lord is not the name of substance but of power. The substance has always existed with its name, which is God; afterwards it was called Lord, the mention of a thing being added. For from the time that there began to be things over which the power of Lord could act, from that time he became Lord and was called Lord, through the addition of power. From here he goes on from God the Lord to God the Father and Judge, and says similar things: because God is also Father, and God is also Judge, yet he is not Father and Judge always merely because he is God always. For he could not be Father before the Son, nor Judge before sin. There was a time when there was neither sin nor Son, which could make God Judge and Father. So also he was not Lord before those things of which he would be Lord, but only going to be Lord at some point, just as he is Father through the Son, and Judge through sin, so he is Lord through those things which he had made to serve him. I do not doubt that if the author had lived after the time of Arius and the disputes with him, he would have written more cautiously on this point. His opinion was never noted or condemned in the Church; rather, it was explained by the constant confession of faith in the Trinity, and by his teaching that the Son is homoousios [ὁμοούσιον], that is, endowed with the same substance. As for what he says about God before the Father existed, I explain it thus: when he denies that God was always Lord, he does not understand it otherwise, nor can he take it otherwise, than that God had not actually ruled, or could not yet rule, over things not yet existing in the world. So too he is not Father simply [ἁπλῶς], but in some respect [κατὰ τι], in that manner: that is, he understands that until the creation of the world and the manifestation of the Son through the creation of the world, God had not yet been Father. For just as someone can be a lord without actually ruling, which is true in other kinds of lordship as well, where we distinguish between possession and action (as an emperor or a prince who does not exercise his power), so God is eternally Lord and has been Lord from eternity, although he only came to rule over the world that was made by him in time. So too the Father, with the Son, from eternity indeed (since he had the Son as the Word in himself, as he says elsewhere), by which reason he was not alone, as he said before; yet the Father was not made manifest except in the Son, through the works and words that were displayed. Hilary, elsewhere, in his book On the Synods, says: If anyone says that the Father is older in time than the Son, who is the only-begotten from himself, and that the Son is younger than the Father, let him be anathema. And our Tertullian, in the following chapter: For what other condition of God is there than eternity? What other state of eternity is there than always to have been and always to be, and the privilege of having no beginning and no end? In chapter 17 he says that the Father established Sophia and begot her in himself, as soon as he perceived her necessary for the works of the world: Let Hermogenes therefore acknowledge that for this reason Sophia also is proclaimed as the born and made of God, lest we believe anything to be unborn and unmade besides God alone. He calls the Son of God made [conditum], following the common use of Prov. 8:22, yet not in the sense that he thinks he was properly created, since he teaches that the Son was born not out of nothing but from God himself and in God himself. Thus the opinion of anyone in this matter is not to be judged by the common and perverse citation of the passage, "God made [ἔκτισε] or founded me." All see that this reading does not agree with the Hebrew, and so it should not be followed. Even if it were retained, some take it of the human nature of Christ and his body, others refer it to the divine nature, and simply take it of generation rather than of creation properly so called; some of them support this use of the word, saying that it is called creation so that the substance and hypostasis of the Word may be signified, and not mere operation. Others take the word to mean to establish, that is, he has established or ordained me. Finally, others take it not of the substantial Word of God, or the Son, but of wisdom, by prosopopoeia, through which God created all things, as an idea. Petavius follows this explanation, in his Tom. II, lib. II, de Trinitate, cap. I, which should be consulted. Certainly the Son is not unbegotten, as God the Father is. For if within the Lord there was nothing without beginning that came from him and was in him, then Sophia, his own, was born and made from the moment she began to be stirred in the mind of God to arrange the works of the world; much more it cannot be that anything existed without beginning which was outside the Lord, which would be the matter of Hermogenes. He denies that the Word was without beginning, since he proceeded from another. He says this harshly, without any regard to the controversies that arose later, only with regard to the matter of Hermogenes, in order to establish that it had its beginning from God and to deny that it lacked a principle. Thus, before a controversy has arisen and been stirred up, men are accustomed to speak more freely, and such words are afterwards wrongly seized upon for a worse sense. Next, our author, in his book against Praxeas, chapter 12, distinguished in a way that was more marvellous than true and accurate between Sophia's being with the Father and her generation as an accomplished fact, as if the generation and being made of her were something new at the time when, in creation, the Father brought forth or manifested the Word through whom he made all things and said that all things should be made. He speaks of this more freely than rightly: first made [conditus] by him in thought under the name of Sophia; then begotten [generatus] in effect. By this kind of generation he makes the Father older: But if Sophia is the same Word of God in sense, and without whom nothing was made, just as nothing was arranged without Sophia, is it right that anything should have existed before the Father, older than the Son of God, the only-begotten and first-begotten Word? And in this way, certainly more nobly, not to mention that what is unborn is stronger than what is born, etc. See the matter of Hermogenes: it would be greater than the Son who was born from God, if it had not been born or made from God, since, as he puts it, the Son is born and made. He applies to the Son words that are applied to matter, but they are not to be understood in the same way.

units.la: Cap. xxxii. habes Sophiam, prior autem abysso genita sum, dicentem; ut credas abyssum quoque genitam, id est, factam, quia & filios facimus, licet generemus.
units.tr: Chapter 32: You have Sophia, saying: "I was begotten before the abyss." So that you may believe that the abyss was also begotten, that is, made, because we also make sons, although we beget them.

units.la: Sub finem denique, hunc in creatione servatum quasi ordinem statuit: ut primo condita fuerit Sophia, tum prolatus Sermo, inde factae res omnes: ut omnino illa considerarit in ordine ad manifestationem in creatione: sed primo Sophiam conditam, initia viarum in opera ipsius: dehinc & sermonem prolatum, per quem omnia facta sunt, & sine quo factum est nihil. Denique sermone ejus coeli confirmati sunt, & Spiritu ipsius universae virtutes eorum. Tandemque Deum in creatione adhibuisse varios animi sui nisus scribit, Sophiam, Valentiam, Sensum, Sermonem, Spiritum, Virtutem: neque sola apparentia, vel appropinquatione ad materiam, mundum condidisse. Per valentiam, intelligit Dei potentiam, sic loquutus paulo ante, valentia facientis terram, intelligentia parantis orbem, & sensu extendentis coelum. Adeo incommodae atque durae Auctoris nostri passim sunt loquutiones: de quibus ex sententia alibi sanius & clarius explicata, non de hac ex illis judicium ferri debet.
units.tr: Finally, toward the end, he lays down an order kept in creation, as follows: first Sophia was made, then the Word was brought forth, and from them all things were made. So he considers all these in relation to their manifestation in creation: But first Sophia was made, the beginnings of the ways in his works; then also the Word was brought forth, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. Finally, the heavens were established by his word, and all their powers by his Spirit. And he writes that God in creation used various efforts of his mind: Sophia, Valentia, Sensus, Sermo, Spiritus, Virtus; and he did not make the world merely by appearance or by approach to matter. By valentia he means the power of God, as he had said a little before: the valentia of the one who makes the earth, the intelligence of the one who prepares the globe, and the sensus of the one who stretches out the heavens. So harsh and awkward are our author's expressions throughout. Judgment on his words should not be passed on the basis of these passages, but on the basis of what he explained more soundly and clearly elsewhere.

units.la: Quod vero Petavium attinet, haec de Tertulliano, aliisque, de quibus hactenus colligentem, & statuentem, in suo, de Dogmatibus Ecclesiasticis, opere, Tom. II. in iis parum aeque cum Petavio agitur: nam ita illa videntur accipi ab Autore Irenici, saltem apud eum, quasi nil aliud de veteribus illis Petavius docuerit, quam ut eos argueret doctrinae minus catholicae, & vel eadem sensisse prorsus cum Arianis post sequutis, vel etiam cum iis, quae hodie Sociniani. Quod aliter se habere, ex iis facile constare potest, quae idem Petavius de iisdem illis autoribus praemittit, in secundi Tomi praefatione: ubi in sententiae & fidei de Trinitate summa, illos probat nobiscum consentire, quamvis in modo loquendi & explicandi diversimode aliquando, & non ita accurate, ut quidem post natas & agitatas controversias, se expediant. Quoties non dicit, non probat hoc Petavius? In Praef. cap. 1. Ac enim complures antiquorum illorum, quos auctores ac testes appellamus fidei nostræ, de plurimis dogmatibus, præ-fertim vero de Trinitate, multum a nobis diversa scripserunt. Verum & pauntiffimi [?] illi sunt, qui in re dissentiunt a communi fide; & , si sinceros purosque catholicos quærimus, omnino nulli. In re ipsa dixi. Nam in loquendi modo paullulum quosdam variasse, in tertio, & quarto capite primi libri de Trinitate monstravimus. Deinde cujusquemodi tandem ipsorum scripta, & testimonia sunt; in præcipuis tamen, & quæ ad summam spectant mysterii totius, ut concordes invicem sunt, ita nobiscum congruunt. Idque duplici ostendit modo. Primum ex aliis priorum sæculorum Patribus, quam quorum in primo de Trinitate libro meminit, & quæ nostep Irenici Autor producit: deinde ex illis ipsis, quos illic adfert. Illud, tum indefinite & universe probat ex Alexandrinæ, & Antiochenæ duplicis Synodi, & ex Athanasii, Basiliique testimoniis; tum signillatim ex trium sæculorum Scriptoribus, Herma, Clemente Romano, Ignatio, Polycarpo; quorum indubitatas, ex quibus vera Trinitatis fides probetur, sententias proponit cap. ii. ex Justino, Irenæo, Athenagora, Theophilo Cæsariensi, cap. iii. ex Hippolyto Portuensi, Clemente Alexandrino, Origene, Dionysiis, Romano, & Alexandrino, Theognosto, Gregorio Thaumaturgo, Methodio, cap. iv. denique & Latinis scriptoribus, Tertulliano, Cypriano, Novatiano, Minutio, Arnobio, & Lactantio, cap. v. Neque vero paucorum vel errata illa, vel παραφθορα[illegible, ~8 letters] perpetuitati traditionis obsunt, aut eam interpellant: vel quia in minutis fere, & incidentibus; non autem in summa, & capite ipso dogmatis, illorum qualiscunque versatur error: vel quia compensatur hoc quidquid est, quod non satis exacte locuti sunt, cum aliis eorum sententiis, in quibus credendæ rei τὰ [illegible, ~10 letters] cernuntur: vel quia longe plures extiterunt, a quibus aut scripto comprehensa; aut sine scripto prædicata fidei veritas permanavit ad posteros. Vide & quæ sequuntur, in Præfat. cap. iii.
units.tr: As for Petavius, the passages about Tertullian and the others that the author of the Irenicum has so far gathered and set down from Petavius's work On the Ecclesiastical Dogmas, vol. II, are not treated with much agreement with Petavius. The Irenicum's author seems to take them as if Petavius had taught nothing about those ancients except to accuse them of less catholic doctrine, and as if they had held exactly the views of the later Arians, or even of those who are Socinians today. That this is not so can easily be seen from what Petavius himself sets out about these same authors in the preface to his second volume. There, in summing up their opinion and faith on the Trinity, he shows that they agree with us, though at times they differ in their manner of speaking and explaining, and not so precisely as they did after the controversies arose and were debated. How often does Petavius not say and prove this? In Praef. cap. 1. For indeed several of those ancients, whom we call the authorities and witnesses of our faith, have written very differently from us on many doctrines, especially on the Trinity. Yet very few of them dissent from the common faith in the matter, and if we seek sincere and pure catholics, there are none at all. I have said so in substance. For that some of them varied somewhat in their manner of speaking, I have shown in the third and fourth chapters of the first book on the Trinity. Next, whatever sort their writings and testimonies are, in the chief points, and those which bear on the sum of the whole mystery, they agree with one another and with us. He shows this in two ways: first from the Fathers of earlier centuries other than those whom he mentions in the first book on the Trinity, and whom the author of the Irenicum cites; and then from those very writers whom he brings forward there. The first he proves both in general terms, from the testimonies of the Alexandrian and Antiochene double synod and of Athanasius and Basil, and specifically from writers of three centuries: Hermas, Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, whose undoubted opinions, by which the true faith in the Trinity is proved, he sets out in chapter 2; from Justin, Irenaeus, Athenagoras and Theophilus of Caesarea in chapter 3; from Hippolytus of Portus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, the two Dionysii, Romanus and the Alexandrian, Theognostus, Gregory Thaumaturgus and Methodius in chapter 4; and finally from the Latin writers, Tertullian, Cyprian, Novatian, Minucius, Arnobius and Lactantius, in chapter 5. Nor do the errors of a few, or that [...] of their corruption, detract from the continuity of the tradition or interrupt it: either because the error, whatever it is, lies almost in minor and incidental matters and not in the main sum and the very heart of the doctrine; or because whatever they did not express quite exactly is made up for by their other opinions, in which the things to be believed are plainly seen; or because there were far more persons, by whom the truth of the faith, either written down or preached without writing, passed on to posterity. See also what follows in the preface, chapter 3.

units.la: Certum est, non tantum plura Veteres scripsisse, quam vulgo exstent, sed in hoc argumento etiam, & pro communi nostra fide. Quod apparet ex posteriorum Patrum ad illorum communem secum doctrinam aliquoties provocantium scriptis, & disputationibus etiam apud Adversarios, hac in re non retusis vel revictis falsi. Et nemo ignorat, ante ortas controversias incuriosius loqui homines solere, quo liberius, quod post motam quæstionem & constitutos disputationum terminos ac apices diligentius observatur cum in rebus, tum etiam loqendi modo. Augustinus, lib. ii. de bono-perfever. cap. xx. Didicimus enim singulas quasque hæreses intulisse Ecclesiæ proprias quæstiones, contra quas diligentius defenderetur Scriptura divina, quam si nulla talis necessitas cogeret. Sic in hoc de Trinitate & Christi Deitate argumento quoque evenit, ut incautius loquuti fuerint Veteres, quam recentiores, & quo antiquiores, eo securiores. Certe, antequam in Alexandria quasi dæmonium meridianum Arius nasceretur, innocenter quædam, & minus caute locuti sunt, & quæ non possint perversorum hominum calumniam declinare, inquit Hieronymus, Apol. ii. contra Rufinum. Denique & Petavius, lib. i. de Trinitate, cap. iii. ex quo, & sequentibus paucis, Autor Irenici disputat, exponit Veterum illorum, qui ante Ariana tempora scripserunt, sententias saltem loquendi usu a communi regula discrepare: alibi & in ista ipsa dissonantia extare vestigia & documenta catholici de Trinitate dogmatis.
units.tr: It is certain that the ancients wrote not only more than what is commonly extant, but also on this subject, and in defence of our common faith. This appears from the writings of later Fathers, who several times appeal to the common doctrine of those ancients, and from disputations, even among our opponents, which in this matter have not been refuted or overcome as false. And no one is unaware that before controversies arose men were accustomed to speak more carelessly, and so more freely; whereas after a question is raised and the limits and precise points of the disputation are set, things are observed more carefully, in substance and also in manner of speaking. Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, book 2, chapter 20: For we have learned that each heresy has brought into the Church its own questions, against which divine Scripture is defended more carefully than it would be if no such necessity compelled us. So also in this argument concerning the Trinity and the Deity of Christ, it happened that the ancients spoke more carelessly than more recent writers, and the earlier they were, the more secure they were. Certainly, before Arius was born in Alexandria like a noonday demon, they spoke some things innocently and less cautiously, things which could not avoid the slander of wicked men, says Jerome, in Apology 2 against Rufinus. Finally, Petavius too, in book 1 on the Trinity, chapter 3, from which and from a few following chapters the author of the Irenicum argues, sets out the opinions of those ancients who wrote before the Arian times: at least in their manner of speaking they depart from the common rule; elsewhere, and even in that very discord, traces and evidences of the catholic doctrine of the Trinity remain.

units.la: Sed ex Philosophia Platonica, quæ tum regnabat, ejusque abusu, Veterum Scriptorum conceptus & sermones in Theologicis & altissimis hisce mysteriis haud parum turbatos fuisse & depravatos, res satis ipsa facit manifestum; adeo ut Tertullinus ipse dicere necesse habuerit, se dolere, doleo, inquit, bona fide Platonem haereticorum omnium condimentarium esse factum. lib. de anima, cap. 23. Praeterea & nimis aliquando Veteres sua, non tantum ex Philosophorum & Poëtarum scriptis probare voluerunt, & sic ostendere quasi sua etiam aliquo modo apud illos reperiri, contra quos agebant, quasi li[?] quid fere simile tinniret in Gentilium scriptis cum doctrina nostra, statim id vel eodem fere, vel probo alias sensu dictum ipsis fuisset, sed & ad eorum stylum & loquendi modum infelicius sua nonnunquam accommodarunt, & intorserunt, ut tacite alios vel lucrifacerent, vel nescio quam intempestivam rerum invicem communionem cupide magis, quam sane, ostentarent. Denique & hanc dat causam Petavius, quod in gratiam infirmiorum & rudiorum, ut in Catecheticis solitum, sæpe res fidei altissimas deumbrarent minus accurate, pro captu magis auditorum, quam sententia prorsus sua. Vide eum in Praefat. cap. iii. Ac mihi videntur illi, cum adversus gentiles doctos, & philosophiae deditos pro Christiana fide disceptarent, quo eam vendibiliorem facerent, ac magis persuaderent, minus accurate, ac subtiliter illius intima, & arcana commisisse libris ipsis, quos emanare in vulgus cuperent: atque ad Platonis decreta, eamque, quam illi combiberant, Theologiae formulam, Christianum illud conformasse mysterium. Quemadmodum dicit Paulum fecisse Athenis, ubi ex inscriptione Arae ignoto Deo, quasi eundem ignorantes coluissent, verum Deum ipsis commonstravit, ac pro Christo causam agens, etiam inscriptionem fortuitam arte torquet in argumentum fidei, sicuti loquitur Hieronymus.
units.tr: But that the concepts and words of the ancient writers in these theological and most lofty mysteries were not a little disturbed and corrupted by the Platonic philosophy, which then reigned, and by its abuse, the matter itself makes plain enough; so much so that Tertullian himself found it necessary to say that he grieved: I grieve, he says, that Plato, in good faith, has been made the seasoner of all heretics. On the Soul, chapter 23. Moreover, the ancients sometimes went too far in wanting to prove their own doctrines from the writings of philosophers and poets, and so to show that their own views could also be found in those whom they were opposing, as if something nearly similar rang out in the writings of the Gentiles with our doctrine. Straightway, what had been said by them in nearly the same or some other, acceptable sense was given to them; and they less happily adapted and twisted their own teaching to the style and manner of speech of those men, either so that they might quietly win over others, or else eagerly rather than soundly displayed some ill-timed fellowship of things. Finally, Petavius also gives this cause: that, for the sake of the weaker and less learned, as was customary in catechetical teaching, they often shaded the highest matters of faith less exactly, to suit the capacity of the hearers rather than their own complete opinion. See him in the preface, chapter 3: And it seems to me that those writers, when they disputed for the Christian faith against learned Gentiles devoted to philosophy, so as to make it more saleable and to persuade more effectively, entrusted to their books, which they wished to be published among the people, its inner and hidden things less accurately and subtly; and they conformed that Christian mystery to Plato's decrees and to the formula of theology which they had imbibed. Just as Paul is said to have done at Athens, where from the inscription To the unknown God, as if they had worshipped him while not knowing him, he showed them the true God, and pleading the cause of Christ, twisted even a chance inscription by art into an argument for the faith, as Jerome puts it.

units.la: Non vero dicit, aut probat Petavius, id quod Autor noster perpetuo colligit, & singulis paginis prænotat, quod solus Pater summus Deus, secundum primorum saeculorum Christianos: non certe sensu eo, quo id putat noster. Nam & duas haereticorum notat sectas, tum eorum, qui unicam tantum divinitatis arbitrabantur personam, quales erant Patripassiani, Noëtus, Sabellius, Paulus Samosatenus, & alii, contra quos agit, lib. 1. de Trinit. cap. xi. tum istorum, qui tres, sed perinde natura, ut proprietatibus distinctas, inter quos Arium, ejusque haeresim, Sabellianæ ex adverso oppositam, persequitur à cap. vii. deinceps: & pro fide Trinitatis disputat late, adversus Arianos, lib. ii. & similis erroris patronos veteres ac hodiernos, tum ἀναςκευαςτικῶς[?], tum καταςκευαςτικῶς[?]. Præterea lib. iii. ex professo refutat Ioh. Crellii librum, de Uno Deo Patre: quod mirum est tanto silentio ad Adversariis præteriri, qui nescio quid non præsidii in libro Petavii secundo putant se reperisse. Denique quamvis Petavius secus aliquid de primorum Christianorum doctrina & fide scripsisset, nos propterea id non obstringeret; & minus mirum in Jesuita videri posset, qui ex dogmatis istius vel declaratione vel expositione aliquid traditionibus suis præter Scripturam, adversus nos, lucratum se facile putaverit. Et quamvis non in illa quorundam sit sen-tentia Petavius, quod dogma Trinitatis merae sit traditionis Ecclesiasticae, & non Scripturari[?], sed in Scriptura doceat contineri ac tradi, attamen neq; traditionum sua-rum prorsus etiam hic est immemor. In Praefat. cap. i. Nempe, quod jam dixi, ad inter-pretandi magistram eundem erit Ecclesiam Catholicam; quæ de locorum illorum Scripturæ hic dubiorum aut controversorum, respondeat. Ea tum vetus, tum hodierna potest esse.
units.tr: But Petavius does not say or prove what our author constantly gathers and notes on every page: that the Father alone is the supreme God, according to the Christians of the first centuries; certainly not in the sense in which our author thinks it. For Petavius also notes two sects of heretics: first, those who held only one person of the Godhead, such as the Patripassians, Noetus, Sabellius, Paul of Samosata and others, against whom he argues in book 1 on the Trinity, chapter 11; and second, those who held three persons but distinguished by nature as by properties, among whom he pursues Arius and his heresy, set against the Sabellian heresy on the other side, from chapter 7 onward. He argues at length for the faith in the Trinity against the Arians in book 2, and against the old and modern patrons of a similar error, both by refutation [ἀναςκευαστικῶς] and by proof [καταςκευαστικῶς]. Moreover, in book 3 he expressly refutes John Crell's book On the One God the Father; it is remarkable that our opponents pass this over in such silence, though they think they have found some kind of help in Petavius's second book. Finally, even if Petavius had written otherwise about the doctrine and faith of the first Christians, that would not bind us; and it might seem less strange in a Jesuit, who, from either the declaration or the exposition of this dogma, may easily have thought he had gained something against us from his traditions beyond Scripture. And although Petavius does not hold the view of some that the dogma of the Trinity is purely of ecclesiastical tradition and not scriptural, but teaches that it is contained and handed down in Scripture, yet he is by no means wholly forgetful of his traditions even here. In Praef. cap. 1: Indeed, as I have already said, the Catholic Church will be the teacher of interpretation in this matter, and will answer concerning those obscure or disputed passages of Scripture. It can be both ancient and modern.

units.la: Quando autem Petavius scribit, lib. iii. de Trinit. cap. iii. §. iii. post Arianam procellam patefactum dogma de Trinitate fuisse, non id istum in sensum accipiendum est, quo Autor Irenici contendit pag. 62. ut tum demum patefactum fuerit, & non ab Apostolis jam retrò traditum: sic enim argumentatur: si tradita fuisset ab Apostolis, his primis sane Christianis omnium primo, & deinde per hos, aliis demum, fuisset patefacta. Atqui patefacta fuit demum, prodit Petavius lib. 1. de Trinit. cap. 3. §. 3. ubi de Expositione fidei, Iustino falso adscripta, agit, iterum expresse loquitur & fatetur, post Arianam procellam. Ubi duplici injuria afficit Petavium. 1. quia quod Petavius de dogmatis illustratione intellexit, ille de mera ejus patefactione accipit. 11. addidit demum fuisse tum demum patefactam illam doctrinam: quod Petavius non dixit. En ista ejus verba, ut argueret Expositionem fidei sub Justini nomine, non posse ejus esse autoris, qua nimis dilertis & terminis demum postea usurpari solitis utitur: ea diserte, ac subtiliter disputat, quae neque ab antiquis caeteris, ante Nicaenum Concilium, usurpata esse constat; neque, nisi patefacto, illustratoque, post Arianam procellam, dogmate isto, scribi potuerunt. Nam contra semper Petavius, & ab Apostolis, & eorum sequacibus, primis etiam ante Nicaenum Concilium temporibus, eandem veritatem agnitam traditamque fuisse, docet.
units.tr: When Petavius writes, in book 3 of De Trinitate, chapter 3, section 3, that the doctrine of the Trinity was made known only after the Arian storm, this must not be taken in the sense in which the author of the Irenicum argues on page 62: that it was made known only then and had not already been handed down by the Apostles. He argues like this: if it had been handed down by the Apostles, it would have been made known first of all to these earliest Christians, and then through them to others. But it was made known only later, as Petavius shows in book 1 of De Trinitate, chapter 3, section 3, where, speaking of the Exposition of the faith falsely ascribed to Justin, he again says expressly and admits that it was after the Arian storm. In this he wrongs Petavius in two ways. First, what Petavius meant of the clarifying of the doctrine, he takes to mean its bare making known. Second, he added the word only, that the doctrine was made known only then, which Petavius did not say. Here are Petavius's own words, where he is arguing that the Exposition of the faith cannot be the work of Justin, since it uses expressions and terms that were only later customary: it argues clearly and subtly on matters which, as is known, were not used by the other ancient writers before the Council of Nicaea, and which could not have been written unless this doctrine had been made known and clarified after the Arian storm. Petavius in fact always teaches the contrary: that this same truth was recognised and handed down both by the Apostles and by their followers, even in the earliest times before the Council of Nicaea.

units.la: Tum quae ex Origene, contra Celsum, Noster [?] profert, pag. 58. neque pro ipso, neque contra nos faciunt. Nam Origenes Celso objicienti, quod praeter unum Deum, etiam ministrum ejus Jesum Christum colerent Christiani, respondet, eo ipso illos non alium Deum colere, sed eundem, quandoquidem Christus dixit, se cum Patre unum esse: quae si consideraffet Celsus, inquit, non putassset nos & alium colere praeter Deum universorum Dominum. Deinde adversus hoc, quod Celsus dixerat, Christianos recens exortum colere; ait, non recens exortum, quasi prius non fuerit, nimiis honoribus extollimus. Credimus enim ejus verbis dicentis; antequam Abraham natus esset, ego sum, Joh. 8.58. — Itaque religiose colimus Patrem veritatis, & veritatem Filium, duos quidem subsistentia, unum vero concordia, consensu, voluntatisque identitate. Eo autem essentiae identitatem non tollit, sed connotat & firmat: ut quoque iis quae sequuntur, quibus Filium scribit, quod sit splendor gloriae, characterque substantiae ejus: vapor potentiae Dei, omnipotentis gloriae sincera promanatio, splendor sempiterni luminis, speculum immaculatum Dei potentiae ac efficaciae, imagoque bonitatis ejus. Deinde quod ait: Esto autem, non deesse quosdam, ut in tam numerosa credentium multitudine, qui discrepantes ab aliis, temere affirmant, quod Servator sit Deus ille universorum Dominus: nos certe hoc non facimus, qui credimus ipsi dicenti, Joh. 14. 28. Pater qui misit me, major me est. Quapropter, quem nunc Patrem vocamus, eum non subjicimus, ut Celsus calumniatur, Deo Filio. Dicitur contra eos, quos & supra aliquoties ab Ignatio, aliisque notatos meminimus, qui Patrem cum Filio confundebant, & eundem esse dicebant, quales fuerunt Patripassiani, & similes. Hoc se facere negat Origenes, nedum ut Patrem Filio subjiceret, aut Filio adstruere imperium in Patrem: sive tale quid ulli inter Christianos ursserint [?], sive potius a se confictum Celsus temere objecerit Christianis: tamen accepit, & non finxit de suo, inquit Origenes. Dixerat Celsus de Christianis, non quod Deum venerentur magnopere, sed quod ipsum extollant plus nimio. Origenes autem, nos enim manifeste praedicamus, Creatoris, qui mundum hunc sensibilem condidit, Filium non esse fortiorem Patre, sed inferiorem. Id quod ex ipsius auctoritate affirmamus, dicente, Pater qui misit me, major me est: Joh. 14.28. Nec est quisquam nostrum tam attonitus, ut dicat, Dominus est Dei hominis Filius. Imperium autem ei, ut Dei Verbo, Sapientiae, Iustitiae, Veritati, asserimus in omnes suscipientes eum hoc nomine; sed non in Deum Patrem omnipotentem. Denique apud Petavium, lib. 1. de Tri-nitat. cap. IV. & in Praefat. cap. IV. vide ex Origene citata, quae recte de Trinitatis fide sonant: uti quando dixit τῇ θεότητι τῆς προσκυνητῆς τριάδος[?], adoranda Trinitatis deitati, & similia.
units.tr: The passages that our author brings from Origen, against Celsus, on page 58, favour neither himself nor us. For when Celsus objected that Christians worshipped Jesus Christ as well as the one God, Origen's minister, Origen replies that by this very fact they do not worship another God, but the same one, since Christ said that he and the Father are one. If Celsus had considered this, he says, he would not have thought that we worship any other God besides the Lord of all. Then, against Celsus's charge that Christians worship someone newly arisen, he says: we do not exalt with excessive honours one who is newly arisen, as though he had not existed before. For we believe his own words, when he says, "Before Abraham was born, I am" (John 8:58). So we devoutly worship the Father of truth and the Truth who is the Son, two in subsistence, but one in agreement, consent and identity of will. He does not by this remove identity of essence, but implies and confirms it, as also in what follows, where he writes that the Son is the brightness of glory and the express image of his substance, the breath of the power of God, the pure emanation of almighty glory, the splendour of eternal light, the unspotted mirror of God's power and efficacy, and the image of his goodness. Then he says: Grant, however, that there may be some, in so large a multitude of believers, who differ from the others and rashly affirm that the Saviour is that God who is Lord of all. We certainly do not do this, since we believe his own words, "The Father who sent me is greater than I" (John 14:28). Therefore the Father, whom we now call the Father, we do not subject, as Celsus falsely charges, to God the Son. The argument is directed against those whom we have noted above several times from Ignatius and others, who confused the Father with the Son and said they were the same, as the Patripassians and similar people did. Origen denies that he does this, let alone that he subjects the Father to the Son or claims for the Son dominion over the Father. Whether some such thing was ever put forward among Christians, or whether Celsus rashly objected to Christians something he had himself invented, yet he received it, and did not make it up himself, says Origen. Celsus had said of the Christians that they do not worship God greatly, but exalt him too much. But Origen says: we openly preach that the Son is not stronger than the Creator who made this sensible world, but inferior to him. We affirm this on his own authority, who says, "The Father who sent me is greater than I" (John 14:28). Nor is any one of us so out of his mind as to say that the Son of the Man is the Lord of God. We assert that dominion belongs to him, as to the Word of God, Wisdom, Righteousness and Truth, over all who receive him under this name; but not over God the Father almighty. Finally, in Petavius, book 1 of De Trinitate, chapter 4, and in the preface, chapter 4, see the passages cited from Origen which speak rightly of faith in the Trinity, as when he said of the adorable Trinity [τῇ θεότητι τῆς προσκυνητῆς τριάδος], to the deity of the adorable Trinity, and similar things.

units.la: Ex istis nunc, quae hactenus allata, facile est respondere ad summaria, quae Autor ex suis perperam adductis repetit, pag. 63. & sequentibus. 1. ex Ignatio: quod reprehendit dicentes, Christum esse Deum super omnes, omniumque creatorem: quo designavit Patrem, & non voluit negare Christum esse Deum; uti suo loco ostendimus: sed duntaxat negavit, illum esse Patrem. II. Quod pro absurdo habuerunt Veteres, dicere Deum omnipotentem in terris unquam apparuisse: item de Patre intellexerunt, & Filio proprium voluerunt, hominibus apparere. Quare III. & bene istam suam sententiam habuerunt non tanquam privatam, sed publicam & communem. Quod vero ex Melitonis addit Chronico Alexandrino, id neque obest nobis: solius Dei, qui ante omnia & super omnia, nos esse cultores, & supra Christum ejus: nam certe super Christum, ut Christum, Deus est, interim & de ipso Christo addit, ὅντως ϑεὸς λόγος πρὸ αἰώνων ἐστὶν θεραπευτής[?], vere qui est Verbum Dei ante secula, sumus cultores: nempe & hujus cultores sumus, uti Patris ministri λειτουργοὶ[?]: & Christus ante secula: & Verbum Dei, cum Patre, a nobis, eodem cultus genere conjungitur. IV. Et quando Veteres dixerunt, Patrem summum Deum, omniumq; creatorem, non certe hoc dixerunt quod hodie Adversarii nostri, sed nihil nobis contrarium.
