Dixerunt, credere se Filium genitum, unigenitum, Sapientiam, & Verbum, ac Virtutem Dei ante saecula, non praecognitione, sed subsistantia, & hypostasi Deum, Dei Filium &c. Qui autem contra dicit, Filium Dei non esse ante constitutionem mundi, dicitque credere, & confiteri esse Deum, non esse aliud, quam duos Deos praedicare; qui Filium Dei non esse Deum praedicat, hunc alienum esse ab Ecclesiastica regula arbitramur. deinde istam suam fidem ac sententiam de Filio Dei esse communem atque catholicam putarunt: & omnes Ecclesiae catholicae nobiscum consentiunt. & Alexandrini, in epistola sua, ita & praedicasse sanctos Patres, & sibi profitendum, credendumque tradidisse. Quod vero Petavius, lib. 1. de Trinitate, cap. IV. & V. nonnulla incommode dicta aliorum notat, non item istorum Antiochenorum Patrum ad Samosatenum Paulum, loquendi usu dicit magis saepe discrepasse, quam animi seu fidei sententia, a nobis. Deum vero universi, seu Patrem, ea enim [illegible, ~9 letters] ipsum vulgo denotant, in se & persona sua hominibus apparuisse, & non Filium, qui propterea etiam Angelus appelletur, recte negant. Neque Hippolyti quae allegat Noster, aliquid continent, quod non in praecedentibus a nobis vindicatum fuit. Non certe istud, quod Deus eorum quae facta sunt, ducem, consiliarium, & operarium genuit filium, nihil sibi coaevum cum haberet, ex mundo videlicet: nam Filium in se habebat, & generando eum, lumen ex lumine generavit, depromens creaturae Dominum, sensum suum. Non duos Deos dicit, sed tanquam lumen ex lumine, & aquam ex fonte, aut radium a sole: una enim virtus ex toto, totum vero Pater, ex quo virtus, Verbum. Omnia igitur per eum facta sunt, ipse solus ex Patre genitus. Quod autem Filium non dicit perfectum ante incarnationem: primo dum incarnationem credit, quantum Nostris hominibus adversetur, patet: deinde id non intelligit respectu Filii, vel generationis ejus in se, cum tamen esset perfectum Verbum, inquit; sed istius, quod ei tandem propter nos & pro muneris sui adimpletione, perficiendum erat. Non ergo haec eo trahenda, ut inaequalitatem Christi ut Dei, doceant a Patre, quod Nostri cupiunt quidem, at non probant. v. Ex Symbolo, quod Apostolicum dicitur, nihil contra nos urgeri potest: quamvis enim non exprimatur aut explice-tur ratio, cur credamus Filium Dei unigenitum, uti illud primis fidei lineamentis antequam haereses natae, non tam distincte & copiose ubivis exponi necesse fuit, ac postea: nihil tamen quod istam expositionem aut sensum in symbolo non ferat, occurrit. Non enim propterea quod incarnatus, hinc demum Christus factus Filius Dei asseritur, sed jam Filius Dei fuisse, antequam conceptus, natus, passus. Quod vero ejus existentia ante mundum, & quod per eum creata omnia, non ita in symbolo exponitur, uti quidem in aliis sequentibus, propter istam rationem factum est, quam diximus: & quomodo in antiquissimo symbolo vel fidei regula dici solitum, reten-tum id deinceps fuit, nam non etiam alia hic variata, quae in symbolis postmodum exposita magis & mutata adversus exortas haereses fuerunt. Certe nihil in Symbolo ostendetur, quod nullam unquam pro aequalitate Filii cum Patre traditionem esse potuisse doceat, vel nec Filium ante mundum conditum a Patre prolatum vel genitum esse: non dicimus, quod Adversarius, paulo ante mundum conditum: quia nulla hic temporis aut momentorum distantia. VI. Denique quod Artemonitarum, qui vixerunt sub annum c L xxx. [?] & Christum docuerunt merum esse hominem, ex Maria natum, non Deum, opiniones, in sententiam suam allegat Noster, eo & sensum suum de Christo prodit, & quam turpiter Deo juxtim ac hominibus illudant isti, dum Christum Deum & verum Deum alias videri volunt fateri; sed & quas in antiquitate partes sectentur, quas item nobis relinquant, suas nempe dum faciunt eas, quas pro haeresibus Ecclesia semper habuit, earumque catalogo propterea inseruit. Neque enim inficiamur, tales semper aliquos extitisse inter Christianos, qui Christo Deitatem inviderent, & propterea tantum esse hominem contenderent; sed istos a melioribus semper notatos rejectosque fuisse, etiam negari haud potest. Et quamvis qui ab Eusebio citatur ad-versum Artemonitas Scriptor, antiquiores ipsorum adversarios notans primum no-minet Justinum, inde Tatianum, Irenaeum &c. non propterea vel negat alios praeter istos extitisse ejusdem fidei, vel ignorare potuit Ignatium illis anteriorem, eundem errorem aliquoties refellere: id est, quotquot dari scriptores hujus argumenti pos-sunt, illam Artemonitarum haeresim quoque condemnarunt. Quemadmodum istum in finem apud Eusebium citantur scripta Justini, Miltiadis, Tatiani, Clementis, & plurimorum aliorum, in quibus omnibus Christus docetur Deus, ὃν τὶς ἁπλῶς θεολογεῖ τῷ ὁ χριστός [?]: Etenim Irenaei, & Melitonis, & caeterorum quos ignorat libros, docentes Christum Deum & hominem esse? Quot item fratrum psalmi & hymni ab initio a fidelibus conscripti Verbum Dei Christum canunt Deum? Jam & tempus, & autorem notant, quando error ille Christum dicens ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον [?] ortus & condemnatus fuit, quantumvis ejus patroni antiquam suam sententiam, & ab ipsis Apostolis natam frustra jactitarent: nempe quod Victor, Ecclesiae Romanae Episcopus, Theodorum coriarium, principem & patrem [illegible, ~16 letters] primum dicentem ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον χριστὸν [?] Christum esse merum hominem, communione privavit. Ista Eusebius, lib. v. cap. xxvii. & Augustinus, de Haeresibus, cap. xl iv. [?] exstinctam fere Artemonis haeresim, a Paulo Samosateno acceptam scribit & resuscitatam: nec Christum aliquid amplius, quam hominem putant. Ista haeresis aliquando cujusdam Artemonis fuit; sed quum defecisset, instaurata est a Paulo; & postea a Photino confirmata, ut Photiniani, quam Paulinani [?] crebrius nuncupentur.
units.tr: From what has been cited so far, it is easy to answer the summaries that the author repeats from his own misquotations, at p. 63 and following. (1) From Ignatius: he rebuked those who said that Christ is God over all and the creator of all. By this he meant the Father, and he did not wish to deny that Christ is God, as we show in its place. He denied only that Christ is the Father. (2) The Ancients thought it absurd to say that God Almighty ever appeared on earth. They understood this of the Father, and they held that it was proper to the Son to appear to men. Therefore (3) they held this view not as a private opinion but as a public and common one. As for what he adds from Melito's Alexandrian Chronicle, that does not harm us. We worship only the God who is before all things and above all things, and above his Christ. For certainly God is above Christ as Christ, and at the same time he says of Christ himself, ὅντως ϑεὸς λόγος πρὸ αἰώνων ἐστὶν θεραπευτής [truly God, the Word, before the ages, is the one we worship]: that is, the Word of God who is before the ages, we are worshippers of him. Indeed we are worshippers of him as well as of the Father, as ministers [λειτουργοὶ] of the Father: and Christ before the ages and the Word of God are joined by us with the Father in the same kind of worship. (4) When the Ancients said that the Father is the highest God and the creator of all, they certainly did not say what our opponents say today, but nothing contrary to us. They said that they believed the Son to be begotten, the only-begotten, the Wisdom and the Word and the Power of God before the ages, not in foreknowledge but in subsistence and hypostasis, God, the Son of God, etc. But whoever says on the contrary that the Son of God did not exist before the foundation of the world, and says that he believes and confesses him to be God, is nothing other than one who preaches two Gods; whoever preaches that the Son of God is not God, we judge to be alien to the ecclesiastical rule. Then they thought that their faith and opinion about the Son of God was common and catholic: and all the catholic Churches agree with us. And the Alexandrians, in their letter, say that the holy Fathers so preached, and handed down that this must be professed and believed by them. As for Petavius, who in his book 1 on the Trinity, chapters 4 and 5, notes that some of the others said things improperly, but not those Antiochene Fathers against Paul of Samosata, he says that they differed more often in the use of words than in the sentiment of mind or faith from us. But they rightly deny that the God of the universe, that is the Father (for this is what the word commonly denotes), appeared to men in his own person, and not the Son, who for that reason is also called the Angel. Nor do the things from Hippolytus which our author cites contain anything that was not vindicated by us in what precedes. Certainly it does not follow from the statement that God begot a son, the leader, counsellor and workman of the things that were made, since he had nothing coeval with himself, that is, from the world: for he had the Son in himself, and by begetting him he begot him, light from light, bringing forth the Lord of creation, his own mind. He does not say two Gods, but, as light from light, and water from a fountain, or a ray from the sun: for the power comes from the whole, and the whole is the Father, from whom comes the power, the Word. Therefore all things were made through him, he alone being begotten of the Father. As to his saying that the Son was not perfect before the incarnation: first, how much this is opposed to our people, while he believes in the incarnation, is plain; next, he does not mean this with respect to the Son, or to his generation in himself, since, he says, he was the perfect Word, but with respect to that which was finally to be perfected in him for our sake and for the fulfilment of his office. Therefore these statements should not be drawn to teach an inequality of Christ as God with the Father, which our people indeed desire but do not prove. (5) Nothing can be urged against us from the so-called Apostles' Creed. For although the reason why we believe the Son of God to be the only-begotten is not expressed or explained in it, just as it was not necessary to set this out at length and in detail everywhere in the first outlines of the faith, before heresies arose, as it was later, nevertheless there is nothing in the creed that does not admit this exposition or sense. For it is not because he was incarnate that Christ is at last asserted to have become the Son of God, but that he was already the Son of God before he was conceived, born, and suffered. As for the fact that his existence before the world, and that all things were created through him, are not set out in the creed in the same way as in some later formulas, this was done for the reason we have mentioned: and just as it was customary to say in the most ancient creed or rule of faith, that was retained afterwards, and other things were not varied here which were later set out more fully and altered against the heresies that arose. Certainly nothing will be shown in the Creed that teaches that no tradition of the equality of the Son with the Father could ever have existed, or that the Son was not brought forth or begotten by the Father before the world was made: we do not say, as our opponent does, shortly before the world was made, because there is no distance of time or moments here. (6) Finally, as for the opinions of the Artemonites, who lived about the year 230 and taught that Christ was merely a man, born of Mary, and not God, which our author cites in support of his own view, by this he also betrays his own sentiment about Christ, and how shamefully these men mock God as well as men, while they want Christ to be seen as professing to be God and true God in other places; and also what parties they follow in antiquity, which they leave to us, namely by making those parties which the Church has always held to be heresies, and for that reason included them in her catalogue. For we do not deny that there have always been some among Christians who grudged Christ his deity and therefore maintained that he was merely a man; but it cannot be denied either that these men were always noted and rejected by the better sort. And although the writer cited by Eusebius against the Artemonites, when he names the older adversaries of these men, names first Justin, then Tatian, Irenaeus, etc., he does not therefore deny that others besides these existed of the same faith, nor could he be ignorant that Ignatius, earlier than them, refuted the same error several times: that is, however many writers of this subject there may be, they all condemned that heresy of the Artemonites too. Just so, for this purpose, the writings of Justin, Miltiades, Tatian, Clement and many others are cited in Eusebius, in all of which Christ is taught to be God, ὃν τὶς ἁπλῶς θεολογεῖ τῷ ὁ χριστός [whom Christ, simply, the one who speaks of God as God]. For what of the books of Irenaeus, and Melito, and the others whom he does not know, teaching that Christ is God and man? What of the psalms and hymns of the brethren, written by the faithful from the beginning, which sing Christ the Word of God as God? Moreover, the time and the author are noted when that error, which calls Christ a mere man, arose and was condemned, however much its patrons vainly boasted of their old opinion, born from the Apostles themselves: namely that Victor, bishop of the Roman Church, cut off from communion Theodotus the tanner, the leader and first father [illegible] of those who said that Christ was a mere man. These things are written by Eusebius, book 5, chapter 27, and by Augustine, in On Heresies, chapter 44: they write that the heresy of Artemon, almost extinguished, was received from Paul of Samosata and revived: nor do they think Christ to be anything more than a man. This heresy was once the heresy of a certain Artemon; but when it had died out, it was restored by Paul, and afterwards confirmed by Photinus, so that they are more often called Photinians than Paulinians.

units.la: Idem respondemus de Nazaræis, sed non prout Christianos illud nomen olim designavit in genere, & qua ratione etiam Paulus, omnesque fideles istius ordinis sunt & cognominis, Act. xxiv. verf. 5. 14. & vel Apostolorum discipulos notat, vel Jerosolymitanos fideles: sed quatenus sectam describit inter Christianos singularem, passim improbatam: & sic, præterquam quod ab aliis ex catalogo hæreticorum omittuntur, non probat Noster, illos omnes promiscue Christum statuisse merum esse hominem: non, idem Jacobum Apostolum docuisse: non, ex Eusebio ista: & denique si illud Nazaræi tenuissent quoque, haud magis nos movere deberet, ac quod iidem legem Mosaicam cum Christiana religione conjungendam esse, & observandam pariter docebant. Quod certe non ab Apostolo Jacobo, vel ab aliis edocti, neque in eo probandi fuerunt aut laudandi. Augustinus, de Hæres. cap. ix. Nazaræi cum Dei Filium confiteantur esse Christum, omnia tamen veteris legis observant, quæ Christiani per Apostolicam traditionem non observare carnaliter, sed spiritualiter didicerunt. Et Hieronymus, epist. lxxxiv. dum volunt Judaei esse & Christiani, nec Judaei sunt, nec Christiani. Nisi ab Ebionitis cum alia, tum hunc quoque errorem assumserint. Nam de Ebione Epiphanius, hæresi xxxix. hic conjunctus illis, & illi huic, utraque pars de propria improbitate alteri impartivit. & horum Ebionæorum consortio vehementer fuisse infamatos Nazaræos, scribit quidem Baronius, Tom. i. ad A. 74. §. 5. non vero vel in laudem eorum speciatim sic dictorum quidpiam, vel de ipsorum ad Artemonitas duratione, vel quod docuerint Christum merum hominem; duntaxat quod nimium sociarint se eum Ebione, & quod hic tandem ex Samaritis, Judaeis, Offenis, Nazaræis, Cerinthianis, Carpocratianis, & aliis unum impietatis compositum corpus. Quæ certe ad commendandos vel Ebionitas, vel Nazaræos, eorumve sententias & dogmata, parum faciunt. Et quemadmodum Augustinus de illis dicit, eos Christum confiteri Dei Filium; ita Epiphanius idem de iis testatur: unum autem Deum profitentur, & hujus Filium Iesum Christum. Porro, de Christo vero non habeo quod dicam, an etiam ipsi prædicta Cerinthi improbitate ducti, nudum hominem ipsum putent: aut, velut veritas ipsa habet, per Spiritum Sanctum ex Maria genitum esse affirment. Quare perperam Nazaræi, qui a Veteribus inter hæreticos collocati, apud nostrum Autorem audiunt primi & veri Apostolorum discipuli, & cum Nazaræis Christianis, in genere sic aliquando, ex odio & contemtu Christi, dictis, confunduntur.
units.tr: We answer the same about the Nazarenes, though not in the sense in which the name "Christians" was once used generally, a sense in which Paul too and all the faithful of that way and name are so called (Acts 24:5, 14), and which denotes either the disciples of the Apostles or the faithful of Jerusalem. The name denotes instead a sect peculiar among Christians and everywhere condemned. Thus, apart from the fact that others omit them from the catalogue of heretics, our author does not prove that all of them indiscriminately held Christ to be a mere man; nor that the Apostle James taught the same; nor does he prove it from Eusebius. Finally, even if the Nazarenes had held that view, it should move us no more than the fact that they also taught that the Mosaic law was to be joined with the Christian religion and observed alongside it. Certainly they had not been taught this by the Apostle James or by others, and in this they were not to be approved or praised. Augustine, On Heresies, ch. 9: Although the Nazarenes confess that the Son of God is Christ, they nevertheless observe all the observances of the old law, which Christians have learned through apostolic tradition not to observe carnally but spiritually. And Jerome, letter 84: While the Jews want to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither Jews nor Christians. Unless they took up this error, along with other things, from the Ebionites. For concerning Ebion, Epiphanius, heresy 39: He was joined to them, and they to him, and each party imparted its own wickedness to the other. That the Nazarenes were greatly discredited by their association with these Ebionites, Baronius writes (vol. 1, on the year 74, §5). But he says nothing in their praise as such, nor about how long they lasted before the Artemonites, nor that they taught that Christ was a mere man; only that they associated themselves too closely with Ebion, and that he at last formed from Samaritans, Jews, Osseans, Nazarenes, Cerinthians, Carpocratians and others one body compounded of impiety. Certainly these points do little to commend either the Ebionites or the Nazarenes, or their opinions and doctrines. And just as Augustine says of them that they confess Christ to be the Son of God, so Epiphanius likewise attests of them: They profess one God and his Son Jesus Christ. Further, concerning Christ I have nothing to say, whether they too, led by the aforementioned wickedness of Cerinthus, think him a bare man, or, as the truth itself has it, affirm that he was begotten of Mary through the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Nazarenes, whom the ancients have placed among the heretics, are wrongly called by our author "the first and true disciples of the Apostles," and are confused with the Nazarene Christians, a name sometimes used in general, out of hatred and contempt for Christ.

units.la: Tandem recurrit ad Baronium, & hunc dicit ad A. 132. in origine doctrinæ de S. Trinitate assignanda, altius quam Petavius, adscendere non potuisse. Sed Petavius ad Scripturam adscendit, & ad primos ab Apostolis scriptores, tam Græcos, quam Latinos. Baronius, defensurus epistolas Pontificum adversus Novatores, quos ita passim & contumeliose nominat, illas in dubium hinc vocantes, quod tam distincte in iis Trinitatis prædicatur unitas, & ad hoc respondens, scribit: quasi novum hoc fuerit in Ecclesia; cum antiquitus in catechizandis mysterium sanctissimæ Trinitatis (quantum homini licet) Catechistas insinuare curasse, etiam Gentiles scriptores, ut impius Lucianus in Philopatre, testes sint. Atque adducit Lucianum, non quasi hoc autore fides Trinitatis nitetur, vel ex illo demum patere conficique traditio de Trinitate posset, uti frustra scribit; sed ut communem Christianorum & antiquam doctrinam etiam hinc evinceret.
units.tr: Finally he has recourse to Baronius, and says that Baronius, in assigning the origin of the doctrine of the Holy Trinity to the year 132, could not go further back than Petavius. But Petavius did ascend to Scripture, and to the first writers after the Apostles, both Greek and Latin. Baronius, meaning to defend the letters of the Pontiffs against the Novatians, whom he everywhere names thus and insultingly, since they call these letters into doubt because the unity of the Trinity is so distinctly proclaimed in them, answers as follows: As if this were something new in the Church; when from of old, in catechizing, the teachers took care to instill the mystery of the most holy Trinity (as far as it is permitted to man), and even pagan writers, such as the impious Lucian in the Philopatris, are witnesses. And he adduces Lucian, not as if the faith of the Trinity would rest on this author, or as if a tradition concerning the Trinity could be established and proved from him alone, as he vainly writes, but to show from him also the common and ancient doctrine of the Christians.

units.la: Quemadmodum idem facit ad A. 325. §. 70. Hanc autem Traditionem plane esse Apostolicam, ut tres personas in una substantia, eandemque unam substantiam in tribus personis distinctam Catholica profiteatur Ecclesia, externi etiam & impii produnt, fidemque faciunt, ut nt illud Luciani (in Philopatr. prope sin. quod suo loco diximus) dum, licet irridens, Christianum introducit catechizantem Ethnicum, de tanto mysterio sic pauca docens: Rogante Ethnico Christianum, atque dicente: Quemnam igitur tibi jurabo? Tryphon respondit: Deum alte regnantem, magnum, aethereum, atque aeternum Filium Patris, & Spiritum Sanctum ex Patre procedentem: Unum ex tribus, & ex uno tria. Hunc tu Jovem[?] puta: hunc Deum existima. Sic apud Lucianum. Sed unde haec blasphemo veritas, nisi ex iis, quae ipse a Christianis, sive Apostolis, sive eorum Discipulis accepisset, de fide Sanctissimae Trinitatis, qua omnes, qui crediturî essent, imbuebantur? ut vel uno hoc argumento ex veteri traditione, atque adeo Apostolorum, deprompto, omnis impietas convicta prorsus remaneat, & extincta. Nam quomodo tres unum sunt, nisi in communicatione substantiae? & quonam pacto unum tres, nisi in distinctione personarum? Ita enim Ecclesiam fideles docuisse[?] tempore Apostolorum (ut vides) Christianae Religionis hostes affirmant. Non quod[?] unum hunc Lucianum, uti Noster vult, ad traditionem illam conficien-dam sufficere, vel eundem velit Baronius affirmare Ecclesiam tempore Apostolorum, Trinitatis doctrinam fideles docuisse; sed quod adeo communis illa fides & profes-sio fuerit, ut neque gentiles latuerit, & in primis rudiorum catechizationibus tradi[?] & tractari consueverit. Nec ibi initium assignatur doctrinae: neque id Lucianus significat: sed quum adeo nota & communis fuerit, & primis doctrinae traditionibus inculcata[?], altius ejus principium, quam pro nuper invento, sed ab Apostolis promanasse, quod adeo commune & certum in Christianis Ethnicus risit, statuendum est.
units.tr: He does the same thing at the year 325, §70: That this tradition is wholly apostolic, that the Catholic Church professes three persons in one substance and the same one substance distinguished in three persons, even outsiders and the impious reveal, and bear witness to it, as in that passage of Lucian (in the Philopatris, near the end, which we have quoted in its place), where, though mocking, he introduces a Christian catechizing a pagan, and teaching a few things about so great a mystery: When the pagan asked the Christian, saying, "By whom then shall I swear to you?" Tryphon answered: "By God reigning on high, great, ethereal and eternal, the Son of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father: one out of three, and three out of one. Consider this to be Jove; consider this to be God." So far Lucian. But whence this blasphemous truth, unless from what he himself had received from the Christians, whether the Apostles or their disciples, concerning the faith of the most holy Trinity, in which all who were to believe were instructed? So that by this one argument alone, drawn from the old tradition, and indeed from the Apostles, all impiety is utterly refuted and remains extinguished. For how are three one, unless in the communion of substance? And how is one three, unless in the distinction of persons? For thus, as you see, the enemies of the Christian religion affirm that the Church taught the faithful in the time of the Apostles. Not that Baronius wishes to affirm that this one Lucian, as our author supposes, is sufficient to establish that tradition, or that the Church in the time of the Apostles taught the doctrine of the Trinity to the faithful on his testimony alone; but that this common faith and profession was so widespread that it did not escape even the Gentiles, and was customarily delivered and discussed especially in the catechizing of the less instructed. Nor is a beginning of the doctrine assigned there, and Lucian does not signify one; but since it was so well known and common, and was inculcated in the first traditions of the teaching, its origin must be placed higher than a recent invention, and it must be held to have come forth from the Apostles, since the pagan laughed at it as something so common and certain among Christians.

units.la: Non vero ideo attulit illa Baronius, ut probaret vocem homoousion seu consubstantia-lem, in sacris literis contineri, sed rem illa significatam vulgo in Ecclesia semper traditam, & hinc ipsis Gentilibus adeo notam fuisse: de voce illa dixerat, Athanasium docuisse, ejus significationem in Sacris reperiri, neque nuper inventam, sed a sanctis-simis quoque Patribus usurpatam, praesertim a Dionysio, Romano Pontifice, Dionysio Alexandrino Episcopo, & ante hos a Theognosto, antiquo Theologo. Et Centuriatores Magdeburgenses, quando censent Decretales Pontificum epistolas esse suppositias, quia clare & explicate loquuntur de Trinitate, non volunt, quod doctrina ista non tum, & semper fuerit tradita in Ecclesiis, nequaquam; sed quod termini & loquendi modi in illis occurrant, qui illo tempore nondum ita noti erant ac pervulgati, & propterea epistolas illas posterioris aevi, & aliorum esse autorum, quam præ se ferunt.
units.tr: Baronius did not, however, adduce those things to prove that the word homoousion, or consubstantial, is contained in the sacred letters, but to show that the thing signified by it was always commonly handed down in the Church, and was from this so well known even to the Gentiles. Concerning that word he had said that Athanasius taught that its meaning is found in the Sacred Scriptures, and that it was not recently invented, but used also by the most holy Fathers, especially by Dionysius, Roman Pontiff, Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, and before these by Theognostus, an ancient theologian. And when the Magdeburg Centuriators judge that the Decretal letters of the Pontiffs are spurious, because they speak clearly and explicitly of the Trinity, they do not mean that this doctrine was not at that time, nor always, handed down in the Churches; by no means. Rather they mean that terms and modes of speaking occur in those letters which at that time were not yet so known and widespread, and that therefore those letters belong to a later age and to other authors than they profess.

units.la: Quod ad aetatem Luciani, parum nos torquet, an Trajani tempore vixerit, an alio vel priore, vel posteriore: neque enim, quod falso Noster, tota simul ei superstructa moles & machina, mysterii scilicet Baroniani fides ac traditio, vel hinc illa corruunt. Mitto irrisionem, Luciano, quam Christiano, in Irenicorum sc. Irenico, magis dignam, mysterii Baroniani. Non illis, vel similibus nititur fides nostra, sed Scripturis: illa faciunt duntaxat ad historiam, & veritatis confirmationem. Neque quod adeo commune & obvium inter Christianos, ut suo demum tempore exortum, commemorat Lucianus, vel Proteus Peregrinus apud eum: tum quae catechismis traduntur, communissima uti passim, ita & antiquissima habentur. Denique accipe simile argumentum, quod ab Ethnico quoque de Christianorum eadem sententia proditum, & tempore Trajani, negari nequit, Plinii videlicet ad Trajanum ipsum epistolam, lib. x. qua testatus fuit nil criminis se in Christianis deprehendisse, ob quod adeo vexandi essent vel interficiendi, carmen autem dicere solitos quovis mane Christo, ut Deo. Illi ergo non ut merum hominem Christum habuerunt, cum Artemonitis, neque ita habendum à proximis Apostolis fuerunt edocti. Et quæ sic de Christianis commemorantur à Gentilibus, tam vitam ipsorum & mores optimos, quam doctrinam concernentia, uti propria & probatissima Christianorum merito habenda sunt.
units.tr: As to the age of Lucian, it troubles us little whether he lived in the time of Trajan or earlier or later. For, contrary to what our author falsely says, the whole structure and machinery built upon it, namely the faith and tradition of the Baronian mystery, does not fall because of this. I pass over the mockery, more fitting for Lucian than for a Christian, in the Irenicum (that is, in the Irenicus), of the "Baronian mystery." Our faith does not rest on such things or the like, but on the Scriptures; these things serve only for history and for confirming the truth. Nor does it matter that Lucian, or Proteus Peregrinus in him, remembers that this doctrine was so common and obvious among Christians that it had arisen only in his own time. For what is taught in the catechisms is held as most universal, and so also as most ancient. Finally, take a similar argument, which is also reported by a pagan concerning the same opinion of the Christians, and which cannot be denied to belong to the time of Trajan: namely the letter of Pliny to Trajan himself, book 10, in which he testified that he had found no crime in the Christians for which they should be so harassed or killed, but that they were accustomed to sing a hymn to Christ as God at dawn on a fixed day. They therefore did not hold Christ as a mere man with the Artemonites, nor had they been taught to hold him so by the Apostles who were close to them. And whatever is recorded of the Christians in this way by the Gentiles, concerning both their life and excellent morals and their doctrine, is rightly to be regarded as proper to the Christians and most approved.

units.la: Jam in priori loco & tomo Baronius, ad A. 132. referens, quomodo prisci Patres opus habuerint Christi divinitatem, eandemque ipsius cum Patre essentiam populum exacte docere, & ex Athanasio id comprobans, qui ad Episcopos Africanos scribens, ait: prisci Episcopi abhinc annis centum & triginta, qui tum Romæ, tum in nostra civitate Episcopatum gesserunt, accusaverunt eos, qui Filium creaturam dicerent, aut qui negarent cum consubstantialem Patri, non vult vel ipse, vel Athanasius, quasi ante illos annos, vel tum demum nata fuisset fides Trinitatis: nihil minus: sed quod, quandocunq; & quamprimum doctrinæ istius orti impugnatores, eam defenderint strenue, & catholicam ac antiquam fidem ab eorum cavillis vindicarint Patres. Quod autem præter & post Scripturam plures in sententiam nostram adduci autores possint, & ex editis qui supersunt, & ex amissis ac non extantibus, tum Græcis tum Latinis, Christianis & Gentilibus S. Trinitatis doctrina & fides adstrui, satis superque ostensum. Quamvis autem in explicando modo variant nonnunquam cum inter se, tum a nobis, summam tamen rei tenent, & dogmatis probant substantiam. Quod hactenus satis est. Hoc in Ignatio ostendimus, Justino, Irenæo, aliisque: nam de sequentibus, & de iis qui a Concilio Nicæno scripserunt, nihil dicere attinet, cum nullum de iis sit dubium, & nil restet Autori nostro, præter calumniam, qua Christianis novi Christi introductionem, quam exiguo vel prorsus nullo pacis studio, ita summa cum veritatis & Christianorum injuria, sub finem suæ scriptionis, impingit. Eadem quippe veritatis, quæ ab illo tempore, quo adversus hæreticos explananda & confirmanda fuit, omni retro Christianismi tempore agnita, credita, scriptisque variis confirmata fuit: quod cum ab aliis, tum a Petavio, adquem frustra hic provocant, & tom. II. Dogmatum Theologicorum, de Trinitate, & tom. IV. de incarnatione, ex Veterum Scriptis abunde expositum fuit: adquæ si ordine, & non desultorie, respondere aggrediantur, tum demum quid rei, quid operis ipsis superfit, deprehendent. Nos & tomo primo, ubi de Trinitate egimus, & hic, ubi de vera & æterna, nam nonalia vera quam æterna, Christi Deitate, id, post alios, pro instituti ratione, putamus præstitisse, judicium porro lectoribus, & ante omnia, Christo Deo committentes. Cujus uti causam egimus hactenus, & acturi porro sumus, ita in eadem placide & toti acquiescimus.
units.tr: Already in the earlier place and volume, Baronius, at the year 132, relates how the ancient Fathers needed to teach the people exactly the divinity of Christ and his very essence together with the Father's, and he confirms this from Athanasius, who, writing to the African bishops, says: The ancient bishops, a hundred and thirty years ago, who held the episcopate both at Rome and in our city, condemned those who called the Son a creature or who denied that he is consubstantial with the Father. Neither he himself nor Athanasius wishes it to be thought that the faith of the Trinity arose only so many years ago, or then for the first time: far from it. Whenever and as soon as opponents of this doctrine arose, the Fathers defended it vigorously and vindicated the catholic and ancient faith from their sophistries. That many authors besides and after Scripture can be brought over to our opinion, both from the extant works and from those lost and no longer existing, Greek and Latin, Christian and Gentile, by which the doctrine and faith of the Holy Trinity is established, has been shown sufficiently and more than sufficiently. Although they sometimes differ among themselves, and from us, in explaining the mode, they nevertheless hold the sum of the matter and prove the substance of the dogma. So far this is enough. We have shown this in Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus and others. As for those who followed, and those who wrote after the Council of Nicaea, there is no need to say anything about them, since there is no doubt concerning them, and nothing is left for our author except calumny, by which, with little or no zeal for peace, and with such great injury to the truth and to the Christians, he assails at the end of his writing the Christians with the introduction of a new Christ. For the same truth, which from that time when it had to be explained and confirmed against heretics, was recognized, believed and confirmed by various writings throughout all earlier Christian time, has been abundantly set out, both by others and by Petavius, to whom they vainly appeal here, in volume II of the Theological Dogmas, on the Trinity, and volume IV, on the incarnation, from the writings of the Ancients. If they set about answering in order and not haphazardly, then at last they will discover what matter and what work is left to them. We, both in the first volume, where we treated of the Trinity, and here, where we treat of the true and eternal Deity of Christ (for he is not true otherwise than eternal), think we have accomplished this, as our plan allowed, after others. We commit the judgment to the readers, and above all to Christ God. Just as we have pleaded his cause so far, and shall plead it further, so in it we rest calmly and wholly.

units.la: CAP. II. De Christi adventu, seu ejus ratione, & necessitate.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. On the coming of Christ, or its reason and necessity.

units.la: CONTROVERSIA: An quamvis homo non peccasset, Christus nihilominus advenisset?
units.tr: CONTROVERSY: Would Christ have come even if man had not sinned?

units.la: Sententia super hac quaestione Scholasticorum, Andreae Osiandri, Smalcii; in quo conveniant, & in quo discrepent. Causae, ob quas ita statuant Sociniani. Sententia nostra. Ejusque argumenta. Ratione Christi, ut talis, promissi post peccatum, & ad istud tollendum. Et in hunc finem a Deo missus. Neque extra hoc adeo necessarius Christi adventus. Testimonia Patrum. Solvuntur objectiones duae.
units.tr: The opinion on this question of the Scholastics, of Andreas Osiander and of Smalcius; in what they agree and in what they differ. The reasons why the Socinians hold their view. Our opinion, and its arguments: that Christ, as such, was promised after the fall and to remove it; and that for this end he was sent by God, and that apart from this his coming was not so necessary. The testimonies of the Fathers. Two objections are answered.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: SECTION ONE.

units.la: Disputant super ista quaestione etiam Scholastici, an, si homo non peccasset, venturus nihilominus in mundum fuisset Dei Filius, & assumturus carnem? affirmant Scotistae: at Thomistae negant. Proque illa sententia, praeter Scotum, stant Alexander Alensis, Pighius, Catharinus, Viguerius, Galatinus etiam; ubi contra Judaeos disputat, Arcan. Cathol. verit. lib. VII. cap. II. Contraria tamen Thomae Aquinatis sententia communis Scholarum est, III. quaest. I. art. III. Becanus, Theol. Scholast. part. III. cap. I. quaerens VII. an Deus fuisset incarnatus, si Adam non peccasset? dupliciter hoc intelligi posse, respondet, nimirum, an si Adam non peccasset, Deus fuisset incarnatus vi illius decreti, quo nunc reipsa incarnatus est? an vero per aliquod aliud decretum fuisset incarnatus? in priori sensu disputatur, inquit, a Theologis. Affirmant Rupertus, Scotus, Albertus, Alexander, Catharinus, Suarez Disp. 5. Sect. 5. Negant D. Thomas, quaest. 1. art. 3. & alii plerique. Et recte negant. Constantius Sarnanus, Cardinalis, in Directorio Theologico, ad mentem Scoti, qu. ult. pag. 252. quaestionem istam facit altissimam, & valde dubiam, & Thomam alicubi dicentem, quod veritatem istius solus ille novit, qui natus & oblatus est, quia ipse voluit. Credo, quia pro Magistro suo magis conatur respondere, quam potest.
units.tr: The Scholastics also dispute this question: if man had not sinned, would the Son of God nevertheless have come into the world and assumed flesh? The Scotists affirm it, but the Thomists deny it. Besides Scotus, Alexander of Hales, Pighius, Catharinus, Viguerius and Galatinus also hold that view, the last where he disputes against the Jews, Arcan. Cathol. verit. lib. VII, cap. II. The opinion of Thomas Aquinas, however, is the common view of the Schools, III, quaest. I, art. III. Becanus, Theol. Scholast. part III, ch. I, question VII, asks whether God would have been incarnate if Adam had not sinned. He answers that this can be understood in two ways: whether, if Adam had not sinned, God would have been incarnate by virtue of that decree by which he is now in fact incarnate, or whether he would have been incarnate by some other decree. It is disputed in the first sense, he says, by the theologians. Rupert, Scotus, Albert, Alexander, Catharinus and Suárez affirm it, Disp. 5, Sect. 5. Thomas denies it, quaest. 1, art. 3, and most others. And they deny it rightly. Constantius Sarnanus, the Cardinal, in his Directorium Theologicum, following the mind of Scotus, last question, p. 252, makes this question very profound and very doubtful, and notes that Thomas somewhere says that only he who was born and offered knows its truth, because he himself willed it. I believe he does this because he strives more to answer for his master than he is able.

units.la: Saeculum est, quod Andreas Osiander in Regiomontana Borussorum Academia idem docuit, Christum, quamvis Adamus lapsus non fuisset, fuisse tamen incarnandum, non vero crucifigendum.
units.tr: It is a novelty that Andreas Osiander, in the Königsberg academy of the Prussians, taught that Christ would have been incarnate even if Adam had not fallen, but would not have been crucified.

units.la: Sociniani similiter, atque ex iis Smalcius, contra Frantzium, Disp. XII. Esto enim, inquit, probari non posse testimonio sacrarum litterarum, decretum Dei fuisse de mittendo Messia, etiamsi primi parentes non peccassent, num propterea falsum est, quod ait Socinus, de praecognito Christo, nempe id eo respectu factum esse, quod venire in mundum debuerit necessario ad servandum homines: morti autem etiam destinatum fuisse sub conditione, si homines peccarent? &c. Ex qua igitur dicet Frantzius consequentia probatis, Christum venturum fuisse, etiamsi primi parentes non peccassent? ex ea, ajo, quod Christus venturus erat ad servandum in æternum homines. Hoc enim ipsum nomen Servatoris, quod Christo proprium quodammodo effectum est, satis superque indicat, & illud; elegit nos in Christo ad adoptionem, ut hac de re luculenter testatur Paulus. Tam vero homines Servatore eguisse, si non peccassent; quam si peccassent, inde conflat, quod omnes ex terra facti erant, ideoque in terram natura sua reversi fuissent, nisi Deus eos per Christum servare decrevisset.
units.tr: The Socinians likewise, and among them Smalcius, against Frantzius, Disp. XII: Granted, he says, that it cannot be proved by the testimony of the Sacred Letters that God's decree to send the Messiah existed even if the first parents had not sinned. Is it therefore false what Socinus says, about the foreknown Christ, namely that this was done with respect to this: that he had necessarily to come into the world to save men, but was also destined for death under the condition that men sinned? etc. From what consequence, then, will Frantzius prove that Christ would have come even if the first parents had not sinned? From this, I say: that Christ was going to come to save men for ever. For the very name of Saviour, which in some sense belongs properly to Christ, sufficiently and more than sufficiently indicates this, as does that text: he chose us in Christ for adoption, as Paul clearly testifies in this matter. Now that men would have needed a Saviour if they had not sinned, just as much as if they had sinned, is clear from the fact that all were made from the earth, and so by their nature would have returned to the earth, unless God had decreed to save them through Christ.

units.la: Omnes qui ejusdem sententiæ, & Scholastici, & Osiander, & Smalcius, dicunt venturum quidem fuisse Christum, at non passurum, non moriturum, si homo non peccasset. Scholastici, venturum in carne non passibili & mortali, sed impassibili. Dicunt illi incarnationem, & incarnandum Christum; quod Socinani negant, qui simpliciter nasciturum hominem, non incarnandum Dei Filium, asse[?]runt. Tum idem quidem hi & illi statuunt, at ob diversas rationes. Hoc videntur quidem commune habere, quod ex ratione, & ordine prædestinationis petunt utrique argumentum, Scholastici ex destinatione Christi, quasi ante prævisum peccatum, sic quippe ii hac in re, quamvis temere, philosophantur, & Socinani: sed in causa finali assignandâ discrepant: Scholasticis dicentibus, facturum hoc fuisse Deum cum propter excellentiam ipsius rei operisque, ut mysterium Filii incarnati orbi exhiberet; tum ad ostendendam suam φιλανθρωπίαν[?], & humanam naturam hac dignitate extollendam, & augendam; Socinianis vero, propter salutem hominum, & salvandos eos à morte, in quam, statu licet integro, per naturam & naturæ corporeæ conditionem, incidissent.
units.tr: All who hold this opinion, both the Scholastics and Osiander and Smalcius, say that Christ would indeed have come, but that he would not have suffered, nor died, if man had not sinned. The Scholastics say he would have come in flesh that was not passible and mortal, but impassible. They speak of incarnation and of the Christ who would be incarnate; the Socinians deny this, asserting that a man would simply have been born, not that the Son of God would have been incarnate. Then indeed these and those hold the same thing, but for different reasons. They seem to share this, that both draw an argument from the order and reason of predestination: the Scholastics from the destination of Christ, as if sin had been foreseen beforehand (for in this matter they philosophise thus, though rashly, as do the Socinians); but they differ in assigning the final cause. The Scholastics say that God would have done this both on account of the excellence of the thing and work itself, so as to display to the world the mystery of the incarnate Son, and to show his love for mankind [φιλανθρωπίαν], and to raise and increase human nature with this dignity. The Socinians say it was for the salvation of men, and to save them from death, into which they would have fallen even in an integral state, through their nature and the condition of their bodily nature.

units.la: Unde patet, quorsum Socinani illud statuant, nempe propter alias theses haud minus heterodoxas. 1. Quia docent, divinitatem Christi in hoc consistere, quod ab æterno à Deo præordinatus fuerit venire in mundum. Non item Dei destinationem extendunt ad futura omnia. Hinc Smalcius dicit, lib. de divinit. Christi, cap. 1. Ea autem prædestinatio ita se habet: Constituerat Deus, qui hominem creaturus erat, & ex materi t mortua, terra nimirum, vivum cum & rationalem productu rus, eidem ita etiam prospicere, ut suo tempore ex hac temporali vita ad aliam, æternam scilicet & immortalem commigrandi, viam & aditum cognitum haberet. Promiserat autem Deus vitam æternam ante tempora sæcularia, & data nobis fuit gratia ante tempora sæcularia, ut ait Apostolus. Ad hoc igitur tam divinum opus elegit Deus Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Hunc ante constitutionem mundi ita dilexit, ut eum & neminem alium voluerit esse tantæ rei & præconem & perfectorem: Per hunc, & neminem alium constituit omnes eos servare quicunque ejus dictis audientes futuri essent. 11. Quia statuunt, hominem primum, etiamsi non peccasset, moriturum quoque fuisse, quare à Christo immortalitate donandum. 111. Quia officium Christi salvatorium non in hoc constituunt, quod proprie nos à peccatis redimat, sed salutis viam duntaxat annunciet. iv. Ac proinde salvatio nostri per Christum non in hoc sita sit, quod à reatu peccati nos vere ac proprie liberet Christus, sed tantum modo à statu vitæ mortali perducat in immortalitatem. v. Ideoque nec officii Christi fuerit, pati & satisfacere pro peccatis nostris. In horum errorum gratiam, quia nihil in Christo ponunt & considerant, quod veram à peccatis redemtionem dicat, nihil etiam obstare vident, quare Christus non etiam venturus fuisse dicatur, peccato quamvis existente nullo. Namque & sic, juxta ipsos, essentialia officii sui peragere etiam apud homines potuisset.
units.tr: From this it is clear why the Socinians hold this, namely on account of other theses no less heterodox. (1) Because they teach that the divinity of Christ consists in this, that from eternity he was preordained by God to come into the world. Nor do they extend God's destination to all future things. Hence Smalcius says, in his book on the divinity of Christ, ch. 1: Now this predestination is as follows. God, who was about to create man, and to produce him living and rational from dead matter, namely earth, had determined to provide for him in such a way that at his proper time he would have a known way and access from this temporal life to another, eternal and immortal. God, moreover, had promised eternal life before the ages of time, and grace was given to us before the ages of time, as the Apostle says. For this so divine a work God therefore chose Jesus Christ our Lord. He loved him before the foundation of the world so much that he willed him, and no one else, to be both herald and perfecter of so great a thing. Through him, and no one else, he decided to save all those who would be obedient to his words. (2) Because they hold that the first man, even if he had not sinned, would also have been destined to die, and so had to be endowed with immortality by Christ. (3) Because they do not make the saving office of Christ consist in this, that he truly redeems us from sins, but only that he announces the way of salvation. (4) And so the salvation of us through Christ does not lie in this, that Christ truly and properly frees us from the guilt of sin, but only that he leads us from a mortal state of life into immortality. (5) Therefore it was not part of Christ's office to suffer and make satisfaction for our sins. Because of these errors, since they posit and consider nothing in Christ that speaks of a true redemption from sins, they also see nothing to prevent Christ from being said to have come even if there were no sin at all. For even so, according to them, he could have performed the essentials of his office among men.

units.la: Contrà nos, quia credimus, Christum, de ratione sui, redemtorem esse & salvatorem à peccatis, Matth. 1. 21. & vocabis nomen ejus Iesum; ipse enim salvabit populum suum à peccatis ipsorum, ideo dicimus, nullam necessitatem atque rationem ejus venturi fuisse, si non peccassent homines. Quia sublato subjecto, & causa, frustranea, vel nulla datur erga illud actio.
units.tr: Against them we, because we believe that Christ, by his very nature, is redeemer and saviour from sins (Matt. 1:21, And you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins), therefore say there was no necessity or reason for his coming if men had not sinned. For when the subject and the cause are removed, any action directed toward it is either futile or non-existent.

units.la: Nempe quaestio non est de possibili, an statu hominis integro non potuisset incarnari Dei Filius; sed de facto, an incarnatus fuisset. Neque enim illud negamus, sed hoc. Sed deinde tum non venisset Dei Filius, ut Christus, id est, ea ratione ac jam post lapsum venit, neque enim futurus fuisset redemtor. Inficiamur, venturum fuisse in carnem, atque ut redemtorem, Christum, siquidem non peccasset homo.
units.tr: The question, namely, is not about what was possible, whether the Son of God could not have been incarnate in man's integral state; it is about what was actual, whether he would have been incarnate. For we do not deny the former, but the latter. But then the Son of God would not have come as Christ, that is, in the manner in which he has come since the fall; for he would not have been a future redeemer. We deny that the Son of God would have come in the flesh, and as the redeemer Christ, if man had not sinned.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA.
units.tr: SECOND SECTION.

units.la: PRobamus autem sententiam nostram. 1. Ex natura & ratione Christi, Salvatoris, ut sic, cujus officium formaliter dicit liberationem à peccatis: ut, si peccatum omne tollas, nec causa, nec ratio, neque conceptus quidem Christi, qualis oportet, dari integer posset. Patet ex loco jam indicato, Matth. 1. 21. vocabis nomen ejus Iesum: nam ipse salvabit populum suum à peccatis ipsorum. 1 Tim. 1. 15. Fidelis sermo, & omni acceptione dignus, quod Christus Iesus venit in mundum, ut peccatores salvaret. Hoc Jesu Christi est, salvare peccatores, salvare homines à peccato: non salvare tantum, sed redimere etiam, hoc est, salvare à peccatis. Adamus salvandus quidem fuerat, utique si perstitisset suo in statu, non autem liberandus, vel redimendus. Atque ita Christo non eguit: Deo quidem Salvatore, non autem mediatore & redemtore Christo, ut per hunc salvari posset. Christi nomen & officium, necessarium atque essentialem respectum habet ad peccatum; nam Mediatorem dicit. Actor. iv. 12. neque est in ullo alio salus: neque enim nomen aliud sub coelo est datum inter homines, in quo nos salvari oportet. Christi nomen est nomen salutis, neque haec alia intelligitur, quam quae à peccatis. Act. 11. 40. [?]σωθῆτε ἀπὸ τῆς σκολιᾶς ταύτης[?]. Matth. XVII. 11. [?]σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός[?]. Rom. v. 5. [?]σωθησόμεθα δι' αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς[?]. Salvare, & salvatio est à peccatis, & eorum poenis. Quare, si salvatio, quam per Christum habemus, non alia uspiam declaratur, quam quae à peccatis est, & talis vi nominis atque officii ejus includitur, necessarium Christus ad peccata respectum habet, ut ab iis nos vindicet; non existente peccato haud magis necessarius, quam aegroto vel morbo nullo, medicus aut sanatio.
units.tr: We prove our view as follows. 1. From the nature and office of Christ as Saviour, whose office, as such, formally means deliverance from sins. If you take away all sin, then neither the cause, nor the reason, nor even the very concept of Christ, as he must be, could be given at all. This is clear from the passage already cited, Matt. 1:21: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." 1 Tim. 1:15: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." This is the work of Jesus Christ: to save sinners, to save men from sin. He does not merely save, but also redeems, that is, saves from sins. Adam indeed would have needed to be saved, certainly if he had persevered in his state, but not delivered or redeemed. And so Christ would not have been needed for this: God would have been the Saviour, but not Christ as Mediator and Redeemer, through whom men could be saved. The name and office of Christ necessarily and essentially refer to sin, for he is called Mediator. Acts 4:12: "Neither is there salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." The name of Christ is the name of salvation, and this salvation is understood as nothing other than salvation from sins. Acts 2:40: "Be saved from this crooked generation" [σώθητε ἀπὸ τῆς γενεᾶς τῆς σκολιᾶς ταύτης]. Matt. 18:11: "to save what was lost" [σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός]. Rom. 5:9: "we shall be saved through him from wrath" [σωθησόμεθα δι' αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς]. To save and salvation are from sins and their punishments. Therefore, if the salvation we have through Christ is declared nowhere else than as salvation from sins, and is included in the very force of his name and office, then Christ necessarily has a reference to sins, so that he may deliver us from them. Where there is no sin, Christ is no more necessary than a physician or a cure is necessary to a patient who has no sickness.

units.la: Secundo. Christus ejusque adventus promissus fuit, à Deo, nec antequam peccasset homo, nec absque respectu ad hominis miseriam & peccata, à quibus eum liberaret: ergo ad peccatum, & peccati antecedentem existentiam necessarium & essentialem respectum habuit ipse, ejusque adventus. Argumentum est bimembre, partim à tempore promissionis, de Christo homini factae sumtum; partim ab ejus relatione ad peccatum perpetuâ. Prima homini promissio de Christo venturo, futuroque semine mulieris facta est post lapsum, Genef. iii. 15, atque in ejus remedium, & solamen. Atque Dan. ix. 24. quod dicitur cum Messiâ expianda iniquitas & adducenda justitia, de fine & causa adventus ejus accipiendum est.
units.tr: Second. Christ and his coming were promised by God, not before man sinned, and not without regard to man's misery and sins, from which he would free him. Therefore he and his coming had a necessary and essential reference to sin and to the prior existence of sin. The argument has two parts: partly from the time of the promise, made to man concerning Christ; partly from his perpetual relation to sin. The first promise to man, concerning Christ who was to come, the future seed of the woman, was made after the fall, Gen. 3:15, as a remedy and comfort for him. And Dan. 9:24, where it is said that with the Messiah iniquity is to be atoned and righteousness brought in, must be understood of the end and cause of his coming.

units.la: Tertio. In Euangelio Christi jam exhibiti causa & finis perpetuo constituitur, hominis redemtio; ergo, nisi homines redimendi fuissent, non advenisset Christus, Matth. ix. 12. non egent sani medico, sed habentes male. Confertur Christus cum medico, atque par utriusque necessitas constituitur in juvandis hominibus; ut, quemadmodum sani homines medicum ignorant, ita nec Christo opus habeant qui sunt integri. Quare, si revera carerent peccato homines, carerent utique & Christo. Ad quid enim illis medicus aut redemtor, qui nec male habent, nec sunt miseri? Matth. xviii. 11. Venit enim Filius hominis servare quod perierat. Ioann. iii. 16. Ita enim Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum miserit, ut quicunque in ipsum credit, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. 1 Timot. i. 15. Christus Iesus in mundum venit ut peccatores servaret. Tit. ii. 14. ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate. Galat. iv. 4. ut redimeret eos qui sub lege erant.
units.tr: Third. The cause and end of Christ, now revealed in the Gospel, is constantly set forth as the redemption of man. Therefore, unless men had needed to be redeemed, Christ would not have come. Matt. 9:12: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." Christ is compared with a physician, and an equal necessity for both is established in helping men: just as healthy men do not know a physician, so those who are whole have no need of Christ. Therefore, if men were truly free from sin, they would certainly be free from Christ also. For what use would a physician or a redeemer be to those who are neither sick nor wretched? Matt. 18:11: "For the Son of man has come to save what was lost." John 3:16: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life." 1 Tim. 1:15: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." Titus 2:14: "that he might redeem us from all iniquity." Gal. 4:4: "that he might redeem those who were under the law."

units.la: Quarto. Si idem Christus Salvator venisset homine integro, qui nunc homine lapso, ergo ad redemtionem hominum nihil fuit necessarium magis Christum venire, & hunc quam alium, nihilque adeo necessarium & proprium egit Christus, quod à se solo praestari debuerit, potueritque: sed si supra illud, quod homine integro praestitisset ad ejus salutem, nunc forte praestitum aliud, vel id non simpliciter necessarium ad salvandos homines fuit, & omitti, vel etiam ab alio praestari potuisset. Quid ni enim vel alius etiam simpliciter mori in bonum aliorum, vel immortalitatem annunciare posset? Verum hoc perquam absurdum, adeo elevare necessitatem solius Christi ad nostram salutem, vel ejus quod in istum finem egit & passus fuit: ergo & antecedens.
units.tr: Fourth. If the same Christ as Saviour had come to a man in integrity as he now comes to a fallen man, then it was no more necessary for Christ, rather than another, to come to redeem men, and nothing that Christ did was so necessary and proper to him that it had to be, and could be, accomplished by him alone. But if what he would have accomplished for man's salvation in his integrity was perhaps something else, or if what he now accomplished was not simply necessary for saving men, then it could have been omitted, or even accomplished by another. For why could not another also simply die for the good of others, or announce immortality? But this is utterly absurd, to diminish so much the necessity of Christ alone for our salvation, or of what he did and suffered for this end. Therefore the antecedent is also true.

units.la: Atque ita in nostram sententiam quoque loquuntur Patres. Irenaeus, lib. v. adverf. haereses, cap. xlv. Si enim non haberet caro salvari, nequaquam verbum Dei caro factum esset: & si non haberet sanguis justorum inquiri, nequaquam sanguinem habuisset Dominus. Origenes, homil. xxxv. in Numer. Si non fuisset peccatum, non necesse fuerat, Filium Dei agnum fieri: sed mansisset hoc, quod in principio erat Deus verbum. Athanasius, Serm. iii. contra Arianos: necessitas quippe indigentiaque hominum anterior est, quam illius naturitas[?], qua sublata carnem non induisset. Ambrosius, de Incarnat. Dominicae mysterio, cap. vi. Nam quae erat causa incarnationis, nisi ut caro quae peccaverat per se redimeretur? Quod peccaverat igitur, hoc redemptum est. Augustinus, in Psalm. 36. Conc. ii. Si tamen ô homo non dimitteres Deum, non fieret pro te Deus homo. Serm. viii. de verbis Apostoli: Venit enim filius hominis quaerere, & salvare quod perierat: si homo non periisset, filius hominis non venisset. Et in seq. Sermone: nulla causa fuit veniendi Christo Domino, nisi peccatores salvos facere. Tolle morbos, tolle vulnera, & nulla est medicinae causa. Idem, lib. de peccat. meritis & remiss. c. xxxvi. Adde Leonem, Serm. iii. in Pentecosten. Cyrillum, lib. v. Dialog. de Trinitate. Gregorium, in iv. Reg. cap. i. aliosque, quos citat Vasquez, in Thomam, part. iii. Tom. x. Disp. x.
units.tr: And so the Fathers also speak in our view. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 5, chapter 45: "For if the flesh were not to be saved, the Word of God would never have been made flesh; and if the blood of the righteous were not to be required, the Lord would never have had blood." Origen, Homily 35 on Numbers: "If there had been no sin, it would not have been necessary for the Son of God to become a lamb; but this would have remained what it was in the beginning, God the Word." Athanasius, Sermon 3 against the Arians: "For the necessity and need of men is prior to his nature, which, if removed, he would not have put on flesh." Ambrose, On the Mystery of the Lord's Incarnation, chapter 6: "For what was the cause of the incarnation, except that the flesh which had sinned might be redeemed through itself? What had sinned, therefore, that has been redeemed." Augustine, on Psalm 36, sermon 2: "Yet if, O man, you had not driven away God, God would not have become man for you." Sermon 8 on the words of the Apostle: "The Son of man has come to seek and to save what had perished: if man had not perished, the Son of man would not have come." And in the following sermon: "The Lord Christ had no cause for coming, except to save sinners. Take away diseases, take away wounds, and there is no cause for medicine." The same, On the Merits and Remission of Sins, chapter 36. Add Leo, Sermon 3 on Pentecost; Cyril, book 5 of the Dialogues on the Trinity; Gregory, on 4 Kings, chapter 1; and others whom Vasquez cites on Thomas, part 3, vol. 10, disputation 10.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: Section Three

units.la: Dices: venisset quidem in statu integro Christus, atque ut Salvator noster, non vero ut redemtor, quare non ista subiturus, aut peracturus, quae jam ex hypothesi peccati praestare eum oportuit, ut differentia quidem accidentalis sit adventus in utroque statu, non essentialis, ac proinde nec hinc illum, nec ex illo istum adventum redargui posse, utpote circumstantiis variantes. Resp. i. Unde vel petis, vel probas discrimen illud Christi Salvatoris, & redemtoris? distincta esse salvare & redimere, posseque salvari, qui non redimatur, quomodo salvati homines fuissent, si non peccassent, scio: at in Christo, ejusque officio ista distingui illa ratione, quin di-vidi & divelli, ut pro illo statu hoc, pro isto aliud fuisset, fecissetque Christus, hoc non comprobatur. II. Non salvare solum, sed & redimere, Christo, ejus nomini & officio est essentiale, non accidentale. III. Totis essentiis differunt, salvare, prout hoc Christo Sociniani tribuunt; & redimere, quod Christo Scriptura attribuit, eique proprium est. IV. Ad nos jam redimendos quid Christus necessario egit, sibique soli proprium fuit, & ejus adventum fecit necessarium, vel propriam & necessariam ad redemtionem nostram relationem & influxum habuit, supra id quod egisset scilicet in statu integro? An quod passus fuit? at hoc, juxta Socini expositionem, & alius quivis Doctor aut martyr potuisset æque subire, ac Christus. Tum nec, juxta eundem, hoc adeo necessarium fuit ad nostram redemtionem, quin constare ea potuisset, absque illa passione, quæ verum redemtionis pretium non continuit, sed exemplum modo fuit, & via Christo ad gloriam, id est, martyrium, non satisfactio, quam Smalcius blaspheme appellat, anile & prophanum commentum. Ut nulla adeo, secundum hæc, necessitas fuerit ipsius Christi, vel passionum ejus ad nostram redemtionem. Quod Christianis auribus & fidei durum atque horrendum merito est.
units.tr: You will say: Christ would indeed have come in the state of integrity, as our Saviour, but not as our redeemer. Why, then, would he not undertake or accomplish those things which, given the hypothesis of sin, he was bound to perform? So the difference in his coming in the two states would be accidental, not essential, and it could not be argued from one state to the other, since the circumstances vary. Answer: (1) Where do you get, or how do you prove, this distinction between Christ the Saviour and Christ the redeemer? I know that to save and to redeem are distinct, and that a man may be saved without being redeemed, as men would have been saved had they not sinned. But that in Christ and his office these things can be so distinguished that, without being divided and torn apart, he would have done one thing in the one state and another in the other, this is not proved. (2) To save only, but also to redeem, is essential to Christ, to his name and his office, not accidental. (3) The two differ in their very essence: to save, which the Socinians attribute to Christ in this way, and to redeem, which Scripture attributes to Christ and which is proper to him. (4) What did Christ do of necessity to redeem us, what was proper to him alone, and what made his coming necessary, or what proper and necessary relation and influence did he have to our redemption, beyond what he would have done in the state of integrity? Was it his suffering? But according to Socinus's explanation, any other teacher or martyr could have undergone this as well as Christ. Moreover, according to the same view, it was not so necessary for our redemption that it could not have been achieved without that suffering, which did not contain the true price of redemption but was only an example and the way for Christ to glory, that is, martyrdom, not satisfaction, which Smalcius blasphemously calls an old wives' and profane fiction. So, on these views, there was no necessity for Christ himself, or for his sufferings, for our redemption. This is rightly hard and horrible to Christian ears and to faith.

units.la: II. Objicientem audivimus Smalcium, Christum homines servare debuisse, utcunque in integritate perstitissent, & liberare à morte, in quam ex conditione naturæ & corporis sui cecidissent, in terram naturâ suâ reversi fuissent, nisi Deus eos per Christum servare decrevisset. Resp. I. Falsa hypothecis, quam alibi profligavimus, hominem in statu integritatis etiam mori potuisse & fuisse moriturum. Ostendimusque, mortem non consequens naturæ, sed pœnam peccati esse. II. Annon tamen in terram naturâ suâ reversi fuissent homines, quamvis (non, nisi) Deus eos per Christum servare decrevisset? Neque enim, juxta Adversarios, naturæ cursum inhibuisset Christus, aut mutasset. III. Ad hoc vero, ut homines absque peccato, in integritate & innocentiâ morientes, in æternum salvasset Deus, & beasset, quid necesse erat Christum venire? IV. Quin revera uti nulla juxta doctrinam Adversariorum necessitas, vel nunc in statu lapsus, ut pro hominibus redimendis Christus veniat, ita minus illam fuisse in innocentiâ, clarum est. Quid autem adeo necessarium fuit, Christum venire, ut viam & modum salutis annunciaret? ut hoc morte obsignaret sua? quum utrumque ab aliis etiam præstari potuisset. Unde multo magis evanescit necessitas Christi venturi sub statu integritatis. V. Jam ergo quia homines nec Servatore eguisse, si non peccassent, neque eum venire in mundum debuisse necessario ad servandum homines, apparet, nec probari possit testimonio nec sacrarum litterarum, decretum Dei fuisse de mittendo Messia, etiamsi primi parentes non peccassent, sequitur imo falsum esse, quod ait Socinus, de præcognito Christo, nempe id eo respectu factum esse, quod venire in mundum debuerit necessario ad servandum homines: morti autem destinatum fuisse sub conditione, si homines peccarent.
units.tr: II. Smalcius, objecting, has told us that Christ ought to have saved men however they had persisted in integrity, and freed them from death, into which they would have fallen by the condition of their nature and body, and they would have returned to the earth by their nature, unless God had decreed to save them through Christ. Answer: (1) The hypothesis is false, which we have overthrown elsewhere: that man in the state of integrity could also die and would have died. And we have shown that death is not a consequence of nature but the punishment of sin. (2) Yet would not men have returned to the earth by their nature, although (unless) God had decreed to save them through Christ? For, according to our opponents, Christ would not have checked or changed the course of nature. (3) But for this purpose, that God would have saved men without sin, dying in integrity and innocence, and would have blessed them for eternity, why was it necessary for Christ to come? (4) Indeed, just as there is, according to the doctrine of our opponents, no necessity for Christ to come now, in the state of the fall, in order to redeem men, so it is clear there was less of one in innocence. But what was so necessary for Christ to come, in order to announce the way and manner of salvation? Or to seal this with his death? Both could have been done by others as well. Hence the necessity of Christ's coming under the state of integrity fades all the more. (5) Therefore, since it appears that men would not have needed a Saviour, had they not sinned, nor ought the Son to have come into the world of necessity to save men, nor can it be proved by the testimony of Holy Scripture that God's decree to send the Messiah would have existed even if our first parents had not sinned, it follows that it is indeed false, what Socinus says, about the foreknown Christ: that it was done with this respect, that he ought to have come into the world of necessity to save men, but was destined for death under the condition that men sinned.

units.la: VI. Quale illud Dei decretum, incertum, suspensum, versatile, destinare Christum morti, vel non, sub conditione rei futuræ, independenter ab omni destinatione Dei? contra Theologiam de Deo pariter, ac illud contra articulum de Christo. Neque aliter oportuit illos in omnia Theologiæ capita incurrere, eaque invertere. Quin & quam jejunas ac frigidas de Christo & tota re Christiana foveant speculationes, sic etiam ostendunt.
units.tr: (6) What sort of divine decree is that: uncertain, suspended, changeable, to destine Christ to death or not, under the condition of a future event, independent of every decree of God? It is contrary to the theology of God alike, and to that article concerning Christ. Nor could they have done otherwise than fall into all the heads of theology and overturn them. Indeed, the barren and frigid speculations they nourish about Christ and the whole Christian cause show this too.

units.la: III. Objiciunt Scholastici, Eph. I. 3. Benedixit nos omni benedictione spirituali in
units.tr: III. The Scholastics object, from Eph. I. 3: He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in

units.la: Tom. 2. Christo: ergo quidquid uspiam benedictionis, & spiritualis, etiam in statu innocentiæ, obvenisset homini, hoc recepisset de Christo: quare & venturus illo etiam fuisset in statu. Resp. Sed additur, quod Deus benedixit in Christo, nobis, sc. peccatoribus: quo ipso ostenditur, Christum esse benedictionem & salutem peccatoribus, nihilque ex hoc loco demonstrari posse, quam venisse propter peccatores, & hos salvandos. Christus in electione constitutus fuit in medium, & mediatorem exequendi electionem, & conferendi electis tum gratiam post peccatum, tum gloriam. Neque alio sensu Apostolus illa de Christo dixit, aut de hominibus aliter, quam in peccato consideratis: non vel de Adamo, vel de nobis in Adamo, ejusque integritate persistentibus.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Christ. Therefore, whatever blessing, even spiritual, would have come to man in the state of innocence, he would have received it from Christ; so Christ too would have come in that state. Answer: But it is added that God blessed us in Christ, us, that is, sinners. By this very fact it is shown that Christ is the blessing and salvation of sinners, and that nothing can be demonstrated from this passage except that he came on account of sinners, and to save them. Christ was appointed in the election as the centre and as mediator to carry out the election, and to confer on the elect both grace after the fall and glory. The Apostle did not speak of Christ in any other sense, nor of men in any other way than as considered in sin; not of Adam, nor of us in Adam, persisting in his integrity.

units.la: CAP. III. De Christi in cœlos assumtione, paulo antequam docere inciperet.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. On Christ's assumption into heaven, shortly before he began to teach.

units.la: CONTROVERSIA:
units.tr: CONTROVERSY:

units.la: Num Christus, tempore quadragesimalis jejunii, in cœlum raptus fuerit, ut ibidem, de doctrinâ hominibus patefaciendâ, instrueretur?
units.tr: Whether Christ, during the forty days' fast, was caught up into heaven, so that there he might be instructed about the doctrine to be revealed to men?

units.la: Figmentum Socini de Christo in cælos subvecto, antequam prophetare inciperet. fere quale Mu-hammedanorum, de suo Muhammede. Exponitur Socinianorum, ex ipsorum scriptis, ista opinio. Nova atque inaudita, fatente Socino. Causæ, cur ista statuant. Argumenta nostra, ex Scri-pturæ silentio: Christi adscensione unicâ: vindicatur Heb. ix. 12. Non necessariæ plures, & anteriores adscensiones. Denique in terra Christus ad officium suum instructus, & imbutus Spiritu fuit. Solvitur, quod objiciunt, ex Joann. iii. 13. 31. & vi. 38. 62. & quod de exemplo Mosis, ac Pauli.
units.tr: This is the fiction of Socinus, that Christ was carried up into heaven before he began to prophesy, much like the Muhammadans' account of their own Muhammad. The Socinians' opinion is set out from their own writings. It is new and unheard of, as Socinus himself admits. The reasons why they hold it are given. Our arguments: from the silence of Scripture; from Christ's single ascension, with Heb. ix. 12 vindicated; and from the fact that several earlier ascensions are not necessary. Finally, Christ on earth was instructed and filled with the Spirit for his office. What they object from John iii. 13, 31 and vi. 38, 62, and from the example of Moses and of Paul, is answered.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: Section One.

units.la: Proximum quidem post personam Christi, & consideratam ejus naturam divinam, esset, ut ejus officia vindicaremus contra errores & corruptelas Socinianorum; nisi aliud, quod interea comminiscuntur, Christum sub exordium muneris prophetici in cœlos sublatum corpore fuisse, ut ibi coram Deo constitutus audiret disceretque, quæ Dei nomine & jussu deinde orbi esset expositurus, primo nobis examinandum esset & repellendum. Figmentum revera, quale in Muhammedanorum Theo-logiâ legas, de Muhammede super jumentum Alborach, in cœlos aliquando subvecto, & haud procul à Dei throno posito, & instituto prius, antequam aliis scilicet vaticinia sua & revelationes Dei communicaret. Atque similis fere figmenti utrobique ratio. De quo diximus in Summa Controvers. de Mu-hammedismo. Sed de Christo nunquam ullus Christianorum illud somniavit, ante Socinum, quod in coelum fuisset assumtus, ut a Deo doceretur, antequam docere inciperet. Et hic tamen palam id scripsit, docuitque. Quasi aliud Euangelium expositurus, & historiam atque Acta Christi. Qualia primis Ecclesiae temporibus multa hinc inde jactata fuerunt apocrypha, Euangelium Petri, Andreae, Jacobi, Barnabae, Thomae, Nicodemi; vel libri, de nativitate, de infantia Salvatoris: vel quasi ad exemplum Apocryphorum, de assumtione Abrahami, Mariae, Pauli, sua excogitaret Socinus, de Christi, tempore quadragesimalis jejunii nempe, in coelos assumtione prima. Ita fere paria facere cum illis Veterum fabulationibus conatus fuit, & post expurgata deletaque illa, aliud ejusdem commatis de suo reproducere. Aut denique ac si ex Schola Gnosticorum, Marcionitarum, aut Valentinianorum fictiones & commenta nova depromeret aliis antiquatis & obsoletis.
units.tr: The next thing to take up, after the person of Christ and the consideration of his divine nature, would be to defend his offices against the errors and corruptions of the Socinians. But first we must examine and refute another notion they are busy inventing: that Christ, at the beginning of his prophetic office, was taken up into heaven in his body, so that there, standing before God, he might hear and learn what he was afterwards to set forth to the world in God's name and by his command. It is a fiction of the kind one reads in the theology of the Muslims, about Muhammad, carried up at some time into heaven on the mule Alborak, set down not far from God's throne, and instructed there before he communicated his prophecies and God's revelations to others. The reasoning behind the two fictions is much the same. I have discussed this in my Summa Controversiarum, under Muhammadanism. But no Christian ever dreamed of Christ being taken up into heaven to be taught by God before he began to teach, before Socinus. Yet he has openly written and taught this. It is as though he were about to set forth another gospel, a history and Acts of Christ. Many such apocryphal writings were tossed about in the earliest times of the Church: the Gospels of Peter, Andrew, James, Barnabas, Thomas and Nicodemus, and books on the nativity and infancy of the Saviour; or, in imitation of the Apocrypha, books on the assumption of Abraham, of Mary, of Paul. Socinus has devised his own, on the first ascension of Christ into heaven, at the time of the forty days' fast. He has tried, more or less, to match those old fables, and, after purging and deleting them, to reproduce another of the same kind from his own invention. Or, finally, it is as though he were drawing new fictions and inventions from the school of the Gnostics, the Marcionites or the Valentinians, after others had been discarded and made obsolete.

units.la: Quare audienda primum illorum sententia vel fabula erit; tum examinanda. Dicunt ergo, Christum, antequam Propheticum inchoaret officium, & docere inciperet, in coelos corporaliter sublatum fuisse; opinantur, tempore quo in deserto per quadraginta dies jejunus agebat: atque in coelos vocatum, ut coram a Deo de voluntate ejus edoceretur, & quid dicere, & agere in mundo deberet, quasi mandati tabulas ac-ciperet. Verum Autores ipsos loquentes introducamus. Primus ergo commenti seu legendae hujus autor, aut certe propalator Socinus, in Catechesi, pag. 127. de ascensu & commoratione Christi hominis in coelo, antequam munus suum in terris obire inciperet, sic loquitur: Nihil verisimilius, & verbis ipsius Christi, & hic & alibi magis consen-taneum fit, quam ipsum Christum, postquam natus est homo, & antequam munus sibi a Deo Patre suo demandatum obire inciperet, in coelo, divino consilio atque opera fuisse, & aliquamdiu ibi commoratum esse, ut illa ab ipso Deo audiret, & praesens apud ipsum, ut ipsa Scriptura loquitur, videret, quae mundo mox annunciaturus & patefacturus ipsius Dei nomine erat. Verba quidem ipsius Christi hoc ipso in loco non minus, quam in superiore, de filio hominis, id est de homine expresse sunt dicta.
