Et si quis vel id animadverterat, quod factum est cum Mose, antequam divina lex tota ipsius ministerio promulgaretur, & manufacta opera, quae ad ipsum divinum cultum pertinerent, cujus materiae, cujusve formae esse deberent, ipsi Mosi a Deo praescriberetur; statim fatebitur (praesertim cum certum alioqui sit, Mosem Christi typum fuisse) nihil convenientius excogitari posse, quam ut Christus ante illud tempus, quod diximus, in coelum ad Deum, idque fortasse non semel ascenderit, ibique aliquamdiu cum eo fuerit. Dicit quidem Socinus verisimile id esse, consentaneum, & conveniens: at tum ex argumentis ad-duxit, & aliorum magis aperta expositione, id pro certo plerique habent. Atque ipse satis peremtorie in Brevi Discursu, de Officio Christi, pag. 17. Hunc Christum [?]cum aetate processisset in coelum accepit, eique ibi omnia ostendit, tum quae ad ipsum in suo mu-nere confirmandum, tum quae ad nos docendos pertinerent, & ita instructum ad nos misit.
units.tr: So the view or fable of these men must first be heard, and then examined. They say, then, that Christ, before he entered upon his prophetic office and began to teach, was bodily taken up into heaven. They suppose this happened at the time when he fasted forty days in the desert, and that he was called up to heaven so that he might be taught by God concerning his will, and what he ought to say and do in the world, as if he were receiving the tables of the law. But let us bring in the authors themselves, speaking. The first author of this invention or legend, or at least its publisher, is Socinus, in his Catechism, p. 127, on the ascent and sojourn of Christ the man in heaven before he began to discharge his office on earth. He speaks thus: Nothing is more likely, and nothing agrees better with the words of Christ himself, here and elsewhere, than that Christ himself, after he was born a man and before he began to discharge the office committed to him by God his Father, was in heaven by the divine counsel and working, and remained there for some time, so that he might hear those things from God himself and see them present with him, as Scripture itself puts it, things which he was about to announce and disclose to the world in God's name. The words of Christ in this very place are, no less than in the earlier passage, expressly spoken of the Son of man, that is, of a man. And if anyone has noted what was done with Moses, before the whole divine law was promulgated through his ministry, and God prescribed to Moses himself the material and form that the handmade works pertaining to the divine worship were to have, he will at once confess (especially since it is otherwise certain that Moses was a type of Christ) that nothing more fitting can be imagined than that Christ, before that time we have mentioned, ascended into heaven to God, and perhaps not only once, and remained there with him for some time. Socinus indeed says that this is likely, consistent and fitting; but since he has adduced arguments, and by the more open exposition of others, most of them hold it for certain. And he himself, quite peremptorily, in his Brief Discourse on the Office of Christ, p. 17: This Christ, when he had come to his age, was taken up into heaven, and there was shown everything, both what pertained to confirming him in his office and what pertained to teaching us; and so instructed, he was sent to us.

units.la: Tum addit, fortasse non semel, sed pluries ita in coelum adscendisse, illo tempo-re, ibique commoratum fuisse. Bis in coelum ingressum Christum, semel, ut a Patre instructus, acceptisque mandatis ad nos mitteretur, iterum ut in throno ac solio status sui con-sideret, scribit Schlichtingius, in Heb. 1.6. Caeterum dubitanter magis de tota re Enjedinus loquitur, in Ioann. xvi. 28. Si admittatur illa, de qua saepe sumus locuti, sententia, Christum in coelo reipsa, post nativitatem, & ante docendi munus fuisse, a qua nos minime abhorremus, &c. Jam Smalcius, lib. de divinitate Christi, cap. 4. plenius haec mysteria exponit, atque confidentius, pag. 11. Denique & hoc ad modum, quo Christus ad munus suum Propheticum initiatus fuit, pertinet, quod non, ut alii ante cum Prophetae & ipse Moses, per angelos aut visiones, id, quod alios docuit edoctus fuit; sed ipse praesens, homo jam natus, patrem suum vidit, & ab eo edoctus fuit omnia, quae deinde nobis exposuit. Et pag. 12. Ergo etiam statuendum est, cum, reipsa & localiter, a Patre venisse in hunc mundum, & consequenter, cum prius in coelo fuisse, quam in mundum veniret. Et pag. 13. Sed praeterea non videtur omnino esse incognitum, quando aut quomodo Dominus Iesus in coelum ascenderit. Quod enim ad modum attinet, nihil absurdi plane in eo est, quod D. Iesus eo raptus fit. Hoc enim modo credimus, eum in coelos post resurrectionem ex mortuis assumptum esse, sicut testatur D. Lucas, eum videntibus Apostolis elevatum esse, & nubem cum suscepisse ab oculis eorum; & idem etiam Angeli repetierunt, dum inquiunt: Hic Iesus, qui assumptus est a vobis in coelum, sic veniet, &c. Quo vero modo Deus semel, in elevando filio suo, usus est, quid prohibet, quominus credamus, isto etiam antea eum usum fuisse? Quod vero ad tempus attinet, plane verisimile (quod nonnulli inter alios Theologos etiam observarunt) illud tunc temporis factum esse, cum Dominus Iesus jam baptizatus, & Spiritu Sancto donatus quidem esset, munus vero suum nondum obire coepisset, cum scilicet quadraginta dies, & totidem noctes, jejunus in deserto consumsit. Quemadmodum enim Moses, tot dies & noctes, absque cibo etiam a Deo conservatus fuerat, antequam legem per eum daret: sic credibile est, D. Iesum, illo cibo caelesti, qui est commercium & conspectus Dei, ita fuisse recreatum, ut nullo naturali alimento, per totum illud tempus, opus habuerit. Tunc enim credibile est, eum patrem suum vidisse, & ab eo doctum fuisse, quod de se utrumque Dominus praedicat. Quae si cui minus probantur, is hoc saltem consideret, nihil a nobis affirmari in hac re, quod cum analogia fidei Christianae pugnet: nobis autem, id plane se ita habere, perfuasissimum est, & hoc mysterium nobis a Deo per sacras literas revelatum esse, plurimum gaudemus. Hic planam plenamque habes mysterii istius revelationem. Adscendisse quidem Christum in coelos dicunt, sed non sua vi ac virtute, uti hoc Christiana credit Ecclesia, sed aliena vi & potentia raptum. De tempore adscensus illius imaginarii ponunt id quod verisimile ipsis videtur, nam & ante dixerat, nihil referre, quod certo id statui non posse videretur. At quod de aliorum Theologorum consensu, inane prorsus est & falsum. Age proferat nonnullos inter Theologos alios qui idem observarint. Sic enim ei fidem habebimus, probanti, non asserenti. Quid in deserto Christus egerit, per quadraginta dies, nostrum non est determinare. Neque hoc scire nos Deus voluit. Temerarium vero supra modum est, quod id ausint nostri homines non definire modo, sed ejusmodi aliquid adferre commentum quod in ipsam omnino impingit fidei analogiam. Dabimus quidem, Christum illo tempore jejunum, cibo spirituali, quem & alias dixit, sustentatu, contemplatione videlicet & studio voluntatis ac mandati Paterni, & instantis muneris: sed ut in coelum subvectus fuerit, ibique divina doctrina imbutus, quasi non jam tum, & aliunde sibi ea constitisset, id vero rejicimus. De eodem Smalcius iterum, lib. de vero & nat. Dei Filio, cap. xii. Et, de verbi incarnat. contra Smiglecium, pag. 35. Atque Oftorodus, Institut. cap. xvi. Smalcius de errorib. Arian. l. ii. cap. ix. & , contra Smiglecium, pag. 74. Oftorod. in Apolog. pag. 31. Contra Tradelum, part. i. cap. x. Volkelius, Instit. lib. iii. cap. v. & lib. v. cap. xiii.
units.tr: He adds that Christ ascended in this way perhaps not once, but several times, at that period, and remained there. Schlichting writes, on Hebrews 1.6: Christ entered heaven twice: once, that he might be instructed by the Father, receive his commands, and be sent to us; and again, that he might sit down on the throne and seat of his status. Enjedinus speaks of the whole matter more doubtfully, on John 16.28: If that opinion is admitted, of which we have often spoken, that Christ was in heaven in reality, after his birth and before his office of teaching, which we by no means abhor, etc. Now Smalcius, in his book on the divinity of Christ, ch. 4, sets out these mysteries more fully and more confidently, p. 11: Finally, this also belongs to the manner in which Christ was initiated into his prophetic office: that, unlike others before him, who were taught by angels or visions, as the prophets and Moses himself were, he was taught what he afterwards taught others; for he himself, present and already born as a man, saw his Father and was taught by him all the things he afterwards set out for us. And on p. 12: Therefore it must also be held that he really and locally came from the Father into this world, and consequently that he was in heaven before he came into the world. And on p. 13: But besides this, it does not seem altogether unknown when or how the Lord Jesus ascended into heaven. As to the manner, there is nothing at all absurd in the idea that the Lord Jesus was caught up thither. For in this way we believe that he was taken up into heaven after his resurrection from the dead, as Luke testifies, that he was lifted up while the Apostles watched, and that a cloud received him from their eyes; and the angels repeated the same thing when they said: This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in this way, etc. But in what manner God once used to lift up his Son, what prevents us from believing that he had used the same before? As to the time, it is quite likely (as some other theologians too have noted) that this happened when the Lord Jesus, already baptized and endowed with the Holy Spirit, had not yet begun to discharge his office, namely when he spent forty days and as many nights fasting in the desert. For just as Moses was kept alive by God for so many days and nights without food before he gave the law through him, so it is credible that the Lord Jesus was so refreshed by that heavenly food, which is the communion and sight of God, that he needed no natural nourishment during all that time. For then it is credible that he saw his Father and was taught by him, as the Lord declares of himself on both counts. If anyone finds these things less convincing, let him at least consider that we affirm nothing in this matter that clashes with the analogy of the Christian faith; and we are wholly persuaded that it is so, and we greatly rejoice that this mystery has been revealed to us by God through the sacred letters. Here you have a plain and full revelation of this mystery. They say that Christ ascended into heaven, but not by his own power and virtue, as the Christian Church believes, but carried up by an alien power and might. As to the time of that imaginary ascent, they put forward what seems likely to them; for he had said earlier that it did not matter that it could not be stated with certainty. But what they say about the agreement of other theologians is utterly empty and false. Come, let him produce some of the other theologians who have noted the same thing. Then we will trust him when he proves it, not merely asserts it. What Christ did in the desert for forty days it is not ours to determine, and God has not willed that we should know it. It is, however, excessively rash that these men not only presume to define it, but bring forward such an invention, which altogether assails the analogy of faith. We will grant that Christ, fasting in that time, was sustained by spiritual food, which he also spoke of elsewhere, namely contemplation and zeal for the will and command of the Father, and for his impending office; but that he was carried up into heaven and there imbued with divine teaching, as if he had not already had that knowledge and got it from elsewhere, that we reject. On the same point, Smalcius again, in his book on the true nature and Son of God, ch. 12, and on the incarnation of the Word, against Smiglecius, p. 35. And Ostorodus, Institutes, ch. 16. Smalcius, on the errors of the Arians, bk. 2, ch. 9, and against Smiglecius, p. 74. Ostorodus, in Apology, p. 31. Against Tradelius, part 1, ch. 10. Volkelius, Institutes, bk. 3, ch. 5, and bk. 5, ch. 13.

units.la: Tantum vero abest, ut alios pro sententia illa nonnullos Theologos adducere queat Smalcius, ut Socinus in hoc potius glorietur, quod nova & inaudita fit. In Catechesi, pag. 128. sententiae quantumvis novae, & majoribus nostris fortassis inauditae. Quam gloriam ei facile concedimus integram.
units.tr: So far is Smalcius from being able to name several theologians who share that opinion, that Socinus instead glories in the fact that it is new and unheard of. In the Catechism, p. 128: "opinions however new, and perhaps unheard of by our forefathers." We readily grant him this glory in full.

units.la: Causa autem, quae ipsos moveat ad hoc statuendum, est, ut & hac ratione Christi Deitatem magis impetant, declinentque locorum Scripturae istorum vim, quae aperte satis dicunt, Christum ante adscensionem à resurrectione, & ante inchoatum munus suum, in coelo, & apud Patrem fuisse, & à Patre exivisse &c. unde Christum in coelis constituendum vident. Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, pag. 11. At Christus reipsa & localiter (ut loquuntur) ex mundo ad Patrem ivit. Ergo etiam statuendum est, eum, reipsa & localiter, à Patre venisse in hunc mundum, & consequenter, cum prius in coelo fuisse, quam in mundum veniret. Unde dicendum ipsis fuit, vel, cum tota Ecclesia Orthodoxa, Christum pro ratione divinae naturae in coelo extitisse, antequam in mundum veniret, & nasceretur; aut alio effugio, & commento eum corporaliter, aut semel, aut pluries in coelum adscendisse: quantumvis unicae adscensionis tantum meminerit Scriptura S. & fides Christiana coluerit hactenus & professa fuerit modo unam. Causam illam cum res ipsa, tum verba eorum testantur. Hinc in Catechesi Socini, pag. 128. dicitur, hac ratione complura sacra testimonia admodum alioqui explicatu difficilia planissima reddi. Nempe quam difficultatem sentiunt in locis explicandis, hoc modo non solvere, sed secare, & involvere amarunt, insuper habentes an cum Scriptura, & fidei communi regula convenirent, an suae modo τῇ ὑπο θέσει viderentur διὰ λόγων. Ita & quis, juxta ipsos, & quando, & quoties, & quam denique ob causam assumtus fuerit in coelum, ante muneris inchoationem, apparet.
units.tr: The reason that moves them to hold this view is that, by this means too, they may attack Christ's deity more effectively and evade the force of those passages of Scripture which state quite plainly that Christ, before his ascension, after his resurrection, and before he began his office, was in heaven and with the Father, and had come out from the Father, and so on; whence they see that Christ must be placed in heaven. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, p. 11: "But Christ in fact and locally (as they say) went from the world to the Father. Therefore it must also be held that he in fact and locally came from the Father into this world, and consequently that he was in heaven before he came into the world." Hence they had to say either, with the whole orthodox Church, that Christ existed in heaven according to his divine nature before he came into the world and was born; or else, by another escape and contrivance, that he ascended into heaven bodily, once or several times. Yet Holy Scripture mentions only one ascension, and Christian faith has hitherto worshipped and professed only one. Both the matter itself and their own words bear witness to this motive. Hence in Socinus' Catechism, p. 128, it is said that "by this means many sacred testimonies, otherwise very difficult to explain, are made perfectly plain." Namely, they felt the difficulty in explaining these passages, and rather than solve it in the right way, they preferred to cut it and tangle it up, caring nothing whether it agreed with Scripture and the common rule of faith, provided it seemed to fit their own hypothesis by arguments [τῇ ὑποθέσει διὰ λόγων]. Thus it also becomes apparent, on their view, who he was, and when, and how often, and finally for what cause he was taken up into heaven before the beginning of his office.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA.
units.tr: SECTION II.

units.la: ADversus quae ita nunc argumentamur. Primò, ex universali Scripturae Sacrae de totâ hac re silentio. Quod, & quam historiam, praesertim Christi, Scriptura nullibi memorat, non certe ubi ejus tradendae locus erat, & tanguntur alia tamen isti connexa, imo minora, illa temere asseritur, aut divinâ accipitur fide: verùm talis est historia de Christi ἀναλήψει Socıniana: ergo. Quis credat, hoc si verum esset, quod Euangelistarum nullus, qui tamen jejunium Christi, & tentationem, aliaque eo spectantia recensent, illud ne verbulo quidem & tanti momenti negotium attigisset? quinimo hoc oportuerat conscribi, si quod aliud, maxime, totius Christi muneris, & fidei habendae, id est, religionis salutisque totius fundamentum. Inde enim omnia pendent, ut, si eum negas Deum, certo tamen constare possit, bene instructum in tradenda doctrina, & fidelem ejus fuisse interpretem. Referunt Euangelistae, Christo è coelis haud unà vice perhibitum à Patre testimonium, quo quis esset, & quantopere audiendus, testatum altâ & coelesti voce fuit: jam autem non semel, sed fortasse aliquoties in coelum evectum, & cum Patre loquutum, doctrinamque & mandata accepisse, ignorasse Discipulos, aut praeterire voluisse, quis credat? certe nemo, nisi qui alteri mancipatus opinioni, propter hanc illud sibi dicendum arbitretur. Nam nec ipsos Socinianos hoc credere propterea quod verum existiment, sed propter aliam thesim, cui illud figmentum accommodarunt, certum. Vel sciverunt Discipuli, & Apostoli illud; vel ignorarunt: Ignorarunt? quorsum id reticuerit Christus, quod tam vehementer faciebat ad personam & officium suum ipsis confirmandum? Unde illud nunc sciunt Socıniani, quod ipsis Christi discipulis olim fuit ignoratum? Quod si ignorarunt, profecto non aliis quibuscunque sermonibus rem significarunt, sibi inauditam & incompertam. Scive-runt: at cur non palam & plane exposuerunt, narrarunt in historiâ, quomodo alia, & nequaquam illo majora? Cur non in concionibus, apologiis, & epistolis, non dico alicubi subindicarunt, sed non saepius exposuerunt, urserunt[?], ut argumentum pro veritate, pro gloria Salvatoris, & impetranda ei fide, tum a Deo ipso erga Chri-stum ostensum, tum a nobis in Evangelii praedicatione inter prima adferendum? Certe aliter egerunt in aliis fidei de Christo articulis, ejus resurrectione, adscensio-ne &c. populo tradendis & exponendis: dubium nulli Christiano esse ut possit, quin si & alias antea, & non semel, sed aliquoties adscendisset in coelos Christus, id etiam certius saepiusque exposuissent, neq; universali & constanti adeo silentio historiam praeterivissent admodum gloriosam, & necessariam. Vim argumenti istius nostri negativi valde confirmat Jonas Schlichtingius, in epist. ad Heb. cap. 1. 5. cui enim dixit aliquando Angelorum: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? ad quae sic, pag. 44. Notari hic debet D. Autorem a negato, ut in Scholis loquuntur, Scripturae testimonio argumentum suum ducere. Ideo enim negat ullum unquam Angelorum hus aut similibus verbis a Deo compellatum fuisse, quod id nusquam in Scriptura sit expressum. Nec enim ex eo quod sibi peculiariter revelatum sit argumentatur; cum & ubique Scripturae testimoniis pugnet, & hoc argumentum per interrogationem ita proponat, ut appareat, etiam illis ipsis ad quos scribit, praesertim ita monitis, rem fore aut esse manifestam: unde autem nisi quia id nusquam Scriptura testetur? Idem facit hoc ipso capite infra v. 13. Simili ratione argumentatur etiam cap. 2. v. 16. cum ait, non enim δήπου[?], id est ullibi sane Angelos apprehendit, q. d. nullo Scripturae loco id continetur, ac proinde nec dici debet. Unde liquet argumenta etiam ex negato Scripturae testimonio aliquando duci posse, nempe cum agitur de rebus haud exigui momenti, quaeque tam insignes sint, ut verisimile non sit eas Spiritum S. praetermissurum fuisse; quippe quarum notitia multum lucis afferre, nosque in divina voluntate aut Majestate cognoscenda haud parum juvare possit. Locus dignus visus, quem totum hic describeremus, tum ad hoc, quod impraesens agitur in nos negotium, tum propter similia quamplurima, quae Socinia-ni, praeter Scripturam, aliquoties comminiscuntur.
units.tr: Against these things we now argue as follows. First, from the complete silence of Holy Scripture on this whole matter. Scripture nowhere records this history, especially of Christ, though it certainly would have been the place to record it. It touches on other things connected with it, and even lesser matters, and the Socinians rashly assert those things or accept them on divine faith. Yet such is the Socinian history of Christ's ascension [ἀναλήψει]. Who would believe that, if it were true, not one of the Evangelists, who nonetheless recount Christ's fast, his temptation, and other events bearing on these, would have touched upon so great a matter even in a single word? Indeed, this above all should have been written down, if anything was, since it is the foundation of the whole office of Christ, of the faith to be held in him, that is, of all religion and salvation. For everything depends on this: if you deny that he is God, it could still be certain that he was well instructed in teaching doctrine and was a faithful interpreter of it. The Evangelists report that a testimony was given to Christ from heaven more than once by the Father, declaring with a loud heavenly voice who he was and how greatly he was to be heard. Now, who would believe that he was lifted up into heaven not once but perhaps several times, spoke there with the Father, and received doctrine and commands, and that the disciples did not know this or wished to pass it over? Certainly no one would, except someone enslaved to another opinion who thinks this must be said for that reason. For it is certain that the Socinians do not believe this because they think it true, but because of another thesis to which they have fitted this fiction. Either the disciples and apostles knew it, or they did not. Did they not know? Why would Christ have kept silent about what so greatly served to confirm his person and office for them? How do the Socinians now know what was unknown to Christ's own disciples long ago? But if they did not know it, they certainly did not signify the matter in any words at all, since it was unheard of and unknown to them. Then they knew it. But why did they not set it out plainly and clearly, and tell it in the history, as they did other things far less important? Why, in sermons, apologies, and letters, did they not, I do not say hint at it somewhere, but set it out and press it more often, as an argument for the truth, for the glory of the Saviour, and for winning faith in him, both as shown by God himself concerning Christ and as something to be brought forward first among us in preaching the Gospel? Certainly they acted otherwise in the other articles of faith about Christ, his resurrection, ascension, and so on, which they taught and expounded to the people. No Christian can doubt that, if Christ had ascended into heaven also earlier, and not once but several times, they would have expounded this too more certainly and more often, and would not have passed over in such universal and constant silence a history so glorious and so necessary. Jonas Schlichting greatly strengthens the force of this negative argument of ours, in his epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, verse 5: "To which of the angels did he ever say: You are my son, today I have begotten you?" On this he says, page 44: "It must be noted here that the author draws his argument from what the schools call a denial of the testimony of Scripture. For he denies that God ever addressed any of the angels in these or similar words, because this is nowhere expressed in Scripture. Nor does he argue from what was revealed to him in particular, since he fights everywhere with the testimonies of Scripture, and he puts this argument as a question in such a way that it appears the matter is or will be plain even to those to whom he writes, especially as they have been so instructed. Whence would it be plain, unless because Scripture nowhere bears witness to it? He does the same in the same chapter below, verse 13. He argues in a similar way also in chapter 2, verse 16, when he says: for surely he does not take hold of [δήπου] angels, that is, nowhere, as if to say: no passage of Scripture contains this, and therefore it ought not to be said. Whence it is clear that arguments can sometimes be drawn even from a denied testimony of Scripture, namely when the matter concerns things of no small moment, and such notable things that it is not likely the Holy Spirit would have omitted them, since knowledge of them could cast much light and help us no little in knowing the divine will and majesty." I thought this passage worth quoting here in full, both for the matter now in hand and because of the very many similar things the Socinians, apart from Scripture, invent from time to time.

units.la: Excipit Socinus, in Catechef. pag. 128. ad interrogationem, quam sic format, tantum dic quaeso, cur Evangelistae in sua historica de Christo narratione, istius ejus in coelum adscensus nullam mentionem fecerunt? respondens : in promptu causa est, cum res ista istiusmodi fuerit, quae a nemine conspecta sit, nec porro plane a quoquam conspici potuerit. & priores quidem tres Evangelistae, ne verba quidem vel ipsius Christi, vel alterius cujuspiam, ulla commemorant, unde res illa intelligi possit; cum tamen quartus & postremus, hoc est Johannes, & ipsius Christi multa, & Johannis Baptistae quaedam recenseat, unde illa aperte intelligitur, si modo ea, ut sonant & proprie accipiantur; ut sane fieri debet, cum aliter fieri debere non constet. qui Johannes Evangelista cum plus non posset, ad fidem tantae rei faciendam satis habuit, & satis omnibus esse debere credidit, testimonia aperta ipsius Christi ejus rei referre. quibus si quis non persuadetur, ne in ipso[?] Evangelistae testimonio minime persuasus fuisset. Resp. 1. Bene quod confiteantur, rem illam a nemine conspectam fuisse, quam illi primi excogitarunt sc. novam & inauditam: quod non conspici a quoquam potuerit, ubi tamen conspecta, & coram testibus contigerit Christi adscensio, Act. 1. 9. videntibus illis sublatus: quod tres Evangelistae nihil commemorent, unde illud colligi possit. Jam vero ecquis vobis dixit, rem istam, si vera, a nemine conspectam fuisse? Scriptura non refert, dices: neque enim aliud tibi reliquum. Accipe ergo nostrum argumentum, quia Scriptura totam rem illam tacet, non modo non conspectam cuiquam fuisse, sed nec contigisse: aeque mihi prorsus eam non contigisse ex illo Scripturae silentio, & regula licet concludere, ac tibi inde, rem non fuisse conspectam. II. Quare non conspici hoc a quoquam potuit, quum postea adscenderit, videntibus discipulis? Imo nunquam Christus magni momenti rem egit aliquam, non adhibitis testibus. Indeque Apostoli testes dicuntur Christi. Act. 1. 8. 11. & Cap. x. 39. & nos fumus testes omnium, quae fecit Jesus in terra Judaeorum, & Jerusalem. Adde 1 Joann. 1. 1. 2. quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod contemplati sumus, &c. Neque quidquam circa Christum contigit, etiam in obscuro, quod nostra refert scire, & non revelatum mox fuerit, uti in nativitate, & sepultura: quare neque ascensio, neque raptus hi corporales ignorati prorsus fuissent, si veri. III. Referunt quidem Evangelistae, quod Diabolus Christum in tentatione παραλαβὲς[?] in montem excelsum: & tacuissent, Christum a Deo raptum in coelos? IV. Maxime quum haec sub idem tempus contigerint, si Socinianorum obtineat sententia: deinde nec etiam ab aliquo conspecta illa res vel tentatio fuerit, & narrata tamen in historia. Ut non hoc causam queat reddere omissae alicujus rei mentionis in Scriptura, quod forte non conspecta fuerit hominibus, vel Scriptoribus. Quae & quanta non sive in V. sive N. T. historia narrantur, nullis visa, vel paucis, denique nec ipsis historicis? V. Vel fac, quod aliud vel Socinus, vel similis ei novator & impostor fingat Christo contigisse, responderetne aliter, ac nunc Socinus? vel cur non eadem posset & alius elabi responsione, & dicere, rem a nemine conspectam fuisse? qualia plani solent passim & mendaces adhibere effugia. Neque alterius census est, quod Socinus impraesentiarum adfert. VI. Tres Evangelistae, ne verba quidem vel ipsius Christi, vel alterius cujuspiam ulla commemorant, unde res ista intelligi possit, non quod non conspexerint eam, sed quod ignorarint, & quod nunquam facta sit, denique a figmentis mendaciisque alieni prorsus fuerint Scriptores Sacri. VII. Videbimus postea, quaenam illa sint vel Christi, vel Johannis dictatem[?] illam testantia, at revera jugulantia. Quod si jam haec tibi videntur aperta esse, quae ut sonant proprie accipiuntur: quare non idem sequutus es in articulo de Christo Deo, aliisque, quae aliter quam sonant & proprie exponi non possunt? Ut sane fieri debet, cum aliter fieri debere non constet. VIII. Quare Johannes Evangelista plus non potuit de illis Christi adscensionibus dicere, siquidem fuerint verae? Jam nihil potuit, quia figmentum est, & nunc denuum in horum hominum cerebro natum.
units.tr: Socinus answers this in his Catechesis, page 128, to the question he frames thus: "Only tell me, please, why did the Evangelists make no mention of this ascent of his into heaven in their historical account of Christ?" He answers: "The reason is ready to hand: since that event was of such a kind that no one saw it, nor indeed could it be seen by anyone at all. And indeed the first three Evangelists record not even words of Christ himself or of anyone else from which that event could be understood; whereas the fourth and last Evangelist, that is John, recounts many things of Christ and certain things of John the Baptist, from which it is clearly understood, provided these are taken as they sound and in their proper sense, as indeed must be done, since it is not established that it should be done otherwise. John the Evangelist, since he could not say more, thought it enough to make faith in so great a matter, and believed it should be enough for all, to report the plain testimonies of Christ himself concerning it. If anyone is not persuaded by these, he would not have been persuaded even by the testimony of the Evangelist himself." Reply. 1. It is good that they confess that this matter was seen by no one, since they first devised it as something new and unheard of. That it could not be seen by anyone, when Christ's ascension nevertheless happened where it could be seen and in the presence of witnesses, Acts 1:9: "while they looked on, he was taken up." That the three Evangelists record nothing from which that could be inferred. But who has told you that this matter, if true, was seen by no one? You will say Scripture does not report it: for you have no other resource. Take then our argument: since Scripture is silent about the whole matter, it follows not only that it was seen by no one, but that it did not happen at all. By that same silence of Scripture and by the same rule I may conclude, just as well as you, that it did not happen, and so that it was not seen. II. Why could it not be seen by anyone, when he afterwards ascended while the disciples looked on? Indeed Christ never did any matter of great importance without witnesses. Hence the apostles are called witnesses of Christ, Acts 1:8, 11, and 10:39: "And we are witnesses of all that he did in the land of the Jews and in Jerusalem." Add 1 John 1:1-2: "what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon," etc. Nor has anything happened concerning Christ, even in obscurity, that it concerns us to know and that was not soon revealed, as in his birth and burial; so that neither his ascension nor these bodily raptures would have been wholly unknown, if they were true. III. Indeed the Evangelists report that the devil took Christ [παραλαβὲς] into a high mountain during the temptation; would they have kept silent about Christ being caught up by God into heaven? IV. Especially since these things would have happened at about the same time, if the opinion of the Socinians held. Moreover, that event or temptation was not seen by anyone, and yet is narrated in the history. So this cannot account for the omission of some mention in Scripture, that perhaps it was not seen by men or by the writers. How many and how great things are narrated in the history of both the Old and New Testaments that were seen by none, or by few, and not even by the historians themselves? V. Suppose that Socinus, or some innovator and impostor like him, invented that some other event happened to Christ: would he answer otherwise than Socinus does now? Or why could not another liar also slip out with the same answer and say that the matter was seen by no one? Such are the evasions that liars commonly use everywhere. Nor is what Socinus brings forward at present of any other sort. VI. "The three Evangelists record not even the words of Christ himself or of anyone else from which that matter could be understood." Not because they did not see it, but because they did not know it, and because it never happened; in short, the sacred writers were altogether free of fictions and lies. VII. We shall see later what those words of Christ or John are, which seem to attest that dictate but in fact cut its throat. But if these things now seem plain, which are taken as they sound and in their proper sense, why have you not followed the same method in the article on Christ as God, and in others which cannot be explained otherwise than as they sound and in their proper sense? As indeed must be done, since it is not established that it should be done otherwise. VIII. Why could John the Evangelist not say more about those ascensions of Christ, if indeed they were true? Now he could say nothing, because it is a fiction, and has only now been born in the brains of these men.

units.la: Non testimonium duntaxat quaerimus, sed historiam: eamque pro more Evangelistarum, qui hujus rei narrationem aeque texuissent ac aliarum. Johannes Evangelista, quando profert aliquid caeteris intactum, tum illud certo, plene, aperteque proponere solet. Postremo ponamus, in silentio reliquorum Evangelistarum, Johannem hanc rem pandere, neque ipsum adeo, ac Christum apud eum aliquibus hoc innuere testimoniis: credis, vel Christum, vel Johannem id non apertius clariusque expositurum fuisse, non obiter in sermone aliquo, & quasi in transcursu, sed ex professo, & plana historia, prout in istis fieri solet? Vel, ut Christus in sermone illa attigisset modo, certe Johannes adjuncta mox latiori expositione rem feciisset planiorem. Nec ullum aut in tota Scriptura, aut quavis probata historia exemplum dari poterit, ubi rei & historiae tantae tam perfunctoria & levis facta mentio, & vix indicata fuerit. Neque solet Deus rerum fidei tam obscura & incerta facere, & vix facere iudicia.
units.tr: We are seeking not merely testimony but history, and history told in the manner of the Evangelists, who would have related this matter as fully as they related the others. When John the Evangelist brings forward something the others left untouched, he is accustomed to set it out certainly, fully and openly. Finally, let us suppose that John alone sets out this matter while the other Evangelists are silent, and that Christ himself hints at it to him in a few passages. Do you believe that either Christ or John would not have expounded it more openly and clearly, not incidentally in some discourse, as if in passing, but deliberately and in plain narrative, as is customary in such matters? Or, if Christ had merely touched on it in a discourse, John would surely have made the matter plainer by adding a fuller exposition. No example can be given, either in all of Scripture or in any approved history, where mention of so great a matter and history has been made so casually and lightly, and barely indicated. Nor is God accustomed to make the matters of faith so obscure and uncertain, or to pronounce his judgments so faintly.

units.la: Secund. arg. Scriptura unius modo adscensus Christi meminit, post resurrectionem; non alterius, alicujus hunc antegressi, non plurium. Quod si semel in coelos Christus adscendit, non ergo bis, non aliquoties: sed tantum semel adscendit. Heb. ix. 12.
units.tr: Second argument. Scripture mentions only one ascension of Christ, after the resurrection: not another preceding it, and not several. If Christ ascended into the heavens once, then he did not ascend twice or several times, but only once. Heb. ix. 12.

units.la: [?] Read in the scan as "dictarem" or "dictatem"; uncertain. per proprium sanguinem introivit ἐφάπαξ semel in sancta, aeterna reperta redemtione. Post impetratam redemtionem adscendit, non sub initium muneris sui; & semel, non aliquoties. Loquimur, uti etiam Adversarii norunt, de adscensione locali, & corporali.
units.tr: "...through his own blood he entered once for all (ἐφάπαξ) into the holy places, having obtained an eternal redemption" [εἰσῆλθεν ἐφάπαξ εἰς τὰ ἅγια]. He ascended after the redemption had been obtained, not at the beginning of his office; and he ascended once, not several times. We speak, as even our opponents know, of a local and bodily ascension.

units.la: Excipit iterum Socinus, Christum quidem ingressum semel in sancta, per suum sanguinem; sed aliter, quam suo sanguine, in coelum pluries. Catechef. pag. 129. Locus ipse, quem intelligis, responsionem secum ad quaestionem iflam affert. Neque enim vel simpliciter ibi dicitur, Christum semel ingressum fuisse in Sancta, vel semel ingressum fuisse, tunc videlicet, cum eo, postquam sanguinem suum fuderat, ingressus est, sed sic verba habent, Per proprium sanguinem introivit semel in Sancta; quae aperte significant, hunc Iesu Christi in coelum ingressum, qui factus est per ipsius sanguinem, semel tantum exitiisse: seu mavis, Christum Iesum per sanguinem suum nonnisi semel in coelum fuisse ingressum. Aharonico enim seu legali Pontifici Christus ibi opponitur; & dicitur, quod ille suum sacrificium ita peragebat, ut per sanguinem hircorum & taurorum in Sancta semel in anno ingrederetur, hic vero suum ita peregit ut per proprium sanguinem semel omnino in vera sancta non manufacta, id est in ipsum coelum ingressui fuerit. Vbi vides, deeo [?] tantum ingressu Christi in coelum verba fieri, qui respondeat ingressui legali Pontificis in Sancta illa manufacta, & ad ipsius Christi sacrificium pertinet, hunc que semel omnino exititisse [?] affirmari. Resp. 1. Locus duo comprehendit, Christum semel in Sancta ingressum, & cum suo sanguine; non ut hoc illud refellat, quemadmodum Socinus id conatur efficere; sed ut elucidet, ac confirmet. Modum ingressus declarat tantum, non vero enervat aut evertit. Quod ex versu 7. apparet, distinete duo illa membra sic observanda esse: in secundum vero semel in anno solus Sacerdos summus ingrediebatur, non sine sanguine. Illud distinctum, utcunque non separatum ab isto, & per se attendi debet, non cum altero commisceri.
units.tr: Socinus objects again: Christ indeed entered once into the holy places through his own blood, but into heaven, in a manner other than through his blood, he entered several times. Catechism, p. 129. "The passage you have in view itself carries its own answer to that question. For it does not simply say that Christ entered the holy places once, or that he entered once, namely at the time when he entered after shedding his blood. The words are rather: 'through his own blood he entered once into the holy places'; which clearly signify that this entry of Jesus Christ into heaven, which was made through his own blood, took place only once. Or, if you prefer, that Christ Jesus, through his own blood, entered heaven only once. For Christ is set here against the Aaronic or legal high priest, and it is said that the latter performed his sacrifice in such a way that he entered the holy place once a year with the blood of goats and bulls, whereas Christ performed his in such a way that through his own blood he entered once altogether into the true holy place, not made with hands, that is, into heaven itself. Here you see that the words concern only Christ's entry into heaven, which answers to the entry of the legal priest into that holy place made with hands, and pertains to the sacrifice of Christ itself; and it is affirmed that this entry took place only once altogether." Reply 1. The passage comprises two things: that Christ entered the holy places once, and that he did so with his own blood. It does not do this in order to refute that, as Socinus tries to make it do, but in order to elucidate and confirm it. It declares only the manner of the entry; it does not weaken or overturn it. This appears from verse 7, where the two clauses are to be observed distinctly in this way: "but into the second only once a year did the high priest alone enter, not without blood." The first clause, though not separated from the second, and though it is connected with it, must be considered in itself and not mixed up with the other.

units.la: II. Ad Socini mentem, loci sensus constare potest absque illo ἐφάπαξ semel: nam in coelum ut Sancta, opposita Sancto legali, tantum ingrediebatur Christus sacrificii peragendi causa, & huius intuitu illud intelligendum venit; quare nulla vel non magna emphasis relinquitur in hoc quod semel ingressus dicitur, nisi accipiatur, nunquam alias ingressum fuisse. III. Atque omnino spectari vocis huius emphasis debet, nempe uti legalis Sacerdos nunquam alias, nec ante, nec post, Sanctum Sanctorum ingrediebatur, quam semel; ita neque Christus pluries illud intravit: & uti ille non absque sanguine alieno, ita nec hic absque suo. IV. Vide uter sensus melius cum verbis, & eorum plenitudine ac emphasi conveniat, intravit Christus semel in coelum, per sanguinem suum, at absque eo quidem alias quoque, & fortasse saepius, inquiunt Adversarii: nos vero sic, uti legalis sacerdos semel omnino, ita Christus semel tantum in Sancta ingressus, idq; tum etiam sanguine suo, non alias, non pluries. Utrum cum vi & sensu verborum magis convenit, per proprium vero sanguinem εἰσῆλθεν ἐφάπαξ εἰς τὰ ἅγια?
units.tr: II. On Socinus's view, the sense of the passage can stand without that word "once for all" (ἐφάπαξ). For Christ entered heaven, the holy place as opposed to the legal holy place, only for the sake of performing his sacrifice, and it is in view of this that the passage must be understood. So little or no emphasis remains in the statement that he entered "once", unless it is taken to mean that he never entered at any other time. III. Indeed, the emphasis of this word must be regarded altogether, namely this: as the legal priest never entered the Holy of Holies at any other time, neither before nor after, but only once, so Christ did not enter it more than once; and as the former did not enter without the blood of another, so neither did the latter enter without his own. IV. Consider which sense agrees better with the words and their fullness and emphasis. Christ entered heaven once through his own blood; but without his blood, our opponents say, he entered other times as well, and perhaps more often. We, however, say that, just as the legal priest entered once altogether, so Christ entered the holy places only once, and that with his own blood, not at other times, not more often. Which agrees better with the force and meaning of the words, "but through his own blood he entered once for all into the holy places" [εἰσῆλθεν ἐφάπαξ εἰς τὰ ἅγια]?

units.la: Accedit ad hoc argumentum autoritas Symboli, quod dicitur, Apostolici, in quo unius tantum adscensus Christi fit professio, ab omnibus Christianis: neque ulli unquam alterum Christi adscensum crediderunt, non illum, qui muneris inchoationem in ipso processisset. Et tamen ad mentem & Theologiam Socini illa prior adscensio, vel adscensiones tam necessariae habendae ad muneris inchoationem, quam alia ad ejus complementum, nec minus articulus in doctrinâ Christi fundamentalis est, si qui fundamentales agnosci debeant.
units.tr: The authority of the creed called the Apostles' Creed adds weight to this argument, since in it the profession is made, by all Christians, of only one ascension of Christ. Nor has anyone ever believed in another ascension of Christ, not even that which began his office. And yet, on Socinus's mind and theology, that earlier ascension, or those ascensions, are as necessary to be held for the beginning of his office as the other is for its completion. Nor is it any less a fundamental article of Christ's doctrine, if any articles are to be recognised as fundamental.

units.la: Excipit Smalcius, Refut. lib. II. de errorib. Arian. cap. IX. in Symbolo autem Apostolico id non contineri, quid mirum? Nec enim omnium mysteriorum de Christo credendorum, sed praecipuorum tantum ibi habetur compendium. At hoc sane ex praecipuis esset, Christum adscendisse in coelos, ad doctrinae suae petendam inde originem & authoritatem, a quo tota religio, & fides, & salus nostra dependet: ut, si quod aliud, hoc saltem praeteriri & dissimulari non debuisset, praesertim ubi & adscensionis Christi fit mentio, & aliorum quae Christi imprimis concernunt personam, & historiam.
units.tr: Smalcius objects, in his Refutation, book II, on the errors of the Arians, chapter IX: "But in the Apostles' Creed, why is it surprising that this is not contained? For there is given there a summary not of all the mysteries to be believed about Christ, but only of the chief ones." But surely this would have been among the chief things: that Christ ascended into the heavens, to derive from there the origin and authority of his doctrine, on which our whole religion, faith and salvation depend. So if anything else, this at least ought not to have been passed over and concealed, especially where mention is made of the ascension of Christ and of other matters which chiefly concern the person and history of Christ.

units.la: Arg. tertium. Christus nihil eguit tali adscensione: superflue igitur a Socinianis asseritur. Nam eo, quod verus, & aeternus Deus est, uti in superioribus adstruximus, & aeterna sapientia, חָכְמָה Prov. VIII. Λόγῳ [?] Ioan. I. non necesse habuit ad accipiendam talem, ac Sociniani volunt, instructionem, in coelos sustolli & rapi primum. Ut haec quaestio a priori dependeat atque decidatur. Non quod negemus, si Deo ita placuisset, quin hoc agere bene quidem potuisset: sed necessarium fuisse, ut proinde tale commentum produci debeat, inficiamur.
units.tr: Third argument. Christ had no need of such an ascension: therefore the Socinians assert it to no purpose. For from the fact that he is true and eternal God, as we have shown above, "and eternal wisdom" [חָכְמָה] (Prov. viii) and "Word" [Λόγος] (John i), he had no need to be lifted up and carried away into heaven first, in order to receive such instruction as the Socinians want. So this question depends upon, and is settled by, what comes before it. We do not deny that, if it had pleased God, he could well have done this; but we deny that it was necessary, and therefore such an invention ought not to be brought forward.

units.la: Quarto. Hic in terrâ Christus Spiritu S. unctus & adimpletus fuit, non in coelo: hic ad Propheticum munus designatus, & sanctificatus; non ibi: ergo propterea nec adscendit, neque adscendere habuit opus. Heb. 1. 6. Quando primogenitum suum introduxit in mundum, &c. verf. 9. Ideo unxit te Deus, Deus tuus oleo laetitiae supra consortes tuos. Jesa. XI. 1, 2. Prodibit virgula e trunco Iesse, &c. super eo quiescet Spiritus Iehovae, Spiritus sapientiae & intelligentiae, Spiritus consilii & potentiae, &c. Luc. II. 40. Puerulus autem crescebat, & corroborabatur Spiritu. Cap. III. 22. In Christum baptizatum descendebat Spiritus corporali specie, tanquam columba. Cap. 4. 1. Iesus autem Spiritu Sancto plenus revertebatur a Iordane. 14. & revertebatur Iesus in virtute Spiritus in Galilaeam. 15. & ipse docebat in Synagogis illorum. Christus docuit, & Propheticum suum munus inchoavit per Spiritum, quem in terris accepit, & peculiari ratione in Baptismo; non ex aliquâ sublatione in coelos. Ioann. II. 34. Quem misit Deus, verba Dei loquitur: non enim dat Spiritum Deus cum mensura. Verba Dei loquitur, & ex Spiritu, quem accepit a Deo, ut missus fuit. Jam autem a Deo missus debuit dici, etiam ante tempus imaginariae istius adscensionis. Act. x. 38. Iesum Nazarenum, ut cum Deus unxit Spiritu Sancto & virtute.
units.tr: Fourth. Here on earth Christ was anointed and filled with the Holy Spirit, not in heaven. Here he was designated and sanctified for the prophetic office, not there. Therefore he did not ascend on that account, nor did he have any work to do by ascending. Heb. i. 6: "When he brought his firstborn into the world, etc." v. 9: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows." Isa. xi. 1, 2: "A shoot shall come forth from the stock of Jesse, etc. Upon him the Spirit of Jehovah shall rest, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, etc." Luke ii. 40: "But the child grew and was strengthened in the Spirit." Ch. iii. 22: "The Spirit descended upon Christ when he was baptised, in bodily form, like a dove." Ch. iv. 1: "But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan." 14: "And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee." 15: "And he himself taught in their synagogues." Christ taught, and began his prophetic office, through the Spirit which he received on earth, and in a special way at baptism; not through any taking up into heaven. John ii. 34: "He whom God has sent speaks the words of God: for God does not give the Spirit by measure." He speaks the words of God, and from the Spirit which he received from God, as one who was sent. Now he ought to have been called one sent by God even before the time of this imaginary ascension. Acts x. 38: "Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power."

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: SECTION THREE.

units.la: Objiciunt omnes, post Socinum, Catechef. pag. 128. & 127. Smalcius, Ostorodus, contra Tradelium, part. I. cap. x. primo, quod Christus dicit Ioann. III. 13. & nemo adscendit in coelum nisi qui descendit de coelo, filius hominis ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ [?]. Idem verf. 31. dicitur ὁ ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος [?], ὁ ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐρχόμενος [?]. Cap. VI. 38. Quia veni de coelo, non ut faciam voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me. 62. si ergo videritis filium hominis adscendentem ubi erat prius? Ex quibus inferunt, Christum ante haec in coelis fuisse. Et bene quidem hoc: sed eo localiter & corporaliter prius adscendisse, quomodo probant? certe id hinc non appareret. Non sane ista sunt clara & aperta Christi testimonia, de quibus gloriati fuere, & quibus totum adscensionum Christi mysterium cupiunt adscribi, II. Illane dicunt, Christum in coelis fuisse ante exorsum munus propheticum, & non etiam ante suum in hunc mundum ingressum, ante nativitatem? Non certe. Ioann. xvi. 28. Exiit a Patre, & veni in mundum. quamprimum in mundum venit, exierat a Patre. III. Filius hominis descendit de coelo: qui, & quando filius hominis, sive quum filius hominis fieret, atque id ut fieret, de coelo descendit: jam ante in coelo existens, atque hanc ob causam descendens, ut filius hominis fieret. Fuit filius hominis, ante munus Propheticum, à nativitate: ergo & tum de coelo jam descenderat. Socinus satis sedulo hoc urget, quod de filio hominis dicitur, de eo ut homine accipi debere, ut enervet quod additur, ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ[?], & ne in hoc Deitatem agnoscere cogatur: agnoscendum est, omnia, quae ipso in loco Christus de se affirmat, optime ipsi, ut homini, convenire, quemadmodum vel ipsa expressa appellatio filii hominis, sub qua Christus ista de se dicit, clare ostendit. Quorsum hoc Socinus urget, mox videbimus; jam, quod: & hoc volumus ut cum antecedenti comparet, non solummodo cum sequenti, observetque antea eum descendisse de coelo, qui filius hominis, id est, homo est & dicitur. IV. vers. 31. dicit, essentiam suam habere è coelo, contra illos qui essentiam habent mere terrestrem: ὁ ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος, ἐπάνω πάντων ἐστίν. ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς γῆς, ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐστι, καὶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς λαλεῖ. ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἐρχόμενος, ἐπάνω πάντων ἐστίν. Opponuntur ἄνωθεν, quodque idem, ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἐρχεσθαι; atque, εἶναι ἐκ τῆς γῆς: loqui coelestia, & loqui terrena: atque utrumque deducitur ex diversa origine, sive coelesti, sive terrena. Quare primo, ἄνωθεν ἐρχέσθαι, & ἄνωθεν εἶναι synonyma sunt. Atque ita Christus non in munere demum, sed essentia existentiaque coelestis fuit: & quod coelestem se ubique exhibuit, tum in doctrina, tum factis, ab illa est origine. 1 Cor. xv. 47. Primus homo ἐκ γῆς, χοϊκός; secundus homo, ὁ Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, dominus de coelo. Quid clarius, ad originem naturae indicandam, non tantum muneris? Quod vero hoc non ita accipiendum sit, quasi humana Christi natura de coelo delata fuerit, & non ex matre concepta, contra quem Anabaptistarum errorem Socinus quoque alibi disputat, est in confesso: sed innuitur, Christum ante ipsam nativitatem extitisse, in coelo, atque hinc venisse, nec tum demum exstitisse coepisse, quando ex Maria nascebatur. V. Sic etiam in alio loco Ioan. vi. 38. 62. Christus dicitur fuisse in coelo prius, quam huc venerit, & missus in mundum sit, atque voluntatem Patris coeperit perficere. Quis autem quaeso ex illis locis extundat, Christum aliquando, ante operis Prophetici initia, in coelos corporaliter sublatum fuisse, & forte pluries? Et tamen haec sola Christi, & Iohannis Baptistae loca sunt, ex quibus se illud confecturos Adversarii sperabant: quaeque putabant perspicue rem illam confectura, clara videlicet, quae in istum sensum nemo Veterum, aut recentiorum Theologorum, & ne hominum quidem aliquis accepit unquam. VI. Quod Socinus tam operose agit, ut Ioann. iii. 3. ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, non accipiatur, qui est in coelo, sed fuit, nullius est. In priore loco ex Graeco ita verba Christi legi possunt, ut dicat, filium hominis non quidem esse in coelo, sed fuisse. Vox enim Graeca ὤν quae per praesens tempus reddita fuit, potest, ut doctissimi aliqui interpretes [?]annotarunt, reddi per praeteritum imperfectum; ut legatur non qui est, sed qui erat in coelo. id autem fieri debere suadent omnino proxime antecedentia, in quibus fatis aperte affirmatur, filium hominis ascendisse in coelum; licet vulgo partim eludere ista Christi verba, ita ut nec dicat se ascendisse in coelum, partim ita interpretari conentur, ut ascensio ista non proprie, sed figurate accipiatur. Unde etiam in versione Racoviensi legunt: Der im Himmel war. Resp. Et legatur ita, non qui est, sed qui erat in coelo, nempe ubi erat prius, antequam hic esset, & degeret: proba, intelligi debere, duntaxat ubi erat priusquam munus inchoaret suum, in coelum sublatus, ut a Patre instrueretur. Si legamus, qui est in coelis, sequitur argumentum pro Christi Deitate, ex ejus omnipraesentia, quod praesens in coelo etiam tum esset: sin qui erat, manet argumentum quoque, ex ejus, ante nativitatem humanam, in coelis existentia. 11. Exivit a Patre, fuit apud Patrem, non aliquando postquam homo fuit, sed ante, & priusquam etiam mundus fieret. Ioann. xvii. 5. gloria, quam habui πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι, παρὰ σοί. Sic quod in textu hic, ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, cap. 1. 18. dicitur, ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός.
units.tr: After Socinus, all of them raise the objection, citing the Catechism, pp. 128 and 127; Smalcius and Ostorodius against Tradelius, part I, chapter 10. First, Christ says in John 3:13, No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven [ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ]. In verse 31 the same person is called the one who comes from above [ὁ ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος] and the one who is from the earth [ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς γῆς]. In chapter 6:38: For I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. In verse 62: If then you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? From these they infer that Christ was in heaven before these things. And indeed this is well said; but how do they prove that he had previously ascended there locally and bodily? Certainly this does not appear from these words. These are not plain and clear testimonies of Christ, in which they have boasted and by which they wish the whole mystery of Christ's ascensions to be ascribed. II. Do they mean that Christ was in heaven before he began his prophetic office, and not also before his entry into this world, before his birth? Certainly not. John 16:28: I went out from the Father and came into the world. As soon as he came into the world, he had already gone out from the Father. III. The Son of Man descended from heaven: he who, and when, was the Son of Man, or when he was becoming the Son of Man, and in order that he might become so, descended from heaven, already existing in heaven before, and descending for this reason, that he might become the Son of Man. He was the Son of Man from his birth, before his prophetic office; therefore he had already descended from heaven at that time too. Socinus urges this quite zealously, that what is said of the Son of Man must be understood of him as man, in order to weaken what is added, who is in heaven [ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ], and so that he may not be compelled to acknowledge deity in this: It must be acknowledged that all the things Christ affirms of himself in that place agree best with him as man, as the very expressed title Son of Man, under which Christ says these things of himself, clearly shows. Why Socinus urges this we shall soon see; for now, we want this to be compared with what precedes, not only with what follows, and it should be noted that he had descended from heaven before, he who is and is called the Son of Man, that is, man. IV. In verse 31 he says that his essence is from heaven, against those who have a purely earthly essence: [ὁ ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος, ἐπάνω πάντων ἐστίν. ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς γῆς, ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐστι, καὶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς λαλεῖ. ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἐρχόμενος, ἐπάνω πάντων ἐστίν.] The terms opposed are "from above" and, what is the same, "to come from heaven"; and "to be from the earth," "to speak earthly things" and "to speak heavenly things"; and both are derived from a different origin, either heavenly or earthly. Therefore, first, "to come from above" and "to be from above" are synonyms. And thus Christ was heavenly not merely in his office, but in his essence and existence, and the fact that he showed himself heavenly everywhere, both in teaching and in deeds, comes from that origin. 1 Cor. 15:47: The first man is of the earth, earthy [ἐκ γῆς, χοϊκός]; the second man, the Lord [ὁ Κύριος], is from heaven [ἐξ οὐρανοῦ], the Lord from heaven. What is clearer for indicating origin of nature, and not merely of office? That this, however, is not to be understood as if the human nature of Christ had been brought down from heaven and not conceived of the mother, which error of the Anabaptists Socinus also disputes elsewhere, is admitted; but it is implied that Christ existed before his very birth, in heaven, and came from there, and did not begin to exist only when he was born of Mary. V. So also in another place, John 6:38, 62, Christ is said to have been in heaven before he came here, and was sent into the world, and began to perform the Father's will. But who, I ask, can squeeze out of those passages that Christ was at some time, before the beginnings of his prophetic work, taken up bodily into heaven, and perhaps several times? And yet these are the only passages of Christ and John the Baptist from which our opponents hoped to establish that, and which they thought would clearly accomplish that matter, clear indeed, which none of the ancient or recent theologians, nor indeed any man, has ever understood in that sense. VI. What Socinus labours so hard to achieve, namely that John 3:13, who is in heaven [ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ], should not be taken as who is in heaven, but was, is nothing. In the former passage, from the Greek, the words of Christ can be read so that he says that the Son of Man is not indeed in heaven, but was there. For the Greek word ὤν, which was rendered by the present tense, can, as some very learned interpreters have noted, be rendered by the imperfect past; so that it is read not who is, but who was in heaven. That this must be done is strongly suggested by the immediately preceding words, in which it is quite plainly affirmed that the Son of Man ascended into heaven; although commonly some men partly evade these words of Christ, so that he does not even say that he ascended into heaven, and partly try to interpret them so that that ascension is taken not properly but figuratively. Hence also in the Racovian version they read: Who was in heaven. Reply. Let it be read thus, not who is, but who was in heaven, namely where he was before he was here and lived: I prove that it must be understood only where he was before he began his office, taken up into heaven so that he might be instructed by the Father. If we read, who is in heaven, the argument for Christ's deity from his omnipresence follows, that he was then present in heaven also; but if who was, the argument also remains, from his existence in heaven before his human birth. 11. He went out from the Father, he was with the Father, not at some time after he was man, but before, and even before the world was made. John 17:5: the glory which I had before the world was [πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι] with you [παρὰ σοί]. So also what is said here in the text, who is in heaven [ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ], in chapter 1:18, is said of him who is in the bosom of the Father [ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός].

units.la: iii. Nihil causae est, quare non τὸ ῥῆμα, & vim vocis servemus, qui est in coelo. Pariter ac in loco Ioann. 1. 18. jam allegato. Vel propter ipsa illa, quae Socinus subjungit: non est, quando hic necessitas nulla id faciendi adest, a verborum proprietate recedendum. Quam inepte, in omnibus aliis vult proprias verborum loquutiones retinendas esse, solum non illo ὁ ὢν, qui est. Tantum ut dictum est, non qui est, sed qui erat in coelo, legendum est. Scilicet quia illa opinioni suae obesse, istud prodesse credit, ad nutum ejus servare aut mutare loquutiones debemus, & sequi pro arbitrio ipsius jam proprias expositiones, tum improprias. At non sibi id in nos, & res nostras imperium esse sciat. iv. Sed antecedentia suadere videntur, ut legatur, qui erat; non, qui est in coelo. eccur? praecedit, filius hominis. Hoc non magis dictat legi debere, qui erat, quam qui est. Dubitas? adorire rem argumento, & videbis: Qui filius hominis est in coelo, vel erat in coelo, ejus est descendere atq; adscendere: fateor, at non propterea qua est filius hominis. Ita, Dominus gloriae dicitur crucifixus, is nempe, qui talis est, non qua talis. Deus sanguine suo redemit Ecclesiam; non, qua Deus, sanguine. Sic dicimus, praestans anima obiit, non qua anima: atque talia innumera. Neque, ad sensum & opinionem tuam potes dicere, Christum, qua filius hominis, in coelos raptum; tantummodo, qui filius hominis erat. v. Non figurate interpretamur verba, qui adscendit, sed proprie, & de vera ac corporali Christi adscensione: non quod illa jam contigisset, sed propter veritatem rei & dogmatis, quod nemini nisi uni utrumque competit, descendere atque adscendere. Denique ita etiam vertit Castellio, homine natus, qui est in coelo. Confer etiam quae habet Christianus Becmannus, Exercitat. Theolog. xiii.
units.tr: III. There is no reason why we should not keep the very word and force of the expression, who is in heaven [ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ], just as in the passage of John 1:18 already cited. Especially because of those very words which Socinus adds: There is no need to depart from the proper meaning of the words where there is no necessity for doing so. How foolishly he wants the proper forms of speech to be retained in all other cases, only not in that ὁ ὢν, who is. Only, as has been said, we must read not who is, but who was in heaven. Clearly, because he believes that the one thing hinders his opinion and the other helps it, we must keep or change expressions at his nod, and follow at our own pleasure now proper and now improper explanations. But let him know that he has no such power over us and our affairs. IV. But the preceding words seem to suggest that it should be read, who was, not who is in heaven. Why? It is preceded by the Son of Man. This does not dictate that it should be read who was rather than who is. Do you doubt it? Attack the matter with an argument and you will see: he who is, or was, the Son of Man in heaven, is the one who descends and ascends: I grant it, but not for that reason, insofar as he is the Son of Man. So the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified, namely he who is such, not as such. God redeemed the Church with his own blood; not, as God, with blood. So we say, a excellent soul died, not as a soul: and countless such things. Nor, according to your sense and opinion, can you say that Christ, as the Son of Man, was taken up into heaven; only that he was who was the Son of Man. V. We do not interpret the words, who ascended, figuratively, but properly, and of the true and bodily ascension of Christ: not because that had already happened, but on account of the truth of the matter and of the doctrine, that to descend and ascend belongs to one alone and to both natures. Finally, Castellio also translates it thus: born of man, who is in heaven. Compare also what Christian Becmann has in his Exercitationes Theologicae, xiii.

units.la: 11. Mosis, & Pauli exempla objiciunt, qui in coelum rapti fuerint. Praeter loca jam allegata, Smalcius lib. de divinit. Christi, cap. iv. Multo magis statuendum est, id Domino Iesu contigisse, quam vel Mosi, vel D. Paulo. Resp. 1. Non fuit Moses in coelum sublatus, duntaxat evocatus in montem. Socinus, Moses, ante primam legis promulgationem, ad Deum in montem Sinai, iter, si quis diligenter advertat, adscendisse legitur: concedi debet, non sublatum fuisse; in montem, non in coelum. 11. Apostolus non corporaliter in coelum se sublatum dicit, sed visione ecstatica, cujus modum ipse non capiebat. Sive in corpore, sive extra corpus, non novi: novit Deus. iii. Nec hic, nec ille ista passi ante exordium muneris, sed in ipso. Denique negatur consequentia, illud Mosi istud Paulo evenit, ergo simile Christo vel evenit, vel evenisse statuendum, aut fingendum nobis est.
units.tr: 11. They object the examples of Moses and Paul, who were caught up into heaven. Besides the passages already cited, Smalcius, in his book on the divinity of Christ, chapter 4: We must hold that this happened to the Lord Jesus far more than to Moses or to St Paul. Reply: (1) Moses was not taken up into heaven, only called up into the mountain. Socinus: If anyone attends carefully, we read that Moses, before the first promulgation of the law, went up the mountain of Sinai to God. It must be conceded that he was not taken up, and that it was a mountain, not heaven. (2) The Apostle does not say that he was taken up bodily into heaven, but that he was carried up in an ecstatic vision, the manner of which he himself did not grasp: Whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know; God knows. (3) Neither the one nor the other suffered these things before the beginning of his office, but in the office itself. Finally, the inference is denied: that what happened to Moses and what happened to Paul happened to one another, therefore something similar happened or must be supposed or invented for Christ.

units.la: LIBER SECUNDUS. DE FIDE PATRUM, sub Vet. Testamento.
units.tr: BOOK TWO. ON THE FAITH OF THE FATHERS UNDER THE OLD TESTAMENT.

units.la: CONTROVERSIA.
units.tr: THE CONTROVERSY.

units.la: An promissio vitæ æternæ, & remissionis peccatorum, ac Spiritus Sancti, & salutis in Christo, Patribus etiam facta & oblata fuerit in Veteri Testamento, ab iisque credita, & proinde eâdem viâ salvati illi fuerint, quâ salvamur nos?
units.tr: Was the promise of eternal life, and of remission of sins, of the Holy Spirit, and of salvation in Christ, also made and offered to the Fathers in the Old Testament, and were they believed by them, so that they were saved in the same way in which we are saved?

units.la: Fœdus[?] Dei cum hominibus varium, operum, vel fidei. Jus Dei omne in creaturas, non nititur Dei in eas beneficiis, sed sua ὑπαρξή[?] & majestate. Quod ostenditur contra Curcellæum. Utriusque fœderis convenientia, & differentia. Vita æterna promissa etiam sub V. Testamento fuit in lege. De religione Veterum ante Abrahamum, præceptis, & promissionibus, ipsis datis. Genesis III. 15. De religione Abrahami, & Mosis. De promissione vitæ æternæ Veteribus factâ; & Christi, ipsorum redemtoris; remissionis peccatorum; & Spiritus sancti. Sententia Remonstrantium. Anabaptistarum, in quo eadem, vel diversa. Argumenta nostra, quæ probant, Patribus in V. T. promissiones etiam datas vitæ æternæ. Quibus & crediderunt Patres, & ipsarum promissa expectarunt. Vindicantur alia, & Act. XV. 11. Promissiones Christi, ipsis factæ. Unica salutis ubique via, & semper, per Christum. Objectiones Adversariorum. Joann. I. 16. 17. & 4. 1 Joann. I. 1. Rom. 1. 2. 3. & XVI. 25. 26. Gal. III. 23. II Tim. I. 9. 10. Heb. II. 3. & cap. VII. 19. & IX. 8. & XI. 39. 40. & VIII. 6. De Spiritu S. Luc. XI. 13. & Joann. VII. 39. Refelliuntur eorum rationes. Sententia Judæorum, de promissâ in lege Mosis vitâ æternâ.
units.tr: God's covenant with men is of two kinds, that of works and that of faith. All of God's right over creatures rests not on his benefits toward them but on his own existence [ὑπαρξή] and majesty. This is shown against Curcellaeus. The agreement and the difference between the two covenants. Eternal life was promised under the Old Testament also, in the law. On the religion of the ancients before Abraham, and on the precepts and promises given to them. Genesis III. 15. On the religion of Abraham and Moses. On the promise of eternal life made to the ancients, and of Christ, their redeemer; of remission of sins; and of the Holy Spirit. The opinion of the Remonstrants, and of the Anabaptists, in what respects it is the same or different. Our arguments, which prove that promises of eternal life were also given to the Fathers under the Old Testament. The Fathers both believed these promises and looked for their fulfilment. Other points are defended, and Acts XV. 11. The promises of Christ made to them. The one way of salvation, everywhere and always, is through Christ. The objections of the adversaries: John I. 16, 17 and IV; I John I. 1; Romans I. 2, 3 and XVI. 25, 26; Galatians III. 23; II Timothy I. 9, 10; Hebrews II. 3, chapter VII. 19, IX. 8, XI. 39, 40 and VIII. 6. On the Holy Spirit: Luke XI. 13 and John VII. 39. Their arguments are refuted. The opinion of the Jews on the eternal life promised in the law of Moses.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: SECTION ONE.

units.la: Plurimum refert in Theologiâ, doctrinam de Dei Fœdere bene explicare & tueri, utpote quæ cor & coagulum σύνδεσμον[?] totius est religionis, in quo Deus & homo concurrunt, & Dei beneficia, & hominis officia, & de ultimo hominis fine ac salute Dei dispositio innotescit, atque œconomia. Uti enim in communione Dei cum homine anima religionis hæret & salutis, ita, quia eam fœdere proposuit Deus ac manifestavit, in hoc rite tum cognoscendo, tum servando summa rei vertitur. Communionis divinæ erga nos primæ sunt ca-pita, quod ad nos loqui, neque hoc solum, sed etiam nobiscum agere, & tractare denique fœdus ipsis placuit. Illud hujus fundamentum, atque principium; hoc, illius vicissim complementum est & κεφάλαιον. Quævis loqui potuisset Deus, ut tamen nihil de fœdere. Imo nec loqui ad nos necesse habuit, sibi nempe; nobis vero quam maxime id fuit utile ac necessarium. Jam & verba Deus facere, & fœdus benigne voluit. Neque alia utriusque causa dari vel fingi potest, quam sola ejus & mera benignitas, pro potestate & dominio, quod in nos habet. Dei fœdus quo cum homi-nibus egit, semper quidem fuit idem; at tradendi ejus ratio haud paulum diversa. Hinc autem ordiri necesse est, ubi de Dei in Ecclesiam beneficiis, vel Christi, verba facere debemus.
units.tr: It matters greatly in theology to explain and defend rightly the doctrine of God's covenant, since it is the heart and the bond [σύνδεσμον] of the whole of religion. In it God and man meet, and in it are made known God's benefits and man's duties, God's arrangement concerning man's final end and salvation, and the economy of salvation. For just as the soul of religion and of salvation lies in communion with God, so the chief concern in knowing and keeping this rightly lies in the fact that God has proposed and revealed this communion to us by covenant. The first heads of divine fellowship toward us are these: that God has willed to speak to us, and not only that but also to deal with us, and finally to enter into a covenant with us. The former is the foundation and principle of this; the latter, in turn, is the completion and the chief point [κεφάλαιον] of the former. God could have spoken without saying anything about a covenant. Indeed, he had no need to speak to us at all, for his own sake; but for us it was most useful and necessary. Now God has both spoken and graciously willed a covenant. No other cause of either can be given or imagined than his sole and pure goodness, according to the power and dominion he holds over us. The covenant of God, by which he dealt with men, has always been the same; but the manner of setting it forth has been quite different. It is from here that we must begin whenever we speak of God's benefits to the Church, or of Christ's.

units.la: Sumitur Dei fœdus vel pro nudo & simplici pacto, quo hoc vel illud facturum in se recipit, estque idem cum simplici Dei promissione: vel pro contractu quasi inter partes, nixo stipulatione officii, & promissione beneficii. Et hoc appellatur fœdus. Quippe inter Deum & hominem non proprie contractus, qualis inter nos, vel pares, initur; sed tamen ad similitudinem ejus, pro quasi contractu, uti in Jure loquuntur, fœdus Dei habetur. Quando enim contractus, ex Theophilo, de obligat. definitur, quod fit duorum pluriumve in idem conventio & consensus, ad constituendam obligationem, & ut alter alteri fiat obnoxius: aliquid hinc ad nostrum quidem negotium assumimus; alia vero linquimus. Neque enim, proprie & stricte loquendo, Dei ulla obligatio est, duntaxat spontanea sui communicatio, ut nullo tamen modo obnoxius fiat suæ, quacum contrahit, creaturæ. Obstringit se sibi, suæ fidelitati & veritati, promissione bonitatis, non nobis. Contrahit tamen, vel contrahere dicitur, fœdere etiam: sed uti quasi contractus, ita & quasi fœdus intelligendum, omni modo impar, neque enim æquo fœdere in amicitiam hic venimus. D. de captivis & postlimin. l. v 11. Stipulatur Deus officium nostrum, pollicetur beneficium suum: & contrarium minatur, siquidem officio nostro desimus. Ut quid a nobis, & quid de nobis fieri velit, inde nempe appareat.
units.tr: The covenant of God is taken either for a bare and simple pact, by which he takes upon himself to do this or that, and which is the same as a simple promise of God; or for a kind of contract between parties, resting on a stipulation of duty and a promise of benefit. It is this that is called a covenant. For between God and man no contract properly so called, such as is made between ourselves who are equals, is entered into; yet, by analogy with it, the covenant of God is regarded as a quasi-contract, as the lawyers speak. For when a contract is defined, according to Theophilus, On obligations, as the agreement and consent of two or more persons to the same thing, in order to establish an obligation and to make one party liable to the other, we take from this something for our present purpose, but leave other things aside. For properly and strictly speaking there is no obligation on God's part, except a spontaneous communication of himself, so that he does not in any way become liable to the creature with whom he contracts. He binds himself, by a promise of goodness, to his own faithfulness and truth, not to us. Yet he does contract, or is said to contract, by covenant too; but this must be understood as a quasi-contract and a quasi-covenant, in every way unequal, for we do not come here into friendship on equal terms (D. On captives and postliminy, l. 5 §1). God stipulates for our duty, and promises his benefit; and he threatens the opposite if we fail in our duty. From this it appears what he wishes to be done by us and concerning us.

units.la: Partes, seu Personæ (non enim improprie dictum fœdus considerámus, seu pactum Dei cum creaturis etiam irrationalibus) sunt Deus, & homo: res Angelorum ignotæ nobis, & propterea prætereundæ. Auctor fœderis, & uti omnium, ita hic, prima causa Deus. Quare nequit non bonum esse fœdus istud, & sapientissimum. Materia, seu argumentum fœderis, quod impræsentiarum attendimus, est hominis summum bonum, & salus æterna, denotata pro phrasi Scripturæ, voce vitæ. Quippe etiam alia fœdera legimus in Scripturis Dei cum homine, de particulari aliquo bono, seu beneficio: vel corporali & terreno, v. g. terra Canaan. Genef. xv. 18. politico, aut dignitate regia in familia conservandâ; aut ecclesiastica & sacerdotali. Num. xxv.12.13. Nehem. xiij. 29. Malach. ii.4.8. Verum hoc loco, non quod aliquos, sed quod omnes homines; & non eorum bonum aliquod, sed summum concernit, spectamus. Atque hoc propter beneficium, ex fœdere & conferendum, & obtinendum.
units.tr: The parties or persons (for we are considering a covenant not improperly so called, or a pact of God with creatures even irrational ones) are God and man; the affairs of angels are unknown to us and therefore to be passed over. The author of the covenant, and of all things, here as elsewhere, is God as first cause. Therefore this covenant cannot but be good and most wise. The matter, or subject of the covenant, which we are now considering, is man's highest good and eternal salvation, expressed in the phrase of Scripture by the word life. For we read of other covenants in the Scriptures between God and man, concerning some particular good or benefit: bodily and earthly, for example the land of Canaan (Gen. 15:18); political, or the preservation of royal dignity in a family; or ecclesiastical and priestly (Num. 25:12–13; Neh. 13:29; Mal. 2:4, 8). But in this place we look at a covenant that concerns not some men but all men, and not some good of theirs but their highest good. And this is the benefit that is to be conferred and obtained by the covenant.

units.la: Stipulationem vero officii quod attinet, estque tertium in præsenti negotio observandum, ea, pro temporis & hominis ratione, varia fuit: nimirum duplex, operum, vel fidei. Illa, ante lapsum; hæc, post. Illa homine integro; hæc, lapso. Illa in homine sita; hæc, extra eum. In Mediatore hæc; illa, sine eo. Fundamentum illius creatio; hujus, Dei singularis gratia. Illa à Deo creatore & justo; hæc, à redemtore benigno. Quare & illa infirmata fuit, antiquataque; hæc vero sola obtinet in perpetuum, solaque superest via, quâ salutem assequi homo queat.
