units.tr: As for the stipulation of duty, which is the third thing to be observed in the present matter, this was varied according to the time and the condition of man: it was twofold, of works or of faith. The former was before the fall, the latter after. The former was with man in his integrity, the latter with man fallen. The former was placed in man himself, the latter outside him. The latter is in a Mediator, the former without one. The foundation of the former is creation; of the latter, God's singular grace. The former comes from God as creator and just; the latter from a kind redeemer. Hence the former was weakened and abolished, but the latter alone holds good forever, and it is the only way left by which man can attain salvation.

units.la: Fœdus Dei operum erat, pactum quo ab homine, à se creato, exigebat perfectam legis obedientiam & justitiam, qua præstita æternum homo beateque vixisset. Juxta formulam ejus, & summam: hoc fac, & vives. Levit. xviii. 5. Jezech. xx. 11. Rom. x. 5. Gal. iii. 12. Cujus sensus est, fac; fac omnia; & constanter in iis mane. ὁ ἐμμ[?]ένων ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς γεγραμμένοις ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ ποιῆσαι αὐτά. Jacob. ii. 10. contrà poena maledictionis constituta in eos, qui non manent in omnibus. Deut. xxvii. 26.
units.tr: The covenant of works was the pact by which God, from man whom he had created, required perfect obedience to the law and righteousness, by performing which man would have lived forever and blessedly. According to its formula and summary: Do this, and you shall live (Lev. 18:5; Ezek. 20:11; Rom. 10:5; Gal. 3:12). Its sense is: do, do all things, and constantly remain in them: "he who abides in all things written in the book of the law to do them" [ὁ ἐμμένων ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς γεγραμμένοις ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ ποιῆσαι αὐτά] (Jas. 2:10). On the contrary, the penalty of the curse is laid upon those who do not remain in all things (Deut. 27:26).

units.la: Iniit hoc fœdus Deus cum homine, à se creato. Non quod creatio, vel beneficia Dei in hominem jus ei fundent legislationis, neutiquam: hoc enim arcessendum à solâ Dei ὑπεροχῇ[?] & majestate: sed quod in creatione hoc manifestatum, ex eaque pendeat quantum à parte nostri, & nostræ tum notitiæ, tum obligationis. Alia, in Deo causa legis dandæ, seu potestatis legislatoriæ; vel in nobis, eam cognoscendæ aut præstandæ. Fundamentum ex quo, vel, fundamentum in quo. Ex quo fœdus Dei fluit, si illud operum consideres, Dei majestas est; sin fidei, gratia. Quod si fundamentum, in quo ponitur utrumque; illud in creaturâ, hoc in Christo, & Dei gratiâ fundatū est. Quamvis hoc ipsum, quod in fœdus ire cum homine Deus vult, benignitatis sit & gratiæ, generatim sumtæ, non semper in Christo: namq; κατ᾽ ἐπαγγελίαν[?] dicit haud minimam, quod quasi contrahere cum creaturâ Creator velit; & pro benevolentia, ei promittere etiam mercedem. Neque enim ad hoc tenetur ulla Deus ratione, aut jure, qui meram à creatura postulare potest obedientiam, absq; ullâ μισθαποδοσία[?]. Jam ei secus placuit, & non injungere homini officium, nisi propositò observantiæ præmio & mercede gratiosa. Jesa. xlv. 29. non dixi Iemini[?] Iacobi, quærite me frustra. & Malach. i. 10. Quare lubet distinguere, fundamentum legislationis; & fundamentum fœderis: hoc illam quidem comprehendit & ponit, eâque ceu conditione nititur, sed in se plus dicit, & promissionem continet: illius fundamentum in Deo est, majestas; hujus insuper, supremi Rectoris benevolentia.
units.tr: God entered into this covenant with man whom he had created. Not that creation or the benefits of God to man, by any means, lay the foundation of his right to legislate; for this must be derived from God's sole supremacy [ὑπεροχῇ] and majesty. But it is that in creation this is made manifest, and from it depends, on our part, as much both our knowledge and our obligation. There is one thing in God, the cause of giving the law, or legislative power; and another in us, the cause of knowing or performing it. The foundation from which, or the foundation in which. The covenant of God flows from which foundation? If you consider the covenant of works, it is God's majesty; if of faith, grace. But if you ask the foundation in which both are placed: the former is founded in the creature, the latter in Christ and the grace of God. Although this very fact, that God wills to enter into covenant with man, belongs to kindness and grace in general, it is not always in Christ; for the Creator, by promise [κατ᾽ ἐπαγγελίαν], shows no small goodwill in willing, as it were, to contract with the creature, and out of benevolence to promise it even a reward. For God is bound by no reason or right to this, since he can demand from the creature pure obedience without any recompense [μισθαποδοσία]. Yet he has otherwise been pleased not to impose a duty on man except with a gracious reward of obedience set before him: "I have not said to the seed of Jacob, Seek me in vain" (Isa. 45:19); and Mal. 1:10. Therefore it is right to distinguish the foundation of legislation from the foundation of the covenant: the latter includes and posits the former, and rests on it as on a condition, but says more in itself, and contains a promise. The foundation of the former is in God's majesty; of the latter, moreover, the benevolence of the supreme Ruler.

units.la: Arminius, in Disput. de Dominio Dei, triplex juris divini in creaturam rationalem fundamentum constituebat: primum, creationem; secundum, contractum cum illâ initum; tertium, peccatum creaturæ. In Examine Thesium Gomari, de Prædestin. pag. 122. Nititur enim omne Dei jus in creaturam vel Dei beneficio erga illam, vel illius in Deum maleficio, vel denique contractu. Quæ eadem habent Remonstrantes, in Scriptis Synodalibus, ad Rom. ix. 21. & prolixè tuetur Stephanus Curcellæus, lib. de jure Dei in creaturas innoc. contra Mosem Amyraldum. Verùm penficulate si rem ponderemus, quamvis jus in creaturam suam Deus habeat etiam ex creatione, & contractu seu fœdere, tum & juste damnandi propter maleficium; non tamen omne Dei jus inde oriri dicendum est. Nempe per creationem Deus jus habet in creaturam, utpote à se factam, & dependentem, sed non id sibi juris ex creationis actione vel beneficio demum acquirit. Creatione quidem ponitur subjectum, quod alias non esset, in quod jus exerceat suum Deus, sed creatura non fundat facultatem juris in Deo; sed egressum, exequutionem, & exercitium ejus in subjecto, in creatura demonstrat. Deus sibi nihil, nihil juris, quod proprietatem dicat divinam, accipit aliunde, vel à creaturâ; sibi est αὐτάρκης[?] & μόνος μακάριος, in se, à se, independenter atque universaliter, אין[?]; sed operari secundum illam proprietatem, vel jus non potest, vel extra se agere quidpiam, nisi intercedat creatio, actio subjectum juris exercendi ponens in creatura, non fundamentum illius habendi in Deo. Similiter ex contractu cum creatura inito nascitur Deo actio, & jus in creaturam (prout in omni hoc contractu solet,) sed non hinc demum jus omne, quod Deus in creaturam, vel illam etiam, cum qua contrahit, habet; vel hoc jus, ut contrahat, vel contrahere demum possit. Contractus Dei cum creatura, dicit quidem quid velit, non adeo quid possit: ergo voluntatis divinae argumentum, foedus est, non ita potestatis, nedum fundamentum.
units.tr: Arminius, in his disputation On the Dominion of God, laid down a threefold foundation of divine right over the rational creature: first, creation; second, the contract entered into with it; third, the sin of the creature. In his Examination of Gomarus's Theses on Predestination, p. 122: For all of God's right over the creature rests either on God's benefit toward it, or on its wrong toward God, or finally on a contract. The Remonstrants hold the same things in their Synodal Writings, on Rom. 9:21, and Stephanus Curcellaeus defends the matter at length in his book On the innocent right of God over creatures, against Moses Amyraldus. But if we weigh the matter more carefully, although God has a right over his creature both from creation and from contract or covenant, and also a right to condemn justly on account of wrong, it must not be said that all of God's right arises from these. For by creation God has a right over the creature, as something made by him and dependent on him; but he does not acquire this right for himself from the act or benefit of creation. By creation indeed there is posited a subject, which otherwise would not exist, on which God may exercise his right; but the creature does not ground the faculty of right in God; it shows rather the going forth, the execution, and the exercise of that faculty in the subject, that is, in the creature. God receives nothing for himself, no right which we call divine property, from elsewhere or from the creature; he is self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης] and "the only blessed" [μόνος μακάριος], in himself, from himself, independently and universally, from nothing [אין]. But he cannot act according to that property, or exercise a right, or do anything outside himself, unless creation intervenes, the act which posits in the creature a subject on which to exercise the right, not the ground of having it in God. Similarly, from a contract entered into with the creature there arises for God an action and a right over the creature (as is usual in every contract), but not from this alone arises every right that God has over the creature, or even over the one with whom he contracts; nor does this right make him able to contract, or ultimately able to contract at all. The contract of God with the creature declares indeed what he wills, not so much what he can do; therefore the covenant is a sign of the divine will, not of his power, much less the foundation of it.

units.la: Qua vero ratione ex creaturae malefício nasci Deo jus potest, id est, ut bene retineamus punctum quaestionis, in Deo? nam si Deo intelligas jus dari hominem puniendi, ex peccato, citra quod cum juste punire non possit, male de jure, & juris in Deo proprietate, quâ de sola quaeritur, accipis, quod de actione dicitur, jus illud exercendi. Uti enim Iudex, ante actionem judicii, atque ante malefactum hominis, quo reus constituitur, justus est, sive justitia & jure praeditus fontem plectendi, ut non ei jus suum tum demum accedat, quidem occasio & subjectum jus & justitiam exercendi; ita in Deo, jus & justitia naturalis est, non demum ἐξωθεν adveniens, ex malefacto creaturae; tantummodo creatura delicto suo facit, non ut Deus justus sit, sed ut justitiam & jus declarare ac exercere in eam queat. Quare altius ascendendum atque juris divini fundamentum arcessendum non extra Deum, creaturâ, sed in ipso Deo constituendum, ejusq; natura. Quia vero jus latissimę est tum significationis, tum extensionis, prout jus δικαίωμα Rom. 1. ult. puniendi malefactorem dicit, sic vindicans seu puniens in Dei justitiâ specificè acceptâ fundatur: prout vero generatim jus agendi ex contractu, in justitiâ generatim sumtâ, seu veritate, & constantiâ Dei: prout deniq; ex creatione (ut species juris divini ab Arminio positas percurramus) cum creaturis agere Deo licet, in ejus situm dominio. Malach. 1.6. Filius patrem honorat, & servus Dominum: quod si pater sum, ubi est honor meus? & si Dominus sum, ubi reverentia mei? ait Iehova exercituum. Jerem. v. 22. an me non reverebimini? dictum Iehovae. an a facie mea non contremiscetis? qui disposui arenam terminum mari, statuto perpetuo, quod non transgredietur. Cap. x. 6,7. Ex eo quod nullus par tibi, o Iehova, maximus, & maximum nomen tuum potentia. Quis non revereatur te Rex gentium? Ex quibus duo consequuntur. 1. In quacunque Dei actione externa, & beneficio, nedum maleficio humano, fundari jus Dei non debere, tanquam radice & fundamento formali, unde Dei pendeat vel sequatur attributum, istud aut proprietas. 11. Sed jus quod habet, & ex quo agit, fundari in ipsa Dei natura, ejusque ὑπεροχὴ & superioritate in omnia.
units.tr: But by what reasoning can a right over God arise from the creature's wrongdoing? To keep the point of the question firmly in view, which concerns God. For if you mean that a right is given to man to punish sin, without which God could not justly punish, you misuse the word "right" and the proper sense of right as it applies to God, which is the only thing in question, and you apply to God's right what is said of action. For just as a judge, before any trial and before the man's crime that makes him a defendant, is just, that is, possesses justice and the right to punish, so that his right does not come to him only then, and the occasion and the subject merely give him the opportunity to exercise his right and justice, so in God right and justice are natural. They do not come to him from outside [ἔξωθεν] from the creature's offence. The creature by its sin does not make God just, but only enables him to declare and exercise justice and right against it. Therefore we must go higher, and seek the foundation of divine right not outside God in the creature, but in God himself and in his nature. For right is very broad both in meaning and in extent. As the right [δικαίωμα] to punish the wrongdoer, mentioned at Rom. 1 at the end, it rests on God's justice taken in the specific sense. As the general right to act from a contract, it rests on justice taken generally, or on God's truth and constancy. Finally, as the right arising from creation (to run through the kinds of divine right laid down by Arminius), God may deal with his creatures because they are in his power and dominion. Mal. 1:6: "A son honours his father, and a servant his lord; if then I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am a lord, where is my reverence? says the LORD of hosts." Jer. 5:22: "Do you not fear me? says the LORD. Do you not tremble before my face, who set the sand as the boundary of the sea, a perpetual decree which it cannot pass?" Ch. 10:6-7: "There is none like you, O LORD; you are great, and your name is great in might. Who would not fear you, O King of the nations?" From these two things follow. 1. In any external action or benefit of God, and much less in human wrongdoing, God's right ought not to be grounded as its root and formal foundation, from which God's attribute, or that property, depends or follows. II. But the right which he has, and by which he acts, is grounded in the very nature of God, in his preeminence [ὑπεροχή] and superiority over all things.

units.la: Non in illo. 1. Quia jus Dei ista antecedit, & prius illis est. Non ergo in iis fundari potest. Antequam Deus aliquid agit, vel creatura existit, quinimo pone quod non existat, neque Deus creet, non caret ideo suo jure, & potestate. Non quis ideo potestatis exsors est, vel jus amittit, quamvis non exerceat, nedum Deus. Qui seipsum privaret suo jure, nisi crearet: quod impossibile. 11. Potestatem Deus habet in facta non solum, sed & facienda, in nondum existentia, ἐξ [?] ποιῆσαι. Rom. ix. 21. Tertio, nihil Deus ab extrinseco acquirit, nihil accedit ei, actione externa sive sua, sive alienâ. Nam hoc contra naturalem ipsius foret αὐτάρκειαν, omnisufficientiam, beatitudinem, primitatem, & immutabilitatem. 1v. Nedum ut ab extrinseco juris sui regulam acciperet, ac mensuram: vel dici deberet, Deo non plus juris esse in creaturam, quam beneficiorum ei contulerit. Quæ hypothesis est Arminii. Fateor equidem, non tuto dici, Deum creaturam insontem infernalibus pœnis subjicere, sed hoc per justitiam suam nequit Deus & bonitatem, non quod re-gulam sui ullam capiat ab externo.
units.tr: Not in those things. 1. Because God's right precedes them and is prior to them. It cannot therefore be grounded in them. Before God does anything, or any creature exists, indeed even supposing that nothing existed and God created nothing, he would not lack his right and power. Nor does anyone lack power or lose a right because he does not exercise it, much less God. He would be depriving himself of his right if he did not create, which is impossible. II. God has power not only over things made, but also over things to be made, over what does not yet exist: to make [ποιῆσαι]. Rom. 9:21. Third, God acquires nothing from outside; nothing comes to him by any external action, whether his own or another's. For this would be contrary to his natural self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν], all-sufficiency, blessedness, primacy and immutability. IV. Still less would he take from outside the rule and measure of his right; otherwise it would have to be said that God has no more right over the creature than the benefits he has conferred on it. This is the hypothesis of Arminius. I admit that it is not safe to say that God subjects an innocent creature to infernal punishments, but God cannot do this consistently with his justice and goodness, not because he takes any rule for himself from something external.

units.la: Attamen, dices, & sic D, Curcellæus, cujus hic primum Dissertationem, argumentatur, beneficia conferunt potestatem & jus benefactori: sic & Deo, procul omni dubio, in creaturam, propter summum primumque beneficium creationis, competit jus suum. Resp. Aliud est, jus alicujus probare etiam aliunde; aliud, inde demum acquirere. Certissimum, quod ex creatione Deus etiam jus habet in creaturam, jus nimirum domini, & factoris: sed non omne suum jus, & non hinc demum acquirit. II. Aliud est, jus primo ortum; aliud, confirmatum. Confirmatur Deo suum ex creatione jus; non primitus inde oritur. III. Aliud, juris est fundamentum; vel, argumentum. Creatio, & reliqua Dei beneficia, totidem argumenta sunt juris postulandi, hominesque ad officium jure debitum commovendi; sed non ideo fundamentum juris primum sunt in Deo. IV. Vel distingue, fundamentum juris habendi, aut exercendi. Illud est, sola Dei ὑπεροχή [?]; hoc, creatio, & creatura. V. Illic formalitas principii attenditur: hic subjectum executionis, & exercitii. VI. Nempe de jure Dei hic quæ-rimus, ut formale dicit in Deo attributum, ac proprietatem; non ut notat juris egres-sum, exercitium, & exequutionem. VII. Negamus, beneficium semper benefactori jus conferre & potestatem in beneficiarium. Puta, si filius beneficium parenti; aut subditus Regi præstet, non tamen ideo hic in Regem, ille in Patrem jus obtinebit. Nisi neges, ista esse beneficia. Aliud est, ubi superioritas præcedit, & jus ex hac ortum, beneficia commendant, confirmantque; vel ubi nihil præter beneficia consideramus: quæ sola jus fundare nec possunt, nec solent. VIII. Jus aliquis habet ante omnia beneficia, forte & absque beneficiis, puta Rex jam electus, qui se nullo adhuc beneficio commendavit.
units.tr: Yet, you will say, and so D. Curcellaeus, whose first Dissertation this is, argues: benefits confer power and right on the benefactor; so too, beyond all doubt, God's own right over the creature rests on his greatest and first benefit, that of creation. Reply. It is one thing to prove a man's right also from elsewhere, another to acquire it from there. It is most certain that from creation God also has a right over the creature, namely the right of lord and maker; but it is not all his right, and he does not acquire it primarily from this. II. It is one thing for a right to have arisen first; another for it to have been confirmed. God's right is confirmed by creation; it does not first arise from it. III. It is one thing for something to be the foundation of a right, another for it to be the argument for it. Creation and God's other benefits are so many arguments for claiming a right and for moving men to a duty owed by right, but for that reason they are not the first foundation of right in God. IV. Or distinguish the foundation of having a right from that of exercising it. The former is God's sole preeminence [ὑπεροχή]; the latter is creation and the creature. V. In the former the formal character of the principle is considered; in the latter the subject of execution and exercise. VI. Indeed we are here inquiring about God's right as it names a formal attribute in God, and a property; not as it denotes the outflow of a right, its exercise and its execution. VII. We deny that a benefit always confers on the benefactor a right and power over the beneficiary. Suppose a son does a service for a parent, or a subject for a king; yet the one does not thereby gain a right over the king, nor the other over the father. Unless you deny that these are benefits. It is different where superiority comes first and the right arises from it, and benefits commend and confirm it; or where we consider nothing but benefits, which alone can neither found a right nor usually do so. VIII. Someone has a right before all benefits, perhaps even without benefits, as a king who has been elected but has not yet commended himself by any benefit.

units.la: Respondet Curcellæus, cap. II. Verum etsi liberi aut subditi, suis in parentes aut reges beneficiis, talem sibi in eos potestatem non acquirunt qualem illi habent, tantam tamen sibi comparant, ut parentes & reges vehementius eos amare, studiosiusque teneantur, quam alios a quibus ejusmodi beneficiis non fuerunt devincti. Resp. Nimirum hoc est dicere, liberos & subditos veram in parentes, & reges potestatem beneficiis suis non acquirere. Quod nos dicimus: ille autem hoc loco impugnat. Nam duo dicit, primo filios & subditos beneficiis suis potestatem non acquirere in reges, & parentes, qualem hi habent: id est, non veram. Quærimus enim non de quantitate potestatis, quam acquirant, sed de veritate, & an ullam veram? Hoc negamus: negat & natura, filium, qua filium, ullis suis beneficiis potestatem acquirere in parentem. Aliud est, si filius evadat Rex, vel alius, qui ex officio jus in parentem habeat, non uti filius in parentem, sed uti rex in subditum. Sic neque subditus in regem ullis beneficiis proprie dictum jus & potestatem impetrare potest, quin non iste rex, vel ille magis subditus futurus est. Ubique videmus, in superioritate jus fundari, non in beneficiis. Deinde dicit, filios & subditos sibi beneficiis suis parentum & regum conciliare affectum & amorem intensiorem, quam alias. Quis nescit, aut negat? Hoc non quæritur, quomodo alicujus devinciri animus queat & amor: quod beneficiis perfici, natura eorum, & a Regibus, parentibusque impetrari, passim omnium sensus docent. Sed de hoc non agamus : at de conciliandâ sibi in beneficiarios verâ potestate & jure. Quod longe aliud est, quam amorem illorum experiri.'Aliud amor, aliud potestas : amor alius erga te : vel potestas tua in alium. Amor parentis in filium : an filii potestas in parentem. Hoc monstri loco est ; illud naturale, & commune. Et sic, vel Regis erga subditos cura & affectus : vel subditorum in Regem vera ac propria potestas, sunt longe diversa. II. Aliud est vinculum obligationis mutuae ; aliud, potestatis. Illud ex mutuis oritur beneficiis, & officiis ; non hoc, sed ex superioritate. Illud effectum amicitiae est, hoc juris. Denique congruum censet parens, censet Rex, ut inferiorum officia remuneretur, non ex illorum in se jure ; sed sua aequitate & amore. Postremo quam haec nullius sunt, inde apparet, quia nemo juris quidpiam in Deum suis officiis adipisci potest, quatenus videatur ejus in se provocare amorem.
units.tr: Curcellaeus replies in chapter II: "Indeed, although children or subjects, by their benefits to parents or kings, do not acquire over them such power as the latter have, yet they gain so much that parents and kings are bound to love them more warmly and to hold them more diligently than others who are not bound to them by such benefits." Reply. Surely this is to say that children and subjects do not acquire by their benefits a true power over parents and kings. That is what we say, but he here attacks it. For he says two things: first, that sons and subjects by their benefits do not acquire over kings and parents a power such as the latter have, that is, not a true one. For we are asking not about the quantity of power that they acquire, but about its truth, and whether any true power at all. This we deny; and nature too denies that a son, as a son, acquires any power over a parent by any of his benefits. It is different if the son becomes king, or someone else who by office has a right over the parent: then he has it not as a son over a parent, but as a king over a subject. So neither can a subject obtain over a king, by any benefits, a right and power properly so called, without this king becoming, or that subject becoming, more of a superior. Everywhere we see that right is grounded in superiority, not in benefits. Next he says that sons and subjects by their benefits win for themselves a greater affection and love from parents and kings than others do. Who does not know this, or deny it? That is not the question: how a man's mind and love can be bound, which is accomplished by benefits, and which the nature of benefits and the common sense of all people teach everywhere, both when they are conferred by kings and parents and when they are received from them. But we are not discussing this; we are discussing the true power and right that a man wins for himself over those who benefit him. That is something quite different from experiencing their love. Love is one thing, power another: the love of another towards you, or your power over another. A parent's love for a son is one thing; the son's power over the parent is another. The one is monstrous, the other natural and common. So too the king's care and affection for his subjects, and the subjects' true and proper power over the king, are far different things. II. The bond of mutual obligation is one thing; power is another. The former arises from mutual benefits and services; the latter does not, but from superiority. The former is an effect of friendship, the latter of right. Finally, a parent thinks, and a king thinks, that it is fitting to reward the services of inferiors not from any right of theirs over him, but from his own equity and love. That these things confer no right at all is shown by this: no one can gain any right over God by his services, even if he seems to provoke God's love towards himself.

units.la: Omnis, inquit Curcellaeus, cui sum obligatus, aliquod in me jus ex illa obligatione habet. Imo cujus generis obligatio est, ejusdem & jus dicitur. Si obligatio sit in potestatem, jus notatur potestatis : quod si obligatio in beneficium, non jus potestatis, sed beneficii repetundi, non ad potestatem spectans & dominium proprie dictum ; sed amicitiam, ex quo fonte obligatio processit, seu beneficium obligationem pariens. Illud autem amicitiae opus, non potestatis fuit : nisi etiam subjectionis fuerit & obedientiae, unde nec in superiorem jus oritur, nec hujus in alterum veri nominis obligatio, tantum modo sic forte dicta ex civilitate & benigna aestimatione accipientis, non proprie dicto jure dantis.
units.tr: Every one to whom I am obliged, says Curcellaeus, has some right over me by virtue of that obligation. Rather, the kind of obligation determines the kind of right that is named. If the obligation is one of power, it is called a right of power. If the obligation arises from a benefit, the right is not a right of power, nor a right of recovering a benefit that looks to power and to dominion properly so called; it looks to friendship, from which source the obligation arose, or to the benefit that creates the obligation. That was the work of friendship, not of power, unless it also involved subjection and obedience. From it, therefore, no right arises over a superior, nor any obligation in the strict sense on the part of the one who receives such a benefit toward another. It is called an obligation only loosely, perhaps, out of courtesy and a kindly estimation on the part of the recipient, not by a right properly so called on the part of the giver.

units.la: Ut, si Titio, addit, sum obligatus ad certam pecuniae summam ei persolvendum, ille etiam jus habet eam a me exigendi : alioqui non vera & proprie dicta obligatio foret. Ratio autem discrepantiae manifesta. Quia obligatio illa, & sic jus ex ea procedens, non ex benefi-cio, sed ex debito est, ideoque verum jus tibi parit adversus debitorem. Nos autem quaerebamus de obligatione, quae nascatur ex meris beneficiis, an illa jus fundaret atque potestatem, per se, sine superioritate. Nam hominis apud Deum illa officia dari non possunt, quo Deum constituunt debitorem. Non Deum potes omnibus tuis officiis, beneficiorum, nedum debitorum reum facere. Denique aliud est, jus gratitu-dinis, sive exigendae, sive praestandae ; aliud, potestatis, vel directi dominii in alium exercendi, de quo hic disputamus. Illud ex beneficiis oritur in alterum collatis ; non istud.
units.tr: Thus, he adds, if I am obliged to pay a certain sum of money to Titius, he too has a right to demand it from me; otherwise it would not be a true and properly so called obligation. The reason for the difference is plain. That obligation, and the right that follows from it, arises not from a benefit but from a debt, and so it gives you a true right against the debtor. But we were asking about an obligation that arises from mere benefits, whether it of itself, without superiority, founds a right and power. For those services cannot be rendered by a man to God in such a way as to make God his debtor. You cannot make God a debtor by all your services, let alone by benefits. Finally, the right of gratitude, whether to be demanded or to be rendered, is one thing; the right of power, or of exercising direct dominion over another, which is what we are discussing here, is another. The former arises from benefits conferred on another; the latter does not.

units.la: Dei autem ὑπεροχὴ & majestas fundamentum est & formalis causa juris, quod habet in omnia, sive quae faciat, sive jubeat, regat, aut quocunque modo de illis disponat, nec potest non semper optime agere & sapientissime. Rom. ix. 21. 20. 19. Matth. xx. 15. Hinc in praeceptis divinis additum illud, ego Iehova. Levit. x. ix, 12. 14. 16. &c. Deut. v. 6. Non quod ideo haec potestas Dei, quamvis αὐτάρκῳ[?] & summa, ad injusta extendi possit vel debeat : quasi Deus praecipere pro absoluto jure contraria praeceptis & virtutibus, etiam amori sui, possit : vel creaturam immerentem poena afficere aeterna : aut quod hoc ex sententia illa sequatur ; aut ex doctrina, quae objectum praedestinationis constituit supra lapsum : vel ii, qui infra lapsum manent, & hinc praedestinationis, atque sententiae suae expositionem inchoant, putent ista ex illo sequi ; quae Remonstrantes praetexunt suae contra nos opinioni. Nam Dei absolutum jus ac potestatem nullo extra se vinculo alligatam tuemur ita, ut interim nihil contra se queat agere, id est, contra sapientiam suam, boni-
units.tr: But the hyperoche [ὑπεροχή] and majesty of God is the foundation and formal cause of the right he has over all things, whether he makes them, commands them, rules them, or disposes of them in any way, and he cannot but always act most excellently and most wisely. Rom. 9:21, 20, 19. Matt. 20:15. Hence the words I am Jehovah are added to the divine precepts. Lev. 10; 9, 12, 14, 16, etc. Deut. 5:6. Not that this power of God, though it is self-sufficient [αὐτάρκης] and supreme, can or ought to be extended to unjust things, as if God could, by an absolute right, command things contrary to his precepts and virtues, even to his own love, or inflict eternal punishment on a creature who has done nothing to deserve it. Nor does this follow from that opinion, or from the doctrine that makes the object of predestination lie above the fall. Nor do those who remain below the fall, and from this begin their account of predestination and their own opinion, suppose that these things follow from it; yet the Remonstrants put forward such things against our opinion. For we maintain God's absolute right and power, bound by no tie outside himself, in such a way that meanwhile he can do nothing against himself, that is, against his own wisdom, goodness, and justice.

units.la: Tom. 2. tatem, atque iustitiam. Deus sibi regula est, non homo Deo: & regulam nescit, qui omnium regula in se solus est ac manet.
units.tr: Vol. 2. God is a rule to himself; man is not a rule to God. And he who is the rule of all things, being alone in himself and remaining so, knows no rule.

units.la: Quando autem dicimus, ὑπεροχὼ [?] & maiestatem Dei fundamentum esse iuris in creaturas, intelligimus a se dependentes in esse possibili, & existentia reali. Atque ita etiam apud nos, non quaevis eminentia potestatem confert in quosvis, sed eminentia dignitatis in inferiores, a nobis, sive natura, sive constitutione, sive alia qua ratione dependentes. Nec dicas, hanc dependentiam inter beneficia recensendam: atq; ita nos incidere in sententiam contrariam. Nam dependentia haec non constituit ius in superiori; sed subiectum duntaxat, in quod superior suum habeat ius. Adeo ut connotetur & includatur dependentia illa ius istud; non vero haec decidat quaestionem: nulla autem ratione pro Adversariis: quia hactenus dependentia ista beneficiis distinguitur, quae illi unicum fundamentum iuris faciunt, & dependentiam consequuntur. Verbi gratia, Rex primum supra populum constitutus, qui nulla adhuc beneficia erogavit, potestatem tamen habet & ius regium. Quamvis alioqui dependentia illa in genus bonorum & beneficiorum etiam sua ratione referri possit: veruntamen magis respiciuntur beneficia dependentiam consequentia, & sic ius, non quod istud demum fundent.
units.tr: When we say that the hyperoche [ὑπεροχή] and majesty of God is the foundation of right over creatures, we mean creatures dependent on him both in possible being and in real existence. And so, among us too, not every eminence confers power over every person, but the eminence of dignity over inferiors who depend on us, whether by nature, by constitution, or by some other cause. Nor should you say that this dependence is to be counted among the benefits, and that we thus fall into the contrary opinion. For this dependence does not constitute a right in the superior; it is only the subject over which the superior has his right. So that dependence is implied and included in that right, and does not itself settle the question. Nor is there any reason for our opponents to claim it, since dependence is distinguished from those benefits which the opponents make the sole foundation of right and which dependence follows. For example, a king newly set over a people, who has not yet conferred any benefits, nevertheless has power and royal right. Although that dependence could also be referred, in its own way, to the class of goods and benefits, yet benefits that follow dependence are more regarded, and so the right, rather than the dependence, is what they ground in the end.

units.la: Hinc commode solvi possunt, quae D. Curcellaeus pro se, adversum nos, adfert, nam dum in hanc materiam incidimus, haud adeo levem & vulgarem, necesse est nervos totius disputationis incidere, & libri ipsius: quod hic nos praestare confidimus. Argumentatur ab exemplo Dei, ptobatque eius solam ἐξοχὴν non posse fundare ius, quia, quum illa ἐξοχὴ referatur ad aliud, quod non existit nisi per creationem, creatio potius iuris illius fundamentum videtur, quam sola excellentia: Finge enim Deum, si fieri posset, infinite perfectiorem esse quam reipsa est, ἐξοχὴν tamen nullam haberet, & consequenter nullum in alios ius, quamdiu solus existeret. Cum igitur creatio sit immediatum potestatis divinae in hominem fundamentum, proprium quoque est: non vero ὑπεροχὴ illa, quae Deo non competit nisi interventu creationis & propter creationem. Resp. 1. Simpliciter nego, ἐξοχὴν habere Deum nullam, quandiu solus. Neque Dei ἐξοχὴ per se & primo dicit respectum ad alia, vel ad alios; sed intimam Dei & essentialem maiestatem, quae semper eadem est, sita in ipsissima divinae naturae immensitate. Quod illam concipimus, & eloquimur ratione habita ad creaturas, non est quod aliter esse nequeat, sed quod iam ita sit, ut & conceptus & sermo noster ex creaturis ad hoc confuerit. Nec vox, aut notio ἐξοχῆς praeiudicare nobis debet, sub qua nil nisi maiestatem & dignitatem, ἀξιότητα Dei contueri animo debemus. II. Deus ante creationem, solus, non habet ius in alios existentes, fateor. At non ideo negandum ei omne ius, quod ipsi intrinsecum; vel etiam in alios possibiles & destinabiles, ad quod Deo placet, ἐξοχῆς ἢ [?] III. Creatio non est immediatum fundamentum potestatis divinae in hominem: sed Dei illa ὑπεροχὴ. adeoque, quod hic dicit, est τὸ ἐν ἐξοχῇ λαμβάνειν [?]. Si vero intelligat immediatum fundamentum exercendae vel exequendae in hominem potestatis, concedimus. Sed hoc praeter quaestionem est, qua inquiritur in fundamentum, non cuius interventu potestatem exerceat Deus, sed ex quo habeat. Et hoc dicimus, antecedere creationem, esseque Deo essentiale æternum, ὑπεροχὴν[?] & majestatem divinam, quæ, quamvis nunquam sequuta suis-set creatio, in se, & ab æterno semper ac necessario in Deo est.
units.tr: Hence what Dr. Curcellaeus brings forward in his own favour against us can be conveniently answered. For since we have come upon this matter, which is not a very slight or commonplace one, it is necessary to attack the sinews of the whole dispute and of his book itself, which we trust we shall do here. He argues from the example of God, and proves that God's excellence alone cannot found a right, because, since that excellence is referred to something else which does not exist except through creation, creation rather than excellence alone seems to be the foundation of that right. For imagine God, if it were possible, to be infinitely more perfect than he really is; he would still have no excellence, and consequently no right over others, as long as he alone existed. Since creation is therefore the immediate foundation of the divine power over man, it is also proper to it; but that hyperoche does not belong to God except through creation and on account of creation. Answer 1. I simply deny that God has no excellence as long as he is alone. Nor does God's excellence, in itself and primarily, refer to other things or other persons, but to the inner and essential majesty of God, which is always the same and lies in the very immensity of the divine nature. That we conceive it and express it with reference to creatures is not because it could not be otherwise, but because it is so, and our concept and speech have become accustomed to proceed from creatures to this. Nor should the word or notion of excellence prejudice us, under which we ought to contemplate nothing but majesty and dignity, the worth [ἀξιότης] of God. II. I grant that God, before creation and alone, has no right over others who exist. But it does not follow that every right intrinsic to him must be denied, or even that right over other possible and destinable beings, to whom God pleases to be [superior by excellence]. III. Creation is not the immediate foundation of the divine power over man; rather it is God's hyperoche. And so what he says is to take the thing in an excellent sense. If, however, he means the immediate foundation of the power that God exercises or carries out over man, we concede it. But that is beside the question, which asks for the foundation, not by whose intervention God exercises his power, but from which he has it. And this we say: that the divine hyperoche and majesty precede creation, and that it is essential and eternal to God; even if creation had never followed, it would be in God, in himself and from eternity, always and necessarily.

units.la: Objicit deinde exemplum Parentum: quorum potestas in filios non videtur niti ὑπερoχῇ[?], sed beneficio generationis: Potest enim fieri, ut filius fit doctus, ingeniosus, probus, robustus, pater contra. Et tamen pater in talem filium, cui tot in rebus est inferior, potestatem non minorem habet, quam si ipsi præfaret. Non ergo ob ἀξιοχρέων[?], sed ob generationis beneficium: quod si dicas parere ἀξιοχρέων[?], cui jus imitatur, id quod una manu videbaris eripere, altera reflituis. Resp. Non est per omnia similis ratio Dei, cum hominibus, in fundamento potestatis apud utrumque. Pater potestatem & dignitatem paternam non habet, nisi post generationem, filio existente: Deus autem divinam, quamvis homo non existat. Tum, non quæritur de potestate, vel jure Dei paterno in suos filios; sed de jure Dei in genere, & abstracte, in se: Dei, ut Dei; non Dei, ut Patris: quamvis hoc ab illo postea sequatur. Etiam potestatis humanæ causa est ὑπεροχή[?]. Atque paterna ὑπεροχή[?], quam Deus parentibus conciliat & attribuit, potestati; paternæ. Licet generatio fundamentum fit paternitatis; non tamen causa est istius eminentiæ, quæ in paternitate solum Deum auctorem habet. Uti homo quidem causa est hominis, ex generatione, non tamen ideo omnis istius præstantiæ quæ in homine generato est: ita generatio est quidem causa relationis, non tamen dignitatis æternæ. Generatio fundamentum est paternitatis, non vero causa proprie dicta & efficiens ἀξιοχρῆς[?], quæ ad paternitatem est in patre. Uti homo causa generationis, quando homo generat hominem, sed non animæ, quæ generatione exiflit, atque in generato est. II. Aliud genus eminentiæ est, virtutum nempe & donorum, quando filius est doctus, dives, &c. ab eminentia potestatis: unde fit, ut ex illo non sequatur jus aut potestas; non, in habentem potestatem, sicuti filio in parentem.
units.tr: He next objects the example of parents, whose power over their children seems to rest not on hyperoche but on the benefit of generation: For it can happen that a son is learned, clever, upright, and strong, and the father the opposite. And yet the father has no less power over such a son, in whom he is inferior in so many things, than if he excelled him. Therefore it is not on account of worth, but on account of the benefit of generation; and if you say that the worth [ἀξιοχρέων] of the parent is the basis, you give back with one hand what you seemed to take away with the other. Answer: The case of God and of men is not altogether similar in the foundation of power in each. A father has paternal power and dignity only after generation, once the son exists; but God has divine power even though man does not exist. Moreover, the question is not about God's paternal power or right over his own children, but about God's right in general, considered abstractly and in itself: God as God, not God as Father, although the latter follows from the former afterwards. The hyperoche is also the cause of human power. And the paternal hyperoche, which God confers on and attributes to parents, is the paternal power. Although generation becomes the foundation of paternity, it is not the cause of that eminence, which has God alone as its author in paternity. Just as a man is indeed the cause of a man by generation, yet not the cause of all the excellence that is in the begotten man, so generation is indeed the cause of the relation, but not of eternal dignity. Generation is the foundation of paternity, but not the cause properly so called and efficient of the worth [ἀξιοχρῆς] that belongs to the father in relation to paternity; just as a man is the cause of generation when a man begets a man, but not of the soul, which comes into existence by generation and is in the begotten. II. There is another kind of eminence, namely of virtues and gifts, when the son is learned, rich, and so on; this is an eminence different from the eminence of power. Hence it follows that no right or power follows from it over the one who has power, as the son has none over the parent.

units.la: III. Generationis beneficium, argumentum quidem filio est præstandi officium atque obedientiam patri; non vero patri fundamentum proprie dictum, ex quo formaliter oriatur sua ipsi potestas. Hæc altioris originis, eamq; à Deo habet Pater, & ejus benedictione qua Patribus, divinæ cujusdam ἀξιοχρῆς[?] referentibus similitudinem, talem concessit potestatem; non à filio, vel suo erga filium beneficio. Confirmat hoc quidem paternam potestatem apud filium; non autem primo & radicaliter fundat. Unde nec dicimus, generationem parere ἀξιοχρῶ[?], sed indicare tantum, cui ea beneficio divino debeatur.
units.tr: III. The benefit of generation is indeed an argument that the son owes the father duty and obedience, but it is not properly the foundation from which the father's own power formally arises. That power has a higher origin. The father has it from God, and God grants such power to fathers by His blessing, since fathers bear a certain likeness to the divine. It does not come from the son or from the father's kindness towards the son. Generation confirms the father's power over the son, but it does not found that power primarily and radically. So we do not say that generation produces authority, but only that it indicates to whom that authority is due by the divine benefit.

units.la: IV. Beneficia à πῶς[?] ἐν ἐξουσίᾳ[?] ἢ ἐξουσίᾳ[?] provenientia, præter beneficium, aliquam trahunt etiam ab autore dignitatem, ut, dum hæc intercurrunt, non ita perspicue appareant limites & ratio utriusque, quam si mera beneficia, ab omni potestate remota, vel mera potestas consideretur, ad internoscendam diversam utriusque formam atque fundamentum.
units.tr: IV. Benefits that arise from [πῶς ἐν ἐξουσίᾳ ἢ ἐξουσίᾳ] carry along with them some dignity from their author as well as the benefit itself. So while these two run together, the limits and the nature of each are not as plainly seen as they would be if we considered pure benefits, apart from any power, or pure power, so as to distinguish the different form and foundation of each.

units.la: Adfert præterea eos, qui, quamvis regiis virtutibus excellant, non ideo tamen potestatem habent regiam, vel ad habenas regni admoventur. Argumento, in ἐξουσίᾳ[?] vel eminentia potestatem non recte à nobis fundari: Hoc volo, illos non continuo potestatem in alios obtinere, qui ita excellunt: imo contra sæpe, ut res humanæ se habent, in pulvere neglectos jacere. Dicam aliquid amplius: Pone quempiam in republica in tantum concives suos animi & corporis dotibus antecellere, ut cæteros omnes longo infra se intervallo relinquat: non tamen tenebuntur eum regem constituere, si democratia ipsis magis quam monarchicum regimen allubescat. Tantummodo si de rege eligendo consultatio iniretur, reliquis propter istam ad imperandum aptitudinem praeferri mererentur. Resp. 1. Non in quavis eminentia dicimus fundari quamcunque potestatem, non in eminentia virtutum, donorum, seu corporis, seu animi; sed in eminentia ἀξιότιμῳ[?] autoritativae: illa est dignitas meritorum; haec, regiminis. II. Aptitudo illa meritoria non fundat potestatem, non ut habeat eam ita meritus, nec ut in minus merentes omnes eam propterea exerceri sequatur: unde nil nisi potestatum omnium confusio oriretur: sed neque, quod plus est, habenti potestatem, fundant eam sua merita, fundamento nimirum, prout hic sumus, originali potestatem obtinendi. Aliud est, ut apte digneque potestatem quis exerceat. Sed pone aptissimum & εἰδῷ[?] ἀξιώτατον[?] eligi in regem, potestatis tamen in eo regiae fundamentum non est illa ejus ad regnum gubernandum aptitudo. Fateor, causam esse, debere saltem esse, quare illum in regem eligant homines: sed electo & constituto non est sua potestas aut a meritis suis, aut a populo; sed a Deo: a populo quidem est, ut rex designetur; sed a Deo, collata ei regia ἀρχή, hinc potestas. Haec non a populo, qui ipse illam nec habet, neque dare potest: sed designat & notati illum, in quem consentit, ut conferatur ipsi a Deo illa dignitas, quam dignitatem ipsi ut θεῖον, non suam, reverenturac colunt. Etenim αἱ ἐξουσίαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ τεταγμέναι εἰσίν[?]: & gratia Dei regunt, qui regni clavo ab hominibus quamvis admoventur. Neque enim est potestas, nisi a Deo. Iterum, quemadmodum in generatione homo corpus praebet & designat quasi, cui Deus ex communi providentia animam increat, quam, qui generatur, a Deo habet, non a parentibus: sic in potestatibus humanis, subjectum designant quidem homines, sed jus tum ἀρχή tum potestas confertur eidem a Deo. Ut non habeant potestatem reges supremam illam regiam ex meritis profluentem, vel populi suffragio, aut aliorum designatione, sed ab eminentia, & authoritate regali, quam iis solus conciliat & tradit Deus.
units.tr: He also brings forward those who, although they excel in royal virtues, do not for that reason have royal power or are not raised to the reins of the kingdom. From this he argues that power is not rightly founded by us on authority or eminence: I maintain that those who excel in this way do not at once obtain power over others; indeed, on the contrary, as human affairs stand, they often lie neglected in the dust. I will say something more. Suppose someone in a commonwealth so surpasses his fellow citizens in gifts of mind and body that he leaves all the rest far beneath him. Yet they will not be bound to make him king, if a democracy pleases them more than monarchy. Only if a consultation were entered upon about choosing a king would the others deserve to be preferred to him on account of his aptitude for ruling. Reply, first: we do not say that every power is founded on every kind of eminence, not on eminence of virtues, gifts, or of body or mind, but on the eminence of authority, which is the dignity of rule; the former is the dignity of merits. Second: that meritorious aptitude does not found power, neither so that the one who has merited it thereby has it, nor so that power should follow to be exercised by all who merit less. From that, nothing but a confusion of all powers would arise. But, what is more, their merits do not found power for the one who already has it, at least not in the sense in which we are speaking, namely as the original ground for obtaining power. It is one thing for someone to exercise power aptly and worthily. But suppose the most fit and most worthy man is chosen king. The foundation of royal power in him is still not that aptitude of his for governing the kingdom. I grant that men have a reason, or at least ought to have one, for choosing him as king. But once he is elected and installed, his power comes neither from his merits nor from the people. It comes from God. It is from the people that he is designated as king, but it is from God that the royal authority is conferred on him, and hence the power. The people do not give it, since they do not themselves have it and cannot give it. They merely designate and mark out the man to whom they consent, so that this dignity may be conferred on him by God; and they honour that dignity as something divine, not as their own. For "the powers that are ordained of God" [αἱ ἐξουσίαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ τεταγμέναι εἰσίν] (Rom. 13. 1), and those who are lifted to the helm of the kingdom by men are governed by the grace of God. For there is no power but of God. Again, just as in generation the man supplies the body and, as it were, designates the one into whom God creates the soul from His common providence, and the one who is begotten has that soul from God and not from his parents, so in human powers men designate the subject, but the right of rule and the power are conferred on him by God. Kings therefore do not have their supreme royal power as flowing from their merits, or from the vote of the people, or from the designation of others, but from the eminence and the royal authority which God alone bestows on them and hands over.

units.la: III. Pari modo dicendum est, non ex beneficiis provenire regiam potestatem. Minus certe, quam ex suis meritis. Quippe nulla adhuc praestiterint beneficia, tamen reges sunt, regiamque obtinent authoritatem. Propter beneficia quae ab iis exspectantur regiam habere potestatem, etiam temere dicitur. Certum est, inquit Curcellaeus cap. II. omnem potestatem conferri aut propter beneficia jam ante accepta, aut propter accipiendi in posterum ipsam. Verum sic aberrat a scopo, non enim finis quaeritur, ob quem regia alicui deferatur dignitas, quidque ab eo exspectetur: sed quodnam fundamentum sit, ex quo potestas, tanquam causa sua antecedente, propria, & adaequata oriatur. Imo Rex potest esse, a quo nullum speres beneficium, sed omnia metuas mala. Etiam, qui nunquam praestet ullum beneficium, & nihilominus Rex erit: ergo hoc non ex beneficiis habet, sed a regia ἀρχή. Et quia familiaribus exemplis uti placet Adversario, fume quod satis obvium est in gradu Doctoratus, qui quando alicui confertur, primum tribuitur ei Doctoralis ἀρχή, & creatur Doctor, inde potestas datur eidem exercendi & faciendi omnia, tum fruendi jure ac privilegiis omnibus, quae illi ἀρχή debentur.
units.tr: III. In the same way it must be said that royal power does not arise from benefits, and certainly less than it arises from their merits. Indeed, kings are kings and hold royal authority even though they have not yet conferred any benefits. It is also rashly said that they have royal power on account of the benefits that are expected from them. It is certain, says Curcellaeus in chapter II, that all power is conferred either on account of benefits already received before, or on account of benefits to be received in future. But in this he misses the point. For the question is not the end for which royal dignity is conferred on someone, or what is expected from him, but what the foundation is from which power, as its antecedent cause, arises as its own and adequate. Indeed, someone may be a king from whom you hope for no benefit, but from whom you fear all kinds of evil. Someone who never confers any benefit will nonetheless be king. Therefore he does not have this from benefits, but from royal authority. And since the Adversary likes to use familiar examples, take what is quite obvious in the degree of Doctor. When this is conferred on someone, first the doctoral authority is given to him, and he is created a Doctor. Then power is given to him to exercise and do all things, and afterwards the right and all the privileges that are owed to that authority.

units.la: Denique ἄγγελος objicit, qui, quantumvis eminentes, nullum tamen in homines obtinent imperium: Sed nihil est quod adeo luculenter offendat solam ὑπεροχὴν nullum in aliis inferioris fortis jus tribuere, atque Angelorum exemplum, qui licet agilitate, robore, sapientia caeterisque virtutibus longe homines superent, nullum tamen in eos imperium obtinent. Sed sunt ministratores spiritus, Hebr. 1. 14. Resp. 1. Quorsum iterum virtutes commemorat? neque nos in illis fundamentum constituimus potestatis, haud magis quam in beneficiis. 11. Ex ὑπεροχῇ, non aut virtutum, aut meritorum, vel beneficiorum, sed authoritatis & dignitatis, sequitur potestas; sed non in omnes, vel omnia ista ὑπεροχὴ quoquomodo minora, vel inferiora, sed sola sub ea constituta, vel ab ea dependentia. Unde Deus qui infinitus & a quo omnia, in omnia potestatem habet, quia uti ab eo, sic etiam sunt sub eo. Angeli vero & homines potestatem habent a Deo limitatam, & in ea modo, quae ab ipsis dependent. Jam autem Deus non subjecit Angelis homines, vel hominibus Angelos, sed hi & illi in ista modo quae a se dependent, potestatem habent a Deo precariam & limitatam. Cui potestatem convenientem ipsis indidit, vel ἡγεμονίαν[?] & dignitatem.
units.tr: Finally, the Angel objects that, however eminent they are, they still have no rule over men: Yet there is nothing that so clearly offends against the view that mere superiority gives no right over those of lower strength, as the example of the angels, who, though they far surpass men in agility, strength, wisdom and other virtues, nevertheless have no rule over them. But they are ministering spirits (Heb. 1. 14). Reply, first: why does he again mention virtues? We do not found power on them, any more than on benefits. Second: power follows from superiority, not of virtues, merits or benefits, but of authority and dignity; yet it follows not over all those who are in some way lesser or inferior in every respect, but only over those who are placed under that superiority or depend on it. Hence God, who is infinite and from whom all things come, has power over all things, because all things both come from Him and are under Him. The angels and men, however, have a power from God that is limited, and only within the sphere that depends on them. Now God has not made men subject to the angels, nor angels subject to men. Rather, each has in those matters that depend on itself a power from God that is precarious and limited, to which He has given the power and dignity that fit them.

units.la: Ex quo jam facile etiam est respondere ad delirum aliorum, quod adjungit, commentum: sequitur ut si mundus a Deo non fuisset conditus, sed ut nonnulli delirarunt, ex fortuito atomorum concursu coagmentatus, Deus in ipsum nullum jure imperium aut potestatem esset habiturus. Delira argumentatio, cui parem potest formare hanc, si alius etiam Deus esset, huic in illum nullum jure competeret imperium aut potestas. Nam facere aliud independens, est facere alium Deum. Apage cum tali hypothesi, quae esse nequit, & turpem ac manifestam involvit contradictionem. Mundus non potest non a Deo dependere. Neque potest nisi unus esse Deus. In mundum Deus potestatem habet. Potestatem habet, non hinc primum quia a Deo dependet, sed dependet a Deo, quia & a Deo, & hic in illum potestatem habet. Potestatem autem habet Deus ex, & a se. Bene tamen dixerimus, quia mundus a Deo dependet, in eum potestatem habet, nempe ut argumentum, ex quo colligere, ut a posteriori, licet, Deum in mundum potestatem habere, non vero ut sit tamquam causa a priori dominium illud primum fundans.
units.tr: From this it is now easy also to answer the nonsense that he adds as a fiction: It follows that if the world had not been created by God, but, as some have raved, had been put together by a chance concourse of atoms, God would have had no rightful rule or power over it. This is a foolish argument, and one can form a similar one: if there were another God, no rightful rule or power would belong to this one over that one. For to make something else independent is to make another God. Away with such a hypothesis, which cannot exist and involves a shameful and manifest contradiction. The world cannot but depend on God, and there can be only one God. God has power over the world. He has this power not first because the world depends on Him, but the world depends on Him because both it is from God and God has power over it. Yet God has power from Himself and of Himself. Still, we may fairly say that, because the world depends on God, He has power over it, namely as an argument from which we may conclude, by way of a posteriori reasoning, that God has power over the world; but it is not as though that dominion, as a cause a priori, were the first thing founding it.

units.la: Unde, quod postremo subjungit, S. Scriptores, fundamentum Dominii Dei in hoc uni-versum ab illius excellentia non petere, sed creatione. Inter alios Davidem, dicentem: verbo Domini caeli confirmati sunt, &c. Psal.33. & Paulus, Deus qui fecit mundum, &c. Act.17. & falsum est, quatenus negat Scriptores Sacros id facere, quod secus se habere modo ostendimus, vel hinc quando Deus rationem mandatorum suorum adferens dicit, quia ego Iehova: & elencho peccat, dum non probat quod probandum erat. Neq; enim sequitur, S. Scriptores inter alia, ad pietatem & religionem moventia, argumentum quoque petunt ex creatione, ergo in creatione constituunt fundamentum potestatis divinae, non in Dei excellentia. Quia aliud est argumentum; aliud, fundamentum. Aliud argumentum apud hominem, quo moveatur: aliud, fundamentum apud Deum, quod eum dicat illum esse, aut hoc & illud habere. Atq; ita occasione data digressionem instituimus haud inutilem vel inconvenientem de fundamento potestatis & juris in Deo, quod situm in ejus ὑπεροχῇ, non beneficiis, aut creatione, vel contractu.
units.tr: Hence, as for what he adds at the end, that the Sacred Writers do not seek the foundation of God's dominion over this universe in his excellence but in creation, citing among others David, who says, By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, etc. (Ps. 33), and Paul, God, who made the world, etc. (Acts 17): this is false, insofar as it denies that the Sacred Writers do what we have just shown to be otherwise, not least where God, giving the reason for his commandments, says, because I am Jehovah. And he errs in his argument, since he does not prove what needed proving. For it does not follow that because the Sacred Writers, among other things that move to piety and religion, also draw an argument from creation, they therefore place the foundation of divine power in creation and not in God's excellence. For argument is one thing, and foundation another. An argument before man is that by which he is moved; a foundation before God is that which makes him to be what he is, or to have this and that. And so, the occasion being given, we have undertaken a digression, not unhelpful or out of place, on the foundation of power and right in God, which lies in his ὑπεροχή, and not in benefits, or creation, or contract.

units.la: Quae quaestio haud minimi momenti est in variis Theologiae capitibus & quaestioni-bus, tum ad hoc quod impraesentiarum tractamus, de contractu, seu foedere divino, ejusque & legislationis, denique vitæ æternæ nobis & promissæ, & exspectatæ, fundamento.
units.tr: This question is of no small importance in various heads and questions of theology, both for the matter we are now treating, concerning the contract or covenant of God, and for its legislation, and finally for the foundation of the eternal life promised to us and expected by us.

units.la: Ergo in fœdere Dei cum homine, primò jus spectamus Dei & potestatem, ex quâ agere cum homine potuit; tum gratiam, qua ita benigne voluit promittere tam amplam mercedem, vitæ, ad stipulationem & conditionem officii, seu justitiæ nostræ. Fœdus operum, aut legis, aut naturæ etiam dicitur: nempe lege præscriptum; operibus observandum; naturæ statim à creatione impressum. Ideoque fœdus est antiquissimum, & universale ad omnes homines æque pertinens, & naturam universam.
units.tr: Therefore, in God's covenant with man, we look first at God's right and the power by which he was able to deal with man; then at his grace, by which he was so kindly pleased to promise so ample a reward, life, on condition of the stipulation and duty, that is, of our righteousness. The covenant is also called the covenant of works, or of law, or of nature: namely, because it was prescribed by law, to be observed by works, and impressed on nature from the moment of creation. Hence the covenant is the most ancient, and universal, pertaining equally to all men and to the whole of nature.

units.la: Fœdus alterum gratia, est pactum, seu quasi contractus Dei cum hominibus peccatoribus, de redemptione & salute æterna, per Christum Mediatorem obtinendâ, si in ipsum credant. Quod dicitur justitia fidei. Convenit utrumque fœdus 1. in Auctore Deo. 11. altera contrahentium parte, homine. 111. in promissione vitæ, in genere. 1v. stipulatione conditionis aliquâ. v. & justitiæ, in genere. v1. denique in fine supremo, qui est Dei gloria. Differunt autem 1. in σχέσει[?] Dei, quam ibi, aut hic habet. Ibi spectatur ut Deus creator; hic ut misericors. 11. Illud cum homine integro initum fuit; hoc, lapso. 111. Illud fundatum in hominis natura; hoc, in Christo. 1v. illud absque; hoc, in Mediatore. v. Stipulatio ibi fuit conditionis justitiæ operum nostrorum perfectæ; hic, fidei. v1. Et promissio illic vitæ simpliciter; hic, illius per redemptionem, ex antecedente miseriâ acquirendæ. v11. Illud tempore antecessit. v111. Fuitque universale cum omnibus hominibus; at hoc particulare est, cum salvandis.
units.tr: The other covenant is that of grace: it is a pact, or quasi-contract, of God with sinful men, concerning redemption and eternal salvation to be obtained through Christ the Mediator, if they believe in him. This is called the righteousness of faith. Both covenants agree (1) in the author, God; (2) in the other party to the contract, man; (3) in the promise of life, in general; (4) in some condition of stipulation; (5) in righteousness, in general; (6) and finally in the supreme end, which is the glory of God. They differ, however, (1) in the relation [σχέσει] which God has there or here. There he is viewed as Creator; here as merciful. (2) The former was entered into with man whole; the latter with man fallen. (3) The former was founded on the nature of man; the latter on Christ. (4) The former was without a Mediator; the latter is through a Mediator. (5) The stipulation there was a condition of the perfect works of our own righteousness; here, of faith. (6) And the promise there was of life simply; here, of life to be acquired through redemption, out of a preceding misery. (7) The former preceded in time. (8) And the former was universal, with all men; but this is particular, with those who are to be saved.

units.la: Nonnulla adhuc obiter ad pleniorem horum explicationem discutienda & enodanda veniunt. Quorum primum, in hac situm quæstione: Quum dicimus homini in fœdere operum promissam vitam, quam intelligamus? an animalem & terrenam in Paradyso degendam; an vero beatam in cœlis? Negant Sociniani, in V. T. factas vitæ æternæ ullibi promissiones: sed Messiæ & Euangelii, temporisque ejus quo Messias venit, proprium esse & solum, vitæ æternæ promissum, nullatenus ante. Ita Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, cap. 11. & vii. Quamvis ajant, ad vitam æternam quidem Patres, atque Adamum, perductos fuisse, sed non ex promissione ulla ipsis hac de re factâ, aut certâ ejus apud illos spe, sed conjecturis modo (ita Smalcius loquitur:) quemadmodum scilicet gentiles, ejus rei ignaros, postea adduxit ad se & salutem Messias. Socinus, contra Puccium, cap. x. pag. 275. Atque ita, non quia homines, si non peccassent, quamvis naturalem mortem experti essent, ad æternam tamen vitam postmodum Dei benignitate (non dicit, ex promissione) perventuri erant. Volkelius, de Religione sua, lib. iii. cap. xi. Rem autem plane, ut dicimus, ita se habere, inde perspicuum est, quod Moses de industria dataque operâ antiqui illius fœderis promissa enumerans, nullam vitæ sempiternæ mentionem facit. & pag. 66. Ex iis, quæ hactenus à nobis disputata sunt, aperte colligitur, non solum in magno errore illos versari, sed in Christum etiam injurios esse, qui primos parentes nostros immortales creatos fuisse contendunt. Hunc enim primum, ut satis jam demonstratum est, immortalitatis & præconem & datorem Deus esse voluit. Quæ quidem laus ei detrahitur, ipsumque immortalitatis bonum valde extenuatur, si antequam Christus & nasceretur, & muneris sui officium fuisset, hominem jam in ipso mundi primordio, naturâ immortalem extitisse affirmatur. Quare constat, Socinianorum sententiam esse, vitâ in legis fœdere promissâ, cœlestem immortalemque illam non significari. Alii, qui quidem dem non negant vitæ æternæ promissionem Patribus sub V. T. factam, in fœdere gratiæ illis proposito, censent tamen, sub promissione vitæ fœderi naturæ addita non cælestem denotari, sed animalem, ejusque beatæ in Paradyso continuationem perpetuam; & prout adjuncta est eadem promissio vitæ, fœderi eidem operum à Mose repetito & sancito cum Israële, designari vitæ fruitionem in terra Canaan. Respondemus, utrosque falli. Socinianos quod attinet, illos forte penitus negaturos fœdus naturæ, quod statuimus: certe negare, vitam æternam Adamo quovis modo promissam: quod in sequentibus erroris studebimus [?] convincere: Jam vero levi brachio ostendendum, fœdus illud naturæ cum Adamo, & omnibus hominibus initum: tum & promissione sancitum, promissione vitæ scilicet cælestis, fuisse. Quod ad primum, Natura rationalis legem justi & æqui inscriptam sibi habet, quam etiam post lapsum retinet, ac sentit: ergo Deus naturæ isti fixit & proposuit. Si jam velint alii negare fœdus naturæ, quia ejus Scriptura in creationis historia expresse non meminit, negent etiam, quod natura neminem negare sinit, legem illam naturæ esse impressam. Nam & natura, & consensus omnium hominum, Gentilium etiam, legem illam testantur. II. Et Scriptura, Rom. II. 14. Quando igitur gentes legem habentes, natura ea quæ legis sunt, faciunt, illi legem non habentes, sibi ipsis lex sunt. Qui ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis. Lex duplici modo homini revelata, in cordibus, & Scripturis: utraq; substantia est eadem. III. Et Socinian ipsi legi naturæ testimonia perhibent: quæ alibi protulimus, Socinianismi Confut. lib. 1. cap. VII. pag. 140. Unde infero, quod eadem sit substantia & materia legis naturæ, & scriptæ, id est, tum ejus quæ in natura hominis est, tum quæ in verbo Dei. Moralis ubiq; eadem. Quod ex collatione capitum & dogmatum utriusque constare potest. Colendum Deum, amandum proximum esse, & justi injustiq; discrimen docet eadem lex: idem natura, idem Scriptura traditur, diverso quidem tradendi modo, non autem rei & legis traditæ. Deinde, uti legis scriptæ promissio est vita, ita, ex præmissis negari nequit, quin eadem sit & legis naturalis. Non modo propter utriusque convenientiam; sed quod non absque promissione soleat lex & fœdus pangi, non à Deo. Per ea, quæ supra allegata fuerunt, ex Jesai. XLV. 19. & Malach. I. Ubi autem lex, & legis pro-missio, vita, ibi & fœdus legis. Quod & in natura fundatum. Superest modo, quid per vitam accipiendum in legis promissione sit? Alterutrum, vel vita animalis intelligenda, in hac terra; vel beata, in cœlis. Beata autem in terris nescio quâ ratione po-natur, quum beatitudinem omnes sciamus & collocandam in cœlis, ἐν ἐπουρανίοις [?]; & sic in Scriptura passim doceri; & terram, aut vitam animalem ejus non esse capacem. Longe enim quid aliud, atque excellentior est visio, seu fruitio Dei, in quâ vera perfectaque beatitudo sita, Psalm. XVI. 11. Matth. v. 8. & XVIII. 10. 1 Cor. XIII. 12. 1 Ioann. III. 2. quam ut in hac vita homini obtingere, vel dari possit.
units.tr: Some further matters come up for discussion and clarification in passing, for a fuller explanation of these points. The first of these lies in this question: when we say that life was promised to man in the covenant of works, what are we to understand by it? Is it the animal and earthly life to be lived in Paradise, or the blessed life in the heavens? The Socinians deny that promises of eternal life are found anywhere in the Old Testament, but say that the promise of eternal life is proper and peculiar to the Messiah, to the Gospel, and to the time when the Messiah came, and by no means before. So Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, chapters 11 and 7. Although, they say, the Fathers and Adam were indeed brought to eternal life, this was not by any promise made to them on this matter, nor by a certain hope of it among them, but only by conjectures (so Smalcius speaks), just as the Messiah afterwards brought the Gentiles, who were ignorant of the matter, to himself and to salvation. Socinus, against Pucci, chapter 10, page 275: And thus it was not that men, had they not sinned, even though they had undergone a natural death, would afterwards by God's kindness come to eternal life (he does not say, by promise). Volkelius, in his On his Religion, book 3, chapter 11: That the matter stands plainly as we say is clear from the fact that Moses, deliberately and purposely enumerating the promises of that ancient covenant, makes no mention of eternal life at all. And on page 66: From what we have argued so far, it is plainly gathered that those who maintain that our first parents were created immortal not only are in great error but also do wrong to Christ. For, as has been sufficiently shown, God willed that he should be the herald and giver of immortality. That praise is taken from him, and the good of immortality itself is greatly diminished, if it is affirmed that man was already immortal by nature at the very beginning of the world, before Christ was born and had begun the office of his work. It is therefore clear that the Socinian view is that the life promised in the covenant of law does not signify that heavenly and immortal life. Others, who indeed do not deny that the promise of eternal life was made to the Fathers under the Old Testament, in the covenant of grace proposed to them, nevertheless hold that under the promise of life added to the covenant of nature, the life denoted is not heavenly but animal, and its perpetual continuation in blessedness in Paradise; and, insofar as the same promise of life is attached to the same covenant of works, repeated and sanctioned by Moses with Israel, it denotes the enjoyment of life in the land of Canaan. We reply that both are mistaken. As for the Socinians, they would perhaps deny altogether the covenant of nature, which we maintain; certainly they deny that eternal life was promised to Adam in any way, which in what follows we shall make an effort to refute. Now we must show with a light arm that that covenant of nature, entered into with Adam and all men, was also sanctioned by a promise, namely a promise of heavenly life. As to the first point: rational nature has the law of the just and the right inscribed upon it, which it retains and perceives even after the fall. Therefore God established and proposed it to nature. If others now want to deny the covenant of nature, because Scripture does not expressly mention it in the account of creation, let them also deny what nature does not allow anyone to deny, that this law of nature has been impressed. For both nature and the consensus of all men, including the Gentiles, bear witness to that law. II. And Scripture, Rom. 2:14: When therefore the Gentiles, who have not the law, do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts. The law is revealed to man in two ways, in the hearts and in the Scriptures; the substance of both is the same. III. And the Socinians themselves bear witness to the law of nature; we have produced these elsewhere, Socinianism Refuted, book 1, chapter 7, page 140. Hence I infer that the substance and matter of the law of nature and of the written law are the same, that is, both that which is in the nature of man and that which is in the word of God. The moral law is everywhere the same, which can be established from comparing the heads and doctrines of each. The same law teaches that God is to be worshipped and one's neighbour loved, and the difference between just and unjust; the same is handed down by nature and by Scripture, in a different manner of handing down, but not in the thing and law handed down. Further, just as the promise of the written law is life, so, from what has been premised, it cannot be denied that the natural law has the same. This is not only because of the agreement between the two, but because a law and covenant are not usually established without a promise, and not by God. From what has been cited above, from Isaiah 45:19 and Malachi 1... Where there is law and a promise of life under the law, there also is the covenant of law, which is also founded in nature. It remains only to ask what is to be understood by life in the promise of the law? Either animal life in this earth is to be understood, or blessed life in the heavens. Yet I do not know on what ground a blessed life should be placed on earth, since we all know that blessedness is to be located in the heavens, in heavenly things [ἐν ἐπουρανίοις], and that Scripture teaches this everywhere, and that the earth, or animal life, is not capable of it. For the vision or enjoyment of God, in which true and perfect blessedness lies, is something far other and more excellent, Ps. 16:11; Matt. 5:8; 18:10; 1 Cor. 13:12; 1 John 3:2, than can be attained or given to man in this life.

units.la: Jam quod illa vita, seu cœlestis, in legis promisso intelligi debeat, probamus, non modo ex simplici vitæ appellatione, quæ omnem illam, id est, beatam etiam comprehendit; sed quoque ejus significatione istum in modum in Sacris explicata. Matth. XIX. 16. 17. Quid boni faciam ut habeam vitam æternam? Si vis intrare in vitam, serva mandata. Quæstionem format ille de vita æterna; Christus respondet simpliciter de vita: ut illa duo in hoc genere pro synonymis haberi significet. Finis observantiæ mandatorum, & expositio vitæ lege promissæ, ponitur vita æterna. Neque ea, vel interrogatione discipuli, aut responsione Christi intelligitur hoc in mundo, aut in terrâ degenda, verum in coelis. Et sic sumendum illud Apostoli, Galat. III. 12. qui fecerit ea homo, vivet in eis. Rom. VII. 10. Mandatum, quod ad vitam erat. Similiter in Veteri Testamento, Levit. XVII. 5. Observabitis statuta mea & judicia mea, quae faciens homo vivet in eis. Jezech. XX. 11. Dedi eis statuta mea & judicia mea, quae faciens homo vivet in eis. Non autem de vita animali, aut in Paradyso, aut Canaan agenda exponere licet, quae in genere de vita Scriptura dicit, non habita ad hunc, vel illum locum restrictione: nam & extra utrumque saepe egerunt homines: & non locus ullus terrenus satisfacere potuit in vitae fruitione, qualem, ex plenitudine promissionis, sibi poterant polliceri undiquaque vitalem & felicem. Neque in Canaan, neque terrarum ullibi illa vitae conditio homini obtingere poterat, quae meram vitam, & beatam, absque miseria, & morte, attulisset. Et vitam tamen simpliciter, id est talem lex promittebat. Denique ex oppositio mortis, legis comminatione expressae, satis dabatur intelligi, qualis e contrario legis promissio, & vitae qualis, esset. Mortem minatam aeternam ipsi Sociniani affirmant, quare ex adverso vita aeterna & coelestis, quae illi opponitur, intelligenda etiam venit.
units.tr: Now we prove that this life, the heavenly one, must be understood in the promise of the law, and this is shown not only by the bare word "life", which includes all that life, that is, the blessed life too, but also by the way the Scriptures explain it. In Matt. 19:16-17 the man asks, "What good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life? ... If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments." He asks about eternal life, and Christ answers simply about life, so that the Lord means these two to be taken as synonyms in this matter. Eternal life is named as the goal of keeping the commandments and as the description of the life promised by the law. Neither in the disciple's question nor in Christ's answer is it understood as life to be lived in this world or on earth, but in heaven. So too must be taken the Apostle's words in Gal. 3:12, "he that doeth them shall live in them", and Rom. 7:10, "the commandment, which was unto life." Similarly in the Old Testament, Lev. 18:5, "Ye shall keep my statutes and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them", and Ezek. 20:11, "I gave them my statutes and shewed them my judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them."* It is not permissible to explain this as animal life to be lived either in Paradise or in Canaan, since Scripture speaks of life in general terms, without any restriction to this or that place. Men often lived outside both. No earthly place could satisfy the enjoyment of life that they could promise themselves, from the fullness of the promise, as life that was altogether vital and happy. Neither Canaan nor any other land could give man that condition of life which would have brought a life that was pure and blessed, without misery and death. Yet the law promised simply life, that is, such life. Finally, from the opposition to death, which the law's threat expressly states, it was sufficiently clear what the promise of the law was, and what life was, by contrast. The Socinians themselves affirm that the death threatened is eternal, so by the same token the eternal and heavenly life that is opposed to it must also be understood.
