units.la: Quaestio secunda, ad expositionem utriusque foederis facit haec: quid inter conditionem foederis hujus & illius, tum operum, tum fidei, adeo interfit, quod differentiam utriusque faciat. Praesertim quum illa dicatur justitia operum, etiam haec fidei. Resp. Imo differentia hic attendenda, eaq; satis magna & clara, qua nititur omne foederis utriusque discrimen. Nempe non est fides redigenda in censum operum: alioqui foedus utrumque, & diversam utriusque naturam aperte confundes: Sed, quantum interest inter dare, & accipere, tantum differentiae videtur inter utramque conditionem, operum, ac fidei. Operibus nostris, & legis ex operibus observantia videmur Deo quasi dare aliquid, nempe id quod operum a nobis exigit, & observationem mandatorum ejus: at fide, primo agnoscimus nos Deo debitum id nostrum ex lege, dare non posse; tum oblatam datamque nobis justitiam Christi, & amorem ac gratiam Dei in eo, nos accipere; amorem Dei nos non mereri, sed gratis in Christo oblatum amplecti. Nos non dare amorem nostrum Deo primum, inde & ejus erga nos consequi, ex legis foedere quasi debitum; sed gratuitum nos Dei, & primum erga nos in Christo amorem applicare nobis, inde sequi nostrum, ut illius effectum, & debitae fructum gratitudinis. Tantum differunt ergo conditio foederis primi, & secundi, operum, ac fidei. Unde etiam patet, quod, quando dicitur justitia fidei, non ita intelligendum hoc sit, quasi fides pro opere, aut justitia operis veniat, quod esset utrumque inter se commiscere foedus, non distinguere; sed, quum in hoc foedere nihil spectetur, quam quod nos accipimus, Jesai. LV. 1. fides hic non operis proprie, ad justitiam legalem spectantis, sed instrumenti oblatam gratiam amplexantis, rationem habet. Rom. III. 25. Phil. III. 9.
units.tr: The second question, bearing on the explanation of each covenant, is this: what difference is there between the condition of this covenant and that one, both of works and of faith, such that they differ so much? This is especially so since the righteousness of works is called that, and the righteousness of faith likewise. Answer: Indeed the difference here must be noted, and it is quite large and clear, and on it rests the whole distinction between the two covenants. Faith is not to be reckoned as a work; otherwise you would plainly confuse the two covenants and their different natures. But just as there is as great a difference between giving and receiving, so there seems to be a difference between the two conditions, that of works and that of faith. By our works, and by keeping the law through works, we seem to give something to God, namely what the works and the observance of his commandments require of us. But by faith, first, we acknowledge that we cannot give God that which we owe him under the law; then we receive the righteousness of Christ offered and given to us, and the love and grace of God in him. We do not merit the love of God, but embrace it offered freely in Christ. We do not first give our love to God, so that his love toward us follows from it as something due under the covenant of law; rather, God's free and first love toward us in Christ is applied to us, and from this our love follows, as its effect and the fruit of a debt of gratitude. So the condition of the first covenant, that of works, and that of the second, that of faith, differ just that much. From this it is also clear that when the righteousness of faith is spoken of, it should not be understood as if faith took the place of a work, or as if righteousness came from works. That would mix the two covenants together rather than distinguish them. Since in this covenant nothing is looked at except what we receive (Isa. 55:1), faith here has the character not of a work, which pertains to legal righteousness, but of an instrument that embraces the grace offered (Rom. 3:25; Phil. 3:9).

units.la: Quaestio tertia fit haec: Quomodo dicamus, foedus operum, seu naturae universale esse, ad omnes spectare homines, & naturam totam; hoc vero gratiae particulare, ad solos salvandos, quum & hoc videatur universale esse, saltem quod ad gratiam, universum omnibus jam ab oeconomia Euangelicae praedicationis, oblatam? Resp. Alia res est externa Euangelii praedicatio, vel foedus ea comprehensum. Aliud, loqui de intentione foedus paciscentis Dei, quam solam hic consideramus, quando foedus gratiae cum nullis aliis inire intendit, quam salvandis electis; aliud, de ministerio homi-num illi foederi exequendo inservientium, qui ignorantes quinam in individuo salvandi illi sint, & scientes ex quavis natione & tribu, Apoc. v. 9. ex universa terra» Matth. xxviii. 19. Deum quosvis in istud foedus adducere, vocant quoscunque, & quibuscunque foederis tabulas proponunt, ut iis, dum non omnes, illi saltem assentiantur, qui ad hoc electi. Matth. xxii. 14. Interim neque haec quidem vocatio aut praedicatio Euangelii universalis est, quamvis fit communis; Deo sua sic moderante, ut vel hinc appareat, foedus hoc non esse, quemadmodum primum illud, universale, sed uti indebitae gratiae, supra peccatum & hominis miseriam supervenientis, ita nec omnium, sed illorum, quibus Deo complacuit. Matth. xi. 26. Luc. xii. 32. Rom. ix. Commune quidem foedus est, ad quoscunque citra discrimen spectans, non autem universale, ad omnes, & singulos in universum. Ita hic distinguimus, inter id quod commune, & quod est universale.
units.tr: The third question is this: how can we say that the covenant of works, or of nature, is universal, pertaining to all men and to the whole of nature, while the covenant of grace is particular, pertaining only to those who are saved, since this covenant too seems to be universal, at least as regards grace, since by the plan of the gospel preaching it is offered to all? Answer: The external preaching of the gospel, or the covenant comprised in it, is one thing. Another thing is the intention of God making the covenant, which alone we consider here, since he intends to enter the covenant of grace with none but the elect who are to be saved. Another thing is the ministry of men serving in the execution of that covenant. They do not know who in particular are to be saved, but knowing that God will bring to this covenant men of every nation and tribe (Rev. 5:9) and from the whole earth (Matt. 28:19), they call whomever they can and set before them the tables of the covenant, so that, though not all assent, at least those who are elect may. (Matt. 22:14.) Yet this calling or preaching of the gospel is not universal, although it is common, since God so governs it according to his own purpose. This shows that this covenant is not, like the first, universal, but is a grace undeserved, coming in above sin and man's misery, and so it belongs not to all but to those in whom God is well pleased (Matt. 11:26; Luke 12:32; Rom. 9). The covenant is indeed common, pertaining to whomever without distinction, but it is not universal, pertaining to all and each in general. So here we distinguish between what is common and what is universal.

units.la: Jam consideranda foederis utriusque est oeconomia, & varia dispensatio, adhibita a Deo sub Veteri, & sub Novo Testamento. Quippe non uno utrobique modo foedus, tum hoc, tum illud administratum fuit, tempore ante Christum exhibitum, & post; sed, quemadmodum alia, ita & hoc, πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως. Utrumque foedus, & utriufq; doctrina, & usus fuit sub Testamento utroque: sed diversimode, tam in foedere hoc, quam illo. Respectu foederis legalis prima ejus periodus attendenda, in prima ejus pactione cum Adamo; fecunda, in illius repetitione & renovatione, per Mosem. Foederis Euangelici prima periodus est, a promissione & promulgatione ejus prima statim a lapsu, Genef. iii. 15. quae variis inde tum promissionibus, tum figuris & caeremoniis confirmata, ad tempora usque Christi exhibiti: & hinc periodus altera: illa proprie προευαγγελίας; haec, Euangelii. Quidquid autem fit de variis utriusque foederis periodis & dispensationibus, utrumque foedus ubique viguit, a lapsu nempe, in Ecclesia; & quidquid fit de accidentali circumstantiarum variatione, substantia & summa eadem fuit, & secum convenit utrobiq; tum hujus temporis, tum illius. Oeconomia & dispensatio foederis, Testamentum vocatur, & quamvis pro foedere ipso vox fumatur, fpeciatim tamen foederis dispensationem respicit: & ita distinctionis ergo, duplex Testamentum, Vetus atque Novum dicimus, dispensationem utriusque foederis, jam, & ante exhibitum Christum, sub Veteri & Novo Testamento. Heb. viii. 7.8.9. Deinde, ratio utriusque Testamenti primo fuit imperfectior, deinde perfectior: tum Testamenti Veteris illa a lapsu, ad Mosem: tum ista, deinceps. Nam ante Mosem quidem disciplina Vet. Testamenti fuit; sed a Mose, quod ad omnes suas leges & δικαιώματα λόγια, in leges & ordinem perfectum relata ac congesta. Euangelii tempora a Christo nato, ad exaltatum, & praedicationem Apostolicam potiora istis fuerunt. Atque ita diversa dispensatio obtinuit cum foedere utroque, ejus primordiis, atque αρχῇ, sub hoc, & illo Testamento. Tertio, discrimen Testamenti utriusque (non dico foederis, de hoc enim jam ante actum, sed oeconomiae utriusque) peti ex duplici causa debet. Primo, Christi promissi, aut exhibiti. Secundo, populi, aut unius Ifraelitici, apud quem olim Ecclesia; vel mundi universi, aut terrae omnis, in quam delata verbi divini doctrina, & Ecclesia postmodum fuit. Ex varia tum hujus, tum illius jam, aut tunc, ratione nascitur utriusque Testamenti diversitas. Quae in hisce consistit. 1. Sub V. T. lex caeremonialis fuit: sub Novo, non. 11. Praedominans tum ministerium legis, & foederis legalis: hodie non. Imo lex non docetur, in ordine ad foedus, aut foedus
units.tr: Now we must consider the economy of each covenant and the varied dispensation that God employed under the Old and the New Testament. For the covenant, both this and that, was not administered in one and the same way on both sides, before Christ was exhibited and after; but, as with other things, so with this also, it was "in many parts and in many ways" [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως]. Each covenant, and the teaching and practice of each, existed under both Testaments, but in different ways, in this covenant as in that. With respect to the legal covenant, its first period is to be noted, namely its first agreement with Adam; the second is in its repetition and renewal through Moses. The first period of the gospel covenant runs from its first promise and promulgation immediately after the fall (Gen. 3:15), which was then confirmed by various promises, and also by types and ceremonies, down to the time of Christ's revelation; and hence the second period. The first is properly the time of the pre-gospel [προευαγγελίας]; the second, of the gospel. Whatever may be the case with the various periods and dispensations of each covenant, each covenant has flourished everywhere in the Church from the fall onward. And whatever variation there is in accidental circumstances, the substance and sum were the same, and in both periods they agreed with one another. The economy and dispensation of a covenant is called a Testament, and although the word is taken for the covenant itself, it properly refers to the dispensation of the covenant. So, for the sake of distinction, we speak of a twofold Testament, Old and New, meaning the dispensation of each covenant, both before and after Christ was revealed, under the Old and the New Testament (Heb. 8:7-9). Next, the form of each Testament was at first more imperfect, and afterwards more perfect: that of the Old Testament from the fall to Moses, and then the later form. For before Moses there was indeed a discipline of the Old Testament; but from Moses on, all its laws and its [δικαιώματα λόγια] were put into a fixed and complete order and arrangement. The times of the gospel from the birth of Christ to his exaltation and to the apostolic preaching were more excellent than those. Thus a different dispensation obtained with each covenant, in its beginnings and its [ἀρχῇ], under this Testament and that. Third, the difference between the two Testaments (I do not mean the covenants, for that has already been treated, but the two economies) must be drawn from a twofold cause. First, from the Christ promised or revealed; second, from the people, either the single Israelite nation among whom the Church once was, or the whole world and all the earth, to which the doctrine of the divine word and the Church were afterwards carried. From the varied circumstances of this and that, of now and then, arises the difference between the two Testaments, which consists in the following points. 1. Under the Old Testament the law was ceremonial; under the New it is not. 2. The ministry of the law and of the legal covenant predominated then; today it does not. Indeed the law is not taught in order to the covenant, or the covenant [the rest of the sentence continues in the original].

units.la: Tom. 2. Nn fœdus legale ; duntaxat ut regula vitæ, & norma sanctitatis ac officii nostri : in ordine ad sanctificationem, non ad justificationem. iii, Hinc status ille pædagogiæ fuit, & servitutis ; Euangelii vero, libertatis est. iv. Obscurior & parcior dispensatio gratiæ, cognitionis & beneficiorum Christi, atque Spiritus S. ibi ; quam temporibus N. Testamenti. v. Etiam angustior & restricta ad unum populum : nunc ad omnis generis homines, sine discrimine, producitur.
units.tr: Vol. 2, Nn. The legal covenant served only as a rule of life and a standard of holiness and of our duty, with respect to sanctification and not to justification. (iii) Hence that state was one of tutelage and servitude, whereas the Gospel is one of liberty. (iv) The dispensation of grace, of the knowledge and benefits of Christ, and of the Holy Spirit was then more obscure and sparing than in the times of the New Testament. (v) It was also narrower and confined to one people, whereas now it is extended to men of every kind without distinction.

units.la: His præmissis, dispiciendum venit, an sub Vet. Test. etiam cognitum fuerit fœdus Euangelicum, seu promissio gratiæ & salutis in Christo,& remissionis peccatorum,& Spir. Sancti: an nota illa Patribus fuerint,qui sub Vet.olim Testamento vixerunt? Socinus differentiam Novi Test. à Veteri constituit in duobus, præceptis nempe, & promissis: in illis quidem,quod V.Testi.quædam præcepta omittat & tollat,alia vero reddat perfectiora scilicet, & veteribus de novo peculiariter addat: quod ad promissa istam facit utriusque differentiam, quod hoc promittat vitam æternam, remissionem peccatorum, & Spir. Sanctum, quæ Vetus Testament. ignoravit, nec cultoribus suis proposuit. Socinus, in Themat. de Officio Christi, Th. xxxiii. Dicimus igitur Novum Fœdus apertissimam vitæ æternæ promissionem nobis attulisse ; præterea promissum remissionis omnium peccatorum, quatenus hoc à vitæ æternæ promissione seu consecutione, per viam intellectus, ut dicitur, distingui potest ; denique promissum, omnibus fidelibus consequendum, Spiritus Sanctus. Quibus omnibus cum Vetus illud Fœdus careat & caruerit, & terrenam felicitatem proposuerit, facile est Novi Fœderis præstantiam hac in parte cognoscere. Quod si illis prorsus caruit Vetus Testamentum, profecto Novi immensa est supra illud præstantia: sed quia vera sine illis religio esse nulla potest, propterea nisi eam omnem veteribus derogare volumus, ista quoque illis deneganda non sunt. Sed de his in sequentibus. Cum autem duplex cum Adversariis hic sit quæstio, de præceptis, quà Veteris, quà N. Testamenti, & promissis, hanc illi præmittere visum,quia annon V. T. habuerit ejusmodi promissiones, ad illud pertinere ; an præcepta alia & per-fectiorem legem Novum Testamentum, ad hoc spectare videtur : & sic ipsa rei tem-porisque inter utrumque Testam. ratio ac ordo exigere, ut de illo prius, antequam de isto, dicamus.
units.tr: Given these points, we must examine whether the Gospel covenant, that is, the promise of grace and salvation in Christ, of the forgiveness of sins and of the Holy Spirit, was also known under the Old Testament, and whether the Fathers who lived under the Old Testament knew it. Socinus establishes the difference between the New Testament and the Old in two things, precepts and promises. As to precepts, the Old Testament omits and abolishes some of them, while the New makes others more perfect and adds some new ones peculiar to itself. As to promises, the difference lies in this: the New promises eternal life, the forgiveness of sins and the Holy Spirit, which the Old Testament did not know and did not set before its worshippers. Socinus, in the Theses on the Office of Christ, thesis 33: We say, therefore, that the New Covenant has brought us the most manifest promise of eternal life; further, the promise of the forgiveness of all sins, insofar as this can be distinguished, by way of the understanding, as it is said, from the promise or attainment of eternal life; lastly, the promise of the Holy Spirit, to be obtained by all the faithful. Since the old covenant lacks all these things, and has lacked them, and has set before us earthly happiness, it is easy to recognise the superiority of the New Covenant in this respect. If the Old Testament entirely lacked these things, then surely the superiority of the New over it is immense. But since true religion cannot exist without them, unless we wish to deny all of this to the ancients, these things too must not be denied to them. But of these matters more will be said below. Since there are two questions here with our opponents, concerning precepts, both of the Old and of the New Testament, and concerning promises, I thought it right to put the latter first, because whether the Old Testament had promises of this kind pertains to the former question, while whether the New Testament has other and more perfect laws seems to belong to the latter. Thus the nature of the matter and the order of time between the two Testaments require that we speak of the former before the latter.

units.la: Primò ergo quæritur : An promissio vitæ æternæ, & remissionis peccatorum, ac Spiritus S. & salutis in Christo, Patribus enim facta & oblata fuerit in Veteri Testamento, ab iisque credita, & proinde eâdem viâ salvati sint, quâ nos ? Affirmat Ecclesia: Sociniani negant. Quorum primùm exponenda est sententia, tum examinanda. Ac illa primum, quam tenent, de variis religionum formis, quas à mundi initio Patribus obtigisse, commemorant. Tum, quod qualibuscunque illis, promissionem tamen vitæ æternæ negant annexam ullibi fuisse.
units.tr: First, then, the question is this: was the promise of eternal life, of the forgiveness of sins, of the Holy Spirit and of salvation in Christ made and offered to the Fathers in the Old Testament, and was it believed by them, so that they were saved by the same way as we are? The Church affirms it; the Socinians deny it. Of these, first their view must be set out, and then examined. And first, that view which they hold concerning the various forms of religion which, they relate, were given to the Fathers from the beginning of the world; then, that whatever these forms were, they maintain that the promise of eternal life was never attached to them anywhere.

units.la: De illo statuunt: Deum, pro temporum diversitate, diversitas sui colendi vias hominum generi ostendisse. Volkelius, lib. ii. cap. viii. diversas Deum colendi vias, & tem-porum religiones appellat. Dispescitque religiones illas in eam, quæ primi mundi fuit, ante Abrahamum ; tum quæ ab Abrahamo; tertio loco ponit Mosaicam; denique, Chri-stianam. In singulis spectat tum præceptiones, seu pietatis officia ; tum promissiones, & minas, vel saltem spem præmiorum, ac pœnarum metum. In prima religione, sic loquitur, quam aliam ponit ante, & post diluvium, homines non tam ex fixis statisque legibus, seu generalibus præceptis, aperte à Deo propositis, quam rectæ rationis judicio, quod singularibus Dei mandatis, ad certas personas, certave negotia pertinentibus non raro instructabatur, firma-
units.tr: Concerning the first, they state: God, according to the diversity of the times, showed mankind a diversity of ways of worshipping him. Volkelius, book 2, chapter 8, calls these diverse ways of worshipping God and religions of the times. He divides those religions into the one which existed before Abraham, at the beginning of the world; then the one from Abraham; third he places the Mosaic; and finally the Christian. In each he considers both the precepts, or duties of piety, and the promises, and threats, or at least the hope of rewards and the fear of punishments. In the first religion, he speaks thus, which he posits before and after the flood, men were instructed not so much by fixed and settled laws, or general precepts, openly proposed by God, as by the judgement of right reason, which was not seldom instructed by particular commands of God, pertaining to certain persons and certain affairs, and was confirmed so as to have composed their life and morals;

units.la: Ex fixis statisque legibus: sic in editione; fixis statisque legibus / seu generalibus. firmabaturque, vt itam ac mores suos composuisse; & nullum reperiri generale Dei praeceptum hominibus propositum. Post diluvium generalia Noacho & posteris ejus tradita praecepta, caeremoniale unum, alterum morale, de non fundendo sanguine humano. Genes. ix. 4. 5. 6.
units.tr: "Ex fixis statisque legibus" stands thus in the edition: "fixis statisque legibus / seu generalibus." ... and was confirmed so as to have composed their life and morals; and no general command of God is to be found that was proposed to men. After the flood, the general precepts given to Noah and his posterity were one ceremonial and the other moral, concerning not shedding human blood. Genesis 9:4, 5, 6.

units.la: Ad quae Respondemus. Teneri ante omnia debere. 1. Religionem, non in duas duntaxat partes, praecepta, & promissiones, sed in tres distingui; addita illis parte prima, quae doctrinam complectitur credendorum. Uti haec alias adstruximus, & probavimus. 11. Religionis distinguenda est essentia, & forma interna; ab externo, & accidentali eam proponendi propagandique modo. Non quamvis hic, illa variat; nec pro diversa ejus exponendae & tradendae formâ constituendae sunt religiones diversae. Non magis quam hominem alium & alium, diversis formis, dicas, qui jam infans, modo vir est, sub quâ similitudine hominum, diversus etiam religionis, sub Vet. & Novo Test. status describi in Sacris solet. Neque enim aetatum & statuum diversitas formam mutat essentialem, sed conditionem duntaxat & habitudinem externam. 111. Vel foederis divini distingue substantiam, ab ejus variâ, quam sortitum est jam vel tum, oeconomiâ & dispensatione. 1v. Aliud est res, & rei factum; aliud, ejus historia. Non, quamvis haec sileat, & mentionem omittat rei, negari ideo facta debet, vel potest. Praesertim in brevi adeo historiâ, ac est primi mundi, tam paucis comprehensa capitibus. Ut quae tum temporis obtinuerit religio, etiam aliunde, quam ex illis solum capitibus, sed vel ex Scripturâ reliquâ, vel analogiâ communi fidei, peti atque dijudicari debeat, v. Aliud est revelatio; aliud, ejus quoque conscriptio, vel Scriptura. Primi aevi Patres non habuerunt quidem Scripturam; sed revelationem, cui innitebantur. In scripta redigere demum Moses jussus fuit: ante cujus tamen tempora Deum πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως etiam loquutum Patribus, ignorare non possumus. Ejusque indicia haud obscura in brevi quamvis istorum temporum historia occurrunt.
units.tr: To these things we reply. First of all, it must be held: 1. that religion is not to be divided into only two parts, precepts and promises, but into three, with the first part, which contains the doctrine of what is to be believed, added to them. As we have argued and proved elsewhere. 2. The essence and internal form of religion must be distinguished from the external and accidental manner of setting it forth and propagating it. Religion does not differ because of this manner, nor are different religions to be posited because of the diverse form in which it is expounded and handed down. No more than one would say that a man is a different man in different forms, who is now an infant and now an adult. By a similar comparison the Scriptures usually describe the diversity in the state of religion under the Old and the New Testament. For the diversity of ages and conditions does not change the essential form, but only the external condition and circumstance. 3. Either the substance of the divine covenant must be distinguished from the varied economy and dispensation it has received now or then. 4. The thing itself and the fact of the thing are one matter; its history is another. The fact is not to be denied, nor can it be denied, because history is silent about it and omits mention of it. Especially in a history so brief as that of the first world, comprised in so few chapters. Nor should the religion that prevailed at that time be sought and judged only from those few chapters, but from the rest of Scripture or from the common analogy of faith. 5. Revelation is one thing; its written record, or Scripture, is another. The Fathers of the first age indeed did not have Scripture, but they had the revelation on which they relied. Moses was at last commanded to commit it to writing; yet we cannot be unaware that before his time God also spoke to the Fathers polymerōs kai polytropōs [in many portions and in many ways]. And clear indications of this occur even in the brief history of those times.

units.la: Atq; ita dicimus. 1. Non ex solo rationis judicio vixisse primaevos patres: utpote quibus, praeter legem naturalem inscriptam cordibus, Rom. 11. 15. etiam de summis mysteriis revelationem factam, Genes. 111. 15. atque ei fidem habuisse ipsos, Heb. xi. 2. id est, substantiam foederis salutisque propositam, non est quod dubitemus. Et quis dicere audeat, illos non ad istam magis vixisse, quam ad sensum ac judicium rationis? Mirum autem, indignumque merito videri debet, quod, cum omnia fere, quae ad religionem istorum hominum, ad praecepta & promissa ipsis facta spectant, recenseat Adversarius, studio omittat praecipuam de futuro Messiâ, ejusque officio, & redemtione promissionem illam, & celeberrimam, quae est Gen. 111. 15. de semine mulieris contrituro serpentis caput. Nisi promissionem illam doleat Patribus factam, quia est contra suas hypotheses, & putet illis à Deo negari debuisse, quod negandum sua censet non sana ratio. Smalcius, lib. de divinitate Christi, cap. 11. & contra Frantzium pag. 95. & 221. locum illum quidem fatetur Christi continere significationem aliquam; sed, Patribus non intellectam.
units.tr: And so we say: 1. The first fathers did not live by the judgement of reason alone. For, besides the natural law written in their hearts (Rom. 2:15), a revelation was also made to them even about the highest mysteries (Gen. 3:15), and that they believed it (Heb. 11:2), that is, the covenant and the salvation proposed in its substance, there is no reason to doubt. And who would dare to say that they lived by this faith less than by the sense and judgement of reason? It must indeed seem strange and rightly unworthy that, although the Adversary recounts almost everything that pertains to the religion of these men, to the precepts and promises made to them, he deliberately omits the chief promise concerning the future Messiah, his office and redemption, the most famous one, which is in Gen. 3:15, about the seed of the woman who will crush the serpent's head. Unless he grieves that this promise was made to the Fathers, because it is against his hypotheses, and thinks that what he considers unsound reason decides should have been denied them by God. Smalcius, in his book on the divinity of Christ, chapter 2, and against Frantzius, pages 95 and 221, admits that this passage does indeed contain some reference to Christ, but that it was not understood by the Fathers.

units.la: Quod ad illa, quae promulgationem legis Resp. Negatur consequentia, Scri-antecesserunt, attinet, haberi quidem potest ptores N. Testamenti locum illum non pro aliqua ejus rei denunciatione, id, quod memorant inter promissiones de Christo Gen. 3. legitur: semen mulieris conteret caput factas; ergo pro promissione haberi non serpentis, quatenus nimirum per Iesum Chri- potuit. Deinde argumentum negatistum aslutia & potentia Satanæ contrita & conculcata est: sed quia nulli virorum sancto-rum novi fœderis, qui promissionum divina-rum antiquitus factarum mentionem faciunt, horum verborum meminit, & non nisi ab A-brahamo illa ordiuntur, pro promissione ca-verba haberi vix possunt, nisi fortassis mystico sensu, qui nunc quidem nobis patet, posteaquam Deus nobis Iesum Christum exhibuit: primis vero parentibus tunc temporis vix ac ne vix quidem patere potuit, nec porro, ut pateret, necesse ullo modo erat. In qua re tanto minus laborandum nobis est, quod multi præstantis-simi Theologi tam vetustiores, quam recentio-res, idem plane de loco isto sentiant.
units.tr: As to those things which preceded the promulgation of the law, it may indeed be held that the things they mention among the promises made concerning Christ are found in Genesis 3: the seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head. Answer: the consequence is denied. The writers of the New Testament do not use that passage as an announcement of that matter, which they recall among the promises of God made of old; the argument from their silence simply does not prove it, unless you show that the writers of the New Testament meant to recount, or did recount, all and each of the promises of the Old Testament, so that from their omission you may conclude that they did not regard it as such a promise. Hence the argument does not follow any more than... it may hardly be held as a promise, except perhaps in a mystical sense, which now indeed lies open to us, since God has shown us Jesus Christ; but to the first parents at that time it could hardly, or scarcely at all, have been open, nor was it at all necessary that it should become open. In this matter we need labour all the less, because many most excellent theologians, both older and more recent, think plainly the same about that passage.

units.la: vum simpliciter non probat: non, nisi ostendas, Scriptores N. Testamenti pro-missiones omnes & singulas V. T. recen-sere voluisse, vel recensuisse; ut tum ex hac omissâ concludas, eam pro tali ab il-lis habitam non fuisse. Quare non magis sequitur argumentatio, quam si inferas, in N. Test. non memoratur ille locus, ergo in Veteri non extat. Præterea neque Scriptores N. Testamenti dicunt locum illum haberi posse pro aliqua ejus rei denun-ciatione, quatenus per Christum aslutia & po-tentia Satanæ contrita & conculcata est: quod tu tamen isto loco contineri dicis: ergo tuo ipsius exemplo, atque explica-tione probas, ex silentio Scriptorum argumentum hac in parte non esse satis validum. iv. Neque distinguere licet, inter denunciationem, & promissionem: quia denunciatio rei bonæ futuræ, qualem ipse hic dicis, nisi de promissione accipi potest. v. Hic illius loci sensus vel constitit Novi fœderis Scriptoribus, vel non. Affirma-bis. Atqui nullus virorum sanctorum novi fœderis, qui promissionum divinarum antiquitus factarum mentionem faciunt, horum verborum meminit: neque etiam ut denunciationem continent Messiæ. Quare quum ex omissa rei mentione arguere nequeas ad Scri-ptores N. Testamenti, quasi illam nesciverint, non ex negata historia, ad negatam notitiam; minus concedetur tibi ut concludas ad homines, qui vixerunt sub Ve-teri Testam. omnes, quasi illud ignorassent, cujus forte probatio non potest peti ex Novo. vi. Accipimus, quod ex Novi Testamenti Scriptura instituis argumenta-tionem ad statum & conditionem Veteris: ut de hoc non ex ejus modo, live V. T. Scriptura, sed quoq; ex Novo, conclusionem fieri, & dignosci illius religionem debe-re, fatearis. vii. Loci Genes. iii. 15. explicatio & applicatio ad Christum vera est, non falsa. At quæro jam, Patres V. Testam. vel veram loci istius expositionem ha-buerunt, vel non. Non habuisse omnino, nullosque ejus ætatis vel Prophetas, vel Doctores, aut fideles verum loci, ejusque adeo illustris & necessarii, scivisse sensum, dici nequit: si vero sciverint, ergo jam intellexerint, denunciatum hoc loco, Diaboli aslutiam & potentiam per Christum conterendam & conculcandam fore. viii. Quotiescunque Christus Abrahamo, vel Davidi postea, & ejus posteris propositus fuit ut semen, ad Abrahamum quidem referri potuit, quod ad distinctam & claram ejus ex Abrahamo prosapiam; non tamen quasi ab eo demum ortam omnem de Christo promissionem; quinimo ut illud quod de Messia semine dictum toties ac repetitu, fundatum fuerit in primâ antiquissimáque Seminis benedicti promissione, primis hominibus facta. ix. Eo magis, quo promissio hæc & sola extat primo mundo, de Christo, facta, præterque eam in Scriptura alia nulla; & amplissimam continet brevi summario de Christi personâ, & officio doctrinam. Neque enim aliàs locum habebit, quod Smalcius hac ead. pag. dicit, Christo omnia à mundi conditione sæcula suo modo occupata fuisse, quodque eum omnes fere singulares & divinæ actiones, quæ ab initio mundi extiterunt, quodammodo figurarunt. x. Frustra nunc ad mysticum recurrit sensum, quasi per mysterium ex loco eruendum quod modo dixit eo denunciatum fuisse, de Christo potentiam Satanae contrituro. Utcunque vero, modo hunc sensum sciverint Patres, & intellexerint. Si omnino mysticum dicas sensum esse, quis ergo fuerit litteralis? Quod primis parentibus vix ac ne vix quidem sensus ille patere potuit, dicit, non vero probat. Minime, quod nec, ut pateret, necesse nullo modo erat. Contra quae necessitas fuit rei denunciandae, fuit & intelligendae. Neque est quod tantam nubem obtendant hoc in loco Patribus Adversarii, quum Judæi infideles, postquam καλύμματα ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν αὐτῶν κεῖται in lectione Mosis, viderunt tamen loco isto Messiam designari. unde Targum Jerosolymitanum locum ita accepit, ויהי כד יהון בניא דאתתא [?] & erit cum mulieris filii operam dabunt legi, & fecerint praecepta, conabuntur tibi percutere caput tuum atque interficere. Cum vero deseruerint filii mulieris praecepta legis, nec servabunt mandata, tu conaberis mordere illos in calcaneis eorum, atque in nocere. Verum remedium erit filiis mulieris; tibi vero serpenti nullum erit remedium. Quandoquidem futurum est, ut curaturi sint quo sibi auferatur morsus calcanei in fine dierum, in diebus regis Messiae, בימי דמלכא משיחא [?], Quod denique de aliis subjungit Theologis, idem de loco illo sentientibus, nullius a nobis fit, dum nec Theologos, nec eorum rationes profert.
units.tr: …simply does not prove it. Unless you show that the writers of the New Testament meant to list, or did list, all and each of the promises of the Old Testament, you cannot conclude from their omission that they did not regard it as such a promise. The argument is therefore no more sound than if you inferred that because that place is not mentioned in the New Testament, it does not exist in the Old. Moreover, the writers of the New Testament do not say that the passage can be taken as a declaration of the thing, that through Christ the cunning and power of Satan have been crushed and trampled, which you nevertheless say is contained in that place. So by your own example and explanation you prove that an argument from the silence of the writers is not strong enough in this respect. (iv) Nor may one distinguish between a declaration and a promise, because a declaration of a future good, such as you here describe, can only be understood as a promise. (v) Either the sense of that passage was established for the writers of the New Testament, or it was not. You will affirm the first. But no holy man of the New Testament who mentions the divine promises made of old recalls these words, nor do they recall it as a declaration concerning the Messiah. Therefore, since you cannot argue from the omission of a matter to the writers of the New Testament, as though they had not known it (from a denied history to a denied knowledge), you will still less be allowed to conclude about all the men who lived under the Old Testament that they were ignorant of it, when proof of this cannot be drawn from the New. (vi) We take it that you draw your argument from the Scripture of the New Testament to the state and condition of the Old, and you must admit that the conclusion about the Old must be drawn not only from its Scripture, that is the Old Testament, but also from the New, and that its religion must be recognised in this way. (vii) The explanation and application of Genesis 3:15 to Christ is true, not false. But I ask now: did the Fathers of the Old Testament have the true exposition of that passage or not? To say that they did not have it at all, and that no prophets, teachers or faithful of that age knew the true sense of a passage so important and necessary, cannot be maintained. But if they did know it, then they already understood that by this passage was declared that the cunning and power of the Devil would be crushed and trampled by Christ. (viii) Whenever Christ was set forth to Abraham, or afterwards to David and his posterity, as the Seed, this could indeed be referred to Abraham, in so far as it refers to his clear and distinct descent; but not as though every promise concerning Christ had arisen from him for the first time. Rather, what was said so often and repeatedly about the Messiah as the Seed was founded on the first and most ancient promise of the blessed Seed, made to the first men. (ix) All the more so, since this promise made to the first world concerning Christ is the only one extant, and there is no other in Scripture; and it contains in a brief summary a most ample teaching about the person and office of Christ. Otherwise, indeed, what Smalcius says on the same page would have no place, that all the ages from the creation of the world were occupied in their own way by Christ, and that almost all the singular and divine actions which have existed from the beginning of the world in some way foreshadowed him. (x) It is in vain that he now has recourse to a mystical sense, as though by a mystery to be drawn out of the passage that he has just said was there declared, concerning Christ who would crush the power of Satan. However that may be, did the Fathers know and understand this sense or not? If you say that the sense is wholly mystical, what then was the literal sense? That the sense could scarcely or not at all be open to the first parents, he says, but does not prove. Not at all, since it was in no way necessary that it be open. On the contrary, there was need for the thing to be declared and to be understood. Nor is there reason for our opponents to throw such a cloud over the Fathers in this place, since the unbelieving Jews, after a veil lies upon their heart [καλύμματα ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν αὐτῶν κεῖται] in the reading of Moses (2 Cor. 3:15), nevertheless saw that the Messiah was designated by that passage. Hence the Jerusalem Targum took the passage thus: And it shall be that when the sons of the woman labour at the law and keep the precepts, they will strive to strike your head and kill you. But when the sons of the woman desert the precepts of the law and do not keep the commandments, you will strive to bite them on the heels and to harm them. Yet there will be a remedy for the sons of the woman; but for you, serpent, there will be no remedy, since it is to be that they will take care to remove the bite of the heel at the end of days, in the days of the King Messiah [בימי דמלכא משיחא]. Finally, as for what he adds about the other theologians who think the same about that passage, it is not something to be dealt with by us, since he produces neither the theologians nor their reasons.

units.la: Ad Volkelium ut revertamur, quaerimus secundo, quomodo sibi ista conveniant, dicere, nullum reperiri Patribus ante diluvium generale Dei praeceptum propositum: & addere, ex quibusdam Dei dictis, quae inibi leguntur, generalia praecepta constituere non esse difficile? An, quod non difficile est ex dictis constituere, in illis non reperiri credendum est? Si variis a Deo admonitionibus eorum temporum homines etiam ante diluvium crebro instructos, ipsisque apparitionibus, ut Deum existere agnoscerent, crederentque, & eum colendum ac metuendum statuerent, edoctos fuisse, tum per se credibile fit, tum ex sacris litteris non obscure colligi possit, uti Volkelius hic loquitur; an dici potest, illos potius ex judicio rationis, quam legibus aut praeceptis generalibus vixisse? Dices, sed, non aperte a Deo propositis: at vero, quod non obscure, non difficile ex dictis colligi & statui potest, aperte etiam positum negari quomodo potest? Si ex iis, quae ibi narrantur, colligi possunt nonnulla pietatis officia, de quibus hominibus generatim omnibus vel constitit, vel constare facile potuit; ergo etiam generalia Dei mandata ad mores pertinentia. Itaque ipse Volkelius. Qui & addit, jam tum patuisse, Deum esse colendum ac metuendum, a malefactis esse abstinendum, recte factis studendum, appetitum esse coercendum, a caede tum aliorum omnium, tum imprimis sanguine junctorum, esse abstinendum; quae ille post diluvium, nos etiam ante illud cognita, & obtinuisse, ex Scriptura tuto asserimus. Quemadmodum ipse etiam ex illis, quae Abrahami aetate gesta, ad tempora & religionem illorum argumentatur: Quamvis autem haec jam Abrahami aetate gesta fuerint, tamen ex religione antea hominibus illis tradita ea manasse & satis per se clarum esse videtur, & inde apertius etiam constat, quo divinus cultus qui una cum Abrahamo incepit, nequaquam communiter, ut prior ille, ad omnes alias, sed ad solam Abrahami familiam revera spectabat. Denique Patrum illorum religio vel fuit mere naturalis, & rationis solius judicio orta & subnixa, vel supranaturalis, & Dei revelatione & praeceptis ordinata: non speciatim de horum aut illorum, sed piorum & fidelium tum omnium, live ecclesiae antediluvianae religione, quaero, ut non singularia, sed generalia ejus praecepta constituamus. Non (opinor) dices merè rationalem, vel naturalem Patrum religionem, aut Dei cultum fuisse, nam apparitionibus instructos, ut Deum existere agnoscerent crederentque, & eum colendum ac metuendum flatuerent, edoctos jam dixisti: quare si illorum religio supranaturalis, uti revera, fuit, non eam rationis judicium moderari potuit; sed fides.
units.tr: To return to Volkelius: we ask, secondly, how these statements agree with one another: that no general command of God is found proposed to the Fathers before the flood, and that he adds: from certain sayings of God which are read there, it is not difficult to establish general precepts? Is it to be believed that what is not difficult to establish from the sayings is not found in them? If, as Volkelius here says, men of those times were taught by God through various admonitions, and by appearances themselves, so that they would recognise that God exists, believe, and resolve to worship and fear him, this is credible in itself and can be gathered not obscurely from the sacred letters; can it be said that they lived by the judgement of reason rather than by general laws or precepts? You will say that these were not openly proposed by God; but how can what can be gathered and established from the sayings not obscurely, not with difficulty be denied to have been openly set forth? If from those things which are narrated there, some duties of piety can be gathered, of which it was or could easily be known to all men in general, then also the general commands of God that pertain to morals. So Volkelius himself. He also adds that it was already plain that God was to be worshipped and feared, that one must abstain from evil deeds, study right conduct, restrain appetite, and abstain from the slaughter of all others, and especially of kinsmen by blood; which things we, too, assert on the authority of Scripture to have been known and held before the flood, as well as after it. Just as he himself argues from what was done in the age of Abraham to the times and religion of those people: although these things were done already in the age of Abraham, nevertheless it seems sufficiently clear of itself that they flowed from the religion previously handed down to those men, and from this it appears more plainly still that the divine worship which began with Abraham did not, as that earlier one did, extend in common to all others, but truly pertained to the family of Abraham alone. Finally, the religion of those Fathers was either purely natural and arose and rested on the judgement of reason alone, or it was supernatural and ordered by God's revelation and precepts. I ask, not of the religion of these or those in particular, but of all the pious and faithful, or of the Church before the flood, so that we may establish not singular but general precepts of it. You will not say (I think) that the religion or worship of God of the Fathers was merely rational or natural, for you have already said that they were taught by appearances to recognise that God exists, to believe, and to resolve to worship and fear him. Therefore, if their religion was supernatural, as in truth it was, the judgement of reason could not govern it, but faith did.

units.la: Caeterum de promissis, illorum temporum hominibus factis, necesse est similiter philosophantem audiamus Volkelium: Restat ut de promissis, idem fere quod & de mandatis primae illius religionis, brevi dicamus: nempe vix aut ne vix quidem generale aliquod illius saeculi hominibus promissum factum: sed minas potius tunc illis metusque propositos fuisse. Neque enim videmus, Deum Adamo, si ab arboris illius fructu sibi temperet, aliquod obedientiae praemium polliceri; sed, nisi dicto audientem praebeat, interim denunciare. Nisi forte, illud unum, quod Caino Deus fecerat, generatim ad omnes respicere volumus. Videtur enim eam rem continere, quae nequaquam unius fit propria, nimirum si recte ageret, futurum fuisse, ut in gratiam reciperetur, & non minus quam Abel, divinam benignitatem experiretur. Nempe hoc vult dicere. 1. Nullum generale. 11. Nullum apertum. 111. De insigni aliquo bono. 1v. Nominatim vitae aeternae promissum; Patribus factum legi. Adde, nec factum fuisse, quia immortalitatis promissio non illius aetatis erat propria, sed ad ultima, nempe Messiae tempora, spectabat.
units.tr: Next we must hear the philosopher Volkelius again on the promises made to men of those times: It remains that, concerning promises, we should say briefly what we said about the commands of that first religion: namely, that hardly any general promise was made to men of that age, but rather threats and fears were set before them. For we do not see that God promised Adam any reward for obedience if he kept himself from the fruit of that tree; rather, unless he gave heed to the word, God only announced punishment. Unless perhaps we want to apply to all in general that one thing God said to Cain. For it seems to contain something that does not belong to him alone: that if he acted rightly, he would be received back into favour and would experience the divine kindness no less than Abel. This is what he means. 1. No general promise. 2. No open promise. 3. Concerning some notable good. 4. Expressly a promise of eternal life, made to the Fathers. Add that it was not made at all, because the promise of immortality did not belong to that age, but looked to the last times, namely the times of the Messiah.

units.la: Adversus quae sic argumentamur. 1. Quibus posita Lex, iisdem propositum est tum mandatum,tum praemium: sed omnibus hominibus vel in natura posita est Lex: ergo omnibus hominibus positum mandatum, & praemium. Omnibus dico, ergo & Adamo, & primaevis hominibus, ac singulis. Quare & mandatum generale, & praemium. Probatur assumtio ex illis, quae antehac pro adstruenda naturali lege attulimus. Jam vero illud τὸ γεγραμμένον ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου, ὅπερ φύσει ποιῷ[?], habet adjunctum sibi conveniens promissum: religionis praescriptioni promissio praemiorum recte factis propositorum conjunctissima, inquit Volkelius: neque haec alia uspiam panditur, vel intelligi datur, quam promissio vitae. Et cujus ea[?] non animalis: eam enim a natura habemus. Non vitae hujus felicitas terrena: habebat & hanc homo, quando ei Lex lata. Tum nec ista satis respondet observationi legis. Et qui legem ad mortem servat, ex sensu promissionis sibi vitam polliceri quidni etiam tum debeat? sed terrenam non ultra tum potest, vel in vanum eam sibi promitteret.
units.tr: Against these claims we argue as follows. (1) To those to whom the Law was given, both a command and a reward were set before them; but the Law was given by nature to all men; therefore a command and a reward were set before all men. I say all: therefore also Adam and the first men, and each one. Hence there was both a general command and a general reward. The assumption is proved from what we brought forward earlier to establish the natural law. Now indeed that "work of the law written in the heart" [τὸ γεγραμμένον ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου, ὅπερ φύσει ποιῷ], has a suitable promise attached to it: "a promise of rewards for right actions is most closely joined to the prescription of religion," says Volkelius; and this promise is nowhere else revealed or can be understood, than the promise of life. And it is not of animal life, for we have that from nature. Nor is it the earthly happiness of this life, for man had that too when the Law was given. Moreover, that does not agree well enough with the keeping of the law. And one who keeps the law unto death, why should he not then also be promised life by the sense of the promise? But he could not then have an earthly life beyond death, or he would promise it to himself in vain.

units.la: Denique, uti comminatio mortis, quae transgressioni posita, intelligitur de morte aeterna, aequum est ut promissio vitae, observationi legis addita, de vita quoque accipiatur aeterna. Unde 11. ita concludimus: Ubi generales minae propositae, ibi necessario & praesupponitur mandatum, & similis conditionis generale intelligi promis-sum debet. Illud, quia minae se habent ad legem consimiliter: quales illae, talis haec accipienda est, aut siquidem illae concernunt omnes homines, & generales sunt, haec non minus generalis quoque esse intelligatur. Istud, quia convenire non videtur, certe non cum solita divinae benignitatis providentia, ut minas aeternae mortis proponat, negato omni in contrarium praemio. Quin imo ex comminata aeterna morte, aeternae vitae promissio colligi tuto potest, ut contrariorum contraria regula solet esse, ac consequentia. 111. Genef. 1v.7. Nonne si bene egeris, שאת[?] exaltatio; si vero non bene egeris, ad fores peccatum excubat? regula est, ex communi jure & conscientia nota: non poena tantum, sed praemio munita, & totius legis argumentum, atque compendium. Hoc, si male; illud, siquidem bene egeris. Hinc exaltatio, inde reatus, & morsus animi, ac damnatio. Iis quidem boni operis gloriam & honorem & incorruptibilitatem quaerentibus, vita aeterna: Istis autem veritati inobedientibus, & iniquitati obedientibus, excandescentia & ira, uti loquitur Apostolus, Rom. 11.7.8. Quare male negatur, praecepta, aut promissa generalia illis temporibus data, aut nota fuisse; maleque asseritur, ex rationis praescripto Patres vixisse, potius quam fixis legibus aut regulis. Nam illud, quod Caino dictum, generatim ad omnes respicere haud negare audet Volkelius. Videtur enim, inquit, eam rem continere, quae nequaquam unius fit propria, nimirum si recte ageret, futurum fuisse, ut in gratiam reciperetur, &, non minus quam Abel, divinam benignitatem experiretur.
units.tr: Finally, just as the threat of death set against transgression is understood to mean eternal death, it is fair that the promise of life added to keeping the law should also be taken to mean eternal life. Hence we conclude thus, (2): where general threats are set forth, there a command is necessarily presupposed, and a promise of a like general condition must be understood. The first, because threats stand in the same relation to the law: whatever kind they are, so must this be understood; if the threats concern all men and are general, this too must be understood to be no less general. The second, because it does not seem to agree, certainly not with the usual providence of divine kindness, that God should set forth threats of eternal death while denying any reward to the contrary. Indeed, from the threatened eternal death the promise of eternal life can safely be inferred, as the rule and consequence of contraries usually is. Genesis 4:7: "Is there not exaltation if you do well; but if you do not do well, sin lies at the door?" [שאת] This is a rule known from common law and conscience: not only punishment but also reward is attached, and it is the argument and summary of the whole law. The one, if you act badly; the other, if you act well. Hence exaltation on one side, guilt, the sting of conscience and condemnation on the other. Indeed, to those who seek glory and honour and incorruptibility in well-doing, eternal life; but to those who disobey the truth and obey unrighteousness, wrath and indignation, as the Apostle says, Romans 2:7, 8. Therefore it is wrongly denied that general commands or promises were given or known in those times, and it is wrongly asserted that the Fathers lived by the prescription of reason rather than by fixed laws or rules. For Volkelius dares not deny that what was said to Cain applies generally to all. For it seems, he says, to contain something that does not belong to him alone: that if he acted rightly, he would be received back into favour and, no less than Abel, would experience the divine kindness.

units.la: Caeterum, quomodo ad Enochi, in coelum a Deo sublati, exemplum, quo doceri caeteri aevi istius, & facti gnari homines de vitae coelestis praemio potuerunt, respondeat Adversarius, etiam perpendendum. Sic ergo: Quod si forte quispiam Enochi in coelum elationem ejusmodi promissionis loco ducendam existimet, qua omnibus cum pietate viventibus eadem felicitas pacta fuerit; is nimirum vehementer errat: cum simplex hoc factum, nulla adjecta ejusdem beneficii oblatione, promissum appellari nequaquam possit. Adde quod res ipsa nequaquam hominibus illis, ex eo quod Enocho singulari de causa contigerat, promissum generale elicere permittebat: cum multi, quos Deus propter singularem potestatem admodum charos habuit, in coelum rapti nequaquam fuerint. Adde etiam, quod immortalitatis promissio non illius aetatis erat propria: sed, ut suo loco demonstrabitur, ad ultima Messiae tempora spectabat. Adeone is vehementer errat, qui ex assumtione Enochi collegerit, vitae coelestis praemium ac fructum pios manere? nae eum oporteat a gravioribus vehementer liberum esse, hic qui tantum errorem, si vel error sit, imaginari sibi possit? Quin vehementer errat, errorem qui hic dicit. II. Ἀνάληψις Enochi, non promissum a nobis appellatur, sed promissi illustris & singularis declaratio atque exhibitio. III. Inque ea duo sunt, assumtio in coelestem vitam; atque modus iste extraordinarius. Illud omnibus piis contingit, ab hac vita: quo enim transferuntur alias, vel translati etiam V. Testamenti illi fuerunt? istud fuit singulare. Neque ex hoc generalem regulam vel promissum aliis elicere licuit: solum in coelestis vitae fide ac spe confirmandi fuerunt, quam singulari illo documento roborare Deus voluit. Omnino debuerunt hinc doceri pii, de vitae coelestis praemio, ac spe:neq;video,qui aliquis tam indignam de Patribus fovere opinionem possit, ut putet, illos videntes aut scientes illam Enochi, viri sanctissimi, μετάθεσιν, non tamen vel in ipso Enocho praemium agnovisse probitatis, vel non etiam alios, quidquid sit de modo illo singulari, simili coelestis vitae, post vitam pie actam, mercedem ex gratia expectare potuisse? Praesertim quum in historia addatur, & immediate praemittatur ejus assumtioni, quod indesinenter ambularat coram Deo. Genef. v. 24. & Hebr. xi. 5. πίστει[?] μετάθεσις αὐτῆς μεμαρτύρηται εὐαρεστηκέναι τῷ Θεῷ. Quod aliis multis est commune, piis vid. omnibus.
units.tr: Moreover, it must also be weighed how the adversary answers the example of Enoch, taken up into heaven by God, by which the others of that age, who knew the facts, could be taught about the reward of heavenly life. His words are: "But if perhaps someone thinks that the elevation of Enoch into heaven should be taken as a promise of this kind, by which the same happiness was pledged to all who live in piety, he certainly greatly errs: since this simple fact, with no offer of the same benefit added, can by no means be called a promise. Add that the thing itself did not permit a general promise to be drawn for those men from what happened to Enoch for a singular reason: since many whom God, on account of a singular power, held very dear, were in no way taken up into heaven. Add also that the promise of immortality did not belong to that age, but, as will be shown in its place, looked to the last times of the Messiah. Does he greatly err who, from the assumption of Enoch, has inferred that the reward and fruit of heavenly life remain for the pious? Indeed, he who can imagine so great an error, if it is even an error, ought to be wholly free from more serious ones?" Indeed, he greatly errs who calls it an error. (1) The taking up of Enoch is not called a promise by us, but a clear and singular declaration and exhibition of the promise. (2) And in it there are two things: the assumption into heavenly life, and that extraordinary manner. The former befalls all the pious from this life: for into what else were the others, or even those of the Old Testament who were taken up, translated? The latter was singular. Nor was it permitted to draw from this a general rule or promise for others: they were only to be confirmed in faith and hope in heavenly life, which God wished to strengthen by that singular proof. Certainly the pious ought to have been taught from this about the reward and hope of heavenly life. And I do not see who could hold so unworthy an opinion of the Fathers as to think that they, seeing or knowing that translation [μετάθεσις] of Enoch, a most holy man, did not recognise a reward of uprightness even in Enoch himself, nor that others too, whatever the singular manner of that translation, could expect from grace a like heavenly life, a reward after a pious life? Especially since in the history it is added, and immediately placed before his assumption, that he walked continually before God: Genesis 5:24; and Hebrews 11:5, "by faith his translation [μετάθεσις] is attested, that he had pleased God" [πίστει μετάθεσις αὐτῆς μεμαρτύρηται εὐαρεστηκέναι τῷ Θεῷ]. This is common to many others, indeed to all the pious.

units.la: Huc accedit, quod salvatos aeterna vita Patres fuisse non negant Adversarii, tantummodo insciis iis, nec tale quid aut credentibus, aut sperantibus id contigisse. Catechesis Racovienfis, capite de Promissio vitae aeternae, qu.v i. Habiturine sunt vitam aeternam ii qui eam sperarunt, licet iis promissa non fuerit? Respondetur, prorsus, at non omnes, verum ii, qui ex animo Deum coluerunt, & dicto audientes ei fuere. Nec etiam obstat quicquam quo minus plus praestet, quam promiserit Deus, & Christus id aperte docet, Luc. 20. verf. 37. 38. cum e verbis ipsius Dei & vere, & subtiliter ratiocinatur, Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Iacobum, resurrecturos a mortuis & victuros. Quem imitatus Autor ad Hebraeos 11. verf. 16. ait, Deum non erubescere eorum vocari Deum, eo quod paraverit iis urbem, & eos aeternum victuros statuerit. Promisisse tamen Deum illis vitam aeternam negant, quia non isti, sed alteri tempori hoc erat proprium: sperasse autem illos vitam aeternam, ajunt, non ex promissione ulla sibi facta, sed rei in se speratae vel expetendae admodum, & credibilis natura, quod illam cultoribus sui vitam daret Deus. Sed unde vel notitiam primum, vel sensum istius habuerunt, vel habere potuerunt, nisi ex divina revelatione? An natura illud docet & mera hominis ratio? Unde hoc, cre-dibile esse, Deum id daturum suis, nisi a Deo ipso, ejusq; revelatione supranaturali du-catur? Vel nullam dic illis factam revelationem. Quid non audent. At quomodo ergo divina revelatione hoc quidem dixit, quod natura? non verbum, quod ratio? non Deus, quod homo? si sperarunt vitam aeternam, ergo & crediderunt. Aeque enim credibilis est, ac speranda vel expetenda illa vita. Si crediderunt rem tantam, & sperarunt, & Deum eam daturum, viderint alii cur negent, aut negare queant, Deum hoc se facturum illis promisisse, & inde id ipsis & credendum fuisse & sperandum. Adeone ergo plus in ipsorum fide & spe fuit, quam in Dei revelatione, verbo, promissis? Et plura nos dicemur apprehendere de Deo, quam ipse declaret, se velle nobis facere? Religio duo significat, doctrinam Dei, de se suaque voluntate; deinde ejus observantiam; illud est a parte Dei; hoc, hominis. Illa objectiva; haec subjectiva. Quid, an in subjectiva plus erit, quam objectiva? & plus in hominis fide, ac spe, quam in Dei doctrina? & homines plus reddent quasi Deo, quam ipsis dederit vel obtulerit primum ipse? Praesertim in illustrem & coelestem Enochi sublatione quando intuemur, quid obsecro aliud ea fuit, quam realis vitae coelestis manifestatio, cujusmodi apparitiones bene possunt haberi pro promissione, vel ejus confirmatione, cujus adeo divinum erant omnibus & publicum documentum.
units.tr: Add to this that the adversaries do not deny that the Fathers were saved to eternal life, only that they were ignorant of it, and that neither believed nor hoped that such a thing would happen. The Racovian Catechism, in the chapter on the promise of eternal life, question 6: "Will those who hoped for eternal life have it, although it was not promised to them?" The answer: "Certainly, though not all, but those who worshipped God from the heart and were obedient to him." Nor does anything stand in the way of God giving more than he promised; and Christ teaches this plainly, Luke 20:37, 38, when from the very words of God he reasons truly and subtly that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will rise from the dead and live. Imitating him, the author to the Hebrews, 11:16, says that God is not ashamed to be called their God, because he has prepared a city for them and has determined that they will live eternally. Yet they deny that God promised them eternal life, because that belonged not to them but to another time; but they say that they hoped for eternal life not from any promise made to them, but from the nature of the thing hoped for and greatly to be desired, and credible, that God would give that life to his worshippers. But whence did they first have, or could they have, knowledge or sense of it, except from divine revelation? Does nature teach this, or does mere human reason? Whence is it credible that God would give this to his own, unless it is led from God himself and his supernatural revelation? Or else say that no revelation was made to them. What do they not dare? But how then did divine revelation say what nature said? Did the word say what reason said? Did God say what man said? If they hoped for eternal life, then they also believed it. For that life is as credible as it is to be hoped for or desired. If they believed so great a thing, and hoped, and that God would give it, let others see why they deny, or can deny, that God promised them that he would do this, and that therefore they both ought to have believed and hoped it. Was there then more in their faith and hope than in God's revelation, word and promises? Are we to be said to grasp more about God than he himself declares he wishes to do for us? Religion signifies two things: the teaching of God concerning himself and his will; then its observance. The former is on God's part, the latter on man's. The former is objective, the latter subjective. Or will there be more in the subjective than in the objective? And will men render more to God, as it were, than God himself first gave or offered to them? Especially when we consider the illustrious and heavenly taking up of Enoch: what, I ask, was it other than a real manifestation of heavenly life? Such appearances may well be regarded as a promise, or a confirmation of a promise, of which they were a divine and public proof to all.

units.la: Inane est, quod dicunt, immortalitatis promissionem illius aetatis non fuisse, sed Messiae. Cujus aetatis quidem est, immortalitatem conferre, non erit istius quoq; eandem promittere? Annon aeque tum, ac postea, ad immortalitatem adspirare debuerunt Patres, & pervenire? Quae igitur repugnantia vel incongruentia, si illa iis promissa quoque fuerit, & gavisi sint cum notitia, & spe, tum promissione quoque, cujus ipsa veritate & beneficio non destituebantur? 11. Ad tempora, & officium Messiae spectavit quidem immortalitatem promereri, & impetrare suis omnibus, tum retro, tum potest victuris; non autem tum demum eam vel promittere, vel largiri.
units.tr: It is empty talk, what they say: that the promise of immortality did not belong to that age but to the Messiah. If it belongs to that age to confer immortality, will it not also belong to it to promise the same? Did not the Fathers then, just as afterwards, aspire to immortality and attain it? What contradiction or incongruity is there, then, if that was promised to them too, and they rejoiced in its knowledge and hope, and in the promise itself, of whose truth and benefit they were not deprived? 11. It pertained indeed to the time and office of the Messiah to merit immortality and to obtain it for all his people, both those who had gone before and those who were yet to live; but not then at last to promise it or bestow it.

units.la: Causam si audire juvet, ob quam dicant Adversarii, Deum illa saeculorum aetate sibi obediri voluisse, nullo fere generali praemio proposito, hanc adferunt: quod Deus in ipso statim mundi primordio, nihil sese cuipiam debere, sed omnium rerum absolutissimum Do-minum esse, omnibus offendere voluerit. Commentum, & satis futile, non ratio. Quasi, quando Deus immortalitatem promittit, ea ostendat se eam cuipiam debere, vel id ulli sanae mentis inde concludant. An ergo quandocunq; eam promisit Deus, significavit tum, se eam hominibus debere? 11. Vel eone promisso negat se absolutissi-mum omnium rerum esse Dominum? Deum esse Dominum ablolutissimum, & nulli quidpiam debere, haud magis jam, quam tum verum est, ac fuit, & semper aeque credendum: nihil ut hinc argui pro vitae immortalis promissione aut faciendâ, aut omittendâ, debeat. Atque ita apparet, quam vana Adversariorum sententia sit, diverdiversam primorum temporum statuentium religionem, totâ formâ & essentiâ aliam à nostrâ, aliam ab eâ quæ vera sit & sola recta, quæ non generalibus præceptis, promissisque, nominatim de vitâ & salute æternâ, sed ex rationis judicio moderata fuerit ac transfacta.
units.tr: If it pleases you to hear the reason why the Adversaries say God wished to be obeyed in that age with almost no general reward set before them, they offer this: that God, at the very beginning of the world, wanted to show everyone that he owed nothing to anyone, but was the most absolute Lord of all things. This is an invention, and a rather flimsy one, not a reasoned argument. As if, when God promises immortality, he thereby shows that he owes it to someone, or any sane person could conclude this from it! Or, whenever God promised it, did he signify that he then owed it to men? 11. Or does he deny that he is the most absolute Lord of all things by making such a promise? That God is the most absolute Lord, and owes nothing to anyone, is no less true now than it was then, and is always to be believed equally. So nothing should be argued from this either for making or for withholding the promise of immortal life. And thus it appears how empty is the view of the Adversaries, who maintain that the religion of the earliest times was entirely different in form and essence from ours, and from that which is true and alone right; a religion which was not governed and shaped by general precepts and promises, named explicitly concerning life and eternal salvation, but by the judgment of reason.

units.la: Ea, quæ de religione hominum primæva, & diversâ illius formâ, ex Adversariorum sententiâ, hactenus vidimus, ad cæteras V. T. juxta ipsos, religiones, utpote Abrahamicam, & Mosaicam, eatenus quoque spectant, quâ nullis earum volunt comprehensam vitæ æternæ, & remissionis peccatorum promissionem fuisse, attamen in hoc ipsas[?] illâ perfectiores, quòd magis generalia continuerint & præcepta, & promissa, sed quævis alia, quam cœlestia. Quid verò adeo refert particularia, an generalia promissa & præcepta tum temporis obtinuerint, & hæc vel illa, si non quòd religionem potissimum fundat, atque animæ necessarium ante omnia est, de eo prospectum ipsis fuerit, de ipsius salutis æternæ certâ notitiâ, spe, & studio? Quod, nisi ex paribus[?] iis sive similis naturæ præceptis & promissis, haberi nequit. Quare, quam propositum fuimus supra quæstionem, hoc nunc loco debitè & plenè examinanda venit, vid. de religione, fide, & salute Patrum sub V. Testamento, sive ii ante Abrahamum vixerint, & ante Noachum, sive posteâ, id est, de Patribus & piis ab Adamo, Noacho, Abrahamo, Mose, ad Christum; an eo (quod ad substantiam religionis, non accidentales differentias attinet, aut circumstantias) quo nos, modo salvati fuerint? Per fidem nimirum, & acceptâ à Deo gratuitâ, per Christum venturum, peccatorum remissione? Vel, an Patribus sub Vet. Test. factæ fuerint rerum spiritualium, salutarium, & cœlestium promissiones? Distinctius, an Patribus factæ promissiones de vitâ æternâ, remissione peccatorum, & Spiritu Sancto, quibus crediderint, & salvati hoc pacto fuerint? Potissimum est, ut probemus, promissiones illius generis ipsis factas: nam hoc ubi constat, facilius dabunt Adversarii, & res clamabit ipsa, creditas fuisse, nec omnes semper illis inobedientes fuisse aut incredulos. Ecclesia affirmativam tuetur; statuitque, eandem, quod ad essentialem formam, religionem, fidem, salutem Patrum fuisse, ac sub Novo Test. nostram. Sociniani[?] negant, & præsertim factas illis vitæ æternæ promissiones.
units.tr: What we have so far seen, from the Adversaries' view, about the primeval religion of men and its different form, also applies, by their own account, to the other Old Testament religions, namely the Abrahamic and the Mosaic, insofar as they deny that any promise of eternal life and remission of sins was comprehended in any of these. Yet in this respect they say these religions were more perfect, because they contained more general precepts and promises, though of anything but heavenly things. But what does it really matter whether particular or general promises and precepts were in force at that time, and whether this or that was provided for them, if it does not found religion chiefly, and if it is not, above all, necessary for the soul: certain knowledge, hope and zeal concerning its own eternal salvation? This cannot be had except from precepts and promises of the same or a similar nature. Therefore the question we proposed above now needs to be examined properly and fully: concerning the religion, faith and salvation of the Fathers under the Old Testament, whether they lived before Abraham and before Noah, or afterwards, that is, concerning the fathers and pious people from Adam, Noah, Abraham and Moses down to Christ. Were they saved in the same way as we were, as regards the substance of religion (not accidental differences or circumstances)? Namely, through faith, and through the free grace received from God, by the coming of Christ, in the remission of sins? Or were promises of spiritual, saving and heavenly things made to the Fathers under the Old Testament? More distinctly: were promises of eternal life, remission of sins and the Holy Spirit made to the Fathers, which they believed and by which they were saved in this way? The chief thing is to prove that promises of that kind were made to them; for once this is established, the Adversaries will more readily concede it, and the matter itself will cry out that they were believed, and that they were not always disobedient or unbelieving. The Church maintains the affirmative, and holds that the Fathers' religion, faith and salvation were, as regards its essential form, the same as ours under the New Testament. The Socinians deny this, and especially that promises of eternal life were made to them.

units.la: Socinus, lib. de officio hominis Christiani, vel, Quod regni Poloniæ, &c. homines omnino deberent se illorum cœtui adjungere, qui in iisdem locis falsò atque immerito Ebionitæ vocantur, nam utroque titulo venit liber, cap. v. inter errores Euangelicorum quamvis leviores, ponit, sexto loco, quem Euangelici (inquit) communem habent cum Pontificiis, quam bene postmodum videbimus, quod existimant, eos, qui sub V. T. coram Deo justi sunt habiti, propterea tales habitos fuisse, & salutis æternæ nobiscum idcirco fore participes, quòd sicut nos in Christum jam exhibitum, sic ipsi in eundem, quem exhibitum iri sperabant, omnino crediderint. Inter Epistol. pag. 405. ad Erasmum Johannis: Nec locus Jezech. 18. qui ad te assertur, contrarium probat; quidquid enim de vitâ ibi dicitur, id pro eo tempore ad æternam vitam referri non potest, cum nondum ea à Deo patefacta fuisset. Contra Palæologum, part. iv. pag. 558. in veteris fœderis promissis nulla æternæ vitæ fit mentio. In Notis, ad Dialog. de Justific. pag. 34. Sub quo V. Test. quidquid multi aliter affirment, nulla certa spes vitæ æternæ facta populo à Deo fuerat.
units.tr: Socinus, in his book on the duty of a Christian man, or, that all men ought altogether to join the assembly of those who in those same places are falsely and undeservedly called Ebionites; for the book has both titles. In chapter 5, among the errors of the Evangelicals, though slight ones, he lists in sixth place what he says the Evangelicals hold in common with the Papists, which we shall soon see he gets wrong: that those who were regarded as righteous before God under the Old Testament were therefore so regarded, and are therefore to be partakers with us of eternal salvation, because, just as we believed in Christ already revealed, so they believed fully in him who they hoped would be revealed. In his letter to Erasmus Johannis, p. 405: Nor does the passage of Ezekiel 18, which is cited against you, prove the contrary; for whatever is said there about life cannot be referred to eternal life for that time, since it had not yet been revealed by God. Against Palaeologus, part 4, p. 558: in the promises of the Old Covenant there is no mention of eternal life. In the Notes on the Dialogue on Justification, p. 34: Under which Old Testament, whatever many may affirm otherwise, no certain hope of eternal life had been given to the people by God.

units.la: Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, cap. ii. pag. 6. Nam neque vitæ æternæ, quæ proprium est Messiæ beneficium, de quo infra suo loco dicemus, mentionem faciebant, vel eam promittebant scripta veteris fœderis. & cap.vii: sunt autem duo potissimum promissa, quæ D. Jesus nobis
units.tr: Smalcius, on the divinity of Christ, chapter 2, p. 6: For the writings of the Old Covenant neither mentioned eternal life, which is the proper benefit of the Messiah, of which we shall speak below in its place, nor promised it. And in chapter 7: there are, however, two chief promises which Lord Jesus has revealed to us

units.la: Tom. 2. revelavit: alterum est vitæ æternæ, alterum Spiritus sancti. Vitam æternam promissum esse Euangelii proprium, quantumvis hodie paucissimi id intelligere videantur, adeo veritati con-sentaneum est, ut aliquid non minimum ad veram Domini Iesu, & muneris ejus cognitionem, deesse illis jure affirmari possit, qui hoc vel ignorant, vel de eo dubitant. Quod duplici modo fit: nempe, dum semel affirmatur, Adamum factum immortalem: & iterum, dum affirma-tur eandem vitam æternam in veteri T. etiam promissam Dei cultoribus fuisse. Quomodo enim d Euangelii proprium esset, quod vel in Adamo naturaliter fuerit: vel alias ante Dominum Iesum revelatum & cognitum fuerit? Vitam æternam esse promissum Euangelii proprium, fatemur. 1. quatenus vita æterna intelligitur peccatoribus promissa ex gratia, atq; dicit ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς ζωῆς [?] junctaque peccatorum remissioni; verum quatenus simpliciter consideratur, & promissa justis, sic etiam lege continetur, uti præmium observantiæ: utroque modo viguit sub V. T. II. vita æterna est promissio Euangelii, quatenus à Christo promerita. Verum aliud est Euangelium considerare pro fœdere Euangelico, cujus proprium est illa promissio, vel pro tempore Euangelii exhibiti: & sic negamus, ad hoc tempus restrictum illud promissum fuisse: sed quatenus Euangelium, quamvis non exhibitum, promissum fuit quoque antea, & à primordio mundi, eatenus ejus promissionem, quæ vitæ æternæ est, semper viguisse etiam, asserendum est. Adamo naturalis fuisset immortalitas, justo nimirum, & in justitia persistenti, quia mors nonnisi ad peccatum posita, & infligenda fuit. Smalcius ibidem: Nos persuasi fuimus, nec in ipsis etiam Prophetarum scriptis, ullum extare apertum promissum vitæ illius beatæ & immortalis, cujus toties repetita promissio in sacris literis novi fœderis inculcatur. Nostri enim cœtus confitentur, & demonstrare parati sunt validissimis testimoniis & rationibus, Iesum Christum primum & solum tantæ rei fuisse præconem. pag. 27. In ea tota versatur res, quod affirmatur, istud bonum vitæ æternæ, nec fœdere inclusum, nec usquam populo aperte promissum fuisse.
units.tr: Vol. 2. one is of eternal life, the other of the Holy Spirit. That eternal life is the proper promise of the Gospel, although very few today seem to understand this, is so consonant with the truth that it may rightly be said that those who either are ignorant of this or doubt it lack something of no small importance for a true knowledge of the Lord Jesus and of his office. This happens in two ways: namely, when it is affirmed once that Adam was made immortal, and again when it is affirmed that this same eternal life was also promised in the Old Testament to the worshippers of God. For how could it be the proper thing of the Gospel if it was already in Adam by nature, or had been otherwise revealed and known before the Lord Jesus? We grant that eternal life is the proper promise of the Gospel: 1. insofar as eternal life is understood as promised to sinners from grace, and joined with remission of sins, [ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς ζωῆς]; but insofar as it is considered simply and promised to the righteous, it is also contained in the law, as the reward of obedience; in both ways it flourished under the Old Testament. 2. Eternal life is the promise of the Gospel insofar as it was merited by Christ. But it is one thing to consider the Gospel as the Gospel covenant, whose proper promise that is, or as the time of the Gospel having been exhibited; and in that sense we deny that this promise was restricted to this time. But insofar as the Gospel, though not yet exhibited, was promised also before, and from the beginning of the world, we must assert that its promise of eternal life has always been in force. Adam would have had natural immortality, that is, if he remained just and persistent in righteousness, because death was posited and to be inflicted only on account of sin. Smalcius in the same place: We were persuaded that not even in the writings of the Prophets is any clear promise of that blessed and immortal life to be found, whose so often repeated promise is inculcated in the sacred writings of the New Covenant.
