For our assembly confesses, and is ready to demonstrate with the strongest testimonies and arguments, that Jesus Christ was the first and only herald of so great a thing, p. 27. The whole matter turns on this, that it is affirmed that this good of eternal life was neither included in a covenant nor openly promised to the people anywhere.

units.la: Deinde, ne putemus Adversarios sub promisso Spiritus S. aliud quid præter id quod vitæ æternæ promissione, & ejus spe continetur, intelligere, non gratiam singularem Spiritus S. nos suâ demum vi sanctificantis & regenerantis, aperte rem sic explicantem audi Smalcium, cap. viii. Sic igitur statuendum est, Spiritum illum Sanctum, qui est promissum N. Fœderis proprium, nihil aliud esse, quam spem vitæ æternæ nobis à Deo promisse, quam in animis nostris sentiamus, certam ac firmam. Propterea enim appellatur, spiritus ille pignus, vel pignus hereditatis nostræ, & simul de eo dicitur, quod in animos nostros infundatur. Extare autem tale promissum, quod omnibus in universum & singulis, qui in Christum credunt, spectandum est, apertissime docent illa Christi verba, si vos, cum mali sitis, nostis bona dona dare filiis vestris, pater vester de cœlo dabit Spiritum Sanctum petentibus se? Quod quidem promissum in Veteri Fœdere omnibus propositum fuisse, nemo opinor affirmabit. Vbi enim tale quid apud Mosem legitur, quod Deus omnibus sibi obedientibus Spiritum sanctum daturus sit? Et certe si tunc Spiritus sanctus promissus & datus fuisset omnibus, non ita impossibile fuisset, ut Lex Dei perfecte observaretur. Quod tamen impossibile fuisse abunde testatur Divus Paulus, cap. 7. & in initio cap. 8. Epist. ad Rom. Resp. Ergo Spiritus S. nihil fere est, quam spes vitæ æternæ. Et tota hæc disputatio figi in hoc debet, quod quæritur de vitâ æternâ. Vbi vero quæso in Scripturâ per Sp. Sanctum spes vitæ æternæ intelligitur? II. Ostende, quid sit in promisso illo Luc. xi. 13. si vos, mali cum sitis, &c. cujus veritas in V. Test. perspecta non fuerit, agnitaque? an bonitatem Dei supra hominum eminentem esse & majorem? vel Deum se petentibus gratiosum esse, atque suas ipsis concedere necessitates? Spiritum S. habuisse Veteres non negat ipse, quum ait, non debet autem aliquis suspicari, nos negare, Deum multis fidelibus Spiritum suum sanctum dedisse sub Veteri etiam foedere. Is enim qui suspicaretur, graviter erraret. Neque dicet, opinor, Veteres non vidisse ac sensisse necessarium sibi ad omnia esse Spiritum sanctum. Unde nec negari potest, illos pro eo rogasse Deum; vel ad eorum petitionem illum ipsis a Deo etiam fuisse concessum.
units.tr: Next, lest we suppose that the Adversaries understand by the promise of the Holy Spirit anything beyond what is contained in the promise of eternal life and the hope of it, and not the singular grace of the Holy Spirit who sanctifies and regenerates us by his own power, listen to Smalcius, who explains the matter plainly in chapter 8: So it must be established that the Holy Spirit, who is the proper promise of the New Covenant, is nothing other than the hope of eternal life promised to us by God, which we feel in our souls to be certain and firm. For this reason that Spirit is called a pledge, or the pledge of our inheritance, and at the same time it is said to be poured into our souls. That there is such a promise, addressed to all in general and to each one who believes in Christ, is most clearly taught by those words of Christ: If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him? Now I think no one will affirm that this promise was set before all in the Old Covenant. For where is anything of the kind read in Moses, that God would give the Holy Spirit to all who obey him? And certainly, if the Holy Spirit had then been promised and given to all, it would not have been so impossible for the Law of God to be perfectly observed. Yet that it was impossible the divine Paul abundantly testifies, in chapter 7 and at the beginning of chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Romans. Answer: So the Holy Spirit is hardly anything but the hope of eternal life. And this whole dispute ought to be fixed on this point, that the question concerns eternal life. But where, I ask, in Scripture is the hope of eternal life understood by the Holy Spirit? II. Show what there is in that promise of Luke 11:13, if you, being evil, etc., whose truth was not perceived and acknowledged in the Old Testament: is it that the goodness of God is above and greater than that of men, or that God is gracious to those who ask him and grants them their needs? The Adversary himself does not deny that the ancients had the Holy Spirit, when he says: Yet no one should suspect that we deny that God gave his Holy Spirit to many believers under the Old Covenant as well. For whoever suspected this would be gravely mistaken. Nor, I think, will he say that the ancients did not see and perceive that the Holy Spirit was necessary to them for everything. Hence it cannot be denied that they asked God for him, or that at their petition he was granted to them by God.

units.la: III. Promissio Spiritus S. non Mosis est, sed Christi; non legis, sed Euangelii, quae quamvis non exprimatur verbis, re tamen ipsa confertur ex Euangelio, credentibus. Gal. III. 2. ex operibus legis spiritum accepistis, an ex auditu fidei? iterum vers. 5. qui ergo vobis concessit spiritum, ex operibus legis, non ex auditu fidei? id est, neutiquam certe ex lege, vel ejus operibus contingit alicui spiritus, sed ex Euangelio, & ejus praedicatione. Ut modo dispiciendum veniat, annon Euangelium sub V. T. hominibus oblatum fuerit traditumque, ex quo tum de Spiritus S. dono & gratia ferendum judicium. IV. Non si tunc Spiritus S. promissus datusque fuit (omnibus non dicimus, sed salvandis & credentibus) sequitur legem ipsis fuisse perfecte servatu possibilem. Non enim hunc in finem Spiritus S. datur, ut legem perfecte servemus, sed ut Deum, recte tamen, quamvis non perfecte, colamus & serviamus.
units.tr: III. The promise of the Holy Spirit belongs not to Moses but to Christ; not to the law but to the Gospel. Although it is not expressed in words, it is nevertheless in fact conferred from the Gospel upon believers. Gal. 3:2: Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Again, verse 5: He who therefore supplies you with the Spirit, does he do it by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? That is, certainly the Spirit does not come to anyone by the law or its works, but by the Gospel and its preaching. So it now comes to be examined whether the Gospel was not offered and delivered to men under the Old Testament, from which judgment is to be drawn about the gift and grace of the Holy Spirit. IV. Even if the Holy Spirit was then promised and given (not to all, we say, but to those who are to be saved and who believe), it does not follow that the law could be perfectly kept by them. For the Spirit is not given for this purpose, that we should keep the law perfectly, but that we should worship and serve God rightly, though not perfectly.

units.la: Catechesis Racoviensis, de Prophetico Christi munere cap. V. Quaest. 1. Exposuisti mihi perfecta Christi mandata, illius quoque promissa exponi velim? Resp. Maximum omnium, quod omnia in se comprehendit, est vita aeterna: verum etiam aliud superest prius obtinendum vehementer pertinens. Quaest. 2. Quod vero istud est? Resp. Donum Spiritus sancti. Quaest. 3. At nonne eadem promissa comprehensa fuerce in lege Mosis? Resp. Imo nullum eorum comprehensum fuit. Etenim nusquam in lege Mosis reperies vel vitam aeternam, vel donum Spiritus sancti, obedientibus legis promissum: quemadmodum in lege per Christum data promissa esse constat. Quaest. VIII. quid vero est is Spiritus sanctus? Resp. Ut facilius intelligas, quid is sit Spiritus sanctus, sic habeto, primum in scripturis Novi foederis Spiritus S. voce designari ipsum Euangelium. 1 Cor. 2. 10. 2 Tim. 1. 10. &c. Deinde ea vox spiritus designat Dei donum, quod certis hominibus datur, quod cum a Scriptura vocetur Arrha, 2 Cor. 1. 22. aut etiam arrha hereditatis nostrae, & simul de eo dicitur, quod in corda nostra infundatur, hinc necessario efficitur, nihil aliud esse, quam firmam & certam vitae aeternae nobis promissae spem, cujus in cordibus nostris gustum, sensumque percipiamus. Quomodo vero id inde concipitur, ut quia Spiritus Sancti vox Euangelium designat, & arrham coelestis vitae, nihil aliud sit, quam ejus firmae spes & certae persuasio? Nam & alia significat illa vox, & si vel illa tantum, non tamen sic sequeretur conclusio. Similia de promisso Spiritus S. Euangelii proprio, Smalcius, de divinitate Christi, cap. IIX.[?] & contra Frantzium, Disp. ult. pag. 459.
units.tr: The Racovian Catechism, on the prophetic office of Christ, chapter 5. Question 1: You have explained to me the perfect commands of Christ; I would like his promises explained too. Answer: The greatest of all, which comprehends all things in itself, is eternal life. But there is also another thing, to be obtained first, which is of great importance. Question 2: What is that? Answer: The gift of the Holy Spirit. Question 3: But were not these same promises contained in the law of Moses? Answer: Indeed none of them was contained there. For nowhere in the law of Moses will you find either eternal life or the gift of the Holy Spirit promised to those who obey the law, as it is established that promises have been given in the law given through Christ. Question 8: What then is this Holy Spirit? Answer: So that you may more easily understand what this Holy Spirit is, hold this: first, in the Scriptures of the New Covenant the word Spirit designates the Gospel itself (1 Cor. 2:10; 2 Tim. 1:10, etc.). Then that word Spirit designates a gift of God, which is given to certain men; since Scripture calls it an earnest (2 Cor. 1:22), or the earnest of our inheritance, and at the same time it is said to be poured into our hearts, it follows necessarily that it is nothing other than a firm and certain hope of the eternal life promised to us, of which we perceive the taste and feeling in our hearts. But how is it inferred from this that, because the word Holy Spirit designates the Gospel, and the earnest of heavenly life, it is nothing other than the firm hope of it and the certain persuasion of it? For that word also has other meanings, and even if it had only this one, the conclusion would still not follow. Similar things are said about the promise of the Spirit, the proper gift of the Gospel, by Smalcius, in his book on the divinity of Christ, chapter 18 (?), and against Frantzius, last disputation, page 459.

units.la: Eademque de promissis praesertim vitae aeternae, tum Spiritus S. nullibi in Veteri, primum & solum in Novo Testamento extantibus, habent Ostorodus, Institut. cap. XXI. Volkelius, lib. II. cap. XIX. & XXI. lib. III. cap. XI. Jonas Schlichtingius, Disput. c. Meisnerum, pag. 682. 683. 684. Autor Dissertationis praemissae Iohannis Cirelli, id est, Crellii Ethicae majori: & alii istius sectae, passim.
units.tr: The same things about the promises, especially of eternal life, and also about the Holy Spirit, which are found nowhere in the Old Testament but first and only in the New, are held by Ostorodt, Institutes, chapter 21; Volkelius, book 2, chapter 19 and book 3, chapter 11 and 21; Jonas Schlichting, Disputation against Meisner, pages 682, 683, 684; the author of the preface to the Dissertation of John Cirellus, that is Crellius, on the Greater Ethics; and others of that sect, everywhere.

units.la: Neque illi soli, sed iis multum colludunt Remonstrantes, in Apol. cap. VII. ubi de tota controversia primum sic pronunciant: quaestionem de fide in Iesum Christum, an & quomodo ea sub Vet. Testamento locum habuerit, inconcinnam, ambiguam, & inutilem esse. tum de ipsa, fidei istius sub Vet. Test. nec in toto Veteri, nec in toto N. Testamento aperta mentio uspiam facta legitur, &c. Cum certum sit locum nullum esse, unde appareat fidem istam sub Vet. Test. praeceptam fuisse, aut viguisse. Tandem revelationis modum distinguunt clarum, vel obscurum, atque ajunt quidem fidem in Iesum Christum nec aperte nec directe, sed tamen indirecte & obscure in V. T. praescriptam fuisse, & viguisse, nempe sub fide generalis Dei favoris & gratiae comprehensam & involutam: Etsi enim credunt fidem in Iesum Christum moriturum directe atque aperte sub V. T. praescriptam, atque exercitam non fuisse, nihilominus tamen statuunt: fidem illam, quae sub V. T. indirecte fidem in Iesum Christum dici posse: quatenus in V. T. gratia & salus per Christum parta, sub generalis gratiae & favoris divini promissio abscondita, & sub typis & umbris, quarum corpus erat Christus, revelata, & rudi veluti Minerva adumbrata fuit. Lex enim umbram rerum futurarum habuit, non ipsam expressam imaginem. Heb. x. 1. Col. 2. 17. Lex Paedagogus fuit in Christum. Gal. 3. 14. unde & fides venisse dicitur sub N. T. ibidem v. 2. aliaque in eandem sententiam. Quod si quis hoc sufficere non credat, ut videat, quomodo ex V. aut N. T. probare possit apertam atque expressam rerum istarum, quae fidei expressae in Christum obiecta sunt, mentionem factam esse sub Vet. Test. Remonstr. fatentur, se id hactenus deprehendere non potuisse: Fidem interim illam, quae in promissionem Dei generalem, queque in typos atque umbras ferebatur, credunt a Deo censitam fuisse, ac censeri recte posse pro fide in Christum, eadem plane ratione, qua Isaac, qui erat semen illud Abrahamo promissum, Christus appellatur, & promissio de semine isto, promissio de Christo, Gal. 3. 16. & 19. imprimis si umbras & typos isti[?] intelligerent, esse umbras & typos venturi Christi, quamquam id paucos admodum intellexisse, verisimile est. Fidem in V. T. ajunt tetendisse praeterquam in specialia nonnulla, in generalem Dei favorem ac benignitatem. Ergo & ejus promissio facta: nam fides nisi in verbum Dei divina non fertur. Atqui sub illa generali promissione, abscònditam specialem de gratia Christi, & involutam, non explicatam, censent. An vero id a Deo nullibi indicatum fuit, sub generalitate illa comprehendi, & promissione illa significatum, ut Patres intelligere potuerint & credere? Si non: unde vos hoc jam scitis & intelligitis? Sin imo, ergo non in generalem solum, sed & specialem gratiam Christi crediderunt illi. Deinde, quae & quorum fides ferebatur in typos atque umbras Christi, non fuit generalis, aut in generalem tantum promissionem directa, sed & specialis: atqui Patrum fides, agnoscente Adversario[?], ferebatur in typos Christi: ergo. Pauci, an multi, vel omnes typos intellexerint[?], haud laboramus, saltem intellexerunt eos aliqui. Unde? vel ex ordinaria, quae in Ecclesia sonabat, doctrina; vel revelatione extraordinaria. Si hoc dicas, proba. Deinde in quaestione de fide ordinaria, & hominum in genere sub V. T. viventium, videris quomodo respondeas extra terminos, de casu extraordinario. Sin illud, ergo viguit tum doctrina quae typos explicaret, prout explicari debent, de Christo, & gratia ac salute per eum obtinenda. Quod si verum, ergo doctrina illa non generalis tantum Dei favoris, sed & de speciali fuit in Christo gratia: quae innitebatur & conformis erat ejusdem generis promissioni. Ei doctrinae quid ni dicas credidisse fideles omnes & pios? Non enim ita frustra in perpetuum sonuit doctrina salutaris, ut non multi quovis tempore ei crediderint & obtemperarint?
units.tr: Nor are they alone in this; the Remonstrants also play along with them a great deal, in their Apology, chapter 7, where they first pronounce on the whole controversy as follows: The question about faith in Jesus Christ, whether and how it had a place under the Old Testament, is ill-conceived, ambiguous, and useless. Then about faith itself, no explicit mention of it is read anywhere in the whole Old Testament or the whole New Testament, etc., since it is certain that there is no place from which it appears that this faith was commanded or flourished under the Old Testament. Finally they distinguish the mode of revelation as clear or obscure, and they say that faith in Jesus Christ was indeed prescribed and flourished under the Old Testament, not openly nor directly, but indirectly and obscurely, namely comprehended and wrapped up in faith in the general favour and grace of God: For although they believe that faith in Jesus Christ who was to die was not prescribed and exercised directly and openly under the Old Testament, nevertheless they hold that that faith which under the Old Testament can be called faith in Jesus Christ indirectly, inasmuch as in the Old Testament grace and salvation won through Christ lay hidden under the promise of God's general grace and favour, and were revealed under types and shadows, of which Christ was the body, and were sketched as if by a rough Minerva. For the law had a shadow of the things to come, not the very express image. (Heb. 10:1; Col. 2:17.) The law was our tutor to bring us to Christ (Gal. 3:24), whence faith is also said to have come under the New Testament (ibid., v. 25), and other passages to the same effect. But if anyone does not think this is sufficient, so that he may see how from the Old or New Testament he can prove that an open and express mention of those things was made under the Old Testament, which are the objects of express faith in Christ, the Remonstrants confess that they have not so far been able to discover it. Meanwhile they believe that that faith which was directed to the general promise of God and to the types and shadows is reckoned by God, and can rightly be reckoned as faith in Christ, in exactly the same way as Isaac, who was the seed promised to Abraham, is called Christ, and the promise concerning that seed is a promise concerning Christ (Gal. 3:16, 19); especially if they understood the types and shadows to be shadows and types of the coming Christ, although it is very probable that very few understood this. They say that faith under the Old Testament was directed, apart from some particular things, to the general favour and kindness of God. Therefore its promise was also made in general, for faith is not carried except to the word of God. But they think that under that general promise the special grace of Christ was hidden and wrapped up, not explained. But has it not been indicated by God anywhere that this special grace was comprehended under that generality and signified by that promise, so that the Fathers could understand it and believe it? If not, how do you now know and understand this? But if so, then those men believed not only in the general but also in the special grace of Christ. Further, the faith which was directed to the types and shadows of Christ, and of those who had it, was not general, nor directed only to a general promise, but also special; but the faith of the Fathers, as the Adversary acknowledges, was directed to the types of Christ: therefore... Whether few, or many, or all understood the types, we do not much care; at least some understood them. From where? Either from the ordinary doctrine which sounded in the Church, or from extraordinary revelation. If you say the latter, prove it. Further, in the question about ordinary faith, and that of men living in general under the Old Testament, see how you will answer, outside the bounds, about an extraordinary case. But if the former, then there flourished at that time a doctrine which explained the types as they ought to be explained, concerning Christ, and the grace and salvation to be obtained through him. And if this is true, then that doctrine was not merely of the general favour of God, but also of the special grace in Christ, which rested on and agreed with promises of the same kind. Why should you not say that all the faithful and pious believed that doctrine? For the saving doctrine has not sounded so vainly for ever that many at every time have not believed it and obeyed it.

units.la: Quomodo de Christo, ejus promissione, & in ipsum fide, ita de vita aeterna in Vet. T. promissa sperataque dogmatizant Remonstrantes. Apol. cap. xv. f. 251. Certum enim est, praeceptum fidei in Iesum Christum nusquam in V. Testamento clare traditum extare, uti neque in terminis promissio vitae aeternae in eo extat. Pariter ergo de utroque philosophantur, visi non quidem aperte negare Christi & vitæ æternæ promissionem in Vet. Testamento extare ullam, quod Sociniani; quàm apertam, claram, directam, & in terminis. Adde, cap. i. f. 26. Neque aliter capere vel conciliare possum quod habent cap. xii. f. 138. Promissionem vitæ æternæ autem sub V. Fœdere factam, aut legę Mosis comprehensam fuisse, non solus, nec primus Socinus, sed eadem multis retro ante sæculis negavit antiquitas: utrumque hoc prolixè varii probarunt, iisque antiquitatum peritissimi scru-tatores: Neutrum affirmant Remonstrantes, neque, ut affirment, necessarium putant; uti jam ante vidimus.
units.tr: In the same way that the Remonstrants teach about Christ, his promise, and faith in him, they also teach about the eternal life promised and hoped for in the Old Testament. Apology, ch. 15, p. 251: For it is certain that the precept of faith in Jesus Christ is nowhere clearly set forth in the Old Testament, just as the promise of eternal life is nowhere found in that Testament in so many words. They therefore reason in the same way about both. They do not indeed openly deny, as the Socinians do, that any promise of Christ or of eternal life is found in the Old Testament; but they deny that it is open, clear, direct, and stated in so many words. Add ch. 1, p. 26. I cannot understand or reconcile what they say in ch. 12, p. 138, any other way. That the promise of eternal life was made under the Old Covenant, or was contained in the law of Moses, was not denied by Socinus alone, nor first by him; antiquity denied it many centuries earlier. Various writers have argued both points at length, and they were most skilled investigators of antiquity. The Remonstrants affirm neither, nor do they think it necessary to affirm either, as we have already seen.

units.la: Quadruplicem faciunt religionem, primam ab Adamo, ad Abrahamum, quam naturalem, & tantum naturalem fuisse, volunt. Episcopius, Instit. lib. i. cap. viii. Atque hæc religio, naturalis plane religio est, quæ rectam solam rationem pro regula ac mensura habet; cujus actus primus est, discrimen recti à prauo. — Ac primo quidem videntur mihi non pauca nec evidentia vestigia apparere, ab ipsis primordiis mundi, cum nulla adhuc lex lata esset, hominesque tantum ad certæ rationis præscriptum vivere, aut saltem vixisse leguntur. Vult homines tum vixisse sine lege lata, & sine promissione, sola duce natura, & naturali ratione. Et sane si sequentia secula, id est fere bis mille annos consecutos videa-mus, ea promissionum expertia fuisse, comperiemus. — aut sine ulla scripta lege, ad normam solius rectæ rationis, absq; ullis promissionibus specialis ac singularis benevolentiæ suæ, primos hominess vivere permiserat.
units.tr: They make four religions. The first, from Adam to Abraham, they want to be natural, and only natural. Episcopius, Institutes, bk. 1, ch. 8: And this religion is plainly a natural religion, which takes right reason alone as its rule and measure, and whose first act is the discernment of right from wrong. — Yet at the outset there seem to me to appear not a few clear traces of this from the very beginnings of the world, when no law had yet been given and men are read to have lived, or at least to have lived, only by the rule of sure reason. He wants men then to have lived without any law given and without any promise, guided by nature alone and by natural reason. And indeed, if we look at the following ages, that is, nearly two thousand years afterwards, we shall find that they were without promises. — or that God allowed the first men to live without any written law, by the standard of right reason alone and without any promises of his special and singular goodwill.

units.la: Hinc Abrahamo factas dicunt promissiones primas, & cum eo Deum inivisse fœdus; quæ secunda religio, vel religionis diversæ forma, ab Abrahamo, ad Mosem. Episcopius, lib. ii. cap. i. Prima revelatio Abrahamo facta, nimirum cum fœderatione conjuncta. — & fœderis quidem sanciti clara atque expressa promissione & stipulatione. Promissiones has constituunt duum generum, communem unam, qua Deus Abrahamo bene se gerenti favorem, gratiam, opem, & auxilium pollicebatur; quod ad omnia sinunt extendi, non temporalia tantum beneficia, sed & æterna, vel quo eum Deus conservaturus, & immunem præstiturus erat ab æternâ morte, vitaque ipsa æterna donaturus. — Generalia enim ejusmodi pronuntiata extendi possunt in inauditum usque, saltem quatenus vis & verborum ipsorum proprietas extendi potest: alteram propriam Abrahamo & peculiarem, i. de terræ Canaan possessione. ii. de semine terræ istius hærede. iii. de seminis istius admirabili multiplicatione, & reductione ex servitute. iv. de seminis benedictione. Et ita quidem promissiones istas accipiendas, pro sensu litterali, sed pro sensu mystico etiam spiritualiter interpretandas, de vero semine benedicto, quod est Christus, & æternæ vitæ, tamquam veri Canaan, possessione: Dico itaque per terram Canaan promissam, Deum significare voluisse cœlum, tamquam Abrahami & fidelium Abrahami vestigiis insistentium patriam, verein[?] seculum sive proprie æternam possidendam. Per semen Abrahamo promissum, Iesum Christum, & populum ejus Christianum, fide Abrahamica Deo adhærentem. Per justificationem Abrahami ante circumcisionem acceptam, & ante legem Mosis latam, justificationem tam gentilium quam Iudeorum sine operibus legis futuram. Sensum hunc mysticum sub promissionibus illis carnalibus Abrahamo factis, veluti sub umbris ac typis comprehensam fuisse, eumque Deum ipsum sub isto verborum corti ce intendisse, nos Christiani ab Apostolis edocti, ex Epist. ad Romanos, ad Heb. & ad Galatas, credimus, & credibile est tum temporis in confesso fuisse apud Hebræos, saltem duos istos priores sensus. Ergo rectè ex Novo Testamento de Veteri judicamus, & bene procedit hinc argumentum: ut quamvis aliquid non totidem verbis in veteri legatur factum, aut creditum fuisse, tamen si ei testimonium perhibeatur in Novo, affirmare de Veteri illud liceat. Deinde credi-bile, plura a veteribus cognita creditaque fuisse, quam quae necesse sit ex ipsius Veteris Testamenti verbis ostendere. Praeterea non tantum ex Veteris foederis promissionibus spiritualia illa & aeterna quovis modo colliguntur, sed a Deo quoque iis ista intentione, haec ut significarent, proposita fuerunt. Deniq;quin proinde clare & aperte, & directe eadem illis fuerint inculcata, haud est quod negent Nostri. Neque dubito, inquit Episcopius, quin Judei hodieque idsint[?] libenter agnituri; qui optima quaeque de Abrahamo & promissionibus Abrahamo factis credunt, & credere paene necesse habent. Ego vero existimo, fideles illos sub V. T. plura, & clarius vidisse in divinis promissionibus, quam hodie faciunt improbi & contumaces Judaei. Praeterea si sua circumcisione quotidie admonebantur Christi, tamquam seminis veri & benedicti, quomodo non dilucide etiam constitisse ipsis promissionem illam dicemus? Atqui id Episcopius agnoscit, lib. 11. cap. x. Quod hoc ipso signo Deus promissionis suae, seu ejus quod Abrahamo promiserat, memoriam extare, & quasi perpetuo ob oculos versari, vel identidem in memoriam revocari voluerit, &c. Circumcisionem itaque instituit, quae non nisi ea parte fit, qua semen prodit. Itaque istud ipsum volebat Deus eo fine isti corporis parti impressum, ut quotiescunque illud intuerentur, aut infantes circumciderent, toties promissi seminis recordarentur; quod pulcherrime in Epistola ad Galatas adnotatum est cap. 3. vers. 16. & 19. Credo equidem: sed non dicam, ut illud ita a Veteribus tum temporis intellectum fuisse, ostendat ex ipsius Veteris T.historia; tantummodo ut ne neget apertam & expressam ergo illorum fidem in Christum fuisse, cujus adeo apertum & expressum gerebant & contuebantur quotidie in carne sua documentum. Quare statim subdit: atque ut hujus feminis promissi memoria semper inhaereret animis populi, hinc circumcisio addita foederi, & seve-re imperata fuit, tanquam signum, promissioni isti designandae & veluti repraesentandae ido-neum, ac tantum non genuinum.
units.tr: From this they say that the first promises were made to Abraham, and that God entered into a covenant with him. This is the second religion, or a different form of religion, from Abraham to Moses. Episcopius, bk. 2, ch. 1: The first revelation made to Abraham, namely one joined with a covenant. — and indeed a covenant sanctioned by a clear and express promise and stipulation. They distinguish these promises into two kinds. One is general, in which God promised Abraham, who behaved well, his favour, grace, help, and assistance; this they allow to extend to all things, not only temporal benefits but also eternal ones, namely that God would keep him and make him immune from eternal death, and would give him eternal life itself. Such general statements can indeed be extended without limit, at least so far as the force and proper meaning of the words themselves allow. The other is proper and peculiar to Abraham, concerning: (i) the possession of the land of Canaan; (ii) a seed who would inherit that land; (iii) the wonderful multiplication of that seed and its deliverance from slavery; (iv) the blessing of that seed. And these promises are to be taken in their literal sense, but also to be interpreted spiritually in their mystical sense, concerning the true blessed seed, which is Christ, and the possession of eternal life as the true Canaan. I say, therefore, that by the land of Canaan promised, God meant to signify heaven, as the homeland of Abraham and of the faithful who walk in the steps of Abraham, to be possessed truly and eternally. By the seed promised to Abraham, he meant Jesus Christ and his Christian people, who cling to God with Abraham's faith. By the justification of Abraham, accepted before circumcision and before the law of Moses was given, he meant a justification without works of the law, to come for Gentiles as well as Jews. We Christians, taught by the Apostles in the Epistles to the Romans, to the Hebrews, and to the Galatians, believe that this mystical sense was comprehended under those carnal promises made to Abraham, as under shadows and types, and that God himself intended it under this outward shell of words; and it is credible that at that time at least these two senses, the first two, were admitted among the Hebrews. Therefore we rightly judge the Old Testament from the New, and the argument proceeds well: that although something is not set down in so many words in the Old Testament as having been done or believed, yet if testimony is borne to it in the New, it is permitted to affirm it of the Old. Further, it is credible that more things were known and believed by the ancients than it is necessary to show from the very words of the Old Testament. Moreover, those spiritual and eternal things are not only gathered in any way from the promises of the Old Covenant, but God also set them before those people with this intention, that they might signify these things. Finally, that these same things were not clearly, openly, and directly impressed upon them is no reason for our opponents to deny it. I do not doubt, says Episcopius, that the Jews even today would gladly acknowledge it, since they believe all the best things about Abraham and the promises made to Abraham, and almost feel bound to believe them. I for my part think that those faithful people under the Old Testament saw more, and more clearly, in the divine promises than the wicked and stubborn Jews do today. Furthermore, if they were daily reminded of Christ by their circumcision, as of the true and blessed seed, how can we say that the promise was not plainly understood by them? Yet Episcopius concedes this, bk. 2, ch. 10: That by this very sign God wished the memory of his promise, or of what he had promised to Abraham, to remain, and as it were to be constantly before the eyes, or to be recalled to memory again and again, etc. He therefore instituted circumcision, which is performed only on that part from which the seed comes forth. Thus God wished that very part of the body to be marked for this end, so that whenever they looked upon it, or circumcised infants, they would be reminded of the promised seed; which is very beautifully noted in the Epistle to the Galatians, ch. 3, verses 16 and 19. I do believe it. But I will not say that it was understood in this way by the ancients at that time, since he does not show it from the history of the Old Testament itself; I say only so that he does not deny that their faith in Christ was clear and express, since they bore and beheld daily in their own flesh so clear and express a token of it. Hence he immediately adds: And so that the memory of this promised seed might always cling to the minds of the people, circumcision was added to the covenant and severely commanded, as a sign suited to designating and, as it were, representing that promise, and virtually not a mere figure.

units.la: Jam quemadmodum diversas religiones Sociniani faciunt, primam Adami, alteram Abrahami, & aevi hujus iistiusque hominum, tertiam Mosaicam; sic & Episcopius: utrumque quartam denique Christi. In promissis foederis Mosaici ille, lib. III. sect.IV. cap. I. iterum alia specialia collocat de bonis terrenis, ea omnia non continent nisi bona terrena, tum ad esse, tum ad bene esse, vitae hujus praesentis pertinentia; alia generalia, sub qui-bus & futurae vitae bona fuerint comprehensa, ex Dei intentione sub litera ista pro isto tempore occultata & nunc clare manifestata: verosimiliter etiam aut intellecta, aut apprehensa a prudentioribus sanctioribusque in populo isto: de quo tamen nolim contendere. Videlicet cum Socinianis. Quoscunque alios oppugnes, modo non istos. Sperata enim & cre-dita fuisse ab iis certum est, si non sub ratione typorum, saltem sub generalitate promissorum. — Atque hoc sensu vix dubium mihi est, quin fideles & sancti in populo Dei sub Veteri Testamento promissa divina acceperint.
units.tr: Just as the Socinians make the religions diverse, the first of Adam, the second of Abraham (and of this age and of these men), the third Mosaic, so also does Episcopius; and he finally makes a fourth, that of Christ. Concerning the promises of the Mosaic covenant, he again, bk. 3, sect. 4, ch. 1, sets out other special promises about earthly goods, which contain only earthly goods, pertaining both to the being and the well-being of this present life; and other general promises, under which the goods of the future life were also included, in God's intention hidden under that letter for that time and now clearly manifested. It is probable that these were also understood or grasped by the wiser and holier men among that people; yet I would not wish to contend this. Namely, I agree with the Socinians, provided you oppose any others but not them. For it is certain that they hoped for and believed these things, if not under the aspect of types, at least under the generality of the promises. — And in this sense I hardly doubt that the faithful and holy people of God under the Old Testament received the divine promises.

units.la: Caeterum quemadmodum Volkelius in religionibus illis passim duo considerat, praecepta primum, seu pietatis officia, & secundo loco promissiones ac minas, vel sal-tem spem praemiorum, ac poenarum metum, ita praesertim in prima illa Adami religio-ne designanda, sive naturali, quam vocant, conveniunt inter se Volkelius, & Episco-pius. Nam & ille dixit, lib. II. cap. VIII. quod eorum temporum homines religiosi non tam ex fixis statisque legibus, seu generalibus praeceptis, aperte a Deo propositis, quam ex certae rationis judicio, vitam ac mores suos composuerunt. De promissis similiter, & eodem capite: Restat ut de promissis idem fere, quod & de mandatis primae illius religionis, dicamus: nempe[?] vix aut ne vix quidem generale aliquod illius saeculi hominibus promissum factum: sed minus potius tunc illis metusque propositos fuisse. Neque aliter Episcopius, & notatu di-gnum est, legem primo homini latam, nulla boni novi aut melioris promissione sancitam fuisse, sed sola malorum aut mortis comminatione.
units.tr: Moreover, just as Volkelius in those religions regularly distinguishes two things, first the precepts or duties of piety, and secondly the promises and threats, or at least the hope of rewards and the fear of punishments, so Episcopius and Volkelius agree with each other, especially in describing the first religion of Adam, the so-called natural religion. For Volkelius says in book 2, chapter 8: "that religious men of those times framed their life and morals not so much from fixed and settled laws, or general precepts openly proposed by God, as from the judgment of a certain reason." And concerning promises, in the same chapter: "It remains that we say about promises nearly the same as about the commands of that first religion: namely, scarcely or not even scarcely any general promise was made to men of that age, but rather fears were set before them then." Episcopius says the same: "And it is worth noting that the law given to the first man was sanctioned by no promise of any new or better good, but only by the threat of evil or death."

units.la: Duo ergo in controversiam hic veniunt, I. annon alia quam naturalis religio primos in mundo homines & Ecclesiam egerit ac gubernarit? II. & nullae adeo ipsis factae fuerint promissiones?
units.tr: Two questions therefore come into dispute here: I. Did some religion other than natural religion guide and govern the first men and the Church? II. And were no promises at all made to them?

units.la: Praesuppono, etiam tum pro ratione Ecclesiae perpetua, & hominum universali conditione, alios fuisse bonos, alios malos. Imo id constat, illos fuisse — contradistincto ad istos habitos, & quid ni sic appellatos tunc quoque? Filios Dei; uti reliquos, filios hominum. Genes. vi. 2. Jam vero in tam brevi historia, & tot tantarumque rerum compendio multum videri debet, si non dissimulatum Dei Verbo, sed vel ex tenui documento illud significatum fuisse quod quaerimus, ostendi queat. Quum longe plura & facta, & docta, & credita fuisse semper, quam singulatim narrentur, sit apertissimum. Hic ergo praeter illa, quae quantumvis tenuiter, ex illa prima primaevi temporis, & fere ἀδήλα[?] historia habentur, addi juste debent, quae sequentium temporum Scriptura, etiam Novi Testamenti, de majorum fide & religione commemorat, tamquam ad priorum temporum ἐξήγησιν & commentarium. Quemadmodum sequentibus temporibus sensim uberior rerum omnium manifestatio in Ecclesia viguit, & Scriptura uti librorum, sic rerum copia magis abundavit: non etiam ac solem cum profecto diei & temporis quaquaversum radios densius emittere, & majorem ubique lucem dispergere, videmus.
units.tr: I presuppose, given the perpetual nature of the Church and the universal condition of mankind, that even then there were some good and some evil. Indeed it is established that those men, in contrast to the others, were, and why should they not then also be called, "sons of God", just as the rest were sons of men (Gen. vi. 2). Now in so brief a history, and a summary of so many and so great matters, much should be expected to appear, if it can be shown that the Word of God did not conceal what we are seeking, but signified it, even from a slight piece of evidence. For it is most evident that far more things were always done, taught and believed than are narrated one by one. Here, therefore, besides those things which, however slightly, are found in that first and almost obscure history of the primeval age, there ought rightly to be added what Scripture of later times, including the New Testament, records of the faith and religion of the forefathers, as an explanation and commentary on the earlier times. Just as in later times a fuller manifestation of all things flourished in the Church, and Scripture, as of books, so the abundance of matters grew greater, just as we see the sun, as the day and the hour advance, send its rays more densely in every direction and spread a greater light everywhere.

units.la: Non vero sequitur, prima illa mundi aetate, homines tantum ad rectae rationis praescriptum vivere jussos, vel vixisse, ideo quod in illorum temporum historia nonnulla legantur, quae cum recta ratione omnino conveniunt; uti, quod Genes. iv. 6. 7. Deus ad Cainum, nonne si bene feceris, erit elevatio? & quod si non beneficeris, pro foribus cu-bat peccatum? qua naturali constant certaque ratione, à conscientia boni & mali sum-ta, & sic alia similia: nam non ea probant, nihil insuper illis hominibus revelatum fuisse, quam quod ex sola natura haberi potest, non magis quam quod revelatio su-pernaturalis talia etiam comprehendat, quae ex natura possunt argui.
units.tr: Yet it does not follow that men in that first age of the world were commanded, or lived, to live only by the prescription of right reason, merely because some things are read in the history of those times which altogether agree with right reason. Such is God's word to Cain in Gen. iv. 6-7: "Shall it not be, if you do well, an uplifting? And if you do not do well, does sin lie crouching at the door?" These words rest on a natural and certain reasoning drawn from the conscience of good and evil, and so do other similar things. For they do not prove that nothing more was revealed to those men than what can be had from nature alone, any more than that supernatural revelation comprehends no things that can also be argued from nature.

units.la: Contrà autem quum negare nemo queat, non etiam Adversarii negent, multiplici modo πολυμερῶς τῇ[?] πολυτρόπως Deum illis quoque loquutum fuisse Patribus, revelavit enim se Adamo, Caino, Enocho, Noë, &c. nihilne credas Deum istis loquutum fuisse, nihil officii aut rei salutaris manifestasse, nisi quod ex natura peteretur, & hinc satis homini constaret? Quare autem sic restringas frequentes & gloriosas Dei ad ipsos revelationes, & tuam de illis fidem, ut de solis naturalibus egerint, & nihil supernaturalis aut officii aut beneficii illis omnibus voluerit attingere? Quo fine vel cohibere se istis terminis voluerit Deus, aut nihil eorum, quae sequentibus saepe, illis aperire constituerit? Nimirum quia sic in ipso statim mundi primordio nihil sese cuiquam debere, sed omnium rerum absolutissimum Dominum esse, omnibus offendere voluit, inquit Volkelius. Quasi vero si Deus spiritualia & salutaria illis jam tum revelarit beneficia, negarit isto modo se absolutissimum omnium esse Dominum, vel id ullo modo obscurarit. Imo eo ipso illud declaravit magis. Vel quando Deus illa post-modum revelavit, uti revelata suo tempore inficiari non possunt, tum vero dissimulavit se Deum, & Dominum esse, qualis est: si quidpiam ex natura constare & probari potest, hoc est, quod Deus omnium est absolutus Dominus: quo ex natura jam cognito, quomodo quod superioris revelationis a Deo est, ejus vim ullo modo vel infringere potest vel obfuscare? quinimo quodcunque ullo unquam tempore revelationi divinae accessit, ad illud confirmandum valuit, & nunquam aliter quam ad ejus corroborandam vim facere apud ullos potuit. Si dicerent, Deum primaevos homines sivisse suo vivere arbitratu, & quemadmodum Gentiles postea, suis incedere viis, nulla eos dignatus sui revelatione, facilius concipi posset, vixisse illos solo rationis suae ductu: at quum nemo ignoret, Deum se multoties iis patefecisse, & de variis loquutum rebus fuisse, hic istas revelationes omnes coercere intra hemispherium rerum naturalium & animalium, ut de coelestibus nō voluerit quidpiam attingere, quod aut praeceptum, aut promissum connotarit altioris supra naturam ordinis, tam contra solitam est Dei benignissimi liberalitatem, quam dignam hominibus θεοσέβειαν [?] religionem ac salutem.
units.tr: On the contrary, since no one can deny, and not even our opponents deny, that God spoke to those fathers too in many and various ways (πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως, Heb. i. 1), for he revealed himself to Adam, Cain, Enoch, Noah, and so on, do you think that God spoke to them, revealing nothing of duty or of saving matter, except what might be sought from nature, and from this it was enough for man to know? Why then do you so restrict God's frequent and glorious revelations to them, and your own belief about them, that they dealt only with natural things, and that God wished to touch on nothing supernatural, of duty or of benefit, in all of them? For what end would God have wished to confine himself to these limits, or decided to reveal none of those things which he often opened up afterwards? Namely, says Volkelius, because thus he wished to show to all men at the very beginning of the world that he owed nothing to anyone, but was the most absolute Lord of all. As if, indeed, had God already then revealed spiritual and saving benefits, he would thereby have denied that he is the most absolute Lord of all, or in any way obscured it. Rather, by that very thing he would have declared it more. Or again, when God afterwards revealed those things, as they cannot deny they were revealed in their time, would he then have hidden that he is God and Lord, as he is? If anything can be established and proved from nature, it is this: that God is the absolute Lord of all. Since this is already known from nature, how can what comes from God by an earlier revelation in any way weaken or obscure its force? Indeed, whatever was added to divine revelation at any time served to confirm that truth, and it could never, for anyone, act in any other way than to strengthen its force. If they said that God allowed the first men to live at their own pleasure, and, like the Gentiles afterwards, to walk their own ways, deigning to give them no revelation of himself, it could more easily be conceived that they lived by the guidance of their reason alone. But since no one is ignorant that God manifested himself to them many times, and spoke to them of various matters, to confine all these revelations within the sphere of natural things and animals, so that he would touch on nothing heavenly which signified a precept or promise of an order higher than nature, is as contrary to the customary liberality of the most kind God as it is to the godliness [θεοσέβειαν] and salvation worthy of men.

units.la: Deinde qui ex fide vivit, ille non vivit ex sola sua ratione: nam uti sensus, externis: ita ratio nititur perceptâ judicio rerum causâ; fides vero auctoritate revelantis & dicentis hoc quod creditur, qui si homo, nascitur inde humana fides, sin Deus, divina: at primi mundi justi vixerunt quoque ex fide: ergo. Justus ex fide vivit: fuerint illi & justi, & fideles. Utrumque probat Epist. ad Hebraeos, cap. xi. Nam quum dixisset Apostolus cap. x, 38. sive initio istius [illegible, ~8 letters]: justus autem ex fide vivet, ex Heb. ii. 4. quod idem Rom. i. 17. Gal. iii. 11. id est, omnium temporum unius veritate. & vers. seq. 39. nos vero non sumus defectionis ad exitium, sed fidei ad redemtionem animae. eo significat, intelligi a se fidem, quae animae salutem secum trahit, sive fidem salutarem. vers. i. cap. xi. est enim fides, speratorum [?] hypostasis, & demonstratio rerum quae non videntur. verbo ut dicam, non rerum simpliciter naturalium.
units.tr: Moreover, he who lives by faith does not live by his reason alone. For just as the senses rest on external things, so reason rests on a judgment of perceived causes; but faith rests on the authority of the one who reveals and says what is believed. If that is a man, human faith arises; if God, divine faith. But the righteous of the first world also lived by faith; therefore they were righteous and faithful too. The Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, proves both. For when the Apostle had said in chapter 10, verse 38, "But the just shall live by faith" (from Hab. ii. 4), which he likewise says in Rom. i. 17 and Gal. iii. 11, that is, the truth of all times is one, and in the following verse, 39, "But we are not of those who draw back to destruction, but of faith to the saving of the soul," he signifies that he means faith which brings the salvation of the soul with it, that is, saving faith. Chapter 11, verse 1: "For faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." In a word, not of merely natural things.

units.la: vers. 2. hujus testimonium acceperunt veteres, ἐν ταύτῃ [?] ἐμαρτυρήθησαν οἱ πρεσ-βύτεροι. de eadem loquitur fide, γὰρ [?]: & innexa adeo argumenta, de unâ eâdemque fide & antiquorum, & praesentium sermonem esse, docent. Quinam isti πρεσβύτεροι seniores? vers. 4. Abel, vers. 5. Enoch, vers. 7. Noach, fide Abel melius sacrificium Deo obtulit prae Caino, per quod testimonium accepit quod esset justus. Justus fuit, ac fidelis, & fide sacrificium obtulit Deo eximium, & gratum, vers. 5. fide translatus fuit Enoch, ne videret mortem: & non repertus fuit, quandoquidem transtulit eum Deus: ante translationem enim testimonium accepit, quod placeret Deo. Hic placuit Deo, per fidem. Et ne singulare id quis putaret, generale interserit axioma Apostolus, sine fide autem impossibile est placere Deo. & tum, & nunc. atqj uti placendum Deo omnino, ita sine fide fieri id prorsus impossibile. Credere autem oportet eum qui accedit ad Deum, quod est, & quaerentibus se est retributor. Non potest non qui in Deum credit, & hoc credere, quod sit gratiose concessurus mercedem. Atque qui Deus dicetur nullam facere iis voluisse μισθαποδότην promissionem? Credent scilicet motu & arbitrariu proprio ac incerto, ὡς εἰς ἀέρα. Et debent tamen hoc aeque credere, Deum esse μισθαποδότην, quam ὅτι ἔστι, Deo & hoc, & istud ipsis revelante: nimirum ut quis talem aliquando mercedem accipiat a Deo, ac Enoch accepit, non quod ad modum μεταθέσεως eandem, sed quod ad rem ac cœlestem apud Deum hæreditatem. vers. 7. fide divinitus admonitus Noë de iis quæ nondum cernebantur, veritus construxit arcam ad salutem domus suæ: per quam condemnavit mundum, & factus est hæres justitiæ quæ secundum fidem est. Quod est elogium Abrahamo, ejusque fidei dari solitum: ut eandem etiam ante ipsum, & fidem, & fidei justitiam viguisse, doceamur. Ex quibus illa jam consequuntur. 1. Non rationem tantum, sed fidem apud Patres illos locum habuisse. 11. & eandem fidem, quæ sequentium, quæ reliquorum fuit, sive in V. sive in N. T. Nam & ejusdem generis ubique ponitur, & eodem modo tum describitur fides, tum commendatur. 111. Speciatim de illa primæ vorum fide dicitur, quod eâ justi fuerint, & grati Deo, ipsi, & facta ipsorum Deo placuerint, quod per eam ad Deum accesserint, & mercedem expectarint Deo dignam, denique & justitiam fidei adepti sint, & hæreditatem, quæ filiorum, uti & filii ipsi. Propterea jam appellantur filii Dei, Genef. vi. 2. Quæ adoptio, & justificatio, & glorificatio ut fidei attribuuntur & fidelibus, sic certe supra naturam adscendunt longè & rationem naturalem.
units.tr: Verse 2: "By this the elders obtained witness" [ἐν ταύτῃ ἐμαρτυρήθησαν οἱ πρεσβύτεροι]. He speaks of that same faith, and the arguments linked together show that the discourse concerns one and the same faith of both the ancients and the present. Who are these elders? Verse 4, Abel; verse 5, Enoch; verse 7, Noah. "By faith Abel offered to God a better sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained witness that he was righteous." He was righteous and faithful, and by faith offered to God an excellent and acceptable sacrifice. Verse 5: "By faith Enoch was translated, that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had translated him; for before his translation he had witness that he pleased God." Here he pleased God through faith. And lest anyone think this was singular, the Apostle inserts a general axiom: "But without faith it is impossible to please God," then as now; and just as it is altogether necessary to please God, so without faith it is utterly impossible. "For he who comes to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him." He who believes in God cannot but believe this, that God will graciously grant a reward. Shall it then be said that God wished to make no promise of reward to them? Would they believe by their own impulse, arbitrarily and uncertainly, as if into the air? Yet they ought equally to believe that God is a rewarder as that he is, God revealing both this and that to them: namely, that someone should receive from God such a reward as Enoch received, not the same by way of translation, but in substance, and the heavenly inheritance with God. Verse 7: "By faith Noah, divinely warned about things not yet seen, moved with reverence, built an ark for the saving of his house, by which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is according to faith." This is a commendation usually given to Abraham and his faith, so that we may be taught that the same faith, and the righteousness of faith, flourished even before him. From these things the following consequences follow. 1. Not reason only, but faith, had its place among those fathers. 2. And it was the same faith that was of the later and other men, whether in the Old or the New Testament; for it is everywhere set down as of the same kind, and faith is both described and commended in the same way. 3. Specifically, it is said of the faith of the first men that by it they were righteous and pleasing to God; they themselves and their deeds pleased God; through it they came to God and expected a reward worthy of God; and finally they obtained the righteousness of faith and the inheritance that belongs to sons, and they were sons themselves. Therefore they are already called sons of God, Gen. vi. 2. Such adoption, justification and glorification, as they are attributed to faith and to the faithful, certainly rise far above nature and natural reason.

units.la: Tertio naturæ, & naturali rationi, uti formali & adæquato principio adscribi nequeunt aliæ, quæ de ipsis dicuntur. Non ipsa primum pietas: quæ non fœtus naturæ est, in homine nunc peccatore, sed ut conditionem, ita vires naturæ supergreditur. Hoc differt vera pietas à naturali Ethica, quod hæc ratione constat, illa superiori principio Spiritus Sancti, & tanto altius hominem provehit, quo altioris est originis & causæ. Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei: nam stultitia ei sunt, & non potest agnoscere, nam spiritualiter dijudicantur. 1 Cor. ii. 15. Homo ψυχικὸς divina nec percipit, nec percipere potest, neque illa quæ Dei sunt, quæ ad eum tendunt, vel gratum Deo hominem efficiunt. Τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ[?] ea quæ Dei nemo novit, nisi Spiritus Dei. vers. 11. & quicunque alii, nonnisi per istum Spiritum. Nobis autem revelavit Deus per Spiritum suum. vers. 10. & 12. Nos autem non accepimus Spiritum mundi, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo: & hinc Dei illa tum capere quadantenus possumus, tum præstare. Cogitatio carnis inimicitia adversus Deum. Rom. viii. x. Deinde filiorum Dei appellatio & vis celsior est, quam ut à naturâ trahat originem. Præterea sacrificandi ratio, & statim ita primis fratribus observata, non ut incertum aliquod, & de quo alter forte ambigeret, sed in quo ambo unanimiter conveniebant, arguit, non solam ipsos in Dei cultu naturam sequutos fuisse. Quomodo enim id dictet statim ratio, Deum præsertim sacrificiis coli, istaq; ei singulariter grata esse, & hinc hominum apparere discrimen? Multo labore hæc ex merâ naturali ratione colligas, non certe tam cito & seliciter, ut ita concordes id primi homines fecerint, quam si ab instituto & revelatione Dei vel Adamo, vel ipsis factâ, illud venire agnoscas. Id quidem ex ratione rectâ colligere Abel potuit, Deum colendum esse rebus, quas habebat, optimis: sed non pariter ex merâ ratione, quod Deus coli vellet sacrificiis: neque in eo præstantia sacrificii unius præ altero fuit sita, quod ex terræ frugibus hoc, istud ex animalibus constabat, sed quod fide præstaret fratre suo Abel. Ergo ex eventu & facto colligere licet de revelatione illis facta: & hoc inter alia re- velatum significatumque ipsis fuisse, ut Deo sacrificarent, ad quod perficiendum tam prompte & alacriter se accinxerint. Non ergo exsola ratione, sed divinâ revelatione religionem instituerunt primi illi suam.
units.tr: Thirdly, the other things said of them cannot be ascribed to nature or to natural reason as their formal and adequate principle. Piety itself is not, first of all, the offspring of nature in man as he is now a sinner; like the condition of grace, it surpasses the powers of nature. True piety differs from natural ethics in this: the latter rests on reason, while the former rests on a higher principle, the Holy Spirit, and it raises man as much higher as its origin and cause is higher. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 Cor. ii. 15. The psychic man [ψυχικὸς] neither perceives nor can perceive the things of God, nor those things which tend toward God or make a man pleasing to God. The things of God no one knows except the Spirit of God. Vers. 11, and likewise whoever else, only through that Spirit. But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit. Vers. 10 and 12. But we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God; and hence we are able, in some measure, both to grasp these things of God and to perform them. The mind of the flesh is enmity against God. Rom. viii. 7. Further, the title and dignity of sons of God are too lofty to derive their origin from nature. Moreover, the manner of sacrificing, observed at once by the first brothers, was not something uncertain about which one of them might perhaps have doubted, but something on which both agreed unanimously; this shows that they did not follow nature alone in the worship of God. For how would reason at once dictate that God is to be worshipped especially by sacrifices, that these are singularly pleasing to him, and that a distinction between men thereby appears? You could gather these things from mere natural reason only with great labour, and certainly not so quickly and happily that the first men would have agreed so well in doing it, as you must acknowledge if you recognise that it came from the institution and revelation of God, given either to Adam or to themselves. Abel could indeed gather from right reason that God is to be worshipped with the best things one has; but not equally from mere reason that God wished to be worshipped with sacrifices. Nor did the excellence of one sacrifice over the other lie in this, that one consisted of the fruits of the earth and the other of animals, but in the fact that Abel excelled his brother by faith. Therefore it is permissible to infer from the outcome and the deed that a revelation was made to them, and that among other things it was revealed and signified to them that they should sacrifice to God, a command they so promptly and eagerly set themselves to perform. Therefore those first men established their religion not from reason alone, but from divine revelation.

units.la: Tom. 2. Ad quod non majus adferri argumentum potest, & quo constat etiam non absque promissio illos vixisse, & generali, & praeclaro, quod sideris instar hinc fulsit perpetuo in Ecclesia, quam Gen. iii. 15. ubi illud semen promisit Deus, quod contereret serpentis caput. Messiam intelligi Christianus nemo negare potest: uti nec, quod praedicatur summa officii ejus, situra in hoc quod aboleret eum, qui mortis habet imperium, sive Diabolum. Hoc quo magis ad primos quoque homines spectare appareret, sub nomine serpentis proterendi, a quo jam tum adeo misere decepti fuerant, proponitur: quod, uti promissum, ita quoque credi oportuit, atque eo ipso fidem ab ipsis postulavit & assensum. Certe summa Euangelii illo vaticinio comprehensa fuit & salutis. Quid pro hominis redemtione facturus erat Deus, quomodo nascitu-rus ex muliere aliquando, qui a serpentis ictu liberaturus & vindicaturus erat hominem, hinc & huic futurum suum semen sanctum, & quod continuam cum serpente foveret inimicitiam, & post luctam cum malo, & sancte custoditas suas partes, in capite illo suo ac duce perpetuum triumpharet. Neque dissitetur Episcopius, quod Christum Servatorem Deus hoc loco significavit, quamvis obscure: Hoc propositum suum Deus obscure primum significare voluit, & quidem sub voce seminis, & seminis quidem mulieris, quod contriturum esset caput serpentis. —— Id vero quod significatum Deus voluit, quid aliud esse posse videtur, quam hoc, quod Deus procuraturus esset suo tempore ut filius hominis Diabolum, qui in Dei horto seu Paradiso per serpentis os causam fuerat casus vel lapsus hominis in mortem, vicissim in horto suo, id est, mundi hujus cujus ipse Deus esse dicitur, obtineret, eique caput comminueret, id est, vim omnem laedendi & perdendi eriperet. Sensum ipsum, Dei sensum fuisse, rei ipsius naturam indicatur postulare, —— & cum non parum confirmat id unum, quod tota Scriptura Veteris Testamenti non videatur esse, adeoque non fit nisi genealogia quaedam, sive series majorum seminis benedicti, id est, Iesu Christi, unde ipsius divini propositi ratio non obscure elucescit. Recte quod ex natura rei heic quoq; argumentetur: & sic certe natura religionis verae exposcit, ut non fit mere naturalis, nec mere naturalis ille Dei cultus, quo flagrarunt primi mundi & Ecclesiae incolę, uti nec mere natura-lis eorum salus. Natura rei postulat illum sensum, atque eadem rei natura sensus illos locorum & testimoniorum Scripturae, quae modo vidimus, de primorum hominum fide ac pietate. Denique & natura rei postulat, ut quomodo illa proposita a Deo fuerunt hominibus, & jugiter ipsis praedicata & inculcata, sic quoq; hi crediderint futura aliquando, in subsidium & salutem omnium eorum, quos a serpente per Chri-stum liberari intererat. Non potest aliter accipi, quam pro promissione: & sic accipere omnes oportuit, ad quos illa facta. Non ergo primum Abrahamo facta promissio de Christo, & femine benedicto fuit. Obscura quamvis nobis videatur, & tam brevi Euangelio indicata magis, quam explicata; nihil tamen est quod dubitemus, & divinarum revelationum frequentia, & vatum ac praeconum, & sacerdotum continua cura magis expositam & elucidatam quotidie fuisse, praesertim ab usu concio-num & cultus divini publico. Jam & non obscure, ait, divini propositi rationem colligi ex tota V. T. historia, quia Christi videatur tantum non esse genealogia aliqua. Multa autem alia, etiam huc spectantia, & in historia fuisse omissa, quae tamen facta & obtinuerunt, credibile est. Et sic a prima aetate, uti observata eadem in genealogia Christi ratio fuit, ita ex eadem de voluntate & proposito divino certiores homines reddi potuerunt, & nos in judicio de illis formando nostro. Quare etiam ad Adamum Lucas Christi genealogiam perducit. Cæterum sententiam suam mediam esse dicit Episcopius inter Socinianos, & Nostros. Se non negare, vitæ æternæ promissionem factam creditamque fuisse etiam sub V. T. & hoc contra Socinianos; sed eam aperte & clare factam, aut viguisse, hoc se inficiari contra Nostros. De re ergo convenit nobiscum, super modo ejus litigat. At cum Socinianis super ipsa re est controversia, an vitæ æternæ notitia, & promissio sub V. T. obtinuerit? an, omnino non? Illi enim non solum non re-velatam fuisse illis vitam æternam contendunt, sed neque etiam debuisse, quia hoc solius sit Christi in carne exhibiti, & post annunciatum Euangelium, vitam manifestare æternam, ejusque promissionem. Promissa de rebus, aut de persona Messiæ etiam fœdere Mosaico contineri credimus, contra quam alii sentiunt, inquit. Neque sub fœdere tantum, vel ejus tempore; sed & ex fœdere ipso constare illa, Episcopius tuetur: promissum de Messiâ tale, ut fœdere divino Mosaico comprehensum dici possit. Tertio, distinguit inter promissa fœderis Mosaici, eaque facit generalia alia, alia speciālia. Specialia dicit nil continuisse nisi bona terrena, tum ad esse, tum ad bene esse vitæ hujus præsentis pertinen-tia: duobus comprehensa capitibus, vid. fixâ sede seu patriâ, templo, ac Republicâ; deinde, valetudine bonâ ac firmâ. Promissa generalia vocat, quæ generalibus termi-nis facta, vel sic concepta ut sub eorum litterâ comprehensa & adumbrata fuerint bona quævis, non hujus tantum vitæ, sed quoque æternæ, atque ita generaliter bona omnia ad felicitatem hujus & futuræ vitæ pertinentia, ex Dei intentione sub litera ista pro isto tempore occultata, & nunc clare manifestata. Quarto, & intellecta à prudentioribus fere concedit, tum ex typis, tum promissionis illâ generalitate: Verosimiliter etiam aut intellecta, aut apprehensa à prudentioribus, sanctioribusque in populo isto: de quo tamen nolim contendere. Sperata tamen & credita fuisse ab iis certum est, si non sub ratione typorum, saltem sub generalitate promissorum. Generalia promissa sunt: Ego ero Deus tuus: vel ego sum Deus tuus: ego ero merces tua multa valde: ego benedicam vobis, &c. Hisce enim promissis sic generatim conceptis atque enunciatis contineri posse quælibet bona, etiam ea quæ non nisi post mortem obveniunt, quis dubitet? Denique promissa generalia typica accipit, tum ratione Testam. Novi typica; tum ipsorum, in Veteri: ut vel significent promissa, quæ typorum instar ac figurarum, sive umbrarum rude atque obscurum aliquod bonorum cœlestium lineamentum habuerunt, quæ temporibus N. T. perfectissime revelata & annunciata sunt: quo sensu totum populum Iudaicum, totam terram Canaan, omniaque bona populo Iudaico in terra ista promissa, typum fuisse aut habuisse populi Christiani, terræ cœlestis, sive cœlestis Canaan, & spiritualium, sive æternorum omnium bonorum in cœlis futurorum, credi merito potest, ac tantum non debet: juxta id quod scriptor ad Hebræos per totam Epistolam, & Paulus ad Galatas, ad Romanos, & ad Colossenses non obscure indicant. Lex enim umbram habuit bonorum futurorum, non ipsam εἰκόνα, sive expressam imaginem. Vel ut significent promissa, quæ non aliter quam typi fuerunt, servieruntque sub V. Test. iis, qui divinæ legi per Mosen latè[?] ob-temperarent, ea tamen non obtinebant à Deo, sed contraria mala experiebantur, aut saltem pluribus malis affligebantur, quam bonis fruebantur. Sub istorum promissorum bonorum cortice, majora bona istis talibus, veluti per transennam ostendere Deus voluit, & cultores ipsi, majora ista bona sub isto cortice latere atque à Deo abscondita esse, sibi persuaserunt. Ad quæ tandem aperte pronunciat, de quæ-stione: ex his facile colligere est, quid statuendum fit, de quæ-stione illa famosa: an vitæ æternæ promissio etiam in V. Fœdere locum habuerit, vel potius in Fœdere ipso comprehensa fuerit? Si enim speciales promissiones in Fœdere ipso Veteri expressæ videantur, fatendum est, nullam vitæ æternæ promissionem disertam in illis reperiri. Si quis contra sentiat, ejus est locum dare, ubi illa exstet, quod puto impossibile esse. Sed vero si promissiones generales videantur, fatendum ex altera parte est, eas tales esse, ut promissio vitae aeternae iis non subesse tantum videatur, sed & Dei intentione eam eis subfuisse etiam credi debeat, uti ex antedictis patet. Quae generalia, utpote obscuriora, à paucis admodum in carnali isto populo intellecta, nec ultra vitae hujus spatium extensa fuisse, existimat: etsi fieri potuisse, ac factum aliquando, fateatur, ut etiam sperarint, post mortem sibi aeternam obventurarit[?] felicitatem; videlicet ne eos suum instar mortuos, omnesque Sadduceos fuisse dicere cogamur: Quod ad meliores, inquit, prudentioresque in populo isto attinet, verosimile est eos seu generalium promissionum vi, seu temporalium bonorum levi aestimatione, seu divinae bonitatis intuitu, seu animae suae, nobilioris quam caduci boni appetentis, consideratione, seu Enochi & Eliae exemplis, ( nota ut istorum exemplum affert ) seu rationibus aliis adductos, credidisse Deum praeter specialia ista bona ad hanc vitam pertinentia, & legibus Mosaicis comprehensa, etiam alia post mortem cultoribus suis fidis largiri velle. Concludit denique: Haec si statuamus, mediam viam ingrediemur inter eos qui apertam claramque, & eos qui nullam prorsus melioris vitae promissionem sub lege aut foedere Mosaico locum habuisse contendunt.
units.tr: Tom. 2. No stronger argument can be brought for this than that the promise was made to those men too, and that it was general and famous, shining like a star in the Church from this point onward. This is the promise in Gen. 3:15, where God promised that seed which would crush the serpent's head. No Christian can deny that the Messiah is meant, nor that the chief office attributed to him is that he would destroy him who has the power of death, namely the Devil. That this was meant to concern the first men as well is made plain by the serpent, whose crushing is proposed to them, the serpent by whom they had already been so wretchedly deceived. This had to be believed as a promise, and so it demanded their faith and assent. Certainly the whole substance of the Gospel and of salvation is contained in that prophecy: what God would do for the redemption of man, how he would one day be born of a woman, who would free and deliver man from the serpent's bite, and that his holy seed, which would keep up a perpetual enmity with the serpent, after the struggle with evil and the faithful performance of his duties, would triumph forever in that head and leader of his. Nor does Episcopius deny that God signified Christ the Saviour in this place, though obscurely: God wished first to signify this purpose of his obscurely, and indeed under the word seed, the seed of the woman, which would bruise the serpent's head. What God wished to be signified seems to be nothing other than this: that God would bring it about in due time that the Son of man would obtain the Devil, who in God's garden or Paradise had been the cause, through the serpent's mouth, of man's fall into death, and in turn would obtain his garden, that is, this world of which he is said to be the god, and would crush his head, that is, would take from him all power to harm and destroy. The sense itself, the sense of God, the nature of the matter itself indicates that it demands, and the fact that the whole of the Old Testament seems to be nothing but a certain genealogy, or series of ancestors of the blessed seed, that is, of Jesus Christ, confirms this not a little, whence the reason of this divine purpose shines forth clearly. Rightly does he argue from the nature of the thing here too; and certainly the nature of true religion requires this, so that it is not merely natural, nor is that worship of God which inflamed the first inhabitants of the world and of the Church merely natural, nor is their salvation merely natural. The nature of the thing demands that sense, and the same nature of the thing demands those senses of the places and testimonies of Scripture which we have just seen, concerning the faith and piety of the first men. Finally, the nature of the thing demands that just as those things were set before men by God and were constantly preached and impressed upon them, so they too believed that they would one day come, for the help and salvation of all those who were to be freed from the serpent through Christ. It cannot be understood otherwise than as a promise, and all to whom those things were made had to understand it so. Therefore the promise concerning Christ and the blessed seed was not first made to Abraham. Although it seems obscure to us, and indicated rather than explained by so brief a gospel, there is nevertheless no reason to doubt that by the frequency of divine revelations, and the continual care of prophets, heralds and priests, it was explained and clarified more and more every day, especially by the practice of sermons and public divine worship. Now too, he says, the reason of the divine purpose is not obscurely gathered from the whole history of the Old Testament, since it seems to be almost a genealogy of Christ. Many other things, also pertaining to this, were omitted from the history, yet it is credible that they were done and took effect. And thus from the earliest age, just as the same method was observed in the genealogy of Christ, so men could be made more certain of the divine will and purpose, and we in forming our judgment of them. For this reason Luke also traces Christ's genealogy back to Adam. Moreover, Episcopius says that his opinion is a middle one between the Socinians and ours. He does not deny that the promise of eternal life was made and believed even under the Old Testament, and this against the Socinians; but he denies that it was made openly and clearly, or flourished, and this against ours. So he agrees with us about the thing itself, but quarrels about the manner of it. But the real controversy with the Socinians is about the thing itself: whether the knowledge and promise of eternal life obtained under the Old Testament at all, or not at all? For they contend not only that eternal life was not revealed to them, but that it ought not to have been, because it belongs only to Christ manifested in the flesh, and after the Gospel was announced, to bring eternal life to light, and its promise. We believe that promises concerning things, or concerning the person of the Messiah, are contained even in the Mosaic covenant, contrary to what others think, he says. And Episcopius maintains that these promises are contained not only in the covenant or in its time, but also from the covenant itself: a promise concerning the Messiah of such a kind that it can be said to be comprehended in the divine Mosaic covenant. Thirdly, he distinguishes among the promises of the Mosaic covenant, and calls some of them general and others special. He says the special ones contain nothing but earthly goods, pertaining both to the being and to the well-being of this present life: comprehended under two heads, namely a fixed seat or homeland, the temple and the commonwealth; then good and firm health. He calls the general promises those which were made in general terms, or so conceived that they were comprehended and foreshadowed under their letter: all good things, not only of this life but also of the eternal, and thus generally all good things pertaining to the happiness of this and of the future life, hidden under that letter for that time from God's intention, and now clearly made manifest. Fourthly, and this he almost concedes from what was understood by the wiser men, both from the types and from the generality of that promise: Probably also understood or grasped by the wiser and holier men among that people, though I would not wish to contend about this. Yet they were certainly hoped for and believed by them, if not under the aspect of types, at least under the generality of the promises. The promises are general: I will be your God; or I am your God; I will be your very great reward; I will bless you, etc. For who would doubt that by promises thus conceived and uttered in general terms, any goods whatever can be contained, even those which come only after death? Finally he takes the general promises as typical, both in respect of the typical nature of the New Testament and of the promises themselves in the Old: so that they either signify promises which, having the character of types and figures, or shadows, had some rough and obscure outline of heavenly goods, which were most perfectly revealed and announced in New Testament times: in which sense the whole Jewish people, the whole land of Canaan, and all the goods promised to the Jewish people in that land, can rightly be believed, and scarcely ought not to be believed, to have been a type of the Christian people, of the heavenly land or heavenly Canaan, and of all spiritual or eternal goods to come in heaven: according to what the writer to the Hebrews throughout his Epistle, and Paul to the Galatians, to the Romans and to the Colossians, indicate not obscurely. For the law had a shadow of good things to come, not the very image, or the express likeness. Or they signify promises which were nothing other than types, and served under the Old Testament those who obeyed the divine law given through Moses, yet these men did not obtain them from God, but experienced contrary evils, or at least were afflicted with more evils than they enjoyed goods. Under the bark of these promised goods, God wished to show greater goods to such men, as it were through a window, and the worshippers themselves were persuaded that those greater goods lay hidden under that bark and were concealed by God. At last he pronounces plainly on the question: from these things it is easy to gather what must be decided about that famous question: whether the promise of eternal life had a place even in the Old Covenant, or rather was comprehended in the covenant itself? For if the special promises seem to be expressed in the Old Covenant itself, it must be admitted that no explicit promise of eternal life is found in them. If anyone thinks otherwise, it is for him to show the place where it is found, which I think is impossible. But if the general promises seem to be such, it must be admitted on the other side that they are of such a kind that the promise of eternal life not only seems to lie under them, but it ought also to be believed that it lay under them by God's intention, as is clear from what has been said above. These general promises, since they are more obscure, he thinks were understood by very few in that carnal people, and were not extended beyond the span of this life: although he admits that it could have happened, and at some time did happen, that they also hoped for eternal happiness to come to them after death, lest we be forced to say that they were like beasts and all the Sadducees. As for the better and wiser men in that people, he says, it is likely that, whether moved by the force of the general promises, or by a slight estimation of temporal goods, or by regard for divine goodness, or by consideration of their own soul, which desires a nobler good than that which perishes, or by the examples of Enoch and Elijah (note how he brings forward their example), or by other reasons, they believed that God wished to bestow on his faithful worshippers, beyond those special goods pertaining to this life and comprehended in the Mosaic laws, other goods after death as well. He concludes at last: If we hold these things, we shall enter a middle way between those who contend that a clear and open promise of a better life had a place under the Mosaic law or covenant, and those who contend that no promise of a better life had any place under the Mosaic law or covenant at all.

units.la: Quae cum ita sint, merito mirum videri potest, quod indigne adeo, de quaestione hac pronunciavit in Apologia, eam inconcinnam, ambiguam, & inutilem esse, quum rem concedat, super qua quaestio agitatur, eamque certe non levem, quae spectat V. Testamenti rationem, & fidem ac religionem Patrum qui tum vixerunt, & nostrae fidei, & Catholicae Ecclesiae magnam confirmationem. De modo duntaxat litem movet nobis, an satis claro apertoque res propósita Patribus fuerit? Saltem rem probat, & causam, quam agimus. Non vero omnino deserendi fuerunt Socinani, vel etiam probandi Nostri. Ergo & hic reperit, quod, istorum in gratiam, nobis aegre diceret, de promissione non clare facta.
