Quibus tamen addere debemus, quod Jonas Schlichtingius, nuperus inter Socinianos scriptor, qui, quantum potest, Socinianā[?] dogmata incrustat, & Remonstranticis accommodat, sua ad mentem Episcopii, uti hic viciissim ad illius, in Commentario ad Hebr. cap. VIII. pag. 359. in hoc ponat quaestionem quoque, quod non aperte vita aeterna olim promissa fit, addens, vitam aeternam in promissis Veteris foederis occulto sensu comprehensam fuisse.
units.tr: Since this is so, it may well seem strange that he rejected this question so contemptuously in his Apology, calling it awkward, ambiguous and useless, when he concedes the matter under dispute, which is certainly no minor one: it concerns the character of the Old Testament, and the faith and religion of the Fathers who lived then, and it greatly strengthens both our faith and the Catholic Church. He only objects to the manner of the question, asking whether the matter was set before the Fathers clearly and openly enough. At least he proves the point and the cause we are pursuing. The Socinians should not have been abandoned, and our own side should not have been approved either. So here too he finds, for the sake of the Socinians, something that he would reluctantly tell us, namely that the promise was not clearly made. To this we must add that Jonas Schlichting, a recent Socinian writer who, as far as he can, dresses up Socinian dogmas and adapts them to the Remonstrants, in his commentary on Hebrews chapter 8, page 359, following Episcopius's view (as Episcopius in turn follows his), likewise raises this question: that eternal life was not openly promised of old, adding that eternal life was contained in the promises of the Old Covenant in a hidden sense.

units.la: Secus ac Socinani disputare hic solent, statuentes, nullam prorsus melioris vitae promissionem sub lege aut foedere Mosaico locum habuisse, quomodo de ipsis loquitur Episcopius: nempe, uti dicunt, non illis temporibus convenientem, sed tempori Christi in totum servatam: atque ita in terminis conveniet saltem Episcopio, cum Schlichtingio, si non cum aliis. Denique idem Schlichtingius, in Epist. ad Gal. II. pag. 71. vitam lege promissam, sensu litterali quidem denotare terrenam hanc, ejusq; felicitatem, at sensu etiam mystico aeternam, ait. Quae est ipsissima Episcopii sententia. Ita ille, sed sensu mystico, vitam illa significabat vitam aeternam; & exsecratio ei oppósita, mortem sempiternam: quemadmodum tum ex epistola inferius constabit: tum ex aliis Novi Testamenti locis, praesertim vero ex epistola ad Romanos cernitur. Contra Meisnerum idem, de Trinitate, pag. 683. affirmat, quod Deus vitam sempiternam sub promissionibus apertis occultavit, & legem servantibus dare apud se constituit. In Commentario ad Hebr. pag. 181. sub involucro autem carnalium promissionum & requietis terrenae latuerunt promissiones spirituales, & requietis coelestis ad semen spirituale Abrahami pertinentes.
units.tr: The Socinians usually argue otherwise here, holding that no promise of a better life was ever given under the law or covenant of Moses, as Episcopius himself describes them: namely, as they say, not suited to those times but kept entirely for the time of Christ. So in these terms Episcopius agrees at least with Schlichting, if not with others. Finally, the same Schlichting, in his Epistle to the Galatians II, page 71, says that the life promised by the law denotes in the literal sense this earthly life and its happiness, but in a mystical sense eternal life. This is exactly Episcopius's view. He, however, in the mystical sense, meant by that life eternal life, and by the opposite curse, everlasting death, as will be clear both from the letter below and from other places of the New Testament, especially from the Epistle to the Romans. Against Meisner the same man, in his work On the Trinity, page 683, asserts that God hid eternal life under open promises and resolved to give it with himself to those who keep the law. In his Commentary on Hebrews, page 181, he says that under the covering of carnal promises and earthly rest, spiritual promises and heavenly rest, pertaining to the spiritual seed of Abraham, lay hidden.

units.la: Jam vero. 1. clarum aliquid dicitur in se; vel ad homines, ad hos, vel istos. Quod respectu nostri luminis, & felicitatis temporum, quâ fruimur, non ita clarum, dici tamen clarum potest fuisse illis, pro istis temporibus, quibus pro statu umbratili clara fuit minor illuminatio, ubi nobis quidem longe major nunc affulsit. Vti ante meridiano tempore dici potest clarus dies, quamvis non ita clarus, ac die adulto. II.
units.tr: Now indeed: 1. something is called clear in itself, or clear to men, to these or to those. With respect to our light and the happiness of the times we enjoy, it is not so clear; yet it can be called clear to them, for those times, when, compared with their shadowy state, there was less illumination, whereas for us now a far greater light has shone forth. Just as the day may be called clear before noon, though not as clear as in full daylight. II.

units.la: Hodie, vel in Euangelio clara, & copiosa est vitæ æternæ promissio, eoque clarior, quo copiosior: in V. T. clara quidem, non ita tamen fuit copiosa. Clarum aliquid intelligitur vel ex solis verborum fœderis terminis; vel in totâ ejus, quæ tum viguit, doctrinâ, quæ qualis fit, non ex solis illis verbis, sed totâ temporis illius, & reliquâ sacra peti debet historiâ. V. c. Episcopius, lib. II. cap. IV. dicit, præceptum Abrahamo propositum quod est Genes. XVII. 1. ambula coram me & esto perfectus, non tum demum ei, sed & antea quoque factum fuisse, quòd licet ei datum legatur cum jam esset nonaginta novem annorum, tamen non tum primum datum ei fuisse verisimile est, sed repetitum tantum & continuatum. Quod non ex verbis Scripturæ, sed natura doctrinæ colligit, Abrahamo notæ & patefactæ. Similiter, cap. VI. verisimile judicat promissionem, quæ est Genes. XV. 1. non tum primum Abrahamo factam, sed repetitam confirmatamque fuisse. At hoc, & similia plura, non ex τῷ ῥητῷ [?] Scripturæ probaverit, verum ex ratione doctrinæ, cujus vim & plenitudinem ex novo petit Testamento. Sic enim loquitur: hæc promissio sive eam hic primo factam Abrahamo, sive repetitam confirmatamque vclimus: quod omnino verisimilius est. Nam scriptor ad Hebr. cap. II. verf. 1. dicit Abrahamum fide audscultasse Deo, ut abiret in locum quem acceptu rus erat in hæreditatem. Ergo tum de amplitudine, tum de claritate promissionis alicujus judicare oportet, præterquam ex fœderis verbis in ipsis tabulis, ex totâ Scripturæ historiâ, & doctrinâ. Unde enim magis typos Christi intellectos Patribus, ex quibus, & generalibus promissis notitiam illorum de vitâ æternâ arcessit, probabis, quàm ex continuâ & jugi, quæ typos comitata fuit, Prophetarum & Sacerdotum doctrina, quæ ita accipiendos illos esse, omnes instruebant? Arminius, in Disput. de legis & Euangelii comparatione, convenientiam utriusque Testamenti, & hactenus bene, in hoc constituit, quod una eademque utriusque materia, fidei scil. obedientia utrobique requisita, & vitæ æternæ hæreditas promissa per justitiæ fidei imputationem, & gratiosam in Christo adoptionem. Unum objectum Christus. Differentia au; em est in accidentalibus nonnullis, quæ nihil derogant unitati substantiali.
units.tr: Today, in the Gospel, the promise of eternal life is clear and abundant, and it is clearer the more abundant it is; in the Old Testament it was clear indeed, but not so abundant. Something is understood to be clear either from the terms of the covenant words alone, or from the whole doctrine of that time, which was in force; and what that doctrine was must be sought not from those words alone, but from the whole history and sacred record of that period. For example, Episcopius, in book II, chapter IV, says that the command given to Abraham, Genesis 17:1, walk before me and be perfect, was not given to him only then, but had been given earlier as well, since, although it is read as given to him when he was already ninety-nine years old, it is nevertheless probable that it was not given to him for the first time then, but only repeated and continued. He draws this not from the words of Scripture but from the nature of the doctrine, known and revealed to Abraham. Similarly, in chapter VI, he judges it probable that the promise in Genesis 15:1 was not made to Abraham for the first time then, but was repeated and confirmed. But this, and many similar things, he does not prove from the literal words [τῷ ῥητῷ] of Scripture, but from the reasoning of doctrine, whose force and fullness he seeks from the New Testament. For he speaks thus: whether we wish this promise to have been first made to Abraham here, or repeated and confirmed, is entirely more probable. For the writer to the Hebrews, chapter II, verse 1, says that Abraham by faith obeyed God, so that he went out into the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. Therefore, both as to the extent and as to the clarity of a promise, one must judge by something other than the words of the covenant in the tablets themselves: by the whole history and doctrine of Scripture. For from what source will you prove more readily that the types of Christ were understood by the Fathers, from which he also derives their knowledge of eternal life from the general promises, than from the continuous and unbroken teaching of the Prophets and Priests that accompanied those types, which instructed all men that they were to be understood in this way? Arminius, in his Disputation on the comparison of Law and Gospel, rightly establishes the agreement of both Testaments in this, that one and the same matter is in both, namely the faith and obedience required on both sides, and the inheritance of eternal life promised through the imputation of the righteousness of faith and the gracious adoption in Christ. One object, Christ. The difference, however, lies in certain accidentals, which do not detract from the substantial unity.

units.la: Inter Anabaptistas esse, qui pariter cum Socinianis statuunt, patet ex Demonstratione Controversiarum inter Reformat. & Anabaptist. Abrah. Dooresaar, & Jacobi Auctrofylvii, art. VIII. thes. I. & art. XIV. pag. 342. Art. XV. thes. III. Præterea contra idem dogma Anabaptistarum disputat Bullingerus, lib. IV, contra Anabapt. cap. V. Kloppenburgius, in Gangrena Anabapt. Jac. Bontemps, in Refutat. Anabaptist. Spanhemius, Disput. Anti-Anabaptistica III. Quamvis Nicolaus Nicolai Cl. Cl. Confessionis, pag. 183. 184. & 196. doceat Israelitas, non terrenas solum, sed & spirituales, cœlestesque promissiones habuisse, & eodem modo justificatos fuisse, quo nos nunc sub N. Testamento, proinde unam ambos facere Ecclesiam Catholicam, & communionem.
units.tr: That there are among the Anabaptists those who, like the Socinians, hold this view is clear from the Demonstration of the Controversies between the Reformed and the Anabaptists by Abraham Dooresaar and Jacob Auctrofylvius, article VIII, thesis I, and article XIV, page 342, article XV, thesis III. Besides, Bullinger disputes against this same Anabaptist doctrine in book IV, against the Anabaptists, chapter V; Kloppenburg, in his Gangrene of the Anabaptists; Jacob Bontemps, in his Refutation of the Anabaptists; Spanheim, in his Anti-Anabaptist Disputation III. Although Nicolaus Nicolai, in the Confession, pages 183, 184 and 196, teaches that the Israelites had not only earthly but also spiritual and heavenly promises, and were justified in the same way as we are now under the New Testament, and so makes both one Catholic Church and one communion.

units.la: Catechismus Tridentinus, pag. 111, de Ecclesia agens ejusque nomine, in hoc dicit Ecclesiam distare à Synagoga, quod hæc Christianorum, illa Judæorum fuerit, quæ terrena & caduca tantum bona spectarit, secus ac Christiani: is optime perspiciet, qui animadverterit, cur olim fidelis populus sub lege positus, synagoga, id est, congregatio diceretur. Nam, ut docet S. Augustinus, hoc ei nomen impositum est, quia pecudum more, quibus magis congregari convenit, terrena, & caduca tantum bona spectaret. Quod vero Augustinum dicit illud statuere, enormis error est, non fallibilitatem, sed falsitatem Conc. Tridentini, & Pii V. quorum nomine, jussuque editus Catechismus, evidenti documento exhibens. Non enim dicit, Synagogam terrena & caduca tantum bona spectasse: quidem, Synagogae vocem Israelitarum coetui convenire; uti nomen Ecclesiae, Christianis: atque illos, alludens ad vim nominis, congregatos instar pecudum, dici posse, non convocari: etiamque pro magnis & summis bonis à Deo carnalia & terrena requisivisse: non vero dicit, terrena & caduca tantum illos spectasse; imo contrarium. In Psalm. LXXI. Quamvis enim proprie dicatur Synagoga Iudaeorum, Ecclesia Christianorum, qua congregatio magis pecorum, convocatio magis hominum intelligi soleat: tamen & illam dictam invenimus Ecclesiam. In Psalm. LXXXI. In Synagoga populum Israel accepimus, quia & ipsorum propria Synagoga dici solet, quamvis & Ecclesia dicta sit. Nostram vero nunquam Apostoli Synagogam dixerunt, sed semper Ecclesiam, sive discernendi causa, sive quod inter congregationem, unde Synagoga, & convocationem, unde Ecclesia nomen accepit, differt aliquid, quod scilicet congregari & pecora solent, atque ipsa propriè, quorum & greges proprie dicimus: convocari autem magis est utentium ratione, sicut sunt homines. Deque illis eodem porro loco dicit: quamvis uni Deo vero mancipatus videretur, pro magnis tamen ac summis bonis ab illo carnalia, terrena, temporalia requirebat. Invenimus etiam saepe eos filios appellatos non ea gratia, quae ad Novum Testamentum pertinet, sed illa, quae ad vetus, quia & ipsa gratia est, qua elegit Abraham. Tum, nisi enim & ipsa esset gratia, non utique de nobis, quibus non terrenum, sed ad regnum coelorum capessendum data est potestas filios Dei fieri, in eodem mox Euangelio, diceretur, quod accepimus gratiam pro gratia, id est, pro promissionibus Testamenti Veteris, promissiones Novi Testamenti. Aliaque in eandem sententiam loca ex Augustino postmodum adferemus, suo loco. Differentiam quidem constituit aliquam, inter tempora Testamenti Veteris, uti etiam constitui debet, & Novi; sed gratiam salutis tamen ubique facit essentiâ eandem, & filios ad eandem pertinere vult Ecclesiam, promissionem, salutem. Neque vel exclusive ad bona coelestia, dicit illos terrena concupivisse, vel nos, exclusive ad illos, bona coelestia affectare, aut non etiam petere posse terrena bona & promissiones. Quod clarius exponit, in Psalm. LXXI. Sed profecto, erant etiam in illo populo, qui intelligerent, habentes fidem, quae postea revelata est, non ad legis literam, sed ad spiritus gratiam pertinentem, non enim sine ipsa fide fuerunt, qui ejus in Christo futuram revelationem praevidere, & pronunciare potuerunt, cum & illa vetera Sacramenta significativa fuerint futurorum. An soli Prophetae habebant hanc fidem, non & populus? imo vero etiam qui Prophetas fideliter audiebant, eadem adjuvabantur gratia, ut intelligerent, quod audiebant. Sed utiq; Sacramentum regni coelorum velabatur in Veteri Testamento, quod plenitudine temporis revelatur in Novo. Nolo enim vos, inquit Apostolus, ignorare fratres, quoniam patres nostri omnes sub nube fuerunt, & omnes mare transierunt, & omnes per Mosen baptizati sunt in nube, & in mari, & omnes eundem cibum spiritualem manducaverunt, & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt. Bibebant enim de spirituali consequente eos petra, petra erat Christus. 1 Cor. x. 1. Idem ita-que in mysterio cibus & potus illorum qui noster, sed significatione idem, non specie: quia idem ille Christus illis in petra figuratus, nobis in carne manifestatus est. Unde omnino apparet, quod alia Augustini fuerit sententia, alia Catechismi Romani, quamq; fallo hic errorem suum authoritate illius obvelare gestiat. Ut & temere Socinus dixerit, in libello ad Polonos, Quod regni Poloniae homines, &c. nos doctrinam hac in parte nostram à Pontificiis, vel cum iis prorsus communem habere.
units.tr: The Catechism of Trent, page 111, speaking of the Church and its name, says that the Church differs from the Synagogue in this: that the one belonged to Christians, the other to Jews, who looked only to earthly and perishable goods, unlike Christians. He will best see this who considers why the faithful people under the law was once called the synagogue, that is, the congregation. For, as Saint Augustine teaches, this name was given to them because, like cattle, which are more suited to being gathered together, they looked only to earthly and perishable goods. But that the Catechism says Augustine held this is a monstrous error, and it shows not the fallibility but the falsity of the Council of Trent and of Pius V, in whose name and by whose command the Catechism was published. For it does not say that the Synagogue looked only to earthly and perishable goods. It says rather that the word Synagogue suits the assembly of the Israelites, as the name Church suits Christians; and that those men, alluding to the force of the name, could be said to be gathered like cattle rather than called together; and that they sought carnal and earthly things from God in place of great and supreme goods. It does not say that they looked only to earthly and perishable things; on the contrary. On Psalm 71: For although the Synagogue is properly said to be of the Jews and the Church of the Christians, since a congregation is usually understood more of cattle and a convocation more of men, nevertheless we find that the former was also called a Church. On Psalm 81: We understand the people of Israel to be in the Synagogue, because it is commonly called their own synagogue, although it was also called a Church. But our own the Apostles never called a Synagogue, but always a Church, either to distinguish them, or because there is a difference between the gathering from which the word Synagogue comes and the calling from which the word Church comes: namely, that cattle are gathered and are properly called flocks, while being called together belongs more to those who use reason, as men do. And of those people in the same place he says further: although they seemed devoted to the one true God, they nevertheless sought from him carnal, earthly and temporal things in place of great and supreme goods. We also often find them called sons, not by the grace that belongs to the New Testament, but by that which belongs to the Old, since that too is grace, by which he chose Abraham. For unless it were also grace, then in the same Gospel it would not be said of us, to whom the power to become sons of God has been given not for an earthly but for a heavenly kingdom, that we have received grace for grace, that is, for the promises of the Old Testament, the promises of the New. We shall later bring forward other passages from Augustine to the same effect, in their proper place. He does indeed set up a certain difference between the times of the Old and New Testaments, as must be done, but he makes the grace of salvation the same in essence everywhere, and wants the sons to belong to the same Church, promise and salvation. Nor does he say that they desired earthly things to the exclusion of heavenly goods, or that we aim at heavenly goods to the exclusion of them, or that we cannot also seek earthly goods and promises. He explains this more clearly on Psalm 71: But truly there were also in that people those who understood, having the faith that was later revealed, which pertains not to the letter of the law but to the grace of the Spirit; for those who foresaw its future revelation in Christ, and could proclaim it, were not without that very faith, since those ancient sacraments were also signs of things to come. Did only the Prophets have this faith, and not the people? Indeed, even those who faithfully heard the Prophets were helped by the same grace to understand what they heard. But certainly the sacrament of the kingdom of heaven was veiled in the Old Testament and revealed in the fullness of time in the New. For I would not have you ignorant, brethren, says the Apostle, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual meat, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ. 1 Cor. 10:1. Thus their food and drink in the mystery is the same as ours, not in appearance but in significance, because that same Christ who was figured in the rock to them has been manifested to us in the flesh. From which it clearly appears that Augustine's opinion was one thing, and that of the Roman Catechism another, which here seeks to cover its error with his authority, though falsely. So also Socinus rashly said, in his little book to the Poles, That the men of the kingdom of Poland, etc., that we have this doctrine on this point either from the Papists or in complete agreement with them.

units.la: Quare ut nos tandem ad ipsam accingamus disputationem primariam, & ad con-flictum argumentorum, unà operâ ostensuri sumus, sub V. Testamento, haud uno loco, modoque, tum vitæ æternæ, tum Christi redemtoris, & remissionis peccatorum, ac Spiritus S. sive bonorum spiritualium & coelestium promissiones Patribus factas fuisse, creditasque. Adversariorum sententiam audivimus: sequitur, ut refutemus. Sed, quemadmodum in omni disputatione, ita & hic, quo ad lineam, quomodo Tertullianus loquitur, congrediamur, praemittenda sunt, quæ ab Adversariis conceduntur, ut ipsum, in quo quæstio vertitur, punctum & cardo distinctius patefiat.
units.tr: Therefore, so that we may at last come to the main dispute itself and the clash of arguments, we will also show at the same time that under the Old Testament, in more than one place and in more than one way, promises were made to the Fathers and believed concerning eternal life, Christ the Redeemer, the forgiveness of sins, and the Holy Spirit, that is, spiritual and heavenly goods. We have heard the opinion of our opponents; it follows that we refute it. But, as in every disputation, so here too, if we are to join battle to the line, as Tertullian puts it, the points that our opponents concede must first be set down, so that the point and hinge on which the question turns may be laid open more clearly.

units.la: Primò ergo, non negatur ipsis, Patres V. T. salvatos à Deo, vel salvandos beatitudine æternâ fuisse. Ne quid dissimulemus, firmiter statuimus, etiamsi promissio nulla aperta extet in Veteri foedere vitæ æternæ: eam tamen aliquando datum iri omnibus illis, quicumque Deo unquam confisi sunt, & eidem obedierunt, inquit Smalcius, de divin. Christi, cap. VII. Catechesis Racov. cap. v. qu. vi. Habiturine sunt vitam æternam ii, qui eam sperarunt, licet iis promissa non fuerit? Resp. Prorsus, at non omnes, verum ii, qui ex animo Deum coluerunt; & dicto audientes ei fuere. Volkelius, lib. III. cap. XI. Haec tamen non perinde à nobis disputantur, quasi illos, qui olim, cum fide justitiaque vixerunt, vitæ æternæ possessione exclusum iri putemus: quin imo ex iis, quæ paulo ante à nobis dicta sunt, cuilibet constare potest, nos plane statuere, Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Iacobum, & his similes, ex mortuis aliquando excitandos, immortalitatisque beneficio ornandos esse. Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum, pag. 683. vitam sempiternam in coelis agendam Deus legem servantibus dare apud se constituit. II. Sic etiam fatentur, Deum etiam remisisse illis peccata, quamvis hoc non promiserit, vel significarit se facturum. A parte Dei constitit ille modus justificandi & salvandi hominis, his licet ignotus, neque ex foedere iis aut debitus, aut concessus. Socinus, de justificatione, pag. 8. Est quidem sub utroque foedere eadem hominis coram Deo justificandi ratio, quatenus utrobique ex parte Dei, peccatorum remissio requiritur. & pag. 46. talis justificatio, & consequenter peccatorum condonatio ejusmodi, ut ea est, quæ post Christum extitit, ipsa lege, ipsoque vetere foedere, non continebatur. Imo neque etiam alibi expresso, atque in perpetuum ejusmodi peccatorum condonatio à Deo proposita ac promissa legitur. Idem, de Servatore part. III. cap. II. pag. 230. seq. Tertio, Christum, & gratiam ac salutem in Christo prædictam in V. T. olim fuisse, nec negant, nec negare possunt. Socinus, Lect. Sacr. pag. 75. Certum est autem, non tantum Christum fuisse revera & esse servatorem nostrum, sed etiam id prædictum per Prophetas fuisse, ut inter alia loca fidem faciunt 23. & 33. cap. Ieremiæ. Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, cap. II. Omnia scripta veteris foederis docebant quidem, Messiam venturum: sed qualis & quantus Messias is futurus esset, non, nisi per involucra, docebant. Beneficium etiam ingens per eum conferendum esse testabantur: sed quale & quantum id futurum esset, non, nisi nimis obscure & mystice, proponebant. Nam non vitæ æternæ, quæ proprium est Messiæ beneficium, de quo infra suo loco dicemus, mentionem faciebant, vel eam promittebant; neque, id quod Messias allaturus erat, ad universos homines, nempe ad extraneas etiam gentes spectare, usquam aperte indicabant. Quæ omnia secus habent, sive quod de promissa vocatione gentium; aut æterna per Christum salute, dicitur. Illud enim, tum contra Iudæos, ex V. Testamento, bene probatur; atque ex eodem, in Novo id factum, ab Apostolo. Istud, in sequentibus, falsi haud uno modo convincemus. IV. Concedunt, Patres quoque notitiam & spem vitae aeternae aliquam habuisse, utcunque ipsis non promissae. Smalcius, de Divinit. cap. vii. pag. 27. Nolumus autem quemquam opinari, nos, dum istud de Christi praestantia dicimus, negare, fideles illos Dei sub Veteri foedere cultores, notitiam aut spem ullam vitae aeternae habuisse. Catechesis Racov. l. c. qu. 4. Attamen prorsus aliquam spem vitae aeternae in Dei populo ante Christum fuisse apparet. Resp. Nihil obstat sperare quidpiam, etiamsi promissio Dei careas, modo res ea sit summopere expetenda, & ejusmodi, quam credibile erat, eam Deum cultoribus suis daturum. Smalcius, conjecturam appellat, vel, quod spes omnis illorum conjecturis, & consideratione justitiae Dei nitebatur. Exigua certe & misera spes, quae pro fundamento, non promissionem, sed conjecturam habet. Socinus ipsis persuasum dicit, sed quemadmodum gentilibus, qui & aliam, post hanc, vitam exspectabant. Ad Dudithium, epist. iii. cum, exceptis Sadducaeis, qui non ita multi erant, caeteri omnes aliam post hanc restare vitam felicitate refertam iis, qui in hac se vita ad normam divinae legis composuissent, persuasum habuerunt. Nec ab illis diversae abibant gentes, quibus post illos eadem promissa oblata fuerunt: jam enim generatim omnibus persuasum erat, hominibus probis post vitam hanc praemium virtuti illorum conveniens repositum esse. unde factum, ut homines generatim, immortalitatis desiderio simul exstimulati, etiam sine ulla, seu promissione vera, seu illius specie, a Deo sibi oblata, aliam sibi quandam vitam cogitatione depinxerint, & satis firmiter persuaserint. v. Quin & exspectasse eos, saltem eorum aliquos Christum, Socinus scribit, in Disputat. cum Erasmo Iohannis, de Filii D. exist. pag. 12. veluti exspectatio illa Christi (quae non semper, ut tibi videtur, sed aliquando, idque sero tandem in Israelis ecclesia fuit.) & epist. ii. ad Radecium, pag. 95. In eo tamen abs te dissentio, quod videris concedere, viros pios, qui sub Vetere Testamento fuerunt, ad Christum in ceremoniis illis & sacrificiis, in quibus adumbratur, respexisse, & in spe illius venturi servatos fuisse, id quod ego mihi persuadere nulla ratione queo, vel ob id, quod expectatio Messiae, sicut nec aperta promissio, non fuit in populo, nisi tandem paullo ante captivitatem Babylonicam, per Hieremiam Prophetam. Et Epist. iii. pag. 137. & 138. Ut enim supra quoque commemoratum fuit, cum novi foederis promissa promulgata sunt, jam tum hac opinione homines isti generatim erant imbuti, post hanc vitam ab eo, quem cura haec tangebat, aliam multo beatissimam iis, qui se probe gessissent, praeparatam atque adornatam esse. vi. Uti de vita aeterna, remissione peccatorum, Christo, ita etiam de Spiritu S. fidelibus sub V. T. dato philosophantur: ut videamus horum omnium, in tota hac disputatione, eandem esse rationem, ideoque, sub nomine spiritualium & coelestium bonorum, tuto a nobis conjungi. Praesertim quando ex praecedentibus tenemus, quid per Spiritum S. intelligant, vid. solam spem vitae aeternae.
units.tr: First, then, it is not denied by them that the Fathers of the Old Testament were saved by God, or were to be saved with eternal blessedness. Lest we conceal anything, we firmly maintain that even if no clear promise of eternal life stands in the Old Covenant, it would nonetheless at some time be given to all those who have ever trusted in God and obeyed him, says Smalcius, De divinitate Christi, chap. 7. Catechism of Racov., chap. 5, question 6: Will those have eternal life who hoped for it, although no promise was made to them? Answer: Assuredly, but not all, only those who worshipped God from the heart and were obedient to him. Volkelius, book 3, chap. 11: Yet these matters are not argued by us as if we thought that those who once lived in faith and righteousness would be shut out from possession of eternal life; indeed, from what we have said a little before, anyone can see that we plainly hold that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their like will at some time be raised from the dead and adorned with the benefit of immortality. Schlichtingius, against Meisner, p. 683: God has determined to give eternal life, to be lived in heaven, to those who keep the law, with himself. II. In the same way they also confess that God forgave them their sins, although he had not promised, or signified, that he would do so. On God's side that method of justifying and saving man stood firm, though it was unknown to them, and was owed to them by no covenant, nor granted by one. Socinus, on justification, p. 8: Indeed under either covenant there is the same way of justifying man before God, insofar as on God's side under both the remission of sins is required. And p. 46: Such a justification, and consequently such a pardon of sins, as is that which arose after Christ, was not contained in the law itself, nor in the Old Covenant itself. Indeed, nowhere else is such a pardon of sins read as having been proposed and promised by God for all time. The same, on the Saviour, part 3, chap. 2, p. 230 f. Third, that Christ, and the grace and salvation in Christ, were once in the Old Testament, they neither deny nor can deny. Socinus, Lectiones sacrae, p. 75: It is certain, however, that Christ was not only truly our Saviour in fact and in being, but that this was also foretold by the Prophets, as the passages of Jeremiah, chapters 23 and 33, among others, bear witness. Smalcius, De divinitate Christi, chap. 2: All the writings of the Old Covenant taught indeed that the Messiah would come; but what and how great the Messiah would be, they taught only through veils. They also testified that a great benefit was to be conferred through him; but what and how great it would be, they set forth only very obscurely and mystically. For they neither mentioned nor promised eternal life, which is the proper benefit of the Messiah (of which we shall speak in its place below); nor did they anywhere plainly indicate that what the Messiah was to bring would concern all men, namely even the foreign nations. All these things stand otherwise, whether it is said of the promised calling of the Gentiles or of eternal salvation through Christ. For the former is well proved, both against the Jews from the Old Testament and, in the New, by the Apostle from the same. The latter we shall refute as false in many ways in what follows. IV. They also concede that the Fathers had some knowledge and hope of eternal life, however it was not promised to them. Smalcius, De divinitate, chap. 7, p. 27: But we do not want anyone to suppose that we, in saying this about the excellence of Christ, deny that those faithful worshippers of God under the Old Covenant had any knowledge or hope of eternal life. Catechism of Racov., loc. cit., question 4: Yet it clearly appears that there was altogether some hope of eternal life among God's people before Christ. Answer: Nothing prevents one from hoping for something even if one lacks God's promise, provided the thing is greatly to be desired and of such a kind that it was credible God would give it to his worshippers. Smalcius calls it a conjecture, or because all their hope rested on conjectures and on the consideration of God's justice. Surely a slight and wretched hope, which has for its foundation not a promise but a conjecture! Socinus says it was persuaded to them, but just as it was to the Gentiles, who also looked for another life after this one. To Dudith, letter 3: with the exception of the Sadducees, who were not very many, all the rest were persuaded that after this life there remains another life full of happiness for those who had conducted themselves in this life according to the rule of the divine law. Nor did the nations that were afterwards offered the same promises differ from them; for already among all men in general it was persuaded that a reward suited to their virtue was laid up for upright men after this life. Hence it came about that men in general, roused at the same time by the desire for immortality, even without any true promise from God, or any semblance of one offered to them by God, pictured to themselves in thought some other life, and persuaded themselves of it quite firmly. v. Indeed Socinus also writes, in his disputation with Erasmus Johannis, On the existence of the Son of God, p. 12, that they looked for Christ, or at least some of them did: as that expectation of Christ (which was not always, as it seems to you, but sometimes, and that late indeed, in the Church of Israel) ; and in letter 2 to Radecki, p. 95: In this, however, I disagree with you, that you seem to concede that pious men who lived under the Old Testament looked to Christ in those ceremonies and sacrifices in which he is foreshadowed, and were saved in the hope of his coming; which I can in no way persuade myself of, since neither the expectation of the Messiah nor any plain promise was in the people until shortly before the Babylonian captivity, through the Prophet Jeremiah. And letter 3, pp. 137 and 138: For as has also been mentioned above, when the promises of the New Covenant were published, these men were already generally imbued with this opinion, that after this life another, far more blessed life had been prepared and made ready by him, whom this concern touched, for those who had conducted themselves well. vi. Just as they speculate about eternal life, the forgiveness of sins and Christ, so too they speculate about the Holy Spirit given to the faithful under the Old Testament. So we see that in this whole dispute the reasoning is the same for all of these, and therefore may safely be joined by us under the name of spiritual and heavenly goods, especially since we hold from what has gone before what they understand by the Holy Spirit, namely only the hope of eternal life.

units.la: - Quid ergo supererst quaestionis, inquies, dum tot ac tanta nonnunquam videntur Adversarii concedere? Vitam aeternam, remissionem peccatorum, Spiritum S. datum etiam Patribus veteri sub Testamento fuisse, & speratam quandoque vitam aeternam, exspectatumque aliquibus Christum? Respondet Smalcius, cap. ii. pag. 27. Sed in eo tota versatur res, quod affirmatur, istud bonum vitae aeternae, nec foedere inclusum, nec usquam populo aperte promissum fuisse. Aequivocatio est in voce aperte, ante etiam notata. Vel dicere debent, rem promissam fuisse quidem in V. foedere; sed modo duntaxat non satis aperto; vel, non promissam omnino. Si hoc, quorsum non aperte promissum criminantur, quod prorsus non promissum statuunt? Si illud, quid ergo tantam nobis litem faciunt, & prorsus non convenisse illis temporibus, solis Messiae posterioribus, promissiones illas contendunt? Sed ex foedere eodem, & gratia gratiâ Dei in Christo servatos omnes, quotquot unquam servantur, sive jam, sive tum, contendimus. Nec simpliciter gratiâ & fœdere apud Deum, & in ejus mente reservato, sed quoque servandis omnibus quovis tempore, at diverso modo, & gradu claritatis copiæque dispari, manifestato. Cui proinde & fidem adhibere debuerunt & obtemperare. Hoc vero factum negant Adversarii, negant unquam jussos, ante Christi tempora, in venturum credere homines, vel hoc modo justifica-tos aut fuisse, aut justificari debuisse. Nec revelatum vel indicatum fuit unquam in sacris literis, nec jussi sunt usquam illi veteres, nedum aliud, sed neque etiam credere Christum venturum. Nam nec invenietur, quod Deus in fœdere, quod cum populo suo sanxit, adventum istum futurum Christi promiserit, aut ulla alia ratione universo populo id per Mosen ita patefecerit, ut aperte ab ipso populo intelligeretur. Quod vero apud Mosen scriptum, vel a Mose populo, Dei nomine promulgatum non invenitur, id universum populum, & singulos ex populo, prorsus ac penitus obligare nullo modo potuit, inquit Socinus, in Fragmentis, de Justificatione.
units.tr: "What then remains of the question," you will say, "when our opponents sometimes seem to concede so many and such great things? That eternal life, the forgiveness of sins, and the Holy Spirit were given also to the Fathers under the Old Testament, and that eternal life was hoped for and Christ looked for by some?" Smalcius answers, chap. 2, p. 27: But the whole matter turns on this, that it is affirmed that this good of eternal life was neither included in the covenant nor anywhere plainly promised to the people. There is an equivocation in the word "plainly", as noted before. They must either say that the thing was indeed promised in the Old Covenant, but only in a not sufficiently plain way; or that it was not promised at all. If it is this, why do they charge that it was not promised plainly, when they hold that it was not promised at all? If it is the other, why do they make such a quarrel with us, and contend that those promises did not at all belong to those times, but only to the later days of the Messiah? But we maintain that all who have ever been saved, whether now or then, were saved by the same covenant and by the grace of God in Christ. Nor was that grace and covenant merely kept with God and in his mind, but was also made known, at every time, to all who were to be saved, though in different ways and with unequal degrees of clarity and fullness. To it therefore they ought also to have given faith and obedience. But our opponents deny that this was done; they deny that before the times of Christ men were ever commanded to believe in one who was to come, or were or ought to have been justified in this way. Nor was it ever revealed or indicated in the sacred letters, nor were those ancients ever commanded anything of the kind, much less to believe that Christ would come. For it will not be found that God promised, in the covenant he made with his people, that this coming of Christ would take place, or that he in any other way made it so plain to the whole people through Moses that it was clearly understood by the people itself. But what is not found written by Moses, or published by Moses in God's name to the people, could in no way bind the whole people, and each of the people, absolutely and fully, says Socinus, in the Fragments, on justification.

units.la: Hinc distinguunt fidem illorum temporum, & nostram: deinde etiam Ecclesiam. Illa ut fides fuerit in Deum simpliciter; hæc etiam in Christum. Smalcius, contra Frantzium, Disp. ult. pag. 459. nec fides illa fuit fides Iesu Christi, sed fides Deo & promissis illius adhibita. De bon. operib. Disp. vi. pag. 198. fides illa nec fidem Christi continebat, nec fœdere inclusa erat, sed ex sola misericordia Dei totum illud negotium pendebat. Quare, tria nunc ad illorum fidem accessisse scribunt, 1. quod sub N. Test. fides fertur in promissionem vitæ æternæ. II. continet obedientiam præceptorum Christi. III. & in Christum non minus tendit, quam in Deum: secus ac olim. Illa fidei essentialia, & ad ejus substantiam pertinentia; hæc accidentalia, appellat, Disp. VI. de bon. operib. pag. 194. adde & Disp. IV. de justific. in initio, pag. 93. Volkelius, lib. IV. cap. III. Utigitur discrimen intelligatur fidei illius, quam Christus nobis præscripsit, à fide illa, per quam prisci illi Dei cultores gratiam ejus & quæsiverunt, & assecuti sunt; animadvertendum est, id triplex potissimum esse. Primum enim fides Christi postulat, ut sibi vitæ sempiternæ, per ipsum nobis apertissime promissæ, animo concipias: id quod ad fidem illam antiquorum constituendam non erat necessarium; cum ejusmodi promisso carerent. Hanc enim Novi fœderis propriam esse suo loco docuimus. Deinde fides Iesu Christi postulat, ut ea præstes omnia, quæ Christus perfectis suis mandatis, de quibus in sequentibus agemus, complexus est; adeoque majorem vitæ pietatem ac sanctimoniam requirit, quam olim à Mose fuit præscriptum. Tertio & illud ad Veterum fidem accessit, quod hodie tam in Christum, quam in Deum credere jubemur: olim vero nequaquam talem fidem extitisse, vel ex eo patet, quod, uti infra suo loco videbimus, Christus tunc nequaquam adhuc extiterit. Quæ singula suis locis examinabimus.
units.tr: Hence they distinguish the faith of those times from ours, and likewise the Church of those times from ours. The former was faith in God simply; ours is faith in Christ as well. Smalcius, against Frantzius, last Disputation, p. 459: "Nor was that faith the faith of Jesus Christ, but faith applied to God and to his promises." On Good Works, Disputation 6, p. 198: "That faith did not contain faith in Christ, nor was it enclosed within the covenant, but the whole matter depended on the mercy of God alone." Therefore they now write that three things were added to the faith of those men: (1) that under the New Testament faith is directed to the promise of eternal life; (2) that it contains obedience to the precepts of Christ; (3) that it is directed to Christ no less than to God, unlike in the past. They call the former the essentials of faith and what belongs to its substance, and the latter accidentals: On Good Works, Disputation 6, p. 194. Add also Disputation 4, On Justification, at the beginning, p. 93. Volkelius, book 4, chapter 3: "If, then, the difference between that faith which Christ prescribed to us and that faith by which those early worshippers of God sought and obtained his grace is to be understood, it must be noted that this difference is chiefly threefold. First, the faith of Christ requires that you conceive in your mind the eternal life promised to us most plainly through him; this was not necessary for constituting the faith of the ancients, since they lacked such a promise. For we have shown in its place that this is proper to the New Covenant. Second, the faith of Jesus Christ requires that you perform all those things which Christ embraced in his perfect commands, which we shall discuss in what follows; and so it requires a greater holiness and purity of life than was prescribed by Moses of old. Third, this also was added to the faith of the ancients: that today we are commanded to believe in Christ as well as in God, whereas in former times no such faith existed at all; this is clear from the fact that, as we shall see in its place below, Christ had not yet come into existence at that time." We shall examine these points individually in their places.

units.la: Atque ita in V. T. fuisse ajunt Ecclesiam Dei; nunc, Christi. Socinus, in Epistolis, ad Eliam Arcifevium, pag. 410. Distinguendum est etiam inter Dei & Christi ecclesiam. Quamvis enim, quæcunque Christi ecclesia est, eadem necessario Dei quoque sit ecclesia, non tamen contra quæ Dei est ecclesia, eadem continuò Christi ut sit ecclesia necesse est. Porrò Dei ecclesiæ invisibilis initium constitui nequit, cum non constet utrum Adamus & Eva, ante susceptos & jam adultos liberos, ex animo unquam Deo confisi fuerint. Duorum enim tantum congregationem, quod idem in hoc proposito nostro est cum Ecclesia, dici posse, docent verba illa Christi. Ubi fuerint duo aut tres congregati in nomine meo, &c. Visibilis autem Dei ecclesiæ initium, tempore Enos filii Seth extitisse dici potest. Atque Ecclesiæ Christi initium con-
units.tr: And so they say that the Church of God existed in the Old Testament, but now it is the Church of Christ. Socinus, in his Letters to Elias Arciszewski, p. 410: "We must also distinguish between the Church of God and the Church of Christ. For although whatever is the Church of Christ must necessarily also be the Church of God, yet conversely, whatever is the Church of God need not for that reason immediately be the Church of Christ. Moreover, the beginning of the invisible Church of God cannot be fixed, since it is not certain whether Adam and Eve, before they had children who were already grown up, ever trusted God from the heart. For the words of Christ teach that only a gathering of two can be spoken of, which in our present purpose is the same as a Church: 'Where two or three are gathered together in my name,' etc. But the beginning of the visible Church of God can be said to have arisen in the time of Enos, son of Seth." And he fixes the beginning of the Church of Christ at the time when the Holy Spirit descended upon the faithful.

units.la: Tom. 2. stituit in id tempus, quo in fideles descendit Spiritus Sanctus. Sic ergo in V. Test. Ecclesiam Christus non habuit.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Thus, then, Christ did not have a Church in the Old Testament.

units.la: Contra autem in V. T. promissiones factas Christi, & vitæ æternæ, omniumque beneficiorum salutarium in eo, & quidem etiam Patribus, ut ad ipsos pertinentes, ex perpetua Euangelici fœderis, & retro & post, vi ac duratione, creditaque ipsis fuisse, ad proprium animarum suarum commodum ac salutem, tuemur: & sive unius, sive alterius promissionem ostenderimus, quum conjunctæ sint rerum spiritualium & salutarium natura, thesim abunde probaverimus, quum pares sint & ejusdem generis, atque quæ vis negatur ab Adversariis in V. T. extare, tantum rerum corporalium promissiones, & fœdus, & bona. Sic ergo nostra probamus.
units.tr: On the contrary, we maintain that in the Old Testament the promises of Christ and of eternal life, and of all saving benefits in him, were made, and indeed to the Fathers too, as belonging to them; that these were entrusted to them, both before and after, by the power and duration of the perpetual evangelical covenant, for the proper advantage and salvation of their souls. And whether we have shown the promise of one or of the other, since they are joined together by the nature of spiritual and saving things, we have sufficiently proved our thesis, since they are equal and of the same kind; whereas our Adversaries deny that there existed in the Old Testament any force of this kind, only promises of corporal things, and a covenant and goods of that sort. Thus we prove our position.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA.
units.tr: Section Two.

units.la: Argumentum primum. In Scripturis V. T. extare salutis æternæ promissiones, a nemine certius doceri possumus, quam ab ipso Christo, sui ipsius teste certissimo, & vitæ æternæ a se dandæ. Ipse utrumque testatur, Ioann. v. 39. scrutamini Scripturas, ñam[?] putatis vos in iis habere vitam æternam: & ipsæ sunt de me testantes. Christus loquitur, ad Judæos, de, & pro se, quem reprehenderant, & confundere perpetuo conabantur. Vers. 31. dixerat, se non testari de semetipso, ne adversus hoc perperam exciperent, sordere proprium testimonium, & laudem; esse alium, qui testetur de se, videlicet Patrem suum cœlestem. Neque egere se Iohannis testimonio, ad quem tamen pro testimonio miserant. vers. 34. ego autem ab homine testimonium non accipio: verum ista dico ut vos salvemini.
units.tr: First argument. That the Scriptures of the Old Testament contain promises of eternal salvation, we can be taught by no one more surely than by Christ himself, the most certain witness both of himself and of the eternal life he gives. He bears witness to both in John 5:39: Search the Scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. Christ speaks to the Jews, about himself and for himself, whom they had reproached and constantly tried to confound. In verse 31 he had said that he does not testify of himself, lest they object that a man's own testimony and praise is worthless; there is another who testifies of him, namely his heavenly Father. Nor did he need the testimony of John, to whom they had nonetheless sent for testimony. Verse 34: But I receive not testimony from man: but these things I say, that ye might be saved.

units.la: Ubi observa, eum de duobus instituere sermonem, de sui nimirum testimonio, & ipsorum salute. Jam ad gravius testimonium provocat, quam illa sint, quæ hactenus dixerat, vel de suo ipsius, vel Iohannis Baptistæ judicio: nimirum ad Patris. Habeo autem testimonium majus Iohanne: opera quæ Pater mihi dedit, ut ea perficerem, ipsa quæ facio opera, testantur de me quod Pater me misit. Et qui misit me Pater, ipse testatus est de me. vers. 36. 37. & 38. atqui verbum ejus non habetis in vobis manens. 39. scrutamini Scripturas, &c. Nempe quia ad Patris testimonium provocarat, & ejus verbum: jam & Scripturas in medium profert, quas recipiebant Judæi; & quidquid ipsis videretur aut de Christi operibus, aut testatione Patris, Scripturas extra dubium ponebant, & sic ex propriis ipsorum δόξας[?] pergit argumentari Christus, ὑμεῖς δο-κεῖτε[?], & scitis, putatis, in illis extare vitam æternam, atque istæ de me testantur.
units.tr: Here observe that he is discussing two matters: his own testimony, and their salvation. Now he appeals to a weightier testimony than those he had so far mentioned, whether his own or John the Baptist's judgment; namely, the Father's. But I have greater witness than that of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me. And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me (verses 36, 37 and 38). And ye have not his word abiding in you. (verse 38). Search the Scriptures, etc. (verse 39). Since he had appealed to the Father's testimony and his word, he now brings forward the Scriptures, which the Jews accepted; and whatever seemed to them to be true, whether about Christ's works or the Father's witness, they placed beyond doubt. So Christ proceeds to argue from their own opinion: ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε [you think], you know, you suppose, that eternal life is in those writings, and these are they which testify of me.

units.la: In terminis nominat Christus vitam æternam: ut hic nihil possit excipi: & prædicatur de Scripturis, quod in istis illa habetur: propterea que jubet illas scrutari: ἐρευνᾶτε, ὅτι, scrutamini, &c.[?] quia. Pro studio vitæ æternæ inquirebant Scripturas, & isto animo, ut eam in ipsis ἐν αὐτοῖς[?] reperirent. Ergo si Christi de Scripturis testimonium verum, in illis vita æterna, & ex illis haberi, & si quæremus, vita æterna iis ostendi potest. De Scripturis autem V. T. loqui eum, certissimum, quia non alium tum extabant, nondum Scripturæ T. Novi, neque ad alias Judæi aut amandari poterant, ut suas, aut de quibus istam foverent opinionem. Hoc ergo ratum, in V. T. Scriptura habeti[?] testimonia pro vitâ æternâ: eaque ab ipsis Judæis palpari posse, quanto magis ab aliis: & satis clara & expressa fuisse, ut quilibet eo fine ac animo Scripturam cum fructu legere possit & indagare.
units.tr: Christ names eternal life explicitly, so that nothing here can be questioned; and of the Scriptures he says that eternal life is to be found in them, and therefore bids them search them: ἐρευνᾶτε [search], ὅτι [because], scrutamini [search], etc. For they searched the Scriptures in pursuit of eternal life, and with that purpose, that they might find it ἐν αὐτοῖς [in them]. Therefore, if Christ's testimony about the Scriptures is true, eternal life is in them and can be had from them, and if we seek it, it can be shown to us in them. That he is speaking of the Scriptures of the Old Testament is most certain, since at that time there were no other Scriptures, the New Testament not yet existing, nor could the Jews appeal to any others as their own or as supporting their opinion. It is therefore established that the Old Testament Scripture contains testimonies to eternal life, and these can be grasped even by the Jews themselves, much more by others; and they were clear and explicit enough that anyone who reads and searches the Scripture with that aim and mind can do so with profit.

units.la: Deinde quamvis non aliter quàm in Christo, & ex eo vita æterna haberi queat, & ipsâ rei veritate ac naturâ hoc satis clarum fit, attamen conjungit Christus, & pleno ore testatur, testimonia sibi in Scripturis illis perhiberi luculentissima: & ista sunt quæ testantur de me. Si testimonium mei quæritis, & non satis vobis sint alia, agite ad Scripturas, quas & ipsi tanti facitis, vosmet recipite, atque illæ testimoniorum affatim suppeditabunt. Quid quærebatur inter Christum, & Judæos? hoc, an Christus Filius Dei esset, & Servator verus? Id vero cum alia, tum Scripturæ illæ confirmabant. Et istius rei ac veritatis probandæ causa, ad illas homines remittuntur. Sive ergo pro Christo cognoscendo, sive habenda vita æterna, ad Scripturam ire, non licet tantum, sed debemus. En Christi præceptum, scrutamini Scripturas; porro & hujus fructum studii, tum ad vitam inde hauriendam æternam, tum cognitionem Christi salutarem.
units.tr: Further, although eternal life cannot be had otherwise than in Christ and from him, and this is made clear enough by the very truth and nature of the matter, nevertheless Christ joins the two and testifies with full voice that the most luminous testimonies to himself are borne in those Scriptures: And these are they which testify of me. If you seek testimony of me, and other things do not suffice for you, go to the Scriptures, which you yourselves value so highly, and receive them; they will supply testimonies in abundance. What was being sought between Christ and the Jews? This: whether Christ was the Son of God and the true Saviour. Now both other things and those Scriptures confirmed this. And to prove this matter and truth, people are sent back to those Scriptures. Therefore, whether for knowing Christ or for obtaining eternal life, it is not merely permitted to go to the Scripture, but we are bound to do so. Here is Christ's command, search the Scriptures; and here is the fruit of this study, both the drawing from it of eternal life and the saving knowledge of Christ.

units.la: Verf. 40. seq. & non vultis venire ad me, ut habeatis vitam. Vide, ut Christus iterum duo illa conjungat, se, atque vitam: habere vitam, in se, & postquam ad se ventum fuerit. Nec dubium potest esse, quin de vita æterna sint accipienda. Atque ita ista conjunguntur cum præcedentibus, ut & unum & alterum in iisdem haberi Scripturis confirment & explanent. Unde Augustinus, lib. xix. contra Faustum Manichæum, cap. ult. Et ipsa vita æterna si non illic in manifesto prædicaretur, non diceret Dominus etiam malis Iudæis, scrutamini Scripturam, in quibus putatis vos vitam æternam habere, ipsæ testimonium perhibent de me. Quo enim nisi ad hoc pertinet, quod ibi scriptum est, Non moriar, sed vivam, & enarrabo opera Domini, & Illumina oculos meos, ne unquam obdormiam in morte; & Iustorum animæ in manu Dei sunt, & non tangit illos tormentum? &c. Illa in sermone Christi satis manifesta, tum versu illo 39. tum antecedentibus & consequentibus, & clare significat Christus in Scripturis contineri, quandoquidem & promiscuam hominum turbam, & Iudæos contestatur, & communem facit inda-gandi Scripturas admonitionem, & illo fine ac fructu commendat, tum ipsorum quoque judicio confirmat & opinione, ut merito videri mirum possit, quid contra hiscere vel excipere Adversarii possint aut velint. Nec acquiescunt tamen: sed
units.tr: Verses 40 following: And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life. See how Christ again joins those two things, himself and life: to have life in him, and this after one has come to him. There can be no doubt that these are to be understood of eternal life. And so these words are connected with what precedes, in such a way that each confirms and explains the other as contained in the same Scriptures. Hence Augustine, in book 19 against Faustus the Manichaean, last chapter: And if eternal life were not openly proclaimed there, the Lord would not say even to the wicked Jews: Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life; they bear witness of me. For to what else does that which is written there pertain, I shall not die but live, and declare the works of the Lord; and, Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death; and, The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and torment does not touch them? etc. These matters are clear enough in Christ's discourse, both in verse 39 and in what precedes and follows; and Christ plainly indicates that they are contained in the Scriptures, since he addresses the mixed crowd and the Jews alike, and makes the admonition to search the Scriptures common, and commends it for that end and fruit; and he also confirms it by their own judgment and opinion, so that it may rightly seem strange what the adversaries can say or wish to object against this. Yet they do not give up, but

units.la: Excipiunt, Christum non dicere, illa in Scripturis revera occurrere, sed id opinari Iudæos, at frustra, quum in Scripturis non habeantur: & sic illum locum nobis non favere, sed esse adversum. Socinus, adversus Palæologum, part. iv. pag. 562.
units.tr: They object that Christ does not say that those things actually occur in the Scriptures, but that the Jews think so, and in vain, since they are not found in the Scriptures; and so that passage is not in our favour but against us. Socinus, against Palaeologus, part 4, page 562.

units.la: Ex quibus non solum intelligitur, Iudæos Resp. Bene quidem Socinus, pro eo quidem existimasse, vitam æternam in Mosis, dem explicat, contineri in Scripturis, & & prophetarum scriptis contineri, id est eam illis promissum fuisse; sed, quod Christum illis promissam fuisse, qui inibi mandata servaf-censet adferre ista non tamquam sua, sed sent, rem tamen aliter se habuisse, verum etiam, Iudæorum propria, non vera, sed falsa, & quid omnino de vetere, novoque fœdere, quod ad propterea non probare, sed improbare sal-vitam æternam attinet, statui debeat, facile tem tacite, in eo magnæ imperitiæ majo-percipitur. Nempe, vitam æternam in vetere rem addit audaciam. 1. Sic enim argu-fœdere, ut dictum est, promissam non fuisse, mento pugnaret Christus, non frivolo nec in illius fœderis scriptis eam contineri, nisi tantum, sed falso, quod nec fecit unquam, quatenus in illis olim promissus, ac prænuncia- nec facere debuit. Arbitramini vos qui-tus fuit Christus, deque ipso illa testantur. ad dem vitam æternam in Scripturis conti-neri,
units.tr: From these words it is understood not only that the Jews thought eternal life was contained in the writings of Moses and the prophets, that is, that it had been promised in them, but also that Christ was promised in those writings and that they bear witness to him; yet Socinus rightly judged that the matter was otherwise. Responding: Socinus indeed rightly judged that the Jews held eternal life to be contained in the writings of Moses and the prophets, that is, promised in them; but he thinks they brought these things forward not as their own but as the Jews' own, not true but false; and what should be decided about eternal life in the Old and New Covenant is easily perceived from this. Namely, as has been said, eternal life was not promised in the Old Covenant, nor is it contained in the writings of that covenant, except only as far as Christ was promised and foretold in it, and those writings bear witness about him. Hence the Jews were unwilling to come to Christ, which is nothing else than to come today to eternal life, if anyone wishes to have it. Not out of respect for Scripture did they refuse to come to Christ. Here Socinus, while not proving but disproving, adds boldness to great ignorance. Thus Christ would be arguing with a frivolous argument, not merely false but one he never made and ought not to have made. Do you think that you who are here in such error, that eternal life is contained in the Scriptures, but rashly and gravely mistaken in this, are

units.la: 1. quem hodie ire oportet, si quis vitam æternam neri, sed temere, & in hoc erratis graviter habere velit. Ad Christum autem ire, quod ii. Neque ex honore Scripturæ est, eam Judæi facere nolebant, nihil aliud est, quam ab commendare argumentis non veris, præipso velle doceri, & porrò illi confidere, eique sertim figmentis & opinionibus falsis Judæorum obdire[?]. quibus rebus summa totius novi fœderis dæorum, & hinc ei pretium quærere velle planè convincitur. Smalcius, adverf. Frant- ac usum. iii. Imo ne conjungi quidem illa zium, Disp. vii. de Bonis operib. pag.22. uno halitu possunt, & commate, Scriptu-Nec enim Christus dicit, in sacris literis V. T. ra Sacra, & falsa Judæorum expositio, esse vitam æternam, sed ait, Judæos putare se quando nihil ultra additur, nihil quod exhabere in iis vitam æternam. Potest autem quis positionem talem aut mendacium coarsputare se aliquid habere, & tamen revera illud guat. Quid paleæ cum frumento? aut non habere. Volckelius, lib. iii. cap. xi. luci cum tenebris? iv. Quorsum Christus pag. 61. Verum id contrarium potius sententiam confirmat, cum Christus nequaquam Scripturas illis vitam æternam contineri, sed eos ita rum? Æque & alia non minus absona po-arbitrari, affirmet. tuisset Christus à Judæis mutuare & commemorare, si voluisset. Nihil autem vel perperam, vel absonum, aut heterogeneum sermoni suo admiscere Christus potuit. v. Nihil tale, quod non aliquo indicio vel argumento contrario redarguisset aut confutasset, si falsum allegasset. vi. Nihil in Christi oratione est, quo significarit, rem aliter se habuisse: nihil quod arguat suam sententiam Judaicæ oppositam. vii. Imo non tacite, sed aperte eam confirmavit, quia de vita æterna agebatur, ejusque studio, quod cum ex sedulâ Scripturarum lectione peterent Judæi, & Christum tamen abominarentur, in quo Scripturæ illam monstrabant, de Christo & salute in eo testificantes, ait, & vos putatis in illis vitam æternam habere, & hoc recte quidem: sed non separanda illa à me, vel extra me quærenda est. viii. Et confirmat illud insuper addita causalis ὅτι, quia: non tantum ad Scripturæ investigationem illos Christus cohortans, sed & propter istam causam, quia nempe in eâ inveniatur æterna vita. Non, inquit, scrutamini Scripturas, putatis in eâ, sed quia, quandoquidem putatis in eâ vitam habere æternam. ix. Uti verum erat, in iis extare testimonium de Christo, ita quoque illud de vitâ æternâ: quæ indivulse conjunguntur, & non hoc magis, quam illud, verum erat certumque, & à Judæis pro vero habitum ubique. x. Quod à Judæis & hodie creditur. Nec denegare Socinus audet, quando adversus Semijudaizantes scripsit, dicant quidquid velint Judæi, nihil unquam Moses promisit præter hujus vitæ bona, & tum alii inter Judæos illud probant, tum Manassé Ben-Israel in libris de resurrectione, qui statim in initio ostendit, dari Resurrectionem mortuorum, autoritate librorum Mosaicorum, deinde & Prophetarum: atque idem in libris de anima Hebraicis. Tum R. Josephus Albo, Ikkarim, part. iii. cap, xxv. Neque ab ullo Christianorum hac in parte Judæi vel accusati erroris fuerunt unquam, vel convicti. xi. δοκεῖτε, putatis, arbitramini, censetis, non significat incertum aliquid, vel falsum, sed pro subjecto, cui adhibetur, sententiam firmam & constantem. Quemadmodum δόγματα[?], κυρίαι δόξαι[?], dogmata & axiomata præcipua & fundamentalia. Actor. xv. 22. ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις, verf. 28. ἔδοξε γὰρ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ ἡμῖν. An hoc est arbitrari, & tantum non putare falsum? Luc. 1. 3. ἔδοξε κἀμοὶ visum & mihi sequuto diligen-ter, &c. Act. xxvi. 9. ἐγὼ μὲν ἐδόξα ἐμαυτῷ[?], ego mihi statueram propter nomen Iesu Nazareni oportere me multa contraria facere. Quibus omnibus locis δόκειν non significat videri hoc quod revera in se falsum, sed firmam sententiam veri, ac boni. Uti & in nostro loco, quod dicitur, ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε[?], non debet exponi de opinione falsi, sed de sententia, pro re cui additur, certa ac gravissima, & quae probatur, non improbatur. Denique si vita aeterna in Veteris T. scriptis continetur saltem, quatenus in Christo, illis olim promisso, ac praenunciato habetur, continetur ergo hactenus: nam non tantum Christum aliquem venturum illa dicunt, sed & exponunt qualis futurus esset, & qualia ejus officia, nimirum salutaria, non ipse animalis vel terrenus aliquis, talis ac Judaei eum faciunt. Et puto, uti Christus, sic & officia ejus ista satis clare ibi doceri, atque salutem ab eo proventuram. Non ergo prorsus negari potuit, vitae aeternae & salutis cognitionem ac promissionem Patribus obti-gisse, quum illi de Christo ipsis factae fuerint promissiones, & ab earum intelligenti-bus Prophetis, & qui exponere easdem ample potuerint, & dilucidare.
units.tr: 1. Whom one must now go to, if anyone wishes to have eternal life. To go to Christ, however, which the Jews were unwilling to do, is nothing other than to wish to be taught by him himself, and further to trust in him and to obey him. By these things it is plainly shown that the sum of the whole New Covenant and its use is here. Smalcius, against Frantzius, Disp. vii, on good works, p. 22. ii. Nor is it for the honour of Scripture to commend it by untrue arguments, especially by the fictions and false opinions of the Jews, and thence to seek esteem and use for it. iii. Indeed, these things cannot even be joined in one breath and one clause with the Holy Scriptures and the false interpretation of the Jews. For Christ does not say that eternal life is in the Old Testament writings, but says that the Jews think they have eternal life in them. One may think oneself to have something and yet in truth not have it. Volckelius, lib. iii, ch. xi, p. 61. Indeed, this rather confirms the contrary opinion: that Christ, when he affirms that the Jews so think, does not affirm that eternal life is contained in the Scriptures. iv. To what purpose? Christ could equally have borrowed from the Jews and mentioned other things no less absurd, had he wished. Yet Christ could mix nothing perverse, absurd, or foreign into his discourse. v. Nothing of that kind is there which he would not have refuted or overthrown by some contrary sign or argument, had he alleged something false. vi. There is nothing in Christ's speech by which he signified that the matter stood otherwise, nothing which argues that his opinion is opposed to the Jewish one. vii. Indeed he did not confirm it tacitly but openly, since eternal life was the subject, and since the Jews, who searched the Scriptures diligently for it and yet abhorred Christ, in whom the Scriptures pointed to that life and testified of Christ and salvation, were the ones concerned. He says: and you think that in them you have eternal life, and this indeed rightly; but that life is not to be separated from me, nor sought outside me. viii. He confirms this further by the added causal ὅτι [because]: Christ urges them to search the Scriptures not only for that purpose, but also for this reason, namely because eternal life is found in them. He says, not "search the Scriptures, which you think to contain it," but because, since you think that in them you have eternal life. ix. Just as it was true that the testimony about Christ is in them, so also was that about eternal life; these are inseparably joined, and it was no more true of the one than of the other, and was held by the Jews everywhere as true. x. This is believed by the Jews today too. Nor does Socinus dare to deny it, when, writing against the semi-Judaizers, he said: Let the Jews say whatever they will; Moses never promised anything except the goods of this life. Other Jews prove the opposite, and Manasseh Ben-Israel in his books on the resurrection, who at the very beginning shows that the resurrection of the dead is given on the authority of the books of Moses and then of the Prophets; and likewise in his Hebrew books on the soul. Then Rabbi Joseph Albo, Ikkarim, part iii, ch. xxv. Nor were the Jews ever accused or convicted of error in this matter by any of the Christians. xi. δοκεῖτε [you think], putatis, arbitramini, censetis, does not signify something uncertain or false, but, with the subject to which it is applied, a firm and settled opinion. Just as δόγματα and κυρίαι δόξαι [dogmas and principal opinions] mean the chief and fundamental dogmas and axioms. Acts 15:22: ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις [it seemed good to the apostles]; verse 28: ἔδοξε γὰρ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ ἡμῖν [for it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us]. Is this to "think," and hardly to suppose false? Luke 1:3: ἔδοξε κἀμοὶ [it seemed good to me also], visum and mihi sequuto diligenter [having followed diligently], etc. Acts 26:9: ἐγὼ μὲν ἐδόξα ἐμαυτῷ [I indeed thought to myself], ego mihi statueram propter nomen Iesu Nazareni oportere me multa contraria facere [I had resolved in myself that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth]. In all these places δόκειν does not mean to seem what is in itself false, but a firm opinion of what is true and good. And so in our passage too, the words ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε [you think] ought not to be taken as an opinion of something false, but as a judgment that is certain and weighty for the matter to which it is added, and which is approved, not disapproved. Finally, if eternal life is contained in the writings of the Old Testament at least insofar as it is held in Christ, who was promised and foretold to them of old, then it is contained so far: for they not only say that Christ was to come, but also set out what sort of person he would be and what his offices would be, namely saving ones, not that of some merely animal or earthly figure, such as the Jews make of him. And I think that, just as Christ himself, so also his offices are taught there clearly enough, and that salvation would come from him. It therefore could not be denied altogether that the knowledge and promise of eternal life and salvation came to the Fathers, since promises were made to them about Christ, and the Prophets who understood them, and who were able to expound and explain them fully, had been given them.

units.la: Smalcius, contra Frantzium, Disp. vii. de Bonis operibus, pag. 222. Quae vero esset merces propositae fidei in Christum, id proprie & manifeste in Euangelio revelatum est. Vitam aeternam ex conjecturis quibusdam, in sacris literis descriptis apparet sibi somniasse Judaeos; sed Christus asserit spem istam vanam esse. Nam quae spes non nititur promissionibus divinis, ea non potest esse absolute certa. Resp. 1. Non negamus, proprie & manifeste in Euangelio revelari & exponi, quae merces proposita fit fidei in Christum; sed quatenus Euangelium etiam in V. T. promulgatum & declaratum fuit, sic & hic illud notum fuit quoque. Euangelium autem etiam tum significatum fuit, quando promissiones de Christo. Nam magnam Veteris Scripturae, & intellectus sani a populo removet partem, qui hoc tantum de Christo putet traditu ibi fuisse, quod aliquando venturus esset, & non quoq; explicatum, quod ejus pro acquirenda hominum salute, futurum fuisset officium. Adeone somniarunt sibi vitam aeternam Judaei, & non crediderunt? & somniarunt ex sacris literis? Scriptura causam suppeditante somnii, vel conjecturae? Res somnii & conjecturae fuit vita aeterna in Veteri populo? Scilicet adeo remota a sensu Scripturae, & fidei articulis, ut non aliter assequi, quam conjectando eam homines potuerint? Imo hoc somnium & Socinianorum, & conjectura non proba de patribus plus hic vigilantibus, & sanis, quam illi. Scilicet somniavit Abraham, somniarunt reliqui, quando vitam aeternam, & coelestem patriam praestolati sunt, & non nisi per somnium ista sibi finxerunt? Si hoc Judaei hodie dicerent, imputaremus eorum caeci-tati & incredulitati: at a Christianis id dici de probis & sanctis viris, qui & vixerunt olim, & non in Scripturis tantum valde praedicantur, sed & ipsi illas scripserunt, tan-tos somniatores fuisse, & conjectores, & fabulatores in re adeo seria & gravi & coe-lesti, id non ferendum arbitror. Somniarint Gentiles, luce divini verbi destituti, & in tenebris aliquid de vita altera & coelis fuerint fabulati: quod tamen, qua parte verum, Hebraeis accepti ferri debet, ut idem quis somniet & fingat de veteribus Prophetis, Patriarchis, & fidelibus omnibus nescio illorum magis, an nostrae religioni probro-sum sit, imprimis si ne illos quidem id adhuc somniasse, aut somnium vidisse putes, quod viderunt infimae aetatis ac fortis Judaei, & in ipsorum scriptis fuisse, quod scriptores ipsos latuerit. Si quae sint indicia in Scripturis, ex quibus posteriores conjicere potuerunt vitam aeternam, multo magis illa viderunt Scriptores ipsi: & si ipsi viderunt, si docuerunt, cur enim non docuissent? si & hinc sciverunt illorum temporum Judaei aeq; ac posteriorum, diceturne totum illud fuisse hominum imperitorum, vel non satis sibi constantium somnium? III. Et hoc non somnium, sed mendacium est satis apertum, scribere quod Christus asserit spem istam vanam esse, quam de vita aeterna ex Scripturis Judaei conceperant: salsissimum est, vel vane illam spem ex Scripturis concipi, vel a Christo id uspiam asseri. IV. Verum quidem est, quod quae spes non nititur promissionibus divinis, non potest esse absolute vera: sed hoc Christus non applicat spei aut fidei Judaeorum, neque de ista verum est: quin contra, quia vitam illam crediderunt & statuerunt, ex Scripturis edocti, teste Christo, promissionibus divinis nixos necesse est. Denique sperasse etiam Veteres vitam aeternam nonnunquam fatentur, uti vidimus, Adversarii, ergo non omnino promissionibus & Scripturis destitutos illos, cogimur fateri. Smalcius, hac ipsa Disp. 220.
units.tr: Smalcius, against Frantzius, Disp. vii, on good works, p. 222. What the reward of faith proposed in Christ is has been revealed properly and plainly in the Gospel. The Jews seem to have dreamed up eternal life from certain conjectures drawn from the holy writings; but Christ declares that this hope is vain. For a hope that does not rest on divine promises cannot be absolutely certain. Reply 1. We do not deny that what reward is offered to faith in Christ is properly and openly revealed and set out in the Gospel; but insofar as the Gospel was also proclaimed and declared in the Old Testament, so here too it was known. Moreover the Gospel was then also signified, when the promises about Christ were made. For he strips the people of a large part of the meaning of the Old Scripture and of sound understanding, who thinks that only this was handed down there about Christ, that he would one day come, and not also explained what his office would be for obtaining the salvation of men. Did the Jews dream up eternal life for themselves, and not believe it? And did they dream it from the holy writings? Did Scripture supply the cause of a dream or a conjecture? Was eternal life in the Old people a matter of dream and conjecture? Surely so far removed from the sense of Scripture and the articles of faith that men could attain it in no other way than by guessing? Indeed this dream is that of the Socinians, and a conjecture not approved of, about the Fathers who were more watchful and sound than they. Surely Abraham dreamed, and the others dreamed, when they waited for eternal life and the heavenly fatherland, and feigned those things for themselves only in a dream? If the Jews said this today, we would impute it to their blindness and unbelief; but that such great dreamers, guessers and fabulists should be said by Christians about upright and holy men, who both lived long ago and are highly praised not only in the Scriptures but who also wrote them, in a matter so serious, weighty and heavenly, I think is not to be borne. The Gentiles, destitute of the light of the divine word, may have dreamed and fabled something in darkness about another life and the heavens; but whatever in that is true should be credited to the Hebrews. That someone should dream and invent the same about the old Prophets, Patriarchs and all the faithful—I do not know whether this is more shameful for them or for our religion, especially if you think they had not even dreamed or seen in a dream what the lowest and most foolish Jews of our own age have seen, and what was in their own writings yet escaped the writers themselves. If there are any indications in the Scriptures from which later men could conjecture eternal life, the writers themselves saw them much more; and if they themselves saw them, if they taught them, why would they not have taught them? And if the Jews of those times knew this as well as those of later times, shall it be said that that whole thing was the dream of unlearned men, or of men not sufficiently consistent with themselves? III. And that this is not a dream but a plain lie, to write that Christ declares this hope vain, which the Jews had conceived about eternal life from the Scriptures: it is most absurd either that this hope is conceived from the Scriptures in vain, or that Christ asserts it anywhere. IV. It is indeed true that a hope that does not rest on divine promises cannot be absolutely true; but Christ does not apply this to the hope or faith of the Jews, nor is it true of it: rather, on the contrary, because they believed and held that life, taught from the Scriptures, as Christ attests, they must have rested on divine promises. Finally, we are compelled to admit, as our opponents also note, that the Ancients sometimes hoped for eternal life, as we have seen; therefore they were not entirely destitute of promises and Scripture. Smalcius, in this same Disp., p. 220.

units.la: Itaque sententiam nostram breviter hic af-scribemus. Resp. I. Vitam aeternam etiam in V.T. scribemus. Vitam aeternam negamus, unquam promissam fuisse, pro conditione tempo-[?]alicui promissam fuisse, nec in ipsa etiam lege rum illorum, satis manifeste & aperte, Mosis, aperte & manifeste: Non negamus au-tem, cum & aliis deinceps sumus ostensuri, omnes pios, qui ante Christum vixerunt, tum ex praesenti loco, & testimonio Christi vitam aeternam consecuturos. Potest enim Deus [?]ipsi est manifestum. Atq; ut nos non posse-plus dare quam promisit: Nec negamus, po-mus loca profetre manifesta & aperta in tuisse homines sperare vitam aeternam, etiamsi terminis id docentia, tamen illa cognita eis promissa non fuerit. Extabant enim quae-dam, quae spem illius excitare poterant. In novo Veteribus fuisse, & ex jugi Prophetarum doctrina piis veritatem illam constitisse, demum foedere[?], vitam aeternam aperte revela- credere oportet, postquam ex Scripto-tam & promissam omnibus in Christum credentibus [?]N. Test. didicimus quam multa V. tibus fuisse, contendimus. Test. infinit argumenta ad probandam veritatem Christi & Evangelii, & commendandam Veterum fidem ac religionem, quae absque hoc nos latuissent. Ubi ergo in N.
