T: dicitur, quod Veteres statuerunt & crediderunt, & sperarunt coelestia, ego malo credere eos istorum habuisse promissiones, quia non potuit esse vana fides illa & incerta, quam negare; quantumvis nequirem tot vel tantas eas ostendere, quae omnium contradictiones compescerent. II. Praesertim ubi addimus, quod iidem illi Prophetae qui ista scripserunt, forte, quod nobis videtur, obscurius, sua optime intelligentes, vivi & continui eorundem fuerunt apud populum interpretes & doctores, qui vel ultro, vel rogati ea expedire, quod ad sensus suos genuinos potuerunt, & populum ubertim erudire. III. Certe Deus plus dat passim, quam promittit, etiam nunc ubi promissiones rerum salutarium fecit satis apertas: verum non mirum tantum, sed parum congruum videtur, Deum sui cultoribus eximiis, & sub multa rerum adversarum acerbitate ipsum sequentibus noluisse vitae aeternae ullam facere manifestationem, quam non per umbram, sed per somnium tantum & conjecturam voluerit illos fingere potius, quam credere. IV. Non potuerunt sperare vitam aeternam, si promissa eis non fuerit; nam quae spes non nititur promissionibus divinis, ea non potest esse absolute certa, imo non vera, non divina, qualem oportet omnino spem istam esse, quam quis concipiat vel foveat aeternae vitae. Certe hic spem facere, qualis somniantium, est in re seria ludere, nisi parum abest a blasphemia.
units.tr: Here, then, we shall briefly set down our view. Reply I. We deny that eternal life was ever promised under the conditions of those times, plainly and clearly, nor even in the law of Moses itself, plainly and manifestly. We do not deny, however, as we shall show elsewhere, that all the godly who lived before Christ will obtain eternal life, as is evident both from the present passage and from the testimony of Christ. For God can give more than he has promised. Nor do we deny that men under the old covenant could hope for eternal life, even though it was not promised to them in express terms. For there were certain things which could arouse that hope. Although we cannot produce passages that teach this in express and manifest terms, we must believe that these things were known to the Fathers, and that by the constant teaching of the prophets the truth was established for the godly. We contend that this is so, since we have learned from the writers of the New Testament how many countless arguments the Old Testament offers for proving the truth of Christ and the Gospel, and for commending the faith and religion of the Fathers, which without this would have remained hidden from us. Therefore, where the New Testament says that the Fathers held, believed and hoped for heavenly things, I prefer to believe that they had promises of these things. For that faith would not have been empty and uncertain, as you would have it, even though I could not show so many or such great promises as would silence every contradiction. II. Especially since we add that the same prophets who wrote these things, perhaps, as seems to us, more obscurely, yet understanding their own words very well, were living and continual interpreters and teachers to the people, who, whether of their own accord or when asked, explained these things as far as they could according to their true sense, and instructed the people abundantly. III. Certainly God everywhere gives more than he promises, even now, when he has made promises of saving things plain enough. But it seems not only strange but altogether unfitting that God should have been unwilling to make any manifestation of eternal life to his outstanding worshippers, who followed him under much bitter adversity, so that he wished them to imagine it, rather than believe it, from a mere shadow, or from a dream and guesswork. IV. They could not have hoped for eternal life if it had not been promised to them; for a hope that does not rest on divine promises cannot be absolutely certain, indeed it cannot be true or divine, which is what this hope must altogether be, if anyone is to conceive or cherish hope of eternal life. Certainly to form a hope of this kind, like that of dreamers, is to trifle in a serious matter, and comes close to blasphemy.

units.la: v. Nunc dicit, quod extabant quaedam quæ ipsum illius excitare poterant, nimirum in Scripturis, vitæ æternæ, & quod ex superioribus repetendum, in ipsa etiam lege Mosis. Hoc vero multum dirimit præsentis controversiæ, extiterunt modo talia in Scripturis. De modo, aperto satis & manifesto, post visuri, ubi in rem fuerit conventum. Et rei tum bonæ, tum futuræ significatio, quam tu inde sperare possis, ut differat à promissione, velim aliquis exponat. Si extant quædam in Scripturis, quæ ipsem vitæ æternæ excitare alicui possint, ergo ea promissa fuit, vel collata, vel aliud, quod eodem trahi apte queat, alioqui ipsem non excitaturum. Et si historia, vel factum, vel veritas aliqua proferatur, non potest aliorum excitare animum vel spem, nisi qua ratione ad eos deduci potest sub ratione promissionis aut expressæ, aut implicitæ, aut alterius, quæ vim tamen eandem habeat, rei. vi. Si in Novo Test. vita æterna promissa omnibus in Christum credentibus; quomodo non eadem vita certo expectanda fuerit in Christum crediturus? Hoc vero debuerunt homines æque, Christo iis quocunque modo revelato, sive venturo, sive exhibito. Semper enim pro modo revelationis divinæ fides ei adhibenda, rei aut futuræ, aut factæ, ne Deum faciamus mendacem, sed ut ejus obsignemus veritatem, tam in promissionibus elucentem, quam rebus ipsis. Postremo Christi ad idem argumentum spectantia videamus verba ultima, verf. 46. 47. Si enim Mosi crederetis, crederetis & mihi, de me enim ille scripsit. Verum ejus scriptis si non credatis, quomodo meis verbis credaretis? Quinque significat. i. Mosem de se scripsisse, & testatum fuisse. ii. Ita aperte, ut hoc cognoscere satis Judæi quivis & legere ex illius scriptis potuerint. iii. & debuerint inde credere. iv. Ejus verbis fidem deberi, quemadmodum & Christi. v. Imo inde evenire quod Christo minus jam crederent, quia Mosis de ipso testimonium non satis digne recipiebant. Suis verbis, atque Mosis scriptis divinam pariter vindicans autoritatem, & fidem. Quare & Abraham ad Divitem, Luc. xvi. 29. 31. habent Mosem, & Prophetas; illos audiant.. Si Mosem & Prophetas non audiunt, neque si vel aliquis ex mortuis resurgat, movebuntur.. Satis in illis erat, quod ad salutem requiri videbatur.
units.tr: V. He now says that certain things which could arouse hope of it existed, namely in the Scriptures of eternal life, and, as is to be repeated from what precedes, in the law of Moses itself. This, however, greatly alters the present controversy: such things existed only in the Scriptures. As to the manner, which is plain and manifest enough, we shall consider it afterwards, when the matter has been discussed. And I would like someone to explain what the signification of a good and future thing is, which you could hope for from that, and how it differs from a promise. If there are in the Scriptures certain things which can arouse hope of eternal life in anyone, then it was either promised or conferred, or something else was promised which can aptly be drawn to the same thing; otherwise it would not arouse hope. And if some history, or fact, or truth is set forth, it cannot arouse the mind or hope of others, unless it can be brought to them under the aspect of a promise, either express or implied, or of some other thing which has the same force. VI. If in the New Testament eternal life is promised to all who believe in Christ, how could that same life not be certainly expected by one who is going to believe in Christ? And men ought to have held this equally, whether Christ was revealed to them in whatever manner, whether as coming or as already exhibited. For faith must always be given to a thing, whether future or past, according to the manner of divine revelation, not so that we make God a liar, but so that we set our seal to his truth, which shines forth as much in his promises as in the things themselves. Finally, let us look at Christ's last words on the same subject, vers. 46, 47: "For if you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote of me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?" These words have five meanings: (1) that Moses wrote about himself and bore witness to it; (2) that he did so so plainly that any Jew could know this and read it from his writings; (3) and ought to have believed it from them; (4) that faith is owed to his words just as it is to Christ's; (5) and indeed that from this it followed that they now believed Christ less, because they did not receive Moses' testimony about him worthily. Christ, by his own words and the writings of Moses, equally claims divine authority and faith. Hence also Abraham to the rich man, Luke 16:29, 31: "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rise from the dead." In those writings there was enough for what seemed required for salvation.

units.la: Jam, quandoquidem ita volunt Adversarii, ostendant nobis apud Mosem loca de Christo adeo aperta & manifesta, qualia à nobis exigunt pro vita æterna; vel admittant, satis nobis debere esse, quod ista à Christo dicuntur, & hæc non exigenda esse ad qualem vel quantamcunque claritatem ac homines aliqui nunc cupiunt, non ut iis credant, sed ut ne credant talia illis tradita fuisse. Deinde observandum, Christum ita dicere illa extare apud Mosem, ut non qualiter cunque inde cognosci, sed & credi debeant: quod ipsum præterquam magnum pro eorum claritate & copia facit argumentum, finem indicat, quem illa dicta apud homines obtinere semper debuerint, ipsorum videlicet fidem & assensum. Neque id tamen tempore Christi, & postea, sed antea quoque, & semper, à quo illa nuncjata vel consignata scripto fuerunt. Nunquam enim non eandem illam suam ἀξίωσιν habuerunt rationem, & necessitatem illis credendi homines: semper oportuit illos Mosi credere: atqui Mosi credentes non potuerunt non credere Christo, nam de Christo ille scripsit. Imo quod Christo non credunt, hinc est quod Mosis scriptis fidem non habent illam, quam debent. Impossibile est ut fidelis in Mose legens Christum, eum fide non apprehendat, non faciat suum. Nisi enim hoc, non erit fidelis; & infidelem se arguet, si minus id faciat. Quid autem est credere, nisi veritatem illam quam tenes, præcipue divinam ac salutarem, tibi applicare, & imbibere? Jam nec possibile est, ut quis quovis wis etiam tempore videns Christum, & cognoscens quid, qualis sit, officia ejus divi-na & salutaria, quin credet ei, & credere tenebitur propter veritatem adeo sibi ne-cessariam & profuam. Denique hoc qui facit, quomodo non in Christo etiam spe-ret vitam æternam, qui eam non modo in se, & suis habet, sed ipse vita est, & via, & veritas, ut quemadmodum ad Patrem nemo quidem venire potest extra eum, sic & ipsum habere nemo, nisi qui & vitæ in eo sit particeps divinæ atque æternæ.
units.tr: Now, since our opponents want it so, let them show us passages about Christ in Moses so plain and manifest as those they demand from us for eternal life; or let them admit that it must be enough for us that these things are said of Christ, and that such passages should not be demanded with any clarity whatever, or with the clarity some men now desire, not so that they may believe them, but so that they may not believe that such things were handed down to them at all. Next, it must be observed that Christ says these things are in Moses in such a way that they should be known from them, not in any manner whatever, but also believed. This, apart from being a great argument for their clarity and abundance, indicates the purpose which those sayings ought always to have had among men, namely their faith and assent. And this was so not only in Christ's time and afterwards, but also before, and always, from the time when those things were announced or committed to writing. For they never lacked the same authority [ἀξίωσιν] and the same reason and necessity for men to believe them; it was always necessary to believe Moses, and those who believe Moses could not fail to believe Christ, for Moses wrote of Christ. Indeed, the fact that they do not believe Christ is the reason why they do not have that faith in Moses's writings which they ought to have. It is impossible that a faithful reader of Christ in Moses should not lay hold of him by faith and make him his own. For unless he does this, he will not be faithful, and he will show himself unbelieving if he does less. And what is it to believe, but to apply to yourself, and to take in, that truth which you hold, especially a divine and saving one? Nor is it possible that anyone, at whatever time, seeing Christ and knowing what he is, and his divine and saving offices, should not believe in him; and he is bound to believe because of a truth so necessary and profitable to himself. Finally, how can one who does this not also hope for eternal life in Christ, since he has it not only in himself and his own, but is himself life, and the way, and the truth, so that just as no one can come to the Father except through him, so no one can possess him unless he also partakes of that divine and eternal life in him?

units.la: Ἐῤῥέθη[?], inquit Smalcius, non sensu imperativo necessario debet accipi, sed modo indicativo etiam potest intelligi, ut sensus sit, non quid deberent facere, sed quid facerent, vos indagatis, non, indagate: Disp. contra Frantz. pag. 222. nam alioquin vox Græca ita converti potest, ut Christus non jubeat quicquam, sed affirmet, Iudæos scrutari scripturam, quæ de se testentur. At non propterea tantum, sed quoque ut in eâ haberent vitam æternam, scrutabantur Scripturam. Legatur indicativo modo: sed quis nescit hoc, pro modo loquendi sacro, in rebus præcepti, imperativi in se vim continere? Atqui legere & scrutari Scripturas, præcepti res est: quare nil obstat ut non imperative legatur, indagate: nam certe justi sunt scrutari Scripturas. Quod præ-ceptum, vel ex eo studium noluit Christus elevare, aut imminuere.
units.tr: The Greek word [ἐραυνᾶτε], says Smalcius, need not be taken in the imperative sense; it can also be understood in the indicative mood, so that the meaning is not what they ought to do but what they do: you search, not search. Disputation against Frantz, p. 222. For otherwise the Greek verb can be rendered so that Christ commands nothing but affirms that the Jews search the Scripture, which bear witness to him. But they did not search the Scriptures for that reason alone; they also searched them because they thought they had eternal life in them. Let it be read in the indicative mood: yet who does not know that, in the manner of sacred speech, things that are commanded carry the force of the imperative within them? Now to read and search the Scriptures is a matter of command. So there is nothing to prevent it being read imperatively, search, for it is certainly right to search the Scriptures. Christ did not wish to weaken or diminish this command, and he showed as much by the zeal he commended.

units.la: Insuper Apostolus II Timoth. III. 15. 16. 17. Scripturas V. T. commendat ab iisdem usibus, quibus Christus, quando ad Timotheum sic loquitur, A pueritia sacras Scripturas nosti, quæ te possunt sapientem reddere ad salutem, per fidem in Christum Iesum. Omnis enim Scriptura divinitus inspirata, & utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam in justitia. Ut perfectus sit vir Dei, ad omne bonum opus in-structus. Scripturas intelligit V. Testamenti: neque alias vel novisse à pueritia Timotheus poterat, vel commendare Apostolus. Vide, quæ de illis testetur, tum quæ in illis contineantur, tum cujus sint usus, & ad quæ valeant. Continentur iis σωτηρία, διὰ πίστεως τῆς[?] ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, & salus, & fides in Christo. Quæ duo illa sunt, quæ in scriptis Mosis haberi, notarat Christus. Quomodo enim sacræ literæ potuissent sapientem reddere unumquemque, & inter alios Timotheum, ad salutem, per fidem in Christo Iesu, nisi illa in se comprehendissent? & illa non comprehenderunt simpliciter, sed potenter, τὰ δυνάμενά σε σοφίσαι. σοφία est supremus gradus scientiæ. Ad hoc ergo copiosæ satis in se valent Scripturæ Sacræ, ut hominem in rebus summis, quales divinæ sunt & Theologicæ, reddant sapientem: sapien-tem vero, ad salutem: & hanc, per fidem in Christum Iesum. Versio Æthiopica legit, quæ potest vivificare te per fidem Iesum Christi. Uti ergo plenæ sapientiâ sunt Scri-pturæ illæ, ita & salute, ita & fide, sive doctrinâ de salute æternâ per fidem in Chri-stum obtinendâ. Hoc sine & Timotheus Scripturas scrutatus ab unguiculis fuit, & calluit, & Paulus eas commendavit. Ergo illæ testantur de Christo, & Timotheus putavit se vitam æternam in iis habere. Jam in usibus Scripturæ commemorandis, per inductionem omnia recenset Apostolus salutaria, ad quæ faciat, è quibus si exi-mantur ea, super quibus controvertimus, certe non potest ita plene ad omnia dici ὠφέλιμος, & ad virum Dei, sive ministrium Dei intelligas ejusque verbi, sive in genere quemvis probum, omni opere bono perficiendum, ac Apostolus hic facit. Versio Æthiopica, ut eruditus sit homo Dei, in omni opere bono, doctor. Hæc sunt argu-menti primi loca, quæ in genere ostendunt V. T. continere promissiones salutis vitæ æternæ, Christi etiam & salutarium in eo beneficiorum, ad omnes spectan-tium, & singulis necessariorum. Jam ad partes descendamus, & rerum in Scripturis commemoratarum species: atque primum dicamus de lege, quæ pars doctrinæ divi-næ prima & antiquissima.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle in 2 Timothy 3:15–17 commends the Old Testament Scriptures for the same uses for which Christ commended them, when he says to Timothy: From childhood you have known the sacred Scriptures, which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. For all Scripture is divinely inspired and is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work. By Scriptures he means the Old Testament; Timothy could not have known any other from childhood, nor could the Apostle commend any other. Consider what he testifies about them, both what is contained in them and what their uses are and what they are good for. In them is contained salvation [σωτηρία], and faith in Christ Jesus [διὰ πίστεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ]: the two things which Christ noted were to be found in the writings of Moses. For how could the holy letters have made each person wise, and Timothy among others, unto salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, unless they contained these things within themselves? And they contain them not merely, but powerfully: which are able [τὰ δυνάμενά] to make you wise [σοφίσαι]. Wisdom [σοφία] is the highest degree of knowledge. Therefore the Holy Scriptures are sufficiently rich in themselves for this purpose, to make a man wise in the highest matters, such as divine and theological matters: wise indeed unto salvation, and this through faith in Christ Jesus. The Ethiopic version reads: which can give you life through faith in Jesus Christ. Thus those Scriptures are as full of wisdom as they are of salvation and of faith, that is, of the teaching about eternal salvation to be obtained through faith in Christ. Timothy searched the Scriptures from his earliest years and became thoroughly versed in them, and Paul commended them. Therefore those Scriptures bear witness to Christ, and Timothy thought that he had eternal life in them. Now in listing the uses of Scripture, the Apostle, by enumeration, recounts all the things that bring salvation, to which Scripture contributes. If those matters over which we are disputing are removed from this list, then certainly it cannot be said so fully that Scripture is profitable [ὠφέλιμος] for all things, and for the man of God, whether you understand by this the minister of God and of his Word, or in general any upright person, to be equipped for every good work, which is what the Apostle here does. The Ethiopic version reads: that the man of God may be learned, a teacher, in every good work. These are the first passages of the argument, which show in general that the Old Testament contains promises of salvation and eternal life, and also of Christ and of the saving benefits in him, which apply to all and are necessary for each. Now let us descend to particulars and to the kinds of things recorded in the Scriptures, and first let us speak of the law, which is the first and most ancient part of divine doctrine.

units.la: Arg. secundum. Quod lex continet, id continet Scriptura Veteris Testamenti: legem enim hæc imprimis tradit & tractat: sed & lex continet promissionem vitæ æternæ: ergo. Vitæ promissionem continere, certum est: quæritur tantum, cujus, & an etiam æternæ? Quod nos asserimus. Lev. xviii. 5. homo qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis. Jezech. xx. 11[?]. 13. quæ qui facit homo, vivit per ea. Rom. x. 5. Moses enim scribit justitiam quæ est ex lege: quod qui fecerit ea homo, vivit in iis. Gal. iii. 11. 12. manifestum vero quod in lege nemo justificatur apud Deum: nam justus ex fide vivet. Lex autem non est ex fide, sed qui fecerit ea homo, vivet in iis.
units.tr: Second argument. What the law contains, the Scripture of the Old Testament contains, for the law is what it chiefly delivers and treats. But the law also contains the promise of eternal life; therefore the Scripture of the Old Testament contains it. That the law contains a promise of life is certain; the question is only whose life it is, and whether it is also eternal life. This is what we assert. Leviticus 18:5: the man who does them shall live by them. Ezekiel 20:11, 13: the man who does them lives by them. Romans 10:5: For Moses writes that the righteousness which is of the law: that the man who does them shall live by them. Galatians 3:11, 12: But that no one is justified before God by the law is evident, for the just shall live by faith. But the law is not of faith, but the man who does them shall live by them.

units.la: Quibus docetur, non vitam tantum promitti in lege aliquam, sed istam, quam alias ex fide habemus: utrobique enim præmium ponitur idem, ibi fidei, hic operum, vivet: diversus duntaxat eam obtinendi, hic & illic, modus. Eadem nempe, sed nunc ex gratia, est merces, æternæ vitæ: qua quia per legem excidimus, de novo beamur[?], ex gratia, in Christo. Rom. viii. 3. quod enim impossibile legi eo quod infirmabatur per carnem, Deus suum ipsius filium mittens effecit. 4. ut justificatio legis in nobis impleretur. non quod ad modum justificationis legalis, sed quod ad rem eandem, & adeptionem vitæ. Quæ ergo vita est ex fide in Christum, eadem in lege promissa fuit operibus. Quamvis autem hac via attingere eam nemo potuit, facta tamen ejus revelatio fuit & promissio hominibus: quâ dum destituebantur ex lege, & desperabant se ista ratione eam assequi posse, hoc ipsum illos docuit, pro eadem impetranda accurrere ad Christum: id est, dum vitam æternam quærebant in Mose, testantem eum de Christo audiverunt, quem pro vita suâ eo fervidius fuerunt amplexi.
units.tr: By these passages it is taught that the law promises not merely some life, but that same life which we have otherwise by faith; for in both places the same reward is set down, life: in the one case for faith, in the other for works. The only difference is the mode of obtaining it, here and there. Indeed the reward is the same, eternal life, though now it is by grace; and since we fell from it through the law, we are restored to blessedness anew by grace, in Christ. Romans 8:3, 4: For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us: not according to the manner of legal justification, but according to the thing itself and the attainment of life. Therefore the life which is from faith in Christ is the same life that was promised to works in the law. Although no one could reach it by that way, nevertheless its revelation and promise were made to men; and while they were deprived of it by the law, and despaired of being able to attain it by that means, this very thing taught them to run to Christ to obtain the same. That is, while they sought eternal life in Moses, they heard him bearing witness to Christ, whom they embraced all the more fervently as their life.

units.la: Hinc illa oppositio frequens apud Apostolum, inter vitam ex lege, & ex fide acquirendam, ut modorum ejusdem rei, vel ad eandem deducentium rem diversissimorum. Rom. x. 4. nam finis legis Christus.
units.tr: Hence comes that frequent opposition in the Apostle between life to be acquired from the law and life to be acquired from faith, as two most different modes of the same thing, or of things leading to the same end. Romans 10:4: For the end of the law is Christ.

units.la: Nequidquam tamen concedunt Adversarii, vitæ mentione in lege, designari æternam: quia vid. non exprimitur. At, neque etiam ea semper exprimitur, quando vita fidei, vel gratiæ refertur in Christo: sæpe enim vita in genere notatur, neque ideo dubium, æternam intelligi. Quod autem æterna etiam in lege intelligenda veniat, hinc constat, quod quum triplex vulgo nota fit vita, naturalis, quam & boni & mali vivunt, vivunt omnes, quâ homines, neque legis est beneficium, sed naturæ; prospera, & felix unicuique in suâ sorte, prout dici solet, quod non vivere, sed valere vita est; denique æterna & beata in cœlis: non potest prima vita intelligi, non sola secunda, sed omnis in universum: quemadmodum notione vitæ quæcumque felicitas ac salus, uti contrà mortis nomine miseriæ quævis denotari solent. Ergo & continuationem vitæ naturalis seu animalis, & prosperitatem ejus, & cœlestis quoque vitæ beatitatem significari promissione vitæ, contendimus. Nam I. æquum est, vitam intelligere maximâ suâ latitudine, & quidquid sub nomine vitæ venire solet ac potest. II. Et non potest terrena sola intelligi, sive naturalis, sive mundana tantum: quia & merces illa tenuior, quam ut sola exhauriat vim promissionis & liberalitatis divinæ, ad præstationem omnis obedientiæ, & augusto illo ac universali nomine vitæ designatæ; deinde cujus piissimi vel non fuerunt participes, qui pertæsi malorum omnium & vitæ suæ passim fuerunt, vel non tanti æstimarunt, neque etiam æstimare debuerunt, ut in eo summam fælicitatis aut benedictionis divinæ constituerent. Quando enim sanctissimi illi vitam duxerunt continuis malis pressam & refertam, quibus non sub mortem magis, quam in vitâ, carebant, quid censebimus ex ob-servatione legis & strictâ pietatis æmulatione ipsos consequutos felicitatem terrenam? sed vero omnia contraria. Deinde considera piissimos, ut sæpe contingit, vitâ adeo brevi mactatos, ut non potuerint hujus vitæ frui gaudiis aut felicitate, quæ sola tamen probitatis præmium à nostris constituitur: ubi tum mansit vita lege pro-missa, vel Dei promittentis veritas? & non potius ludificata fuit eorum spes? neque enim fieri potest, inquit etiam Schlichtingius, in Heb. xi. 35. Ut Deus optimus ac justissimus virtutem ac pietatem omnium maximam, quæ vitæ ipsius, qua nobis nihil est charius, impendio constet, nullo præmio remuneratam dimittat. Ista certe evidenter ostendunt, non posse omnium Dei promissionum Patribus factarum vim collocari in solis bonis terrenis, & temporali eorum usu. Denique, utcunque vixerint, plerosque enim miseram egisse vitam certum est, at sub vitæ finem etiam constanter exercuerunt virtutem, & qui ad extremum infelicis vitæ halitum Deum timebant, & observabant ejus præcepta, quem finem, quam mercedem istius postremæ obedientiæ expectare poterant, si tota vita rebus vanis transfigebatur? vel nulla omnino constantiæ fuit remu-neratio, vel post hanc vitam expectanda: atqui lex dicit vives, æque ad postremum virtutis actum, ac ad primum, imo magis quatenus moribundus in iis manere con-spicitur, ob quæ vitam Deus fuit pollicitus. Neque enim definit hoc, quamvis vitæ suprema tempore, verum esse quod Iesai. iii. 10. dicite justo, quod bonum ei כִּי־טוֹב[?] quod fructum operum suorum comedent. Ubi comedent morientes justi, nisi in vitâ alterâ? vel quâ aliâ ratione eos consolaberis, vel veram & universalem ostendes ubi-que esse promissionem? Quemadmodum contrà quod impiis dicitur, væ malo; nam retributio manuum fiet ei: non potest non accipi quoque de pœna finalis impœnitentiæ atque improbitatis. Istis ergo adigimur, ne putemus solam vitam animalem, vel terrenam lege promitti, sed omnem, eamque maxime, quæ optima, & sola cultores legis consolari potuit & beare. Non tunc tantum, sed semper verum illud Apo-stoli, si in hac tantum vita speraremus, atque addit in Christo, quanto magis extra Christum, essemus omnium hominum miserrimi. 1 Cor. xv. 19. Fac homines sanctissimos vivere extra Christum, extra spem vitæ melioris, & solis hujus vitæ rebus, iisque ca-ducis & miseris lætari; quæ obsecro, & quanta horum optimorum erit miseria? Quare si instemus vel in vitâ veterum fidelium satis miserâ, vel aliorum quoque breviori, vel pietate ad mortem & in eâ constanti, nec vitâ ulteriori hic remuneratâ, videmus vitam lege, ejus observatoribus, promissam non posse esse terrenam & anima-lem, vel aliquam ejus in mundo prosperitatem aut voluptatem. Ne dicam, vel ipsius naturæ & rationis instinctum homines in spem vitæ alterius protrudere; & vel apud Gentiles viguisse, & vigere adhuc passim melioris alicujus post hanc vitam condi-tionis opinionem quamvis vanam. Et tamen si oppositæ ad Israelitas, ipsi uti extor-res testamentorum promissionis, vixisse extra spem perhibentur, spem non habentes, Ephes. ii. 12. ex adverso Israelitæ dicuntur omnia illa habuisset testamenta promissionis & spem, dum de Gentilibus Apostolus loquitur, quod fuerint extranei à politiâ Israelis, & peregrini testamentorum promissionis, spem non habentes: ergo in politiâ Israelis, & apud hos saltem fuerunt fœdera & promissiones, quarum spe fuerint beati. beati, ac felices supra alios, non solis rebus terrenis.
units.tr: Nevertheless, the opponents are wrong to concede that eternal life is meant by the mention of life in the law, on the ground that it is not expressly named. Yet life is not always expressly named even where the life of faith or of grace is referred to in Christ. Life is often mentioned in a general sense, and no one doubts on that account that eternal life is understood. That eternal life is also to be understood in the law is shown by the following. Life is commonly divided into three kinds: first, natural life, which good and bad alike live, and which all men live, as men. This is not a benefit of the law but of nature. Second, prosperous life, a happy life for each person in his own lot, as the saying goes, that life is not living but faring well. Third, eternal and blessed life in heaven. The first kind cannot be meant to the exclusion of the second, nor the second to the exclusion of the rest. Rather, the whole of life in general is meant, just as by the word "life" every kind of happiness and well-being is denoted, and by the word "death" every kind of misery. So we contend that the promise of life signifies both the continuance of natural or animal life and its prosperity, and also the blessedness of heavenly life. For, first, it is only fair to understand "life" in its widest extent, and whatever is ordinarily and properly comprehended under the name of life. Second, the promise cannot be understood of earthly life alone, whether natural or merely worldly. That reward is too meagre to exhaust the force of God's promise and generosity, which was made to secure all obedience, and to be the grand and universal name of life. Moreover, the most pious men either did not share in such a reward, since they were weary of all evils and of their lives and were everywhere beset by them, or they did not value it so highly, nor ought they to have valued it, as to place in it the sum of happiness or of God's blessing. For when those most holy men led lives pressed down and filled with continual evils, from which they were free not so much in death as in life, what shall we think they obtained by keeping the law and by a strict emulation of piety: earthly happiness? Quite the contrary. Again, consider the pious men who, as often happens, were cut off in so short a life that they could not enjoy its joys or happiness, which yet our people set up as the sole reward of uprightness. Where then remained the life promised by the law, or the truth of God who promised it? Was not their hope rather mocked? For, as Schlichting also says on Heb. 11:35, it cannot be that the best and most just God should let go unrewarded the greatest virtue and piety, which costs the very life that is dearer to us than anything. These things plainly show that the force of all God's promises made to the fathers cannot be confined to earthly goods and their temporal use. Finally, however they lived, for it is certain that most of them lived a wretched life, yet at the end of life they steadfastly practised virtue. Those who, at the last breath of an unhappy life, feared God and kept his precepts: what reward could they expect for that final obedience, if their whole life had been spent on vain things? Either there was no reward at all for steadfastness, or it is to be expected after this life. But the law says, "you shall live," with equal force to the last act of virtue as to the first, and even more so, inasmuch as the dying man is seen to persist in those things for which God promised life. Nor does it cease to be true, even at the very end of life, what Isaiah 3:10 says: "Say to the righteous that it is well with him" [כִּי־טוֹב], "for they shall eat the fruit of their works." Where do dying righteous men eat, unless in another life? Or by what other reason will you console them, or show that the promise is true and universal everywhere? Just as, on the contrary, what is said to the wicked, "woe to the wicked, for the recompense of his hands shall be done to him," cannot but be taken also of the punishment of final impenitence and wickedness. We are therefore compelled by these things not to think that the law promises only animal or earthly life, but all life, and that most of all which is best, and which alone could comfort and make blessed the followers of the law. Not only then, but always, is that saying of the Apostle true: "If in this life only we have hope," and he adds "in Christ," how much more, outside Christ, "we would be of all men the most miserable," 1 Cor. 15:19. Suppose the most holy men lived outside Christ, outside the hope of a better life, and rejoiced only in the things of this life, and those fragile and wretched things. Please, what and how great would be the misery of these best of men! Therefore, if we press the point, whether by the life of the old faithful, which was indeed quite wretched, or by that of others, shorter still, or by piety even unto death and steadfast in it, with no further life rewarded here, we see that the life promised by the law to its observers cannot be earthly and animal, or any prosperity or pleasure of it in the world. Not to mention that the very instinct of nature and reason drives men into the hope of another life, and that among the Gentiles the opinion of some better condition after this life, however vain, has flourished and still flourishes everywhere. And yet, if it is said that the Israelites were without hope, as aliens from the covenants of promise, like the Gentiles opposed to them, "having no hope" (Eph. 2:12), on the other hand the Israelites are said to have had all those covenants of promise and hope, since the Apostole speaks of the Gentiles, that they "were aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope." Therefore, in the commonwealth of Israel, and among these at least, there were covenants and promises, in the hope of which they were blessed and happier than others, not in earthly things alone.

units.la: Exc. Attamen locis, quibus promissiones legis exponuntur, inter omnes nullus loquitur de vitâ æternâ. Quemadmodum Levit. xxvi. 3.4. & Deut. xxvii.2. &c.
units.tr: Objection: Yet in the passages where the promises of the law are set out, none of them speaks of eternal life, as in Lev. 26:3-4, Deut. 27:2, etc.

units.la: Resp. Est argumentum negativum, quod non concludit: non commemoratur ibi promissio vitæ æternæ, ergo legem observantibus non fuit promissa? vel, catalogus ibi texitur promissionum & rerum aliquot corporalium, ergo spirituales, vel cœlestes populo, & piis nullæ tum fuerunt factæ? sæpe carnalia beneficia carnali admodum populo offeruntur & exponuntur, at non semper, non ubique ea sola. II.
units.tr: Answer: This is a negative argument, and it does not conclude. Is it therefore not promised to those who keep the law, because the promise of eternal life is not recorded there? Or, because a list of promises and some bodily goods is woven together there, are no spiritual or heavenly ones made to the people and the pious at that time? Carnal benefits are often offered and set forth to a very carnal people, but not always, and not everywhere only these.

units.la: Nonnunquam aut cum, aut sub terrenarum rerum involucro spiritualia etiam significantur, & , quod præsertim apud Prophetas est, panduntur sub iis cœlestia piis atque fidelibus præmia. III. Quando vita simpliciter & absolute promittitur, intelligitur omnis, etiam futura & cœlestis. Quemadmodum Adversarii in commination mortis, quę peccato fit, etiam intelligunt mortem æternam, post hanc corporalem; sic quid ni per vitam, in divinâ promissione, accipiamus quoque æternam? Vel, proferant ex lege locum, ubi mors æterna peccati constituitur pœna, neque inter pœnas, quando recensentur, vel Genes. iii. vel Levit. xxvi. vel Deut. xxvii. mors æterna apparet: & hanc tamen peccati pœnam Adversarii etiam faciunt, nec male: at nec in nobis culpent ergo, quod per vitam in divinis verbis & promissionibus intelligamus quoque æternam, quamvis totidem verbis promissionum catalogo non exprimatur. IV. Quod supra omnem exceptionem est, Christus in tractandâ legis promissione, & vitâ in ea expressâ, significavit pro eodem habendam esse promissionem vitæ, & vitæ æternæ. Matth. xix. 16. 17. ubi Discipulus quærit: Magister bone quid boni faciam ut habeam vitam æternam? hic quæstionem instituit de vitâ æternâ: & Christus ei respondet, si vis intrare in vitam, serva mandata, &c. tantundem est, sive Christus dicat vitam, sive ille vitam æternam: nam non alia intelligitur in observatione præceptorum Dei. Synonyma vel æquipollentia hoc in negotio sunt, vita, & vita æterna. Ille signanter dicit, vitam æternam: Christus satis habet dixisse, vitam, in quæstione de lege, & de legis observatione. Ergo quando lex vitam promittit, non aliter aut acceptum hoc fuit, aut etiam accipi debuit, quam de vitâ æternâ. Tum non obscurum idem, sed clarum apertumque satis fuisse, ex illius interrogatione, & responso Christi nemo est qui non perspiciat. Inde etiam dicitur simpliciter Rom. vii. 10. præceptum ad vitam. Postremo & Targum in Levit. xviii. 5. habet, quæ faciens homo vivet in eis [?]בחיי עלמא [?] vita æterna. Et Targum Jonathanis, quæ si fecerit homo [illegible, ~6 letters] , & portio ejus cum justis. videlicet cum justis in vita illa sæculi, seu æterna. Similiter legit Targum, in Jezech. xx. 2. Versio Arabica, quoniam retributio ejus qui operabitur illa, est ut vivat vitam æternam.
units.tr: Sometimes spiritual things are also signified either together with earthly things or under their covering, and, what is especially found among the Prophets, heavenly rewards are unfolded under them for the pious and faithful. Third: when life is promised simply and absolutely, all life is understood, including future and heavenly life. Just as our opponents, in the threat of death that comes upon sin, also understand eternal death after this bodily death, why should we not likewise understand eternal life by "life" in the divine promise? Or let them produce from the law a passage where eternal death is set as the penalty of sin, and which does not appear among the penalties when they are listed, whether in Gen. 3, Lev. 26 or Deut. 27. Yet our opponents also make this eternal death a penalty of sin, and not wrongly. So let them not blame us that by "life" in the divine words and promises we understand eternal life too, even though it is not expressed in so many words in the catalogue of promises. Fourth, and beyond all exception: Christ, in treating the promise of the law and the life expressed in it, showed that the promise of life and of eternal life are to be held as the same. Matt. 19:16-17: where the disciple asks, "Good Master, what good thing shall I do that I may have eternal life?" he is inquiring about eternal life, and Christ answers him, "If you want to enter into life, keep the commandments," etc. It makes no difference whether Christ says "life" or the other says "eternal life," for in the keeping of God's precepts no other life is understood. In this matter "life" and "eternal life" are synonyms or equivalent. The one expressly says eternal life; Christ is content to have said "life," in a question about the law and about keeping the law. Therefore, when the law promises life, this was not and ought not to be received otherwise than as eternal life. That this was not obscure but quite clear and open is evident to anyone who considers the question and Christ's answer. Hence also Rom. 7:10 simply speaks of "the commandment unto life." Lastly, the Targum on Lev. 18:5 has "which a man doing them shall live in them," bechayei alma, "eternal life." And the Targum of Jonathan, "which if a man shall have done," and "his portion with the righteous," namely with the righteous in that life of the age, or eternal life. The Targum reads similarly on Ezek. 20:2 (Ezek. 20:11?). The Arabic version: "for the reward of him who shall do them is that he shall live eternal life."

units.la: Arg. Tertium peto, ex generalitate promissionis divinæ omnigeni boni, Patribus factæ in Testamento Veteri: sub quâ etiam promissio vitæ æternæ comprehensa & intelligenda fuit. Quemadmodum quando Abrahamo Deus promisit, se fore ei mercedem valde magnam, Genes. xv. 1. vel Deum omnisufficientem, [?]שדי[?], Genes. xvii. 1. Deum ejus, feminisque ejus fœdere æterno. verf. 7. & quæ aliæ promissiones generaliter conceptę, vel generaliter Dei bonitatem & beneficentiam, vel bona omnis generis indifferenter proponebant. Neque aliunde Apostolus habuit, quod dixit I Tim. iv. 8. pietatem habere promissionem vitæ hujus & futuræ. Non indicare poteris promissionem istam in Testamento Veteri: & tamen istam in Novo Testamento nunc adfert Apostolus, tamquam certam fatis, & universaliter notam. Indicat aliquid æternæ veritatis quod pietatis sit, non per temporis aliam & aliam circumstantiam, sed propter ipsam: idem quod Hebræi solent efferre per [illegible, ~3 letters] & [illegible, ~3 letters], ζωῆς τῆς νῦν, τῇ τῆς μελλούσης [?]. Imo, ut videant Adversarii, ipsas verborum literas in hoc urgendas non esse, nullibi ostendent in terminis illam à Deo pietati in Scripturis promissionem factam esse, quam Apostolus hic adeo laudat & commendat. Experiantur & dent operam inquirendi per Scripturam, nihil proferent, quod non in rem nostram futurum sit. An quando Deus ea quæ diximus & istorum similia promisit Abrahamo, & suis, non promisit bona quoque terrena? affirmabis, quinimo dices, sola ea: atqui illa iis non exprimuntur: & quo jure tibi licet generalitatem promissionum restringere ad aliquam, & inferiorem quidem bonorum sortem; nobis non licebit, pro latitudine verborum divinorum, & Dei liberalitate, extendere ad bona quævis alia, & ad cœlestia quoque ac æterna? Episcopius bene, Instit. Theologic. lib. II. cap. VI., hæc promissio, loquitur de Genes. xv. 1. sic generatim concepta ad quemlibet Dei favorem extendi potest: quo videlicet Deus Abrahamum vel protecturus erat [?] ab omni malo temporali, scuti instar, ut locupletaturus mercede multa, id est, bonis omnibus ad vitam hanc bene, commode, felicitérque transigendam pertinentibus: vel qui eum conservaturus, & immunem præstiturus erat ab æterna morte, vitaque ipsa æterna donaturus; vel denique, utroque modo eum beaturus erat. Generalia enim ejusmodi pronunciata extendi possunt in infinitum usque; saltem quousque vis & verborum ipsorum proprietas extendi potest. Quis verò credat, quum vel ipso naturæ rationalis ductu scire potuerint pii animas suas non mori cum corporibus, sed esse immortales, atque ex indiciis saltem multis, & conjecturis, ut Adversariis visum loqui, colligere meliorem ab hac vitam superesse, quod has adeo amplas Dei promissiones, non etiam eo sciverint applicare, & hinc de illius certitudine instrui ac confirmari? præsertim sub vitæ finem, & instantis mortis horam, ubi nullo vitæ hujus desiderio ultra tangi poterant, & quemadmodum Schlichtingius loquitur, in Commentario ad Hebr. pag. 523. hujus etiam terrenæ felicitatis, vergente jam præsertim ætate, vanitatem facile perspicere dabatur.
units.tr: Arg. My third argument is drawn from the generality of God's promise, made to the Fathers in the Old Testament, of every kind of good. Under this promise the promise of eternal life was also included and must be understood to be included. When God promised Abraham that he would be his very great reward (Gen. 15:1), or when God is called All-sufficient (Gen. 17:1), or when he promised to be God to him and to his seed after him in an everlasting covenant (v. 7), and in the other promises conceived in general terms, these either set out God's goodness and beneficence in general, or proposed good things of every kind without distinction. The Apostle had no other source for his words in 1 Tim. 4:8, that godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. You will not be able to show that this promise is found in the Old Testament, and yet the Apostle now brings it forward in the New Testament as something certain and generally known. It signifies an eternal truth belonging to godliness, not one tied to this or that circumstance of time, but to godliness itself. This is what the Hebrews commonly express by the phrases [...] and [...], of the life that now is and of that which is to come [ζωῆς τῆς νῦν, τῆς τῆς μελλούσης]. Indeed, so that our opponents may see that the bare letter of the words is not to be pressed in this matter, they will never show that the promise which the Apostle here so highly praises and commends was made to the godly in express terms in the Scriptures. Let them try, and let them take the trouble to search the Scriptures; they will produce nothing that will not serve our purpose. When God promised Abraham and his people the things we have mentioned, and others like them, did he not also promise earthly goods? You will affirm it; nay, you will say that these alone were promised. But those things are not named in these words. By what right may you restrict the generality of the promises to one particular, and indeed lesser, portion of good things, while we may not, in view of the breadth of God's words and God's liberality, extend them to any other good things, and to heavenly and eternal ones too? Episcopius rightly says, in Institutiones Theologicae, book 2, chapter 6: This promise, spoken of Genesis 15:1, conceived in such general terms, can be extended to any favour of God whatever: whereby God would either protect Abraham from every temporal evil, as a shield, or enrich him with much reward, that is, with all the goods that pertain to living this life well, conveniently and happily; or he would keep him and make him free from eternal death, and give him eternal life itself; or, in short, he would make him blessed in both ways. For general statements of this kind can be extended without limit, at least as far as the force and proper meaning of the words themselves can be extended. But who would believe that, when the godly could know from the light of reason alone that their souls do not die with their bodies but are immortal, and could gather from at least many signs and conjectures (as our opponents like to say) that a better life remains after this one, they did not also apply these so ample promises of God to that life, and so be taught and confirmed about its certainty from them? This is especially so at the end of life, at the hour of impending death, when they could no longer be moved by any desire for this life; and, as Schlichting says in his commentary on Hebrews, p. 523, the vanity of this earthly happiness could easily be seen, especially as age was already advancing.

units.la: Jam & Christus illa sic explicat, atque ad vitam ulteriorem trahit, & quidem mortuorum resurrectionem, apud adversarios, & Sadducæos, illius hostes, probandam. Ergo illis verbis hoc comprehensum, & significatum fuit: alioqui perperam Christus fuisset argumentatus, Matth. xxii. 31. 32. 33. Verum de resurrectione mortuorum nunquid legistis dictum vobis à Deo, inquiente, ego sum Deus Abrahami, & Deus Isaaci, & Deus Iacobi? Deus non est Deus mortuorum, sed viventium. Atque audientes turbæ perculsæ fuerunt de ejus doctrina. Apud Lucam significanter admodum, cap. xx. 36. quod autem mortui resurgunt, & Moses indicavit in rubo, quando Deum dicit Deum Abrahami, & Deum Isaaci, & Deum Iacobi. Satisfecit autem illa argumentatione suâ auditoribus tum suis Christus. videamus, an etiam hominibus nostris. Judæi quidem acquiescere potuerunt, modo idem possint, qui se Christianos etiam appellant, nostri homines Sociniani. Volkelius, lib. iii. cap. xi. pag. 62.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ also explains these words in this way and draws them to a further life, and indeed to the resurrection of the dead, which he sought to prove against the Sadducees, the enemies of that doctrine. So this was included and meant in those words; otherwise Christ would have argued wrongly, Matt. 22:31-33: But as touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. And when the crowds heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. In Luke 20:36, very significantly, and that the dead are raised, even Moses shewed at the bush, when he calleth the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Christ indeed satisfied his hearers of that day with this argument. Let us see whether he also satisfies our people. The Jews could indeed acquiesce, provided that those also who call themselves Christians, our own Socinians, can do so. Volkelius, book 3, chapter 11, p. 62.

units.la: Atqui animadvertendum est, nos in hac disputatione nostra, non ea rei istius testimonia Resp. I. Id propositum Christo, & N. T. Scriptoribus fuisse, ut ex V. T. proferre requirere, quæ tanta sint obscuritate involuta, rent argumenta minus trita, & eadem nihil minus, quam sempiternæ vitæ promissio operâ veritatem inde confirmarent, atque locos sum continere videantur, nec de ea intelligi locos difficiliores enodarent, omnibus, in queant, nisi eorum sensus divinitus nobis ape-riatur: sed quae apertis luculentissimisque verbis, ut in nova scriptura fieri videbimus, hoc ob-servatum. Ut inde non sequatur, haud Dei beneficium nobis polliceantur. Ex quorum alia etiam ejusdem rei in Scripturis exsta-numero hoc, quo de agimus, nequaquam esse re-argumenta, sed ita certam diffusamque hinc patet, quod antequam Christus illud expli-caret, nemo unquam extitit, qui vel suspicari que nos minus putemus ad eam facere, aut auderet, tale quid illo comprehendi. Neque enim adhiberi in disputatione posse.
units.tr: But it must be noted that in this dispute of ours we are not asking for testimonies of this matter [Reply 1.] It was not the purpose of Christ and the New Testament writers to bring forward from the Old Testament arguments that are less worn, or to prove this matter by a promise of eternal life, which is wrapped in such obscurity that it seems to contain nothing of the kind, and whose more difficult passages could not be unfolded by anyone unless their sense were revealed to us by God. Rather, they noted what is made plain in clear and most luminous words, as we shall see in the New Scripture. It does not follow from this that the Scriptures do not promise us this benefit of God. Nor is it clear that the things we are discussing are, in the Scriptures, the subject of a less certain and more diffuse argument. Indeed, it is plain that, before Christ explained that passage, no one ever arose who even suspected, or dared to say, that anything of the kind was contained in it, or that it could be used in disputation. For we do not think it likely that the Pharisees, most skilled in the divine Law, who often, as it seems, disputed sharply with the Sadducees about the resurrection of the dead, would have passed over this passage in silence, if they had noticed that testimony to the matter itself was contained in it.

units.la: II. Istud credibile est, Pharisaeos Legis divinae peritissimos, saepenumero, ut videtur, cum Sadducaeis de mortuorum resurrectione, acerrimeque contendentes, hunc locum silentio praeteriturosfuisse, si rei ipsius testimonium eo contineri animadvertissent. Quid, quod Matthaeus Christum hoc suo responso Sadducaeorum os obturasse apertissime testificatur? ut facile appareat, hanc loci illius explicationem novam plane & inauditam fuisse, & sic verissime a nobis dici, Christum primum extitisse, qui vitae aeternae mysterium nobis explicaverit. Adde, quod in his verbis nulla sit generalis futurae vitae promissio; sed specialis tantum, ad Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Iacobum nominatim spectans.
units.tr: II. It is credible that the Pharisees, most skilled in the divine Law, who often, as it seems, disputed sharply with the Sadducees about the resurrection of the dead, would have passed over this passage in silence, if they had noticed that testimony to the matter itself was contained in it. What of the fact that Matthew most plainly testifies that Christ, by this reply of his, stopped the mouths of the Sadducees? From this it easily appears that this explanation of that passage was entirely new and unheard of, and so we rightly say that Christ was the first to explain to us the mystery of eternal life. Add that in these words there is no general promise of future life, but only a particular one, referring by name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

units.la: III. Dicere, nihil minus, quam sempiternae vitae promissum continere verba illa Dei, ex quibus Christus disputat, est ejus argumentum & vim prorsus destruere: & fac illud Sadducaeos dicere, ut certe si verum dicere aeque possint ac hi, nonne sic egregie prostituitur Christus pugnans apud Adversarios argumento ex re, quae nihil minus dicit, quam quod inde conclusum creditumque cupit?
units.tr: III. To say that the words of God from which Christ argues contain nothing less than a promise of eternal life is to destroy his argument and its force altogether. Suppose the Sadducees had said this, as they certainly could have, if they had been able to speak the truth as well as these people do. Would not Christ then be shamefully exposed, arguing against his opponents from a passage that says nothing less than what he wants to conclude and believe from it?

units.la: IV. Si is verborum eorum sensus divinitus eruitur, ergo verus est, & divinitus quoque a divinis olim Scriptoribus & Prophetis ostendi potuit, quid ni & ostensus fuerit, quibus procul dubio verborum, quae tradiderunt & scripserunt, sensus constitit.
units.tr: IV. If the sense of those words is drawn out divinely, then it is true, and it could also have been shown divinely by the divine writers and prophets of old. Why should it not also have been shown, since without doubt the sense of the words they handed down and wrote was fixed.

units.la: v. An nemo unquam praeter, vel ante Christum, illorum verborum sensum noverit, nunquam probabunt Adversarii, neque temere id dicentibus nos credemus unquam: praesertim quia istam verborum illorum vim esse diffiteri potest nemo. Et num Pharisaei non aliquando isto loco, adversus Sadducaeos usi fuerint, quis dicet? Tum etiamsi nunquam id fecerint, parum ad rem facit. Quum quid illi animadverterint, vel non, haud multum nos torqueat, qui rerum autoritate stamus & pondere, non hominum, non Pharisaeorum, in exponendis Scripturis, acumine aut judicio. Nova fuerit, & inaudita istis hominibus, vel Pharisaeis, vel Sadducaeis, Christi expositio, modo vera & genuina. Neque enim testimonium Christus ab homine recipit, nedum ab inimico.
units.tr: v. Our opponents will never prove that no one, apart from Christ or before him, knew the sense of those words, and we will never rashly believe those who say so. Especially since no one can deny that those words have this force. And will anyone say that the Pharisees never at any time used this passage against the Sadducees? Even if they never did so, it makes little difference. Whether they noticed it or not should not much trouble us, who stand on the authority and weight of the matter, not on the men, nor on the keenness or judgement of the Pharisees in expounding the Scriptures. Christ's exposition may have been new and unheard of to those men, whether Pharisees or Sadducees, provided it is true and genuine. For Christ does not receive testimony from a man, much less from an enemy.

units.la: VI. Quod vero Volkelius tantopere ingeminat de argumento vel conclusione Christi, a nullo praeterea observata, non a Judaeis, Pharisaeis, Sadducaeorum adversariis, praeterquam quod momenti nullius sit, confutat in faciem Judaeus, ex Pharisaeorum gente, Menasse Ben-Israel, in libris de Resurrectione mortuorum, ubi non modo variis, quae Volkelius desiderat, & adferri posse negat, tum ex Mose, tum Prophe-
units.tr: VI. As for Volkelius's constant repetition of the argument or conclusion of Christ, which no one else has noticed, neither the Jews nor the Pharisees nor the Sadducees' adversaries, it is refuted to his face, quite apart from its being of no weight, by the Jew Menasseh Ben-Israel, of the Pharisaic people, in his book on the resurrection of the dead. There he not only denies that the various things Volkelius looks for can be brought forward, both from Moses and from the Prophe-

units.la: Prophetis, probat testimoniis & resurrectionem mortuorum, & vitam æternam, sed quoque, dissimulato quamvis, quod etiam ad rem nostram facit, Christi & nomine, & autoritate, idem tamen inter alia argumentum vidit atque attulit, lib. 1. cap. x. his verbis, cum Mosi primum appareret Dominus dixisse legitur: Ego sum Deus Patrum tuorum, Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci, Deus Iacobi, Exod. 3. 6. Atqui Deus non est Deus mortuorum, quia mortui non sunt: sed viventium, quia vivi exijstunt. Itaque Patriarchæ etiam- num, respectu animæ vivere, ex eo recte infertur.
units.tr: Prophets, he proves by testimonies both the resurrection of the dead and eternal life. But he also, though he conceals it, which bears on our matter too, saw and brought forward the argument of Christ, in his name and authority, among other things, in book 1, chapter 10, in these words: When the Lord first appeared to Moses, it is read that he said: I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, Exod. 3. 6. But God is not the God of the dead, because the dead do not exist; he is the God of the living, because they exist alive. Therefore it is rightly inferred from this that the patriarchs still live, with respect to the soul.

units.la: Eant nunc Sociniani, & vel Christo, ejusque doctrinæ gloriam invideant, quam ei, velint nolint, ne Iudæi quidem negant, vel veritatem illam, quam Iudæi in Scri- pturis vident, diffiteri pergant, & ad Pharisæos, Scripturæ interpretes, & Christiac fidei nostræ, præ ipsis, vindices ultra provocent. Sed de his etiam copiosius, in fine disputationis, adversus Smalcium, dicemus. Omitto, quod idem Menasse, cap. 1. etiam inde argumentatur, quod Exod. 6. 3. Deus inquit, apparui Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Iacobo, in Deo omnipotente, sed nomen meum A. non feci illis notum: nihilominus tamen interpositio fœdere promisi, me daturum illis terram Canaan, in qua peregrini fuerunt. Quia dicit Deus, se illis daturum terram illam, qui nunc omnino erant mortui, atque vivebant tamen, & erant resuscitandi: Probatio luculenta hæc est, inquit, quia Dominus Deus dicit Mosi se iurasse futurum ut stabiliret pactum suum cum Patriarchis initum, dando terram promissam possidendam Patriarcharum filiis, sed dando eam ipsis Patriarchis: uti ex 17. Cap. Genes. videre est, ubi Deus cum Abrahamo loquens, ait, dabo tibi, & semini tuo post te, terram peregrinationis tuæ. Atqui constat Abrahamum, & reliquos Patriarchas eam terram non possedisse: necesse ergo est, ut resuscitentur, quo bonis promissis fruantur: alioquin promissa Dei irrita & falsa forent. Hinc itaque non tantum animæ immortalitas probatur; sed etiam essentiale fundamentum legis, Resurrectio scilicet mortuorum. Iterum, ex Deut. 11. dicit sæpius adversus id genus hominum pugnasse R. Gamalielem: Nam multiplicabuntur dies nostri, & filiorum supra terram, quam iurasit dominus patribus se daturum illis. Ad hæc ait, לתת לחם לא נאמר אלא לכם מכאן לתהית המתים מן התורה (non dicit vobis, sed illis; constat itaque ex lege fore resurrectionem mortuorum.) Eodem argumento uti etiam solet R. Simeon, quemadmodum alias a nobis dictum est. Quo denique confutatur ultimum, quod Volkelius addit, in verbis illis Dei non contineri generalem futuræ vitæ promissionem, sed speciale tantum ad Abrahamum, Isaacum, & Iacobum nominatim spectantem: quia & hæc ipsa sua vi ad eorum posteros quoque extendi debent, & expresse Deus se filiorum eorum Deum testatus sæpe fuit, æque ac parentum & maiorum.
units.tr: Let the Socinians now go and grudge Christ and his doctrine the glory which, whether they like it or not, even the Jews do not deny him. Or let them keep denying that truth which the Jews see in the Scriptures, and appeal beyond them to the Pharisees, the interpreters of Scripture, and to the defenders of our Christian faith before them. But we shall speak of these things more fully at the end of the disputation, against Smalcius. I pass over the fact that the same Menasseh, in chapter 1, also argues from Exod. 6. 3, where God says: I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty, but I did not make my name A. known to them; nevertheless I promised them, by an oath-bound covenant, that I would give them the land of Canaan, in which they were strangers. Since God says that he would give that land to those who were then wholly dead, yet were living and were to be raised: This proof is clear, he says, because the Lord God tells Moses that he swore he would establish his covenant made with the patriarchs, by giving the promised land to be possessed by the sons of the patriarchs, but by giving it to the patriarchs themselves. As may be seen from Genesis 17, where God, speaking with Abraham, says: I will give to you and to your seed after you the land of your sojourning. But it is certain that Abraham and the other patriarchs did not possess that land. It is necessary, therefore, that they be raised, so that they may enjoy the good promises; otherwise the promises of God would be vain and false. Hence not only the immortality of the soul is proved, but also the essential foundation of the law, namely the resurrection of the dead. Again, from Deut. 11 he says that Rabban Gamaliel often fought against this kind of men: For our days will be multiplied, and those of our sons upon the land which the Lord swore he would give to the fathers. To this he adds: it does not say "to you" but "to them"; it is clear therefore from the law that there will be a resurrection of the dead [לתת לחם לא נאמר אלא לכם מכאן לתחית המתים מן התורה]. R. Simeon also is accustomed to use the same argument, as we have said elsewhere. Finally, the last point which Volkelius adds is refuted by this. He claims that those words of God contain no general promise of future life, but only a special one looking to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob by name. But these very words, by their own force, ought to be extended also to their posterity, and God often testified expressly that he was the God of their sons just as of their parents and ancestors.

units.la: Quando testatur, se aliquorum Deum esse, & pro subiecta materia non restringitur vel applicatur, tum pro latitudine sua debet accipi omnimode & ubique Deum se suis ostendere hoc quod est: & non potest non extendi quousque homo est, & quacunque sui parte, in æternum. Non, opinor, dubitarunt Patres, de animarum suarum immortalitate, quare non de perpetua sui existentia: unde nec ambigere potuerunt, se Deo semper & ubique egere. Iam non potuit non huc promissionis illius generalis fieri applicatio, ut crederent se in omnem æternitatem & immortaliter Deum experturos suum, uti promiserat, in morte, atque post eam. Magnam Patrum infscitiam necesse habebis arguere, huius argumenti ut evadas vim, & vel negare, ipsos sciviisse animarum suarum immortalitatem, vel non in ista animarum vita propitio fruituros Deo: quorum tamen illud, vel sola natura duce; & hoc tum ex sensu dividivinæ promissionis, & expertæ semper benignitatis, tum denique fidei suæ, habere potuerunt. Quare quæso desiissent credere, Deo se benigne potituros & in morte, & post eam, quandoquidem tum vel maxime in solum Deum respicere, & fidere nos vel sensus communis jubet & præsens necessitas? Neque Deus vim promissionis illius usquam restrinxit ad mortem, aut cavit, ne ultra se eo consolarentur pii. Quam-obrem ergo illam sibi cum morte amputassent, qui & tum, & semper ejus gustu & vi præsertim pasci se prorsus ac vivere, quod Deum scirent esse suum, experiebantur? An immortaliter bene vivet anima sine Deo, & sancta ac beata anima absque sensu & fruitione favoris ejus? vel nescit forte anima illa seipsam, ac suum Deum, vel in limbo aliquo delitescere debuit omnium rerum ignorans & expers. Deniq;in Apocalypsi, cap.xxi.3.4. exponitur vis phrasis illius, qua dicit Deus se esse suorum Deum, & ad vitam æternam applicatur: & ipsi erunt populus ejus, & ipse Deus cum iis erit, ipsorum Deus. Et absterget omnes lachrymas ab oculis ipsorum, & mors non erit amplius. Plenitudo ergo locutionis illius est, ut quoque vitam comprehendat æternam. & Hebr. xi.16. jam vero meliorem desiderant, id est, cœlestem: ideoque Deum illorum non pudet, vocari ipsorum Deum; paraverat enim iis civitatem. Hæc ratio istius illic denominationis & vis, ad vitam æternam se extendens, ejus promissionem, & dationem. Atque bene hac de re Episcopius, Instit. Theol. lib. iii. sect. iv. cap. i. generalia promissa sunt, inquit, ego ero Deus tuus, vel ego sum Deus tuus; ego ero merces tua multa valde: ego benedicam vobis, &c. hisce enim promissis sic generatim conceptis atque enunciatis contineri posse quælibet bona, etiam ea quæ non nisi post mortem obveniunt, quis dubitet? Deum enim velle Deum alicujus esse, quid aliud est quam Deum velle divina benevolentia aliquem completi? Divina autem benevolentia, sive quæ Deo digna est, quid est aliud quam benevolentia summa, & qua major ulteriorque dari non potest: proinde benevolentia duratione longissima, id est, æterna; effectu potentissima, proinde a morte atque interitu liberans? Certe his verbis utrumque illud non tantum contineri posse, sed etiam contentum fuisse, ex Apostolicis scriptis manifestum est,
units.tr: When he testifies that he is the God of some, and this is not restricted or applied by the subject matter, then in its breadth it must be understood that God shows himself to his own in every way and everywhere as what he is. It cannot but extend as far as the person extends, in every part of him, forever. I suppose the Fathers did not doubt the immortality of their souls, and so could not doubt their perpetual existence; whence they also could not hesitate that they always and everywhere need God. Now the application of that general promise could not but be made to this: that they would believe they would experience their God in all eternity and immortally, as he had promised, in death and after it. You would have to argue a great ignorance in the Fathers in order to escape the force of this argument, and either deny that they knew the immortality of their souls, or deny that they would enjoy the favour of God in that life of the soul. The former they could have from nature alone as their guide; the latter both from the sense of the divine promise and of the goodness always experienced, and finally from their faith. Why, I ask, would they have ceased to believe that they would enjoy God's kindness both in death and after it, since common sense and present necessity bid us especially then to look to God alone and trust him? Nor has God anywhere restricted the force of that promise to death, nor forbidden that the pious console themselves beyond it. Why then would they have cut it off with death, when both then and always they were experiencing that they fed on its taste and power, and so fully lived, because they knew God to be theirs? Or can a soul live well immortally without God, and a holy and blessed soul without feeling and enjoying his favour? Either that soul does not know itself or its God, or it must have lurked in some limbo, ignorant of all things and without any share in them. Finally, in Revelation 21:3-4 the force of that phrase is explained, by which God says he is the God of his people, and it is applied to eternal life: And they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, their God. And he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more. The fullness, therefore, of that expression is that it embraces eternal life too. And Hebrews 11:16: But now they desire a better, that is, a heavenly one; therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city. This is the reason and force of that denomination there, extending to eternal life, both its promise and its gift. Episcopius treats this well in his Institutes of Theology, book 3, section 4, chapter 1: The promises are general, he says, I will be your God, or I am your God; I will be your very great reward; I will bless you, etc. Who would doubt that any goods can be contained in promises so generally conceived and stated, even those which come only after death? For God to will to be someone's God, what else is it than for God to will that someone be completed by divine benevolence? But divine benevolence, or that which is worthy of God, what else is it than the highest benevolence, beyond which no greater or further can be given? Therefore a benevolence of the longest duration, that is eternal, and of the greatest power in its effect, and therefore freeing from death and perishing? Certainly, from the apostolic writings it is clear that both not only could be contained in these words, but were also contained in them.

units.la: Argumentum quartum. Quibus factæ promissiones de Christo Salvatore, iisdem & factæ promissiones rerum salutarium, atque æternarum: sed Patribus in V. T. sunt factæ promissiones de Christo: ergo. Major sua luce est evidens, quia Christus nihil aliud est, quam salvator, & vitæ æternæ verus dator: non enim simpliciter, Christum aliquem venturum, dictum fuit, sed istum, qui salvaret & redimeret a peccatis suos. Hoc & prædictum, & præfiguratum olim multis modis fuit. Neque puto quempiam negaturum Minorem.
units.tr: Fourth argument. To those to whom promises were made concerning Christ the Saviour, to the same were also made promises of saving and eternal things. But promises concerning Christ were made to the fathers in the Old Testament; therefore. The major premise is evident in its own light, because Christ is nothing other than the Saviour and the true giver of eternal life. For it was not simply said that some Christ would come, but that one who would save and redeem his people from their sins. This was both foretold and foreshadowed in many ways of old. Nor do I think anyone will deny the minor premise.

units.la: At excipiunt, illa quidem olim prædicta fuisse, sed ad illos, quibus dicta, non pertinebant, sed ad fideles duntaxat sub N. T. viventes: quemadmodum promissiones de vocatione gentium, nec gentilibus, nec Israelitis aliquid conferebant ante tempora Christi, & Apostolorum: ut sic etiam promissiones reliquæ de Christo, ejusque beneficiis, spectarint ad sola N. T. tempora, non Veteris.
units.tr: But they object that those things were indeed foretold long ago, but that they did not pertain to those to whom they were spoken, and belonged only to the faithful living under the New Testament. Just as the promises about the calling of the Gentiles brought nothing to either Gentiles or Israelites before the time of Christ and the Apostles, so the remaining promises about Christ and his benefits, they say, pertained only to New Testament times and not to the Old.

units.la: Resp. Quasi vero V. T. pii aut prædicere ista potuerint, aut audire, & non ad se quoque applicare? Estne probabile, fieri potuisse, aut debuisse, quod, scientes suas easdem esse necessitates, pro quibus curandis nunciabatur Christus, non voluerint quoque sibi eandem obvenire & contingere curationem ac salutem? Utique se agnoverunt esse peccatores, & hinc misere reos, neque pro meritis exspectare quidpiam posse præter maledictionem: jam vero prædicabatur Christus maledictionem ablaturus, & commutaturus eam benedictione omni spirituali, & hoc futurum certe non ignorabant, neque dissidebant: credebant ergo Christum venturum, & id factu-rum aliquando. Haec vero est fides illa vera in venturum, uti nostra nunc est in eum qui venit. Sic ergo concionabantur Christum, uti Ioannes populo, dicens, ut crederent in eum qui post ipsum venturus erat; hoc est, in Christum Iesum. Act. xix. 4. Aliud est, si vel prohibiti fuissent unquam fidem in Christum sibi annunciatum conjicere, ut in suum quoque bonum; vel res ipsa arguisset ad ipsos nihil istorum facere, quemadmodum non vocatio gentium, ubi sensus erat, gentiles à Christo, & ejus demum tempore vocandas: sed tale nihil in promissionibus de Christo, populo isti factis: nam, & in genere concepte de salute hominibus adferendâ, non restricte ad quoddam tempus; & quia quoq; ad illos spectabant, hinc diserte dictum, quod ipsorum fuerunt promissiones, Rom. ix. 4. qui sunt Israelitae, quorum est adoptio & gloria & testamenta & legislatio & cultus & promissiones. Haec omnia ipsorum fuerunt, & ipsis concessa ac propria; non quae modo in gratiam aliorum portarent, & traderent aliis, haud sibi. Primus certè & proprius illorum usus fuit ad ipsos, tum ad alios. Scilicet tam salutaria bona & beneficia ipsis aeque necessaria & utilia ac aliis, sibi fecissent illicita aut prohibita, à quibus nulla lege vel ratione arcebantur? Tum in praedicatione, illa non proposuerunt ut aliena & extranea, sed communia, sibi & aliis, toti vid. & catholice Dei ecclesiae. Hinc in sua & prima persona eadem identidem annunciarunt, quod ipsi illa viderunt, acceperuntque, non aliter ac sua, nos vidimus eum: morbos nostros pertulit, à defectionibus nostris dolore affectus, ab iniquitatibus nostris attritus, castigatio pacis nostrae ei imposita, & vibice ejus curatio nobis, &c. Iesa. LIII. & sic passim. In quibus observandum, quod in praesenti vel praeterito tempore loquuntur, de re tamen post futurâ; & sibi primum eam applicant in prima persona: utrumq; ad confirmandum quod dicimus, illos existimasse ad se imprimis illa pertinere. Denique & toties, & a primo inde tempore, promissiones illas ingeminatas fuisse: ut eo significetur, non dici ista tantum propter alios longe post demum victuros, sed omni tempore ac loco usum reperisse apud quosvis. Nam & Zacharias in Cantico ait, Luc. i. 69. 70. Suscitavit nobis cornu salutis, in domo David, filii sui. Quemadmodum loquutus est, per os sanctorum, qui ab aevo fuerunt; τ' ἀπ' αἰῶνος[?] — Prophetarum suorum. Christus, Luc. xxiv. Et incipiens à Mose & omnibus Prophetis, interpretatus iis est per omnes scripturas illa quae de ipso, v. 24. & 25. O ignorantes & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus, quae Prophetae dixerunt! annon oportuit illa Christum pati, & sic intrare in gloriam suam? Jam Iohannes, cap. i. 46. Quem scripsit Moses in lege, & Prophetae, invenimus Iesum filium Iosephi à Nazareth. Iterum Christus, loco, quem supra examinavimus, Ioan. v. 39. Scrutamini Scripturas: & illae sunt quae testantur de me. v. 46. Si enim Mosi crederetis, crederetis etiam mihi: de me enim ille scripsit. Et Apostoli, Act. iii. 24. Atque omnes Prophetae à Samuele & deinceps, quotquot loquuti fuerunt, & praenunciarunt hosce dies. Ab omni aevo à Mose, à Samuele, à Prophetis, id est, quovis tempore eadem annunciata, & ab omnibus. Act. x. 43. Huic omnes Prophetae attestantur, remissionem peccatorum accipere per nomen ejus quemcunque in eum credentem. Non exceptis vel negatis ipsis aut Prophetis, aut eorum auditoribus, qui dictis auditisque accommodabant fidem. Uti & de illorum infidelitate subinde graviter conquerebantur. Iesa. LIIII. i. Iterum Act. xiii. 32.[?] Et nos evangelizamus vobis promissionem Patribus factam, quod eam Deus nobis ipsorum filiis adimplevit, resuscitans Iesum. Quemadmodum etiam in secundo Psalmo scribitur. Est promissio non nobis tantum, sed & Patribus facta, utrisque aeque ex bono. Nisi quod his in N. T. impletio πλήρωσις[?] contigit eorum, quorum promissionem illi, at vim habebant utrique. Porro cap. xviii. 28. ostendens per Scripturas, quod Iesus esset Christus. Cap. xxvi. 22. Sed divino praesidio ad hunc usque diem steti, infimos juxta ac summos commonefaciens: neque quicquam extra ea dicens, quæ tum caeteri Vates, tum Moses, futura ante denuntiarunt: videlicet supplicio afficiendum Christum, primumque ex mortuis in vitam revocatum, lucem populo & gentibus nunciaturum. Sic vertit Castellio. Rom. i. 2. Euangelium Dei, quod praenuntiatum per Prophetas in Scripturis sanctis. Non ergo de solo Christo concionati fuerunt Vates, sed ejus quoq; officiis & beneficiis, sive de Euangelio salutis. Quod adhuc clarius ex sequentibus. Cap. iii. 21. Iam ergo justitia Dei manifestatur, a lege ac Vatibus testata: divina justitia, quam fide Iesu Christo habenda consequantur & obtineant omnes credentes. Quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ejus, per condonationem peccatorum τῶν προγεγονότων[?] antea commissorum. Non nostra tantum peccata Christus, sed & veterum expiavit. 1 Cor. xv. 3. 4. Tradidi enim vobis in primis quod etiam accepi, quod Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris, juxta Scripturas. Omnia juxta Scripturas. Jam Ecclesia non doctrinæ tantum Apostolorum, sed & Prophetarum dicitur superædificata: & Christus angularis lapis tum horum, tum illorum. Ephes. ii. 20. Superædificati fundamento Apostolorum, & Prophetarum, angulari lapide existente Iesu Christo. Hebr. ix. 14. 15. Quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum obtulit se Deo irreprehensibilem, &c. Novi Testamenti mediator, ut intervenien-te morte in redemptionem τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων[?] transgressionum sub primo Testamento, promissionem consequerentur vocati ad æternam hæreditatem. Prius illud testamentum est tempus Veteris T. quod apparet cum ex isto, tum antecedenti capite octavo. Quin & Christi jam spiritu actos Veteres Petrus scribit, Doctores, quid ni & auditores, & pios omnes 1 Pet. i. 10. 11. De qua salute inquisiverunt & indagati sunt Prophetæ qui de gratia vobis facta prophetarunt.
