Scrutantes in quod & quale tempus significaret Spiritus in iis Christi, ante testatus Christi passiones, & post illas glorias.
units.tr: Answer. As if the pious of the Old Testament could either foretell these things or hear them without applying them to themselves too! Is it probable that they could have done so, or ought to have done so, knowing that their necessities were the same as those for whose relief Christ was proclaimed, and not wishing that the same cure and salvation should also come to them? They recognised that they were sinners, and therefore miserably guilty, and that by their merits they could expect nothing but a curse. Now Christ was proclaimed as one who would take away that curse and exchange it for every spiritual blessing, and they certainly did not fail to know this or doubt it. They therefore believed that Christ would come and would one day do this. This is that true faith in the one who is to come, just as our faith is now in the one who has come. So they preached Christ, just as John preached to the people, telling them that they should believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus. Acts 19:4. It would be otherwise if they had at any time been forbidden to take up faith in the Christ announced to them as for their own good too, or if the matter itself had shown that they were not to do any of this, as the calling of the Gentiles, where the sense was that the Gentiles were to be called from Christ and only in his time. But nothing of the kind appears in the promises about Christ made to that people. For they were conceived in general terms, as bringing salvation to men, not restricted to a certain time; and because they also pertained to them, it is therefore expressly said that the promises were theirs, Rom. 9:4: who are Israelites, whose is the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises. All these things were theirs, granted to them and their own, not merely to carry them for the benefit of others and hand them on to others, and not for themselves. Their first and proper use was surely for themselves, and then for others. Would God then have made such saving goods and benefits, equally necessary and useful to them as to others, unlawful or forbidden to them, from which no law or reason kept them back? Moreover, in preaching they did not put these things forward as alien and foreign, but as common to themselves and to others, to the whole and catholic Church of God. Hence, in their own first person, they repeatedly announced the same things, which they themselves had seen and received, no differently from their own: we saw him; he bore our diseases, was affected with grief at our defections, was crushed by our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was laid upon him, and by his stripes we are healed, etc. Isaiah 53, and so throughout. In these passages it should be observed that they speak in the present or past tense of a thing that was yet to come, and they apply it first to themselves in the first person; both of these confirm what we are saying, that they judged these things to pertain chiefly to themselves. Lastly, these promises were repeated so often, and from the very first time onward, so that it is thereby signified that these things were not said merely for others who would live far later, but that they had their use at every time and place among any people. For Zachariah also says in the canticle, Luke 1:69-70: He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old [ἀπ' αἰῶνος], his prophets. Christ says, Luke 24: And beginning from Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself, vv. 24-25: O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glory? Again John 1:46: We have found him of whom Moses in the law and the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. Again Christ, in the passage we examined above, John 5:39: Search the Scriptures, for they are they which testify of me. v. 46: For if you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote of me. And the Apostles, Acts 3:24: And all the prophets from Samuel onward, as many as have spoken, have also foretold these days. From all ages, from Moses, from Samuel, from the prophets, that is, at every time the same things were announced, and by all of them. Acts 10:43: To him all the prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him receives remission of sins. No exception is made, nor is any denial made, either of the prophets themselves or of their hearers, who gave faith to what was said and heard. Likewise they sometimes complained gravely of their unbelief, Isaiah 54:1. Again, Acts 13:32: And we bring you the good news of the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled it to us their children, in raising up Jesus, as it is also written in the second Psalm. The promise was made not only to us but also to the fathers, and both share equally in the good. Except that the fulfilment [πλήρωσις] of their promise came to these in the New Testament, while both had the same force. Further, Acts 18:28: showing from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ. Acts 26:22: But by the help of God I have stood until this day, bearing witness both to small and great, saying nothing beyond those things which the prophets and Moses said would come: that Christ should suffer, and that he, first rising from the dead, should proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles. So Castellio translates it. Rom. 1:2: the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures. The prophets therefore did not preach of Christ alone, but also of his offices and benefits, that is, of the gospel of salvation. This is clearer still from what follows. Rom. 3:21: Now the righteousness of God is manifested, witnessed by the law and the prophets; the righteousness of God, which through faith in Jesus Christ is had and obtained by all who believe. Whom God has set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, for the remission of sins that were committed before [τῶν προγεγονότων]. Christ expiated not only our sins but also those of the ancients. 1 Cor. 15:3-4: For I delivered to you first of all what I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. All things according to the Scriptures. Now the Church is said to be built up not only on the teaching of the Apostles but also of the prophets, and Christ is the cornerstone of both. Eph. 2:20: built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone. Heb. 9:14-15: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, etc. And he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, by means of his death for the redemption of the transgressions [τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων] under the first testament, those who are called might receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. That first testament is the time of the Old Testament, as appears both from this passage and from the preceding eighth chapter. Indeed Peter also writes that the prophets of old were moved by the Spirit of Christ, and so were teachers, and why not also hearers and all the pious? 1 Pet. 1:10-11: Concerning this salvation the prophets inquired and searched, who prophesied of the grace that was to come to you; searching what or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ within them signified, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glories after them.

units.la: Hæc vero testimonia quidem ex Novo adducuntur Testamento, sed de Veteri loquuntur: & verissima esse, apud Christianos est indubitatum, quibus perinde est, ex qua Scripturæ parte, sive Novo, sive Veteri adferantur. Nihil quippe Scriptores Novi, de Veteri testari potuerunt voluerunt que, nisi quod verissime iis contineatur: abunde autem, prout multis vidimus, docuerunt, promissiones & ἐπαγγελίαι[?] Patribus de Christo factam, & quod in Novo Testamento εὐαγγέλιον, illis quoque præ-nunciatum fuisse, ὁ προευαγγελισάμενος[?]: ibi ἐπαγγελία, hic εὐαγγέλιον. Rom. i. 1. De Christi pro peccatis morte, resurrectione, redemtione nostri, & cæteris religionis ac fidei nostræ dogmatibus, ex Veteri petuntur ab Apostolis passim testimonia, nihilque præter Scripturas ab ipsis traditur aut docetur: unde illud, secundum Scripturas: vel quod Petrum frequenter in ore habuisse ferunt, κατὰ τὰς γραφάς. Neque prædicta illa modo sub Vet. Testamento, quasi non tum quoque locum habuissent, & duntaxat ad tempora N. Testamenti spectassent, sed & promissa fuerunt iisque ipsis proposita ad salutem, quibus significata. Quod ex superioribus quisque facile colligit & deprehendit. Neque aliud fundamentum est probati, commonstra-tique tique passim N. Testamenti ex Vetere, quam quod illud eo comprehensum, istud ill[?] explicatum sit, instar manus contractę, & exporrectę, eadem utrobique ut salus fuerit & religio.
units.tr: These testimonies are indeed taken from the New Testament, but they speak of the Old, and Christians hold it beyond doubt that they are most true, for whom it makes no difference from which part of Scripture, New or Old, they are drawn. The writers of the New Testament could not testify about the Old, nor wish to, except to what is most truly contained in it. And as we have seen in many places, they taught abundantly that the promises [ἐπαγγελίαι] made to the Fathers concerning Christ, and the gospel [εὐαγγέλιον] of the New Testament, had been announced to them beforehand [ὁ προευαγγελισάμενος]: there the promise, here the gospel (Rom. 1:1). Concerning Christ's death for sins, his resurrection, our redemption, and the other doctrines of our religion and faith, the Apostles everywhere draw their testimonies from the Old, and they hand down and teach nothing apart from the Scriptures. Hence the phrase "according to the Scriptures," or what they say Peter often had on his lips: "according to the Scriptures" [κατὰ τὰς γραφάς]. Nor were these things only under the Old Testament, as though they had no place then and looked only to the times of the New; they were also promised and set before those to whom they were signified, for their salvation. Anyone can easily gather and perceive this from what has gone before. Nor is there any other foundation for the proof, shown everywhere, of the New Testament from the Old, than that the one is contained in the other and the other is explained by it, like a hand drawn together and stretched out, the salvation and the religion being the same in both.

units.la: hoc modo ex necessitate Christi ad salutem absoluta, formamus: si non alia salutis & justificationis via sit, nec fuerit unquam, neque esse possit, quam per Christum, ejus tum gratiam, tum notitiam; ergo in Veteri Testamento qui salvati, fuerunt eodem illo salvati modo, non alio: sed non alia unquam salutis & justificationis via est, aut fuit: ergo. Vel illam habuerunt, vel nullam. Nullam habuisse, non sustinebunt opinor dicere Adversarii: quum & natura, & conditio nostra aliquam salutem effiagitent: & religionem illos habuisse, quæ ad Deum duceret, nulli ignorent. Christus, Ioan. xiv. 6. Ego sum via, veritas, & vita: nemo venit ad Patrem, nisi per me. & Act. iv. 12. Petrus: Non est in alio quopiam salus: neque enim est nomen aliud datum sub cælo, in quo nos oporteat servari.
units.tr: In this way we form the argument for the absolute necessity of Christ for salvation. If there is no other way of salvation and justification, nor ever was, nor can be, than through Christ, both through his grace and through the knowledge of him, then those who were saved under the Old Testament were saved in that same way and no other. But there is and has never been any other way of salvation and justification. Therefore they either had this way or they had none. That they had none, I think the adversaries will not venture to say, since both our nature and our condition demand some salvation, and no one is ignorant that they had a religion which led to God. Christ says (John 14:6): "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no one comes to the Father except through me." And Peter says (Acts 4:12): "Salvation is in no other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."

units.la: Excipit ad locum istum Socinus, debere intelligi de tempore præsenti, non præterito. In lib. Quod Regni Poloniæ, &c.
units.tr: Socinus takes exception to this passage, arguing that it must be understood of the present time, not the past. In the book Quod Regni Poloniæ, etc.

units.la: Verum ipsamet sententia sui ipsius explicationem, & ad ratiocinationem, quę inde vulgò illa dicantur, non tamen ad solum præsens elicitur, responsionem secum affert, cum, nulla tempus restringuntur, vel non etiam præmentione præteriti temporis facta, tantum in terito debent, ac possunt applicari. Nam præsente tempore dicat, nullum aliud nomen valde multa proferuntur passim verbo sub cœlo esse, &c. & proximè ante similiter hujus aut istius temporis, quæ non ideo de præsente tantummodo tempore enunciatum le-singulari isto, sed de omni tempore sunt gatur, in nullo alio esse salutem, addito et-intelligenda. V. g. ne longius abeamus, iam in Græco voci salutis articulo, nempe ut in- hoc eodem capite verf. 2. Apostoli præ-telligatur, de nova, non prius audita, illa salu- dicarunt in Iesu resurrectionem mortuorum: te hic agi, quam proponere populo coeperat Io- an hoc de futuro tantum, vel præsenti,non hannes Baptista, remissione, &c. quorumcun-etiam de præterito tempore accipias, & que, quantumvis gravissimorum, pecca-quocunque tempore mortuis, in Christo torum, & à ventura ira Dei perpetua & tandem resurrecturis? Iterum versu 19. plenissima liberatione, omnibus pœniten-interrogant Apostoli eos, coram quibus tiam agentibus et ventura, & ita animadver-sistebantur: εἰ δίκαιον ἐστιν, num justum tatur, & dictum illud, & sententiam illam, quę fit, illos magis audire, quam Deum? An ideo, statim subjicitur, & in qua ipsius dicti redditur ratio, nullo pacto ad priora illa tempora, sed ad quia in præsenti tempore efferunt, ἐπι nova tantum, pertinere. Similiter respon-dent in Catechef. Racovienf. cap. xi. de justificat. pag. 306.
units.tr: But the very sentence itself, as it is set out and explained, and the reasoning that follows from it, does not refer to the present time alone; it carries its own answer with it. For where no time is restricted, or even where past time is not mentioned, it must and can be applied to the past as well. Many things are said in the present tense throughout Scripture, for example, that there is no other name under heaven, and the like, and just before, similarly of this or that time. Such things are not therefore spoken of the present time only, when it is said that salvation is in no other, even with the addition of this singular word, but must be understood of all time. To take an example, not to go further afield: in this same chapter, verse 2, the Apostles preached in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. Whether you take this of the future only, or of the present, or of the past, and at whatever time the dead, in Christ, are to rise again, is it not still the same? Again, in verse 19 the Apostles ask those before whom they stood whether it is right [εἰ δίκαιον ἐστιν] to hear them rather than God. Is that to be referred only to later times, or to new things alone? It is the same with the sentence that follows, in which the reason of the saying is given, which they express in the present tense. In the same way the Racovian Catechism answers, chapter 11, on justification, page 306.

units.la: cælo. Et non est in alio ullo salus. 11. Æquè possunt argutari Adversarii, in præsenti tempore efferri illa, ergo non intelligi de futuro, ac contra tempus præteritum, ut ne etiam de eo verba intelligantur. 111. universalis, universaliter concepta & intelligenda est, nixa veritate universali ac immutabili, de uno eodemque servatore Iesu Christo. An ergo vel alius servator, vel alia salus fuit sub V.T. aut salutis acquirendæ nomen, quam Iesus Christus? Vel proferant nomen aliud, vel hoc agnoscant unum & perpetuum? An, quando dico, non est alius Deus, quam unus, Pater Domini nostri Iesu, hoc significat, alium vero Deum fuisse, sub Testamento Veteri? Neque semel tantum dicitur in textu, sed bis, & diversis modis eadem veritas profertur & enunciatur, non est in ullo alio salus: neque enim est nomen aliud sub caelo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos servari. Nota, in nullo alio, non est nomen aliud, in genere ullis datum hominibus, uspiam sub universo caelo, nec loco ullo, nec tempore aliud. iv. Futile autem est, quod in articulo quaerunt praesidium hęc salus, ἡ σωτηρία, quasi sit salus alia, vel diversae, & non ubique, non omnibus eadem. Neque articulus ille apud autores semper est ἀλλ[?], aliquando additur citra discrimen, aut omittitur. 1 Cor. vi. 2. ἰδοὺ νῦν ἡμέρα σωτηρίας, non ἡ σωτηρίας, ubi, si articulus hoc praecise notaret, quod volunt, non negligendus fuerat, si uspiam. Hebr. v. 9. αἴτιος σωτηρίας. Cap. vi. 9. ἐχόμενα σωτηρίας. 1 Pet. i. 5. εἰς σωτηρίαν. Hebr. i. 14. κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν. Luc. i. 69. Κέρας σωτηρίας ἡμῖν. 71. 77. γνῶσιν σωτηρίας. Ioan. iv. 21. ὅτι σωτηρία ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐστίν. Hoc ipso libro Act. xvi. 17. οὗτοί εἰσιν ὁδὸν σωτηρίας. Rom. i. 16. σωτηρίαν παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι. cap. x. 1.10. εἰς σωτηρίαν. atque alibi. Sic & Christus jam ὁ σωτήρ, jam absque articulo σωτὴρ dicitur. Luc. ii. 11. ἐτέχθη ὑμῖν σήμερον σωτήρ. Act. v. 31. τῷ σωτῆρι ὑψωσεν τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ. Cap. xiii. 23. ἤγαγε τῷ Ἰσραὴλ σωτῆρα Ἰησοῦν. Ephes. v. 23. αὐτὸς ἐστιν σωτὴρ τοῦ σώματος. atque pluribus in locis ita. Deinde, ponatur emphasis in articulo, sed non propterea erit temporis, quasi significet salutem antea inauditam; verum rei, id est, salutis istius verae, aeternaeque. Tertio, fac ergo eandem significationem articuli additi, hoc in versu, ad ἡ σωτήρ quoque, ἵνα τὸ σωτήριον: quasi scilicet hoc jam coelum aliud fit à priori. iv. Arabs significanter admodum: Nec enim est salus per quemquam neque per alium, neque reperitur nomen aliud concessum, hominibus per quod oportet salvari, nisi per ipsum solum. Sic etiam vertit Castellio, nec est in ullo alio salus. aliisque: & non, haec salus.
units.tr: …heaven. And there is no salvation in any other. II. The adversaries could argue just as well that since those things are expressed in the present tense, they are not to be understood of the future, and conversely that they cannot be understood of the past either. III. The word "universal" must be understood universally, resting on the universal and unchanging truth concerning one and the same Saviour, Jesus Christ. Was there then, under the Old Testament, either another saviour, or another salvation, or another name by which salvation is acquired, than Jesus Christ? Let them either produce another name, or acknowledge this one, and perpetual. When I say there is no other God than the one Father of our Lord Jesus, does this mean that there was another God under the Old Testament? The text says it not once only but twice, and in different ways the same truth is put forward and stated: "there is salvation in no other; for there is no other name given under heaven to men in which we must be saved." Note: in no other; there is no other name given to men in general under the whole heaven, anywhere, or at any time. IV. Moreover, it is futile for them to seek a protection in the article, as if this salvation [ἡ σωτηρία] were another salvation, or a different one, and not the same everywhere and for all. Nor is that article always used in the same way in authors; sometimes it is added without distinction, sometimes omitted. 1 Cor. 6:2: "behold, now is the day of salvation" [ἰδοὺ νῦν ἡμέρα σωτηρίας], not ἡ σωτηρία, where, if the article marked precisely what they want, it would not have been neglected, if anywhere. Heb. 5:9: "the cause of salvation" [αἴτιος σωτηρίας]. Heb. 6:9: "things that accompany salvation" [ἐχόμενα σωτηρίας]. 1 Pet. 1:5: "unto salvation" [εἰς σωτηρίαν]. Heb. 1:14: "to inherit salvation" [κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν]. Luke 1:69: "a horn of salvation for us" [Κέρας σωτηρίας ἡμῖν]. Luke 1:71, 77: "the knowledge of salvation" [γνῶσιν σωτηρίας]. John 4:21: "salvation is of the Jews" [ὅτι σωτηρία ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐστίν]. In this same book, Acts 16:17: "these are the ways of salvation" [οὗτοί εἰσιν ὁδὸν σωτηρίας]. Rom. 1:16: "salvation to everyone who believes" [σωτηρίαν παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι]; Rom. 10:1, 10: "unto salvation" [εἰς σωτηρίαν], and elsewhere. So too Christ is called now "the Saviour" [ὁ σωτήρ], now "Saviour" without the article [σωτὴρ]. Luke 2:11: "a Saviour is born to you today" [ἐτέχθη ὑμῖν σήμερον σωτήρ]. Acts 5:31: "God exalted him at his right hand as Saviour" [τῷ σωτῆρι ὑψωσεν τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ]. Acts 13:23: "he brought to Israel a Saviour, Jesus" [ἤγαγε τῷ Ἰσραὴλ σωτῆρα Ἰησοῦν]. Eph. 5:23: "he himself is the Saviour of the body" [αὐτὸς ἐστιν σωτὴρ τοῦ σώματος], and in many other places in the same way. Next, let the emphasis be put on the article; it will not for that reason be a matter of time, as if it signified a salvation not heard of before, but of the thing itself, that is, of this true and eternal salvation. Third, grant then the same meaning of the article added here to ἡ σωτήρ as well, ἵνα τὸ σωτήριον: as if, forsooth, this were now a different heaven from the former. IV. The Arabic version renders it very expressively: "Nor is there salvation through anyone else, nor is there another name granted to men through which it is fitting to be saved, except through him alone." Castellio too translates it thus: "nor is there salvation in any other," and others: not "this salvation."

units.la: Ad idem argumentum spectat etiam, 1 Tim. ii. 5. Unus etenim Deus, unus etiam Mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus. An dices, quod nunc, tempore Novi Testamenti, Christus Mediator quidem est; at quod non item fuerit sub Test. Veteri? idem ergo & de Deo infer. Ex adverso, quemadmodum non idem solum utrobique & semper Deus, sed unus; pariter & idem, & unus omnibus ubicunque & quandocunque salvandis Mediator, hic ipse Christus Iesus. Ubi notandum insuper, quod locus ille subjungitur testimonio de Dei voluntate salvandi homines; argumento, quod, quemadmodum salutis negotium à Deo uno procedit, ita quoque in uno Mediatore fundatum semper sit. Hebr. xiii. 1. Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem, & in saecula. Non hodie solum, sed & heri, neque jam & tum, vel in praesenti tempore, ac praeterito, sed & in futuro, id est, semper unus idemque Iesus Salvator. Complectitur enim hic dicendi modus omnes temporis differentias. Atque uti futurum tempus se extendit in saecula; ita antecedens heri, se quoque in saecula omnia anteriora.
units.tr: This also bears on the same point, 1 Tim. 2:5: For there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. Will you say that Christ is indeed Mediator now, in the time of the New Testament, but was not so under the Old Testament? Then by the same reasoning you would infer the same about God. On the contrary, just as God is not only the same and always God in both Testaments but also one, so Christ Jesus is likewise the same and one Mediator for all who are to be saved, wherever and whenever they live. It must further be noted that this passage follows the testimony about God's will to save men, to show that just as the business of salvation proceeds from the one God, so it is always founded on the one Mediator. Heb. 13:8: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and for ever. He is not only today but also yesterday, not only now and then, or in the present and the past, but also in the future: that is, Jesus the Saviour is always one and the same. For this manner of speaking embraces all the distinctions of time. And just as the future tense extends into eternity, so the preceding "yesterday" extends into eternity in the sense of all earlier times.

units.la: Unde etiam in Apocalypsi, cap. xiii. 8. Christus dicitur agnus mactatus à mundi fundamento, five primordio: non quidem actu & physice, sed moraliter, quod ad valorem, acceptationem, & certitudinem mactationis suo tempore actu futurae. Quae, uti in contractibus bonae fidei, quando sponsor habetur sufficiens & probus, quamvis solutio nondum revera praestita, propter bonam tamen certamque fidem, habetur rata, valuit etiam tempore omni, a primo promissi Christi exordio. Atque hoc nisi potuisset Christus, id est unica oblatione sanctificare omnes, quandocunque vixerint, oportuisset eum pluries pati σταυρουος ...
units.tr: Hence also in the Apocalypse, ch. 13:8, Christ is called the Lamb slain from the foundation, or beginning, of the world. This is not meant actually and physically, but morally: with respect to the value, acceptance and certainty of a slaying that was to take place in actual fact in its own time. Just as in contracts of good faith, when a surety is held to be sufficient and trustworthy, the payment, though not yet actually made, is nevertheless held to be valid on account of the good and certain faith given, so this slaying had its force at every time from the first beginning of Christ's promise. And if Christ could not have sanctified all men, however long they lived, by a single offering, he would have had to suffer crucifixion over and over again...

units.la: Note: the Greek phrase here is printed as "πολλάκις κατά κόσμο&#x C5;" — see notes. Qui nunc Iesus, & tum fuit Iesus, & erit idem in secula. vi. Articulis istis heri & hodie, & in seculum denotantur omnes temporis differentiae, sunt enim praeteriti, praesentis, & futuri: atque uti hodie, non praecise diem, sed tempus praesens, ita heri omne tempus quod antecedit significat, quod opponitur futuro, in seculum: vis verborum ut sit, a seculo in seculum. Uti enim hodie, est omne tempus praesens, καθ' ἑκάστην [?] ἡμέραν ἄχρις [?] ἂν τὸ σήμερον καλεῖται [?], cap. iii. 13. ita heri significat omnem tempus praeteritum. Non ergo quamvis heri significet proprie proximum diem ante hodiernum, & sic non multo remotum, hic pro recenti sumendum est, quia respicienda hujus latitudo aeque, ac reliquorum articulorum, & oppositio ad descriptionem futuri, quae hic loci est: nam neq; de proximo ante hodiernum tantum accipere ausint Adversarii. Uti ergo quivis antecedentes hodiernum dies sunt hesterni, ita omnes illos accipere convenit, convenienter ad duos reliquos articulos & praesentis temporis, & futuri. vii. Alia est locutio Hebraica, quam hic allegat Smalcius, [?], additumque ut magis constet propinquum & recens tempus notari, [?] a nudiustertius; vel, quod in nostro textu est non ab heri, sed heri: & Job. viii. 9. in [?], subintelligitur [illegible, ~2 letters], ab heri: neque dubium poterit esse, tum ratione loquutionis, tum subjectae materiae brevem illis denotari durationem: hic vero alia est loquutio, & res vel persona designata alia, ad cujus dignitatem & momentum illud dicitur, non vilitatem, uti illud. Quod enim vel Moses inquit, se ab heri & nudiustertius non fuisse virum admodum facundum; & Job, nos esse mortales hesternos, non ad gloriam dicitur, sed vilipendium: at quae Apostolus de Christo, & heri & hodie, & in secula, ad ejus honorem & gloriam faciunt: quare, uti nec loquutio eadem, ita nec pari modo interpretanda. Non dicit, quod Christus ab heri & hodie est, non parvam & momentaneam durationem voluit significare, quorsum enim hoc fecisset? sed durationem ejus in secula, & non per unam, uti in illis locis, sed per omnes temporis differentias, diffusam. Neque tantum, quod denique facit ad locorum dissimilitudinem, quod heri & hodie, & in saecula Christus, sed & idem, non alius & alius, vel nunc, vel tum, vel postea, sed semper & ubique idem Iesus Christus.
units.tr: Who is Jesus now, and was Jesus then, and will be the same for ever. vi. By these words yesterday and today, and for ever, all the distinctions of time are denoted: for they are the past, the present and the future. And just as "today" means not precisely the day but the present time, so "yesterday" means every time that precedes, which is opposed to the future, "for ever": the force of the words is "from age to age." For just as "today" is all the present time, [καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἄχρις οὗ τὸ σήμερον καλεῖται], Heb. 3:13, so "yesterday" signifies all past time. Therefore, although "yesterday" properly means the day just before today, and so not something far off, it must not be taken here as recent, because its breadth must be considered in the same way as that of the other terms, and it is set against the description of the future, which is the point here. For the Adversaries do not dare to take it as only the day before today. Therefore, just as all the days before today are "yesterdays," so it is fitting to take all of them, consistently with the other two terms, the present time and the future. vii. Smalcius cites another Hebrew idiom, [?], and adds, so that it may be clearer that a near and recent time is meant, [?] from the day before yesterday; or, as in our text, not from yesterday but yesterday: and at Job 8:9, in [?], understand [illegible, about two letters], from yesterday. Nor can there be any doubt, both from the manner of speaking and from the matter in hand, that a brief duration is denoted in those places. Here, however, the manner of speaking is different, and so is the thing or person designated, to whose dignity and importance the phrase is applied, not to its meanness. For when Moses says that he was not an eloquent man from yesterday and the day before, and when Job says that we are mortals of yesterday, these are not said to glorify, but to belittle. But what the Apostle says of Christ, yesterday and today, and for ever, serves his honour and glory. Therefore, as the expression is not the same, so it is not to be interpreted in the same way. He does not say that Christ is from yesterday and today, to signify a short and momentary duration; for why would he have done so? He speaks of his duration extending into eternity, not through one moment, as in those places, but through all the distinctions of time. Nor is the difference of the passages merely this, that Christ is yesterday and today and for ever; but also that he is the same, not another and another, now or then or later, but always and everywhere the same Jesus Christ.

units.la: Ad Apoc. xiii. 8. ubi Christus dicitur agnus mactatus ab initio mundi, excipiunt, primo, non mactatum fuisse, sed decretum & destinatum a Deo, ut aliquando suo tempore mactaretur: deinde, verba illa ab initio mundi, non esse connectenda cum proxime praecedentibus agni mactati, sed remotioribus, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae, nempe libro vitae ab initio mundi. Socinus, de Christo Servat. part. ii. cap. xxvi. pag. 216. Si quis primo negaverit istam consecutionem, & dixerit, idcirco potuisse dici, Christum occisum fuisse jam inde ab ipso orbis initio, quia ab ipsis mundi jactis fundamentis, Deus, ut Christus mactaretur, jam decreverat; quemadmodum Paulus dicit, datam nobis fuisse gratiam per Christum ante tempora aeterna, 2 Tim. v. 9. quia, scilicet, eam nobis dare Deus decreverat: quid, quaeso, respondebunt? Nam non modo in eo Pauli loco, sed in aliis compluribus similes loquendi modi inveniuntur. Quod enim Deus facere decrevit, pro jam facto habetur; ut in prophetarum vaticinationibus passim videre est. Deinde animadvertendum fuerat, verba illa, ab origine mundi, non conjungi debere cum proxime antecedentibus, agni mactati, sed cum remotioribus; ut Complutensis editio, quae distinctionem inter utraque verba habet, satis confirmat, & probe animadvertit Sebastianus Castellio, qui hunc locum sic transtulit: Quorum nomina ab orbe condito scripta non sunt in vitae libro agni mactati, edoctus, ut arbitror, ex loco illo cap. 17. verf. 8. ejusdem libri, ubi haec eadem sententia ita scripta est, est, Et mirabuntur inhabitantes terram, quorum non sunt scripta nomina in libro vitæ à constitutione mundi. Ex quibus verbis apparet, verba Græca, quæ utrobique sunt ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [?], in priore loco non ad Christi mactationem, sed ad scriptionem nominum in libro vitæ respicere. Neque vero caret exemplo huiusmodi verborum transpositio apud sacros scriptores. Nam Ioh. 17. vers. 5. scriptum est, Et nunc clarifica me tu Pater apud temetipsum claritate, quam habui priusquam mundus esset, apud te. Vbi nemo non videt Apud te, non cum Esset, cui verborum positione cohæret, sed cum Habui, à quo verbis sequentium est, sensu coniungi debere. Apud Paulum similiter 1 Cor. 15. vers. 19. legitur, εἰ ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ τῇ ἠλπικότες ἐσμὲν ἐν Χριστῷ μόνον, &c. id est, ad verbum, Si in vita hac sperantes sumus in Christo tantum, &c. Perspicuum est autem, adverbium μόνον seu Tantum non ad proxima, sed ad remotiora respicere. Et idcirco rectè vetus interpres hunc locum sic vertit: Si in hac vita tantum in Christo sperantes sumus. Valde autem similis huic nostræ est transpositio illa 2 Par. 20. vers. 7. Nonne tu Deus noster expulisti habitatores terræ hujus à facie populi tui Israelis, & dedisti eam semini Abraham amici tui in seculum? In seculum enim manifestè ad verbum Dedisti, non ad verba Amici tui referendum est. Atque hinc perspicere licet, quantum inveteratæ [?] opiniones nos fallere possint, & quam cautum esse oporteat in fide hominibus sacras litteras vel explanantibus, vel citantibus adhibenda. Non igitur ex hoc Apoc. loco, quicquid vulgus nostrorum theologorum hactenus senserit, probari ulla ratione potest, Christi mortis fructum ad eos fideles etiam, qui ab ipso orbe condito extiterunt, pertinuisse. Similiter Enjedinus, non quidem in Apocalypsin, ubi locum illum non attingit, sed in Ioan. xvii. 5. pag. 248. exponit per trajectionem verborum: uti Socinus istum locum, pro se etiam adfert. Smalcius, contra Smalcium, Disput. iv. de Iustificat. pag. 116. ad probandam istam trajectionem, addit locum Apoc. xvii. 8.
units.tr: Against Apoc. 13:8, where Christ is called the Lamb slain from the beginning of the world, they object: first, that he was not slain, but was decreed and destined by God to be slain at some time in its season; second, that the words from the beginning of the world are not to be joined with the immediately preceding slain Lamb, but with the more remote words, whose names are not written in the book of life, namely, the book of life from the beginning of the world. Socinus, On the Saviour Christ, part 2, ch. 26, p. 216: If someone first denies this sequence, and says that Christ could be said to have been slain from the very beginning of the world because God had already decreed from the foundation of the world that Christ should be slain, just as Paul says that grace was given to us through Christ before the eternal times, 2 Tim. 1:9, because God had decreed to give it to us: what, I ask, will they answer? For not only in that passage of Paul, but in many others, similar modes of speaking are found. For what God has decided to do is held to be already done, as one may see everywhere in the prophets' predictions. Next, it should have been observed that the words from the origin of the world are not to be joined with the immediately preceding words, slain Lamb, but with the more remote ones; as the Complutensian edition, which has a punctuation between the two phrases, sufficiently confirms, and as Sebastian Castellio rightly observed, who translated this passage thus: whose names from the foundation of the world are not written in the book of life of the slain Lamb, taught, as I think, by that passage in ch. 17, verse 8, of the same book, where the same sentiment is written thus: And those who dwell on the earth will marvel, whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. From these words it appears that the Greek words, which in both places are from the foundation of the world, in the first place refer not to Christ's slaying but to the writing of names in the book of life. Nor does such a transposition of words lack precedent among the sacred writers. For John 17:5 says: And now glorify me, Father, with your own self, with the glory which I had before the world was, with you. Here everyone sees that with you is not to be joined with was, to which it stands in word order, but with had, to which it belongs in sense in what follows. Similarly in Paul, 1 Cor. 15:19, we read: If in this life only we have hope in Christ, etc., that is, word for word, if in this life we are hoping in Christ only. It is clear, however, that the adverb only refers not to the immediately preceding words but to the more remote ones. And so the old translator rightly renders this passage: If in this life only we are hoping in Christ. Very similar to this transposition of ours is that in 2 Chron. 20:7: Did you not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it to the seed of Abraham your friend for ever? For for ever manifestly refers to the verb gave, not to the words your friend. From this one may see how far long-held opinions can mislead us, and how cautiously men ought to be heeded, both in explaining and in citing the sacred letters. Therefore, whatever the common run of our theologians has hitherto thought, it cannot be proved by any reasoning from this passage of the Apocalypse that the fruit of Christ's death pertained to those faithful who existed from the very foundation of the world. Likewise Enyedi, not indeed on the Apocalypse, where he does not touch that passage, but on John 17:5, p. 248, explains it by transposition of words, as Socinus also adduces that passage for himself. Smalcius, against Smalcius, Disputation 4, on Justification, p. 116, to prove this transposition, adds the passage Apoc. 17:8.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non negamus, decretam Christi mactationem fuisse, à Deo, & sic datam: & hoc sensu etiam posse dici datam nobis gratiam in Christo Iesu ante tempora sæcularia: sed plus in textu nostro, & aliud quid significari, contendimus, quando Christus dicitur, non datus simpliciter, sed mactatus. Hoc enim aliquid passivum dicit, respectu Christi & quod in eo habemus, non tantummodo quod in intentione Dei fuerit, ejusque decreto. Qui mactatus pro nobis dicitur, idem & datus, sed non viceversa omnis qui datus, vel eo quod datus, mactatus quoque. Ut hoc longe plus dicat, & aliud quid supra illud. 11. Non est in loco Apoc. πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων [?], vel ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, ante originem mundi, vel ante tempora sæcularia; sed, ἀπὸ, ab origine mundi: & perperam Adversarii hic ita loquuntur, ac si vel ejusdem significationis illa essent, vel legeretur, non, ab origine, sed, ante originem mundi. Mactatus Christus dicitur ab origine mundi, non ante. Christus non fuit decretus & constitutus à Deo in Servatorem, post mundi creationem demum, nec quidem juxta Adversarios, qui in eo etiam collocant argumentum divinitatis ejus, quod ab æterno fuit à Deo prædestinatus: non ergo de eo hic sermo quod ei accidisse dicitur post, & à primâ mundi constitutione, tum quod agnus fuit, tum quod etiam habitus quasi vel tum mactatus esset: quorum neutrum de simplice Dei destinatione intelligi debet. Certe, quod Deus facere decrevit, pro jam facto habetur: sed hic non tantum quod Deus, sed Christus facere debuerit, agitur. iv. Imo quemadmodum in Prophetarum vaticinationibus passim videre est promissa & praedicta pro impletis haberi, quia nimirum ita certa sunt: ita ergo & haec futura Christi ma-ctatio, dicitur facta jam à mundi origine, quia tum promissa, & propter suam certi-tudinem pro facto fuit habita & habenda. Mactandus certe fuit, & hoc tam certo, tam infallibiliter, ac si jam omnino mactatus fuit: unde & fructus ex ejus ma-ctatio-ne non jam tum minus certi erant, quam postea. Contrà autem mira adversariorum & inepta expositio eò tendit, ut primùm mactatus, significet datus; tum datus, decretus: ubi, praeterquam quod non possunt locum vel loquutionem dare consimi-lem, ubi mactatus agnus hoc significet, eo tandem redit illa explicatio, ut mactatum ab origine mundi Christum negent, & vel hoc pro certo habitum, creditumque, vel ullam inde vim, fructum, aut consolationem ad pios promanasse, inficientur.
units.tr: Reply 1. We do not deny that Christ's slaying was decreed by God and so given. In this sense it can also be said that grace was given to us in Christ Jesus before the eternal ages. But we maintain that our text means more than this, and something else, when Christ is said not merely to have been given but to have been slain. This phrase refers to something passive, with respect to Christ and to what we have in him, and not only to what was in God's intention and decree. One who is said to have been slain for us is also given, but not conversely: not everyone who is given is also slain. So the phrase says far more, and something further beyond that. 2. The Apocalypse does not have πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων [before the eternal ages] or ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [from the foundation of the world] meaning "before the origin of the world" or "before the ages of time." It has ἀπὸ, "from the origin of the world." Our opponents speak wrongly here, as if these phrases had the same meaning, or as if the text read "before the origin of the world" and not "from the origin of the world." Christ is said to have been slain from the origin of the world, not before it. Christ was not decreed and appointed by God as Saviour only after the creation of the world. Even by the opponents' own view, which places in him the proof of his divinity, he was predestined by God from eternity. So the text is not speaking of something that happened to him after the first constitution of the world. It speaks of his being the Lamb, and of his being regarded as already slain at that time. Neither of these can be understood as a mere divine destination. Certainly what God has decided to do is held as already done. But here the point is not only what God would do, but what Christ was to do. 4. Indeed, just as in the prophetic utterances it is everywhere to be seen that promises and predictions are held as already fulfilled, because they are so certain, so also this future slaying of Christ is said to have been done already from the origin of the world, because it was promised, and on account of its certainty it was and is to be regarded as done. Certainly he was to be slain, and this so surely and infallibly as if he had already been wholly slain. Hence the fruits of his slaying were no less certain then than afterwards. On the other hand, the strange and absurd exposition of our opponents tends to this: that first slain means given, and then given means decreed. But besides the fact that they cannot give a similar place or expression where slain lamb has this meaning, the explanation finally comes to this: they deny that Christ was slain from the origin of the world, and they deny that this was held and believed as certain, or that any force, fruit or comfort flowed from it to the godly.

units.la: Deinde quod ad alteram expositionem, per trajectionem verborum ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου[?]: primùm divellunt illa ex suo loco temere; deinde conjiciunt in locum alium, ubi non conveniunt. Nam 1. Quae aut necessitas, vel autoritas illius antiqui & probati Codicis datur, pro hac nova, mirá, & incondita trajectione? Dicitur in textu, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae agni mactati ab origine mundi. Adversarii ista sic dislocant, quorum nomina sunt scripta in libro vitae ab origine mundi agni mactati. Quis contra Codicum omnium fidem, ex solo ingenii pruritu & pervicacia, ut propriae & pravae serviat hypothesi, concedat ita ludi in sacris, vel haberi pro astragalis? 11. Quid fecerit vel Complutensis editio, vel Castellio parum nos movet, contra omnium sententiam & fidem: & tamen etiam alia ratione, quam quae nunc est Socinianorum, id fecerunt. Spectarunt enim id, quod Apoc. xvii. 8. simpliciter & constanter legitur, quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae ab origine mundi, nullâ mentione facta agni mactati. Verùm si propter istum locum debeas mutare priorem, aeque potes tollere ista agni mactati, quae in altero loco non habentur, quam transponere. Sed & Castellio, qui passim linguae & sermonis sui majorem curam habet, quam sacri, ulterius verba hic projicit, & legit: quorum nomina ab orbe condito scripta non sunt in vitae libro agni mactati. 111. Contrà vero, quemadmodum liber vitae, hic idem est liber agni, & is dicitur mactatus, & post omnia subjungitur, ab origine mundi; ita omnia ut intelligantur istius quoque durationis, & scriptus quasi liber, & agnus, & ejus mactatio, aequum est. Scriptus ab origine mundi dicitur, ratione hominum ab exordio mundi ad librum istum spectantium, non quod tum demum decretum Dei & praedestinatio inceperit, sed quod jam tum fuerit. Aliquando simpliciter dicitur liber vitae. Apoc. iii. 5. & xx. 12. & xxii. 19. Phil. iv. 3. aliquando liber vitae ab origine mundi, qui liber vitae fuit ab origine mundi, Apoc. xvii. 8. Alias, liber vitae agni. Apoc. xxi. 27. Hic, agni mactati ab origine mundi: & liber ab origine mundi; & agni, ab origine mundi; denique & mactati, ab origine mundi: omnia & singula vera, ab origine mundi. Observandum, nullum inter illa in toto sermonis contextu occurrere comma: quo magis liqueat, indivulsa esse: & si constructio formetur ad placitum Adversariorum, neque sic tamen profsus perit argumentum, quia sive istud ab origine mundi praeponatur proxime, sive postponatur verbis agnati mactati, cum iis aeque construi potest, & debet. Sic nihil temeritate sua tamen effecerint Adversarii, nisi injuriam Scripturae magis, quam nobis. Deinde & valde interturbarunt verborum fluxum, & nimis praerupte finiverunt. Quod unicuique facile est obseruare legenti verba, ut Aduersarii transponiunt, ὧν [?] γεγραμμένα τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς [?] τοῦ ἀρνίου ἐσφαγμένου [?] ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. Viderint omnes, an tam bene fluant verba, ac quando manent, prout in textu sunt: ὧν [?] γεγραμμένα τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου [?] ἐσφαγμένου ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. v. Syrus non tantum eo modo legit, sed & in libro vitæ agni illius, sicut quemadmodum & Græci aliqui Codices, ἐσφαγμένου [?] ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. Arabs, in libro vitæ & agni illius occisi antequam esset mundus. Versio Æthiopica, in libro vitæ Agni ejus, qui occisus est, quia creatione mundi erat. vi. Quorsum volunt Aduersarii adeo conjungere ab origine mundi, cum scriptis in libro vitæ, quum non statuant hominum nomina tum iis inscripta fuisse, inscribi demum suo singula tempore, quando actu, & diverso postea tempore credunt? Denique omnes expendant velim, quæ non sequutura sit Scripturæ inversio vulgaris ac petulans, si id semel concedatur, quod hic sibi licere credunt Aduersarii, in transponendis & commutandis verbis. Hoc modo nihil jam erit stabile in tota Scriptura Sacra, nihil quod non ex eâ vel probari possit, vel dirui, ista semel si obtineat pervertendi eam methodus ac ratio.
units.tr: Next, as to the other exposition, by transposition of the words ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [from the foundation of the world]: first, they rashly tear these words from their place, and then they throw them into another place where they do not fit. For, first: what necessity or authority is there for this new, strange and incongruous transposition, against that old and approved manuscript? The text reads whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the origin of the world. Our opponents dislocate these words to read whose names are written in the book of life from the origin of the world of the Lamb slain. Who, against the faith of all the manuscripts, from mere itching of wit and obstinacy, in order to serve his own perverse hypothesis, would allow sacred words to be played with in this way, or regard them as dice? Second: what the Complutensian edition or Castellio did matters little to us, since it is against the view and faith of all. Yet they did it on other grounds than those now used by the Socinians. For they had in view what is simply and consistently read in Revelation 17:8, whose names are not written in the book of life from the origin of the world*, with no mention of the Lamb slain. But if on account of that passage you must change the earlier one, you may as well remove those words of the Lamb slain, which are not found in the other place, as transpose them. Yet Castellio too, who everywhere pays more attention to his own language and style than to Scripture, pushes the words further here and reads: whose names, written from the foundation of the world, are not in the book of life of the Lamb slain. Third: on the contrary, just as the book of life here is the same as the book of the Lamb, and this is said to be slain, and after all these things is added from the origin of the world, so it is fitting that all of these should be understood with the same duration: the book as written, as it were, and the Lamb, and his slaying. The book is said to have been written from the origin of the world with respect to the persons belonging to that book from the beginning of the world. This does not mean that God's decree and predestination only then began, but that they had already been there. Sometimes it is simply called the book of life (Rev. 3:5; 20:12; 22:19; Phil. 4:3), sometimes the book of life from the origin of the world, which was the book of life from the origin of the world (Rev. 17:8), and elsewhere the book of life of the Lamb (Rev. 21:27). Here it is the Lamb slain from the origin of the world, and the book from the origin of the world, and the Lamb from the origin of the world, and finally the slaying from the origin of the world: all and each are true from the origin of the world. It should be observed that there is no comma anywhere in the whole context between these phrases, which makes it clearer that they are inseparable. And even if the construction is shaped according to our opponents' pleasure, the argument is still not wholly lost, since whether this from the origin of the world is placed immediately before, or after the words slain Lamb, it can and must be construed equally with them. So our opponents have accomplished nothing by their rashness except to do more injury to Scripture than to us. Moreover, they have greatly disturbed the flow of the words and ended the sentence too abruptly. Anyone reading the words as our opponents transpose them can easily see this: ὧν γεγραμμένα τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου ἐσφαγμένου ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [whose names are written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world]. Let all judge whether the words flow as smoothly as when they stand as they are in the text: ὧν γεγραμμένα τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου ἐσφαγμένου ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [whose names are written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world]. 5. The Syriac reads not only in this way, but also in the book of life of that Lamb, just as some Greek manuscripts read ἐσφαγμένου ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. The Arabic reads: in the book of life and of the Lamb slain before the world was. The Ethiopic version reads: in the book of life of his Lamb, who was slain, because he was there at the creation of the world. 6. Why do our opponents wish to join from the origin of the world so closely with written in the book of life, when they do not hold that the names of men were then written in it, but that each was written at its own time, when it actually believes, and at a later time? Finally, I would have everyone weigh what a bold and common inversion of Scripture would follow if this were once conceded, which our opponents think they may do in transposing and changing words. In this way nothing in the whole of Holy Scripture will be stable, nothing that could not be either proved or overthrown from it, once such a method and principle of perverting it were allowed.

units.la: Ad similes, quas adferunt, verborum in Scripturâ transpositiones, negamus in iis ullam esse verborum trajectionem; minus talem, atque hic faciunt. Nam Ioann. xvii. 5. & nunc glorifica me tu Pater apud te gloria quam habui antequam hic mundus esset, apud te. nulla est verborum transpositio, sed sive quam habui apud te, priusquam hic mundus esset; sive, quam habui antequam hic mundus esset, apud te, scribatur, eodem redit: & est promiscua ac usitata verborum positio, nulla transpositio: præsertim quum interjectum comma satis declaret, non esse sensum, antequam hic mundus esset apud te; sed, antequam hic mundus esset, habui istam gloriam apud te. In loco vero Apocalypsis nullum aut comma, aut in expositione, nedum verbis, necessaria transpositio.
units.tr: As for the similar transpositions of words they cite from Scripture, we deny that there is any transposition of words in them. They do so less than these men do here. For John 17:5: And now glorify thou me, O Father, with thine own self, with the glory which I had with thee before the world was. There is no transposition of words. Whether one writes "the glory which I had with thee before the world was" or "the glory which I had before the world was, with thee," the meaning is the same. This is a common and ordinary word order, not a transposition. The inserted comma also makes clear that the sense is not "before the world was, with thee," but "before the world was, I had that glory with thee." In the passage of the Apocalypse there is no comma, and no transposition is necessary, either in the exposition or in the words.

units.la: 1 Cor. xv. 19. non est ulla adverbii transpositio, quod promiscue in oratione, citra ullam sermonis differentiam, præponi solet, aliquando postponi: & sive scribatur, si in hac vita tantum sperauemus in Christo, vel, si in hac vita sperauemus in Christo tantum, essemus miserrimi omnium hominum, eodem redit. Tum aliud est, de una voce, vel adverbio quærere, in exponenda oratione; vel, de transponendo integro ejus membro. Idem respondemus ad vocularn vel ad verbum [illegible, ~5 letters] 11 Chron. xx. 7. Ut certe rationem minime habuerit Socinus (nec erit transpositio, si dixero, rationem Socinus habuit minime &c.) dicendi, vulgus Theologorum hactenus male Apocaly-pseos locum legisse, aut fuisse interpretatum: nisi quod, pro more suo, omnes omnium ætatum Theologos, præ se, habere solet & contemnere.
units.tr: In 1 Cor. 15:19 there is no transposition of an adverb. In ordinary speech the adverb is commonly placed before or after the word it modifies with no difference in meaning. Whether one writes "if in this life only we have hope in Christ" or "if in this life we have hope in Christ only," we would be "of all men most miserable" either way. Moreover, it is one thing to ask about a single word or adverb when explaining a sentence, and another to move a whole clause of it. We give the same answer about the little word or the term [illegible] in 11 Chron. xx. 7. Socinus has certainly paid no attention to the manner of speaking (and it will not be a transposition if I say, "Socinus paid little attention to it," etc.). Up to now the common run of theologians has read or interpreted the passage in the Apocalypse badly, except that, as is his habit, he is accustomed to hold all the theologians of every age in contempt and to look down on them.

units.la: Jam ad alterum Hebr. ix. 26. locum, ubi docet Apostolus, quod nisi uno perfectoque sacrificio suo Christus expiasset omnes, decuisset eum sæpius mori, & si sæpius, jam ab origine mundi aliquoties, quo nimirum eorum qui à primo inde tempore vixerunt, quoque expiaret peccata; jam vero contrà eum hoc fecisse semel, unicâ sub mundi finem oblatâ sui hostiâ perfectissimâ, (alioquin oportuisset eum sæpius pati ab origine mundi) jam vero semel in consummatione sæculi, ad abolitionem peccati, per suam hostiam apparuit.
units.tr: Now for the second passage, Heb. 9:26, where the Apostle teaches that unless Christ had made atonement by his one and perfect sacrifice, he would have had to die often, and if often, then several times since the beginning of the world, for those who lived from the first time onward, to make atonement for their sins. But in fact he has done this once, having offered his most perfect victim once at the end of the world. (Otherwise he would have had to suffer often from the beginning of the world.) But now once in the completion of the ages he has appeared, by his own sacrifice, to put away sin.

units.la: Socinus, eodem cap. xxvi. part. ii. de Servatore, pag. 215. sic excipit:
units.tr: Socinus, in the same chapter 26, part 2, on the Saviour, p. 215, replies thus:

units.la: Tantum abesse, ut ex hoc loco probari possit, Christi sacrificium, antequam perageretur, vim expiandi peccata habuisse, & ad priscos illos pertinuisse, ut contrarium potius evidenter in-de colligatur. Nam si virtus sacrificii ad eos etiam pertingere potuit, qui sacrificium ipsum antecesserunt, ut necesse est affirmare, si velimus ad eos, qui ante Christum fuerunt, id per-tinuisse: quid opus erat, etiamsi Christum saepius se offerre oportuisset, ut is a condito orbe saepius pateretur? An non satis superque[?] fuisset, si Christus, postquam in mundum venerat, pati coepisset, & ante extremum illum diem sub-inde passus esset? Cum igitur Apostolus di-cat, necesse futurum, si oportuisset Christum seipsum saepius offerre, ut etiam passus esset ab orbe condito: satis ostendit, sacrificium mortis Christi non debere esse post illos, ad quos ipsius fructus manaturus est. Et propterea, si saepius offerre se debuisset Christus, saepius etiam, ante-quam nos esse desiissemus, ad quos, videlicet, fructus oblationis pertinere debebat, opus fuisse, ut in mortem traderetur. Non solum autem, antequam nos esse desiissemus, dixit, sed, a constitutione mundi; ut quid fieri necesse suis-set, evidentius exprimeret, si quo saepius se ob-tulisset Christus, eo magis nostra peccata ex-piata forent. Quod si necesse est, ut sacrificium mortis Christi non sit post illos, quibus profutu-rum est: certe non modo ad eos pertinere non potest, qui illud tempore praecesserunt, verum etiam alia ratione, quam divinae justitiae satis-faciendo iis, qui post ipsum vel adhuc sunt, vel recens exstiterunt, ipsum prodesse concludendum plane est. Nam, si idcirco hominibus salutem conciliarit, quod divinae justitiae pro peccatis eorum satisfaceret: quid opus esset, ut illos vel praecederet, vel saltem subsequeretur? Dum enim debitum vere solvatur, quid refert quo tempore id fiat, praesertim apud Deum, qui omnia, quae certo futura sunt, comperti ssima[?] habet, & ea singula, tamquam praesentia, per-petuo videt atque intuetur?
units.tr: It is so far from being provable from this passage that the sacrifice of Christ, before it was carried out, had the power of expiating sins and pertained to those of old, that the contrary is plainly inferred from it. For if the power of the sacrifice could reach even those who came before the sacrifice itself, as one must affirm if we want it to have pertained to those who lived before Christ, then what need was there, even if Christ had had to offer himself often, that he should suffer from the foundation of the world? Would it not have been more than enough if Christ, after he had come into the world, had begun to suffer, and had suffered from time to time until that last day? Since the Apostle therefore says that it would have been necessary, if Christ had had to offer himself often, that he should also have suffered from the foundation of the world, he sufficiently shows that the sacrifice of Christ's death ought not to be later than those for whom its fruit was to flow. And so, if Christ had had to offer himself often, it would have been necessary for him to be delivered to death often, before we ceased to exist, that is, for those to whom the fruit of the offering was bound to pertain. And he said not only "before we ceased to exist," but "from the foundation of the world," so as to express more clearly what would have had to happen: the more often Christ offered himself, the more our sins would have been expiated. But if it is necessary that the sacrifice of Christ's death should not be after those for whom it is to profit, then certainly it cannot pertain to those who preceded it in time; and it must be concluded plainly that it profits them by another reason, namely by satisfying the divine justice for those who came after it, or who are still living, or who have recently come into being. For if it had brought salvation to men because it satisfied the divine justice for their sins, what need was there for it to come before them, or at least to follow them? For provided the debt is truly paid, what does it matter at what time this is done, especially with God, who has most certain knowledge of all things that will certainly come to pass, and who always sees and beholds each of them as if present?

units.la: Resp. 1. Quaerit Socinus, si virtus sa-crificii Christi etiam ad eos pertinuit, qui ante Christum vixerunt, quid opus fuit etiam si Christum saepius se offerre oportuisset, ut a condito orbe saepius pateretur? in quo non capit sensum disputationis Apo-stolicae. Nam Apostolus conferens sa-cerdotium Christi cum sacerdotio V. T. Aaronico, inter alia, & hoc urget, quod Christo non necesse fuit saepius offerre, non quotannis, quemadmodum id debuit sub V. T. Sacerdos. Vers. 7. in secundum vero semel in anno solus Sacerdos magnus, non sine sanguine, quem offert pro suis & populi ignorantiis. Christus autem non habuit necesse offerre pro suis peccatis, tantum-modo pro populo suo: non etiam quot-annis: & suo sanguine omnia peregit, non alieno: denique non in terrestre sacrarium ingressus fuit, sed in ipsum coelum. Haec in sequentibus fusius persequitur: & ad secundum istud, quod non quotannis ne-cesse haberet repetere oblationem, verf. 25. ait: neque ut saepius seipsum offerret, quemadmodum sacerdos summus quotannis in sancta ingreditur sanguine alieno: jam verf. 26. (quandoquidem oportuisset eum saepius pati ab origine mundi) nunc vero semel in con-summatione saeculorum, ad abolitionem pecca-torum, per sacrificium suum, apparuit. Pro perfectione & sufficientia unius Christi sacrificii disputat: & si unum illud non suffeciset, infert, ergo pluries, vel quot-annis se debuisset offerre. Jam vero unum illud, ad abolendum peccatum, suffecit. Et certum est, quod si unum sacrificium non suffeciset, plura adhibere oportuis-set, postquam non aliter quam sacrificio, & χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας[?] remissio pec-cati obineri potuit. Et posito quod plu-ribus sacrificiis fuisset opus, iis opus suis-set ab origine mundi, ut peccata tempo-rum, iteratis sacrificiis aboleretur. Jam id non fuit necesse, & praecedentia etiam hominum a mundi origine peccata, uno hoc
units.tr: Reply 1. Socinus asks: if the power of Christ's sacrifice pertained also to those who lived before Christ, what need was there, even if Christ had had to offer himself often, that he should suffer from the foundation of the world? This shows that he does not grasp the sense of the Apostolic argument. For the Apostle, comparing the priesthood of Christ with the Aaronic priesthood of the Old Testament, urges among other things that Christ did not need to offer often, not every year, as the priest under the Old Testament had to. Verse 7: "But into the second only the high priest went once every year, not without blood, which he offered for his own and the people's ignorances." But Christ did not have to offer for his own sins, only for his people, and not yearly; and he accomplished everything with his own blood, not another's. Finally, he entered not into an earthly sanctuary but into heaven itself. He pursues these points more fully in what follows. And for the second point, that he did not need to repeat the offering every year, he says in verse 25: "nor that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters the holy place every year with blood not his own." Then in verse 26: "for then he would have had to suffer often from the foundation of the world; but now once, in the completion of the ages, he has appeared to put away sin by his sacrifice." He argues for the perfection and sufficiency of the one sacrifice of Christ. If that one had not been enough, he infers, then he would have had to offer himself many times, or every year. But that one sufficed to put away sin. And it is certain that if one sacrifice had not sufficed, he would have had to apply several, since forgiveness of sin could be obtained only by sacrifice, and "apart from sin" [χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας]. And granting that several sacrifices would have been needed, they would have been needed from the beginning of the world, so that the sins of each period might be put away by repeated sacrifices. But this was not necessary, and Christ by this one offering of his has blotted out also the sins of men from the beginning of the world.

units.la: Tom. 2. sacrificio suo delevit Christus. Quorsum autem dixit, ab origine mundi? nisi ut denotaret, ipsa ab origine mundi peccata, isto Christi sacrificio expiata fuisse, neque alio eguisse: nisi enim unum Christi sacrificium omnia illa efficere potuisset, hoc iaculo vel tempore vel anno pro istis peccatis, alio pro aliis moriendum ei fuisset; nunc vero unica illa sui hostia, in mundi consummatione, omnia hominum, quibus unquam remittuntur, peccata complexus fuit, & abstersit. Hoc jam ante coeperat dicere, verf. 15. quod Novi Testamenti mediator mortem suam, in remissionem transgressionum sub primo Testamento, interposuerat: & propterea Novi Testamenti mediator est, ut morte facta, εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων, τὴν [?] ἐπαγγελίαν λάβωσιν οἱ κεκλημένοι τῆς αἰωνίου κληρονομίας.
units.tr: Vol. 2. Why does he say "from the beginning of the world"? Only to show that the sins from the beginning of the world were expiated by this sacrifice of Christ, and needed nothing else. For if the one sacrifice of Christ could not have accomplished all this, he would have had to die on one account at one time, and on another for other sins; but now that one sacrifice of himself, at the close of the world, has embraced and wiped away all the sins of men for which forgiveness is ever granted. He had already begun to say this in verse 15, that the Mediator of the New Testament had interposed his death "for the redemption of the transgressions under the first testament," and therefore he is Mediator of the New Testament, so that, death having taken place, "those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance" [εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων, τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν λάβωσιν οἱ κεκλημένοι τῆς αἰωνίου κληρονομίας].

units.la: II. Non vero hoc Apostolus agit, quod Socinus vult, an Christi sacrificium debeat fuisse ante illos, vel post illos, quibus fit profuturum. Quaerit Socinus: Si virtus sacrificii ad eos etiam pertingere potuit, qui sacrificium ipsum antecesserunt; quid opus erat, etiamsi Christum saepius se offerre oportuisset, ut is a condito orbe saepius pateretur? respondeo, mirum illud antecedens, ex quo consequens istud deducitur. Neque enim ita argumentatur Apostolus, vel contra illud disputat, sed an uno sacrificio Christus omnia perficere potuerit, eodemque perfecerit, ut pluribus non fuerit opus? & concludit, vim sacrificii Christi etiam ad anteriora tempora penetrare, ad ipsam usque mundi originem, ut nec inde, nec unquam alias opus fuerit sacrificio expiatorio, praeter istum unum. Annon satis superque fuisset si Christus, postquam in mundum venerat, pati caepisset, & ante extremum illum diem subinde passus fuisset? Non: nam posito quod valuisset ista passio pro peccatis istius aetatis, pro alia aetate alias patiendum ei iterum fuisset, ex hypothesi, de qua disputat Apostolus, quod pluribus sacrificiis fuisset opus, & suum exegissent tempora ab origine mundi, suum iterum consummatio saeculorum aliud.
units.tr: II. Yet the Apostle does not do what Socinus wants, namely ask whether Christ's sacrifice had to take place before those for whom it would be profitable, or after them. Socinus asks: If the power of the sacrifice could reach even those who came before the sacrifice itself, what need was there, even if Christ had had to offer himself many times, for him to suffer again and again from the foundation of the world? I answer that this is a strange premise from which he draws that conclusion. The Apostle does not argue in this way, nor does he dispute against that position. He asks whether Christ could accomplish everything by one sacrifice, and whether he did so, so that there was no need for more. He concludes that the power of Christ's sacrifice reaches even to earlier times, back to the very origin of the world, so that neither then nor at any other time was there need of an expiatory sacrifice apart from that one. Would it not have been more than enough if Christ, after he had come into the world, had begun to suffer and had suffered from time to time until that last day? No. For even granting that his suffering would have availed for the sins of that age, he would then have had to suffer again for another age, and so on, on the hypothesis the Apostle is discussing, namely that many sacrifices would have been needed, and the times from the origin of the world would have demanded one, and the consummation of the ages would have demanded another.

units.la: At dices, si ponat, quod virtus sacrificii ad eos etiam pertingere potest, qui sacrificium ipsum antecesserunt, illud non fuit opus: verum quando praesupponis, quod ad omnes qui antecesserunt, virtus unius sacrificii pertingere potuit, tum disputationi quam Apostolus instituit, non est locus, & habes quaesitum, seu conclusionem. De eo enim agitur, an uno, an variis sacrificiis redemtionem nostram Christus peregerit. Ubi non praesupponitur, sed quaeritur, an, non ad aliquos, sed ad omnes qui antecesserunt, ad originem usque mundi, valere potuerit Christi unica oblatio? Quare suis verbis non significavit Apostolus, sacrificium mortis Christi non debere esse post illos, ad quos ipsius fructus manaturus est: sed imo contrarium, ejus etiam fructum manare ad eos, qui illud tempore antecesserunt, ad ipsam adeo mundi usque originem. Quod si enim Christi sacrificium non posset esse tempore post eos, qui per id redimuntur; ergo nec Iohannem Baptistam, nec alios forte mortuos ante sui oblationem, redimere potuit, solos eos qui post sequuti fuerunt tempore. Quod non tantum nusquam Scriptura significat, sed quoque est contra vim & dignitatem mortis Christi, ejusque ad praecedentia tempora valorem. Imo sic Christus commodissime statim ab origine mundi potius fuisset mortuus, ut sic semel unica oblatione omnes praevertisset, & non in mundi fine, illud si ad mortis ejus vim adeo sit necessarium, ut antecedat, non sequatur. Neq; Apostolus significavit, quo saepius se obtulisset Christus, eo magis nostra peccata expiata forent: qui unica Christi oblatione omnia peccata docet expiata, & redemitos sive anteriores, sive posteriores, à mundi origine ad finem, ἀπὸ καταβολῆς[?], usque ad σωτηρίαν[?]. cap. x. 12. unica pro peccatis oblata hostia. 14. unica enim oblatione τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους[?]. Denique nescio quid sibi fingat Socinus, quando adeo in hoc insistit, an Salvator omnes qui per ipsum salvantur, præcedat, vel subsequatur? Neque enim de eo Apostolus loquitur, vel ut loqueretur præsens urgebat argumentum. Nihil enim ad rem facit, præcedat salutio, an sequatur, dum certo præstatur, & de Sponsoris veritate ac fide nullum posset esse dubium: uti nulla certe de Christi sponsione, apud Deum. Qui quam vere destinatus ab æterno, tam certo promissus fuit in V. Testamento, & vere suo tempore exhibitus: quæ tres ejus sunt periodi, & uti ex destinatione omnia fluunt, ita ante exhibitionem & certo promissus, atque vi exhibitionis infallibiliter futuræ salvati fuerunt à peccatis omnes, pro quibus tandem se Deo obtulit in sacrificium.
units.tr: But you will say: if one holds that the power of the sacrifice can reach even to those who came before the sacrifice itself, then it was not needed. But when you presuppose that the power of the one sacrifice could reach all who went before, then there is no room for the dispute the Apostle undertakes, and you already have the question and its conclusion. For the matter at issue is whether Christ accomplished our redemption by one sacrifice or by many. Here nothing is presupposed; the question is whether Christ's single oblation could avail not for some, but for all who went before, back to the origin of the world. Therefore the Apostle did not mean in his words that the sacrifice of Christ's death ought not to come after those to whom its fruit is to flow. On the contrary, he means the opposite: that its fruit flows even to those who lived before it in time, indeed back to the very origin of the world. For if the sacrifice of Christ could not be effective for those who are redeemed by it at a time later than they, then he could not have redeemed John the Baptist, nor perhaps others who died before his oblation, but only those who came after him in time. This not only is nowhere taught by Scripture, but is also contrary to the power and dignity of Christ's death and to its efficacy for earlier times. Indeed, on that view it would have been far more suitable for Christ to have died at the very origin of the world, so that by one single oblation he might anticipate all; and not at the end of the world, if it is so necessary to the power of his death that it should precede and not follow. Nor did the Apostle mean that the more often Christ had offered himself, the more our sins would have been expiated. He teaches that by the one oblation of Christ all sins are expiated, and that the redeemed, whether earlier or later, are redeemed from the origin of the world to its end, apo katabolēs, up to sōtērian. Chapter 10:12: one sacrifice for sins. Verse 14: for by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified [teteleiōken eis to diēnekes tous hagiazomenous]. Finally, I do not know what Socinus is imagining, when he insists so much on whether the Saviour comes before or after all those who are saved through him. The Apostle is not speaking of this, nor did the present argument require him to. For it makes no difference whether the salvation precedes or follows, provided it is certainly granted, and there can be no doubt about the truth and faithfulness of the Surety; and certainly there was no doubt about Christ's undertaking before God. He was destined from eternity, and was as surely promised under the Old Testament, and truly exhibited at his appointed time. These are his three periods, and just as all things flow from the destination, so those who were surely promised before the exhibition, and by the force of the exhibition that was to come infallibly, were all saved from the sins for which he at last offered himself to God as a sacrifice.

units.la: Arg. quintum est, ex remissione peccatorum quæ Patribus promissa, & contigit sub V. T. & neque extra Christum datur, neque sine vitæ æternæ spe, & gustu. Atque non tantum ex antecedentibus constat, quod ubi Christus cognoscitur, ibi quoque remissio peccatorum est per Christum, sed, præterquam implicite in promissionibus de divina bonitate, vita æterna, & Christo, etiam expresse peccatorum remissionem commemoravit Deus, & annunciavit populo suo Israelitico sæpius. Mich. vii. 18. Quis est Deus par tibi, condonans iniquitatem, & præteriens defectionem reliquiis possessionis tuæ: non retinens in æternum iram suam, eo quod delectetur benignitate. 19. Conversus miserebitur nostri, subiget iniquitates nostras: imo projecturus est in profunda maris omnia peccata istorum. Legitur quidem hoc apud posteriorem aliquem Prophetam, sed neutiquam ut novum aliquod, vel quod prioribus minus notum perspectumque fuerit: quin ex æterna derivatur Dei clementia & benignitate, quæ vnquam non fuit eadem, & celebrata antiquis æque ac posterioribus. Præterquam quod Dei misericordiam & bonitatem adeo prædicat Propheta, credit quoque ita facturum Deum, & condonaturum peccata. Neque nisi ex fide prodire ejusmodi confessio potuit; aut pro remissione impetranda, quæ variis in locis occurrunt, Sanctorum orationes. Ut & promissionem ejus à Deo factam, & fidem à populo ei habitam, & proinde suis precibus insertam ejus mentionem & desiderium, variis Scripturæ locis observemus.
units.tr: The fifth argument is drawn from the remission of sins which was promised to the Fathers, and was granted under the Old Testament, and is given neither apart from Christ nor without the hope and taste of eternal life. Not only does it follow from what has been said that where Christ is known, there also is the remission of sins through Christ; but apart from the fact that it is implied in the promises concerning the divine goodness, eternal life and Christ, God has also expressly recalled the remission of sins and has often announced it to his Israelite people. Micah 7:18: Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over the transgression of the remnant of your inheritance? He does not retain his anger for ever, because he delights in mercy. 19. He will turn again and have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; yes, he will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. This is indeed read in a later Prophet, but by no means as something new, or something less known or understood by the earlier ones. Rather it flows from the eternal clemency and goodness of God, which was never different, and was celebrated by the ancients as much as by the later ones. Besides, the Prophet so proclaims God's mercy and goodness that he also believes God will act so and will forgive sins. Nor could such a confession arise except from faith, or the prayers of the saints for obtaining forgiveness, which occur in various places. Let us observe in various places of Scripture both the promise made by God, and the faith placed in him by the people, and therefore the mention and desire of it inserted into their prayers.

units.la: 1 Reg. viii. 49. 50. Tum exaudis cœlos, statione habitationis tuæ, orationem eorum & deprecationem eorum, ut peragas causam eorum. Ut condones populo tuo quæ peccaverint contra te, & omnes defectiones eorum, quibus defecerint à te. Jesa. lv. 7. Derelinquat impius viam suam; & vir iniquus cogitationes suas, & revertatur ad Dominum, & miserebitur ejus, & ad Deum nostrum, quoniam multus est ad ignoscendum. Quid, annon hoc dictum toti populo? annon promissionem continet remissionis peccatorum impetrandæ ei, etiam iniquissimo, qui se convertat? Neque alteri ea offertur in Euangelio. Et ducto ex divina bonitate argumento, ostenditur, quam perpetuâ nitatur veritate & jure. Jesa. i. 18. Si fuerint peccata vestra ut coccinum, quasi nix dealbabuntur; & si fuerint rubra, quasi vermiculus, velut lana alba erunt. & cap. xliii. 25. Ego sum, ego sum ipse, qui deleo iniqui-tates tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Quibus docetur, non tantum quid Deus fecerit tum temporis, & quod nimirum peccata condonarit, quod quidem Adversarii agnoscunt; sed quoque quod id significarit populo, & palam fecerit se facturum, unde & credere homines id potuerint, & sperare. Cap. xliv. 22. De-levi ut nubem iniquitates tuas, & quasi nebulam peccata tua. Jerem. xxxiii. 8. Et emun-dabo illos ab omni sua iniquitate, in qua peccaverunt mihi, & propitius ero cunctis iniquitatibus eorum.
