Ac propterea David non in futuro tantum, sed praesenti beatitudinem praedicat hominis, cui Deus remisit peccata, & condonavit omnes iniquitates. Psalm. xxxii. 1. 2. & contra quando adversus aliquem vellent orare, & indignum significare divina gratia, precabantur, ne Deus illi remitteret peccata sua, Jerem. xviii. 23. Nam tu Jehova nosti totum consilium eorum contra me ad mortem, ne expiato iniquitatem eorum, & peccatum eorum a conspectu tuo ne deleto.
units.tr: 1 Kings 8:49, 50: Then hear in heaven, the place of your dwelling, their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause. Forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all their transgressions by which they have revolted from you. Isaiah 55:7: Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in pardoning. Is not this saying addressed to the whole people? Does it not contain a promise that forgiveness of sins is to be obtained, even by the most wicked, if he turns? It is not offered to anyone else in the Gospel. And from the argument drawn from the divine goodness, it is shown on what perpetual truth and right it rests. Isaiah 1:18: Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; and though they are red like crimson, they shall be like white wool. And chapter 43:25: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. By these passages it is taught not only what God did at that time, namely that he forgave sins, which indeed the Adversaries acknowledge, but also that he signified this to the people and made it plain that he would do so, whence men could believe it and hope for it. Isaiah 44:22: I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Jeremiah 33:8: And I will cleanse them from all their iniquity, by which they have sinned against me, and I will be propitious to all their iniquities. Therefore David proclaims the blessedness of the man not only in the future but in the present, the man to whom God has remitted sins and forgiven all iniquities: Psalm 32:1, 2. And on the contrary, when they wished to pray against someone and to signify that he was unworthy of divine grace, they prayed that God would not forgive him his sins: Jeremiah 18:23: For you, O Lord, know all their counsel against me to death; do not forgive their iniquity, and do not blot out their sin from your sight.

units.la: Crellius, lib. de Deo, cap. xxviii. Utitur autem Deus priori clementiae effectu, qui in remissione peccatorum cernitur, ergo omnes, qui resipiscunt, & vitam ad normam divinorum mandatorum emendant, ut ex sacris literis cuius liquet. Quamquam haec Dei benignitas novo potissimum foedere est inclusa, & promissis illius comprehensa. Nam quae ante Christum de remissione peccatorum extiterunt promissiones, foederi praesertim antiquo insertae, ea non uno modo restrictae fuerunt. Nam primum ad solos Israelitas revera pertinebant. deinde de remissione poenarum temporalium revera loquebantur: liberationem ab aeterna poena ita significabant, ut ipsum foedus antiquum significabat novum, & populus Israeliticus Christianum; atque adeo respectu illius temporis Deum ad poenam istam ab hominibus auferendam non obligabant. Deniq; respectu peccatorum condonandorum limitatae erant promissiones illae, praesertim si habeatur ratio singulorum ex populo, non populi generatim considerati. quae de re nunc non est fusius dicendi locus. Apud Prophetas ampliores quodammodo extant promissiones: sed in iis divinus spiritus ad novi foederis tempora magis respexit. quatenus autem eaedem ad Veteris tempora spe-ctant, ita sunt accipiendae, ut severitatem quidem illius aliquatenus relaxent, sed non penitus tollant, & sic ipsam foederis rationem evertant. Sufficit nobis, quod fatetur, & ante Christum promissiones de remissione peccatorum extitisse, & foederi quoque antiquo fuisse insertas, quamvis nec negemus in N. T. potissimum illas comprehensas, & ampliores hic occurrere & copiosiores. Ad solos Israelitas illae pertinuerunt sub V. T. quatenus totum Dei verbum ad illos spectabat, & non ad extraneos, Psalm. cxlvii. 19. 20. Deinde loquebantur quidem promissiones illae de remissione poenarum temporalium, sed ita ut nequaquam aeternas excluderent. Et non tantum quatenus vetus foedus novum significabat, vel populus Israeliticus Christianum, remissio poenarum aeternarum nota ibi fuit, sed vi promissionum ipsarum contenta & propo-sita. Tum quid adeo solliciti sunt Adversarii de poenis aeternis, supra temporales, quas in nullo poenarum sensu constituunt, duntaxat in perpetuatione temporalium, ut aeternum maneant homines annihilati? nisi ut quid videantur dicere potius ad-versus nos, quam sententiae suae aliquid explicare. Denique non tantum aliquibus in populo, sed omnibus fuisse eas generatim & promiscue expositas, ex singulis manifestum.
units.tr: Crellius, book on God, chapter 28. God uses the first effect of his clemency, which is seen in the forgiveness of sins; therefore all who repent and amend their lives according to the rule of the divine commandments are forgiven, as is clear from the holy letters. Yet this goodness of God is chiefly enclosed within the New Covenant and comprehended in its promises. For the promises of forgiveness of sins that existed before Christ, especially those inserted into the Old Covenant, were restricted in more than one way. First, they truly belonged only to the Israelites. Second, they truly spoke of the remission of temporal punishments; they signified deliverance from eternal punishment only in the way that the Old Covenant signified the New, and the people of Israel signified the Christian people. And so, with respect to that time, they did not oblige God to remove that punishment from men. Finally, with respect to the forgiveness of sins, those promises were limited, especially if one considers individuals of the people and not the people taken generally. This is not the place to say more about that matter. Among the Prophets the promises are in some way fuller, but in them the divine Spirit looked more towards the times of the New Covenant. Insofar as they refer to the times of the Old, they must be understood so as to relax its severity to some extent, but not to remove it altogether, and so to overturn the very nature of the covenant. It is enough for us that they admit that the promises of forgiveness of sins existed before Christ and were also inserted into the Old Covenant, although we do not deny that they are chiefly comprehended in the New Testament, and that they occur there more fully and more abundantly. Those promises pertained only to the Israelites under the Old Testament, insofar as the whole word of God was directed to them and not to strangers (Psalm 147:19, 20). Next, those promises did indeed speak of the remission of temporal punishments, but in such a way that by no means did they exclude eternal ones. And not only insofar as the Old Covenant signified the New, or the Israelite people signified the Christian people, was the remission of eternal punishments known there, but it was also contained in and set forth by the very force of the promises. Then why are our opponents so anxious about eternal punishments, which they place above temporal ones and which they establish in no sense of punishment, except in the perpetuation of temporal things, so that men remain annihilated forever? Unless perhaps they appear to say something against us rather than to explain their own opinion. Finally, it is clear from individual cases that these promises were set forth not only to some in the people but to all, generally and without distinction.

units.la: Socinus, de Servatore, part. iii. cap. ii. explicans Dei verba ad Cainum. Ge-nes. iv. 7. Nonne, si bene feceris, erit acceptatio? (seu remissio, sive etiam elatio) Gen. 4. v. 7. Ex quibus verbis, quamquam variè ab interpretibus explicatis, manifestè apparet, non alia potissimum ratione Abelem Deo carum fuisse, nisi quia ejus opera erant justa; Cainum vero minimè, quia ejus opera, ut idem Johannes ait, mala erant: Et simul de ea divina liberalitate, de qua agimus, liquidò constat; cum Deus Caino benefacienti, ac resipiscenti veniam delictorum sponte offerat, atque promittat, &c. Quocirca per interrogationem ea sententia expri-mitur: mitur: Nonne;si bene fecerit, &c. quasi hoc natura ipsa omnes docet, videlicet, Deum libe-raliter peccata resipiscentibus condonare. — Quod autem de Abele[?] dictum est, cum jussum fuisse, idem de innumerabilibus aliis scriptum extat. Ex quo aperte colligitur, eos, qui pure & innocenter vivunt, divina benignitate delictorum gratuitam veniam consequi. Si hoc aperte inde colligitur, ergo aperte ibi extat: & proinde in V. T. satis apertae sunt de peccatorum remissione promissiones: & de eo diserte populum a Deo admonitum scri-bit, pag. seq. Porrò autem non satis habuit Deus hac ratione, qua diximus, clementissimum se ab ipso ferme orbe condito delinquentibus praebere; sed sub ipsa Lege voluit etiam tantae suae beneficentiae populum diserte admonere. Nam, tametsi in ipsa Lege ferenda, in ipsoque foedere sanciendo, non nisi quibusdam levioribus delictis, ut supra visum est, expiatoria sacrificia constituisset, caetera vero graviora severe puniri, & vindicari praecepisset; tamen, praeter eas sententias, quas saepius luculentissime populo inculcari voluit, se videlicet tardum ad iram esse, & multum misericordia, tandem, ut Moses populum, postquam illi, nisi a simulacrorum cultu se impollutum conservasset, dispersionem inter populos, & multa alia mala minatus fuerat, ad hunc modum alloqueretur, effecit. Cum fuerit tibi angustia, invenerintque te omnia ista in novissimis diebus; si reversus fueris ad Iehovam Deum tuum, & parueris voci ejus, quia Deus misericors est Iehova Deus tuus, non derelinquet te; nec disperdet te; nec obliviscetur pacti patrum tuorum, de quo juravit illis, Deut. 4. v. 30. Et rursus cap. 30. in ipso initio: Erit autem, cum evenerint tibi omnia verba haec, benedictio, & maledictio, quas proposui tibi, & reduxeris ad cor tuum in cunctis gentibus, ad quas expulerit te Iehova Deus tuus, & conversus fueris ad Iehovam Deum tuum, obedierisque voci ejus per omnia, ut ego praecipio tibi hodie, tu & filii tui toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua; tum reducet Iehova Deus tuus captivitatem tuam, & miserebitur tui, & conversus congregabit te de cunctis populis, ad quos disperserit te Iehova Deus tuus, &c. Promittitur igitur Moses populo, si, postquam Deus eum, pro-pter ipsorum delicta inter gentes dispersisset, & captivum duci voluisset, poenitentiam suorum delictorum egisset, & conversus ad ipsum Deum fuisset, futurum, ut Deus ipsorum misereretur, & a captivitate eos liberaret, & sic eis delicta condonaret. Deinceps adjungit Scri-pturae loca haec, Neh. ix. Psalm. xxxii. Omitto ea, inquit, quae plenissime & apertis-sime hac de re scripta sunt apud Ezechielem cap. 18. & 33. Haec Socinus, quando adver-sus satisfactionem disputat, ut ostendat, Deum liberaliter peccata remittere, absque eâ: è quibus, quae de peccatorum condonatione, in V. T. à Deo promissa, praestitaque, illa nunc capimus, & in praesentem usum applicamus.
units.tr: Socinus, on the Saviour, part 3, chapter 2, explaining God's words to Cain (Genesis 4:7): Shall it not be, if you do well, that you will be accepted? (or forgiven, or even lifted up) (Gen. 4:7). From these words, although explained in various ways by the interpreters, it is plainly evident that Abel was dear to God for no other reason chiefly than that his works were just, whereas Cain's were not at all, because his works were evil, as John also says. And at the same time it is clearly established from them what the divine generosity we are discussing is: since God freely offers and promises pardon of offences to Cain, if he does well and repents, and so on. Hence that sentence is expressed by a question: "Shall it not be, if he does well," and so on, as if nature itself teaches everyone that God freely pardons sins to those who repent. But as to what is said of Abel, that he was commanded to do so, the same is written in the case of countless others. From this it is openly gathered that those who live purely and innocently obtain the free pardon of their offences through the divine kindness. If this is openly gathered from there, then it is openly contained there; and therefore in the Old Testament the promises of forgiveness of sins are sufficiently clear, and he writes that the people were clearly admonished by God about it, on the following page. Moreover, God was not content in this way, as we have said, to show himself most merciful to offenders almost from the very founding of the world; but even under the Law itself he wished to admonish his people plainly of so great a beneficence of his. For although, in enacting the Law itself and sanctioning the covenant itself, he had appointed expiatory sacrifices only for certain lighter offences, as was seen above, and had commanded that the other, graver ones be severely punished and avenged, nevertheless, apart from those sayings which he wished to be most clearly and frequently impressed upon the people, namely that he is slow to anger and abundant in mercy, he finally brought it about, as Moses, after threatening the people with dispersion among the nations and many other evils unless they kept themselves undefiled from the worship of images, addressed them in this way: "When you are in distress, and all these things have found you in the latter days, if you return to Jehovah your God and obey his voice, because Jehovah your God is a merciful God, he will not forsake you, nor destroy you, nor forget the covenant of your fathers, which he swore to them" (Deut. 4:30). And again, chapter 30, at the very beginning: "And it shall be, when all these words, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before you, have come upon you, and you have taken them to heart among all the nations to which Jehovah your God has driven you, and you have returned to Jehovah your God and obeyed his voice in everything, as I command you today, you and your sons, with all your heart and all your soul, then Jehovah your God will restore your captivity, and will have mercy on you, and will gather you again from all the peoples to which Jehovah your God has scattered you," and so on. Moses therefore promises the people that if, after God had scattered them among the nations on account of their sins, and had willed them to be led away captive, they repented of their offences and turned to God himself, God would have mercy on them, deliver them from captivity, and so forgive them their sins. Next he adds these passages of Scripture: Nehemiah 9; Psalm 32. "I omit," he says, "those things which are written most fully and most plainly on this matter in Ezekiel, chapters 18 and 33." So Socinus, when he disputes against satisfaction, in order to show that God freely remits sins without it. From these passages, we now take those things which God promised and granted in the Old Testament concerning the forgiveness of sins, and apply them to our present purpose.

units.la: Ubi est salus hominum peccatorum, ibi est remissio: sed in V. T. fuit illorum salus; ergo & remissio peccatorum. Major certa est & indubitata, quia sine remissio-ne nulla omnino est salus; & David scribit hominis beatitudinem, cui Deus non im-putat peccata. Minor etiam vera: nam salvatos Patres quis dubitet, aut velit credere esse damnatos, quorum vita probata à Deo fuit, & sacris consignata litteris? Imo & perfecta ibi plenaque peccatorum data fuit remissio, quia & plena salus, & perfecta fuit justificatio. Ubi justificatio perfecta, ibi & perfecta est peccatorum remissio: sed in V. T. perfecta fuit justificatio: ergo. Justificatio ubicunque est, perfecta est, quaeque imperfecta non est justificatio. Deus quando peccatorem justificat, justificat eum plene. Non enim quod Pontificii somniant, remissa culpâ Deus poenam retinet, aut non ex animo & prorsus eam delet. Sunt quidem in sanctifica-tione gradus, non vero in justificatione. Et remissionem peccatorum non tantum testamentum varia in V. Testamento, sive promissam variis modis, sive commemoratam & prædicatam, sive rogatam à Deo & petitam, unde tum temporis non ignotum vel negatum ipsis beneficium illud fuisse colligitur, & non tantum respectu eorum qui sub N. T. demum victuri essent, commemoratum: quin istis verbis significatum, expressumque passim fuit, ut perfectam tum etiam temporis viguisse peccatorum remissionem, certum hinc sit atque perspicuum. Dicuntur tecta ipsorum fuisse peccata, deleta, non imputata, oblita Deo, & rejecta post tergum, ac in profundum maris quasi submersa: quæ ubi sunt, quis negat aut remissa fuisse peccata, aut homines perfecte justificatos?
units.tr: Where there is salvation of sinful men, there is remission; but under the Old Testament there was salvation for them; therefore there was also remission of sins. The major premise is certain and indubitable, because without remission there is no salvation at all; and David writes of the blessedness of the man to whom God does not impute sins. The minor premise is also true: for who would doubt, or wish to believe, that the Fathers were damned, whose lives were approved by God and consigned to the holy letters? Indeed, complete and full remission of sins was given there too, because their salvation was full and their justification perfect. Where justification is perfect, there the remission of sins is also perfect; but under the Old Testament justification was perfect; therefore. Wherever there is justification, it is perfect, and whatever is imperfect is not justification. When God justifies a sinner, he justifies him fully. For it is not, as the Papists dream, that after the guilt is remitted God retains the punishment, or does not blot it out wholeheartedly and entirely. There are indeed degrees in sanctification, but not in justification. And the remission of sins was not only testified by the covenant in the Old Testament, whether promised in various ways, or recalled and proclaimed, or asked for and sought from God, from which it is gathered that this benefit was not unknown or denied to them at that time, and that it was recalled not only with respect to those who were to live under the New Testament; but indeed it was signified and expressed by these words, scattered throughout, so that it is certain and clear from this that the full remission of sins flourished at that time too. Their sins are said to have been covered, blotted out, not imputed, forgotten by God, cast behind his back, and as it were sunk into the depths of the sea: where these things are, who denies either that sins were remitted or that men were perfectly justified?

units.la: Nullum ergo, dices, discrimen constituendum inter V. ac N. T. venit? omnino, inquam; sed Euangelii respectu, hic & ibi administrati, circumstantiale & accidentale tantum, non substantiale: non quasi remissio peccatorum, aut quæ per eam fit justificatio, non viguisset etiam illic; sed tum respectu solutionis λύτρᾳ[?], quod solvendum ibi fuit, nunc solutum est; & beneficiorum inde sequutorum claritate, & copia; & communiori ad quascunque gentes & homines diffusione, quæ non item fuerunt sub Testamento veteri. Cętcrum in remissione ipsa, ejusque veritate oppositio Testamenti seu temporis utriusque constituenda non est. Ergo rem distingue, & rei modum: res fuit utrobique ad salvandos homines eadem, modo & œconomiâ dispari. Atque à modo in rem transfire, vel quia non idem dispensatæ gratiæ utrobiq; fuit modus, negare ipsam manifestatam fuisse oblatamque, est perperam transfire de genere in genus.
units.tr: So, you will say, no distinction at all is to be drawn between the Old and New Testaments? Certainly there is, I answer, but with respect to the Gospel, which was administered here and there, the difference is circumstantial and accidental only, not substantial. It is not that forgiveness of sins, or the justification that comes through it, did not flourish back then too. The difference lies in the payment [λύτρᾳ], which had to be paid then and has now been paid; in the brightness and abundance of the benefits that followed from it; and in its wider spread to all nations and peoples, which was not likewise the case under the Old Testament. But the opposition between the Testaments, or between the two periods, must not be set up in the forgiveness itself or in its reality. So distinguish the thing from the manner of the thing. The thing was the same in both for saving men; the manner and economy were different. To move from the manner to the thing, and to deny that the thing itself was revealed and offered, because the manner of dispensing grace was not the same in both, is to pass wrongly from one genus to another.

units.la: Quem proposuit Deus, inquit Apostolus de Christo, Rom. iii. 25. 26. placamentum per fidem in ejus sanguine, ad ostensionem justitiæ suæ, per remissionem παρέσιν peccatorum ante factorum: in Dei longanimitate, ad ostensionem justitiæ ejus, hoc nunc tempore. Christus, qui olim promissus fuit & adumbratus multis modis placamentum ἱλαστή-ριον[?], ἱλασμὸς futurus, tandem id in temporis plenitudine factus fuit præstititq; quod promissum de ipso fuit, & persolvit λύτρον: qua persolutione uti satisfactum divinæ justitiæ, quam in exactione & admissione pretii illius ostendit; sic accepto solutionis, hactenus promissæ, vero nunc pretio, ratihabuit remissionem antea factam, vi hujus certo aliquando futuri λύτρῳ, & sic, uti olim in fidejussione sponsoris certa, ita nunc reali exhibitione πάρεσις fuit τῶν γεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων. Nullo autem modo πάρεσις ista τῇ ἀφέσει opponenda, quum sint synonyma, qualia hujus rei permulta: & πάρεσις hæc non in V. T. sed N. T. dicitur ab Apostolo exhibita in Christo ἱλασηρίῳ ἐν τῷ αἵματι, πρὸς ἔνδειξιν τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐτοῦ, ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ. Quare passim πάρεσιν vertunt remissionem, & exponunt Interpretes non de remissionis modo, qualis fuit in V.T. contradistincte ad Novum, sed de remissione, vel ejus τελείωσιν[?] facta in sanguine Christi jam fuso. Arabs: propter remissionem peccatorum jam commissorum, tolerante Deo, ad patefaciendam justitiam suam in hoc tempore. Quemadmodum Apostolus dixit Heb. ix. 16. in Christi morte factam fuisse ἀπολυτρωσιν τῶν[?] ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παρα-[?] βάσεων[?].
units.tr: "Whom God set forth," says the Apostle of Christ, Rom. 3:25-26, "as a propitiation [ἱλαστήριον] through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness, for the remission [πάρεσις] of sins that are past, in the forbearance of God; to declare, I say, his righteousness at this present time." Christ, who was promised of old and foreshadowed in many ways as the propitiation [ἱλασμός] to come, at last in the fullness of time was made that propitiation and accomplished what had been promised concerning him, and paid the ransom [λύτρον]. By that payment he made satisfaction to divine justice, which he showed in the demanding and accepting of that price. Thus, by accepting the real price of the payment, promised until then, he ratified the remission granted earlier, by virtue of that ransom which was certain to be paid at some time in the future; and so, as once it was certain through the surety's guarantee, now by the actual performance the passing over [πάρεσις] of the sins already committed has taken place. Yet this passing over must in no way be set against forgiveness [ἄφεσις], since they are synonyms, as many such pairs are in this matter. And this passing over is not said by the Apostle to have been displayed under the Old Testament but under the New, in Christ, as a propitiatory [ἱλασηρίῳ] in his blood, to show forth his righteousness at the present time [ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ]. Hence the translators commonly render passing over as remission, and the interpreters explain it not of the mere manner of remission, as it was under the Old Testament in contrast to the New, but of the remission made complete [τελείωσιν] in the blood of Christ now shed. The Arabic version: "On account of the remission of sins already committed, God forbearing, to make known his righteousness in this time." Just as the Apostle said, Heb. 9:15, that in the death of Christ there was made a redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν] of the transgressions [παραβάσεων] committed under the first covenant.

units.la: Denique si distinctio aliqua inter πάρεσιν, quasi V. T. magis propriam ; & ἄφεσιν Novi facere velimus, intelligatur oppositio quod ad modum remissionis non vero quod ad ipsam: neque negetur, remissionem peccatorum tum etiam a Deo donatam fuisse, quamvis non illo modo, qui post actu solutum a Christo pretium, viguit sub Novo.
units.tr: Finally, if we wish to make any distinction between passing over [πάρεσις], as more proper to the Old Testament, and forgiveness [ἄφεσις] of the New, let the opposition be understood as concerning the manner of remission and not the remission itself. Nor is it to be denied that the remission of sins was also granted by God in those days, although not in that manner which, after the price was actually paid by Christ, took effect under the New.

units.la: Heb. x. 2. Quandoquidem cessassent offerri hostiae, propterea quod nullam amplius habuissent peccatorum conscientiam offerrentes, semel purificati: verum in iis hostiis commemoratio peccatorum fiebat quotannis. Quibus exponit, quod dixerat versu praecedente primo, quod ex illa caeremoniali sacrificiotum tantummodo umbram habuerit rerum, & futurorum bonorum, inter quae etiam peccatorum remissio, non hanc ipsam continuerit rem. Quod verissimum, nam ex illa caeremoniarum lege, vel sacrificiis sive quotidianis, sive anniversariis non fluebat remissio: neque enim id poterat sanguis hircorum & taurorum, v. 4. sed ex Evangelio derivabatur ad Patres, & ex Christo ipsis promisso. Pone Patres, & fideles V. T.: his uti salvatio, ita justificatio & remissio peccatorum contigit. at unde? nequaquam vi sacrificiorum propria vel intrinseca: hoc quippe impossibile est ut efficiat sanguis animalium sacrificatorum; sed ex Christo fluxit, & promisso illis, & sacrificiis illis designato: quae propterea habebant non αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα rei aut boni istius salutaris, seu solutionis pro peccato futurae μελλόντων, sed duntaxat σκιὰν: corpus autem erat Christus, Col. ii. Jam quia negatur, ex sacrificiis profluxisse beneficium remissionis, non propterea negandum vel prorsus fuisse ibi, vel fluxisse ex Christo, & promisa certoque futura aliquando ejus solutione & satisfactione. Quod si hostiae potuissent remittere peccata, & mundare sacrificantes, non necesse fuisset illas repeti quotannis. Quae jam repetitio testimonium fuit earum invaliditatis. Uti Christi contra sacrificium semel peractum iterari nil necesse fuit, quia unica oblatione perfecit in perpetuum sanctificatos. verf. 14. Remissio autem peccatorum evenit illis ex promissione Novi foederis, non ex Veteri: illudque Apostolus adfert verf. 17. & peccatorum ipsorum & iniquitatum ipsorum non recordabor amplius. Cujus promissionis vi remissa peccata fuerunt sive olim, sive nunc, quibus ea remittuntur unquam. Eo solum discrimine, quod vi solutionis futurae aut praestandae a Christo remissa fuerint in Test. Veteri; at praestitae vi jam sub Novo. Vbi autem eorum remissio, non ἔτι amplius oblatio pro peccatis. Id est, uti si per oblationes remissio potuisset obtineri, non necesse fuisset illas amplius retineri aut repeti; sic postquam per Christi oblationem ea vere obtenta fuit, nulla amplius opus est: notandum illud ἔτι: quemadmodum verf. 26. οὐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν θυσία. non amplius relinquitur hostia: sed tremenda expectatio judicii, &c.
units.tr: Heb. 10:2: "For would they not have ceased to be offered, because the worshippers, once purified, would have had no more consciousness of sins? But in those sacrifices there is a remembrance of sins made every year." With these words he explains what he had said in the first verse of the previous verse: that the ceremonial sacrifices had only the shadow of the things, and of the good things to come, among which is the remission of sins, but not the very reality itself. This is most true. For from that law of ceremonies, whether from the daily sacrifices or from the yearly ones, remission did not flow; for the blood of goats and bulls could not do it (v. 4). It was derived rather from the Gospel, passed on to the Fathers, and from Christ promised to them. Take the Fathers and the faithful of the Old Testament: for them, as salvation, so justification and remission of sins came about. But how? Certainly not by the proper or intrinsic power of the sacrifices, for it is impossible that the blood of slaughtered animals should effect this; it flowed from Christ, who was promised to them and foreshadowed by those sacrifices. Therefore the sacrifices did not have the very image of that saving good, or of the payment for sin to come [μελλόντων], but only a shadow [σκιὰν]; the body, however, was Christ (Col. 2). Now, because it is denied that the benefit of remission flowed from the sacrifices, it must not be denied either that it existed there at all, or that it flowed from Christ, and from his payment and satisfaction promised and certain to come at some time. But if the victims could have remitted sins and cleansed the worshippers, there would have been no need for them to be repeated every year. That repetition was in fact a witness to their weakness. Just as there was no need at all to repeat the offering of Christ against the sacrifice once made, because by one offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified (v. 14). But remission of sins came to them from the promise of the New Covenant, not of the Old; and the Apostle brings forward that promise in v. 17: and their sins and their iniquities I will remember no more. By virtue of this promise sins were remitted, whether formerly or now, for those to whom they are ever remitted. The only difference is that by virtue of a future payment to be made by Christ they were remitted under the Old Testament, but by virtue of a payment now made under the New. But where there is remission of these, there is no longer any offering for sin. That is, just as if remission could have been obtained through offerings, there would have been no need to keep on or repeat them; so, since through Christ's offering it has truly been obtained, there is no further need. Note the word no longer [ἔτι]: as in v. 26, there remains no longer a sacrifice for sins [οὐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν θυσία]. No further victim remains, but only the dreadful expectation of judgement, etc.

units.la: Peccatorum ἄφεσις consideratur duplici modo, vel qualis fuit ante Christum exhibitum sub V. T. vel qualis post in Novo: ante solutum actu pretium, vel postea: semper autem ex uno Christo, & gratiae in ipso foedere profluxit ea, non aliunde: at prout sub caeremoniarum usu antea impartitus eam fuit Deus, confiscebat cum sacrificiorum jugi oblatione; non vero postea soluto nunc pretio: tum quia perfectio ejus iterationem non permittit, tum quia usus spiritualis, post Christum, ceremoniarum umbras non patitur. Ergo ἀφεσις considerata ab Apostolo in Christo, & in foedere gratiae, prout non in V. T. sed μὴ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας fuit admiadministrata, dicit, eâ politâ non amplius esse hostiam pro peccatis, non aliam post Christum, neque ceremonialis alicujus, uti olim, ultrà usum. Quare versio Æthiopica legit: & ubi ita illis remittitur, non est amplius oblatio pro peccato. Quemadmodum dixit, cap. ix. 8. quod Spiritus significarit, nondum apertam fuisse viam ad sacrarium, stante adhuc priori tabernaculo: quod non est; quod prorsus occlusa via ad cœlum fuerit piis sub V. Test.; sed quod non potuerit ipsis nisi sub obvolucro cæremoniarum & rituum, sub figuris, non ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ [?] πρόσωπῳ [?] patere, uti nobis nunc sub T. N. II Cor. ii. 16. similiter remissio peccatorum aliaque novi fœderis beneficia, non quidem negata illis fuerunt quod ad substantiam, sed quod ad modum, alio modo iis & significata & indulta, ac nobis, nimirum sub σκιαῖς [?] & oneroso rituum variorum ac figurarum apparatu. Ἄφεσις vero uti nunc conceditur, rebus omnibus τελειωμένοις [?], nullam secum patitur ἐπὶ τὴν περιφορὰν [?].
units.tr: The forgiveness of sins [ἄφεσις] may be considered in two ways: either as it was before Christ was exhibited, under the Old Testament, or as it is after him, under the New; before the price was actually paid, or after. Yet in both cases it flowed from Christ alone and from the grace of the covenant in him, and from nowhere else. But in the way God bestowed it before, under the use of ceremonies, it was tied to the continual offering of sacrifices; not so after the price has now been paid. The reasons are, first, that its perfection does not admit of repetition, and second, that spiritual use after Christ does not tolerate the shadows of ceremonies. Therefore the forgiveness [ἄφεσις] considered by the Apostle as in Christ and in the covenant of grace, as it was administered not in the Old Testament but in those days [μὴ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας], says that, once this is in place, there is no longer any offering for sins, no other after Christ, nor any ceremonial one beyond its use, as there was once. Hence the Ethiopic version reads: and where it is thus remitted to them, there is no longer an offering for sin. Just as he said in ch. 9:8, which the Spirit signified, that the way into the sanctuary was not yet opened while the former tabernacle still stood. This does not mean that the way to heaven was utterly closed to the pious under the Old Testament; it means that it could not lie open to them except under the veil of ceremonies and rites, under figures, and not with unveiled face [ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώπῳ], as it lies open to us now under the New Testament (2 Cor. 3:16). Similarly, remission of sins and the other benefits of the New Covenant were not indeed denied to them as to substance, but as to manner: they were signified and granted to them in another way than to us, namely under shadows [σκιαῖς] and the burdensome apparatus of various rites and figures. But forgiveness, as it is now granted, with all things brought to completion [τελειωμένοις], suffers no turning around again [ἐπὶ τὴν περιφορὰν].

units.la: Argum. sextum, ex fide veterum, tantopere in Scripturis commemorata: Quorum fides eadem fuit re & substantia, cum nostra, ii & promissiones re ac substantiâ easdem habuerunt, & religione: sed Patrum in V. T. fides substantiâ eadem fuit, cum nostra: ergo. Probatur assumtio, tum ex communi descriptione & conditione simili ac effectis fidei ipsorum, cum nostra; tum speciatim quia crediderunt quoque in Christum, peccatorum remissionem, & vitam æternam: quare quomodo nos, eodem pacto & illi fuerunt justificati. Hæc vero probanda nunc singulis Scripturæ locis sunt.
units.tr: Sixth argument, from the faith of the ancients, so greatly commemorated in the Scriptures: Their faith was the same as ours in reality and substance, and they had promises that were the same as ours in reality and substance, and in religion. But the faith of the Fathers in the Old Testament was the same in substance as ours. Therefore... The assumption is proved both from the common description, similar condition and effects of their faith compared with ours, and specifically because they too believed in Christ, the remission of sins and eternal life; so they were justified in the same way as we are. These points must now be proved from individual passages of Scripture.

units.la: Ac primum illud quidem constat satis manifeste ex cap. xi. ad Hebræos, ubi Apostolus de fide Veterum integrum texit catalogum, & auream verè Legendam, quę ita ad fideles applicat suos, ut nil distare inter utrorumque fidem evidentissime ostendat. Nam primò cap. x. 38. ubi hujus periodi est exordium, citat illud ex Habakuko Propheta, Iustus fide vivet: quod de fide N. T. dictum etiam nemo potest dissiteri, & fundamentum passim ponitur ab Apostolo disputationis de fide, ac justificatione: & exeo pergit dicere versu seq. ultimo cap. præcedentis, nos sumus non defectionis ad interitum, sed fidei ad redemtionem animæ. Et sic vers. 1. cap. xi. Est autem fides, speratarum rerum hypostasis. Syrus, certitudo de iis rebus, quæ sunt in spe. Sequitur apud Apostolum, rerum non visarum elenchus. Ejus enim testimonium reportarunt antiqui. Connectit Apostolus utrorumque fidem, ut eandem, & naturæ ac definitionis ejusdem. Tum progreditur ad prædicandam fidem Abelis, Enochi, & generale hoc interse- rit axioma, vers. 6. sine fide autem impossibile est placere Deo. Credere enim oportet accedentem Deo, quod est, & quod quærentibus ipsum existit remunerator. Quâ remuneratione, nisi rerum speratarum, nec visarum, quas fide constanti ad finem usque vitæ homo persequitur & ambit? ea etenim quæ videntur, temporaria: quæ vero non videntur, æterna. II Cor. iv. 18. & Hebr. xi. 26. de Mose, quod contemnum Christi præstulerit thesauris Ægypti: respiciebat enim ad remunerationem. De Noacho dicit, quod justitiæ quæ secundum fidem fuerit hæres. vers. 7. de Abrahamo, vers. 10. quod civitatem expectavit habentem fundamenta, cujus artifex & fabricator Deus. id est, ædificium ex Deo, domum non manufactam, æternam in cœlis, II Cor. v. 1. eandem, quam nunc exspectamus & nos. Vers. 13. juxta fidem obierunt omnes isti, non accipientes promissionem, sed de longinquo eas videntes, & crediderunt, & amplexi sunt. vel, salutantes, ut Schlichtingius, in hunc locum, inquit: non autem vel solorum terrenorum & vitæ mundanæ promissiones illis factæ, vel in sola illa intenti fuerunt, sed & salutarium in Christo; quæ procul viderunt, sive cognoverunt, & crediderunt, & amplexi fuerunt ut sua: & declararunt abunde, quod patriam quærerent, vid. illam cœlestem. vers. 14. & meliorem defiderarunt, hoc est coelestem. vers. 14. & propterea se Deus dixit, ipsorum Deum esse, paraverat enim illis civitatem. vers. 16. ut hoc, sive hujus rei promissio verbis illis con-tineatur & significetur. Etiam in resurrectionem mortuorum fide sua respexisse il-los, docet vers. 35. ut meliorem assequerentur liberationem. vers. 39. atque illi omnes testi-monium fidei retulerunt. Videmus ergo, & fidei nomine illos præsertim commendari, & eadem credidisse ac respectasse, quæ nos, & fidei eandem utrobique, quod ad essentialia, esse rationem.
units.tr: First, this is clear enough from chapter 11 of Hebrews, where the Apostle weaves an entire catalogue of the faith of the ancients, a truly golden legend, and applies it to his own believers in such a way that he very plainly shows there is no difference between the faith of the one and the other. For first, in chapter 10, verse 38, where this passage begins, he quotes from the prophet Habakkuk: The just shall live by faith. No one can deny that this was said of New Testament faith, and the Apostle everywhere lays it down as the foundation of his discussion of faith and justification. From this he goes on in the last verse of the preceding chapter: We are not of those who draw back to perdition, but of faith to the saving of the soul. And so in verse 1 of chapter 11: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for. The Syriac has: certainty about those things which are in hope. There follows in the Apostle: the evidence of things not seen, for by it the men of old obtained their testimony. The Apostle links the faith of both, as being of the same nature and definition. Then he proceeds to commend the faith of Abel and Enoch, and inserts this general axiom in verse 6: But without faith it is impossible to please God. For he who comes to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. What is this reward, if not of things hoped for, and not seen, which a man pursues and embraces with steadfast faith until the end of life? For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal (2 Cor. 4:18). And of Moses (Heb. 11:26) that he preferred the reproach of Christ to the treasures of Egypt, for he looked to the reward. Of Noah it says that he became heir of the righteousness which is by faith (v. 7). Of Abraham (v. 10) that he waited for a city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God, that is, a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor. 5:1), the same that we also now look for. Verse 13: According to faith all these died, not having received the promises, but seeing them afar off, and they believed and embraced them; or, greeting them, as Schlichting says on this passage. Nor were the promises made to them only of earthly things and this worldly life, nor were they intent only on those; they also (concerned themselves with) the promises of salvation in Christ, which they saw from afar, or recognised, and believed and embraced as their own; and they declared abundantly that they sought a homeland, namely that heavenly one. Verse 14: and desired a better, that is, a heavenly. Verse 16: and therefore God is said to be their God, for he had prepared for them a city, so that this promise, or the promise of this thing, is contained and signified in those words. He also teaches in verse 35 that they looked, by their faith, to the resurrection of the dead, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Verse 39: and all these bore witness to the faith. We see, therefore, that they are commended especially by the name of faith, that they believed and looked to the same things as we do, and that the faith is of the same nature on both sides, as far as its essentials go.

units.la: Excipiunt, illo capite doceri naturam fidei generalis, non specialis, in Christum Iesum. Smalcius, adversus Frantzium, Disp. vi. de Bon. operib. pag. 207.
units.tr: They object that this chapter teaches the nature of general faith, not of special faith in Christ Jesus. Smalcius, against Frantzius, Disp. 6 on good works, p. 207.

units.la: Thesi autem illa inspecta, manifeste appa-ret, autorem illum naturam & proprietatem fidei generalem, quæ scilicet omnibus Dei cultoribus competat, describere volui te[?]. Quæ est, quod ea, quæ Deus revelat aut promittit, licet nondum apparent[?], vel quæ quis futura speraret, licet ea Deus nec revelaverit, nec promiserit, habeat pro ita certis, ut nihil eorum causa facere detrectet. Hanc fidem in omnibus, quos ibi commemorat, fuisse docet, & tandem etiam Christianis persuadere conatur, ut ex ini-tio cap. 12. quod est conclusio præcedentium, apparet.
units.tr: But if one looks at that thesis, it clearly appears that the author wished to describe the nature and property of general faith, which belongs, namely, to all worshippers of God. It is this: that they hold as so certain those things which God reveals or promises, though they do not yet appear, or which someone would hope for in future, though God has neither revealed nor promised them, that they refuse to do nothing for their sake. He teaches that this faith was in all whom he mentions there, and finally tries to persuade Christians of it too, as appears from the beginning of chapter 12, which is the conclusion of what precedes.

units.la: Resp. Et fidei generalem describit Autor naturam, & applicatam tum promissis quibuscunque aliis, tum etiam spiritualibus in Christo, & salutis, sive patriæ cœlestis ac æternæ. Quando dixit ἐλπι-ζομένων ὑπόστασις, non voluit fidem esse eorum, quæ quis futura sperat, licet ea Deus nec revelaverit, nec promiserit, & tamen habeat pro certis: nam, ut fides, quæ pro basi ponitur eorum, quæ sperantur, nequit esse, nisi reclinet in promissiones; ita spem fundare non potest, nisi sperandorum certitudinem habeat divinam, non certe eorum potest esse hy-poftasis. Etenim intelligitur hic spes & fides divina, quæ proinde divina autoritate rerum ad fidem & spem revelatarum niti prorsus debet. Denique non possunt pro certis haberi in divinis ea quæ Deus nec revelavit, nec promisit: unde enim eorum derivaretur certitudo? Ut enim divina omnino a Deo pendent, ita eorum certitudo aliunde esse nulla potest, nisi ex divina revelatione. Haud magis quam ut in somniis & conjecturis ponas certitudinem, quæ ex cerebro finguntur, & nullam penitus habent hypostasim, non fidem pro hypostasi: atque ita loquuntur Nostri, ut cum vanorum hominum somniis & conjecturis rem illam totam componant.
units.tr: Reply. The author describes the nature of general faith, applied both to any other promises and also to spiritual ones in Christ, and to salvation, or the heavenly and eternal homeland. When he said "the substance of things hoped for", he did not mean that faith is of those things which someone hopes for in future, although God has neither revealed nor promised them, and yet holds them as certain. For faith, which is put as the basis of the things hoped for, cannot be such unless it rests on promises; and so it cannot ground hope unless it has the certainty of the things to be hoped for from divine authority. It certainly cannot be their substance. For here is understood hope and faith that is divine, which must therefore rest entirely on the divine authority of things revealed for faith and hope. Finally, those things which God has neither revealed nor promised cannot be held as certain in divine matters: for from what source would their certainty be derived? As divine matters depend wholly on God, so their certainty can come from nowhere except divine revelation. It is no more possible than to place certainty in dreams and guesses, which are invented by the brain and have no substance at all, and to call faith their substance. And so our opponents speak, as though they put that whole matter together from the dreams and conjectures of vain men.

units.la: Quod si esset, non profecto dixisset Apostolus, fidem esse τ ἐλπιζομένων[?] hypo-stasin vel substantiam, & rerum quæ non videntur, argumentum, seu demonstratio, ubi ex fide nullum pro iis argumentum, nullum ex divina autoritate vel promissio-ne peti potest, sed figmentis omnia constant somniisque. Præterea quod non tantum alia, & generalia fide sua Veteres amplexi fuerunt, sed & specialia ac salutaria in Christo, ex variis in hoc capite locis modo vidimus: etiam æterna, vel coelestia. vers. 16. Christum, vers. 26. & mortuorum resurrectionem, vers. 35. Præsertim in fide Abrahami, fidelium omnium parentis, quæ fuit basis & hypostasis non tantum expectatarum rerum terrenarum & corporearum, sed quoque coelestium.
units.tr: If it were so, the Apostle would certainly not have said that faith is the substance or hypostasis of things hoped for, and the proof of things not seen, when no proof for them can be drawn from faith, and no promise can be sought from divine authority, but everything consists of fictions and dreams. Moreover, that the ancients embraced by their faith not only other and general things, but also special and saving things in Christ, we have just seen from various passages in this chapter: also eternal or heavenly things (v. 16), Christ (v. 26), and the resurrection of the dead (v. 35). Especially in the faith of Abraham, the parent of all believers, which was the basis and substance not only of expected earthly and bodily things, but also of heavenly ones.

units.la: Excipiunt, ad Abrahami istud, non ex ejus intentione id fuisse, sed eventu, non quod ure [?] exspectarit coelestem patriam, sed quod eam Deus non exspectanti, nec spem
units.tr: They object that this was so for Abraham not from his intention but from the outcome: not that he rightly expected the heavenly homeland, but that God at last granted it to him, though he did not expect it and did not extend his hope beyond the riches and happiness of this life.

units.la: Tom. 2. ultra hujus vitæ opes fælicitatemque extendenti, tandem tamen concesserit. Jonas Schlichtingius, in Commentario, ad istum locum, pag. 522.
units.tr: Vol. 2. Jonas Schlichting, in his Commentary on this passage, p. 522.

units.la: Dubitare aliquis posset, an hæc verba de A-brahami intentione & consilio; an vero de eventu tantum accipienda sint? Sane, ut ne-gare nolumus, Abrahamum vitam aliquam ac felicitatem post mortem à Deo sperasse, quippe qui Dei & summam erga suos cultores bonitatem, & summam potentiam, qua etiam mortuos excitare, & sic post mortem suis culto-ribus benefacere posset, cognitam haberet; & hujus etiam terrenæ felicitatis, vergente jam præsertim ætate, vanitatem facile perspicere, & quod omnibus hominibus innatum esse vi-detur, superstitis post funera vitæ desiderium habere posset: si quis tamen historiam sacram consulat, & diligenter legat ac relegat, nihil ea de re scriptum, aut ullo indicio significatum reperiet. At vero Divinus hic Scriptor, ex Sacris Literis eorumque autoritate & fide ex-empla repetens, non alia de viris istis dixisse & asseruisse videtur, quam quæ Sacræ Scriptu-ræ testimonio niti possent. Quod vero Abraha-mus, Isaacus, Jacobus, non tantum vitam ali-quam & felicitatem post mortem, sed etiam il-lam fundamenta habentem civitatem, hoc est, cœlum ipsum, cœlestemque vitam ac felicita-tem nullis unquam seculis finiendam sperarit, & hac ipse cunctas peregrinationis suæ mole-stias, vitæque illius errabundæ fastidia tolerá-rit, Scriptura non prodidit. Quin potius, quas spes aliquando habuerit Abrahamus, inde ap-paret, quod cum Deus ipsum liberis adhuc ca-rentem per visionem allocutus esset, dixisset-que: Noli timere Abraham, ego protector tuus sum, & merces tua magna nimis: ille responderit Deo: Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi? ego vadam absque liberis, & filius procurator domus meæ iste Da-mascus Eliezer: mihi autem non dedisti semen, & ecce vernaculus meus, hæres meus erit. Nonne hic apparet, votorum Abrahami summam in eo fuisse, ut, cum jam bonis omnibus ac divitiis Dei benignitate affluéret, filium & hæredem ex se relinqueret. Num si
units.tr: One might doubt whether these words should be taken of Abraham's intention and purpose, or only of the outcome. Certainly, as we do not wish to deny that Abraham hoped for some life and happiness after death from God, since he knew God's supreme goodness toward his worshippers and his supreme power, by which he could raise the dead and so do good to his worshippers after death; and since he could easily perceive the vanity of this earthly happiness, especially as his years were now declining, and could have a longing for life surviving after burial, which seems innate in all men: yet if anyone consults sacred history, and reads and rereads it diligently, he will find nothing written about this matter, nor any indication of it. But this divine writer, drawing examples from the Sacred Letters and on their authority and faith, seems to have said and asserted about those men nothing other than what could rest on the testimony of Sacred Scripture. But that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob hoped not only for some life and happiness after death, but also for that city having foundations, that is, heaven itself, and heavenly life and happiness never to end, and that for this hope they endured all the troubles of their journey and the weariness of that wandering life, Scripture does not reveal. Rather, what hopes Abraham once had appears from this: when God, while he was still without children, spoke to him in a vision and said, "Fear not, Abraham, I am your protector, and your reward is exceedingly great," he answered God: "Lord God, what will you give me? I shall go without children, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus. To me you have not given offspring, and behold, my home-born servant will be my heir." Does it not appear here that the sum of Abraham's wishes lay in this, that, though he already abounded in all goods and riches by God's kindness, he should leave a son and heir from himself? Whether, if

units.la: Resp. 1. Dubitare, an ex Abrahami in-tentione hoc fuerit verum, est dubitare de veritate verborum, & testimonii Apostolo-lici. Nam non de eo quod Deus fecerit, his verbis, exspectabat enim fundamenta habentem civitatem, agitur, sed Abrahami fide ac spe. Eventum non tollimus: sic enim eventu se res omnino habuit: sed quoq; intentam ab Abrahamo illam fuisse, quando eam exspectavit, clarum est atque evidens. Quomodo enim exspectes, quod non intendas? imo exspectatio nil est aliud, quam animi enixa in rem intentio. Neque semel id hoc in loco dicitur, sed pluries, & aliis atque aliis verbis idem repetitur. 11. Concedit Adversa-rius, Abrahamum vitam aliquam ac felicitatem post mortem à Deo sperasse. An vero aliam, quam Apostolus commemorat? & unde speravit illam? ex bonitate & poten-tia Dei erga suos id collegit, & vitæ hujus, ejusque felicitatis perspecta ipsi vanitate, denique innato vitæ immortalis desiderio: concedimus ista, & facere ad confirma-tionem fidei; sed uti fidem non generant, tantum probabilem aliquam rationem vel conjecturam, ita ultra illa aliquid con-stitui debet, quod fidei fundamentum esse queat; & fides ipsa, exspectationis. Nam de fide Abrahami agitur, non ejus in-genio & sagacitate: & quid fide divina exspectarit, non ratiocinio vel collectio-ne humana aut persuaserit sibi aut finxe-rit. Fides vero divina Dei verbo & testi-monio, ut divina fit, niti debet. Quod autem nostro, vel humano ingenio, tan-tummodo humanum esse poterit, non di-vinum, vel religiosum. III. Nihil est neces-se, ut nos, apud Christianos, laboremus de fide Scriptoris divini, & demonstremus, quod ille nihil attulerit de veteribus quod non certum sit ita se habuisse, sive in tam temporis coelum ipsum & sempiternam il-lam felicitatem firma aliqua ipse praecepisset, Deo sibi mercedem valde magnam promittenti, quid mihi dabis, Domine Deus, respon-didiffet? quibus verbis significat, se bonorum omnium accepisse fatis, & frustra sibi plura promitti, siquidem prolem non habeat cui bona sua reliqu urus effet. Unde apparet, Abraha-mum mercedem illam magnam nimis, quam ipsi Deus promittebat, ultra hujus vitae opes felici-tatemque non extendisse. Itaque verisimilius est, Divinum hunc Autorem his verbis non prodidit, quod Abrahamus, Ifaacus, Iacobum, tam causam reddere voluisse, cur Abrahamus bus, non tantum vitam aliquam & felicitatem infiabilis illius vitae ac peregrinationis tædia post mortem, sed etiam illam fundamenta ha-tanta constantia pertulerit; quam, ut diximus, bentem civitatem, hoc est, coelum ipsum, coele-stemque vitam ac felicitatem nullus unquam se-tario proprioque jure possidendam non dederit, culus finiendam sperarint, & hac spe cunctae non urbes illi incolendas, non sedes stabiles con-peregrinationis suae molestias, vitaeque illius cr-cesserit, sed voluerit, ut in tentoriis, non ipse rabunda fastidia tolerarint. Cui reclamare, tantum, sed cum filio, nepote, pronepotibus de-est ipsi reclamare Scripturae. Tum istud nique suae vitam ibi ageret; nempe quia, ut ex V.T. etiam historia colligit Autor.
units.tr: Answer 1. To doubt whether this was truly Abraham's intention is to doubt the truth of the words and the testimony of the Apostle. For the text does not speak of what God did, in the words "for he was looking for the city having foundations," but of Abraham's faith and hope. We do not deny the outcome: the matter did turn out just so. But that it was also intended by Abraham when he waited for it is clear and evident. For how can you wait for what you do not intend? Indeed, waiting is nothing other than the mind's eager intention toward a thing. Nor is this said only once in this place, but many times, and the same idea is repeated in different words. II. The Adversary concedes that Abraham hoped from God for some life and happiness after death. But was it another life than the one the Apostle mentions? And from where did he hope for it? He gathered it from God's goodness and power toward his own, from the clearly seen vanity of this life and its happiness, and finally from the innate desire for immortal life. We concede these things, and that they serve to confirm faith. But just as they do not generate faith, providing only some probable reason or conjecture, so something beyond them must be posited which can be the foundation of faith; and faith itself is the foundation of expectation. For the matter concerns Abraham's faith, not his talent and shrewdness. What he expected by divine faith he did not persuade himself of, nor fashion by human reasoning or inference. Divine faith, however, must rest on God's word and testimony, if it is to be divine. What can be only human, by our own or human talent, is not divine or religious. III. There is no need for us, among Christians, to labour over the faith of the divine writer and to demonstrate that he has brought forward nothing about the ancients that was not certainly so. He, in the time of the Patriarchs, was looking for the heavens themselves and that eternal happiness, and had been promised by God a very great reward, asked, "What will you give me, Lord God?"; by these words he signifies that he had received the fullness of all good things, and that more is promised to him in vain, since he has no offspring to whom he might leave his goods. Hence it appears that Abraham did not extend that great reward which God promised him beyond the wealth and happiness of this life. Therefore it is more probable that the divine Author did not set forth in these words that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob endured so much with such constancy, as we have said, when they had hoped for no city to be inhabited by them as their own by right, no stable dwelling, but chose to live as wanderers in tents, not only with a certain life and happiness, but with the weariness of that unstable life and pilgrimage; and that they bore with this hope the troubles of their pilgrimage and the restless disgusts of their life. To object to this is to object to Scripture itself. Then that statement, which the Author gathers from the Old Testament history, is not only a bare expression of this life's happiness after death, but of the state of his own life there, namely because (as the Author himself says below, v. 16) God had prepared for them a city...

units.la: infrà v. 16. Autor ipse loquitur, paravit illi Nostrum vero non est assignare locum, ex-Deus civitatem omni illa terra & urbibus in ea quo hauserit. Sufficit, quod id dicat Apo-extructis infinitis partibus majorem ac melio-stolus, quod ex tota Patriarcharum histo-rem.
units.tr: Below, v. 16, the Author himself speaks: God had prepared for them a city. It is not ours to assign the place from which he drew it. It is enough that the Apostle says it: from the whole history of the Patriarchs he promises a greater and better country, built with infinite parts.

units.la: Atque hanc spiritualem felicitatem & ria promit: & quod in ea extent specialia haereditatem divinae illi promissiones Abraha-multa, e quibus hoc tuto colligatur. v. Tu-mo & femini illius datae mystico sensu conti-quando animi sui sollicitudinem de haere-nent. Nam & semen Abrahami, eodem sensu, de expositae Abrahamus Deo, non omnes, spirituale illud omnium credentium fidemque quas unquam habuit, expressit suas spes; Abrahami imitantium semen significat. quod & Deus, uti solet, plura respondit, quam utrunque nos docuit Apostolus in Epist. ad interrogabatur: & ut tum non testatus Rom. cap. 4. v. 11, 12, 13. & ad Gal. 3. fuerit suam spem de coelestibus, quam 5.7. & seq. & 4. 22. & seq. Expectabat ergo conceperat, non magis sequitur, nunquam Abrahamus civitatem illam fundamenta ha-talem habuisse, quam non quoque vitam lentem, magis ratione eventus & consilii di-aliquam ac felicitatem post mortem a Deo spe-rini, quam ratione animi & consilii sui. Nam rafse, quod Abrahamo conceditur ab Ad-& illo sensu saepe cuipiam expectationem rei verfariis, & neque tamen hic confessus alicujus tribuimus. Sic ipse D. Autor cap. fuit. Unde apparet, argumentum ipso-10. v. 27. dixit, voluntarie peccantibus re-rum negativum esse, & non concludere.
units.tr: Indeed, these divine promises given to Abraham and to his seed contain this spiritual happiness and inheritance in a mystical sense, and from them one may safely conclude this. For the seed of Abraham, in the same sense, signifies that spiritual seed of all believers who imitate Abraham's faith, as the Apostle teaches us in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 4, verses 11-13, and in Galatians 3:7 ff. and 4:22 ff. Therefore, if Abraham had expressed his hope about heavenly things when he was asked about his heir, it does not follow that he had no hope of a life and happiness after death from God, which the Adversaries concede to Abraham; and yet this did not stop them from confessing it. Thus the divine Author himself, in chapter 10, verse 27, said that a certain terrible expectation of judgment remains for those who sin wilfully. From this it appears that the argument from silence is negative and does not conclude.

units.la: liftam esse terribilem quandam expectationem De haerede fuit sollicitus: ergo de nulla judicii: cum tamen, si ad eorum consilium ani-re alia? Illud solum nunc exposuit, ergo mique intentionem rem referas, saepe nihil mi-nunquam quidquam majus & coelestius? nus, quam peccatorum poenas expectent. Habe-non sequitur. Votorum Abrahami sum-nus igitur Abrahamus civitatem istam ex-ma hic erat, quod filio carebat haerede: peftasse dicitur, quatenus illum civitas haec ex ergo ea sola summa fuit votorum ejus semper Dei decreto manebat, illíque destinata erat; & semper omnium[?] non certe. De bonis quatenus talis fuit vitæ illius ratio, tam con-terrenis nunc respondit, & hic deficere stans in Deum fides, nullis laboribus, nullis sibi prolem ac hæredem: ergo apparet molestiis fracta ac labefactata, qualis eorum est, Abrahamum mercedem illam magnam nimirum qui hanc fundamenta habentem civitatem di-quam ipsi Deus promittebat, ultra hujus vitæ vina[?] promissione freti, pro laborum suorum opes felicitatemque non extendisse? nulla con-praemio vere expectant: quorum prius illud sequentia. Et fac, ut hic tum vim verbo-rum illorum & promissionis non eo ex-tenderit, non sequitur proinde, aut non istam verborum illorum esse sententiam, aut nunquam ita ab ipso intellectam, creditamque fuisse. Num quia Martha Christi sermonem interrumpens, de curis suis domesticis Dominum interpellat, propterea vel Christi sermo de aliis rebus non fuit, vel illa non alias quoque spiritualia cogitavit vel quaesivit? Et apparet singularis in Abrahami interrogatione Dei providentia, quod de semine vel posteritate difficultatem movit, ut ea occasione ad spirituale semen, quod & cap. xii. Deus significarat, porro sibi explicandum manuduceretur. vi. Non alia est ratio, ob quam verosimile censeat Adversarius, non tam reddi causam ab Apostolo, cur Abrahamus alacriter vitae & peregrinationis suae taedia pertulerit, & Deus ei terram illam jure haereditario non dederit possidendam, quam ut ab Abrahamo ad Deum sermonis sensum deflectens, expositioni suae locum faciat, non tam doceri, quid Abrahamus exspectarit, quam quid Deus ipsi dederit. Quum tamen satis clara sint Apostoli verba in contrarium, & de Abrahamo, ejus fide, & constanti expectatione coelestis patriae loquantur, verss. 8. 9. 10. 13. 14. 16. quo versu non tantum dicitur, quid ei Deus paraverit, sed & exspectarit ipse, νυνὶ ἡ κρείσσονος ὀρέγονται, τάξιν ἐπουράνιον[?]. vii. Bene, continuerint promissiones illae Abrahamo factae spiritualem felicitatem & haereditatem, at & intellexerit istum sensum quoque Abrahamus, credideritque, ad quem capiendum, praeterea ista ratione etiam cogebatur, quod terrenarum rerum minus participabat, & augustam promissionum plenitudinem non satis exprimere nedum exhaurire videbantur solae res terrenae. viii. Ergo non tantum ratione eventus & consilii divini, sed etiam animi & spei suae praestolabatur Abrahamus civitatem illam coelestem: quae & hic, & postea frustra Schlichtingius opponit,pag.538. Apostolum de eventu desiderii ac voti Patrum illorum locutum esse, non vero de animi eorum in coelesti patria quaerenda & appetenda intentione & consilio. Imo quomodo quis eventum talem polliceri sibi potuis-set, nisi ex promissione divina, sibi facta, acceptaque? vel de consilio divino statuere aliquid, in bonum & usum suum, nisi ex divina revelatione? Et si Deus consilium suum, & quod nobis evenire velit, significaverit, nosque crediderimus, quare non pro animo nostro aeque dicemur expectare rem a Deo sic promissam, ac eventu Hebr. x. 27. dicitur, relinqui improbis horribilem expectationem divini judicii, opposite ad sacrificium & expiationem pro peccato: Non relinquitur pro peccatis hostia: sed terribilis quaedam expectatio judicii. At primum & passive hic fit rei sequuturae mentio, ἀπολείπεται[?] ἐκδοχή[?]: in nostro vero loco dicuntur activè ipsi illa ex-pectare. Et quemadmodum manet istos tale tantumq; judicium, ita & expectare illud omnino debent, atque etiam saepe expectant; Abrahamum autem vere expectasse spiritualem felicitatem & hæreditatem nolunt Nostri, sed nescio per quas figuras & metaphoræ, & metonymiæ, citra ullam aut necessitatem, aut veritatem, de eo duntaxat affirmari, quid ipsi evenerit, non quid ipse exspectarit. ix. Nequaquam verò dici potest, hactenus tantum Abrahamum civitatem illam expectasse, quatenus ei divino decreto erat destinata, quod nec scire poterat citra divinam revelationem, neque absque promissione sperare; atque non oppositè & contradistinctè ad eos, qui fundamenta habentem civitatem divina promissione freti, pro laborum suorum præmio vere expectant, sed pari ratione καθ' ὃν τρόπον καὶ κἀκεῖνοι[?], illa expectasse dicendus est Abrahamus, & ex promissione, & vere, non verbo tantum & figurate. Nam & promissionis divinæ constans in hac historia fit mentio; & ita non semel, sed aliquoties, & diversis loquendi modis exspectatio illa exponitur & confirmatur, ut de ejus veritate nemo sanus dubitare, vel invidere istam Patriarchæ, possit.
units.tr: He was anxious about an heir: therefore not about any other matter? He only set this out now: therefore never anything greater and more heavenly? It does not follow. The sum of Abraham's prayers here was that he lacked an heir by his son; therefore that alone was always the sum of his prayers, not certainly. Concerning earthly goods he has now answered, and here he is not failing in the sense of the heir; therefore it appears that Abraham did not extend that great reward which God promised him beyond the wealth and happiness of this life? Not so, following the words. And suppose that here he did not extend the force of those words and the promise to that point, it does not follow that either the meaning of those words is not this, or that it was never so understood and believed by him. Does it follow that because Martha, interrupting Christ's discourse, asks the Lord about her domestic cares, therefore either Christ's discourse was not about other things, or she did not also think or seek spiritual things? And the singular providence of God appears in Abraham's question, in that he raised the difficulty about seed or posterity, so that on that occasion he might be led on to explain the spiritual seed, which God had also signified in chapter 12. Nor is there any other reason why the Adversary thinks it more likely that the Apostle does not give the reason why Abraham bore the weariness of his life and pilgrimage so cheerfully, and why God did not give him that land to possess by hereditary right, than that, by turning the sense of the discourse from Abraham to God, he makes room for his own exposition, and so teaches not so much what Abraham expected as what God gave him. Yet the Apostle's words are clear enough to the contrary, and speak of Abraham, his faith and his constant expectation of the heavenly fatherland, in verses 8, 9, 10, 13, 14 and 16, where it is said not only what God prepared for him but also what he himself looked for: "now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one" [νυνὶ δὲ κρείττονος ὀρέγονται, τουτέστιν ἐπουρανίου]. Granted, those promises made to Abraham contained spiritual happiness and inheritance, and that Abraham understood this sense too and believed it; for grasping this, he was further compelled by this reason, that he had less share in earthly things, and that earthly things alone seemed not to express, let alone exhaust, the august fullness of the promises. Therefore Abraham looked for that heavenly city not only by the outcome and counsel of God, but also by the intention and hope of his own soul. Here and afterwards Schlichting vainly objects (p. 538) that the Apostle spoke of the outcome of the desire and vow of those Patriarchs, not of the intention and purpose of their souls in seeking and desiring the heavenly fatherland. Indeed, how could anyone have promised himself such an outcome, unless from a divine promise made to him and accepted? Or how could he determine anything about God's counsel for his own good and use, unless from divine revelation? And if God has signified his counsel, and what he wishes to come to pass for us, and we have believed it, why should we not be said to expect in our own soul, equally, the thing so promised by God, as with the outcome? Hebrews 10:27 says that a horrible expectation of divine judgment is left to the wicked, set against sacrifice and expiation for sin: "There remains no sacrifice for sins, but a certain terrible expectation of judgment." But there, first, the mention of the coming thing is passive: it is left, ἀπολείπεται, an expectation, ἐκδοχή; while in our passage they are said to expect actively. And just as the wicked remain in such and so great a judgment, so they must expect it entirely, and indeed often do expect it. But that Abraham truly expected spiritual happiness and inheritance our opponents do not want, and by I know not what figures, metaphors and metonymies, without any necessity or truth, they claim this is affirmed of him only as to what happened to him, not what he himself expected. IX. Yet it cannot by any means be said that Abraham expected that city only so far as it was destined for him by God's decree, which he could not know without divine revelation, nor hope for without a promise; and not in opposition and contrast to those who, relying on divine promise, truly expect "the city having foundations" as the reward of their labours. Rather, by the same reasoning, in the manner in which those others also, Abraham must be said to have expected that city, and from the promise, and truly, not merely in word and figuratively. For mention is made in this history of the constant divine promise; and so that expectation is set out and confirmed not once but several times, and in diverse modes of speech, so that no sane person could doubt its truth, or begrudge that hope to the Patriarch.

units.la: Quando autem de Mose dicitur, quod opprobrium Christi pluris æstimavit, quam thesauros Ægypti, excipiunt, Christi nomine hic intelligi, probrum simile illi, quod Christus ejusve populus; qui & ipse Christi nomine aliquando includitur, perpetiatur: vel probrum, quod perpetitur ùs[?], qui Christi ejusve populi typum gerit. Verba sunt Schlichtingii, in Commentario, pag. 553. Respondeo, quomodocunque intelligas, certe nomen Christi in N. T. nunquam sumitur, ut non designet Christi personam, neque sumi aliter debet: præsertim, ubi & probrum ejus additur, atq; ignominia, ipsi propria. Neque aliter exponi potest, quod Moses majores divitias æstimavit τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν τοῦ Χριστοῦ[?], omnibus Ægypti thesauris, ac quod ab eodem hoc Scriptore iisdem verbis dicitur infra, cap. xiii. 13. ut post Christum eamus extra castra, τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν αὐτοῦ φέροντες. Non enim hic habemus manentem civitatem, sed futuram expectamus. Ut videas & verba, & rem eandem esse, quam & hic & ibi tractat Apostolus. Atque ad istum locum Schlichtingius, portare opprobrium Christi est, nihil eorum recusare, quæ Christo contigerunt, Christi causa. Iterum de Christi ὀνειδισμοῖς Apostolus, Rom. xv. 3. οἱ ὀνειδισμοὶ τῶν ὀνειδιζόντων σε, ἐπέπεσον[?] ἐπ' ἐμέ. Tanti ergo Moses fecit opprobria Christi, & portare ea: Christi, id est, in Christo, fide nimirum in eum recumbendo, & cum eo, & deniq; propter eum. Qui semper cupiunt, ut ex V.T. clare & aperte probemus, quæ de eo dicuntur, ostendant nobis in historia V.T. ubi vel Moses putarit se ad similitudinem Christi, & probrorum ejus, cum suis, passi, vel gessisse typum Christi, & hoc eum, & populum scivisse. Denique non simpliciter dicitur, quid Moses passus fuerit ac sustinuerit, sed quid pati potius voluerit, & elegerit, ut quod sibi fieret, ipse quoque intelligeret: ἠρνήσατο[?] noluit dici Pharaonis filius: sed potius elegit cum populo Dei mala perpeti: majores divitias æstimans Christi opprobria: respexit enim ad remunerationem. Quæ omnia probæ notitiæ ac fidei totidem sunt argumenta.
units.tr: When it is said of Moses that he esteemed the reproach of Christ greater than the treasures of Egypt, they object that the name of Christ is here to be understood as a reproach like that which Christ or his people, who is himself sometimes included under the name of Christ, suffers; or a reproach which he suffers who bears the type of Christ or of his people. These are the words of Schlichting, in his Commentary, p. 553. I answer: however you understand it, the name of Christ in the New Testament is never used without designating the person of Christ, nor ought it to be taken otherwise, especially where his own reproach and disgrace are added. Nor can it be explained otherwise that Moses esteemed the reproach of Christ [τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν τοῦ Χριστοῦ] greater than all the treasures of Egypt, or that the same writer says in the same words below, ch. xiii. 13: that we should go forth outside the camp after Christ, bearing his reproach [τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν αὐτοῦ φέροντες]. For we have here no abiding city, but seek one to come. So you may see that the words and the thing itself are the same as the Apostle treats here and there. And on that passage Schlichting says: to bear the reproach of Christ is to refuse nothing of those things which have happened to Christ, for Christ's cause. Again the Apostle speaks of the reproaches of Christ, Rom. xv. 3: "the reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me" [οἱ ὀνειδισμοὶ τῶν ὀνειδιζόντων σε, ἐπέπεσον ἐπ' ἐμέ]. So Moses thought so highly of the reproaches of Christ, and of bearing them: of Christ, that is, in Christ, namely by leaning on him in faith, and with him, and finally on account of him. Those who always want us to prove clearly and openly from the Old Testament what is said of him, let them show us in the Old Testament history where Moses either thought that he had suffered with his people in likeness to Christ and his reproaches, or bore a type of Christ, and that he and the people knew this. Finally, it is not simply said what Moses suffered and endured, but what he chose and preferred to suffer, so that he himself would also understand what was done to him: he refused [ἠρνήσατο] to be called Pharaoh's son, but rather chose to suffer evil with the people of God, esteeming greater riches the reproaches of Christ, for he looked to the recompense. All these things are so many proofs of sound knowledge and faith.

units.la: Ad verf. 35. namque præcipue hoc caput vindicandum nobis est, dicuntur fideles meliorem resurrectionem exspectasse, non accipientes liberationem, ut meliorem repetirent resurrectionem: non ex promissione dicunt Nostri, sed colligentes eam fiduciam ex Dei bonitate, sibi satis perspecta. Schlichtingius, in Commentario, pag. 563. Ut meliorem invenirent resurrectionem. Ostendit, quà ipse quàve fide tam dura pertulerint. Eâ nimirum, quòd crederent longè meliorem sé à Deo resurrectionem consecuturos esse. Vnde vere vero hanc fidem hauserant? non ex ulla aperta ejus rei in lege divina extante promissione, sed sola Dei bonitate, justitia potentiaque freti. Nam cum Deum esse, premiaque iis qui ipsum quaererent retribuere firmiter crederent; & tamen, nisi a lege divina summo cum scelere deficere vellent, maximas calamitates, exilia, carceres, cruciatus, mortem denique truculentam adeundam sibi esse viderent, in eam spem devenerunt, alia virtutis ac pietatis præmia Dei cultoribus post vitæ exitum omnino reposita esse: neque fieri posse, ut Deus optimus ac justissimus virtutem ac pietatem omnium maximam, quæ vitæ ipsius, qua nobis nihil est charius, impendio constet, nullo præmio remuneratam dimittat. Ita ergo Deus, etiam sub veteri fœdere, paulatim populum suum, ad spem alterius vitæ talibus rudimentis exercuit; quanquam minimè dubium est, etiam divino Spiritu duris illis tristibusque persecutionum temporibus servos Dei afflatos, hanc spem animo tanto magis hausisse atque gustasse. Denique, illam ergo umbratilem & fluxam, liberationis a supplicio, resurrectionem contempserunt, quo resurrectionem veram, & cum sempiterna vitæ ac felicitate conjunctam consequerentur.
units.tr: On verse 35, indeed, this chapter must be vindicated by us: the faithful are said to have expected a better resurrection, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Our people say this not from promise, but gathering that confidence from God's goodness, which was sufficiently known to them. Schlichting, in his Commentary, p. 563: that they might find a better resurrection. He shows with what faith, and what faith, they endured such hardships: namely, because they believed that they would obtain from God a resurrection far better. Whence, truly, did they draw this faith? Not from any open promise of that thing in the divine law, but relying on God's goodness, justice and power alone. For since they firmly believed that God exists and rewards those who seek him, and yet saw that, unless they wanted to fall away from the divine law with the greatest wickedness, they must face the greatest calamities, exiles, prisons, tortures and finally a savage death, they came to the hope that other rewards of virtue and piety were wholly reserved for the worshippers of God after the end of life; and that it could not be that the best and most just God would let virtue and piety, the greatest of all, which costs the very life that is dearest to us, go unrewarded. So God, even under the old covenant, gradually trained his people by such rudiments to the hope of another life; although there is no doubt that the servants of God, inspired by the divine Spirit in those hard and sad times of persecution, drew in this hope with all the greater courage and tasted it. Finally, then, they despised that shadowy and fleeting resurrection, a deliverance from punishment, so that they might obtain the true resurrection, joined with everlasting life and happiness.

units.la: Hic vero plura, & longè meliora dicunt, quam vulgo alias. Nam & fidem resurrectionis habuisse Veteres, & spem, agnoscunt, nec resurrectionis tantum, sed & alterius ac melioris vitæ, neque Spiritus divini fuisse omnino exsortes. Quod potissimum est, quod in hac tota disputatione intendimus, ut habuerint modo illa Patres, quomodo, aut unde, nonnisi propter illud, neque adeo anxiè, quærimus. Tum & ipsi fatentur Adversarii, ex divinâ bonitate ac potentia, & bonorum sub extremo vitæ carentiâ, ita collegisse Veteres, & quia Deum esse norant, & se quærentibus benignum remuneratorem. Hoc vero non necesse fuit ex solâ naturâ petere & concludere argumetis adeo artificialibus, quin quoq; exScripturâ potuerint scire, ubi & abunde & clare satis Deus se talem sæpenumero exhibuit, & sub nomine Jehova evidenter fuit complexus: quamvis aperta resurrectionis promissio facta non fuerit expressis verbis. Hæc in vindicationem argumentorum nostrorum, pro fide Patrum sub V. T. ex capite isto Hebr. xi. dicta sunto.
units.tr: Here, however, they say much more, and much better, than they usually do elsewhere.
