For they acknowledge that the Ancients had faith and hope of the resurrection, and not of the resurrection only, but of another and better life, nor were they wholly strangers to the divine Spirit. What we chiefly intend in this whole discussion is only that the Fathers had these things, not how or whence, which we seek only for that reason and not so anxiously. Then the adversaries themselves admit that the Ancients gathered this from the divine goodness and power, and from the lack of good things at the end of life, both because they knew that God exists and that he is a kind rewarder of those who seek him. But it was not necessary to seek this from nature alone, and to conclude it by arguments so artificial; they could also have known it from Scripture, where God very often showed himself abundantly and clearly to be such, and openly embraced himself under the name Jehovah, although an open promise of the resurrection had not been made in express words. These things are to be taken as said in defence of our arguments, for the faith of the Fathers under the Old Testament, from this chapter of Hebrews xi.

units.la: Quibus hæc addimus, idem argumentum confirmantia, Scripturæ loca: & quidem de fide Abrahami præsertim quæ Paulus habet, Rom. iv. 1. 2. 3. & Gal.iii. 6. 7. 8. in explicationem ejus, quod dictum Genef. xv. 6. credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei in justitiam. Quæ ita exponit, ut omnino ad justificationem trahat, & doceat inde non tantum quomodo Abrahamus, sed & quomodo nos justificemur: dum credidit in Deum, non justificantem se ex operibus, ut sic mercedem haberet & gloriationem aliquam; sed fine operibus justificantem impium, qualis ante justificationem homo omnis in se est, & ex gratia; nempe in Deum, uti David explicat justificari fine operibus, remittentem peccata, & obtegentem iniquitates nostras. Quodque Abrahamus fide sua reclinarit in divinam promissionem, non in argumenta aliqua a se facta, vel conjecturas, in Christum denique destinatas, Apostolus exponit Gal. III. ubi & Διαθήκην[?] appellat Abrahamo factam, verf. 15. & ἐπαγγελίαι dicuntur verf. 16. porro verf. 17. Διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην, & ἐπαγγελίας. iterum verf. 18. bis ἐπαγγελία. Si enim ex lege hereditas, non jam ex promissione: Abrahamo autem per promissiones gratificatus Deus fuit. Promissiones intelligit Abrahamo factas de semine, quo & Christus intellectus ac comprehensus fuit. verf. 16. Abrahamo autem dicta fuerunt promissiones, & semini ejus. non dicit: & seminibus, tanquam de pluribus, sed tanquam de uno: & semini tuo, ὅ[?] est Christus. Hoc vero dico, testamentum ante firmatum a Deo in Christum, &c. Ad quae Schlichtingius, vel Crellius, in Commentario Epistolae ad Galatas, pag. 124. Semen enim, ut mox indicat Apostolus, spirituale semen Abrahami declarat, id est, eos omnes, qui Abrahamum fide referunt; qui quidem sunt omnes veri Christiani. Et pag. 126. Possessio terrae Chananaeae, quae typus fuit mundi illius futuri, qui spirituali Abrahami semini destinatus est. Unde Paulus Rom. IV. 13. &c. ubi eadem de re agit, de qua hoc loco, haereditatem mundi, nempe futuri, Abrahamo & feminii[?] ejus promissam esse dicit, non per legem, sed fide obtinendam. Quanquam possessio illius mundi, in benedictione illa mystice sumta, & contra haec in illa, potest comprehendi. Et pag. 127. Nunc autem, cum ubique dicatur semini, uni tantum ea destinata esse indicatur. Iam vero per spirituale illud semen fideles esse intelligendos, supra docuerat Apostolus, qui, ut infra dicetur, multi sunt alii, quam Christus & ejus populus, seu mavis, Christiani cum suo capite conjuncti. Ideo hic ait Apostolus, illud semen esse Christum. Neq; enim hoc loco Christus pro solius Christi persona sumitur, ut ab aliis quoq; est animadversum: sed Christus una cum corpore suo mystico, quod est Ecclesia. totum enim a capite, tanquam praecipua sua parte, denominatur; praesertim quia reliqua membra spiritu illius vivunt, atque ab eo animantur. Sic sumitur Christi nomen apud eundem Apostolum 1 Cor. XII. 12.
units.tr: To these we add Scripture passages confirming the same argument, and especially those which Paul has about the faith of Abraham, Rom. iv. 1, 2, 3, and Gal. iii. 6, 7, 8, in explanation of what is said in Gen. xv. 6: Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. He explains this so as to refer it entirely to justification, and to teach from it not only how Abraham, but how we also are justified: while he believed in God, not justifying himself by works, so as to have a reward and some boasting, but, without works, justifying the ungodly, such as every man is in himself before justification, and by grace; namely in God, as David explains being justified without works, by God forgiving sins and covering our iniquities. And that Abraham by his faith leaned on the divine promise, not on any arguments or conjectures made by himself, finally directed to Christ, the Apostle explains in Gal. iii., where he calls the covenant made with Abraham a covenant [Διαθήκην] in verse 15, and in verse 16 they are called promises [ἐπαγγελίαι]; further in verse 17 a covenant previously ratified [Διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένην] and promises [ἐπαγγελίας]; again in verse 18, twice, a promise [ἐπαγγελία]. For if the inheritance is of the law, it is no longer of promise; but God gave it to Abraham by promise. He means the promises made to Abraham concerning the seed, in which Christ also was understood and comprehended, verse 16: now to Abraham were the promises made, and to his seed. He does not say "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one: "and to thy seed," which is Christ. Now this I say, that the covenant was before confirmed by God in Christ, etc. To which Schlichting, or Crellius, in the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, p. 124, replies: the seed, as the Apostle soon indicates, declares the spiritual seed of Abraham, that is, all those who refer themselves to Abraham by faith, who are indeed all true Christians. And p. 126: the possession of the land of Canaan, which was a type of that future world, is destined for the spiritual seed of Abraham. Whence Paul, Rom. iv. 13, etc., where he treats of the same matter as in this passage, says that the inheritance of the world, namely the future one, was promised to Abraham and his seed, to be obtained not by the law but by faith. Although the possession of that world, taken mystically in that blessing, and against this in that, may be comprehended. And p. 127: now, since it is said everywhere "to the seed," it is indicated that those things are destined for one alone. Now the Apostle had taught above that by that spiritual seed the faithful are to be understood, who, as will be said below, are many others besides Christ and his people, or, if you prefer, Christians joined with their head. Therefore the Apostle says here that that seed is Christ. For Christ is not taken here for the person of Christ alone, as has been noticed by others too, but Christ together with his mystical body, which is the Church; for the whole is named from the head, as from its chief part, especially because the remaining members live by his Spirit and are animated by him. So the name of Christ is used in the same way by the same Apostle, 1 Cor. xii. 12.

units.la: De Abrahamo item Christus, Ioann.viii.56. Abraham Pater vester gestiit videre diem meum, vidit, & gavisus fuit. Adq; Smalcius, adverf. Frantzium, Disp. vi. de Bonis operib. pag. 195. Nonne dies Christi dici potest id tempus, quo aliquid ad honorem Christi extitit, nempe quo Christus in mundo fuit & munere suo perfunctus est? Quemadmodum alibi dies Domini vel Dei id tempus nominatur, quo aliquid in honorem Domini vel Dei extitit, vel exitypum est. Hinc ultimus ille dies judicii, Domini & Dei dies appellatur. Sed ad rem facit, expendere, quam dat loci istius expositionem: Possunt enim illa verba Domini Iesu ita explicari: Abraham pater vester exultasset vel cupivisset diem meum videre, & si eum vidisset, gavisus fuisset, ut supra disput. 3. in respons. ad 101. thesin prolixe docuimus: Videamus quid ibi:
units.tr: Christ also speaks of Abraham at John 8:56: "Abraham your father rejoiced to see my day; he saw it and was glad." And Smalcius, against Frantz, Disp. 6 on good works, p. 195: "Can the day of Christ not be called the time in which something came to the honour of Christ, namely when Christ was in the world and had discharged his office? Just as elsewhere the day of the Lord or of God names the time in which something came to the honour of the Lord or God, or was a type of it. Hence that last day of judgment is called the day of the Lord and of God. But it is to the point to weigh the explanation which he gives of that passage: 'Those words of the Lord Jesus can be explained thus: Abraham your father would have exulted or desired to see my day, and if he had seen it, he would have rejoiced, as we taught at length above in Disp. 3, in reply to the 101st thesis.' Let us see what is there:"

units.la: Abrahamum autem exultasse, ut videret diem Domini, & eum vidisse & gavisum esse, si verba ita, ut vulgo fit, legantur, Christi auctoritate & rei verisimilitudine & sensu gene-rali potius nitebatur, quam aliquo argumen-to vel testimonio. Nihil enim tale expresse us-quam de Abrahamo legitur. Quare credimus haec verba ita etiam posse converti: Abraha-mus pater vester exultasset, ut videret diem meum, & si vidisset, gavisus fuisset, ut sensus fit: quod tantopere & toties jactatum patrem vestrum Abrahamum, id inprimis vos refutare & pudefacere posset, si non omnem pu-dorem profitui isset. Nec enim talis esset A-brahamus, si nunc viveret, quales vos estis. Vos, quibus contigit videre diem meum, de me calumnis & vi opprimendo cogitatis: At A-brahamus, quanto cum desiderio cupiisset vi-dere haec tempora, &, si ipsi id contigisset, quanta laetitia perfusus fuisset? Ita ut Christus
units.tr: "That Abraham exulted to see the day of the Lord, and saw it and rejoiced, if the words are read as is commonly done, rests more on Christ's authority, the probability of the matter and the general sense than on any argument or testimony. For nothing of the kind is expressly read anywhere about Abraham. Therefore we believe these words can also be rendered thus: Abraham your father would have exulted that he might see my day, and if he had seen it, he would have rejoiced, so that the sense is this: that your father Abraham, so greatly and so often boasted of, could especially refute and shame you, if you had not cast off all shame. For Abraham would not be such as you are, were he alive now. You, to whom it has been granted to see my day, plan to oppress me with slanders and violence. But Abraham, with how great a longing would he have desired to see these times, and, had it been granted to him, how great a joy would he have been filled with? So that Christ"

units.la: Resp. 1. Quamvis sic etiam possent exponi Christi verba, uti Socinus vult; non tamen sic debere, hoc ipso loco si-gnificat. Et annon possunt aliter exponi? non simplici sensu, quo & nos, & tota semper Ecclesia verba illa accepit? Addi-mus, & nequaquam illo modo accipi pos-se: propter eas, quas dicemus, rationes.
units.tr: Reply 1. Although Christ's words could be explained in this way, as Socinus wishes, yet they ought not to be so explained, as this very place shows. And can they not be explained otherwise, in the plain sense in which we, and the whole Church always, have understood those words? We add that they cannot be taken in that manner at all, for the reasons we shall give.

units.la: II. Etenim & verbis repugnat singulis ni-mis evidenter; & sensus, quem dat, nullo modo quadrat. Nam non tantum cogi-tur mutare verborum tempora, sed & alia istis addere, praeter textum. Abra-ham pater vester ἠγαλλιάσατο[?], quod proprie est, exultavit, & certum aliquid dicit, in incertum transformat proprio arbitrio, & reddit, gavisus fuisset: qua quaeso necessitate? nisi quia aliter ipsorum thesi adversabitur. Jam si illa probabitur ratio fingendi & refingendi textum, nihil hoc in loco simili modo respondere censendum fit, quo supra verf.40. ubi cum Iudæi dicerent: Pater noster Abraham est. Christus respon-dit: Si filii estis Abrahæ, opera Abra-hami faceretis. Nunc autem quæritis me interficere, hominem, qui illam veritatem locutus sum vobis, quam audivi à Deo. Hoc Abraham non fecit, ut vulgò legitur, sed parum apte. Rectius autem, si sic convertantur verba: Hoc Abraham non fecisset, quod etiam Wolfgangus Musculus, & Henricus Bullingerus observarunt. Notum enim est omnibus, sacrarum literarum studiosis, Hebræos, uno præterito pro omnibus omnium morum præteritis uti; & duabus copulis, duobus verbis additis, idem præstare, ac si priori verbo vel solam, vel post ipsam copulam, particulam conditionalem vel similem addidissent, posterius vero sine ulla copula aut simpliciter aut cum asseverante particula enunciassent. Exempla habes Ierem. 18.7,8,9,10. ubi secundum Hebraicum textum sic legimus: Re-pente loquar adversus gentem & adversus regnum, ut evellam & confringam & perdam, & convertetur gens illa à malo suo, quod locutus sum contra illam, & hoc quidem versu non vult significare. Pœnitebit me super malo, quod cogitavi facere ei. Et repente loquar super gentem & super regnum, ut ædificem & plantem. Si vero converterit se gens illa à malo suo, pœnitebit me, &c. Idem etiam de loco Ioh. 6. 36. Sed dixi vobis, quia & nostro Abrahamo, qui obiit? & Prophetæ vidistis me & non creditis. hoc est, etiamsi obierunt, quem tu teipsum facis? Ibi tum me videritis, tamen non creditis. Sed locus est porro de gloria sua loqui Christus, verf. insignis apud Iacob. cap. 1. 23,24. qui sic 54. si ego meipsum glorifico, gloria mea nihil habet: Si quis auditor verbi est, & non est: Pater est qui me glorificat, quem vos dicitis Deum vestrum. Et relate ad Avultum nativitatis suæ in speculo. Confi-
units.tr: II. For, first, the explanation clearly contradicts the individual words, and the sense it gives does not fit at all. For he is compelled not only to change the tenses of the verbs but also to add other things to the text. "Abraham your father rejoiced" [ἠγαλλιάσατο], which properly means "exulted" and states something certain, he turns into something uncertain by his own judgment, rendering it "would have rejoiced." By what necessity, I ask? Unless because otherwise it would tell against their thesis. Now if that licence of feigning and refashioning the text is accepted, it must be judged that nothing similar is to be answered in this place as at verse 40 above, where the Jews said, "Abraham is our father," and Christ replied: "If you are children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this," as is commonly read, but awkwardly. It is more correct, however, if the words are rendered: "Abraham would not have done this," as Wolfgang Musculus and Heinrich Bullinger also observed. For it is known to all students of the sacred letters that the Hebrews use one past tense for all the past tenses of every mood; and with two conjunctions and two verbs added, they achieve the same effect as if they had added a conditional particle or the like to the first verb, either alone or after the conjunction, and had stated the second without any conjunction, either plainly or with an asseverative particle. You have examples at Jeremiah 18:7, 8, 9, 10, where according to the Hebrew text we read: "Suddenly I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to pluck up, break down and destroy; and that nation will turn from its evil against which I have spoken; and in this verse he does not wish to signify: It will repent me of the evil which I thought to do to it. And suddenly I will speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant. But if that nation turns itself from its evil, it will repent me, etc." The same holds of the passage at John 6:36: "But I said to you, because you have both seen me and do not believe." The sense is: even if they had died, whom do you make yourself? Even though they saw me, they did not believe. But Christ is still speaking about his own glory at John 8:54, the verse noted among Jacob's [writings] ... "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. If anyone is a hearer of the word and is not a doer: it is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God." And with reference to Abraham's [sight] of his nativity in a mirror. Confi-

units.la: iv. Neque sensus, quem verbis ita transformatis dant, huic loco quadrat: nec talis esset Abrahamus, si nunc vos estis. Nam id Christus non vult significare. Sed de præcellentia Christi supra Abrahamum, agebatur. v. Postquam enim Christus verf.18. Patrem suum commemorat, & faciet malum in oculis meis, ut morarat, & quæsivissent Iudæi, verf. 19. ubi est Pater tuus? de Patre suo plura addidit: & quando Iudæi objecerant verf. 33. se esse Abrahami semen; quam degenerare essent Abrahami filii, porro demonstrare instituit, à verf. 37. usque dum Abrahamum cum Christo conferentes, dicerent verf. 53. numquid tu major es patre nostro Abrahamo, qui obiit? & Prophetæ vidistis me & non creditis. hoc est, etiamsi obierunt, quem tu teipsum facis? Ibi tum me videritis, tamen non creditis. Sed locus est porro de gloria sua loqui Christus, verf. 54. si ego meipsum glorifico, gloria mea nihil habet: Si quis auditor verbi est, & non est: Pater est qui me glorificat, quem vos dicitis Deum vestrum. Hic similis est viro consideranti citis, quod est Deus vester. Et relate ad Abrahamum gestiit illum videre diem meum, &c. deravit enim seipsum, & abiit, & statim ille meum videre gestiit, non ego ipsius diem; oblitus est, qualis fuerit, pro eo, quod nos dicemus: nam etiamsi scipsum consideret, tamen quamprimum abierit, oblivisci-tur, qua-lusfuerit[?]. Ubi tria diversa tempora uno tantum praeterito expressa sunt. Et hunc sensum verborum Iohannis, quem nunc innuimus, ad rem accommodatiorem esse, nemo diffitebitur, qui paulo altius rem expenderit. Hoc enim Christus iure dicere poterat, etiamsi nullum de eo extaret testimonium: At illud non ita recte, praesertim apud eos, apud quos nulla tunc erat Christi auctoritas, quique facillime occasionem inde arripere poterant, Christum, tanquam falsa de Abrahamo dicentem, mendacii coarguendi. Quanquam nihil iterum dubitandum est, Christum ita locutum fuisse studio, ut & hoc & illo modo verba ipsius intelligi possent, ut homines improbi, verba non considerantes, haberent, quod speciose carperent. Hic enim Christi mos fuit, homines improbos suis sermonibus quasi intricare, ut ex multis sacrarum literarum testimoniis, maxime vero ex eo, quod cap: 6. apud eundem Iohannem, de mandu-catione carnis & bibitione sanguinis sui, scriptum est, ad oculum apparet. diem: Ille felicem se aestimavit, quod diem meum vidit, & vehementer protinus gavisus fuit, quin & gaudio exultavit. Apparet ergo, quod hic agebatur de collatione Christi & Abrahami inter se; non de Abrahami, & Judaeorum factis, de quibus supra: deinde de Christi supra Abrahamum dignitate, ad-pio-bandum & ostendendum contra Judaeos, quod eo ipso Christus major esset patre ipsorum Abrahamo. Quod etiam patet ex sequentibus, quibus, ex Adversariorum expositione, non est locus; ex nec-stra[?], optime. Nam statim post sequitur, vers. 57. dixerunt ergo ipsi Iudaei, nondum quinquaginta habes annos, & vidisti Abrahamum? Quae non dici potuerunt ab iis, intellectâ Christi praecedente oratione sensu eo, quo dicunt Nostri. Quorsum enim quid facturus fuisset Abrahamus, si vidisset diem Christi, & interim non vidit, nondum quinquaginta annos habes &c. ac disputatio de aetate? Jam vero iis respondit Christus, amen amen dico vobis, antequam Abraham exisseret, ego eram. Ad quae sustulerunt lapides Judaei, quos in eum jacerent.
units.tr: iv. Nor does the sense which they give to the words so changed fit this place; nor would Abraham be such as you are now. For Christ does not wish to signify that. But the discussion was about the pre-eminence of Christ above Abraham. v. For after Christ at verse 18 mentions his Father, and "will do evil in my eyes, so that they might be delayed," and the Jews asked at verse 19, "Where is your Father?", he added more about his Father; and when the Jews objected at verse 33 that they were the seed of Abraham, he set out to show further how far the sons of Abraham had degenerated, from verse 37 onward, until, comparing Abraham with Christ, they said at verse 53: "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died; you have seen me and do not believe." Here he is like a man who considers quickly what is your God. And with reference to Abraham: he longed to see my day, etc. For he departed from himself, and went away, and at once that man longed to see my day, not my day itself; he forgot what sort he was, in contrast to what we shall say: for even if he considers himself, yet as soon as he has departed, he forgets what sort he was. Here three different times are expressed by one past tense alone. And that this sense of John's words, which we now suggest, is better suited to the matter, no one who has weighed the matter a little more deeply will deny. For Christ could rightly say this even if no testimony about it existed; but the other sense is not so right, especially among those to whom at that time there was no authority of Christ, and who could very easily seize on the occasion to convict Christ of lying, as one speaking falsely about Abraham. Yet, again, there is no doubt that Christ spoke deliberately, so that his words could be understood in this way and in that, and wicked men, not considering the words, would have something to carp at speciously. For this was Christ's manner: to entangle wicked men in his speeches, as is plain at a glance from many testimonies of the sacred letters, but especially from what is written in chapter 6 of the same John about eating his flesh and drinking his blood. [Compare also] the day: "He counted himself happy that he saw my day, and at once rejoiced greatly, nay, exulted with joy." It appears, therefore, that what was being discussed here was the comparison of Christ and Abraham with each other, not the deeds of Abraham and the Jews, of which above; and then the dignity of Christ above Abraham, to prove and show against the Jews that by that very fact Christ was greater than their father Abraham. This also appears from what follows, for which there is no place in the explanation of our opponents, but there is in ours, very well. For immediately after it follows, at verse 57: "The Jews therefore said to him, 'You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?'" which they could not have said if they had understood Christ's preceding speech in the sense our side gives. For to what end would Abraham have done what he would have done, had he seen the day of Christ, and meanwhile did not see it, "You are not yet fifty years old," etc., and a dispute about age? Now indeed Christ answered them: "Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am." To which the Jews took up stones to cast at him.

units.la: Audivimus suo loco, qua improbitate ista, antequam Abraham esset, temerent Adversarii, & ut lapidare Christum propter illa verba aeque conentur nunc, ac olim Judaei, quod se ante Abrahamum posuit: sed in verbis proximis, vidit Abraham diem meum &c. pari ludunt audacia. Satis vero manifestum, qua de re agatur, nempe de Christi praestantia supra Abrahamum; non de Abrahami, supra Judaeos. v. Quare non idem, quod verf. 40. argumentum hic a Christo tractari, de Judaeorum vid. indignis erga ipsum operibus, liquet. Ibi enim Christus exserte: hoc Abraham non fecit: hic, nihil simile, sive etiam ibi legatur, hoc Abraham non fecisset; sive, non fecit. Nam eodem redit, ut non opus sit variare verbi tempus, nempe hoc Abraham non fecit, id est, nil tale. vi. Non de eo dicimus, quod Hebraei uno praeterito pro omnibus omnium modorum praeteritis utuntur; sed, similem ac in nostro textu est, locutionem aut verborum acceptionem dari, primum in Graecis, tum Hebraicis, vel propterea nostrum locum ita exponendum esse, negamus. Non enim similis ratio est Jerem. XVIII. 7, 8. 9. 10. ubi tantum in voce שׁוּב & convertitur, obvius est Hebraismus, pro quando convertitur, vel, si vero convertatur: quod non idem est, cum tot praeteritorum primo in alios modos mutatione, tum hypotheticae particulae infertione, quae totum sensum invertit, neque in loco est necessaria. Atqui Jer. XVIII. a re ipsa tale quid exigitur, propter quod reddit nec variat sensum, sed exponit, & omnibus fit manifestum. Tum addita utrobique particula, tamen dissimilis est ratio: nam ibi non est, si se convertisset, uti hic, si vidisset; sed in praesenti, si se convertit; vel, ubi, quando, siquando se convertit. Quare vel si faciamus parem rationem locutionum hic, & ibi, ἵνα ἴδῃ, cum ᾗ[?] εἶδε, argumentum nostrum manebit nihilominus; nempe ibi legitur, quando convertit se gens; hic, quando vidit Abraham diem meum: vel, ubi se convertit gens; ubi vidit Abraham. Neque aliter in loco nostro fumi illa posse, arguit conjunctio, ἵνα ἴδῃ, cum ᾗ[?] εἶδε: quod illis respondet: sic & ἠγαλλιάσατο, vel ἠγαλλιάσατο, ἵνα &c. cum ἐχάρη. vii. Nihil autem in loco Johann. vi. 36. est, quod huc quadret, & vidistis me, & non creditis. Nam quamvis in sensu explanando, huc res redeat, ut significarit Christus, quamvis me videritis, tamen non creditis, non dicit hoc in verbis illis aliquid necessario debere mutari; nam sensus satis fluit & constat, ex retentis ipsis verbis, & vidistis me, & non creditis. Deinde illa variatio esset tantum in copula €, pro etiamsi, & tamen; quae potius explicativa sunt, & addenda copulae, quam ut cum illis commutentur. Denique non est, etiamsi me vidissetis: qualem totam, & sensus, & verborum mutationem nostro loco inferunt, si vidisset, &c. viii. Neque ad rem similiter facit vel Jac. i. 23. 24. vel si aliquando tria diversa tempora uno praeterito exprimuntur. Nam in sensu latine reddendo multa potest esse varietas, quae non ideo est in Graecis, & pendet saepe a particula qua Latine uteris, non ex ipsis Graecis textus verbis: ut, si ubi, vel si uteris Latine, dicis, si se converterit, ubi se converterit, pro ratione particulae in Latina loquutione; vel, quod in Graeco est, abiit, sive Latine reddas, quamprimum abiit, nihil mutat in voce Graeca, utcunque varies in Latinis. Et sensus aeque manet, si retineam Latine eadem tempora, quae in Graecis. Quod non ita est in loco Joann. viii. 56. Ut undique appareat rei & verborum quam multa diversitas. ix. Tandem etiam aperte verba Christi carpere haud erubescunt Adversarii, dum causam contortae suae interpretationis dant, quia alias non ita recte dicere Christus potuisset hoc quod dixit, & videbuntur Christi verba niti rei verisimilitudine potius quam ipsa veritate, vel aliquo argumento aut testimonio Scripturae. Quasi nos debeamus esse solliciti, unde Christus habuerit, quod de Abrahamo testatus fuit, & vacillet ejus fides, nisi locum ostenderimus Testamenti Veteris, unde illud producere potuerit. Quae cura nos non versat. Satis habemus, quod αὐτὸς ἔφα[?], qui nihil dixit, vel dicere potuit, nisi verum. Quare quod de Abrahamo protulit, ita verum mihi est, vidisse illum in fide & prophetiae spiritu diem Christi, eoque exultasse animo, ac quod est verissimum. Et haud semel illum diem sibi praesentem fecit Abraham, sed toties ac Deus de Christo apud ipsum, & semine benedicto verba fecit, vel alias ipse fidem suam in ista explicuit ac exeruit.* Versio Æthiopica: Abraham pater vester desideravit, prophetavit, gavisus est, ut videret diem meum: & vidit eum, & gavisus est. Syriaca, Abraham pater vester cupidus fuit videndi diem meum; viditque, & gavisus est. Arabica, Abraham pater vester exoptavit videre diem meum: viditque, & gavisus est. Persica; Abraham pater vester valde cupidus erat, ut diem meum videret: & videns gavisus est. Nemo aliter locum intellexit, ac nos: Adversariorum sensu nemo. Irenæus, lib. iv. cap. xiii. Propheta ergo cum esset Abraham, & videret in spiritu diem adventus domini, & passionis per quem ipse quoque & omnes qui similiter, ut ipse, crediderit, credunt Deo, salvari inciperent, exultavit ıchementer[?]. Non incognitus igitur erat dominus Abrahæ, cujus diem concupivit videre: sed neque pater domini: didicerat enim à verbo domini, & credidit ei. Quapropter & deputatum est ei ad justitiam[?] à Domino. Denique quod dicunt, Christum intricare verbis suis auditores suos voluisse, iisque objicere quod speciosè carperent, nescio cur, & ad hunc præsertim locum, dicatur: viderint, num satis digne de Christo ejusque tum veritate, tum integritate.
units.tr: We have heard in its place with what wickedness our Adversaries twist those words, "before Abraham was," and how they try to stone Christ now, just as the Jews did of old, because he placed himself before Abraham. But in the words that follow, "Abraham saw my day," etc., they play with the text just as boldly. It is quite clear what the matter is about: Christ's excellence above Abraham, not Abraham's excellence above the Jews. v. So it is plain that Christ is not treating here the same argument as in verse 40, the unworthy deeds of the Jews toward him. There Christ says plainly, "Abraham did not do this"; here there is nothing like that. Whether one reads it there as "Abraham would not have done this," or "did not do it," it comes to the same thing, so there is no need to vary the tense of the verb: "Abraham did not do this," that is, nothing of the kind. vi. We do not say that the Hebrews use one past tense for all the past tenses of every mood. We deny that a usage or meaning of words similar to that in our text is found first in Greek and then in Hebrew, which would justify explaining our passage in this way. For Jeremiah 18:7–10 is not a similar case. There the only Hebraism is in the word שׁוּב [to turn], which is rendered "when it turns" or "if it indeed turns"; the difference is that the change of several past tenses into other moods, together with the insertion of a conditional particle, which reverses the whole sense and is not necessary in this place, is absent there. Yet in Jeremiah 18 the thing itself demands something of the kind, and the rendering does not change the sense but explains it, and this is plain to everyone. Moreover, although a particle is added in both places, the case is still different: there it is not "if it had turned" as here "if he had seen," but in the present passage "if he turns," or "where, when, or whenever he turns." So even if we make the expressions here and there parallel, ἵνα ἴδῃ [that he might see] with ᾗ εἶδε [where he saw], our argument will stand nonetheless: there it reads "when the nation turns," here "when Abraham saw my day"; or "where the nation turns," "where Abraham saw." Nor can the conjunction ἵνα ἴδῃ [that he might see] with ᾗ εἶδε [where he saw] prove that in our passage the past tense is to be taken otherwise; it corresponds to the phrase ἠγαλλιάσατο [he rejoiced] or ἠγαλλιάσατο, ἵνα etc., with ἐχάρη [he was glad]. vii. Nothing in John 6:36 bears on this, "you have seen me and do not believe." For although, in explaining the sense, the matter comes to this, that Christ meant, "though you have seen me, yet you do not believe," it does not follow that the words themselves must be changed; the sense flows and is clear enough from the words as they stand, "you have seen me, and you do not believe." Further, that variation would be only in the copula, "even if" and "yet," which are rather explanatory and are to be added to the copula, not substituted for it. Finally, the text does not say "even if you had seen me," which is the whole change of sense and wording that our passage requires, "if he had seen," etc. viii. Nor does James 1:23–24 help, or the fact that sometimes three different tenses are expressed by one past tense. For in rendering the sense into Latin there can be much variety that is not present in the Greek, and it often depends on the particle used in Latin, not on the words of the Greek text: for example, if you use "where" or "if" in Latin you say "if he turns," "where he turns," according to the particle in the Latin idiom; or, what is in the Greek, ἀπῆλθεν [he went away], whether you render it in Latin "as soon as he went away," this changes nothing in the Greek word, however much you vary the Latin. The sense remains the same if I keep the same tenses in Latin as in the Greek. This is not so in John 8:56. So from every side it appears how great the difference between the thing and the words is. ix. Finally, our Adversaries do not blush to find fault openly with Christ's words, when they give as the reason for their twisted interpretation that otherwise Christ could not properly have said what he said, and that Christ's words would seem to rest on the likelihood of the matter rather than on its truth, or on some argument or testimony of Scripture. As if we ought to be anxious where Christ got what he testified about Abraham, and as if his faith would waver unless we showed a place in the Old Testament from which he could have quoted it. We are not troubled by that concern. It is enough for us that he who said nothing, and could say nothing, except the truth [αὐτὸς ἔφα, "he himself said"]. Therefore what he declared about Abraham is true for me: that Abraham in faith and in the spirit of prophecy saw the day of Christ, and rejoiced in his heart, and this is most true. And Abraham made that day present to himself not once only, but as often as God spoke to him about Christ and about the blessed seed, or otherwise he himself declared and displayed his faith in these things. *Ethiopic version: "Abraham your father desired, prophesied, rejoiced, that he might see my day; and he saw him, and rejoiced." Syriac: "Abraham your father was eager to see my day; and he saw it, and rejoiced." Arabic: "Abraham your father longed to see my day: and he saw it, and rejoiced." Persian: "Abraham your father was very eager to see my day: and seeing it he rejoiced." No one has understood the passage otherwise than we do; none understands it in the Adversaries' sense. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 13: "Abraham, therefore, being a prophet, and seeing in the Spirit the day of the Lord's coming and of his passion, by which he himself and all who likewise believed, as he did, in God, would begin to be saved, rejoiced vehemently. The Lord of Abraham, whose day he desired to see, was therefore not unknown; nor was he the Father of the Lord; for he had learned from the Word of the Lord, and believed him. Wherefore it was also reckoned to him for righteousness by the Lord." Finally, as for their claim that Christ wished to entangle his hearers in his words, and to present them with something they could cavil at, I do not know why this is said, especially about this passage. Let them see whether it is said with sufficient reverence toward Christ, both toward his truth and toward his integrity.

units.la: Adde jam dictis, 1 Cor. x. 3. 4. Et omnes eundem cibum spiritualem ederunt: & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt: biberunt enim ex spirituali sequente eos petra: petra verò illa erat Christus. Syrus, & petra illa erat [illegible, ~2 letters] ipse Christus. Versu. 6. Neque tentemus Christum, quemadmodum ipsorum aliqui tentarunt; atque à serpentibus interierunt. Enjedinus, in illum locum: sensus verborum Pauli est, Petram illam seu aquam ex petra fluentem voco spiritualem, quia significabat Christum. Quod ipse Christus sic explicat Joh. 7. 37. si quis sitit, veniat ad me, & bibat. Qui credit in me, sicut dicit Scriptura: flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ.
units.tr: Add to what has been said 1 Corinthians 10:3–4: "And all ate the same spiritual food; and all drank the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual rock which followed them; and that rock was Christ." The Syriac: "and that rock was [illegible] Christ himself." Verse 6: "Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and perished by the serpents." Enjedinus, on that passage: the sense of Paul's words is that I call that rock, or the water flowing from the rock, spiritual, because it signified Christ. Christ himself explains it in this way in John 7:37–38: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water."

units.la: Psalm. cxvi. 10. & II Cor. IV. 13. habentes autem eundem spiritum fidei, juxta quod scriptum: credidi, ideo loquutus sum; & nos credimus, propterea etiam loquimur. Non eadem solum verba sunt Davidis, & Pauli, vel fidelium sub V. atq; N.T. nam ἡμεῖς nos, inquit Apostolus; sed & idem animus, fides, spiritus. Eadem religio fundat efficitque parem per omnia confessionem. Si diversa fuisset religio, & fides diversa, an dixisset Apostolus, habentes eundem spiritum fidei? an subnasci ex tam diversis, ac illas fuisse volunt Adversarii, religionibus potest nna eademque fidei confessio? Non diceret, eundem, inquit Augustinus, nisi & illorum idem ipse esset spiritus fidei. Sicut autem illi quando idem sacramentum occultum erat, credebant Christi incarnationem futuram, sic & nos credimus factam. Et à nobis autem & ab illis futurus exspectatur ad judicium ejus adventus. Non est enim aliud Dei mysterium nisi Christus, in quo oportet vivificari mortuos in Adam: quia sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, sic & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur.
units.tr: Psalm 116:10 and 2 Corinthians 4:13: "Having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore also speak." These are not only the same words of David and Paul, or of the faithful under the Old and New Testaments; for the Apostle says "we" [ἡμεῖς], but also the same mind, faith, and spirit. The same religion establishes and produces the same confession in all things. If the religion had been different, and the faith different, would the Apostle have said "having the same spirit of faith"? Or can one and the same confession of faith arise from religions so diverse, as our Adversaries wish those to have been? He would not have said "the same," says Augustine, unless their spirit of faith were the same as ours. Just as those, when this sacrament was still hidden, believed that the incarnation of Christ would come, so we believe it has come. And from us as from them his coming to judgment is awaited. For there is no other mystery of God than Christ, in whom the dead must be made alive in Adam; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive.

units.la: Duo, uti vidimus, Adversarii passim regerunt. Primo, Testimonia illa, & argumenta, quibus militamus, petita esse ferè omnia ex N. Testamento, non ex Veteri, de quo tamen est quæstio. Secundò, illam Patrum fidem, fuisse alterius generis à fide nostra in Christum, fuisse generalem, aut in promissiones ipsis à Deo factas, non tamen de Christo Servatore suo, aut salute æterna.
units.tr: As we have seen, the opponents repeat two points everywhere. First, that almost all the testimonies and arguments we use are taken from the New Testament rather than the Old, although that is the very question in dispute. Second, that the faith of the Fathers was of a different kind from our faith in Christ: it was general, or directed only at the promises God made to them, and not at Christ as their Saviour or at eternal salvation.

units.la: Respondimus jam, atque ad illud quidem: Quid ni ex Novo Testamento disputemus, de Veteri? an medium hoc aut fallax videtur, aut impertinens? si verum, quod negare haud sustinent; vera etiam certaque, quam hinc inferimus, conclusio. II. Illud quod dixerunt N. T. Scriptores de Veteri, cum doctrinâ & religione ejus vel convenit, vel non. Si non, falsi ergo fuerunt Scriptores. Sin imo, ergo non solum id quod nos docemus, testati de Vet. Testamento Scriptores Novi T. sunt, sed & doctrinâ in Veteri Test. prædicatâ comprehensum, adeoque traditum, notum, creditumque Patribus illo etiam tempore, ac statu fuit. III. Atqui Scriptores N. T. illa, quæ de Patribus illorum temporum referunt, ex Scripturâ comprobant. Uti inspectis locis allegatis liquet. IV. Nec dicas, nos illorum V. T. locorum sensum illum nunc nosse expositione data in N.T. à posteriori, qui non ita facilis ac manifestus est, si sola loca spectentur uti in Veteri exhibentur historiâ. nam non alium sensum Scriptores N. T. iis attribuerunt, ac inesse voluerunt primi ipsorum autores & dictatores. V. Illud quando objiciunt Adversarii, non attendunt discrimen V. & N. Testamenti, quod in hoc etiam situm, quod res & promissiones salutis per Christum non ita dilucide ac copiose in V. T. exponi debuerunt, ac quidem in Novo. In Novi T. Scriptura hoc unice agitur, ut Evangelium manifestissime explicetur, quod non ita sub V. haberi se debuit: ibi lex & quae legis magis tractabantur; hic, quae promissionis Evangelicae: jam velle ut in V. tam clare omnia extent ac in Novo, est oeconomiam utriusque confundere & in vertere. Uti enim legum expositio magis ex V. T. petenda, quam ex Novo, ita vicissim Evangelii major in N. T. quam V. explicatio facta, & uberior, quum alias utraque & legis, & Evangelii doctrina in utroque etiam legatur V. & N. Test. vi. Quare sufficit, ut aliquo modo in V. T. ostendi possint rei hujus, de qua disputamus, testimonia, licet non tam plura, vel copiosa, uti in Novo extant: scimus autem adfuisse populo tum temporis continuo Prophetas & Sacerdotes, qui de sensu verborum & promissionum divinarum homines jugiter instruere potuerunt ac commonefacere. Multa in N. Testamento referuntur de Veteri, ac Veteribus, quae non ideo minus certa sunt, quia nobis forte non potest ostendi, unde illa habuerint Novae Scripturae Autores; sufficit, sic testatum ab infallibilibus & θεοπνευστίς[?] esse. Quis ostendat in historia, Enochum praedixisse & praedicasse adventum judicis ac judicii, quod Judas commemorat in epistola, verf. 14. 15. an ideo neges septimum ab Adamo Enochum dixisse, ecce venit Dominus, cum sanctis millibus suis, judicium facere de omnibus &c.?
units.tr: We have already answered this. As for the first point, why should we not argue about the Old Testament from the New? Does this method seem to them either deceptive or irrelevant? If so, they cannot deny what is true, and the conclusion we draw from it is also true and certain. (1) What the New Testament writers said about the Old either agrees with its doctrine and religion or it does not. If it does not, then the writers were mistaken. But if it does agree, then the New Testament writers are witnessing not only to what we teach about the Old Testament, but also that the doctrine preached in the Old Testament was contained in it, and so was handed down, known and believed by the Fathers of that time and condition. (2) Yet the New Testament writers confirm from Scripture what they report about the Fathers of those times, as the cited passages make plain. (3) Nor should you say that we now know the sense of those Old Testament passages only from the later explanation given in the New, which is not so easy or plain if the passages are read alone as they appear in the Old Testament history. For the New Testament writers attributed to them no other sense than the one their first authors and inspirers intended. (4) When the opponents raise the objection, they fail to notice the difference between the Old and the New Testament. This difference lies partly in the fact that the matters and promises of salvation through Christ were not to be set out in the Old Testament as clearly and fully as in the New. In the New Testament Scripture is concerned above all to set out the Gospel most plainly, which was not to be done in the same way under the Old. There the law and what pertains to the law were treated mainly; here, the promise of the Gospel. To demand that everything stand out as clearly in the Old as in the New is to confuse the economy of the two and turn it upside down. Just as the exposition of the law is to be sought more from the Old Testament than from the New, so conversely the exposition of the Gospel is fuller and richer in the New than in the Old, although the doctrine of both law and Gospel is read in both Testaments. (5) So it is enough that the testimonies to this matter, which we are discussing, can be shown in some way in the Old Testament, even if they are not as many or as full as they are in the New. We know that at that time there were always prophets and priests among the people, who could continually instruct and remind them of the meaning of the words and divine promises. Much is reported in the New Testament about the Old Testament and its people which is no less certain for this reason: that we may not be able to show where the authors of the New Testament got it. It is enough that it is attested as such by infallible writers and divinely inspired [θεοπνευστίς]. Can anyone show from history that Enoch foretold and preached the coming of the judge and of judgment, which Jude records in his epistle, verses 14 and 15? Will you deny that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, said, Behold, the Lord comes with his holy myriads to execute judgment on all, etc.?

units.la: Ad 11 Exc. Resp. Fides Patrum, tantopere in V. T. laudata, atque in Novo, fuit non generalis modo, & promissionum ipsis in genere factarum; sed & specialis in Christum Messiam, & salutem per eum obtinendam, similis nostrae. 1. Quia hoc exseite Apostolus ostendit, Hebr. xi. 1. ἔστι ἡ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις. Patrum aeque ac nostra, in patriam caelestem extensa, verf. 14. in Deum ipsorum, absolute & semper, verf. 16. ἐπουρανίου[?] qua & Moses Christum spectavit, ejusque ὀνειδισμὸν praetulit omnibus opibus Aegypti, dignitatibusque, verf. 26. qua in ἀπέβλεπεν[?] prospectarunt, quamvis ejus πλεονεξίαν[?] non attingerent Euangelicam. verf. 39. 40. Quorum proinde excemplo hortatur Apostolus, cap. xii. 1. 2. ut suspiciamus εἰς τὸν τῆς πίστεως ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν Ἰησοῦν. Sic & alibi non solum ad eandem fidem cohortatur, qualis Patrum fuit, nominatim Abrahami, sed & nos nostra fide illorum vestigiis insequi docet, quod non esset, si non ejusdem generis esset nostra fides, quae illorum. Rom. iv. 12. τοῖς στοιχοῦσι[?] τῆς ἴχνεσι τῆς ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ πίστεως τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ. Unde etiam Abraham dicitur Pater quorumcunque credentium, verf. 11. & in circumcisione, & in praeputio. Deinde, nisi eadem fides esset, male argumentaretur passim Apostolus, ex illorum fide ad nostram; & justificationem fidei nostram probaret ex illorum exemplo, & fide. Statim enim responderi potuisset, aliam illorum, & nostram sub N. T. esse rationem, fidem aliam, ut minus stringere argumentum ejus videretur. Sed ne semel quidem sibi hoc objiciendum Apostolus exististimavit, unde inoffenso pede disputationem suam hoc ex argumento pertexuit haud semel. Rom. iv. Gal. iii. Denique apertissime in loco modo allegato, eandem fidem appellat, & spiritum fidei, 1 1Cor. iv. 13 iv. 13. habens ergo eundem spiritum fidei, juxta id quod scriptum. Ut & fidem & spiritum eundem Patribus indultum sciamus, (quod utrumque Adversarii negant) sive qui fidelibus contigit sub Test. Veteri, sive Novo.
units.tr: In reply to the eleventh objection of the Exc. Response: the faith of the Fathers, so highly praised in the Old Testament and in the New, was not only general, directed at the promises made to them in general, but was also special, directed at Christ the Messiah and at the salvation to be obtained through him, like ours. (1) This the Apostle shows plainly, Heb. 11:1: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for" [ἔστι ἡ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις]. It was extended to the heavenly fatherland as ours is (v. 14), toward their God, absolutely and always (v. 16) [ἐπουρανίου]. By it Moses also looked to Christ and counted his reproach greater riches than the treasures of Egypt and its dignities (v. 26), by which they looked forward [ἀπέβλεπεν], although they did not attain the fuller Gospel blessing [πλεονεξίαν] (vv. 39, 40). The Apostle therefore urges us to follow their example in chapter 12, verses 1 and 2, that we look to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith [εἰς τὸν τῆς πίστεως ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν Ἰησοῦν]. So too elsewhere he not only exhorts us to the same faith that the Fathers had, namely that of Abraham by name, but teaches us to follow in their footsteps with our faith. He would not do this unless our faith were of the same kind as theirs. Rom. 4:12: "those who walk in the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham, which he had in uncircumcision" [τοῖς στοιχοῦσι τῆς ἴχνεσι τῆς ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ πίστεως τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ]. Hence Abraham is also called the father of all who believe, v. 11, both in circumcision and in uncircumcision. (2) Again, unless the faith were the same, the Apostle would argue badly throughout, inferring our faith from theirs, and proving the justification of our faith by their example and their faith. For it could have been answered at once that the faith and the manner of their faith under the New Testament is different from ours, so that his argument would seem less compelling. But the Apostle did not think that this objection should be raised even once, and he carried on his argument from this example without any stumbling, more than once (Rom. 4; Gal. 3). (3) Finally, in the very passage just cited, he calls it the same faith and the same spirit of faith: 2 Cor. 4:13, having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written. So we know that both the faith and the spirit were granted to the Fathers, which the opponents deny, whether under the Old Testament or the New, just as they were granted to the faithful.

units.la: Arg. septimum, ex Antiquorum petimus. sub V.T. spe: Qui spe divinâ exspectarunt caelestia, illis non tantummodo rerum terrenarum factæ fuerunt promissiones, easque creditæ: sed Patres V.T. spe divinâ exspectarunt cælestia: ergo. De Abrahamo Apostolus, Hebr. xi. 10. Exspectavit enim urbem fundamenta habentem, cujus fab icator Deus. Atque de cæteris Patriarchis Idem, verf. 14. Qui enim illa dicunt, ostendunt quod patriam quærunt. 16. Iam vero meliorem concupiscebant, id est, cælestem. Ideo Deum non pudet (quod eodem versu est) cognominari eorum Deus: nam paraverat in urbem. Non tamquam obscurum vel inusitatum prædicat in Patribus, quod cælestem patriam exspectarunt: nec in uno Abrahamo: denique ex illa id probat promissione, quòd Deus ipsorum esset Deus, quod Abrahami non tantum fuit, sed & reliquorum. Jacobus, Genes. xlix. 18. exclamat ad Deum, ejusque se dicit exspectare salutem לִישׁוּעָתְךָ[?]: non salutem temporariam, inquit Targum Jerof. אָמַר אַבּוּנָן יַעֲקֹב[?] Dixit pater noster Iacob, non liberationem Gideonis, filii Ioasch, exspectat anima mea [illegible, ~6 letters] quæ temporaria neque redemtionem Simsonis, qui fecit redemtionem; sed redemtionem quæ prædicta [illegible, ~4 letters] in verbo tuo, ventura populo tuo filii Israel, istam redemtionem exspectat anima mea. Neque ad aliud Moses respexit, vel respicere potuit, quando ἀπέβλεπε[?] εἰς τὴν μισθαποδοσίαν, Hebr. xi. 26. nam eam hac in vitâ nec quæsivit, verf. 26. nec obtinuit: & in meliorem cœlestemque intentus, vitam hanc plenam molestiis turbisque expertus, quantum ab exspectatâ beatitudine & μισθαποδοσία defuerit, ignorare haud potuit. Jobus apertissimè ac magnificè testatus fuit, se Redemtorem suum nosse, & exspectare salutem, atque resurrectionem corporis beatam, cap. xix. 25. 26. 27. Et ego novi Redemtorem meum vivere: qui postremus insurget in cinerem, atque ubi post pellem contriverint istud, ex carne mea videbo Deum: quem videbo mihi, & videbunt oculi, & non alium: defecerunt renes in sinu meo. Magnum aliquod procul dubio speravit hic & eximium, quo se consolatus fuit & erexit in maximis miseriis, & quam spem suam adeo ex abrupto testatus fuit.
units.tr: The seventh argument we take from the ancients. Under the hope of the Old Testament: those who by divine hope looked for heavenly things were not only given promises of earthly things, and believed them. But the Fathers of the Old Testament, by divine hope, looked for heavenly things. Therefore... About Abraham the Apostle says, Heb. 11:10: For he looked for a city having foundations, whose builder and maker is God. And of the other patriarchs likewise, v. 14: For those who say such things show that they are seeking a fatherland. v. 16: But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly. Therefore God is not ashamed (as it says in the same verse) to be called their God, for he had prepared a city for them. He does not present as obscure or unusual the fact that the Fathers looked for a heavenly fatherland, nor does he mention only Abraham. Finally, from that promise he proves that God was their God, which was true not only of Abraham but of the rest as well. Jacob, Gen. 49:18, cries out to God and says that he looks for salvation from him [לִישׁוּעָתְךָ]. Not a temporary salvation, says the Jerusalem Targum: Our father Jacob said, my soul waits not for the deliverance of Gideon, son of Joash, which was temporary, nor for the redemption of Samson, who wrought a redemption; but for the redemption which was foretold in your word, which is to come to your people the sons of Israel, my soul waits for that redemption. Nor did Moses look to anything else, or could he look to anything else, when he looked [ἀπέβλεπε] to the recompense of reward, Heb. 11:26. For he did not seek it in this life (v. 26), nor did he obtain it; and fixed on the better and heavenly life, having experienced this life full of troubles and disorders, he could not have been ignorant how far it fell short of the expected blessedness and recompense [μισθαποδοσία]. Job most plainly and magnificently testified that he knew his Redeemer and looked for salvation and a blessed resurrection of the body, ch. 19:25–27: And I know that my Redeemer lives, who at last shall rise over the dust; and when they have destroyed this skin, I shall see God from my flesh; whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and no other; my reins are consumed within my bosom. Without doubt he hoped for something great and outstanding here, by which he comforted himself and raised himself up in his greatest miseries, and he so suddenly declared the hope he had.

units.la: Excipiunt. Adversarii, respicere Jobum liberationem suam post sequutam in hac vita; quando dixit se videre Deum, cap. xlii. 5. auditu auris audivi te, nunc autem oculus meus videt te. Volckelius, lib. iii. cap. xi. pag. 59.
units.tr: They object. The adversaries refer Job's deliverance to what followed in this life, when he said that he saw God (ch. 42:5): "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you." Volckelius, bk. 3, ch. 11, p. 59.

units.la: Multò tutius, & ad veritatem firmius su-turum est, si ipsam subjectam materiam secuti, Iobum hoc dicere statuamus: Sese divina ope ex summis afflictionibus, quibus tunc miseran-dum in modum cruciabatur, tandem emersu-rum, & in corpore suo, ad pristinam sanitatem revocato, singularem Dei tum potentiam, tum benignitatem atque clementiam agnituram: quemadmodum sane agnovit: ut ex ultimo libri illius capite perspicuum est.
units.tr: It will be much safer, and more firmly grounded in truth, if we keep to the subject matter itself and hold that Job said this: that by divine help he would emerge from the great afflictions by which he was then cruelly tormented, and that, with his body restored to its former health, he would acknowledge God's singular power, and also his goodness and clemency; just as indeed he did acknowledge, as is clear from the last chapter of that book.

units.la: Resp. Augustiora sunt verba & magis magnifica, quam ut ad solam corporis sa-nitatem restringantur, vel ad istud tem-pus, quo redditus pristinæ valetudini fuit & vigori. Ad ultima se extendit ejus spes & oratio, nempe quæ post exesum cor-pus à vermibus, & in pulverem redactum, expectanda sibi essent. Alias quidem etiam Deum vidit, & singularem ejus expertus gratiam ac præsentiam fuit, sed uti postremam visionem, ita omnium il-lustrissimam nunc notat, majorem quam pro vitæ hujus conditione. Non tantum semel, sed iterum se ista fruiturum gloria designat, videbo Deum, videbo mihi, & videbunt oculi, non alium, non peregrinum. Atque ut corporalis restitutionis ad pristinum statum ac valetudinem non ita erat certus, sic non potuisset tanta cum animi πληροφορίᾳ[?] & jubilo eam exspectare, uti securus coelestium & salutis tandem certo obventurae dicit, quod sui renes exspectant, & exspectando quasi absumuntur.
units.tr: Answer: the words are too weighty and magnificent to be confined to the mere restoration of bodily health, or to the time when he was returned to his former health and vigour. His hope and his speech reach to the last things, namely what was to await him after his body had been eaten away by worms and reduced to dust. He did indeed see God at other times too, and experienced his singular grace and presence; but just as he now marks the final vision, so he marks it as the most illustrious of all, greater than the condition of this life allows. He signifies that he will enjoy that glory not once only but again: "I shall see God; I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall see, and not another, not a stranger." And since he was not so certain of the restoration of his body to its former state and health, he could not have awaited it with such full assurance [πληροφορία] and joy. He speaks as one secure about heavenly things and about salvation that will surely come at last, which his kidneys await, and which wears them away in the waiting.

units.la: Inque eadem bona spes suas produxit David, Psalm. xvi. ult. ostendes mihi viam vitae, satietas gaudiorum in tua facie, jucunditates in dextra tua in aeternum. & Psalm. xxxi. verf. 20. quam multa est benignitas tua, quam reposuisti timentibus te, operatus es fidentibus in te, coram filiis hominum!
units.tr: David too extended his good hope to the same things, Psalm 16 at the end: "You will show me the path of life; in your presence is fullness of joy, at your right hand are pleasures for evermore." And Psalm 31:20: "How great is your goodness, which you have laid up for those who fear you, and wrought for those who trust in you, before the sons of men!"

units.la: Denique Dan.xii.2.3. & multi ex iis qui habitant in pulvere terrae, expergiscentur, hi in vitam aeternam, & isti in contumeliam & opprobrium aeternum. Et qui alios erudierint, splendebunt sicut splendor firmamenti, & qui multos ad justitiam perduxerunt, uti stellae in saeculum & aeternum. Et resurrectionis expressa mentio, & gloriae eam sequuturae. Tria sunt in textu, quae illud probant: quia agitur de habitatoribus in pulvere terrae; tum, quod resurgent; denique resurgent eorum quidam ad vitam aeternam. Hoc vero negant Adversarii, & sermonem esse, aiunt, de liberatione a persecutione Antiochi, eamque metaphorice comparari cum resurrectione. Volkelius, lib. iii. cap. xi.
units.tr: Lastly, Daniel 12:2–3: "And many of those who dwell in the dust of the earth shall awake, these to everlasting life, and those to everlasting shame and reproach. And those who have taught others shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who have turned many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever." Here the resurrection and the glory that will follow it are expressly mentioned. Three things in the text prove this: the subject is those who dwell in the dust of the earth; they will rise; and some of them will rise to eternal life. The adversaries, however, deny this, saying that the discourse concerns deliverance from the persecution of Antiochus, and that this is metaphorically compared with resurrection. Volkelius, bk. 3, ch. 11.

units.la: Primum enim ex praecedentibus verbis apparet, istam resurrectionem ad tempora, quae jam olim praeterierunt, spectare. quandoquidem ea, quae hic recensentur, dicuntur extitura in illo tempore, nempe de quo hucusque sermo fuerat. Sermo autem fuit de tempore Antiochi, qui Iudaicum populum, ut ex Machabaeorum libris constat, gravissime afflixit: a qua tamen tyrannide ac calamitate populus ille postmodum fuit liberatus.
units.tr: For first it appears from the preceding words that this resurrection looks to times that have already long passed, since the things recounted here are said to come about in that time, namely the time of which the discourse has hitherto been. The discourse, however, has been about the time of Antiochus, who grievously afflicted the Jewish people, as is clear from the books of the Maccabees; yet that people was afterwards freed from that tyranny and calamity.

units.la: Resp. Quamvis in praecedentibus, Antiochi, & rerum ejus, tum liberationis ab ejus tyrannide, facta fuit mentio; attamen uti videmus Prophetas persaepe a praesenti suo tempore ad Messiam, & ad ultima vel ejus, vel mundi tempora progredi, & nonnunquam per saltum; sic nihil impedit, ut antecedentia de Antiocho, & haec de ultimo mundi tempore, ac suprema populi Dei liberatione, intelligantur. Praesertim quando ejus rei nota verf. 1.
units.tr: Answer: although mention was made in the preceding words of Antiochus and his affairs, and of the deliverance from his tyranny, yet, just as we see the prophets very often proceed from their present time to the Messiah and to the final times of him or of the world, and sometimes by a leap, so nothing prevents the preceding about Antiochus and this about the last time of the world and the final deliverance of God's people from being understood together. Especially since a mark of this matter appears at verse 1.

units.la: Propheta monere lectores voluit, se ad alia & postrema transfire tempora, quando apertionis libri meminit, ex quo homines sint judicandi, & prout eo continentur, liberandi. Quemadmodum etiam Apoc. xix. 12. cum resurrectione mortuorum junguntur aperiendi libri, & judicabantur mortui ex iis quae in libris erant scripta, & secundum opera opforum.
units.tr: The prophet wished to warn his readers that he was passing to other and final times when he mentions the opening of the book, by which men are to be judged and, according to what is contained in it, delivered. Just so in Rev. 20:12 the opening of books is joined with the resurrection of the dead: "and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works."

units.la: Secundo objicit in textu legi, multos resurrecturos, non omnes:
units.tr: Secondly, they object that the text reads that many will rise, not all.

units.la: Deinde illud quoque docet, de ultima hic ac proprie sic dicta resurrectione sermonem non esse, quod haec futura sit universalis. At in Prophetae verbis non dicitur omnes, sed multos ex iis, qui in pulvere terrae dormiunt, resurrecturos; quod omnino significat, aliquos tunc non resurrecturos. Nam quod quidam dicunt, multos interdum omnes significare, aut in se comprehendere: id hic locum habet nullum. Non enim simpliciter dicitur, multos in pulvere terrae dormientes re-
units.tr: Further, they also teach that the discourse here is not about the last resurrection, properly so called, since that is to be universal. But in the prophet's words it is not said "all", but that many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise, which entirely signifies that some will not rise then. For what some say, that "many" sometimes means all or includes all, has no place here. For it is not simply said, "many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth will re-

units.la: Resp. Dicitur in textu multos, proprie pter resurgentium differentem exitum, & distributionem horum ad vitam aeternam, illorum ad opprobrium & ignominiam. Quod ipsum argumento est, hic agi de resurrectione vitae, uti Christus appellat, Joann. v. 29. & exibunt qui bona fecerunt in resurrectionem vitae; qui vero mala fecerunt in resurrectionem judicii. Nam resurrectio ad vitam aeternam; vel vitas in aeternum, uti est in textu לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם[?], de resursed multos de his, seu ex iis, qui in pulvere terræ dormiunt. quæ loquendi ratio semper distributionem aliquam significat ejus generis, de quo verba fiunt, & non omnes ejus generis res aut personas, sed aliquas tantum intelligendas esse docet. rectione ultima intelligi debet. Libera-ti ab Antiocho neque in pulvere terræ fuerant, neque resurrexerant, nedum in vitam æternam. Atque accipiendo ista de corporali & temporaria liberatione, non minus premit difficultas objecta ex voce multos, atque ex sententia vel expositione nostra, de resurrectione ex mortuis. Nam quomodo, liberatis multis ex ista persequutione, eorum hi ad vitam propterea æternam dicentur liberati, at alii liberati ad ignominiam æternam? Ita enim Græci hic legunt, εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν καὶ εἰς αἰσχύνην αἰώνιον. Sic & Arabs & Syrus, ad interitum & opprobrium sociorum suorum æternum. Quod si de improbis intelligas, quomodo ponuntur inter resuscitatos, vel liberatos? & dein guur[?] liberatorum fit distributio? Nam, qui ut calamitatem effugerent, a lege, a pietate ac virtute desciverant, quomodo una cum aliis poterunt dici resurgere ex dormitione vel habitatione in pulvere? vel non nominandi una cum aliis fuerant, certe non eadem illa locutione. Denique si, quod ait Volkelius, ista ab afflictione atque oppressione liberatio, alii quidem cessura erat in æternam gloriam, iis nimirum qui legi divinæ constanter adhæsissent: — cæteris autem in perpetuum dedecus & ignominiam. hoc uti scire potuerunt isti, & justam exspectare operum & defectionis suæ mercedem; ita illud quoque, fideles alii: & si gloriam æternam, ergo ea ipsis & revelata fuit, & credita, & quare tum ab hac sejungetur necessaria ad eam resurrectio, præsertim cum ejus tam aperte & clare Propheta meminerit? & non semel in hoc capite, sed iterum vers. ult. & tu abi in finem, & quiesce, & resurges in sorte tua, in fine dierum. Quid aliud intelligas, quam resurrectionem significari iltis, & promitti Danieli, in fine dierum mundi exspectandam? Quæ Judæi etiam vident, ad quos nostri aliquando hic provocant. Menaffe ben Israël, lib. 1. de Resurrect. cap. iii. Omnium manifestissima, & nulli præcedentum conferenda ratio petitur ex Danielis cap. xii. Multi qui dormiunt in terræ pulvere, evigilabunt, hi in vitam æternam, illi in opprobrium, ut videant semper. Satis perspicue hinc constat, omnes, qui mortui sunt, resurrecturos esse, alii, ut præmium & gloriam consequantur, alii, ut perpetuo puniantur. Quoniam vero corpora non pereunt in æternum, idcirco mors somno comparatur. Ex hoc loco Rabina quoque ostendit fore resurrectionem; ita enim legitur in Sanhedrin, דבינא אמר מהכא ורבים מיישני אדמת[?] עפר (Rabina ait hinc probatur, & multi, qui dormiunt in terræ pulvere, evigilabunt.) יקיצו R. Asse ex postrema parte hujus capitis, idem etiam colligit: inquit enim, מהכא ואתה לך לקץ (hinc liquet, inquit: Tu autem vade ad præfinitum, & requiesces; & resurges in sorte tua, in fine dierum.) ותנוח ותעמד לגורלך לקץ הימין Procul dubio illic Danieli duo ab Angelo promittuntur. Primo ubi pervenerit ad finem, id est mortem, mors enim est finis ac terminus omnium rerum mortalium, quod requiescet, id est quod tunc anima ejus, in mundo animarum fruetur bonis, quæ reservata sunt justis. Deinde, quod suscitabitur in fine dierum, tempore resurrectionis, & quidem non alium in finem, quam ut, cum omnibus piis probis justis hominibus, in sorte sua beate vivat ea parte, quæ terris condita fuit.
units.tr: Answer: the text says many, properly on account of the differing outcome for those who rise, and the division of these to eternal life and of those to shame and disgrace. This itself is proof that what is at issue is the resurrection of life, as Christ calls it, John 5:29: "and they that have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life; but they that have done evil to the resurrection of judgement." For resurrection to eternal life, or living for ever, as in the text [לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם], is the resurrection of many of these, or from among those, who sleep in the dust of the earth. This manner of speaking always signifies some division within the kind of which the words are spoken, and teaches that not all things or persons of that kind, but only some, are to be understood. It must be understood of the last resurrection. Those freed from Antiochus had neither been in the dust of the earth nor risen, much less to eternal life. And if we take these words of a bodily and temporary deliverance, the difficulty raised from the word "many" presses no less than it does on our explanation of the resurrection from the dead. For how, when many are freed from that persecution, can some of them be said to be freed to eternal life, and others freed to eternal shame? For so the Greeks read here: "to reproach and to everlasting shame" [εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν καὶ εἰς αἰσχύνην αἰώνιον]. So too the Arab and the Syrian: "to the destruction and everlasting reproach of their companions." But if you understand these words of the wicked, how are they placed among the raised or the freed? And then, how is the division of the freed made? For those who had fallen away from the law, from piety and virtue, in order to escape calamity, how can they be said to rise together with others from sleep or from dwelling in the dust? Or if they were not named together with the others, certainly not in that same expression. Finally, if, as Volkelius says, that deliverance from affliction and oppression would indeed in one case issue in eternal glory for those who had constantly clung to the divine law, but for the rest in perpetual disgrace and shame: then those people could know this and expect the just reward of their works and defection; and so could the other faithful. And if eternal glory, then it was also revealed to them and believed. Why then should the resurrection necessary for it be separated from this, especially since the prophet mentions it so plainly and clearly, and not only once in this chapter but again in the last verse: "And go your way to the end, and rest, and you shall rise up for your lot at the end of the days." What else can you understand than that a resurrection is signified to Daniel and promised to him, to be awaited at the end of the days of the world? The Jews also see this, and our people sometimes appeal to them here. Menasseh ben Israel, bk. 1 On the Resurrection, ch. 3: "The most manifest reasoning, to be compared with none of the preceding, is taken from Daniel ch. 12: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, these to everlasting life, those to shame, that they may see for ever. It is quite plainly evident from this that all who have died shall rise, some to receive reward and glory, others to be punished for ever. And since bodies do not perish for ever, death is therefore compared with sleep." From this passage Rabina too shows that there will be a resurrection; for thus it is read in Sanhedrin: "Rabina says: from here it is proved, and many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake" [דבינא אמר מהכא ורבים מיישני אדמת עפר יקיצו]. R. Assi also gathers the same from the last part of this chapter. He says: "hence it is clear: Go thou to the end, and rest, and stand up for your lot at the end of the days" [מהכא ואתה לך לקץ ותנוח ותעמד לגורלך לקץ הימין]. Undoubtedly two things are promised to Daniel here by the angel. First, that when he has come to the end, that is death (for death is the end and limit of all mortal things), he shall rest, that is, that his soul shall then enjoy in the world of souls the good things reserved for the just. Second, that he shall be raised at the end of the days, at the time of the resurrection, and indeed to no other end than that he should live blessedly, together with all the pious, upright and just men, in that lot of his which was assigned to him on earth.

units.la: Quod vero ultimo loco dicit Volkelius, non nisi de iis agi hoc in textu, qui fuerunt ex gente Judaica: quam facile dicitur, à robis[?] quoque potest rejici. Præterquam quod hinc non efficiat, quasi non possint in persona Judæorum, qui mos Prophetis frequens, proponi ista, quæ ad omnes pertinent. Deniq;uti à præsenti suo tempore Propheta transfilit ad finem mundi, ita quid à Judæis ni ad omnes, & hominum omnium postremam conditionem ?
units.tr: As for what Volkelius says in the last place, that this text speaks only of those who were of the Jewish nation: that can be dismissed just as easily. Moreover, it does not follow that these things, which pertain to all, cannot be set forth in the person of the Jews, a practice frequent with the Prophets. Finally, just as the Prophet passes from his own present time to the end of the world, so from the Jews he passes to all, and to the last condition of all men.

units.la: Tandem etiam Adversarii concedunt mystice illa loca de mortuorum resurrectione intelligi posse. Volkelius, Hic verò antequam ad alios sac. literarum locos, qui divinæ huic veritati objici solent, accedamus, hoc admonendum duximus, tria ista superiora divini spiritus testimonia, quamvis, si propriam illorum spectes sententiam, istarum, quas dixi-mus, rerum significationem habeant: mystice tamen ad veram propriamque mortuorum resur-rectionem accommodari posse, ita nimirum, ut illius quamdam contineant adumbrationem. Quo etiam reducit locum Jezech. xxxvii. 12. ecce ego aperiam tumulos vestros, & educam vos de sepulchris vestris, &c.
units.tr: At last the Opponents also concede that those passages about the resurrection of the dead can be understood mystically. Volkelius: "Before we come to the other passages of Holy Scripture that are usually objected to this divine truth, we have thought this must be noted: those three testimonies of the divine Spirit above, although, if you look at their proper sense, they have the meaning of the things we have mentioned, can nevertheless be applied mystically to the true and proper resurrection of the dead, so that they contain a certain foreshadowing of it." To this he also refers Ezek. 37.12: "Behold, I will open your graves, and bring you up out of your sepulchres," etc.

units.la: Præterea Act. xxiv. 14. Apostolus testatur, quod credens omnibus quæ in lege & Prophetis scripta sunt, spem habuit in Deum, quam & ipsi isti exspectant, Judæos designat, resurrectionem futuram mortuorum, iustorum & iniustorum. Loquitur certe de resurrectione ultima & universali, eamque tradi & doceri significat scriptis legis ac Prophetarum, & hinc exspectatam non sibi tantum, sed & cæteris Judæis. Concedunt Adversarii, illos quidem exspectasse resurrectionem, non tamen ex promissione ipsis factâ. Smalcius, contra Frantz. Disp. vii. de bon. operib. pag. 223.
units.tr: Moreover, in Acts 24.14 the Apostol testifies that he, "believing all things which are written in the law and the Prophets, has hope in God, which these men themselves also look for," referring to the Jews, namely the future resurrection of the dead, both of the just and of the unjust. He certainly speaks of the last and universal resurrection, and he says that it is taught and set forth in the writings of the law and the Prophets, and hence was expected not only by himself but by the other Jews as well. Our opponents concede that they indeed looked for the resurrection, but not from a promise made to them. Smalcius, against Frantz, Disputation 7, on good works, p. 223.

units.la: Paulus de se dicit, se in Deo spem habere fore resurrectionem iustorum & iniustorum: de Iudæis vero tantùm dicit, eos exspectare eandem resurrectionem vel spem. Quis vero non videt, quantum differant inter se, spem habere in Deo, futurum aliquid, & simpliciter tantum illud exspectare. Hoc quivis extra ullum promissum facere potest, quia scilicet valde id cupiat: illud non nisi promisso divino nititur. Unde etiam hac phrasi, in Deo spem habere, alibi describitur fides hominum Christianorum. Frantzio autem probandum erat, revelatam & promissam fuisse ante Christum vitam æternam. Itaque turpem committit fallaciam consequentis, dum ex exspectatione revelationem & promissionem concludere nititur. Cui promissa est æterna vita, is eam exspectare iure potest: At non, qui eam exspectat, ei illa propositae est.
units.tr: Paul says of himself that he has hope in God of a resurrection of the just and the unjust; but of the Jews he says only that they look for the same resurrection or hope. Yet who does not see how greatly it differs to have hope in God of something future, and simply to look for it? Anyone can look for a thing without any promise, simply because he desires it greatly; but hope rests only on a divine promise. Hence, too, elsewhere the faith of Christian men is described by this phrase, to have hope in God. But Frantz had to prove that eternal life had been revealed and promised before Christ. Therefore he commits a shameful fallacy of the consequent, when he tries to conclude a revelation and a promise from an expectation. To whom eternal life is promised, he can rightly look for it; but it is not proposed to him who merely looks for it.

units.la: Resp. 1. Paulus pariter de se, ac Judæis inquit, ἀνάστασιν μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι νεκρῶν δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων, & hoc utrisque fuisse creditum, atque ex iisdem fontibus seu principiis Scripturæ, vid. legis, & Prophetarum. II. Quod vero de se dicit, ἐλπίδα ἔχων; de Judæis, ἦν [?] ἐλπίζειν, seu ἐλπίδα ἔχειν, & προσδέχεσθαι, uti ejusdem sunt rei, ita idem denotant; & quo minus de eo dubitemus, jungit se-cum Judæos Apostolus, ἦν [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀντί. Syrus interpres eadem utrobique utitur voce, [illegible, ~5 letters], & qui habeam in Deum spem il-lam quam [?] ii ipsi [illegible, ~4 letters] sperant. Versio Æthiopica, & spero in Deo (quod illi cre-dunt) quod resuscitabuntur iusti & peccatores à mortuis. III. Ego non video tantum inter se differre, spem habere in Deo, futurum aliquid; & simpliciter illud exspectare: nam, quam resurrectionem hi exspectabant, exspectabant certè futuram, μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι, & à quo futuram, nisi à Deo? Non dicitur in textu, quod quia valde cu-piverint, hinc tantùm resurrectionem illam exspectarint Iudæi; non, quod suam il-lam [illegible, ~8 letters] alibi fundarint, quàm in Deo, vel aliunde hauserint, quàm ex ea-dem Scriptura, unde Apostolus, unde quivis habere eam poterat. Phrasi ista, in Deo spem habere, describitur alibi fides hominum Christianorum, 1. Pet. 1. 21. 1. Joann. iii. 3. & quia idem fideles Iudæi, quomodo enim in alio, quàm Deo fidem suam posuissent[?], & spem? propterea eadem ipsorum fides fuit ac exspectatio. IV. Quin æque id Paulo dicere potuisset Smalcius, probandum ipsi, in Legis & Prophetarum scriptis revelatam & promissam vitam æternam, atque resurrectionem mortuorum fuisse, ut inde istam spem & exspectationem tum ipse, tum alii concipere potuissent. Nam præterquam quod manifeste id Apostolus afferat, etiam ex ipsorum exspectatione concludi potest, quandoquidem divina fuit, non humana, rei quæ naturam superabat & conditionem humanam, & in quâ expectandâ noluisset se Apostolus cum iis conjungere, nisi & vere & recte eam exspectare potuissent, idque certo fundamento. Apud Gentiles quidem nonnunquam aliquid dictum forte legitur de mortuorum resurrectione, sed quod forte ipsi non intellexerunt: saltem originem suam habuit à consortio eorum cum Judæis, & propterea Scripturis debetur; sed ipsos quod attinet, longe aliter de istâ veritate ex Dei verbo persuasi Judæi, eandem exspectarunt, ac de eâ incerti prorsus somniarunt Gentiles. Exspectarunt illam Judæi, non Gentiles; ex revelatione Dei in sacro ejus verbo, non solo ingenio vel conjecturâ, à quâ habere non poterant, ut iis exspectationem illam tribuisset Apostolus, aut spem.
units.tr: Answer. 1.
