Paul says in the same way of himself and of the Jews that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and of the unjust [ἀνάστασιν μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι νεκρῶν δικαίων τε καὶ ἀδίκων], and that this was believed by both, and from the same sources or principles of Scripture, namely of the law and the Prophets. 2. As for what he says of himself, "having hope" [ἐλπίδα ἔχων], and of the Jews, "to hope" [ἐλπίζειν], or "to have hope" [ἐλπίδα ἔχειν], and "to await" [προσδέχεσθαι], since these are of the same thing, they mean the same; and lest we doubt this, the Apostle joins himself with the Jews. The Syriac translator uses the same word in both places, and says that he has that hope in God which they themselves [illegible] hope for. The Ethiopic version says: "and I hope in God (as they also believe) that the righteous and the sinners will be raised from the dead." 3. I do not see that there is so great a difference between having hope in God of something future, and simply looking for it. For the resurrection which they looked for, they certainly looked for as future, "about to be" [μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι], and from whom as future, if not from God? The text does not say that the Jews looked for that resurrection only because they greatly desired it, and not because they founded their hope upon God, or drew it from anywhere other than the same Scripture from which the Apostle, and anyone else, could have it. This phrase, to have hope in God, is elsewhere used to describe the faith of Christian men (1 Pet. 1.21; 1 John 3.3); and since the Jewish believers were the same, for in whom else would they have placed their faith and hope? Therefore their faith and their expectation were the same. 4. Indeed Smalcius could just as well say this of Paul: he must prove that eternal life and the resurrection of the dead were revealed and promised in the writings of the law and the Prophets, so that both he and others could conceive that hope and expectation from them. For apart from the fact that the Apostle plainly asserts it, it can also be concluded from their expectation itself, since it was of a divine, not a human, thing, a thing that surpassed nature and the human condition; and the Apostle would not have wished to join himself with them in expecting it unless they could truly and rightly expect it, and on a certain foundation. Among the Gentiles indeed it is sometimes read that something was perhaps said about the resurrection of the dead, but what they perhaps did not understand; at least it had its origin from their association with the Jews, and so is owed to the Scriptures. But as for the Jews themselves, they were persuaded of this truth from God's word in a far different way, and they looked for it, whereas the Gentiles, uncertain about it altogether, dreamed of it. The Jews looked for it, not the Gentiles; from the revelation of God in his holy word, not from mere wit or conjecture, from which they could not have had it; so that the Apostle could have attributed that expectation or hope to them.

units.la: Volkelius, lib. III. cap.XI. pag.64.
units.tr: Volkelius, book 3, chapter 11, page 64.

units.la: Objicitur porrò, veteres illos, & Messiam expectasse, & una cum illo summam quandam felicitatem, idque, ut testis est Petrus, divino spiritu patefaciente. Hic primò respondemus, nequaquam probari posse, omnes illos priscos homines Messiam expectasse; cum nec universo illi populo, nec omni tempore promissum fuerit. Ea enim tantummodo ad universum illum populum, semperque spectabant, quæ fœdere illo per Mosen cum illis facto continebantur. Atqui in horum numero futuri Messiæ promissum nequaquam fuit; cum id nusquam in legis Mosaicâ disertim expressum reperiatur. Quanquam enim Moses prophetam excitandum esse de medio illius populi prænun-ciavit: tamen cum de Josua, deque aliis, qui illum subsecuti fuerunt, verba illa sensu literali intelligi potuerint; quid, quæso, roboris tunc habuerunt, ad faciendam hominibus illius spem futuri Messiæ? Eodem propè modo & de illa Jacobi Patriarchæ vaticinatione judicandum est, quâ sceptrum de Juda auferendum esse negat, donec veniat Silo: cum nec olim verba illa intellecta à Judæis fue-rint, nec hodie ab eodem hominum genere satis
units.tr: It is further objected that those ancients looked for the Messiah, and together with him a certain supreme happiness, and that this was by the revelation of the divine Spirit, as Peter bears witness. Here we first reply that it cannot be proved that all those early men looked for the Messiah, since this was promised neither to that whole people nor at all times. For they always looked only to those things which were contained in the covenant made with them through Moses, and which pertained to that whole people. But the promise of the future Messiah was by no means among these, since it is nowhere expressly stated in the Mosaic law. For although Moses foretold that a prophet would be raised up from the midst of that people, yet since those words could be understood in the literal sense of Joshua and of others who followed him, what, I ask, strength did they then have to create in men the hope of a future Messiah? In much the same way must we judge the prophecy of the Patriarch Jacob, in which he says that the sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah until Shiloh comes; for those words were neither understood by the Jews of old, nor are they today understood sufficiently by that same race of men

units.la: Resp. 1. Certe Messias omni Judæorum populo, atque omni tempore promissus fuit. Uti enim à mundi initio jam sub mulierus[?], tum propiùs sub Abrahami, inde Judæ, denique Davidis semine promissus & prænunciatus fuit, ita non ad certos aliquos singula-riter destinata illa vaticinia fuerunt, sed toti semper populo à vatibus suis expositâ, & nullo non tempore, atque indies & frequentiora & clariora extiterunt. II. Quomodo ea tantummodo ad universum populum semper spectabant, quæ fœdere Mosaico continebantur, quum & longe ante Mosem non populus tantum Dei fuit, sed & eadem de Messiâ ἀπ' αἰῶνος[?] ei fuerint tradita? & tum doctrinâ, tum sacrificiis, & sacramentis ante, ac post Mosem, eadem πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως[?] confirmata? Quod satis clare docetur, Joan. 1. 46. quem scripsit Moses in lege & Prophetæ, invenimus Messiam, filium Josephi Nazarenum. III. Vaticinium Deut. XVIII. 15. 18. si de propheta
units.tr: Answer 1. Certainly the Messiah was promised to the whole Jewish people and at all times. For just as from the beginning of the world he was promised and foretold, first under the woman's seed, then more closely under Abraham, then of Judah, and finally of David's seed, so those prophecies were not singularly destined for certain individuals, but were always set forth by their seers to the whole people, and at no time, and daily, they became both more frequent and clearer. 2. How could those things alone be always looked to by the whole people which were contained in the Mosaic covenant, since not only was the people of God long before Moses, but also the same things about the Messiah were delivered to them from the beginning? And were these not confirmed by teaching, sacrifices and sacraments, both before and after Moses, in many parts and in many ways? This is taught clearly enough in John 1.45: "We have found him of whom Moses in the law and the Prophets did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph." 3. The prophecy in Deut. 18.15, 18, if it is understood of a prophet

units.la: Tom. 2. percipiantur ; tantum abest, ut illis tunc Messiae expectationem movere potuerint. Reliquos vates Messiae adventum praedixisse haud sane diffiteor: verum cum illi nec semper extiterint, nec porro illorum dicta foedere illo, generaliter cum omnibus percusso, comprehensa fuerint; & ideo non ab universis ac singulis audiri potuerint; quam, quasi Christi aliquando mittendi spem atque expectationem Iudaeis generatim omnibus attulisse putabimus? Verum esto, expectaverint sane universi ac singuli Messiae adventum; expectaverint quoque praestantissimum quoddam bonum, quo per eundem Messiam universa Iudaeorum natio mirum in modum locupletanda fuerit: num protinus inde consequitur, expressam illis vitae sempiternae promissionem fuisse? nullo pacto. Nam quale illud bonum futurum esset, & quibus in rebus constitutum, nemo ante Christi tempora clare explicuit. Quid, quod apertissime Petrus Apostolus testificatur, vates illos ista praedicando, non sibi, sed nobis ministrasse; utpote cum ea, quae tunc de conferenda in nos gratia praenunciabant, nequaquam ad illorum, sed ad nostra tempora spectarent.
units.tr: Tom. 2. are understood; so far is it from being the case that they could then have stirred up any expectation of the Messiah. I do not deny that the other prophets foretold the coming of the Messiah. But since they did not always exist, and their sayings were not included in that covenant, which was struck generally with all, and therefore could not be heard by all and each, why should we think they brought to the Jews in general any hope or expectation of Christ's future sending? Grant, however, that all and each certainly looked for the coming of the Messiah; grant also that they looked for some outstanding good, by which the whole Jewish nation was to be enriched in a wonderful way: does it follow at once that a promise of eternal life was expressly made to them? By no means. For no one before Christ's time explained clearly what that good would be or in what things it would consist. What of the fact that the Apostle Peter most plainly testifies that those prophets, in proclaiming these things, ministered not to themselves but to us, since what they then foretold about the grace to be conferred on us did not look to their times but to ours?

units.la: magno inter Judaeos excitando, ut de Iosua, vel aliis eum subsecutis expo-nant Judaei, haud adeo mirum; vel vaticinium Jacobi de adventu Silo, ut dubium reddant, non praeter opi-nionem nobis accidit; sed ut is sermo de locis illis apud Christianos habea-tur, jure merito indignamur. Præ-sertim ubi non tantum ex locis illis ipsis certissima proferuntur argumenta, quibus docetur, non nisi de Messia ac-cipi posse & debere, uti in libris no-stris contra Judaeos copiose ostendi-mus, sed & de magno illo Propheta, qui nec Iosua, nec alius quis aut fuit, aut esse potuit, quum nemo ista emphasi unquam fuerit audiendus, nedum jux-ta, aut supra Mosem, habeamus ex-positionem Apostolicam Act. iii. 22. quae non istum tantum locum nobis confirmat, sed & totum hoc argumen-tum. Nam praeterquam quod Aposto-lus locum illum Christo applicat, ver-sibus 22. & 28. addit vers. 24. & omnes Prophetae a Samuele & deinceps, quotquot loquuti fuerunt, etiam hos praedixerunt dies.
units.tr: That the Jews, in arousing great expectation, expound it of Joshua or of others who followed him, is not very surprising; and that they make doubtful Jacob's prophecy about the coming of Shiloh has not happened beyond our expectation. But we justly and deservedly resent that such talk should be held about those passages among Christians. Especially since we have not only the most certain arguments drawn from those very passages, by which it is shown that they can and must be understood only of the Messiah, as we have shown at length in our books against the Jews, but also of that great Prophet, who neither was nor could be Joshua or anyone else, since no one should ever be heard with such emphasis, let alone set beside or above Moses. We have the apostolic exposition in Acts 3:22, which confirms for us not only that passage but this whole argument. For besides the fact that the Apostle applies that passage to Christ, in verses 22 and 28 he adds, in verse 24, that all the prophets, from Samuel onward, as many as have spoken, also foretold these days.

units.la: Omnes ab illo tempore & deinceps Prophetae euangelium docuerunt, etiam ii apud quos pauca aliàs Christum concernentia te putes reperturum. Vos estis filii Prophetarum & testamenti quod Deus fecit cum Patribus vestris, Abrahamo dicens, & in semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terrae. Hoc argumentum testamenti illius est, quod quia Prophetae continuo annunciarunt & explicarunt, hinc filii Prophetarum, iidem dicuntur & filii testamenti. iv. Admodum iniqua est V. Test. expositio, quae petitur ab hodiernis Judaeis, & hinc velle aut judicare de Scripturae sensu, aut de veterum Israelitarum fide ac religione. Ex adverso verba illa Jacobi à Judaeorum majoribus de Messia intellecta fuisse, ex Chaldaeorum Paraphrasibus, & Talmude, & Scriptoribus aliis probatum dedimus pridem in nostro, contra Judaeos, opere. v. Deinde fatetur Adversarius, reliquos à Mose Prophetas Messiae adventum praedixisse: sed causatur, quod nec semper extiterint: quasi alii semper extitissent: & aut illos necesse fuisset semper exstitere, aut non alii etiam ante eos extitissent. Nec ipsorum dicta fœdere generaliter cum omnibus percusso fuerunt comprehensa: Contrarium testatur Petrus, loco, ex Actis, statim adducto, & quod foedus illud de benedictione omnium gentium in isto semine ad Patres omnes spectarit, omnemque populum; quod illud uti argumentum testamenti, ita Prophetarum fuerit, quod à Sa-muele & deinceps filiis ac posteris suis reliquerunt. Ista certe à Prophetis populo exposita, ab universo illo audiri & intelligi potuerunt, proptereaque & exspectationem Judaeis generatim omnibus facere. Quam universalem gentis Judaicae exspectationem in tempora & adventum Messiae, etiam ex Evange-lio est probare: & ex muliere Samaritana, Ioan. iv. 25. Scio quod Messias venturus est, qui dicitur Christus: ubi ille venerit, annunciabit nobis omnia. Propte-reaque Christus jam appellabatur חמדת כל הגוים desiderium omnium gentium, Hagg. ii. 8. & Judaei dicebantur προσδεχόμενος[?] τὴν παράκλησιν[?] τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ[?], Luc. ii. 25. & apud Malach. iii. 1. & cito venturus est in templum suum Dominus quem quaeritis, ואתם מבקשים, & Angelus faederis quem vos vultis, ומלאך הברית אשר אתם חפצים[?]. Haec universo populo & loquitur Prophetae, & tribuit, exspectationem & desiderium erga Messiam haud uno modo declarantia. vi. Jam & illud videtur liquido satis sequi, quod, ubi tam clara & ante & post, exspectatos à populo Judaico Messiae testimonia, cum quo & praestantissimum quoddam sperarint bonum, quod nec fuit, nec esse potuit, uti Judaei perperam de Messia suo fabulantur, terrenum aliquod & corporale, in Messia propterea etiam promissio vitae aeternae facta debeat intelligi. Quor-sum enim aliter, & propter quod, idemque praestantissimum bonum, Mef-siam tam enixe exspectassent? Nec verum, quod quale illud bonum futurum esset, & quibus in rebus situm, nemo ante Christi tempora clare explicuerit: quum praeter innumera Prophetarum vaticinia, ex iisdem adeo omnia sua confirmant Apostoli, ut nihil extra illa loquutos se palam ausi[?] fuerint testari. Act. xxvi. 22. & xxiv. 14. Denique quando Petrus i. epist. cap. i. 12. dicit, Prophetas ista praedicando, non sibi, sed nobis ministrasse, non hoc vult, istam ab illis praenunciatam gratiam minime ad illorum, sed ad nostra duntaxat tempora spectasse; sed referendum ad καιρὸν τινα ἢ πίστιν[?] exhibitionis, sive Messiae, sive cum ipso gratiae, in quae desiderarint & Angeli introspicere. Hunc singularem, & proprium modum N. Test. fuisse, non Veteris.
units.tr: All the prophets from that time onward, and their sayings, taught the gospel, even those in whom you might think to find few things otherwise concerning Christ. You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant which God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, "And in your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed." This is the argument of that covenant, and because the prophets continually announced and explained it, they are therefore called the sons of the prophets and also the sons of the covenant. (4) The exposition of the Old Testament that is sought from the Jews of today is very unfair, and to wish from it to judge either the sense of Scripture or the faith and religion of the ancient Israelites is wrong. On the contrary, we have already shown, in our work against the Jews, from the Chaldee paraphrases, the Talmud, and other writers, that those words of Jacob were understood by the Jewish forefathers of the Messiah. (5) Next, the Opponent admits that the other prophets after Moses foretold the coming of the Messiah, but he objects that they did not always exist, as if others had not always existed, and as if it were necessary either that they should always have existed, or that others had not existed even before them. Nor were their sayings included in the covenant struck generally with all: Peter testifies to the contrary, in the passage from Acts cited just now, and the covenant concerning the blessing of all nations in that seed looked to all the fathers and the whole people; and as it was the argument of the covenant, so it was the argument of the prophets, which they left from Samuel onward to their sons and descendants. Surely those things, once set out by the prophets to the people, could be heard and understood by all that people, and so they created an expectation among all the Jews in general. That this general expectation of the Jewish nation concerning the time and coming of the Messiah can also be proved from the Gospel: from the Samaritan woman, John 4:25: I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will tell us all things. Therefore Christ was already called chemdat kol hagoyim [חמדת כל הגוים], the desire of all nations, Haggai 2:8, and the Jews were called prosdechomenos tēn paraklēsin tou Israēl [προσδεχόμενος τὴν παράκλησιν τοῦ Ἰσραήλ], Luke 2:25; and in Malachi 3:1, the Lord whom you seek [ואתם מבקשים, ve'attem mevakshim] will soon come to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire [ומלאך הברית אשר אתם חפצים, umal'akh haberit asher attem chafetzim]. These things the prophet speaks to the whole people, and he ascribes to them an expectation and desire for the Messiah that declares itself in more than one way. (6) Now it seems quite clear that, since there is such clear testimony both before and after to the expectation of the Messiah by the Jewish people, and since with it they hoped for some outstanding good, which neither was nor could be what the Jews foolishly fable about their Messiah, namely something earthly and bodily, therefore a promise of eternal life must also be understood to have been made in the Messiah. For why else, and on account of what, would they have so eagerly awaited the Messiah, with that same outstanding good? Nor is it true that no one before Christ's time clearly explained what that good would be or in what things it lay, since, besides the countless prophecies, the Apostles confirm all their own teaching from those same prophecies, so that they openly dared to testify that they had said nothing beyond them (Acts 26:22; 24:14). Finally, when Peter says in 1 Peter 1:12 that the prophets, in proclaiming these things, ministered not to themselves but to us, he does not mean that the grace so foretold by them looked only to our times and not to theirs; rather it must be referred to kairon tina ē pistin [καιρὸν τινα ἢ πίστιν], to some time or manner of the revelation, either of the Messiah or of grace with him, into which even the angels desired to look. This was the singular and proper manner of the New Testament, not of the Old.

units.la: Arg. octavum, ultimumque praebet nobis locus Act. xv. 11. Sed per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi credimus salvari, quo pacto & illi. Collatione inter Patres Veteris, & fideles vel discipulos N. Test. institutä, quatuor de utrisque dicuntur pari ratione. I. Salvatos esse, (σωθέντες)[?]. II. Eodem modo, καθ᾽ ὃν τρόπον.
units.tr: The eighth and last argument is provided by Acts 15:11: But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, in the same way as they. When the fathers of the Old Testament are compared with the faithful, or disciples, of the New Testament, four things are said of both in the same way. I. They were saved [σωθέντες, sōthentes]. II. In the same manner [καθ᾽ ὃν τρόπον, kath' hon tropon].

units.la: III. Perque idem medium, nempe fidei, credimus. Versio Arabica, credimus & certi sumus. Aethiopica: sed quod vivemus per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, credimus, & similiter illi.
units.tr: III. And through the same means, namely faith, we believe. The Arabic version reads: we believe and are certain. The Ethiopic: but that we shall live through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, we believe, and so did they.

units.la: IV. Et per eandem causam; nempe gratiam Domini Jesu Christi. Unde ita argumentamur: Qui salvati pari modo, & per gratiam Christi, ac fidem fuerunt, aeque ac nos jam sub N. Test., illis eadem salus contigit, religio, & foedus, salutaria eadem, coelestiaque: Nam illa, quae de illis hic praedicat Petrus, vera esse & locum habere nequeunt, nisi salutis, Christi, remissionis peccatorum, & omnis gratiae, qua salvari necesse est, facta illis, uti nobis, promissione, eique fide habita pari, constantique. Excipiunt Socinani, sermonem illo loco non esse de Patribus V. Test. sed de Gentilibus, per Euangelii praedicationem ad fidem in Christum accedentibus, & hos intelligi per κακεῖνος. Socinus, lib. Suasorio, ad regni Poloniae Proceres, cap. v.
units.tr: IV. And through the same cause, namely the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Hence we argue thus: those who were saved in the same way, and through the grace of Christ and faith, just as we are now under the New Testament, had the same salvation, religion, and covenant, and the same saving and heavenly things. For what Peter here says about them cannot be true and hold good unless a promise was made to them, as to us, of salvation, of Christ, of the remission of sins, and of all grace, by which it is necessary to be saved, and unless they had equal and constant faith in it. The Socinians object that the discourse in that place is not about the fathers of the Old Testament but about the Gentiles who, through the preaching of the gospel, came to faith in Christ, and that these are understood by ekeinos. Socinus, in his Suasorium addressed to the nobles of the kingdom of Poland, chapter 5.

units.la: Videtur enim, pronomen illi, referri debere ad patres: tum quia proximè fuerant nomi-nati, tum quia gentes, quarum antea mentio fuerat facta, in Graeco sunt generis Neutri, pronomen vero illud relativum generis Masculini. Verùm cùm non admodum raro, & pronomina Relativa non ad proximè, sed ad paulò longinquius nominata, referri debeant; & vocabulum Graecum, quod gentes significat, neutri licet generis pronomine masculini generis relatum inveniatur, sciendum omnino est, pronomen illi non quidem ad Patres, qui obiter ibi sunt nominati, sed ad gentes referri, de quibus expressè agebatur: ad ostendendum, quaenam esset salutis via à Deo per Christum proposita, eamque esse fidem in ipsum Christum, sine operibus legis: quandoquidem gentes, quae in Christum crediderant, sine operibus legis servabantur, id attestante Deo ipso, dato illis Spiritu S. non minus quam Iudaeis, qui Christo fidem habuerant. Idem, Catechesis Racoviensis, cap. xi. de Prophet. Christi munere, pag. 308. Smalcius, contra Frantzium, Disp. vi. de Bonis operibus, pag. 199. & Volkelius, lib. iii. cap. iii. pag. 176.
units.tr: For it seems that the pronoun "they" ought to be referred to the fathers, both because they were named most recently, and because the nations, of which mention had been made earlier, are of the neuter gender in Greek, whereas that relative pronoun is masculine. But since relative pronouns are not infrequently referred not to the nearest noun but to one named a little further back, and since the Greek word that means nations, although it is found with a masculine pronoun referring to it though the pronoun is neuter, one must certainly understand that the pronoun "they" refers not to the fathers, who are named only in passing there, but to the nations, of which the discourse was expressly concerned, to show what way of salvation God set before them through Christ, and that this is faith in Christ himself apart from the works of the law: since the nations who believed in Christ were saved without the works of the law, God himself bearing witness to it by giving them the Holy Spirit no less than to the Jews who had faith in Christ. The same, in the Racovian Catechism, chapter 11, on the prophetic office of Christ, page 308; Smalcius, against Frantz, Disputation 6, on good works, page 199; and Volkelius, book 3, chapter 3, page 176.

units.la: Resp. Dicere quidem instituerat Apostolus de Gentilibus, verf. 7. 8. 9. sed quia quaestio agitabatur, an iis imponenda esset legis caeremonialis observatio, an non, dissuasit illud hoc praesertim argumento, quia legis jugum, nec Patribus, nec ipsis fuerat portandum; quocum connectitur verf. 10. sed per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi credimus salvari, quemadmodum & illi. Ut omnino ad Patres referri debeat, de quibus proximè loquutus fuerat, non ad Gentiles. Rationes sunt, 1. Quia proximè fuerant nominati, fatente Socino. ii. Κακεῖνοι, ad πατέρες, non solum ut proximè praecedens, sed & ejusdem generis, commodius refertur, quam ad ἔθνη, quod verf. 7. Neque enim à communi & planâ expositione facile abeundum, non propter aliquam hypothesim, in quam contra communem sensum verba torqueas, & deflectas. iii. Idem probat adversativum ἀλλὰ, prae-
units.tr: Reply. The Apostle had indeed set out to speak about the Gentiles, in vv. 7, 8 and 9, but since the question was being debated whether the observance of the ceremonial law should be imposed on them or not, he dissuaded it chiefly by this argument: the yoke of the law was to be borne neither by the Fathers nor by themselves. With this is connected v. 10: "but we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also are." So it must altogether be referred to the Fathers, of whom he had spoken most recently, and not to the Gentiles. The reasons are: (1) they had been named most recently, as Socinus admits; (2) "Κακεῖνοι" [and those], when referred to "πατέρες" [fathers], relates not only to the immediately preceding word but also to one of the same kind, and so is more fittingly referred to the fathers than to "ἔθνη" [nations] in v. 7, for one must not lightly depart from the common and plain exposition in favour of some hypothesis into which the words are twisted and bent against their ordinary sense; (3) the adversative "ἀλλὰ" [but] also proves the same, being attached to the preceding words without any major break: the yoke which neither our fathers nor we could bear, "but" [ἀλλὰ] "through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we believe we are saved, just as they also are." Namely, the Fathers.

units.la: cedentibus adjunctum nulla magnâ intervenient distinctione, jugum quod neque Patres nostri neque nos potuimus portare; ἀλλὰ sed per gratiam Domini Jesu Christi credimus salvari, quemadmodum & illi. Illi nempe Patres. iv. Cum sequentibus aliter non cohaerent, nam magna distinctione separantur, & aliud est horum, atque illorum argumentum. Tum quis quaeso sensus in his dictis: nos fideles Christiani credimus salvari, quemadmodum gentiles, vel gentiles conversi? quae orationis vis, aut sapor? quae ad superiora cohaerentia aut sequela? contrà decentissima est oratio, credimus nos salvandos, ad istum modum, quo Patres, nempe absque caeremoniarum jugo, illis juxta ac nobis [illegible, ~9 letters]. v. Siquidem Apostoli se cum gentibus conjungere voluissent, in modo & ratione salutis eadem, dixissent, non, nos credimus salvari, quemadmodum illi, sed vice versa, illi, quemadmodum nos. Apostolorum enim non fuit, Gentiles sequi, & hos sibi in modo salutis proponere in exemplum; sed contrà. Eadem cum nostra fuit antiquorum in Ecclesia, sc. de Patrum sub V. Test. salute, fide, & religione, sententia. Ignatius, epist. ad Philadelphenses: unus enim Deus veteris & Novi Testamenti, unus mediator Dei & hominum ad opificium, intelligentibus & sensibilis creatura, & ad providentiam utilem rebusque accommodam, & unus paracletus qui operatus est in Moyse, & Prophetis & Apostolis. Omnes itaque sancti in Christo salvati sunt sperantes in eum, & illum exspectantes, & per ipsum salutem con-secuti sunt, digni qui amarentur & admirationi nobis essent, à Jesu Christo testimonium adepti in Evangelio spei communis. & postea, hæc est, quæ ad Patrem ducit via, hæc petra, hoc septum, hæc clavis, hic pastor, hæc hostia, hoc cognitionis ostium, ἡ θύρα τῆς γνώσεως, δι᾽ ἧς εἰσῆλθον Ἀβραάμ, καὶ Ἰσαάκ, καὶ Ἰακὼβ, καὶ Μωσῆς, καὶ ὁ σύμπας τῶν Προφητῶν χορὸς, & columnæ mundi Apostoli, & sponsa Domini Ecclesia, pro qua sanguinem suum fudit, ut eam redimeret. Similiter Irenæus, lib. iv. adverf. hæreses, cap. xiii. non modo contendit, eundem Deum esse V. & N.T. sed & eundem cum Patre Filium, Christum, & fœdus ac religionem Chri-sti eandem: inquit enim: Juste autem nos eandem fidem accipientes, quam habuit Abra-ham, tollentes crucem quemadmodum ligna Isaac, sequimur eum. Porro: Propheta ergo quum esset Abraham, & videret in Spiritu diem adventus Domini, & passionis per quem ipse quoque & omnes qui similiter credunt Deo, salvari inciperent, exultavit vehementer. Ejusdem libri, capitis xxi. hoc argumentum est, ostensio unius & ejusdem substantiæ esse quæ secundum legem sunt, & quæ secundum Euangelium, & quemadmodum Novum Testamentum prædicatum est à Prophetis. Cap. xxiv. quod & Prophetæ, & justi ante adventum Domini cognoverunt adventum ejus. Cap. xxvi. Consummata enim vita præcepta in utroque Testamento cum sint eadem, eundem ostenderunt Deum, qui particularia quidem præcepta apta utrisque præceptis, sed eminentiora, & summa, sine quibus salvari non potest, in utroque eadem suasit. Augustinus, de præsentia Dei, ad Dardanum, cap. xvii. erat autem antiquis justis aliquid multum, cum tamen & illi eadem fide salvi fierent, quæ fuerat suo tempore revelanda. Non enim audemus fideles temporis nostri præferre amicis Dei, per quos nobis ista prophetata sunt.
units.tr: (4) Otherwise the following words do not cohere, for they are separated by a major break, and the argument of the one is different from that of the other. What, I ask, is the sense of these words: "we faithful Christians believe we are saved, just as the Gentiles, or converted Gentiles, are"? What force or meaning is there in the sentence? What connection is there with what goes before, or what follows from it? Rather, the sentence is very fitting: "we believe we are to be saved in the manner in which the Fathers were, namely without the yoke of ceremonies, they just as much as we [illegible]." (5) For if the Apostles had wished to join themselves to the Gentiles in the manner and way of salvation, they would have said, not "we believe we are saved, just as they are," but conversely, "they are saved just as we are." For it was not the Apostles' part to follow the Gentiles and set them before themselves as an example in the manner of salvation, but the reverse. The view of the ancients in the Church was the same as ours, namely concerning the salvation, faith and religion of the Fathers under the Old Testament. Ignatius, in his Epistle to the Philadelphians: "For there is one God of the Old and New Testament, one mediator between God and men, for the creation of intelligent and sensible creatures, for a useful providence suited to all things, and one Paraclete who worked in Moses, and in the Prophets and Apostles. All the saints, therefore, were saved in Christ, hoping in him and waiting for him, and obtained salvation through him, being worthy to be loved and to be a wonder to us, having received testimony from Jesus Christ in the Gospel of common hope." And afterwards: "This is the way that leads to the Father, this the rock, this the fold, this the key, this the shepherd, this the sacrifice, this the door of knowledge," [ἡ θύρα τῆς γνώσεως, δι᾽ ἧς εἰσῆλθον Ἀβραάμ, καὶ Ἰσαάκ, καὶ Ἰακὼβ, καὶ Μωσῆς, καὶ ὁ σύμπας τῶν Προφητῶν χορός] "through which entered Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and Moses and the whole chorus of the Prophets, and the pillars of the world, the Apostles, and the bride of the Lord, the Church, for which he shed his blood, that he might redeem her." Similarly Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV, ch. 13, contends not only that the God of the Old and New Testament is one, but also that the Son, Christ, is the same as the Father, and that the covenant and religion of Christ are the same: for he says: "Rightly, then, receiving the same faith that Abraham had, we follow him, taking up the cross as Isaac carried the wood." Further: "Abraham, therefore, being a prophet, and seeing in the Spirit the day of the Lord's coming and his passion, through which he himself and all who similarly believe God were to begin to be saved, rejoiced greatly." The argument of ch. 21 of the same book is "the demonstration that what belongs to the law and what belongs to the Gospel are of one and the same substance, and how the New Testament was preached by the Prophets." Ch. 24: "that both the Prophets and the righteous knew of the Lord's coming before his advent." Ch. 26: "For since the precepts of a perfect life are the same in both Testaments, they show one and the same God, who in both urged particular precepts fitted to each, but the higher and chief precepts, without which one cannot be saved, the same in both." Augustine, On the Presence of God, to Dardanus, ch. 17: "The ancient righteous had something great, yet they too were saved by the same faith that was to be revealed in their time. For we do not dare to set the faithful of our time above the friends of God through whom these things were prophesied to us."

units.la: Pelagius postmodum dixit, Patres sub V. T. per exactam legis observatio-nem justificatos salvatosque esse, non per Christum: sed ante legem Mosis, per naturam: inde, lege tradita, per hanc: demum, per Christum. Contra quod Augustinus, ex sententia Ecclesiæ, docuit, Patres illos eodem, quo nos, pacto, per gratiam Christi, & fidem fuisse salvatos. Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum, lib. i. cap. vii. Pelagiani de Orthodoxis dicebant, quod sanctos in Veteri Testamento non caruisse peccatis, id est, nec per emendationem à criminibus fuisse liberos, immo in reatu à morte fuisse deprehensos, docerent. Ad quod Augustinus respondet: Immo dicimus vel ante legem, vel tempore Veteris Testamenti à peccatis fuisse liberatos non virtute propria, &c. sed liberatos esse per sanguinem ipsius redemptoris, qui est unus Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Jesus. Isti autem inimici gratiæ Dei, quæ data est pu-blicis[?] & magnis, per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, ideo dicunt antiquos homines Dei perfecta fuisse justitia, ne Christi incarnatione, passione, resurrectione, cujus fide salvifacti sunt, credantur eguisse[?]. Cap. xxi. Pelagiani dicunt: Sanctos Veteris Testamenti perfectâ hinc justitia ad æternam transisse vitam, id est, Studio virtutis ab omnibus recessisse peccatis: quia & illi quos legimus aliquid peccasse, postea tamen eos emendasse cognovimus. Respondet Augustinus, Quantalibet fuisse virtutis antiquos prædicces justos, non eos salvos fecit, nisi fides Mediatoris, qui in remissionem peccatorum sanguinem fudit: ipsorum enim vox est: credidi propter quod locutus sum: unde ait & Apostolus Paulus: habentes autem eundem spiritum fidei, secundum quod scriptum est: credidi propter quod locutus sum: & nos credimus, propter quod & loquimur: quid est eundem spiritum, nisi quem justi quoque illi habuerunt, qui ista dixerunt? dicit etiam Apostolus Petrus: quid vultis jugum imponere gentibus, quod neque nos portare potuimus, neque patres nostri? sed per gratiam Domini Nostri Iesu Christi credimus nos salvi fieri quemadmodum & illi: hoc vos non vultis inimici gratia Christi, ut eadem gratia Iesu Christi salvi facti credantur antiqui, sed distribuitis tempora secundum Pelagium, in cujus libro hoc legitur, & ante legem dicitis salvos factos esse per naturam, deinde per legem, postremo per Christum, quasi hominibus, duorum superiorum temporum ante legem scilicet, & in lege sanguis Christi non fuerit necessarius, evacuantes quod dictum est, unus enim Deus, unus & Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Jesus. Diligenter observari volo, ut non eandem modo, quæ nostra est, sententiam & doctrinam propugnet Augustinus, sed & iisdem per omnia argumentis, quibus nos usi sumus ante. Lib. iii. cap. iv. probat, Patres eundem Spiritum S. habuisse, ex promissione, promissionis filios, quem nos jam sub Novo: Quis enim catholicus dicat, quod nos dicere jactitant, Spiritum Sanctum adjutorem virtutis in Veteri Testamento non fuisse?
units.tr: Pelagius afterwards said that the Fathers under the Old Testament were justified and saved through the exact observance of the law, not through Christ: before the law of Moses they were saved through nature, then, once the law was given, through the law, and finally through Christ. Against this, Augustine, following the judgement of the Church, taught that those Fathers were saved in the same way as we are, through the grace of Christ and by faith. Against two letters of the Pelagians, Book I, ch. 7: the Pelagians, speaking of the orthodox, said that they taught "that the saints in the Old Testament were not free from sins, that is, that they were not freed from crimes by amendment, but were found in guilt and liable to death." Augustine replies: "On the contrary, we say that before the law, or in the time of the Old Testament, they were freed from sins not by their own virtue, etc., but were freed through the blood of the Redeemer himself, who is the one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. But those enemies of the grace of God, which was given through Jesus Christ our Lord, say that the ancient men of God had perfect righteousness, so that they should not be thought to have needed the incarnation, passion and resurrection of Christ, through whose faith they were saved [...] facti sunt credantur eguisse[?]." Ch. 21. The Pelagians say: "The saints of the Old Testament passed from this perfect righteousness into eternal life, that is, by zeal for virtue they withdrew from all sins, since we learn that those whom we read to have sinned somewhat afterwards amended themselves." Augustine replies: "However great the virtue of the ancient righteous you proclaim, it did not save them, except the faith of the Mediator, who shed his blood for the remission of sins. For it is their own word: 'I believed, therefore have I spoken'; hence the Apostle Paul also says: 'Having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak.' What is 'the same spirit', if not that which those righteous men also had who said these things? The Apostle Peter also says: 'Why do you wish to put a yoke on the Gentiles, which neither we nor our fathers could bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also are.' You, enemies of the grace of Christ, do not want the ancients to be believed saved by the same grace of Jesus Christ, but you divide the times according to Pelagius, in whose book it is read that before the law you say men were saved through nature, then through the law, and finally through Christ, as if the blood of Christ were not necessary in the two earlier times, namely before the law and under the law, thereby making void what was said: 'For there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.'" I wish it to be carefully observed that Augustine defends not only the opinion and doctrine that is ours, but also with the very same arguments that we used before. In Book III, ch. 4, he proves that the Fathers, as the sons of promise, had the same Holy Spirit that we now have under the New Testament: "For what Catholic would say what they boast we say, that the Holy Spirit was not a helper of virtue in the Old Testament?"

units.la: Deinde, sub gratia vero positi quos vivificat spiritus, ut fide ista faciunt, quæ per dilectionem operatur in spe bonorum, non carnalium, sed spiritualium: non terrenorum, sed cælestium: non temporalium, sed æternorum, præcipue credentes in Mediatorem, per quem sibi non dubitant, & spiritum gratia subministrari, ut bene ista faciant, & ignosci posse cum peccant: Sic pertinent ad Testamentum Novum filii promissionis, & regenerati à Deo patre & libera matre. Hujus generis fuerunt antiqui omnes justi, & ipse Moyses Testamenti minister Veteris, hæres Novi: quia ex fide, qua nos vivimus, una eademque vixerunt, incarnationem, passionem, resurrectionemque Christi credentes futuram, quam nos credimus factam: usque ad ipsum Johannem Baptistam, tanquam præterita dispensationis limitem quendam. Auctor Hypognostic. lib. iii. pag. 1386. Omnes igitur Sancti Dei quos superius memoravi, vel non memoravi, qui ante adventum fuere incarnationis Domini Nostri Iesu Christi, fide non alia, nisi qua nunc est, salvi facti sunt. Atque lib. de Patientia, cap. xxi. sic loquitur: Unde & antiqui justi ante incarnationem verbi, in hac fide Christi, & in hac vera justitia, quod est nobis Christus, justificati sunt, hoc credentes futurum, quod nos credimus factum. Videatur item Augustinus, Lib. x. de Civit. D. cap. xxv. & lib. iv. contra Faustum Manich. cap. xi. Denique Retractat. lib. i. cap. xiii. Nam res ipsa quæ nunc Christiana religio nuncupatur, erat & apud antiquos, nec defuit ab initio generis humani, quousque ipse Christus veniret in carne, unde vera religio quæ jam erat, cœpit appellari Christiana. —— Propterea dixi, hæc est nostris temporibus Christiana religio, non quia prioribus temporibus non fuit, sed quia posterioribus hoc nomen accepit. Superius alia ex ejusdem Commentariis in Psalmos loca attulimus. limus. Hoc & Hieronymus censuit, quando lib. 11. adverf. Iovinianum scripsit: Paulisper de Veteri Testamento exempla distuleram, quia solent, ubicumque contra eos facit, dicere, lex & Prophetae usque ad Johannem. Caeterum quis ignorat sub altera dispensatione Dei, omnes retro sanctos ejusdem fuisse meriti, cujus nunc Christiani sunt. Χριστιανοὶ ἔργῳ, εἰ [?] μὴ ὀνόματι, inquit Eusebius, hist. lib. 1. cap. v.
units.tr: Next: those placed under grace, whom the Spirit quickens, who act by this faith, which works through love in the hope of good things, not carnal but spiritual, not earthly but heavenly, not temporal but eternal, believing above all in the Mediator, through whom they do not doubt that the Spirit of grace is supplied to them so that they may do these things well, and that pardon is available when they sin: thus the children of promise, and those born again of God the Father and of the free mother, belong to the New Testament. All the ancient righteous were of this kind, and Moses himself, minister of the Old Testament and heir of the New, because they lived by the same faith by which we live. They believed that the incarnation, passion and resurrection of Christ would come, as we believe they have come: right up to John the Baptist, who stands as a kind of boundary of the past dispensation. The author of the Hypognosticon, book iii, p. 1386. Therefore all the saints of God whom I have mentioned above, or have not mentioned, who lived before the coming of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, were saved by no other faith than that which exists now. And in the book On Patience, chapter xxi, he speaks thus: Hence the ancient righteous also, before the incarnation of the Word, were justified in this faith of Christ and in this true righteousness, which is Christ to us, believing that to be future which we believe to have been accomplished. Augustine may be consulted likewise: City of God, book x, chapter xxv, and Against Faustus the Manichaean, book iv, chapter xi. Finally, Retractations, book i, chapter xiii: For the very thing which is now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients too, and was not absent from the beginning of the human race, until Christ himself came in the flesh; from which time the true religion, which already existed, began to be called Christian. ... Therefore I said that this is the Christian religion in our times, not because it did not exist in earlier times, but because it received this name in later times. Earlier we brought forward other passages from the same author's Commentaries on the Psalms. Jerome also held this view, when in book ii against Jovinian he wrote: I had for a little while deferred examples from the Old Testament, because they are accustomed, wherever it tells against them, to say, "The Law and the Prophets until John." But who does not know that under the other dispensation of God, all the saints before us were of the same merit as those who are now Christians? Eusebius says, in his History, book i, chapter v: Christians in deed, though not in name [Χριστιανοὶ ἔργῳ, εἰ μὴ ὀνόματι].

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: SECTION THREE.

units.la: SEquitur tandem ut Argumenta, seu Objectiones spectemus Adversariorum, quas pro sua, contra nostram sententiam, adferunt. Quarum prima est, quod promissio vitae aeternae & rerum caelestium ac salutarium in Christo, sub Novo demum Testamento, antea ignorata & occulta, jam revelata dicatur. Et in hoc praestantia ejus prae V. Testamento, & dignitas officii Christi eluceat, quod ad hujus servatum tempora fuerit, tantas res manifestare. Ad quae probanda nonnullis Scripturae locis utuntur, quae singula examinanda. Nam in probatione Assumtionis illius tota vis argumenti haeret, & conclusionis. Secundum argumentum habent, quod Deus Pater, a quo omnia in nos redundant beneficia salutaria, demum in N. Test. notus fuerit ac praedicatus. Tertium, quia praecepta Christi, perfectiora praeceptis Mosaicis Veteris legis, exigere etiam videntur altiores & caelestes promissiones. Quartum, ex consensu & testimonio petunt Judaeorum, pro se, atque errore suo.
units.tr: It remains finally to consider the arguments, or objections, which our opponents bring forward in support of their view against ours. The first is that the promise of eternal life and of heavenly and saving things in Christ was not revealed until the New Testament, having been previously unknown and hidden, and that the excellence of the New Testament over the Old, and the dignity of Christ's office, shine forth in this, that it was reserved for his time to make known such great things. To prove this they use several passages of Scripture, each of which must be examined, for the whole force of the argument rests on the proof of that assumption and of the conclusion. Second, they argue that God the Father, from whom all saving benefits flow to us, was made known and preached only in the New Testament. Third, that the precepts of Christ, which are more perfect than the Mosaic precepts of the Old Law, seem also to require higher and heavenly promises. Fourth, they appeal to the consensus and testimony of the Jews in support of themselves and their error.

units.la: Primi argumenti Scripturae loca, quae adferunt, haec sunt: Joann. 1. 16. 17. & ex plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia. Nam lex per Mosem data est: gratia autem & veritas per Iesum Christum fuit. Hinc ita argumentatur Smalcius, contra Frantzium, Disp. iv. de Justific. pag. 94. Quid enim notius, gratiam pro gratia nobis datam esse, ita ut lex per Mosem data sit, gratia vero & veritas per Iesum Christum facta? Si gratia & veritas per Christum facta est, Christus vero, antequam nasceretur, reipsa non fuit, quomodo gratia & veritas, quae est ipsum Euangelium, antea esse potuit?
units.tr: The passages of Scripture that they cite for the first argument are these: John 1. 16. 17. And of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace. For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Hence Smalcius argues thus against Frantzius, Disp. 4 on Justification, p. 94: For what is more well known than that grace was given to us in place of grace, so that the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ? If grace and truth came through Christ, and Christ did not in fact exist before he was born, how could grace and truth, which is the Gospel itself, have existed before?

units.la: Resp. 1. Opponuntur in loco Euangelistae, Moses, & Christus; lex, & gratia Euangelica; haec Christi, illa Mosis. Nihil vero de tempore, quo gratia Christi viguerit, vel non. Atqui de hoc sola est quaestio: non, an Christus auctor & causa sit salutaris gratiae, & non Moses; & quod lex per Mosem lata, non per Christum: haec enim nota, & in confesso sunt. 11. Moses consideratur dupliciter, vel praecise ut legislator, & sic nihil de Christo, imo Christo opponitur; vel ut Doctor & Propheta in genere, & sic de Christo, & gratia per Christum largienda non minus praedicavit, imo illustrius aliquo modo, quam multi alii. 111. Quin ita argumentor: uti lex, quae per Mosem data, tamen etiam ante Mosem nota fuit & viguit; ita, ut gratia, quae per Christum, etiam ante tempora Euangelica fuerit, nil obstat. 1v. Per gratiam & veritatem hoc in loco potest etiam intelligi non gratia & veritas salutaris simpliciter, sed impletionis & οἰκονομίας Euangelicae, ut sic: plenitudo gratiae, & veritas exhibitionis Euangelii, in plenitudine temporis, per Christum facta. Ut sit ἐξήγησις ejus, & annunciationis Euangelicæ: atqui ea demum per Christum & eo manifestato contigit, quamquam vis & efficacia ejus viguerit omni etiam tempore, ante Christum. Sed gratiæ alia mensura & dispensatio olim fuit, ac hodie. Unde illud ita multi interpretati fuerunt ἀντὶ, gratiam pro gratia, hanc illius loco, & non ad exprimendam duntaxat abundantiam, gratiam ad gratiam. Versio Æthiopica, accepimus nos omnes gratiam pro gratia super gratiam. Quod præcipue significatum videri potest, oppositione gratiæ ad legem, & quod gratiæ adjungitur veritas, quoniam & in Christo omnes promissiones sunt ita & amen, 11, Cor. 1. 2. atque in eo impletæ omnes legis cæremoniæ, ut tum ad has, tum ad illas Christus dicatur veritas: & in quo, cum gratia, nobis veritas obtigit ἐγένετο[?]. v. Negamus, Christum, antequam nasceretur, reipsa aut prorsus non fuisse. Fuit enim Deus. Quemadmodum Johannes verf. anteced. testatus fuit de Christo, ante me factus quia prior me extitit. Et gratia quæ ex ipso fluit, non quà Deus, sed Christus est, eo licet nondum exhibito, etiam esse & operari tamen potuit, quemadmodum nunc postquam natus, ita tunc, scilicet propter veritatem vim ac potentiam nascituri. Quemadmodum in moralibus & contractibus vim suam habent ea quæ in fide & veritate fundata, quamvis nondum exhibita vel præstata sint: ita etiam sponsio Christi, & tota ejus mediatio valuit, à quo tempore prima Christi promissio Patribus facta fuit, quamvis multo demum post Christus in carne manifestaretur vel nasceretur, suffulta nempe Sponsoris fide & veracitate. Nisi enim promissa valerent etiam non exhibita, inter homines quidem omnes mox commercium tolleretur, & societas. Multoque magis fides divina infallibilis idem effectum præstare potest, eandemque merito habet vim.
units.tr: Answer. (1) The passage sets Moses and Christ, the law and the Gospel of grace, over against each other: the one belongs to Christ, the other to Moses. Nothing is said there about the time when the grace of Christ was in force or not. Yet this alone is the question: not whether Christ, and not Moses, is the author and cause of saving grace, and that the law was given through Moses and not through Christ; for these points are known and admitted. (2) Moses may be considered in two ways: either purely as lawgiver, and in that capacity nothing is said of Christ, indeed he is set against Christ; or as teacher and prophet in general, and in that capacity he preached Christ and the grace to be bestowed through Christ no less, and in some respects more clearly, than many others. (3) Indeed I argue thus: just as the law, which was given through Moses, was nevertheless known and in force even before Moses, so there is nothing to prevent the grace which comes through Christ from having existed even before the Gospel times. (4) In this passage, "grace and truth" can also be understood not as saving grace and truth in the simple sense, but of the fulfilment and the Gospel dispensation, so that the meaning is: the fullness of grace and the truth of the Gospel's revelation, brought about through Christ in the fullness of time. Thus it is an explanation and proclamation of the Gospel; and this came to pass only through Christ and when he was made manifest, although its power and efficacy were in force at all times, even before Christ. But the measure and dispensation of grace was once different from what it is today. Hence many have interpreted the word ἀντὶ, "grace for grace," as meaning "in place of," and not merely to express abundance, "grace upon grace." The Ethiopic version reads: we have all received grace for grace upon grace. This can be seen to be chiefly meant by the opposition of grace to law, and by the fact that truth is joined to grace, since in Christ all the promises are yea and amen (2 Cor. 1. 20), and in him all the ceremonies of the law are fulfilled, so that Christ is called the truth with respect to both; and in him, along with grace, truth has fallen to us [ἐγένετο]. (5) We deny that Christ, before he was born, did not in fact exist at all. For he was God. As John testified of Christ in the preceding verse: he was before me, because he was prior to me. And the grace which flows from him, not as God but as Christ, could also be and work even before he was exhibited, just as now, after he was born, so then, by reason of the truth, it had the power and force of him who was to be born. Just as in moral and contractual matters, things founded on faith and truth have their force even when they have not yet been performed or paid, so too the promise of Christ and his whole mediation were effective from the time when the first promise of Christ was made to the Fathers, although Christ was only much later manifested in the flesh or born, being upheld, of course, by the faith and truthfulness of the Surety. For if promises did not have force even when unfulfilled, all commerce and society among men would at once be abolished. How much more, then, can divine and infallible faith produce the same effect, and rightly has the same force.

units.la: Adducit quoque in rem suam Volkelius verba Johannis, cap. hoc primo, verf. 4. in ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum. Quibus & alia addit ex ejusdem Auctoris epistolâ 1. cap. 1. 2.
units.tr: Volkelius also brings forward in his favour the words of John in this first chapter, verse 4: in him was life, and the life was the light of men. To these he adds other passages from the same author's first epistle, chapter 1, verses 1 and 2:

units.la: Annunciamus vobis vitam æternam, quæ erat apud Patrem, & manifestata est nobis: ex quibus constat, vitam æternam ante Christi prædicationem, de quo tempore ibi loquitur, in abdito Dei consilio ac decreto latuisse, nec hominibus fuisse patefactam. Opponit enim inter se illa: erat apud patrem, & manifestata est nobis. Hinc idem Apostolus de Dei sermone, h. e. de Christo, primo perfectæ Dei voluntatis interprete, alibi ait: in ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum, hoc est, ipsi commissa erat vitæ æternæ, & viæ ad eam ducentis annunciatio, quâ hominum animos mirifice collustravit, & ignorantiæ tenebras, quantum in ipso fuit, ab iis depulit. Quod idem alio iterum
units.tr: We announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and has been manifested to us. From these it is clear that eternal life, before the preaching of Christ, of which time he speaks there, lay hidden in the secret counsel and decree of God and was not disclosed to men; for those words, was with the Father and has been manifested to us, are set in opposition to each other. Hence the same apostle, speaking elsewhere of the Word of God, that is of Christ, the first interpreter of the perfect will of God, says: in him was life, and the life was the light of men; that is, to him was committed the proclamation of eternal life and of the way that leads to it, by which he marvellously illuminated the minds of men and drove away, as far as in him lay, the darkness of ignorance. The same is said again elsewhere.

units.la: Resp. 1. Integra ponamus verba. Sic dicitur 1 Joan. 1. 1. quod erat ab initio, quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectavimus, & manus nostræ palparunt de verbo vitæ. (& vita manifestata, ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη & vidimus & testamur, & annuntiamus vobis τὴν ζωὴν τὴν αἰώνιον, qua erat apud Patrem, & manifestata est nobis) Quod vidimus, &c. Ne dicam, Adversarios nunc articulum omittere, in quo alias tantum causæ & responsionis suæ momentum collocant: non est sermo de vita æterna in cœlis, sed in loco edisserit, dum ait: Hoc est testimonium, Christo, vel Christo ipso, qui vita, & (nempe quod Deus testatus est de filio suo) vita aeterna dicitur, quod in & ab ipso vita aeterna fit; per metonymiam cau-sæ. Nam illam vitam, quae manifesta- ta ipsis à Patre, se audivisse, vidisse, & palpasse memorant. Quod non de vita in coelis intelligitur, sed de Christo. Syrus [illegible, ~3 letters], Euangelizamus vobis illum, qui erat in principio. Sic enim convenit cum initio Euangelii ejus, inter quae magna est convenientia. ii Quod utraque locutio addita etiam evincit, fuisse apud Patrem, atque esse manifestum. Quae de Christo, ejusque in mundo manifestatione, usurpari solita. iii.Dato, intelligantur de vitâ caelesti: quid dicitur amplius, quam vitam illam ipsis manifestatam? Quod quis negat? Sed hoc est, jam primum, nec ullo modo ante manifestatam? negamus. Verūm ante manifestationem dicitur apud Patrem fuisse. Nempe quia à Patre prodiit, & hanc unicam habuit suae manifestationis causam atque originem. Nequaqnam vero quod in abdito Dei consilio ac decreto latuerit. Namque Joann. i. i. Christus dicitur fuisse apud Patrem. Quod nec nostro, neque etiam Sociniano sensu intelligitur, in abdito Dei consilio ac decreto latuisse, nec hominibus fuisse patefactum ullo modo. iv.Sit & hoc, ut accipiatur locus de vitâ aeternâ, & quod in abdito Dei consilio hucusque latuerit: respondeo, bene quod ad istum modum manifestationis, in Euangelio luculenter & copiose exhibitum: sive, quod dici solet, secundum quid; & non simpliciter latuit. Quemadmodum 1 Pet. i. 11. dicitur, quibus [?]ἀπεκαλύφθη manifestatum quod non ipsis, sed nobis illa servirent, quae nunc vobis annunciantur &c. in quae desiderant Angeli introspicere. Euangelium vides illis sub V. Test. etiam manifestatum: ergo non simpliciter, neque omni modo latuit, in abdito Dei consilio: sed, quod ad illustrem Euangelicae exhibitionis modum, non ipsis, sed nobis servatum istud: ad quod etiam Angeli, ut novum ipsis atque insolens, praesens contemplandum prurierunt. Hoc Apostolus voluit, Hebr. xi. 40. Deo melius aliquid nobis prospiciente, ne absque nobis perficerentur. Similiter responsum ad caetera loca Ioann. i. 4. & 1 Ioann. v. 10. 11. quibus modo dicitur, quid in Christo fuerit, vel quid ipse, vita nimirum; non quod nullae vitae aeternae promissiones factae fuerint ante ipsum exhibitum. Quod non magis sequitur, quam nullas Christi seu Messiae factas antea promissiones, ideo quia Messias fuit. Denique vita aeterna dupliciter consideratur, vel simpliciter, & sic etiam lege promissa fuit; vel vita aeterna ἀπολυτρώσεως redemtionis, peccatoribus acquisita in Christo: & haec demum ex Euangelio oritur, quovis modo à Deo significato & promisso [?]πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως, posteaque [?]בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים [?]ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν exhibito. Ut utroque modo, & ex lege, & ex Euangelio, quamvis dispari ratione, vita aeterna sub V. Test. promissa fuerit & significata.
units.tr: Answer. (1) Let us set out the words in full. In 1 John 1. 1 it is said: that which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the word of life (and the life was manifested, ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη; and we have seen and testify and announce to you τὴν ζωὴν τὴν αἰώνιον, which was with the Father and has been manifested to us). That which we have seen, and so on. Not to mention that the adversaries now omit the article, on which otherwise they place all the weight of their cause and answer. The discussion is not of eternal life in heaven, but the passage explains itself when it says: "This is the testimony," concerning Christ, or Christ himself, who is life, and (namely, as God has testified of his Son) is called eternal life, because eternal life comes in him and from him; by metonymy of cause. For it is that life which was manifested to them by the Father, which they say they heard, saw and handled. This is not understood of life in heaven, but of Christ. The Syriac version has: we announce to you him who was in the beginning. For thus it agrees with the beginning of his Gospel, with which there is great agreement. (2) Both expressions added there also prove that he was with the Father and has been made manifest, which are commonly used of Christ and of his manifestation in the world. (3) Granting that they are understood of heavenly life: what more is said than that this life was made manifest to them? Who denies it? But this is it: that it was not manifested for the first time, and in no way before? This we deny. Rather it is said to have been with the Father before its manifestation, because it proceeded from the Father and had this one cause and origin of its manifestation. By no means, however, was it hidden in the secret counsel and decree of God. For John 1. 1 says that Christ was with the Father. This is understood neither in our sense nor even in the Socinian sense, that it lay hidden in the secret counsel and decree of God and was in no way disclosed to men. (4) Grant also that the passage is taken of eternal life, and that it has hitherto lain hidden in the secret counsel of God: I answer that it has indeed lain hidden in this way, namely as to the manner of manifestation displayed clearly and abundantly in the Gospel; or, as is commonly said, in a certain respect, and not absolutely. Just as it is said in 1 Pet. 1. 11 that it was revealed to them that they did not minister these things to themselves but to us, which are now announced to you, etc., things into which the angels desire to look. You see that the Gospel was also made manifest to them under the Old Testament; therefore it was not hidden absolutely or in every way in the secret counsel of God, but was reserved, as to the illustrious manner of Gospel exhibition, not for them but for us; and for this the angels too longed to contemplate it present, as something new and strange to them. This is what the apostle meant in Heb. 11. 40: God providing something better for us, that they should not be made perfect without us. A similar answer applies to the other passages, John 1. 4 and 1 John 5. 10, 11, where it is only said what was in Christ, or what he himself is, namely life; not that no promises of eternal life were made before his actual appearance. This does not follow any more than it would follow that no promises of Christ or the Messiah were made before, because the Messiah was. (5) Finally, eternal life is considered in two ways: either simply, and in that sense it was also promised under the law; or as the eternal life of redemption, acquired for sinners in Christ, and this indeed arises from the Gospel, which God has signified and promised in many parts and in many ways [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως], and afterwards exhibited in the latter days [בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים; ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν]. So that in both ways, both from the law and from the Gospel, though in different ways, eternal life was promised and signified under the Old Testament.

units.la: Unde ad sequentia, quae etiam objiciunt, Scripturae loca, facilis responsio.
units.tr: Hence the answer to the following Scripture passages, which they also object, is easy.

units.la: Tom. 2. Rom. 1. 1. 2. 3. segregatus ad Euangelium Dei. (quod προεπηγγείλατο ante annunciatum per Prophetas ejus in Scripturis sanctis) de Filio ejus, &c. Nam locus hic contra Adversarios facit, non pro illis, quoniam ante etiam annunciatum Euangelium dicit. Versio Æthiopica, segregatus ad doctrinam Dei: quam antea annunciaverat per os Prophetarum sacrum, & in Scripturis suis sanctis. Arabica, A Paulo servo Jesu Christi, vocato Apostolo, seletto ad annunciationem Dei, quam antea promiserat per Prophetas suos in Scripturis Sanctorum suorum. Etenim non aliud utriusq; Testamenti, & doctrinae Apostolorum ac Prophetarum discrimen, quam accidentale est, quam inter Διαθήκιον, & εὐαγγελίαν, rei caeteroquin & doctrinae unius ejusdemque; non aliud quam inter promissionem, & impletionem ejus seu exhibitionem, & hujus apertam atque generalem praedicationem. Marc. 1. 1. 2. Initium Euangelii Jesu Christi, filii Dei. Quemadmodum scriptum in Prophetis.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Rom. 1.1–3: "set apart for the gospel of God (which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures [προεπηγγείλατο]) concerning his Son", etc. For this passage works against the adversaries, not for them, since it says the gospel was announced even before. The Ethiopic version reads: "set apart for the teaching of God, which he had announced before through the holy mouth of the prophets and in his holy Scriptures." The Arabic reads: "From Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, chosen for the proclamation of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the Scriptures of his saints." For there is no other difference between the two Testaments and the doctrine of the apostles and prophets than an accidental one, namely the difference between covenant [διαθήκη] and gospel [εὐαγγέλιον], which are otherwise one and the same thing and doctrine. It is nothing other than the difference between a promise and its fulfilment or exhibition, and between that promise's open and general preaching. Mark 1.1–2: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in the prophets."

units.la: Rom. xvi. 25. 26. Qui vos potest roborare juxta Euangelium meum, & praedicationem Jesu Christi, juxta revelationem mysterii saeculis temporum (aeternis temporibus, Castellio) taciti, κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου χρόνοις αἰωνίοις σεσιγημένου. Nunc vero manifestati per scripta etiam Prophetica, juxta &c. Ergo Euangelium temporibus V. Test. latuit, & nulla ratione revelatum fuit. Resp. 1. Hoc contra ipsum hunc textum est, quo dicitur, Euangelium per Scripta Prophetica manifestatum. II. Ergo non fuit σεσιγημένον absolute & simpliciter; sed secundum quid, quod ad exhibitionem ejus & complementum. III. Praesertim quod ad claram ejus divulgationem, & praedicationem Euangelii inter Gentes. ideo subjungit hoc ipso in versu Apostolus, fidei, apud omnes gentes notificata. IV. Sic Apostolus exponit, Ephes. III. 5. quod mysterium Christi seu Euangelium in aliis generationibus non significatum filiis hominum, quemadmodum nunc ὡς νῦν patefactum sanctis Apostolis ejus & Prophetis in spiritu. Ut gentes essent coharedes & concorpores, & participes promissionis ejus in Christo, per Euangelium. Non ergo quod omnino occultatum fuerit Euangelium temporibus priscis, nec manifestatum, sed quod non fuerit manifestatum eo modo quo nunc ὡς νῦν; praesertim quod ad vocationem & coalitionem gentium in nomen & communionem Ecclesiae. Versio Æthiopica: ille autem qui potest nos confirmare juxta illud quod edocui vos, & in gloria Jesu Christi, cujus abscônditus fuit cultus, antequam mundus fuit, At manifestatur per verbum Prophetarum, & praeceptum aeterni Dei.
units.tr: Rom. 16.25–26: "Now to him who is able to establish you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages [κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου χρόνοις αἰωνίοις σεσιγημένου] (eternal times, Castellio), but now made manifest through the prophetic writings, according to", etc. Therefore the gospel lay hidden in the times of the Old Testament and was in no way revealed. Answer. (1) This is against this very text, which says the gospel was made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures. (2) Therefore it was not kept secret absolutely and simply, but only in a certain respect, as regards its exhibition and fulfilment. (3) Especially so as regards its clear publication and the preaching of the gospel among the Gentiles; for this reason the Apostle adds in the same verse, "made known to all nations for the obedience of faith." (4) The Apostle explains it thus in Eph. 3.5: "which mystery of Christ, or gospel, was not made known in other generations to the sons of men, as it is now [ὡς νῦν] revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit, that the Gentiles should be fellow heirs and members of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ through the gospel." Therefore it was not that the gospel was wholly hidden in earlier times, nor that it was not revealed at all, but that it was not revealed in the way it is now [ὡς νῦν], especially as regards the calling and gathering of the Gentiles into the name and fellowship of the Church. The Ethiopic version reads: "But he who is able to confirm us according to what I have taught you, and in the glory of Jesus Christ, whose worship was hidden before the world was, but is now made manifest through the word of the prophets and the command of the eternal God."

units.la: Gal. III. 23. Antequam vero veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur, conclusi in fidem revelandam, εἰς τὸ μέλλοντα πίστιν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι. Locum hunc urget Smalcius, contra Frantzium, pag. 93. Hinc Paulus ait; justitiam ex fide revelatam esse in Euangelio, Rom. 1. 17. & alibi ait: fidem venisse nempe sub Euangelio. Gal. III. 23. Resp. 1. Fides, id est, doctrina fidei venit, & revelata fuit Euangelio: verum hinc non sequitur, eam nulla ratione fuisse revelatam in promissionibus Euangelicis sub T. Veteri. Saepius indicatum sophisma, a dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter: quod passim hic committunt Adverfarii. 11. Negari etenim haud potest, fidem etiam sub V. Teft. viguisse : cum alias, tum quia hinc eam passim probat Apostolus, Rom.1.17. & 1v.3.5. 9.11.12. 1 Cor.1v.13. Gal.111.6.7.8. Hebr.xi. Vel 111. fides est Christus, per metonymiam subjecti,vel habitus pro objecto; fides, id est Christus, quemadmodum spes & amor sæpe pro re sperata, vel amata. Atque ita de Christo commode exponas, quod dicitur venire. Hoc autem non tollit omnem de Christo doctrinam & fidem antegressam, nam lex, quæ tum maxime viguit, dicitur verf. anteced. noster pædagogus ad Christum, ut fc. ex fide justificemur.
units.tr: Gal. 3.23: "But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up to the faith which was to be revealed [εἰς τὸ μέλλοντα πίστιν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι]." Smalcius presses this passage against Frantzius, p. 93: "Hence Paul says that righteousness is revealed from faith in the gospel, Rom. 1.17, and elsewhere says that faith came, namely under the gospel, Gal. 3.23." Answer. (1) Faith, that is the doctrine of faith, came and was revealed under the gospel; but it does not follow from this that it was in no way revealed in the gospel promises under the Old Testament. This is the fallacy often pointed out, the move from a statement made in a certain respect to a statement made absolutely, which the adversaries commit at every turn here. (2) For it cannot be denied that faith also flourished under the Old Testament, both otherwise and because the Apostle everywhere proves it so: Rom. 1.17; 4.3, 5, 9, 11, 12; 1 Cor. 4.13; Gal. 3.6, 7, 8; Heb. 11. Or faith is Christ, by metonymy of the subject, or the habit put for its object: faith, that is Christ, just as hope and love are often used for the thing hoped for or loved. And in this way you may fittingly explain of Christ what is said to "come." This, however, does not remove all doctrine and faith concerning Christ that went before, for the law, which then especially flourished, is called in the preceding verse "our pedagogue to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith."

units.la: Excipit Smalcius, loco citato : Nec quicquam his obstat, quód ex Habacuc Prophetâ afferuntur illa verba à Paulo, justus ex fide vivet. Nam quæ Prophetâ dixerat, ea non poterant haberi pro regula omnibus sequenda, cum, omnibus illud notum fuisse, non constet. Fœdera autem tantum ad omnes pertinent, & cum omnibus pacta sunt : nec quid Deus in universum facturum fe promisisset, Prophetæ annunciavit, sed, quid Deus facturus effet ex mera gratia, spiritu Prophetico prævidit. Deinde etiamsi fide homines olim etiam justificati fuerint, quemadmodum testatur autor Epift. ad Hebr. cap. 11. tamen ista fides, in rebus magni momenti, nihil commune habet cum ea, quâ nunc homines sub N. Teft. justificantur. Primum enim fides illa Deum solum respiciebat ; at nunc requiritur fides in Deum & Christum, five, quod idem reipfa est, fides in Deum per Christum, de qua altum in V. Teft. silentium. Credebant quidem fortassis aliqui, Christum venturum : sed, præterquam quod hoc à nemine requirebatur necessariò, longe illa diversa sunt : Credere aliquem venturum, & credere in aliquem : adeo ut in eum, qui nondum est, nullo modo proprie loquendo, credi possit : eundem verò aliquando præfentem futurum, vere credi possit. Deinde fides illa observatione præceptorum, quæ vel ante legem, vel sub lege proponebantur, contenta erat : At fides, quæ est sub N. Teft. præter ea quæ olim à fidelibus requirebantur, requirit etiam observationem eorum, quæ partim ad legem sunt addita, de quo Matth. 5. 6. 7. & alibi, partim tanquam nova, prorsus à Christo, præcepta, qualia sunt : Abnegatio fui ipsius, portatio crucis suæ, & imitatio Christi, quorum nullum ne vestigium in lege extat, de quo postea.
units.tr: Smalcius, in the place cited: "Nor does it stand in the way of this that Paul quotes the words of the prophet Habakkuk, 'the just shall live by faith.' For what the prophet had said could not be held as a rule to be followed by all, since it is not established that it was known to all. Covenants, however, pertain only to those with whom they were made, and the prophet did not announce what God had promised to do in general, but what God would do out of pure grace, which he foresaw by the prophetic Spirit. Further, even if men were justified by faith in former times, as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, testifies, yet that faith, in matters of great moment, has nothing in common with that by which men are now justified under the New Testament. For first, that faith looked only to God; but now faith is required in God and Christ, or, which is in fact the same thing, faith in God through Christ, of which there is deep silence in the Old Testament. Some perhaps believed that Christ would come; but apart from the fact that this was not necessarily required of anyone, those are very different things: to believe that someone will come, and to believe in someone. Thus in one who is not yet, one cannot believe in any way, properly speaking, whereas one who will at some time be present can truly be believed in. Further, that faith was content with the observance of precepts, which were set forth either before the law or under the law; but the faith which exists under the New Testament, besides those things which were formerly required of the faithful, also requires the observance of those things which were partly added to the law (see Matt. 5, 6, 7 and elsewhere), and partly are new precepts altogether from Christ, such as: denial of oneself, bearing one's cross, and imitation of Christ, of which there is no trace at all in the law, as will be said later."

units.la: Respondet primò ad locum Prophetæ; inde ad fidem, quam habuerunt Patres sub V. Teft. ut ejus discrimen indicet à fide nostrâ. Ad quæ nos. 1. Quare non poterant illa, quæ Propheta dixit de vitâ hominis justi ex fide, haberi pro communi regula omnibus sequenda, vel rem, vel verba, quibus uius [?], ti relpiciamus [?]? Loquitur de justo istorum temporum, de ejus vita, & fide : quodnam horum aut non fuit commune, aut non esse tale debuit? Tum verba nequidquam ita proposita, quasi singulare aliquid significarent, vel quod non quorumcunq; fuerit temporum. Denique Apostolus, quando five hunc, five alia ex V. Teft. loca profert aut exempla, ex quibus doctri-nam fidei explicat, neutiquam ut singularia illa spectavit, & non communem comprehendentia vivendi regulam, sed communia, & sibi æque fa-ventia, atque illis. Et hoc nisi fuisset, non adeo firmiter conclusisset ejus ar-gumentatio. 11. Sed, omnibus illud notum fuisse non constat. Unde constat, vel probatur contrarium? Quare minus nota dicetur fuisse omnibus hæc doctrina Prophetæ, quam reliqua? Imo nulla notior vel fuit, vel esse debuit, propter vim ejus summam necessariam-que ad omnem vitam, bene & feliciter, à quocunque etiam, transfigendam. An hic demum Propheta de fide dicere & docere occœpit? nonne in primis Scripturæ libris & historiâ eadem de fide Patriarcharum occurrunt, & ex totâ ipsorum vitâ colligi possunt ? quod fecit Apostolus, Hebr. xi. 111. Propheta & prævidit quod Deus facturus esset, & annunciavit quid faceret. Non enim illa pugnant, aut se mutuo tollunt. Quemadmodum Gal. iii. 8. 9. Scriptura autem prævidens, quod Deus ex fide justificaturus esset gentes, ante promisit Abrahamo : quod in eo benedicentur omnes gentes. Unde qui ex fide, justificantur cum fideli Abrahamo. Et ex fide justificaturus erat Deus gentes, & ex eadem justificavit Abrahamum, qui proinde Pater dicitur credentium, sive in circumcisione, sive in præputio.
units.tr: He first replies to the prophet's passage, then to the faith which the Fathers had under the Old Testament, so as to point out its difference from our faith. To these we answer. (1) Why could those things which the prophet said about the life of the righteous man by faith not be held as a common rule to be followed by all? Are we looking at the thing or at the words? He speaks of a righteous man of those times, of his life and his faith. Which of these was not common, or ought not to have been so? Then the words are put forward in vain, as if they signified something singular, or something that did not belong to all times. Finally, when the Apostle brings forward this or other passages or examples from the Old Testament by which he explains the doctrine of faith, he by no means regarded them as singular, as if they did not contain a common rule of living, but as common, and as equally applicable to himself as to them. And unless this had been so, his argument would not have been so firmly concluded. (2) But it is not established that it was known to all. How is the contrary established or proved? Why should this doctrine of the prophet be said to have been less known to all than the rest? Indeed none was or ought to have been better known, on account of its supreme force and its necessity for leading every life well and happily. Did the prophet then first begin to speak and teach about faith? Do not the same things about the faith of the Patriarchs occur in the first books of Scripture and in its history, and can they not be gathered from their whole lives, as the Apostle did in Heb. 11? The prophet both foresaw what God would do and announced what he would do. For these do not fight with each other or cancel each other out, just as in Gal. 3.8–9: "But Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, that in him all the nations would be blessed.
