So then those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham." God was going to justify the Gentiles by faith, and by that same faith he justified Abraham, who is therefore called the father of believers, whether in circumcision or in uncircumcision.

units.la: Jam ad illud quod de fide dicit, vel discrimine fidei sub Veteri, ac sub N. Test. Resp. i. Fides sub V. T. nihil commune Adversario dicitur habere cum fide N. T. in rebus magni momenti. ergone in rebus parvi momenti? vel forte nullâ in re. Et si illa justificavit, atque hæc, quod de utrâque scribit Apostolus, annon in re satis magni momenti conveniunt? ii. Nego, quod in V. Test. non requirebatur fides etiam in Christum ; sed venturum. uti nunc in eum qui venit. Namque promissus Christus fuit : quare oportuit promissioni isti habere fidem. Nec in venturum simpliciter requirebatur fides, sed ut in eum, quali futurus esset, id est, in mediatorem ac Salvatorem, eumque, prout est, unicum & necessarium. Nam aliud nomen sub cœlo datum nec est, nec fuit unquam, in quo oporteat salvari, neque alia salutis via, quam per Christum, heri & hodie & in futurum semper eundem. Nec magis dici potest, nullo modo credi in eum posse, qui nondum est, ac non in eum qui fuit, quum non illa temporis circumstantia vel hæc fidem fundet, sed Dei veritas bonitasque, hoc vel illo tempore exhibito Messiâ, ostensa. iii. Mala fidei acceptio est, formam ejus constituere in observatione præceptorum : quum hæc obedientiæ, non vero fidei descripto fit. Tum alia & perfectiora legis præcepta à Christo posita, falsum est, & suo loco discutiemus.
units.tr: Now as to what he says about faith, or the difference between faith under the Old Testament and under the New. Answer. The Adversary says that faith under the Old Testament has nothing in common with New Testament faith in matters of great moment. So is it in matters of small moment? Or perhaps in no matter at all? And if that faith justified, as this faith does, as the Apostle writes of both, do they not agree in a matter of sufficient importance? ii. I deny that faith in the Old Testament was not also required in Christ, but in Christ to come, just as now it is in him who has come. For Christ was promised, so it was necessary that faith should have regard to that promise. Nor was faith required simply in the one to come, but in him as he would be, that is, as Mediator and Savior, and as he really is, the only and necessary one. For there is no other name under heaven given, nor has there ever been, in which we must be saved, and no other way of salvation than through Christ, the same yesterday, today and forever. Nor can it be said more truly that one cannot believe in him who is not yet, than in him who was, since it is not that circumstance of time, whether this or that, which founds faith, but the truth and goodness of God, shown forth at this or that time when the Messiah was revealed. iii. It is a bad understanding of faith to set its form in the observance of precepts, since that describes obedience, not faith. As for the other and more perfect precepts laid down by Christ, that is false, and we shall discuss it in its place.

units.la: ii Tim. i. 9. 10. Qui nos salvat, &c. juxta gratiam datam nobis in Christo Jesu ante tempora sæcularia : nunc vero manifestatam per apparitionem Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi. Resp. Gratiam datam Volkelius etiam exponit, designatam. Quodque per Christum ea dicitur manifestata. in superioribus expositum, non negare simpliciter omnem antea factam manifestationem, sed simpliciter rem ponit, id est, gratiam in Christo reconditam propositamque fuisse ; at antea non exhibitam, uti tempore Evangelii, non tam clare, vel tam illustri ἐπιφανείας[?] φανερωθεῖσαν. Quare aliud est, loqui de gratia in Christo manifestata ; vel de tempore, aut ratione temporis Christum antegressi. Tum aliud, de Christi promissi, vel exhibiti, & quæ hinc oritur temporis utriusque differentia, aut diversa œconomia. Interim illud, quod in textu dicitur, gratiam datam in Christo Jesu ante tempora sæcularia. Versio Æthiopica legit, gratiam in Christo Jesu, qui ante mundum erat.
units.tr: 2 Tim. i. 9, 10. Who saved us, etc., according to the grace given us in Christ Jesus before the ages, but now made manifest by the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ. Answer. The grace given Volkelius also explains as designated. As explained above, he does not simply deny that any manifestation was made before; he simply asserts the thing, that is, that the grace was hidden in Christ and proposed, but not previously exhibited as in the time of the Gospel, not so clearly or so illustriously [ἐπιφανείας] made manifest [φανερωθεῖσαν]. So it is one thing to speak of grace manifested in Christ, and another to speak of the time, or the manner of time, that preceded Christ. Then again it is one thing to speak of Christ promised, or exhibited, and of the difference of time or of the different economy that arises from this. Meanwhile, what the text says is the grace given in Christ Jesus before the ages. The Ethiopic version reads, the grace in Christ Jesus, who was before the world.

units.la: Denique plura ex Epistola ad Hebræos proferunt testimonia. Volkelius, In eandem sententiam, & divinus ille au- thor Epistolae ad Hebraeos multa dicit. Illud enim lus praedicari coepit per Dominum. Non quam luculentum hujus rei testimonium est, quaeritur de initio praedicationis Euan-gelii, sed promissionis; non praedicationis Euangelii exhibiti, sed promissi. Quo salutem nostram praedicationis initium a Domino sumsisse confirmat? Et illud: hoc declaravit Spiritus Sanctus, priore tabernaculo A Christo quidem praedicatum fuisse Euangelium, in N. Test. exordio; sed viam in sacrarium, id est, in caelestè illud a Deo jam promissum idem etiam Tabernaculum, quod Christus primus ingressus est in primordio mundi, & V. Test. est, quodque, dum legis ille cultus durabat, nequaquam apertum erat. Huc & illa ejusdem Authoris verba pertinent: nihil ad perfectum perduxit lex, sed introductio melioris spei, per quam appropinquamus Deo. Loca salus dicitur praedicari coepta per Christum Hebr. 11. 3. & ix. 8. & vii. 19. ftum, non excludit omne tempus, vel praedicationem antegressam: nam Johannes ante Christum praedicare de Christo, & remissione peccatorum, ac regno coelesti coepit.
units.tr: Finally, they bring forward several more testimonies from the Epistle to the Hebrews. Volkelius: To the same effect, that divine author of the Epistle to the Hebrews says many things. For salvation began to be preached through the Lord. How clear a testimony to this is it! The question concerns the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, but of the promise, not of the preaching of the Gospel as exhibited, but as promised. How does that confirm that the beginning of preaching was taken from the Lord? And that other statement: the Holy Spirit declares that under the former tabernacle the Gospel was preached by Christ at the beginning of the New Testament; but the way into the sanctuary, that is, into that heavenly place already promised by God, the same tabernacle which Christ first entered at the beginning of the world and which belongs to the Old Testament, was not at all open while the worship of that law endured. To this also belong those words of the same author: the law brought nothing to perfection, but there was the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God. The passages in Hebrews 11:3, 9:8 and 7:19 say that salvation began to be preached through Christ. But this does not exclude every time, or every earlier preaching; for John began to preach about Christ, and about the remission of sins and the heavenly kingdom, before Christ.

units.la: iv. Oppositio fit inter legem & Euangelium, & argumentatio a minori ad majus, si tam gravis fit transgressio legis, majorem futuram illam Euangelii, nempe quod hoc praedicatum sit a Christo & variis signis atque miraculis confirmatum, quum lex per Angelos tradita sit, & multis modis Euangelio inferior. Jam vero quemadmodum lex quamvis per Mosem, vel per Angelorum ministerium Mosi tradita, antea tamen etiam nota fuit; sic Euangelio, quamvis per Christum praedicari tempore N. Testamenti coepto, non intercedit quod ante hoc tempus etiam innotuerit, & praedicatum quoque olim fit.
units.tr: iv. An opposition is made between the law and the Gospel, and an argument from the less to the greater: if the transgression of the law is so grave, then the transgression of the Gospel will be greater, namely because this was preached by Christ and confirmed by various signs and miracles, whereas the law was delivered through angels and is in many ways inferior to the Gospel. But just as the law, though delivered to Moses, or through the ministry of angels to Moses, was nevertheless known even before, so, although the Gospel began to be preached through Christ at the time of the New Testament, it does not follow that it was not known before this time, and that it was not also preached in former times.

units.la: Hic locus nos juvat, non Adversarios. Lex nihil perficit, ἀδὲν ἐπλείωσεν. Neque eo quo viguit tempore: nam ἀδὲν nihil hoc etiam comprehendit. Ipsaque ejus haec fuit natura, τὴν αὐτῆς ἀσθένειαν καὶ ἀνωφελές. Quapropter alio opus fuit, quod meliorem spem faceret, atque ad Deum accessum, gratia nimirum Jesu Christi. Quia vero illa legis inutilitas ad hoc & impotentia semper fuit, & nunquam non necessaria hominibus melior spes, & ad Deum εἰσαγωγὴ hinc Euangelii gratia semper etiam vigueri necesse est.
units.tr: This passage helps us, not the Adversaries. The law made nothing perfect [οὐδὲν ἐτελείωσεν]. Nor did it do so in the time when it was in force, for nothing [οὐδέν] includes this too. Its very nature was its weakness and unprofitableness [τὴν αὐτῆς ἀσθένειαν καὶ ἀνωφελές]. Therefore something else was needed, which would give a better hope and access to God, namely the grace of Jesus Christ. And since that uselessness and powerlessness of the law has always been the case, and a better hope has always been necessary for men, and the introduction [εἰσαγωγή] to God through the grace of the Gospel must always have been in force.

units.la: Hoc ostendente Spiritu, nondum apertam esse viam in sanctta, stante primo adhuc tabernaculo. Resp. 1. Hunc si ita urgere pergant locum Adversarii, sequetur, stante priori tabernaculo, & ante ingressum Christi in coelos, neminem istuc pervenisse, quod coelestè tabernaculum, dum legis ille cultus durabat, nequaquam apertum erat. Quod nescioan ipsi velint: quemadmodum Pontificii limbum aliquem Patrum fabulantur. Certe in praesenti controversia non de hoc quaeritur, an Patres salvati & coelum ingressi fuerint, sed an salutis ipsis ulla ipsis certa notitia vel promissio contigerit. De hoc vero textus non loqui-
units.tr: The Spirit thus showing that the way into the holy places was not yet opened while the first tabernacle still stood. Answer 1. If the Adversaries persist in pressing this passage, it will follow that, while the first tabernacle stood, and before Christ entered the heavens, no one reached that place, since the heavenly tabernacle was not at all opened while the worship of the law endured. I do not know whether they would want this: just as the Papists invent some limbo of the Fathers. Certainly in the present controversy the question is not whether the Fathers were saved and entered heaven, but whether any certain knowledge or promise of salvation came to them. The text does not speak of this

units.la: {1} Ad Hebr. 11. 3. loquitur. ii. Sensus loci est, stante & vigente priori tabernaculo, viam ad coelestia apertam non fuisse & retectam, sed caeremoniis, figuris, & sacramentali apparatu fuisse quasi obnubilatam. Ideo Apostolus utitur voce πεφανερωσιν[?]. Et quum dicit μηπω πεφανερωσθαι, significat se haec cum tempore N. Test. conferre, quando illae nebulae & umbrae cesserunt claritati Euangelii. Fuit ergo etiam in V. Test. via in coelum, sed via Sacerdotis in sancta obumbrata & significata. Iam discussis & sublatis illis velis ac caeremoniis, salutaria caelestiaque omnia retecta facie intuemur & concupiscimus. Nam quod nunc dicitur aliquid φανερωθῆς, sequitur, id nullo modo antea manifestatum fuisse: nam & Christus novissimo die manifestabitur, ὅταν ὁ Χριστὸς φανερωθῇ, Col. iii. 4. & tamen nunc etiam suo modo, quamvis non isto glorioso, satis est manifestus. iii. Quod enim ad illa quoque tempora spectarit gratia & redemtio per Christum parta, quare & via ad coelum, patet ex verf. 24. 25. 26. ubi Christus ingressus dicitur in ipsum coelum, ut ante faciem Dei appareret pro nobis: neque ut pluries offerret seipsum, quemadmodum Sacerdos &c. (alioquin oportuisset eum pluries pati a primordio mundi) nunc vero semel in fine saeculi, ad peccati abolitionem, per sacrificium suum apparuit, πεφανέρωται.
units.tr: {1} It speaks of Hebrews 11:3. ii. The sense of the passage is that, while the former tabernacle stood and was in force, the way to heavenly things was not opened and revealed, but was as it were veiled by ceremonies, figures and sacramental apparatus. Therefore the Apostle uses the word [φανέρωσιν]. And when he says [μήπω πεφανερῶσθαι], he means that he compares these things with the time of the New Testament, when those clouds and shadows yielded to the brightness of the Gospel. So there was also a way into heaven in the Old Testament, but it was the way of the priest into the holy places, shadowed and signified. Now, with those veils and ceremonies set aside and removed, we look upon and desire all salvation and heavenly things with unveiled face. For when something is now said to be made manifest [φανερωθῇ], it does not follow that it was in no way made manifest before; for Christ too will be revealed on the last day, when Christ shall be made manifest [ὅταν ὁ Χριστὸς φανερωθῇ], Col. 3:4, and yet even now he is sufficiently manifest in his own way, though not in that glorious way. iii. For that the grace and redemption obtained through Christ, and therefore the way to heaven, also pertained to those earlier times, is clear from verses 24, 25 and 26, where Christ is said to have entered into heaven itself, to appear before the face of God for us; not so that he should offer himself many times, as the priest does, etc. (otherwise he would have had to suffer many times from the beginning of the world), but now once at the end of the age, he has appeared [πεφανέρωται] for the abolition of sin through his sacrifice.

units.la: Ubi tria diligenter observanda. i. Unitas sacrificii & passionum Christi. ἅπαξ, non πολλάκις. ii. Ad abolendum peccatum, in genere, εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας. iii. Omnium peccatorum, etiam a primordio mundi commissorum, quae expiata fuerunt hoc uno sacrificio, ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ[?] τῶν αἰώνων oblato.
units.tr: Here three things must be carefully noted. i. The unity of Christ's sacrifice and sufferings: [ἅπαξ], once, not [πολλάκις], many times. ii. For the abolition of sin in general: [εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας]. iii. Of all sins, even those committed from the beginning of the world, which were expiated by this one sacrifice, offered [ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων], at the end of the ages.

units.la: Ex quo colligo, perinde haberi sive Christi sacrificium in mundi exordio, an fine contigerit: & quod hoc uno omnia abolenda vel expianda peccata fuerint, quae a mundi primordio perpetrata, aeque ac postea, & sub finem. Denique, nisi is valor & vis sacrificii Christi in mundi συντελείᾳ[?] fuisset, ut ex-piare potuisset peccata omni tempore commissa, debuisset saepius, & a mundi initio mactatus fuisse Christus. Iam vero hoc nihil necesse fuit, propter summam illius unius vim, se exerentem ad tempora pristina aeque ac futura, ad expiationem sub V. Test. aeque ac N. peragendam. Atque inde dictum Hebr. xii. 22. 23. 24. nos accessisse Zioni monti, & civitati Dei viventis, Ierusalemo caelesti, Panegyri & ecclesiae primogenitorum in coelis scriptorum, Et N. Test. Mediatori Iesu, & sanguini expiationis meliora loquenti, quam Abelis.
units.tr: From this I conclude that it makes no difference whether Christ's sacrifice took place at the beginning of the world or at its end. By this one sacrifice all sins were to be abolished or expiated, those committed from the beginning of the world just as much as those committed afterwards and at the end. Finally, unless the value and power of Christ's sacrifice reached to the consummation [συντελείᾳ] of the world, so that it could expiate sins committed at every time, Christ would have had to be offered more often, and would have had to be slain from the beginning of the world. But this was not necessary at all, because of the supreme power of that one sacrifice, which extends to past times as well as to future ones, to accomplish expiation under the Old Testament as well as under the New. Hence it is said in Hebrews 12:22–24 that we have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to the festal assembly and the church of the firstborn written in heaven, and to Jesus the Mediator of the New Testament, and to the blood of sprinkling, which speaks better than that of Abel.

units.la: Hebr. xi. 39. 40. Atque illi omnes testimonio fidei ornati non reportarunt promissionem, οὐκ ἐκομίσαντο τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν. Deo pro nobis melius quid providente, ne sine nobis perficerentur, ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶσι[?]. Locus intelligendus est, non de promissione vitae aeternae, in coelis obtinendae, sed de promissione aliqua in hac vita, promissione videlicet Christi exhibendi. Non assequuti fuerunt promissionem; id est, rem promissam. Uti amor, pro re amata; spes, pro sperata; fides, pro credita, aliquoties in Sacris usurpantur. Vide Canttic. 11. 7. Col. 1. 27. 1 Cor. ix. 10. Rom. iv. 5. Illa enim ita opponuntur. ἐπαγγελία, & διαθήκιον [?], illud ut sit Christi promissi. & exhibendi ; hoc, exhibiti. Rom. i. 1. 2. Hebr. 11. 2. Καὶ γὰρ ἐσμὲν διαθηκισμένοι [?], καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι. Sed promissionis complementum non attigerunt. hoc cap. verf. 13. Κατὰ πίστιν ἀπέθανον ἅπαντες [?], μὴ λαβόντες τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, ἀλλὰ πόῤῥωθεν αὐτὰς ἰδόντες. Quod ideo verf. 9. vocat συγκληρονόμους τῆς ἐπαγγελίας. Ergo utrumque hoc in cap. de illis docetur, 1. Quod ex fide viventes mortuique vitam caelestem suspexerunt. verf. 14. Qui enim illa dicunt, ostendunt quod patriam quaerunt. 16. Iam vero meliorem appetiverunt, hoc est caelestem. 11. Quod complementum & exhibitionem promissionum sibi hac in vita factarum non attigerunt: alii non illas de possessione terrae Canaan, nulli istas de exhibitione Christi, quam alteri tempori, πληρώματα [?], seu σωτηρίας [?] (namque πλεῖον id dicitur quod πλῆρες, uti in aetate, eruditione, & similibus) τῶν αἰώνων servavit Deus. Sumitur, inquit Jonas Schlichtingius, in hunc locum, vox promissionis hic quoque per metonymiam adjuncti, pro re promissa. Hoc illud est, οὐκ ἀπολαμβάνουσιν [?]. Κομίζεσθαι enim est, rem plene consequi, adipisci, & eâ frui. 1 Pet. 1. 9. Κομιζόμενοι τὸ τέλος fidei. Col. iii. 25. ὁ γὰρ ἀδικῶν κομιεῖται ὃ ἠδίκησε. Sic & Hebr. xi. 13. λαβεῖν τὰς ἐπαγγελίας. verf. 33. ἐπιτυχεῖν ἐπαγγελιῶν. Deinde, ne sine nobis perficerentur, est, ne ante nostra tempora (Schlichtingius: sine nobis, id est, ante nos) gaudérent non modo promissionibus, sed ipsa quoque earum πληρώσεως [?], quae nobis & nostris temporibus reservabatur; pro varia & sapienti Dei in rebus Euangelii administrandis dispensatione, uti hac felicitate hi, illi alia ornarentur. Certe οἰκονομίας illius πληρότητος est cum Christi exhibitione, & statu N. Test. Haec σωτηρίας τῶν αἰώνων, & πληρότητος gratiae Euangelicae. Apostolus, ἐπὶ τὴν πληρότητα φερώμεθα [?]. Hebr. vi. 1. & frequens illa in scriptis T. Test. vocis hujus est usurpatio. Hebr. vii. 19. Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος, ἐπεισαγωγὴ δὲ κρείττονος ἐλπίδος, δι᾽ ἧς ἐγγίζομεν τῷ Θεῷ.
units.tr: Hebrews 11:39–40: "And all these, though they were commended for their faith, did not receive what was promised" [οὐκ ἐκομίσαντο τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν], "God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us" [ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶσι]. The passage must be understood not of the promise of eternal life to be obtained in heaven, but of some promise in this life, namely the promise of the exhibition of Christ. They did not obtain the promise, that is, the thing promised. In the Scriptures, love is used for the beloved thing, hope for the thing hoped for, and faith for the thing believed, in the same way. See Song 1:7; Col. 1:27; 1 Cor. 9:10; Rom. 4:5. For these terms are opposed in this way: promise [ἐπαγγελία] and covenant [διαθήκη]; the former means the thing promised, the Christ who is promised and to be exhibited; the latter, the thing exhibited. See Rom. 1:1–2; Heb. 11:2. "For we have had the gospel preached to us just as they did" [Καὶ γὰρ ἐσμὲν διαθηκισμένοι, καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι]. But they did not attain the fulfilment of the promise, as in this chapter, verse 13: "All of these died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar" [Κατὰ πίστιν ἀπέθανον ἅπαντες, μὴ λαβόντες τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, ἀλλὰ πόῤῥωθεν αὐτὰς ἰδόντες]. For this reason, in verse 9, he calls them "fellow heirs of the promise" [συγκληρονόμους τῆς ἐπαγγελίας]. Therefore both points are taught in this chapter about them: first, that living by faith and dying, they looked up to a heavenly life (verse 14: "For those who say such things show that they are seeking a homeland"; verse 16: "But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one"); second, that they did not attain the fulfilment and exhibition of the promises made to them in this life. Others did not attain them: the promises about possession of the land of Canaan, and none attained those about the exhibition of Christ, which God has reserved for another time, the fulfilments [πληρώματα] or salvation [σωτηρίας] (for the greater is what is full, as in age, learning and the like) of the ages. "The word of promise," says Jonas Schlichting, "is taken here too by metonymy of the adjunct, for the thing promised." This is what is meant by "they did not receive" [οὐκ ἀπολαμβάνουσιν]. For to receive [κομίζεσθαι] is to attain fully, to obtain and to enjoy the thing. 1 Pet. 1:9: "receiving the end of your faith" [Κομιζόμενοι τὸ τέλος τῆς πίστεως]; Col. 3:25: "for he who does wrong will receive back what he has done" [ὁ γὰρ ἀδικῶν κομιεῖται ὃ ἠδίκησε]. So also Heb. 11:13, "to receive the promises" [λαβεῖν τὰς ἐπαγγελίας], and verse 33, "to obtain promises" [ἐπιτυχεῖν ἐπαγγελιῶν]. Next, "that they should not be made perfect without us" means that they should not, before our times (Schlichting: "without us, that is, before us"), enjoy not only the promises but also the very fulfilment of them, which was reserved for us and for our times; so that by the varied and wise dispensation of God in administering the things of the gospel, these were adorned with this happiness, and those with others. Certainly the fulness of that dispensation is bound up with the exhibition of Christ and the state of the New Testament. This is the salvation of the ages and the fulness of evangelical grace. The Apostle says, "let us be carried on to fulness" [ἐπὶ τὴν πληρότητα φερώμεθα] (Heb. 6:1), and this use of the word is frequent in the writings of the New Testament. Heb. 7:19: "For the law made nothing perfect, but there is the bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God" [Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος, ἐπεισαγωγὴ δὲ κρείττονος ἐλπίδος, δι᾽ ἧς ἐγγίζομεν τῷ Θεῷ].

units.la: Hebr. VIII. 6. Iam vero Christus tanto praestantius sortitus est munus, quanto melioris testamenti est mediator, quod melioribus promissis sancitum est. Locum hunc objicit Socinus, in lib. Quod Regni Poloniae, &c. cap. vii. & contra Palaeologum, part. iv. pag. 556. Ostorod. Instit. cap. v. Resp. Non intelligi debet, quasi non etiam in Veteri Foedere promissio fuisset vitae aeternae, nec nota illa, vel praedicata. Quaeso probet Adversarius istam consequentiam: Novum Testamentum, cujus Christus est Mediator, melioribus constat promissionibus: ergo promissio vitæ æternæ nulla fuit in V. Test. Negatur Consequentia. Nam etiam hæc ex novo fœdere gratiæ promissio proposita illo tempore fuit. Oppo-nit Apostolus duplex Testamentum, Vetus Mosaicum, ac Novum Christi; tum utriusque λειτουργίας[?] : ibi Sacerdotes Aaronicos, hic Christum ; qui etiam hujus Mediator, illius Moses. Jam vero illud Testamentum, uti habebat typica omnia, & cæremonialia, ita valebant tantum ad purificationem ex-ternam & cæremonialem carnis, non ad internam animi & conscientiæ, cap. ix. 9. 10. Novum vero Testamentum continet spiritualia & cælestia ipsa, spirituali & copioso modo administrata. Quæ longe meliora sunt illis. Atque uti distinguendum fœdus ipsum, ab ejus administrandi modo; ita quamvis fœ-deris gratiæ substantia & vis etiam fuerit in V. Test. at fuit sub dispensatione vel modo dispensationis Mosaicæ. Testamentum autem prius Mosaicum non tanta continuit bona, ac Testamentum Novum, sub dispensatione & luce Christi. Videlicet hic magis spiritualia, & clara, & copiosa, quam unquam ea fuerunt antea, & fideles N. Test. longe majorem eorum sensum habent ac abundantiam, quam olim Veteres. Vers. x. Apostolus explicaturus novum fœdus, ejusque excellentiam præ Veteri, in eo hoc situm esse docet, quod Deus eorum futurus esset Deus, & ipsi Dei populus. Atqui hoc etiam Deus fnit sui populi in Test. V. at magis tamen Novi. Deinde, non docebunt amplius quisque proximum suum: non quod prorsus id non futurum esset suis in N. T. verum quod minus eo egere viderentur homines, quo futuri, ex uberiore Spiritus copia, doctiores. Denique quod remissurus esset ipsorum peccata: & hoc sub Veteri Testamento etiam fecisse Deum, nemo negat: sed quæ gratia sub N. Test. fuit clarior & abundantior. Quare videmus Apostolum in illa explicatione differentiam testamenti utriusque præsertim ponere in diversis hujus & illius gradibus. Ita habendum, quod duplex est Dei fœdus, legis & operum prius, alterum gratiæ & fidei: deinde duplex utriusque & diversa valde administratio, ante & post Christum, quarum illa appellatur Testamentum Vetus; hæc, Novum. Quocunque modo Novum Testamentum opponitur Veteri, sive in ratione legis ac gratiæ, sive œcono-miæ & dispensationis diversæ, atque hoc melieres[?] longe habet promissiones & res, illo priori. Quamvis etiam toto Veteris Testamenti tempore, sive ante Christum, gratia Novi, pro illorum temporum modo ac mensurâ, viguerit quoque. Arabs sic vertit: nunc autem adeptus est ministerium excellentioris dignitatis, quatenus mediator est præstantissimi fœderis in promissionibus sancitî.
units.tr: Heb. VIII. 6. Now indeed Christ has obtained a ministry so much more excellent, as he is the mediator of a better covenant, which has been enacted on better promises. Socinus objects to this passage in his book Quod Regni Poloniae, etc., ch. 7, and Palaeologus, against it, part 4, p. 556; Ostorod, Instit. ch. 5, replies. It must not be understood as if the promise of eternal life, or its well-known proclamation, had not also existed under the Old Covenant. Let my opponent prove this inference: the New Testament, of which Christ is the Mediator, consists of better promises; therefore there was no promise of eternal life under the Old Testament. I deny the inference. For this promise of grace in the new covenant was also set forth at that time. The Apostle sets two testaments against each other, the old Mosaic and the new of Christ, and likewise the ministry [λειτουργίας] of each: there the Aaronic priests, here Christ, who is also Mediator of this covenant, as Moses was of that one. Now that former testament, as it had all the typical and ceremonial things, so it availed only for the external and ceremonial purification of the flesh, not for the internal purification of the mind and conscience (ch. 9:9–10). But the New Testament contains the spiritual and heavenly things themselves, administered in a spiritual and abundant manner, which are far better than those. And just as the covenant itself must be distinguished from the manner of its administration, so although the substance and power of the covenant of grace was also present under the Old Testament, it was under the dispensation, or manner of dispensation, of Moses. The former Mosaic testament, however, did not contain as many good things as the New Testament, under the dispensation and light of Christ. Clearly the New contains spiritual, clear and abundant things more than ever before, and the faithful of the New Testament have a far greater understanding and abundance of them than the Ancients had. Verse 10: in explaining the new covenant and its excellence above the old, the Apostle teaches that it consists in this, that God would be their God, and they his people. But this God was also indeed the God of his people under the Old Testament, yet more so under the New. Next: "they shall no longer teach each one his neighbour" [not that this would not be the case under the New Testament, but that men would seem to need this less, being more learned from the more abundant outpouring of the Spirit]. Finally, "that he would forgive their sins": nobody denies that God also did this under the Old Testament, but the grace under the New Testament was clearer and more abundant. Therefore we see that in that explanation the Apostle places the difference between the two testaments especially in their different degrees. So it must be held that the covenant of God is twofold: that of law and works, which came first, and that of grace and faith; and again, each of these has a twofold and very different administration, before and after Christ, the former called the Old Testament, the latter the New. However the New Testament is set against the Old, whether in respect of law and grace, or of a different economy and dispensation, it has far better promises and things than the former. Yet even throughout the whole time of the Old Testament, before Christ, the grace of the New also flourished, according to the measure and manner of those times. The Arabic version renders it thus: "Now indeed he has obtained a ministry of more excellent dignity, inasmuch as he is the mediator of the most excellent covenant, which has been enacted on promises."

units.la: Smalcius, contra Frantzium, Disp. vii. de Bon. operib. pag. 220[?]. ex eo[?], quod Christus est mediator fœderis melioris, colligimus, vitam æternam ante Christum nemini promissam fuisse. Alioquin enim non esset melius novum fœdus veteri, si idem, quod in novo promissum est, in veteri promissum fuisset. Nos vero istam colle&ionem dicimus valde esse mancam & infirmam. Imo ex eo ipso contrarium colligimus, ut quia melius istud fœdus etiam vim suam exeruit retro ad tempora Christum antecedentia, etiam vita æterna, vi ejus, & promissa fuerit, & data. Deinde, etiamsi idem quod in novo promissum est, etiam promissum fuerit in Veteri, tamen adhuc dici potest novum melius fuisse veteri. Quia & quidquid boni hujus sub Veteri fuit, id habuit ex Novo: & quamvis Novi illud sub Veteri, non tamen fuit ipsum Novum, sed Vetus Testamentum, id est fœderis gratiæ dispensatio Mosaica, non Christiana, & parcius, & obscurius, & sub jugi legis prædicatione & exactione administrata, quæ se alio modo habuerunt sub Testamento Novo.
units.tr: Smalcius, against Frantzius, Disp. 7 on good works, p. 220: "From this, that Christ is the mediator of a better covenant, we gather that eternal life was promised to no one before Christ. For otherwise the new covenant would not be better than the old, if the same thing which is promised in the new had been promised in the old." But we say that this inference is very lame and weak. Indeed from that very fact we gather the contrary: since that better covenant also exerted its power backwards to the times before Christ, eternal life too was both promised and given by its power. Next, even if the same thing which is promised in the new covenant was also promised in the Old, it could still be said that the new was better than the old. For whatever good there was under the Old came from the New; and although what belonged to the New was present under the Old, it was not the New itself but the Old Testament, that is, the Mosaic dispensation of the covenant of grace, not the Christian one, and was administered more sparingly, more obscurely, and under the yoke of the constant preaching and exaction of the law. These things stood otherwise under the New Testament.

units.la: Smalcius iterum, pag. 167. Quid absurdius, quam sentire eandem esse doctrinam V. & N. Test. ? Cum ipsa nomina Novi & Veteris apertissimam differentiam tacite sonent. Nam si eadem in Novo, quæ in Veteri continentur, quid opus fuit nova hæc appellare? Novum dicitur, propter aliam, quam antea fuit, & longe meliorem gratiæ in Christo, & à legis Mosaicæ vinculis umbrisque liberam dispensationem, & usum.
units.tr: Smalcius again, p. 167. What could be more absurd than to hold that the doctrine of the Old and New Testaments is the same? The very names "New" and "Old" silently signal a most obvious difference. For if the New contains what the Old contains, what was the point of calling it new? It is called New on account of a different, and far better, dispensation and use of grace in Christ, one free from the bonds and shadows of the Mosaic law.

units.la: Speciatim quod in V. T. nulla promissio fuerit Spiritus S. probare se posse autumant Adversarii, ex Luc. xi. 13. Quanto magis pater cælestis Spiritum S. dabit petentibus ipsum? Respondemus 1. Ergo sub V. Test. ille Spiritus non fuit, nec rogatus, nec concessus? quæ sequela? Si vos cum sitis mali, nostis filiis vestris dare dona bona, quanto magis Pater vester cælestis? ergo, vel jam demum sub N. Test. id fecerunt patres suis liberis; vel nunc tandem Deus bona dedit suis, & non item sub Testamento Veteri? Pari enim modo liceret nobis argumentari ita, ac Adversariis. Vel, jam jubentur homines Deum amare, & colere: ergo ejus rei præceptum non extitit sub Veteri Testamento? Appa-ret, quam illa non sequantur. II. Negare haud possunt, Spiritum S. fuisse sub V. Test. & notum satis piis; quum ejus aliquoties fiat mentio, Psalm. li. 13. & cxliii. 20. Jesa. xliv. 3. 4. & liv, 21. Jezech. xxxvi. 27. & xxxvii. 29. &c. III. Ad obedientiam & pietatem, Spiritus S. gratiam vel statuis necessariam, vel non. Si hoc, non erit illa tum spiritualis & vera probitas; sed virtus modo ethica, naturam ejusque vires non supergressa. Et talis Socinianorum est probitas ac religio. Si vero necessaria Spiritus S. gratia & operatio est ad sanctitatem omnem & veram, quomodo eam negabimus Pa-tribus, quos sanctos fuisse & vere pios, negare nullus sustinet? Quare vel pro-bitas requirit donum & gratiam Spiritus S.; & sic eum Patres etiam habuerunt: vel si non, haud potest esse vera & spiritualis, sed erit modo naturalis aliqua & ethica qualitas, quam viribus suis acquirere quivis possit. IV. Quan-doquidem vero gratia illa Spiritus S. ad veram & Deo placentem pietatem est necessaria, ejusque necessitatem non potest non homo ψυχικὸς[?], & suæ miseriæ imbecillitatisque conscius sentire ac agnoscere, qui pote ut non pii sub V. Test. Deum pro illa precati fuerint, &, si precati, eam non adepti, ex eadem ratione, qua hic Christus argumentatus fuit, Si vos, quum mali sitis, noveritis liberis vestris dare dona bona, quanto magis Pater cælestis dabit Spi-ritum S. petentibus ipsum?
units.tr: In particular, the Adversaries think they can prove that there was no promise of the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament, citing Luke 11:13: "How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?" We reply: (1) Then, under the Old Testament, was that Spirit neither asked for nor granted? What follows from this? "If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father...?" So either the fathers gave good things to their children only under the New Testament, and God gave good things to his people only now, and not under the Old Testament? For we could argue in exactly the same way as the Adversaries. Or else: men are now commanded to love and worship God; therefore no precept of this kind existed under the Old Testament? It is clear how little these conclusions follow. (2) They cannot deny that the Holy Spirit was under the Old Testament, and that this is well known to the godly, since his name is mentioned several times: Psalm 51:13; Psalm 143:20; Isaiah 44:3-4; Isaiah 54:21; Ezekiel 36:27; Ezekiel 37:29, etc. (3) For obedience and piety, the grace of the Spirit is either held to be necessary or not. If not, that probity will not be true and spiritual, but merely an ethical virtue that does not rise above nature and its powers. And such is the probity and religion of the Socinians. But if the grace and operation of the Holy Spirit is necessary for all holiness and true holiness, how shall we deny it to the Fathers, whom no one dares deny were holy and truly pious? So either probity requires the gift and grace of the Holy Spirit, and in this way the Fathers also had him; or, if not, it cannot be true and spiritual, but will be only some natural and ethical quality, which anyone could acquire by his own powers. (4) Since indeed that grace of the Holy Spirit is necessary for true piety, which pleases God, and since a man who is psychical [ψυχικὸς] and conscious of his own misery and weakness cannot fail to feel and acknowledge this necessity, how could the pious under the Old Testament have failed to pray to God for it, and, having prayed, have failed to obtain it? By the same reasoning with which Christ argued: "If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Spirit to those who ask him?"

units.la: Adferunt etiam Joann. vii. 39. Hoc vero dixit de Spiritu, quem accepturi essent credentes in ipsum: nondum enim erat Spiritus Sanctus, neque enim Christus adhucdum
units.tr: They also cite John 7:39: "But this he said of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive; for the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Christ was not yet glorified."

units.la: Tom. 2. erat glorificatus. Resp. Non quod omnino non erat, vel minime notus esset Spiritus Sanctus; sed quod illa copia & dona Spiritus S. nondum in homines diffusa erant, uti post ejus glorificationem. Neque enim vel Sociniani negabunt, Spiritum S. sub V. Test. fuisse: & fuisse jam illo tempore, quo Christus haec loquebatur: attamen hic dicitur, non fuisse. Ergo id cogimus exponere κατὰ τι [?] non simpliciter. Quae vero addenda restrictio sit, patet ex subjuncta ratione, nondum Christus erat glorificatus: id est, non is modus diffusi & erogati in omnes Spiritus S. conspiciebatur, qui postmodum, Christo exaltato: non tanta copia, nam ad illud haec per parenthesin adduntur, quod Christus dixerat, si quis in ipsum crederet, quod rivi aquae viventis ex ventre ejus profluerent, verf. 38. quod de Spiritus S. gratia & copia intelligi debuisse, Euangelista obiter exponit.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Reply: this does not mean that the Holy Spirit was altogether absent, or entirely unknown; it means that that abundance and those gifts of the Spirit had not yet been poured out upon men, as they were after his glorification. For not even the Socinians will deny that the Holy Spirit existed under the Old Testament, and that he existed already at the time when Christ spoke these words; yet here it is said that he did not. Therefore we must explain it as true in a certain respect [κατὰ τι], not absolutely. What restriction must be added is clear from the reason subjoined: "Christ was not yet glorified", that is, that mode of the Spirit poured out and dispensed to all, which was seen afterwards when Christ was exalted, was not yet visible; not such an abundance. For to this the evangelist adds in parentheses what Christ had said, that if anyone believed in him, rivers of living water would flow from his belly (verse 38), which the evangelist briefly explains must be understood of the grace and abundance of the Spirit.

units.la: Haec ad Scripturae loca, quae in suam sententiam Adversari adferunt: jam rationes etiam audiamus.
units.tr: So much for the passages of Scripture which the Adversaries bring forward for their opinion. Now let us also hear their arguments.

units.la: Secundum ergo argumentum ex hoc petunt, quod Deus jam demum in Christo Pater noster factus sit, & quod hinc primum promissio vitae aeternae profluat.Volkelius, pag. 57.
units.tr: Accordingly, they derive a second argument from this: that God has only now been made our Father in Christ, and that from this first flows the promise of eternal life. Volkelius, p. 57.

units.la: His omnibus divinis Testimoniis duas evidentes rationes apponendas duximus. Primò enim constat, vitae immortalis spem nobis ostensam, ex Dei cognitione ea ratione pendere, quatenus pater est, id est, quatenus verissimam illam solidissimamque filiis suis hæreditatem donare constituit. Atqui hoc pacto Deus à prisci illis suis cultoribus agnitus non fuit. Tametsi enim Patris quoque nomine illum appellatum tunc fuisse non diffitemur; eam tamen vocabuli istius vim, quam nunc patefaciente Christo tenemus, illis seculis apertam fuisse pernegamus: cum Christus planissime dicat, neminem cognoscere Patrem, nisi filium, & cui filius voluerit revelare. Omnibus igitur ad se veniendum esse ibidem asserit, id est, ipsius disciplinae diligentissimas aures praebendas esse, fidemque firmissimam adhibendam, si animis suis requiem invenire, id est, ad verissimam sempiternae felicitatis spem erigi atque excitari velint.
units.tr: To all these divine testimonies we have thought two clear arguments should be added. For, first, it is certain that the hope of immortal life shown to us depends on the knowledge of God in so far as he is Father, that is, in so far as he has determined to give that most true and most solid inheritance to his sons. But in this way God was not known by those ancient worshippers. For although we do not deny that he was called Father in those times, we deny utterly that the force of this name, which we now hold since Christ has revealed it, was open in those ages, since Christ plainly says that no one knows the Father except the Son, and him to whom the Son wills to reveal him. Therefore he asserts there that all must come to him, that is, that the most diligent ears must be given to his teaching, and the firmest faith applied, if they wish to find rest for their souls, that is, to be raised and stirred up to the most true hope of everlasting happiness.

units.la: Resp. I. Non necesse est ad defendam nostram thesim, ut dicamus cognitionem Dei Patris in Christo, reliquasque istius argumenti relationes in Christo, seculis illis prioribus adeo apertas & familiares fuisse, ac nunc patefaciente eas Christo: sufficit, ut quam Deus gratiam & vitam aeternam fidelibus olim dedit, non nisi per & propter Christum, eam sibi ex illa Dei in promisso Messiâ gratiâ & foedere continere, vi promissionum Euangelica-rum, quae annunciabantur, sciverint istorum temporum fideles ac pii. II. Patris nomine Deum appellatum à Veteribus concedit. Quaero, quâ ratione sic appellatus fuerit ab iis? non propter communem creationem, & pro-videntiam: hoc nimis tenue: ergo pro-pter foedus quod cum ipsis Deus pepi-gerat. Et hinc dicunt Jesa. LXIII. 16:
units.tr: Reply. (1) It is not necessary, in order to defend our thesis, to say that the knowledge of God the Father in Christ, and the other relations of this matter in Christ, were in those earlier ages as open and familiar as they now are since Christ has revealed them. It is enough that the faithful and pious of those times knew, by the force of the gospel promises which were announced, that the grace and eternal life which God once gave to believers were given only through and on account of Christ, and that they were contained in that grace and covenant of God in the promised Messiah. (2) The Ancients concede that God was called Father. I ask: for what reason was he so called by them? Not on account of common creation and providence; that is too slight. Therefore on account of the covenant which God had made with them. And hence they cite Isaiah 63:16: "For you are our Father; for Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O Jehovah, are our Father, our Redeemer; your name is from of old." Jeremiah 64:8 and other passages. (3) Christ indeed says in Matthew 11:27 that no one knows the Father except the Son, and him to whom the Son wills to reveal him; but he does not add that this was revealed to no one under the Old Testament. Yet the controversy turns on this, not on the former point: whether it was not also willed that this be revealed to others under the Old Testament, and not only to those under the New. (4) The fact that Christ now openly stated and proclaimed that all should come to him reflects not a different state of affairs under the Old Testament, but a different season: Christ being incarnate and specifically sent for this office of preaching. This does not weaken or overturn the promises about Christ and eternal life made of old, nor the faith which the Fathers had in them.

units.la: nam tu es Pater noster, nam Abraham non novit nos & Israel non cognoscit nos, tu Jehova Pater noster, [?] redemtor noster, hoc nomen tuum à seculo. Jerem. cap. LXIV. 8. & aliis locis. III. Christus quidem dicit Matth. XI. 27: neminem cognoscere Patrem, nisi Filium, & cui Filius voluerit revelare: sed non addit, hoc nemini revelatum fuisse sub V. Test. : atqui in hoc, non in priori vertitur controversia, annon etiam aliis sub V. Test. hoc voluerit revelari, nisi iis sub Novo. iv. Quod aperte nunc dictum & praedicatum a Christo fuit, ut ad se venirent omnes, non ita sub V. Testam. alia temporis ratio fuit', Christo incarnato, & ad hoc praedicandi officium speciatim misso: quod nec[?] promissiones de Christo, & vitâ aeternâ olim factas, nec fidem illis à Patribus habitam enervat aut evertit.
units.tr: For you are our Father; for Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us. You, O Jehovah, are our Father, [?] our Redeemer; your name is from everlasting. Jer. 64:8, and in other places. III. Christ indeed says in Matthew 11:27 that no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him. But he does not add that this was not revealed to anyone under the Old Testament. Yet the controversy turns on this point, not on the earlier one: whether he may also have wished it to be revealed to others under the Old Testament, and not only to those under the New. IV. What Christ openly declared and preached, that all should come to him, was not the case under the Old Testament. The circumstances of the time were different, since Christ had been made flesh and was specially sent for this office of preaching. This does not weaken or overturn the promises about Christ and eternal life made in former times, nor the faith that the Fathers had in them.

units.la: Tertium argumentum hoc est. Volkelius, Alterum hujus rei argumentum ex Christi praeceptorum perfectione ducitur, quâ, ut suo loco docebimus, omnia antiqua illius legis praecepta superant. Consentaneum enim plane est, ut perfectiori obedientiae perfectioribus mandatis debita, praestantius proponatur praemium. Resp. De hoc in sequenti controversiâ ex professo uberius videbitur; ubi, Christum nec novum, nec perfectiorem legislatorem esse, docebimus. Deinde, nec cum naturâ aut stylo Euangelii convenit, ut praeceptis, sub N. Test. & eorum perfectioni vita aeterna attribuatur, quod in hoc passim legi opponitur, quod ibi vita operibus, hic fidei, ibi ex mercede, hic ex gratiâ, non propter nos, sed Christum, attribuatur.
units.tr: The third argument is this. Volkelius: "The second argument of this matter is drawn from the perfection of Christ's precepts, by which, as we shall show in its place, they surpass all the ancient precepts of that law. For it is entirely fitting that a more perfect obedience should be set before it with a more excellent reward, due to the more perfect commandments." Reply. This will be seen more fully in the following controversy, where we shall show that Christ is neither a new nor a more perfect lawgiver. Further, it does not agree with the nature or manner of the Gospel that eternal life should be attributed to precepts under the New Testament and to their perfection. This is opposed everywhere in the law: there life is ascribed to works and here to faith; there from wages, here from grace, and not on account of us but on account of Christ.

units.la: Tertiò, si vel Christus praecepta alia & perfectiora dedisset, prae prioribus, non sequitur, propterea vitae aeternae promissionem nec potuisse nec debuisse olim fieri, vel ante Christum exhibitum nullam factam fuisse. Probetur (quaesto) ista consequentia. Quia (dicis) perfectiori obedientiae debetur quoque praemium perfectius: Proba & hanc consequentiam, perfectiori obedientiae debetur perfectius praemium, ergo vel isti obedientiae vel gratiae, quae sub V. Test. annunciata & viguit, non potuit proponi praemium vitae aeternae, vel soli id servandum fuit praedicationi quae fuit in T. Novo. Probetur hoc. Quid ni potuisset, dato, ut Christus perfectiora dedisset praecepta, tamen vitae aeternae promissio proponi sub V. Testamento? Vel, utut etiam obedientiae praeceptorum Christi deberetur majus praemium, quid ni constitui hoc in re alia posset etiam, & praemiorum gradibus, ut tamen vita aeterna praedicata & promissa fuerit olim? Denique non probabitur, Deum promissiones suas ita appendere operibus nostris, eorumve merito, ut ex horum aestimatione illas attemperet, nominatim promissionem & praemium vitae aeternae. Neque illam rationem aut censum Deus habet nostrorum operum, vel tanti ea fiunt, praesertim in judicio Dei, ut nobis ullo pacto ad istam rationem divina caelestiaque beneficia commensurare & admetire operibus liceat.
units.tr: Thirdly, even if Christ had given other and more perfect precepts than the earlier ones, it does not follow that the promise of eternal life could not or should not have been made in former times, or that no such promise was made before Christ was revealed. Let the following inference be tested: "Because a more perfect obedience also deserves a more perfect reward." Test this inference too: "A more perfect obedience deserves a more perfect reward; therefore either the promise of eternal life could not be set before that obedience, or before the grace which was announced and flourished under the Old Testament, or it was reserved for the preaching that belonged to the New Testament alone." Let us test this. Why could the promise of eternal life not have been set forth under the Old Testament, even granting that Christ gave more perfect precepts? Or again, even though a greater reward is owed to obedience to Christ's precepts, why could this not have been arranged in another way, and by degrees of reward, so that eternal life was nonetheless preached and promised in former times? Finally, it will not be proved that God so weighs his promises against our works, or their merit, that he adjusts them by the estimate of those works, namely the promise and reward of eternal life. God does not take account of our works in that way, nor do they count for so much, especially in God's judgment, that we may in any way measure and apportion divine and heavenly benefits by our works.

units.la: Ex Judaeorum sententia, sed perperam, ita argumentatur Smalcius, lib. de divinit. Christi, cap. vii.
units.tr: Smalcius argues in this way, though wrongly, from the opinion of the Jews, in his book on the divinity of Christ, chapter 7.

units.la: Quod ad tempora V. Testamenti attinet, Resp. I. Dicunt quidem, Judaeos fatentur hodie omnes Judai, qui legis non omnes hodie ita sentire, sed non pro- possunt esse non peritissimi, & ejusdem obser- bant, ne unius quidem, ex omnibus, vantissimi[?], quosque ideo nihil praetermissuros produco[?] testimonio. II. Neque Ju- plusquam credibile est, quod ad legem Mosai- daeorum hodiernorum testimonio adeo cam ostentandam pertinere posset, quale hoc firma vel certa esse in articulo de reli- esset, si vita aeterna promissum in ea extaret: gione & sententia priscorum sub V. imo quos sibi non defuturos, nec tanta re se ipsos struflaturos certum est, fatentur, in quam, omnes illi Judaei prudentiores, nullum vitae aeternae apertum extare in ipsorum lege, vel, ut apertius loquar, in foedere, quod Deus cum eu per Mosem pepigit promissum. In foedere autem id continere necesse est, & non alibi, quod ad omnes Judaeos in univer-sum pertineat. Idem quoque urget-er,
units.tr: As far as the times of the Old Testament are concerned, I reply: first, they say that the Jews today all think so, but they cannot be other than most skilled and most observant of the same law, and therefore nothing will be omitted by them, of which I can bring forward testimony. Second, it is more than credible that the testimony of today's Jews, which could be brought forward to display the law of Moses, would be firm or certain in the article on the religion and opinion of the ancients under the Old Testament, if eternal life were promised in it. Indeed, all those more prudent Jews, whom it is certain will not be lacking, and who will not wreck themselves in so great a matter, admit that no clear promise of eternal life stands in their law, or, to speak more plainly, in the covenant which God made with them through Moses. Now that promise must be contained in the covenant and nowhere else, since it pertains to all Jews in general. The same point is pressed as well,

units.la: Test. Israelitarum, norunt omnes, qui illos homines, & ipsorum Theologiam hodiernam ac negotia tractarunt.
units.tr: as all who have dealt with that people and with their present theology and affairs know, namely the Testament of the Israelites.

units.la: iii. Ut neque hodie dici queant vel periti adeo vel observantes legis esse, neque hinc tantopere commendari.
units.tr: Third, it cannot be said today that they are so skilled or observant of the law, nor that they are so greatly commended on that account.

units.la: iv. Tum & falsum, Judaeos omnes, quod bis tamen hic refert Smalcius, fateri, nullum vitae aeternae apertum extare in ipsorum lege, vel foedere per
units.tr: Fourth, it is false that all Jews admit that no clear promise of eternal life stands in their law, or in the covenant made

units.la: Mosem ito, promissum. Nisi Sadducaeos putet, qui animarum immortalitatem & vitam futuram, resurrectionemque corporum negarunt, quos Judaei omnes ex tota Scriptura, & lege, gnaviter refellunt. Quod nec facerent, neque facere possent, si nullum vitae aeternae promissum in lege exstare censerent. Unde de Pharisaeis Josephus, lib. xviii. cap. 11. animas credunt esse immortales, & sub terris earum judicia fieri: tum praemia contingere ex virtutis aut malitiae merito, atque hos perpetuis damnari carceribus, illis παραμονὴν & ἀναβίωσιν facilem esse ad vitam reditum. Sadducaeos celeberrimus Judaeorum Doctor Menasseh ben Israel, haud uno in libro, atque cum aliunde, tum ex lege Mosis, convincit, super errore de animarum mortalitate, & negatâ resurrectione, atque vitâ aeternâ, nam illa pariter hic conjunguntur. Quin non habent pro Judaeo, qui articulum hunc negat, & resurrectione faustrandum censent omnes, qui eam negant. Utcunque inter se disputent de articulis religionis Judaicae fundamentalibus, quos Moimonides tredecim, Josephus Albo tres modo facit, in hoc tamen conveninnt, articulum de praemio & poena, tum temporariis, tum aeternis, ex illorum articulorum numero esse, eumque Maimonides in sua serie undecimum, Albo habet tertium. Atque hoc designant per עולם הבא, vel עולם עתיד mundum futurum. Super quibus litem suisse internecinam inter Cainum & Abelem, scribunt in Targum Ierosolymitano, ad Genes. iv. 8. contendente Caino, nec judicium, neque Judicem esse, עולת עלם אוחרן neque saeculum aliud, neque mercedem fore bonam justis, vel ultionem sumendam de impiis. Targum Onkelos Levit. xviii. 5. quod dicitur, qui fecerit illa homo, vivet in eis, exponit בחיי עלמא vitam saeculi, sive aeternam. Frequens apud Hebraeos est, ut dicant, esse bona quaepiam opera, quorum fructum homo percipit in hac vita, fors vero relinquitur ei in vita altera. In Gemara Kiduschin, cap. 1. Hac sunt, quorum fructus homo percipit in hac vita, fors autem manet in vita altera, והקרן קיימת לעולם הבא, nempe, honor parentum, beneficentia, hospitalitas, reconciliatio hominum inter ipsos. Studium vero legis his omnibus aequi paratur. & post illa subjungunt: quod illud igitur est, quod tradit R. Jacobus: Merces praecepti in hac vita non est. Eum n. dixisse accepimus: Nullum praeceptum est, in lege scriptum, cui adjuncta sit μισθαποδοσία, a quo non dependeat resurrectio mortuorum. De observatione parentum legimus: Ut prolongentur dies tui, & bene sit tibi. De dimissione nidi: Ut bene tibi sit & prolonges dies. Quendam jusserat parens pullos ex arce afferre. Is ascendit, pullos capit, matrem dimittit, in reditu lapsus exspirat. Ubi hujus longævitas, ubi prosperitas? Ut bene tibi sit, scil. in seculo, quod totum felix est. Ut longævus sis, in seculo, quod totum longum est. Apud Clariss. virum, & Collegam nostrum D. Coccejum, in Excerptis Gemar. Sanhedrin, pag. 318.
units.tr: through Moses. Unless perhaps he thinks of the Sadducees, who denied the immortality of souls, a future life and the resurrection of bodies, whom all Jews vigorously refute from the whole of Scripture and the law. They would not do this, nor could they, if they judged that no promise of eternal life stood in the law. Hence Josephus, of the Pharisees, book 18, chapter 11: They believe that souls are immortal, and that judgments are made of them under the earth; and that rewards follow according to the merit of virtue or wickedness; and that these are held in perpetual prisons, while the others have an easy passage [paramonen] and a return to life [anabiosin]. The most famous Jewish teacher, Menasseh ben Israel, in more than one book, and from the law of Moses as well as from elsewhere, convicts the Sadducees of the error about the mortality of souls, and of denying the resurrection and eternal life, for these are joined together here. Indeed, they do not count as a Jew anyone who denies this article, and all who deny the resurrection are thought to be cut off from it. However much they dispute among themselves about the fundamental articles of Jewish religion, which Maimonides makes thirteen and Joseph Albo only three, they agree on this point: that the article on reward and punishment, both temporal and eternal, is among the number of those articles, and Maimonides places it eleventh in his series, while Albo has it third. They designate this by olam haba [עולם הבא], or olam atid [עולם עתיד], the world to come. Over these matters, they write in the Jerusalem Targum, on Genesis 4:8, that there was a deadly strife between Cain and Abel, Cain contending that there is neither judgment nor Judge, nor another age, nor a good reward for the just, nor vengeance to be taken on the wicked. Onkelos, on Leviticus 18:5, where it is said, which if a man do, he shall live in them, explains it as bechayei almeta [בחיי עלמא], the life of the age, that is, eternal life. It is common among the Hebrews to say that there are certain good works whose fruit a man receives in this life, but whose principal reward is left to him in the next life. In the Gemara Kiddushin, chapter 1: These are the things whose fruit a man receives in this life, while the principal remains for him in the life to come [veha-keren kayemet le-olam ha-ba], namely, honour of parents, beneficence, hospitality, and reconciliation of men with one another. The study of the law is set equal to all these. And after these things they add: "What, then, is that which R. Jacob hands down? The reward of a precept is not in this life. For we have heard that he said: There is no precept written in the law to which a retribution is attached on which the resurrection of the dead does not depend." Concerning the observance of parents we read: That your days may be prolonged, and that it may be well with you. Concerning sending away the nest: That it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days. A parent had ordered a son to bring young birds from a height. He climbed up, took the young, sent away the mother, and on the way back fell and died. Where, then, is his length of life, where his prosperity? That it may be well with you, namely in the age, which is wholly happy; that you may be long-lived, in the age, which is wholly long. This is in the Excerpts from the Gemara Sanhedrin, page 318, of the most distinguished man and our colleague, Mr. Coccejus.

units.la: R. Menasse ben Israël, in Epist. Dedicatoria ad lib. de Resurrect. inquit, etenim siquis animum diligenter advertat, comperiet præcipua legis dogmata fundata esse in articulo de immortalitate animarum. Et, dogma de immortalitate animarum esse instar baseos[?] ac fundamenti, cui tota lex superinstructa nitatur. Hinc lib. i. cap. i. probat, dari resurrectionem mortuorum, autoritate librorum Mosaicorum; conjuncto passim articulo de vita æterna, utpote quæ se mutuo attingunt in articulis fidei, & innexa sunt. Ut Genes. 11.7[?] dum dicitur Deus formasse Adamum [illegible, ~3 letters] non cum unico, sed duplici, quod superfluum videatur, & præter morem isthoc quoque capite observatum, vers. 19. adfert ex Suorum sententia Judæus, eo designari duas formationes, unam in hac, alteram in sequenti vita, יצירה בעולם הזה ויצירה לעולם הבא. Ad citatum Deut. iv. 4. Vivitis vos omnes hodie, explicari ait, quemadmodum nunc omnes vivitis, ita etiam futuro omnes vivetis sæculo. Quod occurrit in Talmude, Cod. Sanhedrin, cap. chelek. Atque illa non simpliciter doceri in lege, sed manifeste, & evidentissime ex ea ostendi, asserit. Eoque exemplum Henochi, super quo cum Socinianis supra disputavimus, adducit. Cap. x. De Henoch dicitur Genes. 5. v. 24. Quod ambulaverit cum Deo, neque amplius apparuerit, quia tulerat eum Deus. In eandem sententiam loquitur Scriptura de Elia. Quia vero notum est, Eliam cum anima & corpore ex hac vita in aliam transportatum fuisse; inde quoque manifestum fit non aliter Henochum translatum fuisse. Est igitur anima immortalis. Quodque summopere observandum, & propter authoritatem tum Christi, tum Euangelii, atque etiam ad convincendos Adversarios nostros Socinianos valde facit, sic exponit etiam formulam promissionis & fœderis, ego ero Deus vester. Qua de re eodem cap. loquitur, pag. 68. Cum Mosi primum appareret Dominus, dixisse legitur, Ego sum Deus Patrum tuorum, Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci, Deus Jacobi. Atqui Deus non est Deus mortuorum, quia mortui non sunt: sed vivorum, quia vivi exstiunt. Itaque Patriarchas etiamnum, respectu animæ, vivere ex eo recte infertur. Atque integro contra Sadducæos disputavit libro primo, uti fatetur in Præfat. vel Dedic. ad lib.
units.tr: R. Menasseh ben Israel, in the dedicatory epistle to his book on the resurrection, says: For if anyone attends carefully, he will find that the principal doctrines of the law are founded on the article of the immortality of souls. And the doctrine of the immortality of souls is like the base and foundation on which the whole law rests as on a structure. Hence, in book 1, chapter 1, he proves from the authority of the books of Moses that there is a resurrection of the dead, joining throughout the article of eternal life, as things that touch one another among the articles of faith and are bound together. For instance, in Genesis 2:7, where it is said that God formed Adam [illegible], not with one formation but with a double one, which seems superfluous, and contrary to custom observed in this chapter too, verse 19, the Jew brings forward from the opinion of his own people that two formations are designated by it, one in this world and the other in the world to come: yetzirah be-olam ha-zeh and yetzirah le-olam ha-ba [יצירה בעולם הזה ויצירה לעולם הבא]. On the cited Deuteronomy 4:4, You who are alive today, all of you, he says it is explained that just as all of you are now alive, so too all of you will live in the future age. This occurs in the Talmud, Tractate Sanhedrin, chapter Chelek. And he asserts that these things are not taught simply in the law, but are shown from it manifestly and most evidently. He therefore adduces the example of Enoch, about which we disputed above with the Socinians. Chapter 10: Of Enoch it is said in Genesis 5:24, that he walked with God, and was no more, for God took him. Scripture speaks to the same effect of Elijah. Since it is well known that Elijah was carried from this life into another with soul and body, it also becomes manifest that Enoch was translated in no other way. Therefore the soul is immortal. And what must be most carefully noted, and which, on account of the authority both of Christ and of the Gospel, is also very useful for refuting our Socinian adversaries, he likewise explains in this way the formula of promise and covenant, I will be your God. On this matter he speaks in the same chapter, page 68: When the Lord first appeared to Moses, it is read that he said: I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. But God is not the God of the dead, because the dead do not exist, but of the living, because they exist alive. Therefore it is rightly inferred from this that the patriarchs are still living, with respect to the soul. And he disputed at full length against the Sadducees in book 1, as he admits in the preface or dedication to the book.

units.la: II. Nam Sadducæos Mosaicam cum agnosceret legem, præmium & pœnam dum in hoc viverent mundo fore, concedebant; sed nihil post hanc vitam ad sperandum aut metuendum. Cæterum adversus hos clare à nobis prima operis hujus parte disputatum. Disputavit ergo ita pro resurrectione mortuorum, ut quoque pro vita futura, ex lege, & Scriptura tota. Longissime ut à vero absit, quod Smalcius, nescio qua fronte, dicere sustinuit, Judæos omnes negare, vitæ æternæ promissionem in sua lege extare. Quod autem majus ejus, quod dicimus, argumentum esse potest, quam quod inter objectiones Sadducæorum, & atheorum ponit negatam Patribus immortalitatem & vitam æternam, verbis & argumento prorsus eodem, quo Sociniani nostri uti solent? lib. de resurrect. cap v. I. Omnes promissiones & benedictiones, quæ manent cultores legis, sunt temporales: neque ulla vel pœna vel præmium vitæ futuræ in lege expressum est, quod dandum vel exspectandum sit post mortem, observantibus legem. Nam Isac benedicens Jacobo, non alia ei promittit bona, quam caduca & temporalia. Quis autem credat eum, si credisset aliam post hanc vitam esse, etiam non mentionem facturum fuisse vitæ, & istius bonorum ejus spiritualium? Idem Menasse præterea quatuor libros scripsit Hebraice, de Immortalitate animæ: ubi libro primo, cap. II. prorsus refutare se scribit septem rationibus illorum sententiam, חכמי הנים Sapientes Gentium notat, qui docent, Deum in lege Mosaica præmium eam servantibus in futuro sæculo non constituisse. Cum multa, inquit, legis Mosaicæ loca contrarium afferant. Cap. III. Explanantur Pentateuchi loca, quibus Deus mortalibus servatæ legis præmium in futura vita pollicetur. Expressissime contra illud quod de Judæis, & quidem omnibus, perperam testatus Smalcius, & haud semel, fuit. Atque in libello de Termino vitæ, pag. 213. idem Menasse refert, Rabbinos dicere ad Genef. xxxix. 10. de Josepho, & non audivit eam, ut concumberet secum, ut esset cum ea. Noluit dormire cum illa in hoc mundo, ne pœnas daret cum illa in altero. Neque dubito, quin eadem de Judæorum sententia probari possint ex lib. Urielis Hebræi, tit. Examen traditionum Pharisaicarum cum legę scripta collata-rum, contra animæ immortalitatem & altero, de immortalitate animæ, Samuelis de Silva, libris Hispanicis, Amstelodami impressis, apud Paulum Ravenstei-nium: sed qui diligenter è Christianorum manibus arcentur, neque meis triti etiamnum fuerunt.
units.tr: II. For although the Sadducees acknowledged the Mosaic law, they conceded that reward and punishment would come only while men live in this world, and that there was nothing after this life to hope for or fear. Against these men we argued clearly in the first part of this work. He therefore argued for the resurrection of the dead in such a way that he argued also for the future life, from the law and from the whole of Scripture. Far be it from the truth what Smalcius, I know not with what effrontery, ventured to say, that all the Jews deny that the promise of eternal life is found in their law. What greater proof of our point can there be than that, among the objections of the Sadducees and atheists, he sets down the denial of immortality and eternal life to the Fathers, in words and argument entirely the same as those our Socinians are accustomed to use? (Book on the resurrection, ch. 5.) (1) All the promises and blessings that await the keepers of the law are temporal; nor is any penalty or reward of the future life expressed in the law, to be given or expected after death by those who observe the law. For Isaac, blessing Jacob, promises him no other goods than fleeting and temporal ones. But who would believe that, if he had believed there was another life after this one, he would not have made any mention of life, and of those spiritual goods of his? Moreover, the same Menasseh wrote four books in Hebrew, on the Immortality of the soul; in the first book, ch. 2, he writes that he utterly refutes with seven arguments the opinion of those whom he calls חכמי הנים [chachmei ha-nim, the wise men of the nations], the Sages of the Gentiles, who teach that God did not, in the Mosaic law, appoint a reward in the future age for those who keep it. Since, he says, many passages of the Mosaic law assert the contrary. Ch. 3: The passages of the Pentateuch are explained, in which God promises a reward in the future life to mortals who keep the law. This most expressly contradicts what Smalcius, and that more than once, falsely testified about all the Jews. And in the little book On the Term of life, p. 213, the same Menasseh reports that the rabbis say, on Genesis 39:10, concerning Joseph, "he did not listen to her, to lie with her, or to be with her." He refused to sleep with her in this world, lest he be punished with her in the other. Nor do I doubt that the same opinion of the Jews can be proved from the book of Uriel the Hebrew, entitled An examination of Pharisaic traditions collated with the written law, against the immortality of the soul, and from the other book, On the immortality of the soul, by Samuel de Silva, in Spanish, printed at Amsterdam by Paulus Ravensteyn. But these are carefully kept out of Christian hands, and have not yet been worn by my own use.

units.la: Cætera Sociniánorum, quæ in rem suam adferunt, supra à nobis discussa sunt. Inter quæ & hoc, quod quinto alias loco ponere liceret, quod miri-fice facere putent ad commendandam dignitatem & præstantiam Christi, ejusque Euangelii, & religionis, si primus ille promissionem vitæ æternæ pa-tefecisse credatur. Smalcius, lib. de divinit. Christi, pag. 26. Qua igitur hæc amentia est, Christianos, quorum hoc minus interest, quam Judæorum, an in veteri fœdere promissum extet vitæ æternæ: imo quorum interest, Christi Domini sui, & sua etiam præ populo Israëlitico præstantia rationem habere, velle tamen ex sacris litteris V. Testamenti, quod Deus in illo veteri fœdere vitam æternam promiserit? Resp. Non magis hoc Judæorum refert scire, an in V. Test. promissum extet vitæ æternæ, quam nostra. Certe nostra ante omnes: quia illis Patribus nos successisse dicendi sumus, & illorum Testamento, nostrum, quotquot credimus in Deum, & in Christum. II. In hoc Christi præstantia sita est, & excellentia, soli ei debita propriaque, quod vitam æternam promeritus sit. III. Præstantia autem N.T. supra Vetus est, quod ad omnes gratia hic clarius, uberiusque proposita, & ad plures pervenit, quam ibi. IV. Sed utriusque Test. convenientia, & populi fœ-derisque conjunctio, tum vis mortis ac mediationis Christi, fidei, religionis, & salutis utrobique paritas, postulant, ut vitæ æternæ promissio nobis non so-lum, sed & illis facta, & credita, & sperata fuerit, simili fide ac exspecta-tione.
units.tr: The rest of the Socinians' arguments, which they bring forward in their own cause, have been discussed by us above. Among these is also this point, which I could have put in another place as a fifth item, and which they think is wonderfully suited to commending the dignity and pre-eminence of Christ, and of his Gospel and religion, if he is believed to have been the first to reveal the promise of eternal life. Smalcius, in his book on the divinity of Christ, p. 26: What madness, then, is this, that Christians, for whom it matters less than for the Jews whether the promise of eternal life is found in the Old Covenant, or rather, for whom it matters that they take account of the pre-eminence of Christ their Lord, and of their own above the Israelite people, should nevertheless want to hold, from the sacred letters of the Old Testament, that God promised eternal life in that old covenant? Answer: It matters no more to the Jews to know whether eternal life is promised in the Old Testament than it does to us. Certainly it matters more to us than to all others, because we are to be said to have succeeded those Fathers, and we, as many as believe in God and in Christ, have succeeded to their covenant. II. In this lies the pre-eminence and excellence of Christ, which is due to him alone and is his own, that he merited eternal life. III. The pre-eminence of the New Testament over the Old, however, is that grace is here set forth more clearly and more abundantly for all, and reaches more people than there. IV. But the agreement of both Testaments, the unity of the people and of the covenant, and the power of the death and mediation of Christ, and the sameness of faith, religion and salvation on both sides, require that the promise of eternal life was made, and believed, and hoped for, not only to us but also to them, with a like faith and expectation.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM, DE PRÆCEPTIS CHRISTI.
units.tr: CHAPTER II, ON THE PRECEPTS OF CHRIST.

units.la: CONTROVERSIA: Num Christus alia & nova præcepta, seu legem vivendi perfectiorem tulerit, quam fuit antiqua lex moralis?
units.tr: CONTROVERSY: Did Christ bring other and new precepts, or a more perfect rule of living, than the ancient moral law?

units.la: Nexus hujus quæstionis, cum priore. Differentia inter legem Mosis, & doctrinam Christi. Sententiæ Socinianæ radix & fundamentum, in doctrinâ de justificatione, per observationem præceptorum Christi. Præcepta Christi faciunt duum generum, additamenta ad legem, & Christi propria. Quænam ad singula præcepta dicant à Christo addita esse. Propria Christi faciunt moralia tria, de abnegatione sui, tolerantia crucis, & imitatione Christi; atque cæremoniale unum, de S. Cæna. Sententia Anabaptistarum, & Remonstrantium. Præcognita. Argumenta: lex moralis perfecta, & quod ad primam tabulam, vel amorem Dei; & secundam, de amore proximi. Christi officium fuit, salutem promereri, & redimere, non alia nova & graviori lege homines onerare. Quin ejus gratia passim legi opponitur. Iustificatio fit per gratiam in Christo, non per observationem operum. Vindicatur Matthæi quintum caput, quod controversiæ hujus sedes est & argumentum. Examinantur quæ Socinianï dicunt à Christo addita fuisse singulis præceptis legis. De præcepto generali invocandi Deum, quod etiam fuit in Test. Veteri. De Oratione Dominicâ. De invocatione Dei, per Christum. Distinguunt, inter adorationem & invocationem. Fundamentum invocationis Christi est, vera ipsius Deitas. Prætensa additamenta præcepti secundi, de cavendis prorsus idolis, eorumque locis. De temerariis juramentis, ad præceptum tertium. An præceptum quartum fit abrogatum? Ad præceptum quintum, de officiis Magistratuum, & Dominorum. De prohibitâ irâ, contumelia, & vindicta, ad præceptum sextum. Ad septimum, de adspectu fœminæ libidinoso, de divortio, & variis impuritatum carnalium speciebus. De prohibitione avaritiæ, & luxus, ad præceptum octavum: mendacii cujuscunque, ad præceptum nonum. De concupiscentiarum delectatione, ad decimum. De tribus præceptis Christi propriis, abnegatione sui, portatione crucis, atque Christi imitatione.
units.tr: The connection of this question with the previous one. The difference between the law of Moses and the doctrine of Christ. The root and foundation of the Socinian opinion, in the doctrine of justification through the observance of Christ's precepts. Christ's precepts are of two kinds: additions to the law, and Christ's own. What the Socinians say Christ added to each precept. Christ's own precepts comprise three moral ones, concerning self-denial, bearing the cross, and imitation of Christ, and one ceremonial, concerning the Lord's Supper. The opinion of the Anabaptists and the Remonstrants. Preliminary points. Arguments: the moral law is perfect, both as to the first table, the love of God, and as to the second, the love of neighbour. The office of Christ was to merit salvation and to redeem, not to burden men with some other new and heavier law. Indeed, his grace is everywhere set against the law. Justification comes through grace in Christ, not through the observance of works. The fifth chapter of Matthew is vindicated, since it is the seat and proof of this controversy. The things the Socinians say were added by Christ to the individual precepts of the law are examined. On the general precept of calling upon God, which was also in the Old Testament. On the Lord's Prayer. On the invocation of God through Christ. They distinguish between adoration and invocation. The foundation of invoking Christ is his true Deity. The alleged additions to the second precept, on wholly avoiding idols and their places. On rash oaths, under the third precept. Whether the fourth precept has been abrogated. On the fifth precept, concerning the duties of magistrates and masters. On the forbidden anger, contumely and revenge, under the sixth precept. Under the seventh, on the lustful look at a woman, on divorce, and the various kinds of carnal impurity. On the prohibition of avarice and luxury, under the eighth precept; of every kind of lying, under the ninth. On the delight of lusts, under the tenth. On the three precepts peculiar to Christ: self-denial, bearing the cross, and imitation of Christ.

units.la: PARS CAPITIS PRIMA. SECTIO PRIMA
units.tr: PART ONE OF THE CHAPTER, SECTION ONE

units.la: Inter quæstiones de Fœdere Dei, cum Adversariis pertractandas, hæc etiam non minima, quæ de Præceptis Christi est, an vid. Christus præcepta in N. Test. dederit perfectiora, supra moralem legem, & alia à præceptis legis istius? Quam quæstionem eo convenientius cum priori connectimus, quod ex hac ad illam argumentantes audivimus Adversarios. Nempe, quod putent talia à Christo præcepta data esse, quibus demum vitæ æternæ promissionem addiderit, de cætero Patribus sub V. Testam. plane ignoratam. Sic Smalcius, sic Volkelius, & Oftorodus, in Institutionibus: qui cap. xxi. agit de Christi promis-sionibus, tum cap. xii. de Christi præceptis. Nos verò, uti ostendimus, vitæ æternæ promissionem omnino sub Vet. Testamento etiam propositam fuisse, creditamque; ita in præsenti Disputatione ostendemus, frustra Adversarios ex Christo alium facere legislatorum, & perfectiorem ab eo conditam legem, asserere[?].
