units.tr: Among the questions to be treated with our opponents concerning the Covenant of God is this one, which is no small question and concerns the Precepts of Christ: did Christ, in the New Testament, give precepts more perfect than the moral law, above it, and different from the precepts of that law? We link this question more fittingly with the former, because in arguing from the one to the other we have heard our opponents. They think that Christ gave precepts to which he added a promise of eternal life, a promise the Fathers under the Old Testament had plainly not known. So Smalcius, so Volkelius, and Ostorodt in his Institutions, who in chapter 21 treats of Christ's promises and then in chapter 12 of Christ's precepts. We, however, have shown that the promise of eternal life was indeed set before believers under the Old Testament and believed. In the present disputation we will show that our opponents labour in vain to make Christ another lawgiver and to assert that he established a more perfect law.

units.la: Duo autem in hac quæstione inter se conferimus, legem Mosis moralem de diligendo Deum ac proximum; & doctrinam Christi. Illam quum dicimus, intelligimus legem perpetuæ & communis observantiæ, sub N. Test æque ac sub Veteri necessariæ. Ejus præceptis, quia perfectum docent amorem & erga Deum, & proximum, Matth xxii. omnia contineri censemus, quæ officii nostri aut sunt, aut esse possunt. Quid enim ultra illa dici, vel præstari possit? imo quodnam est officium, quod ad illa non referri queat, debeatque?
units.tr: In this question we compare two things: the moral law of Moses concerning the love of God and of neighbour, and the teaching of Christ. When we speak of the former, we mean a law of perpetual and universal observance, necessary under the New Testament as under the Old. We hold that all the duties that are, or can be, required of us are contained in its precepts, since they teach a perfect love both towards God and towards our neighbour (Matt. 22). For what more could be said or done beyond these? Indeed, what duty is there that cannot, and ought not, be referred to them?

units.la: Christi vero doctrina non est doctrina præceptorum primo ac principaliter. Hoc Mosis fuit, præcepta vivendi tradere; quod & tam plene præstitit, copiosaque, ut, quemadmodum perfecto nil addi potest, ita neque illis hoc in genere quidpiam superaddi. Christus vero modum salutis exposuit & redemptionis, & ad hunc tum promerendum seu impetrandum, tum explicandum & (ex eo promerito, uti antea promerendo) applicandum, in mundum venit. Moses legislator: Christus salvator fuit. Salvator non per legem, ejusque opera, ut alia præcepta prioribus addere oportuerit; sed per Euangelium, ejusque meram, & operibus in justificandi modo passim oppositum, gratiam. Uti enim Moses, & Christus, sic lex & Euangelium, gratia & opera in salutis negotio sunt oppositæ. Et hic, alia est justificatio legalis, alia Euangelica. Quoque illa minus possibilis, hoc minus necesse fuit à Christo alia præcepta tradi, vel legem aliam.
units.tr: But the teaching of Christ is not, first and principally, a teaching of precepts. It was Moses' task to deliver precepts for living, and he did this so fully and abundantly that, just as nothing can be added to what is perfect, so nothing further could be added to them in this respect. Christ, however, set out the way of salvation and redemption, and he came into the world both to merit or obtain this, and to explain it and apply it (on the basis of that merit, which he earned beforehand). Moses was the lawgiver; Christ was the Saviour. He saved not through the law and its works, so that it would have been necessary to add other precepts to the earlier ones, but through the Gospel and its grace, which is everywhere set against works in the manner of justification. For just as Moses and Christ are opposed, so law and Gospel, grace and works, are opposed in the matter of salvation. Here too, legal justification is one thing and evangelical justification another. The less possible the former was, the less necessary it was for Christ to deliver other precepts or another law.

units.la: Eumque in finem Socinianithesim[?] illam de lege & præceptis Christi perfectioribus arripuerunt, ut hinc errorem gravissimum in articulo de justificatione hominis statuminarent. Nam quia docent, hominem coram Deo justificari, non quod Ecclesia Orthodoxa, per justitiam Christi nobis imputatam, sed per opera sua, sive obedientiam præceptorum Christi, quo hoc à lege, cui justificationis nostræ per Christum modum opponi passim ignorare non possunt, parumper diverterent, addiderunt, obedientiam præceptorum, non legis tantum, sed & Christi. Hinc disputatio de præceptis Christi, quia per opera nos justificari dictitant: & de præceptis Christi perfectioribus supra legem, ut speciem & colorem quem Justificationis Euangelicæ, à legali sc. distinctæ, servare viderentur. Sed inanem revera speciem, & præter nomen nihil. Nam nihil hoc pacto justitiam nostram, quâ coram Deo, in judicio ejus, subsistimus, constituit, quam legis aut præceptorum observatio, sive à Mose, sive Christo præscripta. Illudque quod materiam justitiæ nostræ præbet, nostrum est totum, & nil nisi operum observatio.
units.tr: To this end they seized upon that Socinian thesis concerning the law and the more perfect precepts of Christ, so that they might establish from it a most grievous error on the article of the justification of man. For because they teach that man is justified before God not, as the Orthodox Church holds, by the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, but by his own works, that is, by obedience to the precepts of Christ, they have added obedience to the precepts, not of the law only but also of Christ. They did this to turn aside a little from the law, through which our justification by Christ is everywhere opposed, as they cannot be ignorant. Hence the dispute about the precepts of Christ, since they keep repeating that we are justified by works, and hence the dispute about the more perfect precepts of Christ above the law. They wish to keep the appearance and colour of an evangelical justification distinct from the legal one. But in truth it is an empty appearance, and nothing but a name. For in this way nothing constitutes our righteousness, by which we stand before God in his judgment, except the observance of the law or of precepts, whether prescribed by Moses or by Christ. And what supplies the material of our righteousness is wholly our own, and nothing but the observance of works.

units.la: Eodem ex fonte nata sunt Pontificiorum Consilia Euangelica, sua Socinianî præcepta appellant, pari omnia modo, fineque, ut justificationem gratuitam obscurent & invertant, doceantque hominem suis operibus & obedientiâ, seu consiliorum illorum, seu præceptorum Euangelicorum, coram Deo justificari. Quare etiam Socinus ad Matth. v. pag. 46. in sententiæ explicatione, illam quoque Pontificiorum adducit, de Consiliis.
units.tr: From the same source arise the Evangelical Counsels of the Papists, which the Socinians call precepts. All of them, in the same way and to the same end, obscure and invert the free justification, and teach that man is justified before God by his works and obedience, whether of those counsels or of those evangelical precepts. For this reason Socinus, in his explanation of the sense of Matthew 5 (p. 46), also brings forward that doctrine of the Papists concerning the Counsels.

units.la: Alio fine est, quod apud nonnullos sive ex Veteribus, sive Hodiernis legas quandoque, Christum nova præcepta dedisse, etiam Matth. v. forte legi Mosis alia majoris perfectionis & sanctitatis addita, quam Mosis quidem lex ab Israelitis exegerit. Quod à multis non dicitur in præjudicium doctrinæ de justificatione, sed ad commendandam altiorem, quam V.T. fuerit sanctitatem, sub Novo. Qua ratione & excusandi veniunt, qui imperitius subinde hic loquuti fuerunt, & defendendi à consensu cum heterodoxiâ Sociniana. Unde responsio sumenda ad illa, quæ pro sua sententia ex Tertulliano adducit Jonas Schlichtingius, in Præfat. Disputat. contra Meisnerum, de Trinitate &c. pag. 60.
units.tr: There is another purpose behind what you sometimes read among some writers, both ancient and modern: that Christ gave new precepts, perhaps even in Matthew 5, which add to the law of Moses a greater perfection and holiness than the law of Moses demanded of the Israelites. Many say this not to the prejudice of the doctrine of justification, but to commend the higher holiness that is required under the New Testament than under the Old. On this ground, those who have sometimes spoken here rather unskilfully can be excused, and defended against the charge of agreeing with Socinian heterodoxy. Hence an answer must be taken from what Jonas Schlichting adduces in support of his view from Tertullian, in the Preface to his Disputation against Meisner, concerning the Trinity, etc., p. 60.

units.la: Præcepta Christi nova duûm faciunt Socinianí generum: alia additamenta Decalogi, ad legem Mosis; alia Christi propria. Nam quædam dicunt à Christo singulis præceptis, excepto quarto, quod totum volunt esse cæremoniale, addita fuisse, ad illorum perfectionem; quædam talia, ut ad præcepta legis referri nequeant, sed uti propria disciplinæ Christi habenda. Socinus, de Officio Christi, themate xi. Excludit autem N. F. præcepta cæremonialia & ut vo-cant judiciaria: hac ratione, ut eis nec ipsi Judæi amplius teneantur. Moralia vero perficit, nempe ea præstantioribus præceptis illustrando, quod nos perfectiora reddidisse intelligi volumus, & mandata quædam peculiariter præscribit, quod addidisse.
units.tr: The Socinians make the new precepts of Christ of two kinds: some are additions to the Decalogue, to the law of Moses; others are proper to Christ. For they say that certain precepts were added by Christ to individual commandments, except the fourth, which they want to be wholly ceremonial, in order to perfect them; and certain others are such that they cannot be referred to the precepts of the law, but must be held as belonging to the proper discipline of Christ. Socinus, On the Office of Christ, thesis 11: The New Covenant, however, excludes the ceremonial and so-called judicial precepts, in such a way that the Jews themselves are no longer bound by them. But it perfects the moral precepts, namely by illustrating them with more excellent precepts, which we want to be understood as having made them more perfect; and it prescribes certain commands peculiarly, which it has added.

units.la: Ad articulos Cuteni, Socinus, th. x. ii. Quamvis Christus suam legem habeat, eamque Dei nomine mundo tulerit, non tamen simpliciter legislator dicitur, cum ejus lex aliud nihil fuerit, quam complementum ac perfectio Mosaicæ legis. Nec sane ob id præcipuè in mundum venit, ut legem ferret, nosterve legislator esset, sed ut nos servaret, in quem etiam finem nobis suam legem dedit. Christi lex, quia, ut diximus, est complementum & perfectio legis Mosaicæ, sine dubio ipsa lege Mosaica est perfectior. Nec tamen negandum est, quin ipsa quoque lex Mosis ab hominibus interiorem probitatem requireret, licet non tam exactam, ut Christi lex requirit, quæ vicissim non minus quam lex Mosis externam probitatem seu sanctitatem postulat, sed multo tamen excellentiorem. Quid verò cau-sæ, quod Christus legem suam habuisse, & tulisse dici tuto possit, non autem legislator fuisse? annon hæc est denominatio ex illo fluens sequensque fundamento? Quid est legislator, nisi qui legem fert? & Christum mundo legem tulisse ais; neque tamen dicendum esse legislatorem. Quo quid ineptius, vel frigidius? Infringe, si potes, argumentum: Qui legem fert, & novam, & aliam à priori, dicendus est legislator: Christus legem fert: ergo est dicendus legislator. Illa propositio est, ex vocis etymologia; ista, ex tuis verbis: conclusio necessaria. ii. Sed quid in nomenclaturâ legislatoris Christo tribuendâ Socinum quæso offendit? quorsum nomen, ubi non rem ipsam, odit? procul dubio quod senserit illud nimis Mosaicum esse, & oppositum veritati ac gratiæ Euangelicæ. Novit scriptum Joann. 1. 17. Nam lex per Mosem data est; gratia
units.tr: On the articles of Cuteni, Socinus, theme x, section ii: Although Christ has his own law, and brought it to the world in God's name, he is not simply called a lawgiver, since his law is nothing other than the completion and perfection of the Mosaic law. Nor indeed did he come into the world chiefly to bring a law or to be our lawgiver, but to save us, and it was for this end that he gave us his law. Christ's law, since, as we have said, it is the completion and perfection of the Mosaic law, is without doubt more perfect than the Mosaic law itself. Yet it must not be denied that the law of Moses also required inner uprightness from men, though not so exact as Christ's law requires, which in turn demands no less than the Mosaic law outward uprightness or holiness, but a far more excellent one. But what reason is there why it may safely be said that Christ had and brought his own law, and yet not that he was a lawgiver? Is this not a designation that flows from and follows upon that very foundation? What is a lawgiver, if not one who brings a law? And you say that Christ brought a law to the world, yet that he is not to be called a lawgiver. What could be more absurd or more feeble? Overturn the argument, if you can: whoever brings a law, and a new one, different from the former, is to be called a lawgiver; Christ brings a law; therefore he is to be called a lawgiver. The first proposition follows from the etymology of the word, the second from your own words; the conclusion is necessary. ii. But I ask, what does Socinus find objectionable in giving Christ the title of lawgiver? Why does he hate the name when he does not hate the thing itself? Doubtless because he thought it too Mosaic, and opposed to the truth and the grace of the Gospel. He knows the Scripture of John 1:17: For the law was given by Moses; but grace

units.la: Tom. 2. autem & veritas per Jesum Christum facta. Quod legis, id ad Mosem spectat: Christi est gratia & veritas. Conturbat illa Adversarius, dum quid aliud per Christum contigisse nobis vult, quam gratiam & veritatem, eaque opposita ad legem: quin dum legem a Christo datam contendet, hac in parte non Mosi oppositum Christum, sed perfectiorem legislatorem fuisse, & Mosem in negotio legum a Christo superatum pluribus aliis legibus, non sola gratia, sequetur.
units.tr: Tom. 2. and truth came by Jesus Christ. What belongs to the law belongs to Moses; grace and truth are Christ's. Your opponent is confounded when he wants something other than grace and truth to have come to us through Christ, and those set against the law. Indeed, while he contends that the law was given by Christ, in this respect it will follow that Christ was not opposed to Moses but was a more perfect lawgiver, and that Moses was surpassed by Christ in the matter of laws, with many other laws, not by grace alone.

units.la: iii. Non potest, inquit, legislator dici Christus, cum ejus lex aliud nihil fuerit, quam complementum & perfectio Mosaica legis. Eo ego dico magis legislator dicendus est, quam Moses ipse: quemadmodum is, qui complementum operi addit, non minus contulisse dicendus est, atque inde denominari etiam poterit, ac is qui nuda modo operis posuit rudimenta.
units.tr: iii. He says Christ cannot be called a lawgiver, since his law was nothing other than the completion and perfection of the Mosaic law. I say on the contrary that he must be called a lawgiver more than Moses himself. Just as one who adds the finishing touch to a work deserves no less credit, and may be named after it, than one who laid only the bare foundations.

units.la: iv. Sed non potest simpliciter dici legislator. eccur minus quam Moses? nam aeque ejus legem nominas, quam Mosis. Et si Moses propter initia potuit dici simpliciter legislator; quare non Christus aeque propter complementum & perfectionem?
units.tr: iv. But he cannot simply be called a lawgiver, he objects. Why less than Moses? For you name it his law just as much as Moses'. And if Moses could be called simply a lawgiver because of the beginnings, why could Christ not equally be called one because of the completion and perfection?

units.la: v. Sed Christus etiam Salvator fuit: non ergo simpliciter legislator. Quali ratione eum Salvatorem statuant Socinani, suo loco videbimus. Pariter & Moses suo modo dici potest ut mediator, ita & salvator, uti illi Christum Salvatorem faciunt. Verum quemadmodum quod Christus Socinianis legislator est, quamvis ita dici eum nolint, non obstat quod non quoque Salvator fuerit; ita nec quod Salvator est impedit, cur non etiam legislator ipsis appelletur.
units.tr: v. But Christ was also a Saviour, so he is not simply a lawgiver. By what reasoning the Socinians make him a Saviour we shall see in its place. Likewise Moses too, in his own way, can be called a mediator and so also a saviour, just as they make Christ a Saviour. But just as the fact that Christ is a lawgiver to the Socinians, though they do not want him so called, is not countered by the fact that he was not also a Saviour; so the fact that he is a Saviour does not prevent him from also being called a lawgiver by them.

units.la: vi. Mox ipse Christum legislatorem vocat, & pro synonymis ponit, Christum ut legem ferret nosterve legislator esset, venisse.
units.tr: vi. Soon he himself calls Christ a lawgiver and sets the two as synonyms, saying that Christ came "to bring a law, that is, to be our lawgiver."

units.la: vii. Christus, inquit, praecipue venit ut nos servaret, in quem etiam finem nobis suam legem dedit. nempe ergo ut nos servaret per legem, & legem suam. Id est, quod jam diximus, Christum ab illis transformari in legislatorem novum; justificationem gratiae, in justificationem operum; Euangelicam, in legalem. Jam, an dicatur, Christum venisse praecipue ut nos per illam suam legem servaret; an, ut legem istam nobis ferret Socioniano sensu, nullus non videt, quam parum distent.
units.tr: vii. Christ, he says, came chiefly to save us, "and to this end also he gave us his law." Namely, then, to save us by the law, and his own law. That is what we have already said: that they transform Christ into a new lawgiver; they change justification by grace into justification by works, and the gospel into a legal system. Now, whether it is said that Christ came chiefly to save us by that law of his, or to bring us that law in the Socinian sense, everyone can see how little the two differ.

units.la: viii. Quin argumentamur a majori: cujus lex est perfectior, is magis dicendus est legislator: verum Christi lex sine dubio, inquit Socinus, ipsa lege Mosaica est perfectior.
units.tr: viii. Indeed we argue from the greater: whose law is more perfect, that man is to be called the more the lawgiver. But Christ's law, says Socinus, is without doubt "more perfect than the Mosaic law itself."

units.la: ix. Lex Mosis requirebat, ais, internam & externam probitatem seu sanctitatem. Verbum addo, & omnem eam, seu internam, seu externam. Nam sic eam explicuit Christus, Matth. xxii. 37. diliges Dominum Deum tuum toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua, & tota cogitatione tua. 39. atque diliges proximum tuum sicuti te ipsum. Quaero, illis verbis aut omnis amor, & sic probitas, quae amore comprehenditur, praescribitur, aut non? Si non, quid latitudini & universalitati verborum aut rei deest? Sin imo, nihil ergo ei in genere praeceptorum addi potuit, neque ipsa supra perfici.
units.tr: ix. The law of Moses, you say, required inward and outward probity or holiness. I add the word all, whether inward or outward. For Christ explained it thus, Matt. 22:37: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind." And verse 39: "and you shall love your neighbour as yourself." I ask: do those words prescribe all love, and so the probity which is comprised in love, or not? If not, what is lacking to the breadth and universality of the words or of the matter? But if so, then nothing could be added to the kind of precepts, nor could it be perfected beyond this.

units.la: Catechesis Racov. de Prophetico Christi munere, cap.1. Quaest.1. Quanam sunt perfecta mandata Dei per Christum patefacta ? Resp. Pars eorum continetur in praeceptis à Mose traditis, una cum iis quae sunt eis in novo foedere addita: pars vero continetur in iis, quae peculiariter ipse Christus praescripsit. Smalcius, de divinit. Christi, cap. V. Praecepta, quae Christus revelavit, duplici modo considerari possunt. Quaedam enim sunt addimenta & perfectiones istius partis legis Mosaicæ, quæ moralis appellatur: quadam vero sunt plane singularia, & quasi nova. Similia habet Ostorodus, Instit. cap. xxii. Volkelius, de Relig. lib. iv. cap. v. Schlichtingius, Disput. contra Meisnerum, art. iv.
units.tr: The Racovian Catechism, on the prophetic office of Christ, ch. 1, question 1: "What are the perfect commandments of God revealed through Christ?" Answer: "Part of them is contained in the precepts handed down by Moses, together with those that were added to them in the New Covenant; but part is contained in those which Christ himself prescribed peculiarly." Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 5: "The precepts which Christ revealed can be considered in two ways. For some are additions and perfections of that part of the Mosaic law which is called moral; but others are altogether singular and, as it were, new." Ostorodt has similar things, Institutes ch. 22; Volkelius, On Religion, book 4, ch. 5; Schlichting, Disputation against Meisner, art. 4.

units.la: Particulatim vero de utroque præceptorum Christi genere ita docent. Præceptis Decalogi addita fuisse in specie hæc. Ad præceptum primum, 1. generale præceptum de faciendis precibus. 11. formulam Orationis Dominicæ. 111. præceptum de invocando Christo. Ad secundum, unum de cavendis idolis, atque idololythis. Ad tertium, 1. ne leviter juremus. 11. ut quoque per Christi nomen liceat jurare. Quartum præceptum totum dicunt esse cæremoniale, & ad Christianos nil pertinere. Ad quintum ajunt additum, quodcunque spectat ad officium Magistratus, & subditorum; maritorum, & uxorem; dominorum, ac servorum. Ad sextum, 1. præceptum de diligendis inimicis. 11. Proximo non irascendum, non conviciandum, vel intentandam esse vindictam. Ad septi-mum, 1. Alienæ uxoris concupiscentiam esse adulterium. 11. Atque Polygamiam, & divortium extra casum adulterii, esse illicita. 111. Scortationem omnem, impuri-tatem, comessationes, turpiloquium, gestus, contrectationes libidinosas &c. damnandas esse. Ad octavum, prohibitam avaritiam. Ad nonum, Mendacium temerarium, simulationes ac dissimulationes, item detractationes & condemnationes temerarias, esse veritas. Ad decimum obiectationem animi in concupiscentiis rerum alienarum, & ejusmodi animo fovere cogitationes, nunc sub Novo demum Test. à Christo pro peccatis habita, & veteri legi accessisse, scribunt. Illis præceptis, dicunt, Chri-stum veterem Mosis moralem legem perfecisse, atque adimplevisse.
units.tr: Particularly, they teach the following about each kind of Christ's precepts. To the precepts of the Decalogue there were added, specifically, these. To the first precept: (1) a general precept about making prayers; (2) the form of the Lord's Prayer; (3) the precept about invoking Christ. To the second: one about avoiding idols and idol-sacrifices. To the third: (1) not to swear lightly; (2) that it is also lawful to swear by the name of Christ. The fourth precept they say is wholly ceremonial and has nothing to do with Christians. To the fifth they say was added whatever concerns the duty of the magistrate and subjects, of husbands and wives, of masters and servants. To the sixth: (1) the precept about loving enemies; (2) that one must not be angry with a neighbour, nor revile him, nor threaten vengeance. To the seventh: (1) that the lust after another's wife is adultery; (2) that polygamy and divorce outside the case of adultery are unlawful; (3) that all fornication, impurity, carousing, filthy speech, gestures, and lewd touching etc. are to be condemned. To the eighth: avarice is forbidden. To the ninth: rash lies, pretences and dissimulations, likewise rash slanders and condemnations, are forbidden. To the tenth: they write that the inward desire for the goods of others, and the cherishing of such thoughts in the mind, were counted as sins only under the New Testament by Christ, and were added to the old law. By these precepts, they say, Christ perfected and fulfilled the old moral law of Moses.

units.la: Propria autem Christi præcepta constituunt tria. 1. sui abnegationem. 11. tolerantiam crucis. 111. imitationem Christi. Hoc omnium præceptorum complexum & syllabus est, quæ Christi lege comprehendunt, aut Christum de novo tulisse arbitrantur. Smalcius, contra Frantzium, Disp. iv. de justifi-sic. pag. 93. At fides, quæ est sub N. F., præter ea, quæ olim à fidelibus requireban-tur, requirit etiam observationem eorum, quæ partim ad legem sunt addita, de quo Matth. v: 6. 7. & alibi, partim tanquam nova prorsus à Christo præcepta, qualia abnegatio sui ipsius, portatio crucis suæ, & imitatio Christi, quorum ne vestigium in lege extat, de quo postea. Sic & alii. Vel distinctius, præcepta ista Christi, absque respectu ad legem, duum faciunt genera, alia moralia, uti tria jam memorata; & cæremoniale unum, de sacra Christi Cœnâ. Socinus, de Officio Christi, them. xxviii. xxix. xxx. Ut autem de iis præceptis jam agere incipiamus, quæ in Novo Fœdere peculiariter sunt tradita, absque respectu Mosaicæ legis, ea duplicia esse censemus, partim bonos mores, partim externas cæremonias concernentia. Quæ ad mores pertinent, sunt, seipsum abnegare, crucem suam tollere, Christum imitari. Cæremoniale unicum est, Sacra nimirum cœna, quæ à Christo est instituta, in commemorationem mortis suæ, id est, ut ipsum etiam Christum solenni laude celebremus, atque pro augusto illo beneficio, & ineffabili ejus amore, quod corpus suum nostra causa contundendum, & sanguinem effundendum tradiderit, gratias ipsi religiose agamus.
units.tr: Christ's own precepts, however, consist of three: (1) self-denial; (2) bearing the cross; (3) imitating Christ. This is the whole compass and summary of those things which they include in the law of Christ, or believe Christ to have newly given. Smalcius, against Frantz, Disputation 4, on justification, p. 93: "But faith, which is under the New Testament, in addition to those things which were formerly required of the faithful, requires also the observance of those things which were partly added to the law (on which see Matt. 5:6, 7 and elsewhere), and partly are precepts entirely new from Christ, such as self-denial, bearing one's own cross, and imitating Christ; of which there is not even a trace in the law, as will be discussed later." So too others. Or, more distinctly, these precepts of Christ, apart from any relation to the law, they make into two kinds: some moral, like the three just mentioned; and one ceremonial, concerning the holy Supper of Christ. Socinus, On the Office of Christ, theses 28, 29, 30: "But to begin to treat of those precepts which are peculiarly handed down in the New Covenant, apart from any regard to the Mosaic law, we judge them to be of two kinds: some concern morals, others external ceremonies. Those which pertain to morals are: to deny oneself, to take up one's cross, to imitate Christ. There is one ceremonial precept, namely the holy supper, which was instituted by Christ in memory of his death; that is, so that we may celebrate Christ himself with solemn praise, and, for that splendid benefit and ineffable love of his, by which he gave up his body to be bruised and his blood to be poured out for our sake, may religiously give thanks to him."

units.la: Cum Socinianis in articulo de præceptis Christi, legem perficientibus, quodque alia Christus in N. Test. supra veterem morum mandata dederit, præsertim Matth. v. sentiunt Anabaptistæ complures, atque Remonstrantes. De illis videndum Dooreslaer, in Tabulâ Controverf. art. xiv. §. 11. & art. viii. §. 1. Isti sic loquuntur in Apologiâ, cap. xxiv, in initio: nihil æque necessarium esse credunt, quamut[?] credatur, Christum novæ legis latorem esse. quod tamen Socinus reformidat dicere. Adde illorum Catechesim, quast. lv. lvi. lxviii. lxxvi. atque Episcopium, Disput. privatâ xvii. thes. i.
units.tr: Several Anabaptists and the Remonstrants agree with the Socinians on the article concerning the precepts of Christ which perfect the law, and that Christ in the New Testament gave other moral commands above the old, especially Matt. 5. On these see Dooreslaer, in his Table of Controversies, art. 14 §11 and art. 8 §1. They speak thus in the Apology, ch. 24, at the beginning: "They believe that nothing is as necessary as that it be believed that Christ is the giver of the new law," which nevertheless Socinus shrinks from saying. Add their Catechism, questions 55, 56, 68, 76, and Episcopius, Private Disputation 17, thesis 1.

units.la: Nostra autem est sententia, legem moralem, à Deo per Mosem traditam, perfectam vitæ, præceptorumque omnium esse regulam, cui nihil hoc in genere apponi potest, neque per Christum appositum in N. Test. fuit; confirmasse quidem Christum moralem legem, ad præstandum Deo secundum eam obedientiam, illamque vindicasse & exposuisse, non vero aliam legem, alia de novo præcepta dedisse, vel veteri legi addenda, vel suæ doctrinæ propria, quæ doctrina gratiæ fuit, Euangelii, & salutis, non novarum legum, afferimus. Socinus adversus Palæologum, part. i. pag. 187. de hoc potissimum disputatur, utrum Christi præcepta interpretamenta, an vero additamenta sunt ad Mosis legem.
units.tr: But our view is that the moral law, delivered by God through Moses, is the perfect rule of life and of all precepts, to which nothing can be added in this respect, and nothing was added through Christ in the New Testament. We affirm that Christ indeed confirmed the moral law, in order to render to God the obedience due according to it, and vindicated and expounded it; but that he did not give another law or new precepts, either to be added to the old law or proper to his own doctrine, which was the doctrine of grace, of the gospel and of salvation, not of new laws. Socinus, against Palaeologus, part 1, p. 187: "The main point of dispute here is whether the precepts of Christ are interpretations or rather additions to the law of Moses."

units.la: Præcognita facimus ante disputationem, ista. 1. Uti leges communiter & ubique, sic divinas, præsertim Decalogi morales, conceptas esse terminis admodum generalibus. ii. Generalia autem sub se continent specialia quæcunque ad generale caput pertinent. Hinc Volkelius, lib. iv. pag. 267. Quid, quod ea etiam prohibita censenda sunt, quæ prohibitis sunt similia, utpote ad rerum interdictarum genus spectantia. Atque in exponendis Christi & N. Test. verbis Adversarii sub eorumdem generalitatem referunt, quæcunque ex rei similitudine eodem pertinent: æquum ergo ut idem observent & in explicandâ lege. Socinus, in Matth. v. pag. 147. prout exempla, quæ Christus subjicit, satis declarant; quæ tamen non eam vim habere debent, ut ad istius generis tantum incommoda, præceptum Christi referatur, sed, ut diximus, ut doceant hic agi de damnis & incommodis hujus vitæ, cujusmodi sunt ea quæ exemplis istis continentur, cum alia interim esse possint ejusdem generis incommoda: nec tamen, quia non sint in istis exemplis expressa, censeri debeat, ea Christi præceptione minime contineri: ad eáve Christi prohibitionem non pertingere; qualia sunt incommoda, quæ ad decus & famam pertinent, quorum in Christi verbis nulla aperta fit mentio. Idem ergo teneatur in expositione legis, ut ad eam etiam, quorum in ea nulla aperta fit mentio, reducantur, & vel præcepta vel prohibita esse censeantur, quæ sunt ejusdem generis. Unde iii. aliud in lege expresse, aliud implicite vulgò continetur. Et quamvis aliquid totidem verbis expressum non sit, haud ideo tamen lege non comprehendi dicendum erit. Volkel. lib. iv. cap. xxiii. pag. 359. Animadvertendum autem hoc loco est, tribus potissimum rationibus fieri posse, ut quis in religionem Christianam peccet, etiamsi id, quod committit, expressis verbis interdictum non legatur. Primum cum id, quod committitur, species universi est generis expresse interdicti, ut peculatus furti, quo interdicto satis etiam ille prohibitus censeri debet. Sic cum impuritas interdicitur, satis omnes ejus species interdicta putanda sunt, etiamsi non omnes forte sint expressa. Secundo, cum ea, quæ admittuntur, prohibitis sunt similia: quo pacto Apostolus, cum recensuisset multa carnis opera, addit, & similia his, de quibus idem fieri vult judicium. Quod si istâ ratione exponenda vobis videantur præcepta N. Testamenti, quare non etiam Veteris ? quare hæc minus suâ generalitate complectentur specialia omnia suâ latitudine comprehensa, quam præcepta vel leges aliæ? Quod si vero admittant de præceptis quoque Veteris legis, uti omnino æquum est, minus negaturi sunt vetita sub V. Test.fuisse, vel legibus illis quoque comprehensa fuisse, quæ jam demum à Christo illis addita frustra contendunt. Volkelius, cap. xvii. pag. 267. Neque enim protinus à prohibitorum numero excludenda ea sunt, quæ expressis litteris non vetantur: cum satis sit hoc implicita quadam ratione fieri. iv. Legis expositio, non est lex alia, neque pro tali unquam apud ullos accipitur. v. Uti nec præceptorum nova determinatio vel applicatio ad aliud & aliud subjectum, ideo lex alia est. vi. Neque varietas legis circumstantialis ejus essentiam mutat, aut tollit. vii. Doctrina Christi consideratur late, vel stricte. Illo modo comprehendit etiam præcepta legis morum, quæ confirmat, & urget, ad vitam digne transfigendam necessaria: stricte quatenus sumitur, & præcisè pro illis quæ solius Christi sunt, exclusive & oppositè ad alia, sic nulla habet per se præcepta, solas autem continet promissiones salutis & gratiæ. Atque ita concilianda sunt, quæ aliquando apud Nonnullos dicta occurrunt de lege & præceptis Christi. Etiam Schlichtingius id agnoscit hactenus in Disp. pro Socino, contra Meisnerum, qu. Unicâ, pag. 7. hoc quidem facile conceditur, Euangelium præcipue & potissimum significare nuntium illum latum de peccatorum remissione & vita æterna.
units.tr: Before the discussion I lay down the following preliminary points. (1) Laws, as is common everywhere, and divine laws especially the moral precepts of the Decalogue, are framed in very general terms. (2) General terms, however, include under them all the specific cases that belong to the general head. Hence Volkelius, book 4, p. 267: What then? Those things are to be counted as forbidden too which are similar to the forbidden things, since they belong to the kind of things that are prohibited. And in explaining the words of Christ and of the New Testament, our opponents bring under their generality whatever belongs to the same thing by likeness. It is only fair, then, that they observe the same rule in explaining the law. Socinus, on Matthew 5, p. 147: As the examples which Christ adds sufficiently show, these examples ought not to have such force that Christ's precept is referred only to that kind of inconvenience. Rather, as we have said, they teach that here it is a question of losses and inconveniences of this life, of the sort contained in those examples, although other inconveniences of the same kind may also exist. Nor should it be thought that, because they are not expressed in those examples, they are in no way contained in Christ's precept or do not fall under Christ's prohibition. Such are the inconveniences which concern honour and reputation, of which no open mention is made in Christ's words. The same therefore must be held in the explanation of the law, so that those things of which no open mention is made in it are also brought back to it, and are judged to be commanded or forbidden if they are of the same kind. (3) Hence, in general, one thing is contained in the law expressly, another implicitly. And although something is not expressed in so many words, we must still say that it is not for that reason excluded from the law. Volkelius, book 4, ch. 23, p. 359: It must be noted here that there are chiefly three ways in which a person may sin against the Christian religion even though what he commits is not forbidden in express words. First, when what is committed is a species of a genus that is expressly forbidden, as theft is of robbery; by that prohibition he too must be considered sufficiently forbidden. So when impurity is forbidden, all its species are sufficiently to be considered forbidden, even if perhaps not all are named. Second, when the things that are permitted are similar to things forbidden; in this way the Apostle, after listing many works of the flesh, adds "and things like these," about which he wishes the same judgement to be made. But if the precepts of the New Testament seem to you to be explained by this method, why not also those of the Old? Why should these not embrace by their generality all the specific cases comprehended in their scope, any more than other precepts or laws do? And if they admit this also for the precepts of the Old Law, as is entirely fair, they will hardly deny that things were forbidden under the Old Testament, or were included in those laws, which they now vainly contend were added to them by Christ. Volkelius, ch. 17, p. 267: For those things which are not forbidden in express letters must not at once be excluded from the number of things forbidden, since it is enough that this is done in some implicit way. (4) An explanation of a law is not another law, nor is it ever taken for one by anyone. (5) Nor is a new determination or application of precepts to one subject or another therefore another law. (6) Nor does a variation of the circumstances of a law change or remove its essence. (7) The teaching of Christ may be considered either broadly or strictly. In the broad sense it also comprehends the precepts of the moral law, which he confirms and urges as necessary for living a life worthy of God. Strictly, as it is taken when it is precisely what belongs to Christ alone, exclusively and in opposition to other things, it has no precepts of its own, but contains only promises of salvation and grace. And so the statements sometimes met with among some men about the law and the precepts of Christ are to be reconciled. Schlichting also acknowledges this so far, in his disputation for Socinus against Meisner, question 1, p. 7: This is readily conceded: the Gospel chiefly and above all signifies that message announced about the forgiveness of sins and eternal life.

units.la: Errorem verò, quem hac in re nos errare Socinus autumat, lib. Quod regni Poloniæ &c. (quem tueri conatur Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum) tantum facit, ut viam salutis impedire, non verò ex eorum numero esse, qui vix ullo modo permittunt ut quis viam salutis insistat, scribat. Quare ? quia hinc potissimum fit, ut ex Euangelicorum doctrina quædam liceant, quæ tamen Christus expresse vetuit, vel certè ipsius Christianæ disciplinæ analogia non permittit. Ecquænam illa ? nullum profert. quasi verò dicere sufficeret. Quodnam, rogo, illud caput est quod nos licitum esse dicimus, contra Christi disciplinam ? quodque tale sit, aut esse debeat, ex sententiâ nostrâ de perfectione legis moralis ? Annon quæ Christus prohibita dicit Matth. v. nos etiam pro talibus habemus ? sola autem inter nos est disputatio, annon etiam sensu legis prohibita fuerint, & non nunc demum ex doctrinâ Christi ? Quod ergo caput est, quod nos contra Christi doctrinam & disciplinam tuemur ? qui fortius quam Sociniani illud dicimus vetitum, ex præcepto legis nimirum etiam, & doctrina Christi, illi modo ex altero capite, nos ex utroque ?
units.tr: But the error which Socinus asserts we commit in this matter, in the book That the kingdom of Poland etc. (which Schlichting tries to defend against Meisner), amounts only to this: that it hinders the way of salvation. It does not place him among those who in no way permit anyone to walk the way of salvation or to write about it. Why not? Because from this above all it comes about that some things are allowed on the basis of the Evangelical teaching which Christ expressly forbade, or at least which the very analogy of Christian discipline does not permit. What are those things? He produces none. As if it were enough simply to say so! Which, I ask, is that point which we say is lawful, against the discipline of Christ, and which is or ought to be such according to our view of the perfection of the moral law? Do we not also regard as forbidden those things which Christ calls forbidden in Matthew 5? The only dispute between us is whether they were also forbidden in the sense of the law, and not only now from the teaching of Christ. What, then, is the point which we defend against the teaching and discipline of Christ? Do we not maintain that it is forbidden more strongly than the Socinians do, namely by the precept of the law as well as by the teaching of Christ, whereas they maintain it only from the one source, and we from both?

units.la: Schlichtingium audiamus, Magistrum suum defendentem, exponentemque. Ita ille, pag. [?]671. Qui enim hanc sententiam imbibit, facile ea omnia, quæ in Veteri Testamento aperta concessa, vel non præcepta fuisse videt, in Novo quoque Testamento vel concessa, vel non præcepta esse putabit: & sic latiorem, ut homines solent, vivendi disciplinam quærens, non ex novo vetus, sed ex vetere novum fœdus interpretabitur. Nonne quotidiana experientia verum id esse docet? quam enim frequenter contingit, ut cum homines ob aliqua vitia in Christiana disciplina haud quaquam concessa arguuntur, puta quod largius bibant, & genio indulgeant, quod tripudient, licita hac olim & à Deo concessa fuisse respondeant. Resp. i. Imo ex illa nostra sententia aliquis videns quid prohiberi, vel praecipi in doctrina N. Test. sciet statim illud quoque in V. Test. & legis generalitate comprehensum, & sive praeceptum, sive vetitum fuisse: unde eo fortius sibi existimabit illud jam quoque prohibitum, vel praeceptum esse. Neque enim nunc aliquis, praecepto Novo, ex V. Test. edoceri cupiet de vita sua ad divinae voluntatis normam instituendam, vel ex Veteri Novum, sed ex Novo illud interpretabitur. Quantumvis enim dicamus, N. Test. non aliam legem vel praecepta continere, quam Vetus, haud tamen negamus hujus doctrinam in Novo saepe exponi clarius explicatiusque. ii. Nemo argumentabitur ex concessis vel permissis sub V. Test. ad se, ut sibi eadem nunc permissa putet, quia non modo cum doctrina Christi, sed legis quoque haud conveniunt: qualia sunt quae Autor hic de luxu, & intemperantia, atque immodestia adscribit. Alia Deus populo illi concesserat, non vero jusserat: & praecepta communia, non indulta particularia pro tempore, & statu populi, vivendi regulam formant, omnibus sequendam. iii. Praeceptum aliud aut prohibitum intelligitur dupliciter, implicite vel explicite, generaliter aut specialiter. Lex non ista solum, quae explicite & speciatim recenset, sed, quia generalibus concepta terminis, omnia comprehendit, quae sub legis aliquo capite continentur: adeo quando ex vi generalis praecepti particularis fit determinatio ad hoc aut illud speciale officium, quamvis ῥητῶς lege non explicatum, vim tamen ejus observandi, illa contentam fuisse censeri omnino debet.
units.tr: Let us hear Schlichting defending and expounding his master. Thus he, p. [?]671: For whoever has imbibed this opinion will easily think that all those things which in the Old Testament are seen to be openly permitted, or not commanded, are also in the New Testament either permitted or not commanded; and so, seeking a broader rule of life, as men usually do, he will interpret not the new from the old but the old from the new covenant. Does not daily experience teach that this is true? For how often it happens that when men are accused of some faults which are by no means permitted in Christian discipline, for example that they drink too freely, indulge their appetite, or dance about, they reply that these things were once lawful and permitted by God. Reply. (1) Indeed, from our opinion, anyone who sees what is forbidden or commanded in the doctrine of the New Testament will know at once that this too is included in the Old Testament under the generality of the law, and was either commanded or forbidden. Therefore he will think it all the more strongly that this is now also forbidden or commanded. For no one now who wishes to order his life according to the norm of the divine will would wish to be taught the New precept from the Old Testament, or to interpret the New from the Old; rather he will interpret the Old from the New. For although we say that the New Testament contains no other law or precepts than the Old, we do not deny that its doctrine is often set out more clearly and explained more fully in the New. (2) No one will argue from things conceded or permitted under the Old Testament that the same things are now permitted to him, because such things agree not only with the teaching of Christ but also with the law; such are the things which this author ascribes to luxury, intemperance and immodesty. God had granted those things to that people, but had not commanded them; and the common precepts, not the particular permissions granted for the time and condition of the people, form the rule of life to be followed by all. (3) A precept is understood to be commanded or forbidden in two ways: implicitly or explicitly, generally or specially. The law is not only that which recites things explicitly and individually, but, since it is framed in general terms, it embraces all things that are contained under any head of the law. Thus when from the force of a general precept a particular determination is made to this or that specific duty, although it is not explained in the law expressly [ῥητῶς], it must nevertheless be judged entirely that the force of observing it was contained in that law.

units.la: Quare ex istis iniquitas judicii Sociniani de sententia nostra est manifesta. Nam i. non negamus illa quae a Christo seu vetita sunt, seu praecepta, pro talibus habenda esse. ii. Sed confirmamus eorum vim, dum sub V. Test. parem sive in genere praecepti, sive prohibiti, docemus illorum fuisse rationem. iii. Et jam in N. Test. majorem requiri a Christianis sanctitatem, quam unquam ab ullis antea. Non tamen plura ideo vel perfectiora statuimus praecepta nunc moralis legis esse, quam olim. Sed erga communia & aeterna legis praecepta, & a pluribus, & major gradus obedientiae hodie exigitur, pro gratiae copiosiori mensura: correctis iis, quae sub oeconomia populo infantili indulta quidem, non praecepta vel probata fuerunt, nobis autem nec permissa.
units.tr: From these points the unfairness of the Socinian judgement about our view is plain. (1) We do not deny that those things which Christ has either forbidden or commanded are to be held as such. (2) But we affirm their force, while we teach that, under the Old Testament, their reason was the same, both in the kind of precept and in the kind of prohibition. (3) And indeed a greater holiness is now required of Christians in the New Testament than was ever required of anyone before. Yet we do not therefore hold that there are now more or more perfect precepts of the moral law than there were before. Rather, both more people and a greater degree of obedience are now demanded, in keeping with the fuller measure of grace, with those things corrected which were indeed granted to the childlike people under the old economy, but were neither commanded nor approved, and are not permitted to us.

units.la: Duo vero praesentis disputationis erunt capita, generale unum, alterum speciale. Primum quaeremus de praeceptis Christi, quae dicunt, in genere: deinde in specie. Hoc ergo videamus, Num Christus alia & nova praecepta, seu ,,legem vivendi perfectiorem tulerit, quam fuit antiqua lex moralis? Nos negamus, & sententiae haec adducimus argumenta. venturus esset, & vocabis nomen ejus Jesus; ipse enim salvabit populum suum a peccatis ipsorum. Salvare a peccatis, aliud quid est, quam leges novasque regulas ferre de peccatis. Et lex quae datur, praesertim additamenta legis moralis debent ad omnes spectare: contra est Euangelium, & Christus; cujus gratia spectat non ad omnes, sed ad Ecclesiam, ad fideles, ad populum suum; non enim est omnibus Jesus, quod designat additum epitheton, & restrictio sui. Matth xx.
units.tr: There will be two heads of this present disputation: one general, the other special. First we shall inquire about the precepts of Christ which speak in general terms, and then about those which speak in particular. Let us therefore consider this: whether Christ has brought in other and new precepts, or a more perfect rule of living, than the old moral law. We deny it, and we bring forward these arguments for our view. "He shall come, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he shall save his people from their sins" (Matth. 1:21). To save from sins is something other than to bring in new laws and new rules concerning sins. And a law that is given, especially additions to the moral law, ought to pertain to all; but it is otherwise with the Gospel and with Christ, whose grace pertains not to all but to the Church, to the faithful, to his people. For Jesus is not for all; the added epithet and the restriction of himself make this plain. Matth. xx.

units.la: 28. Filius hominis non venit ut ei serviatur, sed servitat, atque det animam suam redemptionem pro multis. Luc. iv. 18. 19. 21. Spiritus Domini super me, ideoque unxit me, ut evangelizarem pauperibus misit me, ad sanandum contritos corde, annunciare captivis remissionem, & caecis visum, & ad emittendos confractos in libertatem. Ut praedicem annum Domini acceptum, &c. Coepit autem eis dicere, etenim hodie impleta est in auribus vestris prophetia ista. Certe euangelizare, non est legem ferre. Lex Euangelio, in Scripturis passim opponitur. Neque quidquam hoc in loco, qui petitus ex Jesa. LXI. 1. & quo seu in Vet. Test. praedictione, seu Novi implet-tione, ratio officii Christi expositae est, de lege, lege nova annunciandâ ferendaque. Quae vero hoc in loco, omnia consolationis, gratiae, & salutis sunt, contraria per omnia naturae legis ejusque annuntiationi. Luc. xxii. 20. Poculum hoc est novum testamentum in sanguine meo, qui pro vobis funditur. Haec natura, forma, & ratio est Novi Testamenti, redemtio, & remissio peccatorum in sanguine Christi parta. Joann. i. 15. Johannes testatur de eo & clamavit &c. ex plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus & gratiam pro gratia. Euangelium de Christo, atque in Christo, gratiae est, non legis, gratiae uberrimae & plenissimae, quam liberaliter ex eo omnes haurimus & accipimus. Rom. iii. 24. 25. Justificati gratis ejus gratia, per redemtionem quae est in Christo Jesu: Quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ejus &c. Isti fini est Christus, ut placamentum sit & expiatio pro peccatis nostris, ut gratiam ad nos deferat, non legem. Rom. v. 15. quanto magis gratia Dei, & donum gratia, quae unius hominis Jesu Christi, in multos illos abundabit. 20. 21. Lex autem subintravit, ut abundaret peccatum, superabundavit gratia. Ut, quemadmodum peccatum regnavit in morte, ita gratia regnaret per justitiam in vitam aeternam, per Christum Dominum nostrum. Videmus, nil in Christo praedicari, nihilque ex eo derivari quam gratiam, meram & copiosam gratiam; nam tum gratia, tum donum ejus dicitur, & abundare utrumque ac superabundare. Imo expresse & legi opponitur, quatenus peccatum offendit; Christus autem solam gratiam, omnemque. Atque ejusmodi loca ex toto N. Test. complura adferri possunt, nam ipsum ejus argumentum comprehendunt & summam. Atque illa selegisse suffecerit, quae clare satis abundeque ostendunt, Christum non alio fine venisse in mundum, neque aliud ejus officium fuisse, quam salutis opus perficere, & gratiam ac redemtionem praestare, non aliis legibus nos onerare, & salutem iis adnectere, sed unice se solo totoque homines salvare & reddere Deo, vitaeque. 1 Cor. i. 30. 31. Ex ipso vos estis in Christo Jesu, qui factus nobis est sapientia a Deo, justitia & sanctitas & redemtio. Ut, quemadmodum scriptum, glorians in Domino glorietur. In Christo attenditur quid sit factus nobis, ut in ipso simus & habeamus omnia, non ut in lege nova obserconsummari dixit. Sin ita, ergo omne præceptum lege continetur: nam illud præceptum legis est: & extra id non est præceptum aliud. Namque verba ista, & si quod aliud præceptum, significant, nullum aliud rei cujuscunque speciale mandatum dari posse, quod generali illo legis non includatur. Gal. v. 13.14. Verùm per legem inservite vobis mutuò. Omnis enim lex unico verbo impletur, isto, diliges proximum tuum sicuti teipsum. Adeo in hisce præceptis Apostolus non nisi ad legem provocat, 11. eamque dicit omnia huc spectantia perfecte continere ἐν ἑνὶ λό-γῳ, בדבר אחר[?], sive dicto, sive re, dilectionis proximi, sicuti tui ipsius. legem regiam dicit Jacobus, cap. 11.8. si ergo legem impletis regiam, juxta Scriptu-ram, diliges proximum tuum sicuti teipsum.
units.tr: "The Son of man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Matth. 20:28). Luke 4:18, 19, 21: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he has sent me to heal the broken-hearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord... And he began to say to them, 'Today this scripture is fulfilled in your ears.'" Certainly to preach the gospel is not to bring in a law. The law is commonly set against the Gospel in the Scriptures. Nor does anything in this passage, taken from Isaiah 61:1, and in which, whether in the Old Testament prediction or in the New Testament fulfilment, the office of Christ is set out, concern the law, the announcing and bringing in of a new law. Indeed, everything in this passage is of consolation, grace and salvation, and wholly opposed to the nature of the law and to its proclamation. Luke 22:20: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." This is the nature, form and character of the New Testament: redemption and remission of sins obtained in the blood of Christ. John 1:15, 16: "John bears witness of him, and cried... and of his fullness have we all received, and grace for grace." The Gospel concerning Christ, and in Christ, is of grace, not of law: a most abundant and full grace, which we all draw and receive freely from him. Rom. 3:24, 25: "Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God has set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, etc." This is the end of Christ, that he should be a propitiation and expiation for our sins, and that he should bring grace to us, not law. Rom. 5:15: "How much more did the grace of God, and the gift by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, abound unto many." Verses 20, 21: "Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound; that as sin has reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord." We see that nothing is preached in Christ, and nothing is derived from him, but grace, pure and abundant grace; for it is called both grace and his gift, and both are said to abound and to superabound. Indeed, grace is expressly set against the law, insofar as the law offends by sin, while Christ gives grace alone, and all. Many such passages could be cited from the whole New Testament, for they embrace its very argument and summary. And it will be enough to have selected those which show clearly and abundantly that Christ did not come into the world for any other end, nor was his office anything other than to perform the work of salvation and to bestow grace and redemption; not to burden us with other laws and to attach salvation to them, but solely and wholly to save men and to restore them to God and to life by himself alone. 1 Cor. 1:30, 31: "Of him are you in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption; that, according as it is written, he that glories, let him glory in the Lord." In Christ we are to consider what he has been made for us, so that in him we may have and possess all things, not as if in a new law to be observed... But if so, then every precept is contained in the law; for that is a precept of the law, and there is no other precept outside it. For those words, "and if there is any other precept," signify that no other special command concerning any matter can be given which is not included in that general command of the law. Gal. 5:13, 14: "But by love serve one another. For all the law is fulfilled in one word, namely this: you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Thus in these precepts the Apostle appeals to nothing but the law, and says that it perfectly contains all things pertaining to this in one word [ἐν ἑνὶ λόγῳ], that is, in one saying [bedavar acher, בדבר אחר] or in one matter: the love of one's neighbour, as one's own self. James calls it "the royal law," chap. 2:8: "If you fulfil the royal law according to the Scripture, you shall love your neighbour as yourself."

units.la: Christus interroganti Legulejo, Magister quid faciam ut vitam æternam acquiram? (quærebat de operibus faciendis, τί ποιήσω[?]) respondet, ad legem eum remittens, ut faciendorum perfectum exemplar & canonem, in lege quid scriptum? quomodo legis? respondens autem ille dixit, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo &c. & proximum sicuti teipsum. Dixit autem ei, recte respondisti: id fac, & vives.
units.tr: When the lawyer asked Christ, "Master, what shall I do [τί ποιήσω] to inherit eternal life?" (he was asking about works to be done), Christ answered him by referring him to the law, as the perfect pattern and rule of what is to be done: "What is written in the law? How do you read it?" And he answering said, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, etc., and your neighbour as yourself." And he said to him, "You have answered rightly: do this, and you shall live."

units.la: Nihil præter præcepta legis Christus proponit, quærenti de præceptis, & de præceptis vitæ: ut nec ad vitam, æternam nempe, nec à Christo aliud quid præceptorum doctum fuerit, quam quod lege continetur.
units.tr: Christ sets forth nothing beyond the precepts of the law when he is asked about precepts, and about the precepts of life: so that neither in regard to eternal life, nor from Christ, has anything been taught about precepts other than what is contained in the law.

units.la: Sic summa præceptorum, quæ Christus docuit ad proximum vid. & secundam tabulam spectantia, huc redit, ut, quæcunque quis sibi velit fieri ab hominibus, eadem faciat illis, Matth. vii. 12. Sed hoc Christus dicit medullam legis esse: neque præter vel extra legem præcepta alia proponit. Quæcunque ergo vultis ut vobis faciant homines, sic & vos facite illis: hæc enim est lex & Prophetæ.
units.tr: Thus the sum of the precepts which Christ taught, those pertaining to our neighbour, that is, to the second table, comes to this: whatever you would have men do to you, do the same to them (Matth. 7:12). But Christ says that this is the marrow of the law, and he sets forth no precepts beyond or outside the law. "Therefore whatever you would that men should do to you, do you even so to them; for this is the law and the Prophets."

units.la: Summa legum Novi Testamenti, id est, quæ in Novo Test. traduntur, est quod ad proximum nempe, ejusque dilectionem, facere aliis quæ tibi velis fieri: atqui hæc est summa legum V. T. & legis moralis: ergo eadem utriusque summa, neque alia N. T. præcepta sunt à Veteribus. 1 Tim. 1. 5. Finis autem præcepti est charitas ex puro corde, & conscientia bona, & fide non ficta. Augustinus, lib. vii. contra Faustum, cap. ult. lex Dei tam perfecte commendatur, ut nihil ei addendum minuendumve sit.
units.tr: The sum of the laws of the New Testament, that is, those which are delivered in the New Testament, is this: that, with regard to our neighbour and the love of him, we should do to others what we would have done to ourselves. But this is the sum of the laws of the Old Testament and of the moral law. Therefore the sum of both is the same, and the New Testament precepts are not other than those given by the ancients. 1 Tim. 1:5: "Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned." Augustine, book 7 against Faustus, last chapter: "The law of God is so perfectly commended that nothing is to be added to it or taken from it."

units.la: Secundum argumentum. Cujus officium solum & unicum fuit, salutem impetrare & conferre, à legis maledictione liberare, & redemptionem promereri, exponere, & conferre, ut solâ Dei gratiâ, per remissionem peccatorum, illius sanguine partam, salvaremur; ejus non fuit aliam de novo legem, & graviorem priori ferre, ut per ejus observationem justificaremur & salvaremur: sed, illud Christi fuit officium: ergo. Major certa est, quia id dicitur ejus unicum & solum fuisse officium, oppositè ad novam legislationem. Assumtio probabatur, quia, ubicunque officium Christi describitur, semper hoc inde fit, quod salutis & redemptionis fuit, nuspiam à promulgandâ novâ lege. Perlustremus omnia & singula loca, ea imprimis quæ ex professo hoc argumentum tractant & tradunt, ut ex iis de Christi officio, quodnam fuerit, rite judicemus. Matth. 1. 21[?]. prima nascituri ex Maria annunciatio, declaravit quis, qualis, & quorsum venturus effet, & vocabis nomen ejus Jesus : ipse enim salvabit populum suum a peccatis ipsorum. Salvare à peccatis, aliud quid est,quàm leges novasque regulas ferre de peccatis. Et lex quae datur, praesertim additamenta legis moralis debent ad omnes spectare : contrà est Euangelium, & Christus ; cujus gratia spectat non ad omnes, sed ad Ecclesiam, ad fideles, ad populum suum ; non enim est omnibus Jesus, quod designat additum epitheton, & restrictio sui. Matth xx. 28. Filius hominis non venit ut ei serviatur, sed servitat, atque det animam suam re-demptionem pro multis. Luc. iv. 18. 19. 21. Spiritus Domini super me, ideoque unxit me, ut euangelizarem pauperibus misit me, ad sanandum contritos corde, annunciare captivis remissionem, & cæcis visum, & ad emittendos confractos in libertatem. Ut prædi-cem annum Domini acceptum, &c. Cœpit autem eis dicere, etenim hodie impleta est in auribus vestris prophetia ista. Certe euangelizare, non est legem ferre. Lex Euan-gelio, in Scripturis passim opponitur. Neque quidquam hoc in loco, qui petitus ex Jesa. LXI. 1. & quo seu in Vet. Test. prædictione, seu Novi implete tione, ratio officii Christi expósita est, de lege, lege novâ annunciandâ seren-daque. Quae vero hoc in loco, omnia consolationis, gratiae, & salutis sunt, contraria per omnia naturae legis ejusque annuntiationi. Luc. xxii. 20. Poculum hoc est novum testamentum in sanguine meo, qui pro vobis funditur. Haec natura, forma, & ratio est Novi Testamenti, redemtio, & remissio peccatorum in sanguine Christi parta. Joann. 1. 15. Johannes testatur de eo & clamavit &c. ex plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus & gratiam pro gratia. Euangelium de Christo, atque in Christo, gratiae est, non legis, gratiae uberrimae & plenissimae, quam liberaliter ex eo omnes haurimus & accipimus. Rom. iii. 24. 25. Justificatis gratis ejus gratia, per redemptionem quae est in Christo Jesu : Quem proposuit Deus placa-mentum per fidem in sanguine ejus &c. Isti fini est Christus, ut placamentum sit & expiatio pro peccatis nostris, ut gratiam ad nos deferat, non legem. Rom. v. 15. quanto magis gratia Dei, & donum gratia, quae unius hominis Jesu Christi, in multos illos abundabit. 20. 21. Lex autem subintravit, ut abundaret peccatum, supe-rabundavit gratia. Ut, quemadmodum peccatum regnavit in morte, ita gratia regnaret per justitiam in vitam aeternam, per Christum Dominum nostrum. Videmus, nil in Christo praedicari, nihilque ex eo derivari quàm gratiam, meram & copiosam gratiam ; nam tum gratia, tum donum ejus dicitur, & abundare utrumque ac superabundare. Imo expresse & legi opponitur, quatenus peccatum ostendit ; Christus autem solam gratiam, omnemque. Atque ejusmodi loca ex toto N. Test. complura adferri possunt, nam ipsum ejus argumentum comprehen-dunt & summam. Atque illa selegisse suffecerit, quae clare satis abundeque ostendunt, Christum non alio fine venisse in mundum, neque aliud ejus ossi-cium fuisse, quam salutis opus perficere, & gratiam ac redemtionem praestare, non aliis legibus nos onerare, & salutem iis adnectere, sed unice se solo totoque homines salvare & reddere Deo, vitaeque. 1 Cor. 1. 30. 31. Ex ipso vos estis in Christo Jesu, qui factus nobis est sapientia a Deo, justitia & sanctitas & redemtio. Ut, quemadmodum scriptum, glorians in Domino glorietur. In Christo attenditur quid sit factus nobis, ut in ipso simus & habeamus omnia, non ut in iege nova obser-
units.tr: Second argument. Christ's office was solely and only to obtain and bestow salvation, to free us from the curse of the law, and to win and bestow redemption, so that we might be saved by the grace of God alone, through the forgiveness of sins obtained by his blood. It was not his office to bring a new and heavier law than the former, by whose observance we would be justified and saved. But that was Christ's office; therefore (the conclusion follows). The major premise is certain, since his office is said to have been his one and only office, as opposed to a new legislation. The minor premise is proved as follows: wherever Christ's office is described, it is always stated as the work of salvation and redemption, and nowhere as the promulgation of a new law. Let us go through all the passages, and especially those that treat and set out this argument expressly, so that from them we may rightly judge what Christ's office was. Matt. 1:21 [?]. The first announcement to Mary of the one to be born declared who he was, what sort of person he would be, and to what end he would come: and you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins. To save from sins is something other than to bring laws and new rules about sins. A law that is given, especially additions to the moral law, must concern everyone; but the Gospel and Christ are not of that kind, for his grace concerns not everyone but the Church, the faithful, his own people. Jesus is not for everyone, as the added epithet and the restriction of his person indicate. Matt. 20:28: The Son of man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Luke 4:18, 19, 21: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he has sent me to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and sight to the blind, and to set at liberty those who are bruised; to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord. And he began to say to them, Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing. Certainly, to preach the gospel is not to bring a law. In Scripture the law is everywhere set against the gospel. Nor does the passage from Isaiah 61:1, by which the office of Christ is explained either in the prophecy of the Old Testament or in its fulfilment in the New, say anything about a law, a new law to be proclaimed and established. Everything in this passage is consolation, grace and salvation, which in every respect is contrary to the nature of law and its proclamation. Luke 22:20: This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you. This is the nature, form and character of the New Testament: redemption and forgiveness of sins obtained in the blood of Christ. John 1:15, 16: John bore witness to him and cried out... from his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace. The Gospel about Christ, and in Christ, is grace, not law: abundant and most full grace, which we all draw and receive freely from him. Rom. 3:24, 25: Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, whom God has set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, etc. Christ is for this end, that he may be a propitiation and expiation for our sins, and that he may bring grace to us, not law. Rom. 5:15: how much more did the grace of God, and the gift by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ, abound to many. 5:20, 21: But the law came in, that the offence might abound; but where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. So that, as sin reigned in death, even so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord. We see that nothing is preached in Christ, and nothing is derived from him, except grace: pure and abundant grace. For it is called both grace and his gift, and both are said to abound and to superabound. Indeed, it is expressly set against the law, insofar as the law shows sin, whereas Christ gives grace alone, and all of it. Many such passages can be cited from the whole of the New Testament, for they embrace its very argument and sum. It will suffice to have selected those which clearly and abundantly show that Christ came into the world for no other end, and that his office was no other than to accomplish the work of salvation and to bestow grace and redemption; not to burden us with other laws and attach salvation to them, but to save men and restore them to God and to life by himself alone and wholly. 1 Cor. 1:30, 31: Of him are you in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption; that, as it is written, He that glories, let him glory in the Lord. In Christ, what he has been made for us is noted, so that we may be in him and have all things in him; not so that we may place righteousness in observing a new law, nor glory in that,

units.la: Tom. 2. observandâ iustitiam collocemus, aut in hoc gloriemur, sed in solo Christo. Deus fuit in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians. Non ut legem novam per Christum nobis daret, vel sermonem legis inter nos restitueret. Atque hujusmodi plura in eandem rem ex Sacris proferri facile possunt testimonia.
units.tr: Tom. 2. but glory in Christ alone. God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. He did not give us a new law through Christ, nor did he restore the word of the law among us. Many other testimonies of this kind can easily be brought forward from the Sacred Writings on the same point.

units.la: Tertium argum. Christi officium non solum diversum fuit à lege, sed ei adversum & oppositum, in ordine vid. ad justificationem: ut non dici posset eum in finem venisse, ut legem perfectiorem daret novamque. Etenim tum opponitur Christus legi: tum nos à lege redemisse dicitur; hactenus ut Christo cum lege nil commune fuerit, neque cum ea sibi convenerit. Joann. 1. 17. Nam lex per Mosem data: gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum facta. Opponuntur, Moses, & Christus: utriusque officium, & effectum; illius fuit lex, hujus gratia & veritas. Quemadmodum ergo nequit dici per Mosem gratia contigisse & veritas; ita nec per Christum lex data. Uti Mosis non fuit, gratiam; ita non fuit Christi, legem exhibere. Prout Doctor fuit, & Propheta, legem quidem explicuit & vindicavit: non autem hoc qui facit, legem ferre, nedum novam, censeri debet. Sed non legislator Christus fuit, sed Doctor quidem, sed salvator: & gratia ab eo, quatenus Christus est, non lex.
units.tr: Third argument. Christ's office was not only different from the law but opposed to it and set against it, in respect of justification in particular; so that it could not be said that he came for the purpose of giving a more perfect and new law. For Christ is set in opposition to the law, and we are said to have been redeemed from the law; so that Christ had nothing in common with the law and did not agree with it. John 1:17: For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Moses and Christ are set against each other, as are their offices and effects: the law was the office and effect of the one, grace and truth of the other. Just as it cannot be said that grace and truth came through Moses, so it cannot be said that the law was given through Christ. As it was not Moses' office to bring grace, so it was not Christ's office to set forth the law. Insofar as he was a teacher and a prophet, he explained and vindicated the law; but one who does this should not be considered a maker of law, much less of a new one. Christ was not a lawgiver, but a teacher indeed, but a saviour; and what he gives, insofar as he is Christ, is grace, not law.

units.la: Quod Socinus objicit, contra Palaeologum, pag. 196. locum Pauli, Gal. vi. 2. alter alterius onera portate, & sic adimplete legem Christi. I Cor. ix. 2. ἐννομῷ Χριστῷ, quod vertit, sed in lege essem Christi. & quod praeceptum de charitate dicitur praeceptum novum Christi: ad haec facile respondetur, non quaeri de voce Christi, doctrinae aliquando attributa, sed de rei ipsius proprietate. Nam & Apostolus dicit legem peccati, Rom. vii. 23. non tamen proprie lex peccati est. Sed Christus doctrinâ sua uti confirmavit & expositi legem de amore Dei ac proximi, & praesertim ursit praeceptum illud de charitate, hinc dicitur ejus praeceptum ac lex. At non ab ipso primum lata legislatore: nec ibi loci, ubi Adversarii autumant Christum novas leges dedisse, aut Christi leges appellantur, aut praecepta. Ubi tamen locus erat denominationum istarum, siquidem eo sensu, quo Nostri volunt, essent verae, atque proprie intelligendae.
units.tr: As for what Socinus objects against Palaeologus, p. 196, the passage of Paul, Gal. 6:2: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. And 1 Cor. 9:21, where he translates the Greek ἐννομος Χριστῷ [ennomos Christō] as but I am under the law of Christ, and the precept about charity is called the new precept of Christ: to these things it is easily answered that the question is not about the word "Christ's," which is sometimes attributed to doctrine, but about the proper character of the thing itself. For the Apostle also speaks of the law of sin, Rom. 7:23, and yet it is not properly a law of sin. But Christ, by his teaching, confirmed and expounded the law about the love of God and neighbour, and especially pressed that precept about charity; hence it is called his precept and law. But it was not first brought by him as lawgiver, nor in those places where the adversaries claim that Christ gave new laws are Christ's laws or precepts so called. Yet there was room for these names, since, if they were in the sense our side wants, they would be true and to be understood properly.

units.la: Rom. viii. 2. 3. 4. Lex enim spiritus vitae in Christo Jesu, liberavit me à lege peccati & mortis. Quod enim impossibile legi erat in quo infirmabatur per carnem, fecit Deus suum mittens filium in similitudine carnis peccati, & pro peccato, vel, hostia factus pro peccato, condemnavit peccatum in carne. Ut jus legis impleretur in nobis. Erat in lege nos salvandi & justificandi impossibilitas, ἀδύνατον, ἀθετεῖς [?] ἀνωφελές. Hebr. vii. 18. Hoc ut curaret, & adimpleret, venit Christus. Missâ ergo lege cum suâ impotentiâ, in Christo salus contingit & justificatio. Et promissio vitae vel justificatio, quam lex praeferebat quidem, non autem conferebat, in nobis tamen, sed per Christum est perfecta, Christo eum in finem in carnem misso, & in similitudine carnis peccati expiante & condemnante peccatum nostrum in carne suâ. Quare liberavit nos à lege, & alio, quam per legem, modo nos redemit, & salutis aliam ostendit viam & docuit. Quod vero dicitur lex Spiritus vitæ in Christo, non proprie, sed improprie lex vocatur, & per similitudinem, solâ denominatione externâ: ad significandam duntaxat ejus vim. Quemadmodum cap. præced. vii. 23 dicit, video aliam legem in membris meis belligerantem adversus legem mentis meæ, & captivum me reddentem legi peccati, quæ est in membris meis. per legem peccati, nil intelligit, quam vim peccati. Sic Hebr. vii. 16. qui non factus secundum νόμου legem præcepti carnalis, sed secundum δύναμιν vim vitæ indissolubilis. Quod in uno membro est, secundum legem; in altero est, secundum vim. Alias lex & legis ministerium opponuntur gratiæ ac ministerio Spiritus, tamquam id quod mortis & inefficax per se est, vitæ & justitiæ. 11 Cor. iii. 6. 7. 8. 9. Qui & fecit nos idoneos ut essemus ministri Novi Testamenti, non litteræ, sed spiritus: littera enim occidit, spiritus autem vivificat. Si enim ministerium mortis in litteris, impressum lapidibus, gloriosum fuit, &c. quomodo non magis ministerium Spiritus erit gloriosum? Si enim ministerium condemnationis, cum gloria, quanto magis abundavit ministerium justitiæ in gloria? Si enim quod abrogatur, gloriosum, multo magis id quod manet, gloriosum erit. Confertur atque opponitur inter se, lex & Euangelium. Illa intelligitur lex, quam cum Moses secum de monte ferret, filii Israel faciem ejus intueri non poterant, verf. 7. atque opponitur utriusque ministerium, effecta, usus. Illud littera dicitur; hoc, Spiritus. Illud occidere; hoc, vivificare. Illud mortis & condemnationis esse, hoc vitæ & justitiæ. Illud manere non posse, uti hoc. Apparet ergo quam aliud Christi ministerium, Euangelium, Testamentum sit, ab eo quod Mosis fuit & legis: quamque hæc non diversa solummodo inter se, sed adversa & opposita sint: nempe gratiæ, spiritus, justitiæ, vitæ, & salutis est Christi Testamentum, & hoc est solum totumque. Rabbi Josephus Albo, Ikkarim, ferm. 3. cap. 25. ex interpretatione Genebrardi (qui hoc caput edidit, & confutavit A. 1566.) certe non invenimus Jesum legem tulisse, quin immo ipse per se mandavit servare legem Mosis. Nec Euangelia sunt lex, sed enarratio ortus ejus & signorum, quæ ipsum, dum viveret, edidisse dicunt, qualia comperimus facta per Prophetas, qui legem interea nullam ediderunt. Sic Judæi intelligunt de Christo doceri in Euangelio.
units.tr: Rom. 8:2–4. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death. For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh: that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. There was in the law an impossibility of saving and justifying us [ἀδύνατον], a setting aside [ἀθέτησις] and unprofitableness [ἀνωφελές] (Heb. 7:18). Christ came to remedy this and to fulfil it. The law, therefore, with its impotence set aside, salvation and justification are obtained in Christ. The promise of life, or justification, which the law indeed held out but did not confer, is nevertheless brought to perfection in us, through Christ, who was sent in the flesh to this end, and who, in the likeness of sinful flesh, made atonement for and condemned our sin in his own flesh. Hence he has freed us from the law and redeemed us by another way than through the law, and has shown and taught us another path to salvation. But when the law is called the law of the Spirit of life in Christ, it is not called law in the proper sense but improperly, by way of likeness and by an external designation only, to signify its force alone.
