So also in the preceding chapter, Rom. 7:23, he says: I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members; by the law of sin he means nothing other than the power of sin. So too Heb. 7:16: who is made not after the law [νόμου] of a carnal commandment, but after the power [δύναμιν] of an endless life. In the one member it is "according to law," in the other "according to power." Otherwise law and the ministry of the law are set against grace and the ministry of the Spirit, as that which is deadly and in itself ineffective is set against life and righteousness. 2 Cor. 3:6–9: Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life. But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, … how shall not the ministration of the spirit be rather glorious? For if the ministration of condemnation be glory, much more doth the ministration of righteousness exceed in glory. For even that which was made glorious had no glory in this respect, by reason of the glory that excelleth. For if that which is done away was glorious, much more that which remaineth is glorious. Law and Gospel are compared and set against each other. The law meant here is that which the children of Israel could not look upon when Moses bore it down from the mountain (v. 7), and the ministry of each is opposed in its effect and use. The one is called letter, the other Spirit; the one kills, the other gives life; the one belongs to death and condemnation, the other to life and righteousness; the one cannot remain, whereas the other does. It is plain, then, how different the ministry of Christ is, the Gospel and the Testament, from that which belonged to Moses and the law; and how these are not only different from each other but hostile and opposed: the Testament of Christ is of grace, of the Spirit, of righteousness, of life and salvation, and this alone is the whole of it. Rabbi Joseph Albo, Ikkarim, sermon 3, chapter 25, in the translation of Genebrard (who published and refuted this chapter in 1566): Certainly we do not find that Jesus gave a law; on the contrary, he himself commanded that the law of Moses be kept. Nor are the Gospels a law, but a narrative of his birth and of the signs which they say he performed while he lived, such as we find were done by the prophets, who in the meantime published no law. So the Jews understand that Christ is taught in the Gospel.

units.la: Gal. iii. 2. Ex operibus legis Spiritum accepistis, an ex auditu fidei? 10. Quotquot enim sunt ex operibus legis, sub maledictione legis sunt. 13. Christus nos redemit a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio. Christus ergo, cujus totum ministerium Spiritus est, legis minister non fuit. Ex lege, pro statu hominum in quo natura sumus, maledictio est: in Christo autem, & ex eo solo omnis benedictio: imo liberat nos a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio, ut a lege maledicente redimeret, non eam adgravaret. 14. Ut ad gentiles benedictio Abrahæ pertingeret in Christo Jesu, ut promissionem Spiritus acciperemus per fidem. Nec Spiritus, nec promissio, nec benedictio est per legem, sed per Christum; non per opera, sed per fidem. 18. Si enim ex lege hæreditas, non ex promissione. 19. Quorsum ergo lex? Transgressionum gratia appositæ, usque dum veniret semen cui promissum. 24. Adeo ut lex pædagogus nobis factus sit ad Christum. non Christus ad legem. 28. Veniente autem fide, non amplius sub pædagogo sumus. Ut Christus nos non iterum ad legem reduxerit, & graviorem quidem exactionibus pluribus, duriori-busque pædagogum, quam fuerit olim. Omne istud, ut per fidem justificaremur. verf. 14. 1. Gal. iv. 4. 5. Quando autem venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere, factum sub lege; ut eos qui sub lege redimeret, ut adoptionem accipe-remus.. non ut sub legem nos retraheret.
units.tr: Gal. 3:2: Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? v. 10: For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse of the law. v. 13: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. Christ, therefore, whose whole ministry is that of the Spirit, was not a minister of the law. Under the law, given the state of men in which we are by nature, there is a curse; but in Christ, and from him alone, is every blessing. Indeed he frees us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us, so that he might redeem us from the cursing law, not add to its burden. v. 14: That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Neither the Spirit, nor the promise, nor the blessing is through the law, but through Christ; not by works, but by faith. v. 18: For if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise. v. 19: Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made. v. 24: Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, not Christ to the law. v. 28: But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. So that Christ did not lead us back again to the law, and to a schoolmaster heavier with more exactions and harsher than he was before. All this is that we might be justified by faith (v. 24). Gal. 4:4–5: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons; not so as to draw us back under the law.

units.la: Argument. quartum. Si justificatio nequaquam contingat per opera, vel per observationem præceptorum; ergo nihil necesse est propterea statuere Christum alia de novo præcepta, & legem dedisse perfectiorem, cujus obedientiâ & observatione justificemur: sed verum prius: ergo. Justificatio enim in Euangelio docetur longe alia, quam per legem: imo quæ legi, & operibus è diametro est opposita; eaque plane & prorsus excludens. Rom. i. 17. Justitia enim Dei in eo manifestatur de fide in fidem, quemadmodum scriptum: Justus ex fide vivet. Cap. iii. 21. 22. Jam vero absque lege Justitia Dei manifestatur, testata à lege & prophetis. Justitia autem Dei per fidem Jesu Christi, in omnes & super omnes credentes. 27. Ubi ergo gloriatio? exclusa. Per quam legem? operum? nequaquam: sed per legem fidei. 27. Concludimus autem, fide justificari hominem, absque operibus legis. Cap. iv. 4. Operanti merces imputatur non juxta gratiam, sed debitum. Verum non operanti, credenti autem in eum qui justificat impium, &c. Non ergo opera attenduntur in nostri justificatione, non ipse operans, non debitum, sed pura gratia, & , exclusis operibus, fides. verf. 13. 14. non enim per legem promissio Abrahæ facta, aut semini ejus, hæredem eum futurum mundi, sed per justitiam fidei. Si enim illi qui ex lege, hæredes, vana redditur fides, & exinanitur promissio. Cap. x. 4. 5. 6. Finis enim legis est Christus, ad justitiam omni credenti. Moses enim scribit justitiam quæ ex lege est: quod qui fecerit ea homo, in eis vivet. Verum justitia quæ ex fide est ita inquit: ne dicas in corde tuo, &c. Opponuntur Moses & Christus, lex & fides, tum justitia utriusque. Cap. xi. 6. Si enim gratia, jam non ex operibus: alioqui gratia non esset gratia. Si ex operibus, jam non ex gratia: quoniam opus non esset opus. Gal. iii. 11. &c.
units.tr: Fourth argument. If justification is in no way obtained by works, or by the observance of precepts, then there is no need to assert that Christ gave new precepts and a more perfect law, by whose obedience and observance we are justified. But the first is true; therefore the second is too. For justification is taught in the Gospel as something quite different from that which comes through the law; indeed it is directly opposed to the law and to works, and it utterly and entirely excludes them. Rom. 1:17: For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith; as it is written, The just shall live by faith. Rom. 3:21–22: But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe. v. 27: Where is boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? Nay: but by the law of faith. v. 28: Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. Rom. 4:4–5: Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, &c. Therefore works are not regarded in our justification; neither the one working, nor what is due, but pure grace, and, works being excluded, faith. v. 13–14: For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect. Rom. 10:4–6: For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them. But the righteousness which is of faith speaketh on this wise, Say not in thine heart, &c. Moses and Christ are opposed, the law and faith, and likewise the righteousness of each. Rom. 11:6: And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work. Gal. 3:11, &c.

units.la: Adeo liquet, non convenire utramque Justitiam, operum seu legis, & fidei seu Christi, neque Justificationem Euangelicam cum legali posse confundi, imo nec conjungi. Opponuntur passim in hoc argumento, Moses & Christus; lex & Euangelium: neque Euangelium habendum pro altera vel nova & perfectiori lege, neque Christus pro legislatore, cujus officium quasi fuerit legem aliis præceptis accumulare & perficere, quum satis in hoc genere illa perfecta fuerit in se & consummata, & aliud fuerit Christi officium & opus.
units.tr: It is so clear that the two kinds of righteousness, that of works or of the law and that of faith or of Christ, do not agree, and that evangelical justification cannot be confused with legal justification, nor even joined to it. Throughout this argument Moses and Christ are set against each other, and law and gospel likewise. The gospel is not to be regarded either as another, newer and more perfect law, nor Christ as a lawgiver whose office was, as it were, to pile up and perfect precepts of the law, since in that kind the law was already perfect and complete in itself, and Christ's office and work were something else.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: THIRD SECTION.

units.la: QUidquid autem pro contrariâ sententiâ Adversarii adferunt, quo probent nova Christum præcepta legi addidisse, nititur celebri illo loco Matth. v. cujus proinde expositio sub examen vocanda nunc est. Pars concionis est, vel sermonis Domini in monte, quem habuit, descripti à Matthæo tribus capitibus, v. vi. vii. Illo capite, postquam de beatitudinibus exponendis orsus fuisset Salvator, ad verf. 13. & deinde de Apostolorum officio, compa-rans illos tum sali, tum luci ad verf. 17. nonnihil interferuisset; ad expositio-nem legis progreditur, facto hunc in modum initio: ne putate quod venerim solvere legem aut Prophetas: non veni solvere, sed implere. Quod prosequitur porro argu-mentum ad finem usque capitis.
units.tr: Whatever the Adversaries bring forward for the opposite view, to prove that Christ added new precepts to the law, rests on the famous passage in Matthew 5. Its exposition must therefore now be brought under examination. It is part of the sermon, or discourse, which the Lord gave on the mount, described by Matthew in three chapters, 5, 6 and 7. In that first chapter, after Christ had begun to expound the beatitudes, and had said something about the office of the Apostles (vv. 13ff.), comparing them to salt and to light (v. 17), he goes on to expound the law, beginning in this way: "Do not think that I came to destroy the law or the Prophets; I did not come to destroy, but to fulfil." He then pursues this argument to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Ex quo primum sic argumentantur Sociniani: Qui legem implet, eam perficit: Christus legem implet; ergo perficit. Socinus, in Explicat. Cap. v. Matth. pag. 50. Itaque profitetur in suis verbis Christus, quicquid in lege Mosis ac prophetis continetur ad ipsos mores pertinens, quod quidem præcepti omnino vim habeat, à se nullo pacto abrogatum iri, id est, illud totum integrum ex sua ipsius doctrina permansurum, sed tantummodo aliquid se amplius dicturum, quod ad perfectionem & absolutionem ejus-modi præceptorum pertineat. Prius membrum, eorum quæ hic dicit, lubens admitto, legis moralis nihil quidem per Christum abrogatum, sed totam & integram ex Christi doctrina permanere, hæc enim vis est verborum, non veni solvere legem, sed implere. Verum quod deinceps addit, Christum aliquid amplius dicturum, quod ad perfectionem & absolutionem ejusmodi præceptorum pertineat, præter verba textus est, & contra ea. Neque enim hic sensus est ἐπληρωσῃ [?], cujus vim in superioribus expositerat. Probet, quod, quicunque quovis modo legem dici-tur implere, is eam ex imperfecta reddat perfectam, aut faciat perfectiorem: vel, quomodo dicit Schlichtingius, legis Mosaicæ præcepta novis præceptis à Christo cumulari. Sic iste, pag. 672. contra Meisnerum, Hoc ipsum nos pro sententia nostra urgemus. Nam primò, cur dicit servator: ne putetis, quod venerim solvere legem aut prophetas? nonne his verbis indicat, videri alicui potuisse, licet immeritò, Christum venisse ut legem solveret? at si non alio fine, quod quidem ad doctrinam attinet, venerat, idque etiam profitebatur, quam ut legis interpretem ageret, & erroneas interpretationes à scribis & Pharisæis confictas reprehenderet, ac refutaret, quam quæso huic opinioni ansam vel speciem dedisset? sed quia novam quandam, & legali perfectiorem doctrinam afferre se profitebatur, idque etiam re ipsa faciebat, certè videri (quamvis injuria) poterat, venisse ut legem solveret. Deinde apertissimè dicit Servator, se venisse, ut legem ipsam impleret: de impletione autem, quæ fiat per doctrinam, non quæ fiat per obedientiam, eum præcipuè loqui, sequentia indicant, & omnes agnoscunt. Ipsam ergo legem Christus doctrina sua implebat, id est, (metaphora à vase ducta, quod non parum quidem jam liquoris alicujus contineat, sed qui nondum tamen ad ipsam labrorum extremitatem pertigerit) nova ad illam pietatis præcepta addebat, ut omni ex parte plena & omnium virtutum præceptis exundans esset. At quæso quid ad rem faceret, si post quam dixisset, se venisse, ut legem impleret, non legem ipsam in sequentibus perficeret, & cumulatiorem redderet: sed à perversis interpretationibus tan-tum vindicaret?
units.tr: From this the Socinians first reason as follows: he who fulfils the law perfects it; Christ fulfils the law; therefore he perfects it. Socinus, in his Explanation of Matthew 5, p. 50: "Thus Christ declares in his words that whatever is contained in the law of Moses and the prophets, pertaining to morals, which indeed has the full force of a precept, will by no means be abrogated by him; that is, all of it will remain entire from his own teaching; but he will only say something more, which pertains to the perfection and completion of precepts of this kind." I gladly admit the first part of what he says here: that nothing of the moral law is abrogated by Christ, but that all of it remains whole and entire in the teaching of Christ. For this is the force of the words, "I did not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil." But what he adds next, that Christ will "say something more, which pertains to the perfection and completion of precepts of this kind," is beyond the words of the text, and against them. For this is not the sense of ἐπληρωσῃ [?], whose force he had explained above. Let him prove that whoever is said in any way to fulfil the law makes it from imperfect perfect, or makes it more perfect; or, as Schlichting puts it, "that the precepts of the Mosaic law are heaped up by Christ with new precepts." So he says, p. 672, against Meisner: "This very point we press for our view. For first, why does the Saviour say: 'Do not think that I came to destroy the law or the Prophets'? Does he not by these words indicate that it might have seemed to someone, though undeservedly, that Christ had come to destroy the law? But if, as far as doctrine is concerned, he had come for no other end, and he also professed this, than to act as an interpreter of the law, and to rebuke and refute the erroneous interpretations devised by the scribes and Pharisees, what, I ask, would have given occasion or appearance to this opinion? But because he professed to bring a certain new doctrine, more perfect than the law, and in fact did so, it could certainly seem (though wrongly) that he had come to destroy the law." Next, the Saviour says very plainly that he came to fulfil the law itself. That he is speaking chiefly of a fulfilment which takes place by doctrine, and not one which takes place by obedience, is shown by what follows, and everyone acknowledges it. Christ therefore fulfilled the law itself by his teaching: that is (a metaphor taken from a vessel which already holds a fair amount of some liquid, but has not yet reached the very rim), he added new precepts of piety to it, so that it might be full in every part and overflowing with the precepts of all virtues. But I ask, what would he have done to the point, if, after saying that he had come to fulfil the law, he did not in what follows perfect the law itself and make it fuller, but only defended it against perverse interpretations?

units.la: Resp. Quæstio est, num hoc in loco Christus legem reddiderit aliis præceptis cumulatiorem, quod Sociniani volunt; an verò legem vindicarit, & contra corruptelas Doctorum Judaicorum restituerit integritati suæ & perfectioni, quæ nostra est sententia. Momenta rationum utriusque partis videbimus atque expendemus, ad singulos versus. Hunc verò urgemus pro nostrâ; Sociniani pro sententiâ suâ. Videamus, utri rectius. Duo loci sunt membra. Prius, ne putate quod venerim solvere legem καταλῦσαι. Et hic notandum, quod hoc forte putarent, vel putare potuissent Judaei, quasi Christus soluturus legem accessisset. Verum unde quaeso hoc putarint? numquid occasione ulla ex doctrina, aut vita Christi arrepta? minime. Neque enim ulla ratione ansam isti opinioni praebuisse Christum, dici potest. Ergo ex communi doctrina suorum erat, qui legem suis expositionibus, & vita juxta eas compositā, solvebant: quod idem Christum quoque facturum forte, sperabant. Eo magis, quo putarint rite legem ita solvi, vel exponi. neque in hoc errare aut peccare se, aliosque. Tanta nimirum Doctorum & Pharisaeorum, apud plebem, apud quoscunque erat auctoritas. Quare iis obversaturus Christus dicit, illud de me ne putate, quasi ego legem soluturus venerim, quo pacto vestri eam solvere solent & enervare. Aliter de me existimate, & omnia alia a me exspectatis volo, non veni solvere legem. Quis obsecro alius, vel commodior sensus istorum, μὴ νομίσητε, ne putate? Ut appareat, Christum in hac concione, vel ejus quae sequitur [illegible, ~8 letters], se objicere eorum opinioni: opinioni, quàm imbiberant de legis dissolutione: dissolutioni, quam non vitā magis, quam doctrinā facie- bant, vers. 19. qui ergo unum solverit praeceptorum horum minorum, & sic docuerit homines. Unde duo haec colligimus evidentissima. 1. Christum in toto hoc negotio se opponere illorum opinionibus: quod primā, à qua orsus, ostendit voce, μὴ νομίσητε. 11. non autem legi, sed pro lege agere ipsum & certare. Ex quibus sub ipso jam principio disputationis liquet, vanitas expositionis Socinianae; & contra veritas & certitudo nostrae. Atque in sequentibus idem clarius adhuc sumus ostensuri. Diximus modo de primis verbis μὴ νομίσητε, ne putate.
units.tr: Reply. The question is whether in this passage Christ made the law fuller by adding other precepts, as the Socinians want, or rather defended the law and restored it, against the corruptions of the Jewish teachers, to its integrity and perfection, which is our view. We shall examine and weigh the arguments of each side, verse by verse. We press this passage for our view; the Socinians for theirs. Let us see which is the more correct. There are two members of the passage. The first: "Do not think that I came to destroy the law [καταλῦσαι]." Here it should be noted that the Jews might have thought, or could have thought, that Christ had come to abolish the law. But I ask, from where would they have got this idea? Was there any occasion taken from the teaching or life of Christ? By no means. For it cannot be said that Christ gave any ground for that opinion in any way. Therefore it arose from the common teaching of his people, who by their expositions, and by a life arranged according to them, were dissolving the law, and who perhaps hoped that Christ too would do the same. All the more so because they thought that the law could properly be dissolved or explained in this way, and that they themselves, and others, were not erring or sinning in this. Such, no doubt, was the authority of the teachers and Pharisees among the common people, and among everyone. Therefore Christ, to confront them, says: "Do not think this about me, as if I had come to dissolve the law, in the way that you are accustomed to dissolve and weaken it. Think otherwise of me, and expect from me everything else you like; I did not come to destroy the law." What, I ask, is another or more fitting sense of μὴ νομίσητε, "do not think"? So that it appears that Christ in this discourse, or in what follows [illegible], sets himself against their opinion: the opinion which they had imbibed about the dissolution of the law, a dissolution which they practised not so much by life as by teaching, as verse 19 says: "Whoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so." From which we gather these two most evident points. First, that in this whole matter Christ sets himself against their opinions, which he shows at the very outset by the words "do not think" [μὴ νομίσητε]. Second, that he does not act against the law, but for the law, and contends for it. From these things, already at the very beginning of the discussion, the emptiness of the Socinian exposition is clear, and on the contrary the truth and certainty of ours. And in what follows we shall show the same more clearly still. We have just spoken of the first words, μὴ νομίσητε, "do not think."

units.la: Καταλῦσαι solvere legem. Solvitur lex in aliquo praeceptorum ejus, verf. 19. quicunque solverit μίαν τ ἐντολῶν τύτων unum ex praeceptis illis. Qui in uno deficit, Jac. 11. 10. Joann. v11. 27. Solvere hoc, enervare, luxare est. Duplici autem contingit modo, doctrinā, & vitā. Hic loci illud, si non unice, saltem praesertim intenditur: neque alia prius exprimitur legis solutio, quam si quis ita docuerit homines, nempe vel unum ex praeceptis auferendo seu solvendo. Si quis secundo etiam istam, quae vitā fit, solutionem adjungere cupiat, multum reclamare haud erit operae pretium, neque adeo necesse. Potissimum quum, quidquid sit de verborum & loci sensu, vulgo doctrinam vita sequi soleat: & in membro altero Christus conjungit, qui vero fecerit & docuerit. Socinus, in Eplicatione hujus Capitis, pag. 49. facile ab omnibus intellectum fuit, & in eo fere consensum, quid sit ista legis & prophetarum solutio, quam Christus a se removet; nempe quod sit, ut diximus, istorum, quod ad praecepta attinet, abrogatio. Abrogatio tamen plus videtur dicere, quam solutio. Solvere quis aliquid dici etiam potest, utcunque proprie loquendo non abroget. Solvit, qui vim, necessitatem, usum, integritatem rei quovis modo tollit. Nec difficulter adeo admittent Judaei, se legem solvere: vix item, abrogare. Utcunque, quum Christus tam solemniter hic à se, & bis quidem, amoveat legis solutionem, testeturque se non venisse ut legem solveret; videndum restat, ex nostrâ, an Adversariorum sententiâ magis sequatur, Christum legem solvere. Ex nostrâ certe, nullo colore: neque etiam ab Adversariis id objectum nobis memini. Quum enim doceamus, nihil hic præceptorum à Christo commemorari quod non lege continetur, quodque ei additum dicere haud opus fit, per nostram quidem sententiam legem à Christo solvi, putabit nemo. Verùm ex Adversariorum sententiâ, quæ proinde quam falsa fit hinc liquet, sequitur, Christum legem solvisse, 1. quandoquidem ea ex lege aufert, five præceptorum, five vetitorum, quæ lege omnino continentur. ii. [?] abrogat ex Decalogo totum præceptum quartum. Quod unum uti maximi semper Judæi faciunt, ita objici Christi assertioni vel protestationi haud temere potuisset, de lege per ipsum soluta. Saltem per nostram, & non Adversariorum sententiam, constare Christi verbis & asseveratione suam vim & integritatem, palam est: ne putate quod veni solvere legem.
units.tr: Καταλῦσαι, "to dissolve the law." The law is dissolved in some one of its precepts (v. 19): "whoever shall break [λύσῃ] one of these commandments [μίαν τῶν ἐντολῶν τούτων]," one of those precepts. "Whoever fails in one" (James 2:10; John 7:27). To dissolve is to weaken, to loosen. It happens in two ways, by teaching and by life. In this passage the first, if not exclusively, at least chiefly, is aimed at; nor is any other dissolution of the law stated first than "if anyone so teaches men," namely by removing or dissolving one of the precepts. If someone wishes to add a second dissolution, that which takes place by life, it will not be worth the trouble to object much, nor indeed is it necessary. Especially since, whatever the sense of the words and of the passage, doctrine is commonly followed by life; and in the second member Christ joins, "but whoever does and teaches." Socinus, in his Explanation of this chapter, p. 49: "It has been easily understood by all, and there has been almost universal agreement, what that dissolution of the law and the prophets is which Christ removes from himself; namely that it is, as we have said, the abrogation of their precepts." Yet abrogation seems to say more than dissolution. One may be said to dissolve something even if, strictly speaking, one does not abrogate it. He dissolves who in any way takes away the force, necessity, use or integrity of a thing. Nor would the Jews readily admit that they dissolve the law, and hardly that they abrogate it. However that may be, since Christ so solemnly removes from himself the dissolution of the law, and does so twice, and testifies that he did not come to dissolve the law, it remains to be seen whether, on our view or on the view of the Adversaries, it follows more consistently that Christ dissolves the law. On our view certainly not, on no pretext; nor do I recall that the Adversaries have raised this objection against us. For since we teach that nothing of the precepts mentioned here by Christ is not contained in the law, and that there is no need to say it was added to it, no one will think that by our view the law is dissolved by Christ. But on the view of the Adversaries, and how false it is is clear from this, it follows that Christ dissolved the law: first, because he takes away from the law either precepts or prohibitions which are wholly contained in it; second, he abrogates from the Decalogue the whole fourth precept. This one precept the Jews have always regarded as of the greatest importance, and so it could hardly have been rashly objected to Christ's assertion or protestation about the law dissolved by him. At least by our view, and not by the view of the Adversaries, it is plain that by Christ's words and solemn assurance the law keeps its force and integrity: "Do not think that I came to dissolve the law."

units.la: Legem aut Prophetas. Per legem intelligi præcepta ad mores spectantia, clarum. Sed, quid per Prophetas, haud ita est in confesso. Socinus vult, intelligi per Prophetas nequaquam debere eorum prædictiones, sed solùm moralem doctrinæ ipsorum partem. Ad verf. 18. ubi solius legis redit mentio, Iota unum, aut apex unus non transfibit à lege, inquit, primum igitur statuo, ut dictum ante fuit, simplici legis nomine Prophetas quoque hoc loco intelligi, sed tamen ita, ut non intelligantur Prophetæ, nisi quatenus aliquid dicunt ad præcepta moralia pertinens, vel saltem, quod ad præcepta attinet, non autem quod pertinet ad prædictiones, nihil enim videntur ad propositum Christi facere Prophetarum prædictiones, de quibus videlicet non posset ambigi propter sermonem quem Christus habiturus erat.
units.tr: The Law or the Prophets. That by the Law are meant precepts concerning conduct is clear. But what is meant by the Prophets is not so generally agreed. Socinus holds that by the Prophets we ought not at all to understand their predictions, but only the moral part of their teaching. On verse 18, where mention is made of the Law alone, not one jot or one tittle shall pass from the Law, he says: "First, then, I lay down, as was said before, that under the simple name of the Law the Prophets too are to be understood in this place; but in such a way that the Prophets are not understood except insofar as they say something pertaining to moral precepts, or at least, so far as it concerns precepts and not what pertains to predictions. For the predictions of the Prophets seem to have nothing to do with Christ's purpose, since there could be no doubt about them on account of the discourse Christ was about to give."

units.la: Ego vero non video quare non ἐν πληρῶσαι [?] in omni sua plenitudine accipiatur & vox Prophetæ, & implendi. Ut utrumque significet, & totam Prophetarum doctrinam, ad moralia legis præcepta spectantem, & prophetias seu promissiones de Christo, quam imprimis non solutu-rus, sed impleturus advenerat; & de quibus commodissime & usitatissime tum vox implendi, tum phrasis illa alia, antequam omnia fiant, & sermo præcedens, donec transseat cælum & terra, accipi debent. Et quare hoc non facit ad propositum Christi, ut, dum explicat quorsum venerit, & quid officii sui, vel à se exspectandum sit, præsertim in ordine ad legem & Prophetas, intelligatur quod dicit implere se illa debere, etiam de Prophetarum prædictionibus, quæ διαθηκικῶς [?] Prophetam constituunt & denominant? Haud magis de uno, quam de alio poterat ambigi, an impleturus esset prædictiones omnes Christus, an legem & ejus præcepta? Atque ita propriam & usitatam utriusque vocis, legis & prophetarum servaverimus significationem. A quâ non leviter discedendum; Sociuus monet, hoc ipso in libro, pag. 15. mihi non videtur tantopere audere nos debere, nec sine necessitate aliqua quidquam novi excogitandum esse, aut recedendum ab ea significatione, quæ testimonia satis aperta habet.
units.tr: But I do not see why the word Prophets and the word fulfil [πληρῶσαι] should not be taken in their full sense, so that both are meant: both the whole teaching of the Prophets bearing on the moral precepts of the Law, and the prophecies or promises concerning Christ, which he came not to undo but above all to fulfil. Of these the word fulfil, and that other phrase until all things are done, and the preceding words until heaven and earth pass away, ought to be understood in the most suitable and most usual way. And why should it not bear on Christ's purpose, when he explains what he has come for and what he is to be expected to do in his office, especially in relation to the Law and the Prophets, that he says he must fulfil them, including the predictions of the Prophets, which constitute and name the Prophet covenantally [διαθηκικῶς]? There could be no more doubt about whether Christ would fulfil all the predictions than about whether he would fulfil the Law and its precepts. So we shall keep the proper and usual meaning of both expressions, the Law and the Prophets. We must not depart from this lightly; Socinus himself warns, in this very book, p. 15: "It does not seem to me that we ought to presume so much, nor that anything new should be devised without some necessity, or that we should depart from that meaning which has sufficiently clear testimonies."

units.la: Sed implere, ἀλλὰ πληρῶσαι. Socinus, pag. 44. Sed quid impletio illa sit, ut diximus, non perinde inter omnes convenit, nos illis omnino adharemus, quamvis eos non admodum multos, præsertim inter recentiores, esse credamus, qui statuunt, impletionem istam potissimum perfectionem & absolutionem, metaphora ducta à vase aliquo, seu modio, aut simili aliqua mensura, quæ contineat quidem multum ejus, quod in illam injici solet, sed tamen nondum sit plena nec suum complementum habeat. In voce πληρῶσαι, &c tali, ac Socinus dat, ejus expositione fundant Adversarii quidquid argumenti hoc in loco quæsierunt. Sed 1. πληρῶν non semper significat perficere, absolvere id quod imperfectum est, eique addere suum complementum. Nam & Euangelium dicimur nos implere, Rom. xv. 19. adeo ut ab Hierosolyma & circum usque ad Illyricum impleverim Euangelium Christi. Non certe hoc est, Euangelium perficere & complere, imperfectum, vel incompletum hastenus, sed confirmare. Sic hoc loco, legem implere, est legem confirmare. II. Vel implere Euangelium, intellige fidâ prædicatione: & sic hoc loco legem, id est, fidâ & rectâ expositione: non ut imperfecto, seu Euangelio, seu legi alia addatur de novo perfectio. Uti etiam dicitur Col.1.25. πληρῶσαι τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ [?]. III. πληρῶσαι est perficere opere. Quomodo II Thess. I. 11. dictum, ut Deus πληρώσῃ adimpleat omne beneplacitum bonitatis. non quod beneplacito ejus aliquid desit, vel quod hinc compleatur; sed, ut illud effectum det, & perficiat opere. Quæ eo magis quadrat expositio, quo Socinus sequentia, donec transeat cœlum & terra, Iota unum aut apex unus non transibit à lege, donec omnia fiant, de Christo, ejusque perfectâ legis adimpletione exponit. Sic ille, pag. 51. Is autem sensus est, quod non prius futura esset abrogatio ulla præceptorum illorum, quàm illis plenissima aliqua ratione obtemperatum fuisset, nempe ab aliquo homine præstitum perfectè vel minimum præceptorum istorum, id quod ab ipso Christo factum sine dubio est, dum hic in terris ageret. Et pag. 54. Respondemus satis ad propositum Christi facere, si dicat, tantam esse præstantiam ac firmitatem totius legis Mosaicæ, & ut nihil quantumvis minimum illic scriptum abrogari debeat, donec inventus fuerit, qui, quicquid in eo scriptum est, exactissime serva-verit. IV. πληρῶσαι est implere, tum legis, tum Prophetarum de Christo prædictiones & præfigurationes. Hinc toties in Euangelio, quando aliquid factum narratur, ὅπως πληρωθῇ. Et Socinus, per legem vers. 18. à quâ nihil dicitur transiturum, donec cœlum & terra transeat, intelligit etiam legem cæremonialem, quæ non aliter erat complenda. V. Quomodo aliàs Socinus explicabit, quod dicitur Christus implere Prophetas? nam ad Prophetas æque refertur ac ad legem, non veni solvere, sed implere. & hoc non potest de Prophetis intelligi, quomodo de lege dixit, novâ additione. Si de impletione alia, jam cadit vis argumenti, petita ex solâ voce πληρῶσαι, quasi non aliter intelligi possit quam de tali impletione, quæ per merum fiat earundem rerum, uti in modio vel in mensurâ forte semiplena, additamentum. VI. In nostro loco πληρῶσαι non legi opponitur, sed solutioni legis. Ideoque quum in priori membro dictum fuisset, ne putate quasi venerim solvere legem, & prophetas ; huic nil opponitur, additurve. Mox, non veni solvere, sed implere : simpliciter dicitur solvere, & huic opponitur iterum simpliciter, implere : non addito, vel repetito hoc de lege & Prophetis, ut appareat non legi se opponere Christum, vel istam suam, quam se adferre dicit, impletionem, sed legis solutioni ini-quæ & incongruæ. Ut quemadmodum alii dicuntur veram doctrinam enervare, quod tamen non faciunt quasi hinc veritati periret aliquid in se, sed apud homines duntaxat; ita complere eam ἐδεγλιῶσαν[?] 1 Tim. iii. 15. & πληρῶσαι contra aliorum enervationem, rite dixeris. vii. Denique si velis, Christum legem perfecisse quatenus eam pristino suo juri restituit, & exactæ puritati, nil admittens vel indulgens quod cum ea minus conveniat, & quidem sub V. Test. permissum a Deo præter legem fuerat, quale est negotium repudii, concedimus & sic illam legis perfectionem a Christo factam, sed cum lege, & juxta ejus mentem, non contra eam: quo nec aliud legi præceptum addidit Christus, sed, quod legis erat, ei reddidit & vindicavit. Ut liquidum sit & certissimum, vocem πληρῶσαι, quam pro argumento suo arripiunt Adversarii, nequaquam docere quod contendunt, quasi implere Christi, de sola lege, non de Prophetis, de lege morali, & impletione per solam aliorum præceptorum additionem exponi deberet, & non de alia impletione, oppositá vel simpliciter legis indulto, aut ejus solutioni per doctrinam & vitam Pharisæorum, vel prædictionibus Prophetarum legisque, vid. de impletione observantiæ, tum expositionis, & confirmationis verae. Quibus variis modis, nequaquam præter sensum vocis aut loci, sed ad ejus notandam plenitudinem, exponi verba illa commodé possunt, uti neutiquam ad sententiam Adversariorum. Quibus eo minus displicere debent, quæ, ad illa exponenda, varia hic attulimus, quòd hoc ipso loco scribit Socinus, pag. 52. Jam istius rei, quod verba sacra non unum tantum sensum habeant, quamvis alium alio, vel magis ipsis verbis convenientem, vel magis præcipue a spiritu sancto intellectum, complura sunt exempla in litteris sacris, præsertim ubi aliqua prædictio continentur, quemadmodum hic fit.
units.tr: But to fulfil [ἀλλὰ πληρῶσαι]. Socinus, p. 44: "But what that fulfilling is, as we have said, is not agreed among all; we indeed adhere wholly to those who, though I believe they are not very many, especially among recent writers, maintain that this fulfilling is chiefly a perfecting and completing, a metaphor taken from a vessel, or a measure, or some similar container, which holds much of what is customarily poured into it, but is not yet full nor has its complement." Our opponents base on the word πληρῶσαι, and on such an explanation as Socinus gives, whatever argument they have sought in this place. But: (1) πληρῶν does not always mean to perfect or finish what is imperfect and to add its complement to it. For we are said to fulfil the Gospel, Rom. 15.19: so that from Jerusalem and round about to Illyricum I have fulfilled the gospel of Christ. Certainly this does not mean to perfect and complete a gospel that has been imperfect or incomplete up to then, but to confirm it. So in this place, to fulfil the Law is to confirm the Law. (2) Or by fulfilling the Gospel understand faithful preaching; and so in this place, the Law, that is, by faithful and correct exposition, not as though some new perfection were added to what is imperfect, whether Gospel or Law. So also it is said in Col. 1.25, to fulfil the word of God [πληρῶσαι τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ]. (3) πληρῶσαι means to perfect by deed. As it is said in II Thess. 1.11, that God may fulfil [πληρώσῃ] every good pleasure of goodness, not because anything is lacking to his good pleasure or is completed by this, but so that he may bring it into effect and perfect it by deed. This explanation fits all the better because Socinus, expounding the following words, until heaven and earth pass, not one jot or one tittle shall pass from the Law, until all things are done, refers them to Christ and his perfect fulfilling of the Law. So he says, p. 51: "The sense is that no abrogation of those precepts would take place before they had been obeyed in some fully complete way, namely, perfectly fulfilled by some man in the smallest of those precepts, which was undoubtedly done by Christ himself while he lived on earth." And p. 54: "We reply that it is enough for Christ's purpose if he says that the excellence and firmness of the whole Mosaic Law is such that nothing written in it, however small, ought to be abrogated until someone is found who has kept exactly whatever is written in it." (4) πληρῶσαι means to fulfil the predictions and foreshadowings of the Law and the Prophets concerning Christ. Hence so often in the Gospel, when something is narrated as done, that it might be fulfilled [ὅπως πληρωθῇ]. And Socinus, understanding by the Law in verse 18, of which nothing is said to pass until heaven and earth pass away, also the ceremonial law, which could not otherwise be fulfilled. (5) How else will Socinus explain what is said of Christ fulfilling the Prophets? For he is referred to the Prophets just as to the Law: I came not to destroy, but to fulfil. And this cannot be understood of the Prophets in the way he has said it of the Law, by a new addition. If the fulfilling is of another kind, then the force of the argument drawn from the word πληρῶσαι alone falls, as though it could not be understood otherwise than as a fulfilling which consists in the mere addition of the same things, like a measure or a half-full vessel. (6) In our passage πληρῶσαι is not opposed to the Law but to the dissolving of the Law. Therefore, since in the earlier clause it had been said, do not think that I came to destroy the Law and the Prophets, nothing is opposed to this or added to it. Then: I came not to destroy, but to fulfil. Here simply to destroy is said, and against it is simply set to fulfil, without adding or repeating of the Law and the Prophets, so that it appears Christ is not opposing the Law, or the fulfilling he says he brings, but the unjust and unfitting dissolving of the Law. Just as others are said to weaken true doctrine, yet they do not thereby destroy anything of the truth itself, but only among men; so one may rightly say that the truth is confirmed [ἑδραίωμα, 1 Tim. 3.15] and fulfilled against the weakening of others. (7) Finally, if you wish, we grant that Christ perfected the Law insofar as he restored it to its former right, and to exact purity, admitting or indulging nothing that agrees less with it; and indeed some things had been permitted by God in the Old Testament apart from the Law, such as the matter of divorce. So we grant that Christ made this perfection of the Law, but with the Law and according to its mind, not against it; so that Christ added no new precept to the Law, but restored to it and claimed for it what belonged to the Law. Thus it is clear and most certain that the word πληρῶσαι, which the opponents seize upon for their argument, by no means teaches what they contend: namely, that Christ's fulfilling should be explained as of the Law alone and not of the Prophets, of the moral law, and of fulfilment by the mere addition of other precepts, and not of another kind of fulfilment, opposed either to the indulgence of the Law or simply to its dissolving through the teaching and life of the Pharisees, or to the predictions of the Prophets and of the Law, that is, of fulfilling by observance, of exposition, and of true confirmation. These words can be fittingly explained in these various ways, not beyond the sense of the word or the passage, but to note its fullness; and not at all in the sense of the opponents. The more so should they not displease, since I have brought forward various explanations here for them, because in this very place Socinus writes, p. 52: "Now that sacred words do not have only one sense, though one may be different from another, more suited to the words themselves or more particularly understood by the Holy Spirit, there are many examples of this in the sacred letters, especially where some prediction is contained, as happens here."

units.la: Ex istis, quæ jam diximus ad verf. 17. ubi initium sermonis Christi est de lege, & super eodem disputationis nostræ, luce clarius apparet, Christum nequaquam sibi proponere, adversus legem agere, sed adversus legis solutionem, & contra illorum opinionem legem non solvere, sed implere velle. Alii erant, qui λύσιν τ' ἐντολῶν[?] docebant verf. 19. quos a doctrina falsa, verf. 20. etiam de nomine notat, Pharisæos & Scribas. Atque hoc pro fundamento sermonis Christi tuto ponimus, quod in sequentibus adhuc plenius confirmabitur: Christum legem novis præceptis non complere & adaugere; sed perfectioni & integritati suæ restituere, atque eam vindicare a prava Pharisæorum doctrina & solutione. Verf. 18. Amen dico vobis, usque dum transierit cælum & terra, jota unum vel unus apex non transibit a lege, quousque omnia fiant. Sensus est, nunquam quidquam ex lege periturum, vel transiturum, quod non fiat. Primum statuit Socinus, simplici legis nomine Prophetas quoque hoc loco intelligi. Atque hoc bene. 11. Sed quod ea seu legis, seu Prophetarum sola velit intelligi, quæ ad præcepta moralia pertinent, non quæ ad prædictiones, in eo vim & latitudinem vocis Prophetæ, ne de lege dicam, atque etiam id quod in fine subjungitur , ἕως ἂν [illegible, ~7 letters], non capit, nec exhaurit. 111. Atque ut plenum amphiboliis reddat sermonem Christi Socinus, per legem & Prophetas, in priori versu, praecepta intelligit moralia solum ; in vetsu posteriori, praecepta omnia, caeremonialia & judicialia.
units.tr: From what we have already said at verse 17, where Christ's discourse begins with the law, and on the same point of our argument, it is clearer than light that Christ does not set himself against the law, but against its dissolution. He wills not to dissolve the law, contrary to their opinion, but to fulfil it. There were some who taught the "solution of the commandments" [λύσιν τ' ἐντολῶν?] (verse 19), and in verse 20 he also names them, the Pharisees and Scribes, as the source of the false doctrine. On this we safely build the foundation of Christ's discourse, which will be confirmed even more fully in what follows: Christ does not complete and enlarge the law with new precepts, but restores it to its perfection and integrity, and vindicates it from the perverse doctrine and dissolution of the Pharisees. Verse 18: "Verily I say unto you, till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled." The sense is that nothing will perish or pass away from the law which is not fulfilled. Socinus first holds that by the simple name of "law" the Prophets too are understood here, and this is right. (2.) But that he wishes only those parts of the law or of the Prophets to be understood which pertain to moral precepts, and not to predictions, does not take in the force and breadth of the word "Prophets," not to mention the word "law," nor does it capture or exhaust what is added at the end, ἕως ἂν [illegible]. (3.) And in order to make Christ's words wholly ambiguous, Socinus takes "the law and the Prophets" in the first clause to mean moral precepts only, and in the second clause to mean all precepts, ceremonial and judicial included.

units.la: Verbis autem illis duplicem inesse sensum statuit: cum, quem prima fronte ipsa verba se ferunt, quique Christi propositio magis convenire videatur; tum non hic, sed alius sensus magis secundum veritatem probandus, & quem potissimum Spiritus Sanctus intelligit. Quid ? alius sensus magis probandus, & magis secundum veritatem, quam qui Christi proposito maxime convenit ? Alium sensum Christus ; alium Spiritus Sanct. in Christi ipsius verbis ostendit ? Vin' Christum, & Spiritum inter se committere ? Nullius est, quod in suam expositionem trahere molitur Jobi verba, cap. xiv. 12. ubi legitur, inquit, hominem, postquam mortuus fuerit, nunquam vitae restitutum iri. Locus ita habet : & vir occumbit, & non resurget עד בלחי שמים [?] usque dum non erunt coeli, non excitabuntur, neque expergiscentur a somno suo. Socinus, iis verbis videtur significari, hominem, postquam mortuus fuerit, nunquam vitae restitutum iri. Non hoc simpliciter, sed non in vitam hanc reductum iri. Mihi, addit, qui una cum aliis non paucis credo, hos coelos quos videmus aliquando desituros, multo magis probatur ut dicamus, verum ac praecipuum Spiritus Sancti eo in loco sensum esse, quod, postquam coeli esse desierunt, id est, jam desituri erunt, tum demum, neque ullo modo antea fiet, ut homines a morte in vitam revocentur. Necdum ostendit duplicem eorundem verborum sensum. Nam alia verba primo, alia secundo loco sumit sibi exponenda. Primum, quod dicitur, hominem, postquam occubuit, vitae non iterum restituendum. Deinde, hoc quod additur, quousque non erunt coeli. Jam de hoc non disputatur, an coeli hi interituri sint. Vel sensus loci intelligetur, uti nobis quidem visum, de nunquam futura hominis semel demortui in hanc iterum vitam reductione ; vel de resuscitatione ejus non futura, nisi cum interitu hujus mundi & coelorum, (an totali, & essentiali, an accidentali, jam non disputamus) unus & simplex loci manet sensus, non duplex, non sibi, qualem loco Matth. v. 18. inde conatur dare, parum conveniens. Cui sensum apponit primo hanc, quod nullum Iota neque apex legis periturus sit, quia videlicet fieri nequeat, ut omnia fiant quae sunt scripta in lege. Et hunc tamen sensum, quem verborum illorum dicit esse priorem, quem prima fronte verba ipsa se ferunt, quique Christi propositio magis convenire videatur, & quem in sensum veri simile est Christum ipsum voluisse, ut ipsius verba ab auditoribus acciperentur, negat tamen aperto ore esse verum, non est verus prior ille sensus, non est simpliciter verum. Adeone praeter veritatem Christus quippiam dixit ? & contra veritatem sua verba studiose intelligi voluit ? Hoc demum est ex Christo veteratorem facere, & non fidum satis suorum verborum, nedum legis, interpretem.
units.tr: He holds that these words have a double sense: first, the sense "which the words themselves present at first sight, and which seems more suited to Christ's proposition"; and second, not this, but "another sense, to be proved more in accordance with the truth," and "which the Holy Spirit principally intends." What then? Is another sense to be proved, and one more in accordance with the truth, than that which best suits Christ's purpose? Has Christ shown one sense, and the Holy Spirit another, in Christ's own words? Would you set Christ and the Spirit against each other? He tries to draw into his own exposition the words of Job, chapter 14, verse 12, "where it is read," he says, "that man, after he has died, will never be restored to life." The passage reads: "So man lieth down, and riseth not; till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep" [עד בלחי שמים]. Socinus says: "By these words it seems to be signified that man, after he has died, will never be restored to life." Not simply this, but that he will not be brought back into this life. "To me," he adds, "who together with not a few others believe that these heavens which we see will someday cease, it is much more probable that the true and principal sense of the Holy Spirit in that place is this: that when the heavens have ceased to be, that is, are about to cease, then and not before, men will in no way be called back from death to life." He has not yet shown a double sense of these same words, for he takes one set of words to explain first and another second. First, that it is said that man, once he has died, will not be restored to life again. Then, what is added: till the heavens be no more. Now the question is not whether these heavens will pass away. Either the sense of the passage will be understood, as it seems to us, as the reduction of a man once dead to this life again, which will never happen; or, as concerns his resuscitation not occurring until the passing of this world and the heavens (whether a total and essential or an accidental passing, we do not now discuss), one single and simple sense of the passage remains, not a double one, and not the sort which he tries to give it, which is hardly fitting, as at Matthew 5:18. To this he first appends the sense that not one jot or tittle of the law will perish, because, of course, it cannot happen that "all things be fulfilled which are written in the law." Yet that first sense, which he says is the earlier one, "which the words themselves present at first sight, and which seems more suited to Christ's proposition," and which Christ himself was likely to have meant "so that his words would be understood by his hearers," he nevertheless denies with open mouth to be true: "that earlier sense is not true; it is not simply true." Did Christ say anything beyond the truth? And did he wish his words to be understood against the truth? This is indeed to make Christ a deceiver, and an interpreter of his own words, let alone of the law, who is not sufficiently trustworthy.

units.la: Audiamus etiam secundum sensum, quem facit, verborum Christi: Is autem sensus est, quod non prius futura esset abrogatio ulla quam illis plenissima aliqua ratione obtemperatum fuisset, nempe ab aliquo homine praestitum perfecte vel minimum prapræceptorum istorum, id quod ab ipso Christo factum sine dubio est, dum hic in terris ageret, quo facto & ipso in cælos sublato, tum demum, & non antea abrogatio facta est non paucorum ex illis præceptis, nempe cæremonialium omnium & judicialium. Si bene intelligo, priorum sensum vult, non implenda ab ullo esse omnia legis præcepta de moralibus loquens. Alterum, imo implenda esse, nimirum à solo Christo. Quid vero causæ, quod istorum verborum magis duplicem, & contrarium sensum quærit, quam aliorum? Neque hic locus adeo difficilis est præ reliquis, ut non planum & facilem sui sensum præbeat. Quin eadem fere ratione methodum aperueris, quodvis verbis Christi affingendi, comprehendique quod placuerit. Quin & tertium sensum mox addit, pag. 56. nunquam durante hoc sæculo quidquam ex lege Mosis abrogatum iri. vid. morali lege. Similiter & Jonas Schlichtingius, pag. 675. Sensus autem est, cælum & terram citius interitura, quam ut vel minima in re præcepta legis moralia solvantur, quorum vim & obligationem, ad rerum omnium finem ac confirmationem, durare necesse est. Et pag. 681. Sed id tantum docet, nullum morale legis præceptum, ne minima quidem ex parte, solutum iri ita, ut non amplius homines obligandi vim habeat. Quod hactenus verum quidem, sed cum præcedentibus Socini expositionibus minus quadrat. Adeo quid doceat incertus est Adversarius. Sensus verborum, ἕως ἂν παρέλθῃ donec transierit cælum & terra, non &c. semper talis, ut nihil auferendum legi sit, ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται[?]. Quemadmodum Psalm. LXXII.7. & multitudo pacis erit, עד בלי ירח[?] usque dum non erit luna, id est, semper, nunquam non, ad finem usque. Proverbialis locutio, significans, sic & Socinus ait, pag. 56. nunquam. iv. Invertit postrema verba Socinus, atque hinc omnis confusio, dum ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται[?] vult significare, usque dum omnia observentur, quam sit sensus, usque dum omnia fiant eventu, impletione. Quemadmodum γένηται[?] innumeris in N. Test. locis sumitur. Luc. xxi. 32. 33. Amen dico vobis, quod non transibit generatio hæc, donec omnia fiant ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται[?]. Cœlum & terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt. Notatur, non verborum observatio, sed impletio, ac eventus. Luc. xvi. 17. Facilius est cœlum & terram transire, quam ut unus ex lege cadat apex, ἢ ἕν νόμου μίαν κεραίαν πεσεῖν[?]. hoc est, cadere in terram, pro phrasi Hebræa V. Test. quod opponitur τῷ γενέσθαι[?], & in prædictionibus Prophetarum, eorumque impletionibus, est frequens. v. Ut omnino quod dicitur, prius cœlum & terram interitura, antequam aliquid ex lege excidat, quod non fiat, de firmitate ejus accipiendum sit, & istorum nihil excisurum dicat, quod in lege, & Prophetis dictum, quod fieri oporteat. Nihil de lege cæ. observanda. β. à Christo. γ & quod tum transitura à lege multa, nim. & judicialia & cæremonialia. De quibus hoc in textu nihil, & argumentorum nil à Socino, vel suorum aliquo hactenus allatum.
units.tr: Let us also hear the second sense which he gives to Christ's words: "The sense is this, that there would be no abrogation of anything before some most complete observance had been rendered to these precepts by some man, namely, the perfect performance of the least of them by a man. This was done without doubt by Christ himself while he was living on earth; and when he had been taken up into heaven, then at last, and not before, there was an abrogation of many of those precepts, namely of all the ceremonial and judicial ones." If I understand rightly, he means that the first sense is that not all the precepts of the law about moral matters are to be fulfilled by anyone. The other is that they are indeed to be fulfilled, and by Christ alone. But what reason is there for seeking a double and contrary sense in these words more than in others? This passage is not so difficult compared with the rest that it does not offer its own plain and easy sense. Indeed, by much the same method you could open up a way of attaching to Christ's words whatever you please and of wresting from them whatever pleases you. Indeed he adds a third sense shortly afterwards, at page 56: "that nothing of the law of Moses will be abrogated while this age endures," see the moral law. Similarly Jonas Schlichtingius, page 675: "The sense is, that heaven and earth will pass away more quickly than that the least moral precepts of the law should be dissolved in the smallest matter, whose force and obligation must endure to the end and confirmation of all things." And page 681: "But it teaches only this, that no moral precept of the law, not even in the smallest part, will be dissolved so that it no longer has the power of obliging men." This is true so far, but it fits less well with Socinus's earlier expositions. So uncertain is the adversary about what he teaches. The sense of the words, "ἕως ἂν παρέλθῃ, till heaven and earth pass, not etc.," is always such that nothing is to be taken away from the law, "ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται" [until all things come to pass]. Compare Psalm 72:7, "and abundance of peace, till the moon be no more" [עד בלי ירח], that is, always, never not, until the end. It is a proverbial expression, meaning "never," as Socinus himself says at page 56. (4.) Socinus inverts the final words, and from this comes all the confusion, since by "ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται" he wants to mean "until all things are observed," whereas the sense is "until all things come to pass" in outcome and fulfilment. Thus γένηται is used in countless places in the New Testament. Luke 21:32-33: "Verily I say unto you, this generation shall not pass away till all things be fulfilled [ἕως ἂν πάντα γένηται]. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away." What is noted is not the observance of words but their fulfilment and outcome. Luke 16:17: "It is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than for one tittle of the law to fail" [ἢ ἕν νόμου μίαν κεραίαν πεσεῖν], that is, to fall to the ground, in the Hebrew idiom of the Old Testament, which is opposed to "to come to pass" [τῷ γενέσθαι], and is frequent in the predictions of the Prophets and their fulfilments. (5.) So whatever is said, that heaven and earth will pass away before anything falls from the law which does not come to pass, must be understood of the firmness of the law, and it means that none of those things which were said in the law and the Prophets, and which must come to pass, will fail. (a) Nothing here about the observance of the ceremonial law. (β) By Christ. (γ) And that then many things, namely judicial and ceremonial, will pass from the law. Of these there is nothing in this text, and no argument has so far been brought forward by Socinus or any of his followers.

units.la: Verf. 19. Qui igitur solverit unum ex mandatis istis minimis, & docuerit sic homines, minimus vocabitur in regno cælorum. Socinus hactenus bene: ex hoc quod Christus affirmavit de firmitate & duratione praeceptorum legis Mosaicae, infert ipsemet, quod nulli homini liceat vel minimum ex Mosaicis praeceptis solvere, id est, tamquam id abrogatum esset, de eo non curare, & ne alii curent efficere. Quod minimus vocabitur, expo-nit nullus. Sic vero loquutum fuisse Christum, ut alluderet ad eandem vocem minimi, quae praeceptis in hac verborum comprehensione addita fuerat. Ex adverso, ubi Christus inquit, qui fecerit & docuerit, is magnus appellabitur, id exponit, aliquis vocabitur, id est, erit. fortasse unus est hic locus inter alios, ubi locum habeat phrasis illa hebraica, quod vocari significet esse, tam in prioribus quam in posterioribus Christi verbis. inquit.
units.tr: Vers. 19. Whoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Socinus has so far done well. From what Christ affirmed about the firmness and duration of the precepts of the Mosaic law, he himself infers that no one may break even the least of the Mosaic precepts, that is, treat it as if it had been abrogated, neglect it, and make sure others neglect it too. As for shall be called least, he explains it as shall be nothing. He says Christ spoke this way to play on the same word "least" that had been added to the precepts in this verse. On the other hand, where Christ says whoever shall do and teach them shall be called great, Socinus explains shall be called as shall be. He adds: "Perhaps this is one of the places among others where that Hebrew idiom, by which to be called means to be, applies, in both the earlier and the later words of Christ."

units.la: Verum quod ad filum & scopum disputationis nostræ, in isto etiam versu notandum est, Christum de lege acturum, sermonem suum instituere non adversus legem, sed eos qui solvunt legem, atque sic docent homines. Qui enim solverit unum praeceptorum istorum minimorum, atque ita docuerit homines. Ut, quia hoc singulis in exordio sermonis Christi versibus identidem inculcatur, non in aliâ re ejus argumentum collocari debeat.
units.tr: But, as to the thread and aim of our discussion, it must be noted in this verse too that Christ does not set out his discourse against the law, but against those who break the law and so teach men. For whoever shall break one of these least precepts and so teach men is the wording. Since this is repeated again and again at the opening of Christ's sermon, his argument must not be located in anything else.

units.la: Vers. 20. Dico enim vobis quod nisi justitia vestra abundaverit plus quam justitia Scribarum & Pharisæorum, in regnum cælorum non ingrediemini. Apertissimè ostendit iterum Christus, adversus quos agere instituat, Doctores nempe, Scribas & Pharisaeos, non vitæ solum, sed doctrinâ peccantes, & solventes legem. Nam quod illos non vitæ solum, sed quoque doctrinæ ratione coarguat, Socinus ipse hic fatetur. Quod Schlichtingio reponimus, qui ex adverso argumentatur: Pharisæosne talia docuisse credamus? omnino. Hoc enim Textus, & res ipsa evincit, atque Socinus agnoscit. Neque Schlichtingius negare potest, vers. 19. intelligi solutionem praecepti, sive vitâ, sive doctrinâ. pag. 675.
units.tr: Verse 20. For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Christ shows again, most plainly, whom he means to attack: namely the teachers, the Scribes and Pharisees, who sinned not only in their lives but also in their teaching, and who broke the law. That he rebukes them not only for their lives but also for their doctrine, Socinus himself admits here. We answer Schlichting, who argues the other way: "Should we believe that the Pharisees taught such things?" Certainly. The text itself and the matter prove this, and Socinus acknowledges it. Nor can Schlichting deny that in verse 19 the breaking of a precept is understood as being done either by life or by doctrine. p. 675.

units.la: Et hactenus sermonis Christi exordium. In quo quum tam multa sint, quae ostendunt, ipsum malam Scribarum & Pharisaeorum doctrinam impetere, qui praecepta legis solvebant; nihil vero quod doceat, contra ipsam legem se opponere, eamque arguere, & aliis praeceptis corrigere velle, (quid implere legem sit, suo loco diximus, certe non istud,) pro fundamento expositionis sequentium, & disputationis illud tuto constituere licebit, legem non emendari hic, sed falsas Pharisaeorum expositiones argui atque rejici. Quod in sequentibus planius ostendemus: nam Socinum, uti hactenus, hoc ad Caput pressim sequi, & examinare, in iis vid. quae praesentis controversiae sunt, constitutum est. Cujus sententia est, quod Christus iis, quæ in ipsa lege continebantur, sua opponit, quæ subjicit, quemadmodum loquitur, pag. 63..
units.tr: So far the opening of Christ's sermon. In it there are many things showing that he attacks the bad doctrine of the Scribes and Pharisees, who broke the precepts of the law; but nothing that teaches that he sets himself against the law itself, argues against it, and wishes to correct it by other precepts. (What it is to fulfil the law we have said in its place; certainly not that.) We may safely lay this down as the foundation for explaining what follows and for the discussion: the law is not here being amended, but the false explanations of the Pharisees are being refuted and rejected. We shall show this more plainly in what follows, for it is our plan, as hitherto, to follow Socinus closely chapter by chapter and examine those points that bear on the present controversy. His view is that Christ sets his own sayings against what was contained in the law itself, which he adds, as Socinus puts it, p. 63.

units.la: Vers. 21. Audistis, quod dictum est Antiquis: non occides: qui vero occiderit, reus erit judicii. 22. Ego vero dico vobis, quod quicunque irascitur fratri suo temere, reus erit judicii. Hinc, & ex sequentibus, quae in eundem fere proponuntur modum, dupliciter argumentari solent Adversarii, & concludere, Christum se opponere ipsi Mosis legi, vel iis aliquid addere, non autem falsas interpretationes eorundem praeceptorum, quas Scribae & Pharisaei populo obtrudebant, refellere. 1. Quorsum autem illud non fecisset, qui Pharisaeis nusquam parcere solitus? 11. Quia quæ profert Christus, & exponenda sibi judicat, ipsa legis verba sunt, saltem sententia. Unde constare videatur, Christum sibi ipsam legem objicere, non ejus interpretationes aliquas, & eam perficere atque novis additamentis implere velle. Socinus, pag. 62.
units.tr: Verse 21. You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. 22. But I say to you, that whoever is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment. From this, and from what follows, which is set out in nearly the same way, our opponents usually argue in two ways and conclude that Christ sets himself against the Mosaic law itself, or adds something to it, and does not refute the false interpretations of those same precepts which the Scribes and Pharisees forced on the people. First: why would he not have done so, he who was accustomed never to spare the Pharisees? Second: because what Christ brings forward and judges must be explained are the words of the law itself, or at least their sense. From this it seems clear that Christ sets the law itself against them, not some interpretations of it, and wishes to complete it and fill it with new additions. Socinus, p. 62.

units.la: Iam quod hic Christus in ipso initio ait, & sæpius postea repetit, audistis quod dictum sit antiquis, satis videtur docere, non fuisse Christo propositum Scribarum & Pharisæorum falsas legis interpretationes rejicere, quid enim cum hoc commune habet, quod id cui sua verba hic Christus opponit, audivisset populus dictum fuisse antiquis? annon potius statuendum est, si ita Christi mens fuisset, eum fuisse dicturum, audistis quod dicant Magistri, vel simile quidpiam? certe, si quis non plane prae-fracte veritati reluctari velit, necesse est fateri, Christum sua verba ei opponere hoc in loco & similibus, quæ ab omni antiquitate, postquam lex data & explicata populo fuisset, audita foret; & quid quasi commune habent verba ista, vel sententia hæc tota, quam Christus antiquis dictam fuisse affirmat, cum falsis interpretationibus Scribarum & Pharisaeorum? cum, ut dictum est, partim diserte, partim alioqui satis expresse totum istud in ipsa lege continetur. Idem, contra Palaeologum habet, part. 1. Atq; Schlichtingius, p. 691. Verum enimvero, si Christus non legis ipsius præcepta auget ac perficit; sed legem a Pharisaeorum falsis interpretationibus vindi-cat: quid fit, ut non Pharisaeorum commenta, sed ipsa legis apertissima verba citet, & iis sua dicta opponat? Num sextum præceptum, quod Meisnerus falso, Pontificios imitatus, quintum vocat, non occides, Pharisaeorum commentum erat? Sic & alii istorum, passim argumentantur.
units.tr: Now that Christ at the very beginning says here, and often repeats afterwards, you have heard that it was said to the ancients, seems sufficiently to show that it was not Christ's purpose to reject the false interpretations of the law by the Scribes and Pharisees. For what does it have in common with this, that the people, when Christ sets his words against it, had heard that it was said to the ancients? Ought we not rather to conclude that, if Christ's mind had been so, he would have said you have heard what the Masters say, or something similar? Certainly, unless someone is willing to resist the truth obstinately, he must admit that Christ sets his words against what was heard from all antiquity, since the law was given and explained to the people; and what do these words, or this whole sentence which Christ says was said to the ancients, have in common with the false interpretations of the Scribes and Pharisees? As has been said, this whole matter is contained in the law itself, partly explicitly and partly, otherwise, quite clearly. The same, against Palaeologus, part 1. And Schlichting, p. 691. Yet if Christ does not increase and perfect the precepts of the law itself, but defends the law from the false interpretations of the Pharisees, why is it that he does not quote the commentaries of the Pharisees but the very plainest words of the law, and sets his own sayings against them? Was the sixth precept, you shall not kill, which Meisner falsely calls the fifth, imitating the Papists, a commentary of the Pharisees? So too others of that party argue everywhere.

units.la: Resp. ad prius 1. negari consequentiam. Christus inquit, antiquis dictum fuisse, & non, Pharisaeis; ergo non intelligit Pharisaeos? negatur. Instat Schlichtingius, pag. 680. Pharisaeos non fuisse tum temporis adeo antiquos: Quomodo antiquitus eam traderent, qui antiquitus nondum essent? Nec enim Pharisaei multo ante Christi tempora, ut ex Josepho colligitur, exorti fuerant. Negatur iterum consequentia: Pharisaei pridem orti erant, ergo eorum doctrina non potuit a Christo proponi, ut antiquis tradi-ta, & antiquitatis specie commendari vulgo solita? 11. Ignorant Sociniani rationem & formulam apud Judæos usitatam, qua traditiones & expositiones legis proponere erant soliti, sub nomine majorum & Antiquorum: תנו רבנן tradiderunt, vel docuerunt magi-stri. inde תנאי[?] doctrina, traditio. & תנא[?] doctrina tradita, annunciatia, παραδόσεως πρεσβυ-τέρων[?]. Vel אמרו רבותינו dixerunt magistri, Rabbini nostri. Dices, hæc alia formula est, a nostra, dixerunt Antiqui, ἀρχαῖοι. Respondeo, pro eodem haberi ac poni antiquos, & rabbinos. Sic quod alias dicunt, אמרו רבותינו dixerunt Rabbini nostri; dicunt quoque
units.tr: Reply to the first point: the consequence is denied. Christ says it was said to the ancients, and not to the Pharisees; therefore he does not mean the Pharisees? This is denied. Schlichting presses, p. 680: the Pharisees were not so ancient at that time; how could they have handed it down in antiquity, when they were not yet ancient? For the Pharisees had not arisen long before Christ's time, as is gathered from Josephus. Again the consequence is denied: the Pharisees had arisen long before, therefore their doctrine could not be put forward by Christ as handed down from the ancients and commended under the appearance of antiquity, as was customary with the crowd? Second: the Socinians are ignorant of the method and formula used among the Jews, by which they were accustomed to put forward traditions and explanations of the law under the name of their elders and ancients: תנו רבנן [they taught, our masters], that is, the masters taught. Hence תנאי [tanna], doctrine, tradition, and תנא [tanna], doctrine handed down and announced, παραδόσεως πρεσβυτέρων [the tradition of the elders]. Or אמרו רבותינו [our masters said], that is, our Rabbis said. You will say this is another formula from ours, "the ancients said", ἀρχαῖοι [the ancients]. I answer that the ancients and the rabbis are regarded and used as the same. So when they elsewhere say אמרו רבותינו [our Rabbis said], they also say

units.la: רק דברי הקרמונים[?] זל אמרו antiqui. Aben Ezra, in Exo.xxxiv.27. verum verba Antiquorum beata mem. vera sunt. Sive autem ἐξηγήσῃ[?] τῆς ἀρχαίοις[?] dativo casu exponatur, dictum antiquis, sive ab antiquis, parum ad rem facit, quia antiquis dici nequiit nisi ab antiquis, & non ab antiquis, nisi iterum antiquis. Verbaque utrumque sensum ferunt. Et multa à viris Doctis tum in hanc, tum in illam expositionem adferuntur, quæ pro præsenti negotio tuto præterimus. Videsis Spanhemium, Dub. Euangelic. part. III. Dub. CXIX. Apparet etiam, quare sic loquuti passim fuerunt Traditionarii, dictum esse antiquis, videlicet ut apud populum, nomini & auctoritati majorum suorum supra modum addictum, plus momenti & virium statim acquirerent illa, quae jactabant, dogmata. Neque vel rudiores, vel principes intelligendos putamus per ἀρχαῖς[?]: in quo refutando se occupatum tenet Socinus, pag. 84. 111. Ubi ex lege Christus aliquid allegat, nunquam illa proponit formula, dictum fuisse antiquis. Uti enim hoc loquendi modo suis Dictatis Magisti aliquam conciliare studebant auctoritatem; ita divinis legibus auctoritatem deprecies, si antiquis dictas commemores. Verum lex ubi adducitur, Christus legem ipsam, vel Mosem nominare solet, sic & alii. Quod praecepit Moses, Matth. viii. 4. & xii. 5. an vero non legistis in lege? & xix. 7. Quid ergo Moses jussit? 8. Moses permisit vobis. Marc. xii. 26. annon legistis in libro Mosis? Joann. viii. 5. Verum in lege Mosis praeceptum nobis tales lapidari. 17. & in lege vestra scriptum. Cap. x. 34. annon scriptum est in lege vestra? Luc. ii. 23. Quemadmodum scriptum in lege Domini, & verf. 24. 39. Cap. x. 26. Dixit autem ei Christus, in lege quid scriptum? quomodo legis? 1 Cor. ix. 9. etenim in lege Mosis scriptum. Atque sic semper. Nusquam ubi simpliciter ex lege quid adfert Christus, adfe-runt alii, hac illud praenotatum forma, dictum antiquis, & audiistis dictum antiquis. Quare, quum antiqui hic dicantur a Christo, non lex, vel Moses, quem-admodum semper, & nunquam aliter, ubi legis aliquid occurrit, sed magistri traditionum intelligendi veniunt. Porro Christus ait, dictum antiquis, non scriptum; auditum ipsis, non lectum fuisse, quemadmodum quando de lege[?], dicere solet, legisse illos, sic vel sic scriptum in lege. Adeo plus quam unum argumentum illa praebent pro sententia vel expositione nostra, vid. Christum Pharisaeorum, ab antiquis Rabbinis acceptas, vel antiquitatis nomine jactaras expositiones & traditiones perstringere, non vero ipsi simpliciter semet opponere legi. Ut, quae verba Adversarii pro se facere putarunt atque attulerunt, pro nobis stare, & haud uno modo nostram confirmare sententiam, liqueat iv. Demus & hoc, per antiquos, Israelitas, & dictum iis a Mose intelligi, quemad-modum isto modo etiam nonnulli ex Orthodoxis verba accipiunt: nihil adhuc pro Socinianis sequitur: nam ita dictum quidem antiquis, vid. Israelitis intelligetur, sed non eo, quo id acciperunt sensu Pharisaei. Siquidem ex respon-sione Christi videndum, qua leges exponit, in quam contrariam sententiam illas traxerint Pharisaei. Quodque se Christus non illis, sed contrariae Doc-torum Judaicorum interpretationi opposuerit, etiam inde facile apparet. Neque enim aliter solutam per illos legem, & adversus eam solutionem Christum legem vindicasse, ejusque πλήρωμα[?] ursisse[?], dici potest, quam quatenus illud quod responsio Christi habet, legi addendum[?], vel subintelligendum & comprehendendum ea esse, intelligi debet: & ex Christi conclusione judicandum, de re vel quaestione concludenda. Nisi haud recte satis conclusisse eum, affirmare velimus. Quare non ex verbis, dictum est antiquis, quaestio-nem definire debent Adversarii, sed ad rem ipsam, & tum propositionem Christi reflectere ac responsionem, & videre debent num legem Christus verbis suis petat, corrigatque, an Scribarum doctrinam, & laxas legis divinae expositiones, negantium illa contineri, & seu praecepta seu prohibita fuisse, quæ ad illas Christus refert, & nos illis comprehensa, Sociniani superaddita, autumant.
units.tr: רק דברי הקרמונים זל אמרו [only the words of the ancients, of blessed memory, said], that is, the ancients. Aben Ezra, on Exo.xxxiv.27: only the words of the ancients, of blessed memory, are true. Whether the phrase ἐξηγήσῃ τῆς ἀρχαίοις [the explanation of the ancients] is taken in the dative, said to the ancients, or said by the ancients, matters little to the point, since it could only be said to the ancients by the ancients, and not by the ancients unless again to the ancients. And the words bear either sense. Many things are brought forward by learned men for both this and that explanation, which for the present business we safely pass over. See Spanheim, Dub. Evangel. part III, Dub. CXIX. It also appears why the traditionists everywhere spoke this way, that it was said to the ancients: namely, so that among the people, who were excessively devoted to the name and authority of their forefathers, the things they boasted of would at once gain more weight and strength as doctrines. Nor do we think that the common people or the leaders are to be understood by οἱ ἀρχαῖοι; Socinus occupies himself in refuting this, p. 84, 111. Where Christ cites something from the law, he never uses that formula, it was said to the ancients. For just as the Masters, by this way of speaking, sought to win authority for their dictates, so would they belittle the divine laws if they recalled what was said to the ancients. But where Christ adduces the law, he usually names the law itself or Moses, as do the others: What Moses commanded, Matt. viii. 4 and xii. 5: Have you not read in the law?; xix. 7: Why then did Moses command?; 8: Moses permitted you. Mark xii. 26: Have you not read in the book of Moses? John viii. 5: Now in the law Moses commanded us to stone such. 17: and it is written in your law. Chapter x. 34: Is it not written in your law? Luke ii. 23: as it is written in the law of the Lord, and verse 24, 39. Chapter x. 26: He said to him, What is written in the law? How do you read it? 1 Cor. ix. 9: For it is written in the law of Moses. And so always. Nowhere, when Christ simply brings forward something from the law, do others bring it forward with this prefixed formula, it was said to the ancients, and you have heard that it was said to the ancients. Therefore, since the ancients is here named by Christ, and not the law or Moses, as always and never otherwise when something of the law occurs, the masters of the traditions must be understood.
