Further, Christ says it was said to the ancients, not it was written; heard by them, not read, as when he speaks of the law he is accustomed to say that they had read that it was written so and so in the law. Thus these passages give more than one argument for our view or explanation: that Christ is attacking the explanations and traditions of the Pharisees, received from the ancient Rabbis or boasted of under the name of antiquity, and not setting himself simply against the law itself. So, as to the words which our opponents thought supported them and brought forward, it is clear that they stand for us and in more than one way confirm our opinion. Grant also that by the ancients the Israelites and what was said to them by Moses are meant, as some of the Orthodox also take the words in this way: nothing yet follows for the Socinians. For in that case it is indeed said to the ancients, that is, to the Israelites, but not in the sense the Pharisees took it. For from Christ's reply we must see, by which laws he explains them, into what contrary opinion the Pharisees drew them. And that Christ set himself not against them, but against the contrary Jewish interpretation of the teachers, also appears easily from this. For it cannot be said that the law was dissolved by them, and that Christ defended the law against that dissolution and aimed at its fulfilment [πλήρωμα], except insofar as what Christ's reply contains is understood to be added to the law, or to be implied and included in it; and the conclusion Christ draws must be judged as to the matter or question to be concluded. Unless we wish to affirm that he has concluded rather badly. Therefore our opponents ought not to settle the question by the words it was said to the ancients, but must turn to the matter itself, and reflect on Christ's proposition and reply, and see whether Christ, by his words, attacks and corrects the law itself, or the doctrine of the Scribes and their lax explanations of the divine law, which deny that those things are contained in it, and whether those things to which Christ refers were commanded or forbidden, which the Socinians add over and above what we hold to be comprehended in them.

units.la: Nam, dicunt, & hoc fecundum ipsorum argumentum: ipsa legis verba Christus profert, non occides, non aliquas Scribarum aut Pharisæorum expositiones, ut has exagitare voluerit, & non illam adimplere. Resp. 1. Negatur consequentia: verba legis Christus profert; ergo solam legem petit suâ responsione. 11. Neque ῥητὸν[?] hoc in lege uspiam occurrit: quicunque vero occiderit, reus erit judicii. 111. Ex Christi vero responsione apparet, eum non legem arguere, sed legis istam solutionem, per quam illam sic exponebant, ut solus occisor reus esset judicii, & non quoque temere qui irascceretur fratri. Quare ostendit, ubi homicidium, iram etiam prohiberi, ut quæ ad idem genus malitiæ referatur. Animadvertendum, inquit Socinus, ea, quæ ubique legi Mosis Christus addit, habere conjunctionem quandam cum iis, quæ in lege ipsa continentur, habet enim ira cum odio aliquid commune, etiamsi quiddam valde minus omnino sit, cum homicidium soleat vel ex ira, vel ex odio, quod aliud nihil est quam inveterata ira, plerumque proficisci: statuit igitur Christus eum quoque reum futurum, qui cuiquam temere iratus fuerit, non modo qui illum occiderit. Quare dico, si talia Christus hic urgeat, quæ cum suis apud Mosem legibus habent conjunctionem, & ira cum homicidio illud commune habet, ut soleat ex irâ odioque plerumque proficisci; quid peccat, qui ista legum comprehensa generalitate existimat, & non demum à Christo legi fuisse addita? Præsertim quum omnes ubique leges, & divinæ quoque ita generatim conceptæ videantur, ut non unam speciem, sed istius generis omnia complecti voluisse, hoc ipso evincant. Deinde, ira erga fratrem temeraria, ex quâ homicidium plerumque proficisci solet, vel legitima olim fuit aut licita & bona, vel mala & ἀνεπίληπτον[?] ? Licitam dices, atque ἔννομον[?] fuisse? certe contra ipsam rei lucem id affirmabis, & notitiam vel sensum ipsorum adeo gentilium, qui ex lege naturali illam damnare noverunt, si non etiam contra tuam ipsius conscientiam. Sin aliter, ergo lege prohibita ira illa, & non demum à Christo addita legi prohibitio illa fuit. Denique multis Scripturæ, in lege, & Prophetis locis ira prohibita fuit & damnata. Genes. iv. 5. & xlix. 7. Psalm. v. 15. Quod idem in N. Test adducitur, Ephes. iv. 26. Adde Prov. xv. 18. & xxvi. 21. & xxix. 23. Eccles. vii. 10.
units.tr: For, they say, and this is their second argument, Christ quotes the very words of the law, you shall not kill, and not some exposition of the Scribes or Pharisees, which he would have wished to attack and not fulfil. Reply 1. The inference is denied: Christ quotes the words of the law; therefore by his reply he seeks only the law. 11. No ῥητόν [express word] of this kind occurs anywhere in the law: whoever shall kill shall be liable to judgment. 111. From Christ's reply it appears that he is not impugning the law itself, but that solution of the law by which they explained it so that only the murderer was liable to judgment, and not also whoever rashly grew angry with his brother. Therefore he shows that where murder is forbidden, anger is forbidden too, as referring to the same kind of wickedness. It must be noted, says Socinus, that the things which Christ everywhere adds to the law of Moses have some connection with those things which are contained in the law itself; for anger has something in common with hatred, even though it is altogether something much less, since murder usually arises from anger or from hatred, which is nothing other than long-standing anger: so Christ lays down that he too will be liable who has been rashly angry with anyone, not only he who has killed him. Therefore I say: if Christ here urges such things as have a connection with the laws of Moses, and anger shares with murder this feature, that it usually arises from anger and hatred, what fault is there in one who thinks these included in the general scope of the laws, and not added by Christ at last? Especially since all laws everywhere, and divine ones too, seem to be framed in such general terms that by this very fact they show they wished to embrace not one species but all of that kind. Next, rash anger towards a brother, from which murder usually arises, was either formerly lawful and permitted and good, or evil and [ἀνεπίληπτον: blameless]? Will you say it was lawful and [ἔννομον: in accordance with law]? Surely you would be asserting this against the very light of the matter, and against the knowledge and feeling of the Gentiles themselves, who by the natural law knew how to condemn it, if not also against your own conscience. But if otherwise, then that anger was forbidden by the law, and that prohibition was not something added by Christ at last. Finally, in many places of Scripture, in the Law and the Prophets, anger is forbidden and condemned: Genes. iv. 5 and xlix. 7. Psalm. v. 15. The same is quoted in the New Testament, Ephes. iv. 26. Add Prov. xv. 18, xxvi. 21 and xxix. 23. Eccles. vii. 10.

units.la: Christi responsio docet, iram vel iræ prohibitionem præcepto sexto addendam esse; sed, an supra præceptum, tamquam novum aliquod? an autem ut præcepto ipso intelligendum, & comprehensum? hoc quæritur, neque locus hic præcepto conclusum negat. Sed, in responsione Christi est iræ prohibitio, non in propositione. Negatur consequentia, quod propterea lege connotata non fuerit, uti homicidii causa ac origo. Ipse Socinus, pag. 61. 62. Quamvis enim antea statuerimus, Christi mentem esse illis Mosaicis præceptis aliquid addere, non autem falsas interpretationes eorundem præceptorum, quas Scribæ & Pharisæi populo obtrudebant, refellere; id tamen ita intelligendum est, ut concedamus Christum antiquoties, dum Mosis praeceptorum mentionem facit, cum illis aliquid conjungere, quod expressum diserte in ipsa lege non sit. Sed audiretur tamen, & ab antiquissimis temporibus in populo auditum fuisset, tanquam si germana pars essent ipsius Mosaici praecepti, quae tamen additamenta non abhorrerent ab ipsa legis Mosaicae mente: sed & praeterea id quod diximus intelligendum est, ut interim non negemus, Christum alicubi potuisse tacite recitandis ipsis verbis legis, intelligere una cum illis interpretationem illorum quae in populo resonabat, quam ipse tamen non probaret, quamque iis, quae praecipiendo ipse subjungit, refelleret atque rejiceret; de quibus singulatim suis locis apertius agendum erit.
units.tr: Christ's reply teaches that anger, or the prohibition of anger, is to be added to the sixth precept; but the question is whether it is added above the precept as something new, or is to be understood and comprehended within the precept itself. This passage does not deny that it is contained in the precept. But the prohibition of anger is in Christ's reply, not in his proposition. The inference is denied, that for this reason it was not implied in the law, just as the cause and origin of murder are not stated in it. Socinus himself, p. 61, 62: For although we have said before that Christ's intention is to add something to those Mosaic precepts, and not to refute the false interpretations of the same precepts which the Scribes and Pharisees thrust upon the people; yet this must be understood in such a way that we concede that Christ as often as he makes mention of the precepts of Moses joins to them something which is not expressly stated in the law itself. But it would nevertheless be heard, and from the most ancient times would have been heard among the people, as if they were a genuine part of the Mosaic precept itself; which additions nevertheless did not depart from the very mind of the Mosaic law. But moreover, what we have said must be understood thus, so that meanwhile we do not deny that Christ could somewhere, by silently reciting the very words of the law, have understood along with them the interpretation of them which resounded among the people, which he himself did not approve, and which he refuted and rejected by what he adds in teaching; concerning these things we shall have to speak more openly, one by one, in their own places.

units.la: Quare, quantumvis in Christi propositione, ad mentionem legis, non exser-te id ponatur, quod Christo in animo est reprehendere & corrigere, non pu-tandum ideo, nihil praeter legem eum velle: sed tum ex verbis propositionis, tum responsione ejus colligi potest, aliud quid intendisse eum, praeter legem, quod expressum diserte in ipsa lege non sit, sed audiretur tamen, & ab antiquissimis temporibus in populo auditum fuisset, tamquam si germana pars esset ipsius Mosaici praecepti.
units.tr: Therefore, however much in Christ's proposition, at the mention of the law, it is not expressly stated what Christ has in mind to reprove and correct, we must not think on that account that he wants nothing beyond the law. From the words of his proposition, and from his reply too, it can be gathered that he intended something other than the law: something which is not expressly stated in the law itself, but would nevertheless be heard, and from the most ancient times would have been heard among the people, as if it were a genuine part of the Mosaic precept.

units.la: Tale hoc in loco fuit interpretamentum legi de non occidendo additum, quasi irasci temere non fuisset interdictum ea quoque vel prohibitum, sed tuto hoc licuisset atque impune. Verum hunc in sensum verba Christi accipienda sunt: audiistis pro antiquo jactari, non occides, sed qui occiderit, reum esse judicii; non ita tamen, qui iratus fratri fuerit temere: Ego vero dico, & hoc, & illud esse prohibitum, neque minus judicii reum esse istum, quam illum: utpote quum hoc ad illud praeceptum aeque pertineat, & pari reatu dignus sit uterque, & poena. Hoc est, quod Socinus bene dicit: Christum tacite recitandis ipsis verbis legis, intelligere una cum illis interpretationem illorum quae in populo resonabat, quam ipse tamen non probaret, quamque refelleret atque rejiceret. Et, adversus Palaeologum, part. 1. pag. 157. Extat autem in hoc praecepto de diligendo proximo, quod Christus recitat, cuique sua dicta opponit, aliud proprium indicium praeter id, quod supra commemoravimus, non tam legis ipsius, quam pervulgata in populo praeceptionis rationem habitam fuisse. Ergo fatetur, in Christi sermone aliquando non tam legis ipsius, quam vulgatae hominum in lege exponenda opinionis rationem habitam fuisse. Postremo & hoc docere potest prohibitionem irae spectare ad prohibitionem homicidii, eaque contineri, quia eadem poena utrumque manet, ut, quomodo multa eadem, ita & praecepto comprehendi videantur. Alioquin nisi ejus-dem praecepti essent, & homicidii species aliqua odium vel ira temeraria [illegible, ~3 letters], non eodem involveret fontem reatu & supplicio. Quicunque odit fratrem suum, homicida est. 1 Joann. iv. 15. Si qui odit fratrem, est homicida, quo praecepto homicidium, eodem & prohiberi odium, censendum est.
units.tr: Such an interpretation was added to the law about not killing, as if being rashly angry had not been forbidden, or had been forbidden only in part, and this had been lawful and unpunished. But the words of Christ must be taken in this sense: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, You shall not kill; but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But not so, whoever is rashly angry with his brother. But I say that both this and that are forbidden, and he is liable to judgment no less than the other, since this pertains equally to that precept, and each is worthy of the same guilt and punishment. This is what Socinus rightly says: that Christ, by silently reciting the very words of the law, understood along with them the interpretation of them which resounded among the people, which he however did not approve, and which he refuted and rejected. And against Palaeologus, part 1, p. 157: There is moreover in this precept about loving one's neighbour, which Christ recites, setting his own sayings against each, another distinct indication, besides that which we have mentioned above, that account was taken not so much of the law itself as of the commonly held teaching among the people. Therefore he admits that in Christ's discourse at times account was taken not so much of the law itself as of the common opinion of men on interpreting the law. Lastly, this too can show that the prohibition of anger regards the prohibition of murder, and is contained in it, because the same punishment remains for both; so, just as many things are the same, so they seem to be comprehended in one precept. Otherwise, unless they belonged to the same precept, and some species of murder were hatred or rash anger [illegible], they would not involve the same source of guilt and punishment. Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. 1 Joann. iv. 15. If anyone hates his brother, he is a murderer; by the precept by which murder is forbidden, hatred too must be deemed forbidden.

units.la: Quod de irâ dixi, idem de convitio ac contumelia nescio quis negaturus sit, in Vet. Test. quoque prohibitam & malam fuisse: semper nempe, & naturâ sua, & apud omnes. Atqui & hoc peccatum Christus quoque recensuit, referrque ad summam ejusdem praecepti, de homicidio. Qui dixerit fratri suo demens &c. Ergo non simplex homicidium illo praecepto prohibitum, sed & quaecumque eo spectant, & quae istius generis, seu convitium, seu ira. Nisi putemus vel Simei absque peccato licuisse maledicere Davidi, 11 Sam xvi. s. vel adolescentibus, Elisaeo, 1 Reg. 11. 23.
units.tr: What I have said of anger, someone may deny, if he can, is also true of insult and abuse: that these too were forbidden and evil in the Old Testament, namely always, by their nature, and among all people. Yet Christ also listed this sin, and refers it to the sum of the same precept, about murder: whoever shall say to his brother, Fool, etc. Therefore it is not simple murder alone that is forbidden by that precept, but also whatever pertains to it and is of that kind, whether insult or anger. Unless we think that Shimei could without sin curse David, 2 Sam. xvi. 5, or that the youths could mock Elisha, 1 Reg. ii. 23.

units.la: Idem dicendum de reconciliatione inter fratres instituenda, quam Christus adeo commendat vers. 23. &c. Eam enim vel ratio suadet naturalis, nedum lex Dei scripta. Levit. xix. 17. 18. Adeo nihil quidem Christus hic docuit, atque ad legem seu explicationem de homicidio dixit, quod non ipsa Dei lex, & V. Test. Scriptura habet probatque. Si non verbis legis, saltem ejus sensu, ac re ipsa, implicite & virtualiter, si non explicite & expresse: quamvis ex-presse etiam satis, uti ex annotatis Scripturae locis videre est, illa lege morali comprehenduntur.
units.tr: The same is to be said of the reconciliation of brothers, which Christ so commends in verse 23 and following. For even natural reason suggests this, let alone the written law of God: Levit. xix. 17, 18. So Christ has taught nothing here, nor said anything about the law or its explanation concerning murder, which the law of God and the Scripture of the Old Testament do not contain and approve. If not in the words of the law, then at least in its sense and in fact, implicitly and virtually, if not explicitly and expressly; although also expressly enough, as can be seen from the Scripture passages noted, they are comprehended under that moral law.

units.la: Atque ex hoc uno legis capite est respondere ad reliqua, quae in eun-dem sensum Adversarii de legis aut imperfectione olim, aut adimpletione per Christum, temere adferunt: non ex formula, dictum antiquis, hoc probari; sed nostram prius stabiliri sententiam; non legem Christum aggredi, vel sua dicta Mosis dictis opponere, addereque, uti Socinus loquitur, pag. 82. vel nova pra-cepta dare, & Mosaica legi non pauca addere, eamque suis novis praeceptis perficere, uti pag. 83. sed scita Magistorum, antiquitatis specie & titulo jactata, redarguere & confutare. Praesertim quum, uti huc tota redit disputatio, quae & hinc judicanda & decidenda, ea quae Christus hic respondet, & docet, non nova, & ab eo demum producta sint, sed ipsa antiqua, id est, revera antiquis, in lege & Prophetis dicta praeceptaque fuisse, ostendamus.
units.tr: From this one chapter of the law we can answer the rest that the opponent rashly brings forward to the same effect, whether that the law was once imperfect or that Christ fulfilled it. It does not follow from the formula it was said to the ancients that this is proved. We must first establish our own position: Christ does not attack the law, or oppose his own sayings to the sayings of Moses, and add to them, as Socinus puts it, p. 82, or give new precepts, add not a few things to the Mosaic law, and perfect it by his new precepts, as on p. 83. Rather, he refutes and overturns the traditions of the teachers, which are boasted of under the appearance and title of antiquity. Especially since, as the whole dispute comes down to this, we shall show that what Christ answers and teaches here is not new, nor first produced by him, but is the very old thing: what was in truth said and commanded to the ancients in the law and the Prophets.

units.la: Secundum caput, vel argumentum est, vers. 27. Audivistis, quod dictum est antiquis, non adulterabis. Ad quae Socinus, pag. 87.
units.tr: The second head, or argument, is verse 27: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, You shall not commit adultery. To this Socinus replies, p. 87:

units.la: Resp. 1. In superioribus jam notavimus istam ἀνακολουθίαν: Quod Christus ipsa legis verba & praeceptum citans, proinde praecepto illi vel legi se opponat, ostendimusque ex ipso Socino, mentem Christi & sensum propositionis, ex responso ejus aeque peti debere, ac ex verbis propositionis.
units.tr: Reply 1. Above we have already noted this anacoluthon: that Christ, quoting the very words and precept of the law, thereby sets himself against that precept or law. And we have shown, from Socinus himself, that the mind of Christ and the sense of the proposition ought to be sought from his answer just as much as from the words of the proposition.

units.la: II. Praeceptum non desiderandi mulierem, quomodo ais a Christo tamquam novum praeceptum legi additum, quum id jam lege olim vitium fuerit, praecepto decimo? Quod & Socinus agnoscit haud semel. Pag. 88. Sane jam in ipsa Mosis lege expresse vetitum fuerat, alterius uxorem concupiscere. Atque id hactenus nec quidquam novi esse, ibi-dem fatetur. III. Nulla ratio est, vocem γυναῖκα restringere ad mulierem,
units.tr: II. The precept against coveting a woman: how do you say that it was added by Christ as a new precept to the law, since that was already a sin under the law, in the tenth precept? Socinus himself concedes this more than once. On p. 88: Indeed, in the law of Moses itself it had already been expressly forbidden to covet another's wife. And in the same place he admits that so far there is nothing new in this. III. There is no reason to restrict the word γυναῖκα [gunaika] to a married woman,

units.la: Tom. 2. maritatam, & non potius accipere de muliere quavis, sive maritata, sive alia, ut quamcunque quis adspexerit cupiditate & desiderio potiundi, non liber habeatur atque immunis [illegible, ~3 letters], uti hoc accipiebant Scribae, & Pharisaei. confer Rom. vii. 7. sed reus חַיָּב [?], אָשֵׁם [?], & praecepti violator juxta suam speciem, sive adulterio, sive fornicatione, prout hujus generis sunt quaecunque praecepto illo comprehensa & vetita fuerunt. iv. Christus praecepto addit, inquit, non simpliciter: ergo nec simpliciter vel proprie nova praecepta addit. De quo tamen erat quaestio. v. Addit, juxta Socinum, Christus non quod is peccet, qui ita adspicit, nam id ex legis etiam sententia peccatum esse confitetur, sed quod adulterii reus sit. Verum ita jam Christus non novum praeceptum addidit legis, quod erat τὸ κεφάλαιον [?]; sed praecepto legis reatum novum. Sed in legis manens circuitu, quod vetitum erat, sed praecepto decimo, ad aliud praeceptum revocat, nimirum septimum. Qualis mutatio non est illa innovatio, & additio, vel perfectio legis, certe non in hoc capite, ac de quo quaestio primum propositia fuit & intellecta.
units.tr: vol. 2. and not rather to take it of any woman, whether married or not, so that whoever has looked on any woman with desire to possess her is not regarded as free and exempt. This is how the scribes and Pharisees understood it. Compare Romans 7:7. Rather, he is guilty [ḥayyāv?], [ʾāshēm?], and a violator of the precept according to its kind, whether by adultery or by fornication, as all things of this kind are included in that precept and forbidden. IV. Christ, you say, adds to the precept, not simply: therefore he does not simply or properly add new precepts. Yet this was the very question. V. According to Socinus, Christ adds not that the one who looks in this way sins, for he confesses that this was sin even by the sense of the law, but that he becomes guilty of adultery. But in that case Christ has not added a new precept to the law, which was [to ti kephalaion, the chief point]; he has added a new guilt to the precept of the law. But while remaining within the circuit of the law, he refers what was forbidden in the tenth precept to another precept, namely the seventh. Such a change is not that innovation, addition, or perfection of the law, at least not in this chapter, and this is the matter that was first proposed and understood as the question.

units.la: Socinus: neque id animadverterunt quod diximus, Christum non simpliciter peccatum esse statuere, concupiscentiam iflam, sed eam adulterii loco ducendam esse, quod in ipsa lege neque expresse, nec tacite continebatur. Haec est igitur, ut hinc de hac materia aliquid plenius dicere ordiamur, differentia inter Mosis praeceptum, seu praecepta circa maritatas mulieres, quod Christus pro adulterio habendam esse statuit ipsam talis mulieris potiunda cupiditatem: Moses vero, quamvis cupiditatem iflam diserte prohibeat, non tamen illam adulterii loco ducit: quod cupiditatis istius, quam prohibet, meminit, non modo, ut dictum est, distincte a praecepto non adulterandi, & praeceptum de ea suum, ut diversum ab isto alio, proponit: sed etiam posterioris hujus non statim post prioris propositionem, sed post interposita duo alia praecepta, mentionem facit: quod sane indicat, praeter praeceptorum diversitatem, magnam, quod ad pondus ipsorum attinet, inter utrumque distantiam, id est, multo majus peccatum esse adulterium, quam iflam concupiscentiam.
units.tr: Socinus: They have not noticed what we said, that Christ does not state that this desire is simply a sin, but that it must be counted as adultery, which was contained neither expressly nor tacitly in the law itself. This, then, is the difference, so that we may begin to say something fuller on this matter, between the precept or precepts of Moses concerning married women, and the desire to possess such a woman, which Christ declares must be regarded as adultery. Moses, although he expressly forbids that desire, does not however count it as adultery. He mentions that desire which he forbids not only distinctly from the precept against adultery, and sets down a precept about it as different from that other one; but he also mentions this latter not immediately after the statement of the former, but after two other precepts have been interposed. This indeed indicates that, besides the difference of the precepts, there is a great distance between the two as regards their weight; that is, adultery is a much greater sin than that desire.

units.la: Resp. 1. Ergo non novum praeceptum, vel novam prohibitionem Christus legi addidit, quia ipsa lex, non demum Christus, concupiscentiam alienae mulieris peccatum esse statuit.
units.tr: Reply 1. Therefore Christ did not add a new precept or a new prohibition to the law, because the law itself, not Christ only, declared the desire for another's wife to be sin.

units.la: II. Sub quo autem peccati genere censeri debeat, vel ad quod referatur praecepti genus, attamen non tale est, ut propterea thesim statuere suam queant Adversarii, de legis completione per nova praecepta. Quod ad adulterium referendum illud fit, ipsa res loquitur. Quare dici nequit, in ipsa lege hoc neque expresse, neque tacite contineri. Nempe, concupiscere alienam uxorem, quod ad genus, concupiscentiae nimirum prohibitae, ad praeceptum spectat decimum: sed quod ad concupiscentiae speciem, ad septimum. Legislatori, ob graves certe causas, placuit, non ipsas solum malas actiones prohibere, sed ne quis hoc ignoraret, singulari praecepto, malas quoque concupiscentias: non quasi hoc praeceptum si non esset, concupiscentiae mali bonae fuissent licitae, & non consequenter & implicite aliis quoque praeceptis interdictae; sed quo id manifestius constaret, planiusque, de quo facile dubitare homines, & quod peccatum esse negare malint, quam agnoscere, singulari praecepto cavere voluit, concupiscentiam mali malam esse quoque, & tum in genere prohiberi, tum non ad unam mali speciem, sed ad omnes referri. Attamen speciei vel objecti ratione qui peccat, etiam istorum praeceptorum reus fit, in quae concupiscendo fertur, quaeque sua transgressione violat. Ut qui vult proximo homicidium, etiam, vel quandiu factum non sequitur, homicidium in corde patravit; sic qui adulterium, vel fornicationem, haec corde suo jam peregit, eoque istorum praeceptorum violator habendus est, praecepti non tantum decimi, sed sexti, & septimi, at corde, non opere. Quamobrem Christus dixit, moechatus eam est in corde suo. Aliud est moechari, & sic de reliquis, corde; aliud, opere. Lex hoc prohibens, illud necessario etiam includit, quia non corporalis est, solis actionibus scripta externis, sed & spiritualis, quae cogitationes & interiores voluntates regulat & arguit. Neq; concupiscentia fæminæ, prout est fæminæ alio commodius refertur, quam ad praeceptum septimum; uti bonorum, ad octavum; vitæ, ad sextum, quomodo dictum, quod ad speciem actionis, vel peccati.
units.tr: II. Under what kind of sin it ought to be counted, or to what kind of precept it is referred, is not such that our opponents can therefore establish their thesis of the fulfilling of the law by new precepts. That this is referred to adultery, the matter itself speaks. Hence it cannot be said that this is contained in the law neither expressly nor tacitly. Namely, to covet another's wife belongs, as to the genus of forbidden desire, to the tenth precept; but as to the species of desire, to the seventh. The lawgiver, certainly for weighty reasons, chose not only to forbid the evil actions themselves, but, lest anyone should be ignorant of this, to forbid evil desires also by a separate precept. This is not as if, were this precept absent, evil desires would have been lawful and not consequently and implicitly forbidden by the other precepts too; but in order that this might be more plainly established, and because men easily doubt, and would rather deny that it is a sin than acknowledge it, he chose to guard against it by a particular precept: that the desire for evil is also evil, and is forbidden both in general and is referred not to one species of evil but to all. Yet whoever sins by reason of the species or object is also guilty of those precepts into whose transgression his desire is carried, and which his desire violates. As one who wishes a neighbour dead has committed murder in his heart, even if, while the deed is not done, no killing follows; so one who has already carried out adultery or fornication in his heart is to be regarded as a violator of those precepts: of the tenth, and also of the sixth and seventh, in heart, not in deed. Therefore Christ said, He has committed adultery with her in his heart. To commit adultery, and likewise the other sins, in the heart is one thing; in deed, another. The law forbidding the one necessarily includes the other too, because it is not merely corporeal, written only for external actions, but spiritual, regulating and judging thoughts and inner wills. Nor is a woman's desire, as it is a woman's, more fittingly referred to any precept than to the seventh, just as the desire for goods is to the eighth, and for life to the sixth, as is said with regard to the species of action or sin.

units.la: Diligenter hic sunt consideranda, concupiscere rem vetitam; & rem istam; deniq; concupiscentiam perficere. Hoc est, contra sua singula praecepta, homicidium contra sextum, adulterium contra septimum, & sic de reliquis. Illud, contra praeceptum decimum, atque etiam istud, quandoquidem specificavit concupiscentiam uxoris, proximi, & cujuscunque rei quae proximi est, ita tamen, ut non putare debeamus, quando illa concupiscimus, quae aliis praeceptis vetita, quod liberi sumus a transgressione & reatu illorum quoque praeceptorum. Ratio est, quia lex vetando homicidium, adulterium, furtum, vetat etiam occidendi, adulterandi, & furandi animum. Quod vel negandum tibi hic erit, vel affirmandum. Si affirmas, ergo non actione solum, sed animo & concupiscentia aliquis se homicidii, adulterii, furti reum potest facere, in corde vid. & coram Deo. Illud ipsum, quod Christus dicit, & legi propterea non additur, sed ea continetur. Si neges, tum facile probo. 1. ex praecepti, vel praeceptorum omnium generalitate, quae summatim proposita complectuntur omnia ad suum quaelibet caput specstantia[?]. II. ex legis spiritualitate. Rom. vii. 14. Novimus autem quod lex spiritualis est. Ubi ergo factum aliquod vetat, animum etiam comprehendit, & huic aeque loquitur, atque externo facto & rei. III. ab expositione & sensu legis in Vet. Test. observato, ubi inter peccata primi mundi, diluvium commerita, quum alia generatim referantur, hoc unum in specie notatur, quod filii Dei adspexerunt filias hominum, Genes. vi. 2. Quo procul dubio notantur adulteria & similis generis peccata, sub conspectu mulierum: ergo & jam tum conspectus mulierum illiciti censiti fuere ad praeceptum pertinere de adulterio, vel isto impuritatis capite, quod praecepto illo vetitum etiam dictabat lex naturæ. Quare etiam Iobus dicit, se foedus pepigisse cum oculis suis, ne ad mulierem respiceret. Cap. xxxi. 1. & David, Psalm. cxix. 39. precatur Deum, ut oculos suos avertat, ne vanitatem contueantur. Ergo, quemadmodum qui temere fratri suo irascitur, incurrit in praeceptum sextum, & reatum homicidii; quia qui odit fratrem, jam homicida est, 1 Joann. iv. 15. homicida scilicet in corde, quamvis non opere: ita & qui concupiscit alienam mulierem, praecepti septimi μοιχείας[?], & seu fornicationis seu adulterii, pro re nata, reus est, quia in corde, uti loquitur Christus, adulterium & fornicationem commisit. Quæro, præceptum prohibens adulterium, prohibetne solum adulterium operis, & non etiam cordis? Si ita: ergo, qui corde adulterat, in præceptum illud peccat; & sic nil extra præceptum dicit, qui hominem, dum mulierem adspicit desiderio potiundi, in corde adulterare; docet. Non prohibet adulterium cordis? Sic ergo non omne adulterium. Quum tamen in genere posita lex, adulterium qua patet, in toto ejus decursu, prohibere intelligatur. Vel, an adulterium cordis non est adulterium? quasi animus adulterandi adulteratione expers esse possit. Voluntas peccandi, annon peccatum est? voluntas furandi, adulterandi, quæ voluntatem peccandi specificat, annon voluntas adulterandi dici debet, & proinde adulterium, furtum in voluntate, ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ[?], uti inquit Christus? Hæc cum lex, tum natura rei satis comprobant.
units.tr: Here we must carefully consider three things: to desire a thing forbidden; to desire that thing; and finally, to bring desire to completion. That is, against each of its precepts: murder against the sixth, adultery against the seventh, and so on. The first is against the tenth precept, and also the second, since it specifies the desire for a wife, a neighbour, and whatever belongs to a neighbour; yet we must not think that when we desire those things which are forbidden by other precepts, we are free from transgression and guilt of those precepts too. The reason is that the law, in forbidding murder, adultery and theft, also forbids the intention to kill, to commit adultery, and to steal. Here you must either deny this or affirm it. If you affirm it, then not by action only, but by intention and desire, a person can make himself guilty of murder, adultery, or theft, in heart, and before God. This very thing that Christ says is not added to the law, but is contained in it. If you deny it, I readily prove it: 1. from the generality of the precept, or of all the precepts, which, proposed in summary, embrace all things that pertain to each of their heads. II. From the spirituality of the law: Romans 7:14, For we know that the law is spiritual. Where therefore it forbids some deed, it also comprehends the mind, and speaks to this just as much as to the external deed and thing. III. From the exposition and sense of the law observed in the Old Testament, where, among the sins of the first world that deserved the flood, while other sins are referred to generally, this one alone is noted specifically: that the sons of God saw the daughters of men, Genesis 6:2. By this undoubtedly are noted adulteries and sins of a similar kind, committed under the sight of women. Therefore already at that time the sight of women was judged unlawful and pertaining to the precept about adultery, or to that head of impurity, which the law of nature too forbade by that precept. Hence Job also says that he made a covenant with his eyes, not to look upon a woman, chapter 31:1. And David, Psalm 119:39, prays God to turn his eyes away, lest they look upon vanity. Therefore, just as one who rashly grows angry with his brother falls under the sixth precept and the guilt of murder, because whoever hates his brother is already a murderer, 1 John 4:15, a murderer in heart, though not in deed; so also one who covets another's wife is, according to the occasion, guilty of the seventh precept's [moicheias, adultery] and of either fornication or adultery, since in his heart, as Christ speaks, he has committed adultery and fornication. I ask: does the precept forbidding adultery forbid only adultery of deed, and not also of the heart? If so, then whoever commits adultery in heart sins against that precept, and so he who teaches that a man who looks at a woman with desire to possess her commits adultery in his heart says nothing beyond the precept. If it does not forbid adultery of the heart, then not all adultery is forbidden, although the law, posited in general terms, is understood to forbid adultery throughout its whole course. Or else, is adultery of the heart not adultery? As if the mind's intent to commit adultery could be free of adultery. Is not the will to sin itself a sin? Is not the will to steal or to commit adultery, which specifies the will to sin, to be called the will to commit adultery, and therefore adultery and theft in the will, [en tē kardia, in the heart], as Christ says? These things the law, and the nature of the matter, sufficiently confirm.

units.la: II. Sed, dicit Socinus, Moses cupiditatis istius quam prohibet, meminit, non modo distincte a præcepto non adulterandi, & præceptum de ea suum, ut diversum ab isto alio, proponit: sed etiam posterioris hujus non statim post prioris propositionem, sed post interposita duo alia præcepta, mentionem facit: quod sane indicat, præter præceptorum diversitatem magnam, quod ad pondus ipsorum attinet, inter utrumque distantiam, id est, multo majus peccatum esse adulterium, quam istam concupiscentiam. Conceditur totum. Neque enim de hoc controversia est, an utriusque præcepti esset sua, & magna diversitas, vel an majus esset peccatum adulterium, quam ejus concupiscentia. Quæ quis negat? sed, an idem diversâ sui ratione non possit dici in diversa incurrere præcepta, & concupiscentiam uxoris alienæ, præterquam decimo, damnari etiam præcepto septimo. Adeo ut concupiscens uxorem proximi sui non habeatur liber à transgressione præcepti, quod castimoniæ & puritati thori prospexit in genere, & ex professo?
units.tr: II. But, says Socinus, Moses mentions that lust which he forbids not only distinctly and apart from the precept against adultery, and sets out a precept of its own as different from that other; he also makes mention of this latter not immediately after the first, but after two other precepts have been interposed. This surely indicates that, besides the great difference between the precepts in weight, there is a distance between the two, that is, that adultery is a much greater sin than that concupiscence. I grant the whole. For there is no dispute here, whether each precept has its own place and there is a great difference between them, or whether adultery is a greater sin than the concupiscence of it. Who denies that? But the question is whether the same act, under a different aspect, may not be said to fall under different precepts, so that the coveting of another man's wife is condemned by the seventh commandment as well as by the tenth. Thus one who covets his neighbour's wife is not free from transgression of the precept which provides, in general and expressly, for chastity and purity of marriage.

units.la: Dices, sic præcepta commisceburtur, idemque facinus & ad hoc, & ad illud trahetur præceptum. Resp. Nulla est illa præceptorum commixtio. Neque hoc insolens aut novum, idem delictum variis ex legibus coargui & damnari posse. Præsertim quando naturam præcepti decimi attentius spectamus, quod concupiscentiam prohibens, eorum etiam quæ præcedentibus præceptis notata, expressam facit mentionem: adeo non potes peccare in argumentum præcepti decimi, ut non etiam attingas & incurras in præcepta alia, nempe quod ad speciem peccati & concupiscentiæ.
units.tr: You will say that the precepts would thus be confused, and the same offence would be brought under both this and that precept. I reply: there is no such confusion of precepts. Nor is it unusual or new for the same offence to be charged and condemned under various laws. This is especially so when we look more closely at the nature of the tenth precept, which, in forbidding concupiscence, also expressly mentions those things already noted in the preceding precepts. So you cannot sin against the subject of the tenth precept without also touching and falling under the other precepts, namely as regards the kind of sin and of concupiscence.

units.la: Quid ergo attinuit, dices, præter præcepta priora, decimum addere, quum in prioribus concupiscentia mali, præceptis singulis vetiti, quoque prohibita, vi generalis sanctionis, effet? Resp. Quid attinuit, ut Deus, non contentus unico canone, diliges proximum tuum sicuti teipsum, tot istius argumenti diversasque leges ferret? nempe quamvis illis legibus peccatum aliquod damnat, & omnia etiam coarguit eo spectantia, sic & animum & concupiscen-tiam tiam mali; tamen majoris cautelæ & notitiæ ergo singulatim exprimere præceptorum ultimo voluit quamcunque malorum omnium sibi improbari, non actionem modo, sed concupiscentiam. Idque, ne nescirent homines, expresso & singulari voluit signare præcepto. Eo magis, non modo quod facile lubenterque id ignorent, malintque non esse peccatum, sed quoque, quia hoc ad omnia præcepta sua generalitate spectans, nullius omnino mali habendam fovendamque concupiscentiam esse, in genere cavet. Nullum peccatum committitur contra Dei præcepta, quod non etiam contra decimum: & contra hoc nullum quod ad specificationem actus, quod non referatur etiam ad præcepta alia, horumque peccatorem quoque reum faciat. Ita diversâ ratione eâdem actione homo incurrit in præcepta varia. Aliis præceptis Deus modum & regulam constituit actionibus; ultimo, principaliter cordi & affectibus: ibi mala ne faciamus; hic, ne concupiscamus quoque. Nempe prout Deus, non actionibus solum nostris, sed & cogitationibus sanctificari colique cupit, leges & his dedit, & illis distinctas, variasque; sed omnes ita inter se innexas & conjunctas, ut non modo qui unum, plura facile solvat, sed & in uno transgrediens omnium evadat reus. Jac. 11, 10. Quomodo primum præceptum se habet ad sequentia, ita postremum ad antecedentia. Nemo peccat in præcepta alia, quin etiam in primum, negligens debitum Deo amorem, & cultum. Sic & qui opere quovis peccat, semper animo primum delinquit, & cogitatione, ac concupiscentia. Ut duorum istorum, & primi, & ultimi præcepti generalitate circumvallare reliqua voluerit sapiens legislator. Ne quis ignoraret, uno se peccato diversa transgredi præcepta posse, & plurium simul constitui reum.
units.tr: What, then, you will ask, was the point of adding a tenth precept beyond the earlier ones, since in the earlier ones the concupiscence of evil, forbidden by each single precept, was also prohibited by the force of the general sanction? I reply: what was the point of God, not content with the single rule "You shall love your neighbour as yourself", enacting so many laws of this kind and of diverse content? Although by those laws he condemns some sin and also censures all things tending to it, both the mind and the concupiscence of evil, yet for the sake of greater caution and knowledge he willed to set out in the last precept, one by one, that whatever evil of all kinds is disapproved by him, not only the act but also the concupiscence. He willed to mark this with an express and separate precept, so that men should not be ignorant of it. This is the more necessary, not only because they readily and gladly ignore it and prefer that it not be sin, but also because by its generality, applying to all his precepts, it guards in general against anyone's having or cherishing any concupiscence of any evil at all. No sin is committed against God's precepts that is not also committed against the tenth; and against this one there is no sin, as regards the specific nature of the act, that is not also referred to other precepts, making the sinner guilty of those as well. Thus by a different aspect the same action brings a man under various precepts. By other precepts God has set a measure and rule for actions; by the last, chiefly for the heart and the affections: the former to keep us from doing evil, this to keep us from desiring it too. Indeed, since God wishes to have us sanctified and worshipped not only in our actions but also in our thoughts, he has given laws for both, distinct and various, yet all so interlinked and joined together that whoever breaks one easily breaks many, and whoever transgresses in one becomes guilty of all. (Jas. 2, 10.) As the first precept stands to those that follow, so the last stands to those that go before. No one sins against the other precepts without also sinning against the first, by neglecting the love and worship owed to God. So too, whoever sins by any work always first offends in the mind, in thought and concupiscence. The wise lawgiver therefore willed to surround the remaining precepts with the generality of these two, the first and the last, so that no one should be ignorant that by one sin he can transgress diverse precepts and be made guilty of several at once.

units.la: Instantia. Socinus ita: Si Christi mens fuisset explicare quo sensu accipienda essent legis verba, ac docere, in ipsa lege verbum adulterandi, etiam ipsum desiderium potiunda alicujus nupta mulieris ecmplecti[?].. nullo pacto dixisset, ipso legis præcepto commemorato, ego autem dico vobis, &c. Sic enim plane demonstrat, se non illud explanare velle, sed aliquid diversum ab ipso proponere. Pag. 88. Resp. Negatur sequi. Christus dicens, ego vero &c. adversativum istud non opponit legi, sed Adversariorum opinioni, de qua in initio sermonis dixerat, μὴ νομίσητε[?]; quosque innuit legem solvere, & ita homines docere. Sensus ergo dictorum Christi est, ego vero, contra ac vos opinamini, dico, eum qui mulierem aspexerit, ut ea potiatur, jam adulterium in corde suo commisisse, ejusque apud Deum, nempe adulterii corde commissi, atque ita violatæ legis esse reum. 11. Deinde dari potest, quod aliquid diversum Christus proponat, sed quod tamen latitudine præcepti comprehendatur. Nam quum illa verba, non adulterabis per se notent adulterii actionem, quod nemo nescit: ad eandem tamen legem revocat Christus, & hoc ipsa rei natura, adulterium cordis, quod per se quidem aliqua ratione diversum ab adulterandi actione, attamen ad idem legis caput revocari debet.
units.tr: Objection. Socinus says: "If Christ had intended to explain in what sense the words of the law are to be taken, and to teach that in the law itself the phrase 'commit adultery' embraces even the very desire of possessing a married woman, he would by no means have said, after citing the precept of the law itself, 'But I say to you', etc. For thus he plainly shows that he does not wish to explain it, but to put forward something different from it." p. 88. Reply. This does not follow. Christ, saying "But I say" etc., does not set that adversative against the law, but against the opinion of his opponents, of which he had spoken at the beginning of the sermon, "do not think [μὴ νομίσητε]", and he hints that they supposed he was dissolving the law and so teaching men. The sense of Christ's words is therefore this: "But I say, contrary to what you suppose, that whoever has looked on a woman so as to possess her has already committed adultery in his heart, and is guilty before God of adultery committed in the heart, and so of violating the law." 11. Further, it may be granted that Christ puts forward something different, and yet that it is comprehended within the breadth of the precept. For although the words "you shall not commit adultery" by themselves denote the act of adultery, which nobody fails to know, nevertheless Christ recalls to the same law also adultery of the heart; and the very nature of the matter requires that adultery of the heart, which in some respect is indeed different from the act of adultery, nevertheless be referred to the same head of the law.

units.la: Instant. II, Quomodo potest id esse explanatio, seu ad explanationem pertinere alterius, quod diversum & distinctum quoddam ab eo sit ? Resp. Quid ni ? annon multiplex homicidium, vel diversae & distinctae ejus species, gradus, modi ? sic & furti, & mendacii, & concupiscentiae ad eadem referuntur praecepta: quare non sic etiam adulterium cordis, ad praeceptum generale de adulterio, quamvis diversum & distinctum aliquid ab adulterii actione sit istud quod cordis appellatur ?
units.tr: Objection II. How can that be an explanation, or belong to the explanation of something, if it is something different and distinct from it? Reply. Why not? Is not murder manifold, or are not its species, degrees and modes diverse and distinct? So too theft, lying and concupiscence are referred to the same precepts. Why then should not adultery of the heart likewise be referred to the general precept on adultery, although it is something different and distinct from the act of adultery?

units.la: Denique, tantum abest ut ea, quam Socinus dat, verborum Christi, & legis explanatio, eam augeat ac perficiat, ut ne sic quidem legis vim & plenitudinem capiat. 1. Dum γυναῖκα mulierem in hoc sermone ad maritatam restringit. Nam uti lex, quamvis de adulterio loquatur, fornicationem, & quamcunque ejus generis turpitudinem comprehendit, cum quacunque etiam muliere, sive conjungatâ, sive solutâ, ita in sermone Christi, legis transgressor habetur, qui mulierem concupierit impuro animo, sive maritatam, sive aliam, ut qui cum illâ adulterium, cum aliâ fornicationem committat, in corde suo. 11. Solvit Christi verba Socinus, quando primos concupiscentiae malae motus peccata esse negat. Nam cùm est tantummodo primus quidam motus concupiscendi, tunc nec desiderium, proprie loquendo, dici debet, nec in hominis potestate, qui habitum virtutis castitatis adeptus non fuerit, illo modo esse videtur, & si tamen aliquo modo est, nulla ratione credendum videtur Christum talem cupiditatem adulterii loco duxisse. Illud certum judicio meo est, ejusmodi cupiditatem, cui quis nullo prorsus modo consentiat, non fuisse comprehensam praecepto illo Mosis de non concupiscendo; & vix propter rationem proximè allatam, quod ea non videtur in hominis potestate esse, etiam sub ipso Euangelio, peccati ullam rationem habere, quidquid contrà complures disputent: inquit Adversarius noster, pag.91. Resp. 1. Primus motus concupiscendi quomodocunque appelletur, vel dici debeat, non ideo definit malus esse, quia forte desiderium nominari nequit: neque hinc ratio peccati arcessitur, sed ex ejus ἀνομία. Est motus animi in malum, cum lege non conveniens, & non ad sanctificandum in corde Deum, quod jubemur 1 Petr. iii. 15. ergò est malus. 11. Et ubi est motus concupiscendi alienam uxorem, pertinet ad adulterium certe, ejusque est causa per se, & gradus quidam, formam habens adulterii, sed spiritualis, quod in corde committitur, quale Christus sub adulterio recenset. Alioqui vim sermonis Christi enervabis, & non tantum legis, quando istum concupiscendi motum à peccato, & adulterio τῆς καρδίας, contra tum rei naturam, tum legis, & Christi dictatum, absolvis? iii. Sed non potest proprie dici desiderium. Ecquid tum? quodcunque, vel quomodocunque appelletur. Quare etiam nequit dici desiderium? uti primus motus concupiscendi; ita primus motus sit desiderandi? Si ille motus concupiscentia est, quare non iste desiderium? & quod concupiscentia, quare non est desiderium? vel quod concupiscis, annon suo etiam modo desideras? an tale tantumque horum verborum discrimen est verbale, ut illud peccato obstringat, hoc absolvat? iv. Sed, non sunt illi motus primi in hominis potestate. Hominis in peccato mortui, & irregeniti? haec ipsius culpa est. Regeniti? nego, simpliciter illos haud esse in ejus potestate, ut debitâ curâ, tum implorati in opem Spiritus Sancti, tum vigilantiæ in animum, omnino nequeat mederi & prospicere ei, quamvis non perfectè. Præterea ex malo habitu est, quod motus illi attentionem & consilium prævertunt; & hinc minus videntur esse in nostra potestate. Denique, utcunque subitanei motus sint, non sunt tamen involuntarii in se, sed omnino ex prava voluntate ortum suum habent, affectuque. Atque hoc satis est ad constituendam peccati rationem. v. Non est hæc concupiscentia, neque motus illi concupiscendi, ut quis nullo prorsus modo illis consentiat. Imo consentit, qui eos experitur, dum originaliter ex voluntate fluunt, eamque afficiunt. Neque concupiscere quis potest, ut nullo prorsus modo consentiat. Qua parte concupiscit, ea & consentit. Quare & concupiscentia ista illo Mosis præ-cepto, de non concupiscendo, comprehensa est. Hic jam laxam suam disciplinam & Theologiam ostendunt Sociniani: adeo in vanum est, quod de perfectionibus Christi comminiscuntur. Nam quæ lex, & propria hominis conscientia damnat, motus vid. illos malè concupiscendi, hi, etiam sub Evangelio peccati ullam rationem habere, quidquid contra complures disputent, negant. Scilicet hæc est illa major & perfectior sanctitas, quam Christus docuerit; & quare Christi alia nova & pleniora præcepta præceptis legis addita vociferantur.
units.tr: Finally, so far is the explanation of Christ's words that Socinus gives from enlarging and perfecting it, that even so it does not grasp the force and fullness of the law. 1. He restricts "woman [γυναῖκα]" in this sermon to a married woman. For as the law, although it speaks of adultery, comprehends fornication and every kind of such uncleanness, with any woman whatever, whether married or single, so in Christ's sermon the transgressor of the law is one who has desired a woman with an impure mind, whether she be married or another; just as one who commits adultery with the one, or fornication with the other, commits it in his heart. 11. Socinus undoes Christ's words when he denies that the first motions of evil concupiscence are sins. For when there is only a first motion of desiring, then it ought not properly to be called desire, nor is it in the power of one who has not attained the habit of chastity; and if nevertheless it is in some way, it seems in no way credible that Christ reckoned such a lust as adultery. It is certain in my judgement that a lust of this kind, to which one in no way at all consents, was not comprehended in that precept of Moses about not coveting; and scarcely, for the reason just given, that since it does not seem to be in man's power, even under the Gospel it has any character of sin, whatever many dispute to the contrary: says our adversary, p. 91. Reply. 1. The first motion of concupiscence, however it may be named or ought to be called, does not cease to be evil because perhaps it cannot be called desire. Nor is the character of sin derived from this, but from its lawlessness. It is a motion of the mind towards evil, not agreeing with the law, and not sanctifying God in the heart, which we are commanded to do (1 Pet. 3, 15); therefore it is evil. 11. And where there is a motion of concupiscence towards another man's wife, it certainly pertains to adultery, and is in itself its cause and a certain degree of it, having the form of adultery though spiritual, committed in the heart, such as Christ recounts under adultery. Otherwise you will weaken the force of Christ's words, and not only of the law, when you absolve that motion of concupiscence from sin and from adultery of the heart, against both the nature of the matter and the law and Christ's own teaching. 111. But it cannot properly be called desire. What then? Whatever it be called, or however. Why then can it not be called desire, just as the first motion of concupiscence is a first motion of desiring? If that motion is concupiscence, why is this not desire? And since it is concupiscence, why is it not desire? Or since you covet, do you not in your own way also desire? Is the difference between these words so merely verbal that the one binds to sin and the other absolves? iv. But those first motions are not in man's power. Is this the fault of a man dead in sin and unregenerate? It is; but I deny that for the regenerate those motions are simply not in his power, so that with due care, both by imploring the help of the Holy Spirit and by vigilance over the mind, he cannot altogether remedy them and guard against them, though not perfectly. Moreover, it comes from an evil habit that those motions anticipate attention and deliberation, and for this reason they seem less within our power. Finally, however sudden the motions may be, they are not involuntary in themselves, but have their origin entirely in a depraved will and affection. And this is enough to establish the character of sin. v. That concupiscence and those motions of concupiscence are not such that one in no way at all consents to them. Indeed, he consents who experiences them, since they flow originally from the will and affect it. Nor can one covet in such a way as in no way at all to consent. In whatever part one covets, in that part one also consents. Therefore this concupiscence too is comprehended under that precept of Moses about not coveting. Here the Socinians display their lax discipline and theology; so vain is what they devise concerning the perfections of Christ. For what the law and a man's own conscience condemn, namely those motions of evil concupiscence, they deny to have any character of sin under the Gospel, whatever many dispute to the contrary. Clearly this is that greater and more perfect holiness which Christ taught; and this is why they loudly proclaim other new and fuller precepts added to the precepts of the law.

units.la: Tertio loco venit versus 31. 32. de libello repudii: dictum autem est, si quis dimiserit uxorem suam, det illi libellum repudii. Ego verò dico vobis, &c. Resp. 1.
units.tr: It has been said, "Whoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorce." But I say to you, etc. Reply 1.

units.la: Ipsi Adversarii vident, & agnoscunt, non præceptum fuisse, ut darent-repudii libellum; quamvis id Judæi ita, verùm temerè, acceperunt. Fuit solum permissio, & tolerantia legis, propter eorum σκληροκαρδίαν[?]. Socinus: Itaque breviter statuendum, in ipsa Mosis lege id reipsa fuisse scriptum, quod Christus dictum fuisse hoc loco affirmat, sed tamen nihilominus statuendum simul videtur, Christum hic propterea non dixisse, ut in duobus superioribus locis, Dictum fuisse antiquis, sed simpliciter, Dictum fuisse, propter eam causam, quod diserte in ipsa lege non ita legeretur, ut ejus verba sonant, & vulgò in populo dictum & auditum jam diu fuerat. pag. 99. Resp. Ergo verba illa, dictum esse, vel plene, dictum esse antiquis, non sunt, ut aliàs faciunt Adversarii, eò trahenda, quasi ipsa legis verba sensumque continerent, quem Christus perstringat, aut refigat.
units.tr: The Adversaries themselves see and acknowledge that it was not commanded that they should give a writing of divorce, although the Jews understood it so, rashly. It was only a permission and a toleration of the law, because of their hardness of heart [σκληροκαρδία]. Socinus: Therefore it must briefly be determined that in the law of Moses itself this was in fact written, which Christ affirms was said in this place. Nevertheless, it seems at the same time that it must be determined that Christ did not say here, as in the two preceding places, "It was said to the ancients," but simply, "It was said," for the reason that it was not so read expressly in the law itself as its words sound, and it had long been commonly said and heard among the people. p. 99. Reply: Therefore those words, "It was said," or fully, "It was said to the ancients," are not, as the Adversaries elsewhere do, to be drawn in that direction, as if they contained the very words and sense of the law which Christ would censure or refute.

units.la: II. Res, quam Christus sumit exponendam, non est legis Mosaicæ moralis, sed politicæ: atqui non de istâ, sed illa quæstio nostra est, an Christus illam perfecerit. Lubenter enim fatemur, istam abrogatam, correctamque fuisse. Hoc & Socinus ad hunc locum fatetur. Ideoque alia potius agit, quam ut hinc argumentum formet, vel urgeat. pag 97. Postquam Christus de quibusdam Decalogi ipsius præceptis egit, quibus addere aliquid, eave perficere voluit, ad alia transfit, quæ ad ipsam quidem Mosis legem pertinent, sed in ipso decalogo non habentur, & primo loco agit de divortio seu repudio uxoris. Nil ergo illa ad præsens spectant negotium vel controversiam, quæ est de præceptis Decalogi moralibus, non de aliis. III. Christus quod hic corrigit, ad legem revocat, & ad primam atque moralem conjungit institutionem, ex quâ nec repudiare ob quamvis causam licet[?], neque plures una habere uxores. Matth. xix. 4. 5. 6. legem ergo restituit suo vigori & puritati, contra malam acceptionem & consuetudinem Judæorum; non vero moralem vel castigavit, vel auxit. Adde quæ ad hoc probandum habet Cl. Buxtorfius, in Tractatu, de Sponsalibus & Divortiis, part. 11. à pag. 106. & deinceps. iv. Nam & in polygamia, & repudio, Judæos & Patres, quotquot se eo obstrinxerunt, peccasse contra legem poli, quod dicunt, quamvis non soli, Deo connivente, confert etiam Socinus: Crediderim tamen intelligendum esse, quod attinet ad ipsum civile forum, quod Theologi forum fori appellare solent, licuisse per Mosen ob quamvis causam uxorem dimittere; nec necesse habuisse virum causam dimissionis suæ proferre, & multo minus, eam magistratui approbare, sed, ut dimissio ista juridica esset, satis fuisse, ut id fieret, quod in lege Mosis expressum est, de dando in manus ipsius mulieris libello repudii. Verum, quod attinet ad conscientiam, & ad forum spirituale & divinum, quod forum Poli a Theologis vocitari solet, peccasse etiam sub Mose ipso eum, qui ob causam non legitimam uxorem dimisisset, id est, non talem, quæ vel eadem ipsa sit, vel ei similis quam in ipsa lege scriptam legimus: quæ, ut dictum fuit, est turpitudo aliqua quam in uxore maritus invenerit.
units.tr: II. The matter Christ takes up to explain is not the moral but the political part of the law of Moses. But our question is not about that, but about whether Christ perfected that moral law. For we gladly confess that the political law was abrogated and corrected. Socinus himself concedes this at this passage. So he does something other than form or press an argument from it. p. 97. After Christ had dealt with some of the precepts of the Decalogue itself, to which he wished to add something or to perfect them, he passes on to other matters, which indeed pertain to the law of Moses itself but are not contained in the Decalogue itself, and he first deals with the divorce or repudiation of a wife. Those things therefore have no bearing on the present business or controversy, which concerns the moral precepts of the Decalogue, not others. III. What Christ corrects here he recalls to the law and joins to the first, moral institution, from which it is lawful neither to repudiate a wife for any cause nor to have several wives at once. Matth. xix. 4. 5. 6. He therefore restored the law to its vigour and purity against the Jews' bad interpretation and custom; he neither censured nor increased the moral law. Add what the distinguished Buxtorf has to prove this, in his tractate On Betrothals and Divorces, part 11, from p. 106 onwards. IV. For both in polygamy and in repudiation, the Jews and the Fathers, as many as bound themselves to it, sinned against the law of God, as they say, though not alone, God conniving. Socinus also grants this: I would believe, however, that it must be understood, as regards the civil forum, which theologians are accustomed to call the forum of the forum, that it was permitted through Moses to dismiss a wife for any cause; nor was the husband obliged to state the cause of his dismissal, and much less to have it approved by the magistrate; but for that dismissal to be legal, it was enough that it be done as is expressed in the law of Moses, namely by giving a writing of repudiation into the woman's own hand. But as regards conscience, and the spiritual and divine forum, which theologians are accustomed to call the forum of God, he who had dismissed a wife for a cause not legitimate, that is, not such as is the same as, or similar to, what we read written in the law itself, which, as was said, is some turpitude that the husband has found in the wife, sinned even under Moses himself.

units.la: Quarto loco veniunt ea, quæ de juramento Christus dicit, ad præceptum tertium spectantia. Vers. 33. 34. Iterum audivistis dictum esse antiquis: non perjerabis, reddes autem Domino juramenta tua. Ego vero dico vobis, non jurare omnino, &c. Quum enim ad duo in hisce semper attendendum sit, ad propositionem Christi, seu legem, quam sibi sumit exponendam; & ad responsionem: Socinus, propositionis alteram partem (duabus etenim constat) non perjerabis sumtam dicit ex præcepto Decalogi tertio; alteram, de reddendis Domino juramentis, ex Num. xxx. De priori, dicendum videtur, inquit, in ipso Decalogo præceptum istud expresse contineri, præcepto inquam tertio. pag. 121. & 122. Quidquid fit, illud certissimum est, præceptum non pejerandi isto tertio decalogi mandato plane contineri; unde meritissimo dici posset, ut paulo ante statuimus, Christum priorem partem enunciati sui ex ipso decalogo sumsisse. De parte altera, eadem pag. certissimum est illam ex 30. cap. Numer. esse desumptam, ubi expresse jubetur, ut is, qui ad aliquid faciendum juramento interposito sese obstrinxerit, id omnino reipsa præstare debeat, quod aliud nihil est, quam debere quemlibet juramenta sua domino reddere. Et pag. 123. Itaque merito concludere possumus prædicto loco Numerorum, quamvis non iisdem verbis, quibus hic usus est Christus, tamen eandem sententiam, eamque expressius & clarius, quam in ipsis Christi verbis, contineri.
units.tr: Fourth come the things Christ says about oaths, which pertain to the third commandment. Verses 33, 34: Again you have heard that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not forswear yourself, but shall perform your oaths to the Lord." But I say to you, not to swear at all, etc. For since in these two things must always be attended to, Christ's proposition, or law, which he takes up to explain, and the response: Socinus says that one part of the proposition (for it consists of two) "You shall not forswear yourself" is taken from the third precept of the Decalogue, and the other, about performing oaths to the Lord, from Numbers 30. Of the former, it seems, it must be said that this precept is expressly contained in the Decalogue itself, in the third precept, I mean. p. 121, 122. Whatever the case, this is most certain: the precept against forswearing is plainly contained in that third commandment of the Decalogue, whence it could most deservedly be said, as we stated a little earlier, that Christ took the first part of his statement from the Decalogue itself. Of the other part, on the same page, it is most certain that it is taken from Numbers chapter 30, where it is expressly ordered that he who has bound himself by oath to do something must really perform it, which is nothing other than that everyone must render his oaths to the Lord. And p. 123: Therefore we can rightly conclude that in the said passage of Numbers, although not in the same words as Christ used, the same sentiment is nevertheless contained, and more expressly and clearly than in Christ's own words.

units.la: Quid autem, juxta Socinum, Christus addidit præceptis illis? Primum, non satis esse, ne quis perjuret; sed nec vane, aut temerarie jurandum esse, quod passim appellat voluntarie jurare, pag. 114. Quare, Christi reformatio non ad alia juramenta pertinere dicenda est, quam ad ea quæ plane sunt voluntaria: & censendum, ubi Moses in ejusmodi juramentis perjurium tantum prohibebat, Christum ipsa præterea juramenta vetare; & ubi Moses tantum jubebat ut quis præstaret id quod sua sponte juraret, quod idem est atque in perjurium non incidere (unde multo magis apparet stultitia eorum, qui putarunt alterum alterius esse additamentum) Christus tali præstatione juramenti sui non est contentus, nec vult, ut ea sit causa, quo minus is peccasse dicendus fit, qui ejusmodi voluntaria juramenta fecerit. Pag. 137. Propterea quamtumvis absoluta & generalia sint Jacobi verba, plane voluntaria tamen duntaxat juramenta, non secus ac Christus fecit, eum interdicere voluisse. Pag. 138. Jam quemadmodum videtur nulla causa esse, cur omnia prorsus juramenta interdicta censeri debeant, sed ea omnia posse ac debere concedi, quae aliqua necessitate impellente fiant; sic præter causas ante allatas, quae Christum moverunt ad prorsus voluntaria juramenta interdicenda, &c.– Voluntaria juramenta opponit necessariis, quae ex necessitate fiunt, uti illa quae citra eam. Sed ea non dicenda erant voluntaria juramenta, sed temeraria; nam qui re ita ferente & urgente necessitate, etiam voluntarie jurat, non coacte hoc facit, attamen non jurat temere[?].
units.tr: What then, according to Socinus, did Christ add to those precepts? First, it is not enough that no one forswear himself; one must not swear idly or rashly either, which he everywhere calls swearing voluntarily, p. 114. Therefore Christ's reformation is not to be said to pertain to any oaths other than those which are plainly voluntary; and it is to be judged that where Moses in such oaths only forbade perjury, Christ forbids the oaths themselves besides; and where Moses only commanded that one perform what he swore of his own accord, which is the same as not falling into perjury (whence it appears much more clearly the folly of those who thought the one to be an addition to the other), Christ is not content with such performance of one's oath, nor wills that this be the reason why he who has made such voluntary oaths is said to have sinned. p. 137. Therefore, however absolute and general James's words are, Christ wished to forbid only plainly voluntary oaths, in no other way than he did. p. 138. Now just as there seems to be no reason why all oaths should be absolutely deemed forbidden, but all those which are made from some compelling necessity can and ought to be conceded, so, besides the causes mentioned before, which moved Christ to forbid absolutely voluntary oaths, etc. He opposes voluntary oaths to necessary ones, which are made from necessity, as opposed to those made without it. But those should not be called voluntary oaths but rash ones; for he who, when circumstances and urgent necessity bear it, swears even voluntarily, does not do so under compulsion, yet he does not swear rashly.

units.la: Deinde huc refert juramenta de futuris, quae etiam prohiberi à Christo censet, hactenus saltem, ne cui de eo quod se facturum putat vel statuit, jurare liceat, quasi de futuro, quod in nostra potestate non est, tantummodo de animo præsente erga illud. Pag. 134. Postquam Christus expresse vetuit ne omnino juretur, id est, per nullum jurandi modum, quod ut dictum fuit, de voluntariis & prorsus liberis juramentis intelligendum est, cujusmodi sunt juramenta de futuris rebus, quas videlicet se facturum quis promittat. Et Pag. 140. Nempe, nulli licere de re futura jurare, quod non videtur pugnare cum eo, quod diximus de voluntariis duntaxat juramentis a Christo vetitis, cum juramenta super re futura videantur omnia esse voluntaria; quod tamen diximus de mente Christi circa talia juramenta, ita accipi volumus, ut nos simpliciter jurare non liceat occasione rei, quam quis se facturum non dubitat, tales enim & non aliæ sunt res futuræ super quibus juratur; sed non liceat ita juramentum concipere, ut prorsus quis jurando promittat se aliquid facturum, cum ea quæ futura sunt plane incerta sint, non sit in manu cujusquam absolutè ac penitus positum aliquid facere. Sed interim non vetetur juramentum super re futura præstare, sive vel eo pacto jurisjurandi verba concipiantur, ut jurans de re præsente, id est, de mente ac voluntate sua in eo præstando, quod se facturum jurando promittit, & sic de re sibi comperta juret; vel si non ex ipsis jurisjurandi verbis, aliunde constet, illum non de ipso facto, sed de mente & animo suo id, quod jusjurandum continet, affirmare. Nemo vero qui juramenta probat, vel concipit de futuro, ea absolutè accipit, quasi futurum sit absolutè, aut prorsus, quibus hic verbis Socinus utitur: aut quasi putet in manu aut potestate sua simpliciter situm esse, quod vovet, & non sub conditione polliceatur, sub arbitrio & providentia Dei, ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος θελήσῃ[?]. Jac. iv. 15. sed de mente & proposito præsenti loquitur, qui etiam de futuro jurat, & quo erga rem faciendam sit animo, ut sincere affectus sit, testatur. Uti in contractibus, & fœderibus omnino necesse est ejusmodi de futuro juramenta intercedere, urgente necessitate tantâ quidem, ac ullibi, ubi juramentum probare Sociniani ipsi non nequeunt. Quare illa magis excogita videntur à Socino, ad aliquid dicendum quod legi per Christum additum videri possit, quam quod id res exigeret. Breviter Magistri sui mentem compleditur Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. xiii. Christus dixit, ne jurate omnino, ut ab iis juramentis, quæ nulla postulat necessitas, nos penitus arceat. In antecedentibus enim verbis ex Mose depromtis, quibus sua Christus ita opposuit, ut, quod in illis concediur; in his prohibeatur; voluntaria revera juramenta, & quidem de rebus futuris suscepta,
units.tr: Next he refers here to oaths about future things, which he also thinks Christ forbids, at least so far that no one may swear about what he thinks or has resolved to do, as if about the future, which is not in our power, but only about his present mind towards it. p. 134. After Christ expressly forbade swearing at all, that is, by any manner of swearing, which, as was said, must be understood of voluntary and entirely free oaths, of which kind are oaths about future things, which someone promises he will do. And p. 140. Namely, that it is lawful for no one to swear about a future thing, which does not seem to conflict with what we said about the voluntary oaths alone forbidden by Christ, since oaths about future things all seem to be voluntary. Yet what we said about Christ's mind concerning such oaths we want to be understood thus: it is not lawful for us to swear simply on the occasion of a thing which someone does not doubt he will do, for such, and no others, are the future things about which one swears. But it is not lawful to frame an oath so that by swearing one absolutely promises that he will do something, since future things are wholly uncertain and it is not absolutely and entirely in anyone's hand to do something. But meanwhile swearing about a future thing is not forbidden, whether the words of the oath are framed so that the one swearing swears about a present thing, that is, about his mind and will in doing what he promises by swearing he will do, and so swears about a thing known to himself; or, if it is not clear from the words of the oath itself, it is otherwise evident that he affirms not the fact itself but what the oath contains about his mind and purpose. Yet no one who approves of oaths, or frames them about the future, takes them absolutely, as if the future were absolutely certain, or wholly so, which words Socinus uses here; or as if he thought that what he vows simply lies in his own hand or power, and does not promise it under a condition, under the will and providence of God, if the Lord wills [ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος θελήσῃ]. James 4:15. But he speaks of his present mind and purpose who swears even about the future, and by swearing testifies what disposition he has towards doing the thing, that he be sincerely affected. Just as in contracts and covenants such oaths about the future must of necessity intervene, under as great an urgent necessity as anywhere, where the Socinians themselves cannot do without an oath. Therefore those things seem to have been devised by Socinus rather to say something that could seem to be added to the law by Christ than because the matter demanded it. In brief, Volkelius completes his master's mind, book 4, chapter 13: Christ said, "Swear not at all," so that he might wholly keep us from those oaths which no necessity demands. For in the preceding words taken from Moses, which Christ opposed to his own, so that what is conceded in those is forbidden in these, voluntary oaths, and indeed those taken about future things, are permitted.

units.la: Tom. 2. suscepta, permittuntur. Unde facile apparet, Christum in sequentibus voluntaria jurd-menta, atque ea inprimis, quae de futuris rebus suscipiantur, quaeque ab aliquo impediri queant, penitus prohibere.
units.tr: Vol. 2. are permitted. From this it readily appears that Christ, in what follows, forbids entirely voluntary oaths, and above all those sworn about future matters and those that some circumstance may prevent from being kept.

units.la: Resp. 1. Hoc inter alia argumento, pro se usus, contra nos, Socinus in praesenti negotio fuit, quod dixit ea, quae Christus sibi proponit reforman-da ex lege, eadem contineri, ipsissimaque ejus esse verba: verum quod hic adducit Christus, non pejeratis, &c. istum in modum lege non continetur: ergo. Praeceptum tertium dicit quidem, non sumendum Dei nomen esse לַשָּׁוְא, cujus summa, argumento, & consequentia fateor prohibetur omne non rectum juramentum, omne etiam perjurium; sed tamen non clare & expresse, vel non expressius clariusque illud est in lege, quam ipsis Christi verbis, uti Socinus loquitur, quare neque hinc, quod tertium refigere ac perficere praeceptum Christo propositum fuerit, ullo modo apparet.
units.tr: Reply 1. Socinus, in the present controversy, has used this argument among others in his own favour and against us: that what Christ proposes to reform from the law is contained in the law, and that these are his very words. But what Christ here adduces, "you shall not swear falsely, etc.," is not contained in the law in this way; therefore the conclusion does not follow. The third precept indeed says that the name of God is not to be taken לַשָּׁוְא [in vain]. Its substance, I grant, by argument and consequence, forbids every unlawful oath and every perjury. But it is not clearly and expressly stated in the law, nor is it expressed more plainly there than in Christ's own words, as Socinus puts it. So it does not appear in any way from this that Christ proposed to restore and complete the third precept.

units.la: II. Non nego interim, perjurium praecepto Decalogi tertio prohiberi: sed nemo illud magis isto contineri praecepto dicet, quam irae prohibitionem, sub homicidio; & concupiscentiam mulieris alienae, sub adulterio.
units.tr: II. Meanwhile I do not deny that perjury is forbidden by the third precept of the Decalogue. But no one would say that this precept contains the prohibition of perjury more than the prohibition of anger is contained under the sixth commandment about murder, or the lust after another's wife under the commandment about adultery.

units.la: III. Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum לַשָּׁוְא: ergo, fateor, damnatur etiam perjurium, namque propter hoc vel imprimis illud fit. Sed, perjurium solum illis notari verbis, nemo opinor, dicet: nam & aliis, praeterquam isto modo, nomen Dei prophanari, contra tertium praeceptum, potest. Quare non tertium praeceptum reformare Christus voluit, sed modo aliquid hic dicere de perjurio, vel juramento, praecepti illius parte speciali.
units.tr: III. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain לַשָּׁוְא [in vain]: I grant that perjury is condemned by this, and indeed it is chiefly for this reason that the precept was given.
