But I suppose no one will say that perjury alone is marked by those words, for the name of God can also be profaned against the third precept in other ways than this. Therefore Christ did not wish to reform the third precept, but only to say something here about perjury or oaths, a particular part of that precept.

units.la: IV. Certe sub V. Test. non licuit, temerarie jurare. Socinus dicit, sola falsa juramenta ibi fuisse prohibita, in quibus proprie perjurium locum habet, non item temeraria. In quo valde temerarius ipse est, & fallitur. Nam expresse praecepto tertio dicitur, non sumes nomen Domini Dei tui לַשָּׁוְא, in vanum. Quem istum, ut declinet, negat לַשָּׁוְא significare vanum; vult, falsum notare. Contra communem, verissimamque vocis notationem, solum ut falsae suae succurrat hypothesi. Nam si dicat, temerarium juramentum; lege ergo fuit prohibitum, & non per Christum demum ei additum. Neque habet, quod ei additum dicat, praeterquam id. Quare verbum in alium sensum torquendum omni ratione fuit.
units.tr: IV. Certainly under the Old Testament it was not permitted to swear rashly. Socinus says that only false oaths were forbidden there, those in which perjury properly has its place, and not rash ones. In this he is himself very rash and mistaken. For the third precept expressly says, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God לַשָּׁוְא [in vain]." In order to evade this, he denies that לַשָּׁוְא means "in vain"; he wants it to mean "falsely." This is contrary to the common and most certain meaning of the word, and he does it only to support his own false hypothesis. For if he says that a rash oath is meant, then it was forbidden by the law, and was not added to the law by Christ. Nor has he anything to say was added except that. Therefore the word had to be twisted to another sense by every means.

units.la: Fatetur id ipse his verbis, pag. 139. Nam ut antea dixi, mihi non improbatur illorum sententia, qui tertio decalogi praecepto volunt prohiberi, ne quis nomen Dei sine necessitate assumat, cum ex propria significatione Hebraica vocis, quae reddita est Latine in vanum, mihi persuasum sit ibi tantum vetari, ne, cum quis nomen Dei assumit, i.e. per nomen Dei jurat, quicquam mentiatur; ad quam sententiam amplectendam me etiam id impellit, quod alioqui Christus nihil novi ferme praecepisset; & quod in ipsa lege expresse non contineretur, contra quam verba ejus ferant, quibus ut ante demonstratum est, se legem Mosi in hac juramenti materia non secus atque in aliis quibusdam, reformare velle profitetur, aut certe pra se fert.
units.tr: He himself confesses this in these words, p. 139: "For, as I said before, I do not disapprove of the opinion of those who want the third precept of the Decalogue to forbid anyone to take the name of God without necessity. For from the proper Hebrew meaning of the word that is rendered in Latin 'in vain,' I am persuaded that it forbids only this: that when someone takes the name of God, that is, swears by the name of God, he should not lie anything. What also drives me to embrace this opinion is that otherwise Christ would have commanded almost nothing new, and something that is not expressly contained in the law itself, although his words suggest that, as has been shown before, he professes, or at least displays, that he wishes to reform the law of Moses in the matter of oaths no differently than in certain other matters."

units.la: Quare non probatur ei illorum sententia, qui in praecepto tertio לַשָּׁוְא in vanum interpretantur, & statuunt prohiberi juramenta sine necessitate usurpata? an quia isto modo non prophanatur Dei nomen? hoc respondere debuerat. Vel, cur sibi persuasum, tantum vetari, ut quis per nomen Dei jurans, menmentiatur? nimirum, quod alioqui Christus nihil ferme novi praecepisset, & quod in ipsa lege expresse non continueretur. Vides causam expositionis à se allatæ: exponit ita, non quod verum, vel mens praecepti illa videatur, sed quod ita exigat hypothesis sua, cui necessarium sc. ἀγλόεν[?]. Egregia certe Scripturam explicandi, disputandique methodus! Nempe hi sunt illi ingenui, liberique disputatores! qui omnia facile solvunt & diruunt, Scripturamque pervertunt, in gratiam suarum opinionum, ad quas omnia inflectere oportet, non ipsas Scripturas. Nec Christus leges Mosis se reformare aut perfectiores facere velle profitetur, aut præ se fert; sed hæc Socini perversa glossa est, & commentum, cui statuminando Christum & Mosem servire jubet & invitos suffragari.
units.tr: So the opinion of those who interpret לַשָּׁוְא in the third precept as "in vain," and hold that oaths taken without necessity are forbidden, is not approved by him. Is it because the name of God is not profaned in that way? He ought to have answered that. Or why is it his conviction that only this is forbidden: that someone swearing by the name of God should lie? Clearly, "because otherwise Christ would have commanded almost nothing new, and something not expressly contained in the law itself." You see the reason for the interpretation he has put forward: he explains it thus not because this seems to be the true meaning of the precept, but because his hypothesis requires it, to which the explanation must be necessary [ἀναγκαῖον]. What an excellent method of explaining Scripture and of arguing! Indeed these are those ingenious and free disputants, who easily solve and overturn everything and pervert Scripture for the sake of their own opinions, to which everything must be bent, not the Scriptures themselves. Nor does Christ profess, or display, that he wishes to reform or make more perfect the laws of Moses. This is a perverse gloss and an invention of Socinus, to support which he bids Christ and Moses serve and, though unwilling, lend their support.

units.la: Pag. 121. Interdicitur nomen Dei sumere in vanum, quamvis enim non desint, qui illud in vanum (prout quidem vulgata editio habet) ita interpretentur, ut significet sine necessitate, & quidem viri alioqui linguæ Hebraicæ peritissimi existimati: tamen nos una cum aliis, non paucis, verbum Hebraicum falsitatem ac mendacitatem significare credimus, quemadmodum significat Deut. 5. vers. 20. ubi nonum præceptum de non dicendo falso testimonio, eandem hanc ipsam in Hebraeo vocem habet: qua sola falsitas ista exprimitur: quod si quis nihilominus vulgatam interpretationem in tertio præcepto retinere velit, dicimus, in vanum non significare sine necessitate, sed sine effectu & frustra; ita ut assumtio istius nominis Dei frustranea, ut ita dicam, dici merito possit, quod tunc fit, cum id non præstatur, propter quod nomen Dei assumtum fuit, id quod nihil aliud est, quam merum perjurium.
units.tr: p. 121. "The taking of the name of God in vain is forbidden. For although there are not lacking those who interpret it 'in vain' (as the Vulgate edition indeed has it) so as to mean 'without necessity,' and these men are otherwise thought to be very skilled in the Hebrew language, yet we, together with not a few others, believe that the Hebrew word signifies falsehood and mendacity, as it does in Deut. 5:20, where the ninth precept, about not bearing false witness, has this very same Hebrew word, by which alone that falsity is expressed. But if anyone nevertheless wishes to retain the Vulgate rendering in the third precept, we say that 'in vain' does not mean 'without necessity' but 'without effect and to no purpose'; so that the taking of that name of God may rightly be called, so to speak, frustrated, which happens when that for which the name of God was taken is not accomplished, and this is nothing other than sheer perjury."

units.la: Resp. Quocunque modo, non est accipiendum illud לשוא, nec ut Vulgata, & communiter omnes Interpretes habent, nec ut peritissimi linguæ Hebraicæ existimant, sed ut Socinus jubet, quia alias, Christum nihil novi præcepisse, sequeretur, quod vel contra omnes, omniaque pertinaciter tenendum est. שוא significat vanum: & quia mendacium omne vanum est, hinc non negamus, hoc etiam illo intelligi, sed hoc solum, eo seclusø & negato, quod Socinus vult, nemo dicet, nisi qui ei, vel ejus se mancipaverit opinioni. שוא per antiphrasim videtur dictum à שוא profuit, utile est, nempe quod nullius usus, & frustra, inaniter, ac temere est. א, loco ה radicalis. Ita passim שוא in Sacris sumitur. Job. vii. 3. ירחי שוא menses vanita-tis accepi hæreditate. Cap. xi. 11. מחי שוא, viros vanitatis. & xv. 31. & xxxv. 13. Psalm. cxix. 37. averte oculos meos מראות שוא[?] ne videant vanitatem. Psalm. cxxvii. 1. שוא frustra operantur ædificatores. eoque sensu ter ibi vox illa occurrit. Jesa. i. 13. מנחת שוא oblationem frustraneam. Cap. v. 18. בחבלי השוא funibus vanitatis. Threm. ii. 14. Prophetæ vestri viderunt שוא vanitatem. Jezech. xii. 24. & xiii. 6. 7. 9. & xxii. 28. Malach. iii. 14. dicitur שוא frustra est ut serviamus Deo, & quod lucrum? &c. Atque ita לשוא, quæ constructio hic est, inaniter significat. Psalm. cxxxix. 20. qui extollunt לשוא vane inimicos tuos. Jerem. ii. 30. לשוא frustra percussi filios vestros. & iv. 30. & xviii. 15. & xlvi. 11. לשוא in vanum multiplicas curationes. De-nique distinguuntur aliquando inter se שוא frustra, & כזב, מרמה, מזמה, mendacium. Prov. xxx. 8. שׁוא ודבר כזב[?], vanitatem & verbum mendacii amove à me. Pfalm. xxiv. 4. qui non effert לשוא in vanitatem animam suam, & non jurat למרמה, ad fraudem. Pfalm. xxxix. 20. qui loquuntur de te scelerate למזמה, extollunt לשוא inimicos tuos. Jezech. xiij. 6. vident שוא vanitatem, & divinationem כזב mendacii. Zach. x. 2. Ergo שוא, & לשוא significat vanum; & quia aliquando mendacio contradistinguitur, simpliciter positum, uti fit in praecepto tertio, non potest solum denotare mendacium, & non vanum, quod Socinus, solus omnium, quod scio, Interpretum docet, propter malam hypothesim: sic illa exponens, non sumes nomen Domini Dei tui, mendaci-ter: oppositè & exclusive ad sensum vulgarem, non sumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum: quomodo negat verba exponi posse, certe inaniter valde atque mendaciter simul.
units.tr: Reply. In no way is לשוא to be understood as the Vulgate and all interpreters generally have it, nor as the most skilled in Hebrew think, but as Socinus commands, because otherwise it would follow that Christ commanded nothing new. This must be held against everyone and everything. שוא means "vain." And since every lie is vain, we do not deny that this is also included in that sense; but that this alone is meant, with that other meaning excluded and denied which Socinus wants, no one will say except one who has given himself over to him or to his opinion. שוא, by antiphrasis, seems to be derived from שוא [profit, use], namely that which has no use, and is "frustrated, idle, and rash." The א is in place of the radical ה. Thus שוא is used everywhere in the sacred books. Job 7:3: "months of vanity [ירחי שוא] have been given me as my inheritance." Ch. 11:11: "men of vanity [מחי שוא]." Ch. 15:31 and 35:13. Ps. 119:37: "turn away my eyes [מראות שוא] lest they see vanity." Ps. 127:1: "the builders labour in vain [שוא]," and in that sense the word occurs three times there. Isa. 1:13: "a vain oblation [מנחת שוא]." Ch. 5:18: "with the cords of vanity [בחבלי השוא]." Lam. 2:14: "your prophets have seen vanity [שוא]." Ezek. 12:24, 13:6, 7, 9, and 22:28. Mal. 3:14: "it is vain [שוא] to serve God, and what profit is it?" etc. And so לשוא, which is the construction here, means "in vain." Ps. 139:20: "who lift themselves up in vain [לשוא] against your enemies." Jer. 2:30: "in vain [לשוא] have I struck your sons." Also 4:30, 18:15, and 46:11: "in vain [לשוא] you multiply remedies." Finally, שוא "in vain" and כזב "lie," מרמה "deceit," and מזמה "wicked device" are sometimes distinguished from one another. Prov. 30:8: "remove from me vanity [שׁוא] and the word of lying [דבר כזב]." Ps. 24:4: "who has not lifted up his soul to vanity [לשוא], and has not sworn to deceit [למרמה]." Ps. 139:20 (as cited): "who speak of you wickedly [למזמה] and lift themselves up in vain [לשוא] against your enemies." Ezek. 13:6: "they see vanity [שוא] and divine a lie [כזב]." Zech. 10:2. Therefore שוא and לשוא mean "vain." And since it is sometimes set over against lying, and is used by itself, as it is in the third precept, it cannot denote only lying and not vanity. Socinus alone, so far as I know of all the interpreters, teaches otherwise, because of his false hypothesis: rendering the words "you shall not take the name of the Lord your God mendaciously," opposed and exclusive to the common sense, "you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain." He denies that the words can be so explained, yet to explain them as he does is certainly both vain and mendacious at once.

units.la: Atqui Deut. v. 20.[?] in nono praecepto recitando vox ita accipitur, non re-spondebis contra proximum tuum עד שוא testimonium falsum. quod in Exodo est, עד שוא. Resp. 1. Nos non negamus, שוא tantundem aliquando valere, ac falsum; sed nunquam aliter, nunquam vanum significare, hoc negamus: atque id probandum Socino fuerat, non illud. 11. Deinde loca adferre debuerat, in quibus habeatur, uti nostri in loco, לשוא, adverbialiter, quod est, in vanum. 111. Negatur consequentia, שוא, & לשוא significat alicubi falsum, ergo sic, & non aliter debet sumi praeceptio tertio.
units.tr: Yet in reciting the ninth commandment in Deut. 5:20, the word is taken in this way: "you shall not bear false witness against your neighbour" [עד שוא], "false witness" [עד שוא], as it stands in Exodus. Reply: first, we do not deny that שוא sometimes has the same force as "false"; what we deny is that it ever means "vain" and never anything else. That was what Socinus ought to have proved, not the other point. Second, he ought to have cited passages where לשוא occurs adverbially, as our people do in the passage, meaning "in vain" [לשוא]. Third, the inference is denied: if שוא and לשוא sometimes mean "false", it does not follow that the third commandment must be understood in that sense and in no other.

units.la: Denique concedit Socinus, ut לשוא in vanum, exponatur in praecepto tertio, sed, sineeffectu, quod tum ad mendacium redit, & aliud nihil est quam merum perjurium; non ut sit, sine necessitate. Quasi non aeque in vanum dici debeat, quod sine necessitate est in se, ac quod sine eventu, & non illud aeque frustraneum sit, ac hoc? & שוא, vel לשוא in allegatis Scripturae locis illud significet, & non illud? Indagetur & proferat locum, ubi in vanum significat perjure, ita ut nequeat significare sine necessitate. Imo non solet Scriptura tam leviter loqui de peccato tanto, ac est perjurium, ut simpliciter vanitatem appellet. Praesertim ubi non alia desunt, quibus hoc facinus designetur, vocabula. Denique nec haec alia est, quantumvis videri velit, expositio a priori, quando in vanum ita significat frustra & sine effectu, ut aliud nihil quam merum perju-rium designet.
units.tr: Finally, Socinus concedes that לשוא [in vain] may be rendered "in vain" in the third commandment, but only "without effect", which comes back to lying, and "is nothing other than plain perjury"; he does not allow that it means "without necessity". As if what is done without necessity is not equally called "in vain" as what is done without result, and as if that is not equally empty as this! Does שוא, or לשוא, in the Scripture passages he cites mean that, and not this? Let him search out and produce a passage where "in vain" means "perjuriously", in such a way that it cannot mean "without necessity". Indeed Scripture does not usually speak so lightly of a sin as grave as perjury that it simply calls it "vanity", especially where other words are not lacking to designate this crime. Finally, however much he may wish it to seem so, this is not an argument from cause to effect, when "in vain" means "fruitlessly and without effect" in such a way that it designates nothing other than plain perjury.

units.la: Praeterea sensus tertii praecepti juramentum temerarium prohibet, quia omnem nominis divini prohibet profanationem. Jam vero non perjurio solo, sed etiam aliis modis, quos omnes vetitos hic oportet intelligere, Dei nomen profanatur, aliterque quam decet, sumitur, & inter eos juramento temerario: ergo & hoc illo prohibetur quoque. Sic, ne dicam Commentatores Christianos, qua antiquos, qua recentes, Judaei exponunt, ut temerarium juramentum vetitum eo videant, doceantque. Quare Graeci transtulerunt, ἐπὶ ματαίῳ. Sic & Philo legit, in initio libri, de Specialibus legibus. Aben Ezra, cujus commentarium in Decalogum Munsterus Latine dedit, rationem & gravitatem peccati praecepto illo prohibiti sic exponit: ורבים חושבים, Sunt hic multi, qui putant non magnam esse transgressionem si quis nomen Dei in vanum acceperit. At ego ostendam eis, quod est major & gravior omnibus sequentibus excessibus. Nam qui est occisor aut adulter, quae quidem magnae sunt transgressiones, non potest omni tempore occidere aut mæchari: est enim in timore [illegible, ~4 letters] ’ּ-ע. Qui autem seipsum assuefecit ad vanas dejerationes, committit uno die innumera juramenta, & usque adeo venit in consuetudinem hujus transgressionis, ut non advertat cum jurat. Et si tu eum corripueris, quare nunc sic jurasti? tunc jurat, quod non juraverit,idque pra nimia consuetudine jurandi. Nam tales, antequam aliquod proferant verbum, præmittunt juramentum, elegantiam putantes esse sermonis sic dejerare. Manifestum est, ipsum loqui de juramentis temerariis. Atque similiter præceptum ex Hebræorum mente exponit Johannes Raymondus Merlinus, in expositione Decalogi, Gallice, quam inscripsit Petro Vireto, ediditque Anno MDLXII. præterquam pag. 47. quod prohibeamur, loqui de Deo irreverenter. pag. 128. utrumque sensum probat vocis Hebreæ, pro re vana, seu nullius fructus; atque pro mendacio. In margine pro illa significatione citat Jerem. II. 29. & XLVI. II. Psalm. CXXVII. I. Pro ista, Deut. v. 9. Psalm. xi. 3. Atque ita in utrumque sensum etiam accepit Paraphrastes Chaldæus.
units.tr: Moreover, the sense of the third commandment forbids rash swearing, because it forbids every profanation of the divine name. Now the name of God is profaned, and taken otherwise than is fitting, not only by perjury but also by other means, all of which must be understood to be forbidden here; and among them is rash swearing. Therefore it is forbidden by this commandment as well. Thus the Jews, not to mention the Christian commentators, both ancient and recent, interpret it so that they see and teach that rash swearing is forbidden. For this reason the Greeks translated it "in vain" [ἐπὶ ματαίῳ]. Philo too reads it so, at the beginning of his book On the Special Laws. Aben Ezra, whose commentary on the Decalogue Münster published in Latin, explains the gravity of the sin forbidden by that commandment as follows: "Some here think [ורבים חושבים] that it is not a great transgression if someone takes the name of God in vain. But I will show them that it is greater and more serious than all the following offences. For the one who kills or commits adultery, which are indeed great transgressions, cannot do so at all times; he is in fear [illegible]. But the one who has accustomed himself to vain oaths commits countless oaths in a single day, and comes so much into the habit of this transgression that he does not notice when he swears. And if you rebuke him, saying, 'Why did you swear just now?', then he swears that he did not swear, and that from excessive habit of swearing. For such people, before they utter any word, put an oath in front, thinking it an elegance of speech to swear in this way." It is plain that he is speaking of rash oaths. In the same way, John Raymond Merlin, in his French exposition of the Decalogue, which he addressed to Pierre Viret and published in 1562, explains the precept according to the mind of the Hebrews, except on p. 47, where we are forbidden to speak irreverently of God. On p. 128 he proves both senses of the Hebrew word, "a vain thing, or one of no profit", and "a lie". In the margin, for the first meaning he cites Jer. 2:29 and 46:11, Ps. 127:1; for the second, Deut. 5:9 and Ps. 11:3. And in this double sense the Chaldee paraphrast also takes it.

units.la: Denique rationes ad hominem proferimus, ex ipsis Adversariis, ut probemus, juramenta temeraria, ex lege etiam olim sub V. Test. prohibita fuisse, nimirum illas, ob quas ipsi ista hodie illicita statuunt. Primum Socinus, præter causas, inquit, à Christo allatas, ob quas juramenta voluntaria sint prohibita, etiam est quod petitur ab ipsius Hebraicæ vocis notatione. Sed hæc vim suam semper, proinde & in V. Test. habuit: Præter causas ante allatas, quæ Christum moverant ad prorsus voluntaria juramenta interdicenda, non videtur silentio prætereundum, ejusmodi juramenta usurpanda non esse, vel ex eo constare posse, quod verbum Hebraicum, quod pejerare significat, est passivæ terminationis: vix enim habent Hebraei, quod tamen apud Græcos & Latinos satis frequens est, verbum aliquod passivæ terminationis, quod absolute & simpliciter sit activum, sed semper tali terminatione passiva, si quis verbi significationem accuratissime perpenderit, aliqua passio significari videtur: unde factum est, ut viri, linguæ Hebraicæ peritissimi, non pauci dixerint, propterea verbi juramenti terminationem apud Hebræos passivam esse, ut hac ratione judicetur, in juramento passionem aliquam, ejus qui jurat, semper esse ac coactionem quandam, aut certe esse debere: qualis est cum necessitate aliqua impellente, non autem plane voluntarie juramenta fiunt. Addit, Tametsi id alioqui, in ipsa lege expressum non fuerit. Sentiens videlicet, hoc adversus sententiam suam adferri posse. Sed, quamvis hæc vox in tertio præcepto non occurrat, satis autem per totum V. Test., nullum est dubium, quum quæ de juramento dicenda vel observanda fuerunt, ad tertium pertineant, si sola notatio vocis nulla probet juramenta, nisi quæ necessaria, & non alia, ergo temeraria olim non fuisse licita. Neque hoc argumentum, quod ex ipsius Adversarii petimus observatione, aliquis facile eludet.
units.tr: Finally, we bring forward arguments against the man himself, drawn from our adversaries, to prove that rash oaths were also forbidden under the law even in the Old Testament, namely those very grounds on which they now declare such oaths unlawful. First, Socinus says that, besides the causes alleged by Christ for which voluntary oaths are forbidden, there is also one that is sought from the very meaning of the Hebrew word. But this has always had its force, and therefore also in the Old Testament: Besides the causes alleged above, which moved Christ to forbid wholly voluntary oaths, it does not seem to be passed over in silence that oaths of this kind ought not to be used, and this may be clear from the fact that the Hebrew verb which means "to swear falsely" has a passive ending. For the Hebrews hardly have any verb with a passive ending which is nonetheless absolutely and simply active, as is quite frequent in Greek and Latin; but if one weighs the meaning of the verb most carefully, some passivity always seems to be signified by such a passive ending. Hence it has come about that not a few men most skilled in the Hebrew tongue have said that the verb for swearing has a passive ending among the Hebrews, so that by this reasoning it is judged that in an oath there is always some passivity in the one who swears, and some compulsion, or at least that there ought to be; such as arises from some compelling necessity, and oaths are not made quite voluntarily. He adds, although this is not expressed in the law itself. Evidently he senses that this could be brought against his opinion. But although this word does not occur in the third commandment, it occurs often enough throughout the Old Testament, and there is no doubt that whatever was to be said or observed about oaths pertains to the third commandment. If the bare meaning of the word proves no oaths except necessary ones, and no others, then rash oaths were not lawful even in former times. Nor will anyone easily evade this argument, which we draw from the observation of the adversary himself.

units.la: Addamus alias insuper rationes, quas adscribunt Socinian[?], quare vetita nunc sint juramenta levia & temeraria: videamusque, annon rationes sint juris perpetui & antiqui, quæ etiam viguerint sub V. Test. consequenter illa
units.tr: Let us add, moreover, other reasons which the Socinians give for why light and rash oaths are now forbidden; and let us see whether these reasons are not of perpetual and ancient force, which also held under the Old Testament, and so whether they were then also forbidden.

units.la: [The bottom line of the page, "etiam", is the catchword and is not repeated here.] etiam tum fuerint, prohibita. Smalcius, lib. de Divinit. Christi,cap v. Præcipit lex, ne nomen Domini in falsum, vel vanum assumamus: perfecit eam & implevit D. Jesus, dum nec in rebus veris illud assumere vel invocare permittit (nisi tale quid à nobis exigat gloria Dei) ut ita nomen Dei apud nos sit sacrosanctum & nunquam vilescat: & ne falsè jurando, perjurare etiam assuescamus. Studio dixit, in falsum vel vanum, non in vanum vel falsum, ob rationem quam modo ex Socino audivimus. Verùm hoc missò, si nihil agendum unquam pietas dictaverit & religio, nisi quod à nobis exigat Dei gloria, & nomen Dei semper apud populum suum debu[?] erit esse sacrosanctum, vilescere autem nunquam, & videre debuerint homines, ne, sæpe jurando, pejerare assuescerent, ergo & semper, & olim etiam cavenda fuerunt juramenta temeraria: Sed verùm prius: ergo. Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. xiii. sic ratiocinatur: Causa porro, cur Christus tanta cum sollicitudine à juramentis voluntariis nos dehortetur, duæ potissimum sunt. Prima est, ne summi illius omnium rerum Domini sanctissimum nomen profanum apud nos habeatur, neve nimiâ rei ipsius familiaritate decepti putemus, nos per lusum & jocum cum Deo tanquam socio nostro agere posse, utpote quem, cum libeat, quèamus[?] tanquam dictorum nostrorum testem advocare. Altera causa est, ne sæpe temereque jurando, in perjurium aliquando maximo malo nostro incidamus.
units.tr: [The bottom line of the page, "etiam", is the catchword and is not repeated here.] … also at that time forbidden. Smalcius, in his book on the Divinity of Christ, ch. 5: The law commands that we do not take up the name of the Lord in falsehood or in vanity. Lord Jesus fulfilled and perfected it, while he does not permit that name to be taken up or invoked even in true matters (unless the glory of God requires something of the kind from us), so that the name of God may be held sacred among us and never become cheap, and so that we may not become accustomed to perjury by swearing falsely. He deliberately said "in falsehood or in vanity", not "in vanity or falsehood", for the reason we have just heard from Socinus. But setting this aside: if piety and religion have never dictated that anything be done except what the glory of God requires of us, and the name of God must always be held sacred among his people and never be cheapened, and men ought to see that by swearing often they do not become accustomed to perjury, then rash oaths must always and also formerly have been avoided. But the former is true; therefore the latter. Volkelius, in book 4, ch. 13, reasons thus: Moreover, there are chiefly two reasons why Christ so earnestly dissuades us from voluntary oaths. The first is that the most holy name of that highest Lord of all things should not be held profane among us, nor should we, deceived by too great familiarity with the thing itself, think that we may deal with God in play and jest as with a companion, since we may call him, whenever we please, as a witness of our words. The second reason is that by swearing often and rashly we may at some time fall into perjury, to our very great harm. But these reasons are perpetual, and were to be taught and observed not only under the New Testament but also under the Old, from Moses and the Prophets, and indeed by all the pious. For as regards the first reason, that the most holy name of that highest Lord of all things…

units.la: At istæ causæ perpetuæ, & non N. solum, sed & V. Test. non à Christo demum, sed à Mose & Prophetis, omnibusque adeo piis docendæ semper fuerunt & observandæ. Nam, quod ad primam rationem, ne summi illius omnium rerum Domini sanctissimum nomen profanum apud nos habeatur, quum per juramenta temeraria Dei nomen profanetur, & hoc prohibitum speciali gravique adeo præcepto fuerit, non illa quoque prohibita & illicita fuisse dicemus? Tumne Dei sanctissimum nomen profanare tutò licuit, quod ejusmodi juramentis profanari credis & lædi? An tum licuit cum Deo tanquam cum socio per lusum & jocum agere, vel id, unde hoc facile putetur aliquando licuisse? annon æque cavendum tum perjurium, omnesque ejus committendi occasiones & causæ fuerunt, æque ac hodie? ergo & temeraria juramenta. Quæ si interdicta tum, ergo non Christus ea demum tamquam nova præcepta protulit, legique addidit.
units.tr: But these reasons are permanent, and they have always had to be taught and observed by all the godly, not only under the New Testament, and not only from Christ, but from Moses and the Prophets. As for the first reason, that the most holy name of the Lord of all things not be profaned among us: since God's name is profaned by rash oaths, and this was forbidden by a special and weighty precept, shall we not say that those oaths were also forbidden and unlawful? Was it then lawful to profane God's most holy name safely by such oaths, as you believe they profane and harm it? Or was it then lawful to deal with God in play and jest, as with a companion, or to do something from which it might easily be thought that this was once lawful? Was not perjury, and every occasion and cause of committing it, to be guarded against then just as much as today? Therefore rash oaths were also forbidden then. If these were forbidden then, then Christ did not put them forward as new precepts and add them to the law.

units.la: Quinto loco venit verf. 38. de talione, ubi Christus dicit: audivistis quod dictum est, oculum pro oculo, & dentem pro dente, ego vero dico vobis, &c. Ubi primò iterum observat Socinus, non hic proponi à Christo verba & sensum legis Mosaicæ nude & simpliciter, sed cum ejus sinistra expositione, quam vulgò homines faciebant: contra quam Christus se opponat. Quod causam & disputationem nostram valde juvat. Dicit quidem etiam, Christum quoque legem Mosis corrigere, sed non eam solam, at & malam ejus acceptionem: hoc autem pro nobis est, quod fatetur, Christum hic respicere legis malam interpretationem, adversas quam disputet. Pag. 143. Hic similiter Christus, sicut quando de divortio egit, non dixit, dictum fuisse antiquis, sed simpliciter, dictum fuisse; fortasse ob eam causam, quod etiamsi verba ista, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente, in ipsa Mosis lege legantur, tamen poterant alio sensu accipi, & fortasse accipiebantur, quam eo quo antiquis dicta fuerant, quod scilicet, ubi in Mosis lege agebatur de pœna talionis à Magistratu ipso ipso infligenda, essent, qui carnis sua suasionem secuti, intelligerent ea significare, quod unicuique liceret malum pro malo reddere, modo malum, quod redderetur, esset par; hoc est nihilo majus eo quod acceptum fuisset: quam falsam & a carnali sensu proficiscentem verborum Mosis interpretationem, una cum ipsa re, quae a Mose revera verbis istis permit-tebatur, satis copiose refellit Christus iis, quae statim subjungit. Et pag. 144. Videtur sententiendum, Christum hoc loco dicta sua opponere verbis illis oculum pro oculo, &c. non quatenus simpliciter in Mosis lege scripta inveniuntur, quae lex, ut supra dictum fuit, omnino non privatis, sed magistratui lata est, seu mavis universo populo; sed quatenus a multis, ut supra indicatum est, ita accipiebantur, ut liceret unicuique privatim talionis poenam repetere.
units.tr: Fifthly comes verse 38, on retaliation, where Christ says: You have heard that it was said, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth; but I say to you, etc. Here Socinus first observes again that Christ does not set forth the words and sense of the Mosaic law simply and nakedly, but together with the perverse explanation which people commonly gave, and against which Christ sets himself. This greatly helps our cause and argument. He does say indeed that Christ also corrects the law of Moses, but not that alone; he corrects also its bad interpretation. But this is on our side: he admits that Christ here has in view a bad interpretation of the law, against which he argues. P. 143. Here, as when he spoke about divorce, Christ did not say "it was said to the ancients," but simply "it was said"; perhaps for this reason, that even though those words, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, are read in the very law of Moses, nevertheless they could be understood in another sense, and perhaps were understood, than that in which they had been said to the ancients. That is, where the law of Moses dealt with the penalty of retaliation to be inflicted by the magistrate himself, there were those who, following the persuasion of their own flesh, understood it to mean that each person might return evil for evil, provided the evil returned was equal, that is, no greater than what had been received. Christ thoroughly refutes this false interpretation of Moses' words, which arose from a carnal sense, together with the thing itself which Moses in fact permitted in those words, by what he immediately adds. And on p. 144: It seems that Christ in this place sets his own words against those words, an eye for an eye, etc. not insofar as they are simply found written in the law of Moses, a law which, as was said above, was given not to private persons but to the magistrate, or if you prefer, to the whole people; but insofar as, as was indicated above, they were understood by many in such a way that each person might privately exact the penalty of retaliation.

units.la: Denique, pag. 145. Verum ut huic objectioni respondeamus, considerandum est, cum Christus, ut antea diximus, ipsa verba legis recitet, & nihil prorsus eis addat quibus sua dicta opponat, nulla pacto verisimile esse, quin ipsam legem aliquo modo corrigat; quamvis fieri possit, ut simul falsam interpretationem, quae in populo vigeret, corrigere voluerit.
units.tr: Finally, p. 145: But to answer this objection, it must be considered that since Christ, as we said before, recites the very words of the law and adds nothing at all to them against which he sets his own teaching, it is in no way likely that he does not in some way correct the law itself; although it may be that he also wished to correct the false interpretation which prevailed among the people.

units.la: Sic ergo & nos quoque dicimus, quod Christus hoc in loco, & in aliis, quamvis verba proponat lege Mosis contenta, non ipsam tamen, sed ejus interpretationem respicit, impetritque, quam alii male dabant. Sic hoc loco, non impugnat, quod scriptum in lege erat, oculum pro oculo, & dentem pro dente, sed temerariam falsamque ejus, quae vulgo obtinebat, acceptionem, quasi cuilibet inde liceret pro appetitu & vindicta cupiditate oculum pro oculo suo, & dentem pro dente, ab altero repetere. Quod Moses neque dixit, neque permisit. Atque sic de alio Moses; de alio Christus agit: proindeque inter illos oppositio nulla constitui debet. Deinde non modo vindictam & ulciscendi libidinem non probat Moses, vel imperat, non illis verbis; sed quae dicit, ad Magistratus, & judicum officium referuntur, non ad affectus & jus quorumcunque. Uti ex inspectione locorum manifestum est. Exod. xxi. 22. & dabit בַּפְּלִלִים per judices. verf. 24. 25. Levit xxiv. 19. quemadmodum fecit כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה לּוֹ sic fiet ei. 20. fracturam pro fractura, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente &c. Deut. xix. 18. & accurate indagabuntur judices. 19. & facietis ei, quemadmodum cogitarat facere fratri suo. 21. Neque parcet oculus vester, animam pro anima, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente, manum pro manu, pedem pro pede. Haec de officio Magistratus di-cta, pro administranda in fontes aequa justitia, quilibet ad se male trahebat, & ad affectus vindictae: cui se opponit Christus. Socinus, pag. 144. Nam, quamvis verba ipsius legis non ad privatos, sed ad Magistratum directa sint, qui jubetur in eafibus illis, qui ibi recensentur, poenam talionis ab eo qui laeserit, repetere. 111. Nam etiam vindicta & ulciscendi cupido sub V. Test. mala fuit & prohibita. Ut neutiquam demum a Christo, tanquam novum praeceptum, legi fuisse additum putandum sit. Unde Jacobus Patriarcha, de filiis suis Simeone ad Levi, & exercita contra Sichemitas ultione, Genef. xlix. 5. 6. 7. Simeon & Levi fratres instrumenta violentiae sunt מְכֵרֹתֵיהֶם, vel, gladii, machaerae ipsorum, vel negotia, & negotiationes ipsorum. Non veniat anima mea in arcanum ipsorum, neque honor meus jungatur ipsorum congregationi: quia in ira sua occiderunt virum, & in petulantia sua abripuerunt bovem. Maledicta ira ipsorum, quod fortis, & furor ipsorum, quod durus. Omnia eo tendunt, ut vindictam ipsorum, & hinc orta mala irae, furoris, petulantiae, homihomicidii exaggeret sanctus Parens, & execretur. Illa ergo omnia, ita etiam vindicta, illo tempore pro peccatis habita, & maledicta fuerunt, utcunque lex Mosis nondum fuisset promulgata. Quod si enim lege naturae illud constet, multo magis ex lege scripta. Vindicta nihil est, quam species irae: haec, inimicitiae: quam prohibitam fuisse semper, neque unquam pro bono censitam vel virtute, nescio an ullus ignoret. Levit. xix. 18. 19. non habebis odio fratrem tuum in corde tuo. לא תקום [?], non ulciscēris, neque servabis iram contra filios populi tui, sed diliges socium tuum sicuti temetipsum, ego Jehova. Odium prohibitum, ergo & vindicta; nam hanc odii vel speciem, vel gradum aliquem majorem Socinus definit, in Matth. v. pag. 168. qui vindictā cupiditatem, aut saltem odium adversus inimicum suum retinent. Deut. xxxii. 35. Mea est ultio, & ego retribuam eis. Ad quod Apostolus provocat, Rom. xii. 19. Scriptum est enim, mea est ultio, & ego retribuam, dicit Dominus. adde Jerem. li. 36. Prov. xx. 22. Ne dicas אשלמה רע [?] retribuam malum, expectā Dominum, & salvabit te. Prov. xxiv. 29. Ne dicas, quemadmodum fecit mihi, ita faciam ei, reddam cuique secundum opus suum. Jezech. xxv. 12. Sic loquitur Dominus Deus. Quia fecit Edom בנקום נקם [?] ultionem de domo Jehuda, & peccaverunt delinquendo, & ulti fuerunt de eis: ideo, sic inquit Dominus Deus, convertam manum meam contra Edom. Ergo jam olim, & in V. Test. neque nunc demum a Christo in N. & singularis praecepti additamento supra legem, vindicta pro peccato censita, & prohibita fuit. Quare etiam nihil hoc loco Christus legi de novo addidit, solummodo vindictam execratus [?] fuit, olim non minus doctrina legis & V. Test damnatam, sed quam malā legis expositione sibimet temere indulgebant homines, & putabant licitam.
units.tr: So we too say that Christ in this place, and in others, although he sets out words contained in the law of Moses, nevertheless looks not to the law itself but to its interpretation, and attacks the interpretation which others gave badly. So in this place he does not attack what was written in the law, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, but the rash and false understanding of it which was commonly held, as if anyone might from that take back, according to his appetite and his desire for vengeance, an eye for his eye and a tooth for his tooth from another. Moses neither said nor permitted this. Thus Moses deals with one thing and Christ with another, and therefore no opposition should be set up between them. Next, Moses does not approve or command vengeance or the lust for revenge in those words; rather, what he says is referred to the office of the magistrate and of the judges, not to the feelings and rights of anyone at all. This is clear from looking at the passages. Exod. 21:22: and he shall give [בַּפְּלִלִים] through the judges. Verses 24–25. Lev. 24:19: as he has done [כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה לּוֹ], so shall it be done to him. Verse 20: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, etc. Deut. 19:18: and the judges shall make careful inquiry. Verse 19: and you shall do to him as he had planned to do to his brother. Verse 21: Your eye shall not spare: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot. These things were said about the office of the magistrate, for administering justice fairly in the courts; each person twisted them badly for his own purposes and for his desire for vengeance, and it is against this that Christ sets himself. Socinus, p. 144: For although the words of the law itself are directed not to private persons but to the magistrate, who is commanded in those cases listed there to exact the penalty of retaliation from the one who has done the injury. Verse 111: For vengeance and the desire for revenge were also evil and forbidden under the Old Testament. So it must not be thought that Christ added this to the law as a new precept. Hence the patriarch Jacob, about his sons Simeon and Levi, and the vengeance they carried out against the Shechemites, Gen. 49:5–7: Simeon and Levi are brothers; instruments of violence [מְכֵרֹתֵיהֶם], or swords, their knives, or their dealings and transactions. Let my soul not come into their secret, nor let my honour be joined to their assembly, because in their anger they slew a man, and in their wantonness they hamstrung an ox. Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their fury, for it is harsh. All these things tend to this: that the holy father magnifies and curses their vengeance, and the evils that arose from their anger, fury, wantonness and manslaughter. All these things, therefore, including vengeance, were regarded as sins and were cursed at that time, although the law of Moses had not yet been promulgated. For if this is established by the law of nature, much more is it established by the written law. Vengeance is nothing but a form of anger, and anger is a form of enmity; I do not know whether anyone is ignorant that this has always been forbidden and never regarded as good or as a virtue. Lev. 19:17–18: you shall not hate your brother in your heart; [לא תקום]: you shall not take vengeance, nor keep anger against the children of your people, but you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am the LORD. Hatred is forbidden, therefore vengeance too; for Socinus defines this as a species or some greater degree of hatred, in Matt. 5, p. 168: those who retain the desire for vengeance, or at least hatred, against their enemy. Deut. 32:35: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them. The Apostle appeals to this, Rom. 12:19: For it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. Add Jer. 51:36; Prov. 20:22: Do not say, I will repay evil [אשלמה רע]; wait for the Lord, and he will save you. Prov. 24:29: Do not say, As he has done to me, so will I do to him; I will render to each according to his work. Ezek. 25:12: Thus says the Lord God: Because Edom acted in vengeance against the house of Judah [בנקום נקם], and they sinned by offending, and took vengeance on them; therefore, thus says the Lord God, I will stretch out my hand against Edom. Therefore already long ago, under the Old Testament, vengeance was regarded as sin and forbidden, and it was not first made so by Christ in the New Testament as an addition to the law in a single special precept. For this reason too Christ added nothing new to the law in this place; he only cursed vengeance, which was condemned no less by the doctrine of the law and the Old Testament, but which men, through a bad interpretation of the law, rashly indulged in for themselves and thought lawful.

units.la: Namque Socinus non diffitetur, hoc loco non resistentiam inimici, non jus sua repetendi vel retinendi a Magistratu, per Christum prohiberi, sed vindictam solam: & comparative intelligendum esse quod dicitur, potius quam ut in vindictam concedamus, sinamus injuriam nobis inferri ac damnum, alapam etiam alteram &c. Quare dicit, pag. 148. Deinde intelligendum est, in ipsis etiam hujus vitae incommodis, qua nobis vel inferre conetur, non omnem resistentiam a Christo prohiberi; sed illam, qua vindictam, vindictave, seu ultionis speciem conjunctam habet. Pag. 150. Nec sane ad propositum ipsius Christi quicquam talis praeceptio pertineret, quod satis ostendimus, eam resistentiam prohibere, qua ultionem aliquam secum conjunctam habeat. Pag. 149. Jam hoc ipsum primum exemplum satis nos docere potest, si tum iis conjungatur, qua alibi legimus, Christi verba, non simpliciter, ut sonant, accipienda esse, sed eo sensu, quem diximus; nimirum, ut intelligatur non plane atque absolute ista praecipere, sed jubere ut ista potius fiant, quam ut vindicta sive ultio ulla quaeratur; seu mavis, si fieri non possit, ut vindicta sive ultio non quaeratur, nisi si quis ista faciat, qua Christi praeceptis continentur, tunc debere ista fieri. Pag. 164. Ut hac ratione apertissime ostenderet, quantopere nobis cavendum sit ab omni ultione, cum tam grave damnum nos subire velit potius, quam vindictam nullam quaerere. Eadem habet, in epist. II. ad Statorium.
units.tr: Socinus does not deny that in this place Christ forbids not the resisting of an enemy, nor the claiming or keeping of one's right through the Magistrate, but only vengeance. He also holds that what is said should be understood comparatively, meaning that we should rather let an injury and loss be done to us, and even a second blow to the face, than grant vengeance. So he says on p. 148: Next, it must be understood that, even in the discomforts of this life which someone tries to inflict on us, Christ does not forbid every resistance, but only that which has vengeance, or some form of revenge, attached to it. On p. 150: Nor indeed would such a precept pertain at all to Christ's own purpose, which we have sufficiently shown, namely that it forbids that resistance which has some revenge attached to it. On p. 149: Now this very first example can teach us well enough, if we add to it what we read elsewhere: Christ's words are not to be taken simply as they sound, but in the sense we have stated. That is, it is to be understood that he does not prescribe these things absolutely, but bids that they be done rather than that any vengeance or revenge be sought; or, if you prefer, that vengeance or revenge is not to be sought unless someone does these things which are contained in Christ's precepts, and then these things ought to be done. On p. 164: so that by this reasoning he might most clearly show how carefully we must beware of all revenge, since he wishes us rather to suffer so grave a loss than to seek any vengeance. He says the same in his second letter to Statorius.

units.la: Ut autem videatur ostendere Socinus, quid hoc sit in sermone Christi, quod legi opponat, inquit, in V. Test. concessum fuisse, ut per Magistratum quis vindictam peteret & ultionem, hoc autem in V. Test. à Christo prohiberi. Pag. 148. Necesse est inspicere, quibus Mosaica legis verbis Christus sua dicta opponat, & qua occasione ea praecipiat, qua praecipit. Jam hoc in loco certum est, eum sua dicta opponere Mosaica legi, qua ultionem per Magistratum concedebat, & occasione talis ultionis prohibenda, dicta sunt, sine dubio, à Christo omnia, qua toto hoc loco praecipit. Pag. 152. Sequitur tertium Christi exemplum, ejus quod facere jubet, minime id permittens, quod tacite colligebatur ex ipsa lege Mosis, ut scilicet liceret per Magistratum talionis poenam repetere. Pag. 143. Jam vero id, quod unicuique lege ista sua Moses non obscure permittebat, illud erat, ut liceret, unicuique per Magistratum poenam talionis repetere. Causa sententiae suae eadem est, quae in superioribus, nempe quod alias non posset assignare, in quo Christus legem correxerit auxeritque, quod sibi ostendendum quovis modo, quo jure quave injuria, existimat. Non ergo ita censet, quod videatur rei veritate ad id adigi, sed sua opinione, & hypothesi, cui constitutum [illegible, ~9 letters]. Habe & hic, quemadmodum in argumento praecedenti, ipsa, & expressa ejus verba. Pag. 145. Jam correctio ipsius Mosaica legis in eo est, vel potius in eo omnino esse debet (alioquin nulla correctio effet) quod non liceat per Magistratum, cui lex illa data fuerat, talionis poenam repetere. Hoc est, Mosem & Christum inflectere ad sua placita, non se suamque sententiam illis submittere. Corrigere legem, quia tu corrigendam existimes, non quod corrigenda sit. Et ubi semel dixeris, corrigi à Christo legem, correctionem illam quocunque modo & ubicunque ponere, ne temere illud dixisse aliquando videaris. Hoc autem est, vim Scripturae inferre, eamque pro lubitu quovis trahere, non autem explicare.
units.tr: In order to appear to show what Christ's saying is, which he sets against the Law, he says that in the Old Testament it was permitted to seek vengeance and retribution through the Magistrate, but that Christ forbids this in the Old Testament. On p. 148: It is necessary to examine against which words of the Mosaic law Christ sets his own sayings, and on what occasion he gives the precepts he gives. Now in this place it is certain that he sets his sayings against the Mosaic law, which allowed vengeance through the Magistrate, and that all the things he teaches throughout this passage were undoubtedly spoken by Christ on the occasion of such vengeance being forbidden. On p. 152: There follows the third example of Christ, of what he bids us do, in no way permitting that which was tacitly inferred from the law of Moses itself, namely that it was lawful to seek the penalty of retaliation through the Magistrate. On p. 143: Now indeed, what Moses did not obscurely permit to each person under that law was that each might seek the penalty of retaliation through the Magistrate. The reason for his opinion is the same as in the earlier passages, namely that otherwise he cannot point out in what respect Christ corrected and enlarged the law, which he thinks must be shown by some means, whether by right or wrong. So he does not judge in this way because the truth of the matter compels him to, but because of his own opinion and hypothesis, to which the [illegible, about 9 letters]. Here too, as in the previous argument, take his very words as expressed. On p. 145: Now the correction of the Mosaic law itself lies in this, or rather must wholly lie in this (otherwise there would be no correction), that it is not lawful for a person to seek the penalty of retaliation through the Magistrate to whom that law was given. That is, he bends Moses and Christ to his own pleasures, and does not submit himself and his opinion to them. He corrects the law because you think it should be corrected, not because it needs correction. And once you have said that the law was corrected by Christ, you must set that correction down in whatever way and wherever you can, lest you seem to have said it rashly. But this is to do violence to the force of Scripture, and to drag it about at will, rather than to explain it.

units.la: Lex praescripsit quidem Magistratui, talionem exercere, sed pro justitia, non pro affectu, vel vindicta. Privatis etiam concessum, jus suum per Magistratum experiri; non tamen ex vindicta, vel ulciscendi libidine: qua lex simpliciter, & omnibus ac singulis, qua Magistratui, qua populo interdixit. Quare distinguenda sunt, jus per Magistratum prosequaris tuum, an vindictam: illud licitum, non hoc. Dein, ut Magistratus justitiam exerceat, atque haec talionem praescribat; an propriam vindictam, & ulciscendi cupidinem quisquam sequatur: quod tam injustum, atque illud justum est & necessarium. Denique, quando distingui solet in vindictam publicam, ac privatam, non illa eo modo conceditur vel probatur, quasi vel aliquid propriae vindictae ea palliaretur vel indulgeretur; aut alius quaeterquam in causam affectus, & non in personam, permitteretur: sed nihil illa intelligitur, quam justitiae & aequitatis distributio, citra privatum respectum, affectum, aut vindictam ullam, à Magistratu, (qui θεοῦ διάκονός ἐστι[?]. Rom. xiii[?]. 4.) ad rationem, ac paritatem delicti ferenda, in justa rei causaeque talione. Nullo autem modo, nullibique, sive à Magistratu, sive populo, aut privato quocunque vindicta, simpliciter tendens in malum personae, toleratur aut probatur.
units.tr: The law did indeed prescribe to the Magistrate that he should exercise retaliation, but for the sake of justice, not out of passion or vengeance. It was also granted to private persons to pursue their right through the Magistrate, but not out of vengeance or lust for revenge; the law forbade this simply, and to all and each, both to the Magistrate and to the people. Therefore one must distinguish between pursuing your right through the Magistrate and seeking vengeance: the former is lawful, the latter is not. Again, there is a difference between the Magistrate exercising justice and prescribing this retaliation, and anyone pursuing his own vengeance and desire to take revenge: the one is as unjust as the other is just and necessary. Finally, when it is customary to distinguish between public and private vengeance, the former is not permitted or approved in such a way as if it cloaked or indulged some private vengeance, or were allowed for any cause other than the offence, and not for the person. Rather it means nothing else than the distribution of justice and equity, without any private regard, passion or vengeance, by the Magistrate (who is God's minister [θεοῦ διάκονός ἐστι], Rom. 13.4), to render a penalty matching the offence and its equal, in a just retaliation for the matter and cause. But in no way, and nowhere, whether by the Magistrate, the people, or any private person, is vengeance that aims simply at the harm of another person tolerated or approved.

units.la: Sed, erat, inquit Socinus, omnino repetitio ista talionis, in iis rebus, qua expresse
units.tr: But, says Socinus, that repetition of retaliation was altogether

units.la: Tom. 2. in lege nominantur, & à Christo ex parte commemorantur, mera prorsus ultio. Hoc ego nego. 1. Non loquitur lex de repetitione talionis, sed de poenâ talionis, ex justitiâ, à Magistratu infligenda. 11. Deinde, uti diximus, & punitio illa à Magistratu facta, & repetitio juris sui per Magistratum, vel etiam juris publici, fieri potest, debetque absque ullo ulciscendi vitio. 11. Alia est ultio sui, alia ultio juris, vel injuriae, aut damni facti, quam publica postulat justitia. Haec bona est, illa mala. Neque illam prosequi licet, uti istam.
units.tr: Vol. 2. a mere revenge, in those matters which are expressly named in the law and partly recorded by Christ. I deny this. (1) The law does not speak of the repetition of retaliation, but of the penalty of retaliation, to be inflicted by the Magistrate out of justice. (2) Next, as we have said, that punishment carried out by the Magistrate, and the repetition of one's right through the Magistrate, or even of public right, can and ought to be done without any fault of vengeance. (3) There is one kind of revenge against oneself, another revenge for a right or for an injury or loss suffered, which public justice demands. The latter is good, the former evil. Nor is it lawful to pursue the former as the latter.

units.la: Addit, erat mera prorsus ultio, sine ulla alia certa utilitate vel commodo ea repetentis, quam quod videret eum qui se laeserat, eodem damno sive incommodo affectum, quo ipse ab eo fuerat. pag. 148. Resp. Negatur, nullam aliam hic utilitatem spectari potuisse, quam privatam: publica erat, cujus intuitu illa fiebant. 11. Negatur etiam, cum ἀπηχθεικακίᾳ[?] alicui videre licuisse, aut oblectatione, poenam talionis adversus alium exercerí. 111. Sed poena illa publica, uti debuit, à Magistratu inflicta, timorem accendebat Dei, per ministros judices poenam & talionem justam infligentis. Quod aliud certe commodum est, & utilitas alia, quam simpliciter videre aliquem eo damno affectum, quod tibi destinarat.
units.tr: He adds: it was a mere revenge, without any other certain advantage or benefit to the one seeking it, than that he saw the one who had wronged him afflicted with the same loss or inconvenience by which he himself had been affected by him. p. 148. Reply: it is denied that any other advantage could have been looked for here than a private one; it was a public advantage, for the sake of which those things were done. (2) It is also denied that anyone could have seen, out of ill-will, or with delight, the penalty of retaliation being carried out against another. (3) But that public penalty, as it ought to be, inflicted by the Magistrate, kindled the fear of God, who through his judges and ministers inflicts a just penalty and retaliation. That is surely another benefit and a different advantage, and not simply seeing someone affected by the loss which he had intended for you.

units.la: Quibus accedit, quod ipse Socinus non negat, licere cuivis jus suum prosequi apud Magistratum, & pro damno sibi resarciendo apud illum instare. Pag. 150. Nimirum si quis velit, ut non pauci faciunt, ex verbis ipsius Christi concludere, non licere cuiquam, etiam repetendi sui causa, judicio agere; quod nimis valde absurdum esset, cum repetitiones per ipsum Magistratum fiant dentur, in quibus is, a quo repetitur, nullum damnum sentit: & nisi illa fiant, quispiam maxime laeditur, tum ipse, tum ii qui ejus cura sunt commissi, ab ipsoque alii debent: nec ulla prorsus apparere potest causa, cur Christus ejusmodi repetitiones fieri interdixerit. Pag. 152. Ideoque eam, sicut menti Christi plane adversatur, quae est, omnem vindictam, etiam necessariam, prohibere, sic nihil habere commune cum accusatione illa, in qua nihil praeterea quaeritur, quam rerum sibi acceptarum, aut quoquo modo interversarum, seu retentarum nuda ac simplex repetitio. Pag. 153. Non est autem dubium, quin is, cui vis aliqua infertur, & liber cum sit, ad aliquid faciendum vi cogitur, possit per Magistratum suam hanc injuriam & damnum ulcisci; & quin ejusmodi res naturaliter unumquemque movere soleat, ad vindictam molestia sibi illata quarendam: propterea recte exemplo hoc usus est Christus cum vellet & à publicâ & à privatâ vindictâ, sed potissimum à publica, homines hoc loco deterrere. Epistolâ 11. ad Statorium, pag. 386. Hoc vero nihil commune habet cum sui per Magistratum repetitione. Suum autem appello pecuniam remve suam, & damni injuste accepti (ut sic dixerum) refarcitionem seu compensationem. Atque hoc nos dicimus, licere apud Magistratum cuivis experiri pro damno & incommodo sibi resarciendo, non ex privata aliquâ, aut sui vindictâ & ulciscendi libidine, sed ad prosequendum causam & rem suam, absque sinistro in personam affectu, judicium Deo, ejusque judicium administranti Magistratui, committentes.
units.tr: To this must be added that Socinus himself does not deny that anyone may pursue his right before the Magistrate and press before him for compensation for his loss. On p. 150: Indeed, if someone wishes, as not a few do, to conclude from Christ's own words that it is not lawful for anyone to bring a suit, even for the sake of recovering what is his own; which would be exceedingly absurd, since recoveries are made through the Magistrate himself, in which the one from whom recovery is made feels no loss; and unless these are made, someone is greatly harmed, both himself and those committed to his care, and others owe debts to him: nor can any reason at all appear why Christ should have forbidden such recoveries to be made. On p. 152: Therefore, just as it is wholly contrary to the mind of Christ to forbid all vengeance, even necessary vengeance, so it has nothing in common with that accusation in which nothing is sought beyond the bare and simple recovery of things that were received by him, or in some way taken away or retained. On p. 153: There is no doubt that the one to whom some force is done, and who, being free, is compelled by violence to do something, can through the Magistrate avenge this injury and loss; and that things of this kind naturally move everyone to seek vengeance for the trouble done to him. Therefore Christ rightly used this example when he wished to deter men from both public and private vengeance, but chiefly from public vengeance. In his second letter to Statorius, p. 386: But this has nothing in common with the recovery of one's own through the Magistrate. I call "one's own" my money or my property, and the restitution or compensation (as I may say) for a loss unjustly suffered. And this is what we say: it is lawful for anyone to seek through the Magistrate compensation for his loss and inconvenience, not out of any private passion or lust for vengeance and revenge, but to pursue his cause and his own matter, without an ill-will towards the person, committing the judgment to God and to the Magistrate who administers his judgment.

units.la: Quod vero praeterea Socinus docet, non licere Magistratui Christiano poenam talionis exercere, pag. 156. quod vero attinet ad alterum, utrum, scilicet, possit nihilominus Christianus Magistratus poenam illam talionis inferre; dicendum omnino videtur, eum non posse, cum poena ista omnino cum Christiana charitate pugnet, cumque prudentia, quam Christiana religio nos abundantius docuit, quam Mosaica. Quid enim minus secundum charitatem, minusve prudenter videatur esse factum, quam poenam inferre, qua pertinere debeat ad emendationem, vel compensationem damni ab eo qui punitur accepti; ex qua interim is, qui damnum acceperit, nullum commodum revera sentiat, nullamve damni sibi illati compensationem aut imminutionem? ad id respondeo.
units.tr: As for the further point that Socinus teaches, namely that a Christian magistrate may not exercise the punishment of retaliation (p. 156): as for the other question, namely whether a Christian magistrate may nonetheless inflict that punishment of retaliation, it seems altogether necessary to say that he cannot, since that punishment is wholly opposed to Christian charity, and to the prudence which the Christian religion has taught us more abundantly than the Mosaic religion did. For what could seem less in accordance with charity, or less prudent, than to inflict a punishment which ought to serve the amendment or the compensation of the damage received by the one who is punished, when meanwhile the one who suffered the damage feels no real advantage from it, and no compensation or lessening of the harm done to him? To this I reply.

units.la: I. Negari, poenam talionis non pertinere ad emendationem, vel ad compensationem damni ab eo, qui punitur, accepti: quando talio in pecuniariis, æque ac criminalibus, institui potest. II. Deinde omnis poena tendit ad emendationem rei. III. Respiciendum est bonum publicum, quod juvatur maxime, cum omni præstatione justitiæ, tum imprimis debitæ talionis: ut norint homines, in quod suo peccato incurrant, & propter quod eo abstinere magis debeant, si vitam pro vita, oculum pro oculo debere sciant qui criminis ejusmodi se constituunt reos. Metus peccandi inter illa est, citra quæ Resp. consistere nequit: & propter quem retinendum augendumque poenæ illæ cum valeant, si adhibeantur, tum certe non exiguo fructu afficiunt Rempublicam.
units.tr: I. I deny that the punishment of retaliation does not serve the amendment, or the compensation of the damage received from the one who is punished, since retaliation can be imposed in pecuniary cases just as much as in criminal ones. II. Furthermore, every punishment aims at the amendment of the offender. III. Regard must be had to the public good, which is chiefly served, along with every exercise of justice, and above all by due retaliation, so that men may know into what they run by their sin, and for that reason may abstain from it all the more, if those who make themselves liable to a crime of this kind know that they must give life for life and eye for eye. Fear of sinning is among those things without which the commonwealth cannot stand; and since these punishments, if they are applied, serve to maintain and increase that fear, they certainly bring no small benefit to the commonwealth.

units.la: Ultimum, in quo Socinus dicit, Christum legem Mosis reformasse & adauxisse, est illud de amore quorumcunque hominum, etiam inimicorum, vers. 43. &c. audivistis, quod dictum est: diliges proximum tuum, & odio habebis inimicum tuum: ego vero dico vobis, &c. Fatetur Adversarius, I. operosius aliquanto esse hic discernere, quid Christus supra legem præstiterit, II. an hoc in loco de solis verbis, aut sententia legis reformandâ egerit, an vero præterea, falsa ipsius legis, ejusque mentis interpretamenta retegere ac reticere voluerit, aut etiam an hoc solum facere intellexerit. & pag. 162. facile se dicit posse concedere, quemadmodum & in superioribus quibusdam Christi dictis fecimus, Christum hoc in loco non tantum Mosis legem reformare, sed etiam falsam ejus interpretationem rejicere voluisse. Pag. 163. Causa vero, ut adduci possimus, ut concedamus, Christum hoc loco non modo ipsam legem Mosis reformare, sed etiam falsam ejus interpretationem, interpretationemque istam suis[?] verbis complexum fuisse, non una tantum est, sed ut in quibusdam ex superioribus dictis, quibus Christus sua opponit, omnino duplex. I. Quia non addita est vox antiquis. II. Quia hic quoque ipsa legis verba non plane recitantur, ut in ipsa lege legun-tur. Ergo & hoc concedit III. non disserte in Mosis lege haberi, quod Christus hic sibi proponit sc. reformandum. pag. 159. 163. Satis esse, ex tota ipsa lege sententiam dicto ipso comprehensam, posse colligi.
units.tr: Last, where Socinus says that Christ reformed and enlarged the law of Moses, is the saying about love for all men, even enemies, at v. 43 etc.: you have heard that it was said, you shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy; but I say to you, etc. The opponent confesses, I. that it is somewhat more laborious here to determine what Christ did beyond the law, II. whether in this place he dealt only with the words, or with the sense of the law to be reformed, or whether he also wished to expose and reject the false interpretations of the law itself and of its meaning, or even whether he understood himself to do only this. And at p. 162 he says that he can easily concede, as we did also in some of the earlier sayings of Christ, that Christ in this place wished not only to reform the law of Moses, but also to reject its false interpretation. P. 163. But the reason why we may be brought to concede that Christ in this place wished not only to reform the law of Moses itself, but also its false interpretation, and included that interpretation in his words, is not one only, but, as in some of the earlier sayings in which Christ sets his own against the old, wholly twofold. I. Because the word "to the ancients" has not been added. II. Because here too the words of the law itself are not plainly recited, as they are read in the law itself. Therefore he also concedes, III. that what Christ here proposes to reform is not expressly contained in the law of Moses. P. 159, 163. It is enough that the sense comprehended in the saying can be gathered from the whole law itself.

units.la: Quid jam id sit, ex Socini mente, quod Christus legi huic addidit, & qua parte eam reformavit, videamus. Primum attendenda ejus expositio verborum, quæ Christus adfert, ut antiquis dicta. Deinde, additamentum legis, quod ex ipsius sententia Christus dederit. Illa ita exponit, ut, quod in lege dictum, diliges proximum, solos notasse Israelitas, existimet, & quod non alios diligendos lex præscripserit. Pag. 160. Quod attinet ad nomen proximi, certissimum est, illud significare quempiam ex eodem Israelitico populo, & sane quemlibet talem; sed nulla ratione eum, qui ex eodem populo non esset. Quum vero dicamus, illa quidem verba legis esse, diliges proximum tuum, sed quae subjunguntur, & odio habebis inimicum, non legis, sed falsae expositionis additamentum esse, quodque solum, non illud, perstringat Christus, corrigatque, & id non contra legem, sed juxta eam: Socinus, ut habeat, in quo thesim tamen suam figar[?], quodque in lege emendatum à Christo dicat, statuit, illud quoque legis fuisse, ut inimicum odio haberent: inimicum, id est, inquit, extraneum, non Israelitam. Pag. 161.
units.tr: Let us now see what, according to Socinus's mind, this is which Christ added to this law, and in what part he reformed it. First, his explanation of the words which Christ cites as said to the ancients must be considered. Then, the addition to the law which, in his view, Christ gave. He explains the former so that he thinks the words "you shall love your neighbour" noted only the Israelites, and that the law prescribed the love of no others. P. 160. As to the name of neighbour, it is most certain that it signifies someone from the same Israelite people, and indeed any such person; but by no reasoning does it signify one who is not of the same people. Yet since we say that the words of the law are indeed "you shall love your neighbour", but that what follows, "and hate your enemy", is not of the law but an addition of a false exposition, and that Christ censures and corrects only this and not the other, and does so not against the law but in accordance with it: Socinus, so that he may have something on which to fix his thesis, and so that he may say that what Christ amended in the law, decided that this too belonged to the law, that they should hate their enemy: the enemy, that is, he says, the foreigner, not the Israelite. P. 161.

units.la: Itaque si proximi nomine intelligendus erit is, qui ex eodem sit populo; inimicus intelligendus erit is, qui alienus à populo fuerit, & hostis alio nomine dici potest; ex quo facile constare poterit, istud, quod Christus ait, auditum fuisse de odio adversus inimicum, non esse ex falsa legis interpretatione ipsi legi ad-ditum; sed ex ipsa legis sententia omnino fluere, secundum quam licebat hostes non amare, sed odio habere, & porro eos armis interdum invadere atque delere, penitusque ex-terminare, & alienigenas plane aversari ne-cesse erat.
units.tr: Therefore if the name of neighbour is to be understood of one who is of the same people, the enemy will have to be understood as one who is alien from the people, and can be called by another name, a foe; from which it will be easy to establish that what Christ says was heard, about hatred against the enemy, is not added to the law itself from a false interpretation of the law, but flows entirely from the very sense of the law, according to which it was permitted not to love enemies but to hate them, and further, sometimes to attack them with arms and destroy them, and utterly exterminate them, and it was necessary to shun foreigners altogether.

units.la: Resp. i. Nego, proximum, non quidem, denotasse olim Israelitam; sed hunc solum: vel legem, praescriben-tem amorem proximi, ita Israelitam intellexisse solum, ut excluserit alios homines omnes. ii. Nego, per inimicum, in altero hujus loci membro denotari quemlibet alium extra populum Israeliticum. iii. Nego etiam sequi, si proximi nomine sit intelligendus qui ex eodem populo est Israelita; ergo per inimicos, reliquos om-nes extraneos. Quidni intelligantur, qui hostili aliquâ actione se inimicos faciunt & profitentur, quales quales etiam sint? Quare non vel ex eodem populo poterit dari inimicus tibi qui sit? vel inter extraneos amicior, quam ex populo, & ipsis contribulibus alius? Oportet quidem, & sic vulgo merito accipitur, ut proximi homini & amicissimi sint ejus populares; sed & contingit, ὑπὸ τῶν ἰδίων συμφυλετῶν[?] 1 Thess. ii. 14. affici quempiam majis, uti bonis ab ἀλλυφύλῳ[?]: quo in loco immerito sane hic pro hoste habebitur, & indignus qui diligatur, vel qui diligi nec possit, nec debeat. iv. Non potes dicere, ex ipsa legis sententia fluere, quod Christus dixit auditum fuisse de odio adversus inimicum, quamdiu ex ipsa legis sententia id non probas licitum, quin & praeceptum fuisse. Nam uti illud, diliges proximum, praeceptum fuit; ita & hoc, odio habebis, pro praecepto etiam, si in lege fuerit, uti il-lud, habendum erit. Quod tam alienum est à lege, uti quippiam. Legem odium praecipere, cujus summa & anima est charitas? Ostendat hoc Socinus, & vicerit. Sed satis securi sumus, hanc labem & contumeliam neminem unquam legi Dei impacturum esse. Profer locum, legem profer, secundum quam liceat hostes non amare, sed odio habere: & hoc non solum, sed pro hostibus habendos omnes olim extraneos fuisse, & non licitum, sed jussum fuisse, odio habere omnes homines, praeter Israelitas. Proba, idem esse, hostem & extraneum. Idem esse, non amare, quomodo popularem amas; & odio habere. Idem esse, armis hostem invadere, & habere odio. Proba, licere, vel licuisse olim, quoscunque extraneos, id est, omnes per universum mundum homines armis invadere & delere, penitusque exterminare: omnes enim erant extranei. Proba denique, idem esse, alienigenas aversari, & odio habere. Nihil illorum probat assertor, non disputator, neque probare poterit: absque quibus vana sunt, quæ commentatur omnia.
units.tr: Reply. I. I deny that the name "neighbour" formerly denoted an Israelite only; or that the law prescribing love of neighbour understood the Israelite in such a way as to exclude all other men. II. I deny that "enemy", in the second member of this passage, denotes anyone at all outside the Israelite people. III. I deny also that it follows, if the name neighbour is to be understood as an Israelite of the same people, that the rest of all foreigners are therefore enemies. Why should not those be understood as enemies who make themselves and profess themselves enemies by some hostile act, whatever sort they are? Why can there not be an enemy to you from the same people, or someone more friendly among foreigners than another from the people and from your own fellow-tribesmen? It is indeed proper, and so it is commonly and rightly taken, that one's neighbours and closest friends are one's fellow countrymen; but it also happens that someone is more affected by his own fellow-tribesmen [ὑπὸ τῶν ἰδίων συμφυλετῶν] (1 Thess. ii. 14) than by a foreigner [ἀλλοφύλου]; and in that place such a person will certainly be wrongly regarded as an enemy, and as unworthy of being loved, or as one who neither can nor ought to be loved. IV. You cannot say that it flows from the very sense of the law that Christ said was heard, about hatred against the enemy, so long as you do not prove that it was lawful, nay even commanded, by that very sense of the law. For just as "you shall love your neighbour" was a command, so also "you shall hate" will have to be taken as a command too, if it is in the law. How far this is from the law, as anyone can see! Does the law command hatred, whose sum and soul is charity? Let Socinus show this, and he will have won. But we are quite sure that no one will ever fasten this stain and insult upon the law of God. Produce the passage, produce the law, according to which it is permitted not to love enemies but to hate them; and not only this, but that all foreigners were formerly to be regarded as enemies, and that it was not merely permitted but commanded to hate all men except the Israelites. Prove that enemy and foreigner are the same. Prove that not to love is the same as to love a fellow countryman, and to hate is the same. Prove that to attack an enemy with arms is the same as to hate him. Prove that it was permitted, or had once been permitted, to attack with arms and utterly destroy and exterminate all foreigners whatever, that is, all men throughout the whole world, for all were foreigners. Lastly, prove that to shun foreigners is the same as to hate them. The assertor proves none of these things, and he is not a disputant, nor will he be able to prove them; without them, all that he invents is empty.

units.la: Jam quod à Christo additum legi Adversarius dicit, est, diligendos, non odio habendos, inimicos esse: quasi istud in lege Veteri licitum, in Nova sc. per Christum prohibitum sit, legisque in hoc consistat hic loci reformatio & additio. Pag. 164. Nam pro eo, quod Mosis lex tantum jubebat amare eos, qui ex eodem populo essent, Christus indefinite jubet apare inimicos, & bonum pro malo illis reddere. Pag. 107. ut uno verbo dicere possimus, Mosen proximi tantum amorem praecepisse, Christum vero etiam non proximi. Plus, aliter dicere debet, nisi propriam suam reformidet sententiam. Quippe dicendum[?] ipsi, quum Moses jusserit solos diligi Israelitas, non alios; extraneos omnes, seu reliquos in mundo homines odio haberi: quod Christus illud ita correxit adauxitque, ut omnes homines amari jusserit, atque etiam inimicos. Nos vero non quidem negamus, hanc Christi doctrinam esse: neque de hoc est controversia: sed an illa non etiam legis fuerit doctrina, seu an hoc quod Christus docet, legis sit additamentum, & non ipsa lege contineatur, quæritur. Nos lege contineri dicimus, & Christum nil præter, nedum contra legem, hic præscripsisse. Lex proximum amandum docuit, sed quoque neminem exclusit: odio vero habendum quemquam, nuspiam edixit. De his quæstio est: & nos quidem quod de lege diximus, probamus ita.
units.tr: Now, as to what the Adversary says Christ added to the law, namely that enemies are to be loved and not hated, as if this were permitted under the Old Testament but forbidden in the New by Christ, and as if the reformation and addition here consisted in this. Page 164: "For whereas Moses' law only commanded us to love those who were of the same people, Christ commands us without restriction to love enemies and to render good for evil to them." Page 107: "so that in one word we may say that Moses prescribed love only for the neighbour, but Christ also for the non-neighbour." He would have to say otherwise unless he shrinks from his own opinion. For he must say that, since Moses commanded only Israelites to be loved and not others, all foreigners, that is, the rest of the men in the world, were to be hated; and that Christ corrected and enlarged this so as to command that all men be loved, even enemies. We indeed do not deny that this is Christ's teaching, and the controversy is not about this. The question is whether that teaching was not also the teaching of the law, or whether what Christ teaches is an addition to the law and is not contained in the law itself. We say that it is contained in the law, and that Christ here prescribed nothing beyond the law, let alone anything against it. The law taught that the neighbour is to be loved, but it excluded no one; nowhere did it decree that anyone is to be hated. This is the question, and we prove what we have said about the law as follows.

units.la: Primo. Quæ Dei lex nunquam dixit solos Israelitas amandos esse; illa, quamvis jusserit diligere proximos, hoc non restrinxit ad illos solos. Ubi dixit, vel solos amandos proximos, populares aut conterraneos? vel, solos Israelitas? Si nusquam, cur tute restringis, & ardas præceptum nec limitatum, nec limitandum? Si lex dixit, tabulas profer, & acquiescemus. Israelitas diligendos fuisse, nemo negat vel nescit, eosque præcipue etiam, & ob plurimas rationes fuisse amandos: sed solos illos, & non alios, hoc lege uspiam cautum fuisse, ostendatur.
units.tr: First. The law of God, which never said that only Israelites are to be loved, did not restrict its command to love the neighbour to those alone. Where did it say that only neighbours, fellow-countrymen or compatriots, are to be loved, or only Israelites? If nowhere, why do you yourself restrict it, and presume to add to a precept that is neither limited nor to be limited? If the law says so, produce the tablets, and we will agree.
