No one denies or is ignorant that the Israelites were to be loved, and that they were especially to be loved, and for very many reasons. But let it be shown that the law anywhere laid down that only they, and not others, were to be loved.

units.la: 11 Quin potius, quia proximum diligere lex jubebat, idem erga quemcunq; volebat fieri: quia quilibet homo aliquâ ratione nobis proximus est, atque proximus fieri potest. Quamvis non omnes Israelitæ, omnes tamen Israelitis sunt homines, & quamvis non religione aut loco, aliis possunt officiis illis conjuncti reddi & propinqui: & cur non etiam istâ tum ratione dicentur proximi? Lex, inquis, quum proximum nominat, intelligit Israelitam. esto; sed quando non dicit solum proximum, & in aliis etiam hominibus notæ proximitatis sint, uti hoc non præjudicat proximo ἐξοχῶς[?] dicto, ita nec impedit, ut propter ea etiam colatur ille, qui, quamvis peregrinus, proximum se tamen nobis exhibet. Ut hic omnino etiam parabolam Christi ex Luc.x. 30.v. applicare possimus, atque sic interrogare: pone, quod sub V. Test. homo aliquis Jerusalemo Jerechuntem descendens in latrones inciderit, ab iisque spoliatus, diverberatus, relictus pro semimortuo in via; nec a transeunte Sacerdote, nec Levita fuerit sublevatus, sed a Samaritano: uter istorum trium dicendus homini illi fuisse proximus? certe qui misericordiam exhibuit Sa-maritanus: nec negari posset ab illo Samaritanum pro proximo habendum, diligendumque omnino fuisse, qui tanta propinquitatis praestitisset officia.
units.tr: 11 Rather, because the law commanded us to love the neighbour, it wished the same to be done towards anyone whatever, because every man is in some respect our neighbour, and can become a neighbour. Although not all are Israelites, yet all are men to the Israelites; and although they cannot be made joined and near to us by religion or by place, by other duties, why should they not also be called neighbours on that ground? The law, you say, when it names the neighbour, means an Israelite. Granted. But since it does not say only "neighbour", and since marks of neighbourliness are found in other men too, just as this does not prejudice the term neighbour taken in its eminent sense, so neither does it prevent the one who, though a stranger, shows himself a neighbour to us from being honoured for these things too. Here indeed we may apply the parable of Christ from Luke 10:30, and ask thus: suppose that under the Old Testament some man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers, was stripped and beaten, and was left for half dead on the road; and was helped neither by a passing priest nor by a Levite, but by a Samaritan. Which of those three is to be called the neighbour of that man? Certainly the one who showed mercy, the Samaritan. Nor could it be denied that the Samaritan was to be regarded as a neighbour and wholly to be loved by him, since he had rendered such offices of nearness.

units.la: III. In V. Test. si quis Israelita amasset extraneum, peccasset quaero. nec ne? Si id lex prohibuit, edixitque solum Israelitam diligendum, extraneum quin odio habendum, peccasset certe Israelita extraneum aliquem diligendo; utpote in quo contra legem egisset. At vero quid durius & peregrinum horridumque magis dici potest, quam amando hominem peccare quempiam posse? insuper, amando benefactorem? ideo nempe, quia extraneus est. IV. Atqui dico ego, quod eo magis amandus erat, quia beneficium illud tantumque praestabat extraneus, quo is minus videbatur ad hoc tenerí, vel id praestiturus [?], aut illud exspectandum ab eo erat beneficium. Uti enim virtutis illud majoris, & inusitatae, eo certe plus affectus reciproci etiam merei debuit. V. Vel, an dices, odio habendum fuisse? idque ex lege naturae, & Mosis? Imo teneris id dicere, ex jactá modo hypothesi: quá ex legis praescripto solum diligendum Israelitam, neutiquam extraneum, sed hunc odio habendum, Adversarios statuere coegit mala sua sententia. Quid, non dicam a religione, sed sana mente magis alienum excogitari potest? VI. Certe si hoc sit, jam religio Mosaica Gentili inferior fuit & deterior, quae absque ullo personarum respectu diligendos homines, & benefactores (non dico adhuc de inimicis, quales etiam amore atque beneficiis vincendos & frangendos subinde monuerunt) quoscunque, cujuscunque demum status vel nationis, jussit. Igitur lex Mosaica, docens diligendum proximum, non intellexit id de solis Israelitis. Quod, uti probandum Adversariis ante omnia fuerat, ita nunquam ulla rationis vel minima specie obtinebunt.
units.tr: III. In the Old Testament, if any Israelite had loved a foreigner, had he sinned or not, I ask? If the law forbade this, and decreed that only the Israelite was to be loved and the foreigner hated, then an Israelite certainly would have sinned by loving some foreigner, since in doing so he would have acted against the law. But what could be said that is harsher, stranger, and more horrible than that a man can sin by loving someone? Indeed, by loving a benefactor? Simply because he is a foreigner. IV. Yet I say that he was all the more to be loved, because the foreigner conferred that benefit, and so great a one, the less he seemed bound to it or about to confer it, or the less that benefit was to be expected from him. For just as this is a greater and unusual virtue, so certainly a greater reciprocal affection ought to be earned. V. Or will you say that he was to be hated, and that by the law of nature and of Moses? No, you are compelled to say this by the hypothesis you have just put forward, namely that by the prescription of the law only the Israelite is to be loved, and not at all the foreigner, but he is to be hated. Your bad opinion has forced the Adversaries to this. What, I will not say from religion, but from a sound mind, could be devised that is more alien? VI. Certainly, if this were so, then the Mosaic religion was inferior and worse than the Gentile one, which commanded that men and benefactors be loved without any respect of persons (I do not yet speak of enemies, whom the Gentiles too at times admonished to be overcome and broken by love and benefits), whoever they were and of whatever condition or nation. Therefore the Mosaic law, teaching that the neighbour is to be loved, did not understand this of Israelites alone. This, as the Adversaries ought above all to have proved, they will never establish, not even with the least semblance of reason.

units.la: Secundo. Lex jubens diligere proximum, intellexit per proximum, Israelitam quidem, sed etiam homines in genere omnes. Quod probo, 1. ex ipso legis loco, unde haec citantur, & pro se argumentari Socinus instituit. Levit. xix. 16. 17. 18. non ambulabis ut detractor in populo tuo, non insurges contra sanguinem proximi tui: ego sum Jehova. Non habebis odio fratrem tuum in corde tuo, reprehendendo reprehendes socium tuum, neque feres in eo peccatum. Non ulcisceris, neque servabis iram contra filios populi tui, & diliges proximum tuum, sicut te: ego Jehova. Multa hic praecipiuntur, erga populares & fratres observanda: sed an ideo erga illos solos? & non quoque erga alios? erga omnes? Non licet detrahere populari suo, ergone alteri? quae sequela? annon potius, nec fratri, nec ulli? sic non assurgere contra sanguinem proximi, vid. in judicio, falso adversus eum testimonio, quo interimatur, quod neque in fratrem licet, neque in quemcumque alium. Similiter de odio pronunciandum, & ultione. Quaeque hic praecipiuntur officia, amoris, & amicae reprehensionis, quare non etiam ad quoscunque se extendent? Ut appareat, quamvis aliquid cavea-tur de proximo, non ideo restringi ad quosdam homines, sed ad omnes spectare & referri oportere. II. Et sic passim, in aliis legis praeceptis, quod proximo faciendum dicitur vel minus, haud restringitur ad quosdam, ad populares, vel Israelitas, sed ad omnes etiam pertinet homines. In Decalogo quod dicitur, qui est plenior modo expositio amoris erga proximum, præcepto nono, ne falsum quis proferat testimonium adversus proximum suum, haud permittit ideo, falsum dicere contra extraneum. Annon ubique falsum testimonium prohibetur, & contra omnes? aut quod præcepto decimo dictum, de non concupiscendis rebus proximi, non æque vetat aliorum etiam bona, & res, & personas concupiscere, quam Israelitarum? Ergo quum in lege additur proximus, non restringendum & coërcendum id intra solos Israelitas, sed ad quosvis omnino homines extendendum etiam venit. III. Ubi est generalis ratio & fundamentum dilectionis universalis omnium hominum, ibi præceptum φιλανθρωπίας[?] obtinere æquum est: sed apud omnes homines ratio illa est: ergo. Nempe quia homines omnes sumus: ex uno enim sanguine fecit Deus omnem gentem hominum habitare faciem terræ, ἐν ᾧ[?] γὰρ ζῶμεν[?] καὶ κινούμεθα καὶ ἐσμέν[?]. Act. xvii. 26. 28. Ob quam causam etiam Gentiles sciverunt, amandos promiscue omnes homines esse, quia idem ratio naturalis dictat. IV. Ratio vel modus præcepto additus diligendi proximum, sicuti teipsum, ostendit ita nos aliis facere debere, quomodo velimus agi nobiscum: atque ex hoc pendere universam legem & Prophetas, Christus docuit, Matth. vii. 12. sed vero nos extranei vellemus amari ab aliis, ab omnibus: ergo & amare tales, per legis istud compendium & summam, obstringimur. V. In N. Test. quoties repetitur præceptum legis de amore mutuo, usurpatur eadem vox proximi: ubi tamen notum est, amorem illum se ad omnes homines extendere debere: neque aliud ultra adfertur præceptum, quam illud, diliges proximum sicuti teipsum, nec alio quam proximi nomine, neque alio quam generali de omnibus hominibus sensu. Non aliud nomen aut Christus legi substituit, aut alium sensum. Ita Matth. xix. 19. & xxii. 39. 40. quum de inimicis diligendis Christus loquitur, nomen proximi in lege non immutat. Et Rom. xiii. 8. nemini quidpiam debeatis, nisi invicem diligere: qui enim diligit τὸν ἕτερον alium, legem implevit. Ergo lex jubens diligere proximum, intelligit hoc de dilectione mutua, & proximi, & cujusque alterius: docetque id nos cuivis debere, in genere, non restringere ad aliquod hominum genus, vel ad populares. Nec modo in Nov. Testam. ubi dilectio ad omnes prorsus homines (omnium consensu) extenditur, nil præter veterem legem, ejusque observationem, adfertur; sed & sic explicatur, ut per se ad quoscunque homines referendam eam esse, doceatur. Apostolus, verf. 9. hoc enim, non machaberis; non occides; non furaberis; non falsum dices testimonium; non concupisces, & si quod præceptum aliud ἐντολὴ[?] in hoc verbo continetur, diliges proximum tuum sicuti teipsum. Jam vero illa, non machaberis, non furaberis, haud solum apud Israelitas, sed & extraneos illicita fuerunt, & ubique: ergo hoc, ad quod illa pertinent, & quo comprehenduntur, diliges proximum, non ad solos, vel inter solos Israelitas coarctandum. Verf. 1c. Amor proximo non operatur malum, nam impletio legis charitas est. Hic & τὸ πλησίον non solos Israelitas significat, sed omnes omnino homines; & hic sensus expresse dicitur esse legis. Lex ergo charitatem jubens, eamque proximo impertiendam, intelligit de omnibus omnino & quibuscunque hominibus. Gal. v. 12. 13. Verum per charitatem servite vobis mutuo. Tota enim lex in uno impletur verbo, hoc nempe, diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Nihil iterum praeter legem, & unicum legis verbum, quo omnia nostra officia complentur, de diligendo proximum. Quare sub proximi nomine in lege omnes homines significati fuere.
units.tr: Second. The law bidding us love the neighbour understood by "neighbour" Israelites indeed, but also men in general, all of them. I prove this, first, from the very passage of the law from which these things are cited, and on which Socinus undertook to argue for his own view. Leviticus 19:16–18: "You shall not go about as a slanderer among your people; you shall not stand against the blood of your neighbour: I am Jehovah. You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and shall not bear sin on account of him. You shall not take vengeance, nor keep anger against the children of your people, but you shall love your neighbour as yourself: I am Jehovah." Many things are commanded here to be observed towards fellow-citizens and brothers. But are they therefore to be observed towards them alone, and not also towards others, towards all? It is not permitted to slander one's fellow-countryman; is it therefore permitted to slander another? What follows? Surely rather that it is permitted towards neither a brother nor anyone. Likewise, not to stand against the blood of the neighbour, that is, in judgment, by false testimony against him whereby he is put to death, is forbidden not only towards a brother but towards anyone else. The same must be said of hatred and vengeance. And the duties of love and of friendly rebuke commanded here, why would they not extend to whomsoever? So it appears that although something is laid down concerning the neighbour, it is not therefore restricted to certain men, but must be regarded and referred to all. II. And so throughout, in the other precepts of the law, what is said is to be done or not done to the neighbour is not restricted to certain people, to fellow-countrymen or Israelites, but pertains to all men too. In the Decalogue, the ninth precept, which is a fuller exposition of love towards the neighbour, that no one should bear false witness against his neighbour, does not therefore permit false speech against a foreigner. Is not false testimony forbidden everywhere and against all? Or does the tenth precept, about not coveting the neighbour's goods, not equally forbid coveting the goods and persons of other men as of Israelites? Therefore, when "neighbour" is added in the law, it does not follow that it is to be restricted and confined within Israelites alone, but it must be extended to men of every kind. III. Where there is a general reason and foundation for the universal love of all men, there it is right that the precept of philanthropy should hold; but among all men that reason exists; therefore. Namely, because we are all men: for God "made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on the face of the earth", "for in him [ἐν ᾧ] we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:26, 28). For this reason even the Gentiles knew that all men without distinction are to be loved, because natural reason dictates this. IV. The reason or manner added to the precept of loving the neighbour, "as yourself", shows that we ought to act towards others as we would wish to be dealt with by them. Christ taught that the whole law and the Prophets depend on this (Matthew 7:12). But we, as foreigners, would wish to be loved by others, by all; therefore we are bound, by this summary and sum of the law, to love such people too. V. In the New Testament, whenever the precept of the law about mutual love is repeated, the same word "neighbour" is used, where yet it is known that this love ought to extend to all men. Nor is any other precept brought forward beyond that one, "you shall love your neighbour as yourself", nor under any other name than "neighbour", nor in any other sense than the general sense concerning all men. Neither Christ nor anyone else has substituted another name for the law, or another sense. So in Matthew 19:19 and 22:39–40, when Christ speaks of loving enemies, he does not change the name "neighbour" in the law. And Romans 13:8: "Owe nothing to anyone except to love one another; for he who loves the other [τὸν ἕτερον] has fulfilled the law." Therefore the law bidding us love the neighbour understands this of mutual love, both of the neighbour and of any other person whatever, and teaches that we ought to show it to anyone in general, not restricting it to some kind of men or to fellow-countrymen. Nor is it only in the New Testament, where love is extended to all men absolutely (by universal consent), that nothing is brought forward beyond the old law and its observance; but it is so explained that it is taught to refer of itself to men of every kind. The Apostle, verse 9: "For this, You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment [ἐντολή], it is contained in this word: you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Now "you shall not commit adultery" and "you shall not steal" were unlawful not only among Israelites but among foreigners too, and everywhere. Therefore that to which these pertain, and by which they are comprehended, "you shall love your neighbour", is not to be confined to the Israelites alone, or to be confined among the Israelites alone. Verse 10: "Love does no evil to the neighbour, for love is the fulfilling of the law." Here too τὸ πλησίον [the neighbour] signifies not only Israelites but all men absolutely, and this sense is expressly said to be that of the law. The law, then, which commands charity and enjoins it towards the neighbour, means it of all men absolutely and of any men whatever. Galatians 5:13–14: "But through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, namely this: you shall love your neighbour as yourself." Again, nothing beyond the law, and the one word of the law in which all our duties concerning the love of the neighbour are fulfilled. Hence under the name "neighbour" in the law all men were signified.

units.la: Tertio. Jussit lex etiam inimicos diligere: ergo hoc non demum per Christum legi fuit superadditum. Probatur, ex lege, & legis doctrina, prout in V. Test. viguit: neque enim de legis doctrina ex solis libris Mosis, sed tota historia sacra V. Test. judicium fieri debet: unde Christus hoc in argumento conjungere solet, legem & Prophetas. Matth. v. 17. & vii. 12. & xxii. 40. Luc. xvi. 31. &c. Locus ex V. Test. & lege Mosis, quo probamus, inimicos etiam tum diligeendos fuisse, est Exod. xxiii. 4. 5. Si offenderis bovem inimici tui אֹיִבְךָ[?], aut asinum ejus errantem, omnino reducito eum ad illum. Si videris asinum osoris tui שֹׂנְאֲךָ[?] succumbentem oneri suo, cunctaberis ei omittere tua? omnino derelinques cum eo. Is, cui juberis haec praestare officia, est inimicus & osor tuus, ἐχθρὸς σύ[?]. neque hunc diligere teneris, sed etiam eidem servire, servire ejus jumento, quin & tua in gratiam ejus deferere. Quae nemo aequo animo perpendens, dubitabit, quin lex manifeste satis rigideque amorem imperarit inimici. Cujus asino teneris officia omnia, quae ejus exigit necessitas, illa imprimis ipsi debes: sed inimici asino talia teneris exhibere: ergo multo magis ipsi. Quare alias inimicum & osorem lex exprimat? neque hoc frustra fit, & haud uno verbo, sed, ne dubium sit illum intelligi, quovis designatur, non amicus aut benefactor, proximus vel Israelita, sed inimicus, & osor tuus. Prov. xxv. 22. Si esurierit שֹׂנְאֶךָ[?] osor tuus, ciba eum pane, & si sitierit, pota eum aqua. Quae eo fortius stringunt, quod in N. Test. adducuntur Rom. xii. 20. ut omnino officium dilectionis inimicorum non novum, sed antiquum sit, & tale, quod in N. Test. ex Veteri confirmatur.
units.tr: Third, the law also commanded us to love our enemies; therefore this was not first added to the law through Christ. This is proved from the law and from the teaching of the law as it prevailed in the Old Testament. For judgement on the teaching of the law must be made not from the books of Moses alone but from the whole sacred history of the Old Testament. Hence Christ customarily joins "the law and the Prophets" in this argument: Matt. 5:17; 7:12; 22:40; Luke 16:31, etc. The passage from the Old Testament and the law of Moses by which we prove that enemies were to be loved even then is Exod. 23:4-5: If you meet your enemy's ox [אֹיִבְךָ] or his ass straying, you shall certainly bring it back to him. If you see the ass of him who hates you [שֹׂנְאֲךָ] lying under its burden, will you hold back from helping him? You shall certainly help him with it. The man to whom you are commanded to render these services is your enemy and the one who hates you [ἐχθρὸς σύ]. You are bound not only not to love him but also to serve him, to serve his beast of burden, and even to put aside your own concerns for his sake. No one who weighs this fairly will doubt that the law clearly and sternly enjoined love of an enemy. To his ass you owe all the services which its need requires, and above all these you owe to himself; but to an enemy's ass you are bound to render such services; therefore much more to him. Why then does the law name the enemy and the hater? Not in vain, nor with a single word, but so that there be no doubt that he is meant: he is designated by whatever name, not friend or benefactor, neighbour or Israelite, but your enemy and the one who hates you. Prov. 25:22: If your enemy [שֹׂנְאֶךָ] is hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. These texts bind all the more strongly because they are quoted in the New Testament, Rom. 12:20, so that the duty of love toward enemies is not new but old, and is such a duty as the New Testament confirms from the Old.

units.la: Audiendum nunc, quid ad illa excipiat Socinus: & primo quidem quid ad priorem locum ex Mose; tum quid ad alterum, ex Proverbiis Salomonis. Pag. 167.
units.tr: Let us now hear what Socinus replies to these, first to the earlier passage from Moses, and then to the other, from the Proverbs of Solomon. Page 167.

units.la: Quod si quis ad ostendendum nihilominus beneficiendi praeceptum etiam inimicis suis in Mosis lege contineri, id afferat, quod scriptum est Exod. 23. ubi jubetur unusquisque qui in bovem inimici sui errantem aut asinum incideris, curare ut ad ipsum Dominum reducatur, & si quis viderit asinum illius qui odio habet sub onere succumbentem, jubetur
units.tr: But if someone, to show that the precept of doing good even to one's enemies is nonetheless contained in the law of Moses, adduces what is written in Exodus 23, where each man is commanded, if he comes upon the ox of his enemy straying or his ass, to take care that it is brought back to its owner; and if anyone sees the ass of one who hates him lying under its load, he is commanded

units.la: Resp. 1. Quid inaniter magis dici potest, quam istis officiis etiam erga inimicum jussis, non propterea juberi simpliciter benefacere. Quod non satis intelligo. Non hoc, quod non sit benefacere inimico, qui illa ei praestat officia: quodque lex ea jubens, non juste odio habet sub onere succumbentem, jubetur beat simpliciter benefacere. Ullusne
units.tr: Answer 1. What can be said more idly than that, although these duties are commanded even toward an enemy, it is not for that reason simply commanded to do good to him? This I do not sufficiently understand. It is not that it is not doing good to an enemy to render him those services; nor is it that the law, in commanding them, does not simply command doing good. Is there any mortal who would not interpret those services rendered to him as benefits?

units.la: Ullusne eum non deferere, sed illi auxiliari. Respon-deo, istis officiis, etiam erga inimicum jussis, non propterea juberi simpliciter iis bene face-re; quandoquidem officia ista ab iis tantum negligi solent, qui vindicta cupiditatem, aut saltem odium adversus inimicum suum re-tinent; quod utrumque ab ipso Mose veti-tum fuisse & fatemur, & scriptum esse ipsimet contendimus, nempe supra memorato capite 19. Levit. ut scilicet appareat, ex utro-que isto precepto fluere alia, qua a Mose erga inimicum facienda jubentur, non autem ex eo, quod alioqui ex mente ipsius Mosis tenere-tur quis inimico benefacere. mortalium erit, qui sibi illa præstita, non beneficia interpretetur? Quid sit beneficium, expediat aliquis, vel be-nefacere? ut videamus, annon hæc be-neficia censenda, dicendaque sint- Officia præstare, & inimico, & juva-re eum, juvare ejus asinum, non erit benefacere? Tum ego ignoro quid benefacere, quidve de ratione sit bene-ficii. ii. Officia illa ab iis tantum negligi solent, qui vindicta cupiditatem retinent. Sic ita, an ideo non erit beneficium, ubi ab aliquo præstatur? Quia alter ex odio aut vindicta maleficium patrat, vel officium & beneficium negligit, ideo præstari id non potest, & animo, quali debet, benefaciendi? Videte, quales Scripturæ expositiones rimetur Socinus, subtiliter in speciem, sed audaces supra modum & vanas. Negat beneficium esse, levare alterius jumenta & reducere: negat, hæc tanquam beneficia præ-cepta servandaque fuisse: & tantum illa negat, ne legem talia præcepisse, & non primum à Christo mandata, dicere, contra hypotheses suas cogatur. iii. Quo autem loco habebis, vel quo, obsecro, appellabis nomine & titulo hoc quod lex ibi erga inimicum præscribit officium, si non videatur dicendum benefi-cium esse? certe non est maleficium, neque simplex omissio mali, vel vindi-ctæ, odiive. Quid est quæso, si non beneficium? iv. Mittamus & hoc. virtus an est tibi? hoc enim magis in lege spectamus & prius, virtus an sit aliquid, quam beneficium, seu qualis sit virtus. Neque puto adeo amens quispiam erit, qui dubitabit virtutem dicendam esse: ergo, quidquid sit de beneficio, pro virtute, & lege quidem præscripta, haberi debet. Quod totum id est, quod hic in quæstione, & probandum nobis fuit. v. Negamus, illa erga ini-micum & jumentum officia tantum negligi solere ab iis qui vindictam, aut odium adversus inimicum retinent: nam & ex socordia & incuria, vel malitia, quam ab odio possis distinguere & vindicta, negligentia illa oriri potest. vi. Supra vindictam etiam, a Christo demum damnatam Socinus tu-tatus fuit: ad hoc enim tota ejus expositio & argumentatio redibat, quod vin-dictæ cupiditatem reprehenderet Christus, & legi Mosaicæ de oculo pro ocu-lo, &c. adderet: Jam videt, vindictam in lege etiam prohibitam fuisse: & hactenus bene. vii. Atqui etiam odium erga inimicum. Revera. Ergo lex non dixit, odio habebis inimicum: neque in hoc lex vel impugnanda fuit, vel corri-genda. viii. Quomodo nunc legem Levit. xix. 18. de non ulciscendo, vel retinendo odio, adeo late exponit, ut ex ea fluere velit præceptum de suble-vando inimici jumento, qui alias tam arte singula accipit, & plura, quæ ad aliquod legis antiquæ caput commode reducantnr[?], ut nova præcepta vult-haberi? Atque ita omnia, in quibus dicit Christum novas tulisse leges, ad sua
units.tr: Is there anyone who would not leave it, but help him? I answer: although these duties are commanded even toward an enemy, they are not on that account commanded simply as good deeds to him; since these duties are usually neglected only by those who retain the desire for revenge, or at least hatred toward their enemy. We both admit that Moses himself forbade both, and we contend that it is written in the very chapter 19 of Leviticus cited above, so that it may appear that other things follow from each of these precepts, which Moses commands to be done toward an enemy, and not that from his own mind a man is bound to do good to his enemy. Who could explain what a benefit is, or what it is to do good? Let us see whether these services are not to be counted and called benefits: to render services to an enemy, and to help him, to help his ass, will not be to do good? Then I do not know what doing good is, or what is the nature of a benefit. ii. Are those duties usually neglected only by those who retain the desire for revenge? So, then, is it not a benefit when it is performed by someone? Because another commits an injury out of hatred or revenge, or neglects the service and the benefit, is it on that account impossible for it to be done, and with the spirit with which one ought to do good? See what sort of interpretations of Scripture Socinus digs out: subtle in appearance, but excessively bold and vain. He denies that it is a benefit to lift up another's beasts and bring them back; he denies that these things were commanded as benefits and to be observed as such; and he denies only that the law commanded such things, and that they were first commanded by Christ, which he is forced to say against his own hypotheses. iii. But what place will you give, or by what name and title, I beg you, will you call that duty which the law there prescribes toward an enemy, if it is not to be called a benefit? It is certainly not an injury, nor a simple omission of evil, or of revenge or hatred. What is it, I ask, if not a benefit? iv. Let us also set this aside. Is virtue something for you? For in the law we look more at this, and first, whether virtue is something, than at the benefit, or what kind of virtue it is. Nor do I think anyone so foolish will doubt that it must be called virtue; therefore, whatever is the case with benefit, it must be held as virtue, and indeed as prescribed by the law. This is the whole point that is in question here and that we had to prove. v. We deny that those duties toward an enemy and his beast are usually neglected only by those who retain the desire for revenge or hatred toward the enemy; for that negligence can arise from sloth and carelessness, or from malice, which you cannot distinguish from hatred and revenge. vi. Socinus also thought he had reached beyond revenge, which Christ was the first to condemn; for his whole exposition and argument came to this, that Christ rebuked the desire for revenge and added to the Mosaic law of an eye for an eye, etc. Now he sees that revenge was also forbidden in the law; and so far, well. vii. But also hatred toward an enemy. Indeed. Therefore the law did not say, "You shall hate your enemy"; and in this the law was neither to be attacked nor corrected. viii. How now does he expound Leviticus 19:18, about not taking vengeance or keeping hatred, so widely that he wishes a precept about relieving an enemy's beast to flow from it, when elsewhere he takes each thing so artfully, and wants the many things that can fitly be referred to some chapter of the old law to be held as new precepts? And so all the things in which he says Christ enacted new laws ought rightly to be referred to the precepts of Moses' law, which are referred to kinds of virtues or of vices; and it ought rightly to be charged with ignorance, to put it no more strongly, to make different precepts from them.

units.la: Tom. 2. in Mosis lege praecepta, & seu virtutum, seu vitiorum genera referri merito debent, ut diversa exinde praecepta facere imperitiae, ne quid gravius dicam, accusari jure debeat. Ita quidni quae de ira, vel contumelia, ad praeceptum de non occidendo? quae de concupiscentia mulieris, ad illud de non maechando? de temerario juramento, ad praeceptum tertium, & sic de aliis, referrantur: neque alia diversa, vel nova a Christo Jesu prodita praecepta, dicamus? quum aeque, & magis appareat, ex illis praeceptis fluere ista, ac ex praecepto de non ulciscendo Levit. xix. 18. illud de juvando inimici asino & bove. ix. Nescio quid inepte magis & imperite, pro absurdo habeatur, atque hoc, quod alioqui ex mente ipsius Mosis teneretur quis inimico suo benefaceret. Grande scilicet piaculum! talem si legem Moses dedit, aut hanc ex ejus legibus mentem si quis capiat, vel etiam praeceptum ab eo datum de juvando inimici asino, credat. Judicare quaeso, qualis illa thesis esse debeat, in cujus gratiam cogitur Auctor talia ponere axiomata, & absurda. Nempe, benefacias, atque ex lege Mosis, inimici asino; sed ne inimico ipsi. Hoc scilicet nefas. Annon licuit? vel, si licuit in se; peccatum ergo fuit, ex lege Mosis credere tibi hoc faciendum esse? Pone quis id fecerit olim, id est, benefecerit inimico, eo quod putarit se ex Mosis lege ad hoc teneri, quid dices, ipsum peccasse contra mentem & legem Mosis? Vetuitne Mosis lex, alicui benefacere? benefacere inimico? quum non siverit, sed jusserit benefacere ejus jumento? Ex Mosis lege sublevandus fuit inimici asinus: quid si illum conspexisset quis oneri succumbentem, & non ejus asinum, non tenebatur illum sublevare aeque, si non magis, atque ejus asinum? Nisi neges, beneficium esse ita sublevari, beneficium ex Mosis mente praestandum fuisse inimico etiam, negare haud potes. x. Hoc bonum fuit, benefacere inimico, vel malum. Bonum, dices. Ergo lege Mosis praeceptum, inquam. Quia illa perfecta fuit, & omne continebat bonum, docebatque. Psalm. xix. 8.
units.tr: Vol. 2. Why not likewise refer what is said about anger or insult to the precept about not killing; what is said about a woman's lust to the precept about not committing adultery; what is said about rash oaths to the third precept; and so on for the others? And shall we not call them other or new precepts brought forth by Jesus Christ, since it appears equally, and more clearly, that these follow from those precepts, as from the precept about not taking vengeance in Leviticus 19:18 follows the one about helping the ass and ox of an enemy? ix. I know not what is more foolish and unskilled, and held for absurd, than this: that a man would be bound to do good to his enemy from the mind of Moses himself. A great offence indeed! If Moses gave such a law, or if anyone takes this mind from his laws, or believes even the precept given by him about helping an enemy's ass. Judge, I ask, what that thesis must be, for whose sake the author is forced to lay down such axioms, and absurd ones. Namely: you should do good, and by the law of Moses, to an enemy's ass, but not to the enemy himself. This is surely an abomination. Was it not permitted? Or, if it was permitted in itself, was it then a sin to believe from the law of Moses that you must do this? Suppose someone did it formerly, that is, did good to his enemy, because he thought that he was bound to this by the law of Moses: what will you say, that he sinned against the mind and law of Moses? Did the law of Moses forbid doing good to anyone? Doing good to an enemy? When it did not allow it, but commanded doing good to his beast? By the law of Moses the enemy's ass was to be relieved: what if someone had seen his ass under a load, and not the ass of his enemy? Was he not bound to relieve it equally, if not more, than his enemy's ass? Unless you deny that it is a benefit to be relieved in this way, you cannot deny that a benefit was to be rendered even to an enemy, from the mind of Moses. x. Was it good to do good to an enemy, or evil? Good, you will say. Therefore it was prescribed by the law of Moses, I say. Because that law was perfect, and contained all good and taught it. Ps. 19:8.

units.la: Deinde videamus, ut respondeat ad alterum locum Socinus, ex Proverbiis desumtum. Ita ergo pag. 168.
units.tr: Next let us see how Socinus answers the other passage, the one taken from Proverbs. He says thus on page 168.

units.la: Non etiam cur quis adversus id quod con-clusimus afferat, quod scriptum est a Salomone Proverb. cap. 25. & ab ipso Paulo Apost. ad Rom. 12. usurpatum: sic enim ipsius Salo-monis verba habent: si esuriat osor tuus, ciba eum pane; & si sitiat, da ei bibendam aquam. Quae verba quantumvis praecipiendi modo a Salomone prolata, non possunt habere praecepti vim in ipsa lege contenti, quandoquidem Salomon non profiteatur, se vel Mosis legem explicare, vel praecepta dare ex ipsius divina praescripti atque absoluti jussus mente: sed tantum sicut aliis plerisque in locis illius sui operis, istic etiam monitionem suam ex-ponit, quam sperat atque affirmat utilissimam
units.tr: Nor is there any reason why anyone should bring against what we have concluded the saying written by Solomon in Proverbs chapter 25, which Paul the Apostle himself also uses in Romans 12. For Solomon's own words are: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread; and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink." However much these words are uttered by Solomon in the form of a command, they cannot have the force of a precept contained in the law itself, since Solomon does not profess either to explain the law of Moses or to give precepts by the mind of God's divine prescription and absolute command. He only sets out here, as in many other places of his work, his own admonition, which he hopes and affirms will be most useful.

units.la: Resp. 1. Verba Salomonis praecipiendi modo prolata, & ipsa praecepta sunt, & vim praecepti habent. Sed non in lege contenti, dicit. At ego putabam, nullum alicujus rei & boni operis praeceptum esse, quod non lege comprehenderetur: tum propter legis perfectionem, in genere morum & praeceptorum; tum quod summa illa amandi proximum, sicuti se ipsum, omnia suo ambitu complecteretur; & praesertim hoc de quo Salomon, ex lege Exod. xxiii. 4. 5. ne alia di-cam generaliora, tam commode educi possit, fore, si quis illam sequatur, quemadmodum docent statim sequentia verba, nam prunas coacervabis super caput ejus, & Iehova rependet tibi. Magna igitur utilitas, quae inde consecutura sit si quis ista faciat, movit Salomonem ad ita monendum, non autem quia id censeat in ipsa Dei lege jussum, quondoquidem nihil impedit, quo minus Deus ei rependat qui plus fecerit, quam ipsi praescriptum & absolute jussum ab ipso fuerit; imo hoc ipsum quod Deus dicitur ipsi repensurus, satis indicare potest, benefacta ista erga inimicum suum non fuisse jam tum ab ipso Deo omnino jussa: neque enim videtur ille retributionem a Deo prorsus exspectare debere· qui id facit quod omnino facere jussus est: non loquor jam de totius legis conservatione, sed de re aliqua praestita quae in ipsa lege jussa fuerit. At vero quando id quod quis praestat, excedit ipsius legis praescriptum; & interim est aliquid singulare ac difficile ad praestandum, quodque fidem faciat animi maxime virtute praediti, quale est istud, ipsis inimicis suis benefacere; tunc videtur retributioni omnino locum fore, hic enim fit plus, quam facere quis obstrictus fuerit.
units.tr: Reply 1. Solomon's words, uttered in the form of a command, are both precepts themselves and have the force of a precept. But he says they are not contained in the law. I, however, had thought that there is no precept concerning any matter or good work which is not comprehended in the law: both because of the perfection of the law in the whole field of morals and precepts, and because that highest commandment, to love one's neighbour as oneself, embraces everything within its compass. Especially this precept of which Solomon speaks can be so conveniently drawn from the law, Exodus 23:4-5, to say nothing of more general ones. It will be well for anyone who follows it, as the words that follow teach: "for you will heap coals on his head, and Jehovah will repay you." The great usefulness that will follow if anyone does these things therefore moved Solomon to admonish in this way, not because he judged it commanded in God's own law, since nothing hinders God from repaying one who does more than what has been prescribed and absolutely commanded by Him. Indeed the very fact that God is said to repay him can sufficiently indicate that these good deeds towards his enemy had not yet been wholly commanded by God Himself; for neither does he seem to have any reason to expect a reward from God at all who does only what he was wholly commanded to do. I am not now speaking of keeping the whole law, but of some deed performed which was commanded in the law itself. But when what someone performs exceeds the prescription of the law, and at the same time is something singular and difficult to perform, and which gives proof of a mind especially endowed with virtue, such as doing good to one's enemies, then it seems there will be room for reward altogether, for here more is done than one was bound to do.

units.la: possit, ac illud Exod. xxiii. 4. 5. ex Levit.xix.18. fuere Socinus autumavit. ii. Salomon, inquit, non profitetur, se legem Mosis explicare. Non necesse est, ut hoc expressis verbis praefetur: sufficit ut rem agat, id est, talia praecepta tradat, inculcet, quae ex legis penu & plenitudine sunt petita. Neque enim Prophetae hoc distincte profitentur, qui tamen passim legis doctrinam tradunt, ut conjungi ideo soleant, Moses & Prophetae. iii. Quid hoc est, Salomonem non profiteri se praecepta dare ex ipsius divini praescripti, & absoluti jussus mente? existimatne, Salomonem haec non scripsisse ex instinctu divino? ergo eum obruemus divinitate & authoritate Scripturae totius θεόπνευστος. Quam si everterit, sic demum Theologiae, vel potius Atheologiae suae locum repererit. Si vero Salomon, quemadmodum & reliqui Prophetae, scripserit actus Spiritu divino, non
units.tr: ...can, and that Socinus has asserted that Exodus 23:4-5 is drawn from Leviticus 19:18. ii. Solomon, he says, does not profess that he explains the law of Moses. It is not necessary that this be stated in express words; it is enough that he does the thing, that is, hands down and inculcates such precepts as are drawn from the store and fullness of the law. For the prophets do not profess this distinctly either, although they everywhere teach the doctrine of the law, so that Moses and the Prophets are commonly joined together. iii. What is this, that Solomon does not profess to give precepts from the mind of God's divine prescription and absolute command? Does he think Solomon did not write these things from divine inspiration? Then we will overwhelm him with the divinity and authority of all Scripture, which is God-breathed [θεόπνευστος]. If he overturns that, then at last he will find a place for his Theology, or rather his Atheology. But if Solomon, like the other prophets, wrote things moved by the divine Spirit, not

units.la: θελήματι ἀνθρώπῳ[?], ideoq; & ejus scripta sint οὐκ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, II Pet. 1. 20. 21. quorsum distinguit Salomonis doctrinam, à reliquâ Scripturâ Sacrâ? vel quare illum cum Mose committit? Verum haec minus mirabitur quis à Socino in librum Proverbiorum dicta, qui recolligat animo quae ex Adversariis attulimus, lib. 1. Socinianismi Confutat. cap. 1. in librum illum probrose dicta, quibus ipsorum alios dubitare de ejus authoritate; alios pro apocrypho eum habere, ostendimus. Nimirum propter elegans & augustum de Filio Dei, λόγῳ & Sapientiâ Deo, testimonium, quod eo libro occurrit. Quae testimonia & argumenta eo cariora & validiora haberi debent, quo Adversarii ad eludenda illa operose omnia convellere necesse habent, & ne quidem à turpissimis abstinere. iv. Monitionem exponit Propheta: non etiam legem? quasi monitiones non sint praecepta, vel praeceptis fundatae, & repugnent monitio & lex? atque ex horum distinctione possit negari praeceptum vel legem divinam esse, quod praecipiendi modo ipse dicit prolatum: imo quod omni sua parte legis formam tam habet, ac ullum in lege praeceptum. v. Quod hic Socinus monitionem, consilium appellare solent Pontificii: quae tamen ipse in hoc Commentario rejicit, pag. 46. 47. & plane ortum suum à carne habere asserit. vi. Salomonem, dicit Socinus, sperare atque affirmare, monitionem suam utilissimam fore, si quis illam sequatur. non etiam necessariam? qua tu authoritate legem aut monita Scripturae deprecias, vel solvis unum praeceptorum istorum? quasi non omnes legis monitiones sint utilissimae, & praeterquam necessitate, etiam usu suo commendentur? nequaquam illa inter se opponuntur, vel discrimen faciunt a lege: nec denique Salomonem licet dicere, sola utilitate motum sic edixisse, non quod censuerit id Dei lege iussum fuisse. vii. Nunc aperte Socinus in sui subsidium Pontificiorum themata advocat, docens, hominem plus facere, quam sibi in lege praescriptum sit: quod ne quidem cum sua doctrina satis convenit, nunc statuere hominem non legalem modo perfectionem, sed & plusquam perfectionem praestare potuisse. Agimus enim hic de tempore legis, non Euangelii, ubi justitia & perfectio legalis, non Euangelica (juxta ipsum) considerari debuit. At ex disputationibus contra Pontificios scire debebat, semper homines omnes infra perfectionem longe subsidere, neque praestare nos, quae pro officio legi debemus, posse, nedum illa ut superemus. Nil autem necesse Nostrorum disputationes relegere, aut inferre hic eorum argumenta, quum id ipsum absurdi loco duci debeat, quod in illorum castra, sui defendendi causa, se proripere necesse habeat noster Adversarius. viii. Non sequitur, ex divina remuneratione, quam pollicetur Propheta, quamque exspectar-vir pius in suo officio, ideo id praeter & supra legem esse. Nam ita quaevis officia, praesertim quae fidem faciant animi maxime virtute praediti, uti Socinus loquitur, Deus rependere solet, nec solummodo generalem totius legis observationem (sic dicendum, non conservationem) sed virtutes etiam particulares, praesertim quales sunt, uti hoc, benefacere inimicis suis. Ad omnem quippe religionem, & singula ejus capita referre oportet, quod Apostolus dixit, Hebr. xi. 6. accedentem ad Deum credere oportet, quod est, & quod quaerentibus ipsum sit remunerator. Denique si inimicis suis benefacere, argumentum sit animi maxime quidem virtute praediti, quod Socinus dicit, ergo ipsum illud virtus est haud minima. Quod si, ergo lege fuit praecepta, quae omnem docet virtutem, bonum omne, & justos mores. Quare illud homo praestans, nil supra legem agit, vel plus, quam facere obstrictus fuerit, uti temere Socinus hic loquitur. Qui posset homo plus facere, quam obstrictus sit, quamque teneatur, quum lex omnes hominum ad bene agendum vires postulet, potentiam omnem? Neque solum lex exigit, ut faciamus bona, sed & omnia, & omni modo, vi, gradu: non extensive tantum & objective omnia & singula ut praestemus officia, quae charitas hinc inde jubet, sed & intensive, tot & tantum ac omnino possumus. Ut nihil excogitare possimus, praestare nihil, quod non ex lege debeamus, omne & quousque possumus. Non ferenda ergo sunt, quae Socinus ex Papatu resorbet, & suis iterum propinat, de operibus supererogatoriis. Nam quamvis in aliis rebus Pontificii illa constituant, eodem tamen nituntur fundamento haec & illa, eandemque habent originem, quod sc. homines plus boni praestare queant, quam ipsis per Deum, & in lege sit injunctum. Ne dicam, sic quoque funda-mentum mentum sterni ἐθελοθρησκείας[?], quæ in illis versatur, quæ quis non secundum legem, ejusque jussa, sed propria voluntate aggreditur, & (quomodo de Salomonis monito hic philosophatur Socinus) ubi movetur quis propter summam, quam inde consequuturam sperat, utilitatem.
units.tr: [θελήματι ἀνθρώπῳ], and therefore his writings are not of private interpretation [οὐκ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως], 2 Pet. 1:20-21. Why does he distinguish Solomon's teaching from the rest of Sacred Scripture, or why does he set him against Moses? But no one will be surprised at what Socinus says against the book of Proverbs if he recalls what we showed from our Adversaries, Book 1 of the Socinianismi Confutatio, chapter 1: that some of them doubt its authority, while others hold it apocryphal, and say abusive things against that book. Namely, this is because of the elegant and august testimony concerning the Son of God, the Word [λόγος] and Wisdom of God, which occurs in that book. Those testimonies and arguments ought to be held all the more precious and weighty, the more the Adversaries feel obliged to overthrow all of them with labour in order to evade them, and do not even refrain from the most shameful means. iv. The prophet sets out an admonition, not also the law? As if admonitions were not precepts, or founded on precepts, and admonition and law were opposed? And from this distinction could it be denied that what he himself declares in the form of a command is a divine precept or law? Indeed it has in every part the form of law just as much as any precept in the law. v. What Socinus here calls an admonition, the Papists are accustomed to call counsel; yet he himself rejects this in his Commentary, pages 46-47, and asserts that it has its origin wholly in the flesh. vi. Solomon, says Socinus, hopes and affirms that his admonition will be most useful if anyone follows it. Not also necessary? By what authority do you disparage the law or the admonitions of Scripture, or dissolve one of those precepts? As if all the admonitions of the law were not most useful, and commended by their use as well as by their necessity? Nor are they opposed to one another, or do they make any distinction from the law. Nor finally may it be said that Solomon, moved by utility alone, so ordered, not because he judged it commanded by God's law. vii. Now openly Socinus calls in the themes of the Papists in his own support, teaching that a man does more than is prescribed to him in the law. This does not even agree well enough with his own doctrine, since now he states that man could perform not only legal perfection but even more than perfection. For we are here dealing with the time of the law, not the Gospel, where justice and legal perfection, not evangelical (according to him), ought to be considered. But from the disputations against the Papists he ought to know that men always fall far short of perfection, and that we cannot perform what we owe by duty under the law, much less surpass it. Nor is there any need to reread our disputations or to bring in their arguments here, since that very thing ought to be counted absurd: that our Adversary, to defend himself, must rush into their camp. viii. It does not follow, from the divine reward which the prophet promises and which the pious man awaits in his duty, that this is beyond and above the law. For God is accustomed to repay all duties in this way, and not only the general observance of the whole law (so it should be said, not conservation) but also particular virtues, especially such as this: to do good to one's enemies. For what the Apostle said, Hebrews 11:6, must be referred to all religion and to each of its heads: "he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him." Finally, if doing good to one's enemies is a proof of a mind especially endowed with virtue, as Socinus says, then that very thing is no small virtue. And if it is virtue, then it was commanded by the law, which teaches every virtue, all good, and just morals. Wherefore the excellent man does nothing beyond the law, or "more than he was bound to do," as Socinus rashly says here. How could a man do more than he is bound to, and more than he is obliged to, since the law demands all the strength of men for doing good, every power? Not only does the law require us to do good things, but all things, and in every way, with all vigour and degree: not only extensively and objectively, to perform all and each of the duties which charity enjoins on every side, but also intensively, as much and as greatly as we are altogether able. So that we cannot devise anything, or perform anything, which we do not owe by the law, and we owe everything as far as we are able. Therefore those things which Socinus takes from the Papacy and serves up again to his own people, concerning works of supererogation, are not to be tolerated. For although the Papists establish those things in other matters, these and those rest on the same foundation and have the same origin: namely, that men can perform more good than is enjoined on them by God and in the law. Not to mention that by this also a foundation is laid for self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία], which occurs when someone undertakes, not according to the law and its commands, but by his own will, and (as Socinus here philosophizes about Solomon's admonition) when someone is moved by the great usefulness which he hopes will follow from it.

units.la: Quarto, probamus ea quæ Christus hoc loco proponit, non ita interpretanda esse, quemadmodum Socinus cupit, quia lex Mosis nusquam præcepit odium alicujus hominis, non sui ipsius, non alterius, non inimici; semper charitatem & amorem. Proferat unum, si possit, locum Adversarius, quo mandari odium aliquod ostendat. Non, quo probet averPandos homines aliquos esse, seclu-dendos, armis etiam oppugnandos, delendosque: de hoc non quæritur: sed odio habendos esse, ubi hoc præcipiatur. Nam illa absque odio haberi & fieri posse, ut quem averseris, etiam justo bello exscindas, res satis ostendit. Quemadmodum ubique, & in Ecclesiasticis, politicis, atque domesticis rebus distingui affectus debent in rem, sive causam; & personam: in vitium rei, vel in personam ipsam. Profer, ubi lex dixerit, odio habendum esse hominem aliquem, tum extraneum omnem, sive quemcunque non Israëlitam, id est, plurimam hominum partem. Scio quod nunquam hoc faciet vel Socinus, vel quis alius. Non de illâ hoc probabit lege, quæ tam constanter & copiose amorem urget & loquitur, quamque ipsam, ubi in N. Test de amore agitur, solam seu Christus, seu Apostoli satis habent proferre isto in negotio. Quin & Socinus, pag. 168. odium erga inimicum prohibitum in lege fuisse tandem fatetur, quando quidem officia ista ab iis tantum negligi solent, qui vindicta cupiditatem, aut saltem odium adversus inimicum suum retinent; quod utrumque ab ipso Mose vetitum fuisse, & fatemur, & scriptum esse ipsimet contendimus, nempe supra memorato cap. 19. Levitici. Ergo quod Christus hic adfert, dictum Antiquis, odio habendum inimicum esse, non fuit legis, uti aliàs Socinus contendit.
units.tr: Fourthly, we maintain that the things Christ sets forth in this place are not to be interpreted as Socinus wishes, because the law of Moses nowhere commands hatred of any person: not of oneself, not of another, not of an enemy. It always commands charity and love. Let the Adversary produce, if he can, one passage in which the law enjoins some hatred. I do not mean a passage showing that some men are to be shunned, shut out, attacked even with arms, and destroyed. That is not the question. The question is whether hatred is to be felt where it is commanded. That such things can be done without hatred, and that you may destroy with a just war someone you shun, the matter itself shows well enough. In everything, whether ecclesiastical, political or domestic, feelings must be distinguished according to whether they are directed at the matter or cause, or at the person: at the fault of the thing, or at the person himself. Produce a place where the law says that a certain man is to be hated, and then that every foreigner, or whoever is not an Israelite, that is, the greater part of mankind. I know that neither Socinus nor anyone else will ever do this. He will not prove it from that law, which so constantly and copiously urges and speaks of love, and which, when the New Testament deals with love, Christ or the Apostles alone are content to cite in this matter. Indeed Socinus, on page 168, at last admits that the hatred of an enemy was forbidden in the law, since indeed these duties are usually neglected only by those who retain a desire for revenge, or at least hatred against their enemy; and we both admit that both of these were forbidden by Moses himself, and we contend that it is written in the very chapter 19 of Leviticus mentioned above. Therefore what Christ here adduces, that it was said to the Ancients that one should hate his enemy, was not a precept of the law, as Socinus elsewhere contends.

units.la: Denique & ratio, quam adfert Christus doctrinæ suæ de amandis inimicis, peremtoria est & perpetua, quæque in V. Test. æque valuit, ac sub Novo, videlicet, ut sitis filii Patris vestri cœlestis, qui solem suum exoriri facit supra malos & bonos, &c. Hoc adeo curare & anniti oportuit sub V. Test. viventes illos, æque ac sub Novo jam Test. nos: quare & diligere inimicos, per quod illud obtinetur.
units.tr: Finally, the reason Christ gives for his teaching about loving enemies is decisive and perpetual, and it held as much under the Old Testament as under the New, namely, that you may be sons of your heavenly Father, who makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, etc. Those living under the Old Testament had to take care of this and strive for it just as we now do under the New, and so also to love enemies, by which this is attained.

units.la: Atque ita vindicavimus Matth. cap. v. contra expositionem & disputatio-nem Socini, ostendimusque, Christum sibi non proponere legem Mosis mo-ralem refigere, aliisque præceptis perfectioribus augere, aut cumulare[?], sed legem contra falsas Scribarum, & populi acceptiones & interpreta-tiones veritati & plenitudini suæ restituere. Quod primùm in genere, tum in specie probavimus, de singulis præceptis, quæ Christus adducit, quæque hic tractat, Antiquis dicta: de non occidendo primùm, vers. 21. Deinde, de non machando, vers. 27. Tertio, de non pejerando, vers. 33. Quarto, de talione oculi pro oculo, vers. 38. Denique quinto, de diligendo proximo, & odio habendo inimico, vers. 43: Jam tempus est ut progrediamur, ad singula Decalogi præcepta, visuri & examinaturi ea, quæ Sociniani dicunt addita à Christo sub N. T. fuisse, & quæ alia Christo propria, supra illa etiam, adjecta ajunt prioribus fuisse. Quæ hactenus, in vindicatione cap. v. Matthæi spectavimus, ipsa suis locis eo faciliorem præbebunt operam atque disputationem.
units.tr: And so we have defended Matthew chapter 5 against the exposition and disputation of Socinus, and we have shown that Christ does not propose to restore the moral law of Moses or to enlarge or add to it by more perfect precepts, but to restore the law, against the false acceptations and interpretations of the Scribes and the people, to its truth and fullness. This we proved first in general, and then in particular, for the individual precepts that Christ cites and treats here, which were said to the Ancients: first, concerning not killing, verse 21; second, concerning not committing adultery, verse 27; third, concerning not swearing falsely, verse 33; fourth, concerning retaliation, an eye for an eye, verse 38; and finally, fifth, concerning loving one's neighbour and hating an enemy, verse 43. Now it is time to proceed to the individual precepts of the Decalogue, to look at and examine those things which the Socinians say were added by Christ under the New Testament, and which they say were added to the earlier precepts as things peculiar to Christ beyond those. What we have so far considered in our defence of Matthew chapter 5 will, in their own places, give an easier labour and disputation.

units.la: PARS CAPITIS SECUNDA.
units.tr: SECOND PART OF THE CHAPTER.

units.la: Præcepto autem primo, Sociniani dicunt, per Christum addita fuisse de novo tria. 1. Generale & universale mandatum, de faciendis precibus. 11. Additam dicunt Formulam ac modum Orationis Dominicæ. 111. Præceptum, de invocando Christo. Alias inquiunt, duo à Christo addita: primum, orandi formulam; tum, invocandum etiam esse Christum. Sic Catechesis Racoviensis, cap. 1. de Prophetico Christi munere, pag. 194. Duo etiam Volkelius dicit, lib. iv. cap. 9. sed aliter: primo enim Christus suos preces Deo fundere tum docuit, tum assidue eos hoc facere jussit. Deinde de Deo per semetipsum colendo præcepit. Quorum prius antea Israelitis imperatum minime fuisse, inde constat &c. Ergo sub priori illo comprehendit tum præceptum generale de faciendis Deo precibus, tum formulam Orationis Dominicæ. Commiscet itidem Smalcius, lib. de Divinit. Christi, cap. v. In lege dictum erat, ne alios Deos præter unum haberemus, aut coleremus. Implevit eam & perfecit D. Iesus, dum & modum orationis (qua una ex potissimis cultus divini partibus est) certum, & perpetuum, eumque plane divinum prescripsit: tum etiam modum colendi Deum novum, qui antea plane erat inauditus, revelavit & præcepit. Lex enim nusquam aperte præcipit orationem, nedum, ut certum orandi modum præscribat. Quare nos distinctius tres ponimus quæstiones, revera de tribus, quæ Adversarii statuunt præcepto primo adjecta per Christum fuisse. Et primò quidem de hoc dispiciemus: an nullum in V. Test. de faciendis Deo precibus, extet præceptum; an vero hoc à Christo demum inventum, & legi veteri additum sit? Huc enim tendunt omnia Adversariorum Argumenta, quamvis illud involvere ament, & non denudare. Sic Smalcius, cur oratio in Veteri fœdere præcepta non fuerit, nunc autem præcepta sit, in margine posuit: & hoc primum ostendere satagit, cur in lege oratio præcepta non sit: deinde, quod in Nova fœdere & oratio nobis præcepta est, & modus orationis. Ut idcirco non duo tantum, sed imo tria, prout nos fecimus, à Christo addita hic, ex suo sensu dicere debuerint.
units.tr: The Socinians say that three things were newly added by Christ to the first precept: (1) a general and universal command to make prayers; (2) the form and manner of the Lord's Prayer, which they say was added; (3) a precept to invoke Christ. At other times they say that two things were added by Christ: first, a form of prayer; and then, that Christ too is to be invoked. So the Racovian Catechism, ch. 1, on the prophetic office of Christ, p. 194. Volkelius also speaks of two, book 4, ch. 9, but differently: For first, Christ taught that his followers should pour out their prayers to God, and he repeatedly commanded them to do so. Then he commanded that God be worshipped through himself. That the former was never enjoined on the Israelites is clear from this, etc. So under the former he includes both the general command to make prayers to God and the form of the Lord's Prayer. Smalcius likewise mixes these things together, in his book on the divinity of Christ, ch. 5: In the law it was said that we should not have or worship other gods besides the one. Our Lord Jesus fulfilled and perfected this, when he prescribed both a fixed and perpetual manner of prayer (which is one of the chief parts of divine worship), and that one plainly divine, and also revealed and commanded a new manner of worshipping God, which before had been wholly unheard of. For the law nowhere openly commands prayer, much less prescribes a fixed manner of praying. Therefore we set out three questions more distinctly, concerning the three things which our opponents hold were added by Christ to the first precept. And first we shall examine this: whether there is no precept in the Old Testament concerning making prayers to God, or whether this was first found by Christ and added to the old law. For all the arguments of our opponents tend to this, although they prefer to wrap it up rather than lay it bare. So Smalcius, in the margin, put: why prayer was not commanded in the Old Covenant, but is now commanded; and he labours to show first why prayer was not commanded in the law, then that both prayer and the manner of prayer are commanded to us in the New Covenant. So by their own reckoning they ought to say that not two but even three things were added here by Christ, as we have done.

units.la: Probamus autem, non à Christo demum, vel in N. Test. sed jam olim etiam in V. lege & Test. præceptum viguisse de oratione Deo faciendâ. Pri-mo, ex generali lege de cultu Dei, sub quo non potest non comprehendi & agnosci illud de precibus. Neque enim, opinor, negabunt Adversarii, præcep-tum de colendo Deo extitisse sub V. Test.: vel, hoc argumentum esse primi in Decalogo præcepti. Quod est argumentum, & primum caput cultus naturalis, nedum instituti. Quid ergo negaturi sunt, ex præcepto illo sequi, & invocandum Deum esse? vel, hoc illius vi contineri & summâ? sic certe negabunt aliquid contra manifestissimam rei lucem, & vel Gentilium nocitiam atque Theologiam. Si enim natura sciverunt, colendum Deum esse, ex eodem capite & lege haud ignorarunt, eum quoque esse invocandum. Sciverunt utique: quod ex doctrina, & praxi eorum constat. nec ex alio indicio magis hoc, quam illud, & vicissim: utrumque nempe ex eadem lege, & vel ratione naturali. Quod ergo docuit illos colendum Deum, idem ostendit, & invocandum esse. Praeterquam quod generalia cultus Dei praecepta quando consideramus, ipsa comprehendere quoque orationes liquidem satis fit. Deut.vi.13. Dominum Deum tuum timebis, eique servies, & in nomine ejus jurabis. An juramentum absque invocatione esse potest, vel absque ea vera Dei & plena servitus? עבודה [?] apud Hebraeos, quemadmodum λατρεία [?] apud Graecos, adorationis cultum significat. Jam quis illud praeceptum, ejusque vim digne expendet & explicabit, qui non invocationem, praecipuum cultus divini modum, comprehenderit quoque? Atque ejusmodi loca & praecepta in V. Test. frequenter occurrunt, quae cultum Dei exigant. Omnium loco est primum in Decalogo praeceptum, quod, uti alienos Deos, eorumque cultum damnat, ita unius veri Dei cultum complectitur, & pro suo habet argumento. Quid, dum cultum omnem extraneum vetat, annon etiam falsorum numinum invocationem damnat, quemadmodum secundo praecepto cultum imaginum? ita etiam dum cultum unius Dei verum commendat, non ejus quoque continere invocationem non potest. Accedit consensus Catechesis Racoviensis, pag. 162. quidnam complectitur istud primum praeceptum in se? Resp. Duo, primum, ut Deum pro nostro Deo habeamus, eique divinum honorem praestemus. Alterum, ne alium, praeter eum, pro Deo nostro habeamus, eumque honorem nulli alteri praestemus. Tum quaerens, in quo honore ille consistit? breviter respondendo, consistit in invocatione. Unde pergit, ad naturam invocationis plenius exponendam, aitque, Christum illi praecepto addidisse precationis formam, quam praescripsit. Quare sic argumentamur: Si praeceptum in Decalogo primum, cultum Dei injungendo, praecipue quidem invocationem Dei comprehendat, ut in quo cultus & honor Dei primario consistit; ergo in Veteri lege oratio praecepta fuit: sed verum prius, tum ex natura praecepti, tum doctrina Catechesis: ergo & postremum contra Smalcium, & Socinianos alios.
units.tr: We prove, however, that the precept concerning making prayer to God was in force not only from Christ, or only in the New Testament, but already long ago, even under the law and the Old Testament. First, from the general law concerning the worship of God, under which the precept concerning prayers cannot but be included and recognised. For I suppose our opponents will not deny that a precept concerning worshipping God existed under the Old Testament, or that this is the argument of the first precept of the Decalogue. And this is the argument and first head of natural worship, let alone instituted worship. What then will they deny follows from that precept, namely that God is to be invoked? Or that this is contained in its force and sum? In this way they will certainly deny something contrary to the most manifest light of the matter, and deny the testimony of the Gentiles and of natural theology. For if by nature they knew that God is to be worshipped, they were by no means ignorant, from the same head and law, that he is also to be invoked. They certainly knew this, as is clear from their teaching and practice. Nor is there any sign of the one more than of the other, and vice versa: both, of course, from the same law and from natural reason. Therefore what taught them that God was to be worshipped shows also that he is to be invoked. Besides, when we consider the general precepts of the worship of God, it is quite enough to see that they also clearly include prayers. Deut. 6:13: You shall fear the Lord your God, and serve him, and swear by his name. Can there be swearing without invocation, or true and full service of God without it? The word avodah [עבודה] among the Hebrews, like latreia [λατρεία] among the Greeks, signifies the worship of adoration. Now who will duly weigh and explain that precept and its force, if he does not also include invocation, the chief mode of divine worship? And such passages and precepts, which require the worship of God, occur frequently in the Old Testament. The first precept of the Decalogue stands for all of them: as it condemns strange gods and their worship, so it embraces the worship of the one true God and makes it its own argument. When it forbids every strange worship, does it not also condemn the invocation of false deities, just as the second precept condemns the worship of images? And so, while it commends the worship of the one God, it cannot fail to contain also the invocation of him. To this is added the agreement of the Racovian Catechism, p. 162: What does this first precept embrace in itself? Answer: Two things: first, that we have God as our God, and render him divine honour. Second, that we have no other besides him as our God, and render that honour to no other. Then, asking in what that honour consists?, it answers briefly: It consists in invocation. From there it goes on to explain more fully the nature of invocation, and says that Christ added to that precept the form of prayer which he prescribed. Therefore we argue thus: if the first precept of the Decalogue, enjoining the worship of God, chiefly includes the invocation of God, as the place in which the worship and honour of God primarily consist, then prayer was commanded under the Old Law. But the first is true, both from the nature of the precept and from the teaching of the Catechism. Therefore the last also holds, against Smalcius and the other Socinians.

units.la: Secundum argumentum. Imo & speciales in Vet. Testam. pro faciendis orationibus leges fuerunt, atque praecepta. Psalm. L. 15. Atque invoca me, in die angustia, eripiam te, & glorificabis me. Ibi exsertum invocandi Deum, praeceptum est. Etiam juxta Adversariorum inter adorationem, & invocationem discrimen, quando illam pro cultu civili habent, istam pro religioso, & describunt, quod fit, cum quis in necessitate constitutus, aut aliquid percupiens, confidenter alienam opem & benignitatem imploret. Smalcius de Divinitat. Christi, pag. 141. Atqui hic praecipitur, divinae opis imploratio, in die necessitatis, vel angustiae. Praecipitur etiam laudatio, vel glorificatio Dei, post acceptam liberationem. Quae item pars & species orationis est.
units.tr: Second argument. Indeed there were also special laws and precepts in the Old Testament concerning the making of prayers. Psalm 50:15: And call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. There the duty of invoking God is expressly commanded. Even according to our opponents' distinction between adoration and invocation, when they take the one as civil worship and the other as religious, and describe invocation as what happens when someone, placed in need or desiring something, confidently implores the help and kindness of another, Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, p. 141. But here the imploring of divine help in the day of need or distress is commanded. Also the praise or glorification of God after deliverance is commanded. This too is a part and kind of prayer.

units.la: Quod autem Volkelius excipit, pag. Temere distinguit inter Dei istud Davidis pronunciatum, consilium, quod Psaltes, Dei verbis, pronon mandatum, non legale fuisse: fert ; atque praeceptum: quum revera Dei quasi verbis, atque adeo Dei quoddam praeceptum, tale consilium Dei sit, consilium proferens, juadet, ut illius opem quod à praecepto nihil differt, atque homines afflictionis tempore implorent, certo modo & verbis praecipiendi profera-sibi persuadentes, eum preces illorum audi- tur. ii. Item temere Davidem Mosi, vel Psalmos legi opponit, quasi alia turum. Quod tamen Davidis pronunciatum, ejusmodi mandatum, quale hoc loco commemoramus, minime fuisse, si modo in manda- illic aut isthic praecepta proponantur, tus numerandum est, inde perspicitur, quod & non quae in Psalmis, vel cum lege Deus non in Psalmis praecepta generalia, conveniant, vel in illa fundentur. quibus omnes sub poena comminatione ob- iii. Quare non ex Psalmis & Pro-stringerentur, dedit, sed in ipso foedere per phetis de doctrina & praeceptis V. T. Mosem cum populo illo facto. Itaque haec judicare nobis aeque liceat, ac Adver-Davidis verba, vel consilium tantum conti- fariis, ex scriptis Apostolorum, de do-nent, vel si mandatum continent, illud nequa- ctrina Jesu Christi, & ex illis scilicet quam caeteris praeceptis in ipso foedere com- producere praecepta N.Test. alia supra prehensis par censendum est: ut taceam illud legem solent, & doctrinam Mosis? non perpetuo, omnibusque temporibus ad pre- iv. Praeceptum de Deo invocando, candum homines obstrinxisse: cum hic nonnisi quod est Psalm. l. non est generale? tempus afflictionis, quod Deus sit invocandus, annon omnes concernit, quibuscum-exprimatur. que afflictionibus obsitos, oppressos-que? certe non alia forma conceptum, aut subnixum est re alia, quam generali, & omnibus hominibus conveniente. v. Sin autem istud tale est mandatum, quod lege nulla ratione subnixum fuit, ergo non Euangelium modo dicas, praecepta continere alia & perfectiora à lege, sed idem de Psalmis, aliisque post Mosis legem scriptis pronuncies quoque. vi. Quaero, praeceptum istud orandi Deum, accedit vel ad doctrinam legis, vel Euangelii. Si ad illud, ergo in ipso foedere per Mosem cum populo illo facto continebatur: sin istud, ergo doctrina Euangelii sub V. etiam Testam. patefacta est & viguit. vii. Reprehensionem & comminationem neglecti precum officii sub V. Test. etiam factam, tum res ipsa, tum quae hoc loco adferimus argumenta demonstrant. viii. Quod David, quod alii Prophetae θεόπνευστοι[?] docent, monent, praecipiunt, à Deo est, non minus ac lex Mosis, quare & par ei, ejusdem authoritatis viriumque haberi debet. ix. Quamvis tempus afflictionis commemoretur hoc in praecepto, non tamen ad illud solum restringitur: imo res ipsa docet, & vis loci, quod idem officium nunquam non Deo gratum, & hominibus salutare sit, ideoque assiduo observandum. Nec est aut ullum tempus à Christo expressum, vel causa, aut orandi necessitas, quae non sub V. Testam. fuerit, & tum ex locis, quae adferimus, cognosci potuerit, vel religione Patrum sit observata. Psalm. xxi. 15. invocabit me, & respondebo ei, in tribulatione ero cum eo, eripiam eum, & glorificabo eum. Iesa. lv. 6. quaerite Dominum, dum inveniri potest: invocate eum, dum prope est. Cap. lviii. 9. Tunc invocabis, & Dominus respondebit, clamabis, & dicet, ecce adsum. Psalm. xxvii. 8. Tibi dicit cor meum, dicis, requirite faciem meam ; faciem tuam requiro Domine. Psalm. xxxvii. 4. dabit tibi petitiones cordis tui.
units.tr: As for what Volkelius takes exception to: he rashly distinguishes between that pronouncement of David, which the Psalmist uttered in God's words, as a counsel and not a command, and not a legal precept. He claims that David's pronouncement was not a command of the kind we mention here. Yet it is clear that it is in fact a sort of command of God, as it were in God's words, and so a certain precept of God; such a counsel of God, offering counsel, it persuades people in time of affliction to implore his help, differs in no way from a precept, proposing it in a fixed manner and in words of command, persuading themselves that he will hear their prayers. (ii.) Likewise he rashly sets David against Moses, or the Psalms against the law, as if they put forward other precepts, not those contained in the Law. But if precepts are to be counted among commands only where they are laid down either in the law or in agreement with it, then it appears from this that God did not give general precepts in the Psalms, by which all would be bound under penalty and threat, but in the covenant itself made through Moses with that people. So David's words either contain only a counsel, or if they contain a command, it is by no means to be reckoned equal to the other precepts contained in the covenant itself. Not to mention that it did not bind men perpetually and at all times, since here only the time of affliction is expressed, when God is to be invoked. (iii.) Therefore is it not equally right for us to judge from the Psalms and the Prophets concerning the doctrine and precepts of the Old Testament as it is for our opponents to judge from the writings of the Apostles concerning the doctrine of Jesus Christ, and from them to produce precepts of the New Testament beyond the law and the teaching of Moses? (iv.) Is the precept concerning invoking God, which is in Psalm 50, not general? Does it not concern all, of whatever afflictions they are beset and oppressed? Certainly it is not conceived in another form, nor grounded on another basis, than a general one that suits all men. (v.) But if that is such a command as had no basis in the law, then you will say not only that the Gospel contains precepts other and more perfect than the law, but you will also say the same of the Psalms and other writings after the law of Moses. (vi.) I ask: does this precept of praying to God belong to the doctrine of the law or of the Gospel? If to the law, then it was contained in the covenant itself made through Moses with that people; but if to the Gospel, then the doctrine of the Gospel was also revealed and in force under the Old Testament. (vii.) That under the Old Testament there was also rebuke and threat for neglecting the duty of prayer is shown both by the thing itself and by the arguments we adduce here. (viii.) What David and the other inspired Prophets teach, admonish and command is from God, no less than the law of Moses; hence it must be held equal to it and of the same authority and force. (ix.) Although the time of affliction is mentioned in this precept, it is not restricted to that alone. Indeed the thing itself teaches, and the force of the passage, that this duty is never not pleasing to God and salutary to men, and therefore is to be observed continually. Nor is there any time, or cause, or necessity of praying mentioned by Christ which was not under the Old Testament, and which could not be known from the passages we adduce, or was not observed by the religion of the Fathers. Psalm 91:15: He shall call upon me, and I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him, and glorify him. Isaiah 55:6: Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Isaiah 58:9: Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry, and he will say, Behold, here I am. Psalm 27:8: My heart says to you, Seek my face; your face, Lord, I seek. Psalm 37:4: He will give you the petitions of your heart.

units.la: Arg. tertium. Quæ lex cultum Dei publicum instituit, & oblationem sacrificiorum, eadem præcipit quoque orationes Deo fieri : quia absque orationibus illa peragi nequeunt. Verum lex vetus cultum Dei publicum instituit & præcepit, atque etiam sacrificiorum oblationem : ergo. Adeo quidem cultus Dei publicus in exercitio precum consistit, ut imprimis inde denominetur. Genes. iv. ult. tunc cœptum invocari nomen Domini. Atque hinc denotari & de-scribi solet Patriarcharum religio, quod Deum tum hic, tum ibi, ad hæc vel illa loca, & altaria, in Tabernaculo postmodum, & templo, invocarunt. Vide Deut. xii. 5. 6. 7. & Levit. xvi. 17. 11 Chron. vi. 19. & respicies ad precationem servi tui ; & ad observationem ejus, Domine Deus meus, ad exaudiendum clamorem & orationem quam servus tuus oraverit coram te. Ut sint oculi tui aperti in do-mum hanc die & nocte, in locum, de quo dixisti, quod poneres nomen tuum ibi, ad audiendum orationem, quam oraturus est servus tuus in loco isto. Et audias deprecationes servi tui & populi tui Israël, quas precabuntur versus locum istum, & tu exaudias de loco habitationis tuæ de cælo, & audiens remittas. Cap. vii. 12. Et apparuit Jehova Salomoni nocte illa, & dixit ei, & audivi orationem tuam, & elegi locum hunc mihi in domum sacrificiorum. Si clauso fuerit cœlos, & non fuerit pluvia &c. Et humiliabit se populus meus, super quem invocatur nomen meum, & oraverint, requisiverintque faciem meam, & reversi fuerint a viis suis malis, ego exaudiam e cœlis, & condonabo peccatum eorum, & curabo terram ipsorum. Jam oculi mei aperti erunt, & aures meæ intentæ ad orationem loci hujus, &c. Ex quibus apparet, cultum publicum, & sacrificiorum absque precibus nullum fuisse, & illo instituto, orationes etiam præceptas pro-batasque intelligi. Luc. i. 10. Et omnis multitudo populi erat foris orans tempore suffitus. Prov. xv. 8. sacrificium impiorum abominatio Jehova : oratio autem rectorum beneplacitum ejus.
