Quasi pro synonymis habentur, sacrificium & oratio. Psalm. lxix. 31. 32. Laudabo nomen Dei cantico, & magnificabo eum gratiarum actione. Quæ melior videbitur Jehova, bove, juvenco cornuto, scindente ungulas. Accedit, quod Num. vi. 22. Deus per Mosem Aaroni præscribit rationem benedicendi, & apprecandi à Deo benedictionem populo suo. 27. Et imponent filiis Israelis nomen meum, & ego benedicam eis. Denique non tantum ut pars cultus divini tum cujuscumque in se consideratí, tum publici in Ecclesia, necessaria, & præcipua preces sunt, sed & universus cultus atque religio officio & exercitio orationum denotari solet, in Veteri, atque in Novo Testamento. Unde colligitur, præceptam probatamque orationem fuisse etiam in Veteri, nec tantum in Novo Testam. Nam quod pro tota religione venit, & censeri compendiose solet, etiam in V. Test. qua ratione negari poterit inter præcepta quoque habitum fuisse? Jam vero ita de præcepto & officio precum judicatum in V. Testam. fuisse, ex locis Scripturæ tum citatis, tum citandis, manifestum.
units.tr: Third argument. The law that establishes public worship of God and the offering of sacrifices also commands that prayers be made to God, since those rites cannot be performed without prayers. But the old law established and commanded public worship of God, and also the offering of sacrifices. Therefore it commands prayer. Indeed public worship of God so consists in the practice of prayer that it is named after it above all. Genesis 4, last verse: then men began to call upon the name of the LORD. From this the religion of the patriarchs is also commonly described, because they called upon God here and there, at these or those places and altars, and afterwards in the Tabernacle and the Temple. See Deut. 12:5-7 and Lev. 16:17; 2 Chron. 6:19: Have respect therefore to the prayer of thy servant, and to his supplication, O LORD my God, to hearken unto the cry and the prayer which thy servant prayeth before thee: that thine eyes may be open upon this house day and night, even upon the place of which thou hast said, My name shall be there; that thou mayest hearken unto the prayer which thy servant shall make toward this place. And hear thou the supplications of thy servant, and of thy people Israel, when they shall pray toward this place: and hear thou from thy dwelling place, even from heaven; and when thou hearest, forgive. 2 Chron. 7:12: And the LORD appeared to Solomon by night, and said unto him, I have heard thy prayer, and have chosen this place to myself for an house of sacrifice. If I shut up heaven that there be no rain… If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land. Now mine eyes shall be open, and mine ears attent unto the prayer that is made in this place. From these passages it appears that there was no public worship and no sacrifice without prayers, and that by that institution the prayers commanded and approved are also to be understood. Luke 1:10: And the whole multitude of the people were praying without at the time of incense. Prov. 15:8: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD; but the prayer of the upright is his delight. Sacrifice and prayer are held as if they were synonyms. Ps. 69:30-31: I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving. This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs. Add that in Num. 6:22ff. God, through Moses, prescribes to Aaron the manner of blessing and of invoking a blessing from God upon his people, and at v. 27: And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them. Finally, prayers are not only necessary and chief as a part of divine worship, whether considered in itself or publicly in the Church; the whole worship and religion is also commonly denoted by the office and practice of prayer, in the Old as in the New Testament. Hence it is gathered that prayer was also commanded and approved under the Old Testament, not only under the New. For what stands for the whole of religion, and is commonly reckoned in summary, how can it be denied that it was also counted among the commands even in the Old Testament? Now that this is how the duty and command of prayer was judged under the Old Testament is clear from the passages of Scripture both cited and to be cited.

units.la: Arg. quartum. Cujus rei, vel officii & præcepti promissiones in V. Test. pares, eædemque ac in Novo sunt Testamento, ejus eadem utrobique fuit conditio,
units.tr: Fourth argument. A thing, or duty and command, whose promises are equal in the Old Testament and are the same as in the New, has the same condition and necessity in both.

units.la: Tom. 2. vis, & necessitas : sed precationum eædem utrobique promissiones sunt in Vet. ac in Novo T. : ergo. Promissiones nempe exauditionis, & liberationis, vel beneficii obtinendi. Nec minores aut pauciores in V. Test. occurrunt, quam in Novo: uti ex collatione utrarumque, si cui eam instituere lubitum, apparebit. Si in N. Test. dicitur, petite & dabitur vobis, idem non semel in Veteri. Psalm. xxxvii. 4. Et oblecta te in Jehova, dabitque tibi petitiones cordis tui. & l. 15. invoca me; & eripiam te. & xci. 15. invocabit me, & exaudiam eum, ero cum eo in angustia, eripiam eum, & glorificabit me. Psalm. lvi. 23. & xxxii. 6. & cxlv. 18. 19. Jesa. lv. 6. & lxv. 24. eritque antequam clamabunt, respondebo ipsis; dum adhuc loquuntur, ego exaudiam. Vide 1 Reg. viii. à vers. 28. & deinceps. Quid in N. Testam. aliud super hac re, super precum exauditione, & concessione votorum, scriptum promissumque extat, ac sunt quæ jam ex V. Testam. attulimus? Imo & pluries, & copiosius illa explanantur in V. Testam., quam in Novo.
units.tr: (Vol. 2.) force and necessity. But the promises concerning prayer are the same in the Old and the New Testament. Therefore it has the same condition. These are promises of being heard and delivered, or of obtaining a benefit. Nor do fewer or smaller ones occur in the Old Testament than in the New, as will appear from comparing the two, if anyone cares to make the comparison. If the New Testament says ask, and it shall be given you, the same is said more than once in the Old: Ps. 37:4: Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart. Ps. 50:15: Call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee. Ps. 91:15: He shall call upon me, and I will answer him: I will be with him in trouble; I will deliver him, and honour him. Ps. 56:23; 32:6; 145:18-19; Isa. 55:6; 65:24: And it shall come to pass, that before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear. See 1 Kings 8 from v. 28 onward. What else has been written and promised in the New Testament concerning this matter, the hearing of prayer and the granting of vows, than what we have already brought from the Old Testament? Indeed these things are explained more often and more fully in the Old Testament than in the New.

units.la: Arg. quintum. Etiam praxim si respiciamus precum, in V. Testamento, servata ea fuit æque, ac sub N.Test. Quin plura exempla ex V. Test. hanc in rem, quam ex N. proferre possis. Illic non tantum commemorata precantium, & precum exempla obiter, sed ex professo integri hujus argumenti libri extant: uti Psalmi Davidis: præterquam integra capita, orationum formas & usum exhibentia. Atqui exempla illa omnia nullo nixa præcepto fuerunt? nulla fidei certitudine, quod grata Deo fuerint acceptaque? Num ergo ἐϑελοϑρησκείᾳ & vani cultus habendi fuerunt, nec à Deo præcepti? Quo quid durius, absurdiusque dici possit. Rom. x. 13. 14. 15. Quicunque enim invocaverit nomen Dei salvus erit. Quomodo autem invocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? Quomodo autem credent, de quo non audiverunt? quomodo audient absque prædicante? quomodo vero prædicabunt nisi mittantur? 17. Est autem fides ex auditu: auditus autem per verbum Dei. Nec fides, nec preces possunt non niti verbo Dei. Digna observatu sunt verba Smalcii, quæ habet, cap. xxiv. pag. 142. ubi pro invocatione Christi disputat, hunc in modum: Adeo ut homines isti, non multum intelligere dici possint, qui Spiritu Iudaico inflati, propterea Jesum Christum invocare nolunt, quia scilicet apertum est de re præceptum nullum extet. Est enim invocatio Jesu Christi, ex numero earum rerum, quas præcipere nullo modo opus est: quemadmodum etiam invocatio ipsius Dei, non ideo principaliter nobis incumbit, quia Deus ita præcepit. Nam, ab ipso mundi initio, semper homines pios Deum invocasse, certissimum est, quos tamen, ea de re præceptum à Deo sibi datum ullum habuisse, nemo probare potest. Ad quæ hæc breviter annotamus. 1. Quod si non fit necesse, extare præceptum de invocando Christo, multo minus urgere possunt Adversarii præceptum de invocando Deo. Illud enim obscurius est, & minus notum, quam hoc. Imo nulla ratione notum esse potest, neque ex Scriptura, si Christus non sit Deus, nisi forte, quod Adversarii perperam dicunt, quod Deus jussit illum invocare. 11. Si non necesse est, præceptum extare de Deo, vel Christo invocando, quare in hoc & illo legis præcepta perfecta & adaucta tradunt Adversarii? 111. Quod si incumbit nobis neces-sitas sitas invocandi Deum, etiam citra præceptum, quare pro ejus necessitate præceptum exigunt? iv. Atque aliunde necessitas illa constare & probari poterit, nec ex Dei fœdere? v. Ex quâ ratione pii à condito mundo sciverunt Deum sibi adorandum esse, ex eâdem id habuerunt pro necessario: nec enim arbitrarius ille eorum cultus fuit, sed certus, communis, necessarius, qualis non nisi in præcepto fundari potuit.
units.tr: Fifth argument. If we look also at the practice of prayer, it was kept under the Old Testament just as under the New. Indeed you could bring forward more examples to this purpose from the Old Testament than from the New. There the mentions of those who pray and examples of prayers are not only incidental, but whole books on this very subject exist by design: such as the Psalms of David, besides whole chapters presenting the forms and use of prayers. But were all those examples founded on no command? On no certainty of faith that they were pleasing and acceptable to God? Then were they to be held as will-worship and vain worship, and not commanded by God? Nothing harsher or more absurd could be said. Rom. 10:13-15: For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent? v. 17: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. Neither faith nor prayers can be without the word of God. The words of Smalcius are worth noting, which he has in chapter 24, page 142, where, arguing for the invocation of Christ, he proceeds in this way: So that those men can hardly be said to understand much, who, puffed up with a Jewish spirit, refuse therefore to invoke Jesus Christ, because clearly no command about the matter exists. For the invocation of Jesus Christ is among those things which there is in no way any need to command; just as the invocation of God himself does not rest upon us chiefly because God so commanded. For it is most certain that from the very beginning of the world pious men have always invoked God, yet no one can prove that they had any command given them by God about this matter. To these things we briefly annotate: 1. If it is not necessary that a command concerning the invoking of Christ should exist, much less can the Adversaries press a command concerning the invoking of God. For the former is more obscure and less known than the latter. Indeed it can by no reasoning be known, neither from Scripture, if Christ is not God, except perhaps, as the Adversaries wrongly say, that God commanded us to invoke him. 2. If it is not necessary that a command should exist concerning the invoking of God or Christ, why do the Adversaries hand down the perfected and enlarged precepts of the law in this and that matter? 3. If there lies upon us a necessity of invoking God even without a command, why do they demand a command for his necessity? 4. And that necessity could be established and proved from elsewhere, not even from God's covenant? 5. By whatever reasoning the godly from the creation of the world knew that God was to be worshipped by them, by the same they held it to be necessary. For that worship of theirs was not arbitrary, but certain, common, necessary, such as could be founded only on a command.

units.la: Arg. sextum. Non invocantes Deum reprehensi fuerunt in V. Test. & pro impiis habiti: ergo & peccasse eos, & contra præceptum egisse, tunc etiam temporis constitit. Quomodo alias reprehendi, tam acriter, tantique peccati, aut criminis rei agi potuissent? Psalm.xiv.4. Jehovam non invocant. Jesa.lxiv. 7. Neque ullus est, qui invocet nomen tuum.
units.tr: Argument sixth. Those who did not call upon God were rebuked in the Old Testament and regarded as impious. Therefore it is also established that at that time they sinned and acted against the commandment. For how else could they have been rebuked so sharply, and charged with so great a sin or crime? Ps. 14:4, They do not call upon Jehovah. Isa. 64:7, And there is none that calleth upon thy name.

units.la: Jam & argumenta Adversariorum audiamus, in contrarium: quæ duo fere sunt. Primum hinc petitur, quod cum promissiones Patribus factæ fuerint rerum modo terrenarum, non cœlestium, id est, minores præceptis, ipsis præscriptis, haud necesse visum precibus à Deo implorare, quæ jure omni ipsis debebantur. Quæ quantum Dei & religionis contemtum sapiant, ecquis non videt? Secundum illi par hoc est, quod nullis singularibus ad præstanda præcepta atque obedientiam viribus habuerint opus, nec proinde precibus ad illas impetrandas. Smalcius, de Divinit. Christi, cap. v. pag. 17. Rationes autem, cur in lege oratio præcepta non sit, hæ videntur esse. Primùm, quod promissa omnia in lege pro-posita, non superabant id quod homines facere tenebantur: imo plus lex videbatur præcipe-re, quam promittere. Itaque jure quodam debebatur id, quod lex promittebat, ei, qui illam observaret; nec, ut id præterea oraret, ullo modo opus erat.
units.tr: Let us now hear the opponents' arguments to the contrary, which are about two. The first is drawn from this: since the promises made to the Fathers concerned only earthly things, not heavenly ones, that is, things lesser than the precepts themselves, it seemed scarcely necessary to implore from God by prayer what was owed to them by every right. How much these arguments savour of contempt for God and religion, who does not see? The second is like it: that they had no need of special powers to perform the precepts and obedience, and therefore no need of prayers to obtain them. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 5, p. 17: The reasons why prayer is not commanded in the law seem to be these. First, because all the promises proposed in the law did not exceed what men were bound to do; indeed the law seemed to command more than it promised. Therefore that which the law promised was owed by a certain right to the one who kept it, and there was no need at all for him to pray for it besides.

units.la: Alterum argumentum: Deinde, quod ea, quæ lex præcipiebat, absque singulari ope divina præstari poterant, eo saltem modo, in quo Deus acquiescebat. Nec enim ea alioquin præcipere salva justitia Deus potuisset, si nullo modo præstari potuissent. Similia habet Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. ix.
units.tr: The second argument: Further, because what the law commanded could be performed without special divine help, at least in the manner in which God was content. For otherwise God could not have commanded these things consistently with justice, if they could in no way have been performed. Volkelius has similar points, bk. 4, ch. 9.

units.la: Resp. Perquam multa hic videas, in una re, impietatis (dicendum enim est) Socinianæ argumenta. Non necessario Patres in V. Test. debuisse precari Deum. Tuto hoc, atque absque peccato & transgressione legis, omitti ab illis potuisse. Quinimo ex lege non debuisse illos precari. Non legis mandatum, aut respectum ullum ipsos ad preces adegisse, sed forte præsentem auxilii necessitatem, quum humanum ipsos destituerent. Volkelius: respondemus igitur, ut & supra innuimus, ad id, ut mandatum generale de precum studio detur, non satis esse, interdum ejusmodi tempora incidere, quibus, cum humana ope juvari non possimus, ad divinum præsidium sit confugiendum: cum res ipsa tunc absque ullo mandato præsertim generaliter tradito, hoc effagitare videatur: sed opus esse, ut perpetua quædam rei istius necessitas nobis incumbat, & ex ipso fadere quodammodo profluat: hoc est, ut divino auxilio denudati, neque sederis mandata perficere, nec ejusdem promissa ullo modo assequi possimus. Id est, nulla necessitas tum temporis fuit invocandi Deum, nisi quum humanâ ope destituti ad divinum præsidium confugiendum esset. At quanta illa calumnia in sanctissimam Patrum religionem & pietatem! quasi tali denum tempore ac necessitate ad Deum confugissent, neque extra illud tempus, & non semper orationibus intenti vixissent? Quod res ipsorum precationem efflagitarint, non animus. Non perpetua ipsis incubuerit necessitas precandi: non ex ipso foedere & lege id edocti fuerint, atque ad hoc adstricti. Quod foederis mandata bene praestare potuerint etiam absque divino auxilio, eoque denudati. Ut vid. non magis ipsos Deo, quam Deum ipsis eguisse, videatur. Nec divino auxilio opus habuerint, ad obtinenda legis promissa. Sibi nempe debita, atque à seipsis magis, quam à Deo exspectanda. Quae quam male & improbe dicta sint, contra Deum aeque ac Patres, nemo opinor non videt.
units.tr: Reply. Here you may see a great many arguments of Socinian impiety, in one matter alone (for it must be said). It was not necessary for the Fathers in the Old Testament to pray to God. They could safely, and without sin or transgression of the law, have omitted this. Indeed they ought not to have prayed from the law. It was not a command of the law, nor any regard for it, that drove them to prayer, but perhaps the present need of help when human aid failed them. Volkelius: We reply, therefore, as we also hinted above, that for a general commandment about zeal in prayer to be given, it is not enough that such times should occasionally befall, when, since we cannot be helped by human aid, we must flee to divine protection: since the matter itself then seems to demand this without any commandment, especially one generally delivered; but there must be some perpetual necessity of this thing lying upon us, and flowing in some way from the covenant itself: that is, that stripped of divine help, we could neither perform the covenant's commands nor attain its promises in any way. That is, there was no necessity to call upon God at that time except when, deprived of human aid, one had to flee to divine protection. But how great is that calumny against the most holy religion and piety of the Fathers! As if they had fled to God only at such a time and in such necessity, and had not lived at other times intent on prayer! It was their circumstances, not their disposition, that demanded prayer, they say. No perpetual necessity of praying lay upon them; they were not taught this by the covenant and law itself, nor bound to it. They could perform the covenant's commands well even without divine help, and stripped of it, as if they needed God no more than God needed them. Nor did they need divine help to obtain the promises of the law, which were owed to themselves and to be expected from themselves rather than from God. How badly and wickedly these things are said, against God as much as against the Fathers, I think no one fails to see.

units.la: Negamus, sola terrena bona Patribus promissa fuisse: cujus contrarium suo loco demonstravimus. Negamus, legem plus praecepisse, quam promisisse. Certe hoc ad servi illius nequissimi improbitatem accedit, qui oggerere judici audebat, durum eum esse, atque metere velle ubi non seminasset. Matth. xxv. 24. Negamus, promissa legis non superare nostra officia, id est, Dei benignitatem lege ostensam & promissam non superare hominum observantiam. Titubanter Volkelius, obedientiam lege sancitam vel nihil, vel parum admodum supe-rare visa ejus promissa. Negamus, ullum homini jus esse apud deum, vel observantem legis ex jure posse agere pro mercede, vel pro eo quod lex promittit, quasi suae observantiae debito, nedum quod hoc infra observantiam suam sit.
units.tr: We deny that the Fathers were promised only earthly goods; the contrary we have demonstrated in its place. We deny that the law commanded more than it promised. Certainly this adds to the wickedness of that most wicked servant who dared to tell his master that he was harsh and wished to reap where he had not sown (Matt. 25:24). We deny that the promises of the law do not exceed our duties, that is, that God's kindness shown and promised in the law does not exceed men's observance. Volkelius hesitantly says that its promises seem to exceed the obedience sanctioned by the law either not at all or very little. We deny that man has any right before God, or that one who keeps the law can by right sue for a reward, or for what the law promises as if it were owed to his observance, much less because this lies within his own observance.

units.la: Ut sic homo videatur Deum facere posse debitorem suum, & θεοδιδόναι[?], ad τὸ ἀνταπόδομα[?], quod contra Apostolum est, Rom. xi. 35. Hoc scilicet est Pontificiorum putidissimum atque infame meritum de condigno: quod resumunt & recoquunt nunc hi, qui non modo Reformati audiri cupiunt, sed eorum praecipui, quin & horum, si placet, reformatores. Imo turpius eo meritum est Socinianorum illud, quo non de condigno, sed supra condignum ponunt. Pontificii dare dicunt Deum, quod operibus ipsorum dignum sit: Sociniani, ne quidem illud, atque eorum dignitati non satisfacere. Vel Judaei hac in parte Socinianis meliores, qui Deum nullum opus mercede sua fraudare, communi & obvio axiomate tenent. Aliterque Christus nos docuit, Luc. xvii. verf. 10. quando omnia feceritis qua injuncta vobis, dicite, quod servi inutiles sumus. Dicent contra Sociniani, imo servi utiles sunt qui fecerint omnia, & supra quam utiles, nempe plus meriti, quam lex promittat, & qui de jure plura adhuc a Deo exigere possint vel exspectare, sive Deum facere sibi plurium debitorem. Quam longe aliter Patriarcha dicens, impar sum cunctis his beneficiis ? Genef. xxxii. 10. Denique demus, ut lex ipsis jure debuerit, quod promisit, tamen non hinc sequitur, in quo vis praesentis argumentationis haeret, ut orarent Deum nullo modo opus fuisse. Nam primo, annon alia erant, vel etiam norant ipsi tum bona sibi concedenda, tum avertenda mala, quam terrena & corporalia? & siquidem norant, annon sensus conscientiae & religionis ad precationes pro talibus formandas ipsos adigere poterat & permovere? Tum pro corporalibus bonis non etiam orandum dicemus Deum? vel, quod Volkelius, nec terrena illa felicitas tanta, ut ad eam consequendam, praeter obedientiam, & precibus opus fuerit? quae non merebantur, observantia legis non plenatiâ, ea orare nil opus fuit? an vero putes, omnes legis observatores fuisse perfectos? quo quid imperitius? Pone, perfectos fuisse, atque ita tamen orare Deum illis necesse nihilominus fuit: nempe, ut largiretur, quod gratiose præmium constituerat obedientiæ. Quin pone, mercedem jam adeptos, & quod lex videtur promittere, possedisse; & sic etiam locus precationi, quemadmodum pro pane quotidiano, quamvis eum quis domi, vel manibus suis teneat: nempe, pro benedictione Dei, atque conservatione. Jam quanta impietatum strues hoc in argumento! quas nec numeris suis distinguere potuimus.
units.tr: So man would seem able to make God his debtor, and to repay Him [θεοδιδόναι] with [τὸ ἀνταπόδομα], which is contrary to the Apostle, Rom. 11:35. This is, of course, the foul and infamous merit of condignity of the Papists, which these men now take up and warm over again, men who wish to be heard not only as Reformed, but whose chief reformers, if you like, they are. Indeed the Socinian doctrine of merit is more shameful still, for they place it not of condignity but beyond condignity. The Papists say God gives what is worthy of their works; the Socinians do not even grant that, nor that it satisfies their dignity. In this respect even the Jews are better than the Socinians, holding the common and obvious axiom that God defrauds no work of its reward. Christ taught us otherwise, Luke 17:10: When you have done all the things commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants. The Socinians will reply on the contrary: indeed the servants who have done everything are useful, and more than useful, having merited more than the law promises, and able by right to demand or expect still more from God, thus making God their debtor for more. How differently the Patriarch spoke: I am unworthy of all these mercies (Gen. 32:10). Finally, grant that the law owed them by right what it promised. Still it does not follow, and this is where the force of the present argument hangs, that there was no need at all to pray to God. For first, were there not other goods to be granted and evils to be averted, besides earthly and bodily ones, which they knew? And if they knew them, could not the sense of conscience and religion urge and move them to form prayers for such things? Shall we then say God must not be prayed to even for bodily goods? Or, as Volkelius says, nor was that earthly happiness so great that, besides obedience, prayers were needed to obtain it? Was there no need to pray for what they did not merit, since their observance of the law was not full? Do you really think all observers of the law were perfect? What could be more ignorant than that? Suppose they were perfect; even so it was necessary for them to pray to God, namely that He would bestow what He had graciously appointed as the reward of obedience. Indeed, suppose they had already obtained the reward and possessed what the law seems to promise; there is still room for prayer, just as for daily bread, though one holds it in one's house or hands: namely for God's blessing and preservation. What a heap of impieties in this argument! We could not even count them in order.

units.la: Ad alterum argum. , resp. i. At lex præcipiebat perfectum amorem Dei, & proximi: quem si absque singulari ope divina præstare possimus, tum quid restet, ad quod ope illa egeamus, non video. ii. Neque in alia Deus, secundum legem, observantiâ acquiescebat, quam quæ juxta legis præscriptum esset perfecta. iii. Ostendo ex ea, quam Smalcius hic sequitur, Theologiâ, si ita dicere fas sit, ope divinâ nos ad præstanda officia nullibi egere. Nulla, juxta eos, Deus præcipere, salvâ justitiâ, potest, quæ homini sint impossibilia, vel, quæ nullo modo ab homine præstari possint: verum ad ea, quæ præstare per nos possumus, haud egemus ope: ideo enim dixit, precibus ad observandam legem opus non esse, quia absque Dei ope præstari ejus præcepta queant: ergo, quum nulla Deus alia præcepta (juxta ipsos) proponat, neque etiam proponere possit, quam quæ viribus nostris conveniant, sequitur, alterius, vel Dei ope nullibi nos egere. Non eget homo ope divinâ, in iis, quæ per se ac suis viribus potest: sed omnia præcepta talia sunt, neque per justitiam Deus alia proponere potest: ergo iv. Sequetur, ut olim, ita nec hodie orationes adeo esse necessarias, nempe secundum Adversarios, quia neque jam præcepta illa Deus dedit, quæ nullo modo præstari a nobis possint: præsertim quum nunc, dicant, Deum non illam, nec tantam operum exigere perfectionem, ac olim, non legalem, sed Euangelicam. Quae'quid [?] sibi velint, suo loco plenius examinabimus. v. Atqui simpliciter impossibile fuit, legem observare: ergo, propter contrariam rationem, ac Smalcius adfert, precum tum fuit summa necessitas. Rom. viii. 3. [?]τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον [?] νόμου [?] jugum, quod neque Patres nostri, neque nos potuimus portare. Act. xv. 10.
units.tr: To the second argument I reply. (i) The law commanded perfect love of God and of neighbour. If we can perform this without special divine help, then I do not see what remains for which we need that help. (ii) Nor did God, according to the law, rest content with any observance except one that was perfect according to the law's prescription. (iii) I show from the theology which Smalcius follows here, if it is lawful to speak so, that we nowhere need divine help to perform our duties. According to them, God cannot command anything consistent with justice that is impossible for men, or that cannot in any way be performed by men; but for those things which we can perform through ourselves we need no help. Therefore he said that prayer is not needed for keeping the law, because its precepts can be performed without God's help. So since God, according to them, proposes no precepts other than those that suit our powers, nor can propose any, it follows that we nowhere need the help of God or of another. A man does not need divine help in those things which he can do by himself and with his own powers; but all precepts are of this kind, and God cannot by justice propose others. Therefore (iv) it will follow that prayers are not as necessary now as they were then, namely according to the opponents, because God has not given those precepts which could in no way be performed by us. This is especially so since, they say, God does not now demand such perfection of works as formerly, not the legal but the evangelical perfection. What they mean by this we shall examine more fully in its place. (v) Yet it was simply impossible to keep the law. Therefore, on account of the contrary reason which Smalcius adduces, there was then the greatest necessity of prayer. Rom. 8:3, [τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου], for what the law could not do; a yoke which neither our Fathers nor we were able to bear (Acts 15:10).

units.la: Alterum primi præcepti additamentum Adversarii ponunt Orationem Dominicam, quâ Christus, ceu novo præcepto, primum adauxerit. Catechesis Racoviensis, de Prophetico Christi munere, cap. 1. pag. 164. istud pro primo habet legis, per Christum, auctæ. Quid vero ad hæc addidit Dominus Iesus? Resp. Primum hoc, quod certam nobis orandi formam præscripsit, ad quam orare nos oporteat. Qu. Quaenam illa? Resp. Ea quâ Matth. vi. 9. & Luc. xi. 2. habetur, Pater noster, qui es in cœlis. Smalcius, lib. de Divinit. Christi, cap. v. pag. 17. In lege dictum erat, ne alios Deos præter unum haberemus, aut coleremus. Implevit eam & perfecit D. Iesus, dum & modum orationis (quæ una ex potissimis cultus divini partibus est) certum, & perpetuum, eumque plane divinum præscripsit. Lex enim nusquam aperte præcipit orationem, nedum, ut certum orandi modum præscribat. Idem, contra Frantzium, Disp. vii.
units.tr: The Adversaries put forward the Lord's Prayer as a second addition to the first precept, by which Christ first increased it, as though it were a new commandment. The Racovian Catechism, on the prophetic office of Christ, chapter 1, page 164, takes this as the first point of the law as increased through Christ: "But what did the Lord Jesus add to these things? Answer: First this, that he prescribed to us a fixed form of prayer, which we ought to use. Question: What is that? Answer: The one found in Matthew 6:9 and Luke 11:2, Our Father, who art in heaven." Smalcius, in his book on the Divinity of Christ, chapter 5, page 17: "In the law it was said that we should not have or worship other gods besides the one God. Our Lord Jesus fulfilled and perfected this, while he prescribed a fixed and perpetual manner of prayer (which is one of the chief parts of divine worship), and one that is plainly divine. For the law nowhere expressly commands prayer, much less prescribes a fixed manner of praying." The same author, against Franzius, Disputation 7.

units.la: pag. 229. Deinde gravissime nos cavillatur Franzius, dum ita nos traducit, quasi negemus, quod extent formula certa precum, quibus olim usi sint viri sancti. Nos enim in Catechesi tantum negamus, extitisse antea ullam certam formulam precum, qua omnes sub lege usi fuerint, & necessario uti debuerint, qualis est ea, quam Dominus Iesus nobis praescripsit. Nunc vero, ut apertius dicamus, quod res est, affirmamus, non tantum nullam precandi formulam praescriptam, sed nec precationem ipsam olim praeceptam fuisse in lege. Ex quibus de mente & sententia Adversariorum constat.
units.tr: Page 229: "Then Franzius grievously cavils at us, when he reports us as though we denied that there are fixed forms of prayer which holy men have used in former times. For in the Catechism we deny only this, that before there existed any fixed form of prayer which all under the law used, and were bound to use, such as the one which the Lord Jesus prescribed to us. But now, to say more plainly what the matter is, we affirm that not only was no fixed form of prayer prescribed, but prayer itself was never commanded in the law." From these words the mind and meaning of the Adversaries is clear.

units.la: Praemittendae aliquae ad disputationem distinctiones. 1. In Oratione Dominica considerare est, ejus materiam, rem contentam; & orandi modum, formam, illa serie ordineque a Christo praescriptam. Concedimus, hoc sub V. Test. non fuisse, neque ibi ista formula extitit, aut nota fuit: interim res & materia petitionum usitata, atque Patribus non incognita, non neglecta fuit. II. Ipsa formula Orationis Dominicae, non est quod ad usum absolute & simpliciter necessaria, vel eum in finem praescripta, ut ei omnes omniumque preces ita alligari debeant, quasi absque ea non constarent: quod vel inde patet, quod Apostolos quamvis precatos, non tamen illa precationis formula usos legamus, vel alios quosdam. Notae sunt Brownistarum disputationes, qui nolunt Orationem Dominicam orandi formulam esse, duntaxat exemplar, ad quod precationes nostras formare & instituere oporteat, non ipsam pro oratione dicendam habendamve. Ad quae responsio est, non pugnare, esse aliquid & exemplar, & formulam precandi, imo revera talis est oratio Dominica, nempe utrumque, & exemplar formandae, & formula usurpandae orationis. Non autem formula ita intelligenda vel accipienda est, quae vel sola pro quavis oratione adhibenda sit: qui in aliam partem excessumque error est Pontificiorum, ad quaevis dicentium modo suum Pater noster: oppositae hic extremitates sunt, hinc Pontificiorum, inde Brownistarum: sed pro oratione uti Dominica illa licet: non vero id semper debemus, non vel hac sola uti, aut eandem dicere, vel ad singulas necessario preces adjungere, quasi absque eo invalidas. Hinc Amesius bene, Cas. Consc. lib. iv. cap. xvii. qu. v. Christus illam orationem docens, non voluit nobis praescribere formulam verborum constanter observandam, & quae sequuntur. Certe Christus ex Scriptura, & necessitatibus Sanctorum collegit & conjunxit sua Oratione ea, quae maxime necessaria sunt, ut & quaeramus sedulo, & a Deo impetremus. Breviarium totius Euangelii, Tertullianus merito dixit, lib. de Oratione. Hinc jam multum enervatur thesis Adversariorum, ita disputantium, ac si formula orationis Dominicae praescripta pro lege esset, & necessario semper dicenda. Nam & omittere eam, inter orandum, absque peccato possumus; sed & uti quoque ea, pro re nata. Quidquid autem de illa usus legisve necessitate dicant Adversarii, negamus pro lege nova habendam Orationis Dominicae formulam; vel pro lege, praecepto primo, per Christum, addita.
units.tr: Some distinctions must be laid down before the discussion. I. In the Lord's Prayer we must consider its matter, the content of the petitions, and the manner of praying, its form, in that order and sequence prescribed by Christ. We grant that under the Old Testament this was not so, and that this form did not exist or was not known there; yet the substance and the matter of the petitions was in common use, was not unknown to the Fathers, and was not neglected. II. The very form of the Lord's Prayer is not something absolutely and simply necessary for use, nor was it prescribed for this purpose, that all prayers and everyone's prayers should be so bound to it that they would not stand without it. This is clear from the fact that we read of the apostles praying, and of others, without using that form of prayer. The disputations of the Brownists are well known; they deny that the Lord's Prayer is a form of praying, and say it is only a pattern to which our prayers ought to be shaped and fashioned, and not something to be said as a prayer in itself. To this the answer is that there is no conflict in its being both a pattern and a form of praying; indeed, the Lord's Prayer is truly both: a pattern for forming prayer and a form to be used in prayer. But the form is not to be understood or taken in such a way that it alone must be used for any prayer. That is the error of the Papists, who in the other direction and to excess say their own "Our Father" for any kind of prayer; here the extremes are opposed, on one side the Papists, on the other the Brownists. It is lawful to use that prayer as the Lord's Prayer, but we are not always bound to do so, nor to use it alone or to repeat only it, nor to add it necessarily to every prayer as if without it our prayers were invalid. Hence Amesius rightly says, in Casus Conscientiae, book 4, chapter 17, question 5: "Christ, in teaching that prayer, did not wish to prescribe to us a form of words to be constantly observed," and what follows. Certainly Christ, from Scripture and from the needs of the saints, gathered and joined together in his prayer those things which are most necessary, so that we may both seek them diligently and obtain them from God. Tertullian rightly called it "the summary of the whole Gospel," in his book On Prayer. Hence the adversaries' thesis is greatly weakened, since they argue as if the prescribed form of the Lord's Prayer were a law and must always necessarily be said. For we may omit it in praying without sin, and we may also use it as occasion requires. Whatever the Adversaries say about the necessity of its use or of the law, we deny that the form of the Lord's Prayer is to be regarded as a new law, or as a law, a first precept, added through Christ.

units.la: Quandocunque Orationis istius facimus analysin, & praecipua consideramus capita, pars eorum aliqua Deum, alia nos concernit, nostrasque necessitates, prout in tribus prioribus orationibus dicimus, tum σ̄ σ̄ σ̄[?]; in posterioribus, nobis ἡμῖν , ἡμῖν , ἡμᾶς. precamur ibi Deum, pro nominis sui ho-nore, pro Ecclesia, & cultu suo promovendo, quibus summum nostrum constat bonum: hic, pro corporalibus necessitatibus, & spiritualibus, nempe justificatione, & sanctificatione. At quae omnia in V. Test. Sanctis ubique locorum & temporum non minus necessaria fuerunt & expetenda.
units.tr: Whenever we make an analysis of this prayer and consider its chief parts, some part of them concerns God and another part concerns us and our needs. As we say in the first three petitions "thy" [σου], so in the later ones "us" [ἡμῖν, ἡμῖν, ἡμᾶς]. There we pray to God for the honour of his name, and for the advancement of his Church and his worship, in which our highest good consists; here we pray for bodily needs and for spiritual ones, namely justification and sanctification. Yet all these things were no less necessary and to be desired by the saints of the Old Testament, in every place and time.

units.la: Unde tale instruo argumentum, primum in genere; tum ex inductione singularum partium. Quae argumentum sunt & materia orationis Dominicae, sive honorem & cultum Dei concernant, sive nos & statum nostrum, Patribus sub V. Test. nota etiam fuerunt, & bona, & expetenda; vel non? Si ita, non ergo constituunt novam orationem, Veteribus ignoratam. Si dicas, non sequi: quia utcunque illa usurpata Patribus olim fuerint in precibus, non tamen ex lege aliqua, sed fecisse eos id pro arbitrio; hodie autem ejus latam esse legem, & praeceptum a Christo datum. Ad id respondeo, quodcunque Patres egerunt, & hac etiam in parte, quousque id bonum, cum lege convenerit est necesse, alioqui ἄνομον censebitur, & pro lege prohibita ἐθελοθρησκεία[?]. Deinde, sive praxim & exempla Veterum respiciamus, sive monita eorum & encomia rei hujus, non minus lege contenta censeri debet, ac alia quae lege praescripta esse nullus dubitat, quod ex sequentibus liquebit. Denique conscientia ipsorum, quae dictavit necessarias utilesque esse eas precationes, in generalibus de cultu Dei praeceptis & legibus fundari & potuit, & debuit.
units.tr: Hence I construct such an argument, first in general, and then from the enumeration of the individual parts. The matters and the substance of the Lord's Prayer, whether they concern the honour and worship of God or concern us and our state, were also known to the Fathers under the Old Testament, and were regarded as good and to be desired. Or were they not? If so, then they do not constitute a new prayer unknown to the ancients. If you say that it does not follow, because however much the Fathers used these things in their prayers, they did not do so under any law, but did it of their own free will, whereas today a law has been issued for them and a precept given by Christ: to this I reply that whatever the Fathers did, also in this respect, must be in agreement with the law, insofar as it was good; otherwise it will be counted lawless, and a self-devised worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία], forbidden by law. Further, whether we look at the practice and examples of the ancients, or at their admonitions and praises of this matter, it ought to be judged no less contained in the law than other things which no one doubts were prescribed by the law, as will become clear from what follows. Finally, their conscience, which told them that such prayers were necessary and useful, could and ought to be founded on the general precepts and laws concerning the worship of God.

units.la: Quod si neges, illa Patribus quoque nota fuisse, & quod bona, & quod expetenda fuerint; nega etiam, Patres sollicitos fuisse de honore Dei, de colendo & honorando Deum, de cultu atque honore ejus promovendo apud se, apud alios, de obedientia Deo omni modo praestanda, non pro corporali vita, ejusque bonis Dei implorasse gratiam, in quibus tamen omnes promissiones ipsorum occupatas fuisse dicunt: nil cogitasse illos de peccatis suis aut expiandis, aut sibi condonandis; deque cavendis multis & omittendis: id est, nega religiosos fuisse, aut tales ex lege esse debuisse. Nega denique eos vel ea pro bonis habuisse atque expetendis, quae talia ne Gentiles quidem ignoraruntt. Quod est totam illis adimere religionem atque pietatem. Nam apud Gentiles observare est, scivisse illos Deum quovis modo honorandum, colendumque esse, quaerendam offensarum expiationem & remissionem, mala & peccata omnia vitanda esse, quamvis de modo aut certitudine, uti illa fierent, quae in verbo suo Deus revelavit atque aperuit, essent ignorantes: certe non nescierunt, illa, praesertim corporalia, seu panem & victum quotidianum a Deo petenda esse. Quod an Patres sciverint, quibus & verbum & statuta sua Deus significavit, supra quascunque nationes reliquas, ut est Psalm.cxlvii. 19. 20. hic a Christianus vid. disputatur.
units.tr: But if you deny that these things were also known to the Fathers, and that they were good and to be desired, then deny also that the Fathers were concerned for the honour of God, for worshipping and honouring God, for advancing his worship among themselves and among others, for rendering obedience to God in every way; deny that they implored God's grace not for their bodily life and its goods, although they say that all their promises were occupied with these; deny that they thought of their sins, either of expiating them or of having them forgiven, and of avoiding and putting off many things. That is, deny that they were religious, or that they ought to have been such by law. Finally, deny that they regarded as good and to be desired those things which not even the Gentiles were ignorant of. That would be to strip them of all religion and piety. For among the Gentiles one observes that they knew God must be honoured and worshipped in some way, that the expiation and forgiveness of offences must be sought, and that all evils and sins must be avoided, even if they were ignorant of the manner or the certainty of how these things were to be done, which God revealed and disclosed in his word. Certainly they did not fail to know that these things, especially the bodily ones, namely bread and daily sustenance, were to be asked from God. Whether the Fathers, to whom God made known his word and his statutes above all other nations, as in Psalm 147:19-20, knew this, is a matter debated here among Christians.

units.la: Secundo ex inductione singulorum in Oratione Dominica capitum, ostendimus, eadem precata Patribus fuisse olim quoque sub V. Testamento: ne omissa quidem Orationis praefatione, & exordio. [Πατὴρ ἡμῶν.] Ita dicit Ecclesia, Jesa. LXIII. 16. Tu enim es Pater noster &c. tu Domine es Pater noster. Deut. xxxii. 6. nonne ipse est Pater tuus, qui te acquisivit? Jerem. iii. 4. annon abhinc clamabis ad me, Pater tuus? Ergo hic saltem sermo, & allocutio ad Deum, non nova est & recens, vel in solo demum Nov. Testamento instituta, aut usurpata.
units.tr: Secondly, by going through the individual petitions of the Lord's Prayer one by one, we have shown that the same prayers were used by the fathers under the Old Testament as well, even the preface and opening of the prayer. [Our Father.] Thus the Church speaks in Isaiah 63:16: For thou art our Father etc., thou, O Lord, art our Father. Deut. 32:6: Is not he thy Father who bought thee? Jer. 3:4: Wilt thou not from now on cry to me, My Father? Therefore at least this form of address and speech to God is not new or recent, nor was it introduced or used only in the New Testament.

units.la: Qui in cœlis.] Sic 1 Reg viii. 39. tum tu exaudias in cœlo, loco habitationis tuæ. Jesa lxiii. 15. intuere de cœlo, & vide ex habitaculo sanctitatis tuæ, & ornatus tui, ubi nunc est zelus tuus? Psalm. xi. 4. Jehova, in templo sanctitatis sua, Jehova, cujus solium in cœlis, cujus oculi vident, &c. Psalm. cxv. verf. 3. atqui Deus noster in cœlis est, quodquid placet, facit. Hoc ergo etiam agnovere Veteres, testatique in precibus & cultu divino fuerunt, Deum, Patrem suum, in cœlis esse.
units.tr: Who art in heaven.] So 1 Kings 8:39: then hear thou in heaven, the place of thy dwelling. Isaiah 63:15: Look down from heaven and see from the habitation of thy holiness and thy glory; where is thy zeal now? Ps. 11:4: The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD, whose throne is in heaven, whose eyes behold, etc. Ps. 115:3: But our God is in heaven; he does whatever he pleases. The ancients therefore also acknowledged this, and in their prayers and divine worship testified that God, their Father, is in heaven.

units.la: Sanctificetur nomen tuum.] Num. xiv. 17. nunc igitur magnificetur virtus Domini, quemadmodum pronunciasti, dicendo, Jehova est longanimis &c. Num. xx. 12. Quamobrem dixit Jehova Mosi & Aaroni, quia non credidistis mihi, ut sanctificaretis me ante oculos filiorum Israelis. cap. xxvii. 14. ut me sanctificaretis. Levit. x. 3. illud est, quod dixit Jehova, in appropinquantibus ad me sanctificabor, & ante conspectum totius populi glorificabor. Deut. xxxii. 51. eo quod non sanctificastis me in medio filio-rum Israelis. Ezech. xxxvi. 23. sanctificabo nomen meum maximum, quod prosa-natum fuit in gentibus. Noverunt ergo fideles illi, nomen Dei sanctificari debe-re, & hoc spectandum omnibus, curandumque unice esse, ut sanctificaretur. Psalm. cxv. 1. Non nobis Jehova, non nobis; sed nomini tuo da honorem. Quod quid aliud, quam, sanctificetur nomen tuum? Nihilque frequentius in Psal-mis, & eucharistiis, quam sanctificari Dei nomen. Psalm. ciii. 1. Benedic anima mea Jehova, & omnia intestina mea nomini sanctitatis ejus. Psalm. cxlviii. & cxlix. & cl. & alibi.
units.tr: Hallowed be thy name.] Num. 14:17: Now therefore let the power of the Lord be great, as thou hast spoken, saying, The LORD is longsuffering etc. Num. 20:12: Wherefore the LORD said unto Moses and Aaron, Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel. Num. 27:14: that ye sanctified me. Lev. 10:3: This is it that the LORD spake, saying, I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified. Deut. 32:51: because ye sanctified me not in the midst of the children of Israel. Ezek. 36:23: I will sanctify my great name, which was profaned among the nations. The faithful therefore knew that the name of God must be sanctified, and that this must be the aim of all, and that it must be the sole care that it be sanctified. Ps. 115:1: Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory. What is this but Hallowed be thy name? Nothing is more frequent in the Psalms and in the songs of thanksgiving than that the name of God be sanctified. Ps. 103:1: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Ps. 148, 149, 150, and elsewhere.

units.la: Adveniat regnum tuum.] In nos, atque in alios. Sic sæpe precatos Veteres novimus. Psalm. iv. 7. attolle super nos lucem faciei tuæ Jehova. Psalm. lxvii. 2. Deus gratiosus sit nobis, & benedicat nobis, lucere faciat faciem suam supra nos. Psalm. xxii. 28. 29. Recordabuntur & convertentur ad Jehovam omnes fines terræ, & incurvabunt se coram te omnes familiæ gentium. Quoniam Jehova est regnum. Psalm. xxxiii. 8. Timeat à Jehova omnis terra, ab ipso metuant omnes habitatores orbis. Psalm. xlix. verf. 2. Audite hæc omnes populi: auribus percipite omnes habita-tores mundi.
units.tr: Thy kingdom come.] Upon us, and upon others. We know that the ancients often prayed thus. Ps. 4:6: LORD, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us. Ps. 67:1: God be merciful unto us, and bless us, and cause his face to shine upon us. Ps. 22:27–28: All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD, and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. For the kingdom is the LORD's. Ps. 33:8: Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him. Ps. 49:1–2: Hear this, all ye people; give ear, all ye inhabitants of the world.

units.la: Fiat voluntas tua sicuti in cœlo, ita etiam in terra.] Quod ad voluntatis divi-næ obedientiam, negare haud possunt, eam & præceptam sub V. quoque Testam. fuisse, quare & viguisse, & pro eâ orare Deum fas & æquum fuisse tum etiam, neque minus necessarium. Psalm. xxv. 4. 5. Vias tuas Jehova, notas fac mihi, semitas tuas doce me. Fac incedam in veritate tua, & doce me. Psalm. cxix. 4. 5. & adeo per totum: Tu præcepisti mandata tua observari valde. Utinam comparentur viæ meæ, ad observandum statuta tua. II Sam. xv. 26. quod si ita dixerit, non delector te, ecce me, faciat mihi prout bonum in oculis suis. I Sam. iii. 18. Job. i. 21. Jehova dedit, & Jehova abstulit: sit nomen Jehovæ benedictum.
units.tr: Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.] As to obedience to the divine will, they cannot deny that it was commanded under the Old Testament as well, and therefore that it was in force, and that it was right and proper, and no less necessary, to pray God for it. Ps. 25:4–5: Show me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths. Lead me in thy truth, and teach me. Ps. 119:4–5, and so throughout: Thou hast commanded us to keep thy precepts diligently. O that my ways were directed to keep thy statutes! 2 Sam. 15:26: But if he thus say, I have no delight in thee; behold, here am I, let him do to me as seemeth good unto him. 1 Sam. 3:18; Job 1:21: The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.

units.la: Quod ad additum exemplar & rationem obedientiæ Angelorum, hoc uti præceptum non facit, tantum pro ratione adseritur atque similitudine, ita nec eo modo urgeri potest, uti Smalcius facit: quas[?] unquam in V. Teft. Deum gravit[?], ut ita facerent Dei voluntatem homines, quemadmodum eam faciunt Angeli cœlestes ? contra Frantzium, pag. 231. quandoquidem David se ad cultum, & laudes Dei excitans, Angelos quoque adducit, & postquam dixisset, benedicite Jehova Angeli ejus, ad se rediens, dicit iterum, benedic anima mea Jehova. Psalm. cxiii. 20. 22. Quod revera huc redit, quod sibi voluntatem divinam faciendam existimarit, prout idem Angelis incumbit, atque ab iis præstari solet in cœ-lis. Similiter Psalm. cxlviii. 2. laudate Jehovam cœlites, laudate eum in excelsis. Laudate eum omnes Angeli ejus, laudate eum omnes exercitus ejus. Præterea quomodo vitam suam ad exemplum Angelorum componerent, patet ex comparationi-bus, quas quandoque inter homines & Angelos, in ratione vitæ instituebant. Sic Rex Achis, ad Davidem, 1 Sam. xix. 9. es tu gratiosus in oculis meis, sicuti Angelus Dei. Thechoitis illa, 11 Sam. xiv. 17. Uti Angelus Dei, ita dominus meus rex, ut audiat, quod bonum & malum. Mephiboseth, ad eundem, verum dominus meus rex est uti Angelus Dei. Insuper, non ad Angelorum exemplum, quinimo ipsius Dei jubet lex vitam componere: ergo, uti quod minus majori includi-tur, quum lex istud imperet, imitationem Anglicam non excludit aut amo-vet tanquam alienam, quæ quasi novum aliquod præceptum accedat in Testa-mento Novo. Levit. xix. 2. Sitis sancti: nam ego Jehova Deus vester sanctus sum. & cap. xi. 44. & xx. 7. 26.
units.tr: As to the added example and the ground of the obedience of the angels: this does not make it a command, but is put forward only as a reason and a comparison, and so it cannot be pressed in the way Smalcius presses it: Did God ever seriously urge men in the Old Testament to do God's will as the heavenly angels do? against Frantzius, p. 231. For David, when he stirred himself up to the worship and praises of God, also brings in the angels, and after saying Bless the LORD, ye his angels, turning back to himself he says again, Bless the LORD, O my soul. Ps. 103:20, 22 [cxiii. 20. 22]. In truth this comes to this: he thought that the divine will was to be done by himself just as the angels are charged to do it, and as it is usually performed by them in heaven. Likewise Ps. 148:2: Praise ye the LORD, all his angels; praise ye him, all his hosts. Moreover, how they used to shape their lives on the example of the angels is evident from the comparisons which they sometimes made between men and angels in matters of conduct. So King Achish to David, 1 Sam. 19:9: Thou art good in my sight, as an angel of God. The woman of Tekoa, 2 Sam. 14:17: As an angel of God, so is my lord the king, to discern good and bad. Mephibosheth to the same: But my lord the king is as an angel of God. Furthermore, the law commands us to shape our lives not after the example of angels but after God himself. Therefore, as the lesser is included in the greater, since the law commands this, the imitation of God does not exclude or remove the imitation of angels as something foreign, as though it were some new precept added in the New Testament. Lev. 19:2: Be ye holy, for I the LORD your God am holy. Also Lev. 11:44, 20:7, 26.

units.la: Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie.] Ipsissima oratio extat Prov. xxx. 8. ale me cibo demensi mei. Psalm. cxlv. 15. 16. Oculi omnium ad te spectant, quibus tu das escam suo tempore. Aperis manum tuam, & saturas quidquid vivit ex beneplacito. Genef. xxviii. 20. Si Deus mecum fuerit, & servaverit me in via ista, qua ego profecturus sum, dederitque mihi panem ad comedendum & vestimentum ad induendum. 21. reversusque prospere fuero ad domum patris mei, erit Jehova mihi Deus. Nec puto, pro corporalibus precatos fuisse Veteres, quibus haud alias dicunt contigisse promissiones, Adversarios negaturos. Videri interim & hæc loca possunt, Deut. xxvi. 15. 1 Reg. viii. 35. 36. 11 Chron. vii. 13. 14. Psalm. cxliv. 13. 14. Mirum autem, Smalcium per panem quotidianum in Orat. Dominica intelligere panem spiritualem: qui adeo nihil spirituale in Toto V. Test. promissum videre possunt, hic sub rei corporalis nomine & involucro, spiritualia percipere? Quod nec probamus, quia spiritualia cæteris orationibus comprehensa sunt: & nulla ratio videtur, quare non expresse & distincte Christus id si voluisset, expressisset: & si concedamus, uti plurimis, qua Veteribus, qua recentibus, (quod annotavimus Disp. 11. in Orationem Dominicam) visum, nihil causæ vel thesi nostræ decedit: nam nec negant, corporalem panem etiam comprehendi, Adversatii. Ita Smalcius, pag. 232. Disp. VII. petitio panis illius necessarii, qui non tantum est cibus corporis, sed etiam, isque multo magis, animi, nempe Spiritus Dei. Qua ratione sub pane Spiritum Dei connotatum nunc judi-cant, & in toto V. Test. ubi tamen Spiritus S. frequens mentio, & panis, & multæ petitiones pro pane, inter alia, occurrunt, nihil adeo Spiritus S. pro-missum missum Patribus vident: ut hinc quoque Orationem Dominicam pro novo legis auctario habeant, quod pro Spiritus S. gratia & dono nemo unquam Deum precatus olim fuerit? ita Smalcius, pag. 231. Quis unquam talia ad necessitatem suam pertinere intellexit, ut detur nobis Spiritus S.? cum hoc sit proprium promissum novi foederis, & nemini datus sit Spiritus S. priusquam Jesus glorificaretur? Profanum dogma, nemini datum olim Spiritum S., nemini promissum, im-ploratum a nemine unquam retro fuisse, ante Christum glorificatum: & hoc tamen sub specie panis hic deprehendere possunt? Quasi non Spiritum David petierit, quando dixit, Psalm. LI. 12. 13. cor novum crea in me Deus. quod unde, nisi a Spiritu venit? Jezech. xxxvi. 26. 27. sed & addit ipse: ac spiritum novum renova in medio mei. Ne me rejicias a facie tua, & spiritum tuum sanctum ne auferas a me. Nehem. ix. 20. & spiritum tuum bonum dedisti, qui erudiret eos.
units.tr: Give us this day our daily bread.] The very petition exists in Prov. 30:8: Feed me with food convenient for me. Ps. 145:15–16: The eyes of all wait upon thee, and thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand and satisfiest the desire of every living thing. Gen. 28:20: If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on, 21: so that I come again to my father's house in peace, then shall the LORD be my God. Nor do I think the ancients prayed for bodily things, for which, our opponents will deny, no other promises were made to them. Meanwhile these passages may also be considered: Deut. 26:15; 1 Kings 8:35–36; 2 Chron. 7:13–14; Ps. 144:13–14. It is strange, however, that Smalcius understands the daily bread in the Lord's Prayer to be spiritual bread. Can they who find nothing spiritual promised in the whole of the Old Testament perceive spiritual things here, under the name and covering of a bodily thing? This we do not accept either, because spiritual things are included in the other petitions; and there seems to be no reason why Christ, had he wished this, would not have said it expressly and distinctly. And even if we grant what many, both ancient and modern, have held (which we noted in Disputation 11 on the Lord's Prayer), it does not detract from our thesis or position, for our opponents do not deny that bodily bread is also included. So Smalcius, p. 232, Disp. VII: The petition for that necessary bread, which is not only food for the body but also, and much more, food for the mind, namely the Spirit of God. By what reasoning do they now judge that the Spirit of God is signified under the word bread? And yet in the whole of the Old Testament, where the Holy Spirit is frequently mentioned, and bread and many petitions for bread occur, among other things, they see nothing promised to the fathers of the Holy Spirit. Hence they also hold that the Lord's Prayer is a new addition to the law, since no one ever prayed to God in former times for the grace and gift of the Holy Spirit. So Smalcius, p. 231: Who ever understood such things to pertain to his need, that the Holy Spirit should be given to us? Since this is the proper promise of the new covenant, and the Holy Spirit was given to no one before Jesus was glorified. A profane dogma: that the Holy Spirit was given to no one formerly, promised to no one, and implored by no one before Christ was glorified. And yet they can detect this here under the appearance of bread? As if David had not sought the Spirit when he said, Ps. 51:10–11: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Whence does this come, unless from the Spirit? Ezek. 36:26–27. But he also adds himself: And renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from thy presence, and take not thy holy Spirit from me. Neh. 9:20: Thou gavest also thy good Spirit to instruct them.

units.la: Et remitte nobis debita nostra.] Pro remissione peccatorum precatus Moses fuit, Exod. xxxiv. 9. & dixit, si nunc inveni gratiam in oculis tuis Domine, condones iniquitatem nostram & peccatum nostrum. Num. xiv. 18. 19. Iehova longanimis & mul-tus benignitate condonans iniquitatem & defectionem. Condona quaso iniquitatem populi hujus pro magnitudine benignitatis tua. David, Psalm. xxv. 7. Peccatorum pueritia mea & defectionum mearum ne recorderis. Psalm. xxxii. 5. dixi, confitebor defectiones meas Iehova, & tu sustulisti pœnam peccati mei. Psalm. LI. 3. gratiam hanc mihi, o Deus, secundum benignitatem tuam: secundum amplitudinem miserationum tuarum, dele defectiones meas. Psalm. cxxx. 3. 4. Si iniquitates observes Iah, Domine, quis posset consistere? Verum apud te est condonatio, ut reverenter colaris. Psalm. cxliii. 2. At ne congrediaris judicio cum servo tuo. Adde Rom. iv. 6. 7. 8.
units.tr: And forgive us our debts.] Moses prayed for the forgiveness of sins in Exod. 34:9: "and he said, If now I have found grace in your eyes, Lord, pardon our iniquity and our sin." Num. 14:18-19: "The LORD is longsuffering and of great kindness, forgiving iniquity and transgression. Pardon, I beseech you, the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your kindness." David, Ps. 25:7: "Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions." Ps. 32:5: "I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you took away the punishment of my sin." Ps. 51:3: "Grant me this grace, O God, according to your kindness; according to the greatness of your mercies, blot out my transgressions." Ps. 130:3-4: "If you, LORD, should mark iniquities, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be reverenced." Ps. 143:2: "And enter not into judgment with your servant." Add Rom. 4:6-8.

units.la: Sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris.] Atque hoc etiam præceptum sub V. Test. fuit, ut sibi mutuo remitterent offensas, neque servarent eas animo, vel quovis pacto ulciscerentur. Levit. xix. 18. Prov. xxv. 21.
units.tr: As we also forgive our debtors.] This was also a command under the Old Testament, that they should forgive one another's offences, and not keep them in mind or avenge them in any way. Lev. 19:18; Prov. 25:21.

units.la: Et ne nos inducas in tentationem; sed libera nos a malo.] Quod David precatus est Psalmo xix. 13. 14. Ab occultis meis munda me. Tum a contumaciis subtrahe servum tuum, ne dominentur in me, tunc integer & insons ero a defectione magna. Psalm. LI. 12. 13. & cxix. 36. 37. Flecte animum meum ad statuta tua, non ad avaritiam. Averte oculos meos, ne respiciant vanitatem: in viis tuis fac ut vivam.
units.tr: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.] David prayed this in Ps. 19:13-14: "Cleanse me from my secret faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins, that they may not have dominion over me; then shall I be upright and innocent from great transgression." Ps. 51:12-13; and Ps. 119:36-37: "Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to covetousness. Turn away my eyes from beholding vanity; quicken me in your ways."

units.la: Quia tuum est regnum, & potentia, & gloria in saecula, Amen.] Sic 1. Chron. xxix. 11. David in solemni populi benedictione loquitur, Tua est, o Iehova, magnitudo, & potentia, & gloria, & æternitas, ac majestas, imo omnia in coelo, & in terra: tuum Iehova est regnum. Atque ita ad singula Orationis Dominicæ capita ostendimus, eadem in V. Test. non nota tantum Patribus fuisse, sed commendata, & expetita precibus: nihil ut novum quod ad rem hic a Christo additum legi dicendum sit. Et orationes ipsas, quod ad eatum [?] tum exordium tum conclusionem, argumento veteris legis & Scripturæ contineri atque convenire, probavimus.
units.tr: For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.] So in 1 Chron. 29:11 David speaks in the solemn blessing of the people: "Yours, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the eternity, and the majesty, indeed all things in heaven and on earth; yours, LORD, is the kingdom." Thus, taking each head of the Lord's Prayer in turn, we have shown that these same things were not only known to the Fathers under the Old Testament but also commended and sought in prayer; so that nothing new is to be said to have been added here by Christ. We have also proved that the prayers themselves, both their opening and their closing, are contained in and agree with the argument of the old law and of Scripture.

units.la: Quod autem dicit Smalcius, non quæri, an non suo modo etiam eadem orare potuerint, & oraverint quidam viri sancti sub V. Test. qua in oratione Dominica nobis prae-scribuntur: sed an hic modus orandi præscriptus omnibus generatim fuerit, & an omnes ita vel oraverint, vel orare debuerint, hoc vere in quæstione est. Ego autem nego, hoc, & non istud in quæstione esse: quippe quis dubitet, non hunc orandi modum fuisse præscriptum in V. Test. ? Adeove stolidos nos putat Smalcius, quasi id velimus, quod formula orationis Dominicæ præscripta fuerit olim in V. Test. & majori quidem cum obligatione, ut omnes ita orare debuerint, quam in Novo? Hoc autem quia negare nos & res ipsa loquitur, & Smalcius ignorare nequit, quid superest quod controverti hic possit, quam an materia orationis eadem fuerit in V. Test. seu an eadem etiam oraverint olim viri sancti? Etenim novum hinc præceptum cudere amant Sociniani, vel novum legis additamentum, quod, quando sanctis sub V. lege usurpatum etiam fuit, novum hodie dici non potest. Atque in initio disputationis præmisimus, haud disputare nos de formula, sed materia Orationis Dominicæ: quam, non illam, Patribus olim quoque usurpatam in V. Test. ostendimus. Hoc vero si nobis ex animo concedant, age per nos licet, hæc deleatur quæstio, neque inter alias ultra recenseatur.
units.tr: As to what Smalcius says, that the question is not "whether holy men under the Old Testament could also pray the same things in their own way, and whether some of them did pray the same things that are prescribed to us in the Lord's Prayer; but whether this prescribed manner of praying was prescribed to everyone in general, and whether all either did pray so or ought to have prayed so; this is truly the question." I, however, deny that this is the question and not that other one. For who would doubt that this manner of prayer was not prescribed under the Old Testament? Does Smalcius think us so foolish that we would hold that the form of the Lord's Prayer was prescribed under the Old Testament, and with greater obligation, so that all ought to have prayed in that way, than under the New? Since both the thing itself tells us that we deny this, and Smalcius cannot be ignorant of it, what remains that can be disputed here, except whether the matter of the prayer was the same under the Old Testament, or whether holy men also prayed the same things in former times? For the Socinians like to coin a new precept from this, or a new addition to the law; but since it was also used by the saints under the old law, it cannot today be called new. And at the beginning of the dispute we premised that we are not disputing about the form but about the matter of the Lord's Prayer, and we have shown that it is this matter, not the form, that was used by the Fathers in the Old Testament. If they will grant us this from their hearts, then let it be, by all means, let this question be struck out and not reckoned again among the others.

units.la: Iterum Smalcius, eadem Disp. vii. contra Frantzium, Deinde summam injuriam facit N. Test. Frantzius, dum eadem contineri credit in Psalmis Davidis petitoriis, quæ in oratione Dominica. Quasi insignem ille faciat injuriam Christo & Euangelio, qui dicit, passim à Christo sua ostendi & probari ex Mose, & Prophetis? ita quoque qui orationis Dominicæ summam in Psalmis contineri asserit. Quæ vero sequuntur apud Franzium, quia sunt mera petitiones principii, ejusque quod in quæstione, & à nobis contrarium copiose probatum est, prætermisimus, ne supervacuum laborem nobis aliisque quæsisse, & inutili prolixitati temere studuisse videamur. Sed, dicit, ex Psalmis aliquid probare, non esse idem, quod ex lege. Atque de lege, seu ejus perfectione, ex lege disputandum esse.
units.tr: Again Smalcius, in the same seventh disputation against Frantzius: "Moreover, Frantzius does the New Testament the greatest wrong, since he believes that the same things are contained in the petitionary Psalms of David as in the Lord's Prayer." As if he does a notable wrong to Christ and the Gospel who says that Christ everywhere shows and proves his teaching from Moses and the Prophets; and so too he who asserts that the sum of the Lord's Prayer is contained in the Psalms. What follows in Frantzius, since it is mere begging of the question and of what is in dispute, and what we have copiously proved to be the contrary, we have passed over, lest we seem to have sought superfluous labour for ourselves and others, and rashly aimed at useless prolixity. But, he says, to prove something from the Psalms is not the same as to prove it from the law; and one must dispute about the law, or its perfection, from the law itself.

units.la: Hinc pag. 229. inquit, Primum omnium notandum est, thesim à Frantzio perpetuo immutari. Nos enim affirmamus, præcepta legis esse aucta & perfecta à Christo, hoc est, plus esse à Christo præceptum in Euangelio, quam olim lex per Mosem tradita præciperet. Itaque nisi Frantzius ex ipsa lege Mosis probet, tantum ibi, quantum hic præceptum esse, nihil agit. Prophetæ enim diversum quiddam sunt certo modo à lege, utpote qui non ita ad omnes Iudæos pertinebant, aut pertinere poterant ut lex, quæ omnibus in universum erat tradita: imo erant, & sunt etiamnum multi ex Iudæis, qui Prophetas non recipiebant aut recipiunt, & tamen libros Mosis amplectuntur[?] & amplectuntur[?]. Pag. 231. Deinde quid hoc ad legem habet Mosaicam, quod in uno Davidis individuo singulare apparuit? adde & pag. 248. 249.
units.tr: Hence on p. 229 he says: "First of all it must be noted that Frantzius constantly changes the thesis. For we affirm that the precepts of the law were enlarged and perfected by Christ, that is, that Christ has commanded more in the Gospel than the law delivered through Moses commanded of old. Therefore, unless Frantzius proves from the law of Moses itself that there is commanded there as much as is commanded here, he accomplishes nothing. For the Prophets are in a certain respect something different from the law, inasmuch as they did not pertain, or could not pertain, to all the Jews as the law did, which was delivered to all in general. Indeed there were, and still are, many Jews who did not receive, or do not receive, the Prophets, and yet they embrace the books of Moses." p. 231: "Next, what does this have to do with the Mosaic law, that which appeared singularly in the one individual, David?" Add also pp. 248-249.

units.la: Resp. Etiam in superioribus, si bene memini, ad hoc responsum, quod Prophetas à lege catenus separant Adversarii, quasi non per omnia eadem utriusque doctrina esset, & qui ex Prophetis aliquod probat, non censeatur satis id fecisse quoque ex lege, cujus commentarius apud Prophetas extat. Quum & Christus & Apostoli hoc perinde habeant, & suo exemplo nos docuerint, sive ex lege agere, sive ex Prophetis. Matth. v. 15. & vii. 12. & xxi. 40. Luc. viii. 31. & xxiv 44. Act. xxiv. 14. & xxvi. 22. & xxviii 13.
units.tr: Answer. Also in the earlier passages, if I remember rightly, we have answered this objection, that the Adversaries separate the Prophets from the law to this extent, as though the teaching of both were not in all things the same; and that he who proves something from the Prophets is not thought to have done enough unless he proves it from the law too, whose commentary is found in the Prophets. Since both Christ and the Apostles hold this view, and have taught us by their example, to argue either from the law or from the Prophets: Matt. 5:15; 7:12; 21:40; Luke 8:31; 24:44; Acts 24:14; 26:22; 28:23.

units.la: & Luc. xvi. 29. Habent Mosem & Pro-phetas, audiant illos. Ipse Socinus, Le-ction facrar[?] pag. 35. cum quidquid populo per alium quempiam à Mose Propheram signifisignificabatur, quod pertineret ad rationem & modum ipsi Deo obediendi, nihil esset aliud, quam repetitio, aut declaratio eorum, quæ jam à Mose dicta fuerant. Atque in Maath v. pag. 48. facit mentionem Christus, & legis, & prophetarum, quamvis alioqui solo legis nomine Prophetæ etiam ipsi intelligi solent, quemadmodum præter alia testimonia videtur aperte colligi ex mox sequentibus verbis, in quibus Christus solius legis mentionem facit, cum tamen verisimile admodum sit, eum verbis iis, plane respondere iis, quæ antea dixerat, in quibus, ut dictum est, non legem tantum, sed prophetas quoque nominaverat. Prophetarum vero nominatim Christus ab initio mentionem fecit, ut arbitror, propter hanc causam, quod etiam apud Prophetas multa continentur, quæ pertinent ad Dei legem & ad præcepta ipsa divina, quamvis verisimile sit, ut Iudæi vulgo credunt, in Prophetis, quod ad præcepta divina attinet, nihil revera contineri, quod præceptis ipsis Mosaicis non contineatur; & Prophetas, interpretes & explanatores quosdam, quod huc pertinet, fuisse Mosaicæ legis: quos tamen, præcipue quatenus pertinebat ad præcepta Dei, non recipiebant non pauci ex ipsis Iudæis, ii videlicet, qui Saducæi vocabantur; hodieque sunt inter Iudæos, qui idem sentiunt. Voluit igitur Christus hac ratione indicare, se cum Saducæis non facere. Atque ita vel ex hoc solo Socini testimonio, Smalcio abunde responsum videri debet.
units.tr: And Luke 16:29: "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them." Socinus himself, in Lectio sacrarum p. 35: "Since whatever was signified to the people through any other prophet than Moses, which pertained to the manner and rule of obeying God himself, was nothing other than a repetition or declaration of what had already been said by Moses." And in Matt. 5, p. 48, Christ makes mention both of the law and of the Prophets, although the Prophets are also commonly understood under the name of the law alone; as seems clearly to be gathered, among other testimonies, from the words that follow shortly, in which Christ mentions the law alone, though it is very probable that in those words he plainly answers to what he had said before, in which, as has been said, he named not only the law but the Prophets also. Christ first mentioned the Prophets by name, I think, for this reason, that many things are contained among the Prophets which pertain to the law of God and to the divine precepts themselves; although it is probable, as the Jews commonly believe, that in the Prophets, as far as the divine precepts are concerned, nothing is really contained that is not contained in the Mosaic precepts themselves; and that the Prophets were, as far as this matter goes, certain interpreters and expositors of the Mosaic law. Yet not a few of the Jews themselves did not receive them, especially so far as they pertained to the precepts of God: namely those who were called Sadducees; and there are still among the Jews today those who think the same. Christ therefore wished by this method to show that he does not side with the Sadducees. And thus from this testimony of Socinus alone, Smalcius ought to be thought to have been amply answered.

units.la: 11. Sed, uti Socinus bene observavit, & nos antea annotavimus, sub lege à Christo etiam Prophetæ comprehenduntur, Matth. v. 17. 18. nam illo versu nominat legem & Prophetas, ne putetis quod venerim solvere legem & Prophetas, isto vero satis habet, legem dixisse, non peribit jota unum vel apex à lege. 111. Eandem legis & Prophetarum, in doctrina legis summam constituit Christus, Matth. vii. 12. hæc est lex & Prophetæ. cap. xxii. 40. ab his duobus præceptis pendet tota lex & Prophetæ. iv. Atque ita sub Prophetis olim nihil docere, aut facere licuit, præter vel extra legem. Jesa. viii. 20. ad legem & ad testimonium. Deut. iv. 2. nihil addes, aut demes. cap. xii. 32. Prov. xxx. 6. v. Disputavimus nos atque argumentati sumus non ex solis Psalmis, sed ex lege etiam argumenta protulimus varia. vi. Sociniani, quando nova præcepta à Christo legi addita proferre satagunt, non ex solo Euangelio, sed ex reliqua N. Test. Scriptura, & epistolis Paulinis disputant: æquo jure & nobis, pro perfectione V. Test. agere licet ex scriptis, præterquam legis, etiam Prophetarum.
units.tr: 11. But, as Socinus rightly observed, and as we noted earlier, Christ includes the Prophets under the law, Matt. 5:17–18. In that verse he names "the Law and the Prophets": "Do not think that I came to abolish the Law and the Prophets." In the next verse he is content to say "the Law": "not one jot or one tittle will pass from the Law." 111. Christ sets down the same summary of the Law and the Prophets as the substance of the doctrine of the law, Matt. 7:12: "this is the Law and the Prophets." 22:40: "on these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets." iv. Thus under the Prophets it was never lawful to teach or do anything except within the law or beyond it. Isa. 8:20: "to the law and to the testimony." Deut. 4:2: "you shall add nothing, nor take away." 12:32; Prov. 30:6. v. We have disputed and argued not only from the Psalms but have also brought forward various arguments from the law. vi. When the Socinians strive to produce new precepts added to the law by Christ, they argue not from the Gospel alone but from the rest of the New Testament Scripture and the Pauline epistles. With equal right we may also, for the completion of the Old Testament, argue from the writings beyond the law, namely from the Prophets as well.

units.la: Denique nulla nota, indicium nullum novitatis in Oratione Dominicâ apparet, qualia alias sagaciter Adversarii indagari solent, ut quam speciem opinioni suæ induant, uti quando reperiunt à Christo affirmatum aliquoties, ego vero dico vobis: hic autem nihil omnino occurrit, quod vel novum aliquod, vel veteris augmentum sapiat aut correctionem. Imo quando attendimus ad occasionem, & connexionem traditæ à Christo orationis, cum præcedentibus, egerat de inani Gentilium battologia & polulogia in precibus, quibus Christus suum precandi modum opponit, vers. 8. μὴ οὖν ὁμοιωθῆτε αὐτοῖς [?]. vers. 9. οὕτως οὖν προσεύχεσθε ὑμεῖς [?]. Nihil quod ad Iudæos, nedum eorum legem, vel mutationem ejus aut emendationem aliquam referri videatur.
units.tr: Finally, no mark or sign of novelty appears in the Lord's Prayer, of the kind our opponents are wont to hunt out shrewdly in order to give their opinion some appearance, as when they find it affirmed by Christ several times: "but I say to you."
