Here, however, nothing at all occurs that savours of anything new, or of an enlargement or correction of the old. Indeed, when we attend to the occasion and connection of the prayer delivered by Christ with what precedes, he had spoken of the empty babbling and wordiness of the Gentiles in prayer, and against this Christ sets his own manner of praying. Verse 8: "Therefore do not be like them" [μὴ οὖν ὁμοιωθῆτε αὐτοῖς]. Verse 9: "Pray then in this way" [οὕτως οὖν προσεύχεσθε ὑμεῖς]. Nothing here seems to refer to the Jews, much less to their law, or to any change or emendation of it.

units.la: Tertium, quod præcepto primo, à Christo additum Adversarii, & tanquam novam legem habent, est, de ipso Christo invocando, vel Deo per Christum. Quod in V. Test. ignoratum, saltem in lege non significatum, quæ de Christo nihil, proindeque ceu novum præceptum ei adpositum esse, contendunt. Modum colendi Deum novum, qui antea plane erat inauditus, inquit Smalcius. In Catechesi Racov. Quid praeterea Dominus Iesus huic praecepto primo addidit? Resp. Id, quod etiamnum Dominum Iesum pro Deo cognoscere tenemur, id est, pro eo, qui in nobis potestatem habet divinam, & cui nos divinum exhibere honorem obstricti sumus. Smalcius, de Divinit. Christi, cap. v. Modus colendi Deum novus est, colere eum per Iesum Christum. Quod quidem duplici modo fit. Colimus enim Deum per Iesum Christum, dum cultum divinum Deo Patri tribuimus, non tanquam discipuli vel sectatores Mosis, sed tanquam Christi servi & subditi: Colimus etiam Deum per Iesum Christum, dum ipsum Iesum Christum colimus. Eadem habet & Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. x.
units.tr: Third, what our opponents hold to be a precept added by Christ to the first precept, and as a new law, is the invoking of Christ himself, or of God through Christ. This was unknown in the Old Testament, or at least not signified in the law, which, they contend, says nothing about Christ, and therefore this was added to it as a new precept. "A new mode of worshipping God, which before was quite unheard of," says Smalcius. In the Racovian Catechism: "What else did the Lord Jesus add to this first precept?" Answer: "That we are still bound to acknowledge the Lord Jesus as God, that is, as him who has divine power in us, and to whom we are obliged to render divine honour." Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 5: "The mode of worshipping God is new: to worship him through Jesus Christ. This is done in two ways. For we worship God through Jesus Christ when we ascribe divine worship to God the Father, not as disciples or followers of Moses, but as servants and subjects of Christ. We also worship God through Jesus Christ when we worship Jesus Christ himself." Volkelius has the same, book 4, ch. 10.

units.la: Distinguunt inter adorationem Christi, & invocationem Illa ut sit, quando animum aut corpus coram eo demittimus, & veluti prosternimus, atque ita summum ipsius imperium, & in nos curam agnoscimus, ac, quibus possumus modis, celebramus. Ista, auxilii ejus opisque imploratio, quando eum, quamvis corpore absentem precamur, nobis ut omni ratione succurrere ne dedigne-tur. Utramque Christo attribuunt, sacram & religiosam, non civilem tantummodo, sed plane divini honoris cultum.
units.tr: They distinguish between the adoration of Christ and the invocation of him. The former is when we bow down in mind or body before him and, as it were, prostrate ourselves, and so acknowledge his supreme rule and his care for us, and celebrate him by whatever means we can. The latter is the imploring of his aid and help, when, though we pray to him while bodily absent, we ask that he would not disdain to come to our succour in every way. They attribute both to Christ, as sacred and religious worship, not merely a civil honour but the plainly divine worship of honour.

units.la: Sunt tamen inter Adversarios, qui ei reclamant, & nolunt Christum invocari, nempe quia eum non credunt, non agnoscunt unum illum & verum Deum esse. Atque hoc hactenus bene, quod eum, qui Deus non sit, adorandum negent: sed Christum inficiari verum Deum esse, summa est blasphemia. Soci-niani quamvis in hoc cum iis faciant, quod Christum natura & essentia Deum negent, divino tamen cultu prosequendum docent: in quo, quod alii bene vident, haud consentanea docent, quum qui non est Deus, pro Deo haberi & divino cultu affici, nisi cum summa Dei injuriâ, haud potest. Illius Sectæ sunt Neo-Ariani, qui dicuntur, Franciscus Davidis, Christianus Francken, Budnæus, aliique, quos nec pro Christianis, nec pro fratribus habent Sociniani. Atque de illis dixi, in Apparatu ad Controversias Socinianas.
units.tr: Among our opponents, however, there are some who object to this and do not want Christ to be invoked, namely because they do not believe him, do not acknowledge him, to be that one true God. So far this is well, in that they deny that one who is not God is to be adored. But to deny that Christ is the true God is the greatest blasphemy. The Socinians, although in this they agree with those men in denying that Christ is God by nature and essence, nevertheless teach that he must be pursued with divine worship. In this they teach things that do not agree with each other, which others see well enough: for one who is not God cannot be regarded as God and be given divine worship except with the greatest injury to God. Of that sect are the so-called Neo-Arians: Francis David, Christian Francken, Budnaeus and others, whom the Socinians regard neither as Christians nor as brothers. About them I have spoken in the Apparatus to the Socinian Controversies.

units.la: Fundamentum invocationis Christi ponunt, in donis & potestate ejus; non in natura. Habent eum pro solo natura homine: sed qui multis egregiis divinisque donis à Deo affectus, hoc etiam consequuntur sit, ut religiose adoretur. Quare Christus ipsis novum Numen est, novum σέβασμα[?]: quasi inter Gentiles ageremus, ubi quandoque novi Dii exoriebantur. Et certe non est ipsis Christus nisi homo deificatus, qui per quandam quasi ἀποθέωσιν[?] honorem divinum adeptus sit. Cuditur in ipsorum Theologiâ novum Numen, novum genus cultus religiosi, & nova ejus ratio seu fundamentum: scilicet Christus Deus, Patribus ignotus, nec qui tum fuit Deus: novo à Deo, & inferiori religionis modo colendus: propter novam dignitatem quandam, ei præsertim à morte conciliatam.
units.tr: They lay the foundation of the invocation of Christ in his gifts and power, not in his nature. They hold him to be a man only by nature, but one who, endowed by God with many outstanding and divine gifts, thereby also comes to be religiously adored. Hence Christ is for them a new deity, a new object of worship [σέβασμα], as if we were dealing with the Gentiles, among whom new gods sometimes arose. And indeed Christ for them is nothing but a deified man, who by a certain kind of deification [ἀποθέωσις] has obtained divine honour. In their theology a new deity is coined, a new kind of religious worship, and a new reason or foundation for it: namely, Christ as God, unknown to the Fathers, who was not then God, to be worshipped with a new and lesser mode of religion, on account of a certain new dignity conferred on him, especially from his death.

units.la: Ex adverso causam, fundamentum, & formale objectum adorationis, seu invocationis Orthodoxi constituunt in divinâ naturâ: ut si[?]eam Christus non habet, neque adorari debeat. Et in hoc major propositio in Syllogismo Aria-norum norum vera est; qui non est verus Deus, divino & religioso cultu adorari non debet: verùm assumtio salsissima, quod Christus non sit verus & unus ille Deus. Atque frustra Socinians, Minorem admittentes, in majori mirum in modum se torquent, ut eam servent. Certe nisi Christus verus Deus sit, adorari non debet: si adorari, verus Deus est. reciprocant illa, Dei natura, & adorabilitas, vel adoratio. Neque plumbeum est argumentum, uti Remonstrantes, in gratiam Socinianorum, loquuntur, Apol. cap. xvi. pag. 153. sed certum & validum, quo Ecclesia & contra Arianos, & Photinianos, aliosque Deitatis Christi hostes, ut probaret eum verum Deum, atque adorandum, & ex hoc etiam argumento, Deum esse; atque contra Pontificios, in articulo de Idololatria, semper fuit usa.
units.tr: On the other side, the Orthodox place the cause, foundation and formal object of adoration or invocation in the divine nature, so that, since Christ does not have that nature, neither ought he to be adored. In this respect the major premise of the Arians' syllogism is true: one who is not the true God ought not to be adored with divine and religious worship. But the assumption is most false, that Christ is not the true and only God. In vain the Socinians, admitting the minor, twist themselves in every direction to keep the major. Certainly, unless Christ is true God, he ought not to be adored; if he is adored, he is true God. These things are reciprocal: the nature of God and his adorability, or adoration. Nor is this a leaden argument, as the Remonstrants, to favour the Socinians, put it in their Apology, ch. 16, p. 153. It is a sure and valid argument, which the Church has always used both against the Arians and Photinians and other enemies of Christ's deity, to prove that he is true God and to be adored, and from this argument also that God exists; and it has always been used against the Papists in the article on idolatry.

units.la: Atque ita, uti Christus non novus Deus, aut Deus factus est, sed idem ille aeternus, de cujus cultu primum agit in lege praeceptum, dici quoque nequit, hinc novum legis additamentum factum esse. Idem Deus, qui in lege proponitur, etiam in Euangelio, neque enim alius & alius Deus est, quamvis σχέσις & relatio sit alia: jam vero quemadmodum nec Sociniani dicunt, ideo alium cultum esse Dei, vel aliud novum praeceptum colendi ejus, quamvis sub alia relatione in lege, alia nunc in Euangelio proponatur & colatur; idem dicimus nos de Filio: atque par est utrobique ratio. Filius in V. Test fuit, aeque ac Pater; sed alia ejus relatio seu in lege, seu in Veteri Foederis oeconomia, ac sub Testamento novo, non tamen ideo modus colendi aut Patrem aut Filium novus est, qui antea fuerit inauditus, uti Smalcius dixit. Quotidie obveniunt nobis Dei, divinaeque benignitatis aliae supra alias manifestationes, non tamen inde struimus novos Deum colendi modos, antea inauditos, vel nova praecepta, & ad legem additamenta. Quare quum in praesenti controversia objiciantur nobis Christus, ejus cultus, prout vel olim praescriptus observatusque in Vet. Testamento, vel hodie est sub Novo, ut judicemus, num novum hinc legis praeceptum augmentumque accesserit, probe nonnulla distinguere, ad singula capita, ante alia oportet. Ac primo, Christus consideratur ut Deus, vel ut Mediator.
units.tr: And so, just as Christ is not a new God or a God made, but that same eternal one of whose worship the first precept of the law treats, it cannot be said that a new addition has been made to the law from this. The same God who is set forth in the law is also set forth in the Gospel; for he is not one God and then another, although the relation (σχέσις) is different. Now just as the Socinians do not say that therefore there is another worship of God, or another new precept for worshipping him, although under a different relation he is set forth and worshipped in the law and now in another way in the Gospel, we say the same concerning the Son, and the reasoning is equal on both sides. The Son was in the Old Testament just as the Father was. But his relation, whether under the law or under the economy of the Old Covenant, is different from what it is under the New Testament. Yet for that reason the mode of worshipping either the Father or the Son is not new, or unheard of before, as Smalcius said. Daily other manifestations of God and of divine goodness come to us, one above another, yet we do not from these construct new modes of worshipping God, unheard of before, or new precepts and additions to the law. Therefore, since in the present controversy Christ, and his worship as it was prescribed and observed of old in the Old Testament or as it is today under the New, are brought against us, so that we may judge whether a new precept or addition to the law has thence arisen, we must first properly distinguish several points, one by one. And first, Christ is considered either as God or as Mediator.

units.la: II. Ut Mediator promissus, in V. Testamento; vel exhibitus, in Novo. Neque alia hic novitas vel varietas invocandi Christum, ac Patrem: uti enim Pater, a Veteribus consideraba tur, in ipsorum precibus, ut qui promisisset Filium Mediatorem; jam, ut qui eum exhibuit, absque hoc quod nova cultus ratio erga Patrem hinc statuitur: ita quoque Mediatorem, quem ex revelatione Dei, praenunciabant Veteres, credebantque praenuntiationi, & praenuntiato, ibi ut venturum spectabant, & hac ratione non poterant non colere; sub N. nunc Testamento ut exhibitum veneramur, sine alia nova, nedum inaudita colendi eum ratione, vel praecepto.
units.tr: II. As Mediator, promised in the Old Testament and exhibited in the New. There is no other novelty or variety here in invoking Christ as opposed to the Father. For just as the Fathers regarded the Father in their prayers as the one who had promised the Son as Mediator, and now regard him as the one who has exhibited him, without this establishing any new way of worshipping the Father, so too the Mediator whom the ancients foretold from God's revelation, and in whom they believed as the one to come, they could not but worship in that way, and we now venerate him as one who has been exhibited under the New Testament, with no other new or unheard-of way or rule of worship.

units.la: Modus & gradus revelationis, quibus Deus utitur, sunt varii. Partior[?] fuit sub V.Testamento; clarior & copiosior sub Novo. πολυμερῶς[?] καὶ πολυτρόπως[?], Hebr. 1. 1. & sic religio, fides, & cultus magis manifesta & explicita, sub N. T. nunc sunt, quam olim sub Veteri. Verum ex diversis formis aut modis, non est trahenda realis differentia aut praeceptorum utriusque Test., aut religionis & cultus. Alia est realis differentia; alia modalis: in re diversa, vel in rei ejusdem modo. Et sic novum aliquid potest dici, aut respectu rei, aut revelationis. Et hujus, vel in genere, & ex toto; vel, ex parte. Verbi causa, creatio & lapsus Angelorum, clarius revelantur in N.T. quam in Veteri: non autem hinc sequitur, quod demum sub N. Test. illa contigerint, vel nullo modo nota aut patefacta fuerint sub T. Veteri. Ita clarior omnino, expressior & copiosior doctrina nunc est de Christo, eoque colendo in N. Test. quam Veteri: non proinde sequitur, quod nulla etiam fuerit in Veteri.
units.tr: The modes and degrees of revelation which God uses are various. The revelation was partly under the Old Testament, and clearer and fuller under the New: polymerōs kai polytropōs [πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως], Heb. 1.1. Thus religion, faith and worship are now more manifest and explicit under the New Testament than they were formerly under the Old. But from differences of form or mode we must not infer a real difference either in the precepts of the two Testaments or in religion and worship. One difference is real, another modal: a difference either in the thing itself or in the manner of the same thing. So something may be called new either with respect to the thing or with respect to the revelation, and this either in general and wholly, or in part. For example, the creation and fall of the angels are revealed more clearly in the New Testament than in the Old; but it does not follow that those events happened only under the New Testament, or that they were in no way known or disclosed under the Old. So the doctrine concerning Christ, and the worship of him, is now altogether clearer, more explicit and fuller in the New Testament than in the Old; but it does not follow that there was none of it in the Old.

units.la: Bene & accurate tenenda semper doctrina & differentia legis est, atque Euangelii. In lege nihil de Euangelio, verum est: sed non debet aut potest Euangelium dici complementum aut augmentum moralis legis. Deum colere, lex praescribit: Euangelium offendit Deum nobis reconciliatum, & Mediatorem, quae lex ignorat: quidquid modi aut formae hujus est, ex Euangelio habemus; uti ex lege, Deum, quocunque modo, colendum esse. Quando autem Deus Mediatorem θεάνθρωπον in Euangelio exhibet, legis praecepta huic applicanda etiam, praecepta legis & cultus lege praescripti, nulla nova super eo praecepta aut leges formandae, aut concipiendae veniunt. Aliud est, nova lex; aliud, nova legis ad subjectum applicatio. Lex exigit cultum Dei: Euangelium aliquid de Deo revelat, θεάνθρωπον nempe, qui lege non continetur: hic vero quia Deus est, ad eum legis illud mandatum spectat omnino, atque referendum etiam est. Sed hoc, quamvis non in lege, in doctrina tamen V. Test. comprehensum agnitumque fuit, quatenus ibi quoque viguit doctrina Euangelii: clarius modo, sed non nunc demum, in Novo natum. Non ergo novum hic praeceptum N. Test. quod non etiam in Veteri fuerit; nihilque praecepti, aut ejus quod facere debemus, quod non in lege fundatum sit. Verbi gratia, quidni perspicuitatis ergo rem abunde declaremus? lex jubet Deum colere: accessit modus colendi Deum sub variis olim caeremoniis, quia sic revelarat Deus, coli se velle: an hinc tum novum legis additamentum, ad praeceptum illud additum, de colendo Deum? quis dicet? Ita & hic, ad & post legis dictatum illud, sequutum Euangelium fuit, de colendo Deo suo modo in V. Test., alio in Novo, [illegible, ~4 letters] Patris in Christo, & per Christum: hic autem modus non est dicendus continere novum praeceptum, vel legis majorem quandam perfectionem.
units.tr: The doctrine and the difference between law and Gospel must always be held well and accurately. Nothing about the Gospel is in the law: that is true. But the Gospel ought not, and cannot, be called the complement or augmentation of the moral law. The law prescribes worship of God; the Gospel reveals God reconciled to us, and a Mediator, which the law does not know. Whatever mode or form of this there is, we have it from the Gospel, just as from the law we have that God must be worshipped in whatever way. But when God exhibits the God-man [θεάνθρωπον] as Mediator in the Gospel, the precepts of the law are applied to him, and no new precepts or laws need to be framed or devised concerning him; the precepts of the law and the worship prescribed by the law stand. It is one thing to have a new law; it is another to have a new application of the law to a subject. The law requires the worship of God; the Gospel reveals something about God, namely the God-man, who is not contained in the law. Yet because he is God, that command of the law applies to him altogether and must be referred to him. But although this was not comprehended in the law, it was comprehended and acknowledged in the doctrine of the Old Testament, inasmuch as the doctrine of the Gospel was also in force there: it has been made clearer now, but it was not born only in the New. Therefore the New Testament contains no new precept that was not also in the Old, and nothing of what we must do that is not grounded in the law. For example, why should we not, for the sake of clarity, state the matter fully? The law commands the worship of God. There was added a mode of worshipping God under various ceremonies formerly, because God had so revealed that he wished to be worshipped. Is this a new addition of law to that precept concerning the worship of God? Who would say so? Thus here too, both with and after that dictate of the law, the Gospel followed concerning the worship of God in his own way under the Old Testament and in another way under the New, [illegible, about four letters] of the Father in Christ and through Christ. This mode, however, is not to be said to contain a new precept, or some greater perfection of the law.

units.la: Fateor, si alius pro Deo quis proponatur in Euangelio colendus, ac ille est, quem lex designat colendum, & quidem solum; novum praeceptum hoc tum fore, novam legem, & certe non legis additamentum, sed εὐαγγέλιον [?] & eversionem ejus. Jam vero eundem Deum Euangelium exhibet, quamvis Mediatorem. Non ergo nova hic lex est necessaria, vel praeceptum novum. Contra Adversarii de suo Christo, novo Deo, quem ut Deum coli volunt, quum tamen non sit Deus, non ille legis idem ac solus, aliud praeceptum efficiunt, sed tam legi, quam Euangelio contrarium. Temere autem dogma & thesim suam nobis imputant, qui nullibi alium Deum docemus, aut colimus, quam eundem Legis & Euangelii.
units.tr: I admit that if someone were proposed in the Gospel as the God to be worshipped, other than the one the law designates as to be worshipped, and indeed as the only one, then there would be a new precept here, a new law, and certainly not an addition to the law but a gospel [εὐαγγέλιον] and its overthrow. But in fact the Gospel presents the same God, though as Mediator. So no new law or new precept is necessary here. On the contrary, our adversaries, with their Christ who is a new God, whom they want worshipped as God, although he is not God and is not the same and only one of the law, make a different precept, one contrary to both the law and the Gospel. Yet they rashly impute their own dogma and thesis to us, when we nowhere teach or worship any other God than the same God of Law and Gospel.

units.la: Re hunc in modum enodatâ explicataque, ad argumentationem progredimur. Atque pro nostrâ sententiâ hoc quidem prim. argum. Præceptum, de adorando Deo, non est novum: atqui præceptum de adorando Christo, non est aliud præceptum, quam illud de adorando Deo: ergo non est novum, vel in N. Test. demum natum, notumve. Major certa est, atque in confesso. Minor non minus vera; quia nisi Christus esset verus ille Deus, adorari nec posset, nec deberet; & non est aliud ejus adorandi proprium ac formale objectum, vel causa, quam divina natura. Ubi evicerint, Christum non esse Deum, ultro cedemus: illo vero manente, uti æternæ veritatis est, ideo quoque adorandum dicimus, & tuemur. Ex quo, jure facimus hoc deinde
units.tr: Having thus cleared up and explained the matter, we proceed to the argument. For our view, this is the first argument: the precept concerning the worship of God is not new; but the precept concerning the worship of Christ is not a different precept from that concerning the worship of God; therefore it is not new, nor was it born or made known only in the New Testament. The major premise is certain and admitted. The minor is no less true, because unless Christ were the true God, he could neither be worshipped nor ought to be; and the proper and formal object or cause of his worship is nothing other than the divine nature. If they prove that Christ is not God, we will readily yield; but while he remains God, as is the eternal truth, we say and maintain that he is therefore also to be worshipped. From this we rightly proceed to the following:

units.la: Argum. secundum. Qui est verus Deus, is non demum in N. Test. introducitur, vel proponitur adorandus: sed Christus est verus Deus: ergo. Profecto nisi pro vero illo Deo haberemus eum, non adoraremus. Jam vero quando ut talem accipimus & adoramus, non ex præcepto novo id facere nos, sed veteri, & naturali legis primævæ, consentaneum est. Adeo pendet tota hæc quæstio ex præcedenti, de Christi deitate: hanc si evertere queant, quod nec Diabolus poterit unquam, tum demum in hac quæstione evadent superiores.
units.tr: Second argument. He who is the true God is not introduced or proposed for worship only in the New Testament; but Christ is the true God; therefore. Indeed, unless we held him to be that true God, we would not worship him. And when we accept and worship him as such, it is consistent that we do this not by a new precept but by the old one, and by the natural law of the primeval law. So entirely does this whole question depend on the preceding one, concerning the deity of Christ. If they can overturn this, which the Devil himself will never be able to do, then at last they will prevail in this question.

units.la: III. Arg. Novum Testamentum in hoc etiam confirmat doctrinam Veteris, quod nemo sit adorandus religioso cultu, præter solum & unum Deum, nullaque alia de causa: ergo vel Christus non est Deus; vel propter hoc ado-randus est, & fuit, cultu perpetuo, eodemque. Matth. iv. 10. Scriptum est enim, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli servies. Ubi & hoc notandum, quod quum in lege simpliciter dictum sit, Iehovam colito, Christus id ita accepit & interpretatus fuit, ut excludens alia quævis numina, citarit quasi scriptum, eum solum coles: parem utriusque Testamenti, & in Deo, & solo eo colendo, constituens rationem. Sociniani aliam cultus religiosi causam faciunt in N. Test. quam fuit in Veteri: Scriptura non, sed ubique eandem agnoscit, deitatis nempe: quare, uti haud mirum est, illos, ut figmentis suis paria dicant, suo fictitio & factitio Deo, novum quoque ejus adorandi præceptum introducere: quod, fatemur, debuisset etiam, siquidem novus Deus esset Christus, quia nullo præcepto talis adorari permittitur, nedum ut jubeatur, quod omnibus legis præceptis evertitur & condemnatur: ita quoque convenienter nos Scripturæ sacræ, unam ubique adorationis causam, & perpetuam novimus, Deitatem nempe veram & naturalem, non factitiam, & falsam. Adde Jerem. xvii. 5. Rom. i. 25. Gal. iv. 8. Apoc.xix. 10. & xxii. 6.
units.tr: Third argument. The New Testament also confirms in this the doctrine of the Old, that no one is to be worshipped with religious worship except the one and only God, and for no other reason. Therefore either Christ is not God, or on this account he is to be worshipped, and was worshipped, with the same perpetual worship. Matt. 4.10: "For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve." Here it should also be noted that whereas in the law it is simply said, "Worship Jehovah," Christ took and interpreted it in such a way that, excluding all other divinities, he cited it as if written, "Him only shall you worship", establishing the same basis for both Testaments: in God, and in worshipping him alone. The Socinians make the cause of religious worship in the New Testament different from what it was in the Old. Scripture, however, acknowledges everywhere one and the same cause, namely the deity. Hence it is no wonder that they, so that their own inventions may say like things, introduce also for their fictitious and factitious God a new precept of worshipping him. Yet we confess that they ought to have done this, if Christ were a new God, since no precept permits such a one to be worshipped, let alone commands it; indeed this is overturned and condemned by all the precepts of the law. So, too, in agreement with the holy Scripture, we know that there is everywhere one and perpetual cause of worship, namely the true and natural Deity, not a factitious and false one. Add Jer. 17.5; Rom. 1.25; Gal. 4.8; Rev. 19.10 and 22.6.

units.la: Quarto. Una modo cultus religiosi species est, forma una, & gradus: non alius major, vel minor; superior, inferior; vel supremus, & subordinatus: ergo talis cultus, qualem Christo deferunt Adversarii, utcunque divinum di-cant, cant, natura tamen inferiorem illo, qui vero & uni Deo tribuitur, nullus est, neque in verbo Dei fundatur: quare & frustra pro eo præceptum quærunt, & novum aliquod Novi Testamenti. Qua etenim ratione Pontificiorum explodimus distinctiones & varias cultus sacri formas, δουλείας, ὑπερδουλείας, λατρείας, eadem evertuntur etiam, quæ Sociniani, quamvis non iisdem terminis, de vario tamen Dei cultu pronuntiant.
units.tr: Fourthly. There is only one form, one shape and one degree of religious worship: there is no other greater or lesser, higher or lower, supreme or subordinate kind. So the worship that our opponents pay to Christ, however much they call it divine, is in nature inferior to that which is given to the one true God alone. No such worship exists, and it is not founded in the Word of God. That is why they seek in vain a command for it, and some new precept of the New Testament. By the same reasoning by which we reject the Papists' distinctions and their various forms of sacred worship, dulia [δουλείας], hyperdulia [ὑπερδουλείας] and latria [λατρείας], the same arguments also overturn what the Socinians pronounce about the varying worship of God, though not in the same terms.

units.la: Quinto. Denique Christus etiam in V. Test. ut Mediator propositus fidelibus, acceptus, & cultus fuit: ergo non in N. Test. demum ejus colendi præceptum novum atque inauditum datum est. Probatur illud, quia vel Mediator ipsis apud Deum fuit aliquis, vel nullus. Si nullus, haud potuerunt salvari. Quia extra Mediatorem salus peccatoribus non datur. Si Mediatorem habuerunt; ergo Christum, quia præter eum nullus alius est. Joann. xiv. 6. 1 Tim. ii. 5. 6. Hebr. xiii. 8. Act. xv. 11. Deinde, probamus idem, inductione tum testimoniorum, tum exemplorum, ex Vet. Testamento. Psalm. ii. 12. Osculamini filium. Psalm. xlv. 12. Et delectabitur Rex pulchritudine tua: cumque sit Dominus tuus, incurvate ei. Ad quæ verba notandum, quod habet Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. x. Quanto igitur magis nos, eodem divino ipsius imperio, ad id faciendum astringimur? præsertim quum ipsa quoque Ecclesia, quantumvis sub Salomonis ejusdemque Sponsæ typo, Christum ipsum suum adorare jubeatur. Adde Psalm. cx. Jesa. ix. 6. & Liii. Jerem. xxiii. 6. & xxxiii. 14. De Abrahamo scimus, quod Christus dixit, Joann. viii. 56. exultavit ut videret diem meum, & vidit, & lætatus est. Genef. xviii. adorat Abraham Angelum Jehovam, id est, Angelum fœderis Christum: uti aliàs probavimus. Eundem pro nepotibus suis invocat Jacobus Patriarcha, Genef. xlviii. 16. Confer Exod. xxiii. 21. Jesa. lxiii. 9. Dan. ix. 17. Ausculta Deus noster, &c. propter Dominum. Atque in arca, & sacrificiis spectarunt fideles gratiam & redemtionem in Christo, quem proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον per fidem in sanguine ejus, ad ostensionem justitiæ suæ, ad remissionem peccatorum ante commissorum. Rom. iii. 25. Hactenus de primo Decalogi præcepto, & quod ei additum à Christo Adversarii com-minifcuntur.
units.tr: Fifthly. Finally, Christ in the Old Testament was set forth to the faithful as Mediator, and was accepted and worshipped. So the command to worship him was not given for the first time, as something new and unheard of, in the New Testament. This is proved as follows: either the faithful had some mediator with God, or none. If none, they could not have been saved, since salvation is not given to sinners apart from the Mediator. If they had a mediator, it was Christ, since there is no other beside him: John 14:6; 1 Tim. 2:5, 6; Heb. 13:8; Acts 15:11. Next, we prove the same by an induction from testimonies and examples in the Old Testament. Psalm 2:12: Kiss the Son. Psalm 45:12: And the King shall greatly desire your beauty; for he is your Lord, and you shall bow down to him. On these words we should note what Volkelius says, book 4, chapter 10: How much more, then, are we bound by the same divine command of his to do this, especially since the Church itself, even under the type of Solomon and of his Bride, is commanded to worship Christ himself. Add Psalm 110; Isaiah 9:6 and 53; Jeremiah 23:6 and 33:14. Of Abraham we know what Christ said, John 8:56: Abraham rejoiced to see my day, and he saw it and was glad. In Genesis 18 Abraham worships the Angel Jehovah, that is, the Angel of the covenant, Christ, as we have proved elsewhere. The patriarch Jacob also calls upon the same Angel for his grandsons, Genesis 48:16. Compare Exodus 23:21; Isaiah 63:9; Daniel 9:17: Hear, our God, etc., for the Lord's sake. And in the ark and the sacrifices the faithful looked to grace and redemption in Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness, for the remission of sins previously committed: Romans 3:25. So much concerning the first commandment of the Decalogue, and what the opponents invent as added to it by Christ.

units.la: Ad præceptum legis secundum dicunt, per Christum adjectum fuisse mandatum de cavendis idolis, eorum loco, atque idololythis: id est, de fugiendâ omni omnino idololatriâ, uti loquitur Catechef. Racovienfis, ad hoc adducens 1 Joann. v. 21. filioli, custodite vos ab idolis. 1 Cor. x. 14. ideoque, dilecti mei, fugite idolola-triam. Quod ulterius exponens, ait, ita demum fugere nos idololatriam, si non simus ubi sculptilia & imagines coluntur, & ne participemus ex illis, quæ idolis sunt consecrata. Smalcius, de Divinit. Christi, cap. v. Perfecit eam legem, & implevit D. Jesus, dum per Apostolos omni ratione vitare jubet idola, adeo ut etiam loca illa vitemus, ubi ea coluntur. 1 Cor. x. 14. Quo sive dicas, ad Adversario-rum mentem, præceptum Decalogi auctum, sive hoc ad istud additum, nihil adeo differre existimamus, ut ideo notare Frantzium Smalcius debuerit, Disp. vii. quod dixisset, additum illis videri præceptum hoc, ad illud de Sculptilibus.
units.tr: As to the second commandment of the law, they say that by Christ there was added a command about avoiding idols, in place of them, and idolothytes: that is, about fleeing from every kind of idolatry, as the Racovian Catechism puts it, citing for this 1 John 5:21: Little children, keep yourselves from idols. 1 Cor. 10:14: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. Explaining this further, it says that we flee idolatry only if we are not where graven images and pictures are worshipped, and that we do not partake of things that have been consecrated to idols. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, chapter 5: The Lord Jesus perfected and fulfilled that law, when through the Apostles he commands us to avoid idols by every means, so that we avoid even those places where they are worshipped. 1 Cor. 10:14. Whether you say this is a command of the Decalogue enlarged according to the mind of the opponents, or that this was added to that, we think there is no difference, so that Smalcius ought not to have noted Frantzius for saying, in Disputation 7, that this command seemed to have been added to that one about graven images.

units.la: Tom. 2. nam & adjungi, Volkelius dixit; & ipsa Catechesis exserte, additum five ad-junctum: namque haec aequipollent. was ist in dem newen bunde zu dem gebote gethan? pag. 184. Quod de idolo cavendo, exponunt, de frequentatione istius loci, ubi honorari & religiose coli solent idola, qualia olim erant tempe Ethnica, & hodie sunt Pontificia: non vero de necessaria quandoque inter improbos habitatione, aut conversatione, modo fiat extra periculum seductionis, collusionis, aut scandali. Volkelius, qui ad reliquorum praeceptorum expositionem, dein inquirere solet & proponere quid, ex sua Theologia, Christus illis addiderit, sicco admodum pede illa praeterit in praecepto secundo: post expositum istud, sic inferens: ad hoc autem Dei praeceptum illud quoque adjungendum est, quod tum Paulus, tum Johannes nos admonet, vempe ut fugiamus idola, illorumque cultum; ita nempe, ut non solum idola nequaquam fabricemus, aut colamus; sed etiam tum loca, in quibus ea coluntur, praesertim tunc, cum cultum illum institui novimus, caveamus; tum ab omnibus, qua cum illorum cultu conjunctum quippiam habent, aut quacunque tandem ratione ad illum spectent, abstineamus, ut omnibus hominibus, Deoque ipsi clarissime pateat, quantopere omnia, qua illi improbantur, non solum quod ex se malum est, sed etiam speciem habet, summo studio declinantes. Apparet, quam non illa fiducia hic loquatur de augmento & amplificatione hujus praecepti, atque de aliis. Adjungendum est, inquit, ad fecundum illud praeceptum, quod tum Paulus, tum Johannes nos monent: sed, an adjungendum, tanquam ejus explicatio, an ceu novi praecepti additamentum? hoc quaeritur, non illud. Quod-que non fit haec Veteris legis alia perfectio, seu consummatio, & novum ad eam praeceptum Euangelii, porro ita probamus:
units.tr: Vol. 2. For Volkelius said both adjungi (to be joined) and the Catechism itself says plainly additum or adjunctum (added or joined), since these amount to the same thing. "What has been added to the commandment in the New Covenant?" p. 184. What they say about avoiding idols means frequenting that place where idols are honoured and religiously worshipped, as were formerly the Gentile temples and are now the Papist ones; it does not mean the sometimes necessary dwelling or association with the wicked, provided it is done without danger of seduction, collusion or scandal. Volkelius, who in expounding the other commandments is accustomed to inquire and set out what Christ added to them from his own theology, passes over the second commandment with very dry feet. After expounding it he infers thus: To this command of God, however, must be joined also what both Paul and John admonish us of, namely that we flee idols and their worship: so that we not only never make or worship idols, but also avoid the places in which they are worshipped, especially when we know that such worship is being set up; and that we abstain from everything that has any connection with their worship, or in any way pertains to it, so that it may be most clear to all men, and to God himself, how greatly we, with the utmost zeal, shun everything that is disapproved of there, not only what is evil in itself but also what has the appearance of evil. It is plain that he does not speak here with such confidence about an increase and enlargement of this command, or about other things. It must be joined, he says, to that second commandment, as Paul and John admonish us: but the question is whether it must be joined as its explanation, or as an addition of a new command. Nor is this another perfection or consummation of the Old Law, nor a new precept of the Gospel added to it. We prove this as follows.

units.la: Arg. primum. Quod praeceptum omnem idololatriam prohibet severissime in genere, idem damnat omnes ejus species, modos, capita, & quidquid ullam cum ea habere communionem potest. Per regulam in interpretandis Decalogi praeceptis, quin legibus quibuscunque, apud omnes approbatam, ut generalia completi particularia quaecunque intelligantur. Quod nisi ponas pro certo, jam totidem praecepti cujuscunque augmenta facies novasque leges, quot generalis prohibitionis vel praecepti dari possunt capita aut species singulares. Quod in immensum usque procedet. Quis autem negabit, idololatriam omnem sculptilium vel imaginum prohiberi praecepto secundo? uti quaevis numina, primo? vel, quemadmodum omnis Dei veri cultus includitur praecepto isto; ita quaevis iconolatria vetatur praecepto altero. Volkelius, in expositione praecepti secundi, inquit, antequam augmentum sc. ejus commemorat: Cum igitur, ut ad rem redeamus, Deus idololatriam tantopere aversetur, tamque vehementer vindicet; cavendum est, ne in tantum peccatum ulla ratione incidamus. Hoc si secundo praecepto contineatur, uti revera continetur, tum hoc, fugiendam vid. omni modo idololatriam esse, haud potest constituere praeceptum novum. Et quis, vel cogitatione, vel expositione, aut adhortatione ex praecepto instituta, plenitudinem ejus animo complectatur, qui non hoc posuerit in eo primarium fugiendam prorsus idololatriam omnem esse? Quid autem aliud loca illa, quae huic fini allegare solent, dicunt, 1 Cor. x. 14. 1 Joann. v. 21. quam vel fugite idola? vel, custodite vos ab idolis? Quisquamne est, qui sedata mente ausit profiteri, ista secundo praecepto non contineri? Quod praeceptum dicit, ne idola facias, ne te profernas coram iis, neve ea colas, sed grandi vindicta cavet sui observantiam, non dicere credetur, fugienda idola esse, & idololatriam? Tum nullius praecepti habebitur argumentum & summarium, nullum dabitur, cujus non, haud dico a variis sub eo contentis speciebus, sed ipso ejus argumento, plures formari poterunt additiones, & praecepta alia, illud si obtineat. Etenim hoc, fugere idololatriam non est nova aliqua rei hic vetitae species, sed ipsa: quam si demas, vim praecepti sustuleris. Quisquamne potest satisfacere praecepto, qui idololatriam non fugerit? annon ut caveas idololatriam, praecipitur? potesne cavere, uti oportet, si non quoque fugeris?
units.tr: First argument. The command that forbids all idolatry most severely in general also condemns all its species, modes, heads, and whatever can have any fellowship with it. By the rule, approved by all in interpreting the precepts of the Decalogue, and indeed in any laws, the particulars are understood to be included in the general. Unless you hold this as certain, you will make as many increases of any command, and as many new laws, as there can be single heads or species of a general prohibition or command. And that would proceed to infinity. Who, then, will deny that every idolatry of graven images or pictures is forbidden by the second commandment, just as any gods are forbidden by the first? Or, as all true worship of God is included in that command, so every image-worship is forbidden by the other. Volkelius, in expounding the second commandment, says, before he recounts its enlargement: Since, then, to return to the matter, God so abhors idolatry and punishes it so vehemently, we must take care not to fall into so great a sin in any way. If this is contained in the second commandment, as in truth it is, then this, that idolatry must in every way be fled, cannot constitute a new command. And who, whether in thought, in exposition, or in exhortation drawn from the command, would grasp its fullness in mind, if he had not held that the chief point in it is that all idolatry must altogether be fled? What else do those passages that they are accustomed to allege for this purpose say, 1 Cor. 10:14 and 1 John 5:21, than flee idols or keep yourselves from idols? Is there anyone who, with a calm mind, would dare to profess that these things are not contained in the second commandment? That commandment says, you shall not make idols, nor bow yourself before them, nor serve them; and it guards its observance with a great penalty. Will it not be believed to say that idols and idolatry must be fled? Then there would be no argument or summary of any command, and no command would be left from which, I do not say from its various species contained under it but from its very argument, more additions and other commands could not be formed, if this were allowed. For this, to flee idolatry, is not some new species of the forbidden thing here, but the thing itself: if you take it away, you have destroyed the force of the command. Can anyone satisfy the command who has not fled idolatry? Is it not commanded that you should beware of idolatry? Can you beware as you ought if you have not also fled it?

units.la: Exc. At idolothyta etiam cavenda- & hoc non in Decalogo docetur, sed ab Apostolo 1 Cor. viii. Audiamus Smalcium, contra Frantzium, Disp. VII. pag. 234.
units.tr: Objection: Meat offered to idols must also be avoided, and this is taught not in the Decalogue but by the Apostle in 1 Cor. 8. Let us hear Smalcius against Frantzius, Disp. VII, p. 234.

units.la: Quod quid sit; & quomodo novum aliquid sit, quod in lege non ita strictè prohibitum erat, loca allegata 1 Cor. 8. & 10. offendere poterant, in illis enim Paulus, plane illud, quantumvis per se liceat, non licere docet, si alium offendat, & si quis illud nihilominus faciat, graviter eum peccare, & salutis ja-cturam facere posse prolixe demonstrat, quae res non ita expressa usquam est in V. F. licet enim, ut Frantzius thes. 8o. ostendit, praecepisset Deus, ne nomina Deorum alienorum memorarent Israelitae; & ex eo colligi possit, non licere etiam in locis illis conversari, ubi ea coluntur: tamen hoc non ita precise, nec ob eam causam, quam Paulus affert, interdictum alicui fuisse, apparet. Nam non tantum ob metum seductionis, aut suspicionem collusio-nis, quas causas Frantzius affert, non licet, homini Christiano adesse in locis illis, ubi idola coluntur, sed etiam ideo tantum, si inde scandalum, idque valde subtile, oriri possit. Quod Paulus exprimit 1 Cor. 8. 16. dum ait: Si autem quis viderit te, qui habes scientiam, in idolo recumbentem, nonne conscientia ejus, qui est infirmus, aedificabitur ad idolothyta manducandum? Et perit[?] infirmus frater in tua scientia, propter quem Christus mortuus est, &c. Cur vero periturus sit, ratio reddi-tur alibi, Rom. 14. v. ult. Quia scilicet edet
units.tr: What this is, and how it is something new, when the law did not forbid it so strictly: the passages cited, 1 Cor. 8 and 10, could cause offence. In them Paul plainly teaches that this thing, however lawful in itself, is not lawful if it gives offence to another. He shows at length that if anyone does it nonetheless, he sins gravely and may suffer the loss of salvation. Nowhere in the Old Testament is this matter stated so explicitly. For although, as Frantzius shows in thesis 8, God had commanded that the Israelites not mention the names of foreign gods, and from this it may be inferred that it is not lawful to live in those places where they are worshipped, yet it does not appear that this was forbidden in so precise a way, or for the reason Paul gives. For it is not lawful for a Christian to be present in places where idols are worshipped, not only because of the fear of seduction or the suspicion of collusion, which are the reasons Frantzius gives, but also simply because a scandal, and a very subtle one, may arise from it. Paul expresses this in 1 Cor. 8:16, where he says: "But if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining in an idol's temple, will not the conscience of him who is weak be built up to eat idol meat? And the weak brother perishes by your knowledge, for whom Christ died," and so on. Why he will perish is given elsewhere, Rom. 14, last verse: because, namely, he eats

units.la: Resp. 1. Quod si hoc novum aliquid sit, & in lege non praeceptum, quor-sum vel titubanter adeo in fine vult omnes judicare, an pro auctione, vel augmento praecepti secundi habendum sit; vel pervicaciter tergiversatus fuit cum Frantzio, qui dixerat, hoc additum ipsis praecepto videri? Siquidem novum, certe praecepto additum est.
units.tr: Answer. 1. If this is something new, and not commanded in the law, why does he so hesitantly ask all to judge at the end whether it should be regarded as an enlargement or augmentation of the second precept? Or else he obstinately evaded the point with Frantzius, who had said that this seemed to be added to the precept itself? For if it is new, it is certainly added to the precept.

units.la: II. In lege, inquit, non ita strictè prohibitum fuit. Ergo saltem prohibitum, licet non ita strictè? ergo non novum: ergo lege comprehensum. Et haec est tota controversia. Quippe de re dispu-tamus lege contenta, non de modo, quo contenta fuerit. Modus proponendi vel exponendi strictior aut latior non facit statim praecepta nova. Alio-qui quot sunt libri scriptaque in V. & N. Test. aliis posteriora & copiosiora, toties legem fecerint auctiorem & perfectiorem. Quo quid absurdius? Quid libros dico? capita, & commata quae strictius aliquid proponunt, explicant, aut urgent, nova & nova itera-tum praecepta dare dicenda essent.
units.tr: II. He says that in the law it was not forbidden so strictly. Then at least it was forbidden, though not so strictly? Then it is not new; it is contained in the law. And this is the whole controversy. For we are disputing about a matter contained in the law, not about the manner in which it was contained. A stricter or looser manner of setting forth or explaining a thing does not at once make new precepts. Otherwise, how many books and writings in the Old and New Testament, which are later and fuller than others, would have made the law ever fuller and more perfect, over and over? What could be more absurd? To say nothing of books: chapters and verses which set forth, explain or press something more strictly would have to be said to give new and ever new precepts.

units.la: III. Non licere alium offendere, in quade illis idolothytis adductus non fide, hoc est, non certa persuasione, quod sibi id liceat, sed tantum autoritate fratris, quem id ante se facientem vidit. Quicquid vero fit sine fide, peccatum est. Tam profunda hujus rei consideratio, & ejus tam severa interdictio, quam Paulus tradit, an pro auctione præcepti de sculptilibus non adorandis habenda sit, judicent iterum omnes.
units.tr: III. That one must not give offence to another, in the case of those who, induced by the authority of a brother whom they saw doing this before them, eat such idol meat without faith, that is, without a firm persuasion that it is lawful for them, but only by the authority of a brother. Whatever is done without faith is sin. Let all judge again whether this so profound consideration of the matter, and so severe a prohibition of it, as Paul hands down, should be regarded as an enlargement of the precept about not worshipping graven images.

units.la: quacunque re, non primus, vel solus Paulus docet; sed hæc est lex & Prophetæ, Matth. vii. 12. quæcunque vultis ut vobis faciant homines sic & vos facite illis. Quod etiam est, uti te offendi nolis, ita neque offendere alium. Die mihi, ubi hoc quod Christus dicit summarium esse legis, & Prophetarum, legitur in toto V. Test. vel ita stricte &
units.tr: Paul is not the first or only one to teach this matter in any respect; but this is "the law and the Prophets," Matt. 7:12: "Whatever you want men to do to you, do so to them." This also means: just as you do not wish to be offended, so do not offend another. Tell me, where is what Christ says, that this is the summary of the law and the Prophets, found in the whole Old Testament, either so strictly or so explicitly set forth?

units.la: explicite proponitur? nullum tamen dubium potest esse, quin eo contineatur, quin contineatur regula hæc, diliges proximum, sicut te ipsum. Quemadmodum vero hoc illo contineri, autoritate Christi, & rei ipsius evidentia discimus; ita pari ratione regulis illis, quas diximus, comprehenditur, ne quempiam offendas, præsertim unde salutis jactura sequi queat. Æque, ut ad præceptum recurram, quod præceptum cavendam docet idololatriam, docet quoque fugiendam. iv. Fatetur Smalcius, ex eo quod de idololatria, eaque cavenda, in V. Test. dictum, colligi posse, non licere etiam in locis illis conversari, ubi ea coluntur. atqui hoc totum est, quod quæritur, ex V. nempe Test. colligi illa posse, ut non demum ex Novo constent, vel hujus sint habenda nova ad legem, ex Euangelio, additamenta. Sed non ita præcise, non ita stricte, nec ob eam causam, prohibitum illud olim fuit; ac nunc. Verum hoc non versatur in quæstione, an vel modus proponendi urgendique legem alius aliquando sit, & varius, vel aliæ & plures causæ de virtutibus aut vitiis differendi: sed de re est quæstio, & novo præcepto, veterisque legis perfectione, augmento vel additamento. Hoc vero non probatur ex stricta, aut expressa, vel præcisa ratione proponendi: quinimo contrarium: nam si modus duntaxat proponendi præceptum alius fuit, ergo non ipsum. Quæ absurditas, Paulus ob aliam causam interdictum aliquod urget, quam Moses, ergo prorsus est novum? Quod si & aliam causam alius post Paulum adferat, iterum novum evadet, & præceptum aliud? Nam sane ejusdem rei aut commendandæ aut dehortandæ, variæ pro re nata adferri rationes possunt, & diversi proponendi modi: an toties inde nova nascentur edicta vel interdicta? Ergo quamdiu non probaverint, nil rei istius, sive quod concernit vitationem vel fugam idolorum, in V. lege præceptum dictumve fuisse, nihil effecerint. Nam de re est disputatio. Aut si de modo loquendi velint vitilitigare, obscuriore & generaliore, vel expressiore & clariore, mutetur quæstio, & quæratur, an alius loquendi modus, & doctrinæ modus alius, non ipsa, sub V. T. fuerit, ac sub Novo? Sed quo tum delapsuri sint, viderint: non certe rem obtenturi, de novis à lege præceptis Euangelii. Nam illa loquendi, & argumentandi per varias causas diversa & stricior vel expressior ratio etiam apud singulos Scriptores, non in oppositione tantum utriusque Testamenti, sed divisim in hujus atque illius T. Scripturis, proclive est observare. Idque ubi semel admittetur, quod profundior rei consideratio, aut magis severa interdictio facit novam legem, aut legis, quemadmodum dum Smalcius loquitur, auctionem, quot non novas leges hinc faciemus? certe plures quam adhuc Sociniani Decalogo adfinxerunt, praeter quas quoti-die etiam plures integrum erit fabricare. v. Quod si de scandalo cavendo illud ultra urgeant, quid, annon idem prohibitum quoque fuit sub V. Testamento? annon exserte interdictum, offendiculum ponere cæco? Levit. xix. 14. & reprehensi, qui scandalum dedissent extraneis? 11 Sam. xii. 14. nedum fratri-bus. Denique extra dubium, quod hoc comprehenditur mandato, de dilectione proximi. Vel si illud de scandalo augmentum legis sit, non ad secundum præ-ceptum referri debet, sed ad sequentem tabulam. vii. Proferunt jam Adversarii loca & præcepta ex Paulo; at ex Evangelio, & à Christo dicta pro-ferre deberent, si convenienter loqui vellent & agere suis hypothesibus. Præ-fertim quoniam alios reprehendere solent, qui in doctrina V. Test. plenitudi-nem legis ostendunt ex aliis, præterquam ex libris Mosis. Neque disputamus de Veteri lege, per Apostolos, sed per Christum consummata.
units.tr: Yet there can be no doubt that it is contained in it, that this rule, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself," contains it. Just as we learn by the authority of Christ and the plain evidence of the thing itself that this is contained in that, so by the same reasoning it is comprehended under those rules which we have mentioned: that you should not cause any man to stumble, especially where loss of salvation may follow. Likewise, to come back to the precept, the precept which teaches that idolatry is to be avoided also teaches that it is to be fled from. iv. Smalcius concedes that from what is said in the Old Testament about idolatry, and that it is to be avoided, it can be inferred that it is not lawful to live in those places where they are worshipped. But this whole thing is what is in question: that these things can be inferred from the Old Testament, so that they do not finally rest on the New, or are to be regarded as new additions to the law from the Gospel. But that this was forbidden formerly not so precisely, not so strictly, nor for this reason, as it is now, is not the point. For this does not turn on the question whether the manner of setting forth and urging the law has at some time been different and varied, or whether there are other and more reasons for discussing virtues or vices. The question concerns the thing itself, and a new precept, and the perfecting, augmentation or addition of the old law. And this is not proved from a strict or express or precise way of setting it forth; on the contrary, the opposite follows. For if the manner of setting forth the precept alone was different, then it is not the precept itself. Is it not absurd that Paul urges some prohibition for another reason than Moses did, and therefore it is wholly new? And if someone after Paul gives yet another reason, will it again become new, and a different precept? For surely various reasons may be given, as occasion requires, for commending or dissuading the same thing, and various modes of setting it forth. Will new edicts or prohibitions be born from this so often? Therefore, as long as they have not proved that nothing concerning the avoiding or fleeing of idols, or what concerns that, was commanded or stated in the law of the Old Testament, they have accomplished nothing. For the dispute is about the matter. Or if they wish to quibble about the mode of speaking, whether more obscure and general, or more express and clear, let the question be changed, and let it be asked whether the mode of speaking and of teaching was different under the Old Testament and under the New, not the thing itself. But where they will fall with that, let them see. They will certainly not gain their point, namely new precepts of the Gospel beyond the law. For it is easy to observe that this way of speaking and reasoning, varying and stricter or more express, is found among individual writers, not only in opposition between the two Testaments but separately within the Scriptures of each. And once this is admitted, that a deeper consideration of the matter, or a more severe prohibition, makes a new law, or an enlargement of the law, as Smalcius puts it, how many new laws shall we not make from this? Certainly more than the Socinians have yet attached to the Decalogue, and it will be open to fabricate more of them every day. v. But if they press this further, concerning the avoiding of scandal, what then? Was not the same thing forbidden under the Old Testament as well? Was it not expressly prohibited to put a stumbling block before the blind, Lev. 19:14, and were not those rebuked who gave scandal to strangers, 2 Sam. 12:14, much less to brethren? Finally, beyond doubt this is included in the command about love of neighbour. Or if that about scandal is an augmentation of the law, it ought not to be referred to the second precept but to the following table. vii. The Adversaries now produce passages and precepts from Paul; but if they wished to speak and act consistently with their hypotheses, they ought to produce what was said by Christ and in the Gospel. Especially since they are accustomed to rebuke others who show the fullness of the law in the doctrine of the Old Testament from other sources than the books of Moses. Nor are we disputing about the Old law as consummated through the Apostles, but through Christ.

units.la: Arg. fecundum. In V. Lege plura & graviora extiterunt interdicta idololatriæ, quam quidem in Test. Novo: tamque abunde populo in idololatriam propensio provisum legibus omnem omnino cum idolis atque idololatria communionem prohibentibus fuit, ac in Novo: quare præceptum de fugiendâ Idololatriâ non est novum, & Veteri legi per Apostolos additum, sed ea satis clare & præcise comprehensum, quidquid ad hanc spectare materiam potest. Ut mittam secundum Decalogi præceptum, ex quo modo fuimus argumentati. Ubi jussus severe populus, idola omnia, eorum loca & lucos, memoriam & nomina delere ac detestari, ibi certe interdicta illis omnis cum idololatria communio fuit, & evidenter satis jussi fuerunt fugere omnem, & quovis eam modo devitare: Atqui illud fuerunt jussi sub V. Test. ex lege: ergo. Deut. vii. 25. 26. Sculptiles Deos earum comburite igne: ne concupiscas argentum vel aurum eorum, aut accipias tibi, aut illaqueris eo, nam abominationi est Iehova Deo tuo. Ut ne inferas rem abominabilem in domum tuam sis anathema, sicut ea, omnino detestator eam, & prorsus abominator eam, quia anathema est. Cap. xii. 2. 3. Omnino perdite omnia illa loca, ubi gentes, quas hæreditario jure possessuri estis, coluerunt Deos suos, in singulis montibus excelsis, & in singulis collibus, & sub quaque arbore virente. Diruetis igitur altaria earum, & confringetis statuas earum, & lucos earum comburetis igne, ac sculptiles Deos illarum succidetis: sic perdetis nomen eorum e loco illo. Exod. xxiii. 13. nomen autem Deorum alienorum ne recordamini, ne auditor in ore tuo. Psalm. xvi. 4. non sum libaturus libamina istorum ex sanguine, neque assumturus nomina eorum in labiis meis. Hos. 11. 17. amovebo enim nomina Baalim ab ore ejus, ut non commemorentur amplius nomine suo. De Hiskia, 11 Reg. xviii. 4. ipse amovit excelsa, fregitque statuas, & excidit lucum: contudit etiam serpentem æneum, quem fecerat Moses, eo quod usque ad dies illos Israelitæ adolerent ei, quem vocavit Nechustan. Ex illis quis non videt, propositum in lege Veteri fuisse, mandatumque, ut idola fugerent prorsus & idololatriam, næ is nihil videt. Quæ abominari tenebantur, detestari, diruere, perdere, cum omnibus locis, monumentis, nominibus, totaque eorum memoriâ, an nesciebant fugienda esse? ita ineptos, barbarosque putare Patres illos, quasi dictum sibi ignorassent, ut se custodirent ab idolis, vel idola fugerent? Quod totum est, quod ex Paulo & Johanne Adversarii proferunt, & in quo opinantur, legem veterem fuisse adauctam. Quando contra nos disputant ad Matth. v. ut probent, Christum suam doctrinam legi Mosaicae opponere, non falsae expositioni Pharisaeorum, dicunt, ea quae Christus rejicit, in lege Mosis occurrere vel διαφωνίαν [?], vel saltem quod ad sensum. Quod si ipsis, ut probent, aliqua apud Mosem occurrere, quae revera in lege non continentur, satis videtur, sensum illorum ibi vidisse, in omnibus ipsis praeceptis, quibus Christus sua opposuit, nihil continetur, quod antea in lege Mosaica, vel verbis ipsis, vel sententia non fuerit comprehensum, inquit Volkelius, lib. v. cap. xxiii. an aliquis reperiri poterit, qui sententiam, ne verba dicam, fugiendae penitus idololatriae, locis illis quae in V. Test. indicavimus, quibus & alia addi possunt, non perspexerit? Uti bene alibi Volkelius, lib. iv. cap xvii. pag. 267. neque enim protinus a prohibitorum numero excludenda ea sunt, quae expressis litteris non vetantur: cum satis sit, hoc implicita quadam ratione fieri. Socinus, in Disp. de Adorat. Christi, adverf. Franciscum Davidis, pag. 57. dixi, ad probandum in Sacra Scriptura legi Christum invocatum fuisse, non necesse esse ipsummet vocabulum invocationis, seu verbum invocandi ibi scriptum extare, dummodo ex aequipollentibus verbis eadem sententia eliceretur. Quanto facilius nobis, ex supra allegatis testimoniis evincere, fugiendam idololatriam esse? Et ejusdem libri, seu Fragmenti, pag. 60. Socinus: Quare sic statuendum censeo. Quidquid aut rationibus, aut consequutionibus adeo aperte probatur, ut mens humana necessario acquiescat, id sive deserte scriptum extet, sive minus, credendum & retinendum omnino esse.
units.tr: Second argument. The Old Law contained more and weightier prohibitions of idolatry than the New Testament does. There was such a ready tendency among the people towards idolatry that the laws forbade every communion whatsoever with idols and idolatry, and so amply that nothing more is needed in the New. Therefore the precept about fleeing idolatry is not new, added to the Old Law by the Apostles, but was already stated clearly and precisely enough to cover everything that can bear on this matter. To pass over the second precept of the Decalogue, from which we argued earlier: where the people were strictly commanded to destroy and abhor all idols, their places and groves, their memory and names, there they were certainly forbidden every communion with idolatry, and were plainly enough ordered to flee from it and avoid it in every way. But they were so ordered under the Old Covenant by the law. Deut. 7:25–26: The graven images of their gods shall ye burn with fire: thou shalt not desire the silver or gold that is on them, nor take it unto thee, lest thou be snared therein: for it is an abomination to the LORD thy God. Neither shalt thou bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cast-away like it: thou shalt utterly detest it, and thou shalt utterly abhor it; for it is a cast-away. Ch. 12:2–3: Ye shall utterly destroy all the places wherein the nations which ye shall possess served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree: and ye shall overthrow their altars, and break their images, and burn their groves with fire; and ye shall hew down the graven images of their gods, and destroy the names of them out of that place. Exod. 23:13: And make no mention of the name of other gods, neither let it be heard out of thy mouth. Ps. 16:4: Their drink offerings of blood will I not offer, nor take up their names into my lips. Hos. 11:17: For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name. Concerning Hezekiah, 2 Kings 18:4: He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan. Who does not see from these passages that the Old Law set forth and commanded that idols and idolatry be wholly fled from? Can anyone fail to see it? Were they not bidden to abhor, detest, overthrow and destroy them, together with all their places, monuments and names, and their whole memory? Did they not know that they were to be fled? Must we think those Fathers so foolish and barbarous that they had not understood what was said to them, namely that they should keep themselves from idols or flee them? This is the whole basis on which the Adversaries rely in citing Paul and John, and in thinking that the old law was enlarged. When they dispute against us on Matt. 5, in order to prove that Christ opposed his own teaching to the Mosaic law and not to the false exposition of the Pharisees, they say that the things Christ rejects are found in the law of Moses either as a contradiction [διαφωνίαν] or at least in sense. But even if, to prove their point, they can show that some things are found in Moses which are not really contained in the law, it seems enough to have seen their sense there. Volkelius, book 5, ch. 23: In all those precepts against which Christ set his own, there is nothing contained which was not previously comprehended in the Mosaic law, either in the words themselves or in the sense. Can anyone be found who has not perceived the sense, not to say the words, of fleeing idolatry altogether in the passages from the Old Testament which we have indicated, to which others may be added? As Volkelius rightly says elsewhere, book 4, ch. 17, p. 267: Nor are those things to be excluded at once from the number of prohibited things which are not forbidden in express words, since it is enough that this is done by some implicit reasoning. Socinus, in his disputation on the worship of Christ, against Francis David, p. 57: I said that to prove that Christ was invoked in Holy Scripture, it is not necessary that the very word invocation, or the verb to invoke, be written there, provided the same sense can be drawn from equivalent words. How much more easily, then, can we establish from the testimonies cited above that idolatry is to be fled! And in the same book, or fragment, p. 60, Socinus: Wherefore I judge that it must be decided thus: whatever is so plainly proved by reasons or consequences that the human mind necessarily assents to it, that, whether or not it is expressly written, must wholly be believed and retained.

units.la: De praecepto tertio, vel, quae ejus faciunt Sociniani, additamentis, supra ad Matth. v. diximus: ut inde facilior breviorque nobis hic futura sit disputatio. Contendunt, duo huic praecepto, per Christum addita fuisse. 1. ne leviter aut temere juremus. Quasi hoc licuerit unquam, licuerit sub V. Testamento? II.[?] ut etiam jurare nunc liceat per nomen Christo. Catechef. Racov. pag. 186. qu. LXII. Quid huic praecepto additum, sub novo foedere? Resp. Primo quod non solum Deum, verum etiam Dominum Jesum Christum in testimonium vocare possimus, cum Dominus Iesus corda & renes scrutetur, Apoc. 11. 23. Deinde quod nobis non solum pejerare non liceat; verum etiam ne in veris quidem jurare, nisi longe gravissimis causis adactis, iisque quibus Deigloria nitatur, ad idque non temere, verum cum magno Dei metu & cautione summa accedendum. Istud quoque Smalcius habet, lib. de Divin. Christi, cap. v. pag. 20. & contra Frantz. pag. 396. Volckelius, lib. iv. cap. xiii. Sed jam ponderemus, quae huic praecepto Christus addidit. Ea autem duo potissimum sunt, quorum alterum expressum est, alterum evidentissima ratione adjunctum esse convincitur. Illud est, de cavendis juramentis temerariis. Male passim dicunt, voluntariis: quum non ex voluntate, sed re, ejusque momento temerarium & temeritas, imprimis hoc in argumento, aestimetur. Istud, nos hoc tempore etiam per nomen Christi jurare posse.
units.tr: Concerning the third precept, or the additions which the Socinians make to it, we have spoken above on Matt. 5, so that our discussion here may be easier and shorter. They contend that two things were added to this precept by Christ. 1. That we should not swear lightly or rashly. As if this had ever been allowed, or were allowed under the Old Testament! 2. That now we may even swear by the name of Christ. Racovian Catechism, p. 186, question 62: What was added to this precept under the New Covenant? Answer: First, that we may call to witness not only God but also the Lord Jesus Christ, since the Lord Jesus searches hearts and reins, Rev. 2:23. Next, that we are not only not allowed to forswear ourselves, but not even to swear truly, except when driven by very grave causes, and those on which the glory of God rests; and this is to be done not rashly, but with great fear of God and the utmost caution. Smalcius also has this, in his book on the divinity of Christ, ch. 5, p. 20, and against Frantz, p. 396. Volkelius, book 4, ch. 13. But let us now weigh what Christ added to this precept. There are two things of chief importance: one is expressed, the other is shown to be added by a most evident reasoning. The first concerns avoiding rash oaths. They wrongly say everywhere voluntary oaths, since a rash oath and rashness are judged not by the will but by the matter and its weight, especially in this subject. The second is that we may now swear even by the name of Christ.

units.la: Supra autem ostendimus, falsum esse, quod asserunt, in V. Test temeraria juramenta fuisse licita. Neq; hoc ideo dicunt, quod id probent adeo, vel ostendere annitantur, sed, quod etiam aperte satis fatentur, ut habeant quod Christum addidisse praecepto, & quo correxisse illud, proferre vel jactare queant. Tunc licebat, inquit Smalcius, de V. Test. loquens, Disput. contr. Frantz. pag. 396. quavis de causa jurare, modo quis non pejeraret: nunc vero non tantum pejerare non licet, verum etiam jurare non licet levi de causa, & in quotidiana vita. Quod an falsum magis, an profanum sit afferere, alii judicent. Nos haec opponimus, quae supra latius commonstravimus, ideoque breviter hic per indicem quasi indicasse sufficit.
units.tr: But we have shown above that it is false that they assert that rash oaths were lawful under the Old Testament. They do not say this because they can prove it, or strive to show it, but because, as they also quite openly admit, they have something to bring forward and boast of, namely that Christ added to the precept and corrected it by it. Then it was lawful, says Smalcius, speaking of the Old Testament, Disputation against Frantz, p. 396, to swear for any cause, provided one did not forswear; but now it is not only unlawful to forswear, but it is also unlawful to swear for a slight cause and in everyday life. Whether it is more false or more profane to assert this, let others judge. We set against it what we have shown more fully above, and so it is enough to indicate it briefly here, as in an index.

units.la: 1. Licitum fuisse sub V. Test. quavis & levi de causa jurare, in quotidiana & familiari vita, uti Smalcius ait, probare vel ostendere ullo testimonio, aut ratione Adversarii nequeunt. Et hoc tamen tam libere, tamque audacter affirmant omnes: probare autem satagit nemo. II. Imo lex contrarium dicit, & prohibet non falsa modo juramenta, & perjuria, sed temeraria etiam, & haec quidem primo. Quod ostendimus ex significatione, vi, & usu vocis שָׁוְא [?] in vanum, III. Ex ratione idem, & scopo praecepti, qui est, prohibere profanationem nominis divini: in quod praecipue incurritur, temeraria ejus usurpatione. IV. Idemque ostenditur rationibus iis, quas Socociniani dant, cur non liceat temere jurare, quae tales sunt, ut non in ratione peculiari Novi Test. fundatae sint, sed jure perpetuo, & olim aeque certae, & valuerint, ac hodie: quare & illicita & prohibita ejusmodi juramenta fuisse semper & omni aevo, neque nunc demum, sub N. Testamento, quasi singulari & novo praecepto, sequitur. Quaeque ex Socino, Smalcio, Volkelio supra attulimus, iis nunc addimus Catechef. Racoviensem, pag. 188. Qu. Cur vero Dominus Jesus etiam in verù ultro ac leviter jurare vetat? Resp. Ut nomen Dei altissimi, & ipsius Domini Jesu apud nos sit in summa veneratione: deinde ne levitate jurandi pejerare consuescamus. Annon videndum etiam olim fuit, ne mala vel levi consuetudine in perjuria homines inciderent? annon & tum curari debuit, ut nomen Dei in summa semper esset veneratione?
units.tr: 1. The Adversaries can prove or show by no testimony or reasoning that it was lawful under the Old Testament to swear for any and every slight cause, in everyday and familiar life, as Smalcius says. Yet all of them affirm this so freely and so boldly, while none of them takes the trouble to prove it. II. Indeed the law says the contrary, and forbids not only false oaths and perjuries but also rash ones; and this first from the meaning, force and use of the word שָׁוְא [shav, in vain], which we have shown. III. From the reason and aim of the same precept, which is to forbid the profanation of the divine name, which is chiefly incurred by its rash use. IV. The same is shown by the reasons which the Socinians give why it is not lawful to swear rashly; these are such that they are not founded on any peculiar reason of the New Testament, but on a perpetual law, and were as certain and as valid of old as they are today. It therefore follows that such oaths were illicit and forbidden always and in every age, and not only now under the New Testament as by some singular and new precept. To what we have already quoted from Socinus, Smalcius and Volkelius, we now add the Racovian Catechism, p. 188, question: Why does the Lord Jesus forbid even swearing truly and lightly? Answer: That the name of the Most High God, and that of the Lord Jesus himself, may be held among us in the highest veneration; and then, that by the lightness of swearing we may not become accustomed to perjury. Was it not also necessary in former times to guard against men falling into perjury through an evil, even a light, habit? Was it not also then necessary to take care that the name of God should always be held in the highest veneration?

units.la: Quod ad alterum, de juramento per Christi nomen concipiendo, nihil habent, quod non ad primum praeceptum, ejusque vindicationem, contra fictitium augmentum de cultu Christi, ut Dei, supra discussimus. Neque revera ad hoc praeceptum id potest facere alterum, posito primo illo augmento, de colendo Christum, pro Deo, ad praeceptum primum. Nam id, siquidem ibi pro additione recipiatur, nequit hic iterum facere praeceptum novum, quod modo species illius cultus est, in juratione consistens religiosa. Deinde, quia nos urgent, ut in lege ostendamus expresse & praecise dictum, v. g. fugiendam idololatriam, & similia, quae quia sic in N. Test. occurrunt, hinc praecepta ad veterem legem nova formant; ostendant nunc ipsi, ubi dicatur in N. Test. jurandum per Christi nomen esse. Non quod rem, vel ejus veritatem trahamus in dubium, sed ut ineptam agendi methodum Auctoribus reponamus.
units.tr: As for the other point, about swearing by the name of Christ, they have nothing that we have not already discussed under the first commandment and its defence, against the fictitious addition of worship paid to Christ as God. Indeed, the other point cannot even support this commandment, once that first addition about worshipping Christ as God has been granted under the first commandment. For if that addition is accepted there, it cannot here again make a new commandment, since it is only a form of that worship, consisting in religious swearing. Furthermore, they press us to show in the Law a commandment expressly and precisely stated, for example that idolatry is to be shunned, and similar things, which occur in this way in the New Testament, and from these they form new precepts for the old law. Let them now show where it is said in the New Testament that one must swear by the name of Christ. I do not call the truth of the matter into doubt, but I reproach the Authors for an unsound method of arguing.

units.la: πρὸς Ἀντι[?] Sequitur præceptum Decalogi quartum : super quo nil habent quod dicant, nisi totum cæremoniale, & una cum aliis cæremoniis V. Test. abrogatum prorsus esse, in Novo. Catechesis Racoviensis, pag. 189. ad quæstionem, annon Christus constituerit, ut diem, quem vocamus Dominicum, Sabbati loco observemus? respondet: Nullo modo : cum religio Christi, quemadmodum aliæ cæremonias, uti vocantur, ita deletum dicitur prorsus tollat, uti Col 11. 16. aperte scribit Apostolus. Verum cum diem Dominicum antiquitus celebrari à Christianis videamus, nos eandem libertatem omnibus Christianis permittimus. Smalcius, de Divinit. Christi, pag. 10. Præcepit lex sanctificare diem Sabbati. Hoc præceptum, quia cæremoniale est, D. Iesus non perfecit, sed illud sustulit, ut & alias cæremonias. atque idem pag. 17. Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. xiv. Quartum Decalogi præceptum de Sabbato olim Israelitis traditum erat; esque cæremoniale revera, non morale, ut supra suo loco ostendimus; & porro ad Christi disciplinam nihil quidquam pertinet.
units.tr: Next follows the fourth commandment of the Decalogue. On this they have nothing to say except that the whole ceremonial law was entirely abrogated in the New Testament, together with the other ceremonies of the Old Testament. The Racovian Catechism, p. 189, to the question whether Christ appointed that the day we call the Lord's Day should be observed in place of the Sabbath, answers: By no means: since the religion of Christ does not altogether abolish those so-called ceremonies, which are said to have been removed, as the Apostle plainly writes in Col. 11. 16. Yet since we see that the Lord's Day has been celebrated by Christians from ancient times, we grant this same freedom to all Christians. Smalcius, On the Divinity of Christ, p. 10: The law commanded the sanctification of the Sabbath day. Since this commandment is ceremonial, the Lord Jesus did not fulfil it but abolished it, as he did the other ceremonies. And likewise Volkelius, p. 17, book 4, chapter 14: The fourth commandment of the Decalogue concerning the Sabbath was once given to the Israelites; and it is in truth ceremonial, not moral, as we showed above in its place; and further, it has nothing whatever to do with the discipline of Christ.

units.la: Adeo de duobus hic potissimum disputandum. 1. de observatione Sabbati veteris, olim sub V Test. servati; an tota fuerit mere cæremonialis? ii. de observatione diei Dominicæ, sub N. Test.; an in nullo Dei præcepto fundata, vel Christi, aut Apostolorum authoritate sit, sed tota libera, & sola se defendat Christianorum antiqua consuetudine? Utrumque negamus. Et primum quidem. his argumentis.
units.tr: So there are two points here that must chiefly be disputed: first, concerning the observance of the old Sabbath, once kept under the Old Testament, was it wholly and purely ceremonial? Second, concerning the observance of the Lord's Day under the New Testament: is it founded on no command of God or of Christ or of the Apostles, but is wholly free and defended only by the ancient custom of Christians? We deny both. And first, the former, by these arguments.

units.la: Primo. Quia institutum & observatum Sabbatum fuit ante usum & institutionem cæremoniarum: scilicet à mundi creatione. Genes. 11. 3. Quod & Chrysostomus agnoscit in illum locum, docuisse Deum τὴν μίαν ἡμέραν ἐν τῷ κύκλῳ τῆς ἑβδομάδος ἀπασῶν[?] ἀναλῦσαι καὶ ἀφορίζειν τῇ τῶν πνευματικῶν ἐργασίᾳ, unam integram diem in cyclo septimana consecrare & separare spiritualium operationi.
