units.tr: First. Because the Sabbath was instituted and observed before the use and institution of ceremonies, namely from the creation of the world (Gen. 2. 3). Chrysostom also acknowledges this on that passage, teaching that God τὴν μίαν ἡμέραν ἐν τῷ κύκλῳ τῆς ἑβδομάδος ἀπάσης ἀναλῦσαι καὶ ἀφορίζειν τῇ τῶν πνευματικῶν ἐργασίᾳ [one whole day in the cycle of the week to be set apart and consecrated to spiritual work].

units.la: Secundo, quia præceptum hoc insertum est Decalogo, seu tabulis legis moralis: in quibus uti non fuerunt tradita cæremonialia, quæ sequuntur à cap: xxi. Exodi, sed moralia; sequitur, hoc præceptum illis homogeneum quoque esse morale. Etenim hoc præcepta ista ab aliis distinguuntur, quod inscripta fuerunt tabulis lapideis. Deut. iv. 13. & ipsum vobis indicasse fœdus suum, quo præcipiebat vos observare decem illa verba; & inscripsisse ea duabus tabulis lapideis. Tabulis lapideis inscripsit Deus legem moralem: & hujus quidem capita seu verba decem, non novem. Totidem enim modo forent nobis præcepta, si quartum totum esset cæremoniale, vel inter cæremonialia referendum, non inter moralia Deut. x. 4. Inscripsitque tabulis illis secundum scripturam priorem, eadem decem verba. Cæremonialia & politica, & leges adeo omnes eò quidem possunt referri, tamquam ad materiam æqui omnis & recti, sed non eâ formaliter continentur, reductive tantum ad eam spectant & possunt explicari. Quodque Jacobus, cap. ii. 10. dixit, qui totam legem servet, cadat autem in uno, omnium reus est. Qui enim dixit, non adulterabis, &c. de præceptis Decalogi moralibus intelligendum, ubi qui unum transgreditur, omnium fit reus. Quod obtinere nequit, nisi omnium eadem sit ratio in genere moralitatis, & conjuncta sint pariter vinculo necessariæ observationis. De iisdemque præceptis Christus lo-quutus fuit, quando dixit, non veni legem solvere. Matth. v. 17. Tertio. Nihil est in præcepto quarto, quod ad Christum proprie & per se respiciat, qui tamen corpus fuit cæremoniarum, tanquam umbrarum. Col. 11. 16. Quarto. Ipsum præceptum discutiatur, non cæremonialia, sed moralia sunt, sex dierum operatio, tum requies, & ejus sanctificatio, additumque exemplum quiescentis Dei, ab opere creationis suo. Uti a primo inde creationis tempore distributi dies fuerunt in septimanas, ita æquior, sanctior, melior non potest excogitari temporis, vel dierum distributio, quam in sex dies laboris, & quietis sacræ septimum, ad exemplum laborantis totidem, & quiescentis uno die, Dei. Potuisset quidem Deus post sex laboris dies primum reducere, & non interse-rere septimum, indeque fecisse dierum seximanam, non septimanam, nisi voluisset unum in singulis dierum periodis haberi ἑβδομάδα[?], & post sex laboribus, atque nostris necessitatibus impensos, ultimum sibi, reddi ac esse sacrum. Sapienter autem ita constituit, & ordinavit cum tempus, tum res nostras legi-slator Deus, neque ullus dicere audebit non esse distributionem istam dierum æquissimam & sapientissimam. Unde apud omnes & antiquissimas gentes non tantum dierum in septimanas mansit divisio, sed & diei alicujus in sanctiorem usum sequestratio. Quamvis id pro communi corruptione minus fuerit observatum. Atque illud est quarti in Decalogi præcepti argumentum, dierum nostrorum in communes, & sacrum divisio. Quod tum abrogabitur, ubi aliquis, qui melius ista ordinabit, insurrexerit; & morem tot seculis confirmatum correxerit meliori. Nam vel hæc ipsa duratio æternæ legis, in quâ ille fundatus est, debet esse argumentum. Et ante promulgatum Decalogum, non tantum historia Exod. xvi. manifeste ostendit, sabbatum observatum fuisse, sed præceptorum omnium idem arguit materia, & forma, quâ fuerunt proposita, servata antea fuisse. Nullum præceptorum ita est conceptum, quasi rem aliquam novam ediceret; sed uti de rebus notis, & vel cavendis, vel præstandis, renovant tantum & explicant Dei voluntatem. Sed etiam de Sabbato agitur non uti de re jam demum nata aut orta, sed quæ nota satis, & uti reliqua præceptis suis, confirmata fuit quarto. Et propterea hic singulariter dictum, memento. Duo præcepta, aliis sunt prolixiora, secundum & quartum, adversus quæ maxime homines fremituros prospiciebat Deus. Item duo ex omnibus sunt affirmativa, quaertum vid. & quintum, negativa reliqua. Nec necesse, nec fas est ullum præceptorum tradere hominum pervicaciæ, vel secundum Papistis, vel quartum Socinianis: facile enim & alii aliud exciperent, & mutarent, vel expungerent.
units.tr: Second, because this commandment is inserted in the Decalogue, that is, in the tables of the moral law. In these tables the ceremonial laws, which follow from chapter 21 of Exodus, were not handed down, but moral ones. It follows that this commandment, being of the same kind as the others, is also moral. For these precepts are distinguished from the others in this way, that they were written on stone tablets: Deut. 4. 13: And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to keep, the ten words, and wrote them on two tables of stone. God wrote the moral law on stone tables, and the heads or words of it are ten, not nine. For there would be only nine commandments if the fourth were wholly ceremonial, or to be reckoned among the ceremonial laws and not the moral ones. Deut. 10. 4: And he wrote on those tables, according to the former writing, the same ten words. Ceremonial and civil laws can all indeed be referred to the matter of all equity and righteousness, but they are not formally contained in it; they only relate to it by reduction and can be explained by it. And what James says in chapter 2, verse 10, whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point is guilty of all, must be understood of the moral precepts of the Decalogue, where whoever transgresses one becomes guilty of all. This could not hold unless all have the same reason in the kind of morality and are equally bound by the chain of necessary observance. And Christ spoke of these same precepts when he said, I have not come to destroy the law (Matt. 5. 17). Third, there is nothing in the fourth commandment that properly and in itself relates to Christ, who is nevertheless the body of the ceremonies, as the shadows (Col. 2. 16). Fourth, consider the commandment itself: it is not ceremonial but moral: the working of six days, then rest, and its sanctification, with the added example of God resting from his work of creation. Since from the first time of creation the days have been distributed into weeks, no fairer, holier, or better division of time or of days can be devised than six days of labour and the seventh of sacred rest, following the example of God, who laboured for as many days and rested on one. God could indeed, after six days of labour, have begun again at the first and not inserted a seventh, and so have made a six-day week rather than a seven-day one, unless he willed that one day in each period of days should be a week, and that the last, after six days spent on labours and on our necessities, should be reserved for himself and made holy. But the Lawgiver God wisely ordained both the time and our affairs in this way, and no one will dare to say that this division of days is not most equitable and most wise. Hence among all the most ancient nations there remained not only the division of days into weeks but also the setting apart of one day for a holier use. Although this was less observed because of common corruption. And this is the argument of the fourth commandment: the division of our days into common days and a holy day. This would then be abrogated only when someone arose who would order these things better and corrected the custom confirmed by so many centuries by a better one. For even this long duration of the eternal law, on which it is founded, ought to be an argument. And before the Decalogue was promulgated, the history in Exodus 16 not only plainly shows that the Sabbath was observed, but the matter and form in which all the precepts were proposed indicate that they had been kept before. None of the precepts is so framed as if it were announcing some new thing; but, as concerning things already known and either to be avoided or to be performed, they only renew and explain the will of God. But the Sabbath is also spoken of here not as a thing newly born or arisen, but as one sufficiently known, and, like its other precepts, confirmed by the fourth. And for that reason it is said here with particular emphasis, remember. Two precepts are longer than the others, the second and the fourth, against which God foresaw that men would especially rage. Likewise two of all are affirmative, the fourth and the fifth, the rest negative. Nor is it necessary or lawful to hand over any of the precepts to the obstinacy of men, whether the second to the Papists or the fourth to the Socinians: for others would easily take exception to them in different ways, and change them or strike them out.

units.la: Exceptio. Cæremoniale est, designatio & determinatio illorum, ad certum aliquem diem, nim. septimum. Resp. Non magis temporis ista determinatio præceptum facit totum cæremoniale, ac designatio vel loci, in præcepto quinto istud reddit cæremoniale; vel, quod in omnium exordio est, populi, cui traditæ hæ fuerunt leges, eas reddit cæremoniales aut politicas.
units.tr: Objection. The ceremonial is the designation and determination of these for a certain day, namely the seventh. Answer. The determination of a time does no more make the whole precept ceremonial than the designation of a place makes the fifth precept ceremonial; or, which is at the very beginning, the people to whom these laws were given makes them ceremonial or political.

units.la: Dicunt Socinian, ideo praeceptum istud, quamvis caeremoniale, insertum Decalogo, ut argumentum esset cessaturae legis, meliori & perfectiori legi alteri Iesu Christi. Sic Catechesis, ad quaest. cur vero Decalogo insertum est praeceptum hoc? Resp.
units.tr: The Socinians say that this precept, though ceremonial, was inserted into the Decalogue so that it would serve as a sign that the law was to cease and give way to a better and more perfect law, namely that of Jesus Christ. So the Catechism, in answer to the question, why then was this precept inserted into the Decalogue?, says:

units.la: Ideo, ut absolutissimam legis Mosaicae partem non fuisse patefactam appareret, & quoddam indicium extaret ejus rei, legem successu-ram lege Mosaica longe perfectiorem, legem nempe Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Volkelius: Quod tamen ea de causa in moralium praeceptorum numerum adscriptum esse videtur, quod Sabbathi observatio symbolum erat ac tessera quaedam foederis inter Deum & Israelitas, quos à labore atque ergastulo servitutis Aegyptiacae ad quietem terrenam perduxerat, ut ex Sac. literis constat. Quanquam & ea potest subesse ratio, quod Deus pro summa sua sapientia, etiam Decalogum omni imperfectione nequaquam carere, subindicare voluerit; futurumque tempus illud, cum illi multa adderentur: ut quidem à Christo factum esse, partim jam videmus, partim plenius adhuc intelligemus.
units.tr: So that it might appear that the most complete part of the Mosaic law had not yet been revealed, and so that there might be some indication of this fact, that a law far more perfect than the Mosaic law would succeed it, namely the law of our Lord Jesus Christ. Volkelius: Yet it seems to have been listed among the moral precepts for this reason, that the observance of the Sabbath was a symbol and a certain token of the covenant between God and the Israelites, whom he had led from the labour and bondage of Egyptian slavery to earthly rest, as is clear from the Sacred Writings. Although there may also be this reason, that God, in his great wisdom, wished to signal that the Decalogue was by no means free of all imperfection, and that a time would come when many things would be added to it; which we now partly see has been done by Christ, and will understand more fully still.

units.la: Resp. I. Non sola Sabbati, sed omnium in Decalogo praeceptorum observatio erat symbolum & tessera foederis inter Deum, & Israelitas, à Deo miraculose ex Aegypto liberatos. Quod apparet ex ipso Decalogi proœmio. Ut si argumentum illud valeat, non unum, sed omnia praecepta erunt caeremonialia. Et fac in Decalogi exordio formulam illam de eductione populi insertam non fuisse, res tamen manet, quod & haec, & alia praecepta, eorumque omnium observatio confirmarunt foedus illud Deum inter & populum. Non tamen quod omnia inde fuerint mere caeremonialia. II. Proba Decalogum laborasse sua imperfectio-ne. Quippe si hic imperfectus fuit, quaenam ergo illa lex, cujus perfectionem praedicat David, Psalm. xix? & cui nihil, perfectionis ratione, addi vel tum debuit, vel à Christo etiam additum fuit. Matth. xxii. 37? III. Nugae, hoc pacto significatum esse, legem aliquando à Christo perficiendam fuisse. Eo minus, quo nihil hoc in praecepto à Christo mutatum, eive additum proferre possunt, uti in aliis. Quare correctionis ejusmodi nota potius in aliis praeceptis omnibus extare debuisset, quod tamen in nullis apparet, uti nec in illo. Denique si caeremoniale praeceptum argumentum est mutandae aliquando legis & doctrinae: ergo etiam doctrina Christi non caret omni imperfectione, in quâ praeceptum de S.Coenâ, pro caeremoniali habent Adversarii; illa ergone etiam ulterius mutanda erit atque reformanda?
units.tr: Answer, first: it was not the observance of the Sabbath alone, but the observance of all the precepts in the Decalogue, that was the symbol and token of the covenant between God and the Israelites, whom God had miraculously freed from Egypt. This is clear from the preface of the Decalogue itself. If that argument held, then not one precept but all of them would be ceremonial. Even if the formula about the bringing out of the people had not been inserted at the beginning of the Decalogue, the fact remains that both this precept and the others, and the observance of all of them, confirmed that covenant between God and the people; yet it does not follow that they were all merely ceremonial. Second: prove that the Decalogue suffered from its own imperfection. For if it was imperfect, what then is that law whose perfection David praises, Psalm 19? And to which, as far as perfection goes, nothing ought to have been added at that time, and nothing was in fact added by Christ, Matthew 22:37? Third: it is mere trifling to say that this signified that the law was at some point to be perfected by Christ. All the more so because they cannot point to anything in this precept that Christ changed or added, as they can in other cases. So if a ceremonial precept is a sign that the law and doctrine are to be changed at some point, then a mark of such correction ought rather to appear in all the other precepts, which in fact appears in none of them, not even in this one. Finally, if a ceremonial precept is a sign that the doctrine must be changed, then the doctrine of Christ too is not free from all imperfection. The adversaries count the precept about the Supper as ceremonial; will that doctrine too, then, have to be changed and reformed further?

units.la: Quare quum praeceptum de Sabbato non fit caeremoniale, sed morale, perpetui juris est, & manet, & secundùm substantiam sui, semper est observandum. Videndum verò nunc, an ejus vi & obligatione? tum quâ, an divinâ, seu Christi, seu Apostolorum institutione aut autoritate, dum Dominicum observamus? an verò plane liberum hoc sit, atque à solâ pendeat hominum consuetudine? Nos illud probamus, hoc modo:
units.tr: Therefore, since the precept about the Sabbath is not ceremonial but moral, it is of perpetual right and remains, and in its substance must always be observed. We must now consider whether, by its force and obligation, and by what authority, whether divine, that is by the institution or authority of Christ or of the Apostles, we observe the Lord's day; or whether this is entirely free and depends only on human custom. We prove it as follows:

units.la: Primò, Quia lex Decalogi manet sub N. Test. & tum à Christo, tum ab Apostolis retinetur, docetur, & ab Ecclesiâ Christianâ religiosè servatur: ergo & praeceptum ejus illud quartum. Matth. v. 17. & vii. 12. & xxii. 37. Rom. xiii. 8. 9. Gal. v. 14. Jac. ii. 8. Deinde, Dies Dominicus, sive primus hebdomadæ religiosè habitus fuit à Christo, & Apostolis. Cur enim Dominicus dicatur hic magis, quàm quivis alius? Apoc. i. 10. nisi quâ ratione Cœna Dominica dicitur Apostolo. 1 Cor. xi. 20. neque omnis Cœna est Dominica, ut nec dies. Hunc diem à Christo, in sui, post mortem & resurrectionem, patefactionibus observatum, cur tam insignite historia meminisset? Joann. xx. 19. 26. quod factum itidem ab Apostolis. Act. xx. 7. 1 Cor. xvi. 2. qui amabant Ecclesiis tradere, quod à Christo acceperant. 1 Cor. xi. 23. observaruntque diem illum, sacris solemnibus destinatum: ita enim de eo loquuntur, ut cujus usus jam obtinerer. Et non minus Christus hac in re in domo Dei ordinandâ fidelis fuisse credendus est, ac Moses fuit in aliis, quæ priscam domum concernebant. Hebr. iii. 2. 6. præsertim quum ille non modo filius, ipse servus esset, sed quoque Dominus Sabbati Christus, quod de seipso testatur, Marc. xii. 8. Tertio, Jus & æquitas postulat, ut certum aliquod tempus cultui divino destinatum sit & vacet: quod uti fundamentum est quarti præcepti, in naturali æquitate fundatum, ita perpetui juris est, atque ratio observandæ Dominicæ. Denique, Ecclesia Christiana, jam inde ab Apostolis, diem Dominicum observavit sacrum, non à se institutum, non indifferentem, aut merâ liberâve consuetudine talem, sed profluentem ab Apostolis: uti testantur Ignatius, Justinus, Athanasius, Eusebius, Hilarius, Augustinus, alii, quos adducimus, lib. de sanctificatione dici Dominica.
units.tr: First, because the law of the Decalogue remains under the New Testament, and is retained, taught and religiously observed by Christ and by the Apostles and by the Christian Church; therefore so is its fourth precept. Matthew 5:17; 7:12; 22:37; Romans 13:8–9; Galatians 5:14; James 2:8. Next, the Lord's day, that is the first day of the week, was religiously kept by Christ and the Apostles. For why is this day called the Lord's more than any other? Revelation 1:10. Just as the Lord's Supper is so called by the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 11:20, and not every supper is the Lord's, so not every day is. Why would the history have recorded so notably that Christ observed this day in his appearances after his death and resurrection? John 20:19, 26. That the Apostles did the same is also clear: Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2. They were eager to hand on to the churches what they had received from Christ, 1 Corinthians 11:23, and they observed that day, set apart for the holy solemnities; for they speak of it as a custom already in use. And Christ must be believed to have been no less faithful in this matter, in ordering the house of God, than Moses was in other matters concerning the former house, Hebrews 3:2, 6, especially since he was not only the Son but also the Lord of the Sabbath, as he himself testifies, Mark 2:28. Third, justice and equity require that a certain time be set aside and kept free for divine worship. This is the foundation of the fourth precept, grounded in natural equity, and so it is of perpetual right and is the reason for observing the Lord's day. Finally, the Christian Church, from the time of the Apostles on, has kept the Lord's day as holy, not instituted by itself, not as a thing indifferent or a merely free custom, but flowing from the Apostles, as Ignatius, Justin, Athanasius, Eusebius, Hilary, Augustine and others testify, whom we cite in the book on the sanctification of the Lord's day.

units.la: Objiciunt Adversarii, nullum hac de re Dei mandatum extare. Volkelius: sunt qui Dominum diem, Deo sic ordinante, in Sabbati locum successisse asserant. Verum eos falli, ex eo intelligetur quod nullum hac de re Dei mandatum extet. Resp. Aliud est mandatum explicitum, in terminis & mandandi expressâ forma prolatum; aliud implicitum, ipsâ praxi significatum, confirmatumque: quale hoc est de die Dominico. Nam ipse Volkelius mox ejus celebrationem ab Apostolis repetit, hic verbis: Interim ejus celebrationem, in antiquissimo more positam esse minime diffitemur. Nam etiam Apostolorum ætate eum agitatum in Christi Ecclesia fuisse, certius quibusdam conjecturis assequimur: cùm non solùm primo post Sabbatum die, qui à Johanne dies Dominicus dici videtur, fideles convenisse, scriptum legamus; sed etiam nullum post Apostolos tempus nominari posset, quo idem dies agi caperit. atque annotat in margine, loca, Act. xx. 7. conf. 1 Cor. xvi. 2. Apoc. i. 10. & lib. vi. cap. x. Quod idem & de die Dominico potius, quàm Sabbato celebrando, censemus: quippe cùm Dominicus dies, jam Apostolorum ætate, ad divini cultus exercitia delectus ea fortassis de causa fuerit, ut perpetua Christi resurrectionis, quà eodem die facta est, memoria extaret, quam ob causam & dies Dominicus appellatus videtur.
units.tr: The adversaries object that there is no command of God on this matter. Volkelius: There are those who assert that the Lord's day, by God's ordinance, succeeded to the place of the Sabbath. But that they are mistaken will be understood from the fact that no command of God on this matter exists. Answer: one thing is an explicit command, stated in express terms and in the form of a command; another is an implicit one, signified and confirmed by practice itself, and this is the kind that holds for the Lord's day. For Volkelius himself soon traces its observance back to the Apostles, in these words: Meanwhile we do not deny that its observance was established by a very ancient custom. For by certain rather certain conjectures we infer that it was observed in Christ's Church even in the age of the Apostles; since we read not only that the faithful gathered on the first day after the Sabbath, which John seems to call the Lord's day, but also that no time after the Apostles could be named at which the same day began to be kept. And in the margin he notes the passages Acts 20:7; compare 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10; and book 6, chapter 10. We judge that the same holds for the observance of the Lord's day rather than the Sabbath. For already in the age of the Apostles the Lord's day was chosen for the exercises of divine worship, perhaps for this reason, that a perpetual memory of Christ's resurrection, which took place on that very day, might remain; and for this reason the day seems to have been called the Lord's day.

units.la: Deinde objiciunt, in Catechesi Racovien si, Col. ii. 16. Ne ergo quis vos judicet in cibo aut in potu, aut in parte festi, aut neomenia, aut Sabbatorum. Resp. Per Sabbata ibi intelligi festa cæremonialia: quia hæc demum fuerunt umbra futuri, & ad Christum referebantur, uti suum corpus; non ita Sabbatum hebdomadale Decalogi, ab initio mundi institutum; aut quatenus simpliciter dicit, post sex laborem dies, unum Deo sanctificandum, & proinde feriandum esse. Unde conjunguntur Sabbata cum noviluniis, cum delectu cibociborum, quae erant τὰ ἀσθενῆ[?] καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα, à quibus per Christum liberati sumus. Gal. iv. 9. Non vero id de discrimine diei magis trahi potest ad diem Dominicum, quam quod de cibo & potu dicitur, in praejudicium panis ac vini in S. Coenâ à Christo institutorum, nobisque ex eo observandorum, & respectu istius tum praecepti, tum usus, vulgari sacratiorum[?]. Id est, illa de diebus, cibisque rejiciuntur, quatenus umbratiles caeremoniae fuerunt N. Testamenti; neque in die sanctitas nobis ponitur, sed in diei usu & cultu sacro illo die agitando. Crellius in istum ad Galatas locum, Nam qui vel Sabbatum, vel alium aliquem diem ita observat, ut existimet, eum non esse caeteris sanctiorem aut religiosiorem, interim tamen eum divino cultui consecret; nihil peccat, nec Apostolo contrarius est. Non enim propter diem res divinas tractat; sed propter res divinas diem observat. Sic à Christianis dominicus dies electus est, in quo divino cultui, aliis laboribus & curis sepositis, vacarent. A Christianis nempe, autoritate Apostolica, & manente praecepti quarti ratione morali ac perpetua, uti sex dies laboremus, septimum vero sanctificemus Deo.
units.tr: Next, they object, in the Racovian Catechism, Colossians 2:16: Let no one therefore judge you in meat or drink, or in respect of a feast, or of the new moon, or of the Sabbaths. Answer: the Sabbaths here are to be understood as ceremonial festivals, because these were a shadow of things to come, and referred to Christ, whose body they were; not the weekly Sabbath of the Decalogue, instituted from the beginning of the world, nor insofar as it simply says that after six days of labour one day is to be sanctified to God and therefore kept as a holiday. Hence the Sabbaths are joined with the new moons and with the distinction of foods, which were "the weak and beggarly elements" [τὰ ἀσθενῆ καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα], from which we have been freed through Christ, Galatians 4:9. But this cannot be drawn from the distinction of days to the Lord's day any more than what is said of meat and drink can be drawn to the prejudice of the bread and wine instituted by Christ in the Supper and to be observed by us, and with respect to that precept and use which are commonly regarded as more sacred. That is, those things about days and foods are rejected insofar as they were shadowy ceremonies of the New Testament; and holiness is placed not in the day itself but in the use of the day and in performing sacred worship on it. Crellius, on that passage in Galatians: For whoever observes the Sabbath or any other day in such a way as to think that it is not holier or more sacred than the others, yet dedicates it to divine worship, sins in nothing and is not contrary to the Apostle. For he does not handle divine things because of the day; rather he observes the day because of divine things. Thus the Lord's day was chosen by Christians, that on it, with other labours and cares set aside, they might be free for divine worship. Chosen by Christians, that is, by apostolic authority, and with the moral and perpetual reason of the fourth precept remaining: that we labour six days, and sanctify the seventh to God.

units.la: Quum Meisnerus, contra quem disputat Jonas Schlichtingius, inter peccata moralia adversus legem retulisset quoque Sabbati, apud Christianos, profanationem, regerit ei Schlichtingius, in Disp. super quaestione unica, Num ad Regnum Dei possidendum necesse sit in nullo peccato Euangelicae doctrinae adverso manere? pag. 3.
units.tr: When Meisner, against whom Jonas Schlichting is disputing, had listed among the moral sins against the law the profanation of the Sabbath among Christians, Schlichting replied to him in his Disputation on the single question, Whether it is necessary to remain in no sin contrary to the Evangelical doctrine in order to possess the Kingdom of God? p. 3.

units.la: Patet, eum putare, praeceptum hoc de observando Sabbato adhuc vigere; quod tamen antiquitatum esse res ipsa docet; cum nemo Christianorum Sabbatum observet. Nam si dicas, Christianos pro Sabbato sequentem observare diem. Ego vicissim dico, hinc patere, praeceptum hoc abrogatum esse. quomodo enim pro Sabbato alium observare diem liceret? Num, vigente isto praecepto licuisset Judaeis die Sabbati operari, dummodo alio aliquo die pro Sabbato feriarentur? Deinde quis Christianorum die Dominico ab omni prorsus opere abstinendum sibi ducit, quemadmodum Deus diem Sabbati sanctificare jusserat? Sed & Paulus aperte docet, in Christiana religione, ut ciborum, sic dierum discrimina esse sublata. Rom. 14. Gal. 4. Coloss. 3. quod & ipsa Christianae religionis natura docet, in qua nihil ceremoniale valet, sed tantum fides per charitatem efficax, aut nova creatura. & facies omne opus tuum. at die septimo
units.tr: It is plain that he thinks this precept about observing the Sabbath is still in force; yet the thing itself shows that it has been abrogated, since none of the Christians observes the Sabbath. For if you say that Christians observe the following day in place of the Sabbath, I in turn say that this shows the precept has been abrogated. For how would it be lawful to observe another day in place of the Sabbath? If this precept were still in force, would it have been lawful for the Jews to work on the Sabbath day, provided they rested on some other day instead? Further, which of the Christians thinks himself bound to abstain from every kind of work on the Lord's day, as God commanded the Sabbath day to be sanctified? But Paul also clearly teaches that in the Christian religion the distinction of days, as of foods, has been removed: Rom. 14, Gal. 4, Col. 3. And the very nature of the Christian religion teaches this, in which nothing ceremonial avails, but only faith working through love, or a new creature; and "do all your work," but "on the seventh day"

units.la: Resp. 1. Antiquatum quidem est Sabbatum Judaeorum, sive dies qui pro Sabbato apud Judaeos fuit, & modus eum observandi judaicus: non vero ut post dies sex laboris hebdomadarios, septimus habeatur sacer, cum quiete à labore. Quod argumentum est, & summa moralis praecepti quarti, fundata in summa aequitate, à quo tempore Deo placuit temporis & dierum nostrorum rationem sapientissime ordinare, ut & septem, non sex diebus, rediret primus dierum circulus, & sex labori, unus sacrae vacationi servaretur. In Decalogo dictum, memento diei Sabbati, ut eum sanctifices. Quod est caput & summarium praecepti. Tum pergit lex exponere & sabbatum quod intelligatur, & quae ejus sanctificatio. Sex diebus operaberis Sabbatum Jehova Deo tuo. Hoc est, dies sabbati, est dies septimus, quicunque sequitur ad sex dies laboris & operarum tuarum. Illo vero die nullum facies opus tu &c. Quare ? Provocat lex ad exem-plum Dei, & de opere creationis inquit, quod sex diebus fecit Jehova calum & terram &c. Num post sex illos dies, statim jussit primum redire, ut ita sex, non pluribus diebus constaret ille cyclus ? potuisset utique. Sed non, integrum diem intercedere voluit, quieti sacrum, & ab hoc recurrere operarum dies: & requievit die septimo. Atque inde homini similiter ordinavit dies suos, uti sex operaretur quodcunque sibi faciendum opus esset, septimo autem quiesceret, propterea benedixit Jehova diei sabbati, & sanctificavit eum. Propterea nempe voluit septimum à laboribus esse sabbatum, & sibi sacrum. Sic ab initio operum suorum constituit hominibus Deus, & interpunxit dies nostros labore & otio, sed sacro ac religioso. Atque hoc morale præcepti est, ut dies ille, post sex operarios, sancte observetur. Cæremoniale vero, vel positivum est, quod illo die Judæi Deum coluerunt, suo, quo dictarat[?] modo. Diem vero istum mutare certe Judæis non licuit, ad istum adstrictis. Uti vero Deus sibi servavit præcepto secundo autoritatem definiendi omnia in religione, & modum ejus, uti præcepto quarto, diem, sic in divinâ Christi & Apostolorum praxi, & ordinatione, & usu fundata est diei observatio, quæ apud Christianos inde omnes Dominica appellata fuit. Præterea Christiani diem suum sacrum servant pro sabbato, vel quietis die, & feriatione ab operibus, videlicet uti lege hoc præscribitur ab operibus vocationis temporariæ hebdomadariis, non Judaice, vel quomodo Judæi faciunt, sed pro sensu legis, quæ jubet sex diebus curare res nostras, septimo totos vacare Deo, ejusque cultui. Paulus do-cet quidem, in Christianâ religione sublatum esse discrimen ciborum & dierum Mosaicum cæremoniale, sed non ut, sepositâ Judaicâ dierum diffe-rentiâ, neque habito die uno præ altero ἡμέραν παρ᾽ ἡμέραν [?] sanctiore, illici-tum putetur, post communis laboris dies, unum in hebdomada, ex vi & ratione præcepti quarti, habere sacrum. Et quo minus cæremoniarum est in religione Christianâ, omnia vero ad sanctitatem & cultus spiritualis profes-sionem accommodata, eo magis decet omni genere pietatis exprimere nos-trum zelum & σεβαστὸν [?] supra Judæos, & supra alios omnes, Deumque venerari juxta omnia ejus præcepta, inter quæ & hoc, quod ut infertum ta-bulis moralis legis, & Dei digito lapidi inscriptum prolixiori expressione, & cautione, & ratione allegata, quam in aliis præceptis factum, ita istis quoque modis testari voluit & moralem suam naturalem, & perpetuam durationem.
units.tr: Answer, first: the Sabbath of the Jews has indeed been abrogated, both the day which was the Sabbath among the Jews and the Jewish manner of observing it. But the abrogated thing is not that, after six working days, the seventh should be held sacred, with rest from labour. This is the argument, and the substance of the moral precept of the fourth commandment, founded on the highest equity; from the time when it pleased God to order most wisely the reckoning of our time and days, so that the first circle of days returns after seven days, not six, and one day is kept sacred to rest and six to labour. In the Decalogue it is said: remember the day of the Sabbath, to sanctify it. This is the head and summary of the precept. Then the law goes on to explain what the Sabbath is and what its sanctification is: Six days you shall labour, and do all your work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of Jehovah your God. That is, the Sabbath day is the seventh day, which follows the six days of your labour and work. On that day you shall do no work, etc. Why? The law appeals to the example of God, and says of the work of creation that in six days Jehovah made heaven and earth, etc. Did he not, after those six days, at once order the first day to return, so that this cycle would consist of six days and not more? He certainly could have. But he did not; he willed a whole day to intervene, sacred to rest, and from this the days of work to recur: and he rested on the seventh day. And thence he similarly ordained his days for man, that he should work six days at whatever work was to be done, but rest on the seventh: therefore Jehovah blessed the Sabbath day, and sanctified it. Therefore, of course, he willed the seventh day to be a Sabbath free from labours and holy to himself. Thus God from the beginning of his works appointed for men, and divided our days by labour and leisure, but leisure that is sacred and religious. And this is the moral element of the precept, that this day, after six working days, be kept holy. The ceremonial or positive element, however, is that on that day the Jews worshipped God in their own manner, as it had been prescribed. But to change that day was certainly not lawful for the Jews, who were bound to it. Just as God reserved to himself the authority, under the second precept, of defining all things in religion and their manner, so under the fourth precept the observance of the day has been founded in the divine practice, ordinance and custom of Christ and the Apostles, and that day has been called the Lord's day by all Christians. Moreover, Christians keep their sacred day in place of the Sabbath, or the day of rest, and cease from works, namely from the weekly labours of their temporal calling, as the law prescribes, not in the Jewish manner, nor as the Jews do it, but according to the sense of the law, which bids us attend to our affairs for six days and devote the seventh wholly to God and his worship. Paul indeed teaches that in the Christian religion the Mosaic ceremonial distinction of foods and days has been removed; but not so that, with the Jewish distinction of days set aside, and with one day regarded as holier than another [ἡμέραν παρ᾽ ἡμέραν: day above day], it should be thought unlawful, after the common days of labour, to have one day in the week sacred by the force and reason of the fourth precept. And the less ceremony there is in the Christian religion, and the more everything is adapted to holiness and the profession of spiritual worship, the more it becomes us to express our zeal in every kind of piety, and [σεβαστὸν: reverent] beyond the Jews and beyond all others, and to worship God according to all his precepts; among which is this one, which he wished to be inscribed on the tables of the moral law, and written by God's finger on the stone, with fuller expression, caution and reason than in the other precepts, and so he wished to attest in these ways both its moral, natural and perpetual duration.

units.la: De istis vero alibi disputavimus prolixius: quæ quare. Remonstrantes male habeant, ut in corpore vel farragine Epistolarum in contumeliam virorum optimorum, & qui Ecclesiam in coercendis ipsorum molitionibus & dogmatibus strenue ac fideliter adjutarunt, editâ, ubi & recentes ac nuperi aliquid de suo inter celebriora sc. nomina garrire voluerunt, Næ-ranus nescio quis calumniari nos maluerit, quam aut causam maledicti adfer-re, aut respicere Arminii sui doctrinam de Sabbato, à communi Ecclesia-rum sententiâ hactenus non alienam: nisi vel doleat ipsi Arminium non aliter sensisse, aut non aliam sibi datam vindictæ in nos occasionem, propterea quod in nostro adversus Socinianos opere passim Remonstrantium consonantiam ostendimus cum Socinianis. Quam solam ego causam suspicari possum hominis nominati, & inepte, nempe istius loci erat lemma inserere controversiæ Sabbaticæ, ferocientis. Gratulor autem mihi, quod dignus videar quem tales oderint, à quibus laudari, vereor ne exiguam mihi apud orthodoxos pareret laudem ac gratiam.
units.tr: We have disputed more fully about these matters elsewhere; why the Remonstrants take it ill, in the body or medley of Letters published in insult to excellent men who vigorously and faithfully helped the Church to restrain their schemes and doctrines, where the recent and newly risen men also wished to chatter something of their own among the more famous names, some Naeranus or other preferred to slander us rather than either bring forward a reason for the slander or consider the doctrine of their Arminius about the Sabbath, which hitherto has not differed from the common opinion of the Churches; unless perhaps he is vexed that Arminius did not think otherwise, or that no other occasion of revenge against us was given him, because in our work against the Socinians we everywhere showed the agreement of the Remonstrants with the Socinians. This alone I can suspect as the cause of the man named, who foolishly inserted, in a place where it had no business, a tag of the Sabbath controversy, in a fury. But I rejoice that I seem worthy to be hated by such men; I fear that their praise would bring me little praise or favour among the orthodox.

units.la: Non sane hic aut Arminium, aut Curcellæum facio Socinianos: quorum uterque satis clare idem docet, quod nos, vid. unum diem è septem cultui divino consecrare, esse juris moralis, & perpetui. Arminius, Disp. de quarto præcepto, Jam verò quod ad diem septimum attinet qui sanctificari jubetur; in eo id morale & perpetuum est, ut dies septimus, hoc est, unus ex septem cultui divino consecretur, neque fas sit ulli hominum ullo tempore, quum sex dies animalis vitæ operibus impenderit, septimum in isdem omnibus aut eodem modo continuare. & Curcellæus, singulari de Sabbato Diatribâ, ubi agnoscens, omnes mundi cives ab initio ad Sabbati observationem obligatos fuisse, hæc præterea scribit, Morale autem esse mandatum Sabbati, ostenditur hîs argumentis. Primo, quod in Decalogo continetur. Nam Decalogus, fatentibus omnibus Theologis, summam legis moralis continet, & totus à Iesu Christo ad dilectionem Dei & proximi nostri refertur, Matth. xxii. adeo ut de prima ejus tabula, quæ Deum immediatè spectat, nihil possit eradi, quin dilectioni Deo debitæ multum detrahatur. Inconcinnum verò fuisset inter moralia novem præcepta, unum ceremoniale, & diversi planè generis admiscere. Secundò, ratio illi addita idem suadet, nempe quòd Deus creato sex diebus cœlo, terra & mari, requieverit die septimo, & nos ad exemplum suum velit unum diem è septem ab hujus vitæ laboribus feriari. Nam ea universalis est, & ad omnes mundi incolas, qui Dei sunt opus, pertinet. Nec refert quod Decalogus solis Israëlitis datus esse videatur. Quemadmodum enim reliqua ejus præcepta omnes devinciunt, ita istud quoque, cùm primum à Deo esse profectum scire queunt; saltem nos qui per fidem in Christum in unum corpus cum Israëlitis insiti sumus, & sacras literas ab iis accepimus, quæ nos de voluntate Dei certiores reddunt, nulla cum specie nos ab ejus obedientia subducere possumus. Tertiò, Sabbatum præscriptum fuit Israëlitis, ut servi eorum & ancillæ, sicut ipsi, à laboribus suis quiescerent: Deuter. v. 14. Non minor autem humanitas à dominis requiritur sub Euangelio, erga servos & ancillas suas, quàm olim sub lege; præsertim si Christiani sint, quos tanquam fratres tractare debent.
units.tr: Here I do not indeed make Arminius or the Socinian Curcellaeus my authorities, though each of them teaches clearly enough the same as we do, namely that to consecrate one day in seven to the worship of God is of moral and perpetual right. Arminius, Disputation on the fourth precept: Now as for the seventh day, which is commanded to be sanctified, this is moral and perpetual in that the seventh day, that is, one of the seven, is consecrated to the worship of God, and it is not lawful for any man at any time, when he has spent six days on the works of this animal life, to continue the seventh in the same works or in the same manner. And Curcellaeus, in his singular Diatribe on the Sabbath, where, acknowledging that all citizens of the world were from the beginning bound to observe the Sabbath, he writes further: That the command of the Sabbath is moral is shown by these arguments. First, because it is contained in the Decalogue. For the Decalogue, as all theologians confess, contains the sum of the moral law, and is wholly referred by Jesus Christ to the love of God and of our neighbour, Matth. xxii; so that nothing can be struck from its first table, which immediately regards God, without much being taken away from the love due to God. But it would have been incongruous to mix among the nine moral precepts one ceremonial one of a quite different kind. Second, the reason added to it proposes the same, namely that God, having created heaven, earth and sea in six days, rested on the seventh, and wills us to imitate his example by resting one day in seven from the labours of this life. For this is universal, and pertains to all the inhabitants of the world, who are the work of God. Nor does it matter that the Decalogue seems to have been given to the Israelites alone. For as its other precepts bind all, so this too, once they can know that it came from God; at least we, who through faith in Christ have been grafted into one body with the Israelites, and have received from them the holy writings which make us more certain of the will of God, cannot in any way withdraw ourselves from its obedience. Third, the Sabbath was prescribed to the Israelites so that their menservants and maidservants, like themselves, should rest from their labours: Deut. v. 14. But no less kindness is required of masters under the Gospel towards their menservants and maidservants than under the law of old; especially if they are Christians, whom they ought to treat as brothers.

units.la: Excipitur, rectam rationem non docere unum diem è septem feriandum, & cultui divino impendendum; proinde istud non esse juris naturalis, sed tantùm positivi. Sed resp. Etsi recta ratio id per se non suggerat, ejus tamen agnoscit æquitatem, statim atque ipsi proponitur, & Deo placere audit. Nam cùm ordinis causa certus dies, per vices recurrens, quieti & sacris conventibus destinandus sit, nullus melius isti usui quàm septimus quisque convenire videtur. Et pag. 70. Non oporteret ergo dicere, ut aliqui faciunt, Sabbatum per religionem Christianam esse abrogatum. Mandatum enim quod habemus in Decalogo, ut unum diem è septem quiescamus ab aliis laboribus, & totum cultui divino impendamus, invariatum adhuc manet; cùm nullum extet indicium, unde certi simus nos eo amplius non ieneri. Liberati tantum sumus ab obligatione fervandi Sabbatum quod Israelita in memo-riam Manna, quo Deus ipsos in deserto per xl. annos aluerat, simul & creationis mundi, celebrabant: & à rigida illa exactione quietis à laboribus etiam necessariis, dilationemque vix patientibus; quam tamen aliquando non tam Deus, quam ipsi sibi superstitione sua imposuisse videntur, ut Dominus Iesus ostendit, Luc. vi. 1. & seqq. & xiii. 11. & seqq. xiv. 2. & seqq.
units.tr: It is objected that right reason does not teach that one day in seven should be set aside for rest and devoted to divine worship, and that this is therefore not a matter of natural law but only of positive law. But I answer: although right reason does not suggest this of itself, it nonetheless recognises its fairness as soon as it is put before it, and hears that it pleases God. For since, for the sake of order, a fixed day recurring in turn must be assigned to rest and sacred assemblies, no day seems to fit that use better than every seventh. And on p. 70: It would therefore be wrong to say, as some do, that the Sabbath has been abrogated by the Christian religion. For the command we have in the Decalogue, that we rest from other labours one day in seven and devote the whole of it to divine worship, remains unchanged; since there is no sign from which we could be certain that we are no longer bound by it. We are freed only from the obligation to keep the Sabbath which the Israelites celebrated in memory of the manna, by which God had fed them in the desert for forty years, and at the same time in memory of the creation of the world; and from that rigid exaction of rest even from necessary labours, and from a delay which they could scarcely endure. Yet this was not so much imposed by God as, it seems, imposed by themselves upon themselves through their superstition, as the Lord Jesus showed: Luke 6:1 and following, and 13:11 and following, and 14:2 and following.

units.la: Excipitur 1. Omne discrimen dierum sublatum esse sub novo fœdere. Sic enim docere Apostolum Paulum, cum dicit, Alius judicat diem inter diem: aliis autem judicat omnem diem. Unusquisque in suo sensu abundet. Qui sapit diem, Domino sapit: Rom. xiv. 5. 6. Item, Dies observatis, & menses, & tempora, & annos. Timeo vos, ne forte sine causa laboraverim in vobis. Gal. iv. 11. 11. Resp. Discrimen quod ponitur inter dies ordinis causa, & propter conventus sacros, non esse sublatum: necessarium enim est in Ecclesia. Illud solum est abolitum, quo putatur unus dies alio sanctior esse, aut populum Christianum obligatum esse ad celebrandum certis diebus beneficia quædam Israelitis peculiaria. Sabbatum vero non debemus æstimare propter se, sed propter Dei cultum, & in memoriam creationis mundi, quod est beneficium omnibus hominibus commune. Neque credere oportet cessationem ab hujus vitæ laboribus esse aliquid in se laudabile; sed eam demum quæ pro fine habet exercitiis pietatis tanta diligentius vacare.
units.tr: It is objected, first, that every distinction of days has been abolished under the New Covenant. For so the Apostle Paul is supposed to teach when he says: "One man esteems one day above another; another esteems every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He who regards the day, regards it to the Lord" (Rom. 14:5, 6). Likewise: "You observe days and months and times and years. I am afraid for you, lest I have laboured over you in vain" (Gal. 4:10, 11). I answer: the distinction that is made between days for the sake of order and on account of sacred assemblies has not been abolished, for it is necessary in the Church. Only that has been abolished by which one day is thought to be holier than another, or the Christian people is thought to be bound to celebrate on certain days certain benefits peculiar to the Israelites. Nor ought we to value the Sabbath for its own sake, but for the sake of the worship of God and in memory of the creation of the world, which is a benefit common to all men. Nor should we believe that cessation from the labours of this life is in itself something praiseworthy; rather, it is only that cessation which has as its purpose that we give ourselves more diligently to the exercises of piety.

units.la: Excipitur 2. Apostolum speciatim nos ab obligatione feriandi Sabbatum liberare, dicendo, nemo judicet vos in parte diei festi, aut neomeniæ, aut Sabbatorum: quæ sunt umbra futurorum, corpus autem Christi: Coloff. 11. 16. 17. Resp Nihil esse quod cogat nos per vocem Sabbatorum in plurali intelligere primarium illud Sabbatum in Decalogo imperatum; posse enim eam accipi de aliis festis Iudaicis, quibus nomen Sabbati aliquando in Scriptura tribuitur, ut Levit. xvi. 31. & xxiii. 32. 39. & xxv. 2. 4. Nam alias cur post neomeniam in singulari nominatam, sabbatorum in plurali meminisset, nisi ad illud innuendum? Fac tamen hic de Sabbato proprie dicto agi; non sequetur ex eo quod Chri-stiani non debent alii alios judicare seu damnare propter Sabbata, omnem Sabbati obliga-tionem esse sublatam; quid ni enim potius dicemus Paulum eos solum reprehendere, qui scrupulosam Sabbati observationem, libertati Christianæ contrariam, à fratribus suis exigebant? Christum sane Sabbatum abrogasse non credidit Tertullianus, qui dicit ipsum, Sabbati diem benedictionem Patris à primordio sanctum, benefactione sua effecisse sanctiorem: Adversus Marcionem, lib. iv. cap. 12. Hæc hactenus Curcellæus. Quæ cur non arroserit Næranus, æque ac mea, quæ non alia in toto hoc argumento sunt, haud obscurum est divinare, ex odio mei vid. profecta, satis vehementi illo, at cæco, & suos non minus feriente quos nolit, quam me, nil tale de ipso meritum. Sed ut & ipsi Deus hæc condonet, ex animo precor.
units.tr: It is objected, second, that the Apostle frees us specifically from the obligation to keep the Sabbath, saying: "Let no one judge you in respect of a feast day, or a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ" (Col. 2:16, 17). I answer: there is nothing that compels us, by the word "Sabbaths" in the plural, to understand that chief Sabbath commanded in the Decalogue; for it can be taken of other Jewish feasts, to which the name Sabbath is sometimes given in Scripture, as in Lev. 16:31, 23:32, 39 and 25:2, 4. For otherwise, why would he, having named the new moon in the singular, have mentioned Sabbaths in the plural, unless to hint at those others? Yet grant that the Sabbath properly so called is here meant; it does not follow from the fact that Christians ought not to judge or condemn one another on account of Sabbaths that every obligation of the Sabbath has been abolished. For why should we not rather say that Paul is rebuking only those who demanded from their brothers a scrupulous observance of the Sabbath, contrary to Christian liberty? Certainly Tertullian did not believe that Christ abrogated the Sabbath; he says that Christ, by his beneficence, made holier the day which had been sanctified from the beginning by the Father's blessing: Against Marcion, book 4, chapter 12. So far Curcellaeus. Why Næranus has not approved these things, as he has not approved mine, which contain nothing different on this whole question, is not hard to guess: it arises from his hatred of me, which is quite vehement but blind, and which strikes his own followers no less than me, though they have deserved nothing of the kind from him. But may God forgive him too, this is my heartfelt prayer.

units.la: Progredimur ad secundam Decalogi tabulam, visuri, quæ hic ad singula præcepta, dicant Adversarii, per Christum addita, majoris sc. perfectionis ergo, fuisse: sed primo quæ in genere. De quâ accessione, quæ sc. facta sit secundæ in Decalogo tabulæ, & amori proximi, ita Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. v. ad hanc autem, quam proximo præstare debemus, charitatem, tanta per Christum facta est accessio, ut dici aliqua ratione possit, à nobis hodie postulari, ut eum majore etiam, quàm nos ipsos, amore complectamur id quod duabus potissimum rationibus fieri debet: Primò enim generatim loquendo, multa incommoda subeunda, multa capienda detrimenta, multa devoranda molestia homini Christiano sunt, ut proximo satisfaciat, resque illius in optimo statu collocet. In quo & illud est, quod etiam libertas illa, quam nobis peperit Christus, nequaquam tanti apud nos esse debet, quin charitate, quà fratribus obstricti sumus, postulante, ea nos ipsos spoliemus potius, quàm ad illorum perniciem illa intemperanter abutamur. Atqui Christus ita commemoravit summam illam legis in dilectione positam, ut nihil isti addere se significarit. Nullibi etiam dictum, ut proximum diligamus supra nos ipsos, quo sensu Adversarii hoc volunt esse novum legis additamentum. Nam charitas, quae lege exigitur, quâ nimirum proximum ames, sicuti teipsum, permittit & casu aliquo efflagitat, uti tua posthabeas aliquando commodis proximi, ut multa subeas incommoda, multa capias detrimenta, & devores molestias, quo proximo satisfiat, & illius res statu collocentur optimo: quemadmodum id subinde velimis à proximo fieri erga nos. Et haec est summa legis ac Prophetarum, ut quaecunque vultis vobis faciant homines, eadem faciatis ipsis. Matth vii. 12. Magis vero docet eadem charitatis lex, ut in genere libertatis ea quae libera sunt sepona-mus nonnunquam, & nobis interdicamus eorum usu, quum liberum non tantum sit omittere ea, sed aequum etiam ne ad aliorum perniciem libertate nostrâ utamur. Non addi hoc à Christo necesse fuit tamquam novum, quod & justitiae & charitaris lex sponte docet.
units.tr: We proceed to the second table of the Decalogue, to see what the adversaries say was added by Christ to each of its precepts, for the sake, they say, of greater perfection. But first, in general. Concerning that addition which was made to the second table of the Decalogue, that is, to love of neighbour, Volkelius says as follows, book 4, chapter 5: To this charity, which we owe to our neighbour, so great an addition has been made through Christ that it can in some way be said that we are today required to embrace him with a love even greater than that we have for ourselves; and this must be done chiefly for two reasons. First, speaking generally, the Christian man must undergo many inconveniences, suffer many losses, and endure many troubles, so that he may satisfy his neighbour and set his neighbour's affairs in the best condition. In this too lies the point that the liberty which Christ has won for us ought by no means to be held so dear by us that, when charity, by which we are bound to our brothers, demands it, we should not rather deprive ourselves of it than abuse it intemperately to their ruin. Yet Christ recalled that sum of the law which consists in love in such a way as to signify that he added nothing to it. Nowhere is it said that we should love our neighbour above ourselves, which is the sense in which the adversaries wish this to be a new addition to the law. For the charity which the law requires, namely that you love your neighbour as yourself, permits and at some point demands that you sometimes put your own advantages after those of your neighbour, that you undergo many inconveniences, suffer many losses, and endure troubles, so that your neighbour may be satisfied and his affairs placed in the best condition; just as you would sometimes wish the same from your neighbour towards yourself. "This is the sum of the law and the Prophets: whatever you wish that men should do to you, do so to them" (Matt. 7:12). Indeed, the same law of charity teaches more, namely that in the sphere of liberty we should sometimes set aside what is lawful and forbid ourselves its use, since it is not only lawful to refrain from these things, but also fair not to use our liberty to the destruction of others. There was no need for Christ to add this as something new, which the law of justice and charity teaches of its own accord.

units.la: Alterum, quod Christi ad secundae tabulae summam additamentum habet, est, quod jubemur in N. Test. etiam pro fratre, si opus sit, ponere animam. De quo loquitur, cap. VII. Hac quae de charitate in proximum hactenus diximus, maximum fine dubio momentum continent; sed illud multò gravius est, quod pro fratre vitam etiam in discrimen adducere, atque adeò profundere, si opus sit, jubemur, idque illis Christi verbis: Mandatum novum do vobis, ut diligatis invicem, sicut dilexi vos, ut & vos diligatis invicem. Item illus: Hoc est praeceptum meum, ut diligatis invicem, sicut dilexi vos: Majorem hac dilectione nemo habet, quàm ut animam ponat pro amicis suis. Joann. xiii. 34. & xv. 12. 13. Vitam ponere pro fratre, est argumentum sane charitatis valde excellens, sed tale quod ex vi ejus fluat; & juvetur quidem apud nos exemplo Christi, non verò quod primò demum inde-oriatur[?]. Nam etiam ad commendandum Christi erga nos amorem Apostolus considerat, quod aliquando quis pro viro bono, id est, fratre suo mortem oppetit, quamvis id contingat rarius: fieri tamen aliquando posse. at unde, nisi ex lege mutuae & frarernae charitatis? Quemadmodum exempla ejus occurrunt & extra, & ante Christum. Ut non à Christo demum peti hoc debeat, vel ejus doctrinâ, quod radicem & originem habet altiorem, in ipsius vid. charitatis naturâ. Hinc Ruben filios obsides patri Jacobo offert, pro Benjamino, Genef. xlii. 37. & pro eodem, servum se tradit Juda Josepho, Genef. xliv. 33. Moses & pro, & cum populo se offert aliquoties in mortem: & David mori cupit, pro Abfolomo. Jam quemadmodum ex charitate deducitur, quod Christus pro nobis est mortuus, ita ex eadem derivatur in nobis, ut idem præstemus pro fratribus, quoque ad exemplum Christi: In hoc cognovimus charitatem, quoniam ille animam suam pro nobis posuit, & nos debemus pro fratribus animas ponere. 1 Joann. III. 16.
units.tr: The second addition which Christ has made to the sum of the second table is that in the New Testament we are commanded, if need be, to lay down our lives even for a brother. Of this he speaks in chapter 7: What we have said so far about charity towards a neighbour undoubtedly contains the greatest weight; but that is much more serious, that we are commanded to bring our life into danger for a brother, and indeed to pour it out if need be, and this by those words of Christ: "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another, as I have loved you, that you also love one another." Likewise: "This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you. Greater love has no man than this, that he lay down his life for his friends." (John 13:34; 15:12, 13.) To lay down one's life for a brother is certainly a most excellent argument of charity, but of such a kind as flows from its power; and it is indeed helped among us by the example of Christ, but it does not first arise from that. For even when the Apostle wishes to commend Christ's love towards us, he considers that someone may sometimes die for a good man, that is, for his brother, although this happens rarely; yet that it can sometimes happen. But whence, except from the law of mutual and brotherly charity? Examples of it occur both outside and before Christ. So this must not be sought from Christ alone, or from his teaching, since it has a higher root and origin, in the very nature of charity. Hence Reuben offers his sons as hostages to his father Jacob for Benjamin (Gen. 42:37); and for the same Benjamin Judah gives himself as a slave to Joseph (Gen. 44:33). Moses offers himself several times to death for the people and with the people; and David desires to die for Absalom. Now just as it is from charity that Christ died for us, so from the same charity it is derived in us that we should do the same for our brothers, following the example of Christ: "In this we have known love, because he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers" (1 John 3:16).

units.la: Porro ad singula secundæ tabulæ præcepta, quæ addita à Christo dicunt Adversarii, primùm ad præceptum quintum, ubi liberorum officium præcipitur & præscribitur erga parentes, hæsitant Adversarii, quid dicturi sint, an quid additum isti præcepto sit. Jam ajunt; tum negant. Quod concernit officium Magistratuum, dominorum, & maritorum, vicissim erga illos subditorum, servorum, & uxorum, additum præcepto non audent dicere: ne tamen omnino absque censura abeat præceptum, ajunt huc pertinere aliqua. Catechesis, Quid ergo Christus ei addidit? Resp. Tale quid nihil apparet. Nihilominus tamen ea omnia, quæ de subditis Magistratu, de uxoribus & maritis, de servis & dominis in litteris divinis tradita sunt, huc referenda videntur, quæ mutui officii etiam inter parentes & filios spectantur. Quid id est, huc referri, huc referenda videri? Certè eò referuntur, ut consimiles species, quæcunque similibus officiis constant, ac sunt ista quæ inter parentes & liberos. Hoc Volkelius alibi dixit, quæ propter quandam affinitatem huc referri possunt, de ejusdem præcepti rebus. l. iv. c. xvii. in initio. Quare non iis vel auctum vel perfectum præceptum dici debet. Et tamen de perfectione legis moralis per Christum hic agitur: & Smalcius, lib. de Divinit. pag. 20. in margine, quemadmodum ad cætera præcepta, sic & hic, scribit, perfectio præcepti. En hominis vafritiem. Jam dicit, Præcipit lex, ut honoremus patrem & matrem. Hoc, quia ita comparatum est, ut perfici & augeri non possit, hodie etiam ratum manet. Nulloque interveniente mox addit: auctum verò est & perfectum à Christo, quatenus etiam parentibus, & omnibus aliis, qui parentum loco sunt, utpote, Magistratui, Dominis, maritis, præcipit, quod eis faciendum sit. Si augeri non possit, quomodo auctum est? Si dicas, hoc de officio liberorum erga parentes non est auctum, sed alia accesserunt, non de liberis, sed de parentibus, de Magistratu, &c. eorumque officio erga illos. Sed quid auctum intelligis, quando auctum verò est & perfectum ais aliquod, nonne officium liberorum lege illa præscriptum? ergo præceptum illud. quomodo ergo dixisti, quod perfici, & augeri non possit? auxitne & perfecit Christus, quod augeri perficique non potest? Quando disputamus de augmento & perfectione præceptorum, non intelligitur, an aliquod caput lege præscriptum in se sit auctum, vel perfectum; sed, an præceptum totum? Uti ad tertium præceptum, quo dixerunt, quamvis male, vetari solum perjurium, nihil de perjurio, sed de alia specie juramenti mali, scilicet temerarii, augmentum fecerunt, augmentum tamen intellexerunt præcepti: ita hic, aliis illis honoris vel officiorum speciebus vellent quidem dicere auctum præceptum, sed plane tamen ut affirment, vix à se impetrant. Hinc illa misera apud Smalcium contradictio: apud alios manifesta titubatio. Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. xv. Dicendum nunc de iis esset, quæ Christus huic præcepto addiderit. Verum diligenter licet inquirentibus, nihil tale occurrit. Nisi forte ea, quæ de parentum, Magistratuum, Dominorum,
units.tr: Next, as to the individual precepts of the second table, which our opponents say Christ added to, let us start with the fifth precept, where the duty of children towards their parents is enjoined and prescribed. Here the opponents hesitate over what to say, whether anything was added to that precept. First they say yes, then they say no. As for the duty of magistrates, masters and husbands, and conversely of subjects, servants and wives towards them, they do not dare to say it was added to the precept. Yet, so that the precept is not left entirely without comment, they say some of these things belong here. The Catechism asks: What then did Christ add to it? It answers: Nothing of the kind appears. Nevertheless all those things which are delivered in the divine writings concerning the duty of subjects to the magistrate, of wives and husbands, of servants and masters, seem to be referred here, and these are also considered in the mutual duty between parents and children. What does it mean to say they are referred here, or seem to be referred here? Surely they are referred to it as similar kinds, whatever rests on similar duties, such as those between parents and children. Volkelius said this elsewhere, that they can be referred here on account of a certain affinity, concerning matters of the same precept, book 4, chapter 17, at the beginning. Therefore the precept cannot be said to have been either enlarged or perfected by these. And yet the perfection of the moral law through Christ is what is under discussion here. Smalcius, in his book on the Divinity, page 20, in the margin, writes as for the other precepts, so here too, the perfection of the precept. See the cunning of the man. Now he says: The law commands that we honour father and mother. This, because it is so constituted that it cannot be perfected or increased, still holds today. And without any interval he adds at once: But it has been enlarged and perfected by Christ, in so far as he enjoins on parents, and on all others who stand in the place of parents, such as magistrates, masters and husbands, what is to be done by them to those below them. If it cannot be increased, how has it been increased? If you say that the duty of children towards parents has not been enlarged, but other things have been added, not concerning children but concerning parents, magistrates and so on, and their duty towards those under them: but what do you understand by "enlarged" when you say "but it has been enlarged and perfected" of something? Is not the duty of children prescribed by that law? Then that precept is the thing in question. How, then, did you say it cannot be perfected or increased? Did Christ enlarge and perfect what cannot be enlarged or perfected? When we dispute about the enlargement and perfection of precepts, we do not ask whether some chapter prescribed by the law has been enlarged or perfected in itself, but whether the whole precept has been. As regards the third precept, where they said, though wrongly, that only perjury is forbidden, they made an addition not about perjury but about another kind of wrongful oath, namely a rash one, and yet they understood it as an enlargement of the precept. So here, they would indeed like to say that the precept has been enlarged by these other kinds of honour or duty, but they can scarcely bring themselves to affirm it plainly. Hence that wretched self-contradiction in Smalcius, and in others a manifest hesitation. Volkelius, book 4, chapter 15: It must now be said what Christ has added to this precept. But although we inquire carefully, nothing of the kind occurs. Unless perhaps those things which have been delivered in Holy Writ concerning the duties of parents, magistrates, masters,

units.la: Tom. 2. maritorum: & contra subditorum, servorum, uxorumque officiis, sacris litteris prodita sunt, huc referri posse videantur: qua tamen magna ex parte, vel in ipsa lege fuerunt tradita, vel ipso rationis lumine cognoscuntur. Ecce 1. ut diligenter & anxie inquirant, si quam legis imperfectionem deprehendere queant, vel additiones a Christo factas. 11. nihil tamen occurrit, quod Christus huic praecepto addiderit. Quod, post diligentem inquisitionem, aperte & fortiter asseverant. 111. Subrepit dubitatio, nisi forte de officiis parentum aliquid &c. Sed an additum praecepto? neque id audent dicere. Hoc tamen hic solum quaeritur, & vos tam sedulo inquiritis. Imo an huc referri possit, an huc referri possit videatur? quam stolide. idne est, cur adeo dubitetis, &c. suspenso incedatis gradu, an referri illa ad praeceptum hoc possint? 1v. Iterum & haec ipsa quantulacunque evertunt, mox dicentes, ea in lege fuisse tradita, quin vel rationis lumine cognosci posse. Atqui ea dicetis a Christo demum addita, quae vel ratione cognosci possunt? vel dicere videri velitis, aut dubium saltem hinc aliquod accipere? Quanta ea miseria est; inservire suo errori & hypothesi, non se suaque libenter submittere veritati, & hanc sequi solam? Omnem operam adhibent homines illi, ut quae nova ad singula praecepta a Christo adiecta ad populum queant producere: quae ubi nulla vident, & velint tamen extare, undecunque conantur extundere, etiam quae propria ipsorum mox redarguat conscientia. Parum, vel nihil hic videtur superesse, controversiae: si tamen pergant contendere, merito jubebimus eos primum quaestionem exponere, & aperte formare controversiam. Nos clare satis dicimus, huic praecepto, uti neq; aliis, quidpiam a Christo novi praecepti additum, vel nulla lege auctum perfectumque fuisse. Quod de officio parentum, Magistratus, &c. id omne plenitudine ac vi praecepti contineri, & ex eo doceri posse, non ad illud supervenire tanquam novi quid, vel alterius praecepti, asserimus. Si idem nobiscum sentiant, ergo & loquantur, neque tum ulla hic saltem erit disputatio. Sin aliud, primum se componant cum suis, & varia illa professione, quam notavimus; deinde de nobis sint solliciti. Breviter autem haec ipsis reponimus:
units.tr: Vol. 2. husbands, and conversely of subjects, servants and wives, seem to be able to be referred here; yet these were for the most part either delivered in the law itself, or are known by the very light of reason. See, first, how diligently and anxiously they inquire whether they can detect any imperfection of the law, or any additions made by Christ. Second, nothing nevertheless occurs which Christ added to this precept. This they assert openly and firmly after careful inquiry. Third, doubt creeps in: unless perhaps something about the duties of parents etc. But was it added to the precept? They do not dare to say so. Yet this alone is what is asked here, and you inquire so diligently. Indeed, whether it can be referred here, or seems to be referred here: how foolishly! Is this why you hesitate so much, walking with a suspended step, whether those things can be referred to this precept? Fourth, again, they overturn even these small points, saying at once that these things were delivered in the law, and that they can be known even by the light of reason. But will you say that things which can be known by reason were added by Christ at last? Or do you wish to seem to say this, or at least to derive some doubt from it? How wretched it is to serve one's own error and hypothesis, not gladly to submit oneself and one's own to the truth, and to follow that alone! Those men take every pains to produce whatever new things they can add by Christ to the individual precepts for the people. Where they see none, yet wish them to exist, they try to extract them from anywhere, even things which their own conscience at once refutes. Little or nothing of the controversy seems to remain here. If they nevertheless persist in contending, we shall rightly order them first to set out the question and to frame the controversy plainly. We say clearly enough that to this precept, as to the others, nothing new has been added by Christ as a new precept, nor was it enlarged or perfected by any law. As for the duty of parents, magistrates and so on, we assert that all of it is contained in the fullness and force of the precept, and can be taught from it, and that it does not come upon it as something new or as belonging to another precept. If they feel the same as we do, then let them say so, and there will be no dispute here at least. But if they think otherwise, let them first come to terms with their own people, and with that varied profession which we have noted; then let them be concerned about us. Briefly, however, we reply to them as follows:

units.la: Primum, nihil praecepto quinto additum a Christo, Catechesis totidem verbis dixit. Praeceptum illud perfici & augeri non posse, Smalcius. Quod Christus huic praecepto addiderit, diligenter licet inquirentibus, nihil occurrere, Volkelius. 11. Officia parentum erga liberos, Catechesis directe retulit ad praeceptum quintum, in ejus expositione, pag. 190. antequam pag. 191. inquireret, num quid praecepto huic Christus addidisset. Illud autem Smalcius, lib. de Divinit. Christi, loco jam adducto, & Volkelius, inter illa referunt, in quibus vel auctum & perfectum a Christo videri posset praeceptum, vel saltem eo referri posse, uti Volkelius amat loqui. Expresse iterum Catechesis, ad quaestionem, quid Christus praecepto huic addidit? postquam respondisset, tale quidem nihil apparere, huc tamen referri posse dixit, quae de officiis mutuis subditorum & Magistratus, uxorum & maritorum, servorum & dominorum, in sacris tradita, non addit, quod alii, parentum. Adeo hoc in ipso praecepto contineri statuit, neque dubium esse an ei accesserit. 111. Utcunque, illa tamen officia in ipsa lege fuisse tradita, Volkelius haud dubitanter ait. Dicit quidem magna ex parte: sed qua ex parte non, haud indicavit: neque indicare aliquid poterit, dum vel ex ipso rationis lumine cognosci illa posse, itidem asseruit. Nequaquam ergo talia haec sunt, ut à Christo demum addita censeri possint. Quod tamen solum hic poterit venire in controversiam. iv. Et revera nihil dabunt, nullam officiorum partem, quae non ex lege & doctrinâ V. Testam. comprobari queat: quae proinde Magistratus, & dominos, patrum nomine indigitat, ad significandum, quinto praecepto illorum etiam officia comprehendi, uti Catechesis loquitur Racoviensis, propter communia illorum officia inter se, quae etiam inter parentes liberosque observantur. pag. 191. v. Quomodocunque hoc se habeat, non possunt ostendere, illa à Christo officia praescripta esse, ceu nova praecepta, vel tamquam alia ad quintum additamenta. vi. Apostolus quando illa officia exponit, facit hoc ad legem, & ex praecepto quinto palam educit, Ephes. vi. 1. 2. non ex nova doctrinâ Christi. vii. Quid quod omnia ex unâ lege charitatis trahi commode & explicari possint. Smalcius, de Divinit. pag. 11. Ex eo enim quod lex charitatis exercenda Magistratui in sub-ditos, Dominus in servos, viris in uxores praescribitur, manifeste apparet, omne genus obedientia, honoris, timoris (quod obedientia, honori, & timori Dei non adversatur aut detrahat) deberi à subditis Magistratui, à servis Dominis, ab uxoribus mari-tis. Atque haec ad praeceptum quintum, & Adversariorum, quâ hic utuntur, tergiversationem.
units.tr: First, the Catechism said in so many words that nothing was added by Christ to the fifth precept. Smalcius: that precept cannot be perfected or increased. Volkelius: although they inquire carefully, nothing occurs that Christ added to this precept. Second, the Catechism directly referred the duties of parents towards children to the fifth precept, in its exposition, page 190, before it asked, page 191, whether Christ had added anything to this precept. But Smalcius, in the book on the Divinity of Christ cited above, and Volkelius, count among those things by which the precept might seem to have been enlarged and perfected by Christ, or at least might be referred to it, as Volkelius likes to put it. The Catechism again expressly, to the question, what did Christ add to this precept, after answering that nothing of the kind appears, said that those things delivered in Scripture concerning the mutual duties of subjects and magistrate, wives and husbands, servants and masters, could nevertheless be referred here; it does not add, as others do, of parents. So firmly does it hold that these are contained in the precept itself, and that there is no doubt whether they were added to it. Third, however, Volkelius says without hesitation that those duties were delivered in the law itself. He indeed says for the most part, but in what respect not, he did not indicate; nor will he be able to indicate anything, since he also asserts that these can be known from the very light of reason. Therefore these are by no means such things as can be judged to have been added by Christ at last. Yet this alone can come into controversy here. Fourth, they will in fact give up no part of the duties which cannot be proved from the law and teaching of the Old Testament. These therefore designate magistrates and masters by the name of parents, to signify that their duties are also comprised under the fifth precept, as the Racovian Catechism speaks, because of their common duties among themselves, which are also observed between parents and children. Page 191. Fifth, however this may stand, they cannot show that those duties were prescribed by Christ as new precepts, or as additions to the fifth. Sixth, when the Apostle sets out those duties, he does so in accordance with the law, and plainly draws them from the fifth precept, Ephesians 6:1, 2, not from any new teaching of Christ. Seventh, moreover, everything can conveniently be derived and explained from the one law of charity. Smalcius, on the Divinity, page 11: For from the fact that the law of charity is prescribed to magistrates towards subjects, to the master towards servants, and to husbands towards wives, it clearly appears that every kind of obedience, honour and fear (which does not oppose or detract from the obedience, honour and fear of God) is owed by subjects to magistrates, by servants to masters, and by wives to husbands. So much for the fifth precept, and for the evasion of the Adversaries which they use here.

units.la: In praecepto sexto vindicando jam ante fuimus occupati, ad Matth. v. nam quod illi additum dicunt, hinc petere solent, videlicet tria ferme, quibus Christum praeceptum illud perfecisse, ajunt. Quod iram prohibuit, contume-liam, & vindictam[?]. Sic Catechesis, quid praecepto huic addidit Dominus Jesus? Resp. ne fratri irascamur, neque verbis asperis ex ulciscendi libidine prodeuntibus eum offendamus, qua Dominus Jesus vocibus racha & fatue expressit: quo illa verba pertinent, Ephes. iv. 31. omnis amaritudo & excandescentia, & ira, & clamor, & maledicentia tollatur à vobis cum omni malitia. Qu. Quid praeterea huic praecepto addidit Dominus Jesus? Resp. Inhibuit omne ultionis genus, non solum privatum, verum etiam quod sit per Magistratum: ea ratione, quod siquis vel corpus vel fortunas, vel nomen nostrum laeserit, ut paratiores simus aliam injuriam potius accipere, quam nos ulcisci. Similiter Smalcius, de Divin. pag. 11. Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. xvi. Ostendimus autem suo, quem diximus, loco, illa non minus in V. Lege prohibita & interdicta fuisse, quam in Novo Testamento, à Christo: neque Christum hac in parte correxisse aut perfecisse legem, sed eam à corruptelis Scribarum vindicasse & repurgasse. Quae repetere & ponere eadem nihil est necesse. Non enim novi quid proferatur, quod non ex Matth. v. petitum, & in expositione seu vindicatione loci illius discussum sit.
units.tr: I have already been occupied with vindicating the sixth commandment, at Matt. 5. For what they add to it, they usually take from there, namely roughly three things by which they say Christ perfected that precept: that he forbade anger, insult, and vengeance[?]. Thus the Catechism: What did the Lord Jesus add to this precept? Answer: That we should not be angry with our brother, nor offend him with harsh words spoken out of a desire for revenge, which the Lord Jesus expressed by the words raca and fool. To this belong the words of Ephes. 4:31: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking be put away from you, with all malice." Question: What else did the Lord Jesus add to this precept? Answer: He forbade every kind of revenge, not only private but also that carried out by the magistrate, on the ground that if anyone harms our body, our goods, or our name, we should be readier to receive another injury than to avenge ourselves. Likewise Smalcius, On the Divinity, p. 11; Volkelius, book 4, ch. 16. But we have shown in the place I mentioned that these things were forbidden and prohibited in the Old Testament no less than in the New, and that Christ did not correct or perfect the law in this respect, but cleansed it and freed it from the corruptions of the scribes.
