There is no need to repeat the same things again and set them out. For nothing new is put forward that has not been drawn from Matt. 5 and discussed in the exposition or vindication of that passage.

units.la: Pergimus igitur ad praeceptum septimum, de adulterio. Cui ajunt addita tria. i. Alienae uxoris concupiscentiam, vel aspectum libidinosum, esse adulterium. ii. Divortium, extra casum adulterii, esse illicitum. iii. Atque omnem similiter fornicationem aut impuritatem, turpiloquium, scurrilitatem
units.tr: We proceed therefore to the seventh commandment, concerning adultery. To it, they say, three things were added. First, that the desire for another's wife, or a lustful look, is adultery. Second, that divorce, apart from the case of adultery, is unlawful. Third, and likewise every fornication, impurity, obscene talk, scurrility

units.la: Nota: the printed text ends at "scurrilitatem"; the word "& jocos." below is the catchword and is not repeated here. & jocos. Catechesis: Quid huic praecepto addidit Dominus Jesus? Resp. Primum ne moechemur, non solum reipsa, verum etiam ne mulieren, ita ut concupiscamus, aspiciamus; id innuens, eum, qui eam concupiscit in corde suo, adulterium patravisse. Tertio addidit, eum qui eam dimissam duxerit, eum pariter moechari. Postremo omnem scortationem & impuritatem, ac etiam omnem sermonem turpem & obscænum, & scurrilitatem & jocos nobis interdixit. Ita etiam Smalcius, de Divinit. pag. 21. Ostorodus, Institut. cap. xxiv. addit, per Evangelium etiam praecepto illi appositum esse, ne cui liceat habere concubinam, ex 1 Cor. vii. 9. vel plures simul uxores, juxta Antiquorum Polygamiam. Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. xvii. Sed jam tempus est, ut quae Christus mandato huic adjunxerit, videamus. Ea igitur duplicis sunt generis. Quaedam enim ad animum etiam hominis ab omni adulterii contagione expurgan-dum pertinent: quaedam vero ad corporis ipsius castitatem puritatemque spectant. Illuc refert concupiscentiam alienae uxoris, pro adulterio a Christo habitam: alienae uxoris, aut cujusvis alterius foeminae contrectationem, quae impuram libidinosamque cogitationem in nobis excitat: comessationes, a Christo & Apostolis interdictas. tum subjungit, omnia ista, quae vel expresse, vel implicite nobis interdicta esse hactenus diximus, id est, & comessationes, & eas comitantia, haec nimirum, quae modo enumeravimus, olim Israelitis indulta fuisse. nunc vero ad mentem[?] castitatem tuen-dam, huic Mosis praecepto addita, aut ob affinitatem quandam huc referri jure possunt.
units.tr: & jesting. Catechism: What did the Lord Jesus add to this precept? Answer: First, that we should not commit adultery, not only in deed but also by looking at a woman so as to lust after her, implying that he who desires her in his heart has committed adultery. Third, he added that he who marries a woman who has been put away likewise commits adultery. Lastly, he forbade us every fornication and impurity, and also every foul and obscene speech, and scurrility and jesting. So too Smalcius, On the Divinity, p. 21. Ostorodus, Institutes, ch. 24, adds that through the Gospel it was also joined to that precept that no one may be allowed to keep a concubine, from 1 Cor. 7:9, or several wives at once, in the manner of the polygamy of the ancients. Volkelius, book 4, ch. 17: But now it is time to see what Christ has added to this commandment. These things are of two kinds. For some pertain to cleansing the human mind from every contagion of adultery; others concern the chastity and purity of the body itself. To the former he refers the desire for another's wife, which Christ counted as adultery; the touching of another's wife or of any other woman, which stirs impure and lustful thoughts in us; and drinking parties (comessationes), forbidden by Christ and the Apostles. Then he adds: All these things which we have hitherto said are forbidden to us either expressly or implicitly, that is, both drinking parties and the things accompanying them, namely those we have just listed, were indeed granted to the Israelites of old. But now they may rightly be referred to this precept of Moses, as added to it, for guarding the chastity of the mind, or on account of some kinship with it.

units.la: Quae vero ad corpus ab impuritate confervandum pertinent, censet a Christo addita; interdictum scortationis, aliorumque hujus generis flagitiorum, turpitudinum, immoderati usus connubii, divortii extra casum & causam adulterii, denique polygamiae. Sed quorsum ita distinguat, ut comessationes, ad animum magis quam ad corpus, referat, non adeo exagitabimus, quam quod comessationes illas, aliaque nobis similiter interdicta, Israelitis olim concessa & indulta fuisse, asserit. Ita scilicet illi vixerunt, carni & luxuriae dediti, neque id de facto, sed etiam de jure? videamus.
units.tr: Those things which pertain to keeping the body free from impurity he thinks were added by Christ: the prohibition of fornication and of other shameful acts of this kind, of impurities, of immoderate use of marriage, of divorce apart from the case and cause of adultery, and finally of polygamy. But why he distinguishes things in this way, referring drinking parties to the mind rather than to the body, I shall not press very hard. What I shall pursue is that he asserts those drinking parties and other things likewise forbidden to us were granted and allowed to the Israelites of old. So did they live, given over to the flesh and to lust, not only in fact but also by right? Let us see.

units.la: Quod ad duo priora attinet, quae praecepto huic addita Adversarii dicunt, de iis egimus suo loco, ad Matth. v. ostendimusque, non illa olim ex lege licuisse, sed hanc istis contrariasse: quare nec quae dicunt, a Christo addita demum vel excogitata fuerunt. Jam etiam Volkelius dicit, quod doctrinam suam Christus ex divini instituti ratione deduxit. Eo igitur nititur doctrina Christi, de divortio, pag. 269. quoque de polygamia, pag. 270. non ergo hoc novum quid, & ex natura demum N. Test. derivatur.
units.tr: As for the two former things which the opponents say were added to this precept, we have dealt with them in their place, at Matt. 5, and shown that those things were not once permitted by the law, but that Christ set this against them. Therefore what they say was added, or devised, by Christ was not something new after all. Volkelius also says that Christ derived his teaching from the reason of the divine institution. On that the teaching of Christ about divorce rests, p. 269, and likewise about polygamy, p. 270. So this is not something new, derived only from the nature of the New Testament.

units.la: Quod vero ad reliquas turpitudines spectat, non satis mirari possum hominum improbitatem, quod ausint dicere, talia a Christo demum addita praecepto, & interdicta esse; Patribus vero in V. Test. concessa ac indulta. Quae intoleranda est contumelia, in Patrum probitatem. II. in religionem, quae illa concesserit. III. Deum adeo ipsum, tantarum impuritatum autorem & approbatorem: si nempe Adversarios audimus. Quippe 1. referunt illa omnia sub eorum catalogum & ordinem, quae Dominus Jesus scilicet praecepto huic septimo addiderit, sic Catechesis; adjunxerit, ita Volkelius; quibus id perfecerit & implerit, ut Smalcius, & Ostorodus loquuntur. Non ergo illa praeceptum vetus, vel lex habuit, non interdixit. Sed Christus primus illa expromsit, docuitque in N. Testamento. II. De Patrum turpitudinibus, & turpissimâ religione accipe Volkelium æque aperto ac impudenti ore differentem. Postquam enim comessationes explicuisset, quas à Christo & Apostolis vetitas censet: Ad hunc autem locum non immeritò referri possunt & comessationes, à Christo & Apostolis interdictas: partim quidem, quia eodem cum libidinibus genere continentur, atque ad belluinas corporis voluptates spectant; partim verò, quia libidinum & impurarum cupiditatum solent esse causa. Est autem comessatio in sacris literis interdicta nihil aliud, quàm ejusmodi cibi potusque usus, qui eò revera spectat, ut corpus nostrum voluptate titilletur, non verò ut vires illius reficiantur, ac valetudo confervetur. Usus verò hujusmodi nimium est ac immoderatus; & porrò, ut nihil in omni vita moderatum efficere possit; ita hominum animis maximum turpissimarum cupiditatum affert incendium. pag. 265. Tum ait, illa Veteribus à Deo concessa fuisse: Ut igitur tandem hanc explicationis nostræ partem concludamus; animadvertendum est, omnia ista, quæ vel expressè, vel implicitè nobis interdicta esse hactenus diximus, id est, & comessationes, & eas comitantia, hæc nimirum, quæ modo enumeravimus, olim Israelitis indulta fuisse; quin tunc, nec ad coelestia assiduè contemplanda, abductis animis à rebus terrestribus, incitabantur; nec tantam illis vita continentiam atque castitatem Deus imperabat; nec denique, ut suprà etiam diximus, in assiduo precum studio versari jubebantur. Hodie autem, cum contrà à nobis fieri oporteat, evenit, ut quæ olim in peccatis non habebantur, quæve pœna in lege propositâ non coercebantur, gravissima sæpe peccata existimanda sint.
units.tr: As for the remaining shameful practices, I cannot sufficiently marvel at the wickedness of men who dare to say that such things were added to the precept, and forbidden, only by Christ, whereas they were conceded and granted to the Fathers of the Old Testament. This is an intolerable insult: first, to the probity of the Fathers; second, to the religion which permitted those things; third, to God himself, the author and approver of such great impurities, if we listen to our opponents. For, first, they reckon all those things, which the Lord Jesus, forsooth, added to this seventh precept (so the Catechism), under their own list and order; joined (so Volkelius); by which he perfected and fulfilled it, as Smalcius and Ostorodus put it. So the old precept or law did not contain these things and did not forbid them. But Christ first brought them forth and taught them in the New Testament. Second, concerning the shameful deeds of the Fathers and their most shameful religion, hear Volkelius, speaking with a mouth as open as it is shameless. After he had explained the drinking parties which he holds were forbidden by Christ and the Apostles, he says: To this place can not unfairly be referred also the drinking parties forbidden by Christ and the Apostles, partly because they belong to the same kind as lusts and aim at bestial pleasures of the body, partly because they are wont to be the cause of lusts and impure desires. A drinking party, as forbidden in Holy Scripture, is nothing other than such a use of food and drink as really aims at tickling our body with pleasure, not at restoring its strength and preserving health. Such a use is excessive and immoderate; and further, since it can make nothing moderate in the whole of life, so it kindles in men's minds the greatest fire of most shameful desires. p. 265. Then he says those things were granted to the ancients by God: So then, to conclude this part of our explanation, it must be noted that all those things which we have hitherto said are forbidden to us, either expressly or implicitly, that is, both drinking parties and the things accompanying them, namely those we have just listed, were granted to the Israelites of old. Indeed, then they were not urged to the constant contemplation of heavenly things, their minds being drawn away from earthly things; nor did God command such great continence and chastity of life; nor, lastly, as we also said above, were they bidden to be engaged in constant zeal for prayer. But today, when the contrary ought to be done by us, it happens that things which were formerly not counted as sins, and which the law as proposed did not restrain by penalty, must often be reckoned most grievous sins.

units.la: Omnino autem necesse videtur, hæc distinctius notare & examinare, ad pietatem sc. Adversariorum nostrorum cognoscendam, quâ feruntur erga Patres V. Test. eorumque religionem, dum Deum ajunt, illis indulsisse 1. comessationes, & eas comitantia, quæ enumerarunt, flagitia. II. gravissima quidem ista peccata, olim in peccatis non habita. III. non tantam illis vita continentiam atque castitatem Deum imperasse. IV. omitto, quod de Patribus dicunt, eos ad coelestia assidue contemplanda, abductis animis à rebus terrestribus, non fuisse incitatos, contrà ac Apostolus de illis docet, Hebr. xi. neque in assiduo precum studio versatos, contra totum Psalmorum librum תהלים[?]. v. quin tuto illos & licitè incubuisse omnis generis libidinibus. VI. ad belluinas corporis voluptates. VII. & impuras cupiditates. VIII. nimium & immoderatum usum cibi potusque. IX. & maxima turpissimarum cupiditatum incendia. Eant nunc Patres, & fideles illi V. Test. quos tantæ sanctitatis deptædicat utriusque Testamenti Scriptura, & Ecclesia omnis, Judaica, atque Christiana, & infra non homines, sed ipsas adeo belluas, norint se, per horum hominum theologiam & themata, reduci. Judicent quivis hinc de nostris Adversariis, eorum opinionibus, & probitate, quam tantopere in iis alii efferunt, & de disputationibus. Ego quidem vel ex hoc uno schemate & crimine censeo procul ablegandam esse universam ipsorum doctrinam, quæ tam horrendis modis se defendere cogitur ac stabilire. Certè inter Christianos uti inaudita & abominanda hæc, ita nulli non supremum movere debet fastidium infausta adeo Theologia. De Gentilibus Gentiles ipsi, etiam Christiani honorificentius loquuntur, quam sint ea, quæ nostri de Sanctis V. Test. haud verentur affirmare, & quod durissimum est, de illorum religione, ex quâ ita nequiter vivere licuerit, approbante, & tantum non jubente, Deo. Nos autem aliter à Deo, atque de Deo, de Doctrinâ, & Patribus V. Test. edocti, regerimus ista.
units.tr: It seems altogether necessary to note and examine these things more distinctly, in order to understand the piety of our opponents, by which they are carried towards the Fathers of the Old Testament and their religion, while they say God granted them: first, drinking parties and the vices accompanying them which they listed; second, that those most grievous sins were once not counted as sins; third, that God did not command such great continence and chastity of life; fourth (I pass over what they say of the Fathers, that they were not incited to the constant contemplation of heavenly things, with their minds drawn away from earthly things, contrary to what the Apostle teaches of them, Heb. 11, nor engaged in constant zeal for prayer, against the whole book of the Psalter [תהלים]); fifth, that they were safely and lawfully given over to every kind of lust; sixth, to bestial pleasures of the body; seventh, to impure desires; eighth, to excessive and immoderate use of food and drink; ninth, to the greatest fires of most shameful desires. Let the Fathers go now, and those faithful men of the Old Testament whom the Scripture of both Testaments and the whole Church, Jewish and Christian, proclaims of such great holiness; let them know that, far from being men, they are reduced through the theology and theses of these men to beasts themselves. Let anyone judge from this about our opponents, their opinions and their probity, which others extol so greatly in them, and about their disputations. For my part, I judge that from this single scheme and crime alone the whole of their doctrine, which is compelled to defend and establish itself by such horrible means, is to be banished far away. Surely among Christians this unheard-of and abominable theology, so ill-omened, ought to stir supreme disgust in everyone. Even the Gentiles speak more honourably of the Gentiles than these men dare to assert about the Saints of the Old Testament; and, hardest of all, about their religion, which, with God approving and almost commanding, permitted them to live so wickedly. But we, taught otherwise about God and from God, about doctrine and the Fathers of the Old Testament, reject these claims.

units.la: 1. Flagitia illa (neque aliud sunt, quæ dicunt Adversarii in V. Test. con-cessa, Novo demùm prohibita esse, eamque ipsi hic adhibent nomenclatu-ram) vel ipsa lege naturæ damnantur, & judicio rationis: ergo non potuerunt concessa fuisse in V. Testamento. Consule Gentiles, multa apud eos depre-hendes, contra illa gravissima, uti ipsi hic loquuntur Adversarii, peccata: & Deus illa indulserit suo populo? II. Lex quæcumque honestatis & probitatis, qualis certe fuit Veteris populi, illa improbat & condemnat. III. Lex divina præscribit, ut homines sancti sint, quemadmodum ipse Deus sanctus est. Cum quo impuritas & profanitas illa consistere nullo modo potest. IV. Vetuit omnes omnino mali concupiscentias: ergo & illa, de quibus nunc disputamus. V. Conscientia, vita, & religio Patrum alia fuit, & aliena à flagitiis illis: atque ea detestati fuerunt, & exemplo suo condemnarunt. VI. Doctrina certe alia. Vide quæ adversus scortationem & scorta, Lex dicit, & Salomon in Proverbiis, ibidemque de tota vitâ caste, pure, & sobriè instituendâ. Quæ qui ibi non legit, non certe uti oportet, in Sacris versatur. Exod. xxii. 16. Levit. xix. 29. Num. xv. 39. Deut. xxiii. 17. Jerem. v. 8.9. Prov. vi. 25. & vii. 5. xxiii. 31. 33. Eccles. xi. 9. Neque Socinus diffitetur, fornicationem animi in Veteri Test. fuisse prohibitam, quamvis neget pro adulterio censi-tam fuisse: uti ad Matthæum, eum dicere meminimus. VII. Siquidem concessa illa olim fuissent, & non vetita, Deus haudquaquam tam graviter illa puniisset in isto suo populo, uti Apostolus observat, 1 Cor. x. 7. 8. Denique nec Christus illa novis præceptis prohibuit, neque ex doctrina Christi novas leges promunt Adversarii, vel additiones. Quod eo magis annotamus, quia quando ex Prophetarum scriptus probamus nos, omnes illas impuritates vetitas, ideoque reprehensas fuisse, regerere solent, ex Prophetis illa nostra peti, non ex lege, uti & hoc in casu, apud Smalcium videre est, disp. contra Frantz. pag. 247. & Volkelium, loco mox adducendo. Quasi non eadem utrorumque hac in re fuisset doctrina, legis, & prophetarum: sed nec ipsi semper ex verbis Christi proferunt additiones, quas nomine Christi jactant, & de quibus est controversia, num Christus earum inventor sit & auctor.
units.tr: 1. Those shameful acts (for the Adversaries say nothing else, when they claim that these things were allowed in the Old Testament and were prohibited only in the New, and they use that very terminology here) are condemned even by the law of nature and by the judgment of reason. So they cannot have been permitted in the Old Testament. Consult the Gentiles: you will find many things among them that are condemned, as the Adversaries themselves here call these the most grievous sins. Would God have allowed these things to his own people? II. Every law of honesty and uprightness, which surely belonged to the people of old, disapproves and condemns them. III. The divine law prescribes that men be holy, just as God himself is holy. Such impurity and profanity cannot possibly coexist with that. IV. It forbade absolutely all evil lusts; therefore also those of which we are now disputing. V. The conscience, life, and religion of the Fathers were different, and averse to those shameful acts; they detested them and condemned them by their example. VI. The teaching was certainly different. See what the Law says against whoredom and harlots, and what Solomon says in the Proverbs, and in the same place about ordering one's whole life chastely, purely, and soberly. Whoever does not read these things there, surely does not engage with the Sacred Writings as he should. Exod. 22:16. Lev. 19:29. Num. 15:39. Deut. 23:17. Jer. 5:8, 9. Prov. 6:25; 7:5; 23:31, 33. Eccles. 11:9. Nor does Socinus deny that fornication of the mind was forbidden in the Old Testament, although he denies that it was counted as adultery; as we recall him saying on Matthew. VII. For if those things had once been allowed and not forbidden, God would by no means have punished them so severely in his own people, as the Apostle observes, 1 Cor. 10:7, 8. Finally, Christ did not forbid them by new precepts, nor do the Adversaries bring forth new laws or additions from the teaching of Christ. We note this all the more because, when we prove from the writings of the Prophets that all those impurities were forbidden and therefore reproved, they are accustomed to reply that our proofs are drawn from the Prophets, not from the Law; as may be seen in this very case in Smalcius, disp. contra Frantz. pag. 247, and in Volkelius, in the place about to be cited. As if the teaching of the Law and of the Prophets were not the same on this point in both! Nor, indeed, do they themselves always bring forward from the words of Christ the additions which they boast of in Christ's name, and about which there is controversy: whether Christ is their inventor and author.

units.la: Audiamus, atque examinemus exceptionem Volkelii, ad locum Jesa. v. verf. 11. 22.
units.tr: Let us hear and examine the objection of Volkelius, on Isaiah 5:11, 22.

units.la: Quanquam autem ista olim etiam prohibita fuisse multi censent: tamen secus sese quam simpliciter commessationes ebrietatem habere facile constabit, si illud testimonium justis ponderibus examinabimus, quod opinionis istius confirmanda causa in medium afferri solet. Extat autem locus iste apud
units.tr: Although many think these things were also forbidden of old, it will easily be shown that they concern something other than simple carousing and drunkenness, if we examine with just weights that testimony which is commonly brought forward to confirm this opinion. Now that passage is found in

units.la: Resp. 1. Quid ain' improbè, nequa-quam [?] simpliciter commessationes ebrietatem [?] que prohibitas olim fuisse? non illo lo-nium justis ponderibus examinabimus, quod co? Ego verò dico, quamvis locus ille non extaret, innumera tamen alia tum in specie, tum in genere, & à fiEsaiam Vatem, qui hunc in modum loquitur: Væ, qui consurgitis mane ad ebrietatem fe-standam, & potandum usque ad vesperam, ut vino æstuetis: cithara, & lyra, & tympanum, & tibia, & vinum in conviviis vestris, & opus Domini non respicitis, nec opera manuum ejus consideratis. Item: Væ qui potentes estis ad bibendum vinum, & viri fortes ad miscendam ebrietatem. Quo in loco animadvertendum est, nequaquam sim-pliciter commessationes ebrietatemque prohi-beri; sic enim & usum quoque musicorum instrumentorum interdictum tunc fuisse, pra-sertim in conviviis, concludendum esset, quod nemo, ut arbitramur, concesserit. Ex ea igi-tur parte commessationes illa apud Esaiam vituperantur, quatenus commessatores illi, ut ibidem dicitur, voluptatibus penitus im-mersi, opus Dei non respexerunt, & opera manuum ejus non considerarunt, adeoque Deo metum non præstiterunt, nec illi, qui om-nium bonorum fons origoque est, ut par erat, gratias egerunt. Adde quod, si maxi-me Vates istos, quos alloquebatur, rebus hic memoratis prohibuisset; non tamen protinus ad omnes omnium temporum Israelitas id spe-staret[?]: cum qua Israelitas generatim omnes devincirent, nequaquam ex Vatibus, sed ex fœdere[?] cum omnibus per Mosen factio[?] petenda fuerint. pag. 268.
units.tr: Reply 1. What do you say, that carousing and drunkenness were in no way simply forbidden of old? I, however, say that even if that passage did not exist, there are countless others, both specific and general, from Isaiah the prophet, who speaks in this manner: Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, and drink until evening, so that you grow hot with wine; with lyre and harp, tambourine and flute, and wine at your feasts, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the deeds of his hands. Likewise: Woe to you who are mighty to drink wine, and valiant men to mix strong drink. In this place it must be noted that carousing and drunkenness are not simply forbidden; for then it would have to be concluded that the use of musical instruments was also forbidden at that time, especially at feasts, which, as we think, no one would concede. Therefore those carousings are condemned by Isaiah only in so far as those revellers, as it says there, being wholly immersed in pleasures, did not regard the work of God nor consider the deeds of his hands, and so did not give fear to God, nor give thanks, as was right, to him who is the fount and origin of all good things. Add that, even if the Prophet had forbidden those men he addressed the things mentioned here, it would not immediately follow that this applied to all Israelites of all times, to whom the whole nation was bound by the covenant made through Moses, and which must be sought not from the Prophets but from the covenant made with all people through Moses. p. 268.

units.la: mili adferri posse, quæ turpitudines illas rejiciant & condemnent: neque hoc Scripturam tantum, sed ipsam adeo facere naturam. Quis credidisset unquam homines extituros, qui super eo turbas & controversiam Ecclesiæ moverent, & contenderent, illa olim prohibita non fuisse, quæ inter vitia, nemo quod sciam hominum ratione utentium non posuit? Nonne locus iste apud Iesaiam exserte illos notat, qui surgunt mane ad festandam[?] ebrie-tatem, ad potandum, & potentes sunt ad potum, fortes ad miscendam ebrietatem? & negabis tamen ebrieta-tem illis prohiberi, damnari? Non cen-seo multis operose sententiam illam re-tundendam esse, piis & modestis vel nudâ sui expositione detestandam. ii. Non est, quod vereamur usum tympanorum, & instrumentorum mu-ficorum sic simul interdictum, quia hoc loco non de usu illorum agitur, sed de abusu: atq; hoc rejicitur, quo de nunc disputamus, non aliud. iii. Non autem dici potest, ebrietatis aliquis abusus: ea etenim per se vitiosa est, & nunquam probari potest vel exerceri. iv. Reprehenduntur cantiones & mu-sicalia, propter ebrietatem, cui conci-liandæ vel ornandæ adhibentur: quare ista adhuc magis, & simpliciter damnanda fuit. v. Quam insulse dicitur, comessationes & ebrietatem apud Pro-phetam vituperari, ideo quod voluptati penitus immersi opus Dei non respi-ciunt; quasi comessatores & ebriosi unquam alii sint, vel Dei opus considerent, Deum timeant, aut ei, prout par est, agant gratias? & non omnia con-trario modo apud ebriosos necessario & perpetuo se habeant? Quod si ergo ebrietas hoc proprium habeat, & quamvis (hoc ut demus obiter) non ipsa, illud tamen clare prohibitum sit, nonne sic & ea satis quoque interdicta æsti-mabitur, cui illa tam intrinsece conveniunt & inseparabiliter? vi. Quid iterum hoc, non commune & universalis præcepti, quod Propheta hic habet, sed suæ aut doctrinæ, aut temporis fuisse speciale? Quasi hoc proponat, tamquam particulare aliquod, & non ut juris, vel observantiæ universalis? & quasi non hac ex parte facile revinci potuisset Propheta, si sui temporis ebriosos inaudito & duriori modo excepisset, quam alias, & ex lege quidem licuisset? Denique non audiant hæc Athei, Libertini, Adversarii legis & Prophetarum, vel Gentiles, & Judæi ipsi, ebrietatem, & comessationes non esse in lege, & doctrinâ fœderis antiqui prohibitas. Non enim unum hinc scandalum sequuturum, nemo, credo, non videt. Præsertim quum hæc ipsa inter peccata gravia, & naturâ sua hominem damnantia referat alibi Smalcius, contra Smiglecium, de satisfactione, cap. viii. pag. 241. ubi ita: Equidem gravia peccata ea omnia esse judico, quæ carnis opera appellantur, & de quibus diserte scriptum est, quòd, qui ea faciunt, regnum Dei non sint hæreditaturi, vel simile quid, qualia sunt non tantum idololatria, veneficia, adulteria, homicidia, furta: sed etiam ira, contentio, inimicitia, invidia, convitia, ebrietas, comessatio, potationes, &c. Licet enim hæc ipsa inter se collata, alia aliis sint graviora, alia leviora: sunt tamen naturâ suâ talia, ut, si quis vel in uno illorum hæreat, vitam æternam eripere nobis possint. Atqui illa talia quæ sunt, negabis mala, & illicita, & vetita fuisse, etiam sub V. Test?
units.tr: …could be cited that reject and condemn those vile acts; and this is taught not only by Scripture but by nature itself. Who would ever have believed that there would be men who would stir up tumults and controversy in the Church about this, and contend that those things were not forbidden of old, which, among vices, no one, so far as I know, of men who use reason has ever placed elsewhere? Does not that passage in Isaiah plainly denote those who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, to drink, and who are mighty at drink, valiant in mixing strong drink? And yet you will deny that drunkenness was forbidden to them and condemned? I do not think that opinion needs to be refuted at length; it is to be detested by the pious and moderate even by a bare statement of it. ii. There is no reason to fear that the use of tambourines and musical instruments is thereby forbidden at the same time, because this place does not concern their use but their abuse; and it is this, which we are now disputing, that is rejected, nothing else. iii. Nor can it be said that there is some abuse of drunkenness: for drunkenness is in itself vicious and can never be approved or practised. iv. Songs and music are reproved on account of drunkenness, to which they are applied to promote or adorn it; therefore those things ought to be condemned even more, and absolutely. v. How foolishly it is said that carousing and drunkenness are censured in the Prophet because those wholly immersed in pleasure do not regard the work of God! As if carousers and drunkards were ever otherwise, or considered the work of God, feared God, or gave thanks to him as is right; and as if, among drunkards, all things were not necessarily and perpetually in the opposite state! If therefore drunkenness has this as its own property, and although (to grant this in passing) it is not drunkenness itself but that which is clearly forbidden, will not that also be judged sufficiently forbidden with which drunkenness agrees so intrinsically and inseparably? vi. Again, why is this said to be not a common and universal precept, which the Prophet here gives, but special to his own teaching or time? As if he set it forth as something particular, and not as a matter of universal law or observance? And as if the Prophet could not easily have been refuted on this point, had he treated the drunkards of his own time in an unheard-of and harsher manner than was otherwise permitted by the Law? Finally, let not Atheists, Libertines, adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, or Gentiles and the Jews themselves hear these things, that drunkenness and carousing are not forbidden in the Law and in the teaching of the old covenant. For no one, I think, fails to see that a scandal would follow from this. Especially since Smalcius himself, elsewhere, against Smiglecius, on satisfaction, chapter 8, p. 241, counts these very things among grave sins which condemn a man by their nature, where he says: Indeed I judge those to be grave sins, all those which are called the works of the flesh, and of which it is plainly written that those who do them will not inherit the kingdom of God, or something similar; such are not only idolatry, sorcery, adultery, murder, theft, but also anger, strife, enmity, envy, reproaches, drunkenness, carousing, drinking bouts, etc. For although these, compared with one another, are some more grievous and some lighter, yet they are of such a nature that if anyone clings to even one of them, they can snatch eternal life from us. Now, will you deny that these things, which are such, were evil, unlawful, and forbidden, even under the Old Testament?

units.la: Neque aliter Oftorodus, neque melius philosophatur, Instit. cap. xxx. sed quasi de impietate contenderent inter se non minus Adversarii, ac nobiscum, primo dicit aperte, pag. 219. Deum per Mosen nihil omnino præcepisse, quod modestiam & temperantiam vel sobrietatem concerneret, sed concessisse voluptates ut quærerent in cibo & potu, vestibus & similibus. pag. 220. Nec luxum vestium prohibuisse. pag. 222. Nihil in Mosis præceptis legi, quod Deus inutiles sermones, jocos, urbanitates, quin nec mendacia, juramenta & convitia, lügen / fluchen und schelten aperte prohibuerit. certe horrenda de sanctâ Veterum religione themata. postquam vero ad locum Jesa. v. 11. 12. dixit, quod post eum, & forte ex eo Volkelius; jam etiam pro eo argumentum producere haud erubescit, ex Eccle-siaste, quod enim non simpliciter ejusmodi voluptates fuere prohibita, ex eo manifeste apparet, quod hominem, dum adhuc valet, voluptates sectari, hic illic in suis scriptis admoneant. Eccles. 11. 24. & 111. 12. 13. & v. 17. 18. 19. & viii. 15. & ix. 7. 8. 9. inquit, pag. 221. Quasi aliquis nescit quæcunque hujus rei apud Ecclesiastem occurrunt, non debere intelligi de voluptatibus, quas, ne Scripturam dicam, & Sanctorum etiam Veteris Testament. exempla, ipsa ratio, & vel Ethinicorum ethica coarguunt, id est, immoderatis & luxu ple-nis; sed de bona & læta animi in rebus suis contentatione, & fruitione bono-rum, à Deo concessorum, hilari atque honestâ. Mirum autem ita profane illos ioqui de doctrinâ Veterum, & lege Mosis, in quâ ea videre nequeant, quæ solâ conscientiâ & naturâ duce Gentiles docenda sequendaque esse satis perspexerunt: præsertim quum probaturi illa ex Novo Testamento, ad legem recurrant, & ad generale præceptum atque fundamentum ejus de dilectio-ne. Sic ipse Oftorodus, pag. 222. Quod autem spectat cibum & potum, vestimenta & similia, Christiano haud est integrum excedere modum, qui in N. Test. partim expresse, partim generali præcepto amoris præscriptus est. Atqui amor annon legis est? eum annon Euangelium ex lege Mosis mutuatur? & si eo comprehendi illa dixeris, quæ ex N. Testam. probare intendis, annon tum in lege ea occurrunt eadem ? an etiam de iis dicere sustinebis, nihil omnino istorum in Mosis præceptis legi, quæ tamen perfectum adeo præscribunt amorem & dile-ctionem, cum Dei, tum proximi, ut Christus & Apostoli in N T. non aliunde eam doceant, quam ex lege? Idem iterum, pag.224. Christianum in vestibus cavere duo hæc oportet, luxum, & superbiam. Nempe hoc nos docet magnum in Euangelio præ-ceptum amoris, quod plane etiam ea quæ de cibo ac potu diximus, confirmat. Verum illud magnum præceptum Christus totidem verbis inquit, legis esse, Matth. xxii. Atque tu dices, in lege Mosis, ubi præceptum, & inde præceptum magnum istud petitur, ex quo luxum damnas, nihil de luxu, de superbia, de intemperantia, & immodestia docere aut præscribere ?
units.tr: Ostorodus philosophises no differently and no better in his Institutes, chapter 30. But as though our opponents were disputing about impiety among themselves no less than with us, he first says plainly, p. 219: God through Moses commanded nothing at all that concerned moderation, temperance or sobriety, but allowed people to seek pleasures in food and drink, in clothing and the like. p. 220: Nor did he forbid the luxury of clothing. p. 222: Nothing is read in the precepts of Moses that God openly forbade: useless talk, jokes, witticisms, nor even lies, oaths and abuse (lügen / fluchen und schelten, that is, lying, cursing and scolding). These are dreadful theses about the holy religion of the ancients. After he had turned to Isaiah 5:11-12, which Volkelius perhaps followed after him and from him, he is not ashamed to produce an argument for the same point from Ecclesiastes: that such pleasures were not simply forbidden is clear from the fact that, while a man is still well, the writers here and there in their books advise him to pursue pleasures. Eccles. 2:24, 3:12-13, 5:17-19, 8:15, 9:7-9, p. 221. As if anyone did not know that whatever occurs on this subject in Ecclesiastes must not be understood of pleasures which, not to mention Scripture or the examples of the Old Testament saints, reason itself and even the ethics of the Gentiles condemn, that is, pleasures that are immoderate and full of luxury; rather, they must be understood of a good and cheerful contentment of mind in one's own affairs, and of the joyful and honourable enjoyment of goods granted by God. It is strange, however, that they speak so profanely of the teaching of the ancients and of the law of Moses, in which they cannot see what the Gentiles, guided by conscience and nature alone, have quite clearly seen must be taught and followed. This is especially so since, when they want to prove these things from the New Testament, they have recourse to the law, and to its general precept and foundation, that of love. So Ostorodus himself, p. 222: As for food and drink, clothing and the like, it is not open to the Christian to exceed the measure, which is prescribed in the New Testament partly expressly, partly by the general precept of love. But is love not part of the law? Does the Gospel not borrow it from the law of Moses? And if you say that those things which you intend to prove from the New Testament are comprehended under it, do those same things not occur in the law? Or will you also be bold enough to say that nothing of these is read in the precepts of Moses, although these precepts prescribe such perfect love and dilection, both of God and of neighbour, that Christ and the Apostles in the New Testament teach it from no other source than the law? Again, p. 224: The Christian must be careful about two things in clothing, luxury and pride. For the great precept of love in the Gospel teaches us this, which plainly also confirms what we have said about food and drink. But Christ says in so many words that this great precept is of the law, Matthew 22. And will you say that in the law of Moses, where that precept is found and from which this great precept is drawn, and from which you condemn luxury, there is nothing taught or prescribed about luxury, pride, intemperance and immodesty?

units.la: Præterea, ubi delicias & voluptates in cibo & potu Christiano interdictas probaturus est ex N. Testamento, fatetur, hoc non exserte præcipi, modo ex locorum quorundam N. Test. circumstantiis colligi posse. qui concludendi modus quum non magis in N. quam V. Test. adhiberi & probari debeat, quis tam cæcæ vel obstinatæ mentis est, ut asserere audeat, ex nullius ullorum in V. Test. locorum circumstantiis, ne expressa dicam testimonia, convinci posse, designata illa superius flagitia, de quibus hæc est disputatio, pro peccatis in V. Test. censita fuisse?
units.tr: Moreover, where he intends to prove from the New Testament that delights and pleasures in food and drink are forbidden to the Christian, he admits that this is not expressly commanded, but can only be gathered from the circumstances of certain passages of the New Testament. If this method of inference ought not to be applied and accepted more in the New than in the Old Testament, who is of so blind or obstinate a mind as to dare to assert that from the circumstances of no passage of the Old Testament, not to say express testimonies, can it be shown that those crimes mentioned above, which are the subject of this dispute, were counted as sins under the Old Testament?

units.la: Interim neque placet ipsis, Anabaptistarum in vestimentis anxietas, quos aperte sub nomine <bl>Die Täuffer</bl>[?] taxat Ostorodus, quod jugum imponant aliis non ferendum, & sua singularitate se contemptibiles passim reddant. Concedit etiam ditioribus lautitias in vestibus & cibis, præaliis. pag. 240. Ut quid hic velint, vel quo se distinguant, vix dignoscas: nisi quod contumeliose de V. Test. religione & Patribus loqui, hoc satis habere videantur.
units.tr: Meanwhile the anxiety of the Anabaptists about clothing does not please them either. Ostorodus openly censures them under the name Die Täuffer [the Anabaptists], because they impose a yoke that cannot be borne by others and, by their peculiarity, make themselves contemptible everywhere. He also concedes to the wealthier men luxuries in clothing and food, p. 240. What they want here, or how they distinguish themselves, you can hardly tell, except that they seem to think it enough to speak insultingly of the religion of the Old Testament and of the Fathers.

units.la: Istud vero ad cumulum improbitatis accedit, quod Autor ille, uti de Deo, & religione V. Test. ita & de Scriptura tam contemtim ac indigne loquitur. Pag. 221. præterea & hoc considerandum, quod quando Salomon, vel Syrac (de Syracho non laboramus, sed componi juxta se utrumque Auctorem indignamur) de moribus aliquid dicunt, quod in lege Mosis non expresse præceptum vel prohibitum est, non magis teneat vel obliget, quam alterius cujusque viri sapiens consilium & doctrina: cui siquis obtemperet, bene & recte fecisse, sin contra, non tamen ideo contra Mosis legem peccasse censetur. Hoc scilicet deerat improbitati, ut Salomonis Proverbia, & quidni pari modo aliorum quoque S. scripta de moribus, pro humanis haberentur, non pro divinis & θεόπνευστος[?] de quo etiam diximus, lib. 1. Socin. Confutati, cap. 1.
units.tr: Moreover, to crown his impudence, this author speaks of Scripture as contemptuously and unworthily as he speaks of God and the religion of the Old Testament. Page 221: Furthermore, this also must be considered: when Solomon, or Sirach (we are not concerned with Sirach, but we are indignant at having the two authors set side by side), say something about morals that is not expressly commanded or forbidden in the law of Moses, it does not bind or oblige any more than the wise counsel and teaching of any other man. If anyone follows it, he is said to have done well and rightly; if he does not, he is not thereby considered to have sinned against the law of Moses. Clearly this was all that was lacking to his impudence: that the Proverbs of Solomon, and why not likewise the writings of the other saints on morals, should be regarded as human rather than divine and theopneustos [θεόπνευστος], a point we also made in book 1 of Socinianismi Confutati, chapter 1.

units.la: Ad præceptum octavum de non furando, dicunt per Christum additam fuisse prohibitionem avaritiæ. ex Luc. xii. 15. Ita Catechesis Racoviensi pag. 203. Volkelius duo dicit, avaritiam, & luxum. lib. iv. cap. xviii. Sed jam ea cognoscenda sunt nobis, quæ Christus huic præcepto adjunxit. Intelligendum igitur est, Christum velle, ut ea omnia, quæ honestissimo etiam pacto comparata a nobis sunt, vita tamen nostra necessitates superant, non nostra sed aliorum esse censeamus: quod ut faciamus, charitatis in N. Fœdere nobis præscripta summo jure admonemur. Quod quidem ne a nobis violaretur, Christus ipsiusque Apostoli summopere laboraverunt, tum avaritia cri-
units.tr: Regarding the eighth precept, You shall not steal, they say that Christ added a prohibition of covetousness, from Luke 12:15. So the Racovian Catechism, page 203. Volkelius names two things, covetousness and luxury (book 4, chapter 18). But now we must consider what Christ added to this precept. We should understand, then, that Christ wills that all those things which we have acquired even by the most honourable means, but which exceed the necessities of our life, we should regard as belonging not to us but to others. And that we may do this, we are most rightly admonished by the charity prescribed to us in the New Covenant. Christ and his Apostles laboured greatly that this should not be violated by us, condemning covetousness and all luxury with severity.

units.la: Tom. 2. men , tum luxum omnem severe notando ; qua res dua , cateroquin a se invicem longissi-me distantes , in eo tamen conveniunt , quod liberalitatem pauperibus debitam impediant, quanquam non semper aequaliter. pag. 277. Atqui hac ratione confundit addita-menta septimi praecepti, & octavi. Ibi enim prohibitas dixit comessationes, & ebrietatem : ergo & luxus : namque haec unius & ejusdem generis sunt, & ipse formam ejus consistere in comessatione, aperte testatur, pag. 284. sed, inquit, ad illud praeceptum, de luxu , vel comessatione dictum , quatenus libidinis ministra est ; ad istud, quatenus benignitatem exhaurit : at sic de eadem re , seu virtute seu vitio ad singula fere praecepta agi posset iterum iterumque, quatenus eorum usus ad varios casus, praeceptis singulis notatos , referri sem-per possunt. Smalcius, de Divinit. pag. 21. Prohibet lex , ne furemur : Perfecit eam & implevit D. Jesus , dum non tantum aliena rapere prohibet , & egentem juvare praecipit : verum etiam non permittit , ut quis , quantumvis id absque alicujus injuria facere possit, plus bonorum acquirat , quam ei opus est ad sustentandam hanc vitam : & si tamen plus acquisiverit aut possideat, quam ei opus est , id totum suadet in liberalitatem erga egenos , & in alios usus pios convertere : miram denique & divinam quandam in omni vita temperantiam praescribit, ne ulla ratione id in nosmet ipsos conferamus , quod aliis , jure charitatis , debetur. Non opinor dicit , a Christo demum prohibitam rapinam ; praeceptam eleemosynam vel liberalitatem erga egentes ; denique & in omni vita temperantiam : quae tamen ita conjungit omnia , ut existimare quis possit , eum illa omnia sub perfectione & impletione legis comprehendere , a Christo facta. Ipsam vero avaritiam, quam solam Catechesis nominat , a Christo, ad hoc praeceptum prohibitam , miror quod non exprimat. Quod autem Adversarii dicunt, avaritiam esse , si quis plura possideat, quam ad sustentandam vitam opus sit, & propterea ea quae necessitates illas superant omnia, non nostra esse, sed aliorum , & totum in usus aliorum, sive egenorum erogandum esse, pluribus exponendum videtur, & limitandum.
units.tr: Vol. 2. These two vices, otherwise very far apart from each other, agree in this: that they hinder the liberality owed to the poor, though not always equally, page 277. Yet by this reasoning he confuses the additions to the seventh and the eighth precepts. For there he said that revelling and drunkenness are forbidden; therefore luxury too, for these are of one and the same kind, and he openly testifies that its form consists in revelling, page 284. But, he says, the precept about luxury or revelling is said in so far as it is the servant of lust; the other, in so far as it exhausts kindness. But in this way, the same matter, whether a virtue or a vice, could be discussed again and again in relation to almost every single precept, since their use can always be referred to the various cases noted under each precept. Smalcius, On the Divinity, page 21: The law forbids us to steal. Lord Jesus fulfilled and perfected it, not only by forbidding us to seize what belongs to others and commanding us to help the needy, but also by not permitting anyone, however much he could do so without injury to anyone, to acquire more goods than he needs to sustain this life; and if he has acquired or possesses more than he needs, he urges him to turn all of it to the liberality towards the needy and to other pious uses. Finally, he prescribes a wonderful and divine temperance in the whole of life, so that on no ground do we bestow upon ourselves what by the right of charity is owed to others. I do not think he says that theft was forbidden only by Christ; that almsgiving or liberality towards the needy was commanded; and finally that temperance in the whole of life was required. Yet he so joins all these things together that one might think he comprehends all of them under the perfecting and fulfilling of the law, effected by Christ. But that he does not express covetousness itself, which alone the Catechism names as forbidden by Christ under this precept, I wonder. As for what the opponents say, that covetousness is to possess more than is needed to sustain life, and that therefore all those things which exceed those necessities are not ours but others', and must be spent entirely on the uses of others, or of the needy, this seems to require further explanation and qualification.

units.la: Nimirum 1. Ostorodus magno conatu studet evertere communem avari-tiae definitionem , quod sit immoderata cupiditas habendi bona , & pecuniam. Cujus loco aliam substituit, nim. quod sit cupiditas plura habendi, quam necesse sit. Verum quae definitiones facile conciliari atque in unum redigi possunt. nempe immoderata cupiditas est ea , qua plura cupis quam quidem necesse sit : neque enim aliud & proprior modus dari cupiditati potest, quam τὸ δέον. 11. Duo hic occurrunt termini, qui objectum praebent humanarum cupiditatum, τὸ δέον, & τὸ περισσόν seu περιττόν, necessarium, & superfluum. Illud petere licet, atque teneris, & curare atque anniti quo habeas : istud non. Nemini licet inhiare rebus superfluis, quod Apostolus dixit, βλέπετε ἀπὸ πάσης πλεο-νεξίας, 1 Tim. vi. 9. sed cupiditates & curae coercendae sunt, ἀπὸ τῆς περισσείας, Luc. xii. 15. intra ea quae necessaria, panem ἄρτον [?], לֶחֶם חֻקִּי [?] Prov. xxx. 8. Neque nisi ex intemperantia est, quod homo nisi divitiis contentari nequeat aut nolit. Ut fruftraneam operam agant Adversarii, quando tantis ambagibus probare studeant, cupiditatem ditescendi esse illicitam. Quod nos neutiquam negamus. Neque aliud hoc est, quam cupiditatem immodicam damnare: id quod omnes faciunt. Nam uti ultra modum est [illegible, ~6 letters], ita modo non contentum esse & mediocritate, eoque quod necessitas postulat; sed concupiscere divitias, neque nisi iis saturari, absque peccato non fit. Proinde Syriaca versio Luc. xii. 15. habet, cavete ab omni cupiditate [illegible, ~6 letters], neque enim in abundantia divitiarum est vita. & Persica ibidem: omni malo amorem divitiarum pejorem scitote, & ab eo potissimum cavete: eo quod non in abundantia gregum & animalium vita constat. iii. Aliud autem est, divitias concupiscere, aliud eas habere: uti, si Deus tibi quovis modo, vel labore manuum, aut alia justa vocatione, vel hereditate, donatione, aliisque modis opes adjiciat, caeteroquin forte tua, etiam extra divitias, contento, omnino licet illas pos-sidere, non repuere. Pfalm, lxii. 11. Tertio, neque negamus, avaritiam, praeterquam in cupiditate acquirendi, sed etiam esse in retinendi bona superflua. iv. Nimirum ubi ea retinemus, cum dispendio eorum, quae ad Dei glo-riam, & proximi, praesertim egenorum commodum, eroganda erant, vel, uti loquitur Volkelius, si liberalitatem pauperibus debitam impediant. Atque ita nihil novi hac in parte Adversariis, quod videri tamen volunt, prolatum.
units.tr: Certainly, first, Ostorodus struggles with great effort to overthrow the common definition of covetousness, that it is an immoderate desire for having goods and money. In its place he substitutes another: that it is a desire for having more than is necessary. But these definitions can easily be reconciled and brought into one. For "immoderate" desire is that by which you desire more than is in fact necessary, since no other and closer measure can be set for desire than τὸ δέον [what is needful]. Two terms occur here, which give the object of human desires: τὸ δέον and τὸ περισσόν or περιττόν, that is, "necessary" and "superfluous." It is lawful to seek the first, to hold on to it, and to take care and strive to have it; not the second. No one may lust after superfluous things, as the Apostle said, βλέπετε ἀπὸ πάσης πλεονεξίας [beware of all covetousness], 1 Tim. 6:9. Rather, desires and cares must be restrained from superfluity [ἀπὸ τῆς περισσείας], Luke 12:15, and kept within what is necessary: bread [ἄρτον], לֶחֶם חֻקִּי [bread of my portion], Prov. 30:8. Nor is it only from intemperance that a man cannot, or will not, be content with less than riches. So the Adversaries take useless pains when, with such circumlocutions, they strive to prove that the desire to grow rich is unlawful. We by no means deny this, and it amounts to nothing other than condemning immoderate desire, which everyone does. For just as it is beyond measure to be discontent with moderation and with what necessity requires, so it is not without sin to covet riches and not to be satisfied except with them. Accordingly, the Syriac version of Luke 12:15 reads: "Beware of every covetousness [illegible], for life does not consist in the abundance of riches." And the Persian version in the same place: "Know that the love of riches is worse than every evil, and beware of it above all, because life does not consist in the abundance of flocks and animals." iii. But it is one thing to covet riches and another to have them. If God adds wealth to you in any way, whether by the labour of your hands, by another lawful calling, by inheritance, gift, or other means, then, provided you are otherwise content even apart from riches, it is altogether permitted to possess them and not to reject them. Ps. 62:11. Thirdly, we do not deny that covetousness consists not only in the desire to acquire but also in the retaining of superfluous goods. iv. Namely, this happens when we retain them to the loss of those things which ought to be expended for the glory of God and the benefit of our neighbour, especially the needy; or, as Volkelius puts it, "if they hinder the liberality owed to the poor." And so the Adversaries have put forward nothing new on this point, although they wish it to appear so.

units.la: v. Neque enim volunt, ut quis opes suas statim aliis eroget, & sola praecise necessaria retineat, quamvis Volkelius dixerit, ea omnia quae vitae nostrae necessitates superant, non nostra, sed aliorum esse: quod Oftorodus non de transferenda eorum possessione, sed usu, ubi necesse est, non inhibendo, intelligit. Sic enim loquitur, Instit. cap. xxxi. pag. 238. Unde necessario sequitur, omnes illos, qui superflua non erogant ad honorem Dei promovendum, & proximi juvandas necessitates, pro avaris habendos esse. Quod tamen ita simpliciter & absolute dictum, de usu & redditibus, non de rebus & bonis ipsis, vel eorum summa accipi volumus: quod enim superfluum concernit, tum demum impendendum id censemus, ubi, nisi hoc fieret, neque Dei honor, neque proximi necessitas curaretur, atque ita adversus Dei proximique peccaretur dilectionem. Non enim credimus. eum pro avaro habendum, qui, ubi nec Dei gloria, neque proximi postulat necessitas, superfluum bonorum non divendat ut eorum pretium pauperibus distribuatur: quoniam non dicimus (quod possessionem attinet) eum qui habet, quo etiam carere possit, sed qui omnino illa habere velit, avarum esse &c. neque enim habere, sed quaerere divitias prohibitum. Quo nihil jam dicit, quod non ab omnibus agnoscitur: non, uti in fine capitis loquitur, quod forte a paucis antea rite intelle-ctum. Quis enim ea non capiat? Divitias, uti supra necessitatem & superfluas sunt, concupiscere, & quaerere non licere; at habere quidem. Usum earum non esse, cum Dei & proximi injuria, cohibendum. Summam & sortem ser-vandam esse. Denique, quo omnia illa tendunt, avaritiam esse peccatum. Trita haec, atque omnibus dicta. Interim loqui subinde aliter voluerunt, ut videretur discriminis aliquid, & limites avaritiae ipsis arctius positos, quam vulgo. Quae omnia clarissime revincuntur ex ipsorum praxi. Nam juxta illa themata, opinaretur quis, nullos aut raros apud ipsos esse divites: sed contra est, & multi apud eos opulenti, plura, quam necesse sit, possident, atque erga egenos non aliter se habent, atque vulgò alii. Videtur amplius quid dixisse Volkelius, pag. 278. quod si absque possessionum venditione, pauperibus debitum officium persolvere possumus; intelligendum nihilominus est, omnes superantium bonorum fructus, in illorum usus insumendos esse. Hoc enim perinde quodammodo erit, quasi opes illas vendidissemus; cum illis jam non ut nostris, sed tanquam alienis utamur. quod mox sic exponit, ut totum iterum evanescat. Nam objiciens sibi, quod dicunt homines, futuri etiam temporis habendam rationem esse, quare non statim omnia eroganda aliis, vel pauperibus: praemissa futuri temporis divisione in proximè, & longè futurum; de illo tempore concedit, Christiano in id parare Ilcere[?] ea, quae suppeditent ad cultum, & ad victum, & sibi & liberis. Quod iterum tam incertum est respectu eorum omnium, pro quibus curam rerum suarum conservandarum extendit, & temporis, ut generale illud, quod posuerat axioma, de omnibus quae supersunt bonorum fructibus in pauperes insumendis, adeo hic pereat, ut certi nihil constituatur, praeter generale, quod modo posuimus, ne quis bona sua, non dico eorum modo usum, sed & possessiones atque summam, fortem ipsam retineat, ubi erogationem eorum flagitat vel Dei honor, vel proximi necessitas. Nam & vitae conservationem, quam primo respiciendam ipsi, & ratio monent, ad totam familiam extendunt. Cujus, ut & necessitatis illius termini dum nulli constituuntur certi, res tota relinquitur in medio. Vita verò conservatio, verba sunt Volkelii, cujus in ista avaritia descriptione mentionem fecimus, non unius tantummodo hominis, sed omnium, qui ad illum respiciunt, utpote uxoris, liberorum, familiaeque sustentatione continetur: ita ut tum demum avaritia culpa in aliquem merito conferatur, cum iis, quae ad omnem ejus familiam alendam pertinent, minime contentus, plura cupit, eaque sollicite vel quaerit, vel asservat, nec, cum opus est, in pauperes erogat. Rectè. Ea qui non erogat, quae potest, & tenetur ad sublevandas proximi necessitates, peccat, & avarus est, atque usurpator eorum, quae alterius debebant esse, non sua propria.
units.tr: v. For they do not want a man to give away his wealth to others at once and keep only what is strictly necessary, although Volkelius has said that "all those things which exceed the necessities of our life are not ours but belong to others." Ostorodus understands this not of transferring their ownership but of their use, where necessity requires, without forbidding it. For he speaks thus in the Institutes, chap. 31, p. 238: "Hence it necessarily follows that all those who do not spend their superfluities to promote the honour of God and to help the necessities of their neighbour are to be regarded as covetous." Yet we wish this, said so simply and absolutely, to be taken of use and income, not of the things and goods themselves or their total sum. For as regards what is superfluous, we judge that it is to be spent only when, unless this were done, neither the honour of God nor the need of our neighbour would be cared for, and so we would sin against the love of God and neighbour. For we do not believe that he is to be regarded as covetous who, when neither the glory of God nor the need of a neighbour requires it, does not sell the superfluity of his goods so that their price may be distributed to the poor. For we do not say (as far as possession is concerned) that the man who has something he could even do without is covetous, but that the man who wishes to have it at all costs is covetous, and so on; for it is not forbidden to have riches, but to seek them." Here he says nothing that is not acknowledged by everyone, and nothing, as he says at the end of the chapter, that "perhaps has been properly understood by few before." For who would not grasp it? Riches, insofar as they exceed necessity and are superfluous, may not be coveted or sought; but to have them is not forbidden. Their use is not to be restrained with injury to God and neighbour. Their sum and principal ought to be kept. Finally, to what all those statements tend: covetousness is a sin. These are commonplace, and said by everyone. Yet at times they have wished to speak otherwise, so that there would appear to be some distinction, and limits on covetousness set more narrowly by them than by the common view. All these things are most clearly refuted by their own practice. For according to those theses one would suppose that there are few or no rich men among them. But on the contrary, there are many wealthy among them, who possess more than is necessary, and they treat the needy no differently from others in general. Volkelius seems to have said something further, at p. 278: "If we can discharge our duty to the poor without selling our possessions, it must nevertheless be understood that all the fruits of goods beyond our needs are to be spent on their uses. For this will be in some way just as if we had sold those riches, since we now use them not as our own but as belonging to others." He then explains this in such a way that the whole thing vanishes again. For, raising an objection of his own, that men say that regard must be had for future time, why not give everything to others or to the poor at once, he concedes, after dividing future time into the near and the distant future, that for that time a Christian may lawfully lay aside what suffices for his worship and for his food and that of his children. This is so uncertain with respect to all those for whom he extends the care of preserving one's goods, and so uncertain as to time, that the general principle he had laid down, that all the fruits of goods beyond needs are to be spent on the poor, is so entirely lost here that nothing certain is established beyond the general point we have just stated: that no one should retain his goods, I do not say merely their use, but their possessions and their sum and principal itself, where the honour of God or the need of a neighbour demands their distribution. For they extend the preservation of life, which first of all he himself and reason bid us consider, to his whole household. And since no fixed limits of that necessity are set, the whole matter is left open. "But the preservation of life," in Volkelius's words, which I mentioned in his description of covetousness, "is sustained not only of one man but of all who depend on him, such as wife, children, and family. So fault for covetousness is justly charged against someone only when, not content with what is needed to support his whole family, he desires more, and either seeks or keeps it anxiously, and does not give it to the poor when there is need." Rightly so. Whoever does not give what he is able to give, and is bound to relieve the needs of his neighbour, sins, is covetous, and is a usurper of what ought to belong to another, not his own.

units.la: Ut revertamur, unde defleximus. Negamus prohibitionem avaritiae, ad praeceptum octavum, à Christo nunc demum sub N. Test. factam, & non etiam in V. Test. avaririam pro peccato habitam fuisse. Quod proprie hic controvertitur: si super naturâ aut definitione avaritiae etiam aliud, proponant id prius, quaesit[?], in terminis; atque tum de eo disputiemus. Sententiam verò nostram probamus. 1. Per generale praeceptum, ex quo Ostorodus hic argumentatur, dilectionis; & speciale, de non concupiscendo, quo avarus, eo quod avarus est, transgreditur. II. Idem comprehensum fuit prohibitione usurae, in fratrem egenum. Exod. xxii. 25. Levit. xxv. 36. 37. aliisque locis compluribus. III. Exod. xxiii. 21. jubentur judices probi deligi, osores avaritiae. adde Exod. xxiii. 8. Levit. xix. 13. Quarto probamus pro malo avaritiam & olim censitam fuisse, ex oratione Davidis, Psalm. cxix. 36, qua Deum precatur, ut ne cor suum flectat ad avaritiam. Similiter Prov. xxx. 8. Psalm. lxii. 11. IV. Ex redargutione Propheticâ, Jesa. v. 8. ad eos, qui domum ad domum, agrum ad agrum avare & sine modo congerebant. Proverb. i. 19. & xv. 27. & xxiii. 4. Jesa. i. 23. Jerem. vi. 13. & viii. 10. Hab. ii. 9. 1 Sam. viii. 3. 1 Reg. xxi. 2. 11 Reg. v. 12. quibus tum doctrinis, tum exemplis avaritia improbata & damnata manifeste fuit.
units.tr: To return to where we digressed. We deny that covetousness was forbidden only by Christ under the New Testament, in the eighth commandment, and that it was not also regarded as a sin under the Old Testament. This is the real point in dispute here. If they propose anything else concerning the nature or definition of covetousness, let them first state it clearly in terms, and then we will dispute about it. But we prove our opinion as follows. I. By the general precept of love, on which Ostorodus argues here, and by the particular precept "Thou shalt not covet," by which the covetous man transgresses precisely because he is covetous. II. The same was comprehended in the prohibition of usury against a needy brother: Exod. 22:25; Lev. 25:36, 37, and in many other places. III. Exod. 23:21 orders that upright judges be chosen, "haters of covetousness." Add Exod. 23:8; Lev. 19:13. Fourthly, we prove that covetousness was also judged an evil in former times, from David's prayer, Ps. 119:36, in which he asks God not to incline his heart to covetousness. Similarly Prov. 30:8; Ps. 62:11. IV. From the prophetic rebuke, Isa. 5:8, against those who greedily and without measure gathered house to house and field to field. Prov. 1:19; 15:27; 23:4; Isa. 1:23; Jer. 6:13; 8:10; Hab. 2:9; 1 Sam. 8:3; 1 Kings 21:2; 2 Kings 5:12. By these teachings as well as by these examples, covetousness was manifestly disapproved and condemned.

units.la: Denique, ad hominem, Volkelius, in initio capitis hujus, hoc praecepto quidem interdici furtum ait: veruntamen propter similitudinem quandam revocari huc posse videntur etiam alii modi, quibus commoda aliena intervertuntur, in lege prohibiti directe vel oblique. Si ea ad legem spectent, eâque comprehendantur, quaecumque propter similitudinem aliquam eo revocari possunt, etiam obliquè; sola ergo avaritia eo reduci non poterit? Oftorodus alibi, Instit. cap. xxiv. pag. 160. probaturus polygamiam sub N.Test. prohibitam, inquit, quamvis hoc, nempe plures una habere uxores, expressis verbis in N. Test. non prohibeatur, ex variis tamen circumstantiis videre possumus, omnino tamen id sub Evangelio non convenire. Recte. Sed quod si ex circumstantiis, non verbis modo ipsis, argumentari in N.Test. possumus; quare non etiam in Veteri? Quid, an dicent Adversarii, ex nullis circumstantiis V. Test. colligi posse, avaritiam malam fuisse, & prohibitam? Unde ergo Judaei, avarum satis genus, & hodie norunt avaritiam peccatum esse? Ne de Gentilibus dicam, & olim, & hodie idem peccatum detestantibus. Quodcunque vero dixerint Nostri, parum refert: hoc scio, neminem incorruptæ mentis illis facile assensurum.
units.tr: Finally, to the man himself: Volkelius, at the beginning of this chapter, says that this precept indeed forbids theft, but that because of a certain similarity, other ways by which others' goods are taken away also seem to be brought back here, forbidden in the law directly or indirectly. If those things belong to the law and are comprehended by it, whatever can be referred to it by some similarity, even indirectly, then why can covetousness alone not be brought under it? Ostorodus elsewhere, in his Institutes ch. 24, p. 160, wishing to prove that polygamy is forbidden under the New Testament, says: although this, namely having several wives, is not forbidden in express words in the New Testament, yet from various circumstances we can see that it is altogether unfitting under the Gospel. Rightly so. But if we can argue from circumstances, and not from the words alone, in the New Testament, why not also in the Old? Or will the Adversaries say that from no circumstances of the Old Testament can it be gathered that covetousness was evil and forbidden? Whence then do the Jews, a very covetous race, and today also know that covetousness is sin? I say nothing of the Gentiles, who both formerly and today detest the same sin. Whatever our people have said matters little: this I know, that no one of sound mind will readily agree with them.

units.la: Quod de avaritia, idem de luxu dicimus: utrumque non in Novo magis, quam in V. Test. fuisse prohibitum. Imo si quis horum, aliorumque, quæ Adversarii frustra dicunt, præceptis veteribus à Christo demum addita esse, naturam vitiumque introspexerit, videbit etiam plura in V. Test. occurrere illorum prohibitorum damnatorumque argumenta & exempla, quam in Novo. Quantopere luxus in V. Test. vel lege damnatus fuerit, apparet ex lege de filio immorigero, quem si Parentes luxus in cibo & potu accusassent apud judices, lapidibus obruebatur. Deut. xxi. 20. 21. Confer & Prov. xxiii. 20. Jesa. iii. 16. 17. &c. & v. 11. 12.
units.tr: What we say of covetousness, we say of luxury too: each was forbidden no more in the New Testament than in the Old. Indeed, if anyone looks closely into the nature and the vice of these things, and of the others which the Adversaries vainly say were added by Christ later to the old precepts, he will see that more arguments and examples condemning and forbidding them occur in the Old Testament than in the New. How greatly luxury was condemned even by law in the Old Testament appears from the law concerning the stubborn son, who, if his parents accused him of luxury in food and drink before the judges, was stoned to death. Deut. 21:20, 21. Compare also Prov. 23:20; Isa. 3:16, 17, etc., and 5:11, 12.

units.la: Quod objiciunt, vel annotant Adversarii, ad ea, quæ his locis dicuntur, Luc. 12. 15. Hebr. xiii. 5. 1 Tim. vi. 11. nullius est, nam non negatur, avaritiam, & curas illas rerum terrenarum immodicas prohiberi quoque in N. Test. neque de hoc est quæstio: verum an hic primum, & solum, non quoque in V. Test. prohibita eadem sint, quæritur: quod locis illis non docetur. Quinimo si loca illa debite attendantur, & res, & modus, & ratio interdicti non minus in V. Test. observabitur, quam in Novo.
units.tr: As for what the Adversaries object or remark on the passages cited, Luke 12:15, Heb. 13:5, 1 Tim. 6:11, it counts for nothing. For it is not denied that covetousness and those immoderate cares for earthly things are forbidden in the New Testament too, nor is that the question. The question is whether these same things were forbidden here first and alone, and not also in the Old Testament, which those passages do not teach. Indeed, if those passages are duly attended to, the matter, the manner and the reason of the prohibition will be observed in the Old Testament no less than in the New.

units.la: Præceptum nonum, quo prohibetur falsum de proximo testimonium, perfectum & adimpletum dicunt, prohibitione omnis mendacii. Quod Catechesis ambigue proponit, dicens eam ad præceptum illud pertinere: non autem, quomodo: an ut additamentum vel complementum ejus, an vero ut necessaria expositio rerum sub eo contentarum? Smalcius aperte, lib. de Divinit. pag.
units.tr: The ninth precept, by which false witness against a neighbour is forbidden, they say is perfected and fulfilled by the prohibition of every lie. The Catechism puts this ambiguously, saying that it pertains to that precept, but not how: whether as an addition or complement to it, or rather as a necessary explanation of the things contained under it? Smalcius openly, in his book On the Divinity, p.

units.la: 21. Prohibet lex ne falsum testimonium dicamus adversus proximum. Perfecit eam D. Jesus & implevit, dum omnis generis mendacia & levitates plane tollit; obtrectationes etiam, censuras, judicia & condemnationes à suis cultoribus longissime abesse vult, quae omnia mendacii species sunt. Expressissime Volkelius, dicit per Mosem prohibita quidem fuisse mendacia omnia damnosa; sed per Christum, levia etiam quaeque & temeraria.
units.tr: 21. The law forbids us to bear false witness against our neighbour. Jesus the Lord perfected and fulfilled it, when he entirely removes every kind of lie and levity; he wills that slander, censures, judgments and condemnations, all of which are kinds of lying, be far removed from his worshippers. Volkelius speaks most expressly: he says that through Moses indeed all harmful lies were forbidden, but through Christ also every light and rash lie.

units.la: Restat nunc explicandum, quid huic praecepto in Christi doctrina adjectum censeri queat. Istud autem est, quod Christus etiam illud mendacii genus quod temere profertur, & ex levitate quadam animi proficiscitur, etiamsi alteri non noceat, prohibuerit: cui adjungi possunt ea, quae in gestu factoque aliquo consistunt, simulationes dissimulationesque, frustra sineque justa causa suscepta: & si qua sunt similia. Quae quidem a Christiani hominis gravitate prorsus abhorrent, nec ei conveniunt, qui veritatis esse debet tenacissimus. Imprimis autem huc referri debent damnationes judiciaque illa, quibus apud Matthaeum Christus nos prohibet.
units.tr: It now remains to explain what may be thought to have been added to this precept in the doctrine of Christ. It is this: that Christ also forbade that kind of lie which is uttered rashly and comes from a certain levity of mind, even if it does no harm to another. To this may be joined those things which consist in some gesture or deed, simulations and dissimulations undertaken in vain and without just cause, and whatever is similar. These things indeed are wholly abhorrent from the gravity of a Christian man, nor do they suit one who ought to be most tenacious of the truth. Above all, those condemnations and judgments by which Christ forbids us in Matthew must be referred here.

units.la: Resp. I. Illa praecepto non debent dici addita demum per Christum, quae ad praeceptum vel referuntur, uti Catechesis dicit; vel species sunt mendacii, quod Smalcius: nam mendacia & testimonia falsa in genere lex designat, & prohibet. Vel si, prohibito aut expresso in praeceptis genere, totidem formanda sint praeceptorum additamenta, quot species rei vel praeceptae vel prohibitae, quot non praeceptorum undique supplent additiones? inde est, quod Volkelius dicere debuit, ad recensitas aliquot mendacii species, & si qua sunt similia.
units.tr: Reply I. Those things should not be said to have been added at last by Christ which either are referred to the precept, as the Catechism says, or are kinds of lying, as Smalcius says. For the law designates and forbids lies and false witness in general. Or if, with the kind forbidden or enjoined in the precepts, as many additions of precepts must be framed as there are species of the thing commanded or forbidden, how many additions would then supply what is not in the precepts on every side? Hence Volkelius ought to have said: to the several species of lying listed, and whatever is similar.

units.la: II. Dubitanter admodum rem hanc agunt Adversarii. Volkelius, in omnibus incerto & suspenso incedit gradu. Ubi de praecepto, juxta Mosis mentem exponendo, Moses, inquit, prohibuisse videtur ea falsa testimonia, quae proximum vel in vitae, vel fortunarum, vel honoris discrimen adducunt. Alia vero mendacia, hoc genere minime comprehensa, non usquequaque à Mose interdicta. Ergo aliquatenus saltem. Certe ubi in genere falsum testimonium, seu mendacium prohibetur, quis dubitet eo quascumque etiam mendacii species esse prohibitas, sive ex odio, sive levitate, aut quocunque animo profectas? non unde, vel qua causa, aut ratione oriatur malum, lex attendit, sed ipsum, in sua forma prohibet, vel ἀνομία. Quae mendacii ἀνομία, ubicunque fit, & in quacunque mendacii specie, hic censetur prohibita. Iterum, quando de praeceptis vel rebus à Christo additis, quid huic praecepto, inquit, in Christi doctrina adjectum censeri queat. enumeratis nonnullis levis mendacii speciebus, addit, & si qua sunt similia. Quod si additamentis Christi, quae dicuntur, quaecunque similia licite adjungit: quare non omnia, propter eandem similitudinem, ad ipsum quoque refert praeceptum legis?
units.tr: II. The Adversaries handle this matter very hesitantly. Volkelius walks with an uncertain and wavering step throughout. Where, expounding the precept according to the mind of Moses, he says: Moses seems to have forbidden those false testimonies which bring the neighbour into danger of life, fortune or honour; but other lies, not comprehended under this kind, were not entirely forbidden by Moses. Therefore at least in some measure. Certainly where false witness, or lying in general, is forbidden, who would doubt that all species of lying whatever are forbidden by it, whether they arise from hatred, levity, or any other intention? The law does not attend to whence or from what cause or reason the evil arises, but forbids the thing itself in its form, or lawlessness [ἀνομία]. This lawlessness of lying, wherever it occurs and in whatever species of lying, is here judged forbidden. Again, when he speaks of the things added by Christ, he says: what may be thought to have been added to this precept in Christ's doctrine; after listing some kinds of slight lying he adds and whatever is similar. But if he freely adds whatever similar things to the additions of Christ, which are said to be such, why does he not refer all of them, on account of the same similarity, to the precept of the law itself?

units.la: III. Nullum adducit Christi, de temerariis mendaciis praeceptum, vel prohibitionem. Matth. VII. 1. quae prohibentur judicia & condemnationes aliorum, ipsa lege vetita sunt, quia oriri illa dicit Volkelius, ex charitatis quodam defectu. Charitas autem perfecta lege praescribitur. IV. In Vet. Test. illa, & quaevis mendacii genera imo fuere prohibita. Praeterquam lege, quae generatim loquitur, insuper Levit. xix. 11. non furabimini, לֹא תִגְנֹבוּ & non mentiemini, neque dolose agetis vir cum proximo suo, & vers. 16. non eris detractor in populo populo tuo. Adde Prov. xxxi. 13. & xx. 19. Exod. xxiii. 1. 7. Psal. iv. 3. & xv. 3. & xxxiv. 13. & l. 20. & ci. 5. 7. Prov. iv. 24. & vi. 17. 19. & xii. 22. & xix. 22. & xxx. 8. Jesa. xxxii. 6. Jerem. ix. 6. Jezech. xxii. 9.
units.tr: III. He adduces no precept or prohibition of Christ concerning rash lies. Matt. 7:1, which forbids the judgments and condemnations of others, was itself forbidden by the law, since Volkelius says they arise from a certain defect of charity. But perfect charity is prescribed by the law. IV. In the Old Testament those and every kind of lie were indeed forbidden. Besides the law, which speaks in general terms, add Lev. 19:11, You shall not steal [לֹא תִגְנֹבוּ], and you shall not lie, nor deal falsely, a man with his neighbour, and verse 16, You shall not be a slanderer among your people. Add Prov. 31:13; 20:19; Exod. 23:1, 7; Ps. 4:3; 15:3; 34:13; 50:20; 101:5, 7; Prov. 4:24; 6:17, 19; 12:22; 19:22; 30:8; Isa. 32:6; Jer. 9:6; Ezek. 22:9.

units.la: Et altera hic quæstio movetur, de mendaciis officiosis, num sint licita. Fa nunquam, nec in Vet. nec Nov. Test. censent Adversarii fuisse prohibita. Volkelius, hoc cap. xix.
units.tr: A second question is raised here, about officious lies, whether they are lawful. The Adversaries never think they were forbidden either in the Old or the New Testament. Volkelius, this chapter 19:

units.la: Quin etiam quædam sunt, quæ vulgò officiosa mendacia solent appellari, quæ cum ad injuriam alterius non spectent, interim tamen prodesse cuiquam non parum queant, pro illicitis nunquam fuere habita, nec à nobis habentur: præsertim si videantur necessitate quadam expressa, & ad quempiam vel periculo, vel damno non exiguo liberandum pertineant; modo omne absit juramentum, aut quippiam simile, quod ad divini nominis contumeliam spectare possit.
units.tr: Indeed there are some things which are commonly called officious lies, which, since they do not aim at injury to another, can nevertheless be of no small benefit to someone. These were never held unlawful, nor are they held so by us, especially if they seem to be demanded by some necessity and pertain to freeing someone from danger or no small loss; provided only that every oath, or anything similar which could pertain to the contumely of the divine name, be absent.

units.la: Contrà nos sic argumentatur. 1. Quodcunque in se habet formam peccati & ἁμαρτίας[?], id, quantumcunque officiosum videatur, nunquam potest esse licitum. Non enim ex nostro arbitratu res fiunt licitæ aut illicitæ, vel ex usu, quem videamur facere peccati, eo evadit ipsum nullum, vel justum. Sola Dei lex actionum est regula, cumque eâ illarum vel ἐννομία[?], vel ἀνομία[?] peccatum constituit, aut virtutem. Veritatem sectari jubemur, & mendacium odisse. Ephes. iv. 25. quapropter deponentes mendacium, loquimini veritatem. Alia ex Vet. Test. loca produximus, lib. vii. contra Judæos, cap. viii.
