Jam autem nullum aut lucrum apparens aut damnum efficere potest, ne veritas vel mendacium minus sint hoc quod sunt, nimirum bonum alterum, alterum malum. Nulla peccandi est necessitas, vel utilitas. ii. Nunquam licet mala facere, ut bonum forte inde aliquod sequatur. Num pro Deo loquemini iniquitatem, vel pro eo loquemini dolum? Job. xiii. 7. Rom. iii. 8. Et non (sicuti blasphemamur, & uti quidam ajunt nos dicere) quod faciamus mala, ut eveniant bona.
units.tr: They argue against us thus. (1) Whatever has in itself the form of sin and of error [ἁμαρτίας], can never be lawful, however useful it may seem. For things are not made lawful or unlawful by our judgement, nor does an action that seems to be a sin by our practice turn out to be no sin, or to be just. God's law alone is the rule of actions, and by it those actions are constituted either lawful [ἐννομία] or lawless [ἀνομία], sin or virtue. We are commanded to pursue truth and to hate lying. Eph. 4. 25: therefore putting away lying, speak every man truth. We have brought forward other passages from the Old Testament in Book 7 against the Jews, chapter 8. Now no apparent gain or loss can make truth and lying less than what they are, namely the one good and the other evil. There is no necessity or advantage in sinning. (2) It is never permitted to do evil so that some good may perhaps follow from it. Job 13. 7: Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him? Rom. 3. 8: and not (as we are slandered, and as some affirm that we say) let us do evil that good may come.

units.la: Objicit Volkelius: Atque ad hoc innoxium mendaciorum genus pertinet illud obstetricum Ægyptiacarum, quo Judæorum infantes servabant; & illud factum Rachaha, quæ per mendacium exploratores illos à morte vindicavit: & Micholis prudentia, quæ mendacio maritum conservavit: & denique Jonathani pietas, qui simili ratione ac via Davidem de manibus Sauli liberavit. Exod. i. 19. Jos. ii. 4. 5. 1 Sam. xix. 17. & xx. 6. 28. 29. Resp. Non utcunque aliquod quorundam factum probatur, ideo & agendi modus. Pietas obstetricum Ægyptiacarum commendatur quidem, & opus quod patrabant erga Hebræos, in illis servandis & tuendis à tyrannide Regis, sed non id, quo forte usæ, mendacium. Similiter respondemus de Rahab, & de reliquis.
units.tr: Volkelius objects: To this harmless kind of lie belongs that of the Egyptian midwives, by which they saved the Jewish infants; and that deed of Rahab, who by a lie rescued those spies from death; and the prudence of Michal, who by a lie saved her husband; and finally the piety of Jonathan, who by a similar means and way freed David from the hands of Saul. Exod. 1. 19; Josh. 2. 4, 5; 1 Sam. 19. 17; 20. 6, 28, 29. Answer: The fact that some deed of certain people is approved does not mean that the manner of acting is approved too. The piety of the Egyptian midwives is indeed commended, and the work they performed for the Hebrews in saving and protecting them from the king's tyranny, but not the lie they perhaps used for this. We answer similarly about Rahab and the others.

units.la: Denique ad ultimum in Decalogo præceptum de concupiscentiâ, dicunt à Christo additum, ne tali concupiscentiâ nosmet tacitè oblectemur, neve eam animo concipiamus, aut foveamus. Catechesis: quid in Novo fœdere ei additum? Resp. Non solum ne ita concupiscamus, verum etiam ne rei cupitæ animum ullo modo adjiciamus, quamvis perficere concupiscentiam non constituamus, tamen ne eâ animum titil-lemus. lemus. Quod enim Christiano non convenit facere vel habere, neque concupiscere licet. Tria hic bene distinguenda, ut totidem gradus, rem concupiscere, concupiscen-tiâ delectari, eam perficere & prosequi. Illud quidem lex aperte prohibet. Neque Adversarii negant. Istud videtur Catechesis dicere à Christo additum: sed Smalcius alibi fatetur, lege etiam comprehendi: quod verum est. lib. de Divinit. cap. v. Prohibet denique lex, ne concupiscamus quicquam eorum, quae proximi sunt: perfecit eam D. Jesus & implevit, dum non tantum prohibet, quemadmodum lex prohibebat, ne ejusmodi concupiscentiis delectemur, sed ne unquam apud animos eas nostros concipiamus. Hic primos concupiscentiarum conceptus notat, à Christo prohibitos, non earum delectationes: & has tamen Catechesis designavit, non illas. Haec ejus verba, „Das man nicht allein / also nicht begeren / sondern das man auch sein herz nach den dingen die man begert / nicht hencken soll / ob man schon nicht gedachte die begierde zu vollenziehen / sondern nur sich allein in seinem herzen damit füßele.“ Non adeo primos motus, quam eorum titillationes ponit. Utrumque jungit Volkelius, cap. xx. Huic autem praecepto in novo foedere hoc adjunctum esse videtur, ut non solum ardenti incitatoque studio ea, quae proximi nostri sunt, minime appetamus: sed ne simplicem quidem de iis ad nos pertrahendis cogitationem, quae animis nostris forte obrepere possit foveamus, eave nos oblectemus ac veluti titillemus; sed potius simul ac in animum nostrum illabitur, ilico ei obsistamus, & eam haud secus ac funestissimam pestem ejiciamus. Ergo additum dicunt ad praeceptum illud de concupiscentia, à Christo, ne admittamus vel cogitationem rei concupiscendae, neve ea animum oblectemus, vel istam foveamus.
units.tr: Finally, as to the last commandment of the Decalogue, on concupiscence, they say that Christ added it so that we would not secretly take pleasure in such concupiscence, nor conceive it in our minds, or nurse it. Catechism: What was added to it in the New Covenant? Answer: Not only that we should not so desire, but also that we should in no way admit the desired thing into our minds, even though we do not resolve to carry out the desire; yet that we should not stir up our minds by it. For it is not permitted to a Christian to do or to have, nor even to desire, what is not fitting for him. Three things here must be carefully distinguished, as three degrees: to desire a thing, to take delight in the desire, and to carry it out and pursue it. The law clearly forbids the first. Nor do our opponents deny this. The Catechism seems to say that this is what Christ added; but Smalcius elsewhere admits that it is also contained in the law, which is true. In On the Divinity, chapter 5: Finally the law forbids us to desire anything that belongs to our neighbour; Lord Jesus fulfilled and perfected it, when he forbade not only, as the law forbade, that we should take delight in such desires, but also that we should ever conceive them in our minds. Here he notes the first conceptions of desires, forbidden by Christ, and not their delights; yet the Catechism has designated these, not those. Its words are (German): "That one should not only not so desire, but also should not hang one's heart upon the things one desires, even though one does not intend to carry out the desire, but merely dallies with it in one's heart alone." It sets down not so much the first motions as their titillations. Volkelius joins both, chapter 20: To this precept there seems to be added in the New Covenant this: that we should not only not desire with a burning and eager zeal those things which belong to our neighbour, but that we should not even foster a simple thought of drawing them to ourselves, which might perhaps creep into our minds, nor should we take pleasure in them or, as it were, tickle ourselves; but rather, as soon as it slips into our mind, we should at once resist it, and cast it out no differently than a most deadly plague. Therefore they say that Christ added to the precept on concupiscence that we should not admit even the thought of the thing to be desired, nor take pleasure in it in our minds, nor nurse it.

units.la: Respondeo autem: Verum esse, quod mala illa sint, vid. primam concupiscentiae nefariam, quam lex notat, cogitationem, ejusque apud animum oblectationem admittere. Sed ea ipsa lege, & natura, concupiscentiae comprehenduntur: ut non possis concupiscentiam habere absque illis, vel illa absque concupiscentiâ. Non licet concupiscere, inquit lex: ergo nec cogitationem habere concupiscendi: quomodo enim absque cogitatione concupiscendi, concupiscas? Non licet concupiscere: ergo nec oblectari te concupiscentiâ: ipsa enim actus lubentiae est; neque concupiscis malum, sed bo-num, sed saltem quod tale tibi videatur, ac placeat. Ut omnino impossibile sit naturam concupiscentiae prohibitae ejusve actum habere, absque omni titillatione & oblectatione, utcunque sit levior. Saltem ita & cogitatio, & obectatio concupiscentiae, sunt intrinseca & ei innexa, ut prohibitione con-cupiscentiae inclusa & contenta nemo, extra partes positus, inficiari possit, vel si etiam velit. Neque aliquid Adversarios in istam thesin rapit, quam sola animi pervicacia, volentes per fas & nefas legis imperfectionem arguere, & nova Christi ad leges singulas additamenta vel correctiones undecunque confingere. 11. Neque hic, ut alibi tamen in speciem, ulla Scripturae aut Christi testimonia adducunt, quibus ostendant, id quod probandum ipsis, à Christo demum illa addita legi, & prohibita fuisse. Nec aliquid Christi, aut N.Test. hic proferent, quod non itidem in V.Test. & communibus legis tabulis continetur. iii. Apostolus, quidquid in ratione concupiscentiæ prohibitum vidit, ex lege testatur se didicisse. Rom. vii. 7. quippe concupiscentiam non nôvissem, nisi lex dixisset, non concupisces.
units.tr: I answer, however: it is true that those evils are such, namely that we admit the first thought of the wicked desire, which the law marks, and the pleasure of it in the mind. But these very things are comprehended by the law itself, and by nature: so that you cannot have the desire without them, nor them without the desire. The law says, You shall not desire; therefore neither to have the thought of desiring. For how can you desire without the thought of desiring? You shall not desire; therefore neither take delight in the desire: for delight is itself an act of pleasure; nor do you desire evil, but good, or at least what seems and pleases you as such. So it is altogether impossible to have the nature of forbidden desire, or its act, without some tickling and delight, however slight. So both the thought and the delight of desire are so intrinsic to it and bound up with it, that no one standing outside the parts can deny that they are included and contained in the prohibition of desire, even if he wished to. Nor is anything driving our opponents into this thesis except sheer obstinacy, wishing to argue by fair means or foul that the law is imperfect, and to invent from every quarter new additions or corrections to the individual laws of Christ. (11) Nor do they here, though they do elsewhere, bring forward in appearance any testimonies of Scripture or of Christ, by which they might show what needs to be proved by them: that those things were added to the law by Christ at last, and forbidden. Nor will they bring forward here anything of Christ or of the New Testament that is not likewise contained in the Old Testament and in the common tables of the law. (3) The Apostle testifies that whatever he saw forbidden in regard to concupiscence he learned from the law. Rom. 7. 7: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet.

units.la: Atque hæc dicta sunto de additamentis, vel perfectionibus legum Mosis, & Decalogi, juxta sententiam Adversariorum, à Christo factis. Præter illa, ajunt præcepta esse quædam Christo propria, & singulariter ab eo data: eaq; vel moralia, vel cæremonialia. Cæremoniale dicunt unum, de S. Cœna: de quâ suo dicemus loco. Moralia faciunt tria ista, quæ Christus complexus fuit, Luc. ix. 23. & necessaria fecit suis discipulis, semet abnegare: deinde, ferre crucem suam; tertiò imitari seipsum. Hæc N. Test. & Christi faciunt propria, supra veterem legem addita & introducta. Catechesis Racovien-sis, de Prophetico Christi munere, cap. ii. Smalcius, de Divin. Christi, cap. vi. de præcepti Christi singularibus. Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. xxi. de Christi præceptis seorsim traditis, ita diversimode illa appellant præcepta, quæ vid. seorsim à Christo tradita. Remonstrantes, Apol. cap. xiii. de nostri directione aut abnegatione, de crucis tolerantia, de bonorum ad vitam hanc usu, ne [illegible, ~3 letters] quidem in ea Decalogi lege est.
units.tr: Let these things be said about the additions, or perfections of the laws of Moses and of the Decalogue, made by Christ according to the opinion of our opponents. Besides those, they say there are certain precepts peculiar to Christ and given by him singularly, and these are either moral or ceremonial. They call one ceremonial, concerning the Holy Supper; of which we will speak in its place. They make three moral ones, which Christ comprised in Luke 9. 23, and made necessary for his disciples: to deny oneself; then to bear one's cross; thirdly, to imitate himself. These they make peculiar to the New Testament and to Christ, added and introduced above the old law. The Racovian Catechism, on the prophetic office of Christ, chapter 2; Smalcius, on the Divinity of Christ, chapter 6, on the singular precepts of Christ; Volkelius, book 4, chapter 21, on the precepts of Christ delivered separately: thus variously they name those precepts which are delivered separately by Christ. The Remonstrants, Apology, chapter 13: on the direction or denial of ourselves, on the endurance of the cross, on the use of goods in this life, [illegible] is not even in that law of the Decalogue.

units.la: Nos verò ostendimus, illa non nova & à Christo demum inventa esse: quin cum V. Test. lege convenire, atque in ea fundari. i. In summa legis, diliges Deum ex omni corde tuo, ex omni animo, & totis viribus tuis. Omni tuo in Deum ferri non potes, nisi abnegato teipso, omnibusque quæ illi studio repugnant. Non omni animo Deum colere, nisi etiam lubenti, & tali, ac decet, crucem à Deo impositam patienter feras. Non Deo servire, quin & Christum imiteris: eòdem enim hæc redeunt, si credis in Deum, etiam in Christum crede: si illum colis & imitaris, Christum etiam. Vis & summa mandatorum illorum Christi, non præter legem est, sed eâ nititur atque continetur.
units.tr: But we show that these are not new things discovered only by Christ; indeed they agree with the law of the Old Testament and are grounded in it. (1) In the sum of the law: you shall love God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength. You cannot turn wholly to God unless you deny yourself and all those things that struggle against that zeal. You cannot worship God with all your soul unless you also bear patiently, and willingly, and as is fitting, the cross laid upon you by God. You cannot serve God without also imitating Christ: for these things come back to the same point; if you believe in God, believe in Christ too; if you worship and imitate him, imitate Christ as well. The force and sum of those commandments of Christ is not beyond the law, but rests upon it and is contained in it.

units.la: ii. Neque primis tantum, sed etiam secundis tabulis. Quippe ex vi præcepti sexti, septimi, octavi, noni, decimi, abnegare cupiditates omnes, Deo, cultuique ejus & probitati repugnantes, debemus, præsertim si advertamus ea, quæ Adversarii pro præceptorum additamentis, nos pro partibus habemus: quibus cupiditates, quarum abnegatione singulare hoc præceptum Christi exponunt, refrænantur & repurgantur. ut, nisi abnegatione eorum, illis satisfacere non possis. Quidquid enim in nobis natura est Deo adversum, id totum hac tria verba D. Jesu Christi funditus exturpare valent. Amamus nosmetipsos omnes naturâ, & delectamur nostris cupiditatibus, &c. Sed hoc decimo præcepto funditus extirpa-tur: saltem ejus additamento, ut Adversarii quidam exposuerunt, Cateche-sis nimirum, & Volkelius; Smalcius ipsa lege prohibitum dixit: ergo ejus non novum iterum & singulare Christi præceptum constituendum erat. Volkelius, in expositione præcepti, de abnegatione nostri, consequens est, ut & nos ipsos, qui pulvis & umbra sumus, contemnamus; sic & omnibus cupiditatibus nostris, utpote inanibus, terrenis ac futilibus, abjectis, totam mentem studiumque omne in Deum dirigamus. Quæso te, annon idipsum lege præscribitur, tum secundâ ejus tabulâ, tum primâ? Ut perversissima sit agendi ratio, ad præceptorum à Christo commecommemoratorum praestantiam & perfectionem commendandam, Dei etiam ipsius legem aperte impugnare & criminari, quae eadem illa continet, quae Christus docuit, & latitudine sua omnium officiorum orbitam complectitur. Quis enim aequo animo audiat, quod Smalcius dicit loc. cit. Quicquid divinitatis (ut sic loquar) in doctrina illorum summorum Philosophorum inesse videbatur, & in ipsa lege Mosaica inerat, hic adeo vilescit & obscuratur; ut umbra tantum rei, & ipsissima imperfectio, respectu praeceptorum D. Iesu Christi, jure censeri debeat? De Philosophia haud gravate concedimus: & quis non? sed indignamur vehementer istam comparationem inter Ethnicorum & futilium hominum Philosophiam, & tum doctrinam Mosis, tum Christi. Deinde, divinitatem etiam in illa constitu-tam, deque ea, tum Mosis & Christi, ita loquuntur Auctorem, ac si in ordinem eundem redigi deberent omnes illae, forte gradibus distantes. Quae summa est in Mosem, & in Christum contumelia. Sed & quis ferat, Mosis legem appellari ipsissimam imperfectionem, quae perfectionis suae semper & ubique commendata fuit, variisque modis comprobata?
units.tr: ii. Not only in the first tables but also in the second tables. Indeed, by the force of the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth precepts, we must renounce all desires that oppose God, his worship and uprightness, especially if we consider those things which our opponents hold to be additions to the precepts, and which we hold to be parts of them. By these desires, whose renunciation the Lord's single precept of Christ sets out, they are restrained and purged, so that unless you renounce them you cannot satisfy them. For whatever in us is by nature opposed to God, these three words of our Lord Jesus Christ are able to root out completely. We all love ourselves by nature, and take delight in our desires, etc. But this is utterly rooted out by the tenth precept, at least by its addition, as some of our opponents have explained, namely the Catechism and Volkelius; Smalcius said it was forbidden by the law itself. Therefore there was no need to set up again a new and singular precept of Christ for it. Volkelius, in his exposition of the precept, says: from the renunciation of ourselves it follows that we too, who are dust and shadow, must despise ourselves; so, with all our desires cast off as empty, earthly and worthless, we must direct the whole mind and all our zeal towards God. I ask you, is this not prescribed by the law itself, both in its second table and in its first? It is a most perverse way of proceeding, in order to commend the excellence and perfection of the precepts recalled by Christ, to attack and accuse openly the law of God himself, which contains those very things that Christ taught and embraces in its breadth the whole course of all duties. For who would listen calmly to what Smalcius says in the passage cited: Whatever of divinity (so to speak) seemed to be present in the teaching of those most eminent philosophers, and was present in the Mosaic law itself, here is so cheapened and obscured that, in comparison with the precepts of our Lord Jesus Christ, it ought rightly to be judged only a shadow of the thing and the very imperfection itself? About philosophy we readily concede this, and who would not? But we are vehemently indignant at that comparison between the philosophy of the heathen and of trivial men, on the one hand, and the teaching of Moses and of Christ on the other. Further, they speak of the divinity established in that philosophy, and of that of Moses and of Christ, as if all of them, perhaps differing in degree, ought to be reduced to the same level. This is a great insult to Moses and to Christ. And who could bear the law of Moses being called the very imperfection itself, when its perfection has always and everywhere been commended and proved in various ways?

units.la: Apostolus quidem dicit, Col.11.8.9. Videte ne quis vos rapiat per Philosophiam, & vanam deceptionem, juxta traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, & non secundum Christum. In quo habitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Sed, neque quod Smalcius subjungit, Apostolus divinitatem aliquam in Philosophicis praeceptis agnoscit; quin potius inanem deceptionem. Tum non componit, vel comparat, nedum divinitatis ratione, Philosophiam cum lege, & Christo: sed ab illa dehortatur homines, eamque ne audiendam quidem docet. Denique non intelligit legem Mosis moralem, de cujus praeceptis tota semper fuit nostra disputatio, sed legales caeremonias, quas in hac epistola, & ad Galatas appellare solet τὰ στοιχεῖα [?], & opponere plenitudini, quae est in Christo, verf. 17. quae sunt umbra futurorum, corpus autem Christi. & hic, in quo habitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Bene hactenus Smalcius, corporali-ter, hoc est, inquit, reipsa, non per umbras, ut in lege antea. Legem istam imperfectam fuisse, ipsa testata multis modis fuit, & Apostolus docuit ex professo in epist. ad Hebraeos, atque ad Galatas; verum ut de morali alia dicatur, esse eam ipsissimam imperfectionem, omni tempore in Ecclesia Dei, sive Judaica, sive Christiana inauditum prorsus fuit.
units.tr: The Apostle indeed says, Col. 2:8–9: Take heed lest anyone spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. But neither does the Apostle, as Smalcius adds, acknowledge any divinity in philosophical precepts; rather he calls it empty deceit. Nor does he compare or set philosophy beside the law and Christ, still less in respect of divinity; rather he warns men away from it and teaches that it should not even be heard. Finally, he does not mean the moral law of Moses, on whose precepts our whole discussion has always turned, but the legal ceremonies, which in this epistle, and in that to the Galatians, he is accustomed to call the elements [τὰ στοιχεῖα], and to set against the fullness that is in Christ, v. 17: which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ's; and in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Smalcius is right so far: bodily, that is, he says, in reality, not through shadows, as in the law before. That this law was imperfect the law itself bore witness in many ways, and the Apostle taught it expressly in the epistle to the Hebrews and to the Galatians; but that the moral law should be called the very imperfection itself has never at any time been heard of, either in the Jewish or in the Christian Church of God.

units.la: III. Arg. ad probandum, tria illa Christi monita, non esse nova & singularia praecepta, supra & praeter legem, hoc est: quia in lege dictum fuerat, san-cti sitis, quoniam ego sanctus sum. Levit. xix. 2. quod nec intelligi, nec praestari potest, nisi cum plena & perfecta abnegatione sui, & in omnibus, etiam adversis, submissione in Dei voluntatem, atque adeo ejus imitatione. Non aliud, neque perfectius exemplar Christus in se dedit, quam Dei: & hoc sub Vet. Test. hominibus propositum fuit, ac commendatum quoque. Ergo nec diversa, neque infra Evangelium hactenus fuit lex.
units.tr: III. Argument to prove that those three admonitions of Christ are not new and singular precepts, above and beyond the law. For in the law it was said: Be holy, for I am holy, Lev. 19:2, which cannot be understood or performed except with a full and perfect renunciation of self, and with submission to the will of God in all things, even adverse ones, and therefore with imitation of him. Christ gave himself no other or more perfect pattern than God, and this was set before men under the Old Testament and also commended to them. Therefore the law up to now was neither different nor inferior to the Gospel.

units.la: IV. Arg. Nisi illa sub V. Test. & lege cognita, praecepta & observata fuerint, nulla Veterum fuit religio, pietas, probitas nulla. Quia sine illis esse omnino nequit. Non Deum colere quis potest, nisi resignatis quibusque aliis praeter eum rebus, & cupiditatibus. Nisi ei te subjicias in sustinendis, quae immittit malis; & denique ejus exemplar per omnia imiteris.
units.tr: IV. Argument. Unless those precepts were known and observed under the Old Testament and the law, there was no religion, piety or uprightness among the ancients at all, since without them it is altogether impossible to be. No one can worship God unless he has given up all other things and desires besides him; unless you submit yourself to him in enduring the evils he sends; and finally unless you imitate his pattern in all things.

units.la: v. Arg. Quod ad singula monita. Abnegatio nostri, commendata fuit olim, Deut. xxxiii. 9 qui dicit patri suo & matri suae, non respicio eum, qui fratres suos non agnoscit, & filios suos non recognoscit, quia observant sermonem tuum & foedus tuum custodiunt. Praeter ea, significata eadem fuit circumcisione cordis. Deut.xxx. 6. Jerem. iv. 3. 4. tum omnibus iis in V. Teft. locis, quibus voluptatum, lucri, & superbiae cupiditates rescinduntur, ad quae capita referunt praeceptam nobis abnegationem. Sed illa, quomodo olim etiam fuerint prohibita, supra ad praecepta Decalogi ostendimus. Revera ut Adversarii non modo legis, sed & Christi, ut volunt, praecepta temere multiplicent, & hoc unum operam dedisse videantur, eadem praecepta tanquam varia recensere duntaxat, nulla probare, novo scilicet, & a Christo, jam vel tum, fuisse addita.
units.tr: V. Argument. As to the individual admonitions. The renunciation of ourselves was commended of old, Deut. 33:9: He who says to his father and mother, I do not regard him; who does not acknowledge his brothers, nor recognise his own sons; for they observe your word and keep your covenant. Besides, the same was signified by circumcision of the heart, Deut. 30:6, Jer. 4:3–4, and in all those places of the Old Testament where the desires of pleasure, gain and pride are cut off, to which heads they refer the renunciation enjoined on us. But how those things were also forbidden of old we have shown above, in regard to the precepts of the Decalogue. Indeed, the Opponents, as they wish, rashly multiply not only the precepts of the law but also those of Christ, and seem to have made it their only task to recite the same precepts merely as various ones, without proving any of them, as though they were new and added by Christ, either then or already.

units.la: Deinde quod ad praeceptum de ferenda cruce, atque adversitatibus, hujus qui negat in Scriptura Vet. Teft. documenta extare, & exempla atque monitiones ad crucem patienter sustinendam, is patientiam Jobi non audivit, Jac.v. ii. qui, uti Tertullianus egregie, omnem patientiae speciem adversus omnem Diaboli vim expunxit. non Davidem novit, reliquosque, quorum patientiam & fidem in ferendis adversis, Apostolus in catalogum disposuit, Hebr. xi. & quorum exemplo suam confirmat paraenesim, Hepr. xii. 1. tantam habentes testium circumpositam nubem. Quod si dicas, exempla illa esse, non praecepta, non legis. Atqui, non etiam praecepta illis in libris, vel Jobi, vel Psalmorum, ne alios addam, intercurrunt? eaque an aliena a lege, vel ei adversa sunt, an convenientia & innixa? Impossibile fuit Patribus, & ante Mosis tempora, & sub Mose sustinere omnia illa & perferre, absque magnis assiduisque ad patientiam incitamentis. & sive Jobi historiam ipse conscripserit Moses, vel ex ea consolationem caeperint Israelitae in molesta sua peregrinatione, aut quocunque modo ea res se habuerit, viri illius patientia pro exemplo & lege ab Ecclesia & fidelibus accepta semper fuit. Denique id quod dicitur Prov. iii. ii. correptionem Iehova, fili mi, ne spernito, neque tædeat te correctionis ejus, Apostolus tanquam nobis dictum observat, Hebr. xii. 5.
units.tr: Next, as to the precept of bearing the cross and of adversities: whoever denies that the Old Testament Scriptures contain examples and admonitions to bear the cross patiently has not heard of the patience of Job, James 5:11, who, as Tertullian admirably put it, wiped out every appearance of patience against every power of the Devil. He has not known David, nor the others whose patience and faith in bearing adversities the Apostle set out in a catalogue, Heb. 11, and by whose example he strengthens his exhortation, Heb. 12:1: having so great a cloud of witnesses set around us. But if you say that those were examples, not precepts of the law: are there not also precepts intervening in those books, in Job or in the Psalms, to say nothing of others? And are these foreign to the law or opposed to it, or are they agreeable and grounded in it? The Fathers, both before the time of Moses and under Moses, could not possibly have endured and borne all those things without great and constant incitements to patience. And whether Moses himself wrote the history of Job, or the Israelites took consolation from it in their troublesome pilgrimage, or however that matter stood, the patience of that man was always received by the Church and the faithful as an example and a law. Finally, what is said in Prov. 3:11, My son, do not despise the chastening of Jehovah, nor be weary of his correction, the Apostle notes as said to us, Heb. 12:5.

units.la: Istud de imitando Christum, adeo in V. Teft. neque Mosi ignoratum fuit, ut de eo expresse testetur Apostolus, quod omnia contempserit, ut contumeliam Christi perferret, Heb. xi. 26. Ut in hoc ipso viro, qui, Dei jussu, leges tulit, illustre exemplum habeamus trium illorum praeceptorum fideliter observatorum, abnegationis sui & suorum, toleratae crucis, atque imitationis Christi. Considerat ista in illo Apostolus, versibus, 24. 25. 26. illo, ut se abnegarit, Mo-ses grandis factus abnegavit (ἠρνήσατο [?]) expresse vel recusavit dici filius filia Pha-raonis. Ad crucis portationem haec spectant, verf. 25. Potius eligens simul malis vexari cum populo Dei, quam temporariam habere peccati fruitionem. Denique de imitatione Christi, versus est sequens 26. Majores ducens divitias probrum Christi, quam Ægyptiorum thesauros. Ergo in ipso Veteri legislatore vim trium illorum præceptorum vides, quæ temere Adversarii nova, & à Christo demum suis seorsim tradita, commemorant.
units.tr: That concerning imitating Christ was so far from being unknown to Moses in the Old Testament that the Apostle expressly bears witness of him that he despised all things so that he might bear the reproach of Christ, Heb. 11:26. Thus in this very man, who by God's command gave the laws, we have a notable example of those three precepts faithfully observed: the renunciation of self and of one's own, the bearing of the cross, and the imitation of Christ. The Apostle considers these in him in verses 24–26. As to renouncing himself, Moses, when grown, renounced [ἠρνήσατο] i.e. expressly refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. To the bearing of the cross these things pertain, v. 25: choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin. Finally, the imitation of Christ is the subject of the following verse, 26: esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. Therefore in the very lawgiver of the Old Testament you see the force of those three precepts, which the Opponents rashly recount as new, and delivered separately by Christ himself.

units.la: An dices,quomodo Christum imitari Moses potuit,nondum existentem? Dic tu mihi,quomodo Abraham diem Christi videre potuit, atque eo exultare? non actu erat Christus id, quod postmodum, neque dies ejus; sed in esse fidei, uti Philosophi alias dicunt in esse cognoscibili, præsens Christus & Abrahamo, & Mosi fuit, atque etiam aliis. Certe imitari Christum, non pergit ultra id quod lege præscriptum, de imitando Deum, sitis sancti quia ego sanctus sum. Unde Christus, sitis perfecti quemadmodum Pater vester cœlestis perfectus est. Math. v. 48.
units.tr: Will you say: how could Moses imitate Christ, when Christ did not yet exist? Tell me this: how could Abraham see Christ's day and rejoice in it? Christ was not then actually what he later became, nor was that day yet present; but Christ was present to Abraham, and to Moses, and to others as well, in the being of faith, just as the philosophers elsewhere speak of being knowable. Certainly, to imitate Christ goes no further than what the law prescribes when it bids us imitate God: be holy, for I am holy. Hence Christ says, be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. Matt. 5:48.

units.la: Ut revera Christus, proponens exemplum suum discipulis, nihil à lege diversum, neque supra eam, vel ejus perfectionem dixerit, imo nec dicere potuerit. Viderit Smalcius, an illud præceptum appellari queat ipsissima imperfectio. Præterea virtutum illarum, in quibus exprimendis sitam ajunt Adversarii imitationem Christi, quæ sunt, juxta Catechesim, fiducia in Deum, charitas perfecta, humilitas, in precibus assiduitas perpetua, præterquam quod & re ipsa exigente, & propria ipsorum expositione ad præcepta Decalogi referantur, complura ejus & in lege, & Scripturâ Veteri extant præcepta, & exempla commendata: ut frustra inde nova cudant præcepta Nostri, & nova à novis, id est alia ab additamentis illis novis supra præcepta Decalogi, ad quem, uti locum suum, spectant & pertinent omnia.
units.tr: So in truth Christ, setting forth his own example to his disciples, said nothing different from the law, nothing beyond it or above its perfection; indeed he could not have said such a thing. Let Smalcius see whether that precept can be called sheer imperfection. Moreover, of those virtues in whose expression our opponents say the imitation of Christ consists, which are, according to the Catechism, trust in God, perfect love, humility, and constant perseverance in prayer, not only are they, by the nature of the matter and by the opponents' own explanation, referred to the precepts of the Decalogue, but many such precepts and commended examples of them also exist in the law and in the Old Testament Scripture. So it is in vain that our adversaries fashion new precepts from them, and new ones from new things, that is, precepts other than those additions above the precepts of the Decalogue, to which all these things, as to their proper place, belong and pertain.

units.la: Quod objiciant Adversarii, nihil omnino habent. Nam uti in tota disputatione, ita & hic peccant ignoratione vel dissimulatione elenchi: & probant, quod probandum non est. Non enim quæritur, an ejusmodi præcepta in Nov. Testam. occurrant; sed, an sint nova & propria Novi Testamenti, nec in Vetere etiam Testamento, seu lege tradita? Et hoc nunquam ostendunt: semper circa prius illud occupantur. Atqui non necesse erat, ex Novo Testamento illa comprobare; sed exclusive ad Vet Test. ostendere illa esse singularia, uti appellant, N. Testamenti, & præter aut supra legem, solius Christi, & ab eo demum producta fuisse & instituta.
units.tr: Whatever the opponents object, they have nothing at all. For, as throughout the whole dispute, so here too they err through ignorance or evasion of the point at issue, and they prove what need not be proved. For the question is not whether such precepts occur in the New Testament, but whether they are new and peculiar to the New Testament, and not also delivered in the Old Testament, or in the law. And this they never show; they are always occupied with that first point. Yet it was not necessary to prove those precepts from the New Testament; rather, it was necessary to show, exclusively from the Old Testament, that they are singular, as they call them, to the New Testament, and beyond or above the law, and produced and instituted by Christ alone and only then.

units.la: Sed in V. Lege nihil est de Christo, eoque vel colendo, vel imitando. Resp. Nihil quidem in lege de Christo, qui solo Euangelio innotescit: quamvis & hoc, tempore legis & Vet. Testam. etiam annunciatum fuerit. Sed lex Deum colendum dictitans, includit, ut Deum colamus quocunque is se pacto nobis revelat. Ut in Nov. Testam. vel fœdere quando revelatur Mediator, hoc quidem caput Euangelii, non legis fit; sed tamen cultus ei debitus, non alius est, quam qui lege præscribitur. Id est, legis præceptum, & juxta id observantia applicatur Mediatori, per Euangelium hominibus patefacto. Nihil hic novæ legis aut præcepti, duntaxat veteris ad novum subjectum, nempe lege non contentum, fit applicatio. Uti idem cultus lege præscriptus Deo exhibetur, sive in cæremoniis, uti olim, sive absque iis, uti hodie, honorando. Quod legis moralis nullam arguit variationem, vel præcepta idcirco nova.
units.tr: But in the Old Law there is nothing about Christ, nor about worshipping or imitating him. Answer. Indeed there is nothing in the law about Christ, who is made known by the Gospel alone, although this too was announced in the time of the law and the Old Testament. But the law, which insists that God is to be worshipped, includes that we worship God in whatever way he reveals himself to us. When in the New Testament, or under the covenant, the Mediator is revealed, this indeed is a chief point of the Gospel, not of the law; yet the worship due to him is no other than that which is prescribed by the law. That is, the precept of the law applies to the Mediator, and the observance according to it is applied to him, as made known to men through the Gospel. Here there is no new precept of the new law, only an application of the old to a new subject, namely one not contained in the law. In the same way, the same worship prescribed by the law is offered to God, whether in ceremonies, as formerly, or without them, as today, in honouring him. This argues no variation in the moral law, nor therefore any new precepts.

units.la: Quærit Schlichtingius, quonam referendum sit præceptum de pænitentiâ, ad legem, an ad Euangelium ? adversus Meisnerum, quæst: Num ad regnum Dei possidendum &c. pag. 15. id præterea ex te sciscitari libet, quonam præceptum de pænitentia agenda referas ? num illud plane Euangelicum esse dicas, an legale ? Respondeo, pænitentia si in se spectetur, uti dicit dolorem & remorsum facti perperam commissi, ad legem refertur, quæ uti præcipit bene agere ubique, ita quod proximum est malo operi, ejus pænitere. Nam & natura hoc dictat, & ratio apud Gentiles, pænitentiam utcunque agere peccatorum, qui tamen Euangelio destituebantur. Si verò pænitentiæ attendamus modum, qui est vel legalis prorsus, vel Euangelicus: hunc patimur ad Euangelium reduci, ut tamen præceptum ipsum, quatenus operis est alicujus boni ac necessarii, ad legem.
units.tr: Schlichting asks, against Meisner (question: whether it belongs to the possession of the kingdom of God, etc., p. 15): Moreover, I wish to ask you this: to which law or to which Gospel do you refer the precept concerning the repentance to be performed? Do you say that it is plainly Evangelical, or legal? I answer: repentance, if considered in itself, insofar as it signifies grief and remorse for a deed wrongly committed, is referred to the law, which everywhere prescribes doing well, and so, as what is opposite to evil work, repenting of it. For nature dictates this, and reason among the Gentiles does too, that somehow they should repent of their sins, although they were destitute of the Gospel. But if we attend to the mode of repentance, which is either wholly legal or Evangelical, we allow that this mode is referred to the Gospel; yet the precept itself, insofar as it concerns some good and necessary work, is referred to the law.

units.la: Eademque ratio est fidei, quæ etiam uti in Euangelio præcipitur, non est alia virtus respectu causæ, quam quæ lege exigitur, dum ea jubet Deum colere eo quo se coli vult modo, & in ipsum credere; nisi quod Euangelio alius accedit modus, & determinatio in subjectum aliud, Christum nempe, quem lex ignorat. Ista autem fides, quæ virtus est lege præscripta, & hinc in Deum necessario fertur, Deo in Euangelio Christum revelante, hunc, tum vi generalis de fide Deo ubique habendâ præcepti, tum specialis revelationis Euangelicæ, apprehendit quoque. Quæ erat ratio, quod Christus diceret Joan.xiv.1. credite in Deum, etiam in me credite.
units.tr: The same reasoning holds for faith, which is also commanded in the Gospel. Regarding its cause, it is not a different virtue from that which the law requires, since the law bids us worship God in the way he wishes to be worshipped, and believe in him; except that in the Gospel another mode is added, and a determination to another object, namely Christ, whom the law does not know. That faith, however, which is a virtue prescribed by the law, and hence necessarily directed to God, when God reveals Christ in the Gospel, apprehends him as well, both by virtue of the general precept that God be trusted everywhere, and by virtue of the special Evangelical revelation. This was the reason why Christ said in John 14:1: believe in God, believe also in me.

units.la: Idem respondemus de disciplinâ & præcepto sacramentorum: quæ quatenus gratiæ signa sunt, ad N. pertinent procul dubio Testamentum, & Euangelium: at quatenus præcepta à Deo sunt observari ut bona opera alia, lex hoc exigit ut in omnibus Deo promte perfecteque obediamus.
units.tr: We answer the same concerning the discipline and the precept of the sacraments: insofar as they are signs of grace, they undoubtedly pertain to the New Testament and the Gospel; but insofar as they are things God commands to be observed, like other good works, the law requires that we obey God promptly and perfectly in all things.

units.la: LIBER TERTIVS, DE CHRISTO SERVATORE. CAPUT VNICVM, DE CHRISTI SATISFACTIONE.
units.tr: BOOK THREE, CONCERNING CHRIST THE SAVIOUR. A SINGLE CHAPTER, CONCERNING CHRIST'S SATISFACTION.

units.la: CONTROVERSIA:
units.tr: THE CONTROVERSY:

units.la: An Christus passionibus & morte suâ, pœnas peccatorum nostrorum in se susceperit & sustinuerit, iisque divinæ justitiæ, nostri loco, plene satisfecerit, & expiatis peccatis, veram redemtionem ac salutem nobis acquisierit ?
units.tr: Whether Christ, by his sufferings and his death, took upon himself and bore the punishments of our sins, and by them fully satisfied the divine justice in our place, and, with our sins expiated, obtained for us true redemption and salvation?

units.la: Ravissimæ quæstiones, quæ de Christo agunt, sive ejus persona, sive officio. Triplex Christi officium: sed Regium Sacerdotali præmittunt Adversarii; & utrumque in cœlis demum à Christo peragi volunt, & illud in hoc situm esse, quod Christus opitulari nobis possit, hoc, quod velit. Propositâ quæstione, ostenditur Adversariorum sententia, per partes. Quæ videantur concedere; & satisfactionem ajunt quoque à Christo præstitam, sed divinæ voluntati simpliciter, per obedientiam, non justitiæ, in ferendis pœnis. Verba Crellii, Smalcii, Ruari, Socini. Causæ, ob quas Sociniani Christum dicunt Servatorem, ex ipsorum scriptis exponuntur. Sententia Remonstrantium, de Christo Salvatore, propter præconium ejus, exemplum, & martyrium. Rationes allatæ, contra istas causas. De mortis Christi, ex Adversariorum sententia, finibus: pro confirmandâ doctrinâ suâ, pro dando sui exemplo, & acquirenda sibi in omnia potestate. De Abaillardo: Lælio Socino: Ochino, qui negarint satisfactionem. Status controversiæ. Christum mediatorem quo sensu Adversarii dicant. An Mediator tantùm internuncius, an etiam reconcilians? Disputatur de nominis Mediatorii usu, ex Scripturâ. Gal. iii. 19. 1 Tim. ii. 5. Hebr. viii. 6. & ix. 15. & xii. 24. tum & rationibus ostenditur, quod Christus non tantùm Mediator est internuncii, sed etiam reconciliationis. De necessitate satisfactionis. Proponitur quæstio. Iustitiæ nomen, in Scripturis, quatenus misericordiæ opponitur, & sumitur pro punitivâ. Misericordia Deo naturalis. Probatur idem de justitia vindicatrice, post explicatum quæstionis cardinem. Solvuntur objectiones contrariæ. Expositâ satisfactionis natura. Argumentorum pro Christi satisfactione classes tres. Christus in se suscepit pœnas peccatorum nostras. Explicatur, & vindicatur Isaiæ liii. Portare peccata non simpliciter, nec solum significat auferre, sed quoque in se suscipere, & sustinere. Explicatur Matth. viii. 17. Vindicatur 1 Pet. ii. 24. Christus pro nobis factus peccatum, Iesa. liiii. 10. ii Cor. v. 21. & execratio, Gal. iii. 13. Ex morte peccati pœnâ, quam Christus sustinuit, probatur satisfactio. Tum inde, quia mortuus dicitur pro peccatis, & propter ea. Vindicatur Iesa liiii. 5. Rom. iv. 25. De præpositionibus διὰ, περὶ, ὑπὲρ, ἀντί. Explicatur 1 Ioan. iii. 16. & Col. i. 24. Heb. ii. 9. Ioan. xi. 50. 1 Pet. ii. 21. Ioan. x. 11. 15. Luc. xxii. 19. Christus peccata nostra apud Deum
units.tr: The most weighty questions that deal with Christ concern either his person or his office. The office of Christ is threefold, but our opponents put the kingly office before the priestly, and they want both to be carried out by Christ only in heaven, and his power to help us to rest on his being able to do whatever he wishes. After the question is put, the opinion of the opponents is set out part by part: what they seem to concede, and how they say that satisfaction was also made by Christ, but simply by the will of God, through obedience, and not by justice, in the bearing of punishments. The words of Crellius, Smalcius, Ruarus and Socinus. The reasons why the Socinians call Christ the Saviour are explained from their own writings. The view of the Remonstrants, that Christ is Saviour on account of his preaching, his example and his martyrdom. The arguments brought against these reasons. Concerning the ends of Christ's death according to the opponents' view: to confirm their doctrine, to give an example of himself, and to acquire for himself power over all things. Concerning Abelard, Lelio Sozzini, and Ochino, who denied satisfaction. The state of the controversy. In what sense the opponents call Christ Mediator. Is the Mediator only an intermediary, or also a reconciler? The use of the name Mediator is discussed from Scripture: Gal. iii. 19; 1 Tim. ii. 5; Heb. viii. 6; ix. 15; xii. 24; and it is then shown by arguments that Christ is not only the Mediator of an intermediary, but also of reconciliation. On the necessity of satisfaction. The question is put. The name justice in Scripture, as it is opposed to mercy and is taken as punitive. Mercy is natural to God. The same is proved concerning avenging justice, after the crux of the question has been explained. The contrary objections are answered. With the nature of satisfaction explained, the arguments for Christ's satisfaction fall into three classes. Christ took upon himself our punishments. Isaiah liii is explained and defended. To bear sins does not simply or only mean to take away, but also to take upon oneself and to endure. Matthew viii. 17 is explained. 1 Peter ii. 24 is defended. Christ made sin for us, Isa. liii. 10; 2 Cor. v. 21; and the curse, Gal. iii. 13. Satisfaction is proved from the penalty of death, which Christ endured. Then from this, that he is said to have died for sins and on account of them. Isa. liii. 5 is defended; Rom. iv. 25. On the prepositions dia, peri, hyper, anti [διὰ, περὶ, ὑπὲρ, ἀντί]. John iii. 16; Col. i. 24; Heb. ii. 9; John xi. 50; 1 Pet. ii. 21; John x. 11, 15; Luke xxii. 19 are explained. Christ expiated our sins before God, and made him propitious, and reconciled him to us.

units.la: expiavit, eumque propitium reddidit, & nobis reconciliavit. Ubi de expiatione, & reconciliatione nostri cum Deo. Hebr. i. 3. & ii. 17. & ix. ii:12. 1 Ioan. iv. 10. Apoc. i. 5. Collatio Sacerdotii V Test. cum Novo. Omnia in genere sacrificia expiatoria fuerunt typica Christi, & non tantum anniversarium. Hebr. vii. 27. quotidie, non significat, quod Socinus vult, quotannis. Deinde sacrificia olim non tantum pro levioribus, sed & gravibus peccatis offerebantur. Quomodo pro ignorantiis dicantur fuisse oblata. Exponitur Act. xv. 38. Nulla sacrificia vere expiarunt peccatum, quod ad conscientiam. Christus etiam sacerdos fuit in terris, & in cruce. Chiistus, sui oblatione, placavit Deum: eumque nobis reconciliavit. Exponitur Rom. v. 9. 10. 11 Cor. v. 18. Ephes. ii. 13. &c. Col. i. 20. 21. De redemtione nostri vera, per Christi sanguinem: unde argumentum pro satisfactione. Matth. xx 28. 1 Cor. i. 30. Eph. i. 7. 1 Tim. ii. 6. Hebr. ix. 12. 1 Pet. i. 18. 19. De Christi merito. Hinc dicimur, per & propter eum servari. Quomodo, & quae Christus, dicatur sibi meritus. Objectiones & argumenta Socini, adversus satisfactionem, tria. An possit Deus absque satisfactione peccata remittere? an velit? Ostenditur, remissioni non contrariari satisfactionem. An Christus divinae justitiae satisfacere non potuerit. Exponitur Iezech. xviii. 4. Solvitur denique Socini argumentum, contra Christi meritum.
units.tr: Expiated, and reconciled us to God. Here concerning the expiation and reconciliation of us with God: Heb. i. 3; ii. 17; ix. 11–12; 1 John iv. 10; Rev. i. 5. A comparison of the priesthood of the Old Testament with the New. All the sacrifices of atonement in general were types of Christ, and not only the yearly one. Heb. vii. 27: "daily" does not mean, as Socinus wishes, "yearly." Further, the sacrifices of old were offered not only for lesser but also for grave sins. How they are said to have been offered for ignorances. Acts xv. 38 is explained. No sacrifices truly expiated sin as far as the conscience is concerned. Christ was also a priest on earth, and on the cross. Christ, by the offering of himself, appeased God and reconciled him to us. Rom. v. 9–10; 2 Cor. v. 18; Eph. ii. 13, etc.; Col. i. 20–21 are explained. On our true redemption through the blood of Christ, whence there is an argument for satisfaction: Matt. xx. 28; 1 Cor. i. 30; Eph. i. 7; 1 Tim. ii. 6; Heb. ix. 12; 1 Pet. i. 18–19. On the merit of Christ. Hence we are said to be saved through him and on account of him. In what way, and what merit Christ is said to have earned for himself. The objections and arguments of Socinus against satisfaction, three in number. Whether God could forgive sins without satisfaction, or whether he would. It is shown that satisfaction is not contrary to forgiveness. Whether Christ could not have satisfied the divine justice. Ezek. xviii. 4 is explained. Finally, the argument of Socinus against the merit of Christ is answered.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: SECTION ONE.

units.la: Magni omni ex parte momenti articulus est, qui de Christo agit, de ejus tum persona, tum officiis. Inter haec vero nulla gravior est quaestio, quam qua de Servatore, de eo quod, & qua ratione nos salvat a peccatis nostris, tractatur. Id est, quare appelletur Jesus. Servatorem esse, omnes, quotquot ei nomen dixerunt, agnoscunt: etiam servare eum homines a peccatis. Sed in quo hoc consistat, quidve proprie dicat, haud aeque inter ipsos convenit. Eo tamen nititur tota de Christo tractatio, & hinc tanquam a capite dependet salutis nostrae cognitio, omniumque in hoc genere actionum, tum Dei, tum nostrarum. Quomodo homo coram Deo justificetur, per quam, & cujus justitiam, inde cognoscitur: inde etiam, quae in Christum collocanda fides sit & fiducia. Quare Socinus, in Thematibus de officio Christi, longe perniciosius errari fatetur circa officium Christi, quam circa quaestionem, de ejus natura. Et de Justificatione acturus in Praelectionibus, huc statim deflexit, ut de satisfactione Christi, & contra illam disputet. Neque nisi praemissa hac quaestione, expediri illae ullatenus possunt. Primum ergo videndum, quid Christus nostri loco, & bono nostro egit, passusque fuit: tum, ut per eum justificemur, ac salvemur. Christi officium; deinde ejus beneficium. Utroque Salvator noster, & redemtor est proprie dictus.
units.tr: The article that treats of Christ, both of his person and of his offices, is of great importance in every respect. Among these matters none is weightier than the question that concerns the Saviour: what he does, and in what way he saves us from our sins. That is, why he is called Jesus. All who have given him the name acknowledge that he is Saviour, and that he saves men from their sins. But in what this consists, or what it properly means, they do not agree nearly so well. Yet the whole treatment of Christ rests on this point, and the knowledge of our salvation, and of all actions in this matter, both of God's and of ours, depends on it as on its head. From it we learn how a man is justified before God, through what righteousness and whose; and from it we learn in whom faith and trust are to be placed. Hence Socinus, in his Theses on the office of Christ, admits that men go far more perniciously wrong about the office of Christ than about the question of his nature. And when he was about to treat of justification in his Lectures, he at once turned aside to the satisfaction of Christ and disputes against it. Nor can those matters be disentangled in any way unless this question is settled first. We must therefore first see what Christ did and suffered in our place and for our good, and then how we are justified and saved through him. First Christ's office, then his benefit. By both our Saviour and Redeemer is properly so called.

units.la: Triplex Christi officium confitentur etiam Adversarii, propheticum, sacerdotale, & regium: sed regium sacerdotali praemittunt. Atque sic in Catechesi Racoviensi, primum de Prophetico Christi officio, inde regio agitur, demum de sacerdotali. In rationem postea inquiremus, quae est, quod Christus ipsis statuitur, in coelo sacerdotium orsus, non in terra; post exaltationem & ad-scensionem, non in morte & passionibus. Similiter de Christi regno loquuntur & imperio. Smalcius, de Divinit. Christi, cap. iv. hoc autem munus Christi triplex est, ut S. literae testantur, & omnes hac in re consentiunt Theologi Christiani, Propheticum, Regium, & Sacerdotale. Quorum primum Christus dum in terris fuit, perfecit: ad reliqua vero duo, aditus ei à Deo paratus fuit. Socinus Christi officia dispescit in ea, quae in terris, & illa quae in coelis peragit. Quorum illud sit propheticum; ista, regium, & sacerdotale. De officio Christi them. ii. iii.[?] Atque Smalcius, cap. xiii. breviter exponit utriusque Christi officii, regii, & sacerdotalis differentiam, primum igitur omnium considerandum venit, per Iesu Christi sacerdotium aliud nihil significari, quam quod Christus nostri curam gerere velit, & gerat. Et hoc tantum a regno ejus differt, quod Christus, quatenus rex est potest nostri curam gerere: quatenus vero Pontifex, gerere etiam (ut diximus) vult, & gerit.
units.tr: Even our opponents acknowledge a threefold office of Christ: prophetical, priestly, and kingly; but they place the kingly before the priestly. So in the Racovian Catechism the prophetical office is treated first, then the kingly, and last the priestly. Later we shall inquire into the reason why, for them, Christ began his priesthood in heaven and not on earth, after his exaltation and ascension and not in his death and sufferings. Similarly they speak of Christ's kingdom and rule. Smalcius, in On the Divinity of Christ, chapter 4: This office of Christ is threefold, as the Holy Scriptures testify, and all Christian theologians agree in this, prophetical, kingly, and priestly. Of these, Christ performed the first while he was on earth; for the other two, access was prepared for him by God. Socinus divides the offices of Christ into those he performs on earth and those he performs in heaven. Of these the former is prophetical; the latter are kingly and priestly. On the office of Christ, theses 2 and 3. [?] And Smalcius, in chapter 13, briefly sets out the difference between the kingly and the priestly office of Christ: First of all, then, it must be considered that by the priesthood of Jesus Christ nothing else is meant than that Christ wishes to take care of us, and does so. And this differs from his kingdom only in that Christ, insofar as he is king, is able to take care of us; but insofar as he is high priest, he also wills (as we have said) and does take care of us.

units.la: Propheticum vero Christi officium, hoc ut obiter addamus, in eo constituunt, quod Christus Dei Patris voluntatem perfectè nobis cum revelaverit, tum etiam confirmaverit: Socinus, Themat. v. Revelavit autem in N. demum Testamento, quod à Veteri dicunt distare praeceptis, & promissis. Quod ad praecepta, quod Christus in N. T. & perfectiora reddidit praecepta legis Mosaicae moralis; & praeterea alia addidit singularia. Quod ad promissa N. Test. hic vitae aeternae, & remissionis peccatorum, & Spiritus S. factas promissiones docent, quibus caruerint V. Test. fideles. Confirmavit, dicunt, illam Patris voluntatem Christus, insigni ac perfecta vita innocentia ac sanctitate, tum innumerabilibus ac stupendis miraculis atque prodigiis, tandem morte cruenta, quam jussu & voluntate Patris subiit. Et istam mortis Christi causam statuunt, non, quemadmodum plerique sentiunt, ut justitia divina pro peccatis nostris satisfaceret, vel Deum ex irato & severo judice propitium nobis clementemque patrem redderet. Socinus, them. xxxviii. De illis disputavimus, de promissis, & praeceptis, uti dicunt Adversarii, N. Test. De hoc sequitur deinceps agamus, sive de mortis Christi causa, an fuerit confirmatio doctrinae suae, pro certitudine ejus & promissionum apud animum nostrum; an vera & propria nostri redemtio a peccatis, & peccatorum poenis? Quaeq; nos referimus ad officium Christi sacerdotale; illi referunt ad propheticum: Illi in Christo dun-taxat verum, quamvis excellentiorem forte, martyrem considerant: nos sacerdotem, redemtorem, & servatorem proprium. Regium & sacerdotale Christi officium reipsa faciunt idem. Nam postquam Socinus hunc in modum explicuisset rationem officii sacerdotalis, quod Christus a mortuis excitatus sedeat ad dexteram throni majestatis in excelsis, obtinens omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra, & omne imperium in omnes & spiritus & homines, & vim sibi omnia subjiciendi habens; & praeterea, quod ipsa etiam corda nostra norit, in omnibus nobis calamitatibus subvenire, ab omnibus malis nos afferere, & ab ipsa denique morte nos liberare possit; de regio Christi officio subjungit, them. xlvii. quod ad munus Christi sacerdotale attinet, id quidem non reipsa, sed tamen per viam intellectus a regio ipsius munere distinguimus. Et in hoc distinguit, uti quoque ex Smalcio audivimus, quod pro regio munere possit Christus, pro sacerdotali etiam velit nobis perpetuo opitulari.
units.tr: As for the prophetical office of Christ, to add this in passing, they place it in this, that Christ has fully revealed to us, and also confirmed, the will of the Father. Socinus, Theses 5. He revealed it, however, only in the New Testament, which they say differs from the Old in precepts and promises. As to the precepts: in the New Testament Christ made the precepts of the moral law of Moses more perfect, and besides this added other particular ones. As to the promises of the New Testament: the promises of eternal life, forgiveness of sins, and the Holy Spirit teach that the faithful of the Old Testament lacked them. Christ confirmed that will of the Father, they say, by a remarkable and perfect innocence and holiness of life, then by innumerable and astonishing miracles and wonders, and finally by a bloody death, which he underwent at the command and will of the Father. And they lay down that this was the cause of Christ's death: not, as most think, so that divine justice might be satisfied for our sins, or so that God might be made merciful to us as a father instead of an angry and severe judge. Socinus, Theses 38. We have disputed about those promises and precepts of the New Testament, as our opponents call them. Next we must treat of this: whether the cause of Christ's death was the confirmation of his teaching, for the certainty of his promises in our minds, or whether it was our true and proper redemption from sins and from the punishments of sins? What we refer to the priestly office of Christ, they refer to the prophetical. They regard Christ only as a true martyr, perhaps a more excellent one; we regard him as priest, redeemer, and proper Saviour. In fact, the kingly and priestly offices of Christ they make the same thing. For after Socinus had explained in this way the account of the priestly office, namely that Christ, raised from the dead, sits at the right hand of the throne of majesty on high, holding all power in heaven and on earth, and all dominion over all both spirits and men, and having the power to subject all things to himself; and besides, that he knows our very hearts, can help us in all our calamities, defend us from all evils, and finally free us even from death itself; he adds on the kingly office of Christ, theses 47: As far as the priestly office of Christ is concerned, we distinguish it from his kingly office not indeed in fact, but yet by way of the understanding. And in this he distinguishes, as we have also heard from Smalcius, that for his kingly office Christ is able, but for his priestly office he also wills to help us perpetually.

units.la: Utcunque ergo in eo quidem conveniamus, quod utrimque triplex in Christo officium agnoscitur, propheticum, sacerdotale, & regium; discrepantia tamen est maxima, & circa singulorum officiorum partes, in quo consistant; & ordinem. De Prophetici muneres partibus disputavimus. Sequitur de parte longe maximâ controversia, morte nempe Christi, ejusque causa, & effectu proprio: tum, quo hoc referendum, sive ad quod Christi officium, & quam ad partem. Nos referendum censemus ad officium Christi Sacerdotale; Adversarii, ad Propheticum. II. Quaeritur, an sacerdotale munus Christus etiam in terris obivit; an primum, vel tantum in coelo? Nos illud affirmamus; Adversarii negant. III. Sacerdotale officium an sit praemittendum regio; an vero postponendum? Nos illud; Adversarii istud eligunt. IV. Num sacerdotale Christi officium & regium, sit revera idem, neque plus differant, quam velle, & posse servare? Negamus; Adversarii affirmant. Pendet autem quaestionum illarum decisio ex principali ista de morte Christi, an nempe sit propriè satisfactoria & redemtoria? proque eâ sese habent quaestiones caeterae secundariae, & ex accidenti seu occasione illius agitatae. Namque si mors Christi revera & proprie est expiatoria, & redemtionis nostrae λύτρον, jam in hoc sacrificium Christi situm est, & sacerdotem in eo egit, in terris etiam, atque ante adeptam plene regnandi potestatem, differtque à regali officium illud sacerdotis. Quia autem illud negant Adversarii, in diversa omnia abeundum censuerunt, non adeo ex opinione veritatis, quam ut remotius à principali thesi & veritate distarent. Non enim minus novum fuit, confundere officia Christi sacerdotale & regium, negare Christum in cruce obtulisse sacrificium, & sacerdotem etiam fuisse in terris, quam negare mortem ejus expiatoriam, & redemtionis nostrae verum esse λύτρον. Hinc ergo incipiamus, à quo reliqua dependent.
units.tr: However far we agree on this, that on both sides a threefold office is acknowledged in Christ, prophetical, priestly, and kingly, the disagreement is nevertheless very great, both about the parts of each office, in what they consist, and about the order. We have disputed about the parts of the prophetical office. There follows the part of far the greatest controversy: the death of Christ, its cause, and its proper effect; and to which office this is to be referred, and to which part. We judge that it is to be referred to the priestly office of Christ; our opponents, to the prophetical. II. It is asked whether Christ also performed the priestly office on earth, or only first, or only, in heaven. We affirm the former; our opponents deny it. III. Is the priestly office to be placed before the kingly, or rather after it? We say the former; our opponents choose the latter. IV. Is the priestly office of Christ really the same as the kingly, and do they differ no more than willing and being able to keep? We deny it; our opponents affirm it. The decision of these questions, however, depends on that principal question about the death of Christ: namely, whether it is properly satisfactory and redemptive; and the other, secondary questions stand in relation to it, and are raised incidentally or on occasion of it. For if the death of Christ is truly and properly expiatory, and a ransom [λύτρον] for our redemption, then his sacrifice lies in this, and in it he acted as priest, even on earth and before he had obtained full kingly power; and that priestly office differs from the kingly one. But since our opponents deny this, they have judged that they must go in all directions, not so much from any opinion of the truth, as to be the further removed from the principal thesis and truth. For it was no less novel to confuse the priestly and kingly offices of Christ, to deny that Christ offered a sacrifice on the cross, and that he was even a priest on earth, than to deny that his death is expiatory and a true ransom [λύτρον] for our redemption. Let us therefore begin here, on which the rest depend.

units.la: Quaestio est, de morte Christi, an fuerit pro peccatis nostris satisfactoria? sive, an Christus, passionibus & morte sua, poenas peccatorum nostrorum in se suscepit & sustinuerit, iisque divinae justitiae, nostri loco, plenè satisfecerit, & expiatis peccatis, Deum nobis reconciliarit, & veram redemtionem, ac salutem acquisierit? Affirmamus nos; negant Adversarii. Notanda initio sunt, quae videntur aliquando concedere, & quae ἐξαγωγία; tum, in quibus distinctè haeret controversia. Quod si ullibi, certe hic accurate observandum, ne vel à scopo aberremus, vel vaniloquentiâ nos turbent Adversarii, ubi multa videntur quandoque dicere in speciem & concedere, ut ludum & fucum faciant, atque tantum ut paria ferè putentur dicere cum Orthodoxis, quamvis revera sentiant diversissima.
units.tr: The question is about the death of Christ: was it satisfactory for our sins? That is, did Christ, by his sufferings and death, take upon himself and bear the punishments of our sins, fully satisfy divine justice in our place, expiate our sins, reconcile God to us, and acquire true redemption and salvation? We affirm this; our opponents deny it. First we must note what they seem sometimes to concede, and what is to be drawn out [ἐξαγωγία]; then we must see where the controversy distinctly lies. If ever, it is certainly necessary to observe this carefully here, lest we either stray from the point or be confused by the empty talk of our opponents, who often seem to say and concede much in appearance, playing a game and putting on a show, so that they seem to say almost the same things as the Orthodox, although in truth they hold the most diverse views.

units.la: In confesso est. I. Christum vere passum, ac mortuum. II. Bono nostro. Sed, quâ id ratione? quaeritur. Dicunt Adversarii, mortuum Christum, ut confirmaret veritatem doctrinae suae, nihil ultra. Nam quae adjiciunt, eò solum pertinent, atque inde sequuntur: ut quod fides nostra hinc in doctrinam & promissiones Christi certior redditur ac firmior, usum modo dicit, fructumque illius confirmationis, vel martyrii Christi. Alia mortis Christi effecta, quae dicunt, ad ipsum Christum referuntur, vel ejus resurrectionem. Proprie mortis ejus effectum & usum quod ad nos illud solum est, quod confirmare ea voluerit doctrinam suam.
units.tr: It is agreed: first, that Christ truly suffered and died; second, that he did so for our good. But by what means? That is the question. Our opponents say that Christ died only to confirm the truth of his teaching, and nothing more. For what they add pertains only to this and follows from it: namely, that our faith is thereby made more certain and firm in the doctrine and promises of Christ. They speak only of the use and fruit of that confirmation, or of the martyrdom of Christ. The other effects of Christ's death that they mention are referred to Christ himself, or to his resurrection. Properly speaking, the only effect and use of his death for us is that he willed to confirm his doctrine by it.

units.la: Nos autem non negamus, etiam morte Christi, uti & aliis rebus atque argumentis, confirmatam ejus doctrinam fuisse: sed hoc solum, aut principale mortis ejus effectum fuisse, merito negamus. Dicimus, credimusque, praecipuè mortuum Christum, ut à peccatis nos vere redimeret, ac morte & passionibus suis, tanquam solutionis & satisfactionis pretio, divinæ justitiæ, loco nostro, oblato præstitoque vere liberaret. Quare negant Adversarii, i. Christum poenas fusti-nuisse, vel passionem ejus fuisse vere poenalem. ii. Negant, eum poenas nostras luisse, nostro loco. iii. Pro nobis vere satisfecisse. iv. Divinæ justitiæ. v. ac propterea Deum placasse. vi. vel eum nobis reconciliasse. vii. atque vere nos redemisse: sed, dicunt, redemtionem ejus esse metaphoricam, & eum redemtorem non verum, sed metaphoricum. Probemus, ex Adversariis, singula: ut appareat, recte nos statum controversiæ constituere, & in illis hærere disputa-tionis cardinem.
units.tr: We, however, do not deny that his doctrine was confirmed by the death of Christ, as by his other deeds and arguments; but we rightly deny that this alone, or the principal effect of his death, was that. We say, and believe, that Christ died chiefly so that he might truly redeem us from our sins, and that by his death and sufferings, as the price of a ransom and satisfaction, offered and paid to divine justice in our place, he might truly set us free. Therefore our opponents deny: (i) that Christ bore punishments, or that his passion was truly penal; (ii) that he paid our punishments in our place; (iii) that he truly satisfied for us; (iv) divine justice; (v) and therefore that he appeased God; (vi) or that he reconciled us to God; (vii) and that he truly redeemed us; but, they say, his redemption is metaphorical, and he is a redeemer not in truth but in metaphor. Let us take each point from our opponents, so that it may appear that we rightly set out the state of the controversy, and that the hinge of the dispute lies in these matters.

units.la: Primum diximus, ex mente Adversariorum, Christi passiones non fuisse pœnas. Ita Socinus, in libro de Servatore, part. iii. c. iv. Christi pœnas impropriè dictas contendit, etiamsi ea, qua passus est Christus, poena nomine passus esset, poena tamen simpliciter appellari non deberent, sed potius labores præmia antecedentes. Dein pag. 267. cum quas vos dicitis Christi poenas, non verè & propria sint poenæ. Crellius, contra Grotium, Respons. ad cap. i. pag. 7. Verum Grotius, ut apparet, pœnarum vocem accepit proprie. Pœna vero proprie dicta describitur à I Cr°, vindicta noxæ; consentientibus Græcis, qui κολάσεις ... ἁμαρτημάτων [?] definiunt. Hanc nos Christum, quem Deus infinito præmio ad mortem nostra causa sustinendam hortatus est, eoque reipsa postmodum exhibito, omnes ejus cruciatus abunde compensavit, sustinuisse negamus: improprie dictam, fatemur. postea, vocem pœna proprie huc pertinere non concedimus; & in eum sensum semper verba nostra volumus accipi, cum Christum pœnas pependisse simpliciter negamus.
units.tr: First, we said that, in the opinion of our opponents, the sufferings of Christ were not punishments. So Socinus, in the book De Servatore, part iii, ch. iv: he contends that the punishments of Christ are improperly so called: even though what Christ suffered was suffered under the name of punishment, yet they ought not simply to be called punishments, but rather labours preceding rewards. Then at p. 267: what you call the punishments of Christ are not truly and properly punishments. Crellius, against Grotius, Reply to ch. i, p. 7: But Grotius, as appears, took the word punishment in its proper sense. Punishment properly so called is described by I Cr°, as the vengeance for a wrong, the Greeks agreeing, who define it as ... of sins [?]. We deny that Christ sustained this, whom God urged by an infinite reward to endure death for our cause, and who, when that reward was afterwards actually bestowed, fully compensated all his torments: we admit that it is improperly called so. Later: we do not concede that the word punishment properly applies here; and we always want our words to be taken in that sense, when we simply deny that Christ paid punishments.

units.la: Multo magis negant, Christum poenas pependisse nostro loco. Dicunt quidem Christum mortuum, nostro bono, & causa nostra, uti modo Crellium loquentem audivimus, non vero loco nostro, & hoc sensu pro nobis. Socinus, lib. de Servatore, part. ii. cap. iv. cap. 92. ostenditur, minime concludi debere, Christum omnes poenas pertulisse, quas nos propter peccata nostra pendere debuissemus. Cap. vii. pag. 108. mori propter peccata, seu pro peccatis alicujus, nihil aliud est, quam causa sive occasione peccatorum illius mori. Dixerat, constanter se negare, Christum alicui divinæ justitiæ pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, sive illi id solvisse, quod nos propter peccata nostra solvere debuissemus. Atque postea, neque enim unquam Deus aliena peccata in quoquam vere punit, qui culpa non sit affinis. & cap. seq. viii. demonstrare conatur, dictionem pro hic nullo modo significare vice, seu loco. Similiter Ostorodus, Instit. cap. xxxvii. pag. 319. Alia præterea suo loco infra adducentur.
units.tr: Much more do they deny that Christ paid punishments in our place. They indeed say that Christ died for our good and for our cause, as we have just heard Crellius say, but not in our place, and in this sense not for us. Socinus, book De Servatore, part ii, ch. iv, cap. 92: it is shown that it by no means follows that Christ bore all the punishments which we ought to have paid on account of our sins. Ch. vii, p. 108: to die on account of sins, or for the sins of someone, is nothing else than to die because of, or on the occasion of, that person's sins. He had said that he constantly denies that Christ satisfied divine justice for our sins, or paid to it what we ought to have paid on account of our sins. And afterwards: for God never truly punishes the sins of others in anyone who is not implicated in the guilt. And in the following chapter, viii, he tries to show that the word for [pro] in no way signifies in place of, or instead of. Similarly Ostorodt, Institutes ch. xxxvii, p. 319. Other passages will be adduced below in their place.

units.la: Negant propterea, Christum pro nobis vere satisfecisse. De Servatore, part. iii. cap. ii. Deum voluisse nobis peccata nostra condonare, nulla pro ipsis vera satisfactione accepta. Quod item argumentem est cap. xvii. Præleß. De Servatore, part ii. cap. i. pag. 74. Perlege omnes locos novi Fœderis, in quibus redemtionis fiat mentio: & nullum invenies, ubi de veri alicujus pretii solutione, seu de satisfactione aliqua evidenter agatur. Catechef. Ravov. de Prophetico Christi munere, cap. i. pag. 262. pag. 262. Deus hominibus peccata remittit gratis: cui nihil magis contrarium, quam satisfactio. Inde Smalcius, contra Smiglecium, de satisfact. Christi, in statu quaestionis exponendo, inquit, cap. vii. pag. 225. Christum pro peccatis nostris, & propter peccata nostra, & pro nobis mortuum esse, confitemur omnes & gaudemus; at eum poenas peccatorum nostrorum in se recepisse, & pro illis Deo satisfecisse, hinc consequi, perne-gamus iterum.
units.tr: Therefore they deny that Christ truly satisfied for us. De Servatore, part iii, ch. ii: God wished to forgive us our sins, with no true satisfaction received for them. This is likewise the argument of ch. xvii of the Prelections. De Servatore, part ii, ch. i, p. 74: Read through all the passages of the New Covenant in which redemption is mentioned, and you will find none where the payment of some true price, or any satisfaction, is clearly spoken of. Catechism of Racov, On the Prophetic Office of Christ, ch. i, p. 262: God forgives men's sins freely, to which nothing is more contrary than satisfaction. Hence Smalcius, against Smiglecius, On the Satisfaction of Christ, in setting out the state of the question, says in ch. vii, p. 225: We all confess and rejoice that Christ died for our sins, on account of our sins, and for us; but that he received the punishments of our sins upon himself, and satisfied God for them, we again deny follows from this.

units.la: Præsertim divinae justitiae persolutum λύτρον, aut satisfactum à Christo, inficiantur. Socinus, Themat. XXXVIII. de officio Christi, hanc igitur verissimam Christi mortis causam esse credimus, non quemadmodum plerique sentiunt, ut justitia divina propeccatis nostris satisfecerit. De Servatore, in principio, ubi sententiam suam exponit: divinae autem justitiae, per quam peccatores damnari merentur, pro peccatis nostris neque illum satisfecisse, neque, ut satisfaceret, opus fuisse, affirmo. Crellius, contra Grotium, cap. 1. pag. 8. quod Socinus potissimum sibi oppugnandum sumserat, nempe Christum morte sua justitiae divinae pro peccatis nostris plenissime satisfecisse, hoc est, poenas ejusmodi sustinuisse, quae vi sua delictis omnibus omnium hominum essent aequales.
units.tr: Above all, they deny that a ransom [λύτρον] was paid to divine justice, or that satisfaction was made to it by Christ. Socinus, Thesis XXXVIII, On the Office of Christ: We therefore believe this to be the most true cause of the death of Christ, not, as most think, that divine justice might be satisfied for our sins. In De Servatore, at the beginning, where he sets out his opinion: But I affirm that Christ did not satisfy the justice of God, by which sinners deserve to be condemned, for our sins, nor was it necessary for him to do so in order to satisfy it. Crellius, against Grotius, ch. i, p. 8: What Socinus especially took upon himself to refute, namely that Christ by his death fully satisfied divine justice for our sins, that is, that he endured such punishments as by their force would be equal to all the offences of all men.

units.la: Negant, Deum nobis per Christum placatum. De Servatore, part. 1. cap. viii. pag. 51. docetur, nullo modo consequi, quod Christus ira Dei, pro nobis satisfecerit, eamque placaverit, cap. vii. eadem pag. Christus, ut mediator, Dei iram nobis non placavit.
units.tr: They deny that God was appeased for us through Christ. De Servatore, part i, ch. viii, p. 51: It is taught that it in no way follows that Christ satisfied the wrath of God for us, and appeased it; ch. vii, same page: Christ, as mediator, did not appease the wrath of God for us.

units.la: Negant item, Christum Deum nobis reconciliasse. De Servatore, part. 1. cap. viii. pag. 51. Christum nobis Deum reconciliasse, nusquam scriptum extat. Pag. 63. Per Christum, non Deum nobis, sed nos Deo reconciliatos fuisse, ubique scriptum est. Crellius, contra Grotium, cap. vii. Smalcius, de satisfact. contra Smiglec. cap. 1. pag. 155. Christum sua passione & morte non Deum nobis reconciliasse, vel ex offenso placatum & propitium reddidisse, sed nos Deo reconciliasse, & Deum nobis propitium declarasse.
units.tr: They likewise deny that Christ reconciled God to us. De Servatore, part i, ch. viii, p. 51: That Christ reconciled God to us is nowhere written. P. 63: It is everywhere written that through Christ we were reconciled, not God to us, but us to God. Crellius, against Grotius, ch. vii; Smalcius, On the Satisfaction, against Smiglecius, ch. i, p. 155: that Christ by his passion and death did not reconcile God to us, or make him, who was offended, placated and propitious, but reconciled us to God and declared God propitious to us.
