units.la: Denique & negant, Christum nos vere redemisse. Socinus, de Servatore, part. II. cap. I. pag. 65. redemtionem nostram per Christium factam, esse metaphoricam, id est in ea peragenda nullum verum pretium intervenisse, sive nihil cuiquam pro nobis solutum fuisse. Cap. II. pag. 76. explicatur tota redemtionis nostrae per Christum metaphora. Part. II. cap. xxvi. pag. 218. Nam, quod attinet ad opinionem, de qua disputamus, non solum satisfactionis, seu satisfaciendi verbum, cum de salute nobis per Christum parta agitur, in Sanctis Scripturis, ut ipse fateris, nusquam apparet, sed nihil ejusmodi, ne semel quidem, expresse in eis scriptum reperitur. Quale esset, quod Christus morte sua nobis Deum reconciliasset: vel, quod poenas universas nostris iniquitatibus debitas, moriendo, divinae justitiae persolvisset: vel, quod nos e manibus justitiae divinae, sanguinem suum redemtionis nostrae pretium illi dans, liberasset: vel, quod scelera nostra obedientia sua compensasset: vel, quod, ut remissionem peccatorum nobis Deus largiretur, digne commeritus fuisset: vel denique saltem, quod aliqua ratione Dei iram nobis placasset. Quare, non modo illa negata Adversariis, quae diximus, liquet; sed quoque ubi aliqua istorum probaverimus, quod in sequentibus facturos nos confidimus, conclusionem fecisse atque evicisse nos, apparebit. Neque audienda ea sunt, quae alias magno impetu & φανταςία[?] jactitant de Christi morte & passionibus, tum de ejus redemtione; sed quam metaphoricam habent, non veram, & propriam. Nempe quemadmodum Christus ipsis Deus metaphoricus, non naturâ verus ac unus Deus; ita quoque parem æquum erat habere redemtorem, vid. metaphoricum. Aliquando certe bonis verbis quam proximè ad nos accedere videntur. Crellius, contra Grot. cap. 1. pag. 7. Quod si tamen Grotius ad formam poenæ sufficere putat, relationem nocumenti ad peccatum, & ad bonum commune, atque adeo poenam definit, nocumentum peccati causa cuipiam iustum inflictum, inserviens bono communi, & reatui tollendo; in forma rei, de qua agitur, adeoque in principali quæstione nobis cum ipso convenies, nec nisi forte de voce, controversia nobis ab eo hac in parte movebitur atque hæc, ubi de controversiæ statu dis-ceptatur. Quin ad sententiam, à Grotio propositam, dixit: hæc verba, si dex-tre accipiantur, admitti à nobis possint universa. In libri præfatione: profecto vel id solum tam iniquis aliorum ea in parte iudiciis obstare deberet, quod morti Christi salutem nobis partam adscribimus. Satisfactionem Christi non agnoscere dicimur: nos vero agnoscimus Deo dignam, & S. litteris consentaneam. annotat in margine, libri sui cap 6. disput. partic. 44. & confer cum cap. 1. partic. 1. Capite illo sexto. pag. 343. ali-quam satisfactionem in Christo agnoscit: sed alterius generis satisfactionem, quam usus huius vocis admittat, Socini sententia non tantum non excludit, sed etiam postulat, sive nos respicias, sive Christum. Nam impletio conditionum, quas Deus sive nobis, sive Christo imposuit, quibus intervenientibus peccata nobis reipsa condonare, seu eorum poenas à nobis auferre voluit, satisfactio dici potest. De nobis id docuit Socinus, lib. 3. c. 2. Quod ad Christum attinet, idem ex ejus sententia consequitur. Quod si enim satisfacere cupiam est desiderium ejus implere, ut supra docuimus; Christus, qui desiderium Dei perfectissime implevit, & omnia, quæ salutis nostræ causa ipsi à Deo fuerunt impositia, plene fuit exequn-tus, plenissime etiam Deo satisfecit, idque pro nobis h. e. nostri causa, nostroque summo & sempiterno bono, quanquam non loco ac vice nostra. Ne nomen satisfactionis, si forte apud Adversarios legamus, atque eam videanturdicere, nobis imponat Smal-cius, contra Smiglecium, de Satisfactione, in resp. ad Præfat. pag. 153.
units.tr: Finally, they also deny that Christ truly redeemed us. Socinus, On the Saviour, part II, ch. 1, p. 65: our redemption made through Christ is metaphorical, that is, no true price intervened in accomplishing it, or nothing was paid to anyone on our behalf. Ch. 2, p. 76: the whole metaphor of our redemption through Christ is explained. Part II, ch. 26, p. 218: For as far as the opinion we are discussing is concerned, the word satisfaction, or to satisfy, does not appear anywhere in the Holy Scriptures when the salvation obtained for us through Christ is under discussion, as you yourself admit, and nothing of that kind is found expressly written in them, not even once. What would it be if Christ had reconciled God to us by his death; or if by dying he had paid to divine justice all the punishments due to our iniquities; or if he had freed us from the hands of divine justice by giving his blood as the price of our redemption; or if he had made up for our sins by his obedience; or if he had merited, so that God might grant us the forgiveness of sins; or finally, at least, if he had in some way appeased God's anger towards us. Therefore it is clear that not only are those things, which we have mentioned, denied by our opponents, but also that, when we have proved some of them (which we trust we shall do in what follows), it will appear that we have made and established our conclusion. Nor are those things to be heard which they elsewhere boast about with great vehemence and fancy [φανταςία] concerning the death and sufferings of Christ, and concerning his redemption, which they hold to be metaphorical and not true and proper. Just as Christ is a metaphorical God for them, not truly and by nature the one God, so it was equally fitting that they should have a metaphorical redeemer, as it were. Certainly at times they seem, in good words, to come as close to us as possible. Crellius, against Grotius, ch. 1, p. 7: But if Grotius thinks that the relation of harm to sin and to the common good suffices for the form of punishment, and so defines punishment as harm justly inflicted on someone because of sin, serving the common good and the removal of guilt, then in the form of the matter under discussion, and so in the principal question, he will agree with us; and any controversy raised by him on this point will perhaps be only about a word, and so on, where the state of the controversy is debated. Indeed he said, of the view proposed by Grotius: these words, if taken rightly, can be admitted by us in their entirety. In the preface of his book: Surely this alone, that we ascribe the salvation obtained for us to the death of Christ, ought to be an obstacle to such unfair judgments of others in this matter. We are said not to acknowledge the satisfaction of Christ; yet we acknowledge one worthy of God and agreeing with the Holy Scriptures. He notes in the margin of his book, ch. 6, disp. partic. 44, and compare with ch. 1, partic. 1. In that sixth chapter, p. 343, he acknowledges some satisfaction in Christ: but a satisfaction of a different kind from what the usage of this word admits; the opinion of Socinus not only does not exclude this, but even demands it, whether you look at us or at Christ. For the fulfilment of the conditions which God imposed, either on us or on Christ, and upon which he willed to forgive us our sins in fact, or to remove their punishment from us, can be called satisfaction. Socinus taught this concerning us, book 3, ch. 2. As far as Christ is concerned, the same follows from his opinion. For if to satisfy is to fulfil the desire of another, as we taught above, then Christ, who most perfectly fulfilled the desire of God, and who fully carried out all the things which were imposed on him by God for the sake of our salvation, also most fully satisfied God, and that for us, that is, for our sake and for our highest and everlasting good, although not in our place and stead. Lest, if we perhaps read the name of satisfaction among our opponents and they seem to say it, Smalcius, against Smiglecius, On Satisfaction, in the reply to the preface, p. 153, should impose it on us.

units.la: Ante omnia autem ob rudes & rerum imperitiores dicendum est, quid à nobis impugnetur.
units.tr: But first of all, for the sake of the unlearned and those less versed in the matter, it must be said what is being attacked by us.

units.la: Impugnatur autem non quod Christus omnibus illis satisfecerit, quæ illi à Deo ad salutem nostram procurandam impositia erant: sed quod iustitiæ Dei, ob quam nullum peccatum impu-nitum dimittere posse creditur, satisfecerit, ex irato Deo propitium reddiderit, cum nobis reconciliarit, poenas, quas nos luere debebamus, nostri loco perpessus & salutem nobis meritus sit, & alia his similia. Ruarus, in epistolâ ad amicum: Agnosco etiam obedien-tiam, quam Christus tanquam caput electorum omnium, in vita, & multo magis in morte, summo Deo præstitit, sufficiens esse λύτρον[?] propeccatis nostris; adeoque æquipollens supplicio, quod nos peccatis nostris eramus meriti: non quidem ex sese; ne Deo amoris atque gra-tiæ auferatur gloria, quam sacræ litteræ tantopere nobis inculcant: sed ex clementi Dei accep-tatione: qui obedientiam illam, non tanquam mercenarii ex merito stricte nuncupato; sed tanquam filii unigeniti, effuso in illum amore benigne ponderare, atque æstimare voluit. Cum autem meritum stricte dictum satisfactione excludo: non nego tamen ejus meritum in laxiori significatione: quo pacto nonnulli ex antiquis Ecclesiae patribus (si parva licet componere magnis) piis quoque operibus interdum meriti aliquid adscribunt: non ex proportione operum; sed ex Dei, aut beneplacito, aut promisso mensuratum. Interim fateor Christi meritum, omnia sanctorum (sita [?] lubet appellare) merita tantopere superare: adeoque ad significationem meriti proprie dicti, tanto propius accedere, quanto & perfectior, & omnibus numeris absolutior fuit ejus praestita Deo obedientia, & sublimior natura, & dignitate, is, qui eam praestitit. Poenam pro peccatis nostris a Christo persolutam, vix ausim affirmare; cum ea definiri soleat vindicta noxae: a qua Christus alienus fuit: nec justitia Dei permittat, ut poena nocenti debita, innocenti irrogetur, si laxiori significatione poenam interpreteris sc. perpessionem mali delicti, quamvis alieni causa & occasione cuiquam illatum; de vocabulo nolim esse difficilis. Cum ob peccata generis humani, Christum acerbissima quaeque, Deo ita requirente, sustinuisse, fateor. Tot ac tanta videtur hic Auctor in speciem fateri, & concedere, ut fere dubium sit, quid adeo magni discriminis aut controversiae superfit. Agnoscere se ait, Christi obedientiam esse λύτρον pro peccatis nostris, idque sufficiens, & aequipollens poenis nostris: Christi satisfactionem, & meritum laxe sumtum: poenas etiam, lata significatione; & quae non? promta autem est evasio, ubi illa metaphorice expositerit, quemadmodum totam redemptionis metaphoram Socinus dicit. Similiter Eques Polonus, in nupero ad Ordines Hollandiae scripto, se non negare Christi satisfactionem, non λύτρον pro peccatis nostris, asserit, satisfactionem nempe, qua Christus pro nobis, ad impetrandam peccatorum redemtionem, divinae voluntati ita satisfecerit, ut nihil ad plenissimam satisfactionem insuper requiratur. Atque super Christi merito, testatur, se intelligere perfectam ejus obedientiam & justitiam, ita in nos abundantem, ad vitae aeternae acquisitionem, ac Adami peccatum in posteros, ad ipsorum mortem. Nempe, dicet, exemplariter utrumque, saltem non propria efficientia, & causalitate meritoria: ut quidquid de merito utroque, sive reatus Adami in posteros, sive obedientiae Christi in suos, videtur largiri, meriti rationem enervet non solum, sed tollat. Idemque statuendum de agnita ipsi satisfactione. Non qualiscunque ea intelligenda est, sed vera, & propria; non metaphorica: non qua Christus divinae simpliciter voluntati, sed & justitiae, pro peccatis verum nostri loco λύτρον vel ἀντίλυτρον offerens, satisfecit. De vera satisfactione est quaestio, eaque poenali, divinae justitiae, nostri loco, a Christo, assumtis in se nostris poenis, praestita. Socinus, de Servatore, part. iii. cap. ii. pag. 228. Dixi autem, vera satisfactione, propterea quod dubium non est, quin Deus in iis, quibus peccata condonavit, semper aliquid requisierit, quod fortasse satisfactionis loco fuisse dicipotest; praesertim cum certum sit ea ratione divina voluntati ab eo, cui peccata condonata fuere, ea in parte plene fuisse satisfactum. Hoc autem statuit in nobis esse, vitae puritatem & innocentiam. Quae si praestita a nobis, plene dicant Deo satisfacere, quid adeo mirum, quod in Christi obedientia satisfactionem etiam largiuntur, eamque plenissimam? sed nempe ejusdem generis cum nostra illa. Quodque Socinus illo libro dixit, fortasse satisfactionis loco censeri ista posse; in Praelect. cap. xvii. pag. 88. absolute ponit : veram autem satisfactionem ubique nomino, quia nihil dubito, quin Deus, ab iis, quibus peccata ignovit, semper aliquid requisierit, sive aliquid in ipsis esse voluerit, quod satisfactionis cujusdam loco censeri posset. Id autem breviter nihil aliud est, quam vita pu-ritas atque innocentia. Nos autem veram Christi satisfactionem, verum λύτρον, propitiationem atque redemtionem veram, uti credimus, ita tuemur.
units.tr: What is attacked, however, is not that Christ satisfied all those things which were imposed on him by God for the procuring of our salvation, but that he satisfied the justice of God, by which it is believed that God cannot let any sin go unpunished; that he rendered God, who was angry, favourable, reconciled him to us; that he suffered in our place the punishments which we ought to have paid and so merited our salvation for us; and other things similar to these. Ruarus, in a letter to a friend: I also acknowledge the obedience which Christ, as head of all the elect, rendered to the highest God in his life, and much more in his death, to be a sufficient ransom [λύτρον] for our sins, and so equivalent to the punishment which we had deserved by our sins: not indeed of itself, lest the glory of God's love and grace, which the Holy Scriptures so strongly impress upon us, be taken away; but by the gracious acceptance of God, who was pleased to weigh and value that obedience kindly, not as that of a hired labourer from a strictly named merit, but as that of an only-begotten son, with love poured out upon him. But when I exclude satisfaction from merit taken strictly, I do not deny its merit in a looser sense, in which way some of the ancient Fathers of the Church (if small things may be compared with great) sometimes also ascribe some merit to pious works; not measured by the proportion of the works, but by God's good pleasure or promise. Meanwhile I confess that the merit of Christ far surpasses all the merits of the saints (whatever we like to call them), and so comes so much the nearer to the meaning of merit properly so called, as the obedience rendered by him to God was more perfect and in every way more complete, and he who rendered it was of a more exalted nature and dignity. I would hardly dare to affirm that the punishment for our sins was paid by Christ, since punishment is commonly defined as the vengeance of a crime, from which Christ was free; nor does the justice of God allow that a punishment due to the guilty should be inflicted on the innocent. If, however, in a looser sense you interpret punishment as the suffering of an evil deserved by a crime, even though it was inflicted on someone for the sake and occasion of another, I would not be difficult about the word. I confess that Christ, on account of the sins of the human race, endured the most bitter things, God so requiring. This author seems, in appearance, to confess and concede so many and such great things that it is almost doubtful what great difference or controversy remains. He says he acknowledges that the obedience of Christ is a ransom [λύτρον] for our sins, and that sufficient and equivalent to our punishments: the satisfaction and merit of Christ taken loosely; punishments also in a broad sense; and what not? The way out, however, is ready: where he explains these things metaphorically, just as Socinus says of the whole metaphor of redemption. Likewise the Polish knight, in his recent writing to the States of Holland, asserts that he does not deny the satisfaction of Christ, nor that Christ's ransom [λύτρον] was for our sins; namely, a satisfaction by which Christ, on our behalf, to obtain the redemption of sins, so satisfied the divine will that nothing further is required for a most complete satisfaction. And concerning the merit of Christ, he testifies that he understands his perfect obedience and justice to be so abundant towards us for the acquisition of eternal life, just as the sin of Adam was towards his posterity for their death. Namely, he will say, both are exemplary, at least not by proper efficiency and meritorious causality; so that whatever he seems to concede about either merit, whether the guilt of Adam towards his posterity or the obedience of Christ towards his own, not only weakens the notion of merit but takes it away. The same must be held of the satisfaction he acknowledges. It is not to be understood as any kind whatever, but as true and proper, not metaphorical; not that by which Christ satisfied the divine will simply, but that by which, offering for sins in our place a true ransom [λύτρον] or counter-ransom [ἀντίλυτρον], he satisfied the justice of God too. The question is about true satisfaction, and that a penal one, rendered to divine justice by Christ in our place, with our punishments taken upon himself. Socinus, On the Saviour, part III, ch. 2, p. 228: I have said true satisfaction, because there is no doubt that God, in those to whom he has forgiven sins, has always required something which can perhaps be called instead of satisfaction, especially since it is certain that by that means divine will was fully satisfied on that point by the one to whom the sins were forgiven. But he holds that what is required of us is purity and innocence of life. If these, rendered by us, are said to fully satisfy God, why is it so surprising that they also grant satisfaction in the obedience of Christ, and that the most complete? But of course it is of the same kind as that of ours. And what Socinus said in that book, that those things can perhaps be counted instead of satisfaction, in the Lectures, ch. 17, p. 88, he states absolutely: I call it true satisfaction everywhere, because I do not doubt that God has always required of those whose sins he has pardoned something, or willed something in them, which could be counted in place of some satisfaction. But briefly, that is nothing other than purity and innocence of life. We, however, hold and defend the true satisfaction of Christ, the true ransom [λύτρον], and true propitiation and redemption, as we believe them.

units.la: Atque illa ad statum controversiae constituendum, & eruendam Adversariorum sententiam dicenda fuerunt. Duo restant insuper inquirenda: quid de cau-sis, ob quas Christus Servator est, atque dicitur, Adversarii statuant; deinde, quid de causis, vel finibus mortis ejus, & quam ob causam vel finem mortuus sit.
units.tr: These things had to be said to fix the state of the controversy and to bring out the opponents' opinion. Two matters remain to be examined: what the opponents hold about the causes for which Christ is and is called Saviour, and what they hold about the causes or ends of his death, and why or for what end he died.

units.la: Nos quidem Christum Servatorem credimus, propterea quia a peccatis, seipso, vere & proprie nos redemit, atque servat: non propter ea, quae ad salu-tem nostram quoquomodo faciunt, ut quod doctrinam salutis annunciavit, vel confirmavit, sive miraculis, sive exemplo, aut morte, & denique resurrec-tione sua; non ob praeconium, exemplum, & martyrium: quas causas in Servatore, missa propria & genuina, quod suo pretio nos redemit, & vindicavit, Adversarii ponunt. Quippe sic rationem instituunt, ut primo Christum Servatorem dicant, quia doctrinam Euangelii & salutis annunciavit. Socinus, de Servatore, part. 1. cap. 11. & part. 11. cap. 11. pag. 83. ea praecipue ratione Servatorem nostrum esse contendit, ut intelligamus, non alia ratione magis partam nobis esse salutem per Christum, quam, quod per ipsum Dei voluntatem, in salute nobis conferenda, plenissime assecuti fuerimus, & ipsum Deum quasi praesentem conspexerimus. Cap. xxi. pag. 179. non per satisfactionem divina justitia pro peccatis nostris exhibi-tam, sed per divina voluntatis declarationem, & vita aeterna supremaque potestatis adep-tionem, nos Christus expiavit.
units.tr: We indeed believe that Christ is Saviour because he truly and properly redeems and saves us from our sins by himself. We do not base this on those things which contribute to our salvation in some way: that he announced or confirmed the doctrine of salvation, whether by miracles, by example, or by his death and finally his resurrection; nor on his preaching, example and martyrdom. The opponents set down these causes in the Saviour, leaving out the proper and genuine cause, that he redeemed and vindicated us by his own price. Indeed they reason so that first they call Christ Saviour because he announced the doctrine of the gospel and of salvation. Socinus, On the Saviour, part 1, ch. 11 and part 2, ch. 11, p. 83, argues that our Saviour is so called chiefly for this reason: that we may understand that salvation has been gained for us through Christ by no other means than that through him we have most fully attained God's will in bestowing salvation, and have seen God himself as if present. Ch. xxi, p. 179: Christ atoned for us not by a satisfaction to divine justice exhibited for our sins, but by the declaration of the divine will and by the attaining of eternal life and supreme power.

units.la: Alteram rationem dant, quia salutis illam doctrinam suam, variis modis confirmavit. Part. 1. cap. 111. Christum merito Servatorem nostrum dici eam ab cau-sam, quod salutis aeterna viam nobis confirmaverit. Confirmasse autem dicunt, miraculis, & morte; plenissime vero resurrectione. Pag. seq. Animadvertere autem oportet, non solum miraculis confirmasse Christum viam salutis, quam annunciaverat, sed, vel maxime, sui sanguinis effusione. Pag. 24. Resurrectio Christi plenissima est Euangelii confirmatio. Sed quid dicam de Iesu Christi resurrectione, per quam potissimum & coelesti atque ineffabili ratione ea omnia plenissime ac perfectissime confirmata sunt, qua nobis ille de coelo attulit, atque annunciavit. Pag. 25. Iesum Christum, quia salutis aeterna viam nobis annunciaverit, & confirmaverit, merito servatorem nostrum & dici, & agnosci debere. Idem, de justificatione, pag. 7. Confer etiam Catechef. Racov. de Prophetico Christi munere, cap. vii. Ostorod. Instit. cap. xxxvii. Addunt, & vitae Christi exemplum. Socinus, pag. & loco cit. Quare ad ipsius Iesu Christi vitae exemplum, & a mortuis resurrectionem, quibus in sua ipsius persona viam salutis manifeste eum nobis ostendisse, & ob eam rem servatorem etiam nostrum esse, contendo, excutienda transeamus. Cap. v. pag. 31. explicat, quomodo Christus, a mortuis resurgendo, salutis aeterna viam nobis ostenderit, ac propterea noster servator sit. Pag. 37. Per resurrectionem suam Iesus servator noster factus est.
units.tr: They give a second reason: that he confirmed that doctrine of salvation in various ways. Part 1, ch. 3: Christ is rightly called our Saviour on this account, that he confirmed for us the way of eternal salvation. They say he confirmed it by miracles and by his death, but most fully by his resurrection. Next page: We must notice that Christ confirmed the way of salvation which he had announced not only by miracles, but above all by the shedding of his blood. P. 24: The resurrection of Christ is the fullest confirmation of the gospel. But what shall I say of the resurrection of Jesus Christ, by which, above all, all those things which he brought and announced to us from heaven have been most fully and perfectly confirmed, in a heavenly and ineffable manner? P. 25: Jesus Christ, because he has announced and confirmed for us the way of eternal salvation, ought rightly to be both called and acknowledged as our Saviour. The same, on justification, p. 7. Compare also the Racovian Catechism, on the prophetic office of Christ, ch. vii, and Ostorodt, Institutes, ch. xxxvii. They add also the example of Christ's life. Socinus, p. and place cited: Therefore let us pass over, to be examined, the example of Jesus Christ's own life and his resurrection from the dead, by which I maintain that he clearly showed us the way of salvation in his own person, and for that reason is also our Saviour. Ch. v, p. 31: He explains how Christ, by rising from the dead, showed us the way of eternal salvation, and therefore is our Saviour. P. 37: Through his resurrection Jesus became our Saviour.

units.la: Denique ultimo loco Servatorem Christum ajunt, tum propter adeptam potestatem nos salvandi; tum quod hoc suo tempore revera facturus, nosque actu salvaturum est. Part. II. pag. 179. non per satisfactionem divina justitia pro peccatis nostris exhibitam, sed per divina voluntatis declarationem, & vita aeterna supremaque potestatis adeptionem, nos Christus expiavit. Et part. I. cap. VI. Christum ideo Servatorem nostrum & esse, & nominari, quod ipse vitam aeternam nobis daturus sit.
units.tr: Finally, in the last place, they say Christ is Saviour both because he has obtained the power of saving us and because he will in fact do this in his time, and will actually save us. Part II, p. 179: Christ atoned for us not by a satisfaction to divine justice exhibited for our sins, but by the declaration of the divine will and by the attaining of eternal life and supreme power. And part I, ch. VI: Christ is therefore both our Saviour and is named so, because he himself is going to give us eternal life.

units.la: Propter causas illas, non vero satisfactionem, meritum, aut redemtionem proprie dictam, Servatorem Christum esse, contendunt. Nescio, an satis clare, & justo ordine causas illas exponant, & tractent. Sic potuis dispono illas, ut primo loco dicant Christum Servatorem, ideo quod salutis doctrinam nobis annunciavit. II. atque confirmavit. & hoc tum vita sua. III. tum miraculis. IV. tum morte. V. atque resurrectione. VI. insuper, propter adeptam nos salvandi potestatem. VII. ac denique salutis collationem, sive ipsam salvationem. Et hinc ipsis Salvator appellatur. Ubi duas Frantzius, ex Adversariorum mente, attulisset causas, cur Christum dicant Servatorem, vid. ut voluntatem Dei nobis annunciaret; tum in colligenda Ecclesia eam exequeretur, regerit Smalcius, Disp. VI. de Bonis operib. pag. 166. praeter duas istas causas, & alias a suis addi: Nempe quod salutem aeternam variis modis confirmarit, & in sua ipsius persona ostenderit & ostendat. Quam vero alteram causam affert Frantzius, eam sic intelligimus, quod Iesus Christus, qui nunc potestatem habet absolutam nos servandi, reipsa nos servaturus sit, & vitam aeternam nobis, qui in illum credimus, daturus in extremo illo die.
units.tr: On account of those causes, and not on account of satisfaction, merit, or redemption properly so called, they contend that Christ is Saviour. I do not know whether they set out and treat those causes clearly enough and in a proper order. I could arrange them thus: first, they say Christ is Saviour because he announced to us the doctrine of salvation; (2) and confirmed it, and this both by his life; (3) and by miracles; (4) and by death; (5) and by resurrection; (6) moreover, because of the power he has obtained of saving us; (7) and finally the bestowal of salvation, or salvation itself. And hence he is called Saviour by them. When Frantzius, on behalf of the opponents, had given two reasons why they call Christ Saviour, namely that he might make known God's will to us and then carry it out in gathering the Church, Smalcius, Disp. VI, on good works, p. 166, replied that besides these two reasons others were added by their side: namely that he confirmed eternal salvation in various ways, and has shown and does show it in his own person. But the second reason Frantzius gives we understand thus: that Jesus Christ, who now has absolute power to save us, will in fact save us, and will give eternal life on that last day to us who believe in him.

units.la: Remonstrantes similiter plures modos adsignant, cur Christus Salvator sit, nempe praeconium, exemplum, & martyrium. Apol. cap. VIII. 94. an indignum quippiam Christo aut Christi Salvatoris officio tribuitur, si dicatur pluribus modis, & non uno tantum, id est, si dicatur praeconio, exemplo, & martyrio suo etiam salutem nostram procurasse? Salutem procurare, ambigue dicitur: si intelligatur, quae ad salutem quoquo modo faciunt, haud negamus, Christi etiam doctrinam, & exemplum eo facere. Martyrium vero Christi Jesu mors valde μαρτυρικῶς[?], & inusitate dicitur. Neque Scriptura ita loquitur, quae in Christi morte id ponit, quod ei soli competit, & cum nullius morte commune habet, nempe quod sit ἱλασμός, & λύτρον, quae nullo modo martyribus tribuuntur, aliamque plane à martyrio habent rationem & naturam. Denique nec ejusdem sunt efficaciae vel ordinis ad salutem nostram, cum verâ nostri redemtione, ob quam proprie Christus à Scriptura pariter & nobis Salvator nuncupatur. Nec sufficit, meriti qualem qualem mentionem hic injicere, vel dicere, eo ipso quod Christus, innocentissimus cum esset, mortem tamen violentam subivit, & pretiosum suum sanguinem fudit, ex mandato Patris fui, id effecit & obtinuit a Patre suo, ut Pater isto sanguine, veluti factificio propitiatorio ex manu Christi accepto, cum genere humano adhuc redire voluerit, id est, redierit in gratiam, sic ut justitia ejus, sive amori, quo justitiam amat, & odio habet peccatum, abunde satisfactum fuerit, & impo-sterum cum genere humano propitius, per eundem filium suum, agere decreverit. Quod verbum satisfactionis, & satisfactionem quoque aliquam etiam Sociniani in hoc negotio admittunt, supra vidimus: nec an simpliciter justitiæ divinæ Chri-stus satisfecerit, quæritur, nempe ei, quâ Deus justitiam amat, & odit peccatum; sed an punitivæ & vindicativæ, quæ peccati pœnam efflagitat[?], adeoque an ei sic Christus satisfecerit, ut pœnas nobis debitas in se susceperit, easque exsolverit suâ morte & passionibus: istoque modo nobis Dei gratiam, & gloriam meritus sit, quæritur. Præsertim observanda illa & attendenda, quandoquidem videmus Remonstrantes in Catechesi nimis leviter ac studiose ea præterire. Quæstione etenim 28. ubi interrogant, Per quem, & quomodo Deus hoc liberationis opus effecit? Resp. Per Iesum Christum filium suum unigenitum, quem in mundum misit, non solum ut benignam Dei voluntatem, de remissione peccatorum omnibus pœnitentibus & credentibus annunciaret, eandemque suam doctrinam divinis miraculis confirmaret, verum etiam & præcipue, ut per obedientiam & voluntariam sui ipsius in mortem usque crucis oblationem, simul efficacem operationem sui Spiritus S. eos qui ipsum cognoscentes & in eum credentes viam ab ipso monstratam essent ingressuri, in vitam perduceret æternam.
units.tr: The Remonstrants likewise assign several modes by which Christ is Saviour, namely preaching, example, and martyrdom. Apology, ch. VIII, 94: Is anything unworthy attributed to Christ or to the office of Christ the Saviour if it is said that he did this in several ways and not in one only, that is, if it is said that by his preaching, his example and his martyrdom he also procured our salvation? To procure salvation is said ambiguously: if it is understood as what contributes to salvation in any way, we do not deny that the doctrine and example of Christ also contribute to it. But to call the death of Jesus Christ a martyrdom [μαρτυρικῶς] is very strange and unusual. Nor does Scripture speak so, for Scripture in the death of Christ sets down what belongs to him alone and has nothing in common with anyone else's death: namely that it is an atonement [ἱλασμός] and a ransom [λύτρον]. These are by no means attributed to martyrs, and they have a plainly different character and nature from martyrdom. Finally, they do not have the same efficacy or order toward our salvation as our true redemption, on account of which Christ is properly called Saviour both by Scripture and by us. Nor is it enough to make some mention of merit, of whatever sort, or to say: by the very fact that Christ, though most innocent, nevertheless underwent a violent death and shed his precious blood by the command of his Father, he brought it about and obtained from his Father that the Father, receiving that blood from the hand of Christ as a propitiatory sacrifice, was willing to return to the human race, that is, returned into favour, so that his justice, or the love by which he loves justice and hates sin, was amply satisfied, and he decided henceforth to deal graciously with the human race through the same Son of his. The word satisfaction, and some satisfaction too, the Socinians admit in this business, as we saw above. Nor is the question whether Christ satisfied divine justice simply, that is, that by which God loves justice and hates sin; but whether he satisfied the punitive and vindictive justice, which demands the punishment of sin. The question is whether Christ so satisfied it that he took upon himself the penalties owed by us and paid them off by his death and sufferings, and in this way merited for us God's grace and glory. This is especially to be observed and attended to, since we see the Remonstrants passing over it too lightly and carelessly in their Catechism. For in question 28, where they ask: Through whom, and how, did God accomplish this work of deliverance? the answer is: Through Jesus Christ his only-begotten Son, whom he sent into the world, not only that he might announce God's kindly will concerning the remission of sins to all who repent and believe, and confirm that same doctrine of his by divine miracles, but also, and chiefly, that through obedience and his voluntary offering of himself even to the death of the cross, together with the effective working of his Holy Spirit, he might lead into eternal life those who, knowing him and believing in him, were to enter upon the way shown by him.

units.la: Quid quæso hic est de salvatione aut liberatione nostrâ per Christum, de quo instituta erat interrogatio, quod non Socinianilibenter admittant, atque etiam fateantur, Christum Dei voluntatem, de remissione peccatorum, annunciasse, & confirmasse miraculis, denique salvaturum omnes sibi obtemperantes? Obscura & dubia est constructio, quomodo Christus dicatur per obedientiam & oblationem suiipsius, atque operationem Spiritus S. homines perducere in vitam æternam. Quippe obedientiam Christi, & oblationem sui in crucem, quamvis non pro sacerdocio, & operationem Spiritus S. eamque efficacem, dicent quidem etiam Socinianî. Ita totum silere, & præterire hoc in negotio & quæstione, quidquid est redemtionis & satisfactionis verae? idque ab iis, ubi se etiamnum Reformatos scribunt? Interim & in explicanda liberationis nostræ ratione illas ponere causas salvationis, quas dant Socinianî? neque alias? Qu.
units.tr: What, I ask, has this to do with our salvation or deliverance through Christ, which was the subject of the question? The Socinians do not readily admit this, yet they even confess that Christ announced God's will concerning the forgiveness of sins and confirmed it by miracles, and that he will at last save all who obey him. The construction is obscure and doubtful: how is Christ said to lead men into eternal life through his obedience and through his offering of himself, and through the working of the Holy Spirit? The Socinians too will indeed say that Christ offered obedience and himself on the cross, though not as a priest, and that the Holy Spirit works, and works effectively. Is the whole matter of redemption and true satisfaction, then, to be passed over in silence in this business and question? And is it to be passed over by men who still write of themselves as Reformed? Meanwhile, in explaining the manner of our deliverance, are they to set down only those causes of salvation which the Socinians give, and no others? Qu.

units.la: XXXVI. Breviter ista nunc conjunge in unum, atque dic mihi, quomodo & qua ratione Christum agnoscis tuum redemtorem & servatorem? Resp. Auctor salutis nostræ est, dum doctrinâ suâ viam salutis nobis monstravit: sanctâ vitâ nobis præivit: miraculis suis ac morte doctrinam suam confirmavit, corporis sui ἱλαστηρίῳ[?] salutem nobis impetravit, atque absolutâ auctoritate & potestate nobis vitam æternam confert. En rationes & causas omnes, propter quas etiam Socinianî contendunt Christum esse Servato-rem. Quod additur, corporis sui ἱλαστηρίῳ[?], salutem nobis impetrasse: & impetrasse nobis salutem, haud diffitebuntur Socinianî; neque, opi-nor, negabunt dici posse corporis Christi ἱλαστήριον[?]: uti quando de expiatione & propitiatione per Christum factâ responsiones & exceptiones eorum proferentur, audiemus. Socinus, de Servatore, pag. 82[?]. ait, Iesum Christum esse à Deo pro placamento nobis propositum. Pluraque ejusmodi adducere, in promptu est.
units.tr: XXXVI. Briefly now join these things together, and tell me: how and by what reasoning do you acknowledge Christ as your redeemer and saviour? Answer: He is the author of our salvation, since by his teaching he showed us the way of salvation; he went before us with a holy life; by his miracles and his death he confirmed his teaching; he obtained salvation for us by the propitiatory [ἱλαστηρίῳ] of his body; and by his absolute authority and power he bestows eternal life upon us. Here are all the reasons and causes for which the Socinians too maintain that Christ is the Saviour. As for what is added, that he obtained salvation for us by the propitiatory [ἱλαστηρίῳ] of his body: the Socinians will not deny that he obtained salvation for us, and, I think, they will not deny that the body of Christ can be called a propitiatory [ἱλαστήριον]. We shall hear their answers and objections when the expiation and propitiation made through Christ are brought up. Socinus, on the Saviour, p. 82[?], says that Jesus Christ was set forth by God as a propitiation for us. It is easy to adduce many more statements of this kind.

units.la: Hoc exponendum fuerat, an pœnas peccatorum nostrorum in se sustulerit Christus, & nostri loco eas exsolverit, & sic verâ intercedente satisfactione, ac expiatione delictorum nostrorum, Deo nos reconciliarit, atque redemerit? Certe hoc in loco, ubi omnis Reformata Ecclesia ita loqui & catholicam explicare sententiam consuevit ab iis praesertim illa plenius dicenda erant, qui Socinianismi suspecti, ut suspicionem, siquidem injusta, à se amolirent, saltem ne non etiam loquerentur ex mente & verbis Reformatorum, si magis pro Reformatis, quam, quod nunc egerunt, pro Socinianis loqui ac stare maluissent. De variis autem illis causis, cur Christus Salvator sit, quas Sociniani primum, tum Remonstrantes adferunt, dicimus. 1. non esse dubium, quin illa egerit Christus, & vera in ipso sint; ut quod doctrinam salutis annunciavit, confirmavit, & potestate à Patre acceptâ nos servat. 11. neque negari posse, quin faciant illa ad salutem etiam: ejus doctrinam, vitae exemplum &c 111. Neque disputari, an aliqua inde ratione quis servator, & forte Christus etiam sic dici queat. iv. sed quia Christus non communi aliqua ratione, sed plane singulari, & aliis incommunicabili Salvator est, & appellatur, illa quae etiam in aliis quoquo modo locum habent, ut docere, & doctrinam vel morte confirmare, negamus propriam esse causam, cur ex usu Scripturae, & Ecclesiae, Servator nuncupetur.
units.tr: This should have been explained: whether Christ took upon himself the punishments of our sins and paid them in our place, and so reconciled us to God and redeemed us by a true satisfaction and expiation of our offences? Certainly in this place, where the whole Reformed Church is accustomed to speak in this way and to set out the Catholic doctrine, those especially who are suspected of Socinianism ought to have said this more fully, so that, if the suspicion is unjust, they might remove it from themselves, or at least might not fail to speak in the mind and words of the Reformed, if they preferred to speak and stand for the Reformed rather than, as they have now done, for the Socinians. But concerning those various causes why Christ is the Saviour, which the Socinians first put forward, and then the Remonstrants, we say the following. (1) There is no doubt that Christ did these things, and that they are true in him: that he announced the doctrine of salvation, confirmed it, and with the power received from the Father preserves us. (2) Nor can it be denied that these things also contribute to salvation: his teaching, the example of his life, and so on. (3) It is not disputed whether in some sense a man may be a saviour in this way, and perhaps Christ may also be called so in this sense. (4) But because Christ is the Saviour not by some common reason, but by a wholly singular one, one that cannot be shared with others, we deny that those things which in some way also apply to others, such as teaching, and confirming the teaching even by death, are the proper cause why he is named the Saviour according to the usage of Scripture and of the Church.

units.la: Rationes sunt. 1. Scriptura causam istius nomenclaturae exponit nostri per Christum redemtione: quae ita Christo soli competit, ut in hujus consortium nemo cum illo veniat. Ex proprio & singulari officio, proprium ei quoque nomen. Matth. 1.21. & vocabis nomen ejus Jesum: ipse enim salvabit populum suum a peccatis. Hoc ad redemtionem spectat; non praecise vel proprie ad doctrinam, ejusque confirmationem. Actor. iv. 12. neque est in ullo alio salus: neque etiam nomen est aliud sub caelo datum inter homines, quo nos oportet servari. Ephe. v. 23. & ipse est servator corporis. 25. qui dilexit Ecclesiam, & semetipsum tradidit pro ea. Ut eam sanctificaret, &c. 1. Tim. 1. 15. Fidelis est sermo & omni acceptione dignus, quod Christus Jesus in mundum venit ut peccatores salvaret, quorum ergo primus sum. Heb. ix. 12. per proprium vero sanguinem intravit semel in sancta, aeterna reperta redemtione. 1 Pet. 1, 18. 19. non corruptibilibus, argento aut auro redemti estis, sed pretioso sanguine ut agni inculpati & immaculati Christi. 1 Joan. ii. 1. 2. Jesus Christus, & ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Apocal. v. 9. Dignus es qui accipias librum, & aperias sigilla ejus, quia mactatus es, & emisti nos Deo in sanguine tuo. Ita causa cur Christus Salvator noster & dicitur & est, vel quare redemtor noster, passim in Scripturis constituitur in ejus sanguine, morte, vel redemtione nostra a peccatis, quae morti ejus attribuitur, non doctrinae, ejusve confirmationi, per exemplum, miracula, aut martyrium. 11. Quae propriâ, & reali causalitate salutem non efficiunt, imo quibus positis evenire potest ut tamen homines non salventur, illa propria directa & formalis causa esse nequeunt, cur Christus habeatur Salvator: sed praeconium Christi, & exemplum, & martyrium talia sunt: ergo. 111. Servatorem esse, uti de Christo dicitur, ipsi competit soli, & singulari ratione: ergo etiam causa ejus debet esse aliquid singulare, non hoc quod commune habeat cum pluribus, qualia sunt praeconium, exemplum, & martyrium. Dicuntur quidem & alii Servatores; sed improprie & per metaphoram, non ea ratione, qua Christus, quasi hic excellentissima ratione prae aliis Servator sit, qui propriâ & omnino singulari ratione talis est. quae vel compacompares vel similes proprië nullo modo habet. Talis, qui ab hominibus plane fit κεχωρισμένος[?]. Hebr. vii. 26. Uti Servator noster Christus, ita hoc omni modo solus & unicus est. Æque ac unus mediator, ita & unus Salvator. Unde utrumque conjungit Apostolus, 1 Tim. ii. 5. 6. Unus enim Deus, unus etiam mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Jesus. Qui seipsum dedit redemtionem ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus. Qua ratione seipsum dedit redemtionem, Salvator est, atque unus Salvator, ob causam illam redemtionis sibi singularem & propriam. Quemadmodum nec ob plures causas Dei Filius: ita nec ob alias illas Servator est.. Denique Socinians Christum nequeunt dicere verum & proprium Servatorum. Qui est redemtor metaphoricus, & redemtionem peregit meta-phoricam, is etiam metaphoricus Servator haberi iisdem debet, non proprius: atqui Christus Socinianis est redemtor metaphoricus, ejusque metaphorica redemtio: ergo. Atque hinc, quemadmodum negando veram & propriam Deitatis in Christo rationem necesse putabant confugere ad rationes alias, & plures; ita nunc veram causam Salvationis præteréundo, alias constituunt in Christo, ob quas Servator dicatur, præter & extra veram illam ac genuinam redemtionis. Ut eo minus accedere iis hic oporteat, non ut negemus, quod verum, ut Socino contradicamus, & affirmemus id, quod falsum est, ut ab eo longius recedamus, quemadmodum Remonstrantes nobis exprobrant: sed quia in odium veritatis, veræque redemtionis & salvationis illa confin-guntur a Socinianis, præter sensum Scripturæ, ne temerarii simus in adoptandis alienis, præter Scripturæ & Ecclesiæ sententiam ac consuetudinem, vocabu-lis, & doctrinis.
units.tr: The reasons are these. (1) Scripture sets out the cause of this name in our redemption through Christ, which belongs to Christ alone, so that no one comes into fellowship with him in it. Because of his proper and singular office he also has a proper name. Matt. 1.21: And you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins. This pertains to redemption; it does not pertain precisely or properly to doctrine and its confirmation. Acts 4.12: Neither is there salvation in any other; for neither is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. Eph. 5.23: and he is the Saviour of the body. 25: who loved the Church and gave himself up for it, that he might sanctify it, etc. 1 Tim. 1.15: This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief. Heb. 9.12: but by his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption. 1 Pet. 1.18–19: you were redeemed not with corruptible things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb unblemished and spotless. 1 John 2.1–2: Jesus Christ, and he is the propitiation for our sins. Rev. 5.9: You are worthy to take the book and open its seals, for you were slain and have redeemed us to God by your blood. So the cause why Christ is and is called our Saviour, or why he is our redeemer, is set forth everywhere in the Scriptures as consisting in his blood, his death, or our redemption from sins, which is ascribed to his death; not to his teaching, or its confirmation by example, miracles, or martyrdom. (2) Those things which do not bring about salvation by a proper and real causality, and which, even when they are present, may still leave men unsaved, cannot be the proper, direct and formal cause why Christ is held to be the Saviour. But the proclamation of Christ, his example, and his martyrdom are of this kind; therefore. (3) That he is the Saviour, as is said of Christ, belongs to him alone and for a singular reason; therefore his cause too must be something singular, not something he has in common with many, such as proclamation, example, and martyrdom. Others are indeed also called saviours, but improperly and by metaphor, not for the reason for which Christ is the Saviour, as though he were the Saviour above others by a most excellent reason, who is such by a proper and wholly singular reason, which in no way has equals or similars properly. He is one who is wholly set apart from men [κεχωρισμένος] (Heb. 7.26). As our Saviour Christ is in every way alone and unique, so, as there is one mediator, so there is one Saviour. Whence the Apostle joins both together, 1 Tim. 2.5–6: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for all. Because he gave himself as a redemption, he is the Saviour, and the one Saviour, on account of that redemption which is his own singular and proper cause. Just as the Son of God is not so on many grounds, so he is not Saviour on other grounds. Finally, the Socinians cannot call Christ a true and proper Saviour. One who is a metaphorical redeemer and has accomplished a metaphorical redemption ought to be held a metaphorical saviour, not a proper one; but for the Socinians Christ is a metaphorical redeemer and his redemption is metaphorical; therefore. And hence, just as in denying the true and proper ground of the deity in Christ they felt compelled to take refuge in other and several reasons, so now, passing over the true cause of salvation, they set up in Christ other causes, on account of which he is called Saviour, apart from and outside that true and genuine redemption. We need not go further along this road here, not that we would deny what is true, or contradict Socinus and affirm what is false, so as to recede farther from him, as the Remonstrants reproach us; but because those notions are fabricated by the Socinians out of hatred of the truth and of true redemption and salvation, contrary to the sense of Scripture; and we should not be rash in adopting, beyond the teaching and custom of Scripture and of the Church, the words and doctrines of others.

units.la: Christus autem Servator est, & dicitur, propter opus redemtionis, & salu-tis nostræ, seipso effectum, verâ, propriâ, & reali efficientiâ: ut, quemadmodum hinc salus certo in servandis sequitur, & suâ propriâ vi ac operâ, non solâ morali aliquâ expositione, aut commendatione, ita propter illa Servator agnoscatur, & fit. Nempe, salutis vel redemtionis impetratione, tum etiam applicatione. Quæ duæ partes sunt officii σωτηρικῆς[?], ejusdem dignitatis, effica-ciæ, atque latitudinis. Impetratio fit per satisfactionem, & meritum: Applica-tio autem, per gratiam, & gloriam. Hæc omnia amplitudine redemtionis & sal-vationis continentur, & Christo soli propria sunt, denique verum ac genui-num fundamentum cur dicatur Salvator.
units.tr: Christ is indeed the Saviour, and is so called, because he himself effected the work of redemption and of our salvation by a true, proper and real efficacy. Just as salvation certainly follows from this in preserving us, and does so by its own proper power and work, not merely by some moral exposition or commendation, so Christ is acknowledged and made Saviour on account of those things. Namely, through the impetration of salvation or redemption, and also through its application. These two parts belong to the saving office [σωτηρικῆς], and have the same dignity, efficacy and scope. Impetration takes place through satisfaction and merit; application takes place through grace and glory. All these are contained within the breadth of redemption and salvation, belong to Christ alone, and are finally the true and genuine foundation why he is called Saviour.

units.la: De prioribus illis agendum, disputandumque nobis nunc venit, cum Soci-nianis, qui impetratam, & illo modo, salutem nostram, contumaciter ne-gant. Dumque satisfactionem nos morti Christi, ut proprium effectum attribui-mus, illi quasvis alias causas & fines mortis ejus adferunt, præter illum. Prout de causis cur Servator est, eodem modo de illis, ob quas mortuus Christus, philosophantur. Unde Catechesis Racoviensis cap. 11.[?] de Prophet. Christi munere, pag. 254. utrumque ita conjungit, illius Christi mortis quæ sunt præcipuæ rationes, quemadmodum etiam Dominus Jesus potissimum duplici ratione suorum fidelium Servator est. Primum enim exemplo suo, ut in salutis viâ, quam sunt ingressi, persistant, suos movet. Deinde iisdem in omni tentationum, laborum & periculorum certamine adest, opitulatur, & tandem ab ipsa æterna morte liberat. Quæstio antecesserat hæc: cur necesse erat Christum tot pati, & tam atrocem mortem subire? Resp. Eo quod ab ipso servandi iisdem afflictionibus & morti ejusmodi plerumque sunt obnoxii.
units.tr: We must now deal with and dispute those first matters with the Socinians, who stubbornly deny that our salvation was obtained in this way. While we attribute satisfaction to the death of Christ as its proper effect, they assign to his death various other causes and ends, apart from that one. They philosophise about the reasons why he died in the same way as they do about the reasons why he is Saviour. Hence the Racovian Catechism, ch. 11, on the prophetic office of Christ, p. 254, joins the two together thus: "These are the chief reasons for Christ's death, just as the Lord Jesus is the Saviour of his faithful people chiefly for a twofold reason. For first, by his example he moves his people to persevere in the way of salvation which they have entered. Then he is present in every struggle of temptations, labours and dangers, helps them, and finally frees them from eternal death itself." The question had preceded this: "Why was it necessary for Christ to suffer so much and to undergo so atrocious a death?" Answer: "Because he was to save those who are generally liable to the same afflictions and such a death, from them."

units.la: Prima ergo & potissima mortis Christi causa est exemplaris, juxta Adversarios, & talis ejus fructus atque efficacia, ut pro exemplo faciat fidelibus, in ipsorum afflictionibus & morte. Ubi omnes perpendant, an in hoc, & quidem principaliter, vis & efficacia mortis Christi constituatur in Scripturis? annon in alia, & diversi longe ordinis ac naturæ causa? expiatione videlicet, propitiatione, & redemtione nostrum à peccatis verâ[?]? Sed pergamus in enodandâ Adversariorum sententiâ.
units.tr: The first and chief cause of Christ's death, according to the adversaries, is exemplary, and its fruit and efficacy are such that it serves as an example to the faithful in their afflictions and death. Let everyone weigh whether the power and efficacy of Christ's death, principally and indeed, is set forth in the Scriptures in this, or rather in another cause of a quite different order and nature, namely the expiation, propitiation and true redemption of us from our sins? But let us proceed to unfold the opinion of the adversaries.

units.la: Diversimode se explicant: at huc tendunt, ut tum confirmasse Christum, dicant, doctrinam suam morte; tum sibi acquisivisse potestatem, ad nos salvandum, supremam. Ad prius illud referunt, fidei nostræ in promissiones doctrinæ ejus, per & propter mortem consecutam, confirmationem: deinde efficaciam exempli, in & ex Christi morte, tum resurrectione, & adeptâ cœlesti gloriâ. Catechesis, pag. 257. Qui vero sanguis aut mors Christi nobis voluntatem Dei confirmavit? Resp. Duplici ratione: primum quod nos manifeste de ingenti in nos Dei charitate certos reddiderit, idque adeo, quod Deus nobis velit id donare, quod in novo Fœdere promittat, unde etiam sanguis novi fœderis est dictus, qui præstantiora loquatur, quam sanguis Abel, & ipse Christus testis verax & fidelis dictus est: Deinde quod resurrectione Christi, quæ nonnisi morte ipsius interveniente fieri potuit, de resurrectione nostrâ, & porro vita æterna consequenda certiores facti sumus, si præceptis Domini Jesu pareamus.
units.tr: They explain themselves in various ways, but all tend to this: that Christ, by his death, confirmed his doctrine, and acquired for himself supreme power to save us. To the former they refer the confirmation of our faith in the promises of his doctrine, obtained through and on account of his death; then the efficacy of his example in and from Christ's death, and from his resurrection and the heavenly glory thereby obtained. Catechism, p. 257: "But how did the blood or death of Christ confirm God's will to us?" Answer: "In two ways. First, because it has made us manifestly certain of God's great love towards us, and that God is willing to give us what he promises in the New Covenant; hence the blood is also called the blood of the new covenant, which speaks better things than the blood of Abel, and Christ himself is called a faithful and true witness. Then, because by Christ's resurrection, which could not have occurred except by his death intervening, we have been made more certain of our resurrection and of the eternal life to be attained afterwards, if we obey the precepts of the Lord Jesus."

units.la: Sententiam ita proponit Crellius, contra Grotium, in principio: Christum Servatorem, qui Novi Fœderis Mediator & sponsor est, ideo mortuum esse, ut Novum istud fœdus, promissaque divina in eo comprehensa, quorum potissimum est remissio peccatorum & vita æterna, confirmaret ac sanciret, & sic jus quoddam ad ea obtinenda nobis daret. Deinde ut omnes homines ad conditiones huic fœderi insertas amplectendas & exsequendas adduceret: denique ut hac pacto misericors Pontifex effectus, supremamque in omnia potestatem adeptus, peccata nostra expiaret, ac promissa fœderis, conditiones ejus servantibus reipsa præstaret. Clarè & compendiosè expositâ sententia, ad tres causas fines mortis Christi refert, 1. confirmationem doctrinæ, & promissionum Euangelicarum. 11. movendos & adducendos homines, ad illarum fidem. 111. adeptionem potestatis in Christo. Pluribus ambagibus alibi, & ut putat felicius, quam sui vulgo solent, rem expedit, lib. de causis mortis Christi. Explicaturus enim, qua ratione mors Christi ad remissionem peccatorum nobis comparandam apta, & medium atque instrumentum quoddam, uti loquitur, sit remissionis peccatorum nostrorum perficiendæ, Christum dupliciter considerat, partim ut novi Fœderis Mediatorem, seu sponsorem; partim ut Sacerdotem: quod utrumque munus in Christi morte coiisse dicit, & illud in eâ desiisse; istud vero hinc incepisse, & per illud ad hoc Christum fuisse quodammodo præparatum. Quatenus Mediator, primum morte suâ obstrinxisse dicit, atque obligasse promissorem, ad servanda fæderis promissa. Hoc primum, inquit, nobis præstat mors Christi, fœderi per eum promulgato annexa. Quam rationem consentaneam dicit fini mortis Christi secundo, qui est, ut nos Christo fidem habentes, & in eo spem collocantes, vitam emendemus, & in salutis via ad extremum usque perfistamus. pag. 9. Ubi distinguit, inter mortis Christi vim seu efficaciam, atque scopum, seu finem, in quem efficaciam illam habeat. Illa est, quod tantam Christi mors ad remissionem peccatorum comparandam, respectu Dei, habet potestatem, ut etiam Deum, si forte eum promissionis suæ de remissione peccatorum & liberatione ab interitu nobis concedenda pœ-niteret (utimur phrasi sacris literis usitata) movere atque impellere posset, ne promissum suum rescinderet, sed quod pollicitus esset, reipsa præstaret. Scopus seu finis istius ef-ficaciæ est, ut nos tanto certius credere possemus, nobis in Christum credentibus peccata remissum iri, nosque ab æterno interitu liberandos esse. Atque in eo aliqua videtur discrepantia exponendæ sententiæ, apud Adversarios, qui plerumque primam illam causam efficaciæ mortis Christi ad remissionem peccatorum prætereunt, & hoc quod Crellius secundo loco, pro fine habet, causam mortis Christi faciunt primam. Quæ tamen differentia non est tanti. Deinde con-siderans Christum ut Sacerdotem, finem mortis Christi constituit, ut sibi potestatem acquiretet salvandi.
units.tr: Crellius, against Grotius, sets out the opinion thus at the beginning: "Christ the Saviour, who is the Mediator and surety of the New Covenant, died so that he might confirm and ratify this New Covenant and the divine promises contained in it, of which the chief are the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, and so give us a certain right to obtain them." Next, so that he might lead all men to embrace and carry out the conditions inserted in this covenant; finally, that having become a merciful High Priest by this pact, and having obtained supreme power over all things, he might expiate our sins and actually fulfil the promises of the covenant for those who keep its conditions. Having set out the opinion clearly and briefly, he refers the ends of Christ's death to three causes: 1. the confirmation of the doctrine and of the evangelical promises; 2. moving and bringing men to faith in them; 3. the acquisition of power in Christ. He explains the matter in more roundabout terms elsewhere, and, as he thinks, more happily than their people usually do, in his book On the causes of Christ's death. For intending to explain by what reasoning the death of Christ is suited to procuring the remission of sins for us, and is a certain means and instrument, as he puts it, of bringing about the remission of our sins, he considers Christ in two ways: partly as Mediator or surety of the New Covenant, partly as Priest. He says that these two offices met in Christ's death, and that the former ceased in it, while the latter began from it, and that through the former Christ was in some way prepared for the latter. As Mediator, he says, he first bound himself by his death, and obliged the promiser to keep the promises of the covenant. "This first," he says, "the death of Christ, annexed to the covenant published through him, provides for us." He says this reason agrees with the second end of Christ's death, which is that we, having faith in Christ and placing our hope in him, may amend our lives and persevere to the end in the way of salvation (p. 9). Here he distinguishes between the power or efficacy of Christ's death and the aim, or end, to which that efficacy is directed. The former is that Christ's death has such power with respect to God to procure the remission of sins, that it could move and impel even God, if perhaps he should repent of his promise of the forgiveness of sins and of deliverance from destruction to be granted to us (we use a phrase customary in the sacred writings), not to rescind his promise, but to actually perform what he had pledged. The aim or end of this efficacy is that we might believe all the more surely that sins will be forgiven us who believe in Christ, and that we are to be freed from eternal destruction. In this there seems to be some discrepancy among the adversaries in setting out the opinion, since they mostly pass over that first cause of the efficacy of Christ's death for the remission of sins, and make first the cause which Crellius places second as the end. Yet this difference is not of great importance. Then, considering Christ as Priest, he makes the end of Christ's death that he might acquire for himself the power of saving.

units.la: Confirmatam autem Christi morte doctrinam ejus, & novum fædus, dicit, dupliciter. 1. generaliter, quod fuerit Jesus Christus, Dei Filius. II. magis specialiter id quod dixerit, sive promissa doctrinæ suæ, de remissione, & salute æternâ: quæ confirmarit mortis suæ exemplo, dum post eam perpessam, excitatus à Deo fuit ad vitam sempiternam ac beatam. Quo pacto omnes ipsum sequentes ex mortuis tandem excitabuntur quoque. Unde & tertium sequitur, quo Christi mors confirmarit remissionem peccatorum nobis à Deo oblatam, quia exhibuit insigne documentum singularis ac plane admirabilis Dei ac Christi erga nos charitatis. Hæc, de causis mortis Christi, ita Crellius. Quæ omnia eò tendunt, ut multa quidem proferant Adversarii, obquæ dicunt Christum mortem obiisse, pro confirmandâ veritate doctrinæ in genere, ac in specie remissionis peccatorum gratuitæ, & salutis, ut Deum quasi nobis obstringeret, & sibi viam pararet ad æternam gloriam ac potestatem, quare & exemplo suo nos confirmaret, moveretque omnibus illis, se & doctrinam suam ut sequeremur; de quibus etiam videndus Oftorodus, Inst. cap. xxxvii. sed multa illa talia sunt, ut quidem in speciem videantur aliquid esse, nonnulla nec improbari queant, attamen principalem causam mortis Christi prætereunt, veram nimirum pro peccatis nostris satisfactionem, quæ etiam ea quæ rectè ab illis dicuntur quæcunque complectitur, & istud notat, quod fidei & salutis nostræ est fundamentum. Catechesis Racov. pag. 261. Nonne est etiam aliqua alia mortis Christi causa? Resp. Nulla prorsus. Etsi nunc vulgo Christiani sentiunt, Christum morte sua nobis salutem meruisse, & pro peccatis nostris plenarie satis-fecisse, quæ sententia fallax est, erronea, & admodum perniciosa.
units.tr: He says that Christ's death confirmed his doctrine and the new covenant in two ways: first, generally, that Jesus Christ was the Son of God; second, more specifically, what he said, namely the promises of his doctrine concerning forgiveness and eternal salvation, which he confirmed by the example of his death, since after suffering it he was raised by God to eternal and blessed life. By this way all who follow him will also at last be raised from the dead. Whence there follows a third way, by which Christ's death confirmed the forgiveness of sins offered to us by God, because it displayed a remarkable proof of the singular and altogether admirable love of God and Christ towards us. So Crellius, on the causes of Christ's death. All these things tend to this: that the adversaries bring forward many reasons for which they say Christ died, namely to confirm the truth of his doctrine in general and the forgiveness of sins, freely given, and salvation in particular, so as to bind God to us, as it were, and to prepare for himself a way to eternal glory and power; therefore also to confirm us by his example and to move us to follow him and his doctrine. On these matters see also Ostorodus, Inst. ch. 37. But many of these things are such that they seem to be something in appearance, and some cannot even be disapproved; yet they pass over the principal cause of Christ's death, namely the true satisfaction for our sins, which also embraces whatever they rightly say, and this points to what is the foundation of our faith and salvation. Racovian Catechism, p. 261: "Is there not also some other cause of Christ's death? Answer: None at all. Although Christians now commonly think that Christ by his death merited salvation for us and fully satisfied for our sins, this opinion is false, erroneous and very pernicious."

units.la: Neque magis clementer de nobis, aut sententia nostra loquuntur, quam pro commento non modo habent, quod cum Pontificiorum Purgatorio, auricularis[?] Confessione, mortuorum invocatione, & aliis similibus comparat Socinus, lib. de Servatore, pag. 14. sed & pag. 55. quod absurdum atque impium sit vel dicere, vel cogitare. & pag. 99. humani istius commenti impietatem impie dicit. Ostorodus, pag. 319. & 311. Instit. Opinionus[?] istius falsitatem, & blasphemiam, pueriles & ridendos errores, ac fabulas, & nugas nuncupat. Ut quam modesti sint, & quam probe de nobis sentiant, vel loquantur, sic reddant manifestum.
units.tr: Nor do they treat us more gently, or speak more kindly of our opinion, than they regard as a fiction not only what Socinus, in his book De Servatore, p. 14, compares with the Papists' Purgatory, auricular confession, the invocation of the dead and other similar things, but also what he says on p. 55, that it is absurd and impious even to say or think it, and on p. 99, when he calls the impiety of that human invention impious. Ostorodus, pp. 319 and 311 of the Institutes, calls the falsity and blasphemy of this opinion, puerile and ridiculous errors, fables and trifles. Let them show, then, how modest they are, and how fairly they think or speak of us.

units.la: Neque primi illi sunt, qui satisfactionis vim & veritatem morti Christi derogarunt. Inter Antiquiores, ne de Pelagio dicam, & Pelagianis, qui vim gratiae Christi constituebant in sola doctrina Christi, & exemplo, non in redemtione; Petrus Abaelardus, qui obiit a. MCXLII. xi Kal. Maji, Johannis Rozelini discipulus, atque Magister Petri Lombardi, is, si Bernardo fides, praecipuo ipsius Adversario, cujus maxime instinctu & autoritate condemnatus fuit in Concilio Senonensi, a. MCXL[?]. satisfactionem Christi videtur negasse. Bernardus, epistola exc. ad P. Innocentium, introducit loquentem Abaelardum, novum de veteri magistro Theologum, qui ab ineunte aetate sua in arte Dialectica lusit, & nunc in Scripturis sanctis insanit &c. ideo, inquit, sicut dicunt Doctores, hac necessitate incarnatus est Filius Dei, ut homo, qui aliter liberari non poterat, per mortem innocentis jure liberaretur a jugo Diaboli. Sed, ut nobis videtur, ait, nec Diabolus unquam jus aliquod in homine habuit, nisi forte Deo permittente, ut carcerarius: nec Filius Dei, ut hominem liberaret, carnem assumsit. Quomodo aut qua ratione Diabolus potestatem aliquam in peccatores habuisse, atque ab eâ redem-tos eos, dici possit suo loco postea, ad singularem hac super re Socini obje-ctionem, examinabitur.
units.tr: Nor are they the first to have detracted from the force and truth of Christ's satisfaction. Among the older writers, not to mention Pelagius and the Pelagians, who placed the power of Christ's grace in his doctrine and example alone and not in redemption, Petrus Abaelardus, who died on 21 April 1142 (xi Kal. Maji), a disciple of John Roscelin and the teacher of Peter Lombard, seems, if Bernard is to be trusted, to have denied Christ's satisfaction. Bernard, in his letter to Pope Innocent, introduces Abelard speaking, a new theologian about the old master, who from early youth played at the art of dialectic and now rages in holy Scripture, etc. "Therefore," he says, "as the Doctors say, the Son of God was incarnate out of this necessity: that man, who could not otherwise be freed, might rightly be freed from the yoke of the devil by the death of the innocent. But, as it seems to us," he says, "the devil never had any right over man, except perhaps by God's permission, as a jailer; nor did the Son of God assume flesh in order to free man. How or by what reasoning the devil could be said to have had some power over sinners, and that they were redeemed from it, will be examined in its place later, in connection with Socinus's particular objection on this point.

units.la: Jam vero adversus Petrum illum disputans Bernardus, concludit pro veritate satisfactionis: ut hoc [illegible, ~9 letters] fuisse appareat: Si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt: ut videlicet satisfactio unius omnibus imputetur, sicut omnium peccata unus ille portavit: nec alter jam inveniatur, qui forefecit, (est Gallicum forfait) alter qui satisfecit: quia caput & corpus unus est Christus. Satisfecit ergo caput pro membris. Christus pro vicaribus[?] suis, &c. Utinam ego inveniar in his spoliis quibus spoliata sunt contraria potestates, traductus & ipse in possef-sionem Domini! Pergit, & Abaelardum sic infert loquentem: cum solos electos liberaverit Christus, quomodo eos Diabolus possidebat, sive in hoc saeculo, sive in futuro, magis quam modo? Respondemus, ait Bernardus, imo quia Diabolus electos Dei possidebat, a quo (sicut dicit Apostolus) captivi tenebantur ad ipsius voluntatem, ut Dei propositum de ipsis impleretur, opus fuit liberatore. Oportuit autem liberari in hoc saeculo, ut liberos haberet in futuro, &c. Propterea jam tunc sanguis Christi rorabat etiam Lazaro, ne flammas sentiret, quod & ipse credidisset in eum qui erat passurus. Sic de omnibus electis illius temporis sentiendum, natos quidem & ipsos aeque ut nos sub potestate tenebrarum, propter originale peccatum, sed erutos antequam morerentur, & non nisi in sanguine Christi.
units.tr: Now indeed Bernard, disputing against that Peter, concludes for the truth of satisfaction, so that this [illegible, about nine letters] appears: "If one died for all, then all died": namely, that the satisfaction of one is imputed to all, just as that one bore the sins of all; nor is another found who committed the offence (the French is forfait) and another who made satisfaction, because Christ is one head and body. Therefore Christ as head satisfied for the members, Christ for his vicars, etc. Would that I might be found among those spoils from which the opposing powers have been stripped, and might myself be brought into the possession of the Lord! He goes on and makes Abelard speak thus: "Since Christ freed only the elect, how did the devil possess them, in this age or in the future, any more than now?" We answer, says Bernard, "Nay, because the devil possessed God's elect, by whom (as the Apostle says) they were held captive at his will, so that God's purpose concerning them might be fulfilled, there was need of a deliverer. But they had to be freed in this age, so that they might have their freedom in the future, etc. Therefore the blood of Christ already then dropped even upon Lazarus, lest he feel the flames, since he too had believed in him who was about to suffer. So must we think of all the elect of that time: born indeed, like us, under the power of darkness on account of original sin, but rescued before they died, and only in the blood of Christ."

units.la: Planius mentem Abaelardi exponit porro, de eo sic pergens: Deinde laborans docere & persuadere, Diabolum nullum sibi jus in hominem vindicare potuisse aut debuisse, nisi permissu Dei, & quod sine injuria Diaboli jure Deus profugum suum, si vellet mi-seri, repetere, & solo verbo eripere posset, quasi hoc quis diffiteatur, post multa aliquando infert : qua itaque necessitas, aut qua ratio, aut quod opus fuit, cum sola jus-sione sua divina miseratio liberare hominem a peccato posset, propter redemtionem nostram Filium Dei carne suscepta, tot & tantas inedias, oppropria, flagella, sputa, denique ipsam crucis ignominiosam & asperrimam mortem sustinere, ut cum iniquis patibulum sustineret? respondemus, necessitas nostra fuit, & necessitas dura sedentium in tenebris, & umbra mortis, &c. Quis negat omnipotenti ad manum fuisse alios & alios modos nostra redemtionis, justificationis, liberationis? Verum hoc non praejudicet hujus quem e multus elegit efficatia. Praeterea ait Abaelardus: Quod si tantum fuerat illud Ada peccatum, ut expiari non posset, nisi morte Christi, quam expiationem habebit ipsum homicidium quod in Christum commissum est? Breviter respondemus, ipsum sanguinem quem fuerunt, & interpellationem ipsius quem occiderunt. Denique quod manifestissime mentem ipsius exponit, sic concludit, ut dicat totum esse quod Deus in carne apparuit, nostram de verbo exemplo ipsius institutionem, sive ut postmodum dicit instructionem, totum quod passus & mortuus est, sua erga nos charitatis ostensionem vel commendationem.
units.tr: Abelard sets out his meaning more plainly, continuing about him thus: "Then, labouring to teach and persuade that the devil could claim no right over man, nor ought to, except by God's permission, and that God, without injury to the devil's right, could reclaim his fugitive, if he wished to show mercy, and rescue him by a word alone, as if anyone denied this, after many things he at length infers: what necessity, then, or what reason, or what need was there, since divine mercy could free man from sin by his command alone, for the Son of God, taking flesh for our redemption, to endure so many and such great hungers, reproaches, scourgings, spittings, and finally the shameful and most bitter death of the cross itself, so that he bore the gibbet with the wicked? We answer: it was our necessity, and the hard necessity of those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, etc. Who denies that the Almighty had at hand other and other modes of our redemption, justification and liberation? But this does not prejudge the efficacy of the one he chose." Moreover, Abelard says: "But if that sin of Adam was so great that it could not be expiated except by the death of Christ, what expiation will the homicide itself have, which was committed against Christ? We answer briefly: the very blood which they shed, and the intercession of him whom they killed." Finally, since he most clearly sets out his mind, he concludes thus: "that the whole that God appeared in the flesh is to set before us the example of his teaching from his word, or, as he later says, instruction; and the whole that he suffered and died is a demonstration or commendation of his love towards us."

units.la: Idem : cur per sanguinem, quod potuit facere per sermonem? Et haec ejus sunt verba: cui non crudele & iniquum videtur, ut sanguinem innocentis in pretium aliquod quis requisierit, aut ullo modo ei placuerit, innocentem interfici? nedum Deus tam acceptam filii mortem habuerit, ut per ipsum universo reconciliatus sit mundo? Quae si vera sunt, & sic revera senserit docuerintque Abaelardus, non est quod de ejus mente, vel haeresi amplius dubitemus. Et proferenda haec fuerunt copiosius, quia pro eo absolvendo & defendendo laborant multum, qui opera ipsius nunc demum ediderunt Parisiis, a. MDCXVII. Eundem in finem in Abaelardi Commentario in Epist. ad Rom. annotarunt nonnulla Censores Parisienses: ut quod pag. 549. verba Pauli, ad ostensionem justitiae suae Rom. iii. 25. de charitate & justitia nobis infusa intelligit, cum de charitate Christi, & justitia, qua satisfecit pro nobis, capi praecipue debeant, inquiunt. Similiter observant, illum eodem Commentario, pag. 553. in explicanda redemtione, satisfactionem plane omittere. Neque vel in Apologia sua, vel alibi in Epistolis, aut ipse, aut hyperaspistae ejus, quales habuit praecipuos Berengarium Pictaviensem, Petrum Cluniacensem Abbatem, vel alii, aliquid ad excusationem, aut responsionem, vel dilutionem criminum illorum posuerunt. Quamvis nolim omnibus, quae contra ipsum ab Adversariis arrepta fuerunt, & adducta, credere; nec putem vere ejus ubique sententiam fuisse, quam contra ipsum protulerunt: vel non satisfecisse eum sive in Apologia, quae est Operum ejus pag. 330. sive aliis Scriptis, ac praesertim epistolis. Quod multos contra ipsum incitavit, videtur fuisse inerudito & ferreo illo saeculo resuscitara ab eo imprimis philosophia, forte & periculosae, vel non satis intellectae aliis philosophicae locutiones, & subtilitates. Etenim illud in libro Theologia a se edito conatus fuit, de quo in Epistola ad Amicum, ubi historiam vitae suae pandit, accidit mihi, inquit, ut ad ipsum fidei nostrae fundamentum humanae rationis similitudinibus differendum primo me applicarem, & quendam Theologia tractatum de Unitati & Trinitate divina Scholoribus nostris componerem, qui humanas & philosophicas rationes requiriebant, & plus quam intelligi quam dici possent efflagitabant, &c. Unde de eo Bernardus, in epist. ad Episcopos, & Cardinales Curiæ: irridetur simplicium fides, evisceratur arcana Dei, quæstiones de altissimis rebus temerarie ventilantur, insultatur Patribus, quod eas magis sapiendas quam solvendas censuerint. Sed iterum contra Bernardum Berengarium Scolasticum, mirantur homines in te liberalium disciplinarum ignaro, tantam ubertatem &c. Ut non dubitem, quin ex usu, forte & abusu philosophiæ, istæ ei concitatæ turbæ fuerint. Quod & ipse agnovit, in epist. ad Heloisam suam, odiosum me mundo reddidit Logica. Ajunt enim perversi perverten-tes, quorum sapientia est in perditione, me in Logica præstantissimum esse, sed in Paulo non mediocriter claudicare. Ad quæ, nolo sic esse philosophus, ut recalcitrem Paulo. Non sic esse Aristoteles, ut secludar a Christo &c. Sed de his aliàs, atque de Petro Abaelardo etiam diximus, in Apparatu, ad Controv. Socin. pag. 14.
units.tr: Likewise: "Why by blood, when he could do it by word?" And these are his words: "To whom does it not seem cruel and unjust that someone should demand the blood of an innocent as some price, or that it should please him in any way that the innocent should be killed? Still less that God should have held the death of his Son so acceptable that through him he reconciled the whole world?" If these things are true, and Abelard really so felt and taught, there is no need to doubt further about his mind or his heresy.
