And these things had to be quoted at more length, because those who labour much to absolve and defend him have now at last published his works at Paris, in 1617. To the same end, certain Parisian censors noted several points in Abelard's Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans: for instance, that on p. 549 he understands Paul's words "to show his righteousness" (Rom. 3.25) of the charity and justice infused into us, "whereas what ought chiefly to be understood is the charity of Christ and the justice by which he satisfied for us," they say. Similarly they observe that in the same Commentary, p. 553, in explaining redemption, he plainly leaves out satisfaction. Neither he himself, nor his champions, such as Berengar of Poitiers and Peter, abbot of Cluny, or others, have offered anything by way of excuse, answer or refutation of those charges, either in his Apology or elsewhere in his letters. Although I would not wish to believe everything his adversaries seized upon and brought against him, nor think that the opinion they attributed to him was truly his everywhere, or that he did not make satisfaction, either in the Apology, which is on p. 330 of his Works, or in other writings, and especially his letters. What seems to have stirred many against him was that philosophy, revived above all by him in that unlearned and iron age, perhaps dangerous, and philosophical phrases and subtleties not sufficiently understood by others. For he attempted that in a Theology published by himself, about which, in his letter to a friend, where he unfolds the history of his life, he says: "It happened to me that I first applied myself to explaining the very foundation of our faith by likenesses from human reason, and composed for our students a treatise of theology on the unity and divine Trinity, which demanded human and philosophical reasons and required more to be understood than could be said, etc." Hence Bernard, in his letter to the bishops and cardinals of the Curia: "The faith of the simple is mocked, the hidden things of God are disembowelled, questions about the highest matters are rashly stirred up, and the Fathers are insulted because they judged these things to be to be known rather than resolved." But again, against Bernard, Berengar the scholastic: "men marvel at you, ignorant of the liberal arts, at such abundance, etc." So I do not doubt that these tumults were stirred up against him by the use, and perhaps the abuse, of philosophy. He himself acknowledged this in his letter to his Heloise: "Logic has made me hateful to the world. For the perverse, whose wisdom is in destruction, say, perverting, that I am most outstanding in logic, but that in Paul I limp not a little." To which he replies: "I do not wish to be such a philosopher as to kick against Paul. I do not wish to be such an Aristotle as to be cut off from Christ, etc." But we have spoken of these things elsewhere, and of Peter Abelard too, in Apparatus to the Controversies with Socinus, p. 14.

units.la: Patrum nostrorum ævo, qui Christi satisfactionem impugnavit, fuit Lælius Socinus, cum quo super eodem negotio disputavit Calvinus, epist. a. MDLV. imo jam a. MDLII. uti ex alia Calvini epistola, quam Eques Polonus, in vita Socini exhibuit, ostendi suo loco in Apparatu. etiam Bernardinus Ochinus, quoque Sinensis Italus, veritatem illam convulsit, in Dialogis, de Messia: quod ostendit Gregorius Zarnovecius, cap. 1. libri pro defensione satisfact. Christi.
units.tr: In the age of our fathers, the man who attacked Christ's satisfaction was Lælius Socinus, with whom Calvin disputed on this matter in a letter of 1555, and indeed already in 1552, as another letter of Calvin, which the Polish knight published in the life of Socinus, shows; I have pointed this out in its place in the Apparatus. Bernardino Ochino, the Sienese Italian, also overthrew this truth in his Dialogues On the Messiah, as Gregorius Zarnovecius shows in chapter 1 of his book in defence of Christ's satisfaction.

units.la: Tempus verò est, ut ad disputationem progrediamur, quæ super hoc agitatur: an Christus Mediator in se susceperit pœnas peccatorum, nostro loco ferendas, & exsolvendas? id est, an verè pro nobis Deo, seu divinæ justitiæ satisfecerit, vicariâ pœnarum nostrarum, suâ morte ac passionibus, persolutione; atque ita nos Deo reconciliarit verè, atque redemerit?
units.tr: It is now time to proceed to the disputation that is being carried on about this point: whether Christ the Mediator took upon himself the punishments of sinners, to be borne and paid in our place; that is, whether he truly satisfied God, or divine justice, for us, by his death and sufferings, as a vicarious payment of our punishments, and so truly reconciled us to God and redeemed us?

units.la: Non de eo disputabimus primariò, quod Sociniani affirmant de morte Chri-sti; sed super eo, quod negant. Non, an Christus morte etiam doctrinam confirmarit suam; vel, istâ viâ ad gloriam & potestatem cœlestem conscenderit; aut nobis exemplar passionum reliquerit? sed, num istis, quæ in morte Christi considerant & promunt Adversarii, totum comprehendatur, quod veritas & Scriptura in eâ constituit; annon ejus mors insuper & primariò sit satisfactoria & expiatoria, isto, quo diximus, sensu? Id inquirendum nobis nunc est. Neque est quæstio, an passionibus suis Christus ullo modo satisfece-rit divinæ voluntati, & mandato, etiam legi & justitiæ, sed an justitiæ punienti in Deo, ei quæ pœnas peccatorum nostrorum àChristo exigit, inque ipso vindicarit? Satisfactio ergo intelligitur, non quævis, non mandati simpliciter, utid perfecerit Christus, quod Pater ipsi injunxit, sed satisfactio pœnalis. Christi Mortem quum nominamus, non ea præcise intelligitur, sed una cum omnibus toto vitæ cursu à Christo exantlatis passionibus. Atque ita etiam Sociniani illàm hic accipiunt. Catechef. Racov. de Prophet. Christi munerere, cap. VIII. qu. I.
units.tr: We shall not dispute primarily about what the Socinians affirm concerning the death of Christ, but about what they deny. The question is not whether Christ also confirmed his doctrine by his death, or whether by this way he ascended to glory and heavenly power, or left us an example of suffering. The question is whether everything that truth and Scripture place in his death is comprehended in those things which our adversaries consider and bring forward; or whether his death is not, beyond these, and chiefly, satisfactory and expiatory in the sense we have stated. This is what we must now inquire into. Nor is the question whether by his sufferings Christ in any way satisfied the divine will and command, or the law and justice; but whether he rendered satisfaction to that justice in God which punishes, and which exacts the punishment of our sins from Christ and vindicates it in him. So the satisfaction meant is not any satisfaction whatever, not merely of a command, such as Christ accomplished in doing what the Father enjoined on him, but a penal satisfaction. When we name the death of Christ, what is understood is not that alone, but all the sufferings Christ endured through the whole course of his life. And the Socinians too take it in this way here: Catechesis Racoviensis, On the Prophetic Office of Christ, chapter 8, question 1.

units.la: Mediator Christus est, atque hoc utrimque agnoscitur: sed diverso modo. Quippe Sociniani nihil aliud in Mediatore Christo constituunt, quam quod internuncius divinæ apud nos voluntatis fuerit, per quem nobis ad Deum accessus patet: non verò, quod vel Deum nobis placarit, vel nos ei, tanquam parti summopere offensæ, reconciliarit. Socinus, de Servat. part. I. cap. vii. pag. 45. Covetum deceptum ait, quod Mediatorem vel non dici, nisi qui duos inter se invicem diffidentes componat, & alterum alteri conciliet: vel saltem hanc esse hujus vocabuli praecipuam significationem, existimet. Contra dicit, Mediatoris seu ὁ[?] μεσίτης nomen in sacris litteris nihil aliud significare, quam eum, qui medius quidem inter duos sit, hoc est inter Deum & hominem: non tamen qui Deum iratum homini placet: sed quo Deus ut internuncio atque interprete, ad foedera sua cum hominibus pangenda & sancienda utatur: & per quem illi ad ipsum, ejus voluntatis cognitione instructi, accedere possint. Catechesis Racov. cap. 1. de Proph. Christi munere, pag. 274. Cur Christo nomen Mediatoris Scriptura tribuit? Resp. Propterea quod foedus novum, idque sempiternum nomine Dei cum hominibus sanxerit,& omnem Dei voluntatem, per quam aditus nobis ad Deum patefactus est, exposuerit. Similiter Oftorodus, Inst. cap. xxxvii. pag. 322. Respondemus: in hoc, ut, in aliis, Adversarios id operam dare, ut enervent atque subruant omnes fidei articulos, & hoc iis omnibus auferant, in quo ipsorum vis quidem maxima consistit. Mediatorem esse Christum universa credidit Ecclesia Catholica, non simplicis annunciationis, & praedicationis, sed verae reconciliationis, & redemtionis causa. Illud hi iterum tollunt, atque hoc, quod commune Christo hactenus est cum aliis, voluntatem Dei explicare, ipsi solum relinquunt. Pontificii distinguunt Mediatorem reconciliationis, & intercessionis; istud, praeter Christum, etiam aliis attribuunt; sed illud ei soli reservant. Nihil autem proprium, & omni modo singulare Christo hic vendicant Socinia-ni[?]. Quod Socinus dixit, nos per Christum accedere ad Deum, Catechesis expressit, per voluntatem Dei nobis revelatam patere aditum. Quam voluntatem non à solo Christo, sed & aliis annunciatam fuisse, satis apertum est. Christus Mediator est singulari ratione, non communi; propria, non vulgari: nec propterea solum pro Mediatore habendus, quod doctrinam salutis praedicavit, sed praecipue quia partes adversas composuit & reconciliavit, id est Deo, peccatis nostris juste offenso, nos adduxit, eumque placatum nobis reddidit & propitium. Fatetur adhaec Socinus, vulgarem illam esse & communem vocis Mediatoris acceptionem, quam nos promimus: quod imperitam addit, nescio an quid imperitius dici queat: Vulgari atque imperito loquendi usu; quo factum est, ut is[?] qui pacem inter duos quoquo modo conciliet, mediator appelletur. In vocibus usus spectari solet, tum peritia: jam vero quis, omni praejudicio vacuus, affirmabit, contra peritiam esse, quod nomen Mediatoris significet eum, qui inter duos pacem conciliat? Cedo ullum, qui vocis, hoc usu improprietatem vel incongruitatem observavit? quique non lubenter & recte, ipsa rei natura urgente, illum Mediatorem appellarit?
units.tr: Christ is Mediator, and this is acknowledged on both sides, but in different ways. For the Socinians place nothing else in Christ the Mediator than that he was the messenger of the divine will towards us, through whom access to God lies open to us; not that he appeased God for us, or reconciled us to him as to a party greatly offended. Socinus, On the Saviour, part 1, chapter 7, page 45, says that Covetus is mistaken in thinking that a mediator is not called such unless he reconciles two parties who distrust each other and brings one to the other, or at least that this is the chief meaning of the word. Socinus argues the contrary: that the term mediator (ὁ μεσίτης) in the Sacred Writings signifies nothing other than one who stands between two, that is between God and man, yet not one who makes an angry God pleasing to man; rather one through whom God uses him as messenger and interpreter, to make and ratify his covenants with men, and through whom they may approach him, instructed in the knowledge of his will. Catechesis Racoviensis, chapter 1, On the Prophetic Office of Christ, page 274: "Why does Scripture give Christ the name of Mediator?" Answer: "Because he ratified the new covenant, an everlasting one, between God and men in God's name, and set forth the whole will of God, through which access to God has been opened to us." Likewise Ostorodus, Institutes, chapter 37, page 322. We reply: in this, as in other matters, our adversaries take pains to weaken and undermine all the articles of faith, and to strip away from them that in which their real strength lies. The universal Catholic Church has believed that Christ is Mediator not merely as the cause of simple announcement and preaching, but of true reconciliation and redemption. These men again remove the one and leave to Christ alone the other, which hitherto he shared in common with others: the explaining of God's will. The Papists distinguish a Mediator of reconciliation and a Mediator of intercession; the Papists attribute the latter to others besides Christ, but reserve the former to him alone. The Socinians, however, claim for Christ here nothing proper, nothing singular in any way. What Socinus said, that we come to God through Christ, the Catechism expressed as access opened through the will of God revealed to us. That this will was announced not by Christ alone but also by others is quite plain. Christ is Mediator in a singular way, not a common one; in a proper, not an ordinary sense. Nor is he to be regarded as Mediator only because he preached the doctrine of salvation, but chiefly because he composed and reconciled the opposed parties, that is, because he brought us, who had justly offended God by our sins, to God, and rendered him appeased and propitious toward us. Socinus further admits that the sense of the word Mediator which we put forward is the common one, but he adds something that is hardly to be called anything more inept: "by the common and unskilled usage of speech, by which it has come about that one who in any way reconciles peace between two is called a mediator." In words, usage is customarily regarded as well as skill. Now who, free of all prejudice, will affirm that it is contrary to skill that the name Mediator should signify one who makes peace between two? Name me anyone who has observed impropriety or incongruity in this usage of the word, and who has not gladly and rightly called him Mediator when the very nature of the thing demands it?

units.la: Videamus loca Scripturae, quae Mediatorem Christum dicunt, an intelligant solum Mediatorem internuncium, praeconii; an non praecipue reconciliationis? Atque hac ratione Crellius Socinum tuetur, quod dixit nominis illius usum esse imperitum, quando quis pro conciliatore accipit; nimirum, ex usu Scripturae. Quod proinde videamus, quem usum nomen illud in Scriptura habeat. Interim nec respondet Crellius quidquam ad locum ex Suidâ , à Grotio prolatum , ubi μεσιτεύω voce εἰρηνοποιός interpretatus est.
units.tr: Let us see the passages of Scripture which call Christ Mediator: do they understand only a Mediator as messenger and herald, or not chiefly a Mediator of reconciliation? In this way Crellius defends Socinus, who said that the use of that name is unskilled when someone takes it for a reconciler; namely, by the usage of Scripture. Let us therefore see what use that name has in Scripture. Meanwhile Crellius makes no reply at all to the passage from Suidas cited by Grotius, where he interprets the verb μεσιτεύω [to mediate] by εἰρηνοποιός [peacemaker].

units.la: Primum vox illa reperitur Gal. iii. 19. ubi de Mose sermo est, atque dicitur μεσίτης. Lex ordinata per Angelos, in manu Mediatoris. Mediator autem ὁ [?]δὲ μεσίτης ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστιν· Deus autem unus est. Ubi inquit Socinus, intelligitur non Dei & hominum invicem diffidentium pacificator, sed in promulgandâ lege internuncius. Resp. i. Nec simpliciter internuncius promulgandæ legis intelligitur: nam supra præconem est, quando aliquis etiam dicitur Mediator. Ad promulgationem sufficit præco, absque hoc ut ratio partium habeatur, quod necessarium est in Mediatore. Ideo de Præcone dici nequit, vel legis promulgatore, quod non sit unius, qua ratione de Mediatore dictum, Mediatore autem non est unum. Argumento, Mediatorem plus dicere quam præconem, aut simpliciter internuncium. Quare ubi Mediator intervenit, partes sunt, & non convenientes, quæ per μεσιτεύω componi debent & conjungi. Internuncius est quidem non apud unum, sed alios: at diversa est loquutio, non esse unius: ad hoc necessario subintelligitur pars alia & alia. Ἑνὸς personam respicit, & partam aliam: quare additur, Deus autem est unus. Chrysostomus, ὁ δὲ μεσίτης φησί, δύο τινῶν γίνεται μεσίτης. Præter verba, eorumque vim & connexionem, res ipsa loquitur, Mediatorem esse diffidentium. Nuntio utimur, ubicunque alteri quidpiam significandum venit: Mediatori demum locus est, ubi partes adversæ, interque eas pax reducenda venit & firmanda. ii. Sic hactenus Moses mediator etiam fuit inter Deum & homines, ut inter partes revera diffidentes, quando eo nuntio & Mediatore Deus legem homini proposuit: sed utcunque partium respectu Mediator dici potuerit, & medius inter illas egerit, haud ideo omni, & quæ Christo propria, ratione Mediator fuit. Mediator ergo metaphoricus; non proprius, & plenus: non qui placare Deum, ejusque gratiam nobis reddere potuerit, sed significarit Dei voluntatem parti alteri, quam qui servaret, servaretur. per manum electi versio habet Æthiopica. Uti etiam 1. Tim. ii. 5. electum vertit. & Heb. viii. 6. & ix. 15. at Heb. xii. 24. ducem. iii. Verùm Christus alterius fœderis, & ordinis Mediator, quam Moses, Euangelii, verus, proprius & absolute perfectus fuit, qui inter partes adversas non quoquo modo medius, sed eas seipso reconciliavit verè, proprie, & perfecte. Unde in Scripturis ipsi reconciliatio nostri cum Deo attribuitur: nempe quod eam revera peregit. Non ita Moses, quamvis etiam cum eo comparetur, Heb. iii. 3. sed ita, ut Christus πλείονος δόξης [?]ἠξίωται [?]Μωϋσῆ. Quare, utcunque in loco ad Gal. iii. 19. non agatur de Mediatore vero, Christo, tamen natura Mediatoris in hoc exponitur, quod sit partium inter se diffidentium: quadam quidem specie Moses, ipsa autem veritatis plenitudine, in & de suo, Christus. Quod nec Calvinus, nec Beza, nec Theologorum ullus negavit unquam. iv. Præterquam quod varii hoc etiam
units.tr: First, that word occurs in Galatians 3:19, where Moses is spoken of and is called μεσίτης: "The law was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one [ὁ δὲ μεσίτης ἑνὸς οὐκ ἔστιν], but God is one [ὁ δὲ θεὸς εἷς ἐστιν]." Here, says Socinus, it is understood not as a peacemaker between God and men who distrust each other, but as a messenger in promulgating the law. Reply. (1) Nor is it understood simply as a messenger in promulgating the law, for a person is called Mediator even when he stands above a herald. A herald suffices for promulgation, without any regard being had to the parties, which is necessary in a Mediator. Hence it cannot be said of a herald, or a promulgator of the law, that he is not of one, which is the reason why it is said of the Mediator, "a mediator is not of one." The argument is that a Mediator means more than a herald, or simply a messenger. Therefore where a Mediator intervenes, there are parties, and they are not in agreement, and these must be composed and joined together by the act of mediating (μεσιτεύω). A messenger is indeed not for one party but for others; but the phrase is not of one is a different expression, and necessarily implies one party and another party. "Of one" refers to a person, and to the other party; therefore it is added, "but God is one." Chrysostom: "the mediator, he says, comes to be mediator of two parties" [ὁ δὲ μεσίτης φησί, δύο τινῶν γίνεται μεσίτης]. Apart from the words, their force and connection, the thing itself speaks: a Mediator is of those who distrust one another. We use a messenger wherever something is to be signified to another; a Mediator has his place only where adverse parties are present, and peace must be brought back and established between them. (2) Thus Moses too was in a sense a mediator between God and men, as between parties who in fact distrusted each other, when by that messenger and Mediator God proposed the law to man. But however far a Mediator may be called such with respect to the parties, and however much he acted as a go-between between them, he was not therefore a Mediator in every way, nor in the way proper to Christ. Moses was therefore a metaphorical Mediator, not a proper and full one: not one who could appease God and restore his grace to us, but one who signified God's will to the other party, and who would keep it, and be kept by it. The Ethiopic version has "by the hand of an elect one" [per manum electi]. So also in 1 Timothy 2:5 it translates "elect," and in Hebrews 8:6 and 9:15, while at Hebrews 12:24 it has "leader" [ducem]. (3) But Christ was the Mediator of another covenant and order than Moses, of the Gospel: the true, proper and absolutely perfect one, who did not mediate between the adverse parties in some manner, but reconciled them truly, properly and perfectly by himself. Hence in the Scriptures reconciliation of us with God is attributed to him, namely because he actually accomplished it. This is not how Moses is related, even though he is compared with him in Hebrews 3:3; but rather Christ "has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses" [πλείονος δόξης ἠξίωται Μωϋσῆ]. Therefore, although in the passage at Galatians 3:19 the true Mediator, Christ, is not the subject, yet the nature of a Mediator is explained there as being of parties who distrust each other: in a certain sense Moses was such, but in the fullness of truth, in and concerning his own person, Christ was. This neither Calvin, nor Beza, nor any of the theologians has ever denied. (4) Moreover, various interpreters also understand by "mediator" in this passage not Moses but Christ himself, by whom the law was given to the Church through Moses: Acts 7:38. Chrysostom says: "rightly he calls Christ the mediator, because he gave the law to it" [μεσίτῳ ἡ ἐντάξει τὸν Χριστὸν φησι, δικαίως, ὅτι πρὸς ἡ τὸν νόμον αὐτῆς ἔδωκεν]. Theophylact…

units.la: Tom. 2. etiam loco per μεσίτην, non Mosem, sed ipsum Christum intelligant, à quo lex Mosi tradita fuerit Ecclesiæ. Actorum vii. 38. Chrysostomus, μεσίτῳ ἡ ἐντάξει [?] τὸν Χριστὸν φησι, δικαίως, ὅτι πρὸς [?] ἡ τὸν νόμον αὐτῆς ἔδωκεν. Theophylactus similiter de Christo exponit: Christus itaque quorum Mediator est, Dei videlicet ac hominum. Mediatorem autem egit inter utrosque, εἰρηνίζω ποιήσας [?] ἡ τὴν πόλεμον λύσας, ὡς ἐν τῆς ἀνθρωπίας [?] προσέδωκεν, inquit: quocirca quia mediator & reconciliator ipse, perspicuum est, quod ipse servet, & non lex. Atque alii etiam per Mediatorem hic Christum intelligunt, Hieronymus, Ambrosius, Augustinus. v. Vocem μεσίτης, non internuncii vertunt Interpretes, sed conciliatoris. Sic & Erasmus. Castellio, sequestrem, instituta per genios, lata per sequestrem, sequester autem unius non est. Versio Germanica Racoviensis, eines mittlers. Der mittler aber ist nicht eines einigen.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Even in this passage some understand by the mediator (μεσίτην) not Moses but Christ himself, by whom the law was delivered to the Church (Acts 7:38). Chrysostom says that Christ is rightly called "mediator" [μεσίτης] because he gave the law to it. Theophylact likewise explains this of Christ: "Christ, therefore, is the mediator of those between whom he stands, namely God and men. He acted as mediator between both, making peace [εἰρηνοποιήσας] or ending the war [τὸν πόλεμον λύσας], as he did in the flesh," he says; "therefore, since he is the mediator and reconciler, it is plain that he is the one who keeps the law, and not the law itself." Others too understand the Mediator here to be Christ: Jerome, Ambrose and Augustine. (v.) The interpreters translate the word μεσίτης not as "go-between" but as "reconciler" [conciliatoris]. So too Erasmus. Castellio renders it: "a mediator (sequestrem): the institutions were given through angels, and the law was given through a mediator, but a mediator is not of one party only." The German version of the Racovians reads: "eines Mittlers. Der Mittler aber ist nicht eines einigen" (of a mediator; but a mediator is not of one alone).

units.la: Secundus locus, quo de Mediatore agitur, est 1 Tim. ii. 5. Unus enim Deus; unus & Mediator Dei, & hominum, homo Christus Iesus. Hic iterum μεσίτης solum internuncium significare, non pacificatorem, Socinus contendit. Idque hoc argumento: Internuncium vero, non autem pacificatorem hoc etiam loco Mediatoris nomine significari, argumento esse potest, quod antequam Mediatoris mentio fiat, nihil prorsus dictum fuit de Dei ira adversus hominum scelera; nihil, quare de pacificatione aliqua agendum postea esset, narratum prius, sive conclusum fuerat, nihil denique praecesserat, cur de Christo ut pacificatore mentio injicienda esset. Resp. 1. negari consequentiam. Non, si nihil praecessit de Dei irâ, aut nostro demerito, si nihil dictum de pace inter nos ac Deum ineundâ vel restituenda, nulla Christi, ut pacificatoris, in antecedentibus, facta mentio; ideo non potest vox μεσίτης Christo adscripta notare pacem & reconciliationem per Christum Mediatorem adeptam. Non magis quam quum nec talia antecesserunt, ad quæ hoc, Unus enim Deus, referendum videatur, de unitate Dei propterea istud intelligendum quis ambigat. Annon, quod praecessit de Deo Servatore, quique omnes servari velit, vel jubeat, satis est aptumque ut ei connectatur ratio & modus salvationis, per Mediatorem? Annon praecedenti capite solemniter Apostolus Deo gratias dixit, quod Christum misit in mundum ἁμαρτωλὸς σωτῆρ? quod absque interventu Mediatoris quomodo contingere nequierit, jam docet. Sed fac nihil istorum praecessisse, & ab his verbis non caput, sed epistolam inchoatam, ideo vox Mediatoris significare non poterit intercessorem placationis seu reconciliationis? Quid frigidius? ii. Ex aliis quam plurimis locis, quibus ex professo hoc tractatur argumentum, constare satis potest, Christum reconciliationis mediatorem esse, non solius annunciationis: quem propositut Deus ἱλαστήριον ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι, Rom. iii. 25. ἱλασμόν, 1 Joann. ii. 2. Καταλλαγὴν, ii Corint. v. 18. 19. 20. aliaque de Christo Mediatore dicta satis arguunt homini, fidem ad divina dicta accipienda, non praejudicia adferenti, non solum plus & alia in Mediatore Christo, quam in solo internuntio haberi, sed veram, quam Socinus evertit & plane tollit, reconciliatio-nem. III. Versu seq. explicaturus porro Apostolus, quis Christus, & in quo officium ejus situm sit, immediate subjungit, qui dat semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον pro multis. An internuntius, qua internuntius, se dat ἀντίλυτρον pro iis, ad quos venit? Istud autem de Christo dicitur. Quare omnino Mediator expiationis Christus: & in ipso plus est, quam in internuncio: hoc nimirum quod sui-ipsius λύτρῳ nos propitiavit, & redemit Deo. Quod aliud profecto est, quam internuncium esse, inquit etiam Socinus, ad verf. illum sextum. sed enervat, pro more suo & verba, & rem, dum exponit, Christum non impendisse vitam suam pro liberatione unius aut alterius hominis, unius aut alterius generis personarum: sed pro cunctis indistincte mortuum esse. At vero non simpliciter in Textu dicitur, Christum mortuum fuisse, sed & λύτρον, & ἀντίλυτρον: quae quia emphasim continent, & vim morti Christi propriam, in quibus ratio expiationis haeret & redemtionis, haud neganda Adversario, propter hypothesim adversam fuerant. Addit, nec tamen Mediatoris vocabulum id sua vi significare, sed ex accidente, propter loci circumstantias. Non sequitur. Nam explicatio ista non est praeter vim vocis, sed est ejus ἐξηγητικὴ; ostenditque quem in sensum vox sumi debeat, & soleat. Mediator perfectus est, qui partes componit, non tantum qui officia sua alteri parti annunciat: quippe hoc fieri potest, atque fit saepe, ut omnis mediatio interim reddatur inefficax & frustranea: sed ille demum bene & plene censetur functus mediatione, qui partes junxerit, & gratiam refarcierit ruptam. Quare quum Christus perfectissima ratione sit habendus Mediator, non tantum internuncii, sed reconciliatoris officio, effectuque talis censendus est. Denique, de Beza quod addit, & quod eadem dicat quaedam, quae post eum Socinus, nullius est, quum nec Beza, nec alius quispiam μεσίτην[?] internuncium hic interpretetur; nec aut Beza, aut ullus dubitet, quin Christus haud internuncii solius, sed reconciliationis Mediator sit.
units.tr: The second passage in which the Mediator is spoken of is 1 Tim. 2:5: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Here again Socinus contends that μεσίτης means only a go-between, not a peacemaker. He argues: "That the name of Mediator in this place signifies a go-between and not a peacemaker can be shown by this argument: before the mention of the Mediator, nothing at all was said about God's wrath against the sins of men; nothing had been narrated or concluded beforehand which would require some reconciliation to be dealt with afterwards; nothing, in short, had gone before to make it necessary to bring in a mention of Christ as peacemaker." Reply, first: the consequence is denied. Even if nothing had gone before about God's wrath or our demerit, and nothing had been said about making or restoring peace between us and God, and no mention of Christ as peacemaker had been made in what precedes, it does not follow that the word μεσίτης applied to Christ cannot signify the peace and reconciliation obtained through Christ the Mediator. No one would doubt that "For there is one God" refers to the unity of God, even though nothing of that kind went before to which it could be referred. Does not what precedes, about God as Saviour, who wills, or commands, that all be saved, suffice and fit well to connect with it the reason and manner of salvation through a Mediator? Did not the Apostle, in the preceding chapter, solemnly give thanks to God that he sent Christ into the world as Saviour [σωτὴρ]? He now teaches how this could not happen without the intervention of a Mediator. But suppose nothing of this had gone before, and these words did not begin a chapter but an unfinished letter: would the word Mediator therefore be unable to signify an intercessor of propitiation or reconciliation? What could be more feeble? Second: from very many other places, where this subject is treated expressly, it can sufficiently be established that Christ is the mediator of reconciliation, not merely of announcement. God set him forth as a propitiation [ἱλαστήριον] in his own blood (Rom. 3:25); he is the propitiation [ἱλασμός] for our sins (1 John 2:2); and reconciliation [καταλλαγή] (2 Cor. 5:18-20). These and other things said of Christ the Mediator sufficiently prove to a man who brings no prejudgments to God's words that the Mediator Christ has more and other things in him than a mere go-between, and also that true reconciliation exists, which Socinus overthrows and entirely removes. Third: in the next verse the Apostle, about to explain who Christ is and in what his office consists, immediately adds: "who gave himself a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for all." Does a go-between, as a go-between, give himself as a ransom for those to whom he comes? But this is said of Christ. Therefore Christ is altogether the Mediator of atonement, and there is more in him than in a go-between: namely that by his own ransom [λύτρον] he propitiated us and redeemed us to God. "That is certainly something other than being a go-between," says Socinus himself, on that sixth verse. But, in his usual way, he weakens both the words and the matter when he explains that Christ did not give his life for the deliverance of one or another man, or of one or another class of persons, but died indiscriminately for all. Yet the text does not simply say that Christ died, but uses both λύτρον and ἀντίλυτρον; since these words contain emphasis and the power proper to the death of Christ, on which the reason of atonement and redemption depends, the Adversary ought not to deny them merely because they are against his hypothesis. He adds that the word Mediator does not signify this by its own force, but by accident, because of the circumstances of the passage. This does not follow. For that explanation is not contrary to the force of the word, but explains it, and shows in what sense the word must be taken and is usually taken. A perfect mediator is one who joins the parties, not merely one who announces his own offices to the other party; for that can happen, and often does, so that all mediation meanwhile is rendered ineffective and fruitless. But he is at last rightly judged to have performed mediation well and fully who has joined the parties and repaired the broken favour. Therefore, since Christ is to be regarded as the Mediator in the most perfect way, he is to be judged such not only by the office of a go-between but by the office and effect of a reconciler. Finally, what he adds about Beza, that Beza says some of the same things that Socinus later said, is of no weight, since neither Beza nor anyone else interprets μεσίτην here as a mere go-between; and neither Beza nor anyone else doubts that Christ is the Mediator not merely of a go-between but of reconciliation.

units.la: Tres loci supersunt, in quibus mentio fit Mediatoris, eadem opera examinandi, num Mediator iis significet duntaxat internuncium divinae voluntatis, & non conciliatorem? occurrunt autem in epistola ad Hebreos. Quum enim N. T. propria fere vox Mediatoris sit, in epistola inde, ubi Apostolus ex professo & copiose de officio Christi disputat, aliquoties illa usurpatur. Heb viii. 6. Nunc vero excellentius sortitus est ministerium, quanto & praestantioris est foederis Mediator, quod in praestantioribus promissionibus sanctitum est. Cap. ix. 15. Et ideo Novi Testamenti Mediator est; ut, morte intercedente in redemtionem earum praevaricationum, quae erant sub priore Testamento, repromissionem accipiant, qui vocati sunt, aeternae haereditatis. Vbi enim Testamentum est, mors necesse est intercedat Testatoris. Cap. xii. 24. Et accessistis ad Foederis Novi Mediatorem Jesum. Ad quae loca omnia Socinus respondet, primum Jesus Christus in eis novi & praestantioris foederis, seu testamenti mediator, esse dicitur. quod sane ad Deum nobis placandum non pertinet, sed ad fædus[?] ipsum, de quo agitur. Negatur consequentia, pertinent ad fædus ipsum; ergo non ad placandum nobis Deum. Nota quippe & usitata este regula, quod subordinata non pugnant. Hoc ipsum fædus novum, ejusque natura est, ut placetur nobis morte Filii Deus.
units.tr: Three passages remain in which mention is made of the Mediator; these must be examined at the same time, to see whether in them the Mediator signifies only a go-between of the divine will and not a reconciler. They occur in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Since in the New Testament the word Mediator is almost peculiar to the Christian religion, it is used several times in that epistle, where the Apostle discusses the office of Christ expressly and at length. Heb. 8:6: "But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is also the Mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises." Ch. 9:15: "And for this cause he is the Mediator of the New Testament, so that, by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, those who are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance. For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator." Ch. 12:24: "And you have come to Jesus, the Mediator of the New Covenant." To all these passages Socinus replies: "First, Jesus Christ is said to be the mediator of the new and better covenant or testament in them. This certainly does not pertain to placating God for us, but to the covenant itself of which the passage speaks." The consequence is denied: they pertain to the covenant itself; therefore they do not pertain to placating God for us. For it is a known and common rule that subordinate things do not conflict. This very new covenant, and its nature, is that God is placated toward us by the death of the Son.

units.la: Socinus : deinde epitheta illa Novi, & præstantioris fatis[?] ostendunt, non solum aliud fœdus: quod antiquum appellari posset, & deterius sit, antecessisse; sed illius non minus, quam hujus, aliquem Mediatorem extitisse. Is autem, ut supra vidimus, Moses fuit.
units.tr: Socinus: "Next, those epithets of the new and better covenant show that not only another covenant, which could be called the old one and is inferior, had gone before, but that some mediator of that covenant existed no less than of this one. And that mediator, as we have seen above, was Moses."

units.la: Resp. Negatur iterum consequentia, præcessit aliud fædus ante novum, & cujus Mediator Moses fuit, ergo novi hujus Mediator Christus non fuit reconciliationis Mediator, qui placarit Deum suo sanguine? Negatur, vel parem-utriusque fœderis esse rationem; vel eandem utriusque, Mosis, & Christi. In fœdere legali non Dei gratia proposita fuit, & reconciliatio, uti in Euangelio: nec Moses sanguinem suum pro peccatis fudit, uti Christus, quem nobis Deus constituit placamentum in sanguine ejus. Rom. iii. 25.
units.tr: Reply: the consequence is again denied: "a covenant went before the new one, and Moses was its mediator; therefore Christ was not the Mediator of reconciliation of this new covenant, who placated God by his blood?" It is denied that the reason of both covenants is alike, or that the case of Moses and of Christ is the same. In the legal covenant the grace of God and reconciliation were not set forth as they are in the Gospel; nor did Moses shed his blood for sins as Christ did, whom God set forth as a propitiation in his blood (Rom. 3:25).

units.la: Quod, uti plurima ejusmodi, de Mose, vel eo qui merus divinæ voluntatis mandatique internuncius fit, dici vel concipi nullo modo potest. Ergone sequitur, præcessit aliud fædus ante hoc novum, & illius quadam ratione dictus Mediator, ergo Christus novi Fœderis Mediator nequit esse reconciliationis vel placatonis? Sed in Veteri illo nulla fuit Dei placatio. ergo nec in Novo? quæ sequela. Tute ipse dicis in Veteri nullam promissam fuisse peccatorum remissionem, nullam salutis, & Spiritus S. promissionem, ergo nec in Novo? hoc ipse nolis. Non valet ergo consequentia, vel à fœdere illo, ad istud; vel à Mose, ad Christum.
units.tr: That may be said or conceived of Moses, or of anyone who is merely a messenger of the divine will and command, in no way at all, as with many such things. Does it follow that because another covenant came before this new one, and Moses was in some sense called a mediator of it, therefore Christ, the Mediator of the New Covenant, cannot be a mediator of reconciliation or appeasement? But there was no appeasement of God in that Old Covenant. Therefore neither in the New? What kind of inference is that? You yourself say that in the Old Covenant no forgiveness of sins was promised, and no promise of salvation or of the Holy Spirit, so is there none in the New either? You would not want to say that. The inference therefore fails, whether from that covenant to this one or from Moses to Christ.

units.la: Socinus : Postrema illa eadem epitheta, & id, quod expressius additur ideo fœdus, cujus Jesus Christus Mediator est, excellentius esse, quia in præstantioribus promissionibus fancitum fuerit, nullam in istarum Mediationum (ut ita dicam) modo differentiam esse tacite indicant, qua aliquid momentum habeat: sed differre eas tantummodo, quatenus posterior excellentioris fœderis fuit, & præstantiora promissa continentis, quam prior. Denique & hic negatur consequentia, differt fœdus hoc ab illo, promissionum præstantia, ergo non in mediatione. Quin contrà sic arguimus, quia præstantiores novi Fœderis sunt promissiones, quam Veteris, idque omne ex Mediatore illius Christo, sequitur Mediationis utriusque maximam quidem esse differentiam; tantam ad minimum, quanta est inter utriusque promissiones. Ut promissionum distantia nos ad discrimen mediationis ducat, quum omnes Novi Fœderis promissiones ex Mediatore Christo ortum suum habeant, atque in eo[?] fundamentum. Cernis tu differentiam fœderis utriusque, & promissionum: neque tantam interim inter Christum, & Mosem? Quæ ista vel incredulitas, vel stupor?
units.tr: Socinus: These same final epithets, and the fact that it is added more explicitly that the covenant of which Jesus Christ is Mediator is more excellent because it was ratified with better promises, tacitly indicate that there is no difference of any real weight between these mediations (so to speak), but that they differ only in that the later is the covenant of a more excellent kind and contains the more excellent promises, compared with the earlier. Here too the inference is denied: this covenant differs from that one in the excellence of its promises, therefore not in the mediation. Indeed we argue the contrary: the promises of the New Covenant are more excellent than those of the Old, and it all follows from its Mediator, Christ, that the difference between the two mediations is certainly very great, at least as great as the difference between their promises. The distance between the promises leads us to a distinction of mediation, since all the promises of the New Covenant have their origin in Christ the Mediator and are founded upon him. Do you see a difference between the two covenants and their promises, and yet not so great a difference between Christ and Moses? What unbelief or stupidity is this?

units.la: Quare nos quidem non negamus Christum Mediatorem esse, vel mediationis officio functum etiam in annunciatione divinæ voluntatis & doctrinæ; sed in hoc solo, exclusive ad alia, totam mediationis rationem sitam, uti nunquam probare Socinus vel annititur, vel potest, ita tum perfectioni Mediationis, tum Christo contrariatur, cujus mediationem in hoc constituit Scriptura, non modo doctrina quod fuit, sed etiam quod rei, & circa partem utramque, Deum, & hominem, intra quas medius stetit, aliaque apud homines, alia πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν[?] habuit peragenda. Nempe Mediator quia verus, & perfectus fuit, non tantum internuncii vel testamenti fuit, sed & reconciliationis, qui partes composuit, & , sine quo perfici id non potuit, hominem in gratiam reduxit apud Deum, sui victimâ placatum & sacrificio. Ita ergo Mediator Novi Testamenti, uti id non solum annunciarit, sed effecerit quoque & fundarit, expiatione & reconciliatione seipso facta.
units.tr: Wherefore we do not deny that Christ is Mediator, or that he discharged the office of mediation even in the announcing of the divine will and doctrine. But to place the whole reason of mediation in this alone, to the exclusion of other things, is something Socinus neither attempts nor is able to prove; it is contrary both to the perfection of the mediation and to Christ, whose mediation Scripture defines not only as doctrine, which it was, but also as a matter of fact, and with respect to both parties, God and man, between whom he stood as mediator, and he had other things to accomplish among men and other things toward God [πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν]. Indeed, the Mediator, because he was true and perfect, was not only the messenger or the mediator of the testament, but also of reconciliation, who brought the parties together, and without whom this could not be accomplished; he restored man to favour with God, appeased by his own sacrifice as victim. So the Mediator of the New Testament did not only announce this, but also effected and founded it, having made atonement and reconciliation by himself.

units.la: Quod non eo solum comprobatur, 1. quod solus est Mediator, atque esse solus potest. In annunciatione verò si consistat totum illud mediationis, neque solus est, neque solus esse debuit: nam alii annunciare potuerunt æque ac ille homo, Angeli, hominesque Euangelium: nec hac ratione possset dici, uti unus Deus, ita unum esse Mediatorem. 1 Tim. 11. 5. Deinde perfectus Mediator fuit, revera & effectu ipso partes concilians: quod ad perfectionem illius officii seu actionis requiritur. 111. & ad fiduciam facit, quam plenam in eo ut Mediatore collocamus: ut non modo res scitu necessarias explicuerit, sed nos Deo plenissimè adduxerit quoque & conciliarit. 1v. Sed & illa expendenda, quæ indicant, eum non modo Dei Mediatorem esse apud nos, sed & nostri apud Deum: neque enim Mediator Dei, sed & hominum dicitur, & non unius esse. 1 Tim. 2. 5. Galat. 111. 19. Et v. Mediator in eo, quod se dedit in mortem ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ[?], redemtionis pretium pro nobis. 1. Tim. 11. 6. Novi Testamenti mediator, morte intercedente & redemtionem εἰς ἀπολύ-τρωσιν[?] pravaricationum. Heb. ix. 5. Novi Testamenti mediatori, & sanguini aspersionis meliora loquenti quam Abel. Ex quorum individuo nexu melius fortiusque argumentamur, quàm à pari Socinus, ad 1 Tim. 11. 5. quod nihil de Christi expiatione, in sermone præcesserat.
units.tr: This is proved not only by the following: (1) he is the only Mediator, and he can be the only one. But if the whole of mediation consisted in announcing, he would neither be the only one nor ought he to be the only one, for others could announce the gospel just as well as that man, angels and men alike. Nor could it be said on this ground that, as there is one God, so there is one Mediator (1 Tim. 2. 5). (2) He was a perfect Mediator, truly and in the very effect bringing the parties together, which is required for the perfection of that office or action. (3) This bears on the confidence which we place in him as Mediator in full measure, so that he not only explained the things needful to be known, but also fully brought us to God and reconciled us. (4) Those passages must also be weighed which indicate that he is Mediator not only of God toward us, but also of ours toward God; for he is called the Mediator not of God only but of men, and not of one party only (1 Tim. 2. 5; Gal. 3. 19). (5) He is Mediator in that he gave himself in death as a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for us, the price of redemption (1 Tim. 2. 6). The mediator of the New Testament, by intervening death, for the redemption [εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν] of transgressions (Heb. 9. 15). To Jesus the mediator of the New Testament, and to the sprinkled blood which speaks better than Abel's (Heb. 12. 24). From the inseparable connection of these we argue more soundly and more strongly than Socinus does from the parallel passage, 1 Tim. 2. 5, where nothing had been said beforehand about Christ's atonement in the discourse.

units.la: Hæc in antecessum dicta, ad nomen & naturam Mediatoris, quod non in solo internuncio consistat vel prædicatione, sed quoque morte Christi, & factâ per eam placatione & reconciliatione nostri cum Deo. Cujus controversiæ decisio cum maximè quidem pendeat ex palmariâ quæstione de Christi satisfactione, & morte verè satisfactoriâ, ad illam plenius discutiendam nos, cum Deo, nunc accingimus. Ubi duo agenda, ut probemus satisfactionis 1. ne-cessitatem, quæ fuit. 11. veritatem. Quamvis in isto possemus subsistere: attamen quia nostra, cum plurimis sententia est, Christum satisfecisse non tantum quia ita Deus voluit, jussitque, ut pœnis peccatorum in lege constitutis satisfieret; sed quoque, quia natura & naturalis Dei justitia pœnas, earumque satisfactionem videtur exigere, hoc ex abundanti discutere hic visum. Eo tamen discrimine, ut neutiquam hanc quæstionem, cum ista putemus parem esse Manet enim, quamvis natura Dei punitionem illam non exigeret, necessitas satisfactionis ex hypothesi decreti & voluntatis divinæ, atque eâ fundata satis est illius veritas. Neque ignoramus, in Ecclesia viros esse præstantes & doctissimos, qui veritatem satisfactionis adversus hæreticos nobiscum tuentur, & egregiè vindicant, manentes in sola necessitate ejus hypothetica, ex constitutione divina: quorum certè honori nihil per nos detractum cupimus. Pace illorum, plures novimus istius, quam & nos sequimur, sententiæ, quæ communior est in Ecclesiis & recepta passim, post pressius & accuratius ventila-tam cum Adversariis controversiam. Eo etenim fortius veritas adstruitur arti-culi hujus, quo non modo satisfactum pœnis nostris per earundem solutio-nem, sed & satisfieri debere priusquam liberemur, ex naturâ rei, ostendi-mus. Interim hac in parte libenter Adversarios toleraturi, modo in summâ rei, & veritate Satisfactionis Christi nobiscum amplectendâ, habeamus consentientes.
units.tr: These things have been said in advance concerning the name and nature of the Mediator, that it does not consist in the messenger alone or in preaching, but also in the death of Christ and in the appeasement and reconciliation of us with God effected through it. The decision of this controversy depends very largely on the principal question concerning Christ's satisfaction and his truly satisfying death, and we now set ourselves, with God's help, to discuss that more fully. Here two things must be done, that we may prove (1) the necessity of satisfaction, which is one matter, and (2) its truth. Though we could stop at this, nevertheless, since our view, with most others, is that Christ satisfied not only because God so willed and ordained that the penalties of sins established in the law should be satisfied, but also because the nature and natural justice of God seems to require punishment and its satisfaction, it seemed good to discuss this here over and above what is needed. Yet we do not think this question is on a par with those, by such a distinction that the necessity of satisfaction is in no way... For even if God's nature did not demand that punishment, the necessity of satisfaction remains on the hypothesis of the divine decree and will, and its truth is sufficiently established on that basis. Nor are we unaware that in the Church there are eminent and most learned men who defend the truth of satisfaction along with us against the heretics, and vindicate it splendidly, resting on its merely hypothetical necessity, arising from the divine constitution; we certainly desire that nothing be taken from their honour by us. With their leave, we know many who hold the opinion we also follow, which is more common in the Churches and generally received, after the controversy with the adversaries has been more closely and accurately sifted. For the truth of this article is the more strongly established, since we show from the nature of the matter not only that our penalties have been satisfied by their payment, but also that satisfaction must be made before we are set free. Meanwhile, we shall gladly bear with the adversaries in this part, provided that we have them agreeing with us on the substance of the matter and on the truth of Christ's satisfaction.

units.la: Spectamus ergo primum necessitatem satisfactionis, in se; tum ejus veritatem, in Christo. Atque illud quod attinet, diversimode quæstio proponi potest: An Dei natura vel justitia pœnas exigat, vel exigere velit peccatorum? An ideo tantum Deus puniat, seu velit punire, quia sic libere constituit, an vero ex antecedente æquitate & justitiâ naturali sic velit, ut aliter nolit? An justitia vindicatrix & punitiva Deo sit naturalis, an vero naturæ ipsius indifferens, atque à solâ pendeat divini arbitrii libertate, & decreto? Nos naturalem dicimus, atque à naturâ Dei fluere, non ex mero arbitrio, quod Deus velit punire peccatum. Atque consequenter satisfactionis necessitatem derivamus non ex mero Dei decreto, sed naturâ ejus, & justitia naturali. Multi Theologorum etiam nostrorum aliter hæc explicant, quorum aliquem catalogum producit Joh. Gerh. Vossius, in Respons. ad Ravenspergerum; cap xxviii. quibus & alios adjungere, haud difficile. Rivetus, in Synopsi doctrinæ de Natura & Grat. cap. vi. sententiam illam apud omnes Theologos olim fuisse communem, nullos esse Scholasticos, qui aliter senserint; nec negari posse ita sensisse Calvinum, Musculum, Zanchium, & alios Orthodoxos, etiam ex iis, qui contra Socinum scripserunt, non infimos, dixit. Piscatorem, ajunt Remonstrantes, in Apologiâ, cap. II. pag. 46. tandem in Vorstii sententiam concessisse. Quod an verum sit, nescio. Forte sententia utraque, prout inter Reformatos & Orthodoxos agitatur, conciliari potest. Quod, quia inclinamus ad quæstiones ejus generis componendas magis, quam serendas & propagandas, quoquo tandem modo etiam conamur.
units.tr: We therefore look first at the necessity of satisfaction in itself, and then at its truth in Christ. As to the first, the question may be put in different ways: Does the nature or justice of God demand punishment for sins, or does it wish to demand it? Does God punish, or will he punish, only because he has freely so decreed, or rather does he will it from an antecedent equity and natural justice, so that he would not will otherwise? Is avenging and punitive justice natural to God, or is it indifferent to his nature and dependent solely upon the freedom of the divine will and decree? We say that it is natural, and flows from the nature of God, not from mere arbitrary will that God wills to punish sin. And consequently we derive the necessity of satisfaction not from a mere decree of God, but from his nature and natural justice. Many of our own theologians explain these matters otherwise; John Gerhard Vossius, in Response to Ravensperger, chap. 28, produces a catalogue of some of them, and it would be easy to add others. Rivet, in his Synopsis of the doctrine concerning nature and grace, chap. 6, says that this opinion was formerly common among all theologians, that there were no Schoolmen who thought otherwise, and that it cannot be denied that Calvin, Musculus, Zanchius and other Orthodox writers, including some of no small standing who wrote against Socinus, held this view. The Remonstrants, in their Apology, chap. 2, p. 46, say that Piscator at last conceded to the opinion of Vorstius. I do not know whether this is true. Perhaps the two opinions, as they are debated among the Reformed and the Orthodox, can be reconciled. Since we are inclined to settle questions of this kind rather than to raise and spread them, we try to do so in whatever way we can.

units.la: Justitia Dei, quæ subjectum est quæstionis, alia accipitur universè pro Dei bonitate: uti apud nos justitia universalis, pro qualibet virtute: vel pro Dei veritate, & fidelitate, in servandis dictis suis, atque implendâ voluntate, sive quod ad promissiones, sive minas: tertiò & pro justitiâ judiciariâ, aut punitivâ, vel isto Dei jure, unde æquitas punitionum & pœnarum promanat. Quæ justitia, quia in se virtus est, & seu principium vel proprietas proxima concipitur omnis judicii; per viam causalitatis, & eminentiæ, Deo non potest etiam non attribui. Tum Scriptura quoque illius in Deo juris mentionem facit, in terminis; atque in rei expositione. Psalm. cxix 137. Justus es Deus, & justa judicia tua. Justitia in judiciis est, ex justitia illâ quæ in Deo, vel ipse Deus. Ut justitia ejus, apud nos, non solum conceptum faciat generalis Dei bonitatis; vel veritatis & veracitatis; sed quoque justitiae istius particularis, quae formaliter in judiciis attenditur & poenis. Quod enim poenae justae sunt, ex illa est justitia. Atque in Scriptura veritas & fidelitas Dei a justitia etiam distinguitur. Apoc. xix. 11. πιστὸς [?] ἀληθινὸς, [?] ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ κρίνει.
units.tr: Justice of God, which is the subject of the question, is taken in several senses: in general for the goodness of God, as among us "universal justice" means any virtue; or for the truth and faithfulness of God in keeping his word and fulfilling his will, whether in promises or threats; and thirdly for judicial or punitive justice, that right of God from which the equity of his punishments and penalties proceeds. This justice, since it is itself a virtue and is conceived as the principle or nearest property of all judgment, cannot by way of causality and eminence be denied to God. Scripture also mentions this right of God explicitly, both in its terms and in its account of the matter. Psalm 119:137: You are just, O God, and your judgments are just. Justice in judgments comes from that justice which is in God, or from God himself. So his justice, as we understand it, does not only convey the general idea of God's goodness, or of his truth and veracity, but also that particular justice which is formally regarded in judgments and punishments. For punishments are just because they come from this justice. And in Scripture the truth and faithfulness of God are also distinguished from his justice. Revelation 19:11: πιστὸς [?] ἀληθινὸς, [?] ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ κρίνει [faithful and true; in righteousness he judges].

units.la: Quare frustra est Socinus, quum, de Servat. lib. 1. cap. 1. in eo totus est, & post eum Catechesis Racovien-sis, de Prophetico Christi officio, cap. viii. ut ostendant, in Scriptura nullius divinae justitiae mentionem fieri, quae ita appelletur, quatenus misericordiae opponitur; istam vero in Scripturis, non justitiam appellari, sed vel severitatem Dei, vel iram, indignationem, furorem, vindictam, aut simili quo nomine. Quippe justitia quando dicitur misericordiae opponi, primo non intelligitur, quasi in Deo attributum aliud alteri adversetur, nulla etenim in Deo proprietatum inter se oppositio est, sed in ordine ad effecta dicitur, propter diversas & oppositas Dei operationes, quando miseretur & parcit, ac salvat; sive quando punit, & condemnat. ii. Omnino Scriptura nominat justitiam, ex qua Deus punit, & non modo indignationem, iram &c. Dan. ix. 7. Penes te o Domine est justitia, at penes nos pudor faciei. Ezech. ix. 15. Ius δικαίωμα Dei, quo qui mala faciunt, digni sunt morte, Rom. i. ult. & Actor. xvii. 31. constituit Deus diem, quo judicaturus est orbem terrarum ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, in justitia. non dicit, in furore &c. & δίκαιον παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ rependere afflictionem affligentibus; ii Theff. i. 6. Apoc. xvi. 5. 6. Justus es Domine, quod illa judicaris. nam digni sunt. Tertio, fac quod Scriptura nunquam vocarit eam justitiam, semper autem vel iram, vel indignationem &c. annon res justitiae istis quoque notationibus continetur? si enim res, quid nomen meruit, eam designans, ut saltem isto rem commode exprimamus? Quando indignationem Deus vel iram exercet, oppositam misericordiae, hoc facit pro justitia, vel non? sive, juste sic operatur Deus, aut injuste, neque enim aliud dicere fas est; annon ea est justitia, misericordiae opposita? Si est, quidni ita dicatur, isto-que designetur recto & appositio nomine? Et Scriptura non opponit illa, sed conjungit & pro eodem habet, iram Dei & justitiam. Rom. ii. 5. in die irae ὀργῆς, & revelationis justi Dei judici, δικαιοκρισίας [?] τοῦ Θεοῦ. Cap. iii. 5. 6. Si autem nostra injustitia Dei justitiam commendat, quid dicemus, an injustus Deus iram inferens? secundum hominem loquor: nam quomodo Deus mundum judicaret? Atque ita temere Socinus nomenclaturam justitiae impugnat, & non eam nostro sensu, sive quatenus ex eâ punit Deus, & non miseretur, in Scripturis occurrere, semper iram & similes locutiones, asserit. Imo in verbis illis, ita, indignatio, furor metaphora est, quae non alio nomine proprio exponi potest, quam justitiae. Deus irasci quando dicitur, vel ulcisci, aut quando furor ei adscribitur, nihil aliud hoc, quam justitiae valida est ostensio & executio. Jus suum exequitur tum Deus, & pro merito, ac jure punit, non praeter aut supra jus. Quod si nil præter justitiam in severitate sua præstat, quare severitas justitiæ opponitur, vel alia ab ea esse statuitur, & non idem? Neque in Scriptura, vel alibi, aut ex ipsa rei natura inter se opponuntur ullo modo, Dei justitia, & severitas, ira, vindicta, sed idem rei ubique, diversis quamvis vocibus, forte & pro diversa ejusdem rei, seu justitiæ divinæ manifestatione, majori atque vehementiori, designatur.
units.tr: Socinus, therefore, labours in vain, as does the whole of his De Servatore, book 1, chapter 1, and after him the Racovian Catechism, On the Prophetic Office of Christ, chapter 8, when they try to show that Scripture nowhere mentions a divine justice which is so called as opposed to mercy; they say that what Scripture calls by that name is rather the severity of God, or his wrath, indignation, fury, vengeance, or some similar term. For when justice is said to be opposed to mercy, it is not meant, first, that one attribute in God is opposed to another, since there is no opposition of properties within God; it is said with regard to effects, on account of the different and opposed operations of God, when he shows mercy, pardons and saves, or when he punishes and condemns. Second, Scripture does indeed name a justice by which God punishes, and not merely indignation, wrath and the like. Daniel 9:7: To you, O Lord, belongs justice, but to us shame of face. Ezekiel 9:15. The ordinance (δικαίωμα) of God, by which those who do evil are worthy of death, Romans 1 at the end; and Acts 17:31, where God has appointed a day on which he will judge the world ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, in righteousness, not "in fury" and so on; and it is just (δίκαιον παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ) for God to repay affliction to those who afflict, 2 Thessalonians 1:6; Revelation 16:5, 6: You are just, O Lord, in judging these things, for they are worthy. Third, grant that Scripture never calls it justice but always wrath, indignation and so on: is the thing of justice not contained in these designations as well? For if there is a thing, it has earned a name designating it, or at least we should express the thing fittingly with this name. When God exercises indignation or wrath, opposed to mercy, does he do this for justice or not? Whether God so acts justly or unjustly (for it is not right to say anything else), is it not justice, opposed to mercy? If it is, why should it not be called so and designated by its proper name? And Scripture does not set these against each other but joins them and treats them as the same: the wrath of God and his justice. Romans 2:5: in the day of wrath (ὀργῆς) and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God (δικαιοκρισίας [?] τοῦ Θεοῦ). Chapter 3:5, 6: But if our unrighteousness commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who brings wrath? I speak as a man: for how would God judge the world? And so Socinus rashly attacks the terminology of justice, and asserts that in Scripture we never find it in our sense, that is, insofar as God punishes by it and does not show mercy; he asserts that there are always wrath and similar expressions. Indeed, in those words, indignation and fury are metaphors which cannot be explained by any other proper name than justice. When God is said to be angry, or to take vengeance, or when fury is ascribed to him, this is nothing other than a strong display and execution of justice. God then exercises his own right, and punishes according to merit and right, not beyond or above right. And if in his severity he does nothing except justice, why is severity set against justice, or stated to be something other than it, and not the same? Nor are the justice and severity, wrath and vengeance of God opposed to each other in any way in Scripture, or elsewhere, or by the nature of the thing; rather the same thing is everywhere designated, though by different words, and perhaps as a different and stronger, more vehement manifestation of the same divine justice.

units.la: Non minus justus in exercenda misericordia, quam in ulciscendis injuriis Deus esse dici-tur, inquit Socinus: & quis negat? igitur, non justus dicitur Deus in exercenda misericordia solum, quod in margine ad scripsit, sed etiam in vindicta, & hæc justitiæ uti est, ita quidni etiam dici debet? Misericordiæ divinæ exercitium etiam justitia appellatur, nempe, quia Deus illam suis se præstiturum promisit, estque justitia veracitatis, & fidelitatis, quam supra diximus; non justitiæ judiciariæ, aut vindicatrici, quæ misericordiæ opponitur, quæque in ulciscen-dis injuriis apparet, de quâ hoc loco agimus, vel ejus nomenclaturâ, ut eam ostendamus rite hic adhiberi, & convenienter tum naturæ rei, tum Scripturæ.
units.tr: God is said to be no less just in exercising mercy than in punishing injuries, says Socinus. And who denies it? Therefore God is called just not only in exercising mercy, which he wrote in the margin, but also in vengeance; and since this is justice, why should it not also be called so? The exercise of divine mercy is also called justice, namely because God has promised to show it to his people, and it is the justice of veracity and faithfulness which we spoke of above; it is not judicial or vindictive justice, which is opposed to mercy, and which appears in the punishing of injuries, and about which we are speaking here; or we are naming it so that we may show that its name is rightly used here, both in agreement with the nature of the thing and with Scripture.

units.la: Socinus, justitiæ nomen præcipuè & plerumque rectitudinem & æquitatem significare.
units.tr: Socinus: the name of justice chiefly and usually signifies rectitude and equity.

units.la: Annon etiam justitiam eam, qua in ulciscendis injuriis justum dicimus Deum? An justitia hæc, & rectitudo opponuntur; neque idem cum Dei æquitate est justitia? Æquum enim est, & ideo justum, verba sunt Socini: quæ cur non etiam conjungantur cum justitia ultionis, seu vindicatrice Dei? Ubi enim Deus judiceat, ibi ejus justitia ut sit, necesse est, inquit Idem postea. Cumque ajat ibidem, quid autem divinæ naturæ convenientius, & propterea æquius, ac justius, quam humanum genus miserum atque despectum, immeritum licet, beneficiis afficere, & gloriæ suæ participatione donare? Quare non pari modo liceat nobis dicere, quid etiam divinæ naturæ convenientius, & propterea æquius, ac justius, quam humanum genus pro meritis punire? & hoc quando Deus agit, an minus convenienter naturæ suæ, minus æque ac juste, quam quando benefacit? Quorsum ergo magis hic rejicit denominationem justitiæ, quam illic? & mox addit, quod justitia, quatenus misericordia opponitur, vere justitia non sit. & quod eo nomine in sacris litteris non decoretur, sed potius severitas & vindicta dici debeat. Quæ quam vana sint, ex iis quæ diximus, & porro dicturi sumus, liquebit.
units.tr: Does not justice also mean that by which we call God just in punishing injuries? Are this justice and rectitude opposed, and is justice not the same as the equity of God? For it is equitable, and therefore just, are Socinus's words. Why should these not also be joined with the justice of vengeance, or the vindictive justice of God? For where God judges, it is necessary that his justice be there, he says afterwards. And when he says in the same place, What is more fitting to the divine nature, and therefore more equitable and just, than to bestow benefits on the miserable and despised human race, though undeserving, and to grant them a share in his glory? why may we not in the same way say: what is also more fitting to the divine nature, and therefore more equitable and just, than to punish the human race according to its deserts? And is this less fitting to his nature, less equitable or just, when God does it, than when he does good? Why then does he reject the name of justice more here than there? And he immediately adds that justice, insofar as it is opposed to mercy, is not truly justice, and that in the sacred letters it is not so honoured by that name, but rather severity and vengeance ought to be called it. How vain these things are will be clear from what we have said and shall say further.

units.la: Sed ista ideo, ut neget scilicet, justitiam illam in Deo vere residere, aut ejus esse proprietatem. Quod qualitatem Dei dicit: non admittimus. Agnoscit tamen, quandam justitiam esse misericordiæ oppositam, qua Deus perpetuo utatur. vid. contra peccatores non respipiscentes, quatenus illa justitia vera justitia, hoc est, rectitudini & æquitati debita est ac consentanea. Neque enim, inquit, ideo punit Deus perpetuo peccatores non respipiscentes, quia proprium sit ejus punire eos, qui peccant (hoc namque illud est, quod vere misericordia opponitur, qua per se nihil aliud est quam peccantibus veniam dare, nulla pœnitentia vel contumacia ratione habita) sed quia non respipiscentibus veniam non concedere, id demum natura divina, & decretis ejus, & propterea rectitudini & æquitati debitum est ac consentaneum. Eadem ferme consideratio locum habet in ipsa quoque misericordia, quatenus severitati opposita est, atque vindicta, ut scilicet Dei proprietas non sit, sed effectus tantum voluntatis ejus. Nonnulla primum hic sunt annotanda.*
units.tr: But these things are said so that he may deny that this justice truly resides in God, or is his property. He calls it a quality of God, which we do not admit. Yet he acknowledges that there is a certain justice opposed to mercy, which God uses perpetually, namely against sinners who do not repent, insofar as that justice is true justice, that is, is due and consonant with rectitude and equity. For, he says, God does not punish sinners who do not repent perpetually because it is his property to punish those who sin (for that is what is truly opposed to mercy, which in itself is nothing other than granting pardon to sinners, with no regard to repentance or obstinacy), but because to refuse pardon to those who do not repent is, in the end, due to and consonant with the divine nature, its decrees, and therefore with rectitude and equity. Nearly the same consideration applies to mercy itself, insofar as it is opposed to severity and vengeance, so that it is not a property of God but only an effect of his will. Some points should be noted here first.

units.la: 1. Negat Deo proprium esse, punire peccatores; & tamen non resipiscentes punire ait, non tantum ex decreto, sed quoque natura Dei, istudque tum decretis tum naturae ejus esse consentaneum. Cum enim inquit, natura divina, & decretis, non ex solis decretis, neque primo hinc, sed ex Dei natura fundamentum quaerit divinae vindictae. Consequenter eam non tantum pro effecto habere debet voluntatis divinae, quod paulo ante dixerat, sed & proprietate naturae Deo insita. Et qua ratione, punire non resipiscentes, non demum ex Dei decreto sed natura fluit, & non quoque punire peccatores? Imo quid illud aut dicitur, aut est, nisi hanc ob causam, quia punire peccatores, naturae divinae convenit, & non modo ejus decreto? fundamentum enim puniendi non resipiscentes, in hoc situm est, quod punire velit peccatores. Vel an hoc non aeque rectitudini & aequitati debitum est ac consentaneum, atque illud? II. Ju-stitiam Dei, quae opponitur misericordiae, duplicem Socinus facit, alteram, qua punit impios & non resipiscentes; alteram, qua, si vellet, neque illi ipsi, quos pro sua benignitate justos judicat, ante ejus faciem consistere possent. Quaeso, utraque illa annon huc redit, & in eo primum fundatur, quod peccatores puniat, vel jure eos punire possit, ac velit? Quare impoenitentes? nisi quia peccatores sunt gravissimi. Quare & suos, si vellet? nisi quia interim sunt peccatores. Ergo utrumque in hoc tertio convenit, ceu fundamento, quod Dei justitia fertur in vindictam & punitionem peccatorum. Eaque hactenus misericordiae opponitur. Atque de utraque illa justitia censet in Psalmis agi; de illa Psalm v. uti de ista, Psal. cxxx. aliisque plurimis Scripturae locis, quae adducit pag. 5. Quotsum ergo dixit, pag. 8. quod justitia, quatenus misericordia opponitur, vere justitia non sit. neque eo nomine in sacris litteris decoretur? Si non sit justitia, quare ipse eam sic appellat, atque de eadem agi in variis Scripturae locis affirmat, tanquam de justitia misericordiae opposita? Iterum, si res in Scriptura continetur, quid est, quod vocem eliminemus? qua nulla est proprior & commodior? praeterquam quod eadem, eodemque sensu, vox etiam justitiae in Sacris occurrat. III. Similiter misericordiam Dei constituit duplicem. Unam, qua erga resipiscentes fertur, iis peccata condonat, & salutem largitur, juxta factas ipsis promissiones; alteram, qua homines praevenit, & peccatis adhuc immersos ad se vocat & allicit, & gratuito, ne cogitantibus quidem, delictorum veniam & salutem offert. Quae utraque Dei misericordia a nemine non agnoscitur: atque praecipua ejus dicit effecta ac documenta. Verumenimvero neque & hoc negari potest, misericordiam Dei etiam praeter & extra illa se exerere, erga homines quoscunque, ne bestias dicam atque animalia, & quaecunque miseriae obnoxia sunt: quae omnia Deum servare & regere, omnibusque opem praestare & benedicere uti scimus, ita quoque erga ista Dei misericordiam accipere, & non illa sola bipartita divisione comprehendere, aequum est. Vide Psal. xxxvi. 7. & cvlv. 9. Jon. iv. 1. 11. Luc. vi. 35. 36. Crellius, de Deo & attrib. cap. xxviii. hoc sane modo accipiendum videtur illud Psalmi 146. 9. Suavis, vel, ut in Hebraeo est, bonus Dominus universis, & miserationes, seu misericordia ejus super omnia opera ejus, h. e. Deus misericordiam exercet in omnia sua opera, resve omnes à fe creatas. Vide eundem etiam pag feq· Præterquam quod illa misericordiæ divinæ divisio magis sumatur ex objecto materiali, præcipuo; quam formali, quod non est præcisè homines salvandi, sed creatura misera, quatenus misera. Ut nesciam, quare Socinus dixerit, misericordiam per se nihil aliud esse, quam peccantibus veniam dare, & quidem, quod addit, nulla pœnitentia vel contumacia habita ratione. Jam verò misericordia Dei, prout justitiæ punitrici opponitur, & non ἀνθρωπωπαθῶς[?] affectum aliquem miserendi dicit, sed θεοπρεπῶς[?] & proprie bonitatem, ad benefaciendum creaturæ miseræ, Deo non minus est naturalis atque essentialis, ac justitia, ei oppositæ, punitiva peccatorum. Verùm, uti distinguere omnino hic debemus, atque Socinus ipse distinctè possuit, Dei naturam, & decreta; ita aliud est considerare attributum aliquod Dei, vel ejus egressum, & operationem ad extra, quemadmodum loquuntur, id est, extra Deum. Attributa Deo sunt naturalia, bonitas, potentia, sapientia, justitia, neque illa possunt non esse in Deo, sive Deus non potest concipi sub illorum attributorum negativo, vel contrario: at interim non operatur Deus extra se, juxta & per attributa illa, nisi intercedente consilio atque beneplacito voluntatis suæ. Sic nullâ naturali necessitate extra se producit mundum, eumque regit & conservat; sed posito, quod eum velit creare, & regere, non potest non sapienter, potenter, optimè, ac justè omnia facere. Atque is à nobis dicitur attributorum quasi egressus, in operationibus & operibus divinis, mediante atque antecedente Dei ad operandum voluntate. v. Unde etiam apparet, quod in eodem subjecto perfectè, id est, verè tum justitia Dei, tum misericordia, qua punit & castigat, vel miseretur, exerceri possint, atque eodem tempore, licet non ad idem, eodemque modo, secus ac Socino visum, pag. 6. Neque ideo minus oppositá dicenda, ex justitiâ & misericordiâ, vel punire, & misereri, Socinus, punire eos qui peccant, hoc namque illud est, quod verè misericordiæ opponitur: nam oppositio quævis non in hoc sita, quod non possint eodem tempore opposita in eodem subjecto locum habere, sed quod non ad idem, atque eodem modo. Imo passim Deus illa ita temperat, ut justitiæ & misericordiæ utrobique fere, & iisdem in subjectis, eodemque tempore illustria perhibeat documenta. Psalm. xc. 9. Fuisti eis Deus condonans, etiam quum ultionem sumeres de actionibus eorum. & Thren. iii. 22. 32. 33.
units.tr: 1. He denies that it is proper to God to punish sinners, and yet he says that he punishes those who do not repent, not only by decree but also by the nature of God, and that this is consistent both with his decrees and with his nature. For when he says "the divine nature, and his decrees," he seeks the foundation of divine vengeance not from decrees alone, nor first from them, but from the nature of God. Consequently he must regard vengeance not merely as an effect of the divine will, as he said a little earlier, but also as a property implanted in God's nature. And how is it that the punishing of the impenitent flows from the nature of God and not finally from his decree, while punishing sinners does not? Indeed, what is that statement saying, or what does it mean, except that it is for this reason, namely that punishing sinners agrees with the divine nature and not merely with his decree? For the ground of punishing the impenitent lies in this, that God wishes to punish sinners. Or is this not as much due to and consistent with righteousness and equity as that? II. Socinus makes the justice of God, which is opposed to mercy, twofold: one kind by which he punishes the wicked and the impenitent; the other by which, if he wished, not even those whom by his goodness he judges just could stand before his face. I ask you, does not each of these come back to this, and is it not first grounded in this, that he punishes sinners, or that he can and wills to punish them by right? Why the impenitent? Only because they are the most grievous sinners. Why his own people, if he wished? Only because in the meantime they are sinners. Therefore both agree in this third point, as in a foundation, that the justice of God is directed to the vengeance and punishment of sinners. And so far it is opposed to mercy. And Socinus thinks that both kinds of justice are spoken of in the Psalms: the former in Psalm 5, the latter in Psalm 130 and many other places of Scripture which he adduces at p. 5. Why then did he say at p. 8 that "justice, insofar as it is opposed to mercy, is not truly justice, and is not honoured with that name in the sacred letters"? If it is not justice, why does he himself so call it, and affirm that it is treated in various places of Scripture as justice opposed to mercy? Again, if the thing is contained in Scripture, why do we eliminate the word, when none is more proper and suitable, besides which the same word "justice," with the same sense, also occurs in the Sacred Books? III. Similarly Socinus makes the mercy of God twofold. One kind is directed toward those who repent: it forgives them their sins and bestows salvation, according to the promises made to them; the other anticipates men, and calls and entices them while they are still immersed in sins, and offers forgiveness of offences and salvation freely, even to those not thinking of it. No one fails to acknowledge each of these mercies of God, and he speaks of them as its chief effects and proofs. Yet it cannot be denied that the mercy of God also shows itself beyond and outside those ways, toward men of every kind, not to mention beasts and animals and whatever is subject to misery. We know that God preserves and governs all these things, and grants help and blessing to all; it is fair to understand his mercy toward these things in the same way, and not to comprehend it solely within that twofold division. See Psalm 36:7, Psalm 145:9, Jonah 4:1, 11, Luke 6:35–36. Crellius, On God and his attributes, ch. 28: "Indeed the verse of Psalm 146:9 seems to be understood in this way: The Lord is sweet, or, as it is in the Hebrew, good to all, and his mercies, or mercy, is over all his works, that is, God exercises mercy toward all his works, or all things created by him." See also the following page of the same author. Besides, that division of divine mercy is taken chiefly from the material object rather than the formal one; the formal object is not precisely men to be saved, but a miserable creature insofar as it is miserable. I do not know why Socinus said that mercy in itself is "nothing other than granting pardon to those who sin," and indeed, as he adds, "without regard to repentance or obstinacy." But the mercy of God, as it is opposed to punitive justice, does not express some affection of pity in a human-passion manner [ἀνθρωπωπαθῶς], but in a manner fitting to God [θεοπρεπῶς], and properly goodness to do good to a miserable creature; it is no less natural and essential to God than justice, its opposite, which punishes sins.
