But just as we must here distinguish carefully, and as Socinus himself has distinctly stated, between the nature and the decrees of God, so it is one thing to consider some attribute of God, or its outward going forth and operation, as they say, that is, outside God. The attributes are natural to God: goodness, power, wisdom, justice; nor can they not be in God, nor can God be conceived under the negative or contrary of those attributes. Yet God does not work outside himself according to and through those attributes except by the intervention of the counsel and good pleasure of his will. Thus by no natural necessity does he produce the world outside himself, and govern and preserve it; but, granted that he wills to create and govern it, he cannot but do all things wisely, powerfully, best, and justly. And this we call the going forth, as it were, of the attributes in the divine operations and works, by means of God's will to operate, which is both mediate and antecedent. v. Hence it also appears that in the same subject both the justice of God and the mercy by which he punishes and chastises, or shows pity, can be exercised perfectly, that is, truly, and at the same time, although not toward the same object and in the same way, contrary to what Socinus thought at p. 6. Nor on that account are justice and mercy, or punishing and pitying, to be called less opposed, as Socinus says: "to punish those who sin, for this is what is truly opposed to mercy." For any opposition lies not in this, that they cannot exist together in the same subject at the same time, but in that they are not directed to the same thing and in the same way. Indeed, God often so tempers them that he displays illustrious proofs of justice and mercy on either side, almost in the same subjects and at the same time. Psalm 90:9 (LXX/Vulgate numbering): "You were to them a God forgiving, even when you took vengeance on their deeds"; and Lamentations 3:22, 32–33.

units.la: Schlichtingius, contra Meisnernum, de justificatione: Imo verò nec justitiam, nec misericordiam manifestavit, si vera est vestra sententia. Non justitiam, quia innocentem proprie punivit. Innocens autem nonnisi injuriâ puniri potest: nec misericordiam, quia jure suo non cessit, sed totum jus suum persecutus est. Locus Rom. 3. 25. huc non pertinet. Respondeo: justitiam in Christi morte manifestavit Deus, quatenus pœnam peccatorum exegit. Christus innocens quidem fuit in seipso, sed quatenus statum nostrum subivit nostro loco, & reatum nostrum ac debita persolvenda in se suscepit, in ista ἁμαρτία[?] dicitur factus pro nobis peccatum, utcunque in se peccatum non nosset, ii Cor. v. 21. & κατάρα, maledictio, Gal. iii. 13. [illegible, ~10 letters] ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατά[?] Punivit ergo innocentem quidem in se, non vero innocentem illâ ad nos voluntariâ sui relatione ac surrogatione in locum nostrum : uti quando sponsor fuit pro eo, cujus obivit vadimonium, in se quidem innocens ; non vero innocens ex fidejussione. Misericordia vero suam ostendit Deus, quia Filium suum ad hoc dedit ut puniretur pro nobis, & in eo haberemus redemtionem ac salutem. Ad quod declarandum omnino facit locus Rom.iii.25. quem constituit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad demonstrationem justitiæ suæ Nisi quis dubitet divinæ attribuere erga se misericordiæ, quod Deus & reconciliatur, & placatur: cum quo conjungit Apostolus demonstrationem justitiæ, ut in eodem argumento Deus exhibuerit se summe misericordem, & quoque justum.
units.tr: Schlichting, against Meisner, on justification: "Indeed, if your opinion is true, he has shown neither justice nor mercy. Not justice, because he punished an innocent man properly. But an innocent man can be punished only by injustice; nor mercy, because he did not yield his right but pursued his whole right. The passage Romans 3:25 has nothing to do with this." I answer: God displayed justice in the death of Christ, insofar as he exacted the penalty for sins. Christ was indeed innocent in himself, but insofar as he took on our state in our place, and undertook in himself our debts and the things to be paid, he is said to have been made sin for us in that [ἁμαρτία], although in himself he knew no sin, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and a curse, a maledictio, Galatians 3:13 [illegible, about ten letters] for us. He punished therefore one innocent in himself, but not innocent in that voluntary relation and substitution of himself to us in our place; just as when a surety has been made for one whose bail he has undertaken, he is innocent in himself, but not innocent by virtue of the suretyship. God shows his mercy because he gave his Son to be punished for us, and that in him we might have redemption and salvation. Romans 3:25 altogether serves to declare this, where God "set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, for the demonstration of his justice." Unless someone doubts that it is a mercy of God toward us that God is both reconciled and propitiated; with which the Apostle joins the demonstration of justice, so that in the same argument God has shown himself supremely merciful and also just.

units.la: Denique, quod nec misericordia sit proprietas Dei, sed effectus tantum voluntatis ejus, uti Socinus dicit, haud ita admittimus. Nam, quamvis non negemus, vocem misericordiæ in Deo attributum notat & proprietatem essentialem. ii. Tum formalem misericordiæ rationem Deo non convenire haud ignoramus, quatenus videlicet vel cor, vel cordis affectum notat, sed quod proprie & positive illo attributo continetur, & Deo essentiale, ejus est bonitas & benignitas. iii. Ut quemadmodum, quamvis nulla unquam extitisset, aut à Deo facta fuisset creatura, Deo nihilominus propria essent potentia, sapientia, justitia, ita & bonitas, quæ misericordiâ notatur, etiamsi nunquam aliquis extitisset misericordia: imo vel ne extitisset quidem. Quia attributa relativa non dicuntur tantum ad creaturas existentes, sed & possibiles: & quamvis misericordia non fuisset sub ista nomenclatura & terminatione, fuisset tamen, semperque est in Deo quod adrem, & suum absolutum. iv. Hoc vero est Dei bonitas. Ista ejus proprietas, quæ pro principio naturali omnis benignitatis & beneficentiæ in Deo, ab omnibus adeo hominibus, agnoscitur. Eademque revera in Deo est cum misericordia, sed terminatione discrepat, & effectu, pro objectis diversis. Non potest Deus non bene velle creaturæ, pro naturali sua bonitate: non potest non velle punitionem peccatorum, pro justitia. Psalm. LXXXIX. 15. Justitia & judicium habitaculo folii tui; benignitas & fides præcunt faciei tuæ. Psalm. LXII. 11. Semel loquutus est Deus, duo hæc audivi, quia potestas Dei est, & tibi Domine misericordia: quia tu reddes unicuique juxta opera sua. Psalm. CXVI. 5. Misericors Dominus & justus, & Deus noster miseretur. Utrumque illud Deo naturale est, & proprium. Verum in egressu seu exercitio utriusque proprietatis, Deus hinc bonitatem, inde justitiam ita ostendit, ut pro sapienti consilio, non modo sibi minime officiant, sed conspirent optime; & non omnem ubique mox, & omni ratione vel bonitatem effundit, vel justitiam Deus, sed tali ac tali modo operatur, prout sibi, sapientissimo Moderatori omnium, visum. Quare quamvis Diabolorum non miserentur ad redemtionem & salutem, & non omnes peccatores æquali modo puniat, hoc in præjudicium bonitatis aut justitiæ ejus naturalis trahi non potest: quia utcunque naturaliter quidem bonus est, & justus, attamen nil agit nisi pto sapienti beneplacito. Neque voluntas seu decretum Dei, & natura opponi debent, quasi quod ex decreto,non item ex natura,vel naturali sequatur proprietate ? & quod pro naturae seu bonitate seu justitia, non item ex decreto suo, & libere tum quod ad egressum, tum ejus modum varium, Deus agat: sed decretum, pro natura se habet, atque uti nos pro conceptibus nostris, & in signo rationis loquimur. naturae quasi subordinatur.
units.tr: Finally, we do not accept, as Socinus says, that mercy is not a property of God but only an effect of his will. For although we do not deny that the word mercy signifies an attribute and an essential property in God, ii. we are not unaware that the formal notion of mercy does not belong to God insofar as it denotes either a heart or an affection of the heart. What is properly and positively contained in that attribute, and is essential to God, is his goodness and kindness. iii. Just as power, wisdom and justice would belong to God even if no creature had ever existed or been made by him, so goodness, which is signified by mercy, would belong to him even if no one had ever been an object of mercy, indeed even if mercy had never existed at all. For relative attributes are predicated not only of existing creatures but also of possible ones. Although mercy had not existed under that name and term, it would still have been, and always is, in God as to the thing itself (adrem) and as his absolute attribute. iv. This is God's goodness, that property which is acknowledged by all men, even by all men, as the natural principle of all kindness and beneficence in God. It is really the same in God as mercy, but it differs in its terminus and its effect according to the different objects. God cannot fail to will well to creatures, by his natural goodness; he cannot fail to will the punishment of sinners, by his justice. Psalm 89:15: Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne; kindness and faithfulness go before thy face. Psalm 62:11: God has spoken once; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God, and to thee, O Lord, belongs mercy; for thou renderest to every man according to his work. Psalm 116:5: The Lord is merciful and righteous, and our God is merciful. Both of these attributes are natural to God and proper to him. But in the outgoing or exercise of each property, God displays goodness on the one hand and justice on the other, in such a way that, by his wise counsel, they not only do not hinder each other but agree excellently. God does not pour out goodness or justice everywhere at once and in every way, but works in this or that manner as seemed fitting to him, the most wise Governor of all. Therefore, although he does not show mercy to the devils with a view to redemption and salvation, and does not punish all sinners in the same way, this cannot be drawn to the prejudice of his natural goodness or justice, since, however naturally good and just he is, he nevertheless does nothing except by his wise good pleasure. Nor ought the will or decree of God and his nature to be set against each other, as if what follows from the decree, but not from the nature or natural property, and what follows from his nature, whether goodness or justice, but not from his decree, were in opposition; and as if God acted freely both as to the outgoing and as to its varied manner. Rather, the decree stands in relation to the nature as a kind of subordinate to it, just as we speak of God in our own conceptions and by way of reason's sign.

units.la: Interim pro bonitate & misericordia in Deo naturali, quod non effectum demum voluntatis, sed proprietas divinae sit naturae, faciunt haec. 1. Ea Scripturae loca, quae misericordiam non operibus modo Dei, & effectis voluntatis, sed ipsi ejus natura attribuunt. Exod. xxxiv. 6. 7. Jehova, Jehova, Deus misericors, & gratiosus, longanimis, & multus benignitate ac fide. Custodiens benignitatem, &c. Primum naturam Dei designat, inque ea misericordiam; tum quomodo eandem operibus ostendit, atque excercet. Nehem. ix. 31. sed propter miserationes tuas magnas [?]הָרַבִּים וּבְרַחֲמֶיךָ non fecisti eorum consumtionem, neque dereliquisti eos: quia Deus gratiosus & misericors es, אֵל חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם אַתָּה. Miserationes ex misericordia petit, quia misericors Deus. Deinde misericordia Dei, & gratia seu bonitas idem. 32. Nunc ergo Deus noster servans foedus & benignitatem. Haec effecta voluntatis divinae, ex naturali ipsius misericordia & gratia. Atque illiusmodi plura occurrunt in Scripturis sacris. Indeque dictus Deus Pater miserationum. 2 Cor. 1. 3. Psalm. ciii. 13. Ut miseretur pater filiorum, miseretur Jehova timentium ipsum. Illud certe naturale patribus est, neque nisi cum natura possunt deponere, utcunque pro consilio & beneplacito miserationes suas erga liberos exerceant. Sic etiam Deus natura misericors est, & tamen [illegible, ~14 letters] quemadmodum alia omnia, ita misericordias dispensat. Quis vero dicet, paternam misericordiam in solis operibus consistere, & esse effectum paternae voluntatis, non item naturae ipsius paternae proprietatem? Atque ita Deus non prius operibus quam natura, hac non minus, quam illis, misericors est, & audit. Propterea passim [?]רַחוּם, οἰκτιρμῶν appellatur. Luc. vi. 36. Sitis ergo misericordes, quemadmodum pater vester misericors est. Misericordes nempe non operibus duntaxat, sed & ipso naturae affectu. Atqui Deus solis effectis externis misericors erit, non vero nos interna naturae proprietate? Sic perfectior hactenus in hominibus misericordia, quam in Deo, & quod ad naturam saltem, supra Deum illi erunt misericordes. Deus solis operibus, non vero natura: homines & natura & operibus. Neque quod ad illud Deus ipsis imitandus; vel Dei exemplo ad misericordiam commonefaciendi erunt. Tit. iii. 5. Misericordia sua dicitur, juxta misericordiam suam servavit nos. Certe non ob aliud, quam naturae mesericordiam significandam, tribui Deo possunt σπλάγχνα ἐλέους. Luc. i. 78. per viscera misericordiae Dei nostri, Quamvis bene sciamus, metaphoricam esse locutionem, ubi Deo viscera tribuuntur, attamen quoque intimam iis naturam significari, nemo est qui non sentiat.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the following point supports the claim that goodness and mercy are natural in God, and that they are a property of the divine nature and not merely an effect of his will. 1. Those passages of Scripture which ascribe mercy to God not only in his works and the effects of his will, but to his very nature. Exodus 34:6-7: Jehovah, Jehovah, a merciful and gracious God, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and faithfulness, keeping kindness, &c. The first clause designates the nature of God and mercy within it; then it shows how he displays and exercises the same in his works. Nehemiah 9:31: But for thy great mercies [according to thy great mercies, הָרַבִּים וּבְרַחֲמֶיךָ] thou didst not make an end of them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God [אֵל חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם אַתָּה]. He seeks mercies from mercy, because God is merciful. Then the mercy of God and his grace or goodness are the same. Verse 32: Now therefore, our God, who keepest the covenant and kindness. These are effects of the divine will, arising from his natural mercy and grace. Many passages of this kind occur in the sacred Scriptures, and so God is called the Father of mercies (2 Cor. 1:3). Psalm 103:13: As a father pities his children, so the Lord pities those who fear him. Certainly this is natural to fathers, and they cannot lay it aside except together with their nature, however they may exercise their compassion towards their children according to counsel and pleasure. Thus God too is merciful by nature, and yet, as in all other things, so he dispenses his mercies. Who will say that a father's mercy consists only in his works, and is the effect of paternal will, but not of the paternal nature itself? And so God is merciful and hears not less by nature than by his works; for this reason he is everywhere called [רַחוּם, οἰκτιρμῶν] (merciful). Luke 6:36: Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful. That is, merciful not merely in works, but also in the very affection of his nature. Yet will God be merciful only in external effects, and not in the inner property of his nature? Thus hitherto mercy has been more perfect in men than in God, and, at least as regards nature, men would be merciful beyond God. God is merciful in his works only, not in his nature; men are merciful both in nature and in works. Nor on that account is God to be imitated by them, or are they to be reminded of mercy by God's example. Titus 3:5: He saved us, not by works of righteousness, but according to his mercy. Certainly the phrase tender mercies [σπλάγχνα ἐλέους] can be ascribed to God for no other reason than to signify the mercy of his nature. Luke 1:78: through the tender mercy of our God [διὰ σπλάγχνα ἐλέους θεοῦ ἡμῶν]. Although we know well that the expression is metaphorical when bowels are attributed to God, yet that it signifies his inmost nature, no one can fail to perceive.

units.la: 11. Dei bonitas, benignitas, amor, gratia, unde benefacit hominibus, ipsi naturalis est: neque aliud sub misericordia ejus denotatur. Uti enim apud nos misericordia nihil est, quam amor & benevolentia adversus miserum, idem affectus, quem aliis deferimus, sed qui ex objecti ratione misericordia appellatur; ita etiam in Deo misericordia, in absoluto & proprio conceptu, est bonitas, quæ relata ad objectum, circumstantia miseriæ vestitum, hinc misericordia nominatur, non ex diversitate ulla attributi in Deo, sed objecti in creatura. Atqui bonitatem & amorem Deo esse naturalem, non effectum demum voluntatis, sed naturæ proprietatem, multa cum probent, tum hoc imprimis, quod Deus ipse amor dicitur, 1 Joan. iv. 8. ὅτι ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν. Ephes. ii. 4. Deus autem Ὁ δὲ θεὸς πλούσιος ὢν ἐν ἐλέει, διὰ τὴν πολλὴν ἀγάπην αὐτοῦ ἣν ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς[?] conjungitur misericordia Dei, & amor: atque hic origo omnis exhibiti nobis amoris & misericordiæ. Pro naturali Dei amore copiæ illæ amoris & miserationum in nos profluunt. Rom. v. 8. commendat suam erga nos charitatem Deus, quod nobis etiam peccatoribus Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Joann. iii. 16. Ita Deus dilexit mundum. non quod pro amore suo teneretur nobis Filium dare; sed quod, quum ei istud placuit, non ex alio fonte id fluxerit, quam amoris. Hinc bonitas & beneficentia, ac beneficia Dei ita conjunguntur in Sacris, ut causa & effectum. Psalm. lxxxvi. 5. Tu enim Domine bonus es & condonans. 15. Tu autem Domine Deus misericors & gratiosus, longanimis, & multæ benignitate ac fide. Respice ad me. Psalm cxix. 68. Bonus es & beneficus. Psalm. cxlv. 8 9. Gratiosum & misericordem Jehovam, longanimem & magnum benignitate, Bonum esse Jehovam omnibus, & misericordiam ejus in omnibus operibus ejus. Ideoque Deus solus bonus dicitur. Matth. xix. 17. nemo bonus, nisi unus, Deus. Crellius, lib. de Deo & attrib. cap. xxviii. jure affirmari potest, ubicunque Deus in Sacris literis bonus prædicatur, benignitatem ejus comprehendi, frequentius solam designari. &c. Hinc illud solenne in sacris literis, ac præcipuè in Psalmis: Confitemini Domino, quoniam bonus, quoniam in sæcula misericordia ejus. ubi posteriora verba explicatio sunt priorum. Ex quibus illud quoque intelligitur, etiam misericordiæ nomine hoc Dei attributum venire. Licet enim misericordia affectus sit nomen, sæpe tamen pro ipsa benignitate seu beneficentia sumitur. Quibus nonnihil confirmantur ea, quæ hactenus de attributo misericordiæ, seu bonitatis diximus.
units.tr: 11. The goodness, kindness, love and grace of God, from which he does good to men, is natural to him; and nothing else is denoted under his mercy. For as among us mercy is nothing but love and goodwill towards the wretched, the same affection we show to others, but which is called mercy from the nature of its object, so also in God mercy, in the absolute and proper concept, is goodness, which, when related to an object clothed in the circumstance of misery, is therefore called mercy, not from any diversity in the attribute in God, but from the object in the creature. Now, many things prove that goodness and love are natural to God, and not merely the effect of his will but a property of his nature, and above all this: God himself is called love, 1 John 4:8: God is love [ὅτι ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν]. Ephesians 2:4: But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us [Ὁ δὲ θεὸς πλούσιος ὢν ἐν ἐλέει, διὰ τὴν πολλὴν ἀγάπην αὐτοῦ ἣν ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς]. The mercy and the love of God are joined together, and here is the origin of all the love and mercy shown to us. Out of God's natural love those abundant streams of love and mercies flow towards us. Romans 5:8: God commends his love towards us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. John 3:16: God so loved the world; not because he was bound by his love to give us his Son, but because, when it pleased him to do so, this flowed from no other source than love. Hence goodness and beneficence, and the benefits of God, are so joined together in the Sacred Writings as cause and effect. Psalm 86:5: For thou, Lord, art good and ready to forgive. 15: But thou, O Lord, art a God merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth; O turn unto me. Psalm 119:68: Thou art good and doest good. Psalm 145:8-9: The Lord is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and of great goodness. The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all his works. Therefore God is called alone (solus) good. Matthew 19:17: There is none good but one, that is, God. Crellius, in his book on God and his attributes, chapter 28: It may rightly be affirmed that wherever God is called good in the sacred letters, his kindness is comprehended, and is more often designated alone. Hence the solemn formula in the sacred letters, especially in the Psalms: Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever, where the latter words are an explanation of the former. From which it is also understood that this attribute of God is also expressed by the name of mercy. For although mercy is the name of an affection, it is often taken for kindness or beneficence itself. These points confirm somewhat what we have hitherto said about the attribute of mercy, or goodness.

units.la: Denique Deum natura bonum, clementem, misericordem esse, consensus Gentium attestatur, & tacita animi omnium conscientia. Quando enim operibus cernunt homines & experiuntur adeo abunde benignum Deum, nequeunt non adscendere ad ipsum fontem, eumque in natura ipsa Dei contemplari & ampleƒti. Interroga singulos, & confitebuntur lubenter, Deum natura bonum sibi videri, & misericordem, talemque revera esse. Imo sic debere agnosci, ordine & via tum causalitatis, tum eminentiæ, quia nos natura qualitercunque tales quum simus, & hinc etiam operibus nostris in Deo autem, & ejus natura quia omnino perfectionem dicunt, constituenda quoque veniunt. Neque licet Deum concipere sub contrario boni & misericordis. Quin in natura Dei considerandâ cogimus ista vel imprimis contueri. Quare ergo dicas ad naturam Dei minime pertinere, & esse ejus tantummodo effecta, non proprietates? Inter illa, quae Socinani, de Deo, & ejus essentia necessaria scitu habent, ponunt, quod Deus sit, unus, & aeternus, perfecte justus, sapiens, potens, Catech. Racoviens. de essent Dei, cap. 1. quisautem non merito miretur, bonitatem Dei ab illis omitti, quam cum potentia vel Gentiles passim, & primo semper loco agnoverunt, Deum communi sermone Opt. Max. nuncupantes? Bonitatem illam dicimus, quae cum potentia ejus utrobique ambulat, & ab omnibus statim observatur, ut qua Deus bona nobis vult, altera facit. Crellius, lib. de Deo, & attributis, cap. xxviii. inter attributa Dei ponit etiam benignitatem, & clementiam: Deumque valde propensum facit ad gratiam, favorem, ac benevolentiam hominibus praestandam. Quam definiens, inquit, benignitas Deo in sacris literis attributa, voluntaria est ad benefaciendum propensio. addit, quod benignitas naturae divinae admodum sit consentanea, eaque dignissima. Cur non intrinseca ergo & naturalis proprietas?
units.tr: Finally, that God is good, merciful and kind by nature is attested by the agreement of the Gentiles, and by the tacit conscience of all people. For when men perceive and experience in his works that God is so abundantly kind, they cannot help rising to the very fountain and contemplating and admiring him in the nature of God himself. Question individuals, and they will gladly confess that God seems good by nature to them, and merciful, and that he really is such. Indeed, he must be acknowledged as such, in the order and by the way both of causality and of eminence, because we, being in some measure such by nature, and therefore also good and merciful in our works, must also be placed in God and in his nature, since they are said to be altogether perfection. Nor is it lawful to conceive of God under the contrary of good and merciful. Indeed, in considering the nature of God, we are compelled to contemplate these things above all. Why then do you say that they do not belong to the nature of God at all, and are only his effects, not his properties? Among the things which the Socinians set down as necessary to know about God and his necessary essence, they say that God is, one, and eternal, perfectly just, wise, powerful (Catech. Racov., on the essence of God, ch. 1). But who would not rightly wonder that goodness is left out by them, when even the Gentiles everywhere, and always first of all, have acknowledged it along with power, calling God in common speech the Best and Greatest? We mean that goodness which walks alongside his power in every respect, and is at once observed by all, since what God wills good for us, he also makes it so. Crellius, in his book On God and his attributes, ch. 28, counts kindness and clemency among the attributes of God, and makes God very inclined to show grace, favour and benevolence to men. Defining it, he says: kindness, as ascribed to God in the sacred writings, is a voluntary inclination to do good. He adds that the kindness of the divine nature is very fitting to it, and most worthy of it. Why then is it not an intrinsic and natural property?

units.la: Voluntariam autem propensionem esse diximus, ait: quia ea demum beneficentia vera est, ad quam non necessitas adigit, sed qua libera voluntate suscipitur. Itaque licet benignitas divina natura admodum sit consentanea, eaque dignissima: non tamen simplici atque immutabili necessitati ei est alligata. Alioqui non posset non Deus benigne agere; nec unquam ira ac severitas, quae bonitati seu benignitati ejus aperte in sacris literis opponitur, in illum caderet, aut in ullo ejus opere cerneretur. Neque enim naturalibus Dei proprietatibus quicquam potest in Deum cadere contrarium, aut in ullo ejus opere cerni. Resp. Necessitas alia est voluntati contraria, mera, irrationalis; alia, cum voluntate bene consentiens, eique amica, & ipsa tantum non necessaria: illa a causa procedit mere naturali, atque ad unum determinata; ista vero a natura rationali, quaequidem huc propendet, nihil tamen agit nisi ex ratione. Talis est benignitas, aliaque divinae naturae attributa, quae necessario quidem Deo insunt, utpote perfectionem notantia, non tamen ulla necessitate vel adigunt divinam essentiam, vel, nisi quod libera voluntate suscipitur, praestant. 11. Benignitas naturae divinae consentanea, cur non etiam naturalis dicitur? cur non naturae divinae proprietas? Consentanea. an ut a natura separari possit, esseque aut non consentanea, aut dissentanea? Id est, consentanea aut semper, aut non semper? per se, & natura, an ex accidente? Si illud, ergo naturae est proprietas. Sin istud, cur naturae dicitur ad eam esse propensio? Per hoc enim in natura aliquid constituitur, antecedenter ad voluntatem: ut non sit totum & merum voluntatis effectum. Quid, aut unde ista naturae in benignitatem vel misericordiam propensio, & consentaneitas, liceat ita loqui, naturalis? Formaliter differt benignitas & misericordia, a virtutibus aliis: quod si in natura propensio sit ad illam, unde, nisi quod virtus illa seu attributum Deo est naturale? Vel quodcunque alias dixeris, vide ut inde propensio sit certa & necessaria ad eam. 111. Attributa Dei, simplici atque immutabili necessitate divinae naturae alligata esse, incommode & improprie dicitur: neque de Dei bonitate aut misericordia aliter, quam de caeteris attributis naturalibus, loqui convenit. Quid hoc est, alligatum dici divinae naturae, quod ipsi naturae intrinsecum statuitur, & essentiale? simplici necessitate, quasi exercitium ejus penderet à simplici necessitate, causâ ad agendum determinata, & necessitata, non liberâ & voluntariâ ? Rem secus se habere, contendimus. Utut enim Deus immutabili naturâ bonus est, & misericors, necessitate proprietatis naturalis; attamen in bonitate suâ exercendâ & communicandâ non minus liber est, quam in exercitio potentiæ & sapientiæ, quæ Adversariis quoque agnoscentibus, Deo insunt attributa naturalia, necessitate immutabili. Atque uti de istis, pari modo de bonitate Dei & misericordiâ respondemus. Distinctio ergo certa hic ubique, inter attributa, & eorum egressum; sive proprietatem, & exercitium aut operationem; δύναμιν[?], & actum secundum, qui in agente libero & voluntario sei habet congruenter & consentaneè, uti quoque Adversarii loquuntur, ad naturam & naturalem proprietatem, sive sapientiæ, potentiæ, sive bonitatis, interim & libere, pro beneplacito voluntatis, necessitate liberâ, & libertate necessariâ, utrumque suo modo, illud relate ad naturam, istud ad voluntatem, utrâque mutuo & optimè inter sese conspirante, naturâ cum voluntate. iv. Quare, uti sim-pliciter Deus potest non agere, si velit, ita & potest non benignè agere, siquidem omnino nolit quippiam agere: neque enim necessitatur Deus ad agendum: sed posito quod decrevit agere, non potest non, uti sapienter, ita & bene agere. Iterum, haud tenetur ad illum etiam modum seu gradum sive potentiæ, sapientiæ, aut bonitatis agere: utcunque nil possit contra potentiam, sapientiam, & bonitatem, omnia non nisi pro iis, & naturâ suâ. Puto & ipsi dicent, Deum non posse non agere consentaneè suæ benignitati: hoc autem est quod dicimus, non posse eum non benignè agere. v. Neque etiam sic locus adimitur iræ & severitati, vel iustitiæ Dei vindicatrici: nam in Deo certe ista minimè pugnant, benignitas & iustitia, neque in operibus ejus. Non in Deo, quia attributa in eo omnia identificantur, uti in Scholis loquuntur, seu idem sunt, neque majorem hæc in Deum pugnam inferunt, quam quæ ei pari-ter tribuuntur in Scripturis, amor & odium. In operibus Dei, pro diversitate objectorum, benignitas simul, & iustitia vel ira locum habent: illa in omni-bus, quæ Dei, & prout ejus sunt; ista in peccatis: ubi dum simul, malum creaturæ, & bonum Dei, neque enim datur summum malum, sed hoc sem-per habitat, uti dicunt, in alieno fundo, in eo quod Dei est, Dei unâ benig-nitas atque ira variis modis in operibus ejus cernitur. Ita verò Deus pro arbi-trio dispensat & temperat benignitatem & iustitiam suam, ut nihil clarius ubi-que eluceat, quam mira istorum harmonia & conjugatio. Huc illa faciunt Scripturæ loca, supra à nobis indicata, quibus Dei simul bonitas prædicatur & iustitia, atque in ira ipsâ ejus benignitas & misericordia. Illa enim in effectis quidem varia; in Deo autem unum sunt. Naturalibus Dei proprietatibus nihil quidquam in Deum cadit, vel cadere potest contrarium: neque, prout in Deo, contraria sunt, bonitas & ira, amor & odium, similiaque, quæ in operibus quidem habent effectus contrarios, sed nec affectus, nec proprietates contra-rias in Deo. Quemadmodum eadem sua potentiâ Deus creaturam efficit, de-struitque, quæ valde contraria sunt in opere, non in operante: ita eadem naturâ sua, in quâ ceu distincta quidem attributa concipimus bonitatem, & justitiam, sed quae realiter idem sint, servat & punit, effecta praebet benignita-tis & justitiae, nequicquam variante essentiâ, vel proprietatibus. Atque ita ostendimus, misericordiam seu bonitatem Deo esse naturalem, responsumque obiter ad ea quae in contrarium Crellius adfert, quae eadem sunt cum iis, quae super eadem materiâ extant in Catechesi Racoviensi, cap. VIII. de Prophet. Christi munere. pag. 266. Quibus praemissis, regredimur ad justitiae vindicatricis in Deo explicationem & confirmationem: cujus causa & illa de ejus bonitate ac misericordia naturali disputata fuerunt.
units.tr: We said that it is a voluntary inclination, he says, because that beneficence is truly beneficence only when it is not compelled by necessity, but is undertaken by free will. Therefore, although the kindness of the divine nature is very fitting to it, and most worthy of it, it is nevertheless not bound to it by simple and unchangeable necessity. Otherwise God could not but act kindly, and wrath and severity, which are clearly opposed to his goodness or kindness in the sacred writings, could never fall upon him or be seen in any of his works. For nothing contrary can fall upon God through his natural properties, or be seen in any of his works. Reply: there is one necessity which is contrary to the will, mere and irrational; another which agrees well with the will and is friendly to it, and is itself scarcely a necessity at all. The former proceeds from a purely natural cause and is determined to one thing; the latter, however, proceeds from a rational nature, which inclines this way but acts only from reason. Such is the kindness, and the other attributes of the divine nature, which necessarily belong to God, as they denote perfection, yet by no necessity either compel the divine essence, or produce anything except what is undertaken by free will. 11. Why is the kindness of the divine nature called fitting, and why not also called natural? Why not a property of the divine nature? Is it "fitting" so that it can be separated from the nature, and be either not fitting or unfitting? That is, is it fitting always, or not always? Through itself and by nature, or by accident? If the former, then it is a property of the nature. If the latter, why is an inclination to it said to belong to the nature? For by this something is established in the nature prior to the will, so that it is not wholly and purely an effect of the will. What, or whence, is this inclination and fittingness of the nature to kindness or mercy, which we may so speak, natural? Kindness and mercy differ formally from the other virtues; if there is in the nature an inclination toward them, whence comes it, unless that virtue or attribute is natural to God? Or whatever else you may say, see that from it the inclination to it is certain and necessary. 111. To say that the attributes of God are bound to the divine nature by simple and unchangeable necessity is awkward and improper, and it is not fitting to speak of God's goodness or mercy otherwise than of his other natural attributes. What does it mean to say that something is bound to the divine nature when it is set down as intrinsic to the nature itself and essential, by simple necessity, as if its exercise depended on simple necessity, a cause determined and necessitated to act, and not free and voluntary? We contend that the matter is otherwise. For although God is good and merciful by an unchangeable nature, by the necessity of a natural property, nevertheless in exercising and communicating his goodness he is no less free than in the exercise of his power and wisdom, which, as our opponents also acknowledge, belong to God as natural attributes by unchangeable necessity. And as with those, so in the same way we answer concerning the goodness and mercy of God. There is therefore a sure distinction here everywhere, between the attributes and their going forth, or property and exercise or operation; power and the second act, which in a free and voluntary agent stands congruently and fittingly, as our opponents also speak, with the nature and natural property, whether of wisdom, power or goodness; meanwhile freely, according to the good pleasure of the will, by a free necessity and a necessary freedom, each in its own way: the one relating to the nature, the other to the will, both agreeing together most excellently, nature with will. iv. Wherefore, just as God can simply not act if he wills, so he can also not act kindly, if he altogether wills to do nothing; for God is not compelled to act. But, supposing that he has decreed to act, he cannot but act wisely and also well. Again, he is not bound to act in that mode or degree of power, wisdom or goodness; though he can do nothing against his power, wisdom and goodness, all things come forth only for these, and by his nature. I think even they will say that God cannot but act in agreement with his kindness; but this is what we say, that he cannot but act kindly. v. Nor is room thereby taken away from wrath and severity, or from the avenging justice of God; for in God these certainly do not clash, kindness and justice, nor in his works. Not in God, because all his attributes are identified, as the schools say, or are the same, nor do these bring any greater conflict into God than those which are equally ascribed to him in the Scriptures, love and hatred. In the works of God, according to the diversity of objects, kindness together with justice or wrath has its place: the former in all things which are of God and insofar as they are his; the latter in sins: where, while at once the evil of the creature and the good of God are involved (for there is no supreme evil, but this always dwells, as they say, in another's ground, that is, in that which belongs to God), the one kindness and wrath of God is seen in various ways in his works. Thus God indeed dispenses and tempers his kindness and justice at his pleasure, so that nothing shines more clearly everywhere than the wonderful harmony and joining of these. To this belong the passages of Scripture, cited above by us, in which the goodness and justice of God are proclaimed together, and in his very wrath his kindness and mercy. For these, indeed, are various in their effects, but in God they are one. Nothing contrary can fall upon God through his natural properties, nor can it: nor are goodness and wrath, love and hatred, and the like, contrary in God, as they are in God; in the works they have contrary effects, but in God they have neither contrary affections nor contrary properties. Just as by the same power God creates and destroys a creature, things which are very contrary in the work but not in the worker, so by the same nature, in which we conceive goodness and justice as distinct attributes, yet which are really the same, he both preserves and punishes, bringing forth effects of kindness and justice, with his essence or properties in no way varying. And so we have shown that the mercy or goodness of God is natural to him, and have incidentally answered what Crellius brings forward on the contrary, which are the same things as those which appear on this same matter in the Racovian Catechism, ch. 8, on the office of Christ as Prophet, p. 266. With these things premised, we return to the explanation and confirmation of avenging justice in God, for the sake of which both that discussion of his goodness and mercy as natural was undertaken.

units.la: Quomodo misericordia, seu bonitas Deo naturalis est, ita & justitia: id est, non effecta demum voluntatis divinae sunt, in eo sita, quod Deus actu & opere miseretur, & punit, sed in naturâ fundatam proprietatem habent, hinc justitiae, inde misericordiae, ex quâ operationes illae fluunt. Dicant Adversarii, praeter & supra quasi voluntatem, inesse in naturâ divinâ propensionem ad illa: quae quid sit, velim exponant, si non proprietas dicenda, vel sal-tem sic appellari nobis possit. Nos proprietatem dicimus naturalem, ex quâ Deus velit, tum misereri, tum punire. Neque ea contraria in Deo, utcunque in effectis. Bene quidem, si in Deo, praeter voluntatem puniendi ex justitiâ, aut juste, statueretur voluntas puniendi ex injustitiâ, vel injuste, contraria sic essent: at nunc, voluntas puniendi, ex justitiâ, non repugnat voluntati non puniendi, ex misericordiâ, ubi Deo aequum visum, aut hanc, aut illam sequi. Quod in opere exhibetur nunquam, nisi ex Dei arbitrio & consilio, sic aut nunc illa cupientis manifestare: quae in naturâ fundata sunt, quod ad Deum; & voluntate ejus reguntur, quod ad nos.
units.tr: Just as mercy or goodness is natural to God, so too is justice. That is, these are not attributes that come into being only when God's will acts, in the sense that God shows mercy and punishes by an act and deed. They have a property grounded in his nature: justice on one side, mercy on the other, and from these those operations flow. Let our opponents say what they mean by a propensity to those things, which exists in the divine nature beyond and above the will, as if it were something other than the will. I would like them to explain it, or else let us be allowed to call it a property, or at least something of that kind. We say it is a natural property, from which God is willing both to show mercy and to punish. These are not opposed to each other in God, however they may appear in their effects. It would indeed be a different matter if, in God, besides a will to punish out of justice, or justly, there were posited a will to punish out of injustice, or unjustly; then they would be opposed. As it is, the will to punish out of justice does not conflict with the will not to punish out of mercy, when it seems right to God to follow either the one or the other. This is never displayed in the work except by God's decision and counsel, so that he now manifests the one or the other as he desires. Those things are grounded in his nature as far as God is concerned, and are governed by his will as far as we are concerned.

units.la: Quaeritur ergo, an vero per naturam suam Deus, vel naturalem proprietatem justitiae & misericordiae, non posset pro absolutâ potentiâ & jure omnino non punire, & non misereri? Quod si, jam non dicendae erunt illae proprietates naturales: quia naturam abnegare Deus nunquam potest. Sin secus, adversari videtur absolutae potentiae vel potestati, tum naturae Dei, quae cogi aut necessitari ulla re nequit. Resp. distinguimus, punire & misereri actu, aut velle punire, & misereri. II. Tum, velle punitionem, aut justitiam, ex quâ punitio decernitur, & procedit; quaeque in punitione ipsâ ostenditur. Deus non potest non velle justitiam sibi naturalem: ex eâ vult, seu decernit punitionem, sive justitiae illius exhibitionem & manifestationem, libere simul, & necessario; pro naturâ, & arbitrio. Sequitur punitio ipsa itidem libere, & necessario. Quomodo aliàs explicatur, notumque passim, bene una consistere necessitatem aliquam & libertatem, voluntatem & naturam. III. Potest Deus, non punire, & non velle punire, nempe si decernat ne ponatur subjectum punibile, aut puniendum, sive si nolit hominem condere, & permittere peccatum, quod poenam meretur: at posito subjecto, & decreto de subjecto punibili constituendo, simul etiam est in Deo voluntas justitiam illam suam ostendendi, sive puniendi. Quemadmodum potest quidem Deus nihil facere aut creare extra se, atque decernere ne quid creetur: ubi vero decrevit creare, & jam ex decreto isto creat, simul sapienter & bene omnia facit: neque vel novo decreto ibi opus, post decretum de creatione, quo statuat bene & sapienter omnia facere, vel meri arbitrii hoc & naturae est, quia aliter non potest per naturam, quam bene omnia efficere: ita neque aliter quam juste regere potest Deus, id est, puniendum punire pro merito, posito, quod puniendum velit, quod liberum ei erat velle aut nolle, existere. iv. Neque mera naturae necessitate punit Deus, sed voluntate, naturam sequente: ut, quemadmodum potentiam ubi exerit vel ostendit, quod in omnibus praestat [?] operibus, pro voluntate hoc quidem facit atque arbitrio, non tamen arbitraria proinde sibi est potentia, sed naturalis; ita quoque justitia, qua de hic agi-mus. Non enim opponenda in Deo sunt natura & voluntas, ut quod ex vo-luntate agit, non possit dici fluere ex natura ejus & naturali proprietate. Nihil extra se agit Deus, nisi per voluntatem: hujus opus quodcunque externum, eatenus a libero ejus pendet arbitrio, ut non extra se agere necessitetur ipsi sed posita agendi voluntate, aut actione, natura imperat, ne aliter aliove modo agat, quam pro sua dignitate, jure, id est, potenter, sapienter, juste &c. Est necessitas aliqua naturalis, quae voluntatem omnem excludit, uti in inanimatis & irrationabilibus, quae ad unum ex principio interno determinata, huc caeco & bruto naturae ductu feruntur: atque ea hic locum non habet. Alia est necessitas naturae rationalis & voluntaria, ubi in necessitatem aliquam mire conspirat natura & voluntas, non quod a voluntate pendeat natura vel naturalis proprietas, sed quod voluntas in egressu vel executione & opere, aut desi-nando, aut efficiendo, se habeat pro naturali, inclinatione forte dicent Adver-rii, at nos, proprietate. v Distinguo, in punitione, actionem, & ejus justitiam, si-ve moralitatem actionis. Illa est a voluntate Dei, ut principio imperante; atque vario se habet modo: ista fundatur in Dei natura, unde punire non potest nisi juste, & pro justitia non potest omnino non punire. Quare in concreto quando sumitur punitio, pro actione, & justitia in actione, facile difficultatem movet & objectionem, quomodo non possit Deus non punire? verum, ubi attenditur externa Dei actio in se, vel relata ad ejus voluntatem, videtur hactenus posse non esse; at ubi modus ejus consideratur, & moralitas, quae pro fundamento habet Dei naturam, mox apparet ejus, quam tuemur, necessitas, ut non possit non esse. vi. Quando quaestio appenditur ad Dei potentiam, & quaeritur, annon possit Deus aliter? uti imprimis ibi quidem distinguitur, inter porenriam Dei absolutam, & ordinatam, (de quo vide eximie & Scholastice disputandem Cl. Virum, & Collegam nostrum D. Heereboord, in Meletemat. Philosoph. vol. ii. Disput. xxxviii. & seqq.) atque absolutam se potentiam Dei respicere affirmant alii, qua pro absoluto jure Deus possit justitiam vindicatricem non exercere: ita primo haud lubenter inquirendum nobis putamus in absolutam Dei potentiam, & quaestiones illas, quae ejus summitatem premunt: deinde, non esse praesens argumentum cum Dei absoluta potentia, conjungendum, sed ejus natura, ut non quid Deus pro absoluta potentia sua possit vel non,deci-dendum veniat; sed simpliciter, quid natura ejus exigat vel ferat. vii. In divina
units.tr: It is asked, then, whether God, by his own nature or the natural property of justice and mercy, could not, by his absolute power and right, refrain altogether from punishing and from showing mercy. If he could, those properties would no longer be called natural, because God can never deny his own nature. If not, it seems to conflict with his absolute power or authority, and with the nature of God, which cannot be compelled or necessitated by anything. Answer: we distinguish between punishing and showing mercy in act, and willing to punish and show mercy. II. Next, we distinguish between willing punishment, or justice, from which punishment is decreed and proceeds, and which is displayed in punishment itself. God cannot fail to will his natural justice. From it he wills, or decrees, punishment, or the exhibition and manifestation of that justice, freely and necessarily at once, in accordance with his nature and his will. Punishment itself follows in the same way, both freely and necessarily. How this is explained elsewhere, and is commonly known, is that some necessity and freedom, will and nature, can well exist together. III. God can refrain from punishing and from willing to punish, namely if he decrees that no punishable or liable subject shall be placed in existence, or if he is unwilling to create man and permit the sin which deserves punishment. But once the subject is posited, and the decree to establish a punishable subject is made, there is at the same time in God the will to display and exercise that justice. Just as God can indeed do or create nothing outside himself, and decree that nothing be created; yet when he has decided to create, and now creates in accordance with that decree, he does all things wisely and well at once. Nor is there any need for a new decree after the decree of creation, by which he determines to do all things well and wisely. This belongs to his nature and not to mere arbitrary choice, because by nature he cannot do otherwise than work everything well. So too God can govern only justly, that is, punish a punishable subject according to its desert, once it is posited; for he was free to will or not to will that such a subject should exist. IV. God does not punish by mere necessity of nature, but by a will that follows his nature. Just as, when he exerts or displays his power, which he shows in all his works, he does so by his will and choice, yet his power is not therefore arbitrary but natural, so it is also with the justice of which we are speaking. For in God nature and will are not to be set against each other, so that what he does from will cannot be said to flow from his nature and natural property. God acts outside himself only through his will. Any external work of his depends on his free choice to such an extent that he is not necessitated to act outside himself; but once the will or act of working is posited, nature commands that he not act otherwise or in another way than befits his dignity and right, that is, powerfully, wisely, justly, and so on. There is some natural necessity which excludes all will, as in inanimate and irrational things, which are driven by a blind and brute impulse of nature, determined to one thing by an internal principle. That kind of necessity has no place here. There is another necessity of rational and voluntary nature, where nature and will agree wonderfully in a certain necessity; not because nature or natural property depends on the will, but because the will, in its issue and execution and work, either ceases or acts in a way that is natural. The Adversaries may perhaps call this an inclination, but we call it a property. V. In punishment I distinguish the action and its justice, or the morality of the action. The former is from the will of God as the commanding principle, and it takes various forms. The latter is grounded in the nature of God, and so he can punish only justly, and cannot altogether refrain from punishing for the sake of justice. Therefore, when punishment is taken concretely, as an action, and justice is taken as present in the action, the objection readily arises: how can God not punish? Yet when God's external action is considered in itself, or in relation to his will, it seems that up to this point it might not be; but when its mode and morality are considered, which have God's nature as their foundation, the necessity we defend soon appears, namely that it cannot not be. VI. When the question is raised about God's power, and it is asked whether God could not act otherwise, it is first of all distinguished, as is well known, between God's absolute and ordained power (on which see the distinguished and scholastic disputation of the renowned man and our colleague D. Heereboord, in Meletemat. Philosoph. vol. ii, Disput. xxxviii and following). Others affirm that God's absolute power looks to what by his absolute right God could decline to exercise, namely avenging justice. So we think it not wise to inquire first into God's absolute power and those questions which press upon its height. Then, the present argument should not be joined with God's absolute power, but with his nature, so that the question is not what God can or cannot do by his absolute power, but simply what his nature requires or brings.

units.la: Tom. 1. divinâ punitione attendimus. vel rem simpliciter, ejusque veritatem, id est, ut Deus juste puniat; vel modum punitionis, ejusque gradum. Quando pro naturali Dei justitia disputamus, illud urgere satis est, ut Deus pro naturâ suâ justitiam punientem ostendat; non autem quo modo, aut quo gradu. Ad quae intercedit ejus beneplacitum, ut peccatum in peccatore puniat, vel in vade: forte & quantis poenis, quamvis nunquam supra ipsorum meritum. Ut non sequatur, potest Deus variare in poenarum gradibus, & modo; ergo omnem poenam aut puniendi justitiam aeque omittere in totum. Non sequi, dico. Aliud est, nullo modo velle punire, aut posse velle omnino non punire, quod rejicimus: aliud, quo modo velit punire, quem Dei arbitrio resignamus.
units.tr: Tom. 1. In divine punishment we attend either to the thing itself and its truth, that is, that God punishes justly, or to the mode of punishment and its degree. When we argue for God's natural justice, it is enough to press this: that God, according to his nature, shows a justice that punishes. We do not argue about the mode or degree. His good pleasure intervenes in these matters, so that he punishes sin in the sinner or in the surety; perhaps also with what and how great penalties, although never beyond their own desert. It does not follow that God can vary in the degrees and mode of penalties, and therefore that he can equally omit all penalty or the justice of punishing altogether. I say, it does not follow. It is one thing to will to punish in no way, or to be able to will not to punish at all, which we reject; it is another thing how he is willing to punish, which we leave to God's decision.

units.la: Vorstius, in Notis ad Disp. ix. de Deo, pag. 397. utcunque Deum statuat, posse pro absoluta potestate peccata impunita dimittere, dubitat tamen an omnia: peccata, si non omnia, saltem plurima, sine irrogatione condigna poena, peccantibus condonare posset. viii. Aliud est, justitiam vindicatricem non exercere, & non punire: aliud contrarium ejus posse, aut velle facere. Justitiam non exercere, vel justitiam: misericordiam non ostendere, vel immisericordiam. Quod fie-ret nostro quidem judicio, si immerentem Deus immisericorditer non nisi cru-ciaret, aut ita cruciare posse, diceretur; vel merentem & peccatorem, non dignum poenâ pronunciaret, & juste punire nollet. Quae Deus non potest, quia foret ea sui & naturae suae abnegatio. Sic intelligendum, quando dicitur, Deum aliquid non posse, non quasi potentiam ejus limitemus, vel constringamus, sed quod naturam interpretemur, ejusque vim summam. Quare, Deus non potest non justus esse justitiâ naturali omni, & vindicatrice; non velle, quin justum sit, peccata puniri; & ex justitiâ illâ peccatorem in administra-tione providentiae suae, quocunque modo, punire: etiam, illaesa justitiâ suâ, vel placatâ, non potest non misereri & erga suos esse beneficus. Ut in negotio redemtionis, qui beneficentiam exhibuerat homini in creatione & conserva-tione copiosissimam, & non amare & bonus esse erga μίσημα[?] suum hactenus non poterat, ubi peccavit homo, peccatum probare non potuit: quin etiam extra decretum voluntatis suae, non nisi detestari illud & odisse, atque censere in se & naturâ suâ poenâ dignum, quod proin de nec poterat non pro justitia sua velle punire, & pro sapientia punire aliquando. Hinc autem justitiae satis-faciendum prius fuit, antequam, non omnem & qualemcunque, sed istam peccatori misericordiam ostenderet & praestaret, quae salutem adferret: ut, constituto vade & redemtore Christo, qui nostri loco divinae justitiae, nostra debita, sua morte & passionibus elueret, αἰωνίαν [illegible, ~12 letters], in eo sapientissimus Deus perfectissimum suae pariter justitiae & misericordiae exhiberet exemplar & conjugium. In peccatore sunt duo, peccatum ejus, & miseria: adversus illud insurgit justitia, & hac placatâ, erga miserum ostendit se misericordia. Neutrâ agente in alterius praejudicium, vel laesionem. Uti injustum foret, hominem perdere, etiamsi justitiae esset satisfactum pro eo, vel non omnes istos redimere, pro quibus satisfactum est; ira misericordiâ sal-vare vare non vult promiscue & indiscrete adversus quos inclamat justitia. Senten-tiam nostram de utriusque illius divinæ proprietatis in Christo concursu & combinatione, Catech. ipsa Racoviensis plausibilem fatetur: nos & verissimam in progressu docebimus. Atque ita optimè conspirant hoc in negotio justitia puniens, & misericordia parcens ac salvans; quæque proprietatibus & naturâ in Deo consociantur & idem sunt, effectu & opere quamvis diverso, ad idem ducunt [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: Vorstius, in his Notes on Disputation ix, on God, p. 397, while holding that God can, by absolute power, dismiss sins unpunished, nevertheless doubts whether he could pardon all sins: "sins, if not all, at least very many, without the infliction of a fitting penalty, to sinners." VIII. It is one thing not to exercise avenging justice, and not to punish; it is another to be able or willing to do the opposite. To not exercise justice, or justice; to not show mercy, or to show no mercy. In our judgment this would happen if God were to torment the undeserving without mercy, or were said to be able to torment them so; or if he were to pronounce the deserving and sinful not worthy of punishment, and be unwilling to punish justly. God cannot do these things, because they would be a denial of himself and of his nature. This is how we must understand it when we say that God cannot do something. We do not limit or constrain his power, but interpret his nature and his supreme strength. Therefore God cannot be not just, with all natural and avenging justice; he cannot will that sins not be punished, nor, from that justice, fail to punish the sinner in the administration of his providence, in whatever way. Even with his justice unharmed or satisfied, he cannot fail to show mercy and be beneficent towards his own. So in the business of redemption: he who had shown the most abundant beneficence to man in creation and preservation could not until then fail to love and be good towards his enemy [ἐχθρόν]. When man sinned, God could not approve the sin; indeed, apart from the decree of his will, he could only detest and hate it, and judge that in himself and by his nature it deserved punishment. Hence he could not but will to punish from his justice, and sometimes punish from his wisdom. But justice had to be satisfied before he showed and granted to the sinner not any and every mercy, but that mercy which brings salvation. Thus, with Christ established as surety and redeemer, who by his death and sufferings in our place would wipe away our debts before divine justice, the most wise God would display in him the most perfect pattern and union of his justice and mercy alike [αἰωνίαν]. In the sinner there are two things, his sin and his misery. Justice rises against the former, and when justice is appeased, mercy shows itself towards the wretched. Neither acts to the prejudice or injury of the other. Just as it would be unjust to destroy a man even if satisfaction had been made for him, or not to redeem all those for whom satisfaction was made; so mercy does not wish to save indiscriminately and without distinction those against whom justice cries out. Our opinion about the concurrence and combination of these two divine properties in Christ, the Racovian Catechism itself admits is plausible; we shall teach that it is also most true as we proceed. And so justice punishing and mercy sparing and saving agree most well in this business; and these properties which are joined in God by nature and are the same, though different in effect and work, lead to the same end.

units.la: Quæres: Ergone Deus peccata punit absolutâ necessitate? Resp. Distinguo absolutum, quod dicis: vel intelligitur absolutum à consilio & decreto voluntatis, & sic negatur, Deum absolutè peccata punire; vel absolutum, id est, non in mero Dei arbitrio natum, sed quod in natura, & naturali Dei proprietate fundatum sit: atque hoc sensu asserimus, absolutæ Dei naturæ esse justitiam illam, ex quâ peccata, pro sapienti decreto, suo tempore & modo, vindicat. II. Punit. Tu respicis externam punitionem, puniendi actionem: ista non fluit ex absolutâ Dei naturâ, sed immediatè ex divina voluntate, ut principio executivo, in naturali proprietate fundatâ: nos autem non de punitione externâ disputamus, sed de primo ejus in Deo principio, sive de justitiâ vindicatrice, Deo essentiali. Non punit Deus absolutè, sed quidem absolutè justus est: nos de justitiâ, tu de punitione respondes. Illud naturæ Dei innixum est; hoc à voluntate ejus pendet & dirigitur. Neque dicet ullus nostrum, quod Crellius contra Grotium, cap. 1. pag. 102. & alibi, de Deo pag 268.
units.tr: You will ask: does God punish sins by absolute necessity? I answer by distinguishing the word absolute in your question. (I) If it is taken as absolute from the counsel and decree of the will, then I deny that God punishes sins absolutely. (II) If it means absolute in the sense of not arising from mere divine arbitrariness, but grounded in the nature and natural property of God, then in that sense we assert that the justice by which God avenges sins, according to his wise decree, at his own time and in his own manner, belongs to the absolute nature of God. (III) As for punishes: you are looking at external punishment, the act of punishing. That does not flow from the absolute nature of God but immediately from the divine will, as the executive principle, grounded in a natural property. We, however, are not disputing about external punishment but about its first principle in God, that is, about avenging justice, which is essential to God. God does not punish absolutely, but he is absolutely just. We speak of justice; you speak of punishment. The former rests on the nature of God; the latter depends on and is directed by his will. Nor will any of us say what Crellius says against Grotius, ch. 1, p. 102, and elsewhere, about God, p. 268.

units.la: Deum justitiæ vi ad pœnas exigendas impelli. Non vi aliquâ impellitur Deus, sed liberâ voluntate decernit, pro naturâ suâ, justè agere cum peccatoribus, puniendo ipsos, uti bene & sapienter cum omnibus omnino sive personis, sive rebus. III. Necessitate. Alia est ἄλογῳ[?], mere naturalis, aut coacta: talis nec in Deum, neque divinas actiones cadit: alia cum naturâ rationali, ejusque actionibus optimè consistit & conciliatur. Hujus generis est necessitas illa, quâ Deus vult justitiæ suæ exequutionem, & punitionem, necessitas libera, & libera necessitas, in idem conspirante naturâ & voluntate: naturâ, pro quâ Deus vult; voluntate, ex quâ puniat. Ut justitia vindicatrix non sit meri & solius Dei arbitrii, & effectum voluntatis, quemadmodum Adversarii asse-runt, sed supra, & in signo rationis, ante voluntatem, ejusque decretum, in naturâ radicata: uno verbo, quod sit Deo naturalis, & essentialis. Quemadmodum in differenti exemplo id quidem conspicuum satis est. Sumamus aliquid à merâ pendens divini arbitrii libertate, atque id cum divina punitione inter se conferamus, ut appareat, an ejusdem generis sit & ista. Divina prædestinatio non est naturæ Dei, sed solius beneplaciti, nihilque in toto divinæ naturæ conceptu est, quod hanc prout nunc est urgeat: verùm punitionis attendendo justitiam, ecquis putabit, eam sic in solo Dei consistere aut hærere arbitrio? aut quis non censebit in ipsa Dei naturâ esse, quod jus & justitiam istam dicat, & flagitet? Proinde non, quemadmodum prædestinatio, aliaque quæ actus divinæ voluntatis meri sunt, in eundem ordinem redigi & divina justitia potest. Quæ quod non effectum voluntatis, sed naturæ ipsius divinæ sit proprietas, porro sic probamus, ex S. Scriptura, ex natura Dei, tum virtutis illius, & ratione denique Christi in negotio redemtionis nostræ.
units.tr: That God is driven by the force of justice to exact penalties. God is not driven by any force; by his free will, in accordance with his nature, he decrees to deal justly with sinners by punishing them, just as he deals well and wisely with all persons and things without exception. (III) As for necessity: there is one kind, irrational [ἄλογος], purely natural or compelled; such a kind does not fall upon God or his divine actions. There is another kind which agrees and is well reconciled with a rational nature and its actions. Of this kind is that necessity by which God wills the execution and punishment of his justice: a free necessity, and a necessity that is free, nature and will agreeing together: nature, for which God wills; will, by which he punishes. Thus avenging justice is not merely the effect of the sole arbitrary will of God, as our opponents assert, but is above and before the will and its decree, rooted in nature; in a word, it is natural and essential to God. This is clear enough from a different example. Let us take something that depends on mere freedom of the divine will, and compare it with divine punishment, to see whether the latter is of the same kind. Divine predestination belongs not to the nature of God but to his good pleasure alone, and nothing in the whole concept of the divine nature requires predestination to be as it now is. But if we consider the justice of punishment, who would think that it rests or depends on the sole will of God? Or who would not judge that what claims and demands this right and justice lies in the very nature of God? Therefore divine justice cannot be reduced to the same order as predestination and other acts that are merely of the divine will. That it is a property not of the effect of the will but of the divine nature itself, we further prove in this way: from Holy Scripture, from the nature of God, then from his power, and finally from the role of Christ in the work of our redemption.

units.la: Primùm ex locis S. Scripturæ, quæ docent, & exponunt illam justitiam. Videlicet, 1. adesse & inesse Deo justitiam, peccatorum certam, necessariam, & naturalem vindicem. Quò illa primum faciunt, quæ non Deo attribunt iram, furorem, indignationem; sed, quod Adversarii negant in Scripturis fieri, justitiam peccatis poenas inferentem. Rom. 1. 32. Qui τὸ δικαίωμα [?] jus Dei cognoscentes, (quod qui talia faciunt, ἄξιοι digni morte sunt.) Quæro, unde isthæc poenæ ἀξιότης? An à solâ Dei constitutione, quod peccatum dignum sit morte? ergo minorem, servata dignitate & malitia peccati, potuisset constituere Deus pro arbitrio poenam, nullam, vel minorem ex se merenti. Quod si, jam ultra vel præter ἀξιότητα & condignitatem meriti punit, eam non attendens Deus, leviorem poenam, vel nullam potis statuere, æque juste, atque illam. Quæro, an interno reatu, & malitia suâ peccatum, extra Dei constitutionem, poenam mereatur, vel non? Si non, ergo duriter Deus agit cum creaturâ, quod præter meritum, saltem necessarium, constituit poenas adeo graves peccato. Sin de condigno, naturâ suâ peccatum poenam meretur, idque ex intrinsecâ sua malignitate: non punire ergo Deus non potest, & non comprobare pro sanctitate sua & odio contra peccatum, quod hoc ita malum, & puniendum est: non potest velle ut peccatum vel non, vel minus malum sit, quam revera & naturâ suâ est. Ergo non puræ & arbitrariæ Dei constitutionis est, ut peccatum poenâ dignum, eâ juste plectendum sit. Neque si peccatum mereri de condigno dicamus, sequitur, regulam veri & necessitatis aliquam dari vel exstare ante Deum, siquidem antecedat ejus constitutionem, aut promulgatam legem. Quia, uti peccare creaturam contra Deum, intrinsecâ sua natura malum est, & non demum ex, vel per constitutionem divinam; ut omnino non possit constitui à Deo illud vel non malum, vel bonum esse; ita nec eo, quod dicitur, peccatum ex se punibile esse, & ἄξιον θανάτῳ, hinc antecedens ad naturam Dei regula datur, utcunque ante legislationem. Quia regulæ istius veritas radicatur in ipsâ Dei naturâ, ejus vid. naturali sanctitate & justitia, ut quantumvis ante constitutionem divinæ voluntatis aut legis, naturalem habeat & necessariam in se veritatem hoc quod peccatum ita malum est, tamen eam non nisi à Deo, ejus natura & veritate habeat, in quâ originaliter fundatur. Non potest non peccatum absolute in se malum esse, peccatum non solum contra legem latam, sed naturalem dependentiam creaturæ à Creatore, & ejus bonitatem ac naturam: neque potest non peccatum esse punibile, & puniendum, seu mereri de condigno poenam.
units.tr: First, from the passages of Holy Scripture which teach and explain that justice. Namely: (1) justice belongs to God and dwells in him, as the certain, necessary and natural avenger of sins. This is first shown by those passages which do not ascribe to God wrath, fury and indignation, but, which our opponents deny occurs in Scripture, justice inflicting punishments on sins. Rom. 1.32: "Who, knowing the righteous decree [δικαίωμα] of God (that those who do such things are worthy [ἄξιοι] of death)." I ask, whence comes this worthiness of punishment? Is it only from God's ordinance that sin deserves death? If so, God could have set a smaller punishment, or none, at his pleasure, while keeping the dignity and malice of sin, which deserved none or less. But if he now punishes beyond or apart from the worthiness and condignity of the merit, God, not heeding it, could just as justly set a lighter punishment or none at all. I ask: does sin, by its inner guilt and malice, apart from God's ordinance, deserve punishment or not? If not, then God deals harshly with the creature, since he imposes penalties so grave on sin beyond merit, or at least without necessity. But if sin deserves punishment as condign by its nature, and that from its intrinsic wickedness, then God cannot fail to punish, and cannot fail to approve, for the sake of his holiness and his hatred of sin, that sin is so evil and must be punished. He cannot will that sin be not evil, or less evil, than it truly and by its nature is. Therefore it is not a matter of purely arbitrary divine ordinance that sin, being worthy of punishment, should justly be punished. Nor, if we say that sin deserves punishment as condign, does it follow that some rule of truth and necessity exists or is given before God, since it would precede his ordinance or his promulgated law. For just as it is evil by its intrinsic nature for a creature to sin against God, and not merely from or through a divine ordinance, so that it cannot be made by God to be either not evil or good, so too from the fact that sin is said to be in itself punishable and worthy of death, a rule antecedent to the nature of God is not given, however one might view it before legislation. For the truth of that rule is rooted in the nature of God himself, in his natural holiness and justice; so that, however much before the ordinance of the divine will or law, it has a natural and necessary truth in itself that sin is so evil; yet it has this truth only from God, his nature and truth, in which it is originally grounded. Sin cannot but be evil in itself absolutely, sin being against not only the law given but also the natural dependence of the creature on the Creator, and his goodness and nature; nor can sin fail to be punishable and to be punished, or to deserve punishment as condign.

units.la: II. Observandum, in textu significari, hoc ab Ethnicis, solâ natura magistrâ sciri, peccatores dignos morte esse: quare id sciverunt ex naturâ peccati, non ex lege Dei scriptâ, cap. II. 14. 15. cogitationibus sese mutuo accufantibus. Jefa. LVII 25. nulla est pax improbis, inquit Deus meus. III. Atque illud dicitur δικαιώματα Θεῦ jus Dei. Jus ergo & justitia est, & in Scripturis dicitur, quae poenas peccatorum constituit & exigit, non solummodo furor & indignatio. Δικαίωμα Θεῦ, hoc quod jus Dei constituit, vel quod continet, uti δικαίωμα νόμου, Rom. viii. 4. quod lex facit. Quare Dei jus & justitia est, peccatorem poena & morte dignum, atque puniendum esse. iv. Sed de jure isto suo forte remittere Deum posse, quis dicat. Quamvis detur, remittere posse, non sequitur, omittere vel abnegare posse omnino. Imo abnegare illud jus non potest Deus, quia de natura sua est, de superioritate & potestate in creaturam. Atqui in ea uti essentialiter fundatum est jus in creaturam simpliciter, ita & jus puniendi peccatorem. Illud dominii appellatur, judicii istud. Neque aliter potest dici remittens poenam, remittere de suo jure, nisi jus illud puniendi ipsi competat naturaliter. Quare quando punit, pro jure suo agit & justitia, non pro mero & indifferenti arbitrio. Neque enim remissio voluntatis dicitur, aut ejus quod in voluntate positum, sed juris, quod naturae est.
units.tr: II. It should be observed that the text signifies that the Gentiles, taught by nature alone, knew that sinners are worthy of death. Therefore they knew this from the nature of sin, not from the written law of God, Rom. 2.14, 15, their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another. Isa. 57.21: "There is no peace for the wicked, says my God." III. And that is called the righteous decree of God [δικαίωμα Θεοῦ]. It is therefore law and justice, and Scripture speaks of it as that which constitutes and exacts the penalties of sinners, not merely wrath and indignation. The δικαίωμα Θεοῦ is what the law of God constitutes or contains, just as the δικαίωμα νόμου is what the law requires, Rom. 8.4. Therefore it is the right and justice of God that a sinner is worthy of punishment and death and must be punished. IV. But who would say that God can perhaps remit this right of his? Even if it be granted that he can remit, it does not follow that he can omit or wholly deny it. Indeed God cannot deny that right, because it belongs to his nature, to his superiority and power over the creature. And just as the right over the creature absolutely is essentially grounded in that power, so too is the right to punish the sinner. The former is called dominion, the latter judgment. Nor can one speak of God remitting a punishment, that is, relinquishing something of his right, unless that right of punishing belongs to him by nature. Therefore when he punishes, he acts by his right and justice, not by mere and indifferent arbitrariness. For remission is not said of the will, or of what lies in the will, but of a right, which belongs to nature.

units.la: Quod justitia in Deo sit, quae poenas peccatis constituit, & infert, Apostolus etiam significat, 11 Thess. 1.6. Quandoquidem justum est apud Deum rependere afflictionem affligentibus. Quod si conjunctim spectetur cum sequenti altero membro, & afflictis refocillationem nobiscum, etiam ad divinae voluntatis justam constitutionem referendum; si in se consideretur, pro vindicta peccati simpliciter, in natura Dei fundatum est, & naturali ejus justitia, unde δικαιοκρισία Apostolo dicta, Rom. 11.5. adde & cap. iii. 5. 6.
units.tr: That justice is in God, which establishes and inflicts punishments for sins, the Apostle also indicates in 2 Thess. 1.6: Since it is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you. If this is considered together with the following clause, and to give rest to you who are afflicted with us, it must also be referred to the just ordinance of the divine will. But if it is considered in itself, it is simply founded in the nature of God and in his natural justice, for the vengeance on sin, whence the Apostle calls it δικαιοκρισία [δικαιοκρισία], Rom. 2.5. Add also chap. iii. 5, 6.

units.la: II. Est, diciturque ἐκδίκησις in Scripturis, vindicatio. Rom. xii. 19. Non vos ipsos vindicantes ἐκδικοῦντες, scriptum enim, ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις: ego retribuam ἀνταποδώσω, inquit Dominus. Hoc juris divini est, retribuere & vindicare, potestatis divinae, non humanae, proprietas Dei, non voluntatis, sed naturae. Heb. x 30. 31. Jesa. 1.24. וְאִנָּקְמָה [?] & vindicabor ab inimicis meis. Luc. xxi. 22. ἡμέραι ἐκδικήσεως, dies vindictae, vel vindicationis ipsi.
units.tr: II. In Scripture it is called ἐκδίκησις [ἐκδίκησις], vindication. Rom. 12.19: Do not avenge yourselves [ἐκδικοῦντες], for it is written, Vengeance is mine [ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις], I will repay [ἀνταποδώσω], says the Lord. This is a right that belongs to God: to repay and to avenge belongs to divine power, not human power, and is a property of God not of his will but of his nature. Heb. 10.30, 31. Isa. 1.24: I will be avenged on my enemies [וְאִנָּקְמָה]. Luke 21.22: days of vengeance [ἡμέραι ἐκδικήσεως], or of vindication itself.

units.la: III. Atque propter eam causam Deus dicitur zelotes. Exod. xx. 5. אֵל קַנָּא, Deus zelotes, vindicans peccata. Jos. xxiv. 19. Deus sanctissimus est, Deus zelotes ipse, non feret defectionem vestram. iv. Et non absolvens fontem. Exod. xxxiv. 7. וְנִקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה. Juxta Adversarios, contrarium verum, saepissimeque Deus fontem absolvit, nulla poena postulata, nulla accepta satisfactione. Quod aperte est contra Textum, & non illum modo, sed & Num. xiv. 18. Nah. 1.3. v, Praeterea nec posse aliter quin vindicet, testatur Deus, Jerem. v. 29. Numquid illa non visitarem? inquit Deus. nonne anima mea ulciscereturse de tali gente, ac hac est? impossibilitatem significans omittendae vindictae, & per naturam, לֹא תִתְנַקֵּם נַפְשִׁי [?], nonne vindicaret animo mea? Idem est verf. 9. ejusdem capitis. & cap. ix. 9. Haec ex Scripturae, super ista re, testimoniis.
units.tr: III. For this reason God is called zealous. Exod. 20.5: a zealous God [אֵל קַנָּא], avenging sins. Josh. 24.19: He is a holy God, a jealous God himself; he will not bear your transgression. IV. And he does not acquit [לֹא יְנַקֶּה]. Exod. 34.7: and he will by no means acquit [וְנִקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה]. According to our opponents the opposite is true, and God very often acquits, with no punishment demanded and no satisfaction accepted. This is plainly contrary to the text, and not to this text alone but also to Num. 14.18 and Nah. 1.3. V. Moreover, God testifies that he cannot do otherwise than avenge: Jer. 5.29, Shall I not visit them? says the Lord; shall not my soul avenge itself on such a nation as this? There he signifies the impossibility of omitting vengeance, and this from his nature: [לֹא תִתְנַקֵּם נַפְשִׁי], shall not my soul take vengeance? The same occurs in verse 9 of the same chapter, and in chap. 9.9. These are the testimonies of Scripture on this matter.

units.la: Deinde argumentamur ex natura Dei, ejus imprimis sanctitate, & persectione, quæ justitiam illam vindicatricem omnino efflagitant. Quum enim Deus peccatum omne perfectissime execretur, persequi istud debet omni ratione, qua malum est, neque usquam ad id connivere, non habere vel non malum, vel non puniendum, idque propter absolutam suam sanctitatem, quâ odio habet iniquitatem, Psalm. xlv. 8. & omnes operantes iniquitatem. Psalm. v. 6. & cxxxix. 22. Zach. viii. 17. Hab. i. 13. Purior eo oculis, quam ut adspicias malum. Iof. xxiv. 19. Quod si Deus tantummodo malum haberet peccatum, & non puniendum quoque, quod tamen natura peccati secum fert, non pro tanto id malo videretur habere, ac revera est, sed connivere ad istud, & levius æstimare, quam in se, & à nobis censeri debet. Id quod sanctitati Dei minus congruit, & perfectioni. Sociniani, in Catechesi Racoviensi, de Essentia Dei, cap. 1. qu. Quid hoc est, scire quod Deus sit perfectè justus. Resp. Quod hac sit ipsius natura, æquitatem & justitiam observare. Natura ergo Deus est justus. Æquitatem & justitiam non observans tantum, sed & amans. Amans natura, non indifferenti optione, vel placito. Quia non justus modo, sed propter perfectionem, uti in aliis attributis, ita & hic, est ipsa justitia. Denique, quia perfectè justus, omnem justitiæ veræ & rectæ speciem in se complectitur, id est, vindicatricem quoque. Quare enim hæc minus bona in Deo erit, quam in se est, quam in creaturis, ubi est ex sola communicatione τῆς θείας φύσεως? vid. non formaliter, sed effective. Omnis in actionibus Dei, vel operibus, & creaturis æquitas & justitia est ex divinâ. Neque opponi æquitas voluntatis divinæ, effectumque, naturæ ejus; vel illa ab hac separari debet. Crellius, de Deo, cap xxx. pag. 302. impietas sua natura Dei est odio, & eum ad iram adversus eos, qui illam exercent, exstimulat.
units.tr: Next we argue from the nature of God, above all from his holiness and perfection, which absolutely demand that vindicating justice. For since God utterly abhors every sin, he must pursue it for every reason for which it is evil, and never connive at it, nor regard it as either not evil or not to be punished.
