He does so on account of his absolute holiness, by which he hates iniquity, Ps. 45.8, and all who work iniquity, Ps. 5.6; cf. Ps. 139.22, Zech. 8.17, Hab. 1.13. Too pure are your eyes to look on evil, Josh. 24.19. But if God regarded sin only as evil and not as also deserving punishment, which nevertheless the nature of sin brings with it, he would not regard it as such an evil as it really is, but would connive at it and esteem it more lightly than it ought to be esteemed in itself and by us. This agrees less with the holiness and perfection of God. The Socinians, in the Racovian Catechism, on the Essence of God, chap. 1, question: What does it mean to know that God is perfectly just? Answer: That it is his nature to observe equity and justice. Therefore God is just by nature, and he not only observes equity and justice but loves them: he loves them by nature, not by an indifferent choice or pleasure. For since he is not just merely, but on account of his perfection is justice itself, as in his other attributes, so in this one too, he embraces in himself every true and right form of justice, that is, vindicating justice as well. Why, then, would it be less good in God than it is in itself and in creatures, where it comes only from the communication of the divine nature? I mean not formally but effectively. All equity and justice in God's actions, works and creatures comes from the divine justice. Nor may the equity of the divine will be opposed to its effect, that is, to his nature, nor separated from it. Crellius, On God, chap. 30, p. 302: Impiety is by its nature hateful to God and stirs him to anger against those who practise it.

units.la: III. Ex naturâ virtutis hujus, pro eâ Deo attribuendâ, sic argumentamur. Quod in se simpliciter perfectionis est, non imperfectionis; imo cujus contrarium, vid. injustitia (sive negativum, id est, non justitia; aut contrarium, injustitia, quamvis sæpè coincidant, & non justum tunc sit injustum) imperfectionis est, illud Deo, ordine causalitatis, atque eminentiæ, formaliter attribui debet: sed tale est justitia vindicatrix, in Domino, & judice: ergo Genef. xviii. 25. Iudex totius terra non exerceret jus? item cap. xx. 4. Psalm. xciv. 9. 10. Qui plantavit aurem, non audiret? quique formavit oculum, non videret? qui reprehendit gentes, non castigaret? Supremæ apud homines potestatis adjunctum, non indifferens, sed necessarium est justitia illa: ita ut nec concipi absque ea, nec dari judex aut magistratus queat. Hoc autem divinitatis quoddam quasi χαρακτηρισμα [?], & tale est, ut necessario arguat in naturâ supremi Dei justitiam quoque illam summa suâ perfectione agnoscendam; non verò naturam istâ vacuam. Deinde, nec potes Deum concipere sub contario illius justitiæ: ergo est ei omnino naturalis & necessaria. Rom. iii. 5. numquid injustus Deus? Denique, necessario odit Deus omnem in nobis injustitiam, præsertim vindicatricem si injusta sit, & amat justitiam: non pro libertate vel indifferentia voluntatis, ut possit velle contrarium, sive odisse justitiam, & diligere injustitiam; sed pro natura : ergo non à voluntate solâ, tanquam liberum effectum est Dei justitia, ex quâ is ejus erga virtutem illam amor, sed naturæ.
units.tr: III. From the nature of this virtue we argue as follows, that it must be ascribed to God. What is in itself simply perfection, not imperfection, and whose contrary, injustice (or the negative, that is, non-justice; or the contrary, injustice, although these often coincide, and what is not just is then unjust), is imperfection, must be attributed to God formally, in the order of causality and of eminence. But such is vindicating justice in the Lord and Judge. Therefore: Gen. 18.25, Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? Likewise chap. 20.4; Ps. 94.9, 10: He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? He who formed the eye, shall he not see? He who chastises the nations, shall he not punish? This justice is attached to supreme power among men; it is not indifferent but necessary, so that a judge or magistrate can neither be conceived without it nor exist. This is a kind of quasi-character of divinity, and it is such that it necessarily implies that justice of that kind, to be acknowledged in God's nature in its supreme perfection, and not a nature empty of it. Further, you cannot conceive God under the contrary of that justice; therefore it belongs to him altogether naturally and necessarily. Rom. 3.5: Is God unjust? Finally, God necessarily hates every injustice in us, especially vindicating injustice if it is unjust, and loves justice. He does this not from liberty or indifference of will, so that he could will the opposite, hate justice and love injustice, but from his nature. Therefore the justice of God is not an effect freely produced by the will alone, from which comes his love of that virtue, but is from his nature.

units.la: iv. Denique, nisi justitia vindicatrix Deo sit naturalis, ejusque exercendæ necessitas, ex proprietate Dei fluat essentiali, non apparet, quorsum Deus istam viam inire redemtionis nostræ voluerit, ut cum æque posset, nulla à peccatoribus exactâ pœnâ, vel à vade, omnia etiam illis absolute remittere, Chri-stum tamen adeo diris, pro nobis & nostri loco, cruciatibus subjicere voluerit. Ex adverso si consideremus, justitiam illam Deo naturalem, eique satisfieri debere primum, & judici supremo, ne justitiam minus offendat, quam bonitatem, sed divinam simul utriusque attemperationem, res plana est & evidens, cur tanta pati Christum oportuerit. Luc. xxiv. 26. non tantum ex divino decreto & prædictione variâ; sed natura quoque ipsius justitiæ. Eoque magis sic argumentamur, quod & Socinus inde alias adversum nos, sed perperam, argumentatur, de Servatore, part. iii. cap. iv. pag. 267. respondeo si id verum esset, non opus futurum fuisset, ut Christus tot acerbos cruciatus, & tam diram mortem sustineret: & Deum injustitia aut immanitatis tacite insimulari, qui cum levissima aliqua pœna, dicimus nos nunc, ulla pœna, à Christo sumtâ, sua justitia plene satisfacere posset, ipsum tam atrociter excarnificari voluerit. Adde, quæ idem dicit, part. iv. cap. xi. pag 386[?]. plures una ad beatam immortalitatem vias esse nulla ratio patitur, nec si essent, aut difficiliorem Christum elegisse, qui summam erga nos charitatem pra se tulit, aut faciliorem ignorasse, qui exactissimam divinarum rerum scientiam professus est, nullo pacto credi potest
units.tr: IV. Finally, unless vindicating justice is natural to God, and the necessity of exercising it flows from his essential property, it does not appear why God would wish to take this way of our redemption: when he could equally well, without any penalty exacted from sinners or any surety, remit all things to them absolutely, he nevertheless wished to subject Christ to such dreadful sufferings for us and in our place. On the other hand, if we consider that this justice is natural to God, and that satisfaction must be made to it first, and to the supreme Judge, so that he is not offended in justice less than in goodness, and that the divine reconciliation of both is simultaneously effected, the matter is plain and evident why Christ ought to suffer so much. Luke 24.26: not only from the divine decree and varied prediction, but also from the nature of justice itself. We argue this all the more so because Socinus also argues from it against us in other places, though wrongly, in his book on the Saviour, part iii, chap. iv, p. 267: I answer: if that were true, there would have been no need for Christ to endure so many bitter torments and so dreadful a death; and God would be tacitly accused of injustice or savagery, if he, when Christ had borne even the slightest punishment, (we now say, any punishment), could fully satisfy his justice, yet wished him to be so atrociously tortured. Add what he says in part iv, chap. xi, p. 386: No reason allows that there are several ways to blessed immortality; nor, if there were, can it be believed in any way that Christ chose the harder one, who showed the greatest love towards us, or ignored the easier one, who professed the most exact knowledge of divine things.

units.la: Atque ista quidem argumenta faciunt pro sententia nostra: quæ ex altera parte objiciuntur, aut objici possunt, ne sicco pede transiisse culpemur, discutienda nunc eadem opera sunt. Sic ergo primum argumentantur: Si justitia illa vindicatrix Deo naturalis, nulla posset Deus remittere peccata. Catechesis Racoviensis, cap. viii. de Morte Christi: nam quod attinet ad misericordiam, eam Deo non ita natura inesse, ut isti sentiunt, hinc patet, quod, si natura Deo inesset, non posset Deus nullum peccatum prorsus punire: atque vicissim, si ea justitia natura Deo inesset, ut illi opinantur, nullum peccatum Deus remitteret, sed semper illud puniret. Adversus enim ea, quæ Deo insunt natura, nunquam potest quidquam facere Deus. Exempli causa, cum sapientia inest Deo natura, nunquam contra eam quidquam Deus facit, verùm quæcunque Deus facit, facit sapienter. Verùm cum Deum constet remittere peccata, & punire quando velit, apparet, Deo ejusmodi misericordiam & justitiam, qualem illi opinantur, non inesse natura, sed esse effectus ipsius voluntatis. Resp. i. Negatur consequentia, si misericordia Deo natutalis est, quod ergo nullum peccatum potest punire; si justitia, nullum remittere. Nam & misericordia ipsi est naturalis; sed non in præjudicium, vel cum læsione justitiæ: & justitia ita pœnam exigit, ut relinquat locum divinæ sapientiæ, indagandi viam, quâ misericordiæ & justitiæ simul satisfiat, & utraque in eopem peccatore, admirando & excelso modo, ostendatur. ii. Misericordia Deo naturalis est, sed non ex eâ punire concipitur; itidem justitia, sed non ex hac, illi oppositâ, remittit: verùm remittit ex misericordiâ, & ex justitiâ punit. Quantum ad egressum & executionem istorum attributorum, à Dei voluntate omninò pendet: & quamvis ipsa sint naturalia, effectus tamen & operationes eorum pendent à divino arbitrio, quando, ubi, & quousque velit parcere, aut punire. iii. Adversus attributa sua naturalia, vel naturam, verum est, quod Deus nihil quidquam agat: nec quando miseretur, contra justitiam; aut quando punit, contra miseri cordiam: sed fi injuste Deus aut immisericorditer ageret non misericorditer puniens, aut injuste parcens, hoc sibi foret adversum. Sed jam, ubi pro diversis objectis, in miserum, qua talem, misericordia; in peccatorem, justitia fertur, quae hic quaeso est repugnantia, vel etiam, ubi eundem miserum peccatorem justitia & misericordia sua simul prosequitur? quod facit erga nos in Christo.
units.tr: Those arguments favour our position. But since the opposing objections are, or can be, raised against us, lest we be blamed for passing over them dry-shod, they must now be examined in the same place. They argue as follows: If that avenging justice were natural to God, God could remit no sins. The Racovian Catechism, ch. viii, on the death of Christ: As for mercy, it is not inherent in God by nature, as they think. This is clear because, if mercy were natural to God, God could not punish any sin at all. Conversely, if justice were natural to God in the way they suppose, God would remit no sin but would always punish it. For God can never do anything contrary to what is natural to him. For example, since wisdom is natural to God, he never does anything contrary to it, but whatever he does, he does wisely. But since it is agreed that God forgives sins and punishes when he wills, it is evident that such mercy and justice as they suppose are not natural to God but are effects of his will. Answer. (i) The inference is denied. If mercy is natural to God, it does not follow that he can punish no sin; and if justice is natural to him, it does not follow that he can remit none. For mercy is natural to him, but not to the prejudice or injury of justice; and justice exacts punishment in such a way that it leaves room for divine wisdom to seek out a way by which justice and mercy may both be satisfied, and both may be shown in one and the same sinner in a wonderful and sublime manner. (ii) Mercy is natural to God, but it is not from mercy that he is conceived to punish; likewise justice is natural to him, but it is not from justice, opposed to mercy, that he remits. Rather he remits from mercy and punishes from justice. As to the exercise and execution of these attributes, they depend entirely on the will of God; and although they are natural, their effects and operations depend on the divine decision as to when, where and how far he wills to spare or to punish. (iii) It is true that God does nothing against his natural attributes or nature: he does not act against justice when he shows mercy, nor against mercy when he punishes. But if God acted unjustly, punishing without mercy or sparing unjustly, that would be contrary to himself. But where, in relation to different objects, mercy is directed to the wretched as such, and justice to the sinner, what contradiction, I ask, is there here? Or where does the same wretched sinner receive both justice and mercy at once from him? This he does toward us in Christ.

units.la: Quemadmodum contra sapientiam nihil agere Deus potest, vel insipienter, ita nec contra justitiam, & bonitatem: sed in aliis haec, in aliis illa, & sic, vel aliter manifestat. iv. Quod autem justitiam vindicatricem misericordiae dicimus esse oppositam (quod nec Socino negatur), non intelligitur de attributis, quatenus in Deo sunt, vel quod iis aliquid contrarium sit in creaturis, sed quod diversas & contrarias habeant operationes, in effectis. Ut, contraria sunt punire, & parcere, salvare & damnare, sed contraria inter se, & creaturae; non contraria in Deo justitia & misericordia, vel earum effectus Deo aut alterutri attributo vere & proprie sunt contrarii. Neque contra misericordiam punit Deus; vel contra justitiam est, quando parcit, sed pro misericordia hoc, pro justitia illud, utrumque pro Deo, nil contra eum. Sunt quippe omnes unius perfectissimae simplicissimaeque essentiae operationes; & non tanquam diversa & contraria accidentia concipienda in subjecto uno, Deo. v. Non sequitur, Deus remittit peccata, & punit quando vult, ergo justitia, & misericordia, ex qua, quando vult, remittit & punit, non sunt Deo naturalia effectus voluntatis sunt, remissio & punitio, sed quae voluntas in naturali proprietate justitiae & misericordiae fundatur.
units.tr: Just as God can do nothing against wisdom, either unwisely, so neither can he act against justice and goodness; but he manifests these in some things and those in others, and so on, in one way or another. (iv) When we say that avenging justice is opposed to mercy (which Socinus himself does not deny), this is not to be understood of the attributes as they are in God, or as if anything in them were contrary in creatures, but of their different and contrary operations in their effects. Thus punishing and sparing, saving and condemning, are contraries, but contraries among themselves and in creatures; justice and mercy are not contraries in God, nor are their effects truly and properly contrary to God or to either attribute. God does not punish against mercy, nor is he against justice when he spares; rather this is for mercy and that for justice, and both are for God, nothing against him. Indeed they are all operations of one most perfect and most simple essence, and are not to be conceived as diverse and contrary accidents in one subject, God. (v) It does not follow that because God remits sins and punishes when he wills, therefore justice and mercy, from which he remits and punishes when he wills, are not natural to God; remission and punishment are effects of the will, but the will is grounded in the natural property of justice and mercy.

units.la: Obj. ii. Potest quilibet, ergo etiam Deus, remittere de suo jure, & peccata non punire, in se admissa. Socinus, Praelect. cap. xvi. Deum igitur, contra quam nonnulli sentiant, jure potuisse nobis peccata nostra condonare, nulla à quoquam pro ipsis satisfactione accepta, id manifeste probare videtur, quod peccata nostra nihil aliud sunt, quam offensa majestatis divinae, & debita quaedam, quae cum Deo contrahimus. Sic enim in Sacris literis appellari solent. Atqui nemo est, qui injurias sibi illatas, debitaque secum contracta, summo jure condonare & remittere non queat, nulla vera pro ipsis satisfactione accepta. Igitur, nisi velimus Deo minus concedere, quam hominibus ipsis concedatur, confitendum omnino est, Deum jure potuisse nobis peccata nostra ignoscere, nulla pro ipsis vera satisfactione accepta, &c. Neque enim in Deo ulla justitia est, quae peccata punire omnino jubeat, cui ipse renuntiare non possit. Lib. de Servat. part. i. cap. i. pag. 10. Potest enim Deus, praesertim cum ipse omnium sit Dominus, de suo jure, quantum velit, dimittere. lib. iii. cap. i. Atque idem argumentum, ex potestate Dei, urgent passim alii. Crellius, de Deo, cap xxiii. pag. 182. &c. Resp. i. Peccata nostra debita sunt, non vulgaria; sed & crimina. Haec vero dimittere impunita, non aeque est in potestate ejus, contra quem commiscommissum crimen, ac debita alia. Summum crimen, perpetratum contra supremam potestatem, crimen læsæ majestatis, aliaque gravissima, absque pœna dimitti, salva justitia, non possunt. Injustus foret judex aut Magistra-tus, qui impunita prorsus, & nulla satisfactione accepta, omnia remitteret.
units.tr: Objection. (ii) Anyone can, and so also God, remit something of his right and not punish sins committed. Socinus, Praelections, ch. xvi: Therefore God, contrary to what some think, could justly forgive us our sins without any satisfaction being received from anyone for them. This seems clearly proved by the fact that our sins are nothing other than offences against the divine majesty and certain debts that we contract with God; for so they are customarily called in the Sacred Letters. But there is no one who cannot, by the highest right, condone and remit injuries done to him and debts contracted with him, without any true satisfaction being received for them. Therefore, unless we wish to grant God less than is granted to men themselves, it must be wholly confessed that God could justly forgive us our sins without any true satisfaction received for them, etc. For there is no justice in God that absolutely requires sins to be punished, from which he himself could not withdraw. Book on the Saviour, part i, ch. i, p. 10: For God, especially since he is Lord of all, can remit of his right as much as he wishes. Book iii, ch. i. The same argument, from the power of God, is pressed everywhere by others too: Crellius, On God, ch. xxiii, p. 182, etc. Answer. (i) Our sins are debts, not ordinary ones, but also crimes. But to remit these unpunished is not equally within the power of him against whom the crime was committed, as with other debts. A supreme crime, committed against supreme authority, the crime of high treason, and other most grievous offences, cannot be dismissed without punishment and with justice preserved. A judge or magistrate who remitted everything wholly unpunished and without any satisfaction received would be unjust.

units.la: Igitur antecedens verum non est, quod quilibet injurias sibi illatas, debita, & crimina impunita demittere æque possit. Inter homines, alii non possunt omnia, non exactâ prius pœnâ, remittere; alii non aliter debent, quam nulla postulata ultione condonare: quia hi pro sola agere charitate mutua tenentur, ἐκδίκησιν[?] autem Deo tradere: illi, Dei nomine & loco constituti, pro justitia etiam pœnas exigere: Dei enim minister est magistratus, ἔκδικος[?] εἰς ὀργὴν[?] τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι[?]. Rom. xiii. 4. Cujus rei necessitas non est solum ratione finis, in bono, & conservatione pacis publicæ; sed in ipsa justitiâ, quam Dei nomine & jussu, in istum finem, præstare tenentur, & administrare, vi & natura muneris ac dignitatis suæ. ii. Aliud est, remittere pœnam; aliud, jus puniendi: non statim qui pœnam, ideo jus remittit suum. iii. Aliud est, pœnam aliquam omittere, vel omnem. iv. Iterum aliud est jus acquisitum, aliud naturale: illud, utpote accidentarium, quamvis omittere queas, non tamen ideo istud. v. Denique aliud est, remittere de jure; vel totum mittere, negligere, & abnegare, saltem facto. Deus, utcunque pœnam, non tamen remittit jus suum.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent is not true, that anyone can equally remit injuries done to him, debts, and crimes without punishment. Among men, some cannot remit everything without first exacting a due penalty; others ought to pardon only without demanding any vengeance, because the latter are bound to act from mutual charity alone and to leave vengeance (ekdikēsin [ἐκδίκησιν]) to God; whereas the former, appointed in the name and place of God, also exact penalties for the sake of justice: for the magistrate is God's minister, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil (ekdikos eis orgēn tō to kakon prassonti [ἔκδικος εἰς ὀργὴν τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι]). Rom. xiii. 4. The necessity of this lies not only in the reason of the end, which is the good and the preservation of public peace, but in justice itself, which they are bound to perform and administer in God's name and by his command, for that end, by the force and nature of their office and dignity. (ii) It is one thing to remit a penalty; another to remit the right of punishing. He who remits a penalty does not for that reason remit his right. (iii) It is one thing to omit some penalty, another to omit every penalty. (iv) Again, it is one thing a right acquired, another a natural right: the former, being accidental, you may give up, but not for that reason the latter. (v) Finally, it is one thing to remit something of one's right; another to give up the whole, to neglect and renounce it, at least in practice. God, however much he may remit a penalty, does not remit his right.

units.la: Et pœnam forte aliquam ejusque gradum posset pro beneplacito, & absolutâ potestate omittere: super quo nolo contendere: non ideo tamen omnem. Jus ejus non est accidentarium, vel acquisitum; sed naturale, & necessarium. Et qui de jure utcunque forte posset remittere, negatur tamen, quod omne prorsus abnegare possit, ut nullam omnino justitiam exerceat. Quod etiam Vor-stius dubitavit afferre, an omnia, saltem quod ad plurima peccata, sine irrogatione pœnæ, condonare Deus posset. De jure remisit Deus, certe, & dispensavit, quod peccata nostra, in Vade alio, non in nobis, quod utique jure potuisset, vindicare placuit.
units.tr: Perhaps he could, at his good pleasure and by absolute power, omit some penalty and its degree; but I do not wish to contend about that. Yet he cannot omit every penalty, and so that they may say that he exercises no justice at all. It is not that such a right is accidental or acquired; it is natural and necessary. And although he might perhaps in some way remit a right, it is denied that he could renounce it altogether, so as to exercise no justice whatever. Vorstius too hesitated to affirm whether God could condone all sins, or at least most of them, without the infliction of punishment. God certainly remitted by right, and dispensed, that our sins should be laid on another, not on us, which he could doubtless have avenged by right.

units.la: Neque admitto consequentiam, si Deus, absque læsione justitiæ naturalis, posset forte condonare unum & alterum peccatum impuni-tum, vel gradus pœnarum aliquot, aut remittere quippiam; ergo omnia.
units.tr: I do not accept the inference: if God, without injury to natural justice, could perhaps pardon one or two unpunished sins, or remit some degrees of punishment or something else, it does not follow that he could pardon all.

units.la: Quia aliud est, non ubique jus suum persequi, & de eo remittere posse aliqua: aliud, totum prorsus videri abnegare, & nullum exercere velle: quod cum natu-rali natura & naturali proprietate conciliari nequit. Apud homines, remittere judex de gradu aliquo pœnæ potest; neque ideo ipsam omnem. Licet parenti, licet alteri alapam infligere homini, & pœnam aliquam, non omnem ideo & quantamcumque. Haud valet ergo argumentum à gradu in gradum, vel à gradu ad universum. vi Imo quum dicitur, Deum in remissione peccatorum, extra pœnam, de jure suo remittere, jam agnoscitur jus ejus naturale, ad puniendum peccata. Quorsum alioquidicetur remittere, & de jure? Jus ergo Deo est puniendi: atque istud naturale. Non autem extrinsecus adveniens, vel aliunde quæsitum. Eò hic assurgere debent Adversarii, ut in potestate Dei naturali fundatum dicant jus puniendi: id est, in ejus naturâ. Quod profecto negari nequit. Neque illud jus Deus à se abnegare, vel à natura suâ removere potis est. Est divinæ potestatis, punire peccatores, sed pro, & ex justitiâ: neque enim solum posse, sed juste posse & facere, seu plectere, attendi hic debet Aliter ac in prædestinatione, ubi sola prædestinantis spectatur voluntas, sic pro potestate destinantis: sed voluntas puniendi in Deo, pro potestate, consideratur ut innixa justitiæ suæ naturali. Quare Deus vult punire ?quia justus est. Prædestinavit me ad salutem, quod potuit, quia voluit; neque alia ejus causa est, non naturale aliquod attributum, sive misericordiæ, sive justitiæ, ad mei prædestinationem magis, quam aliorum. Sed, si me punire velit, sola simpliciter consideratâ punitione, aut puniendi voluntate, non in prædestinatione suprema, nec comparatâ ad aliorum electionem, & reprobationem; tum causa illius est ipsa naturæ suæ justitia: si mei miserei, misericordia: cujus utriusque varia dispensatio & destinatio est à voluntate ejus, qui miseretur, quorum vult, & indurat quem vult. Destinatio est à solâ Dei voluntate, sed ex destinatione, aut voluntate istâ est vel misericordiæ, vel justitiæ ostensio. Factâ prædestinatione, pro Dei potestate ex liberrimâ voluntate, sequitur misericordiæ, per eam, demonstratio: & ab altera parte, experimentum justitiæ. Atque justitiam Deus exercet ex justitiâ. Et in hoc discrimen est à natura Dei, prædestinationem inter, & punitionem: quodq; hæc non merae Dei voluntatis, & potestatis solius sit, uti illa; sed intervenientis præterea naturalis proprietatis, justitiæ Saltem etiam juxta Adversarios, jus punitivum Dei, ipsi est naturale, non effectus demum voluntatis. Quod jus, in potestate Dei radicatum, nos inniti dicimus justitiæ naturali, proque ea se habere in exercitio & executione sui vii. Non ideo minus concedimus Deo, quam hominibus, quod negamus, Deum ita de jure suo remittere posse, ut totum obliteret vel exuat quasi, & prorsus non exerat, in punitione justa, ubi objectum ἀξιον[?] providentia divina positum; sed plus eo in Deo agnoscimus, qui se justum esse negare nequit. Uti enim, vel apud nos pater, nato sibi filio, abnegare nequit paternum in filium imperium, narurale istud, quod ei naturâ competit; sic Deus abnegare non potest dominium, quod habet in creaturam à se factam, utcunque omnium dominus, imo ideo quod Dominus, istud suum jus remittere non potest, neque jus, pro justitiâ puniendi. Quæ certè non impotentiam in Deo dicunt, sed perfectionem. Et quo plus in Deo perfectionis, ita minus abnegare illa potest. viii. Certè non potest renuntiare justitiæ in se isti, quæ peccata puniri jubet. Ipsius admirabilis illa proprietas, qua nunquam recedere potest, qua justitia appellatur, & in æquitate ac rectitudine etiam, qua omne in se decorum complectitur, consistit, verba sunt Socini, in Discursu brevi de ratione salutis nostræ, in principio. Quod quare non dicamus pariter de justitiâ Dei vindicatrice? quod sit nempe proprietas, à qua recedere Deus non potest? neque enim minus in æquitate & rectitudine consistit, quam ulla alia justitiæ species. Deinde & omne in se decorum complectitur. Imo in æquitate & rectitudine consistere, neque Adversarii diffitebuntur. Punire, apud Deum, non solius juris est, de quo considerari solet, quid quis remittere possit; sed & justitiæ, admirabilis illius proprietatis, à quâ recedere nunquam Deus potest; non de quo, quan-tum velit, dimittere.
units.tr: For it is one thing not to pursue one's right everywhere and to be able to remit some part of it, and another thing to appear to renounce it altogether and to be unwilling to exercise it at all. The second cannot be reconciled with nature's own nature and with the property natural to him. Among men a judge may remit some degree of punishment, yet not all of it. A parent, or anyone else, may be allowed to strike a man with a slap, and to inflict some punishment, but not for that reason every punishment of any size. So the argument from one degree to another, or from one degree to the whole, is not valid. Indeed, when it is said that God in forgiving sins, apart from punishment, remits something of his right, his natural right to punish sins is already acknowledged. Why else would it be said that he remits, and that it is a matter of right? So God has the right to punish, and this right is natural: it does not come to him from outside or is sought from elsewhere. Here our opponents must rise to the point of saying that the right to punish is founded in God's power as a natural thing, that is, in his nature. This can certainly not be denied. Nor can God renounce that right or remove it from his nature. It belongs to divine power to punish sinners, but for justice and from justice. For here we must consider not only that he can, but that he can and does justly punish. This is unlike predestination, where only the will of the one predestining is regarded, and so it is by the power of the one who destines. The will to punish in God, however, is considered in relation to his power as resting on his natural justice. So God wills to punish because he is just. He predestined me to salvation because he was willing to, and he could do so; there is no other cause for it, and no natural attribute, whether of mercy or of justice, makes him predestine me rather than others. But if he wills to punish me, then, considering punishment or the will to punish simply, and not in the supreme predestination nor in comparison with the election and reprobation of others, its cause is the very justice of his nature. If he shows mercy to me, its cause is mercy. The varied dispensation and destination of each of these is from the will of him who shows mercy to whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills. The destination is from the will of God alone, but from this destination or will there comes a display either of mercy or of justice. Once predestination is made, by God's power and from his most free will, a demonstration of mercy follows through it, and on the other side an experience of justice. And God exercises justice from justice. In this lies the difference in God's nature between predestination and punishment: punishment is not, as predestination is, of God's will and power alone, but there intervenes also his natural property, justice. Even according to our opponents, God's punitive right is natural to him and is not merely the effect of his will. This right, rooted in God's power, we say rests on his natural justice and so stands in the exercise and execution of it. (vii) Nor do we grant less to God than to men when we deny that God can so remit his right as to blot it out or, as it were, strip it off entirely, and not exercise it at all in just punishment, where the object is set by divine providence. Rather, we recognise in God more than that, namely that he cannot deny that he is just. For as a father among us cannot renounce, towards a son born to him, the paternal authority over his son, which belongs to him by nature, so God cannot renounce the dominion which he has over the creature he has made, however much he is the Lord of all; indeed, because he is Lord he cannot remit that right, nor the right to punish in accordance with justice. These things do not speak of impotence in God but of perfection. And the more perfection there is in God, the less he can renounce it. (viii) Certainly he cannot renounce that justice in himself which orders sins to be punished. "That admirable property of his, from which he can never depart, which is called justice, and consists in equity and rectitude, also embracing in itself all that is fitting": these are the words of Socinus, in the short discourse on the reason of our salvation, at the beginning. Why should we not say the same of God's avenging justice? Is it not a property from which God cannot depart? For it consists no less in equity and rectitude than any other species of justice. Moreover, it embraces in itself all that is fitting. Indeed, our opponents will not deny that to consist in equity and rectitude. To punish, with God, is not a matter only of right, about which it is usually considered what someone may remit, but also of that admirable justice from which God can never depart, and which he cannot lay aside at will.

units.la: Alia etiam, quæ objici hic possint, præterire nolumus, ut hoc articulo de necessitate punitionis & satisfactionis rite posito confirmatoque, eo certius & felicius in propugnandâ porro veritate versemur. Sic arguitur. 1. Si Deus ,, non possit peccata sine satisfactione remittere, tum vel quia non potest per ,, potentiam, vel quia non potest per justitiam. At neutrum horum dici potest. ,, Si non per potentiam suam absolutam, tum peccatum condonari, sive non ,, puniri est simpliciter impossibile; ergo peccatum non puniri, constat ex ter-,, minis contradicentibus: oportet ergo ut ostendatur contradictio, cum nulla ,, appareat ex terminis formalibus, & contrà manifestum sit hominem non ,, modo posse, sed & debere inimicis suis in ipsum peccantibus ignoscere. Sed ,, neque congrue dici potest, Deum hoc facere non posse per justitiam, posito ,, quod hoc possit facere per potentiam. Resp. 1. Causa, ob quam Deus pec-cata absque satisfactione non remittit, est quia nec per potentiam potest, neq; per justitiam. Non quasi possit quandoque aliquid per potentiam, quod non potest per justitiam, minime: sed quia quod non potest per justitiam, etiam non possit per potentiam Hoc autem, de quo nunc quærimus, justitiæ ejus repugnat, istique primo & per se contrariatur, non potentiæ: neque ad hanc, sed ad illam refertur præsens quæstio: ideoque haud adeo mirum, si quis præterito primo in dilemmate capite, ad secundum excipiat, & quid debeat fieri attendens magis, quam quid absolute possit, necessitatem satisfactionis tueri satis habeat, ex illâ Dei justitiâ. 11. Atque ita termini contradicentes sunt, non in ordine ad potentiam, sed justitiam, non in hoc, si quis dicat, peccatum condonari, sive non puniri, vel ut plenius loquamur, posse remitti peccata absque satis-factione; sed si quis dicat, posse juste, vel per justitiam Dei remitti peccata citra omnem prorsus punitionem, vel satisfactionem. 111. Quod si ex hominis exemplo ratio adducta sufficiat, Deus non solum poterit, sed debebit etiam remittere peccata: vel saltem potius id volet, quam punire: quum in plurimis tamen creaturis, sive Angelis, sive hominibus, puniat, quam parcat & salvet. Imo nec inter homines, omnes, & præcipui possunt, nedum ut debeant, impunita dimittere crimina, non Judices, aut Magistratus. Sed justi-tiæ primum satisfieri cupiunt, quocunque modo, non autem quovis par-cere. 1v. Bene quidem, non potest dici, Deum facere non posse per justitiam, quod facere possit per potentiam: sed eo non probatur id quod in quæstione est, nimirum Deum posse remittere, per justitiam, peccata, citra omnem omnino punitionem aut satisfactionem. Neque quod ex Scoto adfertur, huc facit: nam ad nullum quidem objectum secundarium ita determinate inclinatur vo-luntas divina, ut sibi repugnet justè inclinari ad oppositum illius: nimirum, quantum ad voluntatem, & id, quod in ipsâ formaliter voluntate situm, vel mere ab ea dependet, vel pro ratione actionis externæ, ut sic: verum talia sunt quædam, in quibus sine contradictione Deus non possit oppositum velle, nedum justè velle: v. g. non potest Deus aliter velle quin sit justus; quin sit talis ac est, quin fit dominus creaturæ suæ ; quin fiat quod dixit, & impleatur quod promisit; quin peccatum malum sit, & pœnâ dignum: ad hæc ergo objecta sic prout vult, volenda, quid ni sic loquar? ita à natura, & naturæ suæ proprietatibus vel attributis veritatis, primitatis, sanctitatis, & justitiæ determinatur, ut per ea, non demum per voluntatem, oppositum illorum velle non possit.
units.tr: We do not wish to pass over the other objections that might be raised here, so that, with the necessity of punishment and satisfaction having been properly established and confirmed in this article, we may proceed more securely and more happily in defending the truth. It is argued thus: (1) If God could not remit sins without satisfaction, then either it is because he cannot by power, or because he cannot by justice. But neither of these can be said. If not by his absolute power, then to pardon sin, or not to punish it, is simply impossible; so that not to punish sin is a contradiction in terms. It is necessary, therefore, that a contradiction be shown, since none appears in the formal terms, and it is plain on the contrary that a man can not only, but ought to forgive his enemies who sin against him. Nor can it fittingly be said that God cannot do this by justice, when he can do it by power. Answer: (1) The reason why God does not remit sins without satisfaction is that he can do so neither by power nor by justice. Not as if he could sometimes do by power what he cannot do by justice; by no means. Rather, what he cannot do by justice he also cannot do by power. But that which we now ask about is repugnant to his justice, and is contrary to it first and of itself, not to his power; and the present question refers not to the power but to the justice of God. So it is not very surprising if someone, passing over the first horn of the dilemma, takes up the second, and, attending to what ought to be done rather than to what could absolutely be done, is content to defend the necessity of satisfaction from God's justice. (2) So the contradictory terms are not in relation to power but to justice. The contradiction does not lie in saying that sin is pardoned, or not punished, or, to speak more fully, that sins can be remitted without satisfaction; it lies in saying that sins can justly, or by the justice of God, be remitted without any punishment or satisfaction at all. (3) But if the reasoning drawn from the example of a man is sufficient, then God will not only be able but will even be bound to remit sins, or at least will rather be willing to do so than to punish. Yet in most creatures, whether angels or men, he punishes rather than spares and saves. Indeed, not all men, not even the most eminent, can, let alone ought, to let crimes go unpunished, nor can judges or magistrates. Rather they desire justice to be satisfied in some way, and not to spare anyone at all. (4) It is indeed true that one cannot say God cannot do by justice what he can do by power; but this does not prove what is in question, namely that God can remit sins by justice without any punishment or satisfaction at all. Nor does what is brought from Scotus bear on this: for the divine will is not so determinately inclined to any secondary object that it would be a contradiction for it to be justly inclined to the opposite. That is to say, as regards the will, and what lies formally in the will itself, or depends merely on it, or relates to the external action as such. But there are some things about which God cannot will the opposite without contradiction, let alone will it justly. For example, God cannot will otherwise than that he is just; that he is such as he is; that he is the Lord of his creature; that what he has said is done and what he has promised is fulfilled; that sin is evil and deserving of punishment. With regard to these objects, which are to be willed as he wills them, why should I not speak thus? They are so determined by his nature, and by the properties or attributes of his nature, of truth, primacy, holiness and justice, that through these, and not merely through the will, he cannot will their opposite.

units.la: ,, II. Arg. Si Deus non potest peccatum impunitum dimittere; tum necesse ,, est ut puniat necessitate absoluta. Quod dici cum ratione non potest. Quan-,, doquidem non semper punit, neque, quantum potest, punit. Resp. 1. Negatur sequi, quod Deus necessitate absoluta puniat, quamvis peccatum impunitum dimitti, natura ejus non ferat. Quia necessitas hæc non est ἀλόγῳ[?], sed naturæ rationalis, atque, quod ad egressum, voluntatis liberrimæ. II. Unde nec semper Deus punit, nec quantum potest: nam spiritus à conspectu meo obrueretur, & anima quas feci. Jesa. LVII. 20. Naturaliter & necessariò Deo in est quidem illa justitia, sed pro eâ non operatur mere naturaliter, & non ex voluntate, vel consilio voluntatis, quo omnia agit. Eph. 1. 11. à quo stat, & quando, & quantum, nunc vel tum, puniat. Simile ab igni eatenus huc non quadrat, quod semper, & quantum potest, urit, quod est agens irrationale, & cæco impetu agens: Deus vero pro ratione se gerit & operatur, etiam quando punitione ostendit se esse ignem consumentem, atque peccatorem justitiæ punienti tanquam paleam adhibet. Deut. iv. 24. & ix. 3. Punit ergo Deus, quando, & quantum, non potest, sed vult, ut tamen punitio justitiâ nitatur, justitia natura & intrinsecâ ejus proprietate.
units.tr: II. Argument. If God cannot dismiss a sin unpunished, then it is necessary that he punish with absolute necessity. This cannot be said with reason, since he does not always punish, nor does he punish as much as he can. Reply 1: It is denied that it follows that God punishes by absolute necessity, even though his nature does not allow sin to go unpunished. For this necessity is not irrational [ἀλόγῳ], but belongs to a rational nature and, as to its outcome, to the most free will. II. Hence God neither always punishes nor punishes as much as he can: for the spirit would be overwhelmed before my face, and the souls which I have made (Isa. 57:20). Justice is indeed in God naturally and necessarily, but he does not act for it merely by nature, and not from will or the counsel of his will, by which he does all things (Eph. 1:11). From that counsel it is settled when, how much, and whether now or then he punishes. The comparison with fire does not fit here in this respect: fire always burns as much as it can, since it is an irrational agent acting with blind impulse. God, however, conducts himself and works according to reason, even when by punishment he shows himself to be a consuming fire, and he uses the sinner, like chaff, for justice that punishes (Deut. 4:24; 9:3). God therefore punishes when and as much as he wills, not as he is unable to do otherwise; yet the punishment rests on justice, on justice by its nature and intrinsic property.

units.la: ,, III. Arg. Potest Deus mitiorem pœnam inferre quam peccatum mere-,, tur: ergo potest pro absoluta sua potentia pœnam universam suspendere. ,, Nam ponantur, si placet, tres gradus pœnæ promeritæ; huic si Deus possit ,, subtrahere gradum unum, cur non & alterum; & si duos possit, cur non ,, simul etiam & reliquum tertium? Resp. Nego consequentiam. Utcunque possit Deus mitius punire, quam pro peccati merito, & gradus pœnæ aliquos demere, non tamen æque omnem omnino pœnam. Quia si prorsum non puni-ret, nulla justitiæ illius punitricis foret declaratio, quod tum aliter exponi quam illius abnegatio, non posset. Atqui hoc impossibile. Non vero ejus periculum est in pœnæ aliquâ remissione, quod potestati divinæ relinquitur, modo non neglectâ prorsus justitiâ, & punitione congrua.
units.tr: III. Argument. God can inflict a milder punishment than sin deserves; therefore by his absolute power he can suspend the whole punishment. For suppose, if you like, three degrees of deserved punishment: if God can remove one degree, why not another; and if he can remove two, why not also the remaining third at the same time? Reply: I deny the consequence. However much God can punish more mildly than the desert of sin, and remove some degrees of punishment, he cannot equally remove the whole punishment altogether. For if he did not punish at all, there would be no declaration of that punishing justice, which could then be explained only as its denial. But this is impossible. Nor is there any danger in some remission of punishment, which is left to the divine power, provided that justice is not wholly neglected and a fitting punishment is inflicted.

units.la: ,, IV. Arg. Potest Deus cruciatum quantumcunque etiam infernalem alicui ,, inferre, citra omne demeritum: ergo etiam potest, non obstante demerito ,, quantocumque quantamcunque pœnam suspendere. Resp. Negatur ante-cedens. Quia uti peccatorem nequaquam velle punire, implicat abnegationem justitiæ; ita immerentem quantocunque cruciatu vexare, videtur secum ferre abnegationem clementiæ & misericordiæ. Quod utrumque æque indignum Deo est, & impossibile.
units.tr: IV. Argument. God can inflict on anyone any torment, even one as great as hellish torment, without any desert; therefore he can also, despite any desert however great, suspend any punishment however great. Reply: I deny the antecedent. Just as to be unwilling ever to punish a sinner implies the denial of justice, so to afflict an undeserving person with any torment whatever seems to carry with it the denial of clemency and mercy. Both are equally unworthy of God and impossible.

units.la: ,, V. Arg. Penes Deum est, utrum velit peccatorem ipsum punire, an vadem & sponsorem ejus: ergo non punit ex absolutā aliquā necessitate. Re-sponsum jam ad id est, de necessitate absolutā: quae fi hoc sensu fumatur ut no-tet necessitatem, quae absque interveniente libera electione fe habet, a nobis rejicitur, qui ad exercitium justitiae omnino dicimus Dei intercedere arbitrium & electionem, non an velit juste agere & punire, posito necessario ejus sub-jecto, sed quo pacto velit, sic an aliter, an in peccatore punire proprio, vel vade.
units.tr: V. Argument. It rests with God whether he wills to punish the sinner himself or his surety and bondsman; therefore he does not punish from any absolute necessity. Reply: This has already been answered, concerning absolute necessity. If it is taken in the sense of a necessity that holds without any intervening free choice, we reject it. For we say that in the exercise of justice God's will and choice do intervene; not whether he wills to act and punish justly, given his necessary nature, but in what manner he wills it, whether so or otherwise, whether to punish in the sinner himself or in a surety.

units.la: vi. Arg. Non impossibile est, ut Deus peccatorem adducat ad poeni-tentiam, ergo neque ut peccatum dimittat impunitum, Resp. Negatur ite-rum consequentia: nam utcunque per poenitentiam & resipiscentiam peccator meliorem vitam degat, pro prioribus tamen peccatis manet ejus debitum, & treatus [?] etiam exsolvendus. Non satis est ad salutem promerendam aliquā vitae parte justum fuisse, nisi omni insons fueris, & perfectè justus. Sine sanctitate enim nemo Deum videbit unquam, vel apud Deum commorari quisquam potest. Quare vel perfecta vitae obedientia, vel satisfactionis praecedere debet, antequam quis salvetur: sola per se non sufficit poenitentia.
units.tr: VI. Argument. It is not impossible for God to bring a sinner to repentance; therefore neither is it impossible for him to dismiss sin unpunished. Reply: Again I deny the consequence. For however much through repentance and repentance-unto-amendment the sinner lives a better life, his debt for former sins remains, and the penalty must still be paid. It is not enough for earning salvation to have been righteous for some part of one's life, unless you are blameless in every respect and perfectly righteous. For no one will ever see God without holiness, nor can anyone dwell with God. Therefore either perfect obedience of life or satisfaction must precede, before anyone is saved; repentance alone is not sufficient.

units.la: vii. Arg. Si necesse sit, ut Deus peccatum puniat, tum vel poena temporariā, vel aeterna: Si temporariā duntaxat; sequetur peccatum non meruisse poenam aeternam. Sin aeterna (quod dicendum est) ergo necesse est, ut peccator in aeternum duret; ergo impossibile est ut annihiletur: Ergo Deus per potentiam suam absolutam non potest annihilare creaturam suam, quam ex nihilo creavit. Resp. 1. Debere puniri peccatum, pro Dei justitiā, statuimus: non vero, quā poenā. Hoc Dei relinquimus arbitrio, quantum, quando, & quomodo puniat, vel cum rigore, vel moderatione, ultra demeritum nunquam, neque etiam ut justitiam suam abneget, omissā omni punitione. Et certe longe aliud est, prorsus non, & nolle punire: vel non tali aut tanto modo. Illud justitia requirit, non adeo istud. Imo apud judices, hoc prudentiae relinquitur, neque dicam injustitiae hinc incurrent, quod in poenis variant, & moderant, uti omnino illam non evaderent, si quidem omnes poenas, & justitiae executionem prorsus omitterent. Multo magis id in Deo est, qui non sibi communicatam & praescriptam habet justitiam aliquam, sed ipsa ejus perfectio est, à se & per essentiam. ii. Negatur sequi, si Deus peccatum punit poena temporariā, ergo non meruit aeternam. Quasi vero judici non sit integrum, punire infra demeritum. iii. Quin Deus possit creatu-tam suam annihilare, quam ex nihilo creavit, nemo unquam dubitat, considerando terminos hic adhibitos, potentiae divinae, & annihilationis, eosque conjungendo: at non de annihilatione disputamus, aut Dei potentiā, ea absolutā, sed de punitione, eaque non ad potentiam Dei, nedum absolutam collata, sed ad justitiam. iv. An vero pro poenā condignā adhibere Deus annihilationem peccatoris queat, non examinamus. Novimus quam, & quantam poenam Deus nunc constituerit peccato; an minorem eā inferre queat, per exceptionem ab ordinatā regula, & mulcta, vel per potentiam absolutam, non disputamus, qui, uti etiam ante dictum, haud juben-tester extremos absolutæ divinæ potentiæ apices in discrimen vocati audimus. Nihil autem ad præsens argumentum inde sequitur, pro negandâ omni punitionis necessitate, si concedamus, posse Deum aliquando leviorem æternâ pœnâ, vel annihilationem inferre. Præsertim juxta istam Aliquorum sententiam, quod non esse deterius sit, quam omnino miserum esse.
units.tr: VII. Argument. If it is necessary for God to punish sin, then the punishment must be either temporal or eternal. If only temporal, it would follow that sin did not deserve eternal punishment. But if eternal (which must be said), then it is necessary that the sinner endure forever; therefore it is impossible for him to be annihilated. Therefore God by his absolute power cannot annihilate the creature whom he created out of nothing. Reply 1: We maintain that sin must be punished according to God's justice, but not with what punishment. This we leave to God's judgment: how much, when, and in what way he punishes, whether with severity or moderation, never beyond desert, nor so as to deny his justice by omitting all punishment. Certainly it is quite different not to punish at all, and to be unwilling to punish, from not punishing in such a way or to such an extent. Justice requires the former, not the latter. Indeed, among judges this is left to prudence, and I will not say that they incur injustice thereby, because they vary and moderate the penalties, just as they would not escape injustice altogether if they omitted all penalties and the execution of justice. Much more is this so in God, who does not have a justice communicated to him and prescribed, but is his very perfection, from himself and by his essence. II. It does not follow, because God punishes sin with temporal punishment, that therefore it did not deserve eternal punishment, as though it were not within the judge's power to punish below desert. III. That God can annihilate the creature whom he created out of nothing no one has ever doubted, if one considers the terms used here, divine power and annihilation, and joins them together. But we are not disputing about annihilation, or about God's power considered as absolute, but about punishment, and that not as compared with God's power, let alone absolute power, but with his justice. IV. Whether God can use annihilation of the sinner as a punishment that fits his guilt, we do not examine. We know what and how great a punishment God has now appointed for sin; whether he can inflict a lesser one, by an exception to the ordained rule and penalty, or by absolute power, we do not dispute, since, as was said before, we do not rashly call into question the outermost reaches of God's absolute power. Nothing follows for the present argument, however, in denying every necessity of punishment, even if we grant that God can sometimes inflict something lighter than eternal punishment, or annihilation. Especially according to the opinion of some, that it is no worse than not being wretched at all.

units.la: „ VIII. Arg. Omne peccatum necesse est, ut puniatur vel in ipso pecca-tore, vel in Christo, ut sic justitiæ satisfiat. Putemus jam electos aliquos partem habuisse in ipsa crucifixione Christi; ergo ipsorum crucifixio Christi punita est in Christo dum crucifigeretur. Non nego ista, ut summè admi-randa, ita etiam & vera esse. Sed qua ratione dicatur necessitate absoluta necesse fuisse, saltem ut hoc modo satisfieret justitiæ divinæ; & interea non posse Deum per absolutam potentiam peccatum aliquod quantulumcunque citra satisfactionem dimittere impunitum, vel etiam minori pœnâ punire, quam æternâ, prorsus non intelligo. Resp. Præter ea, quæ in superioribus discussa, nullum hisce contineri argumentum, vel ipse Autor vidit. Quærit enim, non infert aut concludit. Quodque proponit, & ipse non negat verum esse, vid. inter crucifixores Christi, saltem qui operi isti & facinori se adjunxere socios, fuisse etiam electos & conversos postea, cum ex-Christi pro iis oratione[?], Luc. xxiii. 34. tum ex Act. ii. 23. :6[?]. 38. 39. & iii. 17. colligitur: quorum proinde peccata necessariò, saltem omnium consensu ex necessitate ordinationis divinæ, Christi eâ crucifixione expiata fuerunt. Quærere nunc autem, annon pro absoluta Dei potentiâ res paulo aliter habere se potuerit, ad ea redit, quibus antea respondimus, vel alia petit, de quibus respondere non nostrum, saltem non est præsentis examinis: vid. an alio quo pacto divinæ justitiæ satisfieri potuisset: quæ nos non magis nunc premit quæstio, quam alios.
units.tr: VIII. Argument. Every sin must be punished either in the sinner himself or in Christ, so that justice may be satisfied. Let us now suppose that some of the elect had a part in the very crucifixion of Christ; then their crucifixion of Christ was punished in Christ while he was being crucified. I do not deny these things; they are most admirable, and also true. But how it can be said that it was necessary by absolute necessity, at least that divine justice be satisfied in this way; and at the same time that God, by absolute power, could not dismiss any sin, however small, unpunished without satisfaction, or punish it with a lesser punishment than eternal, I do not at all understand. Reply: Apart from what has been discussed above, the author himself saw that this contains no argument. For he asks; he does not infer or conclude. And what he puts forward, which he himself does not deny to be true, namely that among the crucifiers of Christ, at least those who joined this work and deed as companions, there were also elect persons who were afterwards converted, is gathered both from Christ's prayer for them (Luke 23:34) and from Acts ii. 23, 38, 39 and iii. 17. Therefore their sins were necessarily expiated by that crucifixion of Christ, at least by the consent of all, from the necessity of the divine ordinance. To ask now whether, with respect to absolute divine power, the matter could have stood somewhat differently, comes back to what we answered before, or it asks other things which it is not our business to answer, at least not in the present examination; namely, whether divine justice could have been satisfied in some other way. This question presses on us no more than on others.

units.la: „ IX. Arg. Denique, si Deus puniat peccata necessitate naturali, ut ignis agit ustionem; ergo punitio peccatorum dependet ex liberrimâ Dei voluntate. Nam nisi Deo volente, ne ignis quidem ureret, ut apparet in tribus illis Patritiis à fornace igneo Babylonico intactis. Resp. Concedi totum. Quamvis enim Deo justitia illa sua sit naturalis, atque ex ejus necessitate velit punire; ipsa verò actualis punitio pendet à liberrimâ ipsius voluntate. Liberum quippe dicitur, non respectu proprietatis in Deo naturalis, sed ad egressum ejus, & actiones externas, quæ à Dei voluntate pendent & reguntur.
units.tr: „ IX. Arg. Finally, if God punishes sins by natural necessity, as fire produces burning, then the punishment of sins depends on the most free will of God. For unless God willed it, not even fire would burn, as appears in the three Patricians who were untouched by the Babylonian furnace. Resp. I grant the whole. For although God's justice is natural to him, and he wills to punish from the necessity of his nature, the actual punishment itself depends on his most free will. It is called free not with respect to a property natural in God, but with respect to his outward going forth and external actions, which depend on and are governed by the will of God.

units.la: Atque hæc ad argumenta omnia, quæ scimus in contrarium moveri, responsa sunto. In quo saltem ingenuitatem nostram probare cogentur Adversarii, qui non modo unam alteramque ipsorum objectionem retulimus, sed & plura alia, fortiora etiam, non ab ipsis, sed aliis quandoque prolata: ne argumento ulla ex parte defuisse videamur, sedati candidè omnia & singula, quæ adversum nos facere uspiam possint. Ut ita primò quidem thesim de necessitate satisfactionis, inde de veritate tanto certius confirmaremus. Confirmaremus & fidem hoc in religionis Christianæ articulo nostram tanto evidentius.
units.tr: Let these answers serve for all the arguments which we know are brought against us. In this, at least, our adversaries will be compelled to acknowledge our candour: we have not only set out one or another of their objections, but also many others, stronger ones too, which were sometimes advanced not by them but by others. We have done this so that we might seem to have left nothing undefended on our side, and so that we might candidly address each and every point that could be made against us anywhere. In this way we will first confirm the thesis of the necessity of satisfaction, and then its truth, all the more certainly. We will also confirm our faith in this article of the Christian religion all the more clearly.

units.la: Cæterùm ad conciliationem diversæ inter Orthodoxos, super illâ de justitia vindicatrice Deo naturali, quæstione, hoc addendum duximus: quod agnitâ, asseraque pro certo Satisfactionis per Christum veritate, naturale distingui potest in id, quod à meris & solis pendet fluitque naturæ principiis, in totâ sui actione; quomodo igni naturale est, urere: vel, quod in naturâ quidem, ejusque proprietate essentiali fundatum, non tamen in actionem externam prorumpit, atque operatur, absque interveniente libero arbitrio; uti homini naturale est, ridere; vel propius, uti patri, pro natura paternâ proprium, benignum esse, qui tamen benignitate non utitur erga liberos, nisi pro arbitrio & consilio: Judici naturale, justitiam exercere, quod tamen non facit, nisi ex ratione. Et quia absolutum hic nonnunquam ita interpretantur, quod libertatem arbitrii in executione excludit, nam necessitas absoluta non est, quæ non nisi intercedente libera electione exercetur, inquiunt: proinde necessitatem dicamus hic intercedere quidem, non autem illam absolutam: & naturalem Deo esse justitiam vindicatricem, non primo, sed secundo modo. Qua expositione etiam admittit Twissus, Deo naturale esse peccata punire. Necesse esse, ut omne peccatum Deo displiceat. Scelerate agenti debeti pœnam, & ex natura rei, & ex constitutione divina. Ex naturâ rei, hoc sensu, ut sceleratus evadat dignus, in quem animadvertatur. Fatetur, Deum esse naturaliter justum, sicut etiam est naturaliter misericors & liberalis: sed neque necessitate aliqua fertur ad exercendam suam misericordiam & liberalitatem, neque ad justitiæ suæ specimen exhibendum. Ejusdemque generis apud ipsum & alia. Præsertim vero confitetur in Deo, ad puniendum congruitatem, quod nos dicimus proprietatem naturalem. Hæc ejus verba, loco, quo materiam istam tractat, in Vindiciis, contra Arminium, lib. 1. de Elect. part. 11. Digress. VIII. [?] pag. 28[?]. Interea damus conclusionem, concedimusque Deum, non modo odisse, sed & de facto punire omne peccatum: sed de modo quæritur; nos dicimus hoc fieri naturali quidem non necessitate, sed congruitate, quæ stare potest, imo stat cum liberrima Dei voluntate, liberrimè constituente manifestationem justitiæ suæ. Bené. Sed quod ille congruitatem, obsecro nobis liceat dicere proprietatem naturalem, præsertim quum defendamus, eam cum liberrimâ Dei voluntate stare, quæ constituit manifestare suam justitiam, & negemus, naturalis quamvis sit, esse tamen absolutam talem justitiam, quo sensu vocem absolute hoc in loco alii nonnunquam sumunt.
units.tr: Moreover, for the reconciling of the question, which is disputed among the Orthodox, concerning the natural justice of God as avenger, we have thought the following should be added. Once the truth of satisfaction through Christ has been acknowledged and affirmed as certain, the natural may be distinguished into that which depends wholly and solely on the principles of nature in its whole action, as it is natural to fire to burn; or into that which is indeed grounded in nature and its essential property, but does not break out into external action and operate without the intervention of free choice, as it is natural for a man to laugh; or, more closely, as it is proper to a father, by his paternal nature, to be kind, though he does not use his kindness towards his children except by his own will and counsel; or as it is natural for a judge to exercise justice, which he nevertheless does not do except by reason. And since some people sometimes interpret the absolute in such a way that it excludes freedom of choice in the execution, saying for a necessity is not absolute if it is not exercised except with a free choice intervening, let us therefore say that a necessity does indeed intervene here, but not an absolute one, and that justice as avenger is natural to God not in the first, but in the second way. Twisse also admits this explanation: It is natural for God to punish sins. It is necessary that every sin should displease God. The one who acts wickedly ought to be punished, both from the nature of the thing and from the divine constitution. From the nature of the thing, in this sense, that the wicked man becomes worthy to be punished. He confesses that God is naturally just, just as he is naturally merciful and generous; yet he is not driven by any necessity to exercise his mercy and generosity, nor to display his justice. There are also other things of the same kind in him. Above all, he admits in God a fitness for punishing, which we call natural property. These are his words, in the place where he treats this matter, in the Vindiciae, against Arminius, book 1 on Election, part 11, Digression VIII, [?] page 28[?]. Meanwhile we grant the conclusion, and we concede that God not only hates but in fact punishes every sin; but the question is about the manner. We say that this happens not by natural necessity, but by fitness, which can stand, indeed does stand, together with the most free will of God, who most freely decides to manifest his justice. Well said. But what he calls fitness, I ask leave to call natural property, especially since we maintain that it stands together with the most free will of God, who decides to manifest his justice; and we deny that such justice, though natural, is therefore absolute in the sense in which some people sometimes take the word absolute in this place.

units.la: Positâ ergo sic probatâque justitia vindicatrice in Deo naturali; tum ex eâ, punitionis & satisfactionis necessitate: tempus est, ut ad ostendendam ejus veritatem, sive quod Christus vere pro nobis satisfecit, accingamur. Satisfactionis verbo intelligimus & comprehendimus, quidquid antea diximus controversum inter nos esse: nempe, quod Christus pœnas nostras, nostri loco, exsolverit, divinæ justitiæ, atque ita Deo placato, reconciliatoque, verè nos redemerit. Quo simili ordine nostra hic quoque disponentur argumenta. In verbo satisfactionis non insistimus, modo res teneatur: utimur tamen illo, propter commodam, & emphaticam expressionem. Ad solutionem tenebamur nos propriam & strictam, quam quia Christus ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν præstitit seipso, satisfactio dicitur.
units.tr: Therefore, having thus laid down and proved justice as avenger to be natural in God, and from it the necessity of punishment and satisfaction, it is time to set about showing its truth, that is, that Christ truly made satisfaction for us. By the word satisfaction we understand and include whatever we said earlier was in dispute between us: namely, that Christ, in our place, paid off our penalties to the justice of God, and so, God being appeased and reconciled, truly redeemed us. Our arguments here will be arranged in a similar order. We do not insist on the word satisfaction, provided the matter is kept; yet we use it on account of its convenient and emphatic expression. We were bound to a proper and strict payment, which, because Christ performed it on our behalf [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν] with himself, is called satisfaction.

units.la: Ad cujus exponendam naturam, optime dixit Asconius, satisfacere, esse tantum facere, quantum satis est irato ad vindictam. Thomas Aquinas, in iv. Dist. xv. Satisfactio est illata injuria recompensatio secundum justitiae aequalitatem. In quem eundem locum & Scotus: Satisfactio utique (universaliter accepto vocabulo) redditio est voluntaria aequivalentis, alias indebiti. Non est enim absoluta datio, sed reddi-tio, quae esse debet voluntaria, secus non satisfactio, sed satispassio dicenda foret, qualis reperitur in damnatis. Adhac debet esse aequivalentis, nam hoc justitia requirit, & tale aequivalens debet esse alius indebitum. Si enim foret alia causa debitum, jam non esset hujus satisfactio. Subtiliter. Satisfactio, non absoluta est datio, sed est relativa, redditio. Respectu ejus, qui satisfacit alterius loco, dum non tenetur, est indebita. Debitum quando reddit qui debet, & hoc quod debet, solutio est: etiam quando alius, vel aequivalenti alio satisfacit, solvit. Ad quod requiritur ἐκὼν[?]: & non simpliciter pati, sed voluntarie pati, ne satispassio solum sit, sed satis-factio. Johannes Driedo, de Redemtione, pag. 113. Satisfactio est actio voluntaria, vel passio voluntarie tolerata, qua operans sua sponte tantum facit, quantum ju-stitia sat est, aut solvens creditori, quod illi debuit, aut voluntarie assumens humiliatio-nis disciplinam, quam peccatum commeruit. Sic ratio exsolutionis & liberationis, quae in satisfactione est, a multis exprimitur. Bellarminus, Tom. iii. lib. v. de Poenit. cap. iv. Satisfactio nihil est aliud, nisi actio, qua is qui alterum laesit, tantum facit quantum satis est ad injuriam compensandam: sive quantum is qui laesus est juste exigit. Summa Angelica, quam dicunt, est solutio poenae debita. Navarrus, in Enchirid. Confess. cap. iii. est passio voluntaria poena pro peccato, ad placandum. Toletus, Instruct. Sacerd. lib. iii. cap. xi. Offensa praeterita quo ad poenam recompensatio. Autores isti crebrius illud argumentum tractant, ita ut in naturam rei intenti ea interim ponant, ex quibus humanae ipsorum satisfactiones egregie confunduntur.
units.tr: In explaining its nature, Asconius rightly said that to satisfy is only to do as much as is enough for an angry man to take vengeance. Thomas Aquinas, in book IV, distinction XV: Satisfaction is the recompense of an injury inflicted, according to the equality of justice. In the same place Scotus also says: Satisfaction, taking the word universally, is the voluntary giving back of an equivalent, otherwise not owed. For it is not an absolute giving, but a giving back, which ought to be voluntary; otherwise it would be called not satisfaction but suffering enough, such as is found in the damned. Moreover, it ought to be of an equivalent, for justice requires this, and such an equivalent ought to be something not owed by the one who gives it. For if there were another cause of the debt, it would no longer be the satisfaction of this debt. Subtly put. Satisfaction is not an absolute giving but a relative giving back. With respect to the one who satisfies in another's place, while he is not bound, it is not owed. When the one who owes pays back what he owes, it is a payment; and when someone else, or someone with an equivalent, makes satisfaction, he also pays. For this there is required a willingly [ἑκών]: not merely to suffer, but to suffer voluntarily, so that it is not merely suffering enough, but satisfaction. John Driedo, On Redemption, page 113: Satisfaction is a voluntary action, or a suffering voluntarily endured, by which the one acting, of his own accord, does as much as justice requires, either by paying the creditor what he owed him, or by voluntarily taking upon himself the discipline of humiliation which sin has deserved. In this way the idea of payment and release, which lies in satisfaction, is expressed by many. Bellarmine, vol. III, book V on Penance, chapter IV: Satisfaction is nothing other than an action by which the one who has injured another does as much as is enough to compensate the injury, or as much as the one who was injured justly demands. The so-called Summa Angelica: is the payment of the penalty owed. Navarrus, in the Enchiridion on Confession, chapter III: is a voluntary suffering of punishment for sin, in order to appease. Toletus, Instruction of Priests, book III, chapter XI: a recompense, as to punishment, for a past offence. These authors treat this argument rather often, yet in the meantime they put forward in the nature of the thing such points that their human satisfactions are thoroughly confounded.

units.la: Leges distinguunt, solvere, & satisfacere, & fidejubere. Fidejubet quis se solu-turum: Solvit autem quod debet, vel quovis modo satisfacit. D. quibus modis pign. l. vi. qui vero non solvere, sed satisfacere paratus est, in diversa causa est. De Manum. Testam. l. xli. §. sed si. Si solverit, satisve fecerit. De contrah. empt. l. xix. quod vendidi, non aliter fit accipientis, quam si aut pretium nobis solutum fit, aut satis eo nomine factum, vel etiam fidem habuerimus emtori sine ulla satisfactione. Jam satisfactionem, quamvis propria & stricta solutione inferiorem, tamen pro solutione habent. Satisfactio pro solutione est. D. de solut. l. lii. De verb. signific. cixxvi. solutionis verbo, satisfactionem quoque omnem accipiendam placet. Accedit consensus creditoris, vel domini, ad liberationem. D. de solut. & liberat. l. lviii. si quis offerenti se negotiis alienis, bona fide solverit: quando liberetur? & ait Julianus, cum Dominus ratum habuerit, tunc liberari. C. eod. tit. l. xvii. Instit. quib. mod. tollitur oblig. vel si quis consentiente creditore, aliud pro alio solverit. Debitoris autem nil necesse est attendere voluntatem. Instit. eod. Nec interest quis solvat, utrum ipse qui debet, an alius pro eo, liberatur enim & alio solvente: sive sciente, sive ignorante debitore, vel invito eo, solutio fiat. D. de solut. & liberat. L xxiii. xl. iiii. solvere pro ignorante & invito cuique licet: cum fit jure civili constitutum, licere etiam ignorantis invitique conditionem meliorem facere. Quod in satisfactione Christi, aliisque plurimis Dei in nos beneficiis usu venit, ut ignorantibus, immerentibus, atque vel invitis offerantur & contingant. Rom. v. 8. nobis peccatoribus Christus pro nobis mortuus est. 10 inimici existentes reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus. Adde Eph. ii. 1. 2. 4. 5.
units.tr: The laws distinguish to pay, to satisfy, and to stand surety. Someone stands surety that he will pay; but he pays what he owes, or in some way makes satisfaction. D. On Pledges, book VI: but one who is ready not to pay but to make satisfaction is in a different case. On Manumission of Wills, book XLI, §. but if: If he has paid, or made satisfaction. On Contracting Purchases, book XIX: What I have sold is not transferred to the buyer except as the price has been paid to us, or security given on that account, or indeed we have trusted the buyer without any security. Now, although satisfaction is inferior to proper and strict payment, they nonetheless regard it as payment. Satisfaction is in place of payment. D. On Payment, book LII. On the Meaning of Words, cixxvi: under the word payment it is agreed that all satisfaction is to be understood as well. To this is added the consent of the creditor or owner for release. D. On Payment and Release, book LVIII: If someone, offering himself to another's affairs, pays in good faith, when is he released? And Julian says: when the owner has ratified it, then he is released. C. same title, book XVII. Institutes, by which means an obligation is removed: or if someone, with the creditor consenting, pays one thing in place of another. The will of the debtor, however, need not be considered at all. Institutes, same place: Nor does it matter who pays, whether the debtor himself or another for him, for he is released even by another's paying, whether the debtor knows or does not know, or whether the payment is made against his will. D. On Payment and Release, book XXIII, title XLIV: It is lawful for anyone to pay on behalf of an ignorant and unwilling person, since it is established by civil law that it is also lawful to make the condition of an ignorant and unwilling person better. This happens in the satisfaction of Christ, and in very many other benefits of God toward us: they are offered to us and come to us while we are ignorant, undeserving, and even unwilling. Rom. v. 8: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. 10: while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. Add Eph. ii. 1, 2, 4, 5.

units.la: Debitum quum sit duplex, creditì, & poenæ, & similis hinc obligatio, debitor liberatur, aut solutione, aut fidejussione, & satisfactione sive propriâ, sive alienâ. Creditì solutio fit creditori; poenæ autem, judici. Atque ea est hujus loci: neque enim redemit nos Christus φθαρτῆς[?], ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ. 11 Pet. 1. 18. 19. sed pretioso sanguine. Illa Hebraei in jure suo dicunt, בממונה[?]; ista, בנפשה[?].
units.tr: Since a debt is twofold, a debt of money and a debt of penalty, and a similar obligation arises from each, a debtor is freed either by payment, or by surety and satisfaction, whether made by himself or by another. Payment of a debt of money is made to the creditor; payment of a penalty is made to the judge. And this is the case here, for Christ did not redeem us with corruptible things, with silver or gold [οὐ φθαρτοῖς, ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ] (1 Pet. 1:18, 19) but with precious blood. The Hebrews, in their law, call the former with property [בממונה] and the latter with life [בנפשה].

units.la: In solutione tria occurrunt. 1. Solventis animus, quod intendit & vult solvere. D. de solut. & liber. l. 1. LVI. LVIII. C. eod. l. 1. xv. Deinde solvitur solidum, tantum quantum debetur. D. eod. l. ix. XXXIII. XLVI. Denique & vero creditori. D eod. l. XII. XIV XLIX. Cod. eod. l. iv. l. xi. Christo certe animus solvendi fuit, vel satisfaciendi, & solidum praestitit, vero Domino. Matth. xviii. 23. Non quidem Deo idem solutum quod debebatur, ab iisdem: nos etenim debebamus, aeternas poenas exsolvere: verùm pependit aequivalens Christus. quod alio in casu Marcus cap. xv. 15. dixit, τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι.
units.tr: Three things occur in payment: (1) the mind of the one paying, that is, that he intends and wishes to pay (Dig. de solut. et liber. l. 1, LVI, LVIII; Cod. eod. l. 1, xv); (2) the whole is paid, as much as is owed (Dig. eod. l. ix, XXXIII, XLVI); and (3) it is paid to the true creditor (Dig. eod. l. XII, XIV, XLIX; Cod. eod. l. iv, l. xi). Christ certainly had the intention of paying or satisfying, and he rendered the whole to the true Lord (Matth. 18:23). Not indeed that the same thing was paid to God that was owed, by the same persons: for we were under obligation to pay eternal punishments. But Christ paid an equivalent, which in another place Mark expressed in chapter 15, verse 15, as to do what was sufficient [τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι].

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA.
units.tr: SECOND SECTION.

units.la: UT autem probemus, Christum pro peccatis pretium suâ morte & passionibus verè exsolvisse, & satisfecisse, hoc ordine argumenta disponimus. Primam[?] ut classem faciant eâ, quae docent, Christum in se suscepisse & sustinuisse poenas nostras. Deinde ea, quibus dicitur, pro nobis, & nostro, non solum bono, & causa, sed loco se stitisse, & passum. iii. Quibus Scriptura testatur, eum morte & sanguine suo peccata nostra expiasse, ac Deo, sui oblatione & sacrificio, nos reconciliasse. Denique, & vere nos redemisse.
units.tr: To prove that Christ truly paid and satisfied for sins by his death and sufferings, we arrange our arguments in this order. The first class consists of those passages which teach that Christ took upon himself and bore our punishments. Second, those passages which say that he stood in our place, for us, not only for our good and on our account but in our stead, and suffered. Third, those passages in which Scripture bears witness that he made atonement for our sins by his death and blood, and by his offering and sacrifice reconciled us to God. Finally, that he truly redeemed us.

units.la: Primum, quo manifestissime probatur tota ratio satisfactionis nostrae, & praesertim id, quod in primâ argumentorum classe urgemus, Christum poenas nostras sustulisse, est Euangelicum Jesajae caput liii. Christi, & fidei in ipsum praedicatio valde memoranda, pro isto tempore quae fuit. Unde in primo statim initio, verf. 1. מִי הֶאֱמִין[?] quis credidit? Quippe agi isto capite de passionibus Messiae, haud ita pridem contra Judaeos demonstratum dedimus: ut idem nunc repeti debere, ostendique propter Christianos, merito pudendum sit: argumento huc accedente insuper potissimo ex collatione & confirmatione illius in Novo Testamento: quod variis hinc locis demonstrare cuivis obvium.
units.tr: The first, by which the whole reasoning of our satisfaction is most clearly proved, and especially that point which we press in the first class of arguments, that Christ removed our punishments, is the gospel passage of Isaiah 53, a very notable preaching about Christ and faith in him, and one that was fitting for that time. So at the very start, verse 1: "Who has believed?" [מִי הֶאֱמִין]. For we have already shown, not long ago, against the Jews that this chapter deals with the sufferings of the Messiah; and that the same point should now be repeated, and shown for the sake of Christians, is rightly a matter of shame. The chief argument also comes in from the comparison and confirmation of it in the New Testament, which anyone can easily show from various places.

units.la: At contineri illo capite summam fidei de Christo, ejusque satisfactione & redemtione statim ex analysi apparet. Agitur quippe de Christi utroque statu, humiliationis & mortis; tum exaltationis, & vitae. Quod ad illud, passiones ejus exponit versus 2. non forma ei, neque decor. 3. contemtus & abjectus. 8. ab angustia & judicio, &c.
