Passiones summas & gravissimas, vers. 10. & Jehova placuit conterere eum. 11 מעמל [?], a labore animae suae, &c. Denique, & mortem. vers. 8. excisus est è terra viventium. 12. pro eo quod effudit in mortem animam suam. Atque sepulturam quoque, vers. 9. dederuntque cum improbis sepulchrum ejus, & cum divite fuit in mortibus suis.
units.tr: That the sum of faith concerning Christ, and of his satisfaction and redemption, is contained in that chapter appears at once from an analysis. It deals with both states of Christ: that of humiliation and death; and then that of exaltation and life. As to the former: his sufferings are set out in verse 2, "he had no form nor comeliness"; verse 3, "despised and rejected"; verse 8, "from restraint and judgment," etc.; the greatest and most grievous sufferings, verse 10, "and the LORD was pleased to bruise him"; verse 11, "from the travail of his soul" [מעמל], etc. Finally also his death: verse 8, "he was cut off out of the land of the living"; verse 12, "because he poured out his soul to death." And also his burial, verse 9, "they made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich was he in his deaths."

units.la: . Multum se torquent Interpretes, & alii, in eo quod de divite versu 9. dicitur, cum quo Christus fuerit in suis mortibus: placetque vulgo ad Josephum Arimathaeensem applicare, cujus viri divitis & boni sepulchro Christus usus in historiâ Euangelicâ perhibetur. Praeterquam autem quod ab aliis tunc moveri solet, ita potius dicendum fuisse, cum divite Christum sepulchrum habuisse, quam cum illo fuisse in morte: cum distinctioni, quae hic est, si insistamus, dicatur, cum improbis sepulchrum ejus, & cum divite fuisse ipsum in morte. Dubito autem, annon exile nimis & leve videatur, ad Josephum istum illa referre, aut restringere. Quod si negemus, nulla hic est difficultas, quae omnis ex illâ vulgari oritur applicatione. Certe cum improbis, atque inter eos sepulchrum, etiam mors Christi fuit. Quid igitur אִישׁ עָשִׁיר [?] cum divite ? validos & potentes intellige, quibus in morte fuit traditus: vel idem quod in priori membro intellige, improbos: quemadmodum dicitur mammona iniquitatis, quod iniquitatem sibi vulgo adjunctam habet: sic accipe, cum divite, id est, cum improbo: quemadmodum רָשָׁע [?] apud Hebraeos cauponam, & scortum dicit, quod saepe illa conjungantur: Rahab זוֹנָה [?] Josh. ii. 1. ἡ πόρνη Jacobo, cap. ii. 25. atque ita idem utriusque membri sensus, ut sit, quod improbis & potentibus Christus obsitus ubique fuit & traditus, tum in morte, tum in sepultura. Nam satius est locum indefinite & in genere accipere, & non applicate ad hunc, vel illum.
units.tr: Interpreters and others twist themselves at length over what is said of the rich man in verse 9, that Christ was "with the rich in his deaths." It is the common view to apply this to Joseph of Arimathea, the rich and good man whose tomb Christ is said in the gospel history to have used. Apart from the fact that others commonly object that it should rather have been said that Christ had his tomb with the rich man than that he was with him in death, if we insist on the distinction made here, it reads: "they made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich was he in his death." I doubt whether it is not too slight and trivial to refer or restrict those words to that one Joseph. If we deny this, there is no difficulty here, for all of it arises from that common application. Certainly his death, as well as his grave, was among the wicked. What then is with the rich [אִישׁ עָשִׁיר]? Understand the powerful and mighty, into whose hands he was given up in death; or understand the same as in the first member, the wicked. Just as "mammon of unrighteousness" is so called because unrighteousness is commonly joined to it, so take "with the rich," that is, with the wicked. Thus רָשָׁע among the Hebrews means an innkeeper and a harlot, because these are often joined together: Rahab, a harlot [זוֹנָה], Josh. ii. 1; and [ἡ πόρνη] in James, cap. ii. 25. So the sense of both members is the same: that Christ was everywhere given over to and beset by the wicked and the powerful, both in death and in burial. For it is better to take the expression indefinitely and in general, and not to apply it to this or that particular man.

units.la: Christi exaltationem docet vers. 8. à coarctatione & judicio assumtus est; & generationem ejus quis enarrabit? 10. ubi posuerit animam suam reatum, videbit semen, prolongabit dies. 11. pro labore animae suae videbit & saturabitur. Quae notant duplicem Christi statum, Κενώσεως, & ὑψώσεως. Ad primum spectant ejus passiones, quarum exponit Propheta causam utramque, impulsivam, & finalem. א. causam meritoriam, peccata nostra illas Christo fecerunt angustias & passiones: non ut occasiones, sed causae propriâ & verâ causalitate, mala illa inferentes. vers. 5. & ipse dolore fuit affectus à praevaricationibus nostris, attritus ab iniquitatibus nostris, מְעֹונֹותֵינוּ [?]. 8. à praevaricatione populi mei plaga ei. למו [?] etiam pro singulari masculino tertiae personae, in Scripturâ venire, per epenthesim ת [?], etiam Kimhio observatum, in Grammaticis, ex Job. xxii. 2. & xx. 23. adde Jesa. xliv. 15. ג [?]. inde dicuntur nostri languores, quos Christus pertulit, id est, nobis debiti & commeriti, quos à nobis in se suscepit. vers. 4. revera morbos nostros, species pro genere, id est, languores ipse tulit, & dolores nostros.
units.tr: Christ's exaltation is taught in verse 8: "he was taken from restraint and judgment; and who shall declare his generation?" verse 10: "when he shall have made his soul a guilt offering, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days"; verse 11: "for the travail of his soul he shall see and be satisfied." These mark the twofold state of Christ, of humiliation (κένωσις) and of exaltation (ὕψωσις). His sufferings belong to the first, and the prophet sets out their cause in both respects, the impelling and the final. (1) The meritorious cause: our sins made those distresses and sufferings for Christ, not as occasions but as true causes, bringing those evils upon him by their own proper causality. Verse 5: "he was wounded by our transgressions, bruised by our iniquities" [מְעֹונֹותֵינוּ]. Verse 8: "for the transgression of my people was he stricken." That [למו] also occurs in Scripture for the singular masculine third person, through the epenthetic [ת], as Kimhi observed among the grammarians, from Job xxii. 2 and xx. 23; add Jesa. xliv. 15 [ג]. Hence our sicknesses are said to have been borne by Christ, that is, debts owed and deserved by us, which he took upon himself from us. Verse 4: "surely he bore our diseases," the species put for the genus: "he himself bore our infirmities and our sorrows."

units.la: 3. Qui in illum translati. vers. 5. attritus ab iniquitatibus nostris: castigatio pacis nostra super eum, עָלָיו [?]. 8. Quum exigeretur debitum, ipse afflictus fuit, nec aperuit os suum : os suum : sicut parva pecus ad occisionem ductus fuit. Ita in caput hostiarum olim reatus offerentium quasi manibus imponebatur luendus, caeremonialiter ibi, in Christo vere. 8. a praevaricatione populi mei plaga ei. ה. Christus autem in se omnino insons & absque peccato. verf. 9. violentiam non fecit, nec dolus in ore ejus. ו. Neque temerario casu illa reatus nostri in Christum facta fuit translatio aut delegatio, sed Deo ita volente. verf. 10. & Jehova placuit conterere eum. ז. Qui in Christum, vadem spontaneum & validum conjecit omnia nostra debita. verf. 6. Jehova [?] fecit incurrere in eum iniquitatem omnium nostrum. ח. Eaque Christus portavit lubens, verf. 4. Certe morbos nostros ipse suscepit [?], & dolores nostros portavit eos [?]. 11. Quorum iniquitates & ipse portavit [?]. 12. & ipse peccatum multorum suscepit [?]. ט. Quare ab eo, tanquam sponsore, exegit illa Deus. verf. 7. Vti exactum fuit debitum, & ipse afflictus fuit. י. Et satisfecit Christus, ac expiavit ea. verf. 10. posuit animam suam hostiam pro delicto. כ. atque ita redemit nos, & aeternum salvat. verf. 11. Pro labore animae suae videbit hoc, & saturabitur: scientia sui justificationem conferet justus servus meus plurimis. 12. Nam ipse peccatum multorum tulit, & pro praevaricatoribus intercessit. Ex quibus omnia & singula, quae hujus negotii sunt, liquent: tam quae spectant surrogationem Christi in locum nostrum; ac quae ejus satisfactionem. Qui enim peccata, vel culpas & poenas nostras in se transferri insons cupit, & patitur, volente ita Deo, eaque in ipsum conjiciente, quae portet, quaeque ab ipso Deus exigat, ut eadem tanquam piacularis hostia sua vita vel anima expiet, qui & redimit isto pacto homines, ac salvat; is certe satisfacere credendus est: atqui illa Christum fecisse, ex observatis in Capite illo, apparet: ergo.
units.tr: (3) Those which were imputed to him. Verse 5: "bruised by our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him" [עָלָיו]. Verse 8: "when the debt was exacted he was afflicted, and he did not open his mouth; like a little sheep he was led to slaughter." (4) So formerly, in the case of sacrificial victims, the guilt of the offerers was laid, as it were by hands, upon the head of the beast, to be expiated; ceremonially there, but truly in Christ. Verse 8: "for the transgression of my people was he stricken." (5) Christ, however, was in himself wholly innocent and without sin. Verse 9: "he had done no violence, nor was there deceit in his mouth." (6) That transfer or delegation of our guilt to Christ was not made by chance, but with God willing it so. Verse 10: "and the LORD was pleased to bruise him." (7) He who cast into Christ, as a willing and strong surety, all our debts. Verse 6: "the LORD made to fall on him the iniquity of us all." (8) And Christ bore these gladly. Verse 4: "surely he took up our diseases," and "carried our sorrows"; verse 11: "their iniquities he shall bear"; verse 12: "and he bore the sin of many." (9) Wherefore God exacted them from him as from a surety. Verse 7: "as the debt was exacted, he was afflicted." (10) And Christ satisfied and expiated them. Verse 10: "he made his soul an offering for sin." (20) And so he redeemed us and saves us forever. Verse 11: "for the travail of his soul he shall see this and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many." Verse 12: "for he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors." From these things, all and each of the matters belonging to this business are clear: both what concerns the substitution of Christ in our place, and his satisfaction. For whoever, being innocent, desires and suffers that our sins, or guilt and punishments, be transferred to himself, God so willing and casting upon him what he should bear and what God should exact from him, so that as a propitiatory victim he expiates them by his life or soul, and who in this way redeems and saves men, is surely to be believed to have satisfied. But that Christ did these things appears from what is observed in that chapter. Therefore...

units.la: Socinus autem negat, ex illis evinci posse, Christo a Deo imputata fuisse peccata nostra, & eorum poenas abipso exactas esse. Quod est negare id, quod in Scriptura illa apertissime docetur. Namque ea adeo clare & dilucide traduntur nostro capite, ut clarius dici nil possit. Interrogo Adversarios, omniumque hominum conscientiam, viderint, an si nostrae, quam diximus, sententiae Propheta fuit, alio modo significare & exprimere se debuerit potueritve, quam fecit? Si non, quid est ergo quod non in istam sententiam verba accipiunt, quam habent, & efflagitant? sin secus, age proferant locutiones, quibus putent, Prophetam usurum aliter fuisse. Nos certe non videmus, quibus magis emphaticis sententiam nostram exprimere debuerit, quam iis & vocibus, & phrasibus, quibus hoc egit. Nam non unum aliquod sententiae caput, sed omnia, sed singula, eaque non uno verbo eodemque, sed pluribus, & variis, iisque quibus oportuit, rem proposuit, tractavit, explicuit.
units.tr: Socinus, however, denies that these passages can prove that our sins were imputed to Christ by God, and their punishment exacted from him. This is to deny what is taught most plainly in that Scripture. For the matter is set out so clearly and lucidly in our chapter that nothing clearer could be said. I ask the Adversaries, and the conscience of all people, to consider whether, if the Prophet held the view we have stated, he could have signified and expressed it in any other way than he did. If not, why do they not take the words in the sense they plainly bear, which they resist and try to force? But if they say otherwise, let them produce the phrases by which they think the Prophet would have expressed himself differently. We certainly cannot see by what more emphatic words he could have expressed our view than by those words and phrases he used. For he set out the matter, treated it and explained it, not only one part of the sense but all of it, and each part, and not with one word only, but with several and varied words, and with those that were needed.

units.la: Socinus, de Servat. part. 11. cap. iv. pag. 94. Quod si animadvertisses, ferre & portare in sacris litteris per metonymicam quandam translationem, auferre nonnunquam significare (quod enim alicunde aufertur, abeo, qui aufert, tantisper dum id abjiciat, aut alibi deponat, portatur) nunquam ex illis loquendi modis tantam veritatis sententiae tuae opinionem concepisses: tametsi alioqui haec locutio, portare peccatum, seu iniquitatem, in sacris litteris significare soleat, poenam peccati, seu iniquitatis subire. Resp. 1. En coactam, & praejudicatam expositionem. Fatetur, pro nostra sentensententiâ, stare Scripturam, & Scripturæ consuetudinem, quod portare pec-catum, in sacris litteris significare soleat, poenam peccati, seu iniquitatis subire.
units.tr: Socinus, De Servatore, part 2, chapter 4, page 94: "But if you had noticed that 'to bear' and 'to carry' in the sacred letters sometimes signify, by a certain metonymical transfer, 'to take away' (for what is taken away from somewhere is carried by him who takes it away, for as long as he is putting it down or setting it aside elsewhere), you would never have conceived such confidence in the truth of your opinion from those modes of speaking. Although otherwise this expression, to bear sin or iniquity, in the sacred letters is usually taken to mean to undergo the punishment of sin or iniquity." Reply 1. Here is a forced and prejudiced explanation. He admits that Scripture and the usage of Scripture stand on our side, since to bear sin in the sacred letters usually signifies to undergo the punishment of sin or iniquity.

units.la: Atque eo sensu dicimus, id de Christo hic efferri, quod poenam iniquitatis nostræ subiit. Et hoc non semel de Christo, & hic, & alibi, sed cum pluries, tum aliis iterum & aliis verbis phrasibusque expressum: ut de consuetâ phrasis hic etiam loci acceptione dubium prorsus esse nequeat. ii. Ipse vero alium obtrudit sensum, multâ parte imminutum, & enervatum, cum semper, quousque licet, pro plenitudine sermonis sacri laborare Interpretes, ex communi exponendi Scripturas regulâ, oporteat. Portare peccatum est, inquit, auferre. Sed, per translationem, & quandam, & metonymicam. Ergo, non proprie. Quuum regula itidem nota sit & certa, in exponendâ Scripturâ, à verborum proprietate recedendum non esse, extra necessitatem, quæ id cogat. Hic nulla est, nisi præjudicium opinionis malæ: imo plurima adsunt, quæ sensum proprium omnino postulant. Deinde, nonnunquam, ait, in Scripturis portare significat auferre: non autem semper. Unde quid eum impulerit ad præferendum sensum vocis tropicum, nec frequentem, proprio & usitato, facile est divinare. iii. Nos vero dicimus, quod portare, per se non significat auferre; uti auferre, portare. Non qui portat aliquid, id ideo aufert. Uti qui ægritudinem portat & dolorem sive animi, sive corporis, non aliunde aufert. Qui aufert idem, non tamen semper portat. Quorsum ergo dixit, quod alicunde auferatur, ab eo, qui aufert, tantisper dum id abjiciat, aut alibi deponat, portatur? quod sanè non est verum, neque ullus velit, se id portare debere, quodcunque ab alio aufert vel alteri adimit. Quod nec in physicis, nec in moralibus, nec in pœnis, quas hic spectamus, satis ubique verum. iv. Interim haud negamus, Christum peccata nostra abstulisse: sed etiam portavit, & portando abstulit. Non pugnant ista, nedum ut se perimant in Christo, portare peccata nostra, & auferre. Neque vox portare, suâ natura, aut usu, auferre significat. Sed rei, non vocis vi, in Christo utrumque concurrit, & verum est, quod peccata nostra portavit, abstulitque. Minimè omnium ut portare, solùm auferre significet: & sic, amissâ suâ significatione, transeat in sensum à suo alienum, & suo adversum: nempe ut sit, portavit, id est abstulit tantummodò, & non portavit quoque. Portare peccatum, etiamSocinus agnovit,non ipsum peccatum significare, sed peccati reatum, & pœnam. Hoc ipso in loco, Peccatum, seu prævaricatio, sive iniquitas, in hoc, & similibus locis non delictum ipsum, hoc est, ipsum factum, quod proprie auferri nequit, sed delicti reatum, & pœnam declarat.
units.tr: And in that sense we say that what is here declared of Christ is that he underwent the punishment of our iniquity. And this is said of Christ not once only, here and elsewhere, but many times, and expressed again and again in other words and phrases, so that there can be no doubt about the usual sense of the phrase even in this place. ii. Socinus, however, forces upon us another sense, greatly diminished and weakened, whereas interpreters ought, by the common rule for expounding Scripture, always to labour, as far as they can, for the fullness of the sacred speech. "To bear sin," he says, "is to take away. But by a certain transfer and metonymy." Therefore not in the proper sense. Since the rule is likewise known and certain, that in expounding Scripture one must not depart from the proper meaning of words unless necessity compels it. Here there is no such necessity, except the prejudice of a bad opinion; indeed very many things are present which altogether demand the proper sense. Next, he says that sometimes in Scripture to bear signifies to take away, but not always. Whence it is easy to guess what drove him to prefer the figurative sense of the word, which is not frequent, to the proper and usual one. iii. We, however, say that to bear does not of itself signify to take away, just as to take away does not signify to bear. He who carries something does not for that reason take it away; as he who bears sickness and pain, whether of mind or of body, does not take them away from elsewhere. He who takes away does not always bear. Why then did he say, "that what is taken away from somewhere is carried by him who takes it away, for as long as he is putting it down or setting it aside elsewhere"? which is certainly not true, nor would anyone want to be bound to bear whatever he takes from another or removes from someone else. This holds true neither in physical nor in moral matters, nor in the punishments which we are considering here. iv. Meanwhile we by no means deny that Christ took away our sins; but he also bore them, and by bearing he took them away. These things do not conflict, far less destroy each other, in Christ: to bear our sins and to take them away. Nor does the word to bear, by its nature or usage, signify to take away. But by the force of the thing, not of the word, both come together in Christ, and it is true that he bore our sins and took them away. Least of all does to bear signify only to take away, so that, having lost its own meaning, it passes into a sense alien to its own and opposed to it: namely, that he bore, that is, merely took away, and did not also bear. Socinus himself acknowledged that to bear sin does not signify the sin itself, but the guilt and punishment of sin. In this very place: "Sin, or transgression, or iniquity, in this and similar passages does not declare the offence itself, that is, the deed itself, which strictly cannot be taken away, but the guilt and punishment of the offence."

units.la: Socinus : Interim ferre, seu portare, au-ferendi simpliciter significationem aliquando habere demonstremus. Scriptum est Exod. cap. 34. verf. 7. de Jehova, servans misericor-diam millibus, auferens iniquitatem, & prævaricationem, & peccatum. In Hebræo autem est pro auferens, nõse[?] quod portans proprie significat. Num. 14. 18. Unde Scripto-
units.tr: Socinus: "Meanwhile let us show that to bear, or carry, sometimes simply has the sense of taking away. It is written in Exodus 34:7, of Jehovah, keeping mercy for thousands, taking away iniquity and transgression and sin. But in the Hebrew, instead of taking away, it is nōsē, which properly means bearing. Numbers 14:18. Whence the Scripture-

units.la: Resp. נשא[?] auferendi significa-tionem aliquando habere, haud negamus: illisque & aliis locis Scripturæ significare, pecca​ti pœnam auferre, eamque remittere & condonare: sed nec Socinus, nec quispiam dicet, vocem נשא[?] non pluries significare, vere & proprie aliquid portare, & in humeros
units.tr: Reply: That the verb nāsā [נשא] sometimes has the sense of taking away we do not deny; and in those and other places of Scripture it signifies to take away the punishment of sin, and to remit and forgive it. But neither Socinus nor anyone else will say that the word nāsā [נשא] does not often signify, truly and properly, to carry something on the shoulders

units.la: [The Hebrew words in the reply are written with vowels; the first and second occurrences are both uncertain.] res novi Fœderis & ipsi aliquando βαστά-ζω, quod proprie portare seu bajulare significat, pro auferre usurparunt. Nam Joh. 2. verf. 15. ubi scriptum est, Domine, si tu sustulisti eum, dicito mihi, ubi posuisti eum, in graeco est, κύριε εἰ σὺ ἐβάστασας αὐτόν. Propterea cum apud Esajam legitur de Christo, vere languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse portavit, non intelligendum est, Christum sustinuisse universas poenas, quas nos sustinere debueramus: sed sensus eorum verborum est, Christum a nobis omnes dolo-res & languores nostros abstulisse, & nos (ea ratione potissimum, quam paullo ante expo-suimus) ab omnibus nostris malis redemisse & liberasse. Matth. 8. 16. 17. suscipere : unde משא onus. Adeo ut quando נשא auferre vel remittere pec-catum significat, hoc non vi vocis fiat, sed totius sermonis, ob subjectam ma-teriam, quae commodiorem sensum non fert. נשא ferre significat; & prop-ter rem cui adhibetur, auferre; aliquan-do adferre: quia saltem utrobique inter-cedit latio aliqua: sed in loco Jesajae, neque solum נשא, sed & סבל, & tum res, tum voces illae occurrunt, quae omnino indicant, portandi sen-sum proprium excludi nec posse, nec debere. נשא ibi non conjungitur cum peccatis, non cum פשע, חטא, עון, cum quibus semper sensu remissionis conjungi solet, sed cum doloribus nostris. Ut vel ista diversitas nos in alium sensum ducat, quam Socini est. נשא חלינו הוא morbos nostros ipse tulit, ומכאבינו סבלם, & dolores nostros por-tavit eos. Quae alia est loquutio, quam ubi Scriptura simpliciter dicit, Deum remittere peccata. Nihilque non modo in textu est, quod solam auferendi, vel remittendi (quod praecise hic non respicitur, neque si textum Jesajae, vel Matthaei intueamur; utcumque res quidem cum illo cunjungatur omnino, sive remissio peccatorum, cum illa Christi dolorum nostrorum portatione: quod non negamus) expositionem poscit, sed & vocis נשא nativa & frequentissima significatio, & propria solaque סבל, & morborum dolorumque conjugatio, qui lati & portati à Christo Jesu intelligi debent, omnia eunt incontrarium. Unde Graeci, hoc in loco, αἴρει[?] τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει; non ἀναφέρει. Iterum verf. 11. ועונותם הוא ישא, & iniqui-ates ipsorum ipse portavit, non est נשא, quod de remissione aliquoties adhibetur, sed סבל, quod nunquam non portare significat: ne dubitemus, doceri peccatorum sive poenarum propriam in Christum translationem. 111. עליו super ipsum dicitur castigatio nostra fuisse, verf. 5. & Deus conjecisse in eum peccata nostra, fecit incurrere in eum iniquitatem omnium nostrum, verf. 6. & quando peccatum nostrum exigere Deo placuit, ipse afflictus & contritus fuit, verf. 7. 10. 5. Quarto, imo ubi נשא cum peccatis jungitur, non ubique auferre, sed etiam portare significat: uti in Levitico aliquoties dicitur, de reo quod feret peccatum suum. ישאו עונם, portabunt iniquitatem suam, Levit. xx, 19. & verf. seq. ישאו חטאם, peccatum suum portabunt. Cap. xxii. 9. Num. xiv. 34. & xviii. 1. 2. 3, 32. &c. Ipse hic Socinus: in Hebraeo est nose, quod portans proprie significat, Quinto סבל, quod æque hoc in textu occurrit, ac נשא, numquam simpliciter auferre significat, semper bajulavit, portavit. Unde מַשָּׂא [?] onus, bajulus. Ne unus quidem in contrarium proferri locus potest. Quid ergo ad hoc perversitas excipiet, quando Christus haud semel dicitur portasse, & dolores, & peccata nostra? verf. 4. & 11. Haud metuimus, ut candidus & probus Scripturae ac veritatis sectator malit verbum illud in contrarium sensum trahere, contra suum proprium, naturalem, & perpetuum. Sed qui errare & pervertere data opera velit, sibi dictum, scriptum novit, ὁ ῥυπῶν, ῥυπωσάτω ἔτι. Ergo simpliciter vel tantum abstulit peccata nostra Christus, non quoque bajulavit? Quorsum ergo hac voce, praeter alia eodem facientia, usus Propheta, quae significationem aliam nusquam habent? Ipse iterum Socinus, quemadmodum de נשא, similiter de מַשָּׂא pronunciat, quod proprie portare seu bajulare significat. Nos ergo propriam sequimur significationem, ipse alienam. Cui illam praeferendam passim esse omnes norunt. vi. Quod de scriptoribus N. T. ait, nimis temerarium. Cedo unum locum, ubi βαστάζειν non notet portare. Auferre significat, sed auferre, absque portatione? ut portare excludat, vel ei opponatur? nequaquam. Qui portat, eo quod portat, saepe etiam aufert, atque ita non opponuntur illa, sed conjunguntur; neque vis vocis est, quae auferre dicat, sed rei, cui adhibetur. Atque apud Jesaiam vis βαστάζειν auferre significare, oppositE & exclusive ad portationem? falsum. In N. Test. τὰ [illegible, ~10 letters] βαστάζειν. Matth. iii. 11. τὸ βάρος, cap. xx. 12. κεφάλιον, Marc. xiv. 13. βαστάζων τὴν ὑδρίαν. Luc. vii. 14. βαλλάντιον, cap. x. 4. τὴν [?] σκευήν, cap. xiv. 27. Joan. xix. 17. aliaque istius generis plura sunt: nusquam non βαστάζειν portare significat & bajulare. Joann. xx. 15. εἰ σὺ ἐβάστασάς αὐτόν, non significat, abstulisti absque portatione, sed omnino, si tu asportasti. Ipse quoque Socinus ita vertit, sustulisti, non, abstulisti. Racoviensis versio, hastu ihn weggetragen? vii. Ergo sensus verborum apud Prophetam non est simpliciter Christum a nobis omnes dolores & languores abstulisse, & nos ab omnibus malis nostris redemisse & liberasse, sed primum quidem portasse illos atque in semet suscepisse. Frustra committit inter se Socinus, tanquam ἀντιδιαστολή[?], quae conjuncta sunt. Non negamus ista, quae dicit, vera esse: modo ne neget quoque nostra. Aliquid ille dicit quidem, non omne verum, non illud, quod praesens locus maxime urget, exponit, & exaggerat. Quod ante omnia tollendum negandumque haud fuit. Et quod non ex verbis illis solum, sed toto contextu & capite confirmamus. vii. Matth. viii. 16. 17. Vespere autem facto obtulerunt ei multos daemonia habentes; & ejiciebat spiritus verbo: & omnes male habentes curavit; ut adimpleretur, quod dictum est per Esajam prophetam, ipse infirmitates nostras accepit, & morbos portavit. Primo nec ipse Socinus vult, in hac corporali multorum sanatione adimpletam proprie prophetiam illam esse: nempe quasi hæc de corporalibus infirmitatibus loquuta fuerit, vel de iis sanan-dis aut curandis. Quare nec in eo proprie prophetiæ expositio constituenda est. Verè tamen in eo etiam adimpleta prophetia dicitur, vel potius ad illud: non quod istum in sensum exponenda verba sint; sed quod in illâ re, quam Christus ibi exhibuit, sanatione vid. infirmorum, tanquam in clarissimo documento, apparuit, & eum præsentem esse, quem vaticinatus propheta fuerat, & revera id præstiturum, quod prædixerat, sanationem sc. & liberatio-nem animarum ab omnibus malis & infirmiratibus, quum tam illustre ejus specimen & symbolum jam ibi ostenderet in corporalibus, à nemine quam isto curandis. Adimpletum ergo Prophetæ vaticinium isto facto, non quod ad proprium verborum sensum, sed in applicatione prophetiæ ad personam verè & proprie, ad corporale illud factum symbolice. Non verba respexit Matthæus, sed rem, quæ, pro litterali sensu non accipienda de corporali sa-natione esse, omnes intelligunt. Perperam ergo hîc verbi καταζητεῖ[?] quærit expositionem Socinus, eamque alienam. Verba apud Matthæum nec ponderantur, nec exponuntur; sed simplex est totius sermonis, vel rei eo comprehensæ singu-laris quædam applicatio. Socinus: eadem ratione locum illum ad spirituales nostras infirmitates, & morbos accommodantes, inquit. Perperam iterum: nam ex loci pro-phetici apud Matthæum accommodatione ad infirmitates corporales, ille ad spirituales trahendus non est, qui ipsissimus & proprius prophetiæ sensus; sed de spiritualibus qui omnino accipi debet, ad corporalia à Matthæo accommoda-tus fuit. Expositio loci genuina est de spiritualibus infirmitatibus, earumque per Christum liberatione; & ejus accommodatio ad corporalia: non viceversa. Jam aliquid in portatione spiritualium malorum nostrorum per Christum inter-cessit, quod non item in corporalium; neque integra prophetia, ex quâ argu-mentamur, & non ex non solo commate, quod Matthæus adduxit, ad corpo-ralem sanationem applicari potest: & Socinus de pœnis peccatorum nostro-rum addidit, eas Christum quodammodo in longinquam aliquam regionem secum aspor-tasse. Quod de corporalibus nec dici, nec de pœnis aliis in longinquam regionem asportatis intelligi bene potest.
units.tr: The writers of the New Covenant also sometimes used βαστάζω, which properly means to carry or bear, in the sense of to take away. For in John 2 v. 15, where it is written, "Sir, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him," the Greek is κύριε εἰ σὺ ἐβάστασας αὐτόν. Therefore, when Isaiah says of Christ, "Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows," it is not to be understood that Christ bore all the punishments that we ought to have borne. The sense of those words is rather that Christ has taken away from us all our sorrows and infirmities, and has redeemed and freed us from all our evils, chiefly in the way we explained a little earlier. Matt. 8. 16. 17. Hence the verb נשא [to take up] means to take up, and from it comes משא, a burden. So when נשא means to take away or to forgive sin, this does not happen by the force of the word itself but by that of the whole sentence, because of the matter under discussion, which does not admit a more suitable sense. נשא means to bear, and, according to the thing to which it is applied, to take away, and sometimes to bring: since in each case there is some kind of carrying. But in the passage of Isaiah there occur not only נשא but also סבל, and both the words and the things they refer to clearly show that the proper sense of bearing can be neither excluded nor should be. נשא is not joined there with sins, not with פשע, חטא, or עון, with which it is usually joined in the sense of remission, but with our sorrows. So even this difference should lead us to a sense other than Socinus's: נשא חלינו הוא, he himself bore our sicknesses, and ומכאבינו סבלם, and carried our sorrows. This is a different form of speech from that in which Scripture simply says that God forgives sins. Nothing in the text, not only, the bare sense of taking away or forgiving (which is not precisely in view here, whether we look at the text of Isaiah or of Matthew; although the thing itself is certainly joined with that bearing of our sorrows by Christ, which we do not deny), but also the native and most frequent meaning of the word נשא, and the proper and sole meaning of סבל, and the conjugation of sicknesses and sorrows, which must be understood as taken up and borne by Christ Jesus, all point the other way. Hence the Greeks, in this place, have αἴρει τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει, not ἀναφέρει. Again in verse 11, ועונותם הוא ישא, and he himself shall bear their iniquities: here the word is not נשא, which is sometimes used of forgiveness, but סבל, which always means to bear. Let us not doubt that what is taught is the transfer of sins or punishments to Christ in the proper sense. In verse 5 it is said that our chastisement was upon him, עליו, and in verse 6 that God laid on him the iniquity of us all, and in verse 7 that when it pleased God to exact our debt, he was afflicted and crushed. Fourth, and indeed where נשא is joined with sins, it does not always mean to take away, but also to bear: as in Leviticus it is said several times of the guilty man who shall bear his sin, ישאו עונם, they shall bear their iniquity, Lev. 20:19, and in the following verse ישאו חטאם, they shall bear their sin; Lev. 22:9; Num. 14:34; 18:1, 2, 3, 32, etc. Socinus himself says: in Hebrew it is nose, which properly means bearing. Fifth, סבל, which occurs in this text just as נשא does, never simply means to take away, but always to bear or carry. Hence מַשָּׂא, a burden, a porter. Not even one passage can be brought forward to the contrary. What, then, will perversity object to this, when Christ is said more than once to have borne both our sorrows and our sins? Verses 4 and 11. We are not afraid that a sincere and upright seeker of Scripture and truth would prefer to drag that word into the opposite sense, against its own proper, natural and constant meaning. But whoever wishes to err and pervert on purpose should know what is said: let him who is filthy be filthy still. Did Christ, then, simply or only take away our sins, and not also bear them? Why then did the prophet use this word, along with other words to the same effect, which nowhere have another meaning? Socinus again, just as he says of נשא, says similarly of מַשָּׂא that it properly means to bear or carry. We therefore follow the proper meaning, and he an alien one; and everyone knows that the proper one is everywhere to be preferred. Sixth, what he says about the writers of the New Testament is too rash. Show me one place where βαστάζειν does not mean to carry. It means to take away, but to take away without carrying? So that it excludes carrying or is opposed to it? Not at all. He who carries, by the very fact that he carries, often also takes away; so these things are not opposed but joined; and it is not the force of the word that says "take away," but the force of the thing to which it is applied. And is the force of βαστάζειν in Isaiah to mean to take away, opposed and exclusive to carrying? That is false. In the New Testament we have τὸ βάρος βαστάζειν (Matt. 3:11), τὸ κεφάλιον (Matt. 20:12), βαστάζων τὴν ὑδρίαν (Mark 14:13), βαλλάντιον (Luke 7:14), τὴν σκευήν (Luke 10:4), and (Luke 14:27), and John 19:17, and there are many more of this kind: everywhere βαστάζειν means to carry and to bear. In John 20:15, εἰ σὺ ἐβάστασάς αὐτόν, it does not mean you have taken him away without carrying, but simply, if you have carried him off. Socinus himself also translates it sustulisti, not abstulisti. The Racovian version has hast du ihn weggetragen? Seventh, therefore the sense of the words in the prophet is not simply that Christ took away from us all sorrows and infirmities, and redeemed and freed us from all our evils; but first that he indeed bore them and took them upon himself. Socinus vainly sets against one another, as if they were opposites, things that are joined together. We do not deny that the things he says are true, provided he does not also deny ours. He says something true, but not the whole truth; he does not explain or emphasise what the present passage most urges, which was by no means to be removed or denied first of all. And we confirm this not only from those words but from the whole context and chapter. Seventh, Matt. 8:16, 17: And when evening was come, they brought to him many that were possessed with devils; and he cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all that were sick; that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, He took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses. First, Socinus himself does not wish that prophecy to be properly fulfilled in this bodily healing of many people, as if these words spoke of bodily infirmities, or of healing or curing them. Therefore the proper exposition of the prophecy is not to be founded on that. Yet the prophecy is truly said to be fulfilled in it, or rather to that point: not that the words are to be explained in that sense, but that in the matter which Christ there displayed, namely the healing of the sick, as in a most clear demonstration, he appeared as the one whom the prophet had foretold, and would really accomplish what he had predicted, namely the healing and deliverance of souls from all evils and infirmities, since he had already shown there so illustrious a specimen and symbol of it in bodily things, which no one but he could cure. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled by that deed not in the proper sense of the words, but in the application of the prophecy to the person, truly and properly, while that bodily deed was symbolic. Matthew did not regard the words but the matter, which everyone understands is not to be taken in the literal sense of a bodily healing. Socinus therefore wrongly seeks here an exposition of the word καταζητεῖ, and an alien one at that. The words in Matthew are neither weighed nor expounded; there is simply a certain particular application of the whole discourse, or of the matter comprised in it. Socinus: by the same reasoning he adapts that passage to our spiritual infirmities and sicknesses, he says. Wrongly again: for from the adaptation of the prophetic passage in Matthew to bodily infirmities, it does not follow that it must be dragged to spiritual ones. The most genuine and proper sense of the prophecy is about spiritual infirmities and their deliverance through Christ; it was Matthew who adapted it to bodily things, not the reverse. The genuine exposition of the passage concerns spiritual infirmities and their deliverance through Christ; its adaptation to bodily things is secondary. Moreover, there is something in the bearing of our spiritual evils by Christ that does not equally occur in bodily ones; nor can the whole prophecy, from which we argue, and not merely the one clause Matthew quoted, be applied to bodily healing. And Socinus added, concerning the punishments of our sins, that Christ had carried them off with him in some way into a distant region. This can neither be said of bodily things, nor well be understood of other punishments carried off into a distant region.

units.la: Pergit Socinus, de Servat. part. II. cap. v. & ad alia prophetæ Jesaiæ isto cap. LIII. loca diluenda sic se accingit: nam revera ipsum Prophetam suâ expositione impetunt Adversarii, non adeo nos. Atque versum cap. sextum, ubi dicitur, quod Deus omnium nostrum iniquitatem Christo impegit, imputavit, vel incurrere in eum fecit [illegible, ~4 letters], hunc in modum eludit: non quia illi errata nostra imputata fuerint, vel eorum pœnas ipse vice omnium nostrum subierit; sed quoniam non aliter, atque si super se omnes iniquitates nostras, & supplicia illa divina lege debita habuisset, quam longissime à nobis ea asportavit, atque projecit. Cui fini etiam adhibet ex V. T. similitudinem hirci emissarii, Levit.xvi. ubi quidem dicitur, inquit, Aharonem ponere omnia populi errata super hircum, non quia ipsi hirco imputarentur, aut quia hircus ille pœnas erratis populi debitas penderet: sed quoniam ea secum asportare censebatur, non secus ac si super illum universa posita fuissent. Hæc prima ejus in versum illum expositio.
units.tr: Socinus goes on (De Servatore, part II, chap. 5) and sets about refuting the other passages of this 53rd chapter of the prophet Isaiah in the following way. For our opponents attack the Prophet himself by their interpretation, not so much us. As for the sixth verse, where it is said that God laid the iniquity of us all upon Christ, imputed it, or made it fall upon him [illegible, about 4 letters], he evades it in this manner: not because our errors were imputed to him, or because he himself underwent their punishments in place of us all; but because he carried them very far away from us and cast them off, as if he had had all our iniquities and the punishments due to them by divine law upon himself. To support this purpose he also adduces from the Old Testament the likeness of the scapegoat, Lev. 16, where indeed it is said, he says, that Aaron lays all the errors of the people upon the goat, not because they were imputed to the goat itself, or because that goat paid the punishments due to the people's errors; but because it was supposed to carry them away with it, no differently than if all things had been laid upon it. This is his first interpretation of that verse.

units.la: Resp. 1. Hircus ille non quidem propriâ & reali imputatione imposita sibi habuit peccata populi ; tamen caeremonialiter: & qua ratione auferebat, portabat quoque. Sic enim exserte dicitur, vers. 21. וְסָמַךְ[?] & imponit Aharon linas manus suas super ראש[?] super caput hirci vivenris[?], & confitebitur super ipsum omnes iniquitates filiorum Israëlis, & omnes transgressiones ipsorum, juxta omnia ipsorum peccata, & ponet ea super eaput וְנָתַן אֹתָם עַל־רֹאשׁ, & emittet eum per manum viri prae-sentis in desertum. Ergo ὡς ἐν τύπῳ in eum imponebantur populi peccata, quod ad caeremoniam, non quod ad proprietatem. ii. Quid dices, non aliter etiam fuisse Christo imposita? Christum ergo in ordinem redige τῶν σκιῶν[?] & στοιχείων[?], & non pro corpore umbrarum ipsarum aestima: & Apostolo objice, qui in epistola ad Hebraeos id ex professo agit, ut ostendat, in Christo proprie & perfectissime locum habere, quae caeremoniis V. Test. olim fuerunt adumbrata. Heb. ix. 12. 13. 14. & cap. x 4. 5. &c. Nescio, qui clarius exprimi possit, Christo errata nostra imputata fuisse, & poenas eum nostras subi-isse, quam verbis istis ויהוה הפגיע[?] בו את עון כלנו, Deus fecit occurrere in eum iniquitatem omnium nostrum? Quod aeque est ac si scriptum fuisset, Deum in Christo iniquitatem omnium nostrum, sive poenam iniquitatibus nostris debitam, posuisse: ipse hic ita loqui cogitur Socinus. iii. Et tamen negat, illi errata nostra im-putata. Sed, inquit, non aliter atque si super se omnes iniquitates nostras ha-buisset. Quod quis unquam Christianorum absque stomacho audiat? namque id est Christum, non aliter ac si ex Vet. T. caeremoniis aliquid fuisset, reputare. Ibi obtinebat illa locutio, & sic de hirco, de aliis dici consuevit, non aliter atque si super se iniquitates populi habuissent, eas asportasse atque projecisse. Itane & de Christo ausis tu loqui? Cedo, ubi de Christo, ejus propter peccata nostra passionibus, vel in Vet. vel in N. T. illa aut similis uspiam locutio, non aliter atque si super se iniquitates nostras habuisset. Absolutissime semper & ubique de Christo asseritur, nulla uspiam addita diminuente similitudine aut similitudinis nota, aut quasi per similitudinem fuisset, quod Christus nostra in se suscepit & sustinuit peccata. Repete quam multa hoc uno in capite occurrant, quae id dicunt haud semel, & aliis atque aliis identidem confirmant modis, phrasibusque. Nullibi vel minima dubitandi suspicio, ac si improprie & dicis causa illa de Christo dicta essent, & non proprie atque simpliciter. iv. In textu non dicitur solùm, quod Christus peccata nostra asportavit, sed quod partavit quoque; non projecit duntaxat a nobis, sed quia primum suscepit illa in sese. Portavit, & asportavit. Neque magis illud tibi evacuare licet, per quasi, aut non aliter ac si, quam istud: quin simul potius improprie, & per similitudinem aliquam talem facitote Christum vestrum in hoc, alteroque. Graeci: οὗτος[?] τὰς[?] ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει[?], καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται[?]. Atque postea iterum, vers. 11. καὶ τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν αὐ-τὸς ἀνοίσει[?].
units.tr: Reply. 1. That goat did not indeed have the sins of the people laid upon it by a proper and real imputation, yet it had them ceremonially; and by the same reason by which it carried them away, it also bore them. For it is said expressly in verse 21: "And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the living goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions, according to all their sins; and he shall put them upon the head [וְנָתַן אֹתָם עַל־רֹאשׁ] of the goat, and send it away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness." So the sins of the people were laid upon it as in a figure, as to the ceremony, not as to the reality. ii. What will you say: that they were not also laid upon Christ in the same way? Then reduce Christ to the order of shadows and elements [τῶν σκιῶν, στοιχείων], and do not value him as the substance of those shadows. Object to the Apostle, who in the Epistle to the Hebrews does exactly this, to show that what was once foreshadowed by the ceremonies of the Old Testament has its proper and most perfect fulfilment in Christ: Heb. 9:12, 13, 14, and 10:4, 5, etc. I do not know how it could be expressed more clearly that our errors were imputed to Christ and that he underwent our punishments than by these words: "The LORD made to meet upon him the iniquity of us all" [וַיהוה הִפְגִּיעַ בּוֹ אֶת עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ]. That is just as if it had been written that God placed in Christ the iniquity of us all, that is, the punishment due to our iniquities; and Socinus himself is forced to speak thus here. iii. And yet he denies that our errors were imputed to him. But, he says, "not otherwise than if he had had all our iniquities upon himself." Who of the Christians could hear this without indignation? For that is to think of Christ as "not otherwise than if he had been some ceremony of the Old Testament." There that expression held, and thus it is customary to say of the goat, and of others, "not otherwise than if they had had the iniquities of the people upon themselves, and had carried them away and cast them off." Do you dare to speak thus of Christ? Tell me, where anywhere in the Old or New Testament is there such an expression, or a similar one, said of Christ with respect to his sufferings for our sins: "not otherwise than if he had had our iniquities upon himself"? Absolutely always and everywhere it is asserted of Christ, with no diminishing likeness added anywhere, no mark of similitude, and no hint that it was as if by a likeness, that Christ took our sins upon himself and bore them. Consider how many things occur in this one chapter that say this more than once, and confirm it again and again by different means and phrases. Nowhere is there the least suspicion of doubt, as if those things said of Christ were improper, said for the sake of argument, and not properly and simply. iv. In the text it is said not only that Christ carried away our sins, but that he also bore them; not merely that he removed them from us, but that he first took them upon himself. He bore them and carried them away. Nor may you evacuate this by the words "as if" or "not otherwise than if" any more than you could evacuate that; rather, by doing so you would make your Christ improper and a matter of some likeness in this passage and in the other. Greek: "He bears our sins, and is pained for us" [οὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει, καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται]. And again afterwards, verse 11: "and he himself shall bear their sins" [καὶ τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν αὐτὸς ἀνοίσει].

units.la: 11. Excipit Socinus, alia excogitata verborum expositione, nempe, Et Iehova occurrit per eum, sive potius, cum eo, iniquitati omnium nostrum. Aut, & Iehova occurrere fecit ei iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Priore modo sensus erit, Dum per Christum omnes iniquitates, seu iniquitatum poenas à nobis, illis quodammodo per ipsum, vel cum ipso occurrendo, depulisse. Posteriore autem modo sensus erit, Deum effecisse ut omnium nostrum iniquitates Christo obviam fierent, & ipsum quodammodo aggrederentur, cum nostrarum iniquitatum causa eum mori voluerit. Resp. Er versatile & dolosum infausti hominis ingenium. In primâ exceptione vel responsione non nisi per dubia & impropria se explicuit, non aliter ac si; hic iterum, in unâ & altera responsione, per quodammodo. Quando tandem solidam simplicemque veritatem ingenue & constanter amplectentur isti homines? Quid ni & pari facilitate, & majori jure nobis licet repudiare quidquid tandem ejusmodi responsionum lubricarum adferunt Auctores, quarum nec ipsi certi sunt, nedum alii post illos? An istum in modum vel Scriptura exponi vult, vel veri Expositores eam tractare solent? & non potius firmiter, cumque πληροφορίᾳ[?], absque φλυαρίας[?], dicere convenit, quod Scriptura clare satis & certò docet?
units.tr: 11. Socinus objects, with another contrived interpretation of the words, namely: "And the LORD meets through him, or rather with him, the iniquity of us all." Or: "and the LORD caused the iniquity of us all to meet him." In the former way the sense will be that, through Christ, by meeting them as it were through him or with him, he has driven away from us the iniquities, or the punishments of iniquities. In the latter way the sense will be that God brought it about that the iniquities of us all should meet Christ and somehow assail him, since he willed him to die on account of our iniquities. Answer: what a shifty and deceitful mind this unhappy man has! In his first objection or answer he explains himself only by doubtful and improper terms, "not otherwise than if"; here again, in one answer and the other, by "somehow". When at last will these men sincerely and constantly embrace solid and simple truth? Why should we not, with equal ease and greater right, reject whatever such slippery answers the authors bring, of which they themselves are not sure, let alone others after them? Is this the way Scripture wishes to be explained, or is this how true expositors customarily handle it? Rather it is fitting to say firmly, and with full assurance [πληροφορίᾳ], without idle talk [φλυαρίας], what Scripture clearly and certainly teaches.

units.la: 11. Deinde repugnat sensui verborum, & rei mira expositio utraque. Prior, quia quid illud est, Deum iniquitatibus nostris occurrere quodammodo per ipsum, vel cum ipso Christo? Et alii & alia etiam occurrunt iniquitatibus, si satis sit quoquo modo illa dici. Neque hic docetur, quod Deus peccata à nobis depellit; sed cum iis in Christum incurrit. Altera quod ait expositio, omnium nostrum iniquitates Christo obviam factas, eumque aggressas, quum earum causa moreretur, quid sibi vult, nisi statuamus, imputatas ipsi fuisse, & propterea ipsum mortuum? Quid enim ad mortem Christi faciunt alioqui peccata nostrum omnium? Martyrium Christi, quod illi in ejus morte constituunt, aliquando nobis prædicatum ad peccata deferenda, & fidem ipsi habendam, nihil cum peccatis nostris commune ita habet, ut ea ipsum aggressa dici possint, vel debeant; non collusatus cum iis, vel earum pœnis fuit, si pœnas non sensit. Quanto denique satius est, plana via & catholica locum exponere: fecit Deus occurrere in Christum pœnas omnium nostrum, eas illi imputando, ut sustineret, proque nobis exsolveret? Et sic demum vere & proprie, non imaginario iniquitates nostras Christum aggressas dici poterunt, neque ullo aliter modo. Incurrerunt in Christum, vel Deus fecit ut occurerent in eum, & aggrederentur ipsum: intelligi nequit, nisi quod conjectæ in eum fuerint: & hoc quo, nisi quod ipsi imputatæ? transfierunt, vel translatæ sunt in Christum, non quod ad culpam, sed pœnam: neque enim aliter potuit. Jam vero pœnæ Christum aggredi, invadere, impetere nulla alia ratione possunt, quam per imputationem. Atque hoc modo recte intelligitur, quomodo Deus peccata nostra fecerit incurrere in eum, וַיַּפְגַּע־בּוֹ[?]. Græci: καὶ Κυρίῳ[?] παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν.
units.tr: 11. Next, both of his interpretations are wonderfully at odds with the sense of the words and of the matter. The first, because what is it, that God should meet our iniquities somehow through him, or with him Christ? Other things, and other persons, also meet iniquities, if it is enough that they be said to do so in any way. Nor is it taught here that God drives sins away from us; rather, he runs with them into Christ. The second interpretation, that the iniquities of us all were made to meet Christ and assailed him, when he was dying on their account, what does it mean, unless we suppose they were imputed to him, and so he died? For what else do the sins of us all have to do with Christ's death? The martyrdom of Christ, which they set up in his death as preached to us for the removal of sins and for our faith in him, has nothing in common with our sins such that they can or ought to be said to have assailed him. He did not wrestle with them, or with their punishments, if he did not feel the punishments. Finally, how much better it is to expound the place in the plain and catholic way: God made the punishments of us all meet Christ, imputing them to him, so that he might bear them and pay for us! And so at last our iniquities could truly and properly be said to have assailed Christ, not imaginarily, and in no other way. They ran into Christ, or God made them meet him and assail him; this cannot be understood unless they were cast upon him, and in what sense is this, unless that they were imputed to him? They passed over, or were transferred, into Christ, not as to guilt but as to punishment, for they could not be otherwise. Now punishments can assail, invade, or attack Christ by no other means than by imputation. And in this way it is rightly understood how God made our sins run into him [וַיַּפְגַּע־בּוֹ]. Greek: "and the Lord delivered him up to our sins" [καὶ Κυρίῳ παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν].

units.la: Vers. 5. castigatio pacis nostræ super eum hunc in modum exponit: ut nihil aliud significet, quam Christum flagella & afflictiones subiisse, quæ nobis pacem idest felicitatem, & quietem pepererunt. Resp. מוּסַר[?] castigationem significare, omnes scimus: sed natura rei hoc loco, & subjecta materia non arguit castigationem quæ sit absque punitione, sed eam ipsam. Ne totum capitis contextum dicam, & seu antecedentia, seu consequentia, hoc ipso vertu dicitur affectus à prævaricationibus nostris, attritus ab iniquitatibus nostris. ii. & quod castigatio non fuit ejus, sed nostra, super eum. iii. propterea que ejus vibice nos sanati. Quæ non simpliciter castigatum, sed nostra castigatione, & iniquitatibus confectum dicunt. Castigatio autem non nisi pœnalis fuit. i. propria quia fuit & vera ipsius Christi. ii. in se perfectissime insontis & innocui, & nos nostrumque reatum nulla ratione per se, & extra imputationem, attingentis. iii. attamen & propter nos, lege sponsoris, peccatum factus ii. Cor. v. 21. & qui, quia nostra portavit, inque se suscepit, censitus fuit מכה אלהים casus Dei, & afflictus, verf. superiore. Denique cujus vibice & castigatione salus nobis promerita. Quod nulla alterius, vel simplici castigatione fieri potuit: & certe longe aliud est, quam quod Socinus hac pag. non nisi Christi calamitatibus & morte interveniente, potuisse nos ad cœlestem beatitudinem, tranquillitatemque aspirare. Quasi Christi mors sit causa modò sine qua non, non propriâ & directa causalitate vitam adferens; vel, quæ quoquo modo pacem, id est, felicitatem & quietem pariat nobis, non verâ & propriâ efficientiâ vel merito.
units.tr: Verse 5, "the chastisement of our peace upon him," is explained in this way: so that it signifies nothing more than that Christ underwent scourges and afflictions, which won us peace, that is, happiness and quiet. Reply: we all know that musar [מוּסַר] means chastisement. But the nature of the matter here and the subject under discussion do not point to chastisement that is without punishment; they point to chastisement itself. I need not go through the whole context of the chapter, before and after, where in this same verse it is said that he was bruised for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities (ii), and that the chastisement was not his but ours, upon him (iii), so that by his stripes we are healed. The text does not say he was simply chastised, but that he was chastised with our chastisement and made of our iniquities. Chastisement, however, could only be penal: (i) it was properly his own and truly his; (ii) he was in himself most perfectly innocent and harmless, and he touched us and our guilt in no way by himself, apart from imputation; (iii) yet on our account, by the law of surety, he was made sin (2 Cor. 5:21), and because he bore our burdens and took them upon himself, he was reckoned stricken of God [מכה אלהים], and afflicted, as in the preceding verse. Finally, it is by his stripes and chastisement that salvation was merited for us. This could not be done by any other or by simple chastisement. And it is certainly far different from what Socinus says on this page: that, except through Christ's calamities and the intervening death, we could not aspire to heavenly blessedness and tranquillity. As if Christ's death were merely a cause without which the effect does not follow, bringing life not by proper and direct causality, or as if it somehow produced peace, that is happiness and quiet, for us without true and proper efficacy or merit.

units.la: Socinus: Pax eo loco non reconciliationem, verùm quietem & felicitatem significat. Unde arguit, oppositum ei מוסר non punitionem notare, sed simpliciter afflictionem. Resp. i. Nescio quâ fronte vel animo dicat Socinus, pacem nobis Christi passionibus partâ non reconciliationem comprehendi, & significari. Quorsum opponit reconciliationem: & pacem, quasi unum evertat aut tollat? Omnem felicitatem pacis nomine designant Hebræi: & pro subjectâ materiâ etiam reconciliationem: quæ omnino hic intervenit, ac proinde generali & plenâ vocis acceptione etiam continetur. Quando justificati per fidem in Christum, pacem habere dicimur, Rom. v. 1. an reconciliatio excluditur? Christus pax nostra appellatur, ideo qui ἀποκαταλλάξας [?] reconciliavit nos Deo, per crucem. Ephes. ii. 14. 15. 16. atque hinc βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης. Heb. vii. 2. & in loco Jesajæ, ubi pacis nostræ castigatio super eum fuisse dicitur, reconciliatio intelligi non potest? Scilicet, ne cogatur per castigationem intelligere punitionem. Ergo contra communem Scripturæ, & fidelium sensum neganda quævis sunt, quæ hypothesi incommodant. Quis unquam Christianorum vel loco illo, vel quocumque alio, ubi sermo fit de pace Christi, reconciliationem eliminavit? Quod primus hoc in loco ausus fuit Socinus. Non reconciliationem significat, verùm quietem: imo ideo reconciliationem, quia quietem. Quia hæc abque illâ nulla est. Adeo non se mutuò tollunt, sed ponunt & comprehendunt illa. ii. Nihilo melius quod dixit, מוסר pro flagello seu afflictione sumere, non autem pro vera punitione cogit vox pacis, quæ ei non obscure opponitur. Nempe quia antithesis non est inter punitionem, & pacem, quemadmodum est inter pacem & afflictionem. Cedo cur non quadrat oppositio inter punitionem & pacem, æque ac inter pacem & afflictionem? nem ? Danda ratio fuerat, nec incongruitatis duntaxat, sed impossibilitatis, & ineptitudinis. Præsertim cur oppositio non quadret in Christum, per quem habemus primò recouciliationem[?], inde pacem, cui propriissime punitio opponitur, & non simpliciter afflictio. Ut hoc quidquid est, contra Adversarium faciat, non contra nos. Et id cogit vox pacis ? Quæso, quæ tanta est oppositio, inter afflictionem & pacem, ut illa sola hic valere possit? Per afflictionem promereri pacem magis, quam per punitionem, quis dixerit? De pace reconciliationis contrarium est manifestissimum, nec de quacunque illud minus verum.
units.tr: Socinus: Peace in that place signifies not reconciliation but quiet and happiness. From this he argues that the opposite of musar denotes not punishment but simply affliction. Reply. (i) I do not know with what face or mind Socinus says that the peace obtained for us by Christ's sufferings does not include and signify reconciliation. Why does he set reconciliation against peace, as if the one overturned or removed the other? The Hebrews designate all happiness by the word peace, and, given the subject matter, reconciliation as well, which certainly enters in here and is therefore contained in the general and full sense of the word. When we are said to have peace, being justified by faith in Christ (Rom. 5:1), is reconciliation excluded? Christ is called our peace, and therefore he who reconciled us to God through the cross (Eph. 2:14–16), and hence the king of peace (Heb. 7:2). And in the place of Isaiah where the chastisement of our peace is said to have been upon him, can reconciliation not be understood? Surely only because one would otherwise be forced to understand punishment by chastisement. Therefore whatever is inconvenient for his hypothesis must be denied, contrary to the common sense of Scripture and of the faithful. Which of the Christians, in that passage or anywhere else where Christ's peace is discussed, ever removed reconciliation? Socinus first dared to do this in that place. He says it signifies not reconciliation but quiet: indeed reconciliation precisely because it is quiet, since without reconciliation there is no quiet. So these things do not cancel each other out; they posit and include one another. (ii) What he says next is no better: that taking musar for scourge or affliction rather than true punishment is compelled by the word peace, which is obscurely opposed to it, namely because the antithesis is not between punishment and peace as it is between peace and affliction. I ask, why does the opposition between punishment and peace not fit, just as well as that between peace and affliction? A reason should have been given, not merely of incongruity but of impossibility and unfitness. Especially, why does the opposition not fit Christ, through whom we first have reconciliation and then peace, to which punishment is most properly opposed, and not simply affliction? Whatever this is, it works against the adversary, not against us. And does the word peace compel this? I ask, what opposition is so great between affliction and peace that only the former can hold here? Who would say that peace is merited more by affliction than by punishment? Of the peace of reconciliation the contrary is most manifest, and it is no less true of any peace.

units.la: Ad alterum ejusdem loci testimonium, & in livore ejus sanitas nobis: sive, medicatum est nobis, quomodo Socinus mavult legere, excipit dictum, propterea quod Christus verbera, & vulnera in corpore suo patitur, corpusque ejus totum frangitur, & sauciatur, anima nostra è gravissimis suis malis, & morbis eripitur, & sua vera & perfecta sanitati restituitur. Quem in finem adducit locum Petri, de quo mox singulatim agemus. Resp. Propterea quod Christus passus, non quod simpliciter passus, nam quid merae passiones, si nihil aliud accedat, ad auferenda peccata, & conferendam animabus salutem? sed passiones מַשָּׂאִיו[?] ex peccatis nostris ei עָלָיו[?] illatæ, quas nostri loco sustinuit, & exsolvit, hoc in se & sua virtute continent, ut medeantur nobis. Non passiones, sed tales, & non occasione vel exemplari quâ operatione, sed vi suâ propriâ nos liberant à peccatis, & salvant. Cæterum non ex solis verbis argumentamur, quæ diluere conatus Socinus, sed ex toto capite, & contextu, quod super Christum conjecta omnia peccata nostra, unde ab iis afflictus & attritus fuit, eaque ab ipso exacta, quando se dabat אָשָׁם[?] verè hostiam pro delicto: singula enim commata, & verba totidem præbent argumenta, & argumentorum confirmationes singulares atque valde emphaticas. Glorietur Socinus, uti hoc in loco facit, quod adversus receptissimam sententiam disputet, eamque penitus rejicere audeat: nostra gloriatio in hoc est, quod admodum clara & copiosa vel unum istud Jesajæ caput suppeditat argumenta, ut ad ea vel nil respondere, vel inania prorsus Adversarius inanior potuerit.
units.tr: On the second testimony of the same place, and by his bruise we are healed, or, it has been medicated for us, which Socinus prefers to read, he takes the saying because Christ suffers stripes and wounds in his body, and his body is wholly broken and wounded, our soul is snatched from its gravest evils and diseases and restored to its true and perfect health. To this end he adduces the passage of Peter, which we shall treat individually presently. Reply. The words because Christ suffered do not mean that he simply suffered. For what are mere sufferings, if nothing else is added, for taking away sins and bestowing salvation on souls? Rather, the sufferings laid upon him from our sins, which he endured in our place and paid, contain in themselves and by their own power this: that they heal us. They are not sufferings in general, but such sufferings; and they free us from sins and save us not by occasion or as an example, as a mode of operation, but by their own proper power. Moreover, we do not argue from words alone, which Socinus has tried to dilute, but from the whole chapter and its context, in which all our sins were laid upon Christ, whence he was afflicted and bruised, and they were exacted from him when he gave himself as a guilt offering [אָשָׁם], truly a sacrifice for sin. For each clause and word provides as many arguments, and singular and very emphatic confirmations of those arguments. Let Socinus glory, as he does here, that he disputes against the most received opinion and dares to reject it utterly. Our glorying lies in this: that this one chapter of Isaiah supplies such clear and abundant arguments that the adversary could either answer nothing to them, or, emptier than empty, could offer only utterly empty things.

units.la: Neque silentio prætereundum est Hugonis Grotii commentum, caput illud, contra Christianorum omnium sententiam, exponentis de prophetâ Jeremiâ; typice autem de Christo. Inde ab hujus οἰκονομίας[?] initio. cap. LII. 13. ecce intelliget servus meus] sic commentans: hæc omnia clarissime sibi revelata cognoscet Jeremias: figura Christi, ad quem hæc refert Chaldæus. Fortasse etiam, nisi eò referrer Chaldæus, majus opprobrium hinc veritus, si minus ageret quam Judæus ille, homo Christianus, id non facturus. Sic est, non ad Jeremiam illa refert Paraphrastes Chaldæus, sed ad Messiam. Ista ejus verba, הָא יִצְלַח עַבְדִּי מְשִׁיחָא[?] ecce prosperabitur servus meus Messias, exaltabitur & augebitur, & confortabitur nimis: 14. sicut speraverunt eum domus Israel diebus multis, qui erat pauper inter populos &c. Atque idem Cap. LIII. verf. 8. ex infirmitatibus & ultione congregabit captivitatem nostram: & mirabilia quæ fient nobis in diebus ejus quis poterit enarrare? quia auferet dominium populorum de terra Israel, peccata quæ peccaverunt populus meus, usque ad eos pervenient. & 10. A facie Domini voluntas fuit, ut conflaret & mundaret residuum populi sui, ut purificaret a peccatis animas eorum: videbunt regnum Messiae sui בְּמַלְכוּת מְשִׁיחוֹ[?] , multiplicabunt filios & filias, prolongabuntur dies eorum; & facientes legem Domini, in voluntate ejus dirigentur. A subjectione populorum liberabit animas eorum; videbunt ultionem de inimicis suis, saturabuntur praeda regum eorum. Jeremiam ne nominat quidem, neque ullam ejus prorsus facit mentionem. Sed de Messiâ, & populo ejus, qui futurus diebus ejus sit, locum interpretatur. Uti & de Messiâ locum exposuerunt Judæorum alii. Rabbi Alschech: הָא רַבּוֹתֵינוּ[?] ecce Rabbini nostri p. m. uno ore statuunt, & à majoribus acceperunt, de Rege Messiâ sermonem esse. Atque Abravanel, eam, cum aliorum, tum etiam Chaldaei Paraphraftus teftarur esse sententiam: [illegible, ~4 letters] & certe Jonathan Uzielidis interpretatur de futuro Messiâ, atque etiam est sententia sapientum p. m. in variis eorum expositionibus. Et in Talmude Sanhedrin, & à Maimonide, Menaffe Ben Israël, in Conciliatore Hispanico ad Jefajam, aliisque multis exponitur locus de Messiâ. De Jeremiâ quidem R. Saadiah à Gaon; alii de Abrahamo, de Mose, de Josiâ, passim vero de populo Judaico inter gentes variis modis vexato & oppresso Judæi interpretantur: quos adducimus, lib. vi. contra Judaos, cap. 1. At de Jeremiâ qui locum exposuerit, vel non de solo Christo, ex Christianis novi neminem, praeter unum Grotium. Qui nec aliter locum intellexit, vel ursit[?] olim, contra Socinum quando scribe-ret de satisfactione. Ut nunc doleam virum magnum tam graviter errasse, & tantam nomini suo, aeque ac rei Christianae inussisse maculam, quia summis Christi adversariis Judæis atque Socinianis tam turpiter voluit velificari. Nemo Christianorum caput illud Evangelicum, unde & Propheram[?] ibi Evangelistam potius agere, quam Vatem, haud dubitarunt afferere, intellexit de alio, quam de Christo: neque aliter Judæorum praecipui, & Chaldaeus Paraphrastes: pauciores, de aliis: paucissimi, de[?] Jeremiâ locum accipiendum censuerunt. Cum istis ergo Grotius maluit facere, quam cum aliis omnibus melio-ribus.
units.tr: Nor must the invention of Hugo Grotius be passed over in silence. Against the opinion of all Christians, he explains that chapter as concerning the prophet Jeremiah, though typically concerning Christ. From the beginning of this economy, chapter 52:13, behold, my servant shall understand, he comments thus: Jeremiah would know all these things clearly revealed to him; the Chaldee refers them to Christ, as a figure of him. Perhaps, too, if the Chaldee had not referred them there, he would have feared a greater reproach, and would not have done what that Jew did, though he is a Christian man. So it is: the Chaldee paraphrast does not refer those things to Jeremiah but to the Messiah. His words are: Behold, my servant Messiah shall prosper, shall be exalted and increased and greatly strengthened (52:13). As the house of Israel hoped for him many days, he who was poor among the peoples, etc. (52:14). And likewise in chapter 53, verse 8: He shall gather our captivity out of infirmities and vengeance, and who can tell the wonders that shall be done for us in his days? For he shall take away the dominion of the peoples from the land of Israel; the sins that my people have sinned shall come upon them. And verse 10: From the face of the Lord it was his will to refine and cleanse the remnant of his people, to purify their souls from sins; they shall see the kingdom of his Messiah, they shall multiply sons and daughters, their days shall be prolonged, and those who keep the law of the Lord shall be directed in his will. He shall free their souls from subjection to the peoples; they shall see vengeance on their enemies, and their kings shall be satisfied with spoil. He does not even name Jeremiah, nor make any mention of him at all, but he interprets the place of the Messiah and of the people who will be in his days. Other Jews too have expounded the passage of the Messiah. Rabbi Alshech: Behold, our rabbis of blessed memory with one voice establish, and have received from their fathers, that the discourse concerns the King Messiah. And Abravanel testifies that this is the opinion both of others and of the Chaldee paraphrast: [illegible]. And certainly Jonathan ben Uzziel interprets it of the future Messiah, and it is also the opinion of the wise, of blessed memory, in their various expositions. In the Talmud, Sanhedrin, and by Maimonides, Menasseh ben Israel, in the Spanish Conciliator on Isaiah, and many others, the place is expounded of the Messiah. Of Jeremiah indeed R. Saadiah Gaon speaks; others speak of Abraham, of Moses, of Josiah; but the Jews generally interpret it of the Jewish people, variously harassed and oppressed among the nations. We adduce these in book 6 against the Jews, chapter 1. But among Christians I know of no one, except Grotius alone, who has expounded the place of Jeremiah and not solely of Christ. He did not understand the place otherwise even formerly, when he wrote against Socinus on satisfaction. Now I grieve that so great a man has erred so gravely, and stained both his own name and the Christian cause with so great a blemish, because he wished to sail so shamefully with the chief adversaries of Christ, the Jews and the Socinians. No Christian who has not hesitated to affirm that the Evangelical chapter, where the evangelist rather than the prophet is acting, is about someone other than Christ, understood it otherwise. Nor did the chief Jews or the Chaldee paraphrast; fewer, among others, have taken it of others; very few have thought the passage should be taken of Jeremiah. With these Grotius preferred to side, rather than with all the others, who are better.

units.la: Præterea ad rem ipsam si progredimur, videmus primò, id esse præter morem Prophetarum, ut alius de alio, & suppresso nomine, & tam prolixe, tam augustè vaticinetur. Aliquando quidem fit in sacris libris, ut scriptor alterius autoris vel Scriptoris meminerit, sed breviter admodum, & in transcursu potius, quam ex professo aut data operâ. Habuerunt alia, quae tracta-rent & docerent, spectantia communem statum sive Ecclesiae, sive Reipubli-cae, aut communem fidem & religionem. Vel quando historias interserunt suis vaticiniis, nunquam id aliter, quam expressis fit eorum, quorum res agitur, nominibus: uti in historiâ æquum est. hic vero in tam longo sermone nulla Jeremiae injicitur mentio, nihil occurrit, quod ad eum jubeat referre sermo-nem, vel etiam leviter id suadeat. Deinde quorsum ista de Jeremiâ, ejus captivi-tate, & liberatione, de populi erga eum judicio interserta fuissent à Jesaiâ ? quid hæc tanti, ut tali apparatu & magnificentiâ commemorari debuerint, sive Prophetam aliquem vaticinia de gentis captivitate confirmantem, qualis Jeremias fuit, spectemus; sive etiam populi varium erga ipsum animum? Nam & plures similia docuerunt, & paria a populo fuerunt experti. Nimis particularia ista, & inferiora, quam ut hinc locum in prophetia occupent, & exhauriant praesentis sermonis dignitatem. Insuper nihil omnino in tota sermonis pericope ostendi potest, quod probet debere ad Jeremiam applicari, neque aliter posse. Porro talia multa unusquisque facile observabit, quae non possunt ad prophetam istum, non quoque ad alium referri, & quorum sensus ac vis non constat, nisi attribuantur Christo. Denique nihil apud ipsum Jeremiam occurrit, quod huc referatur, non Jesaiae nomen, non prophetiae hujus quasi de Jeremia futuro vel levissimum indicium: quod tamen maxime fecisset ad sermonis certitudinem, & ipsius Jeremiae confirmationem ac solatium: quem Deus in ingressu Prophetiae, per integrum caput, variis argumentis & signis erigere conatur & roborare, non attulisset has de ipso [illegible, ~12 letters], maxime quidem id apud Prophetam, & populum facturas, quod unice quaerebatur? Quare dum neque apud Jesaiam aliquid extet, quod ad Jeremiam spectat, neque apud hunc de Iesaia aliquid, vel illo ejus vaticinio, non etiam in Scriptura tota, non in hoc sermone, quod istam expositionem, & applicationem flagitet, merito sententiam illam non paradoxam tantum, sed heterodoxam*, & Christo adversam ac Prophetae, rejicimus & condemnamus.
units.tr: Moreover, if we proceed to the matter itself, we see first that it is contrary to the custom of the Prophets for one to prophesy about another, and that without naming him and at such length and with such dignity. It is true that in the sacred books a writer sometimes mentions another author or writing, but very briefly and in passing rather than professedly or deliberately. They had other matters to treat and teach, concerning the common state of the Church or the Commonwealth, or the common faith and religion. When they do weave histories into their prophecies, they never do so without expressly naming the persons whose affairs are being discussed, as is fitting in history. Here, however, in so long a discourse, there is no mention of Jeremiah, nothing occurs that obliges us to refer the discourse to him, or even slightly suggests it. Next, why should Isaiah have inserted those things about Jeremiah, his captivity and deliverance, and the people's judgment of him? Why should these things have been recorded with such display and grandeur, whether we consider a prophet confirming prophecies of the nation's captivity, such as Jeremiah was, or the people's varying attitude toward him? For many others taught similar things and experienced the same from the people. These matters are too particular and too trivial to occupy a place in prophecy here and to exhaust the dignity of the present discourse. Moreover, nothing at all in the whole passage can be shown to prove that it must be applied to Jeremiah, or that it cannot be applied otherwise. Further, anyone will easily observe many such things which cannot be referred to that prophet and not also to another, and whose sense and force are not established unless they are attributed to Christ. Finally, nothing occurs in Jeremiah himself that is related to this; there is not the name of Isaiah, nor even the slightest indication of this prophecy as if concerning a future Jeremiah. Yet this would especially have served the certainty of the discourse and the confirmation and comfort of Jeremiah himself, whom God, at the beginning of the prophecy, strives to raise up and strengthen through an entire chapter with various arguments and signs. Would he not have brought in these things about himself [illegible, about 12 letters], which would especially have accomplished this among the Prophet and the people, since that alone was sought? Therefore, since nothing exists in Isaiah that pertains to Jeremiah, nor anything in Jeremiah about Isaiah, nor, in the whole of Scripture, nor in this discourse, anything that demands this exposition and application, we rightly reject and condemn that opinion, which is not only paradoxical but heterodox, and opposed to Christ and to the Prophet.

units.la: Expendamus singula commata: & quomodo ad Ieremiam contorqueat, a Christo, videamus, inde a cap. LII. versu 13.
units.tr: Let us weigh the individual clauses, and see how he twists them away from Christ and toward Jeremiah, beginning from chapter 52, verse 13.

units.la: ECCE INTELLIGET SERVUS MEUS]
units.tr: BEHOLD, MY SERVANT SHALL UNDERSTAND]

units.la: Haec omnia clarissime sibi revelata cognoscet Jeremias: figura Christi, ad quem haec refert Chaldaeus: inquit Grotius. Majus quid in textu dicitur, quam simpliciter quod aliquis illa clarissime esset cogniturus, הנה ישכיל ecce intelligens erit, vel sapienter ac prudenter aget: uti 1 Sam. XVIII. 30. quin etiam alios erudiet servus meus, cognitione sui justificabit multos, cap. LIII. 11. Vel, proesperabitur, uti est Jerm. XXIII, 5. Quod magis convenit cum verbis mox sequentibus, & cum cap. LIII. 10. Quomodo & Chaldaeus vertit. Quod si vero de servi intelligentia accipiendum putes, uti absolute dictum, ita quoq; exponendum est, ut commendet servum a sapientia; quemadmodum cap. XI. 2. non autem relate aut restricte ad intelligentiam istius prophetiae. Syrus, ecce sapiet servus meus. Arabs: ecce puer meus prudens erit. Puerum etiam vertunt Graeci LXX. [illegible, ~12 letters] praemittitur in Arabico: prophetia de Christo, crucifixione ipsius, & ablatione culparum. Neque servus simpliciter positus alius debet intelligi. Uti quoque cap. LIII. 11. Justus servus meus. & cap. XLII. 1. ecce servus meus. Ubi Chaldaeus etiam, ecce servus meus Messias.
