Grotius autem iterum: LXX. hac de toto populo Judaico intellexerunt, sed bene cuncta intuenti apparebit Dei sermonem redire ad Esaiam, de quo supra XLI. 27. sublimius autem haec impleta in Christo, cujus figuram, quantum potuit, gessit Esaias, ut & Jonas, Jeremias, & alii quidam. Septuaginta quidem hic legunt 'Ιακωβ [illegible, ~6 letters] ὁ παῖς μου[?]. quos & Arabs sequitur, Jacobum puerum meum sustento, & Israel electus meus. praemittitur tamen & hic, tamquam capitis argumentum: prophetia de Christo. Ut dubium fit, annon per filium tamen intellexerint Christum. Quemadmodum Matth. 11. 15. ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum. Certe ad Christum illa referenda esse, sequentia satis indicant, cap XLII. 2. non clamabit, & non elevabit &c. Matthaeus docet, cap. xii. 17. 18. ut impleretur quod dictum per Jesaiam prophetam, ἰδοὺ ὁ παῖς μου &c. Certe servum Christus se praebuit nostri loco, μορφὴν δούλου λαβών, Phil. II. 7. Rom. XV. 8. διάκονον περιτομῆς. Ut revertamur ad Jesa. LII. 13. aeque etiam ad Jonam, vel alios posset applicare Grotius, quam ad Jeremiam. Neque probabit in istis prophetas illos typum Christi gessisse, in quibus vult, saltem ut dicis causa Christo aliquid relinquere videatur. Tria ergo hoc in loco ponit Autor, quorum nullum probat, Servum à Deo designari Jeremiam: quod intelligens exponendum sit restrictè ad res captivitatis Babylonicae: & quod Jeremias figuram Christi gesserit in iis, quae ei contigisse, ex cap. LIII. vult.
units.tr: Jeremiah will know all these things clearly revealed to him, the figure of Christ, to whom the Chaldee paraphrast refers them, says Grotius. Something greater is said in the text than merely that he would know these things most clearly. Ecce intelligens erit [הנה ישכיל], "behold, he will act with understanding," or will act wisely and prudently, as in 1 Sam. 18:30. Indeed, my servant will also instruct others, and will justify many by the knowledge of himself, ch. 53:11. Or he will prosper, as in Jer. 23:5, which agrees better with the words that immediately follow and with ch. 53:10, and this is how the Chaldee also renders it. But if you think the phrase about the servant's understanding should be taken as the text states it absolutely, it must also be explained in that absolute sense, namely that it commends the servant for wisdom, as in ch. 11:2, and not relatively or restrictedly to the understanding of that prophecy. The Syriac has behold, my servant will be wise. The Arabic has behold, my boy will be prudent. The Greek Seventy also render it by "boy" [παῖς]. In the Arabic a heading is placed before the text: prophecy about Christ, his crucifixion, and the removal of sins. Nor should servant, when used without qualification, be understood of anyone else; so also in ch. 53:11, my righteous servant, and in ch. 42:1, behold my servant, where the Chaldee too has behold my servant the Messiah. Grotius, however, says again: the Seventy understood this of the whole Jewish people, but to anyone who looks carefully at everything it will appear that God's word returns to Isaiah, of whom he spoke above in ch. 41:27; yet these things were fulfilled more sublimely in Christ, whose figure Isaiah bore, as far as he could, as did Jonah, Jeremiah, and certain others. Indeed the Seventy here read "Jacob my servant" [Ἰακὼβ ὁ παῖς μου], which the Arab also follows: I uphold Jacob my boy, and Israel my chosen. Yet here too there is prefixed, as it were the argument of the chapter, prophecy about Christ, so that it is doubtful whether they understood Christ by the son as well. Compare Matt. 2:15, out of Egypt I have called my son. That these things must be referred to Christ is certainly sufficiently indicated by what follows, in ch. 42:2, he will not cry out, nor lift up, etc. Matthew teaches, in ch. 12:17–18, that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, "Behold my servant" [ἰδοὺ ὁ παῖς μου], etc. Certainly Christ presented himself as a servant in our place, taking the form of a servant [μορφὴν δούλου λαβών], Phil. 2:7, and a minister of the circumcision [διάκονον περιτομῆς], Rom. 15:8. Grotius could apply Isa. 52:13 to Jonah or other prophets just as well as to Jeremiah, and he will not prove that those prophets bore a type of Christ in the cases where he wishes it, at least so that he seems to leave something to Christ, for the sake of argument. Therefore the author here sets out three things, none of which he proves: that the servant is designated by God as Jeremiah; that understanding is to be explained restrictedly with reference to the affairs of the Babylonian captivity; and that Jeremiah bore the figure of Christ in those things which, according to ch. 53, he wishes to have happened to him.

units.la: EXALTABITUR ET ELEVABITUR, ET SUBLIMIS ERIT VALDE]
units.tr: HE SHALL BE EXALTED AND LIFTED UP, AND SHALL BE VERY HIGH

units.la: in magno honore erit apud ipsos Chaldaeos. Vide Jerem. XXXIX. in fine & XL. Nec applicationem probat, nec restrictionem. Neque tantus honor in Jeremiam collatus à Chaldaeis indicatur illis capitibus, ut vim ac pompam verborum illorum referat vel æquet, vel ut in eo figuram Christi & exaltationis ejus gessisse jure dici debeat. Idem dictum ad gemina quae habet Autor, vers. sequenti. Apertius rem decidit versus 15. ISTE ASPERGET GENTES MULTAS] Multos ex gentibus ab idolorum cultu avertet, similitudo sumta ab aspersionibus legalibus. Non dicitur, multos ex gentibus: sed, gentes multas. Non hoc fecit Ieremias: an multos ex gentibus converterit, nondum vidi probatum. Certe gentilium conversionem quando praedicit Propheta, argumentum habetur, cum loqui de tempore Messiae, neque de alio, quam ipso, cui illa soli potest adscribi.
units.tr: He will be held in great honour among the Chaldeans themselves. See Jer. 39 at the end and chapter 40. He proves neither the application nor the restriction. Nor is such honour, bestowed on Jeremiah by the Chaldeans, shown in those chapters so as to match or equal the force and grandeur of those words, or so that he can rightly be said to have borne the figure of Christ and of his exaltation. The same saying applies to the two things the author mentions in the following verse. The matter is settled more clearly at verse 15: "He shall sprinkle many nations." He will turn many of the Gentiles away from the worship of idols; the likeness is taken from the legal sprinklings. The text does not say "many of the Gentiles" but "many nations." Jeremiah did not do this. I have not yet seen it proved that he converted many of the Gentiles. Certainly, when the Prophet foretells the conversion of the Gentiles, the argument points to the time of the Messiah, and to no other time than to him alone, to whom alone that conversion can be ascribed.

units.la: CONTINEBUNT REGES SUUM]
units.tr: KINGS SHALL SHUT THEIR MOUTHS

units.la: Reges, ut Nabuchodonosor Chaldaeorum, Nechos Ægyptiorum, eorumque Satrapae admirabuntur cum silentio ubi videbunt omnia quae licet Jeremias, ita adamussim, & suis temporibus impleta. Non reges hi, vel isti significantur in textu, sed Reges gentium multarum quivis, uti cap. XLIX. 23. Psalm. LXXII. 10. 11. & incurvabunt se ei omnes reges: omnes gentes ei servient. Quin hoc factum sit à temporibus Messiae, nemo ignorat: quod vero admirati admodum Reges isti fuerint, & eorum Satrapae, quae Jeremias dixerat, non aeque certum vel probatum. Probabilia autem pro certis, leviora pro gravibus, vulgaria & communia spiritualibus substituere, eorum est qui augustissimum & plenum Scripturarum sensum non satis noverunt aut amant. Æque facile idem de aliis hominibus, sive Regibus quoque licebit dicere, quod prophetiarum aliarum veritatem & impletionem fuerint nonnunquam admirati, non minus quam qui hoc in Ieremiâ suspexerint: nam conjecturis & probabilitate agit, & nulla talis profertur ὑποδείξεις[?] aliquorum, in quibus hoc commendet vel deprædicet Sacra Historia, quod possit cum prædictione Iesaiæ jungi merito vel comparari.
units.tr: Kings, such as Nebuchadnezzar of the Chaldeans, Necho of the Egyptians, and their satraps, shall be astonished in silence when they see all those things which Jeremiah foretold, fulfilled so exactly and in their own times. It is not these or those kings that are meant in the text, but kings of many nations in general, as in chapter 49:23 and Psalm 72:10–11: "All kings shall bow down to him; all nations shall serve him." That this was done from the time of the Messiah, no one is unaware; but that those kings and their satraps were greatly astonished at what Jeremiah had said is not equally certain or proved. Yet to substitute probabilities for certainties, and trivial things for weighty ones, and common and ordinary things for spiritual ones, is the mark of those who do not know or love the most lofty and full sense of the Scriptures. In the same way it could easily be said of other men, even of kings, that they sometimes were astonished at the truth and fulfilment of other prophecies, no less than those who admired it in Jeremiah. For he argues from conjectures and probability, and no such indication [ὑποδείξεις] of certain persons is brought forward in which Sacred History commends or proclaims anything that could fairly be joined or compared with the prediction of Isaiah.

units.la: QUIA QUIBUS NON EST NARRATUM DE EO VIDE-RUNT] in Hebræo: quia quod explicatum illis non fuerat (supple ab alio quoquam) id viderunt: per ipsum apertissime prædictum. Atqui de Christo, & regni ejus admirandis, quæ viderunt Gentiles & experti, fuerunt, quum nihil tale ipsis unquam annunciatum à suis fuisset antea, exponit, locum illum adducens, uti apud LXX. legitur, Apostolus, Rom. xv. 21. sed quemadmodum scriptum, quibus non annunciatum de eo, videbunt: & qui non audiverant, intelligent. Confer Iesa. LXV. quæsitus sum iis qui me non interrogaverunt, & inventus sum iis qui me non quæsierunt: dixi, ecce me, ecce me, ad gentem quæ non invocat nomen meum. Quod quamvis Apostolus de vocatione gentium exponat, tempore Messiæ; Grotius tamen etiam ad Antiochi tempora detorquet, & Deum introducit sic loquentem Judæ Maccabæo.
units.tr: "THEY SHALL SEE WHO WERE NOT TOLD OF HIM." In the Hebrew: "that which had not been explained to them (supply: by anyone else) they have seen"; it was foretold most plainly by him. Yet the Apostle, Romans 15:21, explains this of Christ and the wonders of his kingdom, which the Gentiles saw and experienced, although nothing of the kind had ever been announced to them by their own people before. He cites the passage as it is read in the Seventy: "But as it is written, they shall see to whom nothing was announced concerning him, and they who had not heard shall understand." Compare Isaiah 65: "I was sought by those who did not ask for me, and I was found by those who did not seek me. I said, Behold me, behold me, to a nation that does not call upon my name." Although the Apostle explains this of the calling of the Gentiles in the time of the Messiah, Grotius nevertheless turns it also to the times of Antiochus, and introduces God speaking thus to Judas Maccabeus.

units.la: Jam ad caput LIII. verf. 1. QUIS CREDIDIT AUDITUI NOSTRO, ET BRACHIUM DOMINI CUI REVELATUM EST?
units.tr: Now to chapter 53, verse 1: WHO HAS BELIEVED OUR REPORT, AND TO WHOM IS THE ARM OF THE LORD REVEALED?

units.la: Est continuum sermo cum iis quæ præcesserunt capite precedente & commate. 7 Vultis scire, inquit, quis ille sit futurus, de quo cœpi agere, qui & meis prophetiis plenam habebit fidem, & ipse de maximis rebus, quas Dei potentia peraget, revelationes accipiet exactissimas, omnibus circumstantiis additis? dabo vobis geminas ejus notas, unde cognosci possit. Hæ notæ in Ieremiam quidem congruunt primum, sed potius sublimiusque, sæpe & magis [illegible, ~3 letters] λέξιν, in Christum. Quid obsecro tanti referebat, adeo operose describere Ieremiam, quod vid. is esset futurus, qui divinis crederet prophetiis? Nam procul dubio in hoc habuit quidem nonnullos secum sentientes, & socios. Quidve etiam mirum, imo quid necesse est dicere, Prophetam credere prophetiæ? ut id tantopere decantari hoc in loco debuerit. Faciamus sensum Prophetæ Iesaiæ esse: quis credidit sermoni nostro de captivitate Babylonicâ, præterquam Ieremias? Quid hoc tanti? vel cur non clare potius nominasset Prophetam, vel aliquâ certiori notâ designasset? Conquestus quidem de infidelitate & contumaciâ populi erga se, vel doctrinam suam, fuit Ieremias, non adversus Iesaiam. Expostulavit vero de incredulitate Iudæorum Christus, & Apostoli, quod non crederent Prophetis, non Iesaiæ: huc istum ipsum locum adducentes. Ioan. xii. 37. 38. tanta ipso faciente signa coram iis, non crediderunt in ipsum: ut verbum Iesaiæ prophetæ impleretur, quem[?] dixit: Domine quis credidit auditui nostro, & brachium Domini cui revelatum? verf. 41. hæc dixit Iesaias quando gloriam ejus vidit, & de ipso fuit loquutus. Non de Ieremiâ. Rom. x. 16. sed non omnes obedierunt Euangelio. Dicit enim Iesaias: Domine quis credidit auditui nostro. Sermo ergo ille auditus λόγῳ ἀκοῆς περὶ ἡμῶν[?] fuit propheticus de Christo & Euangelio; non de Ieremiâ, & captivitate Babylonicâ. Neque illa prius in Ieremiam quadrant, uti Christi typum, tunc & in illum: nam non probat ex Ieremiâ illam typi rationem Grotius, seu ejus cum hoc capite convenientiam, uti nos eam ostendimus in Christo, ex Euangelio: & typus aut explicatio typica facta vel ficta ex ingenio caret divina illa authentia, quae est in typis ab ipsa Scriptura indicatis. Denique si, & saepe magis, χ̄ λέξιν[?] in Christum illa congruant, quam in Ieremiam, hac saltem ratione non in Ieremiam prius quam in Christum: & vellem ut id saepe in hoc capite ostendisset, & ne nusquam indicasset. Nisi pro forma, uti ajunt, vel in speciem id dixerit, & verba, quam rem, dare Christianis voluerit, caput de solo Christo constanter explicantibus.
units.tr: This is a continuous discourse with what went before, in the preceding chapter and verse 7. "You wish to know," he says, "who that person is to be of whom I have begun to speak, who will have full faith in my prophecies, and who himself will receive the most exact revelations about the greatest things which the power of God will accomplish, with all the circumstances added? I will give you two marks by which he may be recognised." These marks indeed fit Jeremiah first, but more lofty and more fully, often and more so [illegible] literally [κατὰ λέξιν], in Christ. What, I ask, was it worth to describe Jeremiah at such length, to show that he would be the one who believed the divine prophecies? For no doubt in this he had some who agreed with him and were his companions. Or what is even remarkable, or rather what need is there to say, that a prophet believed prophecy, so that it should have been so loudly proclaimed in this place? Let us suppose the sense of the Prophet Isaiah to be: who has believed our report of the Babylonian captivity, except Jeremiah? What is this worth? Or why did he not rather name the Prophet clearly, or mark him by some more certain sign? Jeremiah indeed complained of the unbelief and stubbornness of the people towards himself and his teaching, but not against Isaiah. Christ and the Apostles, on the other hand, complained of the unbelief of the Jews, that they did not believe the Prophets, not Isaiah in particular, citing this very passage. John 12:37–38: "Although he had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, which he spoke: Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?" Verse 41: "Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him." Not of Jeremiah. Romans 10:16: "But not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says: Lord, who has believed our report?" That report heard [λόγῳ ἀκοῆς] concerning us was therefore prophetic, about Christ and the gospel; not about Jeremiah and the Babylonian captivity. Nor do those things fit Jeremiah first, as a type of Christ, and then Christ; for Grotius does not prove from Jeremiah that type-relationship, or its agreement with this chapter, as we show it in Christ from the gospel. And a type, or a typical explanation made or feigned from one's own wit, lacks that divine authority which belongs to the types indicated by Scripture itself. Finally, if those things fit Christ, and often more literally [χ̄ λέξιν] than Jeremiah, at least for this reason they do not fit Jeremiah before Christ. And I would wish he had shown that "often" in this chapter, and not nowhere indicated it. Unless, as they say, he said it for form's sake or in appearance, and wished to give the Christians words rather than the thing itself, those who consistently explain the chapter of Christ alone.

units.la: Porro ista, & brachium Jehova cui revelatum? intellige, ut auditui nostro credat. nam sic exponitur Ioan. xii. 39. statim post allegata illa: & brachium Domini cui revelatum? propterea non potuerunt credere, quia iterum Jesaias inquit, excaecavit eorum oculos, & aggravavit ipsorum cor, ut ne viderent oculis, & cognoscerent corde. Adde Deut xxix. 4. & Ioan. vi. 44. nemo potest venire ad me, nisi pater qui misit me traxerit eum. ut contorta admodum sit expositio, illa de revelationibus Propheticis, vel rebus, quas quis Dei potentia peragat, interpretari. Quae non sunt pro sensu horum verborum, & longe aliis Scriptura exprimeret.
units.tr: Furthermore, as to those words, "and to whom is the arm of Jehovah revealed?" understand them as: that he may believe our report. For so it is explained in John 12:39, immediately after that quotation: "and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah says again: he has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, that they should not see with their eyes and understand with their heart." Add Deuteronomy 29:4 and John 6:44: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." So it is a very strained exposition to interpret those words of prophetic revelations, or of things which someone accomplishes by the power of God. These are not in accord with the sense of these words, and Scripture would have expressed it quite differently.

units.la: 2. ET ADSCENDET SICUT VIRGULTUM CORAM EO]
units.tr: 2. AND HE SHALL GROW UP BEFORE HIM AS A TENDER PLANT]

units.la: Ut hic positum est pro nimirum. Sensus est, Jeremias adhuc puer Deo servire in prophetico munere incipiet. - Sic Dominus Jesus anno aetatis xii. doctores docuit. Quorsum Ieremiae nativitas aut conditio ejus hic memorat fuisset? Christi vero humilis ortus, tum ad salutem hominum, tum ad reliquam ejus historiam facit necessario. Praeter Ieremiam alii plures sunt humili loco nati, & tenuiter educati, atque a primis annis muneri sacro admoti, quibus pari jure illa queas applicare, atque Ieremiae. Tum an Ieremias ita nullius formae ac decoris in vultu, in vita fuerit, macer & maestus, nondum video probatum: certe Christum nulla externa specie & gratia, ac dignitate fuisse commendabilem, sed despectum omnibus, & scandalum propterea Iudaeis, quia formam servi gerebat, uti verissimum, ita scire hoc & credere quam plurimum refert. Et videmus eum, dilutum est, ad Ieremiam referre, quem non Iesaias, nec multi viderunt, nullo suo incommodo: Christum vero vident pii omnes, & Iesaias, ipsum vidit, Ioan. xii. 41.
units.tr: Here "as" is used for "namely." The sense is: Jeremiah, still a boy, begins to serve God in the prophetic office. So the Lord Jesus taught the teachers at the age of twelve. Why would Jeremiah's birth or condition be mentioned here at all? But Christ's lowly birth is necessary both for the salvation of men and for the rest of his history. Besides Jeremiah there are many others born in humble station, raised in poverty, and called to sacred office from their early years, to whom you could apply these words with equal right. Then, I do not yet see it proved that Jeremiah was of such unremarkable form and appearance, thin and sorrowful in countenance and life. Certainly that Christ was commended by no outward beauty, favour or dignity, but was despised by all and therefore a stumbling block to the Jews, "because he had the form of a servant," is as true as it is important to know and believe. And we saw him is referred to Jeremiah, whom Isaiah and many did not see, without any loss to them. But all the godly see Christ, and Isaiah himself saw him, John 12:41.

units.la: 4. VERE LANGUORES NOSTROS IPSE TULIT]
units.tr: 4. SURELY HE HAS BORNE OUR GRIEFS]

units.la: Ille non talia meritus mala tulit quae nos eramus meriti: Haec omnia ait dicturos Iudaeos post captam urbem.
units.tr: He bore evils he had not deserved, which we had deserved. He says the Jews will say all these things after the city is taken.

units.la: ET NOS PUTAVIMUS EUM QUASI LEPROSUM AC PERCUSSUM A DEO ET HUMILIATUM]
units.tr: AND WE ESTEEMED HIM STRICKEN, SMITTEN OF GOD, AND AFFLICTED]

units.la: —Sensus est: nos statuimus Ieremiam merito conjectum in carcerem & lutum, Deo illum exosum habente, ut hostem urbis & templi, ac pseudoprophetam. Vide Ierem. xxvi. Nihil hic de Christo? Cui aperte tamen illa applicat Matthaeus, cap. viii. 17. & Ieremias dolores aliorum tulit? nostrorum omnium? portavit סָבַל[?] ? & vere omnia? Quamvis immerito vexatus, non proprerea aliorum demerita in se transtulit ac suscepit: non τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν ἀνήνεγκεν[?] ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ. 1 Pet. ii. 24. Septuaginta vertunt, ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει[?]. & Symmachus egregie, ὀντως τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνέλαβε. Chaldæus: propterea ipse deprecabitur pro debitis nostris על חובנא[?], & iniquitates nostras propter eum dimittentur. De peccatis agitur vel debitis nostris, à Christo suscepti, & remissis. Arabs similiter: ipse portat peccata nostra, & pro nobis dolore afficitur. Quæ ut omni ratione in Christum quadrant, ita nulla in Ieremiam. Nec tam gravia passus Ieremias fuit, quum in carcerem & lutum conjiciebatur, ut vim hujus vaticinii æquent; neque pro populo passus; quem neque à malis suis redemit, qui illis tandem succubuit & excisus fuit. Nam hæc, ait Grotius, dicturos Iudæos, post urbem captam. Quæ tamen etiam dixisse, non probat. Non legitur Ierem. xxvi. populum credidisse, Deo exosum fuisse Ieremiam, ut hostem urbis & templi, & pseudoprophetam. Imo non tanta illic passus Ieremias, quin adversus vim & calumniam Sacerdotum ac Prophetarum egregie defensus etiam fuit à populo, & vindicatus, simili aliorum Prophetarum exemplo. Adducitur exemplum Prophetæ Uriæ, qui eadem docuerat quæ Ieremias, & graviora quam ille, mortem etiam, propterea pertulerat. Cui quare non prophetia Iesaiæ applicetur tam bene ac Ieremiæ, equidem rationem non video.
units.tr: The sense is: we judged that Jeremiah was rightly thrown into prison and into the mire, God hating him as an enemy of the city and the temple, and a false prophet. See Jer. 26. Nothing here about Christ? Yet Matthew applies these words to him expressly, ch. 8:17. And did Jeremiah bear the sorrows of others, of all of us? Did he carry [Hebrew: sabal]? And did he bear them in truth, all of them? Although he was unjustly harassed, he did not on that account take upon himself and assume the sins of others: he did not "bear our sins in his body" (1 Pet. 2:24) [Greek: anēnenken tas hamartias hēmōn en tō sōmati autou]. The Septuagint translates: "he bears from our sin" [Greek: apo tēs hamartias hēmōn pherei]. Symmachus excellently: "truly he took up our sin" [Greek: ontōs tēs hamartias hēmōn autos anelabe]. The Chaldee: "therefore he himself will pray for our debts" [Hebrew: al chobana], "and our iniquities will be forgiven on account of him." The Arabic similarly: "he himself carries our sins and is afflicted with pain for us." These fit Christ in every respect, but not Jeremiah in any. Nor did Jeremiah suffer so grievously, even when he was cast into prison and the mire, that his suffering equals the force of this prophecy; nor did he suffer for the people, whom he did not redeem from their evils, and who in the end succumbed to them and were cut off. For these things, says Grotius, the Jews will say after the city is taken. Yet that they said these things is not proved. Jeremiah 26 does not say the people believed that Jeremiah was hated by God as an enemy of the city and the temple, and a false prophet. Indeed Jeremiah did not suffer so much there, but was excellently defended and vindicated by the people against the violence and calumny of the priests and prophets, like other prophets. The example of the prophet Uriah is adduced, who taught the same things as Jeremiah and suffered even death for them, things graver than Jeremiah's. Why Isaiah's prophecy should not be applied to Jeremiah as well as Jeremiah's is something I, for my part, do not see.

units.la: 5. IPSE AUTEM VULNERATUS EST PROPTER INIQUITATES NOSTRAS]
units.tr: 5. BUT HE WAS WOUNDED FOR OUR TRANSGRESSIONS]

units.la: Iniquissima de eo sensimus, & propterea crudeliter eum tractavimus: id nunc rebus ipsis apparet. Similia dixerunt Iudai, qui se converterunt die Pentecostes & deinceps. מִשְׁעֲוֹתֵינוּ[?] ab iniquitatibus nostris, vel propter inequitates nostras, non est, nos eum vulneravimus, vel crudeliter tractavimus: quemadmodum etiam quod additur מֵעֲוֹנוֹתֵינוּ[?] ab iniquitatibus nostris attritus est, id est propter eas, eo sensu, quo notant causam passionum meritoriam externam. Neque quid de eo senserint alii, hic significatur. Græci διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν[?], Chaldæus בְּחוֹבֵנָא[?] propter debita nostra. Duo obstant expositioni, quam dat Autor noster, primò verbum passivum vulneratus est, non vero, vulneravimus nos: deinde, à peccatis, vel propter peccata nostra. Atque hoc est, quod dixit Apostolus, Rom. iv. 25. qui traditus est διὰ propter peccata nostra.
units.tr: We thought the most unrighteous things of him, and therefore treated him cruelly. This now appears from the facts themselves. The Jews who were converted on the day of Pentecost and afterwards said similar things. [Hebrew: mishshe'othenu], "from our iniquities" or "on account of our iniquities," does not mean that we wounded him or treated him cruelly, just as the words that follow, [Hebrew: me'avonoteinu], "crushed from our iniquities," mean on account of them, in the sense in which they mark the external meritorious cause of the sufferings. Nor does this express what others thought of him. The Greeks have [Greek: dia tas hamartias hēmōn], and the Chaldee [Hebrew: bechobana], "on account of our debts." Two things stand in the way of the explanation our author gives: first, the passive verb "he was wounded," not "we wounded ourselves"; second, "from sins," or "on account of our sins." And this is what the Apostle said, Rom. 4:25: "who was delivered" [Greek: dia] "on account of our sins."

units.la: DISCIPLINA PACIS NOSTRÆ SUPER EUM]
units.tr: THE CHASTISEMENT OF OUR PEACE WAS UPON HIM]

units.la: Apud eum: id est: monita nobis attulit salutaria, si ea recepissemus. Primum enervat vim vocis מוּסָר[?], quando pro sola disciplina accipit, ejusque monitis, quum, interjectis hinc inde verbis passionem & mala denotantibus, primam & propriam significationem poscat vinculorum & afflictionum, à יָסַר[?] vincivit, ligavit. עָלָיו[?] est super eum, non apud eum, vel cum eo. Et usus præpositionis perpetuus, & totius orationis series non aliam ejus significationem hic poscunt. ἐπ' αὐτὸν, habent Græci. Syrus, castigatio pacis nostræ ipsi imponitur. Sic & Arabs. Kimchi egregie, ad expositionem nempe verborum, quidquid sit de applicatione הַיִּסּוּרִים שֶׁהָיוּ רְאוּיִם לָבֹא עָלֵינוּ כּוּלָּם בָּאוּ עָלָיו[?] castigationes, quæ dignæ erant venire super nos, omnes venerunt super ipsum. Sic Rebecca ad filium Iacobum metuentem, ne doloso artificio Patris in se accerseret maledictionem, loco benedictionis, sic adducam super me [Hebrew: עָלַי מְאֵרָה?] maledictionem, inquit Genes. xxvii. 12. 13. super me [Hebrew: מְאֵרָה?] maledictio tua. Et Iudic. xix. 20. omnis tuus defectus super me veniat, vel imponatur, [Greek: ἐπάλω πᾶν τὸ ὑστέρημά σου ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ?].
units.tr: "Upon him" means: he brought us salutary admonitions, if we had received them. First, he weakens the force of the word [Hebrew: musar], taking it only for discipline and its admonitions, whereas, with words denoting suffering and evils placed on either side, it demands its first and proper meaning of bonds and afflictions, from [Hebrew: yasar], "to bind, to tie." [Hebrew: alav] means "upon him," not "beside him" or "with him." The constant use of the preposition and the whole sequence of the sentence demand no other meaning here. The Greeks have [Greek: ep' auton]. The Syriac: "the chastisement of our peace is laid upon him." So also the Arabic. Kimchi excellently, at least for the explanation of the words, whatever be said of the application: "the chastisements which were worthy to come upon us all came upon him." So Rebekah, when her son Jacob feared that by his father's deceitful device he would bring a curse upon himself instead of a blessing, said: "let your curse be upon me" [Hebrew: alay me'erah], Gen. 27:12–13. And Judg. 19:20: "let all your lack be upon me" [Greek: epalō pan to hysterēma sou ep' eme], or be laid upon me.

units.la: ET LIVORE EJUS SANATI SUMUS] livore ejus (id est, ipsius patientia) nos sanati fuissemus: id est, liberati ab impendentibus malis, si verbis ipsius tanta malorum tolerantia confirmatis habuissemus fidem. Hebraei potentialem modum aliter quam per indicativum exprimere nequeunt, ideo multa adhibenda attentio ad consequendos sensus. Ut contorta & peregrina ubique expositio! livorem, inquit Propheta; iste, patientiam: sanati,ille; sanati fuissemus,hic. Non nescimus, Hebræos non habere modum potentialem, vel optativum, quemadmodum Latini, & pro eo non indicativo, quem quoque non habent, sed infinitivo uti; verum ubi sensus id efflagitat: & hoc obscurum satis esse ipse indicat: sed id hic non est, & obscuritatem loco plano inferre, non est interpretis, sed inversoris: quippe dicitur simpliciter, & livore ejus sanari vel sanatio nobis, [Greek: ἡ τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἰάθημεν?], uti Petrus legit: cujus ipsius vibice sanati estis, non, sanati fuissetis.
units.tr: "And by his bruise we are healed." By his bruise (that is, by his patience) we would have been healed: that is, freed from the threatening evils, if we had had faith in his words confirming such great tolerance of evils. The Hebrews cannot express the potential mood otherwise than by the indicative, so much attention must be given to grasping the sense. How contorted and foreign is this exposition everywhere! "bruise," says the Prophet; this man says "patience"; "healed" is that man's; "we would have been healed" is this. We are not unaware that the Hebrews do not have a potential or optative mood like the Latins, and in its place use not the indicative, which they also lack, but the infinitive. But where the sense demands it, they do so; and this obscurity is itself sufficiently indicated by the author. But here it is not so, and to introduce obscurity into a plain passage is not the work of an interpreter but of a perverter. For it is said simply, "by his bruise we are healed" or "healing comes to us," [Greek: hē tō mōlōpi autou iathēmen], as Peter read it: "by whose stripes you were healed" (1 Pet. 2:24), not "you would have been healed."

units.la: Quæ aptari nullo modo Ieremiæ possunt: cujus nec livore salus vel nobis, vel Iudæis contigit, neque etiam ejus patientiâ sanati fuissent. Iterum alia assumit; & hæc quoque modo potentiali, quorum tamen nullum in Prophetæ verbis vestigium, si verbis ipsius habuissemus fidem. Nam absolute in textu dicitur, vibice ejus fuimus sanati, non conditionaliter fuissemus sanati, neque nisi sub conditione creditarum istarum prophetiarum. Denique si alius hic intelligendus præter Messiam, etiam alius produci deberet quam Ieremias, qui vibices & confractiones passus fuerit, quas illum sustinuisse non legimus. Applicare ad Iohannem Baptistam, vel alium quem similia passum æquò jure posses, ac, quod nunc fecit Grotius, ad Ieremiam.
units.tr: These words can in no way be fitted to Jeremiah, by whose bruise neither we nor the Jews obtained salvation, nor would they have been healed by his patience. Again he assumes other things, and these too in the potential mood, of which there is not the slightest trace in the Prophet's words: "if we had had faith in his words." For the text states absolutely that we were healed by his bruise, not conditionally that we would have been healed, nor except under the condition of believing these prophecies. Finally, if someone other than the Messiah is to be understood here, then another person would have to be produced besides Jeremiah, one who suffered bruises and fractures, which we do not read that Jeremiah endured. You could apply it, with equal right, to John the Baptist or to someone else who suffered similar things, as Grotius now does with Jeremiah.

units.la: 6. OMNES NOS QUASI OVES ERRAVIMUS] Erraveramus jam à Menassis temporibus. Duo committit in paucis adeò verbis: mutat verbi tempus, sine ratione, erravimus, in erraveramus: & restringit tempus vel initium peccatorum, ad Menassis tempora, quod indefinite & absolute ponitur, uti ab omnibus dictum, sic & de omni tempore intelligendum.
units.tr: 6. ALL WE LIKE SHEEP HAVE GONE ASTRAY. We had already gone astray from the time of Manasseh. He commits two faults in so few words: he changes the tense of the verb without reason, from "we have gone astray" to "we had gone astray"; and he restricts the time or beginning of sins to the times of Manasseh, which is stated indefinitely and absolutely, as it is said by all, and so must be understood of every time.

units.la: UNUSQUISQUE IN VIAM SUAM DECLINAVIT] Alii ad alia idola. Adde, & ad peccata quævis alia.
units.tr: EVERYONE HAS TURNED ASIDE TO HIS OWN WAY] Others to other idols. Add also to any other sins.

units.la: ET POSUIT DOMINUS IN EO INIQUITATEM OMNIUM NOSTRUM] Permisit Deus ut ille nostro gravi crimine indignissima pateretur. Ubique necesse habet vim verborum enervare in applicatione instituendâ à Deo ad hominem, à Christo ad Ieremiam. Quum boni expositoris sit, ubique servare sensus amplitudinem, & copiam. Ut nobis hic idem dicere liceat, quod ipse ad vindicandum illum versum, Socino, de Satisf. pag. 25. Non idem est pati, quod pati Deo injiciente iniquitatem, & quamvis quis indignissima, non ideo portat peccata aliorum: vel ubi aliorum indignissima, non ideo peccata omnium nostrum. Satis evidenter notatur occursus Mediatoris, in quem luenda omnium nostrum peccata conjecta a Deo fuerint, non ab hominibus, sed Deo ipsi aliorum imponente peccata. Non sunt indignissima ulla quae homines agant, & putare debeant Deo adscribenda esse, vel eo autore geri. Non permisit hic aliquid Deus, sed fecit, & ipsius efficientia, tanquam in bono punitionis, notatur, non permissio mali peccati, quidque Deus egerit, & erga Mediatorem, non quid proprie homines, nisi quod inique egerunt, at quod istas ipsorum iniquitates conjecerit Deus omnes in Christum. Non satis habet Autor Hebraeum textum enervare, idem & in Vulgato, quem cur sequatur & praefigat semper haud obscurum est, praestat: legit ille, posuit Dominus; hic, permisit. Cedo unum locum ubi [illegible, ~3 letters] hoc significet. Symmachus: Κὐρίῳ καταντήσαι ἐπίησεν εἰς αὐτὸν τῷ ἀνομίαν πάντων ἡμῶν. Versio Syriaca, Dominus autem fecit ut irruerent in eum peccata omnium nostrum.
units.tr: AND THE LORD HAS LAID ON HIM THE INIQUITY OF US ALL] God permitted that he, most unworthily, should suffer for our grave crime. In every place he must weaken the force of the words, in applying to man what God applied to Christ, and to Jeremiah what Christ applied to him. It is the mark of a good expositor to preserve the full range and richness of meaning everywhere. So I may say here what he himself says in defending that verse against Socinus, On Satisfaction, p. 25: it is not the same to suffer as to suffer because God lays iniquity upon one, and although someone suffers most unworthily, he does not therefore bear the sins of others, or, where others suffer most unworthily, the sins of all of us. It is sufficiently clear that the meeting of the Mediator is pointed out, on whom the sins of us all were laid by God, not by men, since God himself laid the sins of others upon him. No deeds of men are so unworthy that they must be ascribed to God or be thought to be done under his authority. God did not here merely permit something, but did it, and his action is indicated, as in a good deed of punishment, not the permission of evil sin. What God did, and toward the Mediator, is what is noted, not what men properly did, except that they acted wickedly; but that God laid all these iniquities of theirs upon Christ. The author does not content himself with weakening the Hebrew text; he does the same with the Vulgate, which he plainly follows and puts first. He reads the Lord laid; the Vulgate reads permitted. Let him show me one passage where [illegible] means this. Symmachus: [Kyriō katantēsai epiēsen eis auton tēn anomian pantōn hēmōn] (the Lord made the lawlessness of us all fall upon him). The Syriac version: And the Lord made the sins of us all rush upon him.

units.la: 7. OBLATUS EST QUIA IPSE VOLUIT, ET NON APERUIT OS SUUM] In Hebræo, oppressus & afflistus fuit, & non aperuit os suum. Sensum bene exprimunt LXX. [?]ὡς αὐτὸς διὰ τὸ κεκακωμένος οὐκ ἤνοιξεν τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ. Etiam tunc cum in carcerem ageretur, & in locum lutosum, nihil fecit dixitve iracunde. Mire hæc omnia invertit Chaldæus, ut Messiam nobis depingat, qualem Judæi volunt. Magis autem invertit ipse, ut Jeremiae adscribat. Qui quamvis nil dixerit iracunde, ubi in carcerem trahebatur ac foveam, non propterea ista ei bene applicari probatur. Non quidem reluctatus divinae voluntati Jeremias fuit, quando pro eo & veritate vaticiniorum pati debuit; at neque admodum obmutuisse legitur, sed adversarios continuo objurgasse & redarguisse, tum sermone, tum factis. Vide cap. xxvi. & seq. Non certe ita ad stuporem tacuit, quemadmodum Christus, quem admirati Judices ipsi fuerunt, quod tam altum sileret, & tacite omnia perferret: quem tamen Grotius ne semel quidem hic commemorat. Apud Matthaeum, cap. xxvi. 62. 63. Cajaphas Christo, nihil respondes? quidquid hi contra testantur? Christus autem tacuit. Tum vix adhibita conjuratione adigere Christum potuit ad dicendum, an esset filius Dei? cui respondit, dixisti. Atque coram Herode, & vexatus multis quaestionibus, nihil vero ipsi respondit. Luc. xxiii. 9. nec magis quando illusus ab eo palam, & veste indutus splendida missus fuit ad Pilatum: & huic etiam Jesus non dabat responsum, dixit ei Pilatus, mihi non loqueris? Joann. xix. 9. 10. Quid, annon haec videntur propiora, quibus illa Jesaiae applicentur, quam ad Jeremiam? Et quando in cruce verba protulit, protulit autem septies, quam pauca, quam gravia, quam de aliis magis, quam de se, & de se ubi semel, ob alios id potius, quam sui causa? Sic loquutus tamen, ut ipsis verbis testaretur silentem Deo animam, & perfecte obsequentem. Quod eo magis mirandum in ipso fuit, quo si voluisset, levi opera & verbulo potuisset, si voluisset, eripere sese, atque hostes omnes suos dissipare, ac conterere, sed noluit & agnum se præbuit, uti vitâ totâ, sic maxime quum tonderetur & tunderetur in judicio atque in morte.
units.tr: 7. HE WAS OFFERED BECAUSE HE HIMSELF WILLED IT, AND DID NOT OPEN HIS MOUTH. In the Hebrew, he was oppressed and afflicted, and did not open his mouth. The Seventy express the sense well [hōs autos dia to kekakōmenos ouk ēnoixen to stoma autou]. Even when he was led into prison and into a miry place, he did nothing and spoke nothing in anger. The Chaldee paraphrast inverts all these things wonderfully, so as to depict for us the Messiah in the way the Jews wish him to be. But the author himself inverts them even more, in order to ascribe them to Jeremiah. Although Jeremiah said nothing in anger when he was dragged into prison and into the pit, it is not thereby proved that these words apply well to him. Jeremiah indeed did not struggle against the divine will when he had to suffer for it and for the truth of his prophecies; yet it is not read that he fell utterly silent, but he constantly rebuked and refuted his adversaries, both in speech and in deeds. See chapter 26 and following. Certainly he did not keep silent to the point of stupor, as Christ did, whom the judges themselves marvelled at, because he was silent to such a degree and bore everything quietly. Yet Grotius does not mention him here even once. In Matthew 26:62-63, Caiaphas said to Christ, Do you answer nothing? What do these men testify against you? But Christ was silent. Then, with hardly any oath, he could only bring Christ to say whether he was the Son of God; to which he answered, You have said it. And before Herod, when he was harassed with many questions, he answered him nothing, Luke 23:9. Nor was he more responsive when he was openly mocked by him and, dressed in a splendid garment, was sent to Pilate; and to him too, Jesus gave no answer. Pilate said to him, Do you not speak to me? John 19:9-10. What? Do not these passages seem closer to those to which that saying of Isaiah should be applied than to Jeremiah? And when he spoke words on the cross, he spoke seven of them: how few, how weighty, how much more about others than about himself, and about himself only once, and that for others rather than for his own sake? Yet he spoke so that by his very words he testified that his soul was silent before God and perfectly obedient. This was all the more remarkable in him, since, if he had willed it, he could have rescued himself with little effort and a single word, and scattered and crushed all his enemies; but he would not, and showed himself a lamb, as he did throughout his whole life, and most of all when he was shorn and beaten in judgment and in death.

units.la: ET QUASI AGNUS] Cum quo ipse Ieremias se comparat XI. 18. Adeo nil meminit Grotius digito ostensum illum à Baptistâ agnum: ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi? Ioan. 1. 29. Vel an similis Eunucho, qui hinc ipsum locum Prophetæ lectitans, erat enim periocha Scripturæ quam legebat hæc: ut ovis ad mactationem ductus: & ut agnus coram tondente se ἄφωνος mutus, sic non aperit os suum: nesciebat de Christo Prophetam loqui? nam rogans, de quo, an de se, an alio quoquam Propheta ista diceret? non responsum, de Ieremiâ sermonem proprie esse, & illum designari agnum; sed annunciabat ipsi Philippus Iesum. Act. viii. 32.34.35. Probet autem prius consequentiam istam suam Grotius, Ieremias comparatur cum agno; ergo ipse per agnum hunc à Iesaiâ intelligitur: æq; uti nos Scripturæ S. divinâ autoritate & consensu probamus consequentiam aut applicationem istius agni ad Christum. Nam & aliis etiam, puta ipsis Babyloniis, à Ieremia adscribitur similitudo agnorum ductorum ad mactationem, cap. L.40. ut singulare id non sit in Ieremiâ: vel ut propterea prophetia Iesaiæ admodum singularis ipsi debeat accommodari. Eadem similitudine Christus dicit se Apostolos mittere, ut agnos. Luc. x.3. Christus vero in N.T. emphatice agnus sæpissime appellatur, præsertim vero in Apocalypsi, & 1 Petr. 1.19.
units.tr: AND AS A LAMB] With which Jeremiah himself compares himself, XI. 18. So little does Grotius remember that lamb pointed out with a finger by the Baptist: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, John 1:29. Or is he like the eunuch, who, reading this very passage of the prophet (for this was the section of Scripture he was reading): He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent [aphōnos], so he does not open his mouth, did not know that the prophet was speaking of Christ? For when he asked of whom the prophet said this, whether of himself or of some other, the answer was not that the discourse was properly about Jeremiah and that he was meant by the lamb; rather Philip announced Jesus to him. Acts 8:32, 34, 35. But first let Grotius prove his inference: Jeremiah is compared with a lamb; therefore he himself is understood by Isaiah through this lamb. In the same way we prove, by the divine authority and consensus of Holy Scripture, the inference or application of that lamb to Christ. For the likeness of lambs led to the slaughter is ascribed by Jeremiah also to others, for instance to the Babylonians themselves, chapter 50:40, so that it is not peculiar to Jeremiah; nor is the prophecy of Isaiah, which is quite singular, therefore to be fitted to him. By the same likeness Christ says that he sends out the Apostles as lambs, Luke 10:3. Indeed, in the New Testament Christ is very often called the Lamb, emphatically, especially in the Apocalypse, and in 1 Peter 1:19.

units.la: 8. DE ANGUSTIA ET DE JUDICIO SUBLATUS EST]
units.tr: 8. CONCERNING THE ANGUISH AND THE JUDGMENT HE WAS TAKEN AWAY

units.la: De carcere & de judicio ablatus est: id est, liberatus tandem. Iudicium vocat hoc, quia specie judicii ipsi hæc mala imposita fuerant. Vide Ierem. xxxii. 3. liberatus autem per Babylonios. Sed quia ita ille liberatus dicitur, ut interim quoque dicatur hoc versu, excisus è terra viventium, quod Ieremiæ non contigit, ideo applicari ei non potest. Quod iterum Grotius sic invertit & evertit: QUIA ABSCISSUS EST DE TERRA VIVENTIUM] nempe cum actus fuit primum in carcerem, deinde in lacum illum canosum, ac rursum in carcerem. Sed hæc non dicuntur excisio è terra viventium, quæ est phrasis morientium. Psalm. lii. 7. Iesa. xxxviii. 11. 12. & Psalm. cxvi. 8. 9. atque de Christo Daniel, & excindetur. cap. ix. 26. Græci, ὅτι ἀφῃρέθη ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ αὐτοῦ. Symmachus, ἀπεσπάσθη γὰρ ἐκ τῆς γῆς ζώντων. Versio Arabica: Vita quidem ipsius ablata est è terra. Quod & confirmatur sequentibus: à defectione populi mei plaga ei. Grotius, in Hebræo est, plaga ipsi, supple evenit, populi summo errore ac crimine, ut & ante dictum est. quidam codices Hebrei hic habuerunt לָמוֹ[?], sed idem significat: neque enim exemplis caret ם[?] ἐπηνθελεκόν[?]. Indicata jam ab aliis exempla, Genes. ix. 26. 27. Iob. xx. 2[?]1. & xxii. 2. Psalm. xi. 7. & xxviii. 8. Iesa. xliv. 15. Sed non interveniente tantum quovis modo aliorum errore & crimine dicitur plaga ipsi fuisse imputata, de quocunq; etiam loquutus Propheta fuerit, sed causâ meritoriâ procatarctica, & revera illam plagam ipsi, pro aliorum salute, inferente: quemadmodum, prophetans de Christi morte Caiaphas, dicebat, expedire ut unus homo moreretur pro populo, & non gens interiret universa. Ioan. xi. 50. 51. Quod vero Iesaias dicit, affectum fuisse plagâ. LXX. reddunt, [?]ἀπὸ τ̃ ἀνομιῶν ἡ λαὸς μου ἤχθη εἰς θάνατον[?]. Neque praetereundum quod in hoc versu quoque est:
units.tr: He was taken away from prison and from judgment: that is, at last set free. He calls it judgment because these evils had been imposed on him under the form of a judicial sentence. See Jer. 32.3. He was set free, however, by the Babylonians. But because he is said to be so set free that at the same time it is said in this verse, cut off from the land of the living, which did not happen to Jeremiah, it cannot be applied to him. Grotius again turns this round and overturns it: "BECAUSE HE WAS CUT OFF FROM THE LAND OF THE LIVING" [namely when he was first put into prison, then into that muddy pit, and again into prison]. But these things are not called a cutting off from the land of the living, which is the phrase for dying. See Ps. 52.7; Isa. 38.11, 12; Ps. 116.8, 9; and of Christ, Daniel: he shall be cut off, ch. 9.26. The Greek reads, "that his life was taken from the earth" [ὅτι ἀφῃρέθη ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ αὐτοῦ]. Symmachus: "for he was torn away from the land of the living" [ἀπεσπάσθη γὰρ ἐκ τῆς γῆς ζώντων]. The Arabic version: His life indeed was taken from the earth. This is confirmed by what follows: for the transgression of my people was the stroke upon him. Grotius: in the Hebrew it is "the stroke to him", supply "fell", namely through the very great error and crime of the people, as was also said before. Some Hebrew manuscripts here have lamo, but it means the same thing, for the ם does not lack examples. Other examples have already been noted: Gen. 9.26, 27; Job 20.21; 22.2; Ps. 11.7; 28.8; Isa. 44.15. But it is not merely through the intervention of someone else's error and crime, in whatever way, that a stroke is said to have been laid upon him, whoever the Prophet may be speaking of; rather it is by a meritorious and procuring cause, and the stroke was truly inflicted on him for the salvation of others, just as Caiaphas, prophesying of Christ's death, said that it was expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish. John 11.50, 51. As for what Isaiah says, that he was afflicted with a stroke, the Seventy render, "the people of mine was led to death for their lawless deeds" [ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνομιῶν τοῦ λαοῦ μου ἤχθη εἰς θάνατον]. Nor should we pass over what is also in this verse:

units.la: GENERATIONEM EJUS QUIS ENARRABIT?] Quis numerare poterit dies vitae ejus? id est, erit valde longaevus. Non adeo longaevus fuit Jeremias, quem vixisse ad annum sexagesimum aetatis Scriptores perhibent: non certe, ut non enarrari posse ejus generationem, vel per interrogationem, ut rem impossibilem nemo id facturus, dici possit. Christo autem ita evidenter haec conveniunt, ut & soli: sive de ipso, & ejus aeterna gloria, Rom. vi. 9. Heb. vii. 14. 15. Apoc. i. 18. sive quoque de fidelibus & Ecclesia ejus intelligantur, quemadmodum vers. 10. videbit semen & prolongabit dies. Psalm. cx. 3. Heb. ii. 10. Apoc. vii. 9. Ne de aeterna & inexplicabili ejus a Patre generatione dicamus, ad quam multi etiam locum referunt. Neque initium dierum, neque vita finem habens, Heb. vii. 3. &c. Graeci, [?]τῶν ἡμερῶν αὐτοῦ τῆς ζωῆς[?].
units.tr: Who will declare his generation? Who can count the days of his life? That is, he will be very long-lived. Jeremiah was not so long-lived, since writers say he lived to about the sixtieth year of his age; certainly not so long-lived that his generation could not be declared, or that it could be said, by way of a question, as an impossible thing which no one would undertake. But these things agree so evidently with Christ that they belong to him alone, whether they are understood of him and of his eternal glory (Rom. 6.9; Heb. 7.14, 15; Rev. 1.18), or also of believers and his Church, as in verse 10: he shall see his seed and prolong his days (Ps. 110.3; Heb. 2.10; Rev. 7.9). Not to speak of his eternal and inexplicable generation from the Father, to which many also refer the passage: having neither beginning of days nor end of life (Heb. 7.3, etc.). The Greek reads, "of his days of life" [τῶν ἡμερῶν αὐτοῦ τῆς ζωῆς].

units.la: ET DABIT IMPIOS PRO SEPULTURA, ET DIVITEM PRO MORTE SVA] illi ipsum etiam interficere voluerant, ut legimus Jerem. xxvi. At Deus ipsius vice viros potentes quidem, sed improbos, sacerdotes nempe mortem Jeremiae machinatos morti dedit per Chaldaeos. II Reg. xxv. 18. 19. 20. 21. Nihil illis divitiae sua profuerunt, quibus redimi se posse speraverant. Sensum hunc bene expresserunt Graeci. Neque tamen intellexerunt illa de Jeremia. Uti neque intelligi possunt, quia non de eo agitur, quem aliqui interficere voluerint, sed revera interfecerint, de ejus morte, atque sepultura. Sic enim & Graeci hic, [?]ὃ δώσω τὰς πλουσίας ἀντὶ τῆς ταφῆς αὐτοῦ, ἢ τὰς πλουσίας ἀντὶ τ̃ θανάτου αὐτοῦ[?]. Caeterum II Reg. xxv. dicitur quidem, quod Praefectus Babylonicus nonnullos e Judaea captivos abduxerit, sed nec solos commemorat Sacerdotes, sed & quosvis alios; neque eos refert fuisse, qui mortem Jeremiae prophetae machinati fuerant; neque etiam opibus suis fidisse, iisque redimi posse se speravisse. Adeo gratis omnia isthaec afferuntur. Et si tantum quaerendus aliquis sit, qui indigna a suis passus fuit, aeque facile Rabbi Alschech interpretabitur illa de Mose, qui sepultus fuit in deserto, cum impio & divite Corah, & aliis istius generis, ac Grotius de Jeremia. Aben Esra, & Christianorum nonnulli [?]בְּמֹתָיו[?] exponunt, non in mortibus ejus, ut ב sit servile, sed radicale, & significet cippum, monumentum sepulchrale, seu sepulchrum ipsum, quod Christiani tum de sepulchro Josephi Arimathaensis, hominis divitis, quod Christo datum fuit, accipiunt, Matth. xxvii. 57.
units.tr: And he gave the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death. They had wanted to kill him too, as we read in Jer. 26. But God, in his stead, gave over to death, through the Chaldeans, the powerful men indeed, but wicked ones, namely the priests who had plotted Jeremiah's death. 2 Kings 25.18–21. Their riches did them no good, by which they had hoped to be able to buy themselves back. The Greek has expressed this sense well. Yet they did not understand these words of Jeremiah. Nor can they be understood so, because the passage is not about the one whom some wanted to kill, but actually killed, about his death and burial. For the Greek here reads, "I will give the rich in exchange for his burial, or the rich in exchange for his death" [ὃ δώσω τὰς πλουσίας ἀντὶ τῆς ταφῆς αὐτοῦ, ἢ τὰς πλουσίας ἀντὶ τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ]. Moreover, 2 Kings 25 does say that the Babylonian commander carried off some captives from Judaea, but it mentions not only the priests but also various others; nor does it report that they were the ones who had plotted the death of the prophet Jeremiah, nor that they had trusted in their wealth and hoped to be redeemed by it. So groundless are all these assertions. And if someone is to be sought who suffered unworthy things at the hands of his own people, Rabbi Alschech would just as easily interpret those words of Moses, who was buried in the wilderness along with the wicked and rich Korah and others of that kind, as Grotius interprets them of Jeremiah. Aben Ezra and some Christians render bemotav [בְּמֹתָיו] not "in his deaths", taking the beth as a servile letter, but as a radical, and meaning a stone pillar, a sepulchral monument, or the sepulchre itself; and Christians then understand this of the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man, which was given to Christ (Matt. 27.57).

units.la: EO QVOD INIQVITATEM NON FECERIT, NEQVE DOLVS FVERIT IN ORE EJVS] Quanquam nihil aliud dixerat: quam quod Deus ei mandaverat. Majus quid verbis illis subest: nam multi quidem nihil aliud dicunt, quam quod Deus ipsis mandavit, haud tamen admitti de illis potest, quod vel iniquitatem non fecerint, vel nullus in ipsorum ore dolus fuerit. Personam haec tangunt & praedicant, atque ejus [?]ἀναμαρτησίαν[?]. Ac propterea soli Christo vindicanda, uti ipsi & verba illa attribuuntur, 1 Pet. ii. 22. II. 22. & res 1 Ioan. iii. 5. Heb. vii. 26. Matth. xxvii. 18.
units.tr: Because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth. Although he had said nothing other than what God had commanded him. Something greater lies beneath those words: for many indeed say nothing other than what God has commanded them, yet it cannot be admitted of them that they did no violence, or that there was no deceit in their mouth. These words touch on a person and proclaim his sinlessness [ἀναμαρτησία]. And therefore they are to be claimed for Christ alone, as these words are attributed to him (1 Pet. 2.22; cf. Isa. 53.9), and the fact is attributed to him in 1 John 3.5, Heb. 7.26 and Matt. 27.18.

units.la: 10. ET DOMINUS VOLUIT CONTERERE EUM IN INFIRMITATE] Tamen Deo visum est eum conterere & infirmare: id est, attenuare fame, illuvie, squallore. Verba activa apud Hebraeos saepe permittendi habent significatum. Causa sequitur cur id Deus permiserit. Per totum caput Grotius necesse habet singula enervare. Quae maximas testantur afflictiones, & personae dignitatem vel rationem plus quam singularem, pro vulgaribus, & quae multis communia sunt, passim accipit. Dominus voluit conterere eum רכא[?], nec tantum fame, illuvie & squallore attenuare.
units.tr: 10. And the Lord was pleased to bruise him with infirmity. Yet it seemed good to God to bruise him and weaken him, that is, to wear him down with hunger, filth and squalor. Active verbs among the Hebrews often have the sense of permitting. The reason follows why God permitted this. Throughout the whole chapter Grotius is compelled to weaken each point. He takes in general terms expressions which attest the greatest afflictions and a dignity or status more than singular, and which are common to many. The Lord was pleased to bruise him, dakka [רכא], and not merely to wear him down with hunger, filth and squalor.

units.la: SI POSUERIT PRO DELICTO ANIMAM SUAM, VIDEBIT SEMEN LONGÆVUM] Verteris recte: ut cum semet ipsum subjecerit poenis, videat semen, diuque vivat. Hebraeis poena etiam injuste irrogata ןוּמ[?] dicitur, quia infligitur, si non sonti, certe quasi sonti. Sic נוּן[?] sumi apparet Genes. xxxi. 39. Zachariae xiv. 19. Vixit diu Jeremias in Aegypto. Nec posuit animam Jeremias. Neque hoc simpliciter est, subjicere se poenis, sed poenae mortis. Non pro delicto, vel suo, aut suorum, quamvis immerens multa, sustinuit. Neque adeo longaevus fuit. Non certe vidit semen longaevum, ἀτέκνα μακρόβιον[?]. Ut neutiquam possint Jeremiae aptari illa: Christo autem debeant.
units.tr: If he shall make his soul a sacrifice for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed. You translate rightly: that when he has subjected himself to punishments, he may see his seed and live long. Among the Hebrews, a punishment even if unjustly inflicted is called [ashmah], because it is laid on, if not on a guilty man, at least as if on a guilty one. So the word appears to be used in Gen. 31.39, and Zech. 14.19. Jeremiah lived long in Egypt. But Jeremiah did not make his soul a sacrifice. Nor does this simply mean subjecting oneself to punishments, but to punishment of death. Jeremiah did not suffer for sin, either his own or that of his people, though he suffered much undeservedly. Nor was he so long-lived. Certainly he did not see a long-lived seed, childless and long-lived [ἄτεκνος μακρόβιος]. So these words cannot in any way be applied to Jeremiah, but they ought to be applied to Christ.

units.la: ET VOLUNTAS DOMINI IN MANU DIRIGETUR] Melius: in manu (ejus scilicet) prosperabitur. Multi per ipsum ad pietatem convertentur. Quod & sequentia explicant. Non hoc unum, ut ad pietatem homines convertat, voluit Deus in, vel cum eo, aut per ipsum: sed quidquid ad nostri redemtionem, & justificationem spectat, & gloriam: ut & sequentia indicant, & antecedentia.
units.tr: And the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. Better: shall prosper in his hand (that is, his). Many will be converted to godliness through him. The following words also explain this. God did not will only this, that he should convert men to godliness, in or with him, or through him; but whatever pertains to our redemption, justification and glory, as both what follows and what precedes indicate.

units.la: 11. VIDEBIT ET SATURABITUR] Videbit diu ad satietatem. Simile loquendi genus in Hebraeo: Gen. xxv. 8. xxxv. 29. 1 Paral. xxiii. 1. xxix. 28. II Paral. xxiv. 14. Sed praemittitur in textu, ἐ labore animae suae[?]. Vel, uti Vulgata habet, pro eo quod laboravit anima. Quae ad sensum loci maxime faciunt.
units.tr: 11. He shall see and be satisfied. He shall see for a long time until he is satiated. A similar mode of speaking in Hebrew: Gen. 25.8; 35.29; 1 Chron. 23.1; 29.28; 2 Chron. 24.14. But in the text there is placed before it, from the travail of his soul [ἀπὸ τοῦ πόνου τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ]. Or, as the Vulgate has it, for what his soul has laboured. These things contribute very much to the sense of the passage.

units.la: IN SCIENTIA SUA] Per eam quam habet Dei cognitionem. Sequentia declarant, accipienda illa esse de notitia ejus, objective, sive de rite eum & cum fide agnoscendo. ἐν ἐπιγνώσει ἐ[?] Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, II Petr. ii. 20. & Phil. iii. 8. διὰ τὸ ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως αὐτοῦ. Ioan. xvii. 3.
units.tr: IN HIS KNOWLEDGE] That is, through the knowledge of God which he has. What follows shows that this must be understood of knowing him objectively, that is, of recognising him properly and with faith. [ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ], 2 Pet. 2:20; and Phil. 3:8, because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of him [διὰ τὸ ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως αὐτοῦ], John 17:3.

units.la: IUSTIFICABIT IPSE SERVUS MEUS MULTOS] Exemplo & institutione sua corriget multos etiam ex gentibus. Hoc est maxime propria verbi צדק[?], & Graece δικαιῶν significatio, quae apparet & Dan. xii. 3. Apoc. xxii. 11. & alibi saepe. Ab hoc significatu proprio alii per similitudinem quandam fluunt. Maxime propria verbi צדיק[?], & Graeci δικαιῶν significatio est forensis & judicialis, opposita condemnationi. Quod patet apud hunc Prophetam, cap. v. 23. & L. 8. tum Deut. xxv. 1. Exod. xxiii. 7. Iob xiii. 18. & xxvii. 5. 1 Reg. viii. 32. Prov. xvii. 15. Matth. xii. 37. & xi. 19. Luc. xvi. 15. Rom. viii. 33. 34. Quodque idem sit loci sensus, manifestum est ex argumento totius capitis, & sequente antiologia, & iniquitates eorum ipse portabit. Tum epitheta & elogia Servi, ac Justi ἐξόχως & absolute positi, Messiam indicant, non Ieremiam.
units.tr: MY SERVANT SHALL JUSTIFY MANY] By his example and teaching he shall correct many, even from among the Gentiles. This is the most proper meaning of the Hebrew צדק and of the Greek δικαιῶν, as appears also in Dan. 12:3, Rev. 22:11, and often elsewhere. Other meanings flow from this proper sense by a certain likeness. The most proper meaning of the Hebrew צדיק and of the Greek δικαιῶν is forensic and judicial, the opposite of condemnation. This is plain in this prophet, ch. 5:23 and 8:? [L. 8.], and then in Deut. 25:1, Exod. 23:7, Job 13:18 and 27:5, 1 Kings 8:32, Prov. 17:15, Matt. 12:37 and 11:19, Luke 16:15, Rom. 8:33-34. That this is the sense of the passage is clear from the argument of the whole chapter and from the following antithesis, and he shall bear their iniquities. Moreover, the titles Servant and Just One, used absolutely and eminently, point to the Messiah, not to Jeremiah.

units.la: ET INIQUITATES EORUM IPSE PORTABIT] id est, auferet, per μετωνυμίαν, quia qui sordes aliquas auferunt, solent eas collo suppositò portare. Sic & נשא pro auferre habes, Num. XVI. 15. II Reg. XX. 17. vertiturque per σκορᾶν, ἀναιρεῖν, ἀφαιρεῖν. Abstulit Ieremias multorum peccata, ita uti diximus, eos corrigendo. Gravis error & in re, & in persona. Nec portavit Ieremias peccata populi, nec abstulit. יסבל est in textu, non נשא, & illud nunquam non asportare, bajulare significat, non simpliciter auferre. Grotius olim, contra Socinum: In Hebraeo est עונם הוא יסבל. Vox autem עון iniquitatem significat: atque etiam iniquitatis poenam, ut 2Reg. VII. 9. Vox autem סבל est sustinere, bajulare, quoties autem bajulare ponitur cum nomine peccati, aut iniquitatis, idin omni lingua & maxime in Hebraismo significat poenas ferre. Nam נשא quidem interdum significat auferre: סבל autem nunquam. Diserte ergo hic dicitur Christus laturus poenas eorum qui justificantur. Haec phrasis nullam aliam interpretationem recipit. Quantum mutatus ab illo!
units.tr: AND HE SHALL BEAR THEIR INIQUITIES] That is, he shall take them away, by metonymy, because those who remove some filth are accustomed to carry it on their neck. So too you find נשא used for to take away, Num. 16:15 and 2 Kings 20:17, and it is rendered by σκορᾶν, ἀναιρεῖν, ἀφαιρεῖν. Jeremiah took away the sins of many, as we have said, by correcting them. A grave error, both in the matter and in the person. Jeremiah neither bore the sins of the people nor took them away. The text has יסבל, not נשא, and that always means to carry off or to bear, not simply to remove. Grotius formerly, against Socinus: in the Hebrew it is עונם הוא יסבל. The word עון means iniquity, and also the punishment of iniquity, as in 2 Kings 7:9. The word סבל means to sustain or bear, and wherever to bear is used with the name of sin or iniquity, in every language and especially in Hebrew idiom it means to bear punishment. For נשא indeed sometimes means to take away, but סבל never does. Therefore it is stated plainly here that Christ will bear the punishments of those who are justified. This phrase admits no other interpretation. How far changed from that!

units.la: 12. IDEO DISPERTIAM EI PLURIMOS] dabo ei partem in multis. Id est, multos servabunt Chaldaei in ipsius gratiam. Vide Jerem. XXXIX. 17. Sed hoc in loco non dicitur, multos propter Jeremiam servatos fuisse; sed Ebedmelechum evasurum, quia confiderat Jehovae. Et quamvis illud esset verum, quid convenit cum verbis Jesaiae? quid cum perpetuo verborum argumento? Quanto rectius Christiani eundem horum sensum faciunt, cum illo Psalmi 11. 8. & dabo gentes hereditatem tuam? adde Psalm. LXXII. 10. 11. & Phil. II. 9. propterea etiam exaltavit eum Deus, & largitus est nomen &c. & Ioan. XVII. 4. 5.
units.tr: 12. THEREFORE I WILL DIVIDE HIM A PORTION among the many: I will give him a portion among the many. That is, the Chaldeans will spare many for his sake. See Jer. 39:17. But in this place it is not said that many were saved on account of Jeremiah; it is said that Ebed-melech would escape because he trusted in Jehovah. And even if that were true, what agrees with the words of Isaiah? What agrees with the consistent argument of the words? How much more rightly do Christians understand the same sense of these words, compared with that of Psalm 2:8, I will give the nations as your inheritance? Add Psalm 72:10-11, Phil. 2:9, therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name, etc., and John 17:4-5.

units.la: ET FORTIUM DIVIDET SPOLIA] Id est, Nabuzardan, magister militum capta urbe de praeda ipsi dona mittet. Jerem. XL. 5. Oblatum etiam ipsi a Chaldaeis terra quantum vellet. Vide & infra XV. Obsecro, quantulum illud, ut praedici, & tanta, non cum emphasi modo, sed gloria, debuerit? Quod ipse ille locus significat satis, ad quem nos remittit: deditque ei Praefectus satellitum viaticum & munus, ac dimisit eum. Quis non ad quosvis fere aut illa ipsa verba, aut alia applicabit, ita in Scripturam commentari si porro libeat? Bene, si in Jeremiâ aliquam hujus Prophetae, aut capitis allegationem ostenderet, vel dictorum explicationem. Jam vero ex cerebro fingere nescio quam coactam & inaudi-tam expositionem aut allegoriam neque ipsum decet, neque nos illis adhibere fidem. Indignum profecto facinus, proferre admiranda Annotata, & non semel probare, quod in istum sensum accipi verba debeant, vel aliter non possint: quod in duris & inusitatis deberet fieri ante omnia. Alioqui quur non cum Christianis vulgo exponas de Christo, ex Col. 11. 15. & Ephes. IV. 8?
units.tr: AND HE SHALL DIVIDE THE SPOILS OF THE STRONG That is, Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard, after the city was taken, will send him gifts from the booty. Jer. 40:5. Also the land was offered him by the Chaldeans, as much as he wished. See also below, ch. 15. I ask you, how small is that, as I have said, and how much ought such a thing to have been, not only with emphasis but with glory? The very passage to which it refers shows this well enough: the captain of the guard gave him provisions and a gift, and let him go. Who would not apply almost any words to almost anything in this way, if one wished to go on commenting on Scripture so? It would be well if he showed some reference from Jeremiah to this prophet, or to the chapter, or an explanation of the sayings. But to invent from his own brain some forced and unheard-of exposition or allegory is neither fitting for him nor something we should give credence to. It is truly an unworthy deed to bring forward wonderful annotations and not once to prove that the words must be taken in that sense, or cannot be taken otherwise; which ought above all to be done in hard and unusual passages. Otherwise, why do you not, as Christians commonly do, expound it of Christ, from Col. 2:15 and Eph. 4:8?

units.la: PRO EO QUOD TRADIDIT IN MORTEM ANIMAM SUAM] In Hebraeo: Quia effudit in mortem animam suam. Id est, periculis mortis semet objecit, colendo veriveritatem qua odium parit. Vide historiam ad hanc rem appositam, Jerem. xxvi. 13. sic ϑέναι ψυχῷ[?] dici pro periculo mortis semet objicere, diximus ad Joh. x. 11. Ita in finem usque pergit Autor evirare Prophetae verba, & extenuare prorsus. Quod de morte dicitur, ille de periculis mortis exponit, & odio, quod quis veritatem dicendo incurrit. Neque Joan. x. 11. ita mortis pericula intelli-guntur, ut non quoque ipsa. μέχρι θανάτου, Phil. ii. 8. Graeci, παρεδόθη εἰς θάνατον ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτῆς. Confer Rom. iv. 25. Accedit, quod in hoc capite non semel fiat mortis mentio, sed aliquoties, ut non nisi de morte perpessa possint intelligi. Denique & phrasis effundendi animam idem evincit. Vide Psalm. xxxi. 14. Sed & hunc quoque Grotius non proprie de Christo, sed Davide exponit, ut Davidis profugi calamitates describentem. Quamvis nec impedire dicat, ut sensu sublimiore ad Messiam respiciat.
units.tr: BECAUSE HE POURED OUT HIS SOUL TO DEATH In the Hebrew: because he poured out his soul to death. That is, he exposed himself to the dangers of death, by cultivating the truth which breeds hatred. See the history relevant to this matter, Jer. 26:13. So θεῖναι ψυχήν is said for to expose oneself to the danger of death, as we said on John 10:11. Thus the author keeps on to the end twisting the prophet's words and weakening them altogether. What is said of death he explains of the dangers of death, and of the hatred which someone incurs by speaking the truth. Nor are the dangers of death in John 10:11 understood so as not also to include death itself: μέχρι θανάτου, Phil. 2:8. The Greek has παρεδόθη εἰς θάνατον ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτῆς; compare Rom. 4:25. Besides, in this chapter mention of death is made not once but several times, so that it can only be understood of death actually suffered. Finally, the phrase of pouring out the soul proves the same thing. See Psalm 31:14. But Grotius also explains this not properly of Christ but of David, as describing the calamities of the fugitive David. Although he does not deny that it may look to the Messiah in a higher sense.

units.la: ET CUM SCELERATIS REPUTATIS EST] Ita est tractatus, quomodo scelerati solent, in carcere, catenis, & barathro, non etiam morte? Nempe ne ad Christum abeat annotatio: qui mortis tempore quidem maxime inter sceleratos, ut eorum princeps & coryphaeus, aestimatus fuit atque pependit. Quare ad hoc Marcus Prophetae illa verba adducit, ut latere Christianum, nisi τῆτο [illegible, ~6 letters] verus sensus non posset, & impleta est Scriptura dicens, & cum impiis putatus est. cap. xv. 28.
units.tr: AND HE WAS COUNTED AMONG THE WICKED Is it treated so as wicked men usually are, in prison, in chains, and in the pit, but not even in death? Surely so that the note does not pass over to Christ, who at the time of his death was indeed counted and hanged among the wicked, as their prince and chief. Therefore Mark applies these words of the prophet to this, so that the Christian could not hide the true sense, unless [illegible] ... and the Scripture was fulfilled which says, and he was counted with the transgressors, ch. 15:28.

units.la: ET IPSE PECCATA MULTORUM TULIT] Pessime tractatus fuit per multorum improbitatem, ut supra 5. Hoc vero aliud quid & minus est, quam aliorum ferre peccata. Non qui ab aliis male excipitur, peccata ipsorum ideo ferr, pro phrasi scripturae, sed qui pro iis luit. Quod non una vice, modoque, in hoc capite notatur, ut dubium amplius esse non queat. Vide Exod. xxviii. 13. Jezech. xviii. 10. Grotius, adversus Socinum, pag. 15. Etiamsi vero ambigua esset harum vocum, ferre peccata, in sacris literis significatio, tamen tum hoc Esaia, tum ipso Petri loco certam faceret interpretationem adjuncta mentio perpessionum Christi & liberationis nostrae. Peccata enim ferre patiendo, atque ita ut inde liberentur alii, aliud indicare non potest, quam poena aliena susceptionem. Apud eundem Esaiam verf. 6. & 7. est: Deus conjecit sive impegit in eum panam omnium nostrum. Exigitur, & ipse affligitur. Hic nullum non lapidem movet Socinus, ut sensum genuinum verbis extorqueat: novamque interpretationem comminiscitur.
units.tr: AND HE BORE THE SINS OF MANY He was very badly treated by the wickedness of many, as above, ch. 5. But this is something other and less than bearing the sins of others. It is not one who is ill-received by others who bears their sins, according to the phrase of Scripture, but one who pays for them. This is noted not once, nor in one manner, in this chapter, so that there can no longer be any doubt. See Exod. 28:13, Ezek. 18:10. Grotius, against Socinus, p. 15: Even if the phrase to bear sins were ambiguous in the meaning of these words in Holy Scripture, yet the mention in Isaiah, and in the very passage of Peter, joined with the sufferings of Christ and our deliverance, would make the interpretation certain. For to bear sins by suffering, and so that others are thereby freed, can indicate nothing other than the taking on of another's punishment. In the same Isaiah, verses 6 and 7: God laid or struck on him the punishment of us all. He is exacted, and he is afflicted. Here Socinus moves every stone to wrest the genuine sense from the words, and devises a new interpretation.

units.la: ET PRO TRANSGRESSORIBUS ROGAVIT] פלל[?] est deprecari, ut exponit ad hunc locum respiciens Scriptor Hebraeus, de vita & morte Mosis. Sensus est; eo ipso tempore, cum tam dura pateretur a populo, non cessavit ad Deum preces pro eo fundere, ut olim Moses in deserto. Vide Jerem. xiv. 7. xxxvii. 3. xxxviii. 17. & xlii. 2. Adeo oblitus nunc est deprecationis, quam Christus pro inimicis fecit in ipso mortis articulo, ut eam ne memorandam quidem censuerit? Etiam Stephanus pro interfectoribus suis oravit: ergo & huic applicetur Jesaiae Prophetia, cujus intercessio, non quum alia, sed crudelem mortem pateretur, magis memorabilis est, quam Jeremiae, locis illis indicata. Quomodo autem Christi hic potuit non meminisse, qui non solum quando diximus, sed in perpetuum apud Patrem, pro transgressoribus intercedit, & vivit ut pro nobis oret? Chaldaeus: & ipse pro peccatis multorum deprecabitur, & transgressoribus dimittetur propter eum.
units.tr: AND HE MADE INTERCESSION FOR THE TRANSGRESSORS פלל means to entreat, as the Hebrew writer explains it in regard to this passage, in his account of the life and death of Moses. The sense is: at that very time, when he suffered such harsh things from the people, he did not cease to pour out prayers to God for them, as once Moses did in the desert. See Jer. 14:7, 37:3, 38:17, and 42:2. Has he now so forgotten the intercession which Christ made for his enemies at the very point of death, that he thinks it is not even worth mentioning? Stephen too prayed for his killers; so the prophecy of Isaiah should be applied to this as well, whose intercession, suffered not in any other way but in a cruel death, is more memorable than Jeremiah's, indicated in those places. But how could Christ here have failed to be remembered, who not only at the time we have mentioned but forever before the Father intercedes for transgressors, and lives to make intercession for us? The Chaldee paraphrast: and he himself shall pray for the sins of many, and the transgressors shall be forgiven because of him.

units.la: Atque ita illustre Prophetae Jesaiae vaticinium Christo vindicavimus, & veritati satisfactionis, per ipsum praestitae, contra Socinum primo, inde etiam contra Grotium. Ad idem vero argumentum alter nunc pro sententia nostra locus est 1 Petr. ii. 14. in quo ita ad Jesaiam respicit, ut ejus quoque adducat verba: qui peccata nostra ipse ἀνήνεγκεν ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ[?] ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον, sustulit in corpore suo, &c. cujus vibice sanati estis. Quod Jesaias dixit, in Christum conjectas nostras iniquitates, easque ipsum portasse, Petrus inquit, sustulisse in corpore suo in lignum. nempe quum אָשָׁם[?] hostia fieret piacularis pro delictis nostris.
units.tr: Thus we have vindicated the illustrious prophecy of Isaiah for Christ, and the truth of the satisfaction made through him, first against Socinus and then also against Grotius. For the same argument there is now another passage that supports our view, 1 Pet. ii. 24, where Peter so refers to Isaiah that he also adduces his words: "who himself bore our sins [ἀνήνεγκεν ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον] in his body on the tree," and "by whose stripes you were healed." What Isaiah said, that our iniquities were laid upon Christ and that he bore them, Peter expresses by saying that he "bore up" (sustulit) them in his body on the wood, namely when he became the guilt offering [אָשָׁם] for our sins.

units.la: Excipit Socinus, de Servat. part. ii. cap. vi. in loco Petri ἀνήνεγκεν non esse pertulit, sed abstulit, uti & Heb. ix. ult. Resp. i. Nullum vero dubium, quin Petrus respexit illa voce ad Hebraeum נָשָׂא[?], & נָשָׂא[?], quibus Propheta usus. Quemadmodum vero ostendimus, quod נשׂא[?] nec solum, nec primo significat abstulit, sed tulit, hinc sustulit, abstulit; ita & vox ἀνήνεγκεν. ii. Eoque magis, quo non simplex ἠνέγκεν dicitur, sed ἀνενέγκεν. Certe ἀναφέρω primum & proprie significat sustollo, sursum fero. Tum, perfero, patior. Etiam, transfero. Nunquam non notat translationem. Propria est illa vocis acceptio, sive compositionem respicias ex ἀνὰ & φέρω; sive usum vocis, apud Scriptores. iii. Jam non modo nulla ratio est, quare non prima, naturalis, & usitata vocis significatio hic retineatur; sed & multa cogunt non aliter accipere. Tum illud, ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτῆ, in corpore suo. Tum, ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον, in lignum. Quae cum voce ἀνήνεγκεν conjuncta, nemini non persuadebunt, sensu proprio sustollendi accipi omnino debere, neque aliter posse. Ut si forte alibi alium in sensum veniret vox illa, certe non hic, ubi tot ac tanta sunt, quae proprium efflagitant, non alienum. Recepit ergo peccata nostra, sive eorum poenas in se Christus, in corpore suo, ad lignum: id est, vere sustulit in se, & pertulit, DWN. Quare ut si vel simplex ἠνέγκεν hic esset, etiam non addita praepositione ἀνὰ sursum, ἀνήνεγκεν, tot circumstantiae satis juberent sensu sustollendi explicare. iv. Sit ita, & significet ἀνήνεγκεν abstulit; an propterea nequit connotare etiam, quod pertulit, vel sustulit? Quid vero magis absonum? Haud pugnant illa. Et abstulit, & sustulit: atque per id quod sustulit prius, abstulit. Non ut nequeat intelligi sustulisse, quia abstulit. Utrumque bene conjungitur, Coloss. ii. 13. 14. Χαρισάμενος[?] vobis omnes transgressiones. Ἐξαλείψας id quod nobis adversum chirographum τοῖς δόγμασιν, & sustulit illud è medio, affigens illud cruci. v. Non vero abstulit Christus illa à se, vel suo corpore: & additur, ἀνενέγκεν [?] ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτῷ. Nequit ergo solo sensu auferendi explicari. vi. In Scripturâ ubiq; habet sensum sustollendi & ferendi sursum. Falliturque Socinus vehementer, quando putat non alibi, in universis Euangelistarum & Apostolorum scriptis, eundem loquendi modum reperiri. ἀναφέρει αὐτὸς εἰς ὄρος ὑψηλόν, Matth. xvii. 1. Καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν. Luc. xxiv. 51. Heb. vii. 27. ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας: & de Pontifice ibidem, quod solitus fuerit θυσίας ἀναφέρειν. & cap. xiii. 12. Jac. ii. 21. ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ. Atque hoc ipso capite Petrus, vers. 5. dixit, ἀνενέγκαι πνευματικὰς θυσίας. Adeo quod semper & ubique significat sursum ferre, offerre, hoc loco non poterit, pro natura, & compositione, & usu suo accipi sensu sustollendi aut ferendi sursum?
units.tr: Socinus objects, in De Servatore, part ii, chapter vi, that in Peter's passage ἀνήνεγκεν does not mean "bore" (pertulit) but "took away" (abstulit), as also in Heb. ix. last verse.
