Answer, first: there is no doubt that Peter was alluding by that word to the Hebrew נָשָׂא, which the prophet used. But as we have shown, נָשָׂא does not primarily or chiefly mean "take away" but "bear," and hence "lift up," "take away"; so too the word ἀνήνεγκεν. Second, all the more so because the simple form ἠνέγκεν is not used but ἀνενέγκεν. Certainly ἀναφέρω first and properly means "to lift up," "to carry upward." Then it means "to bear," "to suffer," and also "to carry across." It never fails to signify transfer. That is the proper sense of the word, whether you look at the composition from ἀνὰ and φέρω or at the usage of the word among writers. Third, there is not only no reason why the first, natural, and common meaning of the word should not be kept here, but many things compel us to take it otherwise. There is the phrase "in his body" (ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ), and there is "on the tree" (ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον). Joined with the word ἀνήνεγκεν, these will persuade anyone that it must be taken in its proper sense of "lifting up," and cannot be taken otherwise. Even if that word happened to have another sense elsewhere, certainly not here, where so many and such weighty things demand the proper sense and not a foreign one. Christ therefore took our sins, or their punishments, upon himself, in his body, to the tree; that is, he truly "bore" them upon himself and endured them, נָשָׂא. So even if the simple ἠνέγκεν stood here, without the preposition ἀνὰ "up," all these circumstances would be enough to direct us to explain it in the sense of lifting up. Fourth, grant that it is so, and that ἀνήνεγκεν means "took away"; can it not also imply that he bore or carried them? What could be more absurd? These senses do not clash. "Took away" and "bore" are both true, and by what he bore he first took away. It does not follow that it cannot be understood as "bore" because it means "took away." Both are well joined in Col. ii. 13, 14: "having forgiven you all trespasses," "blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross" [Χαρισάμενος, Ἐξαλείψας]. Fifth, Christ did not take those sins away from himself or from his body, yet the text adds "in his body" (ἀνενέγκεν ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ). Therefore it cannot be explained by the sense of taking away alone. Sixth, in Scripture the word everywhere has the sense of lifting up and carrying upward. Socinus is gravely mistaken when he thinks that this manner of speaking is not found elsewhere "in the whole writings of the Evangelists and Apostles." "He brought them up (ἀναφέρει) into a high mountain," Matt. xvii. 1; "and he was carried up (ἀνεφέρετο) into heaven," Luke xxiv. 51; Heb. vii. 27, "having offered up himself" (ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας), and of the high priest in the same place, that he was accustomed "to offer up sacrifices" (θυσίας ἀναφέρειν); and chapter xiii. 12; Jas. ii. 21, "having offered up Isaac his son" (ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ). And in this very chapter Peter, verse 5, says "to offer up spiritual sacrifices" (ἀνενέγκαι πνευματικὰς θυσίας). If, then, a word that always and everywhere means to carry up or to offer cannot, by its nature, composition, and use, be taken in this passage in the sense of lifting up or carrying upward, what can?

units.la: Socinus: Hebr. ix. 28. dicitur Christus semel oblatus εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας, ad multorum auferenda peccata. Hic ἀνενεγκεῖν auferre significat, non sustollere in se. Ad quod haud una responsio. i. Detur, hoc solo loco ita accipi: ergo apud Petrum, in eundem sensum, & non illum quem primò, & omnibus aliis Scripturæ locis habet? ii. Sint, quæ suadeant in loco illo ad Hebræos convenire ut sic vertatur: at in loco Petri, propter adjuncta multa, non potest aliter quam communi sua, uti diximus, significatione exponi. iii. In loco Paulino præcesserat ἐσταυρωθείς [?], quod alibi dicitur eadem epist. cap. vii. 27. ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας; ad quod tum sequitur εἰς τὸ ἀνενεγκεῖν, obtulit se, ut auferret. quod utrumque simul complexus Petrus fuit, quando dixit ἀνενέγκεν, non quod vox ista notet auferre, sed res seu ablatio peccatorum eo comprehensa sit, quod Christus peccata nostra in se sustulit. Aliud est, simpliciter dicere ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας, & hoc post memoratam oblationem Christi, eaque comprehensam peccatorum nostrorum in Christum translationem; vel, ἀνενεγκεῖν in suo corpore. Denique nec in loco ad Hebræos, exulat significatio sustollendi, sed præsupponitur & connotatur. Obtulit se Christus Deo in sacrificium expiatorium, eoque peccata nostra in se transtulit, sustinuitque, atque sic à nobis abstulit.
units.tr: Socinus: in Heb. ix. 28 Christ is said to have been offered once "to bear the sins of many" (εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας), "to take away the sins of many." Here ἀνενεγκεῖν means to take away, not to lift up upon oneself. To this there is more than one answer. First, grant that in this one place it is so understood: is it therefore to be understood in the same sense in Peter, and not in the sense which it has first and in all other passages of Scripture? Second, grant that there are reasons that persuade us to render it so in the passage to the Hebrews; yet in Peter's passage, because of the many accompanying words, it cannot be explained otherwise than in its common meaning, as we have said. Third, in Paul's passage the words "having been crucified" (ἐσταυρωθείς) had preceded, and in the same epistle, chapter vii. 27, it is said "having offered up himself" (ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας); and to this follows "to offer" (εἰς τὸ ἀνενεγκεῖν), "that he might bear away" [i.e. "to bear, to take away"]. Peter embraced both together when he said ἀνενέγκεν, not because that word means "take away," but because the thing, namely the removal of sins, is comprehended in it, since Christ bore our sins upon himself. It is one thing to say simply "to bear the sins" (ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας), and that after the mentioned oblation of Christ, which comprehends the transfer of our sins to Christ; it is another to say "to bear in his own body." Finally, the passage to the Hebrews does not exclude the sense of lifting up, but presupposes and implies it. Christ offered himself to God as an expiatory sacrifice, and thereby transferred our sins to himself, sustained them, and so took them away from us.

units.la: Deinde, addit Socinus, præpositionem in, ex Hebraei sermonis proprietate, isto in loco non aliud significare, quàm per: atque ad hunc modum vertendum fuisse Petri locum ipsum, qui peccata nostra ipse abstulit per corpus suum super lignum. Resp. Ut, quibus semel constitutum Scripturam in suam malam pertrahere sententiam, & jubere servire hypothesi, non quiescunt unâ inventâ strophâ! ἀνενεγκεῖν, contrà naturam, & usum vocis non potest Socino significare sustulit. ἐν non in, sed per. Non quidem negamus, apud Hebræos nonnunquam in proper accipi : sed aut debere, aut posse hoc in loco, nullo quidem argumento evincit, quin nec tentat quidem ostendere Adversarius. Profersis ullum, qui ἀνενεγκὰν[?] ἐν τῷ σώματι ita interpretari quiverit. Sanè nobis non est dictator Socinus, non contra Scripturam. Quæ ista verborum perversio, portavit, sustulit in corpore suo, id est, minimè portavit in corpore, sed abstulit per corpus. ii. Repugnat etiam quod additur, in lignum. Nam quando sensu Adversariorum Christus peccata nostra abstulit per corpus, tum à nobis illa abstulit: quorsum vero additur, in lignum? Quid hoc loco tum istud? Quod tantæ hoc in sermone est efficaciæ, & adeo cogitationes nostras ad crucem mox trahit, factamque ibi peccatorum sublationem, ut si concedam verba sic legi debere, qui peccata nostra ipse abstulit per corpus suum super lignum, certus tamen sim à quocunque, præjudiciis adversæ sententiæ modò vacuo, non intellectum id iri aliter, quam uti nos docemus, & quod Socinus impugnat, Christum in cruce sustinuisse peccata nostra. Tanta ubique est veritatis in quocunque verbo vis. iii. Et hoc ipsum sumamus, in quod solum Adversarii identidem se recipiunt, Christum abstulisse peccata nostra: quo id sensu verum habent? non proprio, sed metaphorico, abstulit, id est, doctrinâ suâ viam monstravit quâ à peccatis liberemur, ut sic nobis auferantur ac remittantur. Ubi jam non modo, quod Christum sustulisse dicit Petrus, & in corpore, & in lignum, sed hoc etiam quod solum reliquum habuerunt Nostri, Christum abstulisse peccata, in fumum abit, neque id verâ & propriâ ratione corpori aut cruci Christi relinquitur, ut peccata suâ vi auferat. Neque de martyrio vel martyribus potest dici, quod peccata auferunt, quamvis doctrinam istam sanguine confirment, quæ rationem ostendit ablationis peccatorum, & liberationis ab iisdem.
units.tr: "Further," Socinus adds, "the preposition ἐν, by the peculiarity of the Hebrew idiom, in that place means nothing other than 'through,' and Peter's passage ought to be translated in this way: who himself took away our sins through his body upon the wood." Answer: How restless are those who, once they have settled on dragging Scripture into their own bad opinion and forcing it to serve their hypothesis, do not rest after finding a single trick! ἀνενεγκεῖν, contrary to the nature and use of the word, cannot mean "took" to Socinus. ἐν means not "in" but "through." We do not deny that among the Hebrews ἐν is sometimes taken as "through," but that it ought to be, or can be, so in this place, the Adversary does not prove by any argument; he does not even attempt to show it. Let him produce anyone who has been able to interpret ἀνενεγκὰν ἐν τῷ σώματι in this way. Certainly Socinus is not our dictator; we do not accept him against Scripture. What a perversion of words is this: "bore, took away in his body," that is, not at all "bore in his body," but "took away through his body"! Second, the added words "upon the wood" also clash with this. For if, in the sense of our opponents, Christ took our sins away through his body, then he took them from us; but why is "upon the wood" added? What is that phrase doing here? It has such force in this sentence, and it draws our thoughts at once to the cross and to the removal of sins accomplished there, that even if I grant that the words should be read "who himself took away our sins through his body upon the wood," I am still sure that anyone who is free of prejudice against the opposing view will understand it no differently from the way we teach, and from the way Socinus attacks it: that Christ bore our sins on the cross. Such is the force of truth in every word. Third, let us take even this point, to which our opponents repeatedly retreat alone, that Christ took away our sins. In what true sense do they hold this? Not in the proper sense, but in a metaphorical one: he took them away, that is, by his teaching he showed the way by which we are freed from sins, so that they are taken away from us and remitted. Here not only what Peter says, that Christ bore up our sins both in the body and on the wood, but also the point that our side alone retained, that Christ took away sins, dissolves into smoke; and it is not left to the body or the cross of Christ, in a true and proper way, to take away sins by its own power. Nor can it be said of martyrdom or of martyrs that they take away sins, even though they confirm that doctrine with their blood, which shows the manner of the removal of sins and of deliverance from them.

units.la: Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum, de justificatione, pag. 256. Posterius testimonium sumis ex Petri verbis à nostris jam citatis, cùm ait, Christum peccata nostra sustulisse in corpore suo super lignum, v. 24. Verùm his verbis nihil aliud significatur, quàm quòd Christus peccata nostra veluti suo corpori imposita sursum in crucem secum tulerit, sic ut una cum ipso fuerint extincta & crucifixa, hoc est, crucis mortem subierit, ut peccatorum nostrorum reatum omnem extingueret & aboleret. quod qua ratione citra imputationem aut satisfactionem factum fuerit, alibi ostendimus. Resp. Hoc verò quia nec ostendit alibi, neque ostendere vel ille, vel alius quispiam potest, fieri absque imputatione aut satisfactione, & superioribus verbis modò addimus verè illa sic, uti scribit, se habere, nimirum peccata nostra cum Christo vere fuisse extincta & crucifixa, hoc est, crucis mortem eum subiisse, ut peccatorum nostrorum reatum omnem extingueret & aboleret; sic jam finita est controversia, & habemus quod cupimus.
units.tr: Schlichting, against Meisner, on justification, p. 256. You take the second testimony from Peter's words, which our side has already cited, when he says that Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree, v. 24. But these words signify nothing other than that Christ carried our sins, as if they were laid upon his body, up with him onto the cross, so that they were put to death and crucified together with him; that is, he underwent the death of the cross so as to extinguish and abolish all the guilt of our sins. By what means this was done without imputation or satisfaction, we have shown elsewhere. Reply. But since he has not shown this elsewhere, and neither he nor anyone else can show that it is done without imputation or satisfaction, and since we now add to the words above that he says they are truly so, namely that our sins were truly put to death and crucified with Christ, that is, that he underwent the death of the cross so as to extinguish and abolish all the guilt of our sins, the controversy is thus now settled, and we have what we desire.

units.la: Atque ita fuit classis prima argumentum primum, ostendens, Christum poenas peccatorum nostrorum in se suscepisse ac sustinuisse, ex Iesa. Liii. & 1 Pet. ii. 24. Sequitur alterum, ex eo, quod Christus factus pro nobis sit peccatum, & exsecratio. Qui factus peccatum, & exsecratio, is aliorum in se suscepit sustinuit peccata: Christus factus est peccatum, & execratio: ergo. Major probatur, quia vel in se & propter se illud fuit, vel per & propter alios, causâ aut suâ, aut aliorum: non per, & in se: ergo. Hoc autem significat, quod illis locis additur, ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, pro nobis. Loca sunt Jesa. LIII. 10. II Cor. v. 21. Gal. III. 13.
units.tr: And so the first argument of the first class was that Christ took upon himself and bore the punishments of our sins, from Isaiah 53 and 1 Pet. 2:24. The second follows, from the fact that Christ was made sin and a curse for us. Whoever was made sin and a curse took upon himself and bore the sins of others. Christ was made sin and a curse; therefore. The major premise is proved: he was either so in himself and on his own account, or through and on account of others, either for his own cause or for theirs. Not through and in himself; therefore it was for others. This is what the words added in those places signify, for us (ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν). The passages are Isa. 53:10, 2 Cor. 5:21, Gal. 3:13.

units.la: Jesa. LIII. 10. אם חשים אשם si posuerit peccatum, reatum, hostiam pro peccato & reatu, animam suam, videbit semen. DWN proprie est delictum, ab DWN deliquit, peccavit. per metonymiam significat, oblationem pro delicto. Levit. v. 5. 6. atque erit, si peccaverit, aut reus fuerit אשם unius ex istis, & confiteatur id in quo peccavit, & adducet את אשמו peccatum suum, reatum, oblationem pro reatu suo, Jehova, propter peccatum suum quo peccavit. Similiter vers. 7, 15. Pari modo & Christus אשם dicitur. II Cor. v. 21. Eum qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν, ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in eo. Quo pacto Christus peccatum? num in se? an propter nos? Nimirum fuit hostia pro peccato, non suo, sed nostro. Uti ergo hostia peccatum dicebatur, non propter suum, sed propter ejus, cujus nomine offerebatur, sibi imputatum cæremonialiter, & propter impositum reatum; ita Christus, propter peccata quæ sustinuit nostra, peccatum, vel hostia pro peccato, fuit. Similiter ac ex altera parte nobis injustis imputatur justitia Christi; sic Christus in se justus, propter imputata sibi peccata nostra peccatum censitus fuit. Imputationem etiam Apostolus dicit, vers. Deus fuit in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians, non imputans eis μὴ λογιζόμενος αὐτοῖς τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν[?] peccata ipsorum.
units.tr: Isa. 53:10. If he shall make his soul an offering for sin and guilt, he shall see his seed. [אם תשים אשם] The word for guilt (אשם) properly means a delict, from the verb meaning to offend or sin; by metonymy it signifies an offering for guilt. Lev. 5:5–6: And it shall be, when he is guilty in one of these things, that he shall confess the sin in which he has sinned, and he shall bring his guilt offering to Jehovah for his sin which he has committed. Similarly in verses 7 and 15. In the same way Christ is called a guilt offering (אשם). 2 Cor. 5:21: He who knew no sin he made sin for us (ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν), that we might become the righteousness of God in him. In what way was Christ sin? Was it in himself? Or on account of us? Clearly he was a sacrifice for sin, not for his own sin but for ours. Just as the offering was called sin, not on account of its own sin but on account of him in whose name it was offered, being reckoned to it ceremonially and because of the guilt laid upon it, so Christ, because of the sins which he bore for us, was made sin, or a sacrifice for sin. Similarly, on the other side, the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, who are unrighteous; so Christ, righteous in himself, was reckoned as sin because our sins were imputed to him. The Apostle also speaks of imputation in the verse: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing to them (μὴ λογιζόμενος αὐτοῖς τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν) their sins.

units.la: Socinus, part. I. de Servat. cap. VIII. pag, 56. Non potest vocabulum hostiam pro peccato significare; sed hominem pro peccatore habitum aperte significat; quemadmodum multi clarissimi interpretes annotarunt. Nam, si hostiam pro peccato significaret, quam, obsecro, vim haberent verba illa, qui peccatum non noverat? Quæ enim Dei charitas, quam Paulus Corinthiis proponit ac commendat, & qua eos ad Deo se reconciliandos movere curat, ex eo apparet, quòd hostiam pro peccato fecerit eum, qui peccatum non noverat? Annon necesse est, hostiam pro peccato incontaminatam esse, atque purissimam? Maximam autem vim habebunt, si vocem peccatum, hoc loco, hominem pro peccatore habitum significare dicamus. Ex eo enim Dei charitas vehementer elucet, quòd eum, qui innocentissimus erat, nostri causâ, tamquam pessimum hominem, atroci & infami morte occidi voluerit. Adde, quòd illa interpretatione antithesis manifesta Peccati, & Justitiæ, eaque pulcherrima & elegantissima, penitus corruit atque dissoluitur. Resp. I. Non potest negare Socinus, peccatum etiam significare hostiam pro peccato, sed ut peccatum significet pro peccatore habitum, nullo ostendit exemplo. II. Et si vel peccatum isto sensu veniret unquam, non tamen peccatum fieri. III. non, peccatum fieri à Deo. Non enim quid ab hominibus, sed quod à Deo factum sit, Textus memorat. Deus Christum peccatum fecit. IV. atque ipse Christus se fecit אשם. V. Non id pro nobis dici potest hactenus, quod forte de Christo homines opinati fuerunt. VI. Neque per id facti nos justitia Dei in Christo. Quæ tamen omnia hoc in loco sunt, & sententiam, & argumentum nostrum copiose confirmant. vii. Qui clarissimi interpretes hic annotarunt, signifi-cari Christum pro peccatore habitum, non idcirco negant Christum hostiam fuisse pro peccato: nam utrumque verum est, & quod hostia pro peccato fuit, & pro peccatore habitus. vii. & sic vis sua constat verbis, qui peccatum non noverat, nempe quod is pro peccatore habitus est, & ex imputatis ipsi peccatis nostris (utrumque enim conjungimus) tractatus ut nocentissimus, qui in se revera erat innocentissimus, sanctus, liber a malo, incontaminatus; Hebr. vii. 27.
units.tr: Socinus, part I, On the Saviour, ch. VIII, p. 56: The word cannot signify a sacrifice for sin; it clearly signifies a man regarded as a sinner, as many most distinguished interpreters have noted. For if it signified a sacrifice for sin, what force, I ask you, would the words "who knew no sin" have? For what charity of God, which Paul sets before the Corinthians and commends, and by which he takes care to move them to be reconciled to God, appears from this, that he made a sacrifice for sin of one who knew no sin? Must not a sacrifice for sin be unstained and most pure? But these words will have the greatest force if we say that the word sin here signifies a man regarded as a sinner. For from this the love of God shines forth strongly, that he willed that one most innocent be put to death for our sake, as if he were the worst of men, by an atrocious and infamous death. Add that by that interpretation the manifest and most beautiful and elegant antithesis of sin and righteousness collapses and is wholly dissolved. Reply. (1) Socinus cannot deny that peccatum can also signify a sacrifice for sin, but he shows by no example that it signifies a man regarded as a sinner. (2) Even if the word did ever bear that sense, it would not mean made sin. (3) Nor made sin by God; for the text speaks not of what was done by men but of what was done by God: God made Christ sin. (4) And Christ himself made himself a guilt offering (אשם). (5) It cannot be said that this was done for us merely because men have thought so about Christ. (6) Nor are we made the righteousness of God in Christ by that means. All these things, however, are in this place, and they copiously confirm both our meaning and our argument. (7) The most distinguished interpreters who have noted here that Christ is signified as one regarded as a sinner do not for that reason deny that Christ was a sacrifice for sin: both are true, that he was a sacrifice for sin and that he was regarded as a sinner. (8) And so the force of the words who knew no sin stands: namely, that he was so regarded as a sinner, and treated, with our sins imputed to him (for we join both together), as the most guilty, though in himself he was most innocent, holy, undefiled, unstained (Heb. 7:27).

units.la: ix Et simul hoc charitatem Dei in mittendo Christum, tum Christi erga nos vehementer commendat, quod nullis peccatis commaculatus, tamquam peccatis onustus tamen punitus ac verberatus fuit, insons pro peccatoribus, sanctus pro impiis, & potentissimus Dei filius pro nobis infirmis. Rom. v. 6. 7. Quod si vim habent illa verba, quando vocem peccatum hoc loco hominem pro peccatore habitum significare dicimus; quanto magis, si insuper addimus, & hostiam pro peccato factum, & ut peccatorem, dilaceratum fuisse punitionibus & malis, quæ nos ipsi ferre debuissemus? Adde quod sic etiam magis elucet antithesis manifesta peccati & justitiæ, neque aliter, quam ut intelligatur Christo imputatus noster reatus, & hostia hinc pro peccato factus, unde nobis cederet in justitiam: quia simpliciter id quod pro peccatore aliquis aut habeatur ab hominibus immerito, aut indignissime propterea vexetur & excipiatur, efficere non potest, ut in eo fiamus justitia coram Deo; quod ex imputatione illa quidem. Sic enim inquit Apostolus, eum qui non norat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in eo. Videlicet, non imputans peccata nobis, uti habet vers. 19. quia ea jam imputarat Christo. Syrus, ut nos efficeremur per eum justitia Dei. Arabs, ut nos per ipsum fieremus justitia Deo.
units.tr: And at the same time this greatly commends the charity of God in sending Christ, and Christ's love toward us: that though he was stained by no sins, yet he was punished and beaten as if laden with sins, innocent on behalf of sinners, holy on behalf of the impious, and the mighty Son of God on behalf of us who are weak (Rom. 5:6–7). If those words have force when we say that the word sin in this place signifies a man regarded as a sinner, how much more if we add besides that he was made a sacrifice for sin, and was torn apart as a sinner with the punishments and evils which we ourselves ought to have borne? Add that thus the manifest antithesis of sin and righteousness also shines more clearly, and it cannot be understood otherwise than that our guilt was imputed to Christ, and that he was made a sacrifice for sin from this, whence it would accrue to us for righteousness. For simply that someone is undeservedly regarded by men as a sinner, or is on that account most unworthily harassed and treated, cannot bring it about that we are made the righteousness of God in him; this comes indeed from that imputation. For thus the Apostle says: He who knew no sin he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him. Namely, not imputing their sins to us, as he has it in verse 19, because he had already imputed them to Christ. The Syriac: that we might be made through him the righteousness of God. The Arabic: that through him we might become righteousness to God.

units.la: Galat. iii. 13. Christus nos redemit a maledictione legis ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κα-τάρας τοῦ νόμου, factus pro nobis maledictio, γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα. En veram nostri, per Christum, redemtionem, a maledictione. Quo medio? Per id quod Christus pro nobis factus, factus nimirum maledictio. Id est, nostram maledictionem Christus abstulit, per hoc quod eam in se suscepit, sustinuitque. Cujus documentum fuit, quod ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος pependit in cruce. Nam omnis maledictus, qui in cruce pendet. Pependit autem Christus: sed, pro nobis. Ergo & pro iisdem maledictus, nec simpliciter, sed maledictio, uti peccatum, קְלָלָה [?] : adeo omnem in se nostram portavit maledictionem. Quemadmodum nos justitia Dei in ipso, non vulgariter justi: ita ipse no-stra injustitia, sibi vicissim imputata, peccatum, & maledictione nostra factus fuit maledictio.
units.tr: Gal. 3:13. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law (ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς καταράς τοῦ νόμου), having become for us a curse (γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα). Here is the true redemption of us from the curse, through Christ. By what means? Through this, that Christ became for us, that is, a curse. That is, Christ took away our curse by taking it upon himself and bearing it. The proof of this was that everyone who hangs (ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος) hung on the cross: every one who hangs on a tree is accursed. But Christ hung, and that for us; therefore he was also accursed for them, and not simply accursed but a curse, as sin is sin (קְלָלָה [?]); so entirely did he bear all our curse in himself. As we are made the righteousness of God in him, not merely righteous in a general way, so he himself, with our unrighteousness imputed to him in turn, was made sin, and with our curse was made a curse.

units.la: Socinus, part. ii. cap. i. pag. 73. Christum pro nobis execrationem factum esse, non significat, eam legis execrationem ipsum subiisse, quam nos subire deberemus. Execratio enim, quam nobis lex minabatur, & quam tu intelligis, mors aeterna erat; hanc vero ipse minime subiit. Sed nihil aliud significat, quam Christum, dum ipse nostri causa in quan-dam legis execrationem incidit, nos a vera legis execratione interea liberasse. Amavit enim enim Paulus, ut in aliis sæpe solet, in execrationis verbo argutus esse. Resp. 1. Nem-pe argutias in Paulo observat, qui passim argutias sectatur, ex se Apostolum æstimans, & quasi humanum, aut vulgarem Scriptorem præ manibus haberet loquitur, noster juxta ac Pauli adversarius. Nos Pauli argutias non scimus, sed bene Spiritus per eum loquentis ἐνδείξεως[?]. ii.[?] Paulus, ut Christi pœnas exaggeret & commodius exprimat, maledictionem factum dicit: Socinus contra ut extenuet, quandam legis execrationem, nec factum, sed in eam incidisse, explicat. iii. Et nostri duntaxat eausa, non etiam loco: quum & præpositio ὑπὲρ, & totius orationis contextus hoc loquatur. iv. Et liberasse ab execratione; quum in Textu sit, redemisse. Ut data operâ in id incumbere Adversarios videas, ut Scripturam ubique, & fidem nostram ea fundatam, studiose enervent. v. Non ob aliam causam Christus maledictus, & maledictio, & hoc factus, à Deo pro nobis, dici potest, quam quod eam omnem legis maledictionem subiit, quam nos subire debebamus. vi. Et mortem ideo æternam, non duratione temporis, sed pondere, vi & acerbitate passionis. vii. Non negamus significari, Christum, nostri causâ in legis execrationem incidisse, & nos ab ea liberasse; sed, nihil aliud notari, id negamus. Nam execrationem, à qua nos liberavit & redemit, ipse prius sustinuit, non causâ tantum nostri, sed & loco. Quippe ita oportuit. Christus nos à vera, inquis, execratione liberavit; non ergo quandam, sed veram ipse sustinuit. Quia locus indicat, per hoc nos ab execratione liberari, quod Christus ea pro nobis factus est. Non à quadam nos redemit, sed vera, ergo & veram, non quandam, pro nobis ab illa redimendis, tulit.
units.tr: Socinus, part. ii, chap. i, p. 73: That Christ was made a curse for us does not mean that he underwent that curse of the law which we ought to have undergone. For the curse the law threatened us with, and which you understand, was eternal death, and this he in no way underwent. It signifies only that Christ, while for our sake he fell into a certain curse of the law, meanwhile freed us from the true curse of the law. For he loved Paul, as is often his way elsewhere, to be subtle in the word "curse." Answer 1. Indeed, he finds subtleties in Paul, who everywhere hunts after subtleties, judging the Apostle by himself and speaking as if he had before him a merely human or ordinary writer, as our opponent does just as much as Paul's other adversaries. We do not know Paul's subtleties, but we do know the demonstration [ἐνδείξεως] of the Spirit speaking through him. ii. Paul, to magnify Christ's sufferings and express them more fittingly, says that he was made a curse. Socinus, on the contrary, to diminish them, explains it as a certain curse of the law and says he did not become one but fell into it. iii. It is for our sake only, not also in our place, since both the preposition ὑπέρ [huper] and the whole context of the sentence say so. iv. He freed us from the curse, whereas the text says he redeemed us. So you may see the adversaries deliberately bent on this, namely to weaken studiously Scripture everywhere, and our faith founded on it. v. Christ can be called accursed, and a curse, and made such by God for us, for no other reason than that he underwent the whole curse of the law which we ought to have undergone. vi. And he underwent eternal death not by the length of time but by the weight, force and bitterness of the suffering. vii. We do not deny that it is signified that Christ, for our sake, fell into the curse of the law and freed us from it; what we deny is that nothing else is noted. For the curse from which he freed and redeemed us, he first sustained, not only for our sake but also in our place. Indeed it had to be so. You say Christ freed us from the true curse; therefore he underwent not a certain curse but the true one. For the place indicates that we are freed from the curse by this, that Christ was made a curse for us. He redeemed us not from a certain curse but from the true one; therefore, to redeem us from it, he bore the true curse, not a certain one.

units.la: Arg. tertium. Mors est pœna peccati: Christus tulit mortem: ergo pœnam peccati tulit. Major probata à nobis, Tom. i. Lib. iii. cap. iv. Minor est in confesso. Non ita argumentationem instruimus, uti Socinus, part. iii. cap. vii. pag. 189. facit: Quicumque moritur, aut pro suis, aut pro alienis peccatis moritur: quod argumentum sic totum facile concedit, quasi nihil contra se faciens: omnino contendens, Christum pro peccatis nostris mortuum. Sed sic formamus argumentum: qui mortem sustinet peccati pœnam, eam sustinet vel peccati sui, vel alieni: ne ludum faciat in phrasi, mori pro peccatis, vel peccatorum causa.
units.tr: Third argument. Death is the punishment of sin; Christ underwent death; therefore he underwent the punishment of sin. The major we have proved, Tom. i, Lib. iii, cap. iv. The minor is admitted. We do not frame the argument as Socinus does, part. iii, chap. vii, p. 189: whoever dies, dies either for his own sins or for another's. He readily concedes this argument entire, as if it did nothing against him, while altogether contending that Christ died for our sins. But we frame the argument thus: whoever undergoes death as the punishment of sin undergoes it either for his own sin or for another's. Let him not make a game of the phrase "to die for sins, or on account of sins."

units.la: 1. Exc. Socinus: Innumerabiles moriuntur, qui nec pro suis, nec pro alienis peccatis satisfaciunt. Resp. Si de piis intelligas, & fidelibus qui in Domino moriuntur, mors ipsis non est pœna, per Christum, qui eam morte sua sustulit, ergo mors tua mors. Hi ergo dum moriuntur, pro peccatis suis non satisfaciunt, nedum alienis. Alii vero extra eum, mortem patiuntur, peccati pœnam, non tamen satisfaciunt, quia plura meriti sunt, quam solam illam mortem. Fidelibus in Christo mors non est pœna, quia nullum κατάκριμα iis qui in Christo Jesu, Rom. viii. 1. nulla actualis condemnatio, licet quidem illud quod in se & natura sua, extra Christum, condemnabile in ipsis adhuc reperiatur; sic nec quod pœna vere sit ipsis, quamvis extra Christum pœna omnino esset.
units.tr: First objection. Socinus: Countless people die who make satisfaction neither for their own sins nor for others'. Answer: If you understand this of the godly and the faithful who die in the Lord, death is not a punishment to them, through Christ, who by his death removed it; so your death is death. These, then, while they die, do not make satisfaction for their own sins, much less for others'. But others who die outside him suffer death, the punishment of sin, yet do not make satisfaction, because they have deserved more than that death alone. For believers in Christ death is not a punishment, because there is no condemnation [κατάκριμα] for those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. viii. 1: no actual condemnation, although what is in them condemnable in itself and by its nature, apart from Christ, is still found there. So neither is it truly a punishment to them, although apart from Christ it would be altogether a punishment.

units.la: 11. Exc. Ibidem, pag. 289. Nihil aliud in tua argumentatione concludis, quam, Christum mortuum esse, quia illi aliena peccata imputata fuerint. Sed consequiturne ex hoc, Christum pro nostrum omnium peccatis divinæ justitiæ satisfecisse? Nonne aliena peccata imputata illi dicerentur, si vel unius tantum hominis peccata illi imputata quæ fuissent, propter me mortuus esset? Resp. Quorsum ista faciant, equidem nescio. Nam hoc ex Scriptura satis clarum, non unius, sed plurium hominum peccata, fidelium & salvandorum omnium Christo imposita fuisse. Quid ergo sibi vult hoc, de unius hominis peccatis? Uti unius hominis peccata Christo si imposita fuissent, propter ea mortuus fuisset, sic ex eadem nunc causa mortuus, quia ei imputata peccata populi sui omnia. Nam peccati stipendium mors est. Rom. vi. 23. & per peccatum mors. Rom. v. 12. Atque sic etiam pro unius istius hominis peccatis divinæ justitiæ satisfecisset: nempe quia pœnas ejus tulisset debitas. Quando hic disputamus, an Christus mortis pœnam pro hominum peccatis sustinuit, non spectamus, pro quibus. Illud hactenus probasse impræsen-tiarum suffecerit quod satisfecit, alterius loci est quæreré, pro quibus. Præser-tim quum adeo manifestum sit, non pro unius peccatis ipsum mortuum. Ut mirum videri debeat, Socinum ita hoc loco respondisse, potuisse Christo aliena peccata imputari, & quidem ita, ut pro ipsis satisfecerit, nec tamen inde sequi, illum pro nostris omnium delictis satisfecisse; quia, videlicet, ad istud, unde hoc sequi negamus, confidendum, vel unius tantum peccata illi imputata fuisse sat fuerit. Non hic disputamus, pro quibus; sed, an satisfecerit Christus. Concede, propter imputata sibi pec-cata & mortuum, & satisfecisse: de cæteris postmodum licebit agere. Atque interim ipsius satisfactionis possibilitatem, & veritatem ne exagitent. Imputata Christo fuerunt peccata nostra, ad pœnam, pœnam mortis, quâ divinæ justitiæ satisfecit: atque id hoc loco ostendere nobis propositum, quod unum satis est. Sed demum, inquit Socinus, omnia peccata nostra Christo imputata fuisse, & ob eam rem ipsum mortuum esse, num idcirco pro ipsis peccatis eum satisfecisse, concludendum erit? Omnino: nempe per mortem, uti antea dictum, non intelligendo solam corporalem, sed & cum eâ passiones seu pœnas omnes, quas nostro loco perpessus fuerit. Et quare iis perlatis non dicatur satisfecisse? Sic sequitur, ait, quod quilibet nostrum, qui Christiani sumus, ideo morimur, quia imputantur nobis delicta nostra. Nemo tamen nostrum pro suis delictis, moriendo, satisfacit. Negatur, illud sequi. & hoc, quia mors fidelibus non infligitur in pœnam, uti ante dictum, sed vero est beata missio & transitus in æternam felicitatem. Omnibus autem extra Christum impiis & infidelibus in pœnam cedit, moriuntur in peccatis & reatu suo, qui imputatur ipsis, pro quo quidem singulis pœnis, quas patiuntur, solvunt, at non satisfaciunt, quia æternas meretur peccatum pœnas, quas non sint superando.
units.tr: Eleventh objection. Ibidem, p. 289: In your argument you conclude nothing else than that Christ died because others' sins were imputed to him. But does it follow from this that Christ satisfied divine justice for the sins of us all? Would not others' sins be said to be imputed to him if only the sins of one man had been imputed to him, for whose sake he died? Answer: Why these things bear on the point I truly do not know. For this is clear enough from Scripture: not the sins of one man but of many, of all the faithful and those to be saved, were laid on Christ. What then does this mean about one man's sins? Just as, if one man's sins had been laid on Christ, he would have died on account of them, so now he has died for the same reason, because all the sins of his people were imputed to him. For the wages of sin is death, Rom. vi. 23, and through sin, death, Rom. v. 12. And so he would also have satisfied divine justice for the sins of that one man, namely because he would have borne the penalties due to him. When here we dispute whether Christ underwent the penalty of death for the sins of men, we are not looking at for whom. It is enough for the present to have proved that he made satisfaction; to ask for whom belongs to another place, especially since it is so manifest that he did not die for one man's sins alone. So it ought to seem strange that Socinus has answered here that it could be that others' sins were imputed to Christ, and indeed so that he made satisfaction for them, and yet it does not follow from this that he made satisfaction for the offences of us all; because, namely, it is enough for that consequence, which we deny follows, to be confident that the sins of only one man were imputed to him. We are not disputing here for whom, but whether Christ made satisfaction. Grant that he died and made satisfaction because sins were imputed to him; the rest may be discussed afterwards. Meanwhile let them not harass the very possibility and truth of satisfaction. Our sins were imputed to Christ for punishment, the punishment of death, by which he satisfied divine justice; and this is what we set out to show here, and it is enough. But at last, says Socinus, if all our sins were imputed to Christ and for that reason he died, shall it be concluded that he satisfied for the sins themselves? Certainly: namely through death, as said before, understanding not only the bodily death but with it all the sufferings and penalties which he endured in our place. And why should it not be said that he satisfied, since he bore them? Thus it follows, he says, that each of us who are Christians die because our offences are imputed to us. Yet none of us, by dying, makes satisfaction for his own offences. That this does not follow is denied, and for this reason: death is not inflicted on believers as a punishment, as said before, but is a blessed release and passage into eternal happiness. But for all the impious and unbelievers outside Christ it issues as a punishment; they die in their sins and in the guilt imputed to them. For these they indeed pay, by each of the punishments they suffer, but they do not make satisfaction, because sin deserves eternal punishments, which they are not able to get through.

units.la: Secunda classis argumentorum, pro satisfactione Christi, ex illis petitur Scripturæ S. locis, quæ docent, Christum pro peccatis, propter ea, pro nobis, & loco nostri mortuum fuisse, ὑπὲρ, περὶ [?], ἀντί. Quæ præpositiones junguntur aut peccatis, aut hominibus, pro quibus Christus mortuus: & denotant, tum causam procatarcticam, impulsivam, & meritoriam: tum locum aliorum, quem Christus Christus sustinuit. Unde tale constat nobis argumentum: Qui mortuus est propter peccata hominum, mortem illam merentia & efficientia, & loco seu vice illorum, is poenas eorum sustulit, persolvitque: at Christus ita mortuus est: ergo.
units.tr: The second class of arguments for the satisfaction of Christ is drawn from those places of Holy Scripture which teach that Christ died for sins, on account of them, for us, and in the place of us: for [ὑπέρ], about [περί], instead of [ἀντί]. These prepositions are joined either to sins or to the men for whom Christ died, and they denote both the procatarctic, impulsive and meritorious cause, and the place of others which Christ underwent. Whence this argument is established for us: whoever died on account of men's sins, which deserve and bring about that death, and in the place or stead of them, has borne and paid their punishments; but Christ so died; therefore he bore and paid their punishments.

units.la: Socinus, lib. II. cap. VII. facetur dici posse, Christum pro peccatis, & propter ea mortuum, atque hoc universam satis testari Scripturam. Sed sequi inde negat, Christum divinae justitiae pro peccatis nostris satisfecisse, sive id solvisse, quod nos propter peccara nostra ei solvere debebamus. Mori enim propter peccata, seu pro peccatis alicujus, ut verba ipsa satis indicant, nihil aliud est, quam causa sive occasione peccatorum illius mori. Causa autem, sive occasione peccatorum alicujus is certe moritur, qui ideo moritur, ut quis a peccatis suis retrahatur, utque illi fides fiat, peccata sibi, si ab illis se retraxerit, condonatum iri, ac praterea ut is fructum ejusmodi condonationis, & ita ipsam condonationem reipsa sentiat, & consequatur. Resp.
units.tr: Socinus, book 2, chapter 7, admits that it can be said that Christ died for sins and on account of sins, and that Scripture generally bears witness to this. But he denies that it follows from this that Christ satisfied divine justice for our sins, or paid what we ourselves owed God because of our sins. To die because of sins, or for someone's sins, as the words themselves sufficiently indicate, is nothing other than to die as the cause or occasion of his sins. Now he certainly dies as the cause or occasion of someone's sins who dies so that the person may be drawn back from his sins, so that he may be assured that, if he turns away from them, his sins will be forgiven, and further so that he may actually feel and obtain the fruit of such forgiveness, and thus the forgiveness itself. Reply.

units.la: Id ubique propositum Adversario, res enervare: quod in toto hoc negotio, & Theologia universa, tum in rebus, ab ipsis, fieri, tum verbis, & phrasibus explicandis, observare est. I. Negamus, quod tam audacter affirmat, mori propter peccata, vel pro peccatis, nihil aliud esse, quam causa, sive occasione peccatorum mori. Verum est, quod Christus causa & occasione peccatorum mortuus est, sed nihil ejus praeterea verum esse, pernegamus. II. Causam mortis Christi exponit per occasionem: & sic dicit Christum causa, id est, occasione peccatorum mortuum fuisse. Perquam dilute. Occasio enim causa per accidens est, non per se. Atqui nemo in Sacris legens Christum propter peccata mortuum, intelliget ea leviter ut causam sine qua non, vel per accidens, & occasionem, sed omnino ut causam veram adducci, & meritoriam per se. Hinc & propter peccata, & a peccatis nostris dicitur verberatus מֻכִּים [?]. Quod certe aliud est, quam occasione eorum.
units.tr: The adversary aims everywhere at weakening the matter. This is to be observed throughout this whole question and all of theology, both in the things themselves and in the explanation of words and phrases. I. We deny what he so boldly asserts: that to die because of sins, or for sins, is nothing other than to die as the cause or occasion of sins. It is true that Christ died as the cause and occasion of sins, but we flatly deny that anything else of this is true. II. He explains the cause of Christ's death as an occasion, and so says that Christ died as the cause, that is, the occasion, of sins. This is very weak reasoning. For an occasion is a cause only incidentally, not in itself. Yet no one who reads in the Scriptures that Christ died because of sins will take this lightly as a sine qua non cause or an incidental occasion. Everyone will understand it as a true and meritorious cause in its own right. Hence he is also said to have been smitten [מֻכִּים] because of, and on account of, our sins. This is certainly something other than an occasion of them.

units.la: III. Jam vero explicaturus Socinus, quid sit, quod Christus causa peccatorum nostrorum dicatur mortuus, inquit, ut nos a peccatis retraheremur: ergo ut pro argumento suasionis moralis contra peccatum adferri possit mors Christi, eam subiit: & hoc totum est, quod ejus causa est mortuus? Sic & omnes martyres pro peccatis nostris mortui, quidni & impii, & plurima pro peccatis nostris, & propter ea contingunt, quatenus per ea a peccatis retrahi oportet. Quod quantopere mortem Christi evacuat, & ejus prostituit vim?
units.tr: III. But when Socinus sets out to explain why Christ is said to have died as the cause of our sins, he says that it was so that we might be drawn back from sins. Therefore the death of Christ is to be taken only as an argument for moral persuasion against sin, and he underwent it for that purpose, and this is all that it means that he died for our sins? By that reasoning, all the martyrs also died for our sins, and why not the impious, and many things happen for our sins and on account of them, insofar as through them we ought to be drawn back from sin. How greatly this empties the death of Christ and prostitutes its power!

units.la: IV. Ergo non magis, vel alia causalitate, aut causalitatis influxu putabitur Christus mortuus pro peccatis nostris, quam pro iisdem scriptum Dei verbum, vel habetur praedicatio, aliaque ejusdem generis, quae sunt ut a peccatis retrahamur, & ut fides nobis fiat, peccata, ubi ab iis nos retraxerimus, condonatum iri &c. V. Iterum, per mortem Christi ut quis, sensu Sociniano, condonationem consequatur, illud redolet, quod reprehendi solet, Utinam ne in memore Pelio, &c. ut ei sua verba regeram, quae habet pag. 291. ubi remota causa adfertur pro proxima. Neque enim mors Christi, juxta Adversarios, condonationem peccatorum confert, sed adhibetur tantummodo pro argumento suasivo vel dehortatorio contra peccata: & remissionem, ubi a peccatis conversi ad Deum sumus, per conversionem magis, quam per mortem Christi ita adipiscimur. Ut nobis hæc omnia evenirent, mortuus est Christus. Scilicet eveniunt post Christi mortem, non Christi mors illa efficit. Veluti alibi pag. 101. non nisi Christi calamitatibus & morte interveniente, nos ad cælestia adspirare. Sed sic non Christi morti magis, quam vitæ, quam omnibus quæ dixit, egitque, quæque alii ad salutis nostræ promotionem vel Prophetæ, vel Apostoli, cæterique quibus intervenientibus illam obtinemus, adscribenda erit, salus. Namque ut salutem acquiramus illa & ista interveniunt[?]: si intervenire satis sit, ut pro peccatis fieri[?] aliquid dicatur, & isto quidem modo, quo de Christi morte illud in Scripturis prædicatur.
units.tr: IV. Therefore Christ is no more to be thought to have died for our sins, or by some other kind of causality or causal influence, than the written Word of God, or the preaching, or other things of the same kind, which serve to draw us back from sins and to make us sure that, when we have turned back from them, our sins will be forgiven, and so on. V. Again, by Socinus's sense, one obtains forgiveness through the death of Christ in the way that smells of what is commonly reproved: "Would that the axe had never fallen in the grove of Pelion," to turn his own words back on him, which he has at p. 291, where a remote cause is offered in place of a proximate one. For according to our adversaries, the death of Christ does not bring about the forgiveness of sins. It is used only as an argument of persuasion or dissuasion against sins. We obtain remission, when we have turned from sins to God, through conversion rather than through the death of Christ. Christ died so that all these things might happen to us. Of course these things happen after the death of Christ, but that death does not bring them about. Thus elsewhere, at p. 101, he says that we aspire to heavenly things only when the calamities and death of Christ have intervened. But in that way salvation will be ascribed not to the death of Christ more than to his life, or to everything he said and did, or to what the prophets or apostles or others did to promote our salvation, through whose intervention we obtain it. For in order that we may acquire salvation, these things and those intervene. If it is enough for something to be said to happen for sins merely because it intervenes, then it is so in the way in which Scripture proclaims this of the death of Christ.

units.la: Socinus, part. 111. cap. 11x[?]. pag. 291: affirmat, Christum occasione nostrorum peccatorum mortuum esse: immo etiam causa ipsorum; sive impulsivam, sive finalem causam intelligas. Veruntamen, sicut à finali causa satisfactionem penitus excludo; ita ab impulsiva imputationem quam longissime removeo. Id est, ab utraque, quam dicit, causa ista removet, quæ illam constituunt, ut morti Christi non aliam vim relinquat ad effectum istum amovendorum peccatorum, quam vulgarem & communem rebus etiam multis aliis. Expone impulsivam causam in peccatis ad mortem Christi, negata imputatione; & finalem, negata satisfactione, videbis quantum auferas morti Ghristi pro peccatis nostris, atque nihil ei reliquum facias, quod non aliis quoque sit commune: quum tamen in Scriptura morti Christi peccatorum ablatio adscribatur, modo & ratione singularissima, fundata in imputatione peccatorum, ut pro illis satisfaceret.
units.tr: Socinus, part 3, chapter 11, p. 291, asserts: Christ died on the occasion of our sins, indeed even as their cause, whether you understand the impulsive or the final cause. Yet just as I utterly exclude satisfaction from the final cause, so I remove imputation as far as possible from the impulsive cause. That is, by these two causes which he names as constituting that cause, he removes both, so that the death of Christ is left with no other power to bring about the removal of sins than the common power it has in many other things too. Set out the impulsive cause in sins as related to the death of Christ, with imputation denied, and the final cause with satisfaction denied, and you will see how much you take away from the death of Christ for our sins, and how you leave it nothing that is not common to others also. Yet in Scripture the removal of sins is ascribed to the death of Christ in a most singular manner and way, grounded in the imputation of sins, so that he might satisfy for them.

units.la: Part. II. cap. VII. pag. 109. propter peccata significat tantummodo peccatorum causa. 1 Reg. XIV. 16. Tradetque Jehova Israelem propter peccata Jeroboam, qui peccavit, & peccare fecit Israelem, intelligendum est. Israelem, cum traditus fuit, satisfecisse justitia divina pro peccatis Jeroboami? Nonne patet, propter peccata Jeroboam, nihil aliud significare, quam, causa peccatorum Jeroboami? Resp. 1. Nec ex hoc loco, nec ex aliis infertur, propter peccata significare tantummodo peccatorum causa. II. Causa notatur, non quævis, vel occasio, sed causa meritoria. Non, quemadmodum hic Socinus vult, verba, propter peccata per se nihil aliud unquam significare, quam causam, sive occasionem peccatorum. Propter peccata Jeroboami, scilicet quæ merita istam captivitatem fuerunt. Quemadmodum populus pro merito peccatorum illorum, sic Christus pro merito nostrorum, punitus. Atque istium in modum qui affligitur, pœnam meritorum patitur. III. Confundit Adversarius, punire, & satisfacere. Qui punitur à Deo, ideo non satisfacit, quia nondum omnem pœnam sustinet, non quantum satis est pro demerito peccati. Christus vero non aliquam, sed omnem pœnam nostram tulit, ergo satisfecit, non ita alius. Punitus populus fuit, non autem satisfecit, sive pro suis, sive Jeroboami peccatis, quia non punitus pro iis fuit quantum satis, neque omnes exsuperavit & exsolvit pœnas debitas. Et hoc demum est satisfacere, vel pati.
units.tr: Part 2, chapter 7, p. 109: "Because of sins" signifies only the cause of sins. 1 Kings 14:16: "Jehovah shall give up Israel because of the sins of Jeroboam, who sinned and made Israel to sin." Is it to be understood that Israel, when it was given up, satisfied divine justice for the sins of Jeroboam? Is it not plain that "because of the sins of Jeroboam" signifies nothing other than the cause of Jeroboam's sins? Reply. 1. Neither from this passage nor from others does it follow that "because of sins" signifies only the cause of sins. II. What is indicated is not any cause or occasion, but a meritorious cause. The words "because of sins" do not, as Socinus here wishes, by themselves signify nothing other than the cause or occasion of sins at any time. "Because of the sins of Jeroboam" means those sins which deserved that captivity. Just as the people were punished on account of the merit of their sins, so Christ was punished on account of the merit of ours. And whoever is afflicted in this way suffers the punishment of his merits. III. The adversary confuses to punish and to satisfy. Someone who is punished by God does not thereby satisfy, because he does not yet undergo the whole penalty, that is, as much as is enough for the desert of sin. But Christ bore not some punishment but all our punishment, and therefore he satisfied, which the others did not. The people were punished, but they did not satisfy, whether for their own sins or for the sins of Jeroboam, because they were not punished for them to the full extent, nor did they exhaust and pay all the penalties due. And this is what it finally means to satisfy, or to suffer.

units.la: Ipse Socinus hic subjungit: At dices, ex illis verbis aperte colligi, punitum fuisse populum propter Jeroboamum, unde etiam in locis, de quorum sententia controversia inter nos est, intelligi debeat, Christum punitum fuisse propter peccata nostra. Primum istud longe aliud est, quam satisfacere pro peccatis. potest enim quis puniri propter sua, vel aliena peccata. peccata, nec tamen pro ipsis satisfacere. Omnino. Neque nos volumus, phrasim propter peccata per se significare, satisfacere pro peccatis; tantummodo puniri propter ea. Quod vero de Christo puniri & satisfacere promisimus usurpamus, non est propter loquutionem illam, qua propter peccata nostra passus vel punitus dicitur, sed quod omnes passiones & poenas sustinuit: id est, quia revera non punitum modo, sed & satisfecisse Christum verum est, propter naturam & veritatem rei, non phrasim, hoc di[?]mus: nam propter peccata nostra punitus, etiam pro iis satisfecit, quod non item alii, quamvis pro peccatis puniantur.
units.tr: Socinus himself adds here: But you will say that from those words it is plainly gathered that the people were punished because of Jeroboam, whence also in the passages about whose meaning there is controversy between us, it ought to be understood that Christ was punished because of our sins. This first point is far different from satisfying for sins. For someone can be punished because of his own or others' sins without satisfying for those sins. Certainly. Nor do we want the phrase "because of sins" to signify, by itself, satisfying for sins; only being punished on account of them. But when we claim that Christ was punished and satisfied, we do not rest this on that way of speaking by which he is said to have suffered or been punished for our sins, but on the fact that he bore all sufferings and penalties. That is, it is true, from the nature and truth of the matter and not from the phrase, that Christ not only was punished but also satisfied. For one who is punished because of our sins also satisfied for them, which others do not do, although they are punished for their sins.

units.la: Socinus: Quid? cum David Pf. xxix. 11. scribit, in increpationibus, propter iniquitatem corripis hominem &c. num intelligit increpari & castigari hominem a Deo, ut divina justitia satisfaciat pro iniquitate sua, & non potius causa, & occasione iniquitatis suae hominem a Deo affligi, ut discat ab iniquitate discedere? Resp. Socinani[?] quoque agnoscunt differentiam afflictionis, seu castigationis; & punitionis.
units.tr: Socinus: "What then? When David writes (Ps. xxix. 11), 'with rebukes you correct a man for iniquity,' etc., does he mean that a man is rebuked and chastised by God so that he may satisfy divine justice for his iniquity, and not rather that a man is afflicted by God because of iniquity and on the occasion of it, so that he may learn to turn away from iniquity?" Answer: The Socinians too acknowledge a difference between affliction or chastisement and punishment.

units.la: Utrum Deus faciat, non sola causa occasione (aliquando enim Socinus inquit, causa & occasione; aliquando, causa sive occasione, nec aliud genus causae intelligit, quam occasionem) peccatorum, sed pro merito, sive castigat, sive punit, nam utrumque meretur peccatum, & intelligitur, quando Deus propter peccata homines visitare dicitur. In punitione tamen non satisfaciunt homines, ideo quia non quantum satis est luunt. Divinae autem justitiae poenas dant omnino. Non ita incastigatione, ubi Deus proprie non punit, affligit quidem, & hoc propter peccata; castigat autem ex amore, non ira.
units.tr: Whether God acts not merely on the occasion of sins (for Socinus sometimes says "cause and occasion," and at other times "cause or occasion," and he recognises no kind of cause other than occasion), but in proportion to desert, whether he chastises or punishes, for sin deserves both. This is understood when God is said to visit men because of their sins. In punishment, however, men do not make satisfaction, because they do not pay what is enough. But they fully pay the penalties of divine justice. It is otherwise with chastisement, where God does not properly punish but afflicts, and this because of sins; yet he chastises out of love, not wrath.

units.la: Accedamus vero ad ipsa Scripturæ loca, in quibus Christus pro nobis & peccatis nostris mortuus perhibetur, & expendamus an tantummodo designent occasione eorum Christum mortuum, ut nos a peccatis illo argumento retrahi, & remissionem peccatorum consequi possemus; an autem Christum ita propter illa passum, ut poenas eorum vere sustinuerit, nostri loco: nam & propter peccata, & pro nobis mortuus creditur. Grotius, de satisfact. cap. ix. receptum est in omni lingua, ut cum aliquis aliquid fecit aut passus est vice ac loco alterius, id pro illo passus aut fecisse dicatur. Sic apud Terentium est: pro illo te ducam: ego pro te molam. Adscripsit in exemplari suo propria manu Grotius, quod penes me est: apud Virgilium: meliorem animam pro morte Daretis Persolvo. Item, Unum pro multis dabitur caput.
units.tr: Let us now come to the passages of Scripture themselves, in which Christ is said to have died for us and for our sins, and let us weigh whether they merely indicate that Christ died on the occasion of them, so that we might be drawn back from sins by that example and obtain forgiveness of sins; or rather that Christ suffered on account of them in such a way that he truly bore their penalties in our place. For he is believed to have died both because of sins and for us. Grotius, On Satisfaction, ch. ix: "It is accepted in every language that when someone has done or suffered something in the place and stead of another, it is said to have been done or suffered for him. Thus in Terence: 'I will lead you in his place; I will grind for you.'" Grotius wrote in his own hand in his copy, which is in my possession, "in Virgil: 'I pay a better life for the death of Dares.'" Likewise: "One head will be given for many."

units.la: Quinque præpositiones sunt in præsenti negotio usitatæ. Hebræum בְּ[?]; Græca, διὰ, ὑπὲρ[?], περὶ, ἀντὶ. Illud occurrit Iesa. LIII. 5. & ipse dolore affectus fuit מְחֻלָּל[?] a prævaricationibus nostris, attritus מְדֻכָּא[?], ab iniquitatibus nostris. A prævaricationibus nostris ipse attritus: quod plus est, quam occasione eorum. Occasione peccatorum etiam martyr aliquis moritur, alii alia patiuntur, occasione peccatorum, non tantum suorum, sed & aliorum, non autem ab iis nisi eorum merito, vis & efficacia.
units.tr: Five prepositions are in common use in this matter. The Hebrew ב; the Greek διά, ὑπέρ, περί, ἀντί. The first occurs in Isaiah 53:5: "But he was wounded [מְחֹלָל] for our transgressions, he was bruised [מְדֻכָּא] for our iniquities." He was wounded by our transgressions: which is more than on the occasion of them. A martyr may die on the occasion of sins, and others suffer other things on the occasion of sins, not only their own but also those of others; yet these things have no force or efficacy except by the merit of those sins. [ב]

units.la: Socinus, part. ii. cap. vii. pag. 110. Huc accedit, quod attinet ad locum Esaiae, dictionem Hebraeam, quae reddita est propter, esse min; quae non causam finalem, ut vocant, sed efficientem declarat. Quapropter aliud nihil ex illis verbis colligi potest, quam, Christum a peccatis nostris quodammodo occisum fuisse, sive peccata nostra Christi. mortis causam antecedentem extitisse: non autem ut effectus aliquis ad nostra peccata spectans inde consequeretur, ipsum mortuum esse; quamvis id alioqui verissimum sit. tantum abest, ut ex verbis illis possit colligi, istum effectum ad nostra peccata spectantem propterea ex Christi morte consecutum esse, quod scilicet, pro illis divina justitia Christus, moriendo satisfecerit. Resp. Indignor voces frequenter Adversariis usurpatas, quodammodo, & similes. Numquid dicit Propheta, vel laevissime significat, quodammodo Christum a praevaricationibus nostris, vel ab iniquitatibus attritum? & bis quidem eo loquendi modo utitur: ne, quodammodo, sed verissime Christum ita affectum credamus. II, Et nihil aliud ex Prophetae verbis colligi potest, quam illud quodammodo? Dixisti, לְ[?] hic significare causam efficientem. ergo etiam quodammodo, non omnimodo, efficientem? Jam vel revocare illud videtur, vel extenuare, dicendo causam antecedentem mortis Christi fuisse peccata nostra. Quae omnino apud Prophetam ponuntur mortis Christi causa vera & procatarctica. III. Quo modo, vel qua quaeso vera causalitate peccata nostra mortis Christi causa erunt, vel dicentur, si non effectus aliquis ad nostra peccata spectans inde consequatur? vel a nostris peccatis effectus verus ad Christi mortem? IV. Atque illud si verissimum, uti dicit; quomodo negat tamen quod effectus aliquis ad nostra peccata spectans ex morte Christi consequitur? Annon in loco Prophetae, statim ad expositam mortis Christi ex peccatis nostris causam, subjungitur: castigatio pacificationum nostrarum super eum, & in vibice ejus sanatio nobis? V. Ex quibus & id evidentissime colligitur, Christi morte illum effectum ad nos sequi, eo quod pro peccatis divinae justitiae, moriendo, satisfecit. Nam nostra luit, nostra super eum עָלָיו[?]. Quae dum tulit, satisfecisse quis ambigat? Tulisse autem, tot argumentis, ac poene verba in loco illo sunt, confirmatur.
units.tr: Socinus, part ii, ch. vii, p. 110: "Moreover, as regards the passage of Isaiah, the Hebrew word that is rendered 'because of' is min, which declares not a final but, as they say, an efficient cause. Therefore nothing else can be gathered from those words except that Christ was in some way slain on account of our sins, or that our sins were an antecedent cause of Christ's death; but it cannot be gathered that Christ's death was followed by some effect relating to our sins, namely his own death, although that is otherwise most true. So far is it from the case that from those words it can be gathered that this effect relating to our sins followed from Christ's death for this reason, namely that Christ by dying made satisfaction to divine justice for them." Answer: I am indignant at the word "in some way" [quodammodo] and similar expressions, which our opponents use often. Does the prophet say, or even faintly suggest, that Christ was bruised by our transgressions or by our iniquities "in some way"? And he uses this manner of speaking twice; so we should believe that Christ was so affected not "in some way" but most truly. Second, can nothing else be gathered from the words of the prophet except that "in some way"? You say that the Hebrew lamed here signifies an efficient cause; then is it also "in some way," not "in every way," an efficient cause? Now you seem either to retract that or to weaken it, by saying that our sins were the antecedent cause of Christ's death. Yet in the prophet these things are stated as the true and meritorious cause of Christ's death. III. In what manner, or by what true causality, I ask, will our sins be, or be said to be, the cause of Christ's death, if no effect relating to our sins follows from it? Or will there be a true effect of our sins upon Christ's death? IV. And since you say "most true" of that, how do you nevertheless deny that some effect relating to our sins follows from Christ's death? Does not the prophet, immediately after setting out the cause of Christ's death from our sins, add: "the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed"? V. From which it is also most evidently gathered that this effect for us follows from Christ's death, because by dying he made satisfaction to divine justice for sins. For he bore our sins; "our" [נָּשָׂא] "upon him" [עָלָיו]. Since he bore them, who can doubt that he made satisfaction? And that he bore them is confirmed by so many arguments, almost by the very words in that passage.

units.la: Alia vox, vel praepositio exponenda venit Διά[?]. Rom. IV. 25. qui traditus est Διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν, propter transgressiones nostras. Crellius, contra Grotium, cap. 1. pag. 10. Quod vero Grotius hoc loco asserit, phrasin propter peccata perpessionibus junctam semper causam impulsivam notare, nec unquam aliter sumi, contra quam Socinus opinetur, qui & impulsivam & finalem ea phrasi designari statuit; id locus ab ipsomet Grotio hic allatus dubium reddit. Nam cum in eo loco Christus propter peccata nostra dicitur traditus; hac phrasi causam finalem indicari sequentia verba, resuscitatus propter justificationem nostram, innuere videntur, in quibus causam finalem significari nemo non agnoscit. Quemadmodum 1 Cor. vii. 2. propter stupra unusquisque habeat suam uxorem, id est, propter stupra vitanda. Et sic Rom. IV. propter peccata abolenda. Gal. III. 19. Resp. 1. duo in expositione & Διὰ[?] hoc loco tenenda, quod jungitur cum accusativo; &, quod ad rem vel materiam subjectam, perpessionibus. Qua ratione causam notat impulsivam. Διὰ simpliciter cum accusativo saepius causam efficientem. Διὰ τῶν.[?] διὰ π.[?] διὰ τῷ ἐνίας[?]. Matth. x. 22. eritis exosi omnibus propter nomen meum διὰ τὸ ὄνομά μου. Cap. XIII. 5. exaruit· διὰ διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν propterea quod non habebat terra βάθος. & verf. 6. 21. facta autem persecutione propter verbum, διὰ τ λόγον. 58. neque fecit ibi virtutes multas, propter infidelitatem eorum διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν. & vii. 20. & xxiv. 9. Cap. xiv. 9. διὰ propter juramentum vero & accumbentes. cap. xv. 3. 6. διὰ propter traditionem vestram. Marc. ii. 4. διὰ τὸν ὄχλον, propter turbam. cap. iii. 9. Luc. xxiii. 19. διὰ στάσιν, propter tumultum. Joann. iv. 36. διὰ τὸν λόγον propter sermonem mulieris. 41. 42. & xv. 3. Cap. xix. 38. διὰ τ φόβον propter metum Judaeorum. Cap. xx. 19. Act. xxi. 34. 35. Rom. ii. 24. δι' ὑμᾶς propter vos blasphematur. ii Cor. iv. 11. in mortem tradimur διὰ Ἰησοῦν. Phil. ii. 30. & iii. 7. 8. Col. iv. 3. Apoc. i. 19. & ii. 3. & vi. 9.
units.tr: Another word, or preposition, needs explaining: διά, Rom. iv. 25: "who was delivered [διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν] for our trespasses." Crellius, against Grotius, ch. 1, p. 10: "But that Grotius asserts here that the phrase 'because of sins' joined with sufferings always denotes an impulsive cause, and is never taken otherwise, contrary to what Socinus thinks, who held that both an impulsive and a final cause are designated by that phrase, is made doubtful by the very passage Grotius cites here. For when in that place Christ is said to have been delivered because of our sins, the following words, 'raised again for our justification,' seem to suggest that this phrase indicates a final cause, and no one fails to recognise that a final cause is meant there; just as 1 Cor. vii. 2: 'because of fornications let each man have his own wife,' that is, to avoid fornications. And so Rom. iv: 'because of sins to be abolished.' Gal. iii. 19." Answer: 1. Two things must be held in the explanation of διά in this place: that it is joined with the accusative, and what is the subject matter, namely "sufferings." By this reasoning it denotes an impulsive cause. διά simply with the accusative more often denotes an efficient cause, as in Matt. x. 22: "you will be hated by all men because of my name" [διὰ τὸ ὄνομά μου]; ch. xiii. 5–6: "it withered away, because it had no depth of earth" [διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν βάθος γῆς]; v. 21: "when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word" [διὰ τὸν λόγον]; ch. xiii. 58: "and he did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief" [διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν]; and vii. 20; xxiv. 9; xiv. 9: "because of the oath and those reclining at table" [διὰ τοὺς ὅρκους]; xv. 3, 6: "because of your tradition" [διὰ τὴν παράδοσιν]. Mark ii. 4: "because of the crowd" [διὰ τὸν ὄχλον]; iii. 9. Luke xxiii. 19: "because of the uproar" [διὰ στάσιν]. John iv. 36; iv. 39, 41, 42: "because of the woman's word" [διὰ τὸν λόγον]; xix. 38: "because of fear of the Jews" [διὰ τὸν φόβον]; xx. 19. Acts xxi. 34–35. Rom. ii. 24: "because of you the name of God is blasphemed" [δι᾽ ὑμᾶς]. 2 Cor. iv. 11: "we are delivered to death for Jesus' sake" [διὰ Ἰησοῦν]. Phil. ii. 30; iii. 7–8. Col. iv. 3. Rev. i. 9; ii. 3; vi. 9.

units.la: Quibus locis διὰ causam designat efficientem externam, & impulsivam. ii. Maxime vero ubi passionibus jungitur, causaque earum additur, causam notat impulsivam. Matth. xxvii. 19. multa enim passa sum hodie in somnio διʼ αὐτὸν, propter eum. Joann. x. 32. διὰ ποῖον propter quale eorum opus lapidatis me? Eph, v. 6. διὰ ταῦτα propter ista enim venit ira Dei in filios inobedientiæ. Col. iii. 6. ii Tim. i. 12. δι' ὃν αἰτίαν καὶ ταῦτα πάσχω, propter quam causam etiam illa patior. & ii. 10. διὰ τοῦτο propter id omnia patior. iii. Non negamus, διὰ etiam causæ finalis notam esse, & finem denotare cui, cum accusativo; & propter quos Christus mortuus sit. 1 Cor. viii. 11. δι' οὗ, propter quem Christus mortuus est. ii Cor. viii. 9. nam propter vos δι' ὑμᾶς pauper factus.
units.tr: In these passages διά designates an external and impulsive efficient cause. 2. Especially where it is joined to sufferings and the cause of them is added, it denotes an impulsive cause: Matt. xxvii. 19: "for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him" [διʼ αὐτόν]. John x. 32: "for which of these works do you stone me?" [διὰ ποῖον ἔργον]. Eph. v. 6: "for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience" [διὰ ταῦτα]. Col. iii. 6. 2 Tim. i. 12: "for which cause I also suffer these things" [δι᾽ ὃν αἰτίαν καὶ ταῦτα πάσχω]; ii. 10: "therefore I endure all things" [διὰ τοῦτο]. 3. We do not deny that διά also marks a final cause, and denotes the end, with the accusative, "for whom," and that Christ died for those for whom he died: 1 Cor. viii. 11: "for whom Christ died" [δι᾽ οὗ]; 2 Cor. viii. 9: "for your sake he became poor" [δι᾽ ὑμᾶς].

units.la: iv. Sed plane διὰ significat propter: atq; uti propter apud Latinos jam impulsivam, jam finalem causam notat; iterum impulsivam aliquando, & non finalem, atque vicissim; ita apud Græcos διὰ. Utrumque nunc causam rei, nunc personam: propter quam rem, & quam personam quis aliquid agat, vel patitur. In passionibus Christi, quando propter peccata passus dicitur, uti in omni sermone causam declarat impulsivam, ubi peccata passionum causa memorantur, ita isthic. Verissime ut dictum sit, atque ex omnium sermone & sensu, phrasim propter peccata perpessionibus junctam semper causam denotare impulsivam. Atque sic in nostro argumento. v. In loco Jesa. liii. 5. Græci יָשׁ vertunt per διὰ. αὐτὸς ὁ ἐτραυματίσθη διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, καὶ μεμαλάκισται διὰ τὰς ἀνομίας ἡμῶν: ipse vulneratus est propter peccata nostra, & infirmatus est propter iniquitates nostras, מעונותינו. Quod causam impulsivam denotare, non finalem nullus, credo, ambiget. Quemadmodum διὰ eodem capiere, καὶ αὐτὸς διὰ τὸ κεκακῶσθαι ὃν ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ. Et postea ἐπὶ τ[?] ἀναἀνομιῶν τ' λαῷ μὴ ἠχθῃ εἰς θάνατον[?]. Quæ omnia non nisi causam notant impulsivam. vi. In loco tamen Rom. iv. 25. traditus propter peccata, causam finalem significari, non impulsivam, Sociniani contendunt: hoc sensu, traditus propter abolenda peccata. Verùm sic præpositionis explicatio petitur à verbo, quod ipsi præter textum addunt, non quod in textu est. Alia locutio est, propter peccata quem tradi, affligi, mori; alia, propter peccata abolenda. Istud si fuisset, res clara esset: jam quia non minus clarum, propter peccata tradi, omnibus non aliter sonare & dicere, quam causam impulsivam externam traditionis, hoc tenendum præsertim, quum multis adeo Scripturæ locis confirmetur, peccata nostra causam poni mortis & passionum Christi. vii. Sed in in altero membro, resuscitatus propter justificationem nostram, manifesta causa finalis notatur. Ergo etiam in membro priori? Quæ consequentia? Non negamus διά, propter, causam quandoque finalem significare: sed non semper semper id, non quando propter peccata, tanquam causa passionibus adjungitur, non in primo membro loci controversi. Profer unum locum, non ubi διά finem dicat, sed ubi διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα passionibus, tanquam causa, additum, & διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν passionibus Christi, causam denotet impulsivam meritoriam. Attamen quod διά in altero membro, ubi de Christi resurrectione agitur, finem ejus notat, dispar est ratio, cum priori, uti jam indicatum. viii. Nec sequitur, quod eadem vox eodem in textu, eodem modo sensuque explicari debet. Quod nec Socinianii volunt.
units.tr: iv. But plainly the Greek preposition dia [διὰ] means on account of. Just as propter among the Latins sometimes denotes an impulsive cause and sometimes a final cause, and sometimes an impulsive and not a final cause, and conversely, so it is with dia among the Greeks. It denotes now the cause of a thing, now a person: on account of which thing, and on account of which person, someone does or suffers something. In the sufferings of Christ, when he is said to have suffered on account of sins, the phrase in every discourse declares an impulsive cause, where sins are named as the cause of the sufferings, and so it is here. To put it most truly, and from the sense and usage of all speech, a phrase joining on account of sins to sufferings always denotes an impulsive cause, and so it is in our argument. v. In Isa. 53:5 the Greeks render the Hebrew by dia: "But he was wounded for our transgressions [διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν], and he was bruised for our iniquities [διὰ τὰς ἀνομίας ἡμῶν]," that is, "for our iniquities" (Hebrew מעונותינו). That this denotes an impulsive, not a final, cause, no one, I believe, will doubt. In the same sense the Greek reads, "And he himself, because he was afflicted, did not open his mouth," and afterwards, "from the iniquities of my people he was led to death." All these passages denote only an impulsive cause. vi. Yet in Rom. 4:25, "delivered up on account of our sins," the Socinians contend that a final cause is signified, not an impulsive one, in the sense "delivered up in order to abolish sins." But this takes the explanation of the preposition from a verb which they add beyond the text, and which is not in the text. It is one thing to say "delivered up, afflicted, or dying on account of sins," and another to say "on account of sins to be abolished." Had the text said the latter, the matter would be clear. But since it is no less clear that "delivered up on account of sins" sounds to everyone as nothing other than, and says nothing other than, an external impulsive cause of the delivering up, this must be held all the more because the same is confirmed by so many passages of Scripture, which set our sins as the cause of the death and sufferings of Christ. vii. But in the second member, "raised again for our justification," a final cause is plainly indicated. Therefore also in the first member? What kind of inference is that? We do not deny that dia, on account of, sometimes signifies a final cause; but it does not always do so, and not when it is joined to sufferings as a cause, as with on account of sins in the first member of the disputed passage. Produce one passage where dia states a purpose, not one where dia ta paraptōmata is added to sufferings as a cause, and dia ta paraptōmata hēmōn denotes, of the sufferings of Christ, an impulsive and meritorious cause. Yet that dia in the second member, where the resurrection of Christ is treated, denotes its purpose, is a different case from the first, as has already been pointed out. viii. Nor does it follow that the same word in the same text must be explained in the same way and in the same sense. The Socinians themselves do not want this.

units.la: Vide Joan. i. 10. ubi vox κόσμος bis usurpatur, uno versu, non tamen eodem sensu in mundo erat, & mundus per ipsum factus: & mundus ipsum non cognovit. Sic cap. iv. 34. vox messis. iiCor. v. 21. vox peccati. & talia occurrunt plura. Socinus, in Matth. xv[?]. pag. 103. nec quicquam est absurdi, si unum idemque verbum, in eodem verborum contextu, modo propria ac pleniore, saltem diversa, modo impropria ac minus plena significatione accipiatur. Neque nos hic ex solâ voce arguimus, quæ nunc hanc, nunc illam significationem fert, sed ex phrasi, propter peccata, simpliciter posita, extra additionem Socinianam, quod nusquam phrasis illa aliud significet præter causam impulsivam & meritoriam. ix. 1Cor. vii. 2. διὰ τὴν πορνείας, propter fornicationes vero quilibet propriam habeat uxorem. Ego nego διὰ propter hic causam significare finalem, exclusâ impulsivâ. Imo fornicatio, ejus periculum, causa est antecedens externa consilii de ineundo matrimonio, in quo fateor hoc spectari quoque ut sic extra fornicationem vivatur: quod consequens rei est, ita quidem ut interim quoque fornicatio, ejusque consideratio, & metus antecedens causa, sit impellens animum ad sectandum conjugium. Qui sensus est verborum, διὰ τὰς πορνείας. Ad quam causam, rei vel conjugii iste tum finis sequitur, qui est vers. 5. ne tentet vos Satan διὰ τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν.
