Aliâ cum accusativo vel quarto casu, causam notat antecedentem impulsivam, non finalem verf 9. quod si vero se non contineant, nubant. x. Gal. iii. 19.. Quid ergo lex? τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη, transgressionum gratia adjecta. Quid inde? ergo phrasis propter peccata finem exprimit. Non hoc habet Textus, neque in eo est διὰ propter; sed χάριν. Non perpessionibus jungitur, non Christi. Et denique nec finalem dicit causam, sed impulsivam antecedentem, ob quam Deus legem hominibus per Mosem didit, scilicet propter peccata & trangressiones. Faciamus similiter dictum fuisse de Christo, ejusque passionibus, quod τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν nobis datus fuerit, certe haud aliter istam locutionem acciperemus quam de causa impulsivâ, non finali.
units.tr: See John 1:10, where the word kosmos is used twice in one verse, yet not in the same sense: "He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world did not know him." So in ch. 4:34, the word harvest; in 2 Cor. 5:21, the word sin; and many such occur. Socinus, on Matt. 15 [?], p. 103: "There is nothing absurd if one and the same word, within the same context of words, is taken now in its proper and fuller, or at least different, sense, and now in an improper and less full sense." Nor do we argue here from the word alone, which now bears this meaning and now that, but from the phrase on account of sins, simply stated, apart from the Socinian addition: that this phrase never means anything other than an impulsive and meritorious cause. ix. 1 Cor. 7:2: "On account of fornications [διὰ τὰς πορνείας], let each man have his own wife." I deny that dia, on account of, here signifies a final cause to the exclusion of an impulsive one. Indeed, fornication, and the danger of it, is the antecedent external cause of the counsel to enter marriage, in which I grant that this is also looked at as a means of living outside fornication; that is a consequence of the thing. Yet in the meantime fornication, and the consideration of it, and the fear that precedes it, are the cause which moves the mind to seek marriage. This is the sense of the words on account of fornications. To this cause the purpose of the marriage, or of the thing, follows, which is in verse 5: "that Satan may not tempt you [διὰ τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν] on account of your incontinence." With another case, the accusative, it denotes an antecedent impulsive cause, not a final one, in verse 9: "But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry." x. Gal. 3:19: "What then is the law? It was added because of transgressions [τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν]." What follows? Therefore the phrase on account of sins expresses a final cause? The text does not have this, nor is dia in it; it has charin [χάριν]. It is not joined to sufferings, nor to Christ. And finally it does not state a final cause, but an antecedent impulsive one, on account of which God gave the law to men through Moses, namely on account of sins and transgressions. If it had been said in the same way of Christ and his sufferings, that he was given to us because of transgressions [τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν], we would certainly understand that expression in no other way than of an impulsive, not a final, cause.

units.la: Idem sensus in negotio passionum Christi est ὑπὲρ pro, quando mortuus dicitur pro peccatis; περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, causâ peccatorum, propter ea, vel pro iis. Socino quoque agnoscente, part. ii. cap. vii, nullum vere inter has duas praepositiones, pro, & propter, quod attinet ad eos locos, esse differentiam. Nisi quod addat, quod dictio propter, non solum finalem, sed efficientem quoque causam significare potest. Imo uti ostendimus, & debet: praesertim in nostro hoc negotio. Dictio autem pro semper finalem significat. Hoc falsum esse, nunc ostendemus, & quod pro, quemadmodum propter, aliquando finalem, aliquando efficientem causam significat, & in hac materia, simpliciter posita, atque nostris peccatis, & passionibus Christi addita, 1 Pet. iii. 18. Unde & Christus semel pro peccatis passus est, περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἔπαθε, justus propter injustos ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων. Περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν, & Διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας sunt synonyma. Ut sive pro peccatis, sive propter peccata dicas, causam notet impulsivam antecedentem & hoc, & illud: Rom. viii. 3. Quod enim impossibile legi in quo infirmabatur per carnem, fecit Deus mittens proprium suum filium in similitudine carnis peccati, καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας, condemnavit peccatum in carne. Sive περὶ ἁμαρτίας vertas, propter peccatum, vel hostia propter peccatum, quemadmodum apud Hebraeos חַטָּאת[?] & הַחַטָּאת[?], & Hebr. x. 6. 8. Ὁλοκαυτώματα καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας οὐκ ηὐδόκησας. 11 Cor. v. 21. Eum qui non novit peccatum, ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν: utro modo sumas, vel hostiam pro peccato, vel pro peccato Christum passum, περὶ impulsivam causam denotat, non finalem. 1 Joann. ii. 2. Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Propitiatio peccati, est antecedentis, atque ut antecedenter ad propitiationem considerati. Deinde uti διὰ non solum causam impulsivam, sed & finalem denotare diximus, ita & περὶ, vel hoc ipso loco, non solum pro peccatis nostris, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου, sive pro toto mundo, sive pro peccatis totius mundi. Hebr. v. 3. propterēaque oportuit, καθὼς περὶ [?] λαὸς sicuti pro populo, ita & pro se περὶ ἑαυτῆ offerre ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν pro peccatis. Hoc causam impulsivam; illud finalem denotat. Col. ii. 1. Velim vos scire quantum certamen sustineam περὶ ὑμῶν, καὶ τῶν ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ pro vobis & qui sunt Laodicea. περὶ causa antecedens & impulsiva istius certaminis. Atque ita apparet falsum esse, quod Sociniani asserunt, περὶ pro semper causam finalem significare, non impulsivam. Apud Latinos etiam, & vulgo nota illa, in quibus pro haud aliter accipitur, ut quæ ex Cicerone adduxit Grotius, pro beneficiis gratias agere, aut reddere: ulcisci pro injuriis: pro magnitudine sceleris pœnas persolvere: supplicia pro maleficiis metuere. Ex Plauto: castigare pro commerita noxa. Ex Terentio, pro dictis & factis ulcisci, &c.
units.tr: The same sense holds for hyper, for, in the matter of the sufferings of Christ, when he is said to have died for sins; peri tōn hamartiōn [περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν], that is, on account of sins, because of them, or for them. Socinus too acknowledges, part 2, ch. 7, that "there is truly no difference between these two prepositions, for and on account of, as far as those passages are concerned." Except that he adds that the word on account of "can signify not only a final but also an efficient cause." Indeed, as we have shown, and as it must be taken, especially in this matter of ours. "But the word for," he says, "always signifies a final cause." We shall now show that this is false, and that for, like on account of, sometimes signifies a final and sometimes an efficient cause, and in this matter, when simply stated and joined to our sins and to the sufferings of Christ. 1 Pet. 3:18: "For Christ also suffered once for sins [περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἔπαθε], the just for the unjust [ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων]." Peri hamartiōn and dia tas hamartias are synonyms. So whether you say for sins or on account of sins, the one and the other denote an antecedent impulsive cause. Rom. 8:3: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin [καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας] condemned sin in the flesh." Whether you translate peri hamartias as on account of sin or as a sin-offering, as among the Hebrews חַטָּאת and הַחַטָּאת, and Heb. 10:6, 8: "Burnt offerings and sin-offerings [περὶ ἁμαρτίας] thou hast not delighted in." 2 Cor. 5:21: "He who knew no sin [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν], he made sin for us." In whichever way you take it, whether as a sacrifice for sin or as Christ suffering for sin, peri denotes an impulsive, not a final, cause. 1 John 2:2: "And he is the propitiation for our sins [περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν]." The propitiation for sin is antecedent to the sin, and is considered as antecedent to the propitiation. Next, as we said that dia denotes not only an impulsive but also a final cause, so does peri, and in this very passage: "not only for our sins [ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου], but also for the sins of the whole world." Heb. 5:3: "Therefore he must offer, as for the people, so also for himself, for sins [ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν]." The one denotes an impulsive cause, the other a final cause. Col. 2:1: "I would have you know how great a conflict I have [περὶ ὑμῶν, καὶ τῶν ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ], for you and for those at Laodicea." Peri is the antecedent and impulsive cause of that conflict. And so it appears that the Socinians are wrong when they assert that peri, for, always signifies a final, not an impulsive, cause. Among the Latins too, the familiar usage is the same, as in the examples which Grotius adduced from Cicero: to give thanks or return thanks for benefits; to take vengeance for injuries; to pay penalties for the greatness of a crime; to fear punishments for misdeeds. From Plautus: to chastise for a deserved offence. From Terence: to avenge for words and deeds, etc.

units.la: Sequitur quarta particula vel præpositio, in Sacris ad argumentum nostrum adhiberi solita: ὑπὲρ: tam de re, sic Christus mortuus dicitur ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, pro peccatis; quàm de personis, pro nobis, ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, usurpata. Illud habes 1 Cor. xv. 3. Christus mortuus est ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Gal. i. 4. Qui dedit semetipsum ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, pro peccatis nostris. In quibus ὑπὲρ pro causam notat impulsivam, Uti &c. alias passim. Luc. vi. 28. orate ὑπὲρ pro infestantibus vos. Act. v. 5. Gavisi quod ὑπὲρ pro nomine ejus digni fuissent habiti qui contumelia afficerentur. Cap. ix. 16. qua pati ipsum oportet ὑπὲρ pro nomine meo. Similis locutio, Rom. i. 5. 11 Cor. xii. 10. ὑπὲρ pro Christo. Phil. i. 29. 11 Cor. i. 11. gratia dicantur ὑπὲρ pro nobis. Cap. vii. 4. multa mihi gloriatio ὑπὲρ pro nobis. 12. iterum, pro vobis. Cap. vii. 23. sive ὑπὲρ pro Tito. Cap. ix. 2. ὑπὲρ pro vobis. Ephes. iii. 13. & v. 20. & vi. 11. ὑπὲρ pro me, ut mihi detur sermo, &c. Phil. i. 4. Col. i. 17. Finalem notat, & finem cujus, Joann. vi. 51. Quam ego do ὑπὲρ pro vita mundi. Finem autem cui, Luc. xxii. 19. quod est corpus meum, quod ὑπὲρ pro vobis datur. 20. in sanguine meo, qui ὑπὲρ pro vobis effunditur. 1 Cor. v. 7. etenim Pascha nostrum pro nobis immolatum Christus. Rom. viii. 32. sed ὑπὲρ pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum. In illis etiam, ut & sequentibus ὑπὲρ significat vicarium, loco alterius quid facere: Joann. x. 11. Ego sum bonus ille pastor. Bonus pastor ponit animam suam pro ovibus. 15. & animam meam pono pro ovibus. Cap. xi. 50. conducit nobis ut unus moriatur pro populo, & non tota gens pereat. 52. & non solum pro hac gente, sed ut filios Dei dispersos in unum congreget. & cap. xviii. 14. Cap. xiii. 38. Respondit ei Jesus; animam tuam ὑπὲρ pro me ponês? Rom. v. 6. 7. Vix enim ὑπὲρ pro justo quis moriatur: ὑπὲρ pro bono vero forte quis mori audeat. Exhibet vero Deus charitatem suam nobis, quod nobis peccatoribus Christus ὑπὲρ pro nobis mortuus est. Cap. VIII. 26. quid enim uti oportet precemur ignoramus, ipse vero Spiritus intercedit ὑπὲρ pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus. Cap. xiv. 4. an cibo perdes eum pro quo Christus mortuus est? Cap. xvi. 4. Qui ὑπὲρ pro anima mea suam ipsorum cervicem supposuerunt. Quibus locis ὑπὲρ non simpliciter significat pro, & bono; sed & loco, vice alterius agere, & pati: quod vim locorum & locutionum expendenti non potest non esse manifestum. 11 Cor. v. 20. ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ pro Christo ergo legatione fungimur. Socinus 1. de Servat. cap. viii. pag. 57. Ministrabant ergo, non tantum loquebantur, reconciliationem authoritate Dei ipsi queque Apostoli: quanquam ut supra visum est, vice Christi, & pro Christo. Quare subjungit, pro Christo ergo legatione fungimur, tamquam Deo exhortante per nos. Quare in negotio passionum Christi, quando propter peccata, aut pro nobis passus dicitur, non sola finalis causa intelligi debet, vel levis occasio, uti Socinus exponit, Christum nostri causa passum & mortuum esse, ideo rectissime dicitur, quia ut nos salutem aeternam, quam ipsemet de coelo nobis attulerat, amplecteremur, & consequeremur, mori voluit. de Servat. part. ii. cap. viii. sed, tum peccata nostra veram causam antecedentem, impulsivam procatarticam & meritoriam fuisse passionum; tum & Christum nostri loco istas subiisse.
units.tr: The fourth particle or preposition follows, which is customarily used in Scripture for our subject: hyper [ὑπὲρ]. It is used of the thing, so that Christ is said to have died for sins [ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν], and of persons, for us [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν]. You have the first in 1 Cor. 15:3: Christ died for our sins [ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν]. Gal. 1:4: who gave himself for our sins [ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν]. In these places hyper marks the impulsive cause, as it does elsewhere in many places. Luke 6:28: pray for [ὑπὲρ] those who abuse you. Acts 5:41: rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for [ὑπὲρ] his name. Acts 9:16: how much he must suffer for [ὑπὲρ] my name. A similar expression is Rom. 1:5 and 2 Cor. 12:10, for [ὑπὲρ] Christ. Phil. 1:29 and 2 Cor. 1:11: thanks be given for [ὑπὲρ] us. 2 Cor. 7:4: my great boasting on [ὑπὲρ] your behalf. 7:12: again, for you. 2 Cor. 7:23: whether for [ὑπὲρ] Titus. 2 Cor. 9:2: for [ὑπὲρ] you. Eph. 3:13, 5:20 and 6:11: for [ὑπὲρ] me, that utterance may be given me, etc. Phil. 1:4 and Col. 1:17. It marks the final cause, and the end for which: John 6:51: which I give for [ὑπὲρ] the life of the world. It marks the end to which: Luke 22:19: which is my body, which is given for [ὑπὲρ] you. 22:20: in my blood, which is poured out for [ὑπὲρ] you. 1 Cor. 5:7: for our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed for us. Rom. 8:32: but delivered him up for [ὑπὲρ] us all. In those passages too, and in those that follow, hyper signifies a substitute, doing something in the place of another. John 10:11: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for [ὑπὲρ] the sheep. 10:15: and I lay down my life for [ὑπὲρ] the sheep. John 11:50: it is expedient for us that one man should die for [ὑπὲρ] the people, and that the whole nation should not perish. 11:52: and not for this nation only, but that he might gather together into one the children of God who are scattered. Also John 18:14. John 13:38: Jesus answered him: will you lay down your life for [ὑπὲρ] me? Rom. 5:6–7: For scarcely for [ὑπὲρ] a righteous man will one die; for [ὑπὲρ] a good man perhaps someone would dare to die. But God shows his love for us, in that while we were sinners Christ died for [ὑπὲρ] us. Rom. 8:26: for we do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for [ὑπὲρ] us with groanings that cannot be uttered. Rom. 14:15: will you destroy with your food him for whom [ὑπὲρ] Christ died? Rom. 16:4: who laid down their own necks for [ὑπὲρ] my life. In these places hyper does not simply mean for and for the good of; it also means to act and to suffer in the place of, in the stead of another. Anyone who weighs the force of these places and phrases cannot fail to see this. 2 Cor. 5:20: on behalf of [ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ] Christ, then, we are ambassadors. Socinus, De Servatore 1, ch. 8, p. 57: The apostles, therefore, did not only speak but also minister the reconciliation by the authority of God, though, as has been seen above, in the place of Christ and for Christ. Hence he adds, "we are ambassadors for Christ, as God exhorts through us". Therefore, in the matter of Christ's sufferings, when he is said to have suffered on account of sins, or for us, the final cause alone ought not to be understood, nor a slight occasion, as Socinus explains: that Christ suffered and died for our sake is rightly said, because he wished to die so that we might embrace and obtain the eternal salvation which he himself brought us from heaven (De Servatore, part 2, ch. 8). Rather, our sins were the true antecedent cause, the impulsive, procatarctic and meritorious cause of the sufferings, and Christ underwent them in our place.

units.la: Quod indubitatissime confirmat postrema, quae hic usurpatur particula, ἀντί, quando Christus dicitur ἀντὶ ἡμῶν mortuus: quod ita est pro nobis & vice nostri, ut tum ipsum per se, tum eum praecedentibus junctum haud alio fine adhibitum hac in materia statui debeat, quam ad plenam passionum Christi declarandam vim & efficaciam. Matrh. xx. 28. Quemadmodum filius hominis non venit ut ministraretur ei, sed ut ministraret, atque animam suam daret λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν, lutrum pro multis, loco multorum. Vel simpliciter λύτρον, vel ἀντὶ rem expedivisset; verum non modo ut significaret, verum & copiosissime declararet, nosque minime dubios hac in re relinqueret Servator, emphaticam expressionem utramque adhibuit. Marc. x. 45. Et Ἀντὶ hic est, quod alibi ὑπέρ. Praeter loca adducta, Tit. ii. 14. Qui dedit semetipsum ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, ἵνα λυτρώσηται ἡμᾶς. Λύτρον ἀντὶ, & λύτρον ὑπέρ. Nusquam non ἀντὶ significat vicarium, loco, vice. Quod Syris & Arabibus est פדיון[?]. Hinc ἀντίψυχον. Procopius, in Jesa. lxiii. 6. ἀλλ' ὁ πατὴρ αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀντίψυχον ὥσπερ παρέδωκεν. Sic Eusebius, Demonstrat. Euang. lib. i. cap. x. dicit sacrificia in V. Test. pro transgressionibus oblata fuisse ἀντίψυχα, ψυχὴν ἀντὶ ψυχῆς ἀναφέροντες. Atque illa perpetuus praepositionis ἀντὶ est usus. In N. Test. Matth. ii. 22. dicitur quod Archelaus regnaret ἀντὶ loco Herodis patris sui. Cap. v. 28. oculum ἀντὶ pro, vice oculi, & dentem pro dente. Cap. xvii. 27. flaterem accipiens, da eis ἀντὶ ἐμοῦ καὶ σοῦ, pro me, & te, loco meo, meo, & tuo. Luc. xi. 11. nunquid αντὶ loco piscis, serpentem ei dabit? Rom. xii. 17. malum αντὶ pro malo reddentes. 1 Thess. v. 15. 1 Pet. iii. 9. 1 Cor. xi. 15. nam coma αντὶ pro, loco velaminis ei data. Ephes. v. 31. αντὶ τούτου ejus loco homo relinquet patrem suum & matrem. Hebr. xii. 16. qui αντὶ loco edulii unius tradidit primogenituram suam. Jac. iv. 15. αντὶ ὅ pro eo quod, vel eo loco ut diceretis, siquidem Dominus velit &c. Quid ergo causæ erit, ut ubi vox αντὶ, & natura, & usu suo denotat loco alterius, & sic quoque in Scriptura, non in hac quoque materia, ubi non ea modo voce, sed & consimilibus aliis vocibus, phrasibusque maxime emphaticis, & eodem recurrentibus dicitur Christum ὑπὲρ, αντὶ ἡμῶν mortuum, intelligamus eum loco nostro passum fuisse? præsertim quum non voces & verba, sed res ita perpetuo in Scripturis tradatur, ut nihil omnino omissum sit, quod ad illum sensum & fidem nobis faciendam quisquam, vel Adversariorum, desiderare posset. Et tamen adversus illa excipere non omittunt: quæ jam tempus est ut audiamus.
units.tr: The last of these particles, antí [ἀντί], which is used here, confirms this beyond all doubt, when Christ is said to have died for us [ἀντὶ ἡμῶν]. This means both for us and in our stead, so that in this matter it must be judged to be used, both by itself and when joined to the preceding words, for no other end than to declare the full force and efficacy of Christ's sufferings. Matt. 20:28: Just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom [λύτρον] for [ἀντὶ] many, a ransom for many, in the place of many. The Saviour could have expressed the matter by lytron alone, or by anti alone; but, so that he might not only signify but most fully declare it, and leave us in no doubt on this point, he used both words in an emphatic expression. Mark 10:45 likewise. And anti here is what elsewhere is hyper. Apart from the passages cited, Titus 2:14: who gave himself for [ὑπὲρ] us, that he might redeem [λυτρώσηται] us. Here we have lytron anti and lytron hyper. Everywhere anti signifies a substitute, a place, a stead. The Syrians and Arabs use for this pidyon [פדיון]? Hence antipsychon [ἀντίψυχον], a ransom-life. Procopius, on Isaiah 63:6: But the Father gave him up for us as a ransom-life [ἀντίψυχον]. So Eusebius, Demonstratio Evangelica 1, ch. 10, says that the sacrifices in the Old Testament offered for transgressions were antipsycha, bringing up life for life [ψυχὴν ἀντὶ ψυχῆς]. And that is the constant use of the preposition anti. In the New Testament, Matt. 2:22 says that Archelaus reigned in the place [ἀντὶ] of Herod his father. Matt. 5:38: an eye for [ἀντὶ] an eye, and a tooth for a tooth. Matt. 17:27: taking the stater, give it to them for [ἀντὶ] me and you, in my stead and yours. Luke 11:11: or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of [ἀντὶ] a fish? Rom. 12:17: repaying evil for [ἀντὶ] evil. 1 Thess. 5:15, 1 Pet. 3:9, 1 Cor. 11:15: for her hair is given to her for [ἀντὶ] a covering. Eph. 5:31: for this cause [ἀντὶ τούτου] a man shall leave his father and mother. Heb. 12:16: who for [ἀντὶ] a single meal sold his birthright. James 4:15: instead of [ἀντὶ ὅ] saying, or in place of saying: if the Lord wills, etc. What reason, then, is there, when the word anti by its nature and by its usage signifies the place of another, and so also in Scripture, not only in this matter but where the same phrases recur, and not only with that word but with other similar words and most emphatic phrases, and it is said that Christ died for [ὑπὲρ] us, instead of [ἀντὶ] us, that we should understand that he suffered in our place? Especially since the words and expressions are not the only thing; the matter itself is so continually handed down in Scripture that nothing whatever has been omitted which anyone, even an opponent, could desire to make us believe that sense. And yet they do not fail to object against these. Let us now hear what they say.

units.la: Atque primum objicit Socinus, part. ii. cap° iix. 1 Joann. iii. 16. in hoc cognovimus charitatem, quod ille pro nobis animam suam posuit; & nos debemus pro fratribus animas ponere. Ubi vides, nos quoque mori pro fratribus posse: non tamen quia pro illa divina justitia satisfaciamus: sed quia interdum morimur, dum curamus, ut aliquod longe ab isto diversum beneficium illi sentiant. Resp. i. Neque nos dicimus, simpliciter mori pro aliquo esse divinæ justitiæ satisfacere. Neque hoc ex illa sola phrasi concludimus. Sed mori pro, esse vice alterius mori. Istud arguere hujus loci est. ii. Aliud est mori pro aliquo, aliud pro peccatis aliorum: non illud solum, sed & istud Christus egit proprie & vere, atque eo justitiæ divinæ satisfecit, non per illud quod simpliciter pro aliis, sed & pro aliorum peccatis mortuus fuit. Nos quia quidem possumus aliquando pro aliis mori, ut & Paulus Rom. v. 7. & alia testantur, non tamen pro peccatis aliorum. Hoc solius Christi est. iii. Et mori pro aliquo, aliud, & plus est, quam mori, dum curamus, ut aliquid longe ab isto diversum beneficium quis sentiat. Est enim hic, mori loco alterius. iv. Illo sensu non est mori pro alio, quidem aliquid facere pro alio; & ad quod mors sese habeat per accidens. Morte vero pro alio suscepta intenditur beneficium ex ipsa morte per se sequens. v. Si hoc sit mori pro alio, mori, dum curamus ut aliquid longe ab isto diversum beneficium illi sentiant pro quibus dicimur mori, fere semper debebimur dici mori pro aliis, quod tamen adeo rarum censetur, imo & mori pro improbis, quod vix contingere Apostolus putavit. Secundum illam enim expositionem quo-tidiè fere accidit, ut moriamur, dum curamus, ut aliquod longe ab isto diversum beneficium homines, etiam improbi, sentiant.
units.tr: And first Socinus objects, part 2, ch. 8: 1 John 3:16: "By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers." Here you see that we too can die for the brothers, yet not because we thereby satisfy divine justice, but because sometimes we die while we take care that they perceive some benefit quite different from that. Answer 1: We do not say that to die for someone simply is to satisfy divine justice, nor do we conclude this from that phrase alone. But to die for someone is to die in another's place. To prove that is the business of this passage. 2: To die for someone is one thing; to die for the sins of others is another. Christ did not only do the first but also the second, properly and truly, and so satisfied divine justice; not merely by dying for others in general, but for the sins of others. We indeed can sometimes die for others, as Paul also says in Rom. 5:7 and other passages attest; but not for the sins of others. That belongs to Christ alone. 3: To die for someone is something other and more than to die while we take care that someone perceives a benefit quite different from that. For here it means to die in another's place. 4: In that sense, to die for another is not merely to do something for another, to which death relates only by accident. But when death is undertaken for another, the benefit is aimed at that which follows from death itself. 5: If this were to die for another, we should almost always be said to die for others, because we die while we take care that the persons for whom we are said to die, even wicked persons, perceive some benefit quite different from that. Yet that is considered so rare, and dying even for the wicked is something the Apostle thought scarcely possible. According to that explanation it happens almost every day that we die while we take care that men, even wicked men, perceive some benefit quite different from that.

units.la: II. Obj. Nam & Paulus ad Col. cap. i. 24. ita scribit, Nunc gaudeo in passionibus meis pro vobis, & compleo, quæ desunt afflictionum Christi, in carne mea, pro corpore ipsius, quod est Ecclesia: Non tamen Paulus pro Colossensibus, sive pro Ecclesia Christi ullo modo satisfaciebat, quanquam affligebatur, dum non minimum momentum ad Colossensium, & Christi Ecclesiæ ædificationem offerre curabat. Resp. quod supra. Pro Ecclesia quidem patiebatur Paulus, & communi tum Ecclesiæ, tum Christi causa, non autem pro illorum peccatis. Unde etiam apparet, quando de Christo dicitur, mortuum eum pro nobis, alio id sensu accipiendum esse quam vulgari, sive mortuum simpliciter bono nostro: minime autem ad vulgarem modum vocari debere hoc, quod mortuus est pro peccatis nostris. Quodque Socinus addit, licet ita scriptum reperiatur, non tamen vere, & proprie dici potest, vel fratrem pro fratre mori, vel Paulum pro Colossensibus, aut pro Ecclesia passum fuisse, sicut vere & proprie dici potest, Christum pro nobis passum, & mortuum esse. Id haud recte: nam imo vere illud dicitur, certe ideo quia scriptum, proprie etiam, quamvis non eodem modo, & pari sensu utrobique intelligendum hoc, & illud.
units.tr: II. Objection. Paul also writes in Colossians 1:24: "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh, for his body, which is the Church." Yet Paul did not in any way make satisfaction for the Colossians, or for the Church of Christ, although he suffered, since he took care to offer no small contribution to the building up of the Colossians and of Christ's Church. Answer: as above. Paul did indeed suffer for the Church, and for the common cause of both the Church and Christ, but not for their sins. From this it also appears that when it is said of Christ that he died for us, this must be understood in a different sense from the common one, namely, that he simply died for our good; but what is said, that he died for our sins, ought not to be taken in the common sense. As for what Socinus adds, although it is written thus, it cannot truly and properly be said either that a brother died for a brother, or that Paul suffered for the Colossians or for the Church, just as it can truly and properly be said that Christ suffered and died for us. That is not right. Indeed it is truly said, and certainly because it is written; it is also said properly, although the one expression and the other are not to be understood in the same way and with the same sense in each case.

units.la: III. Obj. Et certe hanc tibi opinionem eximere debuerant ii loci, in quibus, Christum pro peccatis nostris mortuum esse, legitur. Neque enim vice, seu loco peccatorum nostrorum Christus mori potuit. Itaque agnoscere poteras, cum plane verisimile sit, in utrisque locis eandem dictionem pro significationem esse, nihil aliud, pro nobis Christum mortuum esse, significare, quam, nostri causa, quemadmodum pro peccatis nostris mortuum esse Christum, nihil aliud significat, quam peccatorum nostrorum causa, seu propter peccata nostra. Resp. Negamus, eandem & dictionem in utraque locutione adhiberi, & ubi eadem adhibetur, eundem utrobique esse sensum. Pro nobis quando Christus dicitur mortuus, causa finalis denotatur; quando pro peccatis, impulsiva externa. Pro nobis, indicat finem cui; ita ut, ad designandum ipsum loco etiam nostri mortuum esse, adhibeatur dictio ἀντί: quæ nunquam extat ubi pro peccatis nostris mortuus perhibetur, namque sensus ejus est, non solum bono, sed & loco nostro mortuum, quod neutrum locum habet ubi pro peccatis mortuus dicitur. Atque in communi sermone ad denotandum finem tum cujus, tum cui, eandem voculam pro usurpamus: neque ideo sequitur, utrobique eandem dictionis pro significationem esse. Non, opinor, dicent Adversarii, pro alio mori, nunquam, & non posse, significare mori alterius loco. Nam & hoc תחת[?] Hebræis notat: uti celebri illo loco 2 Sam. xviii. ult. utinam mortuus fuissem ego מותי תחתיך[?] pro te, vel loco tuo Absalom fili mi, fili mi. An ergo in tali sermone adhibita vox pro non alium sensum capit, quam simpliciter ubi dicitur quid fieri pro alio? Atque ita de Christo, & ejus pro nobis morte, quia omnes dictiones & loquendi formæ adhibentur, quæ ad sensum istum vicarium excogitari possunt, non est quare non, pro plenitudine sermonis sacri, sic exponamus.
units.tr: III. Objection. Certainly those passages in which it is read that Christ died for our sins ought to have removed this opinion from you. For Christ could not die in the place or stead of our sins. So you could have recognised that, since it is quite probable that the same word has the same meaning in both places, to say that Christ died for us signifies nothing other than that he died on our account, just as to say that Christ died for our sins signifies nothing other than on account of our sins, or because of our sins. Answer: We deny that the same word is used in both expressions, and where the same word is used, we deny that it has the same sense in each. When Christ is said to have died for us, a final cause is denoted; when for our sins, an external impulsive cause. For us indicates the end for whom; so that to designate that he died also in our place, the word ἀντί is used, which never occurs where he is said to have died for our sins, for its sense is not only for our good but in our place, and neither of these applies where he is said to have died for sins. And in common speech we use the little word pro to denote both the end of a thing and the one for whom it is done; but it does not follow that the same meaning of the word pro applies in both cases. I do not think the opponents will say that to die for another can never, and cannot, mean to die in another's place. For the Hebrews also express this by תחת, as in the well-known passage 2 Sam. 18 at the end: "Would that I had died, I, in your place [מותי תחתיך], for you, or in your place, my son Absalom, my son, my son." Is the word pro used in such a statement to have no other sense than where it is simply said that something is done for another? And so, concerning Christ and his death for us, since all the expressions and forms of speech are used that can be devised to convey that vicarious sense, there is no reason why we should not, for the fullness of sacred speech, explain it in this way.

units.la: Pergit excipere Adversarius, ad loca quædam Scripturæ, à Nostris hoc in negotio proferri solita. Heb. ii. 9. ut gratia (seu beneficio) sic ipse Socinus, pro omni ὑπὲρ πάντος[?] gustaret mortem. Quod quid aliud est, inquit, quam, propterea quod Christus mortuus fuerit, omnes nos benignitate divina maximum beneficium consecutos fuisse? Resp. Hoc quidem verum: sed nil aliud verbis illis contineri, negamus. Consequimur maximum per Christi mortem beneficium, sed mortem ὑπὲρ[?] pro & loco nostri perpessam. Et hoc, vimque hujus in expositione suâ Socinus male præterit.
units.tr: The Opponent goes on to take exception to certain passages of Scripture usually brought forward by our side in this matter. Hebrews 2:9: "that by the grace (or benefit) of God he should taste death for every man [ὑπὲρ παντός]." Socinus himself says: What else is this, he asks, than that, because Christ died, all of us obtained the greatest benefit through the divine goodness? Answer: This is indeed true, but we deny that those words contain nothing else. We obtain the greatest benefit through Christ's death, but a death undergone for us and in our place. Socinus wrongly passes over this, and the force of it, in his exposition.

units.la: Inst. Socinus: Quomodo igitur vice & loco nostrum mortuus est Christus, si nos quoque perpetuo eidem mortis generi expositi sumus, & animam nostram effundere non minus, quam ille, parati esse debemus? Si quis vult venire post me (inquit ipse Christus) abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam quotidie, & sequatur me. Luc. 9. v. 23. Resp. I.[?] Eidem mortis generi, quomodo Christus, nos non minus expositos esse, pernegamus. Externa mortis species si consideretur, levius hoc: eidemque expositi fuerunt cum Christo latrones, sed ecquisne propterea dicet, vel istos, vel nos, eidem mortis generi, & per mortem, uti antea constitit, intelligendo omnes Christi passiones, earumque genera, iisdem per omnia subjectos nos esse, uti Christus fuit? II. Animam etiam effundere parati sumus, & pro Christo, pro nomine, pro causa ejus, sed ideone ὑπὲρ[?], ἀντὶ Χριστοῦ[?], perinde, vel non minus ac ille pro nobis? III. Neque hoc vel Luc. ix. 23. vel Hebr. 11.9. docetur, nos pariter pro Christo mori, ac ipse pro nobis: sed crucem portare nos post Christum debere, Luc. ix. 23. & in loco ad Hebræos nihil ferè istorum continetur. Unde quam frustra Adversarius laboret in conquirendis similibus huic locutionibus, mori pro aliquo; & quanto animi ulcere ac præjudicio studeat enervare ea quæ de Christi pro nobis morte in Scriptura plene & copiose admodum traduntur, apparet.
units.tr: Instance. Socinus: How then is Christ said to have died in our stead and place, if we too are constantly exposed to the same kind of death, and ought to be no less ready than he to pour out our soul? "If anyone wishes to come after me," says Christ himself, "let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." Luke 9:23. Answer: First, that we are exposed to the same kind of death as Christ, and no less, we flatly deny. If one considers the outward form of death, this is a lesser matter: thieves were also exposed to the same kind of death with Christ, but will anyone for that reason say that they, or we, are subject in every respect to the same kind of death and sufferings as Christ was, in the sense already established, namely that by death we understand all Christ's sufferings and their kinds? Second, we too are ready to pour out our soul, and for Christ, for his name, for his cause; but is it therefore for [ὑπὲρ] or in the place of [ἀντὶ Χριστοῦ] Christ, in the same way as, or no less than, he died for us? Third, neither Luke 9:23 nor Hebrews 11:9 teaches that we die for Christ in the same way as he died for us; rather, after Christ we ought to carry the cross (Luke 9:23), and in the passage to the Hebrews almost none of these things is contained. Hence it appears how vainly the Opponent labours in seeking similar expressions, to die for someone, and with what a festering spirit and prejudice he strives to weaken what is handed down in Scripture, fully and very copiously, about Christ's death for us.

units.la: Ad alterum ex locis nostris, Joann. x. 50. ubi Cajaphas dixit, expedire ut unus homo moreretur pro populo, neque tota gens periret, excipit, quod Cajaphas nihil aliud sibi voluit, quam, cum aut ipsi periturî essent, si Christum vivere permitterent, aut Christus occidendus foret, si ipsi salvi esse vellent, satius esse, Jesum solum mori, universum populum conservari, quam universum populum perire, & Jesum ipsum vivere. Atque hæc Cajaphæ mens optime per typum ad salutem nostram accommodari potest. Resp. Iterum negamus, quod dicit, Cajapham nihil aliud voluisse: quod quam frequenter Adversario accidat, ut falsitati addat fiduciam, aliquoties observavimus. Tum præsertim ita loquitur, quando vim argumenti & loci prætereuns, aliquid in genere accipit, quod quidem non falsum, & forte illo etiam loco continetur, sed rem vel non tangit, vel saltem non exhaurit.
units.tr: As to the other of our passages, John 11:50, where Caiaphas said that it was expedient for one man to die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish, the Opponent objects that Caiaphas meant nothing other than this: that since either they themselves would perish if they allowed Christ to live, or Christ would have to be killed if they themselves wished to be saved, it was better for Jesus alone to die and the whole people to be preserved, than for the whole people to perish and Jesus himself to live. And this mind of Caiaphas can very well be applied through the type to our salvation. Answer: Again we deny what he says, that Caiaphas meant nothing other; how often this happens to our Opponent, so that he adds confidence to falsehood, we have observed on several occasions. Especially so when he speaks in this way, passing over the force of the argument and of the passage, and takes something in general, which is indeed not false and perhaps is also contained in that passage, but which either does not touch the matter or at least does not exhaust it.

units.la: Vere etenim hoc voluit Cajaphas, cum aut ipsi perituri essent, si Christum vivere permitterent, aut Christum occidi debere, si ipsi salvi esse vellent, satius esse, Jesum solum mori, & universum populum conservari, quam &c. sed non illud solum, vel nihil aliud voluit, verùm Jesum etiam mori pro populo. Non Jesum solum mori & universum populum conservari: sed Jesum mori cupiebat pro populo. Quod quare omittit, quum in eo tota argumenti vis fit? non, quod Christo moriente, quoquomodo servaretur populus; sed quod Christo moriente ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ[?]. Censuit ergo Cajaphas, satius esse, Jesum solum mori pro populo; & populum, istâ Christi morte, conservari. Ad hoc re-pondere Adversarius debuerat. Deinde, quo pacto pro certo habueri potuit, si Christus moreretur, universum populum servati, non moriente, perire. nisi mors ipsius intelligatur piacularis victima loco & vice populi universi? Ut nec Pilatus illa sua verba aliter intelligere potuerit, nec aliter intelligi quam de vicaria occisione debeant: certe ad Christum, prout ex prophetia oportet, applicatum, aliter accipiendum non est, quando pro populo, pro gente, pro filiis Dei mortuus est.
units.tr: For indeed this is what Caiaphas meant: since either they themselves would perish if they allowed Christ to live, or Christ ought to be killed if they themselves wished to be saved, it was better for Jesus alone to die and the whole people to be preserved, and so on. But he did not mean only that, or nothing else; rather he meant that Jesus should also die for the people. Not that Jesus alone should die and the whole people be preserved: but Caiaphas desired that Jesus should die for the people. Why does the Opponent omit this, when the whole force of the argument lies in it? Not that the people would be saved in some way by Christ's dying, but that by Christ's dying for the people [ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ]. Caiaphas therefore judged that it was better for Jesus alone to die for the people, and that the people would be preserved by that death of Christ. The Opponent ought to have answered this. Next, how could it have been held for certain that if Christ died the whole people would be saved, and if he did not die they would perish, unless his death is understood as a propitiatory sacrifice in the place and stead of the whole people? Just as Pilate could not have understood those words of his otherwise, nor can they be understood otherwise than of a vicarious slaying; certainly when applied to Christ, as the prophecy requires, they are not to be taken in any other way when he died for the people, for the nation, for the children of God.

units.la: Tertium testimonium, quod examinat, est 1 Pet. ii. 21. nam & Christus passus est ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν pro vobis, relinquens vobis exemplum &c. Num tibi videtur, inquit Socinus, ex his verbis colligi posse, Christum loco nostrum mortuum esse, cum, moriendo, ad eandem mortem si opus fuerit, subeundam nos invitet, quippe qui nobis, ut insequamur vestigia ipsius, exemplum reliquerit? Resp. Num videtur Tibi, quod haec consequentia procedit? invitamur ad insequendum Christi exemplum, ad mortem etiam usque, ergo Christus pro nobis quando mortuus, hoc non fecit loco nostrum? Nam neque hoc loco expresse invitamur ad mortem pro Christo subeundam; in genere & simpliciter ad imitationem Christi, in quibuscunque etiam adversitatibus, non solis quas pro ipso patimur, sed omnibus: & quamvis pro Christo dicamur mori, non tamen hoc, quod in se nobis reliquit passionum & patientiae exemplar, trahendum eo, ut voluerit Christus, pari modo nos pro se pati. Quod nec dicitur in Textu, nec verum est, vel esse potest. Exemplar didit nobis patientiae, quod imitemur: quod statim sic explicatur & sequentia verba indicant, contumelia affectus non iterum convitiatus fuit &c. sed non in eo proprie constituit exemplar in Christo nostrum Apostolus, quod ille ὑπὲρ pro nobis passus: nam id quidem explicaturus, infert, peccata nostra ipse sustulit in corpore suo ad crucem: quae nulla similitudine ad nos trahi possunt, ut nec eodem sensu dictio pro, si dicamur mori pro Christo. Non ergo ad eandem mortem subeundam pro Christo, quam is pro nobis, invitamur, aut invitari etiam possumus: ad similem quodammodo, non ad eandem. Mirum, Adversarium, quando respondet ad loca Scripturae emphatica illa, quibus docetur Christum ὑπὲρ, ἀντὶ, pro nobis dedisse semetipsum lutrum, & similia, passim enervare illa, exponendo per quodam modo: ut quod Christus vere pro nobis fecit, sibi videatur quodammodo fecisse: interim quando nos ad exemplum Christi, vel pro ejus nomine morimur, hoc ipsum interpretari, quod pro Christo, non quodammodo, sed pari modo idem praestemus, ac Christus fecit pro nobis. Nempe extenuanda & evacuanda fuerunt Dei & Christi erga nos opera ac beneficia; nostra vero Deo exaequanda. Haec adversariorum scilicet est Theologia. Verum est, quod addit Socinus, ex utroque loco & 1 Pet. ii. 21. & Hebr. ii. 9. constare, ideo etiam mortuum fuisse Christum, ut nobis ad quantumvis atrocem mortem subeundam animos adderet, & nobis praeiret: sed non ad subeundam mortem parem, cum sua; non ἀντὶ pro se, qualem quantamque pro nobis sustinuit ipse.
units.tr: The third testimony that he examines is 1 Pet. 2:21: "For Christ also suffered for you [ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν], leaving you an example, etc." Socinus asks: "Does it seem to you that it can be gathered from these words that Christ died in our place, when by dying he invites us to undergo the same death, if need be, since he has left us an example to follow in his steps?" Reply: Does it seem to you that this inference holds? We are invited to follow Christ's example, even to death; therefore, when Christ died for us, he did not do so in our place? For we are not expressly invited here to undergo death for Christ. The invitation is general and simple, to imitate Christ in whatever adversities, not only those we suffer for him, but in all of them. And although we are said to die for Christ, it does not follow that the pattern of suffering and patience he left us in himself must be drawn so that Christ wished us to suffer for him in the same way. This is neither said in the text nor true, nor can it be. He gave us a pattern of patience to imitate, and the following words, when he was reviled, he did not revile again, etc., explain this and show it. But the Apostle does not place the pattern properly in what Christ suffered for us [ὑπὲρ], for when he goes on to explain that, he adds, he himself bore our sins in his body on the cross, which can in no way be drawn to us by similarity, any more than the word for can be taken in the same sense if we are said to die for Christ. Therefore we are not invited to undergo the same death for Christ as he underwent for us, nor can we be invited to it: we are invited to something similar in a way, not the same. It is strange, my opponent, that when he answers those emphatic passages of Scripture by which it is taught that Christ gave himself a ransom for [ὑπὲρ] and instead of [ἀντὶ] us, and similar things, he everywhere weakens them, explaining them away as "in a certain manner," so that what Christ truly did for us seems to him to have been done only in some measure; yet when we die following Christ's example or for his name, he interprets this not as in some measure but as the same thing, in the same way as Christ did for us. Clearly the works and benefits of God and Christ toward us are to be diminished and emptied out, while ours are to be made equal to God's. This, to be sure, is the theology of our opponents. It is true, as Socinus adds, that from both this passage, 1 Pet. 2:21, and Heb. 2:9, it is established that Christ also died so that he might give us courage to undergo however atrocious a death and go before us; but not to undergo a death equal to his own, not instead of [ἀντὶ] himself, such and so great as he himself endured for us.

units.la: Ad quartum testimonium, Joann. x. 11. 15. ubi dicitur, Christum animam suam posuisse pro ovibus suis, excipit: Atqui bonus pastor non ideo dicitur ponere animam suam pro ovibus suis, quia earum loco moriatur: sed quia propter ipsas servandas, si opus est, moritur. Neque enim, quamvis, dum ipse moritur, illa reipsa non servantur, is tamen animam suam pro ovibus suis non posuisse dicetur. Quid quod eo loco: animam po-nere, mori vere non significat, sed, mortis periculum subire? Nam si pastor moriatur, quomodo servabuntur oves, qui scopus est boni pastoris? Resp. 1. Mori propter ipsas servandas, non tollit, mori quoque earundem loco: ita ut pro servandis iis semetipsum earum loco lupo objiciat. Atque hoc vult tum locutio illa, tum parabola. 11. Extra scopum itur, neque enim singula in parabola vexanda & exponenda ad unguem sunt, quando, quid mortuo pastore ovibus fiat, inquiritur: an ovibus tum male sit &c. sed quodnam boni pastoris officium sit erga oves, ut pro illis morti se objiciat, hic exponitur. 111. Ipsi etiam morti, non soli mortis periculo. Namque in illo vis parabolae haeret, & amoris officiique, quod pastor bonus praestat suis ovibus. Et Christus certe non periculum mortis, sed ipsam revera obiit, eandemque intendit, pro ovibus impendere, quae non aliter quam per illam erunt servandae. Quamvis in morte non remansit, vel interiit totum, mortem tamen totam sustinuit, nostri tum bono, tum loco. verf. 17. Propterea diligit me Pater, quia ego pono animam meam, ut iterum su-mam eam.
units.tr: As to the fourth testimony, John 10:11, 15, where it is said that Christ laid down his life for his sheep, he objects: But the good shepherd is not said to lay down his life for his sheep because he dies in their place, but because he dies, if need be, to save them. For although, while he himself dies, they are not in fact saved by it, he will nevertheless not be said to have laid down his life for his sheep. Moreover, does not that expression "to lay down life" in that place mean not truly to die, but to undergo the danger of death? For if the shepherd dies, how will the sheep be saved, since that is the aim of the good shepherd? Reply: (1) To die for the sake of saving them does not exclude also dying in their place, so that, to save them, he exposes himself to the wolf in their stead. This is what both that expression and the parable mean. (2) He goes beyond the point. For the parable is not to be pressed and explained down to the last detail when the question is what would happen to the sheep if the shepherd died, whether it would go badly for the sheep, and so on. Rather, what the duty of the good shepherd toward the sheep is, that he should expose himself to death for them, is what is being explained here. (3) It concerns death itself, not merely the danger of death. For the force of the parable lies in the love and duty that the good shepherd shows his sheep. And Christ certainly did not undergo the danger of death but actually died, and he intended to give himself for the sheep, which they could not be saved except through. Although he did not remain in death, nor perish entirely, he nevertheless endured the whole of death, for our good and in our place. Verse 17: Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.

units.la: Praeterea ad loca Luc. xxi. 19. 1 Cor. xi. 24. hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur, vel frangitur, respondet: quamvis inter testimonia de redemtione numerentur, nihil tamen cum ea commune habere. Nulla enim mentio ibi redemtionis; neque verbum Datur apud Lucam, ad dationem pretii accommodari potest. Quid autem verbum illud significet, satis indicat verbum frangitur, quod a Paulo ejus loco positum est. Ex quo verbo manifestum fit, de traditione, sive datione in mortem ibi agi, non autem de aliqua corporis, seu vitae Christi alicui facta solutione. Resp. 1. Quamvis verbum redemtionis illis locis non occurrat, res modo continetur, satis est. 11. Et certe res continetur, cujus fundamentum memoratur, & formalis causa, corpus, quod pro vobis datur; (sanguis, qui pro vobis effunditur. Quod idem est cum Matth. xx. 28. dare animam suam lutrum pro multis. Quare enim datur, διδόμενον[?] apud Lucam, non aeque ad dationem pretii accommodari potest, ac dare δοῦναι[?] apud Matthaeum? 111. Datur, connotat etiam frangitur, quod apud Paulum est, & traditionem, seu dationem in mortem. Quare non ergo- & solutionem? nam per dationem illam solutio facta est. Dum in mortem se de-dit Christus, pro nobis id quod debebatur, solvit. Illud enim est, dare animam suam, phrasi Scripturae; istud, significatur lutro: quod utrumque in plena oratione Christus conjunxit. Adeo non divellenda, vel opponenda sibi mu-tuo sunt, quod Socinus amat, ut & phrases, & res Scripturae magna opera det eviratas. Quod autem loca Matth. xx. 28. & Tit. ii. 14. ad redemtionem manifeste pertinent, totidem verbis fatetur Socinus. Sed, inquit, vocem pro, non vice seu loco vere significare posse, patet. alioqui Christus vice nostrum captivus remansisset. Quod nullo modo sequitur. Quia non solvere modo nostro loco, sed exsolvere, & liberare Christus debuit. Quodque debuit, revera praestitit, atque effecit.
units.tr: Next, he replies to the passages Luke 22:19 and 1 Cor. 11:24, This is my body, which is given [διδόμενον] or broken for you. Although these passages are counted among the testimonies on redemption, he says they have nothing in common with it. For there is no mention of redemption there; nor does the word "given" in Luke fit the giving of a price. What that word means is sufficiently shown by the word "broken," which Paul puts in that place. From this word it is clear that the passage concerns a handing over, or giving, to death, and not some payment made by Christ's body or life. Reply: (1) Although the word redemption does not occur in those places, the thing itself is contained there, and that is enough. (2) And indeed the thing is contained, since its foundation is mentioned, and its formal cause: the body which is given for you, the blood which is poured out for you. This is the same as Matt. 20:28, to give his life a ransom [λύτρον] for many. For why should "given" [διδόμενον] in Luke not fit the giving of a price as well as "to give" [δοῦναι] in Matthew? (3) "Given" also implies "broken," which is in Paul, and the handing over, or giving, to death. Why then not also payment? For by that giving payment was made. When Christ gave himself to death, he paid for us what was owed. For to give his soul is the expression of Scripture; to be a ransom is what is signified; and Christ joined both in one full sentence. So these things are not to be separated or set against each other, as Socinus likes to do, which makes both the expressions and the realities of Scripture greatly enfeebled. As for the fact that Matt. 20:28 and Titus 2:14 plainly pertain to redemption, Socinus admits this in so many words. But, he says, "that the word 'for' can truly mean not instead of or in place of, is clear. Otherwise Christ would have remained a captive in our place." This does not follow at all. For Christ had to not only pay in our place but to set us free and deliver us, and what he had to do, he truly performed and accomplished.

units.la: Denique ad id, quod apud Matthæum est Græca præpositio ἀντὶ, quæ in locutionibus, ut ista est, dare animam suam redemptionem pro multis, significet debitum aliquod præcessisse, quod persolutum fuerit. ubi apud eundem Matthæum cap. 17. in fine, da eis pro me, & te. ubi pro in Græco est ἀντὶ. Illud enim quod Christus ibi Petrum dare jubet, debebatur ab unoquoque Israelita, qui vigesimum annum explevisset, Exod. 30. 13. respondet, in Matthæi loco, de quo controversia est, agi, ut dictum fuit & apertum est, de redemptione, de qua cum quis loquitur, locus est præpositioni ἀντὶ. Hactenus omnia, & hæc, & illa, bene. etiamsi captivus nihil pro sua redemptione ei debeat, qui ipsum captivum detinet, nimirum propter commutationem illam, quæ in omni redemptione sit. Pretium enim redemptionis datur, & captivus recipitur. & sane in redemptione nostra per Christum facta, licet, ut supra docuimus, metaphorica, hæc commutatio facta est, quod Christus animam suam, ut in loco isto dicitur, dedit, & nos recepit, id est, è peccati servitute liberatos sibi asseruit. Resp. 1. Captivum nihil pro sua redemtione debere ei, qui ipsum detinet, quomodo probat? II. In omni redemtione fit commutatio. Pretium enim redemtionis datur, & captivus recipitur. Sic ergo & in nostrâ redemtione, pretium dedit Christus, atque hoc ἀντὶ ἡμῶν. III. Jam vero omnia conturbat & everrit, quando ait, commutationem factam esse metaphoricam. Quid, an metaphoricè Christus animam dedit, non vere? metaphoricè, & non vere nos liberati, atque vindicati è captivitate spirituali? metaphorica commutatio Christi pro nobis traditi, & nostrum per Christum liberatorum? Habeantur ergo omnia metaphorica, Christus, liberatio, salus, & tota denique religio. IV. Nulla vero in Scripturæ locis, quibus de remtione nostrum agitur, vel levis metaphoræ suspicio aut signum est: quin non uno, sed variis locis; non uno vel modo, vel phrasi, sed diversis res docetur, maximeque emphaticis & propriis locutionibus, quæ nequaquam cedere oportet coactæ & fictitiæ metaphoræ, quâ tota enervatur Scriptura, & nostra fides.
units.tr: Finally, as to the Greek preposition in Matthew, ἀντὶ [instead of, for], which in expressions such as this one, to give his soul a ransom for many, signifies that some debt went before, which was paid. Where in the same Matthew, ch. 17, at the end, give it for me and you, where "for" in the Greek is ἀντὶ [for]. For what Christ there bids Peter give was owed by every Israelite who had completed his twentieth year (Exod. 30:13). Reply: that in the passage of Matthew under dispute it is a question, as has been said and is clear, of redemption, and when one speaks of redemption, there is a place for the preposition ἀντὶ. So far, all these things are good, both these and those. Even though the captive owes nothing to the one who holds him captive for his own redemption, namely because of that exchange which occurs in every redemption. For the price of redemption is given, and the captive is received. And indeed in our redemption through Christ, although, as we taught above, it is metaphorical, this exchange has taken place, in that Christ gave his soul, as is said in that place, and received us, that is, claimed us for himself as freed from the bondage of sin. Reply: (1) How does he prove that a captive owes nothing for his own redemption to the one who holds him? (2) In every redemption there is an exchange. For the price of redemption is given, and the captive is received. So in our redemption too, Christ gave the price, and this instead of us [ἀντὶ ἡμῶν]. (3) Now he throws everything into confusion and sweeps it away when he says the exchange is metaphorical. What, did Christ give his soul only metaphorically, not truly? Were we freed and delivered from spiritual captivity only metaphorically? Is Christ's exchange, his being given up for us and our being freed through him, a metaphor? Then let everything be held to be metaphorical: Christ, deliverance, salvation, and finally the whole of religion. (4) But in the passages of Scripture where our redemption is treated, there is not the slightest suspicion or sign of metaphor; rather, in many places and not just one, in various ways and phrases, the matter is taught, and especially by emphatic and proper expressions, which ought by no means yield to a forced and fictitious metaphor, by which all of Scripture and our faith are enfeebled.

units.la: Atque hactenus fuit secundum Argumentum, sumtum ex illis Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ docent, Christum propter peccata nostra, pro nobis, & loco nostri mortuum fuisse: sequitur tertium, inde petitum, quod Christus, expiatione peccatorum nostrorum seipso facta, Deo nos reconciliavit. Hunc in modum: Qui passionibus & morte suâ peccata nostra verè apud Deum expiavit, eoque reddito nobis propitio, nos cum eo reconciliavit, is pro peccatis nostris omninò satisfecit: atqui Christus illud egit: ergo. Tria argumenti nostri membra, speciatim tractanda sunt; quod expiavit Christus peccata: Deum reddidit propitium; & cum eo nos reconciliavit. Quâ ratione nostra expiavit, propitiavit Deum, & quâ ratione propitiavit, nos cum eo reconciliavit.
units.tr: This is the second argument, drawn from those passages of Scripture which teach that Christ died for our sins, on our behalf and in our place. There follows a third, taken from the fact that Christ, by making expiation for our sins with himself, reconciled us to God. The argument runs thus: whoever truly expiated our sins before God by his sufferings and death, and by making God propitious to us reconciled us to him, has fully satisfied for our sins; but Christ did this; therefore he has fully satisfied for our sins. The three members of this argument must be treated separately: that Christ expiated sins, that he made God propitious, and that by this he reconciled us to God. By what means he expiated our sins and propitiated God, and by what means he propitiated God and reconciled us to him.

units.la: Expiavit peccata nostra seipso, ἑαυτῷ[?] Hebr. 1, 3. id est, passione & morte suâ, vero sui sacrificio. Quare de utroque hujus loci est agere, de expiatione factâ, & per Christi sacrificium. Concedunt Sociniani expiationem no-strũm,per Christum fieri.Socinus eam passim agnoscit,& verbo redemtionis significari vult,deServ. part. ii.cap.xiii.&xiv.Deinde & factam expiationem, per Christioblationem. Cap. xiii. pag. 140. Veram oblationem expiatoriam corporis Christi, inquit. Tertio, perfectam expiationem. Cap. xvi. pag. 154. perpetuam & omnimodam a peccatis expiationem. iv. Peccatorum omnium, praecedentium, & futurorum. Cap. xiv. Christi autem mors, & a praecedentium omnium delictorum, & a futurorum reatu nos liberos reddit, nosque in perpetuum sanctificat, & coram Deo inculpatos in sempiternum efficit. Paulo post, ea, licet futura, divino decreto expiata jam sunt, & ipsis nunquam imputabuntur. v. Christi morte interveniente illam factam. Praeter proximum, quem adduximus; locum, eodem etiam cap. pag. 147. Expiata igitur esse peccata nostra per Christi mortem ex Dei parte, nos ipsi sentimus. Pag. 144. ab ipsa morte Christi in peccatis expiandis. vi. Quod se obtulit Christus in sacrificium, seu victimam. Cap xix. pag. 167. idem & sacerdos & victima. cap. xx. pag. 175. per Christum semetipsum Deo sacrificantem, id est, sanguinem suum, per quem in coelum ingressus est, fundentem. vii. Eaque cumprimis in epistola ad Hebraos doceri, fatetur. Pag. 140. Veram oblationem expiatoriam corporis Christi, quam auctor ad Heb. sacrificiis illis legalibus opponit. Pag. 145. Redemtionis verbum, ab hoc scriptore, pro expiatione usurpatur. Ibidem, vocat auctor ad Heb. hanc peccatorum expiationem aeternam. Pag 155. Denique duplicem peccatorum expiationem, a peccato, & poena, per Christi mortem fieri, ex hoc ad Heb. epist. loco liquet.
units.tr: He expiated our sins by himself [ἑαυτῷ] Heb. 1:3, that is, by his passion and death, by the true sacrifice of himself. Hence we must treat of both parts of this passage: the expiation made, and that it was made through Christ's sacrifice. The Socinians concede that our expiation is made through Christ. Socinus everywhere acknowledges it and wishes it to be signified by the word redemption, De Serv. part. II, cap. xiii and xiv. Next, that the expiation was made by the oblation of Christ. Chapter xiii, page 140: he says, the true expiatory oblation of the body of Christ. Thirdly, a perfect expiation. Chapter xvi, page 154: a perpetual and complete expiation from sins. Fourth, of all sins, past and future. Chapter xiv: the death of Christ frees us both from the guilt of all past offences and of future ones, and makes us holy for ever, and renders us blameless before God for eternity. A little later: these sins, although future, have already been expiated by the divine decree, and will never be imputed to them. Fifthly, that expiation was made with the intervention of Christ's death. Besides the nearer passage that we have cited, in the same chapter at page 147: that our sins have been expiated by the death of Christ on God's part, we ourselves feel. Page 144: from the very death of Christ in the expiating of sins. Sixthly, that Christ offered himself as a sacrifice or victim. Chapter xix, page 167: the same both priest and victim. Chapter xx, page 175: Christ offering himself to God, that is, pouring out his blood, through which he entered into heaven. Seventhly, he admits that this is taught chiefly in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Page 140: the true expiatory oblation of the body of Christ, which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews sets against those legal sacrifices. Page 145: the word redemption is used by this writer for expiation. In the same place: the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews calls this expiation of sins eternal. Page 155: finally, that a twofold expiation of sins, from sin and from punishment, is made by the death of Christ, is clear from this passage of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: Haec quantacunque videri queant, ea tamen non sunt, quae pro ingenue & clare dictis haberi debeant, quaeque proprie Christi morti, peccatorum nostrorum veram expiationem attribuant: imo ne quidem expiationem ipsam intelligunt. Nihil aliud est reipsa peccatorum nostrorum expiatio, quam a morte peccati plena & perpetua liberatio, inquit, cap xiii. pag. 141. Sola & nuda liberatio, non est expiatio; uti nec quodcunque, aut simpliciter liberare, expiare est; sed certi modi liberatio, qui specificam a quavis alia & communi liberatione infert differentiam. Namque expiatio proprie est, purgatio noxae, per poenae luitionem debitam ac justam, ad placandam alterius iram. Jam ex his quidem sequitur liberatio; ipsa vero expiatio, liberatio non est. Liberationem praestat dominus, expiationem reus, vel alius ejus nomine. Et hoc dicitur, luere. Inde poenas luere, luere peccata, & peccati poenas. maculas furtorum & flagitiorum, sociorum innocentium sanguine luere, apud Ciceronem, contra Verrem, Act. vii. Apud Livium, lib. i. debito supplicio scelus luere. Apud Lucanum, lib. xxv. hac cade luatur
units.tr: However great these statements may seem, they are not such as ought to be taken as clearly and openly said, or as properly ascribing to Christ's death a true expiation of our sins. Indeed, they do not even understand expiation itself. "The expiation of our sins in reality is nothing other than a full and perpetual liberation from the death of sin," he says, chapter xiii, page 141. A bare liberation is not expiation, any more than any kind of liberation, or simply to free, is to expiate; it is a liberation of a certain kind which brings a specific difference from any other and general liberation. For expiation properly is the purging of a fault by the bearing of a due and just penalty, in order to appease another's anger. From these things indeed liberation follows; but expiation itself is not liberation. The master grants liberation; the guilty person, or someone on his behalf, makes expiation. And this is called to pay, luere. Hence to pay penalties, to pay for sins, and to pay the penalty of sin: to pay for the stains of thefts and crimes with the blood of innocent allies, in Cicero, Against Verres, Act vii. In Livy, book i: to pay for the crime with due punishment. In Lucan, book xxv: let it be paid for with this slaughter.

units.la: Quidquid Romani meruerunt pendere mores.
units.tr: Whatever the manners of the Romans have deserved to pay.

units.la: Atque hoc proprie piare est, & expiare. Inde piaculum, & piacularis hostia. Plautus,
units.tr: And this is properly to make atonement and to expiate. Hence piaculum and piacularis hostia. Plautus,

units.la: Mene piacularem oportet fieri ob stultitiam tuam, Ut meum tergum stultitia tua subdas succidaneum.
units.tr: Must I be made a scapegoat for your folly, so that your folly lays its blows on my back as a substitute?

units.la: Quod est piaculum fieri, & expiationem pro alio. Livius, lib. i. Itaque ut [?]cædes manifesta aliquo tamen piaculo lueretur, imperatum patri, ut filium expiaret pe-cunia publica. Is quibusdam piacularibus sacrificiis factis &c. Ex quibus locutionibus, quid nimirum expiatio sit, constare potest, an simplex liberatio, an talis, quæ luitione fiat pœnarum? tum quid sit sacrificium piaculare, & quando hoc, pro altero, instituitur? Quid denique, expiationem peccati fieri, aut facere pro alio? Salustius, de Rep. constit. Neque barbaro ritu cæde cædem, sanguine sanguinem expiandum. In expiatione fit purgatio delicti, inde καθαρμός, & καθάρσις dicitur & καθαρμα, devotum, sacrum caput, piamentum, à καθαίρειν purgare, mundare. Item ἁγνισμός, ἁγνίζειν expiare, mundare, ab ἁγνός mundus. Sed est purgatio, quæ fit luitione pœnæ, & afflictionis pro delicto.
units.tr: That is, to be made a piaculum, and to make expiation on behalf of another. Livy, book i: So that a manifest murder might nonetheless be expiated by some sacrifice, the father was ordered to make expiation for his son at public expense. He, having made certain piacular sacrifices, etc. From these expressions it can be established what expiation indeed is: whether a simple liberation, or such as is effected by the paying of penalties? And then what a piacular sacrifice is, and when it is instituted for another? Finally, what it is to make expiation of sin, or to make it on behalf of another? Sallust, On the Constitution of the Republic: nor is murder to be expiated by murder, nor blood by blood, in the barbarous manner. In expiation a fault is purged; hence it is called katharmos and katharsis [καθαρμός, καθάρσις], and katharma, a devoted or sacred offering, piamentum, from kathairein [καθαίρειν], to purge, to cleanse. Likewise hagnismos and hagnizein [ἁγνισμός, ἁγνίζειν], to expiate, to cleanse, from hagnos [ἁγνός], pure. But this is a purging which is effected by the paying of a penalty and of affliction for a fault.

units.la: Socinus expiationem facit duplicem, alteram à peccatis, à peccatorum pœnis alteram. Illam exponit, per sanctificationem, vel resipiscentiam. nisi prius ab ipsis peccatis expiatus fit, id est, à peccando desiterit, part. II. cap. XVI. Istam nihil aliud esse dicit, quam à peccatorum pœna liberationem, quam is, qui à peccando desiterit, propterea consequatur. Revera nec hæc, nec illa expiatio est. Et quantacunque de expiatione dicat, ut in eam resolvat redemtionem, vel, uti improbè solet loqui, redemtionis nostræ metaphoram, nihil præter metaphoram quoque in expiatione facit reliquum. Veritatem ubique odit, & rebus omnibus adimit. Expiatio proprie est à peccati pœnâ, neque fit nisi per succedaneam afflictionem, quâ illa expurgatur, διὰ τὸ ἴσον τῆς ἀντιλήψεως, ἢ ἀνλιδόσεως[?]. Hujus generis sunt sacrificia. Neque sacrificium expiatorium alio modo concipi aut intelligi potest. Minime, dignissimum illud & verissimum sacrificium Christi, atque expiatio, quam nobis peregit. Aliud est remissio, vel liberatio; & aliud expiatio. Levit. v. 6. & adducet reatum suum Jehova propter peccatum suum quo peccavit, &c. ita expiabit eum Sacerdos à peccato suo, 13. Ita expiabit eum Sacerdos à peccato suo, quo peccavit de aliquo ex iis, & remittetur ei. 16. Ita Sacerdos expiabit per arietem illum reatus, & remittetur ei. Item verf. 11. 25. 26. Aliud ergo expiatio est reatus, aliud quæ per & post eam fit, remissio, ac rei liberatio. Cedo unum locum, vel auctorem, qui expiationem intellexerit de resipiscentia; aut abductione vel retractione hominis à peccatis; de liberatione, quæ fiat absque luitione debitæ pœnæ: at liberationem à pœna indicat semper, ubi de sacrificio expiatorio sermo est. Non licet Socino, non licet alicui verbis aliam, à naturali & usitata, significationem aptare, & contra naturalem sensum illa torquere. Expiatio, expiare, proprie & semper significat, pœnæ luitione & solutione, uti sacrificio pro peccato satisfacere, & placare iratum. Sic piabile, & inexpiabile dicitur, & ira inexpiabilis. Ovidius, Fastor. III.
units.tr: Socinus makes expiation twofold: one from sins, the other from the punishments of sins. He explains the former as sanctification or repentance: unless he is first expiated from the sins themselves, that is, has ceased from sinning, Part II, chapter xvi. He says the latter is nothing other than liberation from the punishment of sins, which the one who has ceased from sinning consequently obtains. In truth neither this nor that is expiation. And however much he speaks of expiation, so as to resolve it into redemption, or (as he is wont to speak wrongly) the metaphor of our redemption, he leaves nothing in expiation but a metaphor as well. He hates the truth everywhere and strips it from all things. Expiation properly is from the punishment of sin, and it is not made except by a substituted affliction by which that punishment is purged away, dia to ison tes antilepseos, e antidoseos [διὰ τὸ ἴσον τῆς ἀντιλήψεως, ἢ ἀντιδόσεως]. Sacrifices are of this kind. Nor can a sacrificial expiation be conceived or understood in any other way. Least of all can that most worthy and most true sacrifice of Christ, and the expiation which he accomplished for us, be otherwise. Remission or liberation is one thing; expiation is another. Levit. v. 6. And Jehovah shall bring his guilt for the sin which he has committed, etc. So the priest shall make expiation for him from his sin. 13. So the priest shall make expiation for him from his sin, which he has committed in any of these things, and it shall be forgiven him. 16. So the priest shall make expiation through that ram for the guilt, and it shall be forgiven him. Likewise verses 11, 25, 26. Therefore the guilt is one thing; another is the remission and liberation of the guilty person, which takes place through and after the expiation. Let him name one passage or author who has understood expiation as repentance, or as the turning away or withdrawing of a man from sins, or as a liberation that takes place without the paying of the due penalty; whereas wherever there is discussion of an expiatory sacrifice, it always indicates liberation from punishment. Socinus is not permitted, nor is anyone permitted, to fit words to a meaning other than the natural and usual one, and to twist them against their natural sense. Expiatio, expiare, properly and always signifies the paying and discharge of a penalty, as to satisfy by a sacrifice for sin and to appease an angered one. Thus piabile and inexpiabile are said, and ira inexpiabilis. Ovid, Fasti III:

units.la: Ne nimium terrere, piabile fulmenEst, ait, & sævi flectitur ira Jovis.
units.tr: Lest you terrify too much: a thunderbolt can be expiated, he says, and the anger of savage Jove is appeased.

units.la: Sic & Decii piacula omnia Deorum ira dicuntur Livio, Eximium ex Juvenale locum huic fini adducit Grotius, ut & alia, cap. ix. libri de Satisfactione Christi. Illud dicebant averruncare. Livius, lib. viii. Placuit ad averruncandam Deum iram, victimas caedi. Quod est ἀποτρέπεσθαι[?] Graecis: inde expiationes, ἀπο-τρεπταί[?], & Dii ἀποτρεπαῖοι[?], Latinis averrunci. Hircus expiatorius, ἀποτρεπτικός[?], Levit. xvi.
units.tr: Thus also the piacula of the Decii are all called the anger of the gods by Livy. Grotius adduces a notable passage from Juvenal for this purpose, as well as other things, in chapter ix of the book On the Satisfaction of Christ. They said averruncare. Livy, book viii: It was decided to slaughter victims in order to avert the anger of God. This is apotrepesthai [ἀποτρέπεσθαι] in Greek; hence expiations are apotreptai [ἀποτρεπταί], and the gods apotrepaioi [ἀποτρεπαῖοι], averrunci to the Latins. A scapegoat for expiation, apotreptikos [ἀποτρεπτικός], Lev. xvi.

units.la: Quare falsus est Socinus, quando expiationem de merâ liberatione exponit; omittens illa, in quibus vera & propria expiationis ratio consistit. Mortem Christi quidem intetvenire dicit, pag. 145. expiationem Christi sanguine & morte interveniente factam. & pag. 151. Primum enim sententia mea non sejungit Christi mortem ab ejusdem pro nobis oblatione: immo affero, eum non obtulisse seipsum, nisi per mortem, id est, non nisi morte sua interveniente; quamvis oblatio non ante perfecta fuerit, quam post resurrectionem, & ascensum ipsius in coelum. Mortem intervenisse, ait, sed non ut expiationis causam, quam non in morte factam statuit, sed post Christi mortem, & adscensionem, quam cum sui oblatione in coelum, quando demum incoeperit sacerdotale officium, inchoatam. Sic ut revera mors antecedens remotum, juxta ipsum, fuerit expiationis, non causa: interveniens ad Christum in coelesti gloriâ collocandum, ibique expiationem, seu liberationem nostram procurandam, non tamquam expiationis proprium & formale fundamentum. Unde sic illa explicat, pag. 175. Christum semetipsum Deo sacrificantem, id est, sanguinem suum per quem in coelum ingressus est, fundentem. Sanguis ergo Christi ipsi inserviit, ut per eum in coelum introgrederetur; non nobis, ut per eum expiaremur. Quae naturam expiationis, morti & sanguini illius adscriptae, funditus evertunt. Nam ad expiationem intervenit 1. Afflictio, ut causa ejus. 11. Afflictio poenalis. Expiari crimina, puniri connotat. Cicero, in Pisonem: Tua scelera Dii immortales in nostros milites expiaverunt: id est, etiam puniverunt. 111. Punitio succedanea, pro crimine, vel peccatore, & reo. Sic apud Veteres dictae hostiae succedaneae, ἀντεμψύχων[?] θυσιῶν[?]. Atque in omni piaculari victimâ furrogatio fit, quâ hæc subiditur in locum reatus: unde & ipsa reatus, ἁμαρτία, חטאת[?], & אשם[?] appellatur. iv. Per quam fit, pro crimine & delicto, satisfactio. v. Inde & expurgatio, καθαρσις & καθαρμός. vi. Demum irati placatio, ἱλασμός. vii. Tandem & rei liberatio. Ut Socinus, quando expiationem nihil aliud esse dicit, quam liberationem, totum illud in quo vera & propria ratio expiationis sita est, studiosè & malitiosè transfiliat, id est, veram expiationem. Haec ipsius sunt verba, part. ii. cap. xx. quare dicendum est, Christum quoque peccata nostra expiasse, non quia ex persona sua divina justitia pro eis ulla ex parte satisfecerit, vel Deum nobis placaverit: sed quia ea peregerit, quibus peractis, veniam delictorum nostrorum jam a Deo nobis sponte decretam & promissam consecuti simus, vel etiam, eam veniam nos consecutos esse, declaratum sit. Quod naturam expiationis, & nostrae hinc pendentis salutis, totum invertit, iisque Scripturae locis directè contrariatur, quae verum, hoc est, longe alium ab illo, expiationis nostrae modum docent, & ordinem.
units.tr: Therefore Socinus is wrong when he explains expiation as mere deliverance, leaving out the elements in which the true and proper nature of expiation consists. He does say that Christ's death intervened, p. 145: the expiation made by Christ with his blood and intervening death. And p. 151: For my view does not separate the death of Christ from his offering of himself for us. Indeed I maintain that he did not offer himself except through death, that is, not except with his death intervening, although the offering was not perfected until after the resurrection and his ascension into heaven. He says the death intervened, but not as the cause of expiation, which he holds was not made in the death, but after Christ's death and ascension, which he began with his offering in heaven, when he at last began his priestly office. So, according to him, the preceding death was a remote condition of expiation, not its cause. It intervened to place Christ in heavenly glory, and there to procure our expiation, or deliverance, but not as the proper and formal ground of expiation. Hence he explains it thus, p. 175: Christ offering himself to God, that is, shedding his blood, through which he entered heaven. The blood of Christ therefore served Christ himself, so that he might enter heaven through it; it did not serve us, so that we might be expiated through it. These claims utterly overturn the nature of expiation, which is ascribed to his death and blood. For expiation involves: 1. affliction, as its cause. 2. penal affliction. To expiate crimes implies punishment. Cicero, against Piso: The immortal gods have expiated your crimes upon our soldiers, that is, have punished them. 3. substitute punishment in place of the crime, or of the sinner and the guilty party. So among the ancients sacrifices were called substitute sacrifices, [ἀντεμψύχων θυσιῶν]. In every expiatory victim a substitution takes place, by which the victim is put in the place of the guilt; whence the guilt itself is called sin [ἁμαρτία] and [חטאת] and [אשם]. 4. Through which satisfaction is made for the crime and offence. 5. Hence also purification [καθαρσις and καθαρμός]. 6. Finally the appeasing [ἱλασμός] of the angry party. 7. At last the deliverance of the guilty one. When Socinus says that expiation is nothing other than deliverance, he eagerly and maliciously skips over that whole element in which the true and proper account of expiation lies, that is, true expiation. These are his own words, part II, ch. 20: Wherefore it must be said that Christ also expiated our sins, not because by his divine person he satisfied divine justice in any way for them, or appeased God for us, but because he performed those things by which, once they were performed, we obtained forgiveness of our offences, already decreed and promised by God of his own accord; or it was declared that we had obtained that forgiveness. This overturns the whole nature of expiation, and of our salvation which depends on it, and directly contradicts those passages of Scripture which teach the true manner and order of our expiation, which is quite different from his.

units.la: Inter loca Scripturae, quae id declarant, potiora occurrunt in Epistolâ ad Hebraeos. Statim in initio, ubi Apostolus, post jactam in limine connexionem Veteris Novique Testamenti, verf. 1. πολυμερῶς &c. ὁ θεὸς λα-λήσας τοῖς πατράσιν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις. quod doctrinam & Ecclesiam V.
