T. compendio exhibet. ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ. hoc statum pandit N. T. atque postquam ita Ecclesiam hujus & illius temporis conjunxit, de Christo mox, quis sit, quidque faciat, ut Deus, in mundo creando, & conservando; ut Mediator, verf. 3. exponit', δι' ἑαυτοῦ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. per semetipsum purgatione facta peccatorum nostrorum. Castellio, facta per semetipsum expiatione peccatorum nostrorum.
units.tr: Among the passages of Scripture that declare this, the most important occur in the Epistle to the Hebrews. At the very beginning, where the Apostle, having set out at the threshold the connection of the Old and New Testaments, says in v. 1: "God, having spoken in many parts and in many ways to the fathers by the prophets" [πολυμερῶς ὁ θεὸς λαλήσας τοῖς πατράσιν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις], which briefly presents the teaching and the Church of the Old Testament; "in these last days he has spoken to us in a Son" [ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν υἱῷ], which sets forth the state of the New Testament. Having thus joined the Church of this time to that of the former time, he shortly afterwards describes who Christ is and what he does, as God in creating and preserving the world, and as Mediator, in v. 3: "having made by himself the purification of our sins" [δι' ἑαυτοῦ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν]. Castellio renders it: "having made by himself the expiation of our sins."

units.la: Socinus, de Servat. part II. cap. xx. 175. non poterat divinius, qua ratione Christus, morte sua interveniente, peccata nostra expiarit, explicari, inquit ad illa verba. quae tandem ita exlicat: recte dictum est, eum per semetipsum peccatorum nostrorum purgationem fecisse. Quatenus enim Dei erga nos voluntatem omnem in ipso expressam vidimus, declaratum nobis apertissime est, remissa & deleta esse peccata nostra. Vidimus autem expressam in Christo divinam erga nos voluntatem, non modo quia is, ut supra visum fuit, eam nobis patefecit, sed etiam quia jam in ipso re impletum scimus, quod nobis Deus per ipsum est pollicitus; & certissimum pignus divinae bonitatis nobis patefacta habemus. Quare de expiatione omnium delictorum nostrorum, id est, de liberatione à morte aeterna, quam nobis Christus de coelo attulit, non est, cur jam debitemus. Resp. 1.
units.tr: Socinus, de Servat. part II, ch. 20, p. 175, says on those words: It could not be explained more divinely by what manner Christ expiated our sins, his death intervening. He then explains them thus: It is rightly said that he made the purification of our sins through himself. For inasmuch as we have seen the whole will of God expressed in him, it has been made most clearly known to us that our sins are remitted and blotted out. Now we have seen the divine will toward us expressed in Christ, not only because he, as seen above, revealed it to us, but also because we know that what God promised us through him has already been fulfilled in him, and we have a most certain pledge of the divine goodness revealed to us. Therefore there is no reason for us to doubt about the expiation of all our offences, that is, about deliverance from eternal death, which Christ brought us from heaven. Reply 1.

units.la: Satis tenuiter de Dei verbo, quod recte dictum censet. Nempe postquam ei sensum submisit, sibi magis, quam Scripturae convenientem. Talem videlicet, quae totam expiationis naturam excludat. Nam, nec quod in Christo vidisse dicimur Dei voluntatem, vel declaratum remissa esse peccata nostra, hactenus modum exponit, scilicet fieri remissionem per veram peccatorum expiationem. Aliud est expiatio, aliud voluntas Dei, vel declaratio voluntatis de peccatorum remissione. II. Quid hoc est, in Christo expressam esse Dei voluntatem? nempe ut in hunc sensum trahat verba praecedentia, quibus Christus dicitur ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. Ait Scriptor ille divinus, inquit, Christum splendorem esse gloriae, & expressam imaginem substantiae Dei, hoc est, per Christum nobis Dei gloriam, ipsumque adeo Deum insigniter admodum apparuisse: ita ut ipsummet Deum in Christo conspicere & contemplari nobis licuerit. Quod aliud non est, quam nos Deum, ejusque voluntatem, quatenus nobis haec cognitio salutaris est, per Christum penitus cognovisse, & perspexisse. Iterum istud Socinianum, aliud non esse Christum Dei Patris ἀπαύγασμα resplendescentiam & characterem, quam per eum nos Dei voluntatem cognovisse. Sic enervans illa, quae Christo propria hic tribuuntur, ut si nihil aliud sit, Moses propterea, aliisque Prophetae, & Apostoli, per quos Deum, ejusque voluntatem , quatenus nobis salutaris est , penitus cognovimus & perspeximus, simili nomenclatura insigniri possint, & eodem modo appellari. Quod & contra Apostoli scopum est, Christum omnibus omnino creaturis & Angelis præferentis, & singularia ejus exponentis; & contra rei vetitatem. Ita ergo per solam declarationem divinæ voluntatis, quod tam multis commune est, exponet tum quod de Christo dicitur, eum εἶναι ἀπαύγασμα & χαρακτῆρα, & quod fecit expiationem peccatorum nostrorum seipso? Hoc nimirum est, pro methodo Sociniana, omnium tum verborum, tum rerum vim auferre plane atque destruere. II. Certe non est quod dubitemus, de expiatione delictorum nostrorum omnium per Christum: sed quid hoc est, quod Chri-ftus eam de cœlo attulifte dicit? Ubi hoc Scriptura? Quisve ejus sensus? Man-datum Patris, & doctrinam quidem suam Christus de cœlo attulit: non vero expiationem. Non dicitur, expiationem adferre; sed facere, sed præstare: non, de cœlo. Perfecit eam in terris Christus, quando alta voce exclamavit, πεπλήρωται. III. Ubi etiam dicitur, nos vidisse in Christo expressam Dei voluntatem? ideo nimirum, quod eam patefecit? Habemus in Christo quidem certissimum pignus divinæ bonitatis: sed illa non exponunt vim & naturam expiationis: nec propterea in ipso impleta potest dici expiatio, quidem per ipsum, & hæc, quam Deus nobis per iplum est pollicitus. Non impleta in Chri-sto, eo quod ad sempiternam beatitudinem, uti mox exponit, ipse est perductus, atque omnia regendi potestatem accepit. Sic nihil ejus, quod ad veram expiationem pertinet, hoc in loco commemorat Adversarius, in quo tamen divinissime, qua ratione peccata nostra expiaverit Christus, explicari à Scriptore professus fuerat.
units.tr: This is a rather thin account of the word of God, which he thinks is rightly said. Having subjected its sense to himself, he has fitted it to himself rather than to Scripture, namely in a way that excludes the whole nature of expiation. For neither does what we are said to have seen in Christ, the will of God, nor what is said to have been declared, that our sins are remitted, explain the manner, namely that remission comes about through true expiation of sins. Expiation is one thing; the will of God, or the declaration of his will concerning the remission of sins, is another. II. What does it mean that the will of God was expressed in Christ? Obviously he twists the preceding words, in which Christ is called [ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης] and [χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ], to this sense: That divine writer says that Christ is the splendour of glory and the express image of God's substance, that is, that through Christ the glory of God has been displayed to us, and God himself has appeared most remarkably, so that we have been allowed to behold and contemplate God himself in Christ. This is nothing other than that we have fully known and perceived God, and his will, insofar as this knowledge is saving for us, through Christ. Again, that Socinian claim: Christ is nothing other than the splendour [ἀπαύγασμα] and character of the Father, than that we have known the will of God through him. So he weakens those things that are proper to Christ here, as if they were nothing more than this: Moses, and the other prophets and apostles through whom we have fully known and perceived God and his will, insofar as it is saving for us, could be marked with the same name and called by the same title. This is also contrary to the Apostle's purpose, which is to set Christ above all creatures and angels and to expound his unique qualities, and it is contrary to the truth of the matter. So does he, by the mere declaration of the divine will, which is common to so many, explain both what is said of Christ, that he is [ἀπαύγασμα] and [χαρακτήρ], and that he made the expiation of our sins by himself? This is, by the Socinian method, to remove and utterly destroy the force of both words and things. III. Certainly we have no reason to doubt the expiation of all our offences through Christ; but what does it mean that Christ is said to have brought it from heaven? Where does Scripture say this? And what is its sense? Christ brought his doctrine from heaven, and the commandment of the Father; but not expiation. It is not said that he brought expiation, but that he made it, that he procured it, not from heaven. Christ accomplished it on earth, when he cried with a loud voice: "It is finished" [πεπλήρωται]. Where is it also said that we have seen the will of God expressed in Christ? Surely because he revealed it? We do have in Christ a most certain pledge of the divine goodness; but those things do not set out the force and nature of expiation, nor can expiation be said to have been fulfilled in him, though it was made through him and is what God promised us through him. It was not fulfilled in Christ, in that he was brought, as he soon explains, to everlasting blessedness and received power over all things. So the Adversary here mentions nothing of what pertains to true expiation, though he had professed that the writer had explained most divinely by what method Christ expiated our sins.

units.la: Hebr. 11. 17. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similari, ut misericors fieret (five effet) & fidelis pontifex in iis, qua apud Deum, εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ, ad expiandum peccata populi. Sic ipse Socinus vertit, ut omninò hic agatur de expiatione. ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας, est expiare peccata ἱλάσκεσθαι Θεόν, propitiare Deum. Duo ista significat vox ἱλάσκεσθαι: quia in expiatione, & per eam fit propitiatio: ut non alia expiatio intelligenda fit, quam quâ propitius redditur nobis Deus. Contrà ac Socinus rem accipit, invertitque. Imo prius ἱλάσκομαι placo, & propitium facio significat; inde per metonymiam causæ, expio. ἱλάω enim proprie est, sum propitius.
units.tr: Heb. 11. 17. Wherefore it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make propitiation [εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ] for the sins of the people. So Socinus himself renders it, as if the whole passage were about expiation. To propitiate sins [ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας] means to expiate sins, and to propitiate God [ἱλάσκεσθαι Θεόν] means to appease God. The verb ἱλάσκεσθαι signifies both of these things, because expiation takes place in and through propitiation, so that no other expiation is to be understood than the one by which God is made gracious to us. Socinus takes the matter the other way round and inverts it. Indeed the verb first means to appease and to make propitious, and from this, by metonymy of the cause, to expiate. For ἱλάω properly means to be propitious.

units.la: Excipit Socinus, part. ii. cap. xxi. ad locum illum, Christum, postquam passus est, expiare peccata. Quod certe de perenni vi & efficacitate expiationis, qua in cruce peracta fuerit, intelligi non potest. Quid enim attinuisset commemorare, eum tentatum fuisse, sicut & nos, & ob eam rem misericordem & fidelem esse in expiandis peccatis nostris? Refp. i. Negat Socinus, in cruce peractam à Christo nostri ex-piationem, duntaxat eam peragi, inquiens, postquam passus, & ingressus, ab adscensione, in cœlum fuit. rectum est, immo necessarium, ut non ante facta fuerit expiatio, quam is in coelum assumptus sit. Non factam in cruce expiationem, omnino falsum est: namque passim sanguini & morti adscribitur, hoc etiam in loco, ac capite, haud semel, nec uno modo. Unde debuit fratribus per omnia similari ὁμοιωθῆναι. quod non post adscensionem demum, sed ante eam, & toto vitae cursu, in omnibus, quae Christo contigerunt, perspicuum. Similiter in sui oblatione in cruce, & facta isthoc modo nostrum expiatione apud Deum, apparuit, ejus Sacerdotis sc. summi misericordia ac fidelitas. ἱλάσκεσθαι expiare, in terris intelligitur, atq; hic fieri solet, ubi & peccata populi sunt. Sequitur mox expresse, ἐν ᾧ γὰρ πέπονθεν αὐτὸς πειρασθείς, in quo enim ipse passus est tentatus, sive varias expertus tentationes, potest tentatis opem ferre.
units.tr: Socinus objects, in part II, chapter 21, to that place: Christ, after he had suffered, expiates sins. This certainly cannot be understood of the perpetual power and efficacy of the expiation which was accomplished on the cross. For what would it have served to mention that he was tempted, as we are, and that for this reason he is merciful and faithful in expiating our sins? Answer: Socinus denies that our expiation was accomplished by Christ on the cross, and says that it was carried out only after he had suffered and entered, by his ascension, into heaven. It is right, indeed necessary, that the expiation was not made before he was taken up into heaven. That the expiation was not made on the cross is quite false, for it is ascribed everywhere to his blood and death, in this very place and chapter, and more than once and in more than one way. Wherefore he ought to be made like his brethren in all things [ὁμοιωθῆναι]. It is clear that this likeness was not only after the ascension, but before it, and through the whole course of his life, in all the things that happened to Christ. Similarly, in his offering on the cross, and in the expiation of ours thus made before God, there appeared the mercy and faithfulness of his priesthood. To expiate [ἱλάσκεσθαι] is understood as taking place on earth, and it is here that it is usually done, where the sins of the people are. It follows at once, expressly: for in that he himself hath suffered, being tempted [ἐν ᾧ γὰρ πέπονθεν αὐτὸς πειρασθείς], in that he himself suffered, being tempted, that is, having experienced various temptations, he is able to help those who are tempted.

units.la: Socinus,ut vim vocis πεπονθεν aufugiat,vertit,ex quo ipsi contigit tentatum esse. contra vim, ac usum vocis: πεπονθα enim in praeterito dicitur, pro πεπονθα, tanquam ἀπὸ πάθω, cujus usitatum πάσχω. Sic ἀντιπεπονθότας, ἀντιπεπονθῶς, idem quod ἀντιπαθῶς adverse. Neque minus contra consensum plurimorum interpretum. Castellio, Quoniam enim passus est ipse periclitando. Versio Racoviensis, Denn darinnen er gelitten hat / da er versuchet worden. Erasmus vertit, quod contigit ipsi tentatum esse. magis ad structuram Latini sermonis, quam ut neget passionem notari. Ita, quantum ad verba, pro iisdem quandoque habentur; quid passus, quid contigit ut hoc vel illud faceret quis, aut fieret, Ut nec ista voce qui in tali sermone utuntur, passionem ideo exemtam cupiant. Certe in cruce, maxime tentari contigit Christum. Ut passio ejus non solum verbo πεπονθεν, sed & περιπειρασθείς continetur. Haec autem in terris omnia, non in coelis locum habent. Imo in coelis καταπαυσιν [?] τὴν ἐργῶν αὐτῆ [?], Hebr. iv. 10. expiationis ἔργον in terris perficiendum fuit; in coelos vero εἰς τὴν καταπαυσιν αὐτοῦ intravit. Atque ita expiavit Christus peccata, ἐν ᾧ (addita quippe particula γὰρ) πεπονθεν αὐτὸς πειρασθείς. Vers. 14. ἵνα διὰ τοῦ θανάτου, ut per mortem deleret eum qui potestatem habet mortis, id est, Diabolum. Fuit hoc etiam opus expiationis, quam Socinus exposuit per liberationem à morte, sed Christi morte peractae, & non demum postquam passus est, & in coelum introgressus. Vers. 9. Vidimus Jesum infra Angelos paulo humiliatum, per passionem mortis, gloria & honore coronatum: ut gratia Dei pro omnibus gustaret mortem. 10. Decuit enim eum, &c. ducem salutis ipsorum διὰ παθημάτων τελειῶσαι. Haec isto capite. Ad expiationem, & ejus formam spectat, mortem pro omnibus gustare, atque salutis ducem esse etiam in cruce & passionibus. Hebr. v. 8. 9. Quamvis filius esset, ex iis quae passus est didicit obedientiam. Et consummatus factus est autor salutis aeterna omnibus ei auscultantibus. 11. Non negamus interim, etiam in coelo Christum ea facere quae ad expiationem nostram pertinent, Hebr. vii. 25. sed in terris meritam & acquisitam: quam nobis suo ordine & gradu nunc applicat & confervat. Neque divellenda sunt, officia Christi in terris, tum in coelo quæ peragit, ad idem effectum expiationis conferendum: quum tum expiatio, tum perennis ejus vis atq; efficacia unà hic significentur. 111. Non dicitur in textu, Christum tentatum fuisse, sicut & nos, & ob eam rem misericordem ac fidelem esse in expiandis peccatis nostris, quasi expiatio non illis tentationibus passionibusque fuisset facta: sed dicitur, fidelem esse eum ad succurrendum nobis: hoc est βοηθῆσαι, illud ἱλάσκεσθαι: verf. 16. istud; illud 17. Alrerum fit apud Deum πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι; alterum apud nos, τῆς περιφορᾶς[?]. Imo opitulatio ista est, ex expiatione, propter & post eam. Quod ita explicatum dat Apostolus, Hebr. iv. 15. 16. Non enim habemus Pontificem qui non possit compati infirmitatibus nostris, tentatum in omnibus similiter κατ' ὁμοιότητα, fine peccato. Accedamus ergo cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ, ut accipiamus misericordiam, & gratiam inveniamus εἰς εὔκαιρον βοήθειαν. hoc est illud βοήθειαν, de quo capite fecundo egerat, & utrobique deducit à propria Christi experientiâ, & similitudine passionum aut tentationum ejus, cum nostris. Cap. v. 2: μετριοπαθῆσαι δυνάμενον[?] ἐπεὶ καὶ αὐτὸς περίκειται ἀσθένειαν. 8. Ἐμαθεν ἀφ' ὧν ἔπαθε. Non autem verba illa, cap. iv. 16. ut accipiamus misericordiam & gratiam, de ipsâ exponenda sunt expiatione, quod Socinus fecit: vides, inquit, quid sit peccata nostra expiari à Christo; nempe misericordiam & gratiam ab ipso, sive per ipsum, nobis dari, ut opportuno auxilio non destituamur. Ergo verò nego, hoc esse expiari peccata nostra à Christo: sed ejus esse consequens dico & effectum. Dicitur enim, quid nos accipiamus, non quid Christus faciat. Sic est quidem, dum nos gratiam ejus accipimus, facit ut eam habeamus; tamen aliud est, quod gratiam nobis præstat, vel quod nos eam adipiscimur, atque hoc an illud clare doceatur: imprimis verò, differunt in Christo, expiari peccata, & accipere gratiam ejus, opportunumque auxilium.
units.tr: Socinus, to escape the force of the word πέπονθεν, renders it because it happened to him to be tempted, against the force and usage of the word. For πέπονθα is said in the perfect tense in place of πέπονθα, as if from ἀπὸ πάθω, whose usual form is πάσχω. So ἀντιπεπονθότας and ἀντιπεπονθῶς mean the same as ἀντιπαθῶς, in opposition. Nor is this less contrary to the agreement of most interpreters. Castellio: For since he himself suffered, by putting himself in danger. The Racovian version: Denn darinnen er gelitten hat, da er versuchet worden, that is, for in that he suffered when he was tempted. Erasmus renders it that it happened to him to be tempted, more with regard to the construction of the Latin sentence than to deny that suffering is signified. Thus, as far as the words go, they are sometimes taken as the same: suffered and happened, as when one does or becomes something; and those who use these words in such a discourse do not therefore wish suffering to be removed from it. Certainly on the cross Christ, above all, was tempted. So his passion is contained not only in the word πέπονθεν, but also in περιπειρασθείς. All these things, however, have their place on earth, not in heaven. Indeed, in heaven there is a rest [καταπαυσιν] ... of his works [ἔργων αὐτῆ], Heb. 4. 10. The work of expiation had to be carried out on earth; but he entered into his rest [εἰς τὴν καταπαῦσιν αὐτοῦ] in heaven. And so Christ expiated sins, in that (the particle γὰρ being added) he himself suffered, being tempted [ἐν ᾧ γὰρ πέπονθεν αὐτὸς πειρασθείς]. Verse 14: that through death [ἵνα διὰ τοῦ θανάτου] he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil. This too was a work of expiation, which Socinus explained as liberation from death, but it was accomplished by the death of Christ, and not only after he had suffered and entered heaven. Verse 9: We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death crowned with glory and honour, that by the grace of God he should taste death for every man. Verse 10: For it became him, ... to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings [διὰ παθημάτων τελειῶσαι]. These things are in this chapter. Tasting death for all, and being the captain of salvation even on the cross and in sufferings, belongs to expiation and its manner. Heb. 5. 8, 9: Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him. Meanwhile we do not deny that Christ in heaven also does those things that pertain to our expiation (Heb. 7. 25), but the expiation that he merited and acquired on earth, he now applies to us in its order and degree, and preserves it. Nor are the offices of Christ on earth to be separated from those that he performs in heaven, since both serve the same effect of expiation, because both the expiation and its perpetual power and efficacy are signified here together. III. It is not said in the text that Christ was tempted as we are, and that for this reason he is merciful and faithful in expiating our sins, as if the expiation had not been made by those temptations and sufferings. It is said that he is faithful to help us. That is, to help is βοηθῆσαι, and the other is ἱλάσκεσθαι. Verse 16 gives the former, verse 17 the latter. The one is done before God, πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, to expiate [εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι]; the other is done among us. Indeed that help comes from the expiation, on account of it and after it. The Apostle gives this explanation: Heb. 4. 15, 16: For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need [εἰς εὔκαιρον βοήθειαν]. This is that help [βοήθειαν] of which he had spoken in the second chapter, and in both places he draws it from Christ's own experience and from the likeness of his sufferings or temptations to ours. Chapter 5, verse 2: able to have compassion [μετριοπαθῆσαι δυνάμενον], for that he himself also is compassed with infirmity. Verse 8: he learned from the things which he suffered [ἔμαθεν ἀφ' ὧν ἔπαθε]. But those words of chapter 4, verse 16, that we may obtain mercy and find grace, are not to be explained of expiation itself, as Socinus did: you see, he says, what it is for our sins to be expiated by Christ; namely, that mercy and grace are given to us by him, or through him, so that we are not left without timely help. Therefore I deny that this is to have our sins expiated by Christ; I say rather that it is its consequence and effect. For it is said what we receive, not what Christ does. And so it is indeed, that while we receive his grace, he makes us have it; yet it is one thing that he gives us grace, or that we obtain it, and it is another whether this or that is clearly taught. Above all, to have sins expiated in Christ and to receive his grace and timely help are different things.

units.la: Hebr. IX. 11. 12. Christus autem &c. per amplius & perfectius tabernaculum, non manufactum, id est, non hujus creationis, neque per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum sed per proprium sanguinem introivit semel in sancta, æterna redemtione inventa. Socinus, par. 11. cap. xiv. redemtionis verbum, ab hoc Scriptore pro expiatione usurpatur.
units.tr: Heb. 9. 11, 12: But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building; neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption. Socinus, part II, chapter 14: by this writer the word redemption is used for expiation.

units.la: Atqui expiationem invenit Christus per sanguinem proprium, non hircorum & vitulorum, quo expiatio olim cæremonialis peragebatur, τῶς τῶν ἁγίων[?] καθαρότητα[?]: ad purgandam verò conscientiam valet solus sanguis Christi, verf. 14. Quæ & de purgatione à peccatis ipsis, & de expiatione à peccatorum pœnâ, Socinus accipit, pag. 146. Omnino ergo ipsi sanguini expiatio nostri attribuenda. Unde & postea Apostolus, eodem capite, ut sanguinis aspersioni in Vet. T. omnium rerum & utensilium Tabernaculi adscribit expurgationem καθαρισμόν[?] cæremonialem, ita sanguini Christi expiationem spiritualem. Huc enim illa faciunt, & Tabernaculum & omnia vasa minis-terii aspersit ἐῤῥάντισε[?] similiter sanguine. Et omnia fere secundum legem sanguine purificantur, καθαρίζει[?]: & absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Nostra ergo ἄφεσις, expiatio, καθαρισμὸς, ῥαντισμὸς (cap. x. 22. ἐῤῥαντισμένοι τῆς καρδίας ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως πονηρῆς) ἐν τῷ αἵματι Ἰησοῦ[?], cap. x. 19, vel in αἱματεκχυσία Christi est. καθαρισμὸς enim in hac epistola expiationem connotat. Cap. i. 3 & ix. 13. 22 23. cap x. 2. Cap. x. 4. impossibile enim est sanguinem taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata. Ideo veniens in mundum &c. Socinus, part. 155. in his verbis de expiatione a peccatorum poena praecipue agitur. Sed ea sanguini Christi vere ac proprie, tanquam causae suae attribuitur, uti sanguini animalium derogatur. verf. 4. ἀφαιρεῖν ἁμαρτίας. ιι ἐλθεῖν[?]. 1 Joann. 1. 7. & sanguis Jesu Christi filii ejus καθαρίζει purgat, expiat nos ab omni peccato. quae verba ad expiationis peccatorum nostrorum cognitionem, quam per Christi mortem adepti sumus, pertinere, Socinus fatetur, part. ii. c. xiii. Dein verf. 9. fidelis est Justus, ut remittat nobis peccata, & purget nos καθαρίζῃ ἡμᾶς ab omni iniquitate. scilicet per sanguinem, cujus tacite etiam mentionem facit in illis verbis, fidelis est & justus, inquit Socinus. Non autem ideo, quia sanguis Christi ad Dei promissa firmanda potissimum adhibitus fuit: quod glossema vim sanguinis Christi hoc in negotio totum enervat, qui non ad confirmationem, sed praecipue ad acquisitionem remissionis & expiationis effusus fuit.
units.tr: But Christ has found expiation through his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves, by which the ceremonial expiation was formerly carried out, for the purifying of the flesh [τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα]. Only the blood of Christ avails to purge the conscience (verse 14). Socinus takes this both of the purging from sins themselves and of the expiation from the punishment of sins (p. 146). Therefore expiation of our sins must be wholly attributed to his blood itself. Hence the Apostle, in the same chapter, ascribes to the blood of Christ a spiritual expiation, just as he ascribes a ceremonial cleansing to the sprinkling of blood in the Old Testament, for all the things and utensils of the tabernacle. For these things bear on it: He sprinkled likewise with blood the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry [ἐῤῥάντισε]; and almost all things are by the law purged with blood [καθαρίζει]; and without shedding of blood is no remission. Our remission, then, expiation, cleansing and sprinkling (chapter 10, verse 22: having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience [ἐῤῥαντισμένοι τῆς καρδίας ἀπὸ συνειδήσεως πονηρῆς]), is in the blood of Jesus [ἐν τῷ αἵματι Ἰησοῦ], chapter 10, verse 19, or in the shedding of Christ's blood. For cleansing in this epistle signifies expiation: chapter 1, verse 3; chapter 9, verses 13, 22, 23; chapter 10, verse 2. Chapter 10, verse 4: For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. Wherefore when he cometh into the world, etc. Socinus, part II, p. 155, says that in these words expiation from the punishment of sins is chiefly treated. But this is attributed truly and properly to the blood of Christ as its cause, just as the blood of animals is denied it. Verse 4: to take away sins [ἀφαιρεῖν ἁμαρτίας]. 1 John 1. 7: And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us [καθαρίζει] from all sin. Socinus admits, part II, chapter 13, that these words pertain to the knowledge of the expiation of our sins, which we have obtained through the death of Christ. Then verse 9: He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us [καθαρίσῃ ἡμᾶς] from all unrighteousness. That is, through the blood, of which he also makes silent mention in those words, faithful and just, as Socinus says. But this is not because the blood of Christ was chiefly used to confirm the promises of God. That gloss wholly weakens the power of Christ's blood in this matter, since it was shed not chiefly for the confirmation, but for the acquisition of remission and expiation.

units.la: Socinus: Jam, cum & sanguinem Christi, & Deum emundare nostra peccata dicat, emundandi verbo satisfactionem aliquam non significari liquet. Neque enim Deus peccata nostra emundat, vel potius emundaturus est (nam de futura emundatione ibi expresse agitur) pro peccatis nostris satisfaciendo: sed, ut ibidem ipse Apostolus ait, ea nobis remittendo & condonando. Cujus rei cum nobis Jesu Christi sanguis non dubiam faciat fidem, merito illi peccata emundandi vis attribuitur. Resp 1. Et Deus, & Christi sanguis peccata emundant, nempe Deus per sanguinem Christi, qui in se satisfaciendi vim habet. Non enim proprio suo Filio pro nobis pepercit, sed in mortem pro nobis dedit, eamque satisfactoriam. Quae hic contradictio? vel quare non isto modo Christi sanguis expiat & mundat, quamvis Deus nos quoque expiare & mundare dicatur? nempe Deus, ut causa efficiens principalis; Christi sanguis, ut causa procatarctica meritoria. ii. Deus & emundat peccata nostra, & emundaturus est, atque etiam emundavit, prout aut merita expiatio attenditur in Christi sanguine, aut nobis applicata, & intimata per fidem. Quo sensu admittimus, quod Socinus observat, emundare sapius idem significare, quod mundum pronunciare seu declarare. iii. Non pugnant ista, Deum peccata nostra emundare condonando, & effuso sanguine Filii pro iisdem suae justitiae prius satisfieri. iv. Non ideo Christi sanguini vis attribuitur peccata expiandi, quod remissionis eorum certam nobis facit fidem: id enim & alia quoque praestant, quibus tamen illam
units.tr: Socinus: Now, since he says that both the blood of Christ and God cleanse our sins, it is clear that the word "cleanse" does not signify any satisfaction. For God does not cleanse our sins, or rather is going to cleanse them (for the future cleansing is expressly spoken of there), by making satisfaction for our sins, but, as the Apostle himself says in the same place, by remitting and pardoning them. Since the blood of Jesus Christ does not make this certain for us, the power of cleansing sins is rightly attributed to it. Reply 1. God and the blood of Christ both cleanse sins: God through the blood of Christ, which has in itself the power of satisfaction. For he did not spare his own Son for us, but gave him up to death for us, and that a satisfactory death. What contradiction is there here? Or why may the blood of Christ not be said to expiate and cleanse in the same way that God is said to expiate and cleanse us? God is the principal efficient cause; the blood of Christ is the meritorious procatarctic cause. ii. God both cleanses our sins and will cleanse them, and indeed has cleansed them, insofar as the expiation is regarded as merited in the blood of Christ and is applied and made known to us through faith. In this sense we admit what Socinus observes, that to cleanse often means the same as to pronounce or declare clean. iii. These things do not clash: that God cleanses our sins by pardoning them, and that by the shed blood of his Son satisfaction was first made for them. iv. The blood of Christ is not credited with the power of expiating sins because it makes certain for us the forgiveness of them; for other things also do that, yet it would be wrong to ascribe that power to them. Rather, he has won for us remission and expiation by his own power and merit, and therefore his whole power and efficacy rests in his blood.

units.la: Cap. i. 3 & ix. 13.22 23. cap x. 2. Cap. x. 4. impossibile enim est sanguinem taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata. Ideo veniens in mundum &c. Socinus, part. 155. in his verbis de expiatione a peccatorum poena praecipue agitur. illam vim adscribere nefas sit: sed quod remissionem atque expiationem sua vi, & merito nobis acquisivit. Hinc in sanguine tota ejus vis reponitur & efficacia.
units.tr: Heb. i. 3 and ix. 13, 22, 23; x. 2; x. 4: For it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins. Therefore, coming into the world, etc. Socinus, part 155: In these words the expiation of sin from the punishment of sin is chiefly treated. It would be wrong to ascribe that power to them; rather, he has won for us remission and expiation by his own power and merit. Hence his whole power and efficacy lie in his blood.

units.la: 1 Joann. iv. 1c.[?] in hoc est charitas, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse dilexit nos, misit filium suum propitiationem (sive expiationem, sic Socinus) pro peccatis nostris, ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Quae verba iterum ut eludat, recurrit ad praecedentia, ubi dicitur, quod filium suum unigenitum misit Deus in mundum, ut vivamus per eum. Id est, inquit, expiantur igitur peccata nostra a Christo, non divina alicui justitia satisfaciendo: sed nobis divina voluntate vitam conferendo, & ab aeterna morte nos vindicando. Quae in hac argumentatione sequela? vel quae contradictio inter id, quod Christus divina nobis voluntate vitam confert, & quod divinae etiam justitiae satisfecit? Utrumque verum est, nec alterum alteri ulla ratione adversum. Imo ut per Christum viveremus, propitiatio factus fuit, data vera plenaque pro peccatis nostris primum expiatione. Unde utrumque hoc in loco de Christo docetur. Idem est in hac epistola, cap. 11.2. & ipse est ἱλασμὸς περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Schlichtingius, pro Socino, contra Meisnerum, de Justificatione, pag. 126.
units.tr: 1 Joann. iv. 10: In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation (or expiation, as Socinus puts it) for our sins [ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν]. To escape these words, he turns back to what precedes, where it is said that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. That is, he says, our sins are therefore expiated by Christ, not by making satisfaction to some divine justice, but by conferring life on us by the divine will and rescuing us from eternal death. What is the logical consequence in this argument? Or what contradiction is there between Christ conferring life on us by the divine will, and his having also satisfied divine justice? Both are true, and neither is in any way opposed to the other. Indeed, in order that we might live through Christ, he was made a propitiation, having first been given as the true and full expiation for our sins. So both things are taught about Christ in this passage. It is the same in this epistle, ch. 2.2: and he himself is the propitiation [ἱλασμὸς περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν]. Schlichting, for Socinus, against Meisner, On Justification, p. 126.

units.la: Dicimus, ἱλασμὸν nihil aliud hic significare, quam καθαρισμὸν seu expiationem. Graci enim iique sacri scriptores verbo ἱλάσκεσθαι utuntur ad exprimendam Hebraam vocem kipper, quae expiationem peccatorum significat. Hoc[?] obstat, quod non simpliciter hic dicatur ἱλασμὸς ἁμαρτιῶν, sed interjecta particula περὶ. Haec enim loquendi ratio manavit ex Hebraica consuetudine, qua verba tegendi significationem habentia, quale est kipper, cujus radix est caphar, cum praepositione Hal vel Bead construuntur, quibus in Graca lingua respondet περὶ, vel alia similes particulae. Hinc eodem sensu nunc occurrit phrasis ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας, nunc, idque aliquanto frequentius, ἱλάσκεσθαι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν. Nusquam autem haec vox a sacris scriptoribus de Deo usurpatur passive, quasi ille placatus fuisse dicatur, & ex irato propitius factus: sed semper vel active, ut cum ipse dicitur ἱλάσκεσθαι, expiare peccata; vel absolute & intransitive,
units.tr: We say that ἱλασμὸν here means nothing other than καθαρισμὸν, or expiation. For the Greeks, and those holy writers, use the verb ἱλάσκεσθαι [to propitiate] to express the Hebrew word kipper, which signifies the expiation of sins. There is an objection here: the phrase is not simply ἱλασμὸς ἁμαρτιῶν but has the particle περὶ inserted. This mode of speech comes from Hebrew usage, in which verbs having the sense of covering, such as kipper, whose root is caphar, are construed with the prepositions Hal or Bead, to which in Greek περὶ or other similar particles correspond. Hence in the same sense the phrase ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας occurs at one time, and at another, and rather more frequently, ἱλάσκεσθαι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν. But nowhere do the holy writers use this word of God in the passive, as if he were said to have been placated and to have become propitious from being angry; but always either actively, as when he himself is said ἱλάσκεσθαι, to expiate sins, or absolutely and intransitively,

units.la: Resp. 1. ἱλασμὸν nihil aliud significare, quam καθαρισμὸν, negamus. Plus enim dicit, sive verborum na-turam respicias, aut etymologiam, aut usum. Semper ἱλασμὸς significat propitiationem, uti ἱλάσκεσθαι, a quo venit, placare, & propitiare: καθαρισμὸς vero purgationem, sive rerum, sive personarum aut hominum. Adeo differunt voces in hoc argumento per-sonis, & revera, quod dici solet, toto caelo. Prior etenim Deum respicit aut tangit, posterior homines. Non Deus καθαρίζει[?], sed homo; Deus, autem redditur ἱλεὼς[?]: homo non propitiatur Deo, verum Deus homini. ἱλάσκεσθαι Θεὸν dicunt Graeci, non καθαρίζεσθαι. Atque hinc apparet immanis verborum differentia. Iterum Deus quidem dicitur homines καθα-ρίζειν[?], non autem ἱλάσκεσθαι. Luc. XVIII. ut deponentia multa apud Latinos. unde pro eo nunc ἵλεως εἶναι, nunc ἀφιέναι reponitur. Unde etiam ipse remittendi actus, utpote ex clementia profectus, nulla ejus habita ratione, quòd is, qui remittit, ab aliquo placatus, aut ex irato propitius factus fuerit, ἱλασμὸς dicitur, ut Psal. 130. 4. Sirac. 5. 5. 18.20. Christus ergo ἱλασμὸς περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ideo dicitur, quòd peccata nostra expiet, id est, eorum reatum ac poenas tollat, & sic efficiat, ut Deum propitium ac faventem semper experiamur. Ad peccatorum autem expiationem non opus est poenarum solutione: imò ideo peccata expiantur, ne poenas pro iis pendere sit necesse. Nec tantum poenarum solutione opus non est, sed nec placatione quidem divini numinis, ut scilicet ex irato propitius fiat; cùm saepè ideo tantùm peccata expientur, ut numen propitium esse porrò pergat; nec ut iras deponat, sed ne concipiat. quod in omnibus illis expiationibus accidere necesse est, quas ipse Deus praescripsit ac constituit, qualis vel inprimis est expiatio, quae fit per Christum. Apertissimè istud docet posterior locus apud Johan. cap. 4. in quo eadem extant verba, ubi Deus tùm, cùm filium suum in mundum misit ἱλασμὸν περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν, dicitur nos dilexisse; idque tanquam certissimum admirandae ejus erga nos charitatis argumentum adducitur. Num ergo is, qui tantopere dilexit, ut placaretur iis, quos dilexit, opus habuit? Uno igitur tempore eosdem & impensè amavit, & capitali odio prosecutus est? Quocirca Christus dicitur ἱλασμὸς, quatenus in coelis manens, noster est advocatus apud Patrem, ut istic additur. quo etiam sensu Hebr. 7. 25. dicitur pro nobis intercedere, & 9. 24. dicitur vultui Dei pro nobis apparere, & cap. 2. 17. peccata nostra ἱλάσκεσθαι, hoc est, expiare. Lo-
units.tr: Reply 1. We deny that ἱλασμὸν signifies nothing other than καθαρισμὸν. For it says more, whether you look to the nature of the words, or to their etymology, or to their use. ἱλασμὸς always means propitiation, just as ἱλάσκεσθαι, from which it comes, means to placate and propitiate; but καθαρισμὸς means purgation, whether of things or of persons or of human beings. The words differ so greatly in regard to persons, and indeed, as the saying goes, by the whole heaven. The former regards or touches God, the latter human beings. It is not God who is καθαρίζει [cleansed], but man; God is rendered ἱλεὼς [propitious]: man does not propitiate God, but God man. The Greeks say ἱλάσκεσθαι Θεόν [to propitiate God], not καθαρίζεσθαι. And from this the enormous difference of the words is clear. Again, God is indeed said to cleanse men καθαρίζειν, but not ἱλάσκεσθαι. Luke 18: like the many deponent verbs among the Latins. Hence for this one ἵλεως εἶναι [to be propitious] or ἀφιέναι [to forgive] is sometimes put in its place. Hence also the very act of remitting, since it proceeds from clemency, with no regard to whether he who remits has been placated by someone or has become propitious from being angry, is called ἱλασμὸς, as in Ps. 130.4; Sirach 5.5, 18, 20. Christ therefore is called ἱλασμὸς περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν because he expiates our sins, that is, removes their guilt and punishments, and so brings it about that we always experience God as propitious and favourable. But for the expiation of sins there is no need of payment of punishments; indeed sins are expiated for this very reason, so that it is not necessary to pay penalties for them. Nor is there need only of payment of punishments, but not even of the placation of the divine majesty, namely that it should become propitious from being angry; since often sins are expiated only so that the divine power should go on being propitious, not that it should lay aside wrath, but that it should not conceive it. This must happen in all those expiations which God himself prescribed and established, of which the chief is the expiation which is made through Christ. The later passage in John 4 teaches this most clearly, where the same words occur, in which God is said to have loved us when he sent his Son into the world as ἱλασμὸν περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν; and this is adduced as the most certain proof of his wondrous love towards us. Does then he who loved so greatly have need of placating those whom he loved? Did he at one time both love them intensely and pursue them with deadly hatred? Wherefore Christ is called ἱλασμὸς, insofar as, remaining in heaven, he is our advocate with the Father, as is added there. In this sense too Heb. 7.25 says that he intercedes for us, and 9.24 that he appears before the face of God for us, and ch. 2.17 that he ἱλάσκεσθαι [propitiates] our sins, that is, expiates them.

units.la: xviii. 13. ὁ θεὸς ἱλάσθητί μοι ἁμαρτωλῷ. 11. Videamus, ut probet, ἱλασμὸν nihil aliud hic significare, quam καθαρισμὸν. Graeci enim, inquit, iique sacri scriptores verbo ἱλάσκεσθαι utuntur ad exprimendam Hebraam vocem kipper, quae expiationem peccatorum significat. Sed hoc non quaeritur, adeoque non facit elenchum. Recte Graeci Hebraeum כפר vertunt ἱλάσκεσθαι: sed hoc non dicit aut probat, idem esse ἱλασμὸν, & καθαρισμὸν. ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι. Apud Hebraeos כפר quemadmodum apud Graecos ἱλάσκεσθαι significat placare, & propitiare. Sic illa quidem idem valent, non autem propterea ἱλάσκεσθαι, & καθαρίζειν. Hoc quidem ad illud sequitur etiam, sive Hebraice, sive Graece loquaris, & Deus propitiatus purificat à peccato, non tamen illa idem sunt, vel ἱλασμὸς nihil aliud significat, quam καθαρισμός. Imo hinc nos puros à peccatis praestat, & à poenâ immunes, quia primum placatus & propitius est. In Levitico ἐξιλάσ[?]εται ὑμῶν, καθαρίσει ὑμᾶς. Atq; ita Christus per illa seipso factam expiationem dicitur fecisse δι' ἑαυτοῦ [?] καθαρισμὸν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Hebr. 1. 3. Nam peccatis expiatis, quod sanguine fit, omnia redduntur munda. Hebr. 11. 22. 23. Joan. 1. 7. Tit. 11. 14. Non negamus igitur, per sanguinem Christi nos purgari; sed quod propterea idem sit purgari, & propitiari. purgatur reus; sed antea propiquitur enim illic de expiatione, quam nunc Christus in coelis degens, tanquam summus Pontifex noster, peragit, (quemadmodum textum inspicienti cuivis patet) Christus autem in coelis apud Patrem degens, non aliter peccata nostra expiat, quam quatenus suprema sua potestate, sibi a Patre concessa, nostram salutem procurat, uniceque operam dat, ne peccatorum nostrorum poenas demut [?]. Unde etiam in infirmitatibus nostris, ne propter eas succumbamus, & in aeternum pereamus, auxilium nobis opportunum ferre solet. propitiatur ipsi judex. Atque haec sunt diversa. iii. Quare ubi de sacrificiis expiatoriis & propitiatoriis agitur, in-numeris in locis occurrit ἐξιλάσκε-σθαι, כפר, περὶ αὐτῶν, & περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, praesertim in Levitico, vide modo ejus cap. iv. & v. sensu expiandi, placandi, & propitandi. Nam ita haec se habent ad invicem ut sive vere, sive ceremonialiter, expietur sa-crificio reatus, quo tum placatur, & placatus propitium se gerit, erga reum, judex. Quae significantur primo sensu vocis כפר, sive Graecae ἱλάσκεσθαι, & ἐξιλάσκεσθαι. iv. Nec propriam vocis καθαρισμὸς significationem ponit Schlichtingius, dicendo expiationem. Nam utcunque Christus utrumque suis praestet, expiationem & purgationem, non tamen idem sunt vel vocum significatu, vel re. Nam ἱλασμὸν expiationem praestat Deo περὶ ἡμῶν, & περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν; purgationem autem nobis, & in nobis, ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας, non περὶ ἁμαρτίας. 1 Joan. 1. 7. 9. καὶ καθαρίση ἡμᾶς, ἀπὸ πάσης ἀδι-κίας. at cap. ii. 2. est, ἱλασμὸς περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. v. Vere dicit, modum illud praeponendi περὶ, manare ab usu Hebraeorum, construentium על cum כפר: atqui non alium admittit tum sensum vox כפר quam expiandi. & expiabit pro iis, וכפר עליהם, ἐξιλάσεται περὶ αὐτῶν, Levit. iv. 20. quod plurimis legitur in locis. Cap. xvi. 10. de hirco emissario, sistetur coram Jehova, ad expiandum super ipso לכפר עליו. ἐξιλάσασθαι ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ. Quae sensum renuunt tegendi. Proptereaque additur, quod expiatio fiat coram Jehova, לכפר עליהם לפני יהוה, καὶ ἐξιλάσονται περὶ αὐτῶν ἐναντίον κυρίου. Ita quoque Num. xxxi. 50. jam Kipper, in Piel, significat expiare, placare, propitium reddere, a radice Kaphar, quod significat bituminare: non vero habent tegendi significationem, nisi consequenter. Et Scriptura quando docet tecta esse peccata nostra, dicit כסוי: uti Psalm. xxxii. 1. ὧν ἐπεκα-λύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι. Certe qui expiat peccata, quidem etiam tegit; non tamen voces expiandi & tegendi idem significant, quavis lingua. Quod & derivata confirmant, כפר pretium redemtionis aut expiationis, ἱλαστήριον. dies הכפורים, כפרת, ἱλαστήριον. vi. Falsum vero, quod scribit, nusquam vocem istam a sacris scriptoribus de Deo usurpari passive: quia totidem idlocis fit, ac docetur, sacrificiis apud Deum peccata expiari, & sic tandem eum placati etiam populo. Quod quamvis caeremonialiter tantum per sacrifi-cia contingebat, non propria earum vi, id quod hoc loco non quaeritur, vo-cis saltem כפר signification explicat, veritatem autem rei obtinuisse in Christo. Hebr. ix. 13. 14. Neque alia ratio vel usus expiatoriorum sacrifi-ciorum fuit. Ac propterea non tantum à Deo, active; vel intransitive, ex-piari; sed & passive dicuntur, coram Deo, vel apud Deum ἐναντί Κυρίου [?], uti supra vidimus, expiare. Et proprius vocis usus idem comprobat. Genes. xxxii. 20. quia ecce placabo faciem ejus, אֲכַפְּרָה פָּנָיו [?]. Proverb. xvi. 15. ira regis nuncius mortis, at vir sapiens placabit eam, יְכַפְּרֶנָּה. ἐξιλάσεται αὐτήν. Significat ergo כפר, placare, & ex irato facere propitium. Psalm. cxxx. 4. in Graeco est, ὅτι παρὰ σοὶ ἱλασμός ἐστιν. Hebraice, סליחה. Primò non probat, ἱλασμὸν hic dici, nulla ejus habita ratione, quod is, qui remittit, ab aliquo placatus, aut ex irato propitius factus fuerit: nam uti punire est irae, & irati Dei; ita remittere ac bene facere est placati, cujus ira mutata sit vel aversa, uti alias Scriptura loquitur. Nam ira ejus alias manet super omnem peccatorem inobedientem, impaenitentem, infidelem; gratia vero erga fideles est & pios. Tum hic simpliciter dicitur, quod apud Deum est ἱλασμός, id quod nemo negat, sed modus ejus non exprimitur, qui alibi declaratur, quando vel περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν dicitur ἱλάσκεσθαι, vel esse ἱλασμός. Quod tum plus dicit, & modum etiam sive medium quo, remissionis illius: praesertim ubi additur redemtionis vel placationis & remissionis pretium, sanguis, ἐν τῷ αἵματι. Uti de Christo Rom. iii. 25. quod eum proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον כפרת ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι, εἰς τὴν πάρεσιν propter remissionem peccatorum, or-tam vid. ex illo sanguis propitiatorio. Adversariorum autem perpetua me-thodus est, enervare vim primò verborum sacrorum, inde rerum: contra veram & genuinam interpretationis & fidei sacrae rationem. Est ergo Christus ἱλασμός non tantum active, quod peccata tollat & remittat, sed quoque meritorie, per lutrum sanguinis sui, & περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν. Quomodo non tan-tum remissio denotatur, sed & placatio ac propitiatio, quando Deus dicitur ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, Psalm. lxxvii. 42. & lxxviii. 9. & non modò τὰς ἁμαρτίας. Accedit, quod Christus ista agat tamquam Pontifex apud Deum, πρὸς ἐχιρὸς τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, εἰς τὸ ἐξιλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ, Hebr. ii. 14. quod aliud est, quam quod inde sequitur apud homines & po-pulum, remittere illis peccata. Quemadmodum Levit. xviii. 22. & ego dedi eum vobis super altare, vid. sanguinem, לכפר על נפשתיכם ad expiandum super animas vestras: quia sanguis ipse in anima expiabit יכפר ἐξιλάσκεσθαι περὶ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν τὸ γὰρ αἷμα αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ἐξιλάσκεται. Quod Arabs ita περιφέρει[?] : idcirco constitui illum vobis super altare, ut venia petatur per ipsum pro animabus vestris: nam sanguis hoc pacto expiat animam. alias dicitur λύτρα τῆς ψυχῆς, כֹּפֶר Exod. xxx. 12. & Num. xxxv. 31. כֹּפֶר לַנֶּפֶשׁ, λύτρα περὶ ψυχῆς. In quibus περὶ non notat actionem ad hoc, vel hunc, cui præponitur, sed ab aut pro eo, ad alium, quidem ut expiatio etiam applicetur, sed primò impetretur, & hoc illæ voces & loquitiones volunt, expiare delictum apud judicem, & hinc dare remissionem & veniam iis, pro quibus tali pretio, sacrificio, sanguine expiatum, & propitiatus Deus fuit. Levit. iv. 20. & expiabit pro iis sacerdos, & remittetur iis. Expiatio remissionem ante-cedit, & eam parit. verf. 26. & expiabit eum sacerdos a peccato ejus, & remittetur ei.
units.tr: xviii. 13. God, be merciful to me a sinner [ὁ θεὸς ἱλάσθητί μοι ἁμαρτωλῷ]. 11. Let us see how he proves that ἱλασμός here means nothing other than καθαρισμός [cleansing]. For, he says, the Greeks, and those holy writers, use the verb ἱλάσκεσθαι to express the Hebrew word kipper, which signifies the expiation of sins. But this is not the question, and so it makes no refutation. The Greeks rightly render the Hebrew כפר by ἱλάσκεσθαι; but this does not say or prove that ἱλασμός and καθαρισμός are the same, which was to be shown. Among the Hebrews כפר, as among the Greeks ἱλάσκεσθαι, means to placate and propitiate. So these words do have the same force, but it does not follow that ἱλάσκεσθαι and καθαρίζειν are the same. It does follow from this, whether you speak in Hebrew or in Greek, that God, being propitiated, cleanses from sin; yet these things are not the same, nor does ἱλασμός signify nothing other than καθαρισμός. Indeed, he thereby makes us clean from sins and free from punishment, because he is first placated and propitious. In Leviticus: "he shall make atonement for you, and cleanse you" [ἐξιλάσεται ὑμῶν, καθαρίσει ὑμᾶς]. And so Christ is said to have made, through the expiation he made by himself, "a purification of our sins" [δι' ἑαυτοῦ καθαρισμὸν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν], Heb. 1. 3. For when sins are expiated, which is done by blood, all things are rendered clean, Heb. 11. 22. 23. John 1. 7. Tit. 11. 14. We do not deny, therefore, that we are cleansed through the blood of Christ; but it does not follow that being cleansed and being propitiated are the same. The accused is cleansed; but first the judge is propitiated. For there it speaks of the expiation which Christ now accomplishes, dwelling in heaven as our high priest (as anyone who looks at the text can see). But Christ, dwelling in heaven with the Father, expiates our sins only insofar as, by his supreme power granted to him by the Father, he procures our salvation and devotes his sole care to ensuring that the penalties of our sins do not at last fall upon us. Hence also, in our infirmities, he is wont to bring us timely help, lest we succumb to them and perish forever. The judge himself is propitiated. And these are different things. iii. Wherefore, where expiatory and propitiatory sacrifices are treated, the words ἐξιλάσκεσθαι, כפר, περὶ αὐτῶν, and περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας occur in countless places, especially in Leviticus; see just its chapters 4 and 5, in the sense of expiating, placating and propitiating. For these things stand in such relation to one another that whether guilt is expiated by sacrifice truly or ceremonially, the judge is thereby placated, and being placated he behaves graciously toward the guilty. These are the meanings signified in the primary sense of the Hebrew כפר, or the Greek ἱλάσκεσθαι and ἐξιλάσκεσθαι. iv. Nor does Schlichting give the proper meaning of the word καθαρισμός when he calls it expiation. For although Christ bestows both on his people, expiation and purgation, these are not the same, either in the meaning of the words or in the thing itself. For ἱλασμός is the expiation he makes for us to God [περὶ ἡμῶν, περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν]; but purgation is for us and in us, from sin [ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας], not concerning sin [οὐ περὶ ἁμαρτίας], 1 John 1. 7. 9. "and he will cleanse us from all unrighteousness" [καὶ καθαρίση ἡμᾶς, ἀπὸ πάσης ἀδικίας]. But in ch. ii. 2 it is "ἱλασμός concerning the sins" [ἱλασμὸς περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν]. v. He truly says that this manner of prefixing περί arises from the usage of the Hebrews, who construe על with כפר; but the word כפר admits no sense other than to expiate. "And he shall make atonement for them" [וכפר עליהם, ἐξιλάσεται περὶ αὐτῶν], Lev. iv. 20, which is read in very many places. Lev. xvi. 10, of the scapegoat: it shall be set before the LORD, "to make atonement upon him" [לכפר עליו, ἐξιλάσασθαι ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ]. These expressions reject the sense of covering. Therefore it is also added that the expiation is made before the LORD [לכפר עליהם לפני יהוה, καὶ ἐξιλάσονται περὶ αὐτῶν ἐναντίον κυρίου]. So also Num. xxxi. 50. Now Kipper, in the Piel, signifies to expiate, to placate, to render propitious, from the root Kaphar, which means to smear with bitumen; they have the meaning of covering only as a consequence. And when Scripture teaches that our sins are covered, it says כסוי, as in Ps. xxxii. 1: "whose sins are covered" [ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι]. Certainly, one who expiates sins also covers them; yet the words "to expiate" and "to cover" do not mean the same thing in any language. The derived forms confirm this: כפר is the price of redemption or expiation, ἱλαστήριον; the day of Yom Kippur (הכפורים), כפרת, ἱλαστήριον. vi. But what he writes is false, that this word is nowhere used passively of God by the sacred writers. For in as many places it is done, and taught, that sins are expiated before God by sacrifices, and so at last he is also placated toward the people. Although this happened only ceremonially through sacrifices, and not by their own power (which is not the question here), it at least explains the meaning of the word כפר, and shows that the reality of the thing was attained in Christ, Heb. ix. 13. 14. Nor was there any other reason or use for expiatory sacrifices. And therefore they are said to expiate not only actively or intransitively by God, but also passively before God or with God, as we saw above. And the proper usage of the word confirms the same. Gen. xxxii. 20: for behold, I will appease his face, [אֲכַפְּרָה פָּנָיו]. Prov. xvi. 15: the king's wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will appease it, [יְכַפְּרֶנָּה], [ἐξιλάσεται αὐτήν]. So כפר signifies to placate, and to make propitious one who was angry. Ps. cxxx. 4, in the Greek is "for with you there is ἱλασμός" [ὅτι παρὰ σοὶ ἱλασμός ἐστιν]; in Hebrew, forgiveness [סליחה]. First, it does not prove that ἱλασμός is meant here, without any regard to the fact that the one who forgives has been placated, or made propitious from being angry; for just as to punish belongs to anger and to an angry God, so to forgive and to do good belongs to one who has been placated, whose anger has been changed or turned away, as Scripture speaks elsewhere. For his anger otherwise remains upon every disobedient, unrepentant, unbelieving sinner, but his grace is toward the faithful and the pious. Then, here it is simply said that ἱλασμός is with God, which no one denies; but its mode is not expressed, which is declared elsewhere, where it is said either that one ἱλάσκεσθαι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν, or that there is ἱλασμός. This says more, and also indicates the mode or means by which that remission comes: especially where the price of redemption or placation and remission is added, blood, ἐν τῷ αἵματι. As with Christ in Rom. iii. 25, where God set him forth as ἱλαστήριον [כפרת], "through his blood" [ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι], "for the remission" [εἰς τὴν πάρεσιν] "of sins," that is, as you may see, the mercy seat arising from that blood. But the perpetual method of our opponents is first to weaken the force of the sacred words, and then of the things, which is contrary to the true and genuine rule of interpretation and of sacred faith. Christ is therefore ἱλασμός not only actively, in that he takes away and remits sins, but also meritoriously, through the price of his blood, and "concerning sins" [περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν]. In this way what is signified is not only remission, but also placation and propitiation, when God is said ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας [to propitiate the sins], Ps. lxxvii. 42 and lxxviii. 9, and not merely τὰς ἁμαρτίας. To this is added that Christ does these things as a high priest before God, "in the things pertaining to God, to make expiation for the sins of the people" [πρὸς ἐχιρὸς τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, εἰς τὸ ἐξιλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ], Heb. ii. 14. This is nothing other than what follows from it among men and the people: the remission of their sins to them. As in Lev. xvii. 11 (printed here as xviii. 22): and I have given it to you upon the altar, namely the blood, to make atonement for your souls: for the blood itself will make atonement for the soul, [לכפר על נפשתיכם], [יכפר], [ἐξιλάσκεσθαι περὶ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν· τὸ γὰρ αἷμα αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ ἐξιλάσκεται]. The Arabic version renders this thus: therefore I have appointed it for you upon the altar, that pardon may be sought through it for your souls: for in this way blood makes atonement for the soul. Elsewhere it is called "the ransom of the soul" [λύτρα τῆς ψυχῆς], כֹּפֶר, Exod. xxx. 12, and Num. xxxv. 31: כֹּפֶר לַנֶּפֶשׁ, ransom for a soul, [λύτρα περὶ ψυχῆς]. In these phrases περὶ does not denote an action directed toward this or that person before whom it stands, but on behalf of or in place of that person, toward another; so that the expiation is indeed also applied, but first obtained. These words and phrases mean this: to expiate an offence before the judge, and thence to grant remission and pardon to those for whom God was expiated and propitiated by such a price, sacrifice, or blood. Lev. iv. 20: and the priest shall make atonement for them, and it shall be forgiven them. Expiation goes before remission and brings it forth. Ver. 26: and the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.

units.la: Sic & cap. v. 10. 18. Porro dictantem audimus Schlichtingium multa, parum verò probantem. Quorum hoc primum est, quod ad peccatorum expiatio-nem non opus est pœnarum solutione. Quorsum enim alias Deus olim insti-tuit ritus sacrificiorum, ubi peccatorum pœnæ conjiciebantur in capita animalium, quæ luebant pro iis & solvebant, non quidem verè ad purgationem conscientiarum, sed cæremonialiter, & docebant interim ad expiationem pœnarum solutione opus esse, & Christum suo sanguine id revera præstiturum, quod sanguis taurorum & hircorum deumbrabat. Hebr. ix. 13. 14. Imo, inquit, ideo peccata expiantur, ne pœnas pro iis pendere sit necesse, vid. iis pro quibus fit expiatio, sed quidem illis qui suo sanguine expiant. Sec nec placatione quidem divini numinis opus est, ut scilicet ex irato propitius fiat. Proprie, concedo: nam in Deo nec ira verè, nec mutatio ejus, vel iræ depositio, aut affectus propitius locum habent: sed quod respectu effectus, & sensus nostri alioqui sequuturum fuisset, hoc per placationem & expiationem sublatum est & amovetur.
units.tr: Likewise at chapter 5, verses 10 and 18. Furthermore, we hear Schlichting dictating many things but proving little. The first of these is that the expiation of sins does not need the payment of penalties. For why else did God in former times institute the rites of sacrifice, in which the penalties of sins were laid upon the heads of animals, which bore them and paid them, not truly for the purification of consciences but ceremonially, and which meanwhile taught that expiation requires the payment of penalties, and that Christ would really accomplish with his own blood what the blood of bulls and goats foreshadowed? Hebr. 9. 13. 14. "Indeed," he says, "sins are expiated for this reason, that it should not be necessary to pay penalties for them," namely for those for whom the expiation is made, but indeed for those who expiate with their own blood. "Nor is there any need even of appeasing the divine majesty, namely that from angry it may become propitious." Properly speaking, I concede this: for in God there is neither anger in the true sense, nor change, nor laying aside of wrath, nor a propitious affect. But what would otherwise have followed with respect to the effect and to our perception has been removed and taken away by appeasement and expiation.

units.la: Et sic valde bene utrumque conciliari potest, quod & ex sum-mâ dilectione Deus nobis Filium dedit, & quod is tulerit ea, quibus ira Dei adversus hominum peccata placata est, ne vid. pro eorum culpa & demerito perirent, quibus absque eo pereundum omnino fuisset. Nulli hic in Deo af-sectus concipiendi, nedum contrarii, at quidem effectus diversi, & in iis alii sensus vel amoris quasi erga nos, vel iræ, pro immutabili & indivisibili ubique divina voluntate.
units.tr: And so both can be reconciled very well: that God gave us his Son out of supreme love, and that he bore those things by which the wrath of God against the sins of men was appeased, lest they perish for their guilt and demerit, who without that would have had to perish altogether. Here no affects are to be conceived in God, much less contrary ones; there are indeed different effects, and in them different feelings, or love as it were toward us, or anger, while the divine will remains unchanging and indivisible everywhere.

units.la: Jam tandem definit, quâ ratione Christus sit noster ἱλασμός, vid. in cælis pro nobis intercedens apud Patrem, qui non aliter peccata nostra expiat, quam quatenus suprema sua potestate, à Patre concessa, nostram salutem procurat, uniceque operam dat, ne peccatorum nostrorum pœnas demus. Itane nihil aliud significat Christi expiatio? neque aliter expiat, quam intercedendo, & quæ efficaciam intercessionis istius consequuntur? Primo proba, apud ullum autorem, quavis lingua, expiare nil aliter significare, quam intercedere, & illud quod hic additur. Vel fateatur, in hoc argumento, ubi vocis illius, & similium frequens usus, præter vocis naturam significationem ei obtrudi fictam & novam, quæ vim ejus altera parte minuat & tollat. Nam ut quidem qui peccata expiat pro peccatoribus etiam intercedat, non tamen idem sunt, intercedere & expiare, sed ejusdem operis & τελειώμα[?] distinctæ partes, ubi intercessio non magis antecedaneam expiationem excludit, quam hæc illam. Deinde in sacerdote, & sacrificio expiato-rio, unde illa desumta in hoc argumento, nam & Christus isthæc peragit pro numere sacerdotali, differunt expiare, & intercedere, ut antecedens & consequens, oratio & fundamentum ejus quo intitur, oblatio & fructus qui eam comitatur aut consequitur. Atque ita in Christo, expiatio præmittitur intercessioni, quam peragit in cælis, & sanguini ejusque effusioni attribuitur, quando se in mortem, vel in sacrificium mortis dedit in cruce. Quæ mors in Scripturis consideratur tamquam lutrum expiationis, cujus merito eam perfecit, & quo nititur cælestis pro expiatis suis intercessio, nostram salutem procurans, uniceque operam dans, ne peccatorum nostrorum pœnas demus.
units.tr: At last he defines in what way Christ is our propitiation [ἱλασμός], namely interceding for us in heaven before the Father, who "does not expiate our sins otherwise than insofar as, by his supreme power granted by the Father, he procures our salvation and alone takes care that we do not pay the penalties of our sins." Does Christ's expiation then signify nothing else? Does he expiate in no other way than by interceding, and by what secures the efficacy of that intercession? First prove, from any author in any language, that to expiate signifies nothing else than to intercede, plus what is added here. Or let him admit that in this argument, where that word and similar ones are used frequently, a fictitious and new meaning is foisted upon them, beyond the nature of the word, which diminishes and removes its force on the other side. For although he who expiates sins also intercedes for sinners, to intercede and to expiate are not the same. They are distinct parts of one work, and intercession no more excludes a preceding expiation than the latter excludes the former. Next, in the priest and the expiatory sacrifice, from which the idea is drawn in this argument (for Christ also performs these things in his priestly office), to expiate and to intercede differ as antecedent and consequent: prayer and the foundation on which it rests, the offering and the fruit that accompanies or follows it. And so in Christ, expiation is placed before the intercession which he carries on in heaven, and is attributed to his blood and its shedding, when he gave himself to death, or to the sacrifice of death on the cross. In the Scriptures this death is regarded as the price of expiation, by whose merit he accomplished it, and on which the heavenly intercession for those expiated rests, procuring our salvation and alone taking care that we do not pay the penalties of our sins.

units.la: Quemadmodum in textu conjunguntur, Christum esse paracletum, & quod ipse expiatio pro peccatis nostris: non quod non alia fit expiatio, quam nunc Christus in cælis degens peragit, sed quod fundamentum assignetur intercessionis Christi, vid. quod idem ipse fit expiatio pro peccatis nostris: expia-tio autem non demum in cælis, sed in terrâ quoque in cruce, effuso sanguine pretioso, cujus pretio ἐλυτρώθημεν[?].
units.tr: As in the text are joined that Christ is the advocate and that he himself is the expiation for our sins: not that there is no expiation other than the one Christ now accomplishes while dwelling in heaven, but that the foundation of Christ's intercession is assigned, namely that he himself is the expiation for our sins. Yet expiation is accomplished not only in heaven but also on earth, on the cross, with precious blood poured out, by whose price we were redeemed [ἐλυτρώθημεν].

units.la: Apoc. 1. 5. Qui dilexit nos & lavit nos a peccatis nostris in suo sanguine. Socinus: lavit nos, idem significare potest, quod, nos ablutos esse declaravit. Sit & hoc ita, sed declaravit ablutos solummodo, & non vero lavit quoque? non per sanguinem, verè expiatorium? Socinus: declaratio illa ad divinæ voluntatis patefactionem pertinet &c. Idem videmus plerumque contingere, cum de peccatorum expiatione eadem ratione facta agitur, nimirum ut intelligatur, Dei voluntatem à Christo, dum, sanguine suo interveniente nostra peccata expiat, non conciliatam nobis, sed patefactam fuisse: & verbi expiandi, ac similium significationem illam declarationis non minus Christo, quam legali sacerdoti convenire. Resp. 1. Ita jam tota ratio expiationis Socino definit in declarationem divinæ voluntatis. Quod egregie est fallere & ludere Lectores non minus, quam Scripturam ipsam. Adeo expiare idem, quod declarare? Non negamus, quin Christus voluntatem Dei declararit etiam: sed ut hoc idem sit, cum expiatione peccatorum nostrorum, quam adeo auguste in ipso agnoscit Scriptura & deprædicat, non ferimus.
units.tr: Rev. 1. 5. "Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood." Socinus: "washed us" can mean the same as "declared us to have been washed." Let this also be so; but did he declare us washed only, and not also wash us, through blood that was truly expiatory? Socinus: that declaration "pertains to the manifestation of the divine will, etc. We see the same thing generally happen when the expiation of sins is treated in the same way, namely so that it is understood that the will of God, while Christ expiates our sins by his intervening blood, was not reconciled to us but made manifest; and that the meaning of the word to expiate, and of similar words, as declaration, belongs no less to Christ than to the legal priest." Reply 1. Thus Socinus now defines the whole reason of expiation as a declaration of the divine will. This is an excellent way to deceive and mock readers, no less than Scripture itself. Is to expiate the same as to declare? We do not deny that Christ also declared the will of God; but that this should be the same thing as the expiation of our sins, which Scripture so solemnly acknowledges and proclaims in him, we do not endure.

units.la: Expiatio, & declaratio, præterquam quod totis formis differant & essentiis, illa ὡς τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ[?], ista apud homines fit; illa peccatorum est, ista Dei, divinæque voluntatis: atque commiscebuntur illa, & habebuntur pro eodem? II.
units.tr: Expiation and declaration differ in their whole forms and essences: the one is directed toward God, the other takes place among men; the one belongs to sins, the other to God and the divine will. Are these things to be mixed together and held to be the same? II.

units.la: Similiter & contra veritatem & vim expiationis est, negare, per eam obtentam esse reconciliationem. Alio modo voluntas Dei nobis patefiit; alio, Deus conciliatur: hoc, expiatione peragitur, & veræ expiationis necessarium est effectum ac fructus. Atque inde Socinus male concludit, quod non per satisfactionem, divina justitia pro peccatis nostris adhibitam, sed per divinam voluntatis declarationem, & vita æterna supremaque potestatis adeptionem, nos Christus expiavit. pag. 179. Quis obsecro unquam, vel declarationem alienæ voluntatis, vel potestatis alicujus adeptionem, expiationem appellavit? vel quis nominata expiatione, illa, utcunque diu meditetur, intelligat? & non per expiationem significari sciat luitionem poenae ad satisfactionem, & reconciliationem rei cum suo Domino? Ut utra pars rei veritatem, an sententiae praejudicia sequatur, Nos vel Adversarii, ex hisce satis possit esse manifestum.
units.tr: Likewise it is contrary to the truth and force of expiation to deny that reconciliation is obtained through it. In one way the will of God is made known to us; in another way God is reconciled. The latter is accomplished by expiation, and is the necessary effect and fruit of true expiation. And hence Socinus wrongly concludes "that Christ expiated us not through satisfaction, applied by divine justice for our sins, but through the declaration of the divine will and the attaining of eternal life and supreme power." p. 179. Who, I beg you, has ever called the declaration of another's will, or the attaining of some power, an expiation? Or who, on hearing the word expiation, understands it that way, however long he meditates on it, and does not know that by expiation is signified the bearing of punishment as satisfaction, and the reconciliation of the guilty with his Lord? By these things it may be clear enough to us and to our adversaries which side follows the truth of the matter, and which the prejudices of an opinion.

units.la: Obiicit Socinus, part. II. cap. XXI. Patet, a Christo per satisfactionem peractam non fuisse peccatorum nostrorum expiationem. Si enim per satisfactionem peracta esset: utique ad eam peragendam Deo se in coelis offerre opus non fuisset; sed ante ingressum in coelum, immo statim, morte subsecuta, & ante ipsam resurrectionem a mortuis, expiata fuissent peccata nostra. Resp. Per satisfactionem in morte, facta est peccatorum nostrorum a Christo expiatio; sed ad ejus tum complementum, tum applica-tionem requirebatur insuper ingressus Christi in coelum, pro nobis intercessio, & ad nos regendos potestas ac dominium a Patre ipsi traditum. Quae non di-vellenda, sed conjungenda sunt: haud magis ac in Veterum sacrificiis, eo-rum mactatio & αἱματικχυσία [?], a praesentatione, quae per Pontificis ingressum fiebat in Sacrario. In ipsa Christi morte expiata peccata nostra fuerunt, quod ad satisfactionem: sed hujus tum ratihabitio subsecuta fuit in ejus resurrectione, & sessione ad dexteram: tum denique illorum inde in nobis applica-tio. Praeterea quod Socinus exponit, Christum in coelis perpetuo peccata nostra expiare, a nobis non negatur, modo & ipse non neget, quae Scriptura quoque testatur de expiatione in cruce peracta. Sic autem ille, Christus perpetuo, in coelis ad Dei dexteram collocatus, divina liberalitate nos admonet, & ad eam amplecten-dam jugiter movet, & summa auctoritate, qua apud Deum pollet, hoc est, suprema sibi ab ipso potestate in coelo, & in terra concessa, ab ira, qua adversus impios, & peccatores de coelo identidem exeritur, & in novissimo die simul adversus omnes cumulatissime exeretur, nos & servat, & servaturus est. Quae haud imus inficias.
units.tr: Socinus objects, part II, chapter XXI: "It is evident that the expiation of our sins was not accomplished by Christ through the satisfaction he made. For if it had been accomplished by satisfaction, there would have been no need for him to offer himself to God in heaven in order to accomplish it; our sins would have been expiated before his entry into heaven, indeed immediately upon his death, and before his resurrection from the dead." Reply: By the satisfaction in death, the expiation of our sins was made by Christ; but for its completion as well as its application there was further required Christ's entry into heaven, his intercession for us, and the power and dominion handed to him by the Father, in order to rule us. These are not to be torn apart but joined together, no less than in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, where the slaughter of the victims and the shedding of blood were not separated from the presentation made by the high priest's entry into the sanctuary. In Christ's very death our sins were expiated, as far as satisfaction goes; but its ratification followed in his resurrection and session at the right hand, and finally their application to us. Moreover, that Socinus explains "that Christ in heaven perpetually expiates our sins" is not denied by us, provided he also does not deny what Scripture testifies about the expiation accomplished on the cross. Yet he says: "Christ, perpetually placed in heaven at God's right hand, admonishes us by divine liberality, and continually moves us to embrace it; and by the supreme authority which he has with God, that is, by the supreme power given to him by God in heaven and on earth, both keeps us, and will keep us, from the wrath which is continually poured out from heaven against the impious and sinners, and which will at the last day be poured out most abundantly against all." These things we by no means deny.

units.la: Omnia evadent clariora, ubi, quod Apostolus fecit in epistola ad Hebraeos, Christi expiationem & sacrificium, cum legalibus Vet. T. victimis contuleri-mus, atque examinaverimus. Apostolus autem confert utriusque Testamenti tum sacerdotes, tum sacrificia. Sacerdotium, & sacrificia Levitica, ac Christi. Illi Sacerdotes fuerunt meri homines, ὁ νόμος γὰρ ἀνθρώπους καθίστησιν ἱερεῖς. Hebr. vii. 28. Christus autem fuit Dei filius. Illos lex constituit, & fuerunt κατὰ νόμον [?]. cap. vii. 16. cap. viii. 4. cap. x. 8. Christus μὴ τὸν νόμον. vii. 28. Secundum legem, ordinemque Aaronis illi, κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Ἀαρὼν, cap. vii. 2. Christus autem secundum aliam Melchisedeci, κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ, id est κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα Μελχισεδέκ ἱερεὺς ἔπρᾳ [?]. 15. Sacerdos hic ex tribu Juda; illi ex Levitica. φυλῆς ἐντολῆς [?]. vii. 13. Absque juramento isti, μὴ ὁρκωμοσίας cum juramento ille. vii. 21. 28. Legis carnalis ibi, ἐν τυπικῆς σαρκικῆς [?]. vii. 16. hic κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου. Pro hujus foederis δυνάμει [?]; illius ἀσθενείας. vii. 18. Unus hic; ibi plures. cap. vii. 23. Sacerdos sanctus & perfectus; illi peccatores. vii. 26. Aeternus ille, vel in æteræternum. cap. vii. 17. 24. Διὰ τὸ μένειν αὐτὸν εἰς αἰῶνα, ἀπαράβατον ἔχει τὴν ἱερωσύνην. 28. Isti temporarii, ac mortales. διὰ τὸ θνητὸν κωλύεσθαι [?] παραμένειν. 23.
units.tr: Everything will become clearer if we compare and examine Christ's expiation and sacrifice with the legal victims of the Old Testament, as the Apostle did in the Epistle to the Hebrews. The Apostle compares both the priests and the sacrifices of the two Testaments: the Levitical priesthood and sacrifices on one side, Christ's on the other. Those priests were mere men: "for the law appoints men as high priests" [ὁ νόμος γὰρ ἀνθρώπους καθίστησιν ἱερεῖς], Heb. 7:28. Christ, however, was the Son of God. The law appointed the former, and they served according to the law (7:16; 8:4; 10:8). Christ was not appointed by the law (7:28). The former served according to the order of Aaron (7:2), but Christ according to another order, that of Melchizedek [κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ], that is, after the likeness of Melchizedek he was made priest (7:15). That priest was of the tribe of Judah; the others were of Levi (7:13). The others were made without an oath, but he with an oath (7:21, 28). The former belonged to the carnal law of commandment (7:16), but he to the power of an indestructible life (7:16). The power of this covenant is set against the weakness of that one (7:18). He is one; they were many (7:23). He is a holy and perfect priest; they were sinners (7:26). He is eternal, or for ever (7:17, 24): "because he continues for ever, he holds his priesthood unchangeable" [ἀπαράβατον ἔχει τὴν ἱερωσύνην] (7:24, 28). The others were temporary and mortal, "prevented by death from continuing" (7:23).

units.la: Sacrificium utrobique fuit aliquod. etenim Sacerdotis est offerre. Omnis enim Pontifex ad offerendum dona constituitur & hostias: unde & necesse fuit ipsum habere quoque quod offerret. cap. viii. 3. Offerre Deo. τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν. cap. v. 1. Offerre pro hominibus. Omnis pontifex ex hominibus sumtus, ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καθιστατai [?] τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν. Pro eorum peccato. cap. v. 1. ut offerret dona & hostias pro peccato, ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν. Per sanguinem, χωρὶς αἵματος. cap. ix. 7. cap. ix. 18. ὅθεν οὐδὲ ἡ πρώτη χωρὶς αἵματος ἐγκεκαίνισται. Differentia est, quod Sacerdotes olim offerrent alia, non se. Christus autem semetipsum obtulit Deo in sacrificium. ἑαυτὸν ἀνήνεγκας. vii. 27. hostiam & oblationem non voluisti, corpus vero adaptasti mihi. cap. x. 5. 8. 10. διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς τοῦ σώματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.
