Non sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum Christus, sed proprium dedit, διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος. c. ix. 12. non uti Pontifex olim, ἐν αἵματι ἀλλοτρίῳ. 25. illi, pro suis, & aliorum peccatis; Christus duntaxat pro aliorum obtulit. c. vii. 27. Hic semel, & unicâ sui oblatione consummavit omnia; illi καθ' ἡμέραν sacrificia repetebant. c. vii. 27. c. x. 10. ille ἐφάπαξ. 11. 12. μίαν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν προσενέγκας θυσίαν. 14. μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκές.
units.tr: Both the old and the new priesthood had a sacrifice, for it belongs to the priest to offer. "For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; hence it was necessary for him also to have something to offer" (8:3). He offers to God (5:1), and he offers for men: "every high priest taken from among men is appointed on behalf of men in things pertaining to God" [ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καθίσταται τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν] (5:1). He offers for their sins: "that he might offer gifts and sacrifices for sins" [ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν] (5:1). He offers with blood: "whence not even the first covenant was dedicated without blood" [χωρὶς αἵματος] (9:7, 18). The difference is that the priests of old offered other creatures, not themselves. Christ, however, offered himself to God as a sacrifice [ἑαυτὸν ἀνήνεγκεν] (7:27). "You did not want sacrifice and offering, but a body you prepared for me" (10:5, 8, 10); he offered through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ. Christ gave not the blood of goats and calves but his own blood, "through his own blood" [διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος] (9:12), not as the high priest of old, with the blood of another (9:25). The former offered for their own sins and those of others; Christ offered only for the sins of others (7:27). He, once and by the single offering of himself, completed everything, while the former repeated their sacrifices day by day (7:27; 10:10). He offered once [ἐφάπαξ] (9:11–12), "having offered one sacrifice for sins" (10:12), "for by one offering he has perfected for ever" (10:14).

units.la: Quorsum ergo, & quid fecerunt V. Test. sacrificia? Primum non potuerunt vere expiare peccata. cap. x. 4. ἀδύνατον γὰρ αἷμα ταύρων καὶ τράγων ἀφαιρεῖν ἁμαρτίας. Non mundare & tranquillare conscientias, c. ix. 9. μὴ δυνάμενα κατὰ συνείδησιν τελειῶσαι τὸν λατρεύοντα. non deniq; vitam adferre aeternam, certamque ejus spem valuerunt. c. vii. 19. οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος, ἐπεισαγωγὴ δὲ κρείττονος ἐλπίδος. Quae omnia vere, & plenissime insunt sacrificio Christi. cap. vii. 22. 16. qui non secundum legem carnalis praecepti sunt, sed secundum vim indissolubilis vitae. Sed quam praeter immunditiam & reatum spiritualem in anima, peccata olim attulerunt quoque immunditiam & reatum carnalem, seu caeremonialem, hunc expiare sacrificia V. Test. potuerunt, non illum, quem adumbrabant duntaxat & significabant. Unde dixit Apostolus illa sanctificare, πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα, & δικαιώματα σαρκὸς, cap. ix. 10. δικαιώματα λατρείας. verf. 1. sed μέχρι καιροῦ διορθώσεως, verf. 10. sanguinem vero Christi καθαριεῖ τὴν συνείδησιν. Hebr. ix. 13. 14. cap. vii. 16. ideoque & hunc expiare peccata sub V. Test. commissa. verf. 15. ideoque novi Testamenti mediator est, ut morte intercedente, εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τ᾽ ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων [?]. In quo manifestum utriusque Testamenti discrimen est, quod per hoc demum contingat πλεόνασις, cujus in V. fuit σκιὰ umbra ac typus. cap. viii. 5. & x.*1.
units.tr: Why then, and what did the sacrifices of the Old Testament accomplish? First, they could not truly expiate sins: "for it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins" [ἀδύνατον γὰρ αἷμα ταύρων καὶ τράγων ἀφαιρεῖν ἁμαρτίας] (10:4). Nor could they cleanse and quiet the conscience, being unable "to perfect the worshipper as to conscience" [μὴ δυνάμενα κατὰ συνείδησιν τελειῶσαι τὸν λατρεύοντα] (9:9). Finally, they could not bring eternal life or give a sure hope of it: "for the law perfected nothing, but there was the bringing in of a better hope" (7:19). All these things truly and fully belong to the sacrifice of Christ, who was made "not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life" (7:16, 22). But sins under the old dispensation brought, besides spiritual uncleanness and guilt in the soul, also carnal or ceremonial uncleanness and guilt. The sacrifices of the Old Testament could expiate this, but not the guilt which they only shadowed and signified. Hence the Apostle says that they sanctified "to the purifying of the flesh" [πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα] and were "fleshly ordinances" [δικαιώματα σαρκὸς] (9:10), "ordinances of worship" [δικαιώματα λατρείας] (9:1), "until the time of reformation" [μέχρι καιροῦ διορθώσεως] (9:10). But the blood of Christ "will purge the conscience" [καθαριεῖ τὴν συνείδησιν] (9:13–14; 7:16). He therefore also expiates the sins committed under the Old Testament (9:15): "he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions under the first covenant..." In this lies the clear difference between the two Testaments: only through this does fullness come [πλεόνασις], whose shadow and type was in the Old Testament (8:5; 10:1).

units.la: Σκιὰν umbram ergo lex habens futurorum bonorum, non ipsam εἰκόνα speciem rerum, quotannis iisdem hostiis quas continuo offerunt, δύνανται τὰς προσερχομένους τελειῶσαι [?], nequaquam potest accedentes perficere, id est, uti verf. seq. declaratur, nullam habere ulterius peccati conscientiam ministrantes semel purgatos. Hoc erat τὸ ἀδύνατον sanguinis taurorum & hircorum. verf. 4. Proprium verò sanguinis Christi, in seqq. Non ergo per veterà illa fuit πλεόνασις. cap. vii. 11. 19. οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος [?]. Cujus passim tradit Apostolus τὴν ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελές [?]. cap. vii. 18. ἀδύνατον, μὴ δυνάμεθα, cap. ix. 9. ἀδύνατον, cap. x. 4. Quo sensu intelligendus est, quando dixit, quod prior διαθήκη non fuerit ἀμέμπτος, cap. viii. 7. Secundum autem Christi Testamentum, quod in prioris seu legis locum successit, ideo novum, cap. viii. 13. cap. ix. 15. & melius dicitur. cap. vii. 22. 19. Κεφάλαιον est, quod Christus μιᾷ προσφορᾷ πεπλήρωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους [?]. cap. ix. 15.
units.tr: "The law, having a shadow of good things to come and not the very image of the things, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer continually year by year, make perfect those who draw near" [σκιὰν γὰρ ἔχων ὁ νόμος..., δύναται τοὺς προσερχομένους τελειῶσαι], that is, as the following verse declares, to have no further consciousness of sin for those who minister once purged (10:1–2). This was the impossibility of the blood of bulls and goats (10:4). The proper power of the blood of Christ is set out in what follows. So there was no fullness through those old things (7:11, 19): "for the law perfected nothing." The Apostle teaches its weakness and unprofitableness everywhere (7:18), its impossibility, "we cannot" (9:9), "impossible" (10:4). The sense in which he calls the first covenant not "faultless" (8:7) must be understood in this light. The second covenant of Christ, which took the place of the former or of the law, is therefore called "new" (8:13; 9:15) and "better" (7:22, 19). The sum is that Christ "by one offering has perfected for ever those who are sanctified" [μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκές τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους] (9:15 as cited).

units.la: Cæterum ex illorum comparatione constare poterit, uti Sacerdos in Vet. Test. unusquisque, non solus Pontifex seu Sacerdos supremus, sed sacrificantes quicunque sacrificiis omnibus, & non solo, quamvis præcipue quidem, anniversario, pro peccatis in genere, & non solis levioribus incogitantiis, offerebant, atque tum quum sanguinem fundebant, ac altari imponebant hostiam, non demum quando de sanguine inferebatur in Sanctuarium, quod ejus sacrificii vi expiarunt reatum carnalem, & placarunt cæremonialiter Deum; quod ita Christus Sacerdos noster verus & spiritualis, sui corporis sacrificio, quando pro peccatis nostris omnibus sanguinem effudit, & se in mortem dedit pro expiatione, & propitiatione nostrum perficiendâ apud Deum. Quæ Socino negantur, videlicet, quod sacrificia in genere. Christum respexerunt, sed sola publica, & anniversaria, à summo Pontifice oblata, & quorum sanguis in sancta inferebatnr, non alia, non quæcunque. Part. II. cap. ix. Quare, cum non omnia sacrificia legis, quamvis pro peccatis facta Christi morti, tanquam imago veritati, respondeant: non omnia Christi mortem figurabant. Sed figura mortis Christi erant tantummodo sacrificia illa, quæ publicè, hoc est, pro universo populo, ipso etiam aliquando summo Sacerdote non excluso, & statis quibusdam temporibus fiebant; præsertim verò illud, quod semel in anno summus Sacerdos, in Sancta Sanctorum ingrediens, peragebat, &c. In hoc igitur sacrificio, ut dictum est, potissimum mors Christi, adeoque ipse Christus, quatenus Deo pro nobis sacrificavit, adumbratus fuit. In cæteris verò sacrificiis, quæ pro peccatis fiebant, non figurabatur Christi mors, sed tantum in summi Sacerdotis persona Christus ipse adumbrabatur. Sacrificia autem ipsa, spiritualia nostra sacrificia adumbrabant. Cap. xii. Christi mortis sacrificium non in quibuscunque expia-toriis victimis, sed in iis tantum, qua semel in anno a summo Sacerdote in Sancta Sancto-rum ingrediente pro peccatis immolabantur precipue adumbratum fuisse. Quî quadrant ista, in iis tantum, & precipue?
units.tr: Moreover, from the comparison of these things it will be established that in the Old Testament every person who sacrificed, not only the High Priest or chief priest, but whoever offered sacrifices of every kind, and not only the yearly sacrifice, though that one chiefly, offered for sins in general and not only for slight inadvertences, and that when they poured out the blood and laid the victim on the altar, not only when the blood was carried into the sanctuary, they expiated carnal guilt by the power of that sacrifice and ceremonially placated God. So Christ our true and spiritual priest, by the sacrifice of his body, when he shed his blood for all our sins and gave himself to death, made expiation and accomplished our propitiation before God. Socinus denies these things, namely that sacrifices in general looked to Christ, and holds that only the public and yearly sacrifices offered by the High Priest, whose blood was carried into the holy place, did so, and not others, nor whatever sacrifices. Part II, ch. 9: "Wherefore, since not all the sacrifices of the law, though made for sins, correspond to the death of Christ as image to truth, not all of them figured the death of Christ. But only those sacrifices figured the death of Christ which were made publicly, that is for the whole people, sometimes even with the High Priest not excluded, and at fixed times; especially that which the High Priest once a year performed, entering into the Holy of Holies, etc. In this sacrifice, therefore, as has been said, chiefly the death of Christ, and so Christ himself as he sacrificed for us to God, was foreshadowed. In the other sacrifices which were made for sins the death of Christ was not figured, but only Christ himself was foreshadowed in the person of the High Priest. The sacrifices themselves foreshadowed our spiritual sacrifices." Ch. 12: "The sacrifice of Christ's death was chiefly foreshadowed not in any expiatory victims whatever, but only in those which were offered for sins once a year by the High Priest entering the Holy of Holies." How do these words, "only in those" and "chiefly", fit together?

units.la: Tum non pro gravibus etiam peccatis, sed solis levioribus oblata, five quotidiana, five anniversarium illud, docet. Part.11. cap. 11. pag.231. & cap x. à quibusdam levioribus tantum. Quum revera nulla peccata sint dicenda levia, quidem alia aliis magis vel minus gravia, levia nulla prorsus. Nam levitas de peccato praedicari non potest; gravitas imo, & semper. Jam cap. v. inquit: Verumtamen, quia sacrificia illa levem quandam Dei obedientiam continebant: ut pro levibus duntaxat quibusdam peccatis offerrentur, à Deo instituta fuerant; qua scilicet per incogitantiam & errorem admitterentur. Quod fi pro quibusdam etiam, voluntarijs, five, ut vocant, ultroneis peccatis sacrificia instituta fuerunt, sola sacrificia non ex-piabant; sed ad expiationem peragendam, proximo etiam, qui in eis peccatis lafus fuerat, cumulate satisfaciendum erat. ut videre est in lege sacrificii pro peccato ultroneo, Levit. cap. 6. in principio. Pro gravioribus autem peccatis nullum sacrificium à Deo institutum fuerat. Cap xii pag. 132. Praterea, quod ad ipsum sacrificium attinet, quod in eo folenni festo fiebat, & de quo hic praecipue agitur, dico, illud graviora peccata, qua ad-versus divinam legem ex animi malitia perpetrata effent, non expiaffe, neque pro illis oblatum fuisse; sed pro iis tantum, qua ignorantia appellari possunt, & pro quibus privatorum sacrificia instituta fuerant. Ex quibus verbis (quidquid iidem illi Eruditi viri di-cant) manifestum fit, Pontificem illum non pro omnibus peccatis, sed pro ignorantiis, & erroribus ex infirmitate admissis facrificaffe. Cap. xiv. ignorantias tantum, & quasdam fragilitates, ac delicta quaedam externa, carnem potius, quam animam polluentia. Cap. xviii. cum per immolationes illas ignorantia, & incogitantia, ac leviores quadam fragilitates, & labes quaedam corporis, eademque imaginaria potius, quam vera, expiarentur, & mundarentur. Sic peccata illa, quae expiarint Vet. T. sacrificia, resolvuntur tandem in aliqua imaginaria.
units.tr: Then he teaches that the sacrifices offered not for grave sins but only for lighter ones, whether the daily ones or that yearly one, were offered, citing Part 2, ch. 11, p. 231, and ch. 10, "for certain lighter sins only." Yet no sins should really be called light. Some are more or less grave than others, but none is light at all, for lightness cannot be predicated of sin; gravity can, and always. Next, in ch. 5 he says: "But because those sacrifices contained a certain slight obedience to God, they were instituted by God only to be offered for certain light sins, namely those committed through inadvertence and error. But if sacrifices were also instituted for certain voluntary, or as they call them, deliberate sins, the sacrifices alone did not make atonement; the injured neighbour also had to be fully satisfied for the atonement to be completed, as can be seen in the law of the sacrifice for a deliberate sin, Lev. 6, at the beginning. For graver sins, however, no sacrifice was instituted by God." Ch. 12, p. 132: "Moreover, as to the sacrifice itself, which was made at that solemn feast and of which we are chiefly speaking here, I say that it did not atone for the graver sins committed against the divine law out of malice of mind, nor was it offered for them; it was offered only for those sins which can be called sins of ignorance, and for which private sacrifices had been instituted. From these words (whatever those learned men say) it is clear that the high priest did not offer sacrifice for all sins, but for ignorances and errors committed through weakness." Ch. 14: "only ignorances, certain frailties, and certain external offences, which defile the flesh rather than the soul." Ch. 18: "since by those immolations ignorance and inadvertence, and certain lighter frailties and blemishes of the body, which were imaginary rather than real, were atoned for and cleansed." Thus those sins which the Old Testament sacrifices atoned for are in the end reduced to something imaginary.

units.la: Statuitque Socinus, vere & propria sua vi expiaffe: non ἐν τύπῳ, & per vim sacrificii Christi. Part. 11. cap. xi. Sacrificia tamen non minus pro gravioribus, quam pro levioribus delictis, instituturum Deum fuisse, omnino dicendum videtur, fi sacrificia nullum peccatum vere expiaffent, sed, ut vos dicitis, expiationem tantum per Christum olim faciendam adumbraffent, & à satisfactione, qua pro peccatis noftrus ejus morte peragenda foret, vim omnem sumpsissent. Ibidem, Statuendum omnino est, per sacrificia, victimas illas expiatorias, non modo expiationes, qua sub novo foedere fieri debebant, adumbratas esse, verum etiam peccata ipsa, pro quibus offerebantur, vere ea ratione, qua supra expositum est, expiata fuisse. cap. x. Similitudinem etiam inter le-gales illas purificationes, & purificationem per Christi sanguinem factam eundem auctorem ad Heb. agnovisse, nempe quia non minus per illas, quam per istam, mundatio vere fie-ret, quamvis rerum diversarum-
units.tr: Socinus also states that the sacrifices truly and properly made atonement by their own power, not in a type, and not through the power of Christ's sacrifice. Part 2, ch. 11: "Nevertheless, it seems altogether necessary to say that God would have instituted sacrifices no less for graver than for lighter offences, if the sacrifices had not truly atoned for any sin, but, as you say, had only foreshadowed an atonement to be made once through Christ, and had derived all their force from the satisfaction which was to be made by his death for our sins." In the same place: "It must altogether be held that the sacrifices, those expiatory victims, were not only figures of the atonements which were to be made under the new covenant, but that the sins themselves for which they were offered were truly atoned for in the way explained above." Ch. 10: "The same author in Hebrews also recognised a likeness between those legal purifications and the purification made by the blood of Christ, namely because the cleansing was no less truly effected by those than by this, although the things are different."

units.la: Denique non tum, quum sanguinem suum Christus in terra, & in cruce fudit, aut Sacerdotem fuisse, vel obtulisse sacrificium, sed id demum inchoasse, ac praestitisse in coelis ubi consedit, audacter tradit. Part. II. cap. XV. Per Christi enim oblationem tota illa epistola auctor ille, ut supra monuimus, nihil aliud intelligit, quam per proprii sanguinis fusionem Christi in coelo Deo factam sui ipsius pro nobis (ut ita dicam) praesentationem. &c. Relativa enim sunt Sacerdos, & oblatio. Itaque, ubi verus Sacerdos nondum est, nec vera oblatio esse potest. Ubi autem verus Sacerdos, ibi & vera oblatio fit, necesse est. Christum autem a Scriptore illo ad Hebr. non ante Sacerdotem vere dici, quam post ejus in coelum ascensum, constare potest &c. Capitis XX. argumentum, Christum nostrorum peccatorum expiationem, antequam post mortem suam in coelum ingrederetur, non peregisse. Cap. XXIII. etiam post mortem, antequam coelos conscenderet, Pontifex consecratus non fuit. In Synopsi, de justificatione, pag. 6. Ubi etiam animadvertendum est, quod sicut oblatio antiqui illius anniversarii sacrificii non tunc perficiebatur, cum victima jugulabatur, sed cum jam jugulata sanguis in sancta sanctorum a Pontifice inferebatur, (Scriptum est enim in epist. ad Hebr. 9. 7. Pontificem sanguinem istum pro se & pro ignorantiis populi obtulisse) sic Christi oblatio non tunc perfecta est, cum ipse mactatus & crucifixus fuit, sed cum, postquam crucifixus fuerat, se ipsum in coelum intulit. Si vellet tantum, non fuisse omni modo & parte sua perfectam oblationem, antequam in sancta illatus fuisset ejus a sacerdote sanguis, vel Christus seipsum praesentasset in coelo, facile hic conveniremus, dummodo oblatio mactationis, & sanguinis ibi facta effusio non minus ad sacrificium & ejus oblationem fecisse, ac oblatio praesentationis, vel sanguis oblati postmodum expositus Dei oculis in Sancto, diceretur quoque.
units.tr: Finally, he boldly asserts that Christ was not a priest, nor did he offer a sacrifice, when he shed his blood on earth and on the cross, but that he began and accomplished this only afterwards, in heaven, where he sat down. Part 2, ch. 15: "For by Christ's offering that whole epistle, as we noted above, means nothing other than the presentation of himself, as it were, to God in heaven by the shedding of his own blood for us. For priest and offering are correlative. Therefore, where the true priest is not yet, neither can there be a true offering. But where the true priest is, there of necessity the true offering is also made. Now that Christ is not called a priest by that writer of Hebrews until after his ascent into heaven can be established..." Ch. 20 argues that Christ did not accomplish the expiation of our sins before he entered heaven after his death. Ch. 23: "Even after death, before he ascended to the heavens, the high priest was not consecrated." In the Synopsis, on justification, p. 6: "Here it should also be noted that just as the offering of that ancient annual sacrifice was not completed when the victim was slaughtered, but when the blood, already slain, was carried by the high priest into the holy of holies (for it is written in Hebrews 9:7 that the high priest offered that blood for himself and for the ignorances of the people), so Christ's offering was not completed when he was slain and crucified, but when, after he had been crucified, he carried himself into heaven. If he meant only that the offering was not in every way and part perfect until his blood had been carried by the priest into the holy place, or until Christ had presented himself in heaven, we could easily agree, provided it is also said that the offering of slaughter and the effusion of blood made there contributed no less to the sacrifice and its offering than the offering of presentation, or the blood of the offering afterwards displayed before the eyes of God in the sanctuary."

units.la: Ut quatuor hic potissimum veniant in controversiam. I. Annon omnia Vet. T. sacrificia expiatoria, de aliis non est quaestio, typi fuerint sacrificii Christi? II. Annon pro gravibus etiam peccatis oblata? III. Num vim habuerint veram expiandi? IV. An Christus non etiam in terris Sacerdos fuerit, an demum in coelis, post adscensionem? Nos affirmamus: illi negant.
units.tr: Four points chiefly come into controversy here. I. Were all the Old Testament expiatory sacrifices (I am not asking about others) types of Christ's sacrifice? II. Were they also offered for grave sins? III. Did they have a true power of atonement? IV. Was Christ a priest also on earth, or only in heaven, after his ascension? We affirm; they deny.

units.la: Primum illorum sic probamus. I. Quia tota lex caeremonialis, praecipua sui parte, typica fuit ad Christum: ergo etiam in illis sacrificiis. In genere de illa, variisque aliis, praeter sacrificia, capitibus dixit Apostolus, Col. II. 17. ἅ ἐστι σκιὰ τῶν μελλόντων, τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Simili locutione utitur, Heb. X. I. Σκιὰν γὰρ ἔχων ὁ νόμος futurorum bonorum, non vero ipsam rerum εἰκόνα. cap. IX. 24. ἀντίτυπα τῶν ἀληθινῶν. Socinus, part. II. cap. IX. pag. 118. universum antiquum foedus imago quaedam est novi. II: Praesertim sacrificia peculiarem & propriam relationem habuerunt ad Christum, nempe sacrificia pro peccato. Heb. X. 5. 6. 7. Ideo in mundum veniens, dicit, Hostiam & oblationem non voluisti, corpus vero adaptasti mihi. Holocautomata & pro peccato non petivisti. Tum dixi, ecce venio &c. cap. IX. 23. αὐτὰ ἡ τὰ ἐπουράνια κρείττοσιν θυσίαις παρὰ ταύτας. cap. V. I. & seq. III. Unde & sacerdotes omnes figuram hac ratione quandam gesserunt Christi. Hebr. VIII. 4. 5. Si enim esset in terra, non foret Sacerdos, existentibus Sacerdotibus dona offerentibus juxta legem. Qui ὑποδείγμα-
units.tr: We prove the first point thus. I. Because the whole ceremonial law, in its chief part, was typical of Christ; therefore so were those sacrifices. The Apostle spoke of that law in general, and of various other things besides sacrifices, Col. 2:17: ἅ ἐστι σκιὰ τῶν μελλόντων, τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ ["which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ's"]. He uses similar language in Heb. 10:1: Σκιὰν γὰρ ἔχων ὁ νόμος ["for the law has a shadow"] of good things to come, not the very image of the things themselves. Ch. 9:24: ἀντίτυπα τῶν ἀληθινῶν ["copies of the true things"]. Socinus, Part 2, ch. 9, p. 118: the whole ancient covenant is a certain image of the new. II. Especially sacrifices had a peculiar and proper relation to Christ, namely the sacrifices for sin. Heb. 10:5–7: "Therefore coming into the world he says, Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me. Burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you did not seek. Then I said, Behold I come, etc." Ch. 9:23: αὐτὰ ἡ τὰ ἐπουράνια κρείττοσιν θυσίαις παρὰ ταύτας ["the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these"]. Ch. 5:1ff. III. Hence also all the priests in a certain manner bore a figure of Christ in this respect. Heb. 8:4–5: "For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve [ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ λατρεύουσιν τῶν ἐπουρανίων] a copy and shadow of the heavenly things."

units.la: Tom. 2. ἡ σκιὰ λατρεύσαντ[?] τ[?] ἐπουρανίων. ix. 6. qui in primum tabernaculum continuo ingrediuntur Sacerdotes, cultus perficientes. cap. x. 11. καὶ πᾶς μὲν ἱερεύς. Atque in genere opponit Christo totum Sacerdotium Leviticum, cap. vii. 11. Si enim consummatio esset, per Sacerdotium Leviticum. iv. Hinc communia & quotidiana taurorum, vitulorum, & hircorum sacrificia adducit & urget Apostolus, inter utriusque Vet. ac Nov. Test. sacrificia instituta comparatione. Hebr. ix. 12. 13. & Christus cum agno confertur, Joann. 1. 29. 36. Act. viii. 32. 1 Pet. 1. 19. Apoc. xiii. 8. Quinto, Christus אשם[?] fuit, hostia pro peccato, Jesa. Liii. 10. qualis quotidie offerebatur. Levit. iv. & v. Denique, expresse etiam quotidiana sacrificia cum Christi sacrificio confert Apostolus, Hebr. vii. 27. qui non necesse habet καθ' ἡμέραν quotidie, quemadmodum Pontifices, primum pro suis, inde pro populi peccatis hostias offerre: hoc enim fecit semel, offerens seipsum. cap. ix. 6. iis ita paratis, in primum tabernaculum διὰ παντὸς continuo ingrediebantur Sacerdotes cultus perficientes. cap. x. 11. Et unusquisque quidem Sacerdos stetit καθ' ἡμέραν cultum peragens, easdemque πολλάκις saepe offerens hostias.
units.tr: Vol. 2. ἡ σκιὰ ... τῶν ἐπουρανίων [the shadow of the heavenly things]. Heb. 9:6: "Those who enter continually into the first tabernacle are priests performing the services." Ch. 10:11: καὶ πᾶς μὲν ἱερεύς ["and every priest indeed"]. And in general the Apostle sets the whole Levitical priesthood against Christ, ch. 7:11: "For if perfection were through the Levitical priesthood." IV. Hence the Apostle brings forward and urges the common daily sacrifices of bulls, calves and goats, comparing them with the sacrifices of both the Old and New Testaments, Heb. 9:12–13. Christ is also compared with a lamb: John 1:29, 36; Acts 8:32; 1 Pet. 1:19; Rev. 13:8. Fifth, Christ was an asham [אשם], a victim for sin, Isa. 53:10, such as was offered every day, Lev. 4 and 5. Finally, the Apostle expressly compares the daily sacrifices with the sacrifice of Christ, Heb. 7:27: "who does not need, καθ' ἡμέραν, daily, as the high priests do, to offer sacrifices first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people; for this he did once, offering himself." Ch. 9:6: "With these things so prepared, the priests continually, διὰ παντὸς, enter the first tabernacle, performing the services." Ch. 10:11: "And every priest indeed stands καθ' ἡμέραν daily, performing the service, and often, πολλάκις, offering the same sacrifices."

units.la: Quod autem Socinus excipit, part. ii. cap. xvi. adverbium quotidie non, singulis diebus, sed sape, vel, certo quodam tempore perpetuo, significare. Quotidie dicit, cum tamen id fieret a Sacerdotibus semel tantum quotannis. pro solita sua audacia, qua quidvis in Scriptura solet transponere. Quotidie, inquit Apostolus: reclamat Socinus, & dicit, non quotidie. Singulis diebus, ait Apostolus; jubet eum dicere Socinus, quotannis: belle sane. De quotidiano loquitur Apostolus sacrificio: ille eum loqui vult de solo anniversario. Quasi Apostolus, ubi de isto agit, non novisset κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν dicere? cap. x. 1. 3. & ix. 7. ἅπαξ ἐν ἑαυτῷ μόνῳ ὁ ἀρχιερεύς[?]. Hic vero καθ' ἡμέραν dicit, non semel, sed bis, & expositum per διὰ παντὸς, & πολλάκις, atq; oppositum τῷ ἐφάπαξ, attribuitque Sacerdotibus in communi; & vulgaribus ipsorum λατρείαις, & λειτουργίαις, quas ἐν πρώτῃ σκηνῇ peragebant; non εἰς τὸ δεύτερον, ἅπαξ ἐν ἑαυτῷ. cap. ix. 6. 7. Quodque addit, nusquam legi, summum Sacerdotem in sacrificiis, qua pro populo fiebant, pro se etiam offerre debuisse, nisi in sacrificio illo anniversario. id nec verum, nam etiam extra sacrificium anniversarium, sive pro se, sive pro populo offerebat Pontifex, Levit. iv. 3. 13. neque, si verum, vel sic evinceret, καθ' ἡμέραν non denotare quotidianum sacrificium; vel, id quod pro populi peccatis quotidie offerebatur, non conferri, cum sacrificio Christi, quamvis pro suis populique simul solemniter offerret Pontifex κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν. Nempe significatur, sacrificia pro peccato semper respexisse ad sacrificium Christi, sive quando pro Pontificis, sive populi peccatis, aut seorsim, aut conjunctim, quomodocunque, hostia mactaretur: quo sic vis in opposito membro major atque manifestior, quod non variis, sed uno solo fui sacrificio Christus expiavit omnia, & perfecit. Et quod cap. ix. 9. est, non potest ad anniversarium trahi sacrificium, quia de illis agit, propter quæ quotidie in sanctum ingrediebatur Sacerdos. πῶς ἱερεὺς καθ᾽ ἡμέραν λειτουργῶν, [?]ᾗ πῶς αὐτὰς πολλάκις προσφέρειν θυσίας. uti est cap. x. II.
units.tr: As for what Socinus adds (part 2, ch. 16), that the adverb quotidie ("daily") does not mean each day but often, or at some fixed and perpetual time, and that he says "daily" although the priests did this only once a year, he does so with his usual boldness, by which he is wont to twist anything in Scripture. "Daily," says the Apostle; Socinus objects and says, "not daily." "Each day," says the Apostle; Socinus bids him say "yearly." Very fine indeed! The Apostle speaks of the daily sacrifice; Socinus wants him to speak only of the annual one. As if the Apostle, when treating of that sacrifice, did not know how to say "yearly" [κατ' ἐνιαυτόν]! (Heb. 10.1, 3; and 9.7, "once, the high priest alone by himself" [ἅπαξ ἐν ἑαυτῷ μόνῳ ὁ ἀρχιερεύς].) But here he says "daily" [καθ' ἡμέραν], not once but repeatedly, and explains it by "continually" [διὰ παντὸς] and "often" [πολλάκις], and sets it against "once for all" [ἐφάπαξ]. He ascribes it to the priests in general and to their ordinary services and ministries [λατρείαις, λειτουργίαις], which they performed in the first tabernacle [ἐν πρώτῃ σκηνῇ], not "for the second, once only by himself" [εἰς τὸ δεύτερον, ἅπαξ ἐν ἑαυτῷ] (Heb. 9.6, 7). And what he adds, that it is nowhere read that the high priest had to offer for himself in the sacrifices made for the people, except in that annual sacrifice, is not even true. For apart from the annual sacrifice the high priest offered, whether for himself or for the people (Lev. 4.3, 13). Nor, even if it were true, would it prove either that "daily" does not denote the daily sacrifice, or that what was offered daily for the sins of the people is not compared with the sacrifice of Christ, although the high priest offered solemnly once a year for himself and for the people together. Clearly the meaning is that the sacrifices for sin always looked to the sacrifice of Christ, whether they were offered for the sins of the high priest or of the people, separately or together, however the victim was slain. Thus the force of the opposed member is greater and plainer: Christ by one single sacrifice, not by many, expiated and perfected all things. And as to what is said in Heb. 9.9, that the sacrifice cannot be referred to the annual one, because it deals with those things for which the priest entered daily into the holy place [πῶς ἱερεὺς καθ᾽ ἡμέραν λειτουργῶν], and how he offered the same sacrifices often [πῶς αὐτὰς πολλάκις προσφέρειν θυσίας], as is said in Heb. 10.11.

units.la: Objicit Socinus, part. II. cap. IX. Verùm quia Christi mors non solum pro omnibus, sed pro omnium etiam omnibus peccatis sacrificium fuit: idcirco ea proprie in anniversario illo sacrificio figurabatur, quod solum pro omnium omnibus peccatis fiebat. Catera sacrificia voluntatem populi omnino requirebant, quare populi magis, quam Sacerdotis sacrificia erant. & non pro omnibus, sed singulis fiebant t vel ad summum pro tota Israelis congregatione, tanquam uno quopiam considerata. Haudquaquam negamus, in anniversario sacrificio excellentem sacrificii Christi figuram præcessisse, uti in Sacerdote summo Christi; sed vel proprie in illo, non item in aliis sacrificiis, aut tantum-modo in publicis, quæ pro universo populo fiebant, figuratum sacrificium Christi fuisse, hoc negamus. II. Nulla est consequentia, Christi sacrificium pro omnibus fuit, ergo in privatis olim adumbrari non potuit. Ita enim Christus pro omnibus mortuus, ut pro singulis suis, & quicunque fideles, pro se, de communi illius λυτρῳ participent: ut omnino in singulorum sacrificiis [?]περὶ ἁμαρτίας, Christi verum unicumque sacrificium spectatum etiam fuerit. III. Si solum anniversarium proprie figuravit sacrificium Christi, & non etiam quæ pro singulis fiebant, vel ad summum pro tota Israelis congregatione, tanquam uno quopiam considerata: quare ergo antea ista etiam figuram fecit sacrificii Christi? sed figura mortis Christi erant tantummodo sacrificia illa, quæ publice, hoc est, pro universo populo, ipso etiam aliquando summo Sacerdote non excluso, & statis quibusdam temporibus fiebant; præsertim vero illud quod semel in anno summus Sacerdos, in Sancta Sanctorum ingrediens, peragebat. Si illa sacrificia, præter anniversarium quod præsertim tale, figura Christi fuerunt, & quidem tantummodo illa publica, ut anniversarium ideo rationem figuræ habuisse videatur Adversario, quod publicum, sive pro universo populo fuit; quomodo jam proprie anniversarium, ut pro omnium & omnibus peccatis oblatum, & vi illius argumentationis pro figura sacrificii Christi habetur, & non etiam illud, quod pro tota Israelis congregatione, quantumvis tanquam uno quopiam considerata, oblatum fuit? vel quomodo hoc inter catera sacrificia à figurâ Christi exclusa ponitur, eo quod voluntatem populi requisivit? IV. Voluntas offerentium sacrificia nil tollit de sacrificio, quominus aut sacrificium, aut inter figuras Christi fuerit: nam ea quidem testatissima & respectu Sacerdotis, & populi fuit in anni-versario. V. Nec ideo populi magis, quam Sacerdotis dicenda sacrificia: po-pulus quippe per Sacerdotem, Sacerdos nomine populi λατρείας [?]ἀρχιερεῖ. Atque non à populi voluntate, sed divina ordinatione profluebat sacrificio-num ratio, tam horum, quam illorum. Denique hinc concludimus, quod ergo in Christi morte sacrificium, ipseque Sacerdos in ea fuerit Christus, &c non demum post adscensum in coelos.
units.tr: Socinus objects (part 2, ch. 9): "But because the death of Christ was a sacrifice not only for all, but also for all the sins of all, therefore it was figured properly in that annual sacrifice alone, which was made for all the sins of all. The other sacrifices wholly required the will of the people; hence they were more the sacrifices of the people than of the priest. And they were not made for all, but for individuals, or at most for the whole congregation of Israel, considered as one person." We by no means deny that the excellent figure of Christ's sacrifice went before in the annual sacrifice, just as Christ's high priesthood did. But we deny that the sacrifice of Christ was figured properly in that one alone, and not likewise in the other sacrifices, or only in the public ones which were made for the whole people. (1) There is no consequence in saying: Christ's sacrifice was for all, therefore it could not formerly be shadowed in private sacrifices. For Christ died for all in such a way that his own, each one of the faithful, partake for himself of the common ransom; so that in the sacrifices of individuals, the one true sacrifice of Christ was also regarded (περὶ ἁμαρτίας). (2) If the annual sacrifice alone properly figured the sacrifice of Christ, and not also those offered for individuals, or at most for the whole congregation of Israel considered as one person, then why did those others also formerly figure the sacrifice of Christ? But those sacrifices were figures of Christ's death only, namely those which were made publicly, that is for the whole people, even sometimes with the high priest himself not excluded, and at fixed times; especially that which the high priest, entering into the Holy of Holies once a year, performed. (3) If those sacrifices, besides the annual one (which was especially such), were figures of Christ, and indeed only the public ones, so that the annual one seems to the Adversary to have had the character of a figure because it was public, that is for the whole people, then how is the annual one now properly figured, as offered for all the sins of all, and on the force of that argument held to be a figure of Christ's sacrifice, while that which was offered for the whole congregation of Israel, however considered as one person, is not? Or how is this placed among the other sacrifices excluded from the figure of Christ, on the ground that it required the will of the people? (4) The will of those offering sacrifices takes nothing from the sacrifice, so that it could not be, or be among the figures of Christ; for in the annual sacrifice that will was most manifest, both on the part of the priest and of the people. (5) Nor are sacrifices for that reason to be called more the people's than the priest's. For the people acted through the priest, and the priest in the name of the people [λατρείας ... ἀρχιερεῖ]. And the plan of sacrifices, of these as of those, flowed not from the people's will but from divine ordinance. Finally, we conclude from this that there was a sacrifice in the death of Christ, and that Christ himself was the priest in it, and not only after his ascension into heaven.

units.la: Ad secundam quod spectat quaestionem, & sacrificia olim pro gravibus peccatis, non solis levioribus & ignorantiis, oblata fuisse, probatur, primum ex eo quod sacrificia appellantur in genere pro peccato, sine discrimine θυσίας? ἁμαρτίας, חטא, אשם, non addito quo peccato, vel peccati genere: atque Sacerdos ad hoc dicitur constitui, ex hominibus, ut pro hominibus apud Deum agat, & offerat θυσίας ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν. Hebr. v. 1. 3. Deinde, ex lege appareret, sacrificia etiam pro gravibus peccatis instituta, fuisse: uti pro execratione, קול אלה Levit. v. 1. pro juramento temerario. verf. 4. pro sacrilegio. verf. 15. cap. vi. 2. pro mendacio in deposito, vel rapinâ pro mendacio, & perjurio, verf. 3. 5. adde Num. v. 6. 7. Quae certe non levia, sed atrocia peccata: atque pro illis singula fuerunt ordinata sacrificia. 111. In designatione peccatorum generali, pro quibus sacrificia instituta, ponitur peccatum בשגגה per errorem commissum, מכל מצות יהוה contra quodcunque praeceptum Iehova, quod non oporteret fieri. Levit. iv. 2. 13. cap. v. 17. Num. v. 6. Vir aut mulier quando fecerint, מכל חטאת האדם quodcunque peccatum hominis, transgrediendo contra Jehovam, anima ipsa rea est, atque ei praescribitur sacrificium. Peccatum בשגגה, vel שגגה error, opponitur peccato pervicaci, quod committitur manu excelsa, ביד רמה. Num. xv. 25. 3c. inter quae istud illo quidem gravius, non tamen ita, quin illud etiam peccatum sit. & pro istis sacrificium non ordinatur, quia excisione כרת plectebantur. Denique in anniversario sacrificio fiebat expiatio peccatorum omnium, quorum quis reus esset, ut plenam obtineret remissionem. Levit. xvi. 21. 22. & imponet Aharon binas manus suas supra caput viventis istius hirci, & confitebitur super eo את כל עונות omnes iniquitates filiorum Israel, ובני ישראל ואת כל פשעיהם לכל חטאתם & omnes iniquitates ipsorum, secundum omnia peccata ipsorum: & mittet ea supra caput hirci istius, quem mittet per manum viri praesentis in desertum. ונשא Ita portabit hircus supra se omnes iniquitates ipsorum in terram desertam. Unde & Apostolus dixit in genere, peccatorum ἀνάμνησιν fieri in hostiis καθ' ἐνιαυτὸν. Hebr. x. 3. Quae certe aliud dicunt, quam quod peccata demum levia, nulla gravia fuerint, pro quibus olim factae & ordinatae oblationes; vel, uti Socinus dixit, ignorantiae, ac delicta quaedam externa; carnem potius, quam animam polluentia: incogitantiae, ac leviores fragilitates, & labes quaedam corporis, eaedemque imaginariae potius, quam verae. Ex peccato gravi primum facit leve, ex levi deinde nullum, audacter satis & improbe. Praeterquam quod ipse etiam fatetur, pro quibusdam etiam ultroneis deliciis expiationem per sacrificia concessam fuisse, pag. 135, quae certe omnia non pro levibus vel imaginariis fragilitatibus habenda sunt.
units.tr: As for the second question, that sacrifices were offered formerly for grave sins, not only for lighter ones and for ignorances, this is proved first from the fact that sacrifices are called in general "for sin," without distinction (θυσίας ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν; חטא, אשם), with no addition of what sin or kind of sin, and the priest is said to be appointed from among men to act for men before God and to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins (Heb. 5.1, 3). Second, it appears from the law that sacrifices were also instituted for grave sins: for cursing (קול אלה, Lev. 5.1), for rash swearing (v. 4), for sacrilege (v. 15; 6.2), for lying about a deposit, or robbery, or lying and perjury (vv. 3, 5); add Num. 5.6, 7. These are certainly not light but atrocious sins, and separate sacrifices were ordained for each of them. Third, in the general description of the sins for which sacrifices were instituted, the sin is put as committed "in error" [בשגגה], "against any of the commandments of Jehovah which ought not to be done" [מכל מצות יהוה] (Lev. 4.2, 13; 5.17; Num. 5.6). "When a man or a woman shall have done any sin of men [מכל חטאת האדם], transgressing against Jehovah, that soul is guilty," and a sacrifice is prescribed for him. The sin committed "in error," or "error" [שגגה], is opposed to the sin of obstinacy, which is committed "with a high hand" [ביד רמה] (Num. 15.25 etc.). Of these, the latter is indeed graver, yet not so that the former is not also a sin; and for the latter no sacrifice was ordained, because they were punished with excision [כרת]. Finally, in the annual sacrifice the expiation was made for the sins of all of which anyone was guilty, so that they might obtain full remission. Lev. 16.21, 22: "And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the living goat, and confess over it all the iniquities [את כל עונות] of the children of Israel, and [ובני ישראל] all their transgressions [ואת כל פשעיהם], according to all their sins [לכל חטאתם]; and he shall put them upon the head of the goat, and shall send it away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness [ונשא]; so the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities into a land not inhabited." Hence the Apostle also said, in general, that a "remembrance of sins" [ἀνάμνησιν ἁμαρτιῶν] is made in the sacrifices every year (Heb. 10.3). These certainly say nothing else than that the sins for which sacrifices were formerly made and ordained were only light, none grave; or, as Socinus put it, ignorances and certain external offences, polluting the flesh rather than the soul, thoughtlessness and lighter frailties, and certain stains of the body, and these rather imaginary than real. He makes the grave sin light first, and then from the light makes nothing: boldly enough and wickedly. Besides, he himself admits that atonement by sacrifices was granted for certain even deliberate sins (p. 135), which all certainly are not to be regarded as light or imaginary frailties.

units.la: Neque id docetur illis locis, quibus aut pro peccatis בשגגה per errorem commissis, aut ἀγνοήματα ignorantiis sacrificia aut instituta, aut oblata fuisse, dicuntur. Num. xv. 25. Hebr. ix. 7. Socin. part. ii. cap. xii. Nam, pro illis peccatis; ergo non pro gravibus? negatur. Siquidem & omnia, & gravia peccata etiam ex errore & ignorantia committuntur, qualia recenseri vidimus in catalogo peccatorum, pro quibus sacrificia praescripta. Inde conjungitur, Hebr. v. 2, τοῖς ἀγνοοῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις. & Christi crucifixio dicitur a quam multis κατὰ ἄγνοιαν facta, Petro. Act. iii. 17. 1 Tim. i. 13. ὅτι ἀγνοῶν ἐποίησα. Ephes. iv. 18. διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τὴν οὖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς, διὰ τὴν πώρωσιν τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν. 1 Pet. ii. 15. τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀφρόνων ἀγνωσίαν. 23. eratis ut ἀπειθεῖς, πλανώμενοι. Tit. iii. 2. eramus olim & nos ἀνόητοι, ἀπειθεῖς, πλανώμενοι, servientes cupiditatibus & voluptatibus variis. 11 Pet. ii. 12. ἐν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσι βλασφημοῦντες. Similiter de nobis consideratis ante redemtionem, eramus infirmi, & improbi, ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν καὶ ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν Christus mortuus. Rom. v. 6. Non sequitur ergo, pro ignorantiis, vel infirmitatibus fuerunt vetera sacrificia; ergo non pro peccatis gravibus. Similiter & de peccatis in genere, atque gravioribus dicitur שָׁגָה[?]. Psalm. cxix. 21. Perdis superbos, maledictos הַשֹּׁגִים מִמִּצְוֹתֶיךָ aberrantes a praeceptis tuis. verf. iii. Prov. xix. 27. לִשְׁגוֹת aberrare a sermonibus scientia. Jesa. xxviii. 7. veruntamen isti vino errant שָׁגוּ, & potu inebriante oberrant: praeses ac Prophetae errant potu inebriante. absorbentur a vino; oberrant prae potu inebriante, errant in functione videntis, titubant in judicatione.
units.tr: Nor is this taught by those passages which say that sacrifices were instituted or offered for sins committed through error [בשגגה, bishgagah], or for ignorances [ἀγνοήματα]. Num. xv. 25. Heb. ix. 7. Socinus, part ii, ch. xii. For the argument runs: these sacrifices were for those sins; therefore not for grave ones? This is denied. For all sins, even grave ones, are committed through error and ignorance, as we saw in the catalogue of sins for which sacrifices were prescribed. Hence Heb. v. 2 joins the two: [τοῖς ἀγνοοῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις] "to those who are ignorant and going astray." Peter says that Christ's crucifixion was done by many [κατὰ ἄγνοιαν] "in ignorance." Acts iii. 17. 1 Tim. i. 13: [ὅτι ἀγνοῶν ἐποίησα] "because I did it in ignorance." Eph. iv. 18: [διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τὴν οὖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς, διὰ τὴν πώρωσιν τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν] "because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts." 1 Pet. ii. 15: [τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀφρόνων ἀγνωσίαν] "the ignorance of foolish men." 1 Pet. ii. 23: you were as the disobedient [ἀπειθεῖς], wandering [πλανώμενοι]. Tit. iii. 2: "we ourselves too were once foolish [ἀνόητοι], disobedient [ἀπειθεῖς], going astray [πλανώμενοι], serving our desires and various pleasures." 2 Pet. ii. 12: [ἐν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσι βλασφημοῦντες] "blaspheming in the things they do not understand." Similarly, of us as we were before redemption, when we were weak and ungodly, Christ died [ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν καὶ ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν] "for the ungodly." Rom. v. 6. It does not follow, therefore, that because the old sacrifices were for ignorances or infirmities, they were not for grave sins. Likewise, sins in general, and the more grave ones, are called [שָׁגָה, shagah]. Ps. cxix. 21: "You rebuke the proud and the cursed, who [הַשֹּׁגִים מִמִּצְוֹתֶיךָ, hashogim mimmitzvotecha] wander from your commandments." Verse iii. Prov. xix. 27: [לִשְׁגוֹת] "to wander from the words of knowledge." Isa. xxviii. 7: "But these also [שָׁגוּ, shagu] err through wine, and are led astray through strong drink: the priest and the prophet err through strong drink; they are swallowed up by wine, they go astray through strong drink, they err in seeing visions, they stumble in giving judgment."

units.la: 11. Objicit Socinus, part. ii. cap. x. Paulus Act. 13. 39. ait, in Christum credentes justificari ab omnibus, a quibus lex Mosis justificare non poterat; satis indicans, a quibusdam levioribus tantum, ut ipsosmet Iudaos, quos alloquebatur, optime novisse ibidem innuit, per Mosis legem justificationem contigisse: sed per Christi fidem omnium, etiam gravissimorum, delictorum remissionem dari. Resp. In loco Act. ἀπὸ πάντων, non significat ab aliquibus justificationem illos consecutos per legem Mosis, & non per Christum, sed ab omnibus quibus ἀπὸ πάντων ὧν non potuerunt redimi per Mosem, in Christo liberari. Non fit discrimen peccatorum, vel divisio inter Mosem & Christum, ut ab aliis Moses, ab aliis Christus expiarit: sed soli Christo omnia attribuuntur, ut ab iis solvat, quum ab ipsis non potuerint justificari per Mosem. Sensus est, quod qui a nullis potuerunt per legem absolvi, ab omnibus justificati sint per Christum. Qua ratione dicitur, πᾶσα σὰρξ omnis caro non justificatur ex lege, id est, nulla. Rom. iii. 20. Ad quae etiam hoc observandum, in textu non dici a quibuscunque non potuistis in lege Mosis justificari, ab iis &c. sed in isto quicunque credit justificatur: ut oppositio non fit inter alia & alia peccata, quae vel Mose, vel Christo expientur, sed ut omnium expiatio, quorum nulla per Mosem contigit, per Christum haberi significetur.
units.tr: 11. Socinus objects, part ii, ch. x: Paul says in Acts 13:39 that those who believe in Christ are justified from all things from which the law of Moses could not justify them. This sufficiently indicates that justification came through the law of Moses only from some lighter sins, as he also hints in the same place, which the Jews he was addressing knew very well; but through faith in Christ the remission of all sins, even the most grievous, is given. Answer: In the phrase of Acts, [ἀπὸ πάντων], it does not mean that some were justified by the law of Moses and not by Christ. It means "from all things" [ἀπὸ πάντων ὧν], from which they could not be redeemed through Moses, are set free in Christ. There is no distinction of sins, nor a division between Moses and Christ, as if Moses expiated some sins and Christ others. Rather, all things are attributed to Christ alone, so that he releases from those things from which they could not be justified by Moses. The sense is that those who could be absolved by the law from none have been justified from all by Christ. In the same way it is said that [πᾶσα σὰρξ] "all flesh is not justified by the law," that is, no one is. Rom. iii. 20. On this point it should also be observed that the text does not say "by those things from which you could not be justified in the law of Moses, by these," and so on, but "in this one everyone who believes is justified." So the contrast is not between one sin and another, some to be expiated by Moses and others by Christ. Rather, it is meant to show that the expiation of all sins, none of which came through Moses, is to be had through Christ.

units.la: Quaestio tertia, & quod sacrificia V. Teft. peccata nulla verè expiarint, vid. κατὰ συνείδησιν, probatur 1. ex Hebr. ix. 9. dona & hostia offeruntur, μὴ δυναμένη κατὰ συνείδησιν τελειῶσαι τὴν λατρεύοντα[?]. Cap. x. 1. 3. 4. Alioqui desiissent offerri, propterea quod cultores, semel purificati, nullorum peccatorum amplius sibi essent conscii. At in istis repetita mentio peccatorum quotannis. Ἀ δύνατον γὰρ[?] impossibile enim est sanguinem taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata. 11. Omnis igitur sacerdos adstabat quotidie sacro ministerio defungens, & easdem saepius offerens hostias, quae nequaquam possunt auferre peccata, αἵτινες ἀδύνατοι δύνασθαι[?] περιελεῖν ἁμαρτίας. 11. Solius Christi est, eique soli in Scripturâ attribuitur, expiare sanguine suo peccata. Hebr. x. 5. ideoque veniens in mundum dixit: hostiam & oblationem non voluisti, &c. ecce venio, ut faciam, ô Deus, voluntatem tuam. Aufert primum, ut alterum statuat. In quâ voluntate sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Christi semel. Cap. ix. 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. Christus autem Pontifex factus futurorum bonorum, per melius & perfectius tabernaculum, non manufactum, id est, non hujus factura. Neque per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum, verum per proprium sanguinem semel in Sancta ingressus est, aeterna redemtione inventa. Si enim sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & cinis juvencae adspergens inquinatos, sanctificat ad carnis puritatem: quanto magis sanguis Christi qui per Spiritum aeternum obtulit semetipsum inculpatum Deo, emundabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus, ad colendum Deum vivum? Quibus docemur. i. sacrificia & sanguinem animalium non mundasse conscientiam à peccatis. ii. valuisse tantummodò ad externam quandam, caeremonialem, & carnis puritatem. iii. Neque potuisse quid ultra. iv. Illud verò solius Christi, ejusque sanguinis esse proprium, ut à peccatis expurget, & hominum emundet conscientias.
units.tr: The third question, that the sacrifices of the Old Testament truly expiated no sins, namely in conscience [κατὰ συνείδησιν], is proved first from Heb. ix. 9, where gifts and sacrifices are offered which [μὴ δυναμένη κατὰ συνείδησιν τελειῶσαι τὴν λατρεύοντα] "cannot make the worshipper perfect as regards the conscience." Ch. x. 1, 3, 4: otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, because the worshippers, once purified, would no longer have any consciousness of sins. But in these sacrifices there is a repeated mention of sins every year. [ἀδύνατον γὰρ] "For it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins." 11: "Every priest therefore stood daily, performing his sacred ministry, and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins [αἵτινες ἀδύνατοι δύνασθαι περιελεῖν ἁμαρτίας]." Heb. x. 5 and following: it is Christ alone who expiates sins by his blood, and this is attributed to him alone in Scripture. Therefore, coming into the world, he said: "You did not desire sacrifice and offering," and so on, "Behold, I come to do your will, O God." He takes away the first, that he may establish the second. "By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ once for all." Ch. ix. 11-15: "But Christ, being come as high priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, entered once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption. For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctify to the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" From these passages we are taught: i. that the sacrifices and the blood of animals did not cleanse the conscience from sins; ii. that they availed only for a certain external, ceremonial purity of the flesh; iii. that they could accomplish nothing further; iv. that it is the proper work of Christ alone, and of his blood, to purge from sins and cleanse the consciences of men.

units.la: Denique quod Christus etiam in terris sacerdos fuit, & sui sacrificium Deo in cruce obtulit, sanguinem fundens, probatur. i. quia, uti est Hebr. v. 1. omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumtus, pro hominibus constituitur apud Deum, ut dona efferat & hostias pro peccatis. non in coelis hoc, sed in terrâ. Atqui illud in genere dicitur de Pontificibus, introductionis loco, ut ad Christum adaptetur. ii Hebr. vii. 26. Talis nos decuit Pontifex sanctus, insons, immaculatus, segregatus à peccatoribus, & excelsior factus coelis. Ergo antequam in coelos adscendit, quando insons, sanctus, &c. sacerdos etiam fuit. iii. Quod secundum ordinem Melchisedeci Christus sacerdos, hic in terris fuit. Hebr. vii. 3. sine patre, sine matre, sine genealogia, &c. ii. qua necessitas secundum ordinem Melchisedeci alium exsurgere ἀνίστασθαι[?] sacerdotem? & verf. 15. in terris hoc intelligitur, non in coelo. iv. Ubi est oblatio, & sacrificium, ibi sacerdos: atqui in terris & in cruce Christi fuit oblatio: ergo. Ubi hostia mactatur, & ejus funditur sanguis, ibi quoque sacrificium: sed Christi corpus κλώμενον[?] fractum fuit, & sanguis αἷμα ἐκχυνόμενον[?] in cruce. Luc. xxii. 19. 20. 1 Cor. xi. 24. 25. ergo. Ephes. v. 2. quemadmodum Christus dilexit nos, & semetipsum tradidit pro nobis oblationem & hostiam Deo, in odorem suavitatis. In odorem suavitatis, & hostiam esse, Deo, sacrificium indicant: atqui id fuit Christus tum, quando, nos impensi-fime sime diligens, seipsum tradidit, pro nobis, vid. in mortem. Sensus loci est, inquit Socinus part. 11. cap. xv. Christum ita nos dilexisse, ut & seipsum pro nobis in mortem tradiderit. Ergo non quod Christus oblatio fuerit nonnisi morte sua interveniente, ut primo ad illum locum respondit; sed in ipsa quoque morte. Miserumque effugium, quod secundo loco adfert, dixisse se quidem in epistola ad Hebraeos, oblationem Christi significari in coelis quam peregit demum, non autem ad universa divinorum auctorum scripta se id retulisse. Nam sive hic, sive ibi ita sumatur, dummodo oblationem sacerdotalem peregerit etiam Christus in morte, hoc satis nobis est.
units.tr: Finally, that Christ was also a priest on earth, and offered his sacrifice to God on the cross by shedding his blood, is proved as follows. i. Because, as Heb. v. 1 says, "every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men before God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins," this is not done in heaven but on earth. Yet this is said in general of high priests, by way of introduction, so that it may be applied to Christ. ii. Heb. vii. 26: "Such a high priest became us: holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens." Therefore, before he ascended into the heavens, when he was holy, harmless, and so on, he was also a priest. iii. That Christ was a priest after the order of Melchizedek means that he was a priest on earth. Heb. vii. 3: "without father, without mother, without genealogy," and so on. ii. "What need was there that another priest should arise [ἀνίστασθαι] after the order of Melchizedek?" And verse 15: this is to be understood of the earth, not of heaven. iv. Where there is an offering and a sacrifice, there is a priest. But on earth, and on the cross of Christ, there was an offering. Therefore there was a priest. Where a victim is slain and its blood is poured out, there is also a sacrifice. But Christ's body was [κλώμενον] broken, and his blood [αἷμα ἐκχυνόμενον] poured out, on the cross. Luke xxii. 19, 20; 1 Cor. xi. 24, 25. Therefore Christ was a sacrifice. Eph. v. 2: "as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour." That he was an offering and a sacrifice to God, in a sweet-smelling savour, is shown by the fact that he did this when, loving us most exceedingly, he gave himself up for us, that is, to death. Socinus, part ii, ch. xv, says: "The sense of the passage is that Christ so loved us that he even gave himself up for us to death." So it is not that Christ was an offering only when his death intervened, as he first answered on that passage. Rather, he was an offering in his very death. And the wretched escape he offers next, that he indeed said in the epistle to the Hebrews that the offering of Christ is signified as that which he performed in heaven at last, but that he did not apply this to all the writings of the divinely inspired authors, is no help to him. For whether this is understood here or there, it is enough for us that Christ also performed the sacerdotal offering in his death.

units.la: Denique in σωτηρίᾳ[?] sermonis latibulum reperit, nempe non dici a Paulo, Christum obtulisse se Deo pro nobis, sed semetipsum tradidisse pro nobis quidem, in mortem scilicet, at non tradidisse προσφορὰν ἡ θυσίαν Deo, &c. quare non conjungendum esse παρέδωκεν cum voce προσφορὰν. Sensus igitur huius loci est, inquit, Christum ita nos dilexisse, ut seipsum pro nobis in mortem tradiderit. Deinde, ut Ephesii ad singulare hoc Christi facinus imitandum magis accendantur, per oppositionem subjungitur, hanc ipsius Christi eximiam charitatem, hoc ipsius egregium opus fuisse Deo oblationem & hostiam gratissimam. Resp. 1. locus ita habet, ἡ παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν προσφορὰν ἡ θυσίαν τῷ θεῷ, εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας. nulla distinctio ponitur, nedum tanta, inter παρέδωκεν & προσφοράν. Hoc ergo primum frustra. 11. Sit, ut Tigurini, & Castellio, adde si vis, & alii intercisum fecerint, non tamen ad divellendum eousque sensum & rem eandem hoc textu comprehensam. 111. Si hoc nusquam diceretur, neque verum ulla ratione esset, Christum fuisse pro nobis προσφορὰν ἡ θυσίαν; sed jam istud adeo multis Scripturae testimoniis docetur, ut nec Adversarii quidem negare sustineant. Heb.ix. ult. si Christus semel προσενεχθεὶς, ut multorum ferret peccata. & cap.x. 10· διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς τοῦ σώματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐφάπαξ. 12. αὐτὸς δὲ μίαν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν προσενέγκας θυσίαν. 14. Μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους. iv. Quorsum ergo divellit in textu ea, quae Scriptura, & res ipsa pro individuis habent, factum Christi, actio, seu oblatio, & quod oblatum, Christus ipse? illud erit προσφορά, & θυσία, non item istud? certe utrumque, & hoc, propter illud. v. Neutiquam Apostolo est propositum, Ephesios ad singulare hoc Christi facinus, quale pro nobis edidit, incitare, quod impossibile, & proinde vanum fuisset: sed in genere, ad amorem mutuum. Quare corruit, quae hoc praetextu nititur, coacta nimis expositio. vi. Quid, annon Christus seipsum pro nobis in mortem tradidit? & hoc Deo esse oblationem & hostiam gratissimam, negandum erit? negabis ergo, ipsam Christi mortem, & traditionem sui in eam, fuisse oblationem & gratam hostiam pro nobis? cui, nisi Deo? Negare autem illud nescio quomodo quis sustineat? Quum & illud scriptura, & hoc, praeter ipsam, rei natura satis ostendat. Manet ergo, utcunque magna opera & impudentia textum torqueas, nostrum semper ex eo argumentum, vid. quod Christus in morte oblatio fuit & sacrificium, quare & sacerdos Opt. Maximusque. Socinus, cap. xx. pag. 175.
units.tr: Finally, he finds a hiding-place in the phrase σωτηρίᾳ [σωτηρίᾳ], namely that Paul does not say Christ offered himself to God for us, but that he gave himself up for us, that is, to death, and did not give up an offering or sacrifice [προσφορὰν ἢ θυσίαν] to God. Therefore, he says, παρέδωκεν should not be joined with the word προσφορὰν [προσφορὰν]. "The sense of this passage, then, is that Christ so loved us that he gave himself up to death for us. Next, so that the Ephesians may be more fired up to imitate this singular deed of Christ, it is added by way of contrast that this outstanding love of Christ, this remarkable work of his, was to God an offering and a most acceptable sacrifice." Reply. First, the text reads: "who gave himself up for us as an offering or sacrifice to God, for a fragrant odour" [ἡ παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν προσφορὰν ἢ θυσίαν τῷ θεῷ, εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας]. No distinction is made here, much less such a great one, between παρέδωκεν and προσφοράν. So this first point is in vain. Second, grant that the Tigurines, Castellio, and, if you like, others have made a break in the text; still, that does not justify tearing apart the sense and the one matter embraced in this text. Third, if this were said nowhere, and were in no way true, that Christ was for us an offering or sacrifice [προσφορὰν ἢ θυσίαν]? But this is taught by so many testimonies of Scripture that even the opponents do not venture to deny it. Heb. 9 at the end: Christ, once offered [ἅπαξ προσενεχθείς], to bear the sins of many; and ch. 10:10: through the offering [προσφορᾶς] of the body of Jesus Christ once for all [ἐφάπαξ]; v. 12: but he, having offered one sacrifice [μίαν ... θυσίαν] for sins; v. 14: For by one offering [μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ] he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified. Fourth, why then do you tear apart in the text what Scripture and the thing itself regard as one: the deed of Christ, the action or offering, and the thing offered, Christ himself? Surely the offering and sacrifice is the one, and not the other too? Certainly both, and the one because of the other. Fifth, it is by no means the Apostle's purpose to stir the Ephesians to imitate this singular deed of Christ, such as he performed for us; that would be impossible, and so pointless. Rather, he speaks in general, of mutual love. Hence the forced exposition that rests on this pretext collapses. Sixth, is it not the case that Christ gave himself up for us to death? And must it be denied that this was to God an offering and a most acceptable sacrifice? Will you deny, then, that Christ's death itself, and his surrender of himself to it, was an offering and an acceptable sacrifice for us? To whom, if not to God? But how anyone can bring himself to deny that, I do not know, since both Scripture and the very nature of the matter, apart from the text itself, show it plainly. So it remains that, however greatly you twist the text with labour and impudence, our argument from it stands: that Christ in death was offering and sacrifice, and therefore also the best and greatest priest. Socinus, ch. 20, p. 175.

units.la: Hebr. vii. 27. Qui non necesse habet quotidie, &c. pro peccatis hostias offerre: hoc enim fecit semel, semetipsum offerens. Semetipsum nimirum semel in cruce obtulit: ibi victima, & sacerdos. Cap. ix. 28. Ita Christus semel oblatus ἅπαξ προσενεχθεὶς[?] ut multorum peccata auferret, secundo sine peccato videbitur. Tum quando cum peccatis visus, sibi imputatis, semet obtulit. Quod in terra fuit, praesertim quum in cruce penderet: non in coelo. Cap. x. 10. per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel. Oblatio corporis intelligitur in cruce facta, quando fuit τὸ σῶμα, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον. Luc. xxii. 19. Atque ibi se semel obtulit, qui in coelo se non semel praesentat, sed continuo. Hebr. x. 12. ipse autem μίαν unam pro peccatis offerens hostiam, in perpetuum sedit ad dextram Dei. verf. 14. Oblatio hostiae sessionem ejus antecedit, non sequitur. Illud semel, hoc in perpetuum est.
units.tr: Heb. 7:27: "who has no need daily, etc., to offer sacrifices for sins; for this he did once, offering himself." Namely, he offered himself once on the cross: there he was both victim and priest. Ch. 9:28: "So Christ, offered once [ἅπαξ προσενεχθείς], to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time without sin." Then, when he was seen with sins imputed to him, he offered himself. This happened on earth, especially while he hung on the cross, not in heaven. Ch. 10:10: "through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once." The offering of the body is understood to have been made on the cross, when it was the body which is given for you (Luke 22:19). And there he offered himself once, he who in heaven presents himself not once but continually. Heb. 10:12: "but he, offering one sacrifice [μίαν] for sins, sat for ever at the right hand of God." v. 14: The offering of the victim comes before his session, it does not follow it. The "once" belongs to the one, the "for ever" to the other.

units.la: v. Christus in coelum ingressus fuit, ut in τ̄ κατάπαυσιν αὐτοῦ[?], atque requievit ab operibus suis, quemadmodum à suis, in opere creationis, Deus, testante Apostolo, Hebr. iv. 10. Unde in cruce testatus fuit, consummata fuisse omnia, ὅτι πάντα ἤδη πεπλεσται[?]. Joann. xix. 28. quae est τελείωσις[?], quam toties in epistola ad Hebraeos, Apostolus deprædicat: quare opus oblationis, sacrificii, & sacerdotii non demum exorsus fuit in coelis.
units.tr: v. Christ entered into heaven, to enter into his rest [κατάπαυσιν], and rested from his works, just as God rested from his own works in the work of creation, as the Apostle testifies (Heb. 4:10). Hence on the cross he bore witness that all things were now finished (John 19:28), which is the perfecting [τελείωσις] that the Apostle so often proclaims in the epistle to the Hebrews. Therefore the work of offering, sacrifice, and priesthood did not begin only in the heavens.

units.la: Fatemur quidem, perfici illud continua, quam in coelis peragit, pro nobis intercessione, ad quam vivit nunc in gloria, Hebr. vii. verf. 25. sed hoc complementum est operis in terris inchoati, nituntur que oblatione hic facta. Sacerdotem Christum fatemur in coelis, atque etiamnum esse, sed quoque talem fuisse in terris. Nam & hic obtulit, & pro suis precatus fuit atque intercessit, uti imprimis videre est Joann. xvii. Quemadmodum divina rerum conservatio, post creationem hexaemeri, quieti, ad quam transisse Deus dicitur die septimo, nihil intercedit, nam creationis opus peregerat, & illa tantum est necessaria creatarum rerum, uti loquuntur, manutenentia. Heb. i. 3. sic post dolorem animae, & sui oblationem Christus καθαρισμὸν[?] occupavit, in quo non nova, & quae nunquam antea, sed ea curat applicari & conservari, quae pro nostri redemtione olim laboravit. Ex quibus quam turpis error sit Socini, apparet, asserentis, part. ii. cap. xiii. veram oblationem expiatoriam corporis Christi, quam auctor ad Hebr. sacrificiis illis legalibus opponit, non esse ipsius Christi mortem, sed per mortem ingressum in
units.tr: We indeed admit that what he carries on in heaven, the continual intercession for us, by which he now lives in glory (Heb. 7:25), is perfected; but this is the completion of the work begun on earth, and rests on the offering made here. We confess that Christ is a priest in heaven and is so still, but that he was also such on earth. For he offered here too, and prayed and interceded for his own, as is especially seen in John 17. Just as the divine preservation of things after the creation of the six days does not intervene in the rest to which God is said to have passed on the seventh day, for he had completed the work of creation, and that is only the necessary sustaining, as they call it, of created things (Heb. 1:3); so, after his anguish of soul and his self-offering, Christ entered upon purification [καθαρισμόν], in which he does not bring about new things that never existed before, but takes care that those things which he once laboured for our redemption are applied and preserved. From this we see how base an error Socinus makes, when he asserts (part II, ch. 13) that the true expiatory offering of the body of Christ, which the author of Hebrews sets against those legal sacrifices, is not Christ's death itself, but his entry into

units.la: Utrumque autem quomodo per Christum semetipsum Deo sacrificantem, id est, sanguinem suum per quem in coelum ingressus est, fundentem, &c. cœlum. Quibuscum quomodo convenit, quod alibi dicit, part. II. cap. xxiii[?]. pag. 193. cœpit quidem quodammodo hic in terris Christi sacerdotium, sicut & oblatio cœpit. Sed utrumque in cœlis absolutum fuit? Quod si verè diceret, inchoatum Christi Sacerdotium hic in terris, facilis ad componendam controversiam forer via: sed quodammodo (inquit) cœpit, quæ quid ei significet particula, jam aliquoties audivimus. Dicet forte, præcessisse Christi mortem ad ejus sacerdotium, quemadmodum ad ingressum in cœlum, ubi demum oblationem Christi constituit: in ipsâ verò Christi morte sacerdotium ejus verè situm aut inchoatum fuisse, non dicet.
units.tr: heaven through death. "But how is it that both of these, Christ sacrificing himself to God through the shedding of his own blood, by which he entered heaven, etc." How does this agree with what he says elsewhere (part II, ch. 23, p. 193): "Christ's priesthood indeed began here on earth in a certain way, just as the offering began. But were both completed in heaven?" If he truly said that Christ's priesthood was begun here on earth, the way to settle the controversy would be easy. But he says "in a certain way" it began; we have already heard several times what that particle means to him. Perhaps he will say that Christ's death preceded his priesthood, just as it preceded his entry into heaven, where at last he established Christ's offering; but he will not say that his priesthood was truly located or begun in Christ's very death.

units.la: Atque ita sacerdos Christus in terris fuit, in morte, vel oblatione sui in mortem cruentam, & quemadmodum antiqui sacerdotes typicè, ita Christus verè & plenè, ἑαυτῷ[?] solvens & satisfaciens pro peccatis nostris, ea expiavit, & placatum nobis Deum, ac reconciliatum dedit. Illud Hebræi dicunt כפר. Socinus, part. II. cap. XIII. Usus est autem ea voce redemtionis Scriptor ille ad Heb. pro expiatione, ad exemplum, ut ibi diximus, hebraica vocis copher, quæ & redemtionem, sive redemtionis pretium, & expiationem significat: & propterea, ut supra quoque dictum fuit, possunt commodè loca, quæ de redemptione sanguinis simul facta mentione, loquuntur, de expiatione accipi. præsertim vero locus iste, ubi de ipsorum peccatorum redemtione verba fiunt. Cap. XIX. affirmat verbum istud semper purgandi seu removendi, reatum scilicet, & pœnam peccati, significationem habere. Revera significat expiare, removere peccatum, sed etiam placare, & propitiare. Pagninus, removere iram, removere iniquitatem, & peccatum, expiare. Genes. XXXII. 20. dicebat Jacob, אכפרה placabo vultum ejus במנחה munere quod præcedit ante me, ut postea adspiciam vultum ejus, fortassis suscipiet vultum meum. Exod. XXXII. 32. Prov. XVI. 14. Regis ira nuncius mortis, at vir sapiens יכפרנה placabit eam. Quod est Græcum ἱλάσκεσθαι. Ita כפרת propitiatorium, quod super arcam erat, symbolum propitii Dei, Græcè ἱλαστήριον. Hebr. IX. 5. Qua ratione Christus, illius ἀντίτυπον, vocatur noster ἱλαστήριον. Rom. III. quem proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον, per fidem in sanguine ejus. Scilicet hoc placamine propitiatus nobis Deus. Socinus, part. II. cap. II. ἱλαστήριον, id est, propitiatorium, seu mavis, placamen, sive placamentum; non quia Deum populo Israelitico placaret: sed quia Deus in eo, se propitium populo & placatum præbens, sua responsa dabat; id est, Mosi loquebatur, quæcunque illis significari volebat; uti scriptum est. Exod. XXV. 22. Quo nomine decentissimè hoc loco est Christus à Paulo appellatus. Præterea 1 Joann. IV. 10. & misit filium suum ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Hebr. II. 17. ut misericors esset & fidelis Pontifex τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν in iis quæ apud Deum, εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ. Joann. II. 2. καὶ αὐτὸς ἱλασμός ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν. Quod Hebræi dicunt, כפר על חטאת. Inde est quod ex fœdere Novo, cujus Mediator & fundamentum Christus, Deus promittit, ὅτι ἵλεως ἔσομαι ταῖς ἀδικίαις αὐτῶν. Hebr. viii. 12[?].
units.tr: Thus Christ was a priest on earth, in his death, or in his offering of himself to a bloody death; and just as the ancient priests did so typically, Christ did so truly and fully, paying and satisfying for our sins by himself, and he atoned for them, and gave us God placated and reconciled. The Hebrews call this כפר. Socinus, part II, ch. 13: "That writer to the Hebrews used this word of redemption for expiation, after the example, as we said there, of the Hebrew word copher, which signifies both redemption or the price of redemption, and expiation; and therefore, as was also said above, passages which speak of redemption by blood, while also mentioning forgiveness, can fitly be understood of expiation, especially that passage where the redemption of the sins themselves is spoken of." Ch. 19 affirms that this word always has the meaning of purging or removing, namely the guilt and punishment of sin. In truth it means to expiate, to remove sin, but also to placate and propitiate. Pagninus: "to remove wrath, to remove iniquity and sin, to expiate." Gen. 32:20: Jacob said, I will placate [אכפרה] his face with the gift that goes before me, so that afterwards I may see his face; perhaps he will receive my face. Exod. 32:30; Prov. 16:14: "The anger of a king is a messenger of death, but a wise man will placate it [יכפרנה]." This is the Greek ἱλάσκεσθαι. So also the kapporeth [כפרת], the propitiatory which was above the ark, the symbol of the propitious God, is in Greek ἱλαστήριον (Heb. 9:5). For this reason Christ, its antitype, is called our ἱλαστήριον: Rom. 3: "whom God set forth as a propitiation [ἱλαστήριον] through faith in his blood." Clearly, by this means God is made propitious to us. Socinus, part II, ch. 2: "ἱλαστήριον, that is, propitiatory, or if you prefer, placamen or placamentum; not because it placated God towards the people of Israel, but because God, showing himself propitious and placated to the people in it, gave his answers there; that is, he spoke to Moses whatever he wished to signify to them, as it is written" (Exod. 25:22). "By which name Christ is most fittingly called by Paul in this place." Moreover, 1 John 4:10: "and he sent his Son as a propitiation [ἱλασμὸν] for our sins." Heb. 2:17: "that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in the things pertaining to God, to make propitiation [εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι] for the sins of the people." 1 John 2:2: "and he himself is the propitiation [ἱλασμός] for our sins." What the Hebrews say is כפר על חטאת. Hence it is that in the New Covenant, of which Christ is the Mediator and foundation, God promises that he will be propitious to their iniquities (Heb. 8:12).

units.la: Excipit Socinus, part. ii. cap. ii. nihil inde colligi posse, quam Deum in Christo nobis placatum proponi, non per Christum nobis placatum esse. An continuo inde concludes, à Christo Deum nobis placatum fuisse? Cur non potius, cum de gratia Dei, deque peccatorum condonatione agi videas, inde colliges, Deum per Christum nobis se benignum & placatum ostendisse? &c. Ut ex hoc loco nihil penitus elici possit de placatione aliqua Dei, seu justitia divina per Christum facta; sed tantummodo, si Deum vere, & reipsa placandum habere & experiri velimus, Christo confidendum esse. Resp. Imo in Christo placatus & benignus ostenditur ac proponitur Deus; sed per Christum placatus. Adeo non pugnant illa, aut sibi contrariantur, sed rite & necessario subordinantur. Neque dubium, quin si Deum vere & reipsa placatum experiri velimus, Christo confidendum sit: nempe ei, qui propitium nobis Deum fecit. Quare non exhaurit vim ἱλασμῷ in Christo, qui dicit tantummodo in eo nos Deum placatum habere; & non quoque per Christum placatum nobis redditum. ii. Sic enim ad placandum Deum non plus fecisset Christus, quam olim propitiatorium in arcâ: hoc ostendit exhibuitque Deum placatum, caeremonialiter nimirum & ὡς ἐν τύπῳ, sed Christus revera id effecit, quod illud duntaxat adumbravit & significavit. iii. Quare enim aliàs Christus diceretur propitiatorium in suo sanguine, nisi sanguis ejus propitiationem illam effecisset? quemadmodum & alii sui effectus sanguini adscribuntur. iv. Quemadmodum כפר significationem & vim habet semper activam, expiationis, aut placationis, non nudae declarationis, sic etiam ἱλάσκεσθαι, & ἱλασμός. v. Expressè dicitur, τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, id est, sic expiavit Christus peccata nostra, ut apud Deum, non apud nos: & factâ expiatione placavit Deum nobis, fuerit ἱλασμὸς in iis quae apud Deum pragenda erant. Neque tamen aliquid ex illo loco, de placatione aliqua Dei seu justitia divina per Christum factâ elici potest?
units.tr: Socinus objects, part 2, chapter 2, that nothing can be inferred from this except that God is set forth to us as reconciled in Christ, not that God has been reconciled to us through Christ. Do you at once conclude from this that God was reconciled to us by Christ? Why do you not rather infer, since you see that the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins are being discussed, that through Christ God has shown himself kind and reconciled to us? And so on. So nothing at all can be drawn from this passage about any appeasing of God, or any divine justice satisfied through Christ, but only that, if we wish to have and experience God as truly and actually appeased, we must trust in Christ.
