Reply: Indeed God is shown and set forth as reconciled and kind in Christ, but also as reconciled through Christ. These things do not conflict or contradict one another; they are rightly and necessarily subordinated. There is no doubt that if we wish to experience God as truly and actually reconciled, we must trust in Christ, namely in him who made God favourable to us. Therefore the force of propitiation [ἱλασμός] in Christ is not exhausted by saying only that in him we have God reconciled, and not also that he has been made reconciled to us through Christ. ii. For in that case Christ would have done no more for the appeasing of God than the mercy seat did in the ark of old: it showed and exhibited God as reconciled, ceremonially of course and as in a type [ὡς ἐν τύπῳ], but Christ actually brought about what that only foreshadowed and signified. iii. For why else would Christ be called a propitiatory in his own blood, unless his blood had effected that propitiation? In the same way other effects are also ascribed to his blood. iv. Just as kipper [כפר] always has an active sense and force of expiation or appeasing, and not of mere declaration, so too hilaskesthai and hilasmos [ἱλάσκεσθαι, ἱλασμός]. v. It is expressly said that he was in the things pertaining to God, for the taking away of sins [εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας]; that is, Christ so expiated our sins that the expiation was made before God and not before us, and by making the expiation he appeased God for us, and so he was the propitiation in those things which had to be dealt with before God. Yet can nothing be drawn from that passage about some appeasing of God, or divine justice effected through Christ?

units.la: Atque hæc ad secundum tertiæ classis argumentum, ex eo, quod Christus dicitur esse propitiatorium, & propitiatio nostri apud Deum, quod ostendit, eum nobis Deum placasse & reddidisse propitium atque benignum. Tertium hinc sumitur, quod nos cum Deo verè reconciliavit. Reconciliatos Deo per Christum non quidem negat Adversarius; at reconciliationem ipsam negat, dum Christum nobis Deum reconciliasse, usquam scriptum diffitetur, part. i. cap. ix. quin ei absurdum atque adeo impium vel dicere, vel cogitare, Christo peccata nostra imputata, & ab eo justitiae divinae satisfactum, atque ita Deum nobis reconciliatum esse. Quid ergo? non Deum nobis per Christum, ejusque mortem reconciliatum vult, sed Deum ex se satis placatum, extra & ante Christum, per eum nobis offerre remissionem peccatorum, & reconciliationem sui: atque hoc totum esse: Deum quidem nobis inimicis, non item nos Deo, tanquam nostro adversario, per Christum reconciliari, idcirco reconciliationem per Christum factam non Dei erga nos placationem, sed nostri erga illum conversionem significare; & tantum abesse, ut in reconciliatione hac peragenda Christus nobis Deum placaverit; ut potius eum jam placatum offenderit, & ab eo jam placato ad nos, qui adhuc illius inimici eramus, sibi reconciliandos missus fuerit. Sic confundit nostri reconciliationem, cum conversione, & nisi fimulachrum aliquod reconciliationis, retinet, fecundum dici, non χ̄ τὸ ἐναγές[?]. Quemadmodum nimirum in toto hoc argumento versatur Socinus, ut omnia enervet ac subruat, atque non rem, sed metaphoram retineat redemtionis, expiationis, ita & reconciliationis. Quum tamen reconciliatio natura suâ denotet 1. amicitiae ruptae redintegrationem. 11. inter partem utramque. 111. alteram alteri adversam. 1v. peragendam imprimis apud partem praecipuam, justissimeque offensam. Ille & negare, & invertere omnia, pro more suo, satius habet, ne quid salvum incorruptumque relinquat. Certe per peccatum Deum offendimus gravissime, & nobis fecimus adversarium: peccatis, uti dicitur Jefa. 1x. 2. dirimentibus inter Deum, ac nos, iniquitates vestrae הִיוּ מַבְדִּילִים[?], inter vos & Deum vestrum בֵּינֵיכֶם וּבֵין אֱלֹהֵיכֶם[?], & peccata vestra וְחַטֹּאתֵיכֶם[?] abscondunt faciem à vobis. Quod innumeris praeterea locis confirmari potest. Unde pariter dicimur peccatores esse, inimici Dei, & Christus pro nobis mortuus, ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν, ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν ἀπέθανε. ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν. ἐχθροὶ ὄντες κατηλλάγημεν τῷ Θεῷ[?]. Atque Deus à nobis offensus, ideo nobis etiam infensus, & nos propterea filii irae τέκνα φύσει ὀργῆς, ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποί, dicimur. Ephef. 11.3. Sub irâ Dei esse, cui opponitur, esse sub gratiâ, ἐν χάριτι[?], vid. in Christo: & ira Dei manere super infideles, & inobedientes. Joann. 111. 36. Quo in statu tum inobedientiae, tum irae omnes natura fumus homines. Rom. vi. 32. conclusit Deus omnes εἰς ἀπει-θείαν, ut omnium miseretur. Ista autem Dei ira amovenda fuit, placanda, nosque cum Deo postliminio reducendi in gratiam. Quod Christus egit, Rom. v. 9. justificati nunc per sanguinem ipsius, servabimur per eum ab ira illa. Et nos adducit ad Deum, & Deum ad nos: atque conversio nostri ad Deum, ex illa reconciliatione & placatione oritur. Hinc pro nobis & in terris intercessit apud Patrem, Mediator Christus, Joann. xvii. atque idem in coelis etiamnum peragit, & reconciliationem suâ morte impetratam meritamque confervans, & jugiter applicans. Quod proprium opus atque negotium est ejus, ut Mediatoris. Non quod ira proprie fit in Deo, quae sedanda veniat, illam enim ἀνθρωποπαθῶς[?] de Deo dici, ignorat nemo; sed ut poenae peccatis constitutae primum luendae sint, & auferendae, antequam in gratiam cum Deo redamus. Nec necesse fuit ut actu Christus effet mortuus, antequam ullus gratiam Dei experiretur, sufficiebat sponsorem praestandae aliquando solutionis fidelem esse certumque, cujus vi, uti in moralibus & contractibus civilibus usitatissimum est, ut suam vim habeant etiam ante actualem debiti praestationem, liberati & manumissi sint, quotquot redemti & salvati unquam fuerunt etiam ante. Videamus loca Scripturae, reconciliationem nostri per Christum testantia singula.
units.tr: And this is enough concerning the second argument of the third class, from the fact that Christ is called the propitiatory and the propitiation for us before God, which shows that he has appeased God for us and made him propitious and kind. The third argument is taken from this, that he reconciled us truly to God. The Adversary does not deny that we are reconciled to God through Christ; but he denies the reconciliation itself, while he asserts that it is nowhere written that Christ reconciled God to us (part 1, chapter 9). Indeed he holds it absurd, and even impious, either to say or to think that our sins were imputed to Christ and that satisfaction was made by him to divine justice, and thus that God was reconciled to us. What then? He does not want God to be reconciled to us through Christ and his death, but holds that God, sufficiently appeased of himself, outside and before Christ, offers us through him the forgiveness of sins and his own reconciliation; and that the whole matter is this: God is indeed reconciled to us who are his enemies, but we are not reconciled to God as to our adversary through Christ. Therefore the reconciliation made through Christ signifies not an appeasing of God toward us, but a conversion of ours toward him; and so far is Christ from appeasing God for us in carrying out this reconciliation, that he rather found him already appeased, and was sent by him, already appeased, to reconcile us to himself, who were still his enemies. So he confuses our reconciliation with conversion, and while he retains some image of reconciliation, he keeps (as they say) not the thing itself. This is indeed the whole method of Socinus in this argument: to weaken and undermine everything, and to retain the metaphor of redemption, expiation and likewise reconciliation, but not the thing. Yet reconciliation by its nature denotes: 1. the restoration of a broken friendship; 2. between the two parties; 3. the one being opposed to the other; 4. to be carried out above all before the principal party, the one most justly offended. He prefers, in his usual way, to deny and to overturn everything, so that he may leave nothing safe and uncorrupted. Certainly through sin we have offended God most grievously and made him our adversary. Sins, as it is said in Isaiah 59:2, separate between God and us: your iniquities [הִיוּ מַבְדִּילִים] have separated between you and your God [בֵּינֵיכֶם וּבֵין אֱלֹהֵיכֶם], and your sins [וְחַטֹּאתֵיכֶם] have hidden his face from you. This can moreover be confirmed by countless other passages. Hence likewise we are called sinners, enemies of God, and Christ died for us while we were still weak, for the ungodly [ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν, ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν ἀπέθανε]; while we were still sinners [ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν]; being enemies, we were reconciled to God [ἐχθροὶ ὄντες κατηλλάγημεν τῷ Θεῷ]. And God, offended by us, is therefore also hostile to us, and we are accordingly called children of wrath [τέκνα φύσει ὀργῆς], as the rest are (Ephesians 2:3). To be under the wrath of God is opposed to being under grace [ἐν χάριτι], that is, in Christ; and the wrath of God remains upon the unbelieving and the disobedient (John 3:36). In this state, through disobedience and through wrath, all of us are by nature men. God has shut up all under disobedience [εἰς ἀπειθείαν] so that he may have mercy on all (Romans 11:32). But that wrath of God had to be removed and appeased, and we had to be restored to grace with God. This Christ accomplished: Romans 5:9, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from that wrath. He brings us to God, and God to us, and our conversion to God arises from that reconciliation and appeasing. Hence Christ the Mediator interceded for us with the Father on earth (John 17), and he still does the same in heaven, both preserving the reconciliation obtained and merited by his death and continually applying it. This is his proper work and business as Mediator. Not that wrath properly exists in God, which must be calmed; for no one is ignorant that such a thing is said of God in human terms [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]. Rather, the penalties established for sins must first be paid and removed, before we are restored to favour with God. Nor was it necessary that Christ should actually have died before anyone experienced the grace of God; it was enough that he was a faithful surety, certain at some time to make payment, by whose power (as is most usual in moral matters and civil contracts) those who were ever redeemed and saved, even before, have their force, and are freed and manumitted even before the actual payment of the debt. Let us look at the passages of Scripture that each testify to our reconciliation through Christ.

units.la: Rom. v. 9. 10. Si enim, cum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii ejus, multo magis reconciliati salvi erimus in vita ipsius. 11. Non vero solum, sed & gloriamur in Deo per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, per quem nunc reconciliationem accepimus. Socinus, part. cap. viii. pag. 52. De reconciliatione igitur quam Deus clementissimus per Christum fecerit, aperte loquitur Paulus; qua nos, qui inimici illius eramus, ei reconciliati sumus, hoc est, ad eum conversi, ejus amici evasimus. Itaque sicar-gumentatur Apostolus: Si Deus, cum adhuc essemus peccatores, & ab ipso aversi cum eo bellum quodammodo gereremus, tanta nos charitate complexus est, ut unigenitum filium suum, ut sibi nos reconciliaret, & duritiem animi nostri emolliret, atque adeo amicos suos faceret, morti tradere voluerit; quanto magis nunc, &c. Atque ita hunc locum elegan-tissime inter cateros veteres Theologos interpretatur Joh.Chrysosthomus.Hac autem interpreta-tione, qua sola, ut statim apparebit vera est, retenta, jam constat, reconciliandi verbum hoc loco, non divina alicui justitia satisfaciendi vim habere, sed nostram tantummodo ad Deum conversionem, quam ipse procuravit, atque hac ratione cum eo renovatam, vel potius initam amicitiam, significare. Resp. 1. Certe reconciliationem Deus per Christum fecit, nam omnia sunt ex ipso. Rom. xi. 36. & sic Christi ordinatio, & missio, & quidquid usquam aut egit, aut passus est, a Deo fuit. Ephes. i. 4. 5. Gal. iv. 4. Rom. viii. 32. sed aliter Deus per Christum operatus salutem & reconciliationem nostram fuit, aliter pro eadem laboravit Christus. Non opposita illa; sed subordinata sunt. ii. Proba istam expositionem tuam, ei reconciliati, id est, ad eum conversi. Hoc, & solum quidem, hic dici? Tum statim subjungere, hanc interpretationem solam veram esse? nihil autem istius probare? Apage istam disputandi, & respondendi rationem. iii. Chrysosthomum adducit. Haec jam non ratio; sed authoritas est. Neque dubitat postea afferere, suam illam se interpretationem ex doctissimorum vi-rorum mente attulisse. Mirum vero, illos homines aliorum testimonia adfetre, qui in hoc gloriantur, quod sese omnibus opponunt? Patrum, interque eos Chrysosthomi: qui si redirent, saedam illorum haeresim non minori cum indignatione & cura rejicerent, ac suorum temporum alias fecerunt, similesque. Et Chrysosthomus quid? num reconciliationem nostri, dixit esse conversionem? in quo summa haeret responsionis: nihil omnino. Dicit, Apostolum suos confirmare, futurorum fide, & spe. Quis negat? exaggerat magnam Christi erga nos charitatem, μέγιστον δεῖγμα ἀγάπης γεγυμνασμένον [?]. Quis repugnat? Dicit, duo hic, & tria, quinimo plura esse, πρῶτον μὲν [?], primum quod mortuus est Christus. Deinde, pro impiis. Tertio, quod reconciliavit, quod servavit, quod justificavit, quod immortales, quod filios effecit & haeredes. Hicne ullum est sententiae aut expositionis Socini, in quo glorietur, fundamentum, vel vestigium? Sed nomen illud Chrysosthomi scilicet commemomemorandum erat, ut id saltem emineret, dum quod adferret aliud, non habebat. iv. Verè Deus magnâ nos charitate complexus est, dum aversos & bellum quasi secum gerentes, per Filium sibi reconciliare voluit; sed hoc longe aliud quid & plus est, quam duritiem animi nostri emollire. Neque ex illâ expositione sequitur id quod infert, vid. reconciliandi verbum non divinae alicui justitiae satisfaciendi vim habere, sed nostram tantummodo ad Deum conversionem denotare. v. Non dicitur, reconciliatio nostri facta, aut renovata cum Deo amicitia per nostram conversionem, aut per aliquid nostrum, omnino non; sed per Christum, ejusque sanguinem & mortem. ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτοῦ. verf. 9. [illegible, ~12 letters] θανάτῳ αὐτοῦ. 10. quia Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανε[?]. s. 7. 8. vi. Reconcilia-re, fateor, per se non significat satisfacere, sed placare offensum, & in gratiam cum eo reducere peccantem. Quod in hoc negotio factum fuisse per Christi satisfactionem, multis nunc comprobavimus. vii. Atque illud in textu nostro docetur satis clare, ubi quodcunque in hac relatione necessarium, occurit; nos inimici Dei. verf. 10. in Dei gratiam & pacem adducti, verf. 1. pacem habemus apud Deum, per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum. 2. per quem & accessum habemus fide in gratiam istam, in qua stamus. Per & propter sanguinem, ac mortem Christi. verf. 6. 7. 8. 8. 10. Si enim cum inimici essemus reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii ejus: multo magis reconciliati, salvi erimus in vita ipsius. Atque illa est vera & propria reconciliatio; non autem nostra ad Deum, per resipiscentiam, conversio.
units.tr: Rom. v. 9, 10. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved in his life. 11. And not only so, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation. Socinus, part. ch. viii, p. 52: Paul speaks plainly of the reconciliation which the most merciful God effected through Christ, by which we, who were his enemies, have been reconciled to him, that is, have turned to him and become his friends. So the Apostle reasons thus: If God, when we were still sinners and turned away from him, and were in a sense waging war against him, embraced us with such love that he was willing to deliver up his only-begotten Son to death, so that he might reconcile us to himself, soften the hardness of our hearts, and so make us his friends; how much more now, etc. And in this way the Chrysostom, among the other ancient theologians, most elegantly interprets this passage. With this interpretation retained, which alone, as will shortly appear, is true, it is now plain that the word reconciling in this place does not have the force of satisfying any divine justice, but signifies only our conversion to God, which he himself brought about, and the friendship renewed, or rather begun, with him in this way. Reply. 1. Certainly God effected the reconciliation through Christ, for all things are from him (Rom. xi. 36); and so Christ's appointment and mission, and whatever he did or suffered anywhere, was from God (Eph. i. 4, 5; Gal. iv. 4; Rom. viii. 32). But God worked our salvation and reconciliation through Christ in one way, and Christ laboured for the same end in another way. These are not opposed, but subordinate. 2. Prove your exposition, that to them reconciled, that is, turned to him. Is this, and this alone, what is said here? And then do you immediately add that this interpretation alone is true, while proving nothing of the kind? Away with such a method of arguing and answering! 3. He brings forward Chrysostom. This is not an argument but an appeal to authority. Nor does he hesitate afterwards to assert that he brought forward his own interpretation from the mind of most learned men. But is it strange that those men should cite the testimony of others, who glory in this, that they oppose themselves to all? Of the Fathers, and among them Chrysostom, who, if they returned, would reject that heresy of theirs with no less indignation and care, and who have made others like them in our own times. And what does Chrysostom say? Did he say that the reconciliation of us is conversion? On this the whole weight of the reply rests: he said nothing of the kind. He says that the Apostle strengthens his readers by faith and hope in things to come. Who denies it? He magnifies Christ's great love towards us, μέγιστον δεῖγμα ἀγάπης γεγυμνασμένον [?]. Who opposes it? He says that here there are two things, and three, and indeed more: πρῶτον μὲν [?], first, that Christ died; then, for the ungodly; thirdly, that he reconciled, that he saved, that he justified, that he made us immortal, sons and heirs. Is there any foundation or trace in this of Socinus's exposition, in which he might glory? But the name of Chrysostom had to be mentioned, of course, so that at least this might stand out, since he had nothing else to bring forward. 4. It is true that God embraced us with great love when, although we were turned away and as it were waging war against him, he willed to reconcile us to himself through the Son; but this is something quite different and more than softening the hardness of our hearts. Nor does it follow from that exposition what he infers, namely that the word reconciling does not have the force of satisfying any divine justice, but denotes only our conversion to God. 5. It is not said that the reconciliation of us was made, or friendship renewed with God, through our conversion, or through anything of ours at all; but through Christ, and his blood and death: ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτοῦ [in his blood], v. 9; [illegible] θανάτῳ αὐτοῦ [by his death], v. 10; because Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανε [Christ died for us], vv. 7, 8. 6. I admit that to reconcile does not in itself mean to satisfy, but to appease the one offended and bring back into favour the one who has sinned. That this was done in this business through Christ's satisfaction we have now shown by many proofs. 7. And this is taught quite clearly in our text, where whatever is necessary in this relation occurs: we, enemies of God (v. 10), are brought into the grace and peace of God (v. 1): we have peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ; through whom we also have access by faith into this grace in which we stand. It is through and on account of the blood and death of Christ (vv. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10): For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved in his life. That is the true and proper reconciliation; not our conversion to God through repentance.

units.la: 11 Cor. v. 18. & seq. Omnia autem ex Deo, qui reconciliavit nos sibi per Iesum Christum, dedit que nobis ministerium reconciliationis, quandoquidem Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputans eis peccata ipsorum. Socinus: Ex his verbis liquet primum, ipsum Deum fuisse, qui nos per Christum sibi reconciliavit. Quis vero negat? Pergit: & idcirco reconciliationem per Christum factam, non Dei erga nos placationem, sed nostri erga illum conversionem, unde stabilis cum eo amicitia consecuta fuerit, significare. Hoc autem probet. & tantum abesse, ut in reconciliatione hac peragenda Christus nobis Deum placaverit; ut potius eum jam placatum esse tenderit, & ab eo jam placato ad nos, qui adhuc illius inimici eramus, sibi reconciliandos misit. Non probat illud, quod probandum erat. Non id, quod Christum Deum nobis non placavit; vel, quod reconciliatio nostri nil praeter conversionem ad Deum denotet. Christus Deum placatum ostendit, sed vi oblationis, ac satisfactionis suae praestandae.
units.tr: 2 Cor. v. 18, and following: But all things are of God, who has reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation; since God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not imputing to them their sins. Socinus: From these words it is clear, first, that it was God himself who reconciled us to himself through Christ. Who denies it? He goes on: and therefore the reconciliation made through Christ signifies not God's appeasing towards us, but our turning towards him, whence a stable friendship with him followed. But let him prove this. And so far is it from being the case that in carrying out this reconciliation Christ appeased God for us, that rather he showed that God was already appeased, and sent him, from the God already appeased, to reconcile us, who were still his enemies, to himself. He does not prove what needed proof: that Christ did not appease God for us, or that the reconciliation of us signifies nothing beyond conversion to God. Christ shows God to be appeased, but by the power of his offering and of the satisfaction he rendered.

units.la: Socinus: deinde reconciliationis modo, ne quod dubium superfit, exprimitur, quandoquidem, inquit, Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, &c. Vides, quo pacto nos sibi reconciliaverit Deus per Christum; nimirum scelera nostra, ut per Hieremiam praedixerit, nobis literaliter condonando. Resp. Hoc nihil pugnat cum satisfactione, vel reconciliatione nostri cum Deo, per satisfactionem. Nam quia nos non satisfacimus, atque interim peccavimus, nobis certe remittuntur peccata, quamvis pro illis divinae justitiae, ab alio, quam nobis, fit satisfactum.
units.tr: Socinus: Then, lest any doubt remain, the manner of reconciliation is expressed: since, he says, God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, etc. You see how God reconciled us to himself through Christ, namely by forgiving our sins to us literally, as he foretold through Jeremiah. Reply: This is in no way inconsistent with satisfaction, or with our reconciliation with God through satisfaction. For since we do not make satisfaction, and yet have sinned, our sins are certainly remitted to us, although satisfaction has been made to the divine justice for them by another, not by us.

units.la: Quod vero inquit, Paulum, cum hic de reconciliatione per Christum facta ex pro-fesso agat, satisfactionem praeteriturum non fuisse. ad id respondemus, primò quidem non sequi, aliquid ideo verum non esse, vel non aliis docéri locis, quod alicubi praetereatur, etiam ubi ex professo de illa materia, in quâ id venerit, quodque omnium fit necessarium, habeatur sermo. Est enim argumentum istud negativum, nil afferens vel concludens, ex uno particulari, eoque negativo. Non etiam exserta hic fit mentio sanguinis Christi, quem tamen in hoc negotio intervenisse Socinus profesus fuit. 11. imo illud etiam hic loci haud leviter Apostolus attigit. Commate ultimo, Eum enim qui non noverat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos efficeremur justitia Dei in illo. Socinus, primum non suo loco haec dicta: nimirum quia non isthic, ubi in Christo mundum reconciliasse dicitur, non imputans eis peccata. Scilicet istud vers. 19. illud 21. Magnum videlicet intervallum, ut non loco suo dicta censenda sint, si non ubi illa de modo reconciliationis Apostolus commemoravit. Annon intermedio illo uno versu sermo de reconciliatione nostri cum Deo continuatur? annon proxime praecedentia verba sunt ista, reconciliemini Deo? Ad quae connectit Apostolus, cum enim qui non novit peccatum, &c.
units.tr: As for what he says, that Paul, when he treats expressly here of the reconciliation made through Christ, would not have passed over satisfaction: to this we reply, first, that it does not follow that something is not true, or is not taught in other places, merely because it is passed over somewhere, even where the discourse is expressly on that subject in which it would have come up and which is necessary for all. For this is a negative argument, establishing or concluding nothing, drawn from one particular instance, and a negative one at that. Nor is there here any express mention of the blood of Christ, which Socinus nevertheless professed had intervened in this business. 11. Indeed the Apostle did not lightly touch upon it here as well. In the last clause: For he who did not know sin, he made to be sin for us, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Socinus: first, these words are not in their proper place: namely because they are not there, where it is said that God in Christ reconciled the world, not imputing to them their sins. That is, verse 19 and verse 21. A great interval, evidently, so that the words should not be counted as in their proper place if they were not where the Apostle mentioned the manner of reconciliation. Does the discourse on our reconciliation with God not continue through that one intervening verse? Are not the words immediately preceding these, be reconciled to God? To which the Apostle joins, For he who knew no sin, etc.

units.la: Praeterea negat peccatum hic denotare hostiam pro peccato, sed hominem pro peccatore ab aliis habitum. Jam antea ad hoc respondimus. Nam hic quidem à Deo id factus dicitur, non ab hominibus aestimatus. Idque pro nobis: quod non istud est, quod alii de Christo fuerunt opinati. Nedum ut hoc ipsum, quodcunque alii censuerunt, fecisset ad nostri in eo justitiam, & non revera ad id quod in Christo, à Deo exhibitum fuit, ut in illo fieremus. Socinus: nam si hostiam pro peccato significaret, quam, obsecro, vim haberent verba illa, qui peccatum non noverat? hanc, certè maximam, quod qui insons omnino, ὅσι[?], ἀκακ[?], ἀμίαν[?], κεχωρισμέν[?] ἀπὸ ἁμαρτωλῶν, noštri piacularis victima fieri voluerit, & imputari sibi omnium nostrum peccata. Debuit quidem hostia pro peccato incontaminata esse, atque purissima. Sed quod eam voluerit fieri Christus, cui nulla cum peccatoribus cognatio, aut commercium, id maximam in eo arguit charitatem. Majorem certe, quam quod Christum simpliciter pro tali ab hominibus haberi Deus, & non talem etiam imputatione esse, voluisset.
units.tr: Moreover, he denies that peccatum here means a sacrifice for sin, and holds that it means a man regarded as a sinner by others. We have already answered this objection. For here Christ is said to have been made this by God, not merely judged so by men. And it was done for us, which is not what others have thought about Christ. Still less did it make Christ, whatever others may have thought, to be our righteousness in him, rather than what was in truth exhibited by God in Christ, so that we might be made righteous in him. Socinus: for if it meant a sacrifice for sin, what, I ask you, would the words "who knew no sin" mean? The answer is this, and it is surely the greatest: that he who was altogether innocent, holy, harmless, undefiled, and separated from sinners [ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἄμιαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν; cf. Heb. 7:26] was willing to become our sacrificial victim for sin, and to have the sins of all of us imputed to him. A sin offering ought indeed to be unstained and most pure. But that Christ, who had no kinship or dealings with sinners, was willing to become this, shows the greatest love in him. Certainly it is greater than if God had merely wished Christ to be regarded by men as such, without his actually being such by imputation.

units.la: Socinus: adde, quod illa interpretatione antithesis manifesta peccati & justitia, eaque pulcherrima & elegantissima, penitus corruit atque dissolvitur. Siquidem haec sine dubio est Pauli mens, Deum ita nos amasse, ut filium suum, qui innocens erat, noštrum causa nocentem judicari & tanquam nocentem, occidi voluerit, ut nos, qui vere nocentes eramus, innocentes, & coram ipso Deo justi haberemur, & tanquam justi, aeternam vitam tandem consequeretur. Resp. Imo non constat oppositio, nisi peccatum & justitia, γίνεσθ[?], vel μισθὸς ἁμαρτίας[?], & δικαιοσύνην, utrumque exponatur de verâ imputatione, quâ & Christus peccatum, seu hostia peccati pro nobis, nos justitia Dei in ipso sumus, & non tantum tales opinione & judicio hominum. Atqui ea Pauli mens est, Christum, ad efficiendam noštri cum Deo reconciliationem, non tantum nostrûm causa nocentem judicatum ab hominibus, sed revera talem à Deo factum fuisse, vid. per imputationem, quandoquidem peccatum nullum noverat; & nos contra, ex vere imputatâ nobis ejus justitia, coram Deo justos reddi: imo hoc illius effectum esse & fructum, ad id enim factus Christus à Deo peccatum fuit, ἵνα ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in ipso. Quemadmodum ergo per veram imputa-tionem justitiae Christi, fumus & habemur justi, à Deo; ita & Christus per veram imputationem peccatorum nostrorum factus est, & habitus à Deo, qui ipse id ἐποίησε fecit, peccatum חטאת, seu hostia pro peccato. Atque uti per illam nos juftifi-cationem, non tanquam justi, sed in Christo vere justi, quin δικαιοσύνη, eaque θεῷ, à Deo habemur, non ab hominibus; ita Christus peccatum fa-ctus, non opinione hominum, quodcumque etiam ii judicarint, sed Deo. Denique quod homines Christum tanquam nocentem judicarunt, id hactenus falsum fuit, quod revera voluerunt Christum in fe peccatorem esse & nocentem. Quod nec Deus proinde fecisse dici potest, neque causa fuisse nostrae in ipso justitiae.
units.tr: Socinus: add that on that interpretation the clear and most beautiful and elegant antithesis between sin and righteousness collapses and is wholly dissolved. For this is without doubt Paul's meaning: that God so loved us that he willed his Son, who was innocent, to be judged guilty for our sake and, as if guilty, to be put to death, so that we, who were truly guilty, might be held innocent and just before God himself, and as just might at last attain eternal life. Answer: No, the opposition does not hold, unless both sin and righteousness, namely "he was made sin" or "the wages of sin" [μισθὸς ἁμαρτίας] and "righteousness" [δικαιοσύνη], are understood of true imputation, by which Christ was made sin, or a sin offering, for us, and we are the righteousness of God in him, and not merely such in the opinion and judgment of men. Now Paul's meaning is that Christ, to bring about our reconciliation with God, was not merely judged guilty by men for our sake, but was in truth made such by God, namely by imputation, since he knew no sin; and that on the other hand we, from his righteousness truly imputed to us, are made just before God. Indeed this is its effect and fruit, for Christ was made sin by God for this very purpose, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him [ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ]. Therefore, just as we are made and held righteous by God through the true imputation of Christ's righteousness, so Christ too was made, and held by God, to be sin, through the true imputation of our sins. God himself did this, and made him sin [חטאת], that is, a sin offering. And just as through that justification we are held by God, not by men, as just, not merely as just but truly just in Christ, indeed as righteousness, and that the righteousness of God; so Christ was made sin, not by the opinion of men, whatever they may have judged, but by God. Finally, the men who judged Christ as if he were guilty were wrong in this, that they really wished Christ to be a sinner and guilty in himself. Nor can it be said that God did so, or that it was the cause of our righteousness in him.

units.la: Socinus : postremo, etiamsi concederetur, vocem peccatum hoc loco hostiam pro peccato significare, non tamen continuo sequeretur, Christum pro peccatis nostris divinae alicui justitiae satisfecisse. Quis enim negat, vel negare potest, Christum pro peccatis nostris mortuum fuisse, atque ea ratione nos peccatorum remif-sionem consecutos? Verum hoc non, quia Deum nobis reconciliaverit, aut ju-ftitiae cuiquam divinae pro nobis satisfecerit, scriptum est; sed quia non aliter quam morte ejus interveniente, id peractum & confectum fuit. Resp. Verborum offuciae, Christum pro peccatis nostris mortuum, ut ea ratione peccatorum re-missionem consequeremur, id est, morte interveniente. at quo modo, quo or-dine causalitatis interveniente? duntaxat ut causâ sine quâ non, vel occasio-ne? Scriptura morti Christi remissionem peccatorum attribuit, tanquam verae & propriae causae meritoriae. Hanc dum negant Adversarii, nihil dicunt, quan-tumvis leviter afferant, morte Christi interveniente redimi nos & salvari.
units.tr: Socinus: Finally, even if it were granted that the word "sin" here means a sacrifice for sin, it would not follow at once that Christ made satisfaction to some divine justice for our sins. For who denies, or can deny, that Christ died for our sins, and that in this way we obtained the forgiveness of sins? But it is not written that he did this because he reconciled us to God, or made satisfaction for us to any divine justice; it is written that this was done and accomplished only by his death intervening. Answer: This is a mere veneer of words: that Christ died for our sins, so that in this way we might obtain forgiveness of sins, that is, with death intervening. But in what way, in what order of causality, does it intervene? Only as a cause without which the effect does not follow, or as an occasion? Scripture ascribes the forgiveness of sins to the death of Christ as a true and proper meritorious cause. While the adversaries deny this, they say nothing, however lightly they put it, when they claim that we are redeemed and saved by the death of Christ intervening.

units.la: II. Christus quando peccatum vocatur, vel hostia piacularis pro peccato, proprie significat, expiare, placare, reconciliare, quae intelligi nec explicari aliter possunt, quam ut Deo, ejusque justitiae satisfactum sit: certe non ut perfunctorie dicatur modo, Christi mortem intervenisse. Nam sic in V.T. mors pecudum etiam intercedebat, aliaque ad reconciliationem obtinendam, sive in V. sive N. Testam. III. Hoc non quia Deum nobis reconciliaverit, inquit Socinus: quod est negare aperte, quod fides catholica de Christo, tum ex hoc, tum ex aliis Scripturae locis, tenet. Non alterius generis reconciliationem in Christo ponit Adversarius, quam in Apostolis, vel Doctoribus aliis, saltem martyribus, qui morte sua interveniente, reconciliationem administrant. Hinc ea Socini verba, quae sequuntur, sermo igitur in ministerium reconciliationis, quibus Deus Apostolos instruxerat, nihil aliud erant, quam homines, non secus ac Christus fecerat, rogare, atque Dei nomine hortari, ut ipsi Deo reconciliari vellent, &c. Reconciliati igitur igitur summus Deo per Christum, Deo per ipsum, & per ejus vicarios Apostolos hortante, ut sibi reconciliari velimus. iv. Hoc in loco quod dicitur, ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, pro Christo ergo legatione fungimur, exponit Socinus ὑπέρ vice Christi, & pro Christo. Et tamen quando Christus dicitur ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν pro nobis mortuus, isthic ὑπὲρ pro, non potest ipsi significare vice, & loco nostro.
units.tr: II. When Christ is called sin, or a sin offering for sin, it properly means to expiate, to appease, to reconcile; these things cannot be understood or explained otherwise than that satisfaction has been made to God and to his justice. Certainly it cannot be said in a merely perfunctory way that the death of Christ intervened. For in the Old Testament too the death of beasts intervened, and other things were used to obtain reconciliation, both in the Old and in the New Testament. III. This not because he reconciled us to God, says Socinus: which is plainly to deny what the catholic faith holds concerning Christ, both from this passage and from other passages of Scripture. The adversary posits no other kind of reconciliation in Christ than in the Apostles or other teachers, or at least the martyrs, who by their death intervening administer reconciliation. Hence those words of Socinus that follow: the word of reconciliation, with which God had furnished the Apostles, was nothing other than men, just as Christ had done, begging and exhorting in God's name that they themselves would be reconciled to God, and so on. Therefore we, reconciled to God through Christ, God exhorting us through him and through his vicars the Apostles, that we should be willing to be reconciled to him. IV. In this place, the phrase on behalf of Christ [ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ] in "we are ambassadors for Christ" Socinus explains as in the place of Christ, and on behalf of Christ. And yet when Christ is said to have died for us [ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν], here the word for [ὑπέρ] cannot mean in place of and in our stead.

units.la: Ephes. II. 13. Nunc autem in Christo Jesu, vos qui quondam eratis longinqui, propinqui facti estis in sanguine Christi. 14. Ipse enim est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum, & medium parietem maceriæ diruit. 15. inimicitiam in carne sua, legem mandatorum in dogmatibus abrogans; ut duos conderet in semetipso in unum novum hominem, faciens pacem, 16. & reconciliaret ambos in uno corpore Deo per crucem, perimens inimicitiam per eam. Socinus, in his sane verbis non agitur de dissidio, quod esset inter Deum, & homines; sed de eo, quod inter gentes & Judæos erat, &c. Nam ita interpretor ego illa verba, ut reconciliaret ambos in uno corpore Deo; ut scilicet significent, non quidem reconciliatos Deo ipsos fuisse, sed inter se. Resp. I. Male quidem istud illi opponit, vel secludit, & rejicit, quasi non & inter se reconciliarit Judæos, ac gentes Christus, & cum Deo. Non sejungenda illa, nedum opponenda, sed in unum conjungenda sunt. 2. Non enim solam inimicitiam amborum inter se urget Apostolus, sed præsertim quidem eam, quam cum Deo habebant omnes. Quod ex toto capite apparet. Verf. 3. & eramus natura filii iræ, quemadmodum & reliqui. Deus vero dives in misericordia. II. 12. 13. Quapropter meminisse, quod vos quondam gentes in carne, eratis eo tempore extra Christum, spem non habentes, & absque Deo in mundo. Nunc vero in Christo Jesu. III. Atque declarat, non modo nunc reductos inter se, sed Deo. ὡς τὸν πατέρα, verf. 11. quoniam utrique per ipsum habemus aditum per unum spiritum ad Patrem. 19. Nempe igitur non amplius estis peregrini, sed concives sanctorum, domestici Dei. 20. Superstructi super fundamentum Apostolorum ac Prophetarum, existente angulari lapide Jesu Christo. 22. In quo & vos una ædificamini, ut sitis domicilium Dei per spiritum. 2v. Quare aperte docet reconciliatos, Deo. verf. 16. & utrosque in uno corpore reconciliaret Deo. v. Per Christi sanguinem, cui non adeo attribuitur, quod gentes inter se unum sunt, quam quod apud Deum tales. 13. At nunc in Christo Jesu, vos qui olim eratis longinqui, propinqui facti estis, per sanguinem Christi. Quomodo longinqui olim, μακρὰν, ξένοι, τῆ παροίκοι, à Deo non minus, quam Israële, ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ: ita nunc per Christum ἐγγὺς facti, οἰκεῖοι, ... per Christi sanguinem. 16. ... vi. quem in sensum, nempe in tota sua latitudine accipi debet, quod Christus pax nostra. Nam per hunc habemus imprimis pacem, & ... verf. 18. 14. ipse est enim pax nostra. 15. faciens pacem. 17. evangelizavit pacem. adde Rom. v. 1. 2. & Luc. iv. 18. 19.
units.tr: Ephesians 2:13: But now in Christ Jesus, you who were once far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. 14: For he is our peace, who has made both one, and has broken down the middle wall of partition, 15: having abolished in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments contained in ordinances; that he might create in himself of twain one new man, so making peace; 16: and that he might reconcile both to God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby. Socinus: In these words there is certainly no question of the discord that existed between God and men, but of that which existed between the Gentiles and the Jews, and so on. For I interpret those words as follows, that he reconciled both in one body to God; that is, they mean that the two were not indeed reconciled to God, but to each other. Answer: I. He is wrong to set this against the other, or to exclude and reject it, as though Christ did not reconcile Jews and Gentiles to each other and also to God. These things are not to be separated, much less set against each other; they are to be joined together into one. 2. For the Apostle is urging not only the enmity between the two groups, but chiefly that enmity which all of them had with God. This appears from the whole chapter. Verse 3: and we were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy. 2:12, 13: Remember that you were at that time Gentiles in the flesh, without Christ, having no hope and without God in the world. But now in Christ Jesus. 3: And he declares that they are now brought back not only to each other but to God, verse 18: for through him we both have access by one Spirit to the Father. 19: So then you are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God. 20: Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone. 22: In whom you also are built together for a habitation of God through the Spirit. 2:1. Therefore he clearly teaches that they are reconciled to God: verse 16, and that he might reconcile both in one body to God. 4. Through the blood of Christ, which is not so much ascribed to the Gentiles being one with each other as to their being such before God. 13: But now in Christ Jesus, you who once were far off are made nigh, by the blood of Christ. As they were formerly far off, [μακρὰν, ξένοι, πάροικοι], not less from God than Israel was, and without God in the world [ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ], so now through Christ they are made near [ἐγγύς], fellow citizens and of the household, through the blood of Christ. 16: that is, in the full extent of its meaning, that Christ is our peace. For through him we have above all peace; and verse 14: for he himself is our peace; 15: making peace; 17: he preached peace. Add Romans 5:1, 2, and Luke 4:18, 19.

units.la: Similis est ratio alterius loci, Col. I. 20. 21. & per ipsum reconciliare omnia in ipsum εἰς αὐτὸν, pacificans per sanguinem crucis ejus, per eum, sive qua in terra sunt, sive qua in cœlis. Et vos cum essetis aliquando alienati & inimici mente in operibus malis, nunc vero reconciliavit. 22. in corpore carnis ejus, per mortem, ut sisteret vos sanctos & irreprehensibiles & inculpatos in conspectu suo. Iterum, juxta priorem expositionem, Socinus: reconciliatio, de qua verf. 20. agitur, nihil aliud est, quam omnium rerum non quidem cum Deo, sed secum ipsis per Christum parta concordia. Imo non tantum ipsos inter se, sed & cum Deo, conciliatos indicat, & quia cum Deo, hinc quoque fuerunt reconciliati inter se. Sed verf. 21. addit Socinus, agi de reconciliatione nostri cum Deo: In quibus verbis cum expresse de ea reconciliatione, quam homines Dei amici sunt facti, agatur, satis constat, supra de alia quam de ea actum esse. Quæ, obsecro, ista consequentia? annon potius pro evidenti habebitur, de eadem reconciliatione agi versu utroque? Sed jam istam suam reconciliationem demum exponit per nostri ad Deum conversionem. Quod antea discussimus. Christus enim a sceleribus nostris, mortuisque operibus ad Deum viventem nos convertit, atque, ut supra visum est, eo pacto in Dei stabilem perpetuamque amicitiam, ex voluntate ejus, nos restituit. Verum aliud est, nos convertere ad Deum, aliud reconciliare cum Deo. Illud in nobis: hoc apud Deum peragitur, pro nobis. Illud per Spiritum, ejusque in nobis efficaciam, istud per sanguinem Christi fit, ejusque meritum. Amicitia illa cum Deo, quæ ex conversione oritur, reconciliatione posterior est, atque ejus sensum & intimationem adfert animo. Denique veram nostri cum Deo, per sanguinem Christi placato, reconciliationem, utroque versu doceri, evincimus, i. quia ea demum vera est reconciliatio, hic haud semel nominata. Jam ipse Socinus dicit, pag. 59. neque vero a sermonis proprietate, nisi manifesta ratio subsit, temere est recedendum. ii. Dicitur Deus per Christum ἀποκαταλλάξαι omnia in ipsum, εἰς αὐτὸν; non ergo tantum inter se. iii. Et pacificasse εἰρηνοποιήσας. Christus autem εἰρήνη pax est non tantum hominum inter se, sed imprimis apud Deum. iv. Et hoc magis per sanguinem crucis ejus, per corpus carnis ejus, per mortem fit, quam illud. v. Nihil ejus quidem in textu est, quod vel inimicitiam notet, aut conjunctionem eorum inter se, quæ Christus reconciliasse dicitur. Reconciliavit secum & cum Deo omnia, sive quæ in terra, sive quæ in cœlo; at non dicitur, discordia inter se. Nempe sive qui in cœlo beati, & Ecclesiæ triumphantis membra, sive qui in terris sunt, reconciliavit omnes Deo, per sanguinem crucis. vi. Initio verf. 21. ϰ&[?], indicio est utrumque versum conjungi, cujus idem thema, & verbum utrobique ἀποκαταλλάξαι. vii. Quique reconciliati, antea τοῖς[?] fuerunt abalienati & inimici mente adversus Deum scilicet; cum quo nunc redierunt in gratiam. Uti enim illi inimici Deo, ita eorum inimicitia jure offensus Deus, proindeque placandus iis, & propitiandus vel conciliandus fuit. Postremo nihil est, quod sanguini Christi, & sanguini crucis ejus, adeo pretioso, digne tribui possit, quam nostri reconciliatio cum Deo. Dilutum est, solum sanguinis Christi ponere interventum, & non veram causalitatem, ac meritum. Itaque non vere, & proprie per ipsum fanguinem Christi pacificatio contigit, sed peripsum Christum, sanguinem suum ejus rei occa-sione fundentem. pag. 61. Horrendum in modum audacter & aperte sanguini Christi illud detrahit, quod frequenter Scriptura & clare eidem attribuit. Non vere & proprie per Christi sanguinem pacificatio nostra contigit, inquit Adversarius: quam ubicunque fere memorat Scriptura, eidem adscribit; vel sanguinis Christi ubi meminit, illum ejus effectum quoque adjungit. Sed, non vere ac proprie. Nos sane vere & proprie tot in locis loquutum Spiritum S. cum Christianis omnibus tuemur: de Scriptura statuant Socdiniani, vel eam contorqueant, prout visum. Sub isto nos umbone tutos credimus. Ullibine Scriptura, vel minimo indicio prodit, innumeris fere locis quum de sanguine Christi verba facit, hunc occasione nostrae reconciliationis fusum? Et tamen id ausus fuit Socinus pluribus locis ingerere, atque sensibus Scripturae supponere. De quo certe nos verius pronunciaverimus, quam quod is de nostra sententia, pag. 55. absurdum, atque adeo impium esse illud vel dicere, vel cogitare.
units.tr: A similar argument applies to another passage, Col. 1:20-21: "and through him to reconcile all things to himself [εἰς αὐτὸν], making peace through the blood of his cross, through him, whether the things that are on earth or the things that are in heaven. And you, who were once alienated and enemies in mind through evil works, but now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh, through death, so that he might present you holy and blameless and irreproachable in his sight." Again, following his earlier explanation, Socinus says: "the reconciliation spoken of in verse 20 is nothing other than a concord of all things obtained through Christ, not indeed with God but among themselves." But the text indicates that they were reconciled not only to one another but also to God, and because they were reconciled to God, they were therefore also reconciled to one another. Yet in verse 21 Socinus adds that the reconciliation of us with God is in view: "since in these words the reconciliation by which men are made friends of God is expressly under discussion, it is quite clear that the earlier verse was about another reconciliation." What kind of inference is this, I ask? Would it not rather be held self-evident that both verses speak of the same reconciliation? But he now at last explains his reconciliation as the conversion of ourselves to God, which we have already discussed. "For Christ turns us from our sins and dead works to the living God, and, as has been seen above, in this way restores us, by his will, to the stable and perpetual friendship of God." But it is one thing to convert ourselves to God, and another to be reconciled to God. The former takes place in us; the latter takes place before God, on our behalf. The former is effected through the Spirit and his working in us; the latter is effected through the blood of Christ and his merit. That friendship with God which arises from conversion comes after reconciliation, and it brings the sense and awareness of it to the mind. Finally, we prove that the true reconciliation of us with God, through the blood of Christ as the propitiation, is taught in both verses. (i) Because that is the true reconciliation, which is named here more than once. Socinus himself says, p. 59: "nor indeed should one depart rashly from the proper meaning of the words, unless a clear reason underlies it." (ii) God is said through Christ to reconcile all things to himself [εἰς αὐτὸν]; therefore not only among themselves. (iii) And to have made peace [εἰρηνοποιήσας]. Christ, however, is peace [εἰρήνη] not only of men among themselves but especially before God. (iv) And this is done more through the blood of his cross, the body of his flesh, and death than through the other. (v) There is nothing in the text that denotes either enmity or the union among themselves of those whom Christ is said to have reconciled. He reconciled all things to himself and to God, whether those on earth or those in heaven; but it is not said that they were in discord with one another. Namely, whether those in heaven who are blessed, and the members of the Church triumphant, or those who are on earth, he reconciled them all to God through the blood of the cross. (vi) At the beginning of verse 21 the word "and" indicates that the two verses are joined; their theme is the same, and the verb in both is to reconcile [ἀποκαταλλάξαι]. (vii) Those who have been reconciled were formerly alienated and enemies in mind against God, that is, with whom they have now been restored to favour. For just as they were enemies of God, so God, rightly offended by their enmity, had to be appeased and propitiated, or reconciled, by them. Lastly, there is nothing that can rightly be ascribed to the blood of Christ, and to the blood of his cross, so precious, than our reconciliation with God. It is said that the blood of Christ merely holds the place of an intermediary, and not a true causality and merit. "Thus it is not truly and properly through the blood of Christ itself that the pacification came about, but through Christ himself, who shed his blood on the occasion of that matter." p. 61. He boldly and openly takes away from the blood of Christ, in a horrible manner, what Scripture frequently and clearly attributes to it. The pacification of us did not truly and properly come about through the blood of Christ, says the Adversary; yet wherever Scripture mentions this pacification, it ascribes it to that blood, or wherever it mentions the blood of Christ, it adds this effect to it. "But not truly and properly." We, indeed, truly and properly maintain, together with all Christians, that the Holy Spirit speaks thus in so many places. Let the Socinians pronounce about Scripture, or twist it as they see fit; under that shield we believe we are safe. Does Scripture anywhere, by even the slightest hint, reveal that when it speaks of the blood of Christ, in almost countless places, that blood was shed on the occasion of our reconciliation? And yet Socinus has dared to thrust this into several places and to impose it on the meaning of Scripture. About this we could pronounce more truly than he does about our view, when he says at p. 55 that "it is absurd, and therefore impious, either to say or to think this."

units.la: Quarta classis argumentorum, quae pro veritate satisfactionis Christi adseri-mus, petitur ex redemtione nostri, quam Christus suo sanguine effecit: hunc in modum: Qui nos vere ac proprie redemit, pretium ejus Deo persolvendo, is divinae justitiae pro nobis satisfecit: atqui Christus nos vere ac proprie rede-mit, pretium ejus Deo persolvendo: ergo pro nobis, divinae justitiae satisfe-cit. Major satis clara: nam uti in vera emtione ac redemtione pretium interce-dit, quod pro redimendo solvitur, & qui quod debetur solvit, is satisfacit: ita pro nobis a maledictione & poenis debitis redimendis pretium qui persolvit ju-stum, is certe etiam satisfecit. Neque Socinus in his haeret: quare pro syno-nymis ponit, pag. 69. Deo, sive justitia divina pro peccatis nostris plene satisfecisse, sive id omne persolvisse, quod nos, propter peccata nostra, solvere debuissemus, si Deus summo jure nobiscum agere voluisset. Sed Minorem negat, nempe Christum nos vere & proprie redemisse, pretiumque ejus Deo persolvisse. Sic enim sententiam proponit suam, in initio part. II. de Servat. cap. 1. redemptionem nostram per Christum factam, esse metaphoricam, idest, in ea peragenda nullum verum pretium inter-venisse, sive nihil cuiquam pro nobis solutum fuisse. Quare de duobus ad hoc argu-mentum erit disputatio, de veritate redemtionis per Christum; & dati pretii: quae utraque Socinus negat, & per metaphoram exponit, pag. 75. ego vero non ita hebetem te esse sat scio, ut verbi redimendi metaphora agnita, non vides etiam eadem metaphora Christum dictum fuisse redemtionis nostrae pretium. Unde in Capitis secundi argumento ita loqui ausus fuit: explicatur diligentius tota redemtionis nostrae per Christum metaphora.
units.tr: The fourth class of arguments, which we advance for the truth of Christ's satisfaction, is drawn from the redemption of us, which Christ accomplished by his blood, and runs thus: He who truly and properly redeemed us, by paying its price to God, has made satisfaction to divine justice for us. But Christ truly and properly redeemed us by paying its price to God. Therefore he has made satisfaction to divine justice for us. The major premise is clear enough: for just as in a true purchase and redemption a price intervenes, which is paid for the redeeming, and whoever pays what is owed makes satisfaction, so whoever pays the just price for us, to free us from the curse and the penalties we owed, has certainly also made satisfaction. Nor does Socinus stick at this point; for he treats as synonyms, at p. 69, "to have fully satisfied God, or divine justice, for our sins, or to have paid in full all that we ought to have paid on account of our sins, had God wished to deal with us by the highest right." But he denies the minor premise, namely that Christ truly and properly redeemed us and paid its price to God. For he puts forward his opinion thus, at the beginning of part II, On Salvation, chapter 1: "our redemption made through Christ is metaphorical, that is, in carrying it out no true price intervened, or nothing was paid to anyone for us." So the dispute on this argument concerns two things: the truth of the redemption through Christ, and the price given; Socinus denies both and explains them by metaphor. At p. 75 he says: "I am quite sure you are not so dull that, once the metaphor of the word redeem is recognised, you do not see that by the same metaphor Christ is called the price of our redemption." Hence in the summary of his second chapter he dared to speak thus: "the whole metaphor of our redemption through Christ is explained more carefully."

units.la: Propriam redimendi significationem expositurus, inquit: redimere aliquem nihil aliud proprie significat, quam eum captivum e manibus illius, qui eum detinet, pretio illi dato, liberare. Atque hoc dico, ut propriam simul significationem verborum Hebraicorum padah & gaal, & Graecorum λυτρῶν, seu λυτρωτής, sive ἀπολυτρῶν, de quibus verbis praecipue nobis vere agendum esset, completar[?]. pag. 69. Bene: sed non tantum captivus e manibus custodis, verum & alii, seu rei, seu obaerati, dato dato pretio, verè redimuntur. Æs alienum dissolvere, hastenus quidem non est redimere aliquem, uti nec liberare; at verò ejus fundamentum, quo dato, liberatio sequitur & contingit. Socinus: propriam autem ejus verbi redimendi significationem intelligo, cum verum pretium intervenit. Verum autem pretium voco non pecuniam, sed quidquid, ut ei satisfiat, qui captivum detinet, datur. Rectè. Atqui Scriptura passim pretium redemtionis, lutrum commemorat, uti & redemtionem ipsam. Quare ergo non hoc, & illud proprie accipiamus? Neque verò à sermonis proprietate, nisi manifesta ratio subsit, temere est recedendum, juxta Socinum ipsum, pag. 60. Nulla autem hic ratio, nedum manifesta, urget, cur à propriâ vocis significatione recedamus, quammulta confirmant. Non modo pretii commemoratio, eaque haud semel, sed oppidò plurimis locis, quibus redemtionis nostræ modus ex professo explicatur. Quod cur fieret, siquidem nuda fuisset liberatio, absque vero interveniente pretio? Sed & additur, cujus, & quanti pretii interventu, nimirum sanguinis Christi, pretiosi illius supra aurum & argentum, redemtio contigit. Quæ, quod vera pretii ratio atque æstimatio hic locum habet, ostendunt. Denique, & pro nobis redimendi pretium illud impensum fuisse dicitur. Ergo proprietatem sermonis res ipsa confirmat, junctis ad hæc illis, quæ adduximus supra, argumentis.
units.tr: Intending to set out the proper meaning of redeeming, he says: "to redeem someone properly means nothing other than to free a captive from the hands of the one who holds him, by giving a price to that holder." And he adds: "I say this so that the proper meaning of the Hebrew words padah and gaal, and of the Greek words λυτρῶν, λυτρωτής, or ἀπολυτρῶν, may be made clear, since these words above all we ought to treat truly..." p. 69. Well: but not only a captive is truly redeemed from the hands of a guard by a price given; so are others too, whether debtors or insolvent persons. To pay off a debt is indeed not, so far, to redeem anyone, any more than to free him; but it is the foundation on which, once it is given, liberation follows and takes place. Socinus says: "I understand the proper meaning of the word redeem when a true price intervenes. I call a true price not money, but whatever is given in order to satisfy the one who holds the captive." Rightly so. Yet Scripture everywhere mentions the price of redemption, the lutron [λύτρον], as well as the redemption itself. Why then should we not take both this and that in their proper sense? "Nor indeed should one depart rashly from the proper meaning of speech, unless a clear reason underlies it," as Socinus himself says at p. 60. But no reason here, let alone a clear one, compels us to depart from the proper signification of the word, and many things confirm that signification. Not only is a price mentioned, and not once but in very many places, in which the manner of our redemption is expressly explained. Why would this be so, if it were a bare liberation without a true price intervening? And it is added by what intervention, and of what great price: namely the blood of Christ, that precious thing above gold and silver, by which redemption took place. These things show that a true reckoning and valuation of the price has its place here. Finally, that price is said to have been laid out for us in order to redeem us. So the thing itself confirms the proper sense of the word, together with the arguments we have adduced above.

units.la: Socinus, part. 11. cap. 11. pag.76. Neque aliud in hac liberatione desideratur, ut omnino vera redemtioni respondeat, nisi ut is, qui captivum detinebat, pretium accipiat, &c. Ea siquidem ratione potissimum non vera, sed metaphorica liberatio nostra est, quoniam in eo nemo est, qui pretium accipiat. Si enim id, quod in ipsa pretii loco est, acceptum (ab eo scilicet qui captivum hominem detinebat) fuisset: jam non metaphoricum, sed verum pretium intervenīsset; & propterea vera redemtio esset, secundum ea, quæ à me in principio hujusce disputationis posita sunt. Resp. 1. Redemtio, ejusque pretium aliquando est pecuniarium, aliquando pœnale, ut quis pœnam corpore luat: illic quidem est qui proprie pretium accipit; non eodem modo isthic. Redemtio nostra non pecuniaria fuit, sed pœnalis. In solvendis pœnis, quamvis solutio dicatur, non tamen ita est qui solutionem in manus accipit, ac ubi quis pretium nummarium. Interim & justitiæ ibi solvere reus, aut sponsor dicitur: & sic justitiæ divinæ, pro nobis, persolutum pretium est, atque satisfactum. 11. Et certe Deus accepit pretium, solutionem à Christo, pro nobis: quod ostendit palam in Christi resuscitatione ex mortuis, tamquam apocha, testimonio, & documento reali ac manifesto, sibi satisfactum, & satisfactionem à se acceptatam fuisse. Jesa. LIII. 10. ubi posuerit animam suam hostiam pro reatu, videbit semen. Act. 11. 24. Rom. IV. 25. 1Cor. XV. 17. Si enim Christus non resurrexit, vana fides vestra: quoniam estis in peccatis vestris. III. Solutum autem pretium divinæ justitiæ, non diabolo, vel peccata: quia, uti apud nos non custodi, vel aliis, quam justitiæ publicæ, quæ θεοῦ διάκονός [?] ἐστι, Rom. XIII. 4. ita & Deo, ac divinæ justitiæ tum peccatores pœnam debent, & dant; tum Christus pro nobis peccatoribus plenissime exsolvit. Jam vero non negamus, vocem redemtionis aliquando improprie sumi, pro quavis liberatione: uti quando dicimur, emere sine pecunia, Jesa. LV. 1. Sed hoc quidem nihil praejudicat acceptioni & usui vocis proprio. Quin 1. propria significatione ergo sumi saltem posse, sequitur 11. Nihil adferunt Adversarii, quare non debeat in praesenti nostro argumento. 111. Nos autem ostendimus, haud aliter sumi hic oportere. Idque examine locorum, quibus non de redemtione solum per Christum, sed quoque de pretio ejus agitur. Et vim vocis pro nobis stare, diffiteri Socinus haud poterit. De justificatione, pag. 5.1 redimendi verbum proprie pretio dato liberare significat; immo si ipsius verbi vim spectes, emptionem omnino declarat, qua sine pretio fieri nequit.
units.tr: Socinus, part 2, chap. 11, p. 76. Nor is anything else required in this liberation, in order that it may fully correspond to a real redemption, than that he who was holding the captive receive a price, etc. For chiefly on this ground our liberation is not real but metaphorical, since there is no one in it who receives a price. For if that which stands in the place of the price had been received (namely, from him who held the man captive), then a real price, not a metaphorical one, would have intervened, and therefore it would be a real redemption, according to what I have laid down at the beginning of this disputation. Reply 1. Redemption and its price are sometimes monetary and sometimes penal, as when someone pays the penalty with his body. In the first case there is properly someone who receives the price; in the second it is not the same. Our redemption was not monetary but penal. In paying penalties, although it is called payment, there is not someone who takes the payment into his hands, as there is when someone pays money. Yet in such cases the guilty party, or his surety, is said to pay to justice, and so a price has been paid and satisfaction made to divine justice on our behalf. 2. And certainly God received the price, the payment from Christ on our behalf, which is clearly shown in Christ's resurrection from the dead, as a receipt, a witness, and a real and manifest proof that he was satisfied and that the satisfaction was accepted by him. Isa. 53:10: when he shall have made his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. Acts 2:24. Rom. 4:25. 1 Cor. 15:17: If Christ is not risen, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins. 3. The price was paid to divine justice, not to the devil or to sins; for just as among us the price is not paid to the jailer or to anyone other than public justice, which is God's minister (Rom. 13:4), so sinners owe and give their penalty to God and to divine justice, and Christ on our behalf, as sinners, has paid it in full. Now we do not deny that the word redemption is sometimes used improperly for any kind of deliverance, as when we are told to buy without money (Isa. 55:1). But this does nothing to prejudice the proper meaning and use of the word. Indeed, it follows (1) that it can at least be taken in its proper sense; (2) the Opponents offer nothing to show why it should not be so taken in our present argument; (3) we show that it must be taken in no other way here, and this from an examination of the passages which speak not only of redemption through Christ but also of his price. Socinus will not be able to deny that the force of the word stands for us. On justification, p. 5: the word to redeem properly means to set free by a price given; indeed, if you look at the force of the word itself, it declares a purchase, which cannot be made without a price.

units.la: Matth. xx. 28. Filius hominis non venit ut sibi ministraretur, sed ut ministraret & daret animam suam λύτρον Redemtionis pretium pro multis ἀντὶ πολλῶν. Ministravit Christus, in procuranda salute & redemtione nostra, dando animam, seu vitam suam, loco multorum, pro iis redimendis, pretium verum. Nam quidni verum dicamus? ubi nulla sunt in textu, quae non modo non vera, & propria, sed & non emphatica valde. Socinus, part. 11. cap. 11. pag. 8[?].
units.tr: Matt. 20:28: The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom [λύτρον] for many [ἀντὶ πολλῶν]. Christ ministered, in procuring our salvation and redemption, by giving his soul or life in the place of many, as a true price for redeeming them. For why should we not call it true? In the text there is nothing that is not only not true and proper but also not at all emphatic. Socinus, part 2, chap. 11, p. 8[?].

units.la: Quocirca, cum Christus dixit, daturum se animam suam redemtionis pretium pro multis, non id voluit dicere, scilicet, soluturum se Deo, sive divina justitia vitam suam, ut is, sive illa, quae nos captivos detineret (quod & absurdissimum est dicere, & nusquam quidquam simile in universa Scriptura legitur) justo pretio redemptionis accepto, nos liberos dimitteret: sed se vitam suam daturum, ut inde non minus, quam soluto redemptionis pretio, veris captivis evenire solet, liberationem e spirituali peccati & mortis captivitate nostra consequeremur.
units.tr: Therefore, when Christ said that he would give his soul as a ransom price for many, he did not mean to say that he would pay to God, or to divine justice, his life, so that God, or that justice which held us captive (which is most absurd to say, and nowhere in the whole of Scripture is anything like it to be read), having received a just price of redemption, would let us go free; but that he would give his life so that, no less than when a redemption price is paid and real captives are set free, we should obtain liberation from our captivity to spiritual sin and death.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non minus quam si pretium verum datum esset, pretio sanguinis sui Christum nos redemisse, quid hoc est dicere? Non hic est, haud minus quam, sed, omissis istis, vere soluto redemtionis pretio, nos liberavit. Num Christus subinnuit suis verbis, non minus quam pretio dato? Pretium Christus commemorat. Nec tamen Adversariis illud videtur. Sufficit nobis certe, illud a Christo dictum, datumque. Enervent illi verba, & pretium, & redemtionem Christi, nos pro veritate, proprietate, & vi illorum stabimus usque in perpetuum.
units.tr: Reply 1. No less than: if a real price had been given, with which Christ redeemed us by his blood, what does this saying mean? It is not here no less than; rather, leaving those words aside, he set us free by truly paying the price of redemption. Does Christ hint by his words at no less than a price given? Christ mentions a price. Yet this does not seem so to the Opponents. It is enough for us that the thing was said and given by Christ. Let them weaken the words, both the price and the redemption of Christ; we shall stand for their truth, propriety, and force forever.

units.la: 11. Ostendere debuerat, quare non possint Christi verba proprie accipi, quod in iis signum & argumentum sermonis improprii & metaphorici esset. Negat tantummodo, exponi verba posse, de solutione, pro nobis, divinae justitiae proprie facta. Quo vero argumento? quia, hoc per parenthesim adfert, id absurdissimum. Itane hoc dicere solum? revera est absurdissimum. Nusquam simile quid in Scriptura legitur: Quasi non plurimis in Scriptura locis de Christi redemtione, & pretio legatur. Quae quod nulla ratione ad metaphoram trahenda, sed propriissime intelligenda sint, ipsa sua emphasi insitisque argumentis satis superque confirmant. Quomodo simile quid redemtioni Christi, extra eam, in Scripturis inveniatur, quum simile nec sit ullum, nec dari unquam possit? In genere autem peccatores poenas Deo debere, & dare, notissimum est ex Scriptura: vel ex parabola Matth. xxiii. Quod autem in propria persona alii, Christus ait. ἀντὶ ἡμῶν præstitit, solvitque Domino βασιλεῖ, τὸν τὸ ὀφειλόμενον αὐτῷ. Neque hic nunc quaeritur, utrum reus, an vades solvat, modò cui, & an poena possit dici solvi Domino, ab eoque accipi. Quod probatum dedimus.
units.tr: 2. He ought to have shown why the words of Christ cannot be taken properly, that is, what sign and indication there is in them of an improper and metaphorical manner of speaking. He merely denies that the words can be explained of a payment made properly to divine justice on our behalf. On what argument? Because, as he adds in a parenthesis, this is most absurd. Is that all he has to say? Indeed, it is most absurd. Nothing like it is read in Scripture. As though Scripture did not, in very many places, speak of Christ's redemption and price! That these are not to be drawn into metaphor in any way, but are to be understood most properly, is sufficiently and more than sufficiently confirmed by their own emphasis and by the arguments inherent in them. How can anything like Christ's redemption be found in the Scriptures outside it, since there is nothing like it and never could be? In general, it is most well known from Scripture that sinners owe and give penalties to God, even from the parable in Matt. 18 (not 23). As for Christ himself saying, of himself in his own person, that he gave and paid to the Lord the King what was owed to him [τὸ ὀφειλόμενον αὐτῷ], on our behalf [ἀντὶ ἡμῶν]. Nor is it asked here whether the debtor or the surety pays, provided it can be said to whom, and whether a penalty can be said to be paid to the Lord and received by him. This we have proved.

units.la: III. Non dixit Christus simpliciter, si vitam suam daturum, ut &c. sed se vitam suam daturum lutrum. Et quam verè proprieque illud, pari modo & istud accipiendum est. Nulla non modo inter illa diversitas, sed nec distinctionis ulla est nota. Ἀντὶ ἀντιλύτρον, ὑπὲρ, 1 Tim. 11. 6. ψυχὴ ἀντὶ, quod alias est ἀντίψυχον, non dicitur, nisi intelligatur verum. Quidni enim? Habes eum qui solvit, & quod, quodque in lutrum, & denique pro quibus, quos alterna morte redemit. Quid deest, quod non proprie omnia intelligantur? non æque illud, ac reliqua? Vel si tibi, pro lubitu, aut hypothesi tuâ liceat metaphoram constituere, quidni & alii in aliis idem tentent, & sic tota facile religio in metaphoram vel inane quoddam schema convertatur? v. Veris captivis. Saltem, opinor, dicent, nos vere, quamvis spiritualiter, captivos, atque e spirituali captivitate esse liberatos: cur non ergo & verum lutrum fit, quo liberati, à vero Servatore, dicimur?
units.tr: 3. Christ did not say simply if he would give his life, so that, etc., but that he would give his life as a ransom. And just as truly and properly as that, this must be taken in the same way. There is not only no difference between those expressions, but not even any mark of distinction. Antilutron [ἀντιλύτρον], huper [ὑπὲρ], 1 Tim. 2:6. Psyche anti [ψυχὴ ἀντὶ], which elsewhere is antipsychon [ἀντίψυχον], is not said unless the thing is understood as true. Why not? You have the one who pays, the thing paid, the ransom into which it is paid, and finally the ones for whom, whom he redeemed by a death in exchange. What is lacking here, so that all things are not properly understood? Is that not as true as the rest? Or if it is permitted to you, at your pleasure or to suit your hypothesis, to set up a metaphor, why should not others attempt the same in other places, and so all religion could easily be turned into a metaphor or some empty figure? 4. Real captives. At least, I suppose, they will say that we are truly, though spiritually, captives, and have been set free from spiritual captivity. Why then is the ransom not also real, by which we are said to be set free by the true Saviour?

units.la: 1 Cor. 1. 30. Christus nobis inter alia factus rdemtio ἀπολύτρωσις, id est, in redemtorem, & redemtionem: adeo vera intelligitur ejus, & propria redemtio, ut non tantum redemtor, sed redemtio vocetur. 1 Cor. vi. 20. eam pretio emti estis, ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς. cap. vii. 23. iterum, τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε. Nunc pretium, nunc illa pretii species dicitur, quae lutrum est. ne de re, aut propria ejus veritate ullus addubitet. Gal. iii. 13. Christus nos ἐξηγόρασεν redemit ex maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio. Emit, & redemit: ἠγόρασε, ἐξηγόρασε, factus nostri loco pretium, lutrum, maledictio: pretium lutro, lutrum maledictione, & hoc, ἀντὶ ἡμῶν. Fecit redemtionem δι' ἑαυτοῦ. Hebr. i. 3. Socini exceptionem ad locum Gal. iii. 13. suprà expendimus. Sed nihil aliud significat Apostolus, quam Christum, dum ipse nostri causa in quandam legis execrationem incidit, nos à vera legis execratione interea liberasse. Amavit enim Paulus, ut in aliis sæpe solet, in execrationis verbo argutus esse. Quomodo autem Christi cruce interveniente &c. part. ii. cap. i. Scilicet argute. Nos à vera & propriâ execratione redemti sumus, per id quod Christus vere factus nostro loco; sed Socino nec verum lutrum fuit, nec vera, pro nobis, execratio, sed in quandam incidit Christus, & tota ejus execratio nihil aliud fuit, quam quod cruce interveniente nos liberavit. Quod longe aliud & minus est eo, quod dixit Apostolus, Christum & fa&tum execrationem, & per id nos redemisse.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 1:30. Christ has been made for us, among other things, redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις], that is, redeemer and redemption, so truly and properly is his redemption understood that he is called not only redeemer but redemption. 1 Cor. 6:20: you were bought with a price [ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς]. 1 Cor. 7:23: again, you were bought with a price [τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε]. Now it is called a price, now that kind of price which is a ransom, so that no one should doubt the thing or its real truth. Gal. 3:13: Christ redeemed us [ἐξηγόρασεν] from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. He bought and redeemed: [ἠγόρασε, ἐξηγόρασε], made in our place, price, ransom, curse: price for ransom, ransom for curse, and this in our place [ἀντὶ ἡμῶν]. He made redemption through himself [δι' ἑαυτοῦ] (Heb. 1:3). We examined above Socinus's objection to the passage in Gal. 3:13. But the Apostle means nothing else than that Christ, while for our sake he fell into a certain curse of the law, in the meantime freed us from the true curse of the law. For Paul, as he often does elsewhere, delighted in being clever with the word curse. How, however, by the intervention of Christ's cross, etc. Part 2, chap. 1. Clearly, cleverly. We have been redeemed from the true and proper curse, through the fact that Christ was truly made in our place; but for Socinus there was neither a true ransom nor a true curse for us, but Christ fell into a certain curse, and his whole cursing was nothing else than that by the intervention of the cross he freed us. This is quite different from, and less than, what the Apostle said, that Christ was made a curse and by this redeemed us.

units.la: Ephes. 1. 7. In quo delicto habemus τῷ ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ, redemtionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum. Quae eadem recurrunt in epistolâ, isti ad Ephesios perquam simili, Col. i. 14. in quo habemus bemus redemtionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum. Socinus, part. 11, cap. 11. Explicat Paulus, quid sit ista redemptio nobis, illius sanguinis fusione intervenient, per Christum parta, &c. quo, tamquam pretio, a peccatorum captivitate, in qua detinebamur, id est, a mortis aeterna poena redimeremur. Ostende, ubi Paulus dicat, nos sanguine, tamquam pretio, & non simpliciter nos sanguine, nos pretio redemtos. Ut verè redemti, ex verâ captivitate; ita & vero pretio. Tuum non est enervare illa, & tamquam per similitudinem modò dicta, evertere. Veritas, veritas tenenda, & urgenda est semper ac ubique.
units.tr: Eph. 1. 7. "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins" [ἀπολύτρωσις διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ]. The same words recur in the letter to the Colossians, which is very like this letter to the Ephesians, Col. 1. 14: "in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins." Socinus, part 2, chap. 11: "Paul explains what that redemption is for us, obtained through Christ by the shedding of his blood, by which, as by a price, we were redeemed from the captivity of sins in which we were held, that is, from the punishment of eternal death." Show me where Paul says that we were redeemed by blood "as by a price," and not simply by blood, by a price. Just as they were truly redeemed from a true captivity, so they were redeemed by a true price. It is not for you to weaken these words and reduce them to something "merely said by way of comparison." Truth, the truth must always and everywhere be held and pressed.

units.la: 1 Tim. 11. 6, Dans semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων[?], redemtionis pretium pro omnibus. Heb. ix. 12. non per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum, verum per proprium sanguinem intravit semel in sancta, aeterna facta redemtione αἰωνίαν λύ-τρωσιν εὑράμενος[?]. Socinus, part. 11. cap. 1r, Vide, quomodo Christus in coelum ad gloriam suam penetraverit; nimirum, per sanguinem, & mortem suam. Ex quo aeternam liberationem est adeptus, non solum quia ipse in aeternum vivit, & morti jam non est obnoxius: verum etiam quia nos quoque, qui ejus membra sumus, hac ratione, à morte vindicabit, & una secum in aeternum vivere faciet. Non ista tantum dicuntur ab Apostolo, sed quoque quod redemtionem effecit, & non nudam modò liberationem; redemtionem suo sanguine, id est, eo non tantum intercedente, sed vi, ac pretio, & ejus lutro. Quæ in exponenda redemtionis ratione præterire amat Adversarius, nec tangere, quia ipsum tangunt nimis.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 2. 6: "who gave himself a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for all, the price of redemption for all."
