Heb. 9. 12: "not by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption [αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑράμενος]." Socinus, part 2, chap. 11: "See how Christ entered into heaven to his glory; namely, by his blood and his death. By this he obtained eternal liberation, not only because he himself lives for ever and is no longer subject to death, but also because he will defend us too, who are his members, in this way from death, and will make us live with him for ever." The Apostle says not only these things, but also that he effected a redemption, and not merely a bare liberation: a redemption by his blood, that is, not merely by his intercession, but by force and by a price, and by his ransom. The adversary likes to pass over these things when explaining the nature of redemption, and not to touch them, because they touch him too closely.

units.la: 1 Pet. 1. 18. 18. Scientes, quod non corruptibilibus, argento aut auro ἐλυτρώθητε[?] redemti estis ex vanâ vestra conversatione à Patribus tradita: sed pretioso sanguine τιμίῳ αἵματι[?] tamquam agni irreprehensibilis & immaculati Jesu Christi. Hic, ne verum pretium, & pro pretio Christi sanguinem venisse nescituremus, haud modò τίμιον pretiosum sanguinem dixit Apostolus, & cum ἐλυτρώθητε conjunxit, sed & cum vero rerum aliarum pretio contulit, argento & auro. Socinus, part. 11. cap. 111. Iubet igitur Petrus, ut postquam tanto pretio ex iniquitatibus & ignorantiis nostris redempti sumus, ob eamque rem ei, qui pro nobis id pretium dedit, tantum debemus, eidem illi &c. obediamus. Verum pretium addere debuisset: quod nisi subintelligatur, inanis redditur tota Apostoli ratiocinatio. Ex vana conversatione nostra, non ex divina justitia manibus, cui pretium aliquod pro nobis solvendum esset, redempti sumus. Quin utrumque, & ex poenâ peccati, quam justitiæ divinæ debebamus, & à culpa seu corruptione ipsâ quoque. Et primò quidem ac propriissime à malo poenæ, cujus ratione dicitur lutrum; ex conversatione malâ eximimur, tanquam materiâ ex quâ. Tit. 11. 14. ἵνα λυτρώσηται[?] ἡμᾶς, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purgaret sibi populum peculiarem, zelotem bonorum operum. Quod ex redemtione oritur.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1. 18: "Knowing that you were not redeemed with corruptible things, silver or gold [ἐλυτρώθητε], from your vain conversation handed down from the fathers, but with precious blood [τιμίῳ αἵματι], as of a lamb unblemished and spotless, Jesus Christ." Here, lest we fail to know that the true price, and the blood of Christ as a price, has come, the Apostle not only called the blood precious [τίμιον] and joined it to the word "redeemed" [ἐλυτρώθητε], but also set it against the true price of other things, silver and gold. Socinus, part 2, chap. 3: "Peter therefore commands that, since we have been redeemed at so great a price from our iniquities and ignorances, and since for this reason we owe it to him who gave that price for us, we should obey him, and so on." But he ought to have added the price: unless that is understood, the whole reasoning of the Apostle becomes empty. "From our vain conversation, not by the hands of divine justice, to which some price would have had to be paid for us, were we redeemed." Indeed, we were redeemed from both: from the punishment of sin, which we owed to the justice of God, and from the guilt or corruption itself. First and most properly, from the evil of punishment, by reason of which it is called a ransom; we are freed from our evil conversation, as from the material out of which. Titus 2. 14: "that he might redeem [λυτρώσηται] us from all iniquity, and purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works." This arises from redemption.

units.la: Atque illa Scripturæ loca sunt, quæ veram nostri per Christum redemtionem, & intervenisse lutrum, docent, non demum quod ita dicis causa appelletur modo, sed hoc revera fit, quod dicitur. Socinus, part. II, cap. I. Ut enim metaphorice simplex liberatio redemptio dicitur, quoniam idem effectum est simpli-cis liberationis, qui vera & propria redemptionis, non minus enim hoc, quam illo modo, quis servitute eximitur: sic etiam id, quod in simplici liberatione ad eam peragendam intervenit, per translationem pretium dicitur. Immo tunc demum rite redimendi metaphora procedit, & absolute suis partibus constat, cum in simplici liberatione aliquid intervenit, quod per translationem aliquo pacto pretio respondeat. Resp. I. Nec probat, id quod in simplici liberatione ad eam peragendam intervenit, pretium dici, ubi non veri nominis redemptio est. II. Nec in redemtione nostri per translationem dici Christi pretium. III. Quodque hic per translationem aliquo pacto prerio respondeat, & non tale revera sit. IV. Nempe ut redimendi metaphora procedat, & suis constet partibus. Metaphora scilicet redemtionis, non veritas: qua se objectent miseri homines, veritatem nos sectamur & tenemus. Praesertim quum nullibi Scriptura, in nullo quidem loco, quamvis in valde multis redemtionis meminerit, metaphorae ullum praebeat, vel levissimum, indicium.
units.tr: These are the passages of Scripture which teach that there is a true redemption of us through Christ, and that a ransom intervened; not merely that it is called that for the sake of the expression, but that what is said really happens. Socinus, part 2, chap. 1: "For just as a simple liberation is called redemption metaphorically, since the same effect is produced by simple liberation as by true and proper redemption (for a man is freed from slavery no less in the one way than in the other), so also what intervenes in simple liberation to bring it about is called a price by a figure of speech. Indeed, the metaphor of redeeming then properly applies and is wholly consistent in all its parts, when in simple liberation something intervenes which in some way corresponds by figure to a price." Reply: first, he does not prove that what intervenes in simple liberation to bring it about is called a price, where there is no redemption in the proper sense. Second, nor is Christ's price called by a figure in our redemption. Third, that here it corresponds in some way to a price is not so in fact. Fourth, namely that the metaphor of redeeming applies and is consistent in its parts: a metaphor of redemption, that is, not the truth. Wretched men may object to this, but we pursue and hold the truth. Especially since Scripture nowhere, in no passage, though it mentions redemption in very many places, offers the slightest hint of a metaphor.

units.la: Sic fuerunt pro sententia nostra, & veritate satisfactionis Christi argumenta, vel argumentorum classes quatuor. I. Quod Christus statum & conditionem nostram, debitaque in se suscepit, & luendas poenas. II. Et loco nostro mortuus est. III. Et expiavit peccata apud Deum, eumque nobis placavit & reconciliavit. IV. Et hinc denique nos vere redemit. Quae omnia ita ex Scriptura sacra ostendimus & probata dedimus, ut saepe ἀντιλύτρα, semper quod ad sensum, variis ejus locis & locutionibus, contineri apparuerit. Vulgares ad singula Exceptiones, nominatim Socini, libro de Servatore, discussimus: nam ex ipsa reliqui sua habent, & fere eadem. Tanti quippe Magistrum suum, speciatim illud ejus scriptum faciunt, ut qui illud, eum & reliquos, & caetera pene ejusdem diruisse, haud gravate sint confessuri. Quod praeterquam ex Titulo libri, & inscriptione, in quo dicunt, quod multa, quae apud Evangelicos, & partim etiam apud alios, salutaria Christiana religionis axiomata creduntur, perniciosi errores esse demonstrantur; & tota salutis nostrae per Christum ratio copiose ac dilucide explicantur; etiam ex illis apparet, quae passim Socinus ipse, passim alii de illa, quam eo libro prosequitur, cum Jacobo Coveto, Parisiensi, Theologo Evangelico, disputatione vane gloriantur. Socinus, in epistola Dedicatoria, ad Responsionem primam, contra Andr. Volanum; Elias Arcifevius, in praefat. ad librum Socini, de Christo Servatore: & Joh. Crellius, in praefat. ad Responf. contra Grotium, de Satisfact. pag. 21. audivimus enim ex iis, qui familiariter ipso sunt usi, eum Socinum, quamquam mediocriter de se sentiret & loqueretur, significasse tamen, si, ut tum jactabatur, excellens sibi obtingeret adversarius, qui librum de I. Christo Servatore adoriretur, tum demum se totum hoc argumentum uberrime explicaturum. Adorsi librum illum fuerunt ante me, Viri alii excellentes; ego non quidem singula ἀντιλέγει infequutus, attamen ita me confido praecipuarum cavillationum & argumentationum, quae in illo occurrunt, nervos incidisse, ut haud difficulter ad singula quæque re-sponderi queat. Quæ etiam causa fuit, cur illum potius Autorem imprimis ad partes vocarem, quam alios, quos omnes videbam illo tum scripto, tum scriptore unicè niti. Estque liber ille callide in Belgicum pridem traductus, sub specie Disputationis de Messia, inter Italum, qui Socinus, & Gallum, qui Covetus est, variato titulo, ut incautis eo facilius imponerent.
units.tr: Thus there were four arguments, or classes of arguments, for our view and for the truth of Christ's satisfaction. First, that Christ took upon himself our condition and state, and the debts and penalties to be paid. Second, that he died in our place. Third, that he made atonement for sins before God, and reconciled and appeased him for us. Fourth, and lastly, that from this he truly redeemed us. We have shown all these things from Holy Scripture and given proofs of them, so that, though often under different words, they have always appeared, in sense, to be contained in its various passages and expressions. We have examined the common objections to each point, especially those of Socinus in his book on the Saviour; for the rest of them derive from it and are nearly the same. They hold their master in such esteem, and especially that treatise of his, that they will hardly hesitate to confess that whoever has overthrown it has overthrown him and the others, and almost everything else of the same kind. This appears not only from the title and inscription of the book, in which they say that many things which among Evangelicals, and partly among others, are believed as saving axioms of the Christian religion are shown to be pernicious errors, and that the whole reasoning of our salvation through Christ is explained fully and clearly; it also appears from what Socinus himself everywhere, and others everywhere, boast of vainly concerning the dispute which he carries on in that book with James Covet, a Parisian, an Evangelical theologian. Socinus, in the dedicatory letter to his First Reply against Andrew Wolan; Elias Arcifevius, in the preface to Socinus's book on Christ the Saviour; and John Crell, in the preface to his Replies against Grotius on Satisfaction, p. 21: "For we have heard from those who were on familiar terms with him that Socinus, although he thought and spoke of himself with moderation, nevertheless signified that if, as was then boasted, an excellent adversary should arise to attack his book on Jesus Christ the Saviour, then at last he would explain this whole argument most fully." Other excellent men attacked that book before me. I have not followed each of their contentions, yet I trust that I have struck at the sinews of the chief cavils and arguments which occur in it, so that each can be answered without difficulty. This was also the reason why I preferred to summon that author above all others to the field, rather than the rest, all of whom I saw relied entirely on that writing and that writer. That book was also cunningly translated into Dutch some time ago, under the guise of a disputation on the Messiah between the Italian, who is Socinus, and the Frenchman, who is Covet, with the title changed, so that the unwary might be more easily deceived by it.

units.la: In explicatâ vindicatâque Satisfactionis Christi doctrinâ fundatur ratio me-riti, quod in eo quoque agnoscimus. Nempe quia satisfecit legi perfectissimè, tum pœnis, quas pro nobis tulit, tum observatione, quam præstitit; atque meri-tus nobis est & absolutionem à debitis pœnis, & vitæ, quam lex promittit, nobis verò impossibile erat attingere, Rom. viii. 3. 4. jus in ipso, & ἐξουσίαν[?].
units.tr: The reason of merit, which we also acknowledge in Christ, is grounded in the explained and defended doctrine of Christ's satisfaction. Namely, because he satisfied the law most perfectly, both by the punishments he bore for us and by the observance he rendered, he has merited for us both absolution from the debts of punishment and the life which the law promises, which we could never have attained. Rom. 8:3, 4. Right in him, and authority [ἐξουσίαν].

units.la: Neque enim meriti vox ita accipienda, prout Adversarii volunt, ut solam operis in se condignitatem respiciat, extra omnem divinam promissionem, quasi Deum per se obligaret & constringeret ad mercedem, solâ vi suâ: sic enim rem accipit Socinus, part. iii. cap. vi. & Smalcius, contra Smigle-cium, de satisfact. cap. v. sed meritum, non in ordine ad jus Dei, verum ad legem sumimus, ut is, qui legi à Deo positæ, atque promissione sanctæ satisfecit, promeruisse statuatur? quippe quam, observantibus legem pollicitus fuit-. Non ita in Euangelio, operanti τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ, sed credenti in eum qui pro nobis operatus fuit, salus posita; in lege autem, operanti: illic, κατὰ χάριν[?]; isthic, κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα datur merces. Rom. iv. 4. 5. Ὀφείλημα, non operis, propter suam in se, abstracte, condignitatem; sed ob legis, & promissionis, quam Deus ad eam appendit, sententiam. Ut illa Smalcii hinc corruant, quibus tota ejus nititur disputatio: ubi promissio, quod ibi merito nullus est locus. Nulla enim tandem opus effet promis-sione, si daretur meritum. Imo meritum absolutum, de condigno, rigidè, ab-stractè, & antecedenter ad Dei promissionem, eâque sepositâ, non verò quale duntaxat propugnamus, meritum ad legem, & promissionem. Quod cum promissione ita consistit, ut in eâ totum radicetur.
units.tr: The word merit is not to be taken as our opponents wish, so that it looks only at the intrinsic worthiness of the work, apart from any divine promise, as if it bound and constrained God to reward by its own force alone. That is how Socinus understands it, Part 3, ch. 6, and Smalcius, against Smiglecius, On Satisfaction, ch. 5. Rather, we take merit not with respect to God's right, but with respect to the law: he who satisfied the law laid down by God and sanctified by his promise is held to have deserved, since God promised it to those who keep the law. It is not so in the Gospel: there salvation is set not for the one who works [τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ] but for the one who believes in him who worked for us; in the law, reward is given to the one who works, there according to grace [κατὰ χάριν], here according to what is owed [κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα]. Rom. 4:4, 5. What is owed arises not from the work, taken abstractly in its own worthiness, but from the sentence of the law and of the promise which God attached to it. Thus those arguments of Smalcius, on which his whole disputation rests, collapse: where he says that there is no place for merit if there is a promise. For if merit were given, there would finally be no need of a promise. Indeed, he attacks absolute merit, of condign worth, strictly and abstractly, and prior to God's promise, setting that aside; we do not defend that sort of merit, but merit with respect to the law and the promise. This agrees with the promise in such a way that the whole of it is rooted in the promise.

units.la: Atque sic Christum nobis meruisse salutem & salutaria quæque, negare nemo potest, nisi qui dubitat, eum acquisivisse nobis illa verè, & vi suæ obedientiæ, passionumque. Eo etenim, quod legi absolutè & undequaque satisfecit, meritus illa omnia fuit, sive vi & merito suæ obedientiæ acquisivit nobis liberationem & salutem omnimodam. Mereri enim est, hoc perfectè præstare, propter quod merces, & præmium debetur. Quod Christus perfectè, & abundanter præstitit. Quippe sic Apostolus docet, Rom. v. 18. 19. Nempe igitur, sicuti per unius transgressionem in omnes homines reatus venit ad condemnationem: ita etiam per unius justitiam, gratia in omnes homines ad justificationem vitæ. sicuti enim per inobedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi illi, ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur illi multi, οἱ πολλοί. Opponuntur invicem injustiinjustitia primi, & justitia secundi Adami, cum utriusque in suis effectu & merito. Uti illic, ex antecedente Dei constitutione, transgressio merita fuit reatum mortis in omnes Adami filios; ita, ex alia Dei constitutione, obedientia Christi salutem suis quoq; omnibus, vel multis, pro quibus fuit factus obediens usque ad mortem. Phil.11.8. Rom.vi11.3.4. Quod enim impossibile erat legi in quo infirmabatur per carnem, Deus effecit proprium suum mittens filium in similitudine carnis peccati, & hostia pro peccato condemnavit peccatum in carne. Ut justitia legis impleretur in nobis, ergo ut legi pro nobis satisfaceret, venit Christus: eoque quod praestitit legis justitiae, promissi & vitae evadimus participes, in Christo, qui pro nobis ideo factus a Deo justitia, δικαιοσύνη[?]. 1 Cor. 1. 30. Jerem. xxiii. 6. Rom. x. 4. finis enim legis Christus ad justitiam cuivis credenti. & quae sequuntur. Phil. iii. 9. & comperiar in eo, non habens meam justitiam quae ex lege, sed eam quae est per fidem Christi, justitiam quae ex Deo est per fidem. Gal. iii. 13. 14. Christus nos redemit ex maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio: [?]scriptum est enim &c. Ut ad gentes benedictio Abrahae perveniret in Christo Jesu, ut promissionem spiritus adipisceremur per fidem. Tum ut a malo liberaret nos, tum ut salutem & salutaria acquireret, Christus pro nobis venit, & legi fuit subjectus, cap. iv. 4. 5. factus ex muliere, factus sub lege: ut eos, qui sub lege, redimeret, ut adoptionem adipisceremur. Illud est, vi & merito, non simplici interventu ejus, quod Christus pro nobis praestitit. Hebr. x. 2. 10. Tunc dixit, ecce venio ut faciam, o Deus, voluntatem tuam. In qua voluntate sanctificati sumus, per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel. Apoc. v. 9. 10. nam mactatus es & emisti nos Deo sanguine tuo: & fecisti nos Deo nostro reges & sacerdotes.
units.tr: And so no one can deny that Christ merited salvation and all saving benefits for us, unless he doubts that Christ truly acquired them for us, by the power of his obedience and sufferings. For by the fact that he satisfied the law absolutely and in every respect, he merited all those things; that is, by the power and merit of his obedience he acquired for us liberation and salvation in every way. For to merit is to perform perfectly that for which a wage and reward is due, and this Christ did perfectly and abundantly. So the Apostle teaches, Rom. 5:18, 19: "Therefore, as through the trespass of one man condemnation came upon all men, so through one man's righteousness the free gift came to all men, to justification of life. For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by one man's obedience many will be made righteous" [οἱ πολλοί]. The injustice of the first Adam and the justice of the second are set over against each other, each with its effect and merit. As there, by God's prior appointment, the trespass merited the sentence of death upon all the sons of Adam, so by another appointment of God the obedience of Christ merited salvation for all his own, or for the many for whom he was "made obedient unto death." Phil. 2:8; Rom. 8:3, 4. "For what the law could not do, in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and as an offering for sin he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us; therefore Christ came to satisfy the law for us, and by what he accomplished for the righteousness of the law we become partakers of the promise and of life, in Christ, who for us was made by God righteousness [δικαιοσύνη]." 1 Cor. 1:30; Jer. 23:6; Rom. 10:4: "For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes," and what follows. Phil. 3:9: "and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith." Gal. 3:13, 14: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us; for it is written, etc., so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith." Then, both that he might free us from evil and that he might acquire salvation and saving benefits, Christ came for us and was made subject to the law. Gal. 4:4, 5: "born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive adoption." That is by power and merit, not by his mere intercession, which Christ accomplished for us. Heb. 10:7, 10: "Then I said, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God. By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all." Rev. 5:9, 10: "For you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed us for God, and made us kings and priests to our God."

units.la: Et quia nihil prorsus deliquit, & servavit omnia, ex legis praescripto, ad acquirendam vitam, meruisse eam dicendus est. Crellius, ad Galatas, cap. 11. 16. pag. 70. Hoc vero, natura rei inspecta, duplici potest fieri ratione: vel quia ut, qui justificatur, id plane meritus fuerit, quia nimirum nihil deliquerit. Socinus, de justificatione, pag. 35. qui legem perfectissime servat, is non gratis, sed ex debito justificatur, seu justus pronuntiatur. & pag. 48. Nulla esse opera, quae tanti sint, ut propter ipsorum meritum justificari possimus. Quando scilicet nemo est, qui perfectissime atque integerrime per totam vitam ea opera faciat, quae sive sub vetere sive sub novo Testamento praescripta sunt, id quod tamen omnino requiritur, sive requireretur ad hoc, ut per ipsa opera, tanquam, ejus rei aliquo modo meritoria, justificatio contingeret. Diximus autem, Aliquo modo meritoria, ut ab ipsis operibus excludamus, non modo absolutum & maxime proprium meritum, quod oritur ex ipsa operum praestantia per se considerata, sed etiam illud, quod minus proprie & respective meritum est, quippe, quod non ex ipsa per se operum praestantia, sed ex solo Dei promisso oritur ac proficisci tur, adeo, ut nemo neque per illud, neque per hoc meritum, suorum operum justificationem & absolutionem a peccatis suis adipiscatur. Quamvis autem nos propter opera justificari non possimus, neque per ea mereri, quia non sunt perfecta: Christus autem, quia perfectissime omnia praestitit, hoc ipso meritus dici potest. Ac proinde contumeliose de sententia, quae Christi meritum aliquod dicit, Smalcius, adversus
units.tr: And because he committed no sin at all, and kept all things according to the prescription of the law, he is to be said to have merited life by it. Crellius, on Galatians, ch. 2, v. 16, p. 70: "But this, looking at the nature of the thing, can happen in a twofold way: either because he who is justified has clearly merited it, since he has committed no sin." Socinus, On Justification, p. 35: "He who keeps the law most perfectly is justified, or pronounced righteous, not freely, but from what is owed." And p. 48: "There are no works so great that we can be justified on account of their merit; since there is no one who performs throughout his whole life, most perfectly and most entirely, those works which are prescribed under the Old or the New Testament, which yet is altogether required, or would be required, for justification to come through those works as in some way meritorious of this thing. We said, however, 'in some way meritorious,' so that we exclude from the works themselves not only absolute and most proper merit, which arises from the very excellence of the works considered in themselves, but also that which is less properly and relatively merit, since it does not arise and proceed from the very excellence of the works in themselves, but from God's promise alone; so that no one obtains the justification and absolution of his sins through either that merit or this one." Although we cannot be justified on account of works, nor merit through them, because they are not perfect, Christ, because he performed all things most perfectly, can for that very reason be said to have merited. Therefore Smalcius, in his Disputation 4 on Justification, against Frantzius, Tom. 2, p. 117, unkindly cries out that the opinion which says that "Christ has some merit" is false, absurd and pernicious.

units.la: Tom. 2. Frantzium, Difp. iv. de Justific. pag. 117. clamat, eam esse falsam, absurdam, & pernitiosam.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Against Frantzius, Disp. 4, On Justification, p. 117, he cries out that it is false, absurd, and pernicious.

units.la: Hincper, & propter Christum dicuntur remitti peccata; & propter eum liberari dicimur, & salvari, ita singulariter & energetice, ut simul vim ejus omnino designent meritoriam. Socinus, part. 111. cap. 11. Verum quod praeterea requirimus, cum & inter omnes constet, & ubique scriptum sit, nos per Christum a Deo peccatorum remissionem accepisse &c. Quod vero adjungit, excipitque, haud posse una cum remissione peccatorum stare, Christi pro illis satisfactionem, mox in objectionibus discutiemus.
units.tr: Hence sins are said to be forgiven through God and "on account of Christ," and we are said to be freed and saved on account of him, in such a singular and forceful way that together they plainly signify his meritorious power. Socinus, Part 3, ch. 11: "But what we further require, since it is agreed by all and written everywhere that we have received from God the forgiveness of sins through Christ," etc. What he adds and excepts, that Christ's satisfaction for those sins cannot stand together with the remission of sins, we will discuss shortly among the objections.

units.la: Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum, de justificat. pag. 124.
units.tr: Schlichtingius, against Meisner, On Justification, p. 124.

units.la: Praeterea, si Christi obedientia nostra fuit obedientia, Christi afflictio nostra poena: quomodo ipsi Christo ista, quam praestitit, cum aliis in rebus omnibus, tum etiam ad mortem usque, eamque crucis, obedientia tantum praemium apud Deum & gloriam conciliare potuit? An, si pro afflictione detur praemium, & quidem omnium maximum, non omnis ratio poenae tollitur? Quocirca Christi perpessiones non poenae fuerunt peccatorum, sed labores praemia antecedentes. Et, si pro obedientia alicui conferatur merces, quomodo ista obedientia alterius censeri potest, quam illius ipsius, qui praemium ac mercedem pro ea consecutus est?
units.tr: Furthermore, if Christ's obedience was our obedience, and Christ's affliction our punishment, how could that obedience which he rendered, in all other things and even unto death, and that the death of the cross, win for Christ himself such a reward and glory with God? Or, if a reward is given for affliction, and indeed the greatest of all, is not every reason for punishment taken away? Wherefore the sufferings of Christ were not punishments of sins, but labours preceding a reward. And if a reward is conferred for obedience, how can that obedience be counted as another's than his own, who obtained the prize and wage for it?

units.la: Quomodo, inquit, Christo sua obedientia tantum praemium conciliavit, si fit nostra? vel, si praemium adeptus fuit passione, quomodo haec poena fuit? nam eo ratio poenae videtur tolli, si tantum praemio remuneretur. Resp. Christi obedientia, & poena, fuerunt nostra, reputatione tantum, quatenus quod egit, nostri loco & bono egit: sed per-sonaliter [?] fuerunt Christi, & proinde, quia is tanta pro nobis agere & pati voluit, ideo isto quoque honore & praemio, post labores & obedientiam illam, affectus fuit. Nimirum quia perfectissime omnia praestitit, & pro aliis sive nobis miseris peccatoribus, & ipse quidem tantum, Dei nempe filius, atq; hinc praemio tanto dignus & exornatus fuit, hoc est, pro merito. Utrumque, & poenae fuerunt Christi perpessiones, respectu nostri ac legis, quae transgressoribus illas imponebat; & labores praemium antecedentes, respectu Christi, & promissionis ipsi factae. Quare isto sensu non sublata ex afflictio-nibus ratio poenalitatis fuit; dum eas, nostri loco & causa Christus patiebatur, quamvis post perpessas praemio omnium maximo afficiebatur. Quia ex diversa causa utrumque est, & tum passus debitas poenas fuit, tum legis postulatis & praeceptis perfectissimam detulit obedientiam, ut legis promissio in nobis adimpleri posset, & jus dari vitae. Non simpliciter quando quis patitur, aut punitur, eo meretur, sed in ordine ad legem ejusque promissionem si patiatur; atque uti legi, pro adipiscenda, promissione satisfecit, sic promissum meretur si quidquid lex exigit, rite & perfecte observavit. Denique jam dictum, quomodo alterius censeri possit obedientia, praeterquam illius, qui praemium ac mercedem est consequutus: nimirum imputatione, & ex pacto cum aliis etiam in Vade inito, & cum Vade, illorum respectu ac bono. Nam Christus spectari hic debet, non ut persona singularis, sed communis, uti alter Adam, qui pro se, & suis obedientiam praestitit opposite ad inobedientiam Adami primi, ut ejus obedientiâ constituemur[?] justi, æque ac illius inobedientiâ injusti. Rom. v. 15. & 1 Cor. xv 22. ii. Cor. v. 15. Bernardus, epist. cxc. ad Innocentium: nam si unus, inquit, pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt: ut videlicet satisfactio unius omnibus imputetur, sicut omnium peccata unus ille pertavit[?], nec alter jam inveniatur, qui peccavit, alter qui satisfecit: quia caput & corpus unus est Christus. Satisfecit ergo caput pro membris, Christus pro visceribus suis.
units.tr: They ask: how did Christ's obedience win him so great a reward, if it becomes ours? Or, if he obtained the reward by his passion, how was that passion a punishment? For by this the reason of punishment seems to be removed, if he is rewarded only with a prize. Answer: Christ's obedience and punishment were ours only by reckoning, in so far as he did what he did in our place and for our good. But personally they were Christ's; and therefore, because he willed to do and suffer so much for us, he was also rewarded with this honour and prize after those labours and that obedience. Namely, because he performed all things most perfectly, both for others, that is for us wretched sinners, and for himself alone, being God's Son; and hence he was worthy of and adorned with so great a prize, that is, it was according to merit. Both the sufferings of Christ were punishments, with respect to us and the law which imposed them on transgressors; and labours preceding a reward, with respect to Christ and the promise made to him. Therefore in this sense the reason of penalty was not taken away from the afflictions, since Christ suffered them in our place and cause, although after suffering he was honoured with the greatest of all rewards. Both arise from a different cause: he both suffered the due punishments, and rendered most perfect obedience to the demands and precepts of the law, so that the promise of the law might be fulfilled in us and a right to life be given. A man does not merit simply by suffering or being punished, but in relation to the law and its promise, if he suffers; and just as he satisfied the law in order to obtain the promise, so he merits the promised thing if he has duly and perfectly observed whatever the law requires. Finally, it has been said how the obedience can be counted as another's than his who obtained the prize and wage: namely, by imputation, and by a covenant entered into with others also in the Surety, and with the Surety, for their sake and good. For Christ must be regarded here not as a single person but as a common one, like a second Adam, who rendered obedience for himself and his own, opposite to the disobedience of the first Adam, so that by his obedience we are made righteous, just as by that one's disobedience we were made unrighteous. Rom. 5:15; 1 Cor. 15:22; 2 Cor. 5:15. Bernard, letter 190 to Innocent: For if one died for all, then all died; so that, namely, the satisfaction of one is imputed to all, just as that one bore the sins of all, and no other is found who sinned and another who made satisfaction, since Christ is one head and one body. So the head made satisfaction for the members, Christ for his own inmost members.

units.la: Quibus fateor valde repugnat, quod Adversarii docent, Christum remissionem peccatorum à Deo non impetrasse, duntaxat eam confirmasse: sed etiam repugnat veritati, & Scripturis. Socinus, parr. ii[?]. cap. xvi. pag. 160. Sacrificio corporis Christi attributum, quod peccata nostra expiet, quia nobis remissionis peccatorum in novo fœdere à Deo promissa plenissimam fidem facit: non autem quia eam remissionem nobis à Deo impetraverit. Cap. xix. Christi precibus intervenientibus, Deum peccata nostra reipsa nobis condonasse: non autem, Christi precibus intervenientibus, à Deo impetratum fuisse, ut nobis peccata condonaret. Negant ergo, Christum proprie & vere nobis impetrasse remissionem peccatorum, & salutem, vi obedientiæ, ac sanguinis sui: tantummodò ista intervenisse statuunt, ad remissionem peccatorum confirmandam. Smalcius, contra Smiglecium, de Satisfact. cap. v.
units.tr: To these things I confess that what the Adversaries teach strongly conflicts: that Christ did not obtain remission of sins from God, but only confirmed it. This also conflicts with truth and with Scripture. Socinus, part 2, chap. 16, p. 160: The sacrifice of Christ's body is credited with expiating our sins because it gives full assurance of the remission of sins promised by God in the new covenant to us; not because he obtained that remission for us from God. Chap. 19: By Christ's intercession, God has in fact forgiven us our sins; it is not that, by Christ's intercession, it was obtained from God that he should forgive us our sins. They therefore deny that Christ properly and truly obtained for us the remission of sins and salvation by the power of his obedience and his blood; they hold only that these intervened to confirm the remission of sins. Smalcius, against Smiglecius, on Satisfaction, chap. 5.

units.la: Per sanguinem autem, non est virtute fan-guinis. Nam vox per plerunque causam me-diam, vel instrumentalem denotat. Et si ta-men, sanguine Christi nobis peccata remitti, ea dicere quis velit, & virtute sanguinis Chri-sti, ea id ratione tantum dici posset, quod sanguine facta non fit, nec fieri potuerit remissio, non vero quod sanguis Christi ad remissionem praestandam Deum commoverit aut impulerit? Quo sensu dicitur, nos, jam per fidem, jam fide justificari, vel accessum ad Deum habere; non quod fides sit causa impulsiva in Deo nostræ justificationis: sed quia sine fide (ut Scriptura loquitur) impossibile sit Deo placere, modo scilicet tali, ut quis vitam æternam consequatur.
units.tr: But "through the blood" does not mean "by the virtue of the blood." For the word "through" usually denotes a middle or instrumental cause. And even if someone wishes to say that sins are remitted to us by the blood of Christ, and by the virtue of Christ's blood, this could be said only in this sense: that without the blood the remission is not made, nor could it have been made; not that the blood of Christ moved or impelled God to grant the remission. In the same sense it is said that we are justified now through faith, now by faith, or have access to God; not because faith is the impelling cause in God of our justification, but because without faith (as Scripture puts it) it is impossible to please God, in such a way that someone obtains eternal life.

units.la: Resp. 1. Neque nostra sententia est, Deum proprie impelli aut commoveri re aliquâ, vel sanguine Christi; sed ejus vi, & merito ad legem, & sa-tisfactione ad Dei justitiam, salutem nobis acquiri. 11. Plus passim Scriptu-ra & fides Christo, ejusque sanguini attribuit, quam ut eo duntaxat intermissionem [?] veniente, non autem propria virtute ejus, remissio peccatorum obtigerit: nam multa alia intervenient, sine quibus salus non contingit, haud tamen illis adscribitur, vel adscribi potest: quod indicio est, alio longe pacto Christo, ejusque sanguini remissionem & salutem tribui, quam
units.tr: Answer 1: Our view is not that God is properly impelled or moved by anything, or by the blood of Christ; but that salvation is acquired for us by its power and merit with respect to the law, and by its satisfaction with respect to God's justice. 2: Scripture and faith everywhere attribute more to Christ and his blood than that the remission of sins came about merely by its intervening, and not by its proper virtue. For many other things intervene, without which salvation is not obtained, yet these are not ascribed to it, nor can they be. This is evidence that remission and salvation are attributed to Christ and his blood in a far different way than by mere intervention.

units.la: propter meram intervenientiam. Dicere, quod ea tantum ratione sanguinis Chri-sti liberatio nostra attribuitur, quod sine sanguine facta non fit, facit eum tantum causam sine qua non, non veram. Tantundem olim dicere licuit de sanguine sacrificiorum: hodie de multis aliis rebus, sine quibus salus non habetur, quæ tamen cum sanguine Christi ad liberationem & salutem componere nequeas. Uti, quando Christus dicitur propter peccata nostra mortuus, Adversarii exponunt, nihil aliud esse, quam causam, sive occasione peccatorum mori: ita, nos propter Christi sanguinem salvari, dicunt, occasione vel interventu, & non sine sanguine illo fuso redimi, quamvis non propter eum, uti nec propter peccata mortuus ipsis Christus, tamquam causam mortis meritoriam. Scilicet ubique, & in morte Christi, & salute per eum, causam suam atque veritatem tollunt, id est, religionem Christianam, & praecipua ejus fundamenta emasculant.
units.tr: On account of mere intervention. To say that the deliverance of our race is attributed to the blood of Christ in this sense only, that it is not made without the blood, makes him merely a cause without which not, and not a true cause. The same could once have been said of the blood of the sacrifices, and today of many other things without which salvation is not had; yet these you cannot place alongside the blood of Christ for deliverance and salvation. Just as, when Christ is said to have died for our sins, the Adversaries explain this as nothing other than a cause, or occasion, of sins dying, so they say we are saved on account of Christ's blood by occasion or intervention, and redeemed not without that blood being shed; although Christ did not die on account of it, any more than on account of sins, as a meritorious cause of death. Clearly, everywhere, both in the death of Christ and in salvation through him, they remove their own cause and truth, that is, the Christian religion, and emasculate its chief foundations.

units.la: III. Voculam per causam mediam vel instrumentalem denotare, haud negamus; sed notat etiam meritoriam. Uti quando quis dicitur, per aurum vel argentum, per lutrum redimi. Non ita ubi per fidem dicimur justificari. hic per solum instrumentum denotat, ideo quia nobis, & actionibus seu operibus omnis justificandi vis adimitur, & Christus justitia nostra est, inque eo justitiam habemus, non nostram. Verum alia longe ratione, per sanguinem Christi redimimur: quocum si fidem eadem causalitatis serie colloces, jam nobis haud minus salus attribuenda erit, quam Christo, aut ejus sanguini: quia interventu fidei, & bonorum operum salvamur, nec absque iis salvari datum, aeque ac non sine sanguine Christi in antecessum effuso.
units.tr: III. We do not deny that the little word per denotes a middle or instrumental cause; but it also denotes a meritorious one, as when someone is said to be redeemed through gold or silver, or through a ransom. It is not so where we are said to be justified through faith: here per denotes only an instrument, because all power of justifying is taken away from us and from our actions or works, and Christ is our righteousness, and we have righteousness in him, not our own. But we are redeemed through the blood of Christ by a quite different reason; if you place faith in the same chain of causality with it, then salvation must be attributed to us no less than to Christ or his blood. For we are saved by the intervention of faith and good works, and it is not granted to be saved without them, just as not without the blood of Christ poured out beforehand.

units.la: IV. Contrà autem virtuti sanguinis Christi proprie competit redemtio nostra, ut τιμή, pretio, merito. ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς, 1 Cor. vi. 20. & vii. 23. Quod confertur & opponitur ἀργυρίῳ [?], argento aut auro; sed emti sumus τιμίῳ αἵματι. 1 Petr. i. 18. 19. Quae certe vim, virtutem propriam sanguinis Christi, & meritum designant. Quale est in lutro. Unde Christum lutrum pro nobis, & ἀντίλυτρον dedisse, multis testatum Scripturae locis. Illane nudum interventum sanguinis Christi, & hoc tantum notant? nec veram ejus causalitatem & virtutem propriam? vel, quod illis continetur, meritum? Aut ita de fide nostra loqui fas erit, aliisque causis sine qua non, vel instrumentalibus justificationis, & salutis? Sin, agnoscant ergo sanguini & sacrificio Christi aliam, quam sine qua non, & veram causalitatem deberi, atque impetrationem, & non modo promissionis confirmationem, quae in aliis etiam speciatur seu rebus, seu personis, praeter Christum.
units.tr: IV. On the other hand, redemption properly belongs to the power of Christ's blood, as price (timē), ransom, merit: "For you were bought with a price" [ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς], 1 Cor. 6:20; 7:23. This is compared and opposed to silver or gold [ἀργυρίῳ]; but "you were bought with precious blood" [τιμίῳ αἵματι], 1 Pet. 1:18–19. These certainly designate the proper power and virtue of Christ's blood, and its merit. It is like the ransom [λύτρον]. Hence Scripture in many passages testifies that Christ gave a ransom [λύτρον] and an antiransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for us. Do these words mean only a bare intervention of Christ's blood, and nothing more? Not its true causality and proper virtue? Or the merit contained in them? Or will it be right to speak in this way of our faith, and of other causes without which not, or instrumental causes, of justification and salvation? But if not, let them acknowledge that to the blood and sacrifice of Christ is owed a true causality, other than a cause without which not, and impetration, and not merely the confirmation of a promise, which is also seen in other things or persons besides Christ.

units.la: Sed, nequiit, dicunt Adversarii, pro nobis mereri Christus, quia nec pro se; vel, si quidpiam pro se, idcirco non pro aliis. Socinus, part. iii. cap. v. Quocirca nec etiam pro aliis, magis quam quilibet alius homo, legem divinam confervando, satisfacere potuit, quippe qui ipse eam servare omnino deberet. Johannes certe Calvinus, Christum sibi ipsi meruisse, contra Lombardum, & Scholasticos aperte negat, Institut. lib. 2. cap. 17. sect. 6. At vero si sibi ipsi Christus non meruit, quomodo aliis mereri potuit?
units.tr: But the Adversaries say that Christ could not merit for us, because he did not merit for himself; or, if he did merit something for himself, then not for others either. Socinus, part 3, chap. 5: Wherefore he could not make satisfaction for others any more than any other man, by keeping the divine law, since he himself ought altogether to keep it. John Calvin, moreover, plainly denies, against the Lombard and the Schoolmen, that Christ merited for himself, Institutes, book 2, chap. 17, sect. 6. But if Christ did not merit for himself, how could he merit for others?

units.la: Resp. Primò tamquam improbè dictum notabunt Christiani omnes, quod Christus non magis quam quilibet alius homo potuit. Quod nec aures, nec animi nostri ferunt.
units.tr: Reply. First, all Christians will mark as an improper saying that Christ could no more than any other man do this. Neither our ears nor our minds can bear it.

units.la: ii. Negas, Christum, legem divinam servando, satisfecisse? satisfecisse nimirum obedientiâ legi praestandâ? non potes. Fecit enim in hoc genere quantum satis est. At debebat, certe quia homo, legi quoque erat subjectus. Sed quia sua non intereat, dum in formâ Dei, ἴσος aequalis Deo erat, se exinanire, & formam non modo hominis, sed servi assumere, & hinc obedientem fieri ad ipsam usque mortem crucis, inde nobis ista omnia, & pro nobis praestita fuerunt. Quidquid passus, & passione, tamquam lutro, satisfecit Christus, non pro se, vel crimine suo, sed pro nobis fuit. Quamvis autem humana natura, ut creatura quævis, Deo sublex observantiam debuit, attamen quia nec eam assumere, & talem ejus statum tenebatur, neque simplicis creaturæ obedientia fuit, sed ϑεανθρωπικὴ [?], ideo pro quibus hoc, & istud factum, quidni & satisfecisse pro iisdem dicatur?
units.tr: Second, do you deny that Christ made satisfaction by keeping the divine law? That is, satisfaction by rendering the obedience owed to the law? You cannot. For in this respect he did enough. But he owed it, surely because he was a man and was also subject to the law. Yet since he did not regard his own position as something to be grasped, though he was in the form of God, equal [ἴσος] to God, he emptied himself, and took the form not only of a man but of a servant, and became obedient even unto death, the death of the cross. From this, all these things were done for us and on our behalf. Whatever Christ suffered, and by his suffering, as a ransom, he satisfied, was done not for himself or for his own sin, but for us. Although human nature, like any creature, owed observance to God, yet since it was neither bound to assume that nature nor to hold that state, and since it was not the obedience of a mere creature but theanthropic [ϑεανθρωπικὴ], why should it not be said that he satisfied also for those for whom this and that was done?

units.la: Nihil vero obstat, ut idem, & varia ratione tam huic qui meretur, quam iis, pro quibus, prosit. Uti olim Sacerdos pro se, & populo obtulit: vel Adamus sibi, & posteris primo legem tenuit, tum fregit: ita & Christi obedientia justi constituuntur multi. Rom. v. 18. 19. Probet Adversarius, istud impossibile esse. iii. Calvinus, contra Scholasticos negat, Christum sibi meruisse, nempe contra eorum stultam curiositatem, & temerarias definitiones, uti ibidem loquitur. Annotavit autem Lombardum, iii. Dist. xviii. temere multa effutientem, ut quod Christus a conceptu meruit sibi hoc quod per passionem, & similia. Sed tota illa quæstio pendere videtur ab expositione vocis meriti, quod si, uti alii, & Sociniani videntur accipere, de merito condigni in se capias, extra omnem Dei gratiam & promissionem, quasi per obedientiam Christus sibi a Deo fuisset meritus, & obligasset ejus justitiam ad mercedem exaltationis, eamque sola sua vi & merito, de rigore justitiæ acquisivisset, & non ex Dei promissione: eo sensu non meruisse Christum dicimus, sibi non solum, sed neque nobis: at meritum intelligimus de præstatione & satisfactione conditionis tum lege generatim præscriptæ ad vitam, tum fœdere Mediatorio Dei cum Christo, ut si animam poneret pro multis, quod videret semen, & quam Apostolus appellavit, προκειμένῳ χαρὰν [?], Heb.xii.2. ὑπέμεινεν [?], & ὄνομα ὑπὲρ πᾶν [?] ὄνομα, quod ei Deus ἐχαρίσατο. Phil. ii. 9. pro quibus obtinendis, dum satisfecit Christus conditionibus sibi præscriptis, sive communi lege, sive proprio Mediationis fœdere, potest dici illa meritus, æque ac consecutus. Quum enim Christo in officio Mediatorio peragendo propositæ fuerint, servare legem perfecte, & præterea ea præstare ac pati, quæ ad officium Mediatorium requirebantur, duplex annexum utrique conditioni fuit præmium, vitæ ex lege, & exaltationis ab humiliatione, quibus, dum satisfecit Christus hinc inde conditionibus & regulis, etiam meruit [illegible, ~12 letters] utrimque mercedem & præmium, nempe quod divina bonitas constituerat. Διὸ ᾧ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ [?], ex gratia Deus illa contulit, quæ non absque, sed ex antecedente promissione Christus obtinuit. Nec aliter Christi meritum accipimus, quam quod legi plenissime satisfecit, non solius obedientiæ insita vi ac dignitate ad divini juris rigorem appensa, & hinc quasi debita sibi exaltatione, sed ad legem satisfactoriæ, sic meritus ex divina promissione fuit, non absque eâ. Meritum ad fœdus, non extra illud æstimatur, non ad merum Dei jus, quasi ulla cujusquam actione in rationem debiti trahi posset, Quod nec Socinus ignoravit à Calvino doceri ita & exponi, cujus hæc verba ex Institutionibus, lib. II. cap. XVI. §. I. attulit, part. III. de Servat. cap. IV. pag. 283. Quum ergo de Christi merito agitur, non statuitur in eo principium, sed conscendimus ad Dei ordinationem, qua prima causa est, &c. Et paulo post, Christus non nisi ex Dei beneplacito quicquam mereri potuit. Cæterum plus in merito Christi est, quam nuda præmii consecutio: quia, quemadmodum ex pacto legis & fœderis, pro antecedente observantia, non præmium simplici-ter, sed merces proponitur, ita præstita illa, merces quæ debetur huic obedientiæ propria, pro merito dari dicitur. Etenim non istud solum meritum appellamus, quod dignitate forte sua, citra pactum, sed & quod ex pacto meretur, observata nimirum legis conditione ad mercedem præscripta, hoc si feceris, vives. Τῷ δὲ ἐργαζομένῳ ὁ μισθὸς λογίζεται κατὰ τὸ ὀφει-λημα. Rom. iv. 4. Quamvis mercedis constitutio, & collatio fiat pro Dei benignitate, & hactenus κατὰ χάριν; quod propter antecedentia opera, obtingere dicitur κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα. Ut male inferat Socinus, pag. 180. Ubi debitum, ibi nullum verum & proprium meritum esse. Melius postmodum: potest quidem minus vere & proprie aliquis mereri, quia aliquid fecerit, quamvis id facere teneretur; sed non tamen propter personæ dignitatem aliquam, sed propter promissio-nem, quæ præstiterit. Atque hac ratione & sibi ipsi, & nobis meruisse Christum, ut supra alibi attigimus, recte dici potest. Cum enim Deus, ut ibi explicatum fuit, & decrevisset, & promisisset, si Christus animam suam, ut opus, quod ei mandaverat, peregeret, profudisset, futurum, ut & ipse, & quicunque ei obtemperassent, æternam salutem adipiscerentur, ac præterea ipsemet eam salutem sibi obedientibus dandi potestatem consequeretur; certè, postquam Christus animam suam, & munus sibi a Deo injunctum perficiendo, profudit: dignus fuit, qui ad tantam dignitatem & potentiam eveheretur: & merito nobis, qui illi obedimus, salutis æternæ quemadmodum scriptum est, causa extitit.
units.tr: Nothing stands in the way of the same person both meriting in one way for himself and for those for whom he benefits. Just as the priest once offered for himself and for the people; or as Adam first kept the law for himself and his posterity, and then broke it; so also by the obedience of Christ many are made righteous (Rom. 5:18, 19). Let the Adversary prove that this is impossible. Third, Calvin denies, against the Schoolmen, that Christ merited for himself, namely against their foolish curiosity and rash definitions, as he says in the same place. He noted, moreover, that the Lombard, in book 3, dist. 18, talks rashly, as when he says that Christ merited from the conception what he merited through the passion, and similar things. But that whole question seems to depend on the explanation of the word merit. If you take it, as others and the Socinians seem to, in the sense of merit of condignity in itself, apart from all grace and promise of God, as if Christ by his obedience had merited from God and bound his justice to the reward of exaltation, and had acquired that by the sheer power and merit of strict justice, and not from God's promise, then we say that Christ did not merit in that sense, not for himself only, but not for us either. But we understand merit as the performance and satisfaction of the condition prescribed both generally by the law for life, and by the mediatorial covenant of God with Christ, namely that he should lay down his soul for many, that he should see his seed, and what the Apostle called "the joy set before him, he endured" (Heb. 12:2) [προκειμένῳ χαρὰν; ὑπέμεινεν], and "the name which is above every name," which God graciously bestowed on him (Phil. 2:9) [ὄνομα ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα; ἐχαρίσατο]. For obtaining these, when Christ satisfied the conditions prescribed to him, whether by the common law or by the proper covenant of mediation, he can be said to have merited those things just as much as to have obtained them. For since it was set before Christ, in carrying out the mediatorial office, to keep the law perfectly, and besides to perform and suffer those things which the mediatorial office required, a double reward was attached to each condition: life under the law, and exaltation after humiliation. By satisfying these conditions and rules on both sides, Christ also merited [illegible] the reward and prize on both sides, namely what the divine goodness had appointed. Therefore [διὸ ᾧ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ], God bestowed those things on him out of grace, which Christ obtained not without, but from a prior promise. Nor do we understand Christ's merit otherwise than that he fully satisfied the law, not by the innate power and dignity of obedience weighed against the strictness of divine right, and so by an exaltation owed to himself as if due, but as satisfying the law, and thus he merited from the divine promise, not apart from it. Merit is reckoned in relation to the covenant, not outside it, not in relation to God's mere right, as if by any action of anyone something could be drawn into the reckoning of debt. Socinus did not fail to notice that Calvin teaches and explains it this way; he cited these words of Calvin from the Institutes, book 2, chap. 16, §1, in part 3, on the Preservation, chap. 4, p. 283: When we treat of Christ's merit, no principle is laid down in him, but we rise to the ordinance of God, which is the first cause, etc. And a little later: Christ could merit nothing except by God's good pleasure. Besides, there is more in Christ's merit than the bare obtaining of a reward: for just as, by the covenant of law and grace, upon prior observance, not simply a reward but a wage is proposed, so when that is performed, the reward that is owed to this obedience is said to be given as merit. Indeed we call that merit not only what is meritorious by its own dignity apart from any covenant, but also what is merited by covenant, namely when the condition of the law prescribed for the reward is observed: do this, and you shall live. "To him that worketh, the reward is reckoned not as grace but as debt" (Rom. 4:4) [Τῷ δὲ ἐργαζομένῳ ὁ μισθὸς λογίζεται κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα]. Although the appointment and bestowal of the reward is made by God's kindness, and so far according to grace [κατὰ χάριν], it is said to come about according to debt [κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα] because of the preceding works. So Socinus wrongly infers, p. 180: Where there is debt, there is no true and proper merit. Better afterwards: someone can indeed merit less truly and properly because he did something he was bound to do; yet not on account of some dignity of the person, but on account of the promise which he has fulfilled. And in this way it can rightly be said that Christ merited both for himself and for us, as we touched on elsewhere above. For since God, as was explained there, both decided and promised that, if Christ poured out his soul in carrying out the work which he had commanded him, both he himself and all who obeyed him would obtain eternal salvation, and besides that he himself would obtain the power of giving that salvation to those who obey him; certainly, after Christ poured out his soul and fulfilled the task enjoined on him by God, he was worthy to be raised to such dignity and power; and rightly he became, for us who obey him, the cause of eternal salvation, as it is written.

units.la: Vere & proprie tamen, quamvis Socino minus, meretur, qui perfecte facit quod lex exigit. Ex personæ dignitate est meriti valor; ipsum, ex debita legis observatione; merces, ex promisso. Si recte dicat intelligatque Socinus, Christum & sibi, & nobis meruisse, jam magnam disputationis partem compendio absolverit. Nempe meruit nobis, uti sibi, plena legis satisfactione, præstita nostro nomine & loco, quare & nobis omnino imputandâ, non modo sibi obtemperantibus, sed illâ ejus satisfactione justis & beatis. Quod Christus obedientiâ & morte non tantum consecutus dicitur gloriam sibi destinatam, sed & dignus, qui ad eam eveheretur, meruisse ipsum significat, quâ ratione meritum hic loci accipimus. Quod unice fundatum quum sit in ejus satis-factione, hanc ubi agnoscent Adversarii, erit de quo maxime iis, nobisque gratulabimur. Certe in ratione satisfactionis hæret tota meriti Christi veritas, & explicatio, quod pro nobis Christus præstitit, quidquid fecit, sive patiendo, sive merendo. Ut ex illis, quæ supra disputavimus de satisfactione, tota de merito Christi pendeat, & decidatur quæstio. Quare brevius hic defungimur, quum in illo prolixiores fuimus, atque esse, propter negotii tum gravita-tem, tum copiam, oportuit.
units.tr: Yet truly and properly, though less so in Socinus's view, he merits who perfectly does what the law demands. The value of the merit lies in the dignity of the person; the merit itself in the due observance of the law; the reward in the promise. If Socinus rightly says and understands that Christ merited both for himself and for us, he will have briefly settled a large part of the dispute. For he merited for us, as for himself, by a full satisfaction of the law, performed in our name and place, which therefore must be imputed to us entirely, so that we are just and blessed not only by obeying him but by that satisfaction of his. That Christ is said to have obtained by his obedience and death the glory destined for him, and that he merited to be raised to it, is what the word signifies, and in this sense we take merit here. Since it is founded solely on his satisfaction, when the Adversaries acknowledge this, it will be the thing on which we shall most of all congratulate them and ourselves. Certainly the whole truth and explanation of Christ's merit hangs on the account of satisfaction: that whatever Christ did, whether by suffering or by meriting, he did for us. So from what we have argued above concerning satisfaction, the whole question of Christ's merit depends and is decided. Therefore we dispatch it more briefly here, since we were more lengthy on that, and it had to be so, on account of the weight and the abundance of the matter.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA
units.tr: SECTION THREE

units.la: TAndem, ut ad Objectiones Adversariorum, quibus contra veritatem & doctrinam satisfactionis pugnant, accedamus, est tempus. Suntque illae tres. Primo dicunt, Deum potuisse citra satisfactionem peccata nostra remittere, nosque redimere. Secunda, quia vident non sufficere, si dicatur Deum potuisse illud, voluisse etiam, contendunt. Denique, & satisfactionem per Christum stare non posse, probare conantur. Ad tria illa ipse Socinus sua reducit omnia, quae nobis opponit, Part. III. cap. IV. pag. 367. primum, Deum potuisse, nulla vera pro peccatis nostris satisfactione accepta, ea nobis condonare: deinde, etiam id facere eum voluisse: postremo non potuisse Christum vel sua morte, vel alia ratione divina justitia pro peccatis nostris satisfacere. Part. III. in Praefat. ad cap I. ut assertionis mea veritas magis elucescat, probandum primo erit, potuisse Deum jure nobis peccata nostra ignoscere, nulla vera pro ipsis satisfactione ab ulla persona, ullove modo accepta. Deinde, id facere eum voluisse, demonstrabitur. Quo facto, planum postremo faciam, non potuisse Christum, vel sua morte, vel alia ratione divina justitia satisfacere.
units.tr: At last it is time to come to the objections of our opponents, with which they fight against the truth and doctrine of satisfaction. There are three. First, they say that God could forgive our sins and redeem us without satisfaction. Second, since they see that it is not enough to say that God could do this, they contend that he also willed it. Lastly, they try to prove that satisfaction cannot stand through Christ. Socinus himself reduces all the objections he raises against us to these three, Part III, chap. IV, p. 367: first, that God could forgive us our sins without any true satisfaction being accepted for them; then, that he also willed to do so; last, that Christ could not satisfy divine justice for our sins, either by his death or by any other means. Part III, in the preface to chap. I: So that the truth of my assertion may shine more clearly, it must first be proved that God could justly forgive us our sins, with no true satisfaction for them having been accepted from any person or in any manner. Then it will be shown that he willed to do so. When this is done, I will make it plain at last that Christ could not satisfy divine justice, either by his death or by any other means.

units.la: Eadem, eodemque ordine persequitur in Praelectionibus, in quas illa de verbo ad verbum fere translata sunt. Cap. XVI. Deum nobis peccata jure condonare potuisse, nulla vera pro ipsis a quoquam satisfactione accepta. Cap. XVII. Deum nulla vera satisfactione accepta nobis peccata condonare voluisse. Cap. XVIII. Nullo modo justitia divina salvis nobis pro peccatis nostris satisfieri potuisse, ne ab ipso Christo quidem.
units.tr: He follows the same matters in the same order in his Prelectiones, into which those passages have been translated almost word for word. Chap. XVI: that God could justly pardon us our sins, with no true satisfaction for them having been accepted from anyone. Chap. XVII: that God willed to pardon us our sins with no true satisfaction accepted. Chap. XVIII: that in no way could divine justice be satisfied for our sins, with us remaining safe, not even by Christ himself.

units.la: Deque eodem argumentorum Socini ordine Crellius, contra Grotium, Responf. ad cap IV. pag. 234, 235. Quae singula nunc videamus.
units.tr: Crellius, against Grotius, follows the same order of Socinus' arguments, Response to chap. IV, pp. 234, 235. Let us now look at these one by one.

units.la: Prima ergo objectio est: potuisse Deum, absque ulla interveniente satisfactione, peccata nostra expiare & remittere. Socinus, Part. III. cap. I.
units.tr: The first objection, then, is this: that God could, without any intervening satisfaction, expiate and remit our sins. Socinus, Part III, chap. I.

units.la: Deum nobis ignoscere jure potuisse, nulla pro peccatis nostris vera satisfactione accepta, ex eo constare potest, quod delicta nostra ea-tenus nos Deo obnoxios reddunt, utque pro ipsis ei satisfiat, requirere videri possunt, quatenus offensae sunt majestatis ipsius; ita ut peccatis, vera pro ipsis satisfactione non accepta, Deum ignoscere, nihil aliud fit, quam eum de jure suo remittere. Vnicui-que autem de jure suo quantum velit, re-mittere licet. Deus igitur, vera pro ipsis satisfactione non accepta, peccata nobis con-donare jure potuit. Quocirca Deus in homi-nibus vel puniendis, vel absolvendis, non tamquam judex aliquis statuendus est, qui de alieno jure agat, cuique non liceat a le-gum praescripto recedere; sed tamquam domi-
units.tr: God could justly forgive us without any true satisfaction accepted for our sins. This can be seen from the fact that our sins make us liable to God only so far as they seem to demand that satisfaction be made to him, inasmuch as they are offences against his majesty. So for God to pardon sins without true satisfaction having been accepted is nothing other than for him to remit his own right. But anyone may remit his right as far as he wishes. Therefore God could justly forgive us our sins without a true satisfaction having been accepted. Hence God, in punishing or absolving men, is not to be regarded as some judge acting on another's right, who may not depart from the prescription of the laws; but as a lord and sovereign, whose sole will is the rule of all things, and whose majesty cannot be denied by God.

units.la: Resp. 1. Frustra dicitur, Deum pec-cata remittere posse, nulla facta puni-tione, vel nulla satisfactione accepta: quia res illa non est potentia, ut diju-dicari ex illis debeat, quae Deus potest; sed justitiae: ad hanc,non ad illam exa-minanda quaestio est, non an pro po-tentia Deus possit, neque enim hujus fori est, sed an quidem justitia illud ferat. Nos in principio hujus contro-versiae manifestum fecimus, istam di-vinae justitiae & sanctitatis naturam esse ac vim, ut peccatum omni odio, & poena dignum propterea habeat, ac puniendum peccatorem. Quae illo lo-co abunde firmiterque, uti arbitramur, adstruximus. II. Immo quia peccata nus & princeps, cujus sola voluntas, cum offensæ sunt divinæ majestatis, inulta de ipsius jure tantum agatur, omnium re- ne sinat majestas ejus requirit, quam rum lex est, & perfectissima norma. Idem abnegare Deus haud potest. iii. Re-argumentum prosequitur Socinus, uti mittere de jure suo potest quidem, jam diximus, praefat. cap. xvi. Crellius, de Deo, cap. xxiii. pag. 182. non item totum omittere, non ut nolius, lit jus suum in punitione peccatum 191. Cap. xxv. pag 268. & alii. tum æquâ offendere nulla ratione, nec vindicare, sed ut ne semper, ne ubique, & ad extremum ejus quod posser-.
units.tr: Response 1. It is said in vain that God can remit sins with no punishment inflicted and no satisfaction accepted, because this is not a question of power, to be judged by what God can do, but of justice. The question is to be examined by that standard, not by this one. It is not whether God can do so by his power, for that is not the business of this court, but whether justice allows it. At the beginning of this controversy we made clear that the nature and force of divine justice and holiness is such that sin deserves all hatred and punishment, and that the sinner must therefore be punished. We believe we have established this abundantly and firmly in that place. II. Indeed, since sins offend the divine majesty, that majesty requires that they not go unpunished, and God cannot deny this, since his law is the rule of all things and most perfect. III. Socinus pursues the argument further, as we have already said in the preface to chap. XVI: God can indeed give up his right, but he cannot give up the whole of it, nor leave it entirely aside, so that he would never punish any sin in any way, and never avenge it, and at the very least would not uphold what is due to his majesty. See Crellius, De Deo, chap. XXIII, p. 182, and p. 191; chap. XXV, p. 268, and others.

units.la: Aliud est, remittere suum jus, vel de eo aliquid; deinde, omittere plane, & in totum, ut nec justum te ostendas, nec vindicem. Quin remittere Deus etiam aliqua ratione de illo possit, haud negamus; sed abnegare posse, aut totum praeterire, ne ullo modo, posito ex hypothesi voluntatis permissivæ peccato, jus exercet suum, haud item arbitramur. Quemadmodum, posito quod extra se operatur & producit alia, potest quidem non ad tantum gradum bonitatem suam exercere, & tam bona omnia efficere; sed ut omnino bonitatem suam non ostendat, nec bona sint illa quæ facit, haud potest: simili modo de justitia ejus statuendum, posito peccato. Atque uti æquitas Deo naturalis est, etiam juxta Adversarios, quam non potest non velle & ostendere, dum extra se agere statuit; ita & justitia vindicatrix, posito, ex hypothesi voluntatis & providentiæ divinæ, peccato. iv. Nec verum simpliciter & ubique, quod unicuique de jure suo, quantum velit, remittere liceat. Non certe judici, aut Magistratui, qui singulari & excellenti ratione ad Deum & justitiam ejus accedit, & ex cujus similitudine aut analogia argumentari hic potius convenit quam ex aliis, in communi. v. Deus hic non spectatur ut judex de alieno agens, sed ut judex, & Dominus sui juris. vi. Cujus & voluntas attenditur, & natura, eique insita justitia omnis, & essentialis.
units.tr: It is one thing to remit one's right, or something of it; it is another to give it up entirely and altogether, so that you show yourself neither just nor an avenger. We do not deny that God can in some way remit something of his right; but we do not think that, once sin is assumed under the hypothesis of his permissive will, he can refuse to exercise his right at all, or pass it over entirely in every way. Just as, granted that he works outside himself and produces other things, he can indeed not exercise his goodness to the full extent, and yet cannot fail to show his goodness altogether, nor can what he does be good: in a similar way we must judge of his justice, once sin is granted. And just as equity is natural to God, even according to our opponents, something he cannot but will and show whenever he decides to act outside himself, so also avenging justice, once sin is granted under the hypothesis of God's will and providence. IV. Nor is it true simply and everywhere that anyone may remit his right as much as he wishes. Certainly not a judge or magistrate, who approaches God and his justice in a singular and excellent way, and from whose likeness or analogy it is more fitting to argue here than from others in general. V. God is not regarded here as a judge acting on another's right, but as a judge and lord of his own right. VI. And both his will and his nature are considered here, and all justice that is inborn in him and essential to him.

units.la: Socinus: Quod autem justitia ista in Deo non resideat, præter ea, quæ supra à me disputata sunt, ex eo maxime apparere potest, quod, si ea in Deo resideret, nunquam is, ne minimum quidem delictum, cuiquam condonaret. Nihil enim unquam facit, aut facere potest, quod qualitatibus, quæ in ipso residente, adversetur. Resp. Nullæ in Deo verè sunt, aut residentes qualitates, neque talis est illa, de quâ jam disputatur, Dei justitia[?]. Sed quidquid est in essentiâ Dei, est Deus ipse, neque à natura differunt ipsius attributa. Quia, quod Deus est, per essentiam est, non per aliquod accidens, ipsi superveniens, à quo natura ejus alia, vel illud ab eâ aliud esse queat. ii. De justitia autem vindicatrice in Deo naturali, suo loco à nobis disputatum, & quodcunque à Socino allatum, à nobis discussum fuit, atque ea ipsa ratio, quam hic adfert: ad quam respondemus primo, non facere elenchum: non enim sequitur, si in Deo naturalis est justitia, ergo ne minimum quidem delictum condonabit. Non certe, condonabit, sed propter Christum, satisfactione ab ipso acceptâ, non citra satisfactionem. Concedimus Deum, extra Christum, ejusque satisfactionem & meritum, nemini aut condonare peccata, aut salutem tribuere. Probet vero, non simpliciter ajat, Socinus, istud absurdum esse. Instantiæ, quas forte adfert, ad sequens pertinent argumentum, ubi locum accipient suum, atque simul responsum. Deinde, quamvis nullum delictum Deus condonet, absque Christo, & non nisi vi [illegible, ~12 letters] Christi; at an possit, vel justitia ejus quidem ferat, ut citra omnem punitionem, aut satisfactionem peccata remittantur, hoc de omnibus intelligitur peccatis, non de aliquo: non an in ullo, sed an in remittendis absque punitione & satisfactione peccatis omnibus haud laedatur Dei justitia, quaeritur.
units.tr: Socinus: What, moreover, that justice does not reside in God, apart from what I have argued above, can be seen chiefly from this: if it resided in him, he would never pardon anyone even the least offence. For he never does, or can do, anything that is opposed to the qualities residing in him. Response. In God there are no qualities that are truly distinct or residing in him, nor is the divine justice under discussion such a quality. Whatever is in the essence of God is God himself, and his attributes do not differ from his nature. For what God is, he is by essence, not by some accident that is added to him, by which his nature could be other or differ from it. II. As for avenging justice in God's nature, we have discussed it in its proper place, and whatever Socinus has brought forward on this point has been examined by us, and this very argument he adduces here. To it we reply, first, that it does not prove the point: it does not follow that if justice is natural to God, he will therefore pardon not even the least offence. Certainly he will not pardon, but he will pardon on account of Christ, with satisfaction accepted from him, not without satisfaction. We grant that God, apart from Christ, his satisfaction and merit, grants pardon of sins to no one, nor bestows salvation. But let Socinus prove it, rather than simply assert that this is absurd. The instances he perhaps brings forward belong to the following argument, where they will have their place and their answer. Next, although God forgives no offence without Christ, and only by the power of [illegible] Christ, the question is whether his justice would allow that sins be remitted, all of them, without any punishment or satisfaction. This is what is understood, not whether he could forgive some sin, but whether, in remitting all sins without punishment and satisfaction, the justice of God would not be harmed.

units.la: Secunda objectio est, quod Deus etiam velit, nulla accepta satisfactione, peccata omnia remittere. Quod Socinus, part. III. cap. II. duplicitèr probare instituit, sive quod Deus id consuevit, tum ante Christum exhibitum, tum post. Ad illud, exempla profert divinae bonitatis in condonandis peccatis, etiam citra Christum, primum in Abele, qui justus fuisse, à Christo dicitur, Matth. 23. 35. & Apostolo, Hebr. 11. 4. atqui nemo justus esse potest, cui delicta à Deo non condonentur, Genes. 4. 7. Nonne, si bene fecerit, erit acceptatio? (seu remissio, inquit Soc. sive etiam elatio.) Quasi hoc natura ipsa omnes doceat, videlicet, Deum liberaliter peccata respicientibus condonare. Ut nihil fere magis impium excogitari possit, quam sentire, a Deo peccata non remitti, nisi pro ipsis illi plene satisfiat. 1 Pet. 3. 20. 2 Pet. 3. 9. Non tardat Dominus promissum, ut quidem tarditatem existimant; sed patienter agit erga nos, nolens aliquos perire, sed omnes ad poenitentiam reverti. Exspectabat igitur Deus &c. Ergo, si mundus respuisset, ei Deus diluvium non immisisset; sed hominum delictis gratuito pro liberalitate sua eximia pepercisset. Deinde adfert ad idem probandum, quodque sub ipsa lege Deus liberaliter peccata condonavit, testimonia & exempla, ex Deut. 4. 30. & 30. in initio. Nehem. 9. Psalm. 31. Ezech. 18. & 33. 1 Reg. 19, 16. & 21. 21. 32. Hier. 18.
units.tr: The second objection is that God also wills, without accepting any satisfaction, to forgive all sins. Socinus, in part III, chapter II, sets out to prove this in two ways: that God has done so both before Christ was revealed and after. To show the first, he offers examples of divine goodness in forgiving sins even apart from Christ. The first is Abel, who is said by Christ to have been just (Matt. 23:35) and by the Apostle (Heb. 11:4). But no one can be just to whom God does not forgive sins. (Gen. 4:7): "If you do well, will there not be acceptance?" (or, as Socinus says, forgiveness, or even exaltation). It is as if nature itself taught everyone that God freely forgives sins to those who respect him. So nothing could be more impious to imagine than the view that God does not forgive sins unless full satisfaction is made to him for them. (1 Pet. 3:20; 2 Pet. 3:9): "The Lord does not delay his promise, as some think it slow, but deals patiently with us, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." God therefore waited, etc. So, if the world had rejected him, God would not have sent the flood upon it, but would have spared the sins of men freely, out of his remarkable generosity. He then adduces, to prove the same point, and that under the law itself God freely forgave sins, testimonies and examples from Deut. 4:30 and at the beginning of chapter 30, Neh. 9, Ps. 31, Ezek. 18 and 33, 1 Kings 19:16 and 21:21, 32, Jer. 18.

units.la: Denique, quod etiam in N. Test. Deus per Christum, sine ulla vera satisfactione, peccata condonare velit, arguere conatur, ex verbis foederis, apud Jerem. cap. xxxi. ex quibus constet, in foedere hoc eam vim fuisse, ut in humanis mentibus divina legi parendi & voluntas & vires per ipsum gignerentur, quod satis est ad erratorum veniam plenissimam consequendam, &c. Quia propitius ero iniquitati ipsorum, & peccati eorum non recordabor amplius. Quomodo enim propitius fuisset Deus iniquitatibus nostris, si cum eas nobis, nulla satisfactione interveniente, remittere posset, pro ipsis sibi plenissime satisfieri curasset? addit & alia, eodem spectantia, ad declarandam nimirum summam Dei in N. Foedere liberalitatem in condonandis peccatis. Luc. 1. 77. ubi populo dicuntur remissa esse peccata, propter viscera misericordiae Dei nostri. Quis, inquit, hic satisfactionem ullam intervenisse vel somniare quidem potest? Nonne idem ipse postea, qua ratione hanc, sola Dei misericordia partam nobis, peccatorum remissionem reipsa consequeremur, luculenter expressit, cum poenitentiam agerent, quia regnum coelorum appropinquaret, populo denunciabat. Matth. 3. 2. & baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem peccatorum praedicabat, Marc. 1. 4. Luc. 3. 3. Nihil igitur praeter poenitentiam nostram extra seipsum requisivit Deus, ut peccatorum remissionem nobis in novo foedere oblatam consequeremur &c. Actor. 3. 19. & 36. & cap. 5. 31. & cap. 11. 18. & cap. 17. 30. & cap. 26. 20. Eadem habet Auctor, in Praelect. cap. XVII. Catechesis Racov. cap. VIII. de Prophetico Christi munere, qu. Qui vero Scripturæ repugnat? Resp*. Ad eum modum, quod Scriptura passim Deum peccata hominibus gratuito remittere testentur, potissimum sub novo fœdere. Rom. 3. 24. Ephef. 2. 8. Matth. 18. 23. & seqq. At remissioni gratuitæ nihil adversatur magis, quam satisfactio. Cui enim creditori satisfecit, vel ab ipso debitore vel alio debitoris nomine, de eo non potest vere dici, eum debitum gratuito, ex ipsa gratia remisisse. Eademque urget Crellius, contra Grotium. cap. v. vi.
units.tr: Finally, he tries to argue that even in the New Testament God wishes to forgive sins through Christ without any true satisfaction. He draws this from the words of the covenant in Jeremiah 31, from which, he says, it is clear that this covenant had the force of implanting in human minds both the will and the strength to obey the divine law, which is enough to obtain the most complete pardon for the erring, etc.: "For I will be merciful to their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." For how could God have been merciful to our iniquities if he could have forgiven them to us without any satisfaction intervening, when he had taken care that full satisfaction be made to himself for them? He adds other passages bearing on the same point, namely to declare God's great generosity in forgiving sins under the New Covenant: Luke 1:77, where it is said that sins were forgiven the people because of the tender mercy of our God. "Who," he says, "can even dream that any satisfaction intervened here? Did not the same man later, when he proclaimed to the people that the kingdom of heaven was at hand and that they should repent, clearly express the way in which we would actually obtain this remission of sins, which is obtained by God's mercy alone?" (Matt. 3:2); and he preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3).
