"Therefore God required nothing from outside himself, besides our repentance, in order that we might obtain the remission of sins offered to us in the new covenant, etc." (Acts 3:19, 36; 5:31; 11:18; 17:30; 26:20). The same author has the same in his Lectures, chapter XVII, and in the Racovian Catechism, chapter VIII, on the prophetic office of Christ, question: "But who opposes Scripture?" Answer: In this way, that Scripture everywhere testifies that God forgives sins to men freely, especially under the New Covenant (Rom. 3:24; Eph. 2:8; Matt. 18:23ff.). But nothing is more opposed to free forgiveness than satisfaction. For of a creditor to whom a debt has been paid, whether by the debtor himself or by another on the debtor's behalf, it cannot truly be said that he has remitted the debt freely, out of grace. Crellius presses the same argument against Grotius, chapters 5 and 6.

units.la: Resp. 1. Passim in hac argumentatione committunt Adversarii fallaciam elenchi, nec probant id, quod debent: concludunt enim, Deum liberaliter & gratuito remittere peccata, quod non est in quæstione; sed, an citra Christi satisfactionem Deus condonet peccata, id quæritur: neque hoc ostendunt. Nam quod ajunt, remissionem, & satisfactionem, quomodo utramque nos credimus, non posse concurrere, ajunt modo, non probant. Saltem non probatur ex illis Scripturæ testimoniis, quæ solum illud docent, Deum nempe remittere nobis peccata; non vero, istud pugnare cum satisfactione. Quare nihil ex Scripturæ locis evincunt, quum ex iis constet solum antecedens, de quo non est controversia; non consequens, non consequentis, seu satisfactionis cum remissione repugnantia. Quod sufficere pro responso ad singula ab Adversariis allata posset. 11. Abel justus fuit, aliique multi, quorum meminit Scriptura Sacra, & quorum justitiam commendat. Atqui nemo justus esse potest, cui delicta à Deo non condonentur. Verissimè. Interim, de infantibus, qui salvantur, lubet obiter quærere, pro justis eos habeant, an injustis? si pro injustis: quomodo salvantur? si pro justis, ergo peccata ipsis à Deo condonantur: neque ergo ab omni peccato, & originali, immunes sunt. 111. Condonata certe justis omni seculo fuerunt ipsorum peccata. Sed, quod addit, citra Christum, id unde probat? Eo loci, ubi justus Abel, justi & alii pronunciantur, nihil de Christo adjungitur. Explicans enim auctor ille ad Heb. eam fidem, propter quam & ipse Abel justus habitus à Deo fuerat, & Enochus Deo placuerat: eam iis, quæ jam diximus, contineri dicit; nempe, ut Deus esse credatur, & præmia rependere iis, qui ipsius sunt studiosi. Credidit igitur Abel, non modo Deum esse, sed eos etiam, qui ipsi obedirent, large remunerari. Credidit ista, sed præter ista nihil, neque sub istis etiam alia? Sane, quemadmodum Apostolus ex eo, quod Enochus Deo placuit, rite colligit eum credidisse, quia absque fide Deo placere impossibile sit; ita credisse eum eadem, qua nos, fide, atque eadem Deo placuisse, ex tota argumentatione liquet. Nam quæcunque de fide Patrum longa serie deducit, faciunt ad confirmationem ejus, quod initio capitis dixerat in fidei descriptione, est autem fides; ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων. Quibus, absque dubio, salutem Apostolus innuit, cujus spes basi innititur fidei. Et quod fidem iis describat salvificam, & nostram, qualis est sub N. T. patet tum ex re ipsa; tum ejus cum proxime præcedentibus cennexione, cap. x. 39. nos autem non sumus ὑποστολῆς [?] defectionis ad interitum, sed fidei ad salutis adeptionem. quibus statim subjungit, est autem fides, speratorum hypostasis, Idem confirmat conclufio, cap. XII. iu initio, Ideoque & nos tantam habentes circumstantem nobis testium nubem &c. intuentes in ipsum fidei ducem & consummatorem Iesum &c. Ex quibus constat, ipsum de fide eâdem egisse, quæ nostra est, quæque est in Christum Iesum. Nam non aliter convenient illa, quæ ex V.T. historiâ attulit, vel propositioni, vel conclusioni. Proinde etiam, quæ de fide Veterum, ea & in Christum Iesum referre oportet. Quod non tantum ex iis, quæ diximus, sed & quæ interjungit subinde ad Veterum fidelium exempla, manifestum redditur. Ut quod diserte de Mose, verf. 26. quod ad Christum, ejusque ὀνειδισμὸν [?] respexit, & hinc contemnere omnes Ægypti thesauros potuit: nam & in istam mercedis retributionem fidei suæ defixit oculos, εἰς τὴν μισθαποδοσίαν [?], atq; Christum illum τὴν ἀόρατον [?] ὡς ὁρῶν ἐκαρτέρησε [?].
units.tr: Answer 1. Throughout this argument our opponents commit the fallacy of elenchus, and they do not prove what they ought to prove. For they conclude that God forgives sins freely and graciously, which is not the question; the question is whether God forgives sins without the satisfaction of Christ, and this they do not show. For when they say that remission and satisfaction cannot concur, as we believe both to be the case, they merely say this and do not prove it. At least it is not proved by those testimonies of Scripture which teach only that God forgives us our sins, and not that this conflicts with satisfaction. So they establish nothing from the passages of Scripture, since these establish only the antecedent, about which there is no controversy, and not the consequent, namely the incompatibility of satisfaction with remission. This could suffice as an answer to each of the points our opponents have raised. 2. Abel was just, and many others, whom Holy Scripture mentions and whose righteousness it commends. But no one can be just to whom sins are not forgiven by God. Most true. Meanwhile, concerning the infants who are saved, it is worth asking in passing whether they should be regarded as just or as unjust. If as unjust, how are they saved? If as just, then their sins are forgiven them by God, and therefore they are not free from all sin, original sin included. 3. Certainly the sins of the just were forgiven in every age. But whence does he prove what he adds, apart from Christ? In the passage where Abel is pronounced just, and other just men too, nothing is added about Christ. For that author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, explaining the faith on account of which Abel had been regarded as just by God, and Enoch had pleased God, says that this faith is contained in what we have already said, namely that God is believed to exist and to reward those who seek him. Abel therefore believed not only that God exists, but also that those who obey him are richly rewarded. He believed these things, but did he believe nothing beyond them, nor under them any other things? Certainly, just as the Apostle rightly infers from the fact that Enoch pleased God that he believed, since without faith it is impossible to please God, so it is clear from the whole argument that Enoch believed by the same faith as we do and pleased God by it. For whatever he deduces at length from the faith of the Fathers serves to confirm what he had said at the beginning of the chapter in the description of faith: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" (Heb. 11:1) [ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων]. By this the Apostle undoubtedly hints at salvation, whose hope rests on the foundation of faith. And that he describes this faith as saving, and as ours, such as it is under the New Testament, is evident both from the matter itself and from the connection with what immediately precedes (Heb. 10:39): "But we are not of shrinking back (ὑποστολῆς) to destruction, but of faith to the obtaining of salvation." To which he immediately adds: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for." The conclusion of chapter 12 at the beginning confirms the same: "Therefore we also, having so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, ... looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith" etc. From these it is clear that he was speaking of the same faith that is ours, and that is in Christ Jesus. For those things which he drew from the history of the Old Testament could not otherwise fit either the proposition or the conclusion. Therefore what is said of the faith of the ancients must also be referred to Christ Jesus. This is made plain not only by what we have said, but also by what he adds from time to time as examples of the faithful of old: as, expressly, of Moses (v. 26), who regarded the reproach (ὀνειδισμὸν) of Christ and on that account could despise all the treasures of Egypt; for he also fixed his eyes on the recompense of his faith (εἰς τὴν μισθαποδοσίαν), and endured as seeing him who is invisible (τὴν ἀόρατον ὡς ὁρῶν ἐκαρτέρησε).

units.la: 27. Idem de Abrahamo constat, quando promissum sibi semen spectavit, verf. 18. in Isaaco vocabitur tibi semen. Gal. iii. 16. & semini tuo, qui est Christus. Sic & illum, & fundamenta habentem civitatem exspectavit, cujus fabricator & auctor Deus, verf. 10. id est coelestem. οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ θεοῦ, οἰκίαν ἀχειροποίητον, αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς [?]. IICor. v. 1. Quare fideles illi omnes, eâdem, cum nostrâ, fide prædicti, iisdemque promissis salvati fuerunt. Unde & eadem promissio ipsorum fidei objecta, quæ nostræ, hoc solo discrimine, quod exhibitionem ejus non impetrarint, quæ temporibus N.T. reservabatur, ne sine nobis perficerentur, verf. 39. Et illi omnes μαρτυρηθέντες διὰ τῆς πίστεως, οὐκ ἐκομίσαντο τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν [?]. Promissum non acceperunt, vel reportarunt, quod ad eventum, vel exhibitionem & manifestationem futuri Christi, & status Euangelici, qui cum plenitudine temporis Gal. iv. 4. erat revelandus; ἐπαγγελία tamen ipsis de eo facta, inque eam fide prospexerunt, ac proinde fidei elogio ornati fuerunt, cum quibus, eodemque ac ipsi modo, per fidem in Christum salvatum iri nos credimus, Actor. xv. 11. Sed per gratiam Domini Iesu Christi πιστεύομεν σωθῆναι [?], καθ' ὃν τρόπον κἀκεῖνοι [?]. Habentes eundem spiritum fidei. IICor. iv. 13. Rom. iv. 12. τοῖς στοιχεῖσιν τῆς ἴχνεσιν τῆς ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ πίστεως τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ [?]. Rom. i. 12. Euangelium Dei, (quod prænunciatum ὃ προεπηγγείλατο [?] per Prophetas ejus in Scripturis sa-eris. Atque ideo Christus non nunc modo, sed semper, & heri & hodie idem, & in perpetuum, Hebr. xiii. 8. agnus mactatus à fundatione mundi. Apoc. xiii.
units.tr: 27. The same holds for Abraham, when he looked to the seed promised to him, Heb. 11:18: "In Isaac shall thy seed be called." Gal. 3:16: "and to thy seed, which is Christ." So too he waited for the city that has foundations, whose builder and maker is God, Heb. 11:10, that is, the heavenly one [building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens, 2 Cor. 5:1]. Therefore all those faithful ones, endowed with the same faith as ours, were saved by the same promises. Hence the same promise was the object of their faith as of ours, with this one difference: they did not obtain its fulfilment, which was reserved for the times of the New Testament, so that they should not be made perfect without us, Heb. 11:39. "And all these, having obtained a good report through faith, did not receive the promise" [οὐκ ἐκομίσαντο τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν]. That is, they did not receive or carry back the promise as to its event, or the coming and manifestation of the future Christ and the state of the Gospel, which was to be revealed at the fulness of time, Gal. 4:4. Yet the promise concerning it was made to them, and they looked forward to it in faith, and so they were adorned with the commendation of faith. With them, and in the same way as they, we believe that we shall be saved through faith in Christ, Acts 15:11: "But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, in the same manner as they" [πιστεύομεν σωθῆναι, καθ' ὃν τρόπον κἀκεῖνοι]. "Having the same spirit of faith," 2 Cor. 4:13. Rom. 4:12: "walking in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham which he had while still uncircumcised" [τοῖς στοιχοῦσιν τοῖς ἴχνεσιν τῆς ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ πίστεως τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ]. Rom. 1:2: "the gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand by his prophets in the holy Scriptures" [ὃ προεπηγγείλατο]. And so Christ is not only now but always "the same yesterday, and today, and for ever," Heb. 13:8; "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world," Rev. 13:8.

units.la: 8. Quæ, sive de Christo, sive de Patribus, eorumque fide, relata in Novo Test. quamvis non ita exserte legantur in V.Test., vera tamen sunt, quia in Novo narrantur, quod in hoc non errat, & pro commentario Veteris infallibili haberi ab omnibus debet. Ubi in Veteri ita reperies, quod Abraham, visa per fidem die Christi exultavit, uti hoc in Novo, ab ipso Christo relatum, Ioan. viii. 56. ? vel ubi, quod Moses in Christo ὀνειδισμὸν [?], & futuram illam τὴν μισθαποδοσίαν[?] respexit, quod de eo testatur Apostolus? Hebr. xi. 26 Supra omnem tamen dubitationem illa sunt, & vero veriora. De quibus ex Novo Testamento æque instruendi sumus, atque ex Veteri, & quod omnes Prophetæ à Samuele & deinceps, quotquot loquuti fuerunt, etiam dies prænunciarunt illos Christi, & Euangelii. Act. iii. 24. Nempe in promissionibus, & sacrificiis illa profpectarunt fideles jam inde ab omni ævo, & Abel, & alii, quotquot πίστει θυσίαν[?] Deo obtulerunt, per quam testimonium justitiæ assequuti sunt. Hebr. xi. 4. Sed de illis antea, in disputatione de fœdere Dei abunde dictum.
units.tr: 8. What is related in the New Testament, whether of Christ or of the Fathers and their faith, is true, even though it is not so plainly read in the Old Testament; for it is narrated in the New, which does not err in this, and must be held by all as an infallible commentary on the Old. Where will you find in the Old that Abraham, having seen by faith the day of Christ, rejoiced, as this is reported in the New by Christ himself, John 8:56? Or where is it said that Moses regarded reproach in Christ and the future reward, as the Apostle testifies of him, Heb. 11:26? Yet these things are beyond all doubt, and truer than true. We are instructed about them from the New Testament just as much as from the Old, and all the prophets, from Samuel onward, as many as spoke, also foretold these days of Christ and of the Gospel, Acts 3:24. Indeed the faithful looked for those things from the very beginning of the world, in the promises and sacrifices: Abel and others, as many as offered sacrifice to God by faith [πίστει θυσίαν], through which they obtained testimony of righteousness, Heb. 11:4. But of these things we have spoken at length before, in the disputation on the covenant of God.

units.la: iv. Nunc Socinus ea profert ex V. Test. quæ ostendunt, Patribus constitisse de remissione peccatorum suorum, ex doctrinâ & promissione ipsis tunc factâ. Ad citata ex Deut. 4. & 30. loca, ait, promittit igitur Moses populo, quod, postquam Deus eum, propter delicta inter gentes dispersisset, & captivum duci voluisset, siquando pœnitentiam suorum delictorum ageret, conversus ad ipsum Deum, futurum esset, ut Deus ipsorum misereretur, & à captivi-tate eos liberaret, & sic eis delicta condonaret. Ex cap.9. Neh. & oratione Levitarum ad Deum præcipue idem probat, inque ea & copiosissime & dilucidissime comemorari asserit. Postque adducta verba, quid potuit apertius dici, ut sciremus Dei voluntatem esse, ut peccata pœnitentibus condonentur, & id revera ab ipso præstari? Ad verba Davidis, Psalm. 31. Beatus, cui demissa pravaricatio &c. addit, illis ergo Deus peccata condonat, & iniquitates non imputat. Quibus quomodo conveniant quæ alibi disputant, factas Patribus promissiones rerum corporalium & terrenarum, non item spiritualium & salutarium, ipsi viderint.
units.tr: iv. Now Socinus brings forward passages from the Old Testament which, he says, show that the Fathers were assured of the forgiveness of their sins from the doctrine and promise then made to them. On the passages cited from Deut. 4 and 30, he says: "Moses therefore promises the people that, after God had scattered them among the nations on account of their sins and wished them to be led into captivity, if ever they repented of their sins, turning to God himself, it would come to pass that God would have mercy on them and free them from captivity, and so forgive them their sins." From chapter 9 of Nehemiah, and from the prayer of the Levites to God, he proves the same thing especially, and asserts that it is recalled there both very fully and very clearly. And after the words quoted: "What could have been said more plainly, so that we may know that it is God's will that sins be forgiven to the penitent, and that he really grants this?" On the words of David, Psalm 31: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, etc.," he adds: "God therefore forgives sins to them and does not impute iniquities." How these agree with what he argues elsewhere, that the promises made to the Fathers concerned corporeal and earthly things, not spiritual and saving ones, they themselves may see.

units.la: v. Ergo condonavit Deus hominum peccata liberaliter omni tempore, & hoc se facturum recepit, & crediderunt id quoque fideles, sub V. Test.: sed nec citra Christum remisit illa Deus, neque extra eum remissam obtinuerunt pii, quandoquidem ei omnes Prophetæ attestantur, remissionem peccatorum accipere per nomen ejus quemque credentem in ipsum. Act. x. 43. Textus clarior, quam ut ullâ Adversariorum exceptione possit infringi. Ut enim de remissione peccatorum loquuti fuerunt, ita & de modo ac vitâ eam accipiendi unicâ, per fidem nimirum in Christum. Deque remissione tum ipsis, tum nobis vaticinati fuerunt: quod ex Socini hac disputatione constat. Act. iv. 12. neque est in ullo alio salus: nec nomen aliud datum est sub cœlo hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvari.
units.tr: v. Therefore God forgave men's sins freely at all times, and promised that he would do so, and the faithful under the Old Testament believed this too. But God did not forgive them apart from Christ, nor did the godly obtain forgiveness outside him, since "to him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives remission of sins through his name," Acts 10:43. The text is too clear to be overturned by any objection of the adversaries. For just as they spoke of the forgiveness of sins, so they spoke of the one way and life by which it is received, namely through faith in Christ. And they prophesied of the remission both to them and to us; this is clear from Socinus's own disputation. Acts 4:12: "neither is there salvation in any other; for neither is there any other name under heaven given to men, by which we must be saved."

units.la: vi. Non certe vitæ puritas & innocentia quædam caussa est, ut Deus illis clementer ac benigne peccata condonet. quemadmodum Socinus loquitur. Conditio quidem illa est, requisita in subjecto, cui peccatorum remissio applicetur: non vero causa, ob quam hominibus detur: nisi quod Christi est, nobis, atque operibus nostris arrogare improbè velimus. Resipiscentibus Deus veniam peccatorum pollicetur & præstat, sed non propter causam resipiscentiæ.
units.tr: vi. Certainly the purity and innocence of a life is not a cause why God mercifully and kindly forgives sins, as Socinus puts it. That is indeed a condition required in the subject to whom the remission of sins is applied, but not the cause for which it is given to men, unless we wish wickedly to claim for ourselves and our works what belongs to Christ. God promises and grants pardon of sins to the penitent, but not on account of the cause of repentance.

units.la: vii. Denique sub N. Test. haud aliter Deus remissionem peccatorum aut pollicetur, aut impertit, vel aliter concedenda à fidelibus creditur, quam per & propter Christum, per nihil aliud vel operis meritive nostri, aut alieni. Et Christus quando hic memoratur, pro causa venit, eaque impulsivâ verâ meritoriâ. Neque, nisi iniquior in Christi sanguinem, ejusque pretium dixerit aliquis cum Socino, quod animus parendi legi divinæ satis est ad errantorum veniam plenissimam consequendam. pag. 286. vel, quod nihil præter pœnitentiam nostram extra seipsum requisivit Deus, ut peccatorum remissionem nobis in novo fœdere oblatam consequeremur. Hoc jam est Christum, & sanguinis ejus vim, atque mentionem expungere. Quæ quantopere Christianismum diruant, & nihil reliquum faciant præter vitam quandam ethicam, & pœnitentiam ei similem, qualem ipsi etiam Gentiles tradiderint, per se satis clarum.
units.tr: vii. Finally, under the New Testament God neither promises nor bestows the remission of sins in any other way, nor is it believed to be granted by the faithful in any other way, than through and on account of Christ, and through nothing else, neither our own work or merit nor another's. And when Christ is mentioned here, he comes forward as the cause, and a true impulsive and meritorious cause. Nor would anyone, unless he were more unjust toward the blood of Christ and its price, say with Socinus that the willingness to obey the divine law "is enough to obtain the most full pardon for those who have gone astray," p. 286; or "that God required nothing outside himself besides our repentance, in order that we might obtain the remission of sins offered to us in the new covenant." This is now to erase Christ and the power and mention of his blood. How greatly such views overthrow Christianity, and leave nothing but a certain ethical life and a repentance like that which even the Gentiles taught, is clear enough in itself.

units.la: viii. Non quidem quotiescunque promissio de peccatorum remissione refertur, additur Christi passio, vel satisfactio; nullibi tamen excluditur, vel rejicitur. Et quam frequenter in quibusvis scriptis res aliqua, nec semper ejus causa simul aut modus exponitur?
units.tr: viii. It is true that whenever the promise of the forgiveness of sins is mentioned, the passion or satisfaction of Christ is not always added; yet it is nowhere excluded or rejected. And how often in any writings is some matter set forth without its cause or manner being explained at the same time?

units.la: ix. Revera sola Dei misericordia parta nobis peccatorum remissio est: ea sola ex causa, & fonte unico. Sed cui adeo non repugnat quidquid Christus in salutem nostram egit passusque fuit, ut non aliunde vel ipse derivetur. Ita enim dilexit Deus mundum. Joann. iii. 16. Probavit autem Deus charitatem suam erga nos, quod nobis etiam existentibus peccatoribus Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Rom. v. 8.
units.tr: ix. Truly, the remission of sins won for us is the mercy of God alone: that alone is its cause and its single source. But whatever Christ did and suffered for our salvation is so far from opposing this that it is not itself derived from anywhere else. "For God so loved the world," John 3:16. "But God commends his love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners Christ died for us," Rom. 5:8.

units.la: Socinus: Quid magis remissioni contrarium, quam vera & plena satisfactio? Nam, si dicas, invicem quidem pugnare remissionem & plenam satisfactionem: sed tunc demum, cum satisfactio ab eo ipso proficisci debet, qui remissionem consecutus est: non posse autem ejusdem debiti remissionem, pro quo plene satisfactum fuerit, tunc consistere, cum uni remittitur, alius vero pro eo satisfacit: nihil dixeris. Neque enim illi remittitur, pro quo est qui plene satisfaciat. Nam quid opus est remissione, aut quomodo ea consistere potest, ubi nullum est debitum? Atqui debitum nullum est amplius, ubi jam plene pro ipso satisfactum est. Resp. i. Remissioni non est contraria satisfactio, neque illa huic; verum subordinantur sibi commodè. Uti neque in Deo quæ sunt proprietates, in hoc opere maxime eminentes & energeticæ, & huic respondentes, justitia & misericordia. Utriusque divina sapientia admirandum reperit temperamentum, simul ut justitiæ satisfactum fuerit, & tum in eo, tum ex eo misericordia gloriose eluceat in salvandis redemtis, & redimendis salvandis. Peccatum pœnam merebatur, natura suâ, & divinâ constitutione: ediderat Deus, quod pœnam esset repetiturus à peccatore. Hinc omnes ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, καὶ τὴν κατάραν, & pœnis atq; maledictioni obnoxii. Unde & liberandi erant primum, antequam vitæ participes reddi poterant. Justitia pœnam efflagitabat & satisfactionem: quâ sedatâ locus patuit misericordiæ. Illi viam quærere, quâ placari posset, supra humanam fortem erat. Ideoque Dei Filius venit, ὡς ἐν μορφῇ θεῷ ὑπάρχων, οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ, rapinam non duxit esse [?], verum seipsum ἐκένωσεν, μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν, ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος, καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, humiliavit seipsum, obediens factus usque ad mortem, mortem verò crucis. Phil. ii. 6. 7. 8. atque isto pacto αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑράμενος, Heb. ix. 12. Salvator noster extitit, qui pro nobis divinae justitiae satisfecit, atque ἐξουσίαν[?] accepit remittendi in suo sanguine peccata nostra. Praecessit ergo satisfactio, sed Christi, atque sequuta eam est, ejus vi & merito, peccatorum nostrorum a Deo remissio. Divinissime ergo conspirant illa, non pugnant. Satisfactio remissioni viam stravit, haec satisfactione promerita & impetrata fuit. Quae hic, oblecro, est contrarietas? Opposita debent esse secundum idem, ad idem, eodem modo: quae hic desunt omnia. Justitiae divinae satisfactum, a Christo, pro nobis: unde misericordia remittit peccata, & nobis. Ubique diversa sunt, non eadem, opposita nulla, quamvis quidem subordinata.
units.tr: Socinus: "What is more contrary to remission than true and full satisfaction? For if you say that remission and full satisfaction fight with each other, but only when the satisfaction must come from the very one who has obtained the remission, you would say nothing: for it is not possible that the remission of the same debt, for which full satisfaction has been made, should stand when it is remitted to one person while another makes satisfaction for him. For remission is not granted to the one for whom someone else fully satisfies. For what need is there of remission, or how can it stand, where there is no debt? But there is no debt any longer where full satisfaction has already been made for it." Reply 1: Satisfaction is not contrary to remission, nor remission to satisfaction; rather they are fittingly subordinated to each other. Just as in God there are not opposed properties, but those most prominent and active in this work and corresponding to it, justice and mercy. In these the divine wisdom has found a wonderful temperament, so that justice is satisfied, and in that satisfaction and from it mercy shines forth gloriously in saving the redeemed and redeeming those who are to be saved. By its nature and by the divine constitution, sin deserved punishment: God had declared that he would exact punishment from the sinner. Hence all are under sin and the curse, and liable to penalties and malediction. Whence they had first to be freed, before they could be made partakers of life. Justice demanded punishment and satisfaction; when this was appeased, room was opened for mercy. To seek a way by which God might be appeased was beyond human strength. Therefore the Son of God came, who, "being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man, humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross," Phil. 2:6–8; and in this way, having obtained eternal redemption, Heb. 9:12, he became our Saviour, who made satisfaction for us to divine justice, and received authority [ἐξουσίαν] to remit our sins in his blood. Satisfaction therefore went before, but Christ's satisfaction; and following it came, by its power and merit, the remission of our sins by God. These things therefore agree most divinely; they do not fight. Satisfaction paved the way for remission; remission was merited and obtained by satisfaction. What contrariety is there here, I ask you? Opposites must be in respect of the same thing, to the same thing, in the same way, and all of these are absent here. Divine justice was satisfied for us by Christ; whence mercy remits our sins to us. Everywhere the things are different, not the same; there is no opposition, though they are indeed subordinated.

units.la: 11. Sed, non illi remittitur, pro quo est, qui plene satisfaciat, inquit Socinus. Quod nos plane negamus. Annon est remissio, ubi debita poena alicui non irrogatur, sed & ipsa, & obligario, vel reatus omnis, κατάκριμα[?] perimitur? Istud hic fit. Satisfactio antecedens non est ejus qui peccarat, debitoris ipsius, & cui remittuntur sua; sed alterius. Attamen pro illo praestita, jam proba, quod remissionem interimat, & non possit dici remissum ei debitum, qui ipse nil solvit, atque alienâ solutione liberatur. Posita necessitate solutionis, quam nos in principio adstruximus, vident Adversarii quod forte possit cum ea consistere remissio. Socinus, hoc cap. pag. 236. Primum dico, munificentiam & liberalitatem istam fortasse confisturam, si, ut delicta nostra aliquo modo punirentur, necesse fuisset. hoc vero antea probavimus. Hactenus ergo vident, non adeo ista secum pugnare. Atque etiam pag. 245. ad id, quod dici solet, in ea solutione, quam pro nobis Christus fecit, Dei liberalitatem maximam apparere, cum ipsemet Deus id dederit, quod sibi solvi curavit, respondet itidem Socinus, ejusmodi liberalitates, ut supra a nobis dictum, non exerceri, nisi cum aliter fieri non potest, & nisi aliqua de causa solutionem intervenire necesse fuit.
units.tr: 11. "But it is not remitted to him for whom someone fully satisfies," says Socinus. We flatly deny this. Is it not remission when the debt's penalty is not imposed on someone, but the very obligation, and all guilt, the condemnation [κατάκριμα], is taken away? That is what happens here. The prior satisfaction is not made by the one who sinned, the debtor himself, to whom his sins are remitted, but by another. Yet offered for him, it shows now that it does not destroy remission, and it cannot be said that the debt was remitted to him who pays nothing himself and is freed by another's payment. Granting the necessity of payment, which we laid down at the beginning, our opponents see that remission may perhaps still stand alongside it. Socinus, in this chapter, p. 236: First I say that this kindness and liberality will perhaps hold together, if, in order that our sins might be punished in some way, it had been necessary. But we have already proved this. So far, then, they see that these things do not fight with each other very much. Moreover, on p. 245, in reply to the common saying that in the payment which Christ made for us, God's very great liberality appears, since God himself gave what he arranged to be paid to himself, Socinus again answers: such liberalities, as we said above, are not exercised unless it cannot be otherwise done, and unless for some reason a payment was necessary to intervene.

units.la: 111. Scriptura utrumque conjungit, satisfactionem Christi & remissionem peccatorum nostrorum. Rom. 111. 24. 25. Justificati gratis ipsius gratia, per redemtionem in Jesu Christo. Quem proposuit Deus placamentum ἱλαστήριον[?] per fidem in sanguine ejus, ad demonstrationem justitiae suae, per remissionem peccatorum ante commissorum. Ephes. 1. 7. In quo habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum juxta divitias gratiae ejus.
units.tr: 111. Scripture joins both together, the satisfaction of Christ and the remission of our sins. Rom. 3:24, 25: Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ. Whom God has set forth to be a propitiation [ἱλαστήριον] through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness, for the remission of sins that are past. Eph. 1:7: In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.

units.la: Redemtio per sanguinem, quam ostendimus esse satisfactionem, est ad remissionem peccatorum. Duo ergo illa sunt, debitum satisfactum, & remissum, quae bene consistunt, satisfactum per Christum, & remissum nobis, quia satisfactum prius. Nostra enim erant debita, pro quibus Christus satisfecit, non ejus. Satisfactum justitiae, remissum ex gratia. Denique, eo major est, ex nostra sententia, Dei in remittendis peccatis nostris benignitas, quo non remittit solum ea nobis, sed & per id, seu per Filium, ejusque solutionem, quam ipse de suo nobis donat. Atque ita revera non una, sed duplex Dei liberalitas in peccatorum nostrorum remissione intervenit, una, quod gratis nobis debita remittit: altera, quod per Filium, quem nostri causa acerbissima morti tradidit, & ita seipsum quodammodo graviter ladens, ut nos maxime beneficio afficeret, eum, ut ita dicam, impendere ac profundere non dubitavit. verba sunt Socini, pag. 246. Sed quorsum ista, adeoque acerba, nisi pro debitis nostris solvere Filius voluit, debuitque? licebit enim dicere aliter, quod Socinus, eodem loco, nobis: alioquin enim cur inutili illo circuitu utendum effet, cum simplici debiti remissione, & debitorem liberare, & largitatem suam ostendere creditor posset? Deinde, quid enim causa fuit, ut in istum finem filium suum innocentissimum Deus, tam dira & execrabili morte affici voluerit, cum satisfactione ista nihil opus effet? Et haec Socini verba sunt, pag. 247. quae ipsi ratione longe fortiori merito nunc opponimus.
units.tr: The redemption through blood, which we have shown to be satisfaction, is for the remission of sins. Those two things, therefore, namely the debt satisfied and remitted, agree well: satisfied by Christ, and remitted to us, because it was satisfied first. For the debts were ours, for which Christ satisfied, not his. What is satisfied is justice's due; what is remitted comes from grace. Finally, according to our view, God's kindness in remitting our sins is all the greater, in that he not only remits them to us, but also does so through the Son and his payment, which he himself gives us from his own. And so in truth not one but a double liberality of God intervenes in the remission of our sins: one, that he remits to us debts that we owed without any return; the other, that through the Son, whom for our sake he delivered to a most bitter death, and so, as it were, grievously wounding himself, in order to bestow the greatest benefit upon us, he did not hesitate to spend and pour out, so to speak. These are Socinus's words, p. 246. But why these things, and so harsh, unless the Son was willing and bound to pay for our debts? For one may say otherwise what Socinus, in the same place, says to us: for otherwise why should one use that useless detour, when a creditor could both free the debtor and show his generosity by a simple remission of the debt? Again: for what reason was there that God wished his most innocent Son to be afflicted with such a dire and execrable death for this end, when there was no need of that satisfaction? These are Socinus's words, p. 247, which we now rightly oppose to him with a much stronger argument.

units.la: Socinus: qui, obsecro, eodem tempore & remitti debitum, & pro eo satisfieri potest, si, dum pro eo satisfit, exigitur, dum vero remittitur, condonatur? Resp. 1. Primum satisfit, tum remittitur, non contra. 11. Ubi satisfactum, remittitur, in Christo nempe liberationem merito: remissio peccatorum nostrorum active a Deo facta, id est, remisit Deus in Christo omnibus, pro quibus is satisfecit; quam ex satisfactione remissionem singulis applicatum it passive, tum quando actu existunt & credunt. 111. Ergo & dum satisfacit Christus, debitum ab eo nostrum, tamquam vade, exactum fuit; & nobis in Christo censitis, tamquam in capite condonatum; in persona & actu proprio, nobis condonatur, ubi credimus. Uti Adamus sua παράβασις reatum contraxit sibi, suisque, qui nobis actu imputatur, ubi existimus; sic in Christo, ejusque ὑπακοὴ [?] impetrata nobis redemtio ac salus, applicatur & intimatur tandem in Christum credentibus.
units.tr: Socinus: Pray, how can a debt be both remitted and satisfied for at the same time, if while satisfaction is made it is demanded, and while it is remitted it is pardoned? Reply: (1) First, satisfaction is made, then remission follows, not the reverse. (2) Where satisfaction is made, remission follows in Christ, namely the liberation by merit: the remission of our sins, made by God actively, that is, God remitted in Christ to all for whom he satisfied; this remission, applied to individuals from the satisfaction, takes effect passively when they actually exist and believe. (3) Therefore, while Christ satisfies, the debt of ours was demanded from him as surety, and it was pardoned to us, reckoned in Christ as in the head; in his person and his own act it is pardoned to us when we believe. Just as Adam by his transgression [παράβασις] contracted guilt for himself and his own, which is actually imputed to us when we exist in him, so in Christ, and the redemption and salvation obtained by his obedience [ὑπακοή], are applied to us and finally made known to those who believe in Christ.

units.la: Socinus: Nec vero est, quod quis rursus hic dicat, non eidem condonari, a quo exigitur. Animadvertendum namque est, non posse debitum exigi, nisi ab eo, qui debet. Potest quidem alius pro alio satisfacere. Sed interim non ab eo, qui pro alio fatufacit [?], sed ab eo, pro quo satisfit, debitum exigitur. Resp. Et ab eo qui debet, & a fidejussore ac sponsore debitum exigitur, ubi in ipsum est translatum. Non duplex debitum, vel dupliciter, sed a Vade exigitur, nomine debitoris, cujus causam ille in se suscepit. Atque ita rata, vel praestita satisfactione, tum Vades absolvitur, tum debitor ipse, quia una hi censentur persona. Et nos ita in Christo unum, is pro nobis, nos in eo. Quod praestitit, quod satisfecit, quod absolutus, nostrum est in ipso.
units.tr: Socinus: Nor is there any reason for someone to say again here that it is not pardoned to the same person from whom it is demanded. For it must be noted that a debt cannot be demanded except from the one who owes. Indeed, one person can satisfy for another. But meanwhile the debt is demanded not from the one who satisfies for another, but from the one for whom satisfaction is made. Reply: The debt is demanded both from the one who owes and from the surety and guarantor, once it has been transferred to him. It is not a double debt, nor doubly demanded, but it is demanded from the surety, in the name of the debtor, whose cause he has taken upon himself. And so, once the satisfaction is accepted or made, both the surety is acquitted and the debtor himself, because these are regarded as one person. And we are thus one in Christ, he for us, we in him. What he has paid, what he has satisfied, and what he has been acquitted of, is ours in him.

units.la: Socinus: Ut enim debitum remittatur, non satis est, debitorem, quamvis ipse nihil solverit, liberari: sed necesse est, obligationem illam sola creditoris benignitate omnino extingui: ita ut jam nec ipse debitor, nec alius ejus loco substitutus, creditori quidquam debeat. Si enim alius ejus debitum in se translulerit, non remissum debitum, sed commutatus debitor dicetur. Neque vero dixeris, debitum quidem simpliciter remissum non fuisse: illi tamen remissum esse, qui prior debeat. Non enim illi remissum est debitum: sed ab ipso in alium translatum. Nam, si illi remissum fuisset, illud, ut ipse liberaretur, in alium transferri nec debuisset, nec potuisset. Resp. 1. Remissionis rem invertit Adver-sarius, & quod debitoris est, ad creditorem traducit, ut aliam illius definitionem formet, & negare queat remissum dici debitori debitum, quamvis hic nihil solvit[?], siquando creditori aliâ tamen ratione etiam satisfactum. Cum certe remissionis negotium seu fructus ad debitorem spectet, eaq; remissi vera & propria sit, ubi modò citra solutionem debiti, debitor liberatur. Remissioni opponitur puniri, τῷ ἀφιέντι τὸ κεφάλαιον [?], quorum tota vis & natura ad debitorem spectat, non ad creditorem, aut judicem. Ubi ergo debitor liberatur, nec liberatur solùm, sed ita, ut nihil plane solvat, neque ab eo proprie quidpiam exigat creditor, remissa ipsi debita nemo non statuet. Ita & hic, nostra sunt debita, debemus poenas omnes, quarum nulla nobis imponitur, omnium veniam largitur & impunitatem judex, neque tamen remittere dicetur? ii. Ab alio autem, à Vade debitum exigitur. Ergo id non remittit judex, utcumque remittatur debitori, inquit. Quomodo autem debitori re-mittetur, nisi remittat judex? Dices, quod per novationem quasi mutatâ prioris debitoris personâ, ab aliâ idem tamen exigatur debitum. Nihilominus vera & plena est remissio, debitori quæ contingit. Utcunque justitiæ satisfieri debeat, tamen nec reus, nec alius nisi remissionem interpretari potest, ubi debitor ipse nil luit, & liberatur. iii. Atque hinc etiam verum, quod sola Creditoris benignitate debitum extinguitur. Nam ✱. Deus rationem salutis excogitavit & invenit hominibus, non vero homines sibi ipsis. ʒ. Viam salutis adaperuit, per remissionem & traditionem proprii Filii. ʃ. Atque istam conditionem Filius lubens, sola motus suâ φιλανθρωπία, in se suscepit. ꟻ. Pro hominibus, salute indignis, eamque contemnentibus, sui juxta & Dei inimici. ꟻ. Nihil quidquam debiti solventibus ipsis illis, pro quibus se demittebat. ʔ. Et illam alterius satisfactionem pro nobis acceptam habuit & ratam Deus. ʃ. Denique nec hominum, sed Dei opus quoque est & beneficium, quod ipsis gratia Christi applicatur. Quis hic nisi meram Dei benignitatem ab unâ, ab altera parte remissionem hominibus factam agnoscat? iv. Quare & quamvis commutatus debitor sit, remissum tamen debitum dici potest, verè etenim remissa debitori sunt omnia sua. Et quod ad commutationem, non illam ratihabere, minus ipse eam de suo procurare, Dominus tenebatur. Debitum autem justitia exigebat: quam non minus in negotio hoc, quam benignitatem, extare, intererat. Zaleuci notum exemplum, & hac quoque in re adduci solitum, non repetam. Ex illo tamen constat, etiam in jure humano justitiæ & benignitatis attemperationem maxime prædicari.
units.tr: Socinus: For in order that a debt be remitted, it is not enough that the debtor be freed, although he himself has paid nothing; but it is necessary that that obligation be wholly extinguished by the creditor's kindness alone, so that now neither the debtor himself nor anyone substituted in his place owes anything to the creditor. For if someone else has taken over his debt on himself, it is not a debt remitted, but the debtor is said to have been changed. Nor can you say that the debt was indeed not simply remitted, but was remitted to him who previously owed. For the debt was not remitted to him, but was transferred by him to another. For if it had been remitted to him, it neither ought to nor could have been transferred to another, so that he himself might be freed. Reply: (i) Our opponent turns the matter of remission upside down, and draws to the creditor what belongs to the debtor, so as to form another definition of it, and to be able to deny that a debt is said to be remitted to the debtor, although here he pays nothing, if at any time it is also satisfied to the creditor by some other means. For certainly the business or fruit of remission concerns the debtor, and that remission is true and proper when, apart from any payment of the debt, the debtor is freed. What is opposed to remission is being punished; the whole force and nature of these things relate to the debtor, not to the creditor or judge. Where, therefore, the debtor is freed, and not merely freed but in such a way that he pays nothing at all, and the creditor demands nothing of him in particular, no one would fail to judge the debt to be remitted to him. So also here: our debts are ours, we owe all penalties, none of which is imposed on us, and the judge grants pardon and impunity for all, and yet is not said to remit? (ii) But the debt is demanded from another, from the surety. Therefore the judge does not remit it, however it is remitted to the debtor, he says. But how is it remitted to the debtor, unless the judge remits it? You will say that by novation, as if the prior debtor's person had been changed, the same debt is nevertheless demanded from another. Nonetheless the remission that falls to the debtor is true and full. However justice must be satisfied, neither the guilty party nor anyone else can interpret this except as remission, when the debtor himself pays nothing and is freed. (iii) And hence it is also true that the debt is extinguished by the creditor's kindness alone. For (1) God devised and found the way of salvation for men, not men for themselves. (2) He opened the way of salvation through the remission and surrender of his own Son. (3) And the Son, willingly, moved by his love of mankind alone, took this condition upon himself. (4) For men who were unworthy of salvation and who despised it, and who were enemies both of himself and of God. (5) While those very men for whom he humbled himself had paid nothing of any debt. (6) And God accepted and ratified that other's satisfaction on our behalf. (7) Finally, it is also the work and benefit not of men but of God, which is applied to them by the grace of Christ. Who here would acknowledge anything but God's sheer kindness on the one side, and on the other side remission granted to men? (iv) Therefore, even if the debtor has been changed, the debt can nonetheless be said to be remitted, since truly all his possessions have been remitted to the debtor. And as for the change, God was not bound either to ratify it or to procure it from his own resources. But justice demanded the debt; and it mattered that justice stood in this business no less than kindness. I will not repeat the well-known example of Zaleucus, which is also customarily brought in on this point. From it, however, it is clear that even in human law the tempering of justice and kindness is especially praised.

units.la: Socinus: remissio igitur necessario duas partes habet. Una est, quod is, qui debet, ea obligatione solvitur: altera, quod is, cui debetur, sibi satisfieri non vult. Utraque harum partium deest, remissio nulla est. Resp. i. Partem illam, vel conditionem admittimus, ut, qui debet, obligatione solvatur; atque eatenus fit remissio: non item istam, quasi cum remissione non queat ullo modo, & aliunde consistere satisfactio. ii. Non est ex remissione, quasi hæc sui naturâ satisfactionem postularet aut prærequireret, sed Dei justitia illam flagitat. iii. Non quodcumque creditor requirit, etiam satisfactionis nomine, remissionem interimit, vel ex ipso Socino, qui in initio hujus cap. testatur, Deum in remissione peccatorum aliquid exigere ab iis, quibus peccata remittit, quod satisfactionis loeo[?] haberi queat : dubium non est , quin Deus in iis , quibus peccata condonavit , semper aliquid requisierit , quod fortasse satisfactionis loco fuisse dici potest ; praesertim cum certum sit , ea ratione divinae voluntati ab-eo , cui peccata condonata fuere , ea in parte plene fuisse satisfactum. Exponens autem quod Deus in illis requisierit, inquit, vitae puritatem & innocentiam in iis semper requisivit Deus, quibus peccata ignoscere voluit. ac postea, vitae puritas & innocentia quaedam causa est, ut Deus illis clementer ac benigne peccata condonet. Quod si cum natura & veritate remissionis non pugnet, ut Deus aliqua requirat, quae instar causae sint, cur peccata hominibus condonet, imo & fortasse satisfactionis loco haberi possint, non necessarium est ad remissionem, ut is, cui debetur, sibi omnino non velit satisfieri. Atque si remissionem illa non tollant, quae instar causae & satisfactionis Deus exigit a debitoribus ipsis, quibus condonanda sint peccata, quomodo cum illa non consistet, quod Deus satisfactionis loco exigat non ab illis, sed ab alio, a Vade ? Ut ipsi videre hinc possint, non omnem satisfactionem cum remissione pugnare, neque ad istam requiri, ne creditor sibi velit satisfieri. Non vero ex creditoris, sed debitoris parte remissio aestimanda est, si huic venia delictorum fiat, neque ulla ab eo debiti solutio exigatur. Quodcunque etiam Dominus aut creditor, vel justitia postulet.
units.tr: Socinus: Remission therefore necessarily has two parts. One is that the one who owes is released from the obligation; the other is that the one to whom the debt is owed does not wish to be satisfied. If either of these parts is lacking, there is no remission. Reply: (i) We admit the first part, or condition, that the debtor is released from the obligation, and so far remission takes place. But we do not admit the second, as if satisfaction could in no way stand alongside remission or be consistent with it on other grounds. (ii) It is not that remission by its nature demands or presupposes satisfaction, but God's justice requires it. (iii) Not everything a creditor asks for, even under the name of satisfaction, destroys remission. This is clear from Socinus himself, who at the beginning of this chapter testifies that God, in forgiving sins, requires something from those whose sins he remits, something that can count in place of satisfaction. There is no doubt that God has always required something from those whom he has pardoned, which may perhaps be said to have taken the place of satisfaction, especially since it is certain that in that respect the divine will was fully satisfied by the one whose sins were pardoned. Explaining what God required of them, Socinus says: "God has always required purity and innocence of life from those whom he was willing to forgive sins." And afterwards: "Purity and innocence of life are a certain cause why God pardons sins graciously and kindly." If it does not conflict with the nature and truth of remission that God requires certain things which serve as a cause of his pardoning men's sins, and may even be regarded as in place of satisfaction, then it is not necessary for remission that the one to whom the debt is owed should wish in no way to be satisfied. And if the things which God requires of the debtors themselves, to whom sins are to be forgiven, as a cause and as a kind of satisfaction, do not abolish remission, how will it not be consistent that God requires satisfaction in their place not from them but from another, namely the surety? Let them see from this that not every satisfaction conflicts with remission, nor is it required for remission that the creditor should not wish to be satisfied. Remission is to be judged not from the creditor's side but from the debtor's, if pardon of offences is granted to him and no payment of the debt is demanded from him, whatever the Lord, the creditor, or justice may require.

units.la: Socinus : Jubet Christus , ut quod nobis ab iis , qui nos offenderunt , debetur , illis remittamus , Matth. 18. &c. Primum con-siderandum est, in hac parabola nullam men-tionem fieri satisfactionis , quam rex ille a quoquam pro servo , cui debitum remiserat , aut acceperit , aut requisierit. Quod satis demonstrare videtur , Deum simpliciter pro nobis , quibus peccata remittit , nullam satis-factionem a quoquam vel accepisse , vel re-quisivisse. Deinde observandum est , nos his tacite,in offensis condonandis idem facere ju-bere , quod fecit Deus. Atqui , si Deus pro delictis nostris a Christo , utpote homine , ut nos fumus, sibi satisfieri voluit ; nemo nostrum jure reprehendi posset , modo offensas in iis septies ? & huic rei adhibita parabola ipsis, qui nos offendissent, non ulciscaremur, si interim ab eorum vel propinquis vel amicis illorum poenas repeteremus. &c. Paulus item, ut alibi vidimus, monet nos, ut imitatores Dei simus : & quemadmodum is per faciet, nisi remittat quisque fratri suo ex cor-[?] Christum peccata nobis condonavit, sic nos invicem condonemus. Ephes. 4. 32. & 5. 1. & Dominus dicitur peccata remisisse servo, ad ejus preces, ex mera miseri-cordia , verf. 27. Commiseratione vero motu ... Quod si Deus ita per Christum nobis peccata condonavit, ut interim ab ipso Christo eorum
units.tr: Socinus: Christ commands that what is owed to us by those who have offended us we should remit to them, Matt. 18, etc. First, it must be considered that in this parable there is no mention of any satisfaction which that king accepted or demanded from anyone on behalf of the servant to whom he had remitted the debt. This seems sufficiently to show that God, simply on our behalf, to whom he remits sins, has accepted or demanded no satisfaction from anyone. Next, it must be observed that in forgiving offences we are tacitly bidden to do the same as God did. Yet if God wished satisfaction to be made to himself for our sins by Christ as man, as we are, none of us could rightly be blamed, provided that in such offences [...]. And if the parable applied to this matter were to mean that we should not take vengeance on those who have offended us, we would not, meanwhile, demand penalties from their relatives or friends, etc. Paul likewise, as we have seen elsewhere, warns us to be imitators of God, and as God forgave us our sins in Christ, so let us forgive one another. Eph. 4.32, and 5.1. And the Lord is said to have forgiven the servant's sins at his prayer, out of pure mercy, v. 27. But by compassion moved [...]. If God thus forgave us sins through Christ, that meanwhile by Christ himself their

units.la: Resp. Dissimilia prorsus sunt exempla, de quibus hic Socinus, & longe diversus utrorumque, in ratione remis-sionis , modus. Etenim 1. non debe-mus hic argumentari ab humanis ad di-vina, ab homine ad Deum ; sed contra. 11. Non ex re, ad ejus modum. 111. Quasi modum utrobique & in singulis parem. 1v. A remissione privata sin-gulorum inter se, ad peccatorum re-missionem publicam. Atque de illa re-missione erat Matth. xviii. institutā quaestio, sic Christum interrogante Pe-tro, verf. 21. Domine, quoties in me pec-cabit frater meus, & condonabo ei ? usque ad septies ? Et huic rei adhibita parabola fuit, ut ostenderetur, quam benigne & copiose oporteat remittere proximis peccata sua : quo & conclusio facit, verf. ult. sic & pater meus coelestis vobis de delictis ipsorum. Bene quidem, quod & Dominus dicitur peccata remisisse servo, ad ejus preces, ex mera miseri-cordia, verf. 27. Commiseratione vero poenas repetierit, quid vetat, quo minus motus Dominus servi illius, dimisit eum, & nos, ex Pauli praescripto, Deum imitati, pro mutuum remisisset ei, nulla mentione facta offensis proximi nostri non quidem ab ipso, sed satisfactionis: quia ejus hic meminisse ab alio quopiam, ut modo dicebamus, nobis nil necesse erat, neque faciebat ad satisfieri curemus? scopum: nam, uti non sequitur, praeterita rei mentione, negari eam vel tolli, ita hic non necessarium erat illud exponere, ubi non tractabatur mysterium vel modus redemptionis; sed mutuum modo hominum inter se officium, in remissione debitorum reciproca, Christo erat propositum. Quâ in re ipsam remissionem docere satis erat, quaeque officia ex parte hominis requirantur, tum quod Deus gratis peccata remittat, ad quod exemplum homines se componere debeant: sed ex professo plenam divinae remissionis rationem explicare nihil attinebat, quia nec de eo agebatur hoc loco, neque ad parabolae scopum requirebatur, nec denique modus divinae remissionis cum nostra ubique quadrat & per omnia. Certum enim est, quod inquit Apostolus, Hebr. ix. 22. χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας οὐ γίνεται ἄφεσις[?]. nec nisi per & propter sanguinem Christi peccata nobis remittuntur. Quale nihil, ut alia praeteream, in quibus dissimilitudo etiam ostendi potest, in nostrâ intervenit. Socinus, Deum in remittendis peccatis, ab homine, quasi satisfactionis loco exigere vitae puritatem atque innocentiam, statuit: non tamen idem nobis requirere licet in condonando proximo, sed etiam indignissimo id officii praestare debemus, quousque nos laeserit: neque dicent Adversarii, ita semper Deum remissione suâ praesto esse, uti nos nunquam non, septuagies septies, remittere alteri cogimur. Ex quibus apparet, quod ad modum remissionis, paritatem divinae cum nostra urgeri nullo modo posse, neque hoc ex loco, neque etiam ex Paulino. Namque jubemur quidem hac in re imitari Deum, sed non pari per omnia ratione aut debemus id, aut possumus, sufficit pro nostrâ ratione peccata ingenue condonare aliis, quomodo Deus nobis. Res praecipitur, eamque praestare nostrum est, plene atque ex animo, non verò ad modum agendi nostrum, divinum exigere debemus, aut examinare. Denique proterve sententiam nostram insectatur Socinus, quando Christum pro nobis solvisse, & satisfecisse, cum S. Scripturâ, asserimus, quasi Deus finiastre & inique ab alio id exegisset, quod nobis remittere videtur. Quae non in istum modum accipienda & vexanda sunt: quoniam Christus seipsum vadem pro nobis & sponsorem, qui nostra in se suscepit, pertulitque, non invitus, vel quaesitus, sed lubentissime, nostri loco divinae justitiae objecit, suique ἀντιλύτρῳ redemit nos ac salvat.
units.tr: Reply: The examples are wholly unlike, and the manner of remission in each is very different. For (1) we ought not to argue here from human things to divine, from man to God, but the reverse. (2) Not from the thing to its manner. (3) As if the manner were the same on both sides and in every particular. (4) From the private remission of individuals among themselves to the public remission of sins. Now the question in Matt. 18 concerned that private remission, when Peter asked Christ, v. 21: "Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?" And a parable was applied to this matter, to show how generously and abundantly we ought to forgive our neighbours their sins. The conclusion agrees with this, v. 35: "So also shall my heavenly Father do to you, if you do not forgive from your hearts each one his brother's offences." It is indeed well that the Lord is said to have forgiven the servant's sins at his prayer, out of pure mercy, v. 27. But what prevents us, if the Lord, moved by compassion, dismissed that servant, and we, imitating God according to Paul's precept, forgive our neighbour in mutual remission, with no mention made of offences of our neighbour against us, not indeed by him but in the place of satisfaction; for there was no need for us to mention this by some other person, as we were just saying, nor did it bear on the aim: for as it does not follow that, when a matter is passed over, it is denied or removed, so here it was not necessary to expound that point, since the mystery or manner of redemption was not being treated, but the mutual duty of men toward one another in the reciprocal remission of debts was set before Christ's hearers. In this matter it was enough to teach remission itself and what duties are required on man's part, namely that God forgives sins freely, after whose example men ought to conform themselves. But to set out professedly the full account of divine remission was pointless, because that was not being treated here, nor was it required for the aim of the parable; nor, finally, does the manner of divine remission agree with ours everywhere and in every respect. For it is certain, as the Apostle says, Heb. 9.22, [χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας οὐ γίνεται ἄφεσις], "without shedding of blood there is no remission", and sins are forgiven us only through and on account of the blood of Christ. Something of this kind, to pass over others, in which dissimilarity can also be shown, occurs in our case. Socinus lays down that God, in remitting sins, requires from man purity and innocence of life as if in place of satisfaction. Yet we may not require the same of our neighbour in forgiving him, but must show such kindness even to the most unworthy, for as long as he has wronged us. Nor will the opponents say that God is always present with his remission in the way that we are not always bound to forgive another seventy times seven. From which it appears that as to the manner of remission, parity between the divine and our own cannot be urged in any way, neither from this passage nor from Paul's. For we are indeed bidden to imitate God in this matter, but we neither ought nor are able to do so in every respect by the same reasoning. It is enough that, according to our measure, we freely forgive others their sins as God does to us. The thing is commanded, and it is our part to perform it fully and from the heart; we ought not to demand or examine the divine manner of acting by our own. Finally, Socinus attacks our view insolently when we assert with Holy Scripture that Christ paid and satisfied for us, as if God had unjustly and harshly demanded from another what he seems to remit to us. These things are not to be taken and assailed in that way, since Christ, having offered himself as surety and sponsor for us, who took our debts upon himself and bore them, not unwillingly or under compulsion but most gladly, offered himself to divine justice in our place, and redeems and saves us by his own ransom [ἀντιλύτρῳ].

units.la: Illa, quae adfert Socinus, aliquid videntur dicere, in privatâ vindictâ, ubi quis malâ fide in speciem remittit, sed aliunde sibi, & suis commodis prospicit, vel imò indulget affectui, & ab alio quam oporteat, invito, & ad quem illa non spectent, sibi satisfieri cupit, non pro necessitate justitiae, sed arbitrio, aut ulciscendi voluntate. Quae omnia locum hic non habent, ac propterea Deo, nec praesenti negotio applicari debent. Christus enim Mediatorem se & vadem pro nobis obtulit, nec Patris magis, quam suo consilio in ista ivit, ut simul divinae iustitiae satisfaciendi, & pro misericordia parcendi, viam patefaceret. In humanis negotiis, ubi aliquando Vade & ἀντιψύχοις res agitur, locum illa non habent, quae Socinus adfert, sinistra rei bonae interpretamenta, nedem in divinis, & causa redemtionis per Mediatorem Christum, in quo ideo amorem superéminentem Deus ostendisse dicitur, quod in eum conjecit peccata nostrum omnia. Jes. LIII. & mori eum voluit pro nobis peccatoribus, & inimicis. Rom. 5.8.9.10. Quare & propter Christum peccata nobis condonari, fides tenet catholica.
units.tr: Those arguments of Socinus may seem to say something in the case of private vengeance, where someone pretends to remit a debt in bad faith, but looks out for himself and his own advantage, or even indulges his feelings, and wants satisfaction from another who is unwilling and to whom it does not belong, not out of the necessity of justice but at his own pleasure or from a desire for revenge. None of this applies here, so it should not be applied to God or to the present matter. For Christ offered himself as Mediator and Surety for us, and he undertook this not less on the Father's counsel than on his own, so that he might open a way by which divine justice is satisfied and mercy is shown in forgiving. In human affairs, where a surety and a substitute life are sometimes at stake, the unfavourable interpretations that Socinus brings forward do not apply. Still less do they apply to divine matters and to the cause of redemption through Christ the Mediator, in whom God is said to have shown his surpassing love, in that he laid on him all our sins (Isa. 53), and willed that he die for us sinners and enemies (Rom. 5:8, 9, 10). Therefore the catholic faith holds that our sins are forgiven also on account of Christ.

units.la: Socinus: Id quod scriptum est, Deum nobis per Christum peccata condonasse, non eam vim habere, quasi propter ipsum Christum, qui pro nobis satisfecerit, eam condonationem a Deo consequuti simus; sed a Christo Dei nomine peccatorum condonationem nobis allatam fuisse, per ea verba intelligi debere; ut Paulus ipse elegantur explicat, cum id, quod uno in loco dixerat, sicut & Deus in Christo donavit vobis, Ephes. 4. 32. in alio ita extulit, & Christus donavit vobis, Col. 3. 13.
units.tr: Socinus: That which is written, that God forgave us our sins through Christ, does not have the force that we obtained that forgiveness from God on account of Christ himself, who made satisfaction for us; rather, those words should be understood to mean that the forgiveness of sins was brought to us by Christ in the name of God. Paul himself explains this elegantly: what he had said in one place, "as God in Christ forgave you" (Eph. 4:32), he expressed in another as "Christ forgave you" (Col. 3:13).

units.la: Resp. Deus per Christum, id est, inquit, a Christo, Dei nomine. Quae, obsecro, ista verborum est immutatio? Non quidem negamus, nobis a Christo, Dei nomine, peccata remitti: sed hac ratione phrasis, per Christum, omittitur & non explicatur id, in quo tota vis argumenti sita est. Per Christum hic valet tantundem ac propter Christum: quae nota est causae externae impulsivae, & meritoriae: uti Tit. 1. 13. δὶ ᾧ αἰτίαν. Hebr. 11. 11. & 2.
units.tr: Reply: "God through Christ," that is, "by Christ, in the name of God." What, I ask you, is this change of words? We do not deny that our sins are remitted to us by Christ in the name of God. But by this manner of speaking, "through Christ," is left out, and that is not explained in which the whole force of the argument lies. "Through Christ" here amounts to the same as "on account of Christ." This is the mark of an external, impulsive and meritorious cause, as in Titus 1:13 and Heb. 11:11 and 2, where the Greek has "for which reason" [δὶ ᾧ αἰτίαν].

units.la: Ἀλλὰ τὸ παράπτωμα ἢ θανάτῳ[?]. Neque enim solum dicitur Deus ἐν Χριστῷ, uti Ephes. 4. 32. nobis remittere, vel simpliciter Christus nobis χαρίζεσθαι, Col. iii. 3.[?] sed, ad argumentum nostrum, per & propter Christum constituimur justi, uti per Adamum peccatores, & rei. Rom. v. 17. in vita regnabunt per unum Jesum Christum. per, & propter: sicut per & propter unius transgressionem mors regnavit per unum. 18. 19. 20. 9. multo ergo magis, justificati nunc in sanguine ejus, servabimur per eum ab ira. 1 Thess. v. 9. non posuit nos Deus ad iram, sed ad acquisitionem salutis per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum. Alibi, per sanguinem Christi. Ephes. 1. 7. in quo habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. Col. 1. 14. 20. per sanguinem crucis ejus. 22. per mortem. Hebr. x. 10. per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel. cap. xiii. 12. per proprium sanguinem. Apoc. xii. 11. Ἀλλὰ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀρνίου. Hoc est, per Christum. Non ergo solummodo, quod Christus Dei nomine, sed, sive quo Dei nomine, sive quod Deus per eum peccata remittit, eaque condonantur nobis per & propter Christum, fit hoc omnino per mortem ejus, & passionem satisfactoriam, & meritoriam remissionis, ac gratiae.
units.tr: But the trespass [Ἀλλὰ τὸ παράπτωμα ἢ θανάτῳ]. For God is not only said to remit to us in Christ (Eph. 4:32), or simply Christ to forgive us (Col. 3:13). For our purpose, we are made righteous through and on account of Christ, just as we were made sinners and guilty through Adam (Rom. 5:17): "they shall reign in life through one, Jesus Christ"; through and on account of: "as through the transgression of one, death reigned through one" (Rom. 5:18, 19, 20; 9). "Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from wrath" (Rom. 5:9). "God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thess. 5:9). Elsewhere: through the blood of Christ. "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins" (Eph. 1:7). Col. 1:14, 20: "through the blood of his cross"; 22: "through death"; Heb. 10:10: "through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all"; ch. 13:12: "through his own blood"; Rev. 12:11: "but by the blood of the Lamb" [Ἀλλὰ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀρνίου]. That is, through Christ. It is not, then, only that Christ forgives in the name of God, but whether in the name of God by him, or whether God remits sins through him, and they are forgiven us through and on account of Christ, this happens entirely through his death and his satisfactory and meritorious passion, which is the ground of remission and of grace.

units.la: Atque haec ad objectionem Socini secundam, qua ostendere conatus fuit Deum velle peccata remittere, citra intervenientem satisfactionem ullam veram. Cui suae opinioni adeo mordicus adhaeret, ejusque praejudicio ita excaecatum animum in tota hac disputatione attulit, ut in fine ejus aperto ore dicere non erubescat, pag. 249. Sed nec umquam id disertis verbis à Sacris Scriptoribus dictum fuisse, quod nos sc. credimus, invenimus, quod tamen & sapissime, & difertissime fieri debuerat; nec, si ubique clarissimis verbis testatum reperiremus, sic tamen rem se habere, nobis compertum esset. Mirarisne hominem, cui constitutum rem negare, etiam clarissimis verbis in Scriptura testatam. eam isthic non invenire, utcunque saepissime & difertissime ostensam? Tantum facit praejudicium opinionis, animique ad contradicendum pertinacia. Deum autem veniam peccatorum dare, eo quo Socinus statuit, modo, in divinis monumentis extare, facillime sibi persuaderi, ait, partim quia id rationi maxime consentaneum est; partim quia Christi suscitati, & in coelis sedentis, ipsa satis effecta conspicimus. Primas autem partes ei fert sua ratio, huic cedere cogitur, quidquid minus arridet, utcunque in Scriptura testatissimum. Digna poena pervicaciae, ita cum ratione sc. sua ut insaniant, qui Deum in Scripturis loquentem insuper habent, ubi parum rationis suis congruere videtur.
units.tr: And this is enough for Socinus's second objection, by which he tried to show that God wills to remit sins without any true satisfaction intervening. He clings so stubbornly to his opinion, and has brought to this whole disputation a mind so blinded by prejudice, that at the end he is not ashamed to say openly (p. 249): "But we have found that the sacred writers never said in plain words what we believe, namely, that this should have been said very often and very plainly; nor, if we had found it attested in the clearest words everywhere, would it therefore have been established for us that the matter stands so." Are you surprised that a man who has determined to deny the thing does not find it there, though it is attested in the clearest words in Scripture and very often and very plainly shown? So much does prejudice of opinion and obstinacy of mind to contradict accomplish. He says that it is most easily persuaded to him that God grants forgiveness of sins in the manner Socinus has decided, that it stands in the divine records: partly because this is most consonant with reason, and partly because we see the very satisfaction in Christ raised up and seated in heaven. But his own reason takes first place, and whatever pleases him less he is compelled to yield to it, however plainly attested in Scripture. Such men deserve the penalty of their perversity, who so go mad with their own reason that they despise God speaking in the Scriptures wherever it seems little to agree with their reasoning.

units.la: Sequitur objectio tertia, hinc sumta, quod Christus pro peccatis divina justitia satisfacere non potuerit. quod duplicitèr probare Socinus satagit. 1. Quia nobis non pereuntibus, divinae justitiae pro peccatis satisfieri haud potuerit. 11. Ex Christi persona, qui illud praestare non potuerit.
units.tr: There follows the third objection, drawn from this: that Christ could not satisfy divine justice for sins. Socinus labours to prove this in two ways. First, because divine justice could not have been satisfied for sins without our perishing. Second, from the person of Christ, who could not have performed it.

units.la: Primùm sic argumentatur, part. 111. cap. 111. Si Deus aut non potuisset, aut noluisset citra veram aliquam pro delictis nostris satisfactionem nobis ignoscere, nos ipsi omnino ei satisfacere debuissemus. Neque enim aliquid Deo debebamus, quod alius, qui scilicet non deliquisset, ita nihil ipsi divinae justitiae deberet, pro nobis praestare posset. Resp. 1. Imo si Deus noluisset, (neque enim ad hoc tenebatur, sed meri beneplaciti ac benignitatis res erat) admittere vicariam solutionem, & satisfactionem, nos ipsi omnino satisfacere debuissemus: non, si noluisset simpliciter ignoscere citra satisfactionem. 11. Cerre debebamus Deo permultum, & quod debebamus, alter, neque alius, quam qui absolute insons erat, praestare poterat. Nisi substantiam doctrinae Euangelicae negare constitutum sit, quae Christum ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, & ἀντὶ ἡμῶν, sanctum & perfectè ἀκακον, mortem sustinuisse tradit. 11. Cor. v. 21. eum etenim, qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in ipso.
units.tr: First he argues thus (part 3, ch. 3): "If God either could not, or would not, forgive us our sins without some true satisfaction for our offences, we ourselves would have been bound to satisfy him altogether. For we owed God nothing which another, who of course had not sinned, could thus render to divine justice on our behalf, since he owed nothing to it himself." Reply. First: "Indeed, if God had been unwilling" (for he was not bound to this, but it was a matter of his mere good pleasure and kindness) to admit a vicarious payment and satisfaction, "we ourselves would have been bound to satisfy him altogether." But it would not follow if he had simply been unwilling to forgive without satisfaction. Second: certainly we owed God very much, and what we owed could be paid by no other than one who was absolutely innocent. Unless one has determined to deny the substance of the Gospel doctrine, which teaches that Christ, holy and perfectly blameless, underwent death on our behalf and in our place (2 Cor. 5:21): "For he who knew no sin was made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him."

units.la: Socinus : Poena peccato ipsius Dei voluntate constituta aeterna mors est; quae cum corporalis poena fit, a nemine, praeterquam ab eo ipso, qui peccavit, praestari potest. Pe-cuniaria quidem poena, unius delicto debita, ab alio praestari queunt, &c. At mors unius, sive alia quacunque corporis vexatio alterius effici non potest. neque unquam vel lege, vel consuetudine receptum fuit, ut poenam, quam quis corpore luere teneatur, alius, quisquis tandem ille fit, pro eo pendere pof-sit[?].
units.tr: Socinus: "The punishment established for sin by the will of God itself is eternal death; and since this is a bodily punishment, it can be borne by no one except him who sinned. A pecuniary penalty owed for one man's offence can indeed be paid by another, etc. But the death of one man, or any other bodily suffering, cannot be brought about in another's place; nor has it ever been accepted, either by law or by custom, that anyone, whoever he might be, could pay for another the punishment which that other is bound to bear in his own body."

units.la: Resp. 1. Poena peccato constituta, mors est, quae corporalis, & quoque aeterna: ipsa ergo corporalis, etiam poena: contrà ac alibi disputat Socinus, etiam hominem, si non peccasset, moritu-rum fuisse. Et de ipsa morte, quam Christus sustinuit, hic est quaestio. Ne ad mortis aeternitatem, omissa ipsa, hic confugiat. 11. Mors corporalis, praeterquam ab eo ipso, qui peccavit, praestari, vel subiri, non potest. Ergone Christus peccavit? Quia ergo mortem illam sustinuit is, qui non peccavit, vel hoc ipso sequitur, illam subiisse, pro peccato nostro, sibi imputato. Atque ita patet, quod poenam mortis, nostro loco, persolvit Sponsor noster Christus. Suscipiendo poenam & non suscipiendo culpam, & culpam delevit, & poenam, inquit Augustinus. III.
units.tr: Reply. First: the punishment established for sin is death, which is bodily and also eternal. So the bodily punishment itself is also at issue, contrary to what Socinus argues elsewhere, namely that man would have died even if he had not sinned. And the question here is about that very death which Christ endured; let him not take refuge in the eternity of death while leaving the death itself aside. Second: bodily death cannot be borne or undergone by anyone except him who sinned. Did Christ then sin? Therefore, since he who did not sin underwent that death, it follows from this very fact that he underwent it for our sin, imputed to him. And so it is clear that our Surety Christ paid the punishment of death in our place. "By undertaking the punishment and not undertaking the guilt, he blotted out both the guilt and the punishment," says Augustine (III).

units.la: Uti poenae pecuniariae, ita & corporales, uni debitae, ab alio praestari possunt: modo possit Vades, & velit tum is, tum Dominus, & lex permittat, ex qua poenae illae debentur. Patet hoc ex obsidibus, quos lege & consuetudine receptum est, dari pro aliis; atque ex iis, quos hinc appellant ἀντιψύχους[?].
units.tr: Just as pecuniary penalties owed to one person can be paid by another, so bodily penalties can be paid by another too, provided the surety can and is willing, and both the creditor and the law allow it, the law under which those penalties are owed. This is clear from the hostages who, by law and custom, are given in place of others, and from those whom they call antipsychi [ἀντιψύχους].

units.la: iv. Denique, ut nullum simile exemplum in humanis detur, ulla vel lege vel consuetudine approbatum, quale in Christo poenas nostras persolvente, vel ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ αὐτῷ fuit, inde non periclitatur fidei & doctrinae nostrae veritas: quia ita singulare est Christi pro nobis factum, ut facile concedamus, simile nusquam extare, & tale nec repertum unquam, nec reperiri posse, quod cum eo plane conveniat, nedum ad quod examinari aut conferri debeat. Quod proinde de Zaleuco huc adferri solet, simile quidem aliquâ ratione, multum tamen etiam dissimile negotio nostro, haud diffitemur.
units.tr: iv. Finally, although no similar example is found in human affairs, approved by any law or custom, like Christ paying our penalties on the cross itself [ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ αὐτῷ], the truth of our faith and doctrine is not thereby endangered. What Christ did for us is so unique that we readily concede nothing like it exists anywhere, and nothing has ever been found, or can be found, that agrees with it plainly, let alone anything to which it ought to be examined or compared. What is usually brought forward here about Zaleucus is, in some respects, similar, but we do not deny that it is also quite unlike our case.

units.la: Objicit Socinus, Jezech. xviii. Resp. 1. Quod in lege, vel cap. Je-ubi[?] multis verbis Deus perspicue declarat, se zech. xviii. hac de re dictum extat, nolle iniquitates filiorum in patribus, nec pa-trum in filiis punire, si filii similes patrum dit. Nam agitur illo Cap. de sermone scelestorum non fuerint. ac demum ita conclu-isto[?], quem Judaei inter se habebant, dit: Anima qua peccaverit, ipsa morietur. vice paroemiae, Patres comederunt om-[?] Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris; neque phacem[?], & dentes filiorum obstupuerunt, pater portabit iniquitatem filii. justitia justi super eum erit; & impietas impii super eum erit. Quam sententiam diserte in ipsa quoque scelerum ipsorum injuste poenas dare. lege Moses scriptam legimus, Deut. cap. 24. Hoc autem [illegible, ~4 letters]am & blasphemum- v. 16. idque etiam testatur auctor 2. lib. erat, Deusque acri reprehensione refu-rat, ostendens, se ἀπεσθωσπολίτης[?] judicare, sive patres, sive filios, en omnes anima mea sunt, atque anima patris ac anima filii mea sunt: anima qua peccat, ipsa morietur. verf. 4. Nam quum quis erit justus &c. hic omnino vivet, dictum Domini Jehova. verf. 5. verf ad 9. Quod si genuerit filium effractorem, effusorem sanguinis &c. siccine viveret? non vivet; omnes abominationes istas fecit, moriendo morietur, sanguines ipsius super ipsum erunt דָּמָיו בּוֹ יִהְיוּ[?]. verf. 13. hoc est, ipse peccator, quod justum est, peccata sua luet, atque omnino non vivet, sed morietur. Ex adverso autem si filium natus fuerit probum, qui non faciat secundum illa, &c. hic non morietur propter iniquitatem patris sui, vivendo vivet. 17. 18.
