Pater vero ipsius quia oppressit &c. morietur propter iniquitatem suam. Ergo, hoc vult Deus, probus suae probitatis, improbus vero scelerum, fructus capiet. Jesa. iii. 10. 11. Non vero vel probus, propter alterius improbitatem, vita privabitur; vel improbus sua, quam commeritus est, fraudabitur morte. Pergit Deus, verf. 19. 20. Sed dicitis, qui? annon fert filius propter iniquitatem patris? ut probus filius non vivat, ut moriatur propter delictum patris? negat Deus. anima qua peccat, ipsa morietur: filius non feret propter iniquitatem patris, & pater non feret propter iniquitatem filii, justitia justi cum ipso erit, & improbitas improbi cum ipso erit. Ex quibus perspicitur, agi hic de particulari hominum inter se vita, & propria sive probitate, sive improbitate. II. Unde alter alterum suo singulari facto non posset fontem reddere, vel insontem. III. Nec insons & probus fraudari debeat vita, ex lege sibi promissa. IV. Certe non puniri morte, ob delicta nulla sua, sed aliorum. Verum ista, quae inter homines, communi & ordinaria Dei providentia obtinent, nihil praejudicare Deo possunt, singulari ratione volenti aliquando, ut unus pro alio quid praestet, vel patiatur: quod non ex communi illa lege est, de qua citatis Scripturae locis; sed ex peculiari pacto, quo Deo res, pro beneplacito, ordinare visum. Unde Adamus, ceu caput generis humani, stetit; & omnis natura in eo lapsa, eo transgrediente, fuit. Christus iterum, tamquam alter Adamus, pro nobis passus, mortuus fuit, atque satisfecit. Quae isti regulae de anima, quae peccat, moritura, non contrariantur, quia sub illa non continentur, sed alterius sunt generis, & singularia, in quibus communis lex locum non habet. Neque sibi legem dedit Deus, sed nobis. Idem nempe qui constituit, ut communi certissimoque ordine, unusquisque κομίςη, πρὸς[?] ἃ ἐπραξεν[?], εἴτε ἀγαθὸν, εἴτε κακόν. II. Cor. v. 10. etiam pro singulari sapientia statuit, ut uterque Adamus, suorum caput esset, gereretque personam. Quod argumentum Apostolus tractat cap. v. ad Romanos. Fru-stra autem illa ad communem regulam restringas, à qua eximuntur natura sua: quemadmodum temere vel nativitatem ex virgine, vel assumtionem Eliae, atque Enochi, ex usitato nascendi, & moriendi more, convellas. Neque etiam ita rigide accipi illa possunt apud Jezechielem verba, quia ex lege, & variis Scripturae locis constat. Deum vindicare etiam parentum peccata in liberis. Saepe liberos & innocuos affligi propter parentum, alorumque scelera, notum est. Quod quomodo cum verbis Prophetae conciliari debeat, omnibus videndum. Ita nos respondemus, attendo partim ad peccata, partim ad eorundem poenam: si post peccata parentum, iis se involvant etiam liberi, in communi excidio, & horum, & illorum peccata puniri, omni vacat iniquitate. Sin autem filii insontes & probi sint, sic non ipsi puniuntur, vel moriuntur, aut vita privantur, propter ea, quorum non sunt rei; sed ipsis afflictio, poena est parentibus, qui in illis liberis suis puniuntur. Revera homo uti non in se solum, sed omnibus quae ad se spectant, prospere agit, aut misera, ita & in omnibus iis poenas dat, vel Dei experitur beneficia. Atque ita Rex in subditis, pater in familia & liberis luit, nec tantum ipsi in se. Visitat ergo peccata parentum Deus in liberis, horum afflictione illos puniendo. Poena, ut noxa, caput sequitur: neque aliquis punitur, nisi qui delinquit, & propter sua peccata, non aliorum. Propter aliorum peccata affliguntur & castigantur passim multi: puniuntur, non nisi ob sua, vel solum, vel una cum aliis. Nequaquam vero illa Christi, pro nobis, satisfactioni intercedunt. Sic quidem est, nos pec-caveramus, ac proinde nobis moriendum erat: Christus minime peccavit, & tamen mortuus est. Verum si quid in iis carpendum, eadem vi probaveris, Christum non debuisse mori, qua nobis moriendum fuisse evincis. Quorsum autem, vel unde mortuus Christus, si tantum ipse qui peccat, mori potest, ac debet? Annon pro nostris peccatis, quod ei imputata fuerunt illa omnia, mortuus? Moriendum nobis in aeternum fuerat, nisi Deus aliter providisset. Uti ipsi Adversarii agnoscunt, pereundum nobis ex lege fuisse, nisi gratia remif-sionis succurrisset, quod communis certaque sententiae vim non enervat, *qua maledictus habetur omnis non servans legem. Atque ita manet, quod omni animae peccatrici moriendum sit, nisi in sponsore Christo Deus aliter consti-tuisset. Neque hinc aliqua decreti in Deo mutatio, nec contra suum ipsius decre-tum Deus quippiam commisit: quippe decreti divini est, quod vadem, & satisfactionem in Christo destinavit: atque ex una & immutabili voluntate res una aliam, ac sententia & vis gratiae τὸ κατάκριμα[?] reatus & mortis propriae re-scindit, abrogat, tollit.
units.tr: Socinus objects Ezekiel 18. Answer 1. In that chapter God declares plainly, in many words, that he does not wish the iniquities of sons to be punished in the fathers, nor the fathers' in the sons, if the sons are not like their fathers. For that chapter deals with a saying the Jews had among themselves, used as a proverb: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge. And at last it concludes thus: The soul that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. We read that this same sentence is also set down expressly in the law of Moses, Deut. 24:16. The author of the second book also bears witness to it, and God refutes that saying with sharp rebuke, showing that he judges neither fathers nor sons by such a rule: Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sins, it shall die. Ver. 4. For when a man is just, etc., he shall surely live, saith the Lord Jehovah. Vers. 5 to 9. But if he begets a robber, a shedder of blood, etc. shall he live? He shall not live; having done all these abominations, he shall surely die; his bloods shall be upon him [דָּמָיו בּוֹ יִהְיוּ]. Ver. 13. That is, the sinner himself, so far as is just, shall pay for his own sins, and he shall not live at all, but shall die. On the contrary, if he begets a son who is good, who does not act according to those things, etc., he shall not die for the iniquity of his father; living, he shall live. Vers. 17, 18. But his father, because he oppressed, etc., shall die for his own iniquity. Therefore God wills that the good enjoy the fruit of their goodness and the wicked the fruit of their wickedness (cf. Isa. 3:10, 11). Neither should the good be deprived of life on account of another's wickedness, nor should the wicked be cheated of the death he has deserved by his own. God goes on, vers. 19, 20: But you say, Why? Does not the son bear the iniquity of the father? That a good son should not live, should die for his father's offence? God denies it: the soul that sins, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be with him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be with him. From these words it is clear that the matter here is the particular life of men among themselves, and each man's own conduct, whether uprightness or wickedness. II. Hence one man cannot by his singular deed make another guilty or innocent. III. Nor should the innocent and upright be deprived of life, which the law promised them. IV. Certainly they should not be punished with death for offences not their own, but another's. But those things which hold among men by the common and ordinary providence of God cannot prejudice God, who by a singular reason is willing at times that one should perform or suffer something for another. This is not from that common law of which the cited passages of Scripture speak, but from a peculiar covenant, by which it seemed good to God to order things according to his good pleasure. Hence Adam, as the head of the human race, stood, and all nature fell in him when he transgressed. Christ again, as another Adam, suffered for us, died, and made satisfaction. Those rules about the soul that sins being bound to die are not contrary to this, because they are not contained under that law but are of another kind and singular, in which the common law has no place. Nor did God give a law to himself, but to us. The same God who established, by a common and most certain order, that each one should receive the things done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10), also by a singular wisdom determined that each Adam should be the head of his own and bear their person. The Apostle treats this argument in Romans 5. But it is vain for you to confine those things to the common rule, from which they are exempt by their nature; just as rashly you would overthrow either the birth from a virgin or the taking up of Elijah and Enoch, by appeal to the usual manner of being born and dying. Nor can those words in Ezekiel be taken so rigidly, since it is established both by the law and by various passages of Scripture that God also avenges the sins of parents upon their children. It is well known that children, even innocent ones, are often afflicted on account of the sins of parents and others. How this should be reconciled with the words of the Prophet, let everyone consider for himself. Thus we answer, attending partly to the sins and partly to their punishment: if after their parents' sins the children also are involved in the common ruin, then the punishing of the sins of both is free from all iniquity. But if the sons are innocent and upright, then they are not themselves punished, nor do they die or are deprived of life, on account of things of which they are not guilty; rather, the affliction is a punishment to the parents, who are punished in those children of theirs. Indeed, a man fares well or ill not in himself alone but in all that pertains to him, and so in all those things he pays penalties or experiences God's benefits. Thus a king suffers in his subjects, and a father in his household and children, and not merely in himself. God therefore visits the sins of parents upon the children, punishing the parents by the affliction of these. Punishment, like guilt, follows the head; nor is anyone punished except the one who offends, and on account of his own sins, not those of others. Many are everywhere afflicted and chastised on account of others' sins, but they are punished only for their own, either alone or together with others. Yet those things by no means stand in the way of Christ's satisfaction for us. It is true that we had sinned, and therefore we had to die; Christ did not sin at all, and yet he died. But if anything in these points is to be found fault with, by the same force you would prove that Christ ought not to have died, by which you prove that we had to die. Why, then, or from what cause did Christ die, if only he who sins can and ought to die? Did he not die for our sins, since all of them were imputed to him? We would have had to die forever, unless God had provided otherwise. As the Adversaries themselves acknowledge, we would have perished under the law, unless the grace of forgiveness had come to our aid; this does not weaken the common and certain force of the sentence, Cursed is everyone who does not keep the law. And so it remains that every sinful soul must die, unless God had otherwise appointed a surety in Christ. Nor does this involve any change in God's decree, nor has God done anything against his own decree: for it belongs to the divine decree that he appointed a surety and satisfaction in Christ, and from one and the same unchangeable will, the grace of God cancels, abrogates and removes the one thing by means of the other: the sentence of guilt and of one's own death.

units.la: Socinus: Quanam vindicta, aut peccati punitio est haec, eos, qui peccaverunt, im-punitos dimittere, eum vero, qui nihil mali fecit, gravissimis poenis subjicere? Resp. Non vel ideo quod illi peccaverunt, impune agunt; vel iste, quia nihil mali fecit, punitur: sed, hic quidem, quia se lubens pro vade obtulit ac stitit; & pro illis quia per eum satisfactum, & hi redemti, & punitus ille fuit.
units.tr: Socinus: What kind of vengeance, or punishment for sin, is it to let those who have sinned go unpunished, and to subject to the most severe penalties the one who has done no wrong? Answer: The sinners do not go unpunished for that reason alone, nor is the innocent one punished simply because he has done no wrong. Rather, the one indeed (was punished) because he gladly offered himself and stood as surety; and the others (go free) because through him satisfaction was made, and they were redeemed, while he was punished.

units.la: Socinus: Sed aliam etiam ob caussam, Resp. 1. Mors aeterna duplici modo nobis non pereuntibus, divina justitia vero intelligitur, duratione, ut in omnes[?] pro peccatis nostris satisfieri nullo pacto poterat. aevum duret; & insita gravitate ac ma-lo. Vera enim satisfactio est plena debiti persolu-tio. Unusquisque autem nostrum mortem aeter- durantem mortem sustinuit, sed valore nam divina isti justitia debebat. unusquisque aeternam, intensione, quamvis non igitur nostrum, nisi nos ipsi id facere vole- extensione, & huic quantum defuit, bamus, alium habere debuisset, qui pro ipso illius gravitate compensatum. II. Mors mortem aeternam subiret. Verum id qui fieri aeterna non est corporalis: corporalis poterat, cum omnibus hominibus generatim, quidem etiam ad poenam pertinet, sed si Deus summo jure uti voluisset, aeterna, ea sola, ejusve perpetuitate mors aeter-mors subeunda esset? Quomodo enim potest na non continetur. Quomodo paulo quis eam corporalem poenam, praesertim vero post, pag.256. Socinus inquit, cor-mortem pro alio solvere, quam ipsemet de-porales poenas, qualis aeterna mors est. Sed beat? Unum autem quempiam, qui morti de hoc plenius suo loco. III. Suppo-aeterna, utpote qui nihil deliquisset, mini- nit quidem, at non probat, impossi-me obnoxius inventus fuerit, pro omnibus bile esse, ut, non quivis, sed Chri-satisfacere potuisse, plane ridiculum est cogi- stus, pro alio, pro aliis mortem sol-tare, nedum asserere. Nam perinde est ac si verit. IV. Solvere pro alio mortem, quis diceret, unum, qui nihil ipse debeat, quam quis ipse debeat, locum hic non & centum tantummodo aureos nummos ha- habet, quum Christus eam propter se ipsum beat, quos dare possit, pro innumerabilibus ipsum non debuerit, morti aeterna, ut-aliis, qui singuli aureos nummos centum pote qui nihil deliquisset, minime obnoxius. debeant, posse satisfacere; cum vix pro uno v. Et negatur etiam, simpliciter ve-tantum vere satisfaciendi habeat faculta-rum esse, quod quis pro se debet, nul-tem. la ratione id pro alio quoque valere[?] posse. vi. Quin ideo, quia Christus pro se nil debuit, morti obnoxius ex se non fuit, sed satisfacere bene pro aliis potuit, absque eo ad hoc non valiturus, nec idoneus. vii. Quare & inepta, & falsa est comparatio Christi cum eo, qui centum tantummodo aureos nummos habeat, quos dare possit, quum infinitae potestatis & virtutis Christus sit, ejusque meritum & lutrum pretii infiniti, cum auro argentoque non aestimandi. 1 Pet. 1. 18. 19. quare & contumeliosum est dicere de eo, quod vix pro uno tantum vere satisfaciendi habeat facultatem. quod citra blasphemiam dici non posse, censemus. Denique, saltem pro uno satisfaciendi facultatem habeat Christus: sic certe non pugnat cum natura rei, ut pro altero satisfiat: & si non implicet, pro uno, quare pro pluribus.
units.tr: Socinus: But for another reason also. Answer: (1) Eternal death is understood in two ways: by its duration, that it lasts forever, and by its inherent weight and evil. For true satisfaction is the full payment of what is owed. Each of us indeed had to undergo eternal death, by divine justice, but in its value and intensity, not in its extent. So what was lacking in duration had to be made up for by its weight. Therefore, unless we ourselves were willing to do this, someone else would have had to undergo eternal death for each of us. But how could that be done, when eternal death was owed by all men in general? (2) Death is not only bodily; bodily death also belongs to the penalty, but eternal death is not contained in that bodily death alone or in its duration. This is treated more fully below, at p. 256, where Socinus says that bodily penalties are like eternal death. (3) He suggests, but does not prove, that it is impossible for someone other than Christ to satisfy for others. Yet it is plainly ridiculous to think, let alone assert, that one man, who had committed no sin and was in no way liable to eternal death, could have satisfied for all. (4) To die in the place of another is not the same as dying for what one owes oneself; here the comparison does not hold, since Christ did not owe eternal death on his own account. It is as if someone said that one man, who owed nothing himself but had only a hundred gold coins to give, could pay for countless others, each of whom owed a hundred gold coins; when he can scarcely satisfy for even one. (5) It is also denied that what a man owes for himself can in any way be valid for another. (6) Indeed, because Christ owed nothing on his own account and was not liable to death in himself, he was able to satisfy well for others, and without him they could not be made valid or fit. (7) Therefore the comparison of Christ with a man who has only a hundred gold coins to give is both absurd and false, since Christ has infinite power and virtue, and his merit and ransom are of infinite worth, not to be valued in gold or silver. [1 Pet. 1.18, 19.] Therefore it is also insulting to say that he has scarcely the ability to satisfy truly for one; we judge that this cannot be said without blasphemy. Finally, if Christ has the power to satisfy for at least one, it certainly does not conflict with the nature of the matter that he should satisfy for another; and if it involves no contradiction for one, why not for many?

units.la: Socinus, part. iii. cap. iv. pag. 259. Jam dictum est, poenam, quam unusquisque nostrum propter delicta sua pendere tenebatur, mortem aeternam esse. Hanc profecto Christus non subiit; & si eam subiisset, universa salutis nostra & liberationis a peccatorum poena spes & ratio funditus eversa fuisset. Immo, si jam Christus non resurrexisset, vana, ut inquit Paulus, esset Euangelii praedicatio. Resp. Omnino, nisi Christus resurrexisset. Sed, aliud est, mortem aeternam subire; aliud, in ea, aeternum permanere. Illud quidem Christus pro nobis debuit, quia voluit; istud vero, nec potuit quidem. Aeternam mortem quum Christum sustinuisse dicimus, intelligimus, pondere aeternam, non tempore: immo eo gravior illa fuit, & majoris valoris, quo temporis longinquitatem intensionis gravitate redemit. Nam ita solvendum pro nobis satisfaciendumque erat, ut quoque liberaremur, id est, ut & Christus emergeret, & nos in, ac cum eo. Subeunda ergo nostra conditio, & quoque superanda erat. Mortis quodcumque nos meriti, luendum Christo, sed & resurrectione vincendum absolvendumque fuit.
units.tr: Socinus, part iii, chap. iv, p. 259: It has already been said that the penalty each of us was bound to pay for his own sins is eternal death. Christ certainly did not undergo this; and if he had, the whole hope and ground of our salvation and of our deliverance from the punishment of sin would have been utterly overthrown. Indeed, if Christ had not risen again, as Paul says, the preaching of the Gospel would be in vain. Answer: Certainly, unless Christ had risen. But it is one thing to undergo eternal death, and another to remain in it forever. The former Christ owed for us, because he willed it; the latter he could not do at all. When we say that Christ underwent eternal death, we mean eternal in weight, not in time. Indeed that death was all the more grievous and of greater value, because he redeemed the length of time by the intensity of its weight. For it had to be paid and satisfied on our behalf in such a way that we might also be set free, that is, that Christ might emerge and we with him and in him. Our condition therefore had to be undergone and also overcome. Whatever death had merited for us had to be paid by Christ, and also overcome and absolved by his resurrection.

units.la: Jam non satisfactionem modo, sed & meritum Christi, Socinus hac ratio-ne impugnat, cap. iii. quod supervacaneum videatur, ubi pro aliquo satisfeceris, poenarum solutioni, quas debebat, addi & omnium eorum prae-stationem, quae Dei lex nos facere jubet. Quae pugnare, alterutrum saltem supervacaneum esse, ostendere sic conatur: Pugnant sine dubio haec inter se, pro aliquo satisfacere, id omne faciendo, quod ut facere debuerat, & pro eodem satisfacere, omnes poenas subeundo, quas is, propter delicta sua, subire tenetur. Nam si is omnia fecisse censeatur, quae facere debuerat, fieri non potest ut pro ipso quidquam poena nomine solvatur. Ubi enim nullum delictum, ibi nulla poena. Rursus, si quidquid ille poena nomine debebat, persolvatur, jam pro innocente non habetur. Ubi enim poena persolutio, ibi noxia sit necesse est. Resp. Unica solutione totum id quod adfert, facile diluitur. Loquitur de homine integro, quum & disputatio & res nostra intelligatur de homine lapso. In hoc autem duo consideranda, quod, pro peccatis ejus solvendum fuit, ut liberaretur; tum ut vitae insuper fieret particeps, quod præstari debuit id, ad quod vita promissa erat. Homini integro id modo faciendum erat, quod fieri oportet ad acquirendam vitam, qui si omnia fecisse censeatur, quae facere debuerat, fieri non potest, ut pro ipso quidquam poena nomine solvatur. Ubi enim nullum delictum, ibi nulla poena. Verum peccator, & pro peccato poenas debet, & pro vita adipiscendâ justitiam: neque enim ad salutem ei sufficit, si duntaxat liberetur; sed qui fecerit ea, is demum vivet. Uti quando quis è summâ dignitate in carcerem conjicitur, non satis est liberari è captivitate, nisi etiam in pristinum restituatur locum: ita homo ex paradyso in infernum suo vitio detrusus, ex miseriâ redimendus, & sic in coelo collocandus fuit: utrumque per Christum, illud, ejus satisfactione; istud, merito, sive justitiâ, quâ pro peccatis poenas nostras pertulit, & quâ id omne pro nobis fecit, quod facere nos, ad impetrandam vitam, debebamus. Utrumque Apostolus docet, & conjungit Rom. viii. 3. 4. Quod enim impossibile erat legi, in quo infirmabatur per carnem: quippe impossibile erat attingere & adipisci vitam, lege promissam, & nobis non nisi hac via via acquirendam: hoc fecit Deus filium suum mittens in similitudine carnis peccati. i. e. difficultati vel impossibilitati isti Deus occurrit, juvitque nos per suum Filium, καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας[?], hostia pro peccato, condemnavit peccatum in carne Filii sui, per ejus passionem nempe & satisfactionem. Ut jus legis impleretur in nobis. Nempe non solum per eum à peccato liberati sumus, sed quoque promissionem legis impetravimus. Et hinc Gal. iii. 21. negat Apostolus, legem esse adversus Dei promissiones; sed omnia sub peccato, ait, & reatu teneri, ut promissio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur credentibus. Quare concedimus, quod infert Socinus, si quidquid ille poena nomine debeat, persolvatur, jam pro innocente non habetur. Revera non habetur pro innocente, pro cujus peccatis satisfit, sed pro nocente: & hinc Christus tempestive pro nobis mortuus dicitur, non infirmis tantum, sed impiis.
units.tr: Now Socinus attacks not only the satisfaction but also the merit of Christ, by this argument (chap. iii): it seems superfluous that, when someone has satisfied for another by paying the penalties he owed, the performance of all the things which God's law commands us to do should be added as well. He tries to show that these two things at least are mutually contradictory, or at least that one of them is superfluous: Doubtless these things contradict each other: to satisfy for someone by doing everything that he ought to have done, and to satisfy for the same person by undergoing all the penalties which he is bound to undergo for his sins. For if he is judged to have done all that he ought to have done, it cannot be that anything is paid on his behalf under the name of penalty. For where there is no offence, there is no penalty. Again, if whatever he owed as penalty is paid, he is no longer regarded as innocent. For where the penalty is paid, there the guilty one must be. Answer: The whole of this objection is easily refuted by a single solution. He speaks of a man in his integrity, whereas our dispute and our case concern a fallen man. In the latter case two things must be considered: that for his sins he had to pay, in order to be set free; and that he should also be made a partaker of life, which required that the thing be done on which the promised life depended. A man in integrity had only to do what must be done to acquire life. If he is judged to have done all that he ought to have done, it cannot be that anything is paid on his behalf under the name of penalty. For where there is no offence, there is no penalty. But the sinner both owes penalties for sin and owes righteousness in order to obtain life. For it is not enough for his salvation that he merely be set free; rather, the one who does these things shall live. When someone of high rank is thrown into prison, it is not enough for him to be freed from captivity unless he is also restored to his former position. So man, cast by his own fault out of paradise into hell, had to be redeemed from misery and placed in heaven. Both are accomplished through Christ: the former by his satisfaction, the latter by his merit, or righteousness, by which he bore our penalties for sins and by which he did for us all that we were bound to do in order to obtain life. The Apostle teaches both and joins them in Rom. 8.3, 4: For what the law could not do, in that it was weakened by the flesh, since it was impossible for the law, which promised life and could be obtained by us only by this way, to attain and secure life: God, by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, that is, God met this difficulty or impossibility and helped us through his Son, and concerning sin [καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας], as a sacrifice for sin, condemned sin in the flesh of his Son, namely by his passion and satisfaction; so that the requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us. That is, not only have we been freed from sin through him, but we have also obtained the promise of the law. And hence in Gal. 3.21 the Apostle denies that the law is against God's promises; but he says that all things are held under sin and guilt, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ. Therefore we concede what Socinus infers: If whatever he owed as penalty is paid, he is no longer regarded as innocent. Indeed he is not regarded as innocent for whose sins satisfaction is made, but as guilty; and hence Christ is said to have died for us in due time, not only for the weak, but for the ungodly.

units.la: Rom. v. 6.
units.tr: Rom. v. 6.

units.la: Socinus: Supervacaneum autem alterutrum saltem esse, hoc pacto demonstratur. Nam si delictorum poena penditur, quid attinet eum, pro quo penditur, innocentem haberi? Vel si innocens habetur, quid opus est pro ipsius delictis quidquam poenā nomine solvere? Annon utrumvis istorum per se eum liberat, & ipsius errata prorsus delet? Resp. 1. Non habetur innocens, sed fit, is, pro quo penditur delictorum poenā. 11. Utrumque istorum quidem liberat eum, voce liberationis latius sumtā, non solum pro manumissione ex servitute miseriae, sed quoque restitutione & beatione; distinctè tamen altero errata ejus delentur, atque ita ab iis liberatur; altero jus vitae acquiritur & felicitatis perpetuae: ut ista secum non magis pugnent, vel suorum alterum evincant supervacuum esse, quam redemtio & glorificatio.
units.tr: Socinus: It is shown in this way that it is superfluous for at least one of the two to be present. For if the penalty of sins is paid, what does it matter that the one for whom it is paid be regarded as innocent? Or if he is regarded as innocent, why is there any need to pay anything in punishment for his offences? Does not each of these by itself free him and utterly blot out his errors? Resp. 1. He is not regarded as innocent but made innocent, the one for whom the penalty of the offences is paid. 2. Each of these indeed frees him, if the word "liberation" is taken more broadly, not only for manumission from the slavery of misery but also for restoration and blessing. Yet they act distinctly: by the one his errors are blotted out and he is freed from them; by the other the right to life and perpetual happiness is acquired. So these do not conflict with each other, nor do they prove that either of them is superfluous, any more than redemption and glorification do.

units.la: Socinus: Satis autem fuisse, ut nos justi haberemur, peccata nostra deleri, id apertissime demonstrat, quod in compluribus sanctarum litterarum locis peccatorum remissione universam salutem nostram contineri, si non disertis verbis, at reipsa scriptum extat. Resp. 1. Peccata nostra deleri, ut justi habeamur, omnino est necesse, eoque quod justificamur, peccata remittuntur, namque justificatio consistit partim in re-missione peccatorum, partim in adjudicatione vitæ æternæ, quorum hoc per Christi meritum, illud per satisfactionem contingit. II.[?] Peccatorum remissio-ne sæpe tota salus & μακαρισμὸς[?] describitur, synecdochice, parte pro toto. Quemadmodum in sanguine Christi passim salus nostra, in Scripturis ponitur: quod nec Adversarii interpretabuntur de sanguine aut morte Christi solâ: ita etiam in remissione, quæ χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας ἢ γίνεται[?]: sed non, quasi ista sola omnem salutem comprehenderet, sed quod ad hanc pars necessaria atque primaria fit, absque quâ datur nemini. Cæterum, uti Christus nobis factus & δικαιοσύνη, & ἀπολύτρωσις, ita ad salutem atque justificationem requiritur, præter remissionem peccatorum, etiam justitiæ Christi imputatio, quâ vitæ jus nobis addicitur. Remissio peccatorum exi-mit quidem à reatu & à maledictione liberat, sed uti ad cœlum non satis est extra infernum esse; ita ad vitam in cœlis agendam requiritur justitia, cui de-mum vita pro præmio adscripta fuit. Justitia Christi, quia in eo omnia, quæ ad salutem & justificationem nobis desunt, reperiuntur.
units.tr: Socinus: Moreover, that it was enough for us to be held righteous that our sins be blotted out is most clearly shown by the fact that in many places of Holy Scripture our whole salvation is contained in the remission of sins, if not in express words, yet in fact it stands written. Resp. 1. That our sins must be blotted out if we are to be held righteous is entirely necessary, and by the fact that we are justified, sins are remitted. For justification consists partly in the remission of sins and partly in the adjudication of eternal life; of these, the former comes through Christ's merit, the latter through satisfaction. 2. By the remission of sins the whole salvation and blessedness is often described, by synecdoche, the part standing for the whole. Just as our salvation is placed in the blood of Christ throughout the Scriptures, which even our adversaries will not interpret as the blood or death of Christ alone, so also with remission, which does not happen without the shedding of blood [χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας οὐ γίνεται]. But this is not because remission alone comprehends all salvation; rather, it is a necessary and primary part of it, without which it is given to no one. Moreover, just as Christ is made to us [δικαιοσύνη] and [ἀπολύτρωσις], so for salvation and justification there is required, besides the remission of sins, also the imputation of Christ's righteousness, by which the right to life is adjudged to us. Remission of sins indeed releases us from guilt and frees us from the curse; but just as it is not enough for heaven to be outside hell, so for living a life in heaven righteousness is required, to which life itself is finally assigned as the reward. Christ's righteousness is this, because in him are found all those things that are lacking to us for salvation and justification.

units.la: Socinus: Nihil magis ridiculum excogitari potest, quam, si quis dicat, unius justitiam alterius, qui plane injustus fuerit, justitiam censeri. Parcere quidem Deus multis injustis propter paucos justos consuevit; ut colligitur ex verbis ipsius cum Abrahamo loquentis paullo ante destructionem Sodomæ; ne scilicet una cum impiis pios quoque perdat, aut puniat. Non tamen idcirco injustos, justorum causa, justos censet. Sicut enim impietas impii super eum erit, sic justitia justi super eum futura est, inquit, ut vidimus, ipse Deus apud Ezechielem. Resp. Concedimus omnia, de hominibus vulgo, & inter se. Hic impietas impii super eum, ac pietas pii ad ipsum spectat. Neque Deus injustos, justorum causa, justos censet; nec unius hominis justi-tia, alterius, qui plane injustus fit, censetur. Verùm longè aliter quam pro conditione vulgi, atque uti inter homines solet, res se habet cum Mediatore & salvatore Christo, cujus, & quidem solius, justitia nobis imputatur, quia nobis dicitur factus justitia. 1Cor. 1. 30. ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν δικαιοσύνη[?]. non ita alius quis, aut nobis, aut aliis. Non alius justus, nedum justitia est, non justi-tia mediatoris, qui istum in finem venit, ut justitia ejus justificaret Deus impium. Rom. iv. 5. Non aliis, vel aliorum transgressione constituuntur homines peccatores, uti ex lapsu Adami; ita Christi obedientia, nullius autem alterius, justi fiunt. Quod etiam satis pro responso est ad id, quod sequitur, apud Socinum, ubi inquit: sed finge, unius justitiam, alterius censeri posse; num unius tantum justitia innumerabilium esse censebitur? Quid videtur, annon unius Christi justitia innumerabilium censita fuit? & nonne per Adami inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi? atque ita etiam pro obedientiam unius Christi justi con-stituuntur multi. Rom. v. 19. Quod si enim unius transgressione multi mortui, multo magis gratia Dei & donum gratia unius hominis Jesu Christi abundavit in multos. verf. 15. Tria in Christo bene consideranda, quod Mediator, quod Deus, quod per-sectam praestitit absolutamque omni parte justitiam. Non ergo ejus justitia ex vulgari hominum aliorum aestimanda est. Quia Mediator, pro nobis est quid-quid est, & egit: quia Deus, justitia ejus perfecta, quaeque pro ratione officii praestita, tantarum fuit virium, ut pro omnibus suffecerit, quibus fuit de-stinata.
units.tr: Socinus: Nothing more ridiculous can be imagined than if someone should say that the righteousness of one man is counted as the righteousness of another who has been wholly unrighteous. God indeed is accustomed to spare many unrighteous for the sake of a few righteous, as is gathered from his own words speaking with Abraham shortly before the destruction of Sodom, namely lest he destroy or punish the godly along with the wicked. Yet he does not on that account regard the unrighteous as righteous for the sake of the righteous. For as the impiety of the impious will be upon him, so the righteousness of the righteous will be upon him, says God himself, as we have seen, in Ezekiel. Resp. We concede all of this, as it concerns men commonly and among themselves. Here the impiety of the impious is upon him, and the piety of the pious looks to him. Nor does God regard the unrighteous as righteous for the sake of the righteous, nor is the righteousness of one man counted to another who is wholly unrighteous. But matters stand quite differently with the Mediator and Saviour Christ, and not according to the condition of the common people or as is customary among men: his righteousness, and his alone, is imputed to us, because he is said to be made righteousness to us (1 Cor. 1. 30) [ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν δικαιοσύνη], and not some other man's, either to us or to others. Another is not righteous, much less is he righteousness; it is the righteousness of the Mediator, who came to this end, that God might justify the ungodly through his righteousness (Rom. 4. 5). Men are not constituted sinners by another's transgression or by the transgression of others, as by the fall of Adam; so by the obedience of Christ, and of no other, they are made righteous. This is also enough as an answer to what follows in Socinus, where he says: but suppose that the righteousness of one can be counted to another; will the righteousness of one alone be counted as that of innumerable others? What do you think? Was not the righteousness of the one Christ counted as that of innumerable others? And were not many made sinners through the disobedience of Adam? So also through the obedience of the one Christ many are made righteous. Rom. v. 19. For if through the trespass of the one many died, much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded unto many. Verse 15. Three things in Christ are to be well considered: that he is Mediator, that he is God, and that he performed a perfect righteousness, absolute in every part. Therefore his righteousness is not to be estimated by the common measure of other men. For as Mediator, whatever he is and whatever he did is for us; and as God, his perfect righteousness, performed according to the demands of his office, was of such strength that it sufficed for all for whom it was destined.

units.la: Socinus, part. iii. cap. iv. Vides, quibus philosophicis inventu vobis opus sit, ut istam vestram satisfactionem defendere possitis. Atqui ea, si placet, paullo diligentius examinemus. Quod igitur ad personae dignitatem attinet, primum mihi valde suspectum est, quod pro concesso sumitur, principiis scilicet viri levem poenam ejusdem pretii esse, cujus gravissimam hominis plebeji: quinimmo crediderim, injustam esse eam legem, quae idem delictum in viro principe leviter puniat, in plebejo autem homine gravissime. Resp. I. Non sunt illa philosophica inventa, vel quod Christus Mediator est, aut quod Deus, aut quod perfecta ejus justitia, in Scripturis testatissima, quodque hinc sequitur, illam infiniti esse pretii. Non dicimus, propter personae dignitatem in Christo levius, vel infra condignum vindicata peccata nostra fuisse: sed quum debitas eorum poenas Christus tulerit, ex personae dignitate fluere dicimus, quod justitia ejus tanti habetur, ad nos redimendos, pretii. Duo ergo conjungimus, poenarum justam perfolutionem, & satisfactionis infinitum valorem. Poenas nostras omnes tulit Christus, nec levius in eo punita delicta, quam in aliis, seu in nobis factum fuisset. De quo si quis dubitet, remittimus eum ad cap. LIII. Jesaiae, id ut debite expendat, & conjecta, quae illic dicuntur, in Christum peccata nostrum omnia, quae excepit exfol-vitque. Ut indigne postea Socinus dicat, poenas, quas nostrum caussa pertulit Christus, quamvis per se gravissimas existimari debeant, tamen, si cum iis comparentur, quas nos meriti eramus, multo esse leviores, quam unius diei aut horae exilium, si cum perpetuo exilio comparetur. Non certe tam leves Christi dolores fuerunt & poenae, neque ita per se gravissimae aestimari possent, si nihil aliud fuissent, quam quod unius diei vel horae exilium est, ad perpetuum. Vim perpetui exilii, ut sic loquar, vel eorum quae nos debebamus, Deoque, nisi aliter providisset, luissemus, pertulit Christus ac sustinuit, quodque tempori defuit in diuturnitate, pondere compensatum fuit. Falsumque, quod Socinus ait, quod poenae quas Christus sustinuit, nullam habent ad poenas, quas nos pendere tenebamur, pro-portionem.
units.tr: Socinus, part iii, chap. iv: You see what philosophical inventions you need in order to defend that satisfaction of yours. But let us, if you please, examine them a little more carefully. As for the dignity of the person, first of all it seems to me very suspect that it is taken for granted, on the principles of the man, that a light penalty has the same value as the most grievous penalty for a plebeian. Indeed, I should believe that the law is unjust which punishes the same offence lightly in a prince but most grievously in a plebeian. Resp. 1. Those are not philosophical inventions, whether that Christ is Mediator, or that he is God, or that his perfect righteousness, most clearly attested in Scripture, and that it follows from this that it is of infinite worth. We do not say that on account of the dignity of the person in Christ our sins were punished more lightly, or below what was condign. But since Christ bore their due penalties, we say that it flows from the dignity of the person that his righteousness is held to be of such price for redeeming us. So we join two things: the just full payment of penalties and the infinite value of the satisfaction. Christ bore all our penalties, nor were the offences punished in him more lightly than they would have been in others or in us. If anyone doubts this, we refer him to chapter 53 of Isaiah, so that he may weigh it duly, and the sins laid upon Christ, all of ours, which he took upon himself and paid. Socinus therefore unworthily says that the penalties which Christ endured for our sake, although in themselves they ought to be reckoned most grievous, nevertheless, if they are compared with those which we deserved, are much lighter than the exile of one day or hour when compared with perpetual exile. Certainly Christ's sorrows and penalties were not so light, nor could they be judged so grievous in themselves, if they had been nothing other than the exile of one day or hour set against an everlasting one. The force of perpetual exile, so to speak, or of those things which we owed and would have paid to God had he not otherwise provided, Christ endured and sustained; and what was lacking in duration was made up in weight. False, too, is what Socinus says, that the penalties which Christ sustained have no proportion to the penalties which we were bound to pay.

units.la: Socinus: Et certe si finiti ad infinitum, ut dici solet, nulla est proportio, quaenam poenarum Christi, quae tempore finitae fuere, ad poenas nostris peccatis debitas nunquam tempore finiendas proportio esse potest? Resp. I. Christi poenae tempore quidem & duratione finitae fuerunt, sed gravitate, moraliter ut dici solet, & pretio sunt infinitae. II. An poenarum Christi, quamvis tempore finitarum, nulla est proportio ad hominum annihilationem, si in perpetuum annihilentur? quae illae scilicet poenae Adversariis fuht[?] nullo tempore finiendae.
units.tr: Socinus: And surely, if from finite to infinite, as is commonly said, there is no proportion, what proportion can there be between the penalties of Christ, which were finite in time, and the penalties due to our sins, which are never to be finished in time? Resp. 1. Christ's penalties were indeed finite in time and duration, but in weight, as is commonly said, morally speaking, and in value, they are infinite. 2. Is there no proportion between the penalties of Christ, though finite in time, and the annihilation of men, if they were to be annihilated forever? What penalties, pray, are those which, for the Adversaries, are never to be ended in any time?

units.la: Socinus: Quamvis enim non defuerint, qui, Christum damnatorum poenas passum fuisse, affirmare sint ausi, explosa tamen est sententia ista; & merito quidem, cum propter alia multa, quæ ad eam refellendam afferri solent, tum maxime propter hoc, quod de divina gratia & auxilio desperatio, quæ propria damnatorum est pœna, quam longissime semper à Christo absint. Resp. 1. Christus non est passus pœnas damnatorum, sed damnandorum, id est, eas quas nos alioqui damnandi sustinere debuissemus. Istas omnes tulit, quod ad vim ipsarum, pondus, & substantiam, ut sic di-camus, non quod ad accidentia omnia, & circumstantias. II. Desperatio inter pœnas non venit, quibus à Deo afficiuntur homines, nec proprie ipsa pœna est, sed consequens subjecti, æternum puniendi. III. Quod si de divina gratia & auxilio desperabunt perpetuum damnati, istaque damnato-rum pœna futura sit, jam ergo existent æternum, & sensu afficientur pœna-rum ac cruciatuum infernalium.
units.tr: Socinus: For although there have not been lacking those who have dared to assert that Christ suffered the punishments of the damned, that opinion has been exploded, and rightly so: among many other reasons brought against it, chiefly because the despair concerning divine grace and help, which is the proper punishment of the damned, is always as far as possible from Christ. Reply 1: Christ did not suffer the punishments of the damned, but of those to be damned, that is, the punishments which we, being otherwise bound to damnation, ought to have endured. He bore all of these as regards their force, weight and substance, so to speak, though not as regards all their accidents and circumstances. II. Despair is not among the punishments with which men are afflicted by God, nor is it properly a punishment itself, but a consequence of the subject being destined to eternal punishment. III. But if the damned are to despair of divine grace and help forever, and this is to be their punishment, then they will already exist eternally and be afflicted with the sense of the infernal punishments and torments.

units.la: Socinus : Nunc de vi illa, quam Adversarii adferunt, infinita, eorundem, quæ passus est Christus, disputiamus. Certum est nulla alia ratione posse vim istam infinitam in qua passus est Christus, attribui, nisi quia æternus Deus sit. Sed Christus non potuit, quatenus æternus Deus, quidquam pati. Ergo ad infinitam vim ejus perpessionibus tribuen-dam nihil momenti habet, quod Christus æternus Deus sit. Resp. 1. Negatur consequen-tia, Christus, quatenus est æternus Deus, vel ipsa in eo æterna deitas, pati non potest; ergo nec hæc vim & pretium tribuere perpessionibus potest, quas hu-mana natura, sibi personaliter unita, sustinuit? Christi sunt actiones & passio-nes omnes, sed pro harum conditione, attribuendæ suæ naturæ, ex quâ ortum habent, ut principio, uti ajunt, quo. Quod Deus fuit Christus, tantam passionibus ejus conciliat dignitatem, ut inde dictum, neque temere, Act. xx. 28. quod Deus suo sanguine redemit Ecclesiam. & 1 Joann. 1. 7. sanguis Jesu Christi filii ejus purgat nos ab omni peccato. Duo Christi Deitas huic operi contulit, ut humana natura perferre posset passiones gravissimas, & ut essent tanti valoris; vim patiendi, atque pretium passionum, ipsa Deitate omni mo-do impassibili.
units.tr: Socinus: Now let us dispute about that infinite force which our opponents attribute to the sufferings of Christ. It is certain that this infinite force in which Christ suffered can be attributed only on the ground that he is the eternal God. But Christ, as the eternal God, could suffer nothing. Therefore the fact that Christ is the eternal God has no weight in attributing infinite force to his sufferings. Reply 1: The inference is denied. Christ, as he is the eternal God, or the eternal deity itself in him, cannot suffer; does it follow that this deity cannot give force and worth to the sufferings which the human nature, personally united to it, endured? All the actions and sufferings are Christ's, but they are to be attributed according to their condition to the nature from which they arise, as to their principle, as they say, by which. The fact that Christ was God gives such dignity to his sufferings that it is rightly and not rashly said, Acts 20:28, that God redeemed the Church with his own blood, and 1 John 1:7, the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin. The Deity of Christ contributed two things to this work: that the human nature could bear the most grievous sufferings, and that they would be of such value: the power of suffering and the worth of the sufferings, the Deity itself being in every way impassible.

units.la: Socinus : Ad hæc fingamus, si placet, divinam naturam in Christo verè passam suis-se, num, obsecro, quia divina natura, hoc est, Deus infinita virtutis est, idcirco quacun-que in ipso fiunt, infinita sunt virtutis? Sic enim plerique ex vestris argumentari solent. Maxima omnino est in ista ratiocinatione fallacia. Perinde est enim, ac si quis diceret, quia Deus infinite sapiens est, idcirco quacunque in ipso fiunt, habent sapientiam infini-tam, ex quo concludi posset, (si modo Deum ipsum in Christo vere passum fuisse velimus) Christi perpessiones non infinita virtute tan-tum, sed infinita quoque sapientia prædita esse. quo nihil ineptius dictum excogitari potest. Nec vero in ipsas Christi perpessiones, magus[?] quam
units.tr: Socinus: Furthermore, let us suppose, if you like, that the divine nature in Christ truly suffered. Pray, because the divine nature, that is, God, is of infinite power, are therefore whatever is done in him of infinite power? For this is how many of your people are wont to argue. The fallacy in this reasoning is utterly great. It is just as if someone were to say: because God is infinitely wise, therefore whatever is done in him has infinite wisdom; from which it could be concluded (if we are willing that God himself truly suffered in Christ) that Christ's sufferings are endowed not only with infinite power but also with infinite wisdom. Nothing more absurd than this can be imagined. Nor indeed in Christ's sufferings themselves, more than

units.la: Resp. Quinam nostrum ita argu-mentati fuerunt, uti hic argumentatos Socinus introducit? Non fingendum, quod nec verum, nec dictum fictum-ve nostris unquam fuit, divinam naturam in Christo verè passam fuisse. Quid hoc est, vel ista sibi quid vult-locutio, cui in hac argumentatione totus insistit, in ipso Deo fieri? Deus infinitæ virtutis est, ac proinde quod-cunque in ipso, virtutis ejusdem est, & simul sapientiæ infinitæ: nam Deus sibi ubique Deus est, & idem, & quidquid in eo, simpliciter infinitum est. Chri-stus perpessionibus suis infinitam virtu-tem, id est, valorem addidit, non ita sapientia, cadere potest ea virtus, seu vis sapientiam, quia non sapientiæ, uti ejus generis, cujus illa est, quam in Deo in- virtutis, capaces illæ. Nec virtutem finitam esse omnes consitemur. & , si caderet, suam, prout attributum & proprieta- non id efficeretur, quod quærimus. [illegible, ~8 letters] tem notat divinæ naturæ, in perpessio-nes transfudit, ut idem de sapientiâ inferatur, sed effectivè passionibus suis conciliavit vim, dignitatem, valorem infinitum. Non hæc est infinitas physi-ca, cujus finitum subjectum capax non est; sed moralis, qualis in pretio attendi solet: unde infinitis modis τίμιον αἷμα Χριστοῦ [?] dicitur excellere cor-ruptibilibus, auro & argento. 1 Pet. 1. 18. 19. Interim & vi divinâ infi-nitâ Christus sustinuit humanam naturam, ut tanta pati posset, & perferre, quæ passa, supra quam humana natura in se, & seorsim à divinâ, vel extra unionem personalem cum divinâ, posset. Videns illa Socinus, melius dixit, in fine: non enim quærimus, ut ea quæ Christus passus est, omnia possint, quemadmodum Deus omnia potest (hæc est enim vis illa Dei infinita) sed ut infiniti sint pretii.
units.tr: Reply: Which of us has argued in the way that Socinus here introduces? No one has ever said, or even pretended, that the divine nature truly suffered in Christ, which is neither true nor said. What does this mean, or what does this phrase, on which he rests his whole argument, to happen in God itself, signify? God is of infinite power, and therefore whatever is in him is of the same power, and at the same time of infinite wisdom: for God is everywhere God to himself, and whatever is in him is simply infinite. Christ added to his sufferings an infinite power, that is, worth; this power, or force, cannot fall into wisdom, since those things are not capable of wisdom, as of the kind to which that infinite power in God belongs. Nor do we all confess that power is finite; and if it were, that would not bring about what we seek. [illegible] he transferred his own power, as the attribute and property of the divine nature, into the sufferings, so that the same might be inferred about wisdom; but he effectively gave to his sufferings a force, dignity and infinite worth. This is not physical infinity, to which a finite subject is not capable; but moral infinity, such as is usually considered in worth. Hence in countless ways the precious blood of Christ [τίμιον αἷμα Χριστοῦ] is said to excel corruptible things, gold and silver, 1 Peter 1:18, 19. Meanwhile, also by infinite divine power, Christ sustained the human nature so that it could undergo and endure such great sufferings, more than the human nature could suffer in itself and separately from the divine, or outside personal union with the divine. Socinus, seeing this, said better at the end: for we do not seek that what Christ suffered should be able to do all things, as God can do all things (for that is the infinite power of God), but that they should be of infinite worth.

units.la: Socinus: Alia igitur argumentatione utendum est: hac, videlicet; Deus infiniti pretii est. Christi igitur perpessiones, utpote in ipso Deo factæ, infiniti pretii sunt. Sed rur-sus hac argumentatione nullius ipsa pretii est. Resp. Quem autem nostrum ita argu-mentantem facit? Quis Christi perpessiones, in ipso Deo factas, dixit? vel, Deum esse infiniti pretii? Christi perpessiones, quia Dei sunt, non in ipso Deo, sed in naturâ humanâ, ipsi personaliter unita, unde & Dei, & Filii Dei, & pretiosissimæ, in sacris litteris appellantur, dicimus pretium accipere, ex ratione unionis illius, vel unitæ sibi personaliter naturæ divinæ, quoque infinitum.
units.tr: Socinus: Therefore another argument must be used, namely this: God is of infinite worth. Therefore Christ's sufferings, being made in God himself, are of infinite worth. But again, this argument is of no value at all. Reply: But who among us makes this argument? Who has said that Christ's sufferings were made in God himself, or that God is of infinite worth? Christ's sufferings, because they are God's, are not in God himself but in the human nature personally united to him; hence they are called in Holy Scripture both God's and the Son of God's, and most precious. We say that they receive their worth, which is also infinite, from the reason of that union, that is, of the divine nature personally united to it.

units.la: Socinus: Videmus Dei operationes, quantumvis maximi, non tamen infiniti pretii esse. Operationis autem nomine non operandi actum, sed opus ipsum intelligo, quemadmodum in hac quæstione nostra passionis nomine non patiendi affectum, sed id, quod persona patitur, intelligendum est. Resp. 1. Non est quæstio simpliciter de operatio-nibus Dei, sed de actionibus θεανθρωπικῆς [?], in unione personali Mediatoris Christi. 11. Nec passionibus Christi, solas passiones intelligimus, sed quo-que patiendi affectum; ἐν ᾧ θελήματι [?], qua voluntate sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel factam. Hebr. x. 12.
units.tr: Socinus: We see that the works of God, however great, are nevertheless not of infinite worth. By the name of operation I understand not the act of operating but the work itself, just as in this question of ours by the name of passion we must understand not the affection of suffering but that which the person suffers. Reply 1: The question is not simply about the operations of God, but about the actions [θεανθρωπικῆς] in the personal union of the Mediator Christ. II. Nor by the sufferings of Christ do we mean only the sufferings, but also the affection of suffering; by which will [ἐν ᾧ θελήματι] we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once made, Hebrews 10:12.

units.la: Socinus: Nonne & id quoque, quod unusquisque nostrorum propter delicta sua pati tenebatur, infinitum quiddam erat? &c. Infinitas igitur pretii, quæ in Christi perpessio-nibus, quia divina natura passa fuisset, reperiri posset, pro uno quopiam persolvi potuisset, & unus tantummodo ex nobis, ejus vi, à mortis æternæ reatu liberari. Si quidem, ut dictum est, quilibet ex nobis per se eam pretii infinitatem debebat. Quare totidem pretii pœnarum infinitaies existere opus fuisset, quot nos omnes sumus, non unicam tantum, si omnes, id per alium solvendo, quod nos debebamus, eo nexu liberandi fuissemus. Resp. 1. Non est infinitas in perpessionibus Christi, quia divina natura passa fuerit: neque nos id dicimus: sed persona illa Christus, passa fuit in humanâ naturâ, sola quæ pati potuit: uti passibilitatis, ita passionis omnis exsors est divina.
units.tr: Socinus: Was not even that which each of us was bound to suffer on account of his own sins a certain infinite thing? etc. Therefore the infinity of worth which could be found in Christ's sufferings, because the divine nature would have suffered, could be paid on behalf of one person, and by its power only one of us could be freed from the guilt of eternal death. For, as has been said, each of us by himself would owe that infinity of worth. Wherefore there would have been need for as many infinities of punishments as we all are, not just one, if all of us were to be freed by the bond of another paying what we owed. Reply 1: There is no infinity in Christ's sufferings because the divine nature suffered; nor do we say this. But that person Christ suffered in the human nature, the only nature which could suffer; the divine nature is entirely free both of passibility and of passion.

units.la: 11. Quando de passionibus Christi, earumque vi, & pretio agitur, intueri non solum eas debemus, & personæ infinitatem, sed quoque fœdus Dei, quo Christus ordinatus fuit, ut infinitâ passione non pro uno alteroque, sed innumeris satisfaceret, vitamque mereretur & gratiam. Uti ex Adami peccato, Deo ita ordinante ac pacificente, omnes & singuli homines rei satisfecerunt æternæ damnationis, Rom. v. 12. damnati, antequam nati, inquit Bernardus: nec totidem infinitates distinctæ in unâ primi hominis transgressione constituendæ, quæ ad nos dimanent: ita in Christi obedientiâ temere infinitates debitorum nostrorum segregaveris, quum unâ suâ passione ac morte, pro pœnarum infinitatibus, ut ita loquar, satisfecerit. Istud ex divino pacto, ut ubi animam posuisset, visurus esset semen.
units.tr: II. When we treat of the sufferings of Christ, and of their force and worth, we must consider not only these and the infinity of the person, but also the covenant of God by which Christ was appointed, so that by an infinite passion he might satisfy not for one or another but for countless people, and merit life and grace. Just as through the sin of Adam, God so ordaining and reconciling, all and each of men became guilty of eternal damnation, Romans 5:12; damned before they were born, says Bernard. Nor must we posit as many distinct infinities in the one transgression of the first man as flow down to us; so you cannot rashly separate infinities of our debts in the obedience of Christ, since by his one passion and death he has satisfied, so to speak, for the infinities of punishments. This is from the divine pact, that when he had laid down his soul he would see his seed.

units.la: Atque ita pro Christi satisfactione hactenus à nobis disputatum, defensaque ea adversus omnes, quod scimus, omnium objectiones. Sed pridem aliquam Christi satisfactionem, meritum etiam, lutrum, sacrificium expiatorium, & nescio quæ non agnoscere cæperunt Adversarii. Quæ ne incautis imponant, à nobis ultimo loco supersunt examinanda.
units.tr: So far we have argued for Christ's satisfaction, and defended it against all the objections we know of. But for some time our opponents have begun to deny that Christ made any satisfaction, or merit, ransom, expiatory sacrifice, and I know not what else. Lest they impose these on the unwary, they remain for us to examine in the last place.

units.la: Nemo verò ex Adversariis plausibilibus videtur loquutus fuisse unquam, de Christo, & ejus satisfactione, quam Martinus Ruarus, in epistolâ super hoc argumento scriptâ, a. MDCXLIV. Quæ quia trita multorum manibus, & jactata linguis, digna visa est, quæ hic legeretur, atque expenderetur serio. Sic autem habet:
units.tr: Yet none of our plausible opponents seems ever to have spoken about Christ and his satisfaction as Martinus Ruarus did in a letter on this subject, written in 1644. Since it has been handled by many hands and bandied about on many tongues, it seemed worth quoting here and weighing carefully. It runs thus:

units.la: Quæris ex me, vir Clarissime, quæ mea sit super satisfactione Domini nostri Iesu Christi sententia, cum ob eam pessimè alioquin audiamus, ego verò ingenuè tibi respondeo, ex animo me credere, Dominum Servatorem nostrum Iesum Christum, abunde voluntati sui Patris in omnibus satisfecisse, quæcunque illa generis humani causa & agenda & perpetienda ipsi imposuit, hæcque ab ipso alacriter subita atque tolerata, tanti apud Deum fuisse momenti, ut illorum intuitu miseros mortales, morte æternam ac gehennæ cruciatus meritos in gratiam recipere, & peccatis remissis æternum beare velit, si modo nuncio peccatis remisso reliquum vitæ tempus, in fide Iesu Christi, pro modulo virium, quas ipsemet se invocantibus suggerere vult, cum pietate religiosè exigant. Agnosco etiam obedientiam, quam Christus tanquam caput electorum omnium, in vitâ & multo magis in morte summam Deo præstitit, sufficiens esse lutron pro peccatis nostris, adeoque æquipollens supplicio, quod nos peccatis nostris eramus meriti, non quidem ex sese, ne Deo amoris atque gratiæ auferatur gloria, quod S.S. hic tantopere nobis in-
units.tr: You ask me, most distinguished sir, what my opinion is on the satisfaction of our Lord Jesus Christ, since otherwise we hear it spoken of very badly. I answer you frankly: I believe from my heart that our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ has amply satisfied the will of his Father in all things, whatever was laid upon him to do and to suffer for the cause of the human race; and that these things, cheerfully undertaken and endured by him, were of such weight with God that, for their sake, he is willing to receive wretched mortals, who had deserved eternal death and the torments of hell, into favour, and to bless them eternally with their sins forgiven, provided they spend the rest of their life, with sins remitted, in faith in Jesus Christ, living religiously and piously according to the measure of strength which he himself is willing to supply to those who call upon him. I also acknowledge that the obedience which Christ, as head of all the elect, rendered to God in his life, and much more in his death, is a sufficient ransom for our sins, and so equivalent to the punishment which we had deserved by our sins; not indeed of itself, lest the glory of God's love and grace be taken away, which the Holy Scriptures urge upon us so earnestly in...

units.la: Loquitur de Christi satisfactione primum, & merito; tum de mortis Christi fructibus; atque de salutis nostræ causis. Ibi videtur multa primâ fronte concedere, revera tamen nihil dicit, vel largitur. Testatur quidem Christum voluntati Patris sui in omnibus satisfecisse: generis humani causa passum: & hæc magni apud Deum fuisse momenti: illorum intuitu eum-[?] homines in gratiam recipere, mortem æternam & gehennæ cruciatus meritos: Christi obedientiam sufficiens esse lutron pro peccatis nostris, & æquipollens supplicio, quod eramus meriti: neque negat Christi meritum in latiori quadam significatione: atque eum etiam peccata generis humani acerbissima sustinuisse: seipsum in cruce tanquam piacularem victimam præbuisse; corporis sui per mortem oblatione; & nunc in cœlis Deo apparere ad expiaculum peccatorum populo, eorumque remissionem procurandam. Tres denique causas ad rationem salutis nostræ, ait, culcant , sed ex clementi Dei acceptatione , qui obedientiam illam non tanquam mercena-rii, ex merito strictè nuncupato , sed tanquam Filii unigeniti , ex effuso in illum amore , benignè ponderare atque æstimare voluit. Cum verò meritum strictè dictum ab obedientia Christi excludo , non nego tamen ejus meritum in latiori quádam significatione , quo pasto nonnulli ex antiquis Ecclesiæ Patribus (si parva licet componere magnis) piis quoque fidelium operibus interdum meritum aliquod adscribunt , non ex proportione operum , sed ex Dei promisso , aut beneplacito mensuratum. Interim fateor Christi meritum , omnia fan-storum[?] (si ista licet appellare) merita tantopere superare , adeoque ad significationem meriti proprie dicti tanto proprius accedere , quanto & perfectius , omnibusque numeris absolutior fuit ejus præstita Deo obedientia & sublimior natura , atque dignitate is , qui eam præsti-tit. Pœnam pro peccatis nostris à Christo persolutam vix ausim affirmare , cum ea definiri soleat vindicta noxæ, à qua Christus alienus, nec justitia Dei permittat , ut pœna nocenti debita innocenti irrogetur. Si tamen latiore significatione pœnam interpreteris , perpessionem mali delicti , quamvis alieni , causa , vel occasione cuiquam illatam , de vocabulo nolim esse difficilis , tum ob peccata generis humani acerbissima quæque Christum , Deo ita requirente , sustinuisse , cum S. S. ultro tibi largior. Ut autem sententiam meam de fructibus mortis Christi distinctius tibi promam , existimo eos (quamquam multi , imo plurimi , ex S. S. colligi possunt) ad tres classes referri posse , si quemadmodum & mors se habeat , ad triplex Christi munus consideretur. Cum autem Christus fuerit Propheta Dei summus , & quidem ejusmodi , qui non minus , quam Moses , novam populo Dei legam promulgavit , mors Christi omnium , quæ vivus in isto munere docuit , præcepit , promisit , insignis confirmatio , & quoddam velut signaculum , imo sanctio fuit , qua & nos ad ei credendum , legibusque ejus parendum , & Deus ad præstandum , quæ Christus ejus nomine promisit ,
units.tr: He speaks first of Christ's satisfaction and merit; then of the fruits of Christ's death; and of the causes of our salvation. Here he seems at first sight to concede a great deal, yet in truth he says or grants nothing. He does indeed testify that Christ satisfied the will of his Father in all things and suffered for the cause of the human race, and that these things were of great weight before God; that for their sake he receives men into favour, men who had deserved eternal death and the torments of hell; that Christ's obedience is a sufficient ransom for our sins and equivalent to the punishment we had deserved. Nor does he deny Christ's merit in a broader sense; and that Christ endured the most bitter sins of the human race, that he offered himself on the cross as an expiatory victim, offering his body through death, and that now he appears in heaven before God for the expiation of the people's sins and to procure their forgiveness. Finally, he says that three causes come together in the reckoning of our salvation, but from God's gracious acceptance, who willed to weigh and esteem that obedience kindly, not as a hired labourer's, from merit strictly so called, but as that of his only-begotten Son, from the love poured out upon him. But since I exclude strictly defined merit from the obedience of Christ, I do not deny his merit in a broader sense, in which way some of the ancient Fathers of the Church (if small things may be compared with great) sometimes ascribe some merit to the pious works of believers, measured not by the proportion of the works but by God's promise or good pleasure. Meanwhile I confess that Christ's merit far surpasses all the merits of the saints[?] (if these may be so called), and so comes so much nearer to the meaning of merit properly so called, as his obedience rendered to God was more perfect and in every respect more complete, and he who rendered it more exalted in nature and dignity. I should hardly dare to affirm that the punishment for our sins was paid by Christ, since punishment is usually defined as the vengeance of a crime, from which Christ was free, nor does the justice of God permit that a punishment due to the guilty be inflicted on the innocent. If, however, you understand by punishment, in a broader sense, the suffering of an evil on account of another's fault, or the occasion of such suffering inflicted on anyone, I would not be unwilling to be difficult over the word, since Christ, as God so required, endured the most bitter of the sins of the human race, as I freely grant you, in Holy Scripture. But so that I may set out my opinion on the fruits of Christ's death more distinctly for you, I think they can be referred to three classes (although many, indeed very many, can be gathered from Holy Scripture), if we consider how his death stands in relation to the threefold office of Christ. Since Christ was the highest Prophet of God, and indeed of such a kind that he promulgated a new law to the people of God no less than Moses did, his death was a notable confirmation of all that he taught, commanded and promised while living in that office, and a certain signet, indeed a sanction, by which both we are bound to believe him and obey his laws, and God is bound to perform what Christ promised in his name,

units.la: concurrere , Dei misericordiam , Christi curam , & nostram fidem atque obedientiam: Christi lutron sive sacrificium hic intervenire, & similia: verùm astutè cavet ubique, ne tale quid dicat, vel imo adhibeat verbum ullum , quod sensum orthodoxum , & ingenuam fidei verae confessionem secum trahat: in generalibus vel ambiguis studio captatis hærens, multa profert, modò ne unum , in quo cardo rei versatur, & quo demum sincere comprehendisset quæcunque hic attigit verius , quam explicuit. Nam dum Christum satisfecisse agnoscit voluntati Patris sui in omnibus; de alia prorsus re & satisfactione loquitur, quam de quâ quærimus: & vocem satisfactionis posse se admittere significat, excogitato ei novo sensu, id neutiquam notante quod Theologi omnes eâ designare solent. Quod est ingenii prodere acumen aut versutiam, non sincerum fidei sensum ac veritatem. Quasi de verbis agatur, non rebus, & hoc spectandum in disputatione sit, ut sono earundem vocum non sano callide quis irretiat alium, & intricet, non erudiat.
units.tr: God's mercy, Christ's care, and our faith and obedience, come together; Christ's ransom or sacrifice intervenes here, and the like. But he carefully avoids saying anything of the kind everywhere, or using any word that would carry with it an orthodox sense and the sincere confession of the true faith. Clinging to general or ambiguous terms, which he has deliberately sought out, he brings forward many things, but never the one point on which the whole matter turns, and by which he might at last have explained clearly whatever he touched on here, rather than merely touching on it. For while he acknowledges that Christ satisfied the will of his Father in all things, he speaks of something entirely different from the satisfaction we are asking about; and he signifies that he can admit the word "satisfaction" by devising for it a new sense, which in no way conveys what all theologians are accustomed to designate by it. This is to display the cleverness or cunning of a wit, not a sincere sense of the faith and truth. As if the matter were one of words and not of things, and the aim of the discussion were that someone should cunningly ensnare or entangle another by the sound of the same words, not that he should instruct him by sound doctrine.

units.la: Satisfactio enim intelligitur Theo-logis non in latissimâ vulgi acceptione, pro præstatione officii, ad voluntatem vel jussionem alterius: quomodo nemo non est qui non variis in rebus satisfaciat alteri, imo & sibi: neque aliud [?]tum vox significat, quam morem ge-rere, obedire, præstare officium, voluntati obsecundare, sive propriæ, sive alienæ: etiam ad Deum relatâ acceptione, voluntati ejus quovis modo obtemperare: nam sic non Christus tantum, sed & nos, & omnes pii Deo obedientes, voluntati ejus parere, morem gerere, & satisfacere dicendi: neastringitur. Quod ad Sacerdotale munus atti-net, cum ejus sit orare pro populo, & sacri-ficare, hoc est mactare victimam, eamque deinde lege imperata ad expiationem peccato-rum offerre, Christus ubique, qui & paulo ante mortem pro universo, tum credentium, tum creditururorum cœtu, preces ad Deum ardentissimas effudit, & in cœlos per mortem ingressus, nunc quoque pro ipsis apud Deum intercedit, seipsum in cruce tanquam piacula-rem victimam præbuit, cumque ea victima, corporis sui per mortem oblatione præparata, in cœlos, tanquam in sancta sanctorum ingres-sus, nunc quoque pro iis apud Deum interce-dit, eam ipsam Deo inter Cherubinos, seu po-tius inter Angelorum myriadas sedenti imma-culatum per spiritum æternum obtulit, porroq; in perpetuum coram throno majestatis divi-næ apparet, ad expiaculum peccatorum populo, eorumque remissionem procurandam. Denique
units.tr: For theologians understand satisfaction not in the very broad popular sense, of performing a duty in response to another's will or command. In that sense there is no one who does not satisfy another in various matters, and even himself; nor does the word signify anything other than to comply with, obey, perform a duty, humour a will, whether one's own or another's. Even with God as the object, it means to obey his will in any way at all. For in that sense it is said that not only Christ but also we and all the godly who obey God obey his will, comply and satisfy. As for the priestly office, since it belongs to the priest to pray for the people and to sacrifice, that is, to slay the victim and then offer it, as the law commands, for the expiation of sins, Christ everywhere, who shortly before his death poured out most fervent prayers to God for the whole company of believers and of those who would believe, and who, having entered heaven through death, now also intercedes with God for them, offered himself on the cross as an expiatory victim; and, with that victim prepared by the offering of his body through death, entering heaven as into the holy of holies, he now also intercedes with God for them. He offered that same victim, without blemish, through the eternal Spirit, to God sitting among the Cherubim, or rather among the myriads of angels, and ne astringitur. Quod ad Sacerdotale ... he appears continually before the throne of the divine majesty, to procure the expiation of sins for the people and their forgiveness. Finally

units.la: Domino ac servatori nostro Iesu Christo, ad re-gii muneris obeundam in cœlis functionem, cujus vi omnia quæ ad salutem electorum perti-nent, qua tutando liberandoque eos à malis, qua bonorum eos & spiritualium & cœlestium tandem compotes reddendo, non nisi per obe-dientiam ad mortem usque præstitam, aditus patuit, ut proinde & hoc respectu, non pa-rum, imo omnia Christo, qui eam tam prom-ptè adiit, debeamus. Porro non abs re duco commemorare, hoc in loco triplicis ex mea sententia causæ ad rationem salutis nostræ con-currsum: earumque prima & summa immor-talis Dei misericordia, altera Christi tanquam nostri pro corpore suo suscepta apud Deum cu-ra, tertia fides atque obedientia nostra erga Deum per spiritum regenerationis præstita, sed ut vis tertia à secunda, ita & secunda à pri-ma multum superatur. Princeps autem salutis nostræ causa merito agnoscitur misericordia atque gratia divina, à quâ & cæteræ duæ suo ordine institutæ sapienterque directæ vim suam præcipuam, imò omnem mutuantur. Memini aliquando ex me quæsitum, cur Deus, cum pro jure absoluti Domini peccata pœnitentiam eo-rum agentibus remittere possit, Christianamenque in iis tantum quæ agunt; sed & quæ juxta voluntatem ejus 1 Pet. iii. 17. patiuntur. Unde quid effecit jam suis λόγοις Adversarius, quid singu-lare oblecro dixit, agnoscens Christum voluntati Patris in omnibus satisfecisse? nisi quod talem ipsi satisfactionem ad-scripsit, quæ omnibus sit tribuenda piis, solummodò quod majori gradu & perfectione hoc præstet Christus, quam illi? Quod nemo ignorat. Ve-rum satisfactionis vox hic loci accipi-tur sensu juridico & judiciali, non-ethico, prout in foro usurpatur, non in œconomia & civilitate, atque significat præstationem, vel solutio-nem debiti. An sic Christus satisfecerit, quæritur, solutione debitorum nostro-rum vera & perfecta? non quavis alia latâ & generali vocis acceptione aut-satisfactione, atque utrum illud quis since-re agnoscat, non quodvis aliud, quod novo sensu sibi format aut comminisci-tur. Satisfactio est solutio debiti, vel pœnæ: quæ non significat generalem duntaxat actum obedientiæ, quæ fiat præceptis: quâ ratione omnia nostra opera forent satisfactoria, etiam apud Deum, & non tantum Christi: sed quan-do quis pro transgressione multatur, & pœnam solvit justitiæ, ad compensan-dam injuriam peccato factam & illa-tam legibus, atque ad redintegrandam justitiam & jus, talem satisfactionem hoc in loco confideramus. Non tan-tum obediens fuisse Christus dicitur, atque ad mortem usque, sed de hac ejus morte porro docetur, quod pro solutione fuerit, quod & pro peccatis, & tamquam pretium datum sit, vel pretioso sanguine, pretiosiori longe supra argentum & aurum, nos emti, & redemti, lutron, sive sacrificium hic intervenire volue-rit. Huic interrogationi respondisse memini, quod hic non abs re repetere visum est, cur Deus Abimelecho, de peccato contra Abrahamum, ejusque uxorem admonito, & proinde ab eo-dem abstituro, culpam meditatam non alia ra-tione condonare voluerit, quam si Abrahamus pro eo sibi preces adhiberet. cur Iobi amicos de injuria erga pium amicum confistos non aliter in gratiam recipere voluerit, quam si suppedi-tatæ ab ipsis victimæ Iobo præsente pro ipsis sibi offerrentur, atque ipse Iobus pro ipsis ora-ret. Denique (nec plura exempla congeram) cur Deus non sola sub V. Fœdere delinquen-tium pœnitentia contentus sacrificiorum ex-piatoriorum legem præscripserit, ad quæ & sacerdotum & innoxiorum animantium necem intervenire necesse erat! nam ostendere Deus hoc pacto voluit & quantopere peccatum dete-staretur, cujus veniam eo pollutis, non ad solas eorum preces, aliosque pios assus indul-gere voluerit, nec eorum tamen veniam de-sperandam, cujus per innoxios administros procurandæ ritum certa lege constituerit. Vo-luit quoque simul docere, quanti faceret eos, quos gratiæ suæ proxenetas designaverit, si-mulque hac ratione & illos inter se ad officia mutua, & singulos sibi ad religionis curam ob-stringere.
units.tr: To our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who, in order to discharge the office of his kingly function in heaven, by whose power all things that pertain to the salvation of the elect have been opened up: by protecting and freeing them from evils, and by making them partakers of good things, both spiritual and heavenly at last, which access was granted only through obedience carried to the point of death, so that in this respect too we owe very much, indeed everything, to Christ, who so readily underwent it. I think it is not out of place to recall here that, in my view, three causes concur in the reckoning of our salvation. The first and chief is the immortal mercy of God; the second is the care of Christ, taken before God as the one who cares for his own body; the third is our faith and obedience towards God, offered through the Spirit of regeneration. But just as the third is far surpassed by the second, so the second is much surpassed by the first. The chief cause of our salvation is rightly acknowledged to be the mercy and grace of God, from which the other two, arranged in their proper order and wisely directed, derive their principal force, indeed all of it. I remember that once I was asked by someone why God, who by the right of the absolute Lord can forgive sins to those who repent of them, [...] but only in those things they do, and also in those they suffer according to his will (1 Pet. 3:17).
