Hence, what has the Adversary now achieved with his own words, what singular thing has he said, in acknowledging that Christ has satisfied the will of the Father in all things? Except that he ascribes to Christ a satisfaction of such a kind as is to be given to all the pious, only that Christ performs it to a greater degree and with greater perfection than they do. Nobody is unaware of this. But the word satisfaction is here taken in a juridical and judicial sense, not an ethical one, as it is used in the law courts, not in household management or civil life, and it signifies the rendering or payment of a debt. The question is whether Christ has so satisfied, by the true and perfect payment of our debts, not by any other broad and general meaning of the word satisfaction, and whether one truly acknowledges that, not by some other sense that one invents or devises for oneself. Satisfaction is the payment of a debt or penalty. It does not signify merely a general act of obedience performed in obeying commands, for on that reasoning all our works would be satisfactory, even before God, and not Christ's alone. Rather, when someone is punished for a transgression and pays the penalty to justice, to make up for the injury done by sin and inflicted on the laws, and to restore justice and right, it is such a satisfaction that we are considering here. It is not only said that Christ was obedient, even to death; but it is further taught concerning this death of his that it was given in payment, and that it was given also for sins, and as a price, so that we were bought and redeemed with precious blood, far more precious than silver and gold, and that the Adversary has wished a ransom or sacrifice to intervene here. I remember answering this question, and it seems not out of place to repeat here why God, when he had warned Abimelech about the sin committed against Abraham, and about his wife, and when Abimelech was about to desist, was unwilling to pardon the intended fault by any other means than if Abraham offered prayers for him. Why he was unwilling to receive back into favour the friends of Job, who had done wrong to their pious friend, except that sacrifices supplied by them should be offered for them in Job's presence, and that Job himself should pray for them. Finally (I will not gather more examples), why God, not content with the repentance of offenders alone under the Old Covenant, prescribed the law of expiatory sacrifices, in which the slaughter of priests and of innocent animals had to take part! For God wished to show by this means how greatly he detested sin, whose pardon he was unwilling to grant to those polluted by it merely by their prayers and by other pious assistance; yet neither was their pardon to be despaired of, whose rite of procuring it through innocent ministers he established by a fixed law. He wished also to teach at the same time how highly he valued those whom he had designated as the go-betweens of his grace, and by this means to bind them to mutual duties with one another, and each to the care of religion.

units.la: redemti, & liberati sumus. Hæc lon-ge aliud, & supra generalem obedien-tiam quid dicunt, & ad materiam so-lutionis pertinent; quam Dominus, vel judex exigit, & quæ justitiæ præstatur: sive de tollenda obligatione quæ ex delicto nata hic agitur: tollitur autem omnis obli-gatio solutione ejus quod debetur: vel si quis, consentiente debitore, aliud pro alio solverit.
units.tr: Redeemed, and set free, we are. These words mean something quite different, and go beyond general obedience, and belong to the matter of payment, which the Lord or judge demands, and which is rendered to justice; or they concern the removal of the obligation, arising from a crime, which is what is treated here. Now every obligation is removed by payment of what is owed, or if someone, with the debtor's consent, pays one thing in place of another.

units.la: Multa in hoc genere concurrunt, ad solvendam pœnæ seu reatus obli-gationem; primo, ut quis patiatur: tum & puniatur: nam pati quis potest, uttamen non puniatur; sed si quis pa-tiatur, judice hoc quidquid est inferente, atque in vindictam noxæ, & reddendum jus ac justitiam, hæc punitio est. Jam uti qui punitur, patitur pœnam, ita si quantum satis est, punitur, satisface-re & solvere ita demum intelligitur: sic Christi satisfactio solutio fuit ejus, quod nos debebamus, & quâ præstita nos liberati sumus, nec interest, quis solvat, utrum ipse qui debet, an alius pro eo, libe-ratur enim & alio solvente.
units.tr: Many things concur in this kind of case to discharge the obligation of penalty or guilt. First, that someone suffers; then also that he is punished. For a person can suffer without being punished; but if someone suffers, whatever it is that is inflicted by a judge, and inflicted for the vengeance of the offence and for rendering right and justice, this is punishment. Now, as one who is punished suffers the penalty, so he is understood to satisfy and pay, if he is punished to a sufficient extent. Thus the satisfaction of Christ was the payment of what we owed, and by its being rendered we are set free; nor does it matter who pays, whether the debtor himself or another on his behalf, for one is freed even when another pays.

units.la: Quare non dicat Adversarius tan-tum, quod tenue nimis est, saltem non totum, Christum voluntati Patris sui in omnibus satisfecisse; sed, pro peccatis nostris vere solvendo morte sua & passionibus satisfecisse atque isto nos pretio ut redimeret: nam & hoc de morte Christi non minus testatur Scriptura, quam talem, ac dicit, Christum fuisse in morte, & in vita: sic demum propius rem tetigerit, & satisfecerit quoque quæstioni ac veritati. Dicat & sentiat, non tantum generis humani causa Christum illa egisse, atq; perpessum fuisse, sed & pro peccatis, iisque non tantum intervenientibus ut occasione, sed vera causa meritoria perpessiones istas adfe-rente & inferente, & pro quibus justitiæ divinæ satisfaciendum fuerit, ac propterea dederit Christus verum ac vere sufficiens lutrum pro peccatis nostris, æquipollens supplicio, quod nos eramus commeriti, morte æterna & gehenna cruciatibus luenais[?] par, & sic illa Christum, tamquam peccata nostra acerbissima sustinuisse, sui vere piaculari victima, & per mortem oblatione, ad expiaculum vel expiationem, eorumque remissionem procurandam, mortis suæ non tantum intuitu, sed vero pretio: hæc dico, ubi agnoverit, tum certe erit quod nobis gratulabimur de veritate aquitâ[?] ipsi & confessâ. Sin vero illa non vere intelligat, non vero illo suo sensu, fateatur ergo deprehensam à nobis vafritiem, sub verborum inani schemate latentem, & ludentem. Candide & sincere agendum est, in tanto præsertim argumento, & ubi animi sententiam & confessionem edere rogaris, & hoc te facturum recipis. Nam certe nihil dicit, quod non & aliis, præter Christum, acerba quoque, quamvis non isto gradu, ac ille, perpessis, in hominum gratiam & bonum, pro veritate & fide, vel Prophetis, vel Apostolis, & Martyribus attribui queat, & de illis quoque prædicari. Semper enim patebit evasio, suo modo, & non proprio sensu, sed metaphorico aliquo, illa dici. Atque ita non minus aliis, & nobis, quam Christo, satisfactio & salus poterit adscribi, atque agnoscendi erimus pro salvatoribus, non specie à Christo & toto ordine vel cœlo, sed gradu duntaxat, diversis.
units.tr: Therefore let the Adversary not say merely what is too slight, namely that Christ has satisfied the will of his Father in all things, but rather that by truly paying for our sins with his death and sufferings he made satisfaction, and redeemed us by that price. For Scripture bears witness to this concerning the death of Christ no less than to his being in death and in life; so the Adversary would at last touch the matter more closely, and also satisfy the question and the truth. Let him say and think not only that Christ did and endured those things for the sake of the human race, but also for sins, and not merely intervening as an occasion, but as the true meritorious cause bringing about and inflicting those sufferings, and for which satisfaction had to be made to divine justice; and that therefore Christ gave a true and truly sufficient ransom for our sins, equivalent to the punishment which we had deserved, equal to eternal death and the torments of hell to be paid, and thus that Christ, as one who had sustained our most bitter sins, was truly the sacrificial victim for sin, and was offered through death, for expiation or atonement, and to procure their remission, not merely with regard to his death, but as a true price. If he acknowledges these things, then certainly we shall have reason to rejoice in the truth agreed upon by him and confessed. But if he does not understand them truly, and not in that true sense, let him then confess that we have detected a trickery, lurking and playing under the empty show of words. One must act frankly and sincerely, especially in so great a matter, and when you are asked to set out your opinion and confession, and you undertake to do so. For surely he says nothing that cannot also be attributed, and said, of others besides Christ, who also suffered bitter things, though not to this degree, for the good and favour of men, for the truth and faith, whether of the Prophets, the Apostles, or the Martyrs. There will always be an evasion, in its own way, and these things will be said not in their proper sense but in some metaphorical one. And thus satisfaction and salvation could be ascribed no less to others and to us than to Christ, and we would have to acknowledge them as saviours, not in the same kind as Christ, and not in the whole order of heaven, but in a different degree only.

units.la: Quæ sensisse videtur, quando Christo meritum attribuens, sed in latiori quadam significatione; id ita fe facere dicit, quemadmodum Patres aliquando bonis fidelium operibus meritum adscribunt, quamvis Christi meritum illa istorum longe superet. Nempe quadam demum significatione, eâque latiori, quo pacto hominibus, sic & Christo, & Christi obedientiæ meriti aptatâ voce, conveniente. Quidquid fit de voce meriti, quam scimus à Patribus valde laxo sensu & ἀκυρολόγως sæpe usurpari, & valere idem quod quovis modo consequi, nam non de bonis tantum operibus loquentes vocem illam adhibent, sed etiam de malis, imo culpam Adami felicem appellare audent, quod tantum meruit habere redemtorem, id est, per accidens ad eam confequutus tantus redemtor fuit: quo largo sensu velle explicare rationem meriti in Christo, idem est, ac quod Christi satisfactionem, ex vocis latiori quadam significatione, conatus fuit interpretari, rem interea ipsam declinans & rejiciens. Scilicet nudam verborum sectatus umbram, enervatâ eorum proprietate & vi.
units.tr: This seems to be what he meant when he ascribes merit to Christ, but in a somewhat broader sense. He says he does so in the way the Fathers sometimes ascribe merit to the good works of the faithful, although the merit of Christ far surpasses theirs. Indeed, it is merit only in a certain sense, and a broader one, in which the word can be applied to men, and so also to Christ and to the obedience of Christ. Whatever the case with the word merit, which we know the Fathers often use in a very loose sense, and improperly [ἀκυρολόγως], meaning the same as to obtain in any way, they do not use it only of good works, but also of evil ones. They even dare to call the fall of Adam "happy," because it merited for us so great a Redeemer, that is, through that fall so great a Redeemer came to be ours by chance. To explain the reason of merit in Christ in this loose sense is the same as trying to interpret the satisfaction of Christ by a broader sense of the word, while in fact evading and rejecting the thing itself. He has, of course, pursued the bare shadow of words, having weakened their proper meaning and force.

units.la: Unde fit, ut detractâ hisce externâ verborum specie, & quæ iis ambiebatur quasi nobiscum convenientiâ, nihil rei relinqui, nihil etiam singulare abeo prolatum, nisi verba alia, fit manifestum. Christi quidem meritum non nego pacto & promissione gratiæ Dei niti, quod videlicet ad istam obedientiam & passiones visurus effet femen, & hoc salutem per ipsum, διὸ κῇ, Phil. 11.9. sed tamen vim illæ habuerunt verè meritoriam, quâ omnino destituuntur opera nostra, & quorumcumque hominum, apud Deum. Notissimum est, quomodo Euangelici omnes Pontificiis negent operum bonorum meritum, ut Christo foli vindicent & fervent. An propterea idem Christo aut negandum, aut tribuendum, pari nobiscum modo, saltem quod ad speciem, licet non quod ad gradus eosdem? Nimirum Christus, & ejus justitia, quodque egit & passus fuit, ad nostros modulos exigendum erit, & ad rerum verborumque nostrorum merita. Opera hominum bona sunt quidem necessario antecedentia ad vitam æternam, & media ad eam obtinendam requisita, non verò sunt causa meritoria: quia quamvis homo cum iis salutem consequatur, non tamen propter ea, vel ipsorum ἀξιώσεις meritum, sed gratia Dei præmiat in nobis opus suum, non meritum nostrum, & gratuita est salus, τῇ δὲ χάρισμα δὲ Θεοῦ[?] ζωή[?], vita æterna per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum. Rom. vi. 23.
units.tr: Hence it becomes plain that, once the outward appearance of the words is stripped away, together with the apparent agreement with us which it cloaked, nothing of substance remains, and nothing singular is put forward, but only other words. I do not deny that the merit of Christ rests on the pact and promise of God's grace, namely that he would see his seed through that obedience and those sufferings, and that through him salvation would come, διὸ καὶ, Phil. 11.9. Yet those things had a truly meritorious force, which our works, and those of all men, altogether lack before God. It is well known how all Evangelicals deny the merit of good works to the Papists, in order to claim and preserve it for Christ alone. Should we therefore either deny the same to Christ, or grant it to him in the same way as to us, at least as regards the outward appearance, even if not to the same degrees? Surely Christ, his righteousness, and what he did and suffered, must be measured by our standards, and by the merits of our things and words? Human good works are indeed necessarily antecedent to eternal life, and required as means of obtaining it, but they are not the meritorious cause. For although a man obtains salvation with them, it is not on account of them, nor on account of any merit of their worthiness, but God rewards his own work in us, not our merit, and salvation is a free gift: the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord, Rom. vi. 23. [τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος]

units.la: Atque in Christo solo acquirimus ad vitam istam jus, cujus possessionem adire nemo sine sanctimonia & pace potest. Hebr. xii. 14. At quæ vis merendi (de consequendi vi, ex divina gratia, & voce meriti, cum Patribus, improprie & catachreslice accepta non disputamus) operibus nostris deest, non propterea Christo, & obedientiæ ipsius: verùm propter dignitatem & personæ Christi, & obedientiæ plenæ ac perfectæ, quam, ut totâ vitâ, ita maximè in morte præstitit, vita nobis datur: quod de nostris operibus eorumque dignitate dici non potest: & propterea uti vere solvit Christus pro peccatis nostris, & sic passionibus suis mortiferis à morte nos redemit verè; ita vitam ac ac gloriam quoque meritus verè fuit, quia absolutè præstitit omnia, propter quæ ex divino fœdere debetur illa Christo, & suis. Et hac ratione nos propter Christum adipiscimur salutem, ac vitam, non propter ulla nostra opera. Nec propter Christum simpliciter uti causam quovis modo intervenientem, sed meritoriam, non significatione meriti quadam, sed certâ, non latâ, non impropriâ, sed propriâ & verâ illud consecutus nobis, perfectâ omnium præstatione atque adimpletione, quæ ad hoc requirebatur, fuit. Nostra autem opera omnia sunt imperfectâ, & nemo est qui non peccet, vel peccarit saltem, etiam juxta Adversarios: quare etiam mereri nihil potest, nisi illis suis defectibus & vitiis mortem atque damnationem. Nec tamen Deus obedientiam Christi respexit ut mercenarii, sed obedientis filii, cui pactus præmium salutis omnium suorum æternæ, conditione plenissimæ satisfactionis atque obedientiæ eorum loco præstandæ, hac perfectissimo modo ad impletâ, verè, quatenus meritum dici & dari potest, salutem nobis meruit. Non enim mereri aliquis apud Deum potest, non antecedente pacto & promissione Dei ad hoc liberali, ut mereri per obedientiam propositæ conditionis tale ac tantum bonum possit. Neque Deus obstringi antecedente ullâ alterius actione, non ad remunerationem tantum potest, non præeunte suo ipsius beneplacito, quod talem obedientiam, ad tale præmium assequendum, constituit. Quod mereri quis dicitur operibus & obedientiâ, quando eam examussim, prout lex exigit, præstat. Sic homo, qui perfectè legem servaret, mereretur vitam: si enim Abraham ex operibus justificatus, habet gloriationem. ——operanti autem merces imputatur non secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. Rom. iv. 4. homine autem per peccatum mercede illa destituto, venit Christus, & quod legi erat impos-sibile, quia infirmabatur per carnem, fecit Deus suum ipsius filium mittens, qui plenâ illâ nostri loco obedientiâ fecit, ut jus legis in nobis impleretur, Rom. viii. 3. 4.
units.tr: And in Christ alone we acquire a right to that life, the possession of which no one can attain without holiness and peace, Heb. xii. 14. But the power of meriting, which is lacking in our works (we do not dispute about the power of obtaining through divine grace, nor about the word merit, which with the Fathers is taken improperly and catachrestically), is not therefore lacking in Christ and his obedience. Rather, life is given to us on account of the dignity of the person of Christ and of his full and perfect obedience, which he rendered throughout his life and most of all in his death. This cannot be said of our works or their dignity. Therefore, just as Christ truly paid for our sins, and so truly redeemed us from death by his deadly sufferings, so he also truly merited life and glory, because he absolutely performed all the things on account of which, by the divine covenant, that reward is due to Christ and to his own. In this way we obtain salvation and life on account of Christ, and not on account of any works of ours. Nor is Christ a cause intervening in some general way, on account of which we are saved, but a meritorious cause; he obtained this not by some broad sense of merit, but by a certain, not loose, not improper, but proper and true sense, through the perfect performance and fulfilment of all those things that were required for this. Our works, however, are all imperfect, and there is no one who does not sin, or who has not sinned at least, even according to our opponents. Therefore we can merit nothing by them, except death and damnation on account of their defects and faults. Nor did God regard the obedience of Christ as that of a hired servant, but as that of an obedient son, to whom he had promised the reward of eternal salvation for all his own, on condition that the most complete satisfaction and obedience was rendered in their place. Christ, having fulfilled this most perfectly, merited salvation for us, truly, in so far as merit can be said and given. For no one can merit anything before God unless God, by a free pact and promise, has first made obedience to the stated condition a means of attaining such and so great a good. Nor is God bound by any prior action of another, not only to reward, but also without his own good pleasure preceding, which appointed such obedience as the means of obtaining such a reward. A man is said to merit by works and obedience when he performs it exactly as the law demands. So a man who kept the law perfectly would merit life: for if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of; but to him who works, the wage is reckoned not as grace but as debt, Rom. iv. 4. But since man, through sin, has been deprived of that reward, Christ came, and God, sending his own Son, did what the law could not do, since it was weakened by the flesh, Rom. viii. 3, 4. By that full obedience rendered in our place, he fulfilled the righteous requirement of the law in us.

units.la: Quare nos jam per gratiam salvamur, propter meritum Christi. Unde discrimen in ratione meriti apparet inter Christum, & nos, prorsus essentiale; & quod nitatur semper meritum Dei pacto, atque ejus mensuretur beneplacito & promissione, neque proportio hic alia sit, quam perfectæ obedientiæ & justitiæ, quam Deus constituit ad mercedem adipiscendam. Non antecedens aliqua, quæ Deum extra & ante benignum beneplacitum, possit adigere quasi & obligare, ex solâ rei aut obedientiæ dignitate & pretio, pro justitiâ ad retributionem, nisi velit injustus esse, quomodo meritum suum de condigno Pontificii doctores aliqui exponunt. Perfectio autem operibus seu obedientiae nostrae quia deest, mereri apud Deum nil possumus, neque instamus apud ejus justitiam, pro retributione, sed misericordiam, pro remissione. Et in misericordiam istam, in Christo exhibitam, credimus, hac via justi & beati, non ex operibus, eorum perfectione, justificatione, aut merito. Quae habemus omnia in Christo: nempe obedientiam perfectam, & justitiam, hinc satisfactionem & meritum, atque inde liberationem a malis omnibus, & perfectam beatitudinem in coelis. Etiam apud nos mercenarius non meretur mercedem, nisi ex praevio pacto & promissione, praemium laboris constituente, quem ubi peregit juste, mercedem postulat ex jure. Mercede Christum dignum se praebuisse, post exhaustos illos labores, credo neque Adversarius diffitebitur, neque tamen in censum referet mercenariorum, sic communiter & cum vilipendio dictorum. Mercenarius audit, qui in solam mercedem intuetur, & inhiat, se & commodum suum duntaxat quaerens, & nihil aliud; uti quoq;[?] mercedem qui reddit, solum ejus laborem metitur, non obedientiam, vel animum, quo servierit: at Christus, ut filius, ad obedientiam respexit, Pater ad mercedem obedienti filio reperdendam, animo Christus in officium intento, & placendi alteri, non sibi, Rom. xv. 3. & in commodum ac bonum aliorum versatus hic fuit, posthabito suo, Joann. x. 12. neque usquam ut mercenarium se gessit, etenim mercenarius fugit, quia mercenarius est, & non est sollicitus de ovibus, Christus autem ovium curam habuit perfectam & continuam. Patris erant, sed Pater dederat Christo, & sic ut Patri, ut illis gratificaretur, se impendit totum. Quod profectò non est mercenariorum, quamvis mercedem obedientiae & laborum justam Pater ei rependerit, semen longum, gentes in haereditatem, potestatem in coelum ac terram, nomen supra omne nomen, & gloriam aeternam in coelis.
units.tr: Wherefore we are now saved by grace, on account of the merit of Christ. Hence there appears an essential difference, in the reason of merit, between Christ and us; and merit with God always rests on a pact, and is measured by his good pleasure and promise, and the proportion here is none other than that of the perfect obedience and righteousness which God has appointed for obtaining the reward. No prior thing exists which could, outside and before God's gracious good pleasure, compel or oblige him, as if by the mere dignity and worth of the thing or of obedience, to a righteous recompense, unless he were willing to be unjust, as some of the Papist teachers explain their merit of condignity. But since perfection is lacking in our works or obedience, we can merit nothing before God, nor do we press before his justice for recompense, but for mercy and forgiveness. And in that mercy, displayed in Christ, we believe; by this way we are made righteous and blessed, not by works, their perfection, justification, or merit. All of these we have in Christ: namely, perfect obedience and righteousness, and from these satisfaction and merit, and from these deliverance from all evils and perfect blessedness in heaven. Even among us a hired worker does not merit his wage except by a prior pact and promise establishing the reward for his labour, which, once he has justly completed it, he demands as a right. I believe the Opponent will not deny that Christ, after those labours were exhausted, showed himself worthy of the wage; yet he will not count him among hired men, as those things are commonly and contemptuously said. The hireling is one who looks only to the wage and gapes after it, seeking himself and his own advantage alone, and nothing else; and he who pays the wage measures only the labour, not the obedience or the mind with which it was rendered. But Christ, as a son, regarded obedience; the Father regarded the wage to be repaid to the obedient son. Christ's mind was set on duty and on pleasing another, not himself, Rom. xv. 3, and he lived for the advantage and good of others, setting aside his own, John x. 12. Nowhere did he behave as a hireling: the hireling flees because he is a hireling, and does not care for the sheep; but Christ had a perfect and continual care for the sheep. They were the Father's, but the Father had given them to Christ, and so he devoted himself wholly, as to the Father, so to gratify them. This is surely not the act of hirelings, although the Father repaid him with a just reward for his obedience and labours: a long seed, the nations for an inheritance, power over heaven and earth, the name above every name, and eternal glory in heaven.

units.la: Atque ita ergo Christi satisfactionem & meritum, non nudâ voce, & latiori quadam significatione, sed verâ & propriâ, & ipsa re hoc praestitisse, quod verbis praefertur, agnoscimus. Et si verè in Christo agnosceret Adversarius, quod verbis jactat, haud dubitaret passionibus ejus adscribere rationem poenae, quam pro peccatis nostris sustinuerit, ac persolverit. Nam & vindictam noxae, sed non suae, at nostrae, tulit ipse insons; poenam nobis debitam, in se suscepit, ut hac ratione, imputatione vid. criminum nostrorum nocentem Deus puniret, & nos primo ac proprie nocentes illo absolveret. Nam hinc ad Christi passiones & mortem passim ratio peccatorum nostrorum conjungitur non tantum ut occasio aliqua, sed vera causa meritoria, quia ab illis, & propter ea, & pro iis dicitur passus, & factus peccatum, & hostia pro peccato, & maledictio, denique uti hoc modo nos à maledictione liberaret. Quae sane gravius quid dicunt, quam simpliciter perpessionem mali, ex delicto quavis ratione, vel nudâ occasione, ortam. Dic, perpessionem mali delicti alieni causâ meritoriâ, vel verâ, & non tantum occasione, tanquam causâ finë[?] quâ non, & quae rationem causae vix tueri queat, inflictam. Sed iterum, uti de satisfastione, & merito, sic de pœnis peccatorum nostrorum à Christo latis, latiore significatione, sed non vera, & quæ latâ significatione vim istorum propriam evacuet, loquitur. Justitia Dei, quæ illum qui non norat peccatum, peccatum potuit facere, nostro loco, etiam fecit, ut nos peccatores fiamus justitia Dei in ipso.
units.tr: Thus we acknowledge that Christ has performed the satisfaction and the merit, not in a bare word or in some looser sense, but truly and properly, and in fact, and that he has accomplished what the Adversary merely announces in words. If the Adversary truly recognised in Christ what he boasts of with his lips, he would not hesitate to ascribe to his sufferings the character of punishment, which he bore and paid for our sins. For the innocent one himself bore the penalty of an offence, though not his own but ours, and he took upon himself the punishment owed by us, so that by this reckoning God, imputing our crimes, might punish the guilty and absolve us, who were guilty in the first and proper sense. For from this point on the reckoning of our sins is joined throughout to Christ's sufferings and death, not merely as some occasion but as the true meritorious cause. He is said to have suffered from them, because of them, and for them; he was made sin, a sacrifice for sin, and a curse, in order, in this way, to free us from the curse. Surely these words say something more weighty than merely that the suffering of evil arose from a fault, by whatever reckoning, or by bare occasion. Tell me: is the suffering of evil inflicted by a meritorious or true cause of another's fault, and not merely by occasion, as a cause without which not, a cause that can hardly hold its ground as a cause? But again, as with satisfaction and merit, so with the punishments of our sins borne by Christ, he speaks in a looser sense, not a true one, and in a loose sense that empties their proper force. The justice of God, which made him who knew no sin to be sin, did indeed make him sin in our place, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.

units.la: Quod vero ad sententiam Autoris nostri, de fructibus mortis Christi, pro triplici ejus officio, ad doctrinæ confirmationem, ad ejus in cruce victimam quasi piacularem, & parandum sibi ad regiam in cœlis dignitatem aditum; non negamus quidem Christum etiam morte suâ veritatem doctrinæ obsignasse, sed adeo non inter primos & præcipuos mortis ejus fructus collocari hoc debet, ut Scriptura nusquam fere nos jubeat hoc in morte Christi spectare, sed semper redemtionem nostri à peccatis, ut fructum ejus primum & necessarium, & propter quem mori debuerit, non ob consignandam suam doctrinam, & Salvatorem Christum, non simpliciter martyrem. Altiora in Christo considerare & credere oportet, ad justificationem nostri & salutem, quam id quod cum aliis, qui pro doctrinâ sacrâ mortem obuerunt, habuit commune. Quamvis negemus, hoc eum cum Mose commune habere, quod aliam, non minus quam Mosis, novam populo Dei legem promulgarit. Joann. 1. 17. quia lex per Mosem data: gratia autem & veritas per Jesum Christum facta. Euangelii fuit autor & confirmator, quo homines salvarentur, non per novam legem.
units.tr: As for our author's view of the fruits of Christ's death, under its threefold office: for the confirmation of doctrine, for his cross as a kind of atoning victim, and for preparing for himself an approach to the royal dignity in heaven, we do not deny that Christ also sealed the truth of his doctrine by his death. But this should not be placed among the first and chief fruits of his death, since Scripture almost nowhere bids us look at Christ's death in this light, but always at our redemption from sins as its first and necessary fruit, the reason why he had to die, and not to seal his doctrine or to save Christ as a mere martyr. We ought to consider and believe loftier things in Christ, for our justification and salvation, than what he had in common with others who died for sacred doctrine. Although we deny that he has this in common with Moses, that he promulgated a new law for the people of God, no less than Moses did. John 1:17: For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ. He was the author and confirmer of the gospel, by which men are saved, not of a new law.

units.la: Deinde Christum in morte seipsum non tamquam piacularem victimam præbuisse, sed veram fuisse, agnoscimus. Et hoc si vero sensu, non metaphorico, à Christo præstitum intelligat nobiscum Ruarus, & non iterum latiori aliqua significatione, nempe ut pro sacerdotalis officii partibus vere oravit & adhuc intercedit pro suis, ita quoque vere seipsum in cruce tamquam piacularem victimam præbuerit, non ut martyr, sed salvator, in veram pro peccatis nostris apud Deum expiationem, & remissionem peccatorum, ejus vi[?] & vero lutro ac satisfactione procurandam, bene se habet: etenim in victimâ corporis sui in morte, ejusque oblatione, non præparatâ tum tantum, sed & ibi factâ, pro sacerdotali & sacrificandi munere, non confirmatio doctrinæ potest spectari, quæ ad Propheticum munus pertinuerit, sed expiatio peccatorum vera, uti & vera inde remissio. Atque ita ergo etiam in morte sacerdos Christus, prout obtulit tum victimam, & vere uti victima pro peccatis fuit, ita & expiavit peccata, & reconciliavit peccatores Deo. Hæc si vere teneat Ruarus, en dextram porrigimus; sin minus, agnoscant omnes fucum verbis factum, & negatam callide rem, nempe ipsum Jesu Christi in morte sacrificium expiatorium, seu oblationem, & expiationem. Quæ verba tamen hic adhibuit, ut imponeret scilicet nobis, non vero exponeret sese.
units.tr: Next, we acknowledge that Christ offered himself on the cross not as it were as a propitiatory victim, but truly as one. If Ruarus understands this with us in the true sense, not metaphorically, and not again in some looser meaning, namely that just as he truly prayed in the part of his priestly office and still intercedes for his own, so he truly offered himself on the cross as an atoning victim, not as a martyr but as a Saviour, for a true expiation of our sins before God, and a true remission of sins, to be procured by its power and by a true ransom and satisfaction, then all is well. For in the victim of his body in death, and in its offering, not merely prepared at that time but actually made there, one may consider the sacrificial and priestly office, not the confirmation of doctrine, which belongs to the prophetic office, but a true expiation of sins, and a true remission following from it. Thus also in death Christ was priest, in that he offered the victim, and truly was a victim for sins, and so he expiated sins and reconciled sinners to God. If Ruarus truly holds this, we extend our hand to him; if not, let all acknowledge that a deception has been made with words, and that the thing itself, namely Christ's expiatory sacrifice or offering and expiation in his death, has been craftily denied. Yet he used these words here in order to impose upon us, not to set forth his own mind.

units.la: Denique per mortem quidem aditum sibi fecit Christus in cœlum, & ad cœlestem gloriam, sed non propterea mori debuit, non ista morte maledictâ. Per peccatum mors, & nisi peccata nostra fuissent, Christus non fuisset mortuus, quamvis nunc morte interveniente resurgere, adscendere, ad Dei dexteram sedere, debuit. Eoque respectu, quod pro nobis necesse habuit mori, non pro se, non parum, imo omnia Christo, quod eam tam promte adiit, debere nos, eo evidentius consequitur.
units.tr: Finally, Christ did indeed make for himself an approach into heaven, and to heavenly glory, through his death; but he ought not to have died for this reason, not by that accursed death. Death came through sin, and had not our sins existed, Christ would not have died; yet he had to rise again, ascend, and sit at the right hand of God, with death intervening. From the perspective that he had to die for us, not for himself, it follows all the more clearly that we owe him not a little, indeed everything, because he so readily underwent it.

units.la: Porro nemo dubitat, ad salutem nostram concurrere primo quidem Dei mi-sericordiam, ut causam ejus praecipuam; tum Christi pro nobis curam; denique fidem & obedientiam nostram, duntaxat hanc non ut causam, uti priores illae sunt, sed conditionem, qua Christum accipimus Salvatorem, & ei obedimus, non quod fides sit obedientia, nedum ut ea justificemur, sed quod per istam efficax est & probatur.
units.tr: Moreover, no one doubts that for our salvation there concur, first, the mercy of God as its chief cause; then Christ's care for us; and finally our faith and obedience. The latter alone is not a cause as the former are, but the condition by which we receive Christ as Saviour and obey him; not because faith is obedience, much less that we are justified by it, but because through it obedience is effective and shown to be genuine.

units.la: Ad quaestionem autem, quam facit sibi Autor, vel factam memorat, cur, si Deus pro jure dominii absoluti posset peccata poenitentibus remittere, voluerit Christi tamen lutrum, seu sacrificium hic intervenire? quae respondet, non satisfaciunt. Nisi quod iterum significet, qua mente & quo sensu Christi lutrum dicat & sacrificium; nempe intervenisse quidem ut ritum procurandae saluti destinatum, non vero proprie expiasse peccata, & sacrificium fuisse vere λυτρικόν[?]. Abrahamus intercessit pro Abimelecho, neque antea condonavit ipsi Deus: sic, & non aliter intervenit, ad peccatorum remissionem, Christus? vel, addidit etiam sacrificia pro amicis suis Jobus; neque alio modo se habet sacrificium Christi? aut non aliud fuit, quam V. Test. sacrificia expiatoria? Ubi nunc est Christi satisfactio, & meritum? Simpliciter intervenire satis non est: neque intervenire tantummodo, ut gratum Deo: nam multa alia intervenient ad salutem nostram, vel ab aliis, vel etiam a nobis quae fiunt, ob quae tamen, vel eorum pretium aut meritum non datur salus, uti propter Christum, ejus satisfactionem & obedientiam. Non tantum ergo Christum hic intervenire, dicendum, aut tali modo, quo Abrahami, aut Jobi intercessio in exemplis commemoratis; sed insuper ut verum lutrum, peccata, quomodo dictum, expians & remittens.
units.tr: As for the question which the author poses to himself, or recalls having been asked: why, if God by his right of absolute dominion could forgive sins to the penitent, he nevertheless willed that Christ's ransom, or sacrifice, should intervene here; his answer does not satisfy. Unless he means again in what mind and in what sense he calls Christ's ransom and sacrifice; namely that it intervened indeed as a rite destined for procuring salvation, but did not truly expiate sins, and that the sacrifice was truly a ransom-giving one [λυτρικόν]. Abraham interceded for Abimelech, and God had not forgiven him beforehand; so did Christ intervene for the remission of sins, and in no other way? Or Job also offered sacrifices for his friends; and is Christ's sacrifice in no other position? Or was it nothing more than the sacrifices of expiation of the Old Testament? Where now is Christ's satisfaction and merit? Simply to intervene is not enough, nor merely to intervene as pleasing to God; for many other things intervene for our salvation, whether by others or even by us, and yet salvation is not given in return for their price or merit, as it is on account of Christ, his satisfaction and obedience. Therefore we must say not merely that Christ intervenes in this way, or in the manner of the intercession of Abraham or Job in the examples mentioned, but that he intervenes as a true ransom, expiating and remitting sins, in the sense already stated.

units.la: Caeterum non ingratum nobis erit, si Adversariis placeat porro non inficiari Christi satisfactionem, & meritum; verum docere illa actueri: Christi oblatio-nem, victimam, sacrificium in morte expiatorium, sacerdotem se hic gessisse, & dedisse lutrum non tantum, sed sufficiens pro peccatis, & aequipollens supplicio, quod nos eramus meriti; meritos nos mortem aeternam esse & gehennae cruciatus: cur non, aeternos gehennae cruciatus? generis humani causa non tantum Christum passum, sed & ob peccata generis humani: earumq; passionum intuitu nos justificari & salvari: haec inquam, quae fere sua epistola dicit Ruarus, si docere ament, πάντῃ τρόπῳ, ἐπὶ σωφρόσει[?], ἐπὶ ἀληθείᾳ, hactenus non displicent, non forte fructu suo sunt caritura, quum eventurum nonnunquam sperari possit, quocumque illa sensu dicantur, ut meliori & sinceriori audiantur: quum saepenumero, secundum illud Hilarii, castiores sunt aures auditorum, quam labia sacerdotum. Deinde id boni ex illis dictis confici potest, quod ubi forte tolerari illorum hominum coetus debent, injungatur ipsis secundum illa docere, eaque nullo modo impugnare.
units.tr: Moreover, it will not be unwelcome to us if the Adversaries are willing from now on not to deny Christ's satisfaction and merit, but to teach those things: that Christ's offering, victim and sacrifice in death was expiatory, that he acted here as priest, and gave a ransom not only but one sufficient for sins and equivalent to the punishment which we had deserved: that we deserved eternal death and the torments of hell. Why not eternal torments of hell? That Christ suffered not only for the human race but also on account of the sins of the human race, and that we are justified and saved in view of those sufferings. These things, I say, which Ruarus very nearly states in his letter, if they are willing to teach them, in every way, in soundness, in truth [πάντῃ τρόπῳ, ἐπὶ σωφρόσει, ἐπὶ ἀληθείᾳ], do not displease us so far, and they will not perhaps be without their fruit, since it may sometimes be hoped that, in whatever sense they are said, they will be heard the better and more sincerely; since, according to the saying of Hilary, the ears of hearers are often more chaste than the lips of priests. Further, some good can be drawn from those words: where such assemblies of those men must be tolerated, they should be enjoined to teach these things accordingly, and never to attack them in any way.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM, DE JUSTIFICATIONE.
units.tr: CHAPTER II, ON JUSTIFICATION.

units.la: CONTROVERSIA: Num Deus, propter obedientiam praeceptorum Christi, hominem justificet? An vero propter imputatam ipsi Christi justitiam?
units.tr: DISPUTED QUESTION: Does God justify a man on account of obedience to the precepts of Christ? Or rather on account of the righteousness of Christ imputed to him?

units.la: MOmentum articuli, de justificatione hominis peccatoris, coram Deo. Hujus loci controversiae, de justitia, qua coram Deo justificamur; de ejus imputatione; denique de fide Christum, ejusque justitiam, ad justificationem, apprehendente. Sententia Adversariorum, nos justificari apud Deum, per obedientiam praeceptorum Christi, tamquam justificationis nostrae causam. Doctrina Remonstrantium, & ostenditur, Socinianos in summa rei non convenire cum Orthodoxis. Sententia Arminii. Sociniani justificationem habent pro actione forensi; sed male ejus causam faciunt nostra opera. Conjuncta ea quidem sunt & necessaria justificatis, non autem antecedunt justificationem, ut causa. Justificatio legalis, & Euangelica. Vocis imputandi explicatio. Justitia Christi activa, & passiva. Argumenta nostra. Nullo modo justificari nos per, aut propter opera, Scriptura docet. Sunt illa imperfecta. Et justificatio est gratuita. Fit per remissionem peccatorum. Et justificat Deus impium. Quae opera Apostolus intelligat, quando ea secludit a justificatione. Justificamur per solum Christum: qui nostra, & hoc a Deo factus est, justitia. 1 Cor. 1. 30. Cujus imputatione justificamur, non propria. Vindicantur loca Rom. III. 24. 25. & IV. 24. 25. & V. 1. 2. 9. 19. 21. II Cor. V. 15. Natura fidei justificantis est, credere in Christum, & ejus justitiam, ad justificationem, apprehendere. De loco Joan. 1.12. Gal. II. 20. & III. 26.27. De fide sententia, & concessiones Adversariorum, in specie. Distinguitur, inter credere Christo, confidere, & obtemperare. Atque ostenditur, fidei formam non esse obedientiam: sed fidem hic consideran prout accipit Christum, ejusque obedientiam, seu justitiam. Objectiones Adversariorum diluuntur. Ex exemplo Abrahami, & ejus justificatione. Tum ex Jac. II. 23. Denique quod nostra de justificatione doctrina non tollat bonorum operum studium, ostenditur. Operis conclusio.
units.tr: The weight of the article on the justification of a sinful man before God. The controversy here concerns the righteousness by which we are justified before God, its imputation, and finally faith, which apprehends Christ and his righteousness for justification. The opinion of our opponents: that we are justified before God through obedience to the precepts of Christ, as the cause of our justification. The doctrine of the Remonstrants, and it is shown that the Socinians do not agree with the Orthodox in the main point. The opinion of Arminius. The Socinians regard justification as a forensic act, but wrongly make our works its cause. Works indeed accompany justified persons and are necessary to them, but they do not precede justification as its cause. Legal and evangelical justification. Explanation of the word "to impute." The active and passive righteousness of Christ. Our arguments. Scripture teaches that we are in no way justified by or on account of works. Those works are imperfect. Justification is gratuitous. It takes place through the remission of sins. And God justifies the ungodly. What works the Apostle means when he excludes them from justification. We are justified through Christ alone, who has been made our righteousness by God: 1 Cor. 1:30. We are justified by his imputed, not our own, righteousness. The passages Rom. 3:24, 25; 4:24, 25; 5:1, 2, 9, 19, 21 and 2 Cor. 5:15 are vindicated. The nature of justifying faith is to believe in Christ and to apprehend his righteousness for justification. On the passage John 1:12, Gal. 2:20 and 3:26, 27. The opinion and concessions of our opponents concerning faith, in particular. A distinction is drawn between believing Christ, trusting, and obeying. And it is shown that obedience is not the form of faith; rather, faith is considered here as it receives Christ and his obedience, or righteousness. The objections of our opponents are refuted. From the example of Abraham and his justification. Then from James 2:23. Finally, it is shown that our doctrine of justification does not take away zeal for good works. Conclusion of the work.

units.la: SECTIO PRIMA.
units.tr: SECTION I.

units.la: M[?]Aximi semper suo merito æstimavit Catholica Christi Ec-clesia articulum religionis istum, qui de hominis peccatoris agit coram Deo justificatione: ut à quo reliqua fidei pendent dogmata, & salus ipsa bene percipi non potest, nisi illo fideliter asserto. Hinc adeo solliciti semper extiterunt Theologi Reformati, in conservandâ illius veritate integra, & Lutheri dictum, omnibus facile approbatum fuit, quod in aureo suo in epist. ad Galatas Commentario habet: jacente articulo justifica-tionis, jacent omnia. Unde & Bohaemica Confessio, cap. VI. Hoc caput doctrinae ex omnibus apud nos pro maximo & gravissimo capite habetur, ut in quo summa Euangelii posita est, & quo Christianismus fundatur, & in qua pretiosus, nobilissimusque thesaurus salutis aeternae, unicaque & viva consolatio divina comprehenditur. Itaque in hoc praecipuam operam ponunt Pastores nostri, ut hujus capitis doctrinam in cordibus hominum intimis bene informent, & hiis profunde inferant.
units.tr: The Catholic Church of Christ has always rightly esteemed this article of religion, which treats of the justification of sinful man before God, as of the highest importance: since the other doctrines of the faith depend upon it, and salvation itself cannot be rightly understood unless this is faithfully maintained. Hence the Reformed theologians have always been anxious to preserve its truth entire, and the saying of Luther, which he gives in his golden commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, has been readily approved by all: when the article of justification falls, everything falls. Whence also the Bohemian Confession, ch. VI: Among us this chapter of doctrine is held to be the greatest and most weighty of all, as the sum of the Gospel is set forth in it, Christianity is founded upon it, and in it is contained the precious and most noble treasure of eternal salvation and the only and living divine consolation. Therefore our ministers take especial pains to instruct well the doctrine of this chapter in the inmost hearts of men, and to impress it deeply upon them.

units.la: Quod nec Diabolum latuit, & singulos fere Ecclesiae hostes, qui proinde junctis operis, ab omni tempore, in hoc incubuerunt, ut naturam & vim illius articuli, quantum in se, convellerent, & quidquid alienorum dogmatum est, in hoc tandem exit, ut vel palam, vel per cuniculos, gratuitam nostrum, per Christum, justificationem obruat. Unde, quod mirabile secus videri posset, causa non admodum obscura est, cur omnes extra Ecclesiam & ejus hostes conveniant, ut homini, & suis operibus, quocunque modo appellatis, hac in re, attribuant, quod soli debetur Christo. Plus vel minus omnes, in se suisque, semper plus aequo confidunt, quum e nobis exeundum prorsus fit, ut in solo Christo, ad justificationem deprehendamur. Phil. iii, 9.
units.tr: This did not escape the Devil, nor nearly all the enemies of the Church, who accordingly from every age have joined forces and laboured to overthrow, as far as in them lay, the nature and power of that article; and whatever foreign doctrine there is comes finally to this, that it overwhelms our free justification through Christ, either openly or by secret tunnels. Whence, what might otherwise seem strange, the cause is not very obscure why all those outside the Church and its enemies agree in attributing to man and his works, however they are described, in this matter, what is due to Christ alone. More or less, all trust in themselves and their own, always more than is right, whereas we must altogether go out of ourselves, so as to be found in Christ alone for justification. Phil. iii, 9.

units.la: Socinus, ne & hunc articulum non destrueret, post Christi negatam satisfactionem & meritum, doctrinam gratuitae justificationis necessario quoque impugnandam sibi duxit, ut quae pro illorum ratione se cogitur habere, sic vel aliter. Contraria tamen hic usus, quam ibi, ratione[?]. Etenim veritatem illius negavit, argumento a Dei gratia sumto, quasi in remissione peccatorum nostrorum sic versetur, ut omnem respuat pro peccatis satisfactionem, etiam a Christo praestitam: in justificatione vero, ubi gratiam omnino respicere & praedicare oportebat, ad opera nostra delabitur, eaque, quae hic certe, ubi nostra causa agitur, & a justificatione nostri exulare debebant, gratiae opponit, per nostra nos justificari contendens opera, Euangelica vid. sive per obedientiam praeceptorum Christi.
units.tr: Socinus, so that he might not destroy this article too, after denying Christ's satisfaction and merit, thought he must also attack the doctrine of gratuitous justification, as his system seemed to require him to hold this or that. Yet his method here is the opposite of what it was there. For he denied its truth by an argument drawn from the grace of God, as if the remission of our sins were so arranged that it rejects every satisfaction for sins, even one rendered by Christ. But in justification, where grace ought wholly to be regarded and proclaimed, he slips back to our works, and sets against grace those things which here, where our cause is being argued, ought certainly to have been excluded from justification, contending that we are justified through our works, namely the evangelical ones, that is, through obedience to the precepts of Christ.

units.la: Negat Adversarius, tum materiam justificationis, propter quam justificamur, id est, justitiam, sive satisfactionem, & meritum Christi; tum formam, sive imputationem illius Christi justitiae, quae nobis fiat, quaque absolvamur & justificemur. Utrumque autem, consueto sibi loquendi more, pro commento habet. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. iv. Hinc & fidei justificantis vim plane tollit, sitam in apprehensione justitiae Christi. Smalcius, contra Frantz. Disp. ii. de Peccato orig pag. 55. Apage istud somnium acceptionis meriti Christi per fidem. Quae tria hoc loco praecipue in controversiam veniunt, vid. Christi loco nostro praestita justitia; tum, ejus imputatio, ut nobis fiat; nempe credentibus in Christum, sive istam ejus fide apprehendentibus justitiam. Quamvis de primo, ejusque veritate, in praecedentibus modo disputatum fit, hic tamen idem consideratur, prout justificationem nostram ingreditur, & pro materia venit, vel justitia nobis imputanda.
units.tr: Our opponent denies both the matter of justification, on account of which we are justified, that is, the righteousness, or satisfaction and merit, of Christ, and the form, that is, the imputation of that righteousness of Christ made to us, by which we are absolved and justified. He regards both, in his customary manner of speaking, as an invention. Socinus, de Servat. part iv, ch. iv. Hence he also altogether removes the power of justifying faith, which lies in the apprehension of the righteousness of Christ. Smalcius, against Frantz, Disp. ii, on original sin, p. 55: Away with that dream of the acceptance of Christ's merit through faith. Three things come chiefly into controversy here: namely, the righteousness of Christ rendered in our place; then its imputation to us, that is, to those believing in Christ, or those apprehending that righteousness by faith. Although the first, and its truth, has been discussed in what precedes, it is considered here again insofar as it enters into our justification and comes forward as the matter, that is, the righteousness to be imputed to us.

units.la: Quaeritur ergo, quae sit ea justitia, quae nobis valeat ad justificationem? sive, quid istud, propter quod justificamur? Nos justitiam Christi dicimus, solam: Adversarii, nostram, nempe obedientiam praeceptorum Christi. ii. quaeritur, de justitiae Christi imputatione, quae a Deo nobis contingat, ad nostri justificationem. Adversarii hoc totum negant, nullamque aliam imputationem agnoscunt, quam obedientiae nostrae, quamvis non perfectæ, acceptionem pro justitiâ integrâ. iii. quaestio est, de fide, prout in negotio justificationis in-tervenit, & nos per eam justificari dicimur, an sit nuda Christi, pro justitiâ vel in justitiam, à nobis facta apprehensio; quod Nos tenemus: an vero, quod statuunt Adversarii, obedientia mandatorum Christi? Super illis tota, quae hujus loci est, vertitur controversia.
units.tr: The question, then, is what that righteousness is which avails us for justification, or what that is on account of which we are justified? We say that it is the righteousness of Christ alone; our opponents say it is ours, namely obedience to the precepts of Christ. The second question concerns the imputation of Christ's righteousness, which comes to us from God for our justification. Our opponents deny all of this, and acknowledge no imputation other than the acceptance of our obedience, though it is not perfect, as complete righteousness. The third question concerns faith, insofar as it takes part in the business of justification, and whether we are said to be justified through it, whether it is the mere apprehension of Christ's righteousness as our righteousness, or made by us into righteousness, which we hold; or whether, as our opponents maintain, it is obedience to the commandments of Christ. The whole of the controversy in this place turns upon these matters.

units.la: Quod autem illa Adversariorum sit sententia, hominem coram Deo justifica-ri per obedientiam praeceptorum Christi, luce clarius est. Socinus, de Servat. part. iii. cap. ii. pag. 219. Hi vero non imputat delicta, quibus sunt obnoxii, si respiscant; quia deinceps pure & innocenter vivunt. si in utrisque vitae puritas & innocentia quaedam causa est, ut Deus illis clementer ac benigne peccata condonet. Verum causam exponit alibi non vere efficientem vel impulsivam, sed tantum sine qua non. In Synopsi, de Justificatione, pag. Ut autem cavendum est, ne, ut hodie plerique faciunt, vitae sanctitatem atque innocentiam effectum justificationis nostrae coram Deo esse dicamus, sic diligenter cavere debemus, ne ipsam vitae sanctitatem atque innocentiam, justificationem nostram coram Deo esse credamus, neve illam, nostrae coram Deo justifi-cationis, causam efficientem aut impulsivam esse affirmemus: sed tantummodo causam, sine qua eam justificationem nobis non contingere, decrevit Deus. Nullo autem modo vult causam justificationis esse meritoriam, utcunque aliquo modo causa appellentur. In fragmento, de justific. pag. 48. Quod tamen non eam vim habet, ut à causa justificationis nostrae, omnia quaecunque opera, & quocunque modo considerata, excludere velit Apostolus: sed sensus ipsius est, ut indicavimus, Nulla esse opera, quae tanti sunt, ut propter ipsorum meritum justificari possimus. Quando scilicet nemo est, qui perfectissime atque integerrime per totam vitam ea opera faciat, quae sive sub Vetere sive sub Novo Testamento praescripta sunt, id quod tamen omnino requiritur, sive requireretur ad hoc, ut per ipsa opera, tamquam ejus rei aliquo modo meritoria, justificatio contingeret. Et pag. 49. Ubi considerandum interea est, quod nihilominus merito dici potest, & verissimum est, dari obedientiam, quae possit dici causa justificationis nostrae propter Dei promissum, nec tamen dicendum sit, operum merito tunc justificationem nobis concedi, quippe quod obedientia ista sub ipso novo Testamento, si omnia praecepta in eo nobis data consideren-tur, non posset dici perfecta, quamvis Deus pro sua bonitate velit, si ea praditi fuerimus, nos justificatos pronuntiare. Et pag. 60. Jam igitur ex iis, quae dixi, satis intelligere potes, quid ego bonis operibus tribuam, ejusmodi videlicet operibus, qualia fieri praecepit Jesus Christus, quaeque sub ipsa aeterna vita, ut illi obediatur, fiunt, cum affirmaverim Deum per ipsa nos justificare, id est ea, propter Dei bonitatem ac misericordiam, causam esse, ut ipse Deus nobis peccata nostra ita condonet, ut vitam aeternam largiatur. Quod si causa sint bona opera, quare Deus peccata nobis condonat, quodque per ipsa nos justificat[?], viderit, annon hoc plus dicat, quam causam sine qua non. Alibi iis justificandi vim & efficaciam omnino attribuit. Pag. 55. Haec opera efficaciam habebunt justificandi coram Deo ad vitam aeternam, non quidem ut opera, sed ut fiducia, quae per Christum in Deo colligetur, & quia Deus pro bonitate sua ita vult. Causam, non causam dicit; opera, non opera, pari fide & ingenui-tate,
units.tr: That this is the opinion of our opponents, that a man is justified before God through obedience to the precepts of Christ, is clearer than light. Socinus, de Servat. part iii, ch. ii, p. 219: Those who repent do not have their guilt imputed to them, to which they were liable, since thereafter they live purely and innocently. If in both cases purity and innocence of life is a certain cause, that God graciously and kindly forgives them their sins. But elsewhere he sets out a cause that is not truly efficient or impulsive, but only a cause without which the thing does not happen. In the Synopsis, on Justification, p. But just as we must take care not to say, as most people do today, that the holiness and innocence of life is the effect of our justification before God, so we must carefully take care not to believe that holiness and innocence of life itself is our justification before God, nor affirm that it is the efficient or impulsive cause of our justification before God, but only the cause without which God has decreed that this justification does not come to us. In no way, however, does he wish the cause of justification to be meritorious, however it may be called a cause in some sense. In the fragment on justification, p. 48: Yet this does not have the force that the Apostle wishes to exclude from the cause of our justification all works whatsoever, and considered in whatever way: but his meaning, as we have indicated, is that there are no works so great that we can be justified on account of their merit. Since, namely, there is no one who performs perfectly and most entirely throughout his whole life those works which are prescribed either under the Old or under the New Testament, which nonetheless is wholly required, or would be required, for justification to come through those works as in some way meritorious of it. And p. 49: Here it must meanwhile be considered that it may nonetheless rightly be said, and is most true, that there is an obedience which can be called the cause of our justification on account of God's promise; yet it must not be said that justification is then granted to us on account of the merit of works, since that obedience, under the New Testament itself, if all the precepts given to us in it are considered, could not be called perfect, although God, in his goodness, is willing, if we are endowed with it, to pronounce us justified. And p. 60: From what I have said, therefore, you can already understand well enough what I attribute to good works, namely such works as Jesus Christ commanded to be done, and which are done under eternal life itself in order to obey him; since I have affirmed that God justifies us through them, that is, that they are the cause, on account of God's goodness and mercy, why God himself forgives us our sins in such a way that he bestows eternal life. But if good works are the cause why God forgives us our sins, and why he justifies us through them, let him see whether this says more than a cause without which not. Elsewhere he attributes to them altogether the power and efficacy of justifying. p. 55: These works will have the efficacy of justifying before God unto eternal life, not indeed as works, but as the trust which is gathered in God through Christ, and because God in his goodness so wills. He says "cause," not "cause"; "works," not "works," with equal honesty and candour,

units.la: [The text of the foot line "Tom. 2." is a volume reference and is not part of the main text.] fluctuans ipse, incertos ut per omnia reddat lectores suos. Ibidem, Ita ut opera à fide, reipsa non distinguantur, tunc Christi fides, quam opera subsequentur, aliud nihil erit, quam ipsi Christo confidere, quod sine debito coram Deo justificandi vim habet, & consequenter opera ipsa justificant, quatenus executio sunt ac perfectio, & tamquam forma ipsius fidei. Aperte, pag. seq. fidem & opera ponit, atque hoc pacto fides, id est, Christo confidere, (qui enim in Christum credit, in ipsum Deum credit) & opera, id est, obedientia præceptorum Christi, qua, ut dictum est, executio ac perfectio, & tamquam forma est ipsius fidei, coram Deo nos justificat, seu potius, ut magis proprie, atque ut Scriptura solet, loquamur, Deus per illa, ex illisve nos justificat, sive per illa ex illisve justificamur, & consequenter ex Dei gratia ac bonitate, plurimum valent ad vitam æternam consequendam. Videmus ergo, Socinum justificationem operibus, fidei, obe-dientiæ præceptorum Christi attribuere; quæ omnia ipsi revera sunt idem. In hoc à Pontificiis distans, quod operum meritum negat: cum illis vero consentiens, quod non modo à justificatione, & ejus causa illa non segreget, sed vim, & efficaciam ad justificandum in illis ponat, semota, cui nos solùm & & in solidum justificandi omnem causam, propter quam, assignamus, justitiâ Christi. Nam de causâ efficiente principali, Deo; & proægumena, sive bonitate Dei & gratiâ, non quæritur.
units.tr: [The text of the foot line "Tom. 2." is a volume reference and is not part of the main text.] He himself wavers, so that he makes his readers uncertain in every respect. In the same place: So that works are not really distinguished from faith, then the faith of Christ, which works follow, will be nothing other than trusting in Christ himself, which has the power of justifying before God without any debt, and consequently works themselves justify, insofar as they are the execution and perfection of faith, and as its form. Clearly, on the next page he sets down faith and works, and in this way faith, that is, trusting in Christ (for whoever believes in Christ believes in God himself), and works, that is, obedience to the precepts of Christ, which, as has been said, are the execution and perfection of faith and, as it were, its form, justify us before God. Or rather, to speak more properly and as Scripture usually does, God justifies us through them and from them, or we are justified through them and from them, and consequently, from the grace and goodness of God, they are of great value for attaining eternal life. We see, then, that Socinus attributes justification to works, to faith, to obedience to the precepts of Christ, all of which are in fact the same thing. In this he differs from the Papists in that he denies the merit of works; but he agrees with them in that he does not separate that justification from its cause, and in that he places in works the power and efficacy for justifying, setting aside the justice of Christ, to which alone we assign the whole cause of justification, wholly and entirely. For the principal efficient cause, God, and the antecedent cause, the goodness and grace of God, are not the question here.

units.la: Quæstio autem est, Num Deus propter opera, vel obedientiam præceptorum Christi, vel ex illis, hominem justificet? Quod simpliciter negamus, Adversarii autem affirmant.
units.tr: The question, however, is whether God justifies man on account of works, or the obedience to the precepts of Christ, or from them. We simply deny this; our opponents affirm it.

units.la: Nos, propter Christum, ejus justitiam, sive satisfactionem & meritum, justificari hominem, docemus. Socinus, Præle�why. scriptum obedientem se prabere, idque faciendo ab ipso Christo vita sempiterna coro- nam expectare. Part. iv. cap. ix. ex quibus verissimum id esse liquet, quod jam dudum contendimus, Christi fidem, qua per se, quod ad ea attinet, qua in nobis sunt, nos justi- ficat, seu, ut rectius loquar, qua ipsa per se Deus nos justificat, confidentiam in ipso Christo esse, id est, cum firma spe ea consequendi, qua ipse sibi obedientibus promisit, Christi praeceptorum obedientia. In Synopsi, de Justificat. pag. 8. Ex hominum vero parte requiritur respiscentia, & Dei praeceptorum in posterum obedientia, qua illa fides est vera, qua semper hominem Deo acceptum reddit, & redditura est. Notis, in Dialogum, de Justific. pag. 25. Fides, qua justificamur, non est credere promissionibus divinis; sed est, ipsi Deo confidere: quod ut fiat, propterea sunt a Deo proposita promissa, quibus creditis necessario ipsi Deo considitur. Et idcirco alicubi videtur, fidei isti, quod Dei promissa sunt vera, tribui, quod per eam justificemur; qua fides, obedientiam praeceptorum Dei, non quidem ut effectum suum, sed ut suam substantiam & formam continet atque complectitur. Meminisse enim debemus ejus, quod supra recte conclusum est: fidem, hanc scilicet, qua justificamur, Dei obedientiam esse. Ibidem, omnino fiduciam in ipsum Deum, illamque obedientiam gignant, qua justificamur. Pag. 15. docet, nullo modo fieri posse, ut fides in Christum, qua justificamur, sit credere, quod per ipsius sanguinis fusionem deleta fuerint peccata nostra, sed formam atque essentiam fidei in Christum esse, ejus praeceptis obedire. Adde & pag. 54. 55. 58.
units.tr: We teach that man is justified on account of Christ, on account of his righteousness, that is, his satisfaction and merit. Socinus, in his Praelectiones, says that he shows himself obedient, and that by doing so he expects from Christ himself the crown of eternal life. Part 4, chapter 9. From these passages it is plain that what we have long contended is most true: that the faith of Christ, which, as far as those things go that are in us, justifies us by itself, or, to speak more correctly, by which God himself justifies us, is confidence in Christ himself, that is, with a firm hope of obtaining those things which he himself promised to those who obey him, the obedience of Christ's precepts. In the Synopsis, on Justification, p. 8: On the part of men, however, repentance is required, and obedience to God's precepts in future, which is true faith, which always makes man acceptable to God, and will make him so. In the notes on the Dialogue on Justification, p. 25: The faith by which we are justified is not to believe the divine promises, but is to trust in God himself; and in order that this may happen, the promises have been set forth by God, so that by believing them we necessarily trust in God himself. And so in one place he seems to ascribe to that faith, because God's promises are true, that through it we are justified: which faith contains and embraces the obedience of God's precepts, not indeed as its effect, but as its substance and form. For we must remember what was rightly concluded above: that the faith by which we are justified is the obedience of God. In the same place: they altogether beget confidence in God himself, and that obedience by which we are justified. On p. 15 he teaches that it cannot in any way happen that faith in Christ, by which we are justified, is to believe that our sins have been blotted out by the shedding of his blood, but the form and essence of faith in Christ is to obey his precepts. Add also pp. 54, 55, 58.

units.la: Hic ergo quæritur, num fides, quâ justificamur, nihil fit aliud, quam obedi- entia præceptorum Christi? quod nos negamus. Non quidem hoc, quin fides in Christum vera, conjuncta sibi habeat, & ut necessarium adjunctum consequens bona opera, seu obedientiam, non præceptorum Christi, ut sic, sed Dei: verum in negotio justificationis considerata fides, non pro obedientia venit, quæ ipsa justificet, sed pro instrumento duntaxat, Christum, pro justitia, ac- cipiente: atque ita justificat non in se, sed relative, per suum correlatum, Christum, ejusque justitiam: Christi enim sola justitia nostra est, quæ nos, vi & virtute sua, coram Deo absolvit, præter eam aliud plane nihil.
units.tr: Here, then, the question is whether faith, by which we are justified, is nothing other than the obedience of Christ's precepts. This we deny. Not that true faith in Christ does not have good works joined to it, and as a necessary consequent accompaniment, the obedience not of Christ's precepts as such, but of God's. But in the matter of justification, faith considered in this way does not come forward as an obedience which justifies, but only as an instrument, receiving Christ as righteousness; and so it justifies not in itself but relatively, through its correlate, Christ and his righteousness. For the sole righteousness of Christ is our righteousness, which, by its own power and virtue, absolves us before God; apart from it there is clearly nothing else.

units.la: Quæ Ecclesiarum nostrarum constans est sententia, variis fidei Confessionibus unanimiter testata, & comprobata. Confessio Gallica, ut cæteras præte- ream, art. xviii. omnino virtutum & meritorum opinione abjecta, in sola Jesu Christi obedientia prorsus acquiescimus, quâ quidem nobis imputatur, tum ut tegantur omnia nostra peccata, tum ut gratiam coram Deo nanciscamur. Belgica, art. xxii. Caeterum proprie loquendo, nequaquam intelligimus ipsam fidem per se, seu ex se, nos justificare, ut quæ fit duntaxat veluti instrumentum, quo Christum justitiam nostram apprehendimus. Christus igitur ipse est justitia nostra, qui omnia sua nobis merita imputat, fides vero est instrumentum, quod illi in societatem seu communionem omnium bonorum ipsius copulamur, atque in ea retinemur.
units.tr: This is the constant opinion of our Churches, unanimously attested and approved in various confessions of faith. The French Confession, to pass over the others, art. 18: Having altogether rejected the opinion of virtues and merits, we rest wholly in the obedience of Jesus Christ alone, which is indeed imputed to us, both so that all our sins may be covered, and so that we may obtain grace before God. The Belgic, art. 22: Moreover, speaking properly, we by no means understand that faith itself, by itself or from itself, justifies us, since it is only, as it were, the instrument by which we lay hold of Christ our righteousness. Christ therefore is himself our righteousness, who imputes to us all his merits; but faith is the instrument by which we are joined to him in fellowship and communion of all his goods, and are kept in it.

units.la: Unde, quantopere à veritate, & consensu Ecclesiarum nostrarum, hac etiam in parte, discesserint Remonstrantes, liquet, quando in Apologiâ, cap. x. afferunt, in summa uti pag. 107. & pag. 114. in substantia rei Socinum cum Orthodoxis conspirare in capite de Justificatione. Quod certe nos negamus. Nam quamvis Socinus in hoc cum Orthodoxis faciat, quod justificatio est actus judicialis, non talis quo Deus infundit justitiam peccatori, sed quo peccatorem credentem absolabsolvit, eumque pro justo habet, non in hoc tamen summam rei sitam cognoscimus, sed in justificationis materia, & forma, quam utramque Socinus eversum it[?]. Nec, quod Remonstrantes addunt, similiter in capite de fide, cum Orthodoxis ille conspirat, id est, juxta ipsos, in toto hoc negotio: quia, quamvis fidem non tantum notitiam, sed etiam assensum & fiduciam esse, teneat; attamen cum eam, quatenus justificat, non apprehendere justitiam in Christo, sed nihil aliud esse quam obedientiam praeceptorum Christi, asserit, totam ejus rationem & naturam invertit, nulloque modo in summa rei convenire cum Orthodoxis dici potest. Nisi qua tatione Smalcius, contra Frantzium dixit, Disp. 11. de Poenitentia, postquam aperte professus fuerat suos damnare fidem in meritum Christi, cum nullum meritum Christi agnoscamus, & pro nugatoria fabula id totum habeamus: nota consensum scilicet istorum hominum, in summa rei, cum Orthodoxis: deinde & postquam opera esse formam fidei, & ita ipsam quodammodo fidem, addidisset; intulit, ita ut, quoad verba, idem dicamus cum Lutheranis, fidem, addo etiam, solam fidem, post Dei gratiam, ad salutem requiri. Non ausus vero fuit dicere, se cum Lutheranis in summa rei; sed quoad verba convenire. Non autem qui in verbis, re ideo conveniunt, non certe in summa rei. Ut quidem id de Socinianis, eorumque cum Orthodoxis consensu, jam satis clare ostensum arbitror.
units.tr: From this it is clear how far the Remonstrants have departed from the truth and the agreement of our Churches also in this part, when in their Apology, chap. 10, they assert, in sum, as on pp. 107 and 114, that Socinus agrees with the Orthodox in substance on the chapter of Justification. This we certainly deny. For although Socinus agrees with the Orthodox in this, that justification is a judicial act, not such that God infuses righteousness into the sinner, but such that he absolves the believing sinner and holds him as righteous, we do not recognise the sum of the matter as lying in this, but in the matter and form of justification, both of which Socinus overthrows it[?]. Nor does what the Remonstrants add, that in the same way he agrees with the Orthodox in the chapter on faith, that is, according to them, in the whole of this business, hold: because, although he holds that faith is not merely knowledge but also assent and trust, yet when he asserts that faith, insofar as it justifies, does not lay hold on righteousness in Christ but is nothing other than the obedience of Christ's precepts, he inverts its whole character and nature, and it cannot be said to agree in the substance of the matter with the Orthodox in any way. Smalcius, against Frantzius, said in Disp. 11 on Repentance, after he had plainly professed that his people condemn faith in the merit of Christ, since we acknowledge no merit of Christ, and hold all of it to be a trifling fable, note the agreement of those men with the Orthodox in the substance of the matter; then, after he had added that works are the form of faith, and so in a way faith itself, he inferred: so that, as to words, we say the same as the Lutherans, that faith, and I add, faith alone, after the grace of God, is required for salvation. He did not dare, however, to say that he agrees with the Lutherans in the substance of the matter, but only that he agrees as to words. Yet those who agree in words but not in substance certainly do not agree in the substance of the matter. I think this has now been shown clearly enough concerning the Socinians and their agreement with the Orthodox.

units.la: Non vero id adeo miramur a Remonstrantibus, de Socinianis dictum, quibuscum in summa rei, supra quam oportet, passim convenit, non in aliis tantum, sed & hoc articulo; quum illorum sit sententia, quod non modo fides in negotio justificationis consideranda veniat ut opus, sive actus nostler[?]; sed & exponentes, quomodo fides instrumentum vocatur; ajant, sic fides instrumentum dici potest, quo consequimur remissionem peccatorum, non quasi fides praestita proprie instrumentum fiat, aut instrumentalis sit actio, qua sicut manu apprehendimus aut attrahimus remissionem: Nuga: sed quia ea praestita, non aliter consequimur peccatorum remissionem ex promisso Dei, quam si fides veluti instrumentum a Deo data esset ad consequendam & obtinendam peccatorum remissionem. Quibus paria dicere nil detrectabunt quoque Socinian. Pergunt Remonstrantes, & Confessionum Reformatarum explicaturi sententiam, inquiunt, Verum quidem est Confessiones nonnullae Reformatae ita loqui de fide, ut per eam apprehendi dicant misericordiam, justitiam & remissionem peccatorum: sed nisi istae earum locutiones benigne interpreteris, fieri non potest, ut eas a manifesta absurditate vindices atque absolvas. Quomodo vero? nempe hunc in sensum, quod justitia nobis imputari dicitur propter Christi meritum & obedientiam. In quibus si vel vocem meriti expungas, vel aliqua expositione emollias, quam etiam Socinian non detrectent, nihil adeo quod eos offendat, erit reliquum. Non vero ita, neque is sensus Ecclesiarum Reformatarum est, tantum justitiam nobis imputari, propter Christi meritum & obedientiam; sed hoc ipsum quod Christus nobis meritus, atque quod obedivit Deo, imputari nobis in justitiam: adeoque nos verissime & propriissime per fidem apprehendere misericordiam, justitiam, & remissionem peccatorum. Neque sequitur, quod inferunt Remonstrantes, si utrumque verum esse velimus, necesse esse ut dicamus Justitiam Christi nobis imputari propter justitiam Christi. non, sed justitiam nobis imputari, propter justitiam Christi, sive propter hanc nos justificari. Nec, ubi explicuerunt sententiam Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, dixerunt eam esse, quod justitia Christi nobis imputetur, propter Christi justitiam; sed simpliciter, justitiam propter Christum, ejusque meritum. Quæ quia plenius persequutus est Cl. Vir Samuel Rhætorfortis, 1. Exercit. de divina gratia, Cap. 11. nos facile præterimus.
units.tr: Yet we are not so surprised that the Remonstrants, who in the substance of the matter agree with the Socinians far more than they should, should be said to do so, not only in other points but also in this article. Their view is that faith is to be considered in the business of justification not only as a work or act of ours [?]; and in explaining how faith is called an instrument, they say: "Faith may be called an instrument in this sense, that through it we obtain the forgiveness of sins. Not that faith, once exercised, actually becomes an instrument, or is an instrumental action by which we grasp or draw forgiveness as with the hand. Trifles! Rather, because once faith is exercised we obtain forgiveness of sins from God's promise in no other way than if faith had been given by God as an instrument for obtaining and securing the forgiveness of sins." The Socinians will not hesitate to say the same. The Remonstrants go on, and to explain the view of the Reformed Confessions they say: "It is true that some Reformed Confessions speak of faith in such a way that they say we apprehend through it mercy, righteousness, and the forgiveness of sins. But unless you interpret these expressions favourably, you cannot save them from manifest absurdity and clear them of it." But how? Namely in this sense: that "righteousness is said to be imputed to us on account of Christ's merit and obedience." If you either strike out the word merit or soften it by some explanation, which the Socinians too would not reject, nothing will remain to offend them.
