But that is not so, nor is it the meaning of the Reformed Churches, that only righteousness is imputed to us on account of Christ's merit and obedience; rather, that what Christ merited for us and what he obeyed God in is itself imputed to us as righteousness, and so we most truly and most properly apprehend through faith mercy, righteousness, and the forgiveness of sins. Nor does it follow, as the Remonstrants infer, that if we want both to be true, we must say "that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us on account of the righteousness of Christ." No; righteousness is imputed to us on account of the righteousness of Christ, or we are justified on account of this. Nor, when they explained the view of the Reformed Churches, did they say it was that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us on account of Christ's righteousness; they said simply, righteousness on account of Christ and his merit. Since the distinguished man Samuel Rutherford has pursued this more fully (1. Exercitatio de divina gratia, cap. 11), we pass over it readily.

units.la: Quod porro Remonstrantes ajunt, quod per fidem in negotio justificationis intelligendus (sit actus fidei, quatenus includit in se totam obedientiam hominis Christiani, legem fidei, id est, Evangelio præscriptam. vel controversiam super eo, nil nisi logicam aut Grammaticam esse litem: quid pectore premant, satis indicat. Neque vel verbis aliis sua exprimunt Socinani. Illudque dicere si parum referat, haud video, quorsum adeo Socino negari debeat, formam fidei esse obedientiam. Quod tamen videri volunt facere Remonstrantes. Et mox rident etiam, ut rem nihili. Pag. 114. Quod obedientiam fidei formam vocet Socinus, cum Reformatæ Ecclesiæ eam vocent effectum, fructum, fœtum, sine quo fides esse non potest. Quantulum hoc est? Quis vel ciccum interduit? quod si quis nihilominus magnum hic hiatum esse velit, is doceat intelligibiliter, quid illud reale aut formale sit, quod ista duo tam magno intervallo a se separat ac distare facit. In Confessione jam ante dixerant, Cap. x. §. 2. utique necesse est ut fidei præscriptum non alio modo hic consideretur, quam quatenus proprietate naturali sua obedientiam fidei includit, & tamquam fœcunda bonorum operum mater est, totiusque Christianæ pietatis ac sanctimoniæ fons ac scaturigo: tantum abest, ut huic obedientiæ ac pietati, & ipsa opponi debeat, aut jure possit.
units.tr: Further, when the Remonstrants say that "by faith, in the business of justification, we are to understand the act of faith insofar as it includes in itself the whole obedience of the Christian man, the law of faith, that is, the law prescribed in the Gospel," and that the controversy about this is nothing but a dispute of logic or grammar, what they really think is sufficiently clear. The Socinians do not express their views in other words either. If it makes little difference whether one says this, I do not see why Socinus should be refused the claim that the form of faith is obedience, which the Remonstrants nevertheless want to seem to grant. And soon they even laugh at it, as if it were a trifle. (p. 114) "Because Socinus calls obedience the form of faith, while the Reformed Church calls it the effect, fruit, and offspring, without which faith cannot exist. How trivial is this! Who even grasps a jot of it? But if anyone nonetheless wants to see a great gap here, let him explain intelligibly what that real or formal thing is which separates and makes these two so far apart." Earlier, in their Confession, they had said (ch. 10, §2): "It is necessary that the prescription of faith be considered here only insofar as by its natural property it includes the obedience of faith, and as the fruitful mother of good works, the fount and spring of all Christian piety and holiness. So far is it from being right or possible to set this obedience and piety against faith itself."

units.la: Sententia Arminii erat, imputari nobis in justitiam ipsum actum fidei proprie, non justitiam Christi: quamvis hæc meruerit, ut fides, pro justitia nobis, ex gratuita Dei æstimatione, imputaretur. Asseruit enim, 1. Non ipsam nobis imputari Christi justitiam. 11. Sed fidem. 111. Quæ ex Christi merito, & gratiosa Dei acceptatione id habeat, ut loco legalis justitiæ, quâ destituimur, ipsa pro justitia nostra a Deo censeatur. In epist. ad Hippolytum a Collibus, postremum caput est de justificatione, de quâ hæc mea est sententia: fidem, eamque solam, quamquam sola sine operibus non est, ad justitiam imputari. Hac sola coram Deo justificari, absolvi a peccatis, & justos censeri, pronunciari, declarari a Deo, de gratia tribunali sententiam ferente. Deinde, hoc autem culpant nonnulli, quod ipsum fidei actum, id est τὸ credere dico imputari in justitiam, idque proprio sensu, non metonymice: fateor sane præeunte mihi Apostolo cap. 4. Epistola ad Rom. & sapius istam phrasin usurpante. At quod inde concludunt, nempe sic Christum, ejusque justitiam a justificatione nostra excludi, eamque dignitati fidei nostræ tribui, minime concedo deduci ex mea sententia posse. Vox enim imputandi significat fidem non esse ipsam justitiam, sed gratiose pro justitia haberi: quo ipso dignitas omnis a fide aufertur, nisi quæ est per gratiosam dignationem Dei. Gratiosa autem illa dignatio & æstimatio non est extra Christum, sed respectu Christi, in Christo, & propter Christum: quem constituit Deus placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius. Dico igitur fidem imputari nobis in justitiam, propter Christum & justitiam ejus: in qua enunciatione fides est objectum imputationis, Christus vero & obedientia ejus causa justificationis impetratoria seu meritoria: qui Christus cum obedientia sua objectum est fidei nostrae, at non objectum justificationis seu imputationis divinae, quasi Deus Christum ejusque justitiam nobis imputet in justitiam, quod fieri nequit, quum obedientia Christi sit ipsissima justitia secundum severissimum rigorem legis sumta. Similia habet in Declaratione Sententiae suae ad D D. Ordines, p. 65. Et in Responsi. ad art. xxxi. art. iv. Hinc Bertii epistolica Disceptatio, cum Luberto, super eadem controversia
units.tr: Arminius's view was that the act of faith itself, properly speaking, is imputed to us as righteousness, not the righteousness of Christ; although the latter deserved that faith should be imputed to us as righteousness by God's gracious estimation. For he asserted: (1) that Christ's righteousness itself is not imputed to us; (2) but faith; (3) which, by Christ's merit and God's gracious acceptance, has this effect, that in place of the legal righteousness we lack, it is counted by God as our righteousness. In his letter to Hippolytus a Collibus he writes: "The last chapter is about justification, and my view of it is this: faith, and faith alone, although faith is never alone without works, is imputed to righteousness. By this alone we are justified before God, absolved from sins, and pronounced, declared, and judged righteous by God, who pronounces sentence from the throne of grace." Then: "Some find fault with this, that I say the act of faith itself, that is, the believing, is imputed for righteousness, and in the proper sense, not by metonymy. I confess indeed that I follow the Apostle in Romans 4 and often use that phrase. But that they conclude from this that Christ and his righteousness are thereby excluded from our justification, and that this gives honour to our faith, I by no means concede can be deduced from my view. For the word imputing signifies that faith is not itself righteousness but is held by graceful favour as righteousness; by this very fact all dignity is taken away from faith, except that which comes from God's gracious regard. That gracious regard and estimation, however, is not apart from Christ but has respect to Christ, is in Christ, and is for Christ's sake, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood. I therefore say that faith is imputed to us for righteousness, for the sake of Christ and his righteousness. In this statement faith is the object of imputation, but Christ and his obedience are the impetrating or meritorious cause of justification. This Christ, with his obedience, is the object of our faith, but not the object of justification or of divine imputation, as if God imputed Christ and his righteousness to us for righteousness, which cannot be, since the obedience of Christ is itself righteousness taken according to the strictest rigour of the law." He has similar things in his Declaration of his Opinion to the Lords of the Divinity (p. 65), and in the Response to article 31, article 4. Hence the epistolary Disputation of Bertius with Lubbertus on the same controversy.

units.la: Ex quibus liquet. i. Arminium, & Remonstrantes in summa aut substantia rei convenire cum Socinianis, de justificatione; non hos cum Orthodoxis. ii. Omnesque in eo consentire, contra Reformatos, quod in operibus suis fi-gant causam, propter quam hominem justificari, affirmant. Remonstrantes, in Apol. cap. x. ubi Nostri objecissent, ex sententia illorum sequi, quod homo non ex fide tantum, sed etiam ex operibus justificetur, respondent, istud non tantum absurdum non esse, sed verissimum etiam esse. Socinus, in Synopsi, pag. 55. & consequenter opera ipsa justificant. & pag. seq. Deus per illa, fidem sc. & opera, ex illisve nos justificat, sive per illa ex illisve justificamur.
units.tr: From these things it is clear: (i) that Arminius and the Remonstrants agree with the Socinians, not with the Orthodox, in the sum or substance of the matter of justification; (ii) and that they all agree against the Reformed in this, that they place in their own works the cause on account of which they affirm man is justified. The Remonstrants, in their Apology, ch. 10, where our men had objected that on their view it would follow that man is justified not by faith only but also by works, answer that this is not only not absurd but is even most true. Socinus, in his Synopsis, p. 55: "and consequently the works themselves justify," and on the following page: "God justifies us through those things, namely faith and works, and from them, or we are justified through them and from them."

units.la: Nos vero nihil in nobis causae reperimus, propter quod justificemur, sed unam & solam ejus causam habemus, extra nos, in Christo, qui factus nobis δικαιοσύνη ἡ ἁγιασμὸς[?] καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις[?] ut, quemadmodum scriptum est, qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. 1 Cor. 1. 30. 31. Non autem propter fidei bonum opus, vel actum, vel fiduciam, obedientiam, aut quomodocunque appelletur, justificari hominem posse, censemus.
units.tr: We, however, find in ourselves no cause on account of which we are justified, but we have one and only one cause, outside ourselves, in Christ, who was made for us "righteousness and sanctification and redemption" [δικαιοσύνη ἡ ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις], so that, as it is written, "he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord" (1 Cor. 1:30, 31). We do not think that a man can be justified on account of faith as a good work, or an act, or trust, or obedience, or however else it may be called.

units.la: Hactenus bene Socinus justificationem habet pro actione Dei judicia-li, non qua justitia peccatori infunditur, sed peccatorem credentem in Chri-stum Deus in foro judicii, sed gratuiti, absolvit. De Servat. part. iv. pag. 320. quid aliud reipsa est justificari, quam a peccatis absolvi, & pro justo haberi? Praelect. cap. xiii. & xv. Justificari igitur in sacris litteris, quemadmodum dictum est, justum pronuntiare, proque justo habere proprie significat, id est, tamquam cum justo in sententia ferenda atque exequenda agere. In Synopsi de justificatione, pag. 6. Justificatio nostra coram Deo, ut uno verbo dicam, nihil aliud est, quam a Deo pro justis haberi. Catechesis Racoviensis, cap. xi. Quid vero est justificatio? Resp. Justi-ficatio est, cum nos Deus pro justis habet, quod ea ratione facit, cum nobis & peccata remittit, & nos vita aeterna donat, de quo aperte testatur Paulus, dum ait: Rom. iv. 6. in eo beatudinem hominis consistere, cui Dominus imputat justitiam: deinde e Psalmo addit; Beatus vir, cui non imputat Dominus peccatum. Atque justificare in sacris litteris aliud nihil significare, quam justum pronuntiare, scribit, Notis in Dia-log. de Justific. p. 26. Crellius, in Epist. ad Galat. cap. ii. pag. 10. Justificare in hac disputatione non significat, uti nec alibi in sac. litteris, justum ac sanctum efficere, quandoquidem id pro fructu, sive operum legis, sive fidei in Christum per charitatem efficacis, ponitur, & condemnationi opponitur: sed est vocabulum ex foro & judiciis petitum, significatque justum pronuntiare, vel potius, tamquam justum atque innocentem tractare, ita cum quopiam agere, ut cum justo ac innocente agi convenit. Adde eundem, pag. 70. Deinde, neque id Socinus male, quod sine Christi fide nemini vitam æternam posse contingere, statuit: de fide & operib. pag. 55. Verùm ad tempora hoc restringunt N. Testamenti. Ipse ibidem; & Catechesis Racoviensis: Qu. ergone sine fide in Christum nemo justificatur? Resp. Nemo prorsus. Verum id de eo tempore intelligendum est, quo Christus patefactus est. Sed quod fidei adjungunt aliud, per quod justificemur, quam Christum, & solam ejus justitiam; quodque, ejus loco, nos & nostra opera substituunt, quaestionem facit de re maximâ haud exiguam.
units.tr: Thus far Socinus rightly holds that justification is a judicial act of God, not one by which righteousness is infused into the sinner, but one by which God, in the court of judgement yet a gracious one, absolves the sinner who believes in Christ. On the Saviour, part 4, p. 320: what else is it, in fact, to be justified, than to be absolved from sins and held as righteous? Lectures, chapters 13 and 15: To be justified, then, in the Holy Scriptures, as has been said, properly means to pronounce someone righteous and to hold him as righteous, that is, to deal with him as with a righteous person in pronouncing and carrying out the sentence. In the Synopsis on justification, p. 6: Our justification before God, to say it in one word, is nothing other than being held as righteous by God. The Racovian Catechism, chapter 11: What, then, is justification? Answer: Justification is when God holds us as righteous, which He does by both forgiving us our sins and granting us eternal life, as Paul clearly testifies when he says (Rom. 4:6) that the blessedness of man consists in this, that the Lord imputes righteousness to him; then from the Psalm he adds, Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin. Crellius, in his notes on the Dialogue on Justification, p. 26, writes that to justify in the Holy Scriptures means nothing else than to pronounce righteous. Crellius, on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2, p. 10: To justify in this discussion does not mean, nor does it mean elsewhere in the Holy Scriptures, to make just and holy, since that is put as the fruit of the works of the law or of faith in Christ effective through love, and is opposed to condemnation; rather it is a word taken from the forum and from judgements, and signifies to pronounce righteous, or rather, to treat as righteous and innocent, so as to deal with someone in the way it is fitting to deal with a righteous and innocent person. Add the same author, p. 70. Further, Socinus is not wrong in holding that eternal life can come to no one without faith in Christ, On Faith and Works, p. 55. But they restrict this to the time of the New Testament, as he does in the same place, and so does the Racovian Catechism: Question: Then no one is justified without faith in Christ? Answer: No one at all. But this must be understood of the time in which Christ has been revealed. But when they add to faith something else through which we are justified, other than Christ and His righteousness alone, and in His place substitute ourselves and our works, this raises a question of no small weight.

units.la: Operibus quidem etiam istis, quibus justitiam adscribunt & justificationem, adimunt dignitatem & meritum, quo justificatione in se digna videantur; sed totus iste locus, & genus hoc causalitatis, per quod adferuntur opera in materiam justitiæ, utcunque imperfectæ, negandum fuerat, & caste integreque soli id asservandum Christo.
units.tr: Indeed, to these works, to which they ascribe righteousness and justification, they also take away the worth and the merit by which they might seem worthy of justification in themselves. But that whole argument, and this kind of causality by which works are brought forward as the material of righteousness, however imperfect, ought to have been denied, and this should have been reserved purely and entirely to Christ alone.

units.la: Nos bona opera consideramus ut effectum & fructum justificationis, & consequens justificantis fidei, non tempore ullo ab ea divisum, verum naturâ duntaxat posterius. Uti enim quos vocat Deus, eosdem quoque justificat, Rom. viii. 30. ita Spiritus Christi in vocatione fidem ingenerat, quâ tum justificantur fideles in Christo, id est, ex debitoribus & reis evadunt justificati, absolvuntur à poenis debitis, pronunciantur justi, atque etiam ad præstandam Deo obedientiam, per charitatem omnimodam, quâ fides efficax est, adducuntur.
units.tr: We regard good works as the effect and fruit of justification, and as the consequence of justifying faith, not separated from it by any interval of time, but only later in nature. For just as those whom God calls, He also justifies (Rom. 8:30), so the Spirit of Christ, in calling, engenders faith, by which the faithful are then justified in Christ, that is, they pass from debtors and guilty persons into the justified, are absolved from the penalties they owe, are pronounced righteous, and are also led to render obedience to God through all-embracing love, in which living faith consists.

units.la: Ægre autem fert Socinus, bona opera effecta justificationis haberi, non causam. De justificat. pag. 51. Alterum est extremum, quod vulgò receptum est, non sine summa animarum pernicie, videlicet, ad justificationem nostram nihil prorsus bona opera pertinere, nisi quatenus sunt ipsius justificationis effecta. Ubi, qui ita sentiunt, ceguntur fidem, qua justificamur, ejusmodi intelligere, qua quatenus ab substantiam suam, sive essentiam ac formam, bona opera non requirat. Ex quo consequatur, ut quando certum est, per fidem nos justificari, omnino eveniat, ut isti censeant justificatum esse hominem, etiam antequam boni quicquam faciat, licet postea sit facturus. Quod adversatur totum sacræ scripturæ: quas ut aliam taceam, aperte contestatur, sine panitentia non confiteri, neque existere, peccatorum nostrorum remissionem. Cum & verissimum sit, & isti ipsi idagno-scant, & fateantur, justificationem nostram aliud nihil reipsa esse, quam remissionem peccatorum nostrorum. At Resp. 1. Fatemur, antecedenter & causaliter ad justificationem opera nostra non pertinere; sed esse justificationis ipsius effecta: atque id absque ulla animarum pernicie. Neque enim cum animarum pernicie conjunctum ullatenus dici potest, quod ad animarum salutem omnino requiri-mus, licet non illo loco, quo idipsum Adversarii cupiunt. Sed id animarum perniciem secum trahit, quod, quum requiratur ad salutem, ab Adversariis omnino tollitur, quale est imputatio justitiæ, id est, satisfactionis & meriti Christi, ad justificationem & salutem. Nos vero bonorum operum necessitatem & præsentiam nequidquam tollimus, quamvis non anteponamus justificationi, sed postponamus. Quomodocunque, urgemus bona opera, quantum urgeri possunt, sed suo loco, non ante justificationem, quia nulla ibi sunt; sed post, quando adesse ea simpliciter necessarium est. Quid hinc animæ incommodi, nedum exitii? Adversarii autem, id quod essentiale in toto hoc negotio, & fundamentum unicum est, auferunt, & nullo habent loco: quare ii demum perniciem animabus creare dicendi sunt. ii. Nec fidem nos, etiam qu[?] justificamur, ejusmodi intelligimus, quæ ad substantiam vel complementum suum bona opera non requirat. Contrarium enim apparet ex Disputatio-nibus nostris, contra Pontificios, quando contendimus, fidem à bonis operibus separari non posse. Nobisque gravis fit injuria, in Animadversionibus, adversus Joh. Niemojevium, pro Socino, §. 15. quando dicitur, quod fides nostra sine bonis operibus esse potest. Sed fidem in justificatione, non quatenus bo-na opera secum fert, vel ipsa bonum opus est, sed instrumentaliter & relative, ut amplectentem divitias justitiæ in Christo, contuemur. Aliud est, naturam fidei spectare, in se, quæ omnino requirit, pro vi & ἐνέργεια[?] sua, bona opera, ipsaque singularis virtus est, & ἔργον θεοῦ[?]; aliud eam, in actione hac vel negotio speciali justificationis considerare, ubi nos justificat, quate-nus justitiam Christi apprehendit, uti in sequentibus sumus ostensuri. iii.
units.tr: But Socinus takes it badly that good works are held to be the effects of justification, not its cause. On Justification, p. 51: The other extreme, which is commonly received, not without the greatest ruin of souls, namely that good works contribute absolutely nothing to our justification, except insofar as they are effects of justification itself. Here those who think so are compelled to understand the faith by which we are justified as such that it does not require good works for its substance, that is, its essence and form. From this it follows that, when it is certain that we are justified through faith, it altogether comes about that they hold a man to be justified even before he does any good, although he is going to do it afterwards. This is wholly opposed to Holy Scripture, which, to pass over others, clearly testifies that without repentance there is no confession of, nor existence of, the remission of our sins. And since it is most true, and they themselves acknowledge and confess, that our justification is in fact nothing else than the remission of our sins. But we answer, first: we admit that our works do not contribute to justification antecedently and causally, but are effects of justification itself; and this without any ruin of souls. For what we absolutely require for the salvation of souls cannot in any way be said to be joined with the ruin of souls, although not in the place where our adversaries wish to put it. But what carries ruin of souls with it is that which, since it is required for salvation, is wholly removed by our adversaries, such as the imputation of righteousness, that is, of the satisfaction and merit of Christ, for justification and salvation. We, however, do not in vain remove the necessity and presence of good works, although we do not place them before justification but after it. In any case, we press good works as far as they can be pressed, but in their proper place: not before justification, because there are none there, but after it, when their presence is simply necessary. What harm, let alone destruction, does this bring to the soul? But our adversaries remove what is essential in this whole matter and its sole foundation, and give it no place at all; they are the ones who should be said to bring destruction upon souls. Second: nor do we understand the faith by which we are justified as one that does not require good works for its substance or completion. For the contrary appears from our disputations against the Papists, when we contend that faith cannot be separated from good works. And a grave injustice is done to us, in the Animadversions against John Niemojewski, on behalf of Socinus, §15, where it is said that our faith can be without good works. But we consider faith in justification not insofar as it brings good works with it, nor as itself a good work, but instrumentally and relatively, as embracing the riches of righteousness in Christ. It is one thing to look at the nature of faith in itself, which by its power and energy wholly requires good works, and is itself a singular virtue and a work of God; it is another to consider it in this act or special business of justification, where it justifies us insofar as it lays hold of the righteousness of Christ, as we shall show in what follows. Third.

units.la: Homo justificatus est etiam antequam boni aliquid fecit, id est, boni fidem consequentis, qui ubi credit, justificatur: & illud antequam, & postea, intelligere oportet de ordine naturæ, non temporis. Nam non jam credit homo, ad sui justificationem, & aliquanto tempore post demum in bona incumbit opera; sed quæ gratia hominem ad fidem, eadem illum simul protrudit ad bona quæque opera: & ejusdem spiritus fructus est utrumque. iv. Neque hoc Scripturæ ulli adversatur, quæ testatur quidem ad accipiendam & sentiendam peccatorum remissionem, necessariam esse eorundem poenitentiam, non tamen istam illius, vel justificationis causam esse probat ullo modo. Neque dicit ullibi, nos per poenitentiam justificari, sed per fidem in Christum. Quod satis indicio est, non operibus, propterea quod bona sunt, sed fidei soli, propter Christum, id est, Christo proprie fide verâ apprehen-sio, rationem justificationis attribuendam esse. In subjecto, quod remissionis peccatorum fiat particeps, requiritur poenitentia, non autem ideo ad justifi-cationem Dei, prout ejus actionem dicit, hominem absolventis; bene quidem, prout istius terminationem & sensum passive notat in anima fideli. v. justific. præcipue quidem consistit in remissione peccatorum, complectitur tamen etiam adjudicationem vitæ æternæ, neque nisi ea simul comprehensa dicimus, illam nihil aliud esse quam remissionem peccatorum nostrorum.
units.tr: A man is justified even before he has done any good thing, that is, before the good that follows faith; he who believes is justified. And that "before" and "afterwards" must be understood in the order of nature, not of time. For a man does not first believe for his justification and only some time later apply himself to good works; rather, the same grace that drives a man to faith at the same time drives him to every good work, and both are the fruit of one and the same Spirit. Fourth. Nor does this contradict any passage of Scripture, which indeed testifies that repentance is necessary for receiving and feeling the remission of sins, yet does not prove that repentance is in any way the cause of that remission or of justification. Nor does it say anywhere that we are justified through repentance, but through faith in Christ. This is sufficient indication that the account of justification is to be ascribed not to works, because they are good, but to faith alone, on account of Christ, that is, to the true apprehension of Christ by faith. In the subject, who becomes a partaker of the remission of sins, repentance is required; but this is not on that account the cause of God's justification, as He acts to absolve a man, although it does well enough as it denotes the termination and the passive sense of that justification in the faithful soul. Fifth. Justification consists chiefly in the remission of sins, yet it also embraces the adjudication of eternal life; nor do we say that the former is nothing other than the remission of our sins unless both are taken together.

units.la: Socinus, de fide & operib. pag. 60. Illud certissimum est, non omnia bona opera post justificationem esse, & tamquam ejus appendicem censenda. Quin potius bona opera, quatenus ipsa complementum sunt, & quasi formam fiducia, nec reipsa aliud censeri debent, quam ipsa in Deum fides, ea sunt quibus per Dei gratiam justificamur. Quod autem bona opera non modo appendix quædam justificationis non sint, sed ipsa sint ante justificationem, hinc apparet, quod justificatio nostra nihil aliud reipsa est, quam peccatorum deletio. Peccatorum autem deletionem antecedit pœnitentia, & ad Deum conversio, Act. iii. ii. Sequuntur quidem etiam bona opera justificationem nostram, sed non ut ipsius appendix quaedam. Immo ipsa sunt, quae confervant justificationem, atque ut continuetur efficiunt.
units.tr: Socinus, On Faith and Works, p. 60. This is most certain: not all good works come after justification, nor are they to be regarded as an appendix to it. Rather, good works, insofar as they are its completion and, as it were, the form of faith, ought in fact to be considered nothing other than faith itself in God. These are the things through which we are justified by the grace of God. That good works are not merely some appendix to justification, but actually come before it, is clear from this: our justification is in fact nothing other than the blotting out of sins. Repentance and conversion to God go before the blotting out of sins (Acts 3:19). Good works do indeed follow our justification, but not as some appendix to it. Rather, they are the very things that preserve justification and bring it about that it continues.

units.la: Resp. 1. Quaestio ergo tota in hoc vertitur, an aliqua bona opera justificationem antecedant? tum ob quae, vel per quae Deus homines justificet? uti paulo post Socinus loquitur: jam igitur ex iis, quae dixi, satis intelligere potes, quid ego bonis operibus tribuam, ejusmodi videlicet operibus, qualia fieri praecipit Jesus Christus, quaeque sub spe aeterna vita, ut illi obediatur, fiunt, cum affirmaverim Deum per ipsa nos justificare; id est ea, propter Dei bonitatem ac misericordiam, caussam esse ut ipse Deus nobis peccata nostra ita condonet, ut vitam aeternam largiatur. De justificatione per opera mox sumus disputaturi; jam, quod Euangelica opera ante justificationem collocat, in eo Scripturae adversatur, & rationi: illi, quae a Deo docet justificati impium, Rom. iv. 5. πιστεύοντι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ[?] & justificationem contingere χωρὶς ἔργων νόμου. Rom. iii. 28. & Gal. ii. 16. non justificatur homo ex operibus legis. Rom. xi. 6. si autem ex gratia, jam non ex operibus: quandoquidem gratia jam non est gratia. Si vero ex operibus, jam non est gratia: quandoquidem opus jam non est opus. Rationi adversatur sententia, quia quum fides sit bonorum omnium operum initum, absque qua nemo placere Deo poterit, vel aliquid gratum ipsi praestare, & per eam, statim ac adest, justificamur, jam non antecedere justificationem, uti nec fidem, bona opera possunt, sed tantum sequi. 11. aliqua vero sequi nec Adversarius diffitetur, sed non pro appendice judicanda. Neque nos pro appendice justificationis & fidei habemus bona opera, quae forte abesse queat, vel non admodum sit necessaria; sed pro fructu & adjuncto essentialiter necessario, id est, absque quo nulla unquam habeatur justificatio, & nisi ex fide & justificatione esse ullibi queat. iii. Actor. iii. 19. quidem dicitur, resipiscite ergo & convertite, ut deleantur peccata vestra. Sed jam de Christo, & fide in Christum concionatus fuerat Petrus. Et fac quod non, haud tamen dixit, per resipiscentiam illos justificandos, vel remissionem peccatorum impetraturos. Id quidem verum est, quod nisi resipiscant, partae per Christum, ejusque passiones, ore omnium Prophetarum praedictas, de quo versu immeditate praecedente actum fuerat, remissionis, capaces esse non posse: ut enim ea concedatur, applicetur, intimetur, gratia conversionis & fidei, & bonorum operum donari oportet; tum vim istorum ut exerant, illius vim perspentificere: non autem resipiscentia & conversio justificationem vel meretur, vel impetrat. Socinus, in Notis ad Dial. de justific. respondens ad locum 1 Joann. i. 6. Non est, inquit, haec mens Apostoli: sed hac, docere, quid faciendum nobis sit, (si expiationis omnium peccatorum nostrorum participes esse velimus, quam attulit, seu testatur Christi sanguis. Adeo aliud est, expiatio peccatorum nostrorum, in Christo, quamvis hoc secus ac oportet, exponant; aliud, ejus participatio. iv. Quare aparet hinc necessitas & usus distinctionis, inter justificationem activam, & passivam, uti loquuntur. Nam uti justificatio est peccatorum remissio, haec autem considerari debet veluti impetrata per Christum, ejus passionibus & morte: vel applicata, fide ; quarum illa dicitur actiua , ista passiva , vel applicata in hominum ani-mis ; ita justificatio , vel ex parte Dei spectatur , vel nostri , in nobis & sub-jecto suo terminata. Illa in aeterno Dei decreto nobis destinata est; in promis-sionibus à prima mundi aetate & in Euangelio oblata ; à Christo merita ; ejus re-surrectione confirmata & ratihabita , hastenus actiue: verum passive spectatur, in anima , per fidem, applicata & terminata. v. Et hoc modo gratia remissio-nis peccatorum & justificationis clarius conspicitur, quatenus contingit ho-minibus non mobi nihil boni meritis, sed consistentibus adhuc in reatu & im-probitate; interim cum gratia justificationis, ea etiam sanctificationis praeditis, qua imposterum non improbitati, sed Deo & Christo ex animo vivunt. vi. In nobis nihil omnino est, quo vel mereamur justificationem, vel propter quod nobis applicetur : per fidem quidem ejus reddimur participes, ut instrumentum , quo in Christum respicimus, ὃν προέθετο ὁ θεὸς ἱλαστήριον διὰ τῆς πίστεως [?], Rom. iii. 25. Joann. iii. 14. 15. & antecedentibus bonis operibus apud animum nostrum confirmatur, II Petr. 1. 10. 11. non tamen aut fides, aut bona opera id valent, ut propter ea Deus nos justificet, aut absol-vat: sed ad hoc una sufficit justitia Christi, quae in Dei judicio nos tuetur, no-straque est per fidem. vii. Bona opera si complementum fidei sunt quomodo ergo forma, & nihil aliud quam fides ipsa sunt? viii. Quod si forma fidei, quomodo ergo ante justificationem, id est, ante fidem quoque? nam per fidem, & ad fidem statim justificamur. Non justificamur ante fidem, sed ad fidem, & per fidem : quare, bona opera ponere ante justificationem, est ea ponere ante fidem, sive formam rei ante ipsam. ix. Et tamen dixit Socinus, pag. 55. se quod ad opera attinet, qua fidem antecedunt, nullam eis efficaciam ad vitam aeternam justificandi tribuere. Quae si sint bona opera, & sub Novo nunc Testamento, sic uti oportet, praestita, qua ratione iis vim justificandi adimere, juxta hypotheses suas, potest? x. Denique, qui quaeso una virtus, alterius forma esse potest? unum opus bonum, forma alterius? vel alia quaevis opera, forma fidei? bonum opus quidem genus est singulorum, sed non unum opus specifice consideratum est alterius forma. Ubi non magis unum forma potest esse alterius, ac species una alterius, bestia v. g. hominis, & sic porro.
units.tr: Reply 1. The whole question therefore turns on this: do any good works precede justification? Or are they that by which, or through which, God justifies people? As Socinus says a little later: From what I have said, you can understand well enough what I attribute to good works, namely works of the kind Jesus Christ commands, which are done under the hope of eternal life, so as to obey him. When I have affirmed that God justifies us through them, I mean that they are the cause, on account of God's goodness and mercy, why God himself forgives our sins in such a way as to bestow eternal life. We shall soon be disputing about justification through works. But in placing evangelical works before justification, he contradicts Scripture and reason. Scripture teaches that God justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5), "to him who believes on him who justifies the ungodly" [πιστεύοντι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ], and that justification comes "apart from works of the law" [χωρὶς ἔργων νόμου] (Rom. 3:28; Gal. 2:16): a man is not justified by the works of the law. Rom. 11:6: But if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is by works, then it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work. The opinion is also contrary to reason. Since faith is the beginning of all good works, without which no one can please God or do anything acceptable to him, and since we are justified through faith as soon as it is present, good works cannot precede justification any more than they can precede faith; they can only follow it. 2. Indeed, our opponent does not deny that some good works follow, but he does not judge them to be an appendix. Nor do we regard good works as an appendix to justification and faith, as if they could be absent or were not very necessary. Rather, we regard them as its fruit and as something essentially necessary to it, that is, without which justification is never had, and which can be found nowhere except from faith and justification. 3. It is said in Acts 3:19: Repent therefore and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out. But Peter had already preached about Christ and faith in Christ. Even granting that he had not, he did not say that they would be justified by repentance or obtain the forgiveness of sins through it. It is true that unless they repent, they cannot be capable of the forgiveness of sins procured through Christ and his sufferings, foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, of which the verse immediately before had spoken. For in order that this forgiveness be granted, applied and made known, the grace of conversion and of faith and of good works must be given, and the power of these must be exercised, and the power of that forgiveness perceived. But repentance and conversion do not merit or obtain justification. Socinus, in his Notes on the Dialogue on Justification, replying to 1 John 1:6, says: This is not the mind of the Apostle; but it is to teach what must be done by us if we wish to share in the expiation of all our sins, which the blood of Christ brought or attests. So different is the expiation of our sins in Christ, though they explain it otherwise than they ought, from the participation in it. 4. Hence appears the necessity and use of the distinction between active and passive justification, as they say. For justification is the remission of sins. This is to be considered as procured through Christ, by his sufferings and death, or as applied through faith. The former is called active, the latter passive, or applied in the minds of men. Thus justification is viewed either on God's part or on ours, and is terminated in us and in its subject. On the one hand, it was destined for us in God's eternal decree; it was offered in the promises from the first age of the world and in the Gospel; it was merited by Christ; it was confirmed and ratified by his resurrection. Up to this point it is viewed actively. But it is viewed passively in the soul, through faith, where it is applied and terminated. 5. In this way the grace of the remission of sins and of justification is more clearly seen, inasmuch as it comes to people who have no merit of any good, but who still remain in guilt and wickedness. At the same time, with the grace of justification there is also given sanctification, by which they live from then on not to wickedness, but to God and Christ from the heart. 6. There is absolutely nothing in us by which we might merit justification, or on account of which it is applied to us. Through faith we are indeed made partakers of it, as the instrument by which we look to Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith [ὃν προέθετο ὁ θεὸς ἱλαστήριον διὰ τῆς πίστεως] (Rom. 3:25; John 3:14–15). And it is confirmed in our minds by the good works that precede it (2 Pet. 1:10–11). Yet neither faith nor good works have the power that God should justify or acquit us on their account. For this alone suffices: the righteousness of Christ, which protects us in God's judgment and is ours through faith. 7. If good works are the completion of faith, how then are they its form, and nothing other than faith itself? 8. But if they are the form of faith, how then do they come before justification, that is, before faith too? For we are justified through faith and at once upon faith. We are not justified before faith, but toward faith and through faith. Therefore, to place good works before justification is to place them before faith, that is, before the form of the thing itself. 9. And yet Socinus says, p. 55, that as regards works which precede faith, he attributes to them no efficacy for justifying unto eternal life. But if these are good works, and are performed under the New Testament as they ought to be, by what reasoning can he, according to his own hypotheses, take away from them the power of justifying? 10. Finally, I ask, how can one virtue be the form of another? Can one good work be the form of another? Or can any other works be the form of faith? A good work is indeed the genus of its particular kinds, but one work considered specifically is not the form of another. Just as one thing cannot be the form of another any more than one species can be the species of another—for example, a beast of a man—and so on.

units.la: Atque formaliter differunt credere, & obedire ; nam credere proprie est, fidem vel assensum praebere alicujus dictis, & propterea ipsum habere veracem: uti propterea idem etiam fidei divinae applicatur. Joann. v. 9. 10. Joann. iii. verf. 33. obedire vero, praeceptis ejus obtemperare , & praestare officia, quae imperavit. Ista vero totis formis differunt, utcunque in unum forte concurrant, ut & credas ei, & obtemperes quoque. Praesertim ubi ipsi totum te teneris tradere, & credendo & obtemperando, omnia ab ipso exspectare. Sed non propterea idem dicenda sunt esse, non magis quam virtutes reliquae, quae etiam separari non possunt. v. g. fides & spes; amor Dei & proximi; oratio & patientia, vel patientia & pietas, II Petr. 1. 6. 7. atque similia.
units.tr: And to believe and to obey differ formally. For to believe properly means to give faith or assent to someone's words, and therefore to hold him to be truthful; hence the same term is also applied to divine faith (John 5:9–10; John 3:33). To obey, however, means to comply with his commands and to perform the duties he has enjoined. These differ entirely in form, even though they may perhaps come together in one thing, so that you both believe him and also obey him, especially when you yield yourself wholly to him, expecting everything from him both by believing and by obeying. But they are not therefore to be called the same, any more than the other virtues, which also cannot be separated, are: for example, faith and hope; love of God and of neighbour; prayer and patience, or patience and godliness (2 Pet. 1:6–7), and similar things.

units.la: Habent quidem commune genus omnia, quatenus à Deo praecepta, & sunt bona opera, certe non mala, sed interim differentia inter se distinguuntur & forma sua, neque sunt inter se unum, vel unum per alterum definitur, uti fidem dicunt Adversarii cum obedientia unum esse, & per hanc definiri. Quamvis etiam aliquam fateantur occurrere differentiam, sed rationis tantum. Major tamen illa, quam rationis, est, quae totis formis distat. fides, inquit Smalcius, Disp. vii. de bonis operib. pag. 219. ut antea etiam docuimus, differt ab obedientia, ratione tantum, quatenus mens nostra concipere potest aliud esse, Deo promittenti aliquem confidere, & aliud, ejusdem voluntatem facere: sed reipsa distingui ista non pof-sunt. Quia enim Deus nemini quicquam promittit simpliciter, sed cum hac conditione, si ei obtemperemus, fieri non potest, ut is Deo confidere dici possit, qui ei obedire, eo ipso momento, quo ei confidere incipit, non proponat sibi, & deinde, data Deo obediendi occasione, non obediat. At mens nostra ita concipere potest aliud esse Deo confidere, & ejus praeceptis obedire, ut etiam reipsa distinguantur. Æque ac fides, & spes. Nam etiam Deus nemini promisit bona, nisi in se speranti, & à fide, atque obedientia spes quoque divelli non potest, attamen non sunt ideo unum, vel differunt ratione tantum aliqua, sed formis.
units.tr: They all share a common genus, in that they are commanded by God and are good works, certainly not evil. Yet they are still distinguished from one another by their own forms and are not one thing, nor is one defined through the other, as our adversaries say that faith and obedience are one and are defined by it. They admit that some difference occurs, but only of reason. The difference that is greater than one of reason is the one that differs in whole forms. Faith, says Smalcius, Disp. vii on good works, p. 219, as we taught before, differs from obedience only in reason, insofar as our mind can conceive that to trust God who promises is one thing, and to do his will is another: but in fact these cannot be distinguished. For since God promises nothing to anyone simply, but with this condition, that we obey him, it cannot happen that one can be said to trust God who, at the very moment when he begins to trust him, does not propose to himself to obey him, and then, when the occasion of obeying God is given, does not obey. But our mind can conceive that to trust God is one thing and to obey his precepts is another, so that they are really distinguished, just as faith and hope are. For God promised good things to no one except one who hopes in him, and hope cannot be separated from faith and obedience either. Yet they are not therefore one, or differ only in some respect of reason, but in their forms.

units.la: Et Disp.xii.de causis peccatorum,Smalcius, p.450. Quemadmodum enim anima non est secundarium hominis, sed essentiale & formale: ita opera vel pietas Christiana ipsa sunt fidei Christianae forma & essentia. Ratione quidem aliqua distingui potest, fiducia in Deo per Christum collocata, a vera pietate & obedientia: sed reipsa nullo modo. Nam quandiu deest ipsa pietas & obedientia, tam diu fides illa nondum habet sui experimentum aut complementum, sed adhuc imperfectum est prorsus aliquid. Unde [?]sita non minus arguta quam divina D. Jacobi verba, Vides quod opera cooperabantur fidei illius, & (quod) ex operibus fides consummata est. Quemadmodum autem homo, per animam rationalem est homo, non per hoc quo anima dat sui experimentum; ita quoque non per opera, per quae fides quidem probat & ostendit se veram & rectam, & hoc esse quod est, constituitur, ut per suam forram: forma etenim non sequitur, sed rei ingreditur naturam & eam constituit: fidei vero forma in genere est, assensus; justificantis autem, de qua hic quaerimus, assensus in Christum: quod differt ab obedientia mandatorum Christi, quamvis in subjecto nunquam separari queant. Quamdiu deest pietas & obedientia, fides non modo non habet sui experimentum & complementum, vel est imperfectum aliquid, sed revera nihil, nec vera fides, à qua deesse pietas non aliquamdiu, sed nullo prorsus tempore potest. Non quidem ingrediuuntur opera, cum fide, justificationem; sed à fide tamen ipsa, seu ejus natura neutiquam sejungi possunt. Et sic opera cum fide cooperari συνεργεῖν Apostolus Jacobus dixit, & fidem ex operibus consummari. Nam fides, ut est versu illius capitis ultimo, sine operibus mortua, sive nulla est. Nempe carere bonis operibus fides non potest, uti nec vivum corpus respiratione, neque tamen in illo spiritu seu πνοῆ viventis forma sita est, sed in anima; respiratio autem viventis animae consequens est & effectum. Etiam afflictiones & omnia dicuntur piis cooperari in bonum, Rom. viii. 28. quae a pietate, seu dilectione Dei satis differunt, sed tamen cum eâ, tendunt in commune piorum bonum, uti fides cum operibus, ad probationem & demonstrationem veri fidelis atq; amici Dei. Obedientiam verò, fidei tantùm effectum appellari, non vult Smalcius, pag.152. & 170. opera & fidem non esse ita necessario distincta, ut sunt causa & effectus, quod Frantzius asserit. quamvis Crellius, effectum dicat, lib. de Deo, pag. 180 & Schlichtingius quoque, uti postea videbitur. Atque dum Jacobus de fidei operibus disputat, quasi de ejus effectis loquitur. Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis. Et quae adfert exempla, sive bene quidem volentis pauperi, non vero potrigentis necessaria; vel Abrahami filium offerentis; vel Rahab meretricis exploratores recipientis, effecta totidem fidei sunt, & ut indicia ejus, non tanquam forma, adferuntur.
units.tr: And in Disp. xii on the causes of sins, Smalcius, p. 450: For just as the soul is not an accident of man but is essential and formal, so good works or Christian piety are the form and essence of Christian faith. It can indeed be distinguished in some respect, trust placed in God through Christ, from true piety and obedience: but in fact in no way. For as long as piety and obedience itself is lacking, that faith does not yet have its experience or completion, but is still something altogether imperfect. Whence the words of St. James, no less subtle than divine, are apt: You see that works cooperated with that faith, and that by works faith was consummated. But just as a man is a man through the rational soul, not through that by which the soul gives its experience, so too a thing is constituted not through works, through which faith proves and shows itself to be true and right and to be what it is, as through its form. For form does not follow, but enters into the nature of the thing and constitutes it. The form of faith in general is assent; the form of justifying faith, about which we are inquiring here, is assent to Christ. This differs from obedience to the commands of Christ, although in the subject they can never be separated. As long as piety and obedience are lacking, faith not only lacks its experience and completion, or is something imperfect, but is really nothing, nor is it true faith. Piety cannot be lacking from true faith not for a while, but at no time at all. Works do not enter into justification together with faith, but they cannot be separated from faith itself, or from its nature. And so the Apostle James said that works cooperate with faith [συνεργεῖν] and that faith is consummated by works. For faith, as it is in the last verse of that chapter, without works is dead, that is, it is not at all. Faith certainly cannot lack good works, just as a living body cannot lack breathing; yet the form of the living body does not lie in that breath or πνοή, but in the soul, and the breathing of the living soul is a consequence and an effect. Afflictions too, and all things, are said to work together for good for the pious, Rom. viii. 28. These differ enough from piety or love of God, yet together with it they tend to the common good of the pious, just as faith with works tends to the proof and demonstration of the true faithful friend of God. But Smalcius, p. 152, does not wish obedience to be called merely an effect of faith, and 170: works and faith are not so necessarily distinct as cause and effect, which Frantzius asserts. Although Crellius says effect, in his book on God, p. 180, and Schlichting too, as will be seen later. And while James disputes about the works of faith, he speaks as if of its effects: Show me your faith from your works. The examples he brings, whether of one who kindly wishes well to the poor but does not give what is necessary, or of one offering Abraham's son, or of Rahab the harlot receiving the spies, are so many effects of faith, and are brought forward as its signs, not as its form.

units.la: Volkelius, lib. iv. cap. iii pag. 178. tres fidei distinguit gradus: primum, credere Jesum esse Christum; alterum, ejus disciplinae praebere assensum; tertium, ipsi confidere & obedire: quos tres gradus ratione intellectus, ordinisque natura inter se distinctos quidem ait, reipsa tamen inter se copulatos. Certe copulati inter se sunt, sed non unum propterea, non natura, substantia, & forma idem: quomodo supra loquentes audivimus.
units.tr: Volkelius, book iv, chapter iii, p. 178, distinguishes three degrees of faith: first, to believe that Jesus is the Christ; second, to give assent to his teaching; third, to trust in him and obey. These three degrees he says are distinct from one another by the reason of the intellect and the nature of order, yet in fact are joined together. Certainly they are joined together, but they are not therefore one, nor the same in nature, substance and form, as we heard them speaking above.

units.la: Vocatur quidem fides opus, Joan. vi. 29. & obedientia fidei, Rom. i. 5. non propterea tamen obedientia & fides idem sunt: imo quia obedientia vocatur fidei, eo discrimen notatur, ut quae à fide procedat[?]. Nam credimus, ut quoque obediamus. Quemadmodum obedientia veritatis dicitur, 1 Pet. i. 22. & diversa sunt, obedientia, ac veritas. Vel etiam potest esse, ad obedientiam fidei, id est doctrinae fidei praestandam. Quemadmodum fides saepe doctrinam fidei significat. Gal. i. 23. Sic dicitur Act. vi. 7. magna multitudo sacerdotum crediderunt fidei. & Phil. i. 27. fides Evangelii. Quid si dixisset Apo-stolus, ad obedientiam Evangelii? an propterea obedientiae & Evangelii natura & forma foret eadem? dicit autem Rom. x. 16. non obediverunt Evangelio. adde 11 Thess. i. 8. & cap. ii. 13. inquit, fide veritatis. Nec proinde veritas & fides unum sunt. Ita saepe dicitur Apostolo, justitia fidei, in epistola ad Romanos. spiritus fidei, 11 Cor. iv. 13. gaudium fidei, Phil. i.25. Quod si verò differentia facienda inter obedientiam & fidem, alia constitui non potest, quam ut fides praecedat, obedientia sequatur, ordine naturae; causalitate morali fide obedientiam proferente. Quemadmodum Jacobo dicitur cap. v. 15, oratio fidei, ex fide nimirum proveniens.
units.tr: Faith is indeed called a work, John vi. 29, and obedience of faith, Rom. i. 5, yet obedience and faith are not therefore the same. Indeed, because obedience is called of faith, the difference is marked: obedience proceeds from faith, for we believe so that we may also obey. Just as obedience is called obedience of the truth, 1 Pet. i. 22, and obedience and truth are different. Or it may be meant as rendering obedience to the faith, that is, to the doctrine of faith. Just as faith often signifies the doctrine of faith, Gal. i. 23. So Acts vi. 7 says, a great multitude of priests believed the faith, and Phil. i. 27, the faith of the Gospel. What if the Apostle had said, obedience to the Gospel? Would the nature and form of obedience and of the Gospel therefore be the same? But he says in Rom. x. 16, they did not obey the Gospel. Add 2 Thess. i. 8, and ch. ii. 13, where he says by faith of the truth. Nor therefore are truth and faith one. So the Apostle often speaks of righteousness of faith in the epistle to the Romans, spirit of faith, 2 Cor. iv. 13, joy of faith, Phil. i. 25. But if a difference is to be made between obedience and faith, none other can be established than that faith comes first and obedience follows, in the order of nature, faith producing obedience by moral causality. Just as James, ch. v. 15, speaks of the prayer of faith, that is, arising from faith.

units.la: Jam quod ad remotum genus, fides etiam potest dici obediendia, quemadmodum virtutes omnes, quae ex Dei praecepto praestantur, & sic opus, ac bonum opus sunt. Quamvis opus etiam dicatur, propter ejus ἐνέργειαν. 11 Thess. i. 3. indesinenter memores operis fidei vestrae, & laboris charitatis, & patientiae spei. Nec propterea spes quoq; & patientia idem sunt. Jam vero Joan. vi.29. eo magis opus vocatur, quia hac voce proposita fuerat quaestio, quid faciemus ut operemur opera Dei? Respondit Jesus & dixit iis, hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis &c. Quemadmodum commune est, ut in sermone servetur saepe eadem vox, licet non eodem significatu, quo prius. Sic ubi de lege multum disseruerat Apolus, non tantum legem fidei appellat, Rom. 11 1. 27. sed & legem peccati, alla-sione ad vocem, quâ passim hic utebatur. Rom. v11. 23. 25. & v11. 2. sim-pliciter autem intelligit fidem, & peccatum; & vim illorum connotat, non proprie quod fides, aut peccatum, lex fit. Uti Hebr.*v11. 16. qui non fecundum legem carnalis praecepti factus, sed fecundum vim indissolubilis vitae: ςζ' vcμcv, inquit ibi; hic, ςζ' δωνάμιν. per legem intelligit ubiq; rerum vim atq; efficaciam.
units.tr: As for the remote genus, faith too can be called obedience, just as all virtues which are performed by God's precept are, and so it is a work and a good work. Yet it is also called a work on account of its energy, 1 Thess. i. 3: unceasingly mindful of the work of your faith, and the labour of love, and the patience of hope. Nor therefore are hope and patience the same. Now John vi. 29 calls it a work all the more, because by this word a question had been put: what shall we do that we may work the works of God? Jesus answered and said to them, this is the work of God, that you believe, and so on. It is common for the same word to be kept often in a discourse, though not in the same meaning as before. So when the Apostle had discussed the law at length, he calls it not only law of faith, Rom. iii. 27, but also law of sin, by an allusion to the word he was using everywhere here, Rom. vii. 23, 25. He simply understands faith and sin, and connotes their force; he does not mean that faith or sin properly becomes a law. Likewise Heb. vii. 16: who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life. He says there [νόμον], here [δύναμιν]: everywhere he understands by law the force and efficacy of things.

units.la: Caeterum quatenus fidem contendunt esse obedientiam Adversarii, eâ ratione bona opera completi, & imputari nobis in justificationem quoque afferunt. Quae causa est quod de fidei formâ, & cum obedientiâ operum identitate ita, quomodo audivimus, disputant. Catechesis Racov. cap. ix. de Fide, pag. 281. fides in Christum comprehendit duo. Unum, ne solo Deo, sed etiam domino Jesu Christo confidamus. Alterum, ut Deo obediamus, non tantum in eo quod in lege suâ nobis praecepit, & per Christum non est abolitum, sed & omnibus iis quae Christus legi addidit. Atque fidem completi opera, & obedientiam, passim dicunt. Credendi autem verbo etiam effectus fidei, nempe pietas ei consentanea, includenda est, inquit Crellius, de Deo, cap. xxiii. pag. 180.
units.tr: Moreover, since our opponents contend that faith is obedience, they also assert that good works are fulfilled by faith and are imputed to us for justification. This is why they argue about the form of faith and its identity with the obedience of works in the way we have already heard. Catechesis Racov. ch. 9, On Faith, p. 281: Faith in Christ comprehends two things. The first is that we trust not only in God but also in the Lord Jesus Christ. The second is that we obey God, not only in what he has commanded us in his law, which has not been abolished through Christ, but also in all those things which Christ added to the law. And they say everywhere that faith fulfils works and obedience. Crellius, On God, ch. 23, p. 180: The effect of faith must also be included in believing the word, namely the piety that agrees with it.

units.la: Unde quando propter fidem justificari nos, ajunt, etiam propter opera intelligi hoc debere, liquet. Quamvis cavillum esse Smalcius, contra Frantzium, dicat pag. 212. quando propter bona opera hominem justificari, ex ipsorum sententiâ scribitur. Nempe quia meritum operibus derogant. Interim tamen & Eques Polonus, in Apologiâ inquit, quod Deus fidem nostram in Christum, vivam, & per charitatem efficacem, tanti ex suâ gratiâ & misericordiâ ducit, ut propter eam nos, qui gravissimorum peccatorum reifumus, pro justis habeat. & postea iterum dicit, propter fidem imputari nobis justitiam; tamquam propter aliquod factum. Et Smalcius, contra Frantzium, pag. 104. Non innocentiam, non justitiam Christi Deus imputat credentibus: Sed fidem illorum imputat illis pro justitia, ut Scriptura loquitur. hoc est, etiamsi fides credentium non mereatur vitam aeternam, tamen Deus ita in ea acquiescit, ac si vitam aeternam mereatur. Nempe non propter Christi justitiam, sed nostram, Deus nos justificat; & in nostrâ fide acquiescit, ac si vitam aeternam mereretur, non in merito Christi, quod ibidem calumniatur esse fictitium.
units.tr: Hence it is plain that when they say we are justified on account of faith, this must also be understood as on account of works. Although Smalcius, against Frantzius, p. 212, says that the phrase "when a man is justified on account of good works" is a quibble, it is written in their own opinion. Clearly this is because they detract from the merit of works. Nevertheless, the Polish knight also says in his Apology that God so highly values our faith in Christ, living and effective through love, out of his grace and mercy, that on account of it he regards us, who are guilty of most grievous sins, as righteous. And afterwards he again says that righteousness is imputed to us on account of faith, as though on account of some deed. And Smalcius, against Frantzius, p. 104: God does not impute the innocence or the righteousness of Christ to believers; but he imputes their faith to them as righteousness, as Scripture speaks. That is, even if the faith of believers does not merit eternal life, God nevertheless so rests in it as if it merited eternal life. Clearly, then, God justifies us not on account of the righteousness of Christ but of our own, and he rests in our faith as if it merited eternal life, not in the merit of Christ, which he there slanders as fictitious.

units.la: Quemadmodum & calumnia est Adversariorum, ex sententiâ nostra objicientium, quasi sufficeret imputari nobis justitiam Christi alienam, neque requireretur, ut & ipsi in nobis essemus pii. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. 1. pag. 314. si in salutis nostrae a vobis excogitatâ ratione, non, ut nos vere in nobis ipsis pii simus, requiritur: sed satis est Christi satisfactionem nobis imputari. Hoc quidem dicimus, in negotio justificationis, atque ad justificationem nostram, satis esse justitiam & satisfactionem Christi nobis imputari; non vero, quasi in salutis nostrae ratione totâ, non etiam exigeretur ut revera pii simus. Justificationem & sanctificationem inseparabiliter conjungimus; & Christum pariter esse justitiam credimus, ac sanctitatem; imputari Christi justitiam, & habitualem aliam nobis, ad Christi similitudinem, ingenerari, adeo ut nulla ratio sit salutis adipiscendae, nisi etiam pii vere simus. Ad veram fidem necessa-rio rió vitæ sanctitas sequitur. Ipse Socinus, postquam fidem in præsenti disputatione dixit duplicem habere significationem, primam, quâ significat, credere, Iesum esse Christum, Dei filium, &c. alteram, cum significat confidere Christo, quæ posterior sola fides ipsi est justificans, de prima, vel utriusque nexu tamen pronunciat, quicunque priore hac fide est praditus, altera carere non potest, cum fieri nequeat, ut quisquam ex animo credat, Iesum esse Christum Dei filium, &c. ac consequenter sibi persuadeat, eum habere potestatem dandi vitam æternam iis, qui ipsius præceptis obediverint, nec tamen obediat. Alioqui posset quis sua sponte prudens sciens vitam æternam aspernari, quod tamen fieri nullo modo potest. de fide & operib. pag. 54. Utrique fidei salutem attribuit, priori, quatenus præcedit, & secum necessario trahit posteriorem: posteriori vero, quatenus ea ipsa est revera, quâ justificamur, & Deo ad vitam æternam grati efficimur. Nisi per posteriorem fidem, non tam fidem intelligeret, quam bonorum operum obedientiam, & per eam justificari doceret hominem, & non per justitiam Christi, quæ isthic dicit, haud adeo improbanda viderentur.
units.tr: Just as the objection of our opponents is also a calumny, when they allege our view as if it were enough for the righteousness of Christ to be imputed to us, and it were not required that we ourselves also be godly. Socinus, On the Saviour, part 4, ch. 1, p. 314: If, in the plan of our salvation devised by you, it is not required that we ourselves be truly godly, but it is enough that the satisfaction of Christ be imputed to us. We indeed say this: in the business of justification, and for our justification, it is enough that the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ be imputed to us; but not as though, in the whole plan of our salvation, it were not also required that we really be godly. We inseparably join justification and sanctification, and we believe that Christ is our righteousness and also our holiness: the righteousness of Christ is imputed, and another, habitual righteousness is engendered in us, after the likeness of Christ, so that there is no way of obtaining salvation unless we are also truly godly. Holiness of life necessarily follows true faith. Socinus himself, after saying in the present disputation that faith has a twofold meaning, the first by which we believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, etc., and the second when it means to trust in Christ (which latter alone is justifying faith for him), pronounces concerning the first, or concerning the bond of both: Whoever is endowed with the former faith cannot lack the latter, since it cannot happen that anyone believes from the heart that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, etc., and consequently persuades himself that he has the power of giving eternal life to those who have obeyed his precepts, and yet does not obey. Otherwise someone could knowingly and deliberately, of his own accord, despise eternal life, which cannot in any way happen. On faith and works, p. 54. He ascribes salvation to both kinds of faith: to the former, insofar as it precedes and necessarily draws the latter along with it; to the latter, insofar as it is truly that by which we are justified and made acceptable to God for eternal life. Unless he meant by the latter faith not so much faith as the obedience of good works, and taught that man is justified by these rather than by the righteousness of Christ, which he speaks of there, his statements would not seem so very objectionable.

units.la: Justificatio duplex est, legalis alia, alia Evangelica: illa hominis justi est, siquidem talis daretur, id est, qui legis præcepta ad amussim servaret; ista, peccatoris & rei, qui ex Dei gratia, & liberali peccatorum condonatione, pro justo habetur, propter Christum, id est, justitiæ Christi imputationem.
units.tr: Justification is twofold: one is legal, the other evangelical. The former belongs to a man who is righteous, if such a man could be found, that is, one who kept the precepts of the law exactly; the latter belongs to a sinner and a guilty person, who by God's grace and the free forgiveness of sins is regarded as righteous, on account of Christ, that is, by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ.

units.la: Imputationis in negotio justificationis frequens est mentio, & in eâ multa hujus vertitur expositio: quare in antecessum de eo aliquid dicendum. Socinus part. ix de Servatore, cap. ii. triplicem verbi imputandi facit usum & acceptionem.
units.tr: Mention of imputation is frequent in the business of justification, and much of the discussion turns on it; therefore something must be said about it in advance. Socinus, part 9, On the Saviour, ch. 2, makes a threefold use and sense of the verb to impute.

units.la: Prima est, quando nobis imputari dicitur, quod vere non habemus. Sic, quando justitia peccatoribus imputatur, quâ ipsi in se destituuntur. Vel secundo, quando quod habemus, sed in alium finem imputatur, quam habemus; uti cum peccata, quæ vere habemus, imputantur in pœnam, ut puniantur. Tertio, quando id quod habemus in aliam rem imputatur, quam ipsum proprie est; uti quando fides imputatur pro justitiâ. Probaturus autem, nullo istorum modorum dici posse justitiam Christi nobis imputari, sic infert: non primò; nam & satisfactionem istam ante ejusdem imputationem jam habemus: immo si eam non habemus, ea ne esset quidem, & ita imputari non posset; & post imputationem non eam quidem habere existimamur: sed vere & proprie habemus. Resp. 1. Lusus est in voce habere: quod vel significat, aliquid pro nobis factum aut præstitum; vel idem etiam nobis applicatum, ut possideamus, eoque jam fruamur. Notum, quod non statim habemus, vel possidemus id, quod utcunque nostrum, vel pro nobis est: exempla manifesta sunt in legatis, hæreditatibus, donationibus etiam vulgaribus. Jam verò pro nobis quidem satisfecit Christus, ejusque satisfactio benevolo ejus affectu nobis datur, vel nobis impensa est; sed eam non mox possidemus, eâve, nisi per fidem, fruimur. Quare, uti differunt impetratio, & applicatio, quodque impetratum nobis, & nondum applicatum, etiam nec habere proprie, saltem non plene, dicimur, quemadmodum ubi idem nobis confertur & applicatur: sic non habemus satisfactionem Christi, ante ejus imputationem; at tum censemur habere, & vere etiam ac proprie eam habemus, quum imputatur: illud, quia alie-na, seu Christi est, vel à Christo præstita; istud, quia vere & proprie applicatur, ac fit nostra.
units.tr: The first is when something is said to be imputed to us which we truly do not have. So when righteousness is imputed to sinners, of which they are in themselves destitute. Or secondly, when what we do have is imputed for a different purpose from the one we have it for, as when sins, which we truly have, are imputed for punishment, so that we may be punished. Thirdly, when what we have is imputed for a different thing from what it properly is, as when faith is imputed for righteousness. Intending to prove that the righteousness of Christ cannot be said to be imputed to us in any of these ways, he infers as follows: not in the first, for we already have this satisfaction before its imputation; indeed, if we did not have it, it would not even exist, and so could not be imputed; and after the imputation we are not thought to have it merely, but truly and properly have it. Answer 1: There is a play on the word have, which may mean either that something has been done or rendered for us, or that it has also been applied to us, so that we possess it and now enjoy it. It is well known that we do not immediately have or possess what is in some sense ours or is for us: the examples are plain in legacies, inheritances, and even ordinary gifts. Now Christ has indeed made satisfaction for us, and his satisfaction is given to us by his gracious affection, or has been bestowed upon us; but we do not possess it at once, nor do we enjoy it except through faith. Therefore, just as impetration and application differ, and we are not said to have properly, or at least not fully, what has been obtained for us but not yet applied, just as when the same thing is conferred and applied to us, so we do not have the satisfaction of Christ before its imputation; but then we are reckoned to have it, and we truly and properly have it, when it is imputed: the former because it is another's, that is, Christ's, or was rendered by Christ; the latter because it is truly and properly applied and becomes ours.

units.la: Antequam igitur ea satisfactio nobis imputetur, jam eam habemus; cum ante ipsam imputationem certissimum sit, vere pro nobis satisfactum fuisse. Quod si eam ante non haberemus, nec vere etiam satisfactum ante esset: & sic antea nulla foret satisfactio. Siquidem idem est, satisfactionem esse, & satisfactum fuisse. Resp. 1. At non idem illud est, cum, satisfactionem habere. Distinctio facta fuit, non inter satisfactionem, & satisfactum esse; sed inter id, & satisfactionem habere. Et super eo facta ἔνστασις[?]. 11. ante imputationem certissimum est, verè pro nobis satisfactum esse; at non, eam nos haberi, prout diximus haberi eam, citra imputationem esse, aut dici non debere. Habemus quidem eam apud Deum, & apud Christum; sed in nobis non item, ut qui non tum extitimus, quando à Christo pro nobis satisfactum fuit. Quemadmodum vita nostra & gloria etiam nunc cum Christo abscondita est in Deo, quam nondum tamen habemus; ita satisfactio & justitia nostra in Christo semper fuit, quamvis ante imputationem eam non habeamus. 111. Unde & quam futilis consequentia sit, apparet, si satisfactionem, ante imputationem, non habemus; ergo eam ante imputationem esse nullam. Quasi dicam, gloria cælestis non est, si eam non habemus; nulla hæreditas, quàm non adimus; bonum nullum, quo non actu fruimur. Quæ à ratione & communi sensu sunt remotissima.
units.tr: Therefore, before that satisfaction is imputed to us, we already have it, since it is most certain that satisfaction was truly made for us before the imputation itself. But if we did not have it before, then satisfaction would not truly have been made before either, and thus there would have been no satisfaction before. For to be a satisfaction and to have been made are the same thing. Answer 1: But these are not the same as to have a satisfaction. The distinction drawn was not between a satisfaction and the fact that satisfaction has been made, but between that and having a satisfaction. And an objection [ἔνστασις] was raised about this. Answer 2: Before the imputation it is most certain that satisfaction was truly made for us; but it does not follow that we have it in the sense in which we said it is had, and that it cannot be said to be ours apart from imputation. We indeed have it with God and with Christ, but not in ourselves, since we did not yet exist when satisfaction was made for us by Christ. Just as our life and glory are still hidden with Christ in God, and yet we do not yet possess them, so our satisfaction and righteousness have always been in Christ, although before the imputation we do not have it. Answer 3: From this it is also apparent how futile the inference is: if we do not have satisfaction before imputation, therefore it is nothing before imputation. It would be as if I said, the heavenly glory is not, if we do not have it; there is no inheritance, if we have not yet entered upon it; there is no good, which we do not actually enjoy. These things are most remote from reason and common sense.

units.la: Jam ad alterum modum vel usum imputationis pergens Socinus, ait, nec isto modo dici posse, satisfactionem Christi imputari nobis, quando eam habemus, videlicet, ut in eum finem ea satisfactio nobis imputetur ut justificemur. Nam, inquit, animadvertere debueras, ea quæ aliquis jam habet, & illi in aliquem finem imputantur, ejus generis esse, ut effectum & finem illum alioqui non necessario sint habitura: sed fieri jure posse, ut illo careant. Nam quid imputatione illa effet opus, ut effectus & finis ille consequeretur, si fine illa imputatione, ut consequeretur, necesse esset? Peccata alicui in eum finem imputantur, ut is, prout meritus est, puniatur; quia, ut dictum est, potest ille non puniri, si ipsi peccata non imputentur, id quod à Deo jure fieri potest: cum nemini ea re, ut supra explicatum fuit, ab ipso injuria fiat.
units.tr: Now, passing on to the second mode or use of imputation, Socinus says that Christ's satisfaction cannot be said to be imputed to us in this way either, when we already have it, namely, that the satisfaction is imputed to us to this end, that we may be justified. For, he says, you ought to have noticed that things which someone already has, and which are imputed to him for some end, are of such a kind that they would not necessarily otherwise obtain that effect and end, but may rightly lack it. For what need would there be of that imputation for the effect and end to follow, if it were necessary for it to follow even without that imputation? Sins are imputed to someone for this end, that he may be punished according to what he has deserved; because, as has been said, he may go unpunished if his sins are not imputed to him, which God can rightly do, since, as was explained above, no injury is done to anyone by Him in this matter.

units.la: Resp. 1. Non hoc est de ratione ejus quod imputari dicitur, ut finis, in quem imputatur, sit alterius plane generis, & non necessario consequatur. Neque enim cujus generis hoc, vel istud sit respicimus, sed ut modo in certum finem imputetur. Sic peccata in poenam alicui imputantur. Nam, quod ait, à Deo condonari ea posse neque necessario puniri, præterquam quod supra discussimus, atque aliter quam Socinus vult, se habere ostendimus, certum est quod posita ordinatione & voluntate divina puniri debent, atque tum etiam dicuntur in poenam imputari: quod argumento est, ad imputationis rationem, nedum essentiam, haud requiri, ut id, in quod, vel in quem finem res aliqua cuipiam imputatur, illum non necessario exigat. 11. Imputatione opus est, ut fundamento connexionis & sequelæ, cur illud huc faciat, & unde sequatur; v.g. poena, ad peccatum, propter ejus ad poenam imputationem; justificatio, ad imputationem justitiæ, sive propriæ, sive alienæ. Quemadmodum merces dicitur imputari, non tantum ex gratia, sed etiam ex debito. Rom. iv. 4. Denique imputatur satisfactio Christi in justitiam, quem finem ex se necessario non habet, nam posset Deus satisfactionem ejusmodi pro alio non accipere, sed exigere ab ipsis peccatoribus; magis quam quod ait Socinus, Deum punitionem remittere posse: ergo, etiam juxta illa, locum hic habet imputatio satisfactionis alienæ, ac si nostra esset propria: quam surrogationem instituere & approbare Deus non tenebatur: imo pro suo jure alterius solutionem vel satisfactionem respuere omnino potuisset.
units.tr: Reply 1. It is not part of the nature of what is said to be imputed that the end to which it is imputed should be of a plainly different kind and not follow necessarily. For we do not look at what kind of thing this or that is, but only that it is imputed to a certain end. Thus sins are imputed to someone for punishment. For as to his saying that God can pardon them and that they need not necessarily be punished, we have already examined this above, and have shown that the matter stands otherwise than Socinus wants. It is certain that, once God's ordinance and will are posited, they ought to be punished, and then they are also said to be imputed for punishment. This is evidence that, for the nature of imputation, let alone its essence, it is not required that the end to which something is imputed to someone should necessarily follow. 2. Imputation is needed as the ground of a connection and sequence: why the thing bears on that end and whence it follows. For example, punishment follows sin because of its imputation to punishment; justification follows from the imputation of righteousness, whether one's own or another's. Just as wages are said to be imputed not only by grace but also as a debt (Rom. 4:4). Finally, Christ's satisfaction is imputed for righteousness, an end which it does not of itself necessarily have, for God could refuse to accept such a satisfaction on behalf of another and instead demand it from the sinners themselves. This is more so than Socinus's claim that God can remit punishment. Therefore, even on his own terms, the imputation of another's satisfaction takes place here just as if it were our own. God was not bound to institute and approve this substitution; indeed, in virtue of his right over another, he could have rejected the payment or satisfaction altogether.

units.la: Neque etiam tertio modo imputandi verbo & significationi in justificatione, prout à nobis exponitur, locum esse contendit Socinus, quia, cum quippiam pro alia re imputari dicitur, vult illud tale debere esse, ut ista res nec sit, neque eam vere contineat. Quo sensu ipsi dicitur fides imputari in justitiam. At Christi satisfactio vel ipsa justitia est, vel certe eam vere in se continet. Deletis enim per satisfactionem, & plane obliteratis omnibus peccatis nostris, nos vere justi sumus. Resp. Quomodo probabit Socinus, hoc, quod in aliquam rem imputatur, adeo nihil cum ea commune habere debere, ut eam nulla ratione continere possit, non ea, quâ satisfactio Christi dicitur continere nostram justitiam? Deinde, satisfactio Christi non est justitia nostra; nisi quod in justitiam imputatur. Inter quae nulla tanta est differentia, ut impediat istam, quam dicimus, imputationem. Justitia Christi imputatur nobis, tamquam nostra, ut ea absolvamur & justificemur. Quae hic est repugnantia, vel iniquitas? iii.
