Imo, ut imputatio justa sit & certa, illud, quod imputatur, cum re in quam, debet non communi modo copulari, ut imputationis æquitas appareat, tantum abest, ut pro conditione necessaria ponendum sit, ne rem contineat. Quando Paulus scribit Philemoni, ut, si quid Onesimus ei deberet, sibi imputaretur, se id solutu-rum esse, eone minus satisfactio à Paulo præstita Onesimo imputari potuisset, quia vel eminenter, ut sic loquar, continuisset, vel tam arcto modo contigisset, & causata fuisset liberationem Onesimi? par ratio est cum satisfactione Christi, & nostrâ, quæ ex ejus imputatione, absolutione & justificatione.
units.tr: Nor does Socinus contend that in the third mode of imputing, in the word and its sense in justification as we set it out, there is any place for it. This is because, when something is said to be imputed for another thing, he wants it to be such that the thing neither is nor truly contains that other. In this sense faith is said to be imputed for righteousness. But Christ's satisfaction either is itself righteousness or certainly truly contains it within itself. For with our sins blotted out by the satisfaction, and all of them plainly erased, we are truly righteous. Reply: how will Socinus prove that what is imputed to something must have so little in common with it that it cannot in any way contain it, and not in the sense in which Christ's satisfaction is said to contain our righteousness? Further, Christ's satisfaction is not our righteousness except insofar as it is imputed for righteousness. Between these there is no difference so great as to hinder the imputation we speak of. Christ's righteousness is imputed to us as ours, so that we may be absolved and justified. What contradiction or injustice is there here? 3. Indeed, for an imputation to be just and certain, what is imputed must be joined with the thing to which it is imputed not merely in a general way, so that the equity of the imputation appears. Far from it being required as a necessary condition that it should not contain the thing, it is quite the opposite. When Paul writes to Philemon that, if Onesimus owes him anything, it should be imputed to him, and that he himself will pay it, could the satisfaction made by Paul not be imputed to Onesimus for that reason, namely that it contained it eminently, as I may put it, or was so closely connected with it and caused his release? The case of Christ's satisfaction and ours is similar, which by its imputation issues in absolution and justification.

units.la: Cæterum, si eos, pro quorum peccatis absolute satisfactum est, non vere justos esse, sed tantummodo pro justis haberi contendas; id nihilominus satis est ad istam imputationem excludendam. Resp. Non negamus, vere justos esse, qui pro justis habentur. Nam & vera justitiæ perfectissimæ imputatione, quâ justificantur; & verâ propriâ habituali, quâ sanctificantur, sive duplici modo justi omnino sunt. Committit ergo fallaciam oppositionis Adversarius, atque opponit non opponenda, vid. vere justum esse, & pro justo haberi. Bene, si opponeret illa in eodem genere, nempe pro justo censeri ex imputatione justitiæ Christi, & non esse justum justitiâ propriâ suorum operum. Ista concedimus: non item simpliciter ut opponat, pro justo censeri, & non vere justum esse.
units.tr: Moreover, if you contend that those for whose sins satisfaction has been fully made are not truly righteous but are only held to be righteous, that is nonetheless enough to exclude this imputation. Reply: We do not deny that those who are held to be righteous are truly righteous. For they are wholly righteous in both ways: by the imputation of the most perfect righteousness, by which they are justified, and by their own true inherent righteousness, by which they are sanctified. Therefore the opponent commits the fallacy of opposition, and sets in opposition things that should not be opposed, namely to be truly righteous and to be held righteous. It would be fine if he opposed them within the same genus, namely to be counted righteous through the imputation of Christ's righteousness and not to be righteous by the righteousness of one's own works. We grant this. But we do not grant his simple opposition of being held righteous to being truly righteous.

units.la: Ad instantiam nostram, quod Christi satisfactio imputatur, quasi nostra esset, ipsique pro peccatis nostris satisfecissemus, respondet Socinus, eodem capite II. part. IV. Primum ista imputatione nihil est opus. Nam, si Christus pro peccatis nostris satisfecit: annon hoc satis superque est, ut peccata nostra deleantur? Quid igitur opus est, ut nos ipsi pro illis satisfecisse censeamur? Certe istud, si modo fieri potest, vel sine ulla imputatione ex ipsa Christi satisfactione necessario proficisci tur: vel inutile plane est. Resp. 1. Quod Christus pro peccatis nostris satisfecit, satis ad hoc est ut peccata nostra deleantur, scilicet de jure, ac merito; sed idem quoque ut nobis applicetur, (applicatio autem in justificatione fit per imputationem) requiritur, propter nos, & animi nostri sensum ac tranquillitatem, id est, propter justificationem, quemadmodum supra diximus, passivam, utcunque activae factum satis fuerit, per satisfactionem a Christo praestitam. Omnino ergo opus est illa imputatione, propter nos scilicet, & nostram justificationem. II. Praeter illud non dicimus opus esse, tanquam diversa alia re, ut nos ipsi praeterea pro illis satisfecisse censeamur. Verum in ipsa imputatione id continetur: nam in ista, quasi ipsi satisfecissemus, censetur. III. Neque dicimus, ut dicentes nos facit Socinus, nobis acceptum ferri id, quod Christus pro nobis solvit: neque enim acceptum tulit Deus, quod revera ipsi solutum a Christo fuit, quum acceptilatio fit modo imaginaria solutio, & acceptum ferri dicatur quod vere solutum non est, & cujus obligatio per sola verba tollitur: sed veram & realem satisfactionem Christi, pro nobis, imputat Deus in illum credentibus.
units.tr: To our objection, that Christ's satisfaction is imputed as though it were ours, and as though we ourselves had satisfied for our sins, Socinus replies in the same chapter, part IV, chapter II: First, there is no need for this imputation. For if Christ has satisfied for our sins, is this not more than enough for our sins to be blotted out? Why then is it necessary that we ourselves should be counted as having satisfied for them? Surely this, if it can be done at all, follows of necessity from Christ's own satisfaction without any imputation, or else it is wholly useless. Reply 1. That Christ has satisfied for our sins is enough for them to be blotted out, namely by right and by merit; but the same is also required so that it may be applied to us (and application in justification takes place by imputation), for our sake, and for the sense and tranquillity of our mind, that is, for justification, which, as we said above, is passive, although the active side has been sufficiently accomplished by the satisfaction Christ has rendered. There is therefore entirely a need for that imputation, namely for our sake and for our justification. 2. Apart from this, we do not say that there is a need, as if it were some other different thing, for us to be counted as having ourselves additionally satisfied for them. Rather, this is contained in the imputation itself, for in it we are counted as if we had satisfied. 3. Nor do we say, as Socinus makes us say, that what Christ paid for us is credited to us. For God has not credited to us what was in fact paid to him by Christ, since an acceptilation is merely an imaginary payment, and what is credited is that which has not truly been paid, and whose obligation is removed by words alone. Rather, God imputes to those who believe in him the true and real satisfaction of Christ made for us.

units.la: Atque ita apparet, nullum ex tribus modis, quibus vocem & naturam imputationis Socinus explicuit, nobis repugnare, sed quocunque modo velit, Christi justitiam & satisfactionem nobis imputari, sive applicari: nam non ista inter illa duo, imputari & applicari, quamvis hoc latius se extendat, quam illud, differentia constituenda est, quam Socinus vult, neque difficultate nova illud premit, quam non in antecedentibus sustulimus: nec etiam imputatio tantum est rerum, quae in nobis sunt, & in hunc aut istum finem imputantur, sed & rei extra nos, seu justitiae alienae & Christi, quae nostra fit per imputationem, quod unice hic spectatur.
units.tr: And so it appears that none of the three modes by which Socinus has explained the word and nature of imputation stands against us. However he wishes it, Christ's righteousness and satisfaction are imputed or applied to us. For there is no difference to be drawn between imputing and applying, of the kind Socinus wants, between these two, although the latter extends more widely than the former. Nor does he press any new difficulty which we have not already removed in what precedes. Nor is imputation only of things that are in us, imputed to this or that end, but also of a thing outside us, namely the righteousness and satisfaction of another, Christ's, which becomes ours through imputation. This alone is what is looked at here.

units.la: Denique errant, qui vocem imputationis ita accipiunt, ut hoc demum imputari ad justitiam dicatur, quod in se est imperfectum, quemadmodum fides vel obedientia nostra, at gratiose a Deo quasi pro perfecto habita & aestimata. Quod de materia, vel re nobis in justitiam imputata, negamus. Neque judicis justi foret, pro justitia habere, quod tale omni ex parte non fit. Sed & imputare de re, ut se habet, justa, vel perfecta ad hoc, ad quod imputatur, accipiendum. Uti quando imputari alicui dicuntur peccata; vel etiam non imputari, quod in remissione fit, ad poenam. Et in vulgari sermone dicitur alicui imputari sua culpa. D. de eo per quem. 1. 1. imputare sibi debet, qui crudelis fuit, & Paulus Philemoni, verf. 18. si quod tibi abstulit, aut debet, hoc mihi imputa. & Rom. IV.4. operanti imputatur merces ex debito. Et sic Christo nobis facto justitia, haec nobis imputatur perfecta, non aestimatur ut imperfecta. Phil. III. 9. non habens meam justitiam, quae esset imperfecta: sed illam quae est Christi per fidem, justitiam ex Deo per fidem. Quae est perfectissima, & omnibus numeris absoluta.
units.tr: Finally, those err who take the word imputation in such a way that something is said to be imputed to righteousness only if it is in itself imperfect, as our faith or obedience is, but is regarded and reckoned by God, out of grace, as if it were perfect. We deny this of the matter or thing imputed to us for righteousness. Nor would it be the part of a just judge to count as righteousness something that is not wholly righteous in every respect. Rather, to impute is to reckon a thing as it actually stands, whether just or perfect, to that for which it is imputed. So sins are said to be imputed to someone, or, on the other hand, not imputed, which happens in forgiveness, with respect to punishment. And in common speech a person is said to have his own fault imputed to him. D. de eo per quem, 1. 1: he must impute it to himself who was cruel. And Paul to Philemon, verse 18: if he has wronged you or owes you anything, impute it to me. And Rom. 4. 4: to him who works, the wages are imputed as a debt. So, Christ's righteousness being made ours, this is imputed to us as perfect; it is not reckoned as imperfect. Phil. 3. 9: not having my own righteousness, which would be imperfect, but that which is Christ's through faith, the righteousness which is from God by faith. This is most perfect and complete in every respect.

units.la: Tom. 2. Socinus, ut ostendat, cap. 111. partis iv. perperam dici, Christi satisfactionem nobis per fidem imputari, applicari, sive impartiri, arguit, istud aut seipsum destruere, aut perquam absurdam sententiam continere: & illud quidem hoc modo: etenim nisi nobis ea credenda sunt, quae non sunt vera, & nisi Deus ejusmodi fidem a nobis requirit, quae falsa credat: necesse est, antequam istam fidem habeamus, vere pro nobis jam satisfactum esse. Vere inquam, id est, reipsa: & sic, non sub aliqua conditione, nimirum, si id ipsum crediderimus. Resp. Imo antequam credimus, revera pro nobis satisfactum est a Christo, neque fides nostra facit, ut ei satisfiat, sed credimus, pro nobis satisfactum esse, & non a conditione fidei pendere satisfactionem nostram: sed aliud est, satisfactionem illam nobis imputari, vel applicari, quod a fidei pendet conditione, vel illam demum fieri seu praestari, quod a Christo factum. Atque de eo instituta erat quaestio, num seipsum everteret, quod dicimus, satisfactionem Christi nobis imputari; non, quomodo facta esset. De applicatione satisfactionis quaerebatur, non de ipsa. Facta est a Christo absolute; sed nobis non applicatur citra fidem.
units.tr: In volume 2, chapter 111 of part 4, Socinus, to show that it is wrongly said that Christ's satisfaction is imputed, applied or imparted to us through faith, argues that this either destroys itself or contains a most absurd opinion. He argues thus: For unless we are to believe things that are not true, and unless God requires of us a faith that believes what is false, it is necessary that, before we have this faith, satisfaction has truly been made for us already. Truly, I say, that is, in fact; and so not under any condition, namely, if we believe it. Reply: On the contrary, before we believe, satisfaction has in truth been made for us by Christ, and our faith does not bring it about that satisfaction is made to him; rather we believe that satisfaction has been made for us, and our satisfaction does not depend on the condition of faith. But it is one thing for that satisfaction to be imputed or applied to us, which depends on the condition of faith, and another for it to be made or performed, which was done by Christ. And the question raised was whether what we say, that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us, overturns itself; not how it was made. The question concerned the application of the satisfaction, not the satisfaction itself. It was made by Christ absolutely; but it is not applied to us apart from faith.

units.la: Absurditatem sententiae nostrae probat eodem modo: sed finge, non pugnare hoc inter se, quid alioqui absurdius excogitari potest, quam alicui beneficium dari, si credat, sibi beneficium datum fuisse? Nam, si beneficium datum est, quid opus est, ad ipsum beneficium consequendum, credi datum fuisse? Resp. 1. Absurdum videatur beneficium dari, si credas datum fuisse, ubi dari & datum fuisse, ad idem intelligis, secundum idem, & eodem modo. Sed ubi diversimode, ulla in hoc repugnantia est, vel absurditas, credere beneficium aliquod tibi datum, & dari, & porro datum iri, nimirum ex vi & ratione prioris, quod praecessit.
units.tr: He proves the absurdity of our view in the same way: But grant that these do not conflict with each other. What more absurd can be devised than for a benefit to be given to someone if he believes that a benefit has been given to him? For if the benefit has been given, what need is there to believe that it was given, in order to obtain the benefit itself? Reply 1: It would seem absurd for a benefit to be given if you believe it was given, when to be given and to have been given are understood as the same thing, in the same respect and in the same way. But where they are understood differently, there is no contradiction or absurdity in believing that some benefit has been given to you, and is being given, and will further be given, namely by the force and reason of what went before.

units.la: 11. Tum beneficium datum intelligi potest dupliciter, datum prote, & datum tibi; Christi satisfactio consideratur & creditur a nobis ut beneficium a Christo pro nobis praestitum, non tamen nobis collatum seu datum, nisi quando credimus. Iterum ergo, ejus impetratio in praeterito est, & absoluta; appliatio in praesenti fit, & per fidem; sed ita, ut ab hac nequaquam illius veritas pendeat vel certitudo. III. Opus est ad beneficium consequendum in te, & apud te applicative, ut credas illud datum fuisse, vel impetratum a Christo: non tua fide opus est in Christo, beneficium tibi illud, vel prote consequente. Deni-que, in eo quod credimus, praeteritum & futurum tempus respicimus, be-neficia praeterita & futura, quia & ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις [?] fides est, & πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος [?] οὐ βλεπομένων, etiam in praeterito. Ut non mirum videri Adversario debeat, quod hic etiam allegat, quando fidem, quâ justi-ficamur, Dei promissionibus niti asserimus, quae futurum tempus respiciunt, & quoque in praeteritum: nempe alia, & alia ratione.
units.tr: 11. Then a benefit given can be understood in two ways: as given to the Father and as given to you. Christ's satisfaction is considered and believed by us as a benefit procured by Christ for us, but it is not bestowed or given to us except when we believe. Therefore its procurement lies in the past and is absolute; its application takes place in the present, and through faith; but in such a way that its truth or certainty does not depend on this at all. III. To obtain the benefit in you, and as applied to you, you need to believe that it was given or obtained by Christ; no faith of yours is needed in Christ for the benefit to be yours, with the Father already consenting. Finally, in what we believe we look to both past and future time, to benefits past and future, since faith is the substance of things hoped for [ὑπόστασις ἐλπιζομένων], and the evidence of things not seen [πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων], also in the past (Heb. 11. 1). So it ought not to seem strange to the Opponent that he adduces this also, when we assert that the faith by which we are justified rests on God's promises, which look to future time and also to past time, namely in different ways and for different reasons.

units.la: Jonas Schlichtingius, Disp. pro Socino, contra Meisnerum, de Justificatione, pag. 246. duplicem imputationis dat expositionem, quando alicui aliquid imputari dicitur; vid. ut intelligatur vel simpliciter, vel ad aliquid. Simpliciter dicit alicui imputari justitiam, Rom. iv. 6. & peccatum, verf. 8. Ad aliquid dicit alicui imputari fidem, nempe ad justitiam, vel[?]. 3. 5. Cum igitur justitia alicui imputari dicitur, per justitiam intelligenda est justificatio, inquit, & sensus est, justificationem alicui tribui, nullo ipsius merito, sed ex mera gratia & benignitate. Illud male, quod justitiam dicit esse justificationem: justitia ipsa non est justificatio, sed ad eam; etenim per & propter justitiam, aliquis justificatur. Justificatio est actio Dei; justitia, qua homo justificatur, est extra Deum, & vel propria hominis; vel, eâ ubi destituitur, aliena Salvatoris. Nequaquam vero justitia ipsa est justificatio.
units.tr: Jonas Schlichting, in his Disputation for Socinus, against Meisner, on Justification, p. 246, gives a twofold explanation of what is meant when something is said to be imputed to someone, namely whether it is understood simply or with respect to something. Simply, he says, righteousness is imputed to someone, Rom. 4. 6, and sin, verse 8. With respect to something, faith is imputed to someone, namely for righteousness, Gal. 3. 5. Since therefore righteousness is said to be imputed to someone, he says, righteousness is to be understood as justification, and the sense is that justification is bestowed on someone with no merit of his own, but from sheer grace and kindness. He is wrong in saying that righteousness is justification: righteousness itself is not justification, but is related to it; for a person is justified through and on account of righteousness. Justification is an action of God; the righteousness by which a man is justified is outside God, and is either the man's own or, where he lacks it, the Saviour's. Righteousness itself is by no means justification.

units.la: Justitia Christi vulgo distinguitur in activam, & passivam. Ista in passionibus ejus spectatur, quibus pro peccatis nostris plenissime satisfecit; illa, in obedientiâ vitae, secundum omnia legis officia praestita. Non quod divelli à se queant, nam & per totam vitam passus Christus fuit, & in omni passione omnibus legis praeceptis satisfecit. Ante peccatum tenetur homo duntaxat ad praestationem legis perfectam, ut justificationem mereatur & vitam lege promissam; sed post peccatum, ad poenas tenetur, quas commeritus est; semper autem ad legis conservationem, quatenus est homo. Quare, Christus nostram acturus causam & facturus satis, primum quidem pati & exsolvere poenas nostras debuit, inde etiam legem servare perfectissime, ἵνα τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νό-μου πληρωθῇ ἐν ἡμῖν. Rom. viii. 4.
units.tr: Christ's righteousness is commonly distinguished into active and passive. The latter is seen in his sufferings, by which he fully satisfied for our sins; the former in the obedience of his life, rendered according to all the duties of the law. Not that they can be separated from each other, for Christ suffered throughout his whole life, and in every suffering he also satisfied all the precepts of the law. Before sin, a man is bound only to the perfect performance of the law, so that he may merit justification and the life promised by the law; but after sin he is bound to the punishments he has deserved, and always to the keeping of the law, insofar as he is a man. Therefore Christ, about to plead our cause and make satisfaction, had first of all to suffer and pay the penalties for us, and then also to keep the law most perfectly, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us [ἵνα τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου πληρωθῇ ἐν ἡμῖν] (Rom. 8. 4).

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 120. Euangelici isti, cum quibus Socino res est, hoc est Calviniani, solius satisfactionis Christi per sanguinis fusionem, ut plurimum meminisse solent, cum causam justificationis nostrae coram Deo assignant, & fidem justificare definiunt. Resp. Nec illi, quos Calvinianos probrose nominat Auctor, ut plurimum solius satisfactionis in negotio justificationis meminisse solent; neque id faciunt ideo, quod activam obedientiam excludant; sed ut per synecdochen, unâ specie, vel parte commemorata aliam quoque comprehendant.
units.tr: Schlichting, p. 120: Those evangelicals with whom Socinus has to do, that is the Calvinists, are for the most part accustomed to mention only the satisfaction of Christ through the shedding of blood, when they assign the cause of our justification before God, and when they define that faith justifies. Reply: Neither do those whom the author insults by calling them Calvinists, for the most part, make mention only of satisfaction in the matter of justification; nor do they do so because they exclude active obedience, but because, by synecdoche, mentioning one species or part, they include the other as well.

units.la: Deinde addit, alterutram causam sufficere, utramque autem consistere simul non posse. Si enim, ait, Christus pro omnibus peccatis nostris, & praeteritis, & praesentibus, & futuris, morte sua satisfecit; nihil operis est ut pro nobis justus fuisse dicatur: & vicissim, si Christus pro nobis justus fuit, sic ut ipsius justitia nobis imputari queat, nullus relictus est locus satisfactioni per poenarum solutionem. Ubi enim peccatum non est, ibi nec poena locum habere potest. Resp. 1. Negatur utriusque consequentia. Prioris, quia satisfactione pro peccatis opus fuit, ne illa nos damnarent; justitiâ ut liberati vitam consequeremur: neque enim is, qui à miseriâ liberatur, per hoc omni beatus est felicitate; nec passioni, sed actioni, qui egerit illa, vitae merces attribuitur. Et Socinus in justificatione etiam conjungit, absolvi, & praemium assequi. Notis in Dial. pag. 39. in eo justificando, id est, pro justo habendo ac praemio afficiendo. Crellius distinguit, in epistolam ad Gal. p. 220. justificationis acceptionem facit duplicem, unam, quae significet tantum liberationem à reatu peccatorum, seu absolutionem ab obligatione ad poenam; alteram, quae continet in se non solùm immunitatem à poenis, sed etiam verum & perfectum praemium justitiae, hoc est, salutem aeternam. Posterioris negatur itidem consequentia, quia nec locus justitiae Christi in nobis fuit, nisi ex-solutis solutis primò peccatorum debitis, ut, quemadmodum ibi quid solvi solet, ubi ultimum ligatur, ita reatus primo auferretur, ut vitæ & justitiæ fieret locus. Deinde, verum quidem, ubi justitia est, non requiri satisfactionem, sed ubi peccavit homo, ad restitutionem ejus in integrum, utrumque, satisfactio requiritur, & quoque justitia. Revera, ubi peccatum non est, nec pœnæ locus esse potest: sed ubi jam peccatum præcedit, uti in nobis justificandis & redimendis, primùm solutio priorum exigitur debitorum; inde justitia vitæ, seu præceptorum ac officiorum omnium observatio. Sed per Christi justitiam activam peccatum tollitur. Verùm non actione, sed passione, & pœnæ solutione reatus aufertur: justitia pro se debetur, neque potest pro præteritis delictis impendi. Pœnis debitis, passione; legibus, earundem observatione satisfit & præstatione: non passione, observantiæ præceptorum; neque hac, merito reatui. Adeoque à miseriâ liberamur illo; vitæ verò restituimur, isto modo.
units.tr: Next he adds that either cause suffices, but both cannot stand together. For if, he says, Christ by his death has satisfied for all our sins, past, present and future, there is no point in saying that he was righteous on our behalf; and conversely, if Christ was righteous on our behalf, so that his righteousness can be imputed to us, no place is left for satisfaction by the payment of penalties. For where there is no sin, there can be no place for punishment. Reply 1: The consequence of each is denied. Of the first: satisfaction for sins was needed so that they would not condemn us, and righteousness so that we, being freed, might obtain life; for a man who is freed from misery is not thereby made blessed with every happiness; and the reward of life is attributed not to suffering but to action, to him who has performed those things. And Socinus, in justification, also joins being absolved with obtaining the reward: Notes on the Dialogue, p. 39: in justifying him, that is, in holding him as just and rewarding him. Crell, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, p. 220, distinguishes the acceptance of justification as twofold: one which signifies only liberation from the guilt of sins, or absolution from the obligation to punishment; the other, which contains not only immunity from punishments but also the true and perfect reward of righteousness, that is, eternal salvation. The consequence of the second is likewise denied, because there was no place for Christ's righteousness in us unless first the debts of sins had been paid off; just as, where something is to be paid, the last is loosed first, so guilt had first to be removed so that a place might be made for life and righteousness. Further, it is true that where there is righteousness no satisfaction is required; but where man has sinned, both satisfaction and righteousness are required for his restoration to integrity. Indeed, where there is no sin, there can be no place for punishment; but where sin has already gone before, as in our justification and redemption, first the payment of the earlier debts is demanded, and then the righteousness of life, that is, the keeping of all the precepts and duties. But by Christ's active righteousness sin is not taken away. Guilt is removed not by action but by suffering and the payment of punishment: righteousness is owed for itself, and cannot be offered for past offences. Satisfaction is made to the debts of punishment by suffering, and to the laws by keeping and performing them: not by suffering, the keeping of the precepts; nor by the latter, merit to guilt. Thus we are freed from misery by the one, and restored to life by the other.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 128. Si Christi passiones rationem obedientiæ habent, rationem pœnæ habere non possunt. Obedientia enim virtus, pœna autem propter inobedientiam infligitur. Resp. i. Christi passiones physicè spectatæ non habent rationem obedientiæ, sed in concreto, prout eas Christus sustinuit. ii. Rationem obedientiæ habuerunt, passivæ: uti quis obedientiam Deo probat, non modò agendo, sed etiam bene patiendo. iii. Atque ita in Sacris exserte nominatur ista Christi obedientia. Phil. ii. 1. ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου[?] Hebr. x. 5. &c. iv. Christi passiones rationem pœnæ habuerunt, quatenus à Deo ipsi fuerunt inflictæ; obedientiæ rationem, quatenus à Christo latæ. v. Quomodo rationem afflictionis habere potuerunt & virtutis, quæ Adversarii haud inficiantur; ita rationem habuerunt pœnæ, & virtutis. vi. Quæ illa est illatio, pœna autem propter inobedientiam infligitur? Non enim quæritur, propter quod Christus pœnas passus sit, sed quomodo, & quam obedienter se in iis sustinendis gesserit. Non Christo propter se, vel suam, sed nostram inobedientiam, impactæ fuerunt pœnæ.
units.tr: Schlichting, p. 128: If Christ's sufferings have the character of obedience, they cannot have the character of punishment. For obedience is a virtue, but punishment is inflicted on account of disobedience. Reply: (i) Christ's sufferings, considered physically, do not have the character of obedience, but in the concrete, as Christ endured them, they do. (ii) They had the character of obedience in a passive sense, just as someone proves his obedience to God not only by acting but also by suffering well. (iii) This obedience of Christ is expressly named in Holy Scripture: Phil. ii. 1. [ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου], Hebr. x. 5., etc. (iv) Christ's sufferings had the character of punishment insofar as they were inflicted on him by God, and the character of obedience insofar as they were borne by Christ. (v) How they could have the character of affliction and of virtue, which our opponents do not deny, is how they had the character of both punishment and virtue. (vi) What is the force of that inference, but punishment is inflicted on account of disobedience? For the question is not on account of what Christ suffered punishments, but how, and how obediently he conducted himself in enduring them. The punishments were not laid upon Christ on account of himself or his own disobedience, but on account of ours.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA.
units.tr: SECTION TWO.

units.la: Jam verò argumentis experiamur, an Christi justitiam nobis imputari merum commentum sit, uti Socinus convitiatur, part. iv. de Servat. cap. iv. & quum de duobus potissimum futura sit disputatio, de justificatione, & de fide: de illa agamus prius. Sitque hoc
units.tr: Now let us test by arguments whether the imputation of Christ's righteousness to us is a mere fabrication, as Socinus rails in part iv, On the Saviour, chapter iv. Since the dispute will concern chiefly two things, justification and faith, let us deal first with justification. Let this be our argument.

units.la: Argumentum nostrum primum: Quæ justificatio nullo modo est per, aut propter nostra opera, quomodocunque & qualitercunque considerata, ea nec est per aut propter obedientiam præceptorum Euangelicorum: sed justificatio nostra nullo modo est per aut propter nostra opera: ergo. Probatur Minor, tum locis Scripturæ exsertis; tum iis, quibus hoc in negotio ipsa utitur, argumentis.
units.tr: Our first argument: That justification is in no way through or on account of our works, however and in whatever manner they are considered. That which is not through or on account of our works is not through or on account of obedience to the evangelical precepts. But our justification is in no way through or on account of our works. Therefore, [our justification is not through or on account of obedience to the evangelical precepts]. The minor premise is proved both by express passages of Scripture and by the arguments which Scripture itself uses in this matter.

units.la: Illa sunt, primò quæ affirmant nos non justificari per opera: deinde, justisicari nos fine operibus. Quod si ergo, non per opera, sed imo fine operibus justificamur, non igitur per obedientiam nostram, quorumcunque etiam praeceptorum. Illud haec loca probant: Rom. iii. 20. Propterea ex operibus legis non justificatur ulla caro coram eo, ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ[?], ex Hebraismo כִּי לֹא בָשָׂר[?], id est, nulla caro. Quod autem opera legis exprimuntur, non est ἀγαθῶν[?] operum, uti & postea plenius ostendemus, sed operum quorumvis indicativum, quia certe nisi ex lege sint & ἔννομα, jam non sunt bona, & hoc epitheto, quod Paulus passim adjungit, tacite continetur argumentum, quo pugnabant Adversarii, nimirum opera, quae ad justificationem urgebant, legis esse, à Deo ipso latae. Ergo non ut opera legis ab aliis secernantur, sed ut quaevis opera significentur, illud additum fuit: quae omnia Apostolo, in causa justificationis, rejiciuntur. Deinde Gal. ii. 16. ter uno versu dicitur, ex operibus legis hominem non justificari. Tit. iii. 5. Non ex operibus οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς, verum secundum misericordiam suam salvavit nos. Deinde, & sine operibus justificari dicimur, Rom. iii. 28. Colligimus ergo, fide justificari hominem χωρὶς ἔργων νόμου. Cap. iv. 5. τῷ δὲ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ. 6. ὡς ὁ θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων. Quae legis opera alibi, hic simpliciter opera appellat. Non operanti, haud modo secundum legem: & Deus justitiam imputat, absque operibus, simpliciter quibuscunque. Socinus, in Notis ad Dialog. de Justific. pag. 32. Atqui Paulus cap. 4. ad Rom. affirmat, hominem justificari a Deo sine operibus, non addita voce legis, idque exemplo Abrahami, & testimonio Davidis comprobat. Quorum alter non legitur justificatus fuisse apud Deum operibus, sed fide: Alter vero eos beatos esse testatur, quorum remissae fuerunt iniquitates. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum fit, Paulum negare, non modo ex operibus legis, sed simpliciter ex operibus, nos justificari.
units.tr: These passages are of two kinds: first, those which affirm that we are not justified by works; second, those which affirm that we are justified without works. If therefore we are justified not by works but indeed without works, then we are not justified by our obedience to any precepts whatever. The following passages prove the first point. Rom. 3:20: "Therefore by the works of the law no flesh is justified before him [ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ]," which is the Hebrew idiom "for no flesh" [כִּי לֹא בָשָׂר], that is, no flesh at all. That the works of the law are named here does not refer to good works, as we will also show more fully later, but to works of any kind. For unless they are from the law and lawful [ἔννομα], they are no longer good works at all. The epithet which Paul constantly adds carries a hidden argument, with which the adversaries were contending: namely, that the works which they urged for justification are works of the law given by God himself. So the addition was made not to separate the works of the law from other works, but to signify works of any kind; and all of these are rejected by the Apostle as grounds of justification. Again, Gal. 2:16 says three times in one verse that a man is not justified by the works of the law. Tit. 3:5: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done [οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς], but according to his mercy he saved us." Next, we are said to be justified also without works. Rom. 3:28: "We conclude, therefore, that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law [χωρὶς ἔργων νόμου]." Chapter 4:5: "to him who does not work [τῷ δὲ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ]." Verse 6: "God imputes righteousness without works [ὡς ὁ θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων]." Elsewhere he calls them the works of the law, but here he simply says works: to the one who does not work, not merely not according to the law; and God imputes righteousness without works, simply without any works whatever. Socinus, in his Notes on the Dialogue on Justification, p. 32: "But Paul, in chapter 4 to the Romans, affirms that man is justified by God without works, without adding the word law, and he confirms this by the example of Abraham and the testimony of David. Of these, the former is not read as having been justified before God by works but by faith; the latter testifies that those are blessed whose iniquities have been forgiven. From all these things it is manifest that Paul denies that we are justified not only by the works of the law but simply by works."

units.la: Schlichtingius, pag. 246. Idem indicant addita a Paulo verba, sine operibus, quae nihil aliud significant, quam, etiamsi homo operibus suis justificari non mereatur. quid autem operibus & vita innocentia meremur? certe non vitam innocentiam, sive propriam, sive alienam; sed justificationem, si perfecta sit innocentia. adde, quod haec verba, sine operibus, tacitam quandam oppositionem continent, & indicent, justitiae attributionem sua natura impediri, cum absunt opera, adeo ut, nisi divina gratia accedat, ubi non sint opera, ibi non debeat esse justitia. At vero imputatio innocentiae alienae non habet locum, nisi ibi, ubi non sunt propria opera. Ubi enim est propria innocentia, ibi nihil est opus alienâ. At vero ubi sunt opera, ibi tantum abest, ut locum non habeat haec justitia, ut potius non secundum gratiam imputetur, sed secundum debitum tribuatur, verf. 4.
units.tr: Schlichting, p. 246: "The words which Paul adds, without works, indicate the same thing, which signify nothing other than that, even if a man does not deserve to be justified by his works, what do we deserve by works and innocent life? Certainly not life or innocence, whether our own or another's, but justification, if the innocence be perfect. Add that these words, without works, contain a certain tacit opposition, and indicate that the attribution of righteousness is by its nature hindered when works are absent, so that, unless divine grace comes in, where there are no works there ought not to be righteousness. But the imputation of another's innocence has no place except where there are no works of one's own. For where there is one's own innocence, there is nothing needing another's. But where there are works, this righteousness has so far from no place that it is not imputed according to grace but is rendered according to what is owed, verse 4."

units.la: Resp. i. Verba addita apud Paulum, sine operibus, non modo dicunt, hominem operibus suis justificationem non mereri, sed simpliciter nec justificari. Quid enim in textu est, quod solum meritum impugnat; & non justificationem ex operibus, illis sive meritum novo errore attribuatur, sive minus? sine operibus ergo est, sine operibus quibuscunque, & non demum sine meritis.
units.tr: Reply 1. The words which Paul adds, without works, do not merely say that a man does not merit justification by his works, but that he is not justified at all. For what is in the text that attacks merit alone, and not justification by works? Whether merit is ascribed to them by a new error or less so? So it is without works: without works of any kind, and not merely without merits.

units.la: 11. Opera Apostolus impetit, non meritum, quod imo agnoscit operanti deberi , χ[?] τὸ ὀφείλημα: Sed negat, non merenti, sed operanti justificationem, τῷ δ[?]ὲ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ. Scilicet, quia nemo est, cui ex operibus justitia attribui queat. III. Jam autem Deus non solum ex operibus non justificat, quia non merentur, sed nec quomodocunque consideratis, quia longe contrario modo statuit justificari hominem, scilicet ex fide in Christum Jesum. Tum, non ideo ex operibus, quia non sunt perfecta. Non enim opera si observet Deus, ex iis justum pronunciare potest, nisi qui talis sit; at vero, propter multifarias imperfectiones, non ita sumus justi, quin quoque injusti, & si ex judicio Deus agat nobiscum, nosque justificet, non poterit justos dicere, quin simul etiam injustos, id est, saltem non justificabit ex operibus. IV. Jam & torquet Apostoli verba contra ipsum, & sine operibus vult indicare, non nisi cum operibus. Quod probet. Ait, justitiæ attributionem suâ naturâ impediri, cum absunt opera. An quando absunt in ratione & negotio justificationis? Hoc rectâ est contra Apostolum, qui sine operibus justificari hominem docet, haud semel; & Deum justificare impium. Sic est, imputatio innocentiæ alienæ non habet locum, nisi ubi non sunt propria opera. Ubi enim est propria innocentia, ibi nihil est opus alienâ. Atqui non, ubi sunt opera, ibi locum non habet justitia: sed ubi locum habet ista justitia, ibi non sunt opera. Illud enim, contra rei veritatem, præsupponere videtur, ac si bona opera essent in justificando. Namque si bona opera hic locum haberent, ita ut ex iis justificari homo posset, jam non secundum gratiam, sed debitum eis adscriberetur merces.
units.tr: 2. The Apostle attacks works, not merit, which he in fact acknowledges as owed to the one who works [χ[?] τὸ ὀφείλημα]. But he denies justification not to the one who merits but to the one who works [τῷ δὲ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ]. Clearly, because there is no one to whom righteousness can be attributed on account of works. 3. But God does not justify from works only because they do not merit, but not even when they are considered in any way whatever, since he has decided on the very opposite manner, that man is justified by faith in Christ Jesus. Moreover, he does not justify through works because they are not perfect. For if God observed works, he could pronounce a man just from them only if he were such a man. But on account of their many imperfections we are not so just that we are not also unjust at the same time; and if God were to deal with us according to judgment and justify us, he could not call us just without also calling us unjust at the same time; that is, at least he would not justify us by works. 4. Moreover, he turns the Apostle's words against himself, and by without works he wishes to indicate nothing but with works. Let him prove it. He says that the attribution of righteousness is by its nature hindered when works are absent. But is this when they are absent in the matter and business of justification? This is directly against the Apostle, who teaches more than once that a man is justified without works, and that God justifies the ungodly. Thus: the imputation of another's innocence has no place except where there are no works of one's own. For where there is one's own innocence, there is nothing needing another's. But it is not the case that where there are works, righteousness has no place; rather, where this righteousness has its place, there are no works. For the other claim seems, contrary to the truth of the matter, to presuppose that good works are at work in justifying. For if good works had a place here, so that a man could be justified by them, then the reward would be assigned to them not according to grace but as a debt.

units.la: Deinde, argumenta Scripturæ, confirmantia, hominem ex operibus nullo pacto justificari posse, sunt, 1. quia omnes homines peccarunt, eoque destituuntur gloriâ Dei. Rom. III.23. Gal. III. 10. II.22. sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato, ut promissio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur credentibus. Qui sunt peccatores omnes, eoque sub condemnatione, justificari eatenus non possunt; sed per opera sua omnes homines tales sunt. Verum, propter bona opera, dices, justificabuntur. At bona ista non possunt satisfacere pro malis prioribus, vel illa justificare. Quando autem secundum opera Deus pronunciat, non potest magis secundum bona absolvere, quam juxta mala condemnare: immo, existentibus aliquibus malis, secundum bona non potest justificare, quia maledictus est qui non permanserit in omnibus. In Euangelio, dices, aliter id se habet. Quod ad illam ex operibus justitiam, proba. Quinimo in Euangelio illud confirmatur, operum respectu. Gal. III. 10. ideoque nec eadem via operum, sed diversa longe, fidei nempe per Christum, justificatio hic obtinetur. Quod & verba illa superius adducta commonstrant, conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato, ut promissio ex fide daretur credentibus.
units.tr: Next, the arguments of Scripture confirming that a man can in no way be justified by works are these. 1. Because all men have sinned and therefore fall short of the glory of God: Rom. 3:23; Gal. 3:10; 2:22. "But Scripture has concluded all things under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe." All who are sinners, and therefore under condemnation, cannot be justified to that extent; but all men are such through their works. "But," you will say, "they will be justified on account of good works." But those good works cannot satisfy for the earlier evils, nor justify them. When God pronounces according to works, he cannot absolve according to the good any more than condemn according to the evil. Indeed, while some evils exist, he cannot justify according to the good, because "cursed is he who does not continue in all things." "In the Gospel," you will say, "it is otherwise." Prove that concerning that righteousness from works. Indeed, in the Gospel this is confirmed with respect to works: Gal. 3:10. Therefore justification is obtained here not by the same way of works, but by a far different way, namely by faith through Christ. This the words quoted above also show: "Scripture has concluded all things under sin, so that the promise by faith might be given to believers."

units.la: II. Missis peccatis nostris, quodque omnes sumus peccatores miseri, bona quæ tandem per Dei gratiam præstamus, multis semper imperfectionibus onusta sunt, ut & hac parte etiam illa in censum bonorum per se referri vix queant, non certe justificandorum. Jac. III.2. 1 Joann. 1.8. Rom. VII. 14. &c. Schlichtingius, pag. 134. Falsum est, hominem, qui justificari velit, bona opera interponere non posse, imo non debere. At nulla habet, inquis. Si nulla habet, nec justificabitur. Justificatio enim nec incipit sine fide ac poenitentia; nec durat sine fidei poenitentiaque fructibus atque effectis. At imperfecta sunt. Quid tum, quando Deus pro ineffabili sua benignitate iis vult esse contentus. Alias sunt, inquis, debita. Imo vero non alio fine debentur, quam ut a peccatorum poenis liberi simus. Resp. 1. Si in justificatione interveniant opera nostra bona, jam ergo non sine operibus justificamur. Quod tamen Apostolus docuit. II. Nec interponi debent, propterea ut justificatio omni ex parte sit gratuita. atqui si ex gratia, jam non ex operibus. Rom. xi. 6. III. Ita est, quod nec incipit justificatio sine fide, nec durat sine ejus fructibus continuis; sed proinde non sequitur, opera in justificatione interponi, ad quas Deus in justificatione respiciat, tanquam ad ejus causam veram propriamque. IV. Deum in justificatione nostra, operibus imperfectis contentum esse, ut probas? primo vid. Deum opera requirere? tum imperfecta quamvis, dum propter ea scilicet hominem justificat, admittere in censum justitiae? V. Denique & proba, opera nostra nos a peccatorum poenis, in justificatione, liberare. Quae Euangelio Christi, & doctrinae Apostolicae valde sunt contraria.
units.tr: II. Setting aside our sins, and the fact that we are all wretched sinners, the good works that we at last perform through the grace of God are always burdened with many imperfections, so that on this account too they can hardly be counted among good works in themselves, and certainly not among those by which we are justified. James 3:2; 1 John 1:8; Rom. 7:14, etc. Schlichting, p. 134. It is false that a man who wishes to be justified cannot, indeed ought not, to interpose good works. But, you say, he has none. If he has none, neither will he be justified. For justification neither begins without faith and repentance, nor endures without the fruits and effects of faith and repentance. But they are imperfect. What of it, since God in his ineffable kindness is willing to be content with them? They are owed, you say, for other reasons. Indeed, they are owed for no other end than that we may be free from the punishments of sins. Reply 1. If our good works intervene in justification, then we are not justified without works after all. Yet the Apostle taught this. II. Nor ought they to be interposed, so that justification may be wholly gratuitous. But if by grace, then no longer by works. Rom. 11:6. III. It is true that justification neither begins without faith nor endures without its continual fruits; but it does not follow from this that works are interposed in justification, and that God looks to them in justification as to its true and proper cause. IV. How do you prove that God, in our justification, is content with imperfect works? First, show that God requires works at all; then, even if he justifies a man on account of them, does he admit imperfect works into the reckoning of righteousness? V. Finally, prove also that our works free us from the punishments of sins in justification. These things are very contrary to the Gospel of Christ and to the apostolic doctrine.

units.la: III. Christus docet, post omnia etiam praestita, nos tamen adhuc esse servos inutiles. Lnc. xvii, 10. Ita & vos, ubi feceritis omnia quae praecepta vobis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus, δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοι: quia quod debemus facere, fecimus. tantum abest ut operibus nostris fidamus, vel iis contenti simus, etiam imperfectis, ad justificationem.
units.tr: III. Christ teaches that, even after everything has been done, we are still unprofitable servants. Luke 17:10. So you also, when you have done all the things commanded you, say: we are unprofitable servants [δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοι], because we have done what we ought to do. So far is it from being the case that we trust in our works, or are content with them even when imperfect, for justification.

units.la: IV. Uti Apostolus ideo negat nos ex operibus justificari, ut quoque adimatur homini omnis gloriatio; ita nihil omnino operum retinere debemus, quibus ullo modo justificatio adscribatur, ut plane nullus gloriationi nobis locus superfit. Rom. iii. 29. ubi ergo gloriatio? ἐξεκλείσθη exclusa est. Per quam legem? operum? ἀλλ' [illegible, ~3 letters], nequaquam: sed per legem fidei. Opera gloriationi praebent occasionem, & quousque in hoc argumento servantur, eousque materia gloriationis retinetur, quam omnem Apostolus rescindit, & sublatam funditus cupit. Cap. iv. 2. si enim Abraham ex operibus justificatus, habet gloriationem. 1 Cor. 1. 30. 31. Ex ipso vero vos estis in Christo Jesu, qui factus nobis sapientia a Deo, justitia atque sanctificatio & redemptio: ut, quemadmodum scriptum, qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Ephef.ii.2. Non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur.
units.tr: IV. Just as the Apostle denies that we are justified by works so that all boasting may be taken from man, so we ought to retain absolutely no works to which justification is ascribed in any way, so that no room for boasting is left to us at all. Rom. 3:27, 29: where then is boasting? It is excluded. [ἐξεκλείσθη] By what law? Of works? No, but through the law of faith. Works give occasion for boasting, and as long as they are retained in this matter, so long is the material of boasting retained, which the Apostle cuts away entirely and wishes utterly removed. Rom. 4:2: for if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of. 1 Cor. 1:30–31: But of him you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord. Eph. 2:9: Not of works, lest anyone should boast.

units.la: V. Justificamur gratis, ergo nullo modo ex operibus. Illa duo enim hoc in negotio passim opponuntur. Rom iii. 24. Justificati gratis ejus gratia, δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι, per redemptionem in Christo Jesu. Cap. iv. 4. Operanti vero merces non imputatur κατὰ χάριν secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. At ex gratia nobis merces imputatur, per redemptionem in Christo, uti supra dixit. verf. 16. propterea ex fide, ut secundum gratiam esset. Cap. v. 15. quanto magis gratia Dei & donum in gratia ista unius hominis Jesu Christi in multos illos abundavit. 17. multo magis qui abundantiam gratia & doni justitia accipiunt. 11. Ut quemadmodum peccatum regnavit in morte, ita & gratia regnet per justitiam ad vitam aeternam, per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Cap. vi. 1. Quid ergo dicemus, manebimus in peccato, ut abundet gratia? Cap. xi. 6. Si vero gratia, jam non ex operibus. quandoquidem gratia non foret gratia. si vero ex operibus, jam non est gratia. Socinus, de Justificat. pag. 32. Unde liquet, gratiam & beneficentiam divinam in eo justificando, id est, pro justo habendo ac praemio officiendo intervenisse. Gratia autem locus non est, ubi ex operibus justificatio est. Operanti enim, inquit Paulus, merces debetur, non secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. Et alibi, quippiam esse ex gratia, plane opponit ei, quod est, esse ex operibus. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum fit, Paulum negare, non modo ex operibus legis, sed simpliciter, ex operibus nos justificari. Denique Paulus dicit, Ephef. ii. 8.9. Gratia enim salvati estis per fidem; & hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est: non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur.
units.tr: V. We are justified freely, therefore in no way by works. For these two are constantly set against each other in this business. Rom. 3:24: Justified freely [δωρεὰν] by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Ch. 4:4: To one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace [κατὰ χάριν], but according to debt. But the reward is reckoned to us by grace, through the redemption in Christ, as he said above, v. 16: therefore it is of faith, that it might be according to grace. Ch. 5:15: how much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound unto many. v. 17: much more those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness. v. 21: so that as sin reigned unto death, so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Ch. 6:1: What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? Ch. 11:6: But if by grace, then no longer of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. But if of works, then it is no longer grace. Socinus, de Justificatione, p. 32: Whence it is clear that the grace and beneficence of God intervened in that justifying, that is, in holding a man to be righteous and bestowing a reward. But there is no place for grace where justification is by works. For, says Paul, the reward is owed to one who works, not according to grace but according to debt. And elsewhere he plainly sets being of grace against being of works. From all of which it is manifest that Paul denies that we are justified not only by the works of the law, but simply by works. Finally, Paul says, Eph. 2:8–9: For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, lest anyone should boast.

units.la: vi. Justificat nos Deus, per remissionem peccatorum; ergo non ex operibus. Ubi enim remissione res agitur, judicium ex operibus non instituitur, quibuscunque, vel quomodocunque dictis, legalibus, aut Evangelicis. Rom. iv. 6. 7. Quemadmodum & David beatitudinem hominis dicit, cui Deus justitiam imputat sine operibus: beati quorum remissa peccata &c. Eodem ergo illa spectant in justificatione; nempe sine operibus, & remissione peccatorum absolvi ac haberi pro justo.
units.tr: VI. God justifies us through the remission of sins; therefore not by works. For where the matter concerns remission, judgment is not made according to works, whatever sort they are, or however they are described, legal or evangelical. Rom. 4:6–7: Just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness without works: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, etc. Therefore these things apply in justification alike: namely, that one is absolved and held to be righteous without works, and through the remission of sins.

units.la: vii. Denique, Deus impium dicitur justificare, id est, qui nondum operibus aequisivit, ut pro justo & pio habeatur. Rom. iv. 5.[?] Ei vero qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui justificat impium. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv cap. vii. pag. 362. Deinde, quod attinet ad verba illa, qui justificat impium, considerandum tibi fuerat, eum qui justificatur, id est a reatu suorum peccatorum coram Deo absolvitur, & sic pro justo habetur seu justus pronunciatur, impium a Paulo dici, non quidem quia, postquam justificatus est, adhuc impius perduret: sed quia impius antea fuerat. Resp. Quis autem existimet,impium a Paulo dici justificari,quia post.justificationem etiam impius perdurat; & non , quia impius fuerat, & in ipso actu justificationis non aliter considerari poterat, quam in se reus & impius ? quamvis ea Dei gratia praeditus sit cum justificatione, ex qua pie porro victurus sit: sed hoc nec ante, nec in justificatione: Deus enim χωρὶς ἐργων[?], etiam sine praeeunte pietate hominem absolvit, propter redemtionem in solo Christo. Rom.v.10, quum inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem filii ejus. Col. ii. 13. Vos mortuos in offensis vivificavit, vobis condonatis omnibus offensis. Tit. iii. 3. 4. 5. Eramus quondam & nos amentes, rebelles, servientes cupiditatibus, &c. sed servavit nos ex sua misericordia, non ex operibus justis, quae fecerimus nos. Quo praeter Scripturae loca, etiam faciunt exempla justificatorum impiorum: Rahabae, Mulieris peccatricis, Luc. vii. Pauli, & aliorum. Atque ista pertinent ad illud argumentum, vel primam argumentorum classem, quae docent, nullis nos omnino, etiam qualibuscunque, operibus justificari.
units.tr: VII. Finally, God is said to justify the ungodly, that is, one who has not yet acquired by works that he should be held righteous and pious. Rom. 4:5: But to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly. Socinus, de Servatore, part 4, ch. 7, p. 362: As for the words, who justifies the ungodly, you should have considered that he who is justified, that is, is absolved from the guilt of his sins before God and so is held to be righteous or pronounced just, is called ungodly by Paul, not indeed because, after he has been justified, he remains ungodly still, but because he was ungodly before. Reply. But who would think that Paul calls him ungodly who is justified because, after justification, he still remains ungodly; and not because he was ungodly, and in the very act of justification could be regarded in no other way than as guilty and ungodly in himself? Although he is endowed with the grace of God along with justification, from which he will afterwards live piously, yet this is neither before nor in justification. For God absolves a man without works [χωρὶς ἔργων], even without preceding piety, on account of redemption in Christ alone. Rom. 5:10: When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. Col. 2:13: You, being dead in your offences, he made alive, all your offences having been forgiven. Titus 3:3–5: For we also were once foolish, disobedient, serving lusts, etc., but he saved us according to his mercy, not by works of righteousness which we had done. Besides the passages of Scripture, the examples of justified ungodly persons also confirm this: Rahab, the sinful woman of Luke 7, Paul, and others. These things pertain to that argument, or to the first class of arguments, which teach that we are justified by no works at all, not even by any sort of works whatever.

units.la: Excipiunt Adversarii, Paulo, quando opera a justificatione secludit, intelligi opera, non quaevis, nec legis duntaxat, sed opera perfecta, & meritotia. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. xi. & in Notis ad Dial. pag. 32. dicen-dum, Paulum, operum nomine, non quælibet opera intelligere, nec quolibet modo accepta, sed quæ sua vi hominem justum coram Deo reddere possint; cum negat, nos ex operibus justificari, qualis esset absoluta & perpetua, per totam vitæ curriculum, legis divinæ observatio. Hanc Apostoli mentem esse, & operum simplici nomine, eam perfectam divinorum præceptorum conservationem intelligere, declarat manifeste, quod ait, operanti dari mercedem, non ex gratia, sed ex debito. Et rursum: non operanti, sed credenti in eum, qui justificat impium, imputari fidem ipsius ad justitiam. Et in Fragmentis, de Justific. ibidem, pag. 48. Quod tamen non eam vim habet, ut causa justificationis nostræ, omnino quæcunque opera, & quocunque modo considerata, excludere velit: sed sensus ipsius est, ut indicavimus, Nulla esse opera, quæ tanti sint, ut propter ipsorum meritum justificari possimus. Quando scilicet nemo est qui perfectissime atque integerrime per totam vitam ea opera faciat, quæ sive sub Vetere, sive sub Novo Testamento præscripta sunt, id quod tamen omnino requi-ritur, sive requireretur ad hoc, ut per ipsa opera, tanquam ejus rei aliquo modo merito-ria, justificatio contingeret. In eandem sententiam respondit Schlichtingius, pro Socino, contra Meisnerum, pag. 114. & omnes. Resp. 1. Similiter Pontifi-cii inquiunt, à justificatione excludi quidem opera, non vero quæcunque, sed aliqua duntaxat, sive cæremonialia, sive non renatorum, aut solius liberi arbitrii quæ sunt. 11. Imo Apostolus intelligit perfectam operum observatio-nem; sed non solam. Docet, per legem justificationi aditum non patere, nisi illâ plenissime servatâ; sed nec per eam justificari quempiam prorsus posse. 111. Non perfectis demum; at quibuscunque operibus in genere justifica-tionem derogat. Unde nunquam vel perfecta, vel meritoria nominat opera, sed simpliciter ea, & quæcunque legis sunt, adimit illis omnem justificandi ratio-nem & causam. iv. Atque de operante quando verba facit, tum perfecte operantem, tum simpliciter operibus ad justificationem innitentem intelligit, præsertim ubi dicit, non operanti, sed credenti in eum qui justificat impium. v. Quis existimet, Apostolum, ubi in antecedenti fundamentum jecit de hominum universali corruptione & improbitate, omnes esse peccatores; in sequentibus argumentum justificationis, illâ præmisâ hypothesi, pertractans, sumsisse homines perfectos, & perfecta opera, ut solis iis adimat justificationem, quam fidei adscribat? Quasi, quando concludit, hominem fide justificari, sine operibus legis, voluerit, tantum sine operibus undiquaque perfectis ju-stificari? & excludens gloriationem operum, quod excluserit tantum gloriationem scilicet operum perfectissimorum. Quando de Abrahamo quærit, an ex operibus sit justificatus, potuitne intelligere, vel intelligi de operibus perfectis? & sic de cæteris. Atqui illis omnibus, de quibus loquitur, operibus ju-stificationem abjudicat: quare non perfectis tantum, ut de iis solis accipien-dus esset, sed imo quibuscunque. Denique, quando gratiam & opera opponit, non sola perfecta intelligit, sed quæcunque, quibus justificari homo cupiat. Et hoc Judæi, quos præcipue impugnat, opinabantur, qui certe non sola perfecta crepabant, & pro justitiâ venditabant suâ, sed bona opera quævis. Putamusne, inter Galatas, aliosque dictos Christianos, qui opera &
units.tr: The adversaries make an exception: when Paul excludes works from justification, he is to be understood as meaning not any works, nor the works of the law only, but perfect and meritorious works. Socinus, de Servatore, part 4, ch. 11, and in the Notes on the Dialogue, p. 32: It must be said that by the name of works Paul understands not just any works, nor works taken in just any way, but those which by their own power can render a man righteous before God; when he denies that we are justified by works, he means such as would be an absolute and perpetual observance of the divine law through the whole course of life. That this is the Apostle's mind, and that by the simple name of works he understands that perfect observance of the divine precepts, he declares plainly when he says that the reward is given to one who works not by grace but by debt. And again: his faith is imputed to righteousness not to one who works, but to one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly. And in the Fragments on Justification, ibid., p. 48: This, however, does not have the force of wishing to exclude, as the cause of our justification, all works whatever and considered in any way; rather its sense, as we have indicated, is that there are no works of such worth that we could be justified on account of their merit. Namely, when there is no one who, most perfectly and most entirely, throughout the whole of life, does those works which are prescribed either under the Old or the New Testament, which is nonetheless wholly required, or would be required, in order that justification might come about through those works as in some way meritorious of it. Schlichting, defending Socinus against Meisner, p. 114, and all of them, answered to the same effect. Reply 1. In the same way the Papists say that works are excluded from justification, not indeed all works, but only some, either ceremonial works or those of the unregenerate or of free will alone. II. Indeed the Apostle understands the perfect observance of works, but not only that. He teaches that there is no access to justification through the law unless it is kept most fully, and yet that no one can be justified by it at all. III. He denies justification not only to perfect or meritorious works, but to works in general. Hence he never names works as perfect or meritorious, but simply works, and those that belong to the law, and takes from them every reason and cause of justifying. IV. And when he speaks of the one who works, he means both the one who works perfectly and the one who simply relies on works for justification, especially where he says: to one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly. V. Who would think that the Apostle, having laid in the preceding the foundation of the universal corruption and wickedness of men, that all are sinners, and then, treating the argument of justification on that premise, took perfect men and perfect works, so that he might deny justification to these alone and ascribe it to faith? As if, when he concludes that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law, he wished that he should be justified only without works perfect in every respect? And in excluding the boasting of works, did he exclude only the boasting of most perfect works? When he asks whether Abraham was justified by works, could he have understood, or could it be understood, of perfect works? And so with the rest. Yet he denies justification to all the works of which he speaks; so it should not be taken as referring to perfect works only, but to any works whatever. Finally, when he sets grace and works against each other, he understands not only perfect works, but any by which a man might desire to be justified. And this the Jews, whom he chiefly attacks, supposed, who certainly did not boast of perfect works alone, and did not peddle their own righteousness, but any good works whatever.

units.la: Tom. 2. eorum justitiam objiciebant justificationi per fidem gratuitæ, omnes illos intellexisse perfectam justitiam? Vel, quando ad Ephesios scribit, gratia istiu[?] salvati per fidem, non ex operibus, hoc intellexisse de solis operibus perfectis? Paulus vero omnia opera rejicit, & simpliciter operibus justificandi vim adimit omnem.
units.tr: Tom. 2. Do we suppose that the Galatians and the other so-called Christians, who set their works and their righteousness against justification by free faith, all understood perfect righteousness? Or when he writes to the Ephesians, "by grace you are saved through faith, not of works," do we suppose he meant only perfect works? But Paul rejects all works and simply takes away from works every power of justifying.

units.la: Objicit Schlichtingius, pag. 148. Apostolum alibi ea dicere, quæ ostendant, nos per opera justificari, & servari, quale & illud est, cum docet, in Christo Jesu nihil valere, nisi observationem mandatorum Dei; nisi novam creaturam; nisi fidem, sed per charitatem efficacem, hoc est, cum charitate & bonis operibus conjunctam. Unde etiam apparet, Paulum, cum solam fidem nominat, eique justificationem tribuit, sic eam accipere, ut ejus effectu includat, non secus ac cum dicimus, arborem vel agrum hominem alere. Non enim sola arbor sine fructu, ager sine proventu hominem alit, sed quatenus fructus & segetes producit; sic fides, quatenus ex se uberrimam fructuum justitiæ messem profundit, nos servat & justificat. Resp. I. Nullibi certe Paulus docet, nos per opera justificari: alioqui sibi, qui à negotio justificationis opera omnia constanter excludit, manifeste contradiceret. II. Alius vero sensus eorum est, quum dicit, in Christo nihil valere, quam observationem mandatorum &c. in iis enim agitur de naturâ aut veri fidelis, aut veræ fidei, quam operibus destitui posse negat. Verum de hoc nostra non est disputatio, sed de justificatione, eoque solo, quod causam ejus facit, propter quam homo à Deo justificetur. An dicit uspiam Paulus, propter novam creaturam, vel observata mandata Dei, vel charitatem nos justificari? annon ubique non per opera, & sine operibus, & non operantem justificari gratis asserit, etiam impium? III. Fides non alia justificat, nisi quæ cum charitate & bonis operibus conjuncta est, sed non quatenus talis, aut propter hoc. IV. Quare non dictare, sed probare debuerat Adversarius, Paulum, cum solam fidem nominat in materiâ justificationis, ejus etiam effecta includere. V. Arborem nos alere, vel agrum, id est, cum fructibus, vel per fructus suos, commode dicitur; atque idem quo minus etiam de fide dicatur, haud repugnamus: nimi-rum ut fides nos servet cum fructibus suis, bonis operibus, eo loco & ratione ubi ista requiruntur: nam certe ad salutem etiam sunt necessaria, suo ordine, quamvis non justificent.
units.tr: Schlichting objects, p. 148, that the Apostle elsewhere says things that show we are justified and saved by works. Such is the statement that in Christ Jesus nothing avails except the keeping of God's commandments; except a new creature; except faith, but faith working through love, that is, joined with love and good works. Hence it also appears that Paul, when he names faith alone and attributes justification to it, takes it in such a way that its effect is included, just as when we say that a tree or a field feeds a man. For a tree without fruit, or a field without produce, does not feed a man, but insofar as it bears fruit and crops; so faith, insofar as it pours forth from itself the abundant harvest of the fruits of righteousness, saves us and justifies us. Reply: I. Paul certainly nowhere teaches that we are justified by works; otherwise he would plainly contradict himself, since he constantly excludes all works from the business of justification. II. But their sense is different when he says that in Christ nothing avails except the keeping of the commandments, and so on. For there he is speaking of the nature of a true believer or of true faith, which he denies can be without works. But our dispute is not about this, but about justification, and about that alone which makes the cause for which a man is justified by God. Does Paul anywhere say that we are justified on account of a new creature, or the observance of God's commandments, or love? Does he not everywhere assert that we are justified freely, not by works, and without works, and that the one who does not work, even the ungodly, is justified? III. Faith justifies only as it is joined with love and good works, but not as such, or on account of this. IV. Hence the Adversary ought not merely to assert but to prove that when Paul names faith alone in the matter of justification, he includes its effects as well. V. To say that a tree, or a field, feeds us, that is, with its fruits or through its fruits, is a fair way of speaking; and we do not object to the same being said of faith, namely, that faith preserves us together with its fruits, good works, in the place and manner where these are required. For these are certainly necessary for salvation too, in their own order, though they do not justify.

units.la: Secundum argum. Quemadmodum operibus nostris omnis derogatur justitia, ita Jesu Christo ea tota transferibitur, & quod hac in parte deest nobis, in illo est, qui proinde factus nobis dicitur justitia, quâ coram Deo consistimus. Sic: Qui solus est justitia nostra, quâ justi simus coram Deo, per eum solum, vel illam ejus justitiam justificamur: atqui Christus solus est justitia nostra, quâ coram Deo justi simus: ergo. Probatur Minor, ex Scripturis, haud uno modo. Nam & propter impotentiam nostram dicitur à Deo submissus Chri-stus, ut præstaret & conferret nobis, quod ipsi nequibamus: & singulari ratione justitia nostra: & factus à Deo nobis in justitiam, nosque in eo justitiam habere & fieri: quæ omnia emphatice demonstrant argumenti nostri vim. Videamus singula. Rom. viii. 3. 4. Quod impossibile erat legi in quo infirmabatur per carnem, fecit Deus mittens filium suum in similitudine carnis peccatricis, & pro peccato, condemnavit peccatum in carne. Ut jus legis impleretur in nobis non secundum carnem ambulantibus, sed secundum spiritum. Jus legis erat, ut qui faceret illa homo, is demum viveret: hoc nobis ἀδύνατον. Quam ἀδυναμίαν [?] ut tolleret Christus, in locum nostrum venit, & condemnavit peccatum seu vim condemnandi ei abstulit, & silere jussit, in carne suâ, pro nobis. Ut sic per eum saltem, quia per nos nequibamus, promissae vitae redderemur participes. Ergo justitia, quâ destituimur per nos ipsos, resarcitur nobis in Christo, ipseque nobis justitia est, & vita. Sic ergo contra peccatum, legem, & defectus nostros, habemus omnium istorum supplementum in Christo; & qui per nos, & legem justificari non possumus, justificamur in eo, per id, quod nostro loco fuit, & fecit. Gal. iii. 11. 12. 13. 14. Quod autem in lege nemo justificatur coram Deo, clarum; nam justus ex fide vivet. Lex autem non est ex fide: sed qui fecerit ea homo, in iis vivet. Christus nos redemit ex maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio. Scriptum enim: maledictus quicunque pendet in cruce. Ut ad gentes benedictio Abrahae perveniret in Christo Jesu, ut promissionem spiritus acciperemus per fidem. Cap. iv. 4. 5. Ubi autem venit plenitudo temporis, emisit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere, factum sub lege: ut eos qui sub lege redimeret, ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus. Cap. ii. 16: Scientes quod non justificabitur homo ex operibus legis, sed per fidem Jesu Christi: & nos in Jesum Christum credidimus, ut justificemur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Phil. iii. 8. 9. ut Christum lucrifaciam, & deprehendar in eo, non habens meam justitiam quae ex lege, sed quae per fidem Christi, justitiam ex Deo in fide. Quae omnia ostendunt, in locum legis & legalis justitiae successisse Christum, cum suâ justitiâ, quae nos demum coram Deo justos facit, & ex quâ omnia promissa, & bona, redemtionem ac salutem, adipiscimur.
units.tr: Second argument. Just as all righteousness is taken away from our works, so that whole righteousness is transferred to Jesus Christ, and what is lacking in us is in him, who is therefore said to have been made to us righteousness, by which we stand before God. Thus: whoever alone is our righteousness, by which we are righteous before God, we are justified through him alone, or through that righteousness of his alone; but Christ alone is our righteousness, by which we are righteous before God; therefore. The minor is proved from Scripture in more than one way. For on account of our inability Christ is said to have been sent by God, to accomplish and bestow on us what we could not do ourselves; and he is our righteousness in a unique way; and he was made by God to be righteousness for us, and we have righteousness and are made righteous in him. All these emphatically demonstrate the force of our argument. Let us look at each. Rom. viii. 3, 4: What was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. The requirement of the law was that the man who did those things should live; this was impossible for us. Christ, to remove this inability, came in our place, and condemned sin, or took away its power to condemn, and ordered it to be silent, in his own flesh, on our behalf. So that through him, since we could not through ourselves, we might at least be made partakers of the promised life. Therefore the righteousness we lack through ourselves is restored to us in Christ, and he himself is our righteousness and life. Thus against sin, the law, and our defects, we have the supplement of all these things in Christ; and since we cannot be justified through ourselves or the law, we are justified in him, through what he was and did in our place. Gal. iii. 11-14: That in the law no one is justified before God is clear; for the just shall live by faith. But the law is not of faith; rather, the man who does those things shall live in them. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having been made a curse for us. For it is written: cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. So that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Chap. iv. 4, 5: But when the fullness of time came, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, so that he might redeem those under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. Chap. ii. 16: Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ; and we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ and not by the works of the law. Phil. iii. 8, 9: that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is from God through faith. All these show that Christ has succeeded in the place of the law and of legal righteousness, with his own righteousness, which at last makes us righteous before God, and through which we obtain all the promises and goods, redemption and salvation.

units.la: Deinde, Christus dicitur justitia nostra, quâ aliâ ratione, quam quod justitiam nobis acquisivit, quâ solâ justificamur? annunciare enim, & confirmare doctrinam justitiae, etiam aliorum est: esse verò justitiam, ita soli Christo proprium, ac quod solus est Messias & Servator. Jerem. xxiii. 6. & hoc nomen, quo vocabunt eum יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ [?] Jehova justitia nostra. Praeterea factus nobis dicitur justitia à Deo, 1 Cor. i. 30. Ex ipso autem vos estis in Christo Jesu, ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν σοφία [?] ἀπὸ θεοῦ, δικαιοσύνη καὶ ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις [?], qui factus nobis sapientia à Deo, δικαιοσύνη justitia & sanctificatio, & redemtio. Quemadmodum ergo redemtio, quia nos redimit; sanctificatio, quod sanctificat; ita & justitia, quod justificat. Sapientia certè, quia & sapientes nos reddit, & in eo omnis sapientia reclusa; sic & in ipso omnis nostra justitia, quâ coram Deo justificamur. Socinus, part. iv. de Servat. cap. v.
units.tr: Next, Christ is called our righteousness for what other reason than that he has obtained righteousness for us, through which alone we are justified? For to announce and confirm the doctrine of righteousness belongs also to others; but to be righteousness belongs to Christ alone, in that he alone is the Messiah and Saviour. Jer. xxiii. 6, and the name by which they will call him: Jehovah our righteousness [יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ].
