Moreover, he is said to have been made righteousness to us by God, 1 Cor. i. 30: But of him you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God [ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν σοφία ἀπὸ θεοῦ], and righteousness [δικαιοσύνη] and sanctification and redemption [ἀπολύτρωσις]. Just as redemption is because he redeems us, and sanctification because he sanctifies us, so also righteousness is because he justifies us. Wisdom, certainly, because he also makes us wise, and all wisdom is shut up in him; so also in him is all our righteousness, by which we are justified before God. Socinus, part iv, On Salvation, chap. v.

units.la: Creditis igitur, quia Paulus dixerit, Chri- Resp. 1. Christus factus dicitur no- stum nobis factum fuisse justitiam; ex hoc bis sapientia, & justitia, & redemtio, intelligi par esse, Christum pro nobis justum quorum ista nobis impuratur, quia ea fuisse: & sic ejus justitiam nobis injustè im- justitiae natura est, atque ad id facit, putari. Ergo eadem ratione, qui dixit, Chri-stum factum nobis fuisse sapientiam; intelli-gere oportebit, Christum pro nobis fuisse sa-pientem: & sic ejus sapientiam nobis stultis imputari. Quid de redemtione dicemus? an non eodem modo colligendum erit, Christum pro nobis redemptum fuisse: & sic ejus re-demptionem nobis captivis imputari? At vero quis ita mentis oculis captus est, qui non cer-nat, Christum nobis factum esse sapientiam, & redemptionem idem esse, atque Christi ope nos vere sapientes factos fuisse, & vere re-demptos? Certum igitur esto, ut ad Pauli verba redeam, nihil aliud esse, Christum nobis justitiam a Deo factum fuisse, quam divina providentia per Christum nos id esse consecutos, ut justi coram ipso Deo simus; non secus atque, eundem Christum nobis ab eodem Deo sapientiam, sanctificationem, & redemptionem factum esse, nihil aliud signi-ficat, quam nos divina providentia per Christum id consecutos fuisse, ut sapientes, sancti, & redempti coram ipso Deo simus. ut justos reddat, sui imputatione, non ita alia. Ergo dum illa omnia nobis factus dicitur Christus, sensus est, omnia illa in eo haberi, & sapientiam, & justitiam, & redemtionem, & habere nos illa in eo quo modo omnia potest. Justitia autem suâ natura est ut justos faciat; & aliena hoc non aliter facit, quam imputatione. Sapientia autem, sanctificatio, & redemtio, alio etiam pacto. Quæ diversitas est ex variâ rerum ipsarum naturâ, & applicatione, quæ contingit; non simpliciter ex verbis, quibus Christus ea nobis fa-ctus dicitur. Interim, dum nobis illa factus est, intelligendum nostra fieri plene, singula quo possunt-, omni suo modo, id est, sapientia, ut per eam sapiamus; sanctificatio, per quam sanctificemur; redemtio, quâ redimamur; ita & justitia, ut per eam justificemur. Justificari autem eâ non possumus, quod jam est pro naturâ rei, nisi imputatione. 11. Et quia distinguuntur justitia, quæ Christus factus, & sanctificatio, non pro eodem sumenda sunt, sed uti sanctitas seu inhae-rens nobis justitia, est à Christi ἁγιασμῷ[?]; ita quod ex justitiâ ejus accedit, est justitiæ imputatio, vel justificatio. 111. Longe certe aliud majusque illa Christum nobis factum dicunt, quam simpliciter ejus ope nos illa quomodo-cunque consequi. Quam opem ut iterum emasculent Adversarii, nil necesse hic est pluribus exponere. Et Prophetarum, ac Apostolorum ope nos sapien-tiam, & reliqua etiam obtinemus: an ideo poterunt dici, facti nobis sapien-tia, justitia &c? Vel quis adeo mentis oculis captus, ut non cernat longe augu-stius quid illis significari de Christo, quam quod divina providentia per Chri-stum consequimur, ut simus sapientes, justi, sancti, & redemti?
units.tr: Do you believe, then, that because Paul said that Christ was made righteousness for us, we must understand that Christ was righteous on our behalf, and so his righteousness is unjustly imputed to us? Therefore, by the same reasoning, whoever said that Christ was made wisdom for us must understand that Christ was wise on our behalf, and so his wisdom is imputed to us fools. What shall we say about redemption? Must it not likewise be concluded that Christ was redeemed on our behalf, and so his redemption is imputed to us captives? But who is so blind in mind as not to see that Christ being made wisdom for us and his being redemption amount to the same thing as that by Christ's help we have truly been made wise and truly redeemed? Let it be certain, then, to return to Paul's words, that Christ being made righteousness for us by God means nothing other than that by divine providence, through Christ, we have attained this, that we are righteous before God himself; just as the fact that the same Christ was made for us by the same God wisdom, sanctification, and redemption means nothing other than that we have attained, by divine providence through Christ, that we are wise, holy, and redeemed before God himself. Reply: I. Christ is said to be made wisdom, and righteousness, and redemption for us, of which the first is imputed to us, because righteousness is its nature and it aims at this: to make men righteous by its imputation, and not otherwise. Therefore, while Christ is said to be made all these things for us, the sense is that all of them are had in him, and that we have them in him in whatever way he can give them. Now righteousness by its nature makes men righteous, and an alien righteousness does this only by imputation. But wisdom, sanctification, and redemption do so in another way. This difference arises from the varied nature of the things themselves and the application that takes place, not simply from the words by which Christ is said to be made these things for us. Meanwhile, while he is made these for us, it must be understood that they become ours fully, each in whatever way it can, in its whole manner: wisdom so that we are made wise by it; sanctification by which we are sanctified; redemption by which we are redeemed; and so also righteousness, so that we are justified by it. But we cannot be justified by it except by imputation, which is already required by the nature of the thing. II. And because righteousness, which Christ was made, and sanctification are distinguished, they are not to be taken in the same sense; but as holiness, or righteousness inherent in us, comes from Christ's sanctification, so what comes from his righteousness is the imputation of righteousness, or justification. III. Certainly those words mean something far different and greater about Christ having been made for us, than that we obtain those things in some way simply through his help. As for their attempt to emasculate this help again, there is no need to explain more at length here. And we obtain wisdom and the rest through the help of the Prophets and Apostles too; can they therefore be said to be made wisdom, righteousness, and so on for us? Or who is so blind in mind as not to see that something far more exalted is signified about Christ by those words than that through Christ we attain, by divine providence, to be wise, righteous, holy, and redeemed?

units.la: Rom. iv. 25. Qui traditus est propter transgressiones nostras, & resurrexit propter nostram justitiam, Διὰ[?] τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν. Cap. v. 17. Si enim unius transgressione mors regnavit per illum unum, multo magis qui abundantiam gratiæ & doni τῆς δικαιοσύνης[?] justitiæ acceperunt, in vita regnabunt per unum Jesum Christum. II Cor. v. 21. Eum enim qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos fieri-mus justitia Dei in ipso. Phil. iii. 9. Et reperiar in eo, non habens meam justitiam quæ ex lege, sed eam quæ est per fidem Christi, justitiam ex Deo in fide. Ex quibus conclu-ditur satis manifeste, quod justitia, quâ justificamur coram Deo, non est nostra aliqua, vel operum, sed sola Christi, quam in eo habemus, qui ad hoc nobis à Deo factus datusque, ut justitia nostra esset.
units.tr: Rom. 4:25: who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification [Διὰ τὴν δικαίωσιν ἡμῶν]. Rom. 5:17: For if by one man's offence death reigned by one, much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness [τῆς δικαιοσύνης] shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ. 2 Cor. 5:21: For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Phil. 3:9: And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. From these passages it is clearly enough concluded that the righteousness by which we are justified before God is not any righteousness of our own, or of our works, but only the righteousness of Christ, which we have in him, who was made and given by God to us for this purpose, that he might be our righteousness.

units.la: Arg. tertium. Qui justificamur imputatione justitiæ Christi, non justificamur operibus nostris: sed justificamur imputatione justitiæ Christi: ergo. Minor probatur multis & variis S. Scripturæ locis. Jesa. LIII. 5. castigatio pacis nostræ super eum. 6. Fecit Jehova incurrere in eum iniquitatem omnium nostrum. & quæ in eundem sensum plurima eodem capite. tum sequitur, vers. 11. cognitione sui justificabit servus meus multos, quorum iniquitatem ipse bajulavit. Uti in ipsum conjecta omnia nostrum fuerunt peccata, ea ut lueret; ita per hoc ipsum, & eo, quem pro tali nostro Vade agnoscimus, justificamur. Rom. III. 24 25. Justificati gratis ejus gratia, per redemtionem quæ in Christo Jesu: Quem proposuit Deus placamentum per fidem in ejus sanguine. Habemus hic omnia, in præsenti negotio attendenda: redemtionem in Christo; placationem in ejus sanguine; per fidem acceptam; per quæ justificemur; gratis, sola Dei gratia. id est, placatio, & redemtio, à Christo, ejus sanguine impetrata, applicatur nobis in justificatione fidei, quæ Christum, ut à Deo propositum suo sanguine placamen, respicit & amplexatur.
units.tr: The third argument. We who are justified by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ are not justified by our works; but we are justified by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ; therefore. The minor premise is proved by many and various passages of Holy Scripture. Isa. 53:5: the chastisement of our peace was upon him. 6: The Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. And very many things to the same effect in the same chapter. Then it follows, v. 11: By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities. As all our sins were laid upon him, that he might atone for them, so by this very thing, and by him whom we acknowledge as our surety for this, we are justified. Rom. 3:24-25: Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood. Here we have all the things to be considered in the present matter: redemption in Christ; propitiation in his blood; received through faith; by which we are justified; freely, by the sole grace of God. That is, the propitiation and redemption obtained by Christ through his blood is applied to us in the justification of faith, which looks to and embraces Christ, set forth by God as a propitiation in his blood.

units.la: Quomodo hoc dicto justificatio-nem, quæ per plenam solutionem satisfactio-nemque fiat, complecti potuit Apostolus, in quo aperte dicit, nos justificari gratis? Quomodo alieno merito, si propria Dei gratia? An quia in illo fiat mentio redemtionis in Christo Jesu? At cur redemptionem istam non sic explicas, ut cum gratuita justificatione possit consistere? cur propter redemtionem tollis gratiam? Atque ista redemptio, teste eodem Paulo, peccatorum est remissio. Ephes. 1. 7. Col. 1. 14. Num ergo peccatorum nostrorum solutio, eaque plena, intervenit, ut conse-queretur eorum remissio? Quis talem remissionem fando audivit unquam? Hæc peccatorum remissio, quia & ingentem libera-tionem continet, nimirum ab obligatione & reatu æterna mortis, & liberationem ta-lem, quæ magno impendio constiterit, fusio-ne nempe sanguinis filii Dei, propterea meritò redemptio vocatur. Impendium autem istud non eum in finem factum est, ut Deo pœnas Christus pro nobis proprie loquendo penderet: sed longe alias ob causas, propter quas sapientissimo Dei consilio peccatorum
units.tr: How could the Apostle, in this saying, which plainly says that we are justified freely, embrace a justification that is effected through full payment and satisfaction? How could it be by another's merit, if it is by God's own grace? Or is it because mention is made in it of redemption in Christ Jesus? But why do you not explain that redemption so that it can consist with free justification? Why, on account of redemption, do you take away grace? And that redemption, by the testimony of the same Paul, is the remission of sins. Eph. 1:7; Col. 1:14. Does the full payment of our sins therefore intervene, so that their remission may follow? Who has ever heard of such a remission? This remission of sins, since it also contains a great deliverance, namely from the obligation and guilt of eternal death, and a deliverance of such a kind as has cost a great price, namely the shedding of the blood of the Son of God, is therefore rightly called redemption. But that price was not paid for this end, that Christ might properly speaking pay penalties to God on our behalf; but for quite different causes, on account of which, by the most wise counsel of God, the remission of sins

units.la: Resp. 1. Nihil contra locum nostrum allegatum hic profert Schlichtinngius, quod non in præcedentibus copiose discussum sit, ostensumque 1. satisfactionem Christi nequaquam pugnare cum gratuitâ nostrûm justificatione: quia nec nos satisfecimus, nec Deus alienam nostro loco acceptare solutionem tenebatur, neque eam nobis novo beneficio applicare. II. Neque propter redemtionem in Christo tollimus gratiam; sed imo stabilimus: etenim ex gratia, atque ad gratiam illæ redemtio nostra est. III. Et fundamentum remissionis peccatorum. Ideo conjunguntur hic Dei gratia, & justitia; redemtio per Christi sanguinem, & remissio peccatorum. Justificati gratis ejus gratia per redemtionem quæ in Christo Jesu: Quem proposuit Deus placamen per fidem in ejus sanguine, ad ostensionem justitiæ suæ, per remissionem ante factorem peccatorum. Atque adeo solutio & satisfactio divinæ justitiæ intervenit, ad accipiendam peccatorum remissionem. Qualem remissionem qui ne fando quiremissio sine Christi sanguine nobis non de-buit contingere. dem[?] audivit, nae is parum attente au-divit plurima & gravissima S. Scripturae testimonia, quae, uti antea ostendimus, illud satis docent. iv. Breviter, id discriminis est inter vestram, atque nostram sententiam, quod vos redemptionem vocari asseritis, ac esse metaphoricam; nos vero eam esse veram propriamque affirmamus. v. Quorsum tanto impendio, videlicet fusione sanguinis Filii Dei, constitit peccatorum nostrorum remissio; si nulla eam flagitavit necessitas? Adeone Deus delectari potuit sanguine, & morte Filii sui; qui ne quidem morte improborum delectatur, ut dum non necessario requireretur mors ad nostram liberationem, quin quod morte Christi, idem alio leviori modo etiam peragi potuerit, tamen acerbissimam mortem subire Filium suum voluerit? vi. Quodque eum in finem sanguinem Christus fudit, ut Deo poenas pro nobis penderet, eumque placaret, praeter alia quae ad id probandum afferri possent, inter quae est Jesa. liii. praesens locus satis indicat, quando conjungit haec duo, & Christum esse ait, ἱλαστήριον ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ[?] αἵματι, expiatio, placatio; & in sanguine, id est, per sanguinem, sanguinis fusione placationem illam efficiente.
units.tr: Reply 1. Schlichtingius brings forward nothing against our passage that has not been discussed at length in what precedes, and it has been shown: (1) that the satisfaction of Christ by no means conflicts with our free justification, because we did not satisfy, nor was God bound to accept another's payment in our place, nor to apply it to us as a new benefit. (2) Nor do we take away grace on account of redemption in Christ; rather we establish it, for that redemption of ours is from grace and unto grace. (3) It is also the foundation of the remission of sins. Therefore the grace and justice of God are joined here, and redemption through the blood of Christ and remission of sins. Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; whom God hath set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness, for the remission of sins that are past. And so the payment and satisfaction of divine justice intervenes, so that remission of sins may be received. Whoever has not heard of such a remission, has not heard attentively the very many and very weighty testimonies of Holy Scripture, which, as we showed before, teach this sufficiently. (4) Briefly, the difference between your opinion and ours is this: you assert that redemption is called so and is metaphorical; but we affirm that it is true and proper. (5) To what end did the remission of our sins cost so great a price, namely the shedding of the blood of the Son of God, if no necessity demanded it? Could God take such pleasure in the blood and death of his Son, who does not even take pleasure in the death of the wicked, that, although death was not strictly required for our deliverance, and what was done by the death of Christ could have been accomplished in some other, easier way, he nevertheless willed his Son to undergo a most bitter death? (6) And that Christ shed his blood for this end, to pay penalties to God on our behalf and to appease him, is shown, besides other things that could be brought forward to prove it, among which is Isa. 53, the present passage sufficiently indicates this, since it joins these two things and says that Christ is ἱλαστήριον [propitiation] in his blood, that is, an expiation and propitiation; and in his blood, that is, through the blood, the propitiation being effected by the shedding of blood.

units.la: Rom. iv. 24. 25. Sed & propter nos, quibus imputabitur, credentibus in eum qui Jesum Dominum nostrum suscitavit ex mortuis, qui traditus est propter peccata nostra, & suscitatus propter justificationem nostram. Propter justificationem nostram, id est, ut propter eum, & quod pro nobis traditus, resurrexitque, justificaremur, seu imputaretur nobis justitia. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. iv. pag. 333. certissimum est, non de aliqua ipsius Christi justitia imputatione Apostolum loqui: sed fidem, quam Deo habemus, propterea quod Jesum Dominum & caput nostrum a morte in vitam sempiternam revocavit, nobis justitiae loco ductum iri, afferere: non secus, atque Abrahamo fides, quam Dei verbis habuit, pro justitia imputata fuerat. Resp. i. Quid veritati, obsecro est, convenientius, fidem ipsam nostram, qua credimus Jesum &c. justitiae loco duci, an, ipsum Jesum mortuum, & resuscitatum, fide apprehensum? Quid, tum Christo, tum nobis, & religioni magis congruum est, quam hoc, Christum esse nostram justitiam, non nos, non fidei actum, vel obedientiam nostram? Sic enim & salus vel salutis causa Christo attribuitur, & omnis gloriandi materia homini praescinditur. ii. Si nobis fides, non secus ac Abrahamo ea, quam Dei verbis habuit, imputetur, jam non fides ergo quae obedientia est, quaeque obedientia est praeceptorum Euangelicorum.
units.tr: Rom. 4:24-25: But also for us, to whom it shall be imputed, who believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead; who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. "For our justification," that is, that for his sake, and because he was delivered up for us and rose again, we might be justified, or righteousness might be imputed to us. Socinus, On the Saviour, part 4, ch. 4, p. 333: It is quite certain that the Apostle is not speaking of any imputation of some righteousness of Christ himself, but asserts that the faith which we have in God, because he has raised Jesus our Lord and head from death to eternal life, will be taken to be righteousness for us, just as the faith which Abraham had in God's words was imputed to him for righteousness. Reply 1. I ask you, what is more agreeable to the truth: that our own faith, by which we believe that Jesus, etc., is taken as righteousness, or that Jesus himself, dead and raised again, apprehended by faith? What is more fitting both to Christ and to us, and to religion, than this: that Christ is our righteousness, not we, not an act of faith, or our obedience? For thus both salvation, or the cause of salvation, is attributed to Christ, and all material for boasting is cut off from man. 2. If faith is imputed to us, not otherwise than the faith which Abraham had in God's words, then faith is no longer obedience, and obedience is no longer the obedience of the Gospel precepts.

units.la: Rom. v. 1. 2. Justificati ergo ex fide pacem habemus apud Deum per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum. Per quem accessum habemus fide in gratiam istam, in qua stamus. Chri-sto ergo proprie, non fidei, adscribenda justificationis nostrae, & καύχησις[?] causa, gratiae denique, in qua stamus; fides autem rationem habet instrumenti, & viae, per quam ad Christum, & gratiam pervenimus. Ratio datur, verf. 6. Nam Christus nobis infirmis, suo tempore pro impiis mortuus est. 7. In quo charitatem suam ostendit Deus, quod etiam peccatoribus existentibus nobis Christus pro nobis mortuus est. 9. Multo ergo magis, justificati nunc in ejus sanguine, servabimur per eum ab ira. Apertissime causa justificationis ponitur in ejus sanguine. & vers. seq. Si enim quum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, multo magis reconciliati servabimur in ejus vita. In, & per solum Christum omnia, quae in justificatione obtinemus: reconciliatio nostra per ejus mortem; salus, ejus vita: ipso ergo, & vita, & morte ejus omnia constant, quae salutis sunt. Tum interjecta comparatione Adami, & Christi, illo peccati & mortis auctore, isto gratiae ac salutis, concludit Apostolus, verf. 19. Quemadmodum ergo per inobedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituuntur illi multi, ita & per obedientiam unius justi constituentur isti multi. 21. Ut, quemadmodum peccatum regnavit in morte, ita etiam gratia regnaret per justitiam in vitam aeternam, per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: Rom. 5:1-2: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand. Therefore the justification of ourselves, and the ground of boasting, and finally the grace in which we stand, are to be ascribed properly to Christ, not to faith; faith, however, has the character of an instrument and a way by which we come to Christ and grace. The reason is given in v. 6: For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. 7: In that God commended his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. 9: Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. The cause of justification is most clearly placed in his blood. And in the next verse: For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. All the things we obtain in justification are in Christ alone and through him: our reconciliation through his death, our salvation through his life. Therefore all that belongs to salvation consists in him, in both his life and his death. Then, having interposed a comparison of Adam and Christ, the one the author of sin and death, the other of grace and salvation, the Apostle concludes, v. 19: For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. 21: That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Quid clarius, quam per justitiam Christi constitui justos? per eum nos justitiam obtinere, ex gratia, ad vitam aeternam? Quod argumentum tanti apud Socinum est, ut scribat nullum sibi videri pro sententia nostra majus, lib. IV. de Servat. cap. VI. Nihil in sacris monumentis scriptum esse arbitror, quod vobis majorem errandi occasionem dederit, quam ea cum Adamo Christi collatio, quam idem Paulus instituit, & late persequitur cap. 5. epistola ad Rom. Rem autem ipse satis frigide & dilute exponit; Quemadmodum Adami delicto & inobedientia factum est, ut homines damnarentur ac morerentur; sic Christi justitia, & obedientia factum esse, ut absolvantur & vivant. Non hoc dicendum fuerat, sed qua vi utrumque, & ab Adamo illud, & istud a Christo fieret, explicandum. Pergit, justitia enim & obedientia sua, ex Dei decreto, coelos Christus penetravit, ibi perpetuo regnaturus; & ita & sibi, & suis sempiternam vitam, sempiternamque beatitudinem peperit. Atqui hoc jam non est locum Pauli exponere. Quid in isto illis simile, ut ad ea trahi debeat? De justitia illic Christi agitur, & quomodo per eam obtineamus gratiam, & constituamur justi; non quomodo Christus sibi adeptus fuerit locum & potestatem nos salvandi. Pag. 354. Sicut enim delictum, & inobedientia Adami eum mortis reum peregit: ex quo factum est, ut universum humanum genus, quod post reatum illum ab ipso procreatum & propagatum est, morti penitus obnoxium fit; sic Christi justitia & obedientia sempiternam ipsi Christo vitam peperit; ex quo factum est, ut, quicunque ab ipso procreati & propagati fuerint, spiritualiter scilicet, ejusdem vitae participes sint futuri. Resp. 1. Ratio, quod universum humanum genus ab Adamo morti obnoxium est, nullibi datur in textu, carnalis ex Adamo procreatio, sed quod omnes peccarunt, in Adamo scilicet, nam non omnes peccarunt in se, vel ad similitudinem peccati Adami, etiam qui moriuntur. Quin ne unus quidem versus est in toto sermone, vel collatione Adamum inter & Christum, qui non istam causam memoret, Adami scilicet peccatum. Verf. 12. Atque ita in omnes homines mors pervenit, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. 13. Usque ad legem enim peccatum erat in mundo 14. Sed regnavit mors ab Adamo usque ad Mosem, etiam in eos qui non peccarant in similitudine transgressionis Adami. 15 Si enim unius lapsu multi mortui. Et non uti per unum peccantem, est donum: Reatus enim quidem, ex uno, ad condemnationem. 17. Si enim unius transgressione mors regnavit per unum. 18. Propterea ergo sicut per unius transgressionem in omnes homines, homines, ad condemnationem. 19. Sicuti enim unius hominis inobedientia peccatores con-stituti multi. Adeo singulis versibus notatur causa sequuti in omnes reatus, seu ἁμαρτίας, κατάκριμα[?], καὶ θάνατος, peccatum primi hominis primum; nusquam vero generatio nostra ex eo. Illud autem hujus causa aliter esse nequit, quam per imputationem. 11. Et sic Christus causa & caput constituitur gratiae, justitiae, & salutis aeternae, τῆς χάριτος, δωρεᾶς ἐν χάριτι, τῆς δικαιοσύνης, & δικαιώσεως ζωῆς. Verf. 14. ὃς ἐστι τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος. Atque in comparatione hac Apostolus, ab Adamo ad Christum argumentatur, uti à minori ad majus, πολλῷ μᾶλλον, verf. 15. 17. & 20. ubi enim ἐπλεόνασεν peccatum, ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις. Quocirca, quamvis verum quidem, quod quicunque à Christo spiritualiter procreati, vitae cum eo aeternae sunt participes, & quod Christi justitia ipsi vitam peperit aeternam, istud tamen hoc loco non docetur; sed quod Christi gratia, justitia, & vita in suos abundet, quod cujus justitia δικαίωμα valet εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς, ejus obedientia justi constituantur multi, &c. Quae rationem justificationis nostrae declarant per & propter Christum; uti alia declararant modum κατάκριμα seu condemnationis per & propter peccatum Adami. Quae utriusque causa-litas aliter nec intelligi, nec constare potest, nisi admissa utriusque in suos imputatione, in eos qui Adami, in alios qni Christi sunt. Neque enim actio unius, potest alterius, & plurimorum, vel omnium fieri, nisi per im-putationem.
units.tr: What could be clearer than that we are made righteous through the righteousness of Christ? That through him we obtain righteousness, by grace, unto eternal life? Socinus sets so much store by this argument that he writes that nothing seems to him stronger for our view, Book IV of On Salvation, ch. 6. I think nothing has been written in the sacred records that has given you a greater occasion for error than that comparison of Christ with Adam, which the same Paul draws and pursues at length in Romans 5. He explains the matter himself rather coldly and weakly: As by the offence and disobedience of Adam it came about that men were condemned and died, so by the righteousness and obedience of Christ it came about that they are absolved and live. He should not have said this, but should have explained by what force each of these came about, the one from Adam and the other from Christ. He goes on: For by his righteousness and obedience, according to God's decree, Christ penetrated the heavens, there to reign forever, and so won for himself and his people eternal life and everlasting blessedness. But this is not to expound Paul's passage at all. What in this is like those things, that it should be drawn to them? The passage is about the righteousness of Christ, and how through it we obtain grace and are made righteous; it is not about how Christ himself obtained a place and power to save us. Page 354: For as the offence and disobedience of Adam brought him under the guilt of death, from which it came about that the whole human race, which was born and propagated from him after that guilt, is wholly liable to death; so the righteousness and obedience of Christ won eternal life for Christ himself, from which it came about that whoever are born and propagated from him, spiritually of course, are to be partakers of the same life. Answer 1: That the whole human race is liable to death through Adam is nowhere given in the text as a carnal generation from Adam, but because all sinned, namely in Adam; for not all sinned in themselves, or in the likeness of Adam's sin, even those who die. Indeed there is not even one verse in the whole discourse, or in the comparison between Adam and Christ, which does not mention that cause, namely Adam's sin. Verse 12: And so death came upon all men, because [ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον] all sinned. 13: For until the law sin was in the world. 14: But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam's transgression. 15: For if by the fall of one many died. And the gift is not as through one sinning: for the judgment indeed came from one unto condemnation. 17: For if by one man's transgression death reigned through one. 18: Therefore, as through one man's transgression unto all men, unto condemnation. 19: For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners. So in every single verse the cause is noted of the consequence that extends to all, the guilt, or sin [ἁμαρτίας], condemnation [κατάκριμα], and death [θάνατος]; the sin of the first man is named first, but our generation from him is nowhere mentioned. Now that cause can be nothing other than by imputation. 11: And so Christ is set forth as the cause and head of grace, righteousness, and eternal salvation: of grace [τῆς χάριτος], the gift in grace [δωρεᾶς ἐν χάριτι], of righteousness [τῆς δικαιοσύνης], and of justification of life [δικαιώσεως ζωῆς]. Verse 14: who is a type [ὃς ἐστι τύπος] of the one to come [τοῦ μέλλοντος]. And in this comparison the Apostle argues from Adam to Christ as from the lesser to the greater, much more [πολλῷ μᾶλλον], verses 15, 17, and 20, where sin abounded [ἐπλεόνασεν], grace did abound much more [ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις]. Wherefore, although it is indeed true that whoever are spiritually born of Christ are partakers of eternal life with him, and that Christ's righteousness won eternal life for him, yet this is not taught in this place; rather, it is taught that the grace, righteousness, and life of Christ abound in his own, and that by whose righteous act [δικαίωμα] it is available unto justification of life [εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς], by whose obedience many are made righteous, etc. These declare the ground of our justification through and for the sake of Christ, just as other passages declare the manner of condemnation [κατάκριμα] through and for the sake of Adam's sin. The causality of each of these can be understood and stand in no other way than by admitting the imputation of each to their own: of Adam to those who are Adam's, and of Christ to those who are Christ's. For the act of one person cannot become the act of another, and of many or of all, except by imputation.

units.la: Schlichtingius, contra Meisnerum, pag. 250. Nec enim, ut per Christi justitiam justificemur, opus est, ut illius justitia nostra fiat justitia, sed sufficit, ut Christi justitia causa sit nostra justificationis. & hactenus possumus tibi concedere, Christi justitiam esse nostram justitiam, quatenus nostrum in bonum, justificationemque redundat. Verum tu proprie nostram, id est, nobis attributam adscriptamque intelligis. Ref. 1. Omnino vero. Et tu umbram & improprietatem amplectaris, ut lubet, nos proprietate fruemur & gaudebimus. Notemus autem consuetam Adversariis agendi methodum, primùm multa in speciem magnificè dicere, tandem autem desinere in acceptionem tum vocis, tum rei impropriam. Sic de toto Christo philosophantur: unde quae ipsorum religio, quamque bene Christiana sc. fit, intelligitur.
units.tr: Schlichting, against Meisner, p. 250: For in order that we be justified by the righteousness of Christ, it is not necessary that his righteousness become our righteousness, but it is enough that the righteousness of Christ be the cause of our justification. And so far we can concede to you that the righteousness of Christ is our righteousness, insofar as it redounds to our good and to our justification. But you understand "our" properly, that is, as imputed and ascribed to us. Reply 1: Certainly. But you embrace a shadow and an improper sense as you please; we shall enjoy and rejoice in the proper sense. Let us note the customary method of our adversaries: first they say many things that look grand, and at last they end in an improper meaning of the word and of the thing. Thus they philosophize about the whole of Christ; from which it is understood what their religion is, and how far it is in fact Christian.

units.la: De Christo Deo, redemtione, & expiatione peccatorum nostrorum per eum, nunc & de justificatione, primum talia loquuntur, ut in nullâ fere re videantur à nobis discrepare, & postquam omnia dixerunt, desinunt tandem in locutione aliquâ impropriâ. 11. Non statim id quod in bonum nostrum justificationemque aliquatenus redundat, potest dici aut nostra esse justitia, aut nos justificare. Etiam Scripturae, & multa Dei gratia ac beneficia illum in finem sunt; quae tamen non ideo justificant. 111. Non potest quis per alterius justitiam justificari, non nos justitiâ Christi, nisi nobis imputatâ. Nec si causa sit nostrae justificationis, dici potest, per eam nos justificari, nisi in justitiam imputetur, vel ejus justitia fiat nostra. Non, per Christi justitiam justisicari dicendi sumus, si tantum in bonum nostrum cedat illius justitia, & non vere nobis in justitiam imputetur, quia non alia est vis vel sensus istius phrasis aut causalitatis, quando in hoc negotio legitur, per alicujus justitiam justificari.
units.tr: Concerning Christ as God, the redemption and expiation of our sins through him, and now concerning justification, they first speak in such a way that they seem to differ from us in almost nothing, and after they have said everything, they finally end in some improper expression. 2: That which in some measure redounds to our good and justification cannot at once be called either our righteousness or what justifies us. Even the Scriptures and many gifts and benefits of God are for that end, yet they do not therefore justify. 3: No one can be justified by another's righteousness unless the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us; nor, if it is the cause of our justification, can it be said that we are justified by it, unless it is imputed to us for righteousness or its righteousness becomes ours. We are not to be said to be justified by the righteousness of Christ if his righteousness merely tends to our good and is not truly imputed to us for righteousness, because there is no other force or sense of that phrase of causality, when in this matter it is read that one is justified by someone's righteousness.

units.la: 11 Cor. V. 15. Judicantes hoc, quod si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, jam isti omnes mortui: atque pro omnibus mortuus est &c. 19. Fuit Deus in Christo mundum secum reconcilians, non imputans iis peccata ipsorum. 21. Eum enim qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, ut nos fieremus justitia Dei in ipso. Ergo per solum Christum, ejus mortem, reconciliationem, justitiam, est quod justificamur apud Deum: quod peccata nobis non imputantur, quod reddimur justi, est justitia Dei, id est, Deo placente, atque ab eo nobis ordinata, in Christo.
units.tr: 2 Corinthians 5:14-15, 19, 21: Judging this, that if one died for all, then all have died; and he died for all, etc. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing to them their sins. For he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. Therefore we are justified before God through Christ alone, through his death, reconciliation, and righteousness: that our sins are not imputed to us, and that we are made righteous, is the righteousness of God, that is, what is pleasing to God and ordained by him for us in Christ.

units.la: Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. iv. pag. 334. cum hac imputatione, de qua nimirum in allegato loco, nihil omnino aliena justitia imputatio commercii habet.
units.tr: Socinus, On Salvation, part 4, ch. 4, p. 334: with this imputation, of which in the cited place nothing at all of the imputation of another's righteousness has the character of an exchange.

units.la: Resp. Ostendendum hoc fuerat, non contra nos adeo, ac contra Apostolum; qui uti imputationem intellexit alieni peccati in Christo, quando eum dixit peccatum factum pro nobis; ita nos justitiam fieri in Christo, quia peccata nobis non imputentur propter Christum, intelligit, per imputationem justitiae Christi.
units.tr: Reply: This should have been shown not so much against us as against the Apostle, who, understanding the imputation of another's sin in Christ when he said that he was made sin for us, likewise understands that we are made righteousness in Christ, because our sins are not imputed to us on account of Christ, through the imputation of Christ's righteousness.

units.la: Schlichtingius, pro Socino, con-tra Meisnerum, pag. 257. Atqui nullo congruo sensu diceretur, Deum Christo peccata nostra imputasse in eum finem, ut nobis justitia illius imputaretur. Annon enim justitia Christi nobis imputari potuisset, etiamsi illi peccata nostra non fuissent imputata? vel quomodo ex eo, quod Christo peccata nostra imputata fuerunt, ejus vicissim justitiam nobis imputari consequitur? Adde, quod hoc tanquam omnium efficacissimo argumento movere velit Paulus homines, ut cum Deo reconcilientur, hoc est, inimicitias erga Deum deponant, illum ament, illi serviant, totoque pectore pietatem ac justitiam sectentur. At qua esset ad hanc rem efficacia in eo, quod Christo nostra peccata fuerint imputata, ac vicissim illius justitia nobis?
units.tr: Schlichtingius, for Socinus, against Meisner, p. 257. Yet no fitting sense could be given to the claim that God imputed our sins to Christ in order that his righteousness might be imputed to us. For could not Christ's righteousness have been imputed to us even if our sins had not been imputed to him? Or how does it follow that, because our sins were imputed to Christ, his righteousness is in turn imputed to us? Add that Paul wants to move men by what he regards as the most effective of all arguments to be reconciled to God, that is, to lay aside their enmity toward God, to love him, to serve him, and to pursue piety and righteousness with their whole heart. But what effectiveness would there be for this purpose in the fact that our sins were imputed to Christ, and in turn his righteousness to us?

units.la: Resp. 1. Imo ita oportuit, ex ratione & oeconomia nostrae redemtionis, a Deo constitutâ, ut Christo imputarentur peccata nostra, vid fidejussori & redemtori vero; & nobis ejus justitia, qua absolveremur. Quum enim pro peccatis nostris satisfieri Deo debuit, quod per nullum fieri quam per Christum potuit, primo quidem in eum fecit incurrere Deus omnium nostrum peccata, seu reatum; hoc est, quod factus fuit peccatum, seu hostia pro peccato: deinde, data a Christo, nostri loco, solutione vel satisfactione, haec ceu nostra censeri debuit, nobisque gratiose imputari: quidquid enim Christus aut fuit, aut fecit, nostrum est, & quia pro nobis totus, nostra ei, quaeque ejus, nobis vicissim imputari debuerunt. Atque is sensus dicti Apostolici.
units.tr: Answer 1. Indeed it had to be so, by the reasoning and economy of our redemption as established by God: that our sins be imputed to Christ, as to the true surety and redeemer, and his righteousness to us, by which we would be absolved. For since satisfaction had to be made to God for our sins, which could be made by no one but Christ, God first caused the sins of us all, or the guilt of them, to fall upon him; that is, he was made sin, or a sacrifice for sin. Then, the payment or satisfaction given by Christ in our place ought to be reckoned as ours and graciously imputed to us. For whatever Christ was or did is ours, and since he was wholly for us, our things, and whatever is his, ought in turn to be imputed to us. This is the sense of the apostolic saying.

units.la: Communicavit Christus de malis nostris; nos de ejus bono. Ipse pro nobis peccatum; nos in eo justitia.
units.tr: Christ shared in our evils; we in his good. He was made sin for us; we are made righteousness in him.

units.la: 11. Justitia illa Christi, qua pro nobis satisfecit, non esset, nisi ipsi peccata nostra fuissent imputata; neque alias illa imputari nobis potuisset.
units.tr: 2. The righteousness of Christ, by which he satisfied for us, would not exist unless our sins had been imputed to him; nor could it otherwise have been imputed to us.

units.la: 111. Indeque apparet satis manifeste, quomodo ex eo, quod Christo imputata fuerunt peccata nostra, sequatur, ejus vicissim justitiam imputari nobis, nempe quia nostra est, nostro loco, & pro nobis praestita.
units.tr: 3. From this it appears quite plainly how it follows that, because our sins were imputed to Christ, his righteousness is in turn imputed to us: namely, because it is ours, done in our place and on our behalf.

units.la: Iv. Reconciliari cum Deo, non est inimicitias cum Deo deponere, ei servire &c. sed cum eo in gratiam redire, ejus jam non iram experiri, sed favorem, qui perpetuus sensus est verbi reconciliari cum aliquo: ex quo tum quidem sequitur, ut ei serviatur, nequaquam tamen ut in eo vis & natura reconciliationis constitui aut exponi debeat. v. Jam non necesse est ut vim illationis illius ostendamus, quam Adversarius cupit, quia negamus illud quod ponit consequens, nempe eo, quo facit, sensu expositam reconciliationem. vi. Sed commode atque efficaciter ex eo, quod Christus pro nobis satisfecit, quod in eo Deus mundum secum conciliavit, ille peccata nostra tulit, ut ejus justitiâ absolvamur, hinc monet ac rogat Apostolus, quasi Christi nomine, ut Deo reconciliemur. videlicet, ut favorem & gratiam illam, à Deo factam, & oblatam nobis in Euangelio, τῇ ἀλ[?]γ[?]ῇ τ[?]ς καταλλαγῆς, omni alacritate, fide, animo ampleftamur; dein & digne illâ in perpetuum vivamus cum omni pietate atque justitiâ.ı
units.tr: 4. To be reconciled with God is not to lay aside enmity toward God, to serve him, and so on; it is to return into favour with him, no longer to experience his wrath but his favour. This is the constant sense of the phrase "to be reconciled with someone." From this it does indeed follow that he should be served, but by no means that the force and nature of reconciliation should be located or explained in that. 5. Now we need not show the force of that inference which our opponent wants, since we deny that what he posits as the consequent follows, namely reconciliation explained in the sense in which he does. 6. But it is fitting and effective that, since Christ satisfied for us, and in him God reconciled the world to himself, and he bore our sins so that we might be absolved by his righteousness, the apostle therefore urges and entreats us, as if in Christ's name, to be reconciled to God. That is, that we embrace with all eagerness, faith and sincere mind that favour and grace offered to us by God in the gospel [τῆς καταλλαγῆς], and then live worthily of it forever, with all piety and righteousness.

units.la: Denique, & alia Scripturæ loca sunt, quæ docent, in Christo, perque ejus justitiam, vere & proprie nos justificari. Gal. III.[?] 16. 17. Scientes quod homo non justificatur ex operibus legis, nisi per fidem Jesu Christi; & nos in Christum Jesum credimus, ut justificaremur ex fide Christi &c. Si vero quaerentes justificari in Christo &c. Cap. III. 24. 25. 26. 27. 28. Quandoquidem lex paedagogus noster factus est ad Christum, ut ex fide justificaremur. Veniente autem fide non amplius sumus sub paedagogo. Omnes enim filii Dei estis per fidem in Christo Jesu. Et in sequentibus Apostolus id nominat, in Christum baptizari, Christum induere, in Christo esse. Phil. III. 9. Et reperiar in eo Christo, non habens meam justitiam quæ ex lege, sed eam quæ fidei Christi, justitiam quæ ex Deo est in fide. Nullâ legis, nullâ nostrâ justitia justificamur, sed eâ quæ Dei, quæ Christi, quæ fidei est. Ad hanc in Euangelio adducti sumus, in hac sumus, stamus, vivimus.
units.tr: Finally, there are other passages of Scripture which teach that we are truly and properly justified in Christ and through his righteousness. Gal. 3:16, 17: Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ; and we have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, etc. But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, etc. Gal. 3:24–28: Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. But after faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. And in what follows the apostle calls this being baptized into Christ, putting on Christ, being in Christ. Phil. 3:9: And be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. We are justified not by any righteousness of the law or of our own, but by that which is of God, of Christ, of faith. To this we have been brought in the gospel; in this we stand, live, and remain.

units.la: Et certe nihil est præter eam, quod animum hominis peccatoris securum reddere queat. Destituimur undique, thesaurus iste pretiosissimus tranquillæ conscientiæ nullibi quam in Christo, in eo solo, fide ad justitiam apprehensio, latet. Rom. v. 1. Justificati ergo ex fide, pacem habemus apud Deum per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum; per quem etiam habemus accessum per fidem in gratiam istam in qua stamus. Ut haud immerito hinc Gallica dicat Confessio, art. XVIII. Credimus, non posse nos, si vel tantillum ab hoc fundamento declinemus, repirire ubi conquiescamus, sed potius inquietos semper fore, quoniam pacem cum Deo habere non possumus, donec certo nobis sit persuasum, nos in Jesu Christo diligi, quoniam in nobis ipsis omni odio digni sumus. In quam sententiam loquitur etiam Belgica nostra Confessio, art. XXIV.
units.tr: And certainly there is nothing besides this that can make the mind of a sinful man secure. We are deprived of everything on every side; that most precious treasure of a quiet conscience is found nowhere but in Christ, in him alone, in the grasping of righteousness by faith. Rom. 5:1: Being justified therefore by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ; by whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand. Hence the French Confession rightly says, art. 18: We believe that if we depart even a little from this foundation, we cannot find where to rest, but shall always be restless, since we cannot have peace with God unless it is firmly persuaded to us that we are loved in Jesus Christ, since in ourselves we are worthy of all hatred. Our Belgic Confession, art. 24, speaks to the same effect.

units.la: Arg. quartum, petitur ex natura fidei justificantis. Ut de eo nunc etiam secundo simul loco dicamus. Fidei justificantis objectum est Christus, inde dicitur fides in Christum: atqui in Christum credere, proprie est Christum, & promissionem Euangelii, sive gratiæ & salutis in eo, apprehendere: ergo, proprie dicendo, non per obedientiam nostram justificamur, sed per Christum fide apprehensum. Joann. i. 12. quotquot autem eum acceperunt, [?]ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν, dedit iis potestatem filios Dei fieri, credentibus in ipsius nomen. Credere ergo in Christum, est ipsum accipere.
units.tr: The fourth argument is drawn from the nature of justifying faith. Let us speak of this now, in the second place at the same time. The object of justifying faith is Christ; hence faith is said to be in Christ. But to believe in Christ is properly to lay hold of Christ and the promise of the gospel, that is, of grace and salvation in him. Therefore, properly speaking, we are justified not by our obedience but by Christ apprehended by faith. John 1:12: But as many as received him [ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν], to them he gave power to become the sons of God, to those who believe in his name. To believe in Christ is therefore to receive him.

units.la: Exc. Schlichtingius, pag. 298. Nonne videri potuisti Meisnere, simplex verbum ἔλαβον Hebraico more positum esse pro composito (compositis enim Hebraei destituuntur) παρέλαβον, quemadmodum ex proxime praecedenti versiculo apparet, illius enim loco statim hoc simplex ponitur. At vero Christum ἀπολαμβάνειν, hoc est, recipere, nihil aliud est, quam illius doctrinam complecti, illius discipulum fieri: ideoque credere in nomen Christi, quandoquidem hoc per illud ἔλαβον, ut ipse fateris, explicatur, revera nihil aliud erit, quam Christo adhaerere, illiusque disciplinam ex animo amplecti.
units.tr: Schlichting, against Meisner, p. 298: Could you not see, Meisner, that the simple verb ἔλαβον is used in the Hebrew manner for the compound (for the Hebrews lack compounds) παρέλαβον, as appears from the immediately preceding verse, for in its place this simple form is put at once. But to receive Christ [ἀπολαμβάνειν], that is, to accept him, is nothing other than to embrace his teaching and become his disciple. Therefore to believe in the name of Christ, since, as you yourself admit, this is explained by that ἔλαβον, will in truth be nothing other than to cling to Christ and embrace his discipline from the heart.

units.la: Resp. 1. Sive ἔλαβον, sive παρέλαβον, non negamus, quin etiam notet disciplinam Christi amplecti & sequi, sed nihil aliud significare, hoc negamus.
units.tr: Answer 1. Whether ἔλαβον or παρέλαβον, we do not deny that it also signifies embracing and following the discipline of Christ; but we deny that it signifies nothing else.

units.la: 11. Negabin' illud accipi debere in suâ totâ latitudine, quâ Christus nobis tum offertur, tum accipitur? atqui non pro magistro solum, sed & mediatore ac Salvatore Christus venit, pro eoque agnoscendus, quia talis revera est, quamvis id hoc in loco non distinctè exprimatur.
units.tr: 2. Will you deny that it must be understood in its whole breadth, in which Christ is both offered to us and received? For Christ came not only as teacher but also as mediator and Saviour, and must be acknowledged as such, since he truly is such, even though this is not expressed distinctly in this place.

units.la: 111. Atque illud significatur, tum fide in ejus nomen, tum filiatione eam consequente, quae non sunt eorum, qui simpliciter Christi disciplinam, sed qui totum eum, prout est, accipiunt. Gal. iii. 26. Omnes enim Filii Dei estis fide in Christo Jesu. 1v Et speciatim docetur illo loco, quod Christus, fide in ipsum, accipitur. hoc ἐξήγησις ista continet, credentibus in nomen ejus, per quod prius illud, quotquot eum acceperunt, exponitur. Hoc est credere in Filium. qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam. Joann. iii. 36. Actor. xxvi. 18. [?]ἵνα λαβεῖν αὐτὰς ut accipiant remissionem peccatorum, & fortem inter sanctos, πίστει τῇ εἰς ἐμέ, fide, quae in me. 1 Tim. i. 15. Fidele est verbum, & omni acceptione πίστεως ἀποδοχῆς dignum, quod Jesus Christus in mundum venit ut peccatores servaret. 1 Tim. vi. 12 [?]ἐπιλαβοῦ arripe aeternam vitam. Fit hoc fide, Hebr. xi. Rom. v. 17. multo magis qui abundantiam gratiae, & doni justitiae accipientes, in vita regnabunt per unum Jesum Christum.
units.tr: 3. And this is signified both by faith in his name and by the adoption that follows it, which belong not to those who merely accept Christ's teaching, but to those who receive him wholly, as he is. Gal. 3:26: For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. 4. And specifically that passage teaches that Christ is received by faith in him. This explanation believing in his name contains, by which the earlier phrase as many as received him is explained. That is, to believe in the Son. He who believes in the Son has eternal life. John 3:36. Acts 26:18. that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among the sanctified, [ἵνα λαβεῖν αὐτάς] by faith that is in me [πίστει τῇ εἰς ἐμέ]. 1 Tim. 1:15: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation [πίστεως ἀποδοχῆς] that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners. 1 Tim. 6:12: lay hold on eternal life [ἐπιλαβοῦ]. This is done by faith, Heb. 11. Rom. 5:17: much more those who receive abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness shall reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

units.la: Atque hinc dicimur, justificari fide, πίστει. Rom. iii. 28. & v. 2. ex fide, ἐκ πίστεως. Rom. i. 17. & iii. 30. & v. 1* per fidem, διὰ πίστεως. Rom. iii. 22. 25. 30. Ephes. ii. 8. & passim fidei adscribitur nostra justificatio, fidei in Christum, qua eum accipimus, induimus, uti habetur Gal. iii. 26. 27. Omnes enim filii Dei estis per fidem in Christo Jesu. Quotquot enim in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Ephes. iii. 17. Christum per fidem habitare in cordibus vestris. Inde Apostoli ista gloriatio, Gal. ii. 20. vivo autem, non jam ego, vivit vero in me Christus. quod autem nunc vivo in carne, in fide vivo quae est Filii Dei, qui me dilexit & seipsum pro me tradidit.
units.tr: Hence we are said to be justified by faith [πίστει], Rom. 3:28; 5:2; from faith [ἐκ πίστεως], Rom. 1:17; 3:30; 5:1; through faith [διὰ πίστεως], Rom. 3:22, 25, 30; Eph. 2:8. Throughout Scripture our justification is ascribed to faith, to faith in Christ by which we receive him and put him on, as is stated in Gal. 3:26, 27: "For you are all children of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Eph. 3:17: "that Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts." Hence the Apostle's boast, Gal. 2:20: "I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me."

units.la: Exc. Schlichtingius, pag. 296. Haec verba ad applicationem istam trahere, quid aliud est, quam & verbis vim facere, & id quod in principio petere? Num, quia Christus Paulum dilexit, & se pro Paulum in mortem tradidit, propterea Paulus non aliter in illum credebat, quam illius merita sibi applicando? Resp. 1. Quod si illa Pauli verba non exprimant applicationem singularem, tum quæ hoc factura sint verba, equidem me non posse videre fateor. Dixerat Apostolus, se cum Christo concrucifixum, vivere etiam per ejus vitam, non suam, se ab eo dilectum adeo, ut non dubitarit, quin pro se Christus semet in mortem tradiderit. Neque tamen illa comprehendent applicationem Christi, amoris, mortis, vitæ & beneficiorum ejus? Certe non aliter Paulus in eum credebat, quam ita statuens, uti hic affirmat, illum totum sibi applicando, ergo & beneficia ejus omnia ac merita.
units.tr: Schlichting, p. 296: "To draw these words to that application, what else is it than to do violence to the words and to beg the very question at the start? Because Christ loved Paul and gave himself into death for Paul, does it follow that Paul did not believe in him otherwise than by applying to himself Christ's merits?" Reply: (1) If those words of Paul do not express a personal application, then I confess I cannot see what words would express one. The Apostle had said that he was crucified with Christ, that he lives also by Christ's life and not his own, and that he was loved so much that he did not doubt that Christ had given himself into death for him. Do these words not nevertheless comprehend the application of Christ, of his love, death, life and benefits? Certainly Paul did not believe in him otherwise than by so determining, as he here affirms, by applying him wholly to himself, and therefore also all his benefits and merits.

units.la: Schlichtingius porro: in altero loco dicit Paulus, Quotquot in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Hic similiter principium petis. Quærimus enim, quomodo hic dicatur Christus indui? Tu dicis per applicationem & appropriationem Christi meritorum, nos negamus. Talis enim Christi induitio vera non est, sed imaginaria, & cum ex illa Apostolus colligat, nos esse filios Dei, ut ex præcedenti versiculo apparet, sequeretur etiam nos vere filios Dei non esse, sed tantum per applicationem quandam & imaginationem. Quocirca Christum induere nihil aliud est, quam Christo conformem fieri, & cum illo hac ratione uniri. Resp. 1. Neque etiam induere, applicationem sonat? Quid demum erit sibi aliquid applicare, si non ubi quid induitur? Nec hic de Christi meritis disputatur, sed de Christi, & quidquid nobis habet, meritorum dicas, vel beneficiorum, appropriatione. II. Falsum, induitionem illam non esse veram, sed imaginariam. Ergone quod spirituale, imaginarium vobis est? Dicatur ergo omnis fides, & acceptio Christi, vel donorum ejus Joann. iv. 10. esse tota imaginaria. III. Pari falsitate nititur ea, quam hic instituit, illatio, nos haud vere esse Dei filios, sed tantum per quandam imaginationem. IV. Haud æquipollent ista, per applicationem, & per imaginationem. Applicatio per fidem fit & Spiritum, estque rei certæ & veræ. Nisi velis dicere, remissionem peccatorum, & promissionem divinæ misericordiæ nobis vel non applicari, vel per nudam & temerariam duntaxat imaginationem. Spiritualia dona, & rerum spiritualium gustus, non sunt profecto humanæ imaginationis, nisi arcanum & vim Christianæ religionis infidelibus & atheis deridendam prorsus exhibeas; sed verae, spiritualis, intimæ appropriationis & applicationis. V. Christum induere, non est primo ei conformem fieri, & hac ratione eocum uniri, sed uniri, & sic cum eo conformem reddi, quæ unitio quum per fidem fiat, uti ex adductis Scripturæ locis liquet, Christus nobiscum unitur, nos cum eo, & sic nobis ille primo approximatur & applicatur totus, instar vestis, quæ induitur, sive adjungitur & applicatur corpori; unde tum unio proximè sequitur: atque sic in præsenti negotio, est Christi induitio, unio, conformitas. Applicationem Christi ad animum nostrum nulli negant, nec negare possunt, nisi qui naturam, vim, sensum fidei velint omnino convellere, ac destruere.
units.tr: Schlichting again: "In the other passage Paul says, 'As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.' Here too you beg the question. For we ask how it is said here that Christ is put on. You say by the application and appropriation of Christ's merits; we deny it. For such a putting on of Christ is not true but imaginary, and since the Apostle infers from it that we are sons of God, as appears from the preceding verse, it would follow that we are not truly sons of God either, but only through a certain application and imagination. Therefore to put on Christ is nothing other than to become conformed to Christ, and in this way to be united with him." Reply: (1) Does "to put on" not also mean application? What then would it be to apply something to oneself, if not where something is put on? Nor is the question here about Christ's merits, but about the appropriation of Christ, and of whatever he has, which you may call his merits or benefits. (2) It is false that the putting on is not true but imaginary. Is then whatever is spiritual imaginary for you? Let it be said, then, that all faith and all acceptance of Christ, or of his gifts (John 4:10), is wholly imaginary. (3) The inference he draws here, that we are not truly God's sons but only through some imagination, rests on an equally false basis. (4) "By application" and "by imagination" are not equivalent. Application is made through faith and the Spirit, and is of a thing certain and true. Unless you wish to say that the remission of sins and the promise of divine mercy are either not applied to us, or applied only through a bare and rash imagination. Spiritual gifts and the taste of spiritual things certainly do not belong to human imagination, unless you wish to expose the secret and power of the Christian religion to be utterly mocked by unbelievers and atheists; they belong to a true, spiritual and inward appropriation and application. (5) To put on Christ is not first to be made conformed to him and in this way united with him; rather, one is united with him, and so made conformed to him. This union is made through faith, as is clear from the cited passages of Scripture: Christ is united with us, and we with him. So he first draws near to us and is applied to us wholly, like a garment that is put on, or joined and fitted to the body; from this union follows at once. Thus in the present matter, putting on Christ is union and conformity. No one denies, nor can anyone deny, the application of Christ to our mind, except those who wish utterly to overturn and destroy the nature, power and sense of faith.

units.la: Longe aliter naturam fidei justificantis exponunt Adversarii, nec tamen omnia improbamus, quæ hic tenent. Uti enim ipsi in nobis, sic nos vicissim in ipsis probamus, 1. quod saltem dicunt nobiscum, adversus Pontificios, solam fidem justificare. Schlichting. pag. 290. 11. Quòd fidem ajunt esse assensum animi. Schlichting. pag. 314. Fides, quæ est doctrina Christi assensus. 111. Quòd fidei conjungunt fiduciam, & fidem justificantem tenent esse fiduciam, non assensum tantùm. Schlichting. pag. 293. & 312. Ex assensu autem & deside-rio boni spes oritur ac fiducia: & fiducia quidem assensum magis, spes vero magis desiderium significat. præterea fiducia est assensus firmus rei desiderabilis adipiscendæ in aliquo defixus. 1v. Quòd fidem ferri in divinas promissiones asserunt. v. Eique sic adscribi justificationem. Schlichting. pag. 313. Nam primò opus est, ut divinis promissionibus, etiamsi vel maxime impossibiles nobis videantur, toto pectore assentiamur, & de illarum fide ne tantillum quidem dubitemus. Illi ergo fidei, qua divinis promissionibus firmiter assen-timur, justificatio attribuitur, tum quod initium det justificationi, tum quod ex ea indisso-lubili nexu fluant reliqua, quæ ad justificationeem confervandam, complendam ac perficien-dam requiruntur. Pag. 314. Respondemus enim, fidem justificantem striæte proprieque sumtam non ferri nisi in divinas promissiones nobis per Christum datas. vi. Istamque fidem in nobis necessario producere bona opera agnoscunt. Idem Schlichting. part. 312. Qui enim Christo supremam felicitatem obedientiæ sibi promittenti assentitur, & tanti boni desiderio exardescit, illudque consequi prorsus in animum induxit, fieri non potest quin statim spem ac fiduciam in Christo, & per Christum in Deo collocet. Pag. 313. Fidei namque effecta sunt omnes Christianæ virtutes. Qui namque Christi doctrinæ penitus assentitur, proinde Deo per Christum ex animo confidit, & spem in illo collocat, Deo etiam totum se mancipat, & virtutibus se tradit. Pag. 314. Idem autem contingit etiam fidei effectis, nempe spei, charitati, pietati, sanctimoniæ, vitæ secundum spiritum. Pag. 323. Hæc enim fide in nobis exorta, statim id animis nostris divina promissiones suâ præstantia ac bonitate ardentissimum sui desiderium excitabunt. Inde postea fiet, ut spem & fiduciam in Deo collocemus. Hæc vero posita, quid aliud supererit, quam ut nos toto pectore totisque viribus ad ipsius imperia capescenda, & præcepta exequenda convertamus. & sic nos ei penitus addicamus. Pag. 325. Fides enim in strictâ & propriâ significatione habet se ad obe-dientiam, ut causa ad effectum, ut arbor ad fructum, ut mater ad filiam. Valde bene.
units.tr: The Adversaries explain the nature of justifying faith in a quite different way, yet we do not disapprove of everything they hold here. For just as they approve of us in certain points, so we in turn approve of them: (1) that at least they agree with us, against the Papists, that faith alone justifies (Schlichting, p. 290); (2) that they say faith is an assent of the mind (p. 314): "Faith, which is assent to the doctrine of Christ"; (3) that they join trust to faith, and hold justifying faith to be trust, not merely assent (p. 293 and 312): "From assent and desire for a good thing hope and confidence arise; confidence signifies assent more, hope signifies desire more; moreover, confidence is a firm assent to a desirable thing to be obtained, fixed on something"; (4) that they assert faith is directed to the divine promises; (5) and that justification is ascribed to it (p. 313): "For first it is necessary that we assent with our whole heart to the divine promises, even if they seem to us most impossible, and not doubt even a little of their truth. Justification is therefore ascribed to that faith by which we firmly assent to the divine promises, both because it gives the beginning of justification, and because from it, by an indissoluble bond, the rest flow which are required to preserve, complete and perfect justification." (p. 314): "For we reply that justifying faith, taken strictly and properly, is directed only to the divine promises given to us through Christ." (6) They acknowledge that such faith necessarily produces good works in us. The same Schlichting, p. 312: "For whoever assents to Christ, who promises him supreme happiness for obedience, and burns with desire for so great a good, and has fully resolved to obtain it, cannot but at once place hope and trust in Christ, and through Christ in God." p. 313: "For all Christian virtues are the effects of faith. For whoever fully assents to the doctrine of Christ trusts in God through Christ from the heart, places his hope in him, also surrenders himself wholly to God and gives himself up to the virtues." p. 314: "But the same happens also to the effects of faith, namely hope, charity, piety, holiness, life according to the Spirit." p. 323: "For faith arisen in us will at once stir in our minds a most ardent desire for the divine promises, by their excellence and goodness. Afterwards it will come about that we place hope and trust in God. When these are in place, what else will remain but that we turn ourselves with our whole heart and all our strength to take up his commands and carry out his precepts, and so devote ourselves wholly to him." p. 325: "For faith in its strict and proper sense stands to obedience as cause to effect, as tree to fruit, as mother to daughter." Very well.

units.la: Facile autem dubitarit aliquis, quid ergo quæstionis hic inter nos supersit, vel quomodo in antecentibus diversa ex Socino attulerimus, de operibus, non effectis, sed quasi forma fidei, aliaque quæ in hac disputatione passim in Socinianis impugnavimus, istis quæ jamjam attulimus, parum consentientia? Quos scire oportet, haud nunc demum istam agendi methodum observari in Adversariis, ut multa in speciem dicant, nec tamen multum, vel ut am-ple de multis pronuncient, quæ quis putare possit disputationem allevatura, & proprios illos redditura nobis, at penitus introspecta mox evanescunt, & inani se distinctione occultantes tandem iterum recipiunt ad sua. Ita hic, postquam Socinus haud semel dixisset, fidem nihil aliud esse quam fiduciam, & hanc esse obedientiam; id sibi incrustandum aliquâ ingeniosâ distinctione existimavit Schlichtingius, datâ vocis fidei acceptione strictâ & propriâ, vel latâ & impropriâ, Socinus, de justificat. pag. 25. Quæ fides, obedientiam præ-ceptorum
units.tr: One might easily wonder what question still remains between us here, or how the things we brought forward above from Socinus, about works not as effects but as the form of faith, and the other things we have attacked throughout this disputation in the Socinians, can be reconciled with what has just been cited. Those who ought to know must recognise that this method is not newly observed in the Adversaries: they say many things in appearance, and not much, or they pronounce at length on many matters which one might think would lighten the dispute and bring them over to our side. But when these are looked into thoroughly they soon vanish, and hiding themselves behind an empty distinction, they finally retreat to their own position. So here, after Socinus had said more than once that faith is nothing other than trust, and that this trust is obedience, Schlichting thought he must cover this over with some ingenious distinction, namely by taking the word faith in a strict and proper sense or in a broad and improper one. Socinus, On Justification, p. 25: "Which faith contains the obedience of God's precepts, not indeed as its effect, but as its substance and form contains and embraces it."

units.la: Tttt3 ceptorum Dei, non quidem ut effectum suum, sed ut suam substantiam & formam continet atque complectitur. Meminisse enim debemus, ejus, quod supra recte conclusum est, fidem, hanc scilicet, qua justificamur, Dei obedientiam esse. Pag. 55. Tunc Christi fides, quam opera subsequentur, aliud nihil erit, quam ipsi Christo confidere, quod sine dubio coram Deo justificandi vim habet, & consequenter opera ipsa justificant, quatenus executio sunt ac perfectio, & tamquam forma ipsius fidei. Ibidem. Unde constat, opera nequaquam simpliciter esse fidei fructus, ut vulgo creditur, sed fidei forma perfectionem indere, & vitam (ut sic dixerim) tribuere. Distinctionem adhibet Schlichtingius, quae an possit efficere, ut opera aliquando fidei effectus, aliquando forma dici debeant, videamus. Sic igitur .. pag. 311. Notandum igitur est, fidei, cui justificatio attribuitur, vocem sumi dupliciter: strictius, & latius; & sic proprie, vel improprie. Strictius & proprie sumta, nihil aliud, quam assensum firmum Christi doctrinae prae-bitum significat, & ex eo manantem in Deum & in Christum fiduciam. In hac autem stricta & propria significatione tum sumitur, cum fidei etiam alia ad salutem nobis comparandum pertinentia adjunguntur, quae quanto plura sunt, tanto magis fidei vox restringitur, & ad propriam suam significationem redigitur. Latius autem sumitur tum, cum pauciora illi adjun-guntur: latissime, cum sola ponitur, & tamen illi salus nostra adscribitur. Verbi causa, cum Paulus manere nunc dicit, fidem, spem, charitatem; fidem in stricta & propria significatione sumit, ita ut reliqua duo non complectatur. Cum vero alibi dicit, in Christo Iesu nihil valere, praeter fidem per charitatem efficacem, jam vocem fidei latius extendit, ita ut etiam spem contineat, &c. Similiter Petrus, cum catenam illam veram auream virtutum Christianarum connectit, fidem, quam primo loco nominat, strictissime sumit, sic ut reliquas virtutes, quae illi adduntur, minime complectatur. Divus etiam Iacobus, cum non ex fide tantum, sed etiam ex operibus hominem justificari contendit & evincit, fidem sic sumit, ut reliqua bona opera non contineat. Cum vero sola fides nominatur, eique nulla alia re adjecta salus nostra adscribitur, tum latissime sumitur, sic ut in se ea omnia involvere dicenda sit, quae alibi distincta ac evoluta proponuntur. Solet quippe Scriptura nunc brevius & rotun-dius, nunc plenius & distinctius loqui. Pag. 313. Quocirca si fidei vox stricte sumatur, fides nequaquam est adaequata justificationis nostrae causa, teste Iacobo, qui fidem sine operibus tam esse mortuam docet, quam corpus sine spiritu, proinde ad hominem justificandum prorsus inefficacem. Unde fit: ut fidei alia etiam persæpe [?] tanquam salutis nostrae media adjungantur. Sed quanto latius sumitur, tanto magis justificationi adaequatur; si latissime, adaequatur etiam prorsus. Socinus ergo, cum vellet fidei notionem justificationi nostrae plane adaequatam tradere, praesertim cum de fiducia loqueretur, quae sua natura obedientiam illi, cui fidimus, & cujus bonitati initimur, praestandam, si nimirum eam requirat, secum trahit, fidem in latissima significatione ex Scripturae usu sumsit, & rectissime eo, quo fecit, pacto definivit. Idem videatur quoque Auctor in epist. ad Hebr. pag. 513. Ista latius describenda fuerunt, ut tum de sententia Adversariorum, tum conciliatione eo-rum, quae apud ipsos repugnare sibi invicem videntur, certius constaret.
units.tr: ...the obedience of God's commandments, not indeed as its effect, but as it contains and embraces its own substance and form. For we must remember what was rightly concluded above: that faith, namely that by which we are justified, is the obedience of God. Page 55. Then the faith of Christ, which works follow, will be nothing other than to trust in Christ himself, which without doubt has the power of justifying before God; and consequently the works themselves justify, insofar as they are its execution and perfection, and as it were the form of faith itself. Ibid. Hence it is clear that works are by no means simply the fruits of faith, as is commonly believed, but that they give faith its perfection and, as I may say, impart life to it. Schlichtingius uses a distinction, and let us see whether it can bring it about that works should sometimes be called the effect of faith and sometimes its form. So then, page 311: It must therefore be noted that the word faith, to which justification is ascribed, is taken in two ways: more strictly and more broadly; and so properly or improperly. Taken strictly and properly, it signifies only the firm assent given to the doctrine of Christ, and the trust in God and in Christ that flows from it. This strict and proper sense is used when other things pertaining to the attainment of salvation are added to faith; and the more of these there are, the more the word faith is restricted and reduced to its proper meaning. It is taken more broadly when fewer such things are added to it; most broadly, when it stands alone and yet our salvation is ascribed to it. For example, when Paul says that now faith, hope and charity remain, he takes faith in its strict and proper sense, so that it does not include the other two. But when elsewhere he says that in Christ Jesus nothing avails except faith working through charity, he now extends the word faith more widely, so that it includes hope also, etc. Similarly Peter, when he links that true golden chain of Christian virtues, takes faith, which he names first, in the strictest sense, so that it does not embrace the other virtues which are added to it. The divine James too, when he maintains and proves that a man is justified not by faith only but also by works, takes faith in such a way that it does not contain the other good works. But when faith alone is named, and our salvation is ascribed to it with nothing else added, then it is taken most broadly, so that it must be said to involve in itself all those things which are set out separately and at length elsewhere. Scripture is wont to speak now more briefly and roundly, now more fully and distinctly. Page 313: Wherefore, if the word faith is taken strictly, faith is by no means the adequate cause of our justification, as James teaches, who says that faith without works is as dead as a body without a spirit, and so utterly ineffective for justifying a man. Hence it follows: that other things are also quite often added to faith as means of our salvation. But the more broadly it is taken, the more it is commensurate with justification; and if most broadly, it is entirely commensurate. Socinus, therefore, when he wished to give a notion of faith wholly commensurate with our justification, especially since he was speaking of trust, which by its nature brings with it the obedience to be rendered to the one who is trusted and whose goodness we rely upon, if indeed it requires it, took faith in its broadest sense from the usage of Scripture, and defined it most rightly in the way he did. The same author may also be consulted in the Epistle to the Hebrews, page 513: These things had to be described more broadly, so that it might be more certain both what the opinion of the adversaries is and how those things which among them seem to contradict each other may be reconciled.

units.la: Summa huc redit, fidem proprie sumi, quando assensum firmum Christi doctrinae praebitum significat, & ex eo manantem in Deum & in Christum fiduciam; alia improprie. Ergo nos, in disputatione hac, tenemus fidei propriam iterum significationem, Adversarii vero impropriam. Quod primò caussam nostram haud parum juvat. ii. Impropria fidei acceptio, est vocis duntaxat, & τρόπῳ [?] λέξεως; at non de vocis, aut vocis acceptione, sed de re jam disputamus. Concedimus, voces aliter saepe ac aliter accipi; sed inde in re non debet ea diversitas constitui, ut proinde forma ejus differat; & acceptâ voce fidei late & improprie, ita ut universam comprehendat obedientiam, hinc ut obedientia sit fidei forma. Exempli gratiâ, precatio & invocatio nominis Dei saepe in Scripturis sumitur pro tota religione, & omnium virtutum observantiâ: an ideo haec dicetur orationis esse quasi forma? Joann. ix. 11. conjungitur cum fide adoratio Christi, nam caecus ille credens in Christum, simul adorabat ipsum: non autem inde adoratio fidei est forma. Et sic de aliis.
units.tr: The sum comes to this: faith is properly taken when it signifies the firm assent given to the doctrine of Christ and the trust in God and in Christ flowing from it; otherwise it is improper. So in this dispute we hold to the proper meaning of faith, while our opponents hold to the improper one. This first greatly helps our cause. (2) The improper sense of faith belongs only to the word and to a figure of speech [τρόπῳ λέξεως]; but we are not disputing about the word or the sense of the word, but about the thing itself. We concede that words are often taken in different ways, but from that the difference must not be established in the thing, so that its form would differ accordingly; and, because the word faith is taken broadly and improperly so as to embrace the whole of obedience, it does not follow that obedience is the form of faith. For example, prayer and the invocation of the name of God are often used in Scripture for the whole of religion and the keeping of all the virtues: will this therefore be said to be, as it were, the form of prayer? In John 9:11 the worship of Christ is joined with faith, for that blind man, believing in Christ, at the same time worshipped him; yet the worship is not therefore the form of faith.
