And so with other things.

units.la: Bene dixit [?] Schlichtingius, pag. 328. Licet enim partes ad totum constituendum concurrunt, nihilominus inter se confundi non debent. Ita quamvis ad pietatem, & salutem multae virtutes concurrant, non tamen confundi debent, ut aliae dicantur esse aliarum formae, sed quidem unâ concurrere ad idem complementum. Cum fides sola nominatur, eique nulla alia re adjecta salus nostra adscribitur, tum latissime sumitur, sic ut in se ea omnia involvere dicenda sit, quae alibi distincta ac evoluta proponuntur, inquit pag. 312. Sed vocis fidei significatione, illa per synecdochem partis pro toto, & cum toto, intelligantur, non ideo ipsa, re & natura fide includi, dicenda erunt. De voce, si ita velint, non disputabimus, accipiatur aliquando latius, vel strictius, ipsa tamen fides justificans, ut talis, ea non comprehendat naturâ, vel formâ suâ, ut per ea nos justificet, quae alioqui omnes concedimus, ad fidem sequi, eique in homine, non ita in justificatione, conjungi. iii. Quare bene dixit, ex fide manare fiduciam, & sic reliqua: sed vel ideo non possunt in re, ejus forma ullatenus dici, sed, quod tamen, prout vulgò credi solet, Socinus aperte rejecit, fidei fructus. Socinus, de justificat. pag. 15. quae fides, obedientiam praeceptorum Dei, non quidem ut effectum suum, sed ut suam substantiam & formam continet atque complectitur. iv.
units.tr: Schlichtingius rightly said, page 328: For although parts concur to constitute the whole, nevertheless they ought not to be confused with one another. So although many virtues concur towards piety and salvation, they ought not to be confused, so that some are called the forms of others, but rather they concur into one and the same completion. When faith is named alone, and our salvation is ascribed to it with nothing else added, then it is taken most broadly, so that it must be said to involve in itself all those things which are set out separately and at length elsewhere, he says on page 312. But although by the meaning of the word faith those things are understood by synecdoche, a part for the whole and with the whole, it does not follow that they are to be said to be included in faith itself in fact and nature. About the word we shall not dispute, let it be taken sometimes more broadly or more strictly; yet justifying faith itself, as such, does not comprise by its nature or form those things by which it justifies us, which we all in any case concede to follow faith, and to be joined to it in man, but not in justification. (3) Therefore he rightly said that trust flows from faith, and so on; but for this very reason these things cannot in any way be called its form in reality, but rather, as is commonly believed, its fruits, which Socinus openly rejected. Socinus, On Justification, page 15: which faith, the obedience of God's commandments, not indeed as its effect, but as it contains and embraces its own substance and form. (4)

units.la: Probet auctor notam & regulam istam, quam facit, variae acceptionis fidei, quod quando vox sola ponitur, latissime sumatur; cum alia adjunguntur, & pauciora, latius; quando plura, tum demum proprie & stricte. Nos haec negamus, dicimusque, in materiâ justificationis semper fidem proprie sumi, non prout opera complectitur, vel aliqua, vel omnia, sed assensum firmum Christo, ejusque promissionibus praebitum. Haec, uti id nunc Adversarii ipsi agnoscunt, vocis fidei stricta & propria est significatio, perpetuusque vocis apud omnes usus. Dic, quare fides, quando dicitur Gal. v. 6. in Christo valere fidem per charitatem efficacem, sumatur latius, juxta tuam expositionem, quam 1 Cor. xiii. 13. ubi Apostolus ponit fidem, spem, charitatem? vel etiam quando Petrus in catena virtutum Christianarum vere aurea, primo loco constituit fidem? Detur discriminis ratio, ita vid. ut non incurrat in petitionem principii, vel sophisma ejus, uti dici solet, quod est in quaestione. iv. Sed eò tandem illa faciunt, ut, non manentes in verborum expositione, ad rem transferant, haud aequâ ratione, & caussam justificationis reddant à Scripturâ valde alienam. Nempe ut fides semper habeatur pro causa justificationis, & ubi sola ponitur, pro causâ inadæquatâ; ubi latissime accipitur, cum operum obedientiâ, tum demum pro causâ justificationis adæ-quatâ. Quæ falsa esse multis nunc argumentis evicimus: & sic quomodo in pessimam tandem desinant hypothesim, quæ primo in speciem disseruerunt, multisque dein ambagibus & distinctionibus explicarunt, manifestum.
units.tr: Let the author prove this rule which he makes about the varied sense of faith: that when the word stands alone it is taken most broadly; when other things are added, and fewer, more broadly; when many, then at last properly and strictly. We deny this, and we say that in the matter of justification faith is always taken properly, not insofar as it embraces works, either some or all, but as the firm assent given to Christ and to his promises. This, as our opponents themselves now acknowledge, is the strict and proper meaning of the word faith, and the constant usage of the word among all. Tell us why faith, when it is spoken of in Galatians 5:6 as availing in Christ through charity working, should be taken more broadly according to your exposition, than in 1 Corinthians 13:13, where the Apostle sets down faith, hope and charity? Or also when Peter, in the truly golden chain of Christian virtues, places faith first? Let a reason for the distinction be given, so that it does not fall into begging the question, or into what is commonly called the sophism of the question at issue. (5) But at last those arguments come to this: that, not remaining in the exposition of the words, they transfer the matter to the thing, quite unfairly, and make the cause of justification something very alien to Scripture. Namely, that faith should always be held to be the cause of justification, and where it stands alone, an inadequate cause; where it is taken most broadly, along with obedience to works, only then the adequate cause of justification. We have shown by many arguments that these things are false; and so it is manifest how those who at first argued in appearance, and then explained with many circumlocutions and distinctions, have at last ended in the worst hypothesis.

units.la: Tria hic esse distinguenda, res ipsa monet, neq; Adversarii diffitentur: credere, sive assensum præbere verbis Christi; ei confidere; denique obtemperare. Schlichtingius, pag. 324. Sed quod hinc fiat, ut Christi doctrinæ promissionibusque in ea comprehensis credas, deinde Christo confidas, tandem obedias. In epist. ad Hebræos, cap. xi. pag. 513. Ex hac enim fide vera in Christum fiducia nascitur, secumque naturam suam trahit vitam sanctitatem & innocentiam. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. ix. pag. 370. Animadvertendum autem præterea est, fidei vocabulum, quod attinet ad præsentem disputationem, dupliciter accipi. Neque enim assensum tantummodo alicui rei adhibitum, quæ affirmetur, significat; sed etiam fiduciam seu confidentiam &c. quam in aliquo habemus, declarat. Et cap. xi. pag. 393. Schlichtingius, pag. 314. Præsertim cum de fiducia loqueretur, quæ sua natura obedientiam illi, cui fidimus, & cujus bonitati innitimur, præstandam, si nimirum eam requirat, secum trahit. Pag. 319. Non erat, Meisnere, cur tanto molimine nos doceres, aliud esse formaliter obedire, aliud confidere: cum tam stolidi non simus, ut istud non videamus. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. xi. pag. 386. Sic qui ea, quæ Christus præcipit, facere recusaret, etiamsi ejus verba verissima esse crederet, ei confidere dici tamen non posset. Quamquam ea, quæ sibi obtemperantibus Christus eventura dixit, ejusmodi sunt, ut fieri non possit, quin u[?], qui ejus verba vera esse credat, illi ex animo obediat. & plura istam in rem ibi haud male disserit. Hic fieri non posse bene affirmat Socinus, quin qui verbis Christi credit, ei etiam ex animo obediat: alibi tamen id non necessario sequi scripsit, Notis in Dial. de Justific. pag. 25. Adde, quod credere promissionibus divinis, non quidem necessario, & per se, sed per accidens, gignit fiduciam in ipsum Deum, & ita ejus præceptorum obedientiam. Quod autem fides fiduciam, & hæc bonorum operum observantiam producat, haud uno in loco, neque hactenus male, docet diducitque Schlichtingius. Pag. 291. Non excludit autem ullo pacto opera ex fide provenientia, charitatem, & charitatis fructus, seu veram vitæ sanctimoniam. Pag. 318. Num, verbi causa, plane & vere medico confidet, qui pharmaco, quod propinat medicus, uti nolet? &c. Unde non semel Scriptura eos in Deum credere negat, qui præcepta illius non observant. adde pag. 310. 312.
units.tr: Three things must be distinguished here, as the matter itself shows, and our opponents do not deny it: to believe, that is, to give assent to the words of Christ; to trust in him; and finally to obey. Schlichtingius, p. 324: But from this it follows that you believe the doctrine of Christ and the promises contained in it, then trust in Christ, and finally obey. On the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 11, p. 513: For from this true faith in Christ, trust is born, and it draws with it its own nature, life, holiness and innocence. Socinus, On the Saving (De Servatore), part 4, ch. 9, p. 370: It should further be noted that the word faith, as far as the present dispute is concerned, is taken in two ways. For it does not signify only the assent given to something that is affirmed, but also declares the trust or confidence which we have in someone, etc. And ch. 11, p. 393. Schlichtingius, p. 314: Especially since he was speaking of trust, which by its nature brings with it the obedience that is to be rendered to the one in whom we trust and on whose goodness we rely, if indeed he requires it. P. 319: There was no reason, Meisner, for you to teach us with such great effort that it is one thing to obey formally and another to trust, since we are not so foolish as not to see this. Socinus, On the Saving, part 4, ch. 11, p. 386: Thus one who refused to do what Christ commands, even if he believed his words to be most true, could not for all that be said to trust in him. Yet the things which Christ said would befall those who obey him are of such a kind that it is impossible that he who believes his words to be true should not obey him from the heart. And there he discusses this matter at some length, and not badly. Here Socinus rightly affirms that it is impossible that one who believes the words of Christ should not also obey him from the heart; yet elsewhere he wrote that this does not follow necessarily, in his Notes on the Dialogue on Justification, p. 25: Add that to believe the divine promises does not, indeed, necessarily and of itself, but by accident, produce trust in God himself, and thus obedience to his precepts. That faith produces trust, and this in turn the observance of good works, Schlichtingius teaches and explains in more than one place, and not badly so far. P. 291: However, he by no means excludes the works that proceed from faith, charity, and the fruits of charity, or true holiness of life. P. 318: For example, does not one who refuses to use the medicine which the physician prescribes truly and plainly trust the physician? etc. Hence Scripture more than once denies that those believe in God who do not observe his commandments. Add p. 310, 312.

units.la: Verùm in his ab invicem abimus. 1. Quod fidem justificantem, de eâ quippe agimus, non in promissiones, aliàs dicunt, non tantum in promissiones, sed etiam in præcepta ferri, inquit. Socinus, de Justificat. pag. 25. Fides, quâ justificamur, non est credere promissionibus divinis; sed est, ipsi Deo confidere. Aliter Schlichtingius, in Disput. pro Socino, contra Meisnerum, pag. 324. Respondemus enim, fidem justificantem stricte proprieque sumtam non ferri nisi in divinas promissiones nobis per Christum datas: sed latius, nempe cum suis effectis, & quatenus justificationi nostra plena & perfecta adæquatur, sumtam, hactenus etiam in divina præcepta ferri, & ad eorum executionem sese extendere asserimus. II. Et hinc fidem per ista, quocunque modo, malè definiunt. Schlichtingius, pag. 319. Itaque fidem in Deum & Christum, nec simpliciter per confidere, nec simpliciter per obedire definit Socinus, sed per utrumque, nempe obediendo fidere vel fidendo obedire. III. Unde & obedientiam quasi formam fidei constituunt. Præter superius adducta, Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. xi. pag. 389. Ea siquidem in Deo confidentia, quæ nos coram ipso Deo justos constituit, partim obedientiæ caussa est, partim ipsa obedientia perficitur. Caussa obedientiæ, nam ideo quì obedit, quia confidit. Perficitur autem obedientia, quia nemo vere confidisse dici potest, antequam reipsa obediat, immo ideo confidisse dicitur, quia obedivit. Quæ sic exponit Schlichtingius, pag. 326. nam in hisce haud adeo facile est concordem Adversariorum sententiam deprehendere: Sic & fides non ideo per obedientiam à Socino definitur, quod, formaliter & proprie loquendo, sit obedien-tia partim pars, partim origo & caussa. ideoque etiam in tali definitione fides latius, & ultra suam propriam significationem extenditur. Atque hinc patet, immerito Meisnerum dicere, Socinum fidem proprie dictam, id est, proprie loquendo, definire per obedientiam.
units.tr: But in these matters we part ways. 1. Since we are speaking of justifying faith, they say that it is directed not only to the promises, as they elsewhere say, but also to precepts. Socinus, On Justification, p. 25: The faith by which we are justified is not to believe the divine promises, but is to trust in God himself. Otherwise Schlichtingius, in his Disputation for Socinus against Meisner, p. 324: For we reply that justifying faith, taken strictly and properly, is directed only to the divine promises given to us through Christ; but taken more broadly, namely with its effects, and as far as it is fully and perfectly commensurate with our justification, we assert that it is also directed to the divine precepts and extends itself to their performance. II. From this they also define faith badly by these things, in whatever way. Schlichtingius, p. 319: Thus they define faith in God and Christ neither simply by trusting nor simply by obeying, but by both, namely by trusting by obeying or by obeying by trusting. III. Hence they also make obedience, as it were, the form of faith. Besides what has been cited above, Socinus, On the Saving, part 4, ch. 11, p. 389: That confidence in God which makes us just before God himself is partly the cause of obedience, and partly is itself completed by obedience. It is the cause of obedience, for one who obeys does so because he trusts. But obedience is completed, because no one can truly be said to have trusted before he actually obeys; indeed he is said to have trusted because he has obeyed. Schlichtingius explains these things thus, p. 326, for in these matters it is not very easy to discover the agreement of our opponents' view: Thus faith too is not defined by Socinus through obedience because, speaking formally and properly, it is obedience, partly as a part, partly as the origin and cause. And therefore in such a definition faith is extended more broadly and beyond its proper signification. And from this it is clear that Meisner wrongly says that Socinus defines faith properly so called, that is, properly speaking, through obedience.

units.la: IV. Pejus, per illa nos justificationem apud Deum assequi, contendunt. Schlich-ting. pag. 324. ut Christi doctrinæ, promissionibusque in ea comprehensis credas, deinde Christo confidas, & sic justificationem, ac porro salutem ipsam obtineas. V. Pessimè vero contra apprehensionem Christi, quæ fide fit justificante, disputant Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. xi. pag. 401. præsertim cum ista vestra Christi apprehensio merum humanum commentum, & inanissimum somnium fit. Schlichtingius, pag. 299. At mi Meisnere, doce nos primo, quomodo gratia Dei, seu peccatorum remis-sio, itemque merita Christi, eo quo vos vultú sensu, à nobis apprehendi queant? Idem, pag. 300. 301. 302. Resp. 1. Quomodo docet Socinus, loco modò citato, misericordiam Dei à nobis apprehendi? Dum inquit: at Dei misericordia, obe-dientia ipsi ex Christi præscripto præstita apprehendi rectissime potest, si, se eam præstantibus misericordem reipsa futurum, Deus promiserit; ut certe promisit. II. Et ipse Schlichtingius, Dei promissiones à nobis fide apprehendi, ait. Pag. 301. 302. Non animadvertitis Meisnere, nobis non ipsam peccatorum remissionem, nec ipsam etiam vitam æternam proprie, sed promissionem tantum remissionis peccatorum & vita æterna sub credendi conditione offerri, &c. At vero promissione non rei ipsa nobis porrigitur, sed tantum jus ad rem. Quocirca & fide non ipsam rem apprehendimus, sed jus ad illam. apprehen-dimus autem non alia ratione, quam promissioni credendo, illique penitus assentiendo.
units.tr: IV. Worse, they contend that by these things we obtain justification before God. Schlichtingius, p. 324: so that, by believing the doctrine of Christ and the promises contained in it, and then trusting in Christ, you may thus obtain justification, and further salvation itself. V. Yet more wrongly, they dispute against the apprehension of Christ, which is made by justifying faith. Socinus, On the Saving, part 4, ch. 11, p. 401: especially since this apprehension of Christ of yours is a mere human invention and a most empty dream. Schlichtingius, p. 299: But, my Meisner, teach us first how the grace of God, or the remission of sins, and likewise the merits of Christ, can be apprehended by us in the sense in which you understand them. The same, pp. 300, 301, 302. Reply 1. How does Socinus, in the passage just cited, teach that the mercy of God is apprehended by us? When he says: But the mercy of God can most rightly be apprehended by obedience rendered to him according to Christ's command, if God has promised that he will in fact be merciful to those who perform it; as indeed he certainly has promised. II. And Schlichtingius himself says that the promises of God are apprehended by us through faith. P. 301, 302: You do not notice, Meisner, that what is offered to us is not properly the remission of sins itself, nor eternal life itself, but only the promise of the remission of sins and of eternal life, under the condition of believing, etc. But indeed a promise does not hand the thing itself to us, but only a right to the thing. Wherefore by faith we do not apprehend the thing itself, but the right to it. We apprehend it, however, in no other way than by believing the promise and assenting fully to it.

units.la: III. Denique cum, atque in promissionibus ipsæ etiam res apprehenduntur. Unde fides Apostolo dicitur πραγμάτων ἐλέγχω[?], ipsarum rerum demon-stratio. Hebr. xi. 1. & per totum caput, in ipsas res, per promissiones, fides piorum deducitur.
units.tr: III. Finally, since in the promises the things themselves are also apprehended. Hence faith is called by the Apostle a demonstration of things [ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων], that is, of the things themselves. Hebrews 11:1; and throughout the whole chapter the faith of the godly is led, through the promises, to the things themselves.

units.la: Objeƈtio 1. Schlichtingius, pag. 130 Aut enim fidem instar manus esse vultis, qua munus apprehendimus; aut ipsam apprehensionem muneris, aut ejus dationem; aut denique adeptionem. Si primum, utique fides, qua est id quod est, nempe virtus & bonum opus, justificationis causa erit, non secus ac manus, qua manus est, causa est accepti beneficii. Si secundum, fides justificabit qua est opus, cum apprehensio muneris fit epus.[?] Si tertium, non in nobis, sed in Deo fidei habebit locum. Si denique quartum, fides non officium nostrum erit, sed præmium. Resp. Primo, & secundo modo, fidem dicimus esse instar manus, quâ apprehensio fit. Uti autem in manu, in ordine ad apprehensionem, nihil consideramus quam merum instrumentum, & causalitatem instrumentalem, ita quoque in fide, & ejus apprehensione, quando arripit justitiam & beneficia Christi. Atque uti manus, quâ manus, causa quidem est, instrumentalis nimirum, acceptionis, non autem beneficii; ita fides causa instrumentalis est acceptionis Christi, non verò causa vel Christi, vel ejus quod in Christo, eoque accepto obtinemus, id est, justificationis. Non vel manu, vel acceptione ejus alimur, aut ditamur, sed cibo, vel nummis acceptis: ita non fide, sed Christo, per fidem accepto, justificamur. Simul jam omnes vident, quam rationem apprehensio & applicatio Christi hic habeat.
units.tr: Objection 1. Schlichtingius, p. 130: For you must either regard faith as like a hand, by which we apprehend a gift; or the apprehension of the gift itself; or its giving; or finally its receiving. If the first, then faith, which is what it is, namely a virtue and a good work, will be the cause of justification, just as the hand, which is a hand, is the cause of a benefit received. If the second, faith will justify as it is a work, since the apprehension of the gift is a work. If the third, faith will have its place not in us, but in God. If finally the fourth, faith will not be our duty, but our reward. Reply. In the first and second sense we say that faith is like a hand, by which apprehension takes place. But just as in the hand, in relation to apprehension, we consider nothing but a mere instrument and instrumental causality, so also in faith, and in its apprehension, when it seizes the righteousness and benefits of Christ. And just as the hand, as a hand, is indeed a cause, namely an instrumental cause, of receiving, but not of the benefit, so faith is the instrumental cause of receiving Christ, but not the cause either of Christ or of what we obtain in Christ and by receiving him, that is, of justification. We are nourished or enriched not by the hand, or by its receiving, but by the food or money received; so we are justified not by faith, but by Christ, who is received through faith. All now see at once what place the apprehension and application of Christ has here.

units.la: Object.[?] 11. Schlichtingius, pag. 308. Nonne duas partes religionis Christianæ, proinde & fidei facit Apostolus, 1 Theff. 8. 19. quarum una est servire Deo, altera filium ejus expectare è cœlo: quod quid aliud est, quam sub spe iræ divinæ effugiendæ, & immortalis vitæ consequendæ, Deo & Christo obedire? Resp. 1. Nemo duas illas partes religionis Christianæ, & obedientiæ negat. 11. Sed non loquitur ibi Apostolus de fide. 111. Non de justificante, & prout est justificans. 1v. Fidem, si pro doctrinâ fidei fumas, uti aliquando in Sacris accipitur, non negamus illa continere; sed non fidem, quatenus justificat: & usu vel significatione forensi justificatio sumitur, pro actione Dei judiciali, quemadmodum & Adversarii agnoscunt, non pro justitiâ vitæ.
units.tr: Objection 1. Schlichting, p. 308: Does not the Apostle make two parts of the Christian religion, and so of faith, in 1 Thess. 1:9–10, one of which is to serve God, the other to await his Son from heaven? What is this but, under hope of escaping the wrath of God and obtaining immortal life, to obey God and Christ? Answer 1. No one denies that those two parts of the Christian religion are obedience. 2. But the Apostle is not speaking there of faith. 3. Nor of justifying faith, or faith as it justifies. 4. If you take faith for the doctrine of faith, as it is sometimes used in Holy Writ, we do not deny that it contains those things; but that is not faith as it justifies. And justification, in its forensic use and meaning, is taken for God's judicial act, as the adversaries themselves acknowledge, not for righteousness of life.

units.la: Object. 111. Socinus, de Servat. part. 1v. cap. 1x. pag. 368. Fides in Christum Dei promissione nititur. Verum promissio futurum tempus respicit. Itaque necesse est, fidem in Christum persuasione seu firma opinione alicujus rei, qua futura fit, contineri. At vestra isthac in Christum fides præteritum tempus omnino respicit; & firma opinione ejus rei, qua jam peracta fit, tota continetur. Respondet 1. pro nobis Schlichtingius, & fidem nostram partim etiam præteritum, & præsens respicere, agnoscit; quodque de futuro est, fiduciæ & spei attribuit: id quod nemo diffitetur.
units.tr: Objection 3. Socinus, On the Saviour, part 4, ch. 9, p. 368: Faith in Christ rests on the promise of God. But a promise looks to the future. Therefore faith in Christ must be contained in a persuasion, or firm opinion, of a thing that is going to come about. But your faith in Christ looks wholly to the past, and consists wholly in a firm opinion of a thing that has already been accomplished. Schlichting answers, first, on our side, and he acknowledges that our faith looks partly to the past and the present as well, and he assigns to trust and hope what concerns the future; which no one denies.

units.la: Pag. 304. Verum, ut diximus, talis fiducia & spes non est spes proprie dicta, quæ semper in rem futuram & nondum existentem tendit, & quæ, si nos destitueret ac frustraretur, is, cui vere fidimus, & in quem speramus, nunquam reipsa compleretur & existeret: quod in ista vestra fide, quæ partim præteritum, partim jam reipsa præsens & actu ipso existens creditur, contingere, si modo vera creditis, non potest.
units.tr: P. 304. But, as we have said, such trust and hope is not hope properly so called, which always tends toward a thing future and not yet existing, and which, if it failed us and disappointed us, the one in whom we truly trust, and in whom we hope, would never in fact be fulfilled and come into being. This cannot happen in your faith, which is believed partly as past, partly as already present and existing in act, if you believe true things.

units.la: 11. Fides in præteritum respicit, & præsens, & futurum. In præteritum, ut credamus, quæ Christus pro nobis præstitit, quod nimirum & mortuus propter peccata, & resurrexit propter justitiam nostram. Rom. iv. 2<[?]. In præsenti, Deum nobis misericordem & gratiosum esse. In futuro, nobis propterea largiturum quæcunque promisit, nominatim æternam vitam. Unde & responsum Socino, priora sua utcunque corrigenti, pag. 370. Quamvis autem negari non possit fidem, id est, firmam opinionem alicujus rei qua affirmetur, præteritum tempus non minus, quam futurum, posse respicere: non minus enim certo mihi persuadere possum, aliquid jam fuisse, quam futurum esse ; tamen cum de fide, quæ nos Deo gratos efficiat, sermo est, qualis certe fides in Christum censeri debet: vix invenias de re credenda agi, quæ jam peracta fit, sed semper de futura. Hoc autem omnibus illis Scripturæ S. locis redarguitur, quæ fidem in Christum docent, inque ea, quæ Christus pro nobis passus est, ac fecit-.
units.tr: 2. Faith looks to the past, the present and the future. To the past, that we believe what Christ has done for us, namely that he died for our sins and rose again for our justification (Rom. 4:25). To the present, that God is merciful and gracious to us. To the future, that he will bestow upon us whatever he has promised, above all eternal life. Hence also the answer to Socinus, who in some measure corrects his earlier statements, p. 370: Although it cannot be denied that faith, that is a firm opinion of something affirmed, can look to the past no less than to the future, for I can be no less certainly persuaded that something has already been than that it will be; yet when we speak of the faith that makes us pleasing to God, which faith in Christ must certainly be reckoned to be, you will scarcely find that a thing to be believed is spoken of as already accomplished, but always as future. But this is refuted by all those passages of holy Scripture which teach faith in Christ, and faith in what Christ has suffered and done for us.

units.la: Obj. iv. Quod tota nostra fides justificans videatur esse merè historica. Schlichtingius, pag. 305. Neque tu ullum cordis & voluntatis actum in hac tua fide extendes, qui non possit in historica tantum fide habere locum. Resp. i. In fide historicâ est nudus assensus mentis theoreticus, nullus practicus, qui in fide est justificante. Ille est rei modo in se verae, quod unicum in historiâ spectatur, assensus; iste rei verae & bonae tibi. ii. Actus voluntatis amplexivus & applicativus Christi, est in fide justificante, qui non in historicâ. iii. Etiam conclusivus de salute certo sequuturâ, & per Christum obtinendâ, quum totum toto corde Servatorem amplecteris: qui etiam abest ab historicâ, tam longe ac à Dæmonibus, in quibus fides historica locum habere potest, non item justificans.
units.tr: Objection 4. That our whole justifying faith seems to be purely historical. Schlichting, p. 305: Nor will you extend to this faith of yours any act of the heart or will which could not find a place in historical faith alone. Answer 1. In historical faith there is a bare theoretical assent of the mind, and no practical assent, which is in justifying faith. The former is assent to a thing only as true in itself, which alone is regarded in history; the latter is assent to a thing as true and good for you. 2. An act of the will that embraces and applies Christ is in justifying faith, and not in historical faith. 3. There is also a conclusion, certain of salvation to follow and to be obtained through Christ, when you embrace the Saviour with your whole heart; and this too is absent from historical faith, as far as it is from the demons, in whom historical faith can have a place, but not justifying faith.

units.la: Atque hæc ad argumenta nostra dicta sunto, pro justificatione gratuitâ, per & propter Christi justitiam, fide apprehensam, non per opera nostra qualiacunque; vel fidei, quam dicunt Adversarii, obedientiam. Argumentati autem sumus ex loco quadruplici, i. quod operibus quibuscunque omnis derogatur justitia, & justificandi ratio. ii. Quod soli Christo ea attribuitur. iii. Et imputationi justitiæ ejus nobis factæ. iv. Quâ ratione dicitur fides justificans, ut apprehendens Christi justitiam, non uti obedientiam continens mandatorum, quemadmodum loquuntur, Euangelicorum. Nam illam fidei acceptionem veram & propriam esse, ut assensum denotet, non obedientiam, ipse etiam Socinus vidit ac fassus est. de Seruat. part. iv. cap. xi. pag. 387. Ex quo factum est, ut, Christo, sive Christi verbis credere, idem significet, atque, illi obedire: quamvis per se nihil aliud vere significare possit, quam, ejus verba vera esse, credere: Christo autem, sive ejus verbis non credere, idem sit, atque, illi non obedire. Idem scilicet in rei veritate, quæ postulat utrumque conjungi, credere & obedire: non vero quod vel idem sint, vel credere idem significet, atque obedire.
units.tr: And let these things be said in answer to our arguments, for justification that is free, through and on account of the righteousness of Christ, apprehended by faith, and not through our works of whatever kind, or through the obedience of faith, as the adversaries call it. Now we have argued from four points: 1. that all justice and the manner of justifying is taken away from works of every kind. 2. That it is ascribed to Christ alone. 3. And to the imputation of his righteousness made to us. 4. In what sense faith is called justifying: as apprehending the righteousness of Christ, not as containing obedience to the commandments, as the Evangelicals, so called, speak. For Socinus himself saw and confessed that this acceptance of faith is true and proper, signifying assent, not obedience: On the Saviour, part 4, ch. 11, p. 387: From this it has come about that to believe Christ, or the words of Christ, means the same as to obey him; although in itself it can truly signify nothing else than to believe that his words are true; and not to believe Christ, or his words, is the same as not to obey him. Clearly the same in the truth of the matter, which requires that believing and obeying be joined together; but not that they are the same, or that believing signifies the same as obeying.

units.la: SECTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: SECTION III.

units.la: PErgimus ad Objectiones Adversariorum, proponendas, & diluendas, quas tum pro sententiâ suâ, tum contra nostram, adferunt. Ubi primò advertendum, pari fere modo Socinianos, ac Pontificios, pro suâ causâ tum argumentari, tum excipere, nisi quod illi paullo subtilius, quam isti.
units.tr: We come now to the objections of our opponents, which they bring forward both for their own position and against ours, and to their answers. Here we must first note that the Socinians argue and reply for their cause in almost the same way as the Papists do, except that they do so a little more subtly.

units.la: Objectio prima, ex exemplo Abrahami: Abrahamus fuit justificatus, non autem per fidem in Christum, ejusque justitiam & meritum; per fidem tamen: ergo fides justificans non est, quâ apprehendimus justitiam Christi, vel ut hæc ad justitiam imputetur credentibus; sed sola in Deum, nunc in Christum, fiducia; vera exerens le erga Deum, & Christum, obedientia. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. xi. pag. 388. Deo confidere, semper hominem, pro ipsius Dei benignitate justum coram ipso reddidit, &c. Fragilitatis namque humanæ miserTUS [?] Deus clementissimus, quamvis omnia ejus præcepta perpetuo exactissime non conservemus, id quod ad propriam & absolutam justitiam prorsus necessarium esset; pro perfectè justis nihilominus tamen nos habere voluit; dummodo ipsi confidamus, id est, ei ex animo obedientes, omnem spem nostram in eo collocemus, &c. Nec vero alia fide justificatus est ipse Abrahamus, qui pater omnium credentium est, Rom 4. 11. 16. Resp. 1. Si simpliciter confidere Deo, hominem coram Deo justum reddit, jam extra Christum justificari homo potest, & ille à justificationis nostræ causa ac ratione exulare. Quod necessitatem & vim Christi ac religionis Christianæ penitus evertit. ii. Fragilitatis quidem humanæ misertus in hoc fuit Deus, quod non exactissimam à nobis nunc postulat justitiam, quâ justificemur, quin pro justis censet etiam non plenè justos; sed hoc in Christo, & quidem solo, neutiquam, & nunquam extra eum. iii. Quod si vero loco justitiæ nostræ perfectæ substituamus nostram imperfectam, manemus attamen in nostrâ, & in genere justitiæ operum, quod omnino hoc in negotio rejicere oportet, ut in Christo reperti, justificatione fruamur merè Evangelicâ, id est, legi operibusque oppositâ. iv. Et obedire Deo ex animo debemus, & spem in eo collocare: at non hæc nos justificant, sed fides in Christum, ex quâ tum spes & obedientia emanant. Fides, ut instrumentum; Christus, ut materia justificationis, in hoc opere considerantur. v. Abrahamus eadem fide fuit justificatus, quâ nos. Quod ex scopo & disputatione Pauli apparet, quoties exemplum Abrahami profert ad docendam rationem tum fidei, tum justificationis nostræ. Quæ absque illo non admodum valida essent, nec quadrarent. vi. Quantumvis vero Christus non exprimatur, ubi fidei vel justificationis Abrahami fit mentio, sive apud Mosem, sive Paulum, eo tamen quod credidit, seu objecto fidei ejus comprehensum illum & Paulus innuit, Gal. iii. 16. Abrahamo autem dictæ promissiones, & semini ejus. Non inquit: & feminibus, tamquam de pluribus, sed tamquam de uno, & semini tuo, is est Christus. et Christus significavit, quando Abrahamum gavisum dixit supra modum, conspecto se, & die suo longe. Joann. viii. 56. Quod in V. Test. historiâ expressum temere quæras: nec tamen ideo minus verum haberi debet. Promissionibus autem illis credidit Abraham, & imputatum ipsi fuit in justitiam. Quod enim Socinus, non eo justificatum contendit Abrahamum, quod divinæ promissioni credidit, sed quando immolavit filium, & eo facinore, seu obedientiâ; in eo plane contrariatur Sacris. Pag. 389. Quamvis enim ex Pauli verbis, quæ scripta sunt cap. 4. epist. ad Rom. videatur aperte colligi, fidem qua Abrahamus fuit, fuisse, Deo promittenti, ipsum multarum gentium patrem futurum, & semen suum, sicut stellas cœli numerosum evasurum, fidem alhibuisse, hoc est, eum vera dicere sibi persuasisse; animadvertendum est tamen, rem aliter se habere. Denique Christum, quamvis non ῥητῶς expressum, contineri tamen eâ fide, quâ Abrahamus dicitur fuisse justificatus, eo evidentius contra Socinum asserimus, quo ipse in locutione illâ, credidit Abra-ham ham Deo, causæ tributum ait, quod est effectus: quanto magis dicamus fidei tributum, quod est correlati, sive objecti ejus cum fide, per metonymiam adjuncti? Pag. 392. Verum, quomodo Pauli verba interpretabimur, quibus fidem explicans, qua Abrahamus justificatus est, non ipsius in Deo confidentiam, sed firmam ejus, quod Deus illi promiserat, opinionem commemorat? Sciendum est, Paulum causa id, quod effectus est, tribuisse, ut Abrahami exemplo justificationis nostræ modum, & originem melius exprimeret, & firma illi opinioni, justificandi vim tribuisse, non quia ipsa vere justificatus fuerit Abrahamus, sed quia ex ipsa necessario orta est confidentia, qua vere justificatus est.
units.tr: Objection 1, from the example of Abraham: Abraham was justified, but not by faith in Christ and his righteousness and merit; he was justified by faith, nevertheless. Therefore the justifying faith is not that by which we lay hold of the righteousness of Christ, or by which it is imputed to believers for righteousness, but only a trust in God, now in Christ, together with a true obedience that shows itself towards God and Christ. Socinus, De Servatoribus, part 4, chap. 11, p. 388: To trust in God has always, by God's own kindness, made a man righteous before him, etc. For God, most merciful in regard to human frailty, although we do not perpetually keep all his precepts most exactly, which would be wholly necessary for a perfect and absolute righteousness, has nevertheless willed to hold us as perfectly righteous, provided that we trust in him, that is, obey him from the heart and place all our hope in him, etc. Nor was Abraham himself justified by any other faith, though he is the father of all believers, Rom. 4:11, 16. Answer 1: If merely to trust in God makes a man righteous before God, then a man can already be justified outside Christ, and Christ is banished from the cause and ground of our justification. This utterly overturns the necessity and power of Christ and of the Christian religion. ii. God was indeed merciful to human frailty in this, that he does not now demand from us the most exact righteousness by which we are justified, and yet counts as righteous those who are not fully righteous; but this is in Christ, and in him alone, never apart from him. iii. And if we substitute our imperfect righteousness for the perfect righteousness, we remain in our own righteousness, and in the kind of righteousness that comes from works, which in this matter must altogether be rejected, so that, found in Christ, we may enjoy a justification that is purely evangelical, that is, opposed to the law and to works. iv. We ought indeed to obey God from the heart and to place our hope in him; but these things do not justify us: faith in Christ justifies us, and from it both hope and obedience flow. In this work faith is considered as the instrument, and Christ as the matter of justification. v. Abraham was justified by the same faith by which we are. This is clear from the aim and argument of Paul, whenever he brings forward the example of Abraham to teach the nature both of faith and of our justification. Without that example these arguments would not be very strong, nor would they fit. vi. Yet although Christ is not named wherever mention is made of the faith or justification of Abraham, whether in Moses or in Paul, nevertheless Paul hints that he is included in what Abraham believed, or in the object of his faith, Gal. 3:16: Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He does not say, "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to thy seed," which is Christ. And Christ signified this when he said that Abraham rejoiced exceedingly to see his day, and saw it afar off, John 8:56. This is not something you will easily find expressed in the history of the Old Testament, yet it ought not for that reason to be held any less true. Abraham believed those promises, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. As for Socinus's claim that Abraham was justified not because he believed the divine promise, but when he offered up his son, and by that deed, or obedience, he plainly contradicts the Scriptures, p. 389: For although from the words of Paul, written in chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Romans, it seems clearly to be inferred that the faith by which Abraham was, was that he gave faith to God promising that he would become the father of many nations, and that his seed would become as numerous as the stars of heaven, that is, that he persuaded himself that God was speaking the truth; yet it must be noted that the matter stands otherwise. Finally, we assert all the more clearly against Socinus that Christ, although not expressly named, is nevertheless contained in that faith by which Abraham is said to have been justified: for he himself, in that phrase Abraham believed God, says that the cause is attributed to the effect; how much more may we say that what belongs to the object of faith is attributed to faith, since the object is joined with faith by metonymy? p. 392: But how shall we interpret the words of Paul, in which, explaining the faith by which Abraham was justified, he mentions not his confidence in God, but his firm opinion of what God had promised him? It must be understood that Paul attributed to the cause what is the effect, so that by the example of Abraham he might better express the manner and origin of our justification, and so that he might attribute the power of justifying to that firm opinion; not because Abraham was truly justified by it, but because from it there necessarily arose the confidence by which he was truly justified.

units.la: Objest. II. ex Jac. II. Socinus, de Servat. part. IV. cap. IV. Idem declarant Jacobi verba, qui hominem non fide tantum, sed operibus quoque justificari contendit, Jac. II. 23. Schlichtingius, pag. 291. Non excludit autem ullo pacto opera ex fide provenientia, charitatem, & charitatis fructus, seu veram vitam sanctimoniam; cum innumeris Scriptura locis non minus huic, quam fidei, justificatio & salus adscribatur, & Jacobus apertissime docet, hominem justificari ex operibus, non ex fide tantum. Eundem locum objicere omnes solent; idemque a Remonstrantibus fit, Apol. cap. X. pag. 113. Resp. I. non agitur a Jacobo de justificatione hominis coram Deo, ejusque causa, qua de re disputavit Paulus, & nostra nunc est controversia; sed de natura verae fidei, & hominis fidelis, qui vim & veritatem fidei suae ostendat per bona opera. Ergo nihil hinc Adversarii quicunque, vel adversans Paulo, vel nobis, proferre possunt: quandoquidem aliud est argumentum, quod Jacobus tractat, a nostro. Agere vero ipsum non de justificatione, sed de fide; non de justificatione hominis peccatoris, sed manifestatione hominis fidelis; non de justificatione apud Deum, sed fidei demonstratione in genere, & facto aliquo externo; probatur, ex propositione Apostolicæ disputationis remota, vers. 1. & proxima, vers. 14. Illic inquit, Fratres mei, ne ἐν προσωπολημψίαις in acceptionibus personarum habete fidem Domini nostri Jesu Christi gloriosi. Ibi hic, Qua utilitas, fratres mei, si quis fidem habere dicat, opera vero non habeat: potestne ista fides eum servare? Ex quibus patet, de fide quaestionem fuisse, eaque ostendendā, citra προσωπολημψίαν: de operum necessitate, ad fidem, & salutem: non de justificatione. Ea facta propositione, Apostolus probationes omnes hinc petit, quod fides absque operibus nulla est, quod mortua. vers. 17, 20. Quod dicere & jactare fidem non satis est, ubi probationes exiguntur, ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, & ego tibi ostendam fidem meam ex operibus meis. Vers. 21. Idem confirmat exemplo Abrahami, Abraham Pater noster annon ex operibus justificatus fuit, offerens Isaacum filium suum super altare? &c.
units.tr: Objection 2, from James 2. Socinus, De Servatoribus, part 4, chap. 4: The words of James declare the same thing, who contends that a man is justified not by faith only, but also by works, James 2:23. Schlichting, p. 291: Yet he in no way excludes the works that proceed from faith, charity, and the fruits of charity, or true holiness of life; since justification and salvation are ascribed no less to these than to faith in countless places of Scripture, and James most plainly teaches that a man is justified by works, not by faith only. All of them are accustomed to object this same passage, and the Remonstrants do the same, Apology, chap. 10, p. 113. Answer 1: James is not treating of the justification of a man before God, and its cause, which is what Paul discussed, and which is the present controversy with us; he is treating of the nature of true faith, and of the believing man, who shows the strength and truth of his faith by good works. So our opponents, whether they oppose Paul or us, can bring nothing from this, since the argument James treats is different from ours. That he is speaking not of justification but of faith; not of the justification of a sinful man, but of the demonstration of a believing man; not of justification before God, but of the showing of faith in general and by some outward deed, is proved from the statement at the start of the apostolic discussion, verse 1, and from what comes next, verse 14. There he says: My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons [ἐν προσωπολημψίαις]. And here: What does it profit, my brethren, if a man says he has faith, but does not have works? Can that faith save him? From these words it is plain that the question was about faith, and about showing it, apart from respect of persons; and about the necessity of works for faith and salvation, not about justification. Having laid down this statement, the Apostle seeks all his proofs from the fact that faith without works is nothing, that it is dead, verses 17, 20. It is not enough to say and boast of faith when proofs are demanded: Show me your faith by your works, and I will show you my faith by my works, verse 21. He confirms the same by the example of Abraham: Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he offered Isaac his son upon the altar? etc.

units.la: Vox hic justificationis occurrit quidem, at non proinde de justificatione ea tractat, qua Paulus. Nam & alibi etiam vox illa, extra istud tamen argumentum, adhibetur. A Christo, Matth. XI. 19. justificata est sapientia a filiis ejus. Paulo, 1 Tim. III. 16. ἐδικαιώθη[?] ἐν πνεύματι[?] Christus justificatus Spiritu. Rom. III. 4. ut justificeris in verbis tuis. Neque ideo illis in locis justificatio peccatoris intelligitur coram Deo. Abraham ex operibus fuit justificatus, non coram Deo, in ejus judicio, sed operibus justificatus est esse fidelis ac pius, & fides ejus, uti in seq. versu est, efficax fuit per opera ejus, & perfecta. ἡ πίστις συνηργ[?]εῖ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη[?]. Est justificatio hominis peccatoris coram Deo, sed etiam fidelis, fideique ejus, per opera, quo demonstratur talis revera esse: & de ea hic fit sermo, non de illa. Uti ἀγάπη dicitur πεπληρωμένη[?], 1 Joann. iv. 12. 17. 18. ita fides hic πεπληρωμένη[?], per sua opera. Atque ita impleta fuit Scriptura de Abrahamo, credidit autem Abraham Deo &c. Nempe illo documento operis adeo illustri ἰδεῖξε Abraham, se vere Deo credere, fidelem & justum esse. Unde & amicus Dei appellatus fuit, verf. 24. Videte igitur, quod ex operibus justificatur homo, & non ex fide solum. Nempe vere justus est, & censetur, & declaratur homo, non fide solâ vel sicam habeat, aut habere se dicat, sed operibus, & demonstratione operum. Uti & Rahab meretrix operibus ostendit se justam esse & fidelem. Non quid peccatorem justificet apud Deum; sed qua ratione fidelis justificetur in se, id est, pro tali debeat haberi, hic docetur. Quod denique ex conclusione apparet, verf. ult. Quemadmodum enim corpus sine spiritu mortuum est, ita & fides sine operibus est mortua. De fide concluditur, non de hominis justificatione; de fide, quae sit vera, & vitalis: ergo & de eo in praecedentibus fuerat disputatum. Atque ita nihil hoc ex loco Adversarii quicunque, pro justificatione hominis peccatoris apud Deum, quasi per opera contingat, evincere possunt.
units.tr: The word justification does indeed occur here, but he does not treat of justification in the sense in which Paul does. For that word is used elsewhere too, though outside this argument: by Christ, Matt. 11:19: Wisdom is justified by her children. By Paul, 1 Tim. 3:16: justified in the Spirit [ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι], Christ justified by the Spirit. Rom. 3:4: that you may be justified in your words. Nor in those places is the justification of a sinner before God meant. Abraham was justified by works, not in God's judgment, but he was justified in showing himself faithful and pious, and his faith, as the next verse says, was made effective and perfect through his works: faith worked together with his works, and by works faith was made perfect [ἡ πίστις συνηργεῖ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη]. There is the justification of a sinful man before God, but also of a believer and of his faith, through works, by which it is shown that he is truly such; and it is of this that the discussion here speaks, not of the other. As love is said to be made perfect [πεπληρωμένη], 1 John 4:12, 17, 18, so faith here is made perfect through its works. And so the Scripture was fulfilled concerning Abraham: Abraham believed God, etc. Indeed, by that most illustrious proof of works Abraham showed [ἔδειξε] that he truly believed God and was faithful and righteous. Hence he was also called the friend of God, verse 23. You see, then, that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only, verse 24. That is to say, a man is truly just and is accounted and declared to be so, not by faith alone, or by what he has or says he has, but by works and by the demonstration of works. So too Rahab the harlot showed by her works that she was just and faithful. What justifies a sinner before God is not taught here; what is taught is how a believer is justified in himself, that is, how he ought to be regarded as such. This finally appears from the conclusion, the last verse: For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. The conclusion concerns faith, not the justification of a man: concerns faith that is true and living; so this had been the subject of the preceding discussion. And so our opponents, from this passage, can prove nothing about the justification of a sinful man before God as though it came about by works.

units.la: Objecti. 111. Nostra de Justificatione sententia doctrinam & vim bonorum operum prorsus evertit. Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. iv. pag. 329. Quocunque igitur veritatis, negare non potestis, ex doctrina vestra concludi, non opus esse, ut in iis, qui servandi sunt, vera aliqua vita sanctimonia reperiatur: sed imputativam sufficere, & eos, qui Christo sunt insiti, sine bonis operibus esse posse: immo, quoad in hac mortali vita fuerint, peccati mancipia perpetuo esse, &c. Istam Christi justitia imputationem propter id praecipue a vobis sive adinventam, sive acceptam fuisse, ut hac ratione vitae emendationem, quam ubique Dei spiritus iis, qui Christi beneficium participare volunt, disertis verbis praecipit, atque praescribit, a vobis reipsa indestirpitum evulsam in hominibus inferere videamini. Eadem habet, cap. vii. viii. ix. Volkelius, lib. v. pag. 58[?]. Schlichtingius, pag 11[?]. & passim alii. Eques Polonus, in Apol. Ipsi sunt, qui Dei timorem omnem ex hominum animis vi fucorum dogmatum tollunt. Si enim Christus omnium quaecunque peccare possumus penas dependit, quid Dei timore est opus? Cum & hoc ipsum, Deum non timere, abunde jam a Christo compensatum sit, nec quicquam aliud restet, quam ut arctâ fide nobis id applicemus: quod profecto sine omni Dei timore fieri potest. Resp. 1. hoc profecto est salsissimum, quod id vere credere, sine omni Dei timore esse possit. Imo mera atque horrenda est in doctrinam nostram calumnia, ex ea sequi, non opus esse ut in iis qui servandi sunt, vera aliqua vitae sanctimonia reperiatur. Cui, quantum possumus, reclamamus, & , qua voce, qua vita, obsistimus. 11. Imputativam Christi justitiam sufficere dicimus, ad justificationem. an simpliciter eam sufficere, & ubique? nullo modo. 111. Sed uti praeter justificationem, requiritur etiam sanctificatio, ita ex eâ ponimus vitæ sanctimoniam, non proinde in, vel ad justifi-cationem. Atque ad fidem, & ad salutem necessario requiri bona opera, semper omnes contendimus. Et tamen dicimur ea docere, ex quibus concluditur, non opus esse vitæ sanctimoniâ iis, qui servari cupiunt? Docemus constanter, ad salutem bona opera esse necessaria; necessario conjungi cum fide; esse proprium effectum gratiæ sanctificantis; sine quibus justificatio nec est unquam, nec esse potest: & tamen eorum studium vobis evertimus? tantum ea removemus à causa justificationis. Sed ex aliis illis causis annon satis remanet necessitatis ad bona opera præstanda, & urgenda? An qui triplici illo fune necessitatem operum adstringunt, sanctificationis, fidei, & salutis, urgeri calumniis possunt, quod sine bonis operibus fidelis aliquis & perpetuum peccati mancipium esse possit, vel quod vitæ emendationem stirpitus animis hominum evulsam cupiant? vah blasphemam, & pessimam agendi rationem.
units.tr: Objection III. Our doctrine of justification utterly overthrows the doctrine and force of good works. Socinus, On the Saviour, part iv, chap. iv, p. 329: "Whatever truth you cannot deny, it follows from your doctrine that there is no need for any true holiness of life to be found in those who are to be saved; but imputed righteousness is enough, and those who are implanted in Christ can be without good works; indeed, for as long as they live this mortal life they are perpetually slaves of sin, etc. You seem to have devised or accepted this imputation of Christ's righteousness chiefly for this reason: that by this means you might root out from men's hearts the amendment of life which God's Spirit everywhere commands and prescribes in plain words for those who wish to share in Christ's benefit." He says the same in chaps. vii, viii and ix. Volkelius, bk v, p. 58[?]. Schlichting, p. 11[?]; and many others throughout. The Polish knight, in his Apology: "It is they who, by the poison of their doctrines, remove all fear of God from men's minds. For if Christ pays the penalty for all the sins we can commit, what need is there of the fear of God? Since even not fearing God has already been fully compensated by Christ, and nothing remains but that we apply this to ourselves by a firm faith, which can indeed be done without any fear of God." Answer 1. It is most absurd to say that one can truly believe this without any fear of God. It is also a mere and horrible slander against our doctrine to say that it follows from it that there is no need for some true holiness of life to be found in those who are to be saved. Against this we protest as far as we can, resisting it by our voice and by our life. 2. We say that the imputed righteousness of Christ is sufficient for justification. Is it simply sufficient, and everywhere? By no means. 3. But just as sanctification is required in addition to justification, so from justification we derive holiness of life, not in or for justification. And we have always all contended that good works are necessarily required for faith and for salvation. Yet are we said to teach things from which it follows that there is no need of holiness of life for those who wish to be saved? We constantly teach that good works are necessary for salvation, that they are necessarily joined with faith, that they are the proper effect of sanctifying grace, and that without them justification neither is ever nor can be. And yet do we overthrow zeal for them? We only remove them from the cause of justification. But do not enough other grounds remain for the necessity of performing and urging good works? Or can those who bind the necessity of works with that threefold cord, of sanctification, faith and salvation, be charged with the calumny that some believer can be without good works and be a perpetual slave of sin, or that they desire the amendment of life to be rooted out from men's minds? Oh, what a blasphemous and wicked way of arguing!

units.la: Socinus, de Servat. Sed quod postremo istius vestra in Christum fidei commentum plane retegit, illud est, quod, ut vos ipsi non negatis, ea fides in Christum, qua justificamur, sine bonis operibus esse non potest; ista autem vestra in Christum fides nihil cum bonis operibus commune habet. tantum abest, ut ubicumque illa est, bona opera esse necesse sit. Nam quid (quaso) commune habet, quod quis credat, per Christi mortem universa peccata sua, etiam futura, deleta fuisse, cum eo, quod vitam suam ad Dei normam instituat ac dirigat? Annon potius, si id verum esse sibi omnino persuaserit, segnis & supinus in justitia operibus sectandis fiet: nedum illis, quemadmodum Paulus præcipit, dives fit? Quid enim opus est de peccatis vitandis sollicitum esse, si jam omnia peccata nostra non præterita tantum, sed etiam futura, peni-tus reipsa deleta sunt, nec nobis unquam imputari debent? tamque abundans justificatio aliud quid ex se fundere potest apud animum illius conscium, quam fervidam omnis pietatis æmulationem? Annon ita Christus docuit, Luc. vii. 47. cui multum remittitur, eum etiam multum dilige-re?
units.tr: Socinus, On the Saviour: "But what finally lays bare the fiction of this faith of yours in Christ is that, as you yourselves do not deny, the faith by which we are justified cannot be without good works; yet this faith of yours in Christ has nothing in common with good works. So far is it from being necessary that good works be wherever it is. For what (I ask) does it have in common that someone believes that through Christ's death all his sins, even future ones, have been blotted out, with his ordering and directing his life according to God's norm? Would he not rather, if he has fully persuaded himself that this is true, become slack and idle in pursuing works of righteousness, let alone be rich in them, as Paul enjoins? For why should there be any need to be anxious about avoiding sins, if now all our sins, not only past but also future, have really been wholly blotted out and must never be imputed to us? And can so abundant a justification pour forth anything upon a conscious mind other than a fervent rivalry in all piety? Did not Christ teach this, Luke vii. 47: 'to whom much is forgiven, he also loves much'?"

units.la: Resp. 1. Si nos non negare nosti & fateris, fidem justificantem sine bonis operibus esse non posse, qui dicere potuisti, Christi justitiæ imputationem à nobis adinventam fuisse, ut hac ratione vitæ emendationem stirpitus honminum animis evelleremus? ii. Nonne ergo fidem nihil cum bonis operibus habere commune, tetra est calumnia, doctrinâ & vitâ nostrâ, pietatem inde trahente, juxtâ refutata. Ne dicant, pios nos quidem esse, sed non ex vi doctrinæ illius nostræ: qui nullam aliam pietatem agnoscimus, vel præstamus, quam quæ ex illo doctrinæ & fidei fonte fluit. iii. Imo, quid magis vitam docet jubetque ad Dei normam instituere ac dirigere, quam quod quis credat, per Christi mortem universa peccata sua, etiam quæcunq;, deleta esse? Ista tanta gratia,
units.tr: Answer 1. If you know and admit that we do not deny that justifying faith cannot be without good works, how could you say that we devised the imputation of Christ's righteousness in order that by this means we might tear the amendment of life out from men's hearts? 2. Is it not therefore a foul calumny that faith has nothing in common with good works? This is refuted by our doctrine and by our life, which draws its piety from it. Let them not say that we are indeed pious, but not by the force of our doctrine: for we acknowledge and practise no other piety than that which flows from this fountain of doctrine and faith. 3. Indeed, what teaches and commands us more to order and direct our life according to God's norm than the belief that through Christ's death all one's sins, of whatever kind, have been blotted out? This so great grace,

units.la: & Apostolus, Rom. vi. 1. quid igitur dicemus: manebimus in peccato, ut gratia abundaret? absit: qui mortui sumus peccato &c. Hinc non solum cum justificatione sanctificatio semper individuo nexu copulatur, sed ex illius doctrinâ passim ad sanctitatis studium argumenta quævis deducuntur. iv. Adeo ut impossibile sit, segnem & supinum eum in justitiæ operibus fieri, qui illam justificationem credat & sentiat: impossibile, ne non pro copia remissorum sibi peccatorum, bonis operibus incumbat. Illa enim justificationis gratia, sanctitatem etiam efficit una, & peccata eo cautius vitare hominem docet, quo plenius novit, quantæ gratiæ sit ab iisdem liberari. v. Et præterita & futura peccata per Christi satisfactionem semel expiata sunt omnia, & ablata iis condemnandi vis, illis nimirum qui in Christo Jesu sunt, Rom. viii. 1. quod æque de futuro ac præterito intelligendum est; non ut in futurum securi simus de peccato cavendo; sed, de peccati damnatione. 1 Cor. xv. 55.56.57.
units.tr: And the Apostle, Rom. vi. 1: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. We who are dead to sin, etc." Hence not only is sanctification always joined inseparably with justification, but from this doctrine arguments of every kind for zeal in holiness are drawn everywhere. 4. So that it is impossible for one who believes and feels this justification to be slack and idle in works of righteousness: impossible that he should not, in proportion to the abundance of sins forgiven him, devote himself to good works. For this grace of justification also at once produces holiness, and teaches a man to avoid sins the more carefully the more fully he knows how great a grace it is to be freed from them. 5. Past and future sins have all been expiated once for all through Christ's satisfaction, and the power of condemning them has been taken away from those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. viii. 1. This must be understood of the future no less than of the past: not that we are secure about avoiding sin in future, but about condemnation for sin. 1 Cor. xv. 55, 56, 57.

units.la: Socinus, ibidem: At enim dicere soletis, fieri non posse, ut quis tantam erga se Dei charitatem animo concipiat atque animadvertat, qui peccata ipsius universa delere voluerit, ob eamque causam carissimum Filium acerbissimæ[?] morti tradiderit: & Dei amore non interim ita inflammaretur, ut noctes, diesque de eo, quod illi placeat, faciendo cogitet, universasque actiones suas ad ejus nominis gloriam perpetuo dirigat. Quasi vero nemo ingratus esse possit: & accepti beneficii constans opinio in officio homines necessario contineat? Resp. 1. Imo nemo est, qui non sibi ingratitudinis suæ erga Deum satis sit conscius: interim tamen nemo etiam vera fide præditus, statuit sibi a Deo, per Christum remissa esse peccata omnia, quin velit & debeat quoque gratus esse, proque viribus gratitudinem Deo exhibere & debitam observantiam. ii Cor. v. 15. Judicantes hoc, quod si unus pro omnibus mortuus, jam omnes mortui: & pro omnibus mortuus, ut viventes non amplius sibi vivant, sed ei qui pro ipsis mortuus & resurrexit. Adde 1 Cor. vi. 20. Gal. ii. 20. Deinde, fidem illam, seu assensum Christi promissionibus habitum, ubi verus est, & non in nuda quapiam opinione vel imaginatione consistit, bonorum operum matrem esse & causam, superius ex ipsis Adversariis ostendimus. Qui inde nunc convincuntur, quando fingunt fidem nostram operibus necessario vacuam esse. Præter superius adducta, Socinus, de Servat. part. iv. cap. xi pag. 397. Eadem ratione ea credere, quæ nobis Christus annunciavit, non illa ipsa fides, quæ nos justificat, sed ipsius quasi parens & causa est.
units.tr: Socinus, ibidem: "But you are accustomed to say that it cannot be that someone conceives and perceives in his mind so great a love of God toward himself, since God wished to blot out all his sins and for that reason handed over his most dearly loved Son to a most bitter death, and that in the meantime he is not inflamed with love of God, so that night and day he thinks about doing what pleases Him, and always directs all his actions to the glory of His name. As if indeed no one could be ungrateful, and the constant opinion of a benefit received did not necessarily keep men in their duty!" Answer 1. Indeed there is no one who is not sufficiently aware of his own ingratitude toward God. Yet nevertheless no one endued with true faith, who judges that his sins have all been remitted to him by God through Christ, fails to want to be grateful too, and to show gratitude and due obedience to God according to his powers. 2 Cor. v. 15: "Judging this, that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who died for them and rose again." Add 1 Cor. vi. 20; Gal. ii. 20. Next, we have shown above from the Adversaries themselves that the faith, or assent to Christ's promises, where it is true and does not consist in some bare opinion or imagination, is the mother and cause of good works. They are now convicted of this, when they pretend that our faith is necessarily empty of works. Besides what was adduced above, Socinus, On the Saviour, part iv, chap. xi, p. 397: "By the same reasoning, to believe those things which Christ announced to us is the parent and, as it were, the cause of that very faith which justifies us, and is not itself that faith."

units.la: Socinus: Aut enim ita a nobis opera Deus requirit, ut, si illis careamus, nolit nos caros habere, aut ita requirit, ut gratissimum quidem illi facturi simus, si ejus præcepta servaverimus: cæterum etiamsi id non fecerimus, nos tamen, quia, Christi morte omnia peccata nostra deleta fuisse, firmiter credamus, nihilominus caros habiturus. Si sine bonis operibus illi cari futuri non sumus: falsum esse apparet, nos ea sola fide jam absolute justificatos esse, neque enim perfecte justificatus esse quis potest, quin Deo revera carissimus jam sit. Sin, operibus licet bonis carentes, propter eam fidem caros nihilominus nos est habiturus Deus: non est quod de vita nostra sanctimonia multum laboremus. Resp. 1. Ita a nobis requirit Deus bona opera, ut si iis caruerimus, charos habiturus non sit. 11. Et quamvis absque bonis operibus Deo chari non simus, haud tamen sequitur, iis nos justificari posse. Quia requiruntur in justificato, non justificando; non sunt causa justificationis, sed necessarium ejus consequens; ex gratia sanctificationis in nobis producta, quæ a justificatione divelli prorsus nequit; denique ad salutem necessaria in iis, qui propter Christum justificantur.
units.tr: Socinus: For either God requires good works of us in such a way that, if we lack them, he will not want us as dear to him; or he requires them in such a way that we shall indeed be most pleasing to him if we have kept his precepts, but that even if we have not done so, we shall nevertheless be held dear by him, because we firmly believe that all our sins were blotted out by the death of Christ. If we shall not be dear to him without good works, it appears false that we are now absolutely justified by faith alone; for no one can be perfectly justified without already being truly most dear to God. But if God will hold us dear on account of that faith, even though we lack good works, there is no need for us to labour much over the holiness of our life. Answer. 1. God requires good works of us in such a way that, if we lack them, he will not hold us dear. 2. And although we are not dear to God without good works, it does not follow that we can be justified by them. They are required in the one who is justified, not in the one who justifies; they are not the cause of justification but its necessary consequence, arising from the grace of sanctification produced in us, which can by no means be separated from justification; and finally, they are necessary to salvation in those who are justified for Christ's sake.

units.la: iii. Charissimus Deo quis est in justificatione, charissimus item in sanctificatione, exercitio sanctitatis pietatisque erga Deum: ut tamen hinc non sequatur, per eadem nos justificari, per quæ sancti sumus. Qui justificatur, hoc ipso perfectè justificatur, quia justificatio consistit in perfectâ Dei judicis absolutione, & remissione plane peccatorum omnium; quique justificatur, eo Deo est charissimus. Quid verò hoc obstat, ut idem etiam alio nomine, quamvis ex eodem fundamento præter quod nemo aliud ponere potest, Christo, charissimus Deo sit, nimirum quoque ex genuino sanctitatis studio, per eandem Dei gratiam, in homine qui Dei filius est, atque ex eo genitus, producto? Quemadmodum charissimi sunt & dicuntur filii, ex causâ plus quam unâ. iv. Nunquam verò Deus nos habiturus est charos propter fidem aliquam bonis operibus carentem.
units.tr: iii. He who is justified is dear to God, and likewise he is dear to God in sanctification, in the exercise of holiness and piety towards God; yet it does not follow from this that we are justified by the same things through which we are holy. He who is justified is thereby perfectly justified, because justification consists in the perfect absolution of God the judge and the complete remission of all sins; and he who is justified is thereby most dear to God. But what hinders the same person from also being dear to God under another name, namely to Christ, though from the same foundation, beyond which no one can lay another, and also through the same grace of God, produced in a man who is a son of God and born of him, by the genuine zeal for holiness? Just as sons are and are called dear for more than one reason. iv. Yet God will never hold us dear on account of any faith that lacks good works.

units.la: Jam autem tandem placet concludere, & finire totam de Christo disputationem. Disputavimus autem de Christo, ejus persona, officio, & quod ex officio ejus habemus, beneficio singulari justificationis. Ad personam Christi, de Christo Deo; ad officium ejus, in antecessum quæsivimus, an, si homo non peccasset, tamen venturus in carnem fuisset Christus? atque, ubi venit, an in coelos assumtus, ante prædicationis suæ exordium, tempore quadragesimalis jejunii, fuerit? tum de fœdere gratiæ, an quoque sub V. T. ad Patres pertinuerit, uti ad nos? de doctrinâ Christi, num novis præceptis legem adauxerit, aliaque suis de novo tradiderit? Porro, de ejus satisfactione, & merito: tandem de justificatione nostrâ, per ejus justitiam, disputatum à nobis fuit. Præcipua ubique sectati fuimus, & tum pro veritate confirmandâ, tum errore profligando, ea posuimus, ex quibus non difficulter cætera colligi, & instantias ulteriores, pro re nata, refelli posse, speramus. Quo candore, quaque solertia nihil in Adversariis præterierimus, quod ad causam ipsorum spectare videbatur, judicabunt ii, qui in controversiis his versati, ac scripta Adversariorum legere & expendere fuerint dignati. Idem ille Christus, cujus causam hactenus egimus, pro cujus & veritate, & justitiâ, & fide disputavimus, fecit, ut in nominis sui gloriam cedant omnia, & Ecclesiæ ædificationem, & bonum fidelium: quibus si hæc inserviant, id mihi maxima consolatio, & non laus dico, sed præmium erit, ipse solus merces futurus ampla satis & copiosa. Tibi Christo, Deus, & Salvator meus, obsecro tuam gratiam, laus dicatur etiam à me, indignissimo Majestatis & Nominis tui servo, nunc, & in omnem æternitatem, uti nunquam non sim totus tuus, Tu vicissim mihi primus & ultimus, & justitia, & gaudium, salus denique, & omnia.
units.tr: Now at last it pleases me to conclude and finish the whole disputation about Christ. We have disputed about Christ, his person, his office, and the singular benefit of justification which we have from his office. Concerning the person of Christ, we have treated of Christ as God; concerning his office, we first inquired whether Christ would have come in the flesh even if man had not sinned, and, when he came, whether he was taken up into the heavens before the beginning of his preaching, during the forty days' fast. Then concerning the covenant of grace, whether it also pertained under the Old Testament to the Fathers as it does to us; concerning the doctrine of Christ, whether he increased the law by new precepts and delivered other things anew. Furthermore, we have disputed about his satisfaction and merit; and finally about our justification through his righteousness. Everywhere we have pursued the chief points, and in confirming the truth and overthrowing error we have set down those things from which, we hope, the rest may not be hard to gather, and further objections may, as occasion arises, be refuted. Those who have been versed in these controversies and have deigned to read and weigh the writings of the opponents will judge with what candour and skill we have passed over nothing in our adversaries that seemed to pertain to their cause. That same Christ, whose cause we have so far pleaded, and for whose truth, righteousness and faith we have disputed, has so ordered that all things turn to the glory of his name, the edification of the Church and the good of the faithful. If these serve these ends, this will be my greatest consolation, and I call it not praise but reward; he himself alone will be a sufficiently ample and abundant recompense. To you, Christ, my God and Saviour, I humbly beg that your grace may also be praised by me, the most unworthy servant of your majesty and name, now and throughout all eternity; so that I may never cease to be wholly yours, and you in turn may be to me first and last, both righteousness and joy, salvation in short, and all things.

units.tr: Adversaries: Their false titles given to Christ. p. 3. Their false boasting about the Trinity and the union of persons in Christ. p. 5. Why they claim that Christ is not called the Son of God. p. 6. They make "Son of God" a name of dignity and rule, not of nature and generation. p. 8. Why they deny that Christ is the proper Son of God. p. 22. 24. Why they deny that he is natural. p. 37. 46. Why they deny that he is only-begotten. p. 37. 50. Christ is not an adopted Son of God. p. 47. 48. They also call Christ God. p. 86. They hold that all the names of God, whether Hebrew or Greek, are appellative and common. p. 93. They make a twofold meaning of the divine names. Ibid. They distinguish, in the worship of Christ, between adoration and invocation. p. 142. 443. What is the ground of adoration and invocation in Christ. Ibid. How they assail the incarnation. p. 205. They maintain that Christ would have come into the world even if man had not sinned. p. 253. They affirm that Christ was taken up into heaven shortly before he began to teach. p. 149. They hold that various forms of religion came to the fathers of the Old Testament according to the diversity of times. p. 282. What kind of religion they hold flourished before Abraham, what kind after Abraham, Moses and Christ. p. 289. What they understand by the Holy Spirit. p. 290. What they concede and what they deny in the matter of the faith of the fathers under the Old Testament. p. 303. They distinguish between the faith of the fathers under the Old Testament and present faith, and likewise between that Church and the one that now exists. p. 305. They divide the new precepts of Christ into two kinds: some are additions to the law of Moses from the Decalogue, others are proper to Christ. p. 375. Their catalogue of these. p. 377. They separate the Prophets from the law, so that the teaching is not the same in every respect, and one who proves something from the Prophets is not thought to have proved enough. p. 430. 441. 469. What they think of the fourth commandment and its observance. p. 454. What Christ added in the New Testament to the second table of the Decalogue in general. p. 461. They hesitate whether Christ added anything to the fifth commandment. p. 463. They think that revelries, fornications, obscene speech, lies, etc. were not forbidden to the fathers in the Old Testament. p. 461. 470. They put Christ's kingly office before his priestly office. p. 485. In what they place his prophetic office. 486. They actually confuse the kingly and priestly offices, distinguishing them only in thought. Ibid. What we refer to the priestly office, they refer to the prophetic. Ibid. What causes of Christ's death they make. p. 486. 496. What kind of mediator they make Christ. p. 488. 491. 501. What they deny in the question of Christ's satisfaction. p. 488. Their false boasting about Christ's death, sufferings, satisfaction, redemption, expiation and merit. p. 490. 581. 662. What they mean by satisfaction, when they perhaps concede it. p. 490. 662. Their disagreement about fixing the ends or causes of Christ's death. p. 498. How they say the doctrine and the new covenant are confirmed by the death of Christ. Ibid. They compare our view of Christ's satisfaction, as an invention, with the Papists' purgatory, auricular confession and similar things. Ibid. How they say Christ died for sins and on account of them. p. 566. How they make sin the cause of Christ's death, both impulsive and final. p. 567. units.tr: Slichtingius: why he calls Christ the proper Son of God. p. 22. Why only-begotten. p. 54, 64. His arguments by which he proves that the only and singular Son of God means the same as being Christ. p. 57. He denies that the name God is ever applied to Christ in the subjective case or with the article in Greek. p. 74. As far as he can, he undermines Socinian doctrines and adapts them to the Remonstrants. p. 300. How he sets out the question about the faith of the fathers in the Old Testament. ibid. His agreement with the Bishop. ibid. He gives a twofold acceptation and explanation of imputation. p. 690. Where he places the reconciliation of us with God. p. 705. What it is, according to him, to believe in the name of Christ and to receive Christ. p. 707. He sets out the nature of faith. p. 709. His objections against the apprehension of the forgiveness of sins and of the merits of Christ through faith. p. 713. He is called the most terrible and most pestilential of the Adversaries by the Jesuit Petavius. Prolegomena 2
